studies.title: Returning to the Word
studies.subtitle: Why We Go Back to What God Said
studies.summary: Going back to what the Hebrew and Greek actually say. The original words. The original meaning. Nothing added. Every word examined at its root — explained in everyday English. This opening study traces why the words, context, and meaning of Scripture matter. The next study, The Berean Standard, turns that conviction into a way of reading and testing what we hear.

studies.title: The Berean Standard
studies.subtitle: Examining Scripture the Way Scripture Says To
studies.summary: There is a moment in Acts 17 that most people read past without stopping. Paul and Silas have just arrived in Berea after being driven out of Thessalonica. Paul goes to the synagogue, as was his custom, and begins teaching from Scripture. And the text says something remarkable about what happens next. More noble-minded. That is how the Holy Spirit, through Luke, describes people who refused to simply accept what even an apostle told them — who went back to the text themselves, daily, to see whether it was true. That standard — the Berean standard — is the operating method of this site. It is also one of the most consistently abandoned practices in modern Christianity. And the cost of abandoning it is higher than most people realize.

studies.title: Is the Bible the Inerrant Word of God?
studies.subtitle: A Study on Inspiration, Manuscripts, and Translation
studies.summary: Yes — the Bible is the inspired, inerrant Word of God. But that statement requires a critical clarification that most churches never make: inerrancy belongs to the original Hebrew and Greek texts as God inspired them. Every English translation is a human interpretive act. Some translations carry demonstrable theological and political bias introduced by the very men who produced them. This document examines what inerrancy actually means, the manuscript evidence that supports it, and the documented history of how translation choices have shaped — and in some cases distorted — what ordinary readers encounter when they open their Bibles.

studies.title: Is There a Source of Truth?
studies.subtitle: Manuscripts, Variants, and Why the Bible Can Still Be Trusted
studies.summary: Open two different English Bibles side by side and you'll eventually find a place where they don't say the same thing. One includes a verse the other omits. One says "Son of God," the other doesn't, in a given verse. For a lot of people, that discovery is unsettling — if the Bible has variations across translations, how can anyone trust that any of it is the actual, reliable word of God? It's worth being honest about something before we go any further: we do not possess a single original manuscript of any book of the Bible. Not one autograph, penned by Paul's or John's own hand, has survived. What we have instead are copies — thousands of them, made by hand, across centuries, in different regions, by different scribes. That's not a modern discovery meant to shake your faith. It's simply the historical reality, and it's a reality shaped in part by deliberate, violent effort. In February of 303 AD, the Roman emperor Diocletian ordered the newly built Christian church at Nicomedia razed, its scriptures burned, and its treasures seized — the opening act of what became the most severe, systematic persecution of Christians in Roman history. The edict that followed prohibited Christians from gathering for worship and ordered the destruction of their scriptures, liturgical books, and places of worship across the entire empire. Christians were compelled to hand over their sacred texts to be burned; those who refused were imprisoned, tortured, or killed. It was, by design, an attempt to erase the Bible and the faith built on it entirely. It failed. Diocletian himself abdicated in 305 AD — one of the only Roman emperors in history to leave office alive and by his own choice, rather than by assassination, disease, or battlefield defeat. The faith he tried to erase outlived him, outlived the empire that persecuted it, and became that empire's own religion within a decade of his death. So the question isn't really "why don't we have a perfect original copy." Empires have tried to make sure of that. The real question is: given that reality, can we still trust what we have?

studies.title: The Gospel According to Jesus
studies.summary: There is a word that has been spoken so many times, in so many churches, across so many centuries, that most people assume they know what it means. Gospel. They have heard it from pulpits. They have seen it on signs. They have sung it in songs. And somewhere along the way, the word became familiar enough that the question behind it stopped being asked. What is the gospel, actually? Not what your tradition says it is. Not what you were handed as a child. Not what feels right or what seems loving or what makes the most people comfortable. What does Scripture say it is — in the language it was written in, in the world it was spoken into, from the lips of the ones who first proclaimed it? That question is worth everything. Because the gospel, properly understood, is not one idea among many. It is the central fact of human history. And getting it wrong — even a little — changes everything that follows.

studies.title: Who is The Angel of the Lord?
studies.subtitle: A Study on the Malak Yahweh and the Pre-Incarnate Son
studies.summary: One of the most remarkable figures in the Old Testament is one most people read right past. He appears without introduction, speaks with the full authority of God, receives worship that no created being should receive, and is identified by the text and by those who encounter him as God Himself. He is called the Angel of the Lord — and the closer you look, the clearer it becomes that this is no ordinary messenger.

studies.title: I Am a Disciple
studies.summary: I am a disciple of Jesus Christ. A disciple is a learner who follows the teachings and way of life of Jesus Christ. Through Him I have received salvation by grace through faith. I study His Word, I try to live as a good example for others, and in doing so bear witness to Christ so that others may find Him.

studies.title: Baptism
studies.subtitle: What It Is, What It Does, and How It Should Be Done
studies.summary: Every question about baptism eventually comes back to a single Greek verb, and what it actually meant before any tradition got hold of it. The Greek word translated "baptize" throughout the New Testament is βαπτίζω (baptizō (bap-TID-zoh)). Its lexical meaning is to plunge, immerse, or submerge. In classical Greek it was used to describe dyeing cloth — plunging fabric into dye — and the sinking of ships. The word itself establishes full immersion as the original intent and the normative practice of the early church. The BSB renders the word consistently as "baptize" throughout — preserving the transliteration rather than the meaning, which is itself a translation choice worth knowing. The Greek is baptizō — to immerse or plunge — and the transliteration rather than translation of this word has shaped centuries of theological debate about mode. This matters because the mode of baptism is not arbitrary. The act of going fully under the water and rising out of it carries the entire theological picture baptism is meant to represent. The mode is the meaning.

studies.title: Prayer and Faith
studies.subtitle: What Scripture Actually Teaches About How We Approach God
studies.summary: Most Christians inherit an idea of prayer rather than building one from Scripture. The common assumption is that prayer is a request system — you bring God a need or a desire, you ask sincerely, and if your faith is strong enough or your motives are pure enough, He grants it. When the answer doesn't come, people often reinterpret the outcome to fit what they prayed for, rather than asking whether they understood prayer correctly in the first place. This document works through what the Bible actually says prayer is — not what tradition has assumed it to be. The conclusion is more demanding than the popular view, but it is also more honest to the text: prayer is not a mechanism for securing outcomes. It is communion with God, submission to His will, and dependence on Christ Himself. Every passage below is examined in that light.

studies.title: What Does Prayer Look Like?
studies.subtitle: What Scripture Models — From Jesus, Paul, and the Early Church
studies.summary: The question is not whether to pray. It is what prayer actually is. Scripture never describes prayer as a system for securing outcomes — ask sincerely enough, and the answer arrives. It describes something far more demanding: honest communion with the Father, total surrender to His will, and intercession that asks for the spiritual good of others rather than control over their circumstances. The clearest picture of what this looks like does not come from a theory about prayer. It comes from watching Jesus pray — especially in the moments when prayer cost Him the most.

studies.title: Should We Seek Signs From God?
studies.subtitle: A Study on Coincidence, Confirmation, and Faith
studies.summary: Most of us have heard someone describe an experience like this: a particular bird shows up at just the right moment, a number keeps repeating, a dream feels too vivid to ignore, or something happens right after a prayer that seems to answer it exactly. The person telling the story usually isn't being dishonest or foolish — they're describing something that felt meaningful, often during a hard or emotional time, and they're reaching for language to make sense of it. "God sign," "god-wink," "coincidence that wasn't really a coincidence" — these are common ways people describe it. This study isn't about mocking that impulse or accusing anyone of doing something terrible. It's about asking a more basic question: does Scripture actually describe God working this way as the normal pattern for how He communicates with His people? And if not, what is this impulse, where does it come from, and what does Scripture say we should do with it? As we'll see by the end of this study, the honest answer is that this impulse is far more universal — and far more natural — than most of us realize. That includes the person writing this.

studies.title: The True Church According to Jesus
studies.subtitle: This is where the trail leads.
studies.summary: This is where the trail leads. Strip away the buildings. Silence the stages. Dismantle the systems we've built in His name. What remains? Only what He actually called His Church. Not a place, but a people. Not a performance, but a priesthood. Not a building, but a body — formed by the Spirit, built on the foundation of Christ alone. We are not invited to redesign His Church. We are called to return to it. What follows is not a theory or an ideal — it is the shape of the Church as Jesus declared it. The kind He died to create. The kind that walks in power, because it walks in obedience. This is the Church the gates of hell cannot overcome. This is the Church that still burns with the fire of Acts. This is the Church that knows no altar but the cross. This is the true Church according to Jesus.

studies.title: Who Shepherds the Church?
studies.subtitle: Elders, Overseers, Shepherds, and the Shape of Leadership in the Church
studies.summary: Walk into most churches on a Sunday and the structure tells you everything before a word is said. One man on a stage. A title beneath his name on the sign outside. A congregation seated, facing forward, listening. Somewhere along the way, "elder" became "Pastor," "overseer" became "Bishop," and a room full of believers gathered to wrestle with Scripture together became an audience. We've already made the case elsewhere for what the church actually is at its core — see The True Church According to Jesus for that fuller argument. Here, the question is narrower and more practical: who leads it, and how? Did the New Testament establish titled offices and a chain of command, or something else entirely?

studies.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It
studies.summary: This work draws from the foundational scholarship of Dr. Tom Wadsworth, whose doctoral dissertation A Worship Service or an Assembly: An Investigation of the Terminology Used to Describe Church Meetings in the New Testament (Midwestern Baptist Theological Seminary, 2022) and accompanying video series How We Got Worship Wrong served as a theological catalyst for the deeper study that follows. His examination of the Greek terms behind the English word "worship" confirmed what many believers have long sensed: something essential has been lost in what the modern church calls worship. This document builds on that foundation through continued study of the original languages, the earliest church sources, and the historical forces that shaped what Christianity became. What follows is not a retelling of his research — it is what his work made possible. Each Greek and Hebrew term examined here has been misrepresented by the generic gloss of "worship" in modern Bibles. When restored to its original meaning, each term offers a clearer, deeper invitation — into reverence, into service, into allegiance, into awe. Worship is not a moment, a genre, or a location. It is a life offered wholly to God.

passages.title: Genesis 1:1-31
passages.section_title: The Creation

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth. 2 Now the earth was formless and void, and darkness was over the surface of the deep. And the Spirit of God was hovering over the surface of the waters. 3 And God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light. 4 And God saw that the light was good, and He separated the light from the darkness. 5 God called the light “day,” and the darkness He called “night.” And there was evening, and there was morning—the first day. 6 And God said, “Let there be an expanse between the waters, to separate the waters from the waters.” 7 So God made the expanse and separated the waters beneath it from the waters above. And it was so. 8 God called the expanse “sky.” And there was evening, and there was morning—the second day. 9 And God said, “Let the waters under the sky be gathered into one place, so that the dry land may appear.” And it was so. 10 God called the dry land “earth,” and the gathering of waters He called “seas.” And God saw that it was good. 11 Then God said, “Let the earth bring forth vegetation: seed-bearing plants and fruit trees, each bearing fruit with seed according to its kind.” And it was so. 12 The earth produced vegetation: seed-bearing plants according to their kinds and trees bearing fruit with seed according to their kinds. And God saw that it was good. 13 And there was evening, and there was morning—the third day. 14 And God said, “Let there be lights in the expanse of the sky to distinguish between the day and the night, and let them be signs to mark the seasons and days and years. 15 And let them serve as lights in the expanse of the sky to shine upon the earth.” And it was so. 16 God made two great lights: the greater light to rule the day and the lesser light to rule the night. And He made the stars as well. 17 God set these lights in the expanse of the sky to shine upon the earth, 18 to preside over the day and the night, and to separate the light from the darkness. And God saw that it was good. 19 And there was evening, and there was morning—the fourth day. 20 And God said, “Let the waters teem with living creatures, and let birds fly above the earth in the open expanse of the sky.” 21 So God created the great sea creatures and every living thing that moves, with which the waters teemed according to their kinds, and every winged bird after its kind. And God saw that it was good. 22 Then God blessed them and said, “Be fruitful and multiply and fill the waters of the seas, and let birds multiply on the earth.” 23 And there was evening, and there was morning—the fifth day. 24 And God said, “Let the earth bring forth living creatures according to their kinds: livestock, land crawlers, and beasts of the earth according to their kinds.” And it was so. 25 God made the beasts of the earth according to their kinds, the livestock according to their kinds, and everything that crawls upon the earth according to its kind. And God saw that it was good. 26 Then God said, “Let Us make man in Our image, after Our likeness, to rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the air, over the livestock, and over all the earth itself and every creature that crawls upon it.” 27 So God created man in His own image; in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them. 28 God blessed them and said to them, “Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth and subdue it; rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the air and every creature that crawls upon the earth.” 29 Then God said, “Behold, I have given you every seed-bearing plant on the face of all the earth, and every tree whose fruit contains seed. They will be yours for food. 30 And to every beast of the earth and every bird of the air and every creature that crawls upon the earth—everything that has the breath of life in it—I have given every green plant for food.” And it was so. 31 And God looked upon all that He had made, and indeed, it was very good. And there was evening, and there was morning—the sixth day.

passages.context_html:
Genesis begins with God making the world. Before we meet Abraham and his family, we are shown where the world and everyone in it came from. At first the earth is dark and empty. As God speaks, He gives it order and fills it with life. Throughout the chapter, what He commands happens, and He sees that His work is good.

Notice the order. God separates light from darkness before placing the lights that mark day and night. He separates sky and waters before filling them with birds and sea creatures. Dry land and plants appear before land animals and people. Reading the whole chapter lets us see how these parts belong together. Christians differ over what this pattern tells us about the length of the days, but we should notice the pattern before deciding what it means.

Verses 26-30 give special attention to people. Both male and female are made in God's image. God blesses them and gives them responsibility in the world He has made. At the end, He looks at everything together and calls it very good. The account continues into Genesis 2:1-3, where God finishes His work and blesses the seventh day. We need to read those verses too; the chapter break comes before the story of creation is complete.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The churches discussed here agree that God made the world. Their disagreement is about how we should understand the six days described in this chapter.

Are these six days like ours? Some Christians understand them as six ordinary days, one after another. They point to the numbered days, the repeated evening and morning, and the pattern of six days of work followed by rest in Exodus 20:8-11. The Westminster Confession, chapter 4, and the 1689 Baptist Confession, chapter 4, are church statements of belief that describe a six-day creation. These documents speak for the churches that follow them; Presbyterians and Baptists do not all understand the days in the same way.

Some Christians understand each day as a much longer period of time. Others believe the chapter groups God's work to show how He ordered and filled the world, without giving us the exact order in which every event happened.

Another reading sees God's week as the pattern for our working week: we work and then rest because God did, but His days do not have to be the same length as ours. A report from the Orthodox Presbyterian Church explains these different readings. The report describes views discussed within that church; it does not make every view an official church teaching.

The Catholic Church's teaching guide, the Catechism, 337-339, describes the six days as a picture of God's work. It teaches that God really made the world, that everything depends on Him for its existence, and that what He made has its own goodness.

John Wesley's notes on Genesis 1:31 explain the six days as God's chosen way of working and an example for our work and rest. This is Wesley's explanation, rather than a rule about the days that every Methodist must accept. The Methodist Articles of Religion affirm that God made everything, but do not say how long the creation days lasted.

What about the word day itself? The Hebrew word יוֹם (yôm, YOHM) can refer to daylight, a whole day, or a period of time. The Brown-Driver-Briggs Hebrew dictionary describes these uses. In Genesis 1:5, the word names the light part of the day and then the whole first day, including evening and morning. So looking up the word helps, but it cannot answer the question on its own. We still need to read how it is used in this passage.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The New Testament connects creation directly to Jesus. John 1:1-3, 14 tells us that everything was made through the Word who became flesh. In 2 Corinthians 4:6, Paul looks back to God's command for light to explain how God opens our hearts to recognize His glory in Jesus.

Ephesians 1:9-10 tells us that God's purpose is to bring all things in heaven and on earth together in Christ. Genesis shows us the beginning of that world and our place in it. The God who made it is carrying out His purpose for it through Christ.

passages.title: Genesis 2:1-3
passages.section_title: The Seventh Day

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Thus the heavens and the earth were completed in all their vast array. 2 And by the seventh day God had finished the work He had been doing; so on that day He rested from all His work. 3 Then God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, because on that day He rested from all the work of creation that He had accomplished.
paragraphs: 1 Thus the heavens and the earth were completed in all their vast array. 2 And by the seventh day God had finished the work He had been doing; so on that day He rested from all His work.
3 Then God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, because on that day He rested from all the work of creation that He had accomplished.

passages.context_html:
These verses finish the creation account that began in Genesis 1:1. The six days of work are complete. God rests, blesses the seventh day, and sets it apart as holy. The next passage, Genesis 2:4-25, takes a closer look at human life in the garden. We should read these three verses with the chapter before them, even though they appear at the start of a new chapter.

God rests because His work is finished. He has not worn Himself out; Isaiah 40:28 tells us that the Creator does not grow tired. The seventh day also ends differently from the first six: there is no closing statement about evening and morning. That is worth noticing, but the missing statement alone cannot tell us how long the day lasted.

There is no command to Adam here telling him to keep a weekly day of rest. Later, Exodus 20:8-11 gives Israel that command and points back to God's work and rest at creation. Both passages matter. Genesis tells us what God did; Exodus tells Israel what to do because of it. Christians differ over how that command applies to us today.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians agree that God finished His work and set apart the seventh day. The main question is what that means for us: does God still require a particular day for rest and worship, and if so, which day?

Where do Christians differ? The Westminster Confession, 21.7-8, and the 1689 Baptist Confession, 22.7-8, teach that God still requires one day in every seven for worship and rest. These church statements of belief say that the day was Saturday before Christ's resurrection and Sunday afterward. Churches that follow them often call Sunday the Christian Sabbath. This does not mean that every Presbyterian or Baptist church teaches the same thing.

John Wesley's notes on Genesis 2:2-3 describe God's rest as an example for us to stop working and take delight in our Creator. The Methodist Articles, Article VI, teach that Christians are not required to follow all the old laws about Israel's worship practices, while God's commands about right and wrong still apply. That statement does not itself settle which weekly day Christians should observe.

The Catholic Church teaches that Sunday should be set apart for worship and rest. Sunday celebrates Jesus' resurrection and what the Sabbath pointed toward: our lasting rest in God. Its Catechism, 2174-2185, connects the two while distinguishing Sunday from the Saturday Sabbath.

The Lutheran Large Catechism, Third Commandment, 79-87, teaches that we need time to hear God's Word, worship, and rest. It says that God does not require Christians to do this on one particular day of the week. Sunday is the church's regular day for gathering.

The Seventh-day Adventist Church teaches that God set apart the seventh day for everyone at creation and that we should still keep it. Its statement of belief about the Sabbath identifies Saturday as the day for rest, worship, and serving others. The day remembers God's creation and what He has done to save us through Christ. In this reading, the Sabbath has not moved to Sunday.

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 4:3-11 quotes God's rest on the seventh day and tells its readers that the promise of entering His rest still stands. Joshua had led Israel into the promised land, but that was not the full rest God had promised. Hebrews urges its readers to trust and obey God rather than repeat the unbelief described in Psalm 95.

That connection gives these opening verses a place in the larger story. God finished His work at creation, and He calls His people to share in His rest. The rest we see at the beginning of the Bible helps us understand the rest He still promises His people.

passages.title: Genesis 2:4-25
passages.section_title: Man and Woman in the Garden

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 4 This is the account of the heavens and the earth when they were created, in the day that the LORD God made them. 5 Now no shrub of the field had yet appeared on the earth, nor had any plant of the field sprouted, for the LORD God had not yet sent rain upon the earth, and there was no man to cultivate the ground. 6 But springs welled up from the earth and watered the whole surface of the ground. 7 Then the LORD God formed man from the dust of the ground and breathed the breath of life into his nostrils, and the man became a living being. 8 And the LORD God planted a garden in Eden, in the east, where He placed the man He had formed. 9 Out of the ground the LORD God gave growth to every tree that is pleasing to the eye and good for food. And in the middle of the garden were the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. 10 Now a river flowed out of Eden to water the garden, and from there it branched into four headwaters: 11 The name of the first river is the Pishon; it winds through the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold. 12 And the gold of that land is pure, and bdellium and onyx are found there. 13 The name of the second river is the Gihon; it winds through the whole land of Cush. 14 The name of the third river is the Tigris; it runs along the east side of Assyria. And the fourth river is the Euphrates. 15 Then the LORD God took the man and placed him in the Garden of Eden to cultivate and keep it. 16 And the LORD God commanded him, “You may eat freely from every tree of the garden, 17 but you must not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; for in the day that you eat of it, you will surely die.” 18 The LORD God also said, “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make for him a suitable helper.” 19 And out of the ground the LORD God formed every beast of the field and every bird of the air, and He brought them to the man to see what he would name each one. And whatever the man called each living creature, that was its name. 20 The man gave names to all the livestock, to the birds of the air, and to every beast of the field. But for Adam no suitable helper was found. 21 So the LORD God caused the man to fall into a deep sleep, and while he slept, He took one of the man’s ribs and closed up the area with flesh. 22 And from the rib that the LORD God had taken from the man, He made a woman and brought her to him. 23 And the man said: “This is now bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called ‘woman,’ for out of man she was taken.” 24 For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and they will become one flesh. 25 And the man and his wife were both naked, and they were not ashamed.
