And in the middle of the garden were the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.
10 Now a river flowed out of Eden to water the garden, and from there it branched into four headwaters:
11 The name of the first river is the Pishon; it winds through the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold. 12 And the gold of that land is pure, and bdellium and onyx are found there.
13 The name of the second river is the Gihon; it winds through the whole land of Cush.
14 The name of the third river is the Tigris; it runs along the east side of Assyria. And the fourth river is the Euphrates.
15 Then the LORD God took the man and placed him in the Garden of Eden to cultivate and keep it.

16 And the LORD God commanded him, “You may eat freely from every tree of the garden, 17 but you must not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; for in the day that you eat of it, you will surely die.”
18 The LORD God also said, “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make for him a suitable helper.”

19 And out of the ground the LORD God formed every beast of the field and every bird of the air, and He brought them to the man to see what he would name each one. And whatever the man called each living creature, that was its name. 20 The man gave names to all the livestock, to the birds of the air, and to every beast of the field. But for Adam no suitable helper was found.

21 So the LORD God caused the man to fall into a deep sleep, and while he slept, He took one of the man’s ribs and closed up the area with flesh. 22 And from the rib that the LORD God had taken from the man, He made a woman and brought her to him. 23 And the man said: “This is now bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called ‘woman,’ for out of man she was taken.”
24 For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and they will become one flesh.
25 And the man and his wife were both naked, and they were not ashamed.

passages.context_html:
Genesis 1 surveys the whole creation. This passage brings us into the garden and shows how human life begins there: God forms the man, gives him a home and work to do, speaks a command, and provides the woman. These gifts come before the disobedience in chapter 3. Work and marriage belong to the good world God made; they are not punishments for sin.

The man comes from the ground, yet his life depends on God's breath. He is neither self-made nor self-sustaining. The garden gives him plenty to enjoy, and God's permission to eat comes before the restriction. The forbidden tree raises a question that will drive the next chapter: will people receive what is good from God, or decide for themselves against His word?

The woman answers a need that none of the animals can meet. The Hebrew word עֵזֶר, ʿēzer (AY-zer), means help or someone who helps. Brown–Driver–Briggs lists both this passage and passages describing God as His people's help. The word itself does not mean a servant of lesser worth. Here she is the human companion who corresponds to the man; he recognizes her as his own flesh and bone.

God makes her from the man's צֵלָע, ṣēlāʿ (tsay-LAH), a word Brown–Driver–Briggs gives as rib or side. The point of the scene is their shared life, expressed in the marriage bond of verse 24. Their unashamed nakedness closes the chapter. When chapter 3 ends with hiding and clothing, we are meant to notice how much has changed.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read this as God's provision of human life, meaningful work, and marriage. Jesus Himself uses the creation of male and female and the joining of husband and wife when explaining marriage in Matthew 19:4–6. The union carries responsibilities of faithfulness and care.

Where do traditions differ? Churches following the Westminster Confession, 7.2, describe God's arrangement with Adam as a covenant promising life on the condition of obedience. Genesis 2 gives the command and warning without using that covenant name. The Catholic Catechism, 396, explains the tree as expressing a creature's need to trust God and respect the limits He gives.

The Catholic Church also teaches that marriage between baptized people is a sacrament—a marriage through which Christ gives grace. Its Catechism, 1601, states this, and 1617 explains its connection with Christ and the church. The Methodist Articles, XVI, honor marriage as a scriptural state of life while distinguishing it from the two sacraments of the gospel. The 1689 Baptist Confession, 25.1–2, emphasizes the marriage of one man and one woman and their mutual help. These differences concern the church's understanding of marriage, while the shared starting point is God's creation of the relationship.
passages.current_position_html: As explained in Returning to the Word and Is the Bible the Inerrant Word of God?, our position on the command in verses 16–17 is that God's recorded words must govern how we read the conversation in chapter 3. The command forbids eating from the tree; it contains no prohibition against touching it. We should keep God's words distinct from additions made when those words are retold.

deeper_study.title: Is the Bible the Inerrant Word of God?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 5:25–32 quotes Genesis 2:24 and explicitly connects the marriage union with Christ and the church. Jesus loves His people, gives Himself for them, and cares for them as His own body. Marriage therefore helps explain something larger than the first couple: the faithful love with which Christ joins His people to Himself.

There is a further parallel worth considering. Adam receives his bride through God's work while he sleeps; Christ gives Himself so that His people can belong to Him. Genesis calls Adam's condition sleep, not death, so the correspondence is a picture rather than a claim that every detail predicts the cross. The direct connection rests on Paul's explanation of the marriage union. God's purpose includes a people united to His Son and cared for by Him.

passages.title: Genesis 3:1-7
passages.section_title: The Serpent’s Deception

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now the serpent was more crafty than any beast of the field that the LORD God had made. And he said to the woman, “Did God really say, ‘You must not eat from any tree in the garden?’” 2 The woman answered the serpent, “We may eat the fruit of the trees of the garden, 3 but about the fruit of the tree in the middle of the garden, God has said, ‘You must not eat of it or touch it, or you will die.’” 4 “You will not surely die,” the serpent told the woman. 5 “For God knows that in the day you eat of it, your eyes will be opened and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” 6 When the woman saw that the tree was good for food and pleasing to the eyes, and that it was desirable for obtaining wisdom, she took the fruit and ate it. She also gave some to her husband who was with her, and he ate it. 7 And the eyes of both of them were opened, and they knew that they were naked; so they sewed together fig leaves and made coverings for themselves.
paragraphs: 1 Now the serpent was more crafty than any beast of the field that the LORD God had made. And he said to the woman, “Did God really say, ‘You must not eat from any tree in the garden?’”

2 The woman answered the serpent, “We may eat the fruit of the trees of the garden, 3 but about the fruit of the tree in the middle of the garden, God has said, ‘You must not eat of it or touch it, or you will die.’”
4 “You will not surely die,” the serpent told the woman. 5 “For God knows that in the day you eat of it, your eyes will be opened and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.”

6 When the woman saw that the tree was good for food and pleasing to the eyes, and that it was desirable for obtaining wisdom, she took the fruit and ate it. She also gave some to her husband who was with her, and he ate it.
7 And the eyes of both of them were opened, and they knew that they were naked; so they sewed together fig leaves and made coverings for themselves.

passages.context_html:
The last scene showed the man and woman naked without shame. Now a conversation changes how they hear God's command. The serpent presents God's generous provision as a restriction, then directly denies the warning about death. The temptation is to distrust God's goodness and expect a better life by disobeying Him.

The woman repeats the restriction but adds touching the fruit, which is absent from the command recorded in Genesis 2:16–17. Genesis does not explain where that addition originated. The serpent's reply goes further: what God said would happen, he says will not happen. The woman eats, gives the fruit to her husband, and he eats. The immediate result is shame and an attempt to cover themselves, not the freedom the serpent offered.

The serpent is described as עָרוּם, ʿārûm (ah-ROOM), meaning crafty or shrewd. Brown–Driver–Briggs shows that the word can describe sensible caution elsewhere, but here that cleverness serves deception. Intelligent-sounding words can still lead away from what God has said. Verse 7 must also be read with what follows: covering themselves does not stop them from hiding when God approaches.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians read this as humanity's fall into sin, not simply the discovery of a new kind of knowledge. Romans 5:12–19 connects Adam's disobedience with the sin and death that affect humanity. Christians differ over how to explain our connection with that first sin.

Where do traditions differ? The Westminster Confession, 6.2–4, and 1689 Baptist Confession, 6.2–4, teach that Adam's descendants inherit both the guilt of his sin and a corrupted nature. In these readings, the fall leaves people unable to turn to God without His grace.

The Catholic Catechism, 404–405, describes an inherited loss of humanity's original holiness, while distinguishing that condition from a personal sinful act by each descendant. The Methodist Articles, VII–VIII, emphasize an inherited corruption and our need for God's grace before we can turn toward Him.

The Orthodox Church in America's explanation of original sin emphasizes inherited consequences, especially death, while reserving guilt for Adam and Eve's own act to them.
passages.current_position_html: Returning to the Word and Is the Bible the Inerrant Word of God? use this passage to explain our concern about changing God's words. We should notice both the added restriction in the woman's reply and the serpent's direct contradiction of God's warning. An addition and a denial are different actions, but each changes what was recorded in God's command.

deeper_study.title: Is the Bible the Inerrant Word of God?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Paul does more than look back at the damage. In Romans 5:15–19, he sets Adam's disobedience beside Christ's obedience. One man's act brings condemnation; Christ's obedience brings righteousness and life. The answer to the fall is not a return to the tree to make a better choice, but what God gives through Jesus Christ.

2 Corinthians 11:2–4 also turns Eve's deception into a warning for the church. People who belong to Christ can be led away from devotion to Him by a different message about Jesus. That makes this passage part of both the story of our need for rescue and the continuing call to hold to the truth.

passages.title: Genesis 3:8-13
passages.section_title: God Arraigns Adam and Eve

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 Then the man and his wife heard the voice of the LORD God walking in the garden in the breeze of the day, and they hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God among the trees of the garden. 9 But the LORD God called out to the man, “Where are you?” 10 “I heard Your voice in the garden,” he replied, “and I was afraid because I was naked; so I hid myself.” 11 “Who told you that you were naked?” asked the LORD God. “Have you eaten from the tree of which I commanded you not to eat?” 12 And the man answered, “The woman whom You gave me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it.” 13 Then the LORD God said to the woman, “What is this you have done?” “The serpent deceived me,” she replied, “and I ate.”
paragraphs: 8 Then the man and his wife heard the voice of the LORD God walking in the garden in the breeze of the day, and they hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God among the trees of the garden.
9 But the LORD God called out to the man, “Where are you?”
10 “I heard Your voice in the garden,” he replied, “and I was afraid because I was naked; so I hid myself.”
11 “Who told you that you were naked?” asked the LORD God. “Have you eaten from the tree of which I commanded you not to eat?”
12 And the man answered, “The woman whom You gave me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it.”
13 Then the LORD God said to the woman, “What is this you have done?”
“The serpent deceived me,” she replied, “and I ate.”

passages.context_html:
The promised new wisdom has produced fear. Even after making coverings, the man and woman hide among the trees when they hear God. The garden that had been a place of provision becomes somewhere to avoid the One who provided it. These verses show what their disobedience has done to their relationship with Him and with each other.

God's questions bring the act into the open. He calls the man, asks about his nakedness, and asks directly whether he ate from the forbidden tree. The man points to the woman and reminds God that He gave her to him. The woman points to the serpent. Both acknowledge eating, but their answers also direct attention away from their own choices.

The order matters: God calls and questions them before announcing the consequences. The passage gives us their fear and their answers; it does not supply a full account of their private thoughts or pronounce that blaming another person removes responsibility. The next verses address the serpent, the woman, and the man in turn.
passages.common_interpretations_html: These verses are commonly read as the exposure of sin and the failure of blame to restore a broken relationship with God. Wesley's notes on verses 9–13 understand God's questions as a gracious call to acknowledge wrongdoing, while the Catholic Catechism, 399, describes the fear of God that follows the loss of their original holiness. Both explanations keep responsibility with the people who disobeyed, even though a deceiver and another person were involved.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The hiding here introduces a pattern the rest of Scripture confronts: people try to conceal what God already sees, yet reconciliation requires coming into the light. Hebrews 4:13–16 puts those truths together. Nothing is hidden from God's sight, and through Jesus the high priest, His people are invited to approach Him for mercy and help.

This is a Bible-wide connection, not a claim that God's question in the garden already explained the whole gospel. 1 John 1:8–9 carries the lesson forward: denying sin deceives us; confessing it meets God's promise of forgiveness and cleansing. God's purpose is not served by a better hiding place, but by restored fellowship with Him.

passages.title: Genesis 3:14-15
passages.section_title: The Fate of the Serpent

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 So the LORD God said to the serpent: “Because you have done this, cursed are you above all livestock and every beast of the field! On your belly will you go, and dust you will eat, all the days of your life. 15 And I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed. He will crush your head, and you will strike his heel.”
paragraphs: 14 So the LORD God said to the serpent:
“Because you have done this,
cursed are you above all livestock
and every beast of the field!
On your belly will you go,
and dust you will eat,
all the days of your life.
15 And I will put enmity between you and the woman,
and between your seed and her seed.
He will crush your head,
and you will strike his heel.”

passages.context_html:
God now addresses the serpent, after hearing the man and woman's answers. The first sentence brings humiliation and judgment on the creature that deceived the woman. The next introduces a continuing conflict involving the serpent, the woman, and their offspring. The story moves beyond the fruit already eaten to a struggle that will outlast this encounter.

The Hebrew זֶרַע, zeraʿ (ZEH-rah), can mean seed or offspring. Brown–Driver–Briggs records its use for descendants; the word by itself does not mean a miraculous birth. Here the wording moves from offspring to a particular conflict in which the serpent receives a wound to the head and strikes the heel. To understand the Christian reading, we must follow how later Scripture speaks about the serpent and Christ's victory.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read verse 15 as an early promise that evil will not have the last word and that the woman's offspring points toward Christ. The Westminster Confession, 8.6, identifies the promised offspring with Christ, and Wesley's notes on verse 15 connect the wounds with His suffering and victory. The Catholic Catechism, 410–411, also reads the promise as announcing the Redeemer.

Where do traditions differ? The same Catholic passage also relates the woman to Mary as a new Eve and connects this with Catholic teaching about her freedom from original sin. The Protestant documents cited above develop the promise around Christ without making that additional claim about Mary. The shared reading about Christ should not erase that difference.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Revelation 12:9–17 identifies the ancient serpent as the devil and describes his conflict with the woman and her offspring. Romans 16:20 echoes the crushing language when promising that God will crush Satan under His people's feet. Read together, these passages give a well-supported connection between the conflict announced here and God's victory over the enemy.

Hebrews 2:14–15 explains how Jesus' death defeats the one who holds the power of death and frees people from its fear. His suffering is real, but it does not leave the enemy in control. This is the larger hope Christians see in Genesis 3:15: the judgment at the beginning of the Bible also opens toward the defeat of the deceiver.

passages.title: Genesis 3:16-20
passages.section_title: The Punishment of Mankind

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 To the woman He said: “I will sharply increase your pain in childbirth; in pain you will bring forth children. Your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you.” 17 And to Adam He said: “Because you have listened to the voice of your wife and have eaten from the tree of which I commanded you not to eat, cursed is the ground because of you; through toil you will eat of it all the days of your life. 18 Both thorns and thistles it will yield for you, and you will eat the plants of the field. 19 By the sweat of your brow you will eat your bread, until you return to the ground— because out of it were you taken. For dust you are, and to dust you shall return.” 20 And Adam named his wife Eve, because she would be the mother of all the living.
paragraphs: 16 To the woman He said:
“I will sharply increase your pain in childbirth;
in pain you will bring forth children.
Your desire will be for your husband,
and he will rule over you.”
17 And to Adam He said:
“Because you have listened to the voice of your wife
and have eaten from the tree
of which I commanded you not to eat,
cursed is the ground because of you;
through toil you will eat of it
all the days of your life.
18 Both thorns and thistles it will yield for you,
and you will eat the plants of the field.
19 By the sweat of your brow
you will eat your bread,
until you return to the ground—
because out of it were you taken.
For dust you are,
and to dust you shall return.”
20 And Adam named his wife Eve, because she would be the mother of all the living.

passages.context_html:
The consequences now enter the most familiar parts of life: having children, sharing a marriage, growing food, and facing death. Compare this with the gifts in chapters 1–2. The calling to fill the earth and care for it continues, but pain and frustrated labor now run through those good things.

The ground is cursed because of the man's disobedience. Work itself is not the curse—he already worked in the garden. What changes is the struggle of obtaining food from ground that also produces thorns and thistles. His return to dust answers the warning about death and recalls the material from which God formed him.

The woman's relationship with her husband is also affected. The word תְּשׁוּקָה, tĕšûqāh (teh-shoo-KAH), means longing or desire. Brown–Driver–Briggs lists three uses: here, in Genesis 4:7, and in Song of Solomon 7:10. Those settings involve different relationships, so the word alone cannot settle whether the desire here means affection, dependence, or a wish to control. Its meaning must be weighed with the rest of the sentence.

The section closes with the man naming his wife Eve because she will be the mother of all the living. Death has been announced, yet human life will continue. The following verses show God clothing them and sending them out of the garden.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians read these verses as describing the serious consequences of sin for human relationships, work, and mortality. Where do readings differ? Wesley's notes on verse 16 treat the woman's subjection as part of the punishment that follows the fall. The Catholic Catechism, 400, emphasizes the damage to the couple's original harmony, including lust and domination.

Those readings put different emphasis on the relationship described in verse 16. Neither the announcement of painful consequences nor a theory about the word desire gives husbands permission to be cruel. The New Testament's instruction is explicit: husbands must love their wives and not treat them harshly (Colossians 3:19).
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The struggle described here reaches beyond one family. Romans 8:19–23 describes creation in bondage to decay and speaks of its coming freedom alongside the redemption of God's children. The present pain of the world is not the final shape of God's purpose.

The return to dust also helps us grasp the hope of resurrection. 1 Corinthians 15:42–49 contrasts the body we inherit as people of the dust with the life given through Christ. God addresses the reality of death by raising His people, not by pretending the sentence in Genesis was harmless. At the Bible's close, Revelation 22:3 describes a world where the curse is gone.

passages.title: Genesis 3:21-24
passages.section_title: The Expulsion from Paradise

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 And the LORD God made garments of skin for Adam and his wife, and He clothed them. 22 Then the LORD God said, “Behold, the man has become like one of Us, knowing good and evil. And now, lest he reach out his hand and take also from the tree of life, and eat, and live forever...” 23 Therefore the LORD God banished him from the Garden of Eden to work the ground from which he had been taken. 24 So He drove out the man and stationed cherubim on the east side of the Garden of Eden, along with a whirling sword of flame to guard the way to the tree of life.
paragraphs: 21 And the LORD God made garments of skin for Adam and his wife, and He clothed them.
22 Then the LORD God said, “Behold, the man has become like one of Us, knowing good and evil. And now, lest he reach out his hand and take also from the tree of life, and eat, and live forever...”

23 Therefore the LORD God banished him from the Garden of Eden to work the ground from which he had been taken. 24 So He drove out the man and stationed cherubim on the east side of the Garden of Eden, along with a whirling sword of flame to guard the way to the tree of life.

passages.context_html:
God makes clothing for the man and woman before sending them out of the garden. They had made coverings from leaves; now He provides garments of skin. His care continues, but it does not cancel the consequences of their disobedience. They must leave the home He had given them.

The text states why access to the tree of life is blocked: they must not take its fruit and live forever. The man returns to working the ground from which he was formed. Cherubim and a flaming sword guard the way back. The chapter ends with a real barrier, after beginning with an invitation to distrust a boundary God had already given.

The clothing and the expulsion belong together. Reading only the garments can make the ending sound as though nothing has been lost. Reading only the guarded entrance can miss God's continuing provision. Chapter 4 then follows this family into life outside Eden, where sin's damage spreads into the next generation.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read the expulsion as the loss of humanity's original access to life with God. Some also see the garments as a picture of God providing what people cannot provide for themselves. Wesley's notes on verse 21 go further and suggest an animal sacrifice pointing toward Christ. That is a proposed parallel: Genesis says God made garments of skin, but does not describe an altar, a sacrifice, or a command establishing a sacrificial ritual here.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The guarded tree is not the Bible's last word about life. Revelation 22:1–5, 14 returns to the river, the tree of life, and a world without the curse. God's servants see His face, and those who wash their robes have access to the tree. These shared images form a strong parallel between what is lost at the beginning and the life God gives at the end.

The difference is more than moving back into a garden. Revelation places the throne of God and of the Lamb at the center of that life. The story moves toward fellowship with God in a creation freed from the curse. The clothes in Genesis show His care along the way; the restored access in Revelation shows the larger destination.

passages.title: Genesis 4:1-16
passages.section_title: Cain and Abel

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 And Adam had relations with his wife Eve, and she conceived and gave birth to Cain. “With the help of the LORD I have brought forth a man,” she said. 2 Later she gave birth to Cain’s brother Abel. Now Abel was a keeper of sheep, while Cain was a tiller of the soil. 3 So in the course of time, Cain brought some of the fruit of the soil as an offering to the LORD, 4 while Abel brought the best portions of the firstborn of his flock. And the LORD looked with favor on Abel and his offering, 5 but He had no regard for Cain and his offering. So Cain became very angry, and his countenance fell. 6 “Why are you angry,” said the LORD to Cain, “and why has your countenance fallen? 7 If you do what is right, will you not be accepted? But if you refuse to do what is right, sin is crouching at your door; it desires you, but you must master it.” 8 Then Cain said to his brother Abel, “Let us go out to the field.” And while they were in the field, Cain rose up against his brother Abel and killed him. 9 And the LORD said to Cain, “Where is your brother Abel?” “I do not know!” he answered. “Am I my brother’s keeper?” 10 “What have you done?” replied the LORD. “The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to Me from the ground. 11 Now you are cursed and banished from the ground, which has opened its mouth to receive your brother’s blood from your hand. 12 When you till the ground, it will no longer yield its produce to you. You will be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth.” 13 But Cain said to the LORD, “My punishment is greater than I can bear. 14 Behold, this day You have driven me from the face of the earth, and from Your face I will be hidden; I will be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth, and whoever finds me will kill me.” 15 “Not so!” replied the LORD. “If anyone slays Cain, then Cain will be avenged sevenfold.” And the LORD placed a mark on Cain, so that no one who found him would kill him. 16 So Cain went out from the presence of the LORD and settled in the land of Nod, east of Eden.
paragraphs: 1 And Adam had relations with his wife Eve, and she conceived and gave birth to Cain.
“With the help of the LORD I have brought forth a man,” she said.
2 Later she gave birth to Cain’s brother Abel.

Now Abel was a keeper of sheep, while Cain was a tiller of the soil. 3 So in the course of time, Cain brought some of the fruit of the soil as an offering to the LORD, 4 while Abel brought the best portions of the firstborn of his flock.
And the LORD looked with favor on Abel and his offering, 5 but He had no regard for Cain and his offering. So Cain became very angry, and his countenance fell.

6 “Why are you angry,” said the LORD to Cain, “and why has your countenance fallen? 7 If you do what is right, will you not be accepted? But if you refuse to do what is right, sin is crouching at your door; it desires you, but you must master it.”
8 Then Cain said to his brother Abel, “Let us go out to the field.” And while they were in the field, Cain rose up against his brother Abel and killed him.
9 And the LORD said to Cain, “Where is your brother Abel?”
“I do not know!” he answered. “Am I my brother’s keeper?”

10 “What have you done?” replied the LORD. “The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to Me from the ground. 11 Now you are cursed and banished from the ground, which has opened its mouth to receive your brother’s blood from your hand. 12 When you till the ground, it will no longer yield its produce to you. You will be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth.”

13 But Cain said to the LORD, “My punishment is greater than I can bear. 14 Behold, this day You have driven me from the face of the earth, and from Your face I will be hidden; I will be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth, and whoever finds me will kill me.”
15 “Not so!” replied the LORD. “If anyone slays Cain, then Cain will be avenged sevenfold.” And the LORD placed a mark on Cain, so that no one who found him would kill him.
16 So Cain went out from the presence of the LORD and settled in the land of Nod, east of Eden.

passages.context_html:
The first family now lives outside Eden, and sin reaches into the relationship between brothers. Cain works the soil; Abel keeps flocks. Both bring offerings, but God regards Abel and his offering while rejecting Cain and his offering. Cain's anger, God's warning, and the murder that follows belong to one story. We should not isolate the offerings from the brothers' response to God.

Before Cain kills, God addresses his anger and warns him about sin. The Hebrew חַטָּאת, ḥaṭṭāʾt (khat-TAHT), can mean sin or a sin offering in different settings. Brown–Driver–Briggs recognizes both meanings, but treats the crouching image in verse 7 as sin pictured like a beast. A word's possible meanings are not interchangeable: the surrounding sentence warns Cain about a power that seeks to master him.

After the murder, God's question recalls the questions asked of Adam and Eve. Cain denies knowing where his brother is, but the blood on the ground exposes what he has done. The ground he cultivated will no longer yield its strength to him. He fears being killed, and God gives a protective sign and warns against retaliation. Genesis does not describe the sign's appearance. The account ends with Cain leaving God's presence, not with a license for others to take revenge.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand Abel's acceptance in light of Hebrews 11:4, which emphasizes his faith, and 1 John 3:12, which contrasts the brothers' deeds. The difference is therefore more than a preference for a shepherd's work over a farmer's: the offerings belong to the men's response to God, and Cain's refusal to heed the warning leads to violence.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 12:24 deliberately compares Abel's blood with the blood of Jesus. Abel's shed blood cries out after an injustice; Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, has blood that speaks a better word. The Bible does not leave us with the murderer having the last word or with endless revenge as the answer to bloodshed.

The same reversal appears in 1 John 3:11–18. Cain takes his brother's life; Jesus lays down His life for others. John uses that contrast to call God's children to practical love. God's work through Christ produces a family whose members care for one another instead of treating a brother as a rival to be removed.

passages.title: Genesis 4:17-24
passages.section_title: The Descendants of Cain

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 And Cain had relations with his wife, and she conceived and gave birth to Enoch. Then Cain built a city and named it after his son Enoch. 18 Now to Enoch was born Irad, and Irad was the father of Mehujael, and Mehujael was the father of Methusael, and Methusael was the father of Lamech. 19 And Lamech married two women, one named Adah and the other Zillah. 20 Adah gave birth to Jabal; he was the father of those who dwell in tents and raise livestock. 21 And his brother’s name was Jubal; he was the father of all who play the harp and flute. 22 And Zillah gave birth to Tubal-cain, a forger of every implement of bronze and iron. And the sister of Tubal-cain was Naamah. 23 Then Lamech said to his wives: “Adah and Zillah, hear my voice; wives of Lamech, listen to my speech. For I have slain a man for wounding me, a young man for striking me. 24 If Cain is avenged sevenfold, then Lamech seventy-sevenfold.”
paragraphs: 17 And Cain had relations with his wife, and she conceived and gave birth to Enoch. Then Cain built a city and named it after his son Enoch.

18 Now to Enoch was born Irad, and Irad was the father of Mehujael, and Mehujael was the father of Methusael, and Methusael was the father of Lamech. 19 And Lamech married two women, one named Adah and the other Zillah.
20 Adah gave birth to Jabal; he was the father of those who dwell in tents and raise livestock. 21 And his brother’s name was Jubal; he was the father of all who play the harp and flute.
22 And Zillah gave birth to Tubal-cain, a forger of every implement of bronze and iron. And the sister of Tubal-cain was Naamah.
23 Then Lamech said to his wives:
“Adah and Zillah, hear my voice;
wives of Lamech, listen to my speech.
For I have slain a man for wounding me,
a young man for striking me.
24 If Cain is avenged sevenfold,
then Lamech seventy-sevenfold.”

passages.context_html:
After Cain's departure, Genesis follows his descendants. A city takes his son's name, and the family develops herding, music, and metalworking. The passage records growing human skill alongside growing violence. It does not say that tents, instruments, or tools are evil in themselves, or that technical progress repairs a person's relationship with God.

Lamech takes two wives, then addresses them in a boast about killing someone who wounded him. He appeals to God's earlier protection of Cain but magnifies vengeance for himself. The contrast with chapter 2's marriage and chapter 4's restraint on retaliation matters: Lamech makes his own power the answer to injury.

Several names here also appear, or resemble names, in the next family list. This Lamech belongs to Cain's line; the Lamech in chapter 5 is Noah's father. Keeping the families distinct prevents us from reading the boast of this man into the story of the other. The next two verses return to Adam and Eve and another line of descendants.
passages.common_interpretations_html: This is commonly read as the growth of human culture without a matching cure for sin: skills advance while Lamech openly celebrates retaliation. Wesley's notes on verses 19–24 contrast his multiple wives with the first marriage and describe his boast as a misuse of the protection given to Cain.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
There is a striking parallel in the way Jesus teaches forgiveness. Lamech enlarges a sevenfold claim of vengeance to seventy-sevenfold; in Matthew 18:21–35, Jesus answers Peter's question about forgiving seven times with a far greater measure of forgiveness. The BSB renders the answer as seventy-seven times and notes the alternative calculation of seventy times seven. Either way, the direction is the opposite of Lamech's boast.

This is a comparison between the passages, not an explicit statement by Matthew that Jesus is quoting Lamech. The lesson fits the kingdom Jesus describes: people who have received mercy must show mercy. Romans 12:17–21 carries the same call into Christian life by forbidding personal revenge and urging believers to overcome evil with good.

passages.title: Genesis 4:25-26
passages.section_title: Seth and Enosh

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 25 And Adam again had relations with his wife, and she gave birth to a son and named him Seth, saying, “God has granted me another seed in place of Abel, since Cain killed him.” 26 And to Seth also a son was born, and he called him Enosh. At that time men began to call upon the name of the LORD.
paragraphs: 25 And Adam again had relations with his wife, and she gave birth to a son and named him Seth, saying, “God has granted me another seed in place of Abel, since Cain killed him.”
26 And to Seth also a son was born, and he called him Enosh.
At that time men began to call upon the name of the LORD.

passages.context_html:
The story returns to Adam and Eve after tracing Cain's family. Eve names another son Seth and explicitly sees him as God's provision in place of Abel, whom Cain killed. Abel's death has not ended the family's future. Yet Seth is a new person in the story, not Abel returned to life.

Seth's son Enosh introduces the statement that people began calling on the name of the LORD. The contrast is with the violence and self-exaltation just described. Genesis has already shown people speaking with God and bringing offerings, so this is not the first time anyone has addressed Him. The statement marks a development in the family's worship and prepares for the line followed in chapter 5.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these verses as renewed hope after Abel's murder and a turn toward worshiping God. Wesley's notes on verses 25–26 understand the final line as people gathering to worship and openly identifying themselves with the LORD; Genesis itself supplies no detailed service, place, or ritual.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The family line matters to the larger story. Luke 3:23–38 traces Jesus' ancestry back through Enosh and Seth to Adam. That is a direct New Testament reason to pay attention to these brief birth notices: the family preserved after Abel's death appears in the account of Jesus' human ancestry.

This does not make every later member of Seth's family faithful simply by birth. It shows continuity in God's purpose despite violence and loss. Genesis will follow the family through Noah and then toward Abraham; Luke places Jesus within that long human story.

passages.title: Genesis 5:1-17
passages.section_title: The Descendants of Adam

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 This is the book of the generations of Adam. In the day that God created man, He made him in His own likeness. 2 Male and female He created them, and He blessed them. And in the day they were created, He called them “man.” 3 When Adam was 130 years old, he had a son in his own likeness, after his own image; and he named him Seth. 4 And after he had become the father of Seth, Adam lived 800 years and had other sons and daughters. 5 So Adam lived a total of 930 years, and then he died. 6 When Seth was 105 years old, he became the father of Enosh. 7 And after he had become the father of Enosh, Seth lived 807 years and had other sons and daughters. 8 So Seth lived a total of 912 years, and then he died. 9 When Enosh was 90 years old, he became the father of Kenan. 10 And after he had become the father of Kenan, Enosh lived 815 years and had other sons and daughters. 11 So Enosh lived a total of 905 years, and then he died. 12 When Kenan was 70 years old, he became the father of Mahalalel. 13 And after he had become the father of Mahalalel, Kenan lived 840 years and had other sons and daughters. 14 So Kenan lived a total of 910 years, and then he died. 15 When Mahalalel was 65 years old, he became the father of Jared. 16 And after he had become the father of Jared, Mahalalel lived 830 years and had other sons and daughters. 17 So Mahalalel lived a total of 895 years, and then he died.
paragraphs: 1 This is the book of the generations of Adam. In the day that God created man, He made him in His own likeness. 2 Male and female He created them, and He blessed them. And in the day they were created, He called them “man.”

3 When Adam was 130 years old, he had a son in his own likeness, after his own image; and he named him Seth. 4 And after he had become the father of Seth, Adam lived 800 years and had other sons and daughters. 5 So Adam lived a total of 930 years, and then he died.

6 When Seth was 105 years old, he became the father of Enosh. 7 And after he had become the father of Enosh, Seth lived 807 years and had other sons and daughters. 8 So Seth lived a total of 912 years, and then he died.

9 When Enosh was 90 years old, he became the father of Kenan. 10 And after he had become the father of Kenan, Enosh lived 815 years and had other sons and daughters. 11 So Enosh lived a total of 905 years, and then he died.

12 When Kenan was 70 years old, he became the father of Mahalalel. 13 And after he had become the father of Mahalalel, Kenan lived 840 years and had other sons and daughters. 14 So Kenan lived a total of 910 years, and then he died.

15 When Mahalalel was 65 years old, he became the father of Jared. 16 And after he had become the father of Jared, Mahalalel lived 830 years and had other sons and daughters. 17 So Mahalalel lived a total of 895 years, and then he died.

passages.context_html:
Chapter 4 followed Cain's descendants and ended with Seth and Enosh. Chapter 5 now traces the family line from Adam toward Noah. It repeatedly gives a father's age at a son's birth, mentions other children, and records his total years and death. This is a selected line within a larger family, not a claim that each man had only the one child named.

The opening recalls God making humanity in His likeness, creating male and female, and blessing them. It then describes Seth in Adam's likeness and image. The Hebrew דְּמוּת, dĕmût (deh-MOOT), means likeness or resemblance, and צֶלֶם, ṣelem (TSEH-lem), means image or likeness (Brown–Driver–Briggs, 1823; 6754). Their use here connects the generations; the words do not themselves divide human appearance from a separate spiritual substance.

The repeated deaths carry us back to the warning and sentence in the garden. Long lives do not erase that ending. At the same time, births continue. The chapter holds the continuation of God's blessing and the reality of death together, preparing us to notice Enoch's very different ending in verse 24.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read the list as the continuation of Adam's family under the reality of death, with the chosen line leading toward Noah and eventually Jesus. Wesley's introduction to chapter 5 makes that connection with Luke's account of Jesus' ancestry; the repeated deaths keep the list from being merely a record of impressive ages.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Luke 3:36–38 includes these early generations in Jesus' ancestry, connecting the Savior with the humanity whose beginning Genesis describes. The lists therefore serve more than curiosity about the past: they locate Jesus within the family history of people who need deliverance from sin and death.

Human dignity also remains important after the fall. Genesis 9:6 grounds the value of human life in God's image, and James 3:9–10 condemns cursing people made in God's likeness. The damage caused by sin is real, but it gives us no permission to treat another person's life as worthless.

passages.title: Genesis 5:18-24
passages.section_title: God Takes Up Enoch

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 When Jared was 162 years old, he became the father of Enoch. 19 And after he had become the father of Enoch, Jared lived 800 years and had other sons and daughters. 20 So Jared lived a total of 962 years, and then he died. 21 When Enoch was 65 years old, he became the father of Methuselah. 22 And after he had become the father of Methuselah, Enoch walked with God 300 years and had other sons and daughters. 23 So Enoch lived a total of 365 years. 24 Enoch walked with God, and then he was no more, because God had taken him away.
paragraphs: 18 When Jared was 162 years old, he became the father of Enoch. 19 And after he had become the father of Enoch, Jared lived 800 years and had other sons and daughters. 20 So Jared lived a total of 962 years, and then he died.

21 When Enoch was 65 years old, he became the father of Methuselah. 22 And after he had become the father of Methuselah, Enoch walked with God 300 years and had other sons and daughters. 23 So Enoch lived a total of 365 years.
24 Enoch walked with God, and then he was no more, because God had taken him away.

passages.context_html:
Jared's entry follows the familiar pattern: a son, more children, years of life, and death. Enoch's entry interrupts it. Genesis twice says he walked with God and closes by saying God took him. The expected notice of death is absent. That difference is the main reason this short entry stands out among the surrounding names.

Enoch has a family and walks with God over many years. The passage places that faithfulness within ordinary human life, not apart from it. It does not record the date of his conversion or explain all that happened when God took him. For the Christian explanation of that ending, Hebrews 11 supplies the clearest direct comment.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read Enoch's walk as a life pleasing to God and his being taken as an exception to the deaths around him. Hebrews 11:5–6 states that he was taken without experiencing death and uses him to explain why faith is essential to pleasing God.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Enoch belongs in Hebrews' account of people who trusted God before receiving the full outcome of His promises. Hebrews 11:5–6, 39–40 connects his experience with that larger community of faith and with the better fulfillment God has prepared. Genesis's brief exception is not left as an unexplained curiosity.

There is also a helpful parallel with the promised transformation of believers who are alive when Christ comes. 1 Corinthians 15:51–54 says that not everyone will die, but all will be changed. Enoch's story shows God's power to take a person without death; Paul states the future promise. The comparison does not, by itself, set a timetable for the church's rescue or explain its relation to every future judgment.

passages.title: Genesis 5:25-32
passages.section_title: From Methuselah to Noah

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 25 When Methuselah was 187 years old, he became the father of Lamech. 26 And after he had become the father of Lamech, Methuselah lived 782 years and had other sons and daughters. 27 So Methuselah lived a total of 969 years, and then he died. 28 When Lamech was 182 years old, he had a son. 29 And he named him Noah, saying, “May this one comfort us in the labor and toil of our hands caused by the ground that the LORD has cursed.” 30 And after he had become the father of Noah, Lamech lived 595 years and had other sons and daughters. 31 So Lamech lived a total of 777 years, and then he died. 32 After Noah was 500 years old, he became the father of Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
paragraphs: 25 When Methuselah was 187 years old, he became the father of Lamech. 26 And after he had become the father of Lamech, Methuselah lived 782 years and had other sons and daughters. 27 So Methuselah lived a total of 969 years, and then he died.

28 When Lamech was 182 years old, he had a son. 29 And he named him Noah, saying, “May this one comfort us in the labor and toil of our hands caused by the ground that the LORD has cursed.” 30 And after he had become the father of Noah, Lamech lived 595 years and had other sons and daughters. 31 So Lamech lived a total of 777 years, and then he died.
32 After Noah was 500 years old, he became the father of Shem, Ham, and Japheth.

passages.context_html:
After Enoch's unusual ending, the repeated death notices return. Methuselah lives 969 years, the longest lifespan listed in this chapter, and still dies. His son Lamech also dies. The names and numbers lead toward Noah, the man whose family will carry the narrative through the flood.

This Lamech expresses hope that his son will bring comfort from the painful work caused by the cursed ground. His words reach back to Genesis 3:17–19. They show how heavily that burden weighs on life outside Eden. The text reports the father's expectation; it does not say that Noah himself will remove every consequence of the fall.

The final verse names Noah's three sons and prepares for the family that enters the ark. It need not mean all three were born at once or that their order here settles every question about their ages. The focus is the family through which the account continues.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as the transition from the early family record to Noah, with the father's hope set against the repeated reality of death. Wesley's notes on verses 25–32 likewise connect the family record with Noah's coming role; the promises and judgments in the following chapters show how that role unfolds.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 11:7 explains Noah's part in God's purpose through his response to a warning: he trusts God, builds the ark, and becomes an heir of righteousness by faith. The family introduced here will be preserved through a real judgment. Noah's significance depends on God's warning and provision, not on human longevity alone.

The hope for relief from the cursed ground also remains larger than Noah's lifetime. After the flood, Genesis 9:1–17 describes God's covenant with the surviving family and living creatures. The complete end of the curse appears in Revelation 22:3. Noah has a place in that unfolding story, while the final restoration rests with God.

passages.title: Genesis 6:1-7
passages.section_title: Corruption on the Earth

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now when men began to multiply on the face of the earth and daughters were born to them, 2 the sons of God saw that the daughters of men were beautiful, and they took as wives whomever they chose. 3 So the LORD said, “My Spirit will not contend with man forever, for he is mortal; his days shall be 120 years.” 4 The Nephilim were on the earth in those days—and afterward as well—when the sons of God had relations with the daughters of men. And they bore them children who became the mighty men of old, men of renown. 5 Then the LORD saw that the wickedness of man was great upon the earth, and that every inclination of the thoughts of his heart was altogether evil all the time. 6 And the LORD regretted that He had made man on the earth, and He was grieved in His heart. 7 So the LORD said, “I will blot out man, whom I have created, from the face of the earth—every man and beast and crawling creature and bird of the air—for I am grieved that I have made them.”
paragraphs: 1 Now when men began to multiply on the face of the earth and daughters were born to them, 2 the sons of God saw that the daughters of men were beautiful, and they took as wives whomever they chose.
3 So the LORD said, “My Spirit will not contend with man forever, for he is mortal; his days shall be 120 years.”

4 The Nephilim were on the earth in those days—and afterward as well—when the sons of God had relations with the daughters of men. And they bore them children who became the mighty men of old, men of renown.

5 Then the LORD saw that the wickedness of man was great upon the earth, and that every inclination of the thoughts of his heart was altogether evil all the time. 6 And the LORD regretted that He had made man on the earth, and He was grieved in His heart. 7 So the LORD said, “I will blot out man, whom I have created, from the face of the earth—every man and beast and crawling creature and bird of the air—for I am grieved that I have made them.”

passages.context_html:
The family record in chapter 5 ended with Noah and his sons. This passage explains the world into which his story comes: people multiply, the figures called sons of God take wives as they choose, and human wickedness fills the earth. The description of the human heart in verse 5 is the clearest stated reason for the coming judgment. The difficult opening verses should not distract us from that explanation.

The name נְפִילִים, nĕfîlîm (neh-fee-LEEM), is left as Nephilim in the BSB. Brown–Driver–Briggs describes giants and treats the name's origin as uncertain. A proposed meaning of the name cannot, by itself, establish who their parents were or explain every detail of the passage.

God's grief shows that evil matters to Him. The judgment affects human beings and the other creatures in the world they inhabit. Yet the sentence is immediately followed by the notice that Noah finds favor. The story contains both God's opposition to wickedness and the preservation of life through the man He addresses.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Where do Christian readings differ? One long-standing reading understands the sons of God as heavenly beings who crossed the boundary of their appointed place. Justin Martyr's Second Apology, chapter 5, describes angels taking women and fathering offspring. The US Catholic bishops' Bible notes on Genesis 6:1–4 also identify heavenly beings. These are explanations of the passage, rather than a statement that every Catholic must hold this reading.

Another long-standing reading sees people from the family line associated with God joining themselves to those who had turned from Him. Augustine, City of God 15.22–23, identifies the families of Seth and Cain; Wesley's notes on verse 2 follow that reading. The central concern is the abandonment of faithfulness for the relationships people desire. These named teachers do not speak for every member of a modern denomination.

Readers also differ over the 120 years in verse 3. Wesley's notes take them as a period before judgment; the Catholic bishops' notes take them as a reduction of the human lifespan. The verse's meaning should be considered within the movement toward the flood and the longer lifespans still reported afterward.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus explicitly returns to Noah's days in Matthew 24:37–39. His comparison emphasizes people carrying on with ordinary life until judgment arrives. The warning does not require us to solve every question about the Nephilim before hearing it: a world that ignores God is not made safe by feeling that life will continue as usual.

2 Peter 3:5–13 likewise uses the flood when describing judgment still to come and God's patience before it. The call is to repentance and a life shaped by the promise of a world where righteousness dwells.

passages.title: Genesis 6:8-12
passages.section_title: Noah’s Favor with God

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 Noah, however, found favor in the eyes of the LORD. 9 This is the account of Noah. Noah was a righteous man, blameless in his generation; Noah walked with God. 10 And Noah had three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth. 11 Now the earth was corrupt in the sight of God, and full of violence. 12 And God looked upon the earth and saw that it was corrupt; for all living creatures on the earth had corrupted their ways.
paragraphs: 8 Noah, however, found favor in the eyes of the LORD.
9 This is the account of Noah. Noah was a righteous man, blameless in his generation; Noah walked with God. 10 And Noah had three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
11 Now the earth was corrupt in the sight of God, and full of violence. 12 And God looked upon the earth and saw that it was corrupt; for all living creatures on the earth had corrupted their ways.

passages.context_html:
The word however in verse 8 marks a turn after the announcement of judgment. Noah finds favor with God, walks with Him, and lives differently from the violence around him. His family is named because the account will now follow them through the flood. The surrounding world is described as corrupt in its way of life, not merely damaged in its surroundings.

Favor is חֵן, ḥēn (KHAYN), which Brown–Driver–Briggs gives as favor or grace. Finding favor means being received with kindness. The account places God's favor alongside Noah's actual walk with Him amid the surrounding violence.

The word translated blameless is תָּמִים, tāmîm (tah-MEEM). Brown–Driver–Briggs places Genesis 6:9 among its uses for integrity. This describes Noah's character and way of life, rather than declaring that he has never sinned. The later account of his drunkenness in chapter 9 prevents us from confusing his faithfulness here with moral perfection.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read Noah as a person who receives God's favor and responds in faithfulness amid widespread evil. Wesley's notes on verses 8–9 explain his righteousness through faith and his walk through a changed life, in keeping with the direct New Testament explanation in Hebrews 11:7.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
2 Peter 2:5, 9 names Noah as a preacher of righteousness and uses his preservation to show that God knows how to rescue the godly while judging evil. Noah's difference from the surrounding world therefore matters beyond the survival of one family: God's judgment does not make Him unable to preserve those who belong to Him.

Hebrews 11:7 explains Noah's response as faith in a warning about things not yet seen. The coming ark will be built because God has spoken and Noah trusts Him. Noah's faith takes the form of work in response to God's word, before the danger he has been warned about can be seen.

passages.title: Genesis 6:13-22
passages.section_title: Preparing the Ark

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 Then God said to Noah, “The end of all living creatures has come before Me, because through them the earth is full of violence. Now behold, I will destroy both them and the earth. 14 Make for yourself an ark of gopher wood; make rooms in the ark and coat it with pitch inside and out. 15 And this is how you are to build it: The ark is to be 300 cubits long, 50 cubits wide, and 30 cubits high. 16 You are to make a roof for the ark, finish its walls a cubit from the top, place a door in the side of the ark, and build lower, middle, and upper decks. 17 And behold, I will bring floodwaters upon the earth to destroy every creature under the heavens that has the breath of life. Everything on the earth will perish. 18 But I will establish My covenant with you, and you will enter the ark—you and your sons and your wife and your sons’ wives with you. 19 And you are to bring two of every living creature into the ark—male and female—to keep them alive with you. 20 Two of every kind of bird and animal and crawling creature will come to you to be kept alive. 21 You are also to take for yourself every kind of food that is eaten and gather it as food for yourselves and for the animals.” 22 So Noah did everything precisely as God had commanded him.
paragraphs: 13 Then God said to Noah, “The end of all living creatures has come before Me, because through them the earth is full of violence. Now behold, I will destroy both them and the earth.

14 Make for yourself an ark of gopher wood; make rooms in the ark and coat it with pitch inside and out. 15 And this is how you are to build it: The ark is to be 300 cubits long, 50 cubits wide, and 30 cubits high. 16 You are to make a roof for the ark, finish its walls a cubit from the top, place a door in the side of the ark, and build lower, middle, and upper decks.

17 And behold, I will bring floodwaters upon the earth to destroy every creature under the heavens that has the breath of life. Everything on the earth will perish. 18 But I will establish My covenant with you, and you will enter the ark—you and your sons and your wife and your sons’ wives with you.

19 And you are to bring two of every living creature into the ark—male and female—to keep them alive with you. 20 Two of every kind of bird and animal and crawling creature will come to you to be kept alive. 21 You are also to take for yourself every kind of food that is eaten and gather it as food for yourselves and for the animals.”
22 So Noah did everything precisely as God had commanded him.

passages.context_html:
God tells Noah both what is coming and how life will be preserved. The same speech announces the end of a violent world and gives instructions for building the ark, gathering food, and keeping creatures alive. The warning is not left as a riddle for Noah to solve. He receives work to do in response to God's word.

The dimensions, rooms, covering, entrance, and decks describe a real vessel within the account. The pitch coats it inside and out. The passage does not explain every construction method or identify the wood in terms of a modern species. Its focus is that Noah builds according to God's directions, while God promises a covenant and directs the preservation of the family and animals.

Verse 22 gives Noah's response: he does what God commands. That conclusion belongs with the favor and integrity already described, and with the command to enter in chapter 7. We should read the building, entering, and being preserved as one connected response to God's warning and provision.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read the ark as God's appointed means of preserving Noah's household through the judgment, with Noah's building expressing faith rather than replacing it. Hebrews 11:7 explicitly describes the preparation of the ark in those terms.
passages.current_position_html: Our Baptism study explains the ark as the vessel God appointed to carry Noah's family safely through the water. The wood had no saving power of its own. We draw that limited point from the existing study here: the rescue depends on God's provision, with Noah responding to His instructions in faith.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
1 Peter 3:18–22 connects the days when the ark was being built and the family's passage through water with baptism through Jesus Christ's resurrection. Peter places the rescue inside a larger explanation of Christ suffering for sins to bring people to God. The connection is stated by the New Testament, not inferred from the boat's measurements.

The ark can therefore serve as a helpful picture of rescue God provides when judgment comes. Noah does not make the flood harmless; he receives a way through it. The greater hope in Peter is centered on the risen Jesus and access to God. The story of preservation prepares us to appreciate the greater rescue Peter describes through Jesus' death and resurrection.

passages.title: Genesis 7:1-24
passages.section_title: The Great Flood

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then the LORD said to Noah, “Go into the ark, you and all your family, because I have found you righteous in this generation. 2 You are to take with you seven pairs of every kind of clean animal, a male and its mate; a pair of every kind of unclean animal, a male and its mate; 3 and seven pairs of every kind of bird of the air, male and female, to preserve their offspring on the face of all the earth. 4 For seven days from now I will send rain on the earth for forty days and forty nights, and I will wipe from the face of the earth every living thing I have made.” 5 And Noah did all that the LORD had commanded him. 6 Now Noah was 600 years old when the floodwaters came upon the earth. 7 And Noah and his wife, with his sons and their wives, entered the ark to escape the waters of the flood. 8 The clean and unclean animals, the birds, and everything that crawls along the ground 9 came to Noah to enter the ark, two by two, male and female, as God had commanded Noah. 10 And after seven days the floodwaters came upon the earth. 11 In the six hundredth year of Noah’s life, on the seventeenth day of the second month, all the fountains of the great deep burst forth, and the floodgates of the heavens were opened. 12 And the rain fell upon the earth for forty days and forty nights. 13 On that very day Noah entered the ark, along with his sons Shem, Ham, and Japheth, and his wife, and the three wives of his sons— 14 they and every kind of wild animal, livestock, crawling creature, bird, and winged creature. 15 They came to Noah to enter the ark, two by two of every creature with the breath of life. 16 And they entered, the male and female of every living thing, as God had commanded Noah. Then the LORD shut him in. 17 For forty days the flood kept coming on the earth, and the waters rose and lifted the ark high above the earth. 18 So the waters continued to surge and rise greatly on the earth, and the ark floated on the surface of the waters. 19 Finally, the waters completely prevailed upon the earth, so that all the high mountains under all the heavens were covered. 20 The waters rose and covered the mountaintops to a depth of fifteen cubits. 21 And every living thing that moved upon the earth perished—birds, livestock, animals, every creature that swarms upon the earth, and all mankind. 22 Of all that was on dry land, everything that had the breath of life in its nostrils died. 23 And every living thing on the face of the earth was destroyed—man and livestock, crawling creatures and birds of the air; they were blotted out from the earth, and only Noah and those with him in the ark remained. 24 And the waters prevailed upon the earth for 150 days.
