5 And Noah did all that the LORD had commanded him.

6 Now Noah was 600 years old when the floodwaters came upon the earth. 7 And Noah and his wife, with his sons and their wives, entered the ark to escape the waters of the flood. 8 The clean and unclean animals, the birds, and everything that crawls along the ground 9 came to Noah to enter the ark, two by two, male and female, as God had commanded Noah.

10 And after seven days the floodwaters came upon the earth. 11 In the six hundredth year of Noah’s life, on the seventeenth day of the second month, all the fountains of the great deep burst forth, and the floodgates of the heavens were opened. 12 And the rain fell upon the earth for forty days and forty nights.

13 On that very day Noah entered the ark, along with his sons Shem, Ham, and Japheth, and his wife, and the three wives of his sons— 14 they and every kind of wild animal, livestock, crawling creature, bird, and winged creature. 15 They came to Noah to enter the ark, two by two of every creature with the breath of life. 16 And they entered, the male and female of every living thing, as God had commanded Noah. Then the LORD shut him in.

17 For forty days the flood kept coming on the earth, and the waters rose and lifted the ark high above the earth. 18 So the waters continued to surge and rise greatly on the earth, and the ark floated on the surface of the waters. 19 Finally, the waters completely prevailed upon the earth, so that all the high mountains under all the heavens were covered.

20 The waters rose and covered the mountaintops to a depth of fifteen cubits. 21 And every living thing that moved upon the earth perished—birds, livestock, animals, every creature that swarms upon the earth, and all mankind. 22 Of all that was on dry land, everything that had the breath of life in its nostrils died. 23 And every living thing on the face of the earth was destroyed—man and livestock, crawling creatures and birds of the air; they were blotted out from the earth, and only Noah and those with him in the ark remained.
24 And the waters prevailed upon the earth for 150 days.

passages.context_html:
The preparation becomes an entrance, then a judgment. God tells Noah to bring his household into the ark, specifies the animals to preserve, and announces the approaching rain. The repeated notices of Noah's obedience link the events to chapter 6. The larger number of clean animals also prepares for the offerings after the flood in chapter 8.

The account names water from below and rain from above, then describes it rising over the mountains. The repeated statements about creatures dying make the judgment's seriousness unmistakable. At the same time, the ark is lifted by the water rather than destroyed by it. The very event that brings death outside carries the preserved family through.

God shuts Noah in, and the chapter closes with the waters prevailing for 150 days. The forty days of rain are not the entire length of the family's stay. Chapter 8 will follow the gradual retreat of the water and the much later departure. Genesis supplies a sequence; it does not say that ordinary life resumes as soon as the rain stops.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians read the flood as judgment on evil and the preservation of Noah's family. Where do readings differ? Many take the repeated references to all the mountains and all life on dry land as describing a flood over the whole earth. Augustine, City of God 15.27, defends the reality of water rising above the highest mountains, alongside a further picture of the church's rescue.

Other Christian teachers understand the flood as covering the whole inhabited human world without covering every part of the globe. Hugh Ross's explanation of his reading makes that distinction: universal in its judgment of humanity, geographically limited in extent. That is his organization's interpretation, not an official position shared by all Christians of a denomination. The readings differ over extent while both affirming judgment and preservation.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Matthew 24:37–39 makes the flood a warning about the coming of the Son of Man. The point is the abrupt arrival of judgment upon people who continued ordinary life without recognizing what was coming. Noah's entrance belongs to the contrast between ignoring God's warning and responding to it.

1 Peter 3:20–22 also names the eight people preserved through water and connects this with baptism through Christ's resurrection. These passages give the flood a place in the story of rescue and judgment. They call readers to take God's warning seriously and recognize the rescue He provides.

passages.title: Genesis 8:1-5
passages.section_title: The Ark Rests on Ararat

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 But God remembered Noah and all the animals and livestock that were with him in the ark. And God sent a wind over the earth, and the waters began to subside. 2 The springs of the deep and the floodgates of the heavens were closed, and the rain from the sky was restrained. 3 The waters receded steadily from the earth, and after 150 days the waters had gone down. 4 On the seventeenth day of the seventh month, the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat. 5 And the waters continued to recede until the tenth month, and on the first day of the tenth month the tops of the mountains became visible.
paragraphs: 1 But God remembered Noah and all the animals and livestock that were with him in the ark. And God sent a wind over the earth, and the waters began to subside. 2 The springs of the deep and the floodgates of the heavens were closed, and the rain from the sky was restrained. 3 The waters receded steadily from the earth, and after 150 days the waters had gone down.

4 On the seventeenth day of the seventh month, the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat. 5 And the waters continued to recede until the tenth month, and on the first day of the tenth month the tops of the mountains became visible.

passages.context_html:
The flood's rise has reached its turning point. God remembers Noah and the creatures with him, sends a wind, closes the sources of water, and brings about its retreat. The ark comes to rest, and later the mountain tops become visible. The changes come in stages, while Noah's family remains inside.

The Hebrew verb זָכַר, zākar (zah-KHAR), means remember. Brown–Driver–Briggs includes Genesis 8:1 among uses of God remembering a person with kindness, protection, or deliverance. The following actions explain the statement: God acts for those He has preserved. It is not a notice that Noah had slipped His mind.

The wind is רוּחַ, rûaḥ (ROO-akh), a word that can mean breath, wind, or spirit; Brown–Driver–Briggs identifies wind in this verse. The passage places the ark in the mountains of Ararat without naming an individual peak.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read God's remembering as faithful action for Noah and the creatures, and the retreat of the waters as the beginning of their release. Wesley's notes on verse 1 likewise describe a return of mercy rather than a lapse in God's awareness.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
God remembering and acting to deliver becomes a recurring pattern. In Exodus 2:23–25, He hears the oppressed Israelites and remembers His covenant before the account of their rescue. In Luke 1:68–75, the coming salvation is likewise explained through God's mercy and remembrance of His covenant.

These are connections across the Bible, not statements that each rescue is the same event. They show a consistent feature of God's purpose: He does not abandon His promises while His people wait. The wind and retreating water here are the concrete beginning of that faithfulness becoming visible to Noah.

passages.title: Genesis 8:6-12
passages.section_title: Noah Sends a Raven and a Dove

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 After forty days Noah opened the window he had made in the ark 7 and sent out a raven. It kept flying back and forth until the waters had dried up from the earth. 8 Then Noah sent out a dove to see if the waters had receded from the surface of the ground. 9 But the dove found no place to rest her foot, and she returned to him in the ark, because the waters were still covering the surface of all the earth. So he reached out his hand and brought her back inside the ark. 10 Noah waited seven more days and again sent out the dove from the ark. 11 And behold, the dove returned to him in the evening with a freshly plucked olive leaf in her beak. So Noah knew that the waters had receded from the earth. 12 And Noah waited seven more days and sent out the dove again, but this time she did not return to him.
paragraphs: 6 After forty days Noah opened the window he had made in the ark 7 and sent out a raven. It kept flying back and forth until the waters had dried up from the earth.

8 Then Noah sent out a dove to see if the waters had receded from the surface of the ground. 9 But the dove found no place to rest her foot, and she returned to him in the ark, because the waters were still covering the surface of all the earth. So he reached out his hand and brought her back inside the ark.

10 Noah waited seven more days and again sent out the dove from the ark. 11 And behold, the dove returned to him in the evening with a freshly plucked olive leaf in her beak. So Noah knew that the waters had receded from the earth.
12 And Noah waited seven more days and sent out the dove again, but this time she did not return to him.

passages.context_html:
The ark is resting, but the family has not been told to leave. Noah sends a raven and then a dove to learn about the ground beyond what he can see. The dove's first return shows there is no place for it to settle. Its later return with a fresh olive leaf gives Noah evidence that the waters have retreated further.

The repeated waits are part of the account. Noah does not receive every answer at once, and the leaf is not yet the command to leave. On the next release the dove does not return. In the following verses Noah will look out, and then God will tell the family to go out. Observing the changing conditions and waiting for God's word are presented together.
passages.common_interpretations_html: This is commonly read as Noah patiently testing the conditions as the flood recedes. Wesley's notes on verses 7–12 explain the birds as giving him information about the drying ground and the return of a place to live.

passages.title: Genesis 8:13-19
passages.section_title: Exiting the Ark

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 In Noah’s six hundred and first year, on the first day of the first month, the waters had dried up from the earth. So Noah removed the covering from the ark and saw that the surface of the ground was dry. 14 By the twenty-seventh day of the second month, the earth was fully dry. 15 Then God said to Noah, 16 “Come out of the ark, you and your wife, along with your sons and their wives. 17 Bring out all the living creatures that are with you—birds, livestock, and everything that crawls upon the ground—so that they can spread out over the earth and be fruitful and multiply upon it.” 18 So Noah came out, along with his sons and his wife and his sons’ wives. 19 Every living creature, every creeping thing, and every bird—everything that moves upon the earth—came out of the ark, kind by kind.
paragraphs: 13 In Noah’s six hundred and first year, on the first day of the first month, the waters had dried up from the earth. So Noah removed the covering from the ark and saw that the surface of the ground was dry. 14 By the twenty-seventh day of the second month, the earth was fully dry.

15 Then God said to Noah, 16 “Come out of the ark, you and your wife, along with your sons and their wives. 17 Bring out all the living creatures that are with you—birds, livestock, and everything that crawls upon the ground—so that they can spread out over the earth and be fruitful and multiply upon it.”

18 So Noah came out, along with his sons and his wife and his sons’ wives. 19 Every living creature, every creeping thing, and every bird—everything that moves upon the earth—came out of the ark, kind by kind.

passages.context_html:
Noah sees that the surface is drying before the family leaves. The account distinguishes what he observes in the first month from the dry earth and God's command in the second. His departure follows God's word, just as his entrance did. Preservation in the ark leads to a new responsibility outside it.

God names the whole household and the creatures that are to come out. The purpose is life spreading again: the animals are to breed and multiply on the earth. The closing description of creatures leaving in their groups echoes their ordered entrance. The focus is not merely that Noah has survived, but that the life entrusted to him is released into the world.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as an obedient departure and a renewed beginning for humanity and the other creatures. Wesley's introduction to chapter 8 and notes on verses 13–14 distinguish the appearance of drying ground from its readiness for habitation, while the narrative itself makes God's command the immediate basis for leaving.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The call for living creatures to multiply recalls the blessings of Genesis 1:22, 28. This is a supported parallel with creation: God preserves life through judgment and again directs it to fill the earth. Noah's release is part of that purpose for the world, not simply the end of an individual ordeal.

The renewed beginning is not yet the final freedom of creation. The next chapter still contains sin and death, while Romans 8:19–23 looks toward creation's release from decay along with the redemption of God's children. What God preserves here continues toward a restoration greater than life immediately after the flood.

passages.title: Genesis 8:20-22
passages.section_title: Noah Builds an Altar

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 20 Then Noah built an altar to the LORD. And taking from every kind of clean animal and clean bird, he offered burnt offerings on the altar. 21 When the LORD smelled the pleasing aroma, He said in His heart, “Never again will I curse the ground because of man, even though every inclination of his heart is evil from his youth. And never again will I destroy all living creatures as I have done. 22 As long as the earth endures, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night shall never cease.”
paragraphs: 20 Then Noah built an altar to the LORD. And taking from every kind of clean animal and clean bird, he offered burnt offerings on the altar. 21 When the LORD smelled the pleasing aroma, He said in His heart, “Never again will I curse the ground because of man, even though every inclination of his heart is evil from his youth. And never again will I destroy all living creatures as I have done.
22 As long as the earth endures,
seedtime and harvest,
cold and heat,
summer and winter,
day and night
shall never cease.”

passages.context_html:
After leaving the ark, Noah builds an altar and offers clean animals and birds. The additional clean creatures brought aboard in chapter 7 now have a place in the family's worship. God's acceptance of the offering is followed by His resolve to preserve the world from another destruction of this kind.

The statement about the human heart is important. It still tends toward evil from youth, so the flood has not made the surviving human family incapable of sin. God's promise is given with that condition in view. The regular rhythms of planting, harvest, seasons, day, and night will continue while the earth remains.

Chapter 9 develops this into a covenant with Noah, his descendants, and living creatures. These verses should therefore be read as the beginning of that promise, rather than as a declaration that the earth will exist forever or that humanity no longer needs rescue from evil.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the altar as Noah's worshipful response to preservation and the following promise as an expression of God's patience with a still-sinful humanity. Wesley's notes on verses 20–22 emphasize both the accepted offering and the surprising mercy of preserving people whose hearts remain inclined toward evil.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The accepted offering belongs to a wider biblical pattern of drawing near to God through sacrifice. Ephesians 5:2 describes Christ giving Himself as an offering pleasing to God. This is a connection in the language and theme of sacrifice, rather than an explicit statement that Paul is explaining Noah's particular altar.

The continuing problem of the human heart also keeps this altar from being the end of the story. Hebrews 10:1–14 distinguishes repeated animal offerings from Christ's decisive offering. The world is preserved here so that life continues; the fuller answer to sin comes through the One who gives Himself for His people.

passages.title: Genesis 9:1-17
passages.section_title: The Covenant of the Rainbow

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 And God blessed Noah and his sons and said to them, “Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth. 2 The fear and dread of you will fall on every living creature on the earth, every bird of the air, every creature that crawls on the ground, and all the fish of the sea. They are delivered into your hand. 3 Everything that lives and moves will be food for you; just as I gave you the green plants, I now give you all things. 4 But you must not eat meat with its lifeblood still in it. 5 And surely I will require the life of any man or beast by whose hand your lifeblood is shed. I will demand an accounting from anyone who takes the life of his fellow man: 6 Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man his blood will be shed; for in His own image God has made mankind. 7 But as for you, be fruitful and multiply; spread out across the earth and multiply upon it.” 8 Then God said to Noah and his sons with him, 9 “Behold, I now establish My covenant with you and your descendants after you, 10 and with every living creature that was with you—the birds, the livestock, and every beast of the earth—every living thing that came out of the ark. 11 And I establish My covenant with you: Never again will all life be cut off by the waters of a flood; never again will there be a flood to destroy the earth.” 12 And God said, “This is the sign of the covenant I am making between Me and you and every living creature with you, a covenant for all generations to come: 13 I have set My rainbow in the clouds, and it will be a sign of the covenant between Me and the earth. 14 Whenever I form clouds over the earth and the rainbow appears in the clouds, 15 I will remember My covenant between Me and you and every living creature of every kind. Never again will the waters become a flood to destroy all life. 16 And whenever the rainbow appears in the clouds, I will see it and remember the everlasting covenant between God and every living creature of every kind that is on the earth.” 17 So God said to Noah, “This is the sign of the covenant that I have established between Me and every creature on the earth.”
paragraphs: 1 And God blessed Noah and his sons and said to them, “Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth. 2 The fear and dread of you will fall on every living creature on the earth, every bird of the air, every creature that crawls on the ground, and all the fish of the sea. They are delivered into your hand. 3 Everything that lives and moves will be food for you; just as I gave you the green plants, I now give you all things. 4 But you must not eat meat with its lifeblood still in it. 5 And surely I will require the life of any man or beast by whose hand your lifeblood is shed. I will demand an accounting from anyone who takes the life of his fellow man:
6 Whoever sheds the blood of man,
by man his blood will be shed;
for in His own image
God has made mankind.
7 But as for you,
be fruitful and multiply;
spread out across the earth
and multiply upon it.”

8 Then God said to Noah and his sons with him, 9 “Behold, I now establish My covenant with you and your descendants after you, 10 and with every living creature that was with you—the birds, the livestock, and every beast of the earth—every living thing that came out of the ark. 11 And I establish My covenant with you: Never again will all life be cut off by the waters of a flood; never again will there be a flood to destroy the earth.”

12 And God said, “This is the sign of the covenant I am making between Me and you and every living creature with you, a covenant for all generations to come: 13 I have set My rainbow in the clouds, and it will be a sign of the covenant between Me and the earth.

14 Whenever I form clouds over the earth and the rainbow appears in the clouds, 15 I will remember My covenant between Me and you and every living creature of every kind. Never again will the waters become a flood to destroy all life. 16 And whenever the rainbow appears in the clouds, I will see it and remember the everlasting covenant between God and every living creature of every kind that is on the earth.”
17 So God said to Noah, “This is the sign of the covenant that I have established between Me and every creature on the earth.”

passages.context_html:
God blesses the family He has preserved and repeats the call to fill the earth. He permits animals as food while forbidding meat with its lifeblood. He then requires an accounting for the taking of human life. These instructions hold provision and restraint together: receiving food does not make human beings owners of life without limits.

The reason given for the value of human life reaches back to creation: God made humanity in His image. The fall and flood have not erased that dignity. Verse 6 also gives human beings a role in answering bloodshed, which raises a question Christians continue to discuss about punishment and the protection of life.

God then makes His covenant with Noah's family, their descendants, and the living creatures. The Hebrew בְּרִית, bĕrît (beh-REET), means covenant; Brown–Driver–Briggs identifies this passage as a divine promise with a sign. Its content is stated clearly: God will not again destroy all life by the waters of a flood. The rainbow marks that promise. It is not a promise that no local flood will ever occur.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read the covenant as God's commitment to preserve the world and the commands as requiring respect for life. Where do traditions differ? On verse 6, Wesley's notes understand the punishment of murder as entrusted to human authorities. The Westminster Confession, 23.1, and 1689 Baptist Confession, 24.1, likewise teach that God gives civil rulers the power of the sword to punish wrongdoing; those statements do not prescribe the sentence for every modern case.

The Catholic Church's current Catechism, 2267, teaches that the death penalty is inadmissible and calls for its abolition. It appeals to the continuing dignity of the person and the possibility of protecting society without execution. The disagreement concerns how punishment should protect life; the value of human life remains central to the documents on both sides.

The rainbow's significance is God's promise, rather than a claim about when rainbows first existed. Wesley's notes on verse 13 suggest that an existing rainbow was given a new covenant meaning. Genesis states the sign and its purpose without explaining its first physical appearance.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
In Isaiah 54:9–10, God explicitly recalls the promise to Noah when assuring His people of enduring mercy and a covenant of peace. The earlier promise becomes an example of the trustworthiness of what He says later. God's purpose moves forward through commitments He keeps, not through human confidence that disaster is impossible.

2 Peter 3:5–13 also keeps the flood and the future together. God's patience gives room for repentance, while His promise looks toward a new heaven and earth where righteousness dwells. The Noah covenant preserves the setting in which His continuing work of rescue unfolds; it does not mean that He has ceased to judge evil.

passages.title: Genesis 9:18-25
passages.section_title: Noah’s Shame and Canaan’s Curse

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 The sons of Noah who came out of the ark were Shem, Ham, and Japheth. And Ham was the father of Canaan. 19 These three were the sons of Noah, and from them the whole earth was populated. 20 Now Noah, a man of the soil, proceeded to plant a vineyard. 21 But when he drank some of its wine, he became drunk and uncovered himself inside his tent. 22 And Ham, the father of Canaan, saw his father’s nakedness and told his two brothers outside. 23 Then Shem and Japheth took a garment and placed it across their shoulders, and walking backward, they covered their father’s nakedness. Their faces were turned away so that they did not see their father’s nakedness. 24 When Noah awoke from his drunkenness and learned what his youngest son had done to him, 25 he said, “Cursed be Canaan! A servant of servants shall he be to his brothers.”
paragraphs: 18 The sons of Noah who came out of the ark were Shem, Ham, and Japheth. And Ham was the father of Canaan. 19 These three were the sons of Noah, and from them the whole earth was populated.

20 Now Noah, a man of the soil, proceeded to plant a vineyard. 21 But when he drank some of its wine, he became drunk and uncovered himself inside his tent. 22 And Ham, the father of Canaan, saw his father’s nakedness and told his two brothers outside.

23 Then Shem and Japheth took a garment and placed it across their shoulders, and walking backward, they covered their father’s nakedness. Their faces were turned away so that they did not see their father’s nakedness.
24 When Noah awoke from his drunkenness and learned what his youngest son had done to him, 25 he said,
“Cursed be Canaan!
A servant of servants
shall he be to his brothers.”

passages.context_html:
The account moves from God's covenant to the life of the surviving family. Noah plants a vineyard, becomes drunk, and lies uncovered. Ham sees his father's nakedness and tells his brothers. Shem and Japheth respond differently: they walk backward with a garment and cover their father without looking at him. The contrast concerns how the sons handle another person's exposure and shame.

Genesis does not tell us all that Noah knew about wine or supply a fuller scene inside the tent. It does tell us that he later learns what his youngest son has done. His pronouncement names Canaan, Ham's son, rather than Ham himself. The repeated identification of Ham as Canaan's father prepares for that ending, but the reason for directing the curse to this son is not fully explained.

The curse speaks of Canaan's service to his brothers. Nothing in the words assigns a skin color to anyone, curses all Ham's descendants, or commands the enslavement of an entire modern population. The people named in the passage and the actual terms of the pronouncement must govern how it is read.
passages.common_interpretations_html: A common Christian reading focuses on the contrast between Ham's dishonor and his brothers' care, with the curse anticipating the later place of Canaan's descendants in the story of Israel. Wesley's notes on verses 22–25 develop those themes and relate the service language to Israel's later dealings with the Canaanites, rather than making the passage a decree about every descendant of Ham.

passages.god_plan_html:
The failure after the flood shows a limit of the new beginning: being carried through a judgment has not removed humanity's need for inward renewal. That theme develops in Ezekiel 36:26–27, where God promises a new heart and His Spirit to enable a different way of life.

2 Corinthians 5:17–21 brings new creation and reconciliation together in Christ. The contrast helps explain why the Bible's hope must reach beyond surviving a disaster. God's purpose includes restoring people to Himself.

passages.title: Genesis 9:26-29
passages.section_title: Shem’s Blessing and Noah’s Death

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 26 He also declared: “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Shem! May Canaan be the servant of Shem. 27 May God expand the territory of Japheth; may he dwell in the tents of Shem, and may Canaan be his servant.” 28 After the flood, Noah lived 350 years. 29 So Noah lived a total of 950 years, and then he died.

“Blessed be the LORD, the God of Shem!
May Canaan be the servant of Shem.
27 May God expand the territory of Japheth;
may he dwell in the tents of Shem,
and may Canaan be his servant.”
28 After the flood, Noah lived 350 years. 29 So Noah lived a total of 950 years, and then he died.

passages.context_html:
The blessing begins by naming the LORD as the God of Shem. Japheth is to be enlarged, and the saying includes dwelling in Shem's tents. Canaan's service is repeated. These words turn our attention from the brothers' immediate actions to the families and relationships followed in the next chapters.

The last two verses return to the pattern of the earlier family record: Noah's years are counted, and he dies. Surviving the flood did not make him immortal. The story will continue through his descendants, while the account of the man who built the ark closes with the same human ending seen in chapter 5.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the blessing of Shem in relation to the family through which Abraham and Israel will come, while Japheth receives enlargement and a place in relation to Shem. Wesley's notes on verses 26–27 connect Shem's blessing with Abraham and the honor of belonging to God; the family connections themselves are developed in Genesis 10–11.

passages.god_plan_html:
Luke 3:23–36 explicitly places Shem and Noah in Jesus' ancestry. The family line followed through Shem leads toward the coming of Christ, giving the blessing a place in the larger story of God's rescue.

There is also a useful parallel with the welcome of the nations into God's household. Ephesians 2:11–22 describes people once far away being brought near through Christ and sharing one household. The comparison helps us picture the shared blessing Paul explains: people formerly outside are welcomed into one family through God's Son.

passages.title: Genesis 10:1-32
passages.section_title: The Table of Nations

passages.context_html:
After Noah's death, Genesis follows the families of his three sons as they become peoples with their own lands and languages. This is often called the Table of Nations. Rather than following one line from father to son, as chapter 5 did, it spreads outward across related families. Chapter 11 will return to the question of how their languages became divided.

Several names prepare us for what follows. Nimrod's kingdom begins in Babylon, in Shinar, the setting of the next chapter. Canaan's descendants inhabit the land to which Abram will later be called. Shem's family includes Eber and Peleg; chapter 11 will follow that branch to Abram. The list gives the coming story of one family a place within the story of the nations.

The repeated references to families, lands, and languages hold two things together: these peoples are distinct, and they belong to the same human family. The chapter names ancient peoples and places; it does not give a complete ancestry chart for every modern country or a ranking of people's worth.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this chapter as an account of the nations' shared descent after the flood and as preparation for the story of Abraham and Israel. Wesley's introduction to Genesis 10 also cautions that migration, mixing, and lost records make confident claims about the ancestry of modern populations difficult.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 17:24–27 describes God making every nation from one man and appointing their times and boundaries so that they would seek Him. Paul does not name Genesis 10 there, but his teaching helps us see the larger theme: the nations share one Creator, and their lives matter to Him.

The story will soon narrow to Abram, yet its purpose remains wider than his family. God promises blessing for all the families of the earth in Genesis 12:1–3, and Galatians 3:8–9 connects that promise with the good news reaching the nations through faith. Revelation 7:9–10 shows the destination: people from many nations and languages worshiping God and the Lamb together.

passages.title: Genesis 11:1-9
passages.section_title: The Tower of Babel

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now the whole world had one language and a common form of speech. 2 And as people journeyed eastward, they found a plain in the land of Shinar and settled there. 3 And they said to one another, “Come, let us make bricks and bake them thoroughly.” So they used brick instead of stone, and tar instead of mortar. 4 “Come,” they said, “let us build for ourselves a city with a tower that reaches to the heavens, that we may make a name for ourselves and not be scattered over the face of all the earth.” 5 Then the LORD came down to see the city and the tower that the sons of men were building. 6 And the LORD said, “If they have begun to do this as one people speaking the same language, then nothing they devise will be beyond them. 7 Come, let Us go down and confuse their language, so that they will not understand one another’s speech.” 8 So the LORD scattered them from there over the face of all the earth, and they stopped building the city. 9 That is why it is called Babel, for there the LORD confused the language of the whole world, and from that place the LORD scattered them over the face of all the earth.
paragraphs: 1 Now the whole world had one language and a common form of speech. 2 And as people journeyed eastward, they found a plain in the land of Shinar and settled there.
3 And they said to one another, “Come, let us make bricks and bake them thoroughly.” So they used brick instead of stone, and tar instead of mortar.
4 “Come,” they said, “let us build for ourselves a city with a tower that reaches to the heavens, that we may make a name for ourselves and not be scattered over the face of all the earth.”

5 Then the LORD came down to see the city and the tower that the sons of men were building. 6 And the LORD said, “If they have begun to do this as one people speaking the same language, then nothing they devise will be beyond them. 7 Come, let Us go down and confuse their language, so that they will not understand one another’s speech.”

8 So the LORD scattered them from there over the face of all the earth, and they stopped building the city. 9 That is why it is called Babel, for there the LORD confused the language of the whole world, and from that place the LORD scattered them over the face of all the earth.

passages.context_html:
Chapter 10 described peoples spread across their lands and languages. This passage steps back to explain the scattering. The builders settle in Shinar, make bricks, and plan a city and tower. They tell us what they want: a lasting name for themselves and protection against being scattered. Their determination to stay together stands against God's earlier direction to fill the earth in Genesis 9:1, 7.

Their repeated invitation to act together is answered by God's own decision to come down and confuse their speech. They can no longer understand one another, the work stops, and the scattering they tried to prevent takes place. The description of the LORD coming down to inspect their great tower also puts its supposed greatness in perspective.

The ending uses a Hebrew wordplay. The verb בָּלַל, bālal (bah-LAHL), means to mix or confuse; Brown–Driver–Briggs identifies confusing speech as its use here. The similar sound links Babel with what God does there. Brown–Driver–Briggs on Babel also identifies Babel as Babylon. The point is that the place where people sought lasting fame becomes remembered for confusion and scattering.
passages.common_interpretations_html: A common Christian reading sees pride and resistance to God in the builders' attempt to secure their own greatness and unity. Wesley's notes on Genesis 11:3–9 and the US Catholic bishops' note on Genesis 11:1–9 both emphasize that pride and God's overturning of the project.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
There is a striking contrast with Genesis 12:1–3. The builders try to make their own name great; God promises to make Abram's name great and make him a blessing to all families. The movement is from people securing a name for themselves to a man receiving a promise whose blessing reaches others.

Pentecost offers a helpful parallel. At Babel, confusion of speech ends the shared project and scatters the people. In Acts 2:5–12, people from many places hear God's wonderful works in their own languages. Acts does not call this a direct fulfillment of Babel, and the languages do not disappear. The contrast helps us picture God gathering people through a message they can understand. Revelation 7:9–10 carries that picture further: many peoples and languages united in worship before God and the Lamb.

passages.title: Genesis 11:10-26
passages.section_title: Genealogy from Shem to Abram

Two years after the flood, when Shem was 100 years old, he became the father of Arphaxad. 11 And after he had become the father of Arphaxad, Shem lived 500 years and had other sons and daughters. 12 When Arphaxad was 35 years old, he became the father of Shelah. 13 And after he had become the father of Shelah, Arphaxad lived 403 years and had other sons and daughters. 14 When Shelah was 30 years old, he became the father of Eber. 15 And after he had become the father of Eber, Shelah lived 403 years and had other sons and daughters. 16 When Eber was 34 years old, he became the father of Peleg. 17 And after he had become the father of Peleg, Eber lived 430 years and had other sons and daughters. 18 When Peleg was 30 years old, he became the father of Reu. 19 And after he had become the father of Reu, Peleg lived 209 years and had other sons and daughters. 20 When Reu was 32 years old, he became the father of Serug. 21 And after he had become the father of Serug, Reu lived 207 years and had other sons and daughters. 22 When Serug was 30 years old, he became the father of Nahor. 23 And after he had become the father of Nahor, Serug lived 200 years and had other sons and daughters. 24 When Nahor was 29 years old, he became the father of Terah. 25 And after he had become the father of Terah, Nahor lived 119 years and had other sons and daughters. 26 When Terah was 70 years old, he became the father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran.

passages.context_html:
After the scattering at Babel, the account follows one branch of Noah's family. It begins with Shem, two years after the flood, and moves through Arphaxad, Shelah, Eber, Peleg, Reu, Serug, Nahor, and Terah. Terah's three sons introduce Abram, who will become the central figure in the next part of Genesis.

Chapter 10 traced Eber's descendants through Joktan's many sons; this list takes the other branch, through Peleg. Its repeated pattern of a son's birth, further years, and other children resembles chapter 5. The listed lifespans generally become shorter as the account moves toward Abram, although the change is not an even decline from one generation to the next.

These verses supply names and ages, with few details about the people's lives. Their place in the family record does not establish that every person named was faithful to God. Joshua 24:2–3 later says that Terah's household served other gods before describing God's call of Abraham.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this genealogy as the bridge from Noah's family to Abraham, preparing for God's promises to him. Wesley's notes on Genesis 11:10 emphasize the movement toward Abraham, and the US Catholic bishops' note on Genesis 11:10–26 likewise describes its place at this turning point in the book.

passages.god_plan_html:
Luke 3:34–36 includes these ancestors as it traces Jesus' family back through Abraham, Shem, and Noah. A list that may first look like a pause in the story becomes part of the connection between the earliest generations and the coming of Christ.

There is a detail worth noticing when reading the two lists together: Luke names Cainan between Arphaxad and Shelah, while the Genesis text printed here does not. The US Catholic bishops' note on Genesis 11:12 identifies that additional name in the Greek form of the genealogy. The difference belongs to the history of the texts; the shared line still connects Abraham with the earlier family through whom Luke traces Jesus.

passages.title: Genesis 11:27-32
passages.section_title: Terah’s Descendants

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 27 This is the account of Terah. Terah became the father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran. And Haran became the father of Lot. 28 During his father Terah’s lifetime, Haran died in his native land, in Ur of the Chaldeans. 29 And Abram and Nahor took wives for themselves. Abram’s wife was named Sarai, and Nahor’s wife was named Milcah; she was the daughter of Haran, who was the father of both Milcah and Iscah. 30 But Sarai was barren; she had no children. 31 And Terah took his son Abram, his grandson Lot son of Haran, and his daughter-in-law Sarai the wife of Abram, and they set out from Ur of the Chaldeans for the land of Canaan. But when they arrived in Haran, they settled there. 32 Terah lived 205 years, and he died in Haran.
paragraphs: 27 This is the account of Terah. Terah became the father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran. And Haran became the father of Lot. 28 During his father Terah’s lifetime, Haran died in his native land, in Ur of the Chaldeans.

29 And Abram and Nahor took wives for themselves. Abram’s wife was named Sarai, and Nahor’s wife was named Milcah; she was the daughter of Haran, who was the father of both Milcah and Iscah. 30 But Sarai was barren; she had no children.

31 And Terah took his son Abram, his grandson Lot son of Haran, and his daughter-in-law Sarai the wife of Abram, and they set out from Ur of the Chaldeans for the land of Canaan. But when they arrived in Haran, they settled there. 32 Terah lived 205 years, and he died in Haran.

passages.context_html:
The account now turns from a long family line to the lives of Terah's household. Haran dies while his father Terah is still alive, leaving Lot as his surviving son. Abram marries Sarai, while Nahor marries Milcah, Haran's daughter. These relationships explain why Lot travels with Abram and prepare for the relatives encountered later in Genesis.

The brief notice that Sarai has no children matters enormously. The next chapter promises to make Abram a great nation, yet this family has no child through whom that promise could continue. Genesis introduces the difficulty before it tells us the promise, so we will watch how God meets it.

Terah takes Abram, Sarai, and Lot from Ur of the Chaldeans toward Canaan, but they settle in Haran. Terah dies there. Acts 7:2–4 adds that God first appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia before he lived in Haran. The journey therefore belongs to the beginning of God's call, although Genesis gives the words of that call in the next chapter.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this paragraph as the beginning of Abraham's family story, with the move toward Canaan and Sarai's inability to have children preparing for God's promise. Wesley's notes on Genesis 11:27–32 connect the departure with God's call and explain the relatives' importance for the story that follows.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 7:2–8 explicitly brings this journey and the promise together: God called Abraham before he lived in Haran and promised him descendants even when he had no child. God's purpose begins to take shape while the family is still traveling and the most obvious obstacle remains unresolved.

Hebrews 11:8–12 later remembers both Abraham's journey in faith and Sarah receiving the ability to conceive because she trusted the One who promised. The lesson reaches beyond a successful journey or an unexpected birth: the future of this family rests on God's faithfulness. Their beginning prepares us to see why His promise, rather than their own resources, carries the story forward.

passages.title: Genesis 12:1-9
passages.section_title: The Call of Abram

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then the LORD said to Abram, “Leave your country, your kindred, and your father’s household, and go to the land I will show you. 2 I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you; I will make your name great, so that you will be a blessing. 3 I will bless those who bless you and curse those who curse you; and all the families of the earth will be blessed through you.” 4 So Abram departed, as the LORD had directed him, and Lot went with him. Abram was seventy-five years old when he left Haran. 5 And Abram took his wife Sarai, his nephew Lot, and all the possessions and people they had acquired in Haran, and set out for the land of Canaan. When they came to the land of Canaan, 6 Abram traveled through the land as far as the site of the Oak of Moreh at Shechem. And at that time the Canaanites were in the land. 7 Then the LORD appeared to Abram and said, “I will give this land to your offspring.” So Abram built an altar there to the LORD, who had appeared to him. 8 From there Abram moved on to the hill country east of Bethel and pitched his tent, with Bethel to the west and Ai to the east. There he built an altar to the LORD, and he called on the name of the LORD. 9 And Abram journeyed on toward the Negev.

2 I will make you into a great nation,
and I will bless you;
I will make your name great,
so that you will be a blessing.
3 I will bless those who bless you
and curse those who curse you;
and all the families of the earth
will be blessed through you.”

4 So Abram departed, as the LORD had directed him, and Lot went with him. Abram was seventy-five years old when he left Haran. 5 And Abram took his wife Sarai, his nephew Lot, and all the possessions and people they had acquired in Haran, and set out for the land of Canaan.
When they came to the land of Canaan, 6 Abram traveled through the land as far as the site of the Oak of Moreh at Shechem. And at that time the Canaanites were in the land.
7 Then the LORD appeared to Abram and said, “I will give this land to your offspring.” So Abram built an altar there to the LORD, who had appeared to him.

8 From there Abram moved on to the hill country east of Bethel and pitched his tent, with Bethel to the west and Ai to the east. There he built an altar to the LORD, and he called on the name of the LORD.
9 And Abram journeyed on toward the Negev.

passages.context_html:
God's call follows the account of Terah's family, their move from Ur to Haran, and Sarai's inability to have children. Abram is told to leave the familiar life of his country and father's household for a land God will show him. The promises answer the uncertainty of that departure: God will give him a future, make him a great nation, and make him a blessing to others.

The promise reaches beyond Abram's household to all the families of the earth. This follows the scattering of the nations in chapters 10–11. Where Babel's builders sought to make their own name great, God promises to make Abram's name great so that blessing will reach others. One family now becomes central to a story that still concerns the whole human family.

Abram leaves Haran at seventy-five with Sarai, Lot, their possessions, and the people with them. In Canaan, the presence of the Canaanites reminds us that receiving a promise is different from already possessing its fulfillment. God promises the land to Abram's offspring, while Abram lives in tents, builds altars, and calls on the LORD. His journey becomes a life of worship while he waits.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read Abram's departure as a response of faith to God's call and the promise as blessing that will reach beyond his descendants. Wesley's notes on Genesis 12:1–8 emphasize his trust and obedience, while the Catholic Church's Catechism, 59–60, describes the call of Abraham as part of God's purpose to gather scattered humanity.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Galatians 3:8–14 explicitly connects the promise of blessing for the nations with the good news: through Christ, the blessing promised to Abraham reaches people of other nations, and they receive the Spirit through faith. Abram's call is therefore more than the beginning of Israel's family history. It belongs to the unfolding of God's rescue reaching people from every nation.

Hebrews 11:8–10 also explains Abram's journey as an act of faith. He went without knowing where he was going and lived as a stranger while looking for the city God would build. The tents and altars help us picture that kind of life: acting on what God has said, worshiping Him in the present, and trusting Him for a future not yet in view.

passages.title: Genesis 12:10-20
passages.section_title: Abram and Sarai in Egypt

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 Now there was a famine in the land. So Abram went down to Egypt to live there for a while because the famine was severe. 11 As he was about to enter Egypt, he said to his wife Sarai, “Look, I know that you are a beautiful woman, 12 and when the Egyptians see you, they will say, ‘This is his wife.’ Then they will kill me but will let you live. 13 Please say you are my sister, so that I will be treated well for your sake, and on account of you my life will be spared.” 14 So when Abram entered Egypt, the Egyptians saw that the woman was very beautiful. 15 When Pharaoh’s officials saw Sarai, they commended her to him, and she was taken into the palace of Pharaoh. 16 He treated Abram well on her account, and Abram acquired sheep and cattle, male and female donkeys, menservants and maidservants, and camels. 17 The LORD, however, afflicted Pharaoh and his household with severe plagues because of Abram’s wife Sarai. 18 So Pharaoh summoned Abram and asked, “What have you done to me? Why didn’t you tell me she was your wife? 19 Why did you say, ‘She is my sister,’ so that I took her as my wife? Now then, here is your wife. Take her and go!” 20 Then Pharaoh gave his men orders concerning Abram, and they sent him away with his wife and all his possessions.
paragraphs: 10 Now there was a famine in the land. So Abram went down to Egypt to live there for a while because the famine was severe. 11 As he was about to enter Egypt, he said to his wife Sarai, “Look, I know that you are a beautiful woman, 12 and when the Egyptians see you, they will say, ‘This is his wife.’ Then they will kill me but will let you live. 13 Please say you are my sister, so that I will be treated well for your sake, and on account of you my life will be spared.”

14 So when Abram entered Egypt, the Egyptians saw that the woman was very beautiful. 15 When Pharaoh’s officials saw Sarai, they commended her to him, and she was taken into the palace of Pharaoh. 16 He treated Abram well on her account, and Abram acquired sheep and cattle, male and female donkeys, menservants and maidservants, and camels.

17 The LORD, however, afflicted Pharaoh and his household with severe plagues because of Abram’s wife Sarai. 18 So Pharaoh summoned Abram and asked, “What have you done to me? Why didn’t you tell me she was your wife? 19 Why did you say, ‘She is my sister,’ so that I took her as my wife? Now then, here is your wife. Take her and go!”
20 Then Pharaoh gave his men orders concerning Abram, and they sent him away with his wife and all his possessions.

passages.context_html:
A severe famine interrupts Abram's life in the land God has promised. He goes to Egypt to stay for a while, but fear of being killed because of Sarai's beauty leads him to conceal their marriage. His stated purpose is his own survival. The plan exposes Sarai to the very danger he is trying to escape for himself: she is taken into Pharaoh's household.

Abram receives livestock and servants because of Sarai, yet these gains come while husband and wife are separated. Material increase does not make the situation a success. The LORD intervenes with plagues on Pharaoh's household because of Sarai, and Pharaoh confronts Abram with the deception before sending them away together.

The passage reports Abram's fear, the taking of Sarai, God's intervention, and Pharaoh's rebuke. It does not tell us the nature of the plagues or describe what happened to Sarai inside the palace. The force of the account is already clear without filling in those missing details: the man who has received God's promise endangers his household through a fearful attempt to protect himself.
passages.common_interpretations_html: A common Christian reading sees a serious failure of trust in Abram's deception and God's care in Sarai's deliverance. Wesley's notes on Genesis 12:13–18 stress that even a man known for faith can fall into distrust, and that Pharaoh's rebuke exposes the wrong Abram has done.
passages.current_position_html: Our Prayer and Faith study reads Abram's deception in Egypt as a failure to trust God under pressure. His attempt to protect himself endangers Sarai, and God's intervention, rather than the success of his scheme, brings her back. The study calls us to depend on God instead of using deception to secure the outcome we want.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
There is a useful parallel with the later departure of Abram's descendants from Egypt. Here a famine takes the family to Egypt, Pharaoh's household suffers plagues, and the family leaves with its possessions. In Exodus 12:29–36, judgment on Egypt is followed by Pharaoh sending Israel away, and the people depart with goods. The resemblance helps us recognize a pattern of God bringing His people out of danger; it does not make every detail of the two stories identical.

God's intervention also preserves the family through whom the promised blessing will continue. Galatians 3:8–14 shows the wider reach of that promise in Christ. The future blessing of the nations does not depend on pretending that Abram is consistently brave or honest. Genesis lets us see both his failure and God's continuing work.

passages.title: Genesis 13:1-9
passages.section_title: Abram and Lot Part Ways

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 So Abram went up out of Egypt into the Negev—he and his wife and all his possessions—and Lot was with him. 2 And Abram had become extremely wealthy in livestock and silver and gold. 3 From the Negev he journeyed from place to place toward Bethel, until he came to the place between Bethel and Ai where his tent had formerly been pitched, 4 to the site where he had built the altar. And there Abram called on the name of the LORD. 5 Now Lot, who was traveling with Abram, also had flocks and herds and tents. 6 But the land was unable to support both of them while they stayed together, for they had so many possessions that they were unable to coexist. 7 And there was discord between the herdsmen of Abram and the herdsmen of Lot. At that time the Canaanites and the Perizzites were also living in the land. 8 So Abram said to Lot, “Please let there be no contention between you and me, or between your herdsmen and my herdsmen. After all, we are kinsmen. 9 Is not the whole land before you? Now separate yourself from me. If you go to the left, I will go to the right; if you go to the right, I will go to the left.”
paragraphs: 1 So Abram went up out of Egypt into the Negev—he and his wife and all his possessions—and Lot was with him. 2 And Abram had become extremely wealthy in livestock and silver and gold.

3 From the Negev he journeyed from place to place toward Bethel, until he came to the place between Bethel and Ai where his tent had formerly been pitched, 4 to the site where he had built the altar. And there Abram called on the name of the LORD.

5 Now Lot, who was traveling with Abram, also had flocks and herds and tents. 6 But the land was unable to support both of them while they stayed together, for they had so many possessions that they were unable to coexist. 7 And there was discord between the herdsmen of Abram and the herdsmen of Lot. At that time the Canaanites and the Perizzites were also living in the land.

8 So Abram said to Lot, “Please let there be no contention between you and me, or between your herdsmen and my herdsmen. After all, we are kinsmen. 9 Is not the whole land before you? Now separate yourself from me. If you go to the left, I will go to the right; if you go to the right, I will go to the left.”

passages.context_html:
Abram returns from Egypt with Sarai, Lot, and his possessions. He travels back to the place between Bethel and Ai where he had built an altar, and there he calls on the LORD again. The return brings the story back to his earlier life of worship in the promised land after the danger and deception in Egypt.

Both Abram and Lot have large flocks and herds. Their wealth creates a practical problem: the available land cannot support them together, and their herdsmen begin to quarrel. Other peoples already live in the land as well. The dispute shows that having more possessions can bring pressures that prosperity alone cannot solve.

Abram addresses the conflict before it becomes a lasting breach between them. He appeals to their family relationship and offers Lot the choice of direction, agreeing to take the other way. Separation here is a practical way to preserve peace. Abram does not have to win the first choice in order to keep living in the land God has promised.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read Abram's proposal as a generous effort to protect family peace when their herds can no longer share the same ground. Wesley's introduction to Genesis 13 and notes on verses 6–7 describe the shortage of room and the wisdom of ending a quarrel that could expose the family to danger and public shame.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Abram's willingness to give up the first choice gives a concrete example of the Bible's call to make peace. Jesus blesses peacemakers in Matthew 5:9, and Romans 12:17–21 calls believers to pursue peace as far as it depends on them, leaving judgment to God. Abram takes responsibility for reducing conflict instead of insisting that his own interests come first.

The next part of the chapter will show that letting Lot choose does not put God's promise beyond reach. Abram can act generously while trusting God for the future. The lesson is not that every peaceful choice produces immediate material gain, but that faith gives us reasons to pursue peace beyond what we can secure for ourselves.

passages.title: Genesis 13:10-13
passages.section_title: Lot Proceeds toward Sodom

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 And Lot looked out and saw that the whole plain of the Jordan, all the way to Zoar, was well watered like the garden of the LORD, like the land of Egypt. (This was before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah.) 11 So Lot chose the whole plain of the Jordan for himself and set out toward the east. And Abram and Lot parted company. 12 Abram lived in the land of Canaan, but Lot settled in the cities of the plain and pitched his tent toward Sodom. 13 But the men of Sodom were wicked, sinning greatly against the LORD.
paragraphs: 10 And Lot looked out and saw that the whole plain of the Jordan, all the way to Zoar, was well watered like the garden of the LORD, like the land of Egypt. (This was before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah.) 11 So Lot chose the whole plain of the Jordan for himself and set out toward the east. And Abram and Lot parted company.
12 Abram lived in the land of Canaan, but Lot settled in the cities of the plain and pitched his tent toward Sodom. 13 But the men of Sodom were wicked, sinning greatly against the LORD.

passages.context_html:
Lot looks across the Jordan plain and chooses its well-watered land. The comparison with the garden of the LORD and Egypt emphasizes its visible abundance. For a man with large herds, it appears to offer the resources that were lacking when the two households lived together.

The narrator gives us information that makes the choice troubling. This is the region of Sodom and Gomorrah before their destruction, and the people of Sodom are described as greatly wicked before the LORD. The land's appeal and the city's moral condition stand side by side. Good pasture does not tell the whole story of what it will mean to live there.

Lot settles among the cities of the plain and pitches his tent toward Sodom, while Abram remains in Canaan. The account is beginning to separate not only their grazing grounds but also the settings in which their next decisions will unfold. We will need the later chapters to see the cost of Lot's proximity to Sodom.
passages.common_interpretations_html: A common Christian reading sees a warning about judging a place by its advantages while overlooking the character of life there. Wesley's notes on Genesis 13:10, 13 recognize the plain's garden-like appeal and the open wickedness of its inhabitants.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The New Testament returns to the outcome of this choice. 2 Peter 2:6–9 describes Sodom's judgment and calls Lot a righteous man distressed by the lawless conduct around him. That later description matters: Genesis' warning about his choice should not be turned into a declaration that Lot never belonged to God.

Peter's larger point is that God knows how to rescue the godly and judge wrongdoing. Lot's story will show both the misery of living amid evil and God's power to deliver. The attractive landscape is only the beginning of the account; the ending reveals how much more is at stake than the prosperity Lot first sees.

passages.title: Genesis 13:14-18
passages.section_title: God Renews the Promise to Abram

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 After Lot had departed, the LORD said to Abram, “Now lift up your eyes from the place where you are, and look to the north and south and east and west, 15 for all the land that you see, I will give to you and your offspring forever. 16 I will make your offspring like the dust of the earth, so that if one could count the dust of the earth, then your offspring could be counted. 17 Get up and walk around the land, through its length and breadth, for I will give it to you.” 18 So Abram moved his tent and went to live near the Oaks of Mamre at Hebron, where he built an altar to the LORD.
paragraphs: 14 After Lot had departed, the LORD said to Abram, “Now lift up your eyes from the place where you are, and look to the north and south and east and west, 15 for all the land that you see, I will give to you and your offspring forever.

16 I will make your offspring like the dust of the earth, so that if one could count the dust of the earth, then your offspring could be counted. 17 Get up and walk around the land, through its length and breadth, for I will give it to you.”
18 So Abram moved his tent and went to live near the Oaks of Mamre at Hebron, where he built an altar to the LORD.

passages.context_html:
After Lot leaves, God tells Abram to look in every direction and promises the land to him and his offspring. Lot had looked and chosen what seemed best to him; Abram is now invited to look at what God promises to give. Letting his nephew choose first has not deprived him of God's care.

The promise grows more specific. Abram himself is included with his offspring, and their number is compared with the dust of the earth. Sarai still has no child at this point, so the words ask Abram to trust a future he cannot produce or yet see. He is told to walk through the land, then moves to Hebron and builds another altar.

The word translated forever is עוֹלָם, ʿōlām (oh-LAHM). Brown–Driver–Briggs explains its uses for long duration and enduring existence, including God's covenants and promises. The word does not supply a fixed number of years. Here it stresses the lasting character of what God promises; the wider question of fulfillment involves the rest of Scripture as well.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians agree that God promises Canaan to Abram and his offspring, while explaining the promise's ultimate reach in different ways. Where do readings differ? Some expect a future restoration of Israel to its land when Christ returns. Dallas Theological Seminary's doctrinal statement, Article XX, states that expectation as part of Christ's coming earthly reign.

Reformed teaching often emphasizes how the earthly gift points beyond itself to the lasting inheritance in Christ. The Westminster Confession, 7.5–6, places the Old Testament promises within the same covenant of grace fulfilled under Christ; the Orthodox Presbyterian Church's teaching guide The Covenant of Grace explains Abraham's earthly blessings alongside his hope for the heavenly city in Hebrews 11. For this reading, the promise looks beyond possession of Canaan to lasting life with God.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 11:13–16 explains how the patriarchs could live with promises not fully received in their lifetimes: they welcomed them from afar and sought a better, heavenly country. Abram's tent and altar belong to that life of waiting. Trust does not require him to possess everything immediately before he can worship.

The promise also becomes a source of hope for people beyond Abraham's physical descendants. Romans 4:13–16 connects the inheritance with faith and grace, and Galatians 3:26–29 says that those who belong to Christ are Abraham's offspring and heirs according to the promise. The family God is gathering is larger than Abram could count or see from the place where he stands.

passages.title: Genesis 14:1-9
passages.section_title: The War of the Kings

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 In those days Amraphel king of Shinar, Arioch king of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tidal king of Goiim 2 went to war against Bera king of Sodom, Birsha king of Gomorrah, Shinab king of Admah, Shemeber king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela (that is, Zoar). 3 The latter five came as allies to the Valley of Siddim (that is, the Salt Sea). 4 For twelve years they had been subject to Chedorlaomer, but in the thirteenth year they rebelled. 5 In the fourteenth year, Chedorlaomer and the kings allied with him went out and defeated the Rephaites in Ashteroth-karnaim, the Zuzites in Ham, the Emites in Shaveh-kiriathaim, 6 and the Horites in the area of Mount Seir, as far as El-paran, which is near the desert. 7 Then they turned back to invade En-mishpat (that is, Kadesh), and they conquered the whole territory of the Amalekites, as well as the Amorites who lived in Hazazon-tamar. 8 Then the king of Sodom, the king of Gomorrah, the king of Admah, the king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela (that is, Zoar) marched out and arrayed themselves for battle in the Valley of Siddim 9 against Chedorlaomer king of Elam, Tidal king of Goiim, Amraphel king of Shinar, and Arioch king of Ellasar—four kings against five.
paragraphs: 1 In those days Amraphel king of Shinar, Arioch king of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tidal king of Goiim 2 went to war against Bera king of Sodom, Birsha king of Gomorrah, Shinab king of Admah, Shemeber king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela (that is, Zoar).
3 The latter five came as allies to the Valley of Siddim (that is, the Salt Sea). 4 For twelve years they had been subject to Chedorlaomer, but in the thirteenth year they rebelled.

5 In the fourteenth year, Chedorlaomer and the kings allied with him went out and defeated the Rephaites in Ashteroth-karnaim, the Zuzites in Ham, the Emites in Shaveh-kiriathaim, 6 and the Horites in the area of Mount Seir, as far as El-paran, which is near the desert. 7 Then they turned back to invade En-mishpat (that is, Kadesh), and they conquered the whole territory of the Amalekites, as well as the Amorites who lived in Hazazon-tamar.

8 Then the king of Sodom, the king of Gomorrah, the king of Admah, the king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela (that is, Zoar) marched out and arrayed themselves for battle in the Valley of Siddim 9 against Chedorlaomer king of Elam, Tidal king of Goiim, Amraphel king of Shinar, and Arioch king of Ellasar—four kings against five.

passages.context_html:
Abram and Lot have settled in different places, but the next threat comes from a conflict beyond either household. Four allied kings make war against five kings of the plain, including the rulers of Sodom and Gomorrah. The cause is given plainly: after twelve years of subjection to Chedorlaomer, the five rebel, and the following year he returns with his allies.

The invading force defeats several peoples before meeting the five kings in the Valley of Siddim. The sequence shows the reach of the campaign and prepares us for the defeat of the cities where Lot now lives. The repeated names are not a separate list to memorize; they explain how a regional war will draw Abram's family into danger.

This account also keeps the promised land in view as a place already occupied by peoples and rulers. God's promise to Abram has not removed the conflicts around him. At this point Abram is outside the battle, while Lot's home in the plain places him in its path.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these verses as the political setting for Lot's capture and Abram's rescue of him. Wesley's notes on Genesis 14:1–5 explain the revolt, the invading alliance, and its advance toward the cities of the plain.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.
