passages.title: Genesis 14:10-16
passages.section_title: Abram Rescues Lot

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 Now the Valley of Siddim was full of tar pits, and as the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fled, some men fell into the pits, but the survivors fled to the hill country. 11 The four kings seized all the goods of Sodom and Gomorrah and all their food, and they went on their way. 12 They also carried off Abram’s nephew Lot and his possessions, since Lot was living in Sodom. 13 Then an escapee came and reported this to Abram the Hebrew. Now Abram was living near the Oaks of Mamre the Amorite, a brother of Eshcol and Aner, all of whom were bound by treaty to Abram. 14 And when Abram heard that his relative had been captured, he mobilized the 318 trained men born in his household, and they set out in pursuit as far as Dan. 15 During the night, Abram divided his forces and routed Chedorlaomer’s army, pursuing them as far as Hobah, north of Damascus. 16 He retrieved all the goods, as well as his relative Lot and his possessions, together with the women and the rest of the people.
paragraphs: 10 Now the Valley of Siddim was full of tar pits, and as the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fled, some men fell into the pits, but the survivors fled to the hill country.

11 The four kings seized all the goods of Sodom and Gomorrah and all their food, and they went on their way. 12 They also carried off Abram’s nephew Lot and his possessions, since Lot was living in Sodom.

13 Then an escapee came and reported this to Abram the Hebrew. Now Abram was living near the Oaks of Mamre the Amorite, a brother of Eshcol and Aner, all of whom were bound by treaty to Abram. 14 And when Abram heard that his relative had been captured, he mobilized the 318 trained men born in his household, and they set out in pursuit as far as Dan.

15 During the night, Abram divided his forces and routed Chedorlaomer’s army, pursuing them as far as Hobah, north of Damascus. 16 He retrieved all the goods, as well as his relative Lot and his possessions, together with the women and the rest of the people.

passages.context_html:
The five kings are defeated, and the invading army takes the goods and food of Sodom and Gomorrah. Lot and his possessions are carried away as well. Genesis now says that Lot is living in Sodom, continuing the movement from his earlier choice of the plain and his tent pitched toward the city.

An escapee brings the news to Abram, who is living near Mamre and has allies there. When he hears that his relative has been captured, Abram mobilizes 318 trained men born in his household. He pursues the attackers, divides his forces for a night attack, and drives them beyond Damascus.

The rescue reaches beyond Lot alone. Abram brings back the goods, Lot's possessions, the women, and the other people. The relative from whom he had separated is still someone he will act to save. The next scene will credit God with the victory and show what Abram does with the recovered wealth.
passages.common_interpretations_html: A common Christian reading sees Abram acting out of concern for his captured relative rather than a desire to conquer or enrich himself. Wesley's notes on Genesis 14:13–16 emphasize that charitable purpose; the return of the people and Abram's later refusal of the spoils give it a concrete expression.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Abram's pursuit of a captive relative offers a helpful parallel to God's care for His people. In Matthew 18:12–14, Jesus describes a shepherd searching for a straying sheep to explain the Father's concern that none of His little ones should perish. Abram does not dismiss Lot as someone whose trouble no longer concerns him. He goes after him.

Colossians 1:12–14 describes the Father rescuing His people from the dominion of darkness and bringing them into the kingdom of His Son, where there is redemption and forgiveness. The parallel is the love that acts to rescue, rather than a promise that every military captivity will end as Lot's does. The fuller rescue God gives reaches the power of sin itself.

passages.title: Genesis 14:17-24
passages.section_title: Melchizedek Blesses Abram

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 After Abram returned from defeating Chedorlaomer and the kings allied with him, the king of Sodom went out to meet him in the Valley of Shaveh (that is, the King’s Valley). 18 Then Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine—since he was priest of God Most High — 19 and he blessed Abram and said: “Blessed be Abram by God Most High, Creator of heaven and earth, 20 and blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hand.” Then Abram gave Melchizedek a tenth of everything. 21 The king of Sodom said to Abram, “Give me the people, but take the goods for yourself.” 22 But Abram replied to the king of Sodom, “I have raised my hand to the LORD God Most High, Creator of heaven and earth, 23 that I will not accept even a thread, or a strap of a sandal, or anything that belongs to you, lest you should say, ‘I have made Abram rich.’ 24 I will accept nothing but what my men have eaten and the share for the men who went with me—Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre. They may take their portion.”
paragraphs: 17 After Abram returned from defeating Chedorlaomer and the kings allied with him, the king of Sodom went out to meet him in the Valley of Shaveh (that is, the King’s Valley).
18 Then Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine—since he was priest of God Most High — 19 and he blessed Abram and said:
“Blessed be Abram by God Most High,
Creator of heaven and earth,
20 and blessed be God Most High,
who has delivered your enemies into your hand.”
Then Abram gave Melchizedek a tenth of everything.
21 The king of Sodom said to Abram, “Give me the people, but take the goods for yourself.”

22 But Abram replied to the king of Sodom, “I have raised my hand to the LORD God Most High, Creator of heaven and earth, 23 that I will not accept even a thread, or a strap of a sandal, or anything that belongs to you, lest you should say, ‘I have made Abram rich.’ 24 I will accept nothing but what my men have eaten and the share for the men who went with me—Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre. They may take their portion.”

passages.context_html:
Two kings meet Abram after the rescue. Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, brings bread and wine and blesses him. His blessing credits God, the Creator of heaven and earth, with delivering Abram's enemies into his hand. Abram responds by giving Melchizedek a tenth of everything.

The king of Sodom offers Abram the goods if he will return the people. Abram refuses to let this king claim to have made him rich. He has sworn to the LORD, using the same title for God that Melchizedek used. His refusal makes his dependence clear: he will honor God as the source of his future rather than take wealth on terms that obscure that dependence.

Abram distinguishes his own decision from what belongs to others. He allows for what the men have eaten and for his allies to receive their shares. His personal refusal is not presented as a command that every other participant must refuse the same things. The scene holds together worship, gratitude, and care about the source of his wealth.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly recognize Melchizedek as a king-priest who honors God and blesses Abram. The Catholic Catechism, 58, describes him as an earlier figure pointing to Christ. Where do readings differ? His identity has prompted several proposals. Wesley's notes on Genesis 14:18 record both an identification with Shem and the view that this was an appearance of the Son of God, while declining to decide where Scripture does not expressly identify him.

The bread and wine are also given different emphases. Wesley's notes describe refreshment for Abram and his men. The Catholic Church's Catechism, 1333, also sees Melchizedek's gift as an earlier picture of the Church's offering in the Eucharist, or Lord's Supper. That reading connects the gift with the Church's later worship.
passages.current_position_html: Our Who Shepherds the Church? study draws from Melchizedek's appearance and Hebrews 7 to explain Christ's permanent priesthood. Because Jesus lives forever and intercedes for His people, they can draw near to God through Him. The study concludes that church leaders serve by teaching and caring for believers, rather than becoming an additional priestly class standing between them and God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 7:1–10 explicitly takes up this meeting. It explains Melchizedek's titles in terms of righteousness and peace, points to his blessing of Abraham and receipt of the tenth, and uses his priesthood to show a pattern greater than the later line of Levi. The brief Genesis account becomes important precisely because a priest of God appears before that later priesthood is established.

Hebrews 7:20–28 brings the connection to Jesus: His priesthood is confirmed by God's oath, He continues forever, and He always lives to intercede for those who draw near to God through Him. The earlier king-priest helps us understand the lasting priesthood of Christ. The hope is a living Savior whose help does not end with the death of another human priest.

passages.title: Genesis 15:1-7
passages.section_title: God’s Covenant with Abram

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 After these events, the word of the LORD came to Abram in a vision: “Do not be afraid, Abram. I am your shield, your very great reward.” 2 But Abram replied, “O Lord GOD, what can You give me, since I remain childless, and the heir of my house is Eliezer of Damascus?” 3 Abram continued, “Behold, You have given me no offspring, so a servant in my household will be my heir.” 4 Then the word of the LORD came to Abram, saying, “This one will not be your heir, but one who comes from your own body will be your heir.” 5 And the LORD took him outside and said, “Now look to the heavens and count the stars, if you are able.” Then He told him, “So shall your offspring be.” 6 Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness. 7 The LORD also told him, “I am the LORD, who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans to give you this land to possess.”
paragraphs: 1 After these events, the word of the LORD came to Abram in a vision:
“Do not be afraid, Abram.
I am your shield,
your very great reward.”

2 But Abram replied, “O Lord GOD, what can You give me, since I remain childless, and the heir of my house is Eliezer of Damascus?” 3 Abram continued, “Behold, You have given me no offspring, so a servant in my household will be my heir.”

4 Then the word of the LORD came to Abram, saying, “This one will not be your heir, but one who comes from your own body will be your heir.” 5 And the LORD took him outside and said, “Now look to the heavens and count the stars, if you are able.” Then He told him, “So shall your offspring be.”
6 Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness.
7 The LORD also told him, “I am the LORD, who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans to give you this land to possess.”

passages.context_html:
After the rescue and Abram's refusal of Sodom's wealth, the LORD speaks to him in a vision with reassurance and a promise of reward. Abram answers with the concern that still stands in the way of the promised future: he has no child. As matters stand, a servant in his household will inherit what he has.

God answers that the heir will come from Abram's own body and directs him to the stars as a picture of his future offspring. Abram's question is met with a renewed promise. Verse 6 then states that he believes the LORD and that this is credited to him as righteousness. The account does not hide the questions that accompany his trust.

The verb behind believed comes from אָמַן, ʾāman (ah-MAHN). Brown–Driver–Briggs identifies the form and construction used in Genesis 15:6 as trusting or believing in God. Abram is trusting the One who speaks, not merely agreeing that a large family would be desirable. The LORD then recalls the earlier act of bringing him from Ur and the promise of the land.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians recognize God's grace and Abram's faith as central here, while differing over how to explain being put right with God. Where do traditions differ? The Reformed Westminster Confession, 11.1–2, and 1689 Baptist Confession, 11.1–2, teach that God pardons sinners and accepts them as righteous because of Christ, received through faith alone. They distinguish being accepted by God from being changed inwardly, while insisting that living faith produces love and good works.

The Methodist Articles of Religion, IX–X, likewise teach that people are accounted righteous because of Christ's merit through faith, rather than their own achievements, and that good works follow as the fruit of living faith.

The Catholic Church's Catechism, 1989–1993, teaches that God both forgives people and changes them from within when He puts them right with Himself. Christ's saving work makes this possible, and the gift is given in baptism. God's grace comes first and enables a person's response of faith and love; people do not make themselves righteous by unaided effort.

passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 4:1–12 explicitly quotes Genesis 15:6. Paul contrasts a gift received through trust with wages earned by work, and notes that Abraham was counted righteous before circumcision. This makes Abraham a father of believing people beyond the boundary marked by that later sign.

Paul says the words were written for us too in Romans 4:20–25, connecting faith with the God who raised Jesus from the dead. James 2:21–24 also quotes the verse while describing Abraham's later faith working together with his actions. The New Testament brings this promise into the life of believers through both trust in God's saving work and a faith that becomes visible in how they live.

passages.title: Genesis 15:8-21
passages.section_title: God Confirms His Promise

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 But Abram replied, “Lord GOD, how can I know that I will possess it?” 9 And the LORD said to him, “Bring Me a heifer, a goat, and a ram, each three years old, along with a turtledove and a young pigeon.” 10 So Abram brought all these to Him, split each of them down the middle, and laid the halves opposite each other. The birds, however, he did not cut in half. 11 And the birds of prey descended on the carcasses, but Abram drove them away. 12 As the sun was setting, Abram fell into a deep sleep, and suddenly great terror and darkness overwhelmed him. 13 Then the LORD said to Abram, “Know for certain that your descendants will be strangers in a land that is not their own, and they will be enslaved and mistreated four hundred years. 14 But I will judge the nation they serve as slaves, and afterward they will depart with many possessions. 15 You, however, will go to your fathers in peace and be buried at a ripe old age. 16 In the fourth generation your descendants will return here, for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete.” 17 When the sun had set and darkness had fallen, behold, a smoking firepot and a flaming torch appeared and passed between the halves of the carcasses. 18 On that day the LORD made a covenant with Abram, saying, “To your descendants I have given this land—from the river of Egypt to the great River Euphrates— 19 the land of the Kenites, Kenizzites, Kadmonites, 20 Hittites, Perizzites, Rephaites, 21 Amorites, Canaanites, Girgashites, and Jebusites.”

10 So Abram brought all these to Him, split each of them down the middle, and laid the halves opposite each other. The birds, however, he did not cut in half. 11 And the birds of prey descended on the carcasses, but Abram drove them away. 12 As the sun was setting, Abram fell into a deep sleep, and suddenly great terror and darkness overwhelmed him.

13 Then the LORD said to Abram, “Know for certain that your descendants will be strangers in a land that is not their own, and they will be enslaved and mistreated four hundred years. 14 But I will judge the nation they serve as slaves, and afterward they will depart with many possessions. 15 You, however, will go to your fathers in peace and be buried at a ripe old age. 16 In the fourth generation your descendants will return here, for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete.”

17 When the sun had set and darkness had fallen, behold, a smoking firepot and a flaming torch appeared and passed between the halves of the carcasses. 18 On that day the LORD made a covenant with Abram, saying, “To your descendants I have given this land—from the river of Egypt to the great River Euphrates— 19 the land of the Kenites, Kenizzites, Kadmonites, 20 Hittites, Perizzites, Rephaites, 21 Amorites, Canaanites, Girgashites, and Jebusites.”

passages.context_html:
Abram asks how he can know that he will possess the land. God responds by directing him to bring animals. Abram divides the larger animals and lays the halves opposite each other, leaving the birds whole. As he waits, he drives away birds of prey; at sunset he falls into a deep sleep with terror and darkness.

God tells Abram that the fulfillment will include a long and painful wait. His descendants will live as strangers, suffer enslavement and mistreatment, and later leave with possessions after God judges the nation they serve. Abram himself will die in peace. Their return is also connected with the Amorites' wrongdoing, which has not yet reached its full measure. The promise concerns God's dealings with other peoples as well as this family.

A smoking firepot and a flaming torch pass between the pieces, and the LORD makes the covenant, naming the land and its peoples. Abram is not described as walking between them. Jeremiah 34:18–20 describes another covenant in which people pass between a divided calf and face judgment for breaking their commitment. That later passage helps explain the seriousness of the scene here: God is giving Abram a solemn assurance, not a casual prediction.
passages.common_interpretations_html: A common Christian reading sees God confirming the land promise through a solemn covenant and preparing Abram for the delay before his descendants return. Wesley's notes on Genesis 15:8–18 connect the divided animals with Jeremiah's covenant scene and read the promise of departure with possessions in relation to Israel's later deliverance from Egypt.

passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 7:6–7 explicitly recalls this announcement of foreign residence, oppression, and God's judgment on the enslaving nation. The promised future passes through suffering and deliverance, not an uninterrupted rise in comfort. Exodus 12:29–36 later records judgment on Egypt and the people's departure with possessions, bringing the earlier assurance into the story of Israel's rescue.

The larger theme is God's trustworthy promise through a long wait. Hebrews 6:13–20 appeals to God's later oath to Abraham and describes hope grounded in His unchanging purpose as an anchor for believers. The covenant scene here belongs to that unfolding assurance: God has not forgotten His people when the road to fulfillment includes years they would never have chosen.

passages.title: Genesis 16:1-16
passages.section_title: Hagar and Ishmael

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now Abram’s wife Sarai had borne him no children, but she had an Egyptian maidservant named Hagar. 2 So Sarai said to Abram, “Look now, the LORD has prevented me from bearing children. Please go to my maidservant; perhaps I can build a family by her.” And Abram listened to the voice of Sarai. 3 So after he had lived in Canaan for ten years, his wife Sarai took her Egyptian maidservant Hagar and gave her to Abram to be his wife. 4 And he slept with Hagar, and she conceived. But when Hagar realized that she was pregnant, she began to despise her mistress. 5 Then Sarai said to Abram, “May the wrong done to me be upon you! I delivered my servant into your arms, and ever since she saw that she was pregnant, she has treated me with contempt. May the LORD judge between you and me.” 6 “Here,” said Abram, “your servant is in your hands. Do whatever you want with her.” Then Sarai treated Hagar so harshly that she fled from her. 7 Now the angel of the LORD found Hagar by a spring of water in the desert—the spring along the road to Shur. 8 “Hagar, servant of Sarai,” he said, “where have you come from, and where are you going?” “I am running away from my mistress Sarai,” she replied. 9 So the angel of the LORD told her, “Return to your mistress and submit to her authority.” 10 Then the angel added, “I will greatly multiply your offspring so that they will be too numerous to count.” 11 The angel of the LORD proceeded: “Behold, you have conceived and will bear a son. And you shall name him Ishmael, for the LORD has heard your cry of affliction. 12 He will be a wild donkey of a man, and his hand will be against everyone, and everyone’s hand against him; he will live in hostility toward all his brothers.” 13 So Hagar gave this name to the LORD who had spoken to her: “You are the God who sees me,” for she said, “Here I have seen the One who sees me!” 14 Therefore the well was called Beer-lahai-roi. It is located between Kadesh and Bered. 15 And Hagar bore Abram a son, and Abram gave the name Ishmael to the son she had borne. 16 Abram was eighty-six years old when Hagar bore Ishmael to him.

passages.context_html:
Ten years after Abram's arrival in Canaan, Sarai still has no child. She gives her Egyptian servant Hagar to Abram as a wife, hoping to build a family through her. Hagar conceives, begins to despise Sarai, and becomes the subject of a bitter dispute. Abram leaves Hagar in Sarai's power, and Sarai treats her so harshly that she runs away. The plan produces a pregnancy, but it also tears the household apart.

The angel of the LORD finds Hagar at a spring in the desert. He tells her to return and gives her a promise of many descendants. Her son is to be named Ishmael because the LORD has heard her affliction. Hagar responds by naming the LORD as the God who sees her. In a story where others have treated her as a means to obtain a child, God addresses her personally and speaks about her future.

The word translated angel is מַלְאָךְ, malʾāḵ (mal-AHK), meaning messenger; Brown–Driver–Briggs includes both human messengers and God's angelic messengers among its uses. The word alone does not decide the speaker's identity. Here the speaker promises to multiply Hagar's offspring, and the account then calls the One who spoke to her the LORD. That movement is important to the Christian readings below.

The direction to return is given to Hagar in this particular encounter, together with God's promise for her future. The account describes Sarai's treatment as harsh and Hagar's suffering as affliction. God's attention to Hagar brings that suffering into view. At the chapter's end, she bears the child and Abram names him Ishmael; Abram is eighty-six.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly see the harm caused by the household's attempt to secure a child and God's concern for Hagar in her distress. Where do readings differ? One reading identifies the Angel as the Son of God appearing before His human birth. Hilary of Poitiers, On the Trinity 5.11–13, explicitly reads Hagar's encounter this way, understanding messenger as the Son's task rather than a denial of His divine nature.

Another reading understands such appearances as God speaking through angels who represent Him. Augustine, On the Trinity 3.11.27, explains the appearances to the early fathers through angelic messengers speaking or acting in God's name. The difference concerns how God makes Himself known in the encounter; both readings take His words and care seriously.
passages.current_position_html:
Our What Does Prayer Look Like? study uses Abram and Sarai's plan as a warning against trying to force the outcome we expect instead of trusting God's timing.

Who is The Angel of the Lord? identifies the Angel who speaks with Hagar as the eternal Son appearing before His human birth. The study draws that conclusion from His promise to multiply her offspring and Hagar's recognition of the LORD as the One who spoke to her.

deeper_study.title: Who is The Angel of the Lord?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
There is a striking parallel with the Exodus. Here God hears an Egyptian woman's affliction in Abram's household. In Exodus 3:7–10, He sees Israel's affliction in Egypt, hears their cry, and acts to deliver them. In both scenes, suffering that might be ignored by those with power is heard by God. His concern is not confined to one side of an ethnic boundary.

Galatians 4:21–31 explicitly uses the later story of Hagar, Sarah, and their sons to explain the contrast between slavery under the law and the freedom of children born through God's promise. Paul addresses the way people seek their standing before God. His use of the family story does not cancel the care God shows Hagar and her child in Genesis.

passages.title: Genesis 17:1-8
passages.section_title: Abraham to Father Many Nations

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 When Abram was ninety-nine years old, the LORD appeared to him and said, “I am God Almighty. Walk before Me and be blameless. 2 I will establish My covenant between Me and you, and I will multiply you exceedingly.” 3 Then Abram fell facedown, and God said to him, 4 “As for Me, this is My covenant with you: You will be the father of many nations. 5 No longer will you be called Abram, but your name will be Abraham, for I have made you a father of many nations. 6 I will make you exceedingly fruitful; I will make nations of you, and kings will descend from you. 7 I will establish My covenant as an everlasting covenant between Me and you and your descendants after you, to be your God and the God of your descendants after you. 8 And to you and your descendants I will give the land where you are residing—all the land of Canaan—as an eternal possession; and I will be their God.”
paragraphs: 1 When Abram was ninety-nine years old, the LORD appeared to him and said, “I am God Almighty. Walk before Me and be blameless. 2 I will establish My covenant between Me and you, and I will multiply you exceedingly.”

3 Then Abram fell facedown, and God said to him, 4 “As for Me, this is My covenant with you: You will be the father of many nations. 5 No longer will you be called Abram, but your name will be Abraham, for I have made you a father of many nations.
6 I will make you exceedingly fruitful; I will make nations of you, and kings will descend from you.
7 I will establish My covenant as an everlasting covenant between Me and you and your descendants after you, to be your God and the God of your descendants after you.
8 And to you and your descendants I will give the land where you are residing—all the land of Canaan—as an eternal possession; and I will be their God.”

passages.context_html:
Abram is ninety-nine when God appears again, thirteen years after Ishmael's birth. God introduces Himself as God Almighty and calls Abram to walk before Him and be blameless. The promise of descendants has not been abandoned during the years of waiting, and Abram is still called to a life shaped by the God who has spoken.

Blameless translates תָּמִים, tāmîm (tah-MEEM). Brown–Driver–Briggs places Genesis 17:1 among its uses for soundness and integrity. The command calls for a faithful way of life before God. It does not turn Abram's earlier failures into events that never happened or declare that he has never sinned.

God gives Abram the name Abraham and connects it with becoming the father of many nations. The promise includes fruitfulness, kings, descendants, the land of Canaan, and an enduring relationship in which God will be their God. A new name announces the future God promises while Abraham is still waiting for the son through whom the covenant will continue.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as God reaffirming His covenant and calling Abraham to live faithfully within that relationship. Wesley's notes on Genesis 17:1, 5–8 connect the new name with the promised family and emphasize that the greatest blessing is God giving Himself to be their God.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 4:16–18 explicitly quotes God's words about making Abraham a father of many nations. Paul explains that the promise reaches people who share Abraham's faith, and he describes the God Abraham trusts as the One who gives life to the dead. The new name points to a family God can bring into being when the visible circumstances offer little reason for hope.

The promise that God will be their God also reaches beyond having descendants or land. Hebrews 11:13–16 describes the patriarchs longing for a better country and says that God is not ashamed to be called their God. The lasting goal is life with Him, even when the people receiving His promise spend their present lives waiting.

passages.title: Genesis 17:9-27
passages.section_title: The Covenant of Circumcision

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 God also said to Abraham, “You must keep My covenant—you and your descendants in the generations after you. 10 This is My covenant with you and your descendants after you, which you are to keep: Every male among you must be circumcised. 11 You are to circumcise the flesh of your foreskin, and this will be a sign of the covenant between Me and you. 12 Generation after generation, every male must be circumcised when he is eight days old, including those born in your household and those purchased from a foreigner—even those who are not your offspring. 13 Whether they are born in your household or purchased, they must be circumcised. My covenant in your flesh will be an everlasting covenant. 14 But if any male is not circumcised, he will be cut off from his people; he has broken My covenant.” 15 Then God said to Abraham, “As for Sarai your wife, do not call her Sarai, for her name is to be Sarah. 16 And I will bless her and will surely give you a son by her. I will bless her, and she will be the mother of nations; kings of peoples will descend from her.” 17 Abraham fell facedown. Then he laughed and said to himself, “Can a child be born to a man who is a hundred years old? Can Sarah give birth at the age of ninety?” 18 And Abraham said to God, “O that Ishmael might live under Your blessing!” 19 But God replied, “Your wife Sarah will indeed bear you a son, and you are to name him Isaac. I will establish My covenant with him as an everlasting covenant for his descendants after him. 20 As for Ishmael, I have heard you, and I will surely bless him; I will make him fruitful and multiply him greatly. He will become the father of twelve rulers, and I will make him into a great nation. 21 But I will establish My covenant with Isaac, whom Sarah will bear to you at this time next year.” 22 When He had finished speaking with Abraham, God went up from him. 23 On that very day Abraham took his son Ishmael and all those born in his household or purchased with his money—every male among the members of Abraham’s household—and he circumcised them, just as God had told him. 24 So Abraham was ninety-nine years old when he was circumcised, 25 and his son Ishmael was thirteen; 26 Abraham and his son Ishmael were circumcised on the same day. 27 And all the men of Abraham’s household—both servants born in his household and those purchased from foreigners—were circumcised with him.

12 Generation after generation, every male must be circumcised when he is eight days old, including those born in your household and those purchased from a foreigner—even those who are not your offspring. 13 Whether they are born in your household or purchased, they must be circumcised. My covenant in your flesh will be an everlasting covenant.
14 But if any male is not circumcised, he will be cut off from his people; he has broken My covenant.”

15 Then God said to Abraham, “As for Sarai your wife, do not call her Sarai, for her name is to be Sarah. 16 And I will bless her and will surely give you a son by her. I will bless her, and she will be the mother of nations; kings of peoples will descend from her.”

17 Abraham fell facedown. Then he laughed and said to himself, “Can a child be born to a man who is a hundred years old? Can Sarah give birth at the age of ninety?” 18 And Abraham said to God, “O that Ishmael might live under Your blessing!”

19 But God replied, “Your wife Sarah will indeed bear you a son, and you are to name him Isaac. I will establish My covenant with him as an everlasting covenant for his descendants after him. 20 As for Ishmael, I have heard you, and I will surely bless him; I will make him fruitful and multiply him greatly. He will become the father of twelve rulers, and I will make him into a great nation. 21 But I will establish My covenant with Isaac, whom Sarah will bear to you at this time next year.”
22 When He had finished speaking with Abraham, God went up from him.

23 On that very day Abraham took his son Ishmael and all those born in his household or purchased with his money—every male among the members of Abraham’s household—and he circumcised them, just as God had told him.

24 So Abraham was ninety-nine years old when he was circumcised, 25 and his son Ishmael was thirteen; 26 Abraham and his son Ishmael were circumcised on the same day. 27 And all the men of Abraham’s household—both servants born in his household and those purchased from foreigners—were circumcised with him.

passages.context_html:
God now gives circumcision as the sign of the covenant. The command includes Abraham, his male descendants, and the males of his household, including those born there and those purchased from foreigners. Future sons are to receive the sign at eight days old. The warning about being cut off from the people shows that this sign is a serious covenant obligation.

God also changes Sarai's name to Sarah and identifies her as the mother of the promised son. Abraham laughs at the prospect of a child at their ages and asks for Ishmael to live under God's blessing. God promises blessing for Ishmael, but says the covenant will be established with Isaac, whom Sarah will bear the following year. God's care for Ishmael and His particular promise through Isaac are both stated.

Abraham responds on that very day, circumcising himself, Ishmael, and the men of his household. Ishmael receives the sign even though the promised covenant line is assigned to Isaac. The chapter therefore distinguishes receiving the household sign from being the particular son through whom God says He will establish the covenant.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand circumcision here as the covenant's bodily sign, while Sarah's promised son is distinguished from Ishmael. Where do traditions differ? A major later question is how this household sign relates to baptism and the children of believers.

Reformed teaching includes believers' children within the covenant community. The Westminster Larger Catechism, question 166, says that infants with at least one parent professing faith in Christ are within the covenant and should be baptized. It reads the place of children within God's covenant as continuing into the church.

Reformed Baptist teaching requires a personal profession of repentance and faith for baptism. The 1689 Baptist Confession, 29.2, limits the proper recipients to those who actually profess those things. On this reading, the command to circumcise infants in Abraham's household does not itself authorize baptizing infants in the church.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 4:9–12 explicitly distinguishes Abraham's faith from the later sign. He was counted righteous before circumcision; the sign confirmed the righteousness he already had through faith. Romans 2:28–29 also speaks of a work in the heart by the Spirit. The physical mark has a place in the story, but it cannot stand in for a person's relationship with God.

The promise concerning Sarah and Isaac also matters beyond this household. Romans 9:6–9 uses the distinction between physical descent and the children of promise when explaining why God's word has not failed. God's purposes are not secured simply by human ancestry or by Abraham's understandable desire for Ishmael. They unfold through the promise God Himself gives.

passages.title: Genesis 18:1-8
passages.section_title: The Three Visitors

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then the LORD appeared to Abraham by the Oaks of Mamre in the heat of the day, while he was sitting at the entrance of his tent. 2 And Abraham looked up and saw three men standing nearby. When he saw them, he ran from the entrance of his tent to meet them and bowed low to the ground. 3 “My lord,” said Abraham, “if I have found favor in your sight, please do not pass your servant by. 4 Let a little water be brought, that you may wash your feet and rest yourselves under the tree. 5 And I will bring a bit of bread so that you may refresh yourselves. This is why you have passed your servant’s way. After that, you may continue on your way.” “Yes,” they replied, “you may do as you have said.” 6 So Abraham hurried into the tent and said to Sarah, “Quick! Prepare three seahs of fine flour, knead it, and bake some bread.” 7 Meanwhile, Abraham ran to the herd, selected a tender and choice calf, and gave it to a servant, who hurried to prepare it. 8 Then Abraham brought curds and milk and the calf that had been prepared, and he set them before the men and stood by them under the tree as they ate.

3 “My lord,” said Abraham, “if I have found favor in your sight, please do not pass your servant by. 4 Let a little water be brought, that you may wash your feet and rest yourselves under the tree. 5 And I will bring a bit of bread so that you may refresh yourselves. This is why you have passed your servant’s way. After that, you may continue on your way.”
“Yes,” they replied, “you may do as you have said.”
6 So Abraham hurried into the tent and said to Sarah, “Quick! Prepare three seahs of fine flour, knead it, and bake some bread.”

7 Meanwhile, Abraham ran to the herd, selected a tender and choice calf, and gave it to a servant, who hurried to prepare it. 8 Then Abraham brought curds and milk and the calf that had been prepared, and he set them before the men and stood by them under the tree as they ate.

passages.context_html:
The chapter opens by saying that the LORD appears to Abraham near the Oaks of Mamre. Abraham looks up and sees three men. As the scene unfolds, he welcomes them, offers water and rest, and prepares a meal. The opening tells us that more is happening than an ordinary visit, while the arrival is described in the familiar form of guests at a tent.

Abraham's welcome becomes generous action. He hurries to Sarah about bread, selects a good calf, has it prepared, and sets food before the visitors. He stands nearby while they eat. The repeated haste and the care given to the meal show his eagerness to serve, without requiring us to reconstruct customs the passage does not explain.

The meal prepares for the promise concerning Sarah and then the conversation about Sodom. In the wider scene, two of the visitors go toward Sodom while Abraham remains before the LORD; Genesis 19:1 calls the two who arrive there angels. These details are central to the different Christian explanations of the visitors.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Where do Christian readings differ? One long-standing reading sees the Son of God appearing with two angels. Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho 56, explains the visitor at Mamre as the divine One sent by the Father, distinguished from the two angels who go to Sodom.

Another reading sees God revealing Himself through angelic visitors rather than one visitor being the Son Himself. Augustine, On the Trinity 2.10–12, considers the three visitors as a visible sign of the one God in three persons and compares Abraham's address with Lot's later address to the angels. These are historic Christian readings, rather than a division that every member of a modern denomination follows.
passages.current_position_html: Our Who is The Angel of the Lord? study understands the LORD's visit to Abraham as an appearance of the eternal Son before His human birth. It includes the meal in Genesis 18 among the encounters that show the Son making Himself known before the New Testament account of His birth.

deeper_study.title: Who is The Angel of the Lord?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 13:1–3 calls believers to continue in love and welcome strangers, remembering that some have entertained angels without knowing it. Abraham's meal is a memorable example of that kind of welcome: care takes the form of time, food, effort, and a place to rest. Hospitality becomes part of living before God.

The theme also reaches into service to Christ. In Matthew 25:35–40, Jesus speaks of receiving food, drink, and welcome through what is done for the least of His brothers. His teaching gives acts of care a significance beyond their visible size. Abraham's generous service helps us picture how ordinary provision can become an expression of honor and love.

passages.title: Genesis 18:9-15
passages.section_title: Sarah Laughs at the Promise

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 “Where is your wife Sarah?” they asked. “There, in the tent,” he replied. 10 Then the LORD said, “I will surely return to you at this time next year, and your wife Sarah will have a son!” Now Sarah was behind him, listening at the entrance to the tent. 11 And Abraham and Sarah were already old and well along in years; Sarah had passed the age of childbearing. 12 So she laughed to herself, saying, “After I am worn out and my master is old, will I now have this pleasure?” 13 And the LORD asked Abraham, “Why did Sarah laugh and say, ‘Can I really bear a child when I am old?’ 14 Is anything too difficult for the LORD? At the appointed time I will return to you—in about a year—and Sarah will have a son.” 15 But Sarah was afraid, so she denied it and said, “I did not laugh.” “No,” replied the LORD, “but you did laugh.”
paragraphs: 9 “Where is your wife Sarah?” they asked.
“There, in the tent,” he replied.
10 Then the LORD said, “I will surely return to you at this time next year, and your wife Sarah will have a son!”

Now Sarah was behind him, listening at the entrance to the tent. 11 And Abraham and Sarah were already old and well along in years; Sarah had passed the age of childbearing. 12 So she laughed to herself, saying, “After I am worn out and my master is old, will I now have this pleasure?”

13 And the LORD asked Abraham, “Why did Sarah laugh and say, ‘Can I really bear a child when I am old?’ 14 Is anything too difficult for the LORD? At the appointed time I will return to you—in about a year—and Sarah will have a son.”
15 But Sarah was afraid, so she denied it and said, “I did not laugh.”
“No,” replied the LORD, “but you did laugh.”

passages.context_html:
The visitors ask for Sarah, who is listening at the tent entrance. The LORD promises that she will have a son at the appointed time. The account then tells us why the promise seems impossible to her: both she and Abraham are old, and she is past the age of childbearing.

Sarah laughs inwardly at the prospect. The LORD knows and asks why she laughed, putting the issue plainly: is anything too difficult for Him? The promise is repeated with its time of fulfillment. Sarah denies laughing because she is afraid, but the LORD corrects her. The scene brings her private response into the conversation instead of leaving the promise as something only Abraham hears.

The question about what is too difficult comes from the Hebrew verb פָּלָא, pālāʾ (pah-LAH). Brown–Driver–Briggs places Genesis 18:14 among uses for something beyond a person's power or difficult to do. Here the question directs Sarah from the limits she knows in herself to the power of the One making this particular promise.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read Sarah's laughter as a response to the apparent impossibility of bearing a child at her age, and the LORD's answer as a call to trust His promise. Wesley's notes on Genesis 18:12 describe her doubt about what could happen in the ordinary course of nature; the passage answers that difficulty by directing her to God.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 11:11–12 explicitly remembers Sarah as receiving the ability to conceive through faith because she considered the One who promised faithful. Genesis records her hesitation and correction; Hebrews remembers the faith through which she receives what God has promised. Her story includes growth beyond the first startled response.

There is also a helpful parallel with Luke 1:34–38. Mary hears of Elizabeth's pregnancy in old age and is assured that God's word will not fail as she receives the announcement of Jesus' birth. Sarah's conception in old age and Mary's virginal conception are different events, but both announcements turn attention from human inability to God's faithful power. The promised child advances a purpose larger than the immediate household.

passages.title: Genesis 18:16-33
passages.section_title: Abraham Intercedes for Sodom

Because their sin is so grievous, 21 I will go down to see if their actions fully justify the outcry that has reached Me. Far be it from You! Suppose ten are found there?” And He answered, “On account of the ten, I will not destroy it.” 33 When the LORD had finished speaking with Abraham, He departed, and Abraham returned home.

passages.context_html:
As the visitors leave, the LORD connects His disclosure to Abraham with the purpose of Abraham's calling. His household is to keep the way of the LORD by doing what is right and just, and blessing is to reach the nations through him. What follows is therefore part of learning the character of the God whose promise he carries.

The outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah is great, and the LORD speaks of examining their conduct. Two men go toward Sodom while Abraham remains before the LORD. Abraham asks whether the righteous will be swept away with the wicked and appeals to the Judge of all the earth to do what is right. His concern is expressed as a request to spare the place for the sake of righteous people within it.

The conversation moves from fifty to forty-five, forty, thirty, twenty, and finally ten. Abraham speaks with humility about himself and persistence in asking, and the LORD agrees to spare the place at each stated number. The passage does not tell us why Abraham stops at ten. It ends with the LORD departing and Abraham returning home; the next chapter will show the outcome.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read Abraham's appeal as bold prayer for others grounded in God's justice and mercy. Wesley's notes on Genesis 18:23, 27–33 emphasize his confidence and humility; the Catholic Church's Catechism, 2571, likewise sees Abraham's prayer as sharing God's compassion for people.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The promised blessing of the nations is joined here with teaching a household to do what is right and just. That keeps God's larger purpose connected with the way His people actually live. Acts 17:30–31 later announces that God will judge the world justly through the Man He has appointed, giving assurance through His resurrection. Abraham's appeal to the Judge of the whole earth belongs to a theme that reaches beyond Sodom.

Prayer for others also continues as part of God's people's calling. 1 Timothy 2:1–6 urges prayer for everyone, including rulers, and connects it with God's saving purpose and Christ's work as the one mediator. Abraham's conversation gives an earlier picture of bringing others before God with confidence in His character. The response to approaching judgment includes concern for people, not merely satisfaction that wrong will be punished.

passages.title: Genesis 19:1-11
passages.section_title: Lot Welcomes the Angels

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now the two angels arrived at Sodom in the evening, and Lot was sitting in the gateway of the city. When Lot saw them, he got up to meet them, bowed facedown, 2 and said, “My lords, please turn aside into the house of your servant; wash your feet and spend the night. Then you can rise early and go on your way.” “No,” they answered, “we will spend the night in the square.” 3 But Lot insisted so strongly that they followed him into his house. He prepared a feast for them and baked unleavened bread, and they ate. 4 Before they had gone to bed, all the men of the city of Sodom, both young and old, surrounded the house. 5 They called out to Lot, saying, “Where are the men who came to you tonight? Send them out to us so we can have relations with them!” 6 Lot went outside to meet them, shutting the door behind him. 7 “Please, my brothers,” he pleaded, “don’t do such a wicked thing! 8 Look, I have two daughters who have never slept with a man. Let me bring them to you, and you can do to them as you please. But do not do anything to these men, for they have come under the protection of my roof.” 9 “Get out of the way!” they replied. And they declared, “This one came here as a foreigner, and he is already acting like a judge! Now we will treat you worse than them.” And they pressed in on Lot and moved in to break down the door. 10 But the men inside reached out, pulled Lot into the house with them, and shut the door. 11 And they struck the men at the entrance, young and old, with blindness, so that they wearied themselves trying to find the door.

When Lot saw them, he got up to meet them, bowed facedown, 2 and said, “My lords, please turn aside into the house of your servant; wash your feet and spend the night. Then you can rise early and go on your way.”
“No,” they answered, “we will spend the night in the square.”
3 But Lot insisted so strongly that they followed him into his house. He prepared a feast for them and baked unleavened bread, and they ate.

4 Before they had gone to bed, all the men of the city of Sodom, both young and old, surrounded the house. 5 They called out to Lot, saying, “Where are the men who came to you tonight? Send them out to us so we can have relations with them!”

6 Lot went outside to meet them, shutting the door behind him. 7 “Please, my brothers,” he pleaded, “don’t do such a wicked thing! 8 Look, I have two daughters who have never slept with a man. Let me bring them to you, and you can do to them as you please. But do not do anything to these men, for they have come under the protection of my roof.”

9 “Get out of the way!” they replied. And they declared, “This one came here as a foreigner, and he is already acting like a judge! Now we will treat you worse than them.” And they pressed in on Lot and moved in to break down the door.

10 But the men inside reached out, pulled Lot into the house with them, and shut the door. 11 And they struck the men at the entrance, young and old, with blindness, so that they wearied themselves trying to find the door.

passages.context_html:
The two visitors who left Abraham now arrive in Sodom, where the account identifies them as angels. Lot meets them at the gateway and presses them to stay in his house. Like Abraham, he offers food and shelter, but the setting soon becomes dangerous: men from across the city surround the house and demand the visitors.

Their demand is sexual. The Hebrew verb יָדַע, yādaʿ (yah-DAH), often means know, but Brown–Driver–Briggs identifies sexual relations as its use in verses 5 and 8. The threats, the surrounding mob, and the attempt to break down the door make the violence of the demand clear. They are not simply asking to become acquainted with the guests.

Lot calls their intention wicked, yet offers his daughters in place of the visitors. Protecting one person by exposing another to assault is itself a terrible failure of protection. The angels then rescue Lot from the crowd, shut the door, and strike the attackers with blindness. The people Lot tries to protect become the ones who save him.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read the mob's demand as an intended sexual assault and Lot's offer of his daughters as wrong, even though he is trying to protect his guests. Wesley's note on Genesis 19:8 explicitly rejects doing that wrong in order to prevent another.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Jude 7 explicitly uses Sodom and the neighboring cities as examples of sexual immorality and judgment. Their conduct is treated as morally serious, with consequences beyond what the attackers expect that night.

The wider biblical account also describes Sodom's arrogance, abundance, complacency, and neglect of the poor in Ezekiel 16:49–50. These descriptions belong together: the violent scene here comes from a city whose life has become deeply corrupt. God's concern includes both how people use others and how they disregard those who need help.

passages.title: Genesis 19:12-23
passages.section_title: Lot Flees to Zoar

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 Then the two men said to Lot, “Do you have anyone else here—a son-in-law, your sons or daughters, or anyone else in the city who belongs to you? Get them out of here, 13 because we are about to destroy this place. For the outcry to the LORD against its people is so great that He has sent us to destroy it.” 14 So Lot went out and spoke to the sons-in-law who were pledged in marriage to his daughters. “Get up,” he said. “Get out of this place, for the LORD is about to destroy the city!” But his sons-in-law thought he was joking. 15 At daybreak the angels hurried Lot along, saying, “Get up! Take your wife and your two daughters who are here, or you will be swept away in the punishment of the city.” 16 But when Lot hesitated, the men grabbed his hand and the hands of his wife and his two daughters. And they led them safely out of the city, because of the LORD’s compassion for them. 17 As soon as the men had brought them out, one of them said, “Run for your lives! Do not look back, and do not stop anywhere on the plain! Flee to the mountains, or you will be swept away!” 18 But Lot replied, “No, my lords, please! 19 Your servant has indeed found favor in your sight, and you have shown me great kindness by sparing my life. But I cannot run to the mountains; the disaster will overtake me, and I will die. 20 Look, there is a town nearby where I can flee, and it is a small place. Please let me flee there—is it not a small place? Then my life will be saved.” 21 “Very well,” he answered, “I will grant this request as well, and will not demolish the town you indicate. 22 Hurry! Run there quickly, for I cannot do anything until you reach it.” That is why the town was called Zoar. 23 And by the time the sun had risen over the land, Lot had reached Zoar.

23 And by the time the sun had risen over the land, Lot had reached Zoar.

passages.context_html:
The angels tell Lot to gather his people because the city is about to be destroyed. He warns the men pledged to marry his daughters, but they think he is joking. At daybreak the danger becomes urgent. Even then Lot hesitates, and the angels take him, his wife, and his two daughters by the hand and lead them out. The account gives the reason: the LORD's compassion for them.

Outside the city, the family is told to flee, avoid looking back, and keep moving beyond the plain. Lot fears he cannot reach the mountains and asks to escape to a nearby small town. His request is granted, and that town is spared. He reaches Zoar as the sun rises.

The rescue includes both mercy and a direction to act. Lot's hesitation has not made the danger disappear, and being brought outside the city is followed by the command to keep going. The contrast with the sons-in-law is equally sharp: a warning they take as a joke is the warning that leads the others out.
passages.common_interpretations_html: A common Christian reading emphasizes God's compassion in bringing Lot out despite his hesitation, together with the urgency of responding to the warning. Wesley's notes on Genesis 19:14–17 hold those two themes together.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
2 Peter 2:6–9 explicitly recalls Lot's rescue and concludes that the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials while holding the unrighteous for judgment. Peter calls Lot righteous without treating his decisions as consistently wise. The deliverance shows God's care for someone whose weakness is visible in the account.

Jesus also returns to this escape in Luke 17:28–33. Ordinary buying, selling, planting, and building continued until the day Lot left. Jesus uses the event to call His hearers to readiness when the Son of Man is revealed. The warning is about a response that cannot be postponed indefinitely while people secure the life they already know.

passages.title: Genesis 19:24-29
passages.section_title: The Destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 24 Then the LORD rained down sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah—from the LORD out of the heavens. 25 Thus He destroyed these cities and the entire plain, including all the inhabitants of the cities and everything that grew on the ground. 26 But Lot’s wife looked back, and she became a pillar of salt. 27 Early the next morning, Abraham got up and returned to the place where he had stood before the LORD. 28 He looked down toward Sodom and Gomorrah and all the land of the plain, and he saw the smoke rising from the land like smoke from a furnace. 29 So when God destroyed the cities of the plain, He remembered Abraham, and He brought Lot out of the catastrophe that destroyed the cities where he had lived.
paragraphs: 24 Then the LORD rained down sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah—from the LORD out of the heavens. 25 Thus He destroyed these cities and the entire plain, including all the inhabitants of the cities and everything that grew on the ground.
26 But Lot’s wife looked back, and she became a pillar of salt.

27 Early the next morning, Abraham got up and returned to the place where he had stood before the LORD. 28 He looked down toward Sodom and Gomorrah and all the land of the plain, and he saw the smoke rising from the land like smoke from a furnace.
29 So when God destroyed the cities of the plain, He remembered Abraham, and He brought Lot out of the catastrophe that destroyed the cities where he had lived.

passages.context_html:
The promised judgment now falls. The LORD rains sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah, overthrowing the cities, their inhabitants, and what grows on the plain. Lot's wife looks back in disobedience to the earlier instruction and becomes a pillar of salt. The account moves quickly from escape to the destruction left behind.

Abraham returns to the place where he had stood before the LORD and sees smoke rising from the land. What he sees is the city destroyed, but the narrator tells us more: God remembered Abraham and brought Lot out of the catastrophe. This explicitly links the rescue with Abraham's conversation with God in chapter 18.

The ending keeps judgment and mercy in the same account. Sodom is not spared, and Lot is not abandoned. Abraham's view of the smoke is therefore only part of what God has done. The passage does not tell us exactly when Abraham learns about Lot's escape.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the destruction as God's judgment and Lot's wife's backward look as a serious refusal of the escape instruction. Wesley's notes on Genesis 19:24–29 also connect God's remembering Abraham with mercy shown to Lot.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
In Luke 17:28–33, Jesus explicitly compares the day of Sodom's destruction with the day the Son of Man is revealed and tells His hearers to remember Lot's wife. He joins that warning with the danger of turning back for possessions and trying to preserve one's present life at the cost of the life God gives.

The scene becomes a warning for later hearers, not merely a disaster remembered from another age. Judgment interrupts the assumption that everyday life will always continue on its own terms. At the same time, the account's final word about God remembering Abraham prevents us from losing sight of His mercy within the judgment.

passages.title: Genesis 19:30-38
passages.section_title: Lot and His Daughters

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 30 Lot and his two daughters left Zoar and settled in the mountains—for he was afraid to stay in Zoar—where they lived in a cave. 31 One day the older daughter said to the younger, “Our father is old, and there is no man in the land to sleep with us, as is the custom over all the earth. 32 Come, let us get our father drunk with wine so we can sleep with him and preserve his line.” 33 So that night they got their father drunk with wine, and the firstborn went in and slept with her father; he was not aware when she lay down or when she got up. 34 The next day the older daughter said to the younger, “Look, I slept with my father last night. Let us get him drunk with wine again tonight so you can go in and sleep with him and we can preserve our father’s line.” 35 So again that night they got their father drunk with wine, and the younger daughter went in and slept with him; he was not aware when she lay down or when she got up. 36 Thus both of Lot’s daughters became pregnant by their father. 37 The older daughter gave birth to a son and named him Moab. He is the father of the Moabites of today. 38 The younger daughter also gave birth to a son, and she named him Ben-ammi. He is the father of the Ammonites of today.

35 So again that night they got their father drunk with wine, and the younger daughter went in and slept with him; he was not aware when she lay down or when she got up.

passages.context_html:
Lot leaves Zoar because he is afraid to remain there and settles in a cave with his daughters. The account does not explain exactly what he fears. The older daughter, believing there is no man available to continue their family, proposes getting their father drunk and bearing children through him. The two carry out the plan on successive nights.

The repeated statement that Lot is unaware of their coming and going is important. The daughters arrange these encounters while he is drunk; the account does not describe a knowingly agreed plan between all three. Their intention to preserve the family leads to incest, and both become pregnant.

The sons are named Moab and Ben-ammi, identified as the ancestors of the Moabites and Ammonites. The end of Lot's story thus becomes the beginning of two peoples who will appear repeatedly in Israel's history. Rescue from the destruction has not removed the family's fear or put its life in good order.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a grim family aftermath and an account of the origins of Moab and Ammon. Wesley's notes on Genesis 19:30–38 emphasize the wrongdoing, while the US Catholic bishops' note on Genesis 19:30–38 draws attention to the story's account of Israel's related neighbors.

passages.god_plan_html:
The later story does not reduce every descendant of these sons to the circumstances of their birth. In Deuteronomy 2:9, 19, God tells Israel not to seize the lands He has given to Lot's descendants. His dealings with Moab and Ammon include limits on Israel's actions toward them.

A still larger connection appears through Ruth, a Moabite woman identified in Ruth 1:4. Ruth 4:13–17 places her son Obed in David's family, and Matthew 1:5–6 includes Ruth in Jesus' ancestry. The Bible can tell the shame of a people's beginning truthfully and still show God's grace at work through a woman from that people.

passages.title: Genesis 20:1-18
passages.section_title: Abraham, Sarah, and Abimelech

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now Abraham journeyed from there to the region of the Negev and settled between Kadesh and Shur. While he was staying in Gerar, 2 Abraham said of his wife Sarah, “She is my sister.” So Abimelech king of Gerar had Sarah brought to him. 3 One night, however, God came to Abimelech in a dream and told him, “You are as good as dead because of the woman you have taken, for she is a married woman.” 4 Now Abimelech had not gone near her, so he replied, “Lord, would You destroy a nation even though it is innocent? 5 Didn’t Abraham tell me, ‘She is my sister’? And she herself said, ‘He is my brother.’ I have done this in the integrity of my heart and the innocence of my hands.” 6 Then God said to Abimelech in the dream, “Yes, I know that you did this with a clear conscience, and so I have kept you from sinning against Me. That is why I did not let you touch her. 7 Now return the man’s wife, for he is a prophet; he will pray for you and you will live. But if you do not restore her, be aware that you will surely die—you and all who belong to you.” 8 Early the next morning Abimelech got up and summoned all his servants; and when he described to them all that had happened, the men were terrified. 9 Then Abimelech called Abraham and asked, “What have you done to us? How have I sinned against you, that you have brought such tremendous guilt upon me and my kingdom? You have done things to me that should not be done.” 10 Abimelech also asked Abraham, “What prompted you to do such a thing?” 11 Abraham replied, “I thought to myself, ‘Surely there is no fear of God in this place. They will kill me on account of my wife.’ 12 Besides, she really is my sister, the daughter of my father—though not the daughter of my mother—and she became my wife. 13 So when God had me journey from my father’s house, I said to Sarah, ‘This is how you can show your loyalty to me: Wherever we go, say of me, “He is my brother.”’” 14 So Abimelech brought sheep and cattle, menservants and maidservants, and he gave them to Abraham and restored his wife Sarah to him. 15 And Abimelech said, “Look, my land is before you. Settle wherever you please.” 16 And he said to Sarah, “See, I am giving your brother a thousand pieces of silver. It is your vindication before all who are with you; you are completely cleared.” 17 Then Abraham prayed to God, and God healed Abimelech and his wife and his maidservants, so that they could again bear children— 18 for on account of Abraham’s wife Sarah, the LORD had completely closed all the wombs in Abimelech’s household.

passages.context_html:
Abraham moves to Gerar and again identifies Sarah as his sister, repeating the deception seen in Egypt. Abimelech takes her, but God warns him in a dream that she is married. The account explicitly says he has not gone near her, and God explains that He has kept him from touching her. Sarah is protected before Abraham repairs the situation.

Abimelech confronts Abraham, who explains his fear that people without the fear of God would kill him for his wife. He also says that Sarah is his half-sister and describes their agreement to present him as her brother wherever they travel. That partial truth has concealed the fact that matters here: she is his wife. Abimelech returns her, gives gifts, and publicly clears her.

God calls Abraham a prophet, נָבִיא, nāḇîʾ (nah-VEE), a word Brown–Driver–Briggs explains as spokesman or prophet, expressly including Genesis 20:7. In this scene his role includes praying for Abimelech. The man whose conduct has caused harm is still called to serve God by seeking another household's restoration. Abraham prays, and God heals the household so that its women can again bear children.
passages.common_interpretations_html: A common Christian reading recognizes both Abraham's deceptive conduct and God's intervention to protect Sarah and restore Abimelech's household. Wesley's notes on Genesis 20:6, 9–11 emphasize God's restraint of wrongdoing and challenge Abraham's assumption that no one there fears God.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
God's protection of Sarah preserves the family through whom He has promised the son. The next chapter records Isaac's birth; Hebrews 11:11–12 later remembers that birth in relation to God's faithfulness. The future of the promise continues through God's care even when Abraham's fearful choices endanger the people involved.

There is also a wider lesson about prayer for others. James 5:16–18 joins confession, prayer, and healing, using a human prophet as an example. Abraham's role here is not permission to overlook the wrong he has done. It shows a servant being required to seek the good of people his own conduct has harmed.

passages.title: Genesis 21:1-8
passages.section_title: The Birth of Isaac

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now the LORD attended to Sarah as He had said, and the LORD did for Sarah what He had promised. 2 So Sarah conceived and bore a son to Abraham in his old age, at the very time God had promised. 3 And Abraham gave the name Isaac to the son Sarah bore to him. 4 When his son Isaac was eight days old, Abraham circumcised him, as God had commanded him. 5 Abraham was a hundred years old when his son Isaac was born to him. 6 Then Sarah said, “God has made me laugh, and everyone who hears of this will laugh with me.” 7 She added, “Who would have told Abraham that Sarah would nurse children? Yet I have borne him a son in his old age.” 8 So the child grew and was weaned, and Abraham held a great feast on the day Isaac was weaned.
paragraphs: 1 Now the LORD attended to Sarah as He had said, and the LORD did for Sarah what He had promised. 2 So Sarah conceived and bore a son to Abraham in his old age, at the very time God had promised.

3 And Abraham gave the name Isaac to the son Sarah bore to him. 4 When his son Isaac was eight days old, Abraham circumcised him, as God had commanded him. 5 Abraham was a hundred years old when his son Isaac was born to him.

6 Then Sarah said, “God has made me laugh, and everyone who hears of this will laugh with me.” 7 She added, “Who would have told Abraham that Sarah would nurse children? Yet I have borne him a son in his old age.”
8 So the child grew and was weaned, and Abraham held a great feast on the day Isaac was weaned.

passages.context_html:
The long-awaited birth arrives with repeated emphasis on God's word: He attends to Sarah as He said, does what He promised, and gives the child at the promised time. The opening directs attention to God's faithfulness before describing the family's response. Abraham is a hundred years old when Isaac is born.

Abraham gives the child the name Isaac and circumcises him on the eighth day, as God had commanded. The promise is received with concrete obedience. Sarah's laughter is now the joy of a mother inviting others to rejoice with her, recalling the earlier laughter surrounding the announcement of the birth.

The child grows and is weaned, and Abraham holds a feast. This celebration completes the first part of the account, but it also introduces the setting for the dispute over Ishmael and Isaac that follows. One fulfilled promise brings joy into a household where earlier choices still have consequences.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read Isaac's birth as the fulfillment of God's promise to Abraham and Sarah, with their joy and obedience responding to His faithfulness. The US Catholic bishops' notes on Genesis 21:1–7 likewise identify the promised birth as the central expectation of the preceding chapters now coming true.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 11:11–12 explicitly remembers Sarah's conception through faith in the One who promised. The many descendants begin with this one child, received when the family's own circumstances offered little hope. The account gives faith a definite object: the trustworthiness of what God has actually said.

Galatians 4:22–28 goes on to describe believers as children of promise like Isaac. Paul uses the birth to explain an inheritance received through God's promise rather than secured by placing oneself under the law. The joy in Abraham's tent belongs to a larger story that will reach people who become God's children through Christ.

passages.title: Genesis 21:9-21
passages.section_title: Sarah Turns against Hagar

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 But Sarah saw that the son whom Hagar the Egyptian had borne to Abraham was mocking her son, 10 and she said to Abraham, “Expel the slave woman and her son, for the slave woman’s son will never share in the inheritance with my son Isaac!” 11 Now this matter distressed Abraham greatly because it concerned his son Ishmael. 12 But God said to Abraham, “Do not be distressed about the boy and your maidservant. Listen to everything that Sarah tells you, for through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned. 13 But I will also make a nation of the slave woman’s son, because he is your offspring.” 14 Early in the morning, Abraham got up, took bread and a skin of water, put them on Hagar’s shoulders, and sent her away with the boy. She left and wandered in the Wilderness of Beersheba. 15 When the water in the skin was gone, she left the boy under one of the bushes. 16 Then she went off and sat down nearby, about a bowshot away, for she said, “I cannot bear to watch the boy die!” And as she sat nearby, she lifted up her voice and wept. 17 Then God heard the voice of the boy, and the angel of God called to Hagar from heaven, “What is wrong, Hagar? Do not be afraid, for God has heard the voice of the boy where he lies. 18 Get up, lift up the boy, and take him by the hand, for I will make him into a great nation.” 19 Then God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water. So she went and filled the skin with water and gave the boy a drink. 20 And God was with the boy, and he grew up and settled in the wilderness and became a great archer. 21 And while he was dwelling in the Wilderness of Paran, his mother got a wife for him from the land of Egypt.

Do not be afraid, for God has heard the voice of the boy where he lies. 18 Get up, lift up the boy, and take him by the hand, for I will make him into a great nation.” 19 Then God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water. So she went and filled the skin with water and gave the boy a drink.

20 And God was with the boy, and he grew up and settled in the wilderness and became a great archer. 21 And while he was dwelling in the Wilderness of Paran, his mother got a wife for him from the land of Egypt.

passages.context_html:
At the time of Isaac's celebration, Sarah sees Ishmael mocking and insists that he must not share the inheritance with Isaac. Abraham is deeply distressed because Ishmael is his son too. God tells him to listen to Sarah while distinguishing two promises: the covenant line will be reckoned through Isaac, and Ishmael will also become a nation because he is Abraham's offspring.

Abraham sends Hagar and Ishmael away with bread and water. In the wilderness the water runs out, and Hagar leaves the boy beneath a bush, then sits at a distance because she cannot bear to watch him die. The account stays with her grief rather than treating the departure as a tidy solution to a household dispute.

God hears the boy, and the angel of God addresses Hagar, tells her not to fear, and renews the promise of a great nation. God opens her eyes to a well, and she gives the boy water. The ending says that God is with him as he grows, becomes an archer, lives in Paran, and takes a wife from Egypt through his mother's arrangement. The promised line through Isaac is kept distinct, while Ishmael is cared for.
passages.common_interpretations_html: A common Christian reading distinguishes Isaac's place in the covenant promise from God's continuing mercy toward Ishmael. Wesley's notes on Genesis 21:9, 13, 17 connect the mocking with Galatians and caution against assuming that exclusion from this particular covenant role means exclusion from every mercy of God.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
