passages.god_plan_html:
Galatians 4:21–31 explicitly takes up this separation. Paul uses the slave woman and free woman, their sons, and the inheritance dispute to explain slavery under the law and the freedom of children of promise. He addresses people wanting to be under the law and points believers to the freedom given through Christ in Galatians 5:1. This is Paul's stated connection, rather than a hidden meaning inferred from every object Hagar carries.

Genesis also keeps God's earlier word to Hagar in view. In chapter 16 He heard her affliction and promised a future for her child; here He hears the boy and provides water. God's particular purpose through Isaac and His compassion for Hagar and Ishmael belong in the same story. The distinction between the sons is not a reason to overlook the suffering or the care described here.

passages.title: Genesis 21:22-34
passages.section_title: The Covenant at Beersheba

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 At that time Abimelech and Phicol the commander of his army said to Abraham, “God is with you in all that you do. 23 Now, therefore, swear to me here before God that you will not deal falsely with me or my children or descendants. Show to me and to the country in which you reside the same kindness that I have shown to you.” 24 And Abraham replied, “I swear it.” 25 But when Abraham complained to Abimelech about a well that Abimelech’s servants had seized, 26 Abimelech replied, “I do not know who has done this. You did not tell me, so I have not heard about it until today.” 27 So Abraham brought sheep and cattle and gave them to Abimelech, and the two men made a covenant. 28 Abraham separated seven ewe lambs from the flock, 29 and Abimelech asked him, “Why have you set apart these seven ewe lambs?” 30 He replied, “You are to accept the seven ewe lambs from my hand as my witness that I dug this well.” 31 So that place was called Beersheba, because it was there that the two of them swore an oath. 32 After they had made the covenant at Beersheba, Abimelech and Phicol the commander of his army got up and returned to the land of the Philistines. 33 And Abraham planted a tamarisk tree in Beersheba, and there he called upon the name of the LORD, the Eternal God. 34 And Abraham resided in the land of the Philistines for a long time.

Show to me and to the country in which you reside the same kindness that I have shown to you.”
24 And Abraham replied, “I swear it.”

25 But when Abraham complained to Abimelech about a well that Abimelech’s servants had seized, 26 Abimelech replied, “I do not know who has done this. You did not tell me, so I have not heard about it until today.”

27 So Abraham brought sheep and cattle and gave them to Abimelech, and the two men made a covenant. 28 Abraham separated seven ewe lambs from the flock, 29 and Abimelech asked him, “Why have you set apart these seven ewe lambs?”

30 He replied, “You are to accept the seven ewe lambs from my hand as my witness that I dug this well.” 31 So that place was called Beersheba, because it was there that the two of them swore an oath. 32 After they had made the covenant at Beersheba, Abimelech and Phicol the commander of his army got up and returned to the land of the Philistines.
33 And Abraham planted a tamarisk tree in Beersheba, and there he called upon the name of the LORD, the Eternal God. 34 And Abraham resided in the land of the Philistines for a long time.

passages.context_html:
Abimelech and his commander Phicol approach Abraham because they recognize that God is with him. Abimelech asks for honest and kind treatment of himself and his descendants, recalling the kindness he has shown Abraham. After the deception in chapter 20, the request to avoid false dealing has particular force.

Abraham agrees, but also raises the seizure of a well by Abimelech's servants. Abimelech says he had not known about it. They make a covenant, and Abraham sets apart seven ewe lambs as a witness that he dug the well. The agreement joins peaceful relations with a concrete acknowledgment of the disputed resource. The place is called Beersheba because the two swear an oath there.

Abraham plants a tamarisk and calls upon the LORD as the Eternal God. The Hebrew title is אֵל עוֹלָם, ʾēl ʿōlām (ayl oh-LAHM). Brown–Driver–Briggs cites Genesis 21:33 among uses of the word for God's enduring existence. Abraham's agreement concerns a well and generations of neighbors; his worship looks to the God whose life reaches beyond them.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read the treaty as a peaceful settlement protecting truthful relations and Abraham's claim to the well. Wesley's notes on Genesis 21:31–33 connect the place-name with the oath and Abraham's worship with his continuing life as a stranger in the land.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 11:8–10 describes Abraham living by faith as a stranger in the promised land while looking for the city God would build. This agreement shows the ordinary shape of that waiting: caring for a household's needs, addressing a dispute, keeping peace, and worshiping God. The promise does not make daily responsibilities unimportant.

The title Eternal God also connects with Isaiah 40:28–31, where the everlasting Creator gives strength to the weary who wait for Him. God's enduring life gives His people a hope larger than the span of one treaty or one generation. Abraham can secure an agreement with a neighbor while continuing to place his deeper trust in God.

passages.title: Genesis 22:1-10
passages.section_title: The Offering of Isaac

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Some time later God tested Abraham and said to him, “Abraham!” “Here I am,” he answered. 2 “Take your son,” God said, “your only son Isaac, whom you love, and go to the land of Moriah. Offer him there as a burnt offering on one of the mountains, which I will show you.” 3 So Abraham got up early the next morning, saddled his donkey, and took along two of his servants and his son Isaac. He split the wood for a burnt offering and set out for the place God had designated. 4 On the third day Abraham looked up and saw the place in the distance. 5 “Stay here with the donkey,” Abraham told his servants. “The boy and I will go over there to worship, and then we will return to you.” 6 Abraham took the wood for the burnt offering and placed it on his son Isaac. He himself carried the fire and the sacrificial knife, and the two of them walked on together. 7 Then Isaac said to his father Abraham, “My father!” “Here I am, my son,” he replied. “The fire and the wood are here,” said Isaac, “but where is the lamb for the burnt offering?” 8 Abraham answered, “God Himself will provide the lamb for the burnt offering, my son.” And the two walked on together. 9 When they arrived at the place God had designated, Abraham built the altar there and arranged the wood. He bound his son Isaac and placed him on the altar, atop the wood. 10 Then Abraham reached out his hand and took the knife to slaughter his son.
paragraphs: 1 Some time later God tested Abraham and said to him, “Abraham!”
“Here I am,” he answered.
2 “Take your son,” God said, “your only son Isaac, whom you love, and go to the land of Moriah. Offer him there as a burnt offering on one of the mountains, which I will show you.”

3 So Abraham got up early the next morning, saddled his donkey, and took along two of his servants and his son Isaac. He split the wood for a burnt offering and set out for the place God had designated.

4 On the third day Abraham looked up and saw the place in the distance. 5 “Stay here with the donkey,” Abraham told his servants. “The boy and I will go over there to worship, and then we will return to you.”
6 Abraham took the wood for the burnt offering and placed it on his son Isaac. He himself carried the fire and the sacrificial knife, and the two of them walked on together.
7 Then Isaac said to his father Abraham, “My father!”
“Here I am, my son,” he replied.
“The fire and the wood are here,” said Isaac, “but where is the lamb for the burnt offering?”
8 Abraham answered, “God Himself will provide the lamb for the burnt offering, my son.” And the two walked on together.

9 When they arrived at the place God had designated, Abraham built the altar there and arranged the wood. He bound his son Isaac and placed him on the altar, atop the wood. 10 Then Abraham reached out his hand and took the knife to slaughter his son.

passages.context_html:
The account tells us at the outset that God is testing Abraham. That matters because Abraham has already been told that the promised family will continue through Isaac. Ishmael is also his son, but Isaac is the son through whom this particular promise must be fulfilled. The command seems to put the promise itself in danger.

The Hebrew verb נָסָה, nāsâ (nah-SAH), means to test or put to the proof. Brown–Driver–Briggs specifically includes God's testing of Abraham in this verse. The story is about a trust being tested, rather than God tempting Abraham into wrongdoing.

Abraham sets out promptly, reaches the place on the third day, and tells the servants that he and Isaac will return. Isaac carries the wood while Abraham carries the fire and knife. When Isaac asks about the missing animal, Abraham expresses confidence in God's provision. Yet the tension continues: he builds the altar, binds Isaac, and reaches for the knife.

This passage ends before the resolution. In the next verses God stops Abraham, forbids him to harm Isaac, and provides a ram instead. The whole account must be read together. It does not establish a pattern of offering children to God; Deuteronomy 12:31 explicitly condemns that practice.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as a test of Abraham's trust in God, with obedience making that trust visible. The Catholic Catechism, paragraph 2572, and Wesley's notes on Genesis 22 both connect the test with Abraham's confidence that God could keep His promise even in the face of death.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Worship as the Early Church Knew It uses Genesis 22:5 to explain worship as humble trust expressed in obedience. Abraham calls the journey worship before he knows how the crisis will be resolved. The study draws attention to the surrender involved, rather than reducing worship to music or a meeting.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 11:17–19 directly explains Abraham's reasoning: God had promised descendants through Isaac, so Abraham trusted that God could even raise the dead. His confidence was in the God who had spoken. Hebrews describes receiving Isaac back as, in a sense, receiving him from death.

There is also a long-recognized parallel between Isaac carrying the wood and Jesus carrying His cross in John 19:17, noted in Wesley's explanation of Genesis 22:6. Both scenes place a beloved son on a journey toward sacrifice. That is a comparison between the accounts; John does not explicitly identify Isaac's wood as a prediction. The coming rescue of Isaac also marks a crucial difference: Isaac is spared, while Christ gives His life.

passages.title: Genesis 22:1-18
passages.section_title: Abraham Tested on Mount Moriah

He bound his son Isaac and placed him on the altar, atop the wood. 10 Then Abraham reached out his hand and took the knife to slaughter his son. 11 Just then the angel of the LORD called out to him from heaven, “Abraham, Abraham!” “Here I am,” he replied. 12 “Do not lay a hand on the boy or do anything to him,” said the angel, “for now I know that you fear God, since you have not withheld your only son from me.” 13 Then Abraham looked up and saw behind him a ram in a thicket, caught by its horns. So he went and took the ram and offered it as a burnt offering in place of his son. 14 And Abraham called that place The LORD Will Provide. So to this day it is said, “On the mountain of the LORD it will be provided.” 15 And the angel of the LORD called to Abraham from heaven a second time, 16 saying, “By Myself I have sworn, declares the LORD, that because you have done this and have not withheld your only son, 17 I will surely bless you, and I will multiply your descendants like the stars in the sky and the sand on the seashore. Your descendants will possess the gates of their enemies. 18 And through your offspring all nations of the earth will be blessed, because you have obeyed My voice.”
paragraphs: 1 Some time later God tested Abraham and said to him, “Abraham!”
“Here I am,” he answered.
2 “Take your son,” God said, “your only son Isaac, whom you love, and go to the land of Moriah. Offer him there as a burnt offering on one of the mountains, which I will show you.”

3 So Abraham got up early the next morning, saddled his donkey, and took along two of his servants and his son Isaac. He split the wood for a burnt offering and set out for the place God had designated.

4 On the third day Abraham looked up and saw the place in the distance. 5 “Stay here with the donkey,” Abraham told his servants. “The boy and I will go over there to worship, and then we will return to you.”
6 Abraham took the wood for the burnt offering and placed it on his son Isaac. He himself carried the fire and the sacrificial knife, and the two of them walked on together.
7 Then Isaac said to his father Abraham, “My father!”
“Here I am, my son,” he replied.
“The fire and the wood are here,” said Isaac, “but where is the lamb for the burnt offering?”
8 Abraham answered, “God Himself will provide the lamb for the burnt offering, my son.” And the two walked on together.

9 When they arrived at the place God had designated, Abraham built the altar there and arranged the wood. He bound his son Isaac and placed him on the altar, atop the wood. 10 Then Abraham reached out his hand and took the knife to slaughter his son.
11 Just then the angel of the LORD called out to him from heaven, “Abraham, Abraham!”
“Here I am,” he replied.
12 “Do not lay a hand on the boy or do anything to him,” said the angel, “for now I know that you fear God, since you have not withheld your only son from me.”

13 Then Abraham looked up and saw behind him a ram in a thicket, caught by its horns. So he went and took the ram and offered it as a burnt offering in place of his son. 14 And Abraham called that place The LORD Will Provide. So to this day it is said, “On the mountain of the LORD it will be provided.”

15 And the angel of the LORD called to Abraham from heaven a second time, 16 saying, “By Myself I have sworn, declares the LORD, that because you have done this and have not withheld your only son, 17 I will surely bless you, and I will multiply your descendants like the stars in the sky and the sand on the seashore. Your descendants will possess the gates of their enemies. 18 And through your offspring all nations of the earth will be blessed, because you have obeyed My voice.”

passages.context_html:
God tests Abraham by telling him to offer Isaac, the son through whom He has promised Abraham's descendants. The opening identifies a test; the ending reveals God's provision. Reading the whole movement matters, especially when considering the fearful command at its center.

Abraham prepares for the journey, leaves the servants behind, and goes on with Isaac, who carries the wood. He tells the servants they will return and tells Isaac that God will provide the animal. At the altar he binds his son and reaches for the knife. Genesis does not give Isaac's age or describe his thoughts, so claims about his exact age or his fully informed agreement go beyond the account.

The angel of the LORD calls from heaven and stops the sacrifice. Abraham must not harm the boy. A ram caught in a thicket becomes the offering in Isaac's place, and Abraham names the place for the LORD's provision. The LORD then confirms His promise with an oath: Abraham's descendants will multiply, and blessing will reach all nations through his offspring.

The outcome is a living son and a provided sacrifice. Elsewhere Scripture explicitly condemns offering children to God in Deuteronomy 12:31. This extraordinary test is therefore not permission to harm a child or to treat a private impression as such a command.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand this as a test of Abraham's trust in God, with obedience making that trust visible. The Catholic Catechism, paragraph 2572, and Wesley's notes on Genesis 22 both connect the test with Abraham's confidence that God could keep His promise even in the face of death.

Christians differ over the angel's identity. Wesley, on Genesis 22:11, 15, identifies Him as the eternal Son; Augustine, On the Trinity 3.11.25, understands God to be speaking through an angelic messenger. These are readings offered by Christian teachers, rather than a rule that every member of their respective traditions must interpret this scene in the same way.
passages.current_position_html:
Our study Worship as the Early Church Knew It uses Genesis 22:5 to explain worship as humble trust expressed in obedience. Abraham calls the journey worship before he knows how the crisis will be resolved. The study draws attention to the surrender involved, rather than reducing worship to music or a meeting.

Our study Who is The Angel of the Lord? understands the angel here as the Son of God before His human birth. It points to His speaking as the One from whom Abraham has not withheld his son, followed by the LORD's oath in the first person. This is the study's conclusion about the speaker's identity.

passages.god_plan_html:
The New Testament returns directly to this event. Hebrews 11:17–19 says Abraham believed God could raise Isaac from the dead. James 2:21–23 emphasizes his faith working through his actions and reaching its fulfillment in obedience. The test puts the trust described earlier in Abraham's life into action.

A further parallel helps show the scale of God's love. Abraham is willing to surrender his beloved son, but God stops him. In Romans 8:32, God gives His own Son for us. The Catechism, paragraph 2572, explicitly draws this comparison. Isaac is rescued by an animal dying in his place; Christ actually dies and is raised. The similarities point us toward Christ without making the two events identical.

The oath also reaches beyond Abraham's household. Hebrews 6:13–20 cites God's swearing by Himself to explain why the heirs of the promise can have secure hope. Its conclusion brings that hope to Jesus, who has entered God's presence on our behalf. The foundation is God's unchanging purpose and truthfulness.

passages.context_html:
The call from heaven interrupts Abraham at the moment he is about to kill Isaac. He is told to stop and do nothing to harm the boy. His willingness to surrender the son he loves has demonstrated his fear of God. The story ends with the test answered, rather than with the child's death.

Abraham sees a ram caught by its horns and offers it in Isaac's place. This is a genuine exchange within the account: the animal dies and Isaac lives. Abraham names the place The LORD Will Provide. The verb behind provide is רָאָה, rāʾâ (rah-AH), ordinarily see; Brown–Driver–Briggs includes provide or furnish as its sense in Genesis 22:8. God has seen to the needed offering.

The angel then calls again and declares the LORD's oath. The promises of many descendants and blessing for the nations are confirmed after Abraham's obedience. The wording also raises the question of who is speaking: the angel speaks of Abraham not withholding his son from him, and then delivers the LORD's oath. Abraham returns to the servants and settles in Beersheba.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly see God's rescue of Isaac and provision of an offering as the resolution of Abraham's test. Wesley's notes on Genesis 22:12–14 emphasize both the demonstrated trust and the LORD's provision.

Christians differ over the angel's identity. Wesley, on Genesis 22:11, 15, identifies Him as the eternal Son; Augustine, On the Trinity 3.11.25, understands God to be speaking through an angelic messenger. These are readings offered by Christian teachers, rather than a rule that every member of their respective traditions must interpret this scene in the same way.

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 6:13–20 explicitly takes up this oath. God swears by Himself because there is no greater authority, giving the heirs of His promise strong grounds for hope. Hebrews leads from that assurance to Jesus in God's presence as our high priest. It does not say that the oath requires God to die if He breaks it; its point is that God cannot lie.

The ram's death in Isaac's place also offers a meaningful parallel to God's provision of Christ. John 1:29 identifies Jesus as the Lamb of God who takes away the world's sin. John does not directly quote this scene, and the animal here is a ram, but the comparison is clear: the needed offering comes through God's provision, and another life is given so that the threatened person may live.

passages.section_title: The Sons of Nahor

Milcah bore these eight sons to Abraham’s brother Nahor. 24 Moreover, Nahor’s concubine, whose name was Reumah, bore Tebah, Gaham, Tahash, and Maacah.

23 And Bethuel became the father of Rebekah. Milcah bore these eight sons to Abraham’s brother Nahor. 24 Moreover, Nahor’s concubine, whose name was Reumah, bore Tebah, Gaham, Tahash, and Maacah.

passages.context_html:
After the test on the mountain, Abraham receives news about his brother Nahor's family. Milcah has borne eight sons, and Nahor's concubine Reumah has borne four more children. These names move attention from Abraham's household in Canaan to the relatives from whom Isaac's wife will come.

One detail looks ahead: Bethuel is identified as Rebekah's father. She will become central in chapter 24. The list therefore prepares the next stage of the family story, even though most of the people named will not receive a separate account here. It gives no detailed account of their lives or the timing of Abraham's earlier contact with them.
passages.common_interpretations_html: A common reading is that this family list prepares for Isaac's marriage by introducing Rebekah's relatives. Wesley's note on Genesis 22:20 identifies that connection.

passages.section_title: The Death and Burial of Sarah

passages.context_html:
Sarah dies in Hebron in Canaan at the age of 127, and Abraham mourns and weeps for her. Her death comes after Isaac's birth and before his marriage. The account allows room for Abraham's grief before turning to the practical need for a burial place.

Although God has promised the land to his descendants, Abraham describes himself to the Hittites as a foreigner and outsider. He asks for a burial property and seeks the cave of Machpelah belonging to Ephron. When offered the field and cave, he insists on paying. Ephron names four hundred shekels of silver, and Abraham weighs out that amount in the hearing of the people.

The repeated attention to witnesses and ownership is part of the story. The field, cave, and trees within its boundaries are transferred to Abraham in public at the city gate. Sarah is buried there, and the ending confirms his possession of the burial site. The text gives the price but does not tell us whether it was fair, inflated, or part of a particular tax arrangement.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as an account of genuine grief and a publicly secured burial place in the promised land. Wesley's notes on Genesis 23:2, 4, 20 connect Abraham's mourning with his continuing life as a stranger awaiting the promise.

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 11:13–16 describes the faithful dying without having received the promised fulfillment and acknowledging themselves as strangers on earth. Abraham's situation here makes that waiting concrete. He trusts God's promise about Canaan while still needing to purchase a place to bury Sarah.

Hebrews also says their hope reaches toward a better, heavenly country prepared by God. That hope does not remove the grief of death in Genesis. It gives the waiting a future beyond what Abraham and Sarah have yet seen. Buying the burial site places Sarah's grave in the land of promise while the larger inheritance still lies ahead.

passages.title: Genesis 24:1-14
passages.section_title: A Wife for Isaac

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 By now Abraham was old and well along in years, and the LORD had blessed him in every way. 2 So Abraham instructed the chief servant of his household, who managed all he owned, “Place your hand under my thigh, 3 and I will have you swear by the LORD, the God of heaven and the God of earth, that you will not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites among whom I am dwelling, 4 but will go to my country and my kindred to take a wife for my son Isaac.” 5 The servant asked him, “What if the woman is unwilling to follow me to this land? Shall I then take your son back to the land from which you came?” 6 Abraham replied, “Make sure that you do not take my son back there. 7 The LORD, the God of heaven, who brought me from my father’s house and my native land, who spoke to me and promised me on oath, saying, ‘To your offspring I will give this land’—He will send His angel before you so that you can take a wife for my son from there. 8 And if the woman is unwilling to follow you, then you are released from this oath of mine. Only do not take my son back there.” 9 So the servant placed his hand under the thigh of his master Abraham and swore an oath to him concerning this matter. 10 Then the servant took ten of his master’s camels and departed with all manner of good things from his master in hand. And he set out for Nahor’s hometown in Aram-naharaim. 11 As evening approached, he made the camels kneel down near the well outside the town at the time when the women went out to draw water. 12 “O LORD, God of my master Abraham,” he prayed, “please grant me success today, and show kindness to my master Abraham. 13 Here I am, standing beside the spring, and the daughters of the townspeople are coming out to draw water. 14 Now may it happen that the girl to whom I say, ‘Please let down your jar that I may drink,’ and who responds, ‘Drink, and I will water your camels as well’—let her be the one You have appointed for Your servant Isaac. By this I will know that You have shown kindness to my master.”

10 Then the servant took ten of his master’s camels and departed with all manner of good things from his master in hand. And he set out for Nahor’s hometown in Aram-naharaim. 11 As evening approached, he made the camels kneel down near the well outside the town at the time when the women went out to draw water.

12 “O LORD, God of my master Abraham,” he prayed, “please grant me success today, and show kindness to my master Abraham. 13 Here I am, standing beside the spring, and the daughters of the townspeople are coming out to draw water. 14 Now may it happen that the girl to whom I say, ‘Please let down your jar that I may drink,’ and who responds, ‘Drink, and I will water your camels as well’—let her be the one You have appointed for Your servant Isaac. By this I will know that You have shown kindness to my master.”

passages.context_html:
Abraham, now old, sends the chief servant of his household to seek a wife for Isaac among his relatives. The servant is trusted with Abraham's possessions, but this chapter does not name him. Abraham binds him by an oath, expressed by placing a hand under his thigh. The account records the gesture without explaining all of its cultural meaning.

Two instructions govern the mission: the wife must come from Abraham's kindred rather than the Canaanites, and Isaac must not be taken back to the country Abraham left. Abraham links his confidence to God's promise of this land to his offspring. If the woman is unwilling to come, the servant is released from the oath; he is not authorized to force the outcome.

The servant travels with ten camels to Nahor's town in Aram-naharaim and stops beside the well as women come to draw water. He asks God to show kindness to Abraham by identifying the appointed woman through her offering water to him and his camels. That response would show generous service as well as answer his particular request.

The word translated kindness is חֶסֶד, ḥesed (KHEH-sed). Brown–Driver–Briggs gives kindness and lovingkindness among its meanings and cites this chapter. The servant is asking for God's faithful care toward Abraham to take practical shape in this journey.
passages.common_interpretations_html: A common Christian reading sees prayer for guidance joined with a task carried out under Abraham's instructions. Wesley's notes on Genesis 24:12–15 welcome specific prayer and attention to God's care, while warning against prescribing to God exactly how He must act. The account describes this servant's request; it does not promise that every reader can identify a spouse by arranging the same sort of test.

passages.god_plan_html:
The search serves a purpose larger than finding a suitable household match: the promised family through Isaac must continue. Abraham refuses to secure that future by undoing God's call to the land. His confidence grows from the promise already given, and the servant seeks help while working within that direction.

This also illustrates a theme carried into James 1:5: people who lack wisdom can ask God for it. James encourages that dependence without giving a method of creating signs. The connection is the shared call to seek God's help with a real responsibility, rather than to treat the events at the well as a guaranteed formula for every decision.

passages.title: Genesis 24:15-61
passages.section_title: Rebekah Is Chosen

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 Before the servant had finished praying, Rebekah came out with her jar on her shoulder. She was the daughter of Bethuel son of Milcah, the wife of Abraham’s brother Nahor. 16 Now the girl was very beautiful, a virgin who had not had relations with any man. She went down to the spring, filled her jar, and came up again. 17 So the servant ran to meet her and said, “Please let me have a little water from your jar.” 18 “Drink, my lord,” she replied, and she quickly lowered her jar to her hands and gave him a drink. 19 After she had given him a drink, she said, “I will also draw water for your camels, until they have had enough to drink.” 20 And she quickly emptied her jar into the trough and ran back to the well to draw water, until she had drawn water for all his camels. 21 Meanwhile, the man watched her silently to see whether or not the LORD had made his journey a success. 22 And after the camels had finished drinking, he took out a gold ring weighing a beka, and two gold bracelets for her wrists weighing ten shekels. 23 “Whose daughter are you?” he asked. “Please tell me, is there room in your father’s house for us to spend the night?” 24 She replied, “I am the daughter of Bethuel, the son that Milcah bore to Nahor.” 25 Then she added, “We have plenty of straw and feed, as well as a place for you to spend the night.” 26 Then the man bowed down and worshiped the LORD, 27 saying, “Blessed be the LORD, the God of my master Abraham, who has not withheld His kindness and faithfulness from my master. As for me, the LORD has led me on the journey to the house of my master’s relatives.” 28 The girl ran and told her mother’s household about these things. 29 Now Rebekah had a brother named Laban, and he rushed out to the man at the spring. 30 As soon as he saw the ring, and the bracelets on his sister’s wrists, and heard Rebekah’s words, “The man said this to me,” he went and found the man standing by the camels near the spring. 31 “Come, you who are blessed by the LORD,” said Laban. “Why are you standing out here? I have prepared the house and a place for the camels.” 32 So the man came to the house, and the camels were unloaded. Straw and feed were brought to the camels, and water to wash his feet and the feet of his companions. 33 Then a meal was set before the man, but he said, “I will not eat until I have told you what I came to say.” So Laban said, “Please speak.” 34 “I am Abraham’s servant,” he replied. 35 “The LORD has greatly blessed my master, and he has become rich. He has given him sheep and cattle, silver and gold, menservants and maidservants, camels and donkeys. 36 My master’s wife Sarah has borne him a son in her old age, and my master has given him everything he owns. 37 My master made me swear an oath and said, ‘You shall not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites in whose land I dwell, 38 but you shall go to my father’s house and to my kindred to take a wife for my son.’ 39 Then I asked my master, ‘What if the woman will not come back with me?’ 40 And he told me, ‘The LORD, before whom I have walked, will send His angel with you and make your journey a success, so that you may take a wife for my son from my kindred and from my father’s house. 41 And when you go to my kindred, if they refuse to give her to you, then you will be released from my oath.’ 42 So when I came to the spring today, I prayed: O LORD, God of my master Abraham, if only You would make my journey a success! 43 Here I am, standing beside this spring. Now if a maiden comes out to draw water and I say to her, ‘Please let me drink a little water from your jar,’ 44 and she replies, ‘Drink, and I will draw water for your camels as well,’ may she be the woman the LORD has appointed for my master’s son. 45 And before I had finished praying in my heart, there was Rebekah coming out with her jar on her shoulder, and she went down to the spring and drew water. So I said to her, ‘Please give me a drink.’ 46 She quickly lowered her jar from her shoulder and said, ‘Drink, and I will water your camels as well.’ So I drank, and she also watered the camels. 47 Then I asked her, ‘Whose daughter are you?’ She replied, ‘The daughter of Bethuel son of Nahor, whom Milcah bore to him.’ So I put the ring on her nose and the bracelets on her wrists. 48 Then I bowed down and worshiped the LORD; and I blessed the LORD, the God of my master Abraham, who led me on the right road to take the granddaughter of my master’s brother for his son. 49 Now if you will show kindness and faithfulness to my master, tell me; but if not, let me know, so that I may go elsewhere.” 50 Laban and Bethuel answered, “This is from the LORD; we have no choice in the matter. 51 Rebekah is here before you. Take her and go, and let her become the wife of your master’s son, just as the LORD has decreed.” 52 When Abraham’s servant heard their words, he bowed down to the ground before the LORD. 53 Then he brought out jewels of silver and gold, and articles of clothing, and he gave them to Rebekah. He also gave precious gifts to her brother and her mother. 54 Then he and the men with him ate and drank and spent the night there. When they got up the next morning, he said, “Send me on my way to my master.” 55 But her brother and mother said, “Let the girl remain with us ten days or so. After that, she may go.” 56 But he replied, “Do not delay me, since the LORD has made my journey a success. Send me on my way so that I may go to my master.” 57 So they said, “We will call the girl and ask her opinion.” 58 They called Rebekah and asked her, “Will you go with this man?” “I will go,” she replied. 59 So they sent their sister Rebekah on her way, along with her nurse and Abraham’s servant and his men. 60 And they blessed Rebekah and said to her, “Our sister, may you become the mother of thousands upon thousands. May your offspring possess the gates of their enemies.” 61 Then Rebekah and her servant girls got ready, mounted the camels, and followed the man. So the servant took Rebekah and left.

She was the daughter of Bethuel son of Milcah, the wife of Abraham’s brother Nahor. 16 Now the girl was very beautiful, a virgin who had not had relations with any man. She went down to the spring, filled her jar, and came up again.

21 Meanwhile, the man watched her silently to see whether or not the LORD had made his journey a success.

22 And after the camels had finished drinking, he took out a gold ring weighing a beka, and two gold bracelets for her wrists weighing ten shekels. 23 “Whose daughter are you?” he asked. “Please tell me, is there room in your father’s house for us to spend the night?”

passages.context_html:
Rebekah arrives before the servant has finished praying. She gives him water, then volunteers to draw enough for all ten camels. He watches to see whether the LORD has made his journey successful. He also asks about her family and lodging, learning that she is Bethuel's daughter and belongs to Abraham's kindred. Her kindness and her identity both matter to the mission.

The servant responds by bowing and thanking God for kindness and faithfulness toward Abraham. Rebekah goes home, and Laban comes to welcome the travelers. The servant refuses to eat until he explains why he has come. His long retelling lets the family hear Abraham's instructions, the prayer, and Rebekah's response together, so that the reader sees why he understands the meeting as God's guidance.

Laban and Bethuel recognize the matter as coming from the LORD and agree that Rebekah may become Isaac's wife. The servant worships again and gives gifts to her and her family. The next morning her brother and mother ask for a delay, while the servant wants to leave. Rebekah herself is consulted and agrees to go. Her willingness fulfills the condition Abraham had set before the journey began.

The family sends her away with a blessing for many descendants and victory over enemies, echoing the promise of Genesis 22:17. She travels with her nurse and servant girls, accompanied by Abraham's servant and his men. The chapter describes a consequential decision carried out through prayer, hospitality, conversation, and a willing departure.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the meeting as God's care working through Rebekah's generosity and the servant's faithful work. Wesley's notes on Genesis 24:15, 27, 52, 57 emphasize answered prayer, thanksgiving, and the importance of consulting Rebekah herself. His explanation does not make gratitude a substitute for the practical steps described in the story.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
The repeated prayers of thanks show how the promised future takes shape through ordinary actions. Drawing water, offering a place to stay, explaining a mission honestly, and agreeing to leave become part of the continuation of Abraham's family. God's purpose is being carried forward without a new public miracle like Isaac's birth.

Rebekah's departure also offers a useful parallel to Abraham's earlier willingness to leave a familiar home for the future God opened before him. Hebrews 11:8–10 explicitly describes Abraham's journey as faith. It does not make that same statement about Rebekah, but her decision similarly involves going toward a future she has not yet seen. This is a comparison of the two journeys, rather than a claim that every detail of the servant's mission predicts a later event.

passages.title: Genesis 24:62-67
passages.section_title: Isaac Marries Rebekah

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 62 Now Isaac had just returned from Beer-lahai-roi, for he was living in the Negev. 63 Early in the evening, Isaac went out to the field to meditate, and looking up, he saw the camels approaching. 64 And when Rebekah looked up and saw Isaac, she got down from her camel 65 and asked the servant, “Who is that man in the field coming to meet us?” “It is my master,” the servant answered. So she took her veil and covered herself. 66 Then the servant told Isaac all that he had done. 67 And Isaac brought her into the tent of his mother Sarah and took Rebekah as his wife. And Isaac loved her and was comforted after his mother’s death.
paragraphs: 62 Now Isaac had just returned from Beer-lahai-roi, for he was living in the Negev. 63 Early in the evening, Isaac went out to the field to meditate, and looking up, he saw the camels approaching.
64 And when Rebekah looked up and saw Isaac, she got down from her camel 65 and asked the servant, “Who is that man in the field coming to meet us?”
“It is my master,” the servant answered. So she took her veil and covered herself. 66 Then the servant told Isaac all that he had done.
67 And Isaac brought her into the tent of his mother Sarah and took Rebekah as his wife. And Isaac loved her and was comforted after his mother’s death.

passages.context_html:
The travelers reach Isaac, who is living in the Negev and has returned from Beer-lahai-roi. He is in the field toward evening when he sees the camels approaching. Rebekah sees him, gets down from her camel, and asks the servant who he is. Once told, she covers herself with her veil.

The servant reports what has happened, bringing the mission to its conclusion. Isaac takes Rebekah as his wife and loves her. The account ends by saying that he is comforted after his mother's death, joining this marriage back to Sarah's burial in chapter 23. The next generation's future and a son's grief meet in the same household.

The story tells us what Isaac and Rebekah do at their meeting, but does not explain every meaning of the veil or describe a complete wedding ceremony. Its final emphasis is the marriage, Isaac's love, and the comfort he receives.
passages.common_interpretations_html: A common Christian reading sees a successful conclusion to the servant's mission, with God's care expressed in marriage, love, and comfort after loss. Wesley's overview of Genesis 24 connects Isaac's marriage with Sarah's death and the passing of one generation to the next.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
Scripture uses marriage to help explain Christ's relationship with His people. Ephesians 5:25–32 describes Christ loving the church, giving Himself for her, and preparing her to be with Him. Isaac's love for Rebekah can be read alongside that larger theme: the long search and journey lead to a relationship of love, rather than ending with the delivery of a stranger to a household.

There is also a helpful parallel between Rebekah setting out before she has met Isaac and believers trusting Christ before seeing Him. 1 Peter 1:8–9 describes love and faith directed toward the unseen Christ. Neither passage identifies Rebekah as a prediction of the church. These are comparisons that illuminate the story; they do not require us to identify the unnamed servant as the Holy Spirit or turn the gifts and camels into a hidden timetable.

passages.title: Genesis 25:1-6
passages.section_title: Abraham and Keturah

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now Abraham had taken another wife, named Keturah, 2 and she bore him Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah. 3 Jokshan was the father of Sheba and Dedan. And the sons of Dedan were the Asshurites, the Letushites, and the Leummites. 4 The sons of Midian were Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida, and Eldaah. All these were descendants of Keturah. 5 Abraham left everything he owned to Isaac. 6 But while he was still alive, Abraham gave gifts to the sons of his concubines and sent them away from his son Isaac to the land of the east.
paragraphs: 1 Now Abraham had taken another wife, named Keturah, 2 and she bore him Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah.
3 Jokshan was the father of Sheba and Dedan. And the sons of Dedan were the Asshurites, the Letushites, and the Leummites.
4 The sons of Midian were Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida, and Eldaah.
All these were descendants of Keturah.
5 Abraham left everything he owned to Isaac. 6 But while he was still alive, Abraham gave gifts to the sons of his concubines and sent them away from his son Isaac to the land of the east.

passages.context_html:
Before closing Abraham's story, Genesis records his children through Keturah. Six sons are named, followed by descendants of Jokshan and Midian. Abraham's family extends beyond Isaac and Ishmael, even though the main account will continue through Isaac.

Abraham gives gifts to the sons of his concubines while he is alive and sends them east, away from Isaac. Isaac receives the main inheritance. These different arrangements keep his place as heir distinct while showing that Abraham also provides something for his other sons.

This fits the distinction God had already made in Genesis 17:19–21: He would establish the covenant through Isaac. The additional children do not replace that promise or divide it into competing family lines. Genesis gives these arrangements without explaining every motive behind the marriage or the timing of each child's birth.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these verses as distinguishing Isaac's inheritance from the provision made for Abraham's other sons. Wesley's notes on Genesis 25:5–6 hold those responsibilities together: preserving Isaac's place does not mean giving the other children nothing.

passages.god_plan_html:
The distinction between family descent and the promised inheritance becomes important in the New Testament. Galatians 3:26–29 says that people who belong to Christ are Abraham's offspring and heirs according to the promise. The family story eventually reaches people from different nations through faith in Christ.

The Bible also speaks of that inheritance as something believers still await. Ephesians 1:13–14 describes the Holy Spirit as its pledge, and Hebrews 9:15 connects the promised eternal inheritance with Christ's death. These passages develop the wider inheritance theme; they do not turn each of Keturah's children into a hidden picture of someone rejected by God.

passages.title: Genesis 25:7-11
passages.section_title: The Death of Abraham

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 Abraham lived a total of 175 years. 8 And at a ripe old age he breathed his last and died, old and contented, and was gathered to his people. 9 His sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him in the cave of Machpelah near Mamre, in the field of Ephron son of Zohar the Hittite. 10 This was the field that Abraham had bought from the Hittites. Abraham was buried there with his wife Sarah. 11 After Abraham’s death, God blessed his son Isaac, who lived near Beer-lahai-roi.
paragraphs: 7 Abraham lived a total of 175 years. 8 And at a ripe old age he breathed his last and died, old and contented, and was gathered to his people.

9 His sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him in the cave of Machpelah near Mamre, in the field of Ephron son of Zohar the Hittite. 10 This was the field that Abraham had bought from the Hittites. Abraham was buried there with his wife Sarah.
11 After Abraham’s death, God blessed his son Isaac, who lived near Beer-lahai-roi.

passages.context_html:
Abraham dies at 175, described as old and contented. His life has included long waiting, serious failures, costly tests, and fulfilled promises. The closing description does not claim that everything he did was right; it brings the long account of his life to rest.

Isaac and Ishmael bury him together in the cave of Machpelah, the property he bought when Sarah died. The sons' shared presence at the burial is stated plainly, though the passage does not tell us whether they had fully resolved every earlier family tension. Abraham is buried beside Sarah in Canaan.

The final verse looks forward: God blesses Isaac, who lives near Beer-lahai-roi. Abraham's death therefore closes one life without ending God's work through the family. The promises are not dependent on Abraham remaining alive to carry them forward.
passages.common_interpretations_html: A common Christian reading sees an honorable close to Abraham's life and the continuation of God's blessing through Isaac. Wesley's notes on Genesis 25:8–11 also connect the burial beside Sarah with hope beyond death.

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 11:13–16 describes the faithful dying while still looking toward the fulfillment of God's promises and a better country prepared by Him. Abraham's burial belongs within that larger hope. He has seen Isaac born and established, but his lifetime does not contain everything God has promised.

Jesus later names Abraham when explaining the resurrection in Matthew 22:31–32: God identifies Himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and is the God of the living. Jesus is explaining God's words to Moses rather than quoting this burial scene, but His teaching shows why Abraham's death is not the end of his relationship with God.

passages.title: Genesis 25:12-18
passages.section_title: The Descendants of Ishmael

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 This is the account of Abraham’s son Ishmael, whom Hagar the Egyptian, Sarah’s maidservant, bore to Abraham. 13 These are the names of the sons of Ishmael in the order of their birth: Nebaioth the firstborn of Ishmael, then Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam, 14 Mishma, Dumah, Massa, 15 Hadad, Tema, Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah. 16 These were the sons of Ishmael, and these were their names by their villages and encampments—twelve princes of their tribes. 17 Ishmael lived a total of 137 years. Then he breathed his last and died, and was gathered to his people. 18 Ishmael’s descendants settled from Havilah to Shur, which is near the border of Egypt as you go toward Asshur. And they lived in hostility toward all their brothers.
paragraphs: 12 This is the account of Abraham’s son Ishmael, whom Hagar the Egyptian, Sarah’s maidservant, bore to Abraham. 13 These are the names of the sons of Ishmael in the order of their birth: Nebaioth the firstborn of Ishmael, then Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam, 14 Mishma, Dumah, Massa, 15 Hadad, Tema, Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah.

16 These were the sons of Ishmael, and these were their names by their villages and encampments—twelve princes of their tribes. 17 Ishmael lived a total of 137 years. Then he breathed his last and died, and was gathered to his people.
18 Ishmael’s descendants settled from Havilah to Shur, which is near the border of Egypt as you go toward Asshur. And they lived in hostility toward all their brothers.

passages.context_html:
Genesis briefly follows Ishmael's family before returning to Isaac. It identifies Ishmael as Abraham's son through Hagar, names his twelve sons, and describes them as princes of their tribes. Their villages and encampments show a family that has grown into distinct communities.

The twelve leaders recall God's promise in Genesis 17:20, where He said He would bless Ishmael, multiply his descendants, and make him the father of twelve rulers. That promise is remembered even though the covenant line is traced through Isaac. Being outside that particular line does not mean being outside every kindness God has shown.

Ishmael dies at 137. The account describes his descendants' territory in relation to Egypt and Asshur and, in the BSB, their hostility toward their brothers. It closes this branch of the family history without requiring us to assign the character of these communities to every later person who claims descent from Ishmael.
passages.common_interpretations_html: A common Christian reading sees the twelve princes as fulfillment of God's promise to Ishmael, while the main story continues through Isaac. Wesley's notes on Genesis 25:11, 17 treat Ishmael's growing family and long life as signs of God's care for him.

passages.title: Genesis 25:19-28
passages.section_title: Jacob and Esau

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 This is the account of Abraham’s son Isaac. Abraham became the father of Isaac, 20 and Isaac was forty years old when he married Rebekah, the daughter of Bethuel the Aramean from Paddan-aram and the sister of Laban the Aramean. 21 Later, Isaac prayed to the LORD on behalf of his wife, because she was barren. And the LORD heard his prayer, and his wife Rebekah conceived. 22 But the children inside her struggled with each other, and she said, “Why is this happening to me?” So Rebekah went to inquire of the LORD, 23 and He declared to her: “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples from within you will be separated; one people will be stronger than the other, and the older will serve the younger.” 24 When her time came to give birth, there were indeed twins in her womb. 25 The first one came out red, covered with hair like a fur coat; so they named him Esau. 26 After this, his brother came out grasping Esau’s heel; so he was named Jacob. And Isaac was sixty years old when the twins were born. 27 When the boys grew up, Esau became a skillful hunter, a man of the field, while Jacob was a quiet man who stayed at home. 28 Because Isaac had a taste for wild game, he loved Esau; but Rebekah loved Jacob.
paragraphs: 19 This is the account of Abraham’s son Isaac. Abraham became the father of Isaac, 20 and Isaac was forty years old when he married Rebekah, the daughter of Bethuel the Aramean from Paddan-aram and the sister of Laban the Aramean.
21 Later, Isaac prayed to the LORD on behalf of his wife, because she was barren. And the LORD heard his prayer, and his wife Rebekah conceived.
22 But the children inside her struggled with each other, and she said, “Why is this happening to me?” So Rebekah went to inquire of the LORD, 23 and He declared to her:
“Two nations are in your womb,
and two peoples from within you will be separated;
one people will be stronger than the other,
and the older will serve the younger.”

24 When her time came to give birth, there were indeed twins in her womb. 25 The first one came out red, covered with hair like a fur coat; so they named him Esau. 26 After this, his brother came out grasping Esau’s heel; so he was named Jacob. And Isaac was sixty years old when the twins were born.

27 When the boys grew up, Esau became a skillful hunter, a man of the field, while Jacob was a quiet man who stayed at home. 28 Because Isaac had a taste for wild game, he loved Esau; but Rebekah loved Jacob.

passages.context_html:
The account now turns to Isaac and Rebekah's children. Isaac was forty when they married and sixty when the twins were born, so twenty years passed before they had children. He prays because Rebekah is unable to conceive, and the LORD answers. Genesis tells us about the prayer without saying that Isaac waited twenty years before first asking.

During the pregnancy, Rebekah is troubled by the children's struggle and brings her question to the LORD. His answer reaches beyond a difficult pregnancy: the two children will become two peoples, and the older will serve the younger. Their future is announced before either child has done anything to earn a preferred place.

Esau is born first, red and covered with hair. Jacob follows while grasping his brother's heel, giving the account its explanation for his name. They grow into different ways of life: Esau is a hunter, while Jacob stays among the tents. The Hebrew description of Jacob is תָּם, tām (tahm). Brown–Driver–Briggs gives a sense of sound or wholesome here, while also recording its moral use elsewhere. In this contrast it does not by itself prove that Jacob's later choices are all blameless.

The ending introduces divided affection in the household. Isaac favors Esau and enjoys his game; Rebekah favors Jacob. Those preferences prepare for the conflict in the chapters that follow. Genesis does not tell us whether Rebekah had shared God's message with Isaac.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians agree that God's purpose is not controlled by the twins' birth order. They differ over how His choice here relates to His choice of people for salvation, especially when reading Paul's explanation in Romans 9.

Reformed churches following the Westminster Confession 3.5–6, and Baptists following the 1689 Confession 3.2, 5–6, understand God's choice for salvation as grounded in His grace rather than in faith or good works He foresees in a person. The Baptist confession explicitly cites Romans 9's account of the twins in support.

Wesley's notes on Romans 9:10–13 read the choice here as concerning the promised family line and the peoples descended from Jacob and Esau, rather than a declaration of each man's eternal fate. In his wider explanation, God's mercy receives believers from both Jews and Gentiles; ancestry does not secure that mercy, and faith is not a work that earns it.

The Catholic Church teaches that even the preparation to receive God's grace depends on His help, while His initiative calls for a free human response (Catechism 2001–2002). It also teaches that God predestines no one to hell (Catechism 1037). These are its broader teachings about grace and human response, rather than a detailed ruling on every part of this Genesis scene.
