passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 9:6–13 directly uses Rebekah's twins when answering whether God's word has failed. Paul draws attention to the announcement before their birth or any good or bad deeds. The promised future rests on God's calling rather than being a reward one of the unborn children has earned.

Paul's discussion goes on to people called from both Jews and Gentiles in Romans 9:24–33. He describes Gentiles receiving righteousness by faith and warns against pursuing it as though it came through works. The twins' story thus enters a larger explanation of God's faithfulness, mercy, and the people He gathers. Its reach is greater than the rivalry within one household, even though Christians differ over how all the parts of that explanation fit together.

passages.title: Genesis 25:29-34
passages.section_title: Esau Sells His Birthright

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 29 One day, while Jacob was cooking some stew, Esau came in from the field and was famished. 30 He said to Jacob, “Let me eat some of that red stew, for I am famished.” (That is why he was also called Edom.) 31 “First sell me your birthright,” Jacob replied. 32 “Look,” said Esau, “I am about to die, so what good is a birthright to me?” 33 “Swear to me first,” Jacob said. So Esau swore to Jacob and sold him the birthright. 34 Then Jacob gave some bread and lentil stew to Esau, who ate and drank and then got up and went away. Thus Esau despised his birthright.
paragraphs: 29 One day, while Jacob was cooking some stew, Esau came in from the field and was famished. 30 He said to Jacob, “Let me eat some of that red stew, for I am famished.” (That is why he was also called Edom.)
31 “First sell me your birthright,” Jacob replied.
32 “Look,” said Esau, “I am about to die, so what good is a birthright to me?”
33 “Swear to me first,” Jacob said.
So Esau swore to Jacob and sold him the birthright. 34 Then Jacob gave some bread and lentil stew to Esau, who ate and drank and then got up and went away. Thus Esau despised his birthright.

passages.context_html:
Esau comes in from the field exhausted and hungry while Jacob is cooking stew. He asks for the red food, and the account connects that request with his other name, Edom. Jacob responds with a demand: sell the birthright first. A familiar need for a meal becomes a decision with lasting consequences.

The birthright is the right belonging to the firstborn. The Hebrew noun is בְּכֹרָה, bĕkōrâ (beh-khoh-RAH), which Brown–Driver–Briggs identifies as the right of the firstborn, including its uses in this exchange. It concerns Esau's privileged place in the family, not merely whether he will receive another serving of food.

Esau speaks as though his immediate need makes that future worthless. Jacob requires an oath, Esau swears, and the account explicitly says that he sells the birthright. He receives bread and lentil stew, eats and drinks, gets up, and leaves. The final sentence gives the narrator's assessment: he has despised his birthright.

The verb is בָּזָה, bāzâ (bah-ZAH), meaning despise or regard with contempt; Brown–Driver–Briggs specifically cites this verse. Esau's actions have treated a lasting privilege as worth less than immediate relief. The chapter does not describe every food source available in the camp or settle every question about Jacob's motives.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a warning about treating a lasting privilege as less valuable than immediate satisfaction. Wesley's note on Genesis 25:31 condemns Esau's disregard while also criticizing Jacob for taking advantage of his brother's need; recognizing Esau's failure does not require treating every part of Jacob's bargain as admirable.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 12:14–17 explicitly uses Esau's sale as a warning to its readers. In a call to pursue peace and holiness and not fall short of God's grace, it points to the man who sold his birthright for one meal. A decision that appeared to satisfy the moment led to a loss he later could not simply reverse with tears.

The chapter then describes the believers' privilege of coming to the heavenly Jerusalem, the assembly of the firstborn, and Jesus, the mediator of the new covenant (Hebrews 12:22–24). The warning therefore concerns how people value what God has placed before them. The promised future is worth taking seriously while today's appetites and pressures feel urgent.

passages.title: Genesis 26:1-5
passages.section_title: God’s Promise to Isaac

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now there was another famine in the land, subsequent to the one that had occurred in Abraham’s time. And Isaac went to Abimelech king of the Philistines at Gerar. 2 The LORD appeared to Isaac and said, “Do not go down to Egypt. Settle in the land where I tell you. 3 Stay in this land as a foreigner, and I will be with you and bless you. For I will give all these lands to you and your offspring, and I will confirm the oath that I swore to your father Abraham. 4 I will make your descendants as numerous as the stars in the sky, and I will give them all these lands, and through your offspring all nations of the earth will be blessed, 5 because Abraham listened to My voice and kept My charge, My commandments, My statutes, and My laws.”
paragraphs: 1 Now there was another famine in the land, subsequent to the one that had occurred in Abraham’s time. And Isaac went to Abimelech king of the Philistines at Gerar.

2 The LORD appeared to Isaac and said, “Do not go down to Egypt. Settle in the land where I tell you. 3 Stay in this land as a foreigner, and I will be with you and bless you. For I will give all these lands to you and your offspring, and I will confirm the oath that I swore to your father Abraham. 4 I will make your descendants as numerous as the stars in the sky, and I will give them all these lands, and through your offspring all nations of the earth will be blessed, 5 because Abraham listened to My voice and kept My charge, My commandments, My statutes, and My laws.”

passages.context_html:
Another famine strikes the land, distinct from the one Abraham experienced. Isaac goes to Gerar, where the LORD appears and tells him not to go down to Egypt. He must remain in the land God identifies, trusting the promise of His presence and blessing.

God speaks to Isaac of the same future He promised Abraham: land, many descendants, and blessing for all nations through his offspring. Isaac is addressed personally as an heir of that promise. The difficult circumstances do not mean the promise has been withdrawn.

The LORD also remembers Abraham's obedience. The Hebrew verb שָׁמַע, šāmaʿ (shah-MAH), can mean hear, listen, or obey; Brown–Driver–Briggs includes obedient listening to someone's voice. The list of what Abraham kept makes clear that this was a response expressed in action, rather than merely hearing words. Genesis has already shown his failures as well as his trust, so this commendation does not describe a sinless life.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read God's instruction as a call for Isaac to trust Him in the famine, with the promises to Abraham now confirmed to his son. Wesley's notes on Genesis 26:2, 5 connect God's care with Isaac's responsibility to obey.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Prayer and Faith uses this passage to contrast Isaac's response to famine with Abraham's earlier journey to Egypt. Isaac receives a clear instruction to remain and obeys it. The study draws from this the importance of trusting God's direction through hardship, rather than making survival on our own terms the governing aim.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The promise of blessing for all nations reaches beyond the survival of Isaac's household. Galatians 3:8–9 explicitly connects the promise first given to Abraham with God's bringing Gentiles into blessing through faith. Its renewal to Isaac keeps that worldwide purpose in view.

Hebrews 11:9–10 also names Isaac and Jacob as heirs living in tents with Abraham while awaiting what God would provide. Trust includes continuing to live responsibly in the present while the full inheritance is still ahead. Here, that trust begins with staying where God has told Isaac to remain.

passages.title: Genesis 26:6-11
passages.section_title: Isaac Deceives Abimelech

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 So Isaac settled in Gerar. 7 But when the men of that place asked about his wife, he said, “She is my sister.” For he was afraid to say, “She is my wife,” since he thought to himself, “The men of this place will kill me on account of Rebekah, because she is so beautiful.” 8 When Isaac had been there a long time, Abimelech king of the Philistines looked down from the window and was surprised to see Isaac caressing his wife Rebekah. 9 Abimelech sent for Isaac and said, “So she is really your wife! How could you say, ‘She is my sister’?” Isaac replied, “Because I thought I might die on account of her.” 10 “What is this you have done to us?” asked Abimelech. “One of the people could easily have slept with your wife, and you would have brought guilt upon us.” 11 So Abimelech warned all the people, saying, “Whoever harms this man or his wife will surely be put to death.”
paragraphs: 6 So Isaac settled in Gerar. 7 But when the men of that place asked about his wife, he said, “She is my sister.” For he was afraid to say, “She is my wife,” since he thought to himself, “The men of this place will kill me on account of Rebekah, because she is so beautiful.”

8 When Isaac had been there a long time, Abimelech king of the Philistines looked down from the window and was surprised to see Isaac caressing his wife Rebekah. 9 Abimelech sent for Isaac and said, “So she is really your wife! How could you say, ‘She is my sister’?”
Isaac replied, “Because I thought I might die on account of her.”

10 “What is this you have done to us?” asked Abimelech. “One of the people could easily have slept with your wife, and you would have brought guilt upon us.” 11 So Abimelech warned all the people, saying, “Whoever harms this man or his wife will surely be put to death.”

passages.context_html:
Isaac stays in Gerar as God directed, but his conduct there also reveals fear. When asked about Rebekah, he calls her his sister because he thinks the local men might kill him to obtain her. His decision echoes Abraham's earlier concealment of Sarah's identity, exposing his wife to danger while trying to protect himself.

After a long time, Abimelech sees Isaac caressing Rebekah and recognizes that she is his wife. The Hebrew verb comes from צָחַק, ṣāḥaq (tsah-KHAHK), whose meanings include laughing and playing. Brown–Driver–Briggs specifically identifies marital caresses in this verse. The king sees behavior that contradicts Isaac's account of their relationship.

Abimelech confronts Isaac about the guilt his deception could have brought upon the people. Isaac admits his fear, and the king issues a warning against harming either him or Rebekah. Protection comes despite Isaac's dishonesty. The account shows both his obedience in remaining in the land and his failure to trust God within it.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly see Isaac repeating his father's fear-driven deception and putting Rebekah and others at risk. Wesley's note on Genesis 26:7 treats the concealment as a serious failure by a man who otherwise trusts God.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
God has just promised to be with Isaac, and the story immediately shows how unevenly Isaac lives in that assurance. The promised family is protected through the exposure of his lie and the king's intervention. God's continuing care is visible alongside a needed rebuke, rather than as approval of the deception.

The wider biblical call is for conduct to agree with professed trust. 1 John 2:3–6 joins knowing God with keeping His word and walking as Jesus walked. Isaac's experience helps make that issue concrete: obeying one direction does not remove the need to trust and act truthfully in the next difficulty.

passages.title: Genesis 26:12-25
passages.section_title: Isaac’s Prosperity

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 Now Isaac sowed seed in the land, and that very year he reaped a hundredfold. And the LORD blessed him, 13 and he became richer and richer, until he was exceedingly wealthy. 14 He owned so many flocks and herds and servants that the Philistines envied him. 15 So the Philistines took dirt and stopped up all the wells that his father’s servants had dug in the days of his father Abraham. 16 Then Abimelech said to Isaac, “Depart from us, for you are much too powerful for us.” 17 So Isaac left that place and encamped in the Valley of Gerar and settled there. 18 Isaac reopened the wells that had been dug in the days of his father Abraham, which the Philistines had stopped up after Abraham died. And he gave these wells the same names his father had given them. 19 Then Isaac’s servants dug in the valley and found a well of fresh water there. 20 But the herdsmen of Gerar quarreled with Isaac’s herdsmen and said, “The water is ours!” So he named the well Esek, because they contended with him. 21 Then they dug another well and quarreled over that one also; so he named it Sitnah. 22 He moved on from there and dug another well, and they did not quarrel over it. He named it Rehoboth and said, “At last the LORD has made room for us, and we will be fruitful in the land.” 23 From there Isaac went up to Beersheba, 24 and that night the LORD appeared to him and said, “I am the God of your father Abraham. Do not be afraid, for I am with you. I will bless you and multiply your descendants for the sake of My servant Abraham.” 25 So Isaac built an altar there and called on the name of the LORD, and he pitched his tent there. His servants also dug a well there.
paragraphs: 12 Now Isaac sowed seed in the land, and that very year he reaped a hundredfold. And the LORD blessed him, 13 and he became richer and richer, until he was exceedingly wealthy. 14 He owned so many flocks and herds and servants that the Philistines envied him. 15 So the Philistines took dirt and stopped up all the wells that his father’s servants had dug in the days of his father Abraham.
16 Then Abimelech said to Isaac, “Depart from us, for you are much too powerful for us.”

17 So Isaac left that place and encamped in the Valley of Gerar and settled there. 18 Isaac reopened the wells that had been dug in the days of his father Abraham, which the Philistines had stopped up after Abraham died. And he gave these wells the same names his father had given them.

19 Then Isaac’s servants dug in the valley and found a well of fresh water there. 20 But the herdsmen of Gerar quarreled with Isaac’s herdsmen and said, “The water is ours!” So he named the well Esek, because they contended with him.
21 Then they dug another well and quarreled over that one also; so he named it Sitnah.
22 He moved on from there and dug another well, and they did not quarrel over it. He named it Rehoboth and said, “At last the LORD has made room for us, and we will be fruitful in the land.”

23 From there Isaac went up to Beersheba, 24 and that night the LORD appeared to him and said, “I am the God of your father Abraham. Do not be afraid, for I am with you. I will bless you and multiply your descendants for the sake of My servant Abraham.”
25 So Isaac built an altar there and called on the name of the LORD, and he pitched his tent there. His servants also dug a well there.

passages.context_html:
Isaac's harvest yields a hundredfold, and the account expressly credits the LORD's blessing. His wealth, flocks, herds, and household grow. Yet that prosperity brings envy rather than an easy welcome: the Philistines stop up Abraham's wells, and Abimelech tells Isaac to leave because he has become too powerful.

Isaac moves into the Valley of Gerar and reopens his father's wells. New discoveries of water bring further disputes with local herdsmen. He moves on from the wells called Esek and Sitnah until a third well is left uncontested. He calls it Rehoboth and acknowledges that the LORD has made room for them to live and flourish.

At Beersheba, the LORD appears again and tells Isaac not to fear, renewing His promise of presence, blessing, and descendants for Abraham's sake. Isaac responds by building an altar, calling on the LORD, pitching his tent, and having another well dug. Worship and ordinary provision stand together at the end of the account.
passages.common_interpretations_html: A common Christian reading holds together God's material provision, the opposition it provokes, and Isaac's willingness to keep moving rather than fight over each well. Wesley's notes on Genesis 26:12, 22, 24 emphasize seeking peace and taking courage from God's presence.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 11:9–10 places Isaac among heirs of the promise who live as strangers while looking toward God's lasting city. This story shows what that waiting can involve: receiving real provision without gaining an uncontested claim to everything around him. Blessing and opposition occur within the same life.

Isaac's restraint also belongs alongside the wider call to entrust conflict to God. Romans 12:17–21 calls believers to seek peace where possible and resist repaying evil with evil. 1 Peter 2:21–23 points to Christ, who did not retaliate but trusted the just Judge. Isaac's restraint reflects that wider call to seek peace and trust God when facing opposition.

passages.title: Genesis 26:26-33
passages.section_title: Isaac’s Covenant with Abimelech

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 26 Later, Abimelech came to Isaac from Gerar, with Ahuzzath his adviser and Phicol the commander of his army. 27 “Why have you come to me?” Isaac asked them. “You hated me and sent me away.” 28 “We can plainly see that the LORD has been with you,” they replied. “We recommend that there should now be an oath between us and you. Let us make a covenant with you 29 that you will not harm us, just as we have not harmed you but have done only good to you, sending you on your way in peace. And now you are blessed by the LORD.” 30 So Isaac prepared a feast for them, and they ate and drank. 31 And they got up early the next morning and swore an oath to each other. Then Isaac sent them on their way, and they left him in peace. 32 On that same day, Isaac’s servants came and told him about the well they had dug. “We have found water!” they told him. 33 So he called it Shibah, and to this day the name of the city is Beersheba.
paragraphs: 26 Later, Abimelech came to Isaac from Gerar, with Ahuzzath his adviser and Phicol the commander of his army.
27 “Why have you come to me?” Isaac asked them. “You hated me and sent me away.”

28 “We can plainly see that the LORD has been with you,” they replied. “We recommend that there should now be an oath between us and you. Let us make a covenant with you 29 that you will not harm us, just as we have not harmed you but have done only good to you, sending you on your way in peace. And now you are blessed by the LORD.”

30 So Isaac prepared a feast for them, and they ate and drank. 31 And they got up early the next morning and swore an oath to each other. Then Isaac sent them on their way, and they left him in peace.

32 On that same day, Isaac’s servants came and told him about the well they had dug. “We have found water!” they told him. 33 So he called it Shibah, and to this day the name of the city is Beersheba.

passages.context_html:
Abimelech arrives with his adviser and army commander to seek an agreement. Isaac asks why they have come after treating him with hostility and sending him away. Their answer is that they can plainly see the LORD has been with him, and they want an oath that he will not harm them.

Their description of having done Isaac only good sounds different from Isaac's memory of their treatment and the preceding disputes. The account preserves both voices. Isaac nevertheless prepares a feast, and the next morning they exchange oaths and part in peace.

That same day, Isaac's servants report finding water in the new well. He calls it Shibah, and the account connects the name Beersheba with this event. Chapter 21 has already associated Beersheba with Abraham's oath and well; Isaac's experience continues the family's history of worship, water, and peaceful agreements in that place.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as a settlement that allows Isaac and his neighbors to live in peace after conflict. Wesley's note on Genesis 26:28 emphasizes his willingness to move beyond the injuries he has received.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The neighbors' recognition of the LORD's presence gives Isaac's life a significance beyond his own household. God had promised blessing reaching the nations, and people outside the covenant family now acknowledge His care for Isaac. This agreement is not the full fulfillment of that worldwide promise, but it shows that His work in one family is visible to others.

Isaac responds to that recognition by making peace. Matthew 5:9 identifies peacemakers as people who will be called God's children, while Romans 12:18 calls believers to live at peace as far as it depends on them. The shared theme is a life shaped by God's care that makes room for peace with former opponents.

passages.title: Genesis 26:34-35
passages.section_title: Esau’s Wives

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 34 When Esau was forty years old, he took as his wives Judith daughter of Beeri the Hittite and Basemath daughter of Elon the Hittite. 35 And they brought grief to Isaac and Rebekah.
paragraphs: 34 When Esau was forty years old, he took as his wives Judith daughter of Beeri the Hittite and Basemath daughter of Elon the Hittite. 35 And they brought grief to Isaac and Rebekah.

passages.context_html:
At forty, Esau marries two Hittite women, Judith and Basemath. Genesis says that they bring grief to Isaac and Rebekah, without describing particular conversations or incidents. The short notice interrupts the account of Isaac's outward prosperity with trouble inside his family.

The marriages also prepare for what follows. Abraham had sought a wife for Isaac from his relatives rather than the Canaanites in chapter 24. Rebekah will raise her distress over the Hittite women again in Genesis 27:46, and Isaac will send Jacob away to find a wife among her family. Esau's marriages are therefore part of the setting for Jacob's departure.
passages.common_interpretations_html: A common Christian reading sees Esau's marriages as a source of family grief and a contrast with the concern to preserve the family's calling when choosing a spouse. Wesley's Genesis 26 overview and note on verse 34 make that connection.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Genesis 27:1-29
passages.section_title: Isaac Blesses Jacob

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 When Isaac was old and his eyes were so weak that he could no longer see, he called his older son Esau and said to him, “My son.” “Here I am,” Esau replied. 2 “Look,” said Isaac, “I am now old, and I do not know the day of my death. 3 Take your weapons—your quiver and bow—and go out into the field to hunt some game for me. 4 Then prepare a tasty dish that I love and bring it to me to eat, so that I may bless you before I die.” 5 Now Rebekah was listening to what Isaac told his son Esau. So when Esau went into the field to hunt game and bring it back, 6 Rebekah said to her son Jacob, “Behold, I overheard your father saying to your brother Esau, 7 ‘Bring me some game and prepare me a tasty dish to eat, so that I may bless you in the presence of the LORD before I die.’ 8 Now, my son, listen to my voice and do exactly as I tell you. 9 Go out to the flock and bring me two choice young goats, so that I can make them into a tasty dish for your father—the kind he loves. 10 Then take it to your father to eat, so that he may bless you before he dies.” 11 Jacob answered his mother Rebekah, “Look, my brother Esau is a hairy man, but I am smooth-skinned. 12 What if my father touches me? Then I would be revealed to him as a deceiver, and I would bring upon myself a curse rather than a blessing.” 13 His mother replied, “Your curse be on me, my son. Just obey my voice and go get them for me.” 14 So Jacob went and got two goats and brought them to his mother, who made the tasty food his father loved. 15 And Rebekah took the finest clothes in the house that belonged to her older son Esau, and she put them on her younger son Jacob. 16 She also put the skins of the young goats on his hands and on the smooth part of his neck. 17 Then she handed her son Jacob the tasty food and bread she had made. 18 So Jacob went to his father and said, “My father.” “Here I am!” he answered. “Which one are you, my son?” 19 Jacob said to his father, “I am Esau, your firstborn. I have done as you told me. Please sit up and eat some of my game, so that you may bless me.” 20 But Isaac asked his son, “How did you ever find it so quickly, my son?” “Because the LORD your God brought it to me,” he replied. 21 Then Isaac said to Jacob, “Please come closer so I can touch you, my son. Are you really my son Esau, or not?” 22 So Jacob came close to his father Isaac, who touched him and said, “The voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau.” 23 Isaac did not recognize him, because his hands were hairy like those of his brother Esau; so he blessed him. 24 Again he asked, “Are you really my son Esau?” And he replied, “I am.” 25 “Serve me,” said Isaac, “and let me eat some of my son’s game, so that I may bless you.” Jacob brought it to him, and he ate; then he brought him wine, and he drank. 26 Then his father Isaac said to him, “Please come near and kiss me, my son.” 27 So he came near and kissed him. When Isaac smelled his clothing, he blessed him and said: “Ah, the smell of my son is like the smell of a field that the LORD has blessed. 28 May God give to you the dew of heaven and the richness of the earth— an abundance of grain and new wine. 29 May peoples serve you and nations bow down to you. May you be the master of your brothers, and may the sons of your mother bow down to you. May those who curse you be cursed, and those who bless you be blessed.”

24 Again he asked, “Are you really my son Esau?”
And he replied, “I am.”

Jacob brought it to him, and he ate; then he brought him wine, and he drank.

is like the smell of a field

and the richness of the earth—
an abundance of grain and new wine.

and nations bow down to you.
May you be the master of your brothers,
and may the sons of your mother bow down to you.
May those who curse you be cursed,
and those who bless you be blessed.”

passages.context_html:
Isaac, now old and unable to see clearly, asks Esau to hunt and prepare a meal so that he may bless him before he dies. The family is already divided by the parents' preferences, Esau's sale of his birthright, and his marriages. God's earlier word to Rebekah said that the older son would serve the younger.

Rebekah overhears and prepares a competing plan. Jacob is to bring goats, take Esau's clothes, cover his smooth skin with the goatskins, and carry the prepared meal to Isaac. Jacob fears being exposed and cursed; Rebekah tells him to put that curse on her. Her assurance moves the plan forward, but the account does not say that she can actually remove his responsibility for participating.

Jacob directly claims to be Esau. When Isaac questions the speed of the meal's arrival, Jacob even credits the LORD with bringing it to him. Isaac recognizes Jacob's voice but is persuaded by the hairy hands, the food, the kiss, and Esau's clothing. His uncertainty creates the tension as the deception succeeds.

The blessing includes fruitful land, abundant crops, authority over relatives and peoples, and blessing or curse for those who bless or curse its recipient. That final wording recalls God's promise to Abraham in Genesis 12:3. Jacob receives the blessing, but the means used to obtain it leave the family facing discovery and conflict.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly see the promised line continuing through Jacob while also recognizing the wrongdoing in how the blessing is obtained. Wesley's notes on Genesis 27:6, 19–20 explicitly condemn Rebekah's method and Jacob's lies, including his use of God's name to support the deception; the promised outcome does not make those methods right.

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 11:20 describes Isaac blessing Jacob and Esau by faith concerning the future. Its emphasis is on the future God will bring, rather than approval of every choice made in this episode. Jacob receives the family blessing in keeping with the direction announced before his birth, despite the deeply flawed actions surrounding it.

The Bible repeatedly holds God's purpose and human responsibility together. Acts 2:23 does so most sharply when Peter speaks of Jesus being handed over according to God's plan while still holding His killers responsible. That larger theme also helps us read this family story. God can carry His purpose forward without making deceit or violence good.

passages.title: Genesis 27:30-46
passages.section_title: Esau’s Lost Hope

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 30 As soon as Isaac had finished blessing him and Jacob had left his father’s presence, his brother Esau returned from the hunt. 31 He too made some tasty food, brought it to his father, and said to him, “My father, sit up and eat of your son’s game, so that you may bless me.” 32 But his father Isaac replied, “Who are you?” “I am Esau, your firstborn son,” he answered. 33 Isaac began to tremble violently and said, “Who was it, then, who hunted the game and brought it to me? Before you came in, I ate it all and blessed him—and indeed, he will be blessed!” 34 When Esau heard his father’s words, he let out a loud and bitter cry and said to his father, “Bless me too, O my father!” 35 But Isaac replied, “Your brother came deceitfully and took your blessing.” 36 So Esau declared, “Is he not rightly named Jacob? For he has cheated me twice. He took my birthright, and now he has taken my blessing.” Then he asked, “Haven’t you saved a blessing for me?” 37 But Isaac answered Esau: “Look, I have made him your master and given him all his relatives as servants; I have sustained him with grain and new wine. What is left that I can do for you, my son?” 38 Esau said to his father, “Do you have only one blessing, my father? Bless me too, O my father!” Then Esau wept aloud. 39 His father Isaac answered him: “Behold, your dwelling place shall be away from the richness of the land, away from the dew of heaven above. 40 You shall live by the sword and serve your brother. But when you rebel, you will tear his yoke from your neck.” 41 Esau held a grudge against Jacob because of the blessing his father had given him. And Esau said in his heart, “The days of mourning for my father are at hand; then I will kill my brother Jacob.” 42 When the words of her older son Esau were relayed to Rebekah, she sent for her younger son Jacob and told him, “Look, your brother Esau is consoling himself by plotting to kill you. 43 So now, my son, obey my voice and flee at once to my brother Laban in Haran. 44 Stay with him for a while, until your brother’s fury subsides— 45 until your brother’s rage against you wanes and he forgets what you have done to him. Then I will send for you and bring you back from there. Why should I lose both of you in one day?” 46 Then Rebekah said to Isaac, “I am weary of my life because of these Hittite women. If Jacob takes a Hittite wife from among them, what good is my life?”

passages.context_html:
Esau returns almost as soon as Jacob leaves. Isaac realizes what has happened and trembles violently, yet confirms that the blessing already given will stand. Esau cries out for a blessing of his own and accuses Jacob of taking both his birthright and his blessing. His accusation recalls chapter 25, where the narrator said he had sold the birthright by oath.

Isaac describes what he has granted Jacob and gives Esau a very different prospect: a life away from the land's richness, living by the sword, serving his brother, and eventually breaking his yoke. The words anticipate a history reaching beyond the two men to their descendants, as the earlier announcement about two nations has already indicated.

Esau's grief turns to a murderous resolve against Jacob after Isaac's death. When the threat is reported to Rebekah, she urges Jacob to escape to her brother Laban in Haran until Esau's anger subsides. Her hope is that he can return once the danger has passed.

Rebekah then tells Isaac that she cannot bear the thought of Jacob marrying a Hittite woman like Esau's wives. That concern becomes the stated reason for sending him to her relatives in the next chapter. The immediate result of gaining the blessing is not a peaceful household, but fear, estrangement, and departure.
passages.common_interpretations_html: A common Christian reading sees lasting consequences from the family's choices: Isaac accepts the blessing's outcome, Esau cannot recover what he has lost, and Jacob must leave. Wesley's notes on Genesis 27:33, 45–46 connect the continuing promise with the personal affliction that follows the deception.

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 12:16–17 explicitly recalls Esau's sale and his later tears when seeking the blessing. The warning makes the loss more than an old family dispute: God's people must take seriously the privilege before them, rather than assume that a careless decision can always be reversed when its cost becomes clear.

Hebrews 11:20 also includes both sons when describing Isaac's blessing concerning the future. The promised story continues, but Genesis does not hide the hurt within that continuation. Its outcome gives no encouragement to secure a good end through deception or to answer injury with vengeance.

passages.title: Genesis 28:1-5
passages.section_title: Jacob’s Departure

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 So Isaac called for Jacob and blessed him. “Do not take a wife from the Canaanite women,” he commanded. 2 “Go at once to Paddan-aram, to the house of your mother’s father Bethuel, and take a wife from among the daughters of Laban, your mother’s brother. 3 May God Almighty bless you and make you fruitful and multiply you, so that you may become a company of peoples. 4 And may He give the blessing of Abraham to you and your descendants, so that you may possess the land where you dwell as a foreigner, the land God gave to Abraham.” 5 So Isaac sent Jacob to Paddan-aram, to Laban son of Bethuel the Aramean, the brother of Rebekah, who was the mother of Jacob and Esau.
paragraphs: 1 So Isaac called for Jacob and blessed him. “Do not take a wife from the Canaanite women,” he commanded. 2 “Go at once to Paddan-aram, to the house of your mother’s father Bethuel, and take a wife from among the daughters of Laban, your mother’s brother. 3 May God Almighty bless you and make you fruitful and multiply you, so that you may become a company of peoples. 4 And may He give the blessing of Abraham to you and your descendants, so that you may possess the land where you dwell as a foreigner, the land God gave to Abraham.”
5 So Isaac sent Jacob to Paddan-aram, to Laban son of Bethuel the Aramean, the brother of Rebekah, who was the mother of Jacob and Esau.

passages.context_html:
Isaac now knowingly calls Jacob, blesses him, and sends him to Rebekah's family to seek a wife. The circumstances are very different from the disguised visit in chapter 27. He tells Jacob not to marry a Canaanite woman, but to go to Laban's household in Paddan-aram.

The blessing explicitly names Abraham: fruitfulness, many descendants, and possession of the land in which the family still lives as foreigners. Jacob's departure is therefore not presented as disinheritance. He leaves home bearing the blessing, though the danger and separation caused by the family conflict remain real.

This journey also recalls the search for Isaac's wife in chapter 24. Then a servant went to the relatives and Isaac remained in the land; now Jacob himself must go. The recurring concern is the future of the promised family, while the different journeys show that the next generation's path will not simply repeat the last.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as Isaac openly confirming Jacob as the bearer of Abraham's blessing before sending him away to marry. Wesley's notes on Genesis 28:1, 3–4 emphasize that leaving the land for a time does not cancel the promised inheritance.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
The blessing carries the promise from Abraham through Isaac to Jacob. Hebrews 11:9, 13–16 names these heirs as people who live as strangers while looking toward what God will provide. A journey away from home does not, by itself, mean God has abandoned that future.

The larger promise will also reach beyond physical descent. Galatians 3:26–29 describes those who belong to Christ as Abraham's offspring and heirs according to the promise. Jacob's family remains an essential part of the story through which that blessing reaches others.

passages.title: Genesis 28:6-9
passages.section_title: Esau Marries Mahalath

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 Now Esau learned that Isaac had blessed Jacob and sent him to Paddan-aram to take a wife there, commanding him, “Do not marry a Canaanite woman,” 7 and that Jacob had obeyed his father and mother and gone to Paddan-aram. 8 And seeing that his father Isaac disapproved of the Canaanite women, 9 Esau went to Ishmael and married Mahalath, the sister of Nebaioth and daughter of Abraham’s son Ishmael, in addition to the wives he already had.
paragraphs: 6 Now Esau learned that Isaac had blessed Jacob and sent him to Paddan-aram to take a wife there, commanding him, “Do not marry a Canaanite woman,” 7 and that Jacob had obeyed his father and mother and gone to Paddan-aram.

8 And seeing that his father Isaac disapproved of the Canaanite women, 9 Esau went to Ishmael and married Mahalath, the sister of Nebaioth and daughter of Abraham’s son Ishmael, in addition to the wives he already had.

passages.context_html:
Esau watches Isaac bless Jacob and direct him to seek a wife away from the Canaanites. He also sees Jacob obey his parents and leave for Paddan-aram. The instructions make Isaac's disapproval of Esau's own marriages unmistakable to him.

Esau responds by marrying Mahalath, Ishmael's daughter and Nebaioth's sister. She belongs to Abraham's wider family, but he takes her in addition to the wives he already has. Genesis records the decision without telling us how his parents respond or whether this change resolves any of the existing grief.

The brief account keeps Esau's response in view before following Jacob on his journey. It shows an effort to respond to a recognized family concern, but does not describe a change in the LORD's earlier announcement about the brothers.
passages.common_interpretations_html: A common Christian reading sees Esau responding to his father's displeasure by seeking a wife within Abraham's wider family. Wesley's note on Genesis 28:6 treats Jacob's example as an influence on that decision, without making the new marriage a transfer of Jacob's blessing.

passages.title: Genesis 28:10-17
passages.section_title: Jacob’s Ladder

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 Meanwhile Jacob left Beersheba and set out for Haran. 11 On reaching a certain place, he spent the night there because the sun had set. And taking one of the stones from that place, he put it under his head and lay down to sleep. 12 And Jacob had a dream about a ladder that rested on the earth with its top reaching up to heaven, and God’s angels were going up and down the ladder. 13 And there at the top the LORD was standing and saying, “I am the LORD, the God of your father Abraham and the God of Isaac. I will give you and your descendants the land on which you now lie. 14 Your descendants will be like the dust of the earth, and you will spread out to the west and east and north and south. All the families of the earth will be blessed through you and your offspring. 15 Look, I am with you, and I will watch over you wherever you go, and I will bring you back to this land. For I will not leave you until I have done what I have promised you.” 16 When Jacob woke up, he said, “Surely the LORD is in this place, and I was unaware of it.” 17 And he was afraid and said, “How awesome is this place! This is none other than the house of God; this is the gate of heaven!”
paragraphs: 10 Meanwhile Jacob left Beersheba and set out for Haran. 11 On reaching a certain place, he spent the night there because the sun had set. And taking one of the stones from that place, he put it under his head and lay down to sleep.

12 And Jacob had a dream about a ladder that rested on the earth with its top reaching up to heaven, and God’s angels were going up and down the ladder. 13 And there at the top the LORD was standing and saying, “I am the LORD, the God of your father Abraham and the God of Isaac. I will give you and your descendants the land on which you now lie. 14 Your descendants will be like the dust of the earth, and you will spread out to the west and east and north and south. All the families of the earth will be blessed through you and your offspring. 15 Look, I am with you, and I will watch over you wherever you go, and I will bring you back to this land. For I will not leave you until I have done what I have promised you.”

16 When Jacob woke up, he said, “Surely the LORD is in this place, and I was unaware of it.” 17 And he was afraid and said, “How awesome is this place! This is none other than the house of God; this is the gate of heaven!”

passages.context_html:
Jacob leaves Beersheba for Haran and stops for the night when the sun sets. Away from home and with an uncertain future ahead, he lies down with a stone beneath his head. The account's focus then moves from his vulnerable circumstances to what God reveals while he sleeps.

In the dream, a ladder reaches from earth to heaven, with God's angels ascending and descending. The LORD identifies Himself as the God of Abraham and Isaac, promises Jacob the land and many descendants, and renews the blessing for all families through him and his offspring.

God also addresses the journey itself: He will be with Jacob, watch over him wherever he goes, and bring him back. Jacob is leaving the land, but he is not moving beyond God's presence or care. This assurance comes before Jacob makes any vow in response.

On waking, Jacob recognizes the LORD's presence and responds with awe. He calls the place God's house and heaven's gate. His surprise gives way to reverence: a place where he expected only a night's rest has become the place of a personal encounter with the God of his fathers.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the dream as assurance that God is with Jacob and that heaven is not closed to him. Wesley's notes on Genesis 28:12–17 explain God's care through the angels and also connect the vision with Christ as the way between God and humanity.

passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus takes up the vision's language in John 1:51, speaking of heaven opened and God's angels ascending and descending on the Son of Man. The movement Jacob saw between earth and heaven is now centered on Jesus. Jesus brings the image into His teaching about Himself, showing His central place in God's dealings with His people.

The promise to Jacob also looks outward to all families of the earth. Galatians 3:8–9 identifies the earlier promise of blessing through Abraham with the good news of Gentiles being brought into blessing through faith. Jacob receives a promise that protects him on a difficult journey while serving a purpose much larger than his personal safety.

passages.title: Genesis 28:18-22
passages.section_title: The Stone of Bethel

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 Early the next morning, Jacob took the stone that he had placed under his head, and he set it up as a pillar. He poured oil on top of it, 19 and he called that place Bethel, though previously the city had been named Luz. 20 Then Jacob made a vow, saying, “If God will be with me and watch over me on this journey, and if He will provide me with food to eat and clothes to wear, 21 so that I may return safely to my father’s house, then the LORD will be my God. 22 And this stone I have set up as a pillar will be God’s house, and of all that You give me I will surely give You a tenth.”
paragraphs: 18 Early the next morning, Jacob took the stone that he had placed under his head, and he set it up as a pillar. He poured oil on top of it, 19 and he called that place Bethel, though previously the city had been named Luz.

20 Then Jacob made a vow, saying, “If God will be with me and watch over me on this journey, and if He will provide me with food to eat and clothes to wear, 21 so that I may return safely to my father’s house, then the LORD will be my God. 22 And this stone I have set up as a pillar will be God’s house, and of all that You give me I will surely give You a tenth.”

passages.context_html:
Early the next morning, Jacob sets up the stone as a pillar and pours oil over it. He names the place Bethel, though the city had been called Luz. The name is בֵּית־אֵל, bêt-ʾēl (bayt-AYL), meaning house of God; Brown–Driver–Briggs connects it with this vision. The stone marks the place where God met him.

Jacob then makes a vow concerning God's presence, protection, food, clothing, and a safe return. He says the LORD will be his God, the stone will be God's house, and he will give a tenth of what God gives him. These are concrete promises made in response to a very concrete need for care on the road.

The order matters: God has already promised to be with Jacob and bring him back before Jacob offers anything. His vow therefore responds to an existing promise. The conditional wording also raises a question about his response: is he bargaining for protection, or pledging loyalty as he looks toward the promise being fulfilled?
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly see the pillar and vow as Jacob's response to God's appearance, but differ in how they hear his conditional words. Wesley's notes on Genesis 28:20–22 emphasize a commitment of loyalty and gratitude in response to God's promise.

The US Catholic bishops' Bible note on Genesis 28:20 gives more weight to the condition: Jacob vows to make the God who appeared to him his own if He brings him safely out and back. The two commentaries place different weight on the conditional wording of Jacob's vow.

passages.god_plan_html:
The story later returns to this promise in Genesis 35:1–7. God directs Jacob back to Bethel, and Jacob acknowledges that God answered him in his distress and remained with him wherever he went. What was promised at the beginning of a frightening journey becomes something he can recognize over time.

The wider biblical encouragement rests on that faithfulness. Hebrews 13:5–6 joins contentment and courage with God's promise not to leave or forsake His people. It does not turn Jacob's tenth into a payment for protection. The lasting theme is learning to trust the God who remains with His people through the journey.

passages.title: Genesis 29:1-13
passages.section_title: Jacob Meets Rachel

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Jacob resumed his journey and came to the land of the people of the east. 2 He looked and saw a well in the field, and near it lay three flocks of sheep, because the sheep were watered from this well. And a large stone covered the mouth of the well. 3 When all the flocks had been gathered there, the shepherds would roll away the stone from the mouth of the well and water the sheep. Then they would return the stone to its place over the mouth of the well. 4 “My brothers,” Jacob asked the shepherds, “where are you from?” “We are from Haran,” they answered. 5 “Do you know Laban the grandson of Nahor?” Jacob asked. “We know him,” they replied. 6 “Is he well?” Jacob inquired. “Yes,” they answered, “and here comes his daughter Rachel with his sheep.” 7 “Look,” said Jacob, “it is still broad daylight; it is not yet time to gather the livestock. Water the sheep and take them back to pasture.” 8 But they replied, “We cannot, until all the flocks have been gathered and the stone has been rolled away from the mouth of the well. Then we will water the sheep.” 9 While he was still speaking with them, Rachel arrived with her father’s sheep, for she was a shepherdess. 10 As soon as Jacob saw Rachel, the daughter of his mother’s brother Laban, with Laban’s sheep, he went up and rolled the stone away from the mouth of the well and watered his uncle’s sheep. 11 Then Jacob kissed Rachel and wept aloud. 12 He told Rachel that he was Rebekah’s son, a relative of her father, and she ran and told her father. 13 When Laban heard the news about his sister’s son Jacob, he ran out to meet him. He embraced him and kissed him and brought him to his home, where Jacob told him all that had happened.

And a large stone covered the mouth of the well. 3 When all the flocks had been gathered there, the shepherds would roll away the stone from the mouth of the well and water the sheep. Then they would return the stone to its place over the mouth of the well.
4 “My brothers,” Jacob asked the shepherds, “where are you from?”
“We are from Haran,” they answered.
5 “Do you know Laban the grandson of Nahor?” Jacob asked.
“We know him,” they replied.
6 “Is he well?” Jacob inquired.
“Yes,” they answered, “and here comes his daughter Rachel with his sheep.”
7 “Look,” said Jacob, “it is still broad daylight; it is not yet time to gather the livestock. Water the sheep and take them back to pasture.”
8 But they replied, “We cannot, until all the flocks have been gathered and the stone has been rolled away from the mouth of the well. Then we will water the sheep.”

9 While he was still speaking with them, Rachel arrived with her father’s sheep, for she was a shepherdess. 10 As soon as Jacob saw Rachel, the daughter of his mother’s brother Laban, with Laban’s sheep, he went up and rolled the stone away from the mouth of the well and watered his uncle’s sheep. 11 Then Jacob kissed Rachel and wept aloud. 12 He told Rachel that he was Rebekah’s son, a relative of her father, and she ran and told her father.
13 When Laban heard the news about his sister’s son Jacob, he ran out to meet him. He embraced him and kissed him and brought him to his home, where Jacob told him all that had happened.

passages.context_html:
After God's promise at Bethel, Jacob continues toward Haran and comes to a well where shepherds have gathered their flocks. He asks about Laban and learns that they know him. At that moment Rachel, Laban's daughter, approaches with her father's sheep.

Jacob questions why the sheep have been gathered while there is still time to pasture them. The shepherds explain that they wait until all the flocks arrive before the stone is rolled from the well. When Rachel comes, Jacob moves the stone himself and waters her father's sheep. The account shows his readiness to help, without explaining every reason for the shepherds' arrangement.

Jacob kisses Rachel, weeps, and identifies himself as Rebekah's son. Rachel runs home with the news, and Laban welcomes his sister's son with an embrace and brings him into the household. The scene recalls the servant's arrival at a well when seeking a wife for Isaac in chapter 24. Jacob has reached his relatives, but the welcome is only the beginning of a much longer stay.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly see God's care in Jacob reaching his relatives and being welcomed after his journey. Wesley's notes on Genesis 29:2, 9 connect the meeting with the assurance given at Bethel, while recognizing the resemblance to the earlier search for Rebekah.

passages.title: Genesis 29:14-30
passages.section_title: Jacob Marries Leah and Rachel

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 Then Laban declared, “You are indeed my own flesh and blood.” After Jacob had stayed with him a month, 15 Laban said to him, “Just because you are my relative, should you work for nothing? Tell me what your wages should be.” 16 Now Laban had two daughters; the older was named Leah, and the younger was named Rachel. 17 Leah had weak eyes, but Rachel was shapely and beautiful. 18 Since Jacob loved Rachel, he answered, “I will serve you seven years for your younger daughter Rachel.” 19 Laban replied, “Better that I give her to you than to another. Stay here with me.” 20 So Jacob served seven years for Rachel, yet it seemed but a few days because of his love for her. 21 Finally Jacob said to Laban, “Grant me my wife, for my time is complete, and I want to sleep with her.” 22 So Laban invited all the men of that place and prepared a feast. 23 But when evening came, Laban took his daughter Leah and gave her to Jacob, and he slept with her. 24 And Laban gave his servant girl Zilpah to his daughter Leah as her maidservant. 25 When morning came, there was Leah! “What have you done to me?” Jacob said to Laban. “Wasn’t it for Rachel that I served you? Why have you deceived me?” 26 Laban replied, “It is not our custom here to give the younger daughter in marriage before the older. 27 Finish this week’s celebration, and we will give you the younger one in return for another seven years of work.” 28 And Jacob did just that. He finished the week’s celebration, and Laban gave him his daughter Rachel as his wife. 29 Laban also gave his servant girl Bilhah to his daughter Rachel as her maidservant. 30 Jacob slept with Rachel as well, and indeed, he loved Rachel more than Leah. So he worked for Laban another seven years.

30 Jacob slept with Rachel as well, and indeed, he loved Rachel more than Leah. So he worked for Laban another seven years.

passages.context_html:
After Jacob has stayed a month, Laban asks what wages he should receive for his work. Jacob loves Rachel, the younger daughter, and offers seven years of service for her. His love makes the years seem short, and when the agreed time is complete he asks to marry her.

Laban prepares a feast but brings Leah to Jacob that evening. In the morning Jacob discovers the substitution and confronts him. Laban appeals to a local custom of marrying the older daughter first—an explanation he had not included when agreeing to Jacob's service for Rachel.

Laban offers Rachel as well after Leah's wedding week, in return for another seven years of work. Jacob agrees, completes the week, and marries Rachel before beginning the further service. He does not wait another seven years to receive her. Zilpah is given to Leah as a maidservant, and Bilhah to Rachel; both women will become important in the family story.

The closing statement exposes the coming difficulty: Jacob loves Rachel more than Leah. The man who deceived his father by taking his brother's place has now been deceived through the substitution of an older sister for a younger one. Leah enters a marriage in which she is not the woman her husband wanted, and that unequal affection will shape the household.
passages.common_interpretations_html: A common Christian reading notices the reversal: Jacob, who deceived Isaac, now experiences another person's deception himself. Wesley's notes on Genesis 29:25–27 see a lesson in this while still treating Laban's conduct as wrong and the resulting multiple marriages as a source of trouble.

passages.god_plan_html:
Jacob's experience belongs alongside the Bible's larger teaching that God can train His people through painful circumstances. Hebrews 12:5–11 describes the Father's discipline as serving His children's good and growth in holiness. It does not explicitly identify this wedding as such a lesson, but the reversal invites Jacob—and the reader—to confront what deception does to another person.

The following account also directs attention to God's care for the unloved Leah. Her pain matters in its own right, alongside what Jacob may learn from his experience. God's work in a flawed household includes seeing the person whose pain other people have created.

passages.title: Genesis 29:31-35
passages.section_title: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 31 When the LORD saw that Leah was unloved, He opened her womb; but Rachel was barren. 32 And Leah conceived and gave birth to a son, and she named him Reuben, for she said, “The LORD has seen my affliction. Surely my husband will love me now.” 33 Again she conceived and gave birth to a son, and she said, “Because the LORD has heard that I am unloved, He has given me this son as well.” So she named him Simeon. 34 Once again Leah conceived and gave birth to a son, and she said, “Now at last my husband will become attached to me, because I have borne him three sons.” So he was named Levi. 35 And once more she conceived and gave birth to a son and said, “This time I will praise the LORD.” So she named him Judah. Then Leah stopped having children.
paragraphs: 31 When the LORD saw that Leah was unloved, He opened her womb; but Rachel was barren. 32 And Leah conceived and gave birth to a son, and she named him Reuben, for she said, “The LORD has seen my affliction. Surely my husband will love me now.”
33 Again she conceived and gave birth to a son, and she said, “Because the LORD has heard that I am unloved, He has given me this son as well.” So she named him Simeon.
34 Once again Leah conceived and gave birth to a son, and she said, “Now at last my husband will become attached to me, because I have borne him three sons.” So he was named Levi.
35 And once more she conceived and gave birth to a son and said, “This time I will praise the LORD.” So she named him Judah. Then Leah stopped having children.

passages.context_html:
The LORD sees that Leah is unloved and enables her to have children, while Rachel remains unable to conceive. The account begins with God's notice of Leah's distress, rather than with the sisters' competition. Her place in the household has not made her invisible to Him.

The sons' names give voice to her experience. With Reuben she speaks of the LORD seeing her affliction and hopes Jacob will love her. With Simeon she acknowledges that God has heard she is unloved. With Levi she hopes her husband will become attached to her after the birth of a third son.

At Judah's birth her words turn to praising the LORD. The name is יְהוּדָה, Yĕhûdâ (yeh-hoo-DAH); Brown–Driver–Briggs notes the account's connection with Leah's words of praise. The sequence joins her longing for her husband's affection with recognition of God's attention and generosity. It does not say that every hurt in the marriage has now been resolved.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these births as God's care for Leah in her distress, while the names reveal both her longing for love and her gratitude. Wesley's notes on Genesis 29:31–35 emphasize God's comfort for the less-loved wife and the turn toward praise.

passages.god_plan_html:
Two of these sons become especially important in the Bible's account of worship and salvation. Levi's descendants serve in Israel's priesthood, while Jesus comes from Judah's line. Hebrews 7:11–14 explicitly distinguishes the older Levitical priesthood from the priesthood of the Lord who descended from Judah.

Leah cannot yet see that future in the children she holds. Yet the woman who longs to be valued in her own home becomes an ancestor within the history leading to Christ. God's care in her present pain and His purpose extending across generations belong together; the family's preference for Rachel does not determine whose life matters to Him.

passages.title: Genesis 30:1-8
passages.section_title: Dan and Naphtali

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 When Rachel saw that she was not bearing any children for Jacob, she envied her sister. “Give me children, or I will die!” she said to Jacob. 2 Jacob became angry with Rachel and said, “Am I in the place of God, who has withheld children from you?” 3 Then she said, “Here is my maidservant Bilhah. Sleep with her, that she may bear children for me, so that through her I too can build a family.” 4 So Rachel gave Jacob her servant Bilhah as a wife, and he slept with her, 5 and Bilhah conceived and bore him a son. 6 Then Rachel said, “God has vindicated me; He has heard my plea and given me a son.” So she named him Dan. 7 And Rachel’s servant Bilhah conceived again and bore Jacob a second son. 8 Then Rachel said, “In my great struggles, I have wrestled with my sister and won.” So she named him Naphtali.
paragraphs: 1 When Rachel saw that she was not bearing any children for Jacob, she envied her sister. “Give me children, or I will die!” she said to Jacob.
2 Jacob became angry with Rachel and said, “Am I in the place of God, who has withheld children from you?”
3 Then she said, “Here is my maidservant Bilhah. Sleep with her, that she may bear children for me, so that through her I too can build a family.”

4 So Rachel gave Jacob her servant Bilhah as a wife, and he slept with her, 5 and Bilhah conceived and bore him a son. 6 Then Rachel said, “God has vindicated me; He has heard my plea and given me a son.” So she named him Dan.
7 And Rachel’s servant Bilhah conceived again and bore Jacob a second son. 8 Then Rachel said, “In my great struggles, I have wrestled with my sister and won.” So she named him Naphtali.

passages.context_html:
Rachel sees Leah bearing children and becomes envious. Her demand that Jacob give her children provokes his anger, and he replies that he cannot take God's place. The scene shows how the sisters' unequal circumstances have become a painful conflict within the marriage.

Rachel gives Bilhah, her maidservant, to Jacob as a wife so that she can build a family through her. Bilhah bears two sons, but the account records Rachel naming them and explaining what they mean to her. Bilhah's own thoughts are not reported.

With Dan, Rachel says God has vindicated her and heard her plea. With Naphtali, she speaks of wrestling with her sister and winning. Her explanations show how strongly the rivalry shapes her response to the births. The narrator records what she believes God has done without declaring that God endorses her competition with Leah.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read the scene as showing the harm envy brings into the household and the attempt to secure children through a servant, recalling Sarah and Hagar. Wesley's notes on Genesis 30:1–3 emphasize the rivalry expressed in Rachel's words and naming of the sons.

passages.title: Genesis 30:9-16
passages.section_title: Gad and Asher

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 When Leah saw that she had stopped having children, she gave her servant Zilpah to Jacob as a wife. 10 And Leah’s servant Zilpah bore Jacob a son. 11 Then Leah said, “How fortunate!” So she named him Gad. 12 When Leah’s servant Zilpah bore Jacob a second son, 13 Leah said, “How happy I am! For the women call me happy.” So she named him Asher. 14 Now during the wheat harvest, Reuben went out and found some mandrakes in the field. When he brought them to his mother, Rachel begged Leah, “Please give me some of your son’s mandrakes.” 15 But Leah replied, “Is it not enough that you have taken away my husband? Now you want to take my son’s mandrakes as well?” “Very well,” said Rachel, “he may sleep with you tonight in exchange for your son’s mandrakes.” 16 When Jacob came in from the field that evening, Leah went out to meet him and said, “You must come with me, for I have hired you with my son’s mandrakes.” So he slept with her that night.
paragraphs: 9 When Leah saw that she had stopped having children, she gave her servant Zilpah to Jacob as a wife. 10 And Leah’s servant Zilpah bore Jacob a son. 11 Then Leah said, “How fortunate!” So she named him Gad.
12 When Leah’s servant Zilpah bore Jacob a second son, 13 Leah said, “How happy I am! For the women call me happy.” So she named him Asher.
14 Now during the wheat harvest, Reuben went out and found some mandrakes in the field. When he brought them to his mother, Rachel begged Leah, “Please give me some of your son’s mandrakes.”
15 But Leah replied, “Is it not enough that you have taken away my husband? Now you want to take my son’s mandrakes as well?”
“Very well,” said Rachel, “he may sleep with you tonight in exchange for your son’s mandrakes.”
16 When Jacob came in from the field that evening, Leah went out to meet him and said, “You must come with me, for I have hired you with my son’s mandrakes.” So he slept with her that night.

passages.context_html:
When Leah stops having children, she gives her maidservant Zilpah to Jacob as a wife. Zilpah bears Gad and Asher. Leah's words at their births express good fortune and happiness, while the growing family remains divided by the sisters' competing hopes.

The scene then moves to the wheat harvest. Reuben finds mandrakes and brings them to Leah, and Rachel asks for some. Leah answers with her deeper grievance: Rachel already has the husband whose affection she wants. Their dispute is about much more than plants.

Rachel offers Leah a night with Jacob in exchange for the mandrakes. Leah meets him when he returns from the field and tells him of the arrangement, and he spends the night with her. The next passage expressly credits God with hearing Leah and enabling her to conceive. This exchange does not establish that the plants themselves cause a pregnancy.
passages.common_interpretations_html: A common Christian reading sees rivalry spreading as Leah follows Rachel's example and the sisters bargain over Jacob's company. Wesley's notes on Genesis 30:9, 14 emphasize the damage of that competition, without treating the bargain as a healthy pattern for marriage.

passages.title: Genesis 30:17-21
passages.section_title: Issachar, Zebulun, and Dinah

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 And God listened to Leah, and she conceived and bore a fifth son to Jacob. 18 Then Leah said, “God has rewarded me for giving my maidservant to my husband.” So she named him Issachar. 19 Again Leah conceived and bore a sixth son to Jacob. 20 “God has given me a good gift,” she said. “This time my husband will honor me, because I have borne him six sons.” And she named him Zebulun. 21 After that, Leah gave birth to a daughter and named her Dinah.
paragraphs: 17 And God listened to Leah, and she conceived and bore a fifth son to Jacob. 18 Then Leah said, “God has rewarded me for giving my maidservant to my husband.” So she named him Issachar.
19 Again Leah conceived and bore a sixth son to Jacob. 20 “God has given me a good gift,” she said. “This time my husband will honor me, because I have borne him six sons.” And she named him Zebulun.
21 After that, Leah gave birth to a daughter and named her Dinah.

passages.context_html:
The account says God listens to Leah, and she bears Issachar. She interprets the birth as a reward for giving her maidservant to Jacob. Her own explanation is recorded, but the narrator's emphasis is that God has heard her; it is not a general promise that repeating her arrangement earns a child.

Leah then bears Zebulun and speaks of God's good gift. Even after six sons, she still hopes that her husband will honor her. Gratitude and an unmet longing for respect remain side by side. The births have not simply cured the family's divided affection.

Dinah's birth is noted briefly after the sons. The account does not give a naming explanation for her here, but she will become central in chapter 34. These few verses therefore carry the family story forward while allowing us to hear how Leah understands her life within it.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly see God's care continuing toward Leah, with her words revealing both gratitude and her wish for her husband's regard. Wesley's note on Genesis 30:17 also distinguishes the gift of a son from Leah's conclusion that God is rewarding the earlier arrangement with her maidservant.

passages.god_plan_html:
Zebulun's name will later belong to a tribe and its territory, reaching far beyond the circumstances of his birth. Matthew 4:13–17 places Jesus' ministry in the region of Zebulun and Naphtali and connects it with Isaiah's promise of light dawning on people in darkness.

Matthew is explaining Isaiah's prophecy rather than interpreting Leah's naming of her child. Even so, the later passage lets us follow the family story into God's wider purpose: names first heard amid the troubles of Jacob's household become names associated with the announcement of God's kingdom and the coming of its light.

passages.title: Genesis 30:22-24
passages.section_title: Joseph

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 Then God remembered Rachel. He listened to her and opened her womb, 23 and she conceived and gave birth to a son. “God has taken away my shame,” she said. 24 She named him Joseph, and said, “May the LORD add to me another son.”
paragraphs: 22 Then God remembered Rachel. He listened to her and opened her womb, 23 and she conceived and gave birth to a son. “God has taken away my shame,” she said. 24 She named him Joseph, and said, “May the LORD add to me another son.”

passages.context_html:
God now remembers Rachel, listens to her, and enables her to conceive. Remembering here leads to action on her behalf; it does not mean God had lost track of her while Leah bore children. After the rivalry and the mandrake bargain, the account clearly credits Him with this birth.

Rachel gives birth to Joseph and says that God has taken away her shame. She then asks that the LORD add another son. The explanation of Joseph's name joins gratitude for what she has received with hope for another child. Her words allow us to hear the relief after her earlier distress.

Joseph's birth also marks a transition. Immediately afterward, Jacob asks Laban to let him return to his own homeland. This child will later become central both to the family's conflict and to its survival, though none of that future is explained to Rachel in this scene.
passages.common_interpretations_html: A common Christian reading emphasizes God's answer after Rachel's long distress, together with her gratitude and continuing hope. Wesley's note on Genesis 30:22 connects the name's wordplay with both the removal of shame and the request that God add another son.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Joseph will later tell his brothers that the harm they intended against him became, through God's purpose, a means of preserving many lives (Genesis 50:19–21). His birth is the beginning of a life through which the promised family will be sustained during famine.

Acts 7:9–16 retells that later history: the brothers are jealous of Joseph, but God is with him, and food in Egypt becomes the means of bringing the family there. Rachel's relief is therefore part of a much larger story of God's care. The narrative will again show His purpose advancing through circumstances the family could not have planned or understood at the time.

passages.title: Genesis 30:25-43
passages.section_title: Jacob Prospers

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 25 Now after Rachel had given birth to Joseph, Jacob said to Laban, “Send me on my way so I can return to my homeland. 26 Give me my wives and children for whom I have served you, that I may go on my way. You know how hard I have worked for you.” 27 But Laban replied, “If I have found favor in your eyes, please stay. I have learned by divination that the LORD has blessed me because of you.” 28 And he added, “Name your wages, and I will pay them.” 29 Then Jacob answered, “You know how I have served you and how your livestock have thrived under my care. 30 Indeed, you had very little before my arrival, but now your wealth has increased many times over. The LORD has blessed you wherever I set foot. But now, when may I also provide for my own household?” 31 “What can I give you?” Laban asked. “You do not need to give me anything,” Jacob replied. “If you do this one thing for me, I will keep on shepherding and keeping your flocks. 32 Let me go through all your flocks today and remove from them every speckled or spotted sheep, every dark-colored lamb, and every spotted or speckled goat. These will be my wages. 33 So my honesty will testify for me when you come to check on my wages in the future. If I have any goats that are not speckled or spotted, or any lambs that are not dark-colored, they will be considered stolen.” 34 “Agreed,” said Laban. “Let it be as you have said.” 35 That very day Laban removed all the streaked or spotted male goats and every speckled or spotted female goat—every one that had any white on it—and every dark-colored lamb, and he placed them under the care of his sons. 36 Then he put a three-day journey between himself and Jacob, while Jacob was shepherding the rest of Laban’s flocks. 37 Jacob, however, took fresh branches of poplar, almond, and plane trees, and peeled the bark, exposing the white inner wood of the branches. 38 Then he set the peeled branches in the watering troughs in front of the flocks coming in to drink. So when the flocks were in heat and came to drink, 39 they mated in front of the branches. And they bore young that were streaked or speckled or spotted. 40 Jacob set apart the young, but made the rest face the streaked dark-colored sheep in Laban’s flocks. Then he set his own stock apart and did not put them with Laban’s animals. 41 Whenever the stronger females of the flock were in heat, Jacob would place the branches in the troughs, in full view of the animals, so that they would breed in front of the branches. 42 But if the animals were weak, he did not set out the branches. So the weaker animals went to Laban and the stronger ones to Jacob. 43 Thus Jacob became exceedingly prosperous. He owned large flocks, maidservants and menservants, and camels and donkeys.

passages.context_html:
After Joseph's birth, Jacob asks to return home with his wives and children. Laban wants him to remain because he recognizes that the LORD has blessed him through Jacob. Jacob also acknowledges that blessing, but asks when he can provide for his own household rather than only increasing Laban's wealth.

They agree that Jacob's wages will be identifiable animals within the flock: the specified spotted, speckled, and dark-colored ones. Laban then removes the existing animals of those kinds, entrusts them to his sons, and places three days' distance between them and the flock Jacob tends. That leaves Jacob with a difficult starting point for building his own stock.

Jacob places peeled branches at the watering troughs, separates animals, and gives particular attention to breeding the stronger ones. Over time, the stronger animals become his and the weaker ones Laban's, and Jacob grows prosperous. The account describes what Jacob does without giving a modern biological explanation of the branches.

The following chapter supplies an essential part of the explanation. Jacob tells his wives that God has seen Laban's treatment of him, has prevented harm, and has brought about the increase despite changes to the wages. His work belongs within an account that credits God's care, rather than making the branches a technique that guarantees prosperity to anyone who copies it.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readers commonly connect Jacob's increase with God's promised care and the fuller explanation in Genesis 31. They have explained the branches differently: Wesley's note on Genesis 30:37 describes the older idea that what the animals saw could affect their young.

The US Catholic bishops' note on Genesis 30:32 treats that visual-impression idea as a folk belief and also notes controlled breeding and God's role. These are explanations of the account, not an established scientific mechanism supplied by Genesis.
