passages.god_plan_html:
God's attention to a worker's treatment becomes explicit in the next chapter, when Jacob says the LORD has seen his affliction and labor. James 5:4 carries that concern into the life of God's people by warning that withheld wages cry out to the Lord. The wider theme is that exploitation is not hidden from Him, even when an employer holds greater power.

At the same time, Jacob's prosperity is a particular part of this family's story, not a promise that faithful work always makes someone rich. 1 Timothy 6:6–10 calls believers to contentment and warns of the dangers of making wealth their aim. God's care and the pursuit of ever-greater wealth must not be confused.

passages.title: Genesis 31:1-21
passages.section_title: Jacob Flees from Laban

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now Jacob heard that Laban’s sons were saying, “Jacob has taken away all that belonged to our father and built all this wealth at our father’s expense.” 2 And Jacob saw from the countenance of Laban that his attitude toward him had changed. 3 Then the LORD said to Jacob, “Go back to the land of your fathers and to your kindred, and I will be with you.” 4 So Jacob sent word and called Rachel and Leah to the field where his flocks were, 5 and he told them, “I can see from your father’s countenance that his attitude toward me has changed; but the God of my father has been with me. 6 You know that I have served your father with all my strength. 7 And although he has cheated me and changed my wages ten times, God has not allowed him to harm me. 8 If he said, ‘The speckled will be your wages,’ then the whole flock bore speckled offspring. If he said, ‘The streaked will be your wages,’ then the whole flock bore streaked offspring. 9 Thus God has taken away your father’s livestock and given them to me. 10 When the flocks were breeding, I saw in a dream that the streaked, spotted, and speckled males were mating with the females. 11 In that dream the angel of God said to me, ‘Jacob!’ And I replied, ‘Here I am.’ 12 ‘Look up,’ he said, ‘and see that all the males that are mating with the flock are streaked, spotted, or speckled; for I have seen all that Laban has done to you. 13 I am the God of Bethel, where you anointed the pillar and made a solemn vow to Me. Now get up, leave this land at once, and return to your native land.’” 14 And Rachel and Leah replied, “Do we have any portion or inheritance left in our father’s house? 15 Are we not regarded by him as outsiders? Not only has he sold us, but he has certainly squandered what was paid for us. 16 Surely all the wealth that God has taken away from our father belongs to us and to our children. So do whatever God has told you.” 17 Then Jacob got up and put his children and his wives on camels, 18 and he drove all his livestock before him, along with all the possessions he had acquired in Paddan-aram, to go to his father Isaac in the land in Canaan. 19 Now while Laban was out shearing his sheep, Rachel stole her father’s household idols. 20 Moreover, Jacob deceived Laban the Aramean by not telling him that he was running away. 21 So he fled with all his possessions, crossed the Euphrates, and headed for the hill country of Gilead.

passages.context_html:
Laban's sons accuse Jacob of gaining wealth at their father's expense, and Laban's attitude toward him changes. The LORD tells Jacob to return to his own land and relatives, renewing the promise to be with him. Jacob calls Rachel and Leah into the field to explain the situation and the direction he has received.

He recounts his hard work, Laban's changing wages, and God's protection. In his account of the dream, the angel of God identifies Himself as the God of Bethel, reminds Jacob of the pillar and vow, and tells him to return. The command joins the present move with the promise at the beginning of his journey.

Rachel and Leah agree. They describe their father's treatment of them as that of outsiders and say that what God has given Jacob belongs to them and their children. They tell him to do what God has directed. Jacob then gathers the family, livestock, and possessions and leaves while Laban is away shearing sheep.

Rachel secretly takes her father's household idols. The Hebrew word is תְּרָפִים, tĕrāp̄îm (teh-rah-FEEM); Brown–Driver–Briggs describes these as objects of reverence associated with divination, noting the portable figures here. Jacob does not know she has taken them. He also conceals the departure from Laban, creating the setting for pursuit and confrontation.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read the return as obedience to God's direction amid growing hostility from Laban's household. Wesley's notes on Genesis 31:3, 19 distinguish Jacob's departure, which he regards as a prudent escape from danger, from Rachel's theft of the idols.

passages.god_plan_html:
The return begins with God's promise at Bethel: He would remain with Jacob and bring him back. Now the God who has seen his treatment directs him to leave. The account shows faithfulness expressed through protection, provision, and a call to move when the time has come.

A later, larger departure will carry this same theme. In Exodus 3:7–10, God sees His people's affliction, hears their cries, and acts to bring them out toward the promised land. Jacob's departure is not a detailed prediction of every event in the Exodus, but both accounts reveal the God who sees oppression and keeps His promise to His people.

passages.title: Genesis 31:22-42
passages.section_title: Laban Pursues Jacob

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 On the third day Laban was informed that Jacob had fled. 23 So he took his relatives with him, pursued Jacob for seven days, and overtook him in the hill country of Gilead. 24 But that night God came to Laban the Aramean in a dream and warned him, “Be careful not to say anything to Jacob, either good or bad.” 25 Now Jacob had pitched his tent in the hill country of Gilead when Laban overtook him, and Laban and his relatives camped there as well. 26 Then Laban said to Jacob, “What have you done? You have deceived me and carried off my daughters like captives of war! 27 Why did you run away secretly and deceive me, without even telling me? I would have sent you away with joy and singing, with tambourines and harps. 28 But you did not even let me kiss my grandchildren and my daughters goodbye. Now you have done a foolish thing. 29 I have power to do you great harm, but last night the God of your father said to me, ‘Be careful not to say anything to Jacob, either good or bad.’ 30 Now you have gone off because you long for your father’s house. Have you found anything that belongs to you? Put it here before my brothers and yours, that they may judge between the two of us. 38 I have been with you for twenty years now. But God has seen my affliction and the toil of my hands, and last night He rendered judgment.”

passages.context_html:
Laban learns of the departure on the third day and pursues Jacob until he overtakes him in Gilead. Before the confrontation, God warns Laban in a dream not to speak to Jacob either good or bad. Laban himself later acknowledges that warning as a limit on his power to harm him.

Laban accuses Jacob of carrying off his daughters and depriving him of a farewell, then asks why his gods have been stolen. Jacob explains his fear that Laban would take the daughters back by force. Not knowing about Rachel's theft, he offers a search and declares that anyone found with the idols must not live.

Rachel has hidden them in a camel's saddlebag and sits on them. She tells her father she cannot stand because she is having her period, and the search fails. The reader knows what Jacob does not: the missing objects really are in his camp. His confidence that the search will establish complete innocence exceeds what he knows.

Jacob then confronts Laban about twenty years of service: fourteen for the daughters and six for the flocks. He describes losses he bore, exposure to heat and cold, lost sleep, and changed wages. His final explanation credits the God of Abraham and Isaac with seeing his affliction and preventing Laban from sending him away empty-handed.
passages.common_interpretations_html: A common Christian reading emphasizes God's restraint of Laban, the contrast between the living God and the helpless stolen idols, and Jacob's testimony about his hard service. Wesley's notes on Genesis 31:24, 29–31, 42 draw attention to God's protection while distinguishing Jacob's ignorance from Rachel's actions.

passages.god_plan_html:
The scene sharply contrasts the God who speaks and restrains harm with gods that must be searched for and carried away. Psalm 115:4–8 develops that contrast: manufactured idols cannot see, hear, speak, or act for those who trust them. Laban's search makes their helplessness visible within the story.

God's protection is also the continuation of His word to Jacob at Bethel. The family is still marked by fear, concealment, and unrecognized wrongdoing, yet God has not abandoned the promised return. The account holds His faithfulness and the family's failings together, without treating the successful escape as approval of the theft.

passages.title: Genesis 31:43-55
passages.section_title: Jacob’s Covenant with Laban

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 43 But Laban answered Jacob, “These daughters are my daughters, these sons are my sons, and these flocks are my flocks! Everything you see is mine! Yet what can I do today about these daughters of mine or the children they have borne? 44 Come now, let us make a covenant, you and I, and let it serve as a witness between you and me.” 45 So Jacob picked out a stone and set it up as a pillar, 46 and he said to his relatives, “Gather some stones.” So they took stones and made a mound, and there by the mound they ate. 47 Laban called it Jegar-sahadutha, and Jacob called it Galeed. 48 Then Laban declared, “This mound is a witness between you and me this day.” Therefore the place was called Galeed. 49 It was also called Mizpah, because Laban said, “May the LORD keep watch between you and me when we are absent from each other. 50 If you mistreat my daughters or take other wives, although no one is with us, remember that God is a witness between you and me.” 51 Laban also said to Jacob, “Here is the mound, and here is the pillar I have set up between you and me. 52 This mound is a witness, and this pillar is a witness, that I will not go past this mound to harm you, and you will not go past this mound and pillar to harm me. 53 May the God of Abraham and the God of Nahor, the God of their father, judge between us.” So Jacob swore by the Fear of his father Isaac. 54 Then Jacob offered a sacrifice on the mountain and invited his relatives to eat a meal. And after they had eaten, they spent the night on the mountain. 55 Early the next morning, Laban got up and kissed his grandchildren and daughters and blessed them. Then he left to return home.

48 Then Laban declared, “This mound is a witness between you and me this day.”

Therefore the place was called Galeed. 49 It was also called Mizpah, because Laban said, “May the LORD keep watch between you and me when we are absent from each other. 50 If you mistreat my daughters or take other wives, although no one is with us, remember that God is a witness between you and me.”

51 Laban also said to Jacob, “Here is the mound, and here is the pillar I have set up between you and me. 52 This mound is a witness, and this pillar is a witness, that I will not go past this mound to harm you, and you will not go past this mound and pillar to harm me. 53 May the God of Abraham and the God of Nahor, the God of their father, judge between us.”
So Jacob swore by the Fear of his father Isaac.

54 Then Jacob offered a sacrifice on the mountain and invited his relatives to eat a meal. And after they had eaten, they spent the night on the mountain. 55 Early the next morning, Laban got up and kissed his grandchildren and daughters and blessed them. Then he left to return home.

passages.context_html:
Laban begins by claiming the daughters, children, and flocks as his own, but the confrontation ends with an agreement to part. Jacob sets up a pillar, the relatives gather a mound of stones, and the two men name it as a witness to their covenant. The meal marks the agreement publicly.

Its terms address two concerns. Jacob must not mistreat Laban's daughters or take other wives, and neither man is to cross the boundary to harm the other. The restriction is against crossing for harm, rather than a statement that they may never travel across it for any reason.

The appeal for the LORD to watch between them belongs to that setting of accountability. Even when human witnesses are absent, God sees how they keep the agreement and how the daughters are treated. Jacob swears by the God his father Isaac fears, offers a sacrifice, and shares a meal with his relatives. The next morning Laban blesses his daughters and grandchildren and returns home.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a solemn settlement setting limits after a troubled relationship, with God invoked as witness and judge. Wesley's note on Genesis 31:44 explains the appeal to divine watching in terms of keeping the covenant, rather than simply as a warm farewell saying.

passages.god_plan_html:
The protection of Laban's daughters places marriage within the accountability of life before God. Malachi 2:14 likewise describes the LORD as witness between a husband and his wife and condemns breaking faith with her. An agreement is not only about what one person can enforce when present; it also concerns what God sees when others cannot.

That concern continues in 1 Peter 3:7, where husbands are told to treat their wives with consideration and honor as fellow heirs of life's gracious gift. The passage even connects such treatment with prayer. The wider biblical theme is that honoring God includes how people treat those within their own household.

passages.title: Genesis 32:1-21
passages.section_title: Jacob Prepares to Meet Esau

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Jacob also went on his way, and the angels of God met him. 2 When Jacob saw them, he said, “This is the camp of God.” So he named that place Mahanaim. 3 Jacob sent messengers ahead of him to his brother Esau in the land of Seir, the country of Edom. 4 He instructed them, “You are to say to my master Esau, ‘Your servant Jacob says: I have been staying with Laban and have remained there until now. 5 I have oxen, donkeys, flocks, menservants, and maidservants. I have sent this message to inform my master, so that I may find favor in your sight.’” 6 When the messengers returned to Jacob, they said, “We went to your brother Esau, and now he is coming to meet you—he and four hundred men with him.” 7 In great fear and distress, Jacob divided his people into two camps, as well as the flocks and herds and camels. 8 He thought, “If Esau comes and attacks one camp, then the other camp can escape.” 9 Then Jacob declared, “O God of my father Abraham, God of my father Isaac, the LORD who told me, ‘Go back to your country and to your kindred, and I will make you prosper,’ 10 I am unworthy of all the kindness and faithfulness You have shown Your servant. Indeed, with only my staff I came across the Jordan, but now I have become two camps. 11 Please deliver me from the hand of my brother Esau, for I am afraid that he may come and attack me and the mothers and children with me. 12 But You have said, ‘I will surely make you prosper, and I will make your offspring like the sand of the sea, too numerous to count.’” 13 Jacob spent the night there, and from what he had brought with him, he selected a gift for his brother Esau: 14 200 female goats, 20 male goats, 200 ewes, 20 rams, 15 30 milk camels with their young, 40 cows, 10 bulls, 20 female donkeys, and 10 male donkeys. 16 He entrusted them to his servants in separate herds and told them, “Go on ahead of me, and keep some distance between the herds.” 17 He instructed the one in the lead, “When my brother Esau meets you and asks, ‘To whom do you belong, where are you going, and whose animals are these before you?’ 18 then you are to say, ‘They belong to your servant Jacob. They are a gift, sent to my lord Esau. And behold, Jacob is behind us.’” 19 He also instructed the second, the third, and all those following behind the herds: “When you meet Esau, you are to say the same thing to him. 20 You are also to say, ‘Look, your servant Jacob is right behind us.’” For he thought, “I will appease Esau with the gift that is going before me. After that I can face him, and perhaps he will accept me.” 21 So Jacob’s gifts went on before him, while he spent the night in the camp.

passages.context_html:
As Jacob continues toward Canaan, God's angels meet him, and he names the place Mahanaim after recognizing God's camp. The encounter recalls the angels in his dream at Bethel when he was leaving the land. Now the assurance of God's presence accompanies his return.

Jacob sends messengers to Esau, using respectful language and asking for favor. They return with news that Esau is approaching with four hundred men. The report does not state Esau's intention, but Jacob remembers the earlier threat and is deeply afraid. He divides his people and animals so that one camp might escape if the other is attacked.

His prayer joins God's promise with an honest admission of fear. He recalls the command to return, acknowledges that he has not earned the kindness shown him, and asks for protection for himself, the mothers, and the children. The man who crossed the Jordan with a staff now has a large household whose future concerns him.

Jacob then sends substantial gifts of livestock ahead in separate groups, instructing the servants to identify them as presents for Esau. He hopes to soften his brother's anger before meeting him. Prayer and practical preparations stand together in the account as the encounter draws near.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read Jacob's prayer as humble dependence on God's promise in a frightening situation. Wesley's notes on Genesis 32:7, 9–13 also regard his efforts toward peace as compatible with trust, rather than assuming that taking practical steps necessarily cancels his prayer.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
Jacob appeals to the kindness God has already shown and the word He has already given. The promise has brought him this far, and he now brings his fear into that relationship. His prayer does not claim that his own worth entitles him to a safe outcome.

The New Testament's invitation in Hebrews 4:14–16 similarly joins acknowledged weakness with confidence in God's mercy. Through Jesus, believers can approach for grace and help in need. The shared theme is dependence on God's faithful care, with room to speak honestly about the danger rather than pretending not to be afraid.

passages.title: Genesis 32:22-32
passages.section_title: Jacob Wrestles with God

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 During the night Jacob got up and took his two wives, his two maidservants, and his eleven sons, and crossed the ford of the Jabbok. 23 He took them and sent them across the stream, along with all his possessions. 24 So Jacob was left all alone, and there a man wrestled with him until daybreak. 25 When the man saw that he could not overpower Jacob, he struck the socket of Jacob’s hip and dislocated it as they wrestled. 26 Then the man said, “Let me go, for it is daybreak.” But Jacob replied, “I will not let you go unless you bless me.” 27 “What is your name?” the man asked. “Jacob,” he replied. 28 Then the man said, “Your name will no longer be Jacob, but Israel, because you have struggled with God and with men, and you have prevailed.” 29 And Jacob requested, “Please tell me your name.” But he replied, “Why do you ask my name?” Then he blessed Jacob there. 30 So Jacob named the place Peniel, saying, “Indeed, I have seen God face to face, and yet my life was spared.” 31 The sun rose above him as he passed by Penuel, and he was limping because of his hip. 32 Therefore to this day the Israelites do not eat the tendon attached to the socket of the hip, because the socket of Jacob’s hip was struck near that tendon.
paragraphs: 22 During the night Jacob got up and took his two wives, his two maidservants, and his eleven sons, and crossed the ford of the Jabbok. 23 He took them and sent them across the stream, along with all his possessions.

24 So Jacob was left all alone, and there a man wrestled with him until daybreak. 25 When the man saw that he could not overpower Jacob, he struck the socket of Jacob’s hip and dislocated it as they wrestled. 26 Then the man said, “Let me go, for it is daybreak.” But Jacob replied, “I will not let you go unless you bless me.”
27 “What is your name?” the man asked. “Jacob,” he replied.
28 Then the man said, “Your name will no longer be Jacob, but Israel, because you have struggled with God and with men, and you have prevailed.”
29 And Jacob requested, “Please tell me your name.” But he replied, “Why do you ask my name?” Then he blessed Jacob there.
30 So Jacob named the place Peniel, saying, “Indeed, I have seen God face to face, and yet my life was spared.”

31 The sun rose above him as he passed by Penuel, and he was limping because of his hip. 32 Therefore to this day the Israelites do not eat the tendon attached to the socket of the hip, because the socket of Jacob’s hip was struck near that tendon.

passages.context_html:
During the night, Jacob sends his family and possessions across the Jabbok and is left alone. A man wrestles with him until daybreak. The account introduces the struggle abruptly and lets its meaning become clearer through the encounter, rather than explaining the man's identity at the outset.

Jacob's hip is dislocated, yet he holds on and asks for a blessing. He receives the name Israel, with the explanation that he has struggled with God and with men and prevailed. The blessing comes with an injury: at sunrise he goes on limping, changed by what has happened.

Jacob names the place Peniel because he has seen God face to face and survived. The name is פְּנִיאֵל, Pĕnîʾēl (peh-nee-AYL), face of God; Brown–Driver–Briggs records this meaning. His words identify the encounter as far more than an unexplained fight with a traveler.

Hosea 12:3–6 later describes Jacob struggling with God and the angel, weeping and seeking favor. That explanation brings pleading and dependence into view alongside the physical wrestling. Genesis closes by connecting Jacob's injured hip with an Israelite food restriction that preserves the memory of the event.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly see an encounter with God that also teaches dependence and persistent prayer. Wesley's notes on Genesis 32:24–29 emphasize faith and supplication; the Catholic Catechism, paragraph 2573, likewise treats the scene as a picture of prayer's struggle and perseverance.

Christians differ over the figure's identity. Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho 58, identifies the One who wrestles with Jacob with the divine One who later becomes human in Christ. A different Christian approach understands God to be acting through an angelic representative, consistent with Augustine's broader explanation of the patriarchs' divine appearances in On the Trinity 3.11.27.

A distinct Jewish reading appears in Rashi's commentary on Genesis 32:25, which identifies the wrestler as Esau's guardian angel. These are particular interpretations within their traditions; the passage's importance in prayer and Jacob's changed life is not dependent on every reader giving the same account of the figure.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Hosea does more than recall a remarkable night. After speaking of Jacob's pleading, Hosea 12:6 calls God's people to return to Him, maintain love and justice, and wait for Him. The ancestor's experience becomes a call for the people bearing his name to seek God faithfully.

Jacob also leaves both blessed and weakened. That combination fits the wider theme expressed in 2 Corinthians 12:7–10, where Christ's sufficient grace meets Paul in weakness. The accounts differ, but both direct attention away from strength as the foundation of security and toward the God whose grace sustains His people.

passages.title: Genesis 33:1-17
passages.section_title: Jacob Meets Esau

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now Jacob looked up and saw Esau coming toward him with four hundred men. So he divided the children among Leah, Rachel, and the two maidservants. 2 He put the maidservants and their children in front, Leah and her children next, and Rachel and Joseph at the rear. 3 But Jacob himself went on ahead and bowed to the ground seven times as he approached his brother. 4 Esau, however, ran to him and embraced him, threw his arms around his neck, and kissed him. And they both wept. 5 When Esau looked up and saw the women and children, he asked, “Who are these with you?” Jacob answered, “These are the children God has graciously given your servant.” 6 Then the maidservants and their children approached and bowed down. 7 Leah and her children also approached and bowed down, and then Joseph and Rachel approached and bowed down. 8 “What do you mean by sending this whole company to meet me?” asked Esau. “To find favor in your sight, my lord,” Jacob answered. 9 “I already have plenty, my brother,” Esau replied. “Keep what belongs to you.” 10 But Jacob insisted, “No, please! If I have found favor in your sight, then receive this gift from my hand. For indeed, I have seen your face, and it is like seeing the face of God, since you have received me favorably. 11 Please accept my gift that was brought to you, because God has been gracious to me and I have all I need.” So Jacob pressed him until he accepted. 12 Then Esau said, “Let us be on our way, and I will go ahead of you.” 13 But Jacob replied, “My lord knows that the children are frail, and I must care for sheep and cattle that are nursing their young. If they are driven hard for even a day, all the animals will die. 14 Please let my lord go ahead of his servant. I will continue on slowly, at a comfortable pace for the livestock and children, until I come to my lord at Seir.” 15 “Let me leave some of my people with you,” Esau said. But Jacob replied, “Why do that? Let me find favor in the sight of my lord.” 16 So that day Esau started on his way back to Seir, 17 but Jacob went on to Succoth, where he built a house for himself and shelters for his livestock; that is why the place was called Succoth.

4 Esau, however, ran to him and embraced him, threw his arms around his neck, and kissed him. And they both wept.
5 When Esau looked up and saw the women and children, he asked, “Who are these with you?”

Jacob answered, “These are the children God has graciously given your servant.” 6 Then the maidservants and their children approached and bowed down. 7 Leah and her children also approached and bowed down, and then Joseph and Rachel approached and bowed down.
8 “What do you mean by sending this whole company to meet me?” asked Esau.
“To find favor in your sight, my lord,” Jacob answered.
9 “I already have plenty, my brother,” Esau replied. “Keep what belongs to you.”

10 But Jacob insisted, “No, please! If I have found favor in your sight, then receive this gift from my hand. For indeed, I have seen your face, and it is like seeing the face of God, since you have received me favorably. 11 Please accept my gift that was brought to you, because God has been gracious to me and I have all I need.” So Jacob pressed him until he accepted.
12 Then Esau said, “Let us be on our way, and I will go ahead of you.”

13 But Jacob replied, “My lord knows that the children are frail, and I must care for sheep and cattle that are nursing their young. If they are driven hard for even a day, all the animals will die. 14 Please let my lord go ahead of his servant. I will continue on slowly, at a comfortable pace for the livestock and children, until I come to my lord at Seir.”
15 “Let me leave some of my people with you,” Esau said.
But Jacob replied, “Why do that? Let me find favor in the sight of my lord.”
16 So that day Esau started on his way back to Seir, 17 but Jacob went on to Succoth, where he built a house for himself and shelters for his livestock; that is why the place was called Succoth.

passages.context_html:
Esau arrives with the four hundred men Jacob feared. Jacob arranges the family with the maidservants and their children first, Leah and her children next, and Rachel and Joseph last. He himself goes ahead of them, bowing as he approaches his brother. The unequal order of the household remains visible, but Jacob faces the meeting first.

Esau runs to embrace and kiss him, and both brothers weep. Instead of the attack Jacob feared, he receives a welcome. As Esau asks about the family, Jacob describes the children as gifts God has graciously given him, and they come forward to meet their uncle.

The brothers then discuss the livestock gifts. Esau says he has enough and does not need them, but Jacob presses him to accept. He links the welcome with God's favor and acknowledges that God has been gracious to him. The gift can now be received within a restored relationship rather than remaining only an attempt to prevent an attack.

Esau offers to travel with Jacob, but Jacob points to the needs of the children and nursing animals and declines an escort. Esau returns to Seir, while Jacob goes to Succoth and builds shelters. The narrative records their peaceful parting without describing every later visit or conversation between them.
passages.common_interpretations_html: A common Christian reading emphasizes reconciliation, unexpected kindness, and Jacob's recognition of God's grace in his brother's welcome. Wesley's notes on Genesis 33:3–12 connect the brothers' peace with God's care and regard Jacob's concern for the traveling household as appropriate.

passages.god_plan_html:
The welcome offers a helpful parallel to the larger biblical theme of reconciliation. Jacob approaches afraid of what his past has left between them, and he finds an embrace. Wesley, on Genesis 33:10, already reads Jacob's comparison with seeing God's face in terms of restored peace.

At the greater level, 2 Corinthians 5:18–21 says that God reconciles people to Himself through Christ. Ephesians 2:8–10 distinguishes salvation as God's gift from the good works that follow it. Read alongside that theme, Jacob's insistence on giving after being welcomed helps illustrate generosity as a response to grace, rather than a payment that creates it.

passages.title: Genesis 33:18-20
passages.section_title: Jacob Settles in Shechem

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 After Jacob had come from Paddan-aram, he arrived safely at the city of Shechem in the land of Canaan, and he camped just outside the city. 19 And the plot of ground where he pitched his tent, he purchased from the sons of Hamor, Shechem’s father, for a hundred pieces of silver. 20 There he set up an altar and called it El-Elohe-Israel.
paragraphs: 18 After Jacob had come from Paddan-aram, he arrived safely at the city of Shechem in the land of Canaan, and he camped just outside the city. 19 And the plot of ground where he pitched his tent, he purchased from the sons of Hamor, Shechem’s father, for a hundred pieces of silver. 20 There he set up an altar and called it El-Elohe-Israel.

passages.context_html:
Jacob arrives safely at Shechem in Canaan after his time in Paddan-aram. He camps outside the city and buys the plot where he pitches his tent from the sons of Hamor, Shechem's father. The brief notice places him back in the land God promised to bring him to.

He also builds an altar and names it El-Elohe-Israel, acknowledging God as the God of Israel. The new name he received during the wrestling now appears in his worship. His arrival is marked both by practical arrangements for the household and an acknowledgment of the God who has brought him safely through.

The purchase introduces Hamor's family before the painful events of chapter 34. For the moment, however, the account closes the journey with safe arrival and worship, rather than with Jacob claiming possession of the whole promised land.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a thankful acknowledgment of God's care after a difficult journey. Wesley's notes on Genesis 33:18, 20 join Jacob's safe arrival with worship of the God who has entered into covenant with him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The safe arrival gives concrete expression to God's promise at Bethel to watch over Jacob and bring him back. The altar marks that faithfulness in a real place, even though the purchase is only a small part of the land his descendants are promised.

Hebrews 11:9–10, 13–16 describes the patriarchs as heirs who live as strangers while looking toward what God will provide. Jacob can give thanks for a completed journey while continuing to wait for the larger fulfillment. Gratitude for what God has already done and hope for what remains ahead belong together.

passages.title: Genesis 34:1-12
passages.section_title: The Assault on Dinah

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now Dinah, the daughter Leah had borne to Jacob, went out to visit the daughters of the land. 2 When Shechem son of Hamor the Hivite, the prince of the region, saw her, he took her and lay with her by force. 3 And his soul was drawn to Dinah, the daughter of Jacob. He loved the young girl and spoke to her tenderly. 4 So Shechem told his father Hamor, “Get me this girl as a wife.” 5 Jacob heard that Shechem had defiled his daughter Dinah, but since his sons were with his livestock in the field, he remained silent about it until they returned. 6 Meanwhile, Shechem’s father Hamor came to speak with Jacob. 7 When Jacob’s sons heard what had happened, they returned from the field. They were filled with grief and fury, because Shechem had committed an outrage in Israel by lying with Jacob’s daughter—a thing that should not be done. 8 But Hamor said to them, “My son Shechem longs for your daughter. Please give her to him as his wife. 9 Intermarry with us; give us your daughters and take our daughters for yourselves. 10 You may settle among us, and the land will be open to you. Live here, move about freely, and acquire your own property.” 11 Then Shechem said to Dinah’s father and brothers, “Grant me this favor, and I will give you whatever you ask. 12 Demand a high dowry and an expensive gift, and I will give you whatever you ask. Only give me the girl as my wife!”
paragraphs: 1 Now Dinah, the daughter Leah had borne to Jacob, went out to visit the daughters of the land. 2 When Shechem son of Hamor the Hivite, the prince of the region, saw her, he took her and lay with her by force. 3 And his soul was drawn to Dinah, the daughter of Jacob. He loved the young girl and spoke to her tenderly. 4 So Shechem told his father Hamor, “Get me this girl as a wife.”

5 Jacob heard that Shechem had defiled his daughter Dinah, but since his sons were with his livestock in the field, he remained silent about it until they returned. 6 Meanwhile, Shechem’s father Hamor came to speak with Jacob. 7 When Jacob’s sons heard what had happened, they returned from the field. They were filled with grief and fury, because Shechem had committed an outrage in Israel by lying with Jacob’s daughter—a thing that should not be done.

8 But Hamor said to them, “My son Shechem longs for your daughter. Please give her to him as his wife. 9 Intermarry with us; give us your daughters and take our daughters for yourselves. 10 You may settle among us, and the land will be open to you. Live here, move about freely, and acquire your own property.”

11 Then Shechem said to Dinah’s father and brothers, “Grant me this favor, and I will give you whatever you ask. 12 Demand a high dowry and an expensive gift, and I will give you whatever you ask. Only give me the girl as my wife!”

passages.context_html:
Dinah, Leah and Jacob's daughter, goes out to visit the local women. Shechem, the regional prince and Hamor's son, sees her, takes her, and forces sexual relations on her. Her visit supplies the setting; Shechem is the person the account describes as using force.

The Hebrew verb behind the violation is עָנָה, ʿānâ (ah-NAH). Brown–Driver–Briggs includes mistreatment and, specifically in Genesis 34:2, sexual humiliation. The BSB's wording makes the force explicit. Shechem's subsequent affection and tender speech do not undo what he has done.

Shechem asks his father to obtain Dinah as his wife. Jacob hears what happened and waits until his sons return from the fields. They are grieved and furious, and the account calls the act an outrage that should not be done. Dinah's own words and wishes are not reported.

Hamor proposes a marriage alliance between the communities, access to the land, and the opportunity to settle and trade. Shechem offers whatever payment the family demands. The negotiations move quickly toward what the men want, while the harm done to Dinah remains unresolved. Her brothers' answer in the next passage will turn the proposal into a plan for revenge.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read the scene as a serious violation followed by a marriage proposal that cannot erase the wrong. The US Catholic bishops' note on Genesis 34 identifies the event as rape and reads it together with the violent and unresolved response that follows.

passages.title: Genesis 34:13-31
passages.section_title: The Revenge of Dinah’s Brothers

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 But because Shechem had defiled their sister Dinah, Jacob’s sons answered him and his father Hamor deceitfully. 14 “We cannot do such a thing,” they said. “To give our sister to an uncircumcised man would be a disgrace to us. 15 We will consent to this on one condition, that you become circumcised like us—every one of your males. 16 Then we will give you our daughters and take your daughters for ourselves. We will dwell among you and become one people. 17 But if you will not agree to be circumcised, then we will take our sister and go.” 18 Their offer seemed good to Hamor and his son Shechem. 19 The young man, who was the most respected of all his father’s household, did not hesitate to fulfill this request, because he was delighted with Jacob’s daughter. 20 So Hamor and his son Shechem went to the gate of their city and addressed the men of their city: 21 “These men are at peace with us. Let them live and trade in our land; indeed, it is large enough for them. Let us take their daughters in marriage and give our daughters to them. 22 But only on this condition will the men agree to dwell with us and be one people: if all our men are circumcised as they are. 23 Will not their livestock, their possessions, and all their animals become ours? Only let us consent to them, and they will dwell among us.” 24 All the men who went out of the city gate listened to Hamor and his son Shechem, and every male of the city was circumcised. 25 Three days later, while they were still in pain, two of Jacob’s sons (Dinah’s brothers Simeon and Levi) took their swords, went into the unsuspecting city, and slaughtered every male. 26 They killed Hamor and his son Shechem with their swords, took Dinah out of Shechem’s house, and went away. 27 Jacob’s other sons came upon the slaughter and looted the city, because their sister had been defiled. 28 They took their flocks and herds and donkeys, and everything else in the city or in the field. 29 They carried off all their possessions and women and children, and they plundered everything in their houses. 30 Then Jacob said to Simeon and Levi, “You have brought trouble upon me by making me a stench to the Canaanites and Perizzites, the people of this land. We are few in number; if they unite against me and attack me, I and my household will be destroyed.” 31 But they replied, “Should he have treated our sister like a prostitute?”

Let them live and trade in our land; indeed, it is large enough for them. Let us take their daughters in marriage and give our daughters to them. 22 But only on this condition will the men agree to dwell with us and be one people: if all our men are circumcised as they are. 23 Will not their livestock, their possessions, and all their animals become ours? Only let us consent to them, and they will dwell among us.”
24 All the men who went out of the city gate listened to Hamor and his son Shechem, and every male of the city was circumcised.

25 Three days later, while they were still in pain, two of Jacob’s sons (Dinah’s brothers Simeon and Levi) took their swords, went into the unsuspecting city, and slaughtered every male. 26 They killed Hamor and his son Shechem with their swords, took Dinah out of Shechem’s house, and went away.

27 Jacob’s other sons came upon the slaughter and looted the city, because their sister had been defiled. 28 They took their flocks and herds and donkeys, and everything else in the city or in the field. 29 They carried off all their possessions and women and children, and they plundered everything in their houses.

30 Then Jacob said to Simeon and Levi, “You have brought trouble upon me by making me a stench to the Canaanites and Perizzites, the people of this land. We are few in number; if they unite against me and attack me, I and my household will be destroyed.”
31 But they replied, “Should he have treated our sister like a prostitute?”

passages.context_html:
Jacob's sons answer deceitfully, saying they can agree to intermarriage only if every male in Shechem's community is circumcised. The narrator names the deception before it is carried out. They are using the family's covenant sign to create an opportunity for revenge.

Hamor and Shechem persuade the townsmen by presenting the newcomers as peaceful and stressing the advantages of sharing land, marriages, and wealth. The men agree. Three days later, while they are in pain, Simeon and Levi attack the unsuspecting city, kill its males, and take Dinah out of Shechem's house.

The other sons plunder the city, taking animals, property, women, and children. The violence reaches far beyond Shechem, the man responsible for the assault. Rescue of their sister has become the destruction and captivity of a whole community.

Jacob protests that they have endangered the household by making enemies of the surrounding peoples. The sons answer by asking whether their sister should have been treated like a prostitute. The chapter ends with that sharp exchange, without a peaceful resolution. Later, in Genesis 49:5–7, Jacob explicitly condemns Simeon and Levi's fierce anger and cruelty.
passages.common_interpretations_html: A common Christian reading recognizes both the wrong done to Dinah and the injustice of answering it with deceit, mass killing, and plunder. The US Catholic bishops' note on Genesis 34:1–31 connects the unresolved conflict here with Jacob's later condemnation in chapter 49.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The family was called to a different way. Genesis 18:19 describes God's purpose for Abraham's household in terms of righteousness and justice. Bearing the covenant sign is therefore not permission to turn it into a weapon or to treat everyone around an offender as equally guilty.

The wider biblical call also distinguishes responding to evil from taking unlimited revenge. Romans 12:17–21 tells believers not to repay evil with evil, but to leave judgment with God and overcome evil with good. The passage does not excuse Shechem. It shows why zeal for a wronged family member must still answer to God's standard of justice.

passages.title: Genesis 35:1-15
passages.section_title: Jacob Returns to Bethel

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then God said to Jacob, “Arise, go up to Bethel, and settle there. Build an altar there to the God who appeared to you when you fled from your brother Esau.” 2 So Jacob told his household and all who were with him, “Get rid of the foreign gods that are among you. Purify yourselves and change your garments. 3 Then let us arise and go to Bethel. I will build an altar there to God, who answered me in my day of distress. He has been with me wherever I have gone.” 4 So they gave Jacob all their foreign gods and all their earrings, and Jacob buried them under the oak near Shechem. 5 As they set out, a terror from God fell over the surrounding cities, so that they did not pursue Jacob’s sons. 6 So Jacob and everyone with him arrived in Luz (that is, Bethel) in the land of Canaan. 7 There Jacob built an altar, and he called that place El-bethel, because it was there that God had revealed Himself to Jacob as he fled from his brother. 8 Now Deborah, Rebekah’s nurse, died and was buried under the oak below Bethel. So Jacob named it Allon-bacuth. 9 After Jacob had returned from Paddan-aram, God appeared to him again and blessed him. 10 And God said to him, “Though your name is Jacob, you will no longer be called Jacob. Instead, your name will be Israel.” So God named him Israel. 11 And God told him, “I am God Almighty. Be fruitful and multiply. A nation—even a company of nations—shall come from you, and kings shall descend from you. 12 The land that I gave to Abraham and Isaac I will give to you, and I will give this land to your descendants after you.” 13 Then God went up from the place where He had spoken with him. 14 So Jacob set up a pillar in the place where God had spoken with him—a stone marker—and he poured out a drink offering on it and anointed it with oil. 15 Jacob called the place where God had spoken with him Bethel.

2 So Jacob told his household and all who were with him, “Get rid of the foreign gods that are among you. Purify yourselves and change your garments. 3 Then let us arise and go to Bethel. I will build an altar there to God, who answered me in my day of distress. He has been with me wherever I have gone.”
4 So they gave Jacob all their foreign gods and all their earrings, and Jacob buried them under the oak near Shechem.

5 As they set out, a terror from God fell over the surrounding cities, so that they did not pursue Jacob’s sons. 6 So Jacob and everyone with him arrived in Luz (that is, Bethel) in the land of Canaan. 7 There Jacob built an altar, and he called that place El-bethel, because it was there that God had revealed Himself to Jacob as he fled from his brother.
8 Now Deborah, Rebekah’s nurse, died and was buried under the oak below Bethel. So Jacob named it Allon-bacuth.

9 After Jacob had returned from Paddan-aram, God appeared to him again and blessed him. 10 And God said to him, “Though your name is Jacob, you will no longer be called Jacob. Instead, your name will be Israel.” So God named him Israel.

11 And God told him, “I am God Almighty. Be fruitful and multiply. A nation—even a company of nations—shall come from you, and kings shall descend from you. 12 The land that I gave to Abraham and Isaac I will give to you, and I will give this land to your descendants after you.”
13 Then God went up from the place where He had spoken with him.

14 So Jacob set up a pillar in the place where God had spoken with him—a stone marker—and he poured out a drink offering on it and anointed it with oil. 15 Jacob called the place where God had spoken with him Bethel.

passages.context_html:
After the violence at Shechem, God tells Jacob to go to Bethel and build an altar to the God who met him when he fled Esau. Jacob calls the household to put away foreign gods, purify themselves, and change their clothes. He explains the journey by recalling the God who answered him in distress and has been with him wherever he went.

The household surrenders its idols and earrings, which Jacob buries near Shechem. As they travel, terror from God restrains the surrounding cities from pursuing them. At Bethel, Jacob builds the commanded altar. The account also records the death and burial of Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, preserving the household's grief within the story of return.

God appears again, confirms Jacob's name as Israel, and renews the promises of descendants, nations, kings, and the land given to Abraham and Isaac. The God who has watched over Jacob now reaffirms the same family promise for the generations ahead.

Jacob sets up a stone pillar where God has spoken, pours a drink offering and oil on it, and again names the place Bethel. The return brings the earlier encounter and vow back into view. It also calls the whole household to a loyalty that must affect what they keep and how they live.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the return as a renewal of worship and loyalty to God, accompanied by His confirmation of the promise. Wesley's notes on Genesis 35:1–11 connect the outward removal of idols and preparation for worship with a needed change of heart.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
God's faithfulness calls for a changed life within the people He preserves. Titus 2:11–14 joins saving grace with learning to reject ungodliness and becoming a people eager to do good. That wider theme helps explain why returning to Bethel involves putting away rival gods as well as remembering an earlier blessing.

The promise of kings also reaches forward within the Bible's larger story. Luke 1:31–33 announces Jesus as the Son who receives David's throne and reigns over the house of Jacob forever. Genesis does not yet name those later kings, but the promise to this troubled family belongs to the history that leads to Christ.

passages.title: Genesis 35:16-20
passages.section_title: Benjamin Born, Rachel Dies

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 Later, they set out from Bethel, and while they were still some distance from Ephrath, Rachel began to give birth, and her labor was difficult. 17 During her severe labor, the midwife said to her, “Do not be afraid, for you are having another son.” 18 And with her last breath—for she was dying—she named him Ben-oni. But his father called him Benjamin. 19 So Rachel died and was buried on the way to Ephrath (that is, Bethlehem). 20 Jacob set up a pillar on her grave; it marks Rachel’s tomb to this day.
paragraphs: 16 Later, they set out from Bethel, and while they were still some distance from Ephrath, Rachel began to give birth, and her labor was difficult. 17 During her severe labor, the midwife said to her, “Do not be afraid, for you are having another son.”
18 And with her last breath—for she was dying—she named him Ben-oni. But his father called him Benjamin.
19 So Rachel died and was buried on the way to Ephrath (that is, Bethlehem). 20 Jacob set up a pillar on her grave; it marks Rachel’s tomb to this day.

passages.context_html:
On the journey from Bethel toward Ephrath, Rachel goes into difficult labor. The midwife tells her that she is having another son, but the birth is followed by her death. The account places a new life and a profound loss together without explaining a medical cause.

Rachel calls the child Ben-oni, בֶּן־אוֹנִי, Ben-ʾônî (ben-oh-NEE), son of my sorrow. Jacob calls him Benjamin, בִּנְיָמִין, Binyāmîn (bin-yah-MEEN), son of the right hand. Brown–Driver–Briggs on Ben-oni and Benjamin records these meanings. The two names preserve different responses to the same birth.

Rachel is buried on the way to Ephrath, identified here as Bethlehem, and Jacob sets a pillar on her grave. Like the pillar he set up after God's appearance, this stone preserves a memory, now marked by grief. God's promises to the family continue, but the narrative does not hide the losses they experience along the way.
passages.common_interpretations_html: A common Christian reading recognizes the sorrow of Rachel's death alongside the birth of the final son in Jacob's family. Wesley's notes on Genesis 35:17–20 draw attention to grief, the naming of the child, and the memorial Jacob leaves.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Rachel later becomes a figure of a mother's grief over her people. Jeremiah 31:15–17 pictures her weeping for her children, then speaks of hope and their return. Matthew 2:16–18 takes up Jeremiah's words when Herod kills the children around Bethlehem.

Matthew uses Jeremiah's picture of Rachel to express the grief of later mothers. The connection carries her memory into the story of Christ's coming and the suffering surrounding it. Scripture can hold God's promised future and a family's terrible grief together, giving space to lament rather than treating loss as evidence that the promise has failed.

passages.title: Genesis 35:21-26
passages.section_title: The Sons of Jacob

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 Israel again set out and pitched his tent beyond the Tower of Eder. 22 While Israel was living in that region, Reuben went in and slept with his father’s concubine Bilhah, and Israel heard about it. Jacob had twelve sons: 23 The sons of Leah were Reuben the firstborn of Jacob, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun. 24 The sons of Rachel were Joseph and Benjamin. 25 The sons of Rachel’s maidservant Bilhah were Dan and Naphtali. 26 And the sons of Leah’s maidservant Zilpah were Gad and Asher. These are the sons of Jacob, who were born to him in Paddan-aram.
paragraphs: 21 Israel again set out and pitched his tent beyond the Tower of Eder. 22 While Israel was living in that region, Reuben went in and slept with his father’s concubine Bilhah, and Israel heard about it.
Jacob had twelve sons:
23 The sons of Leah were Reuben the firstborn of Jacob, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun.
24 The sons of Rachel were Joseph and Benjamin.
25 The sons of Rachel’s maidservant Bilhah were Dan and Naphtali.
26 And the sons of Leah’s maidservant Zilpah were Gad and Asher.
These are the sons of Jacob, who were born to him in Paddan-aram.

passages.context_html:
After Rachel's burial, Israel travels on and camps beyond the Tower of Eder. Reuben, his firstborn, sleeps with Bilhah, his father's concubine and the mother of Dan and Naphtali. The account says Israel hears of it, but does not describe an immediate confrontation or tell us Bilhah's response.

The brief notice has lasting significance. Genesis 49:3–4 later recalls Reuben's act when explaining why he will not retain his firstborn preeminence. The silence here therefore does not mean the matter is forgotten.

Genesis then names Jacob's twelve sons by their mothers: Leah, Rachel, Bilhah, and Zilpah. The list gathers the family whose births and conflicts have filled the preceding chapters and prepares the next stage of the story. They are one household, but its history includes both God's gifts and serious failures within it.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read Reuben's act as a grave violation within the family with consequences for his place as firstborn. Wesley's note on Genesis 35:22 connects the brief report with Jacob's later words, while the following list brings all twelve sons into view.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
1 Chronicles 5:1–2 explains the resulting distinctions: Reuben loses the birthright because he defiled his father's bed; the birthright goes to Joseph's sons, while a ruler comes from Judah. These roles should not be flattened into a single privilege automatically held by the oldest son.

Matthew 1:1–3 later follows Jesus' ancestry through Jacob and Judah. God's promise continues through this family, but that continuation does not erase the consequences of its members' actions. The biblical account traces both the lasting purpose and the responsibility of those involved.

passages.title: Genesis 35:27-29
passages.section_title: The Death of Isaac

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 27 Jacob returned to his father Isaac at Mamre, near Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron), where Abraham and Isaac had stayed. 28 And Isaac lived 180 years. 29 Then he breathed his last and died and was gathered to his people, old and full of years. And his sons Esau and Jacob buried him.
paragraphs: 27 Jacob returned to his father Isaac at Mamre, near Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron), where Abraham and Isaac had stayed.
28 And Isaac lived 180 years. 29 Then he breathed his last and died and was gathered to his people, old and full of years. And his sons Esau and Jacob buried him.

passages.context_html:
Jacob comes to his father Isaac at Mamre near Hebron, where Abraham and Isaac had lived. The notice brings him back to his father's household after the long account of his departure, years with Laban, and return to Canaan. It does not give a complete record of every visit that may have happened along the way.

Isaac dies at 180, described as old and full of years, and Esau and Jacob bury him. Their shared action recalls Isaac and Ishmael burying Abraham in Genesis 25. The two brothers who once faced a threat of murder around their father's anticipated death now stand together at his burial.

This closes Isaac's family account before Genesis turns more fully toward Jacob's sons. The promises have passed to another generation, while Isaac's life ends in the land where he lived as an heir still awaiting the larger fulfillment.
passages.common_interpretations_html: A common Christian reading sees an honorable close to Isaac's life, with the brothers cooperating in his burial and the family promise continuing. Wesley's notes on Genesis 35:27–29 emphasize that peaceful ending after the earlier threat and estrangement.

passages.god_plan_html:
Isaac's death does not mark the end of his relationship with God. When Jesus teaches about resurrection in Luke 20:37–38, He recalls God's identification as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and says that God is the God of the living.

Jesus is explaining the burning-bush passage, not commenting directly on this funeral. His teaching nevertheless gives the wider hope in which Isaac's life can be read. The promise extends beyond the years one patriarch lives to see, and the God who has called His people remains their God beyond death.

passages.title: Genesis 36:1-19
passages.section_title: The Descendants of Esau

passages.context_html:
After Isaac's burial, Genesis records Esau's family before returning to Jacob's household. The repeated identification of Esau as Edom connects Jacob's brother with the people who will later appear as Israel's neighbors. The list names his wives, sons, grandsons, and the chiefs descended from them.

Esau moves his household and possessions away from Jacob because their livestock and other property have become too great for them to live together. The explanation recalls Abraham and Lot's separation in Genesis 13. Here, too, the practical needs of large households help explain a lasting division in where the families settle.

Esau settles in the region of Mount Seir. His descendants include Teman and Amalek, names that recur in later biblical history. This family record gives those later names a place in the story rather than treating the peoples around Israel as strangers with no connection to the patriarchs.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as the family history explaining Edom's relationship to Israel and its settlement in Seir. Wesley's introduction and notes on Genesis 36:1–10 also connect Esau's growing family with the earlier promise that Rebekah's sons would become two nations.

passages.god_plan_html:
God's choice of Jacob to carry the covenant promise does not mean that Esau's family is outside His concern. Deuteronomy 2:4–6 calls Esau's descendants Israel's brothers and says God has given Seir to Esau. Israel is told to respect that possession and pay for the food and water it uses.

That later command adds something important to this genealogy: belonging to the chosen family does not give Israel permission to take whatever it wants from its neighbors. God's purpose for His people includes recognizing His dealings with other families and respecting the limits He sets.

passages.section_title: The Descendants of Seir

passages.context_html:
The family record now names the descendants of Seir the Horite, who were already living in the region associated with Edom. Their inclusion shows that the land's history did not begin with Esau's arrival. The passage names their families and chiefs alongside the preceding account of Esau's descendants.

There are family links between the lists. Timna, identified here as Lotan's sister, appears earlier as Eliphaz's concubine and Amalek's mother. Anah and Oholibamah also appear in the surrounding family records. These connections help explain why the ancestry of Seir's people belongs in a chapter about Edom.

The short note about Anah finding hot springs while pasturing donkeys preserves a remembered event within the genealogy. Deuteronomy 2:12, 22 later describes Esau's descendants displacing the Horites. Genesis here concentrates on naming the people and families involved, rather than giving a full account of that change.
passages.common_interpretations_html: A common Christian reading treats this as background to Edom's settlement and its connections with the earlier inhabitants. Wesley's note on Genesis 36:20 likewise reads the list alongside the later account in Deuteronomy. The main point is the relationship of these families to the land and to Esau's descendants.

passages.context_html:
Genesis next lists kings who ruled in Edom before any king ruled over the Israelites. Each king is named in succession, often with a father, home region, or city. A brief notice also remembers Hadad's defeat of Midian in Moab.

The list does not present a simple chain of fathers handing the throne to their sons. Its attention to different places and family names shows a succession of rulers, but it does not explain how each was chosen. The final section returns to chiefs, arranging their names by families, regions, and settlements.

The chapter closes by again identifying Esau as the father of the Edomites. His family has become an established people with territory and rulers. Genesis 37 then returns to Jacob living in Canaan, where the next part of the family's history will unfold through Joseph and his brothers.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the list as a record of Edom's early rulers and settled communities. Wesley's notes on Genesis 36:31, 43 highlight the contrast between Edom already possessing its territory and Jacob's descendants still awaiting the fuller realization of God's land promise.

passages.title: Genesis 37:1-11
passages.section_title: Joseph’s Dreams

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now Jacob lived in the land where his father had resided, the land of Canaan. 2 This is the account of Jacob. When Joseph was seventeen years old, he was tending the flock with his brothers, the sons of his father’s wives Bilhah and Zilpah, and he brought their father a bad report about them. 3 Now Israel loved Joseph more than his other sons, because Joseph had been born to him in his old age; so he made him a robe of many colors. 4 When Joseph’s brothers saw that their father loved him more than any of them, they hated him and could not speak a kind word to him. 5 Then Joseph had a dream, and when he told it to his brothers, they hated him even more. 6 He said to them, “Listen to this dream I had: 7 We were binding sheaves of grain in the field, and suddenly my sheaf rose and stood upright, while your sheaves gathered around and bowed down to mine.” 8 “Do you intend to reign over us?” his brothers asked. “Will you actually rule us?” So they hated him even more because of his dream and his statements. 9 Then Joseph had another dream and told it to his brothers. “Look,” he said, “I had another dream, and this time the sun and moon and eleven stars were bowing down to me.” 10 He told his father and brothers, but his father rebuked him and said, “What is this dream that you have had? Will your mother and brothers and I actually come and bow down to the ground before you?” 11 And his brothers were jealous of him, but his father kept in mind what he had said.
paragraphs: 1 Now Jacob lived in the land where his father had resided, the land of Canaan.

2 This is the account of Jacob. When Joseph was seventeen years old, he was tending the flock with his brothers, the sons of his father’s wives Bilhah and Zilpah, and he brought their father a bad report about them.

3 Now Israel loved Joseph more than his other sons, because Joseph had been born to him in his old age; so he made him a robe of many colors. 4 When Joseph’s brothers saw that their father loved him more than any of them, they hated him and could not speak a kind word to him.

5 Then Joseph had a dream, and when he told it to his brothers, they hated him even more. 6 He said to them, “Listen to this dream I had: 7 We were binding sheaves of grain in the field, and suddenly my sheaf rose and stood upright, while your sheaves gathered around and bowed down to mine.”
8 “Do you intend to reign over us?” his brothers asked. “Will you actually rule us?” So they hated him even more because of his dream and his statements.
9 Then Joseph had another dream and told it to his brothers. “Look,” he said, “I had another dream, and this time the sun and moon and eleven stars were bowing down to me.”

10 He told his father and brothers, but his father rebuked him and said, “What is this dream that you have had? Will your mother and brothers and I actually come and bow down to the ground before you?” 11 And his brothers were jealous of him, but his father kept in mind what he had said.

passages.context_html:
Genesis returns from Esau's descendants to the account of Jacob's family. Joseph is seventeen and tends the flock with his brothers. He brings Jacob a bad report about some of them. The account does not give the report's details, but it soon makes clear how badly the family relationships have deteriorated.

Jacob loves Joseph more than his other sons and gives him a distinctive robe. The brothers recognize the favoritism and cannot speak kindly to Joseph. The BSB calls it a robe of many colors; Brown–Driver–Briggs understands the Hebrew description as a tunic reaching to the palms and soles. Whichever feature of its appearance is emphasized, the narrative itself makes its significance clear: it visibly marks Jacob's special treatment of Joseph.

Joseph's first dream shows his brothers' sheaves of grain bowing to his. They understand it as a claim that he will rule them, and their hatred grows. The second shows the sun, moon, and eleven stars bowing to him. Jacob interprets the figures in terms of the family and rebukes him, yet keeps the matter in mind.

The dreams introduce a future the family finds offensive before anyone knows how it will come about. Later, Genesis 42:6–9 explicitly recalls them when the brothers bow before Joseph in Egypt to buy grain. For now, Joseph has dreams of honor while his daily situation is becoming more hostile.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read the dreams as anticipating Joseph's later authority, while recognizing the harm caused by family favoritism and jealousy. Wesley's notes on Genesis 37:3–10 connect the first dream with the brothers' later bowing in Egypt and distinguish their hostility from Jacob's willingness to remember what Joseph said.
passages.current_position_html: Worship as the Early Church Knew It distinguishes bowing as an act of respect from worship offered to God. Applied here, the bowing in Joseph's dreams expresses the family's submission to his future authority. The scene does not require us to understand them as treating Joseph as God.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
The story begins with a promised future that seems increasingly distant as events unfold. Psalm 105:16–22 later places Joseph's enslavement, hardship, and eventual authority within God's provision before the famine. The dream's grain imagery becomes especially fitting when the family must seek food from the brother it has rejected.

There is also a long-recognized Christian parallel between Joseph's rejection before his rise to authority and Jesus' suffering before His rise to glory; Wesley's introduction to Genesis 37 draws that comparison. Philippians 2:5–11 describes Jesus' suffering and the honor God gives Him. The parallel helps us see how rejection need not defeat God's saving purpose, without turning every detail of Joseph's dreams into a separate prediction about Jesus.

passages.title: Genesis 37:12-30
passages.section_title: Joseph Sold into Egypt

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 Some time later, Joseph’s brothers had gone to pasture their father’s flocks near Shechem. 13 Israel said to him, “Are not your brothers pasturing the flocks at Shechem? Get ready; I am sending you to them.” “I am ready,” Joseph replied. 14 Then Israel told him, “Go now and see how your brothers and the flocks are faring, and bring word back to me.” So he sent him off from the Valley of Hebron. And when Joseph arrived in Shechem, 15 a man found him wandering in the field and asked, “What are you looking for?” 16 “I am looking for my brothers,” Joseph replied. “Can you please tell me where they are pasturing their flocks?” 17 “They have moved on from here,” the man answered. “I heard them say, ‘Let us go to Dothan.’” So Joseph set out after his brothers and found them at Dothan. 18 Now Joseph’s brothers saw him in the distance, and before he arrived, they plotted to kill him. 19 “Here comes that dreamer!” they said to one another. 20 “Come now, let us kill him and throw him into one of the pits. We can say that a vicious animal has devoured him. Then we shall see what becomes of his dreams!” 21 When Reuben heard this, he tried to rescue Joseph from their hands. “Let us not take his life,” he said. 22 “Do not shed his blood. Throw him into this pit in the wilderness, but do not lay a hand on him.” Reuben said this so that he could rescue Joseph from their hands and return him to his father. 23 So when Joseph came to his brothers, they stripped him of his robe—the robe of many colors he was wearing— 24 and they took him and threw him into the pit. Now the pit was empty, with no water in it. 25 And as they sat down to eat a meal, they looked up and saw a caravan of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead. Their camels were carrying spices, balm, and myrrh on their way down to Egypt. 26 Then Judah said to his brothers, “What profit will we gain if we kill our brother and cover up his blood? 27 Come, let us sell him to the Ishmaelites and not lay a hand on him; for he is our brother, our own flesh.” And they agreed. 28 So when the Midianite traders passed by, his brothers pulled Joseph out of the pit and sold him for twenty shekels of silver to the Ishmaelites, who took him to Egypt. 29 When Reuben returned to the pit and saw that Joseph was not there, he tore his clothes, 30 returned to his brothers, and said, “The boy is gone! What am I going to do?”

We can say that a vicious animal has devoured him. Then we shall see what becomes of his dreams!”

21 When Reuben heard this, he tried to rescue Joseph from their hands. “Let us not take his life,” he said. 22 “Do not shed his blood. Throw him into this pit in the wilderness, but do not lay a hand on him.” Reuben said this so that he could rescue Joseph from their hands and return him to his father.

23 So when Joseph came to his brothers, they stripped him of his robe—the robe of many colors he was wearing— 24 and they took him and threw him into the pit. Now the pit was empty, with no water in it.
25 And as they sat down to eat a meal, they looked up and saw a caravan of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead. Their camels were carrying spices, balm, and myrrh on their way down to Egypt.

26 Then Judah said to his brothers, “What profit will we gain if we kill our brother and cover up his blood? 27 Come, let us sell him to the Ishmaelites and not lay a hand on him; for he is our brother, our own flesh.” And they agreed. 28 So when the Midianite traders passed by, his brothers pulled Joseph out of the pit and sold him for twenty shekels of silver to the Ishmaelites, who took him to Egypt.
29 When Reuben returned to the pit and saw that Joseph was not there, he tore his clothes, 30 returned to his brothers, and said, “The boy is gone! What am I going to do?”

passages.context_html:
Jacob sends Joseph to check on his brothers and the flocks near Shechem. After a man directs him to Dothan, Joseph finds them. They see him coming and plan to kill him, dispose of his body, and blame a wild animal. Their reference to his dreams makes their hostility to his anticipated authority explicit.

Reuben intervenes, urging them to put Joseph in a pit without shedding his blood. The narrator tells us his intention is to rescue Joseph and return him to their father. The brothers strip off the distinctive robe and throw Joseph into an empty pit, then sit down to eat. Genesis 42:21 later recalls that they heard his distress and pleas but would not listen.

When traders traveling toward Egypt appear, Judah proposes selling Joseph instead of killing him. The brothers agree and sell him for twenty shekels of silver. Joseph's life is spared, but he is still betrayed and carried away as a slave. Reuben returns to the pit, finds him gone, and tears his clothes in distress.

The passage uses both Ishmaelite and Midianite descriptions for the traders. Its immediate focus is the brothers' wrongdoing and Joseph's removal to Egypt. Their attempt to prevent his dreams from coming true sets him on the road to the place where his later authority will emerge.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a grave betrayal that God will nevertheless turn toward the family's preservation. Wesley's notes on Genesis 37:18–26 emphasize both the brothers' deliberate wrongdoing and the purpose that emerges beyond their intentions. The Catholic Catechism, paragraph 312, also uses Joseph's story to explain that God can bring good from human evil without making the evil itself good.

passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 7:9–10 directly recalls this event: the patriarchs' jealousy leads them to sell Joseph, but God is with him and eventually raises him to authority in Egypt. Stephen later confronts his own hearers over their rejection of the Righteous One in Acts 7:51–53. His speech shows that rejection by people does not mean rejection by God.

The beloved son sent to his brothers and met with a plot against his life also offers a meaningful parallel to Christ's rejection, noted in Wesley's commentary on Genesis 37:21. The connection concerns the pattern of rejection followed by God's saving work. Joseph's suffering will help preserve his family; Christ's saving work reaches further, dealing with sin itself. God's ability to bring good does not excuse the people who betray either of them.

passages.title: Genesis 37:31-36
passages.section_title: Jacob Mourns Joseph

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 31 Then they took Joseph’s robe, slaughtered a young goat, and dipped the robe in its blood. 32 They sent the robe of many colors to their father and said, “We found this. Examine it to see whether it is your son’s robe or not.” 33 His father recognized it and said, “It is my son’s robe! A vicious animal has devoured him. Joseph has surely been torn to pieces!” 34 Then Jacob tore his clothes, put sackcloth around his waist, and mourned for his son many days. 35 All his sons and daughters tried to comfort him, but he refused to be comforted. “No,” he said. “I will go down to Sheol mourning for my son.” So his father wept for him. 36 Meanwhile, the Midianites sold Joseph in Egypt to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh and captain of the guard.

33 His father recognized it and said, “It is my son’s robe! A vicious animal has devoured him. Joseph has surely been torn to pieces!” 34 Then Jacob tore his clothes, put sackcloth around his waist, and mourned for his son many days. 35 All his sons and daughters tried to comfort him, but he refused to be comforted. “No,” he said. “I will go down to Sheol mourning for my son.” So his father wept for him.
36 Meanwhile, the Midianites sold Joseph in Egypt to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh and captain of the guard.

passages.context_html:
After selling Joseph, the brothers slaughter a goat and dip his robe in its blood. They send it to Jacob and ask him to identify it. He recognizes the garment and concludes that a wild animal has killed his son. The robe that displayed Joseph's favored place in the household now becomes the means of deceiving his father.

Jacob tears his clothes, wears sackcloth, and mourns for many days. His children try to comfort him, but he refuses comfort and expects to go to his death still grieving. His sorrow is genuine, though it rests on evidence his sons have deliberately falsified.

Jacob speaks of going down to שְׁאוֹל, Sheʾôl (sheh-OHL), the realm of the dead. Brown–Driver–Briggs specifically includes Genesis 37:35 among passages speaking of descent there at death. Here the word expresses Jacob's expectation of mourning until he dies.

The final verse lets the reader see what Jacob cannot: Joseph is alive and has been sold to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh and captain of the guard. The family believes the story has ended in death, while the narrative has moved to Egypt and the next stage of Joseph's life.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a painful account of deceit and grief, with the closing notice preserving hope that Jacob does not yet have. Wesley's introduction to Genesis 37 and note on verse 35 recognize both the brothers' deception and the depth of their father's mourning.
