passages.god_plan_html:
The closing glimpse of Joseph alive in Egypt shows how limited the family's knowledge is. Psalm 105:16–22 later describes God sending Joseph ahead through circumstances that include enslavement and confinement. What appears to Jacob to be the end is part of a much longer story.

That wider view gives room for hope without requiring us to dismiss the suffering in front of us. Jacob is not comforted here by an explanation of what God is doing. The account allows his grief to remain real while showing the reader that God's care and purpose extend beyond what he can presently see.

passages.title: Genesis 38:1-26
passages.section_title: Judah and Tamar

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 About that time, Judah left his brothers and settled near a man named Hirah, an Adullamite. 2 There Judah saw the daughter of a Canaanite man named Shua, and he took her as a wife and slept with her. 3 So she conceived and gave birth to a son, and Judah named him Er. 4 Again she conceived and gave birth to a son, and she named him Onan. 5 Then she gave birth to another son and named him Shelah; it was at Chezib that she gave birth to him. 6 Now Judah acquired a wife for Er, his firstborn, and her name was Tamar. 7 But Er, Judah’s firstborn, was wicked in the sight of the LORD; so the LORD put him to death. 8 Then Judah said to Onan, “Sleep with your brother’s wife. Perform your duty as her brother-in-law and raise up offspring for your brother.” 9 But Onan knew that the offspring would not belong to him; so whenever he would sleep with his brother’s wife, he would spill his seed on the ground so that he would not produce offspring for his brother. 10 What he did was wicked in the sight of the LORD, so He put Onan to death as well. 11 Then Judah said to his daughter-in-law Tamar, “Live as a widow in your father’s house until my son Shelah grows up.” For he thought, “He may die too, like his brothers.” So Tamar went to live in her father’s house. 12 After a long time Judah’s wife, the daughter of Shua, died. When Judah had finished mourning, he and his friend Hirah the Adullamite went up to his sheepshearers at Timnah. 13 When Tamar was told, “Your father-in-law is going up to Timnah to shear his sheep,” 14 she removed her widow’s garments, covered her face with a veil to disguise herself, and sat at the entrance to Enaim, which is on the way to Timnah. For she saw that although Shelah had grown up, she had not been given to him as a wife. 15 When Judah saw her, he thought she was a prostitute because she had covered her face. 16 Not realizing that she was his daughter-in-law, he went over to her and said, “Come now, let me sleep with you.” “What will you give me for sleeping with you?” she inquired. 17 “I will send you a young goat from my flock,” Judah answered. But she replied, “Only if you leave me something as a pledge until you send it.” 18 “What pledge should I give you?” he asked. She answered, “Your seal and your cord, and the staff in your hand.” So he gave them to her and slept with her, and she became pregnant by him. 19 Then Tamar got up and departed. And she removed her veil and put on her widow’s garments again. 20 Now when Judah sent his friend Hirah the Adullamite with the young goat to collect the items he had left with the woman, he could not find her. 21 He asked the men of that place, “Where is the shrine prostitute who was beside the road at Enaim?” “No shrine prostitute has been here,” they answered. 22 So Hirah returned to Judah and said, “I could not find her, and furthermore, the men of that place said, ‘No shrine prostitute has been here.’” 23 “Let her keep the items,” Judah replied. “Otherwise we will become a laughingstock. After all, I did send her this young goat, but you could not find her.” 24 About three months later, Judah was told, “Your daughter-in-law Tamar has prostituted herself, and now she is pregnant.” “Bring her out!” Judah replied. “Let her be burned to death!” 25 As she was being brought out, Tamar sent a message to her father-in-law: “I am pregnant by the man to whom these items belong.” And she added, “Please examine them. Whose seal and cord and staff are these?” 26 Judah recognized the items and said, “She is more righteous than I, since I did not give her to my son Shelah.” And he did not have relations with her again.

20 Now when Judah sent his friend Hirah the Adullamite with the young goat to collect the items he had left with the woman, he could not find her. 21 He asked the men of that place, “Where is the shrine prostitute who was beside the road at Enaim?” “No shrine prostitute has been here,” they answered.

passages.context_html:
The narrative pauses Joseph's story to follow Judah. He settles near Hirah, marries a Canaanite woman, and has three sons: Er, Onan, and Shelah. Er marries Tamar but dies under God's judgment for wickedness. The account does not identify his specific offense.

Judah tells Onan to provide offspring for his deceased brother through Tamar. Onan has sexual relations with her but deliberately prevents conception because the offspring would not count as his own. God judges his conduct as wicked and puts him to death. A later law in Deuteronomy 25:5–10 also addresses a brother's responsibility to preserve a deceased brother's family name, though Genesis is describing events before that law is given.

Judah sends Tamar back to her father's house to wait for Shelah to grow up, fearing he might also die. Time passes, but Tamar is not given to Shelah even after he is grown. After Judah's wife dies, Tamar disguises herself beside the road to Timnah. Judah mistakes her for a prostitute and has relations with her, leaving his seal, cord, and staff as security for a promised payment.

When Tamar's pregnancy becomes known, Judah demands her death. She sends him the personal items, identifying him as the father. He recognizes them and acknowledges that she is more righteous than he is because he withheld Shelah. The man ready to condemn her is forced to face his own responsibility. The account ends by saying he does not have relations with her again.

This episode belongs beside Joseph's story in more than one way. Judah, who proposed selling Joseph, must now recognize his own wrongdoing. A goat and personal belongings again play a part in a deception, but this time the belongings expose Judah rather than sustaining the lie sent to Jacob.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly recognize Onan's wrongdoing toward his brother and Tamar, Judah's failure to provide what he promised, and the exposure of his double standard. Wesley's notes on Genesis 38:7–23 discuss the family duty, sexual wrongdoing, and Judah's concern for his reputation.

The Catholic Church also draws on Onan's story in its teaching against contraception. Pius XI's Casti connubii, paragraphs 54–56, applies the passage to deliberately preventing conception during sexual intercourse. This extends the application beyond Onan's refusal to provide a child for his brother.

passages.god_plan_html:
Matthew 1:3 explicitly includes Judah, Tamar, and their sons in Jesus' ancestry. This troubling episode therefore belongs to the family history through which the promised Messiah comes. Matthew preserves Tamar's name rather than presenting an ancestry free from wrongdoing and painful circumstances.

The connection shows God's purpose continuing through a family that needs correction and mercy. It does not make Judah's conduct right. His acknowledgment of responsibility matters within the story, while the continuing family line shows that the future promise does not rest on a spotless record of human behavior.

passages.title: Genesis 38:27-30
passages.section_title: The Birth of Perez and Zerah

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 27 When the time came for Tamar to give birth, there were twins in her womb. 28 And as she was giving birth, one of them put out his hand; so the midwife took a scarlet thread and tied it around his wrist. “This one came out first,” she announced. 29 But when he pulled his hand back and his brother came out, she said, “You have broken out first!” So he was named Perez. 30 Then his brother came out with the scarlet thread around his wrist, and he was named Zerah.
paragraphs: 27 When the time came for Tamar to give birth, there were twins in her womb. 28 And as she was giving birth, one of them put out his hand; so the midwife took a scarlet thread and tied it around his wrist. “This one came out first,” she announced. 29 But when he pulled his hand back and his brother came out, she said, “You have broken out first!” So he was named Perez. 30 Then his brother came out with the scarlet thread around his wrist, and he was named Zerah.

passages.context_html:
Tamar gives birth to twins. One child puts out a hand, and the midwife ties a scarlet thread around his wrist to mark him as the first to emerge. He pulls his hand back, however, and his brother is born first.

The firstborn is named Perez, with the midwife's words connecting his name to breaking out ahead. His brother, born with the thread around his wrist, is named Zerah. The brief account preserves the unusual birth order and identifies the two sons who will appear in later family records.

The scene recalls the earlier attention Genesis gives to the birth order of Jacob and Esau. Here the immediate result is the establishment of Judah and Tamar's two sons. Later Scripture will follow Perez's descendants toward David and, eventually, Jesus.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as the birth record of Judah and Tamar's sons, with particular significance because Perez belongs to the ancestry of Christ. Wesley's note on Genesis 38:28 connects the twins with Matthew's genealogy, which names both brothers.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
Ruth 4:12, 18–22 recalls Tamar and traces the family from Perez to David. Matthew 1:3–6 takes up that same line within its account of Jesus' ancestry. The connection is stated in the biblical family records themselves.

This small birth scene thus becomes part of the longer movement from Abraham's family to Israel's king and the Messiah. Its importance comes from the family line Scripture actually follows; the thread and the order of the twins need no additional hidden meaning to give the passage a place in that larger story.

passages.title: Genesis 39:1-12
passages.section_title: Joseph and Potiphar’s Wife

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Meanwhile, Joseph had been taken down to Egypt, where an Egyptian named Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh and captain of the guard, bought him from the Ishmaelites who had taken him there. 2 And the LORD was with Joseph, and he became a successful man, serving in the household of his Egyptian master. 3 When his master saw that the LORD was with him and made him prosper in all he did, 4 Joseph found favor in his sight and became his personal attendant. Potiphar put him in charge of his household and entrusted him with everything he owned. 5 From the time that he put Joseph in charge of his household and all he owned, the LORD blessed the Egyptian’s household on account of him. The LORD’s blessing was on everything he owned, both in his house and in his field. 6 So Potiphar left all that he owned in Joseph’s care; he did not concern himself with anything except the food he ate. Now Joseph was well-built and handsome, 7 and after some time his master’s wife cast her eyes upon Joseph and said, “Sleep with me.” 8 But he refused. “Look,” he said to his master’s wife, “with me here, my master does not concern himself with anything in his house, and he has entrusted everything he owns to my care. 9 No one in this house is greater than I am. He has withheld nothing from me except you, because you are his wife. So how could I do such a great evil and sin against God?” 10 Although Potiphar’s wife spoke to Joseph day after day, he refused to go to bed with her or even be near her. 11 One day, however, Joseph went into the house to attend to his work, and not a single household servant was inside. 12 She grabbed Joseph by his cloak and said, “Sleep with me!” But leaving his cloak in her hand, he escaped and ran outside.

3 When his master saw that the LORD was with him and made him prosper in all he did, 4 Joseph found favor in his sight and became his personal attendant.

Potiphar put him in charge of his household and entrusted him with everything he owned. 5 From the time that he put Joseph in charge of his household and all he owned, the LORD blessed the Egyptian’s household on account of him. The LORD’s blessing was on everything he owned, both in his house and in his field. 6 So Potiphar left all that he owned in Joseph’s care; he did not concern himself with anything except the food he ate.
Now Joseph was well-built and handsome, 7 and after some time his master’s wife cast her eyes upon Joseph and said, “Sleep with me.”

8 But he refused. “Look,” he said to his master’s wife, “with me here, my master does not concern himself with anything in his house, and he has entrusted everything he owns to my care. 9 No one in this house is greater than I am. He has withheld nothing from me except you, because you are his wife. So how could I do such a great evil and sin against God?”

10 Although Potiphar’s wife spoke to Joseph day after day, he refused to go to bed with her or even be near her. 11 One day, however, Joseph went into the house to attend to his work, and not a single household servant was inside. 12 She grabbed Joseph by his cloak and said, “Sleep with me!” But leaving his cloak in her hand, he escaped and ran outside.

passages.context_html:
Genesis returns to Joseph in Egypt, where Potiphar has bought him as a slave. The repeated statement that the LORD is with Joseph explains his success and the trust his master places in him. Potiphar gives him responsibility for the household and possessions, and the household is blessed on Joseph's account.

That trust does not remove Joseph's vulnerability. Potiphar's wife repeatedly demands that he sleep with her. He refuses, explaining both the betrayal of his master's trust and the offense against God. His answer treats the proposed act as wrong even if the people involved could conceal it.

Joseph also avoids being near her. When she finally grabs his cloak while no other servants are inside, he leaves it in her hand and runs outside. He acts decisively to escape her demand. The garment left behind will become central to the false accusation in the next passage.

Read beside Judah's conduct in chapter 38, Joseph's refusal offers a striking contrast. The narrative has shown Judah entering a sexual encounter he later cannot deny; it now shows Joseph refusing one despite repeated pressure from a woman with power over his circumstances.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read Joseph as an example of faithfulness to God, respect for another person's marriage, and decisive resistance to sexual sin. Wesley's notes on Genesis 39:2, 9–12 join God's presence with Joseph's refusal and his escape from the situation.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
The blessing reaches beyond Joseph to an Egyptian household. That is a concrete glimpse of the wider theme in Genesis 12:2–3: God's blessing through Abraham's family is meant to reach others. Joseph is still enslaved, yet God's care for him also brings good to people outside his family.

Joseph's refusal under pressure also offers a useful parallel to Jesus resisting temptation in Matthew 4:1–11. Both accounts show obedience to God taking priority over an offered way forward. The comparison concerns faithful refusal; it does not make their circumstances identical or promise that doing right will immediately make life easier. Joseph's next trial will show the cost his refusal brings.

passages.title: Genesis 39:13-23
passages.section_title: Joseph Falsely Imprisoned

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 When she saw that he had left his cloak in her hand and had run out of the house, 14 she called her household servants. “Look,” she said, “this Hebrew has been brought to us to make sport of us. He came to me so he could sleep with me, but I screamed as loud as I could. 15 When he heard me scream for help, he left his cloak beside me and ran out of the house.” 16 So Potiphar’s wife kept Joseph’s cloak beside her until his master came home. 17 Then she told him the same story: “The Hebrew slave you brought us came to me to make sport of me, 18 but when I screamed for help, he left his cloak beside me and ran out of the house.” 19 When his master heard the story his wife told him, saying, “This is what your slave did to me,” he burned with anger. 20 So Joseph’s master took him and had him thrown into the prison where the king’s prisoners were confined. While Joseph was there in the prison, 21 the LORD was with him and extended kindness to him, granting him favor in the eyes of the prison warden. 22 And the warden put all the prisoners under Joseph’s care, so that he was responsible for all that was done in the prison. 23 The warden did not concern himself with anything under Joseph’s care, because the LORD was with Joseph and gave him success in whatever he did.

He came to me so he could sleep with me, but I screamed as loud as I could. 15 When he heard me scream for help, he left his cloak beside me and ran out of the house.”

16 So Potiphar’s wife kept Joseph’s cloak beside her until his master came home. 17 Then she told him the same story: “The Hebrew slave you brought us came to me to make sport of me, 18 but when I screamed for help, he left his cloak beside me and ran out of the house.”

19 When his master heard the story his wife told him, saying, “This is what your slave did to me,” he burned with anger. 20 So Joseph’s master took him and had him thrown into the prison where the king’s prisoners were confined. While Joseph was there in the prison, 21 the LORD was with him and extended kindness to him, granting him favor in the eyes of the prison warden. 22 And the warden put all the prisoners under Joseph’s care, so that he was responsible for all that was done in the prison. 23 The warden did not concern himself with anything under Joseph’s care, because the LORD was with Joseph and gave him success in whatever he did.

passages.context_html:
Potiphar's wife uses the cloak Joseph left behind to support a false account of what happened. She tells the servants, then her husband, that Joseph approached her sexually and fled when she screamed. The reader has already seen the reverse: she pursued him, and he fled her grasp.

Her accusation repeatedly emphasizes Joseph's identity as a Hebrew and a slave, and she blames her husband for bringing him into the household. Potiphar becomes angry and sends Joseph to the place where the king's prisoners are confined. The account does not tell us all his private conclusions about either Joseph or his wife.

As in the earlier deception of Jacob, a garment becomes supposed evidence for a false story. Joseph loses his place in the household after doing what is right. Yet the account immediately repeats that the LORD is with him, showing kindness and giving him favor with the prison warden.

The Hebrew word for favor is חֵן, ḥēn (khayn). Brown–Driver–Briggs gives the sense of favor or acceptance and specifically cites Genesis 39:21. Here God's care is expressed through the warden's trust: he puts the prisoners and their affairs under Joseph's supervision. God's presence continues inside the prison, before release or vindication comes.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly see unjust suffering alongside God's continuing care. Joseph's imprisonment does not show that God has abandoned him or that his refusal was a mistake. Wesley's notes on Genesis 39:20–21 emphasize that confinement cannot shut out God's presence and connect Joseph's experience with the suffering of Christ.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 7:9–10 directly gathers Joseph's troubles into the larger account of God's presence, eventual rescue, and gift of authority in Egypt. Psalm 105:17–22 likewise places his confinement before his release and appointment to serve. Prison is a real injustice, but it does not put him beyond God's reach or end his role in preserving life.

His suffering after refusing wrong also offers a parallel to the New Testament's account of Christ's faithful endurance. 1 Peter 2:19–24 speaks of suffering for doing good and points to Jesus, who entrusted Himself to the One who judges justly. Christ's bearing of sins is His own saving work; the shared lesson is that God's care and a person's faithful obedience can be present even when the immediate outcome is unjust suffering.

passages.title: Genesis 40:1-23
passages.section_title: The Cupbearer and the Baker

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Some time later, the king’s cupbearer and baker offended their master, the king of Egypt. 2 Pharaoh was angry with his two officers, the chief cupbearer and the chief baker, 3 and imprisoned them in the house of the captain of the guard, the same prison where Joseph was confined. 4 The captain of the guard assigned them to Joseph, and he became their personal attendant. After they had been in custody for some time, 5 both of these men—the Egyptian king’s cupbearer and baker, who were being held in the prison—had a dream on the same night, and each dream had its own meaning. 6 When Joseph came to them in the morning, he saw that they were distraught. 7 So he asked the officials of Pharaoh who were in custody with him in his master’s house, “Why are your faces so downcast today?” 8 “We both had dreams,” they replied, “but there is no one to interpret them.” Then Joseph said to them, “Don’t interpretations belong to God? Tell me your dreams.” 9 So the chief cupbearer told Joseph his dream: “In my dream there was a vine before me, 10 and on the vine were three branches. As it budded, its blossoms opened and its clusters ripened into grapes. 11 Pharaoh’s cup was in my hand, and I took the grapes, squeezed them into his cup, and placed the cup in his hand.” 12 Joseph replied, “This is the interpretation: The three branches are three days. 13 Within three days Pharaoh will lift up your head and restore your position. You will put Pharaoh’s cup in his hand, just as you did when you were his cupbearer. 14 But when it goes well for you, please remember me and show me kindness by mentioning me to Pharaoh, that he might bring me out of this prison. 15 For I was kidnapped from the land of the Hebrews, and even here I have done nothing for which they should have put me in this dungeon.” 16 When the chief baker saw that the interpretation was favorable, he said to Joseph, “I too had a dream: There were three baskets of white bread on my head. 17 In the top basket were all sorts of baked goods for Pharaoh, but the birds were eating them out of the basket on my head.” 18 Joseph replied, “This is the interpretation: The three baskets are three days. 19 Within three days Pharaoh will lift off your head and hang you on a tree. Then the birds will eat the flesh of your body.” 20 On the third day, which was Pharaoh’s birthday, he held a feast for all his officials, and in their presence he lifted up the heads of the chief cupbearer and the chief baker. 21 Pharaoh restored the chief cupbearer to his position, so that he once again placed the cup in Pharaoh’s hand. 22 But Pharaoh hanged the chief baker, just as Joseph had described to them in his interpretation. 23 The chief cupbearer, however, did not remember Joseph; he forgot all about him.

As it budded, its blossoms opened and its clusters ripened into grapes. 11 Pharaoh’s cup was in my hand, and I took the grapes, squeezed them into his cup, and placed the cup in his hand.”

12 Joseph replied, “This is the interpretation: The three branches are three days. 13 Within three days Pharaoh will lift up your head and restore your position. You will put Pharaoh’s cup in his hand, just as you did when you were his cupbearer. 14 But when it goes well for you, please remember me and show me kindness by mentioning me to Pharaoh, that he might bring me out of this prison. 15 For I was kidnapped from the land of the Hebrews, and even here I have done nothing for which they should have put me in this dungeon.”

16 When the chief baker saw that the interpretation was favorable, he said to Joseph, “I too had a dream: There were three baskets of white bread on my head. 17 In the top basket were all sorts of baked goods for Pharaoh, but the birds were eating them out of the basket on my head.”

18 Joseph replied, “This is the interpretation: The three baskets are three days. 19 Within three days Pharaoh will lift off your head and hang you on a tree. Then the birds will eat the flesh of your body.”

20 On the third day, which was Pharaoh’s birthday, he held a feast for all his officials, and in their presence he lifted up the heads of the chief cupbearer and the chief baker. 21 Pharaoh restored the chief cupbearer to his position, so that he once again placed the cup in Pharaoh’s hand. 22 But Pharaoh hanged the chief baker, just as Joseph had described to them in his interpretation.
23 The chief cupbearer, however, did not remember Joseph; he forgot all about him.

passages.context_html:
Two of Pharaoh's officials, his chief cupbearer and chief baker, offend him and are confined in the prison where Joseph is held. The captain of the guard assigns Joseph to attend them. The account does not state their offenses; what matters for the story is that these men from Pharaoh's court now come into contact with Joseph.

Both have troubling dreams on the same night. Joseph notices their distress and asks about it. When they say no interpreter is available, he directs their attention to God as the source of interpretation and invites them to tell him the dreams. He offers to help without presenting the ability as his own independent power.

The cupbearer's dream concerns a vine, grapes, and Pharaoh's cup. Joseph explains that he will be restored to his position in three days. He then asks the man to remember him and mention his case to Pharaoh, explaining that he was kidnapped and has done nothing to deserve imprisonment. His trust in God leaves room to seek release from injustice.

The baker hopes for an equally favorable answer, but his dream of bread baskets and birds has a different meaning. Joseph says he will be executed in three days. At Pharaoh's birthday feast, both interpretations prove true: the cupbearer returns to service, while the baker is hanged.

The chapter ends with disappointment for Joseph. The restored cupbearer forgets him. A real connection to Pharaoh has been made, and Joseph's interpretation has been confirmed, but his request for help brings no immediate release.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly see God's gift at work through Joseph, along with the difficulty of waiting when help seems possible but does not come. Wesley's notes on Genesis 40:8, 14 emphasize both Joseph's crediting God and the legitimacy of his desire for freedom. Faithful service in prison does not require him to approve his wrongful confinement.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
This meeting supplies the human connection that will eventually bring Joseph before Pharaoh. Psalm 105:17–22 places Joseph's confinement and the testing of his word before the king's release and appointment of him. The sequence gives the chapter a place in God's preparation to preserve life through Joseph.

Joseph is also attentive to other people's distress while still suffering himself. That fits the wider theme in 2 Corinthians 1:3–7, where God's comfort in trouble equips His people to care for others. The accounts differ, but both show that someone enduring hardship can still become a means of help to those nearby.

passages.title: Genesis 41:1-13
passages.section_title: The Dreams of Pharaoh

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 After two full years had passed, Pharaoh had a dream: He was standing beside the Nile, 2 when seven cows, sleek and well-fed, came up from the river and began to graze among the reeds. 3 After them, seven other cows, sickly and thin, came up from the Nile and stood beside the well-fed cows on the bank of the river. 4 And the cows that were sickly and thin devoured the seven sleek, well-fed cows. Then Pharaoh woke up, 5 but he fell back asleep and dreamed a second time: Seven heads of grain, plump and ripe, came up on one stalk. 6 After them, seven other heads of grain sprouted, thin and scorched by the east wind. 7 And the thin heads of grain swallowed up the seven plump, ripe ones. Then Pharaoh awoke and realized it was a dream. 8 In the morning his spirit was troubled, so he summoned all the magicians and wise men of Egypt. Pharaoh told them his dreams, but no one could interpret them for him. 9 Then the chief cupbearer said to Pharaoh, “Today I recall my failures. 10 Pharaoh was once angry with his servants, and he put me and the chief baker in the custody of the captain of the guard. 11 One night both the chief baker and I had dreams, and each dream had its own meaning. 12 Now a young Hebrew was there with us, a servant of the captain of the guard. We told him our dreams and he interpreted them for us individually. 13 And it happened to us just as he had interpreted: I was restored to my position, and the other man was hanged.”

Then Pharaoh woke up, 5 but he fell back asleep and dreamed a second time: Seven heads of grain, plump and ripe, came up on one stalk. 6 After them, seven other heads of grain sprouted, thin and scorched by the east wind. 7 And the thin heads of grain swallowed up the seven plump, ripe ones. Then Pharaoh awoke and realized it was a dream.
8 In the morning his spirit was troubled, so he summoned all the magicians and wise men of Egypt. Pharaoh told them his dreams, but no one could interpret them for him.

9 Then the chief cupbearer said to Pharaoh, “Today I recall my failures. 10 Pharaoh was once angry with his servants, and he put me and the chief baker in the custody of the captain of the guard. 11 One night both the chief baker and I had dreams, and each dream had its own meaning. 12 Now a young Hebrew was there with us, a servant of the captain of the guard. We told him our dreams and he interpreted them for us individually. 13 And it happened to us just as he had interpreted: I was restored to my position, and the other man was hanged.”

passages.context_html:
Two full years pass after the cupbearer returns to Pharaoh's service. Joseph remains in prison. The narrative marks the delay before describing the event that finally brings his name before the king: Pharaoh has two dreams that trouble him.

In the first, seven healthy cows come out of the Nile, followed by seven gaunt cows that eat them. In the second, seven full heads of grain are swallowed by seven thin heads scorched by the east wind. The repeated movement from abundance to something that consumes it makes the dreams disturbing, but their meaning has not yet been explained.

Pharaoh summons Egypt's magicians and wise men, but none can interpret the dreams for him. The cupbearer then recalls his earlier failures and tells Pharaoh about the young Hebrew who interpreted the prison dreams. He can report a result the king's court can recognize: one official was restored, and the other was hanged, exactly as Joseph had said.

The forgotten prisoner is now recommended because of a specific, tested experience. The chapter has not yet shown his release, but the failure of Pharaoh's advisers and the cupbearer's recollection bring the story to the threshold of a sudden change.
passages.common_interpretations_html: A common Christian reading sees God bringing the earlier prison encounter into use at the moment Pharaoh needs an answer. Wesley's notes on Genesis 41:8–9 emphasize the failure of the royal advisers and the timing of Joseph's eventual opportunity. The two-year interval makes clear that the answer comes after a substantial wait.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
The delay and the new opportunity belong to the same longer story. Psalm 105:19–22 describes Joseph waiting until his prediction comes true, then being released and placed in authority. What the cupbearer had forgotten becomes relevant again when Pharaoh cannot obtain an answer elsewhere.

God's preparation here reaches beyond improving Joseph's circumstances. The coming famine will threaten many people, including Jacob's household. Acts 7:9–14 later joins Joseph's rescue and appointment with the family's need for food and its move to Egypt. His long-awaited opening is part of provision for others as well as release for himself.

passages.title: Genesis 41:14-36
passages.section_title: Joseph Interprets Pharaoh’s Dreams

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 So Pharaoh sent for Joseph, who was quickly brought out of the dungeon. After he had shaved and changed his clothes, he went in before Pharaoh. 15 Pharaoh said to Joseph, “I had a dream, and no one can interpret it. But I have heard it said of you that when you hear a dream you can interpret it.” 16 “I myself cannot do it,” Joseph replied, “but God will give Pharaoh a sound answer.” 17 Then Pharaoh said to Joseph: “In my dream I was standing on the bank of the Nile, 18 when seven cows, well-fed and sleek, came up from the river and began to graze among the reeds. 19 After them, seven other cows—sickly, ugly, and thin—came up. I have never seen such ugly cows in all the land of Egypt! 20 Then the thin, ugly cows devoured the seven well-fed cows that were there first. 21 When they had devoured them, however, no one could tell that they had done so; their appearance was as ugly as it had been before. Then I awoke. 22 In my dream I also saw seven heads of grain, plump and ripe, growing on a single stalk. 23 After them, seven other heads of grain sprouted—withered, thin, and scorched by the east wind. 24 And the thin heads of grain swallowed the seven plump ones. I told this dream to the magicians, but no one could explain it to me.” 25 At this, Joseph said to Pharaoh, “The dreams of Pharaoh are one and the same. God has revealed to Pharaoh what He is about to do. 26 The seven good cows are seven years, and the seven ripe heads of grain are seven years. The dreams have the same meaning. 27 Moreover, the seven thin, ugly cows that came up after them are seven years, and so are the seven worthless heads of grain scorched by the east wind—they are seven years of famine. 28 It is just as I said to Pharaoh: God has shown Pharaoh what He is about to do. 29 Behold, seven years of great abundance are coming throughout the land of Egypt, 30 but seven years of famine will follow them. Then all the abundance in the land of Egypt will be forgotten, and the famine will devastate the land. 31 The abundance in the land will not be remembered, since the famine that follows it will be so severe. 32 Moreover, because the dream was given to Pharaoh in two versions, the matter has been decreed by God, and He will carry it out shortly. 33 Now, therefore, Pharaoh should look for a discerning and wise man and set him over the land of Egypt. 34 Let Pharaoh take action and appoint commissioners over the land to take a fifth of the harvest of Egypt during the seven years of abundance. 35 Under the authority of Pharaoh, let them collect all the excess food from these good years, that they may come and lay up the grain to be preserved as food in the cities. 36 This food will be a reserve for the land during the seven years of famine to come upon the land of Egypt. Then the country will not perish in the famine.”

I told this dream to the magicians, but no one could explain it to me.”

God has revealed to Pharaoh what He is about to do. 26 The seven good cows are seven years, and the seven ripe heads of grain are seven years. The dreams have the same meaning. 27 Moreover, the seven thin, ugly cows that came up after them are seven years, and so are the seven worthless heads of grain scorched by the east wind—they are seven years of famine.

28 It is just as I said to Pharaoh: God has shown Pharaoh what He is about to do. 29 Behold, seven years of great abundance are coming throughout the land of Egypt, 30 but seven years of famine will follow them. Then all the abundance in the land of Egypt will be forgotten, and the famine will devastate the land. 31 The abundance in the land will not be remembered, since the famine that follows it will be so severe.
32 Moreover, because the dream was given to Pharaoh in two versions, the matter has been decreed by God, and He will carry it out shortly.

33 Now, therefore, Pharaoh should look for a discerning and wise man and set him over the land of Egypt. 34 Let Pharaoh take action and appoint commissioners over the land to take a fifth of the harvest of Egypt during the seven years of abundance. 35 Under the authority of Pharaoh, let them collect all the excess food from these good years, that they may come and lay up the grain to be preserved as food in the cities. 36 This food will be a reserve for the land during the seven years of famine to come upon the land of Egypt. Then the country will not perish in the famine.”

passages.context_html:
Pharaoh sends for Joseph, who is brought quickly from the dungeon, shaves, changes his clothes, and appears before the king. Pharaoh has heard that he can interpret dreams. Joseph immediately gives the credit to God and says that God will provide the answer.

After hearing the dreams, Joseph explains that they carry the same message. The seven healthy cows and full heads of grain represent seven years of abundance. The seven gaunt cows and scorched heads represent seven years of famine so severe that the earlier plenty will be forgotten. The repeated dream means the matter has been settled by God and will happen soon.

Joseph then moves from explaining the warning to proposing a response. He recommends appointing a wise leader and commissioners to collect a fifth of the harvest during the good years. Grain should be stored in the cities under Pharaoh's authority so that reserves will be available when the famine comes.

The interpretation and the proposal belong together, but they are distinct. Joseph explains what the dreams announce, then recommends how the country can prepare. Trust in God's warning leads to careful work with the resources available before the crisis.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as both a God-given warning and an example of wisdom in acting on it. Wesley's notes on Genesis 41:16, 29–30 emphasize Joseph's humility and the provision made possible by abundance arriving before famine. Giving God the credit goes together with responsible preparation.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
God's provision takes a practical form: a warning, an explanation, a plan, and stored grain. Psalm 105:16–22 places Joseph's wisdom and authority within the larger account of famine and God's care. The answer does not remove the need to organize people and prepare before the shortage arrives.

The wider biblical theme is that God gives abilities for service. 1 Corinthians 12:4–7, 11 describes the Spirit's gifts as serving the common good. Paul's subject is the church, while Joseph is serving in Egypt; the shared lesson is that what God gives a person is meant to help others, rather than simply increase that person's standing.

passages.title: Genesis 41:37-45
passages.section_title: Joseph Given Charge of Egypt

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 37 This proposal pleased Pharaoh and all his officials. 38 So Pharaoh asked them, “Can we find anyone like this man, in whom the Spirit of God abides?” 39 Then Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Since God has made all this known to you, there is no one as discerning and wise as you. 40 You shall be in charge of my house, and all my people are to obey your commands. Only with regard to the throne will I be greater than you.” 41 Pharaoh also told Joseph, “I hereby place you over all the land of Egypt.” 42 Then Pharaoh removed the signet ring from his finger, put it on Joseph’s finger, clothed him in garments of fine linen, and placed a gold chain around his neck. 43 He had Joseph ride in his second chariot, with men calling out before him, “Bow the knee!” So he placed him over all the land of Egypt. 44 And Pharaoh declared to Joseph, “I am Pharaoh, but without your permission, no one in all the land of Egypt shall lift his hand or foot.” 45 Pharaoh gave Joseph the name Zaphenath-paneah, and he gave him Asenath daughter of Potiphera, priest of On, to be his wife. And Joseph took charge of all the land of Egypt.
paragraphs: 37 This proposal pleased Pharaoh and all his officials. 38 So Pharaoh asked them, “Can we find anyone like this man, in whom the Spirit of God abides?”

39 Then Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Since God has made all this known to you, there is no one as discerning and wise as you. 40 You shall be in charge of my house, and all my people are to obey your commands. Only with regard to the throne will I be greater than you.”

41 Pharaoh also told Joseph, “I hereby place you over all the land of Egypt.” 42 Then Pharaoh removed the signet ring from his finger, put it on Joseph’s finger, clothed him in garments of fine linen, and placed a gold chain around his neck. 43 He had Joseph ride in his second chariot, with men calling out before him, “Bow the knee!” So he placed him over all the land of Egypt.
44 And Pharaoh declared to Joseph, “I am Pharaoh, but without your permission, no one in all the land of Egypt shall lift his hand or foot.”
45 Pharaoh gave Joseph the name Zaphenath-paneah, and he gave him Asenath daughter of Potiphera, priest of On, to be his wife. And Joseph took charge of all the land of Egypt.

passages.context_html:
Pharaoh and his officials approve Joseph's proposal. Pharaoh recognizes that God has made the matter known to Joseph and that his wisdom fits the responsibility he has described. He places Joseph over his household and all Egypt, reserving only the throne for himself.

The appointment is made public through concrete signs: Pharaoh's signet ring, fine linen, a gold chain, and a ride in the second chariot. People are called to bow before Joseph. These actions give public force to the king's declaration that Joseph's authority must be respected throughout the land.

Pharaoh also gives him an Egyptian name, Zaphenath-paneah, and Asenath, daughter of Potiphera the priest of On, as his wife. The man who entered Egypt as a slave is now entrusted with the nation's preparations for famine. His new place in Egyptian society will also become the setting for the birth of his sons.

The reversal is striking beside the earlier chapters. His brothers stripped him of a robe, and a later garment was used to accuse him falsely. Now he receives clothing and other signs of honor from the king. The authority shown in his youthful dreams is beginning to take a public form, though his family does not yet know what has happened.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the appointment as Joseph's vindication and preparation to preserve life in the famine. Wesley's note on Genesis 41:44 also draws a Christian comparison with the authority given to Christ. The comparison follows the movement from suffering to honor and from personal authority to care for others.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 7:9–10 directly identifies Joseph's appointment as the result of God giving him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh. The man his brothers sold is the one God places in a position that will help them survive. Their rejection has not defeated God's purpose for the family.

Joseph's rise also offers an established parallel to the honor and authority given to Jesus, as Wesley's Genesis 41:44 note recognizes. Philippians 2:8–11 joins Jesus' obedient suffering with God's exalting Him and every knee bowing. Joseph's delegated rule over Egypt helps illustrate the pattern, while Jesus' lordship extends far beyond one nation and one crisis.

passages.title: Genesis 41:46-52
passages.section_title: The Seven Years of Plenty

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 46 Now Joseph was thirty years old when he entered the service of Pharaoh king of Egypt. And Joseph left Pharaoh’s presence and traveled throughout the land of Egypt. 47 During the seven years of abundance, the land brought forth bountifully. 48 During those seven years, Joseph collected all the excess food in the land of Egypt and stored it in the cities. In every city he laid up the food from the fields around it. 49 So Joseph stored up grain in such abundance, like the sand of the sea, that he stopped keeping track of it; for it was beyond measure. 50 Before the years of famine arrived, two sons were born to Joseph by Asenath daughter of Potiphera, priest of On. 51 Joseph named the firstborn Manasseh, saying, “God has made me forget all my hardship and all my father’s household.” 52 And the second son he named Ephraim, saying, “God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction.”
paragraphs: 46 Now Joseph was thirty years old when he entered the service of Pharaoh king of Egypt. And Joseph left Pharaoh’s presence and traveled throughout the land of Egypt.

47 During the seven years of abundance, the land brought forth bountifully. 48 During those seven years, Joseph collected all the excess food in the land of Egypt and stored it in the cities. In every city he laid up the food from the fields around it. 49 So Joseph stored up grain in such abundance, like the sand of the sea, that he stopped keeping track of it; for it was beyond measure.

50 Before the years of famine arrived, two sons were born to Joseph by Asenath daughter of Potiphera, priest of On. 51 Joseph named the firstborn Manasseh, saying, “God has made me forget all my hardship and all my father’s household.” 52 And the second son he named Ephraim, saying, “God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction.”

passages.context_html:
Joseph is thirty when he enters Pharaoh's service and travels through Egypt. During the seven years of abundance, he gathers food and stores it in the cities near the fields that produce it. The amount becomes so great that the account compares it with the sand of the sea and says he stops keeping track.

Before the famine arrives, Asenath bears him two sons. Joseph names the first Manasseh, מְנַשֶּׁה, Mĕnaššeh (meh-nash-SHEH), connecting the name with God making him forget his hardship and his father's household. Brown–Driver–Briggs records the connection with forgetting in Genesis 41:51.

He names the second Ephraim, אֶפְרַיִם, ʾEprayim (ef-RAH-yim), connecting the name with God making him fruitful in the land of his affliction. Brown–Driver–Briggs likewise connects Genesis 41:52 with bearing fruit. Both names acknowledge God in the new life Joseph is building.

The names hold relief and painful history together. Egypt has brought real hardship, and Joseph still calls it the land of his affliction even as he gives thanks for fruitfulness there. Later chapters will show how deeply his family still matters to him. The birth notices prepare for the significant place these two sons will have in Israel's future.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read Joseph's work as faithful preparation and his sons' names as an acknowledgment of God's care after suffering. Wesley's note on Genesis 41:50 emphasizes both meanings while recognizing that relief from misery does not mean Joseph has ceased to care about his father's family.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The stored grain and growing household show provision taking shape before the famine. Psalm 105:16–22 later places Joseph's authority within God's advance care, and Genesis 48:5 will give Ephraim and Manasseh a place among Jacob's own sons. A family established in Egypt will become part of the people who inherit God's promise.

Joseph also gives thanks while naming the place of his earlier pain. That fits the wider theme of God's comfort within affliction in 2 Corinthians 1:3–7. Gratitude for new good does not require the story of suffering to disappear. Scripture can acknowledge both the wound and the care that sustains a life beyond it.

passages.title: Genesis 41:53-57
passages.section_title: The Famine Begins

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 53 When the seven years of abundance in the land of Egypt came to an end, 54 the seven years of famine began, just as Joseph had said. And although there was famine in every country, there was food throughout the land of Egypt. 55 When extreme hunger came to all the land of Egypt and the people cried out to Pharaoh for food, he told all the Egyptians, “Go to Joseph and do whatever he tells you.” 56 When the famine had spread over all the land, Joseph opened up all the storehouses and sold grain to the Egyptians; for the famine was severe in the land of Egypt. 57 And every nation came to Joseph in Egypt to buy grain, because the famine was severe over all the earth.
paragraphs: 53 When the seven years of abundance in the land of Egypt came to an end, 54 the seven years of famine began, just as Joseph had said. And although there was famine in every country, there was food throughout the land of Egypt. 55 When extreme hunger came to all the land of Egypt and the people cried out to Pharaoh for food, he told all the Egyptians, “Go to Joseph and do whatever he tells you.”

56 When the famine had spread over all the land, Joseph opened up all the storehouses and sold grain to the Egyptians; for the famine was severe in the land of Egypt. 57 And every nation came to Joseph in Egypt to buy grain, because the famine was severe over all the earth.

passages.context_html:
The seven good years end, and the famine begins just as Joseph said. The shortage reaches beyond Egypt, but Egypt has food because preparations were made during the abundance. The warnings that sounded remote have become the conditions under which people must now live.

When the Egyptians cry to Pharaoh for food, he directs them to Joseph and tells them to follow his instructions. Joseph opens the storehouses and sells grain. The authority entrusted to him during the years of preparation now becomes responsibility for distributing what has been preserved.

People from other nations also come to Egypt to buy food because the famine is widespread. The account moves from an Egyptian crisis to a need that draws outsiders to Joseph. That prepares the next chapter, where Jacob learns there is grain in Egypt and sends Joseph's brothers to obtain it.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the famine as the fulfillment of the warning and the moment when Joseph's preparation preserves life. Wesley's introduction to Genesis 41 and note on verse 54 connect his appointment with provision for Jacob's family and the surrounding lands.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 7:11–14 explicitly connects the famine with the family's journeys for grain and eventual reunion with Joseph. Psalm 105:16–22 also places the famine and Joseph's advance arrival within God's care. The food available in Egypt becomes a means of preserving the family through which the promise continues.

Joseph's role as the appointed provider of food also offers a helpful Christian parallel to Jesus as the giver of life. Wesley's note on Genesis 41:44 develops Joseph's role as a distributor in its comparison with Christ. In John 6:27–35, Jesus directs people beyond food that perishes to the life the Father gives through Him. Joseph's grain sustains people through famine; the greater gift Jesus offers is eternal life.

passages.title: Genesis 42:1-24
passages.section_title: Joseph’s Brothers Sent to Egypt

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 When Jacob learned that there was grain in Egypt, he said to his sons, “Why are you staring at one another?” 2 “Look,” he added, “I have heard that there is grain in Egypt. Go down there and buy some for us, so that we may live and not die.” 3 So ten of Joseph’s brothers went down to buy grain from Egypt. 4 But Jacob did not send Joseph’s brother Benjamin with his brothers, for he said, “I am afraid that harm might befall him.” 5 So the sons of Israel were among those who came to buy grain, since the famine had also spread to the land of Canaan. 6 Now Joseph was the ruler of the land; he was the one who sold grain to all its people. So when his brothers arrived, they bowed down before him with their faces to the ground. 7 And when Joseph saw his brothers, he recognized them, but he treated them as strangers and spoke harshly to them. “Where have you come from?” he asked. “From the land of Canaan,” they replied. “We are here to buy food.” 8 Although Joseph recognized his brothers, they did not recognize him. 9 Joseph remembered his dreams about them and said, “You are spies! You have come to see if our land is vulnerable.” 10 “Not so, my lord,” they replied. “Your servants have come to buy food. 11 We are all sons of one man. Your servants are honest men, not spies.” 12 “No,” he told them. “You have come to see if our land is vulnerable.” 13 But they answered, “Your servants are twelve brothers, the sons of one man in the land of Canaan. The youngest is now with our father, and one is no more.” 14 Then Joseph declared, “Just as I said, you are spies! 15 And this is how you will be tested: As surely as Pharaoh lives, you shall not leave this place unless your youngest brother comes here. 16 Send one of your number to get your brother; the rest of you will be confined so that the truth of your words may be tested. If they are untrue, then as surely as Pharaoh lives, you are spies!” 17 So Joseph imprisoned them for three days, 18 and on the third day he said to them, “I fear God. So do this and you will live: 19 If you are honest, leave one of your brothers in custody while the rest of you go and take back grain to relieve the hunger of your households. 20 Then bring your youngest brother to me so that your words can be verified, that you may not die.” And to this they consented. 21 Then they said to one another, “Surely we are being punished because of our brother. We saw his anguish when he pleaded with us, but we would not listen. That is why this distress has come upon us.” 22 And Reuben responded, “Didn’t I tell you not to sin against the boy? But you would not listen. Now we must account for his blood!” 23 They did not realize that Joseph understood them, since there was an interpreter between them. 24 And he turned away from them and wept. When he turned back and spoke to them, he took Simeon from them and had him bound before their eyes.

2 “Look,” he added, “I have heard that there is grain in Egypt. Go down there and buy some for us, so that we may live and not die.”
3 So ten of Joseph’s brothers went down to buy grain from Egypt. 4 But Jacob did not send Joseph’s brother Benjamin with his brothers, for he said, “I am afraid that harm might befall him.”
5 So the sons of Israel were among those who came to buy grain, since the famine had also spread to the land of Canaan.

6 Now Joseph was the ruler of the land; he was the one who sold grain to all its people. So when his brothers arrived, they bowed down before him with their faces to the ground. 7 And when Joseph saw his brothers, he recognized them, but he treated them as strangers and spoke harshly to them. “Where have you come from?” he asked.
“From the land of Canaan,” they replied. “We are here to buy food.”
8 Although Joseph recognized his brothers, they did not recognize him. 9 Joseph remembered his dreams about them and said, “You are spies! You have come to see if our land is vulnerable.”
10 “Not so, my lord,” they replied. “Your servants have come to buy food. 11 We are all sons of one man. Your servants are honest men, not spies.”
12 “No,” he told them. “You have come to see if our land is vulnerable.”
13 But they answered, “Your servants are twelve brothers, the sons of one man in the land of Canaan. The youngest is now with our father, and one is no more.”

14 Then Joseph declared, “Just as I said, you are spies! 15 And this is how you will be tested: As surely as Pharaoh lives, you shall not leave this place unless your youngest brother comes here. 16 Send one of your number to get your brother; the rest of you will be confined so that the truth of your words may be tested. If they are untrue, then as surely as Pharaoh lives, you are spies!”

17 So Joseph imprisoned them for three days, 18 and on the third day he said to them, “I fear God. So do this and you will live: 19 If you are honest, leave one of your brothers in custody while the rest of you go and take back grain to relieve the hunger of your households. 20 Then bring your youngest brother to me so that your words can be verified, that you may not die.”
And to this they consented.

21 Then they said to one another, “Surely we are being punished because of our brother. We saw his anguish when he pleaded with us, but we would not listen. That is why this distress has come upon us.”
22 And Reuben responded, “Didn’t I tell you not to sin against the boy? But you would not listen. Now we must account for his blood!”

23 They did not realize that Joseph understood them, since there was an interpreter between them. 24 And he turned away from them and wept. When he turned back and spoke to them, he took Simeon from them and had him bound before their eyes.

passages.context_html:
The famine reaches Jacob's household in Canaan. Hearing that grain is available in Egypt, he sends ten sons to buy food but keeps Benjamin at home because he fears harm may come to him. The brothers arrive among other buyers and bow before Joseph, the ruler responsible for selling grain.

Joseph recognizes them, but they do not recognize him. He remembers his dreams and treats them as strangers, accusing them of spying out the country's weakness. They insist that they are honest men from one family, explaining that the youngest brother remains with their father and another is no more. The reader knows that the brother they describe as gone is standing before them.

Joseph initially proposes sending one brother for Benjamin while the others remain confined. After three days, he changes the arrangement: one will stay, while the rest may carry grain home and return with the youngest brother to verify their account. He states that he fears God and allows food to be taken to their hungry households.

Under this pressure, the brothers speak about what they did to Joseph. They remember his distress and their refusal to hear his pleas, and they connect their present trouble with that guilt. Reuben recalls his warning against harming him. They do not realize Joseph understands because he has been speaking through an interpreter.

Joseph turns away and weeps, then returns and has Simeon bound before them. His hidden emotion shows that the encounter reaches him deeply. The family is confronting its past, but Joseph has not yet disclosed his identity, and the test involving Benjamin remains ahead.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read the encounter as a turning point in the brothers' awareness of their guilt and the beginning of a movement toward reunion. Wesley's notes on Genesis 42:9, 21 understand Joseph as testing them with repentance in view. Wesley also criticizes Joseph's appeal to Pharaoh's life; his reading does not treat every part of Joseph's conduct as beyond criticism.

passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 7:11–13 directly recalls the famine, the first journey for grain, and Joseph making himself known on a later visit. The brother rejected by the family has become the person able to preserve it. Their bowing also recalls the future they once tried to prevent when they rejected his dreams.

The family's preservation includes a confrontation with its wrongdoing. 2 Corinthians 7:9–11 later distinguishes sorrow that produces repentance from sorrow alone. Here the brothers acknowledge what they did; the following events will show whether changed actions accompany that acknowledgment. Their story allows us to see reconciliation developing through truth and responsibility as well as the provision of food.

passages.context_html:
Joseph orders the brothers' bags filled with grain, their silver returned, and provisions supplied for the journey. They leave without knowing about the returned money. At an overnight stop, one brother opens his sack and discovers his silver. The men are frightened and ask what God has done to them.

Back in Canaan, they tell Jacob about the accusation of spying and the demand to bring Benjamin. Simeon has been kept in Egypt while they return with food. As they empty their sacks, every man finds his silver, deepening both their fear and their father's distress.

Jacob sees another threat of loss: Joseph is gone, Simeon is absent, and now Benjamin is being asked for. He concludes that everything is going against him. The reader knows more than he does: Joseph is alive and has supplied the food and money. Jacob must respond without that knowledge.

Reuben offers his own two sons' lives as a guarantee that Benjamin will return. Jacob rejects the proposal and refuses to send Benjamin, fearing that another loss would bring him to his death in sorrow. The chapter ends with food for the present but no resolution of Simeon's confinement or the demand that must be met for a return.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly see fear shaped by the family's unresolved past: the returned money appears threatening, and Jacob cannot bear the possibility of losing another son. Wesley's notes on Genesis 42:28, 38 connect the brothers' alarm with their awakened consciences and Jacob's refusal with his distrust after Joseph's disappearance.

passages.context_html:
The famine continues, and the grain brought from Egypt runs out. Jacob asks his sons to buy more, but Judah reminds him that they cannot appear before the Egyptian ruler without Benjamin. The family cannot avoid the earlier demand simply by waiting or making another purchase.

Jacob asks why they disclosed the existence of another brother. They reply that the ruler questioned them about their father and family and that they could not have anticipated his demand. Judah then offers to take personal responsibility for Benjamin's return. Unlike Reuben's offer involving his sons' lives, Judah places the continuing responsibility on himself.

This is a significant development for the man who proposed selling Joseph in Genesis 37. Judah now promises to protect the other son of Rachel so that the whole household, including its children, may live. His promise will be tested when Benjamin later faces danger.

Jacob finally agrees. He sends gifts from the land, additional silver for food, and the money that had been returned, allowing for the possibility of a mistake. He prays that God Almighty will grant them mercy before the ruler and bring back both Simeon and Benjamin. He acknowledges the possibility of bereavement even as he permits the journey.

The brothers take the gifts, double the silver, and Benjamin, and go down to stand before Joseph. Practical preparations and an appeal for God's mercy accompany a decision Jacob had earlier refused to make.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly recognize Judah's new willingness to accept responsibility and Jacob's difficult step of allowing Benjamin to go. Wesley's notes on Genesis 43:9, 11–14 connect Judah's care for Benjamin with a changed response to his earlier wrong and read Jacob's prayer as an appeal for mercy amid uncertainty.

passages.god_plan_html:
God's care for the promised family includes more than keeping it alive. The men who once abandoned Joseph must now take responsibility for another brother. Judah's commitment gives the story a direction toward restored relationships, while the family's need brings it back to the person God has placed in Egypt to help it.

That movement fits the wider call for repentance to bear fruit. In Luke 3:8, John calls Abraham's descendants to changed conduct instead of resting on their ancestry. Here, too, belonging to the promise family does not remove the need for a different way of treating one another. Judah's words begin to put responsibility where his earlier proposal had put another brother at risk.

passages.context_html:
When Joseph sees Benjamin, he tells his steward to bring the men home and prepare a meal. The brothers interpret the invitation as a threat, fearing that the returned silver will be used as a reason to enslave them. At the entrance they explain what happened and offer the money back, together with payment for more grain.

The steward reassures them, says that their God and their father's God gave them the treasure, and confirms that he received their silver. He brings Simeon out to them. Water is provided for washing their feet, and their donkeys are fed. The reception they feared becomes an unexpected welcome.

The reassurance begins with שָׁלוֹם, šālôm (shah-LOHM), peace or well-being. Brown–Driver–Briggs specifically records this reassuring use in Genesis 43:23. It answers their immediate fear and is followed by actions that give them reason to relax.

When Joseph arrives, the brothers present their gifts and bow before him. He asks about their father's welfare and blesses Benjamin. Seeing his full brother moves him so deeply that he leaves to weep privately, then washes his face and returns to the meal.

Joseph, the brothers, and the Egyptians are served separately; the account explains that the Egyptians regard eating with Hebrews as detestable. The brothers are astonished to find themselves seated in birth order. Benjamin receives five times the portion of the others, yet they feast and drink freely with Joseph. The scene leaves them together in hospitality before the more searching test of the next chapter.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly see a welcome that exceeds the brothers' frightened expectations, along with Joseph's affection and the continuing movement toward reunion. Wesley's notes on Genesis 43:23, 26, 29, 33–34 emphasize the steward's reassurance, the renewed bowing, Joseph's prayer for Benjamin, and the brothers' astonishment and relief.

passages.god_plan_html:
Kindness now joins the pressure that has brought the brothers back. They have spoken of their guilt and fear punishment, yet receive food, reassurance, their brother Simeon, and a place at the table. Joseph's hidden identity does not prevent his care from reaching them.

This offers a clear connection with the wider theme in Romans 2:4: God's kindness leads people toward repentance. Joseph's welcome does not erase the past or finish the reconciliation in this chapter. It shows how generosity can open a way forward as the family's response continues to unfold.

passages.section_title: Benjamin and the Silver Cup

passages.context_html:
Before the brothers leave, Joseph tells his steward to fill their sacks, return their silver, and put his silver cup in Benjamin's sack. The men depart at daybreak. The reader knows the cup has been planted, so the accusation that follows must be understood in that light.

Joseph sends the steward after them with an accusation of repaying kindness with theft. The cup is described in the charge as one used for divination. Joseph has earlier credited God with interpreting dreams; here the narrative reports the claim made about the cup without describing him performing a ritual.

The brothers insist on their innocence and point to their earlier return of the silver. So confident are they that they offer death for whoever has the cup and slavery for the rest. The steward sets a narrower consequence: only the man with the cup will become a slave. The search proceeds from oldest to youngest and ends with the cup in Benjamin's sack.

All the brothers tear their clothes and return to the city. They could leave Benjamin to face the stated penalty alone, but they go back together. Judah speaks for them before Joseph, saying that God has exposed their wrongdoing and offering them all as slaves.

Judah's question about how they can justify themselves uses the verb צָדַק, ṣādaq (tsah-DAHK), to be right or to clear oneself. Brown–Driver–Briggs specifically explains its form in Genesis 44:16 as clearing themselves from suspicion. They have not stolen the cup, but their words recall the real guilt they have already acknowledged concerning Joseph. He answers by again offering to keep only Benjamin and let the others return to their father.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read the episode as a test that reveals whether the brothers will abandon another son of Rachel. Wesley's introduction to Genesis 44 and note on verse 16 connect their return together with a change from their earlier treatment of Joseph. The charge concerning the cup is false, while their remembered wrongdoing against their brother is real.

passages.title: Genesis 44:18-34
passages.section_title: Judah Pleads for Benjamin

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 Then Judah approached Joseph and said, “Sir, please let your servant speak personally to my lord. Do not be angry with your servant, for you are equal to Pharaoh himself. 19 My lord asked his servants, ‘Do you have a father or a brother?’ 20 And we answered, ‘We have an elderly father and a younger brother, the child of his old age. The boy’s brother is dead. He is the only one of his mother’s sons left, and his father loves him.’ 21 Then you told your servants, ‘Bring him down to me so that I can see him for myself.’ 22 So we said to my lord, ‘The boy cannot leave his father. If he were to leave, his father would die.’ 23 But you said to your servants, ‘Unless your younger brother comes down with you, you will not see my face again.’ 24 Now when we returned to your servant my father, we relayed your words to him. 25 Then our father said, ‘Go back and buy us some food.’ 26 But we answered, ‘We cannot go down there unless our younger brother goes with us. So if our younger brother is not with us, we cannot see the man.’ 27 And your servant my father said to us, ‘You know that my wife bore me two sons. 28 When one of them was gone, I said: “Surely he has been torn to pieces.” And I have not seen him since. 29 Now if you also take this one from me and harm comes to him, you will bring my gray hair down to Sheol in sorrow.’ 30 So if the boy is not with us when I return to your servant, and if my father, whose life is wrapped up in the boy’s life, 31 sees that the boy is not with us, he will die. Then your servants will have brought the gray hair of your servant our father down to Sheol in sorrow. 32 Indeed, your servant guaranteed the boy’s safety to my father, saying, ‘If I do not return him to you, I will bear the guilt before you, my father, all my life.’ 33 Now please let your servant stay here as my lord’s slave in place of the boy. Let him return with his brothers. 34 For how can I go back to my father without the boy? I could not bear to see the misery that would overwhelm him.”

33 Now please let your servant stay here as my lord’s slave in place of the boy. Let him return with his brothers. 34 For how can I go back to my father without the boy? I could not bear to see the misery that would overwhelm him.”

passages.context_html:
Judah approaches Joseph respectfully and asks to speak. Rather than trying to explain the cup, he tells the story of Benjamin's place in the family and the difficulty of bringing him to Egypt. Joseph hears how Jacob has lived with the loss of one of Rachel's sons and fears losing the other.

Judah recalls the ruler's insistence that Benjamin come and their father's warning that harm to him would bring overwhelming grief. He now makes his plea personal: he guaranteed Benjamin's return and cannot bear to see what another loss would do to Jacob.

The speech ends with an offer. Judah asks to remain as Joseph's slave in Benjamin's place so that the younger brother can return with the others. His promise to protect Benjamin has become a willingness to bear the cost himself.

This reverses his earlier role in Joseph's sale. In Genesis 37, Judah proposed making another brother a slave. Here he offers his own freedom to prevent that happening to Benjamin. The man who helped bring grief to his father now pleads to spare him further sorrow.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand Judah's appeal as evidence of changed conduct, concern for his father, and willingness to protect his brother at personal cost. Wesley's note on Genesis 44:18 emphasizes the speech's tenderness and Judah's offer to take Benjamin's place. The account shows the earlier guarantee being put into action.

passages.god_plan_html:
Judah's offer provides a meaningful Christian parallel to someone willingly taking another's place. Matthew Henry's commentary on Genesis 44:18–34 explicitly connects his plea and guarantee with Christ. Hebrews 7:14, 22–25 identifies Jesus as descended from Judah and describes Him as the guarantee of a better covenant, always living to speak on behalf of those who approach God through Him.

The comparison reaches further in Jesus' own work. In Mark 10:45, He describes giving His life as a ransom for many. Judah offers his freedom to protect one brother; Jesus gives His life to save others. Judah's plea helps illustrate costly love, while Christ's death and continuing plea on our behalf accomplish the greater rescue the New Testament describes.

passages.title: Genesis 45:1-8
passages.section_title: Joseph Reveals His Identity

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then Joseph could no longer control himself before all his attendants, and he cried out, “Send everyone away from me!” So none of them were with Joseph when he made himself known to his brothers. 2 But he wept so loudly that the Egyptians heard him, and Pharaoh’s household soon heard of it. 3 Joseph said to his brothers, “I am Joseph! Is my father still alive?” But they were unable to answer him, because they were terrified in his presence. 4 Then Joseph said to his brothers, “Please come near me.” And they did so. “I am Joseph, your brother,” he said, “the one you sold into Egypt! 5 And now, do not be distressed or angry with yourselves that you sold me into this place, because it was to save lives that God sent me before you. 6 For the famine has covered the land these two years, and there will be five more years without plowing or harvesting. 7 God sent me before you to preserve you as a remnant on the earth and to save your lives by a great deliverance. 8 Therefore it was not you who sent me here, but God, who has made me a father to Pharaoh—lord of all his household and ruler over all the land of Egypt.

So none of them were with Joseph when he made himself known to his brothers. 2 But he wept so loudly that the Egyptians heard him, and Pharaoh’s household soon heard of it.
3 Joseph said to his brothers, “I am Joseph! Is my father still alive?”
But they were unable to answer him, because they were terrified in his presence.
4 Then Joseph said to his brothers, “Please come near me.” And they did so.

“I am Joseph, your brother,” he said, “the one you sold into Egypt! 5 And now, do not be distressed or angry with yourselves that you sold me into this place, because it was to save lives that God sent me before you. 6 For the famine has covered the land these two years, and there will be five more years without plowing or harvesting. 7 God sent me before you to preserve you as a remnant on the earth and to save your lives by a great deliverance. 8 Therefore it was not you who sent me here, but God, who has made me a father to Pharaoh—lord of all his household and ruler over all the land of Egypt.

passages.context_html:
After Judah's appeal, Joseph can no longer contain his emotion. He sends the attendants away and reveals himself to his brothers, weeping loudly enough for the Egyptians to hear. The ruler before whom they have been pleading identifies himself as the brother they sold.

The brothers are terrified and cannot answer. Joseph calls them closer and repeats who he is. His next words address their distress: God sent him ahead to save lives. The famine has lasted two years, and five more remain. His position in Egypt will preserve the family through the danger still ahead.

Joseph speaks of the same events from two perspectives. His brothers sold him, and he names that action directly. God has brought him to a place where their lives can be preserved. The saving purpose does not make the betrayal disappear; it explains why he can now meet them with reassurance instead of revenge.

He describes his position as a father to Pharaoh, lord of the royal household, and ruler over Egypt. These words convey the influence and responsibility that make his offer of help possible. The family has finally learned what the reader has watched developing through slavery, prison, and appointment.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read Joseph's explanation as God's ability to bring saving good from human wrongdoing, alongside Joseph's willingness to forgive. Wesley's notes on Genesis 45:5–8 distinguish the good God brings from the brothers' sinful intent. The Catholic Catechism, paragraph 312, likewise uses Joseph's story to explain that good brought from evil does not make the evil itself good.
