passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 7:9–14 directly recalls Joseph's rejection, God's presence with him, and his making himself known on the second visit. The rejected brother has become the means of preserving the family. Joseph's explanation here lets them see how the earlier suffering fits into that rescue.

His tears and invitation to draw near also offer a comparison with God's compassion toward returning sinners. Wesley's notes on Genesis 45:1–3 connect the scene with the father's welcome in Luke 15:20–24. The comparison concerns mercy that welcomes people whose wrongdoing is real. Reconciliation becomes possible without pretending that nothing happened.

passages.title: Genesis 45:9-15
passages.section_title: Joseph Sends for His Father

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 Now return quickly to my father and tell him, ‘This is what your son Joseph says: God has made me lord of all Egypt. Come down to me without delay. 10 You shall settle in the land of Goshen and be near me—you and your children and grandchildren, your flocks and herds, and everything you own. 11 And there I will provide for you, because there will be five more years of famine. Otherwise, you and your household and everything you own will come to destitution.’ 12 Behold! You and my brother Benjamin can see that I, Joseph, am the one speaking with you. 13 Tell my father about all my splendor in Egypt and everything you have seen. And bring my father down here quickly.” 14 Then Joseph threw his arms around his brother Benjamin and wept, and Benjamin wept as they embraced. 15 Joseph kissed each of his brothers as he wept over them. And afterward his brothers talked with him.

Come down to me without delay. 10 You shall settle in the land of Goshen and be near me—you and your children and grandchildren, your flocks and herds, and everything you own. 11 And there I will provide for you, because there will be five more years of famine. Otherwise, you and your household and everything you own will come to destitution.’

12 Behold! You and my brother Benjamin can see that I, Joseph, am the one speaking with you. 13 Tell my father about all my splendor in Egypt and everything you have seen. And bring my father down here quickly.”

14 Then Joseph threw his arms around his brother Benjamin and wept, and Benjamin wept as they embraced. 15 Joseph kissed each of his brothers as he wept over them. And afterward his brothers talked with him.

passages.context_html:
Joseph tells his brothers to hurry home and bring Jacob to Egypt. He offers a place in Goshen where the whole household, its children, grandchildren, and livestock can be near him. There are five more years of famine, and he intends to provide for them rather than leave them to be reduced to destitution.

He points to what the brothers, including Benjamin, can see and hear for themselves: Joseph is speaking with them. They are to tell their father about his position and everything they have witnessed, then bring him without delay. The news of his life comes with a practical invitation for the family's future.

Joseph embraces Benjamin, and both weep. He then kisses all his brothers and weeps over them. Finally they talk with him. The men who were unable to answer when he first disclosed his identity can now speak within an openly restored family relationship.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly see reconciliation expressed through affection and concrete care. Wesley's notes on Genesis 45:8, 12 emphasize Joseph's desire to comfort his father, assure the family of his identity, and provide for them during the remaining famine. His authority is being used to bring them near and sustain them.

passages.god_plan_html:
Joseph's invitation offers a Christian parallel between being welcomed and being cared for by the one who has gone ahead. Wesley's note on Genesis 45:12 connects Joseph's desire to have his family with him with Christ's desire for His people to be with Him.

In John 14:1–3, Jesus promises to prepare a place and welcome His disciples into His presence. Joseph's invitation concerns a real household's survival in Egypt; Jesus' promise reaches beyond that immediate need. The shared pattern helps explain the warmth of salvation: rescue includes welcome, belonging, and life with the One who provides it.

passages.title: Genesis 45:16-24
passages.section_title: Pharaoh Invites Jacob to Egypt

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 When the news reached Pharaoh’s house that Joseph’s brothers had come, Pharaoh and his servants were pleased. 17 Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Tell your brothers, ‘Do as follows: Load your animals and return to the land of Canaan. 18 Then bring your father and your families and return to me. I will give you the best of the land of Egypt, and you shall eat from the fat of the land.’ 19 You are also directed to tell them: ‘Take wagons from the land of Egypt for your young children and your wives, and bring your father and come back. 20 But pay no regard to your belongings, for the best of all the land of Egypt is yours.’” 21 So the sons of Israel did as they were told. Joseph gave them wagons as Pharaoh had instructed, and he also gave them provisions for their journey. 22 He gave new garments to each of them, but to Benjamin he gave three hundred shekels of silver and five sets of clothes. 23 And he sent to his father the following: ten donkeys loaded with the best of Egypt, and ten female donkeys loaded with grain and bread and provisions for his father’s journey. 24 Then Joseph sent his brothers on their way, and as they were leaving, he said to them, “Do not quarrel on the way!”
paragraphs: 16 When the news reached Pharaoh’s house that Joseph’s brothers had come, Pharaoh and his servants were pleased.

17 Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Tell your brothers, ‘Do as follows: Load your animals and return to the land of Canaan. 18 Then bring your father and your families and return to me. I will give you the best of the land of Egypt, and you shall eat from the fat of the land.’ 19 You are also directed to tell them: ‘Take wagons from the land of Egypt for your young children and your wives, and bring your father and come back. 20 But pay no regard to your belongings, for the best of all the land of Egypt is yours.’”

21 So the sons of Israel did as they were told. Joseph gave them wagons as Pharaoh had instructed, and he also gave them provisions for their journey. 22 He gave new garments to each of them, but to Benjamin he gave three hundred shekels of silver and five sets of clothes. 23 And he sent to his father the following: ten donkeys loaded with the best of Egypt, and ten female donkeys loaded with grain and bread and provisions for his father’s journey.
24 Then Joseph sent his brothers on their way, and as they were leaving, he said to them, “Do not quarrel on the way!”

passages.context_html:
Pharaoh and his servants are pleased to hear that Joseph's brothers have come. Pharaoh authorizes them to bring their father and families to Egypt, promises good land, and supplies wagons for the children, women, and Jacob. The invitation has the king's support as well as Joseph's affection.

They are told not to be anxious over leaving belongings behind because Egypt's best is available to them. Joseph provides wagons, food, and new garments. Benjamin receives additional clothing and three hundred shekels of silver. Donkeys loaded with Egypt's good things and provisions are sent for Jacob's journey.

The supplies make the invitation something the family can act on. A long move involving an elderly father, children, and possessions will require more than an encouraging message. The brothers return with transport and food already provided.

Joseph's parting instruction is not to quarrel on the way. The old wrong has now been exposed, and the family must carry the news home. Their restored relationship with Joseph calls for a different way of treating one another as they travel.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the gifts and wagons as practical provision for the family's move and Joseph's warning as a call to peace after forgiveness. Wesley's note on Genesis 45:24 applies the instruction to the brothers' need to stop blaming one another and live as a reconciled family.

passages.god_plan_html:
Forgiveness received is meant to change relationships within the whole family. Joseph has welcomed the brothers together, and his warning directs them away from renewing their conflict on the journey. Mercy is to shape what happens after the emotional reunion.

The same wider theme appears in Ephesians 4:29–32: words should build others up, bitterness is to be put away, and believers are to forgive one another as God forgave them in Christ. Joseph's parting instruction gives that theme a concrete family setting. Reconciliation calls for a changed way of speaking as well as a willingness to meet again.

passages.title: Genesis 45:25-28
passages.section_title: The Revival of Jacob

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 25 So the brothers went up out of Egypt and came to their father Jacob in the land of Canaan. 26 “Joseph is still alive,” they said, “and he is ruler over all the land of Egypt!” But Jacob was stunned, for he did not believe them. 27 However, when they relayed all that Joseph had told them, and when he saw the wagons that Joseph had sent to carry him back, the spirit of their father Jacob was revived. 28 “Enough!” declared Israel. “My son Joseph is still alive! I will go to see him before I die.”
paragraphs: 25 So the brothers went up out of Egypt and came to their father Jacob in the land of Canaan. 26 “Joseph is still alive,” they said, “and he is ruler over all the land of Egypt!”

But Jacob was stunned, for he did not believe them. 27 However, when they relayed all that Joseph had told them, and when he saw the wagons that Joseph had sent to carry him back, the spirit of their father Jacob was revived.
28 “Enough!” declared Israel. “My son Joseph is still alive! I will go to see him before I die.”

passages.context_html:
The brothers return to Jacob in Canaan with news he has long believed impossible: Joseph is alive and rules over Egypt. At first he cannot believe them. The shock comes after years of mourning the son whose bloodied robe seemed to establish his death.

The description of Jacob being stunned uses פּוּג, pûg (poog), to grow numb. Brown–Driver–Briggs specifically cites his heart's response in Genesis 45:26. The word helps convey how overwhelming the report is before he can take it in.

The brothers repeat Joseph's words, and Jacob sees the wagons sent to carry him. His spirit revives. The news is accompanied by a visible invitation and the means to make the journey, and he resolves to see his living son before he dies.

The chapter closes with renewed hope and a decision to go. The actual departure will follow God's reassurance in the next chapter. For the moment, the father who refused comfort over Joseph's supposed death is preparing for a meeting he had no longer expected to have.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read the scene as a movement from stunned disbelief to renewed hope. Wesley's notes on Genesis 45:26–27 emphasize that Joseph's being alive matters to Jacob even more than the report of his high position. The father's desire is to see his son.

passages.title: Genesis 46:1-6
passages.section_title: Jacob’s Journey to Egypt

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 So Israel set out with all that he had, and when he came to Beersheba, he offered sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac. 2 And that night God spoke to Israel in a vision: “Jacob, Jacob!” He said. “Here I am,” replied Jacob. 3 “I am God,” He said, “the God of your father. Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt, for I will make you into a great nation there. 4 I will go down with you to Egypt, and I will surely bring you back. And Joseph’s own hands will close your eyes.” 5 Then Jacob departed from Beersheba, and the sons of Israel took their father Jacob in the wagons Pharaoh had sent to carry him, along with their children and wives. 6 They also took the livestock and possessions they had acquired in the land of Canaan, and Jacob and all his offspring went to Egypt.
paragraphs: 1 So Israel set out with all that he had, and when he came to Beersheba, he offered sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac. 2 And that night God spoke to Israel in a vision: “Jacob, Jacob!” He said.
“Here I am,” replied Jacob.

3 “I am God,” He said, “the God of your father. Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt, for I will make you into a great nation there. 4 I will go down with you to Egypt, and I will surely bring you back. And Joseph’s own hands will close your eyes.”

5 Then Jacob departed from Beersheba, and the sons of Israel took their father Jacob in the wagons Pharaoh had sent to carry him, along with their children and wives. 6 They also took the livestock and possessions they had acquired in the land of Canaan, and Jacob and all his offspring went to Egypt.

passages.context_html:
Jacob sets out with all he has and reaches Beersheba, where he offers sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac. The journey toward his living son also means leaving the land promised to his family. The account pauses here for God's reassurance before describing the household's entry into Egypt.

In a night vision, God calls him by name and tells him not to fear going down to Egypt. God will make him a great nation there, go with him, and bring him back. Joseph will close his eyes at death. The promise holds together a new stage for the family and the personal comfort of having his son with him at the end of his life.

Jacob then departs from Beersheba. His sons carry him, their children, and their wives in Pharaoh's wagons. They bring the livestock and possessions acquired in Canaan, and the account emphasizes that all his offspring go with him. This is a household migration, not simply a short visit by one father.

The promise of being brought back reaches beyond Jacob's living journey. Genesis 50:12–13 will record his burial in Canaan, while the following book will tell of his descendants' eventual deliverance from Egypt. His departure does not cancel God's earlier word about the land.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read the vision as reassurance that God's presence and promise continue with Jacob outside Canaan. Wesley's notes on Genesis 46:1–4 understand the return promise in relation both to Jacob's burial and his descendants' return, while Joseph's presence answers the father's personal longing.

passages.god_plan_html:
The family goes into Egypt under God's assurance, not beyond His care. Acts 7:14–15 directly recalls Joseph summoning Jacob and the household's descent to Egypt. Their move belongs to the history through which God preserves and grows the people of His promise.

The promise to go with Jacob also anticipates the assurance given when that people must leave. In Exodus 3:7–12, God declares that He will bring Israel out of oppression and tells Moses He will be with him. The direction of travel changes, but God's faithfulness and presence hold the story together.

passages.section_title: Those Who Went to Egypt

22 These are the sons of Rachel born to Jacob—fourteen in all.
23 The son of Dan: Hushim.
24 The sons of Naphtali: Jahzeel, Guni, Jezer, and Shillem.
25 These are the sons of Jacob born to Bilhah, whom Laban gave to his daughter Rachel—seven in all.

26 All those belonging to Jacob who came to Egypt—his direct descendants, besides the wives of Jacob’s sons—numbered sixty-six persons. 27 And with the two sons who had been born to Joseph in Egypt, the members of Jacob’s family who went to Egypt were seventy in all.

passages.context_html:
The narrative names Jacob's family as it enters Egypt, arranging sons and descendants under Leah, Zilpah, Rachel, and Bilhah. These names connect the household's earlier births and conflicts with the families that will later become Israel's tribes. Dinah and Serah are also remembered within the list.

The record includes reminders of earlier events. Er and Onan are named but identified as having died in Canaan. Manasseh and Ephraim are identified as Joseph's sons born in Egypt. The list therefore gathers the family history rather than simply naming everyone physically seated in the arriving wagons.

The closing totals distinguish sixty-six descendants coming with Jacob, excluding his sons' wives, from the family total of seventy. Joseph's household is already in Egypt. The account gives the starting scale of a family that God has just promised to make into a great nation there.

Readers may notice that Acts 7:14 gives seventy-five. The ancient Greek form of Genesis 46 includes additional descendants in Joseph's branch and gives that total. The biblical family record has come down in more than one textual form; the difference is visible in the texts themselves.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read the list as a record of the small family from which Israel will grow. Wesley's note on Genesis 46:7 explains seventy by adding Jacob, Joseph, and Joseph's two sons to the sixty-six, emphasizing the later growth from this beginning.

The US Catholic bishops' note on Genesis 46:27 draws attention to difficulties in adding every name and reads seventy as expressing the family's completeness. These explanations differ in how they handle the total, while both recognize the list's place in the movement from a household to a people.

passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 7:14–17 places the family migration within the progress of God's promise to Abraham, followed by the people's growth in Egypt. Exodus 1:1–7 likewise begins with the named sons and seventy descendants, then describes the Israelites multiplying greatly.

The family list therefore supplies the beginning against which that growth can be seen. God's promise is carried through particular people with remembered names and relationships. The later nation does not appear without a history; it grows from the household that enters Egypt in need of food and shelter.

passages.title: Genesis 46:28-34
passages.section_title: Jacob Arrives in Egypt

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 28 Now Jacob had sent Judah ahead of him to Joseph to get directions to Goshen. When Jacob’s family arrived in the land of Goshen, 29 Joseph prepared his chariot and went there to meet his father Israel. Joseph presented himself to him, embraced him, and wept profusely. 30 Then Israel said to Joseph, “Finally I can die, now that I have seen your face and know that you are still alive!” 31 Joseph said to his brothers and to his father’s household, “I will go up and inform Pharaoh: ‘My brothers and my father’s household from the land of Canaan have come to me. 32 The men are shepherds; they raise livestock, and they have brought their flocks and herds and all that they own.’ 33 When Pharaoh summons you and asks, ‘What is your occupation?’ 34 you are to say, ‘Your servants have raised livestock ever since our youth—both we and our fathers.’ Then you will be allowed to settle in the land of Goshen, since all shepherds are detestable to the Egyptians.”
paragraphs: 28 Now Jacob had sent Judah ahead of him to Joseph to get directions to Goshen. When Jacob’s family arrived in the land of Goshen, 29 Joseph prepared his chariot and went there to meet his father Israel. Joseph presented himself to him, embraced him, and wept profusely.
30 Then Israel said to Joseph, “Finally I can die, now that I have seen your face and know that you are still alive!”

31 Joseph said to his brothers and to his father’s household, “I will go up and inform Pharaoh: ‘My brothers and my father’s household from the land of Canaan have come to me. 32 The men are shepherds; they raise livestock, and they have brought their flocks and herds and all that they own.’

33 When Pharaoh summons you and asks, ‘What is your occupation?’ 34 you are to say, ‘Your servants have raised livestock ever since our youth—both we and our fathers.’ Then you will be allowed to settle in the land of Goshen, since all shepherds are detestable to the Egyptians.”

passages.context_html:
Jacob sends Judah ahead to Joseph for directions to Goshen. When the family arrives, Joseph prepares his chariot and goes to meet his father. He embraces him and weeps at length. Jacob, who had expected to die without seeing him again, now says he can die knowing his son is alive.

The reunion is followed by arrangements for the household's future. Joseph will tell Pharaoh that his family has arrived from Canaan with flocks, herds, and possessions. He prepares them to answer the king's question about their occupation honestly: they have always raised livestock.

Joseph explains that this will allow them to settle in Goshen because shepherds are detestable to the Egyptians. Their occupation helps account for a distinct place to live within Egypt. The passage supplies that reason without describing every Egyptian religious or social custom behind it.

The family is being welcomed into a foreign land while retaining its identity and work. The next scene will show Pharaoh authorizing the settlement and providing an opportunity for capable men to care for his livestock.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as both an emotional reunion and preparation for the family's distinct settlement in Egypt. Wesley's note on Genesis 46:30 emphasizes Jacob's profound satisfaction in seeing Joseph. The following instructions concern the household's practical place and livelihood in the land.

passages.god_plan_html:
The family can receive help in Egypt without simply disappearing into the surrounding people. Exodus 1:1–7 continues to identify them as Israel's household and describes their growth there. God's promise works through their life in a foreign land.

That situation offers a useful comparison with the wider call to live among others while remaining faithful to God. In John 17:14–19, Jesus asks that His disciples be kept from evil and shaped by God's truth while He sends them into the world. The comparison concerns faithfulness within a surrounding society, rather than treating physical isolation or ancestry as the source of holiness.

passages.title: Genesis 47:1-12
passages.section_title: Jacob Settles in Goshen

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 So Joseph went and told Pharaoh: “My father and my brothers, with their flocks and herds and all they own, have come from the land of Canaan and are now in Goshen.” 2 And he chose five of his brothers and presented them before Pharaoh. 3 “What is your occupation?” Pharaoh asked Joseph’s brothers. “Your servants are shepherds,” they replied, “both we and our fathers.” 4 Then they said to Pharaoh, “We have come to live in the land for a time, because there is no pasture for the flocks of your servants, since the famine in the land of Canaan has been severe. So now, please allow your servants to settle in the land of Goshen.” 5 Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Now that your father and brothers have come to you, 6 the land of Egypt is before you; settle your father and brothers in the best part of the land. They may dwell in the land of Goshen. And if you know of any talented men among them, put them in charge of my own livestock.” 7 Then Joseph brought in his father Jacob and presented him before Pharaoh, and Jacob blessed Pharaoh. 8 “How many years have you lived?” Pharaoh asked. 9 “My travels have lasted 130 years,” Jacob replied. “My years have been few and hard, and they have not matched the years of the travels of my fathers.” 10 Then Jacob blessed Pharaoh and departed from his presence. 11 So Joseph settled his father and brothers in the land of Egypt and gave them property in the best part of the land, the district of Rameses, as Pharaoh had commanded. 12 Joseph also provided his father and brothers and all his father’s household with food for their families.

2 And he chose five of his brothers and presented them before Pharaoh.
3 “What is your occupation?” Pharaoh asked Joseph’s brothers.
“Your servants are shepherds,” they replied, “both we and our fathers.”

4 Then they said to Pharaoh, “We have come to live in the land for a time, because there is no pasture for the flocks of your servants, since the famine in the land of Canaan has been severe. So now, please allow your servants to settle in the land of Goshen.”

5 Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Now that your father and brothers have come to you, 6 the land of Egypt is before you; settle your father and brothers in the best part of the land. They may dwell in the land of Goshen. And if you know of any talented men among them, put them in charge of my own livestock.”
7 Then Joseph brought in his father Jacob and presented him before Pharaoh, and Jacob blessed Pharaoh.
8 “How many years have you lived?” Pharaoh asked.
9 “My travels have lasted 130 years,” Jacob replied. “My years have been few and hard, and they have not matched the years of the travels of my fathers.”
10 Then Jacob blessed Pharaoh and departed from his presence.

11 So Joseph settled his father and brothers in the land of Egypt and gave them property in the best part of the land, the district of Rameses, as Pharaoh had commanded. 12 Joseph also provided his father and brothers and all his father’s household with food for their families.

passages.context_html:
Joseph reports his family's arrival and presents five of his brothers to Pharaoh. They identify themselves as shepherds and explain that the famine has left no pasture for their flocks in Canaan. They ask permission to live in Goshen for a time.

Pharaoh agrees that they may settle in the best part of the land and invites Joseph to place any capable men among them over his own livestock. The king's welcome gives official support to the arrangements Joseph has prepared. The household's occupation can also become a means of service within Egypt.

Joseph then presents Jacob, who blesses Pharaoh. Asked his age, Jacob describes his 130 years as few and hard compared with the lives of his fathers. He blesses Pharaoh again before leaving. His words carry the memory of a difficult life into a meeting with the ruler who can offer the family refuge.

The Hebrew word behind Jacob's description of his travels is מָגוּר, māgûr (mah-GOOR), a stay as a temporary resident. Brown–Driver–Briggs specifically includes Genesis 47:9 as a use covering a person's lifetime. Jacob speaks of life as a journey, even before considering this latest move.

Joseph settles his father and brothers in Goshen, here also called the district of Rameses, and supplies food for their families. The promised care now becomes land to live on and food for the household.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly see God's care expressed through the welcome, Joseph's provision, and Jacob's blessing of Pharaoh. Wesley's notes on Genesis 47:9–10 read Jacob's life as a pilgrimage and his blessing as prayer offered by the patriarch, not simply a courtly greeting.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Jacob receives material help from Pharaoh and also offers him a blessing. This fits the wider purpose in Genesis 12:2–3, where God's blessing of Abraham is intended to reach others. The family arriving in need still has a place in that purpose.

Jacob's description of life as a journey also fits Hebrews 11:9–16, which speaks of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as heirs living as strangers while looking toward what God would provide. Goshen gives genuine relief, but the household's present comfort is not the whole of its hope. God's promise reaches beyond the place where they can now find food.

passages.title: Genesis 47:13-26
passages.section_title: The Famine Continues

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 There was no food, however, in all that region, because the famine was so severe; the lands of Egypt and Canaan had been exhausted by the famine. 14 Joseph collected all the money to be found in the land of Egypt and the land of Canaan in exchange for the grain they were buying, and he brought it into Pharaoh’s palace. 15 When the money from the lands of Egypt and Canaan was gone, all the Egyptians came to Joseph and said, “Give us food. Why should we die before your eyes? For our funds have run out!” 16 “Then bring me your livestock,” said Joseph. “Since the money is gone, I will sell you food in exchange for your livestock.” 17 So they brought their livestock to Joseph, and he gave them food in exchange for their horses, their flocks and herds, and their donkeys. Throughout that year he provided them with food in exchange for all their livestock. 18 When that year was over, they came to him the second year and said, “We cannot hide from our lord that our money is gone and all our livestock belongs to you. There is nothing left for our lord except our bodies and our land. 19 Why should we perish before your eyes—we and our land as well? Purchase us and our land in exchange for food. Then we, along with our land, will be slaves to Pharaoh. Give us seed that we may live and not die, and that the land may not become desolate.” 20 So Joseph acquired for Pharaoh all the land in Egypt; the Egyptians, one and all, sold their fields because the famine was so severe upon them. The land became Pharaoh’s, 21 and Joseph reduced the people to servitude from one end of Egypt to the other. 22 However, he did not acquire the priests’ portion of the land, for it had been given to them by Pharaoh. They ate the rations that Pharaoh supplied; so they did not sell their land. 23 Then Joseph said to the people, “Now that I have acquired you and your land for Pharaoh this day, here is seed for you to sow in the land. 24 At harvest time, you are to give a fifth of it to Pharaoh, and four-fifths will be yours as seed for the field and food for yourselves and your households and children.” 25 “You have saved our lives,” they said. “We have found favor in our lord’s eyes, and we will be Pharaoh’s servants.” 26 So Joseph established a law that a fifth of the produce belongs to Pharaoh, and it is in effect in the land of Egypt to this day. Only the priests’ land does not belong to Pharaoh.

25 “You have saved our lives,” they said. “We have found favor in our lord’s eyes, and we will be Pharaoh’s servants.” 26 So Joseph established a law that a fifth of the produce belongs to Pharaoh, and it is in effect in the land of Egypt to this day. Only the priests’ land does not belong to Pharaoh.

passages.context_html:
The account turns from the family's settlement to the famine's effects on Egypt and Canaan. Joseph sells grain and brings the money into Pharaoh's treasury. When the Egyptians' money is exhausted, they exchange livestock for food. When that resource is gone, they offer their land and themselves rather than starve.

Joseph acquires the land for Pharaoh and reduces the people to servitude. The priests' land is excepted because Pharaoh already provides them with rations. The account thus explains a lasting change in who owns the land and the people's relationship to the crown.

Joseph supplies seed and establishes a share of the harvest: one-fifth for Pharaoh, with four-fifths retained for seed and household food. The people thank him for saving their lives and accept service to Pharaoh. Their survival is preserved at the same time that ownership and power become concentrated in the king's hands.

The policy belongs to this particular famine and royal system. The passage records the people's gratitude as well as their loss of land and freedom. Both are part of understanding what has happened; the closing notice explains the continuing one-fifth obligation and the priests' exception.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
A traditional Christian reading emphasizes Joseph's preservation of life and careful management in an extreme crisis. Wesley's introduction to Genesis 47 reads the arrangement favorably, while his note on verse 21 also acknowledges the hardship of the new servitude and the display of Pharaoh's power.

The narrative itself allows both features to remain visible: the people say their lives have been saved, and they now serve a king who owns their land. Recognizing the rescue does not require treating every consequence of the policy as a rule for governments or relief efforts in other circumstances.

passages.title: Genesis 47:27-31
passages.section_title: The Israelites Prosper in Goshen

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 27 Now the Israelites settled in the land of Egypt, in the region of Goshen. They acquired property there and became fruitful and increased greatly in number. 28 And Jacob lived in the land of Egypt seventeen years, and the length of his life was 147 years. 29 When the time drew near for Israel to die, he called his son Joseph and said to him, “If I have found favor in your eyes, put your hand under my thigh and promise to show me kindness and faithfulness. Do not bury me in Egypt, 30 but when I lie down with my fathers, carry me out of Egypt and bury me with them.” Joseph answered, “I will do as you have requested.” 31 “Swear to me,” Jacob said. So Joseph swore to him, and Israel bowed in worship at the head of his bed.
paragraphs: 27 Now the Israelites settled in the land of Egypt, in the region of Goshen. They acquired property there and became fruitful and increased greatly in number. 28 And Jacob lived in the land of Egypt seventeen years, and the length of his life was 147 years.

29 When the time drew near for Israel to die, he called his son Joseph and said to him, “If I have found favor in your eyes, put your hand under my thigh and promise to show me kindness and faithfulness. Do not bury me in Egypt, 30 but when I lie down with my fathers, carry me out of Egypt and bury me with them.”
Joseph answered, “I will do as you have requested.”
31 “Swear to me,” Jacob said.
So Joseph swore to him, and Israel bowed in worship at the head of his bed.

passages.context_html:
Israel's household settles in Goshen, acquires property, and grows greatly. Jacob lives another seventeen years in Egypt, reaching 147. The family has found security during the famine, but his final request looks beyond the land where that security has been provided.

As death approaches, he calls Joseph and asks for an oath marked by placing a hand under his thigh, recalling the oath Abraham required in Genesis 24. Joseph is to show kindness and faithfulness by carrying him out of Egypt and burying him with his fathers. Joseph agrees and swears to do so.

Jacob then bows in worship at the head of his bed in the BSB. Readers may also remember Hebrews 11:21, which speaks of him worshiping over his staff. The US Catholic bishops' note on Genesis 47:31 explains that the same Hebrew consonants have been read with different vowels as bed or staff, and that the ancient Greek version has staff. This helps explain the wording in the related passages.

The oath keeps the family burial place and God's land promise in view even after years of comfort in Egypt. Jacob accepts care there without making it the final home of his story. His deathbed instructions and the blessings in the following chapters prepare the family's next generation.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the burial request as an expression of faith in God's promise rather than dissatisfaction with Joseph's care. Wesley's note on Genesis 47:29 connects Canaan's significance as the promised land with the larger hope of the better country described in Hebrews. Jacob's worship accompanies his arrangements for death.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 11:21 directly remembers Jacob's dying faith, his blessing of Joseph's sons, and his worship. Its wording brings this closing scene and the following blessing into the larger account of people who trust God's promise at the end of their lives.

The broader explanation in Hebrews 11:13–16 describes people dying in faith while looking toward what they have not yet received. Jacob's burial request fits that hope: the care he has received in Egypt is real, and God's purpose still extends beyond his present circumstances and death. The family must continue to live by the promise after he is gone.

passages.title: Genesis 48:1-22
passages.section_title: Jacob Blesses Ephraim and Manasseh

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Some time later Joseph was told, “Your father is ill.” So he set out with his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim. 2 When Jacob was told, “Your son Joseph has come to you,” Israel rallied his strength and sat up in bed. 3 Jacob said to Joseph, “God Almighty appeared to me at Luz in the land of Canaan, and there He blessed me 4 and told me, ‘Behold, I will make you fruitful and multiply you; I will make you a multitude of peoples, and will give this land to your descendants after you as an everlasting possession.’ 5 And now your two sons born to you in Egypt before I came to you here shall be reckoned as mine; Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine, just as Reuben and Simeon are mine. 6 Any children born to you after them shall be yours, and they shall be called by the names of their brothers in the territory they inherit. 7 Now as for me, when I was returning from Paddan, to my sorrow Rachel died along the way in the land of Canaan, some distance from Ephrath. So I buried her there beside the road to Ephrath” (that is, Bethlehem). 8 When Israel saw the sons of Joseph, he asked, “Who are these?” 9 Joseph said to his father, “They are the sons God has given me in this place.” So Jacob said, “Please bring them to me, that I may bless them.” 10 Now Israel’s eyesight was poor because of old age; he could hardly see. Joseph brought his sons to him, and his father kissed them and embraced them. 11 “I never expected to see your face again,” Israel said to Joseph, “but now God has let me see your children as well.” 12 Then Joseph removed his sons from his father’s knees and bowed facedown. 13 And Joseph took both of them—with Ephraim in his right hand toward Israel’s left hand, and Manasseh in his left hand toward Israel’s right hand—and brought them close to him. 14 But Israel stretched out his right hand and put it on the head of Ephraim, the younger; and crossing his hands, he put his left on Manasseh’s head, although Manasseh was the firstborn. 15 Then he blessed Joseph and said: “May the God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has been my shepherd all my life to this day, 16 the angel who has redeemed me from all harm— may He bless these boys. And may they be called by my name and the names of my fathers Abraham and Isaac, and may they grow into a multitude upon the earth.” 17 When Joseph saw that his father had placed his right hand on Ephraim’s head, he was displeased and took his father’s hand to move it from Ephraim’s head to Manasseh’s. 18 “Not so, my father!” Joseph said. “This one is the firstborn; put your right hand on his head.” 19 But his father refused. “I know, my son, I know!” he said. “He too shall become a people, and he too shall be great; nevertheless, his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his offspring shall become a multitude of nations.” 20 So that day Jacob blessed them and said: “By you shall Israel pronounce this blessing: ‘May God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh.’” So he put Ephraim before Manasseh. 21 Then Israel said to Joseph, “Look, I am about to die, but God will be with you and bring you back to the land of your fathers. 22 And to you, as one who is above your brothers, I give the ridge of land that I took from the Amorites with my sword and bow.”

16 the angel who has redeemed me from all harm— may He bless these boys. And may they be called by my name and the names of my fathers Abraham and Isaac, and may they grow into a multitude upon the earth.”

17 When Joseph saw that his father had placed his right hand on Ephraim’s head, he was displeased and took his father’s hand to move it from Ephraim’s head to Manasseh’s. 18 “Not so, my father!” Joseph said. “This one is the firstborn; put your right hand on his head.”

19 But his father refused. “I know, my son, I know!” he said. “He too shall become a people, and he too shall be great; nevertheless, his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his offspring shall become a multitude of nations.”
20 So that day Jacob blessed them and said: “By you shall Israel pronounce this blessing: ‘May God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh.’” So he put Ephraim before Manasseh.

21 Then Israel said to Joseph, “Look, I am about to die, but God will be with you and bring you back to the land of your fathers. 22 And to you, as one who is above your brothers, I give the ridge of land that I took from the Amorites with my sword and bow.”

passages.context_html:
Hearing that Jacob is ill, Joseph brings Manasseh and Ephraim to him. Jacob recalls God's appearance at Luz and the promise of descendants and land. He then receives Joseph's two sons as his own, giving them a place alongside Reuben and Simeon. Any later children of Joseph will be counted within their brothers' inheritance, rather than creating further tribal shares.

This gives Joseph's family a double place in Israel through his two sons. 1 Chronicles 5:1–2 later distinguishes that birthright from the ruler's line through Judah. Jacob also remembers Rachel's death, bringing the family's sorrow into the moment when her grandsons receive their place in its future.

Jacob's sight is poor, but he embraces the sons and gives thanks that he has seen both Joseph and his children. Joseph places Manasseh, the older, toward Jacob's right hand. Jacob deliberately crosses his hands, giving Ephraim the place Joseph intended for Manasseh. When Joseph objects, Jacob explains that both will become peoples, but the younger will become greater.

In the blessing, Jacob remembers God as the shepherd who has cared for him throughout his life and speaks of the angel who redeemed him from harm. The verb is גָּאַל, gāʾal (gah-AHL), to redeem or rescue. Brown–Driver–Briggs specifically includes Genesis 48:16 under God's rescuing care for a person. The blessing entrusts the next generation to the care Jacob has known himself.

Jacob ends by assuring Joseph that God will be with the family and bring it back to the land of its fathers. He also grants Joseph a special ridge or portion of land. John 4:5 later remembers land Jacob gave Joseph, and Joshua 24:32 records Joseph's burial at Shechem. The precise event behind Jacob's reference to taking it with sword and bow is not narrated earlier in Genesis.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read the chapter as Jacob faithfully passing on the promise, with God's purpose taking priority over the expected order of age. Wesley's notes on Genesis 48:3, 16–21 emphasize the sons' place in the inheritance and the deliberate nature of the crossed hands.

A longstanding Christian reading identifies the redeeming angel with the Son of God. Athanasius, Discourse III Against the Arians 12–13, reads Jacob's prayer as joining the divine Word with the Father in the giving of blessing. Wesley's note on verse 16 also understands the redeemer as Christ. These comments explain that Christian reading rather than making a word's dictionary meaning alone prove the angel's identity.

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 11:21 directly identifies Jacob's blessing of Joseph's sons as an act of faith. He is dying in Egypt, yet speaks confidently about a future God will provide beyond his own remaining years.

The sons' reception into the family also offers a useful comparison with the Bible's wider theme of adoption. Romans 8:15–17 describes believers as God's children and heirs with Christ; Ephesians 1:5 speaks of adoption through Jesus Christ. Jacob's action concerns particular tribal heirs, while the New Testament describes the greater welcome God gives through His Son. In both, an inheritance is received within a relationship the giver establishes.

passages.title: Genesis 49:1-28
passages.section_title: Jacob Blesses His Sons

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then Jacob called for his sons and said, “Gather around so that I can tell you what will happen to you in the days to come: 2 Come together and listen, O sons of Jacob; listen to your father Israel. 3 Reuben, you are my firstborn, my might, and the beginning of my strength, excelling in honor, excelling in power. 4 Uncontrolled as the waters, you will no longer excel, because you went up to your father’s bed, onto my couch, and defiled it. 5 Simeon and Levi are brothers; their swords are weapons of violence. 6 May I never enter their council; may I never join their assembly. For they kill men in their anger, and hamstring oxen on a whim. 7 Cursed be their anger, for it is strong, and their wrath, for it is cruel! I will disperse them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel. 8 Judah, your brothers shall praise you. Your hand shall be on the necks of your enemies; your father’s sons shall bow down to you. 9 Judah is a young lion— my son, you return from the prey. Like a lion he crouches and lies down; like a lioness, who dares to rouse him? 10 The scepter will not depart from Judah, nor the staff from between his feet, until Shiloh comes and the allegiance of the nations is his. 11 He ties his donkey to the vine, his colt to the choicest branch. He washes his garments in wine, his robes in the blood of grapes. 12 His eyes are darker than wine, and his teeth are whiter than milk. 13 Zebulun shall dwell by the seashore and become a harbor for ships; his border shall extend to Sidon. 14 Issachar is a strong donkey, lying down between the sheepfolds. 15 He saw that his resting place was good and that his land was pleasant, so he bent his shoulder to the burden and submitted to labor as a servant. 16 Dan shall provide justice for his people as one of the tribes of Israel. 17 He will be a snake by the road, a viper in the path that bites the horse’s heels so that its rider tumbles backward. 18 I await Your salvation, O LORD. 19 Gad will be attacked by raiders, but he will attack their heels. 20 Asher’s food will be rich; he shall provide royal delicacies. 21 Naphtali is a doe set free that bears beautiful fawns. 22 Joseph is a fruitful vine— a fruitful vine by a spring, whose branches scale the wall. 23 The archers attacked him with bitterness; they aimed at him in hostility. 24 Yet he steadied his bow, and his strong arms were tempered by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob, in the name of the Shepherd, the Rock of Israel, 25 by the God of your father who helps you, and by the Almighty who blesses you, with blessings of the heavens above, with blessings of the depths below, with blessings of the breasts and womb. 26 The blessings of your father have surpassed the blessings of the ancient mountains and the bounty of the everlasting hills. He blessed them, and he blessed each one with a suitable blessing.

passages.context_html:
Jacob gathers his sons to speak about their future. The closing verse identifies them as the twelve tribes of Israel, so these sayings look beyond the men in the room to the peoples bearing their names. The words include rebuke, warning, promise, and blessing; they are not simply compliments offered at a farewell.

Reuben's loss of the leading place among his brothers is tied directly to his violation of his father's bed. Simeon and Levi are addressed together because of their violent anger, recalling the attack on Shechem. Jacob rejects their cruelty and speaks of their scattering. Later, Joshua 19:1 places Simeon's inheritance within Judah, while Deuteronomy 10:8–9 describes Levi's distinct calling to service rather than an ordinary territorial share.

Judah receives the promise of leadership. His brothers will praise and bow before him; the lion, scepter, and staff express strength and rule. The allegiance of nations extends the picture beyond the immediate household. Images of abundant wine and milk describe rich provision alongside that authority.

The brief sayings for Zebulun and Issachar speak of the sea, trade, productive land, and labor. Dan's saying combines justice with the image of a snake overturning a rider. In the middle of these words, Jacob voices his dependence on the LORD's salvation. Gad faces raids and counters them; Asher supplies rich food; Naphtali is pictured as a free doe bearing beautiful fawns.

Joseph's blessing recalls hostility overcome through the help of the Mighty One of Jacob. The fruitful vine, strong arms, shepherd, and rock bring together his hard experience and the care that has sustained him. The blessing asks for abundant life and fruitfulness. Benjamin's wolf image describes a forceful tribe taking and dividing spoil.

The poem links remembered actions with future tribal life, using vivid images that are sometimes difficult to interpret in detail. Its main movements remain clear: wrongdoing has consequences, leadership is associated with Judah, Joseph is richly blessed, and the family must depend on the God whose help Jacob names.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read these sayings as looking forward to the tribes' future, with Judah's royal promise reaching toward Christ. Wesley's notes on Genesis 49:1, 8–10 connect the rule of Judah, David's line, and the Messiah. His explanations of individual images are commentary, not a requirement that every detail have only one possible historical application.

The BSB retains שִׁילֹה, šîlōh (shee-LOH), in verse 10. Its exact meaning is debated. Brown–Driver–Briggs discusses several readings and favors a connection with the one to whom something belongs, while acknowledging uncertainty in the exact translation. The US Catholic bishops' note on Genesis 49:10 likewise discusses different readings while emphasizing Judah and the Davidic dynasty.

The messianic reading also has a Jewish history. Rashi's own commentary on Genesis 49:10 understands Shiloh as the King Messiah to whom the kingdom belongs. Christians identify the promised ruler with Jesus; Rashi's Jewish reading should be recognized on its own terms rather than presented as a Christian identification.

passages.god_plan_html:
Revelation 5:5–10 directly takes up Judah's lion imagery in its description of Jesus, the Lion of the tribe of Judah and Root of David. The vision then shows Him as the slain Lamb whose blood purchases people for God from every tribe, language, people, and nation. The royal promise reaches its Christian fulfillment through the One whose victory includes His self-giving death.

The chapter also keeps different family roles in view. 1 Chronicles 5:1–2 distinguishes Joseph's birthright from the ruler coming through Judah. God's purpose moves through the whole family, with particular responsibilities within it. The warnings against uncontrolled desire and violent anger remain part of that story; receiving a place in the promise does not make the family's wrongdoing harmless.

passages.title: Genesis 49:29-33
passages.section_title: The Death of Jacob

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 29 Then Jacob instructed them, “I am about to be gathered to my people. Bury me with my fathers in the cave in the field of Ephron the Hittite. 30 The cave is in the field of Machpelah near Mamre, in the land of Canaan. This is the field Abraham purchased from Ephron the Hittite as a burial site. 31 There Abraham and his wife Sarah are buried, there Isaac and his wife Rebekah are buried, and there I buried Leah. 32 The field and the cave that is in it were purchased from the Hittites.” 33 When Jacob had finished instructing his sons, he pulled his feet into the bed and breathed his last, and he was gathered to his people.

Bury me with my fathers in the cave in the field of Ephron the Hittite. 30 The cave is in the field of Machpelah near Mamre, in the land of Canaan. This is the field Abraham purchased from Ephron the Hittite as a burial site. 31 There Abraham and his wife Sarah are buried, there Isaac and his wife Rebekah are buried, and there I buried Leah. 32 The field and the cave that is in it were purchased from the Hittites.”
33 When Jacob had finished instructing his sons, he pulled his feet into the bed and breathed his last, and he was gathered to his people.

passages.context_html:
After addressing the tribes' future, Jacob gives his sons instructions about his burial. He is to be placed with his fathers in the cave at Machpelah, near Mamre in Canaan. He identifies the land as the field Abraham purchased from Ephron, recalling the family burial place established in Genesis 23.

He names those already buried there: Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, and Leah. The notice about Leah adds a detail not previously supplied about her death and burial. Rachel remains buried beside the road near Bethlehem, as the earlier account records.

Jacob's instruction to all the sons confirms the request Joseph has already sworn to carry out. When he finishes, he draws his feet into the bed and dies, described as being gathered to his people. The chapter closes his life with the family around him and a clear charge for what they must do next.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the burial instructions as a final expression of Jacob's attachment to God's promise and the family history in Canaan. Wesley's notes on Genesis 49:29, 33 read his death in the hope of belonging with the faithful who have gone before him. The following chapter records the sons' carrying out his charge.

passages.title: Genesis 50:1-14
passages.section_title: Mourning and Burial for Jacob

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then Joseph fell upon his father’s face, wept over him, and kissed him. 2 And Joseph directed the physicians in his service to embalm his father Israel. So they embalmed him, 3 taking the forty days required to complete the embalming. And the Egyptians mourned for him seventy days. 4 When the days of mourning had passed, Joseph said to Pharaoh’s court, “If I have found favor in your eyes, please tell Pharaoh that 5 my father made me swear an oath when he said, ‘I am about to die. You must bury me in the tomb that I dug for myself in the land of Canaan.’ Now let me go and bury my father, and then return.” 6 Pharaoh replied, “Go up and bury your father, as he made you swear to do.” 7 Then Joseph went to bury his father, and all the servants of Pharaoh accompanied him—the elders of Pharaoh’s household and all the elders of the land of Egypt— 8 along with all of Joseph’s household, and his brothers, and his father’s household. Only their children and flocks and herds were left in Goshen. 9 Chariots and horsemen alike went up with him, and it was an exceedingly large procession. 10 When they reached the threshing floor of Atad, which is across the Jordan, they lamented and wailed loudly, and Joseph mourned for his father seven days. 11 When the Canaanites of the land saw the mourning at the threshing floor of Atad, they said, “This is a solemn ceremony of mourning by the Egyptians.” Thus the place across the Jordan is called Abel-mizraim. 12 So Jacob’s sons did as he had charged them. 13 They carried him to the land of Canaan and buried him in the cave at Machpelah in the field near Mamre, which Abraham had purchased from Ephron the Hittite as a burial site. 14 After Joseph had buried his father, he returned to Egypt with his brothers and all who had gone with him to bury his father.
paragraphs: 1 Then Joseph fell upon his father’s face, wept over him, and kissed him.

2 And Joseph directed the physicians in his service to embalm his father Israel. So they embalmed him, 3 taking the forty days required to complete the embalming. And the Egyptians mourned for him seventy days.

4 When the days of mourning had passed, Joseph said to Pharaoh’s court, “If I have found favor in your eyes, please tell Pharaoh that 5 my father made me swear an oath when he said, ‘I am about to die. You must bury me in the tomb that I dug for myself in the land of Canaan.’ Now let me go and bury my father, and then return.”
6 Pharaoh replied, “Go up and bury your father, as he made you swear to do.”

7 Then Joseph went to bury his father, and all the servants of Pharaoh accompanied him—the elders of Pharaoh’s household and all the elders of the land of Egypt— 8 along with all of Joseph’s household, and his brothers, and his father’s household. Only their children and flocks and herds were left in Goshen.

9 Chariots and horsemen alike went up with him, and it was an exceedingly large procession. 10 When they reached the threshing floor of Atad, which is across the Jordan, they lamented and wailed loudly, and Joseph mourned for his father seven days.

11 When the Canaanites of the land saw the mourning at the threshing floor of Atad, they said, “This is a solemn ceremony of mourning by the Egyptians.” Thus the place across the Jordan is called Abel-mizraim.

12 So Jacob’s sons did as he had charged them. 13 They carried him to the land of Canaan and buried him in the cave at Machpelah in the field near Mamre, which Abraham had purchased from Ephron the Hittite as a burial site.
14 After Joseph had buried his father, he returned to Egypt with his brothers and all who had gone with him to bury his father.

passages.context_html:
Joseph responds to Jacob's death with tears and a kiss, then directs his physicians to embalm him. The process takes forty days, and the Egyptians mourn for seventy days. The account records substantial public mourning as well as the son's personal grief.

Joseph asks through Pharaoh's court for permission to honor the oath to bury his father in Canaan. He promises to return, and Pharaoh agrees. A large procession accompanies the family, including royal officials, servants, chariots, and horsemen. Their children and livestock remain in Goshen.

At the threshing floor of Atad, across the Jordan, they hold a further seven-day lament. The Canaanites notice the scale of the Egyptian mourning, and the place is called Abel-mizraim. The account preserves the effect of the funeral on the surrounding people without giving enough detail to settle every question about its route.

Jacob's sons carry him to Machpelah and bury him in the field Abraham purchased. The promise made beside his deathbed has been kept. Joseph and the others then return to Egypt, where the family's story will continue.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as love and grief expressed alongside faithfulness to a dying parent's request. Wesley's notes on Genesis 50:1–5 emphasize Joseph's affection and the preparation for carrying Jacob to Canaan. Mourning and confidence in God's promise stand together rather than canceling one another.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
Jacob's burial in the land preserves the family's connection with the promise even while its living members remain in Egypt. Hebrews 11:13–16 describes the wider hope of those who die in faith while looking beyond what they have received in their lifetime.

The tears also fit the New Testament's account of grief with hope. 1 Thessalonians 4:13–14 does not ask believers to feel no loss; it grounds their hope for the dead in Jesus' death and resurrection. Joseph's mourning is real, and the promise he honors gives the funeral a meaning beyond the separation itself.

passages.title: Genesis 50:15-21
passages.section_title: Joseph Comforts His Brothers

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 When Joseph’s brothers saw that their father was dead, they said, “What if Joseph bears a grudge? Then he will surely repay us for all the evil that we did to him.” 16 So they sent word to Joseph, saying, “Before he died, your father commanded, 17 ‘This is what you are to say to Joseph: I beg you, please forgive the transgression and sin of your brothers, for they did you wrong.’ So now, Joseph, please forgive the transgression of the servants of the God of your father.” When their message came to him, Joseph wept. 18 His brothers also came to him, bowed down before him, and said, “We are your slaves!” 19 But Joseph replied, “Do not be afraid. Am I in the place of God? 20 As for you, what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good, in order to accomplish a day like this—to preserve the lives of many people. 21 Therefore do not be afraid. I will provide for you and your little ones.” So Joseph reassured his brothers and spoke kindly to them.
paragraphs: 15 When Joseph’s brothers saw that their father was dead, they said, “What if Joseph bears a grudge? Then he will surely repay us for all the evil that we did to him.”

16 So they sent word to Joseph, saying, “Before he died, your father commanded, 17 ‘This is what you are to say to Joseph: I beg you, please forgive the transgression and sin of your brothers, for they did you wrong.’ So now, Joseph, please forgive the transgression of the servants of the God of your father.”
When their message came to him, Joseph wept. 18 His brothers also came to him, bowed down before him, and said, “We are your slaves!”

19 But Joseph replied, “Do not be afraid. Am I in the place of God? 20 As for you, what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good, in order to accomplish a day like this—to preserve the lives of many people. 21 Therefore do not be afraid. I will provide for you and your little ones.” So Joseph reassured his brothers and spoke kindly to them.

passages.context_html:
After Jacob's death, the brothers fear that Joseph may now repay them for their earlier evil. They send a message asking forgiveness and reporting that their father had asked for it before he died. Joseph weeps when he hears it. The brothers then come personally, bow before him, and offer themselves as slaves.

Joseph tells them not to fear and asks whether he is in God's place. He names their intention as evil while explaining that God intended good through the same history: many people have been preserved alive. This repeats the saving purpose he described when he first made himself known.

The verb behind preserving life is חָיָה, ḥāyâ (khah-YAH). Brown–Driver–Briggs specifically explains its form in Genesis 50:20 as keeping people alive. Here it concerns survival through the famine, made possible by Joseph's position in Egypt.

His reassurance becomes a promise to provide for them and their little ones. He speaks kindly to them. The death of their father has not undone the forgiveness already offered, and Joseph uses his power to sustain the family rather than take revenge.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly see forgiveness, human responsibility, and God's saving purpose held together here. Wesley's notes on Genesis 50:20–21 emphasize good brought from evil and kindness expressed in both action and speech. The Catholic Catechism, paragraph 312, likewise uses Joseph's explanation while making clear that evil does not become good because God brings good from it.

passages.god_plan_html:
The larger Christian comparison is with God's saving work through Christ's rejection and death. The Catholic Catechism, paragraph 312, explicitly places Joseph's story beside that greater good brought from human evil. Acts 2:22–24 likewise holds together God's purpose, the wrongdoing of those who put Jesus to death, and His resurrection. The comparison preserves responsibility while recognizing a purpose that evil does not defeat.

Joseph's refusal to take revenge also fits Romans 12:17–21, where believers are told to leave judgment with God and answer an enemy's need with practical care. His feeding of the family shows what that can look like after a serious wrong. Mercy is expressed through continued provision, including for children who were not responsible for the betrayal.

passages.title: Genesis 50:22-26
passages.section_title: The Death of Joseph

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 Now Joseph and his father’s household remained in Egypt, and Joseph lived to the age of 110. 23 He saw Ephraim’s sons to the third generation, and indeed the sons of Machir son of Manasseh were brought up on Joseph’s knees. 24 Then Joseph said to his brothers, “I am about to die, but God will surely visit you and bring you up from this land to the land He promised on oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.” 25 And Joseph made the sons of Israel take an oath and said, “God will surely attend to you, and then you must carry my bones up from this place.” 26 So Joseph died at the age of 110. And they embalmed his body and placed it in a coffin in Egypt.
paragraphs: 22 Now Joseph and his father’s household remained in Egypt, and Joseph lived to the age of 110. 23 He saw Ephraim’s sons to the third generation, and indeed the sons of Machir son of Manasseh were brought up on Joseph’s knees.

24 Then Joseph said to his brothers, “I am about to die, but God will surely visit you and bring you up from this land to the land He promised on oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.” 25 And Joseph made the sons of Israel take an oath and said, “God will surely attend to you, and then you must carry my bones up from this place.”
26 So Joseph died at the age of 110. And they embalmed his body and placed it in a coffin in Egypt.

passages.context_html:
Joseph remains in Egypt with his father's household and lives to 110. He sees later generations of Ephraim's family and receives the children of Machir, Manasseh's son, on his knees. The account closes his life with the growing family around him.

As death approaches, he tells his brothers that God will attend to them and bring them to the land sworn to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The promise does not depend on Joseph remaining alive to protect them. God will continue the work after the generation that came to Egypt has died.

Joseph requires an oath that his bones be carried up when that deliverance comes. He is embalmed and placed in a coffin in Egypt. Unlike Jacob's immediate burial in Canaan, his burial there must wait for the family's departure. Genesis ends with a body in Egypt and a promise pointing beyond it.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand Joseph's instructions as confidence in God's promise beyond his own death. Wesley's notes on Genesis 50:24–26 emphasize that Egypt is not the family's final home and that Joseph's remains become a testimony to the return he expects.

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 11:22 directly names this as an act of faith: Joseph speaks of the coming exodus and gives instructions about his bones. His final concern reaches beyond the achievements of his own life to what God has promised the people.

The later narrative follows through. Exodus 13:19 records Moses taking Joseph's bones when Israel leaves Egypt, and Joshua 24:32 records their burial at Shechem. The coffin at Genesis' close therefore looks toward deliverance and inheritance. The book ends with expectation of God's continuing faithfulness.

passages.title: Exodus 1:1-7
passages.section_title: How did Jacob’s family become a people in Egypt?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 These are the names of the sons of Israel who went to Egypt with Jacob, each with his family: 2 Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah; 3 Issachar, Zebulun, and Benjamin; 4 Dan and Naphtali; Gad and Asher. 5 The descendants of Jacob numbered seventy in all, including Joseph, who was already in Egypt. 6 Now Joseph and all his brothers and all that generation died, 7 but the Israelites were fruitful and increased rapidly; they multiplied and became exceedingly numerous, so that the land was filled with them.
paragraphs: 1 These are the names of the sons of Israel who went to Egypt with Jacob, each with his family: 2 Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah; 3 Issachar, Zebulun, and Benjamin; 4 Dan and Naphtali; Gad and Asher. 5 The descendants of Jacob numbered seventy in all, including Joseph, who was already in Egypt.

6 Now Joseph and all his brothers and all that generation died, 7 but the Israelites were fruitful and increased rapidly; they multiplied and became exceedingly numerous, so that the land was filled with them.

passages.context_html:
Exodus begins by naming the sons of Israel who came to Egypt with Jacob. It picks up the family story told in Genesis, where Joseph was already living in Egypt and his relatives joined him during the famine.

The opening count is seventy, with Joseph already in Egypt. The story then moves beyond that generation: Joseph, his brothers and their contemporaries die, while their descendants become numerous and fill the land.

The repeated descriptions of fruitfulness and increase make growth the main event in these verses. The small family has become a people. That growth will soon trouble Egypt’s new king, setting up the conflict that follows.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The shared emphasis is God’s faithfulness to His promises about Abraham’s family. Wesley understands the increase as the result of the promise made to the fathers. The Catholic USCCB notes also connect it with those promises and with the language of blessing and multiplication in Genesis. These explanations share the passage’s movement from one family to a growing people.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
In Genesis 46:2–4, God told Jacob not to fear going to Egypt because He would make him a great nation there. The growth at the opening of Exodus belongs directly with that promise. Egypt is part of the story God has already begun with this family.

Stephen makes the connection explicit in Acts 7:17: the people increased as the time approached for God to fulfill His promise to Abraham. That promise reaches back to Genesis 12:1–3, where the making of a great nation belongs within God’s purpose to bless all the families of the earth.

passages.title: Exodus 1:8-22
passages.section_title: Why did the midwives refuse Pharaoh’s command?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 Then a new king, who did not know Joseph, came to power in Egypt. 9 “Look,” he said to his people, “the Israelites have become too numerous and too powerful for us. 10 Come, let us deal shrewdly with them, or they will increase even more; and if a war breaks out, they may join our enemies, fight against us, and leave the country.” 11 So the Egyptians appointed taskmasters over the Israelites to oppress them with forced labor. As a result, they built Pithom and Rameses as store cities for Pharaoh. 12 But the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied and flourished; so the Egyptians came to dread the Israelites. 13 They worked the Israelites ruthlessly 14 and made their lives bitter with hard labor in brick and mortar, and with all kinds of work in the fields. Every service they imposed was harsh. 15 Then the king of Egypt said to the Hebrew midwives, whose names were Shiphrah and Puah, 16 “When you help the Hebrew women give birth, observe them on the birthstools. If the child is a son, kill him; but if it is a daughter, let her live.” 17 The midwives, however, feared God and did not do as the king of Egypt had instructed; they let the boys live. 18 So the king of Egypt summoned the midwives and asked them, “Why have you done this? Why have you let the boys live?” 19 The midwives answered Pharaoh, “The Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women, for they are vigorous and give birth before a midwife arrives.” 20 So God was good to the midwives, and the people multiplied and became even more numerous. 21 And because the midwives feared God, He gave them families of their own. 22 Then Pharaoh commanded all his people: “Every son born to the Hebrews you must throw into the Nile, but every daughter you may allow to live.”

passages.context_html:
A new king who does not know Joseph sees Israel’s growing population as a threat. He fears that they might join an enemy during war and leave Egypt. Forced labor is his first response: the Israelites build store cities, make bricks and work in the fields under harsh conditions.

The oppression does not achieve its purpose. The people continue to multiply, and Egyptian fear grows. Pharaoh then orders the midwives Shiphrah and Puah to kill Hebrew boys at birth while letting the girls live.

The women fear God and let the boys live. The Hebrew verb can include reverence and honor, as Brown–Driver–Briggs explains under its entry for fearing God, including these verses. Their reverence has a practical result: they refuse the king’s command to kill.

When questioned, they tell Pharaoh that Hebrew women give birth before a midwife arrives. God is good to the midwives, and the people keep growing. The BSB describes God giving the women families of their own. Pharaoh then extends the command to all his people: Hebrew boys are to be thrown into the Nile. The chapter ends with the threat that will surround Moses’ birth.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The main readings commend the women’s fear of God and their protection of the boys. Their reply to Pharaoh receives different explanations. Wesley sees no reason to doubt that the women were telling the truth about the births. Calvin understands the reply as a falsehood, while distinguishing God’s approval of their reverence and mercy from approval of the lie.

Catholic teaching in Catechism 2482–2485 defines lying as intentional deception through falsehood and condemns it. That is a general teaching about truthfulness; those paragraphs do not decide whether the midwives’ particular reply was false.

The women’s identity is also read differently. Calvin takes them as Hebrew women. Wesley understands them as midwives serving the Hebrews who may themselves have been Egyptian. Both identify their fear of God as the reason they resist Pharaoh.

There is a further difference over the households in verse 21. The BSB and Wesley understand the blessing as families given to the midwives. Calvin applies the building of households to the growing families of Israel. Each reading connects the result with God preserving life through the women’s actions.

passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 7:18–22 places this oppression immediately before Moses’ birth and upbringing. The threatened people are the people from whom God is preparing a deliverer. Hebrews 11:23 also remembers Moses’ parents acting in faith despite the king’s edict.

A later parallel appears in Matthew 2:13–18: another ruler orders the killing of boys, while God provides a way for Jesus to be preserved. This is a parallel in the threat and rescue, rather than a claim that the two accounts are identical in every detail.

The women’s choice also recalls the apostles’ response to an order to stop their witness in Acts 5:27–29. Obedience to God takes precedence when a human command directly opposes Him. The larger story shows God preserving His purpose through people whose faithfulness may look small beside royal power.

passages.title: Exodus 2:1-10
passages.section_title: How was Moses preserved under Pharaoh’s decree?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now a man of the house of Levi married a Levite woman, 2 and she conceived and gave birth to a son. When she saw that he was a beautiful child, she hid him for three months. 3 But when she could no longer hide him, she got him a papyrus basket and coated it with tar and pitch. Then she placed the child in the basket and set it among the reeds along the bank of the Nile. 4 And his sister stood at a distance to see what would happen to him. 5 Soon the daughter of Pharaoh went down to bathe in the Nile, and her attendants were walking along the riverbank. And when she saw the basket among the reeds, she sent her maidservant to retrieve it. 6 When she opened it, she saw the child, and behold, the little boy was crying. So she had compassion on him and said, “This is one of the Hebrew children.” 7 Then his sister said to Pharaoh’s daughter, “Shall I go and call one of the Hebrew women to nurse the child for you?” 8 “Go ahead,” Pharaoh’s daughter told her. And the girl went and called the boy’s mother. 9 Pharaoh’s daughter said to her, “Take this child and nurse him for me, and I will pay your wages.” So the woman took the boy and nursed him. 10 When the child had grown older, she brought him to Pharaoh’s daughter, and he became her son. She named him Moses and explained, “I drew him out of the water.”

She named him Moses and explained, “I drew him out of the water.”

passages.context_html:
The order to kill Hebrew boys is still the setting when a Levite couple has a son. His mother hides him for three months. When that is no longer possible, she waterproofs a papyrus basket and places it among the reeds beside the Nile, with his sister watching from a distance.

The Hebrew word for the basket, tebah, is also the word used for Noah’s ark. Brown–Driver–Briggs lists both vessels under that word. The connection draws attention to a protected life in water that otherwise threatens it.

Pharaoh’s daughter finds the crying child, recognizes him as Hebrew and has compassion on him. His sister offers to find a nurse and brings his own mother. The mother who could no longer hide him is now paid to care for him under the princess’s protection.

When he is older, the child becomes Pharaoh’s daughter’s son. She names him Moses, explaining it through his rescue from the water. The household of the king who ordered the boys’ deaths has become the place where this boy will grow up.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The shared reading emphasizes God preserving the future deliverer through his family’s faith and the princess’s compassion. Wesley highlights God’s care in bringing the child to Pharaoh’s daughter. The Catholic USCCB notes emphasize the reversals in the story: the king’s daughter adopts a Hebrew boy and pays his mother to nurse him. Their explanations recognize purpose working through the people’s actions.
