passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 11:23 explicitly remembers the parents hiding Moses as an act of faith despite the king’s command. Acts 7:20–22 carries the story from his birth to his upbringing and education. The preserved child is being prepared for the deliverance Stephen will go on to describe.

The basket also provides a parallel with Genesis 6:14–18, where Noah’s ark preserves life through threatening waters. The vessels and circumstances differ, but the shared word and pattern connect this rescue with an earlier act of preservation in God’s larger story.

passages.title: Exodus 2:11-22
passages.section_title: Why did Moses flee to Midian?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 One day, after Moses had grown up, he went out to his own people and observed their hard labor. He saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, one of his own people. 12 After looking this way and that and seeing no one, he struck down the Egyptian and hid his body in the sand. 13 The next day Moses went out and saw two Hebrews fighting. He asked the one in the wrong, “Why are you attacking your companion?” 14 But the man replied, “Who made you ruler and judge over us? Are you planning to kill me as you killed the Egyptian?” Then Moses was afraid and thought, “This thing I have done has surely become known.” 15 When Pharaoh heard about this matter, he sought to kill Moses. But Moses fled from Pharaoh and settled in the land of Midian, where he sat down beside a well. 16 Now the priest of Midian had seven daughters, and they came to draw water and fill the troughs to water their father’s flock. 17 And when some shepherds came along and drove them away, Moses rose up to help them and watered their flock. 18 When the daughters returned to their father Reuel, he asked them, “Why have you returned so early today?” 19 “An Egyptian rescued us from the shepherds,” they replied. “He even drew water for us and watered the flock.” 20 “So where is he?” their father asked. “Why did you leave the man behind? Invite him to have something to eat.” 21 Moses agreed to stay with the man, and he gave his daughter Zipporah to Moses in marriage. 22 And she gave birth to a son, and Moses named him Gershom, saying, “I have become a foreigner in a foreign land.”

passages.context_html:
As an adult, Moses goes out to his own people and sees their hard labor. When he sees an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, he looks around, kills the Egyptian and hides the body. The next day he tries to stop two Hebrews fighting, but the man in the wrong challenges his authority and mentions the killing.

Moses realizes that the matter is known. Pharaoh seeks his life, and he flees to Midian. His concern for his people has brought him into danger, and they have not recognized him as their ruler or judge.

At a well he again encounters people being mistreated. Shepherds drive away the daughters of the priest of Midian, and Moses helps the women and waters their flock. They describe him to their father Reuel as an Egyptian who rescued them.

Moses is welcomed into the household, marries Zipporah and has a son. He names the child Gershom and explains that he has become a foreigner in a foreign land. The man raised in Egypt’s royal household now lives away from both the court and his own people.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The killing receives different moral explanations. Calvin and Wesley understand Moses as acting under a special divine calling to deliver his people. They distinguish that reading from a general permission for private people to use violence. David Guzik instead understands Moses’ secrecy as a troubled conscience and his action as an attempt to deliver Israel through his own strength. These are the teachers’ readings of his motives and calling.

The household names also receive different explanations. The USCCB notes identify Reuel with Jethro, the name used for Moses’ father-in-law in the next chapter. Wesley suggests that Reuel is the grandfather and Jethro is the immediate father. The narrative here names Reuel and centers on Moses finding welcome and a family in Midian.

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 11:24–26 explains Moses’ choice to identify with God’s people through faith. It connects his willingness to suffer with disgrace for Christ and his hope of reward. That is the New Testament’s own connection between this part of his life and the larger purpose of God.

Acts 7:23–37 explains that Moses expected his people to recognize God’s deliverance through him. Stephen later returns to the challenge about who made him ruler and judge: the rejected Moses is the very one God sends to lead them out. Within Stephen’s address, that pattern leads toward his warning about resistance to God’s messengers and the betrayal of the Righteous One in verses 51–53. The rejection does not cancel God’s purpose for the deliverer.

passages.title: Exodus 2:23-25
passages.section_title: What does it mean that God remembered His covenant?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 23 After a long time, the king of Egypt died. The Israelites groaned and cried out under their burden of slavery, and their cry for deliverance from bondage ascended to God. 24 So God heard their groaning, and He remembered His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. 25 God saw the Israelites and took notice.
paragraphs: 23 After a long time, the king of Egypt died. The Israelites groaned and cried out under their burden of slavery, and their cry for deliverance from bondage ascended to God. 24 So God heard their groaning, and He remembered His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. 25 God saw the Israelites and took notice.

passages.context_html:
Time passes and the king of Egypt dies, but Israel remains enslaved. Their groaning and cry for deliverance rise to God. The change of king has not itself brought freedom.

The account gives a series of responses: God hears, remembers His covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, sees the people and takes notice. Their suffering is brought into direct relationship with the promises He made to their ancestors. The next chapter shows His response taking shape in Moses’ call.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The shared reading understands God remembering as His faithfulness moving toward action. Calvin and Wesley both explain that God has remained mindful of His promise. The language tells the reader that He is attending to the people’s distress and acting on the covenant; it does not describe Him recovering information He had forgotten.

passages.god_plan_html:
Genesis 15:13–16 joins the promised family’s period of oppression with God’s judgment of the oppressing nation and their eventual departure. Exodus now brings the people’s cry and God’s remembrance of that promise together. The deliverance that follows is rooted in His faithfulness.

A later connection appears in Luke 1:68–75, where Zechariah praises God for redemption, mercy and remembrance of His covenant with Abraham. That song looks toward salvation and service to God in holiness. The repeated language links the hope surrounding Jesus with the earlier story of God hearing and delivering His people.

passages.title: Exodus 3:1-22
passages.section_title: Who is the God who sends Moses?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Meanwhile, Moses was shepherding the flock of his father-in-law Jethro, the priest of Midian. He led the flock to the far side of the wilderness and came to Horeb, the mountain of God. 2 There the angel of the LORD appeared to him in a blazing fire from within a bush. Moses saw the bush ablaze with fire, but it was not consumed. 3 So Moses thought, “I must go over and see this marvelous sight. Why is the bush not burning up?” 4 When the LORD saw that he had gone over to look, God called out to him from within the bush, “Moses, Moses!” “Here I am,” he answered. 5 “Do not come any closer,” God said. “Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.” 6 Then He said, “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” At this, Moses hid his face, for he was afraid to look at God. 7 The LORD said, “I have indeed seen the affliction of My people in Egypt. I have heard them crying out because of their oppressors, and I am aware of their sufferings. 8 I have come down to rescue them from the hand of the Egyptians and to bring them up out of that land to a good and spacious land, a land flowing with milk and honey—the home of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites. 9 And now the cry of the Israelites has reached Me, and I have seen how severely the Egyptians are oppressing them. 10 Therefore, go! I am sending you to Pharaoh to bring My people the Israelites out of Egypt.” 11 But Moses asked God, “Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh and bring the Israelites out of Egypt?” 12 “I will surely be with you,” God said, “and this will be the sign to you that I have sent you: When you have brought the people out of Egypt, all of you will worship God on this mountain.” 13 Then Moses asked God, “Suppose I go to the Israelites and say to them, ‘The God of your fathers has sent me to you,’ and they ask me, ‘What is His name?’ What should I tell them?” 14 God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM. This is what you are to say to the Israelites: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’” 15 God also told Moses, “Say to the Israelites, ‘The LORD, the God of your fathers—the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob—has sent me to you.’ This is My name forever, and this is how I am to be remembered in every generation. 16 Go, assemble the elders of Israel and say to them, ‘The LORD, the God of your fathers—the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—has appeared to me and said: I have surely attended to you and have seen what has been done to you in Egypt. 17 And I have promised to bring you up out of your affliction in Egypt, into the land of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites—a land flowing with milk and honey.’ 18 The elders of Israel will listen to what you say, and you must go with them to the king of Egypt and tell him, ‘The LORD, the God of the Hebrews, has met with us. Now please let us take a three-day journey into the wilderness, so that we may sacrifice to the LORD our God.’ 19 But I know that the king of Egypt will not allow you to go unless a mighty hand compels him. 20 So I will stretch out My hand and strike the Egyptians with all the wonders I will perform among them. And after that, he will release you. 21 And I will grant this people such favor in the sight of the Egyptians that when you leave, you will not go away empty-handed. 22 Every woman shall ask her neighbor and any woman staying in her house for silver and gold jewelry and clothing, and you will put them on your sons and daughters. So you will plunder the Egyptians.”

passages.context_html:
While shepherding Jethro’s flock, Moses comes to Horeb and sees a bush burning without being consumed. The angel of the LORD appears in the flame, and God calls to Moses from the bush. Moses is told to remove his sandals because the ground is holy.

The speaker identifies Himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Moses hides his face. The encounter joins God’s holiness with His continuing relationship to the family whose descendants are suffering in Egypt.

God says that He has seen their affliction, heard their cry and come to rescue them. He promises to bring them to a good and spacious land, described through the abundance of milk and honey. Then He sends Moses to Pharaoh to bring His people out.

Moses asks who he is to undertake this task. God answers with the promise that He will be with him, and that the people will worship on this mountain after their deliverance. The assurance rests on God’s presence with Moses.

When Moses asks what name he should give the Israelites, God identifies Himself as I AM WHO I AM and then as the LORD, the God of their fathers. Brown–Driver–Briggs discusses the connection with the Hebrew verb for being and with the promise to be with Moses. In verse 15, LORD represents God’s personal name, written with the Hebrew letters YHWH. The expression ehyeh appears in both the assurance of verse 12 and the answer of verse 14. The name is revealed within a promise of faithful presence.

Moses is to gather the elders and ask Pharaoh to allow a three-day journey into the wilderness for worship. God already knows that Pharaoh will resist and promises to act through wonders that bring about their release. The people will leave with silver, gold and clothing received from their neighbors. Their departure will not be empty-handed.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians differ over the identity and role of the angel in the bush. Calvin identifies Him as the eternal Son making God known before His human birth. Wesley describes an angel making the visible appearance while God speaks. Augustine, On the Trinity 2.13, thinks it could be the Son, but also considers God speaking through an angel without settling which person of the Trinity the messenger represents.

The name also receives several connected emphases. The Catholic Catechism 203–213 and Wesley emphasize that God depends on no one else for His life and remains faithful to His people. Brown–Driver–Briggs also gives attention to the assurance that He will be with Moses. These explanations relate the name both to who God is and to His promised presence.

The request for possessions is read as part of God putting right the people’s oppression. Wesley emphasizes that the women ask for gifts, rather than borrow with an intention not to repay. The BSB likewise says ask. The promised departure with possessions belongs with God’s earlier promise to Abraham.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Who is The Angel of the Lord? reads this encounter as an appearance of the eternal Son before His birth as Jesus. The study points to the angel appearing in verse 2, God speaking in verse 4 and Moses’ fear of looking at God in verse 6. We understand these as one encounter with the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, rather than separate encounters with an ordinary angel and then with God.

deeper_study.title: Who is The Angel of the Lord?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 7:30–37 explicitly recalls the burning bush and God’s commission. Stephen points out that the Moses previously rejected as ruler and judge is the one God sends as ruler and redeemer. God’s choice and presence are decisive even after the earlier rejection.

Jesus quotes God’s identification as the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob when teaching about resurrection in Matthew 22:31–32. He identifies God as the God of the living. The relationship announced at the bush therefore also enters the New Testament’s explanation of hope beyond death.

The promised release with possessions also recalls Genesis 15:13–16. God’s response addresses the oppression, remembers the promised land and prepares His people to worship Him. The scene belongs within a purpose larger than Moses’ ability or Pharaoh’s willingness.

passages.title: Exodus 4:1-5
passages.section_title: How would the people know that God had sent Moses?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then Moses answered, “What if they do not believe me or listen to my voice? For they may say, ‘The LORD has not appeared to you.’” 2 And the LORD asked him, “What is that in your hand?” “A staff,” he replied. 3 “Throw it on the ground,” said the LORD. So Moses threw it on the ground, and it became a snake, and he ran from it. 4 “Stretch out your hand and grab it by the tail,” the LORD said to Moses, who reached out his hand and caught the snake, and it turned back into a staff in his hand. 5 “This is so that they may believe that the LORD, the God of their fathers—the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob—has appeared to you.”
paragraphs: 1 Then Moses answered, “What if they do not believe me or listen to my voice? For they may say, ‘The LORD has not appeared to you.’” 2 And the LORD asked him, “What is that in your hand?” “A staff,” he replied. 3 “Throw it on the ground,” said the LORD. So Moses threw it on the ground, and it became a snake, and he ran from it. 4 “Stretch out your hand and grab it by the tail,” the LORD said to Moses, who reached out his hand and caught the snake, and it turned back into a staff in his hand. 5 “This is so that they may believe that the LORD, the God of their fathers—the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob—has appeared to you.”

passages.context_html:
God has told Moses to return to Egypt, gather the elders and announce the coming deliverance. Moses now asks what will happen if they refuse to believe that the LORD has appeared to him. His concern is how they will recognize the message as coming from God.

God begins with the staff already in Moses’ hand. At His command it becomes a snake, and Moses runs from it. At a second command Moses takes hold of its tail, and it becomes a staff again. The sign is given so the people may believe that the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob has appeared to him. The promise to their ancestors remains at the center of his mission.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The shared reading sees the sign as God confirming Moses’ calling and giving the people a reason to trust his message. Calvin and Wesley both connect the miracle with the authority of the messenger God is sending.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

deeper_study.title: Should We Seek Signs From God?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
God confirming a messenger through signs becomes a theme across Scripture. Acts 2:22 describes Jesus’ miracles as works God performed through Him, and Hebrews 2:3–4 speaks of God confirming the announcement of salvation through signs and wonders.

John 20:30–31 gives the purpose of the signs recorded in that Gospel: that readers may believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life in His name. This is a shared purpose of signs within God’s work: they point people toward the message and the One who sends it.

passages.title: Exodus 4:6-9
passages.section_title: Why did God give Moses more than one sign?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 Furthermore, the LORD said to Moses, “Put your hand inside your cloak.” So he put his hand inside his cloak, and when he took it out, his hand was leprous, white as snow. 7 “Put your hand back inside your cloak,” said the LORD. So Moses put his hand back inside his cloak, and when he took it out, it was restored, like the rest of his skin. 8 And the LORD said, “If they refuse to believe you or heed the witness of the first sign, they may believe that of the second. 9 But if they do not believe even these two signs or listen to your voice, take some water from the Nile and pour it on the dry ground. Then the water you take from the Nile will become blood on the ground.”
paragraphs: 6 Furthermore, the LORD said to Moses, “Put your hand inside your cloak.” So he put his hand inside his cloak, and when he took it out, his hand was leprous, white as snow. 7 “Put your hand back inside your cloak,” said the LORD. So Moses put his hand back inside his cloak, and when he took it out, it was restored, like the rest of his skin. 8 And the LORD said, “If they refuse to believe you or heed the witness of the first sign, they may believe that of the second. 9 But if they do not believe even these two signs or listen to your voice, take some water from the Nile and pour it on the dry ground. Then the water you take from the Nile will become blood on the ground.”

passages.context_html:
God gives Moses another sign. He puts his hand inside his cloak, takes it out diseased and white as snow, then repeats the action and finds it restored. God shows that both the affliction and its removal are under His command.

God then tells him what to do if the people still refuse to believe: take water from the Nile and pour it on dry ground, where it will become blood. That third sign is announced here; it has not yet been performed in this conversation. Each sign answers Moses’ fear that the people will reject his claim to have been sent by God.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The teachers agree that the signs establish Moses’ commission, but give different explanations of the diseased and restored hand. Calvin especially connects it with Moses being restored from obscurity to a position of service. Wesley also sees a picture of Israel being cleansed and delivered from its ruined condition. These are their explanations of what the sign may picture; the stated purpose in verses 8–9 is to bring the people to believe.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

deeper_study.title: Should We Seek Signs From God?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The sign involving Nile water looks ahead to the judgment announced in Exodus 7:14–18. There the river itself will turn to blood as God confronts Pharaoh’s refusal to release His people. What begins as evidence for Israel also points toward the power God will exercise against their oppressor.

A later parallel appears in Revelation 16:4–7, where waters become blood and the judgment is connected with the bloodshed of God’s servants. The repeated image places the Exodus signs within a wider theme: God sees the suffering of His people and holds their persecutors accountable.

passages.title: Exodus 4:10-17
passages.section_title: What if Moses did not feel able to speak?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 “Please, Lord,” Moses replied, “I have never been eloquent, neither in the past nor since You have spoken to Your servant, for I am slow of speech and tongue.” 11 And the LORD said to him, “Who gave man his mouth? Or who makes the mute or the deaf, the sighted or the blind? Is it not I, the LORD? 12 Now go! I will help you as you speak, and I will teach you what to say.” 13 But Moses replied, “Please, Lord, send someone else.” 14 Then the anger of the LORD burned against Moses, and He said, “Is not Aaron the Levite your brother? I know that he can speak well, and he is now on his way to meet you. When he sees you, he will be glad in his heart. 15 You are to speak to him and put the words in his mouth. I will help both of you to speak, and I will teach you what to do. 16 He will speak to the people for you. He will be your spokesman, and it will be as if you were God to him. 17 But take this staff in your hand so you can perform signs with it.”
paragraphs: 10 “Please, Lord,” Moses replied, “I have never been eloquent, neither in the past nor since You have spoken to Your servant, for I am slow of speech and tongue.” 11 And the LORD said to him, “Who gave man his mouth? Or who makes the mute or the deaf, the sighted or the blind? Is it not I, the LORD? 12 Now go! I will help you as you speak, and I will teach you what to say.”

13 But Moses replied, “Please, Lord, send someone else.” 14 Then the anger of the LORD burned against Moses, and He said, “Is not Aaron the Levite your brother? I know that he can speak well, and he is now on his way to meet you. When he sees you, he will be glad in his heart. 15 You are to speak to him and put the words in his mouth. I will help both of you to speak, and I will teach you what to do. 16 He will speak to the people for you. He will be your spokesman, and it will be as if you were God to him. 17 But take this staff in your hand so you can perform signs with it.”

passages.context_html:
Moses turns from the people’s possible unbelief to his own difficulty speaking. The Hebrew description of his mouth and tongue uses a word meaning heavy, which Brown–Driver–Briggs explains here as slow or difficult speech. Moses says the difficulty has remained even since God began speaking with him.

God answers as the Creator of the mouth, hearing and sight. He tells Moses to go and promises to help him speak and teach him what to say. Moses then asks God to send someone else, and the LORD becomes angry.

Even then, God provides Aaron to speak for him. Moses will give Aaron the words, Aaron will address the people, and God will help them both. The comparison between Moses and God in verse 16 describes how the message passes through Moses to Aaron. Moses is to take the staff as well; the calling and the signs remain his responsibility.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The shared reading understands Moses’ final request as an attempt to be excused from the task. Calvin and Wesley both emphasize that God’s promised help answers his weakness, while his continuing refusal brings God’s displeasure. Aaron’s assistance allows the work to go forward.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The exchange has a close parallel in Jeremiah 1:6–9. Jeremiah says he does not know how to speak; God sends him, promises His presence and gives him words. In both callings, the messenger’s confidence rests on the God who sends him.

1 Corinthians 2:1–5 brings that theme into the preaching of Christ. Paul recalls coming in weakness and fear, so that the Corinthians’ faith would rest on God’s power. Across these settings, God’s message reaches people through servants who depend on Him.

passages.title: Exodus 4:18-26
passages.section_title: What did Moses face on the journey back to Egypt?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 Then Moses went back to his father-in-law Jethro and said to him, “Please let me return to my brothers in Egypt to see if they are still alive.” “Go in peace,” Jethro replied. 19 Now the LORD had said to Moses in Midian, “Go back to Egypt, for all the men who sought to kill you are dead.” 20 So Moses took his wife and sons, put them on a donkey, and headed back to Egypt. And he took the staff of God in his hand. 21 The LORD instructed Moses, “When you go back to Egypt, see that you perform before Pharaoh all the wonders that I have put within your power. But I will harden his heart so that he will not let the people go. 22 Then tell Pharaoh that this is what the LORD says: ‘Israel is My firstborn son, 23 and I told you to let My son go so that he may worship Me. But since you have refused to let him go, behold, I will kill your firstborn son!’” 24 Now at a lodging place along the way, the LORD met Moses and was about to kill him. 25 But Zipporah took a flint knife, cut off her son’s foreskin, and touched it to Moses’ feet. “Surely you are a bridegroom of blood to me,” she said. 26 So the LORD let him alone. (When she said, “bridegroom of blood,” she was referring to the circumcision.)
paragraphs: 18 Then Moses went back to his father-in-law Jethro and said to him, “Please let me return to my brothers in Egypt to see if they are still alive.” “Go in peace,” Jethro replied. 19 Now the LORD had said to Moses in Midian, “Go back to Egypt, for all the men who sought to kill you are dead.” 20 So Moses took his wife and sons, put them on a donkey, and headed back to Egypt. And he took the staff of God in his hand.

21 The LORD instructed Moses, “When you go back to Egypt, see that you perform before Pharaoh all the wonders that I have put within your power. But I will harden his heart so that he will not let the people go. 22 Then tell Pharaoh that this is what the LORD says: ‘Israel is My firstborn son, 23 and I told you to let My son go so that he may worship Me. But since you have refused to let him go, behold, I will kill your firstborn son!’”

24 Now at a lodging place along the way, the LORD met Moses and was about to kill him. 25 But Zipporah took a flint knife, cut off her son’s foreskin, and touched it to Moses’ feet. “Surely you are a bridegroom of blood to me,” she said. 26 So the LORD let him alone. (When she said, “bridegroom of blood,” she was referring to the circumcision.)

passages.context_html:
Moses receives Jethro’s permission to return to Egypt and takes his wife, sons and the staff God will use for the signs. The LORD assures him that those who sought his life are dead. The man who fled Egypt is now returning under God’s command.

God also prepares him for resistance. Moses must perform the wonders before Pharaoh, but God says He will harden Pharaoh’s heart. The coming struggle is already within God’s knowledge and purpose. Moses is to tell Pharaoh that Israel is God’s firstborn son and must be released to worship Him. Refusal will bring the death of Pharaoh’s own firstborn.

The journey then takes a startling turn: at a lodging place the LORD confronts Moses and threatens his life. Zipporah circumcises her son, touches the foreskin to Moses’ feet and calls him a bridegroom of blood. The threat ends. Genesis 17:9–14 supplies the covenant background: Abraham’s male descendants were to bear circumcision as its sign.

The Hebrew in verse 24 uses words meaning met him and put him to death, with the person identified from the setting. The BSB names Moses. The brief account does not name the son or explain why his circumcision had been delayed. Its ending directly connects Zipporah’s words with the circumcision.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
There are different readings of God hardening Pharaoh’s heart. The Reformed teacher Calvin understands it as God actively directing the confrontation toward judgment, beyond simply allowing events. Wesley understands it as God eventually permitting Satan to harden a ruler who has repeatedly hardened himself. Both hold Pharaoh responsible, while explaining God’s action differently.

The circumcision scene is commonly read as a confrontation over a neglected covenant obligation. The Catholic USCCB notes, Calvin and Wesley identify Moses as the person threatened. They understand his life as spared when Zipporah circumcises the child.

Zipporah’s words also receive different readings. Wesley takes them as a reproach against Moses over the circumcision. The Baptist commentator John Gill instead understands her as grateful that the blood of circumcision has restored her husband to her. The text reports her words and the end of the threat, but gives little explanation of her feelings.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
God’s description of Israel as His son belongs to a connection the New Testament develops. Hosea 11:1 remembers God calling His son Israel out of Egypt, and Matthew 2:13–15 applies that passage to Jesus’ return from Egypt. Matthew also reports the assurance that those seeking the child’s life have died in verses 19–20, a close parallel with God’s assurance to Moses here.

Romans 9:17–18 directly draws on the confrontation with Pharaoh to explain God displaying His power and making His name known. Paul places the Exodus within his discussion of God’s mercy and purposes, which goes on to speak of people called from both Jews and Gentiles in verses 23–24.

The circumcision scene returns attention to the covenant at the very moment its promised rescue is beginning. Colossians 2:11–14 later uses circumcision language for the work of Christ, joining it with burial and resurrection with Him and the forgiveness of sins. This is a wider connection between God’s covenant people and life through Christ; Colossians does not give a detailed explanation of Zipporah’s actions.

passages.title: Exodus 4:27-31
passages.section_title: How did Israel respond to the news that God had seen their suffering?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 27 Meanwhile, the LORD had said to Aaron, “Go and meet Moses in the wilderness.” So he went and met Moses at the mountain of God and kissed him. 28 And Moses told Aaron everything the LORD had sent him to say, and all the signs He had commanded him to perform. 29 Then Moses and Aaron went and assembled all the elders of the Israelites, 30 and Aaron relayed everything the LORD had said to Moses. And Moses performed the signs before the people, 31 and they believed. And when they heard that the LORD had attended to the Israelites and had seen their affliction, they bowed down and worshiped.
paragraphs: 27 Meanwhile, the LORD had said to Aaron, “Go and meet Moses in the wilderness.” So he went and met Moses at the mountain of God and kissed him. 28 And Moses told Aaron everything the LORD had sent him to say, and all the signs He had commanded him to perform. 29 Then Moses and Aaron went and assembled all the elders of the Israelites, 30 and Aaron relayed everything the LORD had said to Moses. And Moses performed the signs before the people, 31 and they believed. And when they heard that the LORD had attended to the Israelites and had seen their affliction, they bowed down and worshiped.

passages.context_html:
God sends Aaron into the wilderness, where he meets Moses at the mountain of God. Moses tells him what the LORD has commanded him to say and explains the signs. The help God promised is now taking place.

The brothers gather Israel’s elders. Aaron delivers the message, Moses performs the signs, and the people believe. Their response brings the story back to the concern Moses raised at the beginning of the chapter: how would they know God had appeared to him?

What leads them to bow in worship is the news that the LORD has attended to them and seen their affliction. They have not yet left Egypt, but they have heard that their suffering has been seen and that God is acting.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The shared reading sees the meeting as the promised beginning of the mission: the brothers deliver God’s message, the signs confirm it, and Israel responds with belief and worship. Calvin and Gill both connect their thanksgiving with learning that God has taken notice of their suffering.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Rescue and worship belong together in this account. God has already called Israel His son and demanded that Pharaoh release them to worship Him. The people begin to worship while they are still waiting for that freedom.

The theme returns in Luke 1:68–75. Zechariah praises God for visiting and redeeming His people, remembering His covenant with Abraham, and granting deliverance so they may serve Him without fear. The purpose of rescue reaches beyond escape from an enemy into life with God.

passages.title: Exodus 5:1-5
passages.section_title: Why did Pharaoh refuse to listen?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 After that, Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and said, “This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘Let My people go, so that they may hold a feast to Me in the wilderness.’” 2 But Pharaoh replied, “Who is the LORD that I should obey His voice and let Israel go? I do not know the LORD, and I will not let Israel go.” 3 “The God of the Hebrews has met with us,” they answered. “Please let us go on a three-day journey into the wilderness to sacrifice to the LORD our God, or He may strike us with plagues or with the sword.” 4 But the king of Egypt said to them, “Moses and Aaron, why do you draw the people away from their work? Get back to your labor!” 5 Pharaoh also said, “Look, the people of the land are now numerous, and you would be stopping them from their labor.”
paragraphs: 1 After that, Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and said, “This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘Let My people go, so that they may hold a feast to Me in the wilderness.’” 2 But Pharaoh replied, “Who is the LORD that I should obey His voice and let Israel go? I do not know the LORD, and I will not let Israel go.” 3 “The God of the Hebrews has met with us,” they answered. “Please let us go on a three-day journey into the wilderness to sacrifice to the LORD our God, or He may strike us with plagues or with the sword.” 4 But the king of Egypt said to them, “Moses and Aaron, why do you draw the people away from their work? Get back to your labor!” 5 Pharaoh also said, “Look, the people of the land are now numerous, and you would be stopping them from their labor.”

passages.context_html:
After Israel’s believing response, Moses and Aaron deliver God’s demand to Pharaoh: release His people so they can hold a feast to Him in the wilderness. The Hebrew verb for holding a feast, hagag, describes a religious festival; Brown–Driver–Briggs includes this verse under keeping a pilgrim feast. Worship is at the heart of the request.

Pharaoh challenges both the LORD’s identity and His authority. He says he does not know the LORD and will not let Israel go. Moses and Aaron explain that the God of the Hebrews has met with them and ask for a three-day journey to offer sacrifices, warning that failure to worship Him could bring judgment upon them.

Pharaoh treats the request as an interruption of labor. Where God calls Israel His people, Pharaoh sees workers whose time he controls. The confrontation is beginning to show whose claim upon them he will recognize.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The shared reading understands Pharaoh’s reply as a refusal to recognize the LORD’s authority. Wesley and the Catholic USCCB notes both emphasize his defiance: whatever he may have heard about Israel’s God, he rejects the demand to obey Him.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
This confrontation begins a recurring biblical theme: what happens when a ruler’s command conflicts with obedience to God? In Acts 4:18–20, Peter and John are ordered to stop speaking in Jesus’ name and answer that they must heed God. In Acts 5:27–29, the apostles state that obligation directly.

The settings and tasks differ, but the parallel is clear. God’s purpose continues through people who must answer to Him while facing an authority that resists His word. Moses and Aaron’s commission to lead Israel into worship belongs within that wider story of God gathering a people who serve Him.

passages.title: Exodus 5:6-14
passages.section_title: Why did the work become harder after Moses spoke?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 That same day Pharaoh commanded the taskmasters of the people and their foremen: 7 “You shall no longer supply the people with straw for making bricks. They must go and gather their own straw. 8 But require of them the same quota of bricks as before; do not reduce it. For they are lazy; that is why they are crying out, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to our God.’ 9 Make the work harder on the men so they will be occupied and pay no attention to these lies.” 10 So the taskmasters and foremen of the people went out and said to them, “This is what Pharaoh says: ‘I am no longer giving you straw. 11 Go and get your own straw wherever you can find it; but your workload will in no way be reduced.’” 12 So the people scattered all over the land of Egypt to gather stubble for straw. 13 The taskmasters kept pressing them, saying, “Fulfill your quota each day, just as you did when straw was provided.” 14 Then the Israelite foremen, whom Pharaoh’s taskmasters had set over the people, were beaten and asked, “Why have you not fulfilled your quota of bricks yesterday or today, as you did before?”
paragraphs: 6 That same day Pharaoh commanded the taskmasters of the people and their foremen: 7 “You shall no longer supply the people with straw for making bricks. They must go and gather their own straw. 8 But require of them the same quota of bricks as before; do not reduce it. For they are lazy; that is why they are crying out, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to our God.’ 9 Make the work harder on the men so they will be occupied and pay no attention to these lies.”

10 So the taskmasters and foremen of the people went out and said to them, “This is what Pharaoh says: ‘I am no longer giving you straw. 11 Go and get your own straw wherever you can find it; but your workload will in no way be reduced.’” 12 So the people scattered all over the land of Egypt to gather stubble for straw. 13 The taskmasters kept pressing them, saying, “Fulfill your quota each day, just as you did when straw was provided.” 14 Then the Israelite foremen, whom Pharaoh’s taskmasters had set over the people, were beaten and asked, “Why have you not fulfilled your quota of bricks yesterday or today, as you did before?”

passages.context_html:
Pharaoh answers the request for worship by increasing the burden. The people must now gather their own straw for making bricks while still producing the same daily number. He calls them lazy and wants the extra work to keep them from attending to Moses and Aaron’s message.

The order leaves the Israelites searching across Egypt for stubble while the taskmasters continue demanding the full quota. When production falls short, the Israelite foremen are beaten. They are answerable for work their people have been given fewer resources to complete.

The immediate result of God’s message is greater suffering. The promise of deliverance has been announced, but Pharaoh’s response makes the people’s situation worse. This is the pressure behind the complaints in the rest of the chapter.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The shared reading sees Pharaoh deliberately using heavier labor to crush the people’s hope and turn them away from the message of deliverance. Calvin and Wesley both describe the charge of laziness as a pretext for cruelty rather than a fair account of their work.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The oppression in Egypt belongs to a theme Scripture returns to: God hears people whose labor and vulnerability are exploited. James 5:1–6 addresses those who withhold their workers’ wages and says the workers’ cries have reached the Lord. That passage announces accountability for people who use their power to enrich themselves through others’ suffering.

James then calls believers to patience until the Lord’s coming in verses 7–8. That wider horizon helps place Israel’s distress in the larger story. The suffering is real, and the oppressor’s present control will not be the final word.

passages.title: Exodus 5:15-23
passages.section_title: What did Moses do when the promised rescue seemed farther away?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 So the Israelite foremen went and appealed to Pharaoh: “Why are you treating your servants this way? 16 No straw has been given to your servants, yet we are told, ‘Make bricks!’ Look, your servants are being beaten, but the fault is with your own people.” 17 “You are slackers!” Pharaoh replied. “Slackers! That is why you keep saying, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to the LORD.’ 18 Now get to work. You will be given no straw, yet you must deliver the full quota of bricks.” 19 The Israelite foremen realized they were in trouble when they were told, “You must not reduce your daily quota of bricks.” 20 When they left Pharaoh, they confronted Moses and Aaron, who stood waiting to meet them. 21 “May the LORD look upon you and judge you,” the foremen said, “for you have made us a stench before Pharaoh and his officials; you have placed in their hand a sword to kill us!” 22 So Moses returned to the LORD and asked, “Lord, why have You brought trouble upon this people? Is this why You sent me? 23 Ever since I went to Pharaoh to speak in Your name, he has brought trouble on this people, and You have not delivered Your people in any way.”
paragraphs: 15 So the Israelite foremen went and appealed to Pharaoh: “Why are you treating your servants this way? 16 No straw has been given to your servants, yet we are told, ‘Make bricks!’ Look, your servants are being beaten, but the fault is with your own people.” 17 “You are slackers!” Pharaoh replied. “Slackers! That is why you keep saying, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to the LORD.’ 18 Now get to work. You will be given no straw, yet you must deliver the full quota of bricks.” 19 The Israelite foremen realized they were in trouble when they were told, “You must not reduce your daily quota of bricks.”

20 When they left Pharaoh, they confronted Moses and Aaron, who stood waiting to meet them. 21 “May the LORD look upon you and judge you,” the foremen said, “for you have made us a stench before Pharaoh and his officials; you have placed in their hand a sword to kill us!”

22 So Moses returned to the LORD and asked, “Lord, why have You brought trouble upon this people? Is this why You sent me? 23 Ever since I went to Pharaoh to speak in Your name, he has brought trouble on this people, and You have not delivered Your people in any way.”

passages.context_html:
The Israelite foremen appeal to Pharaoh. They explain that they are being beaten for failing to make bricks while being denied the straw needed for the work. Pharaoh repeats his accusation of laziness and refuses to change the quota.

On leaving, the foremen confront Moses and Aaron. They ask the LORD to judge the brothers for making them offensive to Pharaoh and putting their lives in danger. The people who had bowed in worship at the end of chapter 4 are now represented by leaders who blame the messengers for their suffering.

Moses turns back to the LORD with his own anguished questions. Why has God brought trouble upon the people, and why did He send Moses? Since Moses spoke in His name, Pharaoh has done them harm and no deliverance has come. The chapter ends with that unresolved complaint; God’s answer begins in chapter 6.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The teachers agree that Moses is struggling with the gap between God’s promise and the suffering he sees, but assess his response differently. Wesley emphasizes his difficulty reconciling events with the promise and urges people in such distress to turn to God in prayer. Calvin gives a stronger reading: he understands Moses as returning in bitterness and wanting to abandon the commission. These are different assessments of the complaint, whose questions the passage records directly.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Scripture gives other examples of people crying out while they wait for God’s help. Psalm 13 moves from repeated questions about how long God will seem absent to trust in His faithful love. It gives words to suffering that has not yet been resolved.

Romans 8:18–25 places waiting within God’s larger purpose for His children and creation. Believers groan as they wait for the redemption of their bodies, while creation awaits freedom from decay. The Exodus tells of a promised rescue that is still unfolding; Romans looks ahead to a fuller freedom, when suffering and decay themselves are overcome.

passages.title: Exodus 6:1-13
passages.section_title: What did God promise when the people could no longer listen?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 But the LORD said to Moses, “Now you will see what I will do to Pharaoh, for because of My mighty hand he will let the people go; because of My strong hand he will drive them out of his land.” 2 God also told Moses, “I am the LORD. 3 I appeared to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob as God Almighty, but by My name the LORD I did not make Myself known to them. 4 I also established My covenant with them to give them the land of Canaan, the land where they lived as foreigners. 5 Furthermore, I have heard the groaning of the Israelites, whom the Egyptians are enslaving, and I have remembered My covenant. 6 Therefore tell the Israelites: ‘I am the LORD, and I will bring you out from under the yoke of the Egyptians and deliver you from their bondage. I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with mighty acts of judgment. 7 I will take you as My own people, and I will be your God. Then you will know that I am the LORD your God, who brought you out from under the yoke of the Egyptians. 8 And I will bring you into the land that I swore to give to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. I will give it to you as a possession. I am the LORD!’” 9 Moses relayed this message to the Israelites, but on account of their broken spirit and cruel bondage, they did not listen to him. 10 So the LORD said to Moses, 11 “Go and tell Pharaoh king of Egypt to let the Israelites go out of his land.” 12 But in the LORD’s presence Moses replied, “If the Israelites will not listen to me, then why would Pharaoh listen to me, since I am unskilled in speech?” 13 Then the LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron and gave them a charge concerning both the Israelites and Pharaoh king of Egypt, to bring the Israelites out of the land of Egypt.

I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with mighty acts of judgment. 7 I will take you as My own people, and I will be your God. Then you will know that I am the LORD your God, who brought you out from under the yoke of the Egyptians. 8 And I will bring you into the land that I swore to give to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. I will give it to you as a possession. I am the LORD!’” 9 Moses relayed this message to the Israelites, but on account of their broken spirit and cruel bondage, they did not listen to him.

10 So the LORD said to Moses, 11 “Go and tell Pharaoh king of Egypt to let the Israelites go out of his land.” 12 But in the LORD’s presence Moses replied, “If the Israelites will not listen to me, then why would Pharaoh listen to me, since I am unskilled in speech?” 13 Then the LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron and gave them a charge concerning both the Israelites and Pharaoh king of Egypt, to bring the Israelites out of the land of Egypt.

passages.context_html:
God answers Moses’ complaint by promising that Pharaoh will not merely allow Israel to leave: under God’s mighty hand, he will drive them out. The present setback has not changed the outcome God has declared.

God identifies Himself as the LORD and recalls His appearances to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, His covenant to give them Canaan, and the groaning He has heard. He then promises to bring Israel out of bondage, redeem them through judgment, take them as His people and give them the land He swore to their ancestors. Deliverance includes a relationship: He will be their God, and they will know Him through what He does.

The people do not listen because of their broken spirit and cruel bondage. The account describes people weighed down by suffering, struggling to take in the promise. God nevertheless sends Moses back to Pharaoh.

Moses again questions whether anyone will listen to him. The Hebrew expression translated unskilled in speech is literally uncircumcised of lips. Brown–Driver–Briggs identifies it here as a figure for difficulty speaking. God answers by renewing the charge to both Moses and Aaron to bring Israel out.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The shared reading emphasizes God revealing His faithfulness through the promised deliverance. Calvin and Wesley understand the statement about His name in verse 3 as a fuller experience of who He is: the patriarchs knew the name, while their descendants would now witness the rescue He had promised. Genesis 15:7 already records God identifying Himself to Abraham as the LORD.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
The promise that God will be their God and they will be His people continues beyond this rescue. Jeremiah 31:31–34 repeats that relationship in the promise of a new covenant with Israel and Judah, with God’s law written on their hearts and their sins forgiven. Hebrews 8:6–12 quotes that promise while explaining the better covenant Jesus mediates.

Ezekiel 36:22–28 also joins gathering Israel into the land with cleansing, a new heart and God’s Spirit. The purpose reaches into the people themselves: they are to know God and live in His ways. The Exodus begins a story of rescue and belonging that later promises develop more fully.

The same relationship appears in 2 Corinthians 6:16, where believers are called the temple of the living God, and in Revelation 21:3–4, where God dwells with His people and removes death, grief and pain. The larger purpose is a people living with their God.

passages.title: Exodus 6:14-30
passages.section_title: Why pause the account to name Moses and Aaron’s family?

These were the clans of Reuben. 15 The sons of Simeon were Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul, the son of a Canaanite woman. These were the clans of Simeon. 16 These were the names of the sons of Levi according to their records: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. Levi lived 137 years. 17 The sons of Gershon were Libni and Shimei, by their clans. 18 The sons of Kohath were Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. passages.context_html:
The account pauses between God’s renewed command and the next meeting with Pharaoh to identify the men He has sent. It begins with the families of Reuben and Simeon, then gives more detail about Levi’s family. Reuben, Simeon and Levi are the first three sons in the sequence.

Within Levi’s descendants, the record names Amram and Jochebed as the parents of Aaron and Moses. It also names Aaron’s wife Elisheba and their sons, then continues through Eleazar to Phinehas. The genealogy places the brothers within the family of Israel and gives particular attention to Aaron’s line.

Verses 26–27 make the purpose explicit: these are the Aaron and Moses commanded to bring Israel out and sent to speak to Pharaoh. The final verses return to the conversation about that commission. Moses again raises his difficulty speaking, carrying the account into God’s answer in chapter 7.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The shared reading sees the genealogy as establishing the family identity of God’s appointed servants. Wesley and the Catholic USCCB notes explain the opening names as leading to Levi and then to Moses and Aaron.

One family relationship is read differently. Wesley takes the description of Jochebed in verse 20 more broadly as a kinswoman. Calvin and the USCCB notes understand her as Amram’s paternal aunt. The BSB retains the wording his father’s sister. These are different readings of the relationship, rather than a difference about which men God commissioned.

passages.god_plan_html:
The family record helps explain a distinction the New Testament later makes about priesthood. Aaron and his descendants belong to Levi. Hebrews 7:11–17 contrasts the priesthood associated with Aaron with that of Jesus, who comes from Judah and is priest in the order of Melchizedek.

Hebrews grounds Jesus’ priesthood in the power of His indestructible life. Knowing the family line named here helps readers understand that comparison: the later argument is about how Christ’s enduring priesthood differs from a priesthood passed through Aaron’s family.

passages.title: Exodus 7:1-7
passages.section_title: How would Moses and Aaron speak for God before Pharaoh?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 The LORD answered Moses, “See, I have made you like God to Pharaoh, and your brother Aaron will be your prophet. 2 You are to speak all that I command you, and your brother Aaron is to tell Pharaoh to let the Israelites go out of his land. 3 But I will harden Pharaoh’s heart, and though I will multiply My signs and wonders in the land of Egypt, 4 Pharaoh will not listen to you. Then I will lay My hand on Egypt, and by mighty acts of judgment I will bring the divisions of My people the Israelites out of the land of Egypt. 5 And the Egyptians will know that I am the LORD, when I stretch out My hand against Egypt and bring the Israelites out from among them.” 6 So Moses and Aaron did just as the LORD had commanded them. 7 Moses was eighty years old and Aaron was eighty-three when they spoke to Pharaoh.

Then I will lay My hand on Egypt, and by mighty acts of judgment I will bring the divisions of My people the Israelites out of the land of Egypt. 5 And the Egyptians will know that I am the LORD, when I stretch out My hand against Egypt and bring the Israelites out from among them.”
6 So Moses and Aaron did just as the LORD had commanded them. 7 Moses was eighty years old and Aaron was eighty-three when they spoke to Pharaoh.

passages.context_html:
God answers Moses’ concern about speaking by explaining the brothers’ roles again. Moses is to speak what God commands, and Aaron will deliver that message to Pharaoh. Being made like God to Pharaoh describes the authority Moses has been given to represent Him. Aaron is called his prophet because he will speak the message entrusted to Moses.

God also repeats that Pharaoh will not listen. The signs will multiply, judgment will fall upon Egypt, and Israel will be brought out. The declared outcome reaches beyond their freedom: the Egyptians will know that He is the LORD.

Moses and Aaron now do as commanded. Their ages are given as eighty and eighty-three. After the repeated objections, the account turns toward their obedience and the public display of God’s power.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The shared reading understands Moses as God’s authorized representative and Aaron as his spokesman. Calvin, Wesley and Gill all explain the language about Moses being like God through the authority and work entrusted to him.

The difference over hardening continues here. Calvin emphasizes God actively governing the confrontation, while Wesley describes Pharaoh’s heart being allowed to harden. Their explanations agree that Pharaoh’s resistance will not prevent the deliverance God has announced.

passages.god_plan_html:
God says the Egyptians will know Him through His judgment and Israel’s release. Later, in Exodus 9:14–16, He explains that His power will be displayed and His name proclaimed throughout the earth. The confrontation has a purpose beyond settling the immediate dispute with Pharaoh.

Romans 9:17–18 explicitly uses that explanation of Pharaoh’s place in the story. Paul presents God’s power, His mercy and the making known of His name as part of His larger purpose. That New Testament connection places the coming judgments within the wider story of God making Himself known.

passages.title: Exodus 7:8-13
passages.section_title: Why did the magicians’ imitation not settle the question?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 The LORD said to Moses and Aaron, 9 “When Pharaoh tells you, ‘Perform a miracle,’ you are to say to Aaron, ‘Take your staff and throw it down before Pharaoh,’ and it will become a serpent.” 10 So Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and did just as the LORD had commanded. Aaron threw his staff down before Pharaoh and his officials, and it became a serpent. 11 But Pharaoh called the wise men and sorcerers and magicians of Egypt, and they also did the same things by their magic arts. 12 Each one threw down his staff, and it became a serpent. But Aaron’s staff swallowed up the other staffs. 13 Still, Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he would not listen to them, just as the LORD had said.
paragraphs: 8 The LORD said to Moses and Aaron, 9 “When Pharaoh tells you, ‘Perform a miracle,’ you are to say to Aaron, ‘Take your staff and throw it down before Pharaoh,’ and it will become a serpent.” 10 So Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and did just as the LORD had commanded. Aaron threw his staff down before Pharaoh and his officials, and it became a serpent. 11 But Pharaoh called the wise men and sorcerers and magicians of Egypt, and they also did the same things by their magic arts. 12 Each one threw down his staff, and it became a serpent. But Aaron’s staff swallowed up the other staffs. 13 Still, Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he would not listen to them, just as the LORD had said.

passages.context_html:
God prepares Moses and Aaron for Pharaoh to demand a miracle. They follow His instructions, and Aaron’s staff becomes a serpent before Pharaoh and his officials. The Hebrew word here, tannin, can describe several kinds of formidable creatures; Brown–Driver–Briggs lists its use in these verses as serpent.

Pharaoh calls his wise men, sorcerers and magicians, who do the same by their magic arts. The account then gives the decisive difference: Aaron’s staff swallows theirs. The rivals’ apparent success does not erase the superiority displayed through Aaron.

Even after that, Pharaoh refuses to listen. His response is the one God had already announced. The story is moving from the demand for a sign toward the judgments that will follow.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Readers differ over how the magicians’ imitation worked. The Baptist commentator Gill understands it as an illusion. Wesley suggests that evil angels may have substituted real serpents for the staffs. Calvin considers deception probable but also allows that God may have permitted an actual change. These are the teachers’ explanations of a method the passage does not spell out.

Their readings share the central outcome: the imitation fails to match the power shown through Aaron, yet Pharaoh still refuses God’s command.

passages.god_plan_html:
2 Timothy 3:8–9 names Jannes and Jambres as men who opposed Moses and compares them with people who oppose the truth. Their example becomes a warning about deception, along with an assurance that such opposition has limits and its folly will be exposed.

That connection also fits the test given in Deuteronomy 13:1–4: even a sign that comes to pass does not authorize someone to lead people after other gods. The message must be tested by what God has said. The signs in Pharaoh’s court belong within that larger lesson about recognizing God’s truth amid competing claims.

passages.title: Exodus 7:14-25
passages.section_title: What did the judgment on the Nile reveal?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 Then the LORD said to Moses, “Pharaoh’s heart is unyielding; he refuses to let the people go. 15 Go to Pharaoh in the morning as you see him walking out to the water. Wait on the bank of the Nile to meet him, and take in your hand the staff that was changed into a snake. 16 Then say to him, ‘The LORD, the God of the Hebrews, has sent me to tell you: Let My people go, so that they may worship Me in the wilderness. But until now you have not listened. 17 This is what the LORD says: By this you will know that I am the LORD. Behold, with the staff in my hand I will strike the water of the Nile, and it will turn to blood. 18 The fish in the Nile will die, the river will stink, and the Egyptians will be unable to drink its water.’” 19 And the LORD said to Moses, “Tell Aaron, ‘Take your staff and stretch out your hand over the waters of Egypt—over their rivers and canals and ponds and all the reservoirs—that they may become blood.’ There will be blood throughout the land of Egypt, even in the vessels of wood and stone.” 20 Moses and Aaron did just as the LORD had commanded; in the presence of Pharaoh and his officials, Aaron raised the staff and struck the water of the Nile, and all the water was turned to blood. 21 The fish in the Nile died, and the river smelled so bad that the Egyptians could not drink its water. And there was blood throughout the land of Egypt. 22 But the magicians of Egypt did the same things by their magic arts. So Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he would not listen to Moses and Aaron, just as the LORD had said. 23 Instead, Pharaoh turned around, went into his palace, and did not take any of this to heart. 24 So all the Egyptians dug around the Nile for water to drink, because they could not drink the water from the river. 25 And seven full days passed after the LORD had struck the Nile.

Wait on the bank of the Nile to meet him, and take in your hand the staff that was changed into a snake. 16 Then say to him, ‘The LORD, the God of the Hebrews, has sent me to tell you: Let My people go, so that they may worship Me in the wilderness. But until now you have not listened. 17 This is what the LORD says: By this you will know that I am the LORD. Behold, with the staff in my hand I will strike the water of the Nile, and it will turn to blood. 18 The fish in the Nile will die, the river will stink, and the Egyptians will be unable to drink its water.’”

19 And the LORD said to Moses, “Tell Aaron, ‘Take your staff and stretch out your hand over the waters of Egypt—over their rivers and canals and ponds and all the reservoirs—that they may become blood.’ There will be blood throughout the land of Egypt, even in the vessels of wood and stone.” 20 Moses and Aaron did just as the LORD had commanded; in the presence of Pharaoh and his officials, Aaron raised the staff and struck the water of the Nile, and all the water was turned to blood. 21 The fish in the Nile died, and the river smelled so bad that the Egyptians could not drink its water. And there was blood throughout the land of Egypt.

22 But the magicians of Egypt did the same things by their magic arts. So Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he would not listen to Moses and Aaron, just as the LORD had said. 23 Instead, Pharaoh turned around, went into his palace, and did not take any of this to heart. 24 So all the Egyptians dug around the Nile for water to drink, because they could not drink the water from the river. 25 And seven full days passed after the LORD had struck the Nile.

passages.context_html:
After Pharaoh refuses to listen, God sends Moses to meet him beside the Nile in the morning. The demand remains the same: release God’s people to worship Him. This time the warning names a judgment that will make His identity known—water becoming blood.

Aaron strikes the Nile before Pharaoh and his officials. The fish die, the river stinks, and its water becomes undrinkable. The judgment reaches Egypt’s rivers, canals, ponds and reservoirs, even vessels of wood and stone. The Egyptians dig around the river seeking drinking water.

The river also had religious meaning. The Metropolitan Museum of Art describes Hapy as the Egyptian god who personified its annual flooding and was associated with fertility. That background helps explain the force of the judgment: a source associated with life and abundance has become a source of death and distress.

The magicians imitate the sign, and Pharaoh turns back to his palace without taking it to heart. The account closes with seven full days passing after the LORD struck the Nile. The imitation has given him a reason to dismiss the warning, while his people continue facing its consequences.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The shared reading sees the judgment as a display of the LORD’s authority over the water on which Egypt depends. Wesley emphasizes the reversal in a river the Egyptians honored and the failure of the magicians to restore it.

There are different explanations of how the magicians could repeat the sign after the waters had become blood. Gill proposes a small quantity of water, perhaps newly dug or not yet affected, used to produce an appearance of blood. The Catholic USCCB notes instead treat the comparison as an exaggerated description echoing the earlier contest with the staffs. These are different explanations of the scope and wording of their imitation; the narrative reports it without giving its source of water.

passages.god_plan_html:
Scripture later gives the plagues an explicitly religious purpose. Exodus 12:12 announces judgment against Egypt’s gods, and Numbers 33:3–4 recalls that judgment as Israel leaves. The attack on Egypt’s security belongs within God making Himself known as the One who can deliver His people.

A later parallel appears in Revelation 16:4–7, where waters turn to blood and the judgment answers the shedding of the blood of God’s servants. The repeated image connects the Exodus with a wider theme of God judging those who oppress and kill His people.

passages.title: Exodus 8:1-15
passages.section_title: Why did relief from the frogs not lead Pharaoh to keep his word?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then the LORD said to Moses, “Go to Pharaoh and tell him that this is what the LORD says: ‘Let My people go, so that they may worship Me. 2 But if you refuse to let them go, I will plague your whole country with frogs. 3 The Nile will teem with frogs, and they will come into your palace and up to your bedroom and onto your bed, into the houses of your officials and your people, and into your ovens and kneading bowls. 4 The frogs will come up on you and your people and all your officials.’” 5 And the LORD said to Moses, “Tell Aaron, ‘Stretch out your hand with your staff over the rivers and canals and ponds, and cause the frogs to come up onto the land of Egypt.’” 6 So Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters of Egypt, and the frogs came up and covered the land of Egypt. 7 But the magicians did the same thing by their magic arts, and they also brought frogs up onto the land of Egypt. 8 Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said, “Pray to the LORD to take the frogs away from me and my people. Then I will let your people go, that they may sacrifice to the LORD.” 9 Moses said to Pharaoh, “You may have the honor over me. When shall I pray for you and your officials and your people that the frogs (except for those in the Nile) may be taken away from you and your houses?” 10 “Tomorrow,” Pharaoh answered. “May it be as you say,” Moses replied, “so that you may know that there is no one like the LORD our God. 11 The frogs will depart from you and your houses and your officials and your people; they will remain only in the Nile.” 12 After Moses and Aaron had left Pharaoh, Moses cried out to the LORD for help with the frogs that He had brought against Pharaoh. 13 And the LORD did as Moses requested, and the frogs in the houses, the courtyards, and the fields died. 14 They were piled into countless heaps, and there was a terrible stench in the land. 15 When Pharaoh saw that there was relief, however, he hardened his heart and would not listen to Moses and Aaron, just as the LORD had said.

8 Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said, “Pray to the LORD to take the frogs away from me and my people. Then I will let your people go, that they may sacrifice to the LORD.” 9 Moses said to Pharaoh, “You may have the honor over me. When shall I pray for you and your officials and your people that the frogs (except for those in the Nile) may be taken away from you and your houses?” 10 “Tomorrow,” Pharaoh answered. “May it be as you say,” Moses replied, “so that you may know that there is no one like the LORD our God. 11 The frogs will depart from you and your houses and your officials and your people; they will remain only in the Nile.”

12 After Moses and Aaron had left Pharaoh, Moses cried out to the LORD for help with the frogs that He had brought against Pharaoh. 13 And the LORD did as Moses requested, and the frogs in the houses, the courtyards, and the fields died. 14 They were piled into countless heaps, and there was a terrible stench in the land. 15 When Pharaoh saw that there was relief, however, he hardened his heart and would not listen to Moses and Aaron, just as the LORD had said.

passages.context_html:
God again commands Pharaoh to release His people for worship, this time warning of frogs throughout the country. They enter bedrooms, beds, ovens and kneading bowls. The plague carries the disturbance into the most ordinary parts of home life. The magicians bring up more frogs, adding to what is already overwhelming the land.

Frogs also had a place in Egyptian religion. The Global Egyptian Museum describes Heqet as a goddess shown as a frog or with a frog’s head, associated with life and childbirth. That supplies cultural background for the reversal here: creatures associated with new life have become an unbearable intrusion.

Pharaoh now asks Moses and Aaron to pray to the LORD and promises to release the people. Moses lets him choose when the frogs should be removed, so he may know there is no one like the LORD. Pharaoh chooses the next day.

Moses prays, God answers, and the frogs outside the Nile die. Their heaps leave a terrible smell, but the immediate pressure has eased. Pharaoh responds to that relief by hardening his heart and refusing to listen. His promise does not survive the end of the crisis.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The shared reading distinguishes asking for relief from a lasting willingness to obey. Calvin and Wesley both emphasize Pharaoh returning to resistance after the pressure is removed, while God’s answer to Moses demonstrates His authority over the plague.

passages.god_plan_html:
Moses prays for the ruler who is resisting God, and God removes the plague. This is an example of praying on someone else’s behalf. 1 Timothy 2:1–6 later calls believers to pray for everyone, including rulers, and names Christ Jesus as the One who brings people to God and gave Himself as a ransom.

There is also a wider parallel with Christ’s work for His people. Hebrews 7:23–27 describes Jesus as the enduring high priest who always lives to intercede for those who come to God through Him. Moses’ prayer brings temporary relief from a plague; Jesus’ priestly work brings complete salvation. The parallel points toward the fuller help found in Christ.

passages.title: Exodus 8:16-19
passages.section_title: What happened when the magicians could no longer imitate the sign?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 Then the LORD said to Moses, “Tell Aaron, ‘Stretch out your staff and strike the dust of the earth, that it may turn into swarms of gnats throughout the land of Egypt.’” 17 This they did, and when Aaron stretched out his hand with his staff and struck the dust of the earth, gnats came upon man and beast. All the dust of the earth turned into gnats throughout the land of Egypt. 18 The magicians tried to produce gnats using their magic arts, but they could not. And the gnats remained on man and beast. 19 “This is the finger of God,” the magicians said to Pharaoh. But Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he would not listen to them, just as the LORD had said.
paragraphs: 16 Then the LORD said to Moses, “Tell Aaron, ‘Stretch out your staff and strike the dust of the earth, that it may turn into swarms of gnats throughout the land of Egypt.’” 17 This they did, and when Aaron stretched out his hand with his staff and struck the dust of the earth, gnats came upon man and beast. All the dust of the earth turned into gnats throughout the land of Egypt. 18 The magicians tried to produce gnats using their magic arts, but they could not. And the gnats remained on man and beast. 19 “This is the finger of God,” the magicians said to Pharaoh. But Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he would not listen to them, just as the LORD had said.

passages.context_html:
At God’s command Aaron strikes the dust with his staff, and gnats come upon people and animals throughout Egypt. The Hebrew word translated gnats has also been understood as lice. Brown–Driver–Briggs records that uncertainty; the point of the account is an infestation the magicians cannot reproduce.

Their earlier imitations have now reached a limit. They tell Pharaoh that this is the finger of God, acknowledging a power beyond their own. Pharaoh still does not listen. Even the failure of the people he called to oppose Moses does not change his refusal.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The shared reading sees the magicians’ failure and admission as exposing the limits of their power. Calvin, Wesley and the Catholic USCCB notes all understand the finger of God as recognizing divine power at work beyond what they can match.
