deeper_study.title: Should We Seek Signs From God?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The expression finger of God returns in Luke 11:14–23. When Jesus is accused of driving out demons through their ruler, He says that if He does it by the finger of God, God’s kingdom has come upon His hearers. Matthew 12:28 describes that work as being by the Spirit of God.

The language provides a connection between the power recognized in Egypt and the power displayed through Jesus. In Exodus, the magicians admit that they have reached their limit; in the Gospels, Jesus’ victory over demons announces the arrival of God’s kingdom.

passages.title: Exodus 8:20-32
passages.section_title: Why did God distinguish Goshen from the rest of Egypt?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 20 Then the LORD said to Moses, “Get up early in the morning, and when Pharaoh goes out to the water, stand before him and tell him that this is what the LORD says: ‘Let My people go, so that they may worship Me. 21 But if you will not let My people go, I will send swarms of flies upon you and your officials and your people and your houses. The houses of the Egyptians and even the ground where they stand will be full of flies. 22 But on that day I will give special treatment to the land of Goshen, where My people live; no swarms of flies will be found there. In this way you will know that I, the LORD, am in the land. 23 I will make a distinction between My people and your people. This sign will take place tomorrow.’” 24 And the LORD did so. Thick swarms of flies poured into Pharaoh’s palace and into the houses of his officials. Throughout Egypt the land was ruined by swarms of flies. 25 Then Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said, “Go, sacrifice to your God within this land.” 26 But Moses replied, “It would not be right to do that, because the sacrifices we offer to the LORD our God would be detestable to the Egyptians. If we offer sacrifices that are detestable before the Egyptians, will they not stone us? 27 We must make a three-day journey into the wilderness and sacrifice to the LORD our God as He commands us.” 28 Pharaoh answered, “I will let you go and sacrifice to the LORD your God in the wilderness, but you must not go very far. Now pray for me.” 29 “As soon as I leave you,” Moses said, “I will pray to the LORD, so that tomorrow the swarms of flies will depart from Pharaoh and his officials and his people. But Pharaoh must not act deceitfully again by refusing to let the people go and sacrifice to the LORD.” 30 Then Moses left Pharaoh and prayed to the LORD, 31 and the LORD did as Moses requested. He removed the swarms of flies from Pharaoh and his officials and his people; not one fly remained. 32 But Pharaoh hardened his heart this time as well, and he would not let the people go.

Thick swarms of flies poured into Pharaoh’s palace and into the houses of his officials. Throughout Egypt the land was ruined by swarms of flies.

25 Then Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said, “Go, sacrifice to your God within this land.” 26 But Moses replied, “It would not be right to do that, because the sacrifices we offer to the LORD our God would be detestable to the Egyptians. If we offer sacrifices that are detestable before the Egyptians, will they not stone us? 27 We must make a three-day journey into the wilderness and sacrifice to the LORD our God as He commands us.” 28 Pharaoh answered, “I will let you go and sacrifice to the LORD your God in the wilderness, but you must not go very far. Now pray for me.” 29 “As soon as I leave you,” Moses said, “I will pray to the LORD, so that tomorrow the swarms of flies will depart from Pharaoh and his officials and his people. But Pharaoh must not act deceitfully again by refusing to let the people go and sacrifice to the LORD.”

30 Then Moses left Pharaoh and prayed to the LORD, 31 and the LORD did as Moses requested. He removed the swarms of flies from Pharaoh and his officials and his people; not one fly remained. 32 But Pharaoh hardened his heart this time as well, and he would not let the people go.

passages.context_html:
The next warning announces swarms of flies, with a specific distinction: Goshen, where God’s people live, will be spared. God gives the reason—to make Pharaoh know that the LORD is present in the land. The announced timing and boundary make the sign more than a general disaster.

The Hebrew word for these swarms, arob, differs from the word for the gnats in the preceding passage. Brown–Driver–Briggs describes a swarm of stinging flies. The account emphasizes their overwhelming numbers and the ruin they bring.

Pharaoh first offers to let Israel sacrifice within Egypt. Moses objects that their sacrifices would be detestable to the Egyptians and expose them to stoning. He insists on the journey into the wilderness to sacrifice as God commands. Pharaoh then offers to let them go, provided they do not go far, and asks for prayer.

Moses promises to pray and warns Pharaoh against another deceitful refusal. God removes every fly in answer to that prayer, but Pharaoh again hardens his heart and keeps the people in bondage. His concessions have not become obedience.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The distinction between Goshen and Egypt is read as a deliberate display of God’s care and authority. Readers differ over whether that protection also applied to the earlier plagues. Calvin extends it to them, even though it had not been expressly stated. The Catholic USCCB notes describe this as the point where Israel begins to be set apart. The exemption from this plague is explicit in the passage.

Wesley also emphasizes God directing the swarms and hearing Moses’ prayer, alongside Pharaoh’s continued responsibility for breaking his word after relief comes.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
God’s ability to distinguish between those He judges and those He preserves appears elsewhere in Scripture. 2 Peter 2:5–9 recalls Noah’s preservation through the flood and Lot’s rescue from Sodom, then says the Lord knows how to rescue the godly and hold the unrighteous for judgment.

That is a wider parallel with the distinction made here. God’s judgment is not blind to His people. The protection of Goshen makes His knowledge and care visible within this particular act of deliverance, while Peter carries the theme toward the coming day of judgment.

passages.title: Exodus 9:1-7
passages.section_title: What did Pharaoh learn when the livestock were struck?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then the LORD said to Moses, “Go to Pharaoh and tell him that this is what the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, says: ‘Let My people go, so that they may worship Me. 2 But if you continue to restrain them and refuse to let them go, 3 then the hand of the LORD will bring a severe plague on your livestock in the field—on your horses, donkeys, camels, herds, and flocks. 4 But the LORD will make a distinction between the livestock of Israel and the livestock of Egypt, so that no animal belonging to the Israelites will die.’” 5 The LORD set a time, saying, “Tomorrow the LORD will do this in the land.” 6 And the next day the LORD did just that. All the livestock of the Egyptians died, but not one animal belonging to the Israelites died. 7 Pharaoh sent officials and found that none of the livestock of the Israelites had died. But Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he would not let the people go.
paragraphs: 1 Then the LORD said to Moses, “Go to Pharaoh and tell him that this is what the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, says: ‘Let My people go, so that they may worship Me. 2 But if you continue to restrain them and refuse to let them go, 3 then the hand of the LORD will bring a severe plague on your livestock in the field—on your horses, donkeys, camels, herds, and flocks. 4 But the LORD will make a distinction between the livestock of Israel and the livestock of Egypt, so that no animal belonging to the Israelites will die.’” 5 The LORD set a time, saying, “Tomorrow the LORD will do this in the land.” 6 And the next day the LORD did just that. All the livestock of the Egyptians died, but not one animal belonging to the Israelites died. 7 Pharaoh sent officials and found that none of the livestock of the Israelites had died. But Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he would not let the people go.

passages.context_html:
God again demands the release of His people for worship and warns of a severe plague on Egypt’s livestock in the field. Horses, donkeys, camels, herds and flocks are named. The judgment reaches the animals upon which the people’s work and households depend.

A specific time and distinction are announced: the plague will come the next day, and no animal belonging to Israel will die. The event occurs as declared. Pharaoh sends officials to check and learns that Israel’s livestock have indeed been spared.

The investigation confirms what Moses said, but Pharaoh still refuses to release the people. This is another step in the confrontation: he has checked the evidence of the distinction and continues to resist.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The shared reading sees the timing and preservation of Israel’s livestock as demonstrating God’s deliberate action. The description that all the Egyptian livestock died is explained in more than one way, since animals remain in the later account. Wesley understands it as all those in the field, following the scope of the warning in verse 3. Calvin takes it as a broad description of devastating losses throughout the herds, rather than the death of every animal in Egypt.

passages.title: Exodus 9:8-12
passages.section_title: What happened when the magicians themselves were struck?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 Then the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, “Take handfuls of soot from the furnace; in the sight of Pharaoh, Moses is to toss it into the air. 9 It will become fine dust over all the land of Egypt, and festering boils will break out on man and beast throughout the land.” 10 So they took soot from the furnace and stood before Pharaoh. Moses tossed it into the air, and festering boils broke out on man and beast. 11 The magicians could not stand before Moses, because the boils had broken out on them and on all the Egyptians. 12 But the LORD hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he would not listen to them, just as the LORD had said to Moses.
paragraphs: 8 Then the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, “Take handfuls of soot from the furnace; in the sight of Pharaoh, Moses is to toss it into the air. 9 It will become fine dust over all the land of Egypt, and festering boils will break out on man and beast throughout the land.” 10 So they took soot from the furnace and stood before Pharaoh. Moses tossed it into the air, and festering boils broke out on man and beast. 11 The magicians could not stand before Moses, because the boils had broken out on them and on all the Egyptians. 12 But the LORD hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he would not listen to them, just as the LORD had said to Moses.

passages.context_html:
God tells Moses and Aaron to take soot from a furnace, and Moses throws it into the air in Pharaoh’s sight. It becomes fine dust, and festering boils break out on people and animals. The account moves from earlier disturbances and losses into painful affliction of their bodies.

The magicians are affected too and cannot stand before Moses. Those who had tried to match the signs cannot protect themselves from this judgment. The USCCB notes observe that the exact disease is uncertain; the passage describes the sores and their effect.

The LORD hardens Pharaoh’s heart, and he does not listen. This fulfills the warning God gave before Moses returned to confront him.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The magicians’ inability to stand is understood as a public exposure of their limits. The explanation of God hardening Pharaoh remains a point of difference. Calvin emphasizes God actively governing the outcome while Pharaoh remains willingly resistant. Wesley understands it as judgment upon repeated self-hardening, with God giving Pharaoh over and permitting Satan to blind and harden him. These are the teachers’ different explanations of the action named in verse 12.

passages.god_plan_html:
A later parallel appears in Revelation 16:2, where painful sores fall upon those who bear the beast’s mark and worship its image. Both passages use bodily affliction within an account of God judging resistance to Him.

The parallel connects this plague with the wider biblical warning about judgment and misplaced allegiance. In Exodus, the people who had relied on their magic cannot escape the sores themselves; in Revelation, the allegiance attached to the judgment is made explicit. The circumstances differ, but both accounts expose the failure of powers that oppose God.

passages.title: Exodus 9:13-35
passages.section_title: What did the hail reveal about God’s power and Pharaoh’s promises?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 Then the LORD said to Moses, “Get up early in the morning, stand before Pharaoh, and tell him that this is what the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, says: ‘Let My people go, so that they may worship Me. 14 Otherwise, I will send all My plagues against you and your officials and your people, so you may know that there is no one like Me in all the earth. 15 For by this time I could have stretched out My hand and struck you and your people with a plague to wipe you off the earth. 16 But I have raised you up for this very purpose, that I might display My power to you, and that My name might be proclaimed in all the earth. 17 Still, you lord it over My people and do not allow them to go. 18 Behold, at this time tomorrow I will rain down the worst hail that has ever fallen on Egypt, from the day it was founded until now. 19 So give orders now to shelter your livestock and everything you have in the field. Every man or beast that remains in the field and is not brought inside will die when the hail comes down upon them.’” 20 Those among Pharaoh’s officials who feared the word of the LORD hurried to bring their servants and livestock to shelter, 21 but those who disregarded the word of the LORD left their servants and livestock in the field. 22 Then the LORD said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand toward heaven, so that hail may fall on all the land of Egypt—on man and beast and every plant of the field throughout the land of Egypt.” 23 So Moses stretched out his staff toward heaven, and the LORD sent thunder and hail, and lightning struck the earth. So the LORD rained down hail upon the land of Egypt. 24 The hail fell and the lightning continued flashing through it. The hail was so severe that nothing like it had ever been seen in all the land of Egypt from the time it became a nation. 25 Throughout the land of Egypt, the hail struck down everything in the field, both man and beast; it beat down every plant of the field and stripped every tree. 26 The only place where it did not hail was in the land of Goshen, where the Israelites lived. 27 Then Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron. “This time I have sinned,” he said. “The LORD is righteous, and I and my people are wicked. 28 Pray to the LORD, for there has been enough of God’s thunder and hail. I will let you go; you do not need to stay any longer.” 29 Moses said to him, “When I have left the city, I will spread out my hands to the LORD. The thunder will cease, and there will be no more hail, so that you may know that the earth is the LORD’s. 30 But as for you and your officials, I know that you still do not fear the LORD our God.” 31 (Now the flax and barley were destroyed, since the barley was ripe and the flax was in bloom; 32 but the wheat and spelt were not destroyed, because they are late crops.) 33 Then Moses departed from Pharaoh, went out of the city, and spread out his hands to the LORD. The thunder and hail ceased, and the rain no longer poured down on the land. 34 When Pharaoh saw that the rain and hail and thunder had ceased, he sinned again and hardened his heart—he and his officials. 35 So Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he would not let the Israelites go, just as the LORD had said through Moses.

I will let you go; you do not need to stay any longer.” 29 Moses said to him, “When I have left the city, I will spread out my hands to the LORD. The thunder will cease, and there will be no more hail, so that you may know that the earth is the LORD’s. 30 But as for you and your officials, I know that you still do not fear the LORD our God.” 31 (Now the flax and barley were destroyed, since the barley was ripe and the flax was in bloom; 32 but the wheat and spelt were not destroyed, because they are late crops.)

33 Then Moses departed from Pharaoh, went out of the city, and spread out his hands to the LORD. The thunder and hail ceased, and the rain no longer poured down on the land. 34 When Pharaoh saw that the rain and hail and thunder had ceased, he sinned again and hardened his heart—he and his officials. 35 So Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he would not let the Israelites go, just as the LORD had said through Moses.

passages.context_html:
The next warning explains why Pharaoh is still standing. God could already have destroyed him and his people, but has preserved him to display His power and make His name known throughout the earth. The Hebrew verb behind raised you up comes from amad, to stand. Brown–Driver–Briggs explains its use here as maintaining someone rather than overthrowing him. The preceding verse places that preservation in view.

God announces unprecedented hail and also gives a warning that can save lives: bring servants and livestock under shelter. Some of Pharaoh’s officials fear the LORD’s word and act on it. Others leave them in the field. The account distinguishes these responses within Egypt itself.

The hail and lightning devastate what is exposed, while Goshen is spared. Pharaoh confesses that he has sinned, calls the LORD righteous and promises to release Israel. Moses agrees to pray, but tells him that he and his officials still do not fear the LORD.

The account also distinguishes the crops. Flax and barley are destroyed at their more advanced stage, while wheat and spelt remain because they are later crops. This explains why the next plague will still have something to consume.

When Moses prays, the storm ends. Pharaoh and his officials respond by hardening their hearts again. His confession has not led to keeping his promise. The closing refusal confirms what God had already said would happen.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The difference over God’s part in Pharaoh’s hardening continues through this account. Calvin understands God as actively directing the confrontation and connects Pharaoh’s preservation with a purpose determined before his birth. Wesley explains hardening as God giving Pharaoh over after his repeated resistance, permitting Satan to blind him. Both hold Pharaoh responsible for his refusal, while explaining God’s action differently.

They agree on the failure of Pharaoh’s confession to produce lasting obedience. Both point to his return to resistance after the storm ends. The words he says under pressure are tested by what he does when the pressure is removed.

passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 9:17–24 directly quotes God’s explanation to Pharaoh about displaying His power and making His name known. Paul places that event within his discussion of God’s mercy, patience and purposes, including His calling of people from both Jews and Gentiles. The Exodus becomes part of the New Testament’s explanation of God’s wider work.

Pharaoh’s response also illustrates a distinction made in 2 Corinthians 7:8–11: sorrow can lead to repentance, or it can remain sorrow over what has happened. Paul describes a sorrow that produces a changed response. Pharaoh’s story provides a contrasting example—the trouble stops, and his resistance returns. This is a parallel about the response to correction; Paul is addressing the Corinthians in their own circumstances.

passages.title: Exodus 10:1-20
passages.section_title: Why were these events to be remembered by future generations?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then the LORD said to Moses, “Go to Pharaoh, for I have hardened his heart and the hearts of his officials, that I may perform these miraculous signs of Mine among them, 2 and that you may tell your children and grandchildren how severely I dealt with the Egyptians when I performed miraculous signs among them, so that all of you may know that I am the LORD.” 3 So Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and told him, “This is what the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, says: ‘How long will you refuse to humble yourself before Me? Let My people go, so that they may worship Me. 4 But if you refuse to let My people go, I will bring locusts into your territory tomorrow. 5 They will cover the face of the land so that no one can see it. They will devour whatever is left after the hail and eat every tree that grows in your fields. 6 They will fill your houses and the houses of all your officials and every Egyptian—something neither your fathers nor your grandfathers have seen since the day they came into this land.’” Then Moses turned and left Pharaoh’s presence. 7 Pharaoh’s officials asked him, “How long will this man be a snare to us? Let the people go, so that they may worship the LORD their God. Do you not yet realize that Egypt lies in ruins?” 8 So Moses and Aaron were brought back to Pharaoh. “Go, worship the LORD your God,” he said. “But who exactly will be going?” 9 “We will go with our young and old,” Moses replied. “We will go with our sons and daughters, and with our flocks and herds, for we must hold a feast to the LORD.” 10 Then Pharaoh told them, “May the LORD be with you if I ever let you go with your little ones. Clearly you are bent on evil. 11 No, only the men may go and worship the LORD, since that is what you have been requesting.” And Moses and Aaron were driven from Pharaoh’s presence. 12 Then the LORD said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand over the land of Egypt, so that the locusts may swarm over it and devour every plant in the land—everything that the hail has left behind.” 13 So Moses stretched out his staff over the land of Egypt, and throughout that day and night the LORD sent an east wind across the land. By morning the east wind had brought the locusts. 14 The locusts swarmed across the land and settled over the entire territory of Egypt. Never before had there been so many locusts, and never again will there be. 15 They covered the face of all the land until it was black, and they consumed all the plants on the ground and all the fruit on the trees that the hail had left behind. Nothing green was left on any tree or plant in all the land of Egypt. 16 Pharaoh quickly summoned Moses and Aaron and said, “I have sinned against the LORD your God and against you. 17 Now please forgive my sin once more and appeal to the LORD your God, that He may remove this death from me.” 18 So Moses left Pharaoh’s presence and appealed to the LORD. 19 And the LORD changed the wind to a very strong west wind that carried off the locusts and blew them into the Red Sea. Not a single locust remained anywhere in Egypt. 20 But the LORD hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he would not let the Israelites go.

Not a single locust remained anywhere in Egypt. 20 But the LORD hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he would not let the Israelites go.

passages.context_html:
God gives another reason for the signs: Israel is to tell its children and grandchildren what He has done, so they too will know that He is the LORD. The deliverance is to become a remembered and retold part of the people’s life.

Moses warns that locusts will consume what the hail has left. Pharaoh’s officials now urge him to let the people go, saying Egypt lies in ruins. He calls the brothers back but tries to limit who may leave. Moses names everyone—young and old, sons and daughters, along with their animals. Pharaoh offers to release only the men and drives the brothers away.

At God’s command Moses stretches out his staff. An east wind brings locusts in overwhelming numbers, and they consume the remaining plants and fruit. The food that survived the hail is now lost.

Pharaoh hurriedly confesses his sin against the LORD and the brothers, then asks for this death to be removed. Moses prays, and God sends a strong west wind that carries every locust away. The removal is as complete as the invasion was overwhelming, but Pharaoh still refuses to release Israel.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The shared reading sees Pharaoh trying to retain control by offering only part of what is demanded. Calvin and Wesley read his sarcastic words about the LORD being with Israel as a threat, and both emphasize that relief from the plague does not become a lasting willingness to obey.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
The command to tell the coming generations is developed in Deuteronomy 6:20–25. When a child asks about God’s commands, the answer begins with slavery in Egypt and the LORD’s mighty deliverance. Remembering the rescue helps the next generation understand why they belong to Him.

Psalm 78:1–8 gives the purpose of passing on God’s works: children yet to be born are to place their confidence in Him, remember what He has done and keep His commands. The story is meant to shape trust and obedience.

The New Testament also treats Israel’s history as instruction for later readers. In 1 Corinthians 10:1–12, Paul recalls the journey through the sea and the wilderness, explaining that these events were written as examples and warnings for the church. He is discussing later parts of Israel’s story there; the wider connection is that God’s remembered acts continue teaching His people.

passages.title: Exodus 10:21-29
passages.section_title: What did the darkness reveal about Pharaoh’s remaining demands?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 Then the LORD said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand toward heaven, so that darkness may spread over the land of Egypt—a palpable darkness.” 22 So Moses stretched out his hand toward heaven, and total darkness covered all the land of Egypt for three days. 23 No one could see anyone else, and for three days no one left his place. Yet all the Israelites had light in their dwellings. 24 Then Pharaoh summoned Moses and said, “Go, worship the LORD. Even your little ones may go with you; only your flocks and herds must stay behind.” 25 But Moses replied, “You must also provide us with sacrifices and burnt offerings to present to the LORD our God. 26 Even our livestock must go with us; not a hoof will be left behind, for we will need some of them to worship the LORD our God, and we will not know how we are to worship the LORD until we arrive.” 27 But the LORD hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he was unwilling to let them go. 28 “Depart from me!” Pharaoh said to Moses. “Make sure you never see my face again, for on the day you see my face, you will die.” 29 “As you say,” Moses replied, “I will never see your face again.”

Yet all the Israelites had light in their dwellings.

24 Then Pharaoh summoned Moses and said, “Go, worship the LORD. Even your little ones may go with you; only your flocks and herds must stay behind.” 25 But Moses replied, “You must also provide us with sacrifices and burnt offerings to present to the LORD our God. 26 Even our livestock must go with us; not a hoof will be left behind, for we will need some of them to worship the LORD our God, and we will not know how we are to worship the LORD until we arrive.” 27 But the LORD hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he was unwilling to let them go. 28 “Depart from me!” Pharaoh said to Moses. “Make sure you never see my face again, for on the day you see my face, you will die.” 29 “As you say,” Moses replied, “I will never see your face again.”

passages.context_html:
God commands Moses to stretch out his hand, and darkness covers Egypt for three days. It is described as darkness that could be felt. People cannot see one another or leave their places, while the Israelites have light in their dwellings.

Light also mattered in Egypt’s religious life. The Metropolitan Museum of Art describes ancient scarabs bearing inscriptions that sought the protection of the sun god Re. That background gives another dimension to the judgment: Egypt’s religious confidence offers no escape from the darkness God sends.

Pharaoh makes a further offer. The families may go, including the children, but the flocks and herds must remain. Moses insists that the animals must go too, since they will need them for the worship God commands. The terms of that worship are for God to determine.

The LORD hardens Pharaoh’s heart, and he refuses. Pharaoh then threatens Moses with death if he sees him again. Moses accepts that this confrontation is reaching its end. The next chapter brings the announcement of the final judgment.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The shared reading understands the darkness as an extraordinary act of God exposing Egypt’s helplessness and distinguishing Israel’s situation. Calvin and Wesley both connect the judgment and Israel’s light with God’s power and care, while the final exchange shows Pharaoh continuing to resist the full release of the people.

passages.god_plan_html:
A later parallel appears in Revelation 16:10–11, where the beast’s kingdom is plunged into darkness. Its people suffer and curse God, yet still do not repent. Darkness again appears within judgment upon a power that opposes God.

The parallel includes the response as well as the darkness itself. In Egypt, Pharaoh’s control is exposed as powerless to prevent the judgment, but his refusal continues. Revelation likewise shows that suffering under judgment does not by itself produce repentance. Both accounts direct attention to God’s authority over kingdoms that resist Him.

passages.title: Exodus 11:1-10
passages.section_title: What would finally bring Israel’s release?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then the LORD said to Moses, “I will bring upon Pharaoh and Egypt one more plague. After that, he will allow you to leave this place. And when he lets you go, he will drive you out completely. 2 Now announce to the people that men and women alike should ask their neighbors for articles of silver and gold.” 3 And the LORD gave the people favor in the sight of the Egyptians. Moreover, Moses himself was highly regarded in Egypt by Pharaoh’s officials and by the people. 4 So Moses declared, “This is what the LORD says: ‘About midnight I will go throughout Egypt, 5 and every firstborn son in the land of Egypt will die, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sits on his throne, to the firstborn of the servant girl behind the hand mill, as well as the firstborn of all the cattle. 6 Then a great cry will go out over all the land of Egypt. Such an outcry has never been heard before and will never be heard again. 7 But among all the Israelites, not even a dog will snarl at man or beast.’ Then you will know that the LORD makes a distinction between Egypt and Israel. 8 And all these officials of yours will come and bow before me, saying, ‘Go, you and all the people who follow you!’ After that, I will depart.” And hot with anger, Moses left Pharaoh’s presence. 9 The LORD said to Moses, “Pharaoh will not listen to you, so that My wonders may be multiplied in the land of Egypt.” 10 Moses and Aaron did all these wonders before Pharaoh, but the LORD hardened Pharaoh’s heart so that he would not let the Israelites go out of his land.

And when he lets you go, he will drive you out completely. 2 Now announce to the people that men and women alike should ask their neighbors for articles of silver and gold.” 3 And the LORD gave the people favor in the sight of the Egyptians. Moreover, Moses himself was highly regarded in Egypt by Pharaoh’s officials and by the people.

4 So Moses declared, “This is what the LORD says: ‘About midnight I will go throughout Egypt, 5 and every firstborn son in the land of Egypt will die, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sits on his throne, to the firstborn of the servant girl behind the hand mill, as well as the firstborn of all the cattle. 6 Then a great cry will go out over all the land of Egypt. Such an outcry has never been heard before and will never be heard again. 7 But among all the Israelites, not even a dog will snarl at man or beast.’ Then you will know that the LORD makes a distinction between Egypt and Israel. 8 And all these officials of yours will come and bow before me, saying, ‘Go, you and all the people who follow you!’ After that, I will depart.” And hot with anger, Moses left Pharaoh’s presence.

9 The LORD said to Moses, “Pharaoh will not listen to you, so that My wonders may be multiplied in the land of Egypt.” 10 Moses and Aaron did all these wonders before Pharaoh, but the LORD hardened Pharaoh’s heart so that he would not let the Israelites go out of his land.

passages.context_html:
God announces one more plague. After it, Pharaoh will drive the people out completely. Israel is also told to ask its Egyptian neighbors for silver and gold, and the account describes the favor God has given the people and the regard in which Moses is now held.

Moses warns Pharaoh that the LORD will go through Egypt about midnight and every firstborn son will die, from the royal household to the household of the servant girl grinding grain. The firstborn of the cattle are included. Rank and wealth will not shield a household from the coming grief.

The great outcry in Egypt is contrasted with the quiet promised to Israel, expressed through the image of not even a dog snarling at its people or animals. The distinction will make the LORD’s action known. Pharaoh’s own officials will urge Moses and the people to leave.

Moses leaves Pharaoh in anger. The final verses look back over the wonders and the continued refusal: the LORD has hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and the people have not yet been released. The warning now stands immediately before the instructions for Passover.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The shared reading sees the final warning as bringing the confrontation to its announced conclusion. Calvin and Wesley understand Moses’ speech as continuing the final interview described at the end of chapter 10, before he leaves Pharaoh’s presence.

The request for silver and gold receives different explanations. Wesley emphasizes asking rather than borrowing and understands the goods as compensation for the people’s labor. Calvin allows a request made as borrowing, justified by God’s authority to transfer the possessions, and limits his explanation to this particular divine command. Brown–Driver–Briggs notes that the verb can describe borrowing, while also observing that a pretext of temporary use is not clear here. The BSB uses ask.

passages.god_plan_html:
The coming judgment is directly recalled in Hebrews 11:28. It describes Moses keeping the Passover and applying the blood by faith so that Israel’s firstborn would be spared. The instructions that follow in Exodus will show how the people are to trust and act on God’s word.

Jude 1:5 places the wider deliverance within the New Testament’s teaching about Jesus, recalling that He brought His people out of Egypt and later judged unbelief. Rescue and accountability remain together in that recollection. The Exodus becomes both a testimony to God’s saving action and a warning about how His people respond to Him.

passages.title: Exodus 12:1-13
passages.section_title: How were the households to prepare for the Passover?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now the LORD said to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt, 2 “This month is the beginning of months for you; it shall be the first month of your year. 3 Tell the whole congregation of Israel that on the tenth day of this month each man must select a lamb for his family, one per household. 4 If the household is too small for a whole lamb, they are to share with the nearest neighbor based on the number of people, and apportion the lamb accordingly. 5 Your lamb must be an unblemished year-old male, and you may take it from the sheep or the goats. 6 You must keep it until the fourteenth day of the month, when the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel will slaughter the animals at twilight. 7 They are to take some of the blood and put it on the sides and tops of the doorframes of the houses where they eat the lambs. 8 They are to eat the meat that night, roasted over the fire, along with unleavened bread and bitter herbs. 9 Do not eat any of the meat raw or cooked in boiling water, but only roasted over the fire—its head and legs and inner parts. 10 Do not leave any of it until morning; before the morning you must burn up any part that is left over. 11 This is how you are to eat it: You must be fully dressed for travel, with your sandals on your feet and your staff in your hand. You are to eat in haste; it is the LORD’s Passover. 12 On that night I will pass through the land of Egypt and strike down every firstborn male, both man and beast, and I will execute judgment against all the gods of Egypt. I am the LORD. 13 The blood on the houses where you are staying will be a sign; when I see the blood, I will pass over you. No plague will fall on you to destroy you when I strike the land of Egypt.

passages.context_html:
God marks the coming rescue by making this month the beginning of Israel’s year. Each household is to select an unblemished year-old male from the sheep or goats on the tenth day and keep it until the fourteenth, when the animals are to be killed at twilight. Smaller households are to share with their nearest neighbor according to how much they can eat.

The Hebrew word for unblemished, tamim, describes something complete and sound. Brown–Driver–Briggs lists its use for sacrificial animals here. The required condition of the animal is part of God’s instructions for the meal.

The blood is to be put on the sides and top of the doorframe. Inside, the household is to eat the animal roasted, with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, ready for travel. Anything left until morning must be burned. The meal prepares them to leave when God delivers them.

God says He will strike Egypt’s firstborn and execute judgment against its gods. The blood on the houses is the sign He appoints: when He sees it, He will spare those houses. The instructions join a meal, a promised protection and readiness for departure.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The shared Christian reading sees Passover as God’s appointed rescue and as pointing toward Christ. That connection is affirmed in the Catholic Catechism 1340, the Westminster Confession 7.5 and Wesley’s notes, while the New Testament itself provides the foundation for it.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Should We Seek Signs From God? understands the blood on the Passover doorposts as a sign whose meaning God had already given through His word. The instructions and promise came first. The people were called to trust that promise and act on what He had said.

passages.god_plan_html:
1 Corinthians 5:7 explicitly identifies Christ as the Passover lamb who has been sacrificed. The connection between this rescue and Jesus is the New Testament’s own explanation.

1 Peter 1:18–21 describes redemption through Christ’s precious blood, comparing Him with a lamb without blemish or spot. The required soundness of the Passover animal finds a larger connection in the purity of Christ and His saving death.

Hebrews 11:28 remembers Moses keeping Passover and applying the blood by faith. God gives the promise of protection, and faith acts on His instructions. That trust belongs to the account of rescue itself.

passages.title: Exodus 12:14-28
passages.section_title: How would future generations remember the rescue?

passages.context_html:
The night of deliverance is to become a lasting memorial. God commands seven days of unleavened bread, with sacred assemblies on the first and seventh days. Ordinary work stops on those assembly days, with meal preparation permitted. The removal of leaven is treated as a binding covenant obligation.

Moses then gives the elders the instructions for that first night. They are to kill the lambs, use hyssop to apply the blood to the doorframes and remain inside until morning. The LORD will see the blood and prevent the destroyer from entering those houses.

The observance is to continue after they enter the promised land. Children will ask what it means, and the answer is to tell what the LORD did: He struck Egypt and spared Israel’s homes. The people respond by bowing in worship and carrying out the instructions. Memory, explanation and obedience belong together.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The shared reading understands the feast as a binding memorial through which Israel is to remember and teach God’s deliverance. Calvin emphasizes the seriousness of preserving the memory of redemption through the commanded observance; Wesley likewise connects the annual feast with gratitude for the rescue.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Should We Seek Signs From God? understands the blood on the Passover doorposts as a sign whose meaning God had already given through His word. The instructions and promise came first. The people were called to trust that promise and act on what He had said.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
1 Corinthians 5:6–8 applies the removal of leaven to the life of the church. Because Christ has been sacrificed as the Passover lamb, Paul calls believers to put away malice and wickedness and live in sincerity and truth. The remembered rescue leads into a changed way of life.

Luke 22:7–20 places Jesus’ final meal with His apostles within Passover. He gives bread and the cup in connection with His body, His blood and the new covenant, and commands remembrance of Him. 1 Corinthians 11:23–26 explains that this meal proclaims His death until He comes. The memorial of deliverance from Egypt opens into the New Testament’s remembrance of the deliverance accomplished by Christ.

passages.title: Exodus 12:29-30
passages.section_title: What happened when the final warning was fulfilled?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 29 Now at midnight the LORD struck down every firstborn male in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh, who sat on his throne, to the firstborn of the prisoner in the dungeon, as well as all the firstborn among the livestock. 30 During the night Pharaoh got up—he and all his officials and all the Egyptians—and there was loud wailing in Egypt; for there was no house without someone dead.
paragraphs: 29 Now at midnight the LORD struck down every firstborn male in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh, who sat on his throne, to the firstborn of the prisoner in the dungeon, as well as all the firstborn among the livestock. 30 During the night Pharaoh got up—he and all his officials and all the Egyptians—and there was loud wailing in Egypt; for there was no house without someone dead.

passages.context_html:
At midnight, the final judgment occurs as announced. The firstborn males die, from Pharaoh’s household to the household of the prisoner, and among the livestock. The narrative carries the warning of chapter 11 into its fulfillment.

Pharaoh, his officials and the Egyptians rise during the night to a great outcry. The repeated attention to households makes the grief concrete. The next verses describe the release that follows this terrible night.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The shared reading understands the deaths as the fulfillment of God’s final warning and the judgment that brings Israel’s release. Calvin emphasizes the announced timing and the reach from the royal household to the prisoner; Wesley places the event at the turning point from bondage to departure.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 11:28 recalls this same judgment when it describes the firstborn being spared through Passover and the application of blood by faith. The deaths and the protection of Israel’s homes form the setting of the rescue.

The larger question of rescue from judgment continues in Hebrews 9:27–28. There, human death and judgment are set alongside Christ’s once-for-all offering to bear sins and His promised return to bring salvation. The Exodus is a particular historical deliverance; the New Testament takes the need for deliverance into the larger setting of sin, judgment and salvation through Christ.

passages.title: Exodus 12:31-42
passages.section_title: How did Israel finally leave Egypt?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 31 Then Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron by night and said, “Get up, leave my people, both you and the Israelites! Go, worship the LORD as you have requested. 32 Take your flocks and herds as well, just as you have said, and depart! And bless me also.” 33 And in order to send them out of the land quickly, the Egyptians urged the people on. “For otherwise,” they said, “we are all going to die!” 34 So the people took their dough before it was leavened, carrying it on their shoulders in kneading bowls wrapped in clothing. 35 Furthermore, the Israelites acted on Moses’ word and asked the Egyptians for articles of silver and gold, and for clothing. 36 And the LORD gave the people such favor in the sight of the Egyptians that they granted their request. In this way they plundered the Egyptians. 37 The Israelites journeyed from Rameses to Succoth with about 600,000 men on foot, besides women and children. 38 And a mixed multitude also went up with them, along with great droves of livestock, both flocks and herds. 39 Since their dough had no leaven, the people baked what they had brought out of Egypt into unleavened loaves. passages.context_html:
During the night Pharaoh summons Moses and Aaron and orders Israel to leave, taking the families, flocks and herds. He asks for a blessing as well. The Egyptians urge the people to go quickly, afraid that further death will follow if they remain.

Israel leaves in haste, carrying dough before it has been leavened. They also receive silver, gold and clothing from the Egyptians, whose favor the LORD has given them. Their departure with possessions recalls the promise in Genesis 15:13–14.

The journey begins from Rameses to Succoth. The account numbers about 600,000 men, besides women and children, and includes a mixed multitude with them. Their unleavened bread is tied directly to the urgency of leaving before they could prepare provisions.

The account gives 430 years for Israel’s stay in Egypt and emphasizes that the departure takes place to the very day. The night is to be remembered as a vigil to the LORD, who watched over them to bring them out. The ending turns the event into an observance for generations to come.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The chronology is read in two main ways. Keil and Delitzsch understand the 430 years as the time spent in Egypt and allow that genealogies may omit intermediate generations. Calvin and Wesley count the period from the patriarchs’ sojourn through the Exodus, drawing on Galatians 3:17. The BSB retains the statement that Israel’s stay in Egypt was 430 years. These explanations differ over how that statement relates to the other chronological passages.

The shared emphasis is God’s faithfulness in bringing the promised people out. The account also links the haste, the unleavened bread and the possessions they receive with the circumstances of their departure.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
Genesis 15:13–18 had joined oppression, judgment of the enslaving nation, departure with possessions and the promised land. The Exodus brings those promises into view as events begin to unfold.

Galatians 3:15–18 places the promise in a still larger setting. Paul identifies the promised seed with Christ and argues that the law given later does not cancel God’s earlier promise. Beyond the chronological question, the New Testament directs attention to the continuing faithfulness of God and the inheritance He grants through His promise.

passages.title: Exodus 12:43-51
passages.section_title: Who could share in the Passover meal?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 43 And the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, “This is the statute of the Passover: No foreigner is to eat of it. 44 But any slave who has been purchased may eat of it, after you have circumcised him. 45 A temporary resident or hired hand shall not eat the Passover. 46 It must be eaten inside one house. You are not to take any of the meat outside the house, and you may not break any of the bones. 47 The whole congregation of Israel must celebrate it. 48 If a foreigner resides with you and wants to celebrate the LORD’s Passover, all the males in the household must be circumcised; then he may come near to celebrate it, and he shall be like a native of the land. But no uncircumcised man may eat of it. 49 The same law shall apply to both the native and the foreigner who resides among you.” 50 Then all the Israelites did this—they did just as the LORD had commanded Moses and Aaron. 51 And on that very day the LORD brought the Israelites out of the land of Egypt by their divisions.

You are not to take any of the meat outside the house, and you may not break any of the bones. 47 The whole congregation of Israel must celebrate it. 48 If a foreigner resides with you and wants to celebrate the LORD’s Passover, all the males in the household must be circumcised; then he may come near to celebrate it, and he shall be like a native of the land. But no uncircumcised man may eat of it. 49 The same law shall apply to both the native and the foreigner who resides among you.”
50 Then all the Israelites did this—they did just as the LORD had commanded Moses and Aaron. 51 And on that very day the LORD brought the Israelites out of the land of Egypt by their divisions.

passages.context_html:
The final instructions define participation in Passover. An outsider does not eat it simply by being present or employed in the household. Circumcision is required, including for a purchased servant who is to participate.

A foreign resident may join the observance when all the males of his household are circumcised. He is then to be treated like a native of the land, with the same law applying to both. The instructions establish a boundary for the meal and also a way for the foreigner to share in it.

The animal must be eaten within one house, with no meat carried outside and no bones broken. The whole congregation is to observe Passover. The chapter ends with Israel doing as commanded and the LORD bringing them out of Egypt by their divisions.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The shared historical reading understands circumcision as the covenant sign required for participation, while recognizing that a foreigner could enter and be received on the same terms. Calvin and Wesley both emphasize that joining the covenant people opens participation to the outsider.

passages.god_plan_html:
John 19:31–36 draws attention to Jesus’ legs remaining unbroken and identifies this as fulfillment of Scripture. This gives a clear connection with the Passover requirement that the lamb’s bones remain unbroken, alongside Paul’s explicit description of Christ as our Passover lamb in 1 Corinthians 5:7.

The reception of the foreigner also belongs within a wider biblical story. Ephesians 2:11–19 describes Gentiles who were once outsiders being brought near through Christ’s blood and made members of God’s household. Colossians 2:11–14 speaks of a circumcision performed by Christ, joining it with burial and resurrection with Him, faith and forgiveness. The New Testament develops belonging to God’s people around the work of Christ.

passages.title: Exodus 13:1-16
passages.section_title: Why were the firstborn to be set apart for God?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then the LORD said to Moses, 2 “Consecrate to Me every firstborn male. The firstborn from every womb among the Israelites belongs to Me, both of man and beast.” 3 So Moses told the people, “Remember this day, the day you came out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery; for the LORD brought you out of it by the strength of His hand. And nothing leavened shall be eaten. 4 Today, in the month of Abib, you are leaving. 5 And when the LORD brings you into the land of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Hivites, and Jebusites—the land He swore to your fathers that He would give you, a land flowing with milk and honey—you shall keep this service in this month. 6 For seven days you are to eat unleavened bread, and on the seventh day there shall be a feast to the LORD. 7 Unleavened bread shall be eaten during those seven days. Nothing leavened may be found among you, nor shall leaven be found anywhere within your borders. 8 And on that day you are to explain to your son, ‘This is because of what the LORD did for me when I came out of Egypt.’ 9 It shall be a sign for you on your hand and a reminder on your forehead that the Law of the LORD is to be on your lips. For with a mighty hand the LORD brought you out of Egypt. 10 Therefore you shall keep this statute at the appointed time year after year. 11 And after the LORD brings you into the land of the Canaanites and gives it to you, as He swore to you and your fathers, 12 you are to present to the LORD the firstborn male of every womb. All the firstborn males of your livestock belong to the LORD. 13 You must redeem every firstborn donkey with a lamb, and if you do not redeem it, you are to break its neck. And every firstborn of your sons you must redeem. 14 In the future, when your son asks you, ‘What does this mean?’ you are to tell him, ‘With a mighty hand the LORD brought us out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. 15 And when Pharaoh stubbornly refused to let us go, the LORD killed every firstborn in the land of Egypt, both of man and beast. This is why I sacrifice to the LORD the firstborn male of every womb, but I redeem all the firstborn of my sons.’ 16 So it shall serve as a sign on your hand and a symbol on your forehead, for with a mighty hand the LORD brought us out of Egypt.”

passages.context_html:
God commands Israel to consecrate its firstborn males—to set them apart as belonging to Him. The command is joined with another explanation of the rescue from Egypt, the annual observance of unleavened bread and the responsibility to tell children what the LORD has done.

The firstborn are to remind the people of the night when Egypt’s firstborn died and Israel was brought out. The animals offered to God and the sons who are redeemed keep that event before each household. The children’s question is to be answered with the story of deliverance.

The Hebrew word for redeem is פָּדָה, padah (pah-DAH), meaning to ransom; Brown–Driver–Briggs includes these verses under redemption for an assessed price. Here a donkey is to be redeemed with a lamb, and sons must be redeemed. Numbers 18:15–16 later specifies a payment for the redemption of the firstborn son.

The account describes remembrance as a sign on the hand and a reminder on the forehead, with the LORD’s law on their lips. The rescue is to remain part of what they remember, speak about and pass on. These commands are carried into their life in the land God has promised.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The firstborn command is read as an acknowledgment that the people belong to the God who delivered them. Calvin and Wesley both connect the consecration with Israel’s preservation and its responsibility to honor the LORD.

The language about the hand and forehead receives different applications. In the Orthodox Jewish practice described by Chabad, these passages are included in tefillin: small leather boxes containing Scripture, worn on the arm and head. Their explanation joins the physical practice with dedication of thought and action to God. Wesley understands the wording as a proverbial expression for keeping the rescue continually in mind. The Catholic USCCB notes read the feast itself as a visible reminder and also acknowledge the Jewish practice.

passages.god_plan_html:
Luke 2:22–24 explicitly recalls the command about consecrating the firstborn when Mary and Joseph bring Jesus to Jerusalem to present Him to the Lord. Jesus enters the life of Israel within the law and observances given to the people God redeemed.

Galatians 4:4–7 gives the larger purpose: God sent His Son, born of a woman and under the law, to redeem those under the law so they might receive adoption as His children. The Son comes into Israel’s story of redemption and brings people into the fuller relationship with God that Paul describes.

passages.title: Exodus 13:17-22
passages.section_title: Why did God lead Israel along the longer route?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 When Pharaoh let the people go, God did not lead them along the road through the land of the Philistines, though it was shorter. For God said, “If the people face war, they might change their minds and return to Egypt.” 18 So God led the people around by the way of the wilderness toward the Red Sea. And the Israelites left the land of Egypt arrayed for battle. 19 Moses took the bones of Joseph with him because Joseph had made the sons of Israel swear a solemn oath when he said, “God will surely attend to you, and then you must carry my bones with you from this place.” 20 They set out from Succoth and camped at Etham on the edge of the wilderness. 21 And the LORD went before them in a pillar of cloud to guide their way by day, and in a pillar of fire to give them light by night, so that they could travel by day or night. 22 Neither the pillar of cloud by day nor the pillar of fire by night left its place before the people.
paragraphs: 17 When Pharaoh let the people go, God did not lead them along the road through the land of the Philistines, though it was shorter. For God said, “If the people face war, they might change their minds and return to Egypt.” 18 So God led the people around by the way of the wilderness toward the Red Sea. And the Israelites left the land of Egypt arrayed for battle. 19 Moses took the bones of Joseph with him because Joseph had made the sons of Israel swear a solemn oath when he said, “God will surely attend to you, and then you must carry my bones with you from this place.”

20 They set out from Succoth and camped at Etham on the edge of the wilderness. 21 And the LORD went before them in a pillar of cloud to guide their way by day, and in a pillar of fire to give them light by night, so that they could travel by day or night. 22 Neither the pillar of cloud by day nor the pillar of fire by night left its place before the people.

passages.context_html:
God leads the people away from the shorter road through Philistine territory because facing war could make them turn back to Egypt. The longer route is explained through His knowledge of the people’s weakness. He leads them toward the wilderness and the Red Sea.

Moses also carries Joseph’s bones. Joseph had made Israel promise to take them when God attended to the people and brought them out. His long-standing expectation of that departure is now being acted upon.

From Succoth they camp at Etham on the edge of the wilderness. The LORD goes before them in cloud by day and fire by night, giving direction and light. They can travel by day or night, and the visible sign of His guidance remains before them. Their release from slavery is followed by His continuing presence on the journey.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The shared reading sees the route and the cloud and fire as expressions of God’s care for the people He has rescued. Calvin and Wesley both emphasize His continuing guidance and His provision for their weakness. The journey is under His direction even while the people still need to learn to follow Him.

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 11:22 explicitly describes Joseph’s instructions about his bones as an act of faith. Genesis 50:24–26 had connected those instructions with God’s promise to bring the people to the land sworn to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Carrying the bones now makes that earlier trust visible within the promised deliverance.

1 Corinthians 10:1–5 recalls the cloud and the crossing of the sea when it describes Israel being baptized into Moses. Paul places the journey within his instruction to the church, recalling both God’s provision and the people’s later failures. The visible guidance belongs to a story through which later believers are taught to remember God’s faithfulness and respond to Him.

passages.title: Exodus 14:1-14
passages.section_title: Why did God lead Israel into a place that looked like a trap?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then the LORD said to Moses, 2 “Tell the Israelites to turn back and encamp before Pi-hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea. You are to encamp by the sea, directly opposite Baal-zephon. 3 For Pharaoh will say of the Israelites, ‘They are wandering the land in confusion; the wilderness has boxed them in.’ 4 And I will harden Pharaoh’s heart so that he will pursue them. But I will gain honor by means of Pharaoh and all his army, and the Egyptians will know that I am the LORD.” So this is what the Israelites did. 5 When the king of Egypt was told that the people had fled, Pharaoh and his officials changed their minds about them and said, “What have we done? We have released Israel from serving us.” 6 So Pharaoh prepared his chariot and took his army with him. 7 He took 600 of the best chariots, and all the other chariots of Egypt, with officers over all of them. 8 And the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh king of Egypt so that he pursued the Israelites, who were marching out defiantly. 9 The Egyptians—all Pharaoh’s horses and chariots, horsemen and troops—pursued the Israelites and overtook them as they camped by the sea near Pi-hahiroth, opposite Baal-zephon. 10 As Pharaoh approached, the Israelites looked up and saw the Egyptians marching after them, and they were terrified and cried out to the LORD. 11 They said to Moses, “Was it because there were no graves in Egypt that you brought us into the wilderness to die? What have you done to us by bringing us out of Egypt? 12 Did we not say to you in Egypt, ‘Leave us alone so that we may serve the Egyptians’? For it would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the wilderness.” 13 But Moses told the people, “Do not be afraid. Stand firm and you will see the LORD’s salvation, which He will accomplish for you today; for the Egyptians you see today, you will never see again. 14 The LORD will fight for you; you need only to be still.”

Stand firm and you will see the LORD’s salvation, which He will accomplish for you today; for the Egyptians you see today, you will never see again. 14 The LORD will fight for you; you need only to be still.”

passages.context_html:
Israel’s apparent trap is part of the route God commands. He tells Moses to turn back and camp beside the sea, and explains that Pharaoh will take this as a sign that the people are confused and cornered. God will gain honor through what happens to Pharaoh and his army, and the Egyptians will know who the LORD is.

Pharaoh and his officials regret losing Israel’s service. He gathers his chariots and pursues the people, who have been marching out boldly. Their confidence collapses when they see the approaching army. They cry to God, accuse Moses of bringing them out to die and say slavery would have been better.

Moses answers their fear with a promise about this particular rescue: the LORD will fight for them. They are to stand firm and watch what He does. The next part of the account shows how this trust goes together with obedience: when God tells them to move forward, they must go.

The places named in verse 2 have not been definitively identified, as the USCCB study notes acknowledge. The account’s central situation is clear: Israel is beside the sea with an army approaching, and God has brought the people there.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Calvin read Moses’ reassurance as a call to trust God’s power when Israel cannot rescue itself. The people’s fear and complaints are met by a deliverance that depends on the LORD.

The explanation of God hardening Pharaoh differs. Calvin understands God to be actively directing the Egyptians toward the judgment that will display His power. Wesley’s earlier note on Exodus 4:21 describes hardening as God finally permitting Satan to harden a ruler who has repeatedly refused the light already given. These are the two teachers’ explanations of God’s action and Pharaoh’s refusal.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Psalm 106:6–13 looks back on this crisis and says Israel rebelled by the sea. God nevertheless saved the people for the sake of His name, to make His power known. Their rescue displays His faithfulness even when they are frightened and ungrateful; it leads them to believe His promises and sing His praise.

This belongs to a wider biblical theme: God’s rescue reveals His mercy and calls forth a changed life. Ephesians 2:4–10 describes salvation in Christ as God’s gift, through faith, so that no one can boast. Those He makes alive are created in Christ for good works. This is a connection between the two accounts of God’s grace, rather than a claim that every detail of the sea crossing describes a stage of Christian conversion.

passages.title: Exodus 14:15-31
passages.section_title: How did God make a way through the sea?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 Then the LORD said to Moses, “Why are you crying out to Me? Tell the Israelites to go forward. 16 And as for you, lift up your staff and stretch out your hand over the sea and divide it, so that the Israelites can go through the sea on dry ground. 17 And I will harden the hearts of the Egyptians so that they will go in after them. Then I will gain honor by means of Pharaoh and all his army and chariots and horsemen. 18 The Egyptians will know that I am the LORD when I am honored through Pharaoh, his chariots, and his horsemen.” 19 And the angel of God, who had gone before the camp of Israel, withdrew and went behind them. The pillar of cloud also moved from before them and stood behind them, 20 so that it came between the camps of Egypt and Israel. The cloud was there in the darkness, but it lit up the night. So all night long neither camp went near the other. 21 Then Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and all that night the LORD drove back the sea with a strong east wind that turned it into dry land. So the waters were divided, 22 and the Israelites went through the sea on dry ground, with walls of water on their right and on their left. 23 And the Egyptians chased after them—all Pharaoh’s horses, chariots, and horsemen—and followed them into the sea. 24 At morning watch, however, the LORD looked down on the army of the Egyptians from the pillar of fire and cloud, and He threw their camp into confusion. 25 He caused their chariot wheels to wobble, so that they had difficulty driving. “Let us flee from the Israelites,” said the Egyptians, “for the LORD is fighting for them against Egypt!” 26 Then the LORD said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand over the sea, so that the waters may flow back over the Egyptians and their chariots and horsemen.” 27 So Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and at daybreak the sea returned to its normal state. Not one of them survived. 29 But the Israelites had walked through the sea on dry ground, with walls of water on their right and on their left. 30 That day the LORD saved Israel from the hand of the Egyptians, and Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the shore. 31 When Israel saw the great power that the LORD had exercised over the Egyptians, the people feared the LORD and believed in Him and in His servant Moses.

23 And the Egyptians chased after them—all Pharaoh’s horses, chariots, and horsemen—and followed them into the sea. 24 At morning watch, however, the LORD looked down on the army of the Egyptians from the pillar of fire and cloud, and He threw their camp into confusion. 25 He caused their chariot wheels to wobble, so that they had difficulty driving. “Let us flee from the Israelites,” said the Egyptians, “for the LORD is fighting for them against Egypt!” 26 Then the LORD said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand over the sea, so that the waters may flow back over the Egyptians and their chariots and horsemen.” 27 So Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and at daybreak the sea returned to its normal state. As the Egyptians were retreating, the LORD swept them into the sea. 28 The waters flowed back and covered the chariots and horsemen—the entire army of Pharaoh that had chased the Israelites into the sea. Not one of them survived.

29 But the Israelites had walked through the sea on dry ground, with walls of water on their right and on their left. 30 That day the LORD saved Israel from the hand of the Egyptians, and Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the shore. 31 When Israel saw the great power that the LORD had exercised over the Egyptians, the people feared the LORD and believed in Him and in His servant Moses.

passages.context_html:
God tells Moses to send the people forward and stretch out his hand over the sea. The angel of God and the cloud move behind Israel, keeping the two camps apart during the night. The presence that has guided the people now stands between them and the pursuing army.

The LORD drives back the sea with a strong east wind through the night. Israel crosses on dry ground with walls of water on either side. When the Egyptians follow, the LORD throws them into confusion and makes their chariots difficult to drive. The soldiers themselves recognize that He is fighting for Israel.

At God’s command, Moses stretches out his hand again. The water returns and overwhelms the entire pursuing force that entered the sea. Israel reaches safety and sees the Egyptians dead on the shore. The chapter ends with the people fearing the LORD and believing Him and His servant Moses.

The sea’s Hebrew name is יַם־סוּף, yam suph (YAHM SOOHF). Brown–Driver–Briggs explains it as probably meaning sea of reeds and notes that the name is used for both the Gulf of Suez and the Gulf of Aqaba in different passages. The name alone does not identify the crossing site. Here the text emphasizes the dry path God opens, the waters on either side and the destruction of the pursuing army.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley both understand the crossing as a miraculous deliverance: God makes the sea a safe passage for Israel and brings judgment on the pursuing Egyptians. Moses acts at God’s command, and the power that saves the people belongs to God.

There are different explanations of the angel in verse 19. Calvin identifies this leader with God’s Son before His birth as Jesus. The Catholic USCCB study note understands the expression here as God’s power at work, corresponding to the cloud, rather than a separate spiritual being. That is a reading offered in a Catholic Bible’s study notes; it is not presented there as a binding church definition of this verse.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 11:29 explicitly describes Israel’s crossing as an act of faith and contrasts it with the Egyptians’ attempt to follow. Both enter the same path, but the outcome depends on God’s purpose and promise, rather than the strength of the people or their equipment.

1 Corinthians 10:1–12 makes another connection for the church. Paul describes the people as baptized into Moses in the cloud and the sea. Their passage belongs to their shared life under the leader God has given them. Paul then recalls that many later fell into idolatry, disobedience and complaint. His point is a warning to believers: receiving God’s provision is no reason to become careless about following Him.

The rescue also becomes a pattern for later hope. In Isaiah 43:16–21, God recalls the way through the sea and the defeat of chariots as He promises a new work for His people, a way in the wilderness and water in the desert. The God who delivered them before remains able to bring His people where He intends them to go.

passages.title: Exodus 15:1-21
passages.section_title: What does Israel’s song tell us about the God who rescued them?

The horse and rider He has thrown into the sea. 2 The LORD is my strength and my song, and He has become my salvation. He is my God, and I will praise Him, my father’s God, and I will exalt Him. 3 The LORD is a warrior, the LORD is His name. 4 Pharaoh’s chariots and army He has cast into the sea; the finest of his officers are drowned in the Red Sea. 5 The depths have covered them; they sank there like a stone. 6 Your right hand, O LORD, is majestic in power; Your right hand, O LORD, has shattered the enemy. 7 You overthrew Your adversaries by Your great majesty. passages.context_html:
The people who cried out in fear now sing about the LORD’s victory. Moses and Israel recount the destruction of Pharaoh’s army, confess that their strength and rescue come from God, and praise Him as the warrior no enemy can overcome. Miriam, named as a prophetess, leads the women with tambourines and dancing and answers with the song’s opening refrain.

The song retells the crossing through vivid pictures: the enemy sinks like stone and lead, and God’s breath piles up the water. Its paired lines return to the same events from different angles, giving the people words with which to remember and praise. Verse 19 brings the song back to the event itself: the army went into the sea, the water returned and Israel walked through on dry ground.

The song also looks ahead. The people God has redeemed are to be led to His dwelling, while surrounding nations hear and tremble. Joshua 2:8–13 later gives a concrete example: Rahab says Jericho has heard of the crossing and lost courage. Yet she also acknowledges the LORD as God and seeks protection for her household. The news can lead to an appeal for mercy as well as fear.

The praise of God’s rule also speaks into a world with rival claims about divine power. The Metropolitan Museum of Art describes Ugaritic tablets in which Baal defeats the sea god Yamm and gains a royal palace. That is useful cultural background for hearing a song about the LORD’s power over the sea, His dwelling and His reign. The song itself directs Israel’s worship to the LORD who has actually delivered them.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The central reading is praise for God’s saving power and confidence that He will bring His people to the place He has promised. Wesley and Calvin both connect Israel’s thanksgiving with that continuing hope.

There are different ways of relating the poem to the preceding account. Calvin reads it as a poetic celebration confirming the events just narrated. The Catholic USCCB study notes propose that the poem preserves a different telling of the victory, emphasizing a storm at sea. This is a proposal in those study notes, rather than an official definition binding all Catholics.

Miriam’s instruments also receive different applications to later worship. Calvin regards them as belonging to Old Testament ceremonies that Christians should leave behind. The Catholic Church’s Catechism, 1156–1158, describes the church as continuing and developing the older tradition of sacred song and music. Calvin’s application is his own stated position here; it should not be treated as the practice of every Reformed church.
