section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Revelation 15:1–4 explicitly names the song of God’s servant Moses and of the Lamb. Those who have overcome the beast stand beside a sea and praise God’s great works, just ways and holiness. The rescue celebrated in Exodus thus belongs to a larger story of God defeating oppressive powers and bringing His people to worship Him.

Revelation gives the words sung there; they are not simply a repeat of every line in Exodus 15. The connection rests on the named song, deliverance, divine judgment and worship. It does not require treating every image in Israel’s song as a separate prediction.

The hope of being brought to God’s dwelling also reaches beyond the wilderness journey. Hebrews 12:22–24 describes believers as having come to Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant. This is a broader connection in Scripture: God rescues a people and brings them into His presence. Hebrews describes that relationship as already opened to believers through Jesus.

passages.title: Exodus 15:22-27
passages.section_title: What were the people learning at the bitter water?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 Then Moses led Israel from the Red Sea, and they went out into the Desert of Shur. For three days they walked in the desert without finding water. 23 And when they came to Marah, they could not drink the water there because it was bitter. (That is why it was named Marah.) 24 So the people grumbled against Moses, saying, “What are we to drink?” 25 And Moses cried out to the LORD, and the LORD showed him a log. And when he cast it into the waters, they were sweetened. There the LORD made for them a statute and an ordinance, and there He tested them, 26 saying, “If you will listen carefully to the voice of the LORD your God, and do what is right in His eyes, and pay attention to His commands, and keep all His statutes, then I will not bring on you any of the diseases I inflicted on the Egyptians. For I am the LORD who heals you.” 27 Then they came to Elim, where there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, and they camped there by the waters.
paragraphs: 22 Then Moses led Israel from the Red Sea, and they went out into the Desert of Shur. For three days they walked in the desert without finding water. 23 And when they came to Marah, they could not drink the water there because it was bitter. (That is why it was named Marah.) 24 So the people grumbled against Moses, saying, “What are we to drink?” 25 And Moses cried out to the LORD, and the LORD showed him a log. And when he cast it into the waters, they were sweetened. There the LORD made for them a statute and an ordinance, and there He tested them, 26 saying, “If you will listen carefully to the voice of the LORD your God, and do what is right in His eyes, and pay attention to His commands, and keep all His statutes, then I will not bring on you any of the diseases I inflicted on the Egyptians. For I am the LORD who heals you.”
27 Then they came to Elim, where there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, and they camped there by the waters.

passages.context_html:
Three days after leaving the sea, Israel has found no water. The first water they reach is bitter and undrinkable, giving Marah its name. Their question to Moses comes as a complaint, and Moses brings the need to the LORD. God shows him a log; when he throws it into the water, it becomes drinkable.

The account joins this provision to a test. God calls the people to listen carefully, do what is right in His eyes and keep His commands. He promises that, if they listen, He will not bring on them the diseases He inflicted on Egypt. The people who have seen His power against their oppressors now need to learn to live under His direction.

The Hebrew verb רָפָא, rapha (rah-FAH), means to heal. Brown–Driver–Briggs includes both bodily healing and the restoration of a people in its range of uses. Here the LORD identifies Himself as Israel’s healer while supplying water and explaining how they are to live before Him.

The next stop, Elim, has twelve springs and seventy palm trees. They camp beside the water. The passage moves from undrinkable water to water made sweet, and then to a place where they can rest with a plentiful supply. Rescue from Egypt has begun a journey in which dependence on God must be learned in daily needs.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley read the incident as God meeting Israel’s need while teaching obedience. Both connect the warning about disease with the judgments the people have just seen in Egypt.

The role of the wood is explained in different ways. Calvin thinks it may have had a natural property that God made effective beyond its ordinary power. Wesley leaves open whether the wood had such a property or served as a sign of God’s action. The account names God’s direction and the changed water without identifying the kind of wood.

The Baptist teacher John Gill also offers a spiritual comparison: as the wood sweetens bitter water, Christ brings comfort amid His people’s bitter afflictions. This is a devotional application he draws from the event, rather than an explicit New Testament identification of the log with the cross.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
God’s provision in the wilderness is part of teaching His people to depend on Him. Deuteronomy 8:1–5 later describes the wilderness years as a time of humbling, testing and learning to live by God’s word. It compares His discipline to a father’s care for his son. That wider explanation helps place Marah within the journey from being rescued to learning to follow.

James 1:2–5 develops the same theme for believers facing trials: tested faith produces perseverance, and those needing wisdom can ask God. The parallel concerns what trials can teach and how people turn to God within them. The particular promise about Egypt’s diseases belongs to the words God gives Israel here.

passages.title: Exodus 16:1-21
passages.section_title: Why did God give Israel bread one day at a time?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 On the fifteenth day of the second month after they had left the land of Egypt, the whole congregation of Israel set out from Elim and came to the Desert of Sin, which is between Elim and Sinai. 2 And there in the desert the whole congregation of Israel grumbled against Moses and Aaron. 3 “If only we had died by the LORD’s hand in the land of Egypt!” they said. “There we sat by pots of meat and ate our fill of bread, but you have brought us into this desert to starve this whole assembly to death!” 4 Then the LORD said to Moses, “Behold, I will rain down bread from heaven for you. Each day the people are to go out and gather enough for that day. In this way I will test whether or not they will follow My instructions. 5 Then on the sixth day, when they prepare what they bring in, it will be twice as much as they gather on the other days.” 6 So Moses and Aaron said to all the Israelites, “This evening you will know that it was the LORD who brought you out of the land of Egypt, 7 and in the morning you will see the LORD’s glory, because He has heard your grumbling against Him. For who are we, that you should grumble against us?” 8 And Moses added, “The LORD will give you meat to eat this evening and bread to fill you in the morning, for He has heard your grumbling against Him. Who are we? Your grumblings are not against us but against the LORD.” 9 Then Moses said to Aaron, “Tell the whole congregation of Israel, ‘Come before the LORD, for He has heard your grumbling.’” 10 And as Aaron was speaking to the whole congregation of Israel, they looked toward the desert, and there in a cloud the glory of the LORD appeared. 11 Then the LORD said to Moses, 12 “I have heard the grumbling of the Israelites. Tell them, ‘At twilight you will eat meat, and in the morning you will be filled with bread. Then you will know that I am the LORD your God.’” 13 That evening quail came and covered the camp, and in the morning there was a layer of dew around the camp. 14 When the layer of dew had evaporated, there were thin flakes on the desert floor, as fine as frost on the ground. 15 When the Israelites saw it, they asked one another, “What is it?” For they did not know what it was. So Moses told them, “It is the bread that the LORD has given you to eat. 16 This is what the LORD has commanded: ‘Each one is to gather as much as he needs. You may take an omer for each person in your tent.’” 17 So the Israelites did this. Some gathered more, and some less. 18 When they measured it by the omer, he who gathered much had no excess, and he who gathered little had no shortfall. Each one gathered as much as he needed to eat. 19 Then Moses said to them, “No one may keep any of it until morning.” 20 But they did not listen to Moses; some people left part of it until morning, and it became infested with maggots and began to smell. So Moses was angry with them. 21 Every morning each one gathered as much as was needed, and when the sun grew hot, it melted away.

passages.context_html:
One month after the departure from Egypt, Israel reaches the Desert of Sin. Hunger turns their memory of slavery into a story about full meals, and they accuse Moses and Aaron of bringing them out to die. God answers by promising meat in the evening and bread in the morning. His provision will also test whether they follow His instructions.

The cloud reveals the LORD’s glory, quail cover the camp in the evening, and fine flakes appear after the morning dew evaporates. The people’s question is מָן הוּא, man hu (MAHN HOOH), rendered here as “What is it?” Brown–Driver–Briggs explains the connection between that question and the name manna. The name remembers their first puzzlement at the food Moses identifies as God’s gift.

Each household is to gather enough for its members. When the food is measured, those who gathered much have no excess and those who gathered little have no shortfall. The measure is an omer per person; the chapter later explains that an omer is a tenth of an ephah.

The people must trust God for the next day’s supply. Some keep food overnight against the instruction, and it fills with maggots and smells. The remaining manna on the ground melts in the heat. The provision is generous, but it comes with directions: receiving God’s gift includes listening to the One who gives it.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The central reading sees God providing for His people while teaching daily trust and obedience. Wesley and Calvin both connect the food with this test of whether Israel will follow God’s word. His care continues even while their complaints expose how much they still need to learn.
passages.current_position_html: Our Prayer and Faith study understands the manna as pointing forward to Jesus, the living bread. The manna sustained Israel’s bodies for a season; Jesus gives the lasting life to which that provision pointed. The study draws this conclusion from Jesus’ own explanation in John 6.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus explicitly returns to this event in John 6:26–35. When the crowd mentions the manna, He directs them to His Father as its giver and identifies Himself as the bread of life. In verses 47–51, He explains the difference: the ancestors ate manna and eventually died, while He gives life that lasts forever.

The gathering also becomes instruction for the church’s care of people in need. 2 Corinthians 8:12–15 quotes Exodus 16:18 while encouraging generous sharing. Paul calls those who currently have a surplus to supply those who lack, so that provision can be shared as circumstances change. The wilderness gift helps explain how believers should use what God has put in their hands.

passages.title: Exodus 16:22-30
passages.section_title: How did the double portion make rest possible?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 On the sixth day, they gathered twice as much food—two omers per person —and all the leaders of the congregation came and reported this to Moses. 23 He told them, “This is what the LORD has said: ‘Tomorrow is to be a day of complete rest, a holy Sabbath to the LORD. So bake what you want to bake, and boil what you want to boil. Then set aside whatever remains and keep it until morning.’” 24 So they set it aside until morning as Moses had commanded, and it did not smell or contain any maggots. 25 “Eat it today,” Moses said, “because today is a Sabbath to the LORD. Today you will not find anything in the field. 26 For six days you may gather, but on the seventh day, the Sabbath, it will not be there.” 27 Yet on the seventh day some of the people went out to gather, but they did not find anything. 28 Then the LORD said to Moses, “How long will you refuse to keep My commandments and instructions? 29 Understand that the LORD has given you the Sabbath; that is why on the sixth day He will give you bread for two days. On the seventh day, everyone must stay where he is; no one may leave his place.” 30 So the people rested on the seventh day.
paragraphs: 22 On the sixth day, they gathered twice as much food—two omers per person —and all the leaders of the congregation came and reported this to Moses. 23 He told them, “This is what the LORD has said: ‘Tomorrow is to be a day of complete rest, a holy Sabbath to the LORD. So bake what you want to bake, and boil what you want to boil. Then set aside whatever remains and keep it until morning.’” 24 So they set it aside until morning as Moses had commanded, and it did not smell or contain any maggots. 25 “Eat it today,” Moses said, “because today is a Sabbath to the LORD. Today you will not find anything in the field. 26 For six days you may gather, but on the seventh day, the Sabbath, it will not be there.”

27 Yet on the seventh day some of the people went out to gather, but they did not find anything. 28 Then the LORD said to Moses, “How long will you refuse to keep My commandments and instructions? 29 Understand that the LORD has given you the Sabbath; that is why on the sixth day He will give you bread for two days. On the seventh day, everyone must stay where he is; no one may leave his place.” 30 So the people rested on the seventh day.

passages.context_html:
On the sixth day the people gather twice the usual amount. Moses explains that the next day is a holy Sabbath to the LORD. They are to prepare their food and keep the remainder overnight. This time it stays fresh: the supply God has given for the day of rest does not spoil.

Some still go out on the seventh day and find nothing. The LORD challenges their refusal to keep His instructions and reminds them that He has given the Sabbath and the two-day supply. The account ends with the people resting.

The instruction and the provision belong together. God makes it possible for Israel to stop gathering, and they are to trust what He has already supplied. Keeping the extra food is obedience on the sixth day, even though keeping it against His instruction on other days was disobedience. The test is whether they listen to Him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian traditions agree that God commands Israel to rest here; they differ on how that command applies to Christians. Wesley’s note on verse 23 understands the weekly rest as already rooted in creation, rather than a completely new practice invented at this point.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, 21.7–8, and the 1689 Baptist Confession, 22.7–8, teach that God requires one day in seven for worship and rest. They understand the day to have changed from the seventh day to the first after Christ’s resurrection. Both allow duties of necessity and mercy. These are the teachings of these confessions, not a claim that every Presbyterian or Baptist practices alike.

The Catholic Church’s Catechism, 2174–2176, distinguishes Sunday from the Jewish Sabbath and describes Sunday observance as fulfilling its spiritual meaning through Christ’s resurrection. The continuing duty is regular public worship of God, now centered on the Lord’s Day.

The Lutheran Large Catechism, third commandment, distinguishes Israel’s required outward observance from Christian practice. It emphasizes rest, hearing God’s word and gathering for worship. It retains Sunday for an orderly common gathering while saying that no day is inherently better than another.

The Seventh-day Adventist Church’s belief on the Sabbath teaches that the seventh day remains the appointed day of rest and worship for all people. It understands the day as a continuing memorial of creation and a sign of the relationship between God and His people.

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 4:1–11 draws together God’s seventh-day rest, Israel’s wilderness disobedience and the promise of entering God’s rest. It says that Joshua’s bringing the people into the land did not exhaust that promise, and urges its hearers to respond to God in faith rather than repeat the wilderness refusal.

That larger purpose adds depth to the day of rest in this account. God is teaching His rescued people to trust Him, and Scripture carries that theme forward into the call to enter His rest. The explanation in Hebrews reaches beyond deciding which day a congregation meets.

passages.title: Exodus 16:31-36
passages.section_title: Why was some manna kept for later generations?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 31 Now the house of Israel called the bread manna. It was white like coriander seed and tasted like wafers made with honey. 32 Moses said, “This is what the LORD has commanded: ‘Keep an omer of manna for the generations to come, so that they may see the bread I fed you in the wilderness when I brought you out of the land of Egypt.’” 33 So Moses told Aaron, “Take a jar and fill it with an omer of manna. Then place it before the LORD to be preserved for the generations to come.” 34 And Aaron placed it in front of the Testimony, to be preserved just as the LORD had commanded Moses. 35 The Israelites ate manna forty years, until they came to a land where they could settle; they ate manna until they reached the border of Canaan. 36 (Now an omer is a tenth of an ephah.)

It was white like coriander seed and tasted like wafers made with honey. 32 Moses said, “This is what the LORD has commanded: ‘Keep an omer of manna for the generations to come, so that they may see the bread I fed you in the wilderness when I brought you out of the land of Egypt.’” 33 So Moses told Aaron, “Take a jar and fill it with an omer of manna. Then place it before the LORD to be preserved for the generations to come.” 34 And Aaron placed it in front of the Testimony, to be preserved just as the LORD had commanded Moses.
35 The Israelites ate manna forty years, until they came to a land where they could settle; they ate manna until they reached the border of Canaan. 36 (Now an omer is a tenth of an ephah.)

passages.context_html:
The bread receives its name and a description: white, resembling coriander seed, with a taste like honey wafers. God then commands that an omer be kept so later generations can see the food He gave Israel in the wilderness. The daily gift is also to become a lasting reminder.

Aaron places the jar before the Testimony, as commanded. The account looks ahead to the preserved memorial and sums up the long period of provision: Israel eats manna for forty years, until reaching the border of Canaan. God’s care extends through the journey, rather than ending with the first morning’s meal.

Joshua 5:10–12 later records the change after they enter the land. They eat its produce, and the manna ceases. The food has served the purpose God gave it while bringing His people to the place He promised.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The jar is read as a memorial of God’s faithful provision, meant to preserve the story for those who did not gather the food themselves. Calvin and Wesley both understand its preservation as part of the extraordinary provision God wanted later generations to remember.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 9:1–5 explicitly recalls the gold jar of manna among the contents associated with the ark. The remembered wilderness provision becomes part of its description of Israel’s worship and sanctuary.

The manna image also appears in Jesus’ message to the church in Revelation 2:12–17. A congregation facing pressure and teaching that encourages idol food is called to repent and remain faithful; Jesus promises hidden manna to the one who overcomes. The picture of food God gives is carried forward into His assurance to a struggling church. Revelation does not say that the historical jar itself will be opened and handed out.

passages.title: Exodus 17:1-7
passages.section_title: What did Israel’s demand for water reveal?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then the whole congregation of Israel left the Desert of Sin, moving from place to place as the LORD commanded. They camped at Rephidim, but there was no water for the people to drink. 2 So the people contended with Moses, “Give us water to drink.” “Why do you contend with me?” Moses replied. “Why do you test the LORD?” 3 But the people thirsted for water there, and they grumbled against Moses: “Why have you brought us out of Egypt—to make us and our children and livestock die of thirst?” 4 Then Moses cried out to the LORD, “What should I do with these people? A little more and they will stone me!” 5 And the LORD said to Moses, “Walk on ahead of the people and take some of the elders of Israel with you. Take along in your hand the staff with which you struck the Nile, and go. 6 Behold, I will stand there before you by the rock at Horeb. And when you strike the rock, water will come out of it for the people to drink.” So Moses did this in the sight of the elders of Israel. 7 He named the place Massah and Meribah because the Israelites quarreled, and because they tested the LORD, saying, “Is the LORD among us or not?”
paragraphs: 1 Then the whole congregation of Israel left the Desert of Sin, moving from place to place as the LORD commanded. They camped at Rephidim, but there was no water for the people to drink. 2 So the people contended with Moses, “Give us water to drink.” “Why do you contend with me?” Moses replied. “Why do you test the LORD?” 3 But the people thirsted for water there, and they grumbled against Moses: “Why have you brought us out of Egypt—to make us and our children and livestock die of thirst?” 4 Then Moses cried out to the LORD, “What should I do with these people? A little more and they will stone me!”

5 And the LORD said to Moses, “Walk on ahead of the people and take some of the elders of Israel with you. Take along in your hand the staff with which you struck the Nile, and go. 6 Behold, I will stand there before you by the rock at Horeb. And when you strike the rock, water will come out of it for the people to drink.” So Moses did this in the sight of the elders of Israel. 7 He named the place Massah and Meribah because the Israelites quarreled, and because they tested the LORD, saying, “Is the LORD among us or not?”

passages.context_html:
Israel reaches Rephidim by following the LORD’s command, yet there is no water. Being on the commanded route has not removed every need or difficulty. The people turn on Moses, demanding water and accusing him of bringing their families and livestock out to die.

Moses cries to God because their anger threatens his life. God directs him to go ahead with some elders, taking the staff used to strike the Nile. The LORD promises to stand before him by the rock at Horeb. Moses strikes it as commanded, and water comes out before the elders as witnesses.

The names preserve the people’s response as well as the rescue. מַסָּה, Massah (mah-SAH), recalls testing; מְרִיבָה, Meribah (meh-ree-BAH), recalls quarreling. Brown–Driver–Briggs on Massah and Meribah connects the names with this incident. The question behind their complaint is whether the LORD is among them.

The preceding chapter described God testing whether Israel would follow His instructions. Here the people put God to the test, demanding proof of His presence despite the care they have already received. The water meets a real need, while the place names keep the failure of trust in view.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The shared reading sees both Israel’s distrust and God’s patient provision. Wesley and Calvin emphasize that the water comes through God’s power at His command, even while the people quarrel with His servant. The elders witness what He does, and the names preserve a warning for those who come after them.

passages.god_plan_html:
1 Corinthians 10:1–12 explicitly connects the wilderness provision with Christ: Paul identifies the spiritual rock as Christ. He also says these events were written as instruction and warning for the church. Receiving God’s gifts is meant to lead people to trust and obey Him.

Jesus’ invitation in John 7:37–39 carries the water picture into His gift to believers. He calls the thirsty to come to Him and drink, and John explains that the living water concerns the Spirit. The provision of water for physical life helps us understand the greater gift of life from God through Christ.

John Gill also draws a parallel between the rock being struck and Christ suffering for those He saves. Isaiah 53:4–6 describes the servant wounded for others, and 1 Peter 2:21–25 applies that suffering and healing to Christ. This is a further comparison alongside Paul’s explicit identification of the rock; Paul does not explain every action in the scene as a separate prediction.

passages.title: Exodus 17:8-16
passages.section_title: Why did victory depend on more than Joshua’s soldiers?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 After this, the Amalekites came and attacked the Israelites at Rephidim. 9 So Moses said to Joshua, “Choose some of our men and go out to fight the Amalekites. Tomorrow I will stand on the hilltop with the staff of God in my hand.” 10 Joshua did as Moses had instructed him and fought against the Amalekites, while Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the top of the hill. 11 As long as Moses held up his hands, Israel prevailed; but when he lowered them, Amalek prevailed. 12 When Moses’ hands grew heavy, they took a stone and put it under him, and he sat on it. Then Aaron and Hur held his hands up, one on each side, so that his hands remained steady until the sun went down. 13 So Joshua overwhelmed Amalek and his army with the sword. 14 Then the LORD said to Moses, “Write this on a scroll as a reminder and recite it to Joshua, because I will utterly blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven.” 15 And Moses built an altar and named it The LORD Is My Banner. 16 “Indeed,” he said, “a hand was lifted up toward the throne of the LORD. The LORD will war against Amalek from generation to generation.”
paragraphs: 8 After this, the Amalekites came and attacked the Israelites at Rephidim. 9 So Moses said to Joshua, “Choose some of our men and go out to fight the Amalekites. Tomorrow I will stand on the hilltop with the staff of God in my hand.” 10 Joshua did as Moses had instructed him and fought against the Amalekites, while Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the top of the hill. 11 As long as Moses held up his hands, Israel prevailed; but when he lowered them, Amalek prevailed. 12 When Moses’ hands grew heavy, they took a stone and put it under him, and he sat on it. Then Aaron and Hur held his hands up, one on each side, so that his hands remained steady until the sun went down. 13 So Joshua overwhelmed Amalek and his army with the sword.

14 Then the LORD said to Moses, “Write this on a scroll as a reminder and recite it to Joshua, because I will utterly blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven.” 15 And Moses built an altar and named it The LORD Is My Banner. 16 “Indeed,” he said, “a hand was lifted up toward the throne of the LORD. The LORD will war against Amalek from generation to generation.”

passages.context_html:
The Amalekites attack Israel at Rephidim. Deuteronomy 25:17–19 later recalls that they struck the tired and vulnerable people at the rear and did not fear God. Moses appoints Joshua to lead the fighting while he stands on a hill with the staff of God.

Joshua’s men fight, but the account directs attention to Moses’ raised hands. Israel gains ground while they are up and loses ground when he lowers them. When he grows tired, Aaron and Hur give him a seat and support his hands until sunset. The soldiers’ work and the help on the hill belong to the same victory.

God commands Moses to write the event down and repeat the promise of judgment against Amalek to Joshua. Moses also builds an altar naming the LORD as his banner. A banner is a rallying sign; Brown–Driver–Briggs places this verse under that sense. The memorial directs the credit for victory to the LORD.

The raised hands are commonly understood as an appeal to God, although this passage does not explicitly say Moses was praying. What it does show is Israel’s dependence on God and Moses’ need for others to help him continue. The leader on the hill has a task he cannot sustain alone.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley understand Moses’ raised hands as intercession—an appeal to God on behalf of the people fighting below. They read Joshua’s victory as God’s gift, with the fighting and the appeal to Him working together.

The closing image in verse 16 receives different explanations. Calvin understands the hand and throne as God actively exercising His rule against Amalek. A Catholic USCCB study note instead reads the line as a war cry concerning the LORD’s banner, while acknowledging the difficult Hebrew. The BSB’s wording about a hand raised toward the throne is retained in the passage above.

passages.god_plan_html:
Moses’ intercession offers a parallel to Christ’s care for His people, a comparison Calvin also makes. The difference helps explain the fuller hope: Moses grows weary and needs support, while Hebrews 7:23–28 says Jesus lives forever and always intercedes for those who draw near to God through Him. Their lasting help rests in His continuing life.

The New Testament also gives the church a shared responsibility to pray for others. 1 Timothy 2:1–6 calls for prayer for everyone, including rulers, and joins that instruction to God’s desire for people to be saved and to Christ’s role as the one mediator. The account at Rephidim gives a concrete picture of people supporting one another while depending on God; the later instruction extends the call to prayer well beyond one battle or one nation.

passages.title: Exodus 18:1-12
passages.section_title: How did Jethro respond to what God had done for Israel?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now Moses’ father-in-law Jethro, the priest of Midian, heard about all that God had done for Moses and His people Israel, and how the LORD had brought Israel out of Egypt. 2 After Moses had sent back his wife Zipporah, his father-in-law Jethro had received her, 3 along with her two sons. One son was named Gershom, for Moses had said, “I have been a foreigner in a foreign land.” 4 The other son was named Eliezer, for Moses had said, “The God of my father was my helper and delivered me from the sword of Pharaoh.” 5 Moses’ father-in-law Jethro, along with Moses’ wife and sons, came to him in the desert, where he was encamped at the mountain of God. 6 He sent word to Moses, “I, your father-in-law Jethro, am coming to you with your wife and her two sons.” 7 So Moses went out to meet his father-in-law and bowed down and kissed him. They greeted each other and went into the tent. 8 Then Moses recounted to his father-in-law all that the LORD had done to Pharaoh and the Egyptians for Israel’s sake, all the hardships they had encountered along the way, and how the LORD had delivered them. 9 And Jethro rejoiced over all the good things the LORD had done for Israel, whom He had rescued from the hand of the Egyptians. 10 Jethro declared, “Blessed be the LORD, who has delivered you from the hand of the Egyptians and of Pharaoh, and who has delivered the people from the hand of the Egyptians. 11 Now I know that the LORD is greater than all other gods, for He did this when they treated Israel with arrogance.” 12 Then Moses’ father-in-law Jethro brought a burnt offering and sacrifices to God, and Aaron came with all the elders of Israel to eat bread with Moses’ father-in-law in the presence of God.

7 So Moses went out to meet his father-in-law and bowed down and kissed him. They greeted each other and went into the tent. 8 Then Moses recounted to his father-in-law all that the LORD had done to Pharaoh and the Egyptians for Israel’s sake, all the hardships they had encountered along the way, and how the LORD had delivered them. 9 And Jethro rejoiced over all the good things the LORD had done for Israel, whom He had rescued from the hand of the Egyptians. 10 Jethro declared, “Blessed be the LORD, who has delivered you from the hand of the Egyptians and of Pharaoh, and who has delivered the people from the hand of the Egyptians. 11 Now I know that the LORD is greater than all other gods, for He did this when they treated Israel with arrogance.” 12 Then Moses’ father-in-law Jethro brought a burnt offering and sacrifices to God, and Aaron came with all the elders of Israel to eat bread with Moses’ father-in-law in the presence of God.

passages.context_html:
Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law and the priest of Midian, hears about the rescue from Egypt and comes to visit. He brings Zipporah and her two sons, whom he had received after Moses sent her back. Their names recall Moses’ life as a foreigner and God’s help in delivering him from Pharaoh.

Moses welcomes Jethro with affection and respect. Their conversation includes both the great rescue and the hardships along the way. Moses tells how the LORD has delivered Israel through those difficulties; the story has room for what they have suffered as well as what they have received.

Jethro rejoices, blesses the LORD and declares His greatness over other gods. He brings an offering and sacrifices to God, and Aaron and the elders share a meal with him in God’s presence. The deliverance has become something a man from outside Israel hears about, praises God for and celebrates with the people who were rescued.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The visit is read as a response of praise and recognition of the LORD’s power. Wesley understands Jethro’s statement as an existing faith being strengthened: he already knew God, and now knows His greatness more fully. The Catholic USCCB study note also sees his sacrifice as suggesting that he was already a worshiper of Israel’s God.

Calvin agrees that Jethro acknowledges the true God, but thinks the comparison with other gods may show that some belief in lesser gods still remains. He also allows that Jethro’s new knowledge could mean an earlier faith confirmed by experience. These readings differ over how much can be concluded about Jethro’s earlier beliefs; the text clearly records his praise and offering.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Jethro’s joy gives an early example of someone outside Israel sharing in praise for God’s work among His people. That fits the wider promise in Genesis 12:1–3: God will make Abraham’s descendants a blessing, with all the families of the earth in view.

Romans 15:8–12 explains the purpose through Christ. He confirms the promises to the patriarchs so that the Gentiles may glorify God for His mercy; Paul calls on the nations to rejoice with God’s people. Jethro’s response is an earlier example of that shared praise, rather than a claim that Paul is specifically interpreting this visit.

passages.title: Exodus 18:13-27
passages.section_title: Why did Moses need other people to share the work?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 The next day Moses took his seat to judge the people, and they stood around him from morning until evening. 14 When his father-in-law saw all that Moses was doing for the people, he asked, “What is this that you are doing for the people? Why do you sit alone as judge, with all the people standing around you from morning till evening?” 15 “Because the people come to me to inquire of God,” Moses replied. 16 “Whenever they have a dispute, it is brought to me to judge between one man and another, and I make known to them the statutes and laws of God.” 17 But Moses’ father-in-law said to him, “What you are doing is not good. 18 Surely you and these people with you will wear yourselves out, because the task is too heavy for you. You cannot handle it alone. 19 Now listen to me; I will give you some advice, and may God be with you. You must be the people’s representative before God and bring their causes to Him. 20 Teach them the statutes and laws, and show them the way to live and the work they must do. 21 Furthermore, select capable men from among the people—God-fearing, trustworthy men who are averse to dishonest gain. Appoint them over the people as leaders of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens. 22 Have these men judge the people at all times. Then they can bring you any major issue, but all minor cases they can judge on their own, so that your load may be lightened as they share it with you. 23 If you follow this advice and God so directs you, then you will be able to endure, and all these people can go home in peace.” 24 Moses listened to his father-in-law and did everything he said. 25 So Moses chose capable men from all Israel and made them heads over the people as leaders of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens. 26 And they judged the people at all times; they would bring the difficult cases to Moses, but any minor issue they would judge themselves. 27 Then Moses sent his father-in-law on his way, and Jethro returned to his own land.

You cannot handle it alone.

19 Now listen to me; I will give you some advice, and may God be with you. You must be the people’s representative before God and bring their causes to Him. 20 Teach them the statutes and laws, and show them the way to live and the work they must do. 21 Furthermore, select capable men from among the people—God-fearing, trustworthy men who are averse to dishonest gain. Appoint them over the people as leaders of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens. 22 Have these men judge the people at all times. Then they can bring you any major issue, but all minor cases they can judge on their own, so that your load may be lightened as they share it with you. 23 If you follow this advice and God so directs you, then you will be able to endure, and all these people can go home in peace.”

24 Moses listened to his father-in-law and did everything he said. 25 So Moses chose capable men from all Israel and made them heads over the people as leaders of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens. 26 And they judged the people at all times; they would bring the difficult cases to Moses, but any minor issue they would judge themselves. 27 Then Moses sent his father-in-law on his way, and Jethro returned to his own land.

passages.context_html:
Moses spends the next day judging disputes from morning until evening. He explains that people come to inquire of God, and he makes God’s instructions known as he settles their cases. Jethro sees a problem for both the judge and the people waiting for him: the burden is too great for one person.

His proposal preserves Moses’ responsibility to represent the people before God and teach them the way to live. Other capable men can handle ordinary disputes, while the difficult cases come to Moses. The work will be shared so that he can endure and the people can receive judgment without the same exhausting wait.

The Hebrew word חַיִל, chayil (KHAH-yil), has a range that includes strength, ability and worth. Brown–Driver–Briggs places these judges under ability and efficiency, often joined with moral worth. The list in the passage makes that character concrete: they must fear God, be trustworthy and reject dishonest gain.

Jethro places his advice under God’s direction. Moses listens, appoints suitable men over groups of different sizes, and keeps the difficult cases. The change allows others to carry real responsibility while Moses continues the work entrusted to him. Jethro then returns to his own land.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The shared reading sees wise counsel about the limits of one leader and the need for trustworthy helpers. Wesley and Calvin both emphasize the character of those appointed and Moses’ willingness to receive advice. They also take seriously the condition that the arrangement must remain under God’s authority.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
A similar need appears in Acts 6:1–7, when some widows are being overlooked in the daily distribution. The apostles arrange for qualified people to oversee that care so that they can continue in prayer and teaching. Both accounts show work being shared so that people are served and essential responsibilities receive attention. Acts is a later parallel, not an instruction to reproduce Israel’s exact ranks of judges in a church.

Ephesians 4:11–16 gives the larger purpose for the church: Christ gives people to equip others for ministry, and the whole body grows as its members do their part. Shared service is part of how His people mature together. The lesson reaches beyond helping one tired leader; it concerns a community being prepared to carry out its work.

passages.title: Exodus 19:1-15
passages.section_title: What did God call His rescued people to become?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 In the third month, on the same day of the month that the Israelites had left the land of Egypt, they came to the Wilderness of Sinai. 2 After they had set out from Rephidim, they entered the Wilderness of Sinai, and Israel camped there in front of the mountain. 3 Then Moses went up to God, and the LORD called to him from the mountain, “This is what you are to tell the house of Jacob and explain to the sons of Israel: 4 ‘You have seen for yourselves what I did to Egypt, and how I carried you on eagles’ wings and brought you to Myself. 5 Now if you will indeed obey My voice and keep My covenant, you will be My treasured possession out of all the nations—for the whole earth is Mine. 6 And unto Me you shall be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.’ These are the words that you are to speak to the Israelites.” 7 So Moses went back and summoned the elders of the people and set before them all these words that the LORD had commanded him. 8 And all the people answered together, “We will do everything that the LORD has spoken.” So Moses brought their words back to the LORD. 9 The LORD said to Moses, “Behold, I will come to you in a dense cloud, so that the people will hear when I speak with you, and they will always put their trust in you.” And Moses relayed to the LORD what the people had said. 10 Then the LORD said to Moses, “Go to the people and consecrate them today and tomorrow. They must wash their clothes 11 and be prepared by the third day, for on the third day the LORD will come down on Mount Sinai in the sight of all the people. 12 And you are to set up a boundary for the people around the mountain and tell them, ‘Be careful not to go up on the mountain or touch its base. Whoever touches the mountain shall surely be put to death. 13 No hand shall touch him, but he shall surely be stoned or shot with arrows—whether man or beast, he must not live.’ Only when the ram’s horn sounds a long blast may they approach the mountain.” 14 When Moses came down from the mountain to the people, he consecrated them, and they washed their clothes. 15 “Be prepared for the third day,” he said to the people. “Do not draw near to a woman.”

7 So Moses went back and summoned the elders of the people and set before them all these words that the LORD had commanded him. 8 And all the people answered together, “We will do everything that the LORD has spoken.” So Moses brought their words back to the LORD. 9 The LORD said to Moses, “Behold, I will come to you in a dense cloud, so that the people will hear when I speak with you, and they will always put their trust in you.” And Moses relayed to the LORD what the people had said.

10 Then the LORD said to Moses, “Go to the people and consecrate them today and tomorrow. They must wash their clothes 11 and be prepared by the third day, for on the third day the LORD will come down on Mount Sinai in the sight of all the people. 12 And you are to set up a boundary for the people around the mountain and tell them, ‘Be careful not to go up on the mountain or touch its base. Whoever touches the mountain shall surely be put to death. 13 No hand shall touch him, but he shall surely be stoned or shot with arrows—whether man or beast, he must not live.’ Only when the ram’s horn sounds a long blast may they approach the mountain.” 14 When Moses came down from the mountain to the people, he consecrated them, and they washed their clothes. 15 “Be prepared for the third day,” he said to the people. “Do not draw near to a woman.”

passages.context_html:
Israel arrives in the Wilderness of Sinai in the third month after leaving Egypt and camps before the mountain. God’s first message recalls what He has already done: He defeated Egypt, carried the people on eagles’ wings and brought them to Himself. The call to obey follows His rescue and care.

God promises that, if they obey His voice and keep His covenant, the binding agreement He gives them, they will be His treasured possession, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. The Hebrew word סְגֻלָּה, segullah (seh-gooh-LAH), means a valued possession or treasure, as Brown–Driver–Briggs explains. The whole earth belongs to God; Israel is being set apart within it to belong to Him and serve Him.

Moses brings the message to the elders, and the people agree to do what the LORD has spoken. God then promises to speak with Moses in a dense cloud so the people can hear and continue to trust him as the one bringing God’s words to them.

The coming meeting requires preparation. The people are to wash their clothes, refrain from sexual relations for the appointed time and respect a boundary around the mountain. God gives both an invitation to meet Him and instructions for how they may approach. The preparations make clear that this is a meeting with the holy God who has called them.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands the covenant as a gracious invitation to belong to God and serve Him. He reads the kingdom of priests as the whole nation being brought near and devoted to God’s service. Christian traditions differ in how they relate this covenant and its law to life under Christ.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, 7.5–6, understands the time of the law and the time of the gospel as two forms of one saving covenant. Before Christ came, promises, sacrifices and other observances pointed people toward Him; after His coming, the same grace is made known more fully.

The Catholic Church’s Catechism, 1961–1964, describes the law given to Israel as preparation for Christ. It teaches what is good and exposes sin, while the law itself does not supply the Spirit’s power to fulfill it.

A different account appears in Dallas Theological Seminary’s statement, article V. It treats the law, the church and the future kingdom as distinct stages in which God gives people different responsibilities. It explicitly teaches salvation by grace through faith in every period. This is the institution’s stated reading, not a claim that all evangelical churches agree with it.

deeper_study.title: The True Church According to Jesus

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
1 Peter 2:4–12 takes up the language of a royal priesthood, holy nation and people belonging to God when addressing believers in Christ. Their calling includes declaring His goodness and living honorably so that others may glorify Him. Being set apart carries a purpose for how His people live and bear witness.

Revelation 1:4–6 connects this calling with Jesus’ saving work: He loves His people, frees them from their sins by His blood and makes them a kingdom and priests to His God and Father. The purpose of rescue includes service and worship.

Galatians 3:15–29 explains that the later law does not cancel God’s earlier promise to Abraham. It leads the discussion toward Christ and the inheritance received through faith. The covenant at Sinai is part of the story through which Scripture explains God’s promise, human sin and the coming of Christ.

passages.title: Exodus 19:16-25
passages.section_title: Why did the people tremble at the mountain?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 On the third day, when morning came, there was thunder and lightning. A thick cloud was upon the mountain, and a very loud blast of the ram’s horn went out, so that all the people in the camp trembled. 17 Then Moses brought the people out of the camp to meet with God, and they stood at the foot of the mountain. 18 Mount Sinai was completely enveloped in smoke, because the LORD had descended on it in fire. And the smoke rose like the smoke of a furnace, and the whole mountain quaked violently. 19 And as the sound of the ram’s horn grew louder and louder, Moses spoke and God answered him in the thunder. 20 The LORD descended to the top of Mount Sinai and called Moses to the summit. So Moses went up, 21 and the LORD said to him, “Go down and warn the people not to break through to see the LORD, lest many of them perish. 22 Even the priests who approach the LORD must consecrate themselves, or the LORD will break out against them.” 23 But Moses said to the LORD, “The people cannot come up Mount Sinai, for You solemnly warned us, ‘Put a boundary around the mountain and set it apart as holy.’” 24 And the LORD replied, “Go down and bring Aaron with you. But the priests and the people must not break through to come up to the LORD, or He will break out against them.” 25 So Moses went down to the people and spoke to them.
paragraphs: 16 On the third day, when morning came, there was thunder and lightning. A thick cloud was upon the mountain, and a very loud blast of the ram’s horn went out, so that all the people in the camp trembled. 17 Then Moses brought the people out of the camp to meet with God, and they stood at the foot of the mountain. 18 Mount Sinai was completely enveloped in smoke, because the LORD had descended on it in fire. And the smoke rose like the smoke of a furnace, and the whole mountain quaked violently. 19 And as the sound of the ram’s horn grew louder and louder, Moses spoke and God answered him in the thunder. 20 The LORD descended to the top of Mount Sinai and called Moses to the summit. So Moses went up,

21 and the LORD said to him, “Go down and warn the people not to break through to see the LORD, lest many of them perish. 22 Even the priests who approach the LORD must consecrate themselves, or the LORD will break out against them.” 23 But Moses said to the LORD, “The people cannot come up Mount Sinai, for You solemnly warned us, ‘Put a boundary around the mountain and set it apart as holy.’” 24 And the LORD replied, “Go down and bring Aaron with you. But the priests and the people must not break through to come up to the LORD, or He will break out against them.” 25 So Moses went down to the people and spoke to them.

passages.context_html:
On the appointed morning the mountain is covered with cloud, thunder, lightning and a loud ram’s horn. Moses brings the people to its foot to meet God. Smoke rises because the LORD has descended in fire, and the mountain shakes. The people tremble at what they see and hear.

Moses speaks, God answers in the thunder and then calls him to the summit. His ascent follows God’s summons. The people cannot decide for themselves to follow him up the mountain simply because they want to see what is happening.

God sends Moses back to repeat the warning. Even the priests must consecrate themselves, and verse 24 expressly includes them with the people who must not break through. Moses is to bring Aaron with him. The passage distinguishes those whom God summons from those who must remain within the boundary, and shows the care taken to warn everyone of the danger.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The shared reading sees the signs and boundaries as a revelation of God’s holiness and authority that calls for serious attention to His word. Wesley and Calvin both connect the people’s fear with receiving God’s instruction reverently. Calvin also emphasizes that the people are brought to meet God, so the warning and the invitation belong together.

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 12:18–24 explicitly recalls Sinai’s fire, darkness, trumpet and terrifying command about touching the mountain. It then describes believers as having come to heavenly Zion, the gathered people of God and Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant. The scene at Sinai helps explain the significance of the access to God now opened through Him.

The same passage continues with a warning to listen to the One speaking from heaven. In Hebrews 12:25–29, the promise of an unshakable kingdom calls forth gratitude and worship with reverence and awe. Approaching God through Jesus gives confidence and belonging while still calling for a faithful response to His holy word.

passages.title: Exodus 20:1-17
passages.section_title: What kind of life did God call Israel to live?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 And God spoke all these words: 2 “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. 3 You shall have no other gods before Me. 4 You shall not make for yourself an idol in the form of anything in the heavens above, on the earth below, or in the waters beneath. 5 You shall not bow down to them or worship them; for I, the LORD your God, am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on their children to the third and fourth generations of those who hate Me, 6 but showing loving devotion to a thousand generations of those who love Me and keep My commandments. 7 You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain, for the LORD will not leave anyone unpunished who takes His name in vain. 8 Remember the Sabbath day by keeping it holy. 9 Six days you shall labor and do all your work, 10 but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God, on which you must not do any work—neither you, nor your son or daughter, nor your manservant or maidservant or livestock, nor the foreigner within your gates. 11 For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth and the sea and all that is in them, but on the seventh day He rested. Therefore the LORD blessed the Sabbath day and set it apart as holy. 12 Honor your father and mother, so that your days may be long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you. 13 You shall not murder. 14 You shall not commit adultery. 15 You shall not steal. 16 You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor. 17 You shall not covet your neighbor’s house. You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife, or his manservant or maidservant, or his ox or donkey, or anything that belongs to your neighbor.”

8 Remember the Sabbath day by keeping it holy. 9 Six days you shall labor and do all your work, 10 but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God, on which you must not do any work—neither you, nor your son or daughter, nor your manservant or maidservant or livestock, nor the foreigner within your gates. 11 For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth and the sea and all that is in them, but on the seventh day He rested. Therefore the LORD blessed the Sabbath day and set it apart as holy.

12 Honor your father and mother, so that your days may be long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you. 13 You shall not murder. 14 You shall not commit adultery. 15 You shall not steal. 16 You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor. 17 You shall not covet your neighbor’s house. You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife, or his manservant or maidservant, or his ox or donkey, or anything that belongs to your neighbor.”

passages.context_html:
God begins by identifying Himself as the LORD who brought Israel out of slavery. The commandments are spoken to people He has already rescued. They describe the loyalty and conduct that belong to life with Him under the covenant.

The opening commands call Israel to worship the LORD alone, without making an idol to bow before or serve. His jealousy means that He requires their undivided loyalty. The warning about the third and fourth generations stands beside the much longer reach of His loving devotion to a thousand generations. Ezekiel 18:19–20 also teaches this: a son who does what is right is not condemned for his father’s guilt.

The command about God’s name concerns its misuse. The Hebrew word שָׁוְא, shav (SHAHV), includes emptiness and falsehood in Brown–Driver–Briggs. Invoking God’s name falsely or treating it as an empty expression dishonors the One whose name is being used.

The Sabbath sets apart a day of rest in remembrance of God’s completed work of creation. The rest extends through the household to servants, foreigners and livestock. Honoring father and mother comes with a promise concerning life in the land God is giving Israel.

The remaining commands protect life, marriage, another person’s possessions and truthful dealings with neighbors. The final command reaches into desire itself. The verb חָמַד, chamad (khah-MAHD), can mean desire or take pleasure in; Brown–Driver–Briggs identifies the selfish desire for another person’s belongings in this passage. God addresses what people want, as well as what they do.

The chapter presents these words together without numbering them individually. Deuteronomy 4:12–13 explicitly calls them the Ten Commandments and recalls their place in the covenant and on the two stone tablets.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The numbering differs across traditions. The Jewish ordering described by Chabad begins with God identifying Himself as Israel’s God. The Catholic Catechism, 2066, and Luther’s Small Catechism join the prohibitions of other gods and images and count two commands about coveting. The Reformed Westminster Larger Catechism, 103–110, counts other gods and images separately. Each numbering system arranges the commands within this passage.

Christians also differ over images in worship. The Catholic Church’s Catechism, 2129–2132, permits honoring sacred images because the honor is directed to the person portrayed; it distinguishes this from the adoration due to God alone and grounds the practice in the Son becoming human. The Reformed Larger Catechism, question 109, forbids making representations of God and worshiping God through them.

The Sabbath’s Christian application also differs. The Westminster Confession, 21.7–8, teaches a continuing weekly Sabbath now observed on Sunday. The Catholic Catechism, 2174–2176, describes Sunday as fulfilling the Sabbath through Christ’s resurrection. The Lutheran Large Catechism retains Sunday for shared worship and hearing God’s word while saying no day is inherently better than another. The Seventh-day Adventist Church’s Sabbath belief maintains the seventh day as the continuing appointed day.

On the continuing moral commands, the Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 19, and the Methodist Articles, article VI, distinguish these duties from Israel’s ceremonial and civil rules. Both teach that Christians remain bound to moral obedience. The Catholic Catechism, 2068–2072, likewise teaches the commandments’ continuing obligation.

passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus addresses these commands in Matthew 5:17–30. He says He has come to fulfill the Law and the Prophets, and brings anger, reconciliation and lust into the discussion of murder and adultery. God’s purpose includes a heart and relationships brought under His instruction.

Romans 13:8–10 explicitly names the commands against adultery, murder, stealing and coveting, and gathers them under love for the neighbor. Ephesians 6:1–4 also carries the command to honor parents into Christian households, while instructing fathers to nurture children rather than provoke them. The commands become concrete instruction for a people learning to live in love.

In the new-covenant promise recalled in Hebrews 10:15–18, God puts His laws in hearts and minds and remembers sins no more. The chapter joins that promise to Christ’s completed offering. Scripture’s larger movement is toward forgiveness and a people whose life is changed from within.

passages.title: Exodus 20:18-21
passages.section_title: Why did Moses say not to be afraid, yet speak of fearing God?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 When all the people witnessed the thunder and lightning, the sounding of the ram’s horn, and the mountain enveloped in smoke, they trembled and stood at a distance. 19 “Speak to us yourself and we will listen,” they said to Moses. “But do not let God speak to us, or we will die.” 20 “Do not be afraid,” Moses replied. “For God has come to test you, so that the fear of Him may be before you, to keep you from sinning.” 21 And the people stood at a distance as Moses approached the thick darkness where God was.
paragraphs: 18 When all the people witnessed the thunder and lightning, the sounding of the ram’s horn, and the mountain enveloped in smoke, they trembled and stood at a distance. 19 “Speak to us yourself and we will listen,” they said to Moses. “But do not let God speak to us, or we will die.” 20 “Do not be afraid,” Moses replied. “For God has come to test you, so that the fear of Him may be before you, to keep you from sinning.” 21 And the people stood at a distance as Moses approached the thick darkness where God was.

passages.context_html:
The people have heard the words spoken amid thunder, lightning, smoke and the ram’s horn. They tremble and move away, asking Moses to speak to them instead. They fear that hearing God directly will bring death.

Moses reassures them and explains the purpose of the encounter: God has come to test them, and the fear of Him is to help keep them from sin. His reassurance does not treat God’s holiness lightly. He calls them away from expecting immediate destruction and toward a lasting seriousness about listening to Him.

The people remain at a distance while Moses approaches the thick darkness where God is. The one they have asked to speak for them now carries that responsibility. The scene connects the commands with the response God seeks from the people who have heard them.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley and Calvin both distinguish terror that overwhelms the people from a fear of God that humbles them and leads to obedience. They understand the signs as intended to bring Israel to heed His word, with Moses serving as the intermediary the people have requested.

Hebrews 12:18–24 explicitly recalls the voice that made the people ask to hear no more. It places that encounter alongside believers’ approach to heavenly Zion and Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant. Moses’ role in the scene belongs to the larger story of how people come near to God.

Hebrews 10:19–25 describes the confidence now given through Jesus’ blood. Believers are called to draw near with sincere hearts, hold to their hope and encourage one another toward love and good deeds. God’s purpose includes a people who can approach Him in faith and help one another remain faithful.

passages.title: Exodus 20:22-26
passages.section_title: How was Israel to worship the God who had spoken?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 Then the LORD said to Moses, “This is what you are to tell the Israelites: ‘You have seen for yourselves that I have spoken to you from heaven. 23 You are not to make any gods alongside Me; you are not to make for yourselves gods of silver or gold. 24 You are to make for Me an altar of earth, and sacrifice on it your burnt offerings and peace offerings, your sheep and goats and cattle. In every place where I cause My name to be remembered, I will come to you and bless you. 25 Now if you make an altar of stones for Me, you must not build it with stones shaped by tools; for if you use a chisel on it, you will defile it. 26 And you must not go up to My altar on steps, lest your nakedness be exposed on it.’
paragraphs: 22 Then the LORD said to Moses, “This is what you are to tell the Israelites: ‘You have seen for yourselves that I have spoken to you from heaven. 23 You are not to make any gods alongside Me; you are not to make for yourselves gods of silver or gold. 24 You are to make for Me an altar of earth, and sacrifice on it your burnt offerings and peace offerings, your sheep and goats and cattle. In every place where I cause My name to be remembered, I will come to you and bless you. 25 Now if you make an altar of stones for Me, you must not build it with stones shaped by tools; for if you use a chisel on it, you will defile it. 26 And you must not go up to My altar on steps, lest your nakedness be exposed on it.’

passages.context_html:
God reminds Israel that they have heard Him speak from heaven and repeats the prohibition of gods made from silver or gold. The next instructions concern worship directed to the LORD Himself. He gives directions about the altar and the offerings that are to be brought to Him.

The altar may be made from earth or from stones that have not been shaped with tools. God promises to come and bless in the places where He causes His name to be remembered. His presence and blessing are joined to His direction about worship.

The people must not build steps up to the altar that would expose the worshiper’s nakedness. The materials, construction and conduct all fall within the instructions God gives. The focus is a fitting response to the God who speaks and makes His presence known.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley and Calvin understand the plain earth or unworked stone as helping keep worship from becoming attached to shaped images or revered structures. Both read these as directions for the altars used before the later established sanctuary, with God directing the place and manner of worship.

passages.god_plan_html:
The Bible’s account of acceptable worship continues through Christ. Hebrews 10:11–18 explains that His one offering accomplishes what repeated sacrifices could not. Hebrews 13:10–16 then speaks of an altar, Jesus’ suffering and the sacrifices believers now offer through Him: praise, doing good and sharing with others.

In John 4:21–24, Jesus also explains that worship of the Father will not be confined to one mountain or Jerusalem; the Father seeks worshipers in spirit and truth. These passages carry the theme forward from the altar instructions: God makes the way for His people to worship Him, and Christian worship is offered through Jesus in a life that honors God.

passages.title: Exodus 21:1-11
passages.section_title: What did these laws require for Hebrew servants?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 “These are the ordinances that you are to set before them: 2 If you buy a Hebrew servant, he is to serve you for six years. But in the seventh year, he shall go free without paying anything. 3 If he arrived alone, he is to leave alone; if he arrived with a wife, she is to leave with him. 4 If his master gives him a wife and she bears him sons or daughters, the woman and her children shall belong to her master, and only the man shall go free. 5 But if the servant declares, ‘I love my master and my wife and children; I do not want to go free,’ 6 then his master is to bring him before the judges. And he shall take him to the door or doorpost and pierce his ear with an awl. Then he shall serve his master for life. 7 And if a man sells his daughter as a servant, she is not to go free as the menservants do. 8 If she is displeasing in the eyes of her master who had designated her for himself, he must allow her to be redeemed. He has no right to sell her to foreigners, since he has broken faith with her. 9 And if he chooses her for his son, he must deal with her as with a daughter. 10 If he takes another wife, he must not reduce the food, clothing, or marital rights of his first wife. 11 If, however, he does not provide her with these three things, she is free to go without monetary payment.

But in the seventh year, he shall go free without paying anything. 3 If he arrived alone, he is to leave alone; if he arrived with a wife, she is to leave with him. 4 If his master gives him a wife and she bears him sons or daughters, the woman and her children shall belong to her master, and only the man shall go free.

5 But if the servant declares, ‘I love my master and my wife and children; I do not want to go free,’ 6 then his master is to bring him before the judges. And he shall take him to the door or doorpost and pierce his ear with an awl. Then he shall serve his master for life.

7 And if a man sells his daughter as a servant, she is not to go free as the menservants do. 8 If she is displeasing in the eyes of her master who had designated her for himself, he must allow her to be redeemed. He has no right to sell her to foreigners, since he has broken faith with her. 9 And if he chooses her for his son, he must deal with her as with a daughter. 10 If he takes another wife, he must not reduce the food, clothing, or marital rights of his first wife. 11 If, however, he does not provide her with these three things, she is free to go without monetary payment.

passages.context_html:
After the Ten Commandments, God gives Moses laws for particular situations in Israel’s life together. These begin with people living under another person’s authority as servants. The rules concern release, marriage, children and the obligations of a master.

A Hebrew man bought as a servant is to serve six years and go free in the seventh without paying for his release. A wife who came with him leaves with him. But if his master supplied the wife, she and her children remain with the master. The man may choose to stay, and the pierced ear marks that continuing service. His love for his family is part of that decision; leaving would mean leaving them behind.

The daughter sold by her father is dealt with differently because the following instructions concern her place in a marriage. If the master who intended her for himself rejects her, he must permit her redemption and cannot sell her to foreigners. If she is intended for his son, she must be treated as a daughter. Taking another wife does not remove the first wife’s rights to food, clothing and marital relations; withholding them means she goes free without payment.

These are laws regulating human ownership, with limits placed on the owner. They should not be softened into a description of an ordinary job. Elsewhere, Exodus 22:3 allows a thief who cannot repay to be sold, and Leviticus 25:39–46 distinguishes impoverished Israelites from foreign slaves who could become inherited property. Not every case was entered freely, and not every servant had the same right of release.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Readers generally recognize the six-year limit as a protection for the Hebrew man and verses 7–11 as safeguards for the woman’s treatment within the household. Wesley understands the marriage provisions as requiring the master to fulfill the obligations he undertook, rather than discarding the woman when she no longer pleases him.

One difference concerns how long the pierced servant remains. The BSB says “for life.” The Hebrew word עוֹלָם, olam (oh-LAHM), can refer to a continuing duration, including a lifetime; its meaning depends on its setting (Brown–Driver–Briggs). Rashi’s Jewish commentary reads this service as lasting until the Jubilee, when Leviticus 25:10 proclaims release. Wesley allows either the servant’s death or the Jubilee as the endpoint. The BSB wording is retained above, while these readings explain why some interpreters do not understand it as excluding Jubilee release.

passages.god_plan_html:
The larger biblical story uses the difference between slavery and family membership to explain what God gives through His Son. In Galatians 4:1–7, Paul says that God sent Jesus to redeem those under the law so that they might receive adoption. Those who belong to Christ receive His Spirit and can approach God as their Father; they are heirs, not merely people kept in service.

That is a broader biblical connection, rather than Paul giving a verse-by-verse explanation of this household law. It also does not make every form of human ownership an example to imitate. In 1 Corinthians 7:20–24, Paul tells an enslaved believer to take the opportunity for freedom if it becomes available. Belonging to Christ gives a person a standing before God that a human master cannot determine.

passages.title: Exodus 21:12-36
passages.section_title: How did the law deal with violence and responsibility?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 Whoever strikes and kills a man must surely be put to death. 13 If, however, he did not lie in wait, but God allowed it to happen, then I will appoint for you a place where he may flee. 14 But if a man schemes and acts willfully against his neighbor to kill him, you must take him away from My altar to be put to death. 15 Whoever strikes his father or mother must surely be put to death. 16 Whoever kidnaps another man must be put to death, whether he sells him or the man is found in his possession. 17 Anyone who curses his father or mother must surely be put to death. 18 If men are quarreling and one strikes the other with a stone or a fist, and he does not die but is confined to bed, 19 then the one who struck him shall go unpunished, as long as the other can get up and walk around outside with his staff. Nevertheless, he must compensate the man for his lost work and see that he is completely healed. 20 If a man strikes his manservant or maidservant with a rod, and the servant dies by his hand, he shall surely be punished. 21 However, if the servant gets up after a day or two, the owner shall not be punished, since the servant is his property. 22 If men who are fighting strike a pregnant woman and her child is born prematurely, but there is no further injury, he shall surely be fined as the woman’s husband demands and as the court allows. 23 But if a serious injury results, then you must require a life for a life— 24 eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, 25 burn for burn, wound for wound, and stripe for stripe. 26 If a man strikes and blinds the eye of his manservant or maidservant, he must let the servant go free as compensation for the eye. 27 And if he knocks out the tooth of his manservant or maidservant, he must let the servant go free as compensation for the tooth. 28 If an ox gores a man or woman to death, the ox must surely be stoned, and its meat must not be eaten. passages.context_html:
These cases distinguish deliberate violence from an unintended death, and an unexpected accident from a danger someone knowingly failed to prevent. A planned killing cannot be hidden behind religious protection: even the altar is no shelter for the murderer. Striking or cursing parents and kidnapping another person also carry severe penalties.

When an injured person recovers enough to walk, the person who struck him must pay for lost time and healing. The rules for enslaved people are different. An owner who beats a servant to death is subject to punishment; verse 21 withholds that punishment if the servant gets up after a day or two, giving the owner’s property interest as the reason. But destroying a servant’s eye or knocking out a tooth requires the servant’s release. The passage limits a master’s power while still treating the servant as property. Both features need to be faced honestly.

Verses 22–25 address a pregnant woman injured when men fight. The BSB describes a premature birth: if there is no further injury, a court-approved fine is paid; serious injury brings the corresponding penalty. The following eye-for-eye language sets the consequence in relation to the harm done. How this case is understood has been an important point of disagreement.

The animal laws also turn on responsibility. An ox that kills a person must be killed. If its owner knew it was dangerous and failed to restrain it, the owner can also face death, though a ransom may be permitted in that case. A servant’s death brings a fixed payment of thirty shekels to the master. Uncovered pits and injuries between animals require repayment or shared loss, with greater liability when a known danger was neglected. The ransom allowed for the negligent ox owner should not be extended to deliberate murder; Numbers 35:31 expressly forbids accepting a ransom for a murderer.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The distinction between intentional killing, accidental death and preventable harm is widely recognized. Wesley reads the injury penalties as the work of the courts, not permission for an injured person to take revenge. On refuge for an unintended killing, Numbers 35:22–28 later explains both protection from the avenger and release after the high priest’s death; refuge is not described there as imprisonment that can never end.

On the pregnancy case, Calvin understands the serious harm in verses 23–25 to include harm to either the mother or her child. Gill also allows both to be included. In contrast, Rashi understands the fine as payment for the loss of the offspring and the further harm as harm to the woman. These are different readings of what happened and whose injury the next penalty concerns. They should not be presented as a single agreed interpretation, or as every member of a modern denomination speaking with one voice.

There is also a difference over how injury was to be repaid. Calvin describes the corresponding loss of an eye or limb as a judicial penalty, while also speaking of proportionate compensation. The Jewish Mishnah, Bava Kamma 8:1, explains bodily injury through payments for damage, pain, medical care, lost livelihood and humiliation. Its treatment shows that the Jewish legal reading cannot simply be reduced to physically repeating each injury.
