passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus explicitly returns to the eye-for-eye wording in Matthew 5:38–48. He teaches His followers to give up retaliation, respond generously and love their enemies, including praying for those who persecute them. The Father’s goodness toward both the righteous and the unrighteous becomes the pattern for their conduct. This carries the discussion beyond calculating what an offender owes: Jesus calls for people whose response to wrongdoing reflects their Father.

There is another, more sobering connection. Gill draws a parallel between the thirty shekels paid for a servant’s death here and the thirty silver pieces offered for Jesus’ betrayal in Matthew 26:14–16. Matthew does not identify Exodus 21 as a prediction being fulfilled, so this is a parallel rather than an explicit prophecy. Alongside it, Philippians 2:5–11 describes the Son taking a servant’s place and humbling Himself to death, followed by God’s exaltation of Him. The one treated so cheaply is the Lord before whom every knee will bow.

passages.title: Exodus 22:1-15
passages.section_title: What happens when someone steals or damages another person’s property?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 “If a man steals an ox or a sheep and slaughters or sells it, he must repay five oxen for an ox and four sheep for a sheep. 2 If a thief is caught breaking in and is beaten to death, no one shall be guilty of bloodshed. 3 But if it happens after sunrise, there is guilt for his bloodshed. A thief must make full restitution; if he has nothing, he himself shall be sold for his theft. 4 If what was stolen is actually found alive in his possession—whether ox or donkey or sheep—he must pay back double. 5 If a man grazes his livestock in a field or vineyard and allows them to stray so that they graze in someone else’s field, he must make restitution from the best of his own field or vineyard. 6 If a fire breaks out and spreads to thornbushes so that it consumes stacked or standing grain, or the whole field, the one who started the fire must make full restitution. 7 If a man gives his neighbor money or goods for safekeeping and they are stolen from the neighbor’s house, the thief, if caught, must pay back double. 8 If the thief is not found, the owner of the house must appear before the judges to determine whether he has taken his neighbor’s property. 9 In all cases of illegal possession of an ox, a donkey, a sheep, a garment, or any lost item that someone claims, ‘This is mine,’ both parties shall bring their cases before the judges. The one whom the judges find guilty must pay back double to his neighbor. 10 If a man gives a donkey, an ox, a sheep, or any other animal to be cared for by his neighbor, but it dies or is injured or stolen while no one is watching, 11 an oath before the LORD shall be made between the parties to determine whether or not the man has taken his neighbor’s property. The owner must accept the oath and require no restitution. 12 But if the animal was actually stolen from the neighbor, he must make restitution to the owner. 13 If the animal was torn to pieces, he shall bring it as evidence; he need not make restitution for the torn carcass. 14 If a man borrows an animal from his neighbor and it is injured or dies while its owner is not present, he must make full restitution. 15 If the owner was present, no restitution is required. If the animal was rented, the fee covers the loss.

A thief must make full restitution; if he has nothing, he himself shall be sold for his theft. 4 If what was stolen is actually found alive in his possession—whether ox or donkey or sheep—he must pay back double.

5 If a man grazes his livestock in a field or vineyard and allows them to stray so that they graze in someone else’s field, he must make restitution from the best of his own field or vineyard. 6 If a fire breaks out and spreads to thornbushes so that it consumes stacked or standing grain, or the whole field, the one who started the fire must make full restitution.

7 If a man gives his neighbor money or goods for safekeeping and they are stolen from the neighbor’s house, the thief, if caught, must pay back double. 8 If the thief is not found, the owner of the house must appear before the judges to determine whether he has taken his neighbor’s property. 9 In all cases of illegal possession of an ox, a donkey, a sheep, a garment, or any lost item that someone claims, ‘This is mine,’ both parties shall bring their cases before the judges. The one whom the judges find guilty must pay back double to his neighbor.

10 If a man gives a donkey, an ox, a sheep, or any other animal to be cared for by his neighbor, but it dies or is injured or stolen while no one is watching, 11 an oath before the LORD shall be made between the parties to determine whether or not the man has taken his neighbor’s property. The owner must accept the oath and require no restitution. 12 But if the animal was actually stolen from the neighbor, he must make restitution to the owner. 13 If the animal was torn to pieces, he shall bring it as evidence; he need not make restitution for the torn carcass.

14 If a man borrows an animal from his neighbor and it is injured or dies while its owner is not present, he must make full restitution. 15 If the owner was present, no restitution is required. If the animal was rented, the fee covers the loss.

passages.context_html:
These laws continue the question of responsibility raised by the dangerous animals and uncovered pits in the previous chapter. Here the cases involve theft, damage to crops, safekeeping and borrowed animals. The person who suffers the loss is not simply left to absorb it.

A thief who has sold or slaughtered a stolen animal owes more than one who still has it alive. The law requires repayment, and a thief unable to pay can be sold for the theft. It also distinguishes a break-in from killing a thief after sunrise. Theft itself does not give the homeowner an unrestricted right to take the thief’s life.

The cases then move from taking property to harming it or failing a trust. Someone whose livestock stray into another field must repay from the best of his own produce. Someone who starts a fire is answerable when it spreads. Disputed ownership goes before judges; an oath before the LORD and evidence of an animal’s death can also resolve a case. Being entrusted with an animal, borrowing it and hiring it do not all carry identical terms. The details matter because responsibility depends on what happened and what obligation the person had taken on.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The usual reading is that these laws require honest repayment and careful treatment of what belongs to someone else. Wesley emphasizes that carelessness can cause a real wrong even when the damage was not intended. He also sees the borrowing rule as a reason to take particular care with something another person has kindly lent. The passage distinguishes circumstances rather than assigning the same penalty to every loss.

passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus says that love for God and love for one’s neighbor are the two commands on which the Law and the Prophets hang (Matthew 22:34–40). These cases give that love a practical shape: another person’s livelihood and trust must matter to us. This is a connection with the law’s larger purpose, rather than Jesus directly commenting on each repayment amount.

The New Testament carries the theme into changed lives. In Luke 19:1–10, Zacchaeus responds to Jesus by promising generosity to the poor and repayment to people he has cheated. Jesus announces salvation and explains His mission to seek and save the lost. Ephesians 4:25–32 likewise calls the former thief to work and share with someone in need. God’s purpose reaches beyond stopping the theft: the person who once took from others can become someone who provides for them.

passages.title: Exodus 22:16-31
passages.section_title: What did faithfulness to God look like in everyday life?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 If a man seduces a virgin who is not pledged in marriage and sleeps with her, he must pay the full dowry for her to be his wife. 17 If her father absolutely refuses to give her to him, the man still must pay an amount comparable to the bridal price of a virgin. 18 You must not allow a sorceress to live. 19 Whoever lies with an animal must surely be put to death. 20 If anyone sacrifices to any god other than the LORD alone, he must be set apart for destruction. 21 You must not exploit or oppress a foreign resident, for you yourselves were foreigners in the land of Egypt. 22 You must not mistreat any widow or orphan. 23 If you do mistreat them, and they cry out to Me in distress, I will surely hear their cry. 24 My anger will be kindled, and I will kill you with the sword; then your wives will become widows and your children will be fatherless. 25 If you lend money to one of My people among you who is poor, you must not act as a creditor to him; you are not to charge him interest. 26 If you take your neighbor’s cloak as collateral, return it to him by sunset, 27 because his cloak is the only covering he has for his body. What else will he sleep in? And if he cries out to Me, I will hear, for I am compassionate. 28 You must not blaspheme God or curse the ruler of your people. 29 You must not hold back offerings from your granaries or vats. You are to give Me the firstborn of your sons. 30 You shall do likewise with your cattle and your sheep. Let them stay with their mothers for seven days, but on the eighth day you are to give them to Me. 31 You are to be My holy people. You must not eat the meat of a mauled animal found in the field; you are to throw it to the dogs.
paragraphs: 16 If a man seduces a virgin who is not pledged in marriage and sleeps with her, he must pay the full dowry for her to be his wife. 17 If her father absolutely refuses to give her to him, the man still must pay an amount comparable to the bridal price of a virgin.

18 You must not allow a sorceress to live. 19 Whoever lies with an animal must surely be put to death. 20 If anyone sacrifices to any god other than the LORD alone, he must be set apart for destruction.

21 You must not exploit or oppress a foreign resident, for you yourselves were foreigners in the land of Egypt. 22 You must not mistreat any widow or orphan. 23 If you do mistreat them, and they cry out to Me in distress, I will surely hear their cry. 24 My anger will be kindled, and I will kill you with the sword; then your wives will become widows and your children will be fatherless.

25 If you lend money to one of My people among you who is poor, you must not act as a creditor to him; you are not to charge him interest. 26 If you take your neighbor’s cloak as collateral, return it to him by sunset, 27 because his cloak is the only covering he has for his body. What else will he sleep in? And if he cries out to Me, I will hear, for I am compassionate.

28 You must not blaspheme God or curse the ruler of your people. 29 You must not hold back offerings from your granaries or vats. You are to give Me the firstborn of your sons. 30 You shall do likewise with your cattle and your sheep. Let them stay with their mothers for seven days, but on the eighth day you are to give them to Me. 31 You are to be My holy people. You must not eat the meat of a mauled animal found in the field; you are to throw it to the dogs.

passages.context_html:
These instructions bring together sexual conduct, worship, treatment of vulnerable people and the honor owed to God. A man who seduces an unbetrothed woman cannot simply walk away from the consequences. The marriage payment remains due even if her father refuses the marriage. Sorcery, sexual relations with an animal and sacrifice to other gods carry severe penalties under Israel’s covenant law.

Verse 20’s expression “set apart for destruction” comes from חָרַם, charam (khah-RAHM), a Hebrew verb for placing something under a ban or devoting it. In this case it means being devoted to death, not merely being excluded from a gathering (Brown–Driver–Briggs). The wording underlines how seriously the covenant treats worship of another god.

The same God who requires Israel’s exclusive worship forbids them to exploit a foreign resident, widow, orphan or poor borrower. Their own experience in Egypt must shape how they treat foreigners. A creditor must return a poor neighbor’s cloak before night because the person needs it for warmth. God hears the cry of the mistreated and warns the oppressor of judgment. His compassion is given as the reason for protecting the borrower.

The closing instructions require respect for God and rulers, prompt offerings and a distinct way of life. Giving God the firstborn sons must be read with Exodus 13:11–16, which requires their redemption. The instruction does not call for sacrificing children. The rules for firstborn livestock and meat from a mauled animal also belong to the people’s calling to be holy—set apart to God.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Interpreters commonly recognize that devotion to God and justice toward other people belong together here. On lending, Wesley and Calvin understand the interest prohibition as protecting people who borrow out of need. Both distinguish that protection from a ban on every possible interest-bearing arrangement; neither allows profit to excuse exploiting a poor neighbor. These are their readings of the law’s continuing moral purpose, rather than a claim that every Christian tradition has given the same account of lending.

A smaller difference concerns the opening of verse 28. The BSB understands it as a prohibition of blaspheming God. The Catholic Bible’s note likewise reads it as dishonoring God’s authority. Wesley and Calvin take the word there as referring to judges or magistrates, alongside the ruler mentioned next. Both readings require honor for rightful authority; they differ over the first term’s immediate reference.

passages.god_plan_html:
The New Testament takes up both the protection of vulnerable people and the call to honor others. James 1:26–27 joins care for widows and orphans with a life kept faithful to God. James 5:1–6 warns those who enrich themselves by withholding workers’ wages: the workers’ cries have reached the Lord. The God who heard Israel in Egypt still hears people harmed by those with power.

In Acts 23:1–5, Paul explicitly quotes this passage’s command about speaking of a ruler, even after being struck unjustly. 1 Peter 2:11–17 describes honorable conduct as part of God’s people’s witness among the nations. That honor does not make every human demand right: in Acts 5:27–32, the apostles obey God when authorities order them to stop speaking about Jesus. The larger purpose is a people whose loyalty to God shows in compassion, integrity and respect.

passages.title: Exodus 23:1-9
passages.section_title: What does justice require when feelings pull the other way?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 “You shall not spread a false report. Do not join the wicked by being a malicious witness. 2 You shall not follow the crowd in wrongdoing. When you testify in a lawsuit, do not pervert justice by siding with the crowd. 3 And do not show favoritism to a poor man in his lawsuit. 4 If you encounter your enemy’s stray ox or donkey, you must return it to him. 5 If you see the donkey of one who hates you fallen under its load, do not leave it there; you must help him with it. 6 You shall not deny justice to the poor in their lawsuits. 7 Stay far away from a false accusation. Do not kill the innocent or the just, for I will not acquit the guilty. 8 Do not accept a bribe, for a bribe blinds those who see and twists the words of the righteous. 9 Do not oppress a foreign resident, since you yourselves know how it feels to be foreigners; for you were foreigners in the land of Egypt.
paragraphs: 1 “You shall not spread a false report. Do not join the wicked by being a malicious witness. 2 You shall not follow the crowd in wrongdoing. When you testify in a lawsuit, do not pervert justice by siding with the crowd. 3 And do not show favoritism to a poor man in his lawsuit.
4 If you encounter your enemy’s stray ox or donkey, you must return it to him. 5 If you see the donkey of one who hates you fallen under its load, do not leave it there; you must help him with it.

6 You shall not deny justice to the poor in their lawsuits. 7 Stay far away from a false accusation. Do not kill the innocent or the just, for I will not acquit the guilty. 8 Do not accept a bribe, for a bribe blinds those who see and twists the words of the righteous. 9 Do not oppress a foreign resident, since you yourselves know how it feels to be foreigners; for you were foreigners in the land of Egypt.

passages.context_html:
These instructions address the pressures that can bend a person’s judgment: a false report, a powerful crowd, sympathy, hostility or a bribe. A witness must tell the truth even when others are determined to get a different result. Neither poverty nor wealth changes what a just decision requires. Verse 3 forbids favoring a poor person in a lawsuit, and verse 6 forbids denying that person justice.

Fairness also reaches beyond the courtroom. If an enemy’s animal strays or collapses under its load, Israel must help. The owner’s hostility does not cancel the obligation to return the animal or lift its burden. The passage brings truthfulness, fair judgment and practical mercy together.

The warning about foreigners returns to Israel’s own experience: they know how it feels to live as foreigners because they lived in Egypt. That memory is to make them careful with someone else’s vulnerability, rather than give them permission to repeat the treatment they suffered.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The main reading is shared: the law rejects dishonest testimony and favoritism, and requires help even for an enemy. Wesley emphasizes that a crowd’s approval cannot make wrongdoing right and that Israel’s experience as foreigners should lead them to understand a foreigner’s distress. The duties remain when pressure or personal feeling makes them inconvenient.

passages.god_plan_html:
God’s people are to reflect His goodness in the way they treat others. Romans 12:14–21 carries the theme of helping an enemy into Christian life: believers bless persecutors, give food and drink to an enemy in need, and overcome evil with good. Their conduct is not to be controlled by the hostility they receive.

James 2:1–13 likewise connects faith in Jesus with refusing favoritism toward the wealthy and dishonor toward the poor. It calls love of neighbor the royal law and insists that mercy matters in judgment. These passages develop the wider purpose behind the courtroom and animal cases: a community marked by truth, fairness and active love.

passages.title: Exodus 23:10-13
passages.section_title: Who was meant to benefit from Israel’s rest?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 For six years you are to sow your land and gather its produce, 11 but in the seventh year you must let it rest and lie fallow, so that the poor among your people may eat from the field and the wild animals may consume what they leave. Do the same with your vineyard and olive grove. 12 For six days you are to do your work, but on the seventh day you must cease, so that your ox and your donkey may rest and the son of your maidservant may be refreshed, as well as the foreign resident. 13 Pay close attention to everything I have said to you. You must not invoke the names of other gods; they must not be heard on your lips.
paragraphs: 10 For six years you are to sow your land and gather its produce, 11 but in the seventh year you must let it rest and lie fallow, so that the poor among your people may eat from the field and the wild animals may consume what they leave. Do the same with your vineyard and olive grove.

12 For six days you are to do your work, but on the seventh day you must cease, so that your ox and your donkey may rest and the son of your maidservant may be refreshed, as well as the foreign resident. 13 Pay close attention to everything I have said to you. You must not invoke the names of other gods; they must not be heard on your lips.

passages.context_html:
The seventh year is a rest for the land, but its purpose is also about people and animals. The poor may eat what grows, and the wild animals may eat what remains. The vineyard and olive grove are included. Israel’s use of the land must leave room for needs beyond the landholder’s own harvest.

The weekly rest likewise reaches those who could otherwise be kept working: the ox, donkey, servant’s child and foreign resident. The command gives them refreshment. Rest is not reserved for the person with enough power to decide the household’s schedule.

Leviticus 25:18–22 later addresses the question of food during the unsown year. God promises a sixth-year crop sufficient for three years, carrying the people through the return to sowing and the next harvest. Here the rest instructions end with a call to heed everything God has said and refuse the invocation of other gods. Work, provision and loyalty to Him belong together.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Readers generally see care for the poor and rest for dependents alongside trust in God’s provision. Wesley emphasizes that trust: the people must allow the year’s rest without treating constant production as their only security.

Christian traditions differ over the weekly Sabbath’s present observance. The Westminster Confession, 21.7–8, teaches a continuing weekly obligation observed on Sunday. The Seventh-day Adventist statement of belief retains the seventh day. The Catholic Catechism, 2174–2176, explains Sunday worship in relation to Christ’s resurrection and fulfillment of the Sabbath. These differences about Christian practice should be distinguished from the rest this passage explicitly requires for Israel’s land, workers and animals.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
The later history shows that the land’s rest was a serious part of Israel’s covenant responsibility. 2 Chronicles 36:15–23 describes the people’s refusal to hear God’s messengers, the exile and the land enjoying its Sabbath rest during the desolation. The account ends with God opening the way for a return. His dealings include judgment and renewed opportunity, rather than treating the land as something His people possess without responsibility.

The theme also reaches beyond agricultural or weekly rest. Hebrews 4:1–11 joins God’s creation rest, the wilderness warning and the continuing promise of entering His rest. It calls for a response of faith. Hebrews is developing that larger biblical theme, not directly explaining every feature of this seventh-year law.

passages.title: Exodus 23:14-19
passages.section_title: What were Israel’s three yearly festivals meant to remember?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 Three times a year you are to celebrate a feast to Me. 15 You are to keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread as I commanded you: At the appointed time in the month of Abib you are to eat unleavened bread for seven days, because that was the month you came out of Egypt. No one may appear before Me empty-handed. 16 You are also to keep the Feast of Harvest with the firstfruits of the produce from what you sow in the field. And keep the Feast of Ingathering at the end of the year, when you gather your produce from the field. 17 Three times a year all your males are to appear before the Lord GOD. 18 You must not offer the blood of My sacrifices with anything leavened, nor may the fat of My feast remain until morning. 19 Bring the best of the firstfruits of your soil to the house of the LORD your God. You must not cook a young goat in its mother’s milk.
paragraphs: 14 Three times a year you are to celebrate a feast to Me. 15 You are to keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread as I commanded you: At the appointed time in the month of Abib you are to eat unleavened bread for seven days, because that was the month you came out of Egypt. No one may appear before Me empty-handed. 16 You are also to keep the Feast of Harvest with the firstfruits of the produce from what you sow in the field. And keep the Feast of Ingathering at the end of the year, when you gather your produce from the field. 17 Three times a year all your males are to appear before the Lord GOD.

18 You must not offer the blood of My sacrifices with anything leavened, nor may the fat of My feast remain until morning. 19 Bring the best of the firstfruits of your soil to the house of the LORD your God. You must not cook a young goat in its mother’s milk.

passages.context_html:
Israel’s year is to be shaped by worship and remembrance. The Feast of Unleavened Bread recalls the departure from Egypt. The Feast of Harvest brings the firstfruits of the crops, and the Feast of Ingathering comes as the year’s produce is gathered. The people are to acknowledge both the God who rescued them and the God who provides for them.

The later instructions in Exodus 34:18–26 identify the wheat-harvest celebration as the Feast of Weeks. John 7:2 uses the name Tabernacles for the festival associated with booths. The three annual appearances before the Lord are required of Israel’s males, and the worshiper must bring an offering.

The sacrifice must be handled as God directs: no leaven with its blood, no keeping the festival fat until morning, and the best firstfruits brought to the LORD’s house. The last instruction forbids cooking a young goat in its mother’s milk. The passage states that prohibition without explaining its origin.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The festivals are commonly understood as occasions for Israel to remember deliverance and acknowledge God’s provision. Wesley identifies the annual celebrations with Passover and Unleavened Bread, Pentecost, and Tabernacles. Each belongs to Israel’s worship through the year, rather than being a choice of unrelated religious events.

The goat-and-milk instruction has been understood differently. Rashi’s Jewish commentary takes its repetition in the Torah as prohibiting cooking meat with milk, eating the mixture and benefiting from it; he does not restrict the rule to a goat. Calvin relates it to proper sacrifice and the wrongness of using a mother’s milk to cook her young. Wesley raises the concern about cruelty too. These readings should be described on their own terms; the text itself does not state which explanation accounts for the rule.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The New Testament explicitly uses these festival themes to explain Christ and the life of His people. 1 Corinthians 5:6–8 calls Christ the sacrificed Passover lamb and uses unleavened bread to speak of sincerity and truth in place of malice and wickedness. 1 Corinthians 15:20–28 calls the risen Christ the firstfruits of those who have died, with the resurrection of those who belong to Him still to follow. The harvest image points to the resurrection of the people who belong to Him.

Acts 2:1–4 places the coming of the Spirit at Pentecost. At the Feast of Tabernacles, Jesus calls the thirsty to come to Him, and John explains that He is speaking about the Spirit (John 7:37–39). Zechariah 14:16–19 also pictures people from the nations worshiping the LORD as King at that feast. Together these connections widen the view from Israel’s calendar to Christ, resurrection, the gift of the Spirit and worship among the nations.

passages.title: Exodus 23:20-33
passages.section_title: How would God lead Israel into the land He promised?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 20 Behold, I am sending an angel before you to protect you along the way and to bring you to the place I have prepared. 21 Pay attention to him and listen to his voice; do not defy him, for he will not forgive rebellion, since My Name is in him. 22 But if you will listen carefully to his voice and do everything I say, I will be an enemy to your enemies and a foe to your foes. 23 For My angel will go before you and bring you into the land of the Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Canaanites, Hivites, and Jebusites, and I will annihilate them. 24 You must not bow down to their gods or serve them or follow their practices. Instead, you are to demolish them and smash their sacred stones to pieces. 25 So you shall serve the LORD your God, and He will bless your bread and your water. And I will take away sickness from among you. 26 No woman in your land will miscarry or be barren; I will fulfill the number of your days. 27 I will send My terror ahead of you and throw into confusion every nation you encounter. I will make all your enemies turn and run. 28 I will send the hornet before you to drive the Hivites and Canaanites and Hittites out of your way. 29 I will not drive them out before you in a single year; otherwise the land would become desolate and wild animals would multiply against you. 30 Little by little I will drive them out ahead of you, until you become fruitful and possess the land. 31 And I will establish your borders from the Red Sea to the Sea of the Philistines, and from the desert to the Euphrates. For I will deliver the inhabitants into your hand, and you will drive them out before you. 32 You shall make no covenant with them or with their gods. 33 They must not remain in your land, lest they cause you to sin against Me. For if you serve their gods, it will surely be a snare to you.”

And I will take away sickness from among you. 26 No woman in your land will miscarry or be barren; I will fulfill the number of your days.

27 I will send My terror ahead of you and throw into confusion every nation you encounter. I will make all your enemies turn and run. 28 I will send the hornet before you to drive the Hivites and Canaanites and Hittites out of your way. 29 I will not drive them out before you in a single year; otherwise the land would become desolate and wild animals would multiply against you. 30 Little by little I will drive them out ahead of you, until you become fruitful and possess the land.

31 And I will establish your borders from the Red Sea to the Sea of the Philistines, and from the desert to the Euphrates. For I will deliver the inhabitants into your hand, and you will drive them out before you. 32 You shall make no covenant with them or with their gods. 33 They must not remain in your land, lest they cause you to sin against Me. For if you serve their gods, it will surely be a snare to you.”

passages.context_html:
God promises an angel to guard Israel and bring them to the place He has prepared. The people must listen and refuse rebellion because God’s name is in His messenger. Following that voice and doing what God says are presented together. The promise of guidance comes with a serious demand for obedience.

Israel must reject the gods and worship practices of the land’s peoples. Blessings on food, water, health, childbirth and length of life are promised within this covenant setting. These promises address the people’s life in the land; they should not be turned into a diagnosis of an individual believer’s sickness or infertility.

God will act ahead of Israel, but the land will not be emptied in a single year. He gives the reason: rapid abandonment would leave it desolate and allow wild animals to multiply. The gradual pace is part of the promised care. The borders reach from the Red Sea to the Sea of the Philistines and from the desert to the Euphrates. The closing warning concerns the danger of being drawn into the worship of other gods through the relationships Israel forms.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Interpreters differ over the angel’s identity. Calvin and Wesley understand Him as the Son before His human birth. They connect the divine name and authority with Paul’s warning that Israel tested Christ in the wilderness (1 Corinthians 10:9). Rashi instead describes an angelic messenger acting under God’s name and commission, without independent authority to pardon. The difference is whether the messenger is Himself divine or bears the authority of the God who sent him.

The hornet in verse 28 has also been read literally or as an image of the terror that drives the inhabitants away. Calvin and Wesley understand actual hornets; Gill considers both possibilities and favors the literal reading. In either case, the promise emphasizes God’s action ahead of the people and His deliberate pace, rather than Israel succeeding through its own strength alone.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

deeper_study.title: Who is The Angel of the Lord?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The New Testament treats Israel’s wilderness history as a warning for people who have received great gifts from God. 1 Corinthians 10:1–13 recalls the cloud, sea, food and water, yet warns that many still fell through disobedience. Paul specifically speaks of testing Christ. That establishes a connection with Christ in the wilderness story, while the precise identity of this angel remains the interpretive question described above.

Hebrews 3:12–19 likewise calls its readers to keep trusting God and encourage one another rather than become hardened by sin. The warning and the promise belong together: the God who leads His people calls for a lasting response of faith. This is the larger biblical connection, rather than a claim that every feature of Israel’s conquest predicts a separate event in Christian life.

passages.title: Exodus 24:1-11
passages.section_title: How did Israel enter the covenant with God?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then the LORD said to Moses, “Come up to the LORD—you and Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of Israel’s elders—and you are to worship at a distance. 2 Moses alone shall approach the LORD, but the others must not come near. And the people may not go up with him.” 3 When Moses came and told the people all the words and ordinances of the LORD, they all responded with one voice: “All the words that the LORD has spoken, we will do.” 4 And Moses wrote down all the words of the LORD. Early the next morning he got up and built an altar at the base of the mountain, along with twelve pillars for the twelve tribes of Israel. 5 Then he sent out some young men of Israel, and they offered burnt offerings and sacrificed young bulls as peace offerings to the LORD. 6 Moses took half of the blood and put it in bowls, and the other half he splattered on the altar. 7 Then he took the Book of the Covenant and read it to the people, who replied, “All that the LORD has spoken we will do, and we will be obedient.” 8 So Moses took the blood, splattered it on the people, and said, “This is the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you in accordance with all these words.” 9 Then Moses went up with Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel, 10 and they saw the God of Israel. Under His feet was a work like a pavement made of sapphire, as clear as the sky itself. 11 But God did not lay His hand on the nobles of Israel; they saw Him, and they ate and drank.
paragraphs: 1 Then the LORD said to Moses, “Come up to the LORD—you and Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of Israel’s elders—and you are to worship at a distance. 2 Moses alone shall approach the LORD, but the others must not come near. And the people may not go up with him.”

3 When Moses came and told the people all the words and ordinances of the LORD, they all responded with one voice: “All the words that the LORD has spoken, we will do.” 4 And Moses wrote down all the words of the LORD. Early the next morning he got up and built an altar at the base of the mountain, along with twelve pillars for the twelve tribes of Israel. 5 Then he sent out some young men of Israel, and they offered burnt offerings and sacrificed young bulls as peace offerings to the LORD.

6 Moses took half of the blood and put it in bowls, and the other half he splattered on the altar. 7 Then he took the Book of the Covenant and read it to the people, who replied, “All that the LORD has spoken we will do, and we will be obedient.” 8 So Moses took the blood, splattered it on the people, and said, “This is the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you in accordance with all these words.”

9 Then Moses went up with Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel, 10 and they saw the God of Israel. Under His feet was a work like a pavement made of sapphire, as clear as the sky itself. 11 But God did not lay His hand on the nobles of Israel; they saw Him, and they ate and drank.

passages.context_html:
After giving the covenant instructions, God calls Moses, Aaron, Aaron’s sons Nadab and Abihu, and seventy elders to come up and worship. Moses alone may approach more closely. Before the ascent described in verse 9, he tells the people God’s words, writes them down and reads the Book of the Covenant aloud. The people twice declare their intention to obey.

The altar and twelve pillars bring the whole nation into view: the pillars stand for Israel’s twelve tribes. Young men offer burnt offerings and peace offerings. Moses divides the blood between bowls and the altar, then splatters blood on the people and identifies it as the blood of the covenant. The people’s commitment is made in response to words they have heard, and the sacrifice marks the solemn establishment of that relationship.

Moses and the named leaders then go up. The text says they see the God of Israel, describing beneath His feet something like a sapphire pavement, clear as the sky. God does not strike them down; they eat and drink in His presence. The scene combines the seriousness of approaching God with the extraordinary welcome He grants.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The sacrifice, blood and meal are generally understood as the establishment and celebration of the covenant. Wesley emphasizes the commitments of God and the people, and understands the meal as fellowship with God. Calvin likewise describes a sacrificial banquet and stresses that these leaders approach safely because God Himself has called them.

Interpreters differ over the form of the sight granted to the leaders. Calvin understands an appearance of God’s glory suited to what human beings can bear, without a description of God’s full being. Wesley also speaks of a glimpse of glory and understands the description as focusing on the brightness beneath Him. Gill understands a visible appearance of the Son in human form before His birth. These readings take seriously both this passage’s statement that they saw God and the later statement that God is made known through His Son (John 1:18); they differ over what form the encounter took.

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 9:11–24 explicitly recalls Moses proclaiming the commandments and sprinkling the covenant blood. It then explains the greater work of Christ: He enters God’s presence on our behalf through His own blood, secures eternal redemption and cleanses the conscience so that people may serve the living God. His death also redeems transgressions committed under the first covenant, and those called receive the promised eternal inheritance.

Jesus uses the covenant-blood language at the meal before His death. In Matthew 26:26–29, He speaks of His blood poured out for the forgiveness of sins; Luke 22:14–20 calls the cup the new covenant in His blood. The connection reaches beyond the similarity of two ceremonies. The Son gives Himself to bring people into a relationship with God grounded in His completed sacrifice.

passages.title: Exodus 24:12-18
passages.section_title: Why did Moses go further into the cloud?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 Then the LORD said to Moses, “Come up to Me on the mountain and stay here, so that I may give you the tablets of stone, with the law and commandments I have written for their instruction.” 13 So Moses set out with Joshua his attendant and went up on the mountain of God. 14 And he said to the elders, “Wait here for us until we return to you. Aaron and Hur are here with you. Whoever has a dispute can go to them.” 15 When Moses went up on the mountain, the cloud covered it, 16 and the glory of the LORD settled on Mount Sinai. For six days the cloud covered it, and on the seventh day the LORD called to Moses from within the cloud. 17 And the sight of the glory of the LORD was like a consuming fire on the mountaintop in the eyes of the Israelites. 18 Moses entered the cloud as he went up on the mountain, and he remained on the mountain forty days and forty nights.
paragraphs: 12 Then the LORD said to Moses, “Come up to Me on the mountain and stay here, so that I may give you the tablets of stone, with the law and commandments I have written for their instruction.” 13 So Moses set out with Joshua his attendant and went up on the mountain of God. 14 And he said to the elders, “Wait here for us until we return to you. Aaron and Hur are here with you. Whoever has a dispute can go to them.”

15 When Moses went up on the mountain, the cloud covered it, 16 and the glory of the LORD settled on Mount Sinai. For six days the cloud covered it, and on the seventh day the LORD called to Moses from within the cloud. 17 And the sight of the glory of the LORD was like a consuming fire on the mountaintop in the eyes of the Israelites. 18 Moses entered the cloud as he went up on the mountain, and he remained on the mountain forty days and forty nights.

passages.context_html:
God calls Moses to remain on the mountain and receive stone tablets bearing the law and commandments for Israel’s instruction. Moses sets out with Joshua as his attendant, while Aaron and Hur are available to hear disputes among the people. The work of caring for the community continues during his absence.

The cloud covers the mountain for six days. On the seventh day, God calls Moses from within it. The glory of the LORD looks like a consuming fire to the Israelites, and Moses enters the cloud at God’s invitation. He remains on the mountain forty days and forty nights. That extended absence prepares for both the sanctuary instructions in the following chapters and the people’s response while he is away.

The Hebrew word for glory here is כָּבוֹד, kavod (kah-VOHD). It can mean honor or splendor; here it describes the visible display of God’s presence (Brown–Driver–Briggs). The cloud, fire and summons make clear that Moses is approaching the God who has spoken to Israel.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The passage is usually read as confirming Moses’ special responsibility to receive instruction from God. Wesley sees the cloud as both revealing God’s presence and concealing what human beings cannot fully grasp. Calvin emphasizes that the visible glory also gives the people assurance about the source of the law Moses receives. The scene calls for trust in God’s word and reverence before Him.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 12:18–29 returns to Sinai’s fire and fear, then describes believers coming to heavenly Zion and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant. It ends by calling for gratitude, reverence and faithful attention to the God who speaks. Access through Christ brings confidence while preserving the seriousness of listening to God.

The tablets also belong to a larger movement in the Bible. 2 Corinthians 3:1–6 describes Christ’s people as a letter written by the Spirit of the living God on human hearts, rather than on stone tablets. God’s purpose includes His word taking effect within His people, giving them life through the Spirit. The law received on the mountain is part of the story that leads to that new-covenant work.

passages.title: Exodus 25:1-9
passages.section_title: Why did God ask Israel to build a sanctuary?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then the LORD said to Moses, 2 “Tell the Israelites to bring Me an offering. You are to receive My offering from every man whose heart compels him. 3 This is the offering you are to accept from them: gold, silver, and bronze; 4 blue, purple, and scarlet yarn; fine linen and goat hair; 5 ram skins dyed red and fine leather; acacia wood; 6 olive oil for the light; spices for the anointing oil and for the fragrant incense; 7 and onyx stones and gemstones to be mounted on the ephod and breastpiece. 8 And they are to make a sanctuary for Me, so that I may dwell among them. 9 You must make the tabernacle and design all its furnishings according to the pattern I show you.
paragraphs: 1 Then the LORD said to Moses, 2 “Tell the Israelites to bring Me an offering. You are to receive My offering from every man whose heart compels him. 3 This is the offering you are to accept from them: gold, silver, and bronze; 4 blue, purple, and scarlet yarn; fine linen and goat hair; 5 ram skins dyed red and fine leather; acacia wood; 6 olive oil for the light; spices for the anointing oil and for the fragrant incense; 7 and onyx stones and gemstones to be mounted on the ephod and breastpiece.
8 And they are to make a sanctuary for Me, so that I may dwell among them. 9 You must make the tabernacle and design all its furnishings according to the pattern I show you.

passages.context_html:
From within the cloud, God begins giving Moses instructions for the sanctuary and its furnishings. The materials are to come from Israelites whose hearts move them to give. The list includes valuable metals, fabric, leather, wood, oil, spices and stones, each serving the work God is about to describe.

The purpose is stated before the building details: God will dwell among His people. The Hebrew verb שָׁכַן, shakan (shah-KAHN), means to settle, remain or dwell (Brown–Driver–Briggs). Israel is to have a holy place where God makes His presence known among them. The word sanctuary describes a sacred place set apart to Him (Brown–Driver–Briggs).

The willing offering and the prescribed design belong together. The people freely supply the materials, while God shows Moses the pattern for what is to be made. The tabernacle is part of His provision for life with the people He has rescued.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The usual reading is that God is giving Israel an appointed place of worship and a visible assurance of His presence. Wesley emphasizes both willing giving and God’s presence among the people without His being confined to the structure. That distinction is also expressed in 1 Kings 8:27–30: even the heavens cannot contain God, yet He hears His people’s prayers.
passages.current_position_html: As explained in The True Church According to Jesus, God now dwells in His people through His Spirit. That study connects His presence in the tabernacle with His presence in believers, calling for lives made holy by His indwelling.

Worship as the Early Church Knew It

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 8:1–6 explicitly connects the sanctuary’s pattern with the heavenly reality and the greater ministry of Jesus. The earthly priests serve within a copy and shadow; Jesus ministers in the true sanctuary and mediates a better covenant.

God dwelling with His people becomes a central theme in the New Testament. John 1:14–18 describes the Word becoming flesh, dwelling among us and revealing God’s glory. Its verb for dwelling also carries the sense of living in a tent (Thayer). Ephesians 2:19–22 then describes people joined together in Christ as God’s dwelling through the Spirit. Finally, Revelation 21:1–4 announces God dwelling with His people in a world where death and grief are gone. The sanctuary’s stated purpose belongs within that larger story of God bringing people into life with Him.

passages.title: Exodus 25:10-16
passages.section_title: Why was the covenant testimony placed in an ark?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 And they are to construct an ark of acacia wood, two and a half cubits long, a cubit and a half wide, and a cubit and a half high. 11 Overlay it with pure gold both inside and out, and make a gold molding around it. 12 Cast four gold rings for it and fasten them to its four feet, two rings on one side and two on the other. 13 And make poles of acacia wood and overlay them with gold. 14 Insert the poles into the rings on the sides of the ark, in order to carry it. 15 The poles are to remain in the rings of the ark; they must not be removed. 16 And place inside the ark the Testimony, which I will give you.
paragraphs: 10 And they are to construct an ark of acacia wood, two and a half cubits long, a cubit and a half wide, and a cubit and a half high. 11 Overlay it with pure gold both inside and out, and make a gold molding around it. 12 Cast four gold rings for it and fasten them to its four feet, two rings on one side and two on the other.

13 And make poles of acacia wood and overlay them with gold. 14 Insert the poles into the rings on the sides of the ark, in order to carry it. 15 The poles are to remain in the rings of the ark; they must not be removed. 16 And place inside the ark the Testimony, which I will give you.

passages.context_html:
The first furnishing described is an ark—a chest made from acacia wood and overlaid inside and outside with gold. Its gold rings and carrying poles allow it to travel with Israel. The poles must stay in place. The later sanctuary instructions will place the ark in its innermost room.

God tells Moses to put the Testimony inside it. This is the covenant record He will give, the stone tablets already promised in Exodus 24:12. The chest’s central purpose is therefore connected to God’s words and His covenant with Israel. The instructions for its gold covering and the place of meeting follow in verses 17–22.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Calvin emphasize the ark as the appointed place for the covenant tablets and a sign of the honor due God’s word. Calvin cautions against giving every dimension a hidden spiritual meaning.

Gill draws more detailed parallels with Christ, relating the wood and gold to His enduring person and glory. These are devotional readings of the materials. They should be distinguished from the purpose the passage expressly states: the ark is to hold the Testimony God gives Moses.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 9:1–14 recalls the ark, its contents and the arrangement of the sanctuary before explaining Christ’s greater priestly work. The old arrangements taught the seriousness of approaching God, while Christ’s offering cleanses the conscience for service to the living God.

There is also a wider covenant connection. The stone record placed in the ark belongs to the first covenant; Hebrews 8:7–13 speaks of God’s promise to write His laws in people’s minds and hearts, joined with knowing Him and receiving forgiveness. This carries the theme from preserving the covenant words to their inward effect in the people God brings near.

passages.title: Exodus 25:17-22
passages.section_title: What was the mercy seat, and why did it matter?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 And you are to construct a mercy seat of pure gold, two and a half cubits long and a cubit and a half wide. 18 Make two cherubim of hammered gold at the ends of the mercy seat, 19 one cherub on one end and one on the other, all made from one piece of gold. 20 And the cherubim are to have wings that spread upward, overshadowing the mercy seat. The cherubim are to face each other, looking toward the mercy seat. 21 Set the mercy seat atop the ark and put the Testimony that I will give you into the ark. 22 And I will meet with you there above the mercy seat, between the two cherubim that are over the ark of the Testimony; I will speak with you about all that I command you regarding the Israelites.
paragraphs: 17 And you are to construct a mercy seat of pure gold, two and a half cubits long and a cubit and a half wide. 18 Make two cherubim of hammered gold at the ends of the mercy seat, 19 one cherub on one end and one on the other, all made from one piece of gold. 20 And the cherubim are to have wings that spread upward, overshadowing the mercy seat. The cherubim are to face each other, looking toward the mercy seat.

21 Set the mercy seat atop the ark and put the Testimony that I will give you into the ark. 22 And I will meet with you there above the mercy seat, between the two cherubim that are over the ark of the Testimony; I will speak with you about all that I command you regarding the Israelites.

passages.context_html:
The mercy seat is the pure-gold covering set above the ark, matching its length and width. Two gold cherubim are made as part of it, facing one another with their faces turned toward it and their wings spread above it. The covenant Testimony is placed inside the ark beneath it.

God promises to meet Moses there and speak from above the mercy seat, between the cherubim. The place is associated with His presence, His commands and the covenant relationship. The later instructions in Leviticus 16:11–17 add its role on the Day of Atonement, when the high priest brings incense and sacrificial blood into the Most Holy Place.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian commentators commonly connect the mercy seat with Christ’s work of atonement—His dealing with sin so that people can be brought near to God. Wesley and Calvin both make that connection. They understand the covenant testimony and its covering together: the God whose law exposes sin also provides the way for mercy. The cherubim attend His presence; this paragraph does not give a ranking of heavenly beings.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 9:5–14 names the mercy seat and then explains the greater cleansing accomplished through Christ’s own blood. The connection is also reflected in the Greek word ἱλαστήριον, hilasterion (hee-lahs-TAY-ree-on). Thayer’s lexicon explains its use for the ark’s atonement covering in Hebrews 9:5 and for the place or means of atonement in Romans 3:25. The BSB renders the latter as Christ being presented as an atoning sacrifice. The word connection helps explain why Christian readers see this furnishing pointing toward His saving work.

1 John 4:7–12 adds the purpose behind that provision: God’s love is shown in sending His Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and those who receive that love are called to love one another. Atonement begins with God’s loving action and leads to a people who reflect His love.

passages.title: Exodus 25:23-30
passages.section_title: Why was bread kept before God?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 23 You are also to make a table of acacia wood two cubits long, a cubit wide, and a cubit and a half high. 24 Overlay it with pure gold and make a gold molding around it. 25 And make a rim around it a handbreadth wide and put a gold molding on the rim. 26 Make four gold rings for the table and fasten them to the four corners at its four legs. 27 The rings are to be close to the rim, to serve as holders for the poles used to carry the table. 28 Make the poles of acacia wood and overlay them with gold, so that the table may be carried with them. 29 You are also to make the plates and dishes, as well as the pitchers and bowls for pouring drink offerings. Make them out of pure gold. 30 And place the Bread of the Presence on the table before Me at all times.
paragraphs: 23 You are also to make a table of acacia wood two cubits long, a cubit wide, and a cubit and a half high. 24 Overlay it with pure gold and make a gold molding around it. 25 And make a rim around it a handbreadth wide and put a gold molding on the rim. 26 Make four gold rings for the table and fasten them to the four corners at its four legs. 27 The rings are to be close to the rim, to serve as holders for the poles used to carry the table. 28 Make the poles of acacia wood and overlay them with gold, so that the table may be carried with them.

29 You are also to make the plates and dishes, as well as the pitchers and bowls for pouring drink offerings. Make them out of pure gold. 30 And place the Bread of the Presence on the table before Me at all times.

passages.context_html:
The next furnishing is a gold-covered acacia table, with rings and poles so it too can be carried. Gold plates, dishes, pitchers and bowls accompany it. God directs that the Bread of the Presence remain on the table before Him continually.

Leviticus 24:5–9 later explains the practice: twelve loaves are arranged in two rows, replaced every Sabbath and eaten by Aaron and his sons in a holy place. The bread is presented on behalf of Israel. It is an ongoing offering within the covenant worship, with God also providing it as a holy portion for the priests.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The bread is generally understood as a continuing presentation before God, expressing Israel’s relationship with Him. Wesley understands the twelve loaves as representing the tribes and the offering as an acknowledgment of God’s daily provision and fellowship. Calvin similarly emphasizes that the people’s own food comes from God and is to be received in His presence with gratitude. Neither understands the offering as feeding a God who needs human food.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Wesley also reads the bread as a picture of the spiritual provision given through Christ. That is a thematic parallel rather than an explicit New Testament identification of this table with Jesus. In John 6:26–35, Jesus speaks directly about manna and presents Himself as the bread of life who gives lasting life to those who come to Him. God’s provision reaches beyond food that sustains the body to the Son who gives life to the world.

That wider theme also shapes ordinary life. 1 Timothy 6:17–19 tells the wealthy to place their hope in the God who provides and to become generous and ready to share. Acknowledging His gifts is meant to shape how His people use them.

passages.title: Exodus 25:31-40
passages.section_title: What did the seven lamps bring to the sanctuary?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 31 Then you are to make a lampstand of pure, hammered gold. It shall be made of one piece, including its base and shaft, its cups, and its buds and petals. 32 Six branches are to extend from the sides of the lampstand—three on one side and three on the other. 33 There are to be three cups shaped like almond blossoms on the first branch, each with buds and petals, three on the next branch, and the same for all six branches that extend from the lampstand. 34 And on the lampstand there shall be four cups shaped like almond blossoms with buds and petals. 35 For the six branches that extend from the lampstand, a bud must be under the first pair of branches, a bud under the second pair, and a bud under the third pair. 36 The buds and branches are to be all of one piece with the lampstand, hammered out of pure gold. 37 Make seven lamps and set them up on the lampstand so that they illuminate the area in front of it. 38 The wick trimmers and their trays must be of pure gold. 39 The lampstand and all these utensils shall be made from a talent of pure gold. 40 See to it that you make everything according to the pattern shown you on the mountain.

It shall be made of one piece, including its base and shaft, its cups, and its buds and petals. 32 Six branches are to extend from the sides of the lampstand—three on one side and three on the other. 33 There are to be three cups shaped like almond blossoms on the first branch, each with buds and petals, three on the next branch, and the same for all six branches that extend from the lampstand. 34 And on the lampstand there shall be four cups shaped like almond blossoms with buds and petals. 35 For the six branches that extend from the lampstand, a bud must be under the first pair of branches, a bud under the second pair, and a bud under the third pair. 36 The buds and branches are to be all of one piece with the lampstand, hammered out of pure gold.

37 Make seven lamps and set them up on the lampstand so that they illuminate the area in front of it. 38 The wick trimmers and their trays must be of pure gold. 39 The lampstand and all these utensils shall be made from a talent of pure gold. 40 See to it that you make everything according to the pattern shown you on the mountain.

passages.context_html:
The lampstand is made from a single piece of hammered gold, with six branches extending from a central shaft. Cups, buds and petals shaped like almond blossoms give it a branching, flowering form. Its seven lamps are arranged to light the space in front of it; the wick trimmers and trays are also gold.

The instructions end by repeating the requirement to follow the pattern shown to Moses. Leviticus 24:1–4 later describes the people supplying pure olive oil and Aaron tending the lamps from evening until morning before the LORD. Their light is part of the ongoing service in the Holy Place.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The lampstand’s practical purpose is to provide light for the sanctuary. Christian commentators also see in that light a picture of the instruction God gives His people. Wesley connects it with God’s word, while Calvin emphasizes God enlightening His people by His teaching and Spirit. These are theological readings of the furnishing, alongside its stated use as a light.

passages.god_plan_html:
The lampstand image appears again in Zechariah 4:1–14, where the message to Zerubbabel is that God’s work is accomplished by His Spirit. The later vision adds details of its own, but it carries forward the theme of light and provision coming from God.

In Revelation 1:12–20, the risen Christ stands among seven golden lampstands, which He identifies as seven churches. These are separate lampstands, rather than a claim that John sees this one seven-branched furnishing. The image places the churches’ life and witness in relation to their present Lord. Jesus Himself is the light of the world (John 8:12); and in the final vision, God’s glory gives the city light and the Lamb is its lamp (Revelation 21:22–27). The theme reaches from light within Israel’s sanctuary to God’s people living in His light.

passages.title: Exodus 26:1-6
passages.section_title: How did the linen curtains form one tabernacle?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 “You are to construct the tabernacle itself with ten curtains of finely spun linen, each with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and cherubim skillfully worked into them. 2 Each curtain shall be twenty-eight cubits long and four cubits wide —all curtains the same size. 3 Five of the curtains are to be joined together, and the other five joined as well. 4 Make loops of blue material on the edge of the end curtain in the first set, and do the same for the end curtain in the second set. 5 Make fifty loops on one curtain and fifty loops on the end curtain of the second set, so that the loops line up opposite one another. 6 Make fifty gold clasps as well, and join the curtains together with the clasps, so that the tabernacle will be a unit.
paragraphs: 1 “You are to construct the tabernacle itself with ten curtains of finely spun linen, each with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and cherubim skillfully worked into them. 2 Each curtain shall be twenty-eight cubits long and four cubits wide —all curtains the same size. 3 Five of the curtains are to be joined together, and the other five joined as well.

4 Make loops of blue material on the edge of the end curtain in the first set, and do the same for the end curtain in the second set. 5 Make fifty loops on one curtain and fifty loops on the end curtain of the second set, so that the loops line up opposite one another. 6 Make fifty gold clasps as well, and join the curtains together with the clasps, so that the tabernacle will be a unit.

passages.context_html:
After describing the principal furnishings, God gives the instructions for the tent itself. Ten linen curtains are made with blue, purple and scarlet yarn and worked with cherubim. Their equal dimensions allow them to fit together in an ordered design.

Five curtains are joined into each of two sets. Matching blue loops along their edges receive fifty gold clasps, joining the two sets into one tabernacle. The richly worked fabric forms the inner covering, with other layers to be placed over it in the next instructions. The repeated concern is that the separate pieces become one connected structure.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The curtains are commonly read first as the fabric construction of God’s sanctuary, with their skilled work expressing the care given to His dwelling. Christian commentators also draw spiritual comparisons. Wesley connects the joined curtains with the unity of Christ’s churches; Calvin understands the sanctuary’s beauty as pointing toward the spiritual gifts and holiness of God’s people, while cautioning against assigning a secret meaning to every hook and loop.

passages.god_plan_html:
Wesley’s comparison with the church is a parallel, rather than an explicit New Testament explanation of these clasps. It is supported by the larger theme in Ephesians 2:11–22: Christ brings together people once divided, reconciles them to God and builds them into one dwelling through the Spirit.

The point of that connection is the shared life God creates. The joined curtains form one sanctuary; in the New Testament, people from different backgrounds belong to one household in Christ.

passages.title: Exodus 26:7-14
passages.section_title: What covered the tabernacle’s inner curtains?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 You are to make curtains of goat hair for the tent over the tabernacle—eleven curtains in all. 8 Each of the eleven curtains is to be the same size—thirty cubits long and four cubits wide. 9 Join five of the curtains into one set and the other six into another. Then fold the sixth curtain over double at the front of the tent. 10 Make fifty loops along the edge of the end curtain in the first set, and fifty loops along the edge of the corresponding curtain in the second set. 11 Make fifty bronze clasps and put them through the loops to join the tent together as a unit. 12 As for the overlap that remains of the tent curtains, the half curtain that is left over shall hang down over the back of the tabernacle. 13 And the tent curtains will be a cubit longer on either side, and the excess will hang over the sides of the tabernacle to cover it. 14 Also make a covering for the tent out of ram skins dyed red, and over that a covering of fine leather.
paragraphs: 7 You are to make curtains of goat hair for the tent over the tabernacle—eleven curtains in all. 8 Each of the eleven curtains is to be the same size—thirty cubits long and four cubits wide. 9 Join five of the curtains into one set and the other six into another. Then fold the sixth curtain over double at the front of the tent. 10 Make fifty loops along the edge of the end curtain in the first set, and fifty loops along the edge of the corresponding curtain in the second set. 11 Make fifty bronze clasps and put them through the loops to join the tent together as a unit.

12 As for the overlap that remains of the tent curtains, the half curtain that is left over shall hang down over the back of the tabernacle. 13 And the tent curtains will be a cubit longer on either side, and the excess will hang over the sides of the tabernacle to cover it. 14 Also make a covering for the tent out of ram skins dyed red, and over that a covering of fine leather.

passages.context_html:
Eleven curtains of goat hair form a tent over the linen tabernacle. They are longer than the inner curtains and are joined into sets of five and six, with the sixth folded double at the front. Bronze clasps join the sets. The extra material hangs over the back and sides to cover the structure beneath.

Above these curtains are coverings of ram skins dyed red and fine leather. The different layers belong to the tent’s construction and protection. The BSB’s fine leather translates a Hebrew term whose exact material or animal source is uncertain; Brown–Driver–Briggs records several proposals. The instructions do not require us to settle on a particular species to understand how the layers cover the tabernacle.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Readers generally recognize these as the sanctuary’s outer coverings. They differ over spiritual meanings assigned to the materials. Gill sees the protective layers as illustrations of God’s care for His people and connects the covering with Christ’s righteousness and blood. Calvin questions the practice of interpreting the ram skins as Christ’s blood while having no sound explanation for every other layer. His emphasis is restraint in drawing meanings that the text does not state. These are different approaches among individual Christian commentators, not competing descriptions of how the tent was assembled.

passages.title: Exodus 26:15-30
passages.section_title: What held the tabernacle upright and together?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 You are to construct upright frames of acacia wood for the tabernacle. 16 Each frame is to be ten cubits long and a cubit and a half wide. 17 Two tenons must be connected to each other for each frame. Make all the frames of the tabernacle in this way. 18 Construct twenty frames for the south side of the tabernacle, 19 with forty silver bases under the twenty frames—two bases for each frame, one under each tenon. 20 For the second side of the tabernacle, the north side, make twenty frames 21 and forty silver bases—two bases under each frame. 22 Make six frames for the rear of the tabernacle, the west side, 23 and two frames for the two back corners of the tabernacle, 24 coupled together from bottom to top and fitted into a single ring. These will serve as the two corners. 25 So there are to be eight frames and sixteen silver bases—two under each frame. 26 You are also to make five crossbars of acacia wood for the frames on one side of the tabernacle, 27 five for those on the other side, and five for those on the rear side of the tabernacle, to the west. 28 The central crossbar in the middle of the frames shall extend from one end to the other. 29 Overlay the frames with gold and make gold rings to hold the crossbars. Also overlay the crossbars with gold. 30 So you are to set up the tabernacle according to the pattern shown you on the mountain.
paragraphs: 15 You are to construct upright frames of acacia wood for the tabernacle. 16 Each frame is to be ten cubits long and a cubit and a half wide. 17 Two tenons must be connected to each other for each frame. Make all the frames of the tabernacle in this way. 18 Construct twenty frames for the south side of the tabernacle, 19 with forty silver bases under the twenty frames—two bases for each frame, one under each tenon. 20 For the second side of the tabernacle, the north side, make twenty frames 21 and forty silver bases—two bases under each frame.

22 Make six frames for the rear of the tabernacle, the west side, 23 and two frames for the two back corners of the tabernacle, 24 coupled together from bottom to top and fitted into a single ring. These will serve as the two corners. 25 So there are to be eight frames and sixteen silver bases—two under each frame.

26 You are also to make five crossbars of acacia wood for the frames on one side of the tabernacle, 27 five for those on the other side, and five for those on the rear side of the tabernacle, to the west. 28 The central crossbar in the middle of the frames shall extend from one end to the other. 29 Overlay the frames with gold and make gold rings to hold the crossbars. Also overlay the crossbars with gold. 30 So you are to set up the tabernacle according to the pattern shown you on the mountain.

passages.context_html:
The acacia frames provide the upright support for the coverings. Each has two projecting tenons—pieces that fit into the silver bases below. Twenty frames stand on each of the north and south sides. The rear is closed by six frames and two corner frames, with the corner connections joining the structure together.

Gold-covered crossbars pass through gold rings to hold the frames in place, with the central bar extending from end to end. The instructions combine separate supports into a stable structure that can be set up according to the pattern shown to Moses.

Exodus 38:25–28 later identifies the source of the silver: the offering from those counted in Israel. It provides one hundred bases for the sanctuary and inner veil. Exodus 30:12–16 calls that collection atonement money, with the same half-shekel amount required of rich and poor.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The frames, bases and bars are generally understood as the supporting structure for the tent. Gill specifically connects the silver bases with the census collection described in Exodus 38. Calvin stresses following God’s pattern and cautions that the two bases under each frame should not be assigned speculative identities, such as two covenants or two natures of Christ.

passages.god_plan_html:
The use of the atonement collection for the sanctuary’s bases provides a comparison with the wider biblical themes of redemption and foundation. 1 Peter 1:17–21 explicitly says that believers are redeemed through Christ’s precious blood, rather than perishable silver or gold. The saving provision God gives through His Son reaches beyond a monetary offering.

1 Corinthians 3:10–15 also uses a building image, identifying Jesus Christ as the foundation and calling for care in how people build upon Him. These are broader biblical connections, not claims that Peter or Paul directly interprets each silver base. They direct attention to the one on whom God’s people depend and to the responsibility of the work built upon Him.

passages.title: Exodus 26:31-35
passages.section_title: What did the inner veil separate?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 31 Make a veil of blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and finely spun linen, with cherubim skillfully worked into it. 32 Hang it with gold hooks on four posts of acacia wood, overlaid with gold and standing on four silver bases. 33 And hang the veil from the clasps and place the ark of the Testimony behind the veil. So the veil will separate the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place. 34 Put the mercy seat on the ark of the Testimony in the Most Holy Place. 35 And place the table outside the veil on the north side of the tabernacle, and put the lampstand opposite the table, on the south side.
paragraphs: 31 Make a veil of blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and finely spun linen, with cherubim skillfully worked into it. 32 Hang it with gold hooks on four posts of acacia wood, overlaid with gold and standing on four silver bases. 33 And hang the veil from the clasps and place the ark of the Testimony behind the veil. So the veil will separate the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place.

34 Put the mercy seat on the ark of the Testimony in the Most Holy Place. 35 And place the table outside the veil on the north side of the tabernacle, and put the lampstand opposite the table, on the south side.

passages.context_html:
A veil made from the colored yarn and fine linen, worked with cherubim, divides the sanctuary into two rooms. Four gold-covered acacia posts on silver bases support it. The ark and mercy seat are placed behind it in the Most Holy Place.

The table remains outside the veil on the north side of the Holy Place, with the lampstand opposite it to the south. The separation orders the approach to God’s presence. Hebrews 9:6–7 describes the distinction: priests serve regularly in the first room, while the high priest alone enters the second on the yearly occasion, bringing sacrificial blood.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian commentators commonly understand the veil as marking the restricted approach under the first covenant and pointing toward the access Christ opens. Wesley, Calvin and Gill connect it with the New Testament’s account of Christ. Gill particularly emphasizes the connection with His body in Hebrews 10:20. Their further explanations of individual colors or materials go beyond that explicit connection.
passages.current_position_html: As explained in The True Church According to Jesus, Christ’s torn veil means that every believer now has direct access to God and a calling to minister. That existing conclusion guides our application here: access to God through Christ is shared by His people.
