passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 10:19–25 directly speaks of the new and living way into the Most Holy Place through Jesus’ blood and the curtain of His body. Believers are called to draw near in faith, hold to their hope and encourage one another in love and good deeds. The access Christ gives is meant to shape a faithful, caring community.

Matthew 27:45–54 reports the later temple’s veil being torn from top to bottom at Jesus’ death. It is the temple veil in that account, rather than the original wilderness fabric. Read alongside Hebrews, the scene brings the significance of the separation into focus: Christ’s saving work opens the way for people to approach God.

passages.title: Exodus 26:36-37
passages.section_title: How was the entrance to the tent made?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 36 For the entrance to the tent, you are to make a curtain embroidered with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and finely spun linen. 37 Make five posts of acacia wood for the curtain, overlay them with gold, use hooks of gold, and cast five bronze bases for them.
paragraphs: 36 For the entrance to the tent, you are to make a curtain embroidered with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and finely spun linen. 37 Make five posts of acacia wood for the curtain, overlay them with gold, use hooks of gold, and cast five bronze bases for them.

passages.context_html:
A second curtain forms the entrance to the tent. It uses blue, purple and scarlet yarn with finely spun linen and embroidered work. Five gold-covered acacia posts support it with gold hooks and bronze bases.

This is the doorway into the Holy Place, distinct from the inner veil that separates the Most Holy Place. The entrance has five posts on bronze bases; the inner veil has four on silver bases. The instructions complete the enclosed tent while keeping the two places of entry distinct.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The usual reading is that this curtain serves as the tent’s entrance screen. Wesley distinguishes the priests’ regular passage through this entrance from the restricted approach beyond the inner veil. Calvin sees both curtains as teaching reverence in approaching God, while recognizing their different places in the sanctuary.

passages.god_plan_html:
The entrance offers a useful parallel with Jesus’ description of Himself as the gate for the sheep in John 10:7–18. His actual setting is a sheepfold, rather than an explanation of this embroidered curtain. He brings His sheep into life and safety, lays down His life for them and gathers them into one flock.

The larger theme is access through the one God provides. In John 14:1–6, Jesus promises a place with Him and says that people come to the Father through Him. The comparison helps place the sanctuary’s ordered entrance within the broader story of God bringing His people near, as a clearly labeled comparison.

passages.title: Exodus 27:1-8
passages.section_title: What was the bronze altar for?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 “You are to build an altar of acacia wood. The altar must be square, five cubits long, five cubits wide, and three cubits high. 2 Make a horn on each of its four corners, so that the horns are of one piece, and overlay it with bronze. 3 Make all its utensils of bronze—its pots for removing ashes, its shovels, its sprinkling bowls, its meat forks, and its firepans. 4 Construct for it a grate of bronze mesh, and make a bronze ring at each of the four corners of the mesh. 5 Set the grate beneath the ledge of the altar, so that the mesh comes halfway up the altar. 6 Additionally, make poles of acacia wood for the altar and overlay them with bronze. 7 The poles are to be inserted into the rings so that the poles are on two sides of the altar when it is carried. 8 Construct the altar with boards so that it is hollow. It is to be made just as you were shown on the mountain.
paragraphs: 1 “You are to build an altar of acacia wood. The altar must be square, five cubits long, five cubits wide, and three cubits high. 2 Make a horn on each of its four corners, so that the horns are of one piece, and overlay it with bronze. 3 Make all its utensils of bronze—its pots for removing ashes, its shovels, its sprinkling bowls, its meat forks, and its firepans.

4 Construct for it a grate of bronze mesh, and make a bronze ring at each of the four corners of the mesh. 5 Set the grate beneath the ledge of the altar, so that the mesh comes halfway up the altar. 6 Additionally, make poles of acacia wood for the altar and overlay them with bronze. 7 The poles are to be inserted into the rings so that the poles are on two sides of the altar when it is carried. 8 Construct the altar with boards so that it is hollow. It is to be made just as you were shown on the mountain.

passages.context_html:
The instructions move from the enclosed tent to the altar used in the courtyard. It is a square structure of acacia boards covered with bronze, with a horn at each corner. Bronze utensils serve the work of handling sacrifices, blood, fire and ashes. Rings and carrying poles allow the altar to move with the sanctuary.

The Hebrew word מִזְבֵּחַ, mizbeach (miz-BAY-akh), names an altar, a place of sacrifice; it belongs to the word family of slaughtering for sacrifice (Brown–Driver–Briggs; the related verb). This altar’s purpose is bound to the offerings Israel will bring before the LORD.

The structure is hollow, with a bronze grate beneath its ledge and extending halfway up. Moses must follow the pattern shown on the mountain. Leviticus 6:8–13 later describes the priests tending its fire, adding wood and removing ashes. Those repeated duties make the altar an ongoing place of sacrificial service.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The altar is commonly understood as the appointed place for Israel’s sacrifices and, in Christian interpretation, a picture of Christ’s saving death. Wesley connects it with atonement and the acceptance of the people’s service through Christ. Calvin likewise relates the sacrifice to Christ offering Himself through the Spirit, while noting that different offerings involved different portions: not every sacrifice was entirely burned.

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 7:23–28 explains the greater priesthood and sacrifice of Jesus. He lives permanently to intercede for those who approach God through Him, and His offering of Himself is once for all. The repeated service of the altar belongs to the larger story that reaches its completion in His saving work.

Hebrews 13:10–16 also brings together altar, sacrifice and Jesus’ suffering outside the city gate. It calls believers to go to Him and offer praise, do good and share with others. God’s purpose includes a people whose worship continues in faithful allegiance to Christ and practical generosity.

passages.title: Exodus 27:9-19
passages.section_title: How did the courtyard mark out the place of worship?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 You are also to make a courtyard for the tabernacle. On the south side of the courtyard make curtains of finely spun linen, a hundred cubits long on one side, 10 with twenty posts and twenty bronze bases, and silver hooks and bands on the posts. 11 Likewise there are to be curtains on the north side, a hundred cubits long, with twenty posts and twenty bronze bases, and with silver hooks and bands on the posts. 12 The curtains on the west side of the courtyard shall be fifty cubits wide, with ten posts and ten bases. 13 The east side of the courtyard, toward the sunrise, is to be fifty cubits wide. 14 Make the curtains on one side fifteen cubits long, with three posts and three bases, 15 and the curtains on the other side fifteen cubits long, with three posts and three bases. 16 The gate of the courtyard shall be twenty cubits long, with a curtain embroidered with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and finely spun linen. It shall have four posts and four bases. 17 All the posts around the courtyard shall have silver bands, silver hooks, and bronze bases. 18 The entire courtyard shall be a hundred cubits long and fifty cubits wide, with curtains of finely spun linen five cubits high, and with bronze bases. 19 All the utensils of the tabernacle for every use, including all its tent pegs and the tent pegs of the courtyard, shall be made of bronze.
paragraphs: 9 You are also to make a courtyard for the tabernacle. On the south side of the courtyard make curtains of finely spun linen, a hundred cubits long on one side, 10 with twenty posts and twenty bronze bases, and silver hooks and bands on the posts. 11 Likewise there are to be curtains on the north side, a hundred cubits long, with twenty posts and twenty bronze bases, and with silver hooks and bands on the posts. 12 The curtains on the west side of the courtyard shall be fifty cubits wide, with ten posts and ten bases. 13 The east side of the courtyard, toward the sunrise, is to be fifty cubits wide.

14 Make the curtains on one side fifteen cubits long, with three posts and three bases, 15 and the curtains on the other side fifteen cubits long, with three posts and three bases. 16 The gate of the courtyard shall be twenty cubits long, with a curtain embroidered with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and finely spun linen. It shall have four posts and four bases. 17 All the posts around the courtyard shall have silver bands, silver hooks, and bronze bases. 18 The entire courtyard shall be a hundred cubits long and fifty cubits wide, with curtains of finely spun linen five cubits high, and with bronze bases. 19 All the utensils of the tabernacle for every use, including all its tent pegs and the tent pegs of the courtyard, shall be made of bronze.

passages.context_html:
Linen curtains enclose a courtyard one hundred cubits long, fifty wide and five high. Posts stand in bronze bases, with silver hooks and bands supporting the fabric. The eastern entrance has a twenty-cubit embroidered screen made with colored yarn and fine linen. Bronze pegs and utensils complete the instructions.

This enclosure marks out the area around the tent where the people approach for worship and sacrifice. It is distinct from the rooms inside the tabernacle. The later priestly regulations in Numbers 18:1–7 distinguish the work of Aaron’s priestly family from the assistance of the other Levites; belonging to Levi does not by itself authorize all priestly service.

Foreign residents are also addressed in the sacrificial laws. Leviticus 17:8–9 requires a foreigner living among Israel who offers a sacrifice to bring it to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting. Numbers 15:14–16 gives the same offering rule for Israel and the foreign resident. Those instructions belong alongside the boundaries and responsibilities of sanctuary worship.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The courtyard is generally understood as setting apart the place of worship while allowing the people to bring their offerings before God. Wesley also sees it as a picture of God’s people set apart to Him. He carries that comparison forward to the wider gathering of people who call on Christ, rather than treating the courtyard’s physical size as a limit on the people God will bring near.

passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 2:11–22 describes Gentiles who were once far away being brought near through Christ’s blood. Jesus reconciles Jews and Gentiles in one body, and both have access to the Father through one Spirit. They become members of God’s household and a dwelling for His Spirit.

That is a broader biblical connection with the question of belonging and approach to God, not Paul directly explaining this linen fence. The sanctuary’s ordered worship belongs within a story that leads to people from different backgrounds being reconciled to God and to one another through Christ.

passages.title: Exodus 27:20-21
passages.section_title: Who was responsible for keeping the lamps burning?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 20 And you are to command the Israelites to bring you pure oil of pressed olives for the light, to keep the lamps burning continually. 21 In the Tent of Meeting, outside the veil that is in front of the Testimony, Aaron and his sons are to tend the lamps before the LORD from evening until morning. This is to be a permanent statute for the Israelites for the generations to come.
paragraphs: 20 And you are to command the Israelites to bring you pure oil of pressed olives for the light, to keep the lamps burning continually. 21 In the Tent of Meeting, outside the veil that is in front of the Testimony, Aaron and his sons are to tend the lamps before the LORD from evening until morning. This is to be a permanent statute for the Israelites for the generations to come.

passages.context_html:
The people supply pure oil from pressed olives, and Aaron and his sons tend the lamps before the LORD. The lamps stand in the Holy Place, outside the veil in front of the Testimony. These two verses connect the provision of the whole community with the regular service assigned to the priests.

The instruction says to keep the lamps burning continually and to tend them from evening until morning. The same pattern is repeated in Leviticus 24:1–4. Light in the sanctuary requires faithful provision and attention, rather than being a furnishing made once and then forgotten.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian commentators often connect the light with God’s truth and the work of His Spirit. Wesley and Calvin both make that connection, while describing the priests’ responsibility to maintain the lamps.

The word continually has been understood differently in relation to the hours of burning. Rashi understands it as the repeated service every night, comparing other offerings that are continual because they recur regularly. Gill favors light continuing by day and night. The BSB retains both parts of the instruction: continually and from evening until morning.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
The New Testament carries the theme of God-given light into His people’s witness. In Matthew 5:14–16, Jesus calls His followers the light of the world and tells them to let others see their good deeds so that the Father is glorified. The image now reaches beyond the sanctuary into public life.

2 Corinthians 4:5–7 explains the source of that light: God makes the knowledge of His glory shine in the face of Jesus Christ, and His servants proclaim Christ rather than themselves. Their weakness makes clear that the power comes from God. This develops the wider theme of light and faithful service without treating the oil’s preparation as a formula for producing the Spirit’s work.

passages.title: Exodus 28:1-5
passages.section_title: Why did God appoint Aaron and give him special garments?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 “Next, have your brother Aaron brought to you from among the Israelites, along with his sons Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar, to serve Me as priests. 2 Make holy garments for your brother Aaron, to give him glory and splendor. 3 You are to instruct all the skilled craftsmen, whom I have filled with a spirit of wisdom, to make garments for Aaron’s consecration, so that he may serve Me as priest. 4 These are the garments that they shall make: a breastpiece, an ephod, a robe, a woven tunic, a turban, and a sash. They are to make these holy garments for your brother Aaron and his sons, so that they may serve Me as priests. 5 They shall use gold, along with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and fine linen.
paragraphs: 1 “Next, have your brother Aaron brought to you from among the Israelites, along with his sons Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar, to serve Me as priests. 2 Make holy garments for your brother Aaron, to give him glory and splendor. 3 You are to instruct all the skilled craftsmen, whom I have filled with a spirit of wisdom, to make garments for Aaron’s consecration, so that he may serve Me as priest. 4 These are the garments that they shall make: a breastpiece, an ephod, a robe, a woven tunic, a turban, and a sash. They are to make these holy garments for your brother Aaron and his sons, so that they may serve Me as priests. 5 They shall use gold, along with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and fine linen.

passages.context_html:
After describing the sanctuary and its service, God names the family who will serve Him as priests: Aaron and his sons Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar. The appointment comes from God, and Moses is to bring them forward from among Israel.

The garments are holy because they are set apart for this service. The Hebrew verb קָדַשׁ, qadash (kah-DAHSH), used for their consecration, means to set apart or dedicate as sacred (Brown–Driver–Briggs). Skilled craftsmen, whom God has equipped with wisdom for the task, are to make them. Their glory and splendor express the dignity of serving before Him.

The list introduces the breastpiece, ephod, robe, tunic, turban and sash, with instructions for their materials. The chapter will describe Aaron’s special garments and then those of his sons. Their clothing marks the responsibility they receive within Israel’s covenant worship.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The usual reading is that both God’s appointment and the garments set the priests apart for their task. Calvin emphasizes that Aaron does not claim the office for himself. Wesley understands the garments’ beauty as impressing the dignity of the service on both the priests and the people, and sees the craftsmen’s skill as a gift to be used for God.

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 5:1–10 explicitly uses Aaron’s calling to explain that a high priest is appointed by God. It then speaks of Christ being appointed by the Father, with an everlasting priesthood in the order of Melchizedek. Jesus’ priesthood belongs to God’s saving purpose and is not a role He simply claims for Himself.

Hebrews 2:14–18 also explains why He shares our humanity: He becomes a merciful and faithful high priest who makes atonement and helps those who are tempted. The office introduced here leads into the larger biblical account of the Son who represents people before God and brings them the help they need.

passages.title: Exodus 28:6-14
passages.section_title: Why did Aaron carry Israel’s names on his shoulders?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 They are to make the ephod of finely spun linen embroidered with gold, and with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn. 7 It shall have two shoulder pieces attached at two of its corners, so it can be fastened. 8 And the skillfully woven waistband of the ephod must be of one piece, of the same workmanship—with gold, with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and with finely spun linen. 9 Take two onyx stones and engrave on them the names of the sons of Israel: 10 six of their names on one stone and the remaining six on the other, in the order of their birth. 11 Engrave the names of the sons of Israel on the two stones the way a gem cutter engraves a seal. Then mount the stones in gold filigree settings. 12 Fasten both stones on the shoulder pieces of the ephod as memorial stones for the sons of Israel. Aaron is to bear their names on his two shoulders as a memorial before the LORD. 13 Fashion gold filigree settings 14 and two chains of pure gold, made of braided cord work; and attach these chains to the settings.

9 Take two onyx stones and engrave on them the names of the sons of Israel: 10 six of their names on one stone and the remaining six on the other, in the order of their birth. 11 Engrave the names of the sons of Israel on the two stones the way a gem cutter engraves a seal. Then mount the stones in gold filigree settings. 12 Fasten both stones on the shoulder pieces of the ephod as memorial stones for the sons of Israel. Aaron is to bear their names on his two shoulders as a memorial before the LORD. 13 Fashion gold filigree settings 14 and two chains of pure gold, made of braided cord work; and attach these chains to the settings.

passages.context_html:
The ephod is a priestly garment made from finely spun linen worked with gold and the three colored yarns. Shoulder pieces and a woven waistband hold it together. The next instructions provide settings and chains that will connect it with the breastpiece.

Two onyx stones are engraved with the names of Israel’s sons, six on each stone in birth order. Set in gold on the shoulders, they are memorial stones before the LORD. Aaron carries the names as he serves. His place before God concerns the people he represents, whose names are visibly joined to his priestly clothing.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley and Calvin both emphasize representation: Aaron bears Israel before God rather than serving for his own private importance. They also read the shoulder stones as a picture of Christ bearing His people and appearing on their behalf. This is their Christ-centered reading of the priestly pattern, grounded in the later description of His intercession.

passages.god_plan_html:
The representative role reaches its greater fulfillment in Christ. Hebrews 9:24 says that He enters God’s presence on our behalf, and Hebrews 7:23–28 explains that He lives permanently to intercede for those who draw near through Him. The comparison with Aaron’s carried names points toward a living priest who continues to represent His people.

God’s remembrance is also a theme of hope elsewhere in Scripture. When Zion fears she has been forgotten, Isaiah 49:14–16 answers with the image of a mother’s care and God’s people inscribed on His palms. This is a parallel of remembrance, not a description of Jesus literally wearing Aaron’s stones. Together the passages direct hope toward God’s faithful care for the people He has made His own.

passages.title: Exodus 28:15-30
passages.section_title: What did the breastpiece carry before God?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 You are also to make a breastpiece of judgment with the same workmanship as the ephod. Construct it with gold, with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and with finely spun linen. 16 It must be square when folded over double, a span long and a span wide. 17 And mount on it a setting of gemstones, four rows of stones: In the first row there shall be a ruby, a topaz, and an emerald; 18 in the second row a turquoise, a sapphire, and a diamond; 19 in the third row a jacinth, an agate, and an amethyst; 20 and in the fourth row a beryl, an onyx, and a jasper. Mount these stones in gold filigree settings. 21 The twelve stones are to correspond to the names of the sons of Israel, each engraved like a seal with the name of one of the twelve tribes. 22 For the breastpiece, make braided chains like cords of pure gold. 23 You are also to make two gold rings and fasten them to the two corners of the breastpiece. 24 Then fasten the two gold chains to the two gold rings at the corners of the breastpiece, 25 and fasten the other ends of the two chains to the two filigree settings, attaching them to the shoulder pieces of the ephod at the front. 26 Make two more gold rings and attach them to the other two corners of the breastpiece, on the inside edge next to the ephod. 27 Make two additional gold rings and attach them to the bottom of the two shoulder pieces of the ephod, on its front, near its seam just above its woven waistband. 28 The rings of the breastpiece shall be tied to the rings of the ephod with a cord of blue yarn, so that the breastpiece is above the waistband of the ephod and does not swing out from the ephod. 29 Whenever Aaron enters the Holy Place, he shall bear the names of the sons of Israel over his heart on the breastpiece of judgment, as a continual reminder before the LORD. 30 And place the Urim and Thummim in the breastpiece of judgment, so that they will also be over Aaron’s heart whenever he comes before the LORD. Aaron will continually carry the judgment of the sons of Israel over his heart before the LORD.

22 For the breastpiece, make braided chains like cords of pure gold. 23 You are also to make two gold rings and fasten them to the two corners of the breastpiece. 24 Then fasten the two gold chains to the two gold rings at the corners of the breastpiece, 25 and fasten the other ends of the two chains to the two filigree settings, attaching them to the shoulder pieces of the ephod at the front. 26 Make two more gold rings and attach them to the other two corners of the breastpiece, on the inside edge next to the ephod. 27 Make two additional gold rings and attach them to the bottom of the two shoulder pieces of the ephod, on its front, near its seam just above its woven waistband. 28 The rings of the breastpiece shall be tied to the rings of the ephod with a cord of blue yarn, so that the breastpiece is above the waistband of the ephod and does not swing out from the ephod.

Aaron will continually carry the judgment of the sons of Israel over his heart before the LORD.

passages.context_html:
The breastpiece is made with the same materials as the ephod, folded double and fitted with twelve precious stones in four rows. Each stone bears the name of one of Israel’s twelve tribes. Chains, rings and a blue cord secure it to the ephod so that it stays in place.

The people’s names are now carried over Aaron’s heart as well as on his shoulders. The text calls this a continual reminder before the LORD. It also calls the garment the breastpiece of judgment and places the Urim and Thummim within it, associated with the decisions carried before God.

Numbers 27:18–23 later describes Eleazar seeking counsel by the judgment of the Urim for Joshua. 1 Samuel 28:5–7 mentions the Urim among the means by which Saul sought an answer and received none. The purpose is divine counsel for Israel; Exodus does not describe the objects’ exact appearance or the procedure by which an answer was given.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The twelve named stones are commonly understood as presenting the whole people before God through the high priest. Wesley draws attention to the combination of shoulders and heart, reading them as a picture of the strength and love with which Christ represents His people.

The Urim and Thummim have received different explanations. Calvin favors signs of God’s guidance and faithful conduct associated with the breastpiece. Wesley considers several possibilities, including something God supplied or an indication of the priest’s guidance from God. Rashi’s Jewish commentary understands an inscription of God’s name placed within its folds. These are documented readings; the text does not settle the matter by identifying two differently colored stones or describing letters that light up.

passages.god_plan_html:
The theme of God guiding His people reaches a fuller expression in Hebrews 1:1–4. God, who spoke in different ways through the prophets, has spoken through His Son. The Son reveals His nature and, after providing purification for sins, takes His place at God’s right hand. Representation before God and revelation from God come together in Him.

There is also a later parallel in the precious stones and names of Revelation 21:9–21. The holy city bears the names of Israel’s tribes on its gates and the Lamb’s apostles on its jeweled foundations. The arrangements and names on those foundations differ from Aaron’s breastpiece. The shared imagery places God’s people within His promised future: a people remembered, brought near and given a place in the city filled with His glory.

passages.title: Exodus 28:31-43
passages.section_title: How did the rest of the garments mark the priests for holy service?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 31 You are to make the robe of the ephod entirely of blue cloth, 32 with an opening at its top in the center. Around the opening shall be a woven collar with an opening like that of a garment, so that it will not tear. 33 Make pomegranates of blue, purple, and scarlet yarn all the way around the lower hem, with gold bells between them, 34 alternating the gold bells and pomegranates around the lower hem of the robe. 35 Aaron must wear the robe whenever he ministers, and its sound will be heard when he enters or exits the sanctuary before the LORD, so that he will not die. 36 You are to make a plate of pure gold and engrave on it as on a seal: HOLY TO THE LORD. 37 Fasten to it a blue cord to mount it on the turban; it shall be on the front of the turban. 38 And it will be worn on Aaron’s forehead, so that he may bear the iniquity of the holy things that the sons of Israel consecrate with regard to all their holy gifts. It shall always be on his forehead, so that they may be acceptable before the LORD. 39 You are to weave the tunic with fine linen, make the turban of fine linen, and fashion an embroidered sash. 40 Make tunics, sashes, and headbands for Aaron’s sons, to give them glory and splendor. 41 After you put these garments on your brother Aaron and his sons, anoint them, ordain them, and consecrate them so that they may serve Me as priests. 42 Make linen undergarments to cover their bare flesh, extending from waist to thigh. 43 Aaron and his sons must wear them whenever they enter the Tent of Meeting or approach the altar to minister in the Holy Place, so that they will not incur guilt and die. This is to be a permanent statute for Aaron and his descendants.

36 You are to make a plate of pure gold and engrave on it as on a seal: HOLY TO THE LORD. 37 Fasten to it a blue cord to mount it on the turban; it shall be on the front of the turban. 38 And it will be worn on Aaron’s forehead, so that he may bear the iniquity of the holy things that the sons of Israel consecrate with regard to all their holy gifts. It shall always be on his forehead, so that they may be acceptable before the LORD. 39 You are to weave the tunic with fine linen, make the turban of fine linen, and fashion an embroidered sash.

40 Make tunics, sashes, and headbands for Aaron’s sons, to give them glory and splendor. 41 After you put these garments on your brother Aaron and his sons, anoint them, ordain them, and consecrate them so that they may serve Me as priests. 42 Make linen undergarments to cover their bare flesh, extending from waist to thigh. 43 Aaron and his sons must wear them whenever they enter the Tent of Meeting or approach the altar to minister in the Holy Place, so that they will not incur guilt and die. This is to be a permanent statute for Aaron and his descendants.

passages.context_html:
Aaron’s blue robe has a reinforced opening and a hem alternating gold bells with pomegranates worked in colored yarn. Its sound is heard as he enters and leaves the sanctuary. God requires him to wear it in his service, with a warning against approaching contrary to the instruction.

A gold plate on the front of the turban bears the inscription HOLY TO THE LORD. Aaron wears it as he bears the iniquity connected with Israel’s holy gifts, so that they may be accepted before God. The inscription identifies the priest and his service as belonging to the holy God.

Tunics, sashes and headbands are also made for Aaron’s sons. They are to be clothed, anointed, ordained and set apart for priestly service. Linen undergarments cover their bodies from waist to thigh. The clothing requirements apply when they enter the tent or approach the altar; the task must be carried out with the holiness and care God requires.

For the Day of Atonement, Leviticus 16:2–4 separately specifies the linen garments worn for that approach. This helps distinguish those instructions from the blue robe and bells described here.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The garments are generally understood as expressing the holiness of the office and the seriousness of approaching God as He directs. Wesley and Calvin both connect the gold plate and the acceptance of the gifts with Christ’s mediation: the people need more than outwardly impressive offerings to stand before God.

Their readings of the bells differ in emphasis. Wesley understands the sound as alerting worshipers to the priest’s service so that they join in prayer. Calvin draws a spiritual comparison with the proclamation of the gospel. Those applications go beyond the stated requirement that Aaron wear the appointed robe and that its sound be heard in his service.

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 4:14–16 describes the great high priest who is both able to sympathize with human weakness and without sin. Because of Him, believers may approach God’s throne for mercy and help. 1 Peter 2:4–10 then describes God’s people as a holy priesthood offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable through Jesus Christ. What the priestly clothing sets apart for service here leads into the wider theme of a people made fit to serve through Him.

The forehead inscription also has a later parallel in Revelation 22:1–5: God’s servants worship Him, see His face and bear His name on their foreheads. This continues the theme of belonging to God and serving in His presence. The final picture extends that privilege throughout His people in a world freed from the curse.

passages.title: Exodus 29:1-9
passages.section_title: How were Aaron and his sons prepared to serve?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 “Now this is what you are to do to consecrate Aaron and his sons to serve Me as priests: Take a young bull and two rams without blemish, 2 along with unleavened bread, unleavened cakes mixed with oil, and unleavened wafers anointed with oil. Make them out of fine wheat flour, 3 put them in a basket, and present them in the basket, along with the bull and the two rams. 4 Then present Aaron and his sons at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting and wash them with water. 5 Take the garments and clothe Aaron with the tunic, the robe of the ephod, the ephod itself, and the breastplate. Fasten the ephod on him with its woven waistband. 6 Put the turban on his head and attach the holy diadem to the turban. 7 Then take the anointing oil and anoint him by pouring it on his head. 8 Present his sons as well and clothe them with tunics. 9 Wrap the sashes around Aaron and his sons and tie headbands on them. The priesthood shall be theirs by a permanent statute. In this way you are to ordain Aaron and his sons.

Make them out of fine wheat flour, 3 put them in a basket, and present them in the basket, along with the bull and the two rams.

4 Then present Aaron and his sons at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting and wash them with water. 5 Take the garments and clothe Aaron with the tunic, the robe of the ephod, the ephod itself, and the breastplate. Fasten the ephod on him with its woven waistband. 6 Put the turban on his head and attach the holy diadem to the turban. 7 Then take the anointing oil and anoint him by pouring it on his head. 8 Present his sons as well and clothe them with tunics. 9 Wrap the sashes around Aaron and his sons and tie headbands on them. The priesthood shall be theirs by a permanent statute. In this way you are to ordain Aaron and his sons.

passages.context_html:
God now gives the ceremony for setting Aaron and his sons apart as priests. A bull, two unblemished rams and a basket of unleavened bread are prepared for the offerings that follow. At the entrance to the tent, Moses washes the men, clothes them in their appointed garments and pours anointing oil on Aaron’s head.

The washing, clothing and anointing mark their preparation for a responsibility God has given them. Aaron wears the garments described in the previous chapter, while his sons receive their tunics, sashes and headbands. The instructions are given here; their carrying out is later described in Leviticus 8.

The Hebrew expression used for ordaining is מִלֵּא יָד, mille yad (mil-LAY yahd), literally to fill the hand—an idiom for installing someone in priestly office (Brown–Driver–Briggs). Later in this ceremony, offerings are actually placed in their hands. The appointment equips them for service before God.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Calvin understand the preparation as expressing the need for purity and a life set apart to God. They connect the priestly pattern with Christ and the work of God’s Spirit. The outward ceremony belongs to the service God has appointed for Israel.

Christian traditions differ over how that priestly pattern relates to ordained ministry. The Catholic Church sees Aaron’s priesthood as preparing for Christian ordained ministry, while also affirming the priestly calling of all believers; its Catechism, 1541–1547, describes both as sharing in Christ’s one priesthood. It teaches that His one sacrifice is made present in the Eucharist. The Westminster Confession, 27.4 and 29.2, also recognizes ordained ministers, but rejects understanding the Supper as an offering of Christ to the Father. It describes the Supper as commemorating His completed offering and offering praise to God. These are differences in Christian application, rather than disagreement that Aaron’s family receives the office here.

passages.god_plan_html:
The preparation offers a parallel with the way the New Testament describes God making people ready for life with Him. Titus 3:3–8 speaks of salvation by God’s mercy, the washing of new birth and renewal by the Spirit, leading believers to devote themselves to good deeds. Galatians 3:26–29 describes those baptized into Christ as clothed with Him and joined together as heirs of the promise.

2 Corinthians 1:21–22 adds that God establishes His people in Christ, anoints them and gives His Spirit as a pledge. These are broader biblical connections with cleansing, clothing and anointing. The focus is on what God gives so that His people can belong to Him and serve.

passages.title: Exodus 29:10-30
passages.section_title: What did the sacrifices set apart for God?

passages.context_html:
The bull and the two rams have different roles in the ceremony. Aaron and his sons lay their hands on each animal. For the bull, blood is applied to the altar’s horns and poured at its base, selected fat is burned on the altar, and the remaining body is burned outside the camp as a sin offering.

The first ram is a burnt offering: its blood is splattered on the altar, and the whole animal is offered as a pleasing aroma to the LORD. The second is the ram of ordination. Its blood is applied to the priests’ right ears, right thumbs and right big toes, with blood and anointing oil also sprinkled on them and their garments. Their bodies and clothing are set apart for the service they are entering.

Selected portions of the second ram and the bread are placed in their hands, presented before God as a wave offering and burned on the altar. Moses receives the breast as his portion in this ceremony. Verses 27–28 also establish the breast and thigh as the regular priestly portion from Israel’s peace offerings. The closing instructions provide for Aaron’s garments to pass to the son who succeeds him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The sacrifices are generally read as God’s provision for the priests’ own need of atonement and their dedication to Him. Wesley emphasizes both the confession of their need and the giving of their whole selves to God. Calvin reads the ear as representing obedience and the hands and feet as representing conduct and the course of life. On that reading, the marked parts express the dedication of the whole person, rather than only those individual body parts.

The differing treatment of the animals matters: the sin offering, whole burnt offering and ordination offering are not three identical actions. The ceremony distinguishes removal of guilt, dedication and the priest’s participation in the appointed service.

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 9:11–15 explains the greater cleansing accomplished by Christ’s blood: the conscience is purified so that people may serve the living God. It also says that His death redeems transgressions committed under the first covenant. The earlier sacrifices belong within God’s provision that reaches its lasting accomplishment in Him.

Ephesians 5:1–2 describes Christ giving Himself as a fragrant sacrificial offering, then calls His people to walk in love. Romans 12:1–2 calls for their bodies as living sacrifices in response to God’s mercy. These connections carry the theme of whole-person dedication into lives transformed by His saving work.

passages.title: Exodus 29:31-37
passages.section_title: Why did the priests eat a sacred meal and remain for seven days?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 31 You are to take the ram of ordination and boil its flesh in a holy place. 32 At the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, Aaron and his sons are to eat the meat of the ram and the bread that is in the basket. 33 They must eat those things by which atonement was made for their ordination and consecration. But no outsider may eat them, because these things are sacred. 34 And if any of the meat of ordination or any bread is left until the morning, you are to burn up the remainder. It must not be eaten, because it is sacred. 35 This is what you are to do for Aaron and his sons based on all that I have commanded you, taking seven days to ordain them. 36 Sacrifice a bull as a sin offering each day for atonement. Purify the altar by making atonement for it, and anoint it to consecrate it. 37 For seven days you shall make atonement for the altar and consecrate it. Then the altar will become most holy; whatever touches the altar will be holy.

But no outsider may eat them, because these things are sacred. 34 And if any of the meat of ordination or any bread is left until the morning, you are to burn up the remainder. It must not be eaten, because it is sacred.

35 This is what you are to do for Aaron and his sons based on all that I have commanded you, taking seven days to ordain them. 36 Sacrifice a bull as a sin offering each day for atonement. Purify the altar by making atonement for it, and anoint it to consecrate it. 37 For seven days you shall make atonement for the altar and consecrate it. Then the altar will become most holy; whatever touches the altar will be holy.

passages.context_html:
The remaining flesh of the ordination ram is boiled in a holy place. Aaron and his sons eat it with the bread at the entrance to the tent. These are sacred portions connected with their ordination; someone outside that appointed group may not eat them. Anything left until morning is to be burned.

The setting apart of the priests takes seven days, with a bull offered for atonement each day and the altar purified and anointed. The altar becomes most holy. The ceremony concerns both those who serve and the place where they will offer Israel’s sacrifices.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley understands the meal as the priests receiving the benefit of the atonement and enjoying fellowship with God. He sees the seven-day period as giving weight and seriousness to their admission to service. He also connects the repeated sacrifices with the need for the better priesthood and offering of Christ, as explained in Hebrews.

passages.god_plan_html:
The provision of food for those serving at the sanctuary becomes an explicit comparison in 1 Corinthians 9:7–18. Paul recalls that those serving at the altar receive food from its offerings and applies that pattern to support for those who preach the gospel.

Paul also explains why he sometimes chooses not to exercise that right: he wants to remove obstacles to the gospel. The connection brings provision and service together. God’s people can support the work, while the person serving keeps the good of others and the advance of the gospel at the center.

passages.title: Exodus 29:38-44
passages.section_title: Why were lambs offered every morning and evening?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 38 This is what you are to offer regularly on the altar, each day: two lambs that are a year old. 39 Offer one lamb in the morning and the other at twilight. 40 With the first lamb offer a tenth of an ephah of fine flour, mixed with a quarter hin of oil from pressed olives, and a drink offering of a quarter hin of wine. 41 And offer the second lamb at twilight with the same grain offering and drink offering as in the morning, as a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD. 42 For the generations to come, this burnt offering shall be made regularly at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting before the LORD, where I will meet you to speak with you. 43 I will also meet with the Israelites there, and that place will be consecrated by My glory. 44 So I will consecrate the Tent of Meeting and the altar, and I will consecrate Aaron and his sons to serve Me as priests.
paragraphs: 38 This is what you are to offer regularly on the altar, each day: two lambs that are a year old. 39 Offer one lamb in the morning and the other at twilight. 40 With the first lamb offer a tenth of an ephah of fine flour, mixed with a quarter hin of oil from pressed olives, and a drink offering of a quarter hin of wine. 41 And offer the second lamb at twilight with the same grain offering and drink offering as in the morning, as a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD.

42 For the generations to come, this burnt offering shall be made regularly at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting before the LORD, where I will meet you to speak with you. 43 I will also meet with the Israelites there, and that place will be consecrated by My glory. 44 So I will consecrate the Tent of Meeting and the altar, and I will consecrate Aaron and his sons to serve Me as priests.

passages.context_html:
After the ordination instructions comes the regular daily service. Two year-old lambs are offered each day, one in the morning and one at twilight. Each is accompanied by flour, oil and wine. This is a continuing burnt offering at the entrance to the tent.

God joins the offerings with His promise to meet and speak with His people. The place is made holy by His glory. He also declares that He will set apart the tent, altar, Aaron and his sons. The prescribed service is part of the life He establishes with Israel.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The daily offerings are commonly understood as the continuing sacrificial service before God. Wesley reads them as pointing toward Christ’s lasting intercession on the strength of His once-for-all sacrifice. He also draws an application of regular prayer and praise. The repeated lamb offerings belong to Israel’s worship; Christ’s death is not repeated each day.

passages.god_plan_html:
John 1:29–34 identifies Jesus as the Lamb of God who takes away the world’s sin. Hebrews 10:1–18 explains the difference His work makes: priests stand repeatedly offering sacrifices, but Christ offers one sacrifice for sins and sits at God’s right hand. Through that one offering He accomplishes the lasting sanctification the earlier sacrifices could not complete.

The point is more than a contrast between two ways of carrying out a ceremony. Hebrews joins Christ’s completed offering with God’s promise of sins forgiven and His laws written within His people. The daily service belongs within a story that leads to that lasting relationship.

passages.title: Exodus 29:45-46
passages.section_title: Why did God bring Israel out of Egypt?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 45 Then I will dwell among the Israelites and be their God. 46 And they will know that I am the LORD their God, who brought them out of the land of Egypt so that I might dwell among them. I am the LORD their God.
paragraphs: 45 Then I will dwell among the Israelites and be their God. 46 And they will know that I am the LORD their God, who brought them out of the land of Egypt so that I might dwell among them. I am the LORD their God.

passages.context_html:
These closing words state the purpose behind the sanctuary and priesthood instructions: God will dwell among Israel and be their God. He identifies Himself as the LORD who brought them out of Egypt so that He might dwell among them.

Rescue from slavery leads to life with the God who rescued them. The sacrifices, priesthood and sanctuary serve that covenant relationship. Israel is to know who He is through His presence and dealings with them.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The main reading is shared: God’s deliverance and His dwelling among the people belong together. Calvin emphasizes that God is not a deliverer on just one occasion; He continues to care for His people, with the sanctuary serving as a sign of His presence. The promise explains the purpose of the instructions that precede it.
passages.current_position_html: As explained in The True Church According to Jesus, God now dwells in His people through His Spirit. The study connects His presence in the tabernacle with His indwelling in believers and calls for lives made holy by that presence.

passages.god_plan_html:
The New Testament carries this purpose forward through Christ and His people. John 1:14–18 describes the Word becoming flesh and dwelling among us, revealing God’s glory. Ephesians 2:19–22 then describes people joined in Christ as a dwelling for God through His Spirit.

The final vision in Revelation 21:1–4 announces God dwelling with His people, with death, mourning and pain removed. The promise in Exodus contributes to that larger biblical story: God rescues a people to live with Him, and His purpose reaches its fullness in a renewed creation.

passages.title: Exodus 30:1-10
passages.section_title: Why was incense burned before the inner veil?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 “You are also to make an altar of acacia wood for the burning of incense. 2 It is to be square, a cubit long, a cubit wide, and two cubits high. Its horns must be of one piece. 3 Overlay with pure gold the top and all the sides and horns, and make a molding of gold around it. 4 And make two gold rings below the molding on opposite sides to hold the poles used to carry it. 5 Make the poles of acacia wood and overlay them with gold. 6 Place the altar in front of the veil that is before the ark of the Testimony—before the mercy seat that is over the Testimony—where I will meet with you. 7 And Aaron is to burn fragrant incense on it every morning when he tends the lamps. 8 When Aaron sets up the lamps at twilight, he must burn the incense perpetually before the LORD for the generations to come. 9 On this altar you must not offer unauthorized incense or a burnt offering or grain offering; nor are you to pour a drink offering on it. 10 Once a year Aaron shall make atonement on the horns of the altar. Throughout your generations he shall make atonement on it annually with the blood of the sin offering of atonement. The altar is most holy to the LORD.”
paragraphs: 1 “You are also to make an altar of acacia wood for the burning of incense. 2 It is to be square, a cubit long, a cubit wide, and two cubits high. Its horns must be of one piece. 3 Overlay with pure gold the top and all the sides and horns, and make a molding of gold around it. 4 And make two gold rings below the molding on opposite sides to hold the poles used to carry it. 5 Make the poles of acacia wood and overlay them with gold. 6 Place the altar in front of the veil that is before the ark of the Testimony—before the mercy seat that is over the Testimony—where I will meet with you.

7 And Aaron is to burn fragrant incense on it every morning when he tends the lamps. 8 When Aaron sets up the lamps at twilight, he must burn the incense perpetually before the LORD for the generations to come. 9 On this altar you must not offer unauthorized incense or a burnt offering or grain offering; nor are you to pour a drink offering on it. 10 Once a year Aaron shall make atonement on the horns of the altar. Throughout your generations he shall make atonement on it annually with the blood of the sin offering of atonement. The altar is most holy to the LORD.”

passages.context_html:
This smaller altar is made from acacia wood covered with gold, with horns, a molding, rings and carrying poles. It stands in front of the veil, facing the place of meeting above the ark’s mercy seat. Its appointed use differs from the bronze altar in the courtyard.

Aaron burns fragrant incense when tending the lamps in the morning and at twilight. No unauthorized incense, animal offering, grain offering or drink offering is to be presented on it. Its horns do receive blood at the yearly atonement. The distinction concerns its appointed service, with its own requirement for purification.

The instructions join regular worship with approach to the God who meets His people. The altar is most holy, and its use is governed by His command.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian commentators commonly connect the incense with prayer and acceptance before God. Wesley understands the altar as pointing toward Christ’s intercession and the prayers of His people. Calvin likewise emphasizes worship pleasing to God and the connection between prayer and atonement. Psalm 141:1–4 itself compares prayer to incense while asking God to guard the worshiper’s words and heart.

passages.god_plan_html:
Luke 1:5–17 places the praying congregation at the hour when Zechariah offers incense. There the angel announces John’s birth and his work of preparing a people for the Lord. The continuing service of Israel’s sanctuary becomes part of the Gospel’s account of God preparing for the coming of Jesus.

The greater priestly ministry is explained in Hebrews 7:23–28: Jesus lives permanently to intercede for those who approach God through Him, on the basis of His once-for-all offering. The incense’s association with prayer belongs within that larger purpose of bringing people near to God through His Son.

passages.title: Exodus 30:11-16
passages.section_title: Why did the census require a ransom payment?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 Then the LORD said to Moses, 12 “When you take a census of the Israelites to number them, each man must pay the LORD a ransom for his life when he is counted. Then no plague will come upon them when they are numbered. 13 Everyone who crosses over to those counted must pay a half shekel, according to the sanctuary shekel, which weighs twenty gerahs. This half shekel is an offering to the LORD. 14 Everyone twenty years of age or older who crosses over must give this offering to the LORD. 15 In making the offering to the LORD to atone for your lives, the rich shall not give more than a half shekel, nor shall the poor give less. 16 Take the atonement money from the Israelites and use it for the service of the Tent of Meeting. It will serve as a memorial for the Israelites before the LORD to make atonement for your lives.”
paragraphs: 11 Then the LORD said to Moses, 12 “When you take a census of the Israelites to number them, each man must pay the LORD a ransom for his life when he is counted. Then no plague will come upon them when they are numbered. 13 Everyone who crosses over to those counted must pay a half shekel, according to the sanctuary shekel, which weighs twenty gerahs. This half shekel is an offering to the LORD. 14 Everyone twenty years of age or older who crosses over must give this offering to the LORD. 15 In making the offering to the LORD to atone for your lives, the rich shall not give more than a half shekel, nor shall the poor give less. 16 Take the atonement money from the Israelites and use it for the service of the Tent of Meeting. It will serve as a memorial for the Israelites before the LORD to make atonement for your lives.”

passages.context_html:
When Israel is numbered, each person counted is to give a half shekel to the LORD as a ransom for his life, so that no plague comes upon the people. The payment applies from twenty years of age. Rich and poor pay the same amount, and the money supports the service of the Tent of Meeting.

The Hebrew noun כֹּפֶר, kopher (KOH-fer), means a ransom or the price of a life in this setting (Brown–Driver–Briggs). The payment acknowledges life before God and is a memorial for the Israelites. It differs from the earlier sanctuary offering, which people brought as their hearts moved them; here a fixed amount is required from those counted.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin emphasizes that Israel’s people and their lives belong to the God who redeemed them. Wesley draws attention to the equal amount and the equal need of rich and poor.

Wesley also records different readings of how often it was due: at the first census, whenever a census occurred, or as an annual contribution begun at that first counting. The passage itself gives the requirement when the people are numbered. Those proposed later patterns should be distinguished from what this paragraph expressly specifies.

passages.god_plan_html:
A later tax episode in Matthew 17:24–27 draws attention to Jesus’ standing as the Son. He explains that a king’s own sons are exempt, yet provides the payment for Himself and Peter to avoid giving offense. Wesley connects that temple-tax scene with this contribution; the Gospel’s emphasis is Jesus’ relationship to the Father and His willing response.

The New Testament also distinguishes the greater redemption God provides from any monetary payment. 1 Peter 1:17–21 says that believers are redeemed through Christ’s precious blood rather than silver or gold. 1 Timothy 2:1–6 identifies Him as the mediator who gives Himself as a ransom. These are wider biblical connections with the theme of life given and redeemed by God.

passages.title: Exodus 30:17-21
passages.section_title: Why did the priests wash their hands and feet before serving?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 And the LORD said to Moses, 18 “You are to make a bronze basin with a bronze stand for washing. Set it between the Tent of Meeting and the altar, and put water in it, 19 with which Aaron and his sons are to wash their hands and feet. 20 Whenever they enter the Tent of Meeting or approach the altar to minister by presenting a food offering to the LORD, they must wash with water so that they will not die. 21 Thus they are to wash their hands and feet so that they will not die; this shall be a permanent statute for Aaron and his descendants for the generations to come.”
paragraphs: 17 And the LORD said to Moses, 18 “You are to make a bronze basin with a bronze stand for washing. Set it between the Tent of Meeting and the altar, and put water in it, 19 with which Aaron and his sons are to wash their hands and feet. 20 Whenever they enter the Tent of Meeting or approach the altar to minister by presenting a food offering to the LORD, they must wash with water so that they will not die. 21 Thus they are to wash their hands and feet so that they will not die; this shall be a permanent statute for Aaron and his descendants for the generations to come.”

passages.context_html:
A bronze basin on a bronze stand is placed between the courtyard altar and the Tent of Meeting. It holds the water Aaron and his sons use to wash their hands and feet whenever they enter the tent or approach the altar to minister.

This is a repeated requirement during their service, distinct from the washing at their initial ordination in Exodus 29. God attaches a severe warning: they must wash so that they do not die. Their approach to His holy service calls for the care and purity He prescribes.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The basin is generally understood as providing ritual washing and teaching the need for purity before God. Calvin connects hands and feet with actions and the whole course of life. Wesley emphasizes that the priests need continuing cleansing as they serve, and draws an application of renewed repentance and reliance on Christ. These are spiritual applications of the repeated washing, alongside its actual role in sanctuary service.

passages.god_plan_html:
The wider biblical theme of cleansing reaches its greater expression in Christ. Ephesians 5:25–27 describes His love for the church, His giving Himself for her and His cleansing work so that she may be holy and blameless. The focus is the people He makes ready for Himself.

1 John 1:5–10 likewise joins fellowship with God to walking in the light, acknowledging sin and receiving His cleansing. These passages carry the theme into an ongoing life with God, rather than treating purity as something His people can simply put behind them after an initial ceremony.

passages.title: Exodus 30:22-33
passages.section_title: Why was the anointing oil reserved for God’s service?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 Then the LORD said to Moses, 23 “Take the finest spices: 500 shekels of liquid myrrh, half that amount (250 shekels) of fragrant cinnamon, 250 shekels of fragrant cane, 24 500 shekels of cassia —all according to the sanctuary shekel—and a hin of olive oil. 25 Prepare from these a sacred anointing oil, a fragrant blend, the work of a perfumer; it will be a sacred anointing oil. 26 Use this oil to anoint the Tent of Meeting, the ark of the Testimony, 27 the table and all its utensils, the lampstand and its utensils, the altar of incense, 28 the altar of burnt offering and all its utensils, and the basin with its stand. 29 You are to consecrate them so that they will be most holy. Whatever touches them shall be holy. 30 Anoint Aaron and his sons and consecrate them to serve Me as priests. 31 And you are to tell the Israelites, ‘This will be My sacred anointing oil for the generations to come. 32 It must not be used to anoint an ordinary man, and you must not make anything like it with the same formula. It is holy, and it must be holy to you. 33 Anyone who mixes perfume like it or puts it on an outsider shall be cut off from his people.’”

26 Use this oil to anoint the Tent of Meeting, the ark of the Testimony, 27 the table and all its utensils, the lampstand and its utensils, the altar of incense, 28 the altar of burnt offering and all its utensils, and the basin with its stand. 29 You are to consecrate them so that they will be most holy. Whatever touches them shall be holy. 30 Anoint Aaron and his sons and consecrate them to serve Me as priests.

31 And you are to tell the Israelites, ‘This will be My sacred anointing oil for the generations to come. 32 It must not be used to anoint an ordinary man, and you must not make anything like it with the same formula. It is holy, and it must be holy to you. 33 Anyone who mixes perfume like it or puts it on an outsider shall be cut off from his people.’”

passages.context_html:
God gives a particular mixture of spices and olive oil for anointing the sanctuary, its furnishings, Aaron and his sons. A perfumer is to prepare the fragrant blend. Its purpose is to set these people and things apart for His service.

The same formula must not be reproduced for ordinary personal use or applied to someone outside its appointed use. The command is consistent with Aaron and his sons being anointed: their priestly consecration is precisely the purpose God has authorized. The penalty underscores the difference between something dedicated to Him and something people may use as they choose.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The main reading is that the oil marks the people and furnishings as belonging to God’s holy service. Wesley and Calvin also connect anointing with the work and gifts of the Holy Spirit. Calvin emphasizes that the outward service depends on the Spirit’s work; Wesley stresses reverence for what God has appointed.

passages.god_plan_html:
The title Christ comes from the Greek Χριστός, Christos (khrees-TOSS), meaning anointed (Thayer). Acts 10:34–43 explicitly says that God anointed Jesus with the Holy Spirit and power, then recounts His ministry, death, resurrection and the forgiveness received through Him. Luke 3:21–22 also brings together the Father’s declaration about His Son and the Spirit descending upon Him.

The comparison points beyond a sacred material to the person God appoints and empowers. God’s gift remains His to give. In Acts 8:14–24, Peter rebukes Simon for thinking that the power to give the Spirit could be bought. The theme is God’s provision for His work, received in obedience rather than brought under human control.

passages.title: Exodus 30:34-38
passages.section_title: Why could the sacred incense not become an ordinary perfume?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 34 The LORD also said to Moses, “Take fragrant spices—gum resin, onycha, galbanum, and pure frankincense—in equal measures, 35 and make a fragrant blend of incense, the work of a perfumer, seasoned with salt, pure and holy. 36 Grind some of it into fine powder and place it in front of the Testimony in the Tent of Meeting, where I will meet with you. It shall be most holy to you. 37 You are never to use this formula to make incense for yourselves; you shall regard it as holy to the LORD. 38 Anyone who makes something like it to enjoy its fragrance shall be cut off from his people.”
paragraphs: 34 The LORD also said to Moses, “Take fragrant spices—gum resin, onycha, galbanum, and pure frankincense—in equal measures, 35 and make a fragrant blend of incense, the work of a perfumer, seasoned with salt, pure and holy. 36 Grind some of it into fine powder and place it in front of the Testimony in the Tent of Meeting, where I will meet with you. It shall be most holy to you. 37 You are never to use this formula to make incense for yourselves; you shall regard it as holy to the LORD. 38 Anyone who makes something like it to enjoy its fragrance shall be cut off from his people.”

passages.context_html:
The incense is a fragrant blend of gum resin, onycha, galbanum and frankincense in equal measures. It is prepared by a perfumer, seasoned with salt, and ground finely for use before the Testimony where God meets with Moses.

Like the anointing oil, this particular mixture belongs to the appointed worship. The people must regard it as holy to the LORD and must not reproduce it for their own enjoyment. The distinction protects its dedicated purpose within Israel’s life with God.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley and Calvin understand the restriction as preserving reverence for what God has set apart. Calvin also connects the incense’s pleasing fragrance with the acceptance of His people’s prayers. Their emphasis here is on honoring the purpose for which God sets the blend apart.

passages.god_plan_html:
The New Testament explicitly uses incense as an image of God’s people’s prayers. In Revelation 5:6–10, golden bowls of incense are identified with the prayers of the saints before the Lamb, who has redeemed people from every nation and made them a kingdom and priests.

Revelation 8:1–5 presents incense with the saints’ prayers rising before God, followed by fire from the altar cast to the earth. The vision places their prayers within God’s dealings with the world. The worship symbol reaches beyond a fragrance in Israel’s sanctuary to the prayers of the people He redeems and the action of the God who hears them.

passages.title: Exodus 31:1-11
passages.section_title: Who will do the work God has commanded?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then the LORD said to Moses, 2 “See, I have called by name Bezalel son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah. 3 And I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with skill, ability, and knowledge in all kinds of craftsmanship, 4 to design artistic works in gold, silver, and bronze, 5 to cut gemstones for settings, and to carve wood, so that he may be a master of every craft. 6 Moreover, I have selected Oholiab son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan, as his assistant. I have also given skill to all the craftsmen, that they may fashion all that I have commanded you: 7 the Tent of Meeting, the ark of the Testimony and the mercy seat upon it, and all the other furnishings of the tent— 8 the table with its utensils, the pure gold lampstand with all its utensils, the altar of incense, 9 the altar of burnt offering with all its utensils, and the basin with its stand— 10 as well as the woven garments, both the holy garments for Aaron the priest and the garments for his sons to serve as priests, 11 in addition to the anointing oil and fragrant incense for the Holy Place. They are to make them according to all that I have commanded you.”

6 Moreover, I have selected Oholiab son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan, as his assistant. I have also given skill to all the craftsmen, that they may fashion all that I have commanded you: 7 the Tent of Meeting, the ark of the Testimony and the mercy seat upon it, and all the other furnishings of the tent— 8 the table with its utensils, the pure gold lampstand with all its utensils, the altar of incense, 9 the altar of burnt offering with all its utensils, and the basin with its stand— 10 as well as the woven garments, both the holy garments for Aaron the priest and the garments for his sons to serve as priests, 11 in addition to the anointing oil and fragrant incense for the Holy Place. They are to make them according to all that I have commanded you.”

passages.context_html:
God has described the tent, its furnishings, the priests’ clothing, the oil, and the incense. Now He names the people who will make them. Bezalel comes from Judah; Oholiab, his assistant, comes from Dan. The work also involves a wider group of skilled craftsmen. Moses receives the instructions, but he will not carry them out alone.

Being filled with God’s Spirit here includes the ability to design, work metal, cut stones, and carve wood. The passage gives careful craftsmanship a place in serving God. It does not tell us how much training these workers had before this assignment. What it does say is that God supplies the skill needed to carry out His instructions.

The list in verses 7–11 brings the earlier instructions together into one shared task. Their freedom to design and make beautiful things serves a clear purpose: they are to produce what God has commanded. The next passage sets a limit even on this important work—the Sabbath must still be kept.
passages.common_interpretations_html: John Wesley and John Calvin both read these verses as a reminder that practical skill comes from God and should lead to gratitude. Calvin includes the growth of abilities a person already has; neither prayer nor dependence on God makes the actual work unnecessary.

passages.god_plan_html:
The Bible’s opening picture of creation includes the Spirit of God at work over the waters (Genesis 1:1–3). Here the same God equips people to prepare a place for His presence among Israel. This is a useful parallel: God’s Spirit brings the ability to carry out His purpose, including work that others can see and use.

In the New Testament, Paul describes the Spirit giving different gifts for the good of the whole body of Christ. No member can dismiss another as unnecessary (1 Corinthians 12:4–13, 18–27). The craftsmen are not a detailed code for those gifts, but their shared work helps us see the larger pattern: God equips different people to serve His people together. Peter puts the responsibility plainly—use the gift you have received to serve others, with the strength God provides (1 Peter 4:10–11).

passages.title: Exodus 31:12-17
passages.section_title: Why must the builders stop and rest?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 And the LORD said to Moses, 13 “Tell the Israelites, ‘Surely you must keep My Sabbaths, for this will be a sign between Me and you for the generations to come, so that you may know that I am the LORD who sanctifies you. 14 Keep the Sabbath, for it is holy to you. Anyone who profanes it must surely be put to death. Whoever does any work on that day must be cut off from among his people. 15 For six days work may be done, but the seventh day is a Sabbath of complete rest, holy to the LORD. Whoever does any work on the Sabbath day must surely be put to death. 16 The Israelites must keep the Sabbath, celebrating it as a permanent covenant for the generations to come. 17 It is a sign between Me and the Israelites forever; for in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, but on the seventh day He rested and was refreshed.’”
paragraphs: 12 And the LORD said to Moses, 13 “Tell the Israelites, ‘Surely you must keep My Sabbaths, for this will be a sign between Me and you for the generations to come, so that you may know that I am the LORD who sanctifies you. 14 Keep the Sabbath, for it is holy to you. Anyone who profanes it must surely be put to death. Whoever does any work on that day must be cut off from among his people.

15 For six days work may be done, but the seventh day is a Sabbath of complete rest, holy to the LORD. Whoever does any work on the Sabbath day must surely be put to death. 16 The Israelites must keep the Sabbath, celebrating it as a permanent covenant for the generations to come. 17 It is a sign between Me and the Israelites forever; for in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, but on the seventh day He rested and was refreshed.’”

passages.context_html:
Before Moses leaves the mountain, God returns to the Sabbath. Its place here matters. Israel has important work to do for God, but the command to rest still stands. The seventh day belongs to the LORD; building His tent does not make every day a working day.

God calls the Sabbath a sign between Himself and Israel through their generations. It identifies the people He sets apart for Himself and recalls His work in creation. The death penalty shows how seriously this covenant treats its violation. These verses address Israel under that covenant; they do not instruct churches to execute people for working.

The closing description of God being refreshed uses the Hebrew verb נָפַשׁ, naphash (nah-FASH), meaning to take breath or refresh oneself (Brown–Driver–Briggs). The wording gives Israel a pattern of work followed by rest. It should be read alongside Isaiah’s statement that the Creator does not grow tired or weary (Isaiah 40:28). God is not recovering from weakness.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley reads the Sabbath as a sign that God has set Israel apart, with rest serving both His honor and His people’s good. Christian traditions differ over how this command applies after Christ.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, 21.7–8, teaches that God still requires one day in seven for worship and rest, with Sunday now the Christian Sabbath. The Catholic Catechism, 2174–2176, presents Sunday as the fulfillment of the Sabbath through Christ’s resurrection.

Luther’s Large Catechism, 80–90, emphasizes rest and hearing God’s Word; it keeps Sunday for an orderly gathering without making that day intrinsically holier. Seventh-day Adventists retain seventh-day Sabbath observance. These differences concern the command’s continuing application; the passage itself explicitly names Israel as the people receiving this covenant sign.

passages.god_plan_html:
The instructions for God’s dwelling echo the creation account. Across Exodus 25–31, seven separate speeches begin with God speaking to Moses: 25:1; 30:11, 17, 22, 34; and 31:1, 12. The last concerns rest. That arrangement makes a meaningful literary parallel with creation’s six days of work followed by the seventh day of rest (Exodus 25; Exodus 30; Genesis 2:1–3). Both accounts bring work to completion and lead into rest.

Hebrews takes God’s creation rest further. It quotes the seventh day, recalls Israel’s failure to enter because of disobedience, and urges its readers to hear God today and enter His rest through faith (Hebrews 4:1–11). Paul also connects the calendar’s Sabbaths with what finds its substance in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17). Beyond the question of which day to observe, these passages direct us toward God’s purpose of bringing His people into His rest.

passages.title: Exodus 31:18
passages.section_title: Why does God give Moses the commands on stone?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 When the LORD had finished speaking with Moses on Mount Sinai, He gave him the two tablets of the Testimony, tablets of stone inscribed by the finger of God.
paragraphs: 18 When the LORD had finished speaking with Moses on Mount Sinai, He gave him the two tablets of the Testimony, tablets of stone inscribed by the finger of God.

passages.context_html:
The mountain instructions end with something Moses can carry back to Israel: two stone tablets inscribed by God. God has already spoken His commands to the people; now Moses receives their written testimony. Deuteronomy identifies the writing as the Ten Commandments and connects the tablets with the words Israel heard at the mountain (Deuteronomy 4:9–14; 9:9–11).

The chapter closes with God giving His testimony. The next chapter turns to what the people have been doing while Moses is away. That contrast matters: the covenant is not simply an agreement Israel has devised, and the people’s response will be measured against what God has said.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley and Calvin understand God’s finger here as His direct power and authorship: the inscription comes from God. Both also explain the tablets as a lasting witness to His will; the verse does not describe the physical shape of God or state how the commands were divided between the two stones.
