passages.god_plan_html:
Paul later draws an explicit contrast between stone tablets and human hearts. The Corinthians are a letter from Christ, written by the Spirit of the living God on hearts rather than stone (2 Corinthians 3:1–6). He does not dismiss Sinai as something worthless: he calls its ministry glorious, then explains the greater glory of the Spirit’s life-giving work (2 Corinthians 3:7–11).

The connection shows a larger purpose than preserving instructions in writing. Through Christ, God is at work in the people who receive His word, giving life and making them a living testimony that others can read. The stone tablets belong to the unfolding story of that greater work.

passages.title: Exodus 32:1-35
passages.section_title: What happens when Israel turns to the golden calf?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now when the people saw that Moses was delayed in coming down from the mountain, they gathered around Aaron and said, “Come, make us gods who will go before us. As for this Moses who brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has happened to him!” 2 So Aaron told them, “Take off the gold earrings that are on your wives and sons and daughters, and bring them to me.” 3 Then all the people took off their gold earrings and brought them to Aaron. 4 He took the gold from their hands, and with an engraving tool he fashioned it into a molten calf. And they said, “These, O Israel, are your gods, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt!” 5 When Aaron saw this, he built an altar before the calf and proclaimed: “Tomorrow shall be a feast to the LORD.” 6 So the next day they arose, offered burnt offerings, and presented peace offerings. And the people sat down to eat and drink and got up to indulge in revelry. 7 Then the LORD said to Moses, “Go down at once, for your people, whom you brought up out of the land of Egypt, have corrupted themselves. 8 How quickly they have turned aside from the way that I commanded them! They have made for themselves a molten calf and have bowed down to it. They have sacrificed to it and said, ‘These, O Israel, are your gods, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt.’” 9 The LORD also said to Moses, “I have seen this people, and they are indeed a stiff-necked people. 10 Now leave Me alone, so that My anger may burn against them and consume them. Then I will make you into a great nation.” 11 But Moses sought the favor of the LORD his God, saying, “O LORD, why does Your anger burn against Your people, whom You brought out of the land of Egypt with great power and a mighty hand? 12 Why should the Egyptians declare, ‘He brought them out with evil intent, to kill them in the mountains and wipe them from the face of the earth’? Turn from Your fierce anger and relent from doing harm to Your people. 13 Remember Your servants Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, to whom You swore by Your very self when You declared, ‘I will make your descendants as numerous as the stars in the sky, and I will give your descendants all this land that I have promised, and it shall be their inheritance forever.’” 14 So the LORD relented from the calamity He had threatened to bring on His people. 15 Then Moses turned and went down the mountain with the two tablets of the Testimony in his hands. They were inscribed on both sides, front and back. 16 The tablets were the work of God, and the writing was the writing of God, engraved on the tablets. 17 When Joshua heard the sound of the people shouting, he said to Moses, “The sound of war is in the camp.” 18 But Moses replied: “It is neither the cry of victory nor the cry of defeat; I hear the sound of singing!” 19 As Moses approached the camp and saw the calf and the dancing, he burned with anger and threw the tablets out of his hands, shattering them at the base of the mountain. 20 Then he took the calf they had made, burned it in the fire, ground it to powder, and scattered the powder over the face of the water. Then he forced the Israelites to drink it. 21 “What did this people do to you,” Moses asked Aaron, “that you have led them into so great a sin?” 22 “Do not be enraged, my lord,” Aaron replied. “You yourself know that the people are intent on evil. 23 They told me, ‘Make us gods who will go before us. As for this Moses who brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has happened to him!’ 24 So I said to them, ‘Whoever has gold, let him take it off,’ and they gave it to me. And when I threw it into the fire, out came this calf!” 25 Moses saw that the people were out of control, for Aaron had let them run wild and become a laughingstock to their enemies. 26 So Moses stood at the entrance to the camp and said, “Whoever is for the LORD, come to me.” And all the Levites gathered around him. 27 He told them, “This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘Each of you men is to fasten his sword to his side, go back and forth through the camp from gate to gate, and slay his brother, his friend, and his neighbor.’” 28 The Levites did as Moses commanded, and that day about three thousand of the people fell dead. 29 Afterward, Moses said, “Today you have been ordained for service to the LORD, since each man went against his son and his brother; so the LORD has bestowed a blessing on you this day.” 30 The next day Moses said to the people, “You have committed a great sin. Now I will go up to the LORD; perhaps I can make atonement for your sin.” 31 So Moses returned to the LORD and said, “Oh, what a great sin these people have committed! They have made gods of gold for themselves. 32 Yet now, if You would only forgive their sin.... But if not, please blot me out of the book that You have written.” 33 The LORD replied to Moses, “Whoever has sinned against Me, I will blot out of My book. 34 Now go, lead the people to the place I described. Behold, My angel shall go before you. But on the day I settle accounts, I will punish them for their sin.” 35 And the LORD sent a plague on the people because of what they had done with the calf that Aaron had made.

Now I will go up to the LORD; perhaps I can make atonement for your sin.” 31 So Moses returned to the LORD and said, “Oh, what a great sin these people have committed! passages.context_html:
While Moses is on the mountain receiving instructions for God’s dwelling, the people ask Aaron to make gods to go before them. Their stated reason is that Moses has been away and they do not know what has happened to him. Aaron collects their earrings, makes a calf, builds an altar, and announces a feast to the LORD. Giving the celebration God’s name does not make it faithful worship: God says the people have turned aside from His command and bowed down to the calf.

God tells Moses what has happened and announces judgment. Moses pleads for the people by appealing to what God has already done: He rescued them from Egypt, His name is known through that rescue, and He swore promises to Abraham, Isaac, and Israel. Moses does not defend the calf or claim the people deserve protection. Verse 14 says God relents from the threatened destruction.

The Hebrew verb נָחַם, nacham (nah-KHAHM), can describe relenting from a threatened action; the lexicon specifically includes verses 12 and 14 under this use (Brown–Driver–Briggs). The word does not by itself mean that God has confessed a moral wrong. Here the action in view is the calamity He had announced.

Moses then sees the calf and dancing for himself. He breaks the tablets, destroys the calf, and makes the people drink water containing its powder. Aaron’s explanation tries to distance him from the result, but it conflicts with the earlier account: he had deliberately fashioned the calf. The narrator also holds him responsible for letting the people run out of control.

At Moses’ call, the Levites gather to him and carry out a severe judgment in which about three thousand die. The command reaches even close relationships; family loyalty does not excuse this covenant violation. The chapter does not identify every victim or give us a list of ringleaders. This is a particular judgment in Israel’s covenant history, not a command for Christians to use violence against people they consider unfaithful.

The next day Moses returns to ask forgiveness and even offers to be blotted out of God’s book. God holds the sinners accountable rather than accepting Moses’ offer in their place. Israel is told to continue toward the promised destination, but the chapter also records a plague. Being spared total destruction has not made the sin harmless or removed every consequence.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Calvin both see a warning against inventing worship and then using God’s name to justify it. They also take Moses’ prayer seriously. Wesley emphasizes God’s willingness to hear persistent prayer; Calvin explains the relenting as a change in God’s dealings with the people, without a reversal of His settled purpose. Both read the threatened destruction as something God does not carry out after Moses pleads.

Readers differ over how much the feast’s revelry tells us. Wesley sees foolish, sexually improper behavior; Calvin reads the eating and play as the feast and celebrations surrounding idol worship and rejects the claim that the words themselves establish sexual misconduct. The Hebrew word’s range includes play and, in other settings, sexual behavior, so the word alone does not prove that this gathering was a mass orgy. The passage clearly condemns their idolatry.

The book in verses 32–33 is another point of discussion. John Gill surveys a record of earthly life, making Moses’ request an offer to die, and a record of eternal life, making it an expression of his willingness to lose everything for the people. Calvin takes the latter reading but understands the language of erasure as God exposing those who do not truly belong to Him, rather than undoing His choice of the saved. These are commentators’ explanations; the verse itself does not identify the book in greater detail.

Across those readings, Moses’ concern for the people and God’s refusal to ignore their guilt remain central. Moses is a mediator who pleads for mercy, not someone who can make the calf acceptable or compel God to treat the innocent as guilty.

passages.god_plan_html:
Paul explicitly brings this event into his instruction to Christians. In 1 Corinthians 10:1–14, he recalls Israel’s rescue and provision, quotes the description of the feast, and warns against idolatry and overconfidence. Sharing in remarkable gifts from God did not make the people unable to fall. His purpose is practical: believers are to take the warning seriously and flee idolatry, trusting God’s faithfulness in temptation.

Moses’ pleading also gives a meaningful parallel with Christ, while showing the limits of the comparison. Psalm 106:19–23 remembers Moses standing between the people and destruction. Yet this chapter does not say that his own life pays for their sins. The New Testament describes the greater work of Jesus: He is sinless, offers Himself once for all, and lives permanently to intercede for those who come to God through Him (Hebrews 7:23–28). His redemption also reaches transgressions committed under the first covenant (Hebrews 9:11–15).

The timing of the calf exposes a problem that instructions alone cannot cure. Israel has heard God’s commands and still turns away. Paul explains the larger answer in Romans 8:1–4: what the law could not accomplish because of human weakness, God accomplished through His Son, bringing His people into life by the Spirit. God’s purpose reaches beyond identifying wrongdoing to rescuing people from its power.

passages.title: Exodus 33:1-6
passages.section_title: What would the promised land mean without God’s presence?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then the LORD said to Moses, “Leave this place, you and the people you brought up out of the land of Egypt, and go to the land that I promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob when I said, ‘I will give it to your descendants.’ 2 And I will send an angel before you, and I will drive out the Canaanites, Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites. 3 Go up to a land flowing with milk and honey. But I will not go with you, because you are a stiff-necked people; otherwise, I might destroy you on the way.” 4 When the people heard this bad news, they went into mourning, and no one put on any of his jewelry. 5 For the LORD had said to Moses, “Tell the Israelites, ‘You are a stiff-necked people. If I should go with you for a single moment, I would destroy you. Now take off your jewelry, and I will decide what to do with you.’” 6 So the Israelites stripped themselves of their jewelry from Mount Horeb onward.

Now take off your jewelry, and I will decide what to do with you.’” 6 So the Israelites stripped themselves of their jewelry from Mount Horeb onward.

passages.context_html:
After the golden calf, God still directs Israel toward the land He promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. He promises to send an angel and drive out the nations before them. The people’s sin has not made Him forget what He swore to their ancestors.

Yet the announcement includes terrible news: God will not go among this stubborn people, because His presence would expose them to destruction. This reaches the heart of the instructions Israel has just received. The tent was to be a place where God would dwell among them; reaching the land is not the whole purpose of their rescue.

The people mourn and take off their jewelry as God commands. Their response is different from the celebration around the calf. The chapter will now follow Moses’ plea for God to accompany them, so this announcement should be read as part of that unfolding conversation, not as its final outcome.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley and Calvin read the removal of ornaments as an outward expression of humiliation and mourning after sin. The deeper loss is God’s presence among His people: the promise of a destination does not remove their need to be reconciled to Him.

passages.god_plan_html:
These verses raise a question that runs through Scripture: will God’s people receive His gifts while remaining distant from Him? His purpose goes further than providing a place to live. In John 14:15–23, Jesus promises the Spirit’s abiding presence and says He will not leave His disciples as orphans; the Father and Son will make their home with those who love Him and keep His word.

The Bible’s closing vision brings this purpose to its fullness: God dwells with His people, and death, mourning, and pain give way to life with Him (Revelation 21:1–4). That wider theme helps us understand why the threat in Exodus is so serious. God’s presence is central to the rescue, not an optional addition to its benefits.

passages.title: Exodus 33:7-11
passages.section_title: Why is the meeting tent outside the camp?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 Now Moses used to take the tent and pitch it at a distance outside the camp. He called it the Tent of Meeting, and anyone inquiring of the LORD would go to the Tent of Meeting outside the camp. 8 Then, whenever Moses went out to the tent, all the people would stand at the entrances to their own tents and watch Moses until he entered the tent. 9 As Moses entered the tent, the pillar of cloud would come down and remain at the entrance, and the LORD would speak with Moses. 10 When all the people saw the pillar of cloud standing at the entrance to the tent, they would stand up and worship, each one at the entrance to his own tent. 11 Thus the LORD would speak to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend. Then Moses would return to the camp, but his young assistant Joshua son of Nun would not leave the tent.
paragraphs: 7 Now Moses used to take the tent and pitch it at a distance outside the camp. He called it the Tent of Meeting, and anyone inquiring of the LORD would go to the Tent of Meeting outside the camp. 8 Then, whenever Moses went out to the tent, all the people would stand at the entrances to their own tents and watch Moses until he entered the tent. 9 As Moses entered the tent, the pillar of cloud would come down and remain at the entrance, and the LORD would speak with Moses. 10 When all the people saw the pillar of cloud standing at the entrance to the tent, they would stand up and worship, each one at the entrance to his own tent.
11 Thus the LORD would speak to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend. Then Moses would return to the camp, but his young assistant Joshua son of Nun would not leave the tent.

passages.context_html:
Moses pitches the meeting tent at a distance outside the camp. After the calf, that distance makes the broken relationship visible, yet it also leaves a place where people can seek the LORD. In the book’s narrative, the account of constructing the tabernacle still lies ahead; here the emphasis is on meeting God and hearing Him.

The people watch Moses go out, see the cloud at the entrance, and worship from their own tent doors. God continues speaking with Moses, and Joshua remains at the tent when Moses returns to the camp. The passage does not condemn the people’s worship or explain their private motives.

God speaks with Moses as a person speaks with a friend. This describes direct, familiar communication. Later in this same chapter, God tells Moses that he cannot see His face and live. Those two statements need to be read together: close conversation is not the same thing as an unrestricted sight of God’s glory. Numbers 12:5–8 likewise contrasts the clarity of God’s communication with Moses with the dreams and riddles given to other prophets.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Readers differ over which tent this is. Wesley treats it as a meeting place used before the later tabernacle; Gill considers Moses’ own tent or another earlier place of worship. Calvin rejects the private-tent explanation and identifies it as God’s sacred sanctuary, reading the arrangement of these events differently. All three see its distance from the camp as a sign of separation after the calf.

Wesley emphasizes the friendship and kindness in God’s speech to Moses; Calvin also distinguishes such close revelation from seeing God in His fullness. The phrase about speaking face to face need not be turned into a contradiction with verse 20.

passages.god_plan_html:
God’s clear communication with Moses serves the people, not Moses alone. Numbers 12:5–8 describes him as faithful in God’s house. Hebrews 3:1–6 takes up that description and points beyond him: Moses serves within God’s household, while Christ is the Son over it. His faithful service belongs to a larger story whose center is Jesus.

The New Testament also describes a greater nearness for God’s people together. Through Christ, Jews and Gentiles have access to the Father by one Spirit and are being built into a dwelling for God (Ephesians 2:13–22). This does not make every detail of the outside tent a prediction. It shows the wider direction of God’s work: bringing His people near to Himself.

passages.title: Exodus 33:12-23
passages.section_title: How does God answer Moses’ plea to know Him?

versions.text: 12 Then Moses said to the LORD, “Look, You have been telling me, ‘Lead this people up,’ but You have not let me know whom You will send with me. Yet You have said, ‘I know you by name, and you have found favor in My sight.’ 13 Now if indeed I have found favor in Your sight, please let me know Your ways, that I may know You and find favor in Your sight. Remember that this nation is Your people.” 14 And the LORD answered, “My Presence will go with you, and I will give you rest.” 15 “If Your Presence does not go with us,” Moses replied, “do not lead us up from here. 16 For how then can it be known that Your people and I have found favor in Your sight, unless You go with us? How else will we be distinguished from all the other people on the face of the earth?” 17 So the LORD said to Moses, “I will do this very thing you have asked, for you have found favor in My sight, and I know you by name.” 18 Then Moses said, “Please show me Your glory.” 19 “I will cause all My goodness to pass before you,” the LORD replied, “and I will proclaim My name—the LORD—in your presence. I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.” 20 But He added, “You cannot see My face, for no one can see Me and live.” 21 The LORD continued, “There is a place near Me where you are to stand upon a rock, 22 and when My glory passes by, I will put you in a cleft of the rock and cover you with My hand until I have passed by. 23 Then I will take My hand away, and you will see My back; but My face must not be seen.”

How else will we be distinguished from all the other people on the face of the earth?” 17 So the LORD said to Moses, “I will do this very thing you have asked, for you have found favor in My sight, and I know you by name.”

18 Then Moses said, “Please show me Your glory.” 19 “I will cause all My goodness to pass before you,” the LORD replied, “and I will proclaim My name—the LORD—in your presence. I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.” 20 But He added, “You cannot see My face, for no one can see Me and live.”

21 The LORD continued, “There is a place near Me where you are to stand upon a rock, 22 and when My glory passes by, I will put you in a cleft of the rock and cover you with My hand until I have passed by. 23 Then I will take My hand away, and you will see My back; but My face must not be seen.”

passages.context_html:
Moses does not settle for reaching the land without God. He asks to know God’s ways and insists that the people need His presence with them. What distinguishes Israel is not merely where they are going, but the God who goes with them. God agrees to Moses’ request and promises His presence and rest.

The word translated favor is חֵן, chen (KHAYN), meaning favor or grace. Brown–Driver–Briggs includes these verses among examples of finding favor with God. Moses appeals to the relationship God has given him; he does not claim that Israel’s conduct has earned this assurance.

Then Moses asks to see God’s glory. God answers by promising to make His goodness pass before him and to proclaim His name. He also declares His freedom to show mercy and compassion. Knowing God includes learning what He is like, not simply seeing something impressive.

The answer comes with protection and a limit. God places Moses in a cleft of the rock and shields him as His glory passes. Moses may see what God permits, described as His back, but not His face. The passage presents a real encounter while making clear that Moses cannot bear an unlimited sight of God.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley and Calvin both understand the limited sight as an act of kindness toward a human being unable to bear God’s full glory. They also read the promise of mercy as freely given, not something creatures can demand as a debt. Their explanations keep God’s goodness and His freedom together.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
Paul directly quotes God’s declaration to Moses in Romans 9:14–18, explaining that mercy rests on God rather than human desire or effort. The words spoken after Israel’s sin become part of his explanation of God’s mercy in the larger story of salvation.

Moses’ desire to know God also leads us toward what the New Testament says about Jesus. John 1:14–18 describes the Word dwelling among us, revealing glory, grace, and truth, and making the unseen God known. Paul says that God gives the knowledge of His glory in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:3–6). God’s self-revelation reaches beyond this protected glimpse on the mountain.

There is a further parallel in the prayers. Moses pleads for his people to have God’s presence; Jesus prays for His people to be with Him and see His glory (John 17:18–24). The prayers are not identical, but both concern a people brought near to God through the one who pleads for them. Revelation’s closing hope is that God’s servants will see His face (Revelation 22:1–5).

passages.title: Exodus 34:1-9
passages.section_title: What does God reveal when He proclaims His name?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then the LORD said to Moses, “Chisel out two stone tablets like the originals, and I will write on them the words that were on the first tablets, which you broke. 2 Be ready in the morning, and come up on Mount Sinai to present yourself before Me on the mountaintop. 3 No one may go up with you; in fact, no one may be seen anywhere on the mountain—not even the flocks or herds may graze in front of the mountain.” 4 So Moses chiseled out two stone tablets like the originals. He rose early in the morning, and taking the two stone tablets in his hands, he went up Mount Sinai as the LORD had commanded him. 5 And the LORD descended in a cloud, stood with him there, and proclaimed His name, the LORD. 6 Then the LORD passed in front of Moses and called out: “The LORD, the LORD God, is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness, 7 maintaining loving devotion to a thousand generations, forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin. Yet He will by no means leave the guilty unpunished; He will visit the iniquity of the fathers on their children and grandchildren to the third and fourth generations.” 8 Moses immediately bowed down to the ground and worshiped. 9 “O Lord,” he said, “if I have indeed found favor in Your sight, my Lord, please go with us. Although this is a stiff-necked people, forgive our iniquity and sin, and take us as Your inheritance.”

He rose early in the morning, and taking the two stone tablets in his hands, he went up Mount Sinai as the LORD had commanded him.

5 And the LORD descended in a cloud, stood with him there, and proclaimed His name, the LORD. 6 Then the LORD passed in front of Moses and called out: “The LORD, the LORD God, is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness, 7 maintaining loving devotion to a thousand generations, forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin. Yet He will by no means leave the guilty unpunished; He will visit the iniquity of the fathers on their children and grandchildren to the third and fourth generations.”

8 Moses immediately bowed down to the ground and worshiped. 9 “O Lord,” he said, “if I have indeed found favor in Your sight, my Lord, please go with us. Although this is a stiff-necked people, forgive our iniquity and sin, and take us as Your inheritance.”

passages.context_html:
God tells Moses to prepare two new stone tablets like the ones he broke. This is an important answer to the crisis after the calf: God is making a way for the covenant testimony to be restored. Moses goes up alone as commanded, carrying the tablets, and the LORD descends in the cloud.

The proclamation answers Moses’ request to see God’s glory. God declares His name and describes what He is like: compassionate, gracious, patient, faithful, and ready to forgive. This is not an abstract description detached from events. Israel has just sinned grievously, and Moses is seeking forgiveness and God’s continuing presence.

The loving devotion named here is חֶסֶד, chesed (KHEH-sed), a word for kindness or lovingkindness. Brown–Driver–Briggs includes God’s care, redemption, and covenant faithfulness among its uses, and specifically lists its pairing with faithfulness in this verse. The word helps us hear the depth of God’s goodness toward people who need mercy.

The same proclamation says that God does not leave the guilty unpunished and warns of judgment reaching across generations. His forgiveness is not indifference to evil. That warning also needs to be read alongside Ezekiel 18:19–23, where a child who turns from a parent’s wrongdoing is not condemned for that parent’s guilt. Scripture does not treat a family’s history as a reason that repentance and mercy are impossible.

Moses immediately bows down and worships. His next prayer includes himself with the people: he asks pardon for their iniquity and sin, asks God to go with them, and asks that He take them as His inheritance. God’s revealed character becomes the basis of his appeal.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley and Calvin both read the proclamation as holding God’s abundant mercy together with His holiness and justice. They understand Moses’ response as humble reverence and renewed dependence on the God who has made Himself known.
passages.current_position_html: As explained in Worship as the Early Church Knew It, Moses’ immediate bowing shows worship as reverent submission to God. The study uses this passage to show that worship involves the whole person responding to God, rather than simply naming music or an event.

passages.god_plan_html:
This proclamation continues to shape how God’s people approach Him. In Numbers 14:17–24, Moses appeals to these same words when Israel rebels again. God grants pardon while still announcing serious consequences. The name proclaimed on Sinai teaches the people whom they are asking for mercy; it does not become a formula that makes their choices unimportant.

The New Testament brings forgiveness and justice together in Christ. Romans 3:21–26 describes God freely justifying those who believe through Jesus’ redemption, while demonstrating His own righteousness. God’s purpose is not to choose between being merciful and being just. Through His Son, He deals with sin and gives grace to sinners.

John 1:14–18 also describes the Word’s glory in terms of grace and truth, and says that the Son makes God known. This is a meaningful connection with Moses’ encounter: the character God proclaims here is revealed to us through Jesus, who brings us the fullness of grace and truth.

passages.title: Exodus 34:10-35
passages.section_title: How does covenant renewal lead to a greater glory?

And they were afraid to approach him. 31 But Moses called out to them; so Aaron and all the leaders of the congregation returned to him, and Moses spoke to them. 32 And after this all the Israelites came near, and Moses commanded them to do everything that the LORD had told him on Mount Sinai.

And when he came out, he would tell the Israelites what he had been commanded, 35 and the Israelites would see that the face of Moses was radiant. So Moses would put the veil back over his face until he went in to speak with the LORD.

passages.context_html:
God announces covenant renewal and promises wonders among the people. The first commands address the danger they have just demonstrated: turning to other gods. Israel must not make agreements that draw them into the surrounding nations’ worship, share their sacrifices, or enter marriages that lead their children into the same practices. The repeated ban on molten gods speaks directly to the calf.

The instructions then restore the pattern of life God had given them: appointed feasts, redemption of firstborn sons, firstfruits, and Sabbath rest even during the busiest farming seasons. The firstborn sons are to be redeemed, not sacrificed. God also promises to protect their land when the men leave for the three annual appearances before Him. Their worship and ordinary livelihood belong to life under His care.

Moses is instructed to record the covenant words. He remains with the LORD forty days and nights without bread or water, and the tablets again carry the Ten Commandments. Deuteronomy 10:1–5 identifies the LORD as the one who writes the words on the replacement tablets. The covenant is being renewed here; the text does not postpone all renewal until the next generation.

When Moses comes down, his face is radiant from speaking with God, although he does not know it. Aaron and the people are afraid to approach, but he calls them near and gives them God’s commands. He puts on the veil after speaking. When he goes before the LORD, he removes it; when he comes out, the people hear the commands and see the radiance before he covers his face again.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley reads the repeated commands as God renewing the people’s life of worship after their invented feast around the calf. He and Calvin both understand the shining face as an honor God gives to Moses and to the message he brings, and they read the veil in light of Paul’s later explanation about Christ.

passages.god_plan_html:
The warning about sharing sacrifices reaches into the New Testament. Paul tells Christians to flee idolatry and explains that participation at an altar means sharing in its worship; they cannot belong at both the Lord’s table and the table of demons (1 Corinthians 10:14–22). The continuing issue is loyalty to God, not merely avoiding an object shaped like a calf.

The feasts also look beyond themselves in the New Testament. Paul calls Christ the sacrificed Passover lamb and uses unleavened bread to describe a life of sincerity and truth (1 Corinthians 5:6–8). He calls the risen Christ the firstfruits of those who will be raised (1 Corinthians 15:20–23). These are connections Paul himself makes, without requiring us to assign a hidden prediction to every detail of the calendar.

The clearest connection concerns Moses’ face and veil. Second Corinthians 3:7–18 says that the old covenant came with glory, yet the Spirit’s ministry has a greater, lasting glory. Paul describes Moses covering what was fading, then turns the veil into a picture of an inability to see clearly that is removed in Christ. When someone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away. God’s purpose reaches beyond one servant’s radiant face: by the Spirit, His people are being transformed into the Lord’s image and reflect His glory.

passages.title: Exodus 35:1-3
passages.section_title: Why does the work begin with a command to rest?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then Moses assembled the whole congregation of Israel and said to them, “These are the things that the LORD has commanded you to do: 2 For six days work may be done, but the seventh day shall be your holy day, a Sabbath of complete rest to the LORD. Whoever does any work on that day must be put to death. 3 Do not light a fire in any of your dwellings on the Sabbath day.”
paragraphs: 1 Then Moses assembled the whole congregation of Israel and said to them, “These are the things that the LORD has commanded you to do: 2 For six days work may be done, but the seventh day shall be your holy day, a Sabbath of complete rest to the LORD. Whoever does any work on that day must be put to death. 3 Do not light a fire in any of your dwellings on the Sabbath day.”

passages.context_html:
With the covenant renewed, Moses gathers the whole congregation to pass on God’s instructions. Before calling for materials or workers, he repeats the Sabbath command. Even the work of preparing God’s dwelling must fit within the rhythm He has commanded.

The seventh day is set apart for complete rest, with a severe penalty for violation. The prohibition on lighting a fire makes the command concrete within their dwellings. These instructions address Israel’s covenant life; their place here prevents the importance of the building project from becoming a reason to disregard God’s other commands.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley understands the fire restriction as applying to fires used for labor, such as metalworking. Calvin’s discussion reads the restriction more broadly, including food preparation. Both understand the sanctuary work as subject to the Sabbath rather than an exception to it.

passages.god_plan_html: The Bible’s theme of rest reaches beyond stopping a particular task. Hebrews 4:1–11 recalls God’s rest after creation and Israel’s failure to enter through unbelief. It calls its readers to hear God today and enter His rest through faith. The weekly command belongs within that larger story: God is bringing His people into life with Him, and even important service does not replace listening to Him and trusting His promise.

passages.title: Exodus 35:4-9
passages.section_title: What does God ask the people to bring?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 4 Moses also told the whole congregation of Israel, “This is what the LORD has commanded: 5 Take from among you an offering to the LORD. Let everyone whose heart is willing bring an offering to the LORD: gold, silver, and bronze; 6 blue, purple, and scarlet yarn; fine linen and goat hair; 7 ram skins dyed red and fine leather; acacia wood; 8 olive oil for the light; spices for the anointing oil and for the fragrant incense; 9 and onyx stones and gemstones to be mounted on the ephod and breastpiece.
paragraphs: 4 Moses also told the whole congregation of Israel, “This is what the LORD has commanded: 5 Take from among you an offering to the LORD. Let everyone whose heart is willing bring an offering to the LORD: gold, silver, and bronze; 6 blue, purple, and scarlet yarn; fine linen and goat hair; 7 ram skins dyed red and fine leather; acacia wood; 8 olive oil for the light; spices for the anointing oil and for the fragrant incense; 9 and onyx stones and gemstones to be mounted on the ephod and breastpiece.

passages.context_html:
Moses calls for the materials needed to make the dwelling and carry out its service: metals, yarn, linen, skins, wood, oil, spices, and gemstones. The list comes from the earlier instructions; the people are contributing toward a defined task rather than a collection with no stated purpose.

The invitation is directed to those whose hearts are willing. The Hebrew adjective נָדִיב, nadiv (nah-DEEV), can mean willing or generous; Brown–Driver–Briggs specifically lists the willing-heart expression in this verse. The command to make the dwelling is clear, while the contributions are invited as willing gifts.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Calvin emphasizes that the offerings were not extracted by force or necessity. He understands the willing heart as consistent with God’s grace at work within a person, rather than as a gift wrung from an unwilling donor.

passages.god_plan_html:
Paul connects generosity with the grace believers have received through Christ. In 2 Corinthians 8:1–15, the Macedonian churches give willingly, and Jesus’ self-giving becomes the reason for generosity. Paul also says an eager gift is accepted according to what a person has; his goal is to meet needs rather than burden one group to relieve another.

This gives a wider setting for willing contributions. God’s people share what they have because they have received His grace, so that others are served. The value of the response is not reduced to whether everyone can bring the same costly materials.

passages.title: Exodus 35:10-19
passages.section_title: Who will turn these gifts into a place of worship?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 Let every skilled craftsman among you come and make everything that the LORD has commanded: 11 the tabernacle with its tent and covering, its clasps and frames, its crossbars, posts, and bases; 12 the ark with its poles and mercy seat, and the veil to shield it; 13 the table with its poles, all its utensils, and the Bread of the Presence; 14 the lampstand for light with its accessories and lamps and oil for the light; 15 the altar of incense with its poles; the anointing oil and fragrant incense; the curtain for the doorway at the entrance to the tabernacle; 16 the altar of burnt offering with its bronze grate, its poles, and all its utensils; the basin with its stand; 17 the curtains of the courtyard with its posts and bases, and the curtain for the gate of the courtyard; 18 the tent pegs for the tabernacle and for the courtyard, along with their ropes; 19 and the woven garments for ministering in the holy place—both the holy garments for Aaron the priest and the garments for his sons to serve as priests.”
paragraphs: 10 Let every skilled craftsman among you come and make everything that the LORD has commanded: 11 the tabernacle with its tent and covering, its clasps and frames, its crossbars, posts, and bases; 12 the ark with its poles and mercy seat, and the veil to shield it; 13 the table with its poles, all its utensils, and the Bread of the Presence; 14 the lampstand for light with its accessories and lamps and oil for the light;

15 the altar of incense with its poles; the anointing oil and fragrant incense; the curtain for the doorway at the entrance to the tabernacle; 16 the altar of burnt offering with its bronze grate, its poles, and all its utensils; the basin with its stand; 17 the curtains of the courtyard with its posts and bases, and the curtain for the gate of the courtyard; 18 the tent pegs for the tabernacle and for the courtyard, along with their ropes; 19 and the woven garments for ministering in the holy place—both the holy garments for Aaron the priest and the garments for his sons to serve as priests.”

passages.context_html:
The appeal now moves from materials to skilled work. Moses invites the craftsmen to make everything God has commanded: the structure, furnishings, curtains, courtyard, utensils, and priestly garments. Giving supplies is only part of the task; people must also use their abilities to make and assemble them.

The list includes both prominent objects, such as the ark, and easily overlooked necessities, such as pegs and ropes. All belong to the same work. It also distinguishes the garments for Aaron and his sons from the other equipment, keeping the priestly service within the larger preparation of God’s dwelling.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Skilled work is itself part of Israel’s service to God. Calvin’s discussion of the craftsmen treats ordinary practical abilities as God’s gifts, which are to be used gratefully.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The shared work helps illustrate a wider biblical pattern. Romans 12:3–8 describes people who belong to one another in Christ while serving through different gifts—teaching, practical service, giving, leadership, encouragement, and mercy. Paul’s point is not that everyone has the same function, but that each should use what God has given.

The craftsmen are not a hidden list of those New Testament gifts. Their work provides a useful parallel: God’s purpose brings different contributions together. A community needs more than people who can supply resources; it also needs people who faithfully put their abilities to work for others.

passages.title: Exodus 35:20-29
passages.section_title: How do willing hearts become practical generosity?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 20 Then the whole congregation of Israel withdrew from the presence of Moses. 21 And everyone whose heart stirred him and whose spirit prompted him came and brought an offering to the LORD for the work on the Tent of Meeting, for all its services, and for the holy garments. 22 So all who had willing hearts, both men and women, came and brought brooches and earrings, rings and necklaces, and all kinds of gold jewelry. And they all presented their gold as a wave offering to the LORD. 23 Everyone who had blue, purple, or scarlet yarn, or fine linen, goat hair, ram skins dyed red, or articles of fine leather, brought them. 24 And all who could present an offering of silver or bronze brought it as a contribution to the LORD. Also, everyone who had acacia wood for any part of the service brought it. 25 Every skilled woman spun with her hands and brought what she had spun: blue, purple, or scarlet yarn, or fine linen. 26 And all the skilled women whose hearts were stirred spun the goat hair. 27 The leaders brought onyx stones and gemstones to mount on the ephod and breastpiece, 28 as well as spices and olive oil for the light, for the anointing oil, and for the fragrant incense. 29 So all the men and women of the Israelites whose hearts prompted them brought a freewill offering to the LORD for all the work that the LORD through Moses had commanded them to do.
paragraphs: 20 Then the whole congregation of Israel withdrew from the presence of Moses. 21 And everyone whose heart stirred him and whose spirit prompted him came and brought an offering to the LORD for the work on the Tent of Meeting, for all its services, and for the holy garments. 22 So all who had willing hearts, both men and women, came and brought brooches and earrings, rings and necklaces, and all kinds of gold jewelry. And they all presented their gold as a wave offering to the LORD. 23 Everyone who had blue, purple, or scarlet yarn, or fine linen, goat hair, ram skins dyed red, or articles of fine leather, brought them. 24 And all who could present an offering of silver or bronze brought it as a contribution to the LORD. Also, everyone who had acacia wood for any part of the service brought it.

25 Every skilled woman spun with her hands and brought what she had spun: blue, purple, or scarlet yarn, or fine linen. 26 And all the skilled women whose hearts were stirred spun the goat hair. 27 The leaders brought onyx stones and gemstones to mount on the ephod and breastpiece, 28 as well as spices and olive oil for the light, for the anointing oil, and for the fragrant incense. 29 So all the men and women of the Israelites whose hearts prompted them brought a freewill offering to the LORD for all the work that the LORD through Moses had commanded them to do.

passages.context_html:
The congregation leaves Moses, and people return with their contributions. Both men and women bring jewelry and materials. Skilled women spin yarn and goat hair, while the leaders bring stones, spices, and oil. The response includes possessions, practical skill, and time; it is not confined to people able to supply the most expensive items.

The repeated descriptions of willing hearts and stirred spirits show the character of the response. Verse 29 calls it a freewill offering. The Hebrew noun נְדָבָה, nedavah (neh-dah-VAH), means a voluntary offering; Brown–Driver–Briggs specifically includes the gifts for the dwelling in this verse. This is different from a fixed levy.

The passage describes those whose hearts prompted them to give. It should not be turned into a census proving that every individual in Israel contributed. What the account makes clear is that willing people brought what was needed, including work made by their own hands.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley sees willing giving rooted in love for God, gratitude, and desire for His presence. Calvin likewise emphasizes a sincere, voluntary response and explains God’s grace as working within the will rather than dragging an unwilling person. The vocabulary describes willing generosity; it is not, by itself, a complete account of every question about human freedom.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Second Corinthians 9:6–15 carries the theme into Christian giving. Paul asks each person to give from a settled decision rather than regret or compulsion. God supplies what is needed for good works, and generosity becomes more than the transfer of goods: it produces thanksgiving to God and care between His people.

That purpose helps us see what matters in the different gifts listed here. The contribution serves God’s work and other people, while the willing response honors the God who provides. Paul’s vision is a growing harvest of righteousness and generosity, not merely a larger collection.

passages.title: Exodus 35:30-35
passages.section_title: Why does God give the craftsmen the ability to teach?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 30 Then Moses said to the Israelites, “See, the LORD has called by name Bezalel son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah. 31 And He has filled him with the Spirit of God, with skill, ability, and knowledge in all kinds of craftsmanship, 32 to design artistic works in gold, silver, and bronze, 33 to cut gemstones for settings, and to carve wood, so that he may be a master of every artistic craft. 34 And the LORD has given both him and Oholiab son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan, the ability to teach others. 35 He has filled them with skill to do all kinds of work as engravers, designers, embroiderers in blue, purple, and scarlet yarn and fine linen, and as weavers—as artistic designers of every kind of craft.
paragraphs: 30 Then Moses said to the Israelites, “See, the LORD has called by name Bezalel son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah. 31 And He has filled him with the Spirit of God, with skill, ability, and knowledge in all kinds of craftsmanship, 32 to design artistic works in gold, silver, and bronze, 33 to cut gemstones for settings, and to carve wood, so that he may be a master of every artistic craft.

34 And the LORD has given both him and Oholiab son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan, the ability to teach others. 35 He has filled them with skill to do all kinds of work as engravers, designers, embroiderers in blue, purple, and scarlet yarn and fine linen, and as weavers—as artistic designers of every kind of craft.

passages.context_html:
Moses publicly names Bezalel and Oholiab, whose appointment God had already announced in chapter 31. Bezalel is filled with the Spirit of God for design and craftsmanship. The account gives practical work a place in the Spirit’s service: metal, stone, wood, embroidery, and weaving all contribute to the task.

There is an important addition here: God gives both men the ability to teach others. They are not simply to keep their skill to themselves. Their work includes helping others become able to take part, so the project draws on a wider company of workers.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley and Calvin both understand the craftsmen’s exceptional ability as God equipping them for their calling. Calvin also recognizes that they already had abilities that God further supplied; the passage does not require us to assume that they had never trained or worked before.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

deeper_study.title: The True Church According to Jesus

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The ability to teach belongs to a larger pattern of equipping others. In Ephesians 4:7–16, Christ gives gifts so that His people are prepared for service and the whole body grows toward maturity in Him. The gifts equip the whole body to serve and grow.

There is a further parallel in 2 Timothy 2:1–7: Timothy is to entrust what he has learned to faithful people who can teach others in turn. Paul is speaking about gospel teaching, not the tabernacle crafts, but both passages show ability being shared so that others can carry the work forward.

passages.title: Exodus 36:1-7
passages.section_title: Why does Moses stop the people from giving?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 “So Bezalel, Oholiab, and every skilled person are to carry out everything commanded by the LORD, who has given them skill and ability to know how to perform all the work of constructing the sanctuary.” 2 Then Moses summoned Bezalel, Oholiab, and every skilled person whom the LORD had gifted—everyone whose heart stirred him to come and do the work. 3 They received from Moses all the contributions that the Israelites had brought to carry out the service of constructing the sanctuary. Meanwhile, the people continued to bring freewill offerings morning after morning, 4 so that all the skilled craftsmen who were doing all the work on the sanctuary left their work 5 and said to Moses, “The people are bringing more than enough for doing the work the LORD has commanded us to do.” 6 After Moses had given an order, they sent a proclamation throughout the camp: “No man or woman should make anything else as an offering for the sanctuary.” So the people were restrained from bringing more, 7 since what they already had was more than enough to perform all the work.
paragraphs: 1 “So Bezalel, Oholiab, and every skilled person are to carry out everything commanded by the LORD, who has given them skill and ability to know how to perform all the work of constructing the sanctuary.” 2 Then Moses summoned Bezalel, Oholiab, and every skilled person whom the LORD had gifted—everyone whose heart stirred him to come and do the work. 3 They received from Moses all the contributions that the Israelites had brought to carry out the service of constructing the sanctuary. Meanwhile, the people continued to bring freewill offerings morning after morning,

4 so that all the skilled craftsmen who were doing all the work on the sanctuary left their work 5 and said to Moses, “The people are bringing more than enough for doing the work the LORD has commanded us to do.” 6 After Moses had given an order, they sent a proclamation throughout the camp: “No man or woman should make anything else as an offering for the sanctuary.” So the people were restrained from bringing more, 7 since what they already had was more than enough to perform all the work.

passages.context_html:
The appointed craftsmen begin the work with the skill God has given them. Moses calls those who have both the ability and the willingness to serve, and hands over the materials the people have brought. Contributions continue to arrive each morning even after construction begins.

Then the craftsmen leave their work to report that they have more than enough. Moses responds with a public order: people are to stop making further contributions for the sanctuary. The collection has a purpose, and that purpose determines when enough has been received. The materials already supplied are sufficient for the work.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Calvin sees both prudence and honesty here: Moses distributes the materials, the workers begin their task, and they report the surplus instead of quietly accepting more. Wesley also emphasizes the combination of ability and willingness in those called to the work.

deeper_study.title: The True Church According to Jesus

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The New Testament connects giving with meeting needs and handling gifts faithfully. In 2 Corinthians 8:10–24, Paul asks believers to complete a willing gift according to their means, directs surplus toward need, and takes care that the collection is administered honorably before God and people. Generosity and accountability belong together.

The greater goal is what God does among His people. Paul’s prayer in Ephesians 3:14–21 asks for strength through the Spirit, Christ dwelling in their hearts, and a deeper knowledge of His love. God’s ability to do more than we ask serves His glory in the church; the completed material collection is part of service to Him, rather than its final purpose.

passages.title: Exodus 36:8-13
passages.section_title: How do separate curtains become one dwelling?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 All the skilled craftsmen among the workmen made the ten curtains for the tabernacle. They were made of finely spun linen, as well as blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, with cherubim skillfully worked into them. 9 Each curtain was twenty-eight cubits long and four cubits wide; all the curtains were the same size. 10 And he joined five of the curtains together, and the other five he joined as well. 11 He made loops of blue material on the edge of the end curtain in the first set, and also on the end curtain in the second set. 12 He made fifty loops on one curtain and fifty loops on the end curtain of the second set, so that the loops lined up opposite one another. 13 He also made fifty gold clasps to join the curtains together, so that the tabernacle was a unit.
paragraphs: 8 All the skilled craftsmen among the workmen made the ten curtains for the tabernacle. They were made of finely spun linen, as well as blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, with cherubim skillfully worked into them. 9 Each curtain was twenty-eight cubits long and four cubits wide; all the curtains were the same size. 10 And he joined five of the curtains together, and the other five he joined as well.

11 He made loops of blue material on the edge of the end curtain in the first set, and also on the end curtain in the second set. 12 He made fifty loops on one curtain and fifty loops on the end curtain of the second set, so that the loops lined up opposite one another. 13 He also made fifty gold clasps to join the curtains together, so that the tabernacle was a unit.

passages.context_html:
The construction account begins with the inner curtains. Skilled workers make ten curtains of finely spun linen with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn and cherubim worked into them. Their measurements match the instructions Moses received in chapter 26.

Five curtains are joined into each of two sets, then loops and gold clasps connect the sets. The repeated parts become one whole dwelling. The description makes the workers’ obedience visible: the earlier instructions are now being carried out, piece by piece.
passages.common_interpretations_html: In his explanation of the corresponding instructions in chapter 26, Wesley sees the joined curtains as a picture of God’s people united in love and by the Spirit. Calvin emphasizes the exact correspondence between God’s directions and what the workers make.

Worship as the Early Church Knew It

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The joined curtains provide a useful parallel with the unity God creates through Christ. Ephesians 2:13–22 explains how Christ reconciles Jews and Gentiles to God through the cross and gives both access to the Father by one Spirit. Together they become a dwelling for God.

The comparison goes beyond getting separate pieces to fit. God brings people who were divided into a shared life with Himself. The curtains illustrate unity, while the New Testament explains its foundation in Christ’s reconciling work.

passages.title: Exodus 36:14-19
passages.section_title: Why are more coverings placed over the inner curtains?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 He then made curtains of goat hair for the tent over the tabernacle—eleven curtains in all. 15 Each of the eleven curtains was the same size—thirty cubits long and four cubits wide. 16 He joined five of the curtains into one set and the other six into another. 17 He made fifty loops along the edge of the end curtain in the first set, and fifty loops along the edge of the corresponding curtain in the second set. 18 He also made fifty bronze clasps to join the tent together as a unit. 19 Additionally, he made for the tent a covering of ram skins dyed red, and over that a covering of fine leather.
paragraphs: 14 He then made curtains of goat hair for the tent over the tabernacle—eleven curtains in all. 15 Each of the eleven curtains was the same size—thirty cubits long and four cubits wide. 16 He joined five of the curtains into one set and the other six into another. 17 He made fifty loops along the edge of the end curtain in the first set, and fifty loops along the edge of the corresponding curtain in the second set. 18 He also made fifty bronze clasps to join the tent together as a unit.
19 Additionally, he made for the tent a covering of ram skins dyed red, and over that a covering of fine leather.

passages.context_html:
The workers next make the goat-hair tent over the linen dwelling. It has eleven curtains, longer than the inner curtains, arranged in sets of five and six. Loops and bronze clasps join them into a unit, following the instructions already given in chapter 26.

Two further coverings go over the tent: ram skins dyed red and an outer covering of fine leather. The account distinguishes these layers from the decorated linen inside. They belong to the practical completion of a dwelling that will travel with Israel.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley understands the outer covering as protection for the dwelling, while Calvin reads the repeated construction details as evidence of careful obedience.

passages.title: Exodus 36:20-34
passages.section_title: What holds the dwelling together?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 20 Next, he constructed upright frames of acacia wood for the tabernacle. 21 Each frame was ten cubits long and a cubit and a half wide. 22 Two tenons were connected to each other for each frame. He made all the frames of the tabernacle in this way. 23 He constructed twenty frames for the south side of the tabernacle, 24 with forty silver bases to put under the twenty frames—two bases for each frame, one under each tenon. 25 For the second side of the tabernacle, the north side, he made twenty frames 26 and forty silver bases—two bases under each frame. 27 He made six frames for the rear of the tabernacle, the west side, 28 and two frames for the two back corners of the tabernacle, 29 coupled together from bottom to top and fitted into a single ring. He made both corners in this way. 30 So there were eight frames and sixteen silver bases—two under each frame. 31 He also made five crossbars of acacia wood for the frames on one side of the tabernacle, 32 five for those on the other side, and five for those on the rear side of the tabernacle, to the west. 33 He made the central crossbar to run through the center of the frames, from one end to the other. 34 And he overlaid the frames with gold and made gold rings to hold the crossbars. He also overlaid the crossbars with gold.

He made all the frames of the tabernacle in this way. 23 He constructed twenty frames for the south side of the tabernacle, 24 with forty silver bases to put under the twenty frames—two bases for each frame, one under each tenon. 25 For the second side of the tabernacle, the north side, he made twenty frames 26 and forty silver bases—two bases under each frame.

27 He made six frames for the rear of the tabernacle, the west side, 28 and two frames for the two back corners of the tabernacle, 29 coupled together from bottom to top and fitted into a single ring. He made both corners in this way. 30 So there were eight frames and sixteen silver bases—two under each frame.

31 He also made five crossbars of acacia wood for the frames on one side of the tabernacle, 32 five for those on the other side, and five for those on the rear side of the tabernacle, to the west. 33 He made the central crossbar to run through the center of the frames, from one end to the other. 34 And he overlaid the frames with gold and made gold rings to hold the crossbars. He also overlaid the crossbars with gold.

passages.context_html:
The frames now provide the dwelling’s upright structure. Acacia frames stand in silver bases along the south and north sides and at the back, with special arrangements for the corners. Crossbars connect the frames, including a central bar that runs from one end to the other.

The frames and bars are overlaid with gold, and gold rings hold the bars. These are the supports beneath the curtains and coverings just described. The later inventory identifies the silver used for the bases as coming from those counted in the census (Exodus 38:25–28). The gifts are becoming a complete, joined structure.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Calvin reads the repeated measurements and construction details as a record of the workers following God’s design faithfully. The supports are practical parts of the dwelling, and their craftsmanship belongs to the people’s obedience just as much as the more prominent furnishings.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The New Testament uses building language to explain God’s work among His people. In 1 Corinthians 3:10–17, Christ is the foundation, workers must take care how they build, and the community is God’s holy temple because His Spirit dwells among them.

As a broader biblical parallel, a carefully joined dwelling helps us picture a people being built together. Paul directs our attention to Christ as their foundation and to the responsibility of those who serve them.

passages.title: Exodus 36:35-36
passages.section_title: What does the inner veil separate?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 35 Next, he made the veil of blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and finely spun linen, with cherubim skillfully worked into it. 36 He also made four posts of acacia wood for it and overlaid them with gold, along with gold hooks; and he cast four silver bases for the posts.
paragraphs: 35 Next, he made the veil of blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and finely spun linen, with cherubim skillfully worked into it. 36 He also made four posts of acacia wood for it and overlaid them with gold, along with gold hooks; and he cast four silver bases for the posts.

passages.context_html:
The workers make the inner veil from blue, purple, and scarlet yarn and finely spun linen, with cherubim worked into it. Four acacia posts overlaid with gold, supported by silver bases, hold it in place.

This is the partition described in Exodus 26:31–35, separating the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place where the ark belongs. It is different from the entrance curtain made next. Its beauty does not remove the boundary it establishes.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley understands the veil as marking the distance and limited revelation of the old covenant compared with the nearness opened in the New Testament. He also looks toward the fuller knowledge of God that His people will enjoy with Him.
passages.current_position_html: As explained in The True Church According to Jesus, Christ’s torn veil means that every believer now has direct access to God and a calling to minister. That existing conclusion guides our application here: access to God through Christ is shared by His people.

deeper_study.title: The True Church According to Jesus
Worship as the Early Church Knew It

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 10:19–25 makes the connection with Christ explicit. Believers can enter the Most Holy Place by Jesus’ blood, through the living way opened through the curtain of His body. The response is to draw near in faith, hold firmly to hope, and encourage one another in love and good deeds.

The movement is from restricted approach to confident access through Christ. That access also creates responsibility toward other people: Hebrews joins drawing near to God with gathering and encouraging His people.

passages.title: Exodus 36:37-38
passages.section_title: How is the entrance different from the inner veil?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 37 For the entrance to the tent, he made a curtain embroidered with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and finely spun linen, 38 together with five posts and their hooks. He overlaid the tops of the posts and their bands with gold, and their five bases were bronze.
paragraphs: 37 For the entrance to the tent, he made a curtain embroidered with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and finely spun linen, 38 together with five posts and their hooks. He overlaid the tops of the posts and their bands with gold, and their five bases were bronze.

passages.context_html:
The final item in this chapter is the curtain at the tent’s entrance. It uses the same named colors and fine linen as the inner veil, but it is supported by five posts with bronze bases. The inner veil had four posts and silver bases.

This curtain marks the way from the courtyard into the tent, while the inner veil separates the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place. Keeping those locations distinct helps us follow the later arrangement of the furnishings and the different areas of service.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley reads the entrance curtain as dividing the Holy Place from the courtyard. Calvin’s explanation of the chapter keeps the emphasis on carrying out God’s instructions in each part of the dwelling.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The entrance belongs to Scripture’s larger concern with approaching God. Jesus says that people come to the Father through Him (John 14:1–7); Paul describes access to the Father through Christ by one Spirit (Ephesians 2:13–22).

These passages identify the way God brings His people near. The tent’s entrance belongs to the earlier pattern of approach; the New Testament directs our hope toward a life with the Father through His Son.

passages.title: Exodus 37:1-5
passages.section_title: Why does the furniture begin with the ark?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Bezalel went on to construct the ark of acacia wood, two and a half cubits long, a cubit and a half wide, and a cubit and a half high. 2 He overlaid it with pure gold, both inside and out, and made a gold molding around it. 3 And he cast four gold rings for its four feet, two rings on one side and two on the other. 4 Then he made poles of acacia wood and overlaid them with gold. 5 He inserted the poles into the rings on the sides of the ark in order to carry it.
paragraphs: 1 Bezalel went on to construct the ark of acacia wood, two and a half cubits long, a cubit and a half wide, and a cubit and a half high. 2 He overlaid it with pure gold, both inside and out, and made a gold molding around it. 3 And he cast four gold rings for its four feet, two rings on one side and two on the other. 4 Then he made poles of acacia wood and overlaid them with gold. 5 He inserted the poles into the rings on the sides of the ark in order to carry it.

passages.context_html:
With the dwelling’s structure made, the account turns to its furnishings. Bezalel makes the ark from acacia wood, overlays it with gold inside and out, and provides rings and gold-covered poles for carrying it. This is the chest God instructed Moses to make for the covenant testimony in Exodus 25:10–16.

The ark belongs in the innermost room, behind the veil. The next passage describes its golden cover and cherubim. Keeping the ark and its cover together helps us understand their purpose: the testimony of God’s covenant is kept where He promises to meet with His people.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Calvin reads the close match between the command and the finished ark as a testimony to faithful obedience. Gill understands Bezalel’s name as identifying the craftsman directing the work, without requiring the conclusion that he made every part alone.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 9:1–5, 23–28 recalls the ark within the earthly sanctuary, then directs attention to Christ entering heaven itself to appear before God on our behalf. The carefully made furnishings belong to an earlier pattern of worship that points beyond itself to His completed work.

The covenant testimony also belongs within God’s larger purpose for His people. Hebrews 8:8–12 describes the new covenant in terms of God’s laws written in minds and hearts, knowing Him, and receiving forgiveness. God’s aim reaches into the people themselves: His word shapes a people who belong to Him.

passages.title: Exodus 37:6-9
passages.section_title: Why is the ark covered by a mercy seat?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 He constructed a mercy seat of pure gold, two and a half cubits long and a cubit and a half wide. 7 He made two cherubim of hammered gold at the ends of the mercy seat, 8 one cherub on one end and one on the other, all made from one piece of gold. 9 And the cherubim had wings that spread upward, overshadowing the mercy seat. The cherubim faced each other, looking toward the mercy seat.
paragraphs: 6 He constructed a mercy seat of pure gold, two and a half cubits long and a cubit and a half wide. 7 He made two cherubim of hammered gold at the ends of the mercy seat, 8 one cherub on one end and one on the other, all made from one piece of gold. 9 And the cherubim had wings that spread upward, overshadowing the mercy seat. The cherubim faced each other, looking toward the mercy seat.

passages.context_html:
Bezalel makes the ark’s cover from pure gold, with two cherubim formed at its ends. Their wings overshadow the cover and their faces turn toward it. The dimensions match the length and width of the ark.

The BSB calls this cover the mercy seat. In the original instructions, God promises to meet Moses and speak from above it, between the cherubim (Exodus 25:17–22). The description prepares us for worship before a holy God who makes a way for His people to approach Him.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley reads the ark, mercy seat, and cherubim together as a picture of communion with a holy God through a mediator. He connects that reconciliation with Jesus Christ, while Calvin emphasizes the care taken to make the cover as God commanded.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The New Testament gives us an important connection in its wording. Hebrews 9:5 calls the mercy seat ἱλαστήριον, hilastērion (hi-las-TAY-ree-on). Thayer’s lexicon explains that the word can name this cover or the means of dealing with sin. Paul uses the same word for Christ in Romans 3:21–26, where the BSB renders it as an atoning sacrifice.

Readers discuss whether Paul especially has the mercy seat or the sacrifice in view. In either case, his explanation centers on God providing redemption through Jesus’ blood while demonstrating His righteousness. Hebrews 9:11–15 develops that greater work: Christ secures eternal redemption and cleanses the conscience so that His people can serve the living God.

passages.title: Exodus 37:10-16
passages.section_title: What is the table prepared to hold?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 He also made the table of acacia wood two cubits long, a cubit wide, and a cubit and a half high. 11 He overlaid it with pure gold and made a gold molding around it. 12 And he made a rim around it a handbreadth wide and put a gold molding on the rim. 13 He cast four gold rings for the table and fastened them to the four corners at its four legs. 14 The rings were placed close to the rim, to serve as holders for the poles used to carry the table. 15 He made the poles of acacia wood for carrying the table and overlaid them with gold. 16 He also made the utensils for the table out of pure gold: its plates and dishes, as well as its bowls and pitchers for pouring drink offerings.
paragraphs: 10 He also made the table of acacia wood two cubits long, a cubit wide, and a cubit and a half high. 11 He overlaid it with pure gold and made a gold molding around it. 12 And he made a rim around it a handbreadth wide and put a gold molding on the rim. 13 He cast four gold rings for the table and fastened them to the four corners at its four legs. 14 The rings were placed close to the rim, to serve as holders for the poles used to carry the table. 15 He made the poles of acacia wood for carrying the table and overlaid them with gold. 16 He also made the utensils for the table out of pure gold: its plates and dishes, as well as its bowls and pitchers for pouring drink offerings.

passages.context_html:
The table is made of acacia wood overlaid with gold, with a rim, rings, carrying poles, and gold utensils. Like the ark, it is prepared to travel with Israel. Its place is in the Holy Place, where the Bread of the Presence is to be kept before the LORD, as directed in Exodus 25:23–30.

Leviticus 24:5–9 explains the continuing service: twelve loaves are arranged before God, replaced each Sabbath, and eaten by Aaron and his sons in a holy place. The table therefore belongs to an ongoing relationship of worship and provision, not simply the furnishing of an empty room.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley compares the priestly bread with the fellowship offered at Christ’s table in the new covenant. He sees the later table as a fuller enjoyment of what the earlier sanctuary held at a distance.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It
The True Church According to Jesus

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
At the Passover meal, Jesus shares bread and a cup with His apostles and speaks of His body given for them and the new covenant in His blood (Luke 22:14–20). Later in the same conversation, He promises His faithful disciples a place to eat and drink at His table in His kingdom (Luke 22:28–30).

This provides a meaningful parallel with the sanctuary table. God’s purpose includes fellowship with His people, and Jesus connects that fellowship with His self-giving and the coming kingdom. The comparison follows the larger theme of a people welcomed before God.

passages.title: Exodus 37:17-24
passages.section_title: What is the purpose of the lampstand’s light?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 Then he made the lampstand out of pure hammered gold, all of one piece: its base and shaft, its cups, and its buds and petals. 18 Six branches extended from the sides, three on one side and three on the other. 19 There were three cups shaped like almond blossoms on the first branch, each with buds and petals, three on the next branch, and the same for all six branches that extended from the lampstand. 20 And on the lampstand were four cups shaped like almond blossoms with buds and petals. 21 A bud was under the first pair of branches that extended from the lampstand, a bud under the second pair, and a bud under the third pair. 22 The buds and branches were all of one piece with the lampstand, hammered out of pure gold. 23 He also made its seven lamps, its wick trimmers, and trays of pure gold. 24 He made the lampstand and all its utensils from a talent of pure gold.
