deeper_study.title: The True Church According to Jesus

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The New Testament places this period within the story that leads to Jesus. In Acts 13:16–23, Paul recalls the rescue from Egypt, the land, the judges, and the kings, then announces the Savior brought from David’s descendants as God promised. These temporary deliverances belong to God’s unfolding work of rescue.

Hebrews 11:32–40 also honors faith among figures from Judges, including Gideon, Barak, Samson, and Jephthah, while pointing toward the fuller promise. The next chapter directs believers to fix their eyes on Jesus (Hebrews 12:1–3). The Bible recognizes what God accomplished through imperfect servants and places the lasting hope in Christ.

passages.title: Judges 3:1-6
passages.section_title: What will Israel do when its faith is tested?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 These are the nations that the LORD left to test all the Israelites who had not known any of the wars in Canaan, 2 if only to teach warfare to the subsequent generations of Israel, especially to those who had not known it formerly: 3 the five rulers of the Philistines, all the Canaanites, the Sidonians, and the Hivites who lived in the mountains of Lebanon from Mount Baal-hermon to Lebo-hamath. 4 These nations were left to test the Israelites, to find out whether they would keep the commandments of the LORD, which He had given their fathers through Moses. 5 Thus the Israelites continued to live among the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites. 6 And they took the daughters of these people in marriage, gave their own daughters to their sons, and served their gods.
paragraphs: 1 These are the nations that the LORD left to test all the Israelites who had not known any of the wars in Canaan, 2 if only to teach warfare to the subsequent generations of Israel, especially to those who had not known it formerly: 3 the five rulers of the Philistines, all the Canaanites, the Sidonians, and the Hivites who lived in the mountains of Lebanon from Mount Baal-hermon to Lebo-hamath. 4 These nations were left to test the Israelites, to find out whether they would keep the commandments of the LORD, which He had given their fathers through Moses.

5 Thus the Israelites continued to live among the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites. 6 And they took the daughters of these people in marriage, gave their own daughters to their sons, and served their gods.

passages.context_html:
The previous chapter explained why the remaining nations would become a test for Israel. These verses name the peoples involved and describe a generation that had not experienced the earlier wars in Canaan. They would learn warfare, and their response would show whether they would obey the LORD’s commands.

The test concerns loyalty as well as fighting. Israel settles among the surrounding peoples, intermarriages follow, and the Israelites serve their gods. This is the danger named in Deuteronomy 7:1–6: family ties would draw God’s people away from Him into the worship of other gods.

The passage identifies that turning away as the failure. It does not make ancestry alone a measure of faithfulness. Elsewhere, Rahab acknowledges the LORD as God, and Ruth commits herself to Him (Joshua 2:8–14; Ruth 1:14–18). Here, however, the Israelites adopt the worship they had been warned against.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill take the teaching of warfare seriously as practical preparation for a generation without that experience. Wesley also emphasizes their need to stay close to God and depend on His help. Military experience and obedience belong together in this reading; practical skill does not replace trust in God.

Henry draws a further lesson for believers: pressures can reveal what is in the heart and strengthen faith, while comfortable acceptance of unfaithful worship can be more dangerous than open opposition. That is his application to Christian life; Israel’s particular commands in the land remain the immediate setting.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The Bible returns to the question of what testing can produce in God’s people. James 1:2–8 teaches that the testing of faith develops perseverance and calls believers to seek God’s wisdom. First Peter 1:3–9 places trials within the living hope given through Jesus’ resurrection: faith is being proved while believers look toward His appearing and the promised inheritance.

These later passages show a purpose beyond getting through a difficult moment. God forms people who trust Him and remain faithful. The setting has changed from Israel’s wars to life following Christ, but the call to trust and obey continues.

passages.title: Judges 3:7-11
passages.section_title: How does God answer when Israel cries for help?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 So the Israelites did evil in the sight of the LORD; they forgot the LORD their God and served the Baals and the Asherahs. 8 Then the anger of the LORD burned against Israel, and He sold them into the hand of Cushan-rishathaim king of Aram-naharaim, and the Israelites served him eight years. 9 But when the Israelites cried out to the LORD, He raised up Othniel son of Caleb’s younger brother Kenaz as a deliverer to save them. 10 The Spirit of the LORD came upon him, and he became Israel’s judge and went out to war. And the LORD delivered Cushan-rishathaim king of Aram into the hand of Othniel, who prevailed against him. 11 So the land had rest for forty years, until Othniel son of Kenaz died.
paragraphs: 7 So the Israelites did evil in the sight of the LORD; they forgot the LORD their God and served the Baals and the Asherahs. 8 Then the anger of the LORD burned against Israel, and He sold them into the hand of Cushan-rishathaim king of Aram-naharaim, and the Israelites served him eight years.

9 But when the Israelites cried out to the LORD, He raised up Othniel son of Caleb’s younger brother Kenaz as a deliverer to save them. 10 The Spirit of the LORD came upon him, and he became Israel’s judge and went out to war. And the LORD delivered Cushan-rishathaim king of Aram into the hand of Othniel, who prevailed against him. 11 So the land had rest for forty years, until Othniel son of Kenaz died.

passages.context_html:
Israel forgets the LORD and serves the Baals and Asherahs. The account connects this unfaithfulness with eight years under Cushan-rishathaim, king of Aram-naharaim. The Israelites then cry to God, and He raises up Othniel to rescue them. Othniel has already appeared in the account of the capture of Debir and his marriage to Achsah in chapter 1.

The names of the rival gods have a real setting in Canaanite worship. The Metropolitan Museum’s account of Ugaritic texts describes Baal as a storm and fertility god and identifies Athirat with the biblical Asherah. The passage presents Israel’s worship of these gods as abandonment of the LORD, who had rescued them.

The Spirit of the LORD comes upon Othniel, and God gives him victory. The emphasis falls on God’s action: He raises the deliverer, empowers him, and defeats the oppressor through him. The land then has forty years of rest, until Othniel dies. The account gives us the pattern that later rescues will repeat, without describing the battle in detail.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley and Henry understand the Spirit’s coming upon Othniel as God equipping him with wisdom, courage, and power for the work. Both read the rescue as God’s merciful answer to the people’s cry. The victory is more than an impressive leader’s achievement: God supplies the help Israel needs.

deeper_study.title: The True Church According to Jesus

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Othniel’s rescue offers a useful parallel to a larger biblical pattern: people in bondage cry for help, and God provides a deliverer. Jesus identifies a deeper bondage when He teaches that everyone who sins is a slave to sin, and that the Son gives freedom (John 8:31–36). Othniel frees Israel from an earthly oppressor; Jesus addresses the sin that earthly victories cannot remove.

The Spirit’s work also reaches beyond equipping a particular judge for battle. Romans 8:1–17 describes God sending His Son, freeing people from sin and death, and giving His Spirit to those who belong to Christ. They are to put sinful deeds to death through the Spirit and live as God’s children. This is a broader scriptural connection, rather than a claim that every detail of Othniel’s life predicts Jesus.

passages.title: Judges 3:12-30
passages.section_title: How does God bring rescue through Ehud?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 Once again the Israelites did evil in the sight of the LORD. So He gave Eglon king of Moab power over Israel, because they had done evil in the sight of the LORD. 13 After enlisting the Ammonites and Amalekites to join forces with him, Eglon attacked and defeated Israel, taking possession of the City of Palms. 14 The Israelites served Eglon king of Moab eighteen years. 15 And again they cried out to the LORD, and He raised up Ehud son of Gera, a left-handed Benjamite, as their deliverer. So they sent him with tribute to Eglon king of Moab. 16 Now Ehud had made for himself a double-edged sword a cubit long. He strapped it to his right thigh under his cloak 17 and brought the tribute to Eglon king of Moab, who was an obese man. 18 After Ehud had finished presenting the tribute, he ushered out those who had carried it. 19 But upon reaching the idols near Gilgal, he himself turned back and said, “I have a secret message for you, O king.” “Silence,” said the king, and all his attendants left him. 20 Then Ehud approached him while he was sitting alone in the coolness of his upper room. “I have a word from God for you,” Ehud said, and the king rose from his seat. 21 And Ehud reached with his left hand, pulled the sword from his right thigh, and plunged it into Eglon’s belly. 22 Even the handle sank in after the blade, and Eglon’s fat closed in over it, so that Ehud did not withdraw the sword from his belly. And Eglon’s bowels emptied. 23 Then Ehud went out through the porch, closing and locking the doors of the upper room behind him. 24 After Ehud was gone, Eglon’s servants came in and found the doors of the upper room locked. “He must be relieving himself in the cool room,” they said. 25 So they waited until they became worried and saw that he had still not opened the doors of the upper room. Then they took the key and opened the doors—and there was their lord lying dead on the floor. 26 Ehud, however, had escaped while the servants waited. He passed by the idols and escaped to Seirah. 27 On arriving in Seirah, he blew the ram’s horn throughout the hill country of Ephraim. The Israelites came down with him from the hills, and he became their leader. 28 “Follow me,” he told them, “for the LORD has delivered your enemies the Moabites into your hand.” So they followed him down and seized the fords of the Jordan leading to Moab, and they did not allow anyone to cross over. 29 At that time they struck down about ten thousand Moabites, all robust and valiant men. Not one of them escaped. 30 So Moab was subdued under the hand of Israel that day, and the land had rest for eighty years.

passages.context_html:
After Othniel’s death, Israel again does evil. God gives Eglon of Moab power over them, and Eglon joins with the Ammonites and Amalekites to defeat Israel. Eighteen years of subjection follow. When the people cry to the LORD, He raises up Ehud, a Benjamite, as their deliverer.

Ehud is left-handed and carries his concealed sword on his right thigh. The Hebrew description uses אִטֵּר, itter (it-TAIR), explained by Brown–Driver–Briggs as restricted in the right hand, meaning left-handed. This explains the placement and use of his weapon. It does not tell us the medical reason for his handedness.

After presenting the tribute, Ehud returns and obtains a private audience with Eglon. He announces a word from God and kills the king. The locked doors and the servants’ mistaken assumption give him time to escape. He then calls the Israelites together, declares that the LORD has given them victory, and leads them to seize the Jordan crossings. The defeat of the Moabite force brings eighty years of rest.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Gill read Ehud as acting as Israel’s God-raised deliverer and carrying out judgment on its oppressor. Both distinguish this particular rescue from permission for readers to imitate the assassination of a ruler. The narrative’s account of God raising a deliverer is central to their reading.

Wesley emphasizes the practical importance of the concealed weapon and the capture of the crossings, where the Moabites could be prevented from escaping or receiving help. The passage combines Ehud’s planning and Israel’s action with its clear attribution of the rescue to God.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Ehud’s account fits a recurring biblical theme: God’s rescue does not depend on what people expect strength and success to look like. First Corinthians 1:18–31 brings this theme to the cross. Paul proclaims Christ crucified as God’s power and wisdom, and explains that God chooses people the world discounts so that no one can boast before Him.

That connection does not make Ehud’s sword a symbol of Jesus or turn his method into the pattern for advancing Christ’s kingdom. Jesus tells Pilate that His kingdom is not from this world, explaining that His servants would otherwise fight to prevent His arrest (John 18:33–38). The wider story leads us to the Savior whose victory comes through His own death, rather than a repetition of Ehud’s attack.

passages.title: Judges 3:31
passages.section_title: What are we told about Shamgar?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 31 After Ehud came Shamgar son of Anath. And he too saved Israel, striking down six hundred Philistines with an oxgoad.
paragraphs: 31 After Ehud came Shamgar son of Anath. And he too saved Israel, striking down six hundred Philistines with an oxgoad.

passages.context_html:
One verse records Shamgar son of Anath striking down six hundred Philistines with an oxgoad and saving Israel. An oxgoad is a tool for directing oxen; Brown–Driver–Briggs identifies the Hebrew word מַלְמֵד, malmed (mahl-MAID), as an oxgoad. The striking detail is that an agricultural tool serves in this rescue.

The account gives no length for Shamgar’s leadership, no account of his call, and no detailed battle scene. He appears again in Deborah’s song, which recalls the insecurity of travel in his days (Judges 5:6–8). Those few details are worth keeping distinct from reconstructions of his background.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Henry draw attention to God accomplishing rescue through an unlikely means. They compare the oxgoad with Samson’s later use of a donkey’s jawbone: an ordinary object is sufficient when God supplies the strength. Their suggestions that Shamgar had just been plowing explain how the tool might have been at hand, but the verse itself does not describe what he was doing before the encounter.

Gill acknowledges how little is known of Shamgar’s family and tribe. He also discusses different possibilities for fitting his service into the surrounding accounts. The brief notice establishes that he saved Israel; it leaves his full life story and the exact timing unstated.

passages.title: Judges 4:1-16
passages.section_title: How do Deborah and Barak respond to God’s command?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 After Ehud died, the Israelites again did evil in the sight of the LORD. 2 So the LORD sold them into the hand of Jabin king of Canaan, who reigned in Hazor. The commander of his forces was Sisera, who lived in Harosheth-hagoyim. 3 Then the Israelites cried out to the LORD, because Jabin had nine hundred chariots of iron, and he had harshly oppressed the Israelites for twenty years. 4 Now Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth, was judging Israel at that time. 5 And she would sit under the Palm of Deborah between Ramah and Bethel in the hill country of Ephraim, where the Israelites would go up to her for judgment. 6 She summoned Barak son of Abinoam from Kedesh in Naphtali and said to him, “Surely the LORD, the God of Israel, is commanding you: ‘Go and march to Mount Tabor, taking with you ten thousand men of Naphtali and Zebulun. 7 And I will draw out Sisera the commander of Jabin’s army, his chariots, and his troops to the River Kishon, and I will deliver him into your hand.’” 8 Barak said to her, “If you will go with me, I will go; but if you will not go with me, I will not go.” 9 “I will certainly go with you,” Deborah replied, “but the road you are taking will bring you no honor, because the LORD will be selling Sisera into the hand of a woman.” So Deborah got up and went with Barak to Kedesh, 10 where he summoned Zebulun and Naphtali. Has not the LORD gone before you?” So Barak came down from Mount Tabor with ten thousand men following him. 15 And in front of him the LORD routed with the sword Sisera, all his charioteers, and all his army. Sisera abandoned his chariot and fled on foot. 16 Then Barak pursued the chariots and army as far as Harosheth-hagoyim, and the whole army of Sisera fell by the sword; not a single man was left.

passages.context_html:
After Ehud dies, Israel again turns to evil. Jabin of Hazor and his commander Sisera oppress the people for twenty years, supported by nine hundred iron chariots. The Israelites cry to the LORD, and the account introduces Deborah, who is already serving as a prophetess and judge. People come to her to have their disputes heard.

The Hebrew title נְבִיאָה, neviah (neh-vee-AH), means prophetess; Brown–Driver–Briggs lists Deborah alongside other women called by that title. Here she communicates the LORD’s command and promise to Barak: gather the troops, go to Mount Tabor, and God will bring Sisera to the Kishon and give him into Barak’s hand.

Barak agrees to go only if Deborah goes with him. She consents, while announcing that the honor attached to Sisera’s defeat will go to a woman. Barak gathers the men, and when Deborah announces the time to act, he leads them down the mountain. The account credits the LORD with routing Sisera’s forces while also describing Barak’s pursuit. Sisera himself escapes on foot, setting up the next scene.

The brief notice about Heber’s move near Kedesh introduces the household that will become important when Sisera seeks shelter. It belongs to the unfolding account, even though its significance is not yet explained.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Readers recognize Deborah’s significant place in God’s rescue. The Catholic Catechism, paragraph 64, includes her among the holy women who kept Israel’s hope of salvation alive. Henry describes her as speaking God’s message and administering justice, while Wesley emphasizes the authority the people acknowledged in her judging and summoning Barak.

The emphasis differs when readers assess Barak’s condition. Wesley sees both genuine faith in his willingness to go and weakness in his refusal to go without Deborah. Gill also acknowledges weakness but gives more attention to his desire for her counsel, prayer, and reassuring presence. Henry highlights Deborah’s willingness to share the danger and Barak’s concern for the mission’s success over his personal honor. These are readings of his response; his private thoughts are not fully narrated.

passages.god_plan_html:
The New Testament explicitly includes Barak among people remembered for faith. Hebrews 11:32–34 names him in its account of God strengthening people in weakness and giving victories through faith. His need for encouragement does not erase the faith shown when he acts.

Hebrews then leads beyond these earlier servants to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of faith, who endured the cross and is seated at God’s right hand (Hebrews 12:1–3). The larger story honors God’s work through people such as Deborah and Barak while directing our lasting hope and attention to Christ.

passages.title: Judges 4:17-24
passages.section_title: Why does Sisera’s escape end at Jael’s tent?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 Meanwhile, Sisera had fled on foot to the tent of Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, because there was peace between Jabin king of Hazor and the house of Heber the Kenite. 18 Jael went out to greet Sisera and said to him, “Come in, my lord. Come in with me. Do not be afraid.” So he entered her tent, and she covered him with a blanket. 19 Sisera said to her, “Please give me a little water to drink, for I am thirsty.” So she opened a container of milk, gave him a drink, and covered him again. 20 “Stand at the entrance to the tent,” he said, “and if anyone comes and asks you, ‘Is there a man here?’ say, ‘No.’” 21 But as he lay sleeping from exhaustion, Heber’s wife Jael took a tent peg, grabbed a hammer, and went silently to Sisera. She drove the peg through his temple and into the ground, and he died. 22 When Barak arrived in pursuit of Sisera, Jael went out to greet him and said to him, “Come, and I will show you the man you are seeking.” So he went in with her, and there lay Sisera dead, with a tent peg through his temple. 23 On that day God subdued Jabin king of Canaan before the Israelites. 24 And the hand of the Israelites grew stronger and stronger against Jabin king of Canaan until they destroyed him.

Come in with me. She drove the peg through his temple and into the ground, and he died. 22 When Barak arrived in pursuit of Sisera, Jael went out to greet him and said to him, “Come, and I will show you the man you are seeking.” So he went in with her, and there lay Sisera dead, with a tent peg through his temple.
23 On that day God subdued Jabin king of Canaan before the Israelites. 24 And the hand of the Israelites grew stronger and stronger against Jabin king of Canaan until they destroyed him.

passages.context_html:
Sisera seeks shelter with Jael because Jabin and Heber’s household are at peace. Jael welcomes him, covers him, and gives him milk when he asks for water. He asks her to stand at the entrance and deny that anyone is there. Exhausted, he falls asleep.

Jael then kills him with a tent peg and hammer. When Barak arrives in pursuit, she shows him the body. Deborah’s announcement that Sisera would fall into a woman’s hand is fulfilled through Jael, outside the battle Barak has been fighting.

The chapter closes by returning to the wider rescue: God subdues Jabin, and the Israelites press their advantage until his power is destroyed. Sisera’s death is a decisive part of that victory, while the final verses describe continued action against the king.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Readers often ask how to understand Jael’s welcome followed by her killing of Sisera. Wesley recognizes the difficulty of promising safety and then attacking. He considers the possibility that she first intended to shelter Sisera and afterward received divine direction to kill him. Henry and Gill also suggest an initial welcome followed by a divine prompting. The text records her actions but does not explicitly narrate such an instruction or a change of intention.

Within the book, her action contributes to the defeat of Israel’s oppressor, and Deborah’s song calls her blessed (Judges 5:24–27). That praise is an important part of how Judges presents her. The question of exactly when she formed her plan remains open in the account.

passages.god_plan_html:
Later Scripture remembers this rescue as a witness to the LORD’s rule. Psalm 83:9–18 recalls Sisera, Jabin, and the Kishon while praying for God to confront those threatening His people. The prayer also asks that people seek His name and know that He alone is Most High over all the earth.

That purpose reaches beyond relief for one nation. In Revelation 15:3–4, the song of Moses and the Lamb praises God’s just ways and looks toward the nations worshiping Him because His righteous acts have been revealed. These passages place God’s judgments within the larger theme of His name being known and honored throughout the earth.

passages.title: Judges 5:1-31
passages.section_title: Why does Deborah’s song remember both courage and failure?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 On that day Deborah and Barak son of Abinoam sang this song: 2 “When the princes take the lead in Israel, when the people volunteer, bless the LORD. 3 Listen, O kings! Give ear, O princes! I will sing to the LORD; I will sing praise to the LORD, the God of Israel. 4 O LORD, when You went out from Seir, when You marched from the land of Edom, the earth trembled, the heavens poured out rain, and the clouds poured down water. 5 The mountains quaked before the LORD, the One of Sinai, before the LORD, the God of Israel. 6 In the days of Shamgar son of Anath, in the days of Jael, the highways were deserted and the travelers took the byways. 7 Life in the villages ceased; it ended in Israel, until I, Deborah, arose, a mother in Israel. 8 When they chose new gods, then war came to their gates. Not a shield or spear was found among forty thousand in Israel. 9 My heart is with the princes of Israel, with the volunteers among the people. Bless the LORD! 10 You who ride white donkeys, who sit on saddle blankets, and you who travel the road, ponder 11 the voices of the singers at the watering places. There they shall recount the righteous acts of the LORD, the righteous deeds of His villagers in Israel. Then the people of the LORD went down to the gates: 12 ‘Awake, awake, O Deborah! Awake, awake, sing a song! Arise, O Barak, and take hold of your captives, O son of Abinoam!’ 13 Then the survivors came down to the nobles; the people of the LORD came down to me against the mighty. 14 Some came from Ephraim, with their roots in Amalek; Benjamin came with your people after you. The commanders came down from Machir, the bearers of the marshal’s staff from Zebulun. 15 The princes of Issachar were with Deborah, and Issachar was with Barak, rushing into the valley at his heels. In the clans of Reuben there was great indecision. 16 Why did you sit among the sheepfolds to hear the whistling for the flocks? In the clans of Reuben there was great indecision. 17 Gilead remained beyond the Jordan. Dan, why did you linger by the ships? Asher stayed at the coast and remained in his harbors. 18 Zebulun was a people who risked their lives; Naphtali, too, on the heights of the battlefield. 19 Kings came and fought; then the kings of Canaan fought at Taanach by the waters of Megiddo, but they took no plunder of silver. 20 From the heavens the stars fought; from their courses they fought against Sisera. 21 The River Kishon swept them away, the ancient river, the River Kishon. March on, O my soul, in strength! 22 Then the hooves of horses thundered— the mad galloping of his stallions. 23 ‘Curse Meroz,’ says the angel of the LORD. ‘Bitterly curse her inhabitants; for they did not come to help the LORD, to help the LORD against the mighty.’ 24 Most blessed among women is Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, most blessed of tent-dwelling women. 25 He asked for water, and she gave him milk. In a magnificent bowl she brought him curds. 26 She reached for the tent peg, her right hand for the workman’s hammer. She struck Sisera and crushed his skull; she shattered and pierced his temple. 27 At her feet he collapsed, he fell, there he lay still; at her feet he collapsed, he fell; where he collapsed, there he fell dead. 28 Sisera’s mother looked through the window; she peered through the lattice and lamented: ‘Why is his chariot so long in coming? What has delayed the clatter of his chariots?’ 29 Her wisest ladies answer; indeed she keeps telling herself, 30 ‘Are they not finding and dividing the spoil— a girl or two for each warrior, a plunder of dyed garments for Sisera, the spoil of embroidered garments for the neck of the looter?’ 31 So may all Your enemies perish, O LORD! But may those who love You shine like the sun at its brightest.” And the land had rest for forty years.

passages.context_html:
This song looks back on the rescue described in chapter 4. Deborah and Barak praise the LORD while remembering the people who took part, those who stayed away, and the defeat of Sisera. Its poetry adds images and voices to the earlier account, showing what the victory meant for Israel’s life and worship.

The opening recalls God’s majesty at Sinai and contrasts His power with Israel’s earlier insecurity: roads were deserted, village life had broken down, and the people had turned to new gods. Deborah describes herself as a mother in Israel. The song honors leaders who acted and people who freely offered themselves. The Hebrew root נָדַב, nadav (nah-DAHV), expresses willingness; Brown–Driver–Briggs specifically lists volunteering for war in verses 2 and 9.

The middle section remembers the tribes’ different responses. Some joined the danger; others remained with their flocks, ships, or coastal settlements. Meroz is cursed for failing to help. The song therefore joins praise for God with an honest account of His people’s response. His victory does not make courage, service, or refusal unimportant.

The battle is described as reaching beyond the human armies: the stars fight against Sisera, and the Kishon sweeps his forces away. Jael then receives praise for killing the fleeing commander. The final scene turns to Sisera’s mother and her attendants, who explain his delay by imagining him dividing plunder, including captive women. Their expectation of triumph stands against the defeat the reader already knows. The closing prayer asks that God’s enemies perish and that those who love Him shine like the sun; forty years of rest follow.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Henry read the song as grateful praise that gives God the credit while also honoring willing servants. They understand the questions addressed to absent tribes as a challenge to people who prefer safety or their own affairs to helping others. Henry draws attention to the value of ordinary peace for exposed village communities, as well as to the military victory.

Readers explain the battle’s heavenly language in more than one way. Wesley connects it with storms, while Gill discusses both angelic help and the elements acting against Sisera. Henry also suggests that rain swelled the Kishon. The poem plainly credits God and says the river swept the enemy away; the commentators’ proposals about the precise heavenly or weather activity go beyond its brief description.

Wesley and Henry understand the final prayer as reaching toward the lasting honor and joy of those who love God. The song’s contrast is therefore more than a celebration of one side’s military skill: it places the rescue, the people’s response, and their hope before the LORD.

deeper_study.title: The True Church According to Jesus

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The song belongs to a wider biblical pattern in which God brings down the powerful and remembers people who seem unimportant. A later song makes that theme clear when Mary praises God for bringing down rulers, lifting the humble, and remembering His mercy to Israel (Luke 1:46–55). Elizabeth also calls Mary blessed among women, language that recalls the praise of Jael (Luke 1:39–45; Judges 5:24). This is a parallel in the language and theme of the accounts; the women have different roles in God’s work.

The final picture of those who love God shining like the sun also finds a larger setting in Jesus’ teaching. In Matthew 13:36–43, He describes the Son of Man removing evil at the end of the age and the righteous shining like the sun in their Father’s kingdom. The hope reaches beyond a period of peace in the land to God’s final judgment and the life of His kingdom.

passages.title: Judges 6:1-10
passages.section_title: Why does God send a prophet before a deliverer?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Again the Israelites did evil in the sight of the LORD; so He delivered them into the hand of Midian for seven years, 2 and the hand of Midian prevailed against Israel. Because of the Midianites, the Israelites prepared shelters for themselves in the mountains, caves, and strongholds. 3 Whenever the Israelites planted their crops, the Midianites, Amalekites, and other people of the east would come up and invade them, 4 encamping against them as far as Gaza and destroying the produce of the land. They left Israel with no sustenance, neither sheep nor oxen nor donkeys. 5 For the Midianites came with their livestock and their tents like a great swarm of locusts. They and their camels were innumerable, and they entered the land to ravage it. 6 Israel was greatly impoverished by Midian, and the Israelites cried out to the LORD. 7 Now when the Israelites cried out to the LORD because of Midian, 8 He sent them a prophet, who told them, “This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: I brought you up out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. 9 I delivered you out of the hands of Egypt and all your oppressors. I drove them out before you and gave you their land. 10 And I said to you: ‘I am the LORD your God. You must not fear the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you dwell.’ But you did not obey Me.”

passages.context_html:
Israel again does evil, and seven years of Midianite oppression follow. The invaders arrive with allies, livestock, tents, and vast numbers of camels. They destroy crops and leave the Israelites without food or animals. Israel prepares shelters in the mountains and caves, but the repeated devastation brings severe poverty.

When the people cry to the LORD, His first recorded answer is a prophet. The message recalls the rescue from Egypt and the gift of the land. God had told them not to fear the gods of the Amorites, yet they have not obeyed Him. The immediate need is food and safety; the prophet brings the broken relationship with God into view.

The prophet is not named. His message prepares us to understand the rescue that follows: God is addressing Israel’s disobedience as well as its enemies. The story itself explains the reason for this particular oppression; it does not ask us to guess the cause of every hardship from circumstances alone.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley and Henry understand the prophet’s message as part of God’s mercy. The people ask for relief, and He first calls them to recognize their sin and return to Him. They emphasize repentance that grieves disobedience itself, rather than merely wishing its painful consequences would stop.

passages.god_plan_html:
God’s work of rescue includes speaking truth that calls people back to Him. Hebrews 1:1–4 looks back on His many messages through the prophets and announces His fuller speaking through the Son, who provides purification for sins. The hope grows beyond another warning or another temporary escape.

After His resurrection, Jesus joins repentance and forgiveness to the message that will go to all nations in His name (Luke 24:44–49). The prophet’s rebuke belongs to the long story of God confronting sin while making a way for people to return to Him.

passages.title: Judges 6:11-24
passages.section_title: What gives Gideon a reason to go?

versions.text: 11 Then the angel of the LORD came and sat down under the oak in Ophrah that belonged to Joash the Abiezrite, where his son Gideon was threshing wheat in a winepress to hide it from the Midianites. 12 And the angel of the LORD appeared to Gideon and said, “The LORD is with you, O mighty man of valor.” 13 “Please, my Lord,” Gideon replied, “if the LORD is with us, why has all this happened to us? passages.context_html:
Gideon is threshing wheat in a winepress to hide it from the Midianites when the angel of the LORD appears. The greeting names him a mighty man of valor, but his answer expresses the distress of the whole people: if God is with them, where is the rescue their fathers described? The preceding prophet’s message has already supplied the reader with an explanation for Israel’s condition.

The narrative then names the speaker as the LORD, who sends Gideon to save Israel. Gideon points to the weakness of his clan and his place as the youngest in his father’s household. God answers with the promise of His own presence. The call rests on the One sending him, rather than a new claim that Gideon has suddenly become powerful on his own.

Gideon asks for a sign and brings an offering. Fire from the rock consumes it, and the angel vanishes. Gideon becomes afraid that seeing the angel of the LORD will mean his death, but the LORD speaks peace and tells him not to fear. Gideon builds an altar called The LORD Is Peace. The Hebrew שָׁלוֹם, shalom (shah-LOHM), includes peace and well-being; Brown–Driver–Briggs includes the reassurance in verse 23 among its examples.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley, Henry, and Gill identify the angel in this encounter as the divine Son. They point to the movement between the titles angel of the LORD and LORD, together with the supernatural acceptance of the offering. This is their Christian reading of the messenger’s identity.

Henry emphasizes God strengthening someone whose faith needs confirmation. Wesley reads the promise of God’s presence as the source of Gideon’s strength. Their emphasis is on God’s initiative and reassurance, while taking Gideon’s questions seriously.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Who is The Angel of the Lord? identifies the messenger in Gideon’s encounter as the eternal Son appearing before His birth as Jesus. The study draws attention to the account’s movement between the angel of the LORD and the LORD Himself, along with Gideon’s fear and God’s assurance of peace.

deeper_study.title: Who is The Angel of the Lord?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Gideon’s call recalls Moses’ earlier commission. In Exodus 3:7–12, God hears the cries of the oppressed, sends Moses, and answers his question about his own adequacy with the promise to be with him. Gideon’s encounter repeats that pattern of rescue and promised presence.

The theme continues when the risen Jesus sends His disciples to make disciples of all nations and promises to be with them always (Matthew 28:16–20). These servants have different assignments, but the shared assurance points to God accomplishing His purpose through people who depend on Him.

passages.title: Judges 6:25-32
passages.section_title: Why does Gideon’s first task begin at home?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 25 On that very night the LORD said to Gideon, “Take your father’s young bull and a second bull seven years old, tear down your father’s altar to Baal, and cut down the Asherah pole beside it. 26 Then build a proper altar to the LORD your God on the top of this stronghold. And with the wood of the Asherah pole you cut down, take the second bull and offer it as a burnt offering.” 27 So Gideon took ten of his servants and did as the LORD had told him. But because he was too afraid of his father’s household and the men of the city, he did it by night rather than in the daytime. 28 When the men of the city got up in the morning, there was Baal’s altar torn down, with the Asherah pole cut down beside it and the second bull offered up on the newly built altar. 29 “Who did this?” they said to one another. And after they had investigated thoroughly, they were told, “Gideon son of Joash did it.” 30 Then the men of the city said to Joash, “Bring out your son. He must die, because he has torn down Baal’s altar and cut down the Asherah pole beside it.” 31 But Joash said to all who stood against him, “Are you contending for Baal? Are you trying to save him? Whoever pleads his case will be put to death by morning! If Baal is a god, let him contend for himself with the one who has torn down his altar.” 32 So on that day Gideon was called Jerubbaal, that is to say, “Let Baal contend with him,” because he had torn down Baal’s altar.

passages.context_html:
On the same night, the LORD gives Gideon a task within his own community. He must tear down his father’s altar to Baal, cut down the nearby Asherah pole, and build an altar to the LORD. The wood from the pole is to be used for the burnt offering. The coming rescue begins by confronting the worship that helped bring Israel into its present condition.

Gideon takes ten servants and obeys, but does the work at night because he fears his father’s household and the townspeople. Morning reveals how strongly the town is attached to Baal: its men demand Gideon’s death for destroying the altar and pole.

Joash answers by challenging them to let Baal defend himself if he really is a god. Gideon receives the name Jerubbaal, which the passage explains as letting Baal contend with him. The scene exposes the contrast between an idol its worshipers must defend and the LORD who calls Gideon to rescue His people.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry sees grace at work in God raising a reformer from a household involved in idolatry. The rescue requires a return to the LORD, beginning with the worship in Gideon’s own home.

Wesley and Gill give a practical reading of the nighttime action: Gideon fears being prevented from carrying out the command. Gill therefore treats the timing as prudent obedience. The verse explicitly names fear and also says Gideon did what the LORD commanded; these commentators’ explanation differs from readings that treat the nighttime action simply as a failure to obey.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Turning from idols to the living God becomes part of the New Testament’s account of receiving the gospel. First Thessalonians 1:8–10 describes people turning to God from idols, serving Him, and awaiting His risen Son, Jesus, who delivers from the coming wrath.

Titus 2:11–14 connects Christ’s rescue with a changed life: He gives Himself to redeem and purify a people eager to do good. God’s purpose includes both deliverance and renewed loyalty. Gideon’s first task helps us see why rescue and the question of whom people worship belong together.

passages.title: Judges 6:33-40
passages.section_title: What is Gideon asking God to confirm?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 33 Then all the Midianites, Amalekites, and other people of the east gathered together, crossed over the Jordan, and camped in the Valley of Jezreel. 34 So the Spirit of the LORD came upon Gideon, who blew the ram’s horn and rallied the Abiezrites behind him. 35 Calling them to arms, Gideon sent messengers throughout Manasseh, as well as Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali, so that they came up to meet him. 36 Then Gideon said to God, “If You are going to save Israel by my hand, as You have said, 37 then behold, I will place a fleece of wool on the threshing floor. If there is dew only on the fleece and all the ground is dry, then I will know that You are going to save Israel by my hand, as You have said.” 38 And that is what happened. When Gideon arose the next morning, he squeezed the fleece and wrung out the dew—a bowlful of water. 39 Then Gideon said to God, “Do not be angry with me; let me speak one more time. Please allow me one more test with the fleece. This time let it be dry, and the ground covered with dew.” 40 And that night God did so. Only the fleece was dry, and dew covered the ground.

Please allow me one more test with the fleece. This time let it be dry, and the ground covered with dew.” 40 And that night God did so. Only the fleece was dry, and dew covered the ground.

passages.context_html:
The invading coalition gathers in the Valley of Jezreel. The Spirit of the LORD comes upon Gideon, and he sounds the ram’s horn. His own Abiezrite community rallies, and messengers summon men from Manasseh, Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali.

The Hebrew verb לָבֵשׁ, labash (lah-VAHSH), ordinarily concerns putting on clothing. In this verse, Brown–Driver–Briggs describes the Spirit as clothing Himself with Gideon—an image of taking hold of him for the work. The story gives the credit for his ability to lead to God’s Spirit.

Gideon then asks for confirmation of the rescue God has already promised. First he asks for dew on a fleece while the ground remains dry. After receiving that sign, he asks that the fleece be dry while the ground is wet. God grants both requests. Gideon is asking about the promise already spoken to him, not inventing a meaning for an unrelated event.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands the requests as prayer for stronger faith and encouragement for those preparing to fight. He emphasizes God’s tenderness toward weakness. Gill similarly considers encouragement for the soldiers as a possible reason and distinguishes a request for confirmation from complete disbelief in God’s power. The text records Gideon’s repeated requests and God’s patient response without reporting every motive behind them.

Henry also draws an illustration from the wet fleece and ground: God can distinguish the small people He is rescuing from the larger enemy around them. He extends the dew image to God’s blessing reaching beyond Israel. That is his devotional comparison, rather than an explanation the passage itself supplies for each object.

deeper_study.title: The True Church According to Jesus
Should We Seek Signs from God?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The clothing image has a helpful later parallel. After His resurrection, Jesus tells His disciples to remain in Jerusalem until they are clothed with power from on high (Luke 24:44–49). Acts 1:4–8 identifies the promised gift as the Holy Spirit and connects that power with bearing witness to Jesus to the ends of the earth.

The assignment expands from leading a rescue in Israel to announcing the risen Savior among the nations. The common theme is God equipping people for the work He gives them. The shared image helps explain that dependence without making Gideon’s fleece the model for how the disciples must receive guidance.

passages.title: Judges 7:1-8
passages.section_title: Why does God make Gideon’s army smaller?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Early in the morning Jerubbaal (that is, Gideon) and all the men with him camped beside the spring of Harod. And the camp of Midian was north of them in the valley near the hill of Moreh. 2 Then the LORD said to Gideon, “You have too many men for Me to deliver Midian into their hands, lest Israel glorify themselves over Me, saying, ‘My own hand has saved me.’ 3 Now, therefore, proclaim in the hearing of the men: ‘Whoever is fearful and trembling may turn back and leave Mount Gilead.’” So twenty-two thousand of them turned back, but ten thousand remained. 4 Then the LORD said to Gideon, “There are still too many men. Take them down to the water, and I will sift them for you there. If I say to you, ‘This one shall go with you,’ he shall go. But if I say, ‘This one shall not go with you,’ he shall not go.” 5 So Gideon brought the men down to the water, and the LORD said to him, “Separate those who lap the water with their tongues like a dog from those who kneel to drink.” 6 And the number of those who lapped the water with their hands to their mouths was three hundred men; all the others knelt to drink. 7 Then the LORD said to Gideon, “With the three hundred men who lapped the water I will save you and deliver the Midianites into your hand. But all the others are to go home.” 8 So Gideon sent the rest of the Israelites to their tents but kept the three hundred men, who took charge of the provisions and rams’ horns of the others. And the camp of Midian lay below him in the valley.

And the camp of Midian lay below him in the valley.

passages.context_html:
Gideon’s men gather near the spring of Harod, with Midian’s camp below them in the valley. God says the army is too large for the rescue He intends, and gives the reason: Israel might claim that its own strength had saved it. The reduction is meant to make the source of the victory clear.

The fearful are first allowed to leave, as Deuteronomy 20:1–8 had provided for Israel’s armies. Twenty-two thousand depart and ten thousand remain. God then separates them by how they drink at the water. The three hundred who lap with their hands to their mouths are kept; the others return to their tents.

The testing uses the Hebrew verb צָרַף, tsaraph (tsah-RAHF), which can mean to refine metal or to test. Brown–Driver–Briggs specifically identifies the testing of warriors here. God determines whom Gideon is to take and promises to save through those three hundred. The passage explains the choice’s purpose, while leaving much about the men themselves unstated.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley, Henry, and Gill agree on the central purpose: God removes the basis for Israel to boast in its own strength. Dependence on Him is to shape how the people understand the rescue.

The drinking test receives different explanations. Wesley sees the men as hardy and eager to act, taking only a quick drink. Gill discusses both strong-warrior and weak-warrior readings, then emphasizes that the test reduces the number and makes God’s choice known to Gideon. Their explanations should be distinguished from the stated reason for the smaller army; the narrative does not give a full character description of either group.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
God’s power made known through human weakness remains a theme in the New Testament. In Second Corinthians 12:7–10, Paul asks for a painful burden to be removed and instead receives Christ’s assurance that His grace is sufficient and His power is perfected in weakness.

The connection reaches beyond winning a battle. Paul learns to rely on Christ even while difficulty remains. God’s purpose can be served through people whose limitations are still real, with the glory belonging to Him rather than to their apparent strength.

passages.title: Judges 7:9-14
passages.section_title: How does God encourage Gideon before the battle?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 That night the LORD said to Gideon, “Get up and go down against the camp, for I have delivered it into your hand. 10 But if you are afraid to do so, then go down to the camp with your servant Purah 11 and listen to what they are saying. Then your hands will be strengthened to attack the camp.” So he went with Purah his servant to the outposts where armed men were guarding the camp. 12 Now the Midianites, Amalekites, and all the other people of the east had settled in the valley like a swarm of locusts, and their camels were as countless as the sand on the seashore. 13 And as Gideon arrived, a man was telling his friend about a dream. “Behold, I had a dream,” he said, “and I saw a loaf of barley bread come tumbling into the Midianite camp. It struck the tent so hard that the tent overturned and collapsed.” 14 His friend replied: “This is nothing less than the sword of Gideon son of Joash, the Israelite. God has delivered Midian and the whole camp into his hand.”

Then your hands will be strengthened to attack the camp.” So he went with Purah his servant to the outposts where armed men were guarding the camp. 12 Now the Midianites, Amalekites, and all the other people of the east had settled in the valley like a swarm of locusts, and their camels were as countless as the sand on the seashore.

It struck the tent so hard that the tent overturned and collapsed.” 14 His friend replied: “This is nothing less than the sword of Gideon son of Joash, the Israelite. God has delivered Midian and the whole camp into his hand.”

passages.context_html:
That night, the LORD tells Gideon to go against the camp because He has given it into his hand. He also provides reassurance: if Gideon is afraid, he may take his servant Purah down to listen to the enemy. What he hears will strengthen him. God’s response acknowledges his fear and gives him help to act.

The great enemy camp remains in view, with people compared to locusts and camels to the sand on the seashore. At its edge, Gideon hears one man describe a dream in which a barley loaf overturns a tent. The man’s companion interprets it as Gideon’s victory, saying that God has given Midian and the whole camp into his hand.

This exchange confirms the promise Gideon has already received. The assurance comes from an unexpected place: the people he is about to face. The next passage records its effect on him—worship followed by action.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley understands the dream and its interpretation as encouragement God provides through people outside Israel. Henry emphasizes God’s care in bringing Gideon to hear words that strengthen his confidence. The event is read in light of the LORD’s prior promise that this visit would encourage him, rather than as a dream whose meaning Gideon simply invents.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The need for confidence in God’s promise reaches beyond Gideon’s immediate battle. Second Corinthians 4:13–18 grounds Christian courage in the God who raised Jesus and will raise His people with Him. Paul can speak of suffering honestly while looking toward a lasting glory.

Gideon receives reassurance about a particular rescue. Through Jesus’ resurrection, believers receive hope that reaches even beyond death. The larger biblical theme is trust in God’s ability to fulfill what He has promised, with our eyes on the future He has made known.

passages.title: Judges 7:15-25
passages.section_title: How is the victory won with three hundred men?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 When Gideon heard the dream and its interpretation, he bowed in worship. He returned to the camp of Israel and said, “Get up, for the LORD has delivered the camp of Midian into your hand.” 16 And he divided the three hundred men into three companies and gave each man a ram’s horn in one hand and a large jar in the other, containing a torch. 17 “Watch me and do as I do,” Gideon said. “When I come to the outskirts of the camp, do exactly as I do. 18 When I and all who are with me blow our horns, then you are also to blow your horns from all around the camp and shout, ‘For the LORD and for Gideon!’” 19 Gideon and the hundred men with him reached the outskirts of the camp at the beginning of the middle watch, just after the changing of the guard. They blew their horns and broke the jars that were in their hands. 20 The three companies blew their horns and shattered their jars. Holding the torches in their left hands and the horns in their right hands, they shouted, “A sword for the LORD and for Gideon!” 21 Each Israelite took his position around the camp, and the entire Midianite army fled, crying out as they ran. 22 And when the three hundred rams’ horns sounded, the LORD set all the men in the camp against one another with their swords. The army fled to Beth-shittah toward Zererah as far as the border of Abel-meholah near Tabbath. 23 Then the men of Israel were called out from Naphtali, Asher, and all Manasseh, and they pursued the Midianites. 24 Gideon sent messengers throughout the hill country of Ephraim to say, “Come down against the Midianites and seize the waters of the Jordan ahead of them as far as Beth-barah.” So all the men of Ephraim were called out, and they captured the waters of the Jordan as far as Beth-barah. 25 They also captured Oreb and Zeeb, the two princes of Midian; and they killed Oreb at the rock of Oreb and Zeeb at the winepress of Zeeb. So they pursued the Midianites and brought the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to Gideon on the other side of the Jordan.

passages.context_html:
After hearing the dream and its interpretation, Gideon bows in worship and returns ready to lead. He divides the three hundred into three companies, each man carrying a ram’s horn and a jar with a torch inside. They are to follow his signal and call out for the LORD and Gideon.

At the beginning of the middle watch, just after the changing of the guard, they blow the horns and break the jars. The torches become visible, and the men hold their positions around the camp. The enemy flees in panic. The account explicitly says that the LORD turns the men’s swords against one another; the decisive victory is credited to Him.

The action then broadens. Men from Naphtali, Asher, and Manasseh pursue, and Ephraim is called to seize the Jordan waters ahead of the fleeing Midianites. Oreb and Zeeb, two Midianite princes, are captured and killed. The first three hundred have a particular part in the rescue, and other Israelites join in carrying it forward.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley reads the horns, sudden lights, and surrounding groups as a plan that makes Gideon’s force appear much larger. He also sees confusion and darkness contributing to the enemy fighting itself. Those suggestions explain how the attack might work while keeping the account’s central claim that God brings the rout.

Henry draws a lesson from the later cooperation of the tribes: people should be willing to join and complete good work others have begun. He joins recognition of God’s victory with the value of the servants who participate in it.

passages.god_plan_html:
Henry also notices a parallel between the light revealed from the jars and Paul’s picture in Second Corinthians 4:6–12. Paul describes God’s light making Christ known and the treasure carried in jars of clay, so that the extraordinary power is seen to come from God. This is a useful comparison of images, rather than a statement that Paul explicitly identifies Gideon’s jars as a prediction of gospel ministry.

The shared theme is God making His power known through fragile servants. Paul’s account includes pressure, persecution, and the life of Jesus being made visible in mortal people. The wider purpose goes beyond defeating one army: God brings the knowledge of Christ to others through those who depend on Him.

passages.title: Judges 8:1-21
passages.section_title: What happens when the rescue is followed by conflict?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then the men of Ephraim said to Gideon, “Why have you done this to us? Why did you fail to call us when you went to fight against Midian?” And they contended with him violently. 2 But Gideon answered them, “Now what have I accomplished compared to you? Are not the gleanings of Ephraim better than the grape harvest of Abiezer? 3 God has delivered Oreb and Zeeb, the two princes of Midian, into your hand. What was I able to do compared to you?” When he had said this, their anger against him subsided. 4 Then Gideon and his three hundred men came to the Jordan and crossed it, exhausted yet still in pursuit. 5 So Gideon said to the men of Succoth, “Please give my troops some bread, for they are exhausted, and I am still pursuing Zebah and Zalmunna, the kings of Midian.” 6 But the leaders of Succoth asked, “Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your possession, that we should give bread to your army?” 7 “Very well,” Gideon replied, “when the LORD has delivered Zebah and Zalmunna into my hand, I will tear your flesh with the thorns and briers of the wilderness!” 8 From there he went up to Penuel and asked the same from them, but the men of Penuel gave the same response as the men of Succoth. 9 So Gideon told the men of Penuel, “When I return in triumph, I will tear down this tower!” 10 Now Zebah and Zalmunna were in Karkor with their army of about fifteen thousand men—all that were left of the armies of the people of the east. A hundred and twenty thousand swordsmen had already fallen. 11 And Gideon went up by way of the caravan route east of Nobah and Jogbehah, and he attacked their army, taking them by surprise. 12 When Zebah and Zalmunna fled, Gideon pursued and captured these two kings of Midian, routing their entire army. 13 After this, Gideon son of Joash returned from the battle along the Ascent of Heres. 14 There he captured a young man of Succoth and interrogated him. The young man wrote down for him the names of the seventy-seven leaders and elders of Succoth. 15 And Gideon went to the men of Succoth and said, “Here are Zebah and Zalmunna, about whom you taunted me, saying, ‘Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your possession, that we should give bread to your weary men?’” 16 Then he took the elders of the city, and using the thorns and briers of the wilderness, he disciplined the men of Succoth. 17 He also pulled down the tower of Penuel and killed the men of the city. 18 Next, Gideon asked Zebah and Zalmunna, “What kind of men did you kill at Tabor?” “Men like you,” they answered, “each one resembling the son of a king.” 19 “They were my brothers,” Gideon replied, “the sons of my mother! As surely as the LORD lives, if you had let them live, I would not kill you.” 20 So he said to Jether, his firstborn, “Get up and kill them.” But the young man did not draw his sword; he was fearful because he was still a youth. 21 Then Zebah and Zalmunna said, “Get up and kill us yourself, for as the man is, so is his strength.” So Gideon got up and killed Zebah and Zalmunna, and he took the crescent ornaments from the necks of their camels.

passages.context_html:
The pursuit of Midian continues, but conflict now arises among the Israelites. Ephraim protests that Gideon did not call them to the original fight. He answers by honoring their capture of Oreb and Zeeb and acknowledging that God delivered those leaders into their hands. Their anger subsides.

The next encounters are much harsher. Gideon’s exhausted three hundred men cross the Jordan in pursuit of Zebah and Zalmunna. Succoth and Penuel refuse bread because the kings have not yet been captured. Gideon threatens punishment, then surprises the remaining enemy force and takes the kings. On his return he disciplines Succoth’s men with thorns and briers, tears down Penuel’s tower, and kills men of that city.

The last scene reveals a family loss behind the conflict with the kings: they had killed Gideon’s brothers at Tabor. Gideon tells his young firstborn, Jether, to kill them, but the youth is afraid. Gideon carries out the killing himself and takes the ornaments from their camels. The passage brings military victory, disputes within Israel, and personal loss into the same account; it does not report a separate divine command for every action Gideon takes.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Henry praise Gideon’s gentle answer to Ephraim as humility that defuses anger. His acknowledgment of their part in the victory is read as a strength, rather than simply a refusal to confront them.

Readers differ in assessing the later punishments. Henry regards the punishment of Succoth as just and understands the execution of the kings as Gideon acting for his murdered relatives. The Cambridge Bible commentary, especially its note on verse 17, views his treatment of the Israelite towns as vindictive and excessive, while distinguishing it from the execution of the kings. These readings weigh his role as deliverer, the towns’ refusal to help, and the severity of his response differently.

passages.god_plan_html:
The wider biblical story keeps the question of responding to wrong before God’s people. Romans 12:14–21 calls believers to seek peace, reject personal vengeance, and leave judgment to God. It even describes feeding an enemy who is hungry, ending with the call to overcome evil with good.

That teaching gives followers of Jesus clear direction amid hostility. God’s purpose for His people includes a life shaped by mercy and trust in His justice. We can recognize the rescue accomplished in Judges while allowing the later instruction to shape how we ourselves respond to injury and conflict.

passages.title: Judges 8:22-27
passages.section_title: Why does the ephod become a snare?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 Then the Israelites said to Gideon, “Rule over us—you and your son and grandson—for you have saved us from the hand of Midian.” 23 But Gideon replied, “I will not rule over you, nor will my son. The LORD shall rule over you.” 24 Then he added, “Let me make a request of you, that each of you give me an earring from his plunder.” (For the enemies had gold earrings because they were Ishmaelites.) 25 “We will give them gladly,” they replied. So they spread out a garment, and each man threw an earring from his plunder onto it. 26 The weight of the gold earrings he had requested was 1,700 shekels, in addition to the crescent ornaments, the pendants, the purple garments of the kings of Midian, and the chains from the necks of their camels. 27 From all this Gideon made an ephod, which he placed in Ophrah, his hometown. But soon all Israel prostituted themselves by worshiping it there, and it became a snare to Gideon and his household.
paragraphs: 22 Then the Israelites said to Gideon, “Rule over us—you and your son and grandson—for you have saved us from the hand of Midian.” 23 But Gideon replied, “I will not rule over you, nor will my son. The LORD shall rule over you.”

24 Then he added, “Let me make a request of you, that each of you give me an earring from his plunder.” (For the enemies had gold earrings because they were Ishmaelites.) 25 “We will give them gladly,” they replied. So they spread out a garment, and each man threw an earring from his plunder onto it. 26 The weight of the gold earrings he had requested was 1,700 shekels, in addition to the crescent ornaments, the pendants, the purple garments of the kings of Midian, and the chains from the necks of their camels. 27 From all this Gideon made an ephod, which he placed in Ophrah, his hometown. But soon all Israel prostituted themselves by worshiping it there, and it became a snare to Gideon and his household.

passages.context_html:
The Israelites offer Gideon a line of hereditary rulers: he, his son, and his grandson. Their reason credits him with saving them from Midian. He refuses the offer and says that the LORD will rule over them. His words bring the source of their rescue back into view.

Gideon then requests earrings from the plunder. The people give willingly, and he uses the wealth to make an ephod, which he places in Ophrah. The Hebrew אֵפוֹד, ephod (ay-FOHD), is associated with priestly clothing and religious consultation. Brown–Driver–Briggs discusses those uses and the uncertainty about the exact form of Gideon’s object.

The account is clearer about the result than about its construction: Israel worships it, and it becomes a snare to Gideon and his household. The man who tore down Baal’s altar has now made something that draws people into unfaithful worship. Whatever his original intention, the text identifies the outcome as harmful.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley reads Gideon’s refusal of kingship positively, but sees his ephod as an unauthorized religious arrangement that draws people away from the worship God had appointed. Henry and Gill also discuss the possibility of a memorial or an object for seeking divine answers. They recognize that even a respected deliverer can introduce something that misleads others.

The precise shape and intended use remain matters of interpretation. The passage does not say that Gideon wore the ephod or supply a complete account of his reasons for making it. The common concern in these readings is the worship that develops around it and the danger it creates for his own household.

passages.god_plan_html:
The offer of power after a rescue raises a question the Bible will continue to explore: what kind of ruler do God’s people need? Jesus answers His disciples’ desire for status by describing greatness as service. The Son of Man Himself comes to serve and to give His life as a ransom for many (Matthew 20:25–28).

The larger story leads to a Savior whose authority is expressed through giving Himself for others. His example also shapes the people who follow Him: leadership is to serve, rather than become a way to claim honor and power for oneself.

passages.title: Judges 8:28-31
passages.section_title: What does the account tell us about Gideon’s later life?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 28 In this way Midian was subdued before the Israelites and did not raise its head again. So the land had rest for forty years in the days of Gideon, 29 and he—Jerubbaal son of Joash—returned home and settled down. 30 Gideon had seventy sons of his own, since he had many wives. 31 His concubine, who dwelt in Shechem, also bore him a son, and he named him Abimelech.

passages.context_html:
Midian remains subdued, and the land has forty years of rest during Gideon’s lifetime. The phrase about not raising its head describes Midian’s defeat. The rescue has brought a real period of peace, even though the previous verses have already identified trouble around Gideon’s ephod.

The account then introduces his large household: many wives, seventy sons, and another son, Abimelech, born to his concubine at Shechem. A concubine held the status of a secondary wife, as the USCCB’s scholarly note on verse 31 explains. These family details prepare for the struggle over power in the next chapter; they are part of where Gideon’s story leads.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley understands Gideon’s return home as a life between the public service of a judge and the royal court he had declined. Gill notes that the introduction of Abimelech prepares the reader for the following account. These verses report both the lasting relief from Midian and the household from which the next conflict will emerge.

passages.title: Judges 8:32-35
passages.section_title: What does Israel forget after Gideon dies?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 32 Later, Gideon son of Joash died at a ripe old age and was buried in the tomb of his father Joash in Ophrah of the Abiezrites. 33 And as soon as Gideon was dead, the Israelites turned and prostituted themselves with the Baals, and they set up Baal-berith as their god. 34 The Israelites failed to remember the LORD their God who had delivered them from the hands of all their enemies on every side. 35 They did not show kindness to the house of Jerubbaal (that is, Gideon) for all the good things he had done for Israel.
paragraphs: 32 Later, Gideon son of Joash died at a ripe old age and was buried in the tomb of his father Joash in Ophrah of the Abiezrites. 33 And as soon as Gideon was dead, the Israelites turned and prostituted themselves with the Baals, and they set up Baal-berith as their god. 34 The Israelites failed to remember the LORD their God who had delivered them from the hands of all their enemies on every side. 35 They did not show kindness to the house of Jerubbaal (that is, Gideon) for all the good things he had done for Israel.

passages.context_html:
Gideon dies at a ripe old age and is buried in his father’s tomb in Ophrah. Israel then turns again to the Baals and makes Baal-berith its god. The account names the central failure: the people do not remember the LORD who delivered them from their enemies.

Their ingratitude also reaches Gideon’s household. Despite the good he had done for Israel, they do not show his family kindness. The chapter preserves both truths about him: the ephod became a snare, and his service brought genuine good. His death is followed by another departure from the God who had rescued them.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley emphasizes the people’s failure to remain faithful once the judge’s restraining presence is gone. Henry connects forgetting God with forgetting the people through whom help came. He applies the passage by urging patience when service is repaid with ingratitude and by encouraging believers to answer evil with good.

passages.god_plan_html:
The passing of a faithful servant leaves a question the Bible’s larger story addresses: where can God’s people find care that continues beyond a human lifetime? Hebrews 13:7–9 calls believers to remember those who taught them God’s word, imitate their faith, and remain grounded in the unchanging Jesus Christ.

Hebrews 7:23–28 makes a related contrast through the priesthood: human priests die, but Jesus lives forever and continues to intercede for those who draw near to God through Him. The lasting hope rests in the living Son, whose care does not end as the service of mortal leaders does.

passages.title: Judges 9:1-6
passages.section_title: How does Abimelech gain power?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now Abimelech son of Jerubbaal went to his mother’s brothers at Shechem and said to them and to all the clan of his mother, 2 “Please ask all the leaders of Shechem, ‘Is it better for you that seventy men, all the sons of Jerubbaal, rule over you, or just one man?’ Remember that I am your own flesh and blood.” 3 And when his mother’s brothers spoke all these words about him in the presence of all the leaders of Shechem, their hearts were inclined to follow Abimelech, for they said, “He is our brother.” 4 So they gave him seventy shekels of silver from the temple of Baal-berith, with which Abimelech hired some worthless and reckless men to follow him. 5 He went to his father’s house in Ophrah, and on one stone murdered his seventy brothers, the sons of Jerubbaal. But Jotham, the youngest son of Jerubbaal, survived, because he hid himself. 6 Then all the leaders of Shechem and Beth-millo gathered beside the oak at the pillar in Shechem and proceeded to make Abimelech their king.

5 He went to his father’s house in Ophrah, and on one stone murdered his seventy brothers, the sons of Jerubbaal. But Jotham, the youngest son of Jerubbaal, survived, because he hid himself. 6 Then all the leaders of Shechem and Beth-millo gathered beside the oak at the pillar in Shechem and proceeded to make Abimelech their king.

passages.context_html:
The previous chapter introduced Abimelech as Gideon’s son by a concubine who lived in Shechem. After Gideon’s death, Abimelech approaches his mother’s relatives there. He presents a choice between rule by Gideon’s seventy sons and rule by himself, emphasizing that he is their own flesh and blood. The account records his political appeal; it does not say that his brothers had already formed a government.

His relatives persuade Shechem’s leaders to support him. Silver from the temple of Baal-berith pays for reckless followers, whom he leads to his father’s house in Ophrah. He murders his brothers on one stone, while Jotham survives by hiding. The leaders of Shechem and Beth-millo then make Abimelech king.

This rise to power comes through family loyalty, temple money, hired men, and the removal of rivals. The story gives no call from the LORD commissioning him as a deliverer. It continues the account of Israel forgetting both God’s rescue and the good done through Gideon.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley understands the appeal to kinship as persuasion that serves the Shechemites’ own interests. Henry emphasizes that God is not consulted in their choice of king. Both readings treat the episode as a warning about ambition and the harm that can spread through a household and community.

passages.god_plan_html:
Abimelech’s violence makes the question of trustworthy leadership urgent. Jesus describes Himself as the good shepherd who gives life to His sheep and lays down His own life for them (John 10:10–18). The contrast is between taking lives to secure power and giving one’s life for those in one’s care.

The larger biblical hope is more than finding a less violent claimant to the same throne. Jesus speaks of bringing His sheep together as one flock under one shepherd. God’s rescue leads toward people gathered and cared for by the Son who gives Himself for them.

passages.title: Judges 9:7-21
passages.section_title: What does Jotham’s story of the trees expose?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 When this was reported to Jotham, he climbed to the top of Mount Gerizim, raised his voice, and cried out: “Listen to me, O leaders of Shechem, and may God listen to you. 8 One day the trees set out to anoint a king for themselves. They said to the olive tree, ‘Reign over us.’ 9 But the olive tree replied, ‘Should I stop giving my oil that honors both God and man, to hold sway over the trees?’ 10 Then the trees said to the fig tree, ‘Come and reign over us.’ 11 But the fig tree replied, ‘Should I stop giving my sweetness and my good fruit, to hold sway over the trees?’ 12 Then the trees said to the grapevine, ‘Come and reign over us.’ 13 But the grapevine replied, ‘Should I stop giving my wine that cheers both God and man, to hold sway over the trees?’ 14 Finally all the trees said to the thornbush, ‘Come and reign over us.’ 15 But the thornbush replied, ‘If you really are anointing me as king over you, come and find refuge in my shade. But if not, may fire come out of the thornbush and consume the cedars of Lebanon.’ 16 Now if you have acted faithfully and honestly in making Abimelech king, if you have done well by Jerubbaal and his family, and if you have done to him as he deserves— 17 for my father fought for you and risked his life to deliver you from the hand of Midian, 18 but you have risen up against my father’s house this day and killed his seventy sons on a single stone, and you have made Abimelech, the son of his maidservant, king over the leaders of Shechem because he is your brother— 19 if you have acted faithfully and honestly toward Jerubbaal and his house this day, then may you rejoice in Abimelech, and he in you. 20 But if not, may fire come from Abimelech and consume the leaders of Shechem and Beth-millo, and may fire come from the leaders of Shechem and Beth-millo and consume Abimelech.” 21 Then Jotham ran away, escaping to Beer, and he lived there for fear of his brother Abimelech.
