But if not, may fire come out of the thornbush and consume the cedars of Lebanon.’

16 Now if you have acted faithfully and honestly in making Abimelech king, if you have done well by Jerubbaal and his family, and if you have done to him as he deserves— 17 for my father fought for you and risked his life to deliver you from the hand of Midian, 18 but you have risen up against my father’s house this day and killed his seventy sons on a single stone, and you have made Abimelech, the son of his maidservant, king over the leaders of Shechem because he is your brother— 19 if you have acted faithfully and honestly toward Jerubbaal and his house this day, then may you rejoice in Abimelech, and he in you. 20 But if not, may fire come from Abimelech and consume the leaders of Shechem and Beth-millo, and may fire come from the leaders of Shechem and Beth-millo and consume Abimelech.” 21 Then Jotham ran away, escaping to Beer, and he lived there for fear of his brother Abimelech.

passages.context_html:
Jotham speaks from Mount Gerizim to Shechem’s leaders. In his story, the trees seek a king. The olive, fig tree, and vine refuse to abandon the useful produce they already supply. The thornbush accepts, offers shelter in its shade, and threatens fire against the great cedars if the arrangement is not sincere.

The thornbush is the Hebrew אָטָד, atad (ah-TAHD), identified by Brown–Driver–Briggs as a bramble or buckthorn. The contrast in the story is plain: the fruitful plants keep serving, while the plant least able to shelter great trees offers protection backed by a threat.

Jotham then applies the story to Abimelech and Shechem. He recalls his father’s dangerous service and confronts the leaders with their part in the murders. If they have acted faithfully, they may rejoice in their new king. If not, he calls for destructive fire to come from each side against the other. He then escapes to Beer, fearing Abimelech. The rest of the chapter will show what becomes of that warning.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads the fruitful plants as an image of useful service, which can be lost when people pursue status for its own sake. Wesley connects the refusals with Gideon’s refusal of kingship and sees the thornbush as representing Abimelech. Gill emphasizes the emptiness of its promised protection: the apparent refuge itself becomes a danger.

These readings take the story as Jotham’s challenge to this particular choice of ruler. Its direct application concerns whether Abimelech and his supporters have acted faithfully toward Gideon’s house. The story does not require us to assign a hidden prophetic identity to every kind of tree.

passages.god_plan_html:
The contrast between useful service and destructive ambition continues in the New Testament. James 3:13–18 distinguishes wisdom shown through humble good conduct from jealousy and selfish ambition, which bring disorder. Wisdom from above is peace-loving, merciful, sincere, and full of good fruit.

This is a parallel in the moral pattern, rather than a claim that James is explaining Jotham’s trees. It shows what God intends to grow among His people: righteousness and peace, expressed through the lives they lead, rather than a struggle for honor that consumes others.

passages.title: Judges 9:22-29
passages.section_title: Why does the alliance begin to break apart?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 After Abimelech had reigned over Israel for three years, 23 God sent a spirit of animosity between Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem and caused them to treat Abimelech deceitfully, 24 in order that the crime against the seventy sons of Jerubbaal might come to justice and their blood be avenged on their brother Abimelech and on the leaders of Shechem, who had helped him murder his brothers. 25 The leaders of Shechem set up an ambush against Abimelech on the hilltops, and they robbed all who passed by them on the road. So this was reported to Abimelech. 26 Meanwhile, Gaal son of Ebed came with his brothers and crossed into Shechem, and the leaders of Shechem put their confidence in him. 27 And after they had gone out into the fields, gathered grapes from their vineyards, and trodden them, they held a festival and went into the house of their god; and as they ate and drank, they cursed Abimelech. 28 Then Gaal son of Ebed said, “Who is Abimelech, and who is Shechem, that we should serve him? Is he not the son of Jerubbaal, and is not Zebul his officer? You are to serve the men of Hamor, the father of Shechem. Why should we serve Abimelech? 29 If only this people were under my authority, I would remove Abimelech; I would say to him, ‘Muster your army and come out!’”

Is he not the son of Jerubbaal, and is not Zebul his officer? You are to serve the men of Hamor, the father of Shechem. Why should we serve Abimelech? 29 If only this people were under my authority, I would remove Abimelech; I would say to him, ‘Muster your army and come out!’”

passages.context_html:
After three years, the alliance between Abimelech and Shechem’s leaders begins to collapse. The account says that God sends a spirit of animosity between them. It also gives the purpose: the murder of Gideon’s sons is to come to justice, with responsibility falling on both the killer and those who helped him.

The leaders arrange ambushes and rob travelers. Gaal arrives with his brothers and gains their confidence. During a harvest festival in the house of their god, the people curse Abimelech. Gaal challenges his right to rule, invokes Shechem’s connection with Hamor, and says he would remove Abimelech if the people were under his authority.

The motives and competing claims belong to the human conflict, while the narrator identifies a larger judgment at work. The partnership that enabled the murders is becoming a source of danger to its own members.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Readers explain the spirit’s action in different ways. Wesley understands God as allowing the devil to work on their minds. Gill discusses that reading and also the possibility of God giving them over to their own jealousy, hatred, and desire for revenge. The BSB’s wording, a spirit of animosity, highlights the hostility that develops.

Henry emphasizes that the people who helped Abimelech seize power are among the first to suffer under it. The central agreement is that the breakdown serves judgment on their shared guilt. The passage does not give a detailed account of the unseen means by which every suspicion or decision arises.

passages.god_plan_html:
God’s ability to carry out His purposes amid human wrongdoing becomes especially important in the account of Jesus’ death and resurrection. Acts 2:22–24 describes the cross as within God’s plan while still holding the people who killed Jesus responsible. God raises Him from the dead.

The purpose there includes a greater rescue: Peter announces Jesus as Lord and Christ and calls his hearers to repentance and forgiveness in His name (Acts 2:36–39). Human evil is not the final word. God can accomplish judgment and salvation without making the wrongdoing itself good. James 1:13–17 also insists that God does not tempt anyone to evil.

passages.title: Judges 9:30-49
passages.section_title: How does the promised protection become destruction?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 30 When Zebul the governor of the city heard the words of Gaal son of Ebed, he burned with anger. 31 So he covertly sent messengers to Abimelech to say, “Look, Gaal son of Ebed and his brothers have come to Shechem and are stirring up the city against you. 32 Now then, tonight you and the people with you are to come and lie in wait in the fields. 33 And in the morning at sunrise, get up and advance against the city. When Gaal and his men come out against you, do to them whatever you are able.” 34 So Abimelech and all his troops set out by night and lay in wait against Shechem in four companies. 35 Now Gaal son of Ebed went out and stood at the entrance of the city gate just as Abimelech and his men came out from their hiding places. 36 When Gaal saw the people, he said to Zebul, “Look, people are coming down from the mountains!” But Zebul replied, “The shadows of the mountains look like men to you.” 37 Then Gaal spoke up again, “Look, people are coming down from the center of the land, and one company is coming by way of the Diviners’ Oak.” 38 “Where is your gloating now?” Zebul replied. “You said, ‘Who is Abimelech that we should serve him?’ Are these not the people you ridiculed? Go out now and fight them!” 39 So Gaal went out before the leaders of Shechem and fought against Abimelech, 40 but Abimelech pursued him, and Gaal fled before him. And many Shechemites fell wounded all the way to the entrance of the gate. 41 Abimelech stayed in Arumah, and Zebul drove Gaal and his brothers out of Shechem. 42 The next day the people of Shechem went out into the fields, and this was reported to Abimelech. 43 So he took his men, divided them into three companies, and lay in wait in the fields. When he saw the people coming out of the city, he rose up against them and attacked them. 44 Then Abimelech and the companies with him rushed forward and took their stand at the entrance of the city gate. The other two companies rushed against all who were in the fields and struck them down. 45 And all that day Abimelech fought against the city until he had captured it and killed its people. Then he demolished the city and sowed it with salt. 46 On hearing of this, all the leaders in the tower of Shechem entered the inner chamber of the temple of El-berith. 47 And when Abimelech was told that all the leaders in the tower of Shechem were gathered there, 48 he and all his men went up to Mount Zalmon. Abimelech took his axe in his hand and cut a branch from the trees, which he lifted to his shoulder, saying to his men, “Hurry and do what you have seen me do.” 49 So each man also cut his own branch and followed Abimelech. Then they piled the branches against the inner chamber and set it on fire above them, killing everyone in the tower of Shechem, about a thousand men and women.

passages.context_html:
Zebul hears Gaal’s challenge and secretly alerts Abimelech, arranging an ambush. When the troops appear, he first dismisses Gaal’s alarm as shadows, then challenges him to fight the men he has mocked. Gaal is defeated and driven out of Shechem with his brothers.

The next day, the people of Shechem go into the fields. Abimelech attacks them, takes the city, kills its people, demolishes it, and sows it with salt. The account does not identify everyone in the fields as simply Gaal’s expelled fighting force; the violence now falls on the city itself.

The leaders associated with Shechem’s tower seek shelter in the temple of El-berith. Abimelech has his men cut branches and pile them against the inner chamber, then sets it on fire. About a thousand men and women die. The fire Jotham warned of has become a terrible reality: the ruler chosen as protection destroys the community that raised him up.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry distinguishes Abimelech’s aim from God’s judgment. Abimelech attacks those who have turned against him; the narrator places the disaster within the judgment on the earlier murders. Understanding that larger purpose does not require treating Abimelech’s own motives as righteous.

Wesley reads the salt as a sign of intended utter destruction and understands the temple as a place where people expected security. Henry similarly sees the refuge as proving unable to save them. These readings emphasize the failure of the protection the people had trusted.

passages.title: Judges 9:50-57
passages.section_title: How does Abimelech’s rule end?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 50 Then Abimelech went to Thebez, encamped against it, and captured it. 51 But there was a strong tower inside the city, and all the men, women, and leaders of the city fled there. They locked themselves in and went up to the roof of the tower. 52 When Abimelech came to attack the tower, he approached its entrance to set it on fire. 53 But a woman dropped an upper millstone on Abimelech’s head, crushing his skull. 54 He quickly called his armor-bearer, saying, “Draw your sword and kill me, lest they say of me, ‘A woman killed him.’” So Abimelech’s armor-bearer ran his sword through him, and he died. 55 And when the Israelites saw that Abimelech was dead, they all went home. 56 In this way God repaid the wickedness that Abimelech had done to his father in murdering his seventy brothers. 57 And God also brought all the wickedness of the men of Shechem back upon their own heads. So the curse of Jotham son of Jerubbaal came upon them.

They locked themselves in and went up to the roof of the tower. 52 When Abimelech came to attack the tower, he approached its entrance to set it on fire. 53 But a woman dropped an upper millstone on Abimelech’s head, crushing his skull. 54 He quickly called his armor-bearer, saying, “Draw your sword and kill me, lest they say of me, ‘A woman killed him.’” So Abimelech’s armor-bearer ran his sword through him, and he died. 55 And when the Israelites saw that Abimelech was dead, they all went home.

56 In this way God repaid the wickedness that Abimelech had done to his father in murdering his seventy brothers. 57 And God also brought all the wickedness of the men of Shechem back upon their own heads. So the curse of Jotham son of Jerubbaal came upon them.

passages.context_html:
Abimelech next captures Thebez, but the people take refuge in a strong tower. As he approaches to burn its entrance, a woman drops an upper millstone on his head. Mortally injured, he asks his armor-bearer to kill him so that people will not say a woman killed him. The armor-bearer does so, and the army disperses.

His attempt to control his reputation does not erase what happened. The later account in Second Samuel 11:18–21 remembers the woman and the millstone when discussing the danger of approaching a city wall.

The chapter ends with the narrator’s explanation: God repays Abimelech’s wickedness against his father’s household and brings Shechem’s wickedness back upon its leaders. Jotham’s curse has come upon them. The destruction they helped set in motion has reached both parties.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley and Gill notice the fitting reversal: Abimelech killed his brothers on a stone and receives a fatal blow from a stone. Henry emphasizes the end of power gained through wickedness. These readings follow the narrator’s explicit conclusion that God has judged the shared crime, rather than merely describing an unlucky end to a military campaign.

passages.god_plan_html:
The judgment of a violent ruler belongs to a wider biblical assurance that power does not place anyone beyond God’s justice. Acts 17:24–31 announces the Creator’s rule over all nations, calls everyone to repentance, and declares a coming day when He will judge the world through the One He raised from the dead.

Judges records a particular judgment within history. The New Testament points toward judgment through the risen Jesus that reaches the whole world. The hope is not that every wrong will receive an identical visible repayment immediately, but that God’s justice is larger than any ruler’s ability to escape or control the account of his life.

passages.title: Judges 10:1-2
passages.section_title: What are we told about Tola?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 After the time of Abimelech, a man of Issachar, Tola son of Puah, the son of Dodo, rose up to save Israel. He lived in Shamir, in the hill country of Ephraim. 2 Tola judged Israel twenty-three years, and when he died, he was buried in Shamir.
paragraphs: 1 After the time of Abimelech, a man of Issachar, Tola son of Puah, the son of Dodo, rose up to save Israel. He lived in Shamir, in the hill country of Ephraim. 2 Tola judged Israel twenty-three years, and when he died, he was buried in Shamir.

passages.context_html:
After Abimelech’s violent rule, Tola rises to save Israel. He is from Issachar and lives in Shamir, in the hill country of Ephraim. He judges Israel for twenty-three years, then dies and is buried in Shamir.

The notice gives his family, location, purpose, and length of service. It records no particular battle, speech, or dramatic sign. His place in the account shows that the work of a judge can be summarized as years of service, rather than only a single military victory.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley understands Tola’s saving work chiefly as wise government that checks disorder and oppression. Henry reads the brief accounts of Tola and Jair as useful, peaceable service that provides fewer dramatic events to recount. These are explanations of the short notice; the text does not give a detailed record of Tola’s administration.

passages.title: Judges 10:3-5
passages.section_title: What does Jair’s household tell us?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 3 Tola was followed by Jair the Gileadite, who judged Israel twenty-two years. 4 He had thirty sons who rode on thirty donkeys. And they had thirty towns in the land of Gilead, which to this day are called Havvoth-jair. 5 When Jair died, he was buried in Kamon.
paragraphs: 3 Tola was followed by Jair the Gileadite, who judged Israel twenty-two years. 4 He had thirty sons who rode on thirty donkeys. And they had thirty towns in the land of Gilead, which to this day are called Havvoth-jair. 5 When Jair died, he was buried in Kamon.

passages.context_html:
Jair follows Tola and judges Israel for twenty-two years. He is a Gileadite, and his household is described through thirty sons, thirty donkeys, and thirty towns in Gilead. The towns remain associated with his name. He dies and is buried in Kamon.

These details show the extent of his family’s place in the region. The account does not report his battles, name his wives, or tell us how his sons carried out their roles. The brief notice should be read on its own terms before the next passage introduces Israel’s renewed unfaithfulness.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley and Gill suggest that Jair’s sons served as local deputies who traveled to administer justice. That is a possible explanation of the family’s towns and donkeys, rather than a task explicitly assigned to each son in these verses. Henry assesses Jair’s leadership positively as part of a period of useful service. The account’s brevity leaves many details of his family life unknown.

passages.title: Judges 10:6-18
passages.section_title: What changes when Israel turns back to the LORD?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 And again the Israelites did evil in the sight of the LORD. They served the Baals, the Ashtoreths, the gods of Aram, Sidon, and Moab, and the gods of the Ammonites and Philistines. Thus they forsook the LORD and did not serve Him. 7 So the anger of the LORD burned against Israel, and He sold them into the hands of the Philistines and Ammonites, 8 who that very year harassed and oppressed the Israelites, and they did so for eighteen years to all the Israelites on the other side of the Jordan in Gilead, the land of the Amorites. 9 The Ammonites also crossed the Jordan to fight against Judah, Benjamin, and the house of Ephraim, and Israel was in deep distress. 10 Then the Israelites cried out to the LORD, saying, “We have sinned against You, for we have indeed forsaken our God and served the Baals.” 11 The LORD replied, “When the Egyptians, Amorites, Ammonites, Philistines, 12 Sidonians, Amalekites, and Maonites oppressed you and you cried out to Me, did I not save you from their hands? 13 But you have forsaken Me and served other gods, so I will no longer save you. 14 Go and cry out to the gods you have chosen. Let them save you in your time of trouble.” 15 “We have sinned,” the Israelites said to the LORD. “Deal with us as You see fit; but please deliver us today!” 16 So they put away the foreign gods from among them and served the LORD, and He could no longer bear the misery of Israel. 17 Then the Ammonites were called to arms and camped in Gilead, and the Israelites assembled and camped at Mizpah. 18 And the rulers of Gilead said to one another, “Whoever will launch the attack against the Ammonites will be the head of all who live in Gilead.”

10 Then the Israelites cried out to the LORD, saying, “We have sinned against You, for we have indeed forsaken our God and served the Baals.” 11 The LORD replied, “When the Egyptians, Amorites, Ammonites, Philistines, 12 Sidonians, Amalekites, and Maonites oppressed you and you cried out to Me, did I not save you from their hands? 13 But you have forsaken Me and served other gods, so I will no longer save you. 14 Go and cry out to the gods you have chosen. Let them save you in your time of trouble.”

15 “We have sinned,” the Israelites said to the LORD. “Deal with us as You see fit; but please deliver us today!” 16 So they put away the foreign gods from among them and served the LORD, and He could no longer bear the misery of Israel. 17 Then the Ammonites were called to arms and camped in Gilead, and the Israelites assembled and camped at Mizpah. 18 And the rulers of Gilead said to one another, “Whoever will launch the attack against the Ammonites will be the head of all who live in Gilead.”

passages.context_html:
Israel again serves other gods, drawing from the worship of several surrounding peoples and forsaking the LORD. Philistine and Ammonite oppression follow. Gilead suffers for eighteen years, and the Ammonites also cross the Jordan against Judah, Benjamin, and Ephraim. The distress spreads beyond one region.

The people confess that they have forsaken God. His answer recalls the many enemies from whom He has already saved them, then challenges them to ask their chosen gods for rescue. Their repeated rejection of Him is brought into the open. They cannot treat Him as one more source of help while continuing to serve rivals.

The next response includes action: they confess again, submit themselves to His judgment, put away the foreign gods, and serve the LORD. The passage says He can no longer bear Israel’s misery. His compassion is present alongside the rebuke. The armies then gather, and Gilead’s rulers offer leadership over their people to whoever begins the fight against Ammon. The rescue itself remains ahead.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley, Henry, and Gill distinguish words of regret from a return that includes putting away idols. They read the changed worship as evidence that the confession has become more than a request for easier circumstances.

Wesley and Gill understand the refusal to save in verse 13 within that call to genuine repentance, rather than as a promise that God will never help Israel under any circumstances. Henry emphasizes both submission to God’s justice and hope in His mercy. Gill also understands the description of God’s grief as expressing compassion through His dealings with Israel, while affirming that God Himself remains unchanging.

passages.god_plan_html:
The movement from wandering and misery to confession and compassionate welcome has a later parallel in Jesus’ story of the returning son. In Luke 15:11–24, the son comes to his senses, acknowledges his sin, and returns to his father. The father sees him while he is still far away and meets him with compassion.

The situations differ, but the shared pattern helps us see a larger purpose of God’s correction and mercy: a real return to Him, rather than only relief while the old allegiance continues. Jesus’ story presents the joy of receiving the lost one back. The warning against unfaithfulness and the invitation to return belong together.

passages.title: Judges 11:1-28
passages.section_title: Why do Gilead’s leaders turn to the man they rejected?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now Jephthah the Gileadite was a mighty man of valor; he was the son of a prostitute, and Gilead was his father. 2 And Gilead’s wife bore him sons who grew up, drove Jephthah out, and said to him, “You shall have no inheritance in our father’s house, because you are the son of another woman.” 3 So Jephthah fled from his brothers and settled in the land of Tob, where worthless men gathered around him and traveled with him. 4 Some time later, when the Ammonites fought against Israel 5 and made war with them, the elders of Gilead went to get Jephthah from the land of Tob. 6 “Come,” they said, “be our commander, so that we can fight against the Ammonites.” 7 Jephthah replied to the elders of Gilead, “Did you not hate me and expel me from my father’s house? Why then have you come to me now, when you are in distress?” 8 They answered Jephthah, “This is why we now turn to you, that you may go with us, fight the Ammonites, and become leader over all of us who live in Gilead.” 9 But Jephthah asked them, “If you take me back to fight the Ammonites and the LORD gives them to me, will I really be your leader?” 10 And the elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, “The LORD is our witness if we do not do as you say.” 11 So Jephthah went with the elders of Gilead, and the people made him their leader and commander. And Jephthah repeated all his terms in the presence of the LORD at Mizpah. 12 Then Jephthah sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites, saying, “What do you have against me that you have come to fight against my land?” 13 The king of the Ammonites answered Jephthah’s messengers, “When Israel came up out of Egypt, they seized my land, from the Arnon to the Jabbok and all the way to the Jordan. Now, therefore, restore it peaceably.” 14 Jephthah again sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites 15 to tell him, “This is what Jephthah says: Israel did not take away the land of Moab or of the Ammonites. 16 But when Israel came up out of Egypt, they traveled through the wilderness to the Red Sea and came to Kadesh. 17 Then Israel sent messengers to the king of Edom, saying, ‘Please let us pass through your land,’ but the king of Edom would not listen. They also sent messengers to the king of Moab, but he would not consent. So Israel stayed in Kadesh. 18 Then Israel traveled through the wilderness and bypassed the lands of Edom and Moab. They came to the east side of the land of Moab and camped on the other side of the Arnon. But they did not enter the territory of Moab, since the Arnon was its border. 19 And Israel sent messengers to Sihon king of the Amorites, who ruled in Heshbon, and said to him, ‘Please let us pass through your land into our own place.’ 20 But Sihon would not trust Israel to pass through his territory. So he gathered all his people, encamped in Jahaz, and fought with Israel. 21 Then the LORD, the God of Israel, delivered Sihon and all his people into the hand of Israel, who defeated them. So Israel took possession of all the land of the Amorites who inhabited that country, 22 seizing all the land from the Arnon to the Jabbok and from the wilderness to the Jordan. 23 Now since the LORD, the God of Israel, has driven out the Amorites from before His people Israel, should you now possess it? 24 Do you not possess whatever your god Chemosh grants you? So also, we possess whatever the LORD our God has granted us. 25 Are you now so much better than Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab? Did he ever contend with Israel or fight against them? 26 For three hundred years Israel has lived in Heshbon, Aroer, and their villages, as well as all the cities along the banks of the Arnon. Why did you not take them back during that time? 27 I have not sinned against you, but you have done me wrong by waging war against me. May the LORD, the Judge, decide today between the Israelites and the Ammonites.” 28 But the king of the Ammonites paid no heed to the message Jephthah sent him.
paragraphs: 1 Now Jephthah the Gileadite was a mighty man of valor; he was the son of a prostitute, and Gilead was his father. 2 And Gilead’s wife bore him sons who grew up, drove Jephthah out, and said to him, “You shall have no inheritance in our father’s house, because you are the son of another woman.” 3 So Jephthah fled from his brothers and settled in the land of Tob, where worthless men gathered around him and traveled with him.

4 Some time later, when the Ammonites fought against Israel 5 and made war with them, the elders of Gilead went to get Jephthah from the land of Tob. 6 “Come,” they said, “be our commander, so that we can fight against the Ammonites.” 7 Jephthah replied to the elders of Gilead, “Did you not hate me and expel me from my father’s house? Why then have you come to me now, when you are in distress?” 8 They answered Jephthah, “This is why we now turn to you, that you may go with us, fight the Ammonites, and become leader over all of us who live in Gilead.” 9 But Jephthah asked them, “If you take me back to fight the Ammonites and the LORD gives them to me, will I really be your leader?” 10 And the elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, “The LORD is our witness if we do not do as you say.” 11 So Jephthah went with the elders of Gilead, and the people made him their leader and commander. And Jephthah repeated all his terms in the presence of the LORD at Mizpah.

12 Then Jephthah sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites, saying, “What do you have against me that you have come to fight against my land?” 13 The king of the Ammonites answered Jephthah’s messengers, “When Israel came up out of Egypt, they seized my land, from the Arnon to the Jabbok and all the way to the Jordan. Now, therefore, restore it peaceably.” 14 Jephthah again sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites 15 to tell him, “This is what Jephthah says: Israel did not take away the land of Moab or of the Ammonites. 16 But when Israel came up out of Egypt, they traveled through the wilderness to the Red Sea and came to Kadesh. 17 Then Israel sent messengers to the king of Edom, saying, ‘Please let us pass through your land,’ but the king of Edom would not listen. They also sent messengers to the king of Moab, but he would not consent. So Israel stayed in Kadesh. 18 Then Israel traveled through the wilderness and bypassed the lands of Edom and Moab. They came to the east side of the land of Moab and camped on the other side of the Arnon. But they did not enter the territory of Moab, since the Arnon was its border.

19 And Israel sent messengers to Sihon king of the Amorites, who ruled in Heshbon, and said to him, ‘Please let us pass through your land into our own place.’ 20 But Sihon would not trust Israel to pass through his territory. So he gathered all his people, encamped in Jahaz, and fought with Israel. 21 Then the LORD, the God of Israel, delivered Sihon and all his people into the hand of Israel, who defeated them. So Israel took possession of all the land of the Amorites who inhabited that country, 22 seizing all the land from the Arnon to the Jabbok and from the wilderness to the Jordan. 23 Now since the LORD, the God of Israel, has driven out the Amorites from before His people Israel, should you now possess it? 24 Do you not possess whatever your god Chemosh grants you? So also, we possess whatever the LORD our God has granted us.

25 Are you now so much better than Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab? Did he ever contend with Israel or fight against them? 26 For three hundred years Israel has lived in Heshbon, Aroer, and their villages, as well as all the cities along the banks of the Arnon. Why did you not take them back during that time? 27 I have not sinned against you, but you have done me wrong by waging war against me. May the LORD, the Judge, decide today between the Israelites and the Ammonites.” 28 But the king of the Ammonites paid no heed to the message Jephthah sent him.

passages.context_html:
Jephthah is introduced as a capable warrior whose brothers have expelled him because his mother was a prostitute. He settles in Tob, where a band of men gathers around him. When Ammon makes war, Gilead’s elders seek his help. He confronts them with their earlier rejection and asks whether they will truly accept him as leader if the LORD gives him victory.

The elders make their pledge with the LORD as witness. Jephthah returns, is appointed leader and commander, and repeats the terms before the LORD at Mizpah. His appointment answers the question posed at the end of chapter 10, though the account will reveal both his faith and his serious failures.

Before fighting, he sends messengers to Ammon’s king to ask the reason for the invasion. The king claims that Israel took his land during the journey from Egypt. Jephthah replies with an account of Israel avoiding Edom and Moab, seeking passage through Sihon’s territory, and receiving victory when Sihon attacked. His case distinguishes land taken from the Amorites from the Ammonite land now being claimed.

Jephthah also appeals to the LORD’s gift of the land, the precedent of Balak, and Israel’s long occupation. His reference to the opponent’s god Chemosh uses the king’s own religious claims in the exchange; it need not be read as the narrator affirming another god’s real authority. He ends by appealing to the LORD as Judge. The Ammonite king refuses to heed the message.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry emphasizes that a person should not be condemned for his parentage and reads Jephthah’s recognition of the LORD as an acknowledgment that victory depends on God. His difficult beginnings do not prevent him from being used in the rescue.

Wesley and Henry both read the diplomatic exchange positively as an effort to prevent bloodshed. They see a reasonable account of Israel’s claim to the territory, grounded in its history. The failed negotiation does not, in their reading, make the attempt itself a failure of faith.

passages.god_plan_html:
The rejected man being called back to help his people has a parallel elsewhere in the Bible. Acts 7:35–37 recalls that Moses, rejected as ruler and judge, was the very one God sent to lead the rescue. These are different lives, but the repeated pattern warns against assuming that human rejection settles whom God can use.

The pattern reaches its greatest expression in Jesus. Acts 4:8–12 identifies the crucified and risen Jesus as the stone rejected by the builders that becomes the cornerstone, and announces salvation through Him. This is a broader comparison of rejection and God’s saving work, rather than a claim that every part of Jephthah’s life predicts Christ.

passages.title: Judges 11:29-40
passages.section_title: What happens after Jephthah makes his vow?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 29 Then the Spirit of the LORD came upon Jephthah, and he passed through Gilead and Manasseh, then through Mizpah of Gilead. And from there he advanced against the Ammonites. 30 Jephthah made this vow to the LORD: “If indeed You will deliver the Ammonites into my hand, 31 then whatever comes out the door of my house to greet me on my triumphant return from the Ammonites will belong to the LORD, and I will offer it up as a burnt offering.” 32 So Jephthah crossed over to the Ammonites to fight against them, and the LORD delivered them into his hand. 33 With a great blow he devastated twenty cities from Aroer to the vicinity of Minnith, as far as Abel-keramim. So the Ammonites were subdued before the Israelites. 34 And when Jephthah returned home to Mizpah, there was his daughter coming out to meet him with tambourines and dancing! She was his only child; he had no son or daughter besides her. 35 As soon as Jephthah saw her, he tore his clothes and said, “No! Not my daughter! You have brought me to my knees! You have brought great misery upon me, for I have given my word to the LORD and cannot take it back.” 36 “My father,” she replied, “you have given your word to the LORD. Do to me as you have said, for the LORD has avenged you of your enemies, the Ammonites.” 37 She also said to her father, “Let me do this one thing: Let me wander for two months through the mountains with my friends and mourn my virginity.” 38 “Go,” he said. And he sent her away for two months. So she left with her friends and mourned her virginity upon the mountains. 39 After two months, she returned to her father, and he did to her as he had vowed. And she had never had relations with a man. So it has become a custom in Israel 40 that each year the young women of Israel go out for four days to lament the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite.

And he sent her away for two months. So she left with her friends and mourned her virginity upon the mountains. 39 After two months, she returned to her father, and he did to her as he had vowed. passages.context_html:
The Spirit of the LORD comes upon Jephthah before the vow is made. He then promises that, if God gives victory, whatever comes from his house to greet him will belong to the LORD and be offered as a burnt offering. The Hebrew עֹלָה, olah (oh-LAH), is the usual word for a whole burnt offering, as explained by Brown–Driver–Briggs. The LORD gives victory over Ammon, but the account records no divine command to make this vow.

When Jephthah returns, his only child comes out with tambourines and dancing. He tears his clothes in distress and tells her of his promise. She asks for two months with her friends to mourn her virginity. After she returns, the text says he does to her as he vowed, notes that she had never had relations with a man, and records the annual lament for her.

The account does not describe the act in detail, which has led to different readings of what happened. One boundary is clear from the wider law: God forbids the sacrifice of sons and daughters (Deuteronomy 12:29–32; 18:9–13). A military victory and the Spirit’s empowering do not themselves tell us that every action of the deliverer is approved.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The Jewish historian Josephus, in Antiquities 5.7.10, reads the account as Jephthah sacrificing his daughter as a burnt offering. He expressly judges it contrary to the law and unacceptable to God. The scholarly notes published by the USCCB also read the story as a fatal sacrifice. These are interpretations of the account, not a claim that every Jewish or Catholic reader holds the same view.

Wesley takes the other main reading: she is dedicated to remaining unmarried for life. He emphasizes the mourning of her virginity and the statement that she knew no man. The Jewish commentator Radak likewise describes her living separately, with Israelite women visiting her yearly. Henry and Gill discuss the uncertainty and also favor an unmarried dedication rather than her death.

The disagreement concerns what Jephthah did, rather than whether God commanded human sacrifice. Rashi treats the vow as a tragedy that could have been prevented by seeking release from it. The account therefore needs care: Jephthah’s conviction that he cannot take back his words is part of the story, not by itself a declaration that God required a forbidden act.

passages.god_plan_html:
The wider biblical account of sacrifice directs us to what God provides through Christ. Hebrews 10:5–14 presents Jesus willingly doing God’s will and offering Himself once for all. His sacrifice accomplishes the cleansing that repeated offerings cannot secure.

That is the revealed saving purpose to keep before us when reading this painful account. John 10:14–18 also emphasizes Jesus’ willing gift of His own life. Scripture does not identify Jephthah’s daughter as a required sacrifice for Israel’s salvation. The gospel’s assurance rests in Christ’s completed offering, rather than in a bargain a human leader makes to obtain God’s help.

passages.title: Judges 12:1-7
passages.section_title: How does the conflict with Ephraim turn deadly?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then the men of Ephraim assembled and crossed the Jordan to Zaphon. They said to Jephthah, “Why have you crossed over to fight the Ammonites without calling us to go with you? We will burn your house down with you inside!” 2 But Jephthah replied, “My people and I had a serious conflict with the Ammonites, and when I called, you did not save me out of their hands. 3 When I saw that you would not save me, I risked my life and crossed over to the Ammonites, and the LORD delivered them into my hand. Why then have you come today to fight against me?” 4 Jephthah then gathered all the men of Gilead and fought against Ephraim. And the men of Gilead struck them down because the Ephraimites had said, “You Gileadites are fugitives in Ephraim, living in the territories of Ephraim and Manasseh.” 5 The Gileadites captured the fords of the Jordan leading to Ephraim, and whenever a fugitive from Ephraim would say, “Let me cross over,” the Gileadites would ask him, “Are you an Ephraimite?” If he answered, “No,” 6 they told him, “Please say Shibboleth.” If he said, “Sibboleth,” because he could not pronounce it correctly, they seized him and killed him at the fords of the Jordan. So at that time 42,000 Ephraimites were killed. 7 Jephthah judged Israel six years, and when he died, he was buried in one of the cities of Gilead.

We will burn your house down with you inside!” 2 But Jephthah replied, “My people and I had a serious conflict with the Ammonites, and when I called, you did not save me out of their hands. 3 When I saw that you would not save me, I risked my life and crossed over to the Ammonites, and the LORD delivered them into my hand. Why then have you come today to fight against me?”

4 Jephthah then gathered all the men of Gilead and fought against Ephraim. And the men of Gilead struck them down because the Ephraimites had said, “You Gileadites are fugitives in Ephraim, living in the territories of Ephraim and Manasseh.” 5 The Gileadites captured the fords of the Jordan leading to Ephraim, and whenever a fugitive from Ephraim would say, “Let me cross over,” the Gileadites would ask him, “Are you an Ephraimite?” If he answered, “No,” 6 they told him, “Please say Shibboleth.” If he said, “Sibboleth,” because he could not pronounce it correctly, they seized him and killed him at the fords of the Jordan. So at that time 42,000 Ephraimites were killed. 7 Jephthah judged Israel six years, and when he died, he was buried in one of the cities of Gilead.

passages.context_html:
Victory over Ammon is followed by a conflict within Israel. Ephraim’s men accuse Jephthah of fighting without calling them and threaten to burn his house with him inside. He replies that he did call, that they failed to help, and that the LORD gave the victory when he risked his life. The exchange is no longer only about the earlier enemy; fellow Israelites now threaten one another.

Jephthah gathers Gilead’s men and fights Ephraim. The account also records the Ephraimites’ contemptuous description of the Gileadites as fugitives. That insult is not Jephthah’s own explanation of where the tribes live. It is part of the hostility that has developed between them.

The Gileadites control the Jordan crossings and use pronunciation to identify fugitives. The word שִׁבֹּלֶת, shibboleth (shih-BOH-leth), can mean a flowing stream, as Brown–Driver–Briggs notes for this verse. Those who say Sibboleth instead are seized and killed. The passage reports forty-two thousand Ephraimites killed in the conflict. A difference in speech has become a means of deciding who will live and who will die.

The notice then closes Jephthah’s story: he judges Israel for six years, dies, and is buried in Gilead. The rescue from a foreign enemy has been followed by devastating violence among the people themselves.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads the episode as a warning about pride, insulting labels, and rivalry over honor. He compares Ephraim’s complaint with its earlier confrontation with Gideon and urges believers to seek what makes for peace.

Wesley notices the bitter reversal in the repeated word fugitives: those who used it to insult the Gileadites become fugitives themselves. He understands the death toll as covering the conflict, including battle, pursuit, and the crossings.

passages.god_plan_html:
The divisions within Israel make the wider biblical purpose of reconciliation especially significant. Ephesians 2:11–22 describes Christ bringing together people once divided as Jews and Gentiles, reconciling them to God in one body through the cross and giving them access to the Father by one Spirit.

Paul then calls believers to humility, patience, love, and the preservation of that unity in peace (Ephesians 4:1–6). The circumstances differ from Israel’s tribal conflict, but the direction is clear: God forms a people united in Christ, whose shared belonging is to shape how they live together.

passages.title: Judges 12:8-15
passages.section_title: What do we know about Ibzan, Elon, and Abdon?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 After Jephthah, Ibzan of Bethlehem judged Israel. 9 He had thirty sons, as well as thirty daughters whom he gave in marriage to men outside his clan; and for his sons he brought back thirty wives from elsewhere. Ibzan judged Israel seven years. 10 Then Ibzan died, and he was buried in Bethlehem. 11 After Ibzan, Elon the Zebulunite judged Israel ten years. 12 Then Elon the Zebulunite died, and he was buried in Aijalon in the land of Zebulun. 13 After Elon, Abdon son of Hillel, from Pirathon, judged Israel. 14 He had forty sons and thirty grandsons, who rode on seventy donkeys. And he judged Israel eight years. 15 Then Abdon son of Hillel, from Pirathon, died, and he was buried at Pirathon in Ephraim, in the hill country of the Amalekites.

Ibzan judged Israel seven years. 10 Then Ibzan died, and he was buried in Bethlehem.
11 After Ibzan, Elon the Zebulunite judged Israel ten years. 12 Then Elon the Zebulunite died, and he was buried in Aijalon in the land of Zebulun.

13 After Elon, Abdon son of Hillel, from Pirathon, judged Israel. 14 He had forty sons and thirty grandsons, who rode on seventy donkeys. And he judged Israel eight years. 15 Then Abdon son of Hillel, from Pirathon, died, and he was buried at Pirathon in Ephraim, in the hill country of the Amalekites.

passages.context_html:
Three brief notices carry the account forward after Jephthah. Ibzan of Bethlehem judges Israel for seven years. His thirty sons and thirty daughters marry outside their clan, connecting his large household with others. Outside the clan does not itself mean outside Israel.

Elon of Zebulun judges for ten years and is buried at Aijalon in Zebulun. Abdon of Pirathon follows for eight years. His household includes forty sons and thirty grandsons who ride seventy donkeys. He is buried in Pirathon, in Ephraim’s territory.

The account gives lengths of service, family details for two of the men, and burial places. It records no major battle or detailed evaluation of their conduct. Elon’s children are not mentioned. These notices preserve their place in Israel’s story without giving us enough to reconstruct each man’s private life or motives.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry reads these quiet accounts as a reminder of the value of useful, peaceable lives that leave fewer dramatic events to recount. Wesley draws attention to the contrast between Ibzan’s many children marrying and Jephthah’s only daughter remaining unmarried. The differences between the households are noted without treating family size alone as proof of either faithfulness or corruption.

passages.title: Judges 13:1-25
passages.section_title: Why does Samson’s story begin before his birth?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Again the Israelites did evil in the sight of the LORD, so He delivered them into the hand of the Philistines for forty years. 2 Now there was a man from Zorah named Manoah, from the clan of the Danites, whose wife was barren and had no children. 3 The angel of the LORD appeared to the woman and said to her, “It is true that you are barren and have no children; but you will conceive and give birth to a son. 4 Now please be careful not to drink wine or strong drink, and not to eat anything unclean. 5 For behold, you will conceive and give birth to a son. And no razor shall touch his head, because the boy will be a Nazirite to God from the womb, and he will begin the deliverance of Israel from the hand of the Philistines.” 6 So the woman went and told her husband, “A man of God came to me. His appearance was like the angel of God, exceedingly awesome. I did not ask him where he came from, and he did not tell me his name. 7 But he said to me, ‘Behold, you will conceive and give birth to a son. Now, therefore, do not drink wine or strong drink, and do not eat anything unclean, because the boy will be a Nazirite to God from the womb until the day of his death.’” 8 Then Manoah prayed to the LORD, “Please, O Lord, let the man of God You sent us come to us again to teach us how to raise the boy who is to be born.” 9 And God listened to the voice of Manoah, and the angel of God returned to the woman as she was sitting in the field; but her husband Manoah was not with her. 10 The woman ran quickly to tell her husband, “Behold, the man who came to me the other day has reappeared!” 11 So Manoah got up and followed his wife. When he came to the man, he asked, “Are you the man who spoke to my wife?” “I am,” he said. 12 Then Manoah asked, “When your words come to pass, what will be the boy’s rule of life and mission?” 13 So the angel of the LORD answered Manoah, “Your wife is to do everything I told her. 14 She must not eat anything that comes from the vine, nor drink any wine or strong drink, nor eat anything unclean. She must do everything I have commanded her.” 15 “Please stay here,” Manoah said to the angel of the LORD, “and we will prepare a young goat for you.” 16 And the angel of the LORD replied, “Even if I stay, I will not eat your food. But if you prepare a burnt offering, offer it to the LORD.” For Manoah did not know that it was the angel of the LORD. 17 Then Manoah said to the angel of the LORD, “What is your name, so that we may honor you when your word comes to pass?” 18 “Why do you ask my name,” said the angel of the LORD, “since it is beyond comprehension?” 19 Then Manoah took a young goat and a grain offering and offered them on a rock to the LORD. And as Manoah and his wife looked on, the LORD did a marvelous thing. 20 When the flame went up from the altar to the sky, the angel of the LORD ascended in the flame. When Manoah and his wife saw this, they fell facedown to the ground. 21 And when the angel of the LORD did not appear again to Manoah and his wife, Manoah realized that it had been the angel of the LORD. 22 “We are going to die,” he said to his wife, “for we have seen God!” 23 But his wife replied, “If the LORD had intended to kill us, He would not have accepted the burnt offering and the grain offering from our hands, nor would He have shown us all these things or spoken to us this way.” 24 So the woman gave birth to a son and named him Samson. The boy grew, and the LORD blessed him. 25 And the Spirit of the LORD began to stir him at Mahaneh-dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol.

passages.context_html:
Israel again does evil, and the LORD gives the people into Philistine hands for forty years. The account then turns to a childless couple from Dan: Manoah and his wife. It records no national cry for help here. The rescue begins with God sending His messenger to the woman and promising a son who will begin to deliver Israel.

The child is to be a Nazirite from the womb. The Hebrew נָזִיר, nazir (nah-ZEER), means someone devoted or set apart; Brown–Driver–Briggs identifies Samson’s lifelong calling as a special instance. Numbers 6:1–21 describes the usual Nazirite vow for a man or woman, with restrictions concerning grape products, cutting the hair, and contact with a dead body. Samson’s dedication is announced before he can make such a vow himself, and his mother receives instructions to observe during this beginning of his life.

Manoah prays for instruction in raising the child, and God answers by sending the messenger again. The directions already given to his wife are repeated. Manoah offers hospitality, but the messenger directs any burnt offering to the LORD. Asked His name, He says it is beyond comprehension. The Hebrew adjective פִּלְאִי, pili (pil-EE), can mean wonderful or incomprehensible, as Brown–Driver–Briggs explains.

The angel ascends in the flame of the offering, and the couple falls facedown. Manoah fears death because they have seen God. His wife reasons from what God has done: the accepted offering, the promise, and the things shown to them point toward life, rather than their destruction. Samson is born, grows under the LORD’s blessing, and begins to be stirred by His Spirit. The account promises the beginning of rescue; it does not yet describe the defeat of the Philistines.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Henry emphasize God’s initiative in preparing this deliverer and the child’s dedication to His service. Henry treats Manoah’s request for guidance as a good example of parents seeking God’s help, and highlights the wife’s faith as she answers her husband’s fear.

The messenger’s name is read within different understandings of his identity. Rashi explains it as concealed and changing. Wesley identifies the messenger as the divine Son and understands the name as pointing to a nature beyond human comprehension. Henry likewise reads the encounter through Christ and draws attention to God making Himself known through His works. These are the commentators’ readings; their explanations should not be treated as one view shared by every tradition.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Who is The Angel of the Lord? identifies the messenger in Manoah’s encounter as the eternal Son appearing before His birth as Jesus. It draws attention to the extraordinary appearance, the messenger’s words, and Manoah’s recognition that he and his wife have seen God. The study connects these encounters with the Son making the unseen Father known.

passages.god_plan_html:
The promised birth of a child with a God-given mission becomes a familiar pattern in the story leading to Jesus. Luke 1:13–17 announces John’s birth and his work of turning people back to God. The announcement to Mary then promises a Son who will reign forever (Luke 1:26–35). Mary’s virginal conception is distinct from the childlessness of Samson’s mother, but both accounts place the coming child within God’s revealed purpose.

The mission also grows beyond relief from a particular oppressor. Samson will begin Israel’s deliverance from the Philistines; the announcement of Jesus identifies Him as the One who will save His people from their sins (Matthew 1:18–23). This is a broader parallel in promise and rescue, with the lasting hope centered on the Son whose kingdom does not end.

passages.title: Judges 14:1-7
passages.section_title: What do Samson’s parents not yet understand?

Now get her for me as a wife.” 3 But his father and mother replied, “Can’t you find a young woman among your relatives or among any of our people? Must you go to the uncircumcised Philistines to get a wife?” But Samson told his father, “Get her for me, for she is pleasing to my eyes.” 4 (Now his father and mother did not know this was from the LORD, who was seeking an occasion to move against the Philistines; for at that time the Philistines were ruling over Israel.) 5 Then Samson went down to Timnah with his father and mother and came to the vineyards of Timnah. Suddenly a young lion came roaring at him, 6 and the Spirit of the LORD came powerfully upon him, and he tore the lion apart with his bare hands as one would tear a young goat. But he did not tell his father or mother what he had done. 7 Then Samson continued on his way down and spoke to the woman, because she was pleasing to his eyes.

Suddenly a young lion came roaring at him, 6 and the Spirit of the LORD came powerfully upon him, and he tore the lion apart with his bare hands as one would tear a young goat. But he did not tell his father or mother what he had done. 7 Then Samson continued on his way down and spoke to the woman, because she was pleasing to his eyes.

passages.context_html:
Samson sees a Philistine woman in Timnah and asks his parents to arrange the marriage. They object, urging him to choose from his own people. He insists because she is pleasing to his eyes. That emphasis on what he sees and wants appears again after he speaks with her.

The narrator then gives the reader information the parents lack: the matter is from the LORD, who is seeking an occasion to move against the Philistines. They are ruling Israel at this time. Samson’s personal desire is therefore part of a story with a purpose larger than the proposed marriage.

On the journey, a young lion comes against him. The Spirit of the LORD gives him extraordinary strength, and he kills it with his bare hands. He tells neither parent what happened, then continues to meet the woman. The account establishes the source of his strength while leaving the reason for his silence unstated.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Readers differ over how divine purpose relates to Samson’s choice. Wesley and Gill understand this marriage as specially directed by God, with Samson aware of a purpose his parents do not yet know. Wesley therefore treats it as an exceptional action rather than simply a choice driven by appearance.

Henry instead regards Samson’s attraction as foolish and understands God as allowing him to follow his inclinations while bringing good from the outcome. Both readings take verse 4 seriously; they differ over whether Samson’s choice itself has God’s special approval or is a choice through which God brings a larger good.

passages.god_plan_html:
God’s purpose reaching beyond what people can see is a theme elsewhere in Scripture. In Genesis 50:15–21, Joseph distinguishes his brothers’ evil intention from God’s purpose of preserving many lives. The same events involve human responsibility and a saving purpose greater than the people involved had understood.

The New Testament brings this theme to the opposition against Jesus. In Acts 4:24–30, the believers acknowledge rulers conspiring against Him while recognizing that God’s plan is being accomplished. Their response is prayer for faithful witness. The larger story directs attention to God’s rescue through Christ, even amid opposition and confused human choices.

passages.title: Judges 14:8-20
passages.section_title: How does a wedding riddle become a conflict?

passages.context_html:
When Samson returns, he finds bees and honey in the lion’s carcass. He eats some and shares it with his parents without telling them its source. This private experience becomes the basis of his riddle during the wedding feast: something sweet to eat has come from a strong creature that would normally be the eater.

The feast is called a מִשְׁתֶּה, mishteh (mish-TEH), a banquet associated with drinking. Brown–Driver–Briggs specifically lists this wedding feast. The word describes the occasion; the account does not explicitly report Samson drinking wine.

The wager concerns thirty linen garments and thirty sets of clothes. Unable to solve the riddle, the companions threaten to burn Samson’s wife and her father’s household to death. Under that threat, she presses Samson for the answer and passes it to her people. The danger to her family is part of the account and matters when considering her actions.

When the men give the answer, Samson recognizes that they obtained it through his wife. The Spirit of the LORD comes upon him, and he kills thirty men in Ashkelon, taking their apparel to pay the wager. He returns angrily to his father’s house, and his wife is given to one of his companions. The celebration has become a source of violence, anger, and broken relationships.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley reads Samson’s reply about plowing with his heifer as an image of the men using his wife to uncover what was hidden. He connects the comparison with the shared yoke of marriage. The expression identifies the means by which they obtained the answer; it need not become a general statement about women’s character.

Gill understands the attack at Ashkelon as action by a God-empowered judge against Israel’s oppressors. He takes the Spirit’s coming upon Samson as important to that reading. The text records that empowering alongside Samson’s anger, without giving a detailed description of the thirty men’s occupations or the encounter.

Henry draws attention to the riddle’s simple basis in the lion and honey, then makes a devotional comparison with Christ’s victory bringing benefit to His people. That comparison belongs to his wider reading of Scripture rather than to an explanation of the riddle supplied by Samson.

passages.god_plan_html:
Henry’s comparison can be considered alongside the New Testament’s own teaching. First Peter 5:6–10 uses a roaring lion as an image of the devil’s danger. Hebrews 2:14–18 explains that Jesus shares our humanity and, through His death, breaks the devil’s power and frees people from slavery to the fear of death.

The honey illustration brings out a shared theme: an encounter with danger becomes an occasion of benefit. The fulfillment of the Christian hope rests in Jesus’ death and resurrection. First Corinthians 15:54–58 gives thanks for victory over death through Him and calls believers to steadfast service.

passages.title: Judges 15:1-20
passages.section_title: What happens when each side insists on paying the other back?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Later on, at the time of the wheat harvest, Samson took a young goat and went to visit his wife. “I want to go to my wife in her room,” he said. But her father would not let him enter. 2 “I was sure that you thoroughly hated her,” said her father, “so I gave her to one of the men who accompanied you. Is not her younger sister more beautiful than she? Please take her instead.” 3 Samson said to them, “This time I will be blameless in doing harm to the Philistines.” 4 Then Samson went out and caught three hundred foxes. And he took torches, turned the foxes tail-to-tail, and fastened a torch between each pair of tails. 5 Then he lit the torches and released the foxes into the standing grain of the Philistines, burning up the piles of grain and the standing grain, as well as the vineyards and olive groves. 6 “Who did this?” the Philistines demanded. “It was Samson, the son-in-law of the Timnite,” they were told. “For his wife was given to his companion.” So the Philistines went up and burned her and her father to death. 7 And Samson told them, “Because you have done this, I will not rest until I have taken vengeance upon you.” 8 And he struck them ruthlessly with a great slaughter, and then went down and stayed in the cave at the rock of Etam. 9 Then the Philistines went up, camped in Judah, and deployed themselves near the town of Lehi. 10 “Why have you attacked us?” said the men of Judah. The Philistines replied, “We have come to arrest Samson and pay him back for what he has done to us.” 11 In response, three thousand men of Judah went to the cave at the rock of Etam, and they asked Samson, “Do you not realize that the Philistines rule over us? What have you done to us?” “I have done to them what they did to me,” he replied. 12 But they said to him, “We have come down to arrest you and hand you over to the Philistines.” Samson replied, “Swear to me that you will not kill me yourselves.” 13 “No,” they answered, “we will not kill you, but we will tie you up securely and hand you over to them.” So they bound him with two new ropes and led him up from the rock. 14 When Samson arrived in Lehi, the Philistines came out shouting against him. And the Spirit of the LORD came mightily upon him. The ropes on his arms became like burnt flax, and the bonds broke loose from his hands. 15 He found the fresh jawbone of a donkey, reached out his hand and took it, and struck down a thousand men. 16 Then Samson said: “With the jawbone of a donkey I have piled them into heaps. With the jawbone of a donkey I have slain a thousand men.” 17 And when Samson had finished speaking, he cast the jawbone from his hand; and he named that place Ramath-lehi. 18 And being very thirsty, Samson cried out to the LORD, “You have accomplished this great deliverance through Your servant. Must I now die of thirst and fall into the hands of the uncircumcised?” 19 So God opened up the hollow place in Lehi, and water came out of it. When Samson drank, his strength returned, and he was revived. That is why he named it En-hakkore, and it remains in Lehi to this day. 20 And Samson judged Israel for twenty years in the days of the Philistines.

passages.context_html:
Samson returns during the wheat harvest with a young goat, intending to visit his wife. Her father has given her to Samson’s companion because he thought Samson hated her. He offers a younger daughter instead. Samson responds by announcing that this time he will be blameless when he harms the Philistines. That is Samson’s explanation of his actions.

He catches three hundred foxes, ties torches between their tails in pairs, and releases them into the crops. Grain, vineyards, and olive groves burn. The Hebrew word שׁוּעָל, shual (shoo-AHL), can mean fox and may also refer to a jackal. Brown–Driver–Briggs allows that possibility here; the BSB renders it foxes. The account does not explain how long the catching took or whether anyone helped.

The Philistines burn Samson’s wife and her father to death. Samson retaliates with a great slaughter and withdraws to the rock of Etam. Then the Philistines move into Judah to arrest him. Each response spreads the harm beyond the original dispute. The woman who was threatened with burning in chapter 14 now suffers that very fate.

Three thousand men of Judah confront Samson because they fear their Philistine rulers. He agrees to be bound and handed over, provided his own people do not kill him. When the Philistines approach, the Spirit of the LORD comes mightily upon him. He breaks free and strikes down a thousand men with a donkey’s jawbone.

Victory leaves him desperately thirsty. He calls the deliverance God’s work and asks for help; God provides water, and he revives. The chapter closes by saying he judged Israel for twenty years during Philistine rule. His victories begin Israel’s rescue, as the birth announcement promised, but do not yet end that rule.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands Samson’s attacks as the work of a judge avenging injuries against Israel, even though the actions can look like private revenge. Henry likewise sees God using these unlikely means to humble the Philistines. Both place the conflict within Samson’s work against Israel’s oppressors; that is how they explain its purpose.

The distinction between God’s purpose and the people’s stated motives remains important when reading the account. Samson and the Philistines repeatedly explain themselves in terms of paying back what others have done. The narrator explicitly identifies the Spirit’s empowering in verse 14 and God’s provision in verse 19. Those statements should be read alongside the characters’ own explanations.

Wesley and Henry also read Samson’s willingness to be handed over as a picture that points toward Christ. Their comparison draws attention to a rescuer rejected by his own people and willing to be bound. Samson’s later thirst leads them to emphasize that even someone greatly used by God remains dependent on Him. Wesley offers pride as a possible reason for the distress, rather than something the narrator expressly states.

passages.god_plan_html:
The comparison with Jesus becomes clearer when we read Matthew 26:47–56. Jesus could call on His Father for angelic help, yet accepts arrest so that Scripture will be fulfilled. Samson submits to being bound and then fights his way free. Jesus willingly goes further, through suffering and death, to accomplish His saving work. This is a comparison between the accounts; Matthew does not identify Samson’s arrest as a prediction of Jesus’ arrest.

The unlikely weapon and the thirsty victor also bring out a wider biblical theme: the rescue depends on God. First Corinthians 1:26–31 explains that God works through what the world regards as weak so that people boast in Him, and locates our righteousness and redemption in Christ. Second Corinthians 4:7–12 shows the same truth in fragile servants carrying the message of Jesus. God’s power does not make His servants self-sufficient.

For those following Jesus, the response to personal injury is stated directly in Romans 12:17–21: seek peace, leave vengeance to God, and overcome evil with good. Reading the larger story keeps Samson’s particular work as Israel’s judge from becoming a general instruction to repay harm with harm.

passages.title: Judges 16:1-3
passages.section_title: Can great strength hide a serious weakness?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 One day Samson went to Gaza, where he saw a prostitute and went in to spend the night with her. 2 When the Gazites heard that Samson was there, they surrounded that place and lay in wait for him all night at the city gate. They were quiet throughout the night, saying, “Let us wait until dawn; then we will kill him.” 3 But Samson lay there only until midnight, when he got up, took hold of the doors of the city gate and both gateposts, and pulled them out, bar and all. Then he put them on his shoulders and took them to the top of the mountain overlooking Hebron.
paragraphs: 1 One day Samson went to Gaza, where he saw a prostitute and went in to spend the night with her. 2 When the Gazites heard that Samson was there, they surrounded that place and lay in wait for him all night at the city gate. They were quiet throughout the night, saying, “Let us wait until dawn; then we will kill him.” 3 But Samson lay there only until midnight, when he got up, took hold of the doors of the city gate and both gateposts, and pulled them out, bar and all. Then he put them on his shoulders and took them to the top of the mountain overlooking Hebron.

passages.context_html:
Samson goes to Gaza, sees a prostitute, and spends the night with her. When the townspeople learn he is there, they wait at the city gate, planning to kill him at dawn. The danger comes from people who already regard him as their enemy.

He gets up at midnight and removes the gate doors, both posts, and the bar. He carries them to the mountain overlooking Hebron. The narrator describes an extraordinary escape, without explaining how Samson learned of the ambush or how much the gate weighed. The man who can carry away a city’s defenses remains vulnerable in his own choices.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Henry both read the visit to the prostitute as sin. They distinguish Samson’s extraordinary gift from the condition of his heart. His ability to escape does not make the conduct that brought him there right.

Both suggest that his departure may have involved a renewed awareness of guilt or danger. They present possibilities rather than a confession recorded in the passage. The account itself reports what he does at midnight without describing a prayer or stating his motive for getting up.

passages.god_plan_html:
The New Testament connects sexual conduct with belonging to Christ. In 1 Corinthians 6:12–20, Paul explains that believers’ bodies belong to the Lord, that they are joined to Christ, and that God will raise them as He raised Jesus. The call to flee sexual immorality rests on that relationship and future hope.

That adds something beyond the contrast between physical strength and personal weakness: God’s saving work concerns the whole person. Our bodies are part of a life bought for His service, so how we use them matters.

passages.title: Judges 16:4-14
passages.section_title: Why does Samson keep returning to an obvious danger?

versions.text: 4 Some time later, Samson fell in love with a woman in the Valley of Sorek, whose name was Delilah. 5 The lords of the Philistines went to her and said, “Entice him and find out the source of his great strength and how we can overpower him to tie him up and subdue him. Then each one of us will give you eleven hundred shekels of silver.” 6 So Delilah said to Samson, “Please tell me the source of your great strength and how you can be tied up and subdued.” 7 Samson told her, “If they tie me up with seven fresh bowstrings that have not been dried, I will become as weak as any other man.” 8 So the lords of the Philistines brought her seven fresh bowstrings that had not been dried, and she tied him up with them. 9 While the men were hidden in her room, she called out, “Samson, the Philistines are here!” But he snapped the bowstrings like a strand of yarn seared by a flame. So the source of his strength remained unknown. 10 Then Delilah said to Samson, “You have mocked me and lied to me! Now please tell me how you can be tied up.” 11 He replied, “If they tie me up with new ropes that have never been used, I will become as weak as any other man.” 12 So Delilah took new ropes, tied him up with them, and called out, “Samson, the Philistines are here!” But while the men were hidden in her room, he snapped the ropes off his arms like they were threads. 13 Then Delilah said to Samson, “You have mocked me and lied to me all along! Tell me how you can be tied up.” He told her, “If you weave the seven braids of my head into the web of a loom and tighten it with a pin, I will become as weak as any other man.” 14 So while he slept, Delilah took the seven braids of his hair and wove them into the web. Then she tightened it with a pin and called to him, “Samson, the Philistines are here!” But he awoke from his sleep and pulled out the pin with the loom and the web.
paragraphs: 4 Some time later, Samson fell in love with a woman in the Valley of Sorek, whose name was Delilah. 5 The lords of the Philistines went to her and said, “Entice him and find out the source of his great strength and how we can overpower him to tie him up and subdue him. Then each one of us will give you eleven hundred shekels of silver.”

6 So Delilah said to Samson, “Please tell me the source of your great strength and how you can be tied up and subdued.” 7 Samson told her, “If they tie me up with seven fresh bowstrings that have not been dried, I will become as weak as any other man.” 8 So the lords of the Philistines brought her seven fresh bowstrings that had not been dried, and she tied him up with them. 9 While the men were hidden in her room, she called out, “Samson, the Philistines are here!” But he snapped the bowstrings like a strand of yarn seared by a flame. So the source of his strength remained unknown.

10 Then Delilah said to Samson, “You have mocked me and lied to me! Now please tell me how you can be tied up.” 11 He replied, “If they tie me up with new ropes that have never been used, I will become as weak as any other man.” 12 So Delilah took new ropes, tied him up with them, and called out, “Samson, the Philistines are here!” But while the men were hidden in her room, he snapped the ropes off his arms like they were threads.

13 Then Delilah said to Samson, “You have mocked me and lied to me all along! Tell me how you can be tied up.” He told her, “If you weave the seven braids of my head into the web of a loom and tighten it with a pin, I will become as weak as any other man.” 14 So while he slept, Delilah took the seven braids of his hair and wove them into the web. Then she tightened it with a pin and called to him, “Samson, the Philistines are here!” But he awoke from his sleep and pulled out the pin with the loom and the web.

passages.context_html:
Samson falls in love with Delilah in the Valley of Sorek. The Philistine lords offer her eleven hundred shekels of silver each if she discovers how to overpower him. The account gives her name and location but does not identify her ethnicity, call her his wife, or describe her as a prostitute.

She asks directly how he can be bound and subdued. First he names seven fresh bowstrings, then unused ropes. She tries both while men wait in her room, and both attempts fail. Her stated purpose and repeated actions give Samson ample reason to recognize the danger.

His third answer brings his hair into the scheme: she is to weave its seven braids into a loom and fasten them with a pin. Again he breaks free. He continues supplying answers to the person arranging his capture, while she treats his refusal to reveal the truth as a wrong against her.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley calls Samson’s false answers both dishonest and foolish because they encourage a question he should have refused. Henry emphasizes his failure to learn from earlier dangers. Their shared warning concerns his continuing to expose himself to a danger that is becoming increasingly clear.

The sequence also brings the reader closer to what Samson will disclose next. Bowstrings and ropes do not explain his strength; the third attempt already involves his hair. The account has not yet described the decisive breach, but each escape is followed by another attempt rather than an end to the relationship.

This is the third time you have mocked me and failed to reveal to me the source of your great strength!” 16 Finally, after she had pressed him daily with her words and pleaded until he was sick to death, 17 Samson told her all that was in his heart: “My hair has never been cut, because I have been a Nazirite to God from my mother’s womb. passages.context_html:
Delilah presses Samson day after day, questioning his love until he tells her what is in his heart. He connects his uncut hair with being a Nazirite to God from his mother’s womb. נָזִיר, nazir (nah-ZEER), means someone consecrated or devoted. Brown–Driver–Briggs specifically identifies Samson’s dedication from birth, in contrast with the usual voluntary vow for a limited period.

After he falls asleep on her lap, she calls a man to shave off his seven braids. His strength leaves him. Samson expects to escape as before, but the narrator explains what he does not know: the LORD has departed from him. The hair belongs to his consecration; the power is God’s.

The Philistines seize him, gouge out his eyes, take him to Gaza, bind him in bronze shackles, and make him grind grain in prison. Then comes a brief detail that leaves room for what follows: his hair begins growing again. The account has not ended with his capture.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands the hair as a condition attached to Samson’s calling, rather than a substance that produces strength on its own. Henry likewise treats the loss of strength as the consequence of abandoning his dedication to God. Both read his confidence that he can escape again as a warning about not recognizing what has been lost.

They also read the returning hair as a sign of repentance and renewed mercy. The narrator reports the growth without recording a prison confession; the next scene supplies Samson’s prayer. Their reading connects this detail with his later dependence on God, rather than treating hair growth as an automatic way to restore divine power.
