passages.god_plan_html:
The New Testament includes Samson among people commended for faith in Hebrews 11:32–40. His failures are serious, yet they are not the whole account of his relationship with God. Hebrews names him without telling readers to imitate each choice he made.

The next paragraph directs the reader’s attention to Jesus: Hebrews 12:1–3 calls us to lay aside entangling sin, endure, and fix our eyes on the One who begins and completes our faith. The larger story gives both warning and hope, with Jesus as the person to follow.

passages.title: Judges 16:23-31
passages.section_title: How does Samson’s last prayer change the celebration?

passages.context_html:
The Philistine lords gather to sacrifice to Dagon and celebrate Samson’s capture. They credit their god with delivering the enemy who devastated their land. Samson is brought from prison to entertain them and placed between the building’s supporting pillars.

He asks the servant guiding him to let him feel the pillars. The building is full, all the Philistine lords are present, and about three thousand men and women watch from the roof. Samson prays for God to remember and strengthen him once more, asking to avenge the loss of his eyes.

He braces himself against the two central pillars and pushes. The building falls on the lords and the people inside, and Samson dies with them. The narrator says he kills more in his death than during his life. His brothers and his father’s family recover his body and bury him in Manoah’s tomb, closing the account of his twenty years as judge.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Augustine, in City of God 1.21, explains Samson’s death as an exceptional act that can be justified only by special direction from God. His reasoning does not turn Samson’s action into general permission to kill oneself or others. The special direction is Augustine’s explanation; Judges records the prayer and outcome without quoting an additional command.

Wesley and Henry also understand this as a judge acting for God’s honor and Israel’s deliverance, with the answered prayer showing divine approval. They distinguish that purpose from ordinary personal revenge, even though Samson’s recorded request specifically mentions his eyes. These are their readings of the event; the passage supplies both the public setting and his personal words.

Both Protestant commentators also see a comparison with Christ: death becomes the means of defeating an enemy. They regard the final prayer as renewed dependence on God. The story ends with Samson seeking strength from the Lord rather than assuming that past strength guarantees what he can do.

passages.god_plan_html:
The comparison with Jesus is strongest in the outcome: a death that looks like defeat brings victory. Hebrews 2:14–18 states the Christian claim directly—Jesus shares our humanity and through death breaks the devil’s power, releasing people held in fear of death.

The differences matter as well. Samson asks for vengeance for his eyes and dies while destroying his captors. In John 10:11–18, Jesus describes willingly laying down His life for His sheep and taking it up again. Samson’s death brings the account of his service to an end; Jesus’ death and resurrection bring His people lasting rescue. This is a comparison drawn from the two accounts, not a claim that the New Testament explains every detail of Samson’s death as a prediction.

passages.title: Judges 17:1-13
passages.section_title: Does calling something worship make it faithful to God?

passages.context_html:
The last five chapters turn from the accounts of individual judges to two extended stories of life within Israel. Here Micah, who lives in Ephraim’s hill country, admits taking eleven hundred shekels of silver from his mother. She has pronounced a curse over the theft; when he confesses, she blesses him in the LORD’s name.

After the money is returned, she dedicates it to the LORD for making images. Two hundred shekels go to the silversmith, and the images are placed in Micah’s house. He also makes an ephod and household idols, then appoints a son as priest. The word for household idols is תְּרָפִים, teraphim (teh-rah-FEEM). Brown–Driver–Briggs identifies these as objects of reverence also used for seeking guidance; their exact appearance is not described here.

The narrator places this beside the statement that there is no king and everyone does what is right in his own eyes. The family uses the LORD’s name, but Exodus 20:1–6 forbids making and worshiping idols. Deuteronomy 12:1–14 directs Israel to the place God chooses, rather than leaving sacrificial worship to everyone’s preference.

A young Levite from Bethlehem arrives while looking for somewhere to settle. Micah offers him a yearly payment, clothing, and food to become his priest. The young man accepts and is treated like a son. Micah concludes that having a Levite guarantees the LORD’s favor. Yet Numbers 18:1–7 distinguishes the wider tribe’s service from the priesthood entrusted to Aaron and his sons; hiring a Levite does not resolve the problems with this shrine.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Henry both read the story as a warning about mixing religious language with disobedience. Wesley notes that the family means to honor the LORD by the images, rather than simply announcing allegiance to another god. Henry emphasizes how attachment to money leads into corrupted worship. Invoking God’s name does not remove the contradiction with His commands.

They also agree that Micah mistakes a favorable-looking circumstance for God’s approval. A Levite arriving at his door seems to him to confirm that the shrine will prosper. For these readers, his confidence exposes the problem: he treats one outward improvement as though it answers the deeper questions about whom and how he is worshiping.

passages.god_plan_html:
The wider biblical story leads beyond Micah’s attempt to arrange access to God through a private shrine and hired priest. In John 4:19–26, Jesus speaks of the Father seeking worshipers who worship in spirit and truth. He also announces a coming change in the importance of the disputed places of worship and identifies Himself as the Messiah.

Hebrews 7:23–28 explains the lasting access God provides through Jesus: His priesthood continues because He lives forever, and He saves those who draw near to God through Him. The direction of the story is toward God providing the faithful priest and the way to approach Him, rather than people securing His favor by designing their own arrangements.

passages.title: Judges 18:1-13
passages.section_title: Is a reassuring answer enough to show that God approves?

For up to that time they had not come into an inheritance among the tribes of Israel. 2 So the Danites sent out five men from their clans, men of valor from Zorah and Eshtaol, to spy out the land and explore it. “Go and explore the land,” they told them. The men entered the hill country of Ephraim and came to the house of Micah, where they spent the night. 3 And while they were near Micah’s house, they recognized the voice of the young Levite; so they went over and asked him, “Who brought you here? What are you doing in this place? Why are you here?” 4 “Micah has done this and that for me,” he replied, “and he has hired me to be his priest.” 5 Then they said to him, “Please inquire of God to determine whether we will have a successful journey.” 6 And the priest told them, “Go in peace. The LORD is watching over your journey.” 7 So the five men departed and came to Laish, where they saw that the people were living securely, like the Sidonians, quiet and unsuspecting. There was nothing lacking in the land and no oppressive ruler. And they were far away from the Sidonians and had no alliance with anyone. 8 When the men returned to Zorah and Eshtaol, their brothers asked them, “What did you find?” 9 They answered, “Come on, let us go up against them, for we have seen the land, and it is very good. Why would you fail to act? Do not hesitate to go there and take possession of the land! 10 When you enter, you will come to an unsuspecting people and a spacious land, for God has delivered it into your hand. It is a place where nothing on earth is lacking.” 11 So six hundred Danites departed from Zorah and Eshtaol, armed with weapons of war. 12 They went up and camped at Kiriath-jearim in Judah. That is why the place west of Kiriath-jearim is called Mahaneh-dan to this day. 13 And from there they traveled to the hill country of Ephraim and came to Micah’s house.

passages.context_html:
With no king in Israel, a group of Danites searches for territory to occupy. Joshua 19:40–48 has already listed Dan’s allotted territory and records the later move against Leshem. Judges 1:34–35 describes the Amorites pressing Dan into the hill country. The search here belongs to that difficulty in securing a place to live.

Five scouts from Zorah and Eshtaol spend the night near Micah’s house and recognize the young Levite’s voice. After hearing about his employment, they ask him to inquire of God about their journey. He sends them off with reassurance that the LORD is watching over it. The account reports his answer without describing a message from God or how he obtained it.

At Laish they find people living quietly and unsuspectingly in a well-supplied land. The people are far from Sidon and have no alliance to bring help. The scouts return enthusiastically, urging immediate action and saying God has delivered the land into their hands. Six hundred armed Danites then set out and return by way of Micah’s house.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley distinguishes an inheritance allotted to Dan from territory the tribe has actually secured. He also explains the recognized voice through previous acquaintance. Gill gives a similar explanation, while allowing that a distinctive manner of speaking may have helped. The passage does not require a claim that all Levites had a separate accent.

Both commentators question the reliability of the priest’s reassurance. Wesley allows either an answer invented to please the visitors or a deceptive spiritual source; Gill discusses the same possibilities and notes how broadly the words could be understood. These are their explanations of an answer whose source the narrator does not disclose.

The scouts then combine that reassurance with what looks like an easy opportunity. Wesley sees their confidence as resting partly on the supposed promise and partly on the people’s vulnerability. Their conclusion that God has given them the place remains their reported conclusion.

passages.god_plan_html:
The wider biblical call is to test spiritual claims rather than accept them merely because they reassure us. First John 4:1–6 makes confession of Jesus Christ come in the flesh central to discerning truth from deception. The question is whether a message is truly from God, not simply whether it promises what the hearer wants.

First Thessalonians 5:19–24 brings testing together with openness to the Spirit: examine what is said, hold to the good, and reject evil. It also grounds hope in the faithful God who prepares His people for Jesus’ coming. Discernment serves that larger purpose of a people made holy for Him.

passages.title: Judges 18:14-31
passages.section_title: What happens when a stolen god becomes a tribe’s god?

What else do I have? How can you say to me, ‘What is the matter with you?’” 25 The Danites said to him, “Do not raise your voice against us, or angry men will attack you, and you and your family will lose your lives.” 26 So the Danites went on their way, and Micah turned to go back home, because he saw that they were too strong for him. 27 After they had taken Micah’s idols and his priest, they went to Laish, to a quiet and unsuspecting people, and they struck them with their swords and burned down the city. 28 There was no one to deliver them, because the city was far from Sidon and had no alliance with anyone; it was in a valley near Beth-rehob. And the Danites rebuilt the city and lived there. 29 They named it Dan, after their forefather Dan, who was born to Israel—though the city was formerly named Laish. 30 The Danites set up idols for themselves, and Jonathan son of Gershom, the son of Moses, and his sons were priests for the tribe of Dan until the day of the captivity of the land. 31 So they set up for themselves Micah’s graven image, and it was there the whole time the house of God was in Shiloh.
paragraphs: 14 Then the five men who had gone to spy out the land of Laish said to their brothers, “Did you know that one of these houses has an ephod, household gods, a graven image, and a molten idol? Now think about what you should do.” 15 So they turned aside there and went to the home of the young Levite, the house of Micah, and greeted him. 16 The six hundred Danites stood at the entrance of the gate, armed with their weapons of war. 17 And the five men who had gone to spy out the land went inside and took the graven image, the ephod, the household idols, and the molten idol, while the priest stood at the entrance of the gate with the six hundred armed men. 18 When they entered Micah’s house and took the graven image, the ephod, the household idols, and the molten idol, the priest said to them, “What are you doing?” 19 “Be quiet,” they told him. “Put your hand over your mouth and come with us and be a father and a priest to us. Is it better for you to be a priest for the house of one person or a priest for a tribe and family in Israel?” 20 So the priest was glad and took the ephod, the household idols, and the graven image, and went with the people.

21 Putting their small children, their livestock, and their possessions in front of them, they turned and departed. 22 After they were some distance from Micah’s house, the men in the houses near Micah’s house mobilized and overtook the Danites. 23 When they called out after them, the Danites turned to face them and said to Micah, “What is the matter with you that you have called out such a company?” 24 He replied, “You took the gods I had made, and my priest, and went away. What else do I have? How can you say to me, ‘What is the matter with you?’” 25 The Danites said to him, “Do not raise your voice against us, or angry men will attack you, and you and your family will lose your lives.” 26 So the Danites went on their way, and Micah turned to go back home, because he saw that they were too strong for him.

27 After they had taken Micah’s idols and his priest, they went to Laish, to a quiet and unsuspecting people, and they struck them with their swords and burned down the city. 28 There was no one to deliver them, because the city was far from Sidon and had no alliance with anyone; it was in a valley near Beth-rehob. And the Danites rebuilt the city and lived there. 29 They named it Dan, after their forefather Dan, who was born to Israel—though the city was formerly named Laish.

30 The Danites set up idols for themselves, and Jonathan son of Gershom, the son of Moses, and his sons were priests for the tribe of Dan until the day of the captivity of the land. 31 So they set up for themselves Micah’s graven image, and it was there the whole time the house of God was in Shiloh.

passages.context_html:
The scouts tell the armed Danites about Micah’s worship objects. They enter his house and take the images, ephod, and household idols. When the priest objects, they offer him a larger role: priest for a tribe rather than one household. He is glad to join them and carries the objects away.

Micah and his neighbors pursue them. He protests that they have taken the gods he made and his priest, leaving him with nothing. The Danites threaten his family’s life if he continues. Seeing that they are stronger, he turns back. The objects in which he placed his confidence cannot prevent their own theft.

The Danites attack the quiet people of Laish, kill them, and burn the city. No allied force is available to rescue them. The attackers rebuild and rename the city Dan, then establish the stolen image there. What began in one household now has a continuing priesthood.

The BSB identifies the priest as Jonathan, son of Gershom, son of Moses, and says his descendants served until the captivity of the land. The closing verse sets this shrine alongside the house of God at Shiloh. Israel has a place for the worship God commanded, while the Danites maintain Micah’s image.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley reads the priest’s pleasure at the offer as self-interest: a larger position matters more to him than faithfulness. He also points out the contradiction in Micah valuing as gods things he himself made. The account exposes both religious ambition and confidence in objects that others can carry away.

The ending raises a question about how long this priesthood lasted. Wesley takes the captivity of the land to mean the later Assyrian conquest of the northern kingdom, distinguishing the continuing priestly family from the particular image’s duration. Gill favors the earlier capture of the ark by the Philistines, connecting the phrase with the following reference to Shiloh. They agree that the corruption continued; they differ over which captivity marks its endpoint.

The BSB’s reading Moses also gives the genealogy particular force: a descendant of the lawgiver is serving this shrine. Gill discusses the Hebrew spelling behind the older reading Manasseh and the reading Moses. The family connection does not turn the priest’s conduct into faithful service.

passages.god_plan_html:
Micah’s loss raises a larger question: can the Creator be something human beings manufacture and possess? Acts 17:24–31 answers that God gives life to everyone, rather than depending on people to sustain Him. Paul calls people away from images made by human skill toward repentance, and points to the risen Jesus as God’s appointed judge.

The positive direction appears in 1 Thessalonians 1:8–10: people turn from idols to serve the living and true God and await His Son, raised from the dead. The Bible’s answer goes beyond replacing one vulnerable object with another. It is to know and serve the God who gives life and rescues through Jesus.

passages.title: Judges 19:1-30
passages.section_title: What happens when those who should protect someone give her up?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now in those days, when there was no king in Israel, a Levite who lived in the remote hill country of Ephraim took for himself a concubine from Bethlehem in Judah. 2 But she was unfaithful to him and left him to return to her father’s house in Bethlehem in Judah. After she had been there four months, 3 her husband got up and went after her to speak kindly to her and bring her back, taking his servant and a pair of donkeys. So the girl brought him into her father’s house, and when her father saw him, he gladly welcomed him. 4 His father-in-law, the girl’s father, persuaded him to stay, so he remained with him three days, eating, drinking, and lodging there. 5 On the fourth day, they got up early in the morning and prepared to depart, but the girl’s father said to his son-in-law, “Refresh your heart with a morsel of bread, and then you can go.” 6 So they sat down and the two of them ate and drank together. Then the girl’s father said to the man, “Please agree to stay overnight and let your heart be merry.” 7 The man got up to depart, but his father-in-law persuaded him, so he stayed there that night. 8 On the fifth day, he got up early in the morning to depart, but the girl’s father said, “Please refresh your heart.” So they waited until late afternoon and the two of them ate. 9 When the man got up to depart with his concubine and his servant, his father-in-law, the girl’s father, said to him, “Look, the day is drawing to a close. Please spend the night. See, the day is almost over. Spend the night here, that your heart may be merry. Then you can get up early tomorrow for your journey home.” 10 But the man was unwilling to spend the night. He got up and departed, and arrived opposite Jebus (that is, Jerusalem), with his two saddled donkeys and his concubine. 11 When they were near Jebus and the day was almost gone, the servant said to his master, “Please, let us stop at this Jebusite city and spend the night here.” 12 But his master replied, “We will not turn aside to the city of foreigners, where there are no Israelites. We will go on to Gibeah.” 13 He continued, “Come, let us try to reach one of these towns to spend the night in Gibeah or Ramah.” 14 So they continued on their journey, and the sun set as they neared Gibeah in Benjamin. 15 They stopped to go in and lodge in Gibeah. The Levite went in and sat down in the city square, but no one would take them into his home for the night. 16 That evening an old man from the hill country of Ephraim, who was residing in Gibeah (the men of that place were Benjamites), came in from his work in the field. 17 When he looked up and saw the traveler in the city square, the old man asked, “Where are you going, and where have you come from?” 18 The Levite replied, “We are traveling from Bethlehem in Judah to the remote hill country of Ephraim, where I am from. I went to Bethlehem in Judah, and now I am going to the house of the LORD; but no one has taken me into his home, 19 even though there is both straw and feed for our donkeys, and bread and wine for me and the maidservant and young man with me. There is nothing that we, your servants, lack.” 20 “Peace to you,” said the old man. “Let me supply everything you need. Only do not spend the night in the square.” 21 So he brought him to his house and fed his donkeys. And they washed their feet and ate and drank. 22 While they were enjoying themselves, suddenly the wicked men of the city surrounded the house. Pounding on the door, they said to the old man who owned the house, “Bring out the man who came to your house, so we can have relations with him!” 23 The owner of the house went out and said to them, “No, my brothers, do not do this wicked thing! After all, this man is a guest in my house. Do not commit this outrage. 24 Look, let me bring out my virgin daughter and the man’s concubine, and you can use them and do with them as you wish. But do not do such a vile thing to this man.” 25 But the men would not listen to him. So the Levite took his concubine and sent her outside to them, and they raped her and abused her throughout the night, and at dawn they let her go. 26 Early that morning, the woman went back to the house where her master was staying, collapsed at the doorway, and lay there until it was light. 27 In the morning, when her master got up and opened the doors of the house to go out on his journey, there was his concubine, collapsed in the doorway of the house, with her hands on the threshold. 28 “Get up,” he told her. “Let us go.” But there was no response. So the man put her on his donkey and set out for home. 29 When he reached his house, he picked up a knife, took hold of his concubine, cut her limb by limb into twelve pieces, and sent her throughout the territory of Israel. 30 And everyone who saw it said, “Nothing like this has been seen or done from the day the Israelites came out of the land of Egypt until this day. Think it over, take counsel, and speak up!”

passages.context_html:
Another account begins with no king in Israel and a Levite living in Ephraim’s hill country. His concubine, a woman in a recognized but lower-status marital relationship, has returned to her father in Bethlehem. The account calls the Levite her husband. After four months he goes to speak kindly to her and bring her back.

Her father repeatedly persuades him to stay. They finally leave late on the fifth day. The Levite refuses to stop in Jebus because it is a city of foreigners, expecting a safer welcome among Israelites. At Gibeah in Benjamin, however, no one initially offers them shelter.

An older man from Ephraim takes them into his house. The travelers already have food and supplies; they need somewhere to stay. While they eat, men surround the house and demand that the male visitor be brought out for sexual assault. The host objects but offers his daughter and the concubine instead.

The Levite sends his concubine outside. The men rape and abuse her through the night. At dawn she returns and collapses at the doorway, her hands on the threshold. When the Levite tells her to get up, there is no answer. He carries her home, cuts her into twelve pieces, and sends them throughout Israel. The resulting shock leads into the national assembly and civil war in the next chapters.

The woman is never named and her own account is never heard. The chapter gives the acts and words of the men around her. It does not state the exact moment she dies; Judges 20:4–7 calls her murdered and records the Levite’s testimony that the abuse killed her. The next chapter also lets the reader compare that testimony with the events described here.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Readers have differed over the opening separation. The BSB describes her as unfaithful, and Wesley understands adultery. Gill discusses that reading and another that understands the wording as rejection of the husband and departure from him. Both recognize the marital relationship; neither requires inventing an additional wife for the Levite.

The story’s close resemblance to Genesis 19:1–11 is noted in the USCCB Bible study notes: visitors receive shelter, men surround a house demanding its male guests, and a host offers women. These notes emphasize the unfavorable portrait of Gibeah and the wider disorder. They are explanatory notes, rather than a separate church ruling on every detail.

Wesley also interprets the woman’s death as divine punishment for her earlier unfaithfulness. That is his explanation of why she suffers; the narrator does not state that cause. Gill, discussing the host’s offer, says the man has no right to give either woman to the crowd. The account itself describes the demand, the offer, the Levite’s action, and the attackers’ abuse. Keeping those actions in view is essential when considering the different explanations.

The outrage remains a memory of corruption in the prophets. Hosea 9:9 and 10:9 refer back to the days of Gibeah when describing Israel’s wrongdoing. The incident is presented as something that exposes the nation’s need to confront evil.

passages.god_plan_html:
The wider biblical theme of love becomes especially clear against this failure to protect. Ephesians 5:25–30 grounds a husband’s care in Christ’s love: Jesus gives Himself for the church and nourishes and cherishes His people. Here a husband gives another person over to save himself. In the gospel, the Savior gives Himself to bring His people life and holiness.

Jesus also makes mercy concrete in Luke 10:25–37. In His story, the Samaritan stops for an injured stranger, treats his wounds, carries him to shelter, and pays for his care. Hebrews 13:1–3 joins hospitality with remembering the mistreated as though sharing their suffering. The positive purpose is a people whose love takes responsibility for another’s safety and care.

passages.title: Judges 20:1-17
passages.section_title: Will Israel confront the wrongdoers or divide into opposing sides?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then all the Israelites from Dan to Beersheba and from the land of Gilead came out, and the congregation assembled as one man before the LORD at Mizpah. 2 The leaders of all the people and all the tribes of Israel presented themselves in the assembly of God’s people: 400,000 men on foot, armed with swords. 3 (Meanwhile the Benjamites heard that the Israelites had gone up to Mizpah.) And the Israelites asked, “Tell us, how did this wicked thing happen?” 4 So the Levite, the husband of the murdered woman, answered: “I and my concubine came to Gibeah in Benjamin to spend the night. 5 And during the night, the men of Gibeah rose up against me and surrounded the house. They intended to kill me, but they abused my concubine, and she died. 6 Then I took my concubine, cut her into pieces, and sent her throughout the land of Israel’s inheritance, because they had committed a lewd and disgraceful act in Israel. 7 Behold, all you Israelites, give your advice and verdict here and now.” 8 Then all the people stood as one man and said, “Not one of us will return to his tent or to his house. 9 Now this is what we will do to Gibeah: We will go against it as the lot dictates. 10 We will take ten men out of every hundred from all the tribes of Israel, and a hundred out of every thousand, and a thousand out of every ten thousand, to supply provisions for the army when they go to Gibeah in Benjamin to punish them for the atrocity they have committed in Israel.” 11 So all the men of Israel gathered as one man, united against the city. 12 And the tribes of Israel sent men throughout the tribe of Benjamin, saying, “What is this wickedness that has occurred among you? 13 Hand over the wicked men of Gibeah so we can put them to death and purge Israel of this evil.” But the Benjamites refused to heed the voice of their fellow Israelites. 14 And from their cities they came together at Gibeah to go out and fight against the Israelites. 15 On that day the Benjamites mobilized 26,000 swordsmen from their cities, in addition to the 700 select men of Gibeah. 16 Among all these soldiers there were 700 select left-handers, each of whom could sling a stone at a hair without missing. 17 The Israelites, apart from Benjamin, mobilized 400,000 swordsmen, each one an experienced warrior.

passages.context_html:
Israel assembles at Mizpah in response to the dismembered woman. The gathering includes four hundred thousand armed men, and the people ask how the crime happened. The Levite says the men of Gibeah surrounded the house, intended to kill him, and abused his concubine until she died.

His account leaves out an action the reader has already seen: he sent her outside to the men. That omission matters when comparing his testimony with chapter 19. Deuteronomy 19:15–21 calls for established testimony and careful investigation when Israel judges wrongdoing.

The tribes agree to act together against Gibeah and set aside one tenth of their men to supply provisions. Before the fighting, they send messengers through Benjamin asking for the guilty men to be handed over for punishment. Their stated aim is to remove the evil from Israel.

Benjamin refuses to listen and instead gathers to fight the other Israelites. Its force includes twenty-six thousand swordsmen from the cities and seven hundred select men from Gibeah. Seven hundred soldiers are noted for their left-handed skill with the sling. The dispute over a crime has become an armed confrontation between fellow Israelites.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill both regard the demand to hand over the offenders as a proper attempt to distinguish the guilty from the innocent and prevent wider bloodshed. They understand Benjamin’s refusal as protecting the criminals rather than dealing with the wrong.

Wesley sees the large united army as evidence of zeal to punish the crime, while also noting that numbers do not determine success. Gill emphasizes the attempt to settle the matter before war. Neither reading makes loyalty to one’s tribe a reason to shelter those responsible.

The contrast with the previous chapter also invites attention to how the case is presented. The people hear the Levite call for a verdict, while the reader knows more about his own conduct. The fact that a crime requires an answer does not make every person demanding an answer free from responsibility.

passages.god_plan_html:
The New Testament also calls God’s people to confront evil within their community. First Corinthians 5:9–13 distinguishes responsibility within the church from judging everyone outside it. Paul directs the church to remove a persistently wicked member; he does not direct it to wage war.

The purpose of correction includes recovering the person. In Matthew 18:15–20, Jesus describes seeking to win a brother back and establishing matters through witnesses. Galatians 6:1–5 joins restoration with gentleness and self-examination. The larger goal is a community faithful to Christ, willing both to confront wrongdoing and to examine itself.

passages.title: Judges 20:18-48
passages.section_title: Why does victory still leave Israel facing a disaster?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 The Israelites set out, went up to Bethel, and inquired of God, “Who of us shall go up first to fight against the Benjamites?” “Judah will be first,” the LORD replied. 19 The next morning the Israelites set out and camped near Gibeah. 20 And the men of Israel went out to fight against Benjamin and took up their battle positions at Gibeah. 21 And the Benjamites came out of Gibeah and cut down 22,000 Israelites on the battlefield that day. 22 But the Israelite army took courage and again took their battle positions in the same place where they had arrayed themselves on the first day. 23 They went up and wept before the LORD until evening, inquiring of Him, “Should we again draw near for battle against our brothers the Benjamites?” And the LORD answered, “Go up against them.” 24 On the second day the Israelites advanced against the Benjamites. 25 That same day the Benjamites came out against them from Gibeah and cut down another 18,000 Israelites, all of them armed with swords. 26 Then the Israelites, all the people, went up to Bethel, where they sat weeping before the LORD. That day they fasted until evening and presented burnt offerings and peace offerings to the LORD. 27 And the Israelites inquired of the LORD. (In those days the ark of the covenant of God was there, 28 and Phinehas son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron, served before it.) The Israelites asked, “Should we again go out to battle against our brothers the Benjamites, or should we stop?” The LORD answered, “Fight, for tomorrow I will deliver them into your hand.” 29 So Israel set up an ambush around Gibeah. 30 On the third day the Israelites went up against the Benjamites and arrayed themselves against Gibeah as they had done before. 31 The Benjamites came out against them and were drawn away from the city. They began to attack the people as before, killing about thirty men of Israel in the fields and on the roads, one of which led up to Bethel and the other to Gibeah. 32 “We are defeating them as before,” said the Benjamites. But the Israelites said, “Let us retreat and draw them away from the city onto the roads.” 33 So all the men of Israel got up from their places and arrayed themselves at Baal-tamar, and the Israelites in ambush charged from their positions west of Gibeah. 34 Then 10,000 select men from all Israel made a frontal assault against Gibeah, and the battle was fierce. But the Benjamites did not realize that disaster was upon them. 35 The LORD defeated Benjamin in the presence of Israel, and on that day the Israelites slaughtered 25,100 Benjamites, all armed with swords. 36 Then the Benjamites realized they had been defeated. Now the men of Israel had retreated before Benjamin because they were relying on the ambush they had set against Gibeah. 37 The men in ambush rushed suddenly against Gibeah; they advanced and put the whole city to the sword. 38 The men of Israel had arranged a signal with the men in ambush: When they sent up a great cloud of smoke from the city, 39 the men of Israel would turn in the battle. When the Benjamites had begun to strike them down, killing about thirty men of Israel, they said, “They are defeated before us as in the first battle.” 40 But when the column of smoke began to go up from the city, the Benjamites looked behind them and saw the whole city going up in smoke. 41 Then the men of Israel turned back on them, and the men of Benjamin were terrified when they realized that disaster had come upon them. 42 So they fled before the men of Israel toward the wilderness, but the battle overtook them, and the men coming out of the cities struck them down there. 43 They surrounded the Benjamites, pursued them, and easily overtook them in the vicinity of Gibeah on the east. 44 And 18,000 Benjamites fell, all men of valor. 45 Then the Benjamites turned and fled toward the wilderness to the rock of Rimmon, and Israel cut down 5,000 men on the roads. And they overtook them at Gidom and struck down 2,000 more. 46 That day 25,000 Benjamite swordsmen fell, all men of valor. 47 But 600 men turned and fled into the wilderness to the rock of Rimmon, where they stayed four months. 48 And the men of Israel turned back against the other Benjamites and put to the sword all the cities, including the animals and everything else they found. And they burned down all the cities in their path.
paragraphs: 18 The Israelites set out, went up to Bethel, and inquired of God, “Who of us shall go up first to fight against the Benjamites?” “Judah will be first,” the LORD replied. 19 The next morning the Israelites set out and camped near Gibeah. 20 And the men of Israel went out to fight against Benjamin and took up their battle positions at Gibeah. 21 And the Benjamites came out of Gibeah and cut down 22,000 Israelites on the battlefield that day. 22 But the Israelite army took courage and again took their battle positions in the same place where they had arrayed themselves on the first day. 23 They went up and wept before the LORD until evening, inquiring of Him, “Should we again draw near for battle against our brothers the Benjamites?” And the LORD answered, “Go up against them.” 24 On the second day the Israelites advanced against the Benjamites. 25 That same day the Benjamites came out against them from Gibeah and cut down another 18,000 Israelites, all of them armed with swords.

26 Then the Israelites, all the people, went up to Bethel, where they sat weeping before the LORD. That day they fasted until evening and presented burnt offerings and peace offerings to the LORD. 27 And the Israelites inquired of the LORD. (In those days the ark of the covenant of God was there, 28 and Phinehas son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron, served before it.) The Israelites asked, “Should we again go out to battle against our brothers the Benjamites, or should we stop?” The LORD answered, “Fight, for tomorrow I will deliver them into your hand.”

29 So Israel set up an ambush around Gibeah. 30 On the third day the Israelites went up against the Benjamites and arrayed themselves against Gibeah as they had done before. 31 The Benjamites came out against them and were drawn away from the city. They began to attack the people as before, killing about thirty men of Israel in the fields and on the roads, one of which led up to Bethel and the other to Gibeah. 32 “We are defeating them as before,” said the Benjamites. But the Israelites said, “Let us retreat and draw them away from the city onto the roads.” 33 So all the men of Israel got up from their places and arrayed themselves at Baal-tamar, and the Israelites in ambush charged from their positions west of Gibeah. 34 Then 10,000 select men from all Israel made a frontal assault against Gibeah, and the battle was fierce. But the Benjamites did not realize that disaster was upon them. 35 The LORD defeated Benjamin in the presence of Israel, and on that day the Israelites slaughtered 25,100 Benjamites, all armed with swords.

36 Then the Benjamites realized they had been defeated. Now the men of Israel had retreated before Benjamin because they were relying on the ambush they had set against Gibeah. 37 The men in ambush rushed suddenly against Gibeah; they advanced and put the whole city to the sword. 38 The men of Israel had arranged a signal with the men in ambush: When they sent up a great cloud of smoke from the city, 39 the men of Israel would turn in the battle. When the Benjamites had begun to strike them down, killing about thirty men of Israel, they said, “They are defeated before us as in the first battle.” 40 But when the column of smoke began to go up from the city, the Benjamites looked behind them and saw the whole city going up in smoke. 41 Then the men of Israel turned back on them, and the men of Benjamin were terrified when they realized that disaster had come upon them.

42 So they fled before the men of Israel toward the wilderness, but the battle overtook them, and the men coming out of the cities struck them down there. 43 They surrounded the Benjamites, pursued them, and easily overtook them in the vicinity of Gibeah on the east. 44 And 18,000 Benjamites fell, all men of valor. 45 Then the Benjamites turned and fled toward the wilderness to the rock of Rimmon, and Israel cut down 5,000 men on the roads. And they overtook them at Gidom and struck down 2,000 more. 46 That day 25,000 Benjamite swordsmen fell, all men of valor. 47 But 600 men turned and fled into the wilderness to the rock of Rimmon, where they stayed four months. 48 And the men of Israel turned back against the other Benjamites and put to the sword all the cities, including the animals and everything else they found. And they burned down all the cities in their path.

passages.context_html:
Israel asks which tribe should lead the attack, and the LORD names Judah. Yet the first battle costs Israel twenty-two thousand men. After they weep and ask whether to fight again, He tells them to go up. Another eighteen thousand fall on the second day. The first two answers direct their action without promising immediate victory.

The people then gather at Bethel, weep, fast, and offer burnt and peace offerings. The ark is there, with Phinehas son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron, ministering before it. This time they ask whether to continue or stop, and the LORD promises to deliver Benjamin into their hands the next day.

Israel sets an ambush. A retreat draws Benjamin away from Gibeah; the city is attacked, and rising smoke signals the surrounding forces. Benjamin initially expects another victory, then realizes the disaster. The narrator attributes the defeat to the LORD.

The account first summarizes the victory and then describes the fighting and pursuit in more detail. Six hundred Benjamites escape to the rock of Rimmon for four months. Israel turns against the remaining cities, killing and burning what it finds. The next chapter begins with grief over the threat that Benjamin will disappear from Israel. The military victory has left a national crisis.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill read the repeated defeats as humbling Israel’s confidence in its numbers and its cause. They notice the movement from asking who should lead to weeping, fasting, sacrifice, and asking whether to stop. For them, the eventual promise comes as the people learn dependence on God.

Wesley also explains why the promised victory is followed by an ambush: trusting God’s promise does not remove the need to act carefully. The narrator presents both the plan and the LORD’s giving victory, without treating them as competing explanations.

The destruction beyond the battlefield raises a further question. Wesley offers military fury as one explanation, while also considering whether the law concerning an apostate city or Israel’s oath could partly explain it. Gill emphasizes anger after the heavy losses and also discusses the oath. These are attempts to explain the severity; the passage itself records the devastation, and the next chapter shows its consequences.

passages.god_plan_html:
The people approach God with offerings and the ministry of Phinehas, an Aaronic priest. The wider story leads to the lasting priesthood of Jesus. Hebrews 7:11–28 explicitly notes that He comes from Judah and explains that His indestructible life and once-for-all offering give a better hope through which people draw near to God.

This is a connection within the Bible’s larger story of access to God, rather than a prediction hidden in the battle plan. Hebrews 4:14–16 invites those who belong to Jesus to approach with confidence for mercy and help in need. The hope rests on the faithful Son who understands human weakness and intercedes for His people.

passages.title: Judges 21:1-25
passages.section_title: Can Israel repair one tragedy by creating another?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now the men of Israel had sworn an oath at Mizpah, saying, “Not one of us will give his daughter in marriage to a Benjamite.” 2 So the people came to Bethel and sat there before God until evening, lifting up their voices and weeping bitterly. 3 “Why, O LORD God of Israel,” they cried out, “has this happened in Israel? Today in Israel one tribe is missing!” 4 The next day the people got up early, built an altar there, and presented burnt offerings and peace offerings. 5 The Israelites asked, “Who among all the tribes of Israel did not come to the assembly before the LORD?” For they had taken a solemn oath that anyone who failed to come up before the LORD at Mizpah would surely be put to death. 6 And the Israelites grieved for their brothers, the Benjamites, and said, “Today a tribe is cut off from Israel. 7 What should we do about wives for the survivors, since we have sworn by the LORD not to give them our daughters in marriage?” 8 So they asked, “Which one of the tribes of Israel failed to come up before the LORD at Mizpah?” And, in fact, no one from Jabesh-gilead had come to the camp for the assembly. 9 For when the people were counted, none of the residents of Jabesh-gilead were there. 10 So the congregation sent 12,000 of their most valiant men and commanded them: “Go and put to the sword those living in Jabesh-gilead, including women and children. 11 This is what you are to do: Devote to destruction every male, as well as every female who has had relations with a man.” 12 So they found among the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead four hundred young women who had not had relations with a man, and they brought them to the camp at Shiloh in the land of Canaan. 13 Then the whole congregation sent a message of peace to the Benjamites who were at the rock of Rimmon. 14 And at that time the Benjamites returned and were given the women who were spared from Jabesh-gilead. But there were not enough women for all of them. 15 The people grieved for Benjamin, because the LORD had made a void in the tribes of Israel. 16 Then the elders of the congregation said, “What should we do about wives for those who remain, since the women of Benjamin have been destroyed?” 17 They added, “There must be heirs for the survivors of Benjamin, so that a tribe of Israel will not be wiped out. 18 But we cannot give them our daughters as wives.” For the Israelites had sworn, “Cursed is he who gives a wife to a Benjamite.” 19 “But look,” they said, “there is a yearly feast to the LORD in Shiloh, which is north of Bethel east of the road that goes up from Bethel to Shechem, and south of Lebonah.” 20 So they commanded the Benjamites: “Go, hide in the vineyards 21 and watch. When you see the daughters of Shiloh come out to perform their dances, each of you is to come out of the vineyards, catch for himself a wife from the daughters of Shiloh, and go to the land of Benjamin. 22 When their fathers or brothers come to us to complain, we will tell them, ‘Do us a favor by helping them, since we did not get wives for each of them in the war. Since you did not actually give them your daughters, you have no guilt.’” 23 The Benjamites did as instructed and carried away the number of women they needed from the dancers they caught. They went back to their own inheritance, rebuilt their cities, and settled in them. 24 And at that time, each of the Israelites returned from there to his own tribe and clan, each to his own inheritance. 25 In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes.

passages.context_html:
The surviving Benjamites need wives if their tribe is to continue, but the other Israelites have sworn not to give them their daughters. The people weep before God over the loss within Israel and offer sacrifices. Their own oath now stands in the way of the outcome they want.

A second oath threatens death to anyone who failed to attend the assembly at Mizpah. When they discover that Jabesh-gilead sent no one, they dispatch twelve thousand soldiers against it. The soldiers kill the inhabitants except for four hundred young women who have not had relations with a man. These women are taken to Shiloh and then given to the returning Benjamites.

There are still not enough wives. The elders turn to an annual feast of the LORD at Shiloh, where young women come out to dance. They instruct the remaining men to hide in the vineyards and seize women as wives. If fathers and brothers complain, the elders will explain that they did not actually give their daughters and therefore have not broken the oath.

The Benjamites carry out the plan, take the women, and rebuild their cities. Everyone returns to his inheritance. Benjamin survives, but its preservation has involved another massacre and the taking of women by force. The narrator closes with the book’s repeated description: there was no king, and everyone did what was right in his own eyes.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley distinguishes the need to confront Gibeah’s crime from the excessive severity of the response. He regards the war as necessary but reads the grief as recognition that the punishment went too far. His explanation stresses that even justified punishment requires compassion.

Gill explains the elders’ reasoning about the women of Shiloh: because the families did not voluntarily give them, the elders claim the oath has not been broken. The USCCB Bible study notes also explain this distinction between giving and taking, while drawing attention to the disorder of the arrangements. These notes offer an explanation of the passage, rather than a separate church ruling approving its solutions.

The conclusion keeps the reader from treating the survival of a tribe as an uncomplicated happy ending. Israel has found ways around its own restrictions, while more people suffer. No new divine command to attack Jabesh-gilead or seize the dancers is reported. The final statement about everyone’s own judgment invites the reader to assess how this outcome was reached.

passages.god_plan_html:
Judges ends with Israel’s need still unresolved. The account of Ruth begins during the days of the judges, showing another part of life in that troubled period. Its ending traces the family of Ruth and Boaz through Obed and Jesse to David in Ruth 4:13–22. God’s purposes continue amid a history that contains both faithfulness and terrible failure.

Matthew 1:1–6, 16–23 carries that family line forward to Jesus, the son of David, and states His mission: to save His people from their sins. This gives the wider direction of the hope raised by the book’s ending. The answer reaches beyond arranging a political settlement or putting someone on a throne; God provides the Savior who deals with the sin beneath the disorder.

passages.title: Ruth 1:1-5
passages.section_title: Where can hope begin after a family loses so much?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 In the days when the judges ruled, there was a famine in the land. And a certain man from Bethlehem in Judah, with his wife and two sons, went to reside in the land of Moab. 2 The man’s name was Elimelech, his wife’s name was Naomi, and the names of his two sons were Mahlon and Chilion. They were Ephrathites from Bethlehem in Judah, and they entered the land of Moab and settled there. 3 Then Naomi’s husband Elimelech died, and she was left with her two sons, 4 who took Moabite women as their wives, one named Orpah and the other named Ruth. And after they had lived in Moab about ten years, 5 both Mahlon and Chilion also died, and Naomi was left without her two sons and without her husband.
paragraphs: 1 In the days when the judges ruled, there was a famine in the land. And a certain man from Bethlehem in Judah, with his wife and two sons, went to reside in the land of Moab. 2 The man’s name was Elimelech, his wife’s name was Naomi, and the names of his two sons were Mahlon and Chilion. They were Ephrathites from Bethlehem in Judah, and they entered the land of Moab and settled there.

3 Then Naomi’s husband Elimelech died, and she was left with her two sons, 4 who took Moabite women as their wives, one named Orpah and the other named Ruth. And after they had lived in Moab about ten years, 5 both Mahlon and Chilion also died, and Naomi was left without her two sons and without her husband.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The story begins during the days of the judges, when a famine leads Elimelech, Naomi, and their two sons from Bethlehem in Judah to Moab. The setting places this family’s story within the troubled period described in Judges, without naming the particular judge then in office.

Bethlehem is בֵּית לֶחֶם, Beth Lehem (bayt LEH-khem), meaning a place of bread or food. Brown–Driver–Briggs identifies this Bethlehem in Judah and distinguishes it from the town of the same name in Zebulun. The family leaves a town whose name speaks of food because there is not enough to eat.

Elimelech dies in Moab. His sons marry Orpah and Ruth, both Moabite women, and after about ten years the sons also die. Naomi is left without husband or sons, while both daughters-in-law have lost their husbands. The opening moves quickly from a family seeking survival to three bereaved women facing an uncertain future.

The narrator reports the famine, migration, marriages, and deaths without expressly stating why each man dies. Deuteronomy 11:13–17 makes famine part of Israel’s covenant warnings, but Ruth’s opening does not give a separate divine explanation of this family’s losses.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry considers Elimelech’s concern to provide for his family understandable but judges the move to Moab unwise and spiritually dangerous. He reads the losses as a warning that changing one’s surroundings does not necessarily remove life’s trials. This is his assessment of the move, rather than a prohibition quoted from the opening verses.

The marriages also raise questions. Wesley considers whether the women had already embraced Israel’s faith; without that, he reads the marriages and early deaths as sin followed by punishment. Gill discusses both favorable and unfavorable readings and notes that the account will lead to the Messiah’s family line. The passage does not tell us what either woman believed when she married.

The treatment of Moabite women has its own important background. Deuteronomy 23:3–6 restricts Moabite entry into the assembly. In the Jewish legal tradition, Mishnah Yevamot 8:3 applies that restriction to men and permits female converts immediately. That distinction differs from treating every Moabite woman as permanently unable to enter Israel’s community. Ruth’s place in the story should not be reduced to an assumed blanket exclusion.
passages.god_plan_html:
The opening gives no quick answer to the women’s grief, but the book’s ending reveals a purpose they cannot yet see. Ruth 4:13–22 traces Ruth and Boaz’s son to David. Matthew 1:1–6, 16–23 includes Ruth in the family line of Jesus, who comes to save His people from their sins. A bereaved Moabite woman becomes part of that history.

Her inclusion also belongs beside the Bible’s wider account of people from the nations coming near to God. Ephesians 2:11–22 explains how those once distant are brought near through Christ and become members of God’s household. The story helps us see God’s saving purpose reaching people beyond the boundaries they might have expected.

passages.title: Ruth 1:6-14
passages.section_title: What future can Naomi offer the women she loves?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 When Naomi heard in Moab that the LORD had attended to His people by providing them with food, she and her daughters-in-law prepared to leave the land of Moab. 7 Accompanied by her two daughters-in-law, she left the place where she had been living and set out on the road leading back to the land of Judah. 8 Then Naomi said to her two daughters-in-law, “Go back, each of you to your mother’s home. May the LORD show you loving devotion, as you have shown to your dead and to me. 9 May the LORD enable each of you to find rest in the home of your new husband.” And she kissed them as they wept aloud 10 and said, “Surely we will return with you to your people.” 11 But Naomi replied, “Return home, my daughters. Why would you go with me? Are there still sons in my womb to become your husbands? 12 Return home, my daughters. Go on, for I am too old to have another husband. Even if I thought there was hope for me to have a husband tonight and to bear sons, 13 would you wait for them to grow up? Would you refrain from having husbands? No, my daughters, it is much more bitter for me than for you, because the hand of the LORD has gone out against me.” 14 Again they wept aloud, and Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye, but Ruth clung to her.

11 But Naomi replied, “Return home, my daughters. Why would you go with me? Are there still sons in my womb to become your husbands? 12 Return home, my daughters. Go on, for I am too old to have another husband. Even if I thought there was hope for me to have a husband tonight and to bear sons, 13 would you wait for them to grow up? Would you refrain from having husbands? No, my daughters, it is much more bitter for me than for you, because the hand of the LORD has gone out against me.” 14 Again they wept aloud, and Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye, but Ruth clung to her.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Naomi hears that the LORD has provided food for His people, so she prepares to return to Judah. Orpah and Ruth begin the journey with her. Before they go farther, she urges them to return to their mothers’ homes and seek the security of new marriages.

Her blessing recognizes what they have already given: loving devotion to their husbands and to her. The word is חֶסֶד, hesed (KHEH-sed), kindness expressed in faithful care. Brown–Driver–Briggs describes both human kindness and God’s lovingkindness, specifically listing Naomi’s prayer here. She asks God to show them the care they have shown others.

The women weep and initially insist on accompanying her. Naomi explains that she cannot offer them new husbands from her own household. Even the imagined possibility of having sons would leave them waiting far too long. Deuteronomy 25:5–10 gives the background of preserving a deceased brother’s family, but Naomi’s speech shows that no simple solution is available through her.

She describes her own situation as bitter and says the LORD’s hand has gone out against her. Orpah kisses her goodbye, while Ruth clings to her. Naomi’s concern for their future and her sense of personal loss are both present in the conversation.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Henry understand Naomi’s insistence as requiring the women to consider the cost of going with her. They do not read her as merely indifferent to their welfare or faith. Henry draws attention to her prayer when they face separation; Wesley emphasizes her inability to offer a secure future.

Both also use the two women’s choices as an illustration of differing levels of commitment. They compare a sorrowful departure with a loyalty willing to leave familiar surroundings. The narrative gives Orpah’s farewell and Ruth’s decision here; Ruth’s own explanation of her loyalty follows in the next passage.
passages.god_plan_html:
The kindness Naomi asks for belongs to a theme running through Scripture. In Exodus 34:5–9, the LORD declares Himself compassionate and gracious, abundant in loving devotion and faithfulness. Naomi’s prayer seeks care from the God whose character has already been made known to His people.

Titus 3:3–7 brings God’s kindness into the account of salvation through Jesus. He saves according to mercy, renews by the Holy Spirit, and gives the hope of eternal life. The larger purpose reaches beyond finding immediate security: God’s kindness brings people into a renewed life with Him.

passages.title: Ruth 1:15-18
passages.section_title: What is Ruth choosing when she chooses to stay?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 “Look,” said Naomi, “your sister-in-law has gone back to her people and her gods; follow her back home.” 16 But Ruth replied: “Do not urge me to leave you or to turn from following you. For wherever you go, I will go, and wherever you live, I will live; your people will be my people, and your God will be my God. 17 Where you die, I will die, and there I will be buried. May the LORD punish me, and ever so severely, if anything but death separates you and me.” 18 When Naomi saw that Ruth was determined to go with her, she stopped trying to persuade her.
paragraphs: 15 “Look,” said Naomi, “your sister-in-law has gone back to her people and her gods; follow her back home.” 16 But Ruth replied: “Do not urge me to leave you or to turn from following you. For wherever you go, I will go, and wherever you live, I will live; your people will be my people, and your God will be my God. 17 Where you die, I will die, and there I will be buried. May the LORD punish me, and ever so severely, if anything but death separates you and me.” 18 When Naomi saw that Ruth was determined to go with her, she stopped trying to persuade her.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After Orpah leaves, Naomi urges Ruth to follow her back to her people and gods. Ruth refuses. She commits herself to Naomi’s journey, home, people, God, death, and burial. Her answer makes clear that staying is more than continuing a trip together.

The previous verse says Ruth clings to Naomi. The Hebrew verb דָּבַק, dabaq (dah-BAHK), means to cling or remain close. Brown–Driver–Briggs specifically places Ruth’s attachment here among uses expressing loyalty and affection. Her following speech explains the depth of that attachment in her own words.

Ruth invokes the LORD in a solemn pledge that only death will separate them. She accepts a future among Naomi’s people and with Naomi’s God despite the uncertainty Naomi has described. When Naomi sees that she is determined, she stops trying to turn her back.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Henry read Ruth’s words as a deliberate commitment to the God of Israel as well as affection for Naomi. Henry emphasizes God’s grace in her choice; Wesley draws attention to the lasting character of her promise, even concerning burial.

The USCCB Bible study notes likewise explain the speech as a profound oath of loyalty, including belonging with Naomi’s family in death. These readers recognize both parts of the commitment: Ruth attaches herself to a person she loves and to that person’s people and God.

Wesley and Henry also draw a Christian illustration from the contrast with Orpah, comparing attachment that ends when the cost rises with commitment that continues. That illustration is their application. The chapter records Ruth’s confession clearly without telling the later course of Orpah’s life.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ruth’s decision offers a comparison with the costly allegiance Jesus describes in Luke 14:25–33. He calls people to weigh what following Him involves, including claims of family, possessions, and personal safety. Ruth’s pledge is made within her relationship with Naomi; Jesus’ call centers on allegiance to Himself.

This call follows His story of a banquet whose invitation reaches people left outside the expected guest list in Luke 14:15–24. Together, the passages show both welcome and a serious response to it. The wider hope is life in God’s kingdom, with loyalty that reaches beyond what is immediately comfortable or secure.

passages.title: Ruth 1:19-22
passages.section_title: Is Naomi’s emptiness the end of her story?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 So Naomi and Ruth traveled until they came to Bethlehem. When they entered Bethlehem, the whole town was stirred because of them, and the women of the town exclaimed, “Can this be Naomi?” 20 “Do not call me Naomi,” she replied. “Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with me. 21 I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty. Why call me Naomi? After all, the LORD has testified against me, and the Almighty has afflicted me.” 22 So Naomi returned from the land of Moab with her daughter-in-law Ruth the Moabitess. And they arrived in Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest.
paragraphs: 19 So Naomi and Ruth traveled until they came to Bethlehem. When they entered Bethlehem, the whole town was stirred because of them, and the women of the town exclaimed, “Can this be Naomi?” 20 “Do not call me Naomi,” she replied. “Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with me. 21 I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty. Why call me Naomi? After all, the LORD has testified against me, and the Almighty has afflicted me.” 22 So Naomi returned from the land of Moab with her daughter-in-law Ruth the Moabitess. And they arrived in Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Naomi and Ruth arrive in Bethlehem, and the town is stirred by their return. The women ask whether this is Naomi. She answers by asking for a different name: Mara, because she experiences life as bitter under the Almighty’s hand.

The name change expresses her grief. Strong’s entry for Naomi associates her name with pleasantness; Brown–Driver–Briggs explains מָרָא, Mara (mah-RAH), here through the word for bitter. Naomi is saying that the name she bears no longer seems to match what her life has become.

She says she left full and has returned empty, speaking out of the loss of her husband and sons. Yet Ruth is beside her, and they arrive at the beginning of the barley harvest. The narrator places genuine bereavement alongside two details that prepare the next chapter: a faithful companion and food becoming available.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads Naomi’s words as grief that acknowledges God’s rule over her circumstances. He emphasizes the need to bear affliction with humility and hope. Wesley similarly understands her language of God testifying against her as language drawn from judgment.

The USCCB Bible study notes bring out another aspect: her complaint resembles the cries found in the Psalms and Job. Speaking to and about God in this way can express an expectation that He hears and will act, even when His dealings seem unjust to the sufferer. The notes do not treat lament as simply the absence of faith.

The final sentence also keeps Naomi’s own assessment from becoming the last word. Her losses are not undone, but the story has given her a loyal daughter-in-law and brought them home at harvest. Readers can recognize those signs of an opening without asking her to pretend that the grief is small.
passages.god_plan_html:
A later account provides a moving comparison with Naomi’s loss. In Luke 7:11–17, Jesus meets a widow whose only son has died. He has compassion on her, raises the son, and gives him back to his mother. The people recognize God’s care reaching them through Jesus.

That compassion points toward hope stronger than death. Romans 8:18–25 speaks of believers still groaning as they await the redemption of their bodies. Christian hope allows grief and patient expectation to stand together. Naomi’s story is not finished at the harvest’s beginning, and the gospel’s promise reaches beyond even the best restoration this present life can offer.

passages.title: Ruth 2:1-13
passages.section_title: How does Ruth find protection in a stranger’s field?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now Naomi had a relative on her husband’s side, a prominent man of noble character from the clan of Elimelech, whose name was Boaz. 2 And Ruth the Moabitess said to Naomi, “Please let me go into the fields and glean heads of grain after someone in whose sight I may find favor.” “Go ahead, my daughter,” Naomi replied. 3 So Ruth departed and went out into the field and gleaned after the harvesters. And she happened to come to the part of the field belonging to Boaz, who was from the clan of Elimelech. 4 Just then Boaz arrived from Bethlehem and said to the harvesters, “The LORD be with you.” “The LORD bless you,” they replied. 5 And Boaz asked the foreman of his harvesters, “Whose young woman is this?” 6 The foreman answered, “She is the Moabitess who returned with Naomi from the land of Moab. 7 She has said, ‘Please let me glean and gather among the sheaves after the harvesters.’ So she came out and has continued from morning until now, except that she rested a short time in the shelter.” 8 Then Boaz said to Ruth, “Listen, my daughter. Do not go and glean in another field, and do not go away from this place, but stay here close to my servant girls. 9 Let your eyes be on the field they are harvesting, and follow along after these girls. Indeed, I have ordered the young men not to touch you. And when you are thirsty, go and drink from the jars the young men have filled.” 10 At this, she fell on her face, bowing low to the ground, and said to him, “Why have I found such favor in your eyes that you should take notice of me, even though I am a foreigner?” 11 Boaz replied, “I have been made fully aware of all you have done for your mother-in-law since the death of your husband, how you left your father and mother and the land of your birth, and how you came to a people you did not know before. 12 May the LORD repay your work, and may you receive a rich reward from the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have taken refuge.” 13 “My lord,” she said, “may I continue to find favor in your eyes, for you have comforted and spoken kindly to your maidservant, though I am not like one of your servant girls.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The narrator introduces Boaz before Ruth meets him: he is a prominent man of noble character from Elimelech’s clan. Ruth asks Naomi for permission to glean, gathering grain left behind by harvesters. Leviticus 19:9–10 and Deuteronomy 24:19–22 provide for the poor, foreigners, and widows in this way.

She happens to enter Boaz’s part of the field. When he arrives from Bethlehem, he and the workers greet one another in the LORD’s name. The foreman identifies Ruth as the Moabite woman who came with Naomi and reports her request and steady work that morning.

Boaz tells her to stay close to his young women, use his fields, and drink from the jars his workers fill. He has ordered the young men not to touch her. His welcome includes practical safeguards and provision, rather than kind words alone.

Ruth is astonished that he notices her, a foreigner. Boaz explains that he has heard of her care for Naomi and her decision to leave her family and homeland. He prays that the LORD will reward her and describes her as seeking refuge under God’s wings. חָסָה, hasah (khah-SAH), means to seek refuge; Brown–Driver–Briggs specifically connects this verse with the image of shelter under God’s wings.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Henry understand Ruth’s apparently accidental arrival as God’s care working through an ordinary event. Ruth does not first choose the field because she knows its owner’s family connection. The reader, however, has been told why the meeting can matter.

Both emphasize her diligence and Boaz’s kindness. Henry sees the exchange between the owner and workers as evidence that genuine devotion to God affects everyday relationships. He also directly compares Boaz’s care for Ruth with the kindness of Jesus toward people in need.

Wesley and Gill explain the wings as an image of protection, whether recalling a bird sheltering its young or the cherubim associated with God’s presence. The point of the prayer is Ruth’s trust in the God of Israel, expressed through the choices Boaz has heard about.
passages.god_plan_html:
The refuge Boaz describes is part of a wider biblical picture. Psalm 91:1–4 speaks of trust in God through the image of shelter beneath His wings. In Matthew 23:37–39, Jesus uses the image of a hen gathering her young when expressing His longing to gather Jerusalem’s people.

Henry’s comparison with Christ’s kindness also finds a clear invitation in Matthew 11:25–30. Jesus calls the weary to come to Him for rest and learn from His gentleness. Boaz gives Ruth a place to work in safety; Jesus brings people into the deeper rest of knowing the Father through the Son.

passages.title: Ruth 2:14-23
passages.section_title: Why does the name Boaz give Naomi fresh hope?

Do not rebuke her.” 17 So Ruth gathered grain in the field until evening. And when she beat out what she had gleaned, it was about an ephah of barley. 18 She picked up the grain and went into the town, where her mother-in-law saw what she had gleaned. And she brought out what she had saved from her meal and gave it to Naomi. 19 Then her mother-in-law asked her, “Where did you glean today, and where did you work? Blessed be the man who noticed you.” So she told her mother-in-law where she had worked. “The name of the man I worked with today is Boaz,” she said. 20 Then Naomi said to her daughter-in-law, “May he be blessed by the LORD, who has not withdrawn His kindness from the living or the dead.” Naomi continued, “The man is a close relative. He is one of our kinsman-redeemers.” 21 Then Ruth the Moabitess said, “He also told me, ‘Stay with my young men until they have finished gathering all my harvest.’” 22 And Naomi said to her daughter-in-law Ruth, “My daughter, it is good for you to work with his young women, so that nothing will happen to you in another field.” 23 So Ruth stayed close to the servant girls of Boaz to glean grain until the barley and wheat harvests were finished. And she lived with her mother-in-law.

And she lived with her mother-in-law.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Boaz invites Ruth to share the harvesters’ meal. She eats bread and roasted grain, has enough, and saves what remains. Afterward he directs the workers to let her gather among the sheaves and even leave stalks from the bundles for her. They are not to insult or rebuke her.

She works until evening, beats out the grain, and brings about an ephah of barley home. Naomi sees the result and also receives the food Ruth saved from the meal. Her question about where Ruth worked leads to the name she recognizes: Boaz.

Naomi blesses him and speaks of kindness continuing to the living and the dead. She then identifies him as one of their kinsman-redeemers. The word גֹּאֵל, goel (goh-EL), describes a relative acting to redeem or restore what belongs to the family. Brown–Driver–Briggs lists Ruth 2:20 alongside responsibilities such as redeeming family land and freeing a relative from bondage; Leviticus 25:25–28, 47–55 gives those responsibilities.

This family connection opens a possibility beyond food for the day. For now, Ruth continues with Boaz’s young women through the barley and wheat harvests and lives with Naomi. The household is receiving provision while the question of its longer future remains.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Henry emphasize Ruth’s continued work, her sharing with Naomi, and her willingness to accept guidance about where to glean. Gill explains the kindness to the living and dead through care for the surviving women and respect for their deceased family. Their readings connect the present provision with the family ties Naomi has recognized.

Boaz’s welcome at the meal has also prompted readings beyond the immediate event. In the Jewish collection Ruth Rabbah 5:6, one reading connects the bread with the Messiah’s kingship and the vinegar with suffering, citing Isaiah 53:5. The same passage offers several other readings, including the actual harvesters’ meal. This is a Jewish explanation looking toward the Messiah; it does not itself identify Jesus or declare that Boaz performed a Christian ceremony.

The story is also preparing the reader for the responsibilities of a redeemer. Calling Boaz one of them identifies a family relationship and a possible source of help. It does not yet report a completed redemption or a marriage agreement; those questions develop in the following chapters.
passages.god_plan_html:
The responsibility of a relative to act for family provides a useful comparison with Christ’s rescue. Hebrews 2:11–18 says Jesus shares the humanity of those He saves, calls them His brothers, and becomes a merciful and faithful high priest. Through His death He breaks the power of the devil and releases people from slavery to the fear of death.

Galatians 4:4–7 gives the purpose of His coming in terms of redemption and family: God sends His Son to redeem, so that people receive adoption and become heirs. Boaz’s family role introduces a rescue still to unfold in Ruth. The New Testament states the greater rescue through the Son who brings His people into God’s household.
