passages.title: Ruth 3:1-13
passages.section_title: What is Ruth asking Boaz to do?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 One day Ruth’s mother-in-law Naomi said to her, “My daughter, should I not seek a resting place for you, that it may be well with you? 2 Now is not Boaz, with whose servant girls you have been working, a relative of ours? In fact, tonight he is winnowing barley on the threshing floor. 3 Therefore wash yourself, put on perfume, and wear your best clothes. Go down to the threshing floor, but do not let the man know you are there until he has finished eating and drinking. 4 When he lies down, note the place where he lies. Then go in and uncover his feet, and lie down, and he will explain to you what you should do.” 5 “I will do everything you say,” Ruth answered. 6 So she went down to the threshing floor and did everything her mother-in-law had instructed her to do. 7 After Boaz had finished eating and drinking and was in good spirits, he went to lie down at the end of the heap of grain. Then Ruth went in secretly, uncovered his feet, and lay down. 8 At midnight, Boaz was startled, turned over, and there lying at his feet was a woman! 9 “Who are you?” he asked. “I am your servant Ruth,” she replied. “Spread the corner of your garment over me, for you are a kinsman-redeemer.” 10 Then Boaz said, “May the LORD bless you, my daughter. You have shown more kindness now than before, because you have not run after the younger men, whether rich or poor. 11 And now do not be afraid, my daughter. I will do for you whatever you request, since all my fellow townspeople know that you are a woman of noble character. 12 Yes, it is true that I am a kinsman-redeemer, but there is a redeemer nearer than I. 13 Stay here tonight, and in the morning, if he wants to redeem you, good. Let him redeem you. But if he does not want to redeem you, as surely as the LORD lives, I will. Now lie here until morning.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Naomi now seeks a lasting home for Ruth. The word מָנוֹחַ, manoach (mah-NOH-akh), means a resting place or condition of rest. Brown–Driver–Briggs specifically explains its use here as the rest and security sought in marriage. Naomi’s concern extends beyond the food Ruth has obtained during harvest.

She tells Ruth to wash, put on perfume and her best clothes, and approach Boaz after he has finished eating and drinking at the threshing floor. Ruth is to note where he lies, uncover his feet, and lie down. She follows the instructions, and at midnight he wakes in surprise.

Ruth identifies herself and asks him to spread the corner of his garment over her because he is a kinsman-redeemer. כָּנָף, kanaph (kah-NAHF), can mean a wing or the corner of a garment; Brown–Driver–Briggs gives both uses. The request recalls Boaz’s prayer in 2:12 that she find refuge beneath God’s wings. She is asking him to extend care through the family responsibility he can assume.

Boaz blesses her, praises her kindness in not pursuing younger men, and acknowledges that the town knows her noble character. He is willing to act, but another relative has priority. He promises to address that man’s claim in the morning and, if the man declines, to redeem her himself. The response is warm, while the outcome remains subject to a right he will not ignore.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley, Henry, and the USCCB Bible study notes understand Ruth’s request as seeking marriage and read Boaz as treating her honorably. The covering language has a close biblical comparison in Ezekiel 16:8, where the LORD describes spreading His cloak and entering a covenant with Jerusalem.

Gill also reads the action as a marriage request, but acknowledges the risks in Naomi’s unusual plan. He asks how she could be sure the situation would not lead to wrongdoing or misunderstanding. His discussion preserves the honorable purpose without pretending that the approach carried no danger.

These readers also recognize that Boaz’s willingness does not remove the nearer relative’s claim. The scene establishes Ruth’s request and Boaz’s promise to act properly; it does not yet complete the public arrangement described in the next chapter.
passages.god_plan_html:
The sheltering garment belongs beside the Bible’s wider use of marriage to describe God’s covenant care. Ezekiel 16:6–14 portrays the LORD giving life, covering, and dignity to Jerusalem, then pledging Himself to her. The image emphasizes His initiative and care for someone who could not supply those things for herself.

The New Testament brings marriage language to Christ and the church. Ephesians 5:25–33 explains His love through giving Himself to make His people holy and care for them. Revelation 19:6–9 looks toward the joy of the Lamb’s marriage. Ruth’s appeal for a faithful protector and husband fits within that larger theme of belonging secured through faithful love.

passages.title: Ruth 3:14-18
passages.section_title: What can Ruth do while Boaz settles the matter?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 So she lay down at his feet until morning, but she got up before anyone else could recognize her. Then Boaz said, “Do not let it be known that a woman came to the threshing floor.” 15 And he told her, “Bring the shawl you are wearing and hold it out.” When she did so, he poured in six measures of barley and placed it on her. Then he went into the city. 16 When Ruth returned to her mother-in-law, Naomi asked her, “How did it go, my daughter?” Then Ruth told her all that Boaz had done for her. 17 And she said, “He gave me these six measures of barley, for he said, ‘Do not go back to your mother-in-law empty-handed.’” 18 “Wait, my daughter,” said Naomi, “until you find out how things go, for he will not rest unless he has resolved the matter today.”

Then Boaz said, “Do not let it be known that a woman came to the threshing floor.” 15 And he told her, “Bring the shawl you are wearing and hold it out.” When she did so, he poured in six measures of barley and placed it on her. Then he went into the city.

16 When Ruth returned to her mother-in-law, Naomi asked her, “How did it go, my daughter?” Then Ruth told her all that Boaz had done for her. 17 And she said, “He gave me these six measures of barley, for he said, ‘Do not go back to your mother-in-law empty-handed.’” 18 “Wait, my daughter,” said Naomi, “until you find out how things go, for he will not rest unless he has resolved the matter today.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Ruth remains at Boaz’s feet until morning and leaves before others can recognize her. Boaz asks that the visit not become known. He also sends her away with six measures of barley, placed in the shawl she holds out. The unit of measure is not specified in the account.

The BSB then says he goes into the city, preparing the next scene. Ruth returns to Naomi and reports what happened, including Boaz’s message that she should not return to her mother-in-law empty-handed. The gift continues his practical care while the larger question is being settled.

Naomi tells Ruth to wait. Her confidence is in Boaz’s determination: he will not rest until he resolves the matter that day. Ruth has made her request, and the next action belongs to the man who has promised to take responsibility.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley reads the discretion about the visit as concern for both reputations. Gill likewise explains the gift and the prompt action through Boaz’s care and commitment. Gill notes that the six measures do not identify a certain unit; his suggested quantity is an explanation, not a number supplied by the text.

Henry emphasizes patient trust after Ruth has done what she can. He compares her reliance on a willing family redeemer with believers bringing their need to Christ, who shares their humanity. His application invites faith in the Redeemer rather than treating waiting as proof that nothing is happening.
passages.god_plan_html:
The comparison with Christ has a firm basis in what the New Testament says about His work. Hebrews 9:24–28 describes Him appearing before God on His people’s behalf and offering Himself once to bear sins. The decisive sacrifice is already made; those who belong to Him await His return to bring salvation.

Ruth waits for an earthly arrangement still to be completed. Christian hope rests in the Savior whose offering does not need to be repeated and whose promised return is still ahead. The shared lesson is confidence in the one undertaking the rescue, with patience grounded in His faithfulness.

passages.title: Ruth 4:1-12
passages.section_title: What does Boaz accept when the nearer relative refuses?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Meanwhile, Boaz went to the gate and sat down there. Soon the kinsman-redeemer of whom he had spoken came along, and Boaz said, “Come over here, my friend, and sit down.” So he went over and sat down. 2 Then Boaz took ten of the elders of the city and said, “Sit here,” and they did so. 3 And he said to the kinsman-redeemer, “Naomi, who has returned from the land of Moab, is selling the piece of land that belonged to our brother Elimelech. 4 I thought I should inform you that you may buy it back in the presence of those seated here and in the presence of the elders of my people. If you want to redeem it, do so. But if you will not redeem it, tell me so I may know, because there is no one but you to redeem it, and I am next after you.” “I will redeem it,” he replied. 5 Then Boaz said, “On the day you buy the land from Naomi and also from Ruth the Moabitess, you must also acquire the widow of the deceased in order to raise up the name of the deceased on his inheritance.” 6 The kinsman-redeemer replied, “I cannot redeem it myself, or I would jeopardize my own inheritance. Take my right of redemption, because I cannot redeem it.” 7 Now in former times in Israel, concerning the redemption or exchange of property, to make any matter legally binding a man would remove his sandal and give it to the other party, and this was a confirmation in Israel. 8 So the kinsman-redeemer removed his sandal and said to Boaz, “Buy it for yourself.” 9 At this, Boaz said to the elders and all the people, “You are witnesses today that I am buying from Naomi all that belonged to Elimelech, Chilion, and Mahlon. 10 Moreover, I have acquired Ruth the Moabitess, Mahlon’s widow, as my wife, to raise up the name of the deceased through his inheritance, so that his name will not disappear from among his brothers or from the gate of his home. You are witnesses today.” 11 “We are witnesses,” said the elders and all the people at the gate. “May the LORD make the woman entering your home like Rachel and Leah, who together built up the house of Israel. May you be prosperous in Ephrathah and famous in Bethlehem. 12 And may your house become like the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah, because of the offspring the LORD will give you by this young woman.”
paragraphs: 1 Meanwhile, Boaz went to the gate and sat down there. Soon the kinsman-redeemer of whom he had spoken came along, and Boaz said, “Come over here, my friend, and sit down.” So he went over and sat down. 2 Then Boaz took ten of the elders of the city and said, “Sit here,” and they did so. 3 And he said to the kinsman-redeemer, “Naomi, who has returned from the land of Moab, is selling the piece of land that belonged to our brother Elimelech. 4 I thought I should inform you that you may buy it back in the presence of those seated here and in the presence of the elders of my people. If you want to redeem it, do so. But if you will not redeem it, tell me so I may know, because there is no one but you to redeem it, and I am next after you.” “I will redeem it,” he replied.

5 Then Boaz said, “On the day you buy the land from Naomi and also from Ruth the Moabitess, you must also acquire the widow of the deceased in order to raise up the name of the deceased on his inheritance.” 6 The kinsman-redeemer replied, “I cannot redeem it myself, or I would jeopardize my own inheritance. Take my right of redemption, because I cannot redeem it.” 7 Now in former times in Israel, concerning the redemption or exchange of property, to make any matter legally binding a man would remove his sandal and give it to the other party, and this was a confirmation in Israel. 8 So the kinsman-redeemer removed his sandal and said to Boaz, “Buy it for yourself.”

9 At this, Boaz said to the elders and all the people, “You are witnesses today that I am buying from Naomi all that belonged to Elimelech, Chilion, and Mahlon. 10 Moreover, I have acquired Ruth the Moabitess, Mahlon’s widow, as my wife, to raise up the name of the deceased through his inheritance, so that his name will not disappear from among his brothers or from the gate of his home. You are witnesses today.” 11 “We are witnesses,” said the elders and all the people at the gate. “May the LORD make the woman entering your home like Rachel and Leah, who together built up the house of Israel. May you be prosperous in Ephrathah and famous in Bethlehem. 12 And may your house become like the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah, because of the offspring the LORD will give you by this young woman.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Boaz goes to the town gate and invites the nearer relative to sit with him. He gathers ten elders as witnesses, then explains that Naomi is selling the land associated with Elimelech. The nearer man has the first opportunity to redeem it and initially agrees.

Boaz then states that acquiring the land also involves taking Ruth, Mahlon’s widow, to preserve the deceased man’s name through his inheritance. The relative says this would jeopardize his own inheritance. He gives his right of redemption to Boaz instead.

The narrator explains the sandal exchange as a former custom confirming redemption or property exchange. The man removes his sandal, and Boaz publicly accepts the property and Ruth as his wife, stating his purpose of preserving Mahlon’s name. The people affirm that they are witnesses.

Their blessing places this marriage within Israel’s larger family story. They name Rachel and Leah, then Perez, born to Tamar and Judah, and pray for a fruitful household and a lasting name in Bethlehem. The next part of the account will show how far that family’s significance reaches.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley offers more than one explanation for the relative’s concern about inheritance: preserving another man’s name could affect his own line, or added family responsibilities could diminish what he passes on. Gill also discusses the impact of further dependents and children. The narrator gives the concern without spelling out the man’s existing household or exact finances.

Wesley and Gill distinguish the property-confirming sandal custom described here from the particular procedure in Deuteronomy 25 for a brother refusing his deceased brother’s widow. The related concerns are family continuity and inheritance, but the ceremonies are not identical: Ruth’s account does not describe her removing the sandal or spitting.

Henry emphasizes honest, public dealing and draws a warning from the man’s refusal: concern for present possessions can keep people from embracing what is more valuable. That is his application of the contrast with Boaz, who accepts the responsibilities the other man declines.
passages.god_plan_html:
Boaz’s willingness to bear the cost of another household’s future offers a comparison with the greater rescue Jesus undertakes. In Mark 10:42–45, Jesus describes His mission as serving and giving His life to free others. His care involves personal cost rather than using authority for His own advantage.

First Peter 1:18–21 explains that redemption through Christ comes through His precious blood, rather than silver or gold. Boaz settles a family’s earthly need through a witnessed arrangement. Christ’s death and resurrection bring a rescue on which faith and hope in God can rest.

section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Boaz marries Ruth, and the LORD enables her to conceive. Their son’s birth brings a new blessing to Naomi. The women praise God for not leaving her without a redeemer and describe the child as one who will renew her life and support her in old age.

They also recognize Ruth’s love, calling her better to Naomi than seven sons. The foreign daughter-in-law who arrived with her has become central to the household’s renewed future. Naomi takes the child into her lap and cares for him. The neighboring women name him Obed and speak of a son born to Naomi.

The narrator then identifies Obed as the father of Jesse, the father of David. A final genealogy traces the family from Perez through Boaz and Obed to David. The story that began with famine, death, and the threat of a family disappearing ends with life and a place in Israel’s royal history.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The reference to a redeemer in verse 14 has been understood in two ways. Wesley explains the blessing through God not allowing the family’s redeemer to fail in his duty, emphasizing Boaz’s action. Gill acknowledges that reading but favors the newborn child, because the women speak of what has happened that day and of his future care for Naomi.

The USCCB Bible study notes also connect the child with the family’s future care and explain that Naomi’s taking him into her arms need not mean a formal adoption. The account honors her renewed place in the household while still identifying Ruth and Boaz as his parents.

Henry draws out the wider significance of the genealogy: Ruth’s place in David’s family leads toward Christ and the blessing reaching both Jews and Gentiles. The closing names therefore do more than record a private family’s recovery.
passages.god_plan_html:
The New Testament makes that direction explicit. Matthew 1:1–6, 16–23 names Ruth and Boaz in the ancestry of Jesus, the son of David, and identifies His mission as saving His people from their sins. Luke 1:30–33 announces that Jesus will receive David’s throne and reign without end.

The hope also reaches the nations. In Romans 15:8–13, Christ confirms God’s promises and brings Gentiles to praise Him for mercy; Paul points to the Root of Jesse as their hope. Ruth’s place in the family of Jesse and David belongs within that saving purpose. God’s care for these women is part of a story extending far beyond what they could see.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 1:1-8
passages.section_title: What makes Hannah’s sorrow so painful?

passages.context_html:
The book opens inside a troubled household. Elkanah has two wives: Peninnah has children, and Hannah has none. Each year he travels to Shiloh to worship and sacrifice. Eli’s sons, Hophni and Phinehas, serve there as priests. These names introduce the family and the place of worship that will shape Samuel’s early life.

Elkanah loves Hannah and gives her a double portion at the meal. Peninnah turns Hannah’s childlessness into a reason to hurt her. This is repeated cruelty, continuing year after year even during the journey to worship. Hannah reaches the point of weeping and being unable to eat.

The narrator says that the LORD had closed Hannah’s womb. He does not say that she had committed a particular sin or deserved Peninnah’s taunts. Elkanah’s questions draw attention to his love, but they do not remove her grief. His affection and her longing for a child are both real.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The central events are not a major dividing point between Christian traditions: Hannah suffers from childlessness and a rival’s cruelty while her husband continues to love her. Wesley treats Elkanah’s love as something that should remain steady through an affliction Hannah cannot help. He reads the question about ten sons as an appeal to the value of that love.

Henry also emphasizes the harm of adding to someone’s sorrow. He sees Elkanah’s continuing worship amid family conflict as significant. These readings highlight the comfort available to Hannah without making her longing disappear or treating Peninnah’s conduct as justified.

passages.context_html:
This chapter follows Hannah from a painful family situation to the dedication of her son at Shiloh. Peninnah repeatedly taunts her for having no children. Elkanah loves her, yet his affection does not end her grief. The family continues its yearly worship while these wounds remain.

Hannah asks God for a son and promises his lifelong service to the LORD. Eli initially mistakes her silent prayer for drunkenness. After she explains, he blesses her, and she leaves able to eat again. Her relief precedes the answer she hopes for.

The LORD remembers Hannah, and Samuel is born. She nurses him at home before bringing him to Eli. The chapter does not give his exact age. She returns to the place where she prayed, acknowledges God’s answer, and follows through on her promise. The ending is worship rather than a celebration of her own ability to obtain an answer.

The family’s location in Ephraim does not by itself settle its ancestry. First Chronicles 6:33–38 traces Samuel and his father Elkanah through Kohath to Levi. That identifies a Levitical family; it does not make every member a priest descended from Aaron.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The broad reading is shared across Christian traditions: God hears Hannah, Samuel’s birth answers her prayer, and she dedicates him to the LORD. Henry stresses both the freedom to bring a specific need to God and the responsibility to give thanks for what has been received. He also treats Eli’s first response as a warning against judging distress by appearances.

Wesley highlights the lifelong character of Samuel’s dedication and the change in Hannah before the birth. His explanation includes inward assurance from God’s Spirit. The account itself explicitly records her prayer, Eli’s blessing, her changed expression, and God remembering her. Those details should remain distinct from a commentator’s explanation of the parts the narrator leaves unstated.
passages.current_position_html: Our study [Prayer and Faith](../studies/prayer-and-faith.html) reads Hannah’s request as an honest desire placed within God’s purposes. She asks for a son and promises his whole life to God’s service. The account says that God remembered her; it does not make the answer a reward for reaching a certain level of persistence or emotion. Samuel’s life will serve a purpose much larger than the relief of Hannah’s sorrow.

passages.god_plan_html:
Samuel’s story begins with one woman’s anguish, but his life belongs to a larger history. The New Testament explicitly includes Samuel among the prophets whose witness points toward the days of Jesus. In Acts 3:22–26, Peter connects that prophetic witness with God’s promise to Abraham and blessing reaching the families of the earth.

Acts does not turn every action in Hannah’s household into a hidden prediction. It does establish that the child introduced here will belong to the prophetic witness leading toward Christ. God’s answer to a personal prayer becomes part of His work for people far beyond that family.

passages.context_html:
Hannah brings her distress directly to the LORD. She asks for a son and vows to dedicate him to God for his entire life. Her promise that no razor will touch his head marks a life set apart for God; compare the uncut hair in the Nazirite instructions in Numbers 6:1–8. A Nazirite was someone specially dedicated to God under those instructions.

Her prayer is silent: her lips move, but Eli cannot hear her voice. He mistakes this for drunkenness and rebukes her. Hannah explains that she has been pouring out her grief before the LORD. The priest has seen her outward appearance and misunderstood what is happening.

Eli then sends her away in peace and asks that God grant her petition. His words are a blessing, phrased as a request to God. Hannah begins to eat, and her face is no longer downcast. The change comes before she has a child; the narrator does not report that her circumstances have already changed.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads this as a clear example of bringing a particular need to God, rather than speaking only in general terms. He also warns against Eli’s rushed judgment. Hannah’s distress is not proof of drunkenness, and she answers the accusation by explaining herself.

Wesley understands the lifelong dedication as a permanent Nazirite commitment. He also sees God’s Spirit giving Hannah assurance through Eli’s words. That assurance is Wesley’s explanation of her changed expression; the narrator states the visible change without describing every thought or inward experience behind it. Neither the vow nor the blessing supplies a promise that every person who follows the same steps will receive a child.

passages.god_plan_html:
Hannah can speak to God even when the priest misunderstands her. This belongs within the Bible’s wider theme of bringing human weakness before God. Hebrews 4:14–16 presents Jesus as the great high priest who understands our weaknesses and invites His people to approach God for mercy and help.

This is a connection between the passages, rather than a claim that Eli represents Jesus in every detail. Eli misreads Hannah; Jesus’ care rests on His full understanding. The larger hope is access to God through a compassionate and faithful priest, even when other people fail to understand our distress.

Though the boy was still young, she brought him to the house of the LORD at Shiloh. 25 And when they had slaughtered the bull, they brought the boy to Eli. 26 “Please, my lord,” said Hannah, “as surely as you live, my lord, I am the woman who stood here beside you praying to the LORD. 27 I prayed for this boy, and since the LORD has granted me what I asked of Him, 28 I now dedicate the boy to the LORD. For as long as he lives, he is dedicated to the LORD.” So they worshiped the LORD there.
paragraphs: 19 The next morning they got up early to bow in worship before the LORD, and then they returned home to Ramah. And Elkanah had relations with his wife Hannah, and the LORD remembered her. 20 So in the course of time, Hannah conceived and gave birth to a son. She named him Samuel, saying, “Because I have asked for him from the LORD.”

21 Then Elkanah and all his house went up to make the annual sacrifice to the LORD and to fulfill his vow, 22 but Hannah did not go. “After the boy is weaned,” she said to her husband, “I will take him to appear before the LORD and to stay there permanently.” 23 “Do what you think is best,” her husband Elkanah replied, “and stay here until you have weaned him. Only may the LORD confirm His word.” So Hannah stayed and nursed her son until she had weaned him.

24 Once she had weaned him, Hannah took the boy with her, along with a three-year-old bull, an ephah of flour, and a skin of wine. Though the boy was still young, she brought him to the house of the LORD at Shiloh. 25 And when they had slaughtered the bull, they brought the boy to Eli. 26 “Please, my lord,” said Hannah, “as surely as you live, my lord, I am the woman who stood here beside you praying to the LORD. 27 I prayed for this boy, and since the LORD has granted me what I asked of Him, 28 I now dedicate the boy to the LORD. For as long as he lives, he is dedicated to the LORD.” So they worshiped the LORD there.

passages.context_html:
The family worships before leaving Shiloh. Back at home, Hannah conceives and later gives birth to Samuel. The narrator explains the answer in terms of God remembering her. This describes His attention and action on her behalf, rather than suggesting that He had lost track of her.

Hannah connects Samuel’s name with having asked the LORD for him. The Hebrew verb שָׁאַל, sha’al (shah-AHL), means to ask or request. The same root appears again when she dedicates him in verse 28. Brown–Driver–Briggs notes the sense of handing someone over in that verse. What she asked to receive, she now gives into God’s service. The connection with Samuel’s name is wordplay, rather than a simple dictionary translation of the name as “asked of God”; see the name entry.

She first stays home to nurse Samuel, with Elkanah’s agreement. Once he is weaned, she brings him to Shiloh with the offerings. No exact age is given. She identifies herself to Eli and explains that this is the child for whom she prayed. Her dedication is lifelong, and the scene ends in worship.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry emphasizes that caring for the young child at home is itself a faithful responsibility. Hannah’s temporary absence from the annual visit does not cancel her commitment. He also draws out the order of giving: she offers to God a child she first received from Him.

Wesley explains that the older English language of lending Samuel does not mean Hannah plans to reclaim him after a short term. Her commitment is permanent. The BSB expresses this as dedication. Both readings recognize thanksgiving and fulfilled commitment at the center of the scene, rather than a payment that makes God owe her another favor.
passages.current_position_html: Our study [Prayer and Faith](../studies/prayer-and-faith.html) reads Hannah’s request as an honest desire placed within God’s purposes. She asks for a son and promises his whole life to God’s service. The account says that God remembered her; it does not make the answer a reward for reaching a certain level of persistence or emotion. Samuel’s life will serve a purpose much larger than the relief of Hannah’s sorrow.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The passage shows a parent giving a dearly wanted son into a purpose beyond her household. Christians can compare this costly giving with the much greater gift described in John 3:16–18: God gives His Son so that those who believe in Him may have eternal life.

The comparison has limits. Samuel is dedicated to service; this scene does not describe him dying for anyone’s sins. John identifies Jesus as the Son through whom God saves the world. The shared theme is a beloved son given for a purpose reaching beyond one family, while the saving work belongs to Jesus Himself.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 2:1-11
passages.section_title: Why does Hannah’s thanksgiving reach beyond her own family?

versions.label: BSB

My mouth speaks boldly against my enemies, for I rejoice in Your salvation. 2 There is no one holy like the LORD. Indeed, there is no one besides You! And there is no Rock like our God. 3 Do not boast so proudly, or let arrogance come from your mouth, for the LORD is a God who knows, and by Him actions are weighed. 4 The bows of the mighty are broken, but the feeble are equipped with strength. 5 The well-fed hire themselves out for food, but the starving hunger no more. The barren woman gives birth to seven, but she who has many sons pines away. 6 The LORD brings death and gives life; He brings down to Sheol and raises up. 7 The LORD sends poverty and wealth; He humbles and He exalts. 8 He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap. He seats them among princes and bestows on them a throne of honor. For the foundations of the earth are the LORD’s, and upon them He has set the world. 9 He guards the steps of His faithful ones, but the wicked perish in darkness; for by his own strength shall no man prevail. 10 Those who oppose the LORD will be shattered. He will thunder from heaven against them. The LORD will judge the ends of the earth and will give power to His king. He will exalt the horn of His anointed.” 11 Then Elkanah went home to Ramah, but the boy began ministering to the LORD before Eli the priest.

passages.context_html:
Hannah’s prayer turns from the son she has received to the God who gave him. She praises His holiness, knowledge and power to overturn human expectations. The strong can be brought low; the hungry and poor can be raised up. People cannot make themselves secure simply by being powerful.

The repeated horn image may sound unfamiliar. The Hebrew קֶרֶן, qeren (KEH-ren), literally means a horn, but here pictures strength and honor. Brown–Driver–Briggs specifically identifies this use in verses 1 and 10. Hannah begins by thanking God for lifting her up and ends by speaking of His king being strengthened.

The word translated anointed is מָשִׁיחַ, mashiach (mah-SHEE-akh). It describes someone set apart by anointing, including kings and priests; the lexicon lists several such uses. The word alone does not mean every person called anointed is Jesus. Here it introduces a royal hope that reaches beyond Hannah’s immediate circumstances.

The song’s pictures are broader than a report of her family. The seven children of verse 5 are not a claim that she already has seven sons; verse 21 later names three more sons and two daughters. The scene closes with Samuel beginning his service under Eli while Elkanah returns home.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands Hannah’s raised horn as restored strength and honor. He reads the song’s reversals through her own deliverance while also seeing its closing kingly hope as reaching toward Christ. He treats seven as an expression of abundance rather than a literal count of children already born.

Henry likewise emphasizes that Hannah’s joy rests in God Himself, extending beyond the gift of Samuel. He reads the king and anointed language in light of Christ’s kingdom. These are Christian readings of the song within the larger Bible; they do not require every contrast in the poem to describe an event already completed in Hannah’s household.
passages.current_position_html: Our study [Prayer and Faith](../studies/prayer-and-faith.html) points to Hannah’s thanksgiving as evidence of what shaped her request. Her praise centers on God’s holiness, His rule over life and death, and His power to bring down the proud and lift the weak. She responds by worshiping God for who He is, rather than presenting the answer as proof that she had prayed hard enough.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Hannah’s song has a close parallel in Mary’s praise before Jesus’ birth. In Luke 1:46–55, Mary rejoices in God, praises His holiness, and describes the proud brought low, the humble lifted up, and the hungry fed. She connects these reversals with God remembering His promise to Abraham.

This is a shared pattern of praise, rather than a claim that Luke explicitly quotes every line from Hannah. The same chapter’s prophecy speaks of a horn of salvation in David’s house (Luke 1:68–75). Hannah’s thanksgiving opens toward the royal hope; Luke announces God’s promised rescue arriving in the story of Jesus.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 2:12-26
passages.section_title: What is the difference between holding an office and serving God?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 Now the sons of Eli were wicked men; they had no regard for the LORD 13 or for the custom of the priests with the people. When any man offered a sacrifice, the servant of the priest would come with a three-pronged meat fork while the meat was boiling 14 and plunge it into the pan or kettle or cauldron or cooking pot. And the priest would claim for himself whatever the meat fork brought up. This is how they treated all the Israelites who came to Shiloh. 15 Even before the fat was burned, the servant of the priest would come and say to the man who was sacrificing, “Give the priest some meat to roast, because he will not accept boiled meat from you, but only raw.” 16 And if any man said to him, “The fat must be burned first; then you may take whatever you want,” the servant would reply, “No, you must give it to me right now. 18 Now Samuel was ministering before the LORD—a boy wearing a linen ephod. 19 Each year his mother would make him a little robe and bring it to him when she went with her husband to offer the annual sacrifice. 20 And Eli would bless Elkanah and his wife, saying, “May the LORD give you children by this woman in place of the one she dedicated to the LORD.” Then they would go home. 21 So the LORD attended to Hannah, and she conceived and gave birth to three sons and two daughters. Meanwhile, the boy Samuel grew up in the presence of the LORD.

22 Now Eli was very old, and he heard about everything his sons were doing to all Israel and how they were sleeping with the women who served at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting. 23 “Why are you doing these things?” Eli said to his sons. “I hear about your wicked deeds from all these people. 24 No, my sons; it is not a good report I hear circulating among the LORD’s people. 25 If a man sins against another man, God can intercede for him; but if a man sins against the LORD, who can intercede for him?” But they would not listen to their father, since the LORD intended to put them to death. 26 And the boy Samuel continued to grow in stature and in favor with the LORD and with man.

passages.context_html:
Eli’s sons hold priestly office, but the narrator says they have no regard for the LORD. Their servants seize meat from worshipers and demand it before the fat is burned. The threat of force turns worship into an opportunity to take what they want. Their conduct expresses contempt for the LORD’s offering.

Samuel appears in deliberate contrast: he serves before the LORD while still a boy. Hannah continues to care for him, bringing a robe each year. Her dedication has not ended her relationship with him. The LORD also gives her three more sons and two daughters, while Samuel grows in His presence.

The linen ephod is a garment used in worship, not proof that Samuel has become high priest. Second Samuel 6:14 also describes David wearing a linen ephod. Samuel’s service matters here more than any claim to the highest office.

Eli hears of the abuses, including his sons sleeping with the women who serve at the entrance. He rebukes them, but they will not listen. The narrator also says that the LORD intends to put them to death. The closing sentence returns to Samuel growing in favor with God and people, setting his course beside theirs.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley both regard Eli’s response as inadequate: a verbal warning has not restrained ongoing abuses. The later accusation in verse 29 also includes Eli in benefiting from the offerings. This is a concrete failure involving his own household and authority, rather than proof that every parent causes every wrong choice an adult child makes.

On verse 25, Wesley reads the sons’ refusal as the culmination of their prolonged hardening, followed by God giving them over to judgment. Gill also understands a divine judgment that leaves them unresponsive, and retains the connection between their refusal and God’s intention to put them to death. These readings take the narrator’s explanation seriously without treating the sons as innocent people merely caught in a misunderstanding.

Gill does not read Eli’s question about who can intercede as a denial that Christ can save sinners. He distinguishes the severity of these offenses against God’s worship from the hope of mediation through Jesus. Eli’s warning should therefore be read in its immediate setting, rather than turned into a claim that no sin against God can ever be forgiven.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
The description of Samuel growing in stature and favor has a close New Testament parallel. Luke 2:40–52 describes Jesus growing, being found in the temple, and continuing in favor with God and people. Both accounts give a glimpse of a child’s life in relation to God before the work for which he will later be known.

The parallel does not make Samuel equal to Jesus or erase their different callings. It helps place Samuel’s quiet growth within the larger story of God preparing His servants. Luke’s account identifies a greater calling: Jesus speaks of His Father’s house while continuing to live obediently with His parents.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 2:27-36
passages.section_title: What happens when Eli honors his sons above God?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 27 Then a man of God came to Eli and told him, “This is what the LORD says: ‘Did I not clearly reveal Myself to your father’s house when they were in Egypt under Pharaoh’s house? 28 And out of all the tribes of Israel I selected your father to be My priest, to offer sacrifices on My altar, to burn incense, and to wear an ephod in My presence. I also gave to the house of your father all the food offerings of the Israelites. 29 Why then do you kick at My sacrifice and offering that I have prescribed for My dwelling place? You have honored your sons more than Me by fattening yourselves with the best of all the offerings of My people Israel.’ 30 Therefore, the LORD, the God of Israel, declares: ‘I did indeed say that your house and the house of your father would walk before Me forever. But now the LORD declares: Far be it from Me! For I will honor those who honor Me, but those who despise Me will be disdained. 31 Behold, the days are coming when I will cut off your strength and the strength of your father’s house, so that no one in it will reach old age. 32 You will see distress in My dwelling place. Despite all that is good in Israel, no one in your house will ever again reach old age. 33 And every one of you that I do not cut off from My altar, I will cause your eyes to fail and your heart to grieve. All your descendants will die by the sword of men. 34 And this sign shall come to you concerning your two sons Hophni and Phinehas: They will both die on the same day. 35 Then I will raise up for Myself a faithful priest. He will do whatever is in My heart and mind. And I will build for him an enduring house, and he will walk before My anointed one for all time. 36 And everyone left in your house will come and bow down to him for a piece of silver or a morsel of bread, pleading, “Please appoint me to some priestly office so that I can eat a piece of bread.”’”

Despite all that is good in Israel, no one in your house will ever again reach old age. 33 And every one of you that I do not cut off from My altar, I will cause your eyes to fail and your heart to grieve. All your descendants will die by the sword of men. 34 And this sign shall come to you concerning your two sons Hophni and Phinehas: They will both die on the same day.

And I will build for him an enduring house, and he will walk before My anointed one for all time. 36 And everyone left in your house will come and bow down to him for a piece of silver or a morsel of bread, pleading, “Please appoint me to some priestly office so that I can eat a piece of bread.”’”

passages.context_html:
An unnamed man of God brings a message to Eli. The LORD recalls the priestly family’s calling and privileges, then confronts the abuse of those gifts. Eli is accused of honoring his sons above God and joining in the benefits of the offerings they misuse. The warning reaches beyond his failure to speak firmly enough.

The message announces the loss of his family’s strength and standing. His sons Hophni and Phinehas will die on the same day as a sign. Others in his family will experience grief and need. The BSB’s wording in verse 33 describes descendants dying by the sword; the passage should not be reduced to a universal rule about the age at which every priest in the family must die.

Judgment does not leave God’s people without a future. The LORD promises a faithful priest who will carry out His will and an enduring house for him. The closing reversal is sharp: a family that took the best food will have survivors asking for enough bread to eat.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Readings differ in how they connect the promised faithful priest with later history and with Christ. Wesley identifies the priest as Zadok, who replaces Abiathar, while reading the reference to God’s anointed within the larger hope of Christ. Gill also favors Zadok as the historical referent and reports Christian readings that look through that history toward Jesus.

Henry gives the promise a direct Christian application to Jesus, the faithful high priest who perfectly does the Father’s will. These approaches share the hope of faithful service after corruption, but they give different weight to the immediate priestly succession and the fuller Christian reading. The later narrative explicitly connects Abiathar’s removal with the warning against Eli’s house (1 Kings 2:26–27, 35).

passages.god_plan_html:
The historical development is stated in 1 Kings 2:26–27, 35: Solomon removes Abiathar, the narrator calls this a fulfillment of the word against Eli’s house, and Zadok receives the office. The warning has consequences within Israel’s own priestly history.

The Christian comparison with Jesus rests on the New Testament’s account of His priesthood. Hebrews 7:23–28 describes priests whose service ends in death and contrasts them with Jesus, who lives forever, intercedes for those who approach God through Him, and has offered Himself once for all. That passage supplies the larger hope of a priest whose faithfulness and saving work endure. It does not require Eli’s immediate replacement to be skipped or confused with Jesus’ different priesthood.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 3:1-14
passages.section_title: How does Samuel learn who is calling him?

He got up, went to Eli, and said, “Here I am, for you have called me.” Then Eli realized that it was the LORD who was calling the boy. 9 “Go and lie down,” he said to Samuel, “and if He calls you, say, ‘Speak, LORD, for Your servant is listening.’” So Samuel went and lay down in his place. 10 Then the LORD came and stood there, calling as before, “Samuel! Samuel!” And Samuel answered, “Speak, for Your servant is listening.”

11 Then the LORD said to Samuel, “I am about to do something in Israel at which the ears of all who hear it will tingle. 12 On that day I will carry out against Eli everything I have spoken about his house, from beginning to end. 13 I told him that I would judge his house forever for the iniquity of which he knows, because his sons blasphemed God and he did not restrain them. 14 Therefore I have sworn to the house of Eli, ‘The iniquity of Eli’s house shall never be atoned for by sacrifice or offering.’”

passages.context_html:
Samuel continues to serve under Eli during a time when messages and visions from the LORD are rare. At night he hears his name and repeatedly runs to Eli, assuming the priest has called. Eli eventually recognizes what is happening and tells him how to answer. Samuel’s willingness to respond comes before his understanding of who is speaking.

The word translated temple is הֵיכָל, hekal (hay-KAHL), a word used for a palace or temple. Brown–Driver–Briggs specifically lists the pre-Solomon place of worship at Shiloh. This is not Solomon’s later temple in Jerusalem. The word itself does not settle exactly where Samuel’s bed stood.

Verse 7 explains that the LORD’s word had not yet been revealed to Samuel. When he finally listens, the first message is difficult: God will carry out the earlier warning against Eli’s household. Eli knew about his sons’ conduct and did not restrain them. The judgment is confirmed, and sacrifices will not turn it aside.

The account introduces Samuel as a recipient of God’s word. It does not give his exact age or describe a procedure that every person must repeat to hear a private message. The repeated calls belong to this particular encounter.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill understand Samuel’s not yet knowing the LORD as unfamiliarity with this kind of prophetic revelation. Gill explicitly distinguishes this from having no prior knowledge of God or His worship. In that reading, Samuel is learning to recognize God speaking to him in a new way.

Henry emphasizes God’s persistence in calling and Eli’s responsibility to help the younger servant respond. The chapter’s central development is Samuel receiving God’s word; identifying the exact moment when he first possessed saving faith goes beyond what these commentators understand verse 7 to establish.

Wesley reads the statement about sacrifice and offering as confirmation that the announced punishment will occur. Eli’s household cannot avoid it by continuing to offer sacrifices. The warning addresses a known course of wrongdoing and failed restraint, rather than suggesting that performing a ritual can make ongoing abuse acceptable.

passages.god_plan_html:
God making Himself known through His word is a theme that reaches beyond Samuel’s call. Hebrews 1:1–4 looks back on God speaking through the prophets and then announces His speech through the Son. Jesus reveals God and provides purification for sins.

Samuel’s calling belongs within that earlier prophetic history. Hebrews directs the larger story toward Jesus, while distinguishing Him from the prophets who came before. The connection rests on God speaking and making Himself known; it does not depend on identifying the speaker in this scene as an angel when the passage itself does not use that description.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 3:15-21
passages.section_title: Will Samuel tell Eli the whole message?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 Samuel lay down until the morning; then he opened the doors of the house of the LORD. He was afraid to tell Eli the vision, 16 but Eli called to him and said, “Samuel, my son.” “Here I am,” answered Samuel. 17 “What was the message He gave you?” Eli asked. “Do not hide it from me. May God punish you, and ever so severely, if you hide from me anything He said to you.” 18 So Samuel told him everything and did not hide a thing from him. “He is the LORD,” replied Eli. “Let Him do what is good in His eyes.” 19 And Samuel grew, and the LORD was with him, and He let none of Samuel’s words fall to the ground. 20 So all Israel from Dan to Beersheba knew that Samuel was confirmed as a prophet of the LORD. 21 And the LORD continued to appear at Shiloh, because there He revealed Himself to Samuel by His word.
paragraphs: 15 Samuel lay down until the morning; then he opened the doors of the house of the LORD. He was afraid to tell Eli the vision, 16 but Eli called to him and said, “Samuel, my son.” “Here I am,” answered Samuel. 17 “What was the message He gave you?” Eli asked. “Do not hide it from me. May God punish you, and ever so severely, if you hide from me anything He said to you.” 18 So Samuel told him everything and did not hide a thing from him. “He is the LORD,” replied Eli. “Let Him do what is good in His eyes.”

19 And Samuel grew, and the LORD was with him, and He let none of Samuel’s words fall to the ground. 20 So all Israel from Dan to Beersheba knew that Samuel was confirmed as a prophet of the LORD. 21 And the LORD continued to appear at Shiloh, because there He revealed Himself to Samuel by His word.

passages.context_html:
By morning Samuel has received a message he is afraid to deliver. He opens the doors of the LORD’s house and continues his duties. When Eli calls, Samuel answers, and Eli presses him to leave nothing out. Samuel tells him the whole message, despite the pain it concerns.

Eli acknowledges that the message comes from the LORD and places the outcome in His hands. The account records those words without describing every feeling behind them. His earlier failure to restrain his sons remains part of the reason for the judgment.

The closing verses turn from this first encounter to Samuel’s growing recognition as a prophet. The LORD is with him and does not let his words fall to the ground: the messages entrusted to him prove reliable. Israel recognizes his calling, and the LORD continues to reveal Himself at Shiloh.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads Eli’s response as humble repentance and acceptance of a just sentence. Wesley likewise sees submission to God’s rightful judgment, and Gill expressly rejects reading the reply as indifference to his family. These commentators find something faithful in Eli’s response even while recognizing the failure that brought the warning.

Other readers may hear resignation in the same brief reply. The narrator does not directly label Eli’s inward response as either repentance or indifference. His acknowledgment of the LORD and Samuel’s complete delivery of the message are the stated events; conclusions about everything Eli feels should remain distinguishable from them.

On the words not falling to the ground, Wesley and Gill focus on God making good the prophetic messages. Gill discusses a wider application to Samuel’s ordinary speech but favors the fulfillment of prophecy in this setting. The point is God establishing His messenger, rather than a claim that every casual remark Samuel ever made became a prediction.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
The New Testament names Samuel within the prophetic witness that leads toward Jesus. Acts 3:22–26 connects the prophets from Samuel onward with the days of Christ and with God’s promise that Abraham’s offspring would bring blessing beyond one family.

That larger witness also helps explain why receiving God’s word matters here. Samuel must pass on what he has actually been given, including a hard warning. Acts directs the prophetic story toward God’s Servant, who brings blessing by turning people from wickedness. The purpose reaches beyond predicting events to God’s rescue and restoration of His people.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 4:1-11
passages.section_title: Can Israel make God give them victory?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Thus the word of Samuel came to all Israel. Now the Israelites went out to meet the Philistines in battle and camped at Ebenezer, while the Philistines camped at Aphek. 2 The Philistines arrayed themselves against Israel, and as the battle spread, Israel was defeated by the Philistines, who struck down about four thousand men on the battlefield. 3 When the troops returned to the camp, the elders of Israel asked, “Why has the LORD brought defeat on us before the Philistines today? Let us bring the ark of the covenant of the LORD from Shiloh, so that it may go with us to save us from the hand of our enemies.” 4 So the people sent men to Shiloh, and they brought back the ark of the covenant of the LORD of Hosts, who sits enthroned between the cherubim. And the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were there with the ark of the covenant of God. 5 When the ark of the covenant of the LORD entered the camp, all the Israelites raised such a great shout that the ground shook. 6 On hearing the noise of the shout, the Philistines asked, “What is this loud shouting in the camp of the Hebrews?” And when they realized that the ark of the LORD had entered the camp, 7 the Philistines were afraid. “The gods have entered their camp!” they said. “Woe to us, for nothing like this has happened before. 8 Woe to us! Who will deliver us from the hand of these mighty gods? These are the gods who struck the Egyptians with all kinds of plagues in the wilderness. 9 Take courage and be men, O Philistines! Otherwise, you will serve the Hebrews just as they served you. Now be men and fight!” 10 So the Philistines fought, and Israel was defeated, and each man fled to his tent. The slaughter was very great—thirty thousand foot soldiers of Israel fell. 11 The ark of God was captured, and Eli’s two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, died.

And the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were there with the ark of the covenant of God.

5 When the ark of the covenant of the LORD entered the camp, all the Israelites raised such a great shout that the ground shook. 6 On hearing the noise of the shout, the Philistines asked, “What is this loud shouting in the camp of the Hebrews?” And when they realized that the ark of the LORD had entered the camp, 7 the Philistines were afraid. “The gods have entered their camp!” they said. “Woe to us, for nothing like this has happened before. 8 Woe to us! passages.context_html:
After the account of Samuel’s growing recognition, the story turns to war. Israel suffers a defeat in which about four thousand men die. The elders ask why the LORD has allowed this, then decide to bring the ark from Shiloh into the camp. They expect its arrival to save them.

The ark is the ark of God’s covenant, and the LORD is described as enthroned between the cherubim. Yet the elders’ proposal is their own recorded response to defeat; this scene contains no instruction from God to bring it into battle. Hophni and Phinehas accompany it, linking the coming events with the earlier warning about Eli’s sons.

Israel greets the ark with a great shout. The Philistines are frightened and remember reports of the deliverance from Egypt, though they speak of gods in the plural. Their alarm does not end the battle: they urge one another to fight rather than become servants.

The second defeat is worse. Thirty thousand Israelite foot soldiers fall, the ark is captured, and both of Eli’s sons die. Their shared day of death answers the sign announced in 1 Samuel 2:34. The ark’s presence has not guaranteed the outcome the elders expected.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley, Henry and Gill read the elders’ action as misplaced confidence in an outward sign of God’s presence while failing to face their wrongdoing. They distinguish trusting God from expecting possession of the ark to compel His help. That reading concerns the use made of the ark here; it does not require dismissing the ark’s God-given place in Israel’s worship.

The opening sentence leaves a smaller question for interpreters: does Samuel’s word include a command to fight? Wesley understands it that way. Gill discusses that possibility alongside the spread of Samuel’s teaching and prophecy. The verse states that Samuel’s word reached Israel and that Israel went to battle, without reproducing a command to launch this campaign.

The Philistines’ speech also needs to remain their speech. Wesley acknowledges that their recollection may confuse details of Israel’s history. Their fear shows that the reports of God’s power have reached them; it does not make every detail they say a fresh statement by the narrator about where the Egyptian plagues occurred.

passages.god_plan_html:
The danger of presuming on spiritual privileges also appears in 1 Corinthians 10:1–13. Paul recalls Israel’s shared deliverance, food and drink, yet warns that these gifts did not make rebellion harmless. He identifies Christ as their spiritual rock and urges his readers to heed the warning.

Paul is speaking about the wilderness generation, rather than directly explaining this battle. The shared lesson is that God’s gifts are not permission to ignore Him or a means of controlling Him. The larger story calls people to depend on His faithfulness while turning from the conduct He condemns.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 4:12-22
passages.section_title: What does the loss of the ark mean to this family?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 That same day a Benjamite ran from the battle line all the way to Shiloh, with his clothes torn and dirt on his head. 13 When he arrived, there was Eli, sitting on his chair beside the road and watching, because his heart trembled for the ark of God. When the man entered the city to give a report, the whole city cried out. 14 Eli heard the outcry and asked, “Why this commotion?” So the man hurried over and reported to Eli. 15 Now Eli was ninety-eight years old, and his gaze was fixed because he could not see. 16 “I have just come from the battle,” the man said to Eli. “I fled from there today.” “What happened, my son?” Eli asked. 17 The messenger answered, “Israel has fled before the Philistines, and there has been a great slaughter among the people. Your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, are both dead, and the ark of God has been captured.” 18 As soon as the ark of God was mentioned, Eli fell backward from his chair by the city gate, and being old and heavy, he broke his neck and died. And Eli had judged Israel forty years. 19 Now Eli’s daughter-in-law, the wife of Phinehas, was pregnant and about to give birth. When she heard the news of the capture of God’s ark and the deaths of her father-in-law and her husband, she collapsed and gave birth, for her labor pains overtook her. 20 As she was dying, the women attending to her said, “Do not be afraid, for you have given birth to a son!” But she did not respond or pay any heed. 21 And she named the boy Ichabod, saying, “The glory has departed from Israel,” because the ark of God had been captured and her father-in-law and her husband had been killed. 22 “The glory has departed from Israel,” she said, “for the ark of God has been captured.”

And Eli had judged Israel forty years.

When she heard the news of the capture of God’s ark and the deaths of her father-in-law and her husband, she collapsed and gave birth, for her labor pains overtook her. 20 As she was dying, the women attending to her said, “Do not be afraid, for you have given birth to a son!” But she did not respond or pay any heed. 21 And she named the boy Ichabod, saying, “The glory has departed from Israel,” because the ark of God had been captured and her father-in-law and her husband had been killed. 22 “The glory has departed from Israel,” she said, “for the ark of God has been captured.”

passages.context_html:
A survivor brings the news to Shiloh on the same day. His torn clothes and dirt-covered head fit the grief that follows his report. Eli is waiting anxiously for the ark, and the city cries out when the messenger arrives. At ninety-eight, Eli can no longer see and must hear what has happened.

The report moves from Israel’s defeat to the deaths of Hophni and Phinehas, then to the ark’s capture. At that final news Eli falls backward, breaks his neck and dies. The narrator says he was old and heavy and had judged Israel for forty years. The scene does not say he had been sitting on top of a wall or watching the distant fighting.

Phinehas’s wife hears the news and goes into labor. She dies after giving birth, unable to take comfort from the attendants’ announcement of a son. She names the child Ichabod, explaining the name by the departure of Israel’s glory, especially the loss of the ark. Her grief holds a national disaster and devastating family losses together.

The Hebrew for Eli being heavy is כָּבֵד, kaved (kah-VEHD); glory is כָּבוֹד, kavod (kah-VOHD). The similar sounds make a striking contrast alongside the earlier accusation that Eli honored his sons above God and shared in the rich offerings. Brown–Driver–Briggs confirms the ordinary physical meaning of heavy here, while its glory entry connects these closing verses with the ark’s capture. The comparison does not make Eli’s weight itself the definition of his guilt.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Henry read Eli’s concern for the ark as a concern for God’s honor greater even than his concern for his family. Henry does not treat his sudden death as proof of eternal condemnation. The narrative establishes the cause of his fall and his earlier failures; it does not give readers a complete account of his final spiritual state.

The name Ichabod is commonly explained in terms of lost glory. Wesley renders its force as a question about where the glory is; Gill favors the sense of no glory while acknowledging that question form. The lexicon entry also connects the name with the glory going into exile. Both approaches follow the explanation given in the passage itself.

Henry views Phinehas’s wife as grieving the loss of God’s presence in a faithful way. Other readers stress the danger of equating God’s whole presence with possession of the ark. The following story will show God still acting powerfully among the Philistines. The loss is real, but the ark’s capture does not mean Israel’s God has ceased to act.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
The grief over departed glory raises a larger biblical question: how does God make His presence known among people? John 1:14–18 describes the Word becoming flesh, dwelling among us, and revealing the Father’s glory in Jesus. Colossians 2:6–15 places the fullness of God in Christ and calls believers to remain rooted in Him.

These passages do not identify Ichabod’s naming as a direct prediction of Jesus. They show where the Christian account of God’s presence and glory leads: to the Son who makes the Father known, forgives sins, and triumphs through the cross. The answer reaches beyond holding a sacred object to knowing the God who reveals Himself.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 5:1-12
passages.section_title: Has capturing the ark defeated Israel’s God?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 After the Philistines had captured the ark of God, they took it from Ebenezer to Ashdod, 2 carried it into the temple of Dagon, and set it beside his statue. 3 When the people of Ashdod got up early the next morning, there was Dagon, fallen on his face before the ark of the LORD. So they took Dagon and returned him to his place. 4 But when they got up early the next morning, there was Dagon, fallen on his face before the ark of the LORD, with his head and his hands broken off and lying on the threshold. Only the torso remained. 5 That is why, to this day, the priests of Dagon and all who enter the temple of Dagon in Ashdod do not step on the threshold. 6 Now the hand of the LORD was heavy on the people of Ashdod and its vicinity, ravaging them and afflicting them with tumors. 7 And when the men of Ashdod saw what was happening, they said, “The ark of the God of Israel must not stay here with us, because His hand is heavy upon us and upon our god Dagon.” 8 So they called together all the rulers of the Philistines and asked, “What shall we do with the ark of the God of Israel?” “It must be moved to Gath,” they replied. So they carried away the ark of the God of Israel. 9 But after they had moved the ark to Gath, the LORD’s hand was also against that city, throwing it into great confusion and afflicting the men of the city, both young and old, with an outbreak of tumors. 10 So they sent the ark of God to Ekron, but as it arrived, the Ekronites cried out, “They have brought us the ark of the God of Israel in order to kill us and our people!” 11 Then the Ekronites called together all the rulers of the Philistines and said, “Send away the ark of the God of Israel. It must return to its place, so that it will not kill us and our people!” For a deadly confusion had pervaded the city; the hand of God was very heavy upon it. 12 Those who did not die were afflicted with tumors, and the outcry of the city went up to heaven.

passages.context_html:
The Philistines carry the captured ark to Ashdod and place it beside Dagon’s statue. The next morning the statue is facedown before the ark. Its worshipers must put it back in place. On the following morning it has fallen again, this time with its head and hands broken off. The captured ark needs no Israelite army to make the contrast visible.

The narrator connects the broken statue with a continuing practice: people entering Dagon’s temple avoid stepping on the threshold. He does not say they have abandoned the building altogether. The practice remembers the event while worship at the temple continues.

The trouble reaches beyond the statue. The LORD’s hand is described as heavy on Ashdod, then on Gath when the ark is moved there. People suffer tumors and great confusion. When it reaches Ekron, the inhabitants protest that it has been brought to kill them. The rulers are finally asked to send it back to its own place.

The chapter ends with suffering and an outcry reaching heaven. It makes the source of the disaster explicit: the hand of God is against these cities. It does not give a modern medical diagnosis, a statue’s exact height, or a detailed account of how each person dies.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley sees the ark’s placement as the display of a trophy honoring Dagon. Gill discusses both a trophy of victory and the addition of Israel’s ark alongside an existing deity. These are explanations of the Philistines’ purpose; the narrator directly states the placement and what follows without reporting their whole reasoning.

Henry reads the fallen Dagon as a picture of false worship giving way before God. He extends it into a Christian comparison with Christ overturning the idols people cherish in their hearts. That is his application across the Bible, rather than an explanation spoken by a character in the chapter. His reading also recognizes that removing one outward idol does not end the need to resist pride and selfish desire.

The older commentaries often identify the tumors more specifically as hemorrhoids. Brown–Driver–Briggs gives tumor for the written Hebrew term and discusses the alternate reading. The BSB uses tumors. The exact modern disease is not necessary to understand the account’s main point: the people cannot protect themselves merely by moving the ark from one city to another.

passages.god_plan_html:
Henry’s Christian comparison can be tested against the New Testament’s own teaching about Jesus’ victory. Colossians 2:6–15 calls believers to remain rooted in Christ, identifies the fullness of God in Him, and describes Him disarming the powers and authorities through the cross.

The shared theme is God’s victory where human appearances might suggest defeat. The Philistines have captured the ark, yet they have not made God powerless. The New Testament places the decisive saving victory in Christ’s cross, where sins are forgiven and hostile powers are overcome. This is a comparison of the two accounts, rather than a claim that the ark’s movements supply a detailed prediction of every event in Jesus’ death.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 6:1-21
passages.section_title: How does the ark return, and why does joy turn to fear?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 When the ark of the LORD had been in the land of the Philistines seven months, 2 the Philistines summoned the priests and diviners, saying, “What shall we do with the ark of the LORD? Tell us how to send it back to its place.” 3 They replied, “If you return the ark of the God of Israel, do not send it away empty, but by all means return it to Him with a guilt offering. Then you will be healed, and you will understand why His hand has not been lifted from you.” 4 “What guilt offering should we send back to Him?” asked the Philistines. “Five gold tumors and five gold rats,” they said, “according to the number of rulers of the Philistines, since the same plague has struck both you and your rulers. 5 Make images of your tumors and of the rats that are ravaging the land. Give glory to the God of Israel, and perhaps He will lift His hand from you and your gods and your land. 6 Why harden your hearts as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened theirs? When He afflicted them, did they not send the people out so they could go on their way? 7 Now, therefore, prepare one new cart with two milk cows that have never been yoked. Hitch the cows to the cart, but take their calves away and pen them up. 8 Take the ark of the LORD, set it on the cart, and in a chest beside it put the gold objects you are sending back to Him as a guilt offering. Then send the ark on its way, 9 but keep watching it. If it goes up the road to its homeland, toward Beth-shemesh, it is the LORD who has brought on us this great disaster. But if it does not, then we will know that it was not His hand that punished us and that it happened by chance.” 10 So the men did as instructed. They took two milk cows, hitched them to the cart, and penned up their calves. 11 Then they put the ark of the LORD on the cart, along with the chest containing the gold rats and the images of the tumors. 12 And the cows headed straight up the road toward Beth-shemesh, staying on that one highway and lowing as they went, never straying to the right or to the left. The rulers of the Philistines followed behind them to the border of Beth-shemesh. 13 Now the people of Beth-shemesh were harvesting wheat in the valley, and when they looked up and saw the ark, they were overjoyed at the sight. 14 The cart came to the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh and stopped there near a large rock. The people chopped up the cart and offered the cows as a burnt offering to the LORD. 15 And the Levites took down the ark of the LORD and the chest containing the gold objects, and they placed them on the large rock. That day the men of Beth-shemesh offered burnt offerings and made sacrifices to the LORD. 16 And when the five rulers of the Philistines saw this, they returned to Ekron that same day. 17 As a guilt offering to the LORD, the Philistines had sent back one gold tumor for each city: Ashdod, Gaza, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron. 18 The number of gold rats also corresponded to the number of Philistine cities belonging to the five rulers—the fortified cities and their outlying villages. And the large rock on which they placed the ark of the LORD stands to this day in the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh. 19 But God struck down some of the people of Beth-shemesh because they looked inside the ark of the LORD. He struck down seventy men, and the people mourned because the LORD had struck them with a great slaughter. 20 The men of Beth-shemesh asked, “Who can stand in the presence of the LORD, this holy God? To whom should the ark go up from here?” 21 So they sent messengers to the people of Kiriath-jearim, saying, “The Philistines have returned the ark of the LORD. Come down and take it up with you.”

And the large rock on which they placed the ark of the LORD stands to this day in the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh.

19 But God struck down some of the people of Beth-shemesh because they looked inside the ark of the LORD. He struck down seventy men, and the people mourned because the LORD had struck them with a great slaughter. 20 The men of Beth-shemesh asked, “Who can stand in the presence of the LORD, this holy God? To whom should the ark go up from here?” 21 So they sent messengers to the people of Kiriath-jearim, saying, “The Philistines have returned the ark of the LORD. Come down and take it up with you.”

passages.context_html:
After seven months, the Philistines ask their priests and diviners how to return the ark. The advisers call for a guilt offering of gold images representing the tumors and rats that have afflicted the people and land. They urge the rulers to honor Israel’s God and not repeat Pharaoh’s hardening. These are the advisers’ proposals, not instructions given by God in this scene.

The proposed test concerns the source of their suffering. Two milk cows that have never pulled under a yoke are hitched to a new cart, while their calves are kept behind. If the cows go toward Beth-shemesh, the advisers say this will identify the LORD’s hand rather than chance. The cows go straight there, lowing as they travel, with the rulers following to observe.

The people harvesting at Beth-shemesh rejoice. The cart stops in Joshua’s field by a large rock. Levites unload the ark and the gold objects; the cart becomes firewood, and the cows are offered to the LORD. The passage identifies Joshua as the field’s owner, without identifying him as the first person to see the ark or as the priest officiating.

The celebration is followed by judgment when people look inside the ark. The BSB records seventy deaths. The people mourn and ask who can stand before this holy God, then request that Kiriath-jearim receive the ark. Its return has brought genuine joy, but it has not removed the need to treat God as holy.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Henry see the cows’ journey as God directing events rather than a lucky return. Wesley emphasizes the contrast between their route and the pull of their calves at home. Henry contrasts their obedience to their Creator with the earlier failures of Eli’s sons. The account’s observed route supports the test the Philistines proposed; it does not make every detail of their theology or ritual a command for Israel.

The number in verse 19 has prompted different explanations in older commentaries. Gill discusses the larger number found in his translation but gives serious attention to seventy deaths. Henry also recognizes a difficulty in the older wording. This is a textual question, rather than a necessary difference between denominations; the passage above follows the checked BSB reading.

Wesley and Henry understand the closing request to remove the ark as an inadequate response to wrongdoing: the people need to seek peace with God rather than only distance from the object. Numbers 4:5–6, 15, 17–20 also supplies the earlier distinction between preparing the holy objects, carrying them, touching them and looking at them. The rules do not treat every Levite as a priest or permit every carrier to touch an uncovered holy object.
