section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The ark returns before the following chapter describes Israel putting away its idols. This sequence brings together God’s initiative and the need for a fitting response. A wider statement of God acting for people before they have made themselves worthy appears in Romans 5:6–11: Christ dies for sinners and brings reconciliation through His death.

The connection is a shared theme of undeserved divine action, rather than proof that every object in Joshua’s field has a hidden meaning. Hebrews 12:22–29 holds access to God through Jesus together with gratitude, reverence and a warning against refusing God’s voice. Grace and God’s holiness belong together in that larger account.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 7:1-17
passages.section_title: What changes when Israel turns back to the LORD?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then the men of Kiriath-jearim came for the ark of the LORD and took it into Abinadab’s house on the hill. And they consecrated his son Eleazar to guard the ark of the LORD. 2 And from that day a long time passed, twenty years in all, as the ark remained at Kiriath-jearim. And all the house of Israel mournfully sought the LORD. 3 Then Samuel said to all the house of Israel, “If you are returning to the LORD with all your hearts, then put away the foreign gods and Ashtoreths among you, prepare your hearts for the LORD, and serve Him only. And He will deliver you from the hand of the Philistines.” 4 So the Israelites put away the Baals and Ashtoreths and served only the LORD. 5 Then Samuel said, “Gather all Israel to Mizpah, and I will pray to the LORD on your behalf.” 6 When they had gathered at Mizpah, they drew water and poured it out before the LORD. On that day they fasted, and there they confessed, “We have sinned against the LORD.” And Samuel judged the Israelites at Mizpah. 7 When the Philistines heard that the Israelites had gathered at Mizpah, their rulers marched up toward Israel. And when the Israelites learned of this, they feared the Philistines 8 and said to Samuel, “Do not stop crying out to the LORD our God for us, that He may save us from the hand of the Philistines.” 9 Then Samuel took a suckling lamb and offered it as a whole burnt offering to the LORD. He cried out to the LORD on behalf of Israel, and the LORD answered him. 10 As the Philistines drew near to fight against Israel, Samuel was offering up the burnt offering. But that day the LORD thundered loudly against the Philistines and threw them into such confusion that they fled before Israel. 11 Then the men of Israel charged out of Mizpah and pursued the Philistines, striking them down all the way to an area below Beth-car. 12 Afterward, Samuel took a stone and set it up between Mizpah and Shen. He named it Ebenezer, saying, “Thus far the LORD has helped us.” 13 So the Philistines were subdued, and they stopped invading the territory of Israel. And the hand of the LORD was against the Philistines all the days of Samuel. 14 The cities from Ekron to Gath, which the Philistines had taken, were restored to Israel, who also delivered the surrounding territory from the hand of the Philistines. And there was peace between the Israelites and the Amorites. 15 So Samuel judged Israel all the days of his life. 16 Every year he would go on a circuit from Bethel to Gilgal to Mizpah, judging Israel in all these places. 17 Then he would return to Ramah because his home was there, and there he judged Israel and built an altar to the LORD.

passages.context_html:
The ark is taken to Abinadab’s house at Kiriath-jearim, and his son Eleazar is set apart to guard it. After twenty years, Israel is mournfully seeking the LORD. Samuel calls for a concrete response: put away foreign gods, direct their hearts to the LORD, and serve Him alone. The people remove the Baals and Ashtoreths.

At Mizpah they fast, pour out water before the LORD, and confess their sin. Samuel prays for them and acts as judge. When the Philistines approach, the people are afraid again. This time they ask Samuel to keep crying to God for rescue, rather than trying to secure victory by bringing the ark into battle.

Samuel offers a young lamb as a whole burnt offering and prays. The LORD answers with thunder that throws the Philistines into confusion. Israel pursues the fleeing army. The help comes from God, yet the text also describes the Israelites’ own action in the pursuit.

Samuel sets up a stone to remember the LORD’s help. The account describes restored territory and peace, then closes with his continuing work as judge. He travels a regular circuit and returns to Ramah, where he also builds an altar. The chapter joins a moment of deliverance with the steady work of governing and worshiping.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Henry read the return to God as more than sorrow at the loss of the ark. Removing idols and confessing sin give substance to the people’s change. They understand the poured-out water as an expression of humility and repentance. The narrator records the action beside fasting and confession without prescribing it as a ritual every later believer must perform.

Gill likewise interprets the water in terms of repentance, distinguishing it from a celebration or an ordeal in which people drink it. He and Wesley also explain that the twenty years are not necessarily the whole time the ark remains at Kiriath-jearim. The verse marks the period leading into the events narrated here.

The description of Philistine restraint is read in light of later battles under Saul. Wesley and Gill understand it especially in relation to Samuel’s period of sole leadership, rather than claiming that no Philistine force ever appears again during his lifetime. Their reading preserves both this deliverance and the later narrative.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Wesley and Henry draw a Christian comparison from Samuel’s sacrifice and intercession. Samuel stands before God on behalf of a fearful people, and the LORD answers. The comparison directs attention to the greater intercessor described in Hebrews 7:23–28.

Hebrews explains the difference as well as the connection: Jesus lives forever, continually intercedes, and has offered Himself once for all. Samuel offers a lamb and asks for rescue from a particular enemy. Jesus’ priesthood supplies enduring access to God and salvation for those who draw near through Him. The shared pattern of intercession points beyond Samuel without making this battle the whole meaning of Christian salvation.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 8:1-9
passages.section_title: Why is the request for a king a rejection of God?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 When Samuel grew old, he appointed his sons as judges over Israel. 2 The name of his firstborn son was Joel, and the name of his second was Abijah. They were judges in Beersheba. 3 But his sons did not walk in his ways; they turned aside toward dishonest gain, accepting bribes and perverting justice. 4 So all the elders of Israel gathered together and came to Samuel at Ramah. 5 “Look,” they said, “you are old, and your sons do not walk in your ways. Now appoint a king to judge us like all the other nations.” 6 But when they said, “Give us a king to judge us,” their demand was displeasing in the sight of Samuel; so he prayed to the LORD. 7 And the LORD said to Samuel, “Listen to the voice of the people in all that they say to you. For it is not you they have rejected, but they have rejected Me as their king. 8 Just as they have done from the day I brought them up out of Egypt until this day, forsaking Me and serving other gods, so they are doing to you. 9 Now listen to their voice; but you must solemnly warn them and show them the manner of the king who will reign over them.”

They were judges in Beersheba. 3 But his sons did not walk in his ways; they turned aside toward dishonest gain, accepting bribes and perverting justice. 4 So all the elders of Israel gathered together and came to Samuel at Ramah. 5 “Look,” they said, “you are old, and your sons do not walk in your ways. Now appoint a king to judge us like all the other nations.”

6 But when they said, “Give us a king to judge us,” their demand was displeasing in the sight of Samuel; so he prayed to the LORD. 7 And the LORD said to Samuel, “Listen to the voice of the people in all that they say to you. For it is not you they have rejected, but they have rejected Me as their king. 8 Just as they have done from the day I brought them up out of Egypt until this day, forsaking Me and serving other gods, so they are doing to you. 9 Now listen to their voice; but you must solemnly warn them and show them the manner of the king who will reign over them.”

passages.context_html:
As Samuel grows old, he appoints his sons Joel and Abijah as judges in Beersheba. They do not follow his example. They accept bribes, pursue dishonest gain, and twist justice. The elders therefore bring a real problem to Samuel: his sons are unfit to carry on his work.

Their proposed answer is a king who will judge them like the surrounding nations. Samuel is displeased and brings the matter to the LORD. God identifies the deeper issue as the people rejecting Him as their king, continuing a pattern of forsaking Him for other gods.

God tells Samuel to listen to their request, but also to warn them about the king’s conduct. Permission to proceed is not presented as approval of their rejection. The chapter will show the cost of the solution they are determined to receive.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill distinguish the justified concern over Samuel’s sons from the broader demand being made. Replacing corrupt judges would address that concern; choosing a king in order to be like the other nations reaches further. Henry likewise treats God’s granting the request as something that can carry judgment rather than endorsement.

Gill specifically locates the wrong in the manner, reason and timing of this request, rather than treating the existence of kingship as forbidden in every circumstance. Deuteronomy 17:14–20 had already provided for a king chosen by God who remains under His instruction. The problem here must be read alongside that provision, rather than assuming every human king is automatically a replacement for God.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The failure of leaders and the longing for just rule continue through Israel’s story. The larger biblical hope is not fulfilled merely by replacing one flawed family with another ruler. In Luke 1:30–33, Jesus is promised David’s throne and a kingdom that will not end.

This is a connection within the Bible’s royal hope, rather than a claim that this request itself directly predicts every detail of Jesus’ reign. God’s warning about rejecting Him and the later promise of His enduring king belong within the same larger story of learning where faithful rule comes from.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 8:10-18
passages.section_title: What will the king take from the people?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 So Samuel spoke all the words of the LORD to the people who were asking him for a king. 11 He said, “This will be the manner of the king who will reign over you: He will take your sons and appoint them to serve his own chariots and horses, and to run in front of his chariots. 12 He will appoint some for himself as commanders of thousands and of fifties, and others to plow his ground, to reap his harvest, and to make his weapons of war and equipment for his chariots. 13 And he will take your daughters to be perfumers, cooks, and bakers. 14 He will take the best of your fields and vineyards and olive groves and give them to his servants. 15 He will take a tenth of your grain and grape harvest and give it to his officials and servants. 16 And he will take your menservants and maidservants and your best cattle and donkeys and put them to his own use. 17 He will take a tenth of your flocks, and you yourselves will become his slaves. 18 When that day comes, you will beg for relief from the king you have chosen, but the LORD will not answer you on that day.”
paragraphs: 10 So Samuel spoke all the words of the LORD to the people who were asking him for a king. 11 He said, “This will be the manner of the king who will reign over you: He will take your sons and appoint them to serve his own chariots and horses, and to run in front of his chariots. 12 He will appoint some for himself as commanders of thousands and of fifties, and others to plow his ground, to reap his harvest, and to make his weapons of war and equipment for his chariots. 13 And he will take your daughters to be perfumers, cooks, and bakers.

14 He will take the best of your fields and vineyards and olive groves and give them to his servants. 15 He will take a tenth of your grain and grape harvest and give it to his officials and servants. 16 And he will take your menservants and maidservants and your best cattle and donkeys and put them to his own use. 17 He will take a tenth of your flocks, and you yourselves will become his slaves. 18 When that day comes, you will beg for relief from the king you have chosen, but the LORD will not answer you on that day.”

passages.context_html:
Samuel passes on the warning God has given. Its repeated action is taking: the king will take sons for military service and work, daughters for his household, productive land for his servants, and portions of the harvest and flocks. People who hope for a protector will also bear the cost of his power.

The warning moves from particular demands to the people themselves becoming his slaves. The threat is larger than an inconvenient change in administration. Their households, work and possessions will be drawn into serving the ruler they have chosen.

The final warning anticipates their later cry for relief. God says He will not answer them on that day. The words address the consequences of this choice; they should not be detached from the setting and turned into a claim that God never hears anyone who has made a wrong request.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands the warning as describing oppressive demands made for the king’s own advantage. Gill distinguishes the king’s assumed practices from a divine grant of unlimited rights. In this reading, predicting what rulers will do does not make every act of taking morally lawful.

Henry emphasizes the burden of the government the people imagine will solve their problems. He also draws a moral comparison with the harsh mastery of sinful desires. That application extends the warning; the direct subject remains the human king’s claims on Israel’s families, labor and property.

These readings fit the restraint required of the king in Deuteronomy 17:16–20: he must not accumulate power and wealth without limit or consider himself above his fellow Israelites. Samuel’s warning and that instruction should be considered together.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
The ruler who keeps taking provides a strong contrast with Jesus’ account of His own mission. In Mark 10:42–45, Jesus describes rulers who dominate others and tells His disciples to pursue service instead. He gives His own life as a ransom for many.

This is a comparison between ways of exercising authority. Samuel warns of people being used to sustain a ruler; Jesus gives Himself for the people He serves. The New Testament directs the hope of faithful leadership toward His self-giving work, while also shaping the conduct of those who follow Him.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 8:19-22
passages.section_title: Will the people listen to the warning?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 Nevertheless, the people refused to listen to Samuel. “No!” they said. “We must have a king over us. 20 Then we will be like all the other nations, with a king to judge us, to go out before us, and to fight our battles.” 21 Samuel listened to all the words of the people and repeated them in the hearing of the LORD. 22 “Listen to their voice,” the LORD said to Samuel. “Appoint a king for them.” Then Samuel told the men of Israel, “Everyone must go back to his city.”
paragraphs: 19 Nevertheless, the people refused to listen to Samuel. “No!” they said. “We must have a king over us. 20 Then we will be like all the other nations, with a king to judge us, to go out before us, and to fight our battles.” 21 Samuel listened to all the words of the people and repeated them in the hearing of the LORD. 22 “Listen to their voice,” the LORD said to Samuel. “Appoint a king for them.” Then Samuel told the men of Israel, “Everyone must go back to his city.”

passages.context_html:
The warning does not change the people’s answer. They insist on having a king so they can be like the nations, with someone to judge them, lead them and fight their battles. Their desired outcome remains more compelling to them than Samuel’s explanation of its cost.

Samuel repeats their words before the LORD. God again tells him to listen and appoint a king. Samuel then sends the people home. The chapter ends with the request granted in principle, while the choice and appointment of the ruler still lie ahead.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley emphasizes the irony of seeking a military protector after God has just rescued Israel in response to prayer. Henry stresses their refusal to reconsider and the long consequences that can follow an insistent demand.

Both readings distinguish receiving a request from being right to make it. The command to appoint a king stands alongside God’s earlier description of rejection and Samuel’s warning. The text does not invite readers to erase either side of that account.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 9:1-27
passages.section_title: How does a search for donkeys lead Saul to Samuel?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now there was a Benjamite, a powerful man, whose name was Kish son of Abiel, the son of Zeror, the son of Becorath, the son of Aphiah of Benjamin. 2 And he had a son named Saul, choice and handsome, without equal among the Israelites—a head taller than any of the people. 3 One day the donkeys of Saul’s father Kish wandered off, and Kish said to his son Saul, “Take one of the servants and go look for the donkeys.” 4 So Saul passed through the hill country of Ephraim and then through the land of Shalishah, but they did not find the donkeys. He and the servant went through the region of Shaalim, but they were not there. Then they went through the land of Benjamin, and still they did not find them. 5 When they reached the land of Zuph, Saul said to his servant, “Come, let us go back, or my father will stop worrying about the donkeys and start worrying about us.” 6 “Look,” said the servant, “in this city there is a man of God who is highly respected; everything he says surely comes to pass. Let us go there now. Perhaps he will tell us which way to go.” 7 “If we do go,” Saul replied, “what can we give the man? For the bread in our packs is gone, and there is no gift to take to the man of God. What do we have?” 8 The servant answered him again. “Look,” he said, “I have here in my hand a quarter shekel of silver. I will give it to the man of God, and he will tell us our way.” 9 (Formerly in Israel, a man on his way to inquire of God would say, “Come, let us go to the seer.” For the prophet of today was formerly called the seer.) 10 “Good,” said Saul to his servant. “Come, let us go.” So they set out for the city where the man of God was. 11 And as they were climbing the hill to the city, they met some young women coming out to draw water and asked, “Is the seer here?” 12 “Yes, he is ahead of you,” they answered. “Hurry now, for today he has come to the city because the people have a sacrifice on the high place. 13 As soon as you enter the city, you will find him before he goes up to the high place to eat. The people will not eat until he comes, because he must bless the sacrifice; after that, the guests will eat. Go up at once; you will find him.” 14 So Saul and his servant went up toward the city, and as they were entering it, there was Samuel coming toward them on his way up to the high place. 15 Now on the day before Saul’s arrival, the LORD had revealed to Samuel, 16 “At this time tomorrow I will send you a man from the land of Benjamin, and you are to anoint him ruler over My people Israel; he will save them from the hand of the Philistines. For I have looked upon My people, because their cry has come to Me.” 17 When Samuel saw Saul, the LORD told him, “Here is the man of whom I spoke; he shall rule over My people.” 18 Saul approached Samuel in the gateway and asked, “Would you please tell me where the seer’s house is?” 19 “I am the seer,” Samuel replied. “Go up before me to the high place, for you shall eat with me today. And when I send you off in the morning, I will tell you all that is in your heart. 20 As for the donkeys you lost three days ago, do not worry about them, for they have been found. And upon whom is all the desire of Israel, if not upon you and all your father’s house?” 21 Saul replied, “Am I not a Benjamite from the smallest tribe of Israel, and is not my clan the least of all the clans of Benjamin? So why would you say such a thing to me?” 22 Then Samuel took Saul and his servant, brought them into the hall, and seated them in the place of honor among those who were invited—about thirty in all. 23 And Samuel said to the cook, “Bring the portion I gave you and told you to set aside.” 24 So the cook picked up the leg and what was attached to it and set it before Saul. Then Samuel said, “Here is what was kept back. It was set apart for you. Eat, for it has been kept for you for this occasion, from the time I said, ‘I have invited the people.’” So Saul dined with Samuel that day. 25 And after they had come down from the high place into the city, Samuel spoke with Saul on the roof of his house. 26 They got up early in the morning, and just before dawn Samuel called to Saul on the roof, “Get ready, and I will send you on your way!” So Saul got ready, and both he and Samuel went outside together. 27 As they were going down to the edge of the city, Samuel said to Saul, “Tell the servant to go on ahead of us, but you stay for a while, and I will reveal to you the word of God.” So the servant went on.

For I have looked upon My people, because their cry has come to Me.” 17 When Samuel saw Saul, the LORD told him, “Here is the man of whom I spoke; he shall rule over My people.”

18 Saul approached Samuel in the gateway and asked, “Would you please tell me where the seer’s house is?” 19 “I am the seer,” Samuel replied. “Go up before me to the high place, for you shall eat with me today. And when I send you off in the morning, I will tell you all that is in your heart. 20 As for the donkeys you lost three days ago, do not worry about them, for they have been found. And upon whom is all the desire of Israel, if not upon you and all your father’s house?” 21 Saul replied, “Am I not a Benjamite from the smallest tribe of Israel, and is not my clan the least of all the clans of Benjamin? So why would you say such a thing to me?” 22 Then Samuel took Saul and his servant, brought them into the hall, and seated them in the place of honor among those who were invited—about thirty in all. 23 And Samuel said to the cook, “Bring the portion I gave you and told you to set aside.” 24 So the cook picked up the leg and what was attached to it and set it before Saul. Then Samuel said, “Here is what was kept back. It was set apart for you. Eat, for it has been kept for you for this occasion, from the time I said, ‘I have invited the people.’” So Saul dined with Samuel that day.

25 And after they had come down from the high place into the city, Samuel spoke with Saul on the roof of his house. 26 They got up early in the morning, and just before dawn Samuel called to Saul on the roof, “Get ready, and I will send you on your way!” So Saul got ready, and both he and Samuel went outside together. 27 As they were going down to the edge of the city, Samuel said to Saul, “Tell the servant to go on ahead of us, but you stay for a while, and I will reveal to you the word of God.” So the servant went on.

passages.context_html:
Saul is introduced as the son of Kish, a powerful Benjamite. He is strikingly handsome and taller than the other Israelites. His first task in the story is ordinary: his father sends him with a servant to find missing donkeys. After an unsuccessful search, Saul worries that his father will begin worrying about them instead.

The servant suggests consulting a respected man of God in a nearby city and offers a quarter shekel of silver as a gift. Young women drawing water direct them toward Samuel. Their practical decisions bring them to him at the moment he is going to a sacrificial meal.

The title seer does not mean Samuel is a false fortune-teller. Verse 9 explains it as the earlier name for a prophet, and Samuel uses the title for himself in verse 19. The Hebrew רֹאֶה, ro’eh (roh-EH), is identified by Brown–Driver–Briggs as this older prophetic title, including these references to Samuel.

Before Saul arrives, God has already told Samuel to expect him and anoint him ruler. God gives a reason that matters after the previous chapter’s rebuke: He has seen His people and heard their cry. Samuel recognizes Saul, reassures him that the donkeys have been found, and honors him with a place and portion at the meal.

Saul questions how such attention fits his small tribe and family. After the meal he speaks privately with Samuel. The next morning, Samuel sends the servant ahead so Saul can hear God’s word. The chapter prepares for the appointment without yet narrating the anointing.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads Saul’s willingness to search for his father’s animals as commendable obedience. He and Wesley understand the proposed gift as respect for Samuel’s office, rather than proof that genuine prophecy can be bought. The narrator records the proposed gift without saying Samuel demands payment before helping.

The larger movement of events is commonly read as providence: God directing circumstances toward a purpose Saul has not yet understood. Henry emphasizes that God hears Israel’s cry even after granting their request in displeasure. Wesley likewise takes the promised rescue from the Philistines seriously. Saul’s later failures should not be read backward as if this chapter contains no genuine mercy or calling.

Henry also notices Samuel’s willingness to honor the incoming ruler instead of responding with envy. What Samuel and Saul discuss on the roof is not quoted. The setting permits a private conversation, but its full words and Saul’s unspoken reactions remain outside the narrated account.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
God’s purpose is active while Saul is occupied with a smaller problem. More significantly, God hears a people whose request He has just rebuked. The passage holds their need and His mercy together without declaring their rejection good.

A fuller statement of divine mercy toward undeserving people appears in Romans 5:6–11. Christ dies for sinners and reconciles enemies to God. Saul’s appointment is a limited historical rescue, not the final saving work of Jesus. The shared theme is God acting for people who have not first made themselves worthy of His care.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 10:1-8
passages.section_title: How will Saul know that God has called him?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then Samuel took a flask of oil, poured it on Saul’s head, kissed him, and said, “Has not the LORD anointed you ruler over His inheritance? 2 When you leave me today, you will find two men at Rachel’s tomb in Zelzah on the border of Benjamin. They will say to you, ‘The donkeys you seek have been found, and now your father has stopped worrying about the donkeys and started worrying about you, asking, “What should I do about my son?”’ 3 Then you will go on from there until you come to the Oak of Tabor. Three men going up to God at Bethel will meet you there, one carrying three young goats, another carrying three loaves of bread, and another carrying a skin of wine. 4 They will greet you and give you two loaves of bread, which you will accept from their hands. 5 After that you will come to Gibeah of God, where the Philistines have an outpost. As you approach the city, you will meet a group of prophets coming down from the high place, preceded by harps, tambourines, flutes, and lyres, and they will be prophesying. 6 Then the Spirit of the LORD will rush upon you, and you will prophesy with them; and you will be transformed into a different person. 7 When these signs have come, do as the occasion demands, for God is with you. 8 And you shall go before me to Gilgal, and surely I will come to you to offer burnt offerings and to sacrifice peace offerings. Wait seven days until I come to you and show you what you are to do.”

They will say to you, ‘The donkeys you seek have been found, and now your father has stopped worrying about the donkeys and started worrying about you, asking, “What should I do about my son?”’ 3 Then you will go on from there until you come to the Oak of Tabor. Three men going up to God at Bethel will meet you there, one carrying three young goats, another carrying three loaves of bread, and another carrying a skin of wine. 4 They will greet you and give you two loaves of bread, which you will accept from their hands.

5 After that you will come to Gibeah of God, where the Philistines have an outpost. As you approach the city, you will meet a group of prophets coming down from the high place, preceded by harps, tambourines, flutes, and lyres, and they will be prophesying. 6 Then the Spirit of the LORD will rush upon you, and you will prophesy with them; and you will be transformed into a different person. 7 When these signs have come, do as the occasion demands, for God is with you. 8 And you shall go before me to Gilgal, and surely I will come to you to offer burnt offerings and to sacrifice peace offerings. Wait seven days until I come to you and show you what you are to do.”

passages.context_html:
In private, Samuel pours oil on Saul’s head, kisses him, and announces that the LORD has anointed him ruler over His inheritance. Israel still belongs to God. Saul is being appointed to a responsibility over God’s people, rather than receiving them as possessions to use however he wishes.

Samuel then describes three encounters. Two men will report that the donkeys are found and Saul’s father is worried about him. Three men on their way to worship at Bethel will give him bread. A group of prophets will meet him at Gibeah, and the Spirit of the LORD will come upon him so that he prophesies with them.

These signs will confirm the message and God’s presence with him. They are accompanied by an instruction to wait at Gilgal for Samuel to come and show him what to do. Being equipped for kingship does not remove the need to listen and obey.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Henry understand the anointing as a sign of God equipping Saul for his office. Wesley also emphasizes that the people remain God’s inheritance: the appointment is a responsibility under God’s will. The signs give Saul confirmation rather than permission to treat kingship as unrestricted personal power.

The encounters have also prompted devotional comparisons. Wesley and Henry take Rachel’s tomb as a reminder of mortality even while Saul is receiving royal honor. That is a lesson they draw from the setting; Samuel’s explicit words in this scene concern the messengers, the donkeys and Saul’s father. Any further meaning should remain distinguishable from the stated sign.

Wesley understands the prophesying here as potentially including Spirit-prompted praise and speech about God, rather than only predictions of future events. The accompanying instruments and group setting belong to the description, while the exact words Saul will speak are not given.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
The anointing and the Spirit’s enabling lead Wesley and Henry to a larger Christian comparison with Jesus, the anointed one. That connection has a direct New Testament anchor in Luke 4:16–21. Jesus reads Isaiah’s announcement of the Spirit’s anointing for good news and release, and says it is fulfilled in their hearing.

Saul is equipped for a particular task in Israel’s history. Jesus announces a mission of rescue reaching the poor, captives and oppressed. The connection is the pattern of anointing and divine appointment; it does not make Saul’s whole life an example of Jesus’ faithfulness or turn each item carried by the travelers into a hidden prediction.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 10:9-16
passages.section_title: What changes in Saul when the signs come true?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 As Saul turned to leave Samuel, God changed Saul’s heart, and all the signs came to pass that day. 10 When Saul and his servant arrived at Gibeah, a group of prophets met him. Then the Spirit of God rushed upon him, and he prophesied along with them. 11 When all those who had formerly known Saul saw him prophesying with the prophets, they asked one another, “What has happened to the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?” 12 Then a man who lived there replied, “And who is their father?” So the saying became a proverb: “Is Saul also among the prophets?” 13 And when Saul had finished prophesying, he went up to the high place. 14 Now Saul’s uncle asked him and his servant, “Where did you go?” “To look for the donkeys,” Saul replied. “When we saw they were not to be found, we went to Samuel.” 15 “Tell me,” Saul’s uncle asked, “what did Samuel say to you?” 16 And Saul replied, “He assured us that the donkeys had been found.” But Saul did not tell his uncle what Samuel had said about the kingship.
paragraphs: 9 As Saul turned to leave Samuel, God changed Saul’s heart, and all the signs came to pass that day. 10 When Saul and his servant arrived at Gibeah, a group of prophets met him. Then the Spirit of God rushed upon him, and he prophesied along with them. 11 When all those who had formerly known Saul saw him prophesying with the prophets, they asked one another, “What has happened to the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?” 12 Then a man who lived there replied, “And who is their father?” So the saying became a proverb: “Is Saul also among the prophets?” 13 And when Saul had finished prophesying, he went up to the high place.

14 Now Saul’s uncle asked him and his servant, “Where did you go?” “To look for the donkeys,” Saul replied. “When we saw they were not to be found, we went to Samuel.” 15 “Tell me,” Saul’s uncle asked, “what did Samuel say to you?” 16 And Saul replied, “He assured us that the donkeys had been found.” But Saul did not tell his uncle what Samuel had said about the kingship.

passages.context_html:
As Saul leaves Samuel, God changes his heart, and the announced signs take place that day. The account then describes the most public sign: the Spirit of God comes upon him, and he prophesies with the group at Gibeah. People who know him are surprised to see this.

Their question about Saul being among the prophets becomes a proverb. The episode presents something unexpected in a familiar person and credits God with the change. It does not quote the contents of his prophesying or describe the age, dress or appearance of the other prophets.

When Saul’s uncle asks about the journey, Saul reports that Samuel assured him the donkeys had been found. He does not disclose what Samuel said about kingship. The narrator marks that silence, leaving his full reasons unstated.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The significance of the changed heart is an important interpretive question. Wesley explains the change in terms of courage, wisdom and other qualities suited to Saul’s new office. Gill explicitly understands it as preparation for governing, rather than the new heart of conversion.

Henry also cautions against assuming that this surprising religious experience settles Saul’s lasting spiritual condition. His reading distinguishes becoming different in this situation from being made new in the fullest spiritual sense. The text itself states that God changes Saul and empowers his prophesying; conclusions about his final standing before God require a wider interpretation of his story.

On Saul’s silence to his uncle, Wesley sees modesty and a commitment to keeping the matter private. That is an explanation of the omission, rather than an inward motive directly reported by Saul. The scene does not require either immediate condemnation of deceit or a complete verdict on his humility.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 10:17-27
passages.section_title: How does Saul’s private calling become a public appointment?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 After this, Samuel summoned the people to the LORD at Mizpah 18 and said to the Israelites, “This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘I brought Israel up out of Egypt, and I rescued you from the hands of the Egyptians and of all the kingdoms that oppressed you.’ 19 But today you have rejected your God, who saves you from all your troubles and afflictions, and you have said to Him, ‘No, set a king over us.’ Now therefore present yourselves before the LORD by your tribes and clans.” 20 Thus Samuel had all the tribes of Israel come forward, and the tribe of Benjamin was selected. 21 Then he had the tribe of Benjamin come forward by its clans, and the clan of Matri was selected. Finally, Saul son of Kish was selected. But when they looked for him, they could not find him. 22 So again they inquired of the LORD, “Has the man come here yet?” And the LORD replied, “Behold, he has hidden himself among the baggage.” 23 So they ran and brought Saul, and when he stood among the people, he was a head taller than any of the others. 24 Samuel said to all the people, “Do you see the one the LORD has chosen? There is no one like him among all the people.” And all the people shouted, “Long live the king!” 25 Then Samuel explained to the people the rights of kingship. He wrote them on a scroll and laid it up before the LORD. And Samuel sent all the people away, each to his own home. 26 Saul also went to his home in Gibeah, and the men of valor whose hearts God had touched went with him. 27 But some worthless men said, “How can this man save us?” So they despised him and brought him no gifts; but Saul remained silent about it.

20 Thus Samuel had all the tribes of Israel come forward, and the tribe of Benjamin was selected. 21 Then he had the tribe of Benjamin come forward by its clans, and the clan of Matri was selected. Finally, Saul son of Kish was selected. But when they looked for him, they could not find him. 22 So again they inquired of the LORD, “Has the man come here yet?” And the LORD replied, “Behold, he has hidden himself among the baggage.” 23 So they ran and brought Saul, and when he stood among the people, he was a head taller than any of the others. 24 Samuel said to all the people, “Do you see the one the LORD has chosen? There is no one like him among all the people.” And all the people shouted, “Long live the king!”

25 Then Samuel explained to the people the rights of kingship. He wrote them on a scroll and laid it up before the LORD. And Samuel sent all the people away, each to his own home. 26 Saul also went to his home in Gibeah, and the men of valor whose hearts God had touched went with him. 27 But some worthless men said, “How can this man save us?” So they despised him and brought him no gifts; but Saul remained silent about it.

passages.context_html:
Samuel gathers Israel at Mizpah and first recalls God’s rescue of His people. The appointment does not erase the rebuke: in demanding a king, they have rejected the God who saves them from their troubles. Both the warning and the selection remain part of this public event.

The selection narrows from Benjamin to the clan of Matri, then to Saul. When he cannot be found, the people inquire of the LORD and learn that he is hiding among the baggage. They bring him forward, Samuel identifies him as the LORD’s chosen man, and the people acclaim him as king.

Samuel explains the rights of kingship, writes them on a scroll, and places it before the LORD. The exact document is not reproduced here. The scene presents an ordered appointment with stated responsibilities, rather than merely a celebration of Saul’s imposing height.

Saul returns to Gibeah with men whose hearts God has moved to support him. Others despise him and question whether he can save them. Saul remains silent. His public appointment therefore begins with support and resistance side by side.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands the public selection as confirmation of God’s choice that should prevent disputes about Samuel choosing for himself. He reads Saul’s hiding as a sense of unworthiness. Henry also sees reluctance to assume power, while noting that awareness of inadequacy can go too far when someone has been called to a task.

On the written rights of kingship, Wesley connects the rules with the restraints in Deuteronomy 17. Gill discusses the view that Samuel is repeating the abuses warned of in chapter 8, but prefers a distinction: this concerns how the kingdom is to be governed and the duties involved. The document’s full contents are not available in this passage, so these explanations should not be treated as a recovered transcript.

Henry makes a Christian comparison between the different responses to Saul and the different responses to Jesus. Wesley also compares Saul’s restraint with Christ’s silence under opposition. These applications concern particular features of the scene, not a claim that every later act of Saul resembles Christ.

passages.god_plan_html:
Henry’s comparison can be considered alongside John 1:10–13, which describes the world failing to recognize the Word and some receiving Him through faith. The shared theme is a division in response to one whom God has sent; the New Testament makes claims about Jesus that go far beyond Saul’s appointment.

Philippians 2:5–11 directs the larger royal hope toward Jesus’ obedience, death and exaltation, ending with every knee bowing and every tongue confessing Him as Lord. Saul receives a disputed beginning to an earthly reign. Jesus’ final honor rests on the saving path of humble obedience described in that passage.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 11:1-11
passages.section_title: Who will rescue Jabesh-gilead from Nahash?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then Nahash the Ammonite came up and laid siege to Jabesh-gilead. All the men of Jabesh said to him, “Make a treaty with us, and we will serve you.” 2 But Nahash the Ammonite replied, “I will make a treaty with you on one condition, that I may put out everyone’s right eye and bring reproach upon all Israel.” 3 “Hold off for seven days,” replied the elders of Jabesh, “and let us send messengers throughout Israel. If there is no one to save us, we will surrender to you.” 4 When the messengers came to Gibeah of Saul and relayed these words in the hearing of the people, they all wept aloud. 5 Just then Saul was returning from the field, behind his oxen. “What troubles the people?” asked Saul. “Why are they weeping?” And they relayed to him the words of the men from Jabesh. 6 When Saul heard their words, the Spirit of God rushed upon him, and he burned with great anger. 7 He took a pair of oxen, cut them into pieces, and sent them by messengers throughout the land of Israel, proclaiming, “This is what will be done to the oxen of anyone who does not march behind Saul and Samuel.” Then the terror of the LORD fell upon the people, and they came out together as one man. 8 And when Saul numbered them at Bezek, there were 300,000 Israelites and 30,000 men of Judah. 9 So they said to the messengers who had come, “Tell the men of Jabesh-gilead: ‘Deliverance will be yours tomorrow by the time the sun is hot.’” And when the messengers relayed this to the men of Jabesh, they rejoiced. 10 Then the men of Jabesh said to Nahash, “Tomorrow we will come out, and you can do with us whatever seems good to you.” 11 The next day Saul organized the troops into three divisions, and during the morning watch they invaded the camp of the Ammonites and slaughtered them, until the hottest part of the day. And the survivors were so scattered that no two of them were left together.

6 When Saul heard their words, the Spirit of God rushed upon him, and he burned with great anger. 7 He took a pair of oxen, cut them into pieces, and sent them by messengers throughout the land of Israel, proclaiming, “This is what will be done to the oxen of anyone who does not march behind Saul and Samuel.” Then the terror of the LORD fell upon the people, and they came out together as one man. 8 And when Saul numbered them at Bezek, there were 300,000 Israelites and 30,000 men of Judah. 9 So they said to the messengers who had come, “Tell the men of Jabesh-gilead: ‘Deliverance will be yours tomorrow by the time the sun is hot.’” And when the messengers relayed this to the men of Jabesh, they rejoiced.

And the survivors were so scattered that no two of them were left together.

passages.context_html:
Nahash the Ammonite besieges Jabesh-gilead. The men offer to serve him under a treaty, but he demands the loss of everyone’s right eye as a humiliation of all Israel. The elders obtain seven days to seek help. If no rescuer comes, they will surrender.

The report reaches Gibeah and causes public weeping. Saul is returning from the field when he hears it. The Spirit of God comes upon him, and he burns with anger. He cuts up a pair of oxen and sends the pieces with a summons: anyone refusing to follow Saul and Samuel will face the same loss of his own oxen.

The narrator connects the people’s united response with the terror of the LORD falling on them. A force of 300,000 Israelites and 30,000 men of Judah gathers. The threatened city receives the promise of deliverance by the next day’s heat and rejoices.

Saul divides the troops into three groups and attacks during the morning watch. The Ammonites are defeated and scattered. His private anointing and public appointment are now followed by action on behalf of people facing a cruel enemy.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads the rescue as the first fruit of Saul’s rule and emphasizes the courage and readiness that accompany the Spirit’s work. Wesley sees Saul joining Samuel’s name to the summons as reinforcing its authority. Both readings credit God’s enabling while recognizing Saul’s active response.

Wesley understands the threatened mutilation as both humiliation and a means of weakening the people. The explicit reason Nahash gives is reproach upon Israel. The passage does not explain every military effect of losing an eye or establish that this was a universal practice in ancient warfare.

The unity of the response is central to the scene. It contrasts with the fear and helplessness of the opening report. The narrative gives the troop numbers and the outcome without requiring a separate symbolic meaning for each number.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
The Spirit’s enabling is directed toward rescuing threatened people, rather than merely enhancing the king’s reputation. This belongs to the Bible’s wider theme of God appointing a deliverer for those in need. In Luke 4:16–21, Jesus announces the Spirit’s anointing for good news, liberty and release.

The comparison concerns divine appointment serving a rescuing purpose. Saul’s battle is a particular event in Israel’s history; Jesus’ saving mission is greater and is not reduced to military victory. The connection should not turn this campaign into a standing instruction for Christians to repeat Saul’s methods.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 11:12-15
passages.section_title: Will Saul use the victory to kill his opponents?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 Then the people said to Samuel, “Who said that Saul should not reign over us? Bring those men here so we can kill them!” 13 But Saul ordered, “No one shall be put to death this day, for today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel.” 14 Then Samuel said to the people, “Come, let us go to Gilgal and renew the kingship there.” 15 So all the people went to Gilgal and confirmed Saul as king in the presence of the LORD. There they sacrificed peace offerings before the LORD, and Saul and all the Israelites rejoiced greatly.
paragraphs: 12 Then the people said to Samuel, “Who said that Saul should not reign over us? Bring those men here so we can kill them!” 13 But Saul ordered, “No one shall be put to death this day, for today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel.” 14 Then Samuel said to the people, “Come, let us go to Gilgal and renew the kingship there.” 15 So all the people went to Gilgal and confirmed Saul as king in the presence of the LORD. There they sacrificed peace offerings before the LORD, and Saul and all the Israelites rejoiced greatly.

passages.context_html:
After the rescue, the people ask Samuel to produce those who had opposed Saul’s kingship so they can be killed. Saul stops them. He credits the LORD with saving Israel and says no one is to be put to death that day.

Samuel then calls the people to Gilgal to renew the kingship. They confirm Saul as king before the LORD, offer peace sacrifices, and rejoice. The renewal joins recognition of the king with worship of the God Saul has credited for the deliverance.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry sees the benefit of former enemies becoming friends rather than being killed. Gill also recognizes both mercy and prudence in Saul’s restraint, emphasizing that he credits God’s power and goodness rather than his own skill.

Wesley reads the Gilgal gathering as confirmation of the earlier choice, now following Saul’s demonstrated ability to help his people. The text names Samuel as the one who proposes it. It does not describe every dissenter’s attendance, a private bargain for support, or Saul’s entire plan for consolidating power.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Henry extends the scene into a Christian comparison: a formerly despised ruler can receive those who had resisted him. That comparison can be grounded in Romans 5:6–11, where God’s saving mercy reaches sinners and reconciliation reaches His enemies through Christ.

The difference matters. Saul spares opponents after a military rescue; Christ gives His own life to reconcile enemies to God. The shared theme is mercy toward those who have stood in opposition. The Christian hope rests in Jesus’ saving work, rather than in assuming every political opponent of an earthly ruler is God’s enemy.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 12:1-25
passages.section_title: Does having a king change Israel’s responsibility to God?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then Samuel said to all Israel, “I have listened to your voice in all that you have said to me, and I have set over you a king. 2 Now here is the king walking before you, and I am old and gray, and my sons are here with you. I have walked before you from my youth until this day. 3 Here I am. Bear witness against me before the LORD and before His anointed: Whose ox or donkey have I taken? Whom have I cheated or oppressed? From whose hand have I accepted a bribe and closed my eyes? Tell me, and I will restore it to you.” 4 “You have not cheated us or oppressed us,” they replied, “nor have you taken anything from the hand of man.” 5 Samuel said to them, “The LORD is a witness against you, and His anointed is a witness today, that you have not found anything in my hand.” “He is a witness,” they replied. 6 Then Samuel said to the people, “The LORD is the One who appointed Moses and Aaron, and who brought your fathers up out of the land of Egypt. 7 Now present yourselves, so that I may confront you before the LORD with all the righteous acts He has done for you and your fathers. 8 When Jacob went to Egypt, your fathers cried out to the LORD, and He sent them Moses and Aaron, who brought your fathers out of Egypt and settled them in this place. 9 But they forgot the LORD their God, and He sold them into the hand of Sisera the commander of the army of Hazor, and into the hands of the Philistines and the king of Moab, who fought against them. 10 Then they cried out to the LORD and said, ‘We have sinned, for we have forsaken the LORD and served the Baals and Ashtoreths. Now deliver us from the hands of our enemies, that we may serve You.’ 11 So the LORD sent Jerubbaal, Barak, Jephthah, and Samuel, and He delivered you from the hands of your enemies on every side, and you dwelt securely. 12 But when you saw that Nahash king of the Ammonites was moving against you, you said to me, ‘No, we must have a king to rule over us’—even though the LORD your God was your king. 13 Now here is the king you have chosen, the one you requested. Behold, the LORD has placed a king over you. 14 If you fear the LORD and serve Him and obey His voice, and if you do not rebel against the command of the LORD, and if both you and the king who rules over you follow the LORD your God, then all will be well. 15 But if you disobey the LORD and rebel against His command, then the hand of the LORD will be against you as it was against your fathers. 16 Now, therefore, present yourselves and see this great thing that the LORD will do before your eyes. 17 Is it not the wheat harvest today? I will call on the LORD to send thunder and rain, so that you will know and see what a great evil you have committed in the sight of the LORD by asking for a king.” 18 So Samuel called to the LORD, and on that day the LORD sent thunder and rain. As a result, all the people greatly feared the LORD and Samuel. 19 They pleaded with Samuel, “Pray to the LORD your God for your servants so that we will not die! For we have added to all our sins the evil of asking for a king.” 20 “Do not be afraid,” Samuel replied. “Even though you have committed all this evil, do not turn aside from following the LORD, but serve the LORD with all your heart. 21 Do not turn aside after worthless things that cannot profit you or deliver you, for they are empty. 22 Indeed, for the sake of His great name, the LORD will not abandon His people, because He was pleased to make you His own. 23 As for me, far be it from me that I should sin against the LORD by ceasing to pray for you. And I will continue to teach you the good and right way. 24 Above all, fear the LORD and serve Him faithfully with all your heart; consider what great things He has done for you. 25 But if you persist in doing evil, both you and your king will be swept away.”

passages.context_html:
Samuel addresses Israel with its king now in place. He first invites testimony about his own service: has he cheated, oppressed or taken a bribe? The people say he has not. This distinguishes his conduct from the corrupt judging described earlier and establishes the setting for his warning.

He then recalls the LORD’s acts of rescue, from Egypt through the judges. The pattern has included Israel forgetting God, suffering oppression, confessing sin, and receiving deliverance. Their latest demand for a king is set against that history: the LORD was already their king.

The new arrangement does not release either the people or the ruler from obedience. Samuel places both under the call to fear God, serve Him and listen to His voice. He then asks for thunder and rain during the wheat harvest as a public sign of the evil involved in their request. The sign comes, and the people confess and ask for prayer.

Samuel does not tell them that their wrongdoing has made return pointless. They must keep following the LORD, rather than turn to things that cannot save. God will not abandon His people for the sake of His name. Samuel will continue to pray for them and teach them, while urging them to remember God’s great deeds and warning against continued evil.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads Samuel’s public accounting as both a defense against unjust blame and an example for Saul. Wesley likewise understands it as clearing the way to address the people’s responsibility. The testimony concerns Samuel’s treatment of them; it is not a claim that he is without any sin of any kind.

Readers must hold the assurance of verse 22 together with the warning of verse 25. Wesley emphasizes God’s undeserved mercy while retaining the seriousness of people thrusting Him away. Gill stresses that the people were chosen by God’s free favor and that their preservation rests on that same favor. These commentators give different emphasis to human rejection and God’s keeping, while both recognize that Israel’s standing is not earned by merit.

Henry emphasizes Samuel doing more than the people request: he will teach as well as pray. Gill also sees these as continuing responsibilities even with a king in place. Samuel’s change in public role does not mean his service to the people or his duty before God has ended.

passages.god_plan_html:
The promise not to abandon His people rests on God’s name and choice, while the warning calls for a faithful response. A related question appears in Romans 11:1–6: has God rejected His people? Paul answers no, identifies himself as an Israelite, and points to a remnant chosen by grace.

Paul’s discussion is not an explicit quotation of Samuel’s speech, and these verses do not settle every question about later history. They do carry forward the theme of God’s faithfulness amid real human failure. Samuel’s assurance and warning should both remain audible: wrongdoing is no reason to give up following God, and belonging to His people is no reason to treat obedience as optional.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 13:1-7
passages.section_title: What happens when the Philistines answer Jonathan’s attack?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Saul was thirty years old when he became king, and he reigned over Israel forty-two years. 2 He chose for himself three thousand men of Israel: Two thousand were with Saul at Michmash and in the hill country of Bethel, and a thousand were with Jonathan in Gibeah of Benjamin. And the rest of the troops he sent away, each to his own home. 3 Then Jonathan attacked the Philistine outpost at Geba, and the Philistines heard about it. So Saul blew the ram’s horn throughout the land, saying, “Let the Hebrews hear!” 4 And all Israel heard the news: “Saul has attacked an outpost of the Philistines, and now Israel has become a stench to the Philistines!” Then the people were summoned to join Saul at Gilgal. 5 Now the Philistines assembled to fight against Israel with three thousand chariots, six thousand horsemen, and troops as numerous as the sand on the seashore. They went up and camped at Michmash, east of Beth-aven. 6 Seeing that they were in danger because their troops were hard-pressed, the men of Israel hid in caves and thickets, among the rocks, and in cellars and cisterns. 7 Some Hebrews even crossed the Jordan into the land of Gad and Gilead. Saul, however, remained at Gilgal, and all his troops were quaking in fear.

And the rest of the troops he sent away, each to his own home. 3 Then Jonathan attacked the Philistine outpost at Geba, and the Philistines heard about it. They went up and camped at Michmash, east of Beth-aven. 6 Seeing that they were in danger because their troops were hard-pressed, the men of Israel hid in caves and thickets, among the rocks, and in cellars and cisterns. 7 Some Hebrews even crossed the Jordan into the land of Gad and Gilead. Saul, however, remained at Gilgal, and all his troops were quaking in fear.

passages.context_html:
Saul retains three thousand men, dividing them between himself and Jonathan, and sends the rest home. Jonathan attacks a Philistine outpost at Geba. The news spreads as Saul summons Israel to Gilgal, with the attack being reported under the king’s name.

The Philistines assemble at Michmash with chariots, horsemen and an immense body of troops. The BSB gives three thousand chariots and six thousand horsemen. Faced with that force, Israelites hide in caves, thickets and other shelters; some cross the Jordan. Saul stays at Gilgal with people who are trembling.

The opening age and reign figures require care. The BSB footnotes identify differences in the underlying textual witnesses, while Acts 13:21 gives forty years for Saul’s reign. The BSB wording is reproduced above, but this paragraph does not establish an exact date for every event in Saul’s early rule.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley reads the crisis as exposing the limits of confidence in a human king: the people still need God’s help. Henry similarly emphasizes the fear and desertion surrounding Saul. Their readings keep the military danger connected with the larger question of Israel’s trust.

Translations and older commentaries differ over the opening chronology and the number of chariots. The USCCB study notes identify the textual difficulty in verse 1 and the three-thousand reading in some Greek manuscripts. These are questions about the wording transmitted, rather than a necessary division between church traditions. The quotations here follow the checked BSB, without silently replacing its numbers with those of an older commentary.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 13:8-15
passages.section_title: Will Saul wait when his army begins to leave?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 And Saul waited seven days for the time appointed by Samuel, but Samuel did not come to Gilgal, and the troops began to desert Saul. 9 So he said, “Bring me the burnt offering and the peace offerings.” And he offered up the burnt offering. 10 Just as he finished offering the burnt offering, Samuel arrived, and Saul went out to greet him. 11 “What have you done?” Samuel asked. And Saul replied, “When I saw that the troops were deserting me, and that you did not come at the appointed time and the Philistines were gathering at Michmash, 12 I thought, ‘Now the Philistines will descend upon me at Gilgal, and I have not sought the favor of the LORD.’ So I felt compelled to offer the burnt offering.” 13 “You have acted foolishly,” Samuel declared. “You have not kept the command that the LORD your God gave you; if you had, the LORD would have established your kingdom over Israel for all time. 14 But now your kingdom will not endure; the LORD has sought a man after His own heart and appointed him ruler over His people, because you have not kept the command of the LORD.” 15 Then Samuel set out from Gilgal and went up to Gibeah in Benjamin. And Saul numbered the troops who were with him, about six hundred men.

And Saul replied, “When I saw that the troops were deserting me, and that you did not come at the appointed time and the Philistines were gathering at Michmash, 12 I thought, ‘Now the Philistines will descend upon me at Gilgal, and I have not sought the favor of the LORD.’ So I felt compelled to offer the burnt offering.”

13 “You have acted foolishly,” Samuel declared. “You have not kept the command that the LORD your God gave you; if you had, the LORD would have established your kingdom over Israel for all time. 14 But now your kingdom will not endure; the LORD has sought a man after His own heart and appointed him ruler over His people, because you have not kept the command of the LORD.” 15 Then Samuel set out from Gilgal and went up to Gibeah in Benjamin. And Saul numbered the troops who were with him, about six hundred men.

passages.context_html:
Saul waits seven days for the appointed meeting, but Samuel has not arrived and troops are slipping away. Saul orders the offerings brought and offers the burnt offering. Samuel arrives just as he finishes and asks what he has done.

Saul explains the pressure as he saw it: the people were deserting, Samuel had not come, and the Philistines might attack before he sought God’s favor. He describes himself as feeling compelled to act. The explanation shows why he acted; Samuel does not accept it as obedience.

Samuel identifies the offense as failure to keep God’s command. Saul’s kingdom will not endure, and the LORD has sought a ruler after His own heart. The rebuke concerns the future of Saul’s rule and house; Saul does not immediately leave the throne in this scene. After Samuel departs, he counts about six hundred men still with him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill locate the failure in not waiting for Samuel as commanded. They understand the seventh day as not yet completed when Saul acts. That is their explanation of the timing; the narrator directly states the wait, Saul’s action, Samuel’s arrival and the charge that the command was broken.

Gill expressly distinguishes that charge from making the passage solely about a king taking over a priest’s office. He discusses whether Saul performs the act himself or has a priest do it, while keeping the central issue as disregarding the command. The text’s rebuke should remain central when explaining the seriousness of what happens.

The prospect of Saul’s kingdom enduring also receives different explanations. Wesley and Gill understand the duration as a long continuation through his family, allowing for the later kingship of Judah. Wesley also distinguishes this early warning from the later fuller rejection in chapter 15. Those readings address the relationship between the passages; the warning here plainly says that disobedience has cost Saul an enduring kingdom.

passages.god_plan_html:
The New Testament explicitly takes up the description of a man after God’s heart. In Acts 13:21–23, Paul recalls Saul, then David, whom God identifies with that description. He immediately connects David’s descendants with the promised Savior, Jesus.

That connection establishes the larger direction of the royal story without making David sinless or reducing God’s purpose to Saul’s failure. The ruler announced here belongs to the history through which the promised Savior comes. Acts makes the movement toward Jesus explicit rather than leaving it dependent on a guessed symbolic detail.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 13:16-23
passages.section_title: How serious is Israel’s lack of weapons?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 Now Saul and Jonathan his son and the troops with them were staying in Geba of Benjamin, while the Philistines camped at Michmash. 17 And raiders went out of the Philistine camp in three divisions. One headed toward Ophrah in the land of Shual, 18 another toward Beth-horon, and the third down the border road overlooking the Valley of Zeboim facing the wilderness. 19 And no blacksmith could be found in all the land of Israel, because the Philistines had said, “The Hebrews must not be allowed to make swords or spears.” 20 Instead, all the Israelites would go down to the Philistines to sharpen their plowshares, mattocks, axes, and sickles. 21 The charge was a pim for sharpening a plowshare or mattock, a third of a shekel for sharpening a pitchfork or an axe, and a third of a shekel for repointing an oxgoad. 22 So on the day of battle not a sword or spear could be found in the hands of the troops with Saul and Jonathan; only Saul and his son Jonathan had weapons. 23 And a garrison of the Philistines had gone out to the pass at Michmash.
paragraphs: 16 Now Saul and Jonathan his son and the troops with them were staying in Geba of Benjamin, while the Philistines camped at Michmash. 17 And raiders went out of the Philistine camp in three divisions. One headed toward Ophrah in the land of Shual, 18 another toward Beth-horon, and the third down the border road overlooking the Valley of Zeboim facing the wilderness.

19 And no blacksmith could be found in all the land of Israel, because the Philistines had said, “The Hebrews must not be allowed to make swords or spears.” 20 Instead, all the Israelites would go down to the Philistines to sharpen their plowshares, mattocks, axes, and sickles. 21 The charge was a pim for sharpening a plowshare or mattock, a third of a shekel for sharpening a pitchfork or an axe, and a third of a shekel for repointing an oxgoad. 22 So on the day of battle not a sword or spear could be found in the hands of the troops with Saul and Jonathan; only Saul and his son Jonathan had weapons. 23 And a garrison of the Philistines had gone out to the pass at Michmash.

passages.context_html:
Saul and Jonathan remain with their troops at Geba, while the Philistines hold Michmash. Raiding parties leave the Philistine camp in three directions, extending pressure across the surrounding territory. The chapter ends with a Philistine garrison taking the pass at Michmash.

The narrator pauses to explain a serious disadvantage. No blacksmith is available in Israel because the Philistines seek to prevent the Hebrews from making swords and spears. Even sharpening agricultural tools requires going to the Philistines, and the account lists the charges.

When battle comes, only Saul and Jonathan among the troops with them have the weapons described. The statement concerns this force and its swords and spears; it does not require imagining that no Israelite anywhere has a sling, bow or other means of fighting. The situation prepares for Jonathan’s action in the next chapter.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry emphasizes dependence on an enemy even for farming tools. Wesley and Gill both take the weapon shortage seriously while considering how it fits earlier battles. Wesley allows for other kinds of weapons and confines the immediate description to the men with Saul and Jonathan. Gill discusses possible explanations but does not remove the stated disadvantage.

The USCCB study notes see the details as emphasizing the Philistines’ military strength and Israel’s dependence on God for victory. That is consistent with Jonathan’s next words about the LORD being able to save through many or few (1 Samuel 14:1–6). The narrative supplies this contrast without requiring an independently established history of every ancient metalworking technique.

passages.god_plan_html:
The military imbalance leads directly into Jonathan’s confidence that God is not limited by numbers. The following account ultimately credits the LORD with saving Israel (1 Samuel 14:6, 23). Human resources do not set the limit of His ability to rescue.

The same larger theme of unexpected divine power appears in 1 Corinthians 1:18–25. Paul identifies Christ crucified as God’s power and wisdom, despite the weakness and foolishness people imagine they see. This is a comparison of themes, not a claim that a missing sword predicts a particular event at the cross. Christian confidence rests in God’s saving work rather than the outward impressiveness of the means.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 14:1-23
passages.section_title: Can God save through Jonathan and one companion?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 One day Jonathan son of Saul said to the young man bearing his armor, “Come, let us cross over to the Philistine outpost on the other side.” But Jonathan did not tell his father. 2 Meanwhile, Saul was staying under the pomegranate tree in Migron on the outskirts of Gibeah. And the troops who were with him numbered about six hundred men, 3 including Ahijah, who was wearing an ephod. He was the son of Ichabod’s brother Ahitub son of Phinehas, the son of Eli the priest of the LORD in Shiloh. But the troops did not know that Jonathan had left. 4 Now there were cliffs on both sides of the pass that Jonathan intended to cross to reach the Philistine outpost. One was named Bozez and the other Seneh. 5 One cliff stood to the north toward Michmash, and the other to the south toward Geba. 6 Jonathan said to the young man bearing his armor, “Come, let us cross over to the outpost of these uncircumcised men. Perhaps the LORD will work on our behalf. Nothing can hinder the LORD from saving, whether by many or by few.” 7 His armor-bearer replied, “Do all that is in your heart. Go ahead; I am with you heart and soul.” 8 “Very well,” said Jonathan, “we will cross over toward these men and show ourselves to them. 9 If they say, ‘Wait until we come to you,’ then we will stay where we are and will not go up to them. 10 But if they say, ‘Come on up,’ then we will go up, because this will be our sign that the LORD has delivered them into our hands.” 11 So the two of them showed themselves to the outpost of the Philistines, who exclaimed, “Look, the Hebrews are coming out of the holes in which they were hiding!” 12 So the men of the outpost called out to Jonathan and his armor-bearer, “Come on up, and we will teach you a lesson!” “Follow me,” Jonathan told his armor-bearer, “for the LORD has delivered them into the hand of Israel.” 13 So Jonathan climbed up on his hands and feet, with his armor-bearer behind him. And the Philistines fell before Jonathan, and his armor-bearer followed and finished them off. 14 In that first assault, Jonathan and his armor-bearer struck down about twenty men in about half an acre of land. 15 Then panic struck the Philistines in the camp, in the field, and among all the people. Even those in the outposts and raiding parties trembled. Indeed, the earth quaked, and panic spread from God. 16 Now when Saul’s watchmen at Gibeah in Benjamin looked and saw the troops melting away and scattering in every direction, 17 Saul said to the troops who were with him, “Call the roll and see who has left us.” And when they had called the roll, they saw that Jonathan and his armor-bearer were not there. 18 Then Saul said to Ahijah, “Bring the ark of God.” (For at that time it was with the Israelites.) 19 While Saul was talking to the priest, the commotion in the Philistine camp continued to increase. So Saul said to the priest, “Withdraw your hand.” 20 Then Saul and all his troops assembled and marched to the battle, and they found the Philistines in total confusion, with each man wielding the sword against his neighbor. 21 And the Hebrews who had previously gone up into the surrounding camps to join the Philistines now went over to the Israelites who were with Saul and Jonathan. 22 When all the Israelites who had been hiding in the hill country of Ephraim heard that the Philistines were fleeing, they also joined the battle in close pursuit. 23 So the LORD saved Israel that day, and the battle moved on beyond Beth-aven.

passages.context_html:
Jonathan takes his armor-bearer toward the Philistine outpost without telling Saul. His confidence is in what God can do, whether through many or few. Yet he says perhaps the LORD will act: confidence in God’s ability is not the same as claiming advance knowledge of every outcome.

He proposes taking the enemy’s response as a sign. When they call the two men up, Jonathan climbs toward them and attacks, with his companion following. They strike down about twenty men. Panic then spreads through the Philistine force, and the earth quakes; the narrator attributes the panic to God.

Saul’s watchmen see the confusion. He calls the roll to discover who is missing, then speaks to Ahijah. While the commotion increases, Saul cuts short the consultation and leads his troops toward the battle. The Philistines are fighting one another, Hebrews who had been with them change sides, and men previously in hiding join the pursuit.

The conclusion credits the LORD with saving Israel. God’s action works through the people’s fighting and pursuit rather than making those narrated actions unreal. Ahijah’s family also recalls the earlier priestly story: he is Ahitub’s son, and Ahitub is Ichabod’s brother.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley distinguishes Jonathan’s confidence in God’s power from certainty about the particular moment and means of rescue. He and Henry read the initiative as prompted by God. The narrator records Jonathan’s confidence, proposed sign and action, without quoting a separate command that establishes the same method for every later believer.

Henry contrasts Jonathan’s trust with Saul’s haste in ending the consultation when an opening appears. The BSB footnote also records an ark/ephod difference in verse 18. The ephod is the priestly garment used in seeking direction from God. This difference helps explain why commentators may describe the consultation in different terms.

Wesley explains that the LORD saves through the Israelites’ actions. Their pursuit and Jonathan’s fighting are part of the account, even while the panic and deliverance are credited to God. The story does not require choosing between God’s help and the real action of His servants.
