deeper_study.title: Should We Seek Signs From God?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Jonathan’s small beginning shows that the size of a human force does not determine what God can accomplish. A related confidence appears when Jesus addresses His disciples as a little flock in Luke 12:22–34. He calls them away from anxious striving toward trust in their Father and seeking His kingdom.

The connection is a shared theme of dependence on God’s care, not a promise that every small group will win a battle or that every chosen sign must produce a desired result. Jesus’ words direct His followers toward the Father’s kingdom and generosity, extending the hope beyond the military setting of Jonathan’s rescue.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 14:24-36
passages.section_title: What harm does Saul’s oath do to the people?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 24 Now the men of Israel were in distress that day, for Saul had placed the troops under an oath, saying, “Cursed is the man who eats any food before evening, before I have taken vengeance on my enemies.” So none of the troops tasted any food. 25 Then all the troops entered the forest, and there was honey on the ground. 26 And when they entered the forest and saw the flowing honey, not one of them put his hand to his mouth, because they feared the oath. 27 Jonathan, however, had not heard that his father had bound the people with the oath. So he reached out the end of the staff in his hand, dipped it into the honeycomb, and put his hand to his mouth, and his eyes brightened. 28 Then one of the soldiers told him, “Your father bound the troops with a solemn oath, saying, ‘Cursed is the man who eats food today.’ That is why the people are faint.” 29 “My father has brought trouble to the land,” Jonathan replied. “Just look at how my eyes have brightened because I tasted a little of this honey. 30 How much better it would have been if the troops had eaten freely today from the plunder they took from their enemies! Would not the slaughter of the Philistines have been much greater?” 31 That day, after the Israelites had struck down the Philistines from Michmash to Aijalon, the people were very faint. 32 So they rushed greedily to the plunder, taking sheep, cattle, and calves. They slaughtered them on the ground and ate meat with the blood still in it. 33 Then someone reported to Saul: “Look, the troops are sinning against the LORD by eating meat with the blood still in it.” “You have broken faith,” said Saul. “Roll a large stone over here at once.” 34 Then he said, “Go among the troops and tell them, ‘Each man must bring me his ox or his sheep, slaughter them in this place, and then eat. Do not sin against the LORD by eating meat with the blood still in it.’” So that night everyone brought his ox and slaughtered it there. 35 Then Saul built an altar to the LORD; it was the first time he had built an altar to the LORD. 36 And Saul said, “Let us go down after the Philistines by night and plunder them until dawn, leaving no man alive!” “Do what seems good to you,” the troops replied. But the priest said, “We must consult God here.”

passages.context_html:
Saul puts the troops under an oath not to eat until evening, before he has taken vengeance on his enemies. The men fear the oath and leave available honey untouched. Jonathan has not heard the command. He eats some honey and is refreshed, then learns what his father has said.

Jonathan criticizes the restriction because the food would have strengthened the pursuit. The troops continue fighting but become very faint. They then rush to the captured animals and eat meat with the blood still in it. The account identifies that action as sin against the LORD, while the unnecessary food restriction came from Saul.

Saul intervenes by providing a place for the slaughter and telling the people not to eat with the blood. He also builds an altar. When he proposes continuing the pursuit through the night, the priest calls for seeking God’s direction first. The scene places concern for religious actions alongside the damaging consequences of Saul’s own oath.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry regards the order as unwise: any time gained by preventing a meal is offset by the strength lost. Wesley allows that Saul’s intention may have been good, while judging the restriction and threatened punishment too severe. Gill also sees the aim as completing the victory but considers the order harsh and imprudent. These readings do not all assign Saul the same inward motive.

Wesley emphasizes the contrast between fear of the king’s oath and failure to observe God’s command concerning blood. The people’s hunger explains the setting of their action without making Saul’s rule and God’s instruction identical. A leader’s unnecessary demand can make faithful conduct harder for the people under him.

Henry reads Saul’s altar-building critically in the wider account of his conduct. The narrator states that this is his first altar to the LORD. Henry sees a warning here: building something for worship does not by itself show that a ruler is listening to God.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
Saul’s restriction offers a contrast with Jesus’ care for weary people. In Matthew 11:25–30, Jesus invites the burdened to come to Him, describes Himself as gentle and humble, and offers rest under His yoke. His authority gives a different picture from a ruler exhausting people through a needless demand.

This comparison concerns the character and purpose of leadership. It does not call God’s own instructions oppressive or turn every difficult command into a mistake. The larger hope is a Lord who knows His people’s needs and teaches them in gentleness, rather than treating their weakness as an obstacle to His own importance.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 14:37-46
passages.section_title: Must Jonathan die because of Saul’s oath?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 37 So Saul inquired of God, “Shall I go down after the Philistines? Will You give them into the hand of Israel?” But God did not answer him that day. 38 Therefore Saul said, “Come here, all you leaders of the troops, and let us investigate how this sin has occurred today. 39 As surely as the LORD who saves Israel lives, even if it is my son Jonathan, he must die!” But not one of the troops said a word. 40 Then Saul said to all Israel, “You stand on one side, and I and my son Jonathan will stand on the other side.” “Do what seems good to you,” the troops replied. 41 So Saul said to the LORD, the God of Israel, “Why have You not answered Your servant this day? If the fault is with me or my son Jonathan, respond with Urim, but if the fault is with the men of Israel, respond with Thummim.” And Jonathan and Saul were selected, but the people were cleared of the charge. 42 Then Saul said, “Cast the lot between me and my son Jonathan.” And Jonathan was selected. 43 “Tell me what you have done,” Saul commanded him. So Jonathan told him, “I only tasted a little honey with the end of the staff that was in my hand. And now I must die?” 44 And Saul declared, “May God punish me, and ever so severely, if you, Jonathan, do not surely die!” 45 But the people said to Saul, “Must Jonathan die—he who accomplished such a great deliverance for Israel? Never! As surely as the LORD lives, not a hair of his head will fall to the ground, for with God’s help he has accomplished this today.” So the people rescued Jonathan, and he did not die. 46 Then Saul gave up his pursuit of the Philistines, and the Philistines returned to their own land.

43 “Tell me what you have done,” Saul commanded him. So Jonathan told him, “I only tasted a little honey with the end of the staff that was in my hand. And now I must die?” 44 And Saul declared, “May God punish me, and ever so severely, if you, Jonathan, do not surely die!” 45 But the people said to Saul, “Must Jonathan die—he who accomplished such a great deliverance for Israel? Never! As surely as the LORD lives, not a hair of his head will fall to the ground, for with God’s help he has accomplished this today.” So the people rescued Jonathan, and he did not die. 46 Then Saul gave up his pursuit of the Philistines, and the Philistines returned to their own land.

passages.context_html:
God does not answer Saul’s question about pursuing the Philistines. Saul begins an investigation and declares that the offender must die, even if it is Jonathan. The people remain silent. The selection first narrows to Saul and Jonathan, then falls on Jonathan.

Jonathan reports tasting a little honey. In the BSB he asks whether he must now die. Saul insists on the death sentence, but the people refuse it. They point to the deliverance God has brought through Jonathan and insist that he must not be harmed.

The people rescue Jonathan, and he does not die. The Hebrew verb is פָּדָה, padah (pah-DAH), to ransom or rescue. Brown–Driver–Briggs specifically lists this verse as rescue from violence and death. The word does not require inventing a money payment that the narrator never mentions. Saul then ends the pursuit, and the Philistines return to their land.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands Jonathan’s selection as exposing the danger created by Saul’s oath, rather than God endorsing the execution. He takes the people’s appeal to God’s help through Jonathan seriously. Gill likewise regards their intervention as protecting someone who acted without knowing the prohibition and whom God had used to bring deliverance.

Gill reads Jonathan’s reply as willingness to submit, following his older translation. The BSB presents the reply as a question. Both approaches recognize the contrast between the small act of tasting honey and the death Saul demands; the quotation above retains the BSB’s wording.

Henry warns that someone who neglects his own faults can become unusually severe over others’ failures to follow his commands. The account does not quote God ordering Jonathan’s death. It records Saul’s insistence, the people’s resistance, and Jonathan’s rescue. The human oath and God’s own command should remain distinct.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 14:47-52
passages.section_title: What does the summary of Saul’s reign tell us?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 47 After Saul had assumed the kingship over Israel, he fought against all his enemies on every side—the Moabites, the Ammonites, the Edomites, the kings of Zobah, and the Philistines. Wherever he turned, he routed them. 48 He fought valiantly and defeated the Amalekites, delivering Israel from the hands of its plunderers. 49 Now the sons of Saul were Jonathan, Ishvi, and Malchishua. His two daughters were named Merab (his firstborn) and Michal (his younger daughter). 50 His wife’s name was Ahinoam daughter of Ahimaaz. The name of the commander of his army was Abner, the son of Saul’s uncle Ner. 51 Saul’s father Kish and Abner’s father Ner were sons of Abiel. 52 And the war with the Philistines was fierce for all the days of Saul. So whenever he noticed any strong or brave man, Saul would enlist him.

Wherever he turned, he routed them. 48 He fought valiantly and defeated the Amalekites, delivering Israel from the hands of its plunderers.

49 Now the sons of Saul were Jonathan, Ishvi, and Malchishua. His two daughters were named Merab (his firstborn) and Michal (his younger daughter). 50 His wife’s name was Ahinoam daughter of Ahimaaz. The name of the commander of his army was Abner, the son of Saul’s uncle Ner. 51 Saul’s father Kish and Abner’s father Ner were sons of Abiel. 52 And the war with the Philistines was fierce for all the days of Saul. So whenever he noticed any strong or brave man, Saul would enlist him.

passages.context_html:
The chapter closes with a summary of Saul’s wars and household. It names enemies on several sides and credits him with fighting valiantly, defeating Amalekites and rescuing Israel from plunderers. His failings in the preceding scenes do not erase the military help the narrator records.

The summary then names sons, daughters, his wife and the army commander Abner. These names prepare readers for people who will matter later. The list need not be treated as a statement that Saul has no other children anywhere in the wider narrative.

War with the Philistines remains fierce throughout his reign. Saul continues to recruit strong and brave men. The closing picture combines genuine deliverance with continuing conflict; it does not describe a kingdom that has reached lasting peace.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads the summary as a view of Saul’s court and camp, emphasizing how little ease royal status brings him. Wesley and Gill connect the son named Ishvi with Abinadab in later lists, rather than treating every list as naming an entirely different family. Their explanations show why care is needed before declaring the present names an exhaustive account.

Saul has brought real help to Israel, yet the war is far from over. That mixed picture matters as his story continues. Success in battle has not settled the deeper question of whether he will listen to God.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 15:1-9
passages.section_title: Will Saul carry out the command he has been given?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then Samuel said to Saul, “The LORD sent me to anoint you king over His people Israel. Now therefore, listen to the words of the LORD. 2 This is what the LORD of Hosts says: ‘I witnessed what the Amalekites did to the Israelites when they opposed them on their way up from Egypt. 3 Now go and attack the Amalekites and devote to destruction all that belongs to them. Do not spare them, but put to death men and women, children and infants, oxen and sheep, camels and donkeys.’” 4 So Saul summoned the troops and numbered them at Telaim—200,000 foot soldiers and 10,000 men of Judah. 5 Saul came to the city of Amalek and lay in wait in the valley. 6 And he warned the Kenites, “Since you showed kindness to all the Israelites when they came up out of Egypt, go on and get away from the Amalekites. Otherwise I will sweep you away with them.” So the Kenites moved away from the Amalekites. 7 Then Saul struck down the Amalekites all the way from Havilah to Shur, which is east of Egypt. 8 He captured Agag king of Amalek alive, but devoted all the others to destruction with the sword. 9 Saul and his troops spared Agag, along with the best of the sheep and cattle, the fat calves and lambs, and the best of everything else. They were unwilling to devote them to destruction, but they devoted to destruction all that was despised and worthless.

Now therefore, listen to the words of the LORD. 2 This is what the LORD of Hosts says: ‘I witnessed what the Amalekites did to the Israelites when they opposed them on their way up from Egypt. 3 Now go and attack the Amalekites and devote to destruction all that belongs to them. Do not spare them, but put to death men and women, children and infants, oxen and sheep, camels and donkeys.’”

4 So Saul summoned the troops and numbered them at Telaim—200,000 foot soldiers and 10,000 men of Judah. 5 Saul came to the city of Amalek and lay in wait in the valley. 6 And he warned the Kenites, “Since you showed kindness to all the Israelites when they came up out of Egypt, go on and get away from the Amalekites. Otherwise I will sweep you away with them.” So the Kenites moved away from the Amalekites. 7 Then Saul struck down the Amalekites all the way from Havilah to Shur, which is east of Egypt. 8 He captured Agag king of Amalek alive, but devoted all the others to destruction with the sword. 9 Saul and his troops spared Agag, along with the best of the sheep and cattle, the fat calves and lambs, and the best of everything else. They were unwilling to devote them to destruction, but they devoted to destruction all that was despised and worthless.

passages.context_html:
Samuel reminds Saul that the LORD appointed him over His people and tells him to listen. The command concerns Amalek’s attack on Israel after the exodus. Exodus 17:8–16 records that attack and the announced judgment; Deuteronomy 25:17–19 recalls the assault on weary stragglers.

The order is severe and explicit. It includes people of every age, including children and infants, and the livestock. Devoting the people and possessions to destruction means Saul is not being sent to enrich himself with captives or valuable animals. The chapter makes obedience to this particular command its central question.

Saul assembles his troops and warns the Kenites to leave because they had shown kindness to Israel. He then defeats the Amalekites but takes Agag alive. Saul and his troops also keep the best livestock and valuable things, destroying what they consider worthless. They have made their own assessment of what to preserve instead of carrying out the order as given.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Henry read the command as a particular divine judgment linked with Amalek’s earlier violence. They take its severity seriously. In addressing the deaths of children, Wesley appeals to God’s authority over life and the Christian teaching of human sinfulness from birth. That is his theological reasoning about a difficult part of the command, rather than an explanation separately spoken by Samuel in this scene.

Henry also notices the contrast between remembered cruelty and remembered kindness to the Kenites. The USCCB study notes emphasize that the order excludes taking plunder for personal use and that Saul fails to carry it out. Across these readings, the story is more than a report of winning a battle: it exposes selective obedience.

Wesley explicitly warns elsewhere in his comments on this chapter that its extraordinary judgment is not a precedent for private people to take the sword of justice into their own hands. The command belongs to this account and its named recipients; reading it does not give later readers the same commission.

passages.god_plan_html:
The passage connects judgment with God’s earlier promise concerning an enemy that attacked vulnerable people. Within the larger biblical story, evil does not escape God simply because its reckoning is delayed. Revelation 19:11–16 presents the faithful and true rider, identified as the Word of God, judging in righteousness as King of kings.

This is a connection through the theme of divine judgment, rather than a claim that Revelation repeats Saul’s campaign or assigns its command to the church. The New Testament places final judgment under Christ’s authority. It gives the larger hope that violent opposition will not rule forever, while leaving this passage’s difficult details to be faced honestly.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 15:10-23
passages.section_title: Can a sacrifice make up for refusing to listen?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 Then the word of the LORD came to Samuel, saying, 11 “I regret that I have made Saul king, for he has turned away from following Me and has not carried out My instructions.” And Samuel was distressed and cried out to the LORD all that night. 12 Early in the morning Samuel got up to confront Saul, but he was told, “Saul has gone to Carmel, and behold, he has set up a monument for himself and has turned and gone down to Gilgal.” 13 When Samuel reached him, Saul said to him, “May the LORD bless you. I have carried out the LORD’s instructions.” 14 But Samuel replied, “Then what is this bleating of sheep and lowing of cattle that I hear?” 15 Saul answered, “The troops brought them from the Amalekites; they spared the best sheep and cattle to sacrifice to the LORD your God, but the rest we devoted to destruction.” 16 “Stop!” exclaimed Samuel. “Let me tell you what the LORD said to me last night.” “Tell me,” Saul replied. 17 And Samuel said, “Although you were once small in your own eyes, have you not become the head of the tribes of Israel? The LORD anointed you king over Israel 18 and sent you on a mission, saying, ‘Go and devote to destruction the sinful Amalekites. Fight against them until you have wiped them out.’ 19 So why did you not obey the LORD? Why did you rush upon the plunder and do evil in the sight of the LORD?” 20 “But I did obey the LORD,” Saul replied. “I went on the mission that the LORD gave me. I brought back Agag king of Amalek and devoted the Amalekites to destruction. 21 The troops took sheep and cattle from the plunder, the best of the things devoted to destruction, in order to sacrifice them to the LORD your God at Gilgal.” 22 But Samuel declared: “Does the LORD delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices as much as in obedience to His voice? Behold, obedience is better than sacrifice, and attentiveness is better than the fat of rams. 23 For rebellion is like the sin of divination, and arrogance is like the wickedness of idolatry. Because you have rejected the word of the LORD, He has rejected you as king.”

17 And Samuel said, “Although you were once small in your own eyes, have you not become the head of the tribes of Israel? The LORD anointed you king over Israel 18 and sent you on a mission, saying, ‘Go and devote to destruction the sinful Amalekites. Because you have rejected the word of the LORD, He has rejected you as king.”

passages.context_html:
The LORD tells Samuel that He regrets making Saul king because Saul has turned from following Him. Samuel is deeply distressed and cries to God through the night. Meanwhile, Saul has set up a monument for himself and gone to Gilgal.

Saul greets Samuel by claiming to have carried out the command. The sound of the surviving animals exposes the gap between that claim and what happened. Saul says the troops kept them for sacrifice. Samuel brings the issue back to the instruction Saul received and asks why he rushed upon the plunder.

Samuel’s answer sets obedience above sacrifice. The animals are not an acceptable way of compensating for rejecting God’s word. Rebellion and arrogance are compared with divination and idolatry, and Saul is told that his rejection of the word has brought rejection from kingship.

The Hebrew נָחַם, nacham (nah-KHAHM), can express being sorry, grieving or relenting; Brown–Driver–Briggs lists the uses in verses 11, 29 and 35. The chapter speaks of God’s regret while also saying He does not change His mind like a human being. Both statements belong to the story and need to be considered together.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley, Henry and Gill understand God’s regret through the change in His dealings with Saul, rather than God discovering information He did not know. Saul has turned away, and the royal favor he received will not continue in the same way. This reading preserves the seriousness of the response without making God an unreliable human ruler.

On sacrifice, Wesley and Henry emphasize that a religious offering cannot compensate for knowingly refusing the command. Their reading does not treat every sacrifice as worthless. It challenges the attempt to use a worshipful act as a substitute for listening.

The USCCB study notes likewise connect worship with attentiveness to God’s will. In this account Saul’s proposed offering is inseparable from the animals he was told not to keep. Calling the result religious does not change the choice that produced it.

passages.god_plan_html:
The relationship between obedience and sacrifice reaches a fuller expression in Hebrews 10:5–10. Drawing from the Psalms, Hebrews describes Christ coming to do God’s will and offering His own body once for all.

Hebrews is not quoting Samuel’s words here, and Jesus’ offering is not another example of Saul’s failed proposal. It brings obedience and sacrifice together: Christ gives Himself in doing the Father’s will. The larger story points toward a saving offering that fully expresses faithfulness, rather than an offering used to cover refusal.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 15:24-35
passages.section_title: What does Saul’s confession change?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 24 Then Saul said to Samuel, “I have sinned; I have transgressed the LORD’s commandment and your instructions, because I feared the people and obeyed their voice. 25 Now therefore, please forgive my sin and return with me so I can worship the LORD.” 26 “I will not return with you,” Samuel replied. “For you have rejected the word of the LORD, and He has rejected you as king over Israel.” 27 As Samuel turned to go, Saul grabbed the hem of his robe, and it tore. 28 So Samuel said to him, “The LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today and has given it to your neighbor who is better than you. 29 Moreover, the Glory of Israel does not lie or change His mind, for He is not a man, that He should change His mind.” 30 “I have sinned,” Saul replied. “Please honor me now before the elders of my people and before Israel. Come back with me, so that I may worship the LORD your God.” 31 So Samuel went back with Saul, and Saul worshiped the LORD. 32 Then Samuel said, “Bring me Agag king of the Amalekites.” Agag came to him cheerfully, for he thought, “Surely the bitterness of death is past.” 33 But Samuel declared: “As your sword has made women childless, so your mother will be childless among women.” And Samuel hacked Agag to pieces before the LORD at Gilgal. 34 Then Samuel went to Ramah, but Saul went up to his home in Gibeah of Saul. 35 And to the day of his death, Samuel never again visited Saul. Samuel mourned for Saul, and the LORD regretted that He had made Saul king over Israel.
paragraphs: 24 Then Saul said to Samuel, “I have sinned; I have transgressed the LORD’s commandment and your instructions, because I feared the people and obeyed their voice. 25 Now therefore, please forgive my sin and return with me so I can worship the LORD.” 26 “I will not return with you,” Samuel replied. “For you have rejected the word of the LORD, and He has rejected you as king over Israel.” 27 As Samuel turned to go, Saul grabbed the hem of his robe, and it tore. 28 So Samuel said to him, “The LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today and has given it to your neighbor who is better than you. 29 Moreover, the Glory of Israel does not lie or change His mind, for He is not a man, that He should change His mind.”

30 “I have sinned,” Saul replied. “Please honor me now before the elders of my people and before Israel. Come back with me, so that I may worship the LORD your God.” 31 So Samuel went back with Saul, and Saul worshiped the LORD. 32 Then Samuel said, “Bring me Agag king of the Amalekites.” Agag came to him cheerfully, for he thought, “Surely the bitterness of death is past.” 33 But Samuel declared: “As your sword has made women childless, so your mother will be childless among women.” And Samuel hacked Agag to pieces before the LORD at Gilgal. 34 Then Samuel went to Ramah, but Saul went up to his home in Gibeah of Saul. 35 And to the day of his death, Samuel never again visited Saul. Samuel mourned for Saul, and the LORD regretted that He had made Saul king over Israel.

passages.context_html:
Saul confesses that he has sinned, saying that fear of the people led him to listen to them. He asks Samuel for forgiveness and to return with him for worship. Samuel refuses at first and repeats that the LORD has rejected Saul as king.

When Saul grabs Samuel’s robe and tears it, Samuel uses the torn garment to describe the kingdom being taken from him and given to a better neighbor. God’s declaration will not be undone by treating Him as a human being who lies or changes course under pressure.

Saul again admits his sin but also asks to be honored before the elders and Israel. Samuel returns with him, and Saul worships. Samuel then confronts Agag over the bloodshed of his own sword and executes him. The judgment is connected with Agag’s own violence, not only a story of distant ancestors.

Samuel goes home to Ramah, Saul returns to Gibeah, and their visits end. Yet Samuel mourns Saul, and the chapter closes by repeating God’s regret. Rejection from office has not made Saul’s fall an occasion for Samuel to celebrate.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Readers differ over Saul’s confession. Henry and Gill see it as compromised by blame-shifting and concern for public standing. His request for honor helps explain their reading. Wesley disagrees that hypocrisy has been proved: he allows Saul’s admission and request for pardon to be sincere.

Wesley also distinguishes rejection from kingship from a declaration that Saul is rejected from salvation. Whatever judgment a reader reaches about his motives, the sentence stated here concerns his royal office. The passage should not be made to answer every question about his final standing in a single phrase.

Gill reads God’s refusal to lie or change His mind as confirmation of the announced loss of Saul’s kingdom and God’s continuing purpose for His people. The USCCB study notes also emphasize the definitive character of the declaration. Samuel’s eventual return to worship with Saul therefore does not mean the judgment has been canceled.

passages.god_plan_html:
The statement that God does not lie belongs to a wider theme of confidence in His word. Hebrews 6:13–20 recalls the promise to Abraham and grounds the heirs’ encouragement in God’s unchanging purpose and inability to lie.

Hebrews directs that confidence toward the hope opened by Jesus, who has entered God’s presence as forerunner and enduring high priest. Samuel’s statement confirms a judgment; Hebrews confirms a promise of hope. In both settings, God’s word is more dependable than the shifting words and intentions of human beings.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 16:1-13
passages.section_title: Why does God choose the son still out with the sheep?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now the LORD said to Samuel, “How long are you going to mourn for Saul, since I have rejected him as king over Israel? Fill your horn with oil and go. I am sending you to Jesse of Bethlehem, for I have selected from his sons a king for Myself.” 2 “How can I go?” Samuel asked. “Saul will hear of it and kill me!” The LORD answered, “Take a heifer with you and say, ‘I have come to sacrifice to the LORD.’ 3 Then invite Jesse to the sacrifice, and I will show you what you are to do. You are to anoint for Me the one I indicate.” 4 So Samuel did what the LORD had said and went to Bethlehem. When the elders of the town met him, they trembled and asked, “Do you come in peace?” 5 “In peace,” he replied. “I have come to sacrifice to the LORD. Consecrate yourselves and come with me to the sacrifice.” Then he consecrated Jesse and his sons and invited them to the sacrifice. 6 When they arrived, Samuel saw Eliab and said, “Surely here before the LORD is His anointed.” 7 But the LORD said to Samuel, “Do not consider his appearance or height, for I have rejected him; the LORD does not see as man does. For man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart.” 8 Then Jesse called Abinadab and presented him to Samuel, who said, “The LORD has not chosen this one either.” 9 Next Jesse presented Shammah, but Samuel said, “The LORD has not chosen this one either.” 10 Thus Jesse made seven of his sons pass before Samuel, but Samuel told him, “The LORD has not chosen any of these.” 11 And Samuel asked him, “Are these all the sons you have?” “There is still the youngest,” Jesse replied, “but he is tending the sheep.” “Send for him,” Samuel replied. “For we will not sit down to eat until he arrives.” 12 So Jesse sent for his youngest son and brought him in. He was ruddy, with beautiful eyes and a handsome appearance. And the LORD said, “Rise and anoint him, for he is the one.” 13 So Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed him in the presence of his brothers, and the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon David from that day forward. Then Samuel set out and went to Ramah.

passages.context_html:
Samuel is still mourning Saul when the LORD sends him to Jesse’s family in Bethlehem. God has chosen a king from among Jesse’s sons. Samuel fears Saul will kill him if he hears, so God directs him to take a heifer and hold a sacrifice. The visit has a real purpose of worship as well as the appointment God will reveal.

The elders of Bethlehem meet Samuel with fear, but he assures them he comes in peace. Jesse and his sons are prepared for the sacrifice. When Samuel sees Eliab, he thinks he has found the chosen man. God corrects him: appearance and height do not reveal what God sees in the heart.

Seven sons pass before Samuel without being chosen. Only then does Samuel ask whether another remains. The youngest is tending sheep. The gathering waits while he is brought, and the LORD identifies him as the one to anoint.

David is himself described as handsome, with beautiful eyes. The point is that looks do not determine God’s choice, rather than that attractiveness disqualifies someone. Samuel anoints him before his brothers, and the Spirit of the LORD comes upon him. He has been chosen and equipped, but he does not take Saul’s throne that day.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry emphasizes Samuel’s need to learn the lesson he had already seen with Saul: an impressive appearance cannot reveal a person’s heart. Gill likewise contrasts what people can see with the character God knows. The passage challenges a judgment based on appearance, while leaving God’s knowledge greater than ours.

Wesley distinguishes David’s designation for kingship from his later accession. The anointing supplies a real calling and the Spirit’s gifts before his outward circumstances have become royal. The youngest son is still known as a shepherd even after God has chosen him.

Henry reads David as a foreshadowing of Christ, God’s beloved Son. That wider Christian reading is not a claim that David will never sin. It recognizes God beginning a royal story whose full hope extends beyond the young man standing before Samuel.

passages.god_plan_html:
David’s place and work form a well-supported connection with the coming shepherd-king. Matthew 2:1–6 identifies Bethlehem as Jesus’ birthplace and cites the promised ruler who will shepherd Israel. The same town that introduces Jesse’s shepherd son becomes the setting for the birth of the Messiah.

In John 10:11–18, Jesus calls Himself the good shepherd, knows His sheep and gives His life for them. David’s shepherding helps us understand the picture of care, but Jesus carries it further through His willing death and authority to take up His life again. The connection points toward a king whose rule serves and rescues His people.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 16:14-23
passages.section_title: How does David’s music bring him into Saul’s service?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 Now the Spirit of the LORD departed from Saul, and a spirit of distress from the LORD began to torment him. 15 Saul’s servants said to him, “Surely a spirit of distress from God is tormenting you. 16 Let our lord command your servants here to seek out someone who can skillfully play the harp. Whenever the spirit of distress from God is upon you, he is to play it, and you will be well.” 17 And Saul commanded his servants, “Find me someone who plays well, and bring him to me.” 18 One of the servants answered, “I have seen a son of Jesse of Bethlehem who knows how to play the harp. He is a mighty man of valor, a warrior, eloquent and handsome, and the LORD is with him.” 19 So Saul sent messengers to Jesse and said, “Send me your son David, who is with the sheep.” 20 And Jesse took a donkey loaded with bread, a skin of wine, and one young goat and sent them to Saul with his son David. 21 When David came to Saul and entered his service, Saul loved him very much, and David became his armor-bearer. 22 Then Saul sent word to Jesse, saying, “Let David remain in my service, for I am pleased with him.” 23 And whenever the spirit from God came upon Saul, David would pick up his harp and play. Then Saul would find relief and feel better, and the spirit of distress would depart from him.

He is a mighty man of valor, a warrior, eloquent and handsome, and the LORD is with him.”

19 So Saul sent messengers to Jesse and said, “Send me your son David, who is with the sheep.” 20 And Jesse took a donkey loaded with bread, a skin of wine, and one young goat and sent them to Saul with his son David. 21 When David came to Saul and entered his service, Saul loved him very much, and David became his armor-bearer. 22 Then Saul sent word to Jesse, saying, “Let David remain in my service, for I am pleased with him.” 23 And whenever the spirit from God came upon Saul, David would pick up his harp and play. Then Saul would find relief and feel better, and the spirit of distress would depart from him.

passages.context_html:
The story turns from the Spirit coming upon David to the Spirit departing from Saul. A spirit of distress from the LORD torments Saul. The account presents his suffering within the changed relationship between God and the king, rather than treating the loss of royal favor as an empty announcement.

Saul’s servants propose finding a skilled harp player to bring him relief. One recommends Jesse’s son, praising his music, courage, speech and appearance, and saying that the LORD is with him. Saul sends for David, and Jesse sends him with gifts.

Saul welcomes David warmly. He loves him, appoints him as an armor-bearer, and asks Jesse to let him remain. When David plays, Saul finds relief and the distressing spirit departs. The relationship begins with service and affection, even though the reader already knows David has been chosen for the kingship.

The need in Saul’s household opens a place for David’s skill. A young man known for tending sheep is now learning life in the royal court. Neither he nor Jesse is described as arranging a scheme to seize the throne.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill understand the departure of the Spirit especially in terms of the gifts that equipped Saul to rule. They read the distressing spirit as acting under God’s permission in judgment. Their explanation takes the spiritual language seriously while distinguishing God’s authority from approval of evil.

Wesley, Henry and Gill also recognize the relief associated with David’s music. Wesley and Gill allow both the ordinary calming effect of music and God’s particular purpose in bringing David into favor. The chapter describes the relief but does not provide a treatment formula or identify a modern diagnosis for Saul.

Wesley sees providence preparing David for future service through this unexpected opening. Saul’s need and David’s gift bring them together. Saul’s present affection is part of the story and should be allowed its place before their later conflict develops.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
God’s care can reach a troubled person through the gifts and presence of another. David’s music brings real relief even in the household of a failing king. A wider Christian expression of comfort shared through others appears in 2 Corinthians 1:3–7: God comforts His people so they can comfort others, with that comfort overflowing through Christ.

Colossians 3:12–17 brings compassion, patience and the singing of psalms and hymns into the shared life of Christ’s people. These passages do not turn David’s playing into a universal method of driving away spirits. They extend the theme of gifts used in loving service, so that what one person has received becomes help for another.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 17:1-11
passages.section_title: Why does Goliath’s challenge leave Israel afraid?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now the Philistines gathered their forces for war at Socoh in Judah, and they camped between Socoh and Azekah in Ephes-dammim. 2 Saul and the men of Israel assembled and camped in the Valley of Elah, arraying themselves for battle against the Philistines. 3 The Philistines stood on one hill and the Israelites stood on another, with the valley between them. 4 Then a champion named Goliath, who was from Gath, came out from the Philistine camp. He was six cubits and a span in height, 5 and he had a bronze helmet on his head. He wore a bronze coat of mail weighing five thousand shekels, 6 and he had armor of bronze on his legs and a javelin of bronze slung between his shoulders. 7 The shaft of his spear was like a weaver’s beam, and its iron point weighed six hundred shekels. In addition, his shield bearer went before him. 8 And Goliath stood and shouted to the ranks of Israel, “Why do you come out and array yourselves for battle? Am I not a Philistine, and are you not servants of Saul? Choose one of your men and have him come down against me. 9 If he is able to fight me and kill me, then we will be your servants. But if I prevail against him and kill him, then you shall be our servants and work for us.” 10 Then the Philistine said, “I defy the ranks of Israel this day! Give me a man to fight!” 11 On hearing the words of the Philistine, Saul and all the Israelites were dismayed and greatly afraid.

passages.context_html:
The Philistines and Israelites face each other across the Valley of Elah. Goliath comes forward from the Philistine camp with imposing armor, weapons and a shield-bearer. The extended description helps us feel the danger before anyone agrees to fight him.

The Hebrew phrase behind champion is אִישׁ הַבֵּנַיִם, ish habbenayim (eesh hah-beh-NAH-yim). Brown–Driver–Briggs explains it as the man of the space between two armies. Goliath steps into that space and proposes that one man from each side decide the outcome.

His terms concern far more than personal honor: the losing side will serve the winner. He defies Israel and demands an opponent. Saul and the people are dismayed and afraid. The king they wanted to fight their battles is facing a challenge from which the whole army shrinks.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Henry place the army’s fear within the larger question of dependence on God. An impressive king and previous victories do not make the people self-sufficient. Gill explains Goliath’s title in terms of standing between the armies or offering a duel, consistent with the scene’s stated challenge.

There is a difference in the ancient copies over Goliath’s height. The USCCB study notes report four cubits and a span in the Greek text and a Dead Sea Scroll, alongside the six-cubit reading used here in the BSB. Whatever reading is considered, the account describes a formidable opponent and sets his visible strength against the trust in God that David will show.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 17:12-37
passages.section_title: What does David see that the frightened army is missing?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 Now David was the son of a man named Jesse, an Ephrathite from Bethlehem of Judah who had eight sons. And in the days of Saul, Jesse was old and well along in years. 13 The three older sons of Jesse had followed Saul into battle: The firstborn was Eliab, the second was Abinadab, and the third was Shammah. 14 And David was the youngest. The three oldest had followed Saul, 15 but David went back and forth from Saul to tend his father’s sheep in Bethlehem. 16 For forty days the Philistine came forward every morning and evening to take his stand. 17 One day Jesse said to his son David, “Take this ephah of roasted grain and these ten loaves of bread for your brothers and hurry to their camp. 18 Take also these ten portions of cheese to the commander of their unit. Check on the welfare of your brothers and bring back an assurance from them. 19 They are with Saul and all the men of Israel in the Valley of Elah, fighting against the Philistines.” 20 So David got up early in the morning, left the flock with a keeper, loaded up, and set out as Jesse had instructed him. He reached the camp as the army was marching out to its position and shouting the battle cry. 21 And Israel and the Philistines arrayed in formation against each other. 22 Then David left his supplies in the care of the quartermaster and ran to the battle line. When he arrived, he asked his brothers how they were doing. 23 And as he was speaking with them, suddenly the champion named Goliath, the Philistine from Gath, came forward from the ranks of the Philistines and shouted his usual words, which David also heard. 24 When all the men of Israel saw Goliath, they fled from him in great fear. 25 Now the men of Israel had been saying, “Do you see how this man keeps coming out to defy Israel? To the man who kills him the king will give great riches. And he will give him his daughter in marriage and exempt his father’s house from taxation in Israel.” 26 David asked the men who were standing with him, “What will be done for the man who kills this Philistine and removes this disgrace from Israel? Just who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?” 27 The people told him about the offer, saying, “That is what will be done for the man who kills him.” 28 Now when David’s oldest brother Eliab heard him speaking to the men, his anger burned against David. “Why have you come down here?” he asked. “And with whom did you leave those few sheep in the wilderness? I know your pride and wickedness of heart—you have come down to see the battle!” 29 “What have I done now?” said David. “Was it not just a question?” 30 Then he turned from him toward another and asked about the offer, and those people answered him just as the first ones had answered. 31 Now David’s words were overheard and reported to Saul, who sent for him. 32 And David said to Saul, “Let no man’s heart fail on account of this Philistine. Your servant will go and fight him!” 33 But Saul replied, “You cannot go out against this Philistine to fight him. You are just a boy, and he has been a warrior from his youth.” 34 David replied, “Your servant has been tending his father’s sheep, and whenever a lion or a bear came and carried off a lamb from the flock, 35 I went after it, struck it down, and delivered the lamb from its mouth. If it reared up against me, I would grab it by its fur, strike it down, and kill it. 36 Your servant has killed lions and bears; this uncircumcised Philistine will be like one of them, for he has defied the armies of the living God.” 37 David added, “The LORD, who delivered me from the claws of the lion and the bear, will deliver me from the hand of this Philistine.” “Go,” said Saul, “and may the LORD be with you.”

passages.context_html:
David travels between Saul’s service and his father’s sheep. Jesse sends him to carry food to his three oldest brothers and their commander and to bring back news of their welfare. David leaves the flock with a keeper. His arrival at the battle is an act of service to his family.

Goliath has challenged Israel morning and evening for forty days. David hears him and watches the men recoil. The troops describe the reward for defeating him: wealth, marriage to the king’s daughter, and freedom from taxation for the victor’s father’s household. David asks about that offer but also identifies the deeper offense as defying the armies of the living God.

Eliab accuses David of pride and neglecting the sheep. David replies with a question and continues asking the others. His words reach Saul, and he volunteers to fight. Saul sees a young man facing someone trained for war from his youth.

David answers by recalling God’s help while he protected his flock from lions and bears. He does not claim that the danger is imaginary. He believes the LORD who delivered him before will deliver him now. Saul gives permission and sends him with a blessing.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry emphasizes David’s patience under his brother’s anger as well as his courage before Goliath. He sees the timing of Jesse’s errand as God directing ordinary affairs toward a larger purpose. Wesley likewise encourages perseverance when expected supporters become critics.

The shepherding experience is central to Henry’s reading. David has already risked himself to protect animals entrusted to him, and he credits God for the rescue. Henry compares that care with Christ as the good shepherd. David’s readiness grows from remembered help and responsibility, rather than merely a wish to appear brave.

Wesley reads David’s confidence as concern for God and His people. Eliab’s accusation is therefore not treated as the narrator’s verdict on David. The earlier statement that he left a keeper with the sheep also matters when considering the charge of neglect.

passages.god_plan_html:
Henry’s comparison has a clear New Testament anchor in John 10:11–18. Jesus describes the good shepherd staying with the sheep when danger comes, in contrast with the hired hand who abandons them. David’s care for the flock gives a concrete picture of protection that costs the shepherd something.

Jesus carries the picture beyond David’s experience. He willingly lays down His life and takes it up again, gathering His sheep under one shepherd. The connection is about faithful care and rescue, with the greater saving work belonging to Jesus Himself.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 17:38-58
passages.section_title: How does David’s victory become a rescue for the whole army?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 38 Then Saul clothed David in his own tunic, put a bronze helmet on his head, and dressed him in armor. 39 David strapped his sword over the tunic and tried to walk, but he was not accustomed to them. “I cannot walk in these,” David said to Saul. “I am not accustomed to them.” So David took them off. 40 And David took his staff in his hand, selected five smooth stones from the brook, and put them in the pouch of his shepherd’s bag. And with his sling in hand, he approached the Philistine. 41 Now the Philistine came closer and closer to David, with his shield-bearer before him. 42 When the Philistine looked and saw David, he despised him because he was just a boy, ruddy and handsome. 43 “Am I a dog,” he said to David, “that you come at me with sticks?” And the Philistine cursed David by his gods. 44 “Come here,” he called to David, “and I will give your flesh to the birds of the air and the beasts of the field!” 45 But David said to the Philistine, “You come against me with sword and spear and javelin, but I come against you in the name of the LORD of Hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied. 46 This day the LORD will deliver you into my hand. This day I will strike you down, cut off your head, and give the carcasses of the Philistine army to the birds of the air and the creatures of the earth. Then the whole world will know that there is a God in Israel. 47 And all those assembled here will know that it is not by sword or spear that the LORD saves; for the battle is the LORD’s, and He will give all of you into our hands.” 48 As the Philistine started forward to attack him, David ran quickly toward the battle line to meet him. 49 Then David reached into his bag, took out a stone, and slung it, striking the Philistine on the forehead. The stone sank into his forehead, and he fell facedown on the ground. 50 Thus David prevailed over the Philistine with a sling and a stone; without a sword in his hand he struck down the Philistine and killed him. 51 David ran and stood over him. He grabbed the Philistine’s sword and pulled it from its sheath and killed him, and he cut off his head with the sword. When the Philistines saw that their hero was dead, they turned and ran. 52 Then the men of Israel and Judah charged forward with a shout and pursued the Philistines to the entrance of Gath and to the gates of Ekron. And the bodies of the Philistines were strewn along the Shaaraim road to Gath and Ekron. 53 When the Israelites returned from their pursuit of the Philistines, they plundered their camps. 54 David took the head of the Philistine and brought it to Jerusalem, and he put Goliath’s weapons in his own tent. 55 As Saul had watched David going out to confront the Philistine, he said to Abner the commander of the army, “Abner, whose son is this young man?” “As surely as you live, O king,” Abner replied, “I do not know.” 56 “Find out whose son this young man is!” said the king. 57 So when David returned from killing the Philistine, still holding his head in his hand, Abner took him and brought him before Saul. 58 “Whose son are you, young man?” asked Saul. “I am the son of your servant Jesse of Bethlehem,” David replied.

passages.context_html:
David tries Saul’s equipment but takes it off because he is not accustomed to it. He carries his staff, sling and five smooth stones. The account gives the number of stones without explaining a hidden meaning for it.

Goliath despises the young opponent and threatens him. David answers that he comes in the name of the LORD. He declares two purposes for the victory: the world will know there is a God in Israel, and those gathered will learn that the LORD’s saving power does not depend on sword or spear.

David runs forward and strikes Goliath with a sling stone. He then takes Goliath’s sword and cuts off his head. The Philistines flee, and the Israelites pursue and plunder the camp. The victory one man wins changes the position of the army that had been afraid to answer the challenge.

The account records Goliath’s head being brought to Jerusalem and his weapons being kept. It then returns to Saul’s question to Abner as David went out: whose son is he? After the battle, David identifies himself as Jesse’s son from Bethlehem. The question concerns his family, which also matters to the reward described earlier.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill understand David’s rejection of the armor as lack of experience using it. The BSB expresses this as not being accustomed to it. The statement does not require making David’s own untested readiness for kingship the direct meaning of the words.

Henry emphasizes the humility and faith in David’s answer and God receiving the credit for the outcome. He also applies the conflict to Christian resistance against the devil. That is a wider devotional comparison; Goliath remains a human opponent in the story.

The closing family question is explained in different ways. Gill highlights Saul’s need to know the family into which his daughter might marry, while also discussing forgetfulness. Wesley allows several reasons Saul might not recall the earlier servant clearly. The USCCB study notes instead understand parts of the chapter as a different account of David’s introduction brought together with the preceding story. These are explanations of how the accounts fit; Saul’s actual question is about whose son David is.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The victory invites a comparison with rescue won by one on behalf of others. Israel benefits from David defeating the opponent it feared. The New Testament describes a greater deliverance in Hebrews 2:14–18: Jesus shares our humanity, breaks the devil’s power through His death, and frees those enslaved by fear of death.

This is a parallel, rather than a New Testament statement that every weapon or stone predicts a separate event. David defeats an enemy in battle; Jesus overcomes through His own death and saving work. First Corinthians 15:54–58 places the final victory over death in Him and calls His people to steadfast service because of the victory they receive.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 18:1-4
passages.section_title: How does Jonathan welcome the man who could become his rival?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 After David had finished speaking with Saul, the souls of Jonathan and David were knit together, and Jonathan loved him as himself. 2 And from that day Saul kept David with him and did not let him return to his father’s house. 3 Then Jonathan made a covenant with David because he loved him as himself. 4 And Jonathan removed the robe he was wearing and gave it to David, along with his tunic, his sword, his bow, and his belt.
paragraphs: 1 After David had finished speaking with Saul, the souls of Jonathan and David were knit together, and Jonathan loved him as himself. 2 And from that day Saul kept David with him and did not let him return to his father’s house. 3 Then Jonathan made a covenant with David because he loved him as himself. 4 And Jonathan removed the robe he was wearing and gave it to David, along with his tunic, his sword, his bow, and his belt.

passages.context_html:
David has just answered Saul’s question about his family after defeating Goliath. Jonathan, Saul’s son, forms a deep friendship with him. While Saul keeps David at court, Jonathan makes a covenant with him and gives him his robe, tunic and weapons. His love takes the form of a commitment and costly gifts.

The Hebrew verb behind the picture of their souls being knit together is qashar (kah-SHAR), meaning to bind or tie. Brown–Driver–Briggs includes this verse as an expression of strong affection. It helps us picture a close bond, rather than a casual acquaintance.

The reader already knows David has been anointed to replace Saul. That gives the friendship added weight: the king’s son welcomes the young man whose rise could threaten his own future. Jonathan’s generosity will stand in sharp contrast to his father’s growing hostility.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley, Henry and Gill read this as a sincere friendship expressed through a covenant. They emphasize Jonathan’s willingness to honor David rather than resent him. Henry especially sees God’s grace at work in love that is not controlled by the desire for status.

The gifts receive different emphasis. Gill sees Jonathan clothing and equipping David for life at court and in the army. The USCCB Bible notes also see the exchange pointing toward David as the future heir. The scene can carry that larger meaning without describing a formal transfer of the throne at this moment.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Jonathan’s friendship gives a picture of love that willingly gives something up for another. In John 15:12–17, Jesus commands His disciples to love one another as He has loved them, and speaks of laying down one’s life for friends. He brings that love to its fullest expression through His own death.

This is a parallel in the character of love, rather than a claim that John directly interprets Jonathan’s gifts. The connection helps us see why friendship matters in God’s purposes: His people are called to seek another person’s good, even when generosity costs them comfort or standing.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 18:5-16
passages.section_title: Why does David’s success make Saul afraid?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 So David marched out and prospered in everything Saul sent him to do, and Saul set him over the men of war. And this was pleasing in the sight of all the people, and of Saul’s officers as well. 6 As the troops were returning home after David had killed the Philistine, the women came out of all the cities of Israel to meet King Saul with singing and dancing, with joyful songs, and with tambourines and other instruments. 7 And as the women danced, they sang out: “Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands.” 8 And Saul was furious and resented this song. “They have ascribed tens of thousands to David,” he said, “but only thousands to me. What more can he have but the kingdom?” 9 And from that day forward Saul kept a jealous eye on David. 10 The next day a spirit of distress sent from God came upon Saul, and he prophesied inside the house while David played the harp as usual. Now Saul was holding a spear, 11 and he hurled it, thinking, “I will pin David to the wall.” But David eluded him twice. 12 So Saul was afraid of David, because the LORD was with David but had departed from Saul. 13 Therefore Saul sent David away and gave him command of a thousand men. David led the troops out to battle and back, 14 and he continued to prosper in all his ways, because the LORD was with him. 15 When Saul saw that David was very successful, he was afraid of him. 16 But all Israel and Judah loved David, because he was leading them out to battle and back.

And this was pleasing in the sight of all the people, and of Saul’s officers as well. 6 As the troops were returning home after David had killed the Philistine, the women came out of all the cities of Israel to meet King Saul with singing and dancing, with joyful songs, and with tambourines and other instruments. 7 And as the women danced, they sang out: “Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands.” 8 And Saul was furious and resented this song. “They have ascribed tens of thousands to David,” he said, “but only thousands to me. What more can he have but the kingdom?” 9 And from that day forward Saul kept a jealous eye on David.

10 The next day a spirit of distress sent from God came upon Saul, and he prophesied inside the house while David played the harp as usual. Now Saul was holding a spear, 11 and he hurled it, thinking, “I will pin David to the wall.” But David eluded him twice. 12 So Saul was afraid of David, because the LORD was with David but had departed from Saul. 13 Therefore Saul sent David away and gave him command of a thousand men. David led the troops out to battle and back, 14 and he continued to prosper in all his ways, because the LORD was with him. 15 When Saul saw that David was very successful, he was afraid of him. 16 But all Israel and Judah loved David, because he was leading them out to battle and back.

passages.context_html:
David succeeds in the work Saul gives him, and his appointment pleases both the people and Saul’s officers. Then the women celebrating the victory praise David more highly than Saul. Saul hears a threat to his kingdom in their song and begins watching David with jealousy.

The next scene brings that hostility into the house. While David plays the harp, Saul throws his spear at him. David escapes twice. Saul then sends him out to command a thousand men, but distance does not remove Saul’s fear. David continues to succeed, and the people love him as their military leader.

The Hebrew word behind David’s success, sakal (sah-KAHL), can describe acting wisely as well as having success. Brown–Driver–Briggs includes both senses and lists these verses. The picture is of capable, wise service that goes well, with the account repeatedly pointing to the LORD’s presence.

Saul’s response moves in the opposite direction. Instead of welcoming help against Israel’s enemies, he becomes afraid of the man God is helping. David’s growing place among the people and Saul’s loss of favor become increasingly visible.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry emphasizes how quickly celebration becomes danger for David: the praise of others stirs Saul’s envy. Wesley likewise reads Saul’s fear in light of God’s presence with David. The passage presents a king who increasingly treats a faithful servant as a rival.

The BSB says Saul prophesied while the spirit of distress was upon him. Gill discusses several readings, including genuine prophetic speech, imitation of prophetic behavior and disturbed speech or actions; he favors the last. Wesley also reads it as disordered behavior. These are explanations of an unusual scene, rather than a reason to replace the BSB wording or assign Saul a modern medical diagnosis.

Henry contrasts David’s service with Saul’s violence and credits God’s care for David’s safety. David’s restraint matters, and so does his escape. The story does not make remaining within reach of a violent person a condition of faithfulness.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
Henry connects David’s endurance under hostility with the call to consider Christ in Hebrews 12:1–3. David serves while being treated as a threat; Jesus endures the hostility of sinners and the shame of the cross, then sits at God’s right hand.

The parallel points beyond a young commander surviving jealousy. God’s saving purpose reaches its fullness through Jesus, who endures suffering and gives His people reason to keep going. Hebrews calls readers to fix their eyes on Him when opposition makes them weary.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 18:17-30
passages.section_title: How does Saul turn a marriage offer into a trap?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 Then Saul said to David, “Here is my older daughter Merab. I will give her to you in marriage. Only be valiant for me and fight the LORD’s battles.” But Saul was thinking, “I need not raise my hand against him; let the hand of the Philistines be against him.” 18 And David said to Saul, “Who am I, and what is my family or my father’s clan in Israel, that I should become the son-in-law of the king?” 19 So when it was time to give Saul’s daughter Merab to David, she was given in marriage to Adriel of Meholah. 20 Now Saul’s daughter Michal loved David, and when this was reported to Saul, it pleased him. 21 “I will give her to David,” Saul thought, “so that she may be a snare to him, and the hand of the Philistines may be against him.” So Saul said to David, “For a second time now you can be my son-in-law.” 22 Then Saul ordered his servants, “Speak to David privately and tell him, ‘Behold, the king is pleased with you, and all his servants love you. Now therefore, become his son-in-law.’” 23 But when Saul’s servants relayed these words to David, he replied, “Does it seem trivial in your sight to be the son-in-law of the king? I am a poor man and lightly esteemed.” 24 And the servants told Saul what David had said. 25 Saul replied, “Say to David, ‘The king desires no other dowry but a hundred Philistine foreskins as revenge on his enemies.’” But Saul intended to cause David’s death at the hands of the Philistines. 26 When the servants reported these terms to David, he was pleased to become the king’s son-in-law. Before the wedding day arrived, 27 David and his men went out and killed two hundred Philistines. He brought their foreskins and presented them as payment in full to become the king’s son-in-law. Then Saul gave his daughter Michal to David in marriage. 28 When Saul realized that the LORD was with David and that his daughter Michal loved David, 29 he grew even more afraid of David. So from then on Saul was David’s enemy. 30 Every time the Philistine commanders came out for battle, David was more successful than all of Saul’s officers, so that his name was highly esteemed.

So from then on Saul was David’s enemy. 30 Every time the Philistine commanders came out for battle, David was more successful than all of Saul’s officers, so that his name was highly esteemed.

passages.context_html:
Saul offers David his older daughter Merab if David will fight his battles. The account tells us Saul’s hidden intention: he wants the Philistines to kill David for him. David responds with humility about his family’s standing, and Merab is eventually married to someone else.

When Saul learns that Michal loves David, he sees another opportunity. He has his servants encourage the marriage privately. David objects that he is poor and of little standing, so Saul asks for a hundred Philistine foreskins instead of an ordinary marriage payment. The gruesome demand turns enemy deaths into the price of joining the royal family.

Saul hopes David will die trying to meet the terms. Instead, David and his men kill two hundred Philistines, and David presents the full payment. Saul gives him Michal. The attempt to remove David has brought him into Saul’s own family.

The chapter closes with Saul recognizing both the LORD’s presence with David and Michal’s love for him. He becomes still more afraid and remains David’s enemy. David’s continued military success deepens the conflict rather than ending it.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley, Henry and Gill read the marriage offers in light of the intention the passage states openly: Saul is trying to arrange David’s death. His religious language about fighting the LORD’s battles does not make that intention faithful to God.

Henry emphasizes David’s careful conduct under provocation. Wesley also highlights his humility about entering the royal family. Their reading recognizes David’s restraint without turning Saul’s cruelty into an acceptable way for a ruler or parent to behave.

These commentators also see God preserving David through Saul’s schemes. The result reverses the king’s intention: David survives, gains a place in the royal family and grows in public esteem. The account explains this particular turn in David’s calling; it does not promise that every faithful person will gain status through danger.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Saul’s plans cannot stop the royal purpose God has begun with David. A related theme comes into view in Acts 4:24–30, where the believers pray about the rulers who opposed Jesus. They recognize that even the conspiracy against Him did not defeat what God had determined to accomplish.

This is a wider pattern, rather than a claim that Acts identifies Saul’s marriage plot as a direct prediction of the cross. God works through opposition without making the opponents’ cruelty good. For Jesus, that purpose includes suffering and death, followed by resurrection; for the praying believers, it becomes a reason to ask for courage to keep speaking His word.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 19:1-24
passages.section_title: How is David protected when Saul openly orders his death?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then Saul ordered his son Jonathan and all his servants to kill David. But Jonathan delighted greatly in David, 2 so he warned David, saying, “My father Saul intends to kill you. Be on your guard in the morning; find a secret place and hide there. 3 I will go out and stand beside my father in the field where you are, so I can ask about you. And if I find out anything, I will tell you.” 4 Then Jonathan spoke well of David to his father Saul and said to him, “The king should not sin against his servant David; he has not sinned against you. In fact, his actions have been highly beneficial to you. 5 He took his life in his hands when he struck down the Philistine, and the LORD worked a great salvation for all Israel. You saw it and rejoiced, so why would you sin against innocent blood by killing David for no reason?” 6 Saul listened to the voice of Jonathan and swore an oath: “As surely as the LORD lives, David will not be put to death.” 7 So Jonathan summoned David and told him all these things. Then Jonathan brought David to Saul, and David was with Saul as before. 8 When war broke out again, David went out and fought the Philistines and struck them with such a mighty blow that they fled before him. 9 But as Saul was sitting in his house with his spear in his hand, a spirit of distress from the LORD came upon him. While David was playing the harp, 10 Saul tried to pin him to the wall with his spear. But David eluded him and the spear struck the wall. And David fled and escaped that night. 11 Then Saul sent messengers to David’s house to watch him and kill him in the morning. But David’s wife Michal warned him, “If you do not run for your life tonight, tomorrow you will be dead!” 12 So Michal lowered David from the window, and he ran away and escaped. 13 Then Michal took a household idol and laid it in the bed, placed some goat hair on its head, and covered it with a garment. 14 When Saul sent the messengers to seize David, Michal said, “He is ill.” 15 But Saul sent the messengers back to see David and told them, “Bring him up to me in his bed so I can kill him.” 16 And when the messengers entered, there was the idol in the bed with the goat hair on its head. 17 And Saul said to Michal, “Why did you deceive me like this? You sent my enemy away, and he has escaped!” Michal replied, “He said to me, ‘Help me get away, or I will kill you!’” 18 So David ran away and escaped. And he went to Samuel at Ramah and told him all that Saul had done to him. Then he and Samuel went to Naioth and stayed there. 19 When Saul was told that David was at Naioth in Ramah, 20 he sent messengers to seize him. But when they saw the group of prophets prophesying, with Samuel leading them, the Spirit of God came upon them, and Saul’s messengers also began to prophesy. 21 When this was reported to Saul, he sent more messengers, but they began to prophesy as well. So Saul tried again and sent messengers a third time, and even they began to prophesy. 22 Finally, Saul himself left for Ramah and came to the large cistern at Secu, where he asked, “Where are Samuel and David?” “At Naioth in Ramah,” he was told. 23 So Saul went to Naioth in Ramah. But the Spirit of God came upon even Saul, and he walked along prophesying until he came to Naioth in Ramah. 24 Then Saul stripped off his robes and also prophesied before Samuel. And he collapsed and lay naked all that day and night. That is why it is said, “Is Saul also among the prophets?”

Then he and Samuel went to Naioth and stayed there. 19 When Saul was told that David was at Naioth in Ramah, 20 he sent messengers to seize him. So Saul tried again and sent messengers a third time, and even they began to prophesy. 22 Finally, Saul himself left for Ramah and came to the large cistern at Secu, where he asked, “Where are Samuel and David?” “At Naioth in Ramah,” he was told. 23 So Saul went to Naioth in Ramah. But the Spirit of God came upon even Saul, and he walked along prophesying until he came to Naioth in Ramah. 24 Then Saul stripped off his robes and also prophesied before Samuel. And he collapsed and lay naked all that day and night. That is why it is said, “Is Saul also among the prophets?”

passages.context_html:
Saul now tells Jonathan and his servants openly to kill David. Jonathan warns his friend, then appeals to his father: David has served him well, risked his life against Goliath and helped bring deliverance to Israel. Killing him would shed innocent blood. Saul listens and swears that David will not be put to death, allowing a brief return to their earlier relationship.

That peace does not last. After another victory over the Philistines, David is playing the harp when Saul throws his spear. David escapes, but Saul sends men to watch his house and kill him in the morning. Michal warns him and lowers him through a window. She puts a household idol in his bed, adds goat hair and a covering, and says he is ill. The disguise delays the messengers until David has gone.

When Saul confronts her, Michal says David threatened to kill her if she would not help him escape. That is her explanation to Saul; the account has just shown her urging David to flee. The household idol is also an unsettling detail, but the chapter does not identify its owner or explain why it was there.

David reaches Samuel at Ramah, and they stay at Naioth. Saul sends three groups to seize him. Each begins to prophesy when the Spirit of God comes upon them. Finally Saul goes himself, only to be overtaken in the same way. He strips off his robes and lies naked before Samuel through the day and night. The king who came to capture David is unable to carry out his purpose.

The question about Saul being among the prophets recalls his earlier experience in chapter10. Here it comes at a very different point in his life: the Spirit interrupts his pursuit of the man he wants dead. David is protected through Jonathan’s appeal, Michal’s help and an intervention Saul cannot overpower.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley highlights Jonathan’s courage in defending an innocent friend before his own father. He takes Saul’s oath as sincerely intended at that moment. Henry emphasizes the deeper hostility that survives the temporary change. These readings agree about the brief reconciliation while placing different weight on Saul’s immediate intention and lasting character.

Henry distinguishes Michal’s effort to gain time for David from her false statements, especially the claim that he threatened her. Gill also sees that accusation as protecting herself at David’s expense. The rescue is real, but these commentators do not treat every action taken during it as morally approved.

Wesley and Gill explain Saul’s nakedness as the removal of his outer garments. They read the scene as God restraining him long enough for David to escape. The BSB retains the description naked; the commentators’ explanation concerns the extent of undress, rather than a different event.

Henry draws a further distinction between receiving a striking spiritual gift and having a changed heart. Saul’s prophesying does not erase his pursuit of David. The event shows God’s power over him without announcing that his character has been restored.

The USCCB Bible notes see a tension between Saul appearing before Samuel here and the statement in 15:35 that Samuel did not visit Saul again, and read it as evidence of different accounts brought together. Gill’s comment on 15:35 distinguishes Samuel visiting Saul from Saul coming to Samuel. These are explanations of how the accounts relate; the narrative here places Saul before Samuel.
