passages.god_plan_html:
Psalm59 places this danger within David’s life of prayer: its heading identifies the time when Saul sent men to watch his house and kill him. The psalm moves from an urgent plea for rescue to confidence that God is his fortress. David’s innocence of the accusation does not mean he feels no fear or has no need to ask for help.

That theme of refuge reaches further in Hebrews6:17–20. Those who take hold of God’s promised hope are encouraged by His faithfulness, and their secure hope rests in Jesus, who has entered God’s presence on their behalf. This is a shared theme, rather than a claim that Hebrews directly interprets David’s escape.

God’s purpose is larger than keeping one night free from danger. David’s rescue preserves the life of the king God has chosen, while his prayer gives later readers words for trusting God under threat. In Christ, the invitation to seek refuge rests on a hope that reaches beyond immediate circumstances.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 20:1-9
passages.section_title: How can David find out whether he is safe?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then David fled from Naioth in Ramah. He came to Jonathan and asked, “What have I done? What is my iniquity? How have I sinned against your father, that he wants to take my life?” 2 “Far from it!” Jonathan replied. “You will not die. Indeed, my father does nothing, great or small, without telling me. So why would he hide this matter from me? This cannot be true!” 3 But David again vowed, “Your father knows very well that I have found favor in your eyes, and he has said, ‘Jonathan must not know of this, or he will be grieved.’ As surely as the LORD lives and as you yourself live, there is but a step between me and death.” 4 Then Jonathan said to David, “Whatever you desire, I will do for you.” 5 So David told him, “Look, tomorrow is the New Moon, and I am supposed to dine with the king. Instead, let me go and hide in the field until the third evening from now. 6 If your father misses me at all, tell him, ‘David urgently requested my permission to hurry to Bethlehem, his hometown, because there is an annual sacrifice for his whole clan.’ 7 If he says, ‘Good,’ then your servant is safe, but if he is enraged, you will know he has evil intentions. 8 Therefore show kindness to your servant, for you have brought me into a covenant with you before the LORD. If there is iniquity in me, then kill me yourself; why should you bring me to your father?” 9 “Never!” Jonathan replied. “If I ever found out that my father had evil intentions against you, would I not tell you?”

passages.context_html:
David leaves Naioth and goes to Jonathan with a painful question: what has he done to deserve Saul’s pursuit? Jonathan cannot believe his father intends to kill him without first telling him. David answers that Saul knows about their friendship and could be keeping Jonathan in the dark.

They agree to test Saul’s response to David’s absence from the coming New Moon meal. Jonathan is to say that David requested leave for a family sacrifice at Bethlehem. A calm response would point toward safety; anger would reveal a settled intention to harm him.

David appeals to the covenant they made before the LORD. He asks Jonathan to deal kindly and honestly with him. Even his stark offer that Jonathan should kill him if he is guilty presses the same point: he is asking for justice rather than being handed over to someone determined to destroy him.

Jonathan promises to tell him if he discovers danger. Their friendship must now do more than offer reassurance. It must face the evidence about Saul and provide a way for David to act on what they learn.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands Jonathan’s confidence in light of Saul’s oath in chapter19. David’s warning challenges that confidence: a father who once spoke openly may now conceal his intentions. Jonathan’s willingness to investigate matters more than simply repeating that everything will be well.

There are different readings of the Bethlehem explanation. Wesley and Gill allow that David really went there before returning to hide in the field. A reading that takes his hiding as covering the whole interval understands the explanation as a cover story. The passage records the plan and his hiding, without separately narrating a journey to Bethlehem.

Henry sees David’s trials as preparation for the responsibilities ahead and Jonathan’s practical help as true friendship. That reading recognizes a purpose beyond the immediate danger without making Saul’s treatment of an innocent man just.

passages.god_plan_html:
David has been chosen for kingship, but the way ahead includes fear, uncertainty and dependence on help. His calling does not make every difficult question disappear. The larger biblical theme is that God can form faith through trials while bringing His people toward what He has promised.

1 Peter 1:3–9 places that theme in the living hope given through Jesus’ resurrection. Grief and tested faith sit alongside an inheritance God preserves. This does not make Saul’s violence good or promise believers a throne like David’s. It shows how present hardship need not cancel the future God has opened through Christ.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 20:10-29
passages.section_title: What does Jonathan ask David to remember beyond this crisis?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 Then David asked Jonathan, “Who will tell me if your father answers you harshly?” 11 “Come,” he replied, “let us go out to the field.” So the two of them went out into the field, 12 and Jonathan said, “By the LORD, the God of Israel, I will sound out my father by this time tomorrow or the next day. If he is favorable toward you, will I not send for you and tell you? 13 But if my father intends to bring evil on you, then may the LORD punish me, and ever so severely, if I do not tell you and send you on your way in safety. May the LORD be with you, just as He has been with my father. 14 And as long as I live, treat me with the LORD’s loving devotion, that I may not die, 15 and do not ever cut off your loving devotion from my household—not even when the LORD cuts off every one of David’s enemies from the face of the earth.” 16 So Jonathan made a covenant with the house of David, saying, “May the LORD hold David’s enemies accountable.” 17 And Jonathan had David reaffirm his vow out of love for him, for Jonathan loved David as he loved himself. 18 Then Jonathan said to David, “Tomorrow is the New Moon, and you will be missed, because your seat will be empty. 19 When you have stayed three days, hurry down to the place you hid on the day this trouble began, and remain beside the stone Ezel. 20 I will shoot three arrows to the side of it, as if I were aiming at a target. 21 Then I will send a boy and say, ‘Go, find the arrows!’ Now, if I expressly say to him, ‘Look, the arrows are on this side of you; So now, if I have found favor in your eyes, please let me go and see my brothers.’ That is why he has not come to the king’s table.”

24 So David hid in the field, and when the New Moon had come, the king sat down to eat. 25 He sat in his usual place by the wall, opposite Jonathan and beside Abner, but David’s place was empty. 26 Saul said nothing that day because he thought, “Something has happened to David to make him ceremonially unclean—surely he is unclean.” 27 But on the day after the New Moon, the second day, David’s place was still empty, and Saul asked his son Jonathan, “Why hasn’t the son of Jesse come to the meal either yesterday or today?” 28 Jonathan answered, “David urgently requested my permission to go to Bethlehem, 29 saying, ‘Please let me go, because our clan is holding a sacrifice in the city, and my brother has told me to be there. So now, if I have found favor in your eyes, please let me go and see my brothers.’ That is why he has not come to the king’s table.”

passages.context_html:
David asks how he will learn Saul’s answer if it is dangerous for Jonathan to approach him openly. They go into the field, where Jonathan promises before the LORD to investigate and send him away safely if necessary.

Jonathan also asks something for the future: David must continue showing kindness to him and his household, even after David’s enemies are defeated. Their promise now expressly reaches beyond the two friends to their families. Jonathan looks toward David’s future while asking that his own family not be forgotten.

The word translated loving devotion is hesed (KHEH-sed). Brown–Driver–Briggs gives kindness and goodness, and specifically includes these verses among acts of kindness between people. Here the covenant gives that kindness a lasting shape: it must continue when the immediate need has passed.

Jonathan arranges an arrow signal. Arrows on the near side will mean safety; arrows beyond the boy will mean David must leave. At the meal, David’s seat is empty. Saul first assumes he is ceremonially unclean, but on the second day he asks where he is. Jonathan gives the explanation about Bethlehem. Saul’s response comes in the next passage.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill see the covenant extending from the two friends to their households. Their emphasis is on promises that continue beyond a change in power. Jonathan is doing more than securing an immediate escape for David; he asks for kindness that will protect his family’s future.

Gill explains the LORD’s kindness as kindness pleasing to God, modeled on His care and promised before Him. The language holds affection and faithfulness together. It does not reduce the agreement to a useful bargain that either friend can forget once he no longer needs help.

Henry sees Jonathan’s loyalty as love overcoming ambition and self-interest. His future might seem to depend on David failing, yet he binds his family’s hopes to friendship with David. The LORD is repeatedly named as witness, giving the promises a seriousness beyond private convenience.

passages.god_plan_html:
The promise bears fruit in 2 Samuel 9:1–13. David seeks someone from Saul’s household to whom he can show kindness for Jonathan’s sake. He restores land to Jonathan’s son Mephibosheth and welcomes him to eat at his table like one of his own sons. A promise made while David was in danger becomes lasting care when he has power.

There is a helpful parallel with God’s gracious welcome in Ephesians 2:1–10. God makes people alive with Christ and displays His kindness through Him; salvation is His gift, rather than something earned by works. David’s care gives us a human picture of kindness received because of another, while God’s grace in Christ reaches further than any human king’s generosity.

This comparison does not make Mephibosheth’s disability a symbol of personal sin or make every part of the story a hidden code. It draws attention to the welcome itself: faithful love makes room at the table for someone who did not win it through achievement.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 20:30-42
passages.section_title: What does loyalty cost Jonathan and David?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 30 Then Saul’s anger burned against Jonathan, and he said to him, “You son of a perverse and rebellious woman! Do I not know that you have chosen the son of Jesse to your own shame and to the shame of the mother who bore you? 31 For as long as the son of Jesse lives on this earth, neither you nor your kingdom shall be established. Now send for him and bring him to me, for he must surely die!” 32 “Why must he be put to death?” Jonathan replied. “What has he done?” 33 Then Saul hurled his spear at Jonathan to kill him. So Jonathan knew that his father was determined to kill David. 34 Jonathan got up from the table in fierce anger and did not eat any food that second day of the month, for he was grieved by his father’s shameful treatment of David. 35 In the morning Jonathan went out to the field for the appointment with David, and a small boy was with him. 36 He said to the boy, “Run and find the arrows I shoot.” And as the boy ran, Jonathan shot an arrow beyond him. 37 When the boy reached the place where Jonathan’s arrow had fallen, Jonathan called to him, “Isn’t the arrow beyond you?” 38 Then Jonathan cried out, “Hurry! Make haste! Do not delay!” So the boy picked up the arrow and returned to his master. 39 But the boy did not know anything; only Jonathan and David knew the arrangement. 40 Then Jonathan gave his equipment to the boy and said, “Go, take it back to the city.” 41 When the young man had gone, David got up from the south side of the stone, fell facedown, and bowed three times. passages.context_html:
Saul’s anger breaks into insults and a demand for David’s death. He tells Jonathan that David’s survival prevents Jonathan’s kingdom from being established. The choice Saul presents is clear: preserve the family’s claim to power by handing over David.

Jonathan asks again what David has done to deserve death. Saul answers by throwing his spear at his own son. The attack removes Jonathan’s uncertainty about his father’s intention. He leaves the table angry and grieved by Saul’s treatment of David.

The next morning Jonathan uses the agreed signal, shooting an arrow beyond the boy and calling him farther on. After sending the boy back to the city with his equipment, he meets David. David bows, and the friends kiss and weep. Their promise remains, but David must leave.

Jonathan sends him away with the LORD as witness between their families. David departs and Jonathan returns to the city. This painful separation is not their final meeting: 1 Samuel 23:16–18 later describes Jonathan going to encourage David in God.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley highlights the bitter irony in Saul’s actions. He claims to be protecting Jonathan’s future, then tries to kill Jonathan himself. The danger comes from the king’s anger, while the supposed rival is the man Jonathan is protecting.

Henry reads Jonathan’s choice as accepting the cost of identifying with someone God favors. Gill emphasizes the friendship and respect shown in the farewell. David’s tears do not erase his faith or make his loss insignificant; he is leaving people and a life he loves.

Gill reads the final promise as a commitment between both men and their descendants, with God as witness. Separation does not dissolve it. The peace Jonathan speaks concerns that continuing faithfulness, even though he cannot offer David a safe return to Saul’s court.

passages.god_plan_html:
Jonathan refuses to make family advantage a reason to betray an innocent friend. His decision illustrates a wider biblical tension: faithfulness to God can cost a person the approval of those closest to him.

In Matthew 10:34–39, Jesus warns that following Him can bring division within a household and calls His disciples to love Him above even their closest family ties. This is a parallel about costly loyalty, rather than a claim that every family disagreement repeats David’s story. Jesus calls people to follow Him, not to seek conflict or excuse cruelty toward relatives.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 21:1-7
passages.section_title: Why does the priest give David bread reserved for the priests?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then David came to Nob, to Ahimelech the priest. And when Ahimelech met David, he trembled and asked him, “Why are you alone? Why is no one with you?” 2 “The king has given me a mission,” David replied. “He told me no one is to know about the mission on which I am sending you. And I have directed my young men to meet me at a certain place. 3 Now then, what do you have on hand? Give me five loaves of bread, or whatever can be found.” 4 “There is no common bread on hand,” the priest replied, “but there is some consecrated bread—provided that the young men have kept themselves from women.” 5 David answered, “Women have indeed been kept from us, as is usual when I set out. And the bodies of the young men are holy even on common missions. How much more so today!” 6 So the priest gave him the consecrated bread, since there was no bread there but the Bread of the Presence, which had been removed from before the LORD and replaced with hot bread on the day it was taken away. 7 Now one of Saul’s servants was there that day, detained before the LORD. And his name was Doeg the Edomite, the chief shepherd for Saul.
paragraphs: 1 Then David came to Nob, to Ahimelech the priest. And when Ahimelech met David, he trembled and asked him, “Why are you alone? Why is no one with you?” 2 “The king has given me a mission,” David replied. “He told me no one is to know about the mission on which I am sending you. And I have directed my young men to meet me at a certain place. 3 Now then, what do you have on hand? Give me five loaves of bread, or whatever can be found.”

4 “There is no common bread on hand,” the priest replied, “but there is some consecrated bread—provided that the young men have kept themselves from women.” 5 David answered, “Women have indeed been kept from us, as is usual when I set out. And the bodies of the young men are holy even on common missions. How much more so today!” 6 So the priest gave him the consecrated bread, since there was no bread there but the Bread of the Presence, which had been removed from before the LORD and replaced with hot bread on the day it was taken away. 7 Now one of Saul’s servants was there that day, detained before the LORD. And his name was Doeg the Edomite, the chief shepherd for Saul.

passages.context_html:
David comes to Ahimelech the priest at Nob after separating from Jonathan. The priest is alarmed to see him without the company he expects. David says the king has sent him on a secret mission and that his young men are elsewhere. The reader knows he is fleeing from Saul, so the explanation hides the danger surrounding his visit.

David asks for five loaves or whatever food is available. Ahimelech has no ordinary bread on hand, but he has consecrated bread. He asks whether the young men have kept themselves from women, and David assures him that they are holy. The concern is ritual fitness for receiving the sacred food.

The Bread of the Presence had been removed and replaced with fresh bread. Leviticus 24:5–9 directs that twelve loaves be set before the LORD each Sabbath and that the bread belong to Aaron and his sons to eat in a holy place. Ahimelech gives this bread to David in his need.

The account also names a witness: Doeg the Edomite, Saul’s chief shepherd, is there, detained before the LORD. His presence will become important in the next chapter. Here, his reason for being detained is not explained.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Henry read David’s claim of a royal mission as a lie driven by fear. They distinguish his genuine need from the means he uses to obtain help. David’s earlier courage does not make him beyond criticism when he is afraid.

Henry and Gill understand Ahimelech’s gift as mercy responding to necessity. They connect it with Jesus’ later use of this event: the bread’s sacred purpose does not make a hungry person’s need unimportant.

Wesley discusses whether David’s reference to holy vessels concerns bodies or equipment; the BSB uses bodies. The practical issue in the exchange is whether David and the young men are fit to receive the bread. It need not become a judgment that ordinary marriage is sinful.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus Himself brings this event into His teaching in Matthew 12:1–8. When His hungry disciples are accused over picking grain on the Sabbath, He points to David and his companions eating the consecrated bread. He then speaks of the priests’ Sabbath service and declares that One greater than the temple is present.

His conclusion brings mercy and His own authority together: the innocent should not be condemned, and the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath. The story of David’s need helps explain the work of the greater King. God’s holy purposes are not served by using religious observance to overlook people who need mercy.

Jesus’ use of the bread incident does not require approval of David’s misleading account to Ahimelech. It directs our attention to the mercy shown in feeding him and to Jesus’ authority to explain the purpose of the law.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 21:8-15
passages.section_title: Where can David turn when even his escape brings danger?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 Then David asked Ahimelech, “Is there not a spear or sword on hand here? For I have brought neither my sword nor my weapons with me, because the king’s mission was urgent.” 9 The priest replied, “The sword of Goliath the Philistine, whom you killed in the Valley of Elah, is here; it is wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod. If you want, you may take it. For there is no other but this one here.” And David said, “There is none like it; give it to me.” 10 That day David fled from Saul and went to Achish king of Gath. 11 But the servants of Achish said to him, “Is this not David, the king of the land? Did they not sing about him in their dances, saying: ‘Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands’?” 12 Now David took these words to heart and was very much afraid of Achish the king of Gath. 13 So he changed his behavior before them and feigned madness in their hands; he scratched on the doors of the gate and let his saliva run down his beard. 14 Then Achish said to his servants, “Look, you can see that the man is insane! Why have you brought him to me? 15 Am I in need of madmen, that you have brought this man to rave in my presence? Must this man come into my house?”
paragraphs: 8 Then David asked Ahimelech, “Is there not a spear or sword on hand here? For I have brought neither my sword nor my weapons with me, because the king’s mission was urgent.” 9 The priest replied, “The sword of Goliath the Philistine, whom you killed in the Valley of Elah, is here; it is wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod. If you want, you may take it. For there is no other but this one here.” And David said, “There is none like it; give it to me.”

10 That day David fled from Saul and went to Achish king of Gath. 11 But the servants of Achish said to him, “Is this not David, the king of the land? Did they not sing about him in their dances, saying: ‘Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands’?” 12 Now David took these words to heart and was very much afraid of Achish the king of Gath. 13 So he changed his behavior before them and feigned madness in their hands; he scratched on the doors of the gate and let his saliva run down his beard. 14 Then Achish said to his servants, “Look, you can see that the man is insane! Why have you brought him to me? 15 Am I in need of madmen, that you have brought this man to rave in my presence? Must this man come into my house?”

passages.context_html:
David asks Ahimelech for a spear or sword, again saying that the king’s mission was urgent. The only available weapon is Goliath’s sword, wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod. David asks to take it. The weapon recalls the victory that first brought him into national attention.

He then goes to Achish, king of Gath. But Achish’s servants recognize him and repeat the song celebrating his victories. They even call him king of the land. The man escaping Israel’s king is now known among Israel’s enemies, and he becomes deeply afraid.

David pretends to be insane, scratching on the gate doors and letting saliva run down his beard. Achish reacts with irritation and refuses to welcome him into his house. The appearance of helplessness makes David seem unsuitable for the king’s company.

The scene is a sharp change from David facing Goliath. He is still the man God has chosen, but he is now a frightened fugitive whose reputation makes finding safety difficult. The passage shows his actions and fear without giving a full explanation of everything he hoped to achieve by entering Gath.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill see Goliath’s sword as a reminder of God’s earlier deliverance as well as a useful weapon. On that reading, taking the sword need not mean David has abandoned trust in God. The object recalls what God has already done.

Henry views the behavior at Gath as a humiliating sign that David’s faith and courage are wavering. Gill instead allows the disguise as a strategy for escaping an enemy. The difference concerns how to assess his method of escape, rather than whether he pretended: the BSB explicitly says that he feigned madness.

Wesley allows that Achish may have recognized the performance and chosen to dismiss him anyway. Gill treats the king as driving away someone he regards as unfit for his household. The text records Achish’s response without telling us whether he saw through the disguise.

The title king of the land is also read in more than one way. Wesley and Gill discuss David’s prominence as Israel’s victorious commander as well as possible knowledge of his future kingship. The servants’ words show that he is famous; they do not tell us how much the speakers know about Samuel’s anointing.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The headings of Psalm 56 and Psalm 34 connect David’s prayers with danger in Gath and his feigned insanity. Psalm 34 names the ruler Abimelech, while this account calls him Achish. These psalms give us more than the outward scene: David brings fear to God, thanks Him for deliverance and teaches others to seek refuge in Him.

In 1 Peter 3:8–18, Peter takes up Psalm 34’s call to truthful speech, doing good and pursuing peace. He applies it to people facing hostility and directs them to honor Christ as Lord. Their hope rests in the righteous Christ, who suffered for the unrighteous to bring them to God.

This connection allows rescue and growth to stand together. David can thank God for bringing him through danger while learning how to live faithfully. The Christian hope Peter describes likewise includes God hearing His people, a clear conscience under pressure and salvation through Jesus; it does not depend on never feeling afraid.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 22:1-5
passages.section_title: Who joins David when he has a cave instead of a palace?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 So David left Gath and took refuge in the cave of Adullam. When his brothers and the rest of his father’s household heard about it, they went down to him there. 2 And all who were distressed or indebted or discontented rallied around him, and he became their leader. About four hundred men were with him. 3 From there David went to Mizpeh of Moab, where he said to the king of Moab, “Please let my father and mother stay with you until I learn what God will do for me.” 4 So he left them in the care of the king of Moab, and they stayed with him the whole time David was in the stronghold. 5 Then the prophet Gad said to David, “Do not stay in the stronghold. Depart and go into the land of Judah.” So David left and went to the forest of Hereth.

When his brothers and the rest of his father’s household heard about it, they went down to him there. 2 And all who were distressed or indebted or discontented rallied around him, and he became their leader. About four hundred men were with him.

3 From there David went to Mizpeh of Moab, where he said to the king of Moab, “Please let my father and mother stay with you until I learn what God will do for me.” 4 So he left them in the care of the king of Moab, and they stayed with him the whole time David was in the stronghold. 5 Then the prophet Gad said to David, “Do not stay in the stronghold. Depart and go into the land of Judah.” So David left and went to the forest of Hereth.

passages.context_html:
David leaves Gath and takes refuge in the cave of Adullam. His brothers and the rest of his father’s household come to him. Others gather too: people in distress, in debt or discontented. About four hundred men accept him as their leader. The future king’s following begins among people whose lives are already troubled.

David also seeks safety for his parents. He asks the king of Moab to care for them until he learns what God will do for him. They remain there while David is in the stronghold. His own uncertainty does not make him forget their needs.

Then the prophet Gad tells him to leave the stronghold and go into Judah. David follows the direction and goes to the forest of Hereth. He has followers and help, but his circumstances still require movement and dependence rather than a settled royal home.

Psalm 142 is headed as David’s prayer when he was in the cave. It gives voice to being overwhelmed, crying for help and seeking God as refuge. The heading does not name which cave, so the prayer helps us hear David’s experience without fixing its exact moment beyond what it says.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry emphasizes how God begins great work through people who appear weak, and how David cares for his parents while facing danger himself. The followers’ distress does not prevent them from having a place in what God is doing.

Wesley and Gill distinguish gathering indebted people from authorizing injustice. They do not read David’s leadership as permission to evade every rightful obligation. The group is described by its troubles; the account does not declare every man a criminal.

Wesley reads David’s request concerning his parents as trust in God’s wisdom and care while he waits for direction. Henry also sees the concern for them as an example of honoring parents. The king’s future calling does not make ordinary family responsibility beneath him.

passages.god_plan_html:
Henry and Gill draw a comparison between David receiving distressed people and Christ receiving those who come to Him. David’s small, troubled gathering gives a picture of a kingdom whose beginnings do not look impressive by ordinary measures of power.

1 Corinthians 1:26–31 makes the larger principle clear. God’s calling does not depend on worldly wisdom, influence or noble birth. His people receive their righteousness, holiness and redemption in Christ, leaving their boast in the Lord.

This is a parallel, rather than a claim that Paul directly interprets the cave of Adullam. It helps explain why troubled people need not be written off as having nothing to offer. God can make people who need help part of His work of caring for others.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 22:6-23
passages.section_title: What happens when Saul treats help for David as treason?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 Soon Saul learned that David and his men had been discovered. At that time Saul was sitting under the tamarisk tree on the hill at Gibeah, with his spear in hand and all his servants standing around him. 7 Then Saul said to his servants, “Listen, men of Benjamin! Is the son of Jesse giving all of you fields and vineyards and making you commanders of thousands or hundreds? 8 Is that why all of you have conspired against me? Not one of you told me that my own son had made a covenant with the son of Jesse. Not one of you has shown concern for me or revealed to me that my son has stirred up my own servant to lie in wait against me, as is the case today.” 9 But Doeg the Edomite, who had stationed himself with Saul’s servants, answered: “I saw the son of Jesse come to Ahimelech son of Ahitub at Nob. 10 Ahimelech inquired of the LORD for him and gave him provisions. He also gave him the sword of Goliath the Philistine.” 11 Then the king sent messengers to summon Ahimelech the priest, the son of Ahitub, and his father’s whole family, who were priests at Nob. And all of them came to the king. 12 “Listen now, son of Ahitub,” said Saul. “Here I am, my lord,” he replied. 13 And Saul asked him, “Why have you and the son of Jesse conspired against me? You gave him bread and a sword and inquired of God for him so that he could rise up against me to lie in wait, as he is doing today.” 14 Ahimelech answered the king, “Who among all your servants is as faithful as David, the king’s son-in-law, the captain of your bodyguard and honored in your house? 15 Was that day the first time I inquired of God for him? Far be it from me! Let not the king accuse your servant or any of my father’s household, for your servant knew nothing of this whole affair—not in part or in whole.” 16 But the king replied, “You will surely die, Ahimelech, you and all your father’s house!” 17 Then the king ordered the guards at his side, “Turn and kill the priests of the LORD, because they too sided with David. For they knew he was fleeing, but they did not tell me.” But the king’s servants would not lift a hand to strike the priests of the LORD. 18 So the king ordered Doeg, “You turn and strike down the priests!” And Doeg the Edomite turned and struck down the priests himself. On that day he killed eighty-five men who wore the linen ephod. 19 He also put to the sword Nob, the city of the priests, with its men and women, children and infants, oxen, donkeys, and sheep. 20 But one of the sons of Ahimelech son of Ahitub escaped. His name was Abiathar, and he fled to David. 21 And Abiathar told David that Saul had killed the priests of the LORD. 22 Then David said to Abiathar, “I knew that Doeg the Edomite was there that day, and that he was sure to tell Saul. I myself am responsible for the lives of everyone in your father’s house. 23 Stay with me; do not be afraid, for he who seeks your life is seeking mine as well. You will be safe with me.”

On that day he killed eighty-five men who wore the linen ephod. 19 He also put to the sword Nob, the city of the priests, with its men and women, children and infants, oxen, donkeys, and sheep.

20 But one of the sons of Ahimelech son of Ahitub escaped. His name was Abiathar, and he fled to David. 21 And Abiathar told David that Saul had killed the priests of the LORD. 22 Then David said to Abiathar, “I knew that Doeg the Edomite was there that day, and that he was sure to tell Saul. I myself am responsible for the lives of everyone in your father’s house. 23 Stay with me; do not be afraid, for he who seeks your life is seeking mine as well. You will be safe with me.”

passages.context_html:
Saul hears that David and his men have been found. He appeals to his servants as men of Benjamin, asking whether David will give them the land and commands Saul can offer. He accuses them of conspiring against him and claims Jonathan has stirred David to ambush him. These are Saul’s accusations, rather than evidence that David is preparing such an attack.

Doeg reports David’s visit to Ahimelech at Nob: the priest inquired of the LORD for him and gave him food and Goliath’s sword. Saul summons Ahimelech and his family and accuses them of conspiracy. Ahimelech answers that David is a trusted servant and the king’s own son-in-law. He denies knowing anything about the alleged plot.

Saul orders the priests killed. His guards refuse to strike the priests of the LORD, so he turns to Doeg. Doeg kills eighty-five men who wore the linen ephod. He also kills the people of Nob, including women, children and infants, along with their animals. The accusation ends in a massacre of priests and their town.

Abiathar, one of Ahimelech’s sons, escapes and tells David. David accepts responsibility, saying he had known Doeg would tell Saul. He asks Abiathar to stay with him and promises protection because they face the same enemy. The man Saul pursues becomes a refuge for the surviving priest.

Psalm 52 names Doeg’s report in its heading. It condemns destructive speech and confidence in wrongdoing, then turns to trust in God’s enduring loving devotion. It gives the report a moral setting beyond its value as information to a king.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads Saul’s charges as the product of jealous hostility rather than a fair judgment. Gill emphasizes Ahimelech’s innocence of the alleged conspiracy and the guards’ refusal to commit the killing. Royal authority does not make the order right.

Wesley and Gill note the deceit in reporting the assistance without the explanation David had given Ahimelech. Gill allows the inquiry of God to have happened even though chapter21 did not describe it; Ahimelech’s answer in verse15 supports that reading. The priest’s ordinary service to someone he believed loyal is turned into evidence of treason.

Henry and Gill take David’s admission seriously: his concealment and his failure to act on the danger he recognized helped bring others into harm. That does not transfer Saul’s order or Doeg’s killings to David. The account gives space both to David accepting responsibility and to naming those who committed the violence.

Henry sees the shelter offered to Abiathar as a picture of refuge with the Son of David. David promises to care for someone who has suffered because their lives are threatened by the same king. His response moves beyond regret to practical protection.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
This tragedy belongs within the longer account of Eli’s household. 1 Samuel 2:27–36 had announced judgment on that priestly house. Later, 1 Kings 2:26–27 explicitly identifies Solomon’s removal of Abiathar from the priesthood as fulfilling the LORD’s word against Eli’s house. Abiathar’s escape preserves a life whose story continues into that later judgment.

That larger connection does not turn Saul’s cruelty into obedience. God had not commanded him to manufacture a conspiracy charge and slaughter the people of Nob. His purpose can continue through a history in which human beings remain responsible for doing wrong.

The same distinction appears at the center of the gospel in Acts 2:22–24. Peter speaks of Jesus being delivered up according to God’s plan while holding those who crucified Him accountable, and then announces His resurrection. This is a shared theme of God’s purpose continuing through human wrongdoing, rather than a claim that the massacre itself was good or a direct prediction of the cross.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 23:1-6
passages.section_title: Why does David risk helping Keilah while he is being hunted?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now it was reported to David, “Look, the Philistines are fighting against Keilah and looting the threshing floors.” 2 So David inquired of the LORD, “Should I go and attack these Philistines?” And the LORD said to David, “Go and attack the Philistines and save Keilah.” 3 But David’s men said to him, “Look, we are afraid here in Judah; how much more if we go to Keilah against the armies of the Philistines?” 4 Once again, David inquired of the LORD, and the LORD answered him: “Go at once to Keilah, for I will deliver the Philistines into your hand.” 5 Then David and his men went to Keilah, fought against the Philistines, and carried off their livestock, striking them with a mighty blow. So David saved the people of Keilah. 6 (Now Abiathar son of Ahimelech had brought the ephod with him when he fled to David at Keilah.)
paragraphs: 1 Now it was reported to David, “Look, the Philistines are fighting against Keilah and looting the threshing floors.” 2 So David inquired of the LORD, “Should I go and attack these Philistines?” And the LORD said to David, “Go and attack the Philistines and save Keilah.” 3 But David’s men said to him, “Look, we are afraid here in Judah; how much more if we go to Keilah against the armies of the Philistines?” 4 Once again, David inquired of the LORD, and the LORD answered him: “Go at once to Keilah, for I will deliver the Philistines into your hand.” 5 Then David and his men went to Keilah, fought against the Philistines, and carried off their livestock, striking them with a mighty blow. So David saved the people of Keilah. 6 (Now Abiathar son of Ahimelech had brought the ephod with him when he fled to David at Keilah.)

passages.context_html:
David hears that the Philistines are attacking Keilah and looting its threshing floors. Although he is still escaping Saul, he asks the LORD whether he should attack and save the town. The answer is to go.

His men are afraid. They already feel unsafe in Judah, and fighting the Philistine armies seems to add another danger. David asks again rather than simply dismissing their concern. The LORD repeats the direction and promises to deliver the Philistines into his hand.

David and his men go, defeat the attackers and carry off their livestock. Keilah is rescued. The account also reminds us that Abiathar brought the ephod when he fled to David. The surviving priest now accompanies the man Saul is pursuing.

The episode shows David carrying out the work of protecting Israel before he has the throne. His own unsettled circumstances do not keep him from responding to another community’s need.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill understand the second inquiry as reassurance for David’s men. Their fear is answered through another appeal to God and a clearer promise of victory, rather than David relying only on his authority as leader.

Henry emphasizes David’s willingness to act as a protector while being mistreated by the king. He sees an example of continuing to do good when service has brought little gratitude. The rescue directs David’s attention beyond his own danger.

Wesley and Gill associate the ephod with the high priest’s means of seeking God’s direction. The passage identifies Abiathar and the ephod, while leaving the precise way the answer was received undescribed.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
David’s rescue of Keilah shows leadership serving people in need while the leader himself bears hardship. It offers a helpful parallel with the kind of kingship Jesus reveals.

In Mark 10:42–45, Jesus teaches that greatness among His followers takes the form of service. He gives His own mission as the fullest example: He comes to serve and give His life as a ransom for many. David rescues one threatened community; Jesus gives Himself to bring a greater deliverance.

The connection is a parallel in serving and rescuing, rather than a claim that Mark directly identifies Keilah as a prediction. It helps us recognize why David’s care matters before he receives public power: a ruler’s calling is already visible in how he uses what he has for others.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 23:7-29
passages.section_title: How does God sustain David when every hiding place seems unsafe?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 When Saul was told that David had gone to Keilah, he said, “God has delivered him into my hand, for he has trapped himself by entering a town with gates and bars.” 8 Then Saul summoned all his troops to go to war at Keilah and besiege David and his men. 9 When David learned that Saul was plotting evil against him, he said to Abiathar the priest, “Bring the ephod.” 10 And David said, “O LORD, God of Israel, Your servant has heard that Saul intends to come to Keilah and destroy the city on my account. 11 Will the citizens of Keilah surrender me into his hand? Will Saul come down, as Your servant has heard? O LORD, God of Israel, please tell Your servant.” “He will,” said the LORD. 12 So David asked, “Will the citizens of Keilah surrender me and my men into the hand of Saul?” “They will,” said the LORD. 13 Then David and his men, about six hundred strong, set out and departed from Keilah, moving from place to place. When Saul was told that David had escaped from Keilah, he declined to go forth. 14 And David stayed in the wilderness strongholds and in the hill country of the Wilderness of Ziph. Day after day Saul searched for him, but God would not deliver David into his hand. 15 While David was in Horesh in the Wilderness of Ziph, he saw that Saul had come out to take his life. 16 And Saul’s son Jonathan came to David in Horesh and strengthened his hand in God, 17 saying, “Do not be afraid, for my father Saul will never lay a hand on you. And you will be king over Israel, and I will be your second-in-command. Even my father Saul knows this is true.” 18 So the two of them made a covenant before the LORD. And David remained in Horesh, while Jonathan went home. 19 Then the Ziphites came up to Saul at Gibeah and said, “Is not David hiding among us in the strongholds at Horesh, on the hill of Hachilah south of Jeshimon? 20 Now, O king, come down whenever your soul desires, and we will be responsible for delivering him into your hand.” 21 “May you be blessed by the LORD,” replied Saul, “for you have had compassion on me. 22 Please go and prepare further. Investigate and watch carefully where he goes and who has seen him there, for I am told that he is extremely cunning. 23 Observe and find out all the places where he hides. Then come back to me with certainty, and I will go with you. If he is in the land, I will search him out among all the clans of Judah.” 24 So they set out and went to Ziph ahead of Saul. Now David and his men were in the Wilderness of Maon in the Arabah south of Jeshimon, 25 and Saul and his men went to seek him. When David was told about it, he went down to the rock and stayed in the Wilderness of Maon. And when Saul heard of this, he pursued David there. 26 Saul was proceeding along one side of the mountain, and David and his men along the other side. Even though David was hurrying to get away, Saul and his men were closing in on David and his men to capture them. 27 Then a messenger came to Saul, saying, “Come quickly, for the Philistines have raided the land!” 28 So Saul broke off his pursuit of David and went to meet the Philistines. That is why that place is called Sela-hammahlekoth. 29 And David went up from there and lived in the strongholds of En-gedi.

passages.context_html:
Saul hears that David has entered Keilah and thinks its gates and bars will trap him. He claims God has handed David over. David instead asks the LORD what will happen: will Saul come, and will the citizens surrender him? On receiving the warning that they will, David leaves with about six hundred men. Saul then abandons the planned siege.

The pursuit continues in the wilderness. Jonathan comes to Horesh and strengthens David in God, affirming that David will become king. He hopes to serve as David’s second-in-command, and they make a covenant before the LORD. Jonathan then returns home while David remains in hiding.

The Ziphites report David’s whereabouts to Saul and offer to hand him over. Saul blesses them for their concern for him and demands detailed information about the hiding places. He pursues David into the Wilderness of Maon, where the two groups move on opposite sides of a mountain and Saul closes in.

At that moment a messenger reports a Philistine raid. Saul breaks off the pursuit to meet the attackers, and David moves to the strongholds of En-gedi. The escape brings the chapter’s earlier statement into focus: Saul searches day after day, but God does not deliver David into his hand.

The heading of Psalm 54 identifies the Ziphites’ report to Saul. Its plea for rescue and confidence in God as helper give words to faith under this threat.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley, Henry and Gill read the answers at Keilah as describing what would happen if David stayed. His departure changes the circumstances. The warning guides him into action; it is not a prediction that he must remain and be captured.

Henry sees Jonathan’s encouragement as friendship directing David toward God. Wesley reads his expectation of a second place as willingness to accept David’s kingship. Jonathan’s hope for his own role is not fulfilled: 1 Samuel 31:1–6 later records his death before David takes the throne.

Wesley and Gill understand the covenant here as a renewal of their friendship. The passage does not give new terms for a government appointment. Its emphasis is their commitment before the LORD in a time of danger.

Henry contrasts Saul’s religious language with his pursuit of David. Calling the informers blessed does not prove God approves the pursuit. Henry and Gill also see God’s care in the messenger arriving just as David is being surrounded. The needed escape comes through an interruption Saul has to answer.

passages.god_plan_html:
God’s sustaining care reaches David through both encouragement and a way of escape. Jonathan cannot remove the danger, but he helps David remember the future God has opened. The later interruption preserves David when human arrangements appear to be closing around him.

For Christ’s people, Hebrews 10:19–25 joins confidence in God with the work of encouraging one another. Jesus opens the way into God’s presence, God’s faithfulness gives reason to hold firmly to hope, and believers are to spur one another toward love and good deeds.

This is a shared theme of faith sustained in community, rather than a promise that every threatened believer will escape as David did. God’s purpose includes people helping one another keep trusting Him while the outcome is still unseen.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 24:1-15
passages.section_title: Why does David spare Saul when he has the chance to kill him?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 After Saul had returned from pursuing the Philistines, he was told, “David is in the wilderness of En-gedi.” 2 So Saul took three thousand chosen men from all Israel and went to look for David and his men in the region of the Rocks of the Wild Goats. 3 Soon Saul came to the sheepfolds along the road, where there was a cave, and he went in to relieve himself. And David and his men were hiding in the recesses of the cave. 4 So David’s men said to him, “This is the day about which the LORD said to you, ‘Behold, I will deliver your enemy into your hand, that you may do with him as you wish.’” Then David crept up and stealthily cut off a corner of Saul’s robe. 5 Afterward, David’s conscience was stricken because he had cut off the corner of Saul’s robe. 6 So he said to his men, “The LORD forbid that I should do such a thing to my master, the LORD’s anointed. May I never lift my hand against him, since he is the LORD’s anointed.” 7 With these words David restrained his men, and he did not let them rise up against Saul. Then Saul left the cave and went on his way. 8 After that, David got up, went out of the cave, and called out to Saul, “My lord the king!” When Saul looked behind him, David bowed facedown in reverence 9 and said to Saul, “Why do you listen to the words of men who say, ‘Look, David intends to harm you’? 10 Behold, this day you have seen with your own eyes that the LORD delivered you into my hand in the cave. I was told to kill you, but I spared you and said, ‘I will not lift my hand against my lord, since he is the LORD’s anointed.’ 11 See, my father, look at the corner of your robe in my hand. For I cut it off, but I did not kill you. Know and see that there is no evil or rebellion in my hands. I have not sinned against you, even though you are hunting me down to take my life. 12 May the LORD judge between you and me, and may the LORD take vengeance on you, but my hand will never be against you. 13 As the old proverb says, ‘Wickedness proceeds from the wicked.’ But my hand will never be against you. 14 Against whom has the king of Israel come out? Whom are you pursuing? A dead dog? A flea? 15 May the LORD be our judge and decide between you and me. May He take notice and plead my case and deliver me from your hand.”

passages.context_html:
Saul returns from pursuing the Philistines and takes three thousand chosen men to look for David near En-gedi. He enters a cave to relieve himself, unaware that David and his men are hiding farther inside. David’s men interpret the opportunity as the moment to deal with his enemy.

David creeps forward and cuts a corner from Saul’s robe, but afterward his conscience troubles him. The Hebrew word for the garment’s corner is kanaph (kah-NAHF). Brown–Driver–Briggs gives skirt, corner or loose end as its garment sense. The same word describes the hem Saul seized from Samuel in 1 Samuel 15:27–28, when the torn robe accompanied the announcement of Saul’s lost kingdom.

David refuses to lift his hand against the LORD’s anointed and restrains his men. After Saul leaves the cave, David follows and calls to him respectfully. He holds up the piece of robe as evidence that he could have killed Saul but chose to spare him.

He denies intending rebellion or harm and asks the LORD to judge between them, plead his case and deliver him. Calling himself a dead dog or a flea exposes how far the king’s pursuit exceeds the threat David presents. David seeks justice while refusing to make himself Saul’s executioner.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands the men’s appeal to God’s promise as their interpretation of David’s calling, rather than a recorded command to kill Saul. Henry makes the same distinction: the promise of a kingdom does not itself authorize murder as the means of obtaining it.

Gill reads David’s troubled conscience as regret for an indignity toward his sovereign, even though he has refused the greater harm his men urged. David then uses the cut cloth to demonstrate his restraint. His speech to Saul is a defense against treason and murderous intent, rather than an admission that he has been plotting Saul’s death.

Henry emphasizes David’s refusal to avenge himself and his choice to return good for evil. The appeal to God’s judgment makes room for justice without turning the chance to retaliate into a command to do so.

Wesley understands the cave visit as rest or sleep; Gill discusses that reading as well as relieving himself. The BSB uses the latter. The shared point is Saul’s vulnerability and David’s refusal to exploit it by killing him.

passages.god_plan_html:
David’s restraint illustrates the wider biblical call to leave personal vengeance with God. Romans 12:17–21 tells believers to refuse repayment of evil with evil, seek peace where possible and overcome evil with good. David’s appeal for God to judge gives a concrete picture of that trust.

The greater example is Jesus in 1 Peter 2:21–25. He does not retaliate against abuse but entrusts Himself to the One who judges justly, and He bears sins to bring people into a life of righteousness. David spares the king who threatens him; Jesus carries that self-giving faithfulness into His saving death.

This parallel does not make Saul’s conduct acceptable or require someone facing violence to remain within reach of it. David has fled danger and continues to seek deliverance. His refusal of vengeance belongs alongside that pursuit of safety and justice.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 24:16-22
passages.section_title: What changes when Saul sees that David has spared him?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 When David had finished saying these things, Saul called back, “Is that your voice, David my son?” Then Saul wept aloud 17 and said to David, “You are more righteous than I, for you have rewarded me with good, though I have rewarded you with evil. 18 And you have declared this day how you have treated me well, for when the LORD delivered me into your hand, you did not kill me. 19 When a man finds his enemy, does he let him go away unharmed? May the LORD reward you with good for what you have done for me this day. 20 Now I know for sure that you will be king and that the kingdom of Israel will be established in your hands. 21 So now, swear to me by the LORD that you will not cut off my descendants or wipe out my name from my father’s house.” 22 So David gave his oath to Saul. Then Saul returned home, but David and his men went up to the stronghold.

Then Saul returned home, but David and his men went up to the stronghold.

passages.context_html:
Saul answers David with tears and calls him his son. He acknowledges that David has treated him well while he has treated David badly. He recognizes the mercy of being spared and asks the LORD to reward David for it.

He also says that David will surely become king and that Israel’s kingdom will be established in his hands. He asks David to swear that he will not destroy Saul’s descendants or erase his family’s name. David gives his oath.

The encounter ends peacefully, but the two men go separate ways: Saul returns home, and David and his men go to the stronghold. The chapter records a real acknowledgment of David’s righteousness without presenting a return to their former life together.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley emphasizes Saul being moved by David’s kindness and acknowledging both David’s integrity and his own wrong. Henry and Gill stress the difference between being deeply affected and showing lasting repentance. Their caution concerns whether this recognition will change Saul’s conduct.

Wesley and Gill explain David’s return to the stronghold as caution learned from Saul’s earlier changes of mind. Mercy does not require him to assume the danger is over. The peaceful parting leaves room for both the oath and that practical caution.

The promise concerns Saul’s descendants and the preservation of his family’s name. Gill relates it to David’s later care for members of Saul’s house. It asks whether the future king will show mercy once he has power, continuing a concern already raised in David’s covenant with Jonathan.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 25:1
passages.section_title: How does Israel respond to Samuel’s death?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 When Samuel died, all Israel gathered to mourn for him; and they buried him at his home in Ramah. Then David set out and went down to the Wilderness of Paran.
paragraphs: 1 When Samuel died, all Israel gathered to mourn for him; and they buried him at his home in Ramah. Then David set out and went down to the Wilderness of Paran.

passages.context_html:
Samuel dies, and Israel gathers to mourn and bury him at his home in Ramah. The man who served through the end of Eli’s household, the appointment of Saul and the anointing of David is gone. His death marks a major loss in the middle of the unresolved conflict between Saul and David.

David then moves into the Wilderness of Paran. The verse places national mourning beside the continued movement of the fugitive king. It does not say whether David attended the burial or explain his precise reason for leaving.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Henry emphasize Israel’s reason to grieve for someone who had prayed for them and taught them God’s way. Their reading treats the mourning as recognition of faithful service, rather than a passing notice between adventures.

The brief report also closes Samuel’s personal part in the story while leaving the outcome of his work still unfolding. David has been anointed, but he has not yet become king.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 25:2-17
passages.section_title: Why does a request for food turn into a threat against a whole household?

For he is such a scoundrel that nobody can speak to him!”

passages.context_html:
Nabal is a wealthy Calebite with three thousand sheep and a thousand goats. His wife Abigail is intelligent and beautiful; he is harsh and evil in his dealings. During sheep shearing, David sends ten men with a peaceful greeting and asks for whatever food Nabal can spare.

David points to the shepherds’ experience near his men: they have not been harassed or suffered loss. A servant later confirms that David’s men were good to them and protected them day and night. The request comes in the setting of a feast, when Nabal has provisions for his shearers.

Nabal dismisses David as another servant breaking away from his master and refuses to share his food. David responds by arming about four hundred men, leaving two hundred with the supplies. One of Nabal’s servants goes to Abigail because the household is now in danger and Nabal will not listen.

The name Nabal plays an important part in the account. The Hebrew word nabal (nah-BAHL) describes a fool in a moral sense: someone insensitive to what is right, not simply someone who lacks intelligence. Brown–Driver–Briggs explains that sense, while its name entry points to Abigail’s own explanation later in verse25.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry contrasts Nabal’s abundance with his lack of generosity. His wealth cannot tell us whether he is wise or good. Wesley likewise reads David’s request in light of the help his men have given and the opportunity to relieve their need.

Henry also sharply criticizes David’s response. The man who spared Saul is now ready to destroy a household because of insulting words. Nabal’s wrongdoing does not make David’s threatened revenge right.

Wesley reads the servant’s appeal to Abigail as recognition that Nabal cannot be approached reasonably. The contrast places wisdom with the person willing to hear and act before the danger becomes irreversible.

passages.god_plan_html:
Nabal’s wealth and folly bring to mind Jesus’ warning in Luke 12:13–21. In the parable of the rich fool, a man plans security around an abundance of possessions, only to discover that he cannot command the length of his own life. Jesus warns against storing up wealth while failing to be rich toward God.

This is a parallel, rather than a claim that Jesus names Nabal as the man in His parable. Both accounts expose the limits of possessions as a measure of life. God’s purposes call for something deeper than having enough for oneself: wisdom recognizes dependence on Him and responsibility toward others.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 25:18-38
passages.section_title: How does Abigail keep David from shedding innocent blood?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 Then Abigail hurried and took two hundred loaves of bread, two skins of wine, five butchered sheep, five seahs of roasted grain, a hundred clusters of raisins, and two hundred cakes of figs. She loaded them on donkeys 19 and said to her young men, “Go ahead of me. I will be right behind you.” But she did not tell her husband Nabal. 20 As Abigail came riding her donkey into a mountain ravine, she saw David and his men coming down toward her, and she met them. 21 Now David had just said, “In vain I have protected all that belonged to this man in the wilderness. Nothing that belongs to him has gone missing, yet he has paid me back evil for good. 22 May God punish David, and ever so severely, if I let one male belonging to Nabal survive until morning.” 23 When Abigail saw David, she quickly got off the donkey, fell facedown, and bowed before him. 24 She fell at his feet and said, “My lord, may the blame be on me alone, but please let your servant speak to you; hear the words of your servant. 25 My lord should pay no attention to this scoundrel Nabal, for he lives up to his name: His name means Fool, and folly accompanies him. I, your servant, did not see my lord’s young men whom you sent. 26 Now, my lord, as surely as the LORD lives and you yourself live, since the LORD has held you back from bloodshed and from avenging yourself with your own hand, may your enemies and those who seek harm for my lord be like Nabal. 27 Now let this gift your servant has brought to my lord be given to the young men who follow you. 28 Please forgive your servant’s offense, for the LORD will surely make a lasting dynasty for my lord, because he fights the LORD’s battles. So she told him nothing until morning light. 37 In the morning when Nabal was sober, his wife told him about these events, and his heart failed within him, and he became like a stone. 38 About ten days later, the LORD struck Nabal dead.

passages.context_html:
Abigail quickly gathers food and wine, loads donkeys and sends her servants ahead. She follows without telling Nabal. When she meets David, he has already vowed to leave no male in Nabal’s household alive by morning. His anger has put people beyond Nabal himself in danger.

She bows before him and asks that the blame fall on her. She acknowledges Nabal’s folly and offers the provisions David requested. Then she appeals to David’s relationship with the LORD and his future as ruler: needless bloodshed and personal revenge would become a burden on his conscience.

Her image of David’s life held securely in the bundle of the living contrasts God’s care with enemies flung away like stones from a sling. It invites David to trust his life to God instead of securing his honor through killing.

David listens. He praises the LORD for sending Abigail and blesses her discernment in stopping him. He accepts the gift and sends her home in peace. The future king can still be corrected, and he recognizes the correction as a mercy.

At home Abigail finds Nabal very drunk and waits until morning to explain. When he hears, his heart fails within him and he becomes like a stone. About ten days later, the LORD strikes him dead. The account attributes his death to the LORD while leaving David free of the bloodshed he had planned.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill understand Abigail as offering to take Nabal’s blame upon herself while asking David to hear her. Henry emphasizes her humble, practical appeal. She neither excuses Nabal’s behavior nor accepts the destruction of his household as inevitable.

Wesley reads her action without Nabal’s permission in light of the immediate danger to him and the whole household. Her intervention protects lives. The scene calls for wisdom in an emergency rather than turning silence or unquestioning agreement into the measure of faithfulness.

Wesley, Gill and the USCCB Bible notes explain the bundle image as something precious held securely. The sling supplies the opposite picture of being cast away. The meaning concerns God’s keeping, without requiring a hidden meaning for every object.

Henry highlights David’s gratitude for being stopped. Wesley also observes that an oath to do wrong is not made good by carrying it out. David’s vow does not become a duty to kill the people Abigail has come to protect.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
Abigail steps between an angry man and a household facing destruction, offering to bear the blame and pleading for lives. There is a meaningful parallel with Christ’s work for others, provided we keep the difference clear: Abigail wins a reprieve through her appeal; she does not die to atone for Nabal.

1 Peter 3:18 states the greater reality in Jesus: the righteous Christ suffers for the unrighteous to bring people to God. His intervention reaches the problem of sin itself. Abigail’s costly willingness to act for others helps us appreciate self-giving care, while Jesus’ saving work goes beyond the human example.

The passage also shows God restraining the future king from doing evil through a wise person’s courage. David’s calling does not make him beyond correction. Receiving help to turn away from bloodshed is part of becoming fit to care for God’s people.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 25:39-44
passages.section_title: What follows Nabal’s death?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 39 On hearing that Nabal was dead, David said, “Blessed be the LORD, who has upheld my cause against the reproach of Nabal and has restrained His servant from evil. For the LORD has brought the wickedness of Nabal down upon his own head.” Then David sent word to Abigail, asking her to become his wife. 40 When his servants came to Abigail at Carmel, they said, “David has sent us to take you as his wife.” 41 She arose, bowed facedown, and said, “Here is your servant, ready to serve and to wash the feet of my lord’s servants.” 42 So Abigail hurried and got on a donkey, and attended by five of her maidens, she followed David’s messengers and became his wife. 43 David had also married Ahinoam of Jezreel. So she and Abigail were both his wives. 44 But Saul had given his daughter Michal, David’s wife, to Palti son of Laish, who was from Gallim.

For the LORD has brought the wickedness of Nabal down upon his own head.” Then David sent word to Abigail, asking her to become his wife. 40 When his servants came to Abigail at Carmel, they said, “David has sent us to take you as his wife.” 41 She arose, bowed facedown, and said, “Here is your servant, ready to serve and to wash the feet of my lord’s servants.” 42 So Abigail hurried and got on a donkey, and attended by five of her maidens, she followed David’s messengers and became his wife. 43 David had also married Ahinoam of Jezreel. So she and Abigail were both his wives. 44 But Saul had given his daughter Michal, David’s wife, to Palti son of Laish, who was from Gallim.

passages.context_html:
David responds to Nabal’s death by thanking the LORD for upholding his cause and keeping him from evil. He then sends a marriage proposal to Abigail. She accepts with an expression of humble service and follows his messengers, accompanied by five maidens.

The account adds that David has also married Ahinoam of Jezreel. Meanwhile Saul has given Michal, still identified here as David’s wife, to Palti son of Laish. David’s family life is becoming more complicated while his conflict with Saul continues.

The report of multiple wives belongs alongside the warning to Israel’s kings in Deuteronomy 17:16–20, including the command not to take many wives lest the heart go astray. Being chosen to rule does not place a king above the instruction given to him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Gill distinguishes David’s gratitude for being preserved from bloodshed from delight in death simply as revenge. Wesley is more critical of David’s response, calling it another instance of human weakness. The report gives David’s words without requiring readers to treat every part of his reaction as a universal model.

Henry emphasizes Abigail’s willingness to share David’s present troubles because she believes in his future. Gill separately criticizes the practice of multiple wives, even when found among otherwise faithful people. Admiration for Abigail’s wisdom need not become approval of every feature of David’s household.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 26:1-12
passages.section_title: Why does David refuse another chance to kill Saul?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then the Ziphites came to Saul at Gibeah and said, “Is not David hiding on the hill of Hachilah, opposite Jeshimon?” 2 So Saul, accompanied by three thousand chosen men of Israel, went down to the Wilderness of Ziph to search for David there. 3 Saul camped beside the road at the hill of Hachilah opposite Jeshimon, but David was living in the wilderness. When he realized that Saul had followed him there, 4 David sent out spies to verify that Saul had arrived. 5 Then David set out and went to the place where Saul had camped. He saw the place where Saul and Abner son of Ner, the general of his army, had lain down. Saul was lying inside the inner circle of the camp, with the troops camped around him. 6 And David asked Ahimelech the Hittite and Abishai son of Zeruiah, Joab’s brother, “Who will go down with me to Saul in the camp?” “I will go with you,” answered Abishai. 7 That night David and Abishai came to the troops, and Saul was lying there asleep in the inner circle of the camp, with his spear stuck in the ground by his head. And Abner and the troops were lying around him. 8 Abishai said to David, “Today God has delivered your enemy into your hand. Now, therefore, please let me thrust the spear through him into the ground with one stroke. I will not need to strike him twice!” 9 But David said to Abishai, “Do not destroy him, for who can extend a hand against the LORD’s anointed and be guiltless?” 10 David added, “As surely as the LORD lives, the LORD Himself will strike him down; either his day will come and he will die, or he will go into battle and perish. 11 But the LORD forbid that I should extend my hand against the LORD’s anointed. Instead, take the spear and water jug by his head, and let us go.” 12 So David took the spear and water jug by Saul’s head, and they departed. No one saw them or knew about it, nor did anyone wake up; they all remained asleep, because a deep sleep from the LORD had fallen on them.

passages.context_html:
The Ziphites again report David’s location, and Saul brings three thousand chosen men into the wilderness to find him. David confirms the pursuit through spies, locates the camp and sees Saul lying within its inner circle, with Abner and the troops around him.

Abishai volunteers to go down with David at night. Finding Saul asleep with his spear by his head, he offers to kill him with one stroke. He interprets the opportunity as God delivering David’s enemy into his hand.

David refuses. Saul is still the LORD’s anointed, and David will not make himself the one who kills him. He leaves Saul’s end with the LORD, whether through a direct stroke, the ordinary coming of death or battle. They take the spear and water jug instead.

No one sees them or wakes. The account explains that a deep sleep from the LORD has fallen on the camp. Once again Saul is vulnerable and David spares him, now making especially clear that the timing and manner of Saul’s end belong to God.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Henry read this as a refusal to force the promised kingdom into David’s hands through wrongdoing. Abishai’s confidence that the opportunity comes from God does not settle what they should do with it.

Gill understands David’s account of Saul’s possible deaths as reason to wait rather than hurry God’s judgment. It does not supply David with a private date or method of execution.

Henry emphasizes how helpless the powerful camp becomes under God’s hand. Gill likewise recognizes the sleep as the LORD’s action. The miracle leaves David with a choice about how he will treat the king whose life is within reach.

passages.god_plan_html:
Across the cave, Abigail’s intervention and this camp, David faces repeated occasions to decide whether he will trust God or grasp at an outcome through violence. The story gives a concrete picture of faith becoming visible in decisions under pressure.

James 1:2–5 describes tested faith developing perseverance toward maturity and directs those who lack wisdom to ask God. This is a shared theme of growth, rather than a rule that every hardship is a repeated examination with a predictable reward. God’s purpose includes forming people who can act wisely while they wait.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 26:13-20
passages.section_title: What does David’s appeal reveal about the cost of being driven away?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 Then David crossed to the other side and stood atop the mountain at a distance; there was a wide gulf between them. 14 And David shouted to the troops and to Abner son of Ner, “Will you not answer me, Abner?” “Who are you who calls to the king?” Abner replied. 15 So David said to Abner, “You are a man, aren’t you? And who in Israel is your equal? Why then did you not protect your lord the king when one of the people came to destroy him? 16 This thing you have done is not good. As surely as the LORD lives, all of you deserve to die, since you did not protect your lord, the LORD’s anointed. Now look around. Where are the king’s spear and water jug that were by his head?” 17 Then Saul recognized David’s voice and asked, “Is that your voice, David my son?” “It is my voice, my lord and king,” David said. 18 And he continued, “Why is my lord pursuing his servant? What have I done? What evil is in my hand? 19 Now please, may my lord the king hear the words of his servant: If the LORD has stirred you up against me, then may He accept an offering. But if men have done it, may they be cursed in the presence of the LORD! For today they have driven me away from sharing in the inheritance of the LORD, saying, ‘Go, serve other gods.’ 20 So do not let my blood fall to the ground far from the presence of the LORD. For the king of Israel has come out to look for a flea, like one who hunts a partridge in the mountains.”

17 Then Saul recognized David’s voice and asked, “Is that your voice, David my son?” “It is my voice, my lord and king,” David said. 18 And he continued, “Why is my lord pursuing his servant? What have I done? What evil is in my hand? 19 Now please, may my lord the king hear the words of his servant: If the LORD has stirred you up against me, then may He accept an offering. But if men have done it, may they be cursed in the presence of the LORD! For today they have driven me away from sharing in the inheritance of the LORD, saying, ‘Go, serve other gods.’ 20 So do not let my blood fall to the ground far from the presence of the LORD. For the king of Israel has come out to look for a flea, like one who hunts a partridge in the mountains.”

passages.context_html:
From across a wide gulf, David calls to Abner and challenges his failure to protect Saul. The missing spear and water jug show that someone reached the king. David’s words expose the difference between the danger Saul imagines from David and the protection David has actually given him.

Saul recognizes his voice. David asks what evil he has done and why the king is pursuing him. If the LORD is dealing with sin, he appeals for an acceptable offering; if men are stirring up the pursuit, he calls them to account before God.

He describes the cost as being driven away from sharing in the LORD’s inheritance, as though told to serve other gods. His concern reaches beyond losing a comfortable home. The pursuit threatens his place among God’s people and their shared worship.

David again pictures himself as a flea and compares the hunt to chasing a partridge in the mountains. He asks that his blood not be shed far from the LORD’s presence. A king’s campaign against one servant is threatening both his life and his belonging.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley, Henry and Gill read the proposed offering as an appeal to seek peace with God if sin lies behind the conflict. David frames possibilities rather than announcing that he knows a specific hidden offense for which God has ordered Saul to kill him.

Wesley and Gill understand the command to serve other gods as the effect of driving David out, not necessarily words someone has literally spoken. Separation from Israel’s land and worship exposes him to life among idolatrous peoples.

Henry emphasizes the spiritual harm of cutting someone off from worship. The complaint takes belonging seriously, while David’s own prayers throughout his flight show that distance does not place him beyond God’s hearing.
