deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
David’s grief over being pushed away from worship helps us see that God’s purposes concern more than individual survival. His people are called into a shared life before Him, and exclusion from that life is a serious wound.

Jesus opens a further horizon in John 4:19–24. Speaking with the Samaritan woman about the place of worship, He announces worship of the Father in spirit and truth that is not confined to their competing holy places. Salvation comes through the story of Israel, and the Father seeks true worshipers.

This is a wider biblical development, rather than a claim that David’s sentence directly predicts that conversation. It places his longing for access alongside the welcome Jesus announces, in which seeking the Father reaches beyond one location.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 26:21-25
passages.section_title: Why do David and Saul still go separate ways?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 Then Saul replied, “I have sinned. Come back, David my son. I will never harm you again, because today you considered my life precious. I have played the fool and have committed a grave error!” 22 “Here is the king’s spear,” David answered. “Let one of the young men come over and get it. 23 May the LORD repay every man for his righteousness and faithfulness. For the LORD delivered you into my hand today, but I would not extend my hand against the LORD’s anointed. 24 As surely as I valued your life today, so may the LORD value my life and rescue me from all trouble.” 25 Saul said to him, “May you be blessed, David my son. You will accomplish great things and will surely prevail.” So David went on his way, and Saul returned home.

I have played the fool and have committed a grave error!” 22 “Here is the king’s spear,” David answered. “Let one of the young men come over and get it. 23 May the LORD repay every man for his righteousness and faithfulness. For the LORD delivered you into my hand today, but I would not extend my hand against the LORD’s anointed. 24 As surely as I valued your life today, so may the LORD value my life and rescue me from all trouble.” 25 Saul said to him, “May you be blessed, David my son. You will accomplish great things and will surely prevail.” So David went on his way, and Saul returned home.

passages.context_html:
Saul confesses sin, says he has acted foolishly and promises not to harm David again. He recognizes that David valued his life when he could have taken it.

David offers the spear back through one of Saul’s young men. He asks the LORD to repay righteousness and faithfulness, and to value and rescue his life as he has valued Saul’s. Saul blesses him and speaks of his future success, but David goes on his way while Saul returns home.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley takes Saul’s confession here as a particularly sincere acknowledgment of wrong and notes that no further pursuit is recorded. Henry and Gill remain doubtful about lasting repentance. They agree about the words spoken while assessing their depth differently.

Henry directs attention to David’s hope for recompense from the LORD. Saul’s invitation does not become the foundation of his security. Their separate departure allows mercy and caution to remain together, rather than treating the confession as an automatic return to the earlier relationship.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 27:1-12
passages.section_title: What does David gain—and risk—by settling among the Philistines?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 David, however, said to himself, “One of these days now I will be swept away by the hand of Saul. There is nothing better for me than to escape to the land of the Philistines. Then Saul will stop searching for me all over Israel, and I will slip out of his hand.” 2 So David set out with his six hundred men and went to Achish son of Maoch, the king of Gath. 3 David and his men settled in Gath with Achish. Each man had his family with him, and David had his two wives: Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail of Carmel, the widow of Nabal. 4 And when Saul learned that David had fled to Gath, he no longer searched for him. 5 Then David said to Achish, “If I have found favor in your eyes, let me be assigned a place in one of the outlying towns, so I can live there. For why should your servant live in the royal city with you?” 6 That day Achish gave him Ziklag, and to this day it still belongs to the kings of Judah. 7 And the time that David lived in Philistine territory amounted to a year and four months. 8 Now David and his men went up and raided the Geshurites, the Girzites, and the Amalekites. (From ancient times these people had inhabited the land extending to Shur and Egypt.) 9 Whenever David attacked a territory, he did not leave a man or woman alive, but he took the flocks and herds, the donkeys, camels, and clothing. Then he would return to Achish, 10 who would ask him, “What have you raided today?” And David would reply, “The Negev of Judah,” or “The Negev of Jerahmeel,” or “The Negev of the Kenites.” 11 David did not leave a man or woman alive to be brought to Gath, for he said, “Otherwise they will report us, saying, ‘This is what David did.’” And this was David’s custom the whole time he lived in Philistine territory. 12 So Achish trusted David, thinking, “Since he has made himself an utter stench to his people Israel, he will be my servant forever.”

5 Then David said to Achish, “If I have found favor in your eyes, let me be assigned a place in one of the outlying towns, so I can live there. For why should your servant live in the royal city with you?” 6 That day Achish gave him Ziklag, and to this day it still belongs to the kings of Judah. 7 And the time that David lived in Philistine territory amounted to a year and four months.

8 Now David and his men went up and raided the Geshurites, the Girzites, and the Amalekites. (From ancient times these people had inhabited the land extending to Shur and Egypt.) 9 Whenever David attacked a territory, he did not leave a man or woman alive, but he took the flocks and herds, the donkeys, camels, and clothing. Then he would return to Achish, 10 who would ask him, “What have you raided today?” And David would reply, “The Negev of Judah,” or “The Negev of Jerahmeel,” or “The Negev of the Kenites.” 11 David did not leave a man or woman alive to be brought to Gath, for he said, “Otherwise they will report us, saying, ‘This is what David did.’” And this was David’s custom the whole time he lived in Philistine territory. 12 So Achish trusted David, thinking, “Since he has made himself an utter stench to his people Israel, he will be my servant forever.”

passages.context_html:
David tells himself that Saul will eventually kill him and decides that escape to Philistine territory is his best hope. He takes his six hundred men and their families to Achish at Gath. The move stops Saul’s pursuit, but it places the future king of Israel in the service of a Philistine ruler.

At David’s request, Achish gives him Ziklag as a place to live outside the royal city. David remains in Philistine territory for a year and four months. The note that Ziklag still belongs to Judah’s kings reflects the narrator’s own time.

From there David raids the Geshurites, Girzites and Amalekites. He takes livestock and clothing and leaves no man or woman alive. The account gives his reason for leaving no survivors: no one will be able to tell Achish what he has really been doing.

When Achish asks about the raids, David names areas associated with Judah and its neighbors. Achish believes David has turned his own people against him and will therefore remain his servant. The apparent security depends on a deception that will become dangerous when Achish expects him to fight Israel.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Henry criticize David’s fear as distrust of God’s promise after repeated protection. They recognize the immediate shelter he gains while questioning the reasoning that leads him there. The absence of a recorded inquiry contrasts with the earlier decisions he brought to the LORD.

Henry connects the raids with earlier judgment on peoples Israel had been commanded to defeat. That is his reading of their place in Israel’s history. Here the account expressly describes the killing of men and women and David’s concern to prevent reports reaching Gath; it gives no new command for these particular raids.

Wesley and Henry also condemn the misleading answers to Achish. Avoiding a plainly false sentence would not make speech honest if its purpose is to create a false impression. The USCCB Bible notes likewise identify the reports about Judah as deception.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
David’s calling does not remove the need to keep trusting God or to face the harm of his own choices. The chapter is part of a larger story in which God’s purposes continue while the chosen king still needs correction.

Hebrews 3:12–14 brings the danger of unbelief and sin’s deceit into the life of Christ’s people. It calls them to hold firmly to their confidence and to encourage one another daily. This is a shared theme, rather than a claim that Hebrews directly interprets David’s stay at Ziklag: people who have received God’s promises still need help to remain faithful to Him.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 28:1-6
passages.section_title: What happens when both David and Saul face the coming battle?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now in those days the Philistines gathered their forces for warfare against Israel. So Achish said to David, “You must understand that you and your men are to go out to battle with me.” 2 David replied, “Then you will come to know what your servant can do.” “Very well,” said Achish. “I will make you my bodyguard for life.” 3 Now by this time Samuel had died, and all Israel had mourned for him and buried him in Ramah, his own city. And Saul had removed the mediums and spiritists from the land. 4 The Philistines gathered together and camped at Shunem, while Saul gathered all Israel and camped at Gilboa. 5 When Saul saw the Philistine army, he was afraid and trembled violently. 6 He inquired of the LORD, but the LORD did not answer him by dreams or Urim or prophets.
paragraphs: 1 Now in those days the Philistines gathered their forces for warfare against Israel. So Achish said to David, “You must understand that you and your men are to go out to battle with me.” 2 David replied, “Then you will come to know what your servant can do.” “Very well,” said Achish. “I will make you my bodyguard for life.”

3 Now by this time Samuel had died, and all Israel had mourned for him and buried him in Ramah, his own city. And Saul had removed the mediums and spiritists from the land. 4 The Philistines gathered together and camped at Shunem, while Saul gathered all Israel and camped at Gilboa. 5 When Saul saw the Philistine army, he was afraid and trembled violently. 6 He inquired of the LORD, but the LORD did not answer him by dreams or Urim or prophets.

passages.context_html:
The Philistines gather to fight Israel, and Achish tells David that he and his men must march with him. David gives an answer Achish takes as willingness to serve, and the king promises to make him his lifelong bodyguard. The arrangement that offered shelter now requires loyalty in a war against David’s own people.

The scene then turns to Saul. Samuel is dead, and Saul has removed mediums and spiritists from the land. The Philistines camp at Shunem while Saul gathers Israel at Gilboa. Seeing their army, he is terrified.

Saul asks the LORD for guidance, but receives no answer through dreams, Urim or prophets. The chapter places two crises beside each other: David is caught in the obligations of his refuge, and Saul cannot obtain the direction he seeks.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry describes David’s position as a dilemma involving loyalty to Achish and loyalty to Israel. Wesley reads his answer as deliberately ambiguous. Neither the king’s confidence nor David’s wording tells the reader exactly what David intends to do in battle.

Henry connects Saul’s distress with his earlier refusal to heed God’s word. The silence is part of the relationship the narrative has traced, rather than evidence that Saul has never asked God a question before.

The account names the means by which no answer comes. It does not explain the workings of the Urim here or identify a new priest or replacement set of objects serving Saul.

passages.section_title: Can Saul obtain a different answer by seeking Samuel through a medium?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 Then Saul said to his servants, “Find me a woman who is a medium, so I can go and consult her.” “There is a medium at Endor,” his servants replied. 8 So Saul disguised himself by putting on different clothes, and he set out with two of his men. They came to the woman at night, and Saul said, “Consult a spirit for me. Bring up for me the one I name.” 9 But the woman replied, “Surely you know what Saul has done, how he has killed the mediums and spiritists in the land. Why have you set a trap to get me killed?” 10 Then Saul swore to her by the LORD: “As surely as the LORD lives, no punishment shall come upon you for this.” 11 “Whom shall I bring up for you?” the woman asked. “Bring up Samuel,” he replied. 12 But when the woman saw Samuel, she cried out in a loud voice and said to Saul, “Why have you deceived me? You are Saul!” 13 “Do not be afraid,” the king replied. “What do you see?” “I see a god coming up out of the earth,” the woman answered. 14 “What does he look like?” asked Saul. “An old man is coming up,” she replied. “And he is wearing a robe.” So Saul knew that it was Samuel, and he bowed facedown in reverence. 15 Then Samuel said to Saul, “Why have you disturbed me by bringing me up?” “I am deeply distressed,” replied Saul. “The Philistines are fighting against me, and God has turned away from me. He no longer answers me, either by prophets or by dreams. So I have called on you to tell me what to do.” 16 “Why do you consult me,” asked Samuel, “since the LORD has turned away from you and become your enemy? 17 He has done exactly what He spoke through me: The LORD has torn the kingdom out of your hand and given it to your neighbor David. 18 Because you did not obey the LORD or carry out His burning anger against Amalek, the LORD has done this to you today. 19 Moreover, the LORD will deliver Israel with you into the hand of the Philistines, and tomorrow you and your sons will be with me. And the LORD will deliver the army of Israel into the hand of the Philistines.” 20 Immediately Saul fell flat on the ground, terrified by the words of Samuel. And his strength was gone, because he had not eaten anything all that day and night. 21 When the woman came to Saul and saw how distraught he was, she said to him, “Look, your maidservant has obeyed your voice. I took my life in my hands and did as you told me. 22 Now please listen to your servant and let me set a morsel of bread before you so you may eat and have the strength to go on your way.” 23 Saul refused, saying, “I will not eat.” But his servants joined the woman in urging him, and he heeded their voice. He got up from the ground and sat on the bed. 24 The woman had a fattened calf at her house, and she quickly slaughtered it. She also took flour, kneaded it, and baked unleavened bread. 25 She served it to Saul and his servants, and they ate. And that night they got up and left.
paragraphs: 7 Then Saul said to his servants, “Find me a woman who is a medium, so I can go and consult her.” “There is a medium at Endor,” his servants replied. 8 So Saul disguised himself by putting on different clothes, and he set out with two of his men. They came to the woman at night, and Saul said, “Consult a spirit for me. Bring up for me the one I name.” 9 But the woman replied, “Surely you know what Saul has done, how he has killed the mediums and spiritists in the land. Why have you set a trap to get me killed?” 10 Then Saul swore to her by the LORD: “As surely as the LORD lives, no punishment shall come upon you for this.” 11 “Whom shall I bring up for you?” the woman asked. “Bring up Samuel,” he replied.

12 But when the woman saw Samuel, she cried out in a loud voice and said to Saul, “Why have you deceived me? You are Saul!” 13 “Do not be afraid,” the king replied. “What do you see?” “I see a god coming up out of the earth,” the woman answered. 14 “What does he look like?” asked Saul. “An old man is coming up,” she replied. “And he is wearing a robe.” So Saul knew that it was Samuel, and he bowed facedown in reverence.

15 Then Samuel said to Saul, “Why have you disturbed me by bringing me up?” “I am deeply distressed,” replied Saul. “The Philistines are fighting against me, and God has turned away from me. He no longer answers me, either by prophets or by dreams. So I have called on you to tell me what to do.” 16 “Why do you consult me,” asked Samuel, “since the LORD has turned away from you and become your enemy? 17 He has done exactly what He spoke through me: The LORD has torn the kingdom out of your hand and given it to your neighbor David. 18 Because you did not obey the LORD or carry out His burning anger against Amalek, the LORD has done this to you today. 19 Moreover, the LORD will deliver Israel with you into the hand of the Philistines, and tomorrow you and your sons will be with me. And the LORD will deliver the army of Israel into the hand of the Philistines.”

20 Immediately Saul fell flat on the ground, terrified by the words of Samuel. And his strength was gone, because he had not eaten anything all that day and night. 21 When the woman came to Saul and saw how distraught he was, she said to him, “Look, your maidservant has obeyed your voice. I took my life in my hands and did as you told me. 22 Now please listen to your servant and let me set a morsel of bread before you so you may eat and have the strength to go on your way.” 23 Saul refused, saying, “I will not eat.” But his servants joined the woman in urging him, and he heeded their voice. He got up from the ground and sat on the bed. 24 The woman had a fattened calf at her house, and she quickly slaughtered it. She also took flour, kneaded it, and baked unleavened bread. 25 She served it to Saul and his servants, and they ate. And that night they got up and left.

passages.context_html:
Saul seeks a medium at Endor, disguises himself and goes with two men at night. The woman fears a trap because Saul has acted against mediums and spiritists. He swears by the LORD that she will not be punished, then asks her to bring up Samuel.

The narrative calls the figure Samuel. The woman cries out when she sees him and recognizes Saul. She describes an old man wearing a robe, and Saul bows facedown. Her phrase translated a god uses elohim (eh-loh-HEEM). Brown–Driver–Briggs lists this verse under a godlike being, referring to Samuel’s departed spirit. The word here does not by itself identify the figure as God.

Samuel’s message gives Saul no new way around the earlier judgment. The kingdom has been taken from him and given to David because he did not obey the LORD concerning Amalek. He is told that Israel will fall to the Philistines and that he and his sons will join Samuel in death.

Saul falls to the ground in terror, weakened also by having eaten nothing all day and night. The woman and his servants persuade him to eat. She prepares a calf and unleavened bread, and they leave that night. The scene ends with food and human care, while the announced judgment remains.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Henry understand the appearance as the real Samuel, whom God permits to appear beyond the woman’s control. They give weight to the narrative naming him and to the woman’s surprise. This reading does not treat the encounter as permission to consult the dead.

Gill favors a deceptive spirit appearing in Samuel’s likeness. He reasons that God would not answer through a forbidden practice after withholding an answer by the appointed means. He acknowledges the force of the text’s naming Samuel, but interprets the scene as an appearance Saul takes to be the prophet. The disagreement concerns the identity and manner of the appearance, not the fact that Saul has sought a forbidden source of guidance.

Deuteronomy 18:9–14 directly forbids consulting mediums, spiritists and the dead. Saul’s oath to protect the woman does not reverse that instruction. The encounter brings the judgment he wished to escape rather than an alternative plan for winning the battle.

Henry takes the words about being with Samuel as entry into the world of the dead. Wesley allows a hopeful reading but also says the words may concern death alone. They do not settle Saul’s eternal state simply by placing him, his sons and Samuel in the same sentence.

Henry warns against despair while urging any reader still willing to repent to seek God’s mercy. Wesley cautions against claiming certainty about contrition the account does not record. The chapter’s silence about Saul’s inner response leaves more unanswered than the description of his fear.

deeper_study.title: Should We Seek Signs From God?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The encounter shows that seeking extraordinary access cannot make God’s already spoken word disappear. Saul wants direction for danger, but the answer returns to the obedience he had refused. The USCCB Bible notes likewise connect the scene with God’s continuing purpose for David.

The larger biblical movement directs attention to the One through whom God speaks fully. Hebrews 1:1–4 traces God’s speech through the prophets to His Son, who reveals His glory, provides purification for sins and sits at His right hand. The Christian response is to receive God’s revelation in Christ, rather than seek a method of controlling the answer.

This is a shared theme of hearing God’s word, not a claim that Hebrews directly explains the mechanics at Endor. The passage’s importance for God’s plan lies in the word that stands and the kingship moving toward David, rather than in satisfying every curiosity about the unseen world.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 29:1-11
passages.section_title: How does rejection by the Philistine commanders release David?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now the Philistines brought all their forces together at Aphek, while Israel camped by the spring in Jezreel. 2 As the Philistine leaders marched out with their units of hundreds and thousands, David and his men marched behind them with Achish. 3 Then the commanders of the Philistines asked, “What about these Hebrews?” Achish replied, “Is this not David, the servant of King Saul of Israel? He has been with me all these days, even years, and from the day he defected until today I have found no fault in him.” 4 But the commanders of the Philistines were angry with Achish and told him, “Send that man back and let him return to the place you assigned him. He must not go down with us into battle only to become our adversary during the war. What better way for him to regain the favor of his master than with the heads of our men? 5 Is this not the David about whom they sing in their dances: ‘Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands’?” 6 So Achish summoned David and told him, “As surely as the LORD lives, you have been upright, and it seems right in my sight that you should march in and out with me in the army, because I have found no fault in you from the day you came to me until this day. But you are not good in the sight of the leaders. 7 Therefore turn back now and go in peace, so that you will not do anything to displease the leaders of the Philistines.” 8 “But what have I done?” David replied. “What have you found against your servant, from the day I came to you until today, to keep me from going along to fight against the enemies of my lord the king?” 9 Achish replied, “I know that you are as pleasing in my sight as an angel of God. But the commanders of the Philistines have said, ‘He must not go into battle with us.’ 10 Now then, get up early in the morning, along with your master’s servants who came with you, and go as soon as it is light.” 11 So David and his men got up early in the morning to return to the land of the Philistines. And the Philistines went up to Jezreel.

And the Philistines went up to Jezreel.

passages.context_html:
The story returns to the gathering of the Philistine forces at Aphek. David and his men march at the rear with Achish. Other commanders object to the Hebrews being among them, fearing David could regain Saul’s favor by turning against them during battle.

They remember the song celebrating David’s victories. Achish trusts him, but the other leaders do not. Achish repeatedly tells David that he has found no fault in him, then orders him to return because the commanders will not accept his presence.

David protests that he has given no cause for rejection and asks why he cannot fight the enemies of his lord the king. Achish insists. David and his men leave early for Philistine territory while the army goes up to Jezreel. He is released from a battle that would put his loyalties under severe strain.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Henry see God’s care in the commanders’ refusal. Their suspicion frees David from a situation in which serving one side threatens his obligations to the other. What appears to be an unwelcome dismissal becomes a deliverance.

Wesley and Gill read David’s protest as a performance intended to preserve Achish’s trust. Gill thinks David is inwardly relieved. That explains the protest as continued deception, but the narrative itself does not disclose his full battle plan or every private feeling.

Henry emphasizes the danger of coming close to wrongdoing through fear of people. Achish’s favorable opinion is sincere within what he knows; it does not reveal the whole truth about David’s raids or resolve the dilemma.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
David’s release shows how help can come through people who are acting from their own suspicions. Their refusal prevents his involvement in the coming battle and sends him back toward the families who will need rescue.

1 Corinthians 10:12–13 joins a warning against self-confidence with assurance of God’s faithfulness in temptation. He provides a way to endure rather than requiring His people to surrender to wrongdoing. David’s unexpected release offers a human example of receiving a way out of a dangerous entanglement.

This is a parallel about God’s help, rather than a rule that every rejection is a personal message from Him or that every bad decision ends without consequences. The next chapter shows the losses David still has to face.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 30:1-6
passages.section_title: Where does David find strength when his own men turn against him?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 On the third day David and his men arrived in Ziklag, and the Amalekites had raided the Negev, attacked Ziklag, and burned it down. 2 They had taken captive the women and all who were there, both young and old. They had not killed anyone, but had carried them off as they went on their way. 3 When David and his men came to the city, they found it burned down and their wives and sons and daughters taken captive. 4 So David and the troops with him lifted up their voices and wept until they had no strength left to weep. 5 David’s two wives, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail the widow of Nabal of Carmel, had been taken captive. 6 And David was greatly distressed because the people spoke of stoning him, because the soul of every man grieved for his sons and daughters. But David found strength in the LORD his God.
paragraphs: 1 On the third day David and his men arrived in Ziklag, and the Amalekites had raided the Negev, attacked Ziklag, and burned it down. 2 They had taken captive the women and all who were there, both young and old. They had not killed anyone, but had carried them off as they went on their way. 3 When David and his men came to the city, they found it burned down and their wives and sons and daughters taken captive. 4 So David and the troops with him lifted up their voices and wept until they had no strength left to weep. 5 David’s two wives, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail the widow of Nabal of Carmel, had been taken captive. 6 And David was greatly distressed because the people spoke of stoning him, because the soul of every man grieved for his sons and daughters. But David found strength in the LORD his God.

passages.context_html:
David and his men reach Ziklag on the third day and find it burned. Amalekite raiders have taken the women and everyone else captive without killing anyone. The returning men see the ruin before they can know the outcome for their families.

They weep until they have no strength left. David’s own wives have been taken, and the men speak of stoning him because each is grieving for sons and daughters. The danger now comes from the people who have shared his life in the wilderness.

At this point David finds strength in the LORD his God. The loss is not denied or immediately undone. The statement marks where he turns while grief, fear and responsibility press on him together.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley notes that grief does not disgrace even brave people. David and his men genuinely lament their families. Finding strength in God is not presented as having no tears.

Wesley, Henry and Gill understand David’s strength in terms of God’s power, promises and faithfulness. Gill points to remembered mercy and the relationship on which David can rely. The answer to despair begins with turning toward God before the rescue is visible.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
The threatened king’s strength comes from God at a point when his own resources are exhausted. The wider biblical theme is that weakness need not prevent God’s life-giving work.

2 Corinthians 4:7–18 describes God’s power carried in fragile human lives. Paul connects suffering with the death and life of Jesus, and grounds endurance in the promise that God will raise His people with Him. The hope reaches beyond having every present loss repaired.

This is a shared theme, rather than a promise that each crisis will end like Ziklag. David’s tears and his trust can stand together, just as Christian hope can remain alive in people who are still grieving.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 30:7-20
passages.section_title: How does care for an abandoned stranger help lead to rescue?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 Then David said to Abiathar the priest, the son of Ahimelech, “Bring me the ephod.” So Abiathar brought it to him, 8 and David inquired of the LORD: “Should I pursue these raiders? Will I overtake them?” “Pursue them,” the LORD replied, “for you will surely overtake them and rescue the captives.” 9 So David and his six hundred men went to the Brook of Besor, where some stayed behind 10 because two hundred men were too exhausted to cross the brook. But David and four hundred men continued in pursuit. 11 Now his men found an Egyptian in the field and brought him to David. They gave the man water to drink and food to eat— 12 a piece of a fig cake and two clusters of raisins. So he ate and was revived, for he had not had any food or water for three days and three nights. 13 Then David asked him, “To whom do you belong, and where are you from?” “I am an Egyptian,” he replied, “the slave of an Amalekite. My master abandoned me three days ago when I fell ill. 14 We raided the Negev of the Cherethites, the territory of Judah, and the Negev of Caleb, and we burned down Ziklag.” 15 “Will you lead me to these raiders?” David asked. And the man replied, “Swear to me by God that you will not kill me or deliver me into the hand of my master, and I will lead you to them.” 16 So he led David down, and there were the Amalekites spread out over all the land, eating, drinking, and celebrating the great amount of plunder they had taken from the land of the Philistines and the land of Judah. 17 And David struck them down from twilight until the evening of the next day. Not a man escaped, except four hundred young men who fled, riding off on camels. 18 So David recovered everything the Amalekites had taken, including his two wives. 19 Nothing was missing, young or old, son or daughter, or any of the plunder the Amalekites had taken. David brought everything back. 20 And he took all the flocks and herds, which his men drove ahead of the other livestock, calling out, “This is David’s plunder!”

passages.context_html:
David asks Abiathar to bring the ephod and inquires of the LORD about pursuing the raiders. He receives the direction to pursue and the assurance that he will rescue the captives. Six hundred set out, but two hundred are too exhausted to cross the Brook of Besor. Four hundred continue.

They find an Egyptian in a field and give him food and water. After he revives, he explains that he is the slave of an Amalekite who abandoned him when he became ill. He had been with the raiders who burned Ziklag. He agrees to lead David to them if David swears not to kill him or return him to his master.

The raiders are celebrating their plunder when David reaches them. He attacks from twilight until the following evening. Four hundred young men escape on camels, but David recovers everyone and everything taken from his people, including his wives. The outcome matches the promise he received.

The recovered families are accompanied by flocks and herds taken from the raiders. The account now turns from winning the rescue to deciding how its benefits will be shared.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry emphasizes David’s seeking guidance and his refusal to force exhausted men beyond their strength. Wesley likewise treats the return to inquiry as significant. The rescue begins with dependence rather than a claim that urgency leaves no room to ask God.

Henry and Wesley see God working through the abandoned Egyptian. His master’s cruelty leaves the very person who can guide David to the camp. The food and water are given before his information is recorded, allowing kindness a real place in the account.

Henry also compares David’s care for weaker followers with the care of Christ. The men who cannot continue are still his people. Their exhaustion will become the test of generosity after the battle.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Care for someone connected with the enemy becomes part of the rescue. David’s men do not leave the sick Egyptian where his master abandoned him. His life matters, and his help opens the way to the captives.

Luke 6:27–36 carries the wider theme into Jesus’ teaching: His followers are to do good beyond the circle of those who already love them, reflecting the Father’s mercy. The comparison concerns kindness across hostility, rather than approval of every action taken in ancient warfare.

The episode helps us see God’s purposes moving through care for an easily overlooked person. The stranger is not merely an obstacle on the way to helping David’s own people; tending his need becomes part of that help.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 30:21-31
passages.section_title: Why does David share the plunder with those who could not fight?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 When David came to the two hundred men who had been too exhausted to follow him and who were left behind at the Brook of Besor, they came out to meet him and the troops with him. As David approached the men, he greeted them, 22 but all the wicked and worthless men among those who had gone with David said, “Because they did not go with us, we will not share with them the plunder we recovered, except for each man’s wife and children. They may take them and go.” 23 But David said, “My brothers, you must not do this with what the LORD has given us. He has protected us and delivered into our hands the raiders who came against us. 24 Who will listen to your proposal? The share of the one who went to battle will match the share of the one who stayed with the supplies. They will share alike.” 25 And so it has been from that day forward. David established this statute and ordinance for Israel to this very day. 26 When David arrived in Ziklag, he sent some of the plunder to his friends, the elders of Judah, saying, “Here is a gift for you from the plunder of the LORD’s enemies.” 27 He sent gifts to those in Bethel, Ramoth Negev, and Jattir; 28 to those in Aroer, Siphmoth, and Eshtemoa; 29 to those in Racal and in the cities of the Jerahmeelites and Kenites; 30 to those in Hormah, Bor-ashan, and Athach; 31 and to those in Hebron and in all the places where David and his men had roamed.

passages.context_html:
David returns to the two hundred men left at Besor and greets them. Some who fought argue that the exhausted men should receive only their families back and no share of the recovered plunder.

David refuses. The LORD has protected them and given the victory, so the fighters cannot treat its benefits as theirs alone. Those who stayed with the supplies are to share equally with those who went into battle. The decision becomes an ordinance for Israel.

Back at Ziklag, David sends gifts to the elders of Judah and to places where he and his men had roamed. The victory’s benefits reach beyond the raiding force into the wider community that has shared his years of wandering.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill emphasize that the men at Besor had a real place in the work: they remained with the supplies. Their weakness prevented them from continuing; it did not make them enemies or erase their belonging.

Henry and Gill connect generosity with recognizing God as the giver. David’s answer restrains the impulse to claim full credit for the victory and then use that claim to exclude others.

Wesley reads the gifts to Judah as both gratitude for earlier help and a wise way of building goodwill. Those purposes can stand together. The future king uses what he has received to strengthen relationships beyond his immediate company.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
David’s decision gives a picture of a community receiving and sharing what God has supplied. People doing different work remain part of one company, and the most visible contribution is not the whole story.

Romans 12:3–8 develops that theme for the church. Many members form one body in Christ, with differing gifts received by grace. Service, teaching, encouragement, giving, leadership and mercy all have their place.

This is a parallel about belonging and gifts, rather than a command to copy an ancient division of plunder in every setting. It directs attention away from using success to rank people’s worth and toward using God’s gifts for the good of the whole body.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 31:1-6
passages.section_title: How does Saul’s reign come to an end?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now the Philistines fought against Israel, and the men of Israel fled before them, and many fell slain on Mount Gilboa. 2 The Philistines hotly pursued Saul and his sons, and they killed Saul’s sons Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua. 3 When the battle intensified against Saul, the archers overtook him and wounded him critically. 4 Then Saul said to his armor-bearer, “Draw your sword and run me through with it, or these uncircumcised men will come and run me through and torture me!” But his armor-bearer was terrified and refused to do it. So Saul took his own sword and fell on it. 5 When his armor-bearer saw that Saul was dead, he too fell on his own sword and died with him. 6 So Saul, his three sons, his armor-bearer, and all his men died together that same day.

So Saul took his own sword and fell on it. 5 When his armor-bearer saw that Saul was dead, he too fell on his own sword and died with him. 6 So Saul, his three sons, his armor-bearer, and all his men died together that same day.

passages.context_html:
The narrative returns to the battle at Mount Gilboa. Israel flees, and the Philistines kill Saul’s sons Jonathan, Abinadab and Malchishua. The friend who encouraged David in the wilderness dies alongside his brothers.

Saul is critically wounded by archers. Fearing capture and torture, he asks his armor-bearer to kill him. The terrified man refuses, and Saul falls on his own sword. When the armor-bearer sees that he is dead, he also takes his own life.

The same day brings the deaths of Saul, his three sons, his armor-bearer and the men with him. The next passage describes others fleeing, so the statement need not be expanded into a claim that no one in Israel’s whole army survived. The loss ends Saul’s reign and leaves the people facing defeat.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley caution against deciding a person’s eternal state from the manner of death. The account describes what happens to Saul and his sons; it does not give a final verdict on their souls.

Gill takes this narration as Saul’s death by his own hand. In 2 Samuel 1:6–10, an Amalekite later claims that he finished killing Saul. Gill reads that claim as an attempt to win David’s favor, distinguishing a messenger’s account from the narration here.

1 Chronicles 10:13–14 places Saul’s fall within his unfaithfulness and the transfer of kingship to David. That explanation concerns his failed rule before God; it need not make Jonathan’s earlier faithfulness meaningless or give us an unreported reason for each person’s death.

passages.god_plan_html:
The New Testament itself places this change of kings within the story leading to Jesus. In Acts 13:21–23, Paul recalls God giving Israel Saul, removing him and raising up David. He then identifies Jesus as the promised Savior brought from David’s descendants.

The book therefore ends at a transition within a purpose larger than either king. Saul’s failure is real, and David’s reign will have failures of its own. The enduring hope reaches the Savior God brings through David’s line, rather than resting in the idea that another merely human king will solve everything.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 31:7-10
passages.section_title: How does the defeat spread beyond the battlefield?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 When the Israelites along the valley and those on the other side of the Jordan saw that the army of Israel had fled and that Saul and his sons had died, they abandoned their cities and ran away. So the Philistines came and occupied their cities. 8 The next day, when the Philistines came to strip the dead, they found Saul and his three sons fallen on Mount Gilboa. 9 They cut off Saul’s head, stripped off his armor, and sent messengers throughout the land of the Philistines to proclaim the news in the temples of their idols and among their people. 10 They put his armor in the temple of the Ashtoreths and hung his body on the wall of Beth-shan.
paragraphs: 7 When the Israelites along the valley and those on the other side of the Jordan saw that the army of Israel had fled and that Saul and his sons had died, they abandoned their cities and ran away. So the Philistines came and occupied their cities. 8 The next day, when the Philistines came to strip the dead, they found Saul and his three sons fallen on Mount Gilboa. 9 They cut off Saul’s head, stripped off his armor, and sent messengers throughout the land of the Philistines to proclaim the news in the temples of their idols and among their people. 10 They put his armor in the temple of the Ashtoreths and hung his body on the wall of Beth-shan.

passages.context_html:
People along the valley and across the Jordan see Israel’s flight and learn that Saul and his sons are dead. They abandon their cities, and the Philistines occupy them. The defeat brings displacement as well as death.

The next day the Philistines find Saul and his sons among the fallen. They cut off Saul’s head, strip his armor and send news of the victory through their land and the temples of their idols. They place his armor in the temple of the Ashtoreths and hang his body on Beth-shan’s wall.

The treatment turns a military victory into public humiliation of Israel’s king and celebration before Philistine gods. It also prepares for the response of people who remember Saul for more than his final defeat.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands the display as the Philistines crediting their gods with victory. 1 Chronicles 10:8–10 adds that Saul’s head was hung in Dagon’s temple. Both accounts show the defeat being proclaimed as a triumph for their worship.

Henry distinguishes what happens to bodies from what can be known about souls. Public honor or humiliation after death cannot by itself settle a person’s standing before God. Here the account makes the earthly consequences painfully visible.

passages.title: 1 Samuel 31:11-13
passages.section_title: Why do the men of Jabesh-gilead risk recovering the bodies?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 When the people of Jabesh-gilead heard what the Philistines had done to Saul, 12 all their men of valor set out, journeyed all night, and retrieved the bodies of Saul and his sons from the wall of Beth-shan. When they arrived at Jabesh, they burned the bodies there. 13 Then they took their bones and buried them under the tamarisk tree in Jabesh, and they fasted seven days.
paragraphs: 11 When the people of Jabesh-gilead heard what the Philistines had done to Saul, 12 all their men of valor set out, journeyed all night, and retrieved the bodies of Saul and his sons from the wall of Beth-shan. When they arrived at Jabesh, they burned the bodies there. 13 Then they took their bones and buried them under the tamarisk tree in Jabesh, and they fasted seven days.

passages.context_html:
The people of Jabesh-gilead hear what the Philistines have done. Their men of valor travel through the night, recover Saul’s body and those of his sons from Beth-shan’s wall, and bring them back to Jabesh.

They burn the bodies, bury the bones under a tamarisk tree and fast seven days. The book closes with mourning and an act of care for the dead, following the defeat and public disgrace.

Their response recalls 1 Samuel 11, when Saul rescued Jabesh-gilead from Nahash and the Ammonites. Remembering his later failures does not require forgetting the help he once gave them.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley reads the recovery as gratitude for Saul’s rescue of their town. Gill likewise emphasizes their determination to recover the bodies after the Philistines’ treatment. Their courage answers humiliation with care.

Gill discusses possible reasons for burning the bodies, including preventing further abuse and their condition after death. The passage reports the act without specifying the reason. The burning, burial of bones and fasting should each be allowed their place in the account.

In 2 Samuel 2:4–7, David explicitly praises their kindness in burying Saul. The next king recognizes mercy shown to his former pursuer, extending the refusal to let hostility erase respect for a human life.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 1:1-16
passages.section_title: Why doesn’t David reward the messenger who brings Saul’s crown?

When he came to David, he fell to the ground to pay him homage. 3 “Where have you come from?” David asked. “I have escaped from the Israelite camp,” he replied. 4 “What was the outcome?” David asked. “Please tell me.” “The troops fled from the battle,” he replied. “Many of them fell and died. And Saul and his son Jonathan are also dead.” 5 Then David asked the young man who had brought him the report, “How do you know that Saul and his son Jonathan are dead?” 6 “I happened to be on Mount Gilboa,” he replied, “and there was Saul, leaning on his spear, with the chariots and the cavalry closing in on him. 7 When he turned around and saw me, he called out to me, and I answered, ‘Here I am!’ 8 ‘Who are you?’ he asked. So I told him, ‘I am an Amalekite.’ 9 Then he begged me, ‘Stand over me and kill me, for agony has seized me, but my life still lingers.’ 10 So I stood over him and killed him, because I knew that after he had fallen he could not survive. section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Second Samuel continues the story where First Samuel ends. Saul has died in the battle against the Philistines, while David has returned from recovering the families taken from Ziklag. After two days there, David receives a man from Saul’s camp with torn clothes and dust on his head.

The man reports Israel’s defeat and the deaths of Saul and Jonathan. When David asks how he knows, he claims that Saul begged him to end his life and that he did so. He brings Saul’s crown and arm band. This is the messenger’s account; 1 Samuel 31:1–6 has already described Saul dying after falling on his own sword.

David and his men tear their clothes, weep and fast until evening for Saul, Jonathan and Israel’s fallen people. The news could remove the man who pursued David, but David receives it as a national and personal loss.

He then questions the messenger, who identifies himself as the son of a foreigner, an Amalekite. David asks why he did not fear killing the LORD’s anointed, the king God had appointed, and orders his execution. He bases the sentence on the man’s own claim to have killed Saul. The crown brings the messenger no reward.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads David’s mourning as sincere and his response as public justice taking priority over private advantage. David’s future kingship does not make Saul’s death something he must celebrate.

Gill’s earlier comment on Saul’s death treats the Amalekite’s later claim as a false story meant to gain David’s favor. Here Gill again understands the crown and arm band as an appeal to Saul’s successor. On that reading, the messenger has badly misjudged what David values.

Henry judges the sentence by the man’s confession to killing the king. Gill discusses the execution as an exceptional act of royal authority rather than an ordinary rule that any confession automatically warrants death. Those are explanations of David’s judgment in this scene, not instructions for a modern court or private person.
passages.god_plan_html:
David’s grief makes room for the life of someone who has repeatedly harmed him. His calling to become king does not require delight in his pursuer’s death. The scene shows a future ruler sharing the suffering of his people instead of treating their loss only as his own opportunity.

In Matthew 5:43–48, Jesus carries the wider theme into love for enemies and prayer for persecutors, reflecting the Father’s care for both righteous and unrighteous people. The comparison concerns David’s refusal to reduce Saul to an enemy whose death is good news.

This parallel does not make every part of David’s judgment an example to copy. It points to the place of mercy and shared grief within the character of God’s people, a calling Jesus makes explicit.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 1:17-27
passages.section_title: How does David give words to the loss of Saul and Jonathan?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 Then David took up this lament for Saul and his son Jonathan, 18 and he ordered that the sons of Judah be taught the Song of the Bow. It is written in the Book of Jashar: 19 “Your glory, O Israel, lies slain on your heights. How the mighty have fallen! 20 Tell it not in Gath; proclaim it not in the streets of Ashkelon, lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice, and the daughters of the uncircumcised exult. 21 O mountains of Gilboa, may you have no dew or rain, no fields yielding offerings of grain. For there the shield of the mighty was defiled, the shield of Saul, no longer anointed with oil. 22 From the blood of the slain, from the fat of the mighty, the bow of Jonathan did not retreat, and the sword of Saul did not return empty. 23 Saul and Jonathan, beloved and delightful in life, were not divided in death. They were swifter than eagles; they were stronger than lions. 24 O daughters of Israel, weep for Saul, who clothed you in scarlet and luxury, who decked your garments with ornaments of gold. 25 How the mighty have fallen in the thick of battle! Jonathan lies slain on your heights. 26 I grieve for you, Jonathan, my brother. You were delightful to me; your love to me was extraordinary, surpassing the love of women. 27 How the mighty have fallen, and the weapons of war have perished!”

For there the shield of the mighty was defiled, the shield of Saul, no longer anointed with oil.

They were swifter than eagles; they were stronger than lions. 24 O daughters of Israel, weep for Saul, who clothed you in scarlet and luxury, who decked your garments with ornaments of gold. 25 How the mighty have fallen in the thick of battle! Jonathan lies slain on your heights. 26 I grieve for you, Jonathan, my brother. You were delightful to me; your love to me was extraordinary, surpassing the love of women. 27 How the mighty have fallen, and the weapons of war have perished!”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
David composes a lament for Saul and Jonathan and orders that Judah learn it. The account calls it the Song of the Bow and says it is written in the Book of Jashar. The poem turns the news of defeat into something the people can remember and mourn together.

The Hebrew word for this lament is qinah (kee-NAH). Brown–Driver–Briggs identifies it as a dirge, a song of mourning, and lists this verse. Its vivid language gives voice to loss: Israel’s glory lies fallen, the mountains of Gilboa are addressed in grief, and the thought of Philistine celebrations is painful.

David remembers the strength and courage of Saul and Jonathan, the bow and sword that once met the enemy, and the benefits Saul brought Israel. He then speaks directly to Jonathan as his brother, grieving the love and friendship he has lost.

The repeated cry over the fallen mighty men holds public disaster and personal sorrow together. The poem honors what David mourns without retelling every part of Saul’s troubled reign. The earlier narrative remains there for readers who know how much that reign cost.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry takes the Bow as the title of the funeral song. Wesley and Gill discuss teaching the use of the bow as military instruction, with Gill also noting the song-title reading. The BSB presents the instruction as teaching the Song of the Bow.

Wesley and Gill read the wish for no dew or rain on Gilboa as the language of grief. It expresses horror at the loss there, rather than a weather report or a prediction that the hills will never receive rain again.

Henry and Wesley distinguish honoring Saul’s gifts and achievements from praising a devotion to God the story does not demonstrate. The lament need not erase his wrongdoing in order to acknowledge courage, loss and benefits Israel received.

Gill reads the words about Jonathan’s extraordinary love in the setting of a friendship that put David’s good ahead of personal advantage and risked Saul’s anger. Henry also emphasizes the strength of faithful friendship. The comparison with the love of women expresses how deeply David valued that bond.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jonathan’s friendship had become visible through loyalty when David’s future threatened his own prospects. The lament preserves the weight of that love after Jonathan’s death. A well-supported parallel is the self-giving friendship Jesus describes in John 15:12–17.

Jesus commands His disciples to love one another as He has loved them and speaks of laying down one’s life for friends. He carries that love into His own saving death. Jonathan’s loyalty gives a human picture of costly care, while Jesus’ work reaches beyond it: Jonathan did not die to atone for David’s sins.

The connection helps us see friendship as part of the life God forms among His people. Faithful love can shape another person’s life, and grief can honestly acknowledge its loss without undoing trust in God.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 2:1-11
passages.section_title: Why is David king over Judah while another king rules Israel?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Some time later, David inquired of the LORD, “Should I go up to one of the towns of Judah?” “Go up,” the LORD answered. Then David asked, “Where should I go?” “To Hebron,” replied the LORD. 2 So David went there with his two wives, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail the widow of Nabal of Carmel. 3 David also took the men who were with him, each with his household, and they settled in the towns near Hebron. 4 Then the men of Judah came to Hebron, and there they anointed David king over the house of Judah. And they told David, “It was the men of Jabesh-gilead who buried Saul.” 5 So David sent messengers to the men of Jabesh-gilead to tell them, “The LORD bless you, because you showed this kindness to Saul your lord when you buried him. 6 Now may the LORD show you loving devotion and faithfulness, and I will also show you the same favor because you have done this. 7 Now then, be strong and courageous, for though Saul your lord is dead, the house of Judah has anointed me as their king.” 8 Meanwhile, Abner son of Ner, the commander of Saul’s army, took Saul’s son Ish-bosheth, moved him to Mahanaim, 9 and made him king over Gilead, Asher, Jezreel, Ephraim, and Benjamin—over all Israel. 10 Saul’s son Ish-bosheth was forty years old when he began to reign over Israel, and he reigned for two years. The house of Judah, however, followed David. 11 And the length of time that David was king in Hebron over the house of Judah was seven years and six months.

And they told David, “It was the men of Jabesh-gilead who buried Saul.” 5 So David sent messengers to the men of Jabesh-gilead to tell them, “The LORD bless you, because you showed this kindness to Saul your lord when you buried him. 6 Now may the LORD show you loving devotion and faithfulness, and I will also show you the same favor because you have done this. 7 Now then, be strong and courageous, for though Saul your lord is dead, the house of Judah has anointed me as their king.”

8 Meanwhile, Abner son of Ner, the commander of Saul’s army, took Saul’s son Ish-bosheth, moved him to Mahanaim, 9 and made him king over Gilead, Asher, Jezreel, Ephraim, and Benjamin—over all Israel. 10 Saul’s son Ish-bosheth was forty years old when he began to reign over Israel, and he reigned for two years. The house of Judah, however, followed David. 11 And the length of time that David was king in Hebron over the house of Judah was seven years and six months.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After mourning Saul, David asks the LORD whether to return to Judah and where to go. The answer directs him to Hebron. He brings his wives, his men and their households, and the men of Judah anoint him king over their own people.

David then sends thanks to Jabesh-gilead for burying Saul. He asks the LORD to show them loving devotion and faithfulness and promises kindness himself. His message also announces Judah’s decision to make him king. Honoring Saul’s burial and building relationships with Saul’s people go together.

Abner, Saul’s army commander, acts on behalf of a different successor. He takes Saul’s son Ish-bosheth to Mahanaim and makes him king over Israel. Judah follows David, so Saul’s death has not produced immediate agreement about who should rule the whole nation.

The passage gives Ish-bosheth’s age as forty and his reign as two years. David’s rule over Judah at Hebron lasts seven years and six months. The account now follows the struggle between the two royal houses before David’s wider recognition.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley emphasizes David beginning with inquiry rather than simply taking Saul’s death as permission to choose his next move. He also distinguishes Samuel’s earlier anointing, which designated David for kingship, from Judah’s public acknowledgment and the later acknowledgment by all Israel.

Wesley sees the message to Jabesh-gilead as genuine kindness toward people who honored David’s former pursuer. It also offers them the protection and goodwill of Judah’s new king. Political wisdom and respect for their act of mercy need not exclude each other.

Wesley and Gill understand Ish-bosheth’s two years as the period before the war that follows, rather than the whole span of the competing houses. The BSB states the two reign lengths directly; fitting them into a precise calendar involves further interpretation. The central point is clear: David rules Judah while Saul’s house still holds the allegiance of the rest of Israel.
passages.god_plan_html:
Henry sees a parallel between David’s contested kingship and the opposition Christ faces despite being appointed by God. David’s promise does not become immediate national agreement, and the delay does not mean God has abandoned His purpose.

In Acts 4:24–30, believers pray about rulers opposing God’s Anointed and identify that opposition with the conspiracy against Jesus. His suffering does not defeat God’s purpose. The connection points beyond a political contest to the saving work God accomplishes through Christ.

This is a limited parallel about opposition and God’s faithfulness. David’s campaign and Jesus’ saving mission are different events, and the point is not that every political rivalry can be assigned the same meaning. The hope rests in God bringing His purpose to completion.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 2:12-17
passages.section_title: How does a contest become a deadly battle?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 One day Abner son of Ner and the servants of Ish-bosheth son of Saul marched out from Mahanaim to Gibeon. 13 So Joab son of Zeruiah and the servants of David marched out and met them by the pool of Gibeon. And the two groups took up positions on opposite sides of the pool. 14 Then Abner said to Joab, “Let us have the young men get up and compete before us.” “Let them get up,” Joab replied. 15 So they got up and were counted off—twelve for Benjamin and Ish-bosheth son of Saul, and twelve for David. 16 Then each man grabbed his opponent by the head and thrust his sword into his opponent’s side, and they all fell together. So this place, which is in Gibeon, is called Helkath-hazzurim. 17 The battle that day was intense, and Abner and the men of Israel were defeated by the servants of David.

And the two groups took up positions on opposite sides of the pool. 14 Then Abner said to Joab, “Let us have the young men get up and compete before us.” “Let them get up,” Joab replied. 15 So they got up and were counted off—twelve for Benjamin and Ish-bosheth son of Saul, and twelve for David. 16 Then each man grabbed his opponent by the head and thrust his sword into his opponent’s side, and they all fell together. So this place, which is in Gibeon, is called Helkath-hazzurim. 17 The battle that day was intense, and Abner and the men of Israel were defeated by the servants of David.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Abner and Ish-bosheth’s servants come from Mahanaim to Gibeon, where Joab and David’s servants meet them. The groups take positions on opposite sides of the pool. The competing claims to the kingdom now bring their forces face to face.

Abner proposes that the young men compete, and Joab agrees. Twelve men from each side are counted off. Each seizes an opponent by the head and drives a sword into his side, and they all fall together. What follows is an intense battle in which Abner’s side is defeated.

The Hebrew verb behind compete is sahaq (sah-KHAHK). Brown–Driver–Briggs includes making sport and specifically lists this contest. The word helps explain the disturbing contrast: something spoken of as a display or game ends in people killing one another.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley, Henry and Gill criticize the treatment of bloodshed as sport. They read Abner’s proposal as a challenge that opens the way to battle. Joab’s agreement also belongs to the sequence; the deaths do not happen without leaders accepting the contest.

Gill takes all twenty-four men as falling together, consistent with the BSB wording. The USCCB Bible notes caution that the precise nature of the contest is unclear. The violence is explicit even where its intended rules are not.

The account does not describe twelve separate rounds or say that the winning side was promised the right to rule all Israel. It shows the encounter turning from the chosen men’s deaths into a wider clash.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 2:18-32
passages.section_title: When will the pursuit of fellow Israelites end?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 The three sons of Zeruiah were there: Joab, Abishai, and Asahel. Now Asahel was fleet of foot like a wild gazelle, 19 and he chased Abner, not turning to the right or to the left in his pursuit. 20 And Abner glanced back and said, “Is that you, Asahel?” “It is,” Asahel replied. 21 So Abner told him, “Turn to your right or to your left, seize one of the young men, and take his equipment for yourself.” But Asahel would not stop chasing him. 22 Once again, Abner warned Asahel, “Stop chasing me. Why should I strike you to the ground? How could I show my face to your brother Joab?” 23 But Asahel refused to turn away. So Abner thrust the butt of his spear into his stomach, and it came out his back, and he fell dead on the spot. And every man paused when he came to the place where Asahel had fallen and died. 24 But Joab and Abishai pursued Abner. By sunset, they had gone as far as the hill of Ammah opposite Giah on the way to the wilderness of Gibeon. 25 The Benjamites rallied to Abner, formed a single unit, and took their stand atop a hill. 26 Then Abner called out to Joab: “Must the sword devour forever? Do you not realize that this will only end in bitterness? How long before you tell the troops to stop pursuing their brothers?” 27 “As surely as God lives,” Joab replied, “if you had not spoken up, the troops would have continued pursuing their brothers until morning.” 28 So Joab blew the ram’s horn, and all the troops stopped; they no longer pursued Israel or continued to fight. 29 And all that night Abner and his men marched through the Arabah. They crossed the Jordan, marched all morning, and arrived at Mahanaim. 30 When Joab returned from pursuing Abner, he gathered all the troops. In addition to Asahel, nineteen of David’s servants were missing, 31 but they had struck down 360 Benjamites who were with Abner. 32 And they took Asahel and buried him in his father’s tomb in Bethlehem. Then Joab and his men marched all night and reached Hebron at daybreak.
paragraphs: 18 The three sons of Zeruiah were there: Joab, Abishai, and Asahel. Now Asahel was fleet of foot like a wild gazelle, 19 and he chased Abner, not turning to the right or to the left in his pursuit. 20 And Abner glanced back and said, “Is that you, Asahel?” “It is,” Asahel replied. 21 So Abner told him, “Turn to your right or to your left, seize one of the young men, and take his equipment for yourself.” But Asahel would not stop chasing him. 22 Once again, Abner warned Asahel, “Stop chasing me. Why should I strike you to the ground? How could I show my face to your brother Joab?” 23 But Asahel refused to turn away. So Abner thrust the butt of his spear into his stomach, and it came out his back, and he fell dead on the spot. And every man paused when he came to the place where Asahel had fallen and died.

24 But Joab and Abishai pursued Abner. By sunset, they had gone as far as the hill of Ammah opposite Giah on the way to the wilderness of Gibeon. 25 The Benjamites rallied to Abner, formed a single unit, and took their stand atop a hill. 26 Then Abner called out to Joab: “Must the sword devour forever? Do you not realize that this will only end in bitterness? How long before you tell the troops to stop pursuing their brothers?” 27 “As surely as God lives,” Joab replied, “if you had not spoken up, the troops would have continued pursuing their brothers until morning.” 28 So Joab blew the ram’s horn, and all the troops stopped; they no longer pursued Israel or continued to fight. 29 And all that night Abner and his men marched through the Arabah. They crossed the Jordan, marched all morning, and arrived at Mahanaim.

30 When Joab returned from pursuing Abner, he gathered all the troops. In addition to Asahel, nineteen of David’s servants were missing, 31 but they had struck down 360 Benjamites who were with Abner. 32 And they took Asahel and buried him in his father’s tomb in Bethlehem. Then Joab and his men marched all night and reached Hebron at daybreak.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Joab’s brothers Abishai and Asahel are present in the battle. Asahel, noted for his speed, pursues Abner without turning aside. Abner twice warns him to choose another opponent, asking how he could face Joab if he killed his brother.

Asahel refuses to stop. Abner strikes him in the stomach with the butt of his spear, and the blow passes through him. Asahel dies, and those who reach the place pause. Joab and Abishai continue the pursuit until Abner’s Benjamite forces gather on a hill.

Abner then asks whether the sword must devour forever and warns that continued fighting will end in bitterness. Joab answers and sounds the ram’s horn. The pursuit stops, and Abner’s men travel through the night back to Mahanaim.

The cost is counted: nineteen of David’s men besides Asahel are missing, while 360 Benjamites from Abner’s company have fallen. Asahel is buried in his father’s tomb at Bethlehem, and Joab’s men reach Hebron at daybreak. The contest between royal houses has become grief within families.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley see a warning in Asahel’s pursuit: the very ability that makes him confident brings him into danger. The account stresses his speed and refusal to turn aside without giving a full history of his military experience.

Henry emphasizes the bitterness of fighting fellow Israelites. Abner’s appeal speaks a necessary truth even though he helped begin the day’s bloodshed. Recognizing that continued violence will cause harm is a reason to stop before the losses grow.

Wesley and Gill read Joab’s reply as referring back to Abner’s original challenge: without it, the battle need not have begun. The BSB wording instead presents him saying that, without Abner’s appeal to stop, the pursuit would have continued until morning. The readings give the reply a different emphasis, but both leave the halt to fighting clearly in view.
passages.god_plan_html:
The chapter exposes how the pursuit of advantage can leave a people divided and grieving. Its stopping point helps us look beyond which side has more survivors to the kind of wisdom that can interrupt destruction.

James 3:13–18 contrasts jealousy and selfish ambition with wisdom from above, which is peace-loving, gentle, merciful and sincere. God’s purpose for His people includes a harvest of righteousness sown in peace.

This is a shared theme, rather than a claim that James directly interprets the battle at Gibeon. It keeps the larger story of David’s rise from turning every act of violence along the way into something to admire. Faithfulness includes learning when to stop pursuing one another.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 3:1-5
passages.section_title: What changes while the two royal houses remain at war?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now the war between the house of Saul and the house of David was protracted. And David grew stronger and stronger, while the house of Saul grew weaker and weaker. 2 And sons were born to David in Hebron: His firstborn was Amnon, by Ahinoam of Jezreel; 3 his second was Chileab, by Abigail the widow of Nabal of Carmel; his third was Absalom, the son of Maacah daughter of King Talmai of Geshur; 4 his fourth was Adonijah, the son of Haggith; his fifth was Shephatiah, the son of Abital; 5 and his sixth was Ithream, by David’s wife Eglah. These sons were born to David in Hebron.

And David grew stronger and stronger, while the house of Saul grew weaker and weaker. 2 And sons were born to David in Hebron: His firstborn was Amnon, by Ahinoam of Jezreel; 3 his second was Chileab, by Abigail the widow of Nabal of Carmel; his third was Absalom, the son of Maacah daughter of King Talmai of Geshur; 4 his fourth was Adonijah, the son of Haggith; his fifth was Shephatiah, the son of Abital; 5 and his sixth was Ithream, by David’s wife Eglah. section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The struggle between Saul’s house and David’s house continues for a long time. David’s side grows stronger while Saul’s grows weaker. The victory at Gibeon has not brought the divided nation back together.

The account then introduces six sons born to David in Hebron: Amnon, Chileab, Absalom, Adonijah, Shephatiah and Ithream. Each has a different mother. These are members of the family that will stand at the center of the kingdom’s later story.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads the opening as the continuing advance of David’s house despite opposition. He also uses the struggle as an illustration of the conflict between grace and sin in a believer’s life. That is a lesson he draws from the story; the verse itself describes the fortunes of two royal houses.

The growing family should also be read alongside Deuteronomy 17:16–20, where Israel’s king is warned against multiplying wives and turning his heart away from God. Increasing power and a larger household do not by themselves establish that every choice a king makes is wise or faithful.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 3:6-21
passages.section_title: Why does Abner offer to bring Israel over to David?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 During the war between the house of Saul and the house of David, Abner had continued to strengthen his position in the house of Saul. 7 Now Saul had a concubine named Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah. So Ish-bosheth questioned Abner, “Why did you sleep with my father’s concubine?” 8 Abner was furious over Ish-bosheth’s accusation. “Am I the head of a dog that belongs to Judah?” he asked. “All this time I have been loyal to the house of your father Saul, to his brothers, and to his friends. I have not delivered you into the hand of David, but now you accuse me of wrongdoing with this woman! 9 May God punish Abner, and ever so severely, if I do not do for David what the LORD has sworn to him: 10 to transfer the kingdom from the house of Saul and to establish the throne of David over Israel and Judah, from Dan to Beersheba.” 11 And for fear of Abner, Ish-bosheth did not dare to say another word to him. 12 Then Abner sent messengers on his behalf to say to David, “To whom does the land belong? Then Abner said to him, “Go back.” So he returned home. 17 Now Abner conferred with the elders of Israel and said, “In the past you sought David as your king. 18 Now take action, because the LORD has said to David, ‘Through My servant David I will save My people Israel from the hands of the Philistines and of all their enemies.’” 19 Abner also spoke to the Benjamites. Then he went to Hebron to tell David all that seemed good to Israel and to the whole house of Benjamin. 20 When Abner and twenty of his men came to David at Hebron, David held a feast for them. 21 Then Abner said to David, “Let me go at once, and I will gather all Israel to my lord the king, that they may make a covenant with you, and that you may rule over all that your heart desires.” So David dismissed Abner, and he went in peace.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Abner’s influence grows within Saul’s house. When Ish-bosheth accuses him of sleeping with Saul’s concubine Rizpah, Abner responds furiously. He points to his loyalty to Saul’s family and declares that he will now help establish David over Israel and Judah. Ish-bosheth is too afraid of him to answer.

Abner approaches David with an offer to bring Israel to his side. David agrees to a covenant but requires the return of Michal, Saul’s daughter and David’s wife. Ish-bosheth takes her from Paltiel, who follows her in tears until Abner orders him home. The account records Paltiel’s grief but does not tell us how Michal feels about the transfer.

Abner then speaks with Israel’s elders and with Benjamin. He reminds them that they previously wanted David as king and appeals to the LORD’s promise to deliver Israel through him. David welcomes Abner and his twenty companions with a feast. Abner leaves in peace, intending to gather Israel to make a covenant with David.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Gill treats Ish-bosheth’s accusation as something whose truth the account does not establish. Abner’s angry response and change of allegiance are clear; whether he actually slept with Rizpah is not. His acknowledgment of God’s promise also sits beside an immediate personal grievance.

Wesley understands David’s demand for Michal as the recovery of his rightful wife, with both affection and political advantage in view. Henry also treats her return as restoration. Earlier, 1 Samuel 25:44 says Saul gave David’s wife to another man; it does not record David divorcing her.

Deuteronomy 24:1–4 addresses a first husband who divorces his wife and later seeks to remarry her after another marriage. Because the story of Michal does not describe that same sequence, we should not assume that citing the law alone settles every question about this transfer. The political settlement also carries a visible human cost: Paltiel walks behind her weeping.
