passages.title: 2 Samuel 3:22-30
passages.section_title: Why does Joab kill a man David has sent away in peace?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 Just then David’s soldiers and Joab returned from a raid, bringing with them a great plunder. But Abner was not with David in Hebron, because David had sent him on his way in peace. 23 When Joab and all his troops arrived, he was informed, “Abner son of Ner came to see the king, who sent him on his way in peace.” 24 So Joab went to the king and said, “What have you done? Look, Abner came to you. Why did you dismiss him? Now he is getting away! 25 Surely you realize that Abner son of Ner came to deceive you and to track your movements and all that you are doing.” 26 As soon as Joab had left David, he sent messengers after Abner, who brought him back from the well of Sirah. But David was unaware of it. 27 When Abner returned to Hebron, Joab pulled him aside into the gateway, as if to speak to him privately, and there Joab stabbed him in the stomach. So Abner died on account of the blood of Joab’s brother Asahel. 28 Afterward, David heard about this and said, “I and my kingdom are forever guiltless before the LORD concerning the blood of Abner son of Ner. 29 May it whirl over the head of Joab and over the entire house of his father, and may the house of Joab never be without one having a discharge or skin disease, or one who leans on a staff or falls by the sword or lacks food.” 30 (Joab and his brother Abishai murdered Abner because he had killed their brother Asahel in the battle at Gibeon.)

So Abner died on account of the blood of Joab’s brother Asahel.

28 Afterward, David heard about this and said, “I and my kingdom are forever guiltless before the LORD concerning the blood of Abner son of Ner. 29 May it whirl over the head of Joab and over the entire house of his father, and may the house of Joab never be without one having a discharge or skin disease, or one who leans on a staff or falls by the sword or lacks food.” 30 (Joab and his brother Abishai murdered Abner because he had killed their brother Asahel in the battle at Gibeon.)

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Joab returns from a raid after Abner has left. Learning that David welcomed and released him, Joab accuses Abner of coming as a spy. That is Joab’s accusation; the narrator does not confirm it.

Without David’s knowledge, Joab sends messengers to bring Abner back. He takes him aside into the gateway as though for a private conversation, then stabs him. The account names revenge for Asahel’s death as the reason, and it includes Joab’s brother Abishai in responsibility for the murder.

David declares himself and his kingdom innocent of Abner’s blood. He calls down suffering on Joab’s family. His words show how strongly he rejects the killing, but this passage does not report him bringing Joab to trial or removing him from command.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry, Wesley and Gill distinguish this planned killing from Asahel’s death in battle. Abner had warned Asahel to stop pursuing him. Joab now recalls a man who has left under David’s promise of peace and kills him through deception.

Wesley criticizes David’s curse against Joab’s descendants, seeing anger directed toward a family instead of punishment directed toward the murderer. Gill likewise allows that the curse comes from David’s anger rather than a prophetic announcement. Reporting the curse does not require treating every suffering David names as a prediction that God will fulfill.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 3:31-39
passages.section_title: What does David’s mourning show—and what remains unresolved?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 31 Then David ordered Joab and all the people with him, “Tear your clothes, put on sackcloth, and mourn before Abner.” And King David himself walked behind the funeral bier. 32 When they buried Abner in Hebron, the king wept aloud at Abner’s tomb, and all the people wept. 33 And the king sang this lament for Abner: “Should Abner die the death of a fool? 34 Your hands were not bound, your feet were not fettered. As a man falls before the wicked, so also you fell.” And all the people wept over him even more. 35 Then all the people came and urged David to eat something while it was still day, but David took an oath, saying, “May God punish me, and ever so severely, if I taste bread or anything else before the sun sets!” 36 All the people took note and were pleased. In fact, everything the king did pleased them. 37 So on that day all the troops and all Israel were convinced that the king had no part in the murder of Abner son of Ner. 38 Then the king said to his servants, “Do you not realize that a great prince has fallen today in Israel? 39 And I am weak this day, though anointed as king, and these men, the sons of Zeruiah, are too fierce for me. May the LORD repay the evildoer according to his evil!”

May the LORD repay the evildoer according to his evil!”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
David orders Joab and the people to mourn for Abner, and he walks behind the funeral bier himself. At the tomb he weeps and sings a lament. Abner had not been bound as a prisoner; he fell into the hands of wicked men.

David refuses food until sunset. The people take his mourning seriously and become convinced that he had no part in the murder. He tells his servants that a great prince has fallen in Israel.

Yet his closing words leave a problem in view. Though anointed king, David says he is weak and that the sons of Zeruiah are too fierce for him. He appeals to the LORD to repay the evildoer. His innocence of this murder and his ability to govern the men responsible are different questions.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads David’s public grief as sincere and as an important declaration that the king did not authorize the murder. Abner had been an opponent, but David recognizes the loss rather than celebrating an enemy’s death.

Wesley and Gill understand David’s weakness mainly in terms of his unsettled kingdom and the power of Joab and Abishai. They criticize his failure to carry out justice. Henry also regards his handling of Joab as a failure of courage and trust. These readings take David’s difficult circumstances seriously without making them a complete defense of his inaction.
passages.god_plan_html:
Henry looks beyond David’s limited rule to the greater kingship of Christ. Here David can grieve a wrong and condemn it while still struggling to govern the powerful men around him. That leaves us looking for a king whose justice is not held back by such dependence.

Jesus describes His kingdom in John 18:36–37 and connects His mission with bearing witness to the truth. Revelation 19:11–16 presents Him as the faithful and true King who judges righteously. His authority and justice do not depend on protecting a violent commander.

This is a comparison between a limited human king and Christ, rather than a claim that the New Testament directly explains Abner’s funeral. David’s grief gives us something to recognize as good; his unresolved failure also shows why our final hope reaches beyond David himself.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 4:1-4
passages.section_title: What does Abner’s death mean for Saul’s family?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now when Ish-bosheth son of Saul heard that Abner had died in Hebron, he lost courage, and all Israel was dismayed. 2 Saul’s son had two men who were leaders of raiding parties. One was named Baanah and the other Rechab; they were sons of Rimmon the Beerothite of the tribe of Benjamin—Beeroth is considered part of Benjamin, 3 because the Beerothites fled to Gittaim and have lived there as foreigners to this day. 4 And Jonathan son of Saul had a son who was lame in his feet. He was five years old when the report about Saul and Jonathan came from Jezreel. His nurse picked him up and fled, but as she was hurrying to escape, he fell and became lame. His name was Mephibosheth.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
When Ish-bosheth hears that Abner has died, he loses courage, and Israel is dismayed. The king who was afraid to answer Abner now has to face the loss of the commander who supported his rule.

Two leaders of raiding parties are introduced: Baanah and Rechab, brothers from Beeroth, counted here as part of Benjamin. The account pauses to explain the Beerothites’ move to Gittaim before turning to another member of Saul’s family.

Jonathan’s son Mephibosheth was five years old when news of Saul’s and Jonathan’s deaths arrived. His nurse fled with him, and in the hurry he fell and became lame in his feet. This is a look back to the earlier disaster, not a new accident caused by the news of Abner’s death.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill connect this description of Saul’s weakened family with the opportunity the two captains think they see. Ish-bosheth has lost his strongest supporter, and the narrative introduces Jonathan’s injured son before recounting the murder.

The account explains how Mephibosheth came to be injured. It does not blame him for the injury or present it as a measure of his character. Speculation about precisely which bones were damaged goes beyond what these verses tell us.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 4:5-12
passages.section_title: Can murder become good news because it benefits David?

That was his reward for his news! 11 How much more, when wicked men kill a righteous man in his own house and on his own bed, shall I not now require his blood from your hands and remove you from the earth!” 12 So David commanded his young men, and they killed Rechab and Baanah. They cut off their hands and feet and hung their bodies by the pool in Hebron, but they took the head of Ish-bosheth and buried it in Abner’s tomb in Hebron.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Rechab and Baanah enter Ish-bosheth’s house while he is resting at midday. Pretending to get wheat, they stab and kill him, cut off his head, and carry it through the night to David in Hebron.

They present the killing as the LORD’s vengeance on Saul’s family for David’s benefit. David refuses that explanation. He recalls what happened to the messenger who expected a reward for news of Saul’s death, then condemns these men for murdering a righteous man in his own house and bed.

David orders their execution. Their hands and feet are cut off, and their bodies are hung by the pool in Hebron. Ish-bosheth’s head is buried in Abner’s tomb. The violent end of the scene should be read as it is recorded, without turning every detail of an ancient royal punishment into an instruction for readers to imitate.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry understands David’s response as a refusal to gain the kingdom through unlawful help. Trust that God would complete His work did not make another person’s murder acceptable. The captains’ claim that the LORD had acted is their explanation of their crime, not the narrator’s endorsement.

Gill explains David’s description of Ish-bosheth as righteous in relation to this murder: he was killed at home, asleep and defenseless, rather than while fighting these men. David is identifying an innocent victim of their attack, not declaring that Ish-bosheth had never sinned.

Wesley extends the warning to people who use cruelty while claiming to serve Christ. He regards harm done under religious cover as a betrayal of that service. This is his application of the passage; it is not a claim that all churches have issued a distinct official teaching about these captains.
passages.god_plan_html:
The captains confuse an outcome favorable to David with approval from God. David’s answer separates the promised kingdom from their chosen means of advancing it. A person cannot make evil faithful merely by attaching God’s name to the result.

In Romans 3:5–8, Paul rejects the suggestion that human wrongdoing becomes acceptable because God’s truth or righteousness is displayed through it. God’s ability to accomplish good does not remove our responsibility for evil.

This is a theme shared across Scripture, not a claim that Paul is directly commenting on Ish-bosheth’s death. It helps us follow God’s purpose through a troubled history while continuing to call betrayal and murder what they are.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 5:1-5
passages.section_title: Why do all the tribes now recognize David as king?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then all the tribes of Israel came to David at Hebron and said, “Here we are, your own flesh and blood. 2 Even in times past, while Saul was king over us, you were the one who led Israel out and brought them back. And to you the LORD said, ‘You will shepherd My people Israel, and you will be ruler over them.’” 3 So all the elders of Israel came to the king at Hebron, where King David made with them a covenant before the LORD. And they anointed him king over Israel. 4 David was thirty years old when he became king, and he reigned forty years. 5 In Hebron he reigned over Judah seven years and six months, and in Jerusalem he reigned thirty-three years over all Israel and Judah.
paragraphs: 1 Then all the tribes of Israel came to David at Hebron and said, “Here we are, your own flesh and blood. 2 Even in times past, while Saul was king over us, you were the one who led Israel out and brought them back. And to you the LORD said, ‘You will shepherd My people Israel, and you will be ruler over them.’” 3 So all the elders of Israel came to the king at Hebron, where King David made with them a covenant before the LORD. And they anointed him king over Israel. 4 David was thirty years old when he became king, and he reigned forty years. 5 In Hebron he reigned over Judah seven years and six months, and in Jerusalem he reigned thirty-three years over all Israel and Judah.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the deaths of Abner and Ish-bosheth, the tribes come to David at Hebron. They appeal to their shared family identity, remember his leadership during Saul’s reign, and acknowledge the LORD’s appointment of him to shepherd Israel.

David makes a covenant with the elders before the LORD, and they anoint him king over Israel. The recognition that began in Judah now includes the whole nation.

The summary gives David’s age at the beginning of his kingship as thirty. He rules Judah at Hebron for seven years and six months, then all Israel and Judah from Jerusalem for thirty-three years. Thirty is his age when his rule begins, not his age after the years at Hebron.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley emphasizes the shepherd’s responsibility behind the royal title: David is to care for the people rather than use the office simply for his own glory. Gill likewise understands shepherding as the work of a ruler who leads and protects.

Henry sees the gradual recognition of David as a time of preparation and testing. Samuel’s earlier anointing, Judah’s acknowledgment, and now the tribes’ acknowledgment are distinct stages. Delay did not mean that the original appointment had been forgotten.
passages.god_plan_html:
Henry draws a comparison between Israel approaching David as their own flesh and blood and Jesus sharing our humanity. Hebrews 2:11–18 states the greater reality directly: Jesus shares in humanity, calls His people brothers, and helps them through His suffering and saving work.

The shepherd theme also reaches beyond David. In John 10:11–18, Jesus identifies Himself as the good shepherd who knows His sheep and lays down His life for them. God’s care for His people is expressed most fully in the One who gives Himself to save them.

These are supported connections in the larger biblical story, rather than a claim that every detail of David’s coronation predicts an event in Jesus’ life. David is called to care for the people; Christ brings that care to a depth no earthly king can match.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 5:6-10
passages.section_title: How does Jerusalem become the City of David?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 Now the king and his men marched to Jerusalem against the Jebusites who inhabited the land. The Jebusites said to David: “You will never get in here. Even the blind and lame can repel you.” For they thought, “David cannot get in here.” 7 Nevertheless, David captured the fortress of Zion (that is, the City of David). 8 On that day he said, “Whoever attacks the Jebusites must use the water shaft to reach the lame and blind who are despised by David.” That is why it is said, “The blind and the lame will never enter the palace.” 9 So David took up residence in the fortress and called it the City of David. He built it up all the way around, from the supporting terraces inward. 10 And David became greater and greater, for the LORD God of Hosts was with him.
paragraphs: 6 Now the king and his men marched to Jerusalem against the Jebusites who inhabited the land. The Jebusites said to David: “You will never get in here. Even the blind and lame can repel you.” For they thought, “David cannot get in here.” 7 Nevertheless, David captured the fortress of Zion (that is, the City of David). 8 On that day he said, “Whoever attacks the Jebusites must use the water shaft to reach the lame and blind who are despised by David.” That is why it is said, “The blind and the lame will never enter the palace.” 9 So David took up residence in the fortress and called it the City of David. He built it up all the way around, from the supporting terraces inward. 10 And David became greater and greater, for the LORD God of Hosts was with him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
David and his men move against Jerusalem, held by the Jebusites. The defenders mock him by saying that even blind and lame people could keep him out. Despite their confidence, he captures the fortress of Zion and makes it his residence.

The account connects the attack with a water shaft and records a saying about blind and lame people being excluded from the palace. David builds up the fortress, which becomes known as the City of David. The closing explanation for his growing strength is that the LORD God of Hosts is with him.

The Hebrew word rendered water shaft is tsinnor (tsin-NOR). Brown–Driver–Briggs gives meanings such as pipe, spout and conduit, while noting uncertainty about this particular verse. The term supports a connection with a water passage, but it does not give us a complete map of the attack.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley reads the Jebusites’ words as a boast about their defenses. The USCCB Bible notes also consider a mocking or proverbial expression, while acknowledging that the wording of verses 6 and 8 is difficult. It should not be turned into a general statement about the worth of people with disabilities.

Gill surveys several explanations of the passage used in the assault and of the final saying. The BSB translates the latter in relation to the palace. A confident claim that it establishes a rule excluding all Gentiles from the temple goes beyond what this account clearly says.

The parallel account in 1 Chronicles 11:4–9 adds that David promised command to the first man to strike a Jebusite, and that Joab gained that position. It confirms his role without describing each step of a climb through a particular shaft.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 5:11-16
passages.section_title: Who is David’s growing kingdom meant to benefit?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 Now Hiram king of Tyre sent envoys to David, along with cedar logs, carpenters, and stonemasons, and they built a palace for David. 12 And David realized that the LORD had established him as king over Israel and had exalted his kingdom for the sake of His people Israel. 13 After he had arrived from Hebron, David took more concubines and wives from Jerusalem, and more sons and daughters were born to him. 14 These are the names of the children born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon, 15 Ibhar, Elishua, Nepheg, Japhia, 16 Elishama, Eliada, and Eliphelet.
paragraphs: 11 Now Hiram king of Tyre sent envoys to David, along with cedar logs, carpenters, and stonemasons, and they built a palace for David. 12 And David realized that the LORD had established him as king over Israel and had exalted his kingdom for the sake of His people Israel.

13 After he had arrived from Hebron, David took more concubines and wives from Jerusalem, and more sons and daughters were born to him. 14 These are the names of the children born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon, 15 Ibhar, Elishua, Nepheg, Japhia, 16 Elishama, Eliada, and Eliphelet.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Hiram king of Tyre sends messengers, cedar logs and skilled workers who build David a palace. David recognizes that the LORD has established him as king and raised up his kingdom for the sake of Israel.

The account also records more wives and concubines and more sons and daughters after the move from Hebron. Eleven sons are named here, including Nathan and Solomon. The growth of the royal household is part of the description of David’s established rule.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Gill emphasize the purpose David recognizes: his elevation is for the people’s benefit. The palace is a sign of an established kingdom, but the king’s comfort is not the whole point of the kingdom.

Wesley criticizes David’s growing number of wives in light of Deuteronomy 17:17. The command warned a king against multiplying wives and turning his heart away. Recording David’s expanding family does not make all his choices commands or examples for others to follow.

These observations can be held together. God’s care for Israel through David and the need to examine David’s conduct are both part of reading the account carefully.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 5:17-25
passages.section_title: Why does David ask God again before the second battle?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 When the Philistines heard that David had been anointed king over Israel, they all went in search of him; but David learned of this and went down to the stronghold. 18 Now the Philistines had come and spread out in the Valley of Rephaim. 19 So David inquired of the LORD, “Should I go up against the Philistines? Will You deliver them into my hand?” “Go up,” replied the LORD, “for I will surely deliver the Philistines into your hand.” 20 So David went to Baal-perazim, where he defeated the Philistines and said, “Like a bursting flood, the LORD has burst out against my enemies before me.” So he called that place Baal-perazim. 21 There the Philistines abandoned their idols, and David and his men carried them away. 22 Once again the Philistines came up and spread out in the Valley of Rephaim. 23 So David inquired of the LORD, who answered, “Do not march straight up, but circle around behind them and attack them in front of the balsam trees. 24 As soon as you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees, move quickly, because this will mean that the LORD has gone out before you to strike the camp of the Philistines.” 25 So David did as the LORD had commanded him, and he struck down the Philistines all the way from Gibeon to Gezer.
paragraphs: 17 When the Philistines heard that David had been anointed king over Israel, they all went in search of him; but David learned of this and went down to the stronghold. 18 Now the Philistines had come and spread out in the Valley of Rephaim. 19 So David inquired of the LORD, “Should I go up against the Philistines? Will You deliver them into my hand?” “Go up,” replied the LORD, “for I will surely deliver the Philistines into your hand.” 20 So David went to Baal-perazim, where he defeated the Philistines and said, “Like a bursting flood, the LORD has burst out against my enemies before me.” So he called that place Baal-perazim. 21 There the Philistines abandoned their idols, and David and his men carried them away.

22 Once again the Philistines came up and spread out in the Valley of Rephaim. 23 So David inquired of the LORD, who answered, “Do not march straight up, but circle around behind them and attack them in front of the balsam trees. 24 As soon as you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees, move quickly, because this will mean that the LORD has gone out before you to strike the camp of the Philistines.” 25 So David did as the LORD had commanded him, and he struck down the Philistines all the way from Gibeon to Gezer.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Philistines respond to David’s recognition as king by coming against him. When they spread out in the Valley of Rephaim, he asks the LORD whether to attack and whether God will deliver them into his hand. The LORD tells him to go, and David wins.

David compares the victory to water bursting through a barrier and credits the LORD with breaking through his enemies. The Philistines abandon their idols, which David and his men carry away. 1 Chronicles 14:12 adds that David orders them burned.

When the Philistines return, David asks the LORD again. This time the instructions change: circle behind them, approach in front of the balsam trees, and move when the sound of marching is heard in the treetops. David follows the command and defeats them from Gibeon to Gezer. A previous victory does not replace fresh attention to God’s direction.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry stresses David’s dependence on God and his readiness to act when directed. Wesley also sees God’s promise and human action working together: confidence in God does not mean neglecting the task He gives.

Gill discusses the marching sound in relation to wind and angelic help. The USCCB Bible notes understand it as suggestive of the LORD and His heavenly army. The text gives the sign’s meaning clearly—the LORD has gone ahead—without naming every detail of how the sound is produced.
passages.god_plan_html:
Henry compares David waiting for God’s direction with the apostles waiting for the promised Spirit. The shared lesson is dependence on God’s provision rather than confidence that the mission can be carried by human strength alone.

In Acts 1:4–8, Jesus tells His followers to wait for the Father’s gift and promises power from the Holy Spirit to be His witnesses. Their task is to bear witness to Him from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth.

This is a limited parallel about depending on God and then obeying. Israel’s battle is not a pattern authorizing the church to spread the gospel through military force. The apostles receive a mission of witness, with the Spirit’s power for that work.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 6:1-5
passages.section_title: Why does David gather Israel to bring up the ark?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 David again assembled the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand in all. 2 And he and all his troops set out for Baale of Judah to bring up from there the ark of God, which is called by the Name— the name of the LORD of Hosts, who is enthroned between the cherubim that are on it. 3 They set the ark of God on a new cart and brought it from the house of Abinadab, which was on the hill. Uzzah and Ahio, the sons of Abinadab, were guiding the new cart, 4 bringing with it the ark of God. And Ahio was walking in front of the ark. 5 David and all the house of Israel were celebrating before the LORD with all kinds of wood instruments, harps, stringed instruments, tambourines, sistrums, and cymbals.
paragraphs: 1 David again assembled the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand in all. 2 And he and all his troops set out for Baale of Judah to bring up from there the ark of God, which is called by the Name— the name of the LORD of Hosts, who is enthroned between the cherubim that are on it. 3 They set the ark of God on a new cart and brought it from the house of Abinadab, which was on the hill. Uzzah and Ahio, the sons of Abinadab, were guiding the new cart, 4 bringing with it the ark of God. And Ahio was walking in front of the ark. 5 David and all the house of Israel were celebrating before the LORD with all kinds of wood instruments, harps, stringed instruments, tambourines, sistrums, and cymbals.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
David assembles thirty thousand chosen men to bring the ark of God from Baale of Judah. The account identifies it with the name of the LORD of Hosts, enthroned between the cherubim. This is a public act of honoring God, not simply moving an item of royal property.

The ark is placed on a new cart, guided by Uzzah and Ahio from Abinadab’s household. David and Israel celebrate before the LORD with instruments. The joy is unmistakable, but the way they transport the ark will become central to what follows.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry emphasizes the renewed concern to honor the ark after David becomes established. He also warns that the cart does not follow God’s appointed method. Wesley sees the Philistines’ earlier use of a cart as a possible influence, though these verses do not directly explain why David chooses it.

The instructions distinguish the work of priests from the work of the carriers. In Numbers 4:5–15, Aaron and his sons cover the sacred objects before the Kohathites carry them. Numbers 7:9 says the Kohathites are to carry their holy objects on their shoulders. A new cart and enthusiastic celebration do not replace those instructions.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 6:6-11
passages.section_title: Why does the celebration stop at Uzzah’s death?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 When they came to the threshing floor of Nacon, Uzzah reached out and took hold of the ark of God, because the oxen had stumbled. 7 And the anger of the LORD burned against Uzzah, and God struck him down on the spot for his irreverence, and he died there beside the ark of God. 8 Then David became angry because the LORD had burst forth against Uzzah. So he named that place Perez-uzzah, as it is called to this day. 9 That day David feared the LORD and asked, “How can the ark of the LORD ever come to me?” 10 So he was unwilling to move the ark of the LORD to the City of David; instead, he took it aside to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite. 11 Thus the ark of the LORD remained in the house of Obed-edom the Gittite for three months, and the LORD blessed him and all his household.
paragraphs: 6 When they came to the threshing floor of Nacon, Uzzah reached out and took hold of the ark of God, because the oxen had stumbled. 7 And the anger of the LORD burned against Uzzah, and God struck him down on the spot for his irreverence, and he died there beside the ark of God. 8 Then David became angry because the LORD had burst forth against Uzzah. So he named that place Perez-uzzah, as it is called to this day. 9 That day David feared the LORD and asked, “How can the ark of the LORD ever come to me?”

10 So he was unwilling to move the ark of the LORD to the City of David; instead, he took it aside to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite. 11 Thus the ark of the LORD remained in the house of Obed-edom the Gittite for three months, and the LORD blessed him and all his household.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
At Nacon’s threshing floor the oxen stumble. Uzzah reaches out and takes hold of the ark, and God strikes him down. The BSB describes the reason as his irreverence. David becomes angry and afraid, and the journey stops.

David asks how the ark can come to him and takes it instead to Obed-edom’s house. It remains there three months, during which the LORD blesses Obed-edom and his household. The same account that records judgment also records blessing; the ark is not presented as a source of automatic harm to every household near it.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry understands Uzzah’s action as presumption toward something holy. Wesley acknowledges how severe the judgment appears when the apparent intention is to protect the ark, but reads it as a warning against treating God’s holiness lightly. Both go beyond merely describing a transport accident.

The Hebrew expression behind irreverence is difficult. Brown–Driver–Briggs notes disputed explanations, including acting hastily or in error. That uncertainty does not establish that the fault belongs only to David. The parallel in 1 Chronicles 13:10 explicitly connects Uzzah’s death with his putting his hand on the ark.

Leadership responsibility remains part of the story. In 1 Chronicles 15:11–15, David acknowledges that they had not consulted God about the proper order. That passage lets us recognize the wider failure without inventing a complete account of Uzzah’s inner thoughts or declaring him an innocent bystander.
passages.god_plan_html:
The question of approaching a holy God runs through Scripture. Here, the desire to bring the ark near does not erase the boundaries God has given. Yet the blessing on Obed-edom’s household shows that God’s presence is not something His people must simply flee.

Hebrews 12:28–29 calls those receiving God’s kingdom to grateful worship with reverence and awe. Hebrews 4:14–16 also invites believers to approach God’s throne confidently because Jesus is their great high priest.

This is a shared biblical theme, rather than a claim that Hebrews directly interprets Uzzah’s death. Reverence and confidence belong together: we do not make God less holy in order to come near, and through Christ we are invited to seek mercy and help.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 6:12-19
passages.section_title: What changes when the ark’s journey resumes?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 Now it was reported to King David, “The LORD has blessed the house of Obed-edom and all that belongs to him, because of the ark of God.” So David went and had the ark of God brought up from the house of Obed-edom into the City of David with rejoicing. 13 When those carrying the ark of the LORD had advanced six paces, he sacrificed an ox and a fattened calf. 14 And David, wearing a linen ephod, danced with all his might before the LORD, 15 while he and all the house of Israel brought up the ark of the LORD with shouting and the sounding of the ram’s horn. 16 As the ark of the LORD was entering the City of David, Saul’s daughter Michal looked down from a window and saw King David leaping and dancing before the LORD, and she despised him in her heart. 17 So they brought the ark of the LORD and set it in its place inside the tent that David had pitched for it. Then David offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the LORD. 18 When David had finished sacrificing the burnt offerings and peace offerings, he blessed the people in the name of the LORD of Hosts. 19 Then he distributed to every man and woman among the multitude of Israel a loaf of bread, a date cake, and a raisin cake. And all the people departed, each to his own home.

Then David offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the LORD. 18 When David had finished sacrificing the burnt offerings and peace offerings, he blessed the people in the name of the LORD of Hosts. 19 Then he distributed to every man and woman among the multitude of Israel a loaf of bread, a date cake, and a raisin cake. And all the people departed, each to his own home.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
When David hears of the blessing on Obed-edom’s household, he resumes bringing the ark to Jerusalem with joy. This time the account speaks of people carrying it. After six paces, David sacrifices an ox and a fattened calf.

Wearing a linen ephod, David dances before the LORD with all his might, while Israel joins with shouting and the ram’s horn. Michal watches from a window and despises him in her heart. Her response introduces a conflict that will surface when he comes home.

The ark is placed inside the tent David has prepared. He offers burnt offerings and peace offerings, blesses the people in the LORD’s name, and distributes bread, date cakes and raisin cakes to men and women alike. The public celebration ends with people returning to their households.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
1 Chronicles 15:1–15 gives the fuller account of the correction: David appoints Levites, calls them to consecrate themselves, and has the ark carried on shoulders with poles as Moses commanded. Joy and attention to God’s instructions now appear together.

Gill reads the sacrifice after six paces as thanksgiving at the safe beginning of the journey. He questions the idea that it was repeated at every six steps. The BSB describes a sacrifice after six paces; it does not explicitly say every six paces along the entire route.

Wesley and Henry understand David’s linen clothing as a setting aside of royal display in service before God. 1 Chronicles 15:27 also describes his robe of fine linen. The king joins the procession as a worshiper who serves the LORD.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 6:20-23
passages.section_title: Why do David and Michal see the celebration so differently?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 20 When David returned home to bless his own household, Saul’s daughter Michal came out to meet him. “How the king of Israel has distinguished himself today!” she said. “He has uncovered himself today in the sight of the maidservants of his subjects, like a vulgar person would do.” 21 But David said to Michal, “I was dancing before the LORD, who chose me over your father and all his house when He appointed me ruler over the LORD’s people Israel. I will celebrate before the LORD, 22 and I will humiliate and humble myself even more than this. Yet I will be honored by the maidservants of whom you have spoken.” 23 And Michal the daughter of Saul had no children to the day of her death.

I will celebrate before the LORD, 22 and I will humiliate and humble myself even more than this. Yet I will be honored by the maidservants of whom you have spoken.” 23 And Michal the daughter of Saul had no children to the day of her death.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
David returns to bless his household, but Michal greets him with sarcasm. She accuses him of exposing himself before the maidservants in a way unworthy of a king. He answers that his celebration was before the LORD, who appointed him to rule Israel.

David is willing to lower himself further rather than protect his royal dignity at the expense of honoring God. He expects honor from the very women Michal has mentioned. The account closes by saying that Michal had no children to the day of her death.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill read Michal’s accusation in relation to David laying aside royal clothing, rather than as proof that he was literally naked. The USCCB Bible notes likewise connect the dispute with her expectations of how a king should behave.

Henry and Wesley understand her childlessness as judgment for despising David’s worship. That is their reading of the closing note. The BSB states the outcome without explaining its physical cause or saying whether David and Michal continued marital relations.

We can recognize the contrast between David’s joy and Michal’s contempt without turning this account into a general explanation of why someone cannot have children. The passage describes this particular household; it gives us no basis for judging other people’s faith from their fertility.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 7:1-7
passages.section_title: Why does God redirect David’s plan to build Him a house?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 After the king had settled into his palace and the LORD had given him rest from all his enemies around him, 2 he said to Nathan the prophet, “Here I am, living in a house of cedar, while the ark of God remains in a tent.” 3 And Nathan replied to the king, “Go and do all that is in your heart, for the LORD is with you.” 4 But that night the word of the LORD came to Nathan, saying, 5 “Go and tell My servant David that this is what the LORD says: Are you the one to build for Me a house to dwell in? 6 For I have not dwelt in a house from the day I brought the Israelites up out of Egypt until this day, but I have moved about with a tent as My dwelling. 7 In all My journeys with all the Israelites, have I ever asked any of the leaders I appointed to shepherd My people Israel, ‘Why haven’t you built Me a house of cedar?’
paragraphs: 1 After the king had settled into his palace and the LORD had given him rest from all his enemies around him, 2 he said to Nathan the prophet, “Here I am, living in a house of cedar, while the ark of God remains in a tent.” 3 And Nathan replied to the king, “Go and do all that is in your heart, for the LORD is with you.”

4 But that night the word of the LORD came to Nathan, saying, 5 “Go and tell My servant David that this is what the LORD says: Are you the one to build for Me a house to dwell in? 6 For I have not dwelt in a house from the day I brought the Israelites up out of Egypt until this day, but I have moved about with a tent as My dwelling. 7 In all My journeys with all the Israelites, have I ever asked any of the leaders I appointed to shepherd My people Israel, ‘Why haven’t you built Me a house of cedar?’

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
With rest from surrounding enemies, David notices the contrast between his cedar palace and the tent housing the ark. He speaks to Nathan, who encourages him to do what is in his heart because the LORD is with him.

That night, however, the LORD gives Nathan a message for David. God has accompanied Israel from Egypt in a tent and has not demanded a cedar house from the leaders appointed to shepherd His people. The question is no longer simply what David would like to build, but what God Himself intends.

The account distinguishes Nathan’s first advice from the word of the LORD that comes afterward. The prophet must now return with a message that redirects the king’s plan.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry, Wesley and Gill understand Nathan’s first response as his own judgment rather than a revelation from God. His office does not make every personal recommendation a message from the LORD.

David’s desire should not simply be labeled contempt for God’s instructions. In 1 Kings 8:17–20, Solomon recalls that the LORD approved the desire in David’s heart while assigning the building to David’s son. A good intention can be welcomed even when God gives the task to someone else.
passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 7:44–50 directly recalls the tabernacle, David’s desire to provide a dwelling, and Solomon’s building of the house. Stephen then explains that the Most High does not live within the limits of houses made by human hands.

This gives the scene a place in a larger biblical lesson: God’s presence and greatness do not depend on the scale of a building people provide. He accompanied His people before Solomon’s temple existed, and the Creator cannot be contained by what He created.

The connection does not require treating every place built for worship as wrong. It changes where our confidence rests. God makes Himself known and directs His people; a grand structure cannot take His place.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 7:8-17
passages.section_title: What kind of house does God promise to build for David?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 Now then, you are to tell My servant David that this is what the LORD of Hosts says: I took you from the pasture, from following the flock, to be the ruler over My people Israel. 9 I have been with you wherever you have gone, and I have cut off all your enemies from before you. Now I will make for you a name like that of the greatest in the land. 10 And I will provide a place for My people Israel and will plant them so that they may dwell in a place of their own and be disturbed no more. No longer will the sons of wickedness oppress them as they did at the beginning 11 and have done since the day I appointed judges over My people Israel. I will give you rest from all your enemies. The LORD declares to you that He Himself will establish a house for you. 12 And when your days are fulfilled and you rest with your fathers, I will raise up your descendant after you, who will come from your own body, and I will establish his kingdom. 13 He will build a house for My Name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. 14 I will be his Father, and he will be My son. When he does wrong, I will discipline him with the rod of men and with the blows of the sons of men. 15 But My loving devotion will never be removed from him as I removed it from Saul, whom I removed from before you. 16 Your house and kingdom will endure forever before Me, and your throne will be established forever.” 17 So Nathan relayed to David all the words of this entire revelation.

The LORD declares to you that He Himself will establish a house for you.

12 And when your days are fulfilled and you rest with your fathers, I will raise up your descendant after you, who will come from your own body, and I will establish his kingdom. 13 He will build a house for My Name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. 14 I will be his Father, and he will be My son. When he does wrong, I will discipline him with the rod of men and with the blows of the sons of men. 15 But My loving devotion will never be removed from him as I removed it from Saul, whom I removed from before you. 16 Your house and kingdom will endure forever before Me, and your throne will be established forever.” 17 So Nathan relayed to David all the words of this entire revelation.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The LORD reminds David that He took him from caring for sheep and made him ruler of Israel. David’s rise has depended on God’s presence and help. The message also promises a settled place and rest for God’s people.

Then the meaning of house changes. David has proposed a building for God; God promises an enduring family and kingdom for David. A descendant will build a house for God’s name, and God will establish his throne.

The promise includes a father-and-son relationship and discipline when the royal son does wrong. It also distinguishes David’s house from Saul’s: God’s loving devotion will not be withdrawn in the same way. The message ends with the repeated assurance that David’s house, kingdom and throne will endure forever.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley, Henry and the USCCB Bible notes recognize Solomon’s place in the promise while looking beyond him to the lasting kingship of Christ. 1 Chronicles 22:9–10 explicitly names Solomon as the son who will build the house and describes God as his Father. 1 Kings 8:20 treats Solomon’s succession and temple building as God keeping His word.

Wesley applies the warning about wrongdoing to Solomon and other descendants who sin, while understanding the everlasting throne in relation to Christ. Henry also insists that the wrongdoing cannot describe Christ Himself, and extends the lesson of fatherly correction to believers. These readings distinguish the sinless Messiah from the failings of those associated with the royal promise.

It is therefore possible to recognize real events in Solomon’s reign without making his lifetime the whole meaning of an everlasting kingdom. The promise reaches further than any one mortal king.
passages.god_plan_html:
The New Testament makes the connection to Jesus directly. In Luke 1:30–33, the angel announces that God will give Jesus the throne of David and that His kingdom will never end. The enduring kingship promised here is part of the announcement of who Jesus is.

Hebrews 1:1–5 applies the promise of a Father-and-Son relationship to Christ as it explains His greatness above the angels. It uses that promise without assigning the royal descendants’ wrongdoing to Jesus.

In Acts 2:29–36, Peter connects God’s oath about David’s descendant with Jesus’ resurrection and exaltation. David died; Jesus has been raised and declared Lord and Christ. God’s answer to the limits of David’s reign is not merely another brief reign, but the living King whose kingdom endures.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 7:18-29
passages.section_title: How does David respond to a promise he could never earn?

Is this Your custom with man, O Lord GOD? 20 What more can David say to You? For You know Your servant, O Lord GOD. 21 For the sake of Your word and according to Your own heart, You have accomplished this great thing and revealed it to Your servant. 22 How great You are, O Lord GOD! section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
David goes in and sits before the LORD, amazed at what God has done for him and promised for his family’s future. He does not begin by listing his achievements. He asks who he and his household are to have received such generosity.

His thanks moves from his own house to Israel. He praises the LORD as the one true God who redeemed a people from Egypt and established them as His own. The promise to David belongs within that larger history of God’s care.

David then asks God to confirm His word, magnify His name and bless the house of His servant. The promise gives him courage to pray. He rests his request on God’s truthfulness rather than his ability to control the future.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley emphasize David’s humble recognition that these gifts come from God’s generosity, not from a claim that God owes him a dynasty. His prayer responds to what God has already said.

Wesley also stresses that the prayer comes from David’s heart rather than merely his lips. Henry sees assurance in the relationship between God’s word and His action: the One who promises can be trusted to do as He has said.

David’s confidence should not turn this particular royal promise into a guarantee that every reader’s family will receive a throne or earthly prosperity. The prayer shows us how he receives God’s word with thanks and brings that word back to God in prayer.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 8:1-6
passages.section_title: How does the account describe David’s expanding rule?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Some time later, David defeated the Philistines, subdued them, and took Metheg-ammah from the hand of the Philistines. 2 David also defeated the Moabites, made them lie down on the ground, and measured them off with a cord. He measured off with two lengths those to be put to death, and with one length those to be spared. So the Moabites became subject to David and brought him tribute. 3 David also defeated Hadadezer son of Rehob, king of Zobah, who had marched out to restore his dominion along the Euphrates River. 4 David captured from him a thousand chariots, seven thousand charioteers, and twenty thousand foot soldiers, and he hamstrung all the horses except a hundred he kept for the chariots. 5 When the Arameans of Damascus came to help King Hadadezer of Zobah, David struck down twenty-two thousand of their men. 6 Then he placed garrisons in Aram of Damascus, and the Arameans became subject to David and brought him tribute. So the LORD made David victorious wherever he went.

He measured off with two lengths those to be put to death, and with one length those to be spared. So the Moabites became subject to David and brought him tribute.

3 David also defeated Hadadezer son of Rehob, king of Zobah, who had marched out to restore his dominion along the Euphrates River. 4 David captured from him a thousand chariots, seven thousand charioteers, and twenty thousand foot soldiers, and he hamstrung all the horses except a hundred he kept for the chariots. 5 When the Arameans of Damascus came to help King Hadadezer of Zobah, David struck down twenty-two thousand of their men. 6 Then he placed garrisons in Aram of Damascus, and the Arameans became subject to David and brought him tribute. So the LORD made David victorious wherever he went.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The chapter surveys David’s victories beyond Israel’s borders. He subdues the Philistines and takes Metheg-ammah. The parallel in 1 Chronicles 18:1 names Gath and its villages.

The defeat of Moab includes a grim division: people are made to lie on the ground and measured with a cord, with some put to death and others spared. Those left become subject to David and pay tribute. The violence is part of the account and should not disappear behind a general description of national success.

David also defeats Hadadezer of Zobah and the Arameans who come to help him. He disables captured chariot horses while keeping a hundred, places garrisons in Aram of Damascus, and receives tribute. The summary credits the LORD with making David victorious.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry understands the measuring in Moab as two parts put to death and one spared. Gill reports that reading and an alternative in which the full line marks the larger group spared. The USCCB Bible notes also discuss the uncertainty about the proportions.

The BSB states the division by lengths without explaining a height or age test. We should therefore avoid confidently saying that only adult men were killed while children were spared.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 8:7-14
passages.section_title: What does David do with the wealth that comes from victory?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 And David took the gold shields that belonged to the officers of Hadadezer and brought them to Jerusalem. 8 And from Betah and Berothai, cities of Hadadezer, King David took a large amount of bronze. 9 When King Toi of Hamath heard that David had defeated the entire army of Hadadezer, 10 he sent his son Joram to greet King David and bless him for fighting and defeating Hadadezer, who had been at war with Toi. Joram brought with him articles of silver and gold and bronze, 11 and King David dedicated these to the LORD, along with the silver and gold he had dedicated from all the nations he had subdued— 12 from Edom and Moab, from the Ammonites and Philistines and Amalekites, and from the spoil of Hadadezer son of Rehob, king of Zobah. 13 And David made a name for himself when he returned from striking down eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt. 14 He placed garrisons throughout Edom, and all the Edomites were subject to David. So the LORD made David victorious wherever he went.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
David brings Hadadezer’s gold shields to Jerusalem and takes bronze from two of his cities. Toi of Hamath, who had also been at war with Hadadezer, sends his son Joram with congratulations and gifts of silver, gold and bronze.

David dedicates these gifts to the LORD along with wealth from the peoples he has subdued. The survey then records victory over eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt and garrisons throughout Edom. Once again, it credits the LORD with David’s success.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry connects the dedicated wealth with preparations for the temple. The parallel in 1 Chronicles 18:8 specifically says that Solomon used the captured bronze for temple furnishings. David’s part in the work extends beyond what he builds during his own lifetime.

1 Chronicles 18:12–13 names Abishai in the Edomite victory that this passage credits to David. The USCCB Bible notes also note the different attribution. A royal summary can credit a king with his forces’ achievement without saying he personally delivered every blow.

Toi’s gift is presented as a response to the defeat of a common opponent. The passage does not describe the terms of a separate covenant or tell us the private motives behind every diplomatic gesture.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 8:15-18
passages.section_title: What is David’s government meant to provide for the people?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 Thus David reigned over all Israel and administered justice and righteousness for all his people: 16 Joab son of Zeruiah was over the army; Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was the recorder; 17 Zadok son of Ahitub and Ahimelech son of Abiathar were priests; Seraiah was the scribe; 18 Benaiah son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and Pelethites; and David’s sons were priestly leaders.
paragraphs: 15 Thus David reigned over all Israel and administered justice and righteousness for all his people: 16 Joab son of Zeruiah was over the army; Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was the recorder; 17 Zadok son of Ahitub and Ahimelech son of Abiathar were priests; Seraiah was the scribe; 18 Benaiah son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and Pelethites; and David’s sons were priestly leaders.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The account moves from victories abroad to the work of governing at home. David rules over Israel and administers justice and righteousness for his people. Strength is not described only in terms of land, tribute or an army.

The summary names his leading officials: Joab over the army, Jehoshaphat as recorder, Zadok and Ahimelech as priests, Seraiah as scribe, and Benaiah over the Cherethites and Pelethites. It also gives David’s sons a place in the leadership.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry emphasizes the king’s responsibility to attend to justice rather than leave people’s claims unanswered. The verse describes the character of David’s administration; it does not say he never makes a wrong decision elsewhere in the book.

The description of David’s sons needs care. The Hebrew word kohen (koh-HEN) normally means priest, and the BSB calls them priestly leaders. Brown–Driver–Briggs includes this verse under chiefs who exercise priestly functions. Gill instead emphasizes their role as senior royal officials, comparing 1 Chronicles 18:17, which places them at the king’s side. The main difference is whether their title points to religious duties or senior service in the royal court.
passages.god_plan_html:
The connection between David’s throne and justice continues in Isaiah 9:6–7. The promised ruler will sustain his kingdom with justice and righteousness, and his government and peace will not end. The hope reaches beyond winning a battle to the lasting character of the King’s rule.

Luke 1:32–33 identifies Jesus as the One who receives David’s throne and reigns forever.

David’s rule gives a real picture of justice being administered, but the rest of his story shows its limits. The enduring hope is in the King whose rule will not fail or end.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 9:1-13
passages.section_title: Why does David welcome Jonathan’s son to his table?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then David asked, “Is there anyone left from the house of Saul to whom I can show kindness for the sake of Jonathan?” 2 And there was a servant of the house of Saul named Ziba. They summoned him to David, and the king inquired, “Are you Ziba?” “I am your servant,” he replied. 3 So the king asked, “Is there anyone left of the house of Saul to whom I can show the kindness of God?” Ziba answered, “There is still Jonathan’s son, who is lame in both feet.” 4 “Where is he?” replied the king. And Ziba said, “Indeed, he is in Lo-debar at the house of Machir son of Ammiel.” 5 So King David had him brought from the house of Machir son of Ammiel in Lo-debar. 6 And when Mephibosheth son of Jonathan, the son of Saul, came to David, he fell facedown in reverence. Then David said, “Mephibosheth!” “I am your servant,” he replied. 7 “Do not be afraid,” said David, “for surely I will show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan. I will restore to you all the land of your grandfather Saul, and you will always eat at my table.” 8 Mephibosheth bowed down and said, “What is your servant, that you should show regard for a dead dog like me?” 9 Then the king summoned Saul’s servant Ziba and said to him, “I have given to your master’s grandson all that belonged to Saul and to all his house. 10 You and your sons and servants are to work the ground for him and bring in the harvest, so that your master’s grandson may have food to eat. But Mephibosheth, your master’s grandson, is always to eat at my table.” Now Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants. 11 And Ziba said to the king, “Your servant will do all that my lord the king has commanded.” So Mephibosheth ate at David’s table like one of the king’s own sons. 12 And Mephibosheth had a young son named Mica, and all who dwelt in the house of Ziba were servants of Mephibosheth. 13 So Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem, because he always ate at the king’s table, and he was lame in both feet.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
David asks whether anyone remains from Saul’s house to whom he can show kindness for Jonathan’s sake. Ziba, a servant of Saul’s household, tells him about Jonathan’s son Mephibosheth, who is living with Machir in Lo-debar and is lame in both feet.

David has Mephibosheth brought to him, calls him by name and tells him not to fear. He promises to restore Saul’s land and give him a continuing place at the royal table. Mephibosheth responds with astonished humility, referring to himself as a dead dog. Those are his words about himself, not a judgment the narrator asks us to make about his worth.

David assigns Ziba, his fifteen sons and twenty servants to cultivate the land. Mephibosheth lives in Jerusalem and eats at the king’s table like one of David’s own sons. His young son Mica is also mentioned. The chapter ends by again noting his disability; his welcome has not depended on its removal.

The word translated kindness is hesed (KHEH-sed). Brown–Driver–Briggs includes kindness expressed in favors and benefits, and specifically lists this chapter. Here it takes practical form: property, provision and a place at the table.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads David’s action as faithfulness to his friendship and promises to Jonathan. Gill also connects it with the pledge not to cut off kindness from Jonathan’s household. That promise is recorded in 1 Samuel 20:12–17. The passage presents David seeking an opportunity for kindness rather than a reason to eliminate a rival.

Gill understands eating like one of the king’s sons as a high honor and a continuing expression of friendship. The land’s produce supports Mephibosheth’s household even while he regularly eats with David. Both provision and personal welcome matter.

His disability is stated plainly, but the account does not equate it with guilt, uselessness or a lesser human value. David’s kindness is tied to Jonathan and the promise he made, not to a test of Mephibosheth’s physical ability.
passages.god_plan_html:
Henry draws a limited comparison between David’s kindness and the kindness of God our Savior. Mephibosheth does not arrive with an achievement that purchases his place. The king takes the initiative and gives him a welcome rooted in a relationship and promise that came before this meeting.

Ephesians 2:4–10 describes God’s mercy and kindness in Christ: salvation is His gift, received through faith rather than earned by works, and it leads into the good works He prepares. The connection is the generosity of the giver, not a claim that a physical disability represents sin.

The table also offers a meaningful parallel of welcome. In Luke 22:28–30, Jesus promises His faithful disciples a place at His table in His kingdom. That is a different promise in a different setting, but both scenes help us see the honor of being received by the king.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 10:1-5
passages.section_title: How does an offer of kindness become a public humiliation?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Some time later, the king of the Ammonites died and was succeeded by his son Hanun. 2 And David said, “I will show kindness to Hanun son of Nahash, just as his father showed kindness to me.” So David sent some of his servants to console Hanun concerning his father. But when they arrived in the land of the Ammonites, 3 the princes of the Ammonites said to Hanun their lord, “Just because David has sent you comforters, do you really believe he is showing respect for your father? Has not David instead sent his servants to explore the city, spy it out, and overthrow it?” 4 So Hanun took David’s servants, shaved off half of each man’s beard, cut off their garments at the hips, and sent them away. 5 When this was reported to David, he sent messengers to meet the men, since they had been thoroughly humiliated. The king told them, “Stay in Jericho until your beards have grown back, and then return.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the Ammonite king dies, his son Hanun succeeds him. David sends servants to console him, intending to return the kindness his father Nahash had shown him. Hanun’s advisers interpret the visit as a plan to spy out the city and overthrow it.

Hanun accepts that suspicion and humiliates the messengers: he has half of each man’s beard shaved and their clothes cut at the hips. David responds to their shame by allowing them to remain in Jericho until their beards grow back. His concern reaches the men themselves, not only the insult to his royal standing.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads the episode as an example of goodwill being distorted by suspicion. The advisers’ accusation is reported as their reasoning; the narrator has introduced David’s purpose as kindness and consolation.

Wesley and Gill emphasize the disgrace intended by the treatment of the men. Henry also highlights David’s care for them afterward. The account describes a deliberate insult and a considerate response without requiring a full reconstruction of the messengers’ clothing or a universal rule about ancient grooming.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 10:6-14
passages.section_title: How do Joab and Abishai face a battle on two fronts?

And if the Ammonites are too strong for you, then I will come to your rescue. 12 Be strong and let us fight bravely for our people and for the cities of our God. So Joab returned from fighting against the Ammonites and came to Jerusalem.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Realizing how badly they have offended David, the Ammonites hire troops from several neighboring kingdoms. David sends Joab with his mighty men. The Ammonites take position at the city gate while their allies remain in the open country.

With enemy lines in front and behind, Joab divides his forces. He takes selected men against the Arameans, and Abishai commands the rest against the Ammonites. Each agrees to come to the other’s aid if needed.

Joab urges courage for their people and God’s cities, then entrusts the outcome to what the LORD sees as good. When the Arameans flee, the Ammonites withdraw into the city. Joab returns to Jerusalem, but the wider conflict is not yet over.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Gill see Joab’s words as joining practical duty with trust in God. They prepare, encourage one another and act, while acknowledging that the outcome belongs to the LORD.

The account records this appeal to God even though it does not describe David making a separate inquiry before sending the army. Silence about an inquiry does not establish that he never prayed. Nor does Joab’s return, after forcing the opposing troops to retreat, automatically turn the encounter into a failure.
passages.god_plan_html:
Henry draws a lesson for believers from the brothers’ readiness to strengthen one another. The connection is mutual support in serving God, rather than treating Israel’s battle as the church’s method of spreading its faith.

Galatians 6:1–5 gives that responsibility a clear form in the life of the church: restore a person gently, watch against temptation, and carry one another’s burdens. Each person remains responsible for their own conduct while also being ready to help.

This is a shared theme of responsible care, not a claim that Paul is explaining Joab’s tactics. The larger lesson is that dependence on God can include accepting responsibility for one another instead of leaving someone to face every difficulty alone.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 10:15-19
passages.section_title: What happens when the Arameans gather to fight again?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 When the Arameans saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they regrouped. 16 Hadadezer sent messengers to bring more Arameans from beyond the Euphrates, and they came to Helam with Shobach the commander of Hadadezer’s army leading them. 17 When this was reported to David, he gathered all Israel, crossed the Jordan, and went to Helam. Then the Arameans arrayed themselves against David and fought against him. 18 But the Arameans fled before Israel, and David killed seven hundred charioteers and forty thousand foot soldiers. He also struck down Shobach the commander of their army, who died there. 19 When all the kings who were subject to Hadadezer saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they made peace with Israel and became subject to them. So the Arameans were afraid to help the Ammonites anymore.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The defeated Arameans regroup. Hadadezer brings additional troops from beyond the Euphrates, led by Shobach, to Helam. This time David gathers Israel, crosses the Jordan and leads the encounter.

Israel defeats them, and Shobach dies. The BSB records seven hundred charioteers and forty thousand foot soldiers killed. The kings subject to Hadadezer make peace with Israel, and the Arameans become afraid to help the Ammonites again.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley read the defeat as part of God establishing Israel’s promised reach and overcoming opposition to David’s rule. The immediate result named here is the loss of the Ammonites’ Aramean support.

The chapter does not yet describe the capture of the Ammonite capital. The next scene begins with a renewed campaign and the siege of Rabbah. Distinguishing the defeated allies from the remaining Ammonite stronghold helps explain why fighting continues into chapter 11.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 11:1-5
passages.section_title: How does David use his power when he sees Bathsheba?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 In the spring, at the time when kings march out to war, David sent out Joab and his servants with the whole army of Israel. They destroyed the Ammonites and besieged Rabbah, but David remained in Jerusalem. 2 One evening David got up from his bed and strolled around on the roof of the palace. And from the roof he saw a woman bathing—a very beautiful woman. 3 So David sent and inquired about the woman, and he was told, “This is Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam and the wife of Uriah the Hittite.” 4 Then David sent messengers to get her, and when she came to him, he slept with her. (Now she had just purified herself from her uncleanness.) Then she returned home. 5 And the woman conceived and sent word to David, saying, “I am pregnant.”
paragraphs: 1 In the spring, at the time when kings march out to war, David sent out Joab and his servants with the whole army of Israel. They destroyed the Ammonites and besieged Rabbah, but David remained in Jerusalem. 2 One evening David got up from his bed and strolled around on the roof of the palace. And from the roof he saw a woman bathing—a very beautiful woman. 3 So David sent and inquired about the woman, and he was told, “This is Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam and the wife of Uriah the Hittite.” 4 Then David sent messengers to get her, and when she came to him, he slept with her. (Now she had just purified herself from her uncleanness.) Then she returned home. 5 And the woman conceived and sent word to David, saying, “I am pregnant.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
While Joab and Israel’s army besiege Rabbah, David remains in Jerusalem. One evening he rises from his bed, walks on the palace roof and sees a beautiful woman bathing. He inquires and learns that she is Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah the Hittite.

David sends messengers to get her and sleeps with her. The BSB notes that she had just purified herself from her uncleanness. She returns home, then later sends word that she is pregnant. David has acted despite being told that she is married to a man serving in his army.

The account tells us what David sees, asks and sends others to do. It does not report Bathsheba’s private intentions while bathing or describe the conversation when she is brought to him. Those gaps should remain gaps rather than become an invented explanation that she set out to tempt him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley see a warning in David’s remaining at home while the army is away and then pursuing what he sees. The danger develops through choices: learning that the woman is married does not cause him to stop.

Interpreters differ about Bathsheba’s part. Gill and Wesley infer that she was persuaded and consented. Bob Deffinbaugh challenges readings that assign her the role of seducer and emphasizes David’s abuse of royal power. These are individual readings, not official teachings shared by every church in their traditions.

The text itself does not give us Bathsheba’s consent or intentions. It does clearly make David the king who sends for a married woman. The note about purification describes ritual cleanness; it does not establish a plan by Bathsheba to make sexual wrongdoing acceptable through a later washing.
passages.god_plan_html:
James 1:13–15 describes desire drawing a person toward sin and sin growing toward death. It also says that God does not tempt people to evil. That distinction matters as we follow a story in which God’s chosen king acts so destructively.

This is a biblical pattern illustrated by David’s choices, not a claim that James directly comments on this encounter. God’s work through David does not excuse his pursuit of another man’s wife or make the harm part of a good example.

The story calls for attention to the point where desire is becoming deliberate action. David has the authority to send for people, but authority gives him responsibility to protect them rather than freedom to take what he wants.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 11:6-13
passages.section_title: Why will Uriah not go home?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 At this, David sent orders to Joab: “Send me Uriah the Hittite.” So Joab sent him to David. 7 When Uriah came to him, David asked how Joab and the troops were doing and how the war was going. 8 Then he said to Uriah, “Go down to your house and wash your feet.” So Uriah left the palace, and a gift from the king followed him. 9 But Uriah slept at the door of the palace with all his master’s servants; he did not go down to his house. 10 And David was told, “Uriah did not go home.” “Haven’t you just arrived from a journey?” David asked Uriah. “Why didn’t you go home?” 11 Uriah answered, “The ark and Israel and Judah are dwelling in tents, and my master Joab and his soldiers are camped in the open field. How can I go to my house to eat and drink and sleep with my wife? As surely as you live, and as your soul lives, I will not do such a thing!” 12 “Stay here one more day,” David said to Uriah, “and tomorrow I will send you back.” So Uriah stayed in Jerusalem that day and the next. 13 Then David invited Uriah to eat and drink with him, and he got Uriah drunk. And in the evening Uriah went out to lie down on his cot with his master’s servants, but he did not go home.
