How can I go to my house to eat and drink and sleep with my wife? As surely as you live, and as your soul lives, I will not do such a thing!” 12 “Stay here one more day,” David said to Uriah, “and tomorrow I will send you back.” So Uriah stayed in Jerusalem that day and the next. 13 Then David invited Uriah to eat and drink with him, and he got Uriah drunk. And in the evening Uriah went out to lie down on his cot with his master’s servants, but he did not go home.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
David recalls Uriah from the army, asks about Joab and the campaign, then sends him home with a gift. Uriah instead sleeps at the palace entrance with the king’s servants. David asks why he has not gone to his house.

Uriah answers that the ark and the people are in tents and his commander and fellow soldiers are in the open field. He will not enjoy food, drink and his wife at home while they remain in those conditions. David keeps him another day and gets him drunk, but Uriah still does not go home.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands David’s arrangements as an attempt to make the pregnancy appear to be Uriah’s child. Uriah’s answer frustrates the plan. His concern for the people serving away from home contrasts with David’s use of the king’s comforts.

Gill emphasizes Uriah’s solidarity with those exposed to danger. He also discusses whether Uriah suspected David, but the account does not say that he knew about Bathsheba. We can understand his stated reason without inventing a secret accusation.

Henry stresses the seriousness of David making another person drunk as part of his wrongdoing. Uriah is being treated as a means of hiding what the king has done, while the repeated refusal to go home leaves David’s concealment unsuccessful.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 11:14-27
passages.section_title: Can David hide murder inside the losses of war?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 The next morning David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it with Uriah. 15 In the letter he wrote: “Put Uriah at the front of the fiercest battle; then withdraw from him, so that he may be struck down and killed.” 16 So as Joab besieged the city, he assigned Uriah to a place where he knew the strongest enemy soldiers were. 17 And when the men of the city came out and fought against Joab, some of David’s servants fell, and Uriah the Hittite also died. 18 Joab sent to David a full account of the battle 19 and instructed the messenger, “When you have finished giving the king a full account of the battle, 20 if the king’s anger flares, he may ask you, ‘Why did you get so close to the city to fight? Did you not realize they would shoot from atop the wall? 21 Who struck Abimelech son of Jerubbesheth? Was it not a woman who dropped an upper millstone on him from the wall, so that he died in Thebez? Why did you get so close to the wall?’ If he asks you this, then you are to say, ‘Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead as well.’” 22 So the messenger set out and reported to David all that Joab had sent him to say. 23 The messenger said to David, “The men overpowered us and came out against us in the field, but we drove them back to the entrance of the gate. 24 Then the archers shot at your servants from the wall, and some of the king’s servants were killed. And your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead as well.” 25 Then David told the messenger, “Say this to Joab: ‘Do not let this matter upset you, for the sword devours one as well as another. Strengthen your attack against the city and demolish it.’ Encourage him with these words.” 26 When Uriah’s wife heard that her husband was dead, she mourned for him. 27 And when the time of mourning was over, David had her brought to his house, and she became his wife and bore him a son. But the thing that David had done was evil in the sight of the LORD.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
David sends Joab a letter carried by Uriah himself, ordering that Uriah be placed in the fiercest fighting and left exposed so that he will die. Joab assigns him to a dangerous position. Enemy soldiers come out, and Uriah dies along with other men from David’s forces.

Joab prepares a messenger to explain the battlefield losses. He anticipates that David might question why the troops went so close to the wall, recalling Abimelech’s death at Thebez. The messenger is to report Uriah’s death as well. David responds by minimizing the loss as something the sword does to one person as to another and urges Joab to continue the attack.

Bathsheba mourns her husband. After the mourning, David brings her into his house, marries her, and she bears a son. The chapter’s final judgment cuts through the appearance that the matter has been settled: what David has done is evil in the LORD’s sight.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill understand the order as murder designed to conceal the earlier wrongdoing. Uriah’s death in a real battle does not turn David’s intended killing into an innocent wartime loss. Other soldiers also die in the operation.

Henry emphasizes how one wrongdoing is used to cover another. Gill contrasts David’s dismissal of these deaths with his earlier sensitivity over harming Saul. The account allows the king’s moral decline to be seen instead of protecting his reputation.

The closing verdict belongs to the LORD, not to the success or failure of the cover-up. David’s marriage to Bathsheba does not erase Uriah’s death, and the son born here is not named Solomon. The consequences and the confrontation with David follow in the next chapter.
passages.god_plan_html:
David uses royal authority to arrange the death of a man serving him. That gives a painful contrast with the kingship Jesus describes in Mark 10:42–45. Jesus warns against ruling by lording power over others and calls His followers to serve.

He then explains His own mission as giving His life as a ransom for many. David sacrifices a servant’s life to protect himself; Jesus gives His own life to save others. This is a contrast grounded in Scripture, not a claim that Uriah’s murder was secretly a righteous act.

The larger story therefore gives us reason to look beyond David to Christ. A king’s appointment does not make his abuse of power good. The saving King shows the proper direction of His authority through service and self-giving.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 12:1-6
passages.section_title: Why can David see the rich man’s cruelty so clearly?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then the LORD sent Nathan to David, and when he arrived, he said, “There were two men in a certain city, one rich and the other poor. 2 The rich man had a great number of sheep and cattle, 3 but the poor man had nothing except one small ewe lamb that he had bought. He raised it, and it grew up with him and his children. It shared his food and drank from his cup; it slept in his arms and was like a daughter to him. 4 Now a traveler came to the rich man, who refrained from taking one of his own sheep or cattle to prepare for the traveler who had come to him. Instead, he took the poor man’s lamb and prepared it for his guest.” 5 David burned with anger against the man and said to Nathan: “As surely as the LORD lives, the man who did this deserves to die! 6 Because he has done this thing and has shown no pity, he must pay for the lamb four times over.”

He raised it, and it grew up with him and his children. It shared his food and drank from his cup; it slept in his arms and was like a daughter to him. 4 Now a traveler came to the rich man, who refrained from taking one of his own sheep or cattle to prepare for the traveler who had come to him. section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The LORD sends Nathan to David with a story. A rich man has many animals, while a poor man cherishes one ewe lamb as part of his household. When a traveler arrives, the rich man takes the poor man’s lamb for the meal instead of using his own.

David burns with anger, declares that the man deserves to die, and orders repayment four times over. He recognizes the cruelty of someone who has plenty taking another person’s treasured possession. He has not yet recognized himself in the story.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads the story as a careful way of bringing David to judge his own conduct before he realizes the application. Nathan approaches the king indirectly, then will identify the wrong plainly.

Wesley notes the contrast between David’s severity toward another person and his indulgence toward himself. The fourfold repayment fits Exodus 22:1, but David’s declaration that the man deserves death goes beyond that law’s penalty for taking a sheep. His anger at another person’s lack of pity stands beside his own treatment of Uriah.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 12:7-14
passages.section_title: What happens when Nathan names David’s wrongdoing?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 Then Nathan said to David, “You are that man! This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘I anointed you king over Israel, and I delivered you from the hand of Saul. 8 I gave your master’s house to you and your master’s wives into your arms. I gave you the house of Israel and Judah, and if that was not enough, I would have given you even more. 9 Why then have you despised the command of the LORD by doing evil in His sight? You put Uriah the Hittite to the sword and took his wife as your own. You have slain him with the sword of the Ammonites. 10 Now, therefore, the sword will never depart from your house, because you have despised Me and have taken the wife of Uriah the Hittite to be your own.’ 11 This is what the LORD says: ‘I will raise up adversity against you from your own house. Before your very eyes I will take your wives and give them to another, and he will lie with them in broad daylight. 12 You have acted in secret, but I will do this thing in broad daylight before all Israel.’” 13 Then David said to Nathan, “I have sinned against the LORD.” “The LORD has taken away your sin,” Nathan replied. “You will not die. 14 Nevertheless, because by this deed you have shown utter contempt for the word of the LORD, the son born to you will surely die.”

This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘I anointed you king over Israel, and I delivered you from the hand of Saul. 8 I gave your master’s house to you and your master’s wives into your arms. I gave you the house of Israel and Judah, and if that was not enough, I would have given you even more. 9 Why then have you despised the command of the LORD by doing evil in His sight? You put Uriah the Hittite to the sword and took his wife as your own. You have slain him with the sword of the Ammonites. 10 Now, therefore, the sword will never depart from your house, because you have despised Me and have taken the wife of Uriah the Hittite to be your own.’

Before your very eyes I will take your wives and give them to another, and he will lie with them in broad daylight. 12 You have acted in secret, but I will do this thing in broad daylight before all Israel.’” 13 Then David said to Nathan, “I have sinned against the LORD.” “The LORD has taken away your sin,” Nathan replied. “You will not die. 14 Nevertheless, because by this deed you have shown utter contempt for the word of the LORD, the son born to you will surely die.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Nathan identifies David as the man. He speaks the LORD’s reminder of what David has received: kingship, rescue from Saul and rule over Israel and Judah. David has despised God’s command by killing Uriah through the Ammonites and taking his wife.

The announced consequences reach David’s household. Violence will remain within it, and wrongdoing he tried to hide will be answered by public calamity. David confesses that he has sinned against the LORD. Nathan announces that God has taken away his sin and that David will not die, then says that the child will die.

Forgiveness and the announced consequences appear together. The text does not describe the child’s death as a payment David must make to obtain forgiveness; Nathan has already announced that his sin has been taken away.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley emphasize David’s confession without an attempt to excuse himself. They also distinguish pardon from the painful consequences that follow. Being forgiven does not make Uriah’s death or the harm to the household disappear.

The reference to Saul’s wives has prompted questions about what David received. Gill understands it as their being placed under David’s authority, noting that the narrative does not describe him marrying Saul’s wives. The BSB retains the word wives. The statement concerns the abundance given to David and exposes how little excuse he had for taking Uriah’s wife.
passages.god_plan_html:
The need to confess rather than conceal sin continues in 1 John 1:8–10. God calls people into truth about themselves and promises forgiveness and cleansing, rather than inviting them to maintain an appearance of innocence.

1 John 2:1–2 identifies Jesus Christ as the advocate before the Father and the atoning sacrifice for sins. That gives the larger story its saving center: our hope for forgiveness rests in Christ.

This is a connection through the biblical theme of confession and mercy, not a claim that John directly explains Nathan’s visit. David’s child is not assigned Jesus’ saving role. The account’s painful consequences should not obscure where the New Testament places the work that brings forgiveness.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 12:15-23
passages.section_title: Why does David plead for the child and then rise to worship?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 After Nathan had gone home, the LORD struck the child that Uriah’s wife had borne to David, and he became ill. 16 David pleaded with God for the boy. He fasted and went into his house and spent the night lying in sackcloth on the ground. 17 The elders of his household stood beside him to help him up from the ground, but he was unwilling and would not eat anything with them. 18 On the seventh day the child died. But David’s servants were afraid to tell him that the child was dead, for they said, “Look, while the child was alive, we spoke to him, and he would not listen to us. So how can we tell him the child is dead? He may even harm himself.” 19 When David saw that his servants were whispering to one another, he perceived that the child was dead. So he asked his servants, “Is the child dead?” “He is dead,” they replied. 20 Then David got up from the ground, washed and anointed himself, changed his clothes, and went into the house of the LORD and worshiped. Then he went to his own house, and at his request they set food before him, and he ate. 21 “What is this you have done?” his servants asked. “While the child was alive, you fasted and wept, but when he died, you got up and ate.” 22 David answered, “While the child was alive, I fasted and wept, for I said, ‘Who knows? The LORD may be gracious to me and let him live.’ 23 But now that he is dead, why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? I will go to him, but he will not return to me.”

The LORD may be gracious to me and let him live.’ 23 But now that he is dead, why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? I will go to him, but he will not return to me.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After Nathan leaves, the LORD strikes the child with illness. David pleads with God, fasts and lies on the ground through the night. His household cannot persuade him to get up and eat. On the seventh day the child dies.

The servants fear telling David, but he notices their whispering and asks directly. Once they confirm the death, he washes, changes his clothes, worships and eats. They are puzzled because he had fasted and wept while the child lived.

David explains that while the child was alive he hoped the LORD might show mercy and spare him. Now he cannot bring him back. David will go to the child, but the child will not return to him. His answer explains why he ends this particular fast; it need not mean that his love or grief has ended.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The Hebrew word for child is yeled (YEH-led). Brown–Driver–Briggs shows that it can describe children across a range of ages, including the young Moses in Exodus 2. It does not prove that David’s son was an older boy or establish a delay of several years before Nathan came.

Wesley and Gill understand David’s words about going to the child as including hope of reunion with him in heaven. The verse itself does not name heaven or set out a complete account of the destiny of every child. Their hopeful reading should be distinguished from what the sentence states explicitly.

The narrator directly connects this illness and death with the LORD’s announcement to David. That makes this a difficult account of a specific judgment; it does not give readers a rule that a child’s illness reveals a parent’s particular sin, or a timetable that other grieving parents must follow.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Thessalonians 4:13–18 places Christian hope in Jesus’ death and resurrection and in the future resurrection of those who belong to Him. Paul speaks of grief with hope and calls believers to encourage one another.

This supplies a clear New Testament foundation for hope beyond death without turning David’s brief answer into a complete explanation of every question about a child’s future. The passage about David does not state the child’s personal response to God.

The connection is the larger theme of death, grief and hope in God. It leaves room to face the loss honestly. Confidence in resurrection does not require pretending that death is painless or judging someone whose mourning takes a different course.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 12:24-25
passages.section_title: What does Solomon’s birth reveal after the loss?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 24 Then David comforted his wife Bathsheba, and he went to her and lay with her. So she gave birth to a son, and they named him Solomon. Now the LORD loved the child 25 and sent word through Nathan the prophet to name him Jedidiah because the LORD loved him.
paragraphs: 24 Then David comforted his wife Bathsheba, and he went to her and lay with her. So she gave birth to a son, and they named him Solomon. Now the LORD loved the child 25 and sent word through Nathan the prophet to name him Jedidiah because the LORD loved him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
David comforts Bathsheba, and afterward she gives birth to another son, Solomon. The account expressly says that the LORD loves this child and sends word through Nathan to name him Jedidiah.

Brown–Driver–Briggs gives the name Jedidiah the meaning beloved of Yah, referring to the LORD. The name expresses the love the narrative has just announced. This is another child, not a new name for the son who died.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley read the announcement as a sign of God’s continuing favor toward David’s family. The loss and the wrongdoing have not become the whole future of the household.

The description focuses on God’s love for Solomon and the comfort David gives Bathsheba. It does not ask us to treat one child as interchangeable with another or to assume that a later birth removes their grief.
passages.god_plan_html:
Matthew 1:6–7, 16–17 explicitly includes Solomon in the family line leading to Jesus. It also recalls his mother as Uriah’s wife, keeping the painful history in view as it traces God’s work toward the Christ.

This is a direct connection to God’s saving purpose. The family’s story continues toward Jesus, while the account of David’s wrongdoing remains on the page. God’s faithfulness reaches through a damaged history without requiring us to rename its wrongs as good.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 12:26-31
passages.section_title: How does the campaign against Rabbah finally end?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 26 Meanwhile, Joab fought against Rabbah of the Ammonites and captured the royal fortress. 27 Then Joab sent messengers to David to say, “I have fought against Rabbah and have captured the water supply of the city. 28 Now, therefore, assemble the rest of the troops, lay siege to the city, and capture it. Otherwise I will capture the city, and it will be named after me.” 29 So David assembled all the troops and went to Rabbah; and he fought against it and captured it. 30 Then he took the crown from the head of their king. It weighed a talent of gold and was set with precious stones, and it was placed on David’s head. And David took a great amount of plunder from the city. 31 David brought out the people who were there and put them to work with saws, iron picks, and axes, and he made them work at the brick kilns. He did the same to all the Ammonite cities. Then David and all his troops returned to Jerusalem.

Otherwise I will capture the city, and it will be named after me.”

29 So David assembled all the troops and went to Rabbah; and he fought against it and captured it. 30 Then he took the crown from the head of their king. It weighed a talent of gold and was set with precious stones, and it was placed on David’s head. And David took a great amount of plunder from the city. 31 David brought out the people who were there and put them to work with saws, iron picks, and axes, and he made them work at the brick kilns. He did the same to all the Ammonite cities. Then David and all his troops returned to Jerusalem.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Joab captures Rabbah’s royal fortress and water supply, then calls David to bring the rest of the troops and complete the capture. He warns that if he takes the city himself, the credit and its name will belong to him.

David comes, captures the city and takes its crown and plunder. The BSB describes the people being put to work with saws, picks and axes and at brick kilns, and says David does the same in the other Ammonite cities. He and his troops then return to Jerusalem.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley reads Joab’s message as an opportunity for David to receive the honor of the final capture. The narrative returns to the campaign introduced before the account of Bathsheba and Uriah, bringing that unfinished battle to its close.

The treatment of the captives has been read in different ways. Wesley, following wording about placing people under saws and through a kiln, understands severe executions and criticizes David’s cruelty. Gill discusses that reading but also accepts a translation describing compulsory labor. The BSB follows the labor reading, and Henry calls the result slavery and criticizes its severity.

The difference matters: these readings describe different acts, even though both involve the harsh exercise of power over defeated people. The passage should be explained with its translation questions visible rather than made into a simple claim that everything in the victory was merciful.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 13:1-14
passages.section_title: How does Amnon turn a request for care into an attack on Tamar?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 After some time, David’s son Amnon fell in love with Tamar, the beautiful sister of David’s son Absalom. 2 Amnon was sick with frustration over his sister Tamar, for she was a virgin, and it seemed implausible for him to do anything to her. 3 Now Amnon had a friend named Jonadab, the son of David’s brother Shimeah. Jonadab was a very shrewd man, 4 and he asked Amnon, “Why are you, the son of the king, so depressed morning after morning? Won’t you tell me?” Amnon replied, “I am in love with Tamar, my brother Absalom’s sister.” 5 Jonadab told him, “Lie down on your bed and pretend you are ill. When your father comes to see you, say to him, ‘Please let my sister Tamar come and give me something to eat. Let her prepare it in my sight so I may watch her and eat it from her hand.’” 6 So Amnon lay down and feigned illness. When the king came to see him, Amnon said, “Please let my sister Tamar come and make a couple of cakes in my sight, so that I may eat from her hand.” 7 Then David sent word to Tamar at the palace: “Please go to the house of Amnon your brother and prepare a meal for him.” 8 So Tamar went to the house of her brother Amnon, who was lying down. She took some dough, kneaded it, made cakes in his sight, and baked them. 9 Then she brought the pan and set it down before him, but he refused to eat. “Send everyone away!” said Amnon. And everyone went out. 10 Then Amnon said to Tamar, “Bring the food into the bedroom, so that I may eat it from your hand.” Tamar took the cakes she had made and went to her brother Amnon’s bedroom. 11 And when she had brought them to him to eat, he took hold of her and said, “Come lie with me, my sister!” 12 “No, my brother!” she cried. “Do not violate me, for such a thing should never be done in Israel. Do not do this disgraceful thing! 13 Where could I ever take my shame? And you would be like one of the fools in Israel! Please speak to the king, for he will not withhold me from you.” 14 But Amnon refused to listen to her, and being stronger, he violated her and lay with her.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Amnon desires Tamar, Absalom’s sister and his own half-sister. His cousin Jonadab suggests a plan: pretend to be ill and ask David to send Tamar to prepare food. David agrees, and Tamar comes to care for her brother.

Amnon refuses the food, dismisses everyone else, then asks Tamar to bring it into the bedroom. He takes hold of her and demands sex. She clearly refuses, calls the act disgraceful, and appeals to him to think of the harm to her and the dishonor to himself.

Tamar also asks him to speak to the king rather than do this. Amnon refuses to listen. He overpowers and rapes her. The account makes his choice and her refusal explicit; her obedience to her father’s request is not consent to what Amnon does.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry connects the violence within David’s family with the earlier announcement that his household would suffer. Wesley emphasizes how Tamar appeals to the duty a brother should have to protect her. The story exposes the betrayal of that duty rather than excusing Amnon’s desire.

Tamar’s request about speaking to the king has been read in different ways. Wesley thinks she hoped David would make an exception permitting marriage; Gill considers several explanations, including a desperate attempt to delay the attack. Leviticus 18:9 and 20:17 prohibit sexual relations between half-siblings; the second passage also expressly describes such a marriage as disgraceful.

Whatever Tamar thought the king might do, she is trying to prevent the violation. Her plea should be heard in that danger, rather than used as a general rule requiring an assaulted person to marry the attacker.
passages.god_plan_html:
Amnon describes his desire as love, but his behavior disregards the person he claims to love. The contrast helps us recognize a theme Scripture develops more fully: love seeks another person’s good rather than using them to satisfy a desire.

1 Corinthians 13:4–7 describes love as patient and kind, opposed to self-seeking and wrongdoing, and joined to truth. That gives a clear measure for the difference between love and a claim of love used to take control.

This is a shared biblical theme, not a claim that Paul is directly interpreting Amnon’s words. God’s purpose for relationships calls people toward care and faithfulness. A powerful desire does not make an act loving when it overrides another person’s refusal.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 13:15-22
passages.section_title: Who listens to Tamar after the assault?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 Then Amnon hated Tamar with such intensity that his hatred was greater than the love he previously had. “Get up!” he said to her. “Be gone!” 16 “No,” she replied, “sending me away is worse than this great wrong you have already done to me!” But he refused to listen to her. 17 Instead, he called to his attendant and said, “Throw this woman out and bolt the door behind her!” 18 So Amnon’s attendant threw her out and bolted the door behind her. Now Tamar was wearing a robe of many colors, because this is what the king’s virgin daughters wore. 19 And Tamar put ashes on her head and tore her robe. And putting her hand on her head, she went away crying aloud. 20 Her brother Absalom said to her, “Has your brother Amnon been with you? Be quiet for now, my sister. He is your brother. Do not take this thing to heart.” So Tamar lived as a desolate woman in the house of her brother Absalom. 21 When King David heard all this, he was furious. 22 And Absalom never said a word to Amnon, either good or bad, because he hated Amnon for violating his sister Tamar.

Now Tamar was wearing a robe of many colors, because this is what the king’s virgin daughters wore. 19 And Tamar put ashes on her head and tore her robe. And putting her hand on her head, she went away crying aloud.

20 Her brother Absalom said to her, “Has your brother Amnon been with you? Be quiet for now, my sister. He is your brother. Do not take this thing to heart.” So Tamar lived as a desolate woman in the house of her brother Absalom. 21 When King David heard all this, he was furious. 22 And Absalom never said a word to Amnon, either good or bad, because he hated Amnon for violating his sister Tamar.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Amnon’s desire turns into intense hatred. He orders Tamar away and refuses to listen when she protests that sending her out adds another great wrong. His attendant puts her outside and bolts the door.

Tamar tears the robe that marks her place among the king’s virgin daughters, puts ashes on her head and goes away crying aloud. Absalom asks whether Amnon has been with her, tells her to be quiet for now, and takes her into his house. She remains there desolate.

David hears and is furious, but this account reports no punishment of Amnon by him. Absalom says nothing to Amnon while hating him for what he has done. Tamar’s distress is visible while the men’s responses leave the wrong unresolved.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands Tamar’s second protest as a response to added cruelty and public disgrace. Her words do not make the rape a small matter; they show how Amnon compounds the harm by throwing her out.

Henry and Wesley criticize David’s failure to deal adequately with his son. Gill also observes that the account records anger without reporting punishment. Their explanations of David’s motives vary; the absence of a reported action should not become certainty about every private thought he had.

Absalom provides a home, but his instruction to keep quiet is his response within this story. It is not a command from God to people who have been assaulted. Tamar’s desolation describes what she suffers, not a loss of her human worth or a share in Amnon’s guilt.
passages.god_plan_html:
Psalm 34:18 speaks of the LORD being near to the brokenhearted. 2 Corinthians 1:3–4 calls God the Father of compassion and describes His comfort flowing through His people to others in trouble.

This broader theme supplies something the responses around Tamar leave painfully incomplete: wounded people need compassionate care rather than dismissal. God’s people are called to share the comfort they receive, with attention to the person who is suffering.

This is a connection through Scripture’s account of God’s character and His people’s calling. It is not a claim that Tamar’s suffering was good or that a promise of comfort removes the need to face the wrong done to her.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 13:23-29
passages.section_title: What does Absalom arrange at the sheep-shearing feast?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 23 Two years later, when Absalom’s sheepshearers were at Baal-hazor near Ephraim, he invited all the sons of the king. 24 And he went to the king and said, “Your servant has just hired shearers. Will the king and his servants please come with me?” 25 “No, my son,” the king replied, “we should not all go, or we would be a burden to you.” Although Absalom urged him, he was not willing to go, but gave him his blessing. 26 “If not,” said Absalom, “please let my brother Amnon go with us.” “Why should he go with you?” the king asked. 27 But Absalom urged him, so the king sent Amnon and the rest of his sons. 28 Now Absalom had ordered his young men, “Watch Amnon until his heart is merry with wine, and when I order you to strike Amnon down, you are to kill him. Do not be afraid. Have I not commanded you? Be courageous and valiant!” 29 So Absalom’s young men did to Amnon just as Absalom had ordered. Then all the other sons of the king got up, and each one fled on his mule.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Two years later, Absalom invites the king’s sons to his sheep-shearing gathering. He first urges David to come. David declines, saying that bringing everyone would burden him, but gives his blessing.

Absalom then asks specifically for Amnon. David questions the request but eventually allows Amnon and the other sons to go. Absalom has already ordered his servants to wait until Amnon is merry with wine and then kill him at his command.

The servants carry out the order. The remaining princes flee on their mules. The long silence between the brothers has ended in a planned killing, not a public hearing or a restoration of Tamar.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley reads the two-year delay as a sign of settled revenge and careful planning. Henry emphasizes that Absalom draws his servants into the killing, assuring them with his own authority. A prince’s command does not make the servants’ participation innocent.

Henry also connects this violence with David’s failure to address the earlier wrong. The connection helps explain how the situation has grown; it does not transfer responsibility for Absalom’s order away from Absalom or make murder the only possible answer to an injustice.
passages.god_plan_html:
The scene brings the difference between facing evil and taking private revenge into view. Anger at what happened to Tamar does not by itself make Absalom’s secret order a faithful act.

Romans 12:17–21 tells believers not to repay evil with evil or avenge themselves, but to leave vengeance to God and overcome evil with good. This is a larger biblical direction for our response, rather than a claim that Paul directly comments on Absalom’s feast.

It does not turn the earlier assault into something to ignore. The need to address wrongdoing remains, while this path of revenge adds another death and further tears apart the household.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 13:30-39
passages.section_title: How does the report of Amnon’s death leave the family divided?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 30 While they were on the way, a report reached David: “Absalom has struck down all the sons of the king; not one of them is left!” 31 Then the king stood up, tore his clothes, and lay down on the ground. And all his servants stood by with their clothes torn. 32 But Jonadab, the son of David’s brother Shimeah, spoke up: “My lord must not think they have killed all the sons of the king, for only Amnon is dead. In fact, Absalom has planned this since the day Amnon violated his sister Tamar. 33 So now, my lord the king, do not take to heart the report that all the sons of the king are dead. Only Amnon is dead.” 34 Meanwhile, Absalom had fled. When the young man standing watch looked up, he saw many people coming down the road west of him, along the side of the hill. And the watchman went and reported to the king, “I see men coming from the direction of Horonaim, along the side of the hill.” 35 So Jonadab said to the king, “Look, the sons of the king have arrived! It is just as your servant said.” 36 And as he finished speaking, the sons of the king came in, wailing loudly. Then the king and all his servants also wept very bitterly. 37 Now Absalom fled and went to Talmai son of Ammihud, the king of Geshur. But David mourned for his son every day. 38 After Absalom had fled and gone to Geshur, he stayed there three years. 39 And King David longed to go to Absalom, for he had been consoled over Amnon’s death.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
A report reaches David saying that Absalom has killed all the king’s sons. David and his servants tear their clothes, and he lies on the ground. Jonadab counters that only Amnon is dead and connects the killing with Absalom’s purpose since Tamar’s assault.

The other sons arrive, confirming that the first report was exaggerated. They and David weep bitterly. Absalom has fled to Talmai king of Geshur, where he remains three years.

The chapter ends with David’s longing for Absalom after he has been consoled over Amnon’s death. One son is dead, another is in exile, and Tamar’s desolation has not been resolved. A corrected report spares David one imagined loss while leaving real grief and division.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Gill considers whether Jonadab’s confident answer suggests prior knowledge of the plot. That is an inference about how he knew, not something the narrator independently establishes. His earlier advice to Amnon is explicit; a second detailed conspiracy should not be supplied as a proven fact.

The final verse has also been understood differently. Wesley follows the longing-for-Absalom reading reflected in the BSB. Gill also discusses older readings in which David ceases going out against Absalom. The readings differ over pursuit and desire, but both leave a separation that the next chapter takes up.

Being consoled over Amnon’s death does not mean David is said to celebrate his murder. The account has just shown the family weeping. Its closing words describe a change over time in grief and in David’s attitude toward his absent son.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 14:1-20
passages.section_title: How does Joab persuade David to bring Absalom back?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now Joab son of Zeruiah perceived that the king’s heart longed for Absalom. 2 So Joab sent to Tekoa to bring a wise woman from there. He told her, “Please pretend to be a mourner; put on clothes for mourning and do not anoint yourself with oil. Act like a woman who has mourned for the dead a long time. 3 Then go to the king and speak these words to him.” And Joab put the words in her mouth. 4 When the woman from Tekoa went to the king, she fell facedown in homage and said, “Help me, O king!” 5 “What troubles you?” the king asked her. “Indeed,” she said, “I am a widow, for my husband is dead. 6 And your maidservant had two sons who were fighting in the field with no one to separate them, and one struck the other and killed him. 7 Now the whole clan has risen up against your maidservant and said, ‘Hand over the one who struck down his brother, that we may put him to death for the life of the brother whom he killed. Then we will cut off the heir as well!’ So they would extinguish my one remaining ember by not preserving my husband’s name or posterity on the earth.” 8 “Go home,” the king said to the woman, “and I will give orders on your behalf.” 9 But the woman of Tekoa said to the king, “My lord the king, may any blame be on me and on my father’s house, and may the king and his throne be guiltless.” 10 “If anyone speaks to you,” said the king, “bring him to me, and he will not trouble you again!” 11 “Please,” she replied, “may the king invoke the LORD your God to prevent the avenger of blood from increasing the devastation, so that my son may not be destroyed!” “As surely as the LORD lives,” he vowed, “not a hair of your son’s head will fall to the ground.” 12 Then the woman said, “Please, may your servant speak a word to my lord the king?” “Speak,” he replied. 13 The woman asked, “Why have you devised a thing like this against the people of God? When the king says this, does he not convict himself, since he has not brought back his own banished son? 14 For we will surely die and be like water poured out on the ground, which cannot be recovered. Yet God does not take away a life, but He devises ways that the banished one may not be cast out from Him. 15 Now therefore, I have come to present this matter to my lord the king because the people have made me afraid. Your servant thought, ‘I will speak to the king. Perhaps he will grant the request of his maidservant. 16 For the king will hear and deliver his maidservant from the hand of the man who would cut off both me and my son from God’s inheritance.’ 17 And now your servant says, ‘May the word of my lord the king bring me rest, for my lord the king is able to discern good and evil, just like the angel of God. May the LORD your God be with you.’” 18 Then the king said to the woman, “I am going to ask you something; do not conceal it from me!” “Let my lord the king speak,” she replied. 19 So the king asked, “Is the hand of Joab behind all this?” The woman answered, “As surely as you live, my lord the king, no one can turn to the right or to the left from anything that my lord the king says. Yes, your servant Joab is the one who gave me orders; he told your maidservant exactly what to say. 20 Joab your servant has done this to bring about this change of affairs, but my lord has wisdom like the wisdom of the angel of God, to know everything that happens in the land.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Joab perceives David’s longing for Absalom and arranges an indirect appeal. He brings a wise woman from Tekoa, tells her to dress as a mourner, and gives her the words she is to say. Her account of a family crisis is part of Joab’s plan.

She presents herself as a widow whose two sons fought, leaving one dead. The clan now demands the survivor’s death, which would end her husband’s family line. David promises protection and eventually swears that her remaining son will not be harmed.

The woman then applies the decision to David’s own banished son. She appeals to the shortness of life and to God’s provision for restoring those who have been cast out. David asks whether Joab is behind the appeal, and she acknowledges that he is. He has been led to compare a staged case with his own household.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley points out that the two cases differ: the woman describes a fatal fight, while Absalom planned Amnon’s killing. Her appeal is persuasive, but the comparison does not settle every question about Absalom’s responsibility.

Gill discusses her statement about God sparing life and restoring the banished in connection with mercy and the cities of refuge. The USCCB Bible notes also suggest a possible reference to refuge provisions for an unintentional killing. These are explanations of her reasoning, not proof that those provisions automatically clear Absalom.

Henry draws attention to mercy while insisting that God’s pardon does not dishonor justice or encourage wrongdoing. The speech should be read within its setting: a woman coached by Joab is seeking a particular decision from the king. Her words are not a stand-alone claim that God never takes life in judgment.
passages.god_plan_html:
The hope that those estranged from God can be restored is stated clearly in 2 Corinthians 5:18–21. God reconciles people to Himself through Christ and entrusts His people with the message of reconciliation.

Romans 3:21–26 joins that saving grace with God’s righteousness. Through Christ’s atoning work, God is just and justifies those who have faith in Jesus. Mercy does not depend on pretending that wrongdoing never mattered.

This is a connection through the wider biblical theme of restoration, rather than a claim that the woman’s whole appeal is a direct prophecy of the gospel. Her attempt to secure Absalom’s return raises questions the larger story answers more fully in Christ.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 14:21-27
passages.section_title: What kind of return does David allow Absalom?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 Then the king said to Joab, “I hereby grant this request. Go, bring back the young man Absalom.” 22 Joab fell facedown in homage and blessed the king. “Today,” said Joab, “your servant knows that he has found favor in your eyes, my lord the king, because the king has granted his request.” 23 So Joab got up, went to Geshur, and brought Absalom to Jerusalem. 24 But the king added, “He may return to his house, but he must not see my face.” So Absalom returned to his own house, but he did not see the face of the king. 25 Now there was not a man in all Israel as handsome and highly praised as Absalom. From the sole of his foot to the top of his head, he did not have a single flaw. 26 And when he cut the hair of his head—he shaved it every year because his hair got so heavy—he would weigh it out to be two hundred shekels, according to the royal standard. 27 Three sons were born to Absalom, and a daughter named Tamar, who was a beautiful woman.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
David grants Joab’s request, and Joab brings Absalom back from Geshur to Jerusalem. But the permission has a limit: Absalom may go to his house and must not see the king’s face. Return to the city has not yet become a personal reunion with his father.

The narrative then describes Absalom’s appearance and family. He is highly praised for his beauty, and his heavy hair is weighed when cut each year. Three sons and a daughter named Tamar are mentioned. Public admiration stands beside the unresolved relationship at the center of the story.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill understand David’s restriction as a way of showing that Absalom’s crime has not been approved, and possibly of encouraging deeper humility. Those are explanations of his decision; the account does not report David giving a complete account of his motives.

Henry notes that the praise here concerns Absalom’s looks rather than wisdom or godliness. His attractive appearance gives readers no reason to assume that the problems revealed by his earlier actions have been resolved.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 14:28-33
passages.section_title: How does Absalom force an audience with the king?

So Absalom sent a second time, but Joab still would not come. 30 Then Absalom said to his servants, “Look, Joab’s field is next to mine, and he has barley there. Go and set it on fire!” And Absalom’s servants set the field on fire. 31 Then Joab came to Absalom’s house and demanded, “Why did your servants set my field on fire?” 32 “Look,” said Absalom, “I sent for you and said, ‘Come here. I want to send you to the king to ask: Why have I come back from Geshur? It would be better for me if I were still there.’ So now, let me see the king’s face, and if there is iniquity in me, let him kill me.” 33 So Joab went and told the king, and David summoned Absalom, who came to him and bowed facedown before him. Then the king kissed Absalom.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Absalom lives in Jerusalem for two years without seeing David. Twice he sends for Joab to seek an audience with the king, and twice Joab refuses to come. Absalom then orders his servants to burn Joab’s neighboring barley field.

The fire brings Joab to his house. Absalom demands to know why he was brought back from Geshur only to remain excluded, and asks either to see the king or be put to death if he is guilty. Joab conveys the message, David summons Absalom, and Absalom bows before him. The king kisses him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry criticizes the pressure Absalom uses to gain what he wants. Wesley also sees a son pressing his own justification rather than plainly confessing his wrongdoing. The success of the demand does not make burning Joab’s field a good example.

Gill understands David’s kiss as a sign of reconciliation. That is an important change from exclusion, but the account records no confession by Absalom and gives no assurance that every conflict between father and son has ended.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 15:1-12
passages.section_title: How does Absalom turn popular approval into a rebellion?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Some time later, Absalom provided for himself a chariot with horses and fifty men to run ahead of him. 2 He would get up early and stand beside the road leading to the city gate. Whenever anyone had a grievance to bring before the king for a decision, Absalom would call out and ask, “What city are you from?” And if he replied, “Your servant is from one of the tribes of Israel,” 3 Absalom would say, “Look, your claims are good and right, but the king has no deputy to hear you.” 4 And he would add, “If only someone would appoint me judge in the land, then everyone with a grievance or dispute could come to me, and I would give him justice.” 5 Also, when anyone approached to bow down to him, Absalom would reach out his hand, take hold of him, and kiss him. 6 Absalom did this to all the Israelites who came to the king for justice. In this way he stole the hearts of the men of Israel. 7 After four years had passed, Absalom said to the king, “Please let me go to Hebron to fulfill a vow I have made to the LORD. 8 For your servant made a vow while dwelling in Geshur of Aram, saying: ‘If indeed the LORD brings me back to Jerusalem, I will worship the LORD in Hebron.’” 9 “Go in peace,” said the king. So Absalom got up and went to Hebron. 10 Then Absalom sent spies throughout the tribes of Israel with this message: “When you hear the sound of the horn, you are to say, ‘Absalom reigns in Hebron!’” 11 Two hundred men from Jerusalem accompanied Absalom. They had been invited as guests and they went along innocently, for they knew nothing about the matter. 12 While Absalom was offering the sacrifices, he sent for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David’s counselor, to come from his hometown of Giloh. So the conspiracy gained strength, and Absalom’s following kept increasing.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Absalom surrounds himself with a chariot, horses and fifty runners, then positions himself where people come with cases for the king. He approves their claims, says no royal deputy will hear them, and promises that he would give them justice. Warm gestures accompany the criticism of David’s administration.

The narrator describes the result as stealing the hearts of Israel. After four years, Absalom asks to go to Hebron to fulfill a vow to the LORD. With David’s permission he leaves, but he has arranged for messengers to announce him as king when the horn sounds.

Two hundred invited men go with him without knowing the plot. Absalom also summons Ahithophel, David’s counselor. Sacrifices and a stated religious purpose provide the setting for a conspiracy that continues to gain support.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley reads Absalom’s treatment of petitioners as a calculated way of winning allegiance. His promise that everyone will receive justice from him is part of his campaign; the narrator does not independently confirm every accusation he makes against David’s government.

Henry emphasizes the misuse of an appearance of devotion and the danger of drawing unsuspecting people into wrongdoing. The invited men’s ignorance matters: being present with Absalom does not prove that all two hundred knowingly joined the rebellion.

The BSB gives four years. Gill discusses that reading alongside the forty years in older translations and the attempts to explain the longer number. The translation difference need not obscure the movement of the story: Absalom has patiently cultivated support before announcing a rival claim to the throne.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 15:13-23
passages.section_title: Who stays with David when he leaves Jerusalem?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 Then a messenger came to David and reported, “The hearts of the men of Israel are with Absalom.” 14 And David said to all the servants with him in Jerusalem, “Arise and let us flee, or we will not escape from Absalom! We must leave quickly, or he will soon overtake us, heap disaster on us, and put the city to the sword.” 15 The king’s servants replied, “Whatever our lord the king decides, we are your servants.” 16 Then the king set out, and his entire household followed him. But he left behind ten concubines to take care of the palace. 17 So the king set out with all the people following him. He stopped at the last house, 18 and all his servants marched past him—all the Cherethites and Pelethites, and six hundred Gittites who had followed him from Gath. 19 Then the king said to Ittai the Gittite, “Why should you also go with us? Go back and stay with the new king, since you are both a foreigner and an exile from your homeland. 20 In fact, you arrived only yesterday; should I make you wander around with us today while I do not know where I am going? Go back and take your brothers with you. May the LORD show you loving devotion and faithfulness.” 21 But Ittai answered the king, “As surely as the LORD lives, and as my lord the king lives, wherever my lord the king may be, whether it means life or death, there will your servant be!” 22 “March on then,” said David to Ittai. So Ittai the Gittite marched past with all his men and all the little ones who were with him. 23 Everyone in the countryside was weeping loudly as all the people passed by. And as the king crossed the Kidron Valley, all the people also passed toward the way of the wilderness.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
News of Absalom’s support reaches David, and he orders a hurried departure to avoid being trapped and to spare the city an attack. His household and loyal servants leave with him, while ten concubines remain to care for the palace. His guards and six hundred men who followed him from Gath pass before him.

David gives Ittai, a foreigner and recent arrival, freedom to stay rather than join his uncertain journey. Ittai refuses. He pledges to remain wherever David is, whether that means life or death. David accepts him, and Ittai’s men and dependents pass on with the company.

The countryside weeps as David crosses the Kidron Valley toward the wilderness. The king who once entered Jerusalem in strength now leaves it with an uncertain destination and people choosing whether to share his danger.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry sees care for others in David’s willingness to release Ittai from joining his trouble. Wesley and Gill emphasize Ittai’s steady loyalty in adversity. The oath expresses a commitment that does not depend on David’s present comfort or popularity.

The narrative names loyal people from outside Israel as well as royal servants and, in the next scene, priests. It does not reduce everyone’s loyalty to payment or ethnic background. Ittai’s willingness is stated directly; his exact financial arrangements are not.
passages.god_plan_html:
Wesley and Henry draw a parallel between Ittai’s loyalty to David and a believer’s attachment to Christ. The connection is the willingness to remain faithful when following brings hardship rather than advantage.

In Luke 9:57–62, a person offers to follow Jesus wherever He goes. Jesus answers by making the cost of following Him clear, including the absence of a settled place to rest. The call to follow is more than enthusiasm while the journey looks promising.

This is a limited parallel, not a claim that Ittai’s oath was a direct prediction of those conversations. Nor does it turn loyalty to an earthly leader into an unlimited duty. The greater commitment is to Christ, whose calling is the measure for His followers.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 15:24-29
passages.section_title: Why does David send the ark back to Jerusalem?

And they set down the ark of God, and Abiathar offered sacrifices until all the people had passed out of the city. 25 Then the king said to Zadok, “Return the ark of God to the city. If I find favor in the eyes of the LORD, He will bring me back and let me see both it and His dwelling place again. 26 But if He should say, ‘I do not delight in you,’ then here I am; let Him do to me whatever seems good to Him.” 27 The king also said to Zadok the priest, “Are you not a seer? section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Zadok, Abiathar and the Levites are present with the ark as the people leave the city. David orders the ark returned. If he finds favor with the LORD, he trusts that God can bring him back to see it and its dwelling place again.

David also acknowledges that the outcome belongs to God even if it is not what he wants. He arranges for the priests and their sons to provide news while he waits near the wilderness. Zadok and Abiathar return the ark to Jerusalem and remain there.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley emphasize David’s concern for the ark and his willingness to submit his own future to God. He does not insist that the sacred object must follow his flight in order for God to help him.

The practical arrangement also matters: the priests’ sons can carry information to David. Trust in God’s decision does not keep him from making careful preparations.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 15:30-37
passages.section_title: How does David respond to betrayal on the Mount of Olives?

versions.label: BSB

Send them to me with everything you hear.” 37 So David’s friend Hushai arrived in Jerusalem just as Absalom was entering the city.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
David climbs the Mount of Olives weeping, barefoot and with his head covered. His companions also weep. When he learns that Ahithophel has joined Absalom, he asks the LORD to turn the counselor’s advice into foolishness.

At the summit Hushai meets him with torn clothing and dust on his head. David sends him back to Jerusalem, telling him to offer his service to Absalom so that he can counter Ahithophel’s counsel. The priests and their sons will help send reports. Hushai enters the city as Absalom arrives.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads the prayer as an appeal against Ahithophel’s counsel rather than an attack on his person. David then takes practical steps toward the outcome he has requested by sending Hushai back.

That strategy is not praised without qualification by every commentator. Wesley criticizes the deceptive offer of service David tells Hushai to make. Henry likewise observes the imperfect mixture in David’s conduct and contrasts it with Christ’s perfect response to treachery. The narrative’s unfolding help for David does not require us to call every tactic faultless.
passages.god_plan_html:
Wesley notes the shared setting of David’s crossing the Kidron and Jesus’ journey toward His suffering. John 18:1–4 places Jesus across that valley with His disciples as Judas brings those who will arrest Him.

Luke 22:39–46 also places Jesus on the Mount of Olives, praying in anguish and submitting His will to the Father. The geographical and personal parallels make a meaningful comparison: betrayal, sorrow and prayer appear in both accounts.

The difference is just as important to the comparison. David’s story includes consequences of his own failures; Jesus faces His saving work in innocence. This is a supported parallel, not a claim that every person in David’s escape represents someone in Jesus’ story. It directs our attention to the faithful Son of David whose obedience remains whole under betrayal.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 16:1-4
passages.section_title: What does David accept when Ziba brings supplies?

He had a pair of saddled donkeys loaded with two hundred loaves of bread, a hundred clusters of raisins, a hundred summer fruits, and a skin of wine. 2 “Why do you have these?” asked the king. Ziba replied, “The donkeys are for the king’s household to ride, the bread and summer fruit are for the young men to eat, and the wine is to refresh those who become exhausted in the wilderness.” 3 “Where is your master’s grandson?” asked the king. section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Just beyond the summit, Ziba meets David with donkeys and substantial supplies for the journey. He explains that they are for the royal household and those becoming exhausted in the wilderness.

When David asks about Mephibosheth, Ziba claims that he has remained in Jerusalem hoping to regain Saul’s kingdom. David immediately assigns Mephibosheth’s property to Ziba. The gift brings practical help, but the decision also accepts a serious accusation while the accused man is absent.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Gill understand Ziba’s report as slander. Wesley criticizes David’s judgment as hasty because he condemns Mephibosheth without hearing him. In 2 Samuel 19:24–30, Mephibosheth later gives a different account, saying that Ziba deceived and slandered him.

This scene itself reports what Ziba says, not independent proof that Mephibosheth is plotting to take the throne. Reading the accusation as an accusation preserves the question that David should have examined before awarding the estate.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 16:5-14
passages.section_title: Why does David refuse to strike back at Shimei?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
At Bahurim, Shimei, a man from Saul’s family, curses David and throws stones at him and his servants. He calls David a man of bloodshed and interprets Absalom’s rise as the LORD repaying him for the blood of Saul’s house.

Abishai offers to kill Shimei, but David refuses. With his own son seeking his life, he will not answer this abuse by another immediate killing. He speaks of accepting what the LORD has allowed and hopes that God will see his affliction and repay him with good.

Shimei continues alongside them, cursing and throwing stones and dust. David and his people eventually stop to recover from exhaustion. The refusal to retaliate does not make the treatment painless or cause it to stop at once.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry contrasts David’s patience under abuse with his readiness to believe Ziba’s flattering report. David is capable of responding well to an openly hostile man even after making a rash judgment about an absent friend.

Which events Shimei means by Saul’s blood is not settled by the speech. Wesley discusses Abner and Ish-bosheth as well as Saul’s descendants in chapter 21; the USCCB Bible notes favor the latter connection. Shimei is giving his interpretation of David’s troubles, not delivering a new prophetic verdict endorsed by the narrator.

Wesley and Gill understand David’s statement about the LORD telling Shimei to curse in terms of God’s rule over the circumstances, while keeping responsibility for the wrongdoing with Shimei. They distinguish what God allows and uses from a command making the abuse morally right.
passages.god_plan_html:
Henry compares David’s restraint with Christ’s response to those who mistreated Him. The fuller account appears in 1 Peter 2:21–25: Jesus does not retaliate under abuse, but entrusts Himself to the One who judges justly.

The comparison has an important limit. David has wrongs of his own to face; Peter expressly describes Jesus as sinless and speaks of Him bearing our sins. Christ’s patience belongs to His saving work as well as providing an example for His followers.

This is a supported parallel, not a rule that anyone being abused has caused it through their own sin. It points to trust in God’s judgment rather than the desire to make every insult end in vengeance.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 16:15-23
passages.section_title: How does Absalom make the break with David public?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 Then Absalom and all the men of Israel came to Jerusalem, and Ahithophel was with him. 16 And David’s friend Hushai the Archite went to Absalom and said to him, “Long live the king! Long live the king!” 17 “Is this the loyalty you show your friend?” Absalom replied. “Why did you not go with your friend?” 18 “Not at all,” Hushai answered. “For the one chosen by the LORD, by this people, and by all the men of Israel—his I will be, and with him I will remain. 19 Furthermore, whom should I serve if not his son? As I served in your father’s presence, so also I will serve in yours.” 20 Then Absalom said to Ahithophel, “Give me counsel. Such was the regard that both David and Absalom had for Ahithophel’s advice.

As I served in your father’s presence, so also I will serve in yours.”

When all Israel hears that you have become a stench to your father, then the hands of all who are with you will be strengthened.” 22 So they pitched a tent for Absalom on the roof, and he slept with his father’s concubines in the sight of all Israel. 23 Now in those days the advice of Ahithophel was like the consultation of the word of God. Such was the regard that both David and Absalom had for Ahithophel’s advice.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Absalom enters Jerusalem with Ahithophel. Hushai greets him as king, and Absalom questions why he has left his friend David. Hushai speaks of serving the one chosen by the LORD and Israel and of serving the son as he served the father. Readers already know that David has sent him to work against Ahithophel’s counsel.

Ahithophel advises Absalom to sleep with the concubines David left to care for the palace. He explains the intended effect: an unmistakable breach with David will strengthen Absalom’s supporters. A tent is set up on the roof, and Absalom carries out the advice publicly.

The chapter closes by describing the extraordinary trust both David and Absalom had placed in Ahithophel’s counsel. Its reputation helps explain why such a destructive proposal is followed.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Gill understands Hushai’s answer as deliberately ambiguous and criticizes its deception. His words can be heard by Absalom as loyalty while Hushai remains committed to David. The strategy’s service to David does not make its moral questions disappear.

Henry and Wesley read Ahithophel’s advice as an attempt to make reconciliation between father and son seem impossible, securing the commitment of Absalom’s party. The women left in the palace are being drawn into the struggle for power.

Wesley also connects the public act with Nathan’s earlier announcement in 2 Samuel 12:11–12. That connection explains its place in the story of judgment without making the advice morally good. Being regarded like an answer from God is a description of Ahithophel’s influence, not a declaration that everything he says is God’s word.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 17:1-14
passages.section_title: Why does Absalom choose the plan that gives David time?

versions.label: BSB

You seek the life of only one man; then all the people will be at peace.” 4 This proposal seemed good to Absalom and all the elders of Israel. 5 Then Absalom said, “Summon Hushai the Archite as well, and let us hear what he too has to say.” 6 So Hushai came to Absalom, who told him, “Ahithophel has spoken this proposal. Should we carry it out? If not, what do you say?” 7 Hushai replied, “This time the advice of Ahithophel is not sound.” 8 He continued, “You know your father and his men. They are mighty men, and as fierce as a wild bear robbed of her cubs. Moreover, your father is a man of war who will not spend the night with the troops. 9 Surely by now he is hiding in a cave or some other location. If some of your troops fall first, whoever hears of it will say, ‘There has been a slaughter among the troops who follow Absalom.’ 10 Then even the most valiant soldier with the heart of a lion will melt with fear, because all Israel knows that your father is a mighty man who has valiant men with him. 11 Instead, I advise that all Israel from Dan to Beersheba—a multitude like the sand on the seashore—be gathered to you, and that you yourself lead them into battle. 12 Then we will attack David wherever we find him, and we will descend on him like dew on the ground. And of all the men with him, not even one will remain. 13 If he retreats to a city, all Israel will bring ropes to that city, and we will drag it down to the valley until not even a pebble can be found there.” 14 Then Absalom and all the men of Israel said, “The advice of Hushai the Archite is better than that of Ahithophel.” For the LORD had purposed to thwart the good counsel of Ahithophel in order to bring disaster on Absalom.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Ahithophel proposes an immediate pursuit with twelve thousand men. He expects to find David weary, scatter his supporters and kill the king, bringing the rest back under Absalom. Absalom and the elders approve.

Absalom nevertheless asks Hushai for advice. Hushai stresses David’s experience and the danger of attacking a fierce and hidden enemy. He urges Absalom to gather a much larger force and lead it personally, promising an overwhelming victory.

Absalom and his supporters prefer Hushai’s advice. The narrator then gives the deeper explanation: the LORD has purposed to thwart Ahithophel’s effective counsel and bring disaster on Absalom. The delay serves David’s escape rather than the quick victory Ahithophel intended.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands Hushai’s proposal as a way of gaining time for David to prepare. Its promise of a great army and a victory personally led by Absalom also offers the kind of public glory that can make delay seem attractive.

Henry and Gill emphasize the LORD’s overruling of the competing plans. Gill explains the good counsel as advice well suited to Absalom’s aim. Calling a plan effective is different from approving the murder it seeks to accomplish.

Hushai’s confident description of David’s hiding place is part of his persuasive speech. The narrator does not independently confirm every cave, expected attack or promised result he describes.
passages.god_plan_html:
The chapter directly states that the contest of counselors remains within God’s purpose. The revolt does not become beyond His reach because a skilled adviser has devised a dangerous plan.

Ephesians 1:9–11 gives the wider saving purpose its center: God brings all things together in Christ and works according to His will. That is a larger horizon than either side’s immediate struggle for a throne.

This is a connection through Scripture’s account of God’s purpose, not a claim that Paul directly interprets this council meeting. It gives grounds for confidence in God without requiring us to approve every human scheme.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 17:15-23
passages.section_title: How does the warning reach David in time?

Otherwise the king and all the people with him will be swallowed up.’” 17 Now Jonathan and Ahimaaz were staying at En-rogel, where a servant girl would come and pass along information to them. They in turn would go and inform King David, for they dared not be seen entering the city. 18 But a young man did see them and told Absalom. So the two left quickly and came to the house of a man in Bahurim. He had a well in his courtyard, and they climbed down into it. 19 Then the man’s wife took a covering, spread it over the mouth of the well, and scattered grain over it so nobody would know a thing. 20 When Absalom’s servants came to the woman at the house, they asked, “Where are Ahimaaz and Jonathan?” “They have crossed over the brook,” she replied. The men searched but did not find them, so they returned to Jerusalem.

21 After the men had gone, Ahimaaz and Jonathan climbed up out of the well and went to inform King David, saying, “Get up and cross over the river at once, for Ahithophel has given this advice against you.” 22 So David and all the people with him got up and crossed the Jordan. By daybreak, there was no one left who had not crossed the Jordan. 23 When Ahithophel saw that his advice had not been followed, he saddled his donkey and set out for his house in his hometown. He put his affairs in order and hanged himself. So he died and was buried in his father’s tomb.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Hushai reports both plans to the priests and urges that David cross the river without delay. Jonathan and Ahimaaz receive information through a servant girl because they cannot safely appear in the city.

When a young man notices them and reports them to Absalom, they hide in a well at Bahurim. A woman covers the opening with a cloth and grain, then tells the searchers the men have crossed the brook. After the searchers leave, the messengers reach David.

David and everyone with him cross the Jordan before daybreak. Meanwhile Ahithophel, seeing that his advice has not been followed, returns home, puts his affairs in order and takes his own life. He is buried in his father’s tomb.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands the urgent warning as necessary because Absalom might still change course and pursue quickly. The accepted delay does not lead Hushai to assume that David can safely remain where he is.

Wesley also calls the woman’s answer to the searchers a lie. Her help preserves the messengers, but the account of their escape is not a blanket endorsement of every deception used in wartime.

Henry and Gill think Ahithophel recognized that Absalom’s cause was likely to fail and feared what would follow. Those are explanations of his response; the text itself connects his death with the rejection of his counsel without revealing every motive.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 17:24-29
passages.section_title: Who provides for David’s exhausted people?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
David reaches Mahanaim while Absalom crosses the Jordan and camps in Gilead. Absalom has appointed Amasa to command the army in Joab’s place. The conflict is moving toward another encounter.

At Mahanaim, Shobi, Machir and Barzillai bring beds, vessels and plentiful food for David’s people. Their reason is direct: the people are hungry, exhausted and thirsty after the wilderness journey. Before the next battle, they need somewhere to rest and something to eat.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley see encouragement in help that comes to David from outside his immediate household while his own son pursues him. Loyalty appears in ordinary provision as well as in military decisions.

Machir is the man who had housed Mephibosheth before David brought him to Jerusalem in 2 Samuel 9:4–5. The reappearance connects this help with a person already known for caring for someone in need.

The scene gives the names and the provisions without explaining every private motive or political bargain. The practical point remains clear: these men recognize suffering and use what they have to sustain the people who arrive.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 18:1-8
passages.section_title: What does David ask of the army before the battle?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then David reviewed his troops and appointed over them commanders of thousands and of hundreds. 2 He sent out the troops, a third under Joab, a third under Joab’s brother Abishai son of Zeruiah, and a third under Ittai the Gittite. And the king said to the troops, “I will surely march out with you as well.” 3 But the people pleaded, “You must not go out! For if we have to flee, they will not care about us. Even if half of us die, they will not care. But you are worth ten thousand of us. It is better now if you support us from the city.” 4 “I will do whatever seems best to you,” the king replied. So he stood beside the gate, while all the troops marched out by hundreds and by thousands. 5 Now the king had commanded Joab, Abishai, and Ittai, “Treat the young man Absalom gently for my sake.” And all the people heard the king’s orders to each of the commanders regarding Absalom. 6 So David’s army marched into the field to engage Israel, and the battle took place in the forest of Ephraim. 7 There the people of Israel were defeated by David’s servants, and the slaughter was great that day—twenty thousand men. 8 The battle spread over the whole countryside, and that day the forest devoured more people than the sword.
