section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
David organizes his forces under Joab, Abishai and Ittai, giving each command of a third. He offers to go with them, but they urge him to remain in the city because the enemy’s main target is the king. David accepts their advice.

As the troops leave, David publicly orders the commanders to treat Absalom gently for his sake. Everyone hears. The battle in the forest of Ephraim ends in a major defeat for Absalom’s forces, with twenty thousand men killed. The account says the forest devours more people than the sword, emphasizing the danger of the scattered fighting.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry highlights the contrast between Absalom wanting David killed and David wanting Absalom spared. He sees mercy toward a son who has acted as an enemy.

Wesley gives several possible reasons for David’s order, including affection, awareness of his own failures and a desire to leave time for repentance. He also includes a criticism of mercy that fails to confront a violent rebel. The tension between David’s concern as a father and his responsibility as king is real; interpreters do not all put the same emphasis on it.

The forest’s role is stated without a full explanation of how each death happens. Detailed accounts of hidden pits, wild animals or particular escape routes are possible reconstructions, not a description supplied by the narrator.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 18:9-18
passages.section_title: Why does Joab kill Absalom despite the king’s command?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 Now Absalom was riding on his mule when he met the servants of David, and as the mule went under the thick branches of a large oak, Absalom’s head was caught fast in the tree. The mule under him kept going, so that he was suspended in midair. 10 When one of the men saw this, he told Joab, “I just saw Absalom hanging in an oak tree!” 11 “You just saw him!” Joab exclaimed. “Why did you not strike him to the ground right there? I would have given you ten shekels of silver and a warrior’s belt!” 12 The man replied, “Even if a thousand shekels of silver were weighed out into my hands, I would not raise my hand against the son of the king. For we heard the king command you and Abishai and Ittai, ‘Protect the young man Absalom for my sake.’ 13 If I had jeopardized my own life—and nothing is hidden from the king—you would have abandoned me.” 14 But Joab declared, “I am not going to wait like this with you!” And he took three spears in his hand and thrust them through the heart of Absalom while he was still alive in the oak tree. 15 And ten young men who carried Joab’s armor surrounded Absalom, struck him, and killed him. 16 Then Joab blew the ram’s horn, and the troops broke off their pursuit of Israel because Joab had restrained them. 17 They took Absalom, cast him into a large pit in the forest, and piled a huge mound of stones over him. section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
While riding beneath a large oak, Absalom catches his head in the tree and is left suspended as the mule continues. A soldier sees him and reports it to Joab. Asked why he did not kill him, the man points to David’s public command and says that even Joab would abandon him if the king called him to account.

Joab refuses to wait. He thrusts three spears through Absalom while he is still alive in the tree, and ten armor-bearers then strike and kill him. Joab sounds the horn to stop the pursuit. Absalom is thrown into a pit under a mound of stones.

The account contrasts that end with the pillar Absalom had set up to preserve his own name, saying he had no son to do so. The monument he arranged for himself is different from the grave his enemies give him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The BSB says Absalom’s head catches in the tree. Wesley thinks his hair was probably involved, while Gill considers either tangled hair or the head being caught in a fork of the branches. The familiar picture of hanging by his hair is therefore a reading of the scene, not the verse’s exact wording.

The soldier’s refusal and Joab’s response place the king’s command directly before the reader. The killing ends the immediate threat from Absalom, but it also disregards the instructions everyone heard. A successful outcome does not remove that conflict.

The earlier description names three sons of Absalom in 2 Samuel 14:27. Gill explains the statement about having no son by supposing they had died. The account does not give the dates or story of their deaths, so that explanation should remain an inference.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 18:19-33
passages.section_title: Why is news of victory devastating to David?

You may do it another day, but you must not do so today, because the king’s son is dead.” 21 So Joab said to a Cushite, “Go, tell the king what you have seen.” The Cushite bowed to Joab and took off running. 22 Ahimaaz son of Zadok, however, persisted and said to Joab, “No matter what, please let me also run behind the Cushite!” “My son,” Joab replied, “why do you want to run, since you will not receive a reward?” 23 “No matter what, I want to run!” he replied. “Then run!” Joab told him. So Ahimaaz ran by way of the plain and outran the Cushite. 24 Now David was sitting between the two gates when the watchman went up to the roof of the gateway by the wall, looked out, and saw a man running alone. 25 So he called out and told the king. “If he is alone,” the king replied, “he bears good news.” As the first runner drew near, 26 the watchman saw another man running, and he called out to the gatekeeper, “Look! section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Ahimaaz wants to carry news of victory, but Joab initially refuses because the king’s son is dead. He sends a Cushite instead. Ahimaaz keeps asking and is eventually allowed to run; he takes the way of the plain and reaches David first.

David hears that runners are approaching and expects good news. Ahimaaz announces that the LORD has delivered him from his enemies. When David asks about Absalom, however, he says he saw a disturbance but does not know what it was.

The Cushite arrives with the same announcement of deliverance. Asked about Absalom, he answers indirectly, wishing the king’s enemies to share the young man’s fate. David understands. He goes up to the chamber above the gate and weeps, repeatedly calling Absalom his son and wishing he had died instead.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Gill criticizes Ahimaaz’s answer as evasion: Joab had already told him that the king’s son was dead. The scene shows the distance between reporting a military victory and answering the question the father most wants answered.

Henry and Wesley see a serious conflict between David’s grief for Absalom and his duty toward the people who have saved him. They also discuss whether his wish reflects concern about his son’s future beyond death or the intensity of his immediate sorrow. The verse gives his cry, not a complete declaration about Absalom’s eternal state.

The loss is genuine even though Absalom has done great harm. The chapter allows that grief to be heard in David’s own repeated words. The consequences for the returning soldiers and David’s next responsibility are taken up in chapter 19.
passages.god_plan_html:
Henry sees a limited picture of the Savior’s love in a father grieving for a son who has become his enemy. David wishes he could die in Absalom’s place, but his wish cannot undo the death.

Romans 5:6–10 describes what Christ actually does: He dies for the ungodly, and enemies are reconciled to God through His death. The saving work goes far beyond the love expressed in David’s cry.

This is a comparison, not a claim that David’s grief itself accomplishes salvation or that every detail of Absalom’s story predicts Christ. It helps us see the greater wonder of a love that gives itself to bring enemies into peace with God.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 19:1-8
passages.section_title: Why does Joab urge the grieving king to face his people?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then it was reported to Joab, “The king is weeping and mourning over Absalom.” 2 And that day’s victory was turned into mourning for all the people, because on that day they were told, “The king is grieving over his son.” 3 So they returned to the city quietly that day, as people steal away in humiliation after fleeing a battle. 4 But the king covered his face and cried out at the top of his voice, “O my son Absalom! O Absalom, my son, my son!” 5 Then Joab went into the house and said to the king, “Today you have disgraced all your servants who have saved your life and the lives of your sons and daughters, of your wives, and of your concubines. 6 You love those who hate you and hate those who love you! For you have made it clear today that the commanders and soldiers mean nothing to you. I know today that if Absalom were alive and all of us were dead, it would have pleased you! 7 Now therefore get up! Go out and speak comfort to your servants, for I swear by the LORD that if you do not go out, not a man will remain with you tonight. This will be worse for you than all the adversity that has befallen you from your youth until now!” 8 So the king got up and sat in the gate, and all the people were told: “Behold, the king is sitting in the gate.” So they all came before the king. Meanwhile, the Israelites had fled, each man to his home.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Word of David’s mourning reaches the returning army. Instead of entering the city as victors, the soldiers come quietly and ashamed, while David continues crying for Absalom.

Joab confronts him, saying he has disgraced the people who saved him and his household. He accuses David of caring more for Absalom than for all his loyal servants and warns that they will abandon him if he does not speak to them.

David rises and sits in the gate, where the people come before him. He resumes his public responsibility without the account saying that his private grief has simply vanished.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry thinks David needed to respond to the people, but also criticizes the disrespect in Joab’s rebuke. A necessary point can be made in a way that deserves criticism itself.

Wesley explicitly treats Joab’s claim that David would prefer all his servants dead as an overstatement rather than an exact description of David’s wishes. The sharp language aims to awaken the king to how his behavior is affecting those who served him.

The scene presents a leader’s responsibilities during personal loss. It does not establish that grieving for a wayward child is itself wrong or that every bereaved person should respond on the same schedule.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 19:9-15
passages.section_title: How does David invite Judah to receive him again?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 And all the people throughout the tribes of Israel were arguing, “The king rescued us from the hand of our enemies and delivered us from the hand of the Philistines, but now he has fled the land because of Absalom. 10 But Absalom, the man we anointed over us, has died in battle. So why do you say nothing about restoring the king?” 11 Then King David sent this message to Zadok and Abiathar, the priests: “Say to the elders of Judah, ‘Why should you be the last to restore the king to his palace, since the talk of all Israel has reached the king at his quarters? 12 You are my brothers, my own flesh and blood. So why should you be the last to restore the king?’ 13 And say to Amasa, ‘Aren’t you my flesh and blood? May God punish me, and ever so severely, if from now on you are not the commander of my army in place of Joab!’” 14 So he swayed the hearts of all the men of Judah as though they were one man, and they sent word to the king: “Return, you and all your servants.” 15 So the king returned, and when he arrived at the Jordan, the men of Judah came to Gilgal to meet him and escort him across the Jordan.

So why do you say nothing about restoring the king?”

11 Then King David sent this message to Zadok and Abiathar, the priests: “Say to the elders of Judah, ‘Why should you be the last to restore the king to his palace, since the talk of all Israel has reached the king at his quarters? 12 You are my brothers, my own flesh and blood. So why should you be the last to restore the king?’ 13 And say to Amasa, ‘Aren’t you my flesh and blood? May God punish me, and ever so severely, if from now on you are not the commander of my army in place of Joab!’” 14 So he swayed the hearts of all the men of Judah as though they were one man, and they sent word to the king: “Return, you and all your servants.” 15 So the king returned, and when he arrived at the Jordan, the men of Judah came to Gilgal to meet him and escort him across the Jordan.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Across Israel the people debate what to do after Absalom’s death. They remember David’s deliverance of the nation and ask why nothing is being done to bring him back. The defeat of the rebellion has not yet produced an orderly restoration.

David sends the priests to Judah’s elders, appealing to them as his own flesh and blood. He also promises Amasa command of the army in place of Joab. The message wins Judah’s support, and the people invite David and his servants to return. They come to Gilgal to escort him across the Jordan.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill understand the offer to Amasa as both a way of bringing former opponents into David’s support and a way of replacing Joab after his offenses. The offer is a significant act toward the commander of the defeated side.

Henry emphasizes the movement of the people toward receiving their king. The invitation is not only imposed by David: verses 9–10 already report discussion of his return among Israel, before his message to Judah.

Winning support and securing lasting unity are different tasks. The favorable response here is real, but the chapter’s closing quarrel will show how much remains unsettled.
passages.god_plan_html:
David’s return offers a limited comparison with the biblical hope of the coming King. His people call him back after a rebellion; Christians look forward to the return of the One whose kingship will endure.

Luke 1:32–33 identifies Jesus as the heir of David’s throne whose kingdom has no end. In Revelation 22:12–20, Jesus promises His coming, and the response is a call for Him to come.

This is a comparison of welcome and hope, not a timetable drawn from each step of David’s journey. Jesus’ promised return rests on His own word. The disputes that remain under David also keep our hope looking beyond the limits of an earthly restoration.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 19:16-23
passages.section_title: Why does David spare Shimei when he returns?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 Then Shimei son of Gera, a Benjamite from Bahurim, hurried down with the men of Judah to meet King David, 17 along with a thousand men of Benjamin, as well as Ziba the steward of the house of Saul and his fifteen sons and twenty servants. They rushed down to the Jordan before the king 18 and crossed at the ford to carry over the king’s household and to do what was good in his sight. When Shimei son of Gera crossed the Jordan, he fell down before the king 19 and said, “My lord, do not hold me guilty, and do not remember your servant’s wrongdoing on the day my lord the king left Jerusalem. May the king not take it to heart. 20 For your servant knows that I have sinned, so here I am today as the first of all the house of Joseph to come down to meet my lord the king.” 21 But Abishai son of Zeruiah said, “Shouldn’t Shimei be put to death for this, because he cursed the LORD’s anointed?” 22 And David replied, “Sons of Zeruiah, what have I to do with you, that you should be my adversaries today? Should any man be put to death in Israel today? Am I not indeed aware that today I am king over Israel?” 23 So the king said to Shimei, “You shall not die.” And the king swore an oath to him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Shimei, who cursed David as he left Jerusalem, hurries to meet him with the men of Judah. A thousand Benjamites are present, along with Ziba and his household. They help bring the king’s household across the Jordan.

Shimei falls before David, acknowledges his wrongdoing and asks him not to hold it against him. Abishai again calls for his death because he cursed the LORD’s anointed. David rejects that course for the day of his restoration and swears to Shimei that he will not die.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley sees both mercy and concern for reconciliation in David’s answer. Beginning his return with an execution could deepen the fear of those who had opposed him. Having received mercy himself, David has reason to show it to another.

The account records Shimei’s confession and David’s oath. It does not give a complete view of Shimei’s heart or make every member of Benjamin responsible for his earlier actions.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 19:24-30
passages.section_title: What does Mephibosheth say about Ziba’s accusation?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 24 Then Mephibosheth, Saul’s grandson, went down to meet the king. He had not cared for his feet or trimmed his mustache or washed his clothes from the day the king had left until the day he returned safely. 25 And he came from Jerusalem to meet the king, who asked him, “Mephibosheth, why did you not go with me?” 26 “My lord the king,” he replied, “because I am lame, I said, ‘I will have my donkey saddled so that I may ride on it and go with the king.’ But my servant Ziba deceived me, 27 and he has slandered your servant to my lord the king. Yet my lord the king is like the angel of God, so do what is good in your eyes. 28 For all the house of my grandfather deserves death from my lord the king, yet you have set your servant among those who eat at your table. What further right, then, do I have to keep appealing to the king?” 29 The king replied, “Why say any more? I hereby declare that you and Ziba are to divide the land.” 30 And Mephibosheth said to the king, “Instead, since my lord the king has safely come to his own house, let Ziba take it all!”

Yet my lord the king is like the angel of God, so do what is good in your eyes. 28 For all the house of my grandfather deserves death from my lord the king, yet you have set your servant among those who eat at your table. What further right, then, do I have to keep appealing to the king?”

29 The king replied, “Why say any more? I hereby declare that you and Ziba are to divide the land.” 30 And Mephibosheth said to the king, “Instead, since my lord the king has safely come to his own house, let Ziba take it all!”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Mephibosheth comes to meet David, having neglected his feet, mustache and clothing throughout the king’s absence. David asks why he did not accompany him. Mephibosheth says that Ziba deceived him when he wanted a donkey prepared and then slandered him.

He recalls David’s kindness in giving him a place at the royal table and submits the matter to the king. David ends the discussion by ordering that he and Ziba divide the land. Mephibosheth answers that Ziba may have it all, since David has returned safely.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley reads Mephibosheth’s neglected appearance as mourning that supports his account of loyalty. The scene gives him the opportunity to answer the accusation David accepted in 2 Samuel 16:1–4.

Wesley and Gill understand the division as returning to the earlier arrangement in which Ziba works the estate and shares its proceeds. The BSB states David’s ruling directly without explaining all its practical terms. The narrative also gives no further hearing in which Ziba answers the charge of slander.

Henry emphasizes Mephibosheth’s joy at the king’s return. Whatever happens to the land, his final words place David’s safety above winning the dispute. That is the loyalty his reply expresses.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 19:31-40
passages.section_title: How does David honor Barzillai’s help?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 31 Now Barzillai the Gileadite had come down from Rogelim to cross the Jordan with the king and send him on his way from there. 32 Barzillai was quite old, eighty years of age, and since he was a very wealthy man, he had provided for the king while he stayed in Mahanaim. 33 The king said to Barzillai, “Cross over with me, and I will provide for you at my side in Jerusalem.” 34 But Barzillai replied, “How many years of my life remain, that I should go up to Jerusalem with the king? 35 I am now eighty years old. Can I discern what is good and what is not? Can your servant taste what he eats or drinks? Can I still hear the voice of singing men and women? Why should your servant be an added burden to my lord the king? 36 Your servant will go with the king only a short distance past the Jordan; why should the king repay me with such a reward? 37 Please let your servant return, that I may die in my own city near the tomb of my father and mother. But here is your servant Chimham. Let him cross over with my lord the king, and do for him what is good in your sight.” 38 The king replied, “Chimham will cross over with me, and I will do for him what is good in your sight, and I will do for you whatever you desire of me.” 39 So all the people crossed the Jordan, and then the king crossed over. The king kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and Barzillai returned home. 40 Then the king crossed over to Gilgal, and Chimham crossed over with him. All the troops of Judah and half the troops of Israel escorted the king.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Barzillai, who provided for David at Mahanaim, accompanies him to the Jordan. He is eighty and wealthy enough to have sustained the king. David invites him to Jerusalem and offers to provide for him there.

Barzillai declines, describing the limits of his strength and enjoyment and asking to return to his own city near his parents’ tomb. He instead commends Chimham to David. The king agrees to care for Chimham and promises to honor Barzillai’s wishes.

David kisses and blesses Barzillai before he returns home. Chimham continues with the king to Gilgal. Care given in David’s need is remembered after the danger has passed.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry sees humility in Barzillai’s surprise at the reward offered for his service. Wesley emphasizes his recognition that the pleasures and demands of court life no longer suit him.

Barzillai speaks about his own condition, not a rule that every eighty-year-old is unable to contribute or enjoy life. His generosity has already proved valuable. Declining one invitation does not cancel the service he has given or the honor David shows him.
passages.god_plan_html:
Henry compares Barzillai’s response with the surprise of the righteous in Matthew 25:34–40. In Jesus’ description, the King remembers food, drink, welcome and care given to the least of His brothers as service to Himself.

The comparison places practical generosity within the larger calling to serve the King. Help that seems ordinary to the giver can matter greatly to those who receive it and can be remembered far beyond the moment of need.

This is a supported comparison, not a claim that David’s arrangements for Chimham describe every feature of the coming kingdom. It turns our attention toward the value God places on faithful care rather than only public power or recognition.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 19:41-43
passages.section_title: Why does the welcome turn into another quarrel?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 41 Soon all the men of Israel came to the king and asked, “Why did our brothers, the men of Judah, take you away secretly and bring the king and his household across the Jordan, together with all of David’s men?” 42 And all the men of Judah replied to the men of Israel, “We did this because the king is our relative. Why does this anger you? Have we ever eaten at the king’s expense or received anything for ourselves?” 43 “We have ten shares in the king,” answered the men of Israel, “so we have more claim to David than you. Why then do you despise us? Were we not the first to speak of restoring our king?” But the men of Judah spoke more fiercely than the men of Israel.
paragraphs: 41 Soon all the men of Israel came to the king and asked, “Why did our brothers, the men of Judah, take you away secretly and bring the king and his household across the Jordan, together with all of David’s men?” 42 And all the men of Judah replied to the men of Israel, “We did this because the king is our relative. Why does this anger you? Have we ever eaten at the king’s expense or received anything for ourselves?” 43 “We have ten shares in the king,” answered the men of Israel, “so we have more claim to David than you. Why then do you despise us? Were we not the first to speak of restoring our king?” But the men of Judah spoke more fiercely than the men of Israel.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The men of Israel accuse Judah of taking the king across the Jordan without them. Judah answers that David is their relative and denies receiving special benefits. Israel claims a larger share in the king and says its people were first to speak of bringing him back.

The narrator ends by saying that Judah answers more fiercely. Both sides claim loyalty to David, but their words expose rivalry over recognition and influence. The king is returning; the nation’s division is still present.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Gill connects Israel’s claim of having spoken first with the discussion already recorded earlier in the chapter. It is not simply a claim the story has given no reason to consider.

Henry emphasizes the harm of pride and harsh speech, while Wesley links the dispute with the rebellion that follows. The closing scene qualifies the chapter’s welcome: support for the same king has not yet become patient regard for one another.
passages.god_plan_html:
The quarrel shows how people can speak for a common cause while competing for priority within it. Scripture’s larger purpose for God’s people includes a different way of belonging together.

Ephesians 4:1–6 calls believers to humility, gentleness, patience and a diligent effort to preserve unity through peace. The unity is grounded in one Lord, one faith and one God, rather than in a contest over who deserves the greater share of honor.

This is a shared theme, not a claim that Paul directly interprets Judah’s argument or that the church and the tribes have identical political arrangements. It shows why loyalty to the King should shape how His people speak to one another.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 20:1-7
passages.section_title: Why does another rebellion begin as David returns?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now a worthless man named Sheba son of Bichri, a Benjamite, happened to be there, and he blew the ram’s horn and shouted: “We have no share in David, no inheritance in Jesse’s son. Every man to his tent, O Israel!” 2 So all the men of Israel deserted David to follow Sheba son of Bichri. But the men of Judah stayed by their king all the way from the Jordan to Jerusalem. 3 When David returned to his palace in Jerusalem, he took the ten concubines he had left to take care of the palace, and he placed them in a house under guard. He provided for them, but he no longer slept with them. They were confined until the day of their death, living as widows. 4 Then the king said to Amasa, “Summon the men of Judah to come to me within three days, and be here yourself.” 5 So Amasa went to summon Judah, but he took longer than the time allotted him. 6 And David said to Abishai, “Now Sheba the son of Bichri will do us more harm than Absalom. Take your lord’s servants and pursue him, or he will find fortified cities and elude us.” 7 So Joab’s men, along with the Cherethites, the Pelethites, and all the mighty men, marched out of Jerusalem in pursuit of Sheba son of Bichri.

Every man to his tent, O Israel!” 2 So all the men of Israel deserted David to follow Sheba son of Bichri. But the men of Judah stayed by their king all the way from the Jordan to Jerusalem. 3 When David returned to his palace in Jerusalem, he took the ten concubines he had left to take care of the palace, and he placed them in a house under guard. He provided for them, but he no longer slept with them. They were confined until the day of their death, living as widows.

4 Then the king said to Amasa, “Summon the men of Judah to come to me within three days, and be here yourself.” 5 So Amasa went to summon Judah, but he took longer than the time allotted him. 6 And David said to Abishai, “Now Sheba the son of Bichri will do us more harm than Absalom. Take your lord’s servants and pursue him, or he will find fortified cities and elude us.” 7 So Joab’s men, along with the Cherethites, the Pelethites, and all the mighty men, marched out of Jerusalem in pursuit of Sheba son of Bichri.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The quarrel at the end of chapter 19 becomes an opening for another revolt. Sheba, a Benjamite, sounds the ram’s horn and calls Israel away from David. Israel follows him, while Judah remains with the king on the journey to Jerusalem.

The Hebrew word behind the description of Sheba as worthless is beliyyaal, pronounced beh-lee-YAH-al. Brown–Driver–Briggs includes this verse among its examples of a base or wicked person. The description concerns his character and conduct.

Back in Jerusalem, David places the ten concubines under guard and provides for them, but no longer sleeps with them. Their confinement lasts for the rest of their lives. The consequences of Absalom’s actions in chapter 16 continue after his death.

David orders Amasa to gather Judah’s men within three days. When he takes longer, David sends Abishai and the troops already available. He fears Sheba will reach fortified cities and become an even greater danger than Absalom.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry connects the revolt with the pride and angry exchanges that came before it. A dispute among the king’s supporters creates an opportunity for someone who wants to reject the king altogether.

Wesley understands the statement about all Israel as referring to the general body of Israelites present. The scene describes the division at David’s return, rather than giving a separate account of every individual in every tribe.

Gill leaves the reason for Amasa’s delay uncertain: he considers Amasa’s own slowness, reluctance among the people and insufficient time. The text reports the delay without explaining its cause.

The women’s situation also deserves attention. They receive material support, but lose their freedom and their former life. The account records what David does; it does not record their consent to Absalom’s actions or tell us what each woman thought.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 20:8-13
passages.section_title: How does Joab take command again?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 And while they were at the great stone in Gibeon, Amasa joined them. Now Joab was dressed in military attire, with a dagger strapped to his belt. And as he stepped forward, he slipped the dagger from its sheath. 9 “Are you well, my brother?” Joab asked Amasa. And with his right hand Joab grabbed Amasa by the beard to kiss him. 10 Amasa was not on guard against the dagger in Joab’s hand, and Joab stabbed him in the stomach and spilled out his intestines on the ground. And Joab did not need to strike him again, for Amasa was dead. Then Joab and his brother Abishai pursued Sheba son of Bichri. 11 One of Joab’s young men stood near Amasa and said, “Whoever favors Joab, and whoever is for David, let him follow Joab!” 12 But Amasa wallowed in his blood in the middle of the road, and when the man saw that all the troops were stopping there, he dragged the body off the road into a field and threw a garment over it. 13 As soon as Amasa’s body was removed from the road, all the men went on with Joab to pursue Sheba son of Bichri.

And with his right hand Joab grabbed Amasa by the beard to kiss him. 10 Amasa was not on guard against the dagger in Joab’s hand, and Joab stabbed him in the stomach and spilled out his intestines on the ground. And Joab did not need to strike him again, for Amasa was dead. Then Joab and his brother Abishai pursued Sheba son of Bichri.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Amasa meets the troops at Gibeon. Joab approaches him with a friendly question and reaches for his beard as if to kiss him. Amasa is not watching the dagger in Joab’s hand. Joab stabs him, killing him with a single blow.

Joab and Abishai continue after Sheba. One of Joab’s men calls on those who support Joab and David to follow. When the soldiers keep stopping at Amasa’s body, he moves it off the road and covers it. The troops then continue behind Joab.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry treats the killing as murder driven by personal revenge. Joab’s pursuit of a rebel does not excuse his own violence against the man David appointed.

Wesley also refuses to let the practical result hide the crime. Moving and covering the body allows the army to march on, but does not remove the guilt of shedding Amasa’s blood.

The scene recalls Joab’s earlier killing of Abner in chapter 3: apparent friendliness creates an opening for a deadly attack. Here again, military strength and service to David coexist with conduct the reader has reason to condemn.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 20:14-22
passages.section_title: How does a wise woman save her city from destruction?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 Sheba passed through all the tribes of Israel to Abel-beth-maacah and through the entire region of the Berites, who gathered together and followed him. 15 And Joab’s troops came and besieged Sheba in Abel-beth-maacah and built a siege ramp against the outer rampart of the city. As all the troops with Joab were battering the wall to topple it, 16 a wise woman called out from the city, “Listen! Listen! Please tell Joab to come here so that I may speak with him.” 17 When he had come near to her, the woman asked, “Are you Joab?” “I am,” he replied. “Listen to the words of your servant,” she said. “I am listening,” he answered. 18 Then the woman said, “Long ago they used to say, ‘Seek counsel at Abel,’ and that is how disputes were settled. 19 I am among the peaceable and faithful in Israel, but you are trying to destroy a city that is a mother in Israel. Why would you swallow up the LORD’s inheritance?” 20 “Far be it!” Joab declared. “Far be it from me to swallow up or destroy! 21 That is not the case. But a man named Sheba son of Bichri, from the hill country of Ephraim, has lifted up his hand against the king, against David. Deliver him alone, and I will depart from the city.” “Look,” the woman replied, “his head will be thrown to you over the wall.” 22 Then the woman went to all the people with her wise counsel, and they cut off the head of Sheba son of Bichri and threw it to Joab. So he blew the ram’s horn and his men dispersed from the city, each to his own home. And Joab returned to the king in Jerusalem.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Sheba reaches Abel-beth-maacah, and Joab’s army besieges the city. The troops build a ramp and batter the wall. A wise woman calls for Joab and asks him to listen.

She appeals to Abel’s reputation as a place where disputes were settled and identifies herself with the peaceable and faithful in Israel. She challenges Joab’s attack on a city that belongs to the LORD’s inheritance.

Joab says his target is Sheba alone and offers to withdraw if the city hands him over. The woman takes the matter to the people. They cut off Sheba’s head and throw it over the wall. Joab sounds the horn, ends the siege and returns to Jerusalem.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley emphasizes that the decisive wisdom comes from a woman whom the account does not name. Her ability to speak and act wisely matters more than whether she holds a position usually associated with men.

Henry draws attention to the value of making the actual dispute clear. Joab seeks one rebel; the woman speaks for a city that does not want to be destroyed with him. Their conversation makes an agreement possible.

The outcome is severe: Sheba is killed. The woman’s intervention saves the city from the wider destruction the siege threatened. Both parts belong to the account.
passages.god_plan_html:
This scene connects with the Bible’s wider teaching about wisdom that makes peace. The woman listens, identifies the issue and speaks to protect her people. Wisdom becomes visible in what she does.

James 3:13–18 contrasts jealousy and selfish ambition with wisdom that is humble, peace-loving and full of mercy. It adds a question for readers of this chapter: do our words and decisions stir up conflict, or help bring it to an end?

James does not interpret this siege or give Christians instructions to copy its execution. The connection is the value of practical wisdom that seeks peace amid destructive conflict.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The chapter closes with the people responsible for David’s army, bodyguard, forced labor, records, writing and priestly service. Joab is again named over the whole army. Amasa is gone.

The list recalls the officials named in 2 Samuel 8:15–18. David’s rule continues after the rebellions, but the story of Joab’s return to command makes this a troubled restoration.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley sees Joab’s military success and strong support as reasons David could not safely remove him. Gill likewise connects his continued command with his influence and the defeat of the rebellion. These are explanations of the political situation, not declarations that Joab’s murder was right.

There is also a difference in how Ira’s role is understood. The BSB calls him David’s priest; Gill takes the title here to mean a high official close to the king. This resembles the question about the title given to David’s sons in chapter 8.

Whatever the precise duties of each office, the list shows that governing the kingdom involves more than the king alone. It also leaves the reader facing a difficult fact: an effective commander can remain in power after doing great wrong.
passages.god_plan_html:
The survival of David’s kingdom is important, but its survival is not the same as perfect rule. The promises connected with his throne reach beyond the weaknesses of this court.

Isaiah 9:6–7 describes a ruler on David’s throne whose government is sustained by justice and righteousness, with peace that does not end. Luke 1:32–33 identifies Jesus as the Son who receives David’s throne and reigns forever.

That promise gives the larger hope alongside this unsettled ending. David’s officials keep a kingdom functioning; Jesus is the King whose lasting rule fulfills God’s promise.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 21:1-9
passages.section_title: Why does David seek to make amends to the Gibeonites?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 During the reign of David there was a famine for three successive years, and David sought the face of the LORD. And the LORD said, “It is because of the blood shed by Saul and his family, because he killed the Gibeonites.” 2 At this, David summoned the Gibeonites and spoke to them. (Now the Gibeonites were not Israelites, but a remnant of the Amorites. The Israelites had taken an oath concerning them, but in his zeal for Israel and Judah, Saul had sought to kill them.) 3 So David asked the Gibeonites, “What shall I do for you? How can I make amends so that you may bless the inheritance of the LORD?” 4 The Gibeonites said to him, “We need no silver or gold from Saul or his house, nor should you put to death anyone in Israel for us.” “Whatever you ask, I will do for you,” he replied. 5 And they answered the king, “As for the man who consumed us and plotted against us to exterminate us from existing within any border of Israel, 6 let seven of his male descendants be delivered to us so that we may hang them before the LORD at Gibeah of Saul, the chosen of the LORD.” “I will give them to you,” said the king. 7 Now the king spared Mephibosheth son of Jonathan, the son of Saul, because of the oath before the LORD between David and Jonathan son of Saul. 8 But the king took Armoni and Mephibosheth, the two sons whom Rizpah daughter of Aiah had borne to Saul, as well as the five sons whom Merab daughter of Saul had borne to Adriel son of Barzillai the Meholathite. 9 And he delivered them into the hands of the Gibeonites, and they hanged them on the hill before the LORD. So all seven of them fell together; they were put to death in the first days of the harvest, at the beginning of the barley harvest.

So all seven of them fell together; they were put to death in the first days of the harvest, at the beginning of the barley harvest.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
A three-year famine leads David to seek the LORD. The answer identifies bloodshed by Saul and his family against the Gibeonites, a people Israel had sworn to protect. The episode is placed during David’s reign without an exact date.

The background is Joshua 9:14–21. Although the Gibeonites deceived Israel about where they came from, Israel’s leaders made a treaty to let them live. After discovering the deception, the leaders still recognized their obligation to keep the oath.

David asks the Gibeonites how he can make amends. The Hebrew verb is kaphar, pronounced kah-FAR. Brown–Driver–Briggs includes this verse under dealing with guilt without a sacrificial rite. David’s question concerns the wrong done to this people and how it can be addressed.

The Gibeonites reject payment and ask for seven male descendants of Saul. David agrees, while sparing Jonathan’s son Mephibosheth because of his oath to Jonathan. The seven handed over include two sons of Rizpah and five sons of Merab. Rizpah’s son Mephibosheth is a different man from Jonathan’s son.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry understands Saul’s family as sharing his violent conduct. On that reading, the deaths address wrongdoing in the household as well as Saul’s own offense.

Wesley and Gill, however, describe the seven as dying for Saul’s sin rather than for personal crimes of their own. They understand the episode as an exceptional judgment authorized by God. Both infer that authorization from God’s response to the land; a separate command naming these seven men is not recorded.

That difference matters because Deuteronomy 24:16 says that children are not to be executed for their fathers’ sins. The chapter identifies the bloodguilt of Saul’s house but gives no individual account of what each of the seven did. Readers should distinguish the facts the narrator supplies from the explanations commentators offer.
passages.god_plan_html:
This episode belongs to the Bible’s wider concern for faithfulness to promises. Saul’s zeal for Israel does not cancel Israel’s obligation toward outsiders. David also recognizes his promise to Jonathan while dealing with the wrong done to the Gibeonites.

Matthew 5:33–37 takes truthfulness into everyday speech: Jesus teaches His followers to give a dependable yes or no. The connection is the seriousness of keeping one’s word, even when circumstances change.

That shared theme does not make this execution a pattern for settling broken promises today. It directs attention to the faithfulness owed both to God and to people who depend on what we have said.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 21:10-14
passages.section_title: What does Rizpah do for the men who have died?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 And Rizpah the daughter of Aiah took sackcloth and spread it out for herself on a rock. From the beginning of the harvest until the rain from heaven poured down on the bodies, she did not allow the birds of the air to rest on them by day, nor the beasts of the field by night. 11 When David was told what Saul’s concubine Rizpah, daughter of Aiah, had done, 12 he went and took the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan from the men of Jabesh-gilead, who had stolen them from the public square of Beth-shan where the Philistines had hung the bodies after they had struck down Saul at Gilboa. 13 So David had the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan brought from there, and they also gathered the bones of those who had been hanged. 14 And they buried the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan in Zela in the land of Benjamin, in the tomb of Saul’s father Kish. After they had done everything the king had commanded, God answered their prayers for the land.

12 he went and took the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan from the men of Jabesh-gilead, who had stolen them from the public square of Beth-shan where the Philistines had hung the bodies after they had struck down Saul at Gilboa. 13 So David had the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan brought from there, and they also gathered the bones of those who had been hanged. 14 And they buried the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan in Zela in the land of Benjamin, in the tomb of Saul’s father Kish. After they had done everything the king had commanded, God answered their prayers for the land.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Rizpah spreads sackcloth on a rock and keeps watch over the exposed bodies, preventing birds and wild animals from feeding on them. She remains from the beginning of harvest until rain falls on the bodies.

When David hears what she has done, he retrieves the bones of Saul and Jonathan from Jabesh-gilead. The bones of the executed men are gathered too. Saul and Jonathan are buried in the tomb of Saul’s father Kish at Zela.

After the king’s instructions have been carried out, God answers the prayers for the land. The episode ends with burial and answered prayer, while Rizpah’s persistent care remains central to the story.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley sees Rizpah’s example as prompting David to give Saul and Jonathan an honorable burial. Her grief and care for the dead move the king to act.

Gill notes the difficulty created by the exposed bodies, since Deuteronomy 21:22–23 requires burial on the day of execution. He treats the prolonged display as an exceptional case under divine permission. That permission is his explanation of the event, rather than an instruction quoted in this chapter.

The passage shows consequences reaching beyond the people who first committed the violence. Rizpah’s care refuses to let the dead be forgotten. The narrator also places God’s answer after the acts David orders, without giving a general rule that every unanswered prayer proves someone has failed to obey.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 21:15-22
passages.section_title: Why do David’s men tell him to stop going into battle?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 Once again the Philistines waged war against Israel, and David and his servants went down and fought against the Philistines. But David became exhausted. 16 Then Ishbi-benob, a descendant of Rapha, whose bronze spear weighed three hundred shekels and who was bearing a new sword, resolved to kill David. 17 But Abishai son of Zeruiah came to his aid, struck the Philistine, and killed him. Then David’s men swore to him, “You must never again go out with us to battle, so that the lamp of Israel may not be extinguished.” 18 Some time later at Gob, there was another battle with the Philistines. At that time Sibbecai the Hushathite killed Saph, a descendant of Rapha. 19 Once again there was a battle with the Philistines at Gob, and Elhanan son of Jair the Bethlehemite killed the brother of Goliath the Gittite, the shaft of whose spear was like a weaver’s beam. 20 And there was also a battle at Gath, where there was a man of great stature with six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot—twenty-four in all. He too was descended from Rapha, 21 and when he taunted Israel, Jonathan the son of David’s brother Shimei killed him. 22 So these four descendants of Rapha in Gath fell at the hands of David and his servants.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
During another battle with the Philistines, David becomes exhausted. Ishbi-benob intends to kill him, but Abishai comes to his aid and kills the attacker. David’s men then insist that he must no longer go out with them to battle. They describe his life as the lamp of Israel.

The remaining accounts name other victories by Sibbecai, Elhanan and Jonathan, the son of David’s brother Shimei. The closing summary credits David and his servants together. The king’s earlier victories do not mean he can now fight without help.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry emphasizes help arriving when David’s strength fails. The scene gives proper place to both the king’s weakness and the servants who protect him.

There is a question about the wording of verse 19. The BSB says that Elhanan killed the brother of Goliath, matching the relationship stated in 1 Chronicles 20:5. Gill also reads Samuel with that parallel account. This is a different victory from David’s killing of Goliath in 1 Samuel 17.

The account honors the men who stand beside David. Recognizing limits and accepting help can protect the work entrusted to a leader.
passages.god_plan_html:
David’s need for help connects with the wider biblical lesson that serving God does not mean having unlimited strength. Here, his life is preserved through another person’s timely action.

In 2 Corinthians 12:7–10, Paul describes a weakness that remains even after repeated prayer. Christ’s answer teaches him to depend on grace and on power that is made known in weakness.

Paul is speaking about his own experience, not interpreting David’s battle. The shared lesson is dependence on God when personal strength is insufficient. It leaves room for receiving help rather than treating the need for it as failure.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 22:1-7
passages.section_title: Why does David describe God as his rock and refuge?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 And David sang this song to the LORD on the day the LORD had delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul. 2 He said: “The LORD is my rock, my fortress, and my deliverer. 3 My God is my rock, in whom I take refuge, my shield, and the horn of my salvation. My stronghold, my refuge, and my Savior, You save me from violence. 4 I will call upon the LORD, who is worthy to be praised; so shall I be saved from my enemies. 5 For the waves of death engulfed me; the torrents of chaos overwhelmed me. 6 The cords of Sheol entangled me; the snares of death confronted me. 7 In my distress I called upon the LORD; I cried out to my God. And from His temple He heard my voice, and my cry for help reached His ears.
paragraphs: 1 And David sang this song to the LORD on the day the LORD had delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul. 2 He said: “The LORD is my rock, my fortress, and my deliverer. 3 My God is my rock, in whom I take refuge, my shield, and the horn of my salvation. My stronghold, my refuge, and my Savior, You save me from violence. 4 I will call upon the LORD, who is worthy to be praised; so shall I be saved from my enemies.

5 For the waves of death engulfed me; the torrents of chaos overwhelmed me. 6 The cords of Sheol entangled me; the snares of death confronted me. 7 In my distress I called upon the LORD; I cried out to my God. And from His temple He heard my voice, and my cry for help reached His ears.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The narrative pauses for David’s song of deliverance. A closely related version appears as Psalm 18. David looks back on rescue from his enemies, naming Saul in particular, and addresses his thanks to the LORD.

The opening pictures gather around safety: rock, fortress, shield, stronghold and refuge. David’s confidence is personal. He has known danger and has come to depend on God for deliverance.

He describes that danger as overwhelming water and the cords and snares of death. In distress he cries to God, and his cry is heard. The thanksgiving remembers both the fear of the crisis and the help that followed.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads the chapter as thanksgiving that names particular acts of God’s mercy. Remembering the rescue gives shape to the praise.

Gill, commenting on the matching words in Psalm 18:6, understands God’s temple here as His heavenly dwelling. The reference does not require Solomon’s later temple to have already been built.

The language of refuge helps the reader hear what rescue meant to David. His praise grows out of distress he actually experienced, rather than denying that he had been afraid.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 22:8-20
passages.section_title: What does the storm picture tell us about God’s rescue?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 Then the earth shook and quaked; the foundations of the heavens trembled; they were shaken because He burned with anger. 9 Smoke rose from His nostrils, and consuming fire came from His mouth; glowing coals blazed forth. 10 He parted the heavens and came down with dark clouds beneath His feet. 11 He mounted a cherub and flew; He soared on the wings of the wind. 12 He made darkness a canopy around Him, a gathering of water and thick clouds. 13 From the brightness of His presence coals of fire blazed forth. 14 The LORD thundered from heaven; the voice of the Most High resounded. 15 He shot His arrows and scattered the foes; He hurled lightning and routed them. 16 The channels of the sea appeared, and the foundations of the world were exposed at the rebuke of the LORD, at the blast of the breath of His nostrils. 17 He reached down from on high and took hold of me; He drew me out of deep waters. 18 He rescued me from my powerful enemy, from foes too mighty for me. 19 They confronted me in my day of calamity, but the LORD was my support. 20 He brought me out into the open; He rescued me because He delighted in me.

13 From the brightness of His presence coals of fire blazed forth. 14 The LORD thundered from heaven; the voice of the Most High resounded. 15 He shot His arrows and scattered the foes; He hurled lightning and routed them. 16 The channels of the sea appeared, and the foundations of the world were exposed at the rebuke of the LORD, at the blast of the breath of His nostrils.

17 He reached down from on high and took hold of me; He drew me out of deep waters. 18 He rescued me from my powerful enemy, from foes too mighty for me. 19 They confronted me in my day of calamity, but the LORD was my support. 20 He brought me out into the open; He rescued me because He delighted in me.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The song moves from David’s cry to a powerful picture of God’s response. Earth and heaven shake. Fire, darkness, wind, thunder and lightning accompany His coming. Even the sea’s channels and the world’s foundations are exposed.

Then the picture becomes close and personal: God reaches down, takes hold of David and draws him out of deep waters. His enemies were too strong for him, but the LORD supported him and brought him into the open.

The scene expresses the greatness of the Rescuer and David’s inability to save himself. The One whose power shakes creation also takes hold of a person in danger.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The USCCB notes read the storm scene as a poetic portrayal of God coming to David’s aid. The thunder, clouds and shaking earth communicate the power of His intervention.

The song itself connects these images to rescue from human enemies in verses 17–19. It does not identify a separate occasion when David literally saw every detail of the scene. Poetry gives voice to the meaning of the deliverance.
passages.god_plan_html:
The picture recalls God’s earlier rescue of Israel. In Exodus 14:21–31, the sea is driven back, dry ground appears and the people are saved from an enemy they could not defeat alone.

The shaking, smoke and thunder also recall God’s coming at Sinai in Exodus 19:16–19. These are parallels in the language and events: the God David praises is the God who delivered Israel and made Himself known to them.

David’s personal rescue thus sits within the larger story of God caring for His people. His experience becomes another occasion to remember the LORD’s power and faithfulness.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 22:21-30
passages.section_title: How should we understand David’s claim to clean hands?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 The LORD has rewarded me according to my righteousness; He has repaid me according to the cleanness of my hands. 22 For I have kept the ways of the LORD and have not wickedly departed from my God. 23 For all His ordinances are before me; I have not disregarded His statutes. 24 And I have been blameless before Him and kept myself from iniquity. 25 So the LORD has repaid me according to my righteousness, according to my cleanness in His sight. 26 To the faithful You show Yourself faithful, to the blameless You show Yourself blameless; 27 to the pure You show Yourself pure, but to the crooked You show Yourself shrewd. 28 You save an afflicted people, but Your eyes are on the haughty to bring them down. 29 For You, O LORD, are my lamp; the LORD lights up my darkness. 30 For in You I can charge an army; with my God I can scale a wall.
paragraphs: 21 The LORD has rewarded me according to my righteousness; He has repaid me according to the cleanness of my hands. 22 For I have kept the ways of the LORD and have not wickedly departed from my God. 23 For all His ordinances are before me; I have not disregarded His statutes. 24 And I have been blameless before Him and kept myself from iniquity. 25 So the LORD has repaid me according to my righteousness, according to my cleanness in His sight.

26 To the faithful You show Yourself faithful, to the blameless You show Yourself blameless; 27 to the pure You show Yourself pure, but to the crooked You show Yourself shrewd. 28 You save an afflicted people, but Your eyes are on the haughty to bring them down. 29 For You, O LORD, are my lamp; the LORD lights up my darkness. 30 For in You I can charge an army; with my God I can scale a wall.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
David says that the LORD has rewarded him according to his righteousness and the cleanness of his hands. He speaks of keeping God’s ways, attending to His commands and turning from wrongdoing.

The song then describes God’s dealings with the faithful, the pure and the crooked. God saves afflicted people and brings down the proud. David calls the LORD his lamp and credits Him with strength to face an army or scale a wall.

These statements belong beside the rest of Samuel’s account of David. The same book records his grave wrongdoing, Nathan’s rebuke and David’s confession. His words here need to be understood within that fuller picture.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Gill, on Psalm 18:20, understands David’s clean hands in relation to the accusations and persecution he faced, especially his refusal to kill Saul when he had the chance. On this reading, David is speaking of the rightness of his cause rather than claiming a sinless life.

Gill also reads the language more fully in relation to Christ, whose obedience is complete. That is his further reading of the song; it should be distinguished from what the narrative records about David himself.

Verses 26–30 keep attention on God’s response to human conduct and on the help David receives. The king who speaks of obedience still depends on God for light and strength.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 22:31-46
passages.section_title: Who gives David the strength to win?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 31 As for God, His way is perfect; the word of the LORD is flawless. He is a shield to all who take refuge in Him. 32 For who is God besides the LORD? And who is the Rock except our God? 33 God is my strong fortress, and He makes my way clear. 34 He makes my feet like those of a deer and stations me upon the heights. 35 He trains my hands for battle; my arms can bend a bow of bronze. 36 You have given me Your shield of salvation, and Your gentleness exalts me. 37 You broaden the path beneath me so that my ankles do not give way. 38 I pursued my enemies and destroyed them; I did not turn back until they were consumed. 39 I devoured and crushed them so they could not rise; they have fallen under my feet. 40 You have armed me with strength for battle; You have subdued my foes beneath me. 41 You have made my enemies retreat before me; I destroyed those who hated me. 42 They looked, but there was no one to save them— to the LORD, but He did not answer. 43 I ground them as the dust of the earth; I crushed and trampled them like mud in the streets. 44 You have delivered me from the strife of my people; You have preserved me as the head of nations; a people I had not known shall serve me. 45 Foreigners cower before me; when they hear me, they obey me. 46 Foreigners lose heart and come trembling from their strongholds.

And who is the Rock except our God? 33 God is my strong fortress, and He makes my way clear. 34 He makes my feet like those of a deer and stations me upon the heights. 35 He trains my hands for battle; my arms can bend a bow of bronze. 36 You have given me Your shield of salvation, and Your gentleness exalts me. 37 You broaden the path beneath me so that my ankles do not give way.

38 I pursued my enemies and destroyed them; I did not turn back until they were consumed. 39 I devoured and crushed them so they could not rise; they have fallen under my feet. 40 You have armed me with strength for battle; You have subdued my foes beneath me. 41 You have made my enemies retreat before me; I destroyed those who hated me. 42 They looked, but there was no one to save them— to the LORD, but He did not answer. 43 I ground them as the dust of the earth; I crushed and trampled them like mud in the streets.

44 You have delivered me from the strife of my people; You have preserved me as the head of nations; a people I had not known shall serve me. 45 Foreigners cower before me; when they hear me, they obey me. 46 Foreigners lose heart and come trembling from their strongholds.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
David praises God’s perfect way and flawless word. He describes God as his fortress, the One who gives him sure footing, trains his hands and shields him. Even David’s greatness is credited to God’s gentleness.

The next lines recount the defeat of enemies in forceful language. David pursues, crushes and puts them to flight. Yet he repeatedly names God as the source of the strength and success.

The song also remembers conflict among David’s own people and his authority over other nations. Foreigners submit and emerge trembling from their strongholds. This is the victory song of Israel’s king after real conflict.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Gill, on Psalm 18:32, understands the secure way God gives David as protection and success in his path, rather than a claim that every act of his life was morally perfect.

On Psalm 18:35, Gill emphasizes God’s goodness in raising David from a low position. The king’s strength and standing are received gifts. Henry likewise sees the song as returning the glory for deliverance to God.

The strong language about defeated enemies should be read in its setting. David is recounting royal warfare, with God receiving the credit for his victories.
passages.god_plan_html:
The broader lesson of strength received from God also appears in Ephesians 6:10–18. Paul tells believers to be strong in the Lord and describes the protection God supplies through truth, righteousness, faith, salvation and His word.

The distinction is important: Paul says the struggle is not against flesh and blood. The Christian response he describes includes standing firm, prayer and readiness with the gospel of peace.

The shared dependence on God carries forward, while the New Testament identifies the kind of struggle and faithfulness required of Christ’s people. David’s battle song is not an instruction to attack people who oppose us.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 22:47-51
passages.section_title: Why does David’s praise reach beyond Israel?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 47 The LORD lives, and blessed be my Rock! And may God, the Rock of my salvation, be exalted— 48 the God who avenges me and brings down nations beneath me, 49 who frees me from my enemies. You exalt me above my foes; You rescue me from violent men. 50 Therefore I will praise You, O LORD, among the nations; I will sing praises to Your name. 51 Great salvation He brings to His king. He shows loving devotion to His anointed, to David and his descendants forever.”
paragraphs: 47 The LORD lives, and blessed be my Rock! And may God, the Rock of my salvation, be exalted— 48 the God who avenges me and brings down nations beneath me, 49 who frees me from my enemies. You exalt me above my foes; You rescue me from violent men.

50 Therefore I will praise You, O LORD, among the nations; I will sing praises to Your name. 51 Great salvation He brings to His king. He shows loving devotion to His anointed, to David and his descendants forever.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The song closes by blessing the living LORD, the Rock who rescues David and gives him victory. David promises to praise Him among the nations.

The final line remembers God’s loving devotion to His anointed king, David, and to his descendants forever. Loving devotion translates hesed, pronounced KHEH-sed. Brown–Driver–Briggs gives the central meaning as goodness or kindness. Here it describes God’s faithful care for David and his line.

The ending looks back to the promise of an enduring house and kingdom in 2 Samuel 7:12–16. David’s thanksgiving reaches beyond one rescue and one lifetime.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Gill, on Psalm 18:49–50, reads the praise as public acknowledgment that David’s victories came from God. He also connects the closing promise to the Messiah descended from David.

Henry similarly understands the song’s ultimate hope as reaching the Redeemer. These readings preserve the thanksgiving of David while looking beyond the limits of his reign.
passages.god_plan_html:
The New Testament itself takes up this song. In Romans 15:7–13, Paul quotes its promise of praise among the nations, also found in Psalm 18:49, as part of his explanation that Gentiles glorify God for His mercy.

Paul places that praise alongside God’s faithfulness to His promises and the hope of people from the nations in the Root of Jesse. The movement is wider than conquered nations acknowledging David’s power: people from the nations come to share in praise and hope through Christ.

That is an explicit New Testament connection. David’s song becomes part of Paul’s call for believers to welcome one another and glorify God together.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 23:1-7
passages.section_title: What hope does David express in his last words?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 These are the last words of David: “The oracle of David son of Jesse, the oracle of the man raised on high, the one anointed by the God of Jacob, and the sweet psalmist of Israel: 2 The Spirit of the LORD spoke through me; His word was on my tongue. 3 The God of Israel spoke; the Rock of Israel said to me, ‘He who rules the people with justice, who rules in the fear of God, 4 is like the light of the morning at sunrise of a cloudless dawn, the glistening after the rain on the sprouting grass of the earth.’ 5 Is not my house right with God? For He has established with me an everlasting covenant, ordered and secured in every part. Will He not bring about my full salvation and my every desire? 6 But the worthless are all like thorns raked aside, for they can never be gathered by hand. 7 The man who touches them must be armed with iron or with the shaft of a spear. The fire burns them to ashes in the place where they lie.”
paragraphs: 1 These are the last words of David: “The oracle of David son of Jesse, the oracle of the man raised on high, the one anointed by the God of Jacob, and the sweet psalmist of Israel: 2 The Spirit of the LORD spoke through me; His word was on my tongue. 3 The God of Israel spoke; the Rock of Israel said to me, ‘He who rules the people with justice, who rules in the fear of God, 4 is like the light of the morning at sunrise of a cloudless dawn, the glistening after the rain on the sprouting grass of the earth.’

5 Is not my house right with God? For He has established with me an everlasting covenant, ordered and secured in every part. Will He not bring about my full salvation and my every desire? 6 But the worthless are all like thorns raked aside, for they can never be gathered by hand. 7 The man who touches them must be armed with iron or with the shaft of a spear. The fire burns them to ashes in the place where they lie.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
David’s last words are introduced as an oracle. The Hebrew word is neum, pronounced neh-OOM. Brown–Driver–Briggs describes it as an utterance or declaration and explicitly includes this verse. David says that the Spirit of the LORD spoke through him.

The message describes a ruler who acts with justice and in the fear of God. Such rule is compared to a clear sunrise and the brightness after rain on growing grass. Right government is a blessing to the people under it.

David then speaks of God’s everlasting covenant with his house. His confidence rests on that ordered and secure promise. The closing picture contrasts this hope with the wicked, who are like harmful thorns gathered for burning.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands last words as David’s final inspired testimony, rather than the last sounds he ever spoke. He takes the description of just rule as instruction about a king’s duties toward God and people.

Gill also sees instruction for rulers, including Solomon, and reads its fullest expression in the Messiah. The duties of a present king and the hope of a greater King need not be separated into competing readings.

Verse 5 has been worded differently in English translations. The older wording followed by Wesley and Gill begins by acknowledging the shortcomings of David’s house; the BSB presents a question expressing confidence in its standing with God. In their comments, both writers place David’s hope in God’s covenant despite the failures within his family.
passages.god_plan_html:
The hope of righteous rule and an enduring house reaches beyond David’s own achievements. Jeremiah 23:5–6 promises a righteous Branch raised up for David, a King who will act wisely and administer justice.

Luke 1:32–33 identifies Jesus as the Son who receives David’s throne and whose kingdom has no end. These passages help place David’s confidence within the larger promise of a lasting, righteous King.

This connection rests on the promises Scripture gives. It does not require treating David’s own reign as flawless or making every detail of the morning picture a separate prediction.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 23:8-12
passages.section_title: Why are these three warriors remembered?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 These are the names of David’s mighty men: Josheb-basshebeth the Tahchemonite was chief of the Three. He wielded his spear against eight hundred men, whom he killed at one time. 9 Next in command was Eleazar son of Dodo the Ahohite. As one of the three mighty men, he went with David to taunt the Philistines who had gathered for battle at Pas-dammim. The men of Israel retreated, 10 but Eleazar stood his ground and struck the Philistines until his hand grew weary and stuck to his sword. The LORD brought about a great victory that day. Then the troops returned to him, but only to plunder the dead. 11 And after him was Shammah son of Agee the Hararite. When the Philistines had banded together near a field full of lentils, Israel’s troops fled from them. 12 But Shammah took his stand in the middle of the field, defended it, and struck down the Philistines. So the LORD brought about a great victory.

He wielded his spear against eight hundred men, whom he killed at one time. 9 Next in command was Eleazar son of Dodo the Ahohite. As one of the three mighty men, he went with David to taunt the Philistines who had gathered for battle at Pas-dammim. The men of Israel retreated, 10 but Eleazar stood his ground and struck the Philistines until his hand grew weary and stuck to his sword. The LORD brought about a great victory that day. Then the troops returned to him, but only to plunder the dead.

When the Philistines had banded together near a field full of lentils, Israel’s troops fled from them. 12 But Shammah took his stand in the middle of the field, defended it, and struck down the Philistines. So the LORD brought about a great victory.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The chapter turns from David’s oracle to accounts of the men who served with him. Josheb-basshebeth is named chief of the Three and remembered for a great victory against eight hundred men.

Eleazar stands his ground with David when Israel’s troops retreat. He fights until his hand is weary and sticks to his sword. The troops return afterward to take the spoil.

Shammah likewise defends a field of lentils when others flee. In both accounts, the narrator explicitly credits the LORD with bringing about the victory. The men’s courage is remembered alongside God’s help.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley emphasizes the repeated statement about the LORD’s victory. The warriors truly fight, but the praise for the outcome belongs to God.

That balance shapes the account: it neither erases the men’s actions nor credits their strength alone. Their names and deeds are preserved because their service mattered in David’s kingdom.
