passages.title: 2 Samuel 23:13-17
passages.section_title: Why does David pour out the water his men bring him?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 At harvest time, three of the thirty chief men went down to David at the cave of Adullam, while a company of Philistines was encamped in the Valley of Rephaim. 14 At that time David was in the stronghold, and the garrison of the Philistines was at Bethlehem. 15 David longed for water and said, “Oh, that someone would get me a drink of water from the well near the gate of Bethlehem!” 16 So the three mighty men broke through the Philistine camp, drew water from the well near the gate of Bethlehem, and brought it back to David. But he refused to drink it; instead, he poured it out to the LORD, 17 saying, “Far be it from me, O LORD, to do this! Is this not the blood of the men who risked their lives?” So he refused to drink it. Such were the exploits of the three mighty men.
paragraphs: 13 At harvest time, three of the thirty chief men went down to David at the cave of Adullam, while a company of Philistines was encamped in the Valley of Rephaim. 14 At that time David was in the stronghold, and the garrison of the Philistines was at Bethlehem. 15 David longed for water and said, “Oh, that someone would get me a drink of water from the well near the gate of Bethlehem!”

16 So the three mighty men broke through the Philistine camp, drew water from the well near the gate of Bethlehem, and brought it back to David. But he refused to drink it; instead, he poured it out to the LORD, 17 saying, “Far be it from me, O LORD, to do this! Is this not the blood of the men who risked their lives?” So he refused to drink it. Such were the exploits of the three mighty men.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Three men come to David at the cave of Adullam while the Philistines occupy Bethlehem. David longs for a drink from the well near Bethlehem’s gate.

The three break through the Philistine camp, draw the water and bring it back. David refuses to drink it. He sees the water in terms of the lives they risked and pours it out to the LORD.

What began as a longing for water becomes an act of worship. The men’s costly loyalty and David’s recognition of its cost are both remembered.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands David’s words as a wish rather than an order that his men risk their lives. He reads the refusal to drink as David refusing to put his own appetite above their lives.

Henry is more critical of the original longing, seeing a careless desire David corrects by denying himself. He also draws attention to the men’s readiness to serve.

The pouring out honors the value of what was brought. It does not mean the men’s lives or their effort were unimportant to David.
passages.god_plan_html:
A useful comparison appears in Mark 14:3–9, where a woman pours expensive perfume on Jesus. Others call it waste, but Jesus recognizes its value and says her deed will be remembered.

The circumstances differ: David pours out water because of the lives risked to obtain it; Jesus receives an act that prepares His body for burial. The parallel is costly devotion being recognized and remembered.

This is a comparison between the accounts, rather than a claim that Mark identifies the water as a prediction. It invites readers to consider the value of devotion beyond its price or immediate practical use.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 23:18-23
passages.section_title: How are Abishai and Benaiah honored for their service?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 Now Abishai, the brother of Joab and son of Zeruiah, was chief of the Three, and he wielded his spear against three hundred men, killed them, and won a name along with the Three. 19 Was he not more honored than the Three? And he became their commander, even though he was not included among the Three. 20 And Benaiah son of Jehoiada was a man of valor from Kabzeel, a man of many exploits. He struck down two champions of Moab, and on a snowy day he went down into a pit and killed a lion. 21 He also struck down an Egyptian, a huge man. Although the Egyptian had a spear in his hand, Benaiah went against him with a club, snatched the spear from his hand, and killed the Egyptian with his own spear. 22 These were the exploits of Benaiah son of Jehoiada, who won a name along with the three mighty men. 23 He was most honored among the Thirty, but he did not become one of the Three. And David appointed him over his guard.

And he became their commander, even though he was not included among the Three.

He struck down two champions of Moab, and on a snowy day he went down into a pit and killed a lion. 21 He also struck down an Egyptian, a huge man. Although the Egyptian had a spear in his hand, Benaiah went against him with a club, snatched the spear from his hand, and killed the Egyptian with his own spear. 22 These were the exploits of Benaiah son of Jehoiada, who won a name along with the three mighty men. 23 He was most honored among the Thirty, but he did not become one of the Three. And David appointed him over his guard.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Abishai is remembered for killing three hundred men and becoming a commander, while remaining distinct from the Three previously named. His reputation and position are recorded together.

Benaiah is remembered for overcoming two Moabite champions, killing a lion in a pit on a snowy day and defeating an Egyptian with the man’s own spear. David appoints him over his guard.

The account recognizes both men’s achievements without making them identical. Each has a name, a record of service and a particular responsibility.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Gill distinguishes the first group of three from the men discussed afterward. He understands Benaiah’s appointment as command of David’s bodyguard.

Wesley likewise reads the distinctions as differences in military honor and ability. The text remembers more than one level of recognition within the group of warriors.

The passage gives the basis for their reputation in concrete deeds. It does not supply a complete chart explaining every rank in the army.
passages.god_plan_html:
Recognition of faithful service also appears in Jesus’ parable in Luke 19:11–27. A returning ruler calls his servants to account, and faithful servants receive further responsibility.

That offers a limited comparison with David recognizing men who served and entrusting them with command. The larger biblical lesson is that service matters to the King and carries responsibility.

Luke does not present David’s military list as a map of future offices. The comparison encourages faithfulness without turning each warrior’s place into a prediction about a Christian’s rank.

passages.section_title: Why does this list of names matter?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The chapter preserves the names and origins of more men who served with David. Most receive no account of an individual exploit here, but they are still included in the record of the Thirty.

Asahel appears near the beginning of the list, and Uriah the Hittite stands at its end. Both have already died in the narrative. The list looks back across David’s years of leadership rather than describing only the men alive at one final gathering.

Its closing total is thirty-seven. Behind the larger story of David’s reign are many people whose service the narrator does not leave unnamed.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley points to Asahel and Uriah as evidence that the list reaches back to earlier service. He also notes that the related list in 1 Chronicles 11 contains differences and additional names.

Gill identifies the final Uriah as Bathsheba’s husband. That name recalls the painful contrast between Uriah’s faithful service in chapter 11 and David’s treatment of him.

Remembering these men adds depth to the story of the kingdom. Its achievements belong to many servants, and its record includes people whom the king himself failed.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 24:1-9
passages.section_title: Why does David insist on counting the troops?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Again the anger of the LORD burned against Israel, and He stirred up David against them, saying, “Go and take a census of Israel and Judah.” 2 So the king said to Joab the commander of his army, who was with him, “Go now throughout the tribes of Israel from Dan to Beersheba and register the troops, so that I may know their number.” 3 But Joab replied to the king, “May the LORD your God multiply the troops a hundred times over, and may the eyes of my lord the king see it. But why does my lord the king want to do such a thing?” 4 Nevertheless, the king’s word prevailed against Joab and against the commanders of the army. So Joab and the commanders of the army departed from the presence of the king to register the troops of Israel. 5 They crossed the Jordan and camped near Aroer, south of the town in the middle of the valley, and proceeded toward Gad and Jazer. 6 Then they went to Gilead and the land of Tahtim-hodshi, and on to Dan-jaan and around to Sidon. 7 They went toward the fortress of Tyre and all the cities of the Hivites and Canaanites. Finally, they went on to the Negev of Judah, to Beersheba. 8 At the end of nine months and twenty days, having gone through the whole land, they returned to Jerusalem. 9 And Joab reported to the king the total number of the troops. In Israel there were 800,000 men of valor who drew the sword, and in Judah there were 500,000.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The final chapter opens with the LORD’s anger against Israel and David being stirred to take a census. The reason for the anger against Israel is not specified. David orders Joab to register the troops throughout the land.

Joab wishes that God would multiply the people but questions why David wants the count. The king overrules him and the commanders. They travel through the land and return after nine months and twenty days.

The report gives eight hundred thousand men of valor in Israel and five hundred thousand in Judah. The following verses show David recognizing the census as a serious wrong.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry understands David’s sin as pride and reliance on military strength. This reading focuses on the confidence behind the count, rather than treating every census as forbidden.

The USCCB notes place another emphasis on royal power: a count equips a king to impose demands on the people. The people belong to God, and royal control over them has limits. This is an explanation of the census’s significance, rather than a motive David explicitly states.

Gill reads the opening alongside 1 Chronicles 21:1, which names Satan as the one inciting David. Henry describes David as being left to act wrongly under God’s judgment. These readings distinguish God’s rule over events from David’s responsibility for the act.

James 1:13–15 also matters when reading this difficult opening: God does not tempt anyone to evil, and people are accountable for the desires that lead them into sin.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 24:10-14
passages.section_title: Where does David turn when his conscience troubles him?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 After David had numbered the troops, his conscience was stricken and he said to the LORD, “I have sinned greatly in what I have done. Now, O LORD, I beg You to take away the iniquity of Your servant, for I have acted very foolishly.” 11 When David got up in the morning, the word of the LORD had come to Gad the prophet, David’s seer: 12 “Go and tell David that this is what the LORD says: ‘I am offering you three options. Choose one of them, and I will carry it out against you.’” 13 So Gad went and said to David, “Do you choose to endure three years of famine in your land, three months of fleeing the pursuit of your enemies, or three days of plague upon your land? Now then, think it over and decide how I should reply to Him who sent me.” 14 David answered Gad, “I am deeply distressed. Please, let us fall into the hand of the LORD, for His mercies are great; but do not let me fall into the hands of men.”

Now, O LORD, I beg You to take away the iniquity of Your servant, for I have acted very foolishly.” 11 When David got up in the morning, the word of the LORD had come to Gad the prophet, David’s seer: 12 “Go and tell David that this is what the LORD says: ‘I am offering you three options. Choose one of them, and I will carry it out against you.’”

13 So Gad went and said to David, “Do you choose to endure three years of famine in your land, three months of fleeing the pursuit of your enemies, or three days of plague upon your land? Now then, think it over and decide how I should reply to Him who sent me.” 14 David answered Gad, “I am deeply distressed. Please, let us fall into the hand of the LORD, for His mercies are great; but do not let me fall into the hands of men.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the count, David’s conscience is stricken. He confesses that he has sinned greatly and acted foolishly, and asks the LORD to take away his guilt.

God sends the prophet Gad with three choices: three years of famine, three months fleeing enemies or three days of plague. David is deeply distressed and asks to fall into the LORD’s hand because His mercies are great, rather than into human hands.

Confession does not make the consequences disappear. Yet David’s response turns from insisting on his own decision to depending on God’s mercy.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry emphasizes both awakened conscience and trust in mercy. He understands David’s choice as placing him under the same danger as the people, rather than choosing a hardship from which a king might shelter himself.

Gill likewise understands the plague as David’s choice from his words and the event that follows, although David does not expressly name that option. The clearest reason he states is his confidence in the LORD’s great mercy.
passages.god_plan_html:
David’s confession connects with the wider biblical call to acknowledge sin honestly before God. In 1 John 1:8–10, denying sin is self-deception; confession meets God’s faithfulness and forgiveness.

That passage gives Christian readers grounds for coming into the light rather than hiding their wrongdoing. David’s story also reminds us that forgiveness and the removal of every earthly consequence are different things.

The connection is confession and dependence on mercy. Samuel’s account of David receiving three choices does not promise that everyone will be offered a choice of consequences.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 24:15-17
passages.section_title: What does David ask when he sees the people suffering?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 So the LORD sent a plague upon Israel from that morning until the appointed time, and seventy thousand of the people from Dan to Beersheba died. 16 But when the angel stretched out his hand to destroy Jerusalem, the LORD relented from the calamity and said to the angel who was destroying the people, “Enough! Withdraw your hand now!” At that time the angel of the LORD was by the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite. 17 When David saw the angel striking down the people, he said to the LORD, “Surely I, the shepherd, have sinned and acted wickedly. But these sheep, what have they done? Please, let Your hand fall upon me and my father’s house.”
paragraphs: 15 So the LORD sent a plague upon Israel from that morning until the appointed time, and seventy thousand of the people from Dan to Beersheba died. 16 But when the angel stretched out his hand to destroy Jerusalem, the LORD relented from the calamity and said to the angel who was destroying the people, “Enough! Withdraw your hand now!” At that time the angel of the LORD was by the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite. 17 When David saw the angel striking down the people, he said to the LORD, “Surely I, the shepherd, have sinned and acted wickedly. But these sheep, what have they done? Please, let Your hand fall upon me and my father’s house.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The plague kills seventy thousand people across Israel. As the angel stretches out his hand toward Jerusalem, the LORD stops the destruction. The angel is beside Araunah’s threshing floor.

The Hebrew verb behind relented is naham, pronounced nah-KHAHM. Brown–Driver–Briggs includes this verse among uses concerning calamity brought on others. In the account, the LORD’s response is made clear by His command to withdraw the destroying hand.

David then appeals to the LORD, identifying himself as the shepherd who sinned and the people as sheep. He asks that the judgment fall on him and his father’s house. The king takes responsibility and pleads for the people under his care.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry understands the LORD’s relenting as a change in the judgment being carried out, rather than God repenting of moral wrongdoing. The narrative presents mercy in the midst of severe judgment.

Gill reads David’s appeal as an expression of affection and sympathy for his people. David is absorbed with his own guilt. The opening verse also speaks of anger against Israel, so his question about the sheep should be heard as his plea, rather than a complete explanation of every person’s standing before God.
passages.god_plan_html:
Henry and Gill both see a shepherd comparison here. David is willing to bear the consequence rather than see his people destroyed. In John 10:11–18, Jesus identifies Himself as the good shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep.

The difference gives the comparison its force. David is confessing his own wrongdoing and asking to bear judgment; Jesus gives His life for others. 1 Peter 2:21–24 describes Him as without sin and as bearing our sins.

This is a supported parallel between shepherds, not a claim that John directly identifies David’s prayer as a prediction. It directs hope beyond the failure of an earthly shepherd to the saving work of Christ.

passages.title: 2 Samuel 24:18-25
passages.section_title: Why does David insist on paying for the altar site?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 And that day Gad came to David and said to him, “Go up and build an altar to the LORD on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.” 19 So David went up at the word of Gad, just as the LORD had commanded. 20 When Araunah looked out and saw the king and his servants coming toward him, he went out and bowed facedown before the king. 21 “Why has my lord the king come to his servant?” Araunah said. “To buy your threshing floor,” David replied, “that I may build an altar to the LORD, so that the plague upon the people may be halted.” 22 Araunah said to David, “May my lord the king take whatever seems good to him and offer it up. Here are the oxen for a burnt offering and the threshing sledges and ox yokes for the wood. 23 O king, Araunah gives all these to the king.” He also said to the king, “May the LORD your God accept you.” 24 “No,” replied the king, “I insist on paying a price, for I will not offer to the LORD my God burnt offerings that cost me nothing.” So David bought the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver. 25 And there he built an altar to the LORD and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings. Then the LORD answered the prayers on behalf of the land, and the plague upon Israel was halted.

22 Araunah said to David, “May my lord the king take whatever seems good to him and offer it up. Here are the oxen for a burnt offering and the threshing sledges and ox yokes for the wood. 23 O king, Araunah gives all these to the king.” He also said to the king, “May the LORD your God accept you.” 24 “No,” replied the king, “I insist on paying a price, for I will not offer to the LORD my God burnt offerings that cost me nothing.” So David bought the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver. 25 And there he built an altar to the LORD and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings. Then the LORD answered the prayers on behalf of the land, and the plague upon Israel was halted.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Gad instructs David to build an altar on Araunah’s threshing floor. David goes in obedience to the LORD’s command and explains that he wants to buy the place so that the plague may be halted.

Araunah offers the ground, oxen and equipment for the offering. David insists on paying: he will not present burnt offerings to the LORD that cost him nothing. He buys the threshing floor and oxen for fifty shekels of silver.

He builds the altar and offers burnt offerings and peace offerings. God answers the prayers for the land, and the plague is halted. The book ends with judgment restrained and worship offered in response to God’s instruction.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry understands David’s refusal as a matter of honoring God with his own resources. Gill likewise sees a willing cost in David’s worship. The point is personal participation, rather than passing the whole burden to someone else.

The price differs from 1 Chronicles 21:25, which records six hundred shekels of gold for the site. Gill proposes that the larger sum concerns a wider purchase, while Samuel concerns the threshing floor and oxen. That is a proposed explanation; neither account gives a separate description confirming two transactions.

Samuel’s emphasis is clear even with that question remaining: David obeys, pays for what he offers and seeks the LORD on behalf of the land.
passages.god_plan_html:
The site has a stated place in the next stage of Israel’s worship. 2 Chronicles 3:1 identifies Solomon’s temple site on Mount Moriah with the threshing floor prepared by David.

The larger story of sacrifice then reaches Christ. Hebrews 9:11–14, 24–28 explains that Jesus offers Himself once for all and enters God’s presence on our behalf. The connection is the biblical movement from sanctuary and repeated sacrifice to His completed offering.

David’s altar prepares ground for the temple; it is not itself the final answer to human sin. The book’s closing scene of mercy, sacrifice and answered prayer belongs within that larger hope.

passages.title: 1 Kings 1:1-4
passages.section_title: Why is Abishag brought to care for David?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now King David was old and well along in years, and though they covered him with blankets, he could not keep warm. 2 So his servants said to him, “Let us search for a young virgin for our lord the king, to attend to him and care for him and lie by his side to keep him warm.” 3 Then they searched throughout Israel for a beautiful girl, and they found Abishag the Shunammite and brought her to the king. 4 The girl was unsurpassed in beauty; she cared for the king and served him, but he had no relations with her.
paragraphs: 1 Now King David was old and well along in years, and though they covered him with blankets, he could not keep warm. 2 So his servants said to him, “Let us search for a young virgin for our lord the king, to attend to him and care for him and lie by his side to keep him warm.” 3 Then they searched throughout Israel for a beautiful girl, and they found Abishag the Shunammite and brought her to the king. 4 The girl was unsurpassed in beauty; she cared for the king and served him, but he had no relations with her.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Kings begins with David still on the throne but physically weak. Even under blankets he cannot keep warm. His servants seek a young woman to attend him and lie beside him for warmth.

Abishag the Shunammite is brought to him and cares for him. The narrator expressly says that David has no sexual relations with her. The scene establishes the king’s frailty before turning to the question of who will succeed him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill understand Abishag’s place in the household as that of a wife, while recognizing that the relationship is not consummated. Their reading also looks ahead to the dispute over marrying her in chapter 2.

The present account emphasizes her care and David’s weakness. It names no particular disease and gives no marriage ceremony. Those details should be distinguished from the explanations readers may draw from the wider story.

passages.title: 1 Kings 1:5-10
passages.section_title: How does Adonijah try to make himself king?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 At that time Adonijah, David’s son by Haggith, began to exalt himself, saying, “I will be king!” And he acquired chariots and horsemen and fifty men to run ahead of him. 6 (His father had never once reprimanded him by saying, “Why do you act this way?” Adonijah was also very handsome, born next after Absalom.) 7 So Adonijah conferred with Joab son of Zeruiah and with Abiathar the priest, who supported him. 8 But Zadok the priest, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, Nathan the prophet, Shimei, Rei, and David’s mighty men would not join Adonijah. 9 And Adonijah sacrificed sheep, oxen, and fattened calves near the stone of Zoheleth, which is next to En-rogel. He invited all his royal brothers and all the men of Judah who were servants of the king. 10 But he did not invite Nathan the prophet, Benaiah, the mighty men, or his brother Solomon.
paragraphs: 5 At that time Adonijah, David’s son by Haggith, began to exalt himself, saying, “I will be king!” And he acquired chariots and horsemen and fifty men to run ahead of him. 6 (His father had never once reprimanded him by saying, “Why do you act this way?” Adonijah was also very handsome, born next after Absalom.) 7 So Adonijah conferred with Joab son of Zeruiah and with Abiathar the priest, who supported him. 8 But Zadok the priest, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, Nathan the prophet, Shimei, Rei, and David’s mighty men would not join Adonijah.

9 And Adonijah sacrificed sheep, oxen, and fattened calves near the stone of Zoheleth, which is next to En-rogel. He invited all his royal brothers and all the men of Judah who were servants of the king. 10 But he did not invite Nathan the prophet, Benaiah, the mighty men, or his brother Solomon.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Adonijah, David’s son by Haggith, declares that he will be king. He gathers chariots, horsemen and fifty runners, recalling Absalom’s earlier display in 2 Samuel 15:1.

The narrator notes that David has never reprimanded him. Adonijah is handsome and was born after Absalom. He gains the support of Joab and Abiathar, but Zadok, Benaiah, Nathan and other servants of David do not join him.

Adonijah holds a sacrificial feast near En-rogel and invites the royal sons and the king’s servants from Judah. Solomon and several of David’s leading supporters are left out. A claim to the throne is taking shape without David’s authorization.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley reads the failure to correct Adonijah as David’s serious error and a source of his son’s presumption. The account places that failure beside Adonijah’s confidence and public display.

Wesley gives more than one possible reason for Joab and Abiathar’s support: they may have considered Adonijah entitled to the throne, or may have sought to protect their own interests. The narrative names their support without disclosing all their motives.

The contrast is between Adonijah promoting himself and the decision David has yet to make public. The outward signs of a royal following do not settle who has authority to reign.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Kings 1:11-27
passages.section_title: How do Nathan and Bathsheba bring the danger to David’s attention?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Nathan warns Bathsheba that Adonijah has become king without David knowing. He urges her to act for her own safety and Solomon’s. She is to remind David of his oath that Solomon will succeed him; Nathan will come in and confirm her report.

Bathsheba follows that plan. She describes the feast and Solomon’s exclusion, and says Israel is looking to David to name his successor. If the matter is left unresolved, she fears that she and Solomon will be treated as criminals after David dies.

Nathan then arrives and asks whether David has authorized Adonijah’s rise. His report presses the same question: who is to sit on David’s throne? The king can no longer leave the issue unaddressed.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Gill points out that the earlier oath is confirmed by David himself in verse 30. Its absence from the preceding narrative does not mean Nathan and Bathsheba invent it.

The wider account also identifies Solomon as chosen to succeed David: 1 Chronicles 22:6–10 and 28:4–7 record David’s statements about God’s choice of Solomon.

Henry emphasizes David’s continuing responsibility even as his strength declines. Nathan and Bathsheba’s intervention brings a real danger before him and calls for action on the commitment he has already made.

passages.title: 1 Kings 1:28-40
passages.section_title: How does David make Solomon’s kingship public?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
David recalls the LORD who has redeemed his life from distress and renews his oath to Bathsheba. Solomon will sit on his throne, and David will act that very day.

He orders Zadok, Nathan and Benaiah to take Solomon to Gihon on his own mule. Solomon is to be anointed, proclaimed king and brought back to sit on David’s throne. Benaiah prays that God will be with Solomon and make his throne greater than David’s.

The instructions are carried out. Zadok anoints Solomon, the ram’s horn sounds and the people rejoice loudly. Unlike Adonijah’s self-promotion, this public action carries the reigning king’s express authorization.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill understand the use of David’s own mule as a sign of his consent to Solomon’s succession. The significance lies especially in whose animal it is.

Wesley reads Solomon’s taking the throne while David is alive as delegated rule that becomes sole kingship after David’s death. Henry stresses the people’s joy at Solomon’s elevation.

The scene brings together David’s decision, the priest’s anointing, the prophet’s participation and the people’s welcome. It answers the question that has driven the chapter.
passages.god_plan_html:
This royal entry offers a useful comparison with Jesus entering Jerusalem in Matthew 21:1–11. The people there acclaim Him as the Son of David, and Matthew identifies His coming with the promised gentle King.

The animals are different: Solomon rides David’s mule, while Matthew describes a donkey and her colt. Matthew explicitly connects Jesus’ entry with the prophetic promise he quotes; he does not say that Solomon’s procession is that prophecy.

The parallel concerns the public welcome of a Davidic king. Alongside it stands Luke 1:32–33, which promises Jesus David’s throne and a kingdom without end. Solomon’s succession continues the family line; Jesus is the King whose reign endures.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Kings 1:41-53
passages.section_title: What becomes of Adonijah’s claim to the throne?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The noise reaches Adonijah’s feast. Jonathan, Abiathar’s son, reports that David has made Solomon king. He recounts the anointing, Solomon’s place on the throne and David’s thanksgiving that he has lived to see his successor.

Adonijah’s guests scatter in terror. Adonijah takes hold of the altar’s horns and asks Solomon to swear that he will not put him to death.

Solomon spares him on the condition that he proves a man of character, warning that further evil will bring death. Adonijah is brought down, bows before Solomon and is sent home. The immediate contest ends with Solomon’s authority recognized.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Gill understands Adonijah’s action at the altar as seeking refuge. He notes that the text does not identify exactly which altar is meant.

Gill reads Solomon’s answer as pardon tied to future conduct as a subject. Wesley understands the instruction to go home as a direction to live privately and stop interfering in the kingdom’s affairs.

Adonijah is given his life, but not a share in the throne. His bow acknowledges the king he had tried to displace. The account records that outward submission without claiming to disclose everything in his heart.
passages.god_plan_html:
Solomon’s restraint raises the wider biblical theme of mercy toward people who have opposed the king. The terms of this political pardon are specific to Adonijah’s situation.

God’s mercy in Christ goes further. Ephesians 2:1–9 describes people formerly living in disobedience being made alive with Christ because of God’s great love. Salvation is received by grace through faith as God’s gift.

The comparison helps us recognize mercy without making the two situations identical. Solomon conditions continued safety on Adonijah’s conduct; Paul expressly says that salvation is not earned by works.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Kings 2:1-4
passages.section_title: What does David say Solomon needs most as king?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 As the time drew near for David to die, he charged his son Solomon, 2 “I am about to go the way of all the earth. So be strong and prove yourself a man. 3 And keep the charge of the LORD your God to walk in His ways and to keep His statutes, commandments, ordinances, and decrees, as written in the Law of Moses, so that you may prosper in all you do and wherever you turn, 4 and so that the LORD may fulfill His promise to me: ‘If your descendants take heed to walk faithfully before Me with all their heart and soul, you will never fail to have a man on the throne of Israel.’
paragraphs: 1 As the time drew near for David to die, he charged his son Solomon, 2 “I am about to go the way of all the earth. So be strong and prove yourself a man. 3 And keep the charge of the LORD your God to walk in His ways and to keep His statutes, commandments, ordinances, and decrees, as written in the Law of Moses, so that you may prosper in all you do and wherever you turn, 4 and so that the LORD may fulfill His promise to me: ‘If your descendants take heed to walk faithfully before Me with all their heart and soul, you will never fail to have a man on the throne of Israel.’

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
As death approaches, David charges Solomon to be strong and take up his responsibility. He directs him to keep the LORD’s ways and the commands written in the Law of Moses.

David connects the future of his house with wholehearted faithfulness to God. Solomon’s task is more than holding power: he is to govern under the word of the LORD.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands the call to strength as the courage and sound judgment required to govern according to God’s law. David’s charge makes obedience central to that responsibility.

Henry distinguishes the promised coming of the Messiah from the faithfulness required of the kings in David’s line. On his reading, the final promise rests on God’s purpose, while the kings remain accountable for how they rule.
passages.god_plan_html:
Obedience as an expression of faithfulness continues in the New Testament. In John 14:15–21, Jesus connects love for Him with keeping His commands and promises His followers the Spirit’s presence.

The settings differ: David is charging Israel’s next king; Jesus is speaking to His disciples. The shared concern is that devotion to God shapes how people live and carry out what He entrusts to them.

The connection does not turn Israel’s royal promises into a guarantee of wealth or political success for every Christian. It calls attention to love expressed in obedience and dependence on God.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Kings 2:5-9
passages.section_title: Why are David’s instructions about Joab and Shimei debated?

He killed them in peacetime to avenge the blood of war. He stained with the blood of war the belt around his waist and the sandals on his feet. 6 So act according to your wisdom, and do not let his gray head go down to Sheol in peace. 7 But show loving devotion to the sons of Barzillai the Gileadite, and let them be among those who eat at your table, because they stood by me when I fled from your brother Absalom. 8 Keep an eye on Shimei the son of Gera, the Benjamite from Bahurim who is with you. He called down bitter curses against me on the day I went to Mahanaim, but when he came down to meet me at the Jordan, I swore to him by the LORD: ‘I will never put you to the sword.’ 9 Now therefore, do not hold him guiltless, for you are a wise man. You know what you ought to do to him to bring his gray head down to Sheol in blood.”

You know what you ought to do to him to bring his gray head down to Sheol in blood.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
David reminds Solomon that Joab killed Abner and Amasa in peacetime. He tells his son to deal with Joab according to wisdom and not let him go to the grave in peace.

He also asks Solomon to show kindness to Barzillai’s sons because of their help during Absalom’s rebellion. They are to have a place at the royal table.

David then recalls Shimei’s bitter curses and his own oath not to put Shimei to the sword. Despite that oath, he tells Solomon not to hold Shimei guiltless and speaks of bringing him to death. The relationship between the oath and this instruction is an important question in reading the passage.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry defends the instructions as concern for the security of Solomon’s throne rather than personal resentment. He considers Joab’s murders and Shimei’s hostility continuing matters of public responsibility.

Wesley sharply questions the instruction about Shimei. Reading David’s earlier oath in 2 Samuel 19:23 as an absolute promise, he considers this dying charge a serious failure in David’s life.

These readings differ over whether the instructions carry out public justice or compromise a promise already made. The text records David’s words; the fact that he gives them does not make the question about his oath disappear.

passages.title: 1 Kings 2:10-12
passages.section_title: What does David’s death mean for the promise to his house?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 Then David rested with his fathers and was buried in the City of David. 11 The length of David’s reign over Israel was forty years—seven years in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem. 12 So Solomon sat on the throne of his father David, and his kingdom was firmly established.
paragraphs: 10 Then David rested with his fathers and was buried in the City of David. 11 The length of David’s reign over Israel was forty years—seven years in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem. 12 So Solomon sat on the throne of his father David, and his kingdom was firmly established.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
David dies and is buried in the City of David. The account summarizes his forty-year reign: seven years in Hebron and thirty-three in Jerusalem.

Solomon sits on his father’s throne, and his kingdom is described as firmly established. David’s life ends, but the story of the house God promised him continues.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley, in his comments on David’s approaching death, emphasizes that even kings and prophets share humanity’s mortality. Their position does not exempt them from death.

The short notice closes one reign and opens another. It asks the reader to hold together the death of the king and the continuation of his line.
passages.god_plan_html:
The New Testament expressly draws attention to David’s death and burial. In Acts 13:32–39, Paul says that David served God’s purpose in his generation, died and underwent decay.

He contrasts David with Jesus, whom God raised from the dead and who did not undergo decay. Paul connects that resurrection with God’s promises and the forgiveness proclaimed through Jesus.

The lasting hope therefore reaches beyond a succession of kings who eventually die. David’s son Solomon continues the line; the risen Jesus brings the promised salvation that death cannot end.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Kings 2:13-25
passages.section_title: Why does a request to marry Abishag lead to Adonijah’s death?

versions.text: 13 Now Adonijah son of Haggith went to Bathsheba the mother of Solomon, and she asked, “Do you come in peace?” “Yes, in peace,” he replied. 14 Then he said, “I have something to tell you.” “Say it,” she answered. 15 “You know that the kingship was mine,” he said. “All Israel expected that I should reign, but the kingship has turned to my brother, for it has come to him from the LORD. 16 So now I have just one request of you; do not deny me.” “State your request,” she told him. 17 Adonijah replied, “Please speak to King Solomon, since he will not turn you down. Let him give me Abishag the Shunammite as my wife.” 18 “Very well,” Bathsheba replied. “I will speak to the king for you.” 19 So Bathsheba went to King Solomon to speak to him for Adonijah. The king stood up to greet her, bowed to her, and sat down on his throne. Then the king had a throne brought for his mother, who sat down at his right hand. 20 “I have just one small request of you,” she said. “Do not deny me.” “Make your request, my mother,” the king replied, “for I will not deny you.” 21 So Bathsheba said, “Let Abishag the Shunammite be given to your brother Adonijah as his wife.” 22 King Solomon answered his mother, “Why do you request Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? Since he is my older brother, you might as well request the kingdom for him and for Abiathar the priest and for Joab son of Zeruiah!” 23 Then King Solomon swore by the LORD: “May God punish me, and ever so severely, if Adonijah has not made this request at the expense of his life. 24 And now, as surely as the LORD lives—the One who established me, who set me on the throne of my father David, and who founded for me a dynasty as He promised—surely Adonijah shall be put to death today!” 25 So King Solomon gave orders to Benaiah son of Jehoiada, and he struck down Adonijah and he died.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Adonijah approaches Bathsheba, saying that the kingdom had been expected to be his but has come to Solomon from the LORD. He asks her to request Abishag as his wife.

Bathsheba agrees to speak for him. Solomon receives his mother with honor, but reacts strongly to the request. He links it with the kingdom itself and names Adonijah’s earlier supporters, Abiathar and Joab.

Solomon declares that Adonijah has made the request at the cost of his life. He orders Benaiah to kill him. The marriage request is thus treated by the king as a renewed threat to his rule.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads the request as another attempt to gain the throne and considers Adonijah a continuing danger. Solomon’s own response in verse 22 explicitly links Abishag with the claim to the kingdom.

Wesley is less certain: he questions whether Adonijah intended wrongdoing and whether Solomon’s execution of him was right. Clarke is more directly critical, emphasizing that Adonijah is killed on suspicion without a recorded hearing.

The difference concerns how confidently to infer Adonijah’s purpose and how to judge Solomon’s response. His earlier ambition is part of the context, but this scene gives no separate speech in which he explains a secret plan to seize power.

passages.title: 1 Kings 2:26-27
passages.section_title: Why does Solomon spare Abiathar but remove him from the priesthood?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 26 Then the king said to Abiathar the priest, “Go back to your fields in Anathoth. Even though you deserve to die, I will not put you to death at this time, since you carried the ark of the Lord GOD before my father David, and you suffered through all that my father suffered.” 27 So Solomon banished Abiathar from the priesthood of the LORD and thus fulfilled the word that the LORD had spoken at Shiloh against the house of Eli.
paragraphs: 26 Then the king said to Abiathar the priest, “Go back to your fields in Anathoth. Even though you deserve to die, I will not put you to death at this time, since you carried the ark of the Lord GOD before my father David, and you suffered through all that my father suffered.” 27 So Solomon banished Abiathar from the priesthood of the LORD and thus fulfilled the word that the LORD had spoken at Shiloh against the house of Eli.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Solomon sends Abiathar back to his fields at Anathoth. He says that Abiathar deserves death, but remembers his service with David: he carried the ark and shared David’s hardships.

Abiathar’s life is spared, but his priestly office is taken away. The narrator expressly identifies this removal as fulfillment of the LORD’s earlier word against Eli’s house at Shiloh.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley see mercy joined with judgment. Abiathar’s recent conduct is addressed without erasing the help he gave David in earlier years.

Gill connects the removal with 1 Samuel 2:27–36, where Eli’s house is warned about losing its place. The fulfillment is stated by Kings itself, rather than supplied only by a later commentator.
passages.god_plan_html:
The earlier warning includes God’s promise to raise up a faithful priest in 1 Samuel 2:35. This chapter will name Zadok in Abiathar’s place. Within Israel’s story, that change answers the failure of Eli’s house.

The wider biblical hope of faithful priesthood reaches further. Hebrews 7:23–28 contrasts priests limited by weakness and death with Jesus, whose priesthood is permanent and whose offering is complete.

Hebrews does not identify Abiathar’s dismissal as a direct prediction of Jesus. The connection is the larger need for faithful priestly service and the final confidence Christians place in the living High Priest.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Kings 2:28-35
passages.section_title: Why does the altar not protect Joab from judgment?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 28 When the news reached Joab, who had conspired with Adonijah but not with Absalom, he fled to the tent of the LORD and took hold of the horns of the altar. 29 It was reported to King Solomon: “Joab has fled to the tent of the LORD and is now beside the altar.” So Solomon sent Benaiah son of Jehoiada, saying, “Go, strike him down!” 30 And Benaiah entered the tent of the LORD and said to Joab, “The king says, ‘Come out!’” But Joab replied, “No, I will die here.” So Benaiah relayed the message to the king, saying, “This is how Joab answered me.” 31 And the king replied, “Do just as he says. Strike him down and bury him, and so remove from me and from the house of my father the innocent blood that Joab shed. 32 The LORD will bring his bloodshed back upon his own head, for without the knowledge of my father David he struck down two men more righteous and better than he when he put to the sword Abner son of Ner, commander of Israel’s army, and Amasa son of Jether, commander of Judah’s army. 33 Their blood will come back upon the heads of Joab and his descendants forever; but for David, his descendants, his house, and his throne, there shall be peace from the LORD forever.” 34 So Benaiah son of Jehoiada went up, struck down Joab, and killed him. He was buried at his own home in the wilderness. 35 And the king appointed Benaiah son of Jehoiada in Joab’s place over the army, and he appointed Zadok the priest in Abiathar’s place.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the news reaches him, Joab flees to the tent of the LORD and takes hold of the altar’s horns. He refuses Benaiah’s instruction to come out, saying that he will die there.

Solomon tells Benaiah to carry out the sentence and bury him. He names the innocent blood of Abner and Amasa and says that Joab’s guilt must be removed from David’s house.

Benaiah kills Joab, who is buried at his own home in the wilderness. Solomon appoints Benaiah over the army and Zadok in Abiathar’s place. The two senior offices are now held by men who supported Solomon.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The law gives a relevant distinction in Exodus 21:12–14: someone who deliberately schemes to kill a neighbor may be taken even from God’s altar to face death. Seeking the altar does not make a planned killing cease to matter.

Henry reads Joab’s case in light of that limit on refuge. Gill sees the judgment as addressing bloodshed that David’s administration had left unresolved.

The account connects Joab’s death with both the earlier murders and Solomon’s consolidation of power. Military usefulness and long service do not erase the deaths of Abner and Amasa.

passages.title: 1 Kings 2:36-46
passages.section_title: Why is Shimei executed after leaving Jerusalem?

And Shimei was told, “Look, your slaves are in Gath.” 40 So Shimei saddled his donkey and set out to Achish at Gath in search of his slaves, and he brought them back from Gath. 41 When Solomon was told that Shimei had gone from Jerusalem to Gath and had returned, 42 the king summoned Shimei and said to him, “Did I not make you swear by the LORD and warn you, ‘On the day you leave and go elsewhere, know for sure that you will die’? section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Solomon requires Shimei to live in Jerusalem and not go elsewhere, warning him about leaving and crossing the Kidron Valley. Shimei accepts the terms and remains in the city.

Three years later, two of his slaves flee to Gath. Shimei goes there and brings them back. Solomon summons him, recalls the restriction and oath, and asks why he has disobeyed.

Solomon also recalls Shimei’s earlier treatment of David and orders his execution. Benaiah kills him. The chapter closes by saying that the kingdom is firmly established in Solomon’s hand.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley reads the restriction as general: Shimei is not to leave Jerusalem for any destination. On that reading, the named Kidron crossing does not limit the command to one route. Gill understands the breach as disobedience to the king and violation of the oath.

The USCCB notes question Solomon’s justification. They read the explicit death warning as tied to crossing the Kidron and observe that the earlier conversation does not expressly record Shimei taking an oath. They understand the old offense against David as the real reason for the execution.

These readings differ over the force of the original warning and Solomon’s later account of it. The narrative records the removal of another threat to the throne; assessing the fairness of the act requires attention to those details.

passages.title: 1 Kings 3:1-5
passages.section_title: What kind of beginning does Solomon make?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Later, Solomon formed an alliance with Pharaoh king of Egypt by marrying his daughter. Solomon brought her to the City of David until he had finished building his palace and the house of the LORD, as well as the wall around Jerusalem. 2 The people, however, were still sacrificing on the high places because a house for the Name of the LORD had not yet been built. 3 And Solomon loved the LORD and walked in the statutes of his father David, except that he sacrificed and burned incense on the high places. 4 Now the king went to Gibeon to sacrifice there, for it was the great high place. Solomon offered a thousand burnt offerings on the altar there. 5 One night at Gibeon the LORD appeared to Solomon in a dream, and God said, “Ask, and I will give it to you!”
paragraphs: 1 Later, Solomon formed an alliance with Pharaoh king of Egypt by marrying his daughter. Solomon brought her to the City of David until he had finished building his palace and the house of the LORD, as well as the wall around Jerusalem. 2 The people, however, were still sacrificing on the high places because a house for the Name of the LORD had not yet been built. 3 And Solomon loved the LORD and walked in the statutes of his father David, except that he sacrificed and burned incense on the high places.

4 Now the king went to Gibeon to sacrifice there, for it was the great high place. Solomon offered a thousand burnt offerings on the altar there. 5 One night at Gibeon the LORD appeared to Solomon in a dream, and God said, “Ask, and I will give it to you!”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Solomon forms an alliance with Egypt by marrying Pharaoh’s daughter. She lives in the City of David while his palace, the LORD’s house and Jerusalem’s wall are being completed.

The narrator says that Solomon loves the LORD and follows David’s statutes, while also noting his sacrifices and incense at the high places. The temple has not yet been built.

Solomon goes to Gibeon, the great high place, and offers a thousand burnt offerings. 2 Chronicles 1:3–6 explains that the Tent of Meeting and its bronze altar are there. At night, God appears to Solomon in a dream and invites him to ask for a gift.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry criticizes Solomon’s choice of a foreign wife. Wesley and Gill instead suppose that Pharaoh’s daughter first adopted Israel’s faith. The narrative itself records the alliance and marriage without describing her conversion.

Wesley also criticizes the wider use of high places, since the tabernacle already provided an appointed place for sacrifice. Gill distinguishes Gibeon’s importance by the presence of that tabernacle and its altar.

These details make the opening more than a simple account of success. Solomon’s love for the LORD is affirmed, while choices about marriage and worship remain matters the reader must follow through the rest of his reign.

passages.title: 1 Kings 3:6-15
passages.section_title: Why does Solomon ask for an understanding heart?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 Solomon replied, “You have shown much loving devotion to Your servant, my father David, because he walked before You in faithfulness, righteousness, and uprightness of heart. And You have maintained this loving devotion by giving him a son to sit on his throne this very day. 7 And now, O LORD my God, You have made Your servant king in my father David’s place. But I am only a little child, not knowing how to go out or come in. 8 Your servant is here among the people You have chosen, a people too numerous to count or number. 9 Therefore give Your servant an understanding heart to judge Your people and to discern between good and evil. For who is able to govern this great people of Yours?” 10 Now it pleased the Lord that Solomon had made this request. 11 So God said to him, “Since you have asked for this instead of requesting long life or wealth for yourself or death for your enemies—but you have asked for discernment to administer justice— 12 behold, I will do what you have asked. I will give you a wise and discerning heart, so that there will never have been another like you, nor will there ever be. 13 Moreover, I will give you what you did not request—both riches and honor—so that during all your days no man in any kingdom will be your equal. 14 So if you walk in My ways and keep My statutes and commandments, just as your father David did, I will prolong your days.” 15 Then Solomon awoke, and indeed it had been a dream. So he returned to Jerusalem, stood before the ark of the covenant of the Lord, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings. Then he held a feast for all his servants.
paragraphs: 6 Solomon replied, “You have shown much loving devotion to Your servant, my father David, because he walked before You in faithfulness, righteousness, and uprightness of heart. And You have maintained this loving devotion by giving him a son to sit on his throne this very day. 7 And now, O LORD my God, You have made Your servant king in my father David’s place. But I am only a little child, not knowing how to go out or come in. 8 Your servant is here among the people You have chosen, a people too numerous to count or number. 9 Therefore give Your servant an understanding heart to judge Your people and to discern between good and evil. For who is able to govern this great people of Yours?”

10 Now it pleased the Lord that Solomon had made this request. 11 So God said to him, “Since you have asked for this instead of requesting long life or wealth for yourself or death for your enemies—but you have asked for discernment to administer justice— 12 behold, I will do what you have asked. I will give you a wise and discerning heart, so that there will never have been another like you, nor will there ever be. 13 Moreover, I will give you what you did not request—both riches and honor—so that during all your days no man in any kingdom will be your equal. 14 So if you walk in My ways and keep My statutes and commandments, just as your father David did, I will prolong your days.” 15 Then Solomon awoke, and indeed it had been a dream. So he returned to Jerusalem, stood before the ark of the covenant of the Lord, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings. Then he held a feast for all his servants.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Solomon begins by thanking God for the loving devotion shown to David and for placing David’s son on the throne. He then admits how unequal he feels to the task of governing so many people.

His request is for an understanding heart that can judge rightly. The Hebrew description draws on shama, pronounced shah-MAH, meaning to hear or listen. Brown–Driver–Briggs specifically lists this verse under attentive listening. Solomon needs a heart that listens so he can discern good and evil and serve the people well.

God is pleased that he asks for justice rather than wealth, long life or the death of enemies. He grants wisdom and adds riches and honor. The promise to prolong Solomon’s days is expressly connected with walking in God’s ways.

Solomon awakes, returns to Jerusalem and offers sacrifices before the ark. He then gives a feast for his servants.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Gill emphasizes the request’s practical setting: Solomon needs to hear cases, distinguish right from wrong and govern justly. His wisdom is to benefit the people entrusted to him.

Henry and Wesley draw attention to Solomon’s humility. Calling himself a little child expresses his sense of inexperience and dependence, rather than claiming that the work of a king is easy.

The dream is presented as an encounter in which God answers Solomon. The gifts are real, but receiving wisdom does not remove his responsibility to remain faithful. Verse 14 keeps that responsibility in view.
passages.god_plan_html:
Solomon’s request belongs with the Bible’s wider invitation to seek wisdom from God. James 1:5–8 tells those who lack wisdom to ask the God who gives generously, and to ask in faith.

The connection concerns dependence on God for the wisdom needed to live and serve faithfully. Solomon asks for help with the responsibility before him; Christian readers are likewise invited to bring their need for wisdom to God.

James does not promise every believer Solomon’s wealth or position. The encouragement is to ask for wisdom rather than pretend we already have all we need.

passages.title: 1 Kings 3:16-28
passages.section_title: How does Solomon recognize the child’s mother?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 At that time two prostitutes came to the king and stood before him. 17 One woman said, “Please, my lord, this woman and I live in the same house, and I gave birth while she was in the house. 18 On the third day after I gave birth, this woman also had a baby. We were alone, with no one in the house but the two of us. 19 During the night this woman’s son died because she rolled over on him. 20 So she got up in the middle of the night and took my son from my side while I was asleep. She laid him in her bosom and put her dead son at my bosom. 21 The next morning, when I got up to nurse my son, I discovered he was dead. But when I examined him, I realized that he was not the son I had borne.” 22 “No,” said the other woman, “the living one is my son and the dead one is your son.” But the first woman insisted, “No, the dead one is yours and the living one is mine.” So they argued before the king. 23 Then the king replied, “This woman says, ‘My son is alive and yours is dead,’ but that woman says, ‘No, your son is dead and mine is alive.’” 24 The king continued, “Bring me a sword.” So they brought him a sword, 25 and the king declared, “Cut the living child in two and give half to one and half to the other.” 26 Then the woman whose son was alive spoke to the king because she yearned with compassion for her son. “Please, my lord,” she said, “give her the living baby. Do not kill him!” But the other woman said, “He will be neither mine nor yours. Cut him in two!” 27 Then the king gave his ruling: “Give the living baby to the first woman. By no means should you kill him; she is his mother.” 28 When all Israel heard of the judgment the king had given, they stood in awe of him, for they saw that the wisdom of God was in him to administer justice.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Two women, identified as prostitutes, bring a dispute to Solomon. One says that they gave birth three days apart in the same house, with no one else present. She says the other child died during the night and that the babies were exchanged while she slept. The other woman denies it.

Solomon calls for a sword and orders the living child divided. The true mother immediately asks that the child be given to the other woman rather than killed. The other woman agrees to the division.

The account describes the mother’s deep compassion for her son. The Hebrew verb used for this stirring of feeling is kamar, pronounced kah-MAR. Brown–Driver–Briggs describes it as growing warm and tender and explicitly includes this verse.

Solomon gives the living child to the woman who pleaded for his life. Israel hears the judgment and stands in awe, recognizing God’s wisdom in the king’s administration of justice.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry understands the test as revealing which woman loves the child. The decisive question becomes whose concern for his life is greater than her desire to win the dispute.

Wesley and Gill likewise understand the mother’s plea as the clue Solomon recognizes. His order brings out the contrasting responses; his final ruling expressly forbids killing the child.

The episode demonstrates the wisdom just promised to Solomon. Its outcome preserves the child’s life and restores him to his mother. It is a particular account of judgment, not an instruction to threaten children when settling disputes.
passages.god_plan_html:
The mother’s compassion has a meaningful place beside the Bible’s pictures of God’s care. In Isaiah 49:14–16, God answers Zion’s fear of being forgotten by asking whether a nursing mother could forget her child. Even if a mother could forget, He will not forget His people.

Hosea 11:8–9 also describes God’s deeply stirred compassion toward Israel. The verb used for that stirring is the same one used here for the mother’s feeling. The parallel helps us see the strength of the care being described.

These passages do not identify this woman as a prediction or make every mother’s experience identical. They use the recognizable depth of compassionate love to help readers grasp God’s faithful concern for His people.

passages.title: 1 Kings 4:1-6
passages.section_title: Who helps Solomon govern the kingdom?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 So King Solomon ruled over Israel, 2 and these were his chief officials: Azariah son of Zadok was the priest; 3 Elihoreph and Ahijah, the sons of Shisha, were secretaries; Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was the recorder; 4 Benaiah son of Jehoiada was in charge of the army; Zadok and Abiathar were priests; 5 Azariah son of Nathan was in charge of the governors; Zabud son of Nathan was a priest and adviser to the king; 6 Ahishar was in charge of the palace; and Adoniram son of Abda was in charge of the forced labor.
paragraphs: 1 So King Solomon ruled over Israel, 2 and these were his chief officials: Azariah son of Zadok was the priest; 3 Elihoreph and Ahijah, the sons of Shisha, were secretaries; Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was the recorder; 4 Benaiah son of Jehoiada was in charge of the army; Zadok and Abiathar were priests; 5 Azariah son of Nathan was in charge of the governors; Zabud son of Nathan was a priest and adviser to the king; 6 Ahishar was in charge of the palace; and Adoniram son of Abda was in charge of the forced labor.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The chapter names Solomon’s chief officials. Priestly service, writing, records, the army, supervision of governors, the palace and forced labor all have people assigned to them.

Some names continue from David’s reign, including Jehoshaphat and Benaiah. Others mark the developing organization under Solomon. Two men named Azariah appear, one identified as Zadok’s son and the other as Nathan’s son.

The list shows that the rule of one king depends on the work of many people. It also identifies the offices through which royal decisions are put into practice.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry sees wisdom in the appointment of officials and notes continuity with David’s administration. Different responsibilities require people to carry them out.

Abiathar’s name raises a question after his removal in chapter 2. Wesley understands the list as including successive holders of priestly office. Gill also considers the possibility that Abiathar retained the title after his removal. The verse names him without saying he has been restored to his former position.

passages.title: 1 Kings 4:7-19
passages.section_title: How is the royal household supplied?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Twelve governors are responsible for supplying food for Solomon and his household, each for one month of the year. The list names the areas from which those provisions come.

Two governors are also identified as sons-in-law of Solomon: Ben-abinadab is married to Taphath, and Ahimaaz to Basemath. The BSB ends the list with a further reference to a governor in Judah.

The arrangement makes the resources of different parts of the land available to the royal household. It explains how the large daily provisions described in the next section can be maintained.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry understands the rotation as a way to share the burden so that one part of the country is not exhausted by supplying the court.

The USCCB notes place more emphasis on an unequal burden, reading Judah’s separate administration as favorable to Solomon’s own tribe. That reading looks ahead to the later division of the kingdom.

The monthly system is clear, but its effects on the people require the wider narrative too. In 1 Kings 12:1–16, the people will ask Solomon’s son to lighten the heavy burden his father placed on them. Court organization and the experience of those who support it are both part of the story.

passages.title: 1 Kings 4:20-28
passages.section_title: What does peace under the vine and fig tree mean?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 20 The people of Judah and Israel were as numerous as the sand on the seashore, and they were eating and drinking and rejoicing. 21 And Solomon reigned over all the kingdoms from the Euphrates to the land of the Philistines, as far as the border of Egypt. These kingdoms offered tribute and served Solomon all the days of his life. 22 Solomon’s provisions for a single day were thirty cors of fine flour, sixty cors of meal, 23 ten fat oxen, twenty range oxen, and a hundred sheep, as well as deer, gazelles, roebucks, and fattened poultry. 24 For Solomon had dominion over everything west of the Euphrates —over all the kingdoms from Tiphsah to Gaza—and he had peace on all sides. 25 Throughout the days of Solomon, Judah and Israel dwelt securely from Dan to Beersheba, each man under his own vine and his own fig tree. 26 Solomon had 4,000 stalls for his chariot horses and 12,000 horses. 27 Each month the governors in turn provided food for King Solomon and all who came to his table. They saw to it that nothing was lacking. 28 Each one also brought to the required place their quotas of barley and straw for the chariot horses and other horses.

These kingdoms offered tribute and served Solomon all the days of his life. 22 Solomon’s provisions for a single day were thirty cors of fine flour, sixty cors of meal, 23 ten fat oxen, twenty range oxen, and a hundred sheep, as well as deer, gazelles, roebucks, and fattened poultry. 24 For Solomon had dominion over everything west of the Euphrates —over all the kingdoms from Tiphsah to Gaza—and he had peace on all sides. 25 Throughout the days of Solomon, Judah and Israel dwelt securely from Dan to Beersheba, each man under his own vine and his own fig tree.

26 Solomon had 4,000 stalls for his chariot horses and 12,000 horses. 27 Each month the governors in turn provided food for King Solomon and all who came to his table. They saw to it that nothing was lacking. 28 Each one also brought to the required place their quotas of barley and straw for the chariot horses and other horses.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Judah and Israel are described as numerous, eating, drinking and rejoicing. Solomon rules over kingdoms that bring tribute, and peace surrounds his realm.

The daily food required for his court is substantial. The governors supply it in turn and also provide feed for the horses. The account presents both the prosperity of the land and the resources needed to maintain the king’s household.

The image of each person under his own vine and fig tree gives that peace a homely setting. People can enjoy what grows around their homes without living in fear of attack.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands the vine and fig tree as a picture of enjoying the fruit of one’s work in safety and comfort. Security extends beyond defended cities into the countryside.

Henry sees the prosperity and peace as part of the brightness of Solomon’s reign, and draws a further comparison with the peace of Christ’s kingdom.

The scene describes a high point in Israel’s life under Solomon. Its gifts should be read alongside the responsibilities and burdens that the rest of Kings will continue to show.
passages.god_plan_html:
The description of people as numerous as the seashore’s sand recalls God’s promise to Abraham in Genesis 22:17–18. The nation’s growth belongs within the story of God’s faithfulness, while the promise also reaches to blessing for all nations.

The vine and fig tree picture appears again in Micah 4:1–4. There, God teaches the nations, settles disputes and brings an end to training for war. Each person sits without fear under a vine and fig tree.

Solomon’s peace offers a limited comparison with that larger hope. Micah looks beyond the success of one royal household to peace among peoples under God’s instruction. The shared picture helps readers recognize what safe and settled life is meant to be.

passages.title: 1 Kings 4:29-34
passages.section_title: Why do people from other nations come to hear Solomon?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 29 And God gave Solomon wisdom, exceedingly deep insight, and understanding beyond measure, like the sand on the seashore. 30 Solomon’s wisdom was greater than that of all the men of the East, greater than all the wisdom of Egypt. 31 He was wiser than all men—wiser than Ethan the Ezrahite, and wiser than Heman, Calcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol. And his fame spread throughout the surrounding nations. 32 Solomon composed three thousand proverbs, and his songs numbered a thousand and five. 33 He spoke of trees, from the cedar in Lebanon to the hyssop growing in the wall, and he taught about animals, birds, reptiles, and fish. 34 So men of all nations came to listen to Solomon’s wisdom, sent by all the kings of the earth, who had heard of his wisdom.

And his fame spread throughout the surrounding nations. 32 Solomon composed three thousand proverbs, and his songs numbered a thousand and five. 33 He spoke of trees, from the cedar in Lebanon to the hyssop growing in the wall, and he taught about animals, birds, reptiles, and fish. 34 So men of all nations came to listen to Solomon’s wisdom, sent by all the kings of the earth, who had heard of his wisdom.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
God gives Solomon wisdom, deep insight and understanding beyond measure. His reputation surpasses the wisdom of the East and Egypt, and his fame spreads through the surrounding nations.

The account describes three thousand proverbs and a thousand and five songs, along with teaching about plants and animals. His learning reaches across many parts of life.

People sent by other kings come to hear him. The gift requested so that he could govern God’s people has become known beyond Israel.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry considers Solomon’s wisdom a greater glory than his wealth. He emphasizes using great gifts for the good of others.

Wesley also sees value in Solomon’s wide learning, while noting that his discourses about the natural world have not all been preserved. The biblical record describes a body of teaching larger than the writings we now possess.

The source of the gift remains central: the passage begins by saying that God gave this wisdom. Solomon’s fame leads readers back to the One who answered his request.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus explicitly compares Himself with Solomon in Matthew 12:42. He recalls the Queen of the South coming to hear Solomon’s wisdom and says that One greater than Solomon is present.

Colossians 2:2–3 places the treasures of wisdom and knowledge in Christ. Solomon’s gifted understanding provides a point of comparison, while Jesus is the greater One to whom readers are directed.

This connection does not depend on treating every later decision of Solomon as wise. The rest of his story will show why God’s gift and a person’s faithful use of it must be kept together.
