passages.title: 1 Kings 5:1-6
passages.section_title: Why can Solomon now prepare to build the LORD’s house?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now when Hiram king of Tyre heard that Solomon had been anointed king in his father’s place, he sent envoys to Solomon; for Hiram had always been a friend of David. 2 And Solomon relayed this message to Hiram: 3 “As you are well aware, due to the wars waged on all sides against my father David, he could not build a house for the Name of the LORD his God until the LORD had put his enemies under his feet. 4 But now the LORD my God has given me rest on every side, and there is no adversary or crisis. 5 So behold, I plan to build a house for the Name of the LORD my God, according to what the LORD said to my father David: ‘I will put your son on your throne in your place, and he will build the house for My Name.’ 6 Now therefore, order that cedars of Lebanon be cut down for me. My servants will be with your servants, and I will pay your servants whatever wages you set, for you know that there are none among us as skilled in logging as the Sidonians.”
paragraphs: 1 Now when Hiram king of Tyre heard that Solomon had been anointed king in his father’s place, he sent envoys to Solomon; for Hiram had always been a friend of David. 2 And Solomon relayed this message to Hiram:

3 “As you are well aware, due to the wars waged on all sides against my father David, he could not build a house for the Name of the LORD his God until the LORD had put his enemies under his feet. 4 But now the LORD my God has given me rest on every side, and there is no adversary or crisis. 5 So behold, I plan to build a house for the Name of the LORD my God, according to what the LORD said to my father David: ‘I will put your son on your throne in your place, and he will build the house for My Name.’ 6 Now therefore, order that cedars of Lebanon be cut down for me. My servants will be with your servants, and I will pay your servants whatever wages you set, for you know that there are none among us as skilled in logging as the Sidonians.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Hiram king of Tyre sends envoys after hearing that Solomon has succeeded David. His friendship with David provides the setting for Solomon’s request.

Solomon explains that David’s wars prevented him from building a house for the LORD’s Name. God has now given rest, and Solomon intends to carry out the promise that David’s son would build it.

The word for an adversary in verse 4 is satan, pronounced sah-TAHN. Brown–Driver–Briggs lists this passage under the ordinary sense of a personal or national opponent. Solomon is describing the peace that makes the building work possible.

He asks for cedars from Lebanon and the help of skilled Sidonian workers, offering to pay their wages. The earlier timber Hiram sent David had been for David’s own house, as 2 Chronicles 2:3 makes clear. Solomon is now requesting help for the LORD’s house.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Gill understands Solomon’s rest as freedom from opposition that would hinder the work. Henry emphasizes using such an opportunity to proceed with what God has promised.

Wesley sees the assistance of non-Israelites as significant in the building of the temple. Skills beyond Israel are being put to use in this work. His further comparison with God’s gathering of the nations should be distinguished from the immediate account of timber and labor.
passages.god_plan_html:
The desire for God to dwell among His people runs through the Bible. In Exodus 29:45–46, the LORD says that He brought Israel out of Egypt so that He might dwell among them.

The temple project belongs to that larger story. In Ephesians 2:19–22, the picture reaches people joined together in Christ: they become a holy temple and a dwelling place for God in His Spirit, with Jesus as the cornerstone.

This is a connection across the biblical story, not an identification of each construction detail as a prediction. The enduring purpose is God dwelling with His people, and the New Testament shows how people from beyond Israel are included in that household through Christ.

passages.title: 1 Kings 5:7-12
passages.section_title: What agreement do Solomon and Hiram reach?

There I will separate the logs, and you can take them away. 10 So Hiram provided Solomon with all the cedar and cypress timber he wanted, 11 and year after year Solomon would provide Hiram with 20,000 cors of wheat as food for his household, as well as 20,000 baths of pure olive oil. 12 And the LORD gave Solomon wisdom, as He had promised him. There was peace between Hiram and Solomon, and the two of them made a treaty.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Hiram rejoices at Solomon’s message and blesses the LORD for giving David a wise son. He agrees to supply cedar and cypress timber, moving the logs to the sea and floating them as rafts to the place Solomon specifies.

In return, Solomon is to provide food for Hiram’s household. The account records yearly supplies of wheat and pure olive oil.

The passage concludes by naming the LORD as the giver of Solomon’s wisdom and by recording peace and a treaty between the two kings. Preparation for the temple involves negotiation, supplied materials and an ongoing exchange.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry emphasizes mutual dependence: one country supplies the skills and timber, while the other supplies food. Each has something the other needs.

The USCCB notes pay closer attention to the negotiation. Hiram answers Solomon’s offer of workers’ wages with a request for provisions for his own household. They read his reply as securing terms favorable to Tyre.

Gill sees practical wisdom in Solomon’s preparations and the maintenance of peaceful relations. Hiram’s blessing acknowledges Israel’s God, but the account does not describe a full change in his religious allegiance.
passages.god_plan_html:
The benefits of the agreement cross Israel’s borders. Hiram receives provisions, Solomon receives materials and skilled help, and a foreign king voices praise for the LORD’s gift of wisdom.

That wider outlook belongs beside God’s promise in Genesis 12:1–3 that Abraham would become a blessing and that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him. The blessing was never described as being for his family alone.

Galatians 3:8–14 identifies the promise’s reach to the nations with the gospel and the blessing received through Christ by faith. This trade agreement is a limited example of benefit reaching beyond Israel; the New Testament explains the greater blessing that comes through Christ.

passages.title: 1 Kings 5:13-18
passages.section_title: Who does the work of preparing the temple materials?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 Then King Solomon conscripted a labor force of 30,000 men from all Israel. 14 He sent them to Lebanon in monthly shifts of 10,000 men, so that they would spend one month in Lebanon and two months at home. And Adoniram was in charge of the forced labor. 15 Solomon had 70,000 porters and 80,000 stonecutters in the mountains, 16 not including his 3,300 foremen who supervised the workers. 17 And the king commanded them to quarry large, costly stones to lay the foundation of the temple with dressed stones. 18 So Solomon’s and Hiram’s builders, along with the Gebalites, quarried the stone and prepared the timber and stone for the construction of the temple.

And Adoniram was in charge of the forced labor. 15 Solomon had 70,000 porters and 80,000 stonecutters in the mountains, 16 not including his 3,300 foremen who supervised the workers.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.context_html:
Solomon conscripts thirty thousand men from Israel. They serve in Lebanon in shifts of ten thousand, spending one month there and two months at home. Adoniram supervises this forced labor.

The account also names seventy thousand porters, eighty thousand stonecutters and thirty-three hundred foremen. Large, costly stones are quarried and dressed for the foundation.

Solomon’s builders work with Hiram’s builders and the Gebalites to prepare the timber and stone. The temple requires a large workforce as well as a royal decision to build it.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Gill distinguishes the Israelite levy, which works in rotation, from the porters and stonecutters. He reads the latter alongside 2 Chronicles 2:17–18, which identifies those workers as foreigners living in the land.

1 Kings 9:20–22 also distinguishes the continuing forced labor of the remaining non-Israelite peoples from the status of Israelites. The arrangements should not all be treated as the same kind of service.

The shifts give the Israelite men time at home, but the text still calls their work conscription and forced labor. The sacred purpose of the building and the demands made on the workers both belong in our reading.

passages.title: 1 Kings 6:1-10
passages.section_title: How is the temple’s main structure built?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 In the four hundred and eightieth year after the Israelites had come out of the land of Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon’s reign over Israel, in the month of Ziv, the second month, he began to build the house of the LORD. 2 The house that King Solomon built for the LORD was sixty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high. 3 The portico at the front of the main hall of the temple was twenty cubits long, extending across the width of the temple and projecting out ten cubits in front of the temple. 4 He also had narrow windows framed high in the temple. 5 Against the walls of the temple and the inner sanctuary, Solomon built a chambered structure around the temple, in which he constructed the side rooms. 6 The bottom floor was five cubits wide, the middle floor six cubits, and the third floor seven cubits. He also placed offset ledges around the outside of the temple, so that nothing would be inserted into its walls. 7 The temple was constructed using finished stones cut at the quarry, so that no hammer or chisel or any other iron tool was heard in the temple while it was being built. 8 The entrance to the bottom floor was on the south side of the temple. A stairway led up to the middle level, and from there to the third floor. 9 So Solomon built the temple and finished it, roofing it with beams and planks of cedar. 10 He built chambers all along the temple, each five cubits high and attached to the temple with beams of cedar.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Solomon begins the temple in his fourth year, in Ziv, the second month. The narrator also dates the work from Israel’s departure from Egypt: four hundred and eighty years earlier. The new house belongs within the story of the people God brought out of slavery.

The main building measures sixty by twenty by thirty cubits. Using the approximate measurements given in the BSB notes, that is about ninety feet long, thirty feet wide and forty-five feet high. A porch stands at the front, and rooms are arranged in three levels along the sides.

Ledges support the side structure so that its beams do not have to be inserted into the temple walls. The stones are finished at the quarry, so no hammer, chisel or iron tool is heard in the temple during construction. Cedar beams and planks form the roof.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The time from the Exodus is read in different ways. Wesley takes the four hundred and eighty years as a count of elapsed years and works out a total from Israel’s earlier history. The USCCB notes understand it as a rounded count of twelve generations of forty years each. Both readings recognize that the date deliberately connects the temple with the Exodus.

Henry draws a further lesson from the quiet building work: care and peace suit the service of God. That is his application of the detail about tools, rather than a new rule that all worship must be silent.

passages.title: 1 Kings 6:11-14
passages.section_title: What matters more than the building Solomon is making?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 Then the word of the LORD came to Solomon, saying: 12 “As for this temple you are building, if you walk in My statutes, carry out My ordinances, and keep all My commandments by walking in them, I will fulfill through you the promise I made to your father David. 13 And I will dwell among the Israelites and will not abandon My people Israel.” 14 So Solomon built the temple and finished it.
paragraphs: 11 Then the word of the LORD came to Solomon, saying: 12 “As for this temple you are building, if you walk in My statutes, carry out My ordinances, and keep all My commandments by walking in them, I will fulfill through you the promise I made to your father David. 13 And I will dwell among the Israelites and will not abandon My people Israel.” 14 So Solomon built the temple and finished it.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The construction account pauses for a word from the LORD. Solomon is to walk in God’s statutes, carry out His ordinances and keep His commandments.

God connects that obedience with fulfilling His promise to David through Solomon. He promises to dwell among Israel and not abandon His people. The account then returns to the building work.

The interruption makes the central concern plain. The house is being built for the LORD, and the life of its king must answer to the LORD’s word.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley emphasize that the expense of the temple cannot excuse disobedience or shield the people from its consequences.

Gill likewise connects the promise with the faithfulness required of Solomon, his successors and the people. The message concerns an ongoing relationship with God, rather than the completion of a building alone.
passages.god_plan_html:
The promise of God’s dwelling among His people reaches a new expression in John 1:14: the Word becomes flesh and makes His dwelling among us. The Greek verb is skēnoō, pronounced skay-NO-oh. Thayer’s lexicon connects it with living in a tent or tabernacle, as well as dwelling more generally.

John 14:23–24 also joins love, obedience and God’s presence: Jesus speaks of the Father and Son making their home with the person who loves Him and keeps His word.

These are connections in the larger biblical story, not a claim that John directly quotes Solomon’s instructions. God’s purpose is to be with His people, and the New Testament brings that presence into focus through Jesus.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Cedar lines the walls, and cypress boards cover the floor. A room twenty cubits long is set apart at the rear as the Most Holy Place, with a forty-cubit main hall in front of it.

The inner room is a cube, twenty cubits in each direction, prepared to receive the ark of the covenant. Gold covers the interior surfaces. Two large cherubim made of olive wood stand there, each ten cubits high, with wings spread across the room and meeting in the middle.

Cherubim, palm trees and open flowers are carved into the walls, and gold covers the floor. The account gives particular attention to the room prepared for the ark and to the care with which it is set apart.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill distinguish these large wooden cherubim from the smaller gold cherubim made with the ark’s mercy seat. They are additional figures in the inner room.

Wesley understands the figures as representing God’s heavenly attendants, rather than objects to be worshipped. The honor of the place is directed toward the God whose covenant ark is to be brought there.

Henry reads the temple in relation to the wider biblical teaching about Christ and God’s people as His dwelling. Such connections should be supported from Scripture rather than assigned to every measurement or material separately.
passages.god_plan_html:
The separated inner room helps us understand the biblical concern with approaching a holy God. Hebrews 9:1–8, describing the tabernacle arrangement that preceded the temple, explains that access to the Most Holy Place was restricted.

Hebrews 10:19–22 then calls believers to draw near with confidence through Jesus and His blood. The larger movement is from restricted access to the way Christ opens for His people.

Jesus also speaks of the temple of His own body in John 2:19–22. The connection is centered on Him: the temple’s holiness and the hope of drawing near to God help readers grasp the significance of His death and resurrection. The text does not require a separate prediction hidden in each piece of gold or wood.

passages.section_title: How is the temple brought to completion?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Olive-wood doors lead into the inner sanctuary, while folding cypress doors mark the other sanctuary entrance. The carved cherubim, palm trees and flowers continue on the doors, covered with gold.

The inner courtyard is built with dressed stone and trimmed cedar. The account ends by returning to the dates: the foundation was laid in Solomon’s fourth year, in the second month, and the work was finished in his eleventh year, in the eighth month.

The concluding summary says that Solomon built the temple in seven years and that it was completed in every detail according to its specifications.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Gill understands the seven years as a rounded account of the period. The more detailed dates extend from the second month of one year to the eighth month seven years later.

Wesley emphasizes the scale and care of the whole project when explaining why it took time. The notice is about sustained work brought to completion.

The final attention to details and dates closes the description of the building itself. The next chapter will turn to other royal construction and the temple’s furnishings.

passages.title: 1 Kings 7:1-12
passages.section_title: What does Solomon build for the royal household?

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The account of the temple pauses to describe Solomon’s palace complex, which takes thirteen years to complete. It includes the House of the Forest of Lebanon, a colonnade, the Hall of Justice, Solomon’s residence and a residence for Pharaoh’s daughter.

The House of the Forest measures a hundred by fifty by thirty cubits. The colonnade has different dimensions, fifty by thirty cubits. The Hall of Justice is where the king judges. These are distinct parts of the royal complex.

Costly dressed stones and cedar are used throughout, with courtyards linking the buildings. Royal life, public administration and judgment all require space in the account.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Gill read the longer time spent on the palace as consistent with greater urgency about the LORD’s house. On their reading, building the temple first shows the priority Solomon gives it.

The USCCB notes place a different emphasis on the contrast: the narrator highlights that Solomon spends almost twice as long on his own house. They also see the repeated mention of Pharaoh’s daughter as keeping the question of his foreign marriage before the reader.

The difference concerns what the comparison of building times suggests about Solomon’s priorities. The narrative records the scale and duration of both projects without directly explaining every motive behind them.

passages.title: 1 Kings 7:13-22
passages.section_title: Who makes the bronze pillars, and why are they named?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Solomon brings Huram, a skilled bronze craftsman, from Tyre. He is distinct from the king of Tyre who arranged the supplies. His mother is identified here as a widow from Naphtali and his father as a Tyrian bronze worker.

Huram makes two decorated bronze pillars for the temple entrance. Their capitals carry chainwork, pomegranates and lily shapes. The pillar to the south is named Jachin, and the one to the north Boaz.

Jachin, pronounced YAH-keen, means he will establish, according to Brown–Driver–Briggs. The account preserves the names as well as the pillars’ size and workmanship, but gives no separate speech explaining their dedication.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Henry connect the strength and stability of the pillars with dependence on God to establish and sustain His people.

Gill also develops that comparison, while rejecting the idea that the name Boaz must commemorate David’s ancestor. The exact meaning of the pillar’s name is less certain than such a connection might suggest: Brown–Driver–Briggs records several proposals.

The immediate emphasis is the skilled work that marks the entrance to the LORD’s house. The further lessons about stability should be recognized as comparisons drawn from that setting.
passages.god_plan_html:
The temple-pillar picture appears in Jesus’ promise in Revelation 3:12. The one who overcomes is made a pillar in God’s temple, never again to leave, and receives the names associated with God and His city.

Gill sees an allusion to the named pillars here. That offers a supported comparison: strength and an established place at the temple help express lasting belonging in God’s presence.

Revelation gives the promise its own meaning and setting. The connection encourages confidence in Christ’s keeping, rather than making the two bronze pillars a code for every detail of the vision.

passages.title: 1 Kings 7:23-39
passages.section_title: What are the great Sea and the ten smaller basins for?

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.context_html:
Huram makes a large circular bronze reservoir called the Sea, supported by twelve bronze oxen facing the four directions. Its rim has the shape of a lily blossom.

Its capacity is given as two thousand baths. A bath is an ancient liquid measure, as Brown–Driver–Briggs explains; the number describes how much water the vessel holds.

Ten smaller bronze basins stand on decorated wheeled supports, five on each side of the temple. 2 Chronicles 4:6 explains their uses: the offering portions are rinsed in the smaller basins, while the priests use the Sea for washing.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley distinguishes the cleansing of the priests from the washing associated with sacrifices. The vessels serve the work of worship, rather than being ornaments alone.

The parallel account gives the Sea’s capacity as three thousand baths in 2 Chronicles 4:5. Gill proposes that two thousand describes an ordinary filling and three thousand the full capacity. That is a possible explanation; the accounts do not expressly state that distinction.

Henry draws a further comparison between the washing arrangements and the cleansing people need before God. The New Testament gives the basis for developing that theme.
passages.god_plan_html:
The washing arrangements belong to a wider biblical concern with being clean for God’s service. Hebrews 9:13–14 distinguishes outward cleansing under the old order from what Christ’s offering accomplishes for the conscience.

Its emphasis is not merely on being washed on the outside. Christ offers Himself so that people can be cleansed from works of death and serve the living God.

This is a broader connection with the worship system, not a claim that Hebrews assigns a separate meaning to every wheel or bronze ox. The goal of cleansing comes into focus through the work of Jesus.

passages.context_html:
The narrator gathers Huram’s completed bronze work into a final inventory: pillars, capitals, decorated networks, stands, basins, the Sea, oxen and utensils. The bronze has been cast in the Jordan plain, and its total weight is left unrecorded because of its abundance.

The gold furnishings are then named, including the altar, the table for the Bread of the Presence, ten lampstands, vessels, tools and door hinges.

Finally, Solomon brings in the silver, gold and furnishings his father David dedicated and places them in the temple treasuries. The building and its equipment are ready for the dedication that follows.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands the stored silver, gold and vessels as the resources David had dedicated that remained available after the work. The new king carries his father’s preparations into the completed house.

Henry turns the inventory toward the worship it serves, drawing attention to giving ourselves and what we have to God. The value of the objects points beyond possession and display to their use in His service.
passages.god_plan_html:
The background to David’s dedicated resources appears in 1 Chronicles 29:1–9. David gives from his own treasures, the leaders give willingly, and the people rejoice at their wholehearted response.

A related theme appears in 2 Corinthians 9:6–12: giving is to come from a willing heart, with God supplying what enables generosity. The result includes needs being met and thanksgiving offered to God.

The settings are different—preparing a temple and helping believers in need—but both connect resources with service and grateful generosity. The point is larger than amassing precious objects: what is given is put to use in honoring God and serving His purposes.

passages.section_title: What happens when the ark enters the temple?

So the priests and Levites carried them up. 5 There, before the ark, King Solomon and the whole congregation of Israel who had assembled with him sacrificed so many sheep and oxen that they could not be counted or numbered. 6 Then the priests brought the ark of the covenant of the LORD to its place in the inner sanctuary of the temple, the Most Holy Place, beneath the wings of the cherubim. 7 For the cherubim spread their wings over the place of the ark and overshadowed the ark and its poles. 8 The poles extended far enough that their ends were visible from the Holy Place in front of the inner sanctuary, but not from outside the Holy Place; and they are there to this day. 9 There was nothing in the ark except the two stone tablets that Moses had placed in it at Horeb, where the LORD had made a covenant with the Israelites after they had come out of the land of Egypt. 10 And when the priests came out of the Holy Place, the cloud filled the house of the LORD 11 so that the priests could not stand there to minister because of the cloud. section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The temple is ready, and Solomon gathers Israel’s leaders to bring the ark from the City of David to its new place. Priests and Levites also bring the Tent of Meeting and its sacred furnishings. Sacrifices accompany the gathering.

The priests place the ark in the Most Holy Place, beneath the wings of the large cherubim. Its carrying poles remain with it. Inside are the two stone tablets Moses placed there at Horeb, the reminder of the covenant God made with Israel after bringing them out of Egypt.

When the priests come out, a cloud fills the temple. They cannot continue their service because the glory of the LORD fills the house. The account moves from what the builders have completed to what God Himself does.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill understand the cloud as a sign of God’s presence and His acceptance of the house dedicated to Him. The furnishings alone do not account for the significance of this moment; God makes His presence known.

Henry draws a further comparison between the cloud and the limits of what people can presently see of God’s glory. That is a lesson he draws from the scene. The narrative itself identifies the cloud with the LORD’s glory and describes its effect on the priests.
passages.god_plan_html:
This scene closely parallels the completion of the tabernacle in Exodus 40:34–35. There, too, a cloud covers the place of worship, the LORD’s glory fills it, and even Moses cannot enter. The temple continues the story of God dwelling among the people He brought out of Egypt.

That theme reaches beyond either building. Revelation 21:3–4 describes God dwelling with His people in the new creation, where death and mourning are gone. This is a connection across the Bible’s story: God’s purpose includes His people living in His presence.

passages.title: 1 Kings 8:12-21
passages.section_title: Why does Solomon begin by remembering God’s promise?

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Solomon responds to the cloud, then turns to bless the gathered people. He gives the LORD the credit for bringing this day about: what God promised to David, He has now carried out.

David wanted to build a house for the LORD’s Name. God welcomed that desire but appointed David’s son to do the building. Solomon now sits on David’s throne and has completed the house, with a place for the covenant ark.

The emphasis is on a promise kept. Solomon’s work has a place in the account because God spoke first. The tablets in the ark also keep Israel’s covenant with the LORD at the center of the dedication.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill read the completed temple as the fulfillment of the promise that David’s son would build it. Henry emphasizes the same direction of thought: Solomon points to what God has done, rather than treating the ceremony simply as a celebration of his own achievement.

Gill understands Solomon’s language about a lasting dwelling in contrast with the movable tabernacle. The words should also be read alongside Solomon’s acknowledgment in verse 27 that even the heavens cannot contain God. A settled place of worship does not make Him small enough to be enclosed in a building.

passages.title: 1 Kings 8:22-30
passages.section_title: How can God hear prayer at a house that cannot contain Him?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 Then Solomon stood before the altar of the LORD in front of the whole assembly of Israel, spread out his hands toward heaven, 23 and said: “O LORD, God of Israel, there is no God like You in heaven above or on earth below, keeping Your covenant of loving devotion with Your servants who walk before You with all their hearts. 24 You have kept Your promise to Your servant, my father David. What You spoke with Your mouth You have fulfilled with Your hand this day. 25 Therefore now, O LORD, God of Israel, keep for Your servant, my father David, what You promised when You said: ‘You will never fail to have a man to sit before Me on the throne of Israel, if only your descendants guard their way to walk before Me as you have done.’ 26 And now, O God of Israel, please confirm what You promised to Your servant, my father David. 27 But will God indeed dwell upon the earth? The heavens, even the highest heavens, cannot contain You, much less this temple I have built. 28 Yet regard the prayer and plea of Your servant, O LORD my God, so that You may hear the cry and the prayer that Your servant is praying before You today. 29 May Your eyes be open toward this temple night and day, toward the place of which You said, ‘My Name shall be there,’ so that You may hear the prayer that Your servant prays toward this place. 30 Hear the plea of Your servant and of Your people Israel when they pray toward this place. May You hear from heaven, Your dwelling place. May You hear and forgive.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Solomon begins his public prayer before the altar with his hands spread toward heaven. He praises the LORD’s unmatched faithfulness and asks Him to continue keeping His promise to David. The prayer also remembers the responsibility of David’s descendants to walk faithfully before God.

Then comes a question that explains how Solomon understands the temple: if even the highest heavens cannot contain God, how could this house do so? Yet Solomon asks God to watch over this place, where He has chosen to put His Name.

The king asks for himself and for the people who will pray toward the temple. God is to hear from heaven and forgive. The house gives their worship a place of focus, while the One they call on remains greater than the whole creation.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill both explain that Solomon does not imagine God confined within the temple. God graciously makes His presence known there while remaining beyond the limits of any place.

Henry sees the fulfilled promise to David as grounds for continuing prayer: what God has already done encourages Solomon to depend on Him for what comes next. Forgiveness is central to the request, alongside confidence in God’s faithfulness.

These readings hold together two features of the passage: the temple genuinely matters in Israel’s worship, and God hears from heaven. The direction of prayer expresses dependence on the God who made the promise.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Acts 7:44–50, Stephen recalls the tabernacle, David’s desire for a dwelling place and Solomon’s building of the house. He then makes the same essential point Solomon makes here: the Most High cannot be enclosed in something human hands have built.

Stephen supports that point from the prophets, describing heaven as God’s throne and earth as His footstool. The New Testament therefore carries this warning forward directly: honoring a place of worship must go together with recognizing the greatness of the God to whom it belongs.

passages.title: 1 Kings 8:31-32
passages.section_title: Who can judge rightly when people dispute what happened?

May You judge Your servants, condemning the wicked man by bringing down on his own head what he has done, and justifying the righteous man by rewarding him according to his righteousness.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Solomon’s prayer turns to particular situations the people may face. The first concerns a person who has sinned against a neighbor and is required to take an oath before the temple altar.

The king asks God to hear from heaven and judge rightly: let wrongdoing fall back on the wrongdoer, and let the person in the right be vindicated. The appeal is to God’s ability to establish the truth and act justly.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill understand this as a disputed case brought before God, especially when the available testimony does not settle it. The oath is a solemn appeal to Him as witness and judge.

On that reading, the request concerns justice between neighbors. The prayer asks God to distinguish guilt from innocence; it does not say that taking an oath makes a dishonest person truthful or guarantees that every human verdict is correct.

passages.title: 1 Kings 8:33-40
passages.section_title: What does Solomon ask when sin brings defeat or distress?

versions.text: 33 When Your people Israel are defeated before an enemy because they have sinned against You, and they return to You and confess Your name, praying and pleading with You in this temple, 34 then may You hear from heaven and forgive the sin of Your people Israel. May You restore them to the land You gave to their fathers. 35 When the skies are shut and there is no rain because Your people have sinned against You, and they pray toward this place and confess Your name, and they turn from their sins because You have afflicted them, 36 then may You hear from heaven and forgive the sin of Your servants, Your people Israel, so that You may teach them the good way in which they should walk. May You send rain on the land that You gave Your people as an inheritance. 37 When famine or plague comes upon the land, or blight or mildew or locusts or grasshoppers, or when their enemy besieges them in their cities, whatever plague or sickness may come, 38 then may whatever prayer or petition Your people Israel make—each knowing his own afflictions and spreading out his hands toward this temple— 39 be heard by You from heaven, Your dwelling place. And may You forgive and act, and repay each man according to all his ways, since You know his heart—for You alone know the hearts of all men— 40 so that they may fear You all the days they live in the land that You gave to our fathers.

May You send rain on the land that You gave Your people as an inheritance.

And may You forgive and act, and repay each man according to all his ways, since You know his heart—for You alone know the hearts of all men— 40 so that they may fear You all the days they live in the land that You gave to our fathers.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Solomon next prays about defeat by enemies and a lack of rain because Israel has sinned against the LORD. He asks that when the people turn back, confess and pray, God will forgive, restore and teach them how to live.

These requests fit the warnings given to Israel in Leviticus 26:14–20, where breaking the covenant brings defeat and failing harvests. The prayer also reaches into famine, disease, crop damage and siege, including the afflictions known to each person.

God alone knows every heart. Solomon asks Him to hear, forgive and act with that complete knowledge, so the people will live in reverence for Him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley highlights the order of the request: forgiveness and learning the right way come before the plea for rain. The need is deeper than relief from the immediate hardship.

Henry and Gill take the language about the heart’s affliction as an invitation to recognize and confess inward sin. Gill also notes the parallel wording in Chronicles about a person’s own grief and trouble.

The stated setting is Israel’s covenant life in the land. The passage calls for honest repentance and trust in God’s knowledge of the heart. It does not give readers the knowledge to identify a particular sin behind every other person’s illness or hardship.
passages.god_plan_html:
A broader theme comes into view in Hebrews 12:5–11: God’s correction is directed toward the good of His children, so that they share in His holiness and learn to live rightly. The settings differ, but in both, the purpose reaches beyond ending the pain.

1 John 1:7–9 also connects honest acknowledgment of sin with forgiveness and cleansing through Jesus. Together these passages show why turning to God involves more than asking circumstances to improve. It includes receiving His mercy and learning His ways.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Kings 8:41-43
passages.section_title: Why does Solomon pray for people from other nations?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 41 And as for the foreigner who is not of Your people Israel but has come from a distant land because of Your name— 42 for they will hear of Your great name and mighty hand and outstretched arm—when he comes and prays toward this temple, 43 then may You hear from heaven, Your dwelling place, and do according to all for which the foreigner calls to You. Then all the peoples of the earth will know Your name and fear You, as do Your people Israel, and they will know that this house I have built is called by Your Name.
paragraphs: 41 And as for the foreigner who is not of Your people Israel but has come from a distant land because of Your name— 42 for they will hear of Your great name and mighty hand and outstretched arm—when he comes and prays toward this temple, 43 then may You hear from heaven, Your dwelling place, and do according to all for which the foreigner calls to You. Then all the peoples of the earth will know Your name and fear You, as do Your people Israel, and they will know that this house I have built is called by Your Name.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The prayer now looks beyond Israel. Solomon imagines a foreigner coming from a distant country after hearing about the LORD’s great name and power.

He asks God to hear that person’s prayer toward the temple. The purpose is clear: people throughout the earth are to know and revere the LORD, just as Israel does, and recognize that this house bears His Name.

The foreigner’s presence is welcomed into the prayer. God’s dealings with Israel are meant to make Him known beyond Israel’s borders.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley emphasizes the generous scope of Solomon’s request and sees it as an early indication of God’s welcome to people from the nations. Gill likewise connects the prayer with people outside Israel being drawn to worship Israel’s God.

The request is for a person who comes because of the LORD’s name. Its aim is knowledge of and reverence for Him. The promise of being heard is therefore set within coming to the living God, rather than treating the temple as a source of benefits detached from Him.
passages.god_plan_html:
This prayer belongs within the wider promise of blessing reaching the nations. In Genesis 12:1–3, God promises that all the families of the earth will be blessed through Abraham. Solomon’s concern that the nations know the LORD fits that larger purpose.

Galatians 3:6–9 explicitly connects the promise to Abraham with God bringing people from the nations into a right relationship with Himself through faith. Solomon’s prayer is not the whole fulfillment of that promise, but it points in the same direction: the blessing is to reach beyond one people.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Kings 8:44-53
passages.section_title: Can God hear His people when they are far from home?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 44 When Your people go to war against their enemies, wherever You send them, and when they pray to the LORD in the direction of the city You have chosen and the house I have built for Your Name, 45 then may You hear from heaven their prayer and their plea, and may You uphold their cause. 46 When they sin against You—for there is no one who does not sin—and You become angry with them and deliver them to an enemy who takes them as captives to his own land, whether far or near, 47 and when they come to their senses in the land to which they were taken, and they repent and plead with You in the land of their captors, saying, ‘We have sinned and done wrong; we have acted wickedly,’ 48 and when they return to You with all their heart and soul in the land of the enemies who took them captive, and when they pray to You in the direction of the land that You gave to their fathers, the city You have chosen, and the house I have built for Your Name, 49 then may You hear from heaven, Your dwelling place, their prayer and petition, and may You uphold their cause. 50 May You forgive Your people who have sinned against You and all the transgressions they have committed against You, and may You grant them compassion in the eyes of their captors to show them mercy. 51 For they are Your people and Your inheritance; You brought them out of Egypt, out of the furnace for iron. 52 May Your eyes be open to the pleas of Your servant and of Your people Israel, and may You listen to them whenever they call to You. 53 For You, O Lord GOD, have set them apart from all the peoples of the earth as Your inheritance, as You spoke through Your servant Moses when You brought our fathers out of Egypt.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Solomon asks God to uphold the people when they go to battle where He sends them. Their dependence on Him is to continue even when they are away from the temple.

Then the prayer faces the possibility of sin, defeat and captivity. Solomon acknowledges that no one is without sin. If the captives come to their senses, confess their wrongdoing and turn wholeheartedly to God, he asks that God hear, forgive and move their captors to show compassion.

They may be far from home, but they remain the people God brought out of Egypt. Solomon appeals to that history and to God’s choice of Israel as His own inheritance. Distance does not put their prayer beyond His hearing.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill stress that going to battle here is subject to God’s direction. Prayer expresses dependence on Him, rather than making any war someone chooses to fight automatically righteous.

For the captives, both commentators emphasize a sincere return to God. Gill also notes that the compassion requested involves God working on the hearts of those holding them. The king asks for mercy in the very place where the consequences of sin have taken them.
passages.god_plan_html:
The pattern of prayer from exile later appears in Daniel 9:3–19. Daniel confesses the people’s sin, acknowledges the justice of what has happened and appeals to God’s compassion for His people and Jerusalem.

This is a later biblical parallel to what Solomon anticipates. The people’s failure does not make repentance pointless. Their hope rests in the mercy of the God who brought them out of Egypt, not in a claim that they have earned rescue by their own righteousness.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Kings 8:54-61
passages.section_title: What should the people carry home from this prayer?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 54 Now when Solomon had finished praying this entire prayer and petition to the LORD, he got up before the altar of the LORD, where he had been kneeling with his hands spread out toward heaven. 55 And he stood and blessed the whole assembly of Israel in a loud voice, saying: 56 “Blessed be the LORD, who has given rest to His people Israel according to all that He promised. Not one word has failed of all the good promises He made through His servant Moses. 57 May the LORD our God be with us, as He was with our fathers. May He never leave us or forsake us. 58 May He incline our hearts to Himself, to walk in all His ways and to keep the commandments and statutes and ordinances He commanded our fathers. 59 And may these words with which I have made my petition before the LORD be near to the LORD our God day and night, so that He may uphold the cause of His servant and of His people Israel as each day requires, 60 so that all the peoples of the earth may know that the LORD is God. There is no other! 61 So let your heart be fully devoted to the LORD our God, as it is this day, to walk in His statutes and to keep His commandments.”

59 And may these words with which I have made my petition before the LORD be near to the LORD our God day and night, so that He may uphold the cause of His servant and of His people Israel as each day requires, 60 so that all the peoples of the earth may know that the LORD is God. There is no other! 61 So let your heart be fully devoted to the LORD our God, as it is this day, to walk in His statutes and to keep His commandments.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Solomon rises from kneeling before the altar and blesses the assembly. He praises the LORD for giving Israel rest and keeping the good promises spoken through Moses.

He asks God to stay with His people and turn their hearts toward Him, so they will walk in His ways. He also asks for help with each day’s needs, with a wider purpose: all the peoples of the earth are to know that the LORD alone is God.

The blessing ends with a call for wholehearted devotion. The dedication is to shape how the people live after the gathering ends.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill understand the request about the heart as asking God Himself to help the people love and obey Him. The command to obey is accompanied by dependence on His help.

Wesley explains wholehearted devotion as obedience that is sincere, undivided and lasting. Henry similarly holds together the people’s responsibility to respond and their need for God to enable that response. The point is a life directed toward Him, not merely an impressive ceremony.
passages.god_plan_html:
The need for God’s work within His people continues in Jeremiah 31:31–34. God promises a new covenant with Israel and Judah in which His law is written on their hearts, they know Him, and their sins are forgiven.

Hebrews 8:6–13 quotes that promise while explaining the better covenant Jesus mediates. This develops the concern heard in Solomon’s blessing: God’s purpose involves people who know Him from the heart and live in response to His mercy.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Kings 8:62-66
passages.section_title: How does the dedication become a shared celebration?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 62 Then the king and all Israel with him offered sacrifices before the LORD. 63 And Solomon offered as peace offerings to the LORD 22,000 oxen and 120,000 sheep. So the king and all the Israelites dedicated the house of the LORD. 64 On that same day the king consecrated the middle of the courtyard in front of the house of the LORD, and there he offered the burnt offerings, the grain offerings, and the fat of the peace offerings, since the bronze altar before the LORD was too small to contain all these offerings. 65 So at that time Solomon and all Israel with him—a great assembly of people from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of Egypt—kept the feast before the LORD our God for seven days and seven more days—fourteen days in all. 66 On the fifteenth day Solomon sent the people away. So they blessed the king and went home, joyful and glad in heart for all the good things that the LORD had done for His servant David and for His people Israel.

So the king and all the Israelites dedicated the house of the LORD. 64 On that same day the king consecrated the middle of the courtyard in front of the house of the LORD, and there he offered the burnt offerings, the grain offerings, and the fat of the peace offerings, since the bronze altar before the LORD was too small to contain all these offerings.

65 So at that time Solomon and all Israel with him—a great assembly of people from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of Egypt—kept the feast before the LORD our God for seven days and seven more days—fourteen days in all. 66 On the fifteenth day Solomon sent the people away. So they blessed the king and went home, joyful and glad in heart for all the good things that the LORD had done for His servant David and for His people Israel.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The king and the people offer sacrifices together. The peace offerings include twenty-two thousand oxen and one hundred twenty thousand sheep. With more offerings than the bronze altar can hold, Solomon consecrates the middle of the courtyard for this occasion.

The gathering includes people from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of Egypt. The celebration lasts fourteen days. At its close the people bless the king and go home joyful because of the LORD’s goodness to David and Israel.

The account ends with that shared gratitude. The temple has been built, the ark brought in, God’s glory made known, and the people called to wholehearted faithfulness.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Gill distinguishes the seven days of dedication from the seven days of the Feast of Tabernacles. He also connects the feasting with the portions of the peace offerings shared by the worshippers.

Henry emphasizes how the people leave: their joy gives way to grateful life at home. The scale of the gathering matters in the narrative, while its closing emphasis is the goodness of God that the people celebrate.

passages.title: 1 Kings 9:1-9
passages.section_title: What does God promise, and what does He warn Solomon about?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now when Solomon had finished building the house of the LORD and the royal palace, and had achieved all that he had desired to do, 2 the LORD appeared to him a second time, as He had appeared to him at Gibeon. 3 And the LORD said to him: “I have heard your prayer and petition before Me. I have consecrated this temple, which you have built, by putting My Name there forever; My eyes and My heart will be there for all time. 4 And as for you, if you walk before Me as your father David walked, with a heart of integrity and uprightness, doing all I have commanded you, and if you keep My statutes and ordinances, 5 then I will establish your royal throne over Israel forever, as I promised your father David when I said, ‘You will never fail to have a man on the throne of Israel.’ 6 But if indeed you or your sons turn away from following Me and do not keep the commandments and statutes I have set before you, and if you go off to serve and worship other gods, 7 then I will cut off Israel from the land that I have given them, and I will banish from My presence this temple I have sanctified for My Name. Then Israel will become an object of scorn and ridicule among all peoples. 8 And when this temple has become a heap of rubble, all who pass by it will be appalled and will hiss and say, ‘Why has the LORD done such a thing to this land and to this temple?’ 9 And others will answer, ‘Because they have forsaken the LORD their God who brought their fathers out of the land of Egypt, and have embraced other gods, worshiping and serving them—because of this, the LORD has brought all this disaster upon them.’”

6 But if indeed you or your sons turn away from following Me and do not keep the commandments and statutes I have set before you, and if you go off to serve and worship other gods, 7 then I will cut off Israel from the land that I have given them, and I will banish from My presence this temple I have sanctified for My Name. Then Israel will become an object of scorn and ridicule among all peoples. 8 And when this temple has become a heap of rubble, all who pass by it will be appalled and will hiss and say, ‘Why has the LORD done such a thing to this land and to this temple?’ 9 And others will answer, ‘Because they have forsaken the LORD their God who brought their fathers out of the land of Egypt, and have embraced other gods, worshiping and serving them—because of this, the LORD has brought all this disaster upon them.’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After Solomon’s building work is complete, the LORD appears to him again, as He did at Gibeon. He tells Solomon that He has heard his prayer and consecrated the temple for His Name.

The assurance comes with a call to faithfulness. Solomon is to walk before God with integrity, keeping His commands. Turning to other gods would bring severe consequences for both the royal house and the people.

The warning includes removal from the land and the rejection of the temple itself. Passersby would ask why such destruction had happened, and the answer would point to the people abandoning the LORD who brought their ancestors out of Egypt. The temple cannot shield them from the consequences of rejecting Him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry emphasizes that even building and dedicating the temple gives Solomon no permission to sin. Past service does not remove the need for continuing faithfulness.

Wesley highlights the condition attached to the royal promise here. Gill reads God’s continuing regard for the temple together with the warning against corrupting its worship. Both resist treating the assurance of God’s presence as a guarantee that this building will stand regardless of how the people live.
passages.god_plan_html:
The warning closely follows the pattern in Deuteronomy 29:22–28: other nations see the ruined land, ask why, and learn that Israel abandoned the covenant. The possible ruin of the temple belongs within that larger covenant warning.

A later parallel appears in Jesus’ lament over Jerusalem in Matthew 23:37–39. He speaks of the city’s refusal to receive those sent to it and of its house being left desolate. This is a supported comparison across the story, rather than a claim that Jesus directly quotes this passage. A place associated with God does not make refusal to listen to Him harmless.

passages.title: 1 Kings 9:10-14
passages.section_title: Why is Hiram disappointed with Solomon’s gift?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 Now at the end of the twenty years during which Solomon built these two houses, the house of the LORD and the royal palace, 11 King Solomon gave twenty towns in the land of Galilee to Hiram king of Tyre, who had supplied him with cedar and cypress logs and gold for his every desire. 12 So Hiram went out from Tyre to inspect the towns that Solomon had given him, but he was not pleased with them. 13 “What are these towns you have given me, my brother?” asked Hiram, and he called them the Land of Cabul, as they are called to this day. 14 And Hiram had sent the king 120 talents of gold.
paragraphs: 10 Now at the end of the twenty years during which Solomon built these two houses, the house of the LORD and the royal palace, 11 King Solomon gave twenty towns in the land of Galilee to Hiram king of Tyre, who had supplied him with cedar and cypress logs and gold for his every desire. 12 So Hiram went out from Tyre to inspect the towns that Solomon had given him, but he was not pleased with them. 13 “What are these towns you have given me, my brother?” asked Hiram, and he called them the Land of Cabul, as they are called to this day. 14 And Hiram had sent the king 120 talents of gold.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Twenty years have gone into the temple and royal palace. Hiram has supplied timber and gold, and Solomon gives him twenty towns in Galilee.

Hiram inspects the towns and is not pleased. His question to Solomon expresses that disappointment, and the district becomes known as the Land of Cabul. The account also records the hundred twenty talents of gold Hiram had sent.

The name fits the story’s unhappy response, though its exact meaning is uncertain. Brown–Driver–Briggs offers as good as nothing as a possible explanation of the name in this setting.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads the episode as a mismatch between the gift and Hiram’s interests. Gill likewise considers the towns unsuitable for Hiram, without concluding that they were necessarily worthless to everyone.

Gill discusses whether Solomon transferred the towns themselves or their revenues. He favors an actual grant; Wesley also understands a transfer of territory. Their explanations about the towns’ earlier population and status go beyond what this short account directly supplies.

The clear point is the strain in an otherwise productive partnership: the king who supplied Solomon’s projects is dissatisfied with what he receives.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Kings 9:15-23
passages.section_title: Who carries the burden of Solomon’s building projects?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 This is the account of the forced labor that King Solomon imposed to build the house of the LORD, his own palace, the supporting terraces, and the wall of Jerusalem, as well as Hazor, Megiddo, and Gezer. 16 Pharaoh king of Egypt had attacked and captured Gezer. He had set it on fire, killed the Canaanites who lived in the city, and given it as a dowry to his daughter, Solomon’s wife. 17 So Solomon rebuilt Gezer, Lower Beth-horon, 18 Baalath, and Tamar in the Wilderness of Judah, 19 as well as all the store cities that Solomon had for his chariots and horses —whatever he desired to build in Jerusalem, Lebanon, and throughout the land of his dominion. 20 As for all the people who remained of the Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites (the people who were not Israelites)— 21 their descendants who remained in the land, those whom the Israelites were unable to devote to destruction—Solomon conscripted these people to be forced laborers, as they are to this day. 22 But Solomon did not consign any of the Israelites to slavery, because they were his men of war, his servants, his officers, his captains, and the commanders of his chariots and cavalry. 23 They were also the chief officers over Solomon’s projects: 550 supervisors over the people who did the work.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The account lists the work supported by Solomon’s labor force: the temple, palace, supporting terraces, Jerusalem’s wall, rebuilt towns and storage facilities for chariots and horses. Gezer comes into his possession after Pharaoh captures it and gives it as a dowry to his daughter.

Descendants of the remaining Canaanite peoples are conscripted as forced laborers. The passage distinguishes their status from that of the Israelites, who serve as soldiers, royal officials and commanders. Five hundred fifty supervisors oversee the work.

This distinction should be read alongside 1 Kings 5:13–14, which already described an Israelite labor levy working in rotations. Saying that Solomon did not make Israelites slaves does not mean that no Israelite had to perform compulsory work.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill distinguish the continuing servitude imposed on the remaining peoples from the service of the Israelites. Gill also connects the wider levy with the men and resources needed for Solomon’s projects.

Henry emphasizes the prosperity and building achievements in the account. Reading the labor details alongside those achievements keeps both parts visible: the kingdom’s expansion depends on people bearing its workload.

The narrative describes how the projects are accomplished. It does not make every treatment of laborers a model for later rulers or employers.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Kings 9:24-25
passages.section_title: How are Solomon’s household and temple worship put in order?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 24 As soon as Pharaoh’s daughter had come up from the City of David to the palace that Solomon had built for her, he built the supporting terraces. 25 Three times a year Solomon offered burnt offerings and peace offerings on the altar he had built for the LORD, burning incense with them before the LORD. So he completed the temple.
paragraphs: 24 As soon as Pharaoh’s daughter had come up from the City of David to the palace that Solomon had built for her, he built the supporting terraces. 25 Three times a year Solomon offered burnt offerings and peace offerings on the altar he had built for the LORD, burning incense with them before the LORD. So he completed the temple.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Pharaoh’s daughter moves from the City of David into the residence Solomon has built for her. The account then notes his work on the supporting terraces.

Solomon also provides burnt offerings and peace offerings three times a year, with incense before the LORD. The closing statement about completing the temple brings together the finished building and the worship conducted there.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Gill links the move of Pharaoh’s daughter with 2 Chronicles 8:11, where Solomon explains that the places entered by the ark are holy. The parallel supplies the reason Kings leaves unstated.

Wesley and Gill connect the three annual occasions with the major festivals. Gill understands Solomon’s offerings and incense as provided through the priests, rather than as the king personally taking over their work. His reading of completion includes putting the temple service into operation.

passages.title: 1 Kings 9:26-28
passages.section_title: How does Solomon’s partnership with Hiram bring in more wealth?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 26 King Solomon also assembled a fleet of ships at Ezion-geber, which is near Eloth in Edom, on the shore of the Red Sea. 27 And Hiram sent his servants, sailors who knew the sea, to serve in the fleet with Solomon’s servants. 28 They sailed to Ophir and imported gold from there—420 talents—and delivered it to Solomon.
paragraphs: 26 King Solomon also assembled a fleet of ships at Ezion-geber, which is near Eloth in Edom, on the shore of the Red Sea. 27 And Hiram sent his servants, sailors who knew the sea, to serve in the fleet with Solomon’s servants. 28 They sailed to Ophir and imported gold from there—420 talents—and delivered it to Solomon.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Solomon assembles a fleet at Ezion-geber, near Eloth in Edom on the Red Sea. Hiram supplies experienced sailors to work alongside Solomon’s servants.

They sail to Ophir and bring Solomon four hundred twenty talents of gold. The episode adds sea trade to the account of the kingdom’s resources and shows the continuing partnership with Hiram despite the earlier disagreement over the towns.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry sees the trade as part of Solomon’s prosperity, while reminding readers that wisdom is more valuable than silver and gold. The USCCB notes emphasize the way this part of the narrative turns attention toward the wealth and luxury of Solomon’s court.

Gill records several proposed locations for Ophir. The account itself does not give enough detail to choose confidently among them. The source of the shipment is named; its precise place on a modern map remains a separate question.
passages.god_plan_html:
The gold should be read beside the instructions for Israel’s king in Deuteronomy 17:16–20. A king is warned against accumulating great wealth and exalting himself above his own people. Material success still leaves the question of faithful use.

A related concern appears in 1 Timothy 6:17–19. Those with wealth are called to place their hope in God, do good and be generous. This is a broader biblical theme, not a claim that Paul is explaining Solomon’s voyage: resources bring responsibility, while trust belongs in God.

passages.title: 1 Kings 10:1-9
passages.section_title: What does the queen of Sheba discover about Solomon’s wisdom?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now when the queen of Sheba heard about the fame of Solomon concerning the name of the LORD, she came to test him with difficult questions. 2 She arrived in Jerusalem with a very large caravan—with camels bearing spices, gold in great abundance, and precious stones. And she came to Solomon and spoke to him all that was on her mind. 3 And Solomon answered all her questions; nothing was too difficult for the king to explain. 4 When the queen of Sheba saw all the wisdom of Solomon, the palace he had built, 5 the food at his table, the seating of his servants, the service and attire of his attendants, his cupbearers, and the burnt offerings he presented at the house of the LORD, it took her breath away. 6 She said to the king, “The report I heard in my own country about your words and wisdom is true. 7 But I did not believe these things until I came and saw with my own eyes. Indeed, not even half was told to me. Your wisdom and prosperity have far exceeded the report I heard. 8 How blessed are your men! How blessed are these servants of yours who stand continually before you and hear your wisdom! 9 Blessed be the LORD your God, who has delighted in you to set you on the throne of Israel. Because of the LORD’s eternal love for Israel, He has made you king to carry out justice and righteousness.”

How blessed are these servants of yours who stand continually before you and hear your wisdom! 9 Blessed be the LORD your God, who has delighted in you to set you on the throne of Israel. Because of the LORD’s eternal love for Israel, He has made you king to carry out justice and righteousness.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The queen of Sheba hears of Solomon’s fame in connection with the LORD and comes to test him with difficult questions. She brings a great caravan of gifts and speaks freely about what is on her mind. Solomon answers every question.

The Hebrew word behind difficult questions is chidah, pronounced khee-DAH. Brown–Driver–Briggs explains that it can refer to a riddle or a perplexing question, and specifically identifies the queen’s questions here. Her visit puts the reports of Solomon’s wisdom to a real test.

She is overwhelmed by both his answers and what she sees of his household and worship. The report was true, she says, and still did not tell half the story. Her praise ends with the LORD: His love for Israel has placed Solomon on the throne to carry out justice and righteousness.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Henry emphasize the queen’s desire to hear wisdom and learn. Henry also follows Jesus’ use of her journey as a challenge to people who will not listen to Him.

Gill stresses the purpose she names for Solomon’s kingship: justice for the people, rather than rule for personal pleasure. The USCCB notes similarly draw attention to her reminder of that responsibility amid the splendor of the court.

These emphases help keep the visit centered on more than wealth. The queen recognizes wisdom, but she also identifies what such a gifted ruler is meant to do.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus directly returns to this visit in Matthew 12:38–42. When some scribes and Pharisees ask for a sign, He recalls the Queen of the South coming from far away to hear Solomon’s wisdom. Her response will stand as a rebuke to people refusing to receive what is before them.

Jesus then identifies Himself as greater than Solomon. The connection is stated by the New Testament itself: this queen’s willingness to seek wisdom helps expose the responsibility to listen when the greater King is present. The story leads beyond admiration of Solomon to the question of how people respond to Jesus.

passages.title: 1 Kings 10:10-13
passages.section_title: What do the royal gifts add to the account?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 Then she gave the king 120 talents of gold, a great quantity of spices, and precious stones. Never again were spices in such abundance brought in as those the queen of Sheba gave to King Solomon. 11 (The fleet of Hiram that brought gold from Ophir also brought from Ophir a great cargo of almug wood and precious stones. 12 The king made the almug wood into steps for the house of the LORD and for the king’s palace, and into lyres and harps for the singers. Never before had such almug wood been brought in, nor has such been seen again to this day.) 13 King Solomon gave the queen of Sheba all she desired—whatever she asked—besides what he had given her out of his royal bounty. Then she left and returned to her own country, along with her servants.

Never before had such almug wood been brought in, nor has such been seen again to this day.) 13 King Solomon gave the queen of Sheba all she desired—whatever she asked—besides what he had given her out of his royal bounty. Then she left and returned to her own country, along with her servants.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The queen gives Solomon a hundred twenty talents of gold, precious stones and an extraordinary quantity of spices. The narrator pauses to mention another rich supply: Hiram’s fleet brings gold, almug wood and precious stones from Ophir.

Solomon uses the wood for steps at the temple and palace and for musical instruments. The queen, in turn, receives what she asks for as well as gifts from Solomon’s royal generosity, then returns home with her servants.

These exchanges place the visit within the wider account of Solomon’s international connections. Wisdom brings people to his court, and their arrival is accompanied by remarkable gifts.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry sees the queen’s gift as a generous response to her visit and draws a lesson about gratitude. Gill distinguishes the things she requests from what Solomon gives freely in addition.

The narrative describes mutual generosity without recording the terms of a commercial treaty. Its brief account should not be expanded into a detailed agreement that it does not supply.

passages.title: 1 Kings 10:14-22
passages.section_title: How does the account picture the scale of Solomon’s wealth?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 The weight of gold that came to Solomon each year was 666 talents, 15 not including the revenue from the merchants, traders, and all the Arabian kings and governors of the land. 16 King Solomon made two hundred large shields of hammered gold; six hundred shekels of gold went into each shield. 17 He also made three hundred small shields of hammered gold; three minas of gold went into each shield. And the king put them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon. 18 Additionally, the king made a great throne of ivory and overlaid it with pure gold. 19 The throne had six steps, and its back had a rounded top. There were armrests on both sides of the seat, with a lion standing beside each armrest. 20 Twelve lions stood on the six steps, one at either end of each step. Nothing like this had ever been made for any kingdom. 21 All King Solomon’s drinking cups were gold, and all the utensils of the House of the Forest of Lebanon were pure gold. There was no silver, because it was accounted as nothing in the days of Solomon. 22 For the king had the ships of Tarshish at sea with Hiram’s fleet, and once every three years the ships of Tarshish would arrive bearing gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Solomon receives six hundred sixty-six talents of gold each year, apart from other revenue. Gold goes into hundreds of shields, an ivory throne overlaid with gold, drinking cups and the furnishings of the House of the Forest of Lebanon.

The throne has six steps, lions beside its armrests and twelve more lions along the steps. The narrator presents it as unmatched among the kingdoms. Sea trade also brings precious metals, ivory and animals.

The repeated descriptions make the scale of royal wealth unmistakable. Silver counts for little in this setting because gold is so abundant.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley treats the golden shields as part of royal display. Henry sees the wealth as evidence of the prosperity promised to Solomon, while asking readers to value wisdom and God’s gifts above possessions.

The USCCB notes read a warning in the emphasis on luxury at the palace, compared with earlier descriptions of prosperity shared across the kingdom. These are different emphases in reading the same inventory: the abundance is real, while its purpose and effect on the king still matter.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ecclesiastes 2:4–11 considers a life filled with building projects, treasures and pleasures. Looking back over all that achievement, its speaker finds that abundance does not deliver the lasting gain he sought.

Jesus develops the concern in Luke 12:15–21. His account of the rich man with overflowing storehouses shows why possessions cannot secure a person’s life before God. This is a wider biblical connection, not a claim that the parable names Solomon. Royal splendor leaves unanswered the question of what a person ultimately lives for.
