passages.title: 1 Kings 10:23-25
passages.section_title: Why do people keep coming to Solomon’s court?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 23 So King Solomon surpassed all the kings of the earth in riches and wisdom. 24 The whole world sought an audience with Solomon to hear the wisdom that God had put in his heart. 25 Year after year, each visitor would bring his tribute: articles of silver and gold, clothing, weapons, spices, horses, and mules.
paragraphs: 23 So King Solomon surpassed all the kings of the earth in riches and wisdom. 24 The whole world sought an audience with Solomon to hear the wisdom that God had put in his heart. 25 Year after year, each visitor would bring his tribute: articles of silver and gold, clothing, weapons, spices, horses, and mules.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The narrator brings the accounts of wisdom and wealth together: Solomon surpasses the kings of the earth in both. People seek an audience to hear the wisdom God has put in his heart.

The visitors bring gifts year after year—silver, gold, clothing, weapons, spices, horses and mules. Solomon’s renown brings an ongoing flow of people and resources to the court.

Even at this height of fame, the source of his wisdom is expressly named. It is something God has given him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands the broad description of visitors as rulers from the surrounding world. Henry reads Solomon’s greatness in light of God’s promise to give him wisdom and riches.

The account celebrates the reach of Solomon’s reputation while giving God the credit for the wisdom people come to hear. Fame is a response to a gift received; it does not make Solomon its ultimate source.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Kings 10:26-29
passages.section_title: What concern is raised by Solomon’s horses and chariots?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 26 Solomon accumulated 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horses, which he stationed in the chariot cities and also with him in Jerusalem. 27 The king made silver as common in Jerusalem as stones, and cedar as abundant as sycamore in the foothills. 28 Solomon’s horses were imported from Egypt and Kue; the royal merchants purchased them from Kue. 29 A chariot could be imported from Egypt for six hundred shekels of silver, and a horse for a hundred and fifty. Likewise, they exported them to all the kings of the Hittites and to the kings of Aram.
paragraphs: 26 Solomon accumulated 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horses, which he stationed in the chariot cities and also with him in Jerusalem. 27 The king made silver as common in Jerusalem as stones, and cedar as abundant as sycamore in the foothills. 28 Solomon’s horses were imported from Egypt and Kue; the royal merchants purchased them from Kue. 29 A chariot could be imported from Egypt for six hundred shekels of silver, and a horse for a hundred and fifty. Likewise, they exported them to all the kings of the Hittites and to the kings of Aram.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Solomon accumulates fourteen hundred chariots and twelve thousand horses, stationing them in chariot cities and Jerusalem. The account adds another picture of abundance: silver is as common as stones and cedar as plentiful as sycamore.

Royal merchants import horses from Egypt and Kue. The narrator gives the prices of imported chariots and horses and notes their export to Hittite and Aramean kings.

The trade belongs beside Deuteronomy 17:16–17, where Israel’s king is warned against multiplying horses, returning to Egypt to obtain them and accumulating great wealth. The inventory therefore raises a question about obedience alongside its picture of success.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Gill explicitly notes the tension between importing horses from Egypt and the command in Deuteronomy. He also reads the closing verse as describing royal merchants buying and exporting the animals and chariots.

The USCCB notes emphasize the way chariots and horses become another traded commodity in this account. Read with the law for Israel’s king, material and military strength cannot simply be taken as proof that every royal decision is faithful.

passages.title: 1 Kings 11:1-8
passages.section_title: How does Solomon’s heart turn away from the LORD?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 King Solomon, however, loved many foreign women along with the daughter of Pharaoh—women of Moab, Ammon, Edom, and Sidon, as well as Hittite women. 2 These women were from the nations about which the LORD had told the Israelites, “You must not intermarry with them, for surely they will turn your hearts after their gods.” Yet Solomon clung to these women in love. 3 He had seven hundred wives of royal birth and three hundred concubines—and his wives turned his heart away. 4 For when Solomon grew old, his wives turned his heart after other gods, and he was not wholeheartedly devoted to the LORD his God, as his father David had been. 5 Solomon followed Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians and Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites. 6 So Solomon did evil in the sight of the LORD; unlike his father David, he did not follow the LORD completely. 7 At that time on a hill east of Jerusalem, Solomon built a high place for Chemosh the abomination of Moab and for Molech the abomination of the Ammonites. 8 He did the same for all his foreign wives, who burned incense and sacrificed to their gods.
paragraphs: 1 King Solomon, however, loved many foreign women along with the daughter of Pharaoh—women of Moab, Ammon, Edom, and Sidon, as well as Hittite women. 2 These women were from the nations about which the LORD had told the Israelites, “You must not intermarry with them, for surely they will turn your hearts after their gods.” Yet Solomon clung to these women in love. 3 He had seven hundred wives of royal birth and three hundred concubines—and his wives turned his heart away.

4 For when Solomon grew old, his wives turned his heart after other gods, and he was not wholeheartedly devoted to the LORD his God, as his father David had been. 5 Solomon followed Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians and Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites. 6 So Solomon did evil in the sight of the LORD; unlike his father David, he did not follow the LORD completely. 7 At that time on a hill east of Jerusalem, Solomon built a high place for Chemosh the abomination of Moab and for Molech the abomination of the Ammonites. 8 He did the same for all his foreign wives, who burned incense and sacrificed to their gods.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The account now makes Solomon’s failure explicit. He loves many foreign women and takes seven hundred royal wives and three hundred concubines. As he grows old, his wives turn his heart toward other gods.

The warning in Deuteronomy 7:3–4 explains the danger as being drawn away to serve other gods. Here that danger becomes reality: Solomon follows Ashtoreth and Milcom and builds places of worship for Chemosh and Molech, as well as providing for the worship of his other wives.

The text says Solomon clung to these women in love. The Hebrew verb dabaq, pronounced dah-BAHK, means to cling or hold close. Brown–Driver–Briggs lists this verse under the word’s use for attachment and loyalty. The account makes the direction of that attachment—and its effect on his devotion to God—the central concern.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads Solomon’s actions as participation in idol worship and warns that great wisdom and age do not protect someone from an unguarded heart. Wesley emphasizes the permission Solomon gives to this worship and considers his participation in its outward acts possible, while stopping short of saying he changed his beliefs about which God is true.

The difference concerns how to describe Solomon’s inward beliefs and involvement. The narrative itself is unambiguous about his responsibility: he follows other gods, establishes their worship and does evil in the LORD’s sight.
passages.god_plan_html:
Solomon’s divided devotion belongs within a wider biblical warning about competing loyalties. In Matthew 6:24, Jesus explains that a person cannot serve two masters. His immediate example is God and money, but the principle helps explain why devotion cannot simply be divided without consequence.

This is a connection in theme, rather than a claim that Jesus is interpreting Solomon’s marriages. God’s purpose for His people calls for wholehearted faithfulness, and Solomon’s story shows what happens when another attachment takes priority.

passages.title: 1 Kings 11:9-13
passages.section_title: What judgment does Solomon face, and what mercy remains?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 Now the LORD grew angry with Solomon, because his heart had turned away from the LORD, the God of Israel, who had appeared to him twice. 10 Although He had warned Solomon explicitly not to follow other gods, Solomon did not keep the LORD’s command. 11 Then the LORD said to Solomon, “Because you have done this and have not kept My covenant and My statutes, which I have commanded you, I will tear the kingdom away from you and give it to your servant. 12 Nevertheless, for the sake of your father David, I will not do it during your lifetime; I will tear it out of the hand of your son. 13 Yet I will not tear the whole kingdom away from him. I will give one tribe to your son for the sake of My servant David and for the sake of Jerusalem, which I have chosen.”
paragraphs: 9 Now the LORD grew angry with Solomon, because his heart had turned away from the LORD, the God of Israel, who had appeared to him twice. 10 Although He had warned Solomon explicitly not to follow other gods, Solomon did not keep the LORD’s command. 11 Then the LORD said to Solomon, “Because you have done this and have not kept My covenant and My statutes, which I have commanded you, I will tear the kingdom away from you and give it to your servant. 12 Nevertheless, for the sake of your father David, I will not do it during your lifetime; I will tear it out of the hand of your son. 13 Yet I will not tear the whole kingdom away from him. I will give one tribe to your son for the sake of My servant David and for the sake of Jerusalem, which I have chosen.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The LORD’s anger is directed at Solomon because his heart has turned away. God had appeared to him twice and explicitly warned him not to follow other gods, but he has not kept that command.

The consequence is the tearing away of the kingdom and its transfer to a servant. Yet the judgment has limits: for David’s sake it will happen in the next generation, and Solomon’s son will retain a tribe for the sake of David and Jerusalem.

The same announcement holds together the seriousness of Solomon’s failure and the LORD’s continuing regard for His earlier promise.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill connect the mercy shown for David’s sake with God’s promise to him. The delay and the remaining royal rule are not presented as rewards for Solomon’s idolatry.

Gill discusses several ways of understanding the reference to one tribe alongside Judah and Benjamin. The central point of the announcement is clear without settling every detail of that count: much of the kingdom will be taken away, while David’s royal house will continue.

passages.title: 1 Kings 11:14-25
passages.section_title: How do old conflicts return to trouble Solomon?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 Then the LORD raised up against Solomon an adversary, Hadad the Edomite, from the royal line of Edom. 15 Earlier, when David was in Edom, Joab the commander of the army had gone to bury the dead and had struck down every male in Edom. 16 Joab and all Israel had stayed there six months, until he had killed every male in Edom. 17 But Hadad, still just a young boy, had fled to Egypt, along with some Edomites who were servants of his father. 18 Hadad and his men set out from Midian and went to Paran. They took men from Paran with them and went to Egypt, to Pharaoh king of Egypt, who gave Hadad a house and land and provided him with food. 19 There Hadad found such great favor in the sight of Pharaoh that he gave to him in marriage the sister of Queen Tahpenes, his own wife. 20 And the sister of Tahpenes bore Hadad a son named Genubath. Tahpenes herself weaned him in Pharaoh’s palace, and Genubath lived there among the sons of Pharaoh. 21 When Hadad heard in Egypt that David had rested with his fathers and that Joab, the commander of the army, was dead, he said to Pharaoh, “Let me go, that I may return to my own country.” 22 But Pharaoh asked him, “What have you lacked here with me that you suddenly want to go back to your own country?” “Nothing,” Hadad replied, “but please let me go.” 23 And God raised up against Solomon another adversary, Rezon the son of Eliada, who had fled from his master, Hadadezer king of Zobah, 24 and had gathered men to himself. When David killed the Zobaites, Rezon captained a band of raiders and went to Damascus, where they settled and gained control. 25 Rezon was Israel’s enemy throughout the days of Solomon, adding to the trouble caused by Hadad. So Rezon ruled over Aram with hostility toward Israel.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The LORD raises up two adversaries against Solomon. Hadad is an Edomite prince who escaped to Egypt as a child during Joab’s campaign in Edom. Pharaoh provides for him, and he marries into the Egyptian royal household. After hearing that David and Joab have died, Hadad asks to return to his country.

Rezon has fled from Hadadezer king of Zobah, gathered a band of raiders and gained control in Damascus. His hostility adds to the trouble caused by Hadad.

The Hebrew word for adversary is satan, pronounced sah-TAHN. Brown–Driver–Briggs specifically lists these verses under its ordinary meaning of a personal or national opponent. The account is naming human enemies, whose histories reach back into David’s reign.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Gill understand the rise of these opponents as God’s correction of Solomon. Human conflicts become part of the consequences the LORD has announced.

Gill places their active opposition in the period following Solomon’s turn to idolatry, reading it alongside the earlier description of peace. The USCCB notes emphasize that the enemies’ histories go back to the beginning of his reign and question how complete that earlier picture of peace was.

The difference concerns the timing and extent of the opposition. In both readings, these accounts qualify the picture of an untroubled kingdom and show that Solomon’s power cannot keep every threat at bay.

passages.title: 1 Kings 11:26-39
passages.section_title: What does Ahijah’s torn cloak announce to Jeroboam?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 26 Now Jeroboam son of Nebat was an Ephraimite from Zeredah whose mother was a widow named Zeruah. Jeroboam was a servant of Solomon, but he rebelled against the king, 27 and this is the account of his rebellion against the king. Solomon had built the supporting terraces and repaired the gap in the wall of the city of his father David. 28 Now Jeroboam was a mighty man of valor. So when Solomon noticed that the young man was industrious, he put him in charge of the whole labor force of the house of Joseph. 29 During that time, the prophet Ahijah the Shilonite met Jeroboam on the road as he was going out of Jerusalem. Now Ahijah had wrapped himself in a new cloak, and the two of them were alone in the open field. 30 And Ahijah took hold of the new cloak he was wearing, tore it into twelve pieces, 31 and said to Jeroboam, “Take ten pieces for yourself, for this is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘Behold, I will tear the kingdom out of the hand of Solomon, and I will give you ten tribes. 32 But one tribe will remain for the sake of My servant David and for the sake of Jerusalem, the city I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel. 33 For they have forsaken Me to worship Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians, Chemosh the god of the Moabites, and Milcom the god of the Ammonites. They have not walked in My ways, nor done what is right in My eyes, nor kept My statutes and judgments, as Solomon’s father David did. 34 Nevertheless, I will not take the whole kingdom out of Solomon’s hand, because I have made him ruler all the days of his life for the sake of David My servant, whom I chose because he kept My commandments and statutes. 35 But I will take ten tribes of the kingdom from the hand of his son and give them to you. 36 I will give one tribe to his son, so that My servant David will always have a lamp before Me in Jerusalem, the city where I chose to put My Name. 37 But as for you, I will take you, and you shall reign over all that your heart desires, and you will be king over Israel. 38 If you listen to all that I command you, walk in My ways, and do what is right in My sight in order to keep My statutes and commandments as My servant David did, then I will be with you. I will build you a lasting dynasty just as I built for David, and I will give Israel to you. 39 Because of this, I will humble David’s descendants—but not forever.’”

Solomon had built the supporting terraces and repaired the gap in the wall of the city of his father David. 28 Now Jeroboam was a mighty man of valor. section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jeroboam is an industrious official whom Solomon has placed over the labor force of the house of Joseph. He too rebels against the king. Away from Jerusalem, the prophet Ahijah meets him and tears his own new cloak into twelve pieces.

Ahijah tells Jeroboam to take ten pieces. God will give him ten tribes because Solomon and the people have turned to other gods. The kingdom will be divided after Solomon’s lifetime, while David’s house retains rule in Jerusalem.

Jeroboam receives a promise with a clear responsibility: listen to God, walk in His ways and keep His commands. God will then be with him and establish his dynasty. The judgment on David’s descendants will not last forever.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads the announcement as both an opportunity and a warning for Jeroboam: his rise does not remove his obligation to obey God. Gill similarly emphasizes the condition attached to the promise of a lasting royal house.

Gill understands the lamp promised to David as the continuation of his royal line. The picture is of a successor remaining before God in Jerusalem, even while most of the kingdom is taken away.
passages.god_plan_html:
The image of a continuing lamp also appears in Psalm 132:11–18. The psalm remembers God’s oath to David, His choice of Zion and His provision of a lamp for His anointed one. It joins royal hope to God’s faithfulness.

Luke 1:30–33 identifies Jesus as the Son who receives David’s throne and whose kingdom has no end. Gill connects the promise here with that New Testament hope. The judgment on Solomon’s house therefore sits within a larger story: its failures do not bring God’s purpose through David’s line to an end.

passages.title: 1 Kings 11:40-43
passages.section_title: How does Solomon’s reign come to an end?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 40 Solomon therefore sought to kill Jeroboam. But Jeroboam arose and fled to Egypt, to Shishak king of Egypt, where he remained until the death of Solomon. 41 As for the rest of the acts of Solomon—all that he did, as well as his wisdom—are they not written in the Book of the Acts of Solomon? 42 Thus the time that Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel was forty years. 43 And Solomon rested with his fathers and was buried in the city of his father David. And his son Rehoboam reigned in his place.

But Jeroboam arose and fled to Egypt, to Shishak king of Egypt, where he remained until the death of Solomon. 41 As for the rest of the acts of Solomon—all that he did, as well as his wisdom—are they not written in the Book of the Acts of Solomon? 42 Thus the time that Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel was forty years. 43 And Solomon rested with his fathers and was buried in the city of his father David. And his son Rehoboam reigned in his place.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Solomon tries to kill Jeroboam, who escapes to Shishak king of Egypt and remains there until Solomon’s death. The ruler who once received wisdom to govern now seeks the life of the man named to receive much of his kingdom.

The narrator refers readers to the Book of the Acts of Solomon for the rest of his deeds and wisdom. His reign over all Israel lasts forty years. He is buried in the City of David, and his son Rehoboam succeeds him.

The notice closes Solomon’s reign with both his achievement and his failure in view. The announced division of the kingdom remains ahead.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill believe Solomon repented, treating Ecclesiastes as evidence of his return after his fall. Henry, in his comments on verses 9–13, allows hope for repentance but emphasizes that Scripture does not expressly record it here.

This is a real difference in how confidently the writers draw a conclusion beyond the closing notice. Kings records the reign, death, burial and succession; it leaves Solomon’s final inward response unstated.

passages.title: 1 Kings 12:1-5
passages.section_title: What do the people ask of their new king?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then Rehoboam went to Shechem, for all Israel had gone there to make him king. 2 When Jeroboam son of Nebat heard about this, he was still in Egypt where he had fled from King Solomon and had been living ever since. 3 So they sent for Jeroboam, and he and the whole assembly of Israel came to Rehoboam and said, 4 “Your father put a heavy yoke on us. But now you must lighten the burden of your father’s service and the heavy yoke he put on us, and we will serve you.” 5 Rehoboam answered, “Go away for three days and then return to me.” So the people departed.

But now you must lighten the burden of your father’s service and the heavy yoke he put on us, and we will serve you.” 5 Rehoboam answered, “Go away for three days and then return to me.” So the people departed.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Rehoboam goes to Shechem, where the people have gathered to make him king. Jeroboam returns from Egypt after being summoned, and joins the assembly in bringing a request to Solomon’s son.

The people describe Solomon’s service as a heavy yoke—a burden they have had to carry. They offer to serve Rehoboam if he lightens it. He asks for three days before giving his answer.

The request brings another side of Solomon’s great projects into view. The new king faces a decision about the people who sustain the kingdom, not merely about the position he inherits.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands the complaint as concerning heavy taxes and royal expenses. Henry is more skeptical: he considers the charges false or exaggerated in light of the prosperity under Solomon.

The USCCB notes instead treat Solomon’s oppression as a real source of discontent that Rehoboam’s response will intensify. These readings differ over the fairness of the complaint. The narrative records the people’s plea and then makes the king’s response central.

passages.title: 1 Kings 12:6-15
passages.section_title: Will Rehoboam serve the people or try to intimidate them?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 Then King Rehoboam consulted with the elders who had served his father Solomon during his lifetime. “How do you advise me to respond to these people?” he asked. 7 They replied, “If you will be a servant to these people and serve them this day, and if you will respond by speaking kind words to them, they will be your servants forever.” 8 But Rehoboam rejected the advice of the elders; instead, he consulted the young men who had grown up with him and served him. 9 He asked them, “What message do you advise that we send back to these people who have spoken to me, saying, ‘Lighten the yoke your father put on us’?” 10 The young men who had grown up with him replied, “This is how you should answer these people who said to you, ‘Your father made our yoke heavy, but you must make it lighter.’ This is what you should tell them: ‘My little finger is thicker than my father’s waist! 11 Whereas my father burdened you with a heavy yoke, I will add to your yoke. Whereas my father scourged you with whips, I will scourge you with scorpions.’” 12 After three days, Jeroboam and all the people returned to Rehoboam, since the king had said, “Come back to me on the third day.” 13 And the king answered the people harshly. He rejected the advice of the elders 14 and spoke to them as the young men had advised, saying, “Whereas my father made your yoke heavy, I will add to your yoke. Whereas my father scourged you with whips, I will scourge you with scorpions.’”

He rejected the advice of the elders 14 and spoke to them as the young men had advised, saying, “Whereas my father made your yoke heavy, I will add to your yoke. Whereas my father scourged you with whips, I will scourge you with scorpions.” 15 So the king did not listen to the people, and indeed this turn of events was from the LORD, to fulfill the word He had spoken to Jeroboam son of Nebat through Ahijah the Shilonite.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The elders who served Solomon advise Rehoboam to answer kindly and serve the people. In their judgment, meeting the present need will win lasting loyalty.

Rehoboam rejects their advice and turns to the men who grew up with him. They recommend a boast about greater strength and a threat of harsher treatment. When the assembly returns, he repeats that threat instead of offering relief.

The narrator gives two levels of explanation together: Rehoboam refuses to listen, and this turn of events fulfills the LORD’s word through Ahijah about Jeroboam. The king’s harsh choice becomes part of the announced judgment on Solomon’s house.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Gill sees the elders’ advice as a call to humble, gentle government that wins the people’s attachment. Henry reads the rejection of that advice as pride and a desire for unchecked power.

Gill and Wesley explain verse 15 in terms of God allowing Rehoboam to follow his own folly while bringing the earlier prophecy to fulfillment. This reading keeps the human decision and God’s purpose in view together; it does not make the harsh answer wise or kind.
passages.god_plan_html:
The elders’ call for a king to serve the people has a clear later counterpart in Mark 10:42–45. Jesus contrasts rulers who dominate others with the way His disciples are to lead: greatness is expressed in service.

Jesus then gives Himself as the fullest example, serving and giving His life as a ransom for many. This is a connection in theme, not a claim that Mark quotes Rehoboam’s story. The contrast shows why the need for a faithful ruler reaches deeper than strength or inherited office.

passages.title: 1 Kings 12:16-20
passages.section_title: How does the kingdom break apart?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 When all Israel saw that the king had refused to listen to them, they answered the king: “What portion do we have in David, and what inheritance in the son of Jesse? To your tents, O Israel! Look now to your own house, O David!” So the Israelites went home, 17 but Rehoboam still reigned over the Israelites living in the cities of Judah. 18 Then King Rehoboam sent out Adoram, who was in charge of the forced labor, but all Israel stoned him to death. And King Rehoboam mounted his chariot in haste and escaped to Jerusalem. 19 So to this day Israel has been in rebellion against the house of David. 20 When all Israel heard that Jeroboam had returned, they summoned him to the assembly and made him king over all Israel. Only the tribe of Judah followed the house of David.

And King Rehoboam mounted his chariot in haste and escaped to Jerusalem. 19 So to this day Israel has been in rebellion against the house of David. 20 When all Israel heard that Jeroboam had returned, they summoned him to the assembly and made him king over all Israel. section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The people answer Rehoboam’s refusal by rejecting the house of David and returning home. Rehoboam continues to rule the Israelites in Judah’s cities, but the wider union has broken.

He sends Adoram, the official responsible for forced labor, and the people stone him to death. Rehoboam escapes to Jerusalem in his chariot. The northern assembly then makes Jeroboam king.

The dispute over service has become a lasting political division, with a killing at the point of rupture. Solomon’s son retains rule, but no longer over all the people his father governed.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill distinguish God’s purpose in the division from approval of the people’s motives and conduct. Gill expressly condemns the killing of Adoram, while recognizing that the separation fulfills the announced judgment.

Henry focuses on the rejection of David’s house and the need to face loss without revenge. The following scene makes the practical question immediate: will Rehoboam try to restore the kingdom by force?

passages.title: 1 Kings 12:21-24
passages.section_title: Why does Rehoboam call off the planned war?

versions.text: 21 And when Rehoboam arrived in Jerusalem, he mobilized the whole house of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin—180,000 chosen warriors—to fight against the house of Israel and restore the kingdom to Rehoboam son of Solomon. 22 But the word of God came to Shemaiah the man of God: 23 “Tell Rehoboam son of Solomon king of Judah, all the house of Judah and Benjamin, and the rest of the people 24 that this is what the LORD says: ‘You are not to go up and fight against your brothers, the Israelites. Each of you must return home, for this is My doing.’” So they listened to the word of the LORD and turned back according to the word of the LORD.

Each of you must return home, for this is My doing.’” So they listened to the word of the LORD and turned back according to the word of the LORD.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Back in Jerusalem, Rehoboam gathers a hundred eighty thousand chosen warriors from Judah and Benjamin. The plan is to fight Israel and restore his rule over the whole kingdom.

Before the campaign begins, God sends a word through Shemaiah. The king and people are not to fight their fellow Israelites. Each man is to go home, because the division has come from God.

This time they listen. The force turns back, and the attempt to reverse the separation by war stops at God’s command.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry understands the response as submitting to God even when His word crosses the king’s wishes. Gill likewise reads an attack to recover the kingdom as resisting the judgment God has just announced.

The command is specific to this threatened conflict between the two parts of Israel. Its force in the story is that Rehoboam’s claim to restore his power must yield to what God has said.

passages.title: 1 Kings 12:25-33
passages.section_title: Why does Jeroboam create another system of worship?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 25 Then Jeroboam built Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim and lived there. And from there he went out and built Penuel. 26 Jeroboam said in his heart, “Now the kingdom might revert to the house of David. 27 If these people go up to offer sacrifices in the house of the LORD at Jerusalem, their hearts will return to their lord, Rehoboam king of Judah; then they will kill me and return to Rehoboam king of Judah.” 28 After seeking advice, the king made two golden calves and said to the people, “Going up to Jerusalem is too much for you. Here, O Israel, are your gods, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt.” 29 One calf he set up in Bethel, and the other in Dan. 30 And this thing became a sin; the people walked as far as Dan to worship before one of the calves. 31 Jeroboam also built shrines on the high places and appointed from every class of people priests who were not Levites. 32 And Jeroboam ordained a feast on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, like the feast that was in Judah, and he offered sacrifices on the altar; he made this offering in Bethel to sacrifice to the calves he had set up, and he installed priests in Bethel for the high places he had set up. 33 On the fifteenth day of the eighth month, a month of his own choosing, Jeroboam offered sacrifices on the altar he had set up in Bethel. So he ordained a feast for the Israelites, offered sacrifices on the altar, and burned incense.

So he ordained a feast for the Israelites, offered sacrifices on the altar, and burned incense.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jeroboam establishes himself at Shechem and builds Penuel, but fear soon drives his decisions. He reasons that worship at Jerusalem will draw the people back to Rehoboam and lead to his own death.

After taking advice, he makes two golden calves and places them at Bethel and Dan, telling the people they need not travel to Jerusalem. The narrator calls this a sin. Jeroboam also builds shrines and appoints priests who are not Levites.

He establishes a festival like the one in Judah, but in a month of his own choosing, and offers at the altar in Bethel. Worship is being shaped around the king’s concern to keep the people’s loyalty.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley, Henry and Gill understand the calves as intended representations for worship of Israel’s God, rather than necessarily an announcement that the LORD is being replaced by Baal. They nevertheless regard the practice as disobedient worship.

This reading explains why language about the exodus and a familiar-looking feast could make the change appear acceptable. The narrator’s judgment remains clear: the calves, the priesthood and the king’s chosen arrangements lead the people into sin.
passages.god_plan_html:
The scene deliberately recalls Exodus 32:1–8: a golden calf, an altar, a feast and the claim that this is the god who brought Israel out of Egypt. Jeroboam’s words repeat the earlier failure instead of learning from it.

In 1 Corinthians 10:6–14, Paul treats the wilderness failures, including the calf’s feast, as warnings for believers and calls them to flee idolatry. Paul is explaining that earlier history, not directly commenting on Jeroboam. The recurring pattern shows why receiving God’s help must be joined with continuing to trust and obey Him.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

passages.title: 1 Kings 13:1-10
passages.section_title: What warning interrupts Jeroboam’s worship at Bethel?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Suddenly, as Jeroboam was standing beside the altar to burn incense, there came a man of God from Judah to Bethel by the word of the LORD. 2 And he cried out against the altar by the word of the LORD, “O altar, O altar, this is what the LORD says: ‘A son named Josiah will be born to the house of David, and upon you he will sacrifice the priests of the high places who burn incense upon you, and human bones will be burned upon you.’” 3 That day the man of God gave a sign, saying, “The LORD has spoken this sign: ‘Surely the altar will be split apart, and the ashes upon it will be poured out.’” 4 Now when King Jeroboam, who was at the altar in Bethel, heard the word that the man of God had cried out against it, he stretched out his hand and said, “Seize him!” But the hand he stretched out toward him withered, so that he could not pull it back. 5 And the altar was split apart, and the ashes poured out, according to the sign that the man of God had given by the word of the LORD. 6 Then the king responded to the man of God, “Intercede with the LORD your God and pray for me that my hand may be restored.” So the man of God interceded with the LORD, and the king’s hand was restored to him as it was before. 7 Then the king said to the man of God, “Come home with me and refresh yourself, and I will give you a reward.” 8 But the man of God replied, “If you were to give me half your possessions, I still would not go with you, nor would I eat bread or drink water in this place. 9 For this is what I was commanded by the word of the LORD: ‘You must not eat bread or drink water or return by the way you came.’” 10 So the man of God went another way and did not return by the way he had come to Bethel.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
A man of God from Judah arrives while Jeroboam is at the altar in Bethel. He announces that a future son of David named Josiah will bring judgment on this worship. A sign is given for that day: the altar will split and its ashes spill out.

Jeroboam orders the man seized, but his outstretched hand withers and the altar splits. He then asks the messenger to pray for his recovery. The prayer is answered, and his hand is restored.

The king offers hospitality and a reward. The man refuses because God has commanded him not to eat or drink there and to return by another route. He leaves according to those instructions.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Gill distinguish Jeroboam’s request for his hand to be healed from a request for forgiveness or a changed heart. The scene shows both a warning and mercy, but the king’s lasting response remains in question.

Wesley and Gill understand the refusal of a meal as part of the messenger’s separation from the condemned worship. The refusal carries out a specific command; he will not set it aside even for the king’s reward.
passages.god_plan_html:
The later account in 2 Kings 23:15–20 identifies the fulfillment. Josiah destroys Jeroboam’s altar at Bethel and defiles it with human bones, just as the earlier message announced.

The later king also recognizes the messenger’s tomb and leaves his bones undisturbed. This connection is supplied by Scripture itself. The messenger’s death does not cancel the word he delivered, and a royal system of worship cannot make that warning disappear.

deeper_study.title: Should We Seek Signs From God?

passages.title: 1 Kings 13:11-19
passages.section_title: Why does a claim about an angel lead the messenger astray?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 Now a certain old prophet was living in Bethel, and his sons came and told him all the deeds that the man of God had done that day in Bethel. They also told their father the words that the man had spoken to the king. 12 “Which way did he go?” their father asked. And his sons showed him the way taken by the man of God, who had come from Judah. 13 So the prophet said to his sons, “Saddle the donkey for me.” Then they saddled the donkey for him, and he mounted it 14 and went after the man of God. He found him sitting under an oak tree and asked, “Are you the man of God who came from Judah?” “I am,” he replied. 15 So the prophet said to the man of God, “Come home with me and eat some bread.” 16 But the man replied, “I cannot go home with you, and I will not eat bread or drink water with you in this place. 17 For I have been told by the word of the LORD: ‘You must not eat bread or drink water there or return by the way you came.’” 18 Then the prophet replied, “I too am a prophet like you, and an angel spoke to me by the word of the LORD, saying, ‘Bring him back with you to your house, so that he may eat bread and drink water.’” The old prophet was lying to him, 19 but the man of God went back with him, ate bread in his house, and drank water.

He found him sitting under an oak tree and asked, “Are you the man of God who came from Judah?” “I am,” he replied.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
An old prophet in Bethel hears from his sons what has happened and follows the man from Judah. He finds him resting under an oak and invites him home to eat.

The man repeats the command he has received from God. The old prophet then claims that an angel has brought a different instruction: bring him back so he can eat and drink. The narrator expressly says this is a lie.

The man goes back and shares the meal. A claim to speak for God has persuaded him to act against the command already given to him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry emphasizes how an appearance of holiness can make deception persuasive. Gill identifies the angel-message as the old prophet’s invention, rather than a genuine change of instruction.

The writers differ in how confidently they describe the old prophet’s overall character. Henry calls him ungodly; Gill sees troubling actions alongside signs of respect for God’s messenger and leaves the wider question open. Neither reading makes the lie truthful or the invitation authorized.
passages.god_plan_html:
The need to test claims of divine authority continues in the New Testament. In Galatians 1:6–9, Paul insists that even a message presented by an angel must be rejected if it contradicts the gospel already received.

1 John 4:1–6 likewise calls believers to test spiritual claims, with the truth about Jesus and the apostolic witness at the center. These are broader connections, not direct quotations of this story. A messenger’s impressive claim does not remove the responsibility to weigh what is said against what God has made known.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Kings 13:20-25
passages.section_title: What consequence follows the messenger’s disobedience?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 20 While they were sitting at the table, the word of the LORD came to the prophet who had brought him back, 21 and the prophet cried out to the man of God who had come from Judah, “This is what the LORD says: ‘Because you have defied the word of the LORD and have not kept the commandment that the LORD your God gave you, 22 but you went back and ate bread and drank water in the place where He told you not to do so, your body shall never reach the tomb of your fathers.’” 23 And after the man of God had finished eating and drinking, the old prophet who had brought him back saddled the donkey for him. 24 As he went on his way, a lion met him on the road and killed him, and his body was left lying in the road, with the donkey and the lion standing beside it. 25 And there were men passing by who saw the body lying in the road with the lion standing beside it, and they went and reported this in the city where the old prophet lived.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
At the table, a genuine word from the LORD comes to the prophet who brought the man back. He announces that the man from Judah has disobeyed God’s command and will not be buried in his ancestors’ tomb.

After the meal, the man departs on a donkey. A lion meets him on the road and kills him. Passing travelers see his body with the lion and donkey standing nearby, and report it in the city.

The account makes the announced consequence part of the same story as the deception. The messenger who delivered God’s warning also had to heed the command given to him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley emphasizes the seriousness of disregarding a direct command, rather than judging the act only by how ordinary a meal may seem. Henry also sees a warning that a person’s office or earlier service does not make disobedience harmless.

Both writers address the difficult question of why the deceiver is not shown receiving the same immediate punishment. They look beyond present events to God’s final judgment. The narrative does not supply the old prophet’s whole future, and its silence should not be turned into approval of his lie.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Kings 13:26-32
passages.section_title: Why does the old prophet bury him and ask to share his tomb?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 26 When the prophet who had brought him back from his journey heard this, he said, “It is the man of God who disobeyed the command of the LORD. Therefore the LORD has delivered him to the lion, and it has mauled him and killed him, according to the word that the LORD had spoken to him.” 27 Then the old prophet instructed his sons, “Saddle the donkey for me.” So they saddled it, 28 and he went and found the body lying in the road, with the donkey and the lion standing beside it. The lion had not eaten the body or mauled the donkey. 29 So the old prophet lifted up the body of the man of God, laid it on the donkey, and brought it back to his own city to mourn for him and bury him. 30 Then he laid the body in his own tomb, and they lamented over him, “Oh, my brother!” 31 After he had buried him, the prophet said to his sons, “When I die, you must bury me in the tomb where the man of God is buried. Lay my bones beside his bones, 32 for the message that he cried out by the word of the LORD against the altar in Bethel and against all the shrines on the high places in the cities of Samaria will surely come to pass.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The old prophet recognizes the reported death as the fulfillment of the warning spoken at his table. He goes to the road and finds the body still beside the lion and donkey. The lion has eaten neither the man nor the donkey.

He carries the body back, mourns over the man and lays him in his own tomb. He then instructs his sons to bury his bones beside the man’s bones when he dies.

His reason points back to the original message: the word against Bethel’s altar and the high-place shrines will certainly come true. Burial and grief do not erase that announcement.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill see the lion’s unusual restraint as a sign that this death belongs to the announced judgment, rather than simply an ordinary attack for food.

Gill connects the request for shared burial with the later preservation of both men’s bones in 2 Kings 23:17–18. The old prophet’s confidence in the warning is clear. The text describes his mourning and his words without separately narrating every motive behind them.

passages.title: 1 Kings 13:33-34
passages.section_title: Do these warnings change Jeroboam’s course?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 33 Even after these events, Jeroboam did not repent of his evil ways, but again he appointed priests for the high places from every class of people. He ordained anyone who desired to be a priest of the high places. 34 And this was the sin of the house of Jeroboam that led to its extermination and destruction from the face of the earth.
paragraphs: 33 Even after these events, Jeroboam did not repent of his evil ways, but again he appointed priests for the high places from every class of people. He ordained anyone who desired to be a priest of the high places. 34 And this was the sin of the house of Jeroboam that led to its extermination and destruction from the face of the earth.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The account returns to Jeroboam after the events surrounding the two prophets. Despite what has happened, he does not turn from his evil ways.

He continues appointing priests for the high places from every class of people, accepting anyone who wants the role. The narrator identifies this sin as the course that leads to the destruction of his royal house.

The contrast with the opening promise to Jeroboam is sharp. He had been offered an enduring dynasty with faithfulness to God; he persists in the worship arrangements created to secure his rule.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill read the closing notice as continued refusal despite repeated warning. Henry draws attention to the failure of Jeroboam’s plan: the sinful means intended to preserve his family’s throne become the cause of its ruin.

The healing and signs have not produced the repentance the narrative calls for. Receiving help and changing direction remain distinct responses.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Kings 14:1-6
passages.section_title: Can Jeroboam’s disguise hide the truth from God?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 At that time Abijah son of Jeroboam became ill, 2 and Jeroboam said to his wife, “Now get up, disguise yourself so they will not recognize you as my wife, and go to Shiloh. For Ahijah the prophet is there; it was he who spoke about my kingship over this people. 3 Take with you ten loaves of bread, some cakes, and a jar of honey, and go to him. He will tell you what will become of the boy.” 4 Jeroboam’s wife did as instructed; she arose and went to Shiloh and arrived at Ahijah’s house. Now Ahijah could not see, for his eyes were dim because of his age. 5 But the LORD had said to Ahijah, “Behold, the wife of Jeroboam is coming to ask you about her son, for he is ill. Why are you disguised? For I have been sent to you with bad news.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jeroboam’s son Abijah becomes ill. The king sends his wife to Ahijah, the prophet who announced his kingship, to ask what will happen to the boy. He tells her to disguise herself and take bread, cakes and honey.

Ahijah can no longer see because of his age, but the LORD tells him who is coming and gives him a message for her. When he hears her footsteps, he addresses her as Jeroboam’s wife and asks why she is disguised.

The contrast is striking: the prophet cannot see her, yet she is already known. The visit will bring a word about much more than the question the king has sent her to ask.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill see the disguise exposed as evidence that the couple cannot conceal themselves from God. The prophet’s knowledge depends on what the LORD reveals, rather than his eyesight.

Henry emphasizes the attempt to seek reassuring information without facing the need for change. The message refuses that restriction: Jeroboam’s conduct and the future of his household will be addressed.
passages.god_plan_html:
A related theme appears in Hebrews 4:12–16. God’s word reaches the thoughts and intentions of the heart, and nothing is hidden from His sight.

That passage also directs people to Jesus, the sympathetic and sinless high priest, and invites them to seek mercy and help. This is a wider connection, not an identification of Ahijah with Christ. Being fully known by God gives people reason to approach Him honestly and seek grace, rather than rely on concealment.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Kings 14:7-16
passages.section_title: What does Ahijah announce about Jeroboam’s house and Israel?

versions.text: 7 Go, tell Jeroboam that this is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘I raised you up from among the people and appointed you ruler over My people Israel. 8 I tore the kingdom away from the house of David and gave it to you. You have proceeded to make for yourself other gods and molten images to provoke Me, and you have flung Me behind your back. 10 Because of all this, behold, I am bringing disaster on the house of Jeroboam: I will cut off from Jeroboam every male, both slave and free, in Israel; I will burn up the house of Jeroboam as one burns up dung until it is gone! 11 Anyone belonging to Jeroboam who dies in the city will be eaten by dogs, and anyone who dies in the field will be eaten by the birds of the air.’ For the LORD has spoken. 12 As for you, get up and go home. When your feet enter the city, the child will die. 13 All Israel will mourn for him and bury him. section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The message begins with what the LORD has done for Jeroboam: He raised him up and gave him rule over Israel. In return, Jeroboam has made images, led the people into other worship and cast God aside.

Judgment will fall on his royal house. His ill son will die when his mother returns, yet this boy is distinguished from the coming destruction: Israel will mourn and bury him because God has found good in him.

The warning then reaches beyond one family. Another king will end Jeroboam’s dynasty, and Israel will eventually be uprooted from the land and scattered beyond the Euphrates. The people share in the idolatry their king has encouraged.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry understands the boy’s death as removal from the evil coming on the household, with his burial showing the regard God has for him. Gill emphasizes the good disposition toward God that sets him apart within the family.

The text gives that distinction but does not answer every question about why he dies. Its own description prevents his death from being read as proof that he was the worst member of the household.

Wesley also emphasizes the wider responsibility of a ruler who draws others into sin. The judgment concerns both Jeroboam’s own choices and the destructive course he establishes for the people.
passages.god_plan_html:
Two later passages show how the warning unfolds. 1 Kings 15:25–30 recounts Baasha killing Nadab and destroying Jeroboam’s household, expressly connecting the event with Ahijah’s word.

2 Kings 17:7–23 later explains Israel’s exile in terms of persistent idolatry, including the course introduced by Jeroboam. The larger story therefore joins a leader’s choices, the people’s response and the long consequences of refusing repeated calls to return to God.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Kings 14:17-20
passages.section_title: What happens when Jeroboam’s wife returns home?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 Then Jeroboam’s wife got up and departed for Tirzah, and as soon as she stepped over the threshold of the house, the boy died. 18 And they buried him, and all Israel mourned for him, according to the word that the LORD had spoken through His servant Ahijah the prophet. 19 As for the rest of the acts of Jeroboam, how he waged war and how he reigned, they are indeed written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel. 20 And the length of Jeroboam’s reign was twenty-two years, and he rested with his fathers, and his son Nadab reigned in his place.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jeroboam’s wife returns to Tirzah. As she crosses the threshold of the house, the boy dies. He is buried, and Israel mourns for him, as Ahijah had announced.

The narrator then closes the account of Jeroboam’s reign, referring to the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel for his other deeds and wars. He reigns twenty-two years, dies, and is succeeded by his son Nadab.

The boy’s death and the public mourning confirm the immediate part of Ahijah’s message. The rest of the warning still stands over the dynasty Nadab inherits.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill read the precise return and death as confirmation of the prophetic word. They distinguish the royal chronicles mentioned here from the biblical books bearing the name Chronicles.

The account’s focus is selective: the king’s other deeds are acknowledged, while the narrative keeps the consequences of his religious choices before the reader.

passages.title: 1 Kings 14:21-24
passages.section_title: Does having the temple keep Judah faithful?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The account turns to Rehoboam in Judah. He begins to reign at forty-one and rules seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city chosen for the LORD’s Name. His mother is Naamah the Ammonite.

Judah nevertheless does evil in God’s sight. High places, sacred pillars and Asherah poles spread through the land, and the account also names male shrine prostitutes. The people imitate the practices of the nations previously driven out.

The chosen city and temple remain important, but their presence has not kept the people’s devotion faithful. The southern kingdom faces the same need to obey the LORD.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry emphasizes the limits of outward religious advantages: the temple and its ceremonies cannot by themselves change the heart. He sees the need for God’s work within the people.

Gill likewise treats the chosen city as making Judah’s failure more serious. The account gives no basis for treating the north as capable of failure while the south is automatically protected from it.

passages.section_title: What is lost when Shishak attacks Jerusalem?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
In Rehoboam’s fifth year, Shishak king of Egypt attacks Jerusalem and takes the treasures of the temple and palace, including Solomon’s gold shields. Rehoboam replaces those shields with bronze ones, which the guards carry when he enters the LORD’s house.

The contrast makes the loss visible. The royal ceremony continues, but the wealth that once marked Solomon’s court has been carried away.

The closing notice names continuing war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam, refers to further royal records, and records Rehoboam’s death and burial. His son Abijam succeeds him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Henry read the bronze replacements as a picture of diminished royal glory. The loss of the gold is part of the cost attached to the kingdom’s unfaithfulness.

Wesley and Gill suggest smaller or defensive conflicts as a way to understand the continuing war after the earlier decision against an invasion. That is an explanation they offer; this passage does not give a full account of the campaigns.
passages.god_plan_html:
The parallel in 2 Chronicles 12:1–12 explains more of the event. Shemaiah identifies the attack with Judah’s unfaithfulness. When the king and leaders humble themselves, God grants deliverance from complete destruction, though they still face subjection to Shishak.

The stated purpose is that they learn the difference between serving God and serving other kings. That adds something beyond the lost treasure: correction is meant to teach, and mercy can be present even while consequences remain. This is the explanation given by the parallel account, rather than a rule for diagnosing every later defeat.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Kings 15:1-8
passages.section_title: Why does David’s royal line continue through an unfaithful king?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 In the eighteenth year of the reign of Jeroboam son of Nebat, Abijam became king of Judah, 2 and he reigned in Jerusalem three years. His mother’s name was Maacah daughter of Abishalom. 3 And Abijam walked in all the sins that his father before him had committed, and his heart was not as fully devoted to the LORD his God as the heart of David his forefather had been. 4 Nevertheless, for the sake of David, the LORD his God gave him a lamp in Jerusalem by raising up a son to succeed him and to make Jerusalem strong. 5 For David had done what was right in the eyes of the LORD and had not turned aside from anything the LORD commanded all the days of his life, except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite. 6 And there was war between the houses of Rehoboam and Jeroboam all the days of Abijam’s life. 7 As for the rest of the acts of Abijam, along with all his accomplishments, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? And there was war between Abijam and Jeroboam. 8 And Abijam rested with his fathers and was buried in the City of David, and his son Asa reigned in his place.

His mother’s name was Maacah daughter of Abishalom. 3 And Abijam walked in all the sins that his father before him had committed, and his heart was not as fully devoted to the LORD his God as the heart of David his forefather had been. 4 Nevertheless, for the sake of David, the LORD his God gave him a lamp in Jerusalem by raising up a son to succeed him and to make Jerusalem strong. 5 For David had done what was right in the eyes of the LORD and had not turned aside from anything the LORD commanded all the days of his life, except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite.

6 And there was war between the houses of Rehoboam and Jeroboam all the days of Abijam’s life. 7 As for the rest of the acts of Abijam, along with all his accomplishments, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? And there was war between Abijam and Jeroboam. 8 And Abijam rested with his fathers and was buried in the City of David, and his son Asa reigned in his place.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Abijam succeeds Rehoboam and reigns three years in Jerusalem. The account measures his life by devotion to the LORD: he continues his father’s sins rather than following David’s example of wholehearted faithfulness.

Yet the LORD gives David’s house a continuing lamp in Jerusalem by raising up a son to succeed Abijam. The reason named is God’s regard for David, not approval of Abijam’s conduct.

The account explicitly remembers David’s grave sin concerning Uriah the Hittite. Its comparison is therefore not a claim that David never sinned. After a reign marked by continuing war with Jeroboam, Abijam dies and his son Asa succeeds him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill understand the lamp as a son and successor through whom David’s royal line continues. Henry connects that continuing line with God maintaining His purpose despite the failure of particular rulers.

Wesley reads the assessment of David as describing the overall direction of his loyalty, while recognizing the deliberate and sustained wrongdoing concerning Uriah. The favorable comparison does not make that wrong disappear.
passages.god_plan_html:
The continuing royal line matters within the promise of a lasting kingdom through David’s descendant. In Luke 1:30–33, the angel announces that Jesus will receive David’s throne and reign without end.

This gives the preserved line its wider significance in the Bible’s story. God’s purpose through David reaches beyond the short and troubled reign of any one successor. The New Testament directs that hope toward Jesus, rather than treating Abijam himself as the faithful king the people ultimately need.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Kings 15:9-15
passages.section_title: What does Asa change when he becomes king?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 In the twentieth year of Jeroboam’s reign over Israel, Asa became king of Judah, 10 and he reigned in Jerusalem forty-one years. His grandmother’s name was Maacah daughter of Abishalom. 11 And Asa did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, as his father David had done. 12 He banished the male shrine prostitutes from the land and removed all the idols that his fathers had made. 13 He also removed his grandmother Maacah from her position as queen mother because she had made a detestable Asherah pole. Asa chopped down the pole and burned it in the Kidron Valley. 14 The high places were not removed, but Asa’s heart was fully devoted to the LORD all his days. 15 And he brought into the house of the LORD the silver and gold and the articles that he and his father had dedicated.

Asa chopped down the pole and burned it in the Kidron Valley.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Asa reigns forty-one years in Jerusalem and receives a different assessment from his father: he does what is right in the LORD’s sight. He removes idols and male shrine prostitutes from the land.

The changes reach his own household. He removes his grandmother Maacah from her position as queen mother because of the Asherah pole she has made, then cuts it down and burns it. He also brings the dedicated silver, gold and articles into the LORD’s house.

The account includes a limit: the high places are not removed. Even with that unfinished work, it describes Asa’s heart as fully devoted to the LORD.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry emphasizes that reform begins at home. Asa’s family relationship does not prevent him from acting against worship that dishonors God.

Wesley and Gill distinguish high places used for worship of the LORD from those dedicated to foreign gods. They use that distinction to read Kings alongside 2 Chronicles 14:2–5, which describes Asa removing foreign worship and high places.

That is an explanation they offer for the accounts’ different statements. Kings itself records both the remaining high places and Asa’s wholehearted devotion, holding a favorable assessment together with a limit to the reform.

passages.title: 1 Kings 15:16-22
passages.section_title: Does Asa’s successful strategy also show faithful trust?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 Now there was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel throughout their days. 17 Baasha king of Israel went to war against Judah and fortified Ramah to prevent anyone from leaving or entering the territory of Asa king of Judah. 18 So Asa withdrew all the silver and gold that remained in the treasuries of the house of the LORD and the royal palace. He entrusted it to his servants and sent them with this message to Ben-hadad son of Tabrimmon, the son of Hezion, the king of Aram, who was ruling in Damascus: 19 “Let there be a treaty between me and you as there was between my father and your father. See, I have sent you a gift of silver and gold. Now go and break your treaty with Baasha king of Israel, so that he will withdraw from me.” 20 And Ben-hadad listened to King Asa and sent the commanders of his armies against the cities of Israel, conquering Ijon, Dan, Abel-beth-maacah, and the whole land of Naphtali, including the region of Chinnereth. 21 When Baasha learned of this, he stopped fortifying Ramah and withdrew to Tirzah. 22 Then King Asa summoned all the men of Judah, with no exceptions, and they carried away the stones of Ramah and the timbers Baasha had used for building. And with these materials King Asa built up Geba of Benjamin, as well as Mizpah.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Baasha king of Israel fortifies Ramah to restrict movement into and out of Asa’s territory. Asa responds by sending silver and gold from the temple and palace treasuries to Ben-hadad king of Aram.

He asks Ben-hadad to break his treaty with Baasha and attack Israel. The plan works: the attack draws Baasha away from Ramah. Asa then summons Judah’s men to remove its building materials and uses them to strengthen Geba and Mizpah.

The episode records an effective political and military response. The parallel account asks a further question about the trust behind it.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill criticize the use of dedicated treasures to purchase the breaking of another treaty. Henry also sees the alliance as showing a failure to trust the LORD.

This concern is explicit in 2 Chronicles 16:7–9, where Hanani confronts Asa for relying on Aram instead of the God who had helped him before. Immediate success does not settle the question of whether the means were faithful.

passages.title: 1 Kings 15:23-24
passages.section_title: What final note closes Asa’s reign?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 23 Now the rest of the acts of Asa, along with all his might, all his accomplishments, and the cities he built, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? In his old age, however, he became diseased in his feet. 24 And Asa rested with his fathers and was buried with them in the city of his father David, and his son Jehoshaphat reigned in his place.
paragraphs: 23 Now the rest of the acts of Asa, along with all his might, all his accomplishments, and the cities he built, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? In his old age, however, he became diseased in his feet. 24 And Asa rested with his fathers and was buried with them in the city of his father David, and his son Jehoshaphat reigned in his place.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The narrator refers to the royal records for Asa’s other accomplishments, his strength and the cities he built. Alongside those achievements comes a personal detail: in old age he becomes diseased in his feet.

Asa dies and is buried in the City of David. His son Jehoshaphat succeeds him. The brief notice closes a long reign without removing either its good work or its weaknesses.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Gill connects the illness with the fuller account in 2 Chronicles 16:12–14. Chronicles says that even then Asa did not seek the LORD, but relied only on physicians.

The concern is the absence of seeking God, continuing the issue raised by his alliance with Aram. The account does not identify the disease in medical terms or promise that a different response would necessarily have brought physical recovery.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Kings 15:25-34
passages.section_title: Does a new royal house bring a new direction for Israel?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 25 In the second year of Asa’s reign over Judah, Nadab son of Jeroboam became king of Israel, and he reigned two years. 26 And he did evil in the sight of the LORD and walked in the way of his father and in his sin, which he had caused Israel to commit. 27 Then Baasha son of Ahijah of the house of Issachar conspired against Nadab, and Baasha struck him down at Gibbethon of the Philistines while Nadab and all Israel were besieging the city. 28 In the third year of Asa’s reign over Judah, Baasha killed Nadab and reigned in his place. 29 As soon as Baasha became king, he struck down the entire household of Jeroboam. He did not leave to Jeroboam anyone who breathed, but destroyed them all according to the word that the LORD had spoken through His servant Ahijah the Shilonite, 30 because of the sins Jeroboam had committed and had caused Israel to commit, and because he had provoked the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger. 31 As for the rest of the acts of Nadab, along with all his accomplishments, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel? 32 And there was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel throughout their days. 33 In the third year of Asa’s reign over Judah, Baasha son of Ahijah became king of all Israel, and he reigned in Tirzah twenty-four years. 34 And Baasha did evil in the sight of the LORD and walked in the way of Jeroboam and in his sin, which he had caused Israel to commit.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The account returns to the north during Asa’s reign. Nadab son of Jeroboam reigns two years and continues the sin his father introduced. While Israel besieges the Philistine town of Gibbethon, Baasha kills him and takes the throne.

Baasha then destroys Jeroboam’s household. The narrator expressly identifies this with the word the LORD spoke through Ahijah about Jeroboam’s sin and its effect on Israel.

Yet the new dynasty does not bring faithfulness. Baasha reigns twenty-four years and follows the same course of worship as the family he has destroyed. The rulers change while the central sin continues.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill distinguish the fulfillment of God’s warning from Baasha’s motives in carrying out the killings. Gill sees ambition and the removal of rivals, rather than a desire to end idolatry.

Henry likewise reads the upheaval as human wrongdoing within a history in which God’s announced word comes to pass. Baasha’s continuation of Jeroboam’s ways prevents the coup from being mistaken for spiritual reform.
passages.god_plan_html:
The next chapter makes an essential distinction explicit. In 1 Kings 16:1–7, God holds Baasha accountable for leading Israel into sin and for striking down Jeroboam’s house.

The judgment previously announced against Jeroboam does not make Baasha’s conduct righteous simply because it helps bring that judgment about. Across these linked passages, God’s purposes and human responsibility remain together: a person used within the course of events is still answerable for what he does.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Kings 16:1-7
passages.section_title: Why does Baasha face the judgment he brought on Jeroboam’s house?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then the word of the LORD came to Jehu son of Hanani against Baasha, saying: 2 “Even though I lifted you out of the dust and made you ruler over My people Israel, you have walked in the way of Jeroboam and have caused My people Israel to sin and to provoke Me to anger by their sins. 3 So now I will consume Baasha and his house, and I will make your house like that of Jeroboam son of Nebat: 4 Anyone belonging to Baasha who dies in the city will be eaten by dogs, and anyone who dies in the field will be eaten by the birds of the air.” 5 As for the rest of the acts of Baasha, along with his accomplishments and might, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel? 6 And Baasha rested with his fathers and was buried in Tirzah, and his son Elah reigned in his place. 7 Moreover, the word of the LORD came through the prophet Jehu son of Hanani against Baasha and his house, because of all the evil he had done in the sight of the LORD, provoking Him to anger with the work of his hands and becoming like the house of Jeroboam, and also because Baasha had struck down the house of Jeroboam.
