section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The LORD sends Jehu son of Hanani to Baasha. God raised Baasha to rule over Israel, but the king has continued Jeroboam’s course and led the people into sin. His house will now face the same destruction as Jeroboam’s.

The notice of Baasha’s death and Elah’s succession is followed by a further explanation of his guilt. It includes both the evil he has encouraged and his destruction of Jeroboam’s house.

The account does not let Baasha claim that his rise to power makes him exempt from judgment. He is responsible for his actions and for the worship he promotes.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill distinguish God’s purpose in transferring rule from Baasha’s ambition and conduct. The fulfillment of a warning against Jeroboam does not make every action of the man who brings it about righteous.

Henry emphasizes the repeated pattern: Baasha resembles the family he destroyed in the very sins for which it was judged. His opportunity to govern becomes a responsibility he fails to meet.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Kings 16:8-14
passages.section_title: How does the judgment on Baasha’s house unfold?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 In the twenty-sixth year of Asa’s reign over Judah, Elah son of Baasha became king of Israel, and he reigned in Tirzah two years. 9 However, while Elah was in Tirzah getting drunk in the house of Arza the steward of his household there, Elah’s servant Zimri, the commander of half his chariots, conspired against him. 10 So in the twenty-seventh year of Asa’s reign over Judah, Zimri went in, struck Elah down, and killed him. And Zimri reigned in his place. 11 As soon as Zimri began to reign and was seated on the throne, he struck down the entire household of Baasha. He did not leave a single male, whether a kinsman or friend. 12 So Zimri destroyed the entire household of Baasha, according to the word that the LORD had spoken against Baasha through Jehu the prophet. 13 This happened because of all the sins Baasha and his son Elah had committed and had caused Israel to commit, provoking the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger with their worthless idols. 14 As for the rest of the acts of Elah, along with all his accomplishments, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Elah son of Baasha reigns two years in Tirzah. While he is getting drunk in his steward Arza’s house, Zimri, commander of half the royal chariots, conspires against him and kills him.

Zimri takes the throne and destroys Baasha’s household, including its male relatives and friends. The narrator connects this with the word spoken through Jehu.

The reason given includes the sins of both Baasha and Elah and their influence on Israel. Another violent transfer of power ends a royal house without first ending the worship that brought it under judgment.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill explain the description of the idols as worthless: they cannot provide the help their worshippers seek. Henry likewise connects the destruction with the kings’ continuing religious choices.

The repeated judgment shows the failure of a dynasty to learn from its predecessor. Zimri’s seizure of the throne will itself be judged in the next part of the account.
passages.god_plan_html:
The wider Bible addresses more than the repetition of one sinful pattern after another. In Romans 6:15–23, Paul contrasts slavery to sin with the freedom God gives for wholehearted obedience and a life of righteousness.

This is a connection in theme, not Paul’s explanation of Elah’s assassination. The history shows the destructive course of entrenched sin; the New Testament announces the possibility of a different allegiance through God’s gift of life in Christ.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Kings 16:15-20
passages.section_title: Why does Zimri’s reign last only seven days?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 In the twenty-seventh year of Asa’s reign over Judah, Zimri reigned in Tirzah for seven days. Now the troops were encamped against Gibbethon of the Philistines, 16 and the people in the camp heard that Zimri had conspired against the king and struck him down. So there in the camp that very day, all Israel proclaimed Omri, the commander of the army, king over Israel. 17 Then Omri and all the Israelites marched up from Gibbethon and besieged Tirzah. 18 When Zimri saw that the city was captured, he entered the citadel of the royal palace and burned it down upon himself. So he died 19 because of the sins he had committed, doing evil in the sight of the LORD and following the example of Jeroboam and the sin he had committed and had caused Israel to commit. 20 As for the rest of the acts of Zimri and the treason he committed, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
News of Zimri’s coup reaches the army encamped at Gibbethon. The troops proclaim their commander Omri king, then march with him against Tirzah.

When Zimri sees that the city has fallen, he enters the palace citadel and burns it down upon himself. His reign has lasted seven days.

The narrator connects his end with his own sin and his continuation of Jeroboam’s example. Taking the throne by violence has not given him either lasting security or a different direction for the kingdom.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill understand the reference to Zimri’s sins as reaching beyond the few days of his reign. They consider his earlier life and his support of the existing worship part of the assessment.

Their reading explains why a short reign still receives a moral evaluation. The narrative’s central concern is not how long he possesses power, but the course he follows with it.

passages.title: 1 Kings 16:21-28
passages.section_title: What does Omri establish, and what does he fail to change?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 At that time the people of Israel were divided: Half of the people supported Tibni son of Ginath as king, and half supported Omri. 22 But the followers of Omri proved stronger than those of Tibni son of Ginath. So Tibni died and Omri became king. 23 In the thirty-first year of Asa’s reign over Judah, Omri became king of Israel, and he reigned twelve years, six of them in Tirzah. 24 He bought the hill of Samaria from Shemer for two talents of silver and built a city there, calling it Samaria after the name of Shemer, who had owned the hill. 25 But Omri did evil in the sight of the LORD and acted more wickedly than all who were before him. 26 For he walked in all the ways of Jeroboam son of Nebat and in his sins, which he caused Israel to commit, provoking the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger with their worthless idols. 27 As for the rest of the acts of Omri, along with his accomplishments and the might he exercised, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel? 28 And Omri rested with his fathers and was buried in Samaria, and his son Ahab reigned in his place.

So Tibni died and Omri became king. 23 In the thirty-first year of Asa’s reign over Judah, Omri became king of Israel, and he reigned twelve years, six of them in Tirzah. 24 He bought the hill of Samaria from Shemer for two talents of silver and built a city there, calling it Samaria after the name of Shemer, who had owned the hill.

25 But Omri did evil in the sight of the LORD and acted more wickedly than all who were before him. 26 For he walked in all the ways of Jeroboam son of Nebat and in his sins, which he caused Israel to commit, provoking the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger with their worthless idols. 27 As for the rest of the acts of Omri, along with his accomplishments and the might he exercised, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel? 28 And Omri rested with his fathers and was buried in Samaria, and his son Ahab reigned in his place.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Israel is divided between supporters of Tibni and Omri. Omri’s supporters prevail, Tibni dies, and Omri becomes king. His twelve-year reign includes six years in Tirzah.

Omri buys a hill from Shemer for two talents of silver and builds a city there, naming it Samaria after the former owner. He is eventually buried in that city, and his son Ahab succeeds him.

The account recognizes his building work and might but gives a severe assessment of his devotion: he does more evil than his predecessors and continues Jeroboam’s ways. Establishing a city does not establish faithfulness to God.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill count Omri’s reign from the earlier struggle for power, explaining the dates in terms of a contested period followed by sole rule.

Henry emphasizes that power and renown can coexist with serious wrongdoing. The account measures Omri by his response to God, alongside the strength and accomplishments mentioned in his royal record.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Kings 16:29-34
passages.section_title: How does Ahab deepen Israel’s departure from God?

versions.label: BSB

34 In Ahab’s days, Hiel the Bethelite rebuilt Jericho. At the cost of Abiram his firstborn he laid its foundation, and at the cost of Segub his youngest he set up its gates, according to the word that the LORD had spoken through Joshua son of Nun.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Ahab son of Omri reigns twenty-two years in Samaria and exceeds his predecessors in evil. He marries Jezebel, daughter of Ethbaal king of the Sidonians, and proceeds to worship Baal.

He builds a temple and altar for Baal in Samaria and sets up an Asherah pole. The account presents this as a further step beyond Jeroboam’s sin, provoking the LORD more than the earlier kings had done.

A final notice records Hiel rebuilding Jericho at the cost of his sons Abiram and Segub. The narrator expressly connects those losses with the word God had spoken through Joshua.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley distinguish Ahab’s worship of other gods from the earlier attempt to worship Israel’s God through the calves. The new king does not merely preserve the existing departure; he deepens it.

Wesley and Gill read Hiel’s losses as the fulfillment of Joshua’s warning. The account places this disregard of an earlier word alongside the king’s disregard of the LORD. It records the cost to Hiel’s sons without describing the manner of their deaths.
passages.god_plan_html:
The earlier word is found in Joshua 6:26, which specifically warns of the cost to the firstborn and youngest son of the person who rebuilds Jericho. Kings explicitly identifies the connection.

Hebrews 11:30 recalls the other side of Jericho’s story: its walls fell through faith as the people followed God’s direction. Read together, these passages present a meaningful contrast between responding to God in faith and pressing ahead against His warning.

passages.title: 1 Kings 17:1-7
passages.section_title: Who sustains Elijah when the rain stops?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now Elijah the Tishbite, who was among the settlers of Gilead, said to Ahab, “As surely as the LORD, the God of Israel, lives, before whom I stand, there will be neither dew nor rain in these years except at my word!” 2 Then a revelation from the LORD came to Elijah: 3 “Leave here, turn eastward, and hide yourself by the Brook of Cherith, east of the Jordan. 4 And you are to drink from the brook, and I have commanded the ravens to feed you there.” 5 So Elijah did what the LORD had told him, and he went and lived by the Brook of Cherith, east of the Jordan. 6 The ravens would bring him bread and meat in the morning and evening, and he would drink from the brook. 7 Some time later, however, the brook dried up because there had been no rain in the land.
paragraphs: 1 Now Elijah the Tishbite, who was among the settlers of Gilead, said to Ahab, “As surely as the LORD, the God of Israel, lives, before whom I stand, there will be neither dew nor rain in these years except at my word!”

2 Then a revelation from the LORD came to Elijah: 3 “Leave here, turn eastward, and hide yourself by the Brook of Cherith, east of the Jordan. 4 And you are to drink from the brook, and I have commanded the ravens to feed you there.” 5 So Elijah did what the LORD had told him, and he went and lived by the Brook of Cherith, east of the Jordan. 6 The ravens would bring him bread and meat in the morning and evening, and he would drink from the brook. 7 Some time later, however, the brook dried up because there had been no rain in the land.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Elijah the Tishbite appears before Ahab and announces that neither dew nor rain will come except at his word. He speaks as a servant of the living LORD, the God of Israel, in the setting of Ahab’s turn to Baal.

The drought fits the warning in Deuteronomy 11:16–17: turning to other gods would bring the shutting of the heavens and the loss of the land’s produce.

The LORD then sends Elijah into hiding beside the Brook of Cherith, east of the Jordan. Ravens bring bread and meat morning and evening, and he drinks from the brook. Eventually it dries up too. God’s servant is being sustained within the same drought he has announced.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill connect Elijah’s announcement with his prayer, drawing on James’ later account. They read his words as service to God’s purpose, rather than independent control of the weather.

Henry emphasizes the unexpected provision through ravens and the need for continuing dependence when the brook dries. The supply comes as God directs it, and Elijah must continue following His word as circumstances change.
passages.god_plan_html:
James 5:16–18 explicitly returns to Elijah’s prayer. James stresses that Elijah was a person like other believers, yet his earnest prayer was effective: rain stopped, and later prayer accompanied its return.

The New Testament therefore presents the episode as encouragement to pray, with the power resting in God. Elijah’s place in the story is that of a servant whose prayer matters within what God is doing, not a man possessing a power separate from Him.
passages.current_position_html: Our [Prayer and Faith](../studies/prayer-and-faith.html) study reads Elijah’s prayer as a response to God’s declared purposes, rather than a way of producing whatever outcome a person wants. The drought belongs to God’s warning about idolatry; Elijah serves the word of the God to whom he prays.

passages.title: 1 Kings 17:8-16
passages.section_title: How can a widow with almost nothing provide for Elijah?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 Then the word of the LORD came to Elijah: 9 “Get up and go to Zarephath of Sidon, and stay there. Behold, I have commanded a widow there to provide for you.” 10 So Elijah got up and went to Zarephath. When he arrived at the city gate, there was a widow gathering sticks. Elijah called to her and said, “Please bring me a little water in a cup, so that I may drink.” 11 And as she was going to get it, he called to her and said, “Please bring me a piece of bread.” 12 But she replied, “As surely as the LORD your God lives, I have no bread—only a handful of flour in a jar and a little oil in a jug. Look, I am gathering a couple of sticks to take home and prepare a meal for myself and my son, so that we may eat it and die.” 13 “Do not be afraid,” Elijah said to her. “Go and do as you have said. But first make me a small cake of bread from what you have, and bring it out to me. Afterward, make some for yourself and your son, 14 for this is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘The jar of flour will not be exhausted and the jug of oil will not run dry until the day the LORD sends rain upon the face of the earth.’” 15 So she went and did according to the word of Elijah, and there was food every day for Elijah and the woman and her household. 16 The jar of flour was not exhausted and the jug of oil did not run dry, according to the word that the LORD had spoken through Elijah.

Look, I am gathering a couple of sticks to take home and prepare a meal for myself and my son, so that we may eat it and die.”

13 “Do not be afraid,” Elijah said to her. “Go and do as you have said. But first make me a small cake of bread from what you have, and bring it out to me. Afterward, make some for yourself and your son, 14 for this is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘The jar of flour will not be exhausted and the jug of oil will not run dry until the day the LORD sends rain upon the face of the earth.’” 15 So she went and did according to the word of Elijah, and there was food every day for Elijah and the woman and her household. 16 The jar of flour was not exhausted and the jug of oil did not run dry, according to the word that the LORD had spoken through Elijah.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
God sends Elijah to Zarephath of Sidon and tells him a widow there will provide for him. At the city gate he finds her gathering sticks and asks for water and bread.

Her situation is desperate. She has only a handful of flour and a little oil, enough for what she expects to be a last meal for herself and her son. Elijah tells her not to fear and asks her to make him a small cake first.

The request comes with a specific word from the LORD: her flour and oil will not run out before the rain returns. She acts on that word, and her household and Elijah have food day after day. The provision matches the promise.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley, Henry and Gill understand the widow’s response as trust in the promise brought by Elijah. Her lack of resources makes the dependence especially clear.

The promise is essential to the scene. Elijah is not merely demanding that a hungry household feed him without assurance; he brings a word that God will sustain them. That particular promise should govern how the request is understood.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus expressly recalls this widow in Luke 4:24–30. Speaking in Nazareth, He notes that many widows were in Israel during the famine, yet Elijah was sent to the widow in Zarephath of Sidon.

His example makes the reach of God’s mercy unmistakable. God’s work is not something a hometown or a nation can possess as its exclusive claim. In the larger story, this household outside Israel receives His help, and Jesus uses that history to challenge the expectations of His own hearers.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Kings 17:17-24
passages.section_title: What happens when the widow’s son dies?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 Later, the son of the woman who owned the house became ill, and his sickness grew worse and worse, until no breath remained in him. 18 “O man of God,” said the woman to Elijah, “what have you done to me? Have you come to remind me of my iniquity and cause the death of my son?” 19 But Elijah said to her, “Give me your son.” So he took him from her arms, carried him to the upper room where he was staying, and laid him on his own bed. 20 Then he cried out to the LORD, “O LORD my God, have You also brought tragedy on this widow who has opened her home to me, by causing her son to die?” 21 Then he stretched himself out over the child three times and cried out to the LORD, “O LORD my God, please let this boy’s life return to him!” 22 And the LORD listened to the voice of Elijah, and the child’s life returned to him, and he lived. 23 Then Elijah took the child, brought him down from the upper room into the house, and gave him to his mother. “Look, your son is alive,” Elijah declared. 24 Then the woman said to Elijah, “Now I know that you are a man of God and that the word of the LORD from your mouth is truth.”

21 Then he stretched himself out over the child three times and cried out to the LORD, “O LORD my God, please let this boy’s life return to him!” 22 And the LORD listened to the voice of Elijah, and the child’s life returned to him, and he lived. 23 Then Elijah took the child, brought him down from the upper room into the house, and gave him to his mother. “Look, your son is alive,” Elijah declared. 24 Then the woman said to Elijah, “Now I know that you are a man of God and that the word of the LORD from your mouth is truth.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the household has been sustained through the famine, the widow’s son becomes gravely ill and dies. In her grief she asks whether Elijah has come to bring her sin to remembrance and cause her son’s death. Those are her anguished questions, not a separate explanation supplied by the narrator.

Elijah carries the boy to his room and cries out to the LORD. He stretches himself over the child three times and asks that the boy’s life return. The LORD hears, and the child lives.

Elijah gives him back to his mother. Her final response brings the chapter’s focus into view: she now knows that he is a man of God and that the LORD’s word from his mouth is true.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley emphasizes that faithful service does not prevent severe affliction. Henry likewise begins by acknowledging that faith and obedience do not exclude suffering and death.

Gill reads the event as an actual return from death and the widow’s closing words as renewed certainty about Elijah’s message. The account locates the power in the LORD hearing prayer; it gives no instruction to turn Elijah’s posture or the number three into a technique for controlling life and death.
passages.god_plan_html:
A closely related scene appears in Luke 7:11–17. Jesus meets a widow whose only son has died, acts with compassion, raises the young man and gives him back to his mother. The people recognize a great prophet and praise God for visiting His people.

The parallel connects care for a grieving widow with God’s power over death. It also brings Jesus’ authority into view: Elijah pleads with the LORD, while Jesus directly commands the young man to rise. The earlier account prepares readers to recognize both the compassion and the greater authority shown in Jesus.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Kings 18:1-16
passages.section_title: Why is Obadiah afraid to tell Ahab that Elijah has returned?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 After a long time, in the third year of the drought, the word of the LORD came to Elijah: “Go and present yourself to Ahab, and I will send rain upon the face of the earth.” 2 So Elijah went to present himself to Ahab. The famine was severe in Samaria, 3 and Ahab summoned Obadiah, who was in charge of the palace. (Now Obadiah greatly feared the LORD, 4 for when Jezebel had slaughtered the prophets of the LORD, Obadiah had taken a hundred prophets and hidden them, fifty men per cave, providing them with food and water.) 5 Then Ahab said to Obadiah, “Go throughout the land to every spring and every valley. Perhaps we will find grass to keep the horses and mules alive so that we will not have to destroy any livestock.” 6 So they divided the land to explore. Ahab went one way by himself, and Obadiah went the other way by himself. 7 Now as Obadiah went on his way, Elijah suddenly met him. When Obadiah recognized him, he fell facedown and said, “Is it you, my lord Elijah?” 8 “It is I,” he answered. “Go tell your master, ‘Elijah is here!’” 9 But Obadiah replied, “How have I sinned, that you are handing your servant over to Ahab to put me to death? 10 As surely as the LORD your God lives, there is no nation or kingdom where my lord has not sent someone to search for you. When they said, ‘He is not here,’ he made that kingdom or nation swear that they had not found you. 11 And now you say, ‘Go tell your master that Elijah is here!’ 12 I do not know where the Spirit of the LORD may carry you off when I leave you. Then when I go and tell Ahab and he does not find you, he will kill me. But I, your servant, have feared the LORD from my youth. 13 Was it not reported to my lord what I did when Jezebel slaughtered the prophets of the LORD? I hid a hundred prophets of the LORD, fifty men per cave, and I provided them with food and water. 14 And now you say, ‘Go tell your lord that Elijah is here!’ He will kill me!” 15 Then Elijah said, “As surely as the LORD of Hosts lives, before whom I stand, I will present myself to Ahab today.” 16 So Obadiah went to inform Ahab, who went to meet Elijah.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The LORD tells Elijah to present himself to Ahab and promises to send rain. The famine is severe, and Ahab and his palace official Obadiah are searching for grass to keep the livestock alive.

The narrator introduces an important distinction within the royal household: Obadiah greatly fears the LORD. When Jezebel killed God’s prophets, he hid a hundred of them, fifty in each cave, and supplied food and water.

Elijah meets Obadiah and asks him to announce his presence. Obadiah fears that Elijah may disappear before Ahab arrives and that the king will kill him for the failed report. Elijah gives a solemn assurance that he will meet Ahab that day. Obadiah then carries the message.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Henry emphasize Obadiah’s protection of God’s servants in an unexpected and dangerous setting. His place in Ahab’s household does not erase the narrator’s testimony to his faithfulness.

Gill understands his fear in light of the king’s search for Elijah and the risk attached to an apparently false report. The exchange shows a faithful servant facing real danger, rather than simply someone indifferent to God.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Kings 18:17-24
passages.section_title: Why must the people stop wavering between the LORD and Baal?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 When Ahab saw Elijah, he said to him, “Is that you, O troubler of Israel?” 18 “I have not troubled Israel,” Elijah replied, “but you and your father’s house have, for you have forsaken the commandments of the LORD and have followed the Baals. 19 Now summon all Israel to meet me on Mount Carmel, along with the four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal and the four hundred prophets of Asherah who eat at Jezebel’s table.” 20 So Ahab summoned all the Israelites and assembled the prophets on Mount Carmel. 21 Then Elijah approached all the people and said, “How long will you waver between two opinions? If the LORD is God, follow Him. But if Baal is God, follow him.” But the people did not answer a word. 22 Then Elijah said to the people, “I am the only remaining prophet of the LORD, but Baal has four hundred and fifty prophets. 23 Get two bulls for us. Let the prophets of Baal choose one bull for themselves, cut it into pieces, and place it on the wood but not light the fire. And I will prepare the other bull and place it on the wood but not light the fire. 24 Then you may call on the name of your god, and I will call on the name of the LORD. The God who answers by fire, He is God.” And all the people answered, “What you say is good.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Ahab calls Elijah the troubler of Israel. Elijah answers that the king’s house has caused the trouble by abandoning the LORD’s commands and following the Baals. He calls for the people and the rival prophets to gather at Mount Carmel.

Elijah challenges the people’s divided loyalty. The Hebrew verb behind waver is pasach, pronounced pah-SAHKH. Brown–Driver–Briggs identifies its use here as a picture of limping. The people are trying to move between loyalties instead of following the LORD wholeheartedly.

The test will involve two bulls and two altars, with neither party lighting a fire. The God who answers by fire is to be acknowledged as God. The people agree to the proposal.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry understands the challenge as a call to settle both belief and practice: acknowledging the LORD means following Him. Gill similarly emphasizes that the people cannot keep alternating their allegiance.

Wesley reads Elijah’s statement about being alone as referring to the prophet openly present for this confrontation. The earlier account of the hundred hidden prophets already shows that he is not literally the only living servant of the LORD.

passages.title: 1 Kings 18:25-29
passages.section_title: What happens when Baal’s prophets call for an answer?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 25 Then Elijah said to the prophets of Baal, “Since you are so numerous, choose for yourselves one bull and prepare it first. Then call on the name of your god, but do not light the fire.” 26 And they took the bull that was given them, prepared it, and called on the name of Baal from morning until noon, shouting, “O Baal, answer us!” But there was no sound, and no one answered as they leaped around the altar they had made. 27 At noon Elijah began to taunt them, saying, “Shout louder, for he is a god! Perhaps he is deep in thought, or occupied, or on a journey. Perhaps he is sleeping and must be awakened!” 28 So they shouted louder and cut themselves with knives and lances, as was their custom, until the blood gushed over them. 29 Midday passed, and they kept on raving until the time of the evening sacrifice. But there was no response; no one answered, no one paid attention.
paragraphs: 25 Then Elijah said to the prophets of Baal, “Since you are so numerous, choose for yourselves one bull and prepare it first. Then call on the name of your god, but do not light the fire.” 26 And they took the bull that was given them, prepared it, and called on the name of Baal from morning until noon, shouting, “O Baal, answer us!” But there was no sound, and no one answered as they leaped around the altar they had made. 27 At noon Elijah began to taunt them, saying, “Shout louder, for he is a god! Perhaps he is deep in thought, or occupied, or on a journey. Perhaps he is sleeping and must be awakened!” 28 So they shouted louder and cut themselves with knives and lances, as was their custom, until the blood gushed over them. 29 Midday passed, and they kept on raving until the time of the evening sacrifice. But there was no response; no one answered, no one paid attention.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The prophets of Baal choose their bull and prepare it without lighting the wood. From morning until noon they call for an answer and move around the altar, but there is no response.

Elijah taunts them with possibilities that expose the absence of an answer: perhaps their god is occupied, away or asleep. They cry louder and cut themselves, continuing until the time of the evening sacrifice.

The narrator closes the scene with repeated silence. Their effort has not produced a voice, an answer or attention from the god they call upon.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill read the escalating cries and actions as unsuccessful attempts to obtain a response. Henry contrasts them with the prayer Elijah will offer for God’s glory and the people’s good.

The account makes the absence of an answer the central fact. The number of worshippers, the intensity of their efforts and the length of the ceremony cannot establish Baal’s power.

passages.title: 1 Kings 18:30-40
passages.section_title: What does Elijah ask God to make known?

Then he dug a trench around the altar large enough to hold two seahs of seed. 33 Next, he arranged the wood, cut up the bull, placed it on the wood, 34 and said, “Fill four waterpots and pour the water on the offering and on the wood.” “Do it a second time,” he said, and they did it a second time. “Do it a third time,” he said, and they did it a third time. 35 So the water ran down around the altar and even filled the trench. 36 At the time of the evening sacrifice, Elijah the prophet approached the altar and said, “O LORD, God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, let it be known this day that You are God in Israel and that I am Your servant and have done all these things at Your command. 37 Answer me, O LORD! section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Elijah repairs the LORD’s broken altar with twelve stones, explicitly corresponding to the tribes descended from Jacob. The political division of the kingdoms has not removed that shared identity.

He prepares the sacrifice and has water poured over it repeatedly until the trench is filled. His prayer asks that the people know the LORD is God, that Elijah is His servant and that these actions follow God’s command. He asks for their hearts to be turned back.

Fire consumes the sacrifice, wood, stones, dust and water. The people fall facedown and acknowledge the LORD as God. Elijah then has the prophets of Baal seized and brings them to the Kishon Valley, where they are killed.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley sees the twelve stones as recalling the covenant with all the tribes. Gill emphasizes that Elijah’s prayer claims obedience to God’s command, rather than a display arranged for his own importance.

Henry distinguishes the crowd’s acknowledgment from certainty that every individual has undergone lasting conversion. Their words are significant, while the continuing story will show how deeply the response takes root.

Gill understands the execution of Baal’s prophets within Israel’s covenant judgment against those leading the people to other gods, described in Deuteronomy 13:1–5. He treats Elijah as acting in a specific prophetic role within that setting.
passages.god_plan_html:
The aim of the prayer is a return of the heart, not simply astonishment at fire. A related purpose appears in 1 Thessalonians 1:8–10, where the believers’ response is described as turning from idols to serve the living and true God and await His Son, Jesus.

The settings differ, but the direction is shared: people leave false worship and give their allegiance to God. The New Testament places that response within the hope of the risen Son and His deliverance. The greater purpose is a people who know whom they serve.

passages.title: 1 Kings 18:41-46
passages.section_title: How does the rain return after the long drought?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 41 And Elijah said to Ahab, “Go up, eat and drink, for there is the sound of a heavy rain.” 42 So Ahab went up to eat and drink. But Elijah climbed to the summit of Carmel, bent down on the ground, and put his face between his knees. 43 “Go and look toward the sea,” he said to his servant. So the servant went and looked, and he said, “There is nothing there.” Seven times Elijah said, “Go back.” 44 On the seventh time the servant reported, “There is a cloud as small as a man’s hand rising from the sea.” And Elijah replied, “Go and tell Ahab, ‘Prepare your chariot and go down before the rain stops you.’” 45 Meanwhile, the sky grew dark with clouds and wind, and a heavy rain began to fall. So Ahab rode away and went to Jezreel. 46 And the hand of the LORD came upon Elijah, and he tucked his cloak into his belt and ran ahead of Ahab all the way to Jezreel.
paragraphs: 41 And Elijah said to Ahab, “Go up, eat and drink, for there is the sound of a heavy rain.” 42 So Ahab went up to eat and drink. But Elijah climbed to the summit of Carmel, bent down on the ground, and put his face between his knees. 43 “Go and look toward the sea,” he said to his servant. So the servant went and looked, and he said, “There is nothing there.” Seven times Elijah said, “Go back.” 44 On the seventh time the servant reported, “There is a cloud as small as a man’s hand rising from the sea.” And Elijah replied, “Go and tell Ahab, ‘Prepare your chariot and go down before the rain stops you.’”

45 Meanwhile, the sky grew dark with clouds and wind, and a heavy rain began to fall. So Ahab rode away and went to Jezreel. 46 And the hand of the LORD came upon Elijah, and he tucked his cloak into his belt and ran ahead of Ahab all the way to Jezreel.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Elijah tells Ahab that heavy rain is coming. While the king goes to eat and drink, Elijah climbs Carmel and bows low to the ground with his face between his knees.

He sends his servant to look toward the sea. At first there is nothing to report. On the seventh visit, the servant sees a small cloud. Elijah tells him to warn Ahab to leave before the rain delays him.

The sky darkens, wind rises and heavy rain falls. Ahab heads to Jezreel, and the LORD strengthens Elijah to run ahead of him. The rain promised at the beginning of the chapter has come.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Gill read Elijah’s low posture and repeated watching as earnest, continuing prayer. His confidence concerns the rain God has already said He will send.

Wesley also emphasizes God’s strengthening in the final scene. The account joins the prophet’s obedience and prayer with the LORD’s power to end the drought.
passages.god_plan_html:
James 5:17–18 explicitly connects both the drought and its ending with Elijah’s prayer. The heavens give rain again, and the earth produces its crops.

That connection shows why the promise of rain and the act of praying belong together. God announces what He will do, and Elijah continues to seek it from Him. James uses this history to encourage prayer by ordinary believers; the power is God’s, and the servant’s dependence is real.
passages.current_position_html: Our [Prayer and Faith](../studies/prayer-and-faith.html) study understands Elijah’s effective prayer in terms of alignment with God’s declared will. Here God promises rain before Elijah returns to Ahab. His prayer expresses dependence on that promise, rather than an attempt to create a result apart from God’s purpose.

passages.title: 1 Kings 19:1-8
passages.section_title: How does God care for Elijah when he has had enough?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now Ahab told Jezebel everything that Elijah had done and how he had killed all the prophets with the sword. 2 So Jezebel sent a messenger to Elijah, saying, “May the gods deal with me, and ever so severely, if by this time tomorrow I have not made your life like the lives of those you killed!” 3 And Elijah was afraid and ran for his life. When he came to Beersheba in Judah, he left his servant there, 4 while he himself went a day’s journey into the wilderness. He sat down under a broom tree and prayed that he might die. “I have had enough, LORD,” he said. “Take my life, for I am no better than my fathers.” 5 Then he lay down under the broom tree and fell asleep. Suddenly an angel touched him and said, “Get up and eat.” 6 And he looked around, and there by his head was a cake of bread baked over hot coals, and a jar of water. So he ate and drank and lay down again. 7 A second time the angel of the LORD returned and touched him, saying, “Get up and eat, or the journey will be too much for you.” 8 So he got up and ate and drank. And strengthened by that food, he walked forty days and forty nights until he reached Horeb, the mountain of God.

When he came to Beersheba in Judah, he left his servant there, 4 while he himself went a day’s journey into the wilderness. 5 Then he lay down under the broom tree and fell asleep. Suddenly an angel touched him and said, “Get up and eat.” 6 And he looked around, and there by his head was a cake of bread baked over hot coals, and a jar of water. So he ate and drank and lay down again. 7 A second time the angel of the LORD returned and touched him, saying, “Get up and eat, or the journey will be too much for you.” 8 So he got up and ate and drank. And strengthened by that food, he walked forty days and forty nights until he reached Horeb, the mountain of God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jezebel hears what has happened to Baal’s prophets and threatens Elijah’s life. Afraid, he runs to Beersheba, leaves his servant there and goes farther into the wilderness.

Under a broom tree he asks the LORD to take his life. The account allows his exhaustion and despair to be heard after the public confrontation on Carmel.

An angel wakes him and provides food and water. After more sleep, the angel of the LORD returns and tells him to eat because the journey is too much for him. Strengthened by that food, Elijah travels forty days and nights to Horeb. God cares for the servant who feels he can go no further.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry sees Elijah’s flight as a failure of confidence after his bold service on Carmel. Wesley explicitly resists blaming him for fleeing persecution and points to the angel’s provision as evidence of God’s care for his journey.

These readings differ over how to assess the flight. Both recognize that the prophet’s strength is dependent on God. The text gives particular attention to the food, rest and help he receives in his weakness.
passages.god_plan_html:
Elijah’s forty-day wilderness journey and the care of angels have a later counterpart in Matthew 4:1–11. Jesus spends forty days and nights fasting in the wilderness, remains faithful under temptation, and is ministered to by angels afterward.

This is a parallel, with different circumstances and a different order of events. It places Elijah’s experience within a wider story of wilderness testing and God’s provision, while the account of Jesus brings the Son’s faithful obedience into view.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Kings 19:9-14
passages.section_title: Why does God speak after the wind, earthquake and fire?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 There Elijah entered a cave and spent the night. And the word of the LORD came to him, saying, “What are you doing here, Elijah?” 10 “I have been very zealous for the LORD, the God of Hosts,” he replied, “but the Israelites have forsaken Your covenant, torn down Your altars, and killed Your prophets with the sword. I am the only one left, and they are seeking my life as well.” 11 Then the LORD said, “Go out and stand on the mountain before the LORD. Behold, the LORD is about to pass by.” And a great and mighty wind tore into the mountains and shattered the rocks before the LORD, but the LORD was not in the wind. After the wind there was an earthquake, but the LORD was not in the earthquake. 12 After the earthquake there was a fire, but the LORD was not in the fire. And after the fire came a still, small voice. 13 When Elijah heard it, he wrapped his face in his cloak and went out and stood at the mouth of the cave. Suddenly a voice came to him and said, “What are you doing here, Elijah?” 14 “I have been very zealous for the LORD, the God of Hosts,” he replied, “but the Israelites have forsaken Your covenant, torn down Your altars, and killed Your prophets with the sword. I am the only one left, and they are seeking my life as well.”

I am the only one left, and they are seeking my life as well.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
At Horeb, Elijah spends the night in a cave. God asks what he is doing there. Elijah describes his zeal, Israel’s rejection of the covenant and the threat to his life. He says he is the only one left.

God tells him to stand before Him. A powerful wind, an earthquake and fire pass, but the LORD is not in those events. Afterward comes a still, small voice. Elijah covers his face and stands at the cave’s entrance.

The question is repeated, and Elijah repeats his complaint. God has met him, and the answer that follows will address both his task and his sense of being alone.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry hears correction in God’s question and sees the gentle voice as carrying a power the terrifying events do not. Wesley reads the scene as showing that God accomplishes His work in His own way, by His Spirit.

Gill notes that Scripture elsewhere does associate God’s presence with wind, fire and earthquake. The point here is how God chooses to meet Elijah in this scene. It cannot be made into a rule that He always speaks through one kind of experience.
passages.god_plan_html:
The setting recalls Moses’ encounter with God in Exodus 33:18–23: the LORD passes by, and Moses is sheltered as His glory is revealed. The parallels include the mountain setting, God’s passing presence and the servant’s limited ability to behold Him.

Later, Moses and Elijah appear together with Jesus in Luke 9:28–36, speaking about His coming departure at Jerusalem. The voice from the cloud directs the disciples to listen to God’s Son. These earlier servants who encountered God are brought into a scene centered on Jesus and what He will accomplish.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Kings 19:15-18
passages.section_title: Is Elijah really the only faithful person left?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 Then the LORD said to him, “Go back by the way you came, and go to the Desert of Damascus. When you arrive, you are to anoint Hazael as king over Aram. 16 You are also to anoint Jehu son of Nimshi as king over Israel and Elisha son of Shaphat from Abel-meholah to succeed you as prophet. 17 Then Jehu will put to death whoever escapes the sword of Hazael, and Elisha will put to death whoever escapes the sword of Jehu. 18 Nevertheless, I have reserved seven thousand in Israel—all whose knees have not bowed to Baal and whose mouths have not kissed him.”
paragraphs: 15 Then the LORD said to him, “Go back by the way you came, and go to the Desert of Damascus. When you arrive, you are to anoint Hazael as king over Aram. 16 You are also to anoint Jehu son of Nimshi as king over Israel and Elisha son of Shaphat from Abel-meholah to succeed you as prophet. 17 Then Jehu will put to death whoever escapes the sword of Hazael, and Elisha will put to death whoever escapes the sword of Jehu. 18 Nevertheless, I have reserved seven thousand in Israel—all whose knees have not bowed to Baal and whose mouths have not kissed him.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The LORD gives Elijah a further assignment: return and appoint Hazael as king of Aram, Jehu as king of Israel and Elisha as the prophet who will succeed him. God’s response includes continuing work, coming judgment and a successor.

Then comes the correction to Elijah’s isolation: God has reserved seven thousand in Israel who have not bowed to Baal or kissed him in worship.

Elijah does not see the whole picture. The LORD knows the people who remain faithful, and the future of His work does not depend on this one servant carrying it alone.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry emphasizes that God’s faithful people may be hidden from the prophet’s view. Wesley likewise reads the answer as correcting Elijah’s belief that he alone remains.

Gill discusses the preservation of these worshippers in connection with the judgment to come as well as the answer to Elijah’s present complaint. The assurance stands beside the announcement of judgment: God is still preserving people for Himself.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 11:1–6 directly quotes Elijah’s complaint and God’s answer about the seven thousand. Paul uses the passage while denying that God has rejected His people.

He then identifies a continuing remnant chosen by grace in his own day. The New Testament itself supplies the larger connection: widespread unfaithfulness does not mean God has lost sight of His people or that His gracious purpose has failed. Elijah’s limited view is corrected by what God has preserved.

passages.title: 1 Kings 19:19-21
passages.section_title: What does Elisha leave behind when he follows Elijah?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 So Elijah departed and found Elisha son of Shaphat. He was plowing with twelve teams of oxen, and he was with the twelfth team. Elijah passed by him and threw his cloak around him. 20 So Elisha left the oxen, ran after Elijah, and said, “Please let me kiss my father and mother goodbye, and then I will follow you.” “Go on back,” Elijah replied, “for what have I done to you?” 21 So Elisha turned back from him, took his pair of oxen, and slaughtered them. Using the oxen’s equipment for fuel, he cooked the meat and gave it to the people, and they ate. Then he set out to follow and serve Elijah.
paragraphs: 19 So Elijah departed and found Elisha son of Shaphat. He was plowing with twelve teams of oxen, and he was with the twelfth team. Elijah passed by him and threw his cloak around him. 20 So Elisha left the oxen, ran after Elijah, and said, “Please let me kiss my father and mother goodbye, and then I will follow you.” “Go on back,” Elijah replied, “for what have I done to you?” 21 So Elisha turned back from him, took his pair of oxen, and slaughtered them. Using the oxen’s equipment for fuel, he cooked the meat and gave it to the people, and they ate. Then he set out to follow and serve Elijah.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Elijah finds Elisha son of Shaphat plowing with twelve teams of oxen, working with the twelfth. He throws his cloak around him, and Elisha understands that he is being called to follow.

Elisha asks to bid his parents goodbye. He then slaughters his pair of oxen, uses their equipment as fuel, cooks the meat and shares it with the people.

He sets out to follow and serve Elijah. The departure is concrete: the work and equipment that occupied him are left behind as he begins the service God has named for him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill understand the destruction of the working equipment and the shared meal as a decisive departure from Elisha’s earlier occupation. His response expresses willingness to undertake the new service.

Henry emphasizes that he is called while doing ordinary, honest work. He leaves it to accompany Elijah, beginning with service and learning as the older prophet’s companion.
passages.god_plan_html:
The combination of a plow, a family farewell and a call to follow appears again in Luke 9:57–62. Jesus speaks of the urgency of God’s kingdom and warns against putting a hand to the plow while looking back.

The scenes offer a clear parallel in the cost and direction of following. Elisha’s departure shows a real change of commitment; Jesus calls His followers to a similarly undivided response to the kingdom He proclaims. The focus is the response to the call, rather than one outward action every disciple must reproduce.

passages.title: 1 Kings 20:1-12
passages.section_title: Why does Ahab refuse Ben-hadad’s increasing demands?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now Ben-hadad king of Aram assembled his entire army. Accompanied by thirty-two kings with their horses and chariots, he marched up, besieged Samaria, and waged war against it. 2 Then he sent messengers into the city to Ahab king of Israel, 3 saying, “This is what Ben-hadad says: ‘Your silver and gold are mine, and your best wives and children are mine!’” 4 And the king of Israel replied, “Just as you say, my lord the king: I am yours, along with all that I have.” 5 The messengers came back and said, “This is what Ben-hadad says: ‘I have sent to you to demand your silver, your gold, your wives, and your children. 6 But about this time tomorrow I will send my servants to search your palace and the houses of your servants. They will seize and carry away all that is precious to you.’” 7 Then the king of Israel summoned all the elders of the land and said, “Please take note and see that this man is looking for trouble, for when he demanded my wives, my children, my silver, and my gold, I did not deny him.” 8 And the elders and the people all said, “Do not listen to him or consent to his terms.” 9 So Ahab answered the messengers of Ben-hadad, “Tell my lord the king, ‘All that you demanded of your servant the first time I will do, but this thing I cannot do.’” So the messengers departed and relayed the message to Ben-hadad. 10 Then Ben-hadad sent another message to Ahab: “May the gods deal with me, and ever so severely, if enough dust remains of Samaria for each of my men to have a handful.” 11 And the king of Israel replied, “Tell him: ‘The one putting on his armor should not boast like one taking it off.’” 12 Ben-hadad received this message while he and the kings were drinking in their tents, and he said to his servants, “Take your positions.” So they stationed themselves against the city.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Ben-hadad king of Aram brings an army and thirty-two allied kings against Samaria. He demands Ahab’s silver, gold, wives and children. Ahab initially submits.

The demands then expand: Ben-hadad will send servants to search the palace and the houses of Ahab’s servants and take what they value. Ahab consults the elders, who advise him to refuse.

Ben-hadad responds with a boast about overwhelming Samaria. Ahab answers with a warning against celebrating victory before the battle is fought. Ben-hadad, drinking with his allies, orders his forces into position.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill understand Ahab’s first answer as accepting subordinate status, rather than necessarily agreeing to hand over his whole household immediately. The next message makes the threatened seizure unmistakable.

Henry emphasizes the danger of Ben-hadad’s confidence and recognizes the sense in Ahab’s reply: the outcome has not yet been decided. The king who sounds strongest before the battle may not be the one who prevails.

passages.title: 1 Kings 20:13-22
passages.section_title: Why does God promise victory to an unfaithful king?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 Meanwhile a prophet approached Ahab king of Israel and declared, “This is what the LORD says: ‘Do you see this entire great army? Behold, I will deliver it into your hand this very day, and you will know that I am the LORD.’” 14 “By whom?” Ahab asked. And the prophet replied, “This is what the LORD says: ‘By the young officers of the district governors.’” “Who will start the battle?” asked Ahab. “You will,” answered the prophet. 15 So Ahab assembled the young officers of the district governors, and there were 232 men. And after them, he assembled the rest of the Israelite troops, 7,000 in all. 16 They marched out at noon while Ben-hadad and the 32 kings allied with him were in their tents getting drunk. 17 And the young officers of the district governors marched out first. Now Ben-hadad had sent out scouts, who reported to him, “Men are marching out of Samaria.” 18 “If they have marched out in peace,” he said, “take them alive. Even if they have marched out for war, take them alive.” 19 Meanwhile, these young officers of the district governors marched out of the city, with the army behind them, 20 and each one struck down his opponent. So the Arameans fled, with the Israelites in pursuit. But Ben-hadad king of Aram escaped on horseback with the cavalry. 21 Then the king of Israel marched out and attacked the horses and chariots, inflicting a great slaughter on the Arameans. 22 Afterward, the prophet approached the king of Israel and said, “Go and strengthen your position, and take note what you must do, for in the spring the king of Aram will come up against you.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
An unnamed prophet brings Ahab a promise: the LORD will deliver the great opposing army into his hand so that he will know who the LORD is. Ahab asks who will lead the action and is told that the young officers of the district governors will go first, with Ahab initiating the battle.

Two hundred thirty-two officers lead out, followed by seven thousand Israelite troops. Ben-hadad is getting drunk with his allies and orders the approaching men captured alive. Instead, the Israelites strike their opponents and the Arameans flee.

Ben-hadad escapes. After the victory, the prophet warns Ahab to strengthen his position because the enemy will return in the spring. Receiving help does not remove the need to heed God’s next word.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley emphasizes that God helps Ahab despite being neglected by him. The purpose includes making the LORD known and preserving His people, rather than rewarding the king’s worthiness.

Gill likewise understands the victory as a demonstration that the LORD can save through a small force. Henry contrasts the confident invaders with the unexpectedly victorious Israelites. The outcome points beyond the apparent balance of power.
passages.god_plan_html:
The purpose of making God known appears elsewhere alongside undeserved help. In Ezekiel 36:22–23, God says He will act for the holiness of His Name, which His people have profaned, so the nations will know Him.

Romans 5:6–10 brings undeserved mercy into focus through Christ dying for the ungodly and reconciling people who were enemies. These are connections in theme, not an equation between military victory and salvation. God’s kindness can come before a person has made himself worthy of it, calling for a response to the One who gives it.

passages.title: 1 Kings 20:23-30
passages.section_title: Can the LORD’s power be confined to the hills?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 23 Meanwhile, the servants of the king of Aram said to him, “Their gods are gods of the hills. That is why they prevailed over us. Instead, we should fight them on the plains; surely then we will prevail. 24 So do this: Dismiss all the kings from their positions and replace them with other officers. 25 And you must raise an army like the one you have lost—horse for horse and chariot for chariot—so we can fight the Israelites on the plain, where we will surely prevail.” And the king approved their plan and acted accordingly. 26 In the spring, Ben-hadad mobilized the Arameans and went up to Aphek to fight against Israel. 27 The Israelites also mobilized, gathered supplies, and marched out to meet them. The Israelites camped before them like two small flocks of goats, while the Arameans covered the countryside. 28 Then the man of God approached the king of Israel and said, “This is what the LORD says: ‘Because the Arameans have said that the LORD is a god of the hills and not of the valleys, I will deliver all this great army into your hand. Then you will know that I am the LORD.’” 29 For seven days the armies camped opposite each other, and on the seventh day the battle ensued, and the Israelites struck down the Arameans—a hundred thousand foot soldiers in one day. 30 The rest of them fled into the city of Aphek, where the wall fell on twenty-seven thousand of the remaining men. Ben-hadad also fled to the city and hid in an inner room.

The Israelites camped before them like two small flocks of goats, while the Arameans covered the countryside. 28 Then the man of God approached the king of Israel and said, “This is what the LORD says: ‘Because the Arameans have said that the LORD is a god of the hills and not of the valleys, I will deliver all this great army into your hand. Then you will know that I am the LORD.’” 29 For seven days the armies camped opposite each other, and on the seventh day the battle ensued, and the Israelites struck down the Arameans—a hundred thousand foot soldiers in one day. 30 The rest of them fled into the city of Aphek, where the wall fell on twenty-seven thousand of the remaining men. Ben-hadad also fled to the city and hid in an inner room.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Ben-hadad’s advisers explain their defeat by claiming that Israel’s gods are gods of the hills. They recommend replacing the allied kings with officers, rebuilding the army and fighting on the plains.

In the spring the armies meet at Aphek. Israel’s force looks like two small flocks of goats beside the Aramean multitude. A man of God declares that the LORD will give victory precisely because the enemy has denied His power in the valleys.

After seven days the battle begins. The account records a hundred thousand Aramean foot soldiers struck down and a wall falling on twenty-seven thousand more at Aphek. Ben-hadad hides in the city. The proposed boundary around God’s power has failed.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley, Henry and Gill read the advisers’ explanation as a misunderstanding of the LORD: His power is not restricted to one kind of terrain.

Gill emphasizes that God is defending the honor of His Name, rather than acting because Ahab has become faithful. The prophet’s stated aim is knowledge of the LORD. Changing the battlefield cannot change who He is.
passages.god_plan_html:
A broader statement of God’s rule appears in Acts 17:24–31. Paul describes the God who made the world as Lord of heaven and earth, giving life to all and ordering the times and places of the nations.

His purpose is that people seek Him, and Paul calls them to repentance in view of the judgment God will carry out through the risen Jesus. The connection extends the concern here beyond one battlefield: God is greater than the limits people assign to Him, and knowing that calls for a response.

passages.title: 1 Kings 20:31-34
passages.section_title: What agreement does Ahab make with the defeated king?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 31 Then the servants of Ben-hadad said to him, “Look now, we have heard that the kings of the house of Israel are merciful. Let us go out to the king of Israel with sackcloth around our waists and ropes around our heads. Perhaps he will spare your life.” 32 So with sackcloth around their waists and ropes around their heads, they went to the king of Israel and said, “Your servant Ben-hadad says, ‘Please spare my life.’” And the king answered, “Is he still alive? He is my brother.” 33 Now the men were looking for a sign of hope, and they quickly grasped at this word and replied, “Yes, your brother Ben-hadad.” “Go and get him!” said the king. Then Ben-hadad came out, and Ahab had him come up into his chariot. 34 Ben-hadad said to him, “I will restore the cities my father took from your father; you may set up your own marketplaces in Damascus, as my father did in Samaria.” “By this treaty I release you,” Ahab replied. So he made a treaty with him and sent him away.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Ben-hadad’s servants appeal to the reputation of Israel’s kings for mercy. Wearing sackcloth and ropes, they ask Ahab to spare their master’s life.

Ahab responds by calling Ben-hadad his brother. The servants seize on the hopeful word, and the defeated king is brought up into Ahab’s chariot.

Ben-hadad offers to return towns taken by his father and allow Ahab marketplaces in Damascus. Ahab makes a treaty and releases him. The next scene will judge that decision in light of what God had determined.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry emphasizes the reversal from Ben-hadad’s proud demands to his plea for life. Wesley reads Ahab’s welcome as giving him both pardon and honor.

Wesley also questions the agreement’s failure to address the dishonor done to God and the harm to Israel. The immediate result is a royal settlement, but political terms alone will not settle the question raised by the prophetic word.

passages.title: 1 Kings 20:35-43
passages.section_title: How does a disguised prophet lead Ahab to judge his own action?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 35 Meanwhile, by the word of the LORD, one of the sons of the prophets said to his companion, “Strike me, please!” But the man refused to strike him. 36 Then the prophet said to him, “Because you have not obeyed the voice of the LORD, as soon as you depart from me a lion will kill you.” And when he left, a lion found him and killed him. 37 Then the prophet found another man and said, “Strike me, please!” So the man struck him and wounded him, 38 and the prophet went and waited on the road for the king, disguising himself with a bandage over his eyes. 39 As the king passed by, he cried out to the king: “Your servant had marched out into the middle of the battle, when suddenly a man came over with a captive and told me, ‘Guard this man! If he goes missing for any reason, your life will be exchanged for his life, or you will weigh out a talent of silver.’ 40 But while your servant was busy here and there, the man disappeared.” And the king of Israel said to him, “So shall your judgment be; you have pronounced it on yourself.” 41 Then the prophet quickly removed the bandage from his eyes, and the king of Israel recognized him as one of the prophets. 42 And the prophet said to the king, “This is what the LORD says: ‘Because you have let slip from your hand the man I had devoted to destruction, your life will be exchanged for his life, and your people for his people.’” 43 Sullen and angry, the king of Israel went home to Samaria.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
By the LORD’s word, a member of the prophetic company asks a companion to strike him. When the man refuses, a warning follows and he is killed by a lion. Another man does strike and wound the prophet, who disguises himself with a bandage.

He then tells Ahab a story about losing a captive he had been ordered to guard, under a penalty of his own life or a talent of silver. Ahab pronounces judgment on the careless guard.

The prophet removes the disguise and delivers the application: Ahab has released the man God had devoted to destruction, and his own life and people will bear the consequence. The king returns to Samaria sullen and angry.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Gill compares the story’s method with Nathan confronting David: the king first judges another person’s case, then discovers its bearing on himself. Henry likewise reads it as a parable designed to expose Ahab’s failure.

Wesley connects the initial refusal and the later royal decision as acts judged by the specific command of God. The scene concerns more than whether sparing someone appears generous; the prophet identifies what Ahab was responsible to do in this case.

The narrative gives the closing verdict without recording every earlier instruction about Ben-hadad. Its clear emphasis is that Ahab cannot treat the victory as permission to set God’s word aside.

passages.title: 1 Kings 21:1-7
passages.section_title: Why does Naboth refuse Ahab’s offer for his vineyard?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Some time after these events, Naboth the Jezreelite owned a vineyard in Jezreel next to the palace of Ahab king of Samaria. 2 So Ahab said to Naboth, “Give me your vineyard to use as a vegetable garden, since it is next to my palace. I will give you a better vineyard in its place—or if you prefer, I will give you its value in silver.” 3 But Naboth replied, “The LORD forbid that I should give you the inheritance of my fathers.” 4 So Ahab went to his palace, sullen and angry because Naboth the Jezreelite had told him, “I will not give you the inheritance of my fathers.” He lay down on his bed, turned his face away, and refused to eat. 5 Soon his wife Jezebel came in and asked, “Why are you so sullen that you refuse to eat?” 6 Ahab answered, “Because I spoke to Naboth the Jezreelite and told him, ‘Give me your vineyard for silver, or if you wish, I will give you another vineyard in its place.’ And he replied, ‘I will not give you my vineyard!’” 7 But his wife Jezebel said to him, “Do you not reign over Israel? Get up, eat some food, and be cheerful, for I will get you the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite.”

Get up, eat some food, and be cheerful, for I will get you the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Naboth owns a vineyard beside Ahab’s palace in Jezreel. The king wants it for a vegetable garden and offers either a better vineyard or payment in silver.

Naboth refuses in the LORD’s name because the vineyard is his ancestral inheritance. The background is the concern for family land in Leviticus 25:23–28 and Numbers 36:7–9: the land belongs to God, and Israel’s inherited holdings are not simply possessions to transfer without regard to that gift.

Ahab returns home sullen and angry, lies down and refuses food. Jezebel responds by questioning whether he really rules Israel and promises to obtain the vineyard for him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill understand Naboth’s refusal as concern for God’s law and his family’s inheritance. They recognize that temporary sale could occur under the law, while a transfer into royal possession could put the family’s recovery of the land in doubt.

Henry focuses on Ahab’s discontent: the resources of a kingdom do not satisfy him while this one desired property remains unavailable. The conflict begins with the king’s unwillingness to accept a limit.

passages.title: 1 Kings 21:8-16
passages.section_title: How are worship and legal procedure used to destroy an innocent man?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 Then Jezebel wrote letters in Ahab’s name, sealed them with his seal, and sent them to the elders and nobles who lived with Naboth in his city. 9 In the letters she wrote: “Proclaim a fast and give Naboth a seat of honor among the people. 10 But seat two scoundrels opposite him and have them testify, ‘You have cursed both God and the king!’ Then take him out and stone him to death.” 11 So the elders and nobles who lived in Naboth’s city did as Jezebel had instructed in the letters she had written to them. 12 They proclaimed a fast and gave Naboth a seat of honor among the people. 13 And the two scoundrels came in and sat opposite Naboth, and these men testified against him before the people, saying, “Naboth has cursed both God and the king!” So they took him outside the city and stoned him to death. 14 Then they sent word to Jezebel: “Naboth has been stoned to death.” 15 When Jezebel heard that Naboth had been stoned to death, she said to Ahab, “Get up and take possession of the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite, who refused to give it to you for silver. For Naboth is no longer alive, but dead.” 16 And when Ahab heard that Naboth was dead, he got up and went down to take possession of the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jezebel writes in Ahab’s name and seals the letters with his seal. She instructs Naboth’s local elders and nobles to proclaim a fast, give him a prominent seat and arrange for two men to accuse him of cursing God and the king.

The officials carry out the instructions. The false testimony is given, Naboth is taken outside the city and stoned, and his death is reported to Jezebel. She then tells Ahab to take the vineyard, and he goes to possess it.

The use of two witnesses imitates a safeguard in Israel’s law while defeating its purpose. Deuteronomy 19:15–21 requires sufficient testimony and investigation of false accusations. Here the accusation and outcome have been arranged in advance.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry emphasizes that the wrongdoing wears the appearance of both religion and justice. A fast and a formal accusation do not make the proceeding righteous.

Wesley and Gill likewise see the charges as a means to remove Naboth and obtain the property. The narrative exposes the cooperation of royal authority, local officials and false witnesses in carrying out the wrong.
passages.god_plan_html:
The pattern of false testimony used to secure the death of an innocent person appears again in the proceedings against Jesus in Mark 14:55–65. Witnesses give false and inconsistent accounts, and the hearing ends with a condemnation for blasphemy.

This is a comparison of the injustice shown in the two accounts. Naboth’s story helps readers recognize how religious language and proceedings can be turned against the innocent. In the Gospel, that wrong is directed against Jesus Himself, bringing the need for truthful judgment into still sharper focus.

passages.title: 1 Kings 21:17-26
passages.section_title: Why does God hold Ahab responsible for Naboth’s death?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 Then the word of the LORD came to Elijah the Tishbite, saying, 18 “Get up and go down to meet Ahab king of Israel, who is in Samaria. See, he is in the vineyard of Naboth, where he has gone to take possession of it. 19 Tell him that this is what the LORD says: ‘Have you not murdered a man and seized his land?’ Then tell him that this is also what the LORD says: ‘In the place where the dogs licked up the blood of Naboth, there also the dogs will lick up your blood—yes, yours!’” 20 When Elijah arrived, Ahab said to him, “So you have found me out, my enemy.” He replied, “I have found you out because you have sold yourself to do evil in the sight of the LORD. 21 This is what the LORD says: ‘I will bring calamity on you and consume your descendants; I will cut off from Ahab every male in Israel, both slave and free. 22 I will make your house like that of Jeroboam son of Nebat and like that of Baasha son of Ahijah, because you have provoked My anger and caused Israel to sin.’ 23 And the LORD also speaks concerning Jezebel: ‘The dogs will devour Jezebel by the wall of Jezreel.’ 24 Anyone belonging to Ahab who dies in the city will be eaten by dogs, and anyone who dies in the field will be eaten by the birds of the air.” 25 (Surely there was never one like Ahab, who sold himself to do evil in the sight of the LORD, incited by his wife Jezebel. 26 He committed the most detestable acts by going after idols, just like the Amorites whom the LORD had driven out before the Israelites.)
