section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The LORD sends Elijah to meet Ahab at the vineyard he has gone to possess. God’s question joins the two acts: murder and taking the land. Ahab is confronted as responsible, even though Jezebel wrote the instructions and the local men carried them out.

Elijah announces judgment against Ahab’s royal house, comparing its coming end with those of Jeroboam and Baasha. Jezebel is also named in the warning: dogs will devour her at Jezreel.

The narrator acknowledges Jezebel’s influence while still describing Ahab as one who sold himself to do evil. Being urged on by another person does not remove the king’s responsibility for what he accepts and gains.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Gill connects Ahab’s guilt with his coveting and his taking possession after the murder. He considers further knowledge or consent likely, while the narrative itself makes the king’s responsibility explicit.

Wesley emphasizes that another person’s temptation does not excuse the one who yields to it. Henry likewise reads Ahab’s course as willing involvement in evil, rather than something that merely happened to him.
passages.god_plan_html:
The later story returns directly to Naboth’s ground. In 2 Kings 9:24–26, Jehu orders the body of Ahab’s son Joram thrown into Naboth’s field and recalls God’s word about the blood of Naboth and his sons.

That continuation shows why taking the vineyard was not the final word. What royal power concealed or treated as settled remained known to God. The Bible carries the account forward as a reckoning with the wrong done, including the family members the earlier scene did not describe.

passages.title: 1 Kings 21:27-29
passages.section_title: What does God do when Ahab humbles himself?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 27 When Ahab heard these words, he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, and fasted. He lay down in sackcloth and walked around meekly. 28 Then the word of the LORD came to Elijah the Tishbite, saying: 29 “Have you seen how Ahab has humbled himself before Me? Because he has humbled himself before Me, I will not bring the calamity during his days, but I will bring it upon his house in the days of his son.”
paragraphs: 27 When Ahab heard these words, he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, and fasted. He lay down in sackcloth and walked around meekly. 28 Then the word of the LORD came to Elijah the Tishbite, saying: 29 “Have you seen how Ahab has humbled himself before Me? Because he has humbled himself before Me, I will not bring the calamity during his days, but I will bring it upon his house in the days of his son.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Ahab responds to the warning by tearing his clothes, putting on sackcloth and fasting. He lies in sackcloth and goes about meekly.

The LORD draws Elijah’s attention to that response. Because Ahab has humbled himself before Him, the announced calamity upon his house will come in his son’s days rather than his own.

The closing word is a postponement of the royal house’s judgment. God takes notice of Ahab’s humbling even after the severe assessment of his life.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley describes the humbling as real but not lasting and sees God’s response as evidence of His readiness to show mercy. Henry and Gill judge it to be outward or incomplete, rather than a thorough change of heart.

The difference concerns how deeply and enduringly Ahab’s response reaches. All recognize the reprieve stated in the passage. The text reports God acknowledging his humbling and delaying the judgment; it does not announce that every earlier consequence has been canceled.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 2:4–6 explains that God’s kindness, patience and tolerance are meant to lead people to repentance. It also warns against a hardened response that stores up judgment.

This broader teaching helps explain the significance of a reprieve. Mercy calls for a changed response to God; delay is not a reason to dismiss His judgment or continue the wrong. Ahab’s humbling and the word of postponement keep both mercy and accountability before the reader.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Kings 22:1-12
passages.section_title: Does a united answer mean the prophets are speaking for God?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then three years passed without war between Aram and Israel. 2 However, in the third year, Jehoshaphat king of Judah went down to visit the king of Israel, 3 who said to his servants, “Do you not know that Ramoth-gilead is ours, but we have failed to take it from the hand of the king of Aram?” 4 So he asked Jehoshaphat, “Will you go with me to fight against Ramoth-gilead?” Jehoshaphat answered the king of Israel, “I am as you are, my people are your people, and my horses are your horses.” 5 But Jehoshaphat also said to the king of Israel, “Please inquire first for the word of the LORD.” 6 So the king of Israel assembled the prophets, about four hundred men, and asked them, “Should I go to war against Ramoth-gilead, or should I refrain?” “Go up,” they replied, “and the Lord will deliver it into the hand of the king.” 7 But Jehoshaphat asked, “Is there not still a prophet of the LORD here of whom we can inquire?” 8 The king of Israel answered, “There is still one man through whom we can inquire of the LORD, but I hate him because he never prophesies anything good for me, but only bad. He is Micaiah son of Imlah.” “The king should not say that!” Jehoshaphat replied. 9 So the king of Israel called one of his officials and said, “Bring Micaiah son of Imlah at once.” 10 Dressed in royal attire, the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah were sitting on their thrones at the threshing floor by the entrance of the gate of Samaria, with all the prophets prophesying before them. 11 Now Zedekiah son of Chenaanah had made for himself iron horns and declared, “This is what the LORD says: ‘With these you shall gore the Arameans until they are finished off.’” 12 And all the prophets were prophesying the same, saying, “Go up to Ramoth-gilead and triumph, for the LORD will deliver it into the hand of the king.”

He is Micaiah son of Imlah.” “The king should not say that!” Jehoshaphat replied. 9 So the king of Israel called one of his officials and said, “Bring Micaiah son of Imlah at once.”

10 Dressed in royal attire, the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah were sitting on their thrones at the threshing floor by the entrance of the gate of Samaria, with all the prophets prophesying before them. 11 Now Zedekiah son of Chenaanah had made for himself iron horns and declared, “This is what the LORD says: ‘With these you shall gore the Arameans until they are finished off.’” 12 And all the prophets were prophesying the same, saying, “Go up to Ramoth-gilead and triumph, for the LORD will deliver it into the hand of the king.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After three years without war between Aram and Israel, Ahab raises the question of recovering Ramoth-gilead. Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, agrees to join him but also asks that they first seek the LORD’s word.

About four hundred prophets promise success. Jehoshaphat nevertheless asks for a prophet of the LORD. Ahab names Micaiah son of Imlah, then explains his dislike: Micaiah brings him bad news rather than the good news he wants.

The kings sit in royal dress at Samaria’s gate while the prophets repeat their assurances. Zedekiah adds a visible sign, iron horns, claiming that Ahab will gore the Arameans. The scene brings together agreement, ceremony and confidence before the reader has heard the message Micaiah will give.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley emphasize the danger of fitting a religious message to the wishes of a ruler. Jehoshaphat’s request for God’s word is commendable, while his willingness to ally himself with Ahab exposes him to danger.

Gill likewise regards these as Ahab’s false prophets. Their agreement is part of the problem: the king is being encouraged in the course he already desires. The use of the LORD’s name does not settle whether He has spoken.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Kings 22:13-18
passages.section_title: Why does Micaiah first repeat the promise of victory?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 Then the messenger who had gone to call Micaiah instructed him, “Behold now, with one accord the words of the prophets are favorable to the king. So please let your words be like theirs, and speak favorably.” 14 But Micaiah said, “As surely as the LORD lives, I will speak whatever the LORD tells me.” 15 When Micaiah arrived, the king asked him, “Micaiah, should we go to war against Ramoth-gilead, or should we refrain?” “Go up and triumph,” Micaiah replied, “for the LORD will deliver it into the hand of the king.” 16 But the king said to him, “How many times must I make you swear not to tell me anything but the truth in the name of the LORD?” 17 So Micaiah declared: “I saw all Israel scattered on the hills like sheep without a shepherd. And the LORD said, ‘These people have no master; let each one return home in peace.’” 18 Then the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “Did I not tell you that he never prophesies good for me, but only bad?”
paragraphs: 13 Then the messenger who had gone to call Micaiah instructed him, “Behold now, with one accord the words of the prophets are favorable to the king. So please let your words be like theirs, and speak favorably.” 14 But Micaiah said, “As surely as the LORD lives, I will speak whatever the LORD tells me.” 15 When Micaiah arrived, the king asked him, “Micaiah, should we go to war against Ramoth-gilead, or should we refrain?” “Go up and triumph,” Micaiah replied, “for the LORD will deliver it into the hand of the king.” 16 But the king said to him, “How many times must I make you swear not to tell me anything but the truth in the name of the LORD?”

17 So Micaiah declared: “I saw all Israel scattered on the hills like sheep without a shepherd. And the LORD said, ‘These people have no master; let each one return home in peace.’” 18 Then the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “Did I not tell you that he never prophesies good for me, but only bad?”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The messenger urges Micaiah to agree with the other prophets and give the king a favorable answer. Micaiah replies that he will speak what the LORD tells him.

His first answer repeats their promise of success. Ahab immediately demands the truth, showing that he does not receive this as Micaiah’s serious message. Micaiah then describes Israel scattered on the hills like sheep without a shepherd, with permission for each person to return home.

The picture points to the loss of the king rather than the promised triumph. Ahab responds by treating the warning as further evidence that Micaiah is against him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill read Micaiah’s initial answer as irony: he echoes the answer Ahab wants before making the true warning clear. Their reading follows the contrast between that first response and the king’s immediate demand to hear the truth.

Henry emphasizes that warning someone of danger is an act of kindness. An unwelcome message is not necessarily an unkind one, and the hearer’s dislike does not make it false.
passages.god_plan_html:
The image of people without a shepherd continues through Scripture. In Mark 6:30–44, Jesus sees the crowd in that condition, has compassion, teaches them and provides food.

This is a broader biblical connection, rather than a claim that Micaiah is directly predicting that scene. Here the people face the loss of their king. In John 10:11–18, Jesus describes Himself as the good shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep. His care supplies a striking contrast to leadership that leaves people exposed.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Kings 22:19-23
passages.section_title: How should we understand the vision of the lying spirit?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 Micaiah continued, “Therefore hear the word of the LORD: I saw the LORD sitting on His throne, and all the host of heaven standing by Him on His right and on His left. 20 And the LORD said, ‘Who will entice Ahab to march up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?’ And one suggested this, and another that. 21 Then a spirit came forward, stood before the LORD, and said, ‘I will entice him.’ ‘By what means?’ asked the LORD. 22 And he replied, ‘I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouths of all his prophets.’ ‘You will surely entice him and prevail,’ said the LORD. ‘Go and do it.’ 23 So you see, the LORD has put a lying spirit in the mouths of all these prophets of yours, and the LORD has pronounced disaster against you.”
paragraphs: 19 Micaiah continued, “Therefore hear the word of the LORD: I saw the LORD sitting on His throne, and all the host of heaven standing by Him on His right and on His left. 20 And the LORD said, ‘Who will entice Ahab to march up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?’ And one suggested this, and another that. 21 Then a spirit came forward, stood before the LORD, and said, ‘I will entice him.’ ‘By what means?’ asked the LORD. 22 And he replied, ‘I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouths of all his prophets.’ ‘You will surely entice him and prevail,’ said the LORD. ‘Go and do it.’ 23 So you see, the LORD has put a lying spirit in the mouths of all these prophets of yours, and the LORD has pronounced disaster against you.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Micaiah now describes the LORD on His throne with the host of heaven around Him. In the vision, a spirit proposes to entice Ahab by becoming a lying spirit in the mouths of his prophets. The LORD permits the plan to proceed and declares that it will succeed.

Micaiah tells Ahab that this explains the assurances he has received. The LORD has pronounced disaster against him. Ahab hears both the false promise and the warning that exposes it before he chooses to go to battle.

The scene raises a serious question about God’s rule and the lies of others. It should be read alongside Scripture’s direct statements that God cannot lie, in Titus 1:1–3, and that He does not tempt anyone to evil, in James 1:13–18.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands the permission as God giving Ahab and the prophets over to their own chosen course. Gill likewise describes God allowing an evil spirit to work through prophets disposed to flatter the king.

Henry emphasizes that the vision presents heavenly matters in a form people can understand. He cautions against imagining that God needs advice or becomes the author of sin.

The wider traditions agree that God’s rule does not make Him the source of moral evil. The Catholic Church teaches that God permits the evil choices of His creatures and can bring good from them, while remaining entirely good (Catechism 311–312).

Reformed accounts place particular emphasis on God actively limiting and governing evil toward His holy purposes, rather than merely allowing it. Both the Westminster Confession 5.4 and the 1689 Baptist Confession 5.4 make that distinction while saying that the sin belongs to the creatures, not to God. These statements explain the traditions’ broader approach; they do not identify the unnamed spirit or define every detail of Micaiah’s vision.
passages.god_plan_html:
A related pattern appears in 2 Thessalonians 2:9–12: people refuse the love of the truth, delight in wickedness and come under a judgment in which they believe a lie. The surrounding passage also announces that the Lord Jesus will bring the lawless one to an end.

The connection is the warning about rejecting truth and embracing deception, not an identification of Ahab with a future figure. In both passages, deception remains under God’s rule and does not give evil the final word.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Kings 22:24-29
passages.section_title: Can silencing a prophet change the truth of his warning?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 24 Then Zedekiah son of Chenaanah went up, struck Micaiah in the face, and demanded, “Which way did the Spirit of the LORD go when He departed from me to speak with you?” 25 Micaiah replied, “You will soon see, on that day when you go and hide in an inner room.” 26 And the king of Israel declared, “Take Micaiah and return him to Amon the governor of the city and to Joash the king’s son, 27 and tell them that this is what the king says: ‘Put this man in prison and feed him only bread and water until I return safely.’” 28 But Micaiah replied, “If you ever return safely, the LORD has not spoken through me.” Then he added, “Take heed, all you people!” 29 So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah went up to Ramoth-gilead.
paragraphs: 24 Then Zedekiah son of Chenaanah went up, struck Micaiah in the face, and demanded, “Which way did the Spirit of the LORD go when He departed from me to speak with you?” 25 Micaiah replied, “You will soon see, on that day when you go and hide in an inner room.”

26 And the king of Israel declared, “Take Micaiah and return him to Amon the governor of the city and to Joash the king’s son, 27 and tell them that this is what the king says: ‘Put this man in prison and feed him only bread and water until I return safely.’” 28 But Micaiah replied, “If you ever return safely, the LORD has not spoken through me.” Then he added, “Take heed, all you people!” 29 So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah went up to Ramoth-gilead.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Zedekiah strikes Micaiah and challenges his claim to speak by the LORD’s Spirit. Micaiah replies that Zedekiah will discover the answer when he hides in an inner room.

Ahab orders Micaiah imprisoned on bread and water until the king returns safely. Micaiah makes the outcome the test of his message: if Ahab returns safely, the LORD has not spoken through him.

This recalls the concern in Deuteronomy 18:20–22 that a claim to speak for God must answer to whether the word comes true. Ahab and Jehoshaphat then proceed to Ramoth-gilead.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry notes that Micaiah does not answer Zedekiah’s blow with another blow. He leaves the claim to be tested by what happens. Wesley likewise understands the coming danger as the event that will expose the false assurance.

Gill reads the imprisonment and restricted food as punishment meant to keep Micaiah suffering. The king can confine the messenger, but the narrative leaves his prediction in place for the reader to test.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Kings 22:30-40
passages.section_title: Does Ahab’s disguise keep him safe?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 30 And the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “I will disguise myself and go into battle, but you wear your royal robes.” So the king of Israel disguised himself and went into battle. 31 Now the king of Aram had ordered his thirty-two chariot commanders, “Do not fight with anyone, small or great, except the king of Israel.” 32 When the chariot commanders saw Jehoshaphat, they said, “Surely this is the king of Israel!” So they turned to fight against him, but Jehoshaphat cried out. 33 And when the chariot commanders saw that he was not the king of Israel, they turned back from pursuing him. 34 However, a certain man drew his bow without taking special aim, and he struck the king of Israel between the joints of his armor. So the king said to his charioteer, “Turn around and take me out of the battle, for I am badly wounded!” 35 The battle raged throughout that day, and the king was propped up in his chariot facing the Arameans. And the blood from his wound ran out onto the floor of the chariot, and that evening he died. 36 As the sun was setting, the cry rang out in the army: “Every man to his own city, and every man to his own land!” 37 So the king died and was brought to Samaria, where they buried him. 38 And the chariot was washed at the pool of Samaria where the prostitutes bathed, and the dogs licked up Ahab’s blood, according to the word that the LORD had spoken. 39 As for the rest of the acts of Ahab, along with all his accomplishments and the ivory palace and all the cities he built, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel? 40 And Ahab rested with his fathers, and his son Ahaziah reigned in his place.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Ahab disguises himself for battle while Jehoshaphat wears his royal robes. The Aramean chariot commanders have been ordered to pursue the king of Israel, so they initially turn toward Jehoshaphat. When he cries out and they recognize their mistake, they stop pursuing him.

An unnamed archer, taking no special aim, strikes Ahab between the joints of his armor. The wounded king remains propped up in his chariot during the battle and dies that evening. A cry then sends the men back to their own cities and lands.

Ahab is buried in Samaria. When his chariot is washed there, dogs lick up his blood. The narrator identifies this as happening according to the LORD’s word. The report closes with Ahab’s accomplishments and the succession of his son Ahaziah.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Gill see Ahab’s arrangement as protecting himself while exposing Jehoshaphat to danger. For Jehoshaphat’s rescue, 2 Chronicles 18:28–34 adds explicitly that the LORD helped him and drew the attackers away.

Wesley emphasizes the contrast between the apparently unplanned arrow and the announced outcome. The disguise does not prevent Ahab’s death, and the scattering of the army brings Micaiah’s warning into view. The account’s focus is the fulfillment of the word Ahab had rejected.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Kings 22:41-50
passages.section_title: How does Jehoshaphat’s reign combine faithfulness with compromise?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 41 In the fourth year of Ahab’s reign over Israel, Jehoshaphat son of Asa became king of Judah. 42 Jehoshaphat was thirty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem twenty-five years. His mother’s name was Azubah daughter of Shilhi. 43 And Jehoshaphat walked in all the ways of his father Asa; he did not turn away from them, but did what was right in the eyes of the LORD. The high places, however, were not removed; the people still sacrificed and burned incense on the high places. 44 Jehoshaphat also made peace with the king of Israel. 45 As for the rest of the acts of Jehoshaphat, along with the might he exercised and how he waged war, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? 46 He banished from the land the male shrine prostitutes who remained from the days of his father Asa. 47 And there was no king in Edom; a deputy served as king. 48 Jehoshaphat built ships of Tarshish to go to Ophir for gold, but they never set sail, because they were wrecked at Ezion-geber. 49 At that time Ahaziah son of Ahab said to Jehoshaphat, “Let my servants sail with your servants,” but Jehoshaphat refused. 50 And Jehoshaphat rested with his fathers and was buried with them in the city of his father David. And his son Jehoram reigned in his place.

His mother’s name was Azubah daughter of Shilhi. 43 And Jehoshaphat walked in all the ways of his father Asa; he did not turn away from them, but did what was right in the eyes of the LORD. The high places, however, were not removed; the people still sacrificed and burned incense on the high places. 44 Jehoshaphat also made peace with the king of Israel.

And his son Jehoram reigned in his place.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The account returns to Judah and summarizes Jehoshaphat’s twenty-five-year reign. He follows his father Asa in doing what is right in the LORD’s eyes, but the high places remain in use. His peace with Israel also belongs to this mixed picture.

The king removes the remaining male shrine prostitutes. The account then mentions Edom’s deputy ruler and Jehoshaphat’s unsuccessful shipping venture: ships intended to obtain gold from Ophir are wrecked at Ezion-geber. He refuses Ahaziah’s offer to have their servants sail together.

2 Chronicles 20:31–37 provides further detail, connecting the loss of the ships with a rebuke for an alliance with Ahaziah. Jehoshaphat’s son Jehoram succeeds him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry emphasizes the overall good character of Jehoshaphat’s reign. Wesley also takes the favorable assessment seriously while treating the alliance with Ahab as a blemish with consequences for the family.

Wesley and Gill read the refusal of Ahaziah’s proposal in light of the earlier failed partnership described in Chronicles. The two accounts together explain why this king can be commended for faithfulness while still needing correction.
passages.god_plan_html:
The consequences of this family alliance continue beyond Jehoshaphat’s death. 2 Chronicles 21:1–7 explains that Jehoram married a daughter of Ahab and followed the ways of Ahab’s house. It then says the LORD did not destroy David’s house because of His covenant with David.

That continuation places the flawed reigns within the larger story of God keeping His promise. The covenant does not make the kings’ evil acceptable; it explains why their failures do not simply bring David’s family line to an end.

passages.title: 1 Kings 22:51-53
passages.section_title: What does Ahaziah carry forward from his parents?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 51 In the seventeenth year of Jehoshaphat’s reign over Judah, Ahaziah son of Ahab became king of Israel, and he reigned in Samaria two years. 52 And he did evil in the sight of the LORD and walked in the ways of his father and mother and of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had caused Israel to sin. 53 Ahaziah served and worshiped Baal, provoking the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger, just as his father had done.
paragraphs: 51 In the seventeenth year of Jehoshaphat’s reign over Judah, Ahaziah son of Ahab became king of Israel, and he reigned in Samaria two years. 52 And he did evil in the sight of the LORD and walked in the ways of his father and mother and of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had caused Israel to sin. 53 Ahaziah served and worshiped Baal, provoking the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger, just as his father had done.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The book closes by returning to Israel. Ahaziah, Ahab’s son, begins to reign in Samaria and is credited with a two-year reign.

His conduct is measured against both his parents and Jeroboam: he continues the ways that had led Israel into sin. The particular act named is his service and worship of Baal.

This brief ending leaves the account of his reign unfinished; it continues in 2 Kings. A new ruler has taken the throne, but the change of name has not brought a change in worship.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry emphasizes Ahaziah’s failure to learn from what had happened to his father. Wesley draws attention to the limit of family example: following parents does not justify conduct opposed to God’s word.

Gill likewise reads the summary as a continuation of Ahab’s and Jezebel’s practices. These readings focus on the choices the text names, rather than treating a king’s ancestry as removing his responsibility.

passages.title: Ezra 1:1-4
passages.section_title: How does the return from exile begin?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, to fulfill the word of the LORD spoken through Jeremiah, the LORD stirred the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia to send a proclamation throughout his kingdom and to put it in writing as follows: 2 “This is what Cyrus king of Persia says: ‘The LORD, the God of heaven, who has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, has appointed me to build a house for Him at Jerusalem in Judah. 3 Whoever among you belongs to His people, may his God be with him, and may he go to Jerusalem in Judah and build the house of the LORD, the God of Israel; He is the God who is in Jerusalem. 4 And let every survivor, wherever he lives, be assisted by the men of that region with silver, gold, goods, and livestock, along with a freewill offering for the house of God in Jerusalem.’”
paragraphs: 1 In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, to fulfill the word of the LORD spoken through Jeremiah, the LORD stirred the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia to send a proclamation throughout his kingdom and to put it in writing as follows: 2 “This is what Cyrus king of Persia says: ‘The LORD, the God of heaven, who has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, has appointed me to build a house for Him at Jerusalem in Judah. 3 Whoever among you belongs to His people, may his God be with him, and may he go to Jerusalem in Judah and build the house of the LORD, the God of Israel; He is the God who is in Jerusalem. 4 And let every survivor, wherever he lives, be assisted by the men of that region with silver, gold, goods, and livestock, along with a freewill offering for the house of God in Jerusalem.’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Ezra opens with a proclamation from Cyrus king of Persia permitting God’s people to return to Jerusalem and rebuild the temple. The opening sentence explains the event through God’s action: He stirs Cyrus’s spirit to fulfill the word spoken through Jeremiah.

The Hebrew verb behind this stirring is עוּר, ur, pronounced OOR. Brown–Driver–Briggs explains its use here as rousing someone to action. The same verb appears when God stirs the returning people in verse 5: both the royal permission and the people’s response belong to the beginning of the restoration.

Cyrus invites those who belong to God’s people to go, and directs their neighbors to provide practical support. The aim is specific: rebuilding the house of the LORD in Jerusalem, rather than simply allowing a change of residence.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The main reading is straightforward: the proclamation is presented as God fulfilling His promise through a Persian ruler. Henry and Gill emphasize God moving the king to act, while Wesley connects the opening with the promised end of captivity. The passage does not describe how Cyrus first learned of that promise.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jeremiah 29:10–14 promises a return after Babylon’s seventy years and calls the exiles to seek God. Ezra explicitly identifies the proclamation as a fulfillment of Jeremiah’s word.

The same larger purpose appears in Isaiah 44:24–28 and 45:1–7, where Cyrus is named in connection with Jerusalem and the temple. God’s purposes for His people can advance through a ruler who does not yet know Him. The return therefore begins with His faithfulness, not with a claim that the Persian king has become Israel’s promised savior.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezra 1:5-11
passages.section_title: Who responds, and what goes back to Jerusalem?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 So the family heads of Judah and Benjamin, along with the priests and Levites—everyone whose spirit God had stirred—prepared to go up and rebuild the house of the LORD in Jerusalem. 6 And all their neighbors supported them with articles of silver and gold, with goods and livestock, and with valuables, in addition to all their freewill offerings. 7 King Cyrus also brought out the articles belonging to the house of the LORD that Nebuchadnezzar had carried away from Jerusalem and placed in the temple of his gods. 8 Cyrus king of Persia had them brought out by the hand of Mithredath the treasurer, who counted them out to Sheshbazzar the prince of Judah. 9 This was the inventory: 30 gold dishes, 1,000 silver dishes, 29 silver utensils, 10 30 gold bowls, 410 matching silver bowls, and 1,000 other articles. 11 In all, there were 5,400 gold and silver articles. Sheshbazzar brought all these along when the exiles went up from Babylon to Jerusalem.

Sheshbazzar brought all these along when the exiles went up from Babylon to Jerusalem.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Family heads from Judah and Benjamin, together with priests and Levites, prepare to return. They are described as people whose spirit God has stirred to rebuild His house. Their neighbors provide silver, gold, goods, livestock and freewill offerings.

Cyrus also returns temple articles that Nebuchadnezzar had taken from Jerusalem. Mithredath the treasurer counts them out to Sheshbazzar, the prince of Judah, who brings them with the returning exiles.

The return includes both people and the objects associated with their worship. What had been carried away in conquest is being brought back for the rebuilding work.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Gill see God’s initiative in both the decision to return and the provision for the work. They also note that the temple articles have been preserved through the captivity.

Some details remain debated. Wesley and Gill identify Sheshbazzar with Zerubbabel, while the USCCB study notes discuss a different possible identification and regard it as uncertain. Gill takes the stated total of 5,400 articles to include items not separately listed; the USCCB editors consider a copying problem in one or more of the figures possible. The passage does not explain the difference between the listed amounts and the total.
passages.god_plan_html:
The return has a clear parallel with the departure from Egypt. In Exodus 12:35–36, the Israelites leave with silver, gold and clothing provided by their neighbors. Here, too, those leaving captivity receive material support.

Exodus 35:20–29 then describes willing people whose hearts are stirred bringing gifts for the tabernacle. The parallel connects freedom from captivity with restored worship and willing participation. It does not make every later building project a promise of unlimited funding.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The list identifies people returning from the captivity Nebuchadnezzar had imposed, each to a town in Jerusalem or Judah. Zerubbabel and Jeshua appear among the leaders, followed by family groups and people associated with particular towns.

These names show continuity between the community that was carried away and the community now settling again. The restoration concerns actual families and places, rather than an unnamed crowd.

A related list appears in Nehemiah 7:5–7, where Nehemiah says he found the register of those who first returned. The two lists have differences in some names and numbers; Ezra does not supply an explanation for each one.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley and Gill understand the entries as family descent and connections with former towns. Henry also reads the list as a record of the families returning from captivity. Explanations of the differences from Nehemiah include changes in the groups counted, but these are proposed explanations rather than events narrated here.
passages.god_plan_html:
Zerubbabel also appears in the line leading to Jesus in Matthew 1:11–17. Matthew’s account moves through the exile, names Shealtiel and Zerubbabel after it, and continues toward the birth of Christ.

That New Testament connection gives these returning families a place in the larger story. Exile has not brought the line of David to an end. The return is part of the history through which the Gospel later presents Jesus as the son of David and the son of Abraham.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The register turns from the general population to groups associated with temple service. Four priestly family groups are listed, followed by Levites, singers, gatekeepers and temple servants.

Descendants of Solomon’s servants are listed as another group. Together with the temple servants, they number 392. The passage preserves distinctions between the groups rather than treating everyone as a priest.

The rebuilding needs more than royal permission or a supply of gold. A community must return with people able to carry out the worship and service for which the temple exists.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley and Gill read these as the various groups needed for the restored worship. They discuss possible origins of the temple servants, but the passage itself is clearest about their place in the returning community. The main point is the return of people with distinct responsibilities, not a definition of offices in a later Christian church.

passages.title: Ezra 2:59-63
passages.section_title: What happens when a family cannot establish its priestly descent?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 59 The following came up from Tel-melah, Tel-harsha, Cherub, Addan, and Immer, but they could not prove that their families were descended from Israel: 60 the descendants of Delaiah, the descendants of Tobiah, and the descendants of Nekoda, 652 in all. 61 And from among the priests: the descendants of Hobaiah, the descendants of Hakkoz, and the descendants of Barzillai (who had married a daughter of Barzillai the Gileadite and was called by their name). 62 These men searched for their family records, but they could not find them and so were excluded from the priesthood as unclean. 63 The governor ordered them not to eat the most holy things until there was a priest to consult the Urim and Thummim.
paragraphs: 59 The following came up from Tel-melah, Tel-harsha, Cherub, Addan, and Immer, but they could not prove that their families were descended from Israel: 60 the descendants of Delaiah, the descendants of Tobiah, and the descendants of Nekoda, 652 in all.

61 And from among the priests: the descendants of Hobaiah, the descendants of Hakkoz, and the descendants of Barzillai (who had married a daughter of Barzillai the Gileadite and was called by their name). 62 These men searched for their family records, but they could not find them and so were excluded from the priesthood as unclean. 63 The governor ordered them not to eat the most holy things until there was a priest to consult the Urim and Thummim.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Some returning groups cannot prove that their families descend from Israel. The account then identifies priestly families who search for their records but cannot find them.

Those unable to establish priestly descent are excluded from the priesthood and from eating the most holy things while the matter remains unresolved. The governor directs them to wait for a priest who can consult the Urim and Thummim.

The stated restriction concerns priestly standing and its privileges. The passage does not say that everyone with missing ancestry records is expelled from the returning population, nor does it describe how the Urim and Thummim would provide an answer.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley and Gill understand the decision as protecting the requirements of priestly service until the question can be settled. Henry also draws a spiritual lesson about needing a true relationship with God rather than merely claiming its privileges. That is his application beyond the immediate issue of the families’ records.
passages.god_plan_html:
The importance of descent for this priesthood provides background for the different basis of Jesus’ priesthood in Hebrews 7:11–28. Hebrews explicitly says He belongs to Judah, a tribe from which Moses did not appoint priests, and grounds His permanent priesthood in God’s oath and His enduring life.

This is a wider connection, not a claim that Ezra directly predicts Jesus in the missing records. It helps explain why the New Testament gives careful attention to how Jesus can serve as high priest and why people draw near to God through Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.section_title: How does the returning community begin to rebuild?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The account gives a total assembly of 42,360, alongside 7,337 male and female servants and 200 singers. It also records the animals that accompany them.

On arrival at the temple site, some family heads give freewill offerings for rebuilding. The gifts include gold, silver and priestly garments, and the giving is described as according to their ability.

The chapter ends with the people settling in their towns. They have returned and begun to provide for the work, but the temple has not yet been rebuilt.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry emphasizes that the acceptability of the offerings is connected with the people’s ability, rather than whether their gifts equal the wealth of earlier generations. Gill and Wesley understand arrival at the house of God as arrival at its site or ruins, not at an already restored temple. The scene marks a beginning made through willing gifts and settlement.

passages.title: Ezra 3:1-6
passages.section_title: Why does worship begin before the temple is rebuilt?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 By the seventh month, the Israelites had settled in their towns, and the people assembled as one man in Jerusalem. 2 Then Jeshua son of Jozadak and his fellow priests, along with Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and his associates, began to build the altar of the God of Israel to sacrifice burnt offerings on it, as it is written in the Law of Moses the man of God. 3 They set up the altar on its foundation and sacrificed burnt offerings on it to the LORD—both the morning and evening burnt offerings—even though they feared the people of the land. 4 They also celebrated the Feast of Tabernacles in accordance with what is written, and they offered burnt offerings daily based on the number prescribed for each day. 5 After that, they presented the regular burnt offerings and those for New Moons and for all the appointed sacred feasts of the LORD, as well as all the freewill offerings brought to the LORD. 6 On the first day of the seventh month, the Israelites began to offer burnt offerings to the LORD, although the foundation of the temple of the LORD had not been laid.

4 They also celebrated the Feast of Tabernacles in accordance with what is written, and they offered burnt offerings daily based on the number prescribed for each day. 5 After that, they presented the regular burnt offerings and those for New Moons and for all the appointed sacred feasts of the LORD, as well as all the freewill offerings brought to the LORD. 6 On the first day of the seventh month, the Israelites began to offer burnt offerings to the LORD, although the foundation of the temple of the LORD had not been laid.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
In the seventh month, the people gather in Jerusalem. Jeshua and the priests, together with Zerubbabel and his associates, rebuild the altar so that offerings can begin according to the Law of Moses.

They offer the morning and evening sacrifices despite their fear of the surrounding peoples. The account also records the Feast of Tabernacles, the regular offerings and freewill gifts. The temple’s foundation has not yet been laid.

The festival recalls Israel’s life in booths after leaving Egypt, as explained in Leviticus 23:33–43. For this returning community, keeping it means resuming the worship Scripture prescribes while much of the rebuilding still lies ahead.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry, Wesley and Gill emphasize that the people begin with the worship they can offer rather than wait for a completed temple. Their fear is real, but it does not prevent them from rebuilding the altar and following the written instructions.
passages.god_plan_html:
The wider biblical story continues the question of how people approach God. In John 4:19–26, Jesus tells the Samaritan woman of worship in spirit and truth that will not be confined to Jerusalem or her mountain.

Romans 12:1–2 calls believers to offer their bodies as living sacrifices in response to God’s mercy. These passages develop the theme beyond the altar here: worship reaches the whole life of those who belong to God. They do not turn Ezra’s prescribed offerings into meaningless ceremonies; they show how the New Testament describes worship through Christ.

passages.title: Ezra 3:7-9
passages.section_title: How is the rebuilding work organized?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The people pay masons and carpenters and provide food, drink and oil to people from Sidon and Tyre in exchange for cedar from Lebanon. The timber is to come by sea to Joppa under Cyrus’s authorization.

The work begins in the second month of the second year after their arrival. Zerubbabel, Jeshua and the returning community appoint Levites aged twenty and above to supervise it. Several families share that responsibility.

The cedar arrangements recall Solomon’s preparations in 1 Kings 5:1–12. The returnees are beginning again with materials, payments and people assigned to oversee the work.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Gill reads the arrangements as preparation for the foundation and rebuilding, while Wesley emphasizes the supervisors’ task of encouraging the work forward. Shared participation is guided by named supervisors.

passages.title: Ezra 3:10-13
passages.section_title: Why do joy and tears meet at the new foundation?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 When the builders had laid the foundation of the temple of the LORD, the priests in their apparel with trumpets, and the Levites (the sons of Asaph) with cymbals, took their positions to praise the LORD, as David king of Israel had prescribed. 11 And they sang responsively with praise and thanksgiving to the LORD: “For He is good; for His loving devotion to Israel endures forever.” Then all the people gave a great shout of praise to the LORD, because the foundation of the house of the LORD had been laid. 12 But many of the older priests, Levites, and family heads who had seen the first temple wept loudly when they saw the foundation of this temple. Still, many others shouted joyfully. 13 The people could not distinguish the shouts of joy from the sound of weeping, because the people were making so much noise. And the sound was heard from afar.

12 But many of the older priests, Levites, and family heads who had seen the first temple wept loudly when they saw the foundation of this temple. Still, many others shouted joyfully. 13 The people could not distinguish the shouts of joy from the sound of weeping, because the people were making so much noise. And the sound was heard from afar.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
When the foundation is laid, the priests and Levites take their places with trumpets and cymbals. They praise the LORD according to David’s directions and give thanks for His goodness and enduring devotion to Israel.

The response is mixed. Many shout for joy, while older priests, Levites and family heads who had seen the first temple weep loudly. The combined sound travels so far that the cries of joy and grief cannot be distinguished.

The same event carries both hope for what is beginning and memory of what was lost. The narrative records both responses without supplying each person’s thoughts.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry understands the tears largely through comparison with the former temple. He allows that grief over the sin behind the loss can be fitting, while warning against despising the present beginning.

Wesley and Gill also emphasize the contrast with the former temple’s glory. Wesley additionally sees the scene as an example of joy and sorrow mingled in earthly life. The text identifies those weeping as people who had seen the earlier house, but does not record a speech explaining every reason for their tears.
passages.god_plan_html:
Haggai 2:1–9 later addresses people who remember the former temple’s glory and find the present work small by comparison. God calls Zerubbabel, Joshua and the people to be strong and work, assuring them that His Spirit remains with them.

Haggai connects that assurance with the promise made when Israel came out of Egypt and looks toward glory and peace still to come. This places the small beginning within God’s continuing purpose to dwell among His people. Their future rests on His presence and promise, not merely on how impressive the building appears at this stage.

passages.title: Ezra 4:1-5
passages.section_title: Why do the leaders refuse the offer of help?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 When the enemies of Judah and Benjamin heard that the exiles were building a temple for the LORD, the God of Israel, 2 they approached Zerubbabel and the heads of the families, saying, “Let us build with you because, like you, we seek your God and have been sacrificing to Him since the time of King Esar-haddon of Assyria, who brought us here.” 3 But Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the other heads of the families of Israel replied, “You have no part with us in building a house for our God, since we alone must build it for the LORD, the God of Israel, as Cyrus king of Persia has commanded us.” 4 Then the people of the land set out to discourage the people of Judah and make them afraid to build. 5 They hired counselors against them to frustrate their plans throughout the reign of Cyrus king of Persia and down to the reign of Darius king of Persia.
paragraphs: 1 When the enemies of Judah and Benjamin heard that the exiles were building a temple for the LORD, the God of Israel, 2 they approached Zerubbabel and the heads of the families, saying, “Let us build with you because, like you, we seek your God and have been sacrificing to Him since the time of King Esar-haddon of Assyria, who brought us here.” 3 But Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the other heads of the families of Israel replied, “You have no part with us in building a house for our God, since we alone must build it for the LORD, the God of Israel, as Cyrus king of Persia has commanded us.”

4 Then the people of the land set out to discourage the people of Judah and make them afraid to build. 5 They hired counselors against them to frustrate their plans throughout the reign of Cyrus king of Persia and down to the reign of Darius king of Persia.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The narrator introduces the visitors as enemies of Judah and Benjamin. They offer to help build, saying that they seek the same God and have sacrificed to Him since an Assyrian king brought them into the region.

Zerubbabel, Jeshua and the family heads refuse to share the project. They appeal to their commission to build the LORD’s house under Cyrus’s command. The visitors then work to discourage and frighten the builders, hiring counselors to frustrate the work.

For background, 2 Kings 17:24–41 describes people settled in Samaria who worshiped the LORD alongside their own gods. That account helps explain why a claim to worship the same God need not mean agreement about worship.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry, Wesley and Gill understand the offered partnership in light of the visitors’ mixed worship and the hostility that follows. They read the refusal as protecting the assigned work, rather than as a rejection of help merely because help comes from outside Judah. The narrative itself begins by identifying these particular visitors as opponents.
passages.god_plan_html:
This conflict is not the Bible’s final word about Samaria. Jesus speaks with a Samaritan woman about the Father seeking worshipers in spirit and truth in John 4:9,19–26. In Acts 8:4–17,25, Samaritans receive the message of Christ, and Peter and John later preach in Samaritan villages.

The wider story therefore holds together the need for true worship and the welcome extended through the gospel. Ezra’s account of particular opponents is not a permanent judgment that people from Samaria can never belong among God’s people.

passages.title: Ezra 4:6-24
passages.section_title: How do the letters against Jerusalem fit the story?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 At the beginning of the reign of Xerxes, an accusation was lodged against the people of Judah and Jerusalem. 7 And in the days of Artaxerxes king of Persia, Bishlam, Mithredath, Tabeel, and the rest of his associates wrote a letter to Artaxerxes. It was written in Aramaic and then translated. 8 Rehum the commander and Shimshai the scribe wrote the letter against Jerusalem to King Artaxerxes as follows: 9 From Rehum the commander, Shimshai the scribe, and the rest of their associates—the judges and officials over Tripolis, Persia, Erech and Babylon, the Elamites of Susa, 10 and the rest of the peoples whom the great and honorable Ashurbanipal deported and settled in the cities of Samaria and elsewhere west of the Euphrates. 11 (This is the text of the letter they sent to him.) To King Artaxerxes, From your servants, the men west of the Euphrates: 12 Let it be known to the king that the Jews who came from you to us have returned to Jerusalem and are rebuilding that rebellious and wicked city. They are restoring its walls and repairing its foundations. 13 Let it now be known to the king that if that city is rebuilt and its walls are restored, they will not pay tribute, duty, or toll, and the royal treasury will suffer. 14 Now because we are in the service of the palace and it is not fitting for us to allow the king to be dishonored, we have sent to inform the king 15 that a search should be made of the record books of your fathers. In these books you will discover and verify that the city is a rebellious city, harmful to kings and provinces, inciting sedition from ancient times. That is why this city was destroyed. 16 We advise the king that if this city is rebuilt and its walls are restored, you will have no dominion west of the Euphrates. 17 Then the king sent this reply: To Rehum the commander, Shimshai the scribe, and the rest of your associates living in Samaria and elsewhere in the region west of the Euphrates: Greetings. 18 The letter you sent us has been translated and read in my presence. 19 I issued a decree, and a search was conducted. It was discovered that this city has revolted against kings from ancient times, engaging in rebellion and sedition. 20 And mighty kings have ruled over Jerusalem and exercised authority over the whole region west of the Euphrates; and tribute, duty, and toll were paid to them. 21 Now, therefore, issue an order for these men to stop, so that this city will not be rebuilt until I so order. 22 See that you do not neglect this matter. Why allow this threat to increase and the royal interests to suffer? 23 When the text of the letter from King Artaxerxes was read to Rehum, Shimshai the scribe, and their associates, they went immediately to the Jews in Jerusalem and forcibly stopped them. 24 Thus the construction of the house of God in Jerusalem ceased, and it remained at a standstill until the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The chapter records an accusation in the reign of Xerxes and a letter to Artaxerxes. The letter concerns Jerusalem’s walls and the claim that a rebuilt city will refuse taxes and threaten Persian control west of the Euphrates.

The king orders an archive search, receives a report of Jerusalem’s earlier rebellions and commands the rebuilding of the city to stop until he issues another order. The officials then use force to stop the work.

It helps to distinguish the city and its walls from the temple project. Xerxes and Artaxerxes belong to a later period than the Darius named at the chapter’s end; the sequence of Persian kings is given in the USCCB introduction to Ezra. On the reading that these letters illustrate later opposition, verse 24 returns to the earlier interruption of temple building, which lasts until Darius’s second year.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Readers differ over the timeline. Wesley and Gill identify the royal names in a way that puts the letters before Darius, treating the chapter as a continuing sequence. They connect the order against the city with the stopping of temple work.

The Cambridge commentary instead identifies the rulers as Xerxes and Artaxerxes I and reads verses 6–23 as later examples of opposition before the account returns to the temple in verse 24. The reference to city walls is an important part of that reading.

Henry emphasizes the letters’ use of political suspicion to obstruct the work. Past rebellion becomes the basis for predicting future disloyalty. Whatever view is taken of the timeline, the royal reply answers the accusations presented to the king; it does not establish that the returnees had actually planned the future tax revolt alleged against them.

passages.title: Ezra 5:1-5
passages.section_title: What helps the people begin again?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Later, the prophets Haggai and Zechariah son of Iddo prophesied to the Jews in Judah and Jerusalem in the name of the God of Israel, who was over them. 2 Then Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Jeshua son of Jozadak rose up and began to rebuild the house of God in Jerusalem. And the prophets of God were with them, helping them. 3 At that time Tattenai the governor of the region west of the Euphrates, Shethar-bozenai, and their associates went to the Jews and asked, “Who authorized you to rebuild this temple and restore this structure?” 4 They also asked, “What are the names of the men who are constructing this building?” 5 But the eye of their God was on the elders of the Jews, so that they were not stopped until a report was sent to Darius and written instructions about this matter were returned.
paragraphs: 1 Later, the prophets Haggai and Zechariah son of Iddo prophesied to the Jews in Judah and Jerusalem in the name of the God of Israel, who was over them. 2 Then Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Jeshua son of Jozadak rose up and began to rebuild the house of God in Jerusalem. And the prophets of God were with them, helping them.

3 At that time Tattenai the governor of the region west of the Euphrates, Shethar-bozenai, and their associates went to the Jews and asked, “Who authorized you to rebuild this temple and restore this structure?” 4 They also asked, “What are the names of the men who are constructing this building?” 5 But the eye of their God was on the elders of the Jews, so that they were not stopped until a report was sent to Darius and written instructions about this matter were returned.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Haggai and Zechariah prophesy to the people in Judah and Jerusalem in the name of Israel’s God. Zerubbabel and Jeshua resume the temple work, with the prophets alongside them to help.

Tattenai, governor of the region west of the Euphrates, arrives with other officials to ask who authorized the work and who is responsible for it. The questioning does not immediately stop construction: God watches over the elders while the matter is referred to Darius.

Haggai 1:1–15 gives more of the prophetic message. The people are called to consider their priorities, hear God’s assurance that He is with them, and return to the work.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry, Wesley and Gill emphasize the practical help the prophets give through correction, encouragement and God’s promise. Henry and Gill read God’s watching eye as protection and favorable care: the inquiry proceeds, but the work is allowed to continue.
passages.god_plan_html:
Zechariah 4:6–10 addresses Zerubbabel directly, grounding the work in God’s Spirit rather than human might and promising that the hands which laid the foundation will complete it. The small beginning is part of a purpose God has not abandoned.

The larger theme of God forming a dwelling among His people continues in Ephesians 2:19–22, where people are joined together in Christ as a dwelling for God in His Spirit. That is a connection across the biblical story, rather than a claim that Ezra’s builders were constructing the later church.

passages.title: Ezra 5:6-17
passages.section_title: How do the elders explain the work to the Persian officials?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 This is the text of the letter that Tattenai the governor of the region west of the Euphrates, Shethar-bozenai, and their associates, the officials in the region, sent to King Darius. 7 The report they sent him read as follows: To King Darius: All peace. 8 Let it be known to the king that we went into the province of Judah, to the house of the great God. The people are rebuilding it with large stones and placing timbers in the walls. This work is being carried out diligently and is prospering in their hands. 9 So we questioned the elders and asked, “Who authorized you to rebuild this temple and restore this structure?” 10 We also asked for their names, so that we could write down the names of their leaders for your information. 11 And this is the answer they returned: “We are servants of the God of heaven and earth, and we are rebuilding the temple that was built many years ago, which a great king of Israel built and completed. 12 But since our fathers angered the God of heaven, He delivered them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, the Chaldean who destroyed this temple and carried away the people to Babylon. 13 In the first year of his reign, however, Cyrus king of Babylon issued a decree to rebuild this house of God. 14 He also removed from the temple of Babylon the gold and silver articles belonging to the house of God, which Nebuchadnezzar had taken and carried there from the temple in Jerusalem. section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Tattenai’s report describes substantial construction being carried out diligently. It records the officials’ questions and gives the elders’ answer rather than simply repeating an accusation of rebellion.

The elders identify themselves as servants of the God of heaven and earth. They explain that the former temple was destroyed when their ancestors provoked God’s anger, and that Cyrus later authorized rebuilding and returned its articles through Sheshbazzar.

Their answer acknowledges both the reason for the earlier destruction and the permission under which they are working. Tattenai asks Darius to search the archives for Cyrus’s decree and send a decision.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Gill notes that the officials transmit the elders’ account fairly and fully. Wesley contrasts this with the misleading presentation of the earlier opposition. Henry emphasizes being ready to explain what one is doing in God’s service and why.

The account distinguishes an inquiry from a verdict against the builders. Tattenai asks the king to check the authorization, while the elders give an answer that can be checked against the royal records.

passages.title: Ezra 6:1-5
passages.section_title: What does the archive search uncover?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Thus King Darius ordered a search of the archives stored in the treasury of Babylon. 2 And a scroll was found in the fortress of Ecbatana, in the province of Media, with the following written on it: Memorandum: 3 In the first year of King Cyrus, he issued a decree concerning the house of God in Jerusalem: Let the house be rebuilt as a place for offering sacrifices, and let its foundations be firmly laid. It is to be sixty cubits high and sixty cubits wide, 4 with three layers of cut stones and one of timbers. The costs are to be paid from the royal treasury. 5 Furthermore, the gold and silver articles of the house of God, which Nebuchadnezzar took from the temple in Jerusalem and carried to Babylon, must also be returned to the temple in Jerusalem and deposited in the house of God.

3 In the first year of King Cyrus, he issued a decree concerning the house of God in Jerusalem: Let the house be rebuilt as a place for offering sacrifices, and let its foundations be firmly laid. It is to be sixty cubits high and sixty cubits wide, 4 with three layers of cut stones and one of timbers. The costs are to be paid from the royal treasury. 5 Furthermore, the gold and silver articles of the house of God, which Nebuchadnezzar took from the temple in Jerusalem and carried to Babylon, must also be returned to the temple in Jerusalem and deposited in the house of God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Darius orders a search of the archives associated with Babylon’s treasury. A memorandum is found at the fortress of Ecbatana in Media.

The document confirms Cyrus’s order that the temple be rebuilt for sacrifice. It records dimensions and construction details, directs that costs be paid from the royal treasury, and requires the return of the gold and silver temple articles.

The elders’ claim now has a written royal record behind it. The narrative moves from their report of Cyrus’s permission to the discovery of the permission itself.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley and Gill understand the search as extending beyond Babylon to the place where the memorandum is found. Both discuss the temple’s dimensions, offering different ways of relating them to Solomon’s building. The clearest point of the document for the story is its confirmation of permission, funding and the returned articles.

passages.title: Ezra 6:6-12
passages.section_title: How does Darius’s reply change the situation?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 Therefore Darius decreed: To Tattenai governor of the region west of the Euphrates, Shethar-bozenai, and your associates and officials in the region: You must stay away from that place! 7 Leave this work on the house of God alone. Let the governor and elders of the Jews rebuild this house of God on its original site. 8 I hereby decree what you must do for these elders of the Jews who are rebuilding this house of God: The cost is to be paid in full to these men from the royal treasury out of the taxes of the provinces west of the Euphrates, so that the work will not be hindered. 9 Whatever is needed—young bulls, rams, and lambs for burnt offerings to the God of heaven, as well as wheat, salt, wine, and oil, as requested by the priests in Jerusalem—must be given to them daily without fail. 10 Then they will be able to offer sacrifices of a sweet aroma to the God of heaven and to pray for the lives of the king and his sons. 11 I also decree that if any man interferes with this directive, a beam is to be torn from his house and raised up, and he is to be impaled on it. And his own house shall be made a pile of rubble for this offense. 12 May God, who has caused His Name to dwell there, overthrow any king or people who lifts a hand to alter this decree or to destroy this house of God in Jerusalem. I, Darius, have issued the decree. Let it be carried out with diligence.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Darius tells the regional officials to leave the temple work alone and allow the Jewish governor and elders to rebuild on its original site. He also orders the full cost paid from regional tax revenue so that the work will not be hindered.

The decree supplies animals and other materials needed for the offerings, according to the priests’ requests. Darius gives a purpose for this support: sacrifices to the God of heaven and prayers for the lives of the king and his sons.

The order ends with a severe penalty for interference and a call for God to overthrow anyone who tries to destroy His house. It is the Persian king’s decree protecting this rebuilding project.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry emphasizes help arriving through a ruler from whom it might not have been expected. Gill draws attention to the expanded practical support: the officials must provide resources for the work, not simply stop obstructing it. He also connects the requested prayers with prayer for rulers under whom God’s people live.
passages.god_plan_html:
Prayer for rulers also appears in 1 Timothy 2:1–6. Believers are urged to pray for kings and everyone in authority, with a view to peaceful, godly lives. Paul places this within God’s desire that people come to the knowledge of the truth and the work of Jesus Christ as mediator.

The wider connection moves beyond the welfare of one royal family. God’s people can pray for public authorities while seeking the good of others and the spread of the truth about Christ.

passages.title: Ezra 6:13-18
passages.section_title: How is the completed temple dedicated?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 In response, Tattenai the governor of the region west of the Euphrates, Shethar-bozenai, and their associates diligently carried out what King Darius had decreed. 14 So the Jewish elders built and prospered through the prophesying of Haggai the prophet and Zechariah son of Iddo. They finished building according to the command of the God of Israel and the decrees of Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes, kings of Persia. 15 And this temple was completed on the third day of the month of Adar, in the sixth year of the reign of King Darius. 16 Then the people of Israel—the priests, the Levites, and the rest of the exiles—celebrated the dedication of the house of God with joy. 17 For the dedication of the house of God they offered a hundred bulls, two hundred rams, four hundred lambs, and a sin offering for all Israel of twelve male goats, one for each tribe of Israel. 18 They also appointed the priests by their divisions and the Levites by their groups to the service of God in Jerusalem, according to what is written in the Book of Moses.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Tattenai and his associates carry out Darius’s instructions. The elders continue building, encouraged by Haggai and Zechariah, and the temple is completed on the third day of Adar in Darius’s sixth year.

The account places God’s command alongside the Persian royal decrees. The people then celebrate the dedication with joy, offering bulls, rams and lambs, together with twelve male goats as a sin offering for all Israel, one for each tribe.

Priests and Levites are assigned to their groups for service according to the Book of Moses. Completion means the restoration of an ordered place of worship, not merely finishing a building.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley emphasizes that the success belongs to God, who both sends the prophets and moves the ruler to support the work. Gill reads the twelve goats as expressing concern for all Israel, including people from beyond Judah and Benjamin.

Readers also discuss why Artaxerxes is named in the summary of royal decrees before the completion date under Darius. Gill considers several possibilities and favors treating the name as another title of Darius; the Cambridge commentary understands it as a reference to later royal help included in the summary. The completion date itself is explicitly given as Darius’s sixth year.

passages.title: Ezra 6:19-22
passages.section_title: Why does the account end this stage with Passover?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 On the fourteenth day of the first month, the exiles kept the Passover. 20 All the priests and Levites had purified themselves and were ceremonially clean. And the Levites slaughtered the Passover lamb for all the exiles, for their priestly brothers, and for themselves. 21 The Israelites who had returned from exile ate it, together with all who had separated themselves from the uncleanness of the peoples of the land to seek the LORD, the God of Israel. 22 For seven days they kept the Feast of Unleavened Bread with joy, because the LORD had made them joyful and turned the heart of the king of Assyria toward them to strengthen their hands in the work on the house of the God of Israel.

And the Levites slaughtered the Passover lamb for all the exiles, for their priestly brothers, and for themselves. 21 The Israelites who had returned from exile ate it, together with all who had separated themselves from the uncleanness of the peoples of the land to seek the LORD, the God of Israel. 22 For seven days they kept the Feast of Unleavened Bread with joy, because the LORD had made them joyful and turned the heart of the king of Assyria toward them to strengthen their hands in the work on the house of the God of Israel.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The returned exiles keep Passover on the fourteenth day of the first month. The priests and Levites have purified themselves, and the Levites prepare the Passover lambs for the people, the priests and themselves.

The meal includes the returning Israelites and those who have separated themselves from the surrounding peoples’ uncleanness to seek the LORD. Seven days of Unleavened Bread follow with joy.

The closing explanation gives God credit for their joy and for turning royal power toward the work. The ruler is called the king of Assyria, even though the narrative has been describing Persian rule.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry emphasizes serving God with joy as worship is restored. Gill reads those joining the returnees as people leaving idolatry to seek Israel’s God.

Wesley and Gill explain the title king of Assyria through the Persian ruler’s possession of the earlier empire’s territory. Their emphasis is the reversal: power associated with past oppression now helps support the rebuilding.
passages.god_plan_html:
Passover reaches back to God delivering Israel from Egypt in Exodus 12:1–20. After another captivity, the people again remember that deliverance as their life of worship is renewed.

The New Testament carries the Passover theme to Christ. In 1 Corinthians 5:6–8, Paul identifies Christ as the sacrificed Passover lamb and calls for lives marked by sincerity and truth. Ezra records the restored celebration; Paul shows how the feast’s language helps explain Christ’s sacrifice and the life that follows it.
