passages.title: Ezra 7:1-10
passages.section_title: What kind of teacher is Ezra?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Many years later, during the reign of Artaxerxes king of Persia, Ezra son of Seraiah, the son of Azariah, the son of Hilkiah, 2 the son of Shallum, the son of Zadok, the son of Ahitub, 3 the son of Amariah, the son of Azariah, the son of Meraioth, 4 the son of Zerahiah, the son of Uzzi, the son of Bukki, 5 the son of Abishua, the son of Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron the chief priest— 6 this Ezra came up from Babylon. He was a scribe skilled in the Law of Moses, which the LORD, the God of Israel, had given. The king had granted Ezra all his requests, for the hand of the LORD his God was upon him. 7 So in the seventh year of King Artaxerxes, he went up to Jerusalem with some of the Israelites, including priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, and temple servants. 8 Ezra arrived in Jerusalem in the fifth month of the seventh year of the king. 9 He had begun the journey from Babylon on the first day of the first month, and he arrived in Jerusalem on the first day of the fifth month, for the gracious hand of his God was upon him. 10 For Ezra had set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, to practice it, and to teach its statutes and ordinances in Israel.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The account moves many years beyond the temple’s completion and introduces Ezra during the reign of Artaxerxes. His family line is traced back to Aaron, and he is described as a scribe skilled in the Law of Moses.

Ezra travels from Babylon with Israelites and people associated with temple service. He arrives in Jerusalem in the fifth month of the king’s seventh year, and the account repeatedly gives God credit for the favor and help he receives.

His purpose is stated in verse 10: he has set his heart to study the LORD’s Law, practice it and teach its instructions in Israel. Knowing, doing and teaching belong together in his preparation for the task.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley and Gill emphasize the order: Ezra seeks to understand God’s word, lives by it and then teaches others. Henry also emphasizes the favor God gives him for the journey and service. His expertise is presented alongside his commitment to obey, rather than as knowledge alone.
passages.god_plan_html:
The connection between hearing and doing continues in James 1:19–27, which warns against hearing the word without acting on it. In Matthew 28:16–20, Jesus commissions His disciples to teach people to obey what He has commanded.

2 Timothy 3:14–17 places Scripture’s teaching, correction and training within salvation through faith in Christ and preparation for good works. These are broader connections with Ezra’s pattern of study and obedience, not a claim that every believer holds Ezra’s particular office.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezra 7:11-20
passages.section_title: What does the king authorize Ezra to do?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 This is the text of the letter King Artaxerxes had given to Ezra the priest and scribe, an expert in the commandments and statutes of the LORD to Israel: 12 Artaxerxes, king of kings. section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Artaxerxes’s letter allows willing Israelites, priests and Levites to go with Ezra to Jerusalem. The king and his seven counselors commission him to examine the situation in Judah and Jerusalem according to God’s Law.

Ezra is also to carry the king’s gifts and the people’s freewill offerings. The money is assigned first to animals and accompanying offerings for the temple altar, with remaining funds to be used according to God’s will.

Temple articles must be delivered, and further needs may be supplied from the royal treasury. The letter gives both permission for the journey and practical means for the work Ezra is to undertake.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry emphasizes the generosity of a foreign king toward the worship of Israel’s God. Gill and Wesley understand the inquiry as examining the people’s life against the Law Ezra knows. The commission joins material support with responsibility for instruction and conduct.

passages.title: Ezra 7:21-26
passages.section_title: How far does Ezra’s royal commission extend?

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Artaxerxes directs the treasurers west of the Euphrates to supply Ezra promptly, within stated amounts of silver, wheat, wine and oil, with salt unrestricted. He also exempts temple personnel from the specified taxes.

The decree authorizes Ezra to appoint magistrates and judges and to teach those who do not know God’s laws. It closes with penalties under the law of God and the king, ranging from imprisonment and confiscation to banishment and death.

These instructions describe the legal authority the Persian king grants Ezra for this setting. They form part of the royal letter rather than a separate instruction from Jesus to His disciples.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley and Gill connect the wisdom entrusted to Ezra with his knowledge of God’s Law and the need for informed judgment. Henry distinguishes this royal authority from Christian ministry, which he describes in terms of faithful teaching, holy conduct, prayer and patient endurance. That distinction matters when applying a Persian decree beyond its original setting.

passages.title: Ezra 7:27-28
passages.section_title: Why does Ezra interrupt the account to give thanks?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 27 Blessed be the LORD, the God of our fathers, who has put into the heart of the king to so honor the house of the LORD in Jerusalem, 28 and who has shown me favor before the king, his counselors, and all his powerful officials. And because the hand of the LORD my God was upon me, I took courage and gathered the leaders of Israel to return with me.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the king’s letter, Ezra speaks in the first person and blesses the LORD. He credits God with putting the desire to honor the Jerusalem temple into the king’s heart.

He also gives thanks for favor before the king, counselors and officials. God’s hand upon him gives him courage, and he gathers Israelite leaders to go with him.

The letter is therefore followed by the account’s own explanation of its significance: Ezra sees God’s kindness at work in the opportunity and support he has received.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry, Wesley and Gill read this as gratitude for both the commission and the encouragement to carry it out. Ezra’s courage is described as a response to God’s help, and the favorable royal decision becomes a reason for thanksgiving.

passages.title: Ezra 8:1-14
passages.section_title: Who travels with Ezra?

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.context_html:
Ezra records the family heads and genealogical enrollment of those returning with him from Babylon under Artaxerxes. The list begins with descendants of Phinehas, Ithamar and David, then identifies further family groups and the men registered with them.

This is another company of returnees after the earlier group in chapter 2. The repeated family names show continuing ties within the people who have lived away from Judah.

The numbers here record men, while the later prayer for their children in verse 21 shows that the journey includes families. The list should not be mistaken for a complete description of every traveler.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley notes that the named men travel with families, and Henry emphasizes the gathering of people to accompany Ezra in the work. The family record makes this a return involving identifiable households, continuing the earlier restoration rather than beginning with an unrelated population.

passages.title: Ezra 8:15-20
passages.section_title: Why does Ezra pause to recruit Levites?

passages.context_html:
The company camps for three days by the canal flowing to Ahava. When Ezra reviews those assembled, he finds priests but no other Levites.

He sends leaders and teachers to Iddo at Casiphia with a request for ministers for God’s house. Sherebiah’s group and Hashabiah’s group then join them, together with 220 temple servants.

Ezra again credits God’s gracious hand for the response. He also records the practical steps taken: reviewing the company, identifying the need and sending a specific request.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley and Gill distinguish the missing Levites from the priests who are already present. They see God’s help in supplying people for the needed service. Henry draws attention to the importance of asking people to take part: the need becomes an occasion for a direct invitation.

passages.title: Ezra 8:21-23
passages.section_title: Why do the travelers fast before setting out?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 And there by the Ahava Canal I proclaimed a fast, so that we might humble ourselves before our God and ask Him for a safe journey for us and our children, with all our possessions. 22 For I was ashamed to ask the king for an escort of soldiers and horsemen to protect us from our enemies on the road, since we had told him, “The hand of our God is gracious to all who seek Him, but His great anger is against all who forsake Him.” 23 So we fasted and petitioned our God about this, and He granted our request.
paragraphs: 21 And there by the Ahava Canal I proclaimed a fast, so that we might humble ourselves before our God and ask Him for a safe journey for us and our children, with all our possessions. 22 For I was ashamed to ask the king for an escort of soldiers and horsemen to protect us from our enemies on the road, since we had told him, “The hand of our God is gracious to all who seek Him, but His great anger is against all who forsake Him.” 23 So we fasted and petitioned our God about this, and He granted our request.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Ezra proclaims a fast by the Ahava Canal so that the company can humble themselves before God and ask for a safe journey for themselves, their children and their possessions.

He explains that he had been ashamed to ask the king for a military escort after speaking of God’s gracious care for those who seek Him. The group fasts and prays, and Ezra reports that God grants their request.

The account describes a particular decision made in light of Ezra’s testimony to the king. Nehemiah 2:1–9 later records another servant praying, receiving royal help and traveling with officers and cavalry.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry understands Ezra’s choice as concern that a lawful advantage might undermine his witness in this situation. He emphasizes seeking wisdom about when to use or decline such help. Gill likewise connects the choice with what Ezra had already said about God’s care. The fast expresses dependence on God as the company faces a real need.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus’ teaching in Matthew 6:16–18 also directs fasting toward the Father rather than toward an audience. The wider theme is an honest turning to God, not a performance designed to impress others.

In Matthew 26:36–46, Jesus brings His distress and request to the Father while submitting to His will. Ezra records a granted request for safe travel; Jesus’ prayer shows why trust reaches deeper than receiving the particular outcome requested.

passages.title: Ezra 8:24-30
passages.section_title: Why are the gifts weighed and placed in named hands?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 24 Then I set apart twelve of the leading priests, together with Sherebiah, Hashabiah, and ten of their brothers, 25 and I weighed out to them the contribution of silver and gold and the articles that the king, his counselors, his leaders, and all the Israelites there had offered for the house of our God. 26 I weighed out into their hands 650 talents of silver, articles of silver weighing 100 talents, 100 talents of gold, 27 20 gold bowls valued at 1,000 darics, and two articles of fine polished bronze, as precious as gold. 28 Then I told them, “You are holy to the LORD, and these articles are holy. The silver and gold are a freewill offering to the LORD, the God of your fathers. 29 Guard them carefully until you weigh them out in the chambers of the house of the LORD in Jerusalem before the leading priests, Levites, and heads of the Israelite families.” 30 So the priests and Levites took charge of the silver and gold and sacred articles that had been weighed out to be taken to the house of our God in Jerusalem.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Ezra sets apart leading priests together with Sherebiah, Hashabiah and their brothers. He weighs out to them the silver, gold and articles offered for God’s house by the king, his officials and the Israelites.

He reminds them that both they and the articles are set apart to the LORD. They must guard the gifts until they can be weighed before the leaders in Jerusalem.

Trust in God is accompanied by named responsibility and a check on delivery. The gifts belong to the purpose for which they were offered, and their care can be accounted for.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry connects the concern for God’s gifts with faithful care for what belongs to Him. Gill emphasizes that the same weight is to be delivered in the presence of witnesses. The procedure protects the offering and gives the carriers a clear responsibility.
passages.god_plan_html:
A related concern appears in 2 Corinthians 8:16–24. Paul arranges for trusted people to accompany a generous offering and explains that care is being taken to do what is right before both God and other people.

The parallel is responsible care for gifts entrusted to ministry. In both settings, confidence in God goes together with arrangements other people can see and assess. Practical accountability serves the generosity rather than detracting from it.

passages.title: Ezra 8:31-36
passages.section_title: What happens when the travelers reach Jerusalem?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 31 On the twelfth day of the first month we set out from the Ahava Canal to go to Jerusalem, and the hand of our God was upon us to protect us from the hands of the enemies and bandits along the way. 32 So we arrived at Jerusalem and rested there for three days. 33 On the fourth day, in the house of our God, we weighed out the silver and gold and sacred articles into the hand of Meremoth son of Uriah, the priest. Eleazar son of Phinehas was with him, along with the Levites Jozabad son of Jeshua and Noadiah son of Binnui. 34 Everything was verified by number and weight, and the total weight was recorded at that time. 35 Then the exiles who had returned from captivity sacrificed burnt offerings to the God of Israel: 12 bulls for all Israel, 96 rams, 77 lambs, and a sin offering of 12 male goats. All this was a burnt offering to the LORD. 36 They also delivered the king’s edicts to the royal satraps and governors of the region west of the Euphrates, who proceeded to assist the people and the house of God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The group leaves the Ahava Canal on the twelfth day of the first month. Ezra gives God credit for protecting them from enemies and bandits along the way. After reaching Jerusalem, they rest for three days.

On the fourth day, the gifts are weighed into the care of priests and Levites at the temple. Everything is checked by number and weight, and the total weight is recorded.

The returnees then offer sacrifices, including offerings for all Israel, and deliver the king’s orders to the regional authorities. Those officials assist the people and God’s house. The journey ends with worship, an accounted-for delivery and the royal commission put into effect.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry and Gill emphasize God’s protection and the people’s thankful response. Gill also notes the officials’ assistance after receiving the royal orders. The events complete the preparations described earlier: the people arrive, the gifts are received and the work gains its authorized support.

passages.title: Ezra 9:1-4
passages.section_title: Why does the report about these marriages horrify Ezra?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 After these things had been accomplished, the leaders approached me and said, “The people of Israel, including the priests and Levites, have not kept themselves separate from the surrounding peoples whose abominations are like those of the Canaanites, Hittites, Perizzites, Jebusites, Ammonites, Moabites, Egyptians, and Amorites. 2 Indeed, the Israelites have taken some of their daughters as wives for themselves and their sons, so that the holy seed has been mixed with the people of the land. And the leaders and officials have taken the lead in this unfaithfulness!” 3 When I heard this report, I tore my tunic and cloak, pulled out some hair from my head and beard, and sat down in horror. 4 Then everyone who trembled at the words of the God of Israel gathered around me because of the unfaithfulness of the exiles, while I sat there in horror until the evening offering.
paragraphs: 1 After these things had been accomplished, the leaders approached me and said, “The people of Israel, including the priests and Levites, have not kept themselves separate from the surrounding peoples whose abominations are like those of the Canaanites, Hittites, Perizzites, Jebusites, Ammonites, Moabites, Egyptians, and Amorites. 2 Indeed, the Israelites have taken some of their daughters as wives for themselves and their sons, so that the holy seed has been mixed with the people of the land. And the leaders and officials have taken the lead in this unfaithfulness!”

3 When I heard this report, I tore my tunic and cloak, pulled out some hair from my head and beard, and sat down in horror. 4 Then everyone who trembled at the words of the God of Israel gathered around me because of the unfaithfulness of the exiles, while I sat there in horror until the evening offering.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Leaders report that people, priests and Levites have not kept themselves separate from the surrounding peoples and their practices. They have taken foreign wives for themselves and their sons, and officials have led the way in what the report calls unfaithfulness.

The expression holy seed uses the Hebrew זֶרַע, zera, pronounced ZEHR-ah, which can mean offspring or descendants. Brown–Driver–Briggs places this particular expression among uses describing the character of a people or community. Here it concerns Israel as a people set apart to God, with the report tying the marriages to the surrounding peoples’ abominations.

The background includes Exodus 34:10–17 and Deuteronomy 7:1–6, where marriage with the named peoples is connected with being led away to other gods. Ezra tears his clothing, pulls hair from his head and beard, and remains in horror until the evening offering. Others who tremble at God’s word gather around him.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry and Gill understand the report through the covenant commands and the danger of renewed idolatry. Gill notes that Ezra’s list includes peoples beyond those expressly named in Deuteronomy 7 and relates the wider concern to the same danger. The leaders’ participation makes the breach especially serious: those responsible for guiding the people have taken part in it.
passages.god_plan_html:
The wider biblical story includes people from outside Israel who turn to the LORD. Ruth 1:15–18 records Ruth’s commitment to Naomi’s people and God. Hebrews 11:31 names Rahab as someone who did not perish because she acted in faith.

Galatians 3:6–14 explains the promise to Abraham as reaching the nations through faith in Christ. These passages keep Israel’s call to holiness within God’s larger purpose to bring blessing to the nations. The concern for faithfulness here does not establish that ancestry places someone beyond God’s mercy.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezra 9:5-15
passages.section_title: Why does Ezra confess the people’s guilt as our guilt?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 At the evening offering, I got up from my humiliation with my tunic and cloak torn, and I fell on my knees, spread out my hands to the LORD my God, 6 and said: “O my God, I am ashamed and embarrassed to lift up my face to You, my God, because our iniquities are higher than our heads, and our guilt has reached the heavens. 7 From the days of our fathers to this day, our guilt has been great. Because of our iniquities, we and our kings and priests have been delivered into the hands of the kings of the earth and subjected to the sword and to captivity, to pillage and humiliation, as we are this day. 8 But now, for a brief moment, grace has come from the LORD our God to preserve for us a remnant and to give us a stake in His holy place. Even in our bondage, our God has given us new life and light to our eyes. 9 Though we are slaves, our God has not forsaken us in our bondage, but He has extended to us grace in the sight of the kings of Persia, giving us new life to rebuild the house of our God and repair its ruins, and giving us a wall of protection in Judah and Jerusalem. 10 And now, our God, what can we say after this? For we have forsaken the commandments 11 that You gave through Your servants the prophets, saying: ‘The land that you are entering to possess is a land polluted by the impurity of its peoples and the abominations with which they have filled it from end to end. 12 Now, therefore, do not give your daughters in marriage to their sons or take their daughters for your sons. Would You not become so angry with us as to wipe us out, leaving no remnant or survivor? 15 O LORD, God of Israel, You are righteous! For we remain this day as a remnant. Here we are before You in our guilt, though because of it no one can stand before You.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
At the evening offering Ezra kneels and spreads his hands before God. He prays as part of the guilty community, using our and we rather than speaking only about other people’s wrongdoing.

He recalls the long history of sin and its consequences, but also the grace that has preserved a remnant and made a return possible. Even under Persian rule, the people have received help to rebuild God’s house and begin again.

That mercy makes renewed disobedience more troubling. Ezra acknowledges that God has punished them less than they deserved and ends by admitting that the people cannot defend themselves before Him. The prayer offers confession rather than an excuse.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill understand Ezra’s language as identifying himself with the nation and its guilt; it is not a claim that he personally entered one of the marriages being reported. Henry emphasizes shame over sin, recognition of past mercy and reliance upon God rather than a defense of the wrongdoing.

Wesley and Gill also understand the wall of protection in verse 9 as security through God’s care and Persian favor. They do not take it as proof that Jerusalem’s physical walls have already been rebuilt.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ezra’s prayer belongs to the biblical theme of a priest speaking before God on behalf of the people. The New Testament develops priestly intercession in Hebrews 7:23–28, where Jesus lives continually to intercede for those who draw near to God through Him.

The connection includes an important difference: Ezra prays from within a sinful community, while Hebrews describes Jesus as holy and undefiled, offering Himself for sin once for all. The connection is between intercession for guilty people and Christ’s enduring priesthood.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezra 10:1-5
passages.section_title: What response does Shecaniah propose?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 While Ezra prayed and made this confession, weeping and falling facedown before the house of God, a very large assembly of Israelites—men, women, and children—gathered around him, and the people wept bitterly as well. 2 Then Shecaniah son of Jehiel, an Elamite, said to Ezra: “We have been unfaithful to our God by marrying foreign women from the people of the land, yet in spite of this, there is hope for Israel. 3 So now let us make a covenant before our God to send away all the foreign wives and their children, according to the counsel of my lord and of those who tremble at the command of our God. Let it be done according to the Law. 4 Get up, for this matter is your responsibility, and we will support you. Be strong and take action!” 5 So Ezra got up and made the leading priests, Levites, and all Israel take an oath to do what had been said. And they took the oath.

Let it be done according to the Law. 4 Get up, for this matter is your responsibility, and we will support you. Be strong and take action!”
5 So Ezra got up and made the leading priests, Levites, and all Israel take an oath to do what had been said. And they took the oath.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
As Ezra prays and weeps before God’s house, a large gathering of men, women and children joins him in bitter weeping. Shecaniah son of Jehiel acknowledges the unfaithfulness but also says there is still hope for Israel.

He proposes a covenant to send away the foreign wives and their children, according to the counsel of those who tremble at God’s command, and calls Ezra to lead. Ezra then requires the leading priests, Levites and people to take an oath to act on the proposal.

The proposal involves an actual separation of families, not simply an expression of regret. The following verses describe the assembly and investigation through which the matter is addressed.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry, Wesley and Gill see the response as moving from sorrow to action under the covenant requirements. They understand the marriages in question as unlawful in that setting.

Henry also distinguishes that setting from marriage after the gospel’s removal of the separation between Jews and Gentiles. The New Testament directly addresses a Christian married to an unbeliever: if the unbelieving spouse is willing to remain, the believer must not divorce that spouse (1 Corinthians 7:10–16). Ezra’s account therefore needs to be read alongside those instructions when considering Christian marriage.

passages.title: Ezra 10:6-17
passages.section_title: How is the decision investigated and carried out?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 Then Ezra withdrew from before the house of God and walked to the chamber of Jehohanan son of Eliashib. And while he stayed there, he ate no food and drank no water, because he was mourning over the unfaithfulness of the exiles. 7 And a proclamation was issued throughout Judah and Jerusalem that all the exiles should gather at Jerusalem. 8 Whoever failed to appear within three days would forfeit all his property, according to the counsel of the leaders and elders, and would himself be expelled from the assembly of the exiles. 9 So within the three days, all the men of Judah and Benjamin assembled in Jerusalem, and on the twentieth day of the ninth month, all the people sat in the square at the house of God, trembling regarding this matter and because of the heavy rain. 10 Then Ezra the priest stood up and said to them, “You have been unfaithful by marrying foreign women, adding to the guilt of Israel. 11 Now, therefore, make a confession to the LORD, the God of your fathers, and do His will. Separate yourselves from the people of the land and from your foreign wives.” 12 And the whole assembly responded in a loud voice: “Truly we must do as you say! 13 But there are many people here, and it is the rainy season. We are not able to stay out in the open. Nor is this the work of one or two days, for we have transgressed greatly in this matter. 14 Let our leaders represent the whole assembly. Then let everyone in our towns who has married a foreign woman come at an appointed time, together with the elders and judges of each town, until the fierce anger of our God in this matter is turned away from us.” 15 (Only Jonathan son of Asahel and Jahzeiah son of Tikvah, supported by Meshullam and Shabbethai the Levite, opposed this plan.) 16 So the exiles did as proposed. Ezra the priest selected men who were family heads, each of them identified by name, to represent their families. On the first day of the tenth month they launched the investigation, 17 and by the first day of the first month they had dealt with all the men who had married foreign women.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Ezra continues mourning without food or water. A proclamation summons the exiles to Jerusalem within three days, with forfeiture of property and exclusion from the assembly threatened for failure to appear.

The people gather in the ninth month, trembling over the matter and in heavy rain. Ezra calls for confession and separation from the foreign wives. The assembly agrees, while asking for appointed hearings because many people are involved and the matter cannot be settled in one or two days.

The BSB records four men opposing the plan. Ezra and selected family heads begin examining cases on the first day of the tenth month and finish by the first day of the first month. The account describes a sustained investigation rather than a single decision made for every household in the rain.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry emphasizes the need for the decision to be carried out carefully. Gill likewise understands the appointed times and involvement of local elders and judges as the means of investigating the cases.

There is a difference over verse 15. Wesley understands the four named men as officials administering the matter. Gill discusses that reading but also considers the reading that they opposed it probable; this latter reading is the one used in the BSB. Either way, the narrative then moves to the named representatives and the investigation.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.context_html:
The closing list begins with priests, including men from Jeshua’s family. They pledge to send their wives away and present a ram as a guilt offering. Levites, singers, gatekeepers and other Israelites follow in the list.

The order makes clear that the matter reaches people in religious service as well as the wider community. The report names those involved rather than leaving the breach as an accusation against an anonymous group.

The final verse adds that some had children by these wives. The book ends at that point. It records the men’s responsibility and the presence of children without giving a full account of the later circumstances of the affected families.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Gill read the list as the identified cases addressed in the reform, with the priests’ pledge and guilt offering leading the account.

Readers draw different conclusions about the children. Wesley understands them as excluded from Israel’s community but thinks provision was probably made for them. Gill notes that the closing account does not repeat the proposal to send the children away and suggests they were retained and cared for. These are the commentators’ proposed conclusions; the narrative does not follow the families’ later lives.
passages.god_plan_html:
The priests’ guilt offering belongs to the sacrificial setting of Israel’s Law. Hebrews 10:1–18 explains the limits of repeated animal offerings and presents Christ’s offering of Himself as the sacrifice for sins given once for all.

That wider teaching distinguishes acknowledging guilt and responding to it from the ultimate ground of forgiveness. Ezra’s ending shows a community confronting unfaithfulness. Hebrews directs readers to Christ’s completed offering, through which God provides the forgiveness the sacrifices could not finally accomplish.

passages.title: Nehemiah 1:1-4
passages.section_title: Why does the news from Jerusalem move Nehemiah to tears?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 These are the words of Nehemiah son of Hacaliah: In the month of Chislev, in the twentieth year, while I was in the citadel of Susa, 2 Hanani, one of my brothers, arrived with men from Judah. So I questioned them about the remnant of the Jews who had survived the exile, and also about Jerusalem. 3 And they told me, “The remnant who survived the exile are there in the province, in great trouble and disgrace. The wall of Jerusalem is broken down, and its gates have been burned with fire.” 4 When I heard these words, I sat down and wept. I mourned for days, fasting and praying before the God of heaven.
paragraphs: 1 These are the words of Nehemiah son of Hacaliah: In the month of Chislev, in the twentieth year, while I was in the citadel of Susa, 2 Hanani, one of my brothers, arrived with men from Judah. So I questioned them about the remnant of the Jews who had survived the exile, and also about Jerusalem. 3 And they told me, “The remnant who survived the exile are there in the province, in great trouble and disgrace. The wall of Jerusalem is broken down, and its gates have been burned with fire.”
4 When I heard these words, I sat down and wept. I mourned for days, fasting and praying before the God of heaven.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Nehemiah is in the citadel of Susa when Hanani and other men arrive from Judah. He asks about both the Jewish people who have survived the exile and the condition of Jerusalem.

The answer is troubling: the people are in distress and disgrace, the city wall is broken down and the gates have been burned. A return to the land has taken place, but important needs remain.

Nehemiah sits down and weeps. His grief continues for days and becomes fasting and prayer before the God of heaven. The book begins with attention to other people’s condition before it describes the work he will undertake.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry emphasizes that distance and a position at court have not removed Nehemiah’s concern for his people. Gill likewise reads the report as the distress of a vulnerable community. His mourning and prayer show that the inquiry is more than an interest in news.

passages.title: Nehemiah 1:5-11
passages.section_title: How does God’s promise shape Nehemiah’s prayer?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 Then I said: “O LORD, God of heaven, the great and awesome God who keeps His covenant of loving devotion with those who love Him and keep His commandments, 6 let Your eyes be open and Your ears attentive to hear the prayer that I, Your servant, now pray before You day and night for Your servants, the Israelites. I confess the sins that we Israelites have committed against You. Both I and my father’s house have sinned. 7 We have behaved corruptly against You and have not kept the commandments, statutes, and ordinances that You gave Your servant Moses. 8 Remember, I pray, the word that You commanded Your servant Moses when You said, ‘If you are unfaithful, I will scatter you among the nations, 9 but if you return to Me and keep and practice My commandments, then even if your exiles have been banished to the farthest horizon, I will gather them from there and bring them to the place I have chosen as a dwelling for My Name.’ 10 They are Your servants and Your people. You redeemed them by Your great power and mighty hand. 11 O Lord, may Your ear be attentive to my prayer and to the prayers of Your servants who delight to revere Your name. Give Your servant success this day, I pray, and grant him mercy in the sight of this man.” (At that time I was the cupbearer to the king.)

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Nehemiah begins with God’s greatness and faithfulness to His covenant. He confesses the sins of Israel and explicitly includes his own sins and those of his family.

He then recalls the warning that disobedience brings scattering and the promise that God will gather His people when they return to Him. The language draws on the promise in Deuteronomy 30:1–10, including gathering people from the farthest horizon.

The prayer ends with a concrete request for success and mercy before a particular man. The final sentence explains why: Nehemiah is the king’s cupbearer. His concern for Jerusalem is moving toward an approach to the king.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry and Gill emphasize confession, God’s covenant promise and His past redemption of the people. Nehemiah’s confidence rests on who God is and what He has said, while his immediate request concerns the opportunity before him at court.
passages.god_plan_html:
The promise in Deuteronomy 30:1–10 reaches beyond a change of location: it includes a people returning to God, loving Him and obeying Him. Nehemiah prays within that larger purpose of restored relationship and service.

The song at John the Baptist’s birth in Luke 1:68–79 also celebrates God remembering His covenant, bringing redemption and enabling His people to serve Him in holiness. Luke carries the hope forward toward salvation through the promised Savior and the forgiveness of sins. This is a broader connection with covenant faithfulness, not a claim that rebuilding Jerusalem’s wall is the whole fulfillment of that hope.

passages.title: Nehemiah 2:1-8
passages.section_title: What does Nehemiah ask when the king notices his sadness?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now in the month of Nisan, in the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes, when wine was set before him, I took the wine and gave it to the king. I had never been sad in his presence, 2 so the king said to me, “Why is your face sad, though you are not ill? This could only be sadness of the heart.” I was overwhelmed with fear 3 and replied to the king, “May the king live forever! Why should I not be sad when the city where my fathers are buried lies in ruins, and its gates have been destroyed by fire?” 4 “What is your request?” replied the king. So I prayed to the God of heaven 5 and answered the king, “If it pleases the king, and if your servant has found favor in your sight, I ask that you send me to Judah, to the city where my fathers are buried, so that I may rebuild it.” 6 Then the king, with the queen seated beside him, asked me, “How long will your journey take, and when will you return?” So it pleased the king to send me, and I set a time. 7 I also said to him, “If it pleases the king, may letters be given to me for the governors west of the Euphrates, so that they will grant me safe passage until I reach Judah. 8 And may I have a letter to Asaph, keeper of the king’s forest, so that he will give me timber to make beams for the gates of the citadel to the temple, for the city wall, and for the house I will occupy.” And because the gracious hand of my God was upon me, the king granted my requests.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
In the month of Nisan, Nehemiah serves wine to Artaxerxes. The king notices his sad face and asks what is wrong. Nehemiah is afraid, but he explains the condition of the city where his ancestors are buried.

When the king asks what he wants, Nehemiah prays to the God of heaven and requests permission to go to Judah and rebuild. The king asks about the journey and his return, and Nehemiah gives him a time.

He also asks for letters granting passage through the region and timber for the gates, wall and his lodging. The king grants the requests, and Nehemiah attributes the favorable answer to God’s gracious hand upon him.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry and Gill understand the prayer in verse 4 as a brief turning to God in the midst of the conversation. It follows the longer prayer already described. Both emphasize that dependence on God is joined with a direct and practical request to the king.
passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 4:14–16 gives the New Testament ground for approaching God confidently in need: Jesus, the great high priest, understands human weakness and has remained without sin.

Nehemiah turns to God while facing an earthly ruler. Hebrews develops the wider invitation to seek mercy and timely help at God’s throne of grace through Jesus. The connection is access to God in need, with confidence grounded in His provision rather than in the petitioner’s status at court.

passages.title: Nehemiah 2:9-16
passages.section_title: Why does Nehemiah inspect the walls before announcing his plan?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 Then I went to the governors west of the Euphrates and gave them the king’s letters. The king had also sent army officers and cavalry with me. 10 But when Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite official heard about this, they were deeply disturbed that someone had come to seek the well-being of the Israelites. 11 After I had arrived in Jerusalem and had been there three days, 12 I set out at night with a few men. I did not tell anyone what my God had laid on my heart to do for Jerusalem. The only animal with me was the one on which I was riding. 13 So I went out at night through the Valley Gate toward the Well of the Serpent and the Dung Gate, and I inspected the walls of Jerusalem that had been broken down and the gates that had been destroyed by fire. 14 Then I went on to the Fountain Gate and the King’s Pool, but there was no room for the animal under me to get through; 15 so I went up the valley by night and inspected the wall. Then I headed back and reentered through the Valley Gate. 16 The officials did not know where I had gone or what I was doing, for I had not yet told the Jews or priests or nobles or officials or any other workers.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Nehemiah delivers the king’s letters to the regional governors and travels with army officers and cavalry. Sanballat and Tobiah are disturbed that someone has come to seek the Israelites’ well-being.

After three days in Jerusalem, Nehemiah goes out at night with a few men. He has not yet told the local officials what God has laid on his heart to do. He follows a route past gates and pools, examining the broken walls and burned gates.

At one point his animal cannot get through, so he continues his inspection by the valley and returns through the Valley Gate. The officials and prospective workers still do not know where he has gone or what he is preparing.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Gill understands the small company and nighttime visit as a way of keeping the plan private until Nehemiah is ready. Henry emphasizes that he considers the situation before asking the people to join him. The narrative clearly records the inspection and temporary secrecy, while leaving several possible reasons for the precise arrangements unstated.

passages.title: Nehemiah 2:17-20
passages.section_title: How does Nehemiah invite the people to share the work?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 Then I said to them, “You see the trouble we are in. Jerusalem lies in ruins, and its gates have been burned down. Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem, so that we will no longer be a disgrace.” 18 I also told them about the gracious hand of my God upon me, and what the king had said to me. “Let us start rebuilding,” they replied, and they set their hands to this good work. 19 But when Sanballat the Horonite, Tobiah the Ammonite official, and Geshem the Arab heard about this, they mocked us and ridiculed us, saying, “What is this you are doing? Are you rebelling against the king?” 20 So I answered them and said, “The God of heaven is the One who will grant us success. We, His servants, will start rebuilding, but you have no portion, right, or claim in Jerusalem.”

Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem, so that we will no longer be a disgrace.” 18 I also told them about the gracious hand of my God upon me, and what the king had said to me. “Let us start rebuilding,” they replied, and they set their hands to this good work.

19 But when Sanballat the Horonite, Tobiah the Ammonite official, and Geshem the Arab heard about this, they mocked us and ridiculed us, saying, “What is this you are doing? Are you rebelling against the king?” 20 So I answered them and said, “The God of heaven is the One who will grant us success. We, His servants, will start rebuilding, but you have no portion, right, or claim in Jerusalem.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Nehemiah puts the city’s condition before the people and invites them to rebuild together. He speaks of the trouble they are in as a shared concern and tells them about God’s gracious hand and the king’s support.

The people respond by committing themselves to the work. Sanballat, Tobiah and Geshem then mock the undertaking and suggest that the builders are rebelling against the king.

Nehemiah answers with confidence in the God of heaven. He identifies the builders as God’s servants who will begin the work and rejects the opponents’ claim to a share, right or standing in Jerusalem.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry emphasizes that Nehemiah does not undertake the work without the people: he encourages them to act with him. Gill likewise reads the account of God’s help and the royal commission as encouragement for their response.

Gill understands the opponents’ question as a threat to portray the project as rebellion. He reads Nehemiah’s answer as both confidence in God and a denial that these opponents have authority over the undertaking. The accusation is made after the account has already described the king’s permission.
passages.god_plan_html:
The concern for leadership that serves others continues in Luke 22:24–27. Jesus answers His disciples’ concern about greatness by placing Himself among them as one who serves.

Ephesians 4:11–16 describes leaders equipping God’s people for service so that the whole body grows in love under Christ. This is a wider connection with shared service and growth: Nehemiah calls people into the rebuilding, while the New Testament describes people building one another up as Christ’s body.

passages.title: Nehemiah 3:1-32
passages.section_title: Whose hands rebuild Jerusalem’s wall?

versions.text: 1 At the Sheep Gate, Eliashib the high priest and his fellow priests began rebuilding. They dedicated it and installed its doors. After building as far as the Tower of the Hundred and the Tower of Hananel, they dedicated the wall. 2 The men of Jericho built next to Eliashib, and Zaccur son of Imri built next to them. 3 The Fish Gate was rebuilt by the sons of Hassenaah. They laid its beams and installed its doors, bolts, and bars. 4 Next to them, Meremoth son of Uriah, the son of Hakkoz, made repairs. Next to him, Meshullam son of Berechiah, the son of Meshezabel, made repairs; and next to him, Zadok son of Baana made repairs as well. 5 Next to him, the Tekoites made repairs, but their nobles did not put their shoulders to the work under their supervisors. 6 The Jeshanah Gate was repaired by Joiada son of Paseah and Meshullam son of Besodeiah. They laid its beams and installed its doors, bolts, and bars. 7 Next to them, repairs were made by Melatiah the Gibeonite, Jadon the Meronothite, and the men of Gibeon and Mizpah, who were under the authority of the governor of the region west of the Euphrates. 8 Next to them, Uzziel son of Harhaiah, one of the goldsmiths, made repairs. They rebuilt it, installed its doors, bolts, and bars, and repaired a thousand cubits of the wall as far as the Dung Gate. 14 The Dung Gate was repaired by Malchijah son of Rechab, ruler of the district of Beth-haccherem. He rebuilt it and installed its doors, bolts, and bars. 15 The Fountain Gate was repaired by Shallun son of Col-hozeh, ruler of the district of Mizpah. He rebuilt it, roofed it, and installed its doors, bolts, and bars. He also repaired the wall of the Pool of Shelah near the king’s garden, as far as the stairs that descend from the City of David. 16 Beyond him, Nehemiah son of Azbuk, ruler of a half-district of Beth-zur, made repairs up to a point opposite the tombs of David, as far as the artificial pool and the House of the Mighty. 17 Next to him, the Levites made repairs under Rehum son of Bani, and next to him, Hashabiah, ruler of a half-district of Keilah, made repairs for his district. 18 Next to him, their countrymen made repairs under Binnui son of Henadad, ruler of the other half-district of Keilah. 19 And next to him, Ezer son of Jeshua, ruler of Mizpah, repaired another section opposite the ascent to the armory, near the angle in the wall. 20 Next to him, Baruch son of Zabbai diligently repaired another section, from the angle to the doorway of the house of Eliashib the high priest. 21 Next to him, Meremoth son of Uriah, the son of Hakkoz, repaired another section, from the doorway of the house of Eliashib to the end of the house. 22 And next to him, the priests from the surrounding area made repairs. 23 Beyond them, Benjamin and Hasshub made repairs in front of their house, and next to them, Azariah son of Maaseiah, the son of Ananiah, made repairs beside his house. 24 After him, Binnui son of Henadad repaired another section, from the house of Azariah to the angle and the corner, 25 and Palal son of Uzai made repairs opposite the angle and the tower that juts out from the upper palace of the king near the courtyard of the guard. Next to him, Pedaiah son of Parosh 26 and the temple servants living on the hill of Ophel made repairs opposite the Water Gate toward the east and the tower that juts out. 27 And next to them, the Tekoites repaired another section, from a point opposite the great tower that juts out to the wall of Ophel. 28 Above the Horse Gate, each of the priests made repairs in front of his own house. 29 Next to them, Zadok son of Immer made repairs opposite his house, and next to him, Shemaiah son of Shecaniah, the guard of the East Gate, made repairs. 30 Next to him, Hananiah son of Shelemiah, as well as Hanun the sixth son of Zalaph, repaired another section. Next to them, Meshullam son of Berechiah made repairs opposite his own quarters. 31 Next to him, Malchijah, one of the goldsmiths, made repairs as far as the house of the temple servants and the merchants, opposite the Inspection Gate, and as far as the upper room above the corner. 32 And between the upper room above the corner and the Sheep Gate, the goldsmiths and merchants made repairs.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The account follows the work around the city, beginning and ending at the Sheep Gate. It records who takes responsibility for neighboring sections, gates, towers and stretches beside homes.

The people include priests, Levites, district rulers, goldsmiths, a perfumer, merchants and Shallum’s daughters. Several groups repair sections near their own homes, while some undertake another section as well. The Tekoites appear twice, even though their nobles refuse to join the work under their supervisors.

The repeated word for repairs comes from Hebrew חָזַק, chazaq, pronounced khah-ZAHK. Brown–Driver–Briggs specifically lists its use in this chapter for repairing Jerusalem’s walls. Here the work is making the damaged defenses firm again, section by section.

The list makes the shared undertaking concrete. Nehemiah’s invitation is followed by the names and places of the people who carry it forward, together with the notice that some do not participate.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry emphasizes divided responsibilities serving a common good: each person or group attends to work within reach, and some take on more. Gill likewise highlights the Tekoites’ continued work in contrast with their nobles’ refusal. The nobles’ refusal is recorded alongside the work other Tekoites undertake.
passages.god_plan_html:
The wider theme of different people serving a shared purpose appears in 1 Corinthians 12:4–27. God gives different gifts for the common good, and the members of Christ’s body need and care for one another.

This is a connection between shared work here and the mutual service described in the New Testament. The wall needs its neighboring sections joined together; Christ’s body grows through people whose different contributions matter. The passage gives the reader names to remember where a summary might have mentioned only the leader.

passages.title: Nehemiah 4:1-6
passages.section_title: How does Nehemiah respond to the mockery?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now when Sanballat heard that we were rebuilding the wall, he was furious and filled with indignation. He ridiculed the Jews 2 before his associates and the army of Samaria, saying, “What are these feeble Jews doing? Can they restore the wall by themselves? Will they offer sacrifices? Will they complete it in a day? Can they bring these burnt stones back to life from the mounds of rubble?” 3 Then Tobiah the Ammonite, who was beside him, said, “If even a fox were to climb up on what they are building, it would break down their wall of stones!” 4 Hear us, O God, for we are despised. Turn their scorn back upon their own heads, and let them be taken as plunder to a land of captivity. 5 Do not cover up their iniquity or let their sin be blotted out from Your sight, for they have provoked the builders. 6 So we rebuilt the wall until all of it was joined together up to half its height, for the people had a mind to work.

He ridiculed the Jews 2 before his associates and the army of Samaria, saying, “What are these feeble Jews doing? Can they restore the wall by themselves? Will they offer sacrifices? Will they complete it in a day? Can they bring these burnt stones back to life from the mounds of rubble?” 3 Then Tobiah the Ammonite, who was beside him, said, “If even a fox were to climb up on what they are building, it would break down their wall of stones!”

4 Hear us, O God, for we are despised. Turn their scorn back upon their own heads, and let them be taken as plunder to a land of captivity. 5 Do not cover up their iniquity or let their sin be blotted out from Your sight, for they have provoked the builders. 6 So we rebuilt the wall until all of it was joined together up to half its height, for the people had a mind to work.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Sanballat ridicules the Jews before his associates and Samaria’s army, questioning their strength, materials and ability to finish. Tobiah adds that even a fox could break down their wall.

Nehemiah turns to God with a severe prayer. He asks that the scorn return upon the opponents and that their wrongdoing not be covered or erased from God’s sight. The prayer does not soften the hostility the builders are facing.

The account then returns to the work: the whole wall is joined to half its height because the people are willing to work. The ridicule has not brought construction to an end.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry understands the severity of the prayer in light of hardened opposition. Gill reads it as concern for God’s justice rather than a private grudge, and additionally takes it as a prophetic judgment. These are explanations of the harsh petition the narrative records; the words are presented as an appeal to God.
passages.god_plan_html:
The New Testament joins concern for justice with a call to bless persecutors. Romans 12:14–21 forbids personal revenge, leaves judgment to God and calls believers to meet an enemy’s need.

1 Peter 2:21–25 gives Christ’s response to abuse as the example: He entrusted Himself to the One who judges justly and bore sins so that people might live in righteousness. These teachings develop the question raised by Nehemiah’s prayer: how God’s people can bring wrongdoing before Him while following Christ’s way toward those who oppose them.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Nehemiah 4:7-14
passages.section_title: What changes when mockery becomes a threat of attack?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 When Sanballat and Tobiah, together with the Arabs, Ammonites, and Ashdodites, heard that the repair to the walls of Jerusalem was progressing and that the gaps were being closed, they were furious, 8 and all of them conspired to come and fight against Jerusalem and create a hindrance. 9 So we prayed to our God and posted a guard against them day and night. 10 Meanwhile, the people of Judah said: “The strength of the laborer fails, and there is so much rubble that we will never be able to rebuild the wall.” 11 And our enemies said, “Before they know or see a thing, we will come into their midst, kill them, and put an end to the work.” 12 At that time the Jews who lived nearby came and told us ten times over, “Wherever you turn, they will attack us.” 13 So I stationed men behind the lowest sections of the wall, at the vulnerable areas. I stationed them by families with their swords, spears, and bows. 14 After I had made an inspection, I stood up and said to the nobles, the officials, and the rest of the people, “Do not be afraid of them. Remember the Lord, who is great and awesome, and fight for your brothers, your sons and your daughters, your wives and your homes.”

I stationed them by families with their swords, spears, and bows. 14 After I had made an inspection, I stood up and said to the nobles, the officials, and the rest of the people, “Do not be afraid of them. Remember the Lord, who is great and awesome, and fight for your brothers, your sons and your daughters, your wives and your homes.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
As the gaps in the wall close, the opponents conspire to fight against Jerusalem and disrupt the work. The people pray and post a guard day and night.

Pressure also appears within the workforce. The laborers are exhausted and the rubble seems overwhelming. Repeated warnings from Jews living near the opponents add urgency to the threat.

Nehemiah stations families with weapons at vulnerable sections of the wall. He tells the people to remember the great and awesome Lord and to defend their brothers, children, spouses and homes. His response addresses their fear as well as the exposed places in the defenses.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry and Gill emphasize prayer together with watchfulness and practical measures. Turning to God does not prevent Nehemiah from posting guards or organizing the people. The account treats their weariness and the danger as real needs requiring a response.

passages.title: Nehemiah 4:15-23
passages.section_title: How do the people keep building while remaining ready?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 When our enemies heard that we were aware of their scheme and that God had frustrated it, each of us returned to his own work on the wall. 16 And from that day on, half of my servants did the work while the other half held spears, shields, bows, and armor. The officers stationed themselves behind all the people of Judah 17 who were rebuilding the wall. The laborers who carried materials worked with one hand and held a weapon with the other. 18 And each of the builders worked with his sword strapped at his side. But the trumpeter stayed beside me. 19 Then I said to the nobles, the officials, and the rest of the people: “The work is great and extensive, and we are spread out far from one another along the wall. 20 Wherever you hear the sound of the horn, rally to us there. Our God will fight for us!” 21 So we continued the work, while half of the men held spears from the break of dawn until the stars came out. 22 At that time I also said to the people, “Let every man and his servant spend the night inside Jerusalem, so that they can stand guard by night and work by day.” 23 So neither I nor my brothers nor my servants nor the guards with me changed out of our clothes; each carried his weapon, even to go for water.

21 So we continued the work, while half of the men held spears from the break of dawn until the stars came out. 22 At that time I also said to the people, “Let every man and his servant spend the night inside Jerusalem, so that they can stand guard by night and work by day.” 23 So neither I nor my brothers nor my servants nor the guards with me changed out of our clothes; each carried his weapon, even to go for water.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The opponents learn that their plan is known and has been frustrated. The workers return to their sections, and Nehemiah gives God credit for the outcome.

From then on, half of his servants work while the other half remain armed. The carriers keep weapons to hand, the builders wear swords and the trumpeter stays beside Nehemiah. Because the workers are spread along the wall, a horn signal will call them together wherever needed.

The work continues from dawn until the stars appear. People are told to stay inside Jerusalem overnight so that they can guard as well as work. Nehemiah and those with him remain dressed and ready, even carrying weapons when going for water.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Gill emphasizes readiness for both labor and defense, understanding the one-handed work language as expressing preparedness for both duties. Henry also draws a spiritual lesson about remaining watchful while serving God. The immediate account distinguishes the carriers’ equipment, the builders’ swords and the plan to assemble at the horn.
passages.god_plan_html:
Nehemiah’s assurance that God will fight for the people belongs to the wider biblical theme of trusting God under threat. Romans 8:31–39 gives Christian confidence its ground in God giving His Son, Christ’s death and resurrection, and His continuing prayer for His people.

Paul names persecution, danger and the sword among the troubles believers may face, yet says that nothing can separate them from God’s love in Christ. That carries the theme beyond one city’s defense: confidence in God’s faithful care endures even through suffering.

passages.title: Nehemiah 5:1-5
passages.section_title: Why are families crying out against their own countrymen?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 About that time there was a great outcry from the people and their wives against their fellow Jews. 2 Some were saying, “We and our sons and daughters are numerous. We must get grain in order to eat and stay alive.” 3 Others were saying, “We are mortgaging our fields, our vineyards, and our homes to get grain during the famine.” 4 Still others were saying, “We have borrowed money to pay the king’s tax on our fields and vineyards. 5 We and our children are just like our countrymen and their children, yet we are subjecting our sons and daughters to slavery. Some of our daughters are already enslaved, but we are powerless to redeem them because our fields and vineyards belong to others.”
paragraphs: 1 About that time there was a great outcry from the people and their wives against their fellow Jews. 2 Some were saying, “We and our sons and daughters are numerous. We must get grain in order to eat and stay alive.” 3 Others were saying, “We are mortgaging our fields, our vineyards, and our homes to get grain during the famine.” 4 Still others were saying, “We have borrowed money to pay the king’s tax on our fields and vineyards. 5 We and our children are just like our countrymen and their children, yet we are subjecting our sons and daughters to slavery. Some of our daughters are already enslaved, but we are powerless to redeem them because our fields and vineyards belong to others.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The account turns from threats outside the city to an outcry within the community. Some families need grain to feed their many children. Others mortgage fields, vineyards and homes during famine, while others borrow to pay the king’s taxes.

The consequences reach the children: sons and daughters are being brought into slavery, and families cannot redeem them because their land is already in other hands. The complaint stresses that these are fellow people and fellow children, not lives of lesser worth.

The Law provides the relevant background. Exodus 22:25–27 protects poor borrowers, while Leviticus 25:35–43 calls for support of a destitute countryman and forbids harsh treatment of those whom God brought out of Egypt.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry emphasizes compassion for the oppressed and the disgrace of exploiting fellow people. Gill reads the complaints through debt, famine and the loss of the means to recover the children. Their shared membership in the people makes the hardship a concern for the whole community.
passages.god_plan_html:
The Law connects care for the poor with God’s own redemption: those He brought out of Egypt are not to be treated harshly (Leviticus 25:35–43). Freedom received from God is meant to shape life together.

In the New Testament, Galatians 5:13–15 joins freedom with serving one another in love. 1 John 3:16–18 grounds that love in Jesus laying down His life and asks how love can remain where a person with resources closes his heart to a brother in need. The larger purpose is a people whose practical treatment of one another reflects the God who has loved and redeemed them.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Nehemiah 5:6-13
passages.section_title: What does Nehemiah require beyond a promise to do better?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 When I heard their outcry and these complaints, I became extremely angry, 7 and after serious thought I rebuked the nobles and officials, saying, “You are exacting usury from your own brothers!” So I called a large assembly against them 8 and said, “We have done our best to buy back our Jewish brothers who were sold to foreigners, but now you are selling your own brothers, that they may be sold back to us!” But they remained silent, for they could find nothing to say. 9 So I continued, “What you are doing is not right. Shouldn’t you walk in the fear of our God to avoid the reproach of our foreign enemies? 10 I, as well as my brothers and my servants, have been lending the people money and grain. Please, let us stop this usury. 11 Please restore to them immediately their fields, vineyards, olive groves, and houses, along with the percentage of the money, grain, new wine, and oil that you have been assessing them.” 12 “We will restore it,” they replied, “and will require nothing more from them. We will do as you say.” So I summoned the priests and required of the nobles and officials an oath that they would do what they had promised. 13 I also shook out the folds of my robe and said, “May God likewise shake out of his house and possessions every man who does not keep this promise. May such a man be shaken out and have nothing!” The whole assembly said, “Amen,” and they praised the LORD. And the people did as they had promised.

We will do as you say.” So I summoned the priests and required of the nobles and officials an oath that they would do what they had promised. 13 I also shook out the folds of my robe and said, “May God likewise shake out of his house and possessions every man who does not keep this promise. May such a man be shaken out and have nothing!” The whole assembly said, “Amen,” and they praised the LORD. And the people did as they had promised.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Nehemiah becomes angry at the complaints, gives the matter serious thought and rebukes the nobles and officials for charging their own brothers interest. He contrasts their conduct with the effort to buy back Jews who had been sold to foreigners.

He says that he and his household are also lending money and grain, and calls on them to stop charging interest. He requires the immediate return of fields, vineyards, olive groves, houses and the amounts being assessed.

The creditors agree to restore what has been taken and require nothing more. Nehemiah brings in the priests to confirm the promise by oath, then shakes out his robe as a warning of what should happen to anyone who breaks it. The assembly praises God, and the people act on the promise.

The prohibition of interest on a loan to a brother appears in Deuteronomy 23:19–20. Deuteronomy 15:1–18 also joins debt release and care for servants with the memory that Israel was once enslaved and redeemed.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry emphasizes that fear of God should change how people use their rights and resources toward their neighbors. Gill likewise understands the response as the return of property confirmed by an oath. The account’s emphasis is on returning what has been taken and following through, rather than ending with words alone.

passages.title: Nehemiah 5:14-19
passages.section_title: Why does Nehemiah decline the governor’s allowance?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 Furthermore, from the day King Artaxerxes appointed me to be their governor in the land of Judah, from his twentieth year until his thirty-second year (twelve years total), neither I nor my brothers ate the food allotted to the governor. 15 The governors before me had heavily burdened the people, taking from them bread and wine plus forty shekels of silver. Their servants also oppressed the people. But I did not do this, because of my fear of God. 16 Instead, I devoted myself to the construction of the wall, and all my servants were gathered there for the work; we did not acquire any land. 17 There were 150 Jews and officials at my table, besides the guests from the surrounding nations. 18 Each day one ox, six choice sheep, and some fowl were prepared for me, and once every ten days an abundance of all kinds of wine was provided. But I did not demand the food allotted to the governor, because the burden on the people was so heavy. 19 Remember me favorably, O my God, for all that I have done for this people.

But I did not demand the food allotted to the governor, because the burden on the people was so heavy. 19 Remember me favorably, O my God, for all that I have done for this people.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Nehemiah looks back over twelve years as governor and explains that he and his brothers did not take the food allowance assigned to the office. Earlier governors and their servants had burdened the people; he chooses differently because he fears God.

He continues with the wall work, gathers his servants to it and does not acquire land. He also hosts 150 Jews and officials, along with other visitors, without demanding the allowance because the people’s burden is already heavy.

The account gives both his reason and his appeal: consideration for the people shapes his use of office, and he asks God to remember him favorably for what he has done for them.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry and Gill understand the example as refusing to enrich oneself at the people’s expense. They read the closing prayer as dependence on God’s gracious recognition, rather than a claim that God owes salvation as payment for service. The stated reason for declining the allowance is the weight already resting on the community.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus describes leadership through service in Mark 10:42–45, grounding it in His own coming to serve and give His life as a ransom. The needs of those served take priority over personal advantage.

Paul also distinguishes a right to material support from the choice to set that right aside for the gospel in 1 Corinthians 9:3–18. The broader connection is freely accepting a cost for the good of others. It does not make receiving legitimate support inherently wrong; Paul expressly affirms that support while explaining his own choice.

passages.title: Nehemiah 6:1-9
passages.section_title: How does Nehemiah respond to repeated attempts to draw him away?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 When Sanballat, Tobiah, Geshem the Arab, and the rest of our enemies heard that I had rebuilt the wall and not a gap was left—though to that time I had not yet installed the doors in the gates— 2 Sanballat and Geshem sent me this message: “Come, let us meet together in one of the villages on the plain of Ono.” But they were planning to harm me. 3 So I sent messengers to them, saying, “I am doing a great work and cannot come down. Why should the work stop while I leave it to go down to you?” 4 Four times they sent me the same message, and each time I gave the same reply. 5 The fifth time, Sanballat sent me this same message by his young servant, who had in his hand an unsealed letter 6 that read: “It is reported among the nations—and Geshem agrees—that you and the Jews are plotting to revolt, and this is why you are building the wall. According to these reports, you are to become their king, 7 and you have even appointed prophets in Jerusalem to proclaim on your behalf: ‘There is a king in Judah.’ Soon these rumors will reach the ears of the king. So come, let us confer together.” 8 Then I sent him this reply: “There is nothing to these rumors you are spreading; you are inventing them in your own mind.” 9 For they were all trying to frighten us, saying, “Their hands will be weakened in the work, and it will never be finished.” But now, my God, strengthen my hands.
