section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The wall’s gaps have been closed, although the gate doors have not yet been installed. Sanballat and Geshem repeatedly invite Nehemiah to a meeting outside Jerusalem. Nehemiah recognizes an intention to harm him and refuses to leave the work.

After four invitations receive the same answer, Sanballat sends an unsealed letter. It alleges that Nehemiah intends to rebel, become king and have prophets proclaim him. Nehemiah denies the allegations as inventions. The account presents the letter as an attempt to frighten the workers into giving up.

Nehemiah answers briefly and turns to God for strength to continue. The passage moves from an invitation that would remove him from the work to an accusation designed to make staying at it appear dangerous.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Gill understand the invitations and letter as connected efforts to stop the rebuilding. Gill sees the unsealed letter as a way to spread the allegation more widely. Both emphasize Nehemiah’s steady attention to the task and his reliance on God.

The account gives specific reasons for recognizing this plot: the intention to harm him and the accusations he identifies as fabricated. It does not treat every question or criticism of a leader as the same kind of threat.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Nehemiah 6:10-14
passages.section_title: How does Nehemiah recognize counsel that would lead him into sin?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 Later, I went to the house of Shemaiah son of Delaiah, the son of Mehetabel, who was confined to his house. He said: “Let us meet at the house of God inside the temple. Let us shut the temple doors because they are coming to kill you— by night they are coming to kill you!” 11 But I replied, “Should a man like me run away? Should one like me go into the temple to save his own life? I will not go!” 12 I realized that God had not sent him, but that he had uttered this prophecy against me because Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him. 13 He had been hired to intimidate me so that I would sin by doing as he suggested, so they could give me a bad name in order to discredit me. 14 O my God, remember Tobiah and Sanballat for what they have done, and also Noadiah the prophetess and the other prophets who tried to intimidate me.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Shemaiah urges Nehemiah to hide inside the temple and shut its doors, claiming that men are coming to kill him that night. Nehemiah refuses to flee or enter the temple to save his life.

He recognizes that God has not sent the message: Tobiah and Sanballat have hired Shemaiah to frighten him into sin and provide grounds to discredit him. Nehemiah asks God to remember their actions, together with those of Noadiah and the other prophets who sought to intimidate him.

The threat comes wrapped in a claim of prophetic insight and an offer of safety. Nehemiah judges the proposed action rather than accepting the message simply because someone presents it as a warning from God.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Gill read Shemaiah’s proposal as a religious trap. Gill connects the proposed entrance into the sanctuary with the restriction on unauthorized approach in Numbers 18:1–7. On that reading, the refuge being offered would involve crossing a boundary God had established.

The narrative itself identifies the intended result: fear, sin and damage to Nehemiah’s reputation. A claim to speak for God does not make the advice trustworthy.
passages.god_plan_html:
Testing claims to speak for God remains a concern in the New Testament. 1 John 4:1–6 tells believers to test the spirits because false prophets have gone out into the world, and connects that testing with the truth about Jesus Christ.

1 Thessalonians 5:19–22 joins openness to prophecy with examining everything and holding to what is good. The broader theme is a people who listen carefully and test what they hear, so that a religious claim does not turn them away from faithfulness to God.

passages.title: Nehemiah 6:15-19
passages.section_title: What changes when the wall is finished, and what trouble remains?

versions.label: BSB

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The wall is completed on the twenty-fifth of Elul, after fifty-two days. The surrounding nations lose confidence because they recognize that the work has been accomplished with God’s help.

The completion does not end every source of pressure. Nobles in Judah exchange letters with Tobiah, and many are bound to him by oath through family connections. They praise him to Nehemiah and report Nehemiah’s words back to him.

Tobiah continues sending letters to intimidate Nehemiah. The passage sets a completed wall beside relationships within the community that still give an opponent influence.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry and Gill emphasize God’s help in completing the wall despite sustained opposition. They also notice the continuing danger from those within Judah who favor Tobiah. Success in the building work has exposed the opponents’ failure without bringing every divided loyalty to an end.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
With the wall rebuilt and its doors installed, Nehemiah appoints gatekeepers, singers and Levites. He entrusts responsibility for Jerusalem to Hanani and Hananiah, describing Hananiah as faithful and especially reverent toward God.

The instructions for opening, closing and guarding the gates make the city’s protection an ongoing responsibility. Residents are to serve as guards, including near their own homes.

The city is spacious, but its population is small and houses remain unbuilt. Nehemiah says God puts it into his heart to assemble the people for registration by family. He finds the register of those who returned at the beginning; the long list that follows comes from that earlier return.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry emphasizes the choice of trustworthy people and the continuing need for care after construction. Gill relates the small population to the many returnees who lived in other towns. Both read the register as a record of the first return, which Nehemiah finds useful for the needs of the community in his own time.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jerusalem’s restored defenses meet an immediate need, but the wider biblical hope reaches beyond a city that must keep watch against attack. Revelation 21:1–4, 22–27 describes the new Jerusalem where God dwells with His people, death and mourning are gone, and the gates never close because there is no night.

The connection is the larger hope of God living with His people in lasting safety. Nehemiah’s guards and gate instructions show what protection requires in a threatened city; Revelation places that hope’s fulfillment in God’s presence and the Lamb.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.context_html:
The register recalls people whom Nebuchadnezzar had carried away and who returned to Jerusalem and Judah, each to their own town. It names the leaders associated with that return, including Zerubbabel and Jeshua, then records families and people grouped by towns.

This is the earlier return also recorded in Ezra 2, not a new company of travelers arriving with Nehemiah. The two lists preserve many of the same names while differing in a number of their figures.

The names and counts keep the restoration tied to actual households and places. The community Nehemiah is helping rebuild has a history that reaches back through exile to the return God made possible.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry understands the repeated record as honoring the return and preserving the people’s family history. Gill also connects it with Ezra’s register and discusses differences between the lists. Explanations involving changes among the families have been proposed, but the passage does not supply a separate explanation for every differing number.
passages.god_plan_html:
Zerubbabel’s place in this return also connects with the New Testament’s account of Jesus’ family line. Matthew 1:11–17 traces that line through the exile, then through Shealtiel and Zerubbabel, and onward to Jesus the Messiah.

Matthew gives an explicit connection between the history preserved here and the coming of Christ. The return is part of the setting in which God carries forward that family line after the upheaval of exile.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The register turns to priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, temple servants and the descendants of Solomon’s servants. Worship in the restored community involves many different responsibilities.

Some returnees cannot establish their family’s descent from Israel. A further group claiming priestly descent cannot find the records confirming it. They are excluded from the priesthood as unclean and told not to eat the most holy food until a priest can decide the matter with the Urim and Thummim.

The restriction concerns eligibility for priestly service and its holy food. The account does not say that every family whose ancestry is uncertain is expelled from the returning community.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry and Gill understand the disputed priestly records as a reason to withhold priestly privileges until the matter can be settled. The careful registration protects the responsibilities attached to the priesthood. Neither the list nor its ruling describes the ancestry uncertainty as proof of the individuals’ personal wickedness.
passages.god_plan_html:
The question of who may serve as priest also helps bring out the distinction made in Hebrews 7:11–28. Under the earlier arrangement, descent from Levi mattered. Jesus comes from Judah, and Hebrews grounds His priesthood in God’s oath and the power of an indestructible life.

This is a connection between the earlier priesthood’s requirements and the different basis of Christ’s priesthood. Hebrews directs confidence toward the Son who lives forever and is able to save completely those who come to God through Him.

passages.context_html:
The register gives a total assembly of 42,360, along with servants, singers and animals. It then records gifts for the work from the governor, heads of families and the rest of the people. The contributions include gold, silver and priests’ garments.

The priests, Levites and other returning people settle in their towns. The closing notice that the Israelites are in their towns by the seventh month prepares for the next scene, where the people gather to hear the Law.

These totals and gifts conclude the register Nehemiah found. They belong with its account of the earlier return rather than describing a new migration of that size under Nehemiah.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry emphasizes both the willingness to return and the gifts supporting the work. Gill compares the closing figures and contributions with Ezra’s account. The register closes by showing the returning community established in its towns, with resources given toward the shared undertaking.

passages.section_title: Why do the people ask to hear the Law explained?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The people gather at the Water Gate and ask Ezra to bring out the Law of Moses. On the first day of the seventh month, men, women and all who can understand listen from daybreak until noon.

Ezra stands on a wooden platform with others beside him. When he opens the book, the people stand; they praise God, lift their hands and bow in worship. The Levites help them understand what is being read.

The setting recalls Deuteronomy 31:9–13, where Moses commands a public reading of the Law at the Feast of Tabernacles in the year of debt release, so that the people and their children may learn to follow God. Here, attention is given to understanding as well as hearing.

One word used for the reading comes from Hebrew פָּרַשׁ, parash, pronounced pah-RAHSH. Brown–Driver–Briggs gives the sense of making something distinct or clear and lists this verse under that use. The aim in the passage is that the people grasp what the Law is saying.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry emphasizes that teachers should explain Scripture so that its hearers understand it, and that explanations should themselves be tested by Scripture. Gill discusses whether the reading involved translating Hebrew into the language the returnees used. He favors clear, distinct reading followed by explanation, rather than treating translation as necessary here. Both understand the scene as making God’s instruction intelligible to the people.
passages.god_plan_html:
The theme of Scripture being opened to understanding continues in Luke 24:25–27, 44–49. Jesus explains what Moses and the Prophets wrote about Him, then opens His disciples’ minds to understand the Scriptures.

Luke brings that understanding to a definite focus: Christ’s suffering and resurrection, and the proclamation of repentance and forgiveness to all nations in His name. Hearing Scripture serves God’s purpose when people come to understand what He has made known and respond to it.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Nehemiah 8:9-12
passages.section_title: Why are the people told to rejoice when the Law has moved them to tears?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 Nehemiah the governor, Ezra the priest and scribe, and the Levites who were instructing the people said to all of them, “This day is holy to the LORD your God. Do not mourn or weep.” For all the people were weeping as they heard the words of the Law. 10 Then Nehemiah told them, “Go and eat what is rich, drink what is sweet, and send out portions to those who have nothing prepared, since today is holy to our Lord. Do not grieve, for the joy of the LORD is your strength.” 11 And the Levites calmed all the people, saying, “Be still, since today is holy. Do not grieve.” 12 Then all the people began to eat and drink, to send out portions, and to rejoice greatly, because they understood the words that had been made known to them.

Do not mourn or weep.” For all the people were weeping as they heard the words of the Law. 10 Then Nehemiah told them, “Go and eat what is rich, drink what is sweet, and send out portions to those who have nothing prepared, since today is holy to our Lord. Do not grieve, for the joy of the LORD is your strength.” 11 And the Levites calmed all the people, saying, “Be still, since today is holy. Do not grieve.” 12 Then all the people began to eat and drink, to send out portions, and to rejoice greatly, because they understood the words that had been made known to them.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The people weep as they hear the Law, but Nehemiah, Ezra and the teaching Levites tell them that this day is holy to God and should be celebrated. Leviticus 23:23–25 identifies the first day of the seventh month as a sacred assembly announced by trumpet blasts.

Nehemiah sends them to enjoy a meal and share portions with those who have nothing prepared. Their celebration is to include people who would otherwise go without.

The people leave rejoicing because they have understood the words explained to them. Their tears are followed by a welcome to find strength in joy before God; confession will receive its own place later in the month.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry sees the tears as evidence of tender hearts and stresses the generosity that should accompany the feast. Gill understands joy directed toward God and received from Him as renewing the people’s strength to serve. Neither treats the call to rejoice on this holy day as a denial that sin needs to be confessed.
passages.god_plan_html:
The movement from sorrow to joy has a wider biblical parallel. Zechariah 12:10–14 describes mourning over the pierced One, and John 19:34–37 connects the pierced One with Jesus’ crucifixion.

Jesus also tells His disciples that their grief will turn to joy when they see Him again (John 16:16–22). These are parallels in the way God brings people through sorrow into joy, rather than a statement that Nehemiah’s gathering is itself a prediction of those events. The New Testament grounds that lasting joy in Christ.

passages.section_title: What happens when the people put what they have learned into practice?

versions.text: 13 On the second day of the month, the heads of all the families, along with the priests and Levites, gathered around Ezra the scribe to study the words of the Law. 14 And they found written in the Law, which the LORD had commanded through Moses, that the Israelites were to dwell in booths during the feast of the seventh month, 15 and that they should proclaim this message and spread it throughout their towns and in Jerusalem, saying, “Go out to the hill country and bring back branches of olive, wild olive, myrtle, palm, and other leafy trees, to make booths, as it is written.” 16 And the people went out, brought back branches, and made booths on their own rooftops, in their courtyards, in the courts of the house of God, and in the squares by the Water Gate and by the Gate of Ephraim. 17 The whole assembly that had returned from exile made booths and lived in them. From the days of Joshua son of Nun until that day, the Israelites had not celebrated like this. And there was great rejoicing. 18 Day after day, from the first day to the last, Ezra read from the Book of the Law of God. The Israelites kept the feast for seven days, and on the eighth day they held an assembly, according to the ordinance.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The following day, family heads, priests and Levites gather around Ezra to study further. They find the command to live in booths during the seventh-month feast and spread instructions to gather branches.

The people make these temporary shelters on rooftops, in courtyards, in the temple courts and in the public squares. Leviticus 23:33–43 explains their purpose: later generations are to remember that God made Israel dwell in booths when He brought them out of Egypt.

The whole returning assembly participates with great joy. Ezra reads from the Law each day through the seven-day feast, followed by the assembly on the eighth day. Learning leads to a shared act of remembrance and obedience.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Gill understands the statement that Israel had not celebrated like this since Joshua as describing the celebration’s particular thoroughness and joy. He notes earlier observances, including Ezra 3:4. Henry emphasizes putting the recovered instruction into practice and connects the temporary shelters with the life of God’s people as travelers who depend on Him.
passages.god_plan_html:
The Feast of Tabernacles also appears in Zechariah 14:9, 16–21, where the Lord is King over all the earth and survivors from the nations come to worship Him and celebrate the feast.

This is a scriptural connection through the same feast. In Nehemiah, the returned community remembers God’s care on the journey from Egypt; Zechariah places the feast within a larger picture of the nations honoring the Lord as King. The worship described there reaches beyond the community gathered here.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Nehemiah 9:1-5
passages.section_title: How does the gathering change from celebration to confession?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 On the twenty-fourth day of the same month, the Israelites gathered together, fasting and wearing sackcloth, with dust on their heads. 2 Those of Israelite descent separated themselves from all the foreigners, and they stood and confessed their sins and the iniquities of their fathers. 3 While they stood in their places, they read from the Book of the Law of the LORD their God for a quarter of the day, and they spent another quarter of the day in confession and worship of the LORD their God. 4 And the Levites—Jeshua, Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah, Bunni, Sherebiah, Bani, and Chenani—stood on the raised platform and cried out in a loud voice to the LORD their God. 5 Then the Levites—Jeshua, Kadmiel, Bani, Hashabneiah, Sherebiah, Hodiah, Shebaniah, and Pethahiah—said, “Stand up and bless the LORD your God from everlasting to everlasting: Blessed be Your glorious name, and may it be exalted above all blessing and praise.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
On the twenty-fourth day of the month, after the feast, the Israelites gather with fasting, sackcloth and dust on their heads. They separate themselves from the foreigners and confess both their own sins and those of their fathers.

They spend a quarter of the day reading the Law and another quarter confessing and worshiping. The Levites cry out to God and call the people to bless His name.

The pattern has a foundation in Leviticus 26:39–45, which speaks of confession, humbled hearts and God remembering His covenant after His people have suffered because of their unfaithfulness. The gathering looks honestly at sin while turning toward the God whose faithfulness has preserved them.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry emphasizes how Scripture directs prayer by bringing both sin and God’s mercy into view. Gill links the mourning with the end of the festival and reads the separation in light of the concern about foreign marriages. The verse itself states the separation and confession without detailing a new set of individual marriage cases.

passages.title: Nehemiah 9:6-15
passages.section_title: Why does the prayer begin with creation, Abraham and the exodus?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The prayer begins with God as the only Lord, Creator and giver of life. It then recalls His choosing Abram, bringing him from Ur, naming him Abraham and keeping the promise to give the land to his descendants.

The people remember God seeing their ancestors’ affliction, delivering them through the sea and guiding them with cloud and fire. At Sinai He gives just laws and makes His Sabbath known; in the wilderness He provides food and water.

These memories establish the prayer’s starting point: God has acted faithfully and generously. The confession that follows is measured against the goodness the people have already received.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry understands the remembrance of mercy as deepening confession rather than excusing sin. Gill likewise emphasizes God’s creation, covenant faithfulness and care. The prayer makes God’s character visible through what He has done, before describing how the people have responded.
passages.god_plan_html:
The same themes of covenant, mercy and deliverance appear when Zechariah speaks about the coming salvation in Luke 1:67–79. He praises the God of Israel for remembering His covenant and the oath to Abraham, so that His people may serve Him without fear.

Luke connects that hope with the coming Lord and the knowledge of salvation through forgiveness of sins. The larger story moves from recalling God’s earlier acts of rescue to announcing the salvation that comes through Christ.

passages.title: Nehemiah 9:16-25
passages.section_title: What does God’s continued care reveal when the people rebel?

They stiffened their necks and appointed a leader to return them to their bondage in Egypt. But You are a forgiving God, gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and rich in loving devotion, and You did not forsake them. 18 Even when they cast for themselves an image of a calf and said, ‘This is your God who brought you up out of Egypt,’ and when they committed terrible blasphemies, 19 You in Your great compassion did not forsake them in the wilderness. By day the pillar of cloud never turned away from guiding them on their path; and by the night the pillar of fire illuminated the way they should go. 20 You gave Your good Spirit to instruct them. You did not withhold Your manna from their mouths, and You gave them water for their thirst. 21 For forty years You sustained them in the wilderness, so that they lacked nothing. Their clothes did not wear out and their feet did not swell. 22 You gave them kingdoms and peoples and allotted to them every corner of the land. section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The prayer contrasts God’s gifts with the ancestors’ refusal to listen. They become stubborn, seek a return to slavery and make a golden calf, dishonoring the God who rescued them.

Yet God does not abandon them. His guidance continues; His good Spirit instructs them; manna and water sustain them through forty years. The account goes on to remember victory over Sihon and Og, multiplied descendants and the possession of a fruitful land.

The people receive houses, wells, vineyards and trees they did not have to create from nothing. The prayer places rebellion and patient generosity side by side, so that the abundance they enjoyed cannot be mistaken for something they earned by consistent obedience.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry highlights God’s patience alongside the people’s stubbornness. Gill reads the continuing guidance and provision as evidence of the forgiving character described in verse 17. The prayer remembers both the seriousness of the rebellion and God’s refusal to bring the people’s story to an end there.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Corinthians 10:1–14 returns to the same wilderness history: the cloud, the sea, food and drink, and the turn to idolatry. Paul says these events were written as warnings for those who come afterward and identifies the spiritual rock with Christ.

The New Testament uses this history to call believers away from misplaced confidence and toward faithfulness to God. Shared blessings do not make rebellion harmless. God’s faithfulness remains the ground for resisting temptation rather than a reason to take it lightly.

passages.title: Nehemiah 9:26-31
passages.section_title: Why does the prayer keep returning to both rebellion and mercy?

versions.text: 26 But they were disobedient and rebelled against You; they flung Your law behind their backs. They killed Your prophets, who had admonished them to return to You. They committed terrible blasphemies. 27 So You delivered them into the hands of enemies who oppressed them, and in their time of distress they cried out to You. From heaven You heard them, and in Your great compassion You gave them deliverers who saved them from the hands of their enemies. 28 But as soon as they had rest, they again did evil in Your sight. So You abandoned them to the hands of their enemies, who had dominion over them. When they cried out to You again, You heard from heaven, and You delivered them many times in Your compassion. 29 You admonished them to turn back to Your law, but they were arrogant and disobeyed Your commandments. They sinned against Your ordinances, by which a man will live if he practices them. They turned a stubborn shoulder; they stiffened their necks and would not obey. 30 You were patient with them for many years, and Your Spirit admonished them through Your prophets. Yet they would not listen, so You gave them into the hands of the neighboring peoples. 31 But in Your great compassion, You did not put an end to them; nor did You forsake them, for You are a gracious and compassionate God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The prayer recalls the people rejecting the Law and killing prophets sent to turn them back to God. Oppression follows, but God hears their cries and gives deliverers. Once they have relief, they do evil again.

The pattern continues over many years. God warns them by His Spirit through the prophets, but they will not listen, and they come under the rule of other peoples.

Even then, the prayer gives thanks that God has not destroyed or abandoned them completely. The community now praying exists because His compassion has outlasted their repeated unfaithfulness.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry emphasizes that the prophets’ warnings came through God’s Spirit, while mercy remained the people’s hope. Gill traces the repeated rescues and the preservation of a people through conquest and exile. The prayer does not minimize judgment; it recognizes that judgment has not canceled every expression of God’s compassion.
passages.god_plan_html:
Stephen returns to this pattern in Acts 7:35–53. He recalls the rejection of Moses, the golden calf and the persecution of the prophets, then confronts his hearers with the betrayal and killing of the Righteous One.

This is a connection through the same repeated rejection of God’s messengers, brought to its most serious point in the rejection of Christ. Remembering earlier failures is meant to lead to listening now, rather than assuming that knowing the history has already made the response faithful.

passages.title: Nehemiah 9:32-38
passages.section_title: What do the people ask for while acknowledging that God is just?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 32 So now, our God, the great and mighty and awesome God who keeps His gracious covenant, do not view lightly all the hardship that has come upon us, and upon our kings and leaders, our priests and prophets, our ancestors and all Your people, from the days of the kings of Assyria until today. 33 You are just in all that has befallen us, because You have acted faithfully, while we have acted wickedly. 34 Our kings and leaders and priests and fathers did not obey Your law or listen to Your commandments and warnings that You gave them. 35 For even while they were in their kingdom, with the abundant goodness that You had given them, and in the spacious and fertile land that You had set before them, they would not serve You or turn from their wicked ways. 36 So here we are today as slaves in the land You gave our fathers to enjoy its fruit and goodness— here we are as slaves! 37 Its abundant harvest goes to the kings You have set over us because of our sins. And they rule over our bodies and our livestock as they please. We are in great distress. 38 In view of all this, we make a binding agreement, putting it in writing and sealing it with the names of our leaders, Levites, and priests.”

And they rule over our bodies and our livestock as they please. We are in great distress. 38 In view of all this, we make a binding agreement, putting it in writing and sealing it with the names of our leaders, Levites, and priests.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The prayer reaches the community’s present distress. The people ask the great and faithful God not to regard their hardships as a small matter, naming the suffering of rulers, priests, prophets, ancestors and the whole people.

They acknowledge that God has dealt faithfully while they have acted wickedly. Even in the land given to their fathers, they remain subject to kings who take its produce and rule over their bodies and livestock.

The prayer ends with a binding written agreement, sealed with the names of leaders, Levites and priests. Confession is to be followed by a recorded commitment to obey; the names and promises are set out in the next chapter.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry reads the appeal as dependence on undeserved mercy, with responsibility for sin honestly acknowledged. Gill explains the continuing servitude in relation to Persian rule and understands the written agreement as a binding promise to observe God’s Law. Returning to the land has not yet removed every form of hardship or foreign control.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The chapter supplies the names attached to the written agreement announced at the end of the prayer. Nehemiah the governor appears first, followed by priests, Levites and leaders of the people.

The list gives the community’s commitment identifiable witnesses. Its setting is the confession of chapter 9: God has been faithful, the people have been unfaithful, and they are now recording their intention to follow His Law.

The promises themselves follow the names. The next verses also make clear that the wider community joins the commitment, including wives and children who are able to understand.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Gill understands the names as the leaders who seal the agreement on behalf of the community. Henry reads the chapter as a renewed commitment to the whole of God’s instruction. The record joins identifiable leadership with the people’s own participation, rather than leaving the response as an unnamed promise.

passages.title: Nehemiah 10:28-31
passages.section_title: What changes do the people promise in their everyday lives?

section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The rest of the community joins the nobles in a sworn commitment to obey the Law given through Moses. The account includes the people serving at the temple, their wives, and sons and daughters who can understand what they are undertaking.

They promise not to arrange marriages with the surrounding peoples. The Law’s warning in Deuteronomy 7:1–6 connects prohibited marriages with the danger of turning away to serve other gods.

They also promise not to buy goods on the Sabbath or a holy day, and to observe the seventh year’s rest for the land and cancellation of debts. Exodus 23:10–12 and Deuteronomy 15:1–11 show how these commands protect rest and provide for neighbors in need. Their commitment reaches family decisions, trade, farming and lending.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry emphasizes turning from the surrounding way of life toward conduct directed by God’s word. Gill understands the oath as the wider community’s agreement with the leaders, and the specific promises as obedience in matters where the people were vulnerable to failure. He also notes that the marriage problem appears again in chapter 13. The vow expresses a serious intention without making later failure impossible.
passages.god_plan_html:
The concern with covenant faithfulness reaches a further point in Hebrews 8:6–13. Hebrews describes Jesus as the One who brings a better covenant and repeats God’s promise to put His laws in the people’s minds and write them on their hearts.

That promise also includes knowing God and receiving forgiveness. The wider story addresses the need exposed by repeated broken commitments: God’s purpose reaches the heart, and confidence rests in what He promises through Christ.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The people undertake a yearly contribution of a third of a shekel for temple service, including the bread, regular offerings, appointed feasts and sacrifices for sin. Families are assigned times to bring wood for the altar.

They also promise firstfruits, firstborn offerings and the tithes supporting the Levites and priests. Numbers 18:8–32 explains the background: firstborn sons are redeemed, the Levites receive a tenth of the produce, and they in turn give a tenth of what they receive.

A priest is to accompany the Levites collecting the tithe. The goods go into the temple storerooms, supporting the service and those who carry it out. The closing promise brings all the arrangements together: the house of God is not to be neglected.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry emphasizes that turning from wrong must be accompanied by taking up neglected duties. Gill reads the provisions as practical support for worship and for the people who serve. The commitment includes money, produce, materials, schedules and oversight, making the promise concrete.
passages.god_plan_html:
The repeated sacrifices supported here belong to the earlier worship described in Hebrews 10:1–25. Hebrews points to Christ’s one offering for sins and the access to God that comes through Him.

The passage then calls believers to draw near, hold to their hope, encourage love and good deeds, and continue meeting together. The wider connection is care for worship and for one another, now grounded in Christ’s completed offering. The New Testament gives that call its own foundation rather than simply transferring the temple’s supply arrangements to a church building.

passages.title: Nehemiah 11:1-2
passages.section_title: Why are some people asked to make Jerusalem their home?

versions.text: 1 Now the leaders of the people settled in Jerusalem, and the rest of the people cast lots to bring one out of ten to live in the holy city of Jerusalem, while the remaining nine were to dwell in their own towns. 2 And the people blessed all the men who volunteered to live in Jerusalem.
paragraphs: 1 Now the leaders of the people settled in Jerusalem, and the rest of the people cast lots to bring one out of ten to live in the holy city of Jerusalem, while the remaining nine were to dwell in their own towns. 2 And the people blessed all the men who volunteered to live in Jerusalem.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The leaders settle in Jerusalem, while lots select one in ten of the other people to live there. The remaining nine stay in their own towns. This addresses the need already noted in Nehemiah 7:4: the city has room, but too few people.

The people also bless those who volunteer to settle in Jerusalem. A rebuilt wall needs a community living within it, and the account recognizes both the organized resettlement and the willingness of those who offer to go.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Gill distinguishes people selected by lot from those who volunteer, and understands the move as accepting a cost for the community’s good. Henry likewise stresses willingness to serve beyond personal convenience. On this reading, the blessing honors those who help meet the city’s need.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 12:1–13 describes a life offered to God in response to His mercy, then turns to the different gifts and practical care within Christ’s body. Giving, leading, serving and hospitality all contribute to the good of others.

The connection is willing service that may change a person’s own arrangements for the sake of the community. Nehemiah’s account concerns settling a city; Paul’s teaching shows the wider pattern of people using what God gives them to serve one another.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.context_html:
The register identifies families of Judah and Benjamin living in Jerusalem, along with priests, Levites and gatekeepers. It records names, family connections, numbers and responsibilities, giving a fuller picture of the community within the rebuilt walls.

The work includes temple service, care for work outside the house of God, thanksgiving, prayer and watching the gates. The temple servants live on Ophel. Uzzi oversees the Levites in Jerusalem, and the singers’ daily activities are regulated by a royal command.

Pethahiah is named as the king’s agent in matters concerning the people. The register shows the city functioning through many kinds of responsibility, alongside the households and temple workers who remain in the other towns.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Gill reads the list as an account of residents and the responsibilities supporting the temple and community. He discusses whether the command concerning the singers should be connected with David or the Persian king, favoring the latter. The verse itself mentions a royal command without naming that king.

[Henry]({H11}) draws attention to usefulness in the place a person has been given. The named responsibilities make clear that sustaining Jerusalem involves more than one leader or one kind of service.

passages.context_html:
The account turns from Jerusalem to the villages and fields where other people live. It names settlements associated with Judah and then those associated with Benjamin, and notes Levite divisions settling in Benjamin.

The list describes an inhabited region around the city, with households living on their land. The restoration includes these towns and their fields as well as Jerusalem and its temple.

The two settings belong together: chapter 10 describes produce coming from the towns to support temple service, while chapter 11 records both the people living in Jerusalem and those established beyond its walls.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Gill understands the Levites’ distribution among the people as helping provide instruction. Henry emphasizes faithfulness and usefulness in differing places. Their readings bring attention to the people outside Jerusalem as participants in the community’s life, with their own homes and responsibilities.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The register begins with priests and Levites who returned with Zerubbabel and Jeshua. It then traces the family from Jeshua through Joiakim, Eliashib, Joiada, Jonathan and Jaddua, and names priestly family heads serving in Joiakim’s time.

Further notices record the keeping of family lists, the arrangement of praise and thanksgiving in alternating groups, and the gatekeepers guarding the storerooms. The section ends by naming the periods of Joiakim, Nehemiah and Ezra.

The lists show continuity in the community’s worship across changing generations. The restoration depends on people carrying forward responsibilities they have received, rather than beginning every task anew.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry reads the record as a reason to remember faithful predecessors and learn from their example. Gill understands the family line as the succession of high priests and discusses whether some notices extend beyond Nehemiah’s own lifetime. The named periods make this a record spanning generations, rather than a list of everyone serving at one moment.
passages.god_plan_html:
The succession of priests provides a point of comparison with Hebrews 7:11–28. Hebrews explains that the earlier priests were many because death prevented them from continuing, while Jesus lives forever and holds His priesthood permanently.

This comparison brings the larger hope into focus: access to God finally rests in the Son who offered Himself and continues to pray for those who draw near through Him. The continuing work recorded across these generations meets its lasting answer in a priest whose life does not end.

And they stopped at the Gate of the Guard. 40 The two thanksgiving choirs then stood in the house of God, as did I, along with the half of the officials accompanying me, 41 as well as the priests with their trumpets—Eliakim, Maaseiah, Miniamin, Micaiah, Elioenai, Zechariah, and Hananiah— 42 and also Maaseiah, Shemaiah, Eleazar, Uzzi, Jehohanan, Malchijah, Elam, and Ezer. Then the choirs sang out under the direction of Jezrahiah. 43 On that day they offered great sacrifices, rejoicing because God had given them great joy. The women and children also rejoiced, so that the joy of Jerusalem was heard from afar.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Levites and singers are gathered from their homes around Jerusalem for the wall’s dedication. The priests and Levites purify themselves, the people, the gates and the wall before the celebration.

Nehemiah appoints two thanksgiving choirs to proceed along the wall in opposite directions. Ezra leads one procession, and Nehemiah follows the other with part of the people. The routes lead the two companies to stand in the house of God.

Priests sound trumpets, the singers sing, and great sacrifices are offered. Women and children share the rejoicing. The account gives God credit for their great joy and says that Jerusalem’s celebration can be heard from afar.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry emphasizes that those who share in God’s kindness should join in giving thanks. Gill understands the dedication as embracing the city and its defenses, with the people praising God for the safety provided. The completed work becomes an occasion to honor God together, rather than simply to commend the builders.
passages.god_plan_html:
The theme of a restored people proclaiming God’s goodness continues in 1 Peter 2:4–12. Peter describes believers as living stones built into a spiritual house through Jesus Christ and as a people called to proclaim the virtues of the One who brought them out of darkness.

This is a connection through thanksgiving and the purpose of God’s people, rather than a claim that the singers on Nehemiah’s wall are the stones Peter means. Hebrews 13:15–16 likewise joins praise offered through Jesus with doing good and sharing. God’s work in a people is to become visible in their praise and life together.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

passages.title: Nehemiah 12:44-47
passages.section_title: How is the celebration followed by continuing support?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 44 And on that same day men were appointed over the rooms that housed the supplies, contributions, firstfruits, and tithes. The portions specified by the Law for the priests and Levites were gathered into these storerooms from the fields of the villages, because Judah rejoiced over the priests and Levites who were serving. 45 They performed the service of their God and the service of purification, along with the singers and gatekeepers, as David and his son Solomon had prescribed. 46 For long ago, in the days of David and Asaph, there were directors for the singers and for the songs of praise and thanksgiving to God. 47 So in the days of Zerubbabel and Nehemiah, all Israel contributed the daily portions for the singers and gatekeepers. They also set aside daily portions for the Levites, and the Levites set aside daily portions for the descendants of Aaron.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Men are appointed over the rooms holding contributions, firstfruits and tithes. The portions specified for priests and Levites are gathered from the villages, with Judah rejoicing over those who serve.

The account connects the arrangements for singers, gatekeepers and purification with David and Solomon. It recalls daily support in the periods of Zerubbabel and Nehemiah, including the Levites setting aside portions for Aaron’s descendants.

The thanksgiving is followed by attention to the work that must continue after the public celebration. Appointed responsibilities and regular supplies support that ongoing service.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry emphasizes thanksgiving that leads to more willing attention to duty. Gill similarly connects appreciation for the ministry with providing the portions assigned to its workers. The scene shows practical support accompanying the joy, although the next chapter will reveal that such arrangements still need faithful follow-through.

passages.title: Nehemiah 13:1-3
passages.section_title: Why does another reading of the Law lead to separation?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 At that time the Book of Moses was read aloud in the hearing of the people, and in it they found the passage stating that no Ammonite or Moabite should ever enter the assembly of God, 2 because they had not met the Israelites with food and water, but had hired Balaam to call down a curse against them (although our God had turned the curse into a blessing). 3 As soon as the people heard this law, they excluded from Israel all of foreign descent.
paragraphs: 1 At that time the Book of Moses was read aloud in the hearing of the people, and in it they found the passage stating that no Ammonite or Moabite should ever enter the assembly of God, 2 because they had not met the Israelites with food and water, but had hired Balaam to call down a curse against them (although our God had turned the curse into a blessing). 3 As soon as the people heard this law, they excluded from Israel all of foreign descent.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
A public reading brings the people to the restriction concerning Ammonites and Moabites in Deuteronomy 23:3–5. The reason recalled is their failure to bring food and water and their hiring of Balaam to curse Israel. God had turned the curse into a blessing.

The people respond by excluding those of foreign descent from Israel. The passage presents this as a response to the Law they have heard, continuing the book’s concern that the community’s life be shaped by God’s instruction.

The wider scriptural setting also includes Ruth, a Moabite woman who commits herself to Israel’s people and God and becomes part of the family line recorded in Matthew 1:5. Her story matters when considering what Scripture says about foreigners and belonging.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Gill understands entering the assembly here in connection with marriage and reads the separation in that setting. Henry emphasizes the distinction between Israel and the surrounding nations and the way hearing Scripture exposes neglected duties. These readings focus on the community’s covenant responsibilities; the passage does not describe every possible case involving a foreigner.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 2:11–22 explicitly addresses Gentiles once separated from Israel’s commonwealth and the covenants of promise. Through Christ’s blood, those who were far away are brought near.

Paul describes Jews and Gentiles reconciled to God in one body through the cross, with access to the Father by one Spirit. The larger story of belonging therefore reaches its center in Christ, who makes those formerly called foreigners members of God’s household.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Nehemiah 13:4-9
passages.section_title: Why does Nehemiah remove Tobiah’s belongings from the temple?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 4 Now before this, Eliashib the priest, a relative of Tobiah, had been put in charge of the storerooms of the house of our God 5 and had prepared for Tobiah a large room where they had previously stored the grain offerings, the frankincense, the temple articles, and the tithes of grain, new wine, and oil prescribed for the Levites, singers, and gatekeepers, along with the contributions for the priests. 6 While all this was happening, I was not in Jerusalem, because I had returned to Artaxerxes king of Babylon in the thirty-second year of his reign. Some time later I obtained leave from the king 7 to return to Jerusalem. Then I discovered the evil that Eliashib had done on behalf of Tobiah by providing him a room in the courts of the house of God. 8 And I was greatly displeased and threw all of Tobiah’s household goods out of the room. 9 Then I ordered that the rooms be purified, and I had the articles of the house of God restored to them, along with the grain offerings and frankincense.

Some time later I obtained leave from the king

7 to return to Jerusalem. Then I discovered the evil that Eliashib had done on behalf of Tobiah by providing him a room in the courts of the house of God. 8 And I was greatly displeased and threw all of Tobiah’s household goods out of the room. 9 Then I ordered that the rooms be purified, and I had the articles of the house of God restored to them, along with the grain offerings and frankincense.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The account looks back to something done while Nehemiah was away. Eliashib, the priest responsible for the temple storerooms and a relative of Tobiah, has prepared a large room for him. It had previously held offerings, temple articles and supplies assigned to the workers.

Nehemiah explains that he had returned to Artaxerxes in the thirty-second year of the king’s reign and later obtained permission to come back to Jerusalem. On returning, he learns what Eliashib has done.

Greatly displeased, Nehemiah throws Tobiah’s household goods out, orders the rooms purified and restores the temple articles, grain offerings and frankincense. The space is returned to the purpose for which it had been set apart.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry and Gill understand Tobiah’s room as a misuse of space belonging to God’s house. Henry also draws a personal lesson about removing what sustains sin and making room for what serves God. The immediate action concerns a governor correcting the use of temple storerooms during his absence.
passages.god_plan_html:
There is a clear parallel with Jesus’ action in the temple courts in John 2:13–22. Jesus drives out the trading activity and objects to His Father’s house becoming a marketplace.

The accounts share concern for the proper use of God’s house; John does not identify Nehemiah’s action as a prediction of Jesus’ action. John then takes the theme further: Jesus speaks of the temple of His body, and His disciples understand His words after His resurrection.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Nehemiah 13:10-14
passages.section_title: What happens when the people who serve are left without support?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 I also learned that because the portions for the Levites had not been given to them, all the Levites and singers responsible for performing the service had gone back to their own fields. 11 So I rebuked the officials and asked, “Why has the house of God been neglected?” Then I gathered the Levites and singers together and stationed them at their posts, 12 and all Judah brought a tenth of the grain, new wine, and oil into the storerooms. 13 I appointed as treasurers over the storerooms Shelemiah the priest, Zadok the scribe, and Pedaiah of the Levites, with Hanan son of Zaccur, the son of Mattaniah, to assist them, because they were considered trustworthy. They were responsible for distributing the supplies to their fellow Levites. 14 Remember me for this, O my God, and do not blot out my deeds of loving devotion for the house of my God and for its services.
paragraphs: 10 I also learned that because the portions for the Levites had not been given to them, all the Levites and singers responsible for performing the service had gone back to their own fields. 11 So I rebuked the officials and asked, “Why has the house of God been neglected?” Then I gathered the Levites and singers together and stationed them at their posts, 12 and all Judah brought a tenth of the grain, new wine, and oil into the storerooms. 13 I appointed as treasurers over the storerooms Shelemiah the priest, Zadok the scribe, and Pedaiah of the Levites, with Hanan son of Zaccur, the son of Mattaniah, to assist them, because they were considered trustworthy. They were responsible for distributing the supplies to their fellow Levites. 14 Remember me for this, O my God, and do not blot out my deeds of loving devotion for the house of my God and for its services.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Nehemiah discovers that the Levites and singers have not received their assigned portions. They have returned to their fields, leaving the service without the people needed to carry it out.

He rebukes the officials, brings the workers back to their posts and restores the collection of the grain, wine and oil. He appoints men considered trustworthy to oversee the storerooms and distribute the supplies.

The correction addresses both the missing resources and responsibility for handling them. Nehemiah closes with a prayer that God remember his care for the house and its services.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry emphasizes that neglecting the workers has led to neglecting the work. Gill likewise understands the move back to the fields as a need to obtain a living. Both read Nehemiah’s prayer as an appeal to God’s gracious acceptance, rather than a claim that service has earned a debt God must pay.
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul makes a direct comparison between temple workers sharing in the offerings and those preaching the gospel receiving support in 1 Corinthians 9:3–18. He affirms that right even while explaining why he has chosen to forgo it.

The wider theme is that a community’s response to spiritual service includes material care. Paul’s example also keeps that support connected with the good of the gospel, rather than making financial advantage the purpose of the work.

passages.title: Nehemiah 13:15-22
passages.section_title: Why does Nehemiah close the gates before the Sabbath?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 In those days I saw people in Judah treading winepresses on the Sabbath and bringing in grain and loading it on donkeys, along with wine, grapes, and figs. All kinds of goods were being brought into Jerusalem on the Sabbath day. So I warned them against selling food on that day. 16 Additionally, men of Tyre who lived there were importing fish and all kinds of merchandise and selling them on the Sabbath to the people of Judah in Jerusalem. 17 Then I rebuked the nobles of Judah and asked, “What is this evil you are doing—profaning the Sabbath day? 18 Did not your forefathers do the same things, so that our God brought all this disaster on us and on this city? And now you are rekindling His wrath against Israel by profaning the Sabbath!” 19 When the evening shadows began to fall on the gates of Jerusalem, just before the Sabbath, I ordered that the gates be shut and not opened until after the Sabbath. I posted some of my servants at the gates so that no load could enter on the Sabbath day. 20 Once or twice, the merchants and those who sell all kinds of goods camped outside Jerusalem, 21 but I warned them, “Why are you camping in front of the wall? If you do it again, I will lay hands on you.” From that time on, they did not return on the Sabbath. 22 Then I instructed the Levites to purify themselves and guard the gates in order to keep the Sabbath day holy. Remember me for this as well, O my God, and show me mercy according to Your abundant loving devotion.

All kinds of goods were being brought into Jerusalem on the Sabbath day. And now you are rekindling His wrath against Israel by profaning the Sabbath!”

19 When the evening shadows began to fall on the gates of Jerusalem, just before the Sabbath, I ordered that the gates be shut and not opened until after the Sabbath. I posted some of my servants at the gates so that no load could enter on the Sabbath day. 20 Once or twice, the merchants and those who sell all kinds of goods camped outside Jerusalem, 21 but I warned them, “Why are you camping in front of the wall? If you do it again, I will lay hands on you.” From that time on, they did not return on the Sabbath. 22 Then I instructed the Levites to purify themselves and guard the gates in order to keep the Sabbath day holy. Remember me for this as well, O my God, and show me mercy according to Your abundant loving devotion.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Nehemiah sees winepresses being worked and loads of produce brought into Jerusalem on the Sabbath. Traders from Tyre also sell fish and other goods to the people of Judah. These practices violate the commitment the people made in Nehemiah 10:31.

He rebukes the nobles and reminds them that their ancestors’ disregard for the Sabbath contributed to the disaster that fell on the city. As evening shadows approach before the Sabbath, he orders the gates closed until it is over and stations his servants to stop loads entering.

When traders camp outside the wall, he warns them against returning. He also instructs the Levites to purify themselves and keep guard for the holiness of the Sabbath. His closing prayer asks God for remembrance and mercy according to His great loving devotion.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry emphasizes the seriousness of disregarding the Sabbath after earlier judgment. Gill also stresses the corrective action and understands the request for mercy as recognition that Nehemiah depends on God’s grace. Gill distinguishes the servants guarding the city gates from what he reads as the Levites’ responsibility at the temple gates. The account’s main concern is restoring observance of the time the community has promised to keep holy.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Nehemiah 13:23-29
passages.section_title: Why does Nehemiah point to Solomon when confronting these marriages?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 23 In those days I also saw Jews who had married women from Ashdod, Ammon, and Moab. 24 Half of their children spoke the language of Ashdod or of the other peoples, but could not speak the language of Judah. 25 I rebuked them and called down curses on them. I beat some of these men and pulled out their hair. Then I made them take an oath before God and said, “You must not give your daughters in marriage to their sons or take their daughters as wives for your sons or for yourselves! 26 Did not King Solomon of Israel sin in matters like this? There was not a king like him among many nations, and he was loved by his God, who made him king over all Israel—yet foreign women drew him into sin. 27 Must we now hear that you too are doing all this terrible evil and acting unfaithfully against our God by marrying foreign women?” 28 Even one of the sons of Jehoiada son of Eliashib the high priest had become a son-in-law to Sanballat the Horonite. Therefore I drove him away from me. 29 Remember them, O my God, because they have defiled the priesthood and the covenant of the priesthood and of the Levites.
paragraphs: 23 In those days I also saw Jews who had married women from Ashdod, Ammon, and Moab. 24 Half of their children spoke the language of Ashdod or of the other peoples, but could not speak the language of Judah. 25 I rebuked them and called down curses on them. I beat some of these men and pulled out their hair. Then I made them take an oath before God and said, “You must not give your daughters in marriage to their sons or take their daughters as wives for your sons or for yourselves! 26 Did not King Solomon of Israel sin in matters like this? There was not a king like him among many nations, and he was loved by his God, who made him king over all Israel—yet foreign women drew him into sin. 27 Must we now hear that you too are doing all this terrible evil and acting unfaithfully against our God by marrying foreign women?”

28 Even one of the sons of Jehoiada son of Eliashib the high priest had become a son-in-law to Sanballat the Horonite. Therefore I drove him away from me. 29 Remember them, O my God, because they have defiled the priesthood and the covenant of the priesthood and of the Levites.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Nehemiah sees Jews married to women from Ashdod, Ammon and Moab. Half of the children speak the languages of those peoples and cannot speak the language of Judah. He confronts the men, calls down curses, beats some and pulls out their hair, then requires an oath against arranging such marriages.

He appeals to Solomon’s example. 1 Kings 11:1–13 recounts how Solomon’s wives turned his heart toward other gods despite the favor God had shown him. Nehemiah’s warning concerns unfaithfulness to God, not an assumption that Solomon lacked intelligence or standing.

The problem reaches the priestly family: a son of Jehoiada, grandson of Eliashib the high priest, is Sanballat’s son-in-law. Nehemiah drives him away and appeals to God concerning the defilement of the priesthood.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Gill understand the marriages as breaches of the community’s obligations and read the beating as punishment administered under Nehemiah’s authority as governor. The narrative records severe measures alongside his warning from Solomon’s failure.

The New Testament gives instructions for Christian marriages in their own setting. 1 Corinthians 7:10–16 tells a believer not to divorce an unbelieving spouse who is willing to remain. That instruction must be heard when considering the relationship between this ancient community’s reforms and Christian family life.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Nehemiah 13:30-31
passages.section_title: What does Nehemiah leave in place, and what does he leave with God?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 30 Thus I purified the priests and Levites from everything foreign, and I assigned specific duties to each of the priests and Levites. 31 I also arranged for contributions of wood at the appointed times, and for the firstfruits. Remember me, O my God, with favor.
paragraphs: 30 Thus I purified the priests and Levites from everything foreign, and I assigned specific duties to each of the priests and Levites. 31 I also arranged for contributions of wood at the appointed times, and for the firstfruits. Remember me, O my God, with favor.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The book ends with a brief summary: Nehemiah purifies the priests and Levites from what is foreign, assigns their duties and arranges the wood contributions and firstfruits.

His final words are a prayer asking God to remember him with favor. After walls, registers, promises, celebrations and renewed failures, he ends by placing his work before God.

The restored arrangements matter, but the closing chapter has shown that a past promise or celebration does not make continued faithfulness automatic. The book leaves the reader with both the responsibilities that must be carried forward and the appeal to God’s care.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry understands the closing request as humble dependence on God after imperfect service. Gill connects it with God graciously remembering the particular work Nehemiah has described. Both read the ending as an appeal to God’s favor rather than a declaration that every problem has been permanently solved.
passages.god_plan_html:
The need for God’s continuing work within His people is expressed in the prayer of Hebrews 13:20–21. It asks the God who raised Jesus, the great Shepherd, to equip His people to do His will and work in them what pleases Him through Christ.

This is the larger theme to which Nehemiah’s unfinished struggle points: faithful service matters, and God’s people continue to need His help. The New Testament grounds that hope in the risen Shepherd and God’s work through Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Psalm 22:1
passages.context_html: Psalm 22 moves from abandonment and suffering into vindication and praise before the nations. When its opening cry appears on Jesus' lips, the whole psalm stands behind the citation, not merely its first line in isolation.
passages.common_interpretations_html: This is the rawest prayer in the Bible. Jesus is not asking God to stop what is happening. He is not requesting relief. He is bringing the full, unfiltered weight of what He is experiencing into words, directed at the Father, in the darkest moment any human being has ever faced. The Father does not answer immediately. He does not remove the suffering. The cup is drunk to the last drop. If Jesus could bring this kind of honesty before God without it being unfaithful, so can we.
passages.current_position_html: No defined position is stated here yet beyond the common interpretations above. As related study develops, this section will be updated where the text warrants a clearer conclusion.

passages.title: Psalm 31:5
passages.context_html: Psalm 31 is a prayer of trust from the midst of distress, slander, and danger. Its language of entrusting oneself to God belongs to a larger movement of refuge, deliverance, and steadfast confidence in the Lord.
passages.common_interpretations_html: His final words are not a request at all. They are pure release — Himself, placed entirely into the Father's hands, with nothing held back and nothing left to ask for. Intercession without control. Anguish without demand. Surrender without condition. These three prayers, spoken in the worst hours of His life, are the same prayer Gethsemane modeled — just carried all the way through to the end.
passages.current_position_html: No defined position is stated here yet beyond the common interpretations above. As related study develops, this section will be updated where the text warrants a clearer conclusion.

passages.title: Psalm 46:10
passages.context_html: Psalm 46 proclaims God's presence and stability when nations rage and the earth shakes. Its stillness language belongs to a psalm about God's sovereign rule and refuge, not to a merely inward or sentimental quietism.
passages.common_interpretations_html: This topic connects directly to the broader question of how prayer and faith are described in Scripture — particularly the difference between faith that rests in what God has already done and said, versus prayer that seeks ongoing outward confirmation. See the companion documents Prayer and Faith and What Does Prayer Look Like? for more on that distinction, especially the discussion of the woman with the issue of blood and the pattern of faith without a requested sign. Also connected: the companion document What Does Prayer Look Like? addresses the question of sitting quietly and waiting for a feeling as God's answer — and why Psalm 46:10, often cited in support of that practice, actually says something very different in the Hebrew. This study didn't start as an abstract topic. It started with a conversation. Someone close to me shared something good — an eagle, flying low, maybe chasing something in the yard. A genuinely nice moment. But the conversation didn't stop there. It moved into stories about dreams — reports of people having visions of Jesus, especially in certain countries — and something about that didn't sit right with me. It felt like it was reaching for more than Scripture actually supports. That feeling is what sent me into this study in the first place. So I started digging into what the Bible actually says about signs, dreams, and how God communicates. And partway through that study, while I was working through the very passages about sign-seeking, I stopped. Because I remembered something I'd said in that same conversation, before any of this started — something about the eagle. I'd made a comment that maybe this was God's way of showing us a heads-up about something coming. I said I was being facetious. But I'd said it.
passages.current_position_html: No defined position is stated here yet beyond the common interpretations above. As related study develops, this section will be updated where the text warrants a clearer conclusion.

passages.title: Psalm 95:6
passages.context_html: Psalm 95:6 should be read within the flow of its chapter and the larger argument of Psalm.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Restored reading: "Come, let us bow down and fall prostrate; Let us kneel before Yahweh our Maker." Shachah appears alongside "bow down" and "kneel" — not redundant phrases but reinforcements of the same truth: worship is a posture of the whole self. The people do not stand and observe — they fall and adore. Worship here is not passive; it is participatory.
passages.current_position_html: No defined position is stated here yet beyond the common interpretations above. As related study develops, this section will be updated where the text warrants a clearer conclusion.

passages.title: Psalm 110:4
passages.context_html: Psalm 110:4 should be read within the flow of its chapter and the larger argument of Psalm.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The book of Hebrews spends its middle chapters establishing that Jesus is a priest "according to the order of Melchizedek" (Hebrews 5:6, quoting Psalm 110:4) rather than according to the order of Levi. Melchizedek appears once in Genesis, blessing Abraham — a king and priest with no recorded genealogy, no predecessor, no successor (Genesis 14:18-20; see also Hebrews 7:1-3). The writer of Hebrews uses that silence deliberately: a priesthood that isn't passed down, isn't inherited, isn't mediated through a class of men set apart by birth. Then comes the argument that matters most for this study: A change in priesthood. A change in law. The old covenant required a mediating class — men set apart, functioning between God and the people, offering sacrifices the people themselves could not offer. Hebrews' whole argument is that this pointed forward to something, and that something has already arrived:

passages.title: Psalm 119:105
passages.context_html: Psalm 119:105 should be read within the flow of its chapter and the larger argument of Psalm.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The Word itself. Psalm 119:105 — "Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path." Scripture is not a static document awaiting supplementation by personal signs. It is living and active (Hebrews 4:12), sufficient to equip the believer for every good work (2 Timothy 3:16-17). Prayer and wisdom. James 1:5 — "But if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all generously and without reproach, and it will be given to him." The gift promised in response to asking is wisdom — the sanctified judgment to navigate circumstances — not a sign pointing to a predetermined answer. The counsel of others. Proverbs 15:22 — "Without consultation, plans are frustrated, but with many counselors they succeed." The community of believers, grounded in the same Word, is itself a means of guidance.

versions.text: 1 My son, do not forget my teaching, but let your heart keep my commandments; 2 for they will add length to your days, years and peace to your life. 3 Never let loving devotion or faithfulness leave you; bind them around your neck, write them on the tablet of your heart. 4 Then you will find favor and high regard in the sight of God and man. 5 Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and lean not on your own understanding; 6 in all your ways acknowledge Him, and He will make your paths straight. 7 Be not wise in your own eyes; fear the LORD and turn away from evil. 8 This will bring healing to your body and refreshment to your bones. 9 Honor the LORD with your wealth and with the firstfruits of all your harvest; 10 then your barns will be filled with plenty, and your vats will overflow with new wine. 11 My son, do not reject the discipline of the LORD, and do not loathe His rebuke; 12 for the LORD disciplines the one He loves, as does a father the son in whom he delights.

passages.context_html: In Proverbs 3, wisdom is presented as a way of life marked by trust, humility, correction, and submission to the Lord's ordering of the path. Its language about trusting and acknowledging God belongs to a whole chapter about wise dependence rather than self-direction.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Proverbs 3:5-6 speaks to the limits of human judgment. The passage calls for trust in the LORD precisely because we do not see enough of the path to direct it wisely on our own. That matters for prayer as well. The warning against leaning on our own understanding cuts against the assumption that we are equipped to decide in advance which specific outcome would best serve God's purpose.
passages.current_position_html: This site's current position is that Proverbs 3:5-6 calls for more than emotional confidence that God will back the path we prefer. It calls for surrender of self-direction itself. In the context of prayer, that means trust is not insisting on a chosen outcome and then asking God to authorize it. Trust is acknowledging Him precisely where our own understanding proves insufficient.
