passages.god_plan_html:
The image of people hiding among rocks before divine judgment appears again in Revelation 6:12–17. Kings, commanders, the wealthy, slaves and free people seek shelter from the One on the throne and the wrath of the Lamb.

This is a scriptural parallel in the language and scope of judgment. Human rank and resources cannot provide refuge from God. Revelation carries the theme into its vision of the Lamb’s authority.

passages.title: Isaiah 3:1-15
passages.section_title: What becomes of a community when its support and leadership collapse?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 For behold, the Lord GOD of Hosts is about to remove from Jerusalem and Judah both supply and support: the whole supply of food and water, 2 the mighty man and the warrior, the judge and the prophet, the soothsayer and the elder, 3 the commander of fifty and the dignitary, the counselor, the cunning magician, and the clever enchanter. 4 “I will make mere lads their leaders, and children will rule over them.” 5 The people will oppress one another, man against man, neighbor against neighbor; the young will rise up against the old, and the base against the honorable. 6 A man will seize his brother within his father’s house: “You have a cloak—you be our leader! Take charge of this heap of rubble.” 7 On that day he will cry aloud: “I am not a healer. I have no food or clothing in my house. Do not make me leader of the people!” 8 For Jerusalem has stumbled and Judah has fallen because they spoke and acted against the LORD, defying His glorious presence. 9 The expression on their faces testifies against them, and like Sodom they flaunt their sin; they do not conceal it. Woe to them, for they have brought disaster upon themselves. 10 Tell the righteous it will be well with them, for they will enjoy the fruit of their labor. 11 Woe to the wicked; disaster is upon them! For they will be repaid with what their hands have done. 12 Youths oppress My people, and women rule over them. O My people, your guides mislead you; they turn you from your paths. 13 The LORD arises to contend; He stands to judge the people. 14 The LORD brings this charge against the elders and leaders of His people: “You have devoured the vineyard; the plunder of the poor is in your houses. 15 Why do you crush My people and grind the faces of the poor?” declares the Lord GOD of Hosts.
paragraphs: 1 For behold, the Lord GOD of Hosts is about to remove from Jerusalem and Judah both supply and support: the whole supply of food and water, 2 the mighty man and the warrior, the judge and the prophet, the soothsayer and the elder, 3 the commander of fifty and the dignitary, the counselor, the cunning magician, and the clever enchanter. 4 “I will make mere lads their leaders, and children will rule over them.” 5 The people will oppress one another, man against man, neighbor against neighbor; the young will rise up against the old, and the base against the honorable.

6 A man will seize his brother within his father’s house: “You have a cloak—you be our leader! Take charge of this heap of rubble.” 7 On that day he will cry aloud: “I am not a healer. I have no food or clothing in my house. Do not make me leader of the people!” 8 For Jerusalem has stumbled and Judah has fallen because they spoke and acted against the LORD, defying His glorious presence. 9 The expression on their faces testifies against them, and like Sodom they flaunt their sin; they do not conceal it. Woe to them, for they have brought disaster upon themselves.

10 Tell the righteous it will be well with them, for they will enjoy the fruit of their labor. 11 Woe to the wicked; disaster is upon them! For they will be repaid with what their hands have done. 12 Youths oppress My people, and women rule over them. O My people, your guides mislead you; they turn you from your paths.

13 The LORD arises to contend; He stands to judge the people. 14 The LORD brings this charge against the elders and leaders of His people: “You have devoured the vineyard; the plunder of the poor is in your houses. 15 Why do you crush My people and grind the faces of the poor?” declares the Lord GOD of Hosts.

passages.context_html:
The warning moves from misplaced trust in people to the removal of the things Judah depends on: food, water, experienced leaders, military strength and counsel. The list also includes people claiming spiritual powers.

The result is disorder and mutual oppression. Leadership becomes so desperate that merely having a cloak seems a reason to be put in charge. The person approached refuses, lacking the resources to repair the ruin.

The passage connects Jerusalem’s condition with words and actions opposed to the Lord. It distinguishes the outcome of the righteous from that of the wicked, then confronts guides who mislead the people.

The Lord stands to bring His charge against elders and leaders. Those who should protect the people have consumed the vineyard and filled their own houses with goods taken from the poor. The accusation names the harm directly: they are crushing God’s people.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands the would-be healer as someone being asked to repair the ruined state. Henry emphasizes the accountability of those entrusted with wealth and power and the particular wrong of making people poor and then oppressing them.

Readings differ about the historical reach of the disaster. The NABRE notes connect the loss of leading people with deportation and the upheaval it causes. Gill instead directs the passage particularly toward Jerusalem’s later destruction by Rome. The chapter itself names Judah and Jerusalem and makes their rebellion and unjust leadership central to the warning.

passages.context_html:
The warning turns to the proud daughters of Zion: their looks, movements and ornaments display the importance they place on appearance. The long list of clothing, jewelry and accessories makes their outward splendor vivid.

The announced judgment reverses that condition. Fragrance gives way to stench, fine dress to sackcloth and styled hair to baldness. The things used to display status cannot protect them from loss and humiliation.

The scene widens to fallen warriors and Zion herself sitting destitute, with her gates mourning. The loss belongs to the disaster overtaking the city, continuing the chapter’s warning against pride and the misuse of advantage.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry emphasizes the neglect of devotion, generosity and justice while time and resources are spent on display. Gill similarly begins with pride as the source of the behavior described.

The NABRE notes place these women within the ruling class and note that many terms in the clothing list are rare and difficult to identify precisely. The overall reversal remains clear even where the exact shape of an accessory is uncertain: the city’s finery will become mourning.

passages.god_plan_html:
The wider question of what God values appears in 1 Peter 3:1–6. Peter directs attention to the enduring beauty of the heart and a gentle spirit precious to God, in a passage where conduct may lead an unbelieving spouse toward faith.

1 Timothy 2:8–10 joins prayer without anger among men with modesty, self-control and good deeds among women. The connection is a people whose worship becomes visible through character and conduct. Outward display cannot supply the inward faithfulness that makes such a witness possible.

passages.title: Isaiah 4:1-6
passages.section_title: How does the promise of shelter follow the city’s disgrace?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 In that day seven women will take hold of one man and say, “We will eat our own bread and provide our own clothes. Just let us be called by your name. Take away our disgrace!” 2 On that day the Branch of the LORD will be beautiful and glorious, and the fruit of the land will be the pride and glory of Israel’s survivors. 3 Whoever remains in Zion and whoever is left in Jerusalem will be called holy— all in Jerusalem who are recorded among the living— 4 when the Lord has washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion and cleansed the bloodstains from the heart of Jerusalem by a spirit of judgment and a spirit of fire. 5 Then the LORD will create over all of Mount Zion and over her assemblies a cloud of smoke by day and a glowing flame of fire by night. For over all the glory there will be a canopy, 6 a shelter to give shade from the heat by day, and a refuge and hiding place from the storm and the rain.
paragraphs: 1 In that day seven women will take hold of one man and say, “We will eat our own bread and provide our own clothes. Just let us be called by your name. Take away our disgrace!”

2 On that day the Branch of the LORD will be beautiful and glorious, and the fruit of the land will be the pride and glory of Israel’s survivors. 3 Whoever remains in Zion and whoever is left in Jerusalem will be called holy— all in Jerusalem who are recorded among the living— 4 when the Lord has washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion and cleansed the bloodstains from the heart of Jerusalem by a spirit of judgment and a spirit of fire.

5 Then the LORD will create over all of Mount Zion and over her assemblies a cloud of smoke by day and a glowing flame of fire by night. For over all the glory there will be a canopy, 6 a shelter to give shade from the heat by day, and a refuge and hiding place from the storm and the rain.

passages.context_html:
The opening verse completes the picture of loss at the end of chapter 3. Seven women seek one man’s name while offering to provide their own food and clothing. Their appeal shows the desperation produced by the city’s disaster.

The tone then changes. The Branch of the Lord and the land’s fruit become the survivors’ glory. Those left in Zion are called holy after the Lord washes away the city’s filth and bloodshed through judgment and fire.

The Hebrew צֶמַח, tsemach, pronounced TSEH-makh, means sprout or growth. Brown–Driver–Briggs lists this verse under growth, while also recording the word’s use for a future ruler in other passages. The word alone does not settle whether the image here describes the land’s renewed growth or points to the coming Messiah.

The promise ends with cloud and fire over Zion’s assemblies and shelter from heat, storm and rain. These are pictures of God’s presence and protection for a people He has cleansed, following the earlier warnings about their exposure and shame.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Readers differ over the Branch. The NABRE notes recognize that the word can refer to the future Davidic king, but favor renewed growth here because it stands beside the land’s fruit. Henry and Wesley read the Branch as Christ, connecting the passage with His kingdom and the good He brings to His people.

The royal reading also draws on passages such as Jeremiah 23:5–6 and Zechariah 3:8–10, which use Branch language for God’s promised ruler or servant. These readings differ over the image’s immediate reference while recognizing that the cleansing and shelter come from the Lord.

passages.god_plan_html:
The cloud and fire recall God guiding His people out of Egypt in Exodus 13:20–22. Isaiah uses that familiar picture of divine presence in a promise concerning Zion’s restored community.

A further parallel appears in Revelation 7:9–17. People from every nation stand before God and the Lamb, their robes washed in the Lamb’s blood. God spreads His tabernacle over them, and the Lamb shepherds them beyond hunger, thirst and scorching heat. The shared themes are cleansing, God dwelling with His people and the shelter He provides.

passages.title: Isaiah 5:1-7
passages.section_title: What went wrong with the carefully tended vineyard?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 I will sing for my beloved a song of his vineyard: My beloved had a vineyard on a very fertile hill. 2 He dug it up and cleared the stones and planted the finest vines. He built a watchtower in the middle and dug out a winepress as well. He waited for the vineyard to yield good grapes, but the fruit it produced was sour! 3 “And now, O dwellers of Jerusalem and men of Judah, I exhort you to judge between Me and My vineyard. 4 What more could have been done for My vineyard than I have done for it? Why, when I expected sweet grapes, did it bring forth sour fruit? 5 Now I will tell you what I am about to do to My vineyard: I will take away its hedge, and it will be consumed; I will tear down its wall, and it will be trampled. 6 I will make it a wasteland, neither pruned nor cultivated, and thorns and briers will grow up. I will command the clouds that rain shall not fall on it.” 7 For the vineyard of the LORD of Hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah are the plant of His delight. He looked for justice, but saw bloodshed; for righteousness, but heard a cry of distress.

Why, when I expected sweet grapes, did it bring forth sour fruit? 5 Now I will tell you what I am about to do to My vineyard: I will take away its hedge, and it will be consumed; I will tear down its wall, and it will be trampled. 6 I will make it a wasteland, neither pruned nor cultivated, and thorns and briers will grow up. I will command the clouds that rain shall not fall on it.”

7 For the vineyard of the LORD of Hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah are the plant of His delight. He looked for justice, but saw bloodshed; for righteousness, but heard a cry of distress.

passages.context_html:
Isaiah sings of a beloved owner who gives his vineyard everything needed to flourish: fertile ground, cleared stones, choice vines, a watchtower and a winepress. Yet it produces sour fruit instead of the good grapes expected.

The word behind that disappointing fruit is Hebrew בְּאֻשִׁים, beushim, pronounced beh-oo-SHEEM. Brown–Driver–Briggs describes stinking or worthless things and lists the wild grapes of this vineyard. The image stresses the fruit’s bad quality after such careful attention.

The owner invites Jerusalem and Judah to judge the matter. He then announces that he will remove the vineyard’s protection and care, leaving it trampled, overgrown and without rain.

The final verse explains the song: the vineyard is Israel, and the people of Judah are the planting God delights in. The fruit He sought was justice and righteousness; what appeared was bloodshed and the cry of those in distress. The problem is exposed through the difference between His care and their conduct.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley understand the careful planting as the advantages and instruction God gave His people, and the bad fruit as their failure to respond faithfully. Gill likewise connects the expected grapes with justice and care for the vulnerable.

The song gives its own explanation rather than leaving the reader to invent a meaning for every item. Its central charge is that a people so carefully provided for have produced the opposite of the justice God seeks.

passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus’ parable of the tenants draws on the same vineyard picture in Matthew 21:33–46 and Mark 12:1–12: an owner plants a vineyard, provides its wall, winepress and tower, and seeks its fruit.

Jesus brings the account to the tenants’ rejection of the owner’s servants and finally his beloved son. The leaders recognize that He is speaking about them. This is a strong connection through shared imagery, with the New Testament bringing the question of faithfulness to its climax in the response to the Son. Responsibility for God’s gifts calls for the fruit He seeks.

passages.title: Isaiah 5:8-30
passages.section_title: What does the vineyard’s bad fruit look like in everyday life?

passages.context_html:
The warnings now name the conduct pictured by the bad grapes. People accumulate houses and fields until others have no room, pursue drink from morning into night, and fill their feasts with pleasure while disregarding the Lord’s work.

The promised reversal touches the things in which they take pride: great houses stand empty, crops fail, and honor and revelry give way to hunger, thirst, exile and death. God’s justice exposes the limits of their security.

Further warnings confront those who pull sin along behind them, mock the announcement of God’s work, reverse good and evil, trust their own wisdom, and use their power to drink heavily and pervert justice for bribes. Their rejection of God’s instruction is the stated reason for judgment.

The ending describes distant nations summoned with a banner and a whistle. The advancing force is swift, ready and fierce as a lion, carrying off its prey. The chapter closes with darkness over the land instead of the fruitful vineyard with which it began.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Gill distinguish owning property from an appetite to acquire more without regard for others. Henry likewise distinguishes music itself from pleasure that draws the heart away from God. The warnings concern the conduct described, rather than making every house purchase or celebration a sin.

The readers also differ over the distant invading force. Wesley connects it with the Chaldeans, while Gill directs it toward Rome; Henry sees the pattern in both earlier and later invasions. The prophecy does not name the force here. Its emphasis is that those who dismiss God’s word cannot prevent the judgment He summons.

passages.title: Isaiah 6:1-13
passages.section_title: How is Isaiah cleansed and sent into a ministry people will resist?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 In the year that King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord seated on a throne, high and exalted; and the train of His robe filled the temple. 2 Above Him stood seraphim, each having six wings: With two wings they covered their faces, with two they covered their feet, and with two they were flying. 3 And they were calling out to one another: “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Hosts; all the earth is full of His glory.” 4 At the sound of their voices the doorposts and thresholds shook, and the temple was filled with smoke. 5 Then I said: “Woe is me, for I am ruined, because I am a man of unclean lips dwelling among a people of unclean lips; for my eyes have seen the King, the LORD of Hosts.” 6 Then one of the seraphim flew to me, and in his hand was a glowing coal that he had taken with tongs from the altar. 7 And with it he touched my mouth and said: “Now that this has touched your lips, your iniquity is removed and your sin is atoned for.” 8 Then I heard the voice of the Lord saying: “Whom shall I send? Who will go for Us?” And I said: “Here am I. Send me!” 9 And He replied: “Go and tell this people, ‘Be ever hearing, but never understanding; be ever seeing, but never perceiving.’ 10 Make the hearts of this people calloused; deafen their ears and close their eyes. Otherwise they might see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their hearts, and turn and be healed.” 11 Then I asked: “How long, O Lord?” And He replied: “Until the cities lie ruined and without inhabitant, until the houses are left unoccupied and the land is desolate and ravaged, 12 until the LORD has driven men far away and the land is utterly forsaken. 13 And though a tenth remains in the land, it will be burned again. As the terebinth and oak leave stumps when felled, so the holy seed will be a stump in the land.”

5 Then I said: “Woe is me, for I am ruined, because I am a man of unclean lips dwelling among a people of unclean lips; for my eyes have seen the King, the LORD of Hosts.” 6 Then one of the seraphim flew to me, and in his hand was a glowing coal that he had taken with tongs from the altar. 7 And with it he touched my mouth and said: “Now that this has touched your lips, your iniquity is removed and your sin is atoned for.”

8 Then I heard the voice of the Lord saying: “Whom shall I send? Who will go for Us?” And I said: “Here am I. Send me!” 9 And He replied: “Go and tell this people, ‘Be ever hearing, but never understanding; be ever seeing, but never perceiving.’ 10 Make the hearts of this people calloused; deafen their ears and close their eyes. Otherwise they might see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their hearts, and turn and be healed.”

11 Then I asked: “How long, O Lord?” And He replied: “Until the cities lie ruined and without inhabitant, until the houses are left unoccupied and the land is desolate and ravaged, 12 until the LORD has driven men far away and the land is utterly forsaken. 13 And though a tenth remains in the land, it will be burned again. As the terebinth and oak leave stumps when felled, so the holy seed will be a stump in the land.”

passages.context_html:
The account now describes Isaiah’s vision in the year King Uzziah dies. The earthly king’s death stands beside the sight of the Lord enthroned, with His robe filling the temple. Heavenly attendants called seraphim cover their faces and feet as they proclaim His holiness; their voices shake the thresholds, and smoke fills the temple.

Isaiah responds by confessing his own unclean lips and his place among a people with the same uncleanness. He has seen the King and recognizes his unfitness to stand before Him. One of the seraphim touches his mouth with a coal from the altar and announces that his guilt is removed and his sin atoned for.

Only then does Isaiah hear the call for a messenger and offer himself. The commission is sobering: his hearers will keep hearing and seeing without understanding. His message will be bound up with the hardening of their hearts, rather than producing the widespread turning he might have hoped for.

When Isaiah asks how long, the answer is devastation, empty houses, a ravaged land and people driven far away. Even a remaining tenth faces further burning. Yet the final image is a stump that remains after a tree is felled: the holy seed is still there.

The chapter joins God’s holiness, Isaiah’s cleansing, his willingness to serve and the painful outcome of speaking to a resistant people. The surviving stump keeps the final word from being complete destruction.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads the vision in light of John 12:41, which connects it with Christ’s glory, and understands the coal as assurance of pardon through Christ’s work. Wesley likewise sees the touch as a sign of pardon and cleansing. Their readings emphasize that Isaiah is made ready by God’s mercy before he is sent.

On the hardening, Henry and Wesley both connect the judgment with people who have refused to listen. Wesley describes God continuing to send His word while withdrawing the help they have resisted. The Reformed Westminster Confession 5.6 and the 1689 Baptist Confession 5.6 similarly describe God judging earlier sin by withholding or withdrawing help, while people harden themselves through what softens others.

These explanations take both the divine judgment and the people’s refusal seriously. They do not turn the promise of a surviving holy seed into an announcement that everyone responds in exactly the same way. The closing image preserves hope within a severe commission.

passages.god_plan_html:
The New Testament directly connects this chapter with Jesus. John 12:37–43 quotes the hardening words and says Isaiah spoke because he saw Jesus’ glory. The vision therefore belongs to the New Testament’s account of who Jesus is, as well as its explanation of unbelief in the face of His signs.

Jesus quotes the passage when explaining His use of parables in Matthew 13:10–17; the connection also appears in Mark 4:10–12 and Luke 8:9–10. Hearing the message and understanding it are not treated as the same response.

Paul quotes the passage in Acts 28:23–28, after some hearers are persuaded about Jesus and others refuse to believe. He then announces that God’s salvation has been sent to the Gentiles. Isaiah’s commission becomes part of the explanation of the gospel’s reception and its movement among the nations.

Romans 11:1–12, 17–32 adds an essential part of that larger picture. Paul rejects the claim that God has rejected His people, speaks of a remnant by grace and a hardening in part, and warns Gentile believers against boasting. God’s purpose includes mercy toward people who have been disobedient; the account calls for humility and faith, rather than superiority toward others.

passages.title: Isaiah 7:1-9
passages.section_title: What is Ahaz being asked to trust when Jerusalem is threatened?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now in the days that Ahaz son of Jotham, the son of Uzziah, was king of Judah, Rezin king of Aram marched up to wage war against Jerusalem. He was accompanied by Pekah son of Remaliah the king of Israel, but he could not overpower the city. 2 When it was reported to the house of David that Aram was in league with Ephraim, the hearts of Ahaz and his people trembled like trees in the forest shaken by the wind. 3 Then the LORD said to Isaiah, “Go out with your son Shear-jashub to meet Ahaz at the end of the aqueduct that feeds the upper pool, on the road to the Launderer’s Field, 4 and say to him: Calm down and be quiet. Do not be afraid or disheartened over these two smoldering stubs of firewood—over the fierce anger of Rezin and Aram and of the son of Remaliah. 5 For Aram, along with Ephraim and the son of Remaliah, has plotted your ruin, saying: 6 ‘Let us invade Judah, terrorize it, and divide it among ourselves. Then we can install the son of Tabeal over it as king.’ 7 But this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘It will not arise; it will not happen. 8 For the head of Aram is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin. Within sixty-five years Ephraim will be shattered as a people. 9 The head of Ephraim is Samaria, and the head of Samaria is the son of Remaliah. If you do not stand firm in your faith, then you will not stand at all.’”
paragraphs: 1 Now in the days that Ahaz son of Jotham, the son of Uzziah, was king of Judah, Rezin king of Aram marched up to wage war against Jerusalem. He was accompanied by Pekah son of Remaliah the king of Israel, but he could not overpower the city. 2 When it was reported to the house of David that Aram was in league with Ephraim, the hearts of Ahaz and his people trembled like trees in the forest shaken by the wind.

3 Then the LORD said to Isaiah, “Go out with your son Shear-jashub to meet Ahaz at the end of the aqueduct that feeds the upper pool, on the road to the Launderer’s Field, 4 and say to him: Calm down and be quiet. Do not be afraid or disheartened over these two smoldering stubs of firewood—over the fierce anger of Rezin and Aram and of the son of Remaliah. 5 For Aram, along with Ephraim and the son of Remaliah, has plotted your ruin, saying: 6 ‘Let us invade Judah, terrorize it, and divide it among ourselves. Then we can install the son of Tabeal over it as king.’

7 But this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘It will not arise; it will not happen. 8 For the head of Aram is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin. Within sixty-five years Ephraim will be shattered as a people. 9 The head of Ephraim is Samaria, and the head of Samaria is the son of Remaliah. If you do not stand firm in your faith, then you will not stand at all.’”

passages.context_html:
Ahaz faces an alliance between Rezin of Aram and Pekah of Israel, also called Ephraim. Their attack has not overpowered Jerusalem, but news of the alliance leaves the king and people shaking with fear.

The Lord sends Isaiah and his son Shear-jashub to meet Ahaz near the upper pool. Isaiah is to tell him to be calm: the two threatening kings are like smoldering pieces of wood, and their plan to replace him with the son of Tabeal will not stand.

The message addresses the house of David as well as the immediate military threat. It limits the two kings’ power and announces Ephraim’s coming collapse. Ahaz must stand firm in faith rather than treating the threat as greater than God’s promise.

2 Kings 16:5–9 supplies the wider setting: Ahaz appeals to Assyria for rescue and sends silver and gold from the temple and palace. His fear is part of a real political crisis, and his response reveals where he looks for security.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley emphasize the contrast between the enemies’ threatening appearance and God’s assurance that their plan will fail. Wesley connects the message with God’s commitment to David’s house and reads the warning about faith against Ahaz’s decision to seek Assyrian help.

The call concerns trusting a particular word God has given in this crisis. It is not a general promise that any plan a person believes in strongly enough must succeed.

passages.god_plan_html:
The threat to David’s house belongs to the larger story of God keeping His promise concerning that royal line. In Luke 1:26–38, Gabriel announces that Jesus will receive David’s throne and reign over Jacob’s house forever.

Luke 1:67–75 likewise joins salvation from David’s house with God remembering His holy covenant. The connection reaches beyond Ahaz’s own character: God carries forward the promise that comes to its center in Christ.

passages.title: Isaiah 7:10-16
passages.section_title: What does God’s sign of Immanuel mean?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 Again the LORD spoke to Ahaz, saying, 11 “Ask for a sign from the LORD your God, whether from the depths of Sheol or the heights of heaven.” 12 But Ahaz replied, “I will not ask; I will not test the LORD.” 13 Then Isaiah said, “Hear now, O house of David! Is it not enough to try the patience of men? Will you try the patience of my God as well? 14 Therefore the Lord Himself will give you a sign: Behold, the virgin will be with child and give birth to a son, and will call Him Immanuel. 15 By the time He knows enough to reject evil and choose good, He will be eating curds and honey. 16 For before the boy knows enough to reject evil and choose good, the land of the two kings you dread will be laid waste.
paragraphs: 10 Again the LORD spoke to Ahaz, saying, 11 “Ask for a sign from the LORD your God, whether from the depths of Sheol or the heights of heaven.” 12 But Ahaz replied, “I will not ask; I will not test the LORD.” 13 Then Isaiah said, “Hear now, O house of David! Is it not enough to try the patience of men? Will you try the patience of my God as well?

14 Therefore the Lord Himself will give you a sign: Behold, the virgin will be with child and give birth to a son, and will call Him Immanuel. 15 By the time He knows enough to reject evil and choose good, He will be eating curds and honey. 16 For before the boy knows enough to reject evil and choose good, the land of the two kings you dread will be laid waste.

passages.context_html:
The Lord invites Ahaz to ask for a sign, with no limit set by depth or height. Ahaz refuses, saying that he will not test God. Deuteronomy 6:16–19 does forbid testing the Lord, but Isaiah rebukes this refusal: here the invitation has come from God Himself.

The address broadens to the house of David. God will give His own sign: the virgin will bear a son called Immanuel. The next words connect a child’s early years with the approaching end of the two kings whose lands Ahaz fears.

The Hebrew עַלְמָה, almah, pronounced al-MAH, describes a young woman of marriageable age. Brown–Driver–Briggs includes a maiden or newly married woman in its definition. That range matters when considering the sign’s immediate setting; the word alone does not answer every question about the child’s identity.

The passage therefore needs to be read with both its promise to David’s house and its time reference to the present threat in view. Matthew’s account of Jesus’ birth supplies an explicit New Testament connection.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The Catholic Catechism 496–497, Reformed Westminster Confession 8.2, 1689 Baptist Confession 8.2 and Methodist Article II share the teaching that Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the virgin Mary. The Catechism explicitly identifies this with Isaiah’s promise. There is no need to present these traditions as disagreeing about the virgin birth.

Christian readers do differ over how the sign relates to Ahaz’s own time. The NABRE notes emphasize a child-sign reassuring the king during the current danger and connect its ultimate Christian meaning with God coming to be with His people in Christ.

Henry and Wesley read the promised virgin-born Son as the future Messiah, whose coming guarantees that David’s house will survive this threat. They understand the boy in verse 16 as Isaiah’s son Shear-jashub, present at the meeting, marking the nearer deadline. That identification is their explanation of the passage; verse 16 does not name the boy.

deeper_study.title: Should We Seek Signs From God?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
Matthew 1:18–25 explicitly says that Jesus’ birth fulfills the promise. Mary conceives through the Holy Spirit before she and Joseph come together, and Matthew explains Immanuel as God with us.

The meaning reaches beyond rescue from the two kings. The child is named Jesus because He will save His people from their sins. At the Gospel’s close, the risen Jesus sends His disciples to all nations and promises His continuing presence with them (Matthew 28:16–20). God’s presence with His people becomes central to the salvation and mission accomplished through Christ.

passages.title: Isaiah 7:17-25
passages.section_title: Why will the power Ahaz seeks for help become a source of humiliation?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 The LORD will bring on you and on your people and on the house of your father a time unlike any since the day Ephraim separated from Judah—He will bring the king of Assyria.” 18 On that day the LORD will whistle to the flies at the farthest streams of the Nile and to the bees in the land of Assyria. 19 And they will all come and settle in the steep ravines and clefts of the rocks, in all the thornbushes and watering holes. 20 On that day the Lord will use a razor hired from beyond the Euphrates—the king of Assyria—to shave your head and the hair of your legs, and to remove your beard as well. 21 On that day a man will raise a young cow and two sheep, 22 and from the abundance of milk they give, he will eat curds; for all who remain in the land will eat curds and honey. 23 And on that day, in every place that had a thousand vines worth a thousand shekels of silver, only briers and thorns will be found. 24 Men will go there with bow and arrow, for the land will be covered with briers and thorns. 25 For fear of the briers and thorns, you will no longer traverse the hills once tilled by the hoe; they will become places for oxen to graze and sheep to trample.
paragraphs: 17 The LORD will bring on you and on your people and on the house of your father a time unlike any since the day Ephraim separated from Judah—He will bring the king of Assyria.” 18 On that day the LORD will whistle to the flies at the farthest streams of the Nile and to the bees in the land of Assyria. 19 And they will all come and settle in the steep ravines and clefts of the rocks, in all the thornbushes and watering holes. 20 On that day the Lord will use a razor hired from beyond the Euphrates—the king of Assyria—to shave your head and the hair of your legs, and to remove your beard as well.

21 On that day a man will raise a young cow and two sheep, 22 and from the abundance of milk they give, he will eat curds; for all who remain in the land will eat curds and honey. 23 And on that day, in every place that had a thousand vines worth a thousand shekels of silver, only briers and thorns will be found. 24 Men will go there with bow and arrow, for the land will be covered with briers and thorns. 25 For fear of the briers and thorns, you will no longer traverse the hills once tilled by the hoe; they will become places for oxen to graze and sheep to trample.

passages.context_html:
The warning names Assyria as a coming calamity for Ahaz, his people and his father’s house. Relief from the two immediate enemies will not mean freedom from the consequences of seeking security elsewhere.

God summons forces associated with Egypt and Assyria as easily as calling flies and bees. Assyria becomes a hired razor, stripping away hair and beard in an image of humiliation and thorough loss. Ahaz’s payment to the Assyrian king in 2 Kings 16:7–9 makes the description especially pointed.

The land’s changed condition completes the warning. Survivors live from a few animals and their milk, while valuable vineyards become briers and thorns. Cultivated hills are given over to grazing and trampling. Curds and honey appear within this picture of a countryside whose settled farming life has been disrupted.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads the passage as a warning that rejecting God’s assurance leads into the calamities now announced. Wesley emphasizes the reversal in the hired razor: the power Ahaz pays for help becomes the means of his people’s suffering.

The animals, milk, thorns and abandoned vineyards describe life after devastation. There is food for those who remain, yet it comes amid the loss of the land’s former cultivation and wealth. The immediate escape from one threat has not made Ahaz’s chosen source of confidence safe.

passages.title: Isaiah 8:1-10
passages.section_title: What does Isaiah’s son announce about the approaching invasion?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then the LORD said to me, “Take a large scroll and write on it with an ordinary stylus: Maher-shalal-hash-baz. 2 And I will appoint for Myself trustworthy witnesses—Uriah the priest and Zechariah son of Jeberekiah.” 3 And I had relations with the prophetess, and she conceived and gave birth to a son. The LORD said to me, “Name him Maher-shalal-hash-baz. 4 For before the boy knows how to cry ‘Father’ or ‘Mother,’ the wealth of Damascus and the plunder of Samaria will be carried off by the king of Assyria.” 5 And the LORD spoke to me further: 6 “Because this people has rejected the gently flowing waters of Shiloah and rejoiced in Rezin and the son of Remaliah, 7 the Lord will surely bring against them the mighty floodwaters of the Euphrates— the king of Assyria and all his pomp. It will overflow its channels and overrun its banks. 8 It will pour into Judah, swirling and sweeping over it, reaching up to the neck; its spreading streams will cover your entire land, O Immanuel! 9 Huddle together, O peoples, and be shattered; pay attention, all you distant lands; prepare for battle, and be shattered; prepare for battle, and be shattered! 10 Devise a plan, but it will be thwarted; state a proposal, but it will not happen. For God is with us.”
paragraphs: 1 Then the LORD said to me, “Take a large scroll and write on it with an ordinary stylus: Maher-shalal-hash-baz. 2 And I will appoint for Myself trustworthy witnesses—Uriah the priest and Zechariah son of Jeberekiah.” 3 And I had relations with the prophetess, and she conceived and gave birth to a son. The LORD said to me, “Name him Maher-shalal-hash-baz. 4 For before the boy knows how to cry ‘Father’ or ‘Mother,’ the wealth of Damascus and the plunder of Samaria will be carried off by the king of Assyria.”

5 And the LORD spoke to me further: 6 “Because this people has rejected the gently flowing waters of Shiloah and rejoiced in Rezin and the son of Remaliah, 7 the Lord will surely bring against them the mighty floodwaters of the Euphrates— the king of Assyria and all his pomp. It will overflow its channels and overrun its banks. 8 It will pour into Judah, swirling and sweeping over it, reaching up to the neck; its spreading streams will cover your entire land, O Immanuel!

9 Huddle together, O peoples, and be shattered; pay attention, all you distant lands; prepare for battle, and be shattered; prepare for battle, and be shattered! 10 Devise a plan, but it will be thwarted; state a proposal, but it will not happen. For God is with us.”

passages.context_html:
Isaiah is told to write a name on a large scroll with an ordinary stylus, with Uriah and Zechariah appointed as trustworthy witnesses. The prophetess then conceives and bears a son, whom the Lord tells Isaiah to give the same name.

The Hebrew name מַהֵר שָׁלָל חָשׁ בַּז, Maher-shalal-hash-baz, pronounced mah-HARE sha-LAHL khash BAZ, announces swift plunder. Brown–Driver–Briggs explains its words in terms of speed, booty and prey. Before the child can call for his father or mother, Assyria will carry away the wealth of Damascus and the spoil of Samaria.

The warning expands through a water picture. The people reject Shiloah’s gentle flow, and the Lord brings the mighty floodwaters of the Euphrates—the king of Assyria and his forces. The flood reaches into Judah up to the neck, filling the land addressed as Immanuel’s.

The final challenge reaches the distant peoples: their military preparations and plans will be shattered because God is with His people. The passage places the real danger of invasion beside the limit God sets on hostile plans.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads the gentle water as a picture of mild government and the flood as the overwhelming power of a conqueror. Wesley likewise connects the rising river with Assyria’s expansion and the threat reaching Judah.

They do not all identify the rebuked people in verse 6 in the same way. Wesley understands them as northern Israel, rejoicing in its king and Syrian ally, while the NABRE notes apply the warning to Judah’s rejection of God’s protection. Both readings see the water imagery exposing the danger of rejecting the security God provides.

passages.god_plan_html:
The failure of hostile plans belongs to a wider biblical theme. Psalm 2 describes nations plotting against the Lord and His Anointed One, while God establishes His King on Zion.

The believers in Acts 4:23–31 apply that psalm to the gathering against Jesus. They recognize that even the opposition involved in His death did not defeat God’s purpose, and ask for boldness to keep speaking His word. This is a connection through God carrying His purpose forward amid opposition, rather than a promise that His people never face danger or loss.

passages.title: Isaiah 8:11-18
passages.section_title: How can the Lord be both a sanctuary and a stumbling stone?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 For this is what the LORD has spoken to me with a strong hand, instructing me not to walk in the way of this people: 12 “Do not call conspiracy everything these people regard as conspiracy. Do not fear what they fear; do not live in dread. 13 The LORD of Hosts is the One you shall regard as holy. Only He should be feared; only He should be dreaded. 14 And He will be a sanctuary— but to both houses of Israel a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense, to the dwellers of Jerusalem a trap and a snare. 15 Many will stumble over these; they will fall and be broken; they will be ensnared and captured.” 16 Bind up the testimony and seal the law among my disciples. 17 I will wait for the LORD, who is hiding His face from the house of Jacob. I will put my trust in Him. 18 Here am I, and the children the LORD has given me as signs and symbols in Israel from the LORD of Hosts, who dwells on Mount Zion.
paragraphs: 11 For this is what the LORD has spoken to me with a strong hand, instructing me not to walk in the way of this people: 12 “Do not call conspiracy everything these people regard as conspiracy. Do not fear what they fear; do not live in dread. 13 The LORD of Hosts is the One you shall regard as holy. Only He should be feared; only He should be dreaded. 14 And He will be a sanctuary— but to both houses of Israel a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense, to the dwellers of Jerusalem a trap and a snare. 15 Many will stumble over these; they will fall and be broken; they will be ensnared and captured.”

16 Bind up the testimony and seal the law among my disciples. 17 I will wait for the LORD, who is hiding His face from the house of Jacob. I will put my trust in Him. 18 Here am I, and the children the LORD has given me as signs and symbols in Israel from the LORD of Hosts, who dwells on Mount Zion.

passages.context_html:
The Lord strongly warns Isaiah not to follow the people’s way of thinking or share their fears. He is not to label everything a conspiracy merely because others do. The Lord Himself is the One to regard as holy and to fear.

The same Lord will be a sanctuary and a stone over which people stumble. Both houses of Israel and the inhabitants of Jerusalem come within the warning: many will fall and be caught. Their relationship to God is the decisive question amid the political threats.

The testimony and instruction are to be bound and sealed among the disciples. Isaiah declares that he will wait for and trust the Lord even while God hides His face from Jacob. He presents himself and the children God has given him as signs and symbols from the Lord.

The response is therefore more than refusing panic. It is holding to the message already given and continuing to trust God when His favor is not plainly visible.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley emphasize that reverence for God provides a different ground for confidence from fear of human power. They understand the sanctuary and stumbling stone as different responses to the same Lord.

The conspiracy language receives more specific explanations. Wesley reads it as a warning against joining the proposed Assyrian alliance. The NABRE notes understand Isaiah and his followers as being accused of conspiracy because they oppose that policy. The main instruction in either reading is to resist the surrounding fear and give God His rightful place.

Henry emphasizes the children’s names as reminders of God’s message. Gill reads the speaker in verse 18 as Christ presenting the people God has given Him, appealing to Hebrews’ use of the words. These readings differ over how the immediate voice relates to the later application to Christ.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
The New Testament directly uses these words to speak about Christ. Romans 9:30–33 and 1 Peter 2:4–10 apply the stumbling-stone language to the response to Him. Peter also echoes the call to fear rightly and regard the Lord as holy when he tells believers to honor Christ as Lord in their hearts (1 Peter 3:14–16).

Hebrews 2:10–18 places the words about trust and God-given children on Jesus’ lips. It then explains that He shares their humanity, frees them through His death from slavery to the fear of death, and becomes a merciful and faithful high priest.

These are connections made by the New Testament itself. The sanctuary promised amid fear takes on fuller meaning in the Son who shares His people’s life, deals with their sins and brings them to glory.

passages.title: Isaiah 8:19-22
passages.section_title: Where should people turn for guidance when fear and darkness grow?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 When men tell you to consult mediums and spiritists who whisper and mutter, shouldn’t a people consult their God instead? Why consult the dead on behalf of the living? 20 To the law and to the testimony! If they do not speak according to this word, they have no light of dawn. 21 They will roam the land, dejected and hungry. When they are famished, they will become enraged; and looking upward, they will curse their king and their God. 22 Then they will look to the earth and see only distress and darkness and the gloom of anguish. And they will be driven into utter darkness.
paragraphs: 19 When men tell you to consult mediums and spiritists who whisper and mutter, shouldn’t a people consult their God instead? Why consult the dead on behalf of the living? 20 To the law and to the testimony! If they do not speak according to this word, they have no light of dawn.

21 They will roam the land, dejected and hungry. When they are famished, they will become enraged; and looking upward, they will curse their king and their God. 22 Then they will look to the earth and see only distress and darkness and the gloom of anguish. And they will be driven into utter darkness.

passages.context_html:
The passage anticipates pressure to consult mediums and spiritists. Its answer is a pair of questions: should a people not consult their God, and why seek the dead on behalf of the living?

The call to the law and testimony directs the hearers back to God’s instruction. The same concern appears in Deuteronomy 18:9–14, which forbids consulting mediums, spiritists and the dead.

The chapter closes with hunger, anger and cursing of king and God. Looking upward or down to the earth brings no relief, only distress and darkness. These verses describe the grim outcome of turning away from the light of God’s word, before the next chapter’s announcement of light in the darkness.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley read the appeal to the law and testimony as the answer to seeking guidance from forbidden spiritual sources. Their emphasis is on God’s revealed instruction as the standard by which counsel is tested.

The closing distress gives the warning its urgency. The issue is where people place their confidence when hardship exposes the failure of the guidance they have chosen.

passages.title: Isaiah 9:1-7
passages.section_title: Who brings light into the darkness and peace that lasts?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Nevertheless, there will be no more gloom for those in distress. In the past He humbled the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, but in the future He will honor the Way of the Sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations: 2 The people walking in darkness have seen a great light; on those living in the land of the shadow of death, a light has dawned. 3 You have enlarged the nation and increased its joy. The people rejoice before You as they rejoice at harvest time, as men rejoice in dividing the plunder. 4 For as in the day of Midian You have shattered the yoke of their burden, the bar across their shoulders, and the rod of their oppressor. 5 For every trampling boot of battle and every garment rolled in blood will be burned as fuel for the fire. 6 For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given, and the government will be upon His shoulders. And He will be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace. 7 Of the increase of His government and peace there will be no end. He will reign on the throne of David and over his kingdom, to establish and sustain it with justice and righteousness from that time and forevermore. The zeal of the LORD of Hosts will accomplish this.
paragraphs: 1 Nevertheless, there will be no more gloom for those in distress. In the past He humbled the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, but in the future He will honor the Way of the Sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations: 2 The people walking in darkness have seen a great light; on those living in the land of the shadow of death, a light has dawned.

3 You have enlarged the nation and increased its joy. The people rejoice before You as they rejoice at harvest time, as men rejoice in dividing the plunder. 4 For as in the day of Midian You have shattered the yoke of their burden, the bar across their shoulders, and the rod of their oppressor. 5 For every trampling boot of battle and every garment rolled in blood will be burned as fuel for the fire.

6 For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given, and the government will be upon His shoulders. And He will be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace. 7 Of the increase of His government and peace there will be no end. He will reign on the throne of David and over his kingdom, to establish and sustain it with justice and righteousness from that time and forevermore. The zeal of the LORD of Hosts will accomplish this.

passages.context_html:
The darkness at the end of chapter 8 gives way to a promise of light. Zebulun and Naphtali, lands that had known humiliation, will receive honor. The change reaches beyond private relief: the nation grows, joy returns, and the burden of oppression is broken.

The reference to the day of Midian recalls God’s deliverance through Gideon in Judges 6–7. Isaiah uses that remembered rescue to describe the defeat of an oppressor. Boots and bloodstained clothing become fuel for the fire; the equipment of war has no further use.

The reason for this hope is a child born and a son given. He will carry the responsibility of government, with names describing extraordinary wisdom, divine might, enduring fatherly care and peace. His rule on David’s throne will grow in justice and righteousness, without an end. The final assurance rests on the Lord’s determination to accomplish it.

The Hebrew פֶּלֶא, pele, pronounced PEH-leh, means a wonder. Brown–Driver–Briggs explains its use here as describing the promised king as a wonderful counselor. The title points to the exceptional character of His counsel, rather than simply giving Him an ordinary personal name.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley read this as a promise of Christ and His kingdom. They connect the light with His coming and the release from oppression with His victory over sin. Henry includes both the peace Christ gives His people now and the final peace of His completed kingdom.

There is also discussion of the setting in which Isaiah first spoke. The NABRE notes suggest that the description of the child may reflect a king’s coronation rather than the moment of his birth. This concerns the immediate royal setting of the words; the New Testament’s application to Jesus is explicit in Matthew 4.

Gill explains Everlasting Father in terms of Christ’s lasting care for His people and His relation to eternal life. In this reading the title does not mean that the Son is the same person as God the Father. The title describes the promised ruler’s character and relationship to those He governs.
passages.current_position_html: In [Who is The Angel of the Lord?](../studies/angel-of-the-lord.html), we connect Isaiah 9:6 with the Angel’s answer about His name in Judges 13:18. That study understands the Angel as the eternal Son appearing before He came as a man.

deeper_study.title: Who is The Angel of the Lord?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Matthew 4:12–17 directly identifies Jesus’ ministry in Galilee as the fulfillment of Isaiah’s promise of light in Zebulun and Naphtali. Matthew places the quotation beside Jesus’ announcement that the kingdom of heaven is near. The light arrives in a Person who calls people to repent.

The promise concerning David’s throne also appears in Gabriel’s announcement to Mary. Luke 1:30–33 says that her Son Jesus will receive David’s throne and reign forever. Together these passages identify the King and the lasting rule through which God carries His promise forward.

passages.title: Isaiah 9:8-12
passages.section_title: What happens when a warning is met with pride?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 The Lord has sent a message against Jacob, and it has fallen upon Israel. 9 All the people will know it— Ephraim and the dwellers of Samaria. With pride and arrogance of heart they will say: 10 “The bricks have fallen, but we will rebuild with finished stone; the sycamores have been felled, but we will replace them with cedars.” 11 The LORD has raised up the foes of Rezin against him and joined his enemies together. 12 Aram from the east and Philistia from the west have devoured Israel with open mouths. Despite all this, His anger is not turned away; His hand is still upraised.
paragraphs: 8 The Lord has sent a message against Jacob, and it has fallen upon Israel. 9 All the people will know it— Ephraim and the dwellers of Samaria. With pride and arrogance of heart they will say: 10 “The bricks have fallen, but we will rebuild with finished stone; the sycamores have been felled, but we will replace them with cedars.”

11 The LORD has raised up the foes of Rezin against him and joined his enemies together. 12 Aram from the east and Philistia from the west have devoured Israel with open mouths. Despite all this, His anger is not turned away; His hand is still upraised.

passages.context_html:
The focus turns to a message against Jacob and Israel, with Ephraim and Samaria named directly. These are the people of the northern kingdom. Their response to loss is proud confidence that they can replace what has fallen with something better.

The fallen bricks and felled sycamores become a boast about finished stone and cedars. The problem is the attitude expressed in the rebuilding: the people answer a warning with confidence in their own ability to recover, while refusing to face what has gone wrong before God.

The Lord raises up enemies, and Israel is attacked by Aram from the east and Philistia from the west. The closing line says His anger has not turned away and His hand remains upraised. This refrain returns in verses 17 and 21, holding the warnings together.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley understand the rebuilding speech as a refusal to be humbled. Wesley describes the speakers as expecting to repair their losses to their own advantage; Henry stresses the danger of remaining proud under circumstances meant to turn people back to God.

The NABRE notes likewise read these verses as part of a series of judgments against the northern kingdom, with continued rebellion explaining the repeated refrain. The central issue across these readings is the people’s response to God, rather than the choice of building materials.

passages.title: Isaiah 9:13-17
passages.section_title: Why are the leaders and the people both held responsible?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 But the people did not return to Him who struck them; they did not seek the LORD of Hosts. 14 So the LORD will cut off Israel’s head and tail, both palm branch and reed in a single day. 15 The head is the elder and honorable man, and the tail is the prophet who teaches lies. 16 For those who guide this people mislead them, and those they mislead are swallowed up. 17 Therefore the Lord takes no pleasure in their young men; He has no compassion on their fatherless and widows. For every one of them is godless and wicked, and every mouth speaks folly. Despite all this, His anger is not turned away; His hand is still upraised.
paragraphs: 13 But the people did not return to Him who struck them; they did not seek the LORD of Hosts. 14 So the LORD will cut off Israel’s head and tail, both palm branch and reed in a single day. 15 The head is the elder and honorable man, and the tail is the prophet who teaches lies.

16 For those who guide this people mislead them, and those they mislead are swallowed up. 17 Therefore the Lord takes no pleasure in their young men; He has no compassion on their fatherless and widows. For every one of them is godless and wicked, and every mouth speaks folly. Despite all this, His anger is not turned away; His hand is still upraised.

passages.context_html:
The people do not return to the One who struck them or seek the Lord. The warning therefore reaches the whole community, pictured as head and tail, palm branch and reed. Verse 15 explains the head as the elder and honored man, and the tail as the prophet who teaches lies.

Their guides lead them astray, and those who follow are swallowed up. Misleading leadership is a serious part of the failure, but the passage also describes corruption spreading through the people themselves.

The warning becomes especially severe when it names young men, fatherless children and widows. Even the groups normally associated with strength or particular need do not escape this judgment. The stated reason is the community’s pervasive godlessness, wrongdoing and corrupt speech. The refrain again announces that the Lord’s anger has not turned away.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley emphasize the harm done by leaders who make people comfortable in wrongdoing. They read the loss of both high and low as a warning that rank will provide no shelter when the nation is judged.

Wesley understands the sweeping description of wickedness as a statement about the body of the people, rather than a claim that God has no faithful person left anywhere. He also notes that fatherless children and widows are ordinarily special objects of God’s care. Their inclusion makes this particular warning more severe.

passages.god_plan_html:
The failure of these guides belongs to Scripture’s wider concern with people being lost under harmful leadership. John 10:1–18 presents a sharply different shepherd: Jesus knows His sheep, leads them, and lays down His life for them instead of abandoning them to danger.

This is a contrast between the passages, not a claim that John directly quotes Isaiah 9. It shows how God’s answer goes beyond exposing failed guides: the Son gathers His people and gives His own life for their salvation.

passages.title: Isaiah 9:18-21
passages.section_title: How does wickedness turn a people against itself?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 For wickedness burns like a fire that consumes the thorns and briers and kindles the forest thickets, which roll upward in billows of smoke. 19 By the wrath of the LORD of Hosts the land is scorched, and the people are fuel for the fire. No man even spares his brother. 20 They carve out what is on the right, but they are still hungry; they eat what is on the left, but they are still not satisfied. Each one devours the flesh of his own offspring. 21 Manasseh devours Ephraim, and Ephraim Manasseh; together they turn against Judah. Despite all this, His anger is not turned away; His hand is still upraised.
paragraphs: 18 For wickedness burns like a fire that consumes the thorns and briers and kindles the forest thickets, which roll upward in billows of smoke. 19 By the wrath of the LORD of Hosts the land is scorched, and the people are fuel for the fire. No man even spares his brother.

20 They carve out what is on the right, but they are still hungry; they eat what is on the left, but they are still not satisfied. Each one devours the flesh of his own offspring. 21 Manasseh devours Ephraim, and Ephraim Manasseh; together they turn against Judah. Despite all this, His anger is not turned away; His hand is still upraised.

passages.context_html:
Wickedness spreads like fire from thorns and briers into the forest. The picture then includes the wrath of the Lord: the land is scorched and the people themselves become fuel. Human wrongdoing and God’s judgment meet in the destruction described here.

The violence reaches the closest relationships. No one spares his brother; grabbing and eating bring no satisfaction, and the language even speaks of devouring one’s own offspring. The closing verse names Manasseh and Ephraim consuming one another, then joining against Judah.

This is a community destroying itself from within while also turning against its neighbor. The repeated words about the Lord’s anger leave the warning unresolved: the damage has not brought the people back to Him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Gill emphasize the fighting and plundering through which people consume their own relatives and neighbors. Gill connects the devouring language with the conflict between Manasseh and Ephraim in the final verse.

The NABRE notes also identify civil conflict in the northern kingdom as the setting of the warning. Across these readings, the fire and devouring images expose how wrongdoing destroys the bonds that should hold a people together.

passages.god_plan_html:
A related warning appears in Galatians 5:13–26. Paul warns believers that biting and devouring one another can end in mutual destruction. The verbal picture resembles Isaiah’s warning, though Paul does not identify it as a quotation.

Paul also sets out a different way of life: people called to freedom in Christ are to serve one another in love and walk by the Spirit. Love, patience, kindness and self-control replace the rivalries that consume a community. The connection carries the theme from the ruin caused by sin to the life God produces among His people.

passages.title: Isaiah 10:1-4
passages.section_title: Who will help those who use the law to oppress others?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Woe to those who enact unjust statutes and issue oppressive decrees, 2 to deprive the poor of fair treatment and withhold justice from the oppressed of My people, to make widows their prey and orphans their plunder. 3 What will you do on the day of reckoning when devastation comes from afar? To whom will you flee for help? Where will you leave your wealth? 4 Nothing will remain but to crouch among the captives or fall among the slain. Despite all this, His anger is not turned away; His hand is still upraised.
paragraphs: 1 Woe to those who enact unjust statutes and issue oppressive decrees, 2 to deprive the poor of fair treatment and withhold justice from the oppressed of My people, to make widows their prey and orphans their plunder.

3 What will you do on the day of reckoning when devastation comes from afar? To whom will you flee for help? Where will you leave your wealth? 4 Nothing will remain but to crouch among the captives or fall among the slain. Despite all this, His anger is not turned away; His hand is still upraised.

passages.context_html:
The warning continues the judgment announced in chapter 9, ending with the same refrain about the Lord’s anger and upraised hand. It now names people who write unjust laws and oppressive decrees.

Their decisions deny fair treatment to the poor and turn widows and orphans into people to be exploited. The problem is built into the way authority is exercised: those responsible for protecting others use their position to take from them.

The coming day of reckoning reverses their apparent security. They must answer where they will find help and leave their wealth when devastation arrives. Their power cannot save them from captivity or death, and the warning ends without announcing an end to God’s anger.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry applies the warning to both those who devise unjust decrees and the officials who put them into effect. Wesley similarly identifies rulers and judges who make unjust laws or hand down unjust decisions.

Their shared emphasis is that legal authority does not make injustice right. The people who deny others a fair hearing will themselves have to answer to God, and neither wealth nor office will provide an escape.

passages.title: Isaiah 10:5-19
passages.section_title: How can God use Assyria and still judge its king?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 Woe to Assyria, the rod of My anger; the staff in their hands is My wrath. 6 I will send him against a godless nation; I will dispatch him against a people destined for My rage, to take spoils and seize plunder, and to trample them down like clay in the streets. 7 But this is not his intention; this is not his plan. For it is in his heart to destroy and cut off many nations. 8 “Are not all my commanders kings?” he says. 9 “Is not Calno like Carchemish? Is not Hamath like Arpad? Is not Samaria like Damascus? 10 As my hand seized the idolatrous kingdoms whose images surpassed those of Jerusalem and Samaria, 11 and as I have done to Samaria and its idols, will I not also do to Jerusalem and her idols?” 12 So when the Lord has completed all His work against Mount Zion and Jerusalem, He will say, “I will punish the king of Assyria for the fruit of his arrogant heart and the proud look in his eyes. 13 For he says: ‘By the strength of my hand I have done this, and by my wisdom, for I am clever. I have removed the boundaries of nations and plundered their treasures; like a mighty one I subdued their rulers. 14 My hand reached as into a nest to seize the wealth of the nations. Like one gathering abandoned eggs, I gathered all the earth. No wing fluttered, no beak opened or chirped.’” 15 Does an axe raise itself above the one who swings it? Does a saw boast over him who saws with it? It would be like a rod waving the one who lifts it, or a staff lifting him who is not wood! 16 Therefore the Lord GOD of Hosts will send a wasting disease among Assyria’s stout warriors, and under his pomp will be kindled a fire like a burning flame. 17 And the Light of Israel will become a fire, and its Holy One a flame. In a single day it will burn and devour Assyria’s thorns and thistles. 18 The splendor of its forests and orchards, both soul and body, it will completely destroy, as a sickness consumes a man. 19 The remaining trees of its forests will be so few that a child could count them.

It would be like a rod waving the one who lifts it, or a staff lifting him who is not wood! 16 Therefore the Lord GOD of Hosts will send a wasting disease among Assyria’s stout warriors, and under his pomp will be kindled a fire like a burning flame. 17 And the Light of Israel will become a fire, and its Holy One a flame. In a single day it will burn and devour Assyria’s thorns and thistles. 18 The splendor of its forests and orchards, both soul and body, it will completely destroy, as a sickness consumes a man. 19 The remaining trees of its forests will be so few that a child could count them.

passages.context_html:
Assyria is called the rod of God’s anger, an instrument He uses in judgment. But verse 7 immediately distinguishes God’s purpose from the king’s intention. The king aims to destroy nations and enlarge his own power.

His boast treats conquered cities as proof that Jerusalem must fall as well. He speaks as though the Lord can be measured alongside the idols of defeated kingdoms. Then God declares that, after completing His work concerning Zion and Jerusalem, He will punish the king’s arrogance.

The axe and saw expose the mistake. A tool cannot rightly boast over the person using it, yet the king credits his own strength and wisdom with everything he has gained. The image does not remove his responsibility; his proud words and destructive purpose are precisely what bring judgment.

The army’s strength is then pictured as a forest that will burn away, leaving so few trees that a child could count them. The empire that appears unstoppable remains subject to the Lord.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley both distinguish God’s purpose in correcting His people from the conqueror’s ambition. They understand Assyria as serving a purpose it neither recognizes nor shares.

Gill likewise says that God’s use of the king does not mean the king consciously intends to obey Him. Across these readings, being used in God’s judgment gives the king no excuse for cruelty or pride. The Lord who governs his success can also bring him down.

passages.god_plan_html:
God’s purpose can move forward even through people whose intentions are evil. A major example appears in Acts 4:23–31: the believers name the rulers and peoples who gathered against Jesus, then acknowledge that the events of His death carried out what God had determined beforehand.

This is a shared biblical theme, rather than a claim that Assyria’s king represents Jesus or that Acts directly quotes this passage. In the account of Christ, human opposition becomes part of the saving work it seeks to stop. God’s rule over events does not turn the opponents’ hostility into faithful obedience.

passages.title: Isaiah 10:20-34
passages.section_title: Where will the survivors place their trust?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 20 On that day the remnant of Israel and the survivors of the house of Jacob will no longer depend on him who struck them, but they will truly rely on the LORD, the Holy One of Israel. 21 A remnant will return —a remnant of Jacob— to the Mighty God. 22 Though your people, O Israel, be like the sand of the sea, only a remnant will return. Destruction has been decreed, overflowing with righteousness. 23 For the Lord GOD of Hosts will carry out the destruction decreed upon the whole land. 24 Therefore this is what the Lord GOD of Hosts says: “O My people who dwell in Zion, do not fear Assyria, who strikes you with a rod and lifts his staff against you as the Egyptians did. 25 For in just a little while My fury against you will subside, and My anger will turn to their destruction.” 26 And the LORD of Hosts will brandish a whip against them, as when He struck Midian at the rock of Oreb. He will raise His staff over the sea, as He did in Egypt. 27 On that day the burden will be lifted from your shoulders, and the yoke from your neck. The yoke will be broken because your neck will be too large. 28 Assyria has entered Aiath and passed through Migron, storing their supplies at Michmash. 29 They have crossed at the ford: “We will spend the night at Geba.” Ramah trembles; Gibeah of Saul flees. 30 Cry aloud, O Daughter of Gallim! Listen, O Laishah! O wretched Anathoth! 31 Madmenah flees; the people of Gebim take refuge. 32 Yet today they will halt at Nob, shaking a fist at the mount of Daughter Zion, at the hill of Jerusalem. 33 Behold, the Lord GOD of Hosts will lop off the branches with terrifying power. The tall trees will be cut down, the lofty ones will be felled. 34 He will clear the forest thickets with an axe, and Lebanon will fall before the Mighty One.

He will raise His staff over the sea, as He did in Egypt. 27 On that day the burden will be lifted from your shoulders, and the yoke from your neck. The yoke will be broken because your neck will be too large.

28 Assyria has entered Aiath and passed through Migron, storing their supplies at Michmash. 29 They have crossed at the ford: “We will spend the night at Geba.” Ramah trembles; Gibeah of Saul flees. 30 Cry aloud, O Daughter of Gallim! Listen, O Laishah! O wretched Anathoth! 31 Madmenah flees; the people of Gebim take refuge. 32 Yet today they will halt at Nob, shaking a fist at the mount of Daughter Zion, at the hill of Jerusalem.

33 Behold, the Lord GOD of Hosts will lop off the branches with terrifying power. The tall trees will be cut down, the lofty ones will be felled. 34 He will clear the forest thickets with an axe, and Lebanon will fall before the Mighty One.

passages.context_html:
The survivors of Israel will no longer depend on the power that struck them. They will truly rely on the Lord, the Holy One of Israel. A remnant—a surviving part of the people—will return to the Mighty God, even though the nation had been as numerous as the sand of the sea.

The Lord tells His people in Zion not to fear Assyria. He recalls His earlier victories over Midian and Egypt and promises to remove the burden and yoke from His people. The same God who judged them also sets the limit on their oppression.

The final scene makes the threat feel close. An army passes through a series of towns until it shakes its fist at Jerusalem. Then the image changes to a forest being cut down: the Lord fells the lofty trees and clears the thickets.

The movement of the passage is from threatened destruction to a changed dependence. The survivors are not merely people who escaped a stronger army; they are people who turn back to the Lord.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley emphasize genuine reliance on God in place of reliance on the power that had oppressed the people. They connect the closing forest image with God bringing down the army threatening Jerusalem.

There are differences over how closely the named route describes a particular campaign. Henry and Wesley describe it as Sennacherib’s march. The NABRE notes read it as a poetic advance toward Jerusalem and distinguish it from the route of Sennacherib’s troops. Either way, the scene brings the threat to the city’s doorstep before the Lord intervenes.

Verse 27 also has a long history of different explanations. Henry and Wesley develop an anointing reading that points toward the Messiah. The BSB instead pictures a neck grown too large for its yoke. The Hebrew word שֶׁמֶן, shemen, pronounced SHEH-men, can mean fat or oil; Brown–Driver–Briggs places this verse under fatness and notes that the expression is difficult. These explanations differ over the picture, while the promise that the burden will be broken remains clear.

passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 9:27–28 directly quotes Isaiah’s words about the remnant and God carrying out His sentence. Paul uses them while discussing God’s mercy, the inclusion of Gentiles and the response of Israel. His argument goes on to contrast seeking righteousness by works with receiving it through faith.

Romans 11:1–12 makes clear that this does not mean God has simply rejected His people: Paul points to himself and to a remnant chosen by grace. He later warns Gentile believers against boasting over the branches and speaks of God’s power to graft them in again (Romans 11:17–32).

Isaiah’s surviving people therefore belong to a larger account of judgment and mercy that the New Testament itself develops. The response called for is faith and humility before God, rather than confidence in numbers, ancestry or superiority over others.

passages.title: Isaiah 11:1-16
passages.section_title: What kind of King can bring justice, peace and a people together?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then a shoot will spring up from the stump of Jesse, and a Branch from his roots will bear fruit. 2 The Spirit of the LORD will rest on Him— the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and strength, the Spirit of knowledge and fear of the LORD. 3 And He will delight in the fear of the LORD. He will not judge by what His eyes see, and He will not decide by what His ears hear, 4 but with righteousness He will judge the poor, and with equity He will decide for the lowly of the earth. He will strike the earth with the rod of His mouth and slay the wicked with the breath of His lips. 5 Righteousness will be the belt around His hips, and faithfulness the sash around His waist. 6 The wolf will live with the lamb, and the leopard will lie down with the goat; the calf and young lion and fatling will be together, and a little child will lead them. 7 The cow will graze with the bear, their young will lie down together, and the lion will eat straw like the ox. 8 The infant will play by the cobra’s den, and the toddler will reach into the viper’s nest. 9 They will neither harm nor destroy on all My holy mountain, for the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the sea is full of water. 10 On that day the Root of Jesse will stand as a banner for the peoples. The nations will seek Him, and His place of rest will be glorious. 11 On that day the Lord will extend His hand a second time to recover the remnant of His people from Assyria, from Egypt, from Pathros, from Cush, from Elam, from Shinar, from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea. 12 He will raise a banner for the nations and gather the exiles of Israel; He will collect the scattered of Judah from the four corners of the earth. 13 Then the jealousy of Ephraim will depart, and the adversaries of Judah will be cut off. Ephraim will no longer envy Judah, nor will Judah harass Ephraim. 14 They will swoop down on the slopes of the Philistines to the west; together they will plunder the sons of the east.
