He will split it into seven streams for men to cross with dry sandals. 16 There will be a highway for the remnant of His people who remain from Assyria, as there was for Israel when they came up from the land of Egypt.

passages.context_html:
Chapter 10 ended with lofty trees being cut down. Now a new shoot grows from Jesse’s stump. Jesse was David’s father, so the picture returns to the family from which David’s kingship began. Where the previous scene showed proud power brought low, this one presents new life and a different kind of ruler.

The Hebrew word for Branch here is נֵצֶר, netser, pronounced NAY-tser. Brown–Driver–Briggs explains it as a sprout or shoot. The image is of life growing from roots that remain, rather than another imposing tree already standing at full height.

The Spirit of the Lord rests on this ruler, giving wisdom, understanding, counsel, strength, knowledge and reverence for God. He judges fairly for the poor and lowly instead of deciding by appearances or rumors. His word has power to carry out judgment; righteousness and faithfulness belong to the way He rules.

The peace is pictured through animals and children living without danger from one another. The explanation reaches beyond the animals: the earth will be full of the knowledge of the Lord. The Root of Jesse stands as a banner whom the nations seek.

The Lord also gathers the scattered of Israel and Judah. Their jealousy ends, and they stand together against their enemies. Obstacles to their return are removed, with a highway compared to Israel’s way out of Egypt. The chapter holds together righteous rule, the end of destructive hostility, and the gathering of God’s people.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry, Wesley and Gill identify the promised ruler as Christ. They connect the shoot from Jesse with the house of David brought low and renewed through Him. The NABRE notes likewise describe the hope for a new Davidic king who fulfills the ideals the historical kings failed to embody.

Readers differ over the animals living in peace. Gill understands them as pictures of people changed by grace: former persecutors become gentle toward those they once harmed. Henry also emphasizes changed human character while looking toward a fuller peace still to come. Irenaeus, in Against Heresies 5.33.4, accepts the connection with changed people but also expects the named animals themselves to live peacefully in a restored creation.

The gathering and victories also receive different explanations. Wesley reads the conquest language in terms of the Messiah’s spiritual victory through the spread of the gospel. The NABRE notes emphasize God restoring the scattered people to their land and ending the hostility between Israel and Judah. These readings place different emphasis on how the promised restoration takes shape; they agree that the passage looks toward God overcoming division and opposition.

passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 15:7–13 directly quotes Isaiah 11:10 about the Root of Jesse ruling the nations and becoming their hope. Paul uses the promise to explain why Jewish and Gentile believers should welcome one another: Christ confirms God’s promises and brings the nations into praise for His mercy.

The ruler’s powerful word also finds a close New Testament echo in 2 Thessalonians 2:8, where the Lord Jesus destroys the lawless one with the breath of His mouth. The promised King is not powerless before the wickedness He judges.

The peace of creation belongs beside the wider hope described in Romans 8:18–25: creation waits to be freed from decay as God brings His children into glory. Paul does not directly quote Isaiah’s animals there, but both passages place God’s saving purpose beyond private relief, reaching toward a creation freed from destruction.

passages.title: Isaiah 12:1-6
passages.section_title: What do God’s people sing when His anger gives way to comfort?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 In that day you will say: “O LORD, I will praise You. Although You were angry with me, Your anger has turned away, and You have comforted me. 2 Surely God is my salvation; I will trust and not be afraid. For the LORD GOD is my strength and my song, and He also has become my salvation.” 3 With joy you will draw water from the springs of salvation, 4 and on that day you will say: “Give praise to the LORD; proclaim His name! Make His works known among the peoples; declare that His name is exalted. 5 Sing to the LORD, for He has done glorious things. Let this be known in all the earth. 6 Cry out and sing, O citizen of Zion, for great among you is the Holy One of Israel.”
paragraphs: 1 In that day you will say: “O LORD, I will praise You. Although You were angry with me, Your anger has turned away, and You have comforted me. 2 Surely God is my salvation; I will trust and not be afraid. For the LORD GOD is my strength and my song, and He also has become my salvation.” 3 With joy you will draw water from the springs of salvation,

4 and on that day you will say: “Give praise to the LORD; proclaim His name! Make His works known among the peoples; declare that His name is exalted. 5 Sing to the LORD, for He has done glorious things. Let this be known in all the earth. 6 Cry out and sing, O citizen of Zion, for great among you is the Holy One of Israel.”

passages.context_html:
This short song follows the promise of gathering and deliverance in chapter 11. The singer praises the Lord because His anger has turned away and He has brought comfort. Fear gives way to trust in God as salvation.

The words about the Lord being strength, song and salvation recall Israel’s song after the sea crossing in Exodus 15:1–3. Once again, rescue leads to praise of the One who accomplished it.

The picture of drawing water from the springs of salvation expresses joyful refreshment from God. The song then opens outward: His works are to be made known among the peoples and throughout the earth. Zion’s joy rests on the presence of the Holy One of Israel among His people.

The movement is from receiving comfort to making God known. The people do more than celebrate the end of danger; they call others to recognize the Lord’s greatness.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley reads the song in connection with Israel’s restoration and the gathering of Gentiles. He stresses that the salvation comes from God’s power and explains the water as God’s grace and comfort refreshing thirsty souls.

Gill similarly connects it with salvation through Christ and notices its links with the song after the Red Sea. He reads the call to make God’s works known as including the announcement of Christ’s saving work among the nations. Both readings see received salvation becoming thankful worship and public witness.

passages.god_plan_html:
The picture of God giving life through water continues in John 7:37–39. Jesus invites the thirsty to come to Him and drink, and John explains that He is speaking about the Spirit whom believers will receive. This is a related biblical picture, rather than a claim that John identifies Isaiah 12 as his sole source.

Revelation 7:9–17 brings the themes of this song together in a larger scene: a multitude from every nation praises God and the Lamb for salvation, and the Lamb leads them to springs of living water. Isaiah’s call for God’s saving works to be known throughout the earth belongs within that wider hope of people gathered into His presence and praise.

passages.title: Isaiah 13:1-22
passages.section_title: What happens when Babylon’s greatness meets the Lord’s judgment?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 This is the burden against Babylon that Isaiah son of Amoz received: 2 Raise a banner on a barren hilltop; call aloud to them. Wave your hand, that they may enter the gates of the nobles. 3 I have commanded My sanctified ones; I have even summoned My warriors to execute My wrath and exult in My triumph. 4 Listen, a tumult on the mountains, like that of a great multitude! Listen, an uproar among the kingdoms, like nations gathered together! The LORD of Hosts is mobilizing an army for war. 5 They are coming from faraway lands, from the ends of the heavens— the LORD and the weapons of His wrath— to destroy the whole country. 6 Wail, for the Day of the LORD is near; it will come as destruction from the Almighty. 7 Therefore all hands will fall limp, and every man’s heart will melt. 8 Terror, pain, and anguish will seize them; they will writhe like a woman in labor. They will look at one another, their faces flushed with fear. 9 Behold, the Day of the LORD is coming— cruel, with fury and burning anger— to make the earth a desolation and to destroy the sinners within it. 10 For the stars of heaven and their constellations will not give their light. The rising sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light. 11 I will punish the world for its evil and the wicked for their iniquity. I will end the haughtiness of the arrogant and lay low the pride of the ruthless. 12 I will make man scarcer than pure gold, and mankind rarer than the gold of Ophir. 13 Therefore I will make the heavens tremble, and the earth will be shaken from its place at the wrath of the LORD of Hosts on the day of His burning anger. 14 Like a hunted gazelle, like a sheep without a shepherd, each will return to his own people, each will flee to his native land. 15 Whoever is caught will be stabbed, and whoever is captured will die by the sword. 16 Their infants will be dashed to pieces before their eyes, their houses will be looted, and their wives will be ravished. 17 Behold, I will stir up against them the Medes, who have no regard for silver and no desire for gold. 18 Their bows will dash young men to pieces; they will have no mercy on the fruit of the womb; they will not look with pity on the children. 19 And Babylon, the jewel of the kingdoms, the glory of the pride of the Chaldeans, will be overthrown by God like Sodom and Gomorrah. 20 She will never be inhabited or settled from generation to generation; no nomad will pitch his tent there, no shepherd will rest his flock there. 21 But desert creatures will lie down there, and howling creatures will fill her houses. Ostriches will dwell there, and wild goats will leap about. 22 Hyenas will howl in her fortresses and jackals in her luxurious palaces. Babylon’s time is at hand, and her days will not be prolonged.

Ostriches will dwell there, and wild goats will leap about. 22 Hyenas will howl in her fortresses and jackals in her luxurious palaces. Babylon’s time is at hand, and her days will not be prolonged.

passages.context_html:
This chapter begins a series of messages concerning other nations. The first is identified as a burden against Babylon received by Isaiah son of Amoz. An army gathers at the Lord’s command, and the Day of the Lord is announced as a time of terror and destruction.

The language reaches from trembling hearts to darkened stars, sun and moon. God declares that He will punish evil, end arrogance and bring down the ruthless. What had seemed secure becomes a place from which people try to flee.

Verse 17 names the Medes as attackers. Wealth will not secure safety, and the description of the assault includes the killing of children and sexual violence. These are part of the horror of the announced judgment, not scenes of a clean or painless transfer of power.

The closing picture reverses Babylon’s splendor. The jewel of kingdoms becomes like Sodom and Gomorrah, with deserted houses and palaces occupied by wild creatures. Human pride cannot preserve what the Lord has marked for destruction.

For the historical background, Cyrus captured Babylon in 539 BC. The Metropolitan Museum’s account of the Cyrus Cylinder describes the capture and the establishment of Persian rule. The cylinder also records building work in Babylon, so the capture of the city and its complete desolation should not be treated as the same event without further explanation.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry, Wesley and Gill connect the chapter with Babylon’s defeat by the Medes and Persians. They understand the darkened heavens as prophetic pictures of overwhelming disaster. Gill explains the final desolation as something completed over time rather than all occurring at the moment of capture.

A future reading places greater weight on the worldwide judgment and permanent desolation. In discussing Revelation 18, Walvoord presents the reading that Babylon must be rebuilt and finally destroyed at Christ’s return, and finds that explanation preferable in several respects. He also acknowledges readings in which Babylon represents a wider political and religious power. These are differences among interpreters, rather than a single official position shared by all Christians.

passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus uses Isaiah’s language about the darkened sun and moon when speaking about the coming of the Son of Man (Matthew 24:29–31; Mark 13:24–27). The New Testament carries this language of judgment into its account of His coming and the gathering of His people.

Revelation 18:1–8, 20–24 also takes up Babylon’s fall, its desolation and its connection with the blood of God’s people. God calls His people away from sharing in its sins and judges the power that has enriched itself through evil.

These connections show that Babylon’s judgment belongs to Scripture’s larger account of God ending proud, destructive rule. The New Testament use of the images does not, by itself, settle every question about the timing or location of Isaiah’s fulfillment.

passages.title: Isaiah 14:1-2
passages.section_title: What does Babylon’s fall mean for the people it oppressed?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 For the LORD will have compassion on Jacob; once again He will choose Israel and settle them in their own land. The foreigner will join them and unite with the house of Jacob. 2 The nations will escort Israel and bring it to its homeland. Then the house of Israel will possess the nations as menservants and maidservants in the LORD’s land. They will make captives of their captors and rule over their oppressors.
paragraphs: 1 For the LORD will have compassion on Jacob; once again He will choose Israel and settle them in their own land. The foreigner will join them and unite with the house of Jacob. 2 The nations will escort Israel and bring it to its homeland. Then the house of Israel will possess the nations as menservants and maidservants in the LORD’s land. They will make captives of their captors and rule over their oppressors.

passages.context_html:
The warning against Babylon is followed by a promise of compassion for Jacob. The Lord will choose Israel again and settle the people in their own land. Foreigners will join them, and the nations will help bring them home.

The reversal includes hard language about service and captivity: Israel will possess servants and make captives of those who had held them captive. The focus is the overturning of the relationship between an oppressed people and their oppressors.

These verses introduce the rest from pain and forced labor described in verse 3. Babylon’s loss of power means more than the fall of a ruler; it opens the way for the people he oppressed to return.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Gill understands the first setting as Israel’s return from captivity, with foreigners joining the restored community. He also sees a wider application to Gentiles joining believing Jews in the people gathered through the gospel.

Wesley likewise distinguishes a historical reversal from a fuller spiritual application in the gospel’s spread. Henry emphasizes God’s mercy in restoring His people and urges the church to receive those whom God receives. These applications extend the passage toward the gathered people of God; they do not all work out the details of the reversal in the same way.

passages.title: Isaiah 14:3-23
passages.section_title: How far can a proud ruler fall?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 3 On the day that the LORD gives you rest from your pain and torment, and from the hard labor into which you were forced, 4 you will sing this song of contempt against the king of Babylon: How the oppressor has ceased, and how his fury has ended! 5 The LORD has broken the staff of the wicked, the scepter of the rulers. 6 It struck the peoples in anger with unceasing blows; it subdued the nations in rage with relentless persecution. 7 All the earth is at peace and at rest; they break out in song. 8 Even the cypresses and cedars of Lebanon exult over you: “Since you have been laid low, no woodcutter comes against us.” 9 Sheol beneath is eager to meet you upon your arrival. It stirs the spirits of the dead to greet you— all the rulers of the earth. It makes all the kings of the nations rise from their thrones. 10 They will all respond to you, saying, “You too have become weak, as we are; you have become like us!” 11 Your pomp has been brought down to Sheol, along with the music of your harps. Maggots are your bed and worms your blanket. 12 How you have fallen from heaven, O day star, son of the dawn! You have been cut down to the ground, O destroyer of nations. 13 You said in your heart: “I will ascend to the heavens; I will raise my throne above the stars of God. I will sit on the mount of assembly, in the far reaches of the north. 14 I will ascend above the tops of the clouds; I will make myself like the Most High.” 15 But you will be brought down to Sheol, to the lowest depths of the Pit. 16 Those who see you will stare; they will ponder your fate: “Is this the man who shook the earth and made the kingdoms tremble, 17 who turned the world into a desert and destroyed its cities, who refused to let the captives return to their homes?” 18 All the kings of the nations lie in state, each in his own tomb. 19 But you are cast out of your grave like a rejected branch, covered by those slain with the sword, and dumped into a rocky pit like a carcass trampled underfoot. 20 You will not join them in burial, since you have destroyed your land and slaughtered your own people. The offspring of the wicked will never again be mentioned. 21 Prepare a place to slaughter his sons for the iniquities of their forefathers. They will never rise up to possess a land or cover the earth with their cities. 22 “I will rise up against them,” declares the LORD of Hosts. “I will cut off from Babylon her name and her remnant, her offspring and her posterity,” declares the LORD. 23 “I will make her a place for owls and for swamplands; I will sweep her away with the broom of destruction,” declares the LORD of Hosts.

22 “I will rise up against them,” declares the LORD of Hosts. “I will cut off from Babylon her name and her remnant, her offspring and her posterity,” declares the LORD. 23 “I will make her a place for owls and for swamplands; I will sweep her away with the broom of destruction,” declares the LORD of Hosts.

passages.context_html:
The passage identifies itself as a song of contempt against the king of Babylon, to be sung when the Lord gives His people rest from forced labor. The oppressor’s staff is broken, the earth rests, and even the trees rejoice that he can no longer cut them down.

The scene then moves to Sheol, the realm of the dead. Former rulers greet the arriving king with the discovery that he is now as weak as they are. His royal display has become a bed of maggots and a blanket of worms.

The fallen king is addressed as the day star, son of the dawn. The Hebrew הֵילֵל, helel, pronounced hay-LALE, is explained by Brown–Driver–Briggs as a shining one or morning star, used here as a title for Babylon’s king. The picture contrasts his brilliant height with his collapse.

His repeated plans to ascend end with being brought down to the Pit. Those who see him ask whether this is the man who shook kingdoms and refused to release his captives. Even the honor of a royal burial is withheld.

The judgment reaches his dynasty and Babylon itself. The Lord declares that He will cut off its name and descendants and sweep it away. The end of this ruler’s power is presented as the Lord’s action, not merely a change in political fortune.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill read the morning-star language as a picture of the king of Babylon falling from royal glory. Gill explicitly distinguishes that immediate reading from an account of Satan’s original fall, though he allows a connection with it.

Another longstanding Christian reading sees Satan’s fall in these words. Origen, in On First Principles 1.5.5, uses Isaiah’s description together with Jesus’ words about Satan falling from heaven in Luke 10:18. His concern is that the devil fell from an earlier good condition, rather than being created evil.

The difference concerns how far the speech reaches beyond its named human ruler. The immediate setting is a taunt against Babylon’s king; the further application to Satan is an interpretation of the ruler’s pride and fall. The Hebrew title itself does not settle that further question.

passages.god_plan_html:
The proud ruler’s demand to rise like the Most High provides a contrast with the way of Christ in Philippians 2:5–11. Jesus takes the form of a servant and humbles Himself in obedience to death; God then exalts Him, and every knee will bow before Him.

This is a contrast between the passages, rather than a claim that Paul directly quotes Isaiah 14. Scripture’s larger account of rightful rule centers on the obedient Son, whose exaltation brings glory to the Father. The proud ruler who destroys others cannot keep the height he claims for himself.

passages.title: Isaiah 14:24-27
passages.section_title: Who can overturn what the Lord has purposed?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 24 The LORD of Hosts has sworn: “Surely, as I have planned, so will it be; as I have purposed, so will it stand. 25 I will break Assyria in My land; I will trample him on My mountain. His yoke will be taken off My people, and his burden removed from their shoulders.” 26 This is the plan devised for the whole earth, and this is the hand stretched out over all the nations. 27 The LORD of Hosts has purposed, and who can thwart Him? His hand is outstretched, so who can turn it back?
paragraphs: 24 The LORD of Hosts has sworn: “Surely, as I have planned, so will it be; as I have purposed, so will it stand. 25 I will break Assyria in My land; I will trample him on My mountain. His yoke will be taken off My people, and his burden removed from their shoulders.” 26 This is the plan devised for the whole earth, and this is the hand stretched out over all the nations. 27 The LORD of Hosts has purposed, and who can thwart Him? His hand is outstretched, so who can turn it back?

passages.context_html:
The focus shifts to Assyria. The Lord swears that what He has planned will stand: He will break Assyria in His land and remove the burden from His people’s shoulders.

The language recalls chapter 10, where the Lord uses the Assyrian king and then judges his arrogance. The empire is powerful, but its power does not give it control over God’s purpose.

The closing questions widen the view to the earth and the nations. If the Lord has purposed it and stretched out His hand, who can turn Him back? The assurance concerns His declared action, rather than human confidence in what an empire can accomplish.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads this as comfort for God’s people and a warning to those who make themselves a burden upon them. Wesley connects the Assyrian defeat with assurance that the judgment on Babylon will also stand.

Gill also distinguishes the Assyrian warning from the preceding Babylon oracle, connecting it with the threat described earlier in Isaiah. Their shared emphasis is that the Lord’s purpose is secure against the power of those He judges.

passages.god_plan_html:
The certainty of God’s purpose appears in a fuller account of His saving work in Ephesians 1:7–14. Paul describes forgiveness through Christ’s blood and God’s plan to bring all things in heaven and on earth together in Him.

Isaiah’s assurance about Assyria is not a prediction of every detail Paul later explains. The shared theme is that the purpose belongs to God and does not depend on the strength of a human ruler. Ephesians shows that purpose reaching its center in Christ and the inheritance God promises His people.

passages.title: Isaiah 14:28-32
passages.section_title: Why should Philistia hold back its celebration?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 28 In the year that King Ahaz died, this burden was received: 29 Do not rejoice, all you Philistines, that the rod that struck you is broken. For a viper will spring from the root of the snake, and a flying serpent from its egg. 30 Then the firstborn of the poor will find pasture, and the needy will lie down in safety, but I will kill your root by famine, and your remnant will be slain. 31 Wail, O gate! Cry out, O city! Melt away, all you Philistines! For a cloud of smoke comes from the north, and there are no stragglers in its ranks. 32 What answer will be given to the envoys of that nation? “The LORD has founded Zion, where His afflicted people will find refuge.”
paragraphs: 28 In the year that King Ahaz died, this burden was received: 29 Do not rejoice, all you Philistines, that the rod that struck you is broken. For a viper will spring from the root of the snake, and a flying serpent from its egg. 30 Then the firstborn of the poor will find pasture, and the needy will lie down in safety, but I will kill your root by famine, and your remnant will be slain.

31 Wail, O gate! Cry out, O city! Melt away, all you Philistines! For a cloud of smoke comes from the north, and there are no stragglers in its ranks. 32 What answer will be given to the envoys of that nation? “The LORD has founded Zion, where His afflicted people will find refuge.”

passages.context_html:
This message is dated to the year King Ahaz died. Philistia is warned not to celebrate the breaking of the rod that struck it. The succession of snake, viper and flying serpent pictures a threat becoming more dangerous.

The contrast is between refuge for the needy and famine and destruction for Philistia. Smoke approaches from the north, with no stragglers in the ranks. What looked like a reason for celebration is followed by a call to wail.

The closing answer to the envoys centers on the Lord’s founding of Zion. His afflicted people find refuge there. The message directs attention away from a change of ruler as a guarantee of safety and toward what the Lord has established.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry connects the stronger threat with Hezekiah succeeding rulers under whom the Philistines had gained confidence. Wesley discusses several possible identities for the broken rod and favors the weakened royal line of Judah, followed by Hezekiah’s renewed power.

Gill also discusses both Judean and Assyrian identifications, and connects the final northern threat with Babylon. These differences matter when identifying each image with a particular ruler; the commentators nevertheless agree on the warning against premature confidence and the closing promise of refuge for God’s people.

passages.title: Isaiah 15:1-9
passages.section_title: Why does the prophet grieve over Moab’s ruin?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 This is the burden against Moab: Ar in Moab is ruined, destroyed in a night! Kir in Moab is devastated, destroyed in a night! 2 Dibon goes up to its temple to weep at its high places. Moab wails over Nebo, as well as over Medeba. Every head is shaved, every beard is cut off. 3 In its streets they wear sackcloth; on the rooftops and in the public squares they all wail, falling down weeping. 4 Heshbon and Elealeh cry out; their voices are heard as far as Jahaz. Therefore the soldiers of Moab cry out; their souls tremble within. 5 My heart cries out over Moab; her fugitives flee as far as Zoar, as far as Eglath-shelishiyah. With weeping they ascend the slope of Luhith; they lament their destruction on the road to Horonaim. 6 The waters of Nimrim are dried up, and the grass is withered; the vegetation is gone, and the greenery is no more. 7 So they carry their wealth and belongings over the Brook of the Willows. 8 For their outcry echoes to the border of Moab. Their wailing reaches Eglaim; it is heard in Beer-elim. 9 The waters of Dimon are full of blood, but I will bring more upon Dimon— a lion upon the fugitives of Moab and upon the remnant of the land.

Moab wails over Nebo, as well as over Medeba. Every head is shaved, every beard is cut off. 3 In its streets they wear sackcloth; on the rooftops and in the public squares they all wail, falling down weeping. 4 Heshbon and Elealeh cry out; their voices are heard as far as Jahaz. Therefore the soldiers of Moab cry out; their souls tremble within.

5 My heart cries out over Moab; her fugitives flee as far as Zoar, as far as Eglath-shelishiyah. With weeping they ascend the slope of Luhith; they lament their destruction on the road to Horonaim. 6 The waters of Nimrim are dried up, and the grass is withered; the vegetation is gone, and the greenery is no more. 7 So they carry their wealth and belongings over the Brook of the Willows. 8 For their outcry echoes to the border of Moab. Their wailing reaches Eglaim; it is heard in Beer-elim. 9 The waters of Dimon are full of blood, but I will bring more upon Dimon— a lion upon the fugitives of Moab and upon the remnant of the land.

passages.context_html:
This message concerns Moab, and it continues into chapter 16. The opening announces the sudden ruin of Ar and Kir. The sound that follows is mourning: people weep at their places of worship, wear sackcloth in the streets and cry out from rooftops and public squares.

The shaved heads and cut beards belong to the scene of grief, as the NABRE notes explain. Even the soldiers tremble. The repeated place names let the reader hear distress spreading across the country.

The speaker’s own heart cries out over Moab while fugitives escape with their belongings. Water dries up, vegetation disappears, and wealth must be carried away. The disaster affects the homes, food and security on which ordinary life depends.

The closing warning announces still more danger for those who escape. Yet the passage does not celebrate their suffering: the voice that announces the judgment also laments what is happening to them.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry understands the grief as compassion for people who, though enemies of Israel, remain fellow human beings. Gill likewise reads verse 5 as the prophet pitying Moab, while noting that other interpreters understand it as the Moabites voicing their own sorrow.

The final lion is read in more than one way. Wesley understands actual lions finding those who escaped the invading army. Gill includes that reading but also reports the interpretation of a further conquering king. The shared warning is that fleeing the first disaster will not necessarily bring safety.

passages.title: Isaiah 16:1-14
passages.section_title: Can proud Moab find refuge under a just ruler?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Send the tribute lambs to the ruler of the land, from Sela in the desert to the mount of Daughter Zion. 2 Like fluttering birds pushed out of the nest, so are the daughters of Moab at the fords of the Arnon: 3 “Give us counsel; render a decision. Shelter us at noonday with shade as dark as night. Hide the refugees; do not betray the one who flees. 4 Let my fugitives stay with you; be a refuge for Moab from the destroyer.” When the oppressor has gone, destruction has ceased, and the oppressors have vanished from the land, 5 in loving devotion a throne will be established in the tent of David. A judge seeking justice and hastening righteousness will sit on it in faithfulness. 6 We have heard of Moab’s pomposity, his exceeding pride and conceit, his overflowing arrogance. But his boasting is empty. 7 Therefore let Moab wail; let them wail together for Moab. Moan for the raisin cakes of Kir-hareseth, you who are utterly stricken. 8 For the fields of Heshbon have withered, along with the grapevines of Sibmah. The rulers of the nations have trampled its choicest vines, which had reached as far as Jazer and spread toward the desert. Their shoots had spread out and passed over the sea. 9 So I weep with Jazer for the vines of Sibmah; I drench Heshbon and Elealeh with my tears. Triumphant shouts have fallen silent over your summer fruit and your harvest. 10 Joy and gladness are removed from the orchard; no one sings or shouts in the vineyards. No one tramples the grapes in the winepresses; I have put an end to the cheering. 11 Therefore my heart laments for Moab like a harp, my inmost being for Kir-heres. 12 When Moab appears on the high place, when he wearies himself and enters his sanctuary to pray, it will do him no good. 13 This is the message that the LORD spoke earlier concerning Moab. 14 And now the LORD says, “In three years, as a hired worker counts the years, Moab’s splendor will become an object of contempt, with all her many people. And those who are left will be few and feeble.”

passages.context_html:
The message to Moab turns to tribute, counsel and refuge. Lambs are to be sent toward Zion, and the daughters of Moab are pictured as birds pushed from their nest. The request is urgent: hide the refugees and do not betray the person who flees.

In the BSB, the appeal in verse 4 asks for refuge for Moab. It is followed by the prospect of oppression ending and a throne established in loving devotion in David’s house. The ruler is marked by faithfulness, justice and readiness to do what is right.

Then Moab’s excessive pride and empty boasting come back into view. Vineyards are trampled, harvest celebrations fall silent, and the speaker weeps and laments for the devastated country. Turning wearily to its sanctuary does not bring Moab the help it seeks.

The final verses distinguish an earlier message from a fresh announcement: within three years, counted as carefully as a hired worker counts a term of work, Moab’s splendor will be brought low. Those who remain will be few and weak. The judgment has an announced limit in time, even though the passage does not name its starting year.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Readers differ over who is asking whom for shelter. The Cambridge commentary reads the speech as Moab appealing to Judah for protection. Wesley and Gill, following a different reading of verse 4, understand it as a call for Moab to shelter Israelite fugitives. The difference affects the direction of the appeal; both explanations center on protection for people driven from home.

The throne in David’s house is also read at more than one level. Henry and Gill connect it with Hezekiah, while seeing a greater fulfillment in Christ’s just rule. The Cambridge commentary recognizes the language of the promised king but reads its place in the speech as an appeal to the Davidic dynasty.

Henry reads the later mourning as real concern over a country’s desolation, alongside the warning that pride refuses needed counsel. The closing three-year limit is understood by Wesley and Gill as a definite period, though they discuss different possible historical settings rather than agreeing on one exact campaign.

passages.god_plan_html:
The promise of a faithful ruler in David’s house belongs to the wider hope taken up in Luke 1:30–33, where Gabriel announces that Jesus will receive David’s throne and reign forever. This connects the theme of righteous Davidic rule with Christ without claiming that Luke directly quotes Isaiah 16.

An earlier story also provides a useful parallel to Moab’s need for refuge. In Ruth 2:10–12, a Moabite woman who has joined Israel receives kindness and is described as taking refuge under the Lord’s wings. Ruth lived before Isaiah, so her story is an illustration of refuge, not a fulfillment of this prophecy.

Matthew 1:1–6 names Ruth in the family line leading to David and ultimately to Jesus. Scripture’s larger account therefore includes a woman from Moab receiving refuge and becoming part of the family through which the promised King comes.

passages.title: Isaiah 17:1-14
passages.section_title: What remains when strong cities and handmade gods fail?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 This is the burden against Damascus: “Behold, Damascus is no longer a city; it has become a heap of ruins. 2 The cities of Aroer are forsaken; they will be left to the flocks, which will lie down with no one to fear. 3 The fortress will disappear from Ephraim, and the sovereignty from Damascus. The remnant of Aram will be like the splendor of the Israelites,” declares the LORD of Hosts. 4 “In that day the splendor of Jacob will fade, and the fat of his body will waste away, 5 as the reaper gathers the standing grain and harvests the ears with his arm, as one gleans heads of grain in the Valley of Rephaim. 6 Yet gleanings will remain, like an olive tree that has been beaten— two or three berries atop the tree, four or five on its fruitful branches,” declares the LORD, the God of Israel. 7 In that day men will look to their Maker and turn their eyes to the Holy One of Israel. 8 They will not look to the altars they have fashioned with their hands or to the Asherahs and incense altars they have made with their fingers. 9 In that day their strong cities will be like forsaken thickets and summits, abandoned to the Israelites and to utter desolation. 10 For you have forgotten the God of your salvation and failed to remember the Rock of your refuge. Therefore, though you cultivate delightful plots and set out cuttings from exotic vines— 11 though on the day you plant you make them grow, and on that morning you help your seed sprout— yet the harvest will vanish on the day of disease and incurable pain. 12 Alas, the tumult of many peoples; they rage like the roaring seas and clamoring nations; they rumble like the crashing of mighty waters. 13 The nations rage like the rush of many waters. He rebukes them, and they flee far away, driven before the wind like chaff on the hills, like tumbleweeds before a gale. 14 In the evening, there is sudden terror! Before morning, they are no more! This is the portion of those who loot us and the lot of those who plunder us.

passages.context_html:
The message is headed against Damascus, but it also names Ephraim and Jacob. The connection recalls the alliance of Aram and Israel against Judah. Second Kings 16:5–9 records that alliance and the Assyrian king’s capture of Damascus after Ahaz appealed to him.

The fading glory of Jacob is pictured as a body wasting away and a field harvested until only gleanings remain. A few olives left on a tree provide a second picture of the small number who survive.

The passage then describes people looking to their Maker and the Holy One of Israel instead of the altars and objects they made with their own hands. Alongside that change comes the explanation for the disaster: they forgot the God of their salvation and the Rock of their refuge.

Careful planting cannot secure the hoped-for harvest. The final scene turns from cultivation to the roar of nations, like mighty waters. God rebukes them, and they are driven away as easily as chaff before the wind. Terror in the evening gives way to their disappearance before morning; this is the announced portion of those who plunder God’s people.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry, Wesley and Gill connect the opening warning with Assyrian conquest and understand the remaining olives as a small surviving part of the people. Wesley and Gill explicitly connect the threat against Damascus with the capture recorded in 2 Kings 16:9.

They read verses 7–8 as a genuine turning toward God and away from idols. Henry emphasizes a remnant awakened to return; Wesley describes sincere trust and worship. The loss of false security is understood as leading people back to their Maker.

There are differences over the planting image. Henry reads the foreign plants as a picture of imported idolatrous worship; Wesley emphasizes the valued plants people cultivate, only to lose the harvest. For the closing nations like waters, Henry and Gill connect God’s rebuke with the defeat of the Assyrian threat against Jerusalem.

passages.god_plan_html:
Turning from handmade gods to the living God remains a major theme in the New Testament. First Thessalonians 1:8–10 describes people turning from idols to serve the living and true God and to await His Son, Jesus, raised from the dead and rescuing them from the coming wrath.

This is a shared theme, not a claim that Paul directly quotes Isaiah 17. The New Testament account carries the movement beyond the collapse of false objects of trust: people are brought into service of the true God and hope in His risen Son.

passages.title: Isaiah 18:1-7
passages.section_title: What happens while the Lord quietly watches the nations?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Woe to the land of whirring wings, along the rivers of Cush, 2 which sends couriers by sea, in papyrus vessels on the waters. Go, swift messengers, to a people tall and smooth-skinned, to a people widely feared, to a powerful nation of strange speech, whose land is divided by rivers. 3 All you people of the world and dwellers of the earth, when a banner is raised on the mountains, you will see it; when a ram’s horn sounds, you will hear it. 4 For this is what the LORD has told me: “I will quietly look on from My dwelling place, like shimmering heat in the sunshine, like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest.” 5 For before the harvest, when the blossom is gone and the flower becomes a ripening grape, He will cut off the shoots with a pruning knife and remove and discard the branches. 6 They will all be left to the mountain birds of prey, and to the beasts of the land. The birds will feed on them in summer, and all the wild animals in winter. 7 At that time gifts will be brought to the LORD of Hosts— from a people tall and smooth-skinned, from a people widely feared, from a powerful nation of strange speech, whose land is divided by rivers— to Mount Zion, the place of the Name of the LORD of Hosts.

Go, swift messengers, to a people tall and smooth-skinned, to a people widely feared, to a powerful nation of strange speech, whose land is divided by rivers. 3 All you people of the world and dwellers of the earth, when a banner is raised on the mountains, you will see it; when a ram’s horn sounds, you will hear it.

4 For this is what the LORD has told me: “I will quietly look on from My dwelling place, like shimmering heat in the sunshine, like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest.” 5 For before the harvest, when the blossom is gone and the flower becomes a ripening grape, He will cut off the shoots with a pruning knife and remove and discard the branches. 6 They will all be left to the mountain birds of prey, and to the beasts of the land. The birds will feed on them in summer, and all the wild animals in winter.

7 At that time gifts will be brought to the LORD of Hosts— from a people tall and smooth-skinned, from a people widely feared, from a powerful nation of strange speech, whose land is divided by rivers— to Mount Zion, the place of the Name of the LORD of Hosts.

passages.context_html:
The chapter addresses a land associated with the rivers of Cush and couriers traveling in papyrus vessels. The NABRE notes locate the ancient kingdom in the Upper Nile region, centered in what is now Sudan. Its boundaries should not simply be equated with those of modern Ethiopia.

The messengers are directed to a people described as tall, smooth-skinned, widely feared and speaking a strange language. Then the address widens: all the world is to watch for a banner and listen for a ram’s horn.

The Lord says He will quietly look on from His dwelling place. His quietness does not mean events have escaped His notice. Before the harvest is gathered, He cuts the shoots and branches away; the scene ends with what has fallen left to birds and beasts.

The final verse returns to the description of the people from the opening. Gifts now come from them to the Lord at Mount Zion. The chapter moves from international activity and interrupted expectations to homage offered at the place of His name.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The precise political setting and some of the images have received different explanations. Wesley connects the couriers with attempts to build alliances and reads the cutting down as judgment on the people addressed. The NABRE notes understand the setting as a Cushite approach to Judah and regard the later destructive harvest as probably directed against Assyria.

The heat and dew in verse 4 are also understood differently. Henry sees timely comfort for God’s people, while Wesley sees the Lord withholding help from the threatened people. Gill discusses both comforting and judging readings, favoring the latter in this setting.

For the final gifts, Wesley and Gill see people turning to the Lord and offering themselves in worship. The different explanations of the preceding judgment do not erase the closing movement toward acknowledging Him.

passages.god_plan_html:
The movement of the nations toward God also appears in Psalm 68:31–35, which speaks of Egypt’s envoys and Cush stretching out her hands to God. The psalm calls the kingdoms of the earth to praise Him.

Acts 8:26–40 provides a concrete New Testament example of that wider movement: an Ethiopian court official returns from worshiping in Jerusalem, hears the good news about Jesus from Philip, and is baptized. Philip explains a different passage of Isaiah—the suffering servant passage—so Acts is not claiming to quote or directly fulfill Isaiah 18.

The connection is the wider gathering of people from the nations to the Lord. The final homage in Isaiah belongs alongside the gospel reaching a man whose journey of worship becomes a joyful response to Christ.

passages.title: Isaiah 19:1-15
passages.section_title: What can Egypt’s idols, river and advisers do when judgment comes?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 This is the burden against Egypt: Behold, the LORD rides on a swift cloud; He is coming to Egypt. The idols of Egypt will tremble before Him, and the hearts of the Egyptians will melt within them. 2 “So I will incite Egyptian against Egyptian; brother will fight against brother, neighbor against neighbor, city against city, and kingdom against kingdom. 3 Then the spirit of the Egyptians will be emptied out from among them, and I will frustrate their plans, so that they will resort to idols and spirits of the dead, to mediums and spiritists. 4 I will deliver the Egyptians into the hands of a harsh master, and a fierce king will rule over them,” declares the Lord GOD of Hosts. 5 The waters of the Nile will dry up, and the riverbed will be parched and empty. 6 The canals will stink; the streams of Egypt will trickle and dry up; the reeds and rushes will wither. 7 The bulrushes by the Nile, by the mouth of the river, and all the fields sown along the Nile, will wither, blow away, and be no more. 8 Then the fishermen will mourn, all who cast a hook into the Nile will lament, and those who spread nets on the waters will pine away. 9 The workers in flax will be dismayed, and the weavers of fine linen will turn pale. 10 The workers in cloth will be dejected, and all the hired workers will be sick at heart. 11 The princes of Zoan are mere fools; Pharaoh’s wise counselors give senseless advice. How can you say to Pharaoh, “I am one of the wise, a son of eastern kings”? 12 Where are your wise men now? Let them tell you and reveal what the LORD of Hosts has planned against Egypt. 13 The princes of Zoan have become fools; the princes of Memphis are deceived. The cornerstones of her tribes have led Egypt astray. 14 The LORD has poured into her a spirit of confusion. Egypt has been led astray in all she does, as a drunkard staggers through his own vomit. 15 There is nothing Egypt can do— head or tail, palm or reed.

passages.context_html:
The message against Egypt opens with the Lord riding on a swift cloud. Its idols tremble, and the people lose heart. The Lord announces conflict within the country, failed plans, resort to forbidden spiritual counsel, and rule by a harsh master.

The drying of the Nile reaches through the fields and working life of the land. Fishermen mourn, plants wither, and those who work in flax and cloth lose their livelihood. The passage makes the disruption visible through the people and occupations affected by it.

The warning then confronts Pharaoh’s counselors. Their claims to wisdom cannot reveal what the Lord has planned, and those who should guide Egypt instead lead it astray. Confusion is pictured as a drunkard staggering through his own vomit.

The closing line includes head and tail, palm and reed: Egypt is helpless across its ranks. The chapter has exposed the failure of its religious, material and political sources of confidence before turning to a different future in the following verses.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley read the civil conflict, harsh rule and failed counsel as the Lord’s judgment on Egypt’s false security. Both emphasize that celebrated human wisdom cannot protect a people whose plans stand against Him.

There is less agreement on the ruler in verse 4. Wesley identifies Psammetichus; Gill discusses that identification alongside other proposed rulers. The text itself leaves the harsh master unnamed, so the warning can be explained without treating one historical identification as certain.

Wesley and Gill also discuss whether the river language is a picture of lost power and trade or a description of the Nile’s waters failing. Both give weight to the physical effects described in the following verses.

passages.title: Isaiah 19:16-25
passages.section_title: How can Egypt and Assyria become a blessing alongside Israel?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 In that day the Egyptians will be like women. They will tremble with fear beneath the uplifted hand of the LORD of Hosts, when He brandishes it against them. 17 The land of Judah will bring terror to Egypt; whenever Judah is mentioned, Egypt will tremble over what the LORD of Hosts has planned against it. 18 In that day five cities in the land of Egypt will speak the language of Canaan and swear allegiance to the LORD of Hosts. One of them will be called the City of the Sun. 19 In that day there will be an altar to the LORD in the center of the land of Egypt, and a pillar to the LORD near her border. 20 It will be a sign and a witness to the LORD of Hosts in the land of Egypt. When they cry out to the LORD because of their oppressors, He will send them a savior and defender to rescue them. 21 The LORD will make Himself known to Egypt, and on that day Egypt will acknowledge the LORD. They will worship with sacrifices and offerings; they will make vows to the LORD and fulfill them. 22 And the LORD will strike Egypt with a plague; He will strike them but heal them. They will turn to the LORD, and He will hear their prayers and heal them. 23 In that day there will be a highway from Egypt to Assyria. The Assyrians will go to Egypt, and the Egyptians to Assyria. passages.context_html:
The threat against Egypt gives way to a striking promise. Fear of the Lord’s action is followed by cities speaking the language of Canaan and swearing allegiance to Him. An altar and a pillar become a sign and witness to the Lord within Egypt.

When the Egyptians cry out because of their oppressors, the Lord sends a savior and defender. He makes Himself known to them, they worship Him, and they fulfill their vows. The passage describes Him striking and healing: they turn to Him, He hears, and He heals.

The promise then reaches beyond Egypt. A highway links Egypt and Assyria, and the two peoples worship together. Israel joins them as a blessing upon the earth.

The final declaration gives each a place in that blessing. Egypt is called God’s people, Assyria His handiwork, and Israel His inheritance. Nations known in these chapters as threats and oppressors are now included in worship and favor from the Lord.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry, Wesley and Gill emphasize the gathering of Gentiles with Jews through the gospel. They read the altar and sacrifices as language for worship through Christ, including prayer and praise. In this reading, people formerly divided by hostility are united in serving God.

A future kingdom reading places more emphasis on these named nations in their lands. Walvoord, in The Nations in Prophecy, understands the later part of the chapter as reaching its ultimate fulfillment in Christ’s future reign, with Egypt, Assyria and Israel sharing in its blessing.

The readings differ over when and how the details take shape. Both recognize that the promise goes beyond Egypt merely surviving: the Egyptians know the Lord, turn to Him and join others in His worship.

passages.god_plan_html:
The promise that former enemies will worship together belongs to Scripture’s wider purpose of reconciliation. Ephesians 2:11–22 explains that Gentiles once far away are brought near through Christ’s blood. He makes peace and reconciles Jews and Gentiles to God in one body through the cross.

Paul does not directly quote Isaiah 19 here or explain the highway’s geography. He does explain the saving work through which divided peoples receive access to the Father by one Spirit and become members of God’s household.

The connection carries the hope beyond a political alliance: God brings people who were estranged into His presence together. Isaiah’s final blessing on Egypt, Assyria and Israel is an especially vivid expression of that wider biblical hope.

passages.title: Isaiah 20:1-6
passages.section_title: What does Isaiah’s unsettling sign expose about misplaced hope?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Before the year that the chief commander, sent by Sargon king of Assyria, came to Ashdod and attacked and captured it, 2 the LORD had already spoken through Isaiah son of Amoz, saying, “Go, remove the sackcloth from your waist and the sandals from your feet.” And Isaiah did so, walking around naked and barefoot. 3 Then the LORD said, “Just as My servant Isaiah has gone naked and barefoot for three years as a sign and omen against Egypt and Cush, 4 so the king of Assyria will lead away the captives of Egypt and the exiles of Cush, young and old alike, naked and barefoot, with bared buttocks—to Egypt’s shame. 5 Those who made Cush their hope and Egypt their boast will be dismayed and ashamed. 6 And on that day the dwellers of this coastland will say, ‘See what has happened to our source of hope, those to whom we fled for help and deliverance from the king of Assyria! How then can we escape?’”
paragraphs: 1 Before the year that the chief commander, sent by Sargon king of Assyria, came to Ashdod and attacked and captured it, 2 the LORD had already spoken through Isaiah son of Amoz, saying, “Go, remove the sackcloth from your waist and the sandals from your feet.” And Isaiah did so, walking around naked and barefoot. 3 Then the LORD said, “Just as My servant Isaiah has gone naked and barefoot for three years as a sign and omen against Egypt and Cush, 4 so the king of Assyria will lead away the captives of Egypt and the exiles of Cush, young and old alike, naked and barefoot, with bared buttocks—to Egypt’s shame.

5 Those who made Cush their hope and Egypt their boast will be dismayed and ashamed. 6 And on that day the dwellers of this coastland will say, ‘See what has happened to our source of hope, those to whom we fled for help and deliverance from the king of Assyria! How then can we escape?’”

passages.context_html:
The chapter connects Isaiah’s sign with the Assyrian capture of Ashdod by a commander sent by Sargon. The Lord had told Isaiah to remove his sackcloth and sandals, and Isaiah obeyed, walking naked and barefoot.

The Lord explains the sign in terms of Egypt and Cush. As Isaiah has gone exposed and barefoot for three years, Assyria will lead away their captives, young and old, in humiliating exposure. The description includes bared buttocks and Egypt’s shame.

The final verses address those who had made Cush their hope and Egypt their boast. The failure of the powers they trusted leaves them asking how they themselves can escape.

The sign therefore confronts more than Egypt’s coming humiliation. It makes the people watching reconsider the strength on which they have based their own safety.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley understand Isaiah’s exposure as going without his outer garment rather than complete nakedness. They read the action as a visible representation of the shame of captives. This explanation should not hide the severity of verse 4, which explicitly describes the prisoners’ uncovered bodies.

Gill discusses different ways of relating the three years to the sign and the coming judgment. The BSB attaches the period to Isaiah’s action. Across these readings, the main warning remains the same: Egypt and Cush cannot be a secure refuge if they themselves are being led into captivity.

passages.title: Isaiah 21:1-10
passages.section_title: What does the watchman announce about Babylon?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 This is the burden against the Desert by the Sea: Like whirlwinds sweeping through the Negev, an invader comes from the desert, from a land of terror. 2 A dire vision is declared to me: “The traitor still betrays, and the destroyer still destroys. Go up, O Elam! Lay siege, O Media! I will put an end to all her groaning.” 3 Therefore my body is filled with anguish. Pain grips me, like the pains of a woman in labor. I am bewildered to hear, I am dismayed to see. 4 My heart falters; fear makes me tremble. The twilight I desired has turned to horror. 5 They prepare a table, they lay out a carpet, they eat, they drink! Rise up, O princes, oil the shields! 6 For this is what the Lord says to me: “Go, post a lookout and have him report what he sees. 7 When he sees chariots with teams of horsemen, riders on donkeys, riders on camels, he must be alert, fully alert.” 8 Then the lookout shouted: “Day after day, my lord, I stand on the watchtower; night after night I stay at my post. 9 Look, here come the riders, horsemen in pairs.” And one answered, saying: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon! All the images of her gods lie shattered on the ground!” 10 O my people, crushed on the threshing floor, I tell you what I have heard from the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel.

Go up, O Elam! Lay siege, O Media! I will put an end to all her groaning.” 3 Therefore my body is filled with anguish. Pain grips me, like the pains of a woman in labor. I am bewildered to hear, I am dismayed to see. 4 My heart falters; fear makes me tremble. The twilight I desired has turned to horror. 5 They prepare a table, they lay out a carpet, they eat, they drink! Rise up, O princes, oil the shields!

6 For this is what the Lord says to me: “Go, post a lookout and have him report what he sees. 7 When he sees chariots with teams of horsemen, riders on donkeys, riders on camels, he must be alert, fully alert.” 8 Then the lookout shouted: “Day after day, my lord, I stand on the watchtower; night after night I stay at my post. 9 Look, here come the riders, horsemen in pairs.” And one answered, saying: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon! All the images of her gods lie shattered on the ground!” 10 O my people, crushed on the threshing floor, I tell you what I have heard from the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel.

passages.context_html:
The message opens with a desert storm and a distressing vision. Elam and Media are summoned to advance, while the speaker is seized by anguish and fear. The name of the city under judgment is withheld until the watchman’s report.

A scene of eating and drinking is interrupted by a call to the princes to rise and oil their shields. The Lord then tells the prophet to post a lookout. The repeated attention to watching, by day and night, prepares for the announcement that follows.

The riders arrive, and the report is unmistakable: Babylon has fallen, and the images of its gods lie shattered. The city’s religious objects cannot preserve its power.

The closing words address a people crushed on the threshing floor. The prophet assures them that the message comes from the Lord, the God of Israel. The news of Babylon’s fall is therefore also a message to people who have suffered under oppression.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry, Wesley and Gill connect the vision with Babylon’s defeat through the Medes and Persians. The NABRE notes also link the interrupted feast with Daniel 5.

The final threshing-floor image is understood differently. Henry and Gill apply it to God’s afflicted people, receiving assurance of deliverance. Wesley considers Babylon itself the people being threshed, while understanding the report as a message given for Israel’s benefit.

Henry and Gill also connect Babylon’s fall with the later Babylon of Revelation. This extends the passage’s significance beyond one empire without requiring every detail of the first vision to have the same setting as the later book.

passages.god_plan_html:
Revelation 18:2–8 takes up the announcement of Babylon’s fall. It describes a power marked by corrupt wealth and influence and calls God’s people away from sharing in its sins.

The connection places the watchman’s announcement within Scripture’s larger account of God judging the powers that oppress and corrupt. The same Lord who exposes the failure of Babylon’s idols also calls His people to faithfulness while they await His judgment.

passages.title: Isaiah 21:11-12
passages.section_title: What does the watchman mean by morning and night?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 This is the burden against Dumah: One calls to me from Seir, “Watchman, what is left of the night? Watchman, what is left of the night?” 12 The watchman replies, “Morning has come, but also the night. If you would inquire, then inquire. Come back yet again.”
paragraphs: 11 This is the burden against Dumah: One calls to me from Seir, “Watchman, what is left of the night? Watchman, what is left of the night?” 12 The watchman replies, “Morning has come, but also the night. If you would inquire, then inquire. Come back yet again.”

passages.context_html:
This brief message is headed against Dumah, and the caller speaks from Seir. The repeated question asks the watchman how much of the night remains. It sounds like a request for news or relief from a period of danger.

The answer gives no simple assurance that trouble is over. Morning comes, but night comes too. The caller is invited to inquire and return again.

The short exchange leaves much unexplained. Its urgency is clear, but it does not give a detailed timetable or identify all the events represented by morning and night.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley connects Dumah with Edom because of Seir. He reads the exchange as people anxiously asking about danger, with the reply warning that relief will not remove every reason for further inquiry. The NABRE notes discuss Dumah as a north Arabian oasis while also identifying the caller with Edom.

Henry develops the passage as a call to make good use of an opportunity before another season of trouble. Gill includes an invitation to repentance in the closing words, alongside the ordinary sense of returning to ask again. The interpreters do not agree on one detailed sequence of events behind this short answer.

passages.title: Isaiah 21:13-17
passages.section_title: What happens when the caravans themselves need refuge?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 This is the burden against Arabia: In the thickets of Arabia you must lodge, O caravans of Dedanites. 14 Bring water for the thirsty, O dwellers of Tema; meet the refugees with food. 15 For they flee from the sword— the sword that is drawn— from the bow that is bent, and from the stress of battle. 16 For this is what the Lord says to me: “Within one year, as a hired worker would count it, all the glory of Kedar will be gone. 17 The remaining archers, the warriors of Kedar, will be few.” For the LORD, the God of Israel, has spoken.
paragraphs: 13 This is the burden against Arabia: In the thickets of Arabia you must lodge, O caravans of Dedanites. 14 Bring water for the thirsty, O dwellers of Tema; meet the refugees with food. 15 For they flee from the sword— the sword that is drawn— from the bow that is bent, and from the stress of battle.

16 For this is what the Lord says to me: “Within one year, as a hired worker would count it, all the glory of Kedar will be gone. 17 The remaining archers, the warriors of Kedar, will be few.” For the LORD, the God of Israel, has spoken.

passages.context_html:
The message concerns Arabia and addresses caravans of Dedanites forced to lodge in thickets. The people of Tema are called to bring water and food to those fleeing the sword, the drawn bow and the pressure of battle.

The scene moves from travelers’ vulnerability to a definite warning about Kedar. Within one year, carefully counted as a hired worker counts time, its glory will fail and only a few of its warriors will remain.

The final assurance is that the Lord, the God of Israel, has spoken. The strength of archers cannot guarantee safety against the judgment announced, and people on the move need practical help with food and water.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry, Wesley and Gill understand the passage as a warning of war bringing loss and flight among the Arabian peoples. Wesley and Gill connect the threat with Assyrian invasion, while treating the year as a definite limit.

Henry emphasizes how quickly wealth and military strength can fail. The call to feed the refugees keeps the warning grounded in human need: those who appear secure may find themselves depending on the kindness of others.

passages.title: Isaiah 22:1-14
passages.section_title: Why do Jerusalem’s preparations fail to answer God’s warning?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 This is the burden against the Valley of Vision: What ails you now, that you have all gone up to the rooftops, 2 O city of commotion, O town of revelry? Your slain did not die by the sword, nor were they killed in battle. 3 All your rulers have fled together, captured without a bow. All your fugitives were captured together, having fled to a distant place. 4 Therefore I said, “Turn away from me, let me weep bitterly! Do not try to console me over the destruction of the daughter of my people.” 5 For the Lord GOD of Hosts has set a day of tumult and trampling and confusion in the Valley of Vision— of breaking down the walls and crying to the mountains. 6 Elam takes up a quiver, with chariots and horsemen, and Kir uncovers the shield. 7 Your choicest valleys are full of chariots, and horsemen are posted at the gates. 8 He has uncovered the defenses of Judah. On that day you looked to the weapons in the House of the Forest. 9 You saw that there were many breaches in the walls of the City of David. You collected water from the lower pool. 10 You counted the houses of Jerusalem and tore them down to strengthen the wall. 11 You built a reservoir between the walls for the waters of the ancient pool, but you did not look to the One who made it, or consider Him who planned it long ago. 12 On that day the Lord GOD of Hosts called for weeping and wailing, for shaven heads and the wearing of sackcloth. 13 But look, there is joy and gladness, butchering of cattle and slaughtering of sheep, eating of meat and drinking of wine: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die!” 14 The LORD of Hosts has revealed in my hearing: “Until your dying day, this sin of yours will never be atoned for,” says the Lord GOD of Hosts.

Do not try to console me over the destruction of the daughter of my people.”

5 For the Lord GOD of Hosts has set a day of tumult and trampling and confusion in the Valley of Vision— of breaking down the walls and crying to the mountains. 6 Elam takes up a quiver, with chariots and horsemen, and Kir uncovers the shield. 7 Your choicest valleys are full of chariots, and horsemen are posted at the gates.

You collected water from the lower pool. 10 You counted the houses of Jerusalem and tore them down to strengthen the wall. 11 You built a reservoir between the walls for the waters of the ancient pool, but you did not look to the One who made it, or consider Him who planned it long ago.

passages.context_html:
The Valley of Vision is identified within the passage by the City of David and the houses of Jerusalem. The opening confronts a noisy, celebrating city with death, flight and capture. The prophet responds with bitter grief over his own people.

The threat grows visible in chariots, horsemen and exposed defenses. The people inspect weapons, collect water, count houses and demolish buildings to strengthen the wall.

Verse 11 names the failure behind these preparations: they do not look to the One who made and planned it. Their activity does not become dependence on God. When the Lord calls for mourning and repentance, they answer with feasting and the thought that death may come tomorrow.

The closing declaration makes their response a grave matter. This is not an ordinary celebration misunderstood by an anxious observer; it is refusal of the Lord’s call in the face of judgment.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Gill emphasize misplaced confidence. Gill explicitly says that the preparations themselves are not the fault; the people trust their defenses while failing to look to God.

The historical setting is discussed differently. Wesley connects the captured rulers with Zedekiah and the Babylonian crisis. Gill reads the threat in the setting of Sennacherib’s invasion during Hezekiah’s reign. Both readings identify Jerusalem’s refusal to respond rightly to God as the central issue.

Henry and Gill connect the defiant feast with living as though there is no life beyond death. Their emphasis is on the refusal to repent, rather than a general condemnation of food, drink or practical preparations.

passages.god_plan_html:
First Corinthians 15:32–34 directly uses the words about eating and drinking because tomorrow brings death. Paul sets that reasoning against the truth of resurrection and urges the believers to stop sinning.

His wider argument is that Christ’s resurrection changes everything: if Christ has not been raised, faith is futile and the dead have perished (1 Corinthians 15:12–19). Isaiah’s exposed attitude therefore becomes part of the New Testament’s explanation of why hope beyond death matters for how people live now.

passages.title: Isaiah 22:15-25
passages.section_title: What does the key of David say about entrusted authority?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 This is what the Lord GOD of Hosts says: “Go, say to Shebna, the steward in charge of the palace: 16 What are you doing here, and who authorized you to carve out a tomb for yourself here—to chisel your tomb in the height and cut your resting place in the rock? 17 Look, O mighty man! The LORD is about to shake you violently. He will take hold of you, 18 roll you into a ball, and sling you into a wide land. There you will die, and there your glorious chariots will remain—a disgrace to the house of your master. 19 I will remove you from office, and you will be ousted from your position. 20 On that day I will summon My servant, Eliakim son of Hilkiah. 21 I will clothe him with your robe and tie your sash around him. I will put your authority in his hand, and he will be a father to the dwellers of Jerusalem and to the house of Judah. 22 I will place on his shoulder the key to the house of David. What he opens no one can shut, and what he shuts no one can open. 23 I will drive him like a peg into a firm place, and he will be a throne of glory for the house of his father. 24 So they will hang on him all the glory of his father’s house: the descendants and the offshoots—all the lesser vessels, from bowls to every kind of jar. 25 In that day, declares the LORD of Hosts, the peg driven into a firm place will give way; it will be sheared off and fall, and the load upon it will be cut down.” Indeed, the LORD has spoken.

The LORD is about to shake you violently. He will take hold of you, 18 roll you into a ball, and sling you into a wide land. There you will die, and there your glorious chariots will remain—a disgrace to the house of your master. 19 I will remove you from office, and you will be ousted from your position.

20 On that day I will summon My servant, Eliakim son of Hilkiah. 21 I will clothe him with your robe and tie your sash around him. I will put your authority in his hand, and he will be a father to the dwellers of Jerusalem and to the house of Judah. 22 I will place on his shoulder the key to the house of David. What he opens no one can shut, and what he shuts no one can open.

23 I will drive him like a peg into a firm place, and he will be a throne of glory for the house of his father. 24 So they will hang on him all the glory of his father’s house: the descendants and the offshoots—all the lesser vessels, from bowls to every kind of jar. 25 In that day, declares the LORD of Hosts, the peg driven into a firm place will give way; it will be sheared off and fall, and the load upon it will be cut down.” Indeed, the LORD has spoken.

passages.context_html:
The Lord sends the prophet to Shebna, the steward in charge of the palace. The rebuke challenges the grand tomb he is cutting for himself. Instead of securing his place in Jerusalem, he will be removed from office and die in a distant land.

Eliakim son of Hilkiah is appointed in his place. The robe, sash and authority pass to him, and he is to care for Jerusalem and Judah as a father. The key of David’s house expresses authority to open and shut.

Eliakim is then pictured as a peg fixed firmly enough to carry his family’s honor and dependents. But the final verse announces that a firmly fixed peg will fall, taking its load with it. Readers differ over which official is in view at that closing point.

Second Kings 18:17–18 later names Eliakim as palace administrator and Shebnah as scribe among the officials who meet the Assyrian delegation. It confirms the change of roles without giving a full account of Shebna’s later fate.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry, Wesley and Gill understand the key as entrusted authority and see Eliakim’s appointment as a contrast to Shebna’s pride. For the final fallen peg, Wesley and Gill return to Shebna. The Cambridge commentary instead reads it as the eventual fall of Eliakim’s family’s position.

The key also has a place in differing Christian accounts of church authority. A Catholic reading is illustrated by Benedict XVI’s homily of 29 June 2012, which connects Eliakim’s key with the keys promised to Peter in Matthew 16. The Catholic Church teaches that Peter’s pastoral office continues in the bishops under the Pope’s primacy (Catechism 881–882).

The Reformed Westminster Confession 30.1–2 places the keys of the kingdom in the hands of church officers; its chapter 25.6 rejects papal headship. The 1689 Baptist Confession 26.4 likewise affirms Christ’s supreme authority and rejects papal headship. Those confessions state their teaching about the church; they do not give a separate detailed explanation of every verse in Isaiah 22.

These differences concern the later application of entrusted authority. The direct New Testament use of the key of David for Christ himself appears in Revelation 3:7.

passages.god_plan_html:
Revelation 3:7–13 directly places Isaiah’s language on Jesus’ lips: He holds the key of David, and no one can reverse His opening and shutting. He addresses a church with little strength that has kept His word.

The connection carries the image from an appointed royal steward to the Lord who governs access in His kingdom. The church’s security rests in His authority, rather than its own power.

The same message promises a lasting place in God’s temple to the one who overcomes. Isaiah’s picture of entrusted authority reaches forward, through Revelation’s own use of it, to Christ’s authority to keep and welcome His people.

passages.title: Isaiah 23:1-18
passages.section_title: What becomes of Tyre’s wealth when the Lord brings down its pride?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 This is the burden against Tyre: Wail, O ships of Tarshish, for Tyre is laid waste, without house or harbor. Word has reached them from the land of Cyprus. 2 Be silent, O dwellers of the coastland, you merchants of Sidon, whose traders have crossed the sea. 3 On the great waters came the grain of Shihor; the harvest of the Nile was the revenue of Tyre; she was the merchant of the nations. 4 Be ashamed, O Sidon, the stronghold of the sea, for the sea has spoken: “I have not been in labor or given birth. I have not raised young men or brought up young women.” 5 When the report reaches Egypt, they will writhe in agony over the news of Tyre. 6 Cross over to Tarshish; wail, O inhabitants of the coastland! 7 Is this your jubilant city, whose origin is from antiquity, whose feet have taken her to settle far away? 8 Who planned this against Tyre, the bestower of crowns, whose traders are princes, whose merchants are renowned on the earth? 9 The LORD of Hosts planned it, to defile all its glorious beauty, to disgrace all the renowned of the earth. 10 Cultivate your land like the Nile, O Daughter of Tarshish; there is no longer a harbor. 11 The LORD has stretched out His hand over the sea; He has made kingdoms tremble. He has given a command that the strongholds of Canaan be destroyed. 12 He said, “You shall rejoice no more, O oppressed Virgin Daughter of Sidon. Get up and cross over to Cyprus— even there you will find no rest.” 13 Look at the land of the Chaldeans— a people now of no account. The Assyrians destined it for the desert creatures; they set up their siege towers and stripped its palaces. They brought it to ruin. 14 Wail, O ships of Tarshish, for your harbor has been destroyed! 15 At that time Tyre will be forgotten for seventy years—the span of a king’s life. But at the end of seventy years, it will happen to Tyre as in the song of the harlot: 16 “Take up your harp, stroll through the city, O forgotten harlot. Make sweet melody, sing many a song, so you will be remembered.” 17 And at the end of seventy years, the LORD will restore Tyre. Then she will return to hire as a prostitute and sell herself to all the kingdoms on the face of the earth. 18 Yet her profits and wages will be set apart to the LORD; they will not be stored or saved, for her profit will go to those who live before the LORD, for abundant food and fine clothing.
