passages.context_html:
The message against Tyre reaches across the sea to the ships, traders and neighboring peoples connected with its trade. News of its ruined harbor brings mourning. The grain of the Nile had made Tyre a merchant of the nations; the loss therefore reaches beyond one city.

The central question asks who planned this against a city whose merchants were treated like princes. The answer is the Lord of Hosts. The judgment exposes the pride attached to beauty, reputation and wealth.

The warning includes flight toward Cyprus and a reference to the Chaldeans and Assyrian devastation. Even a move overseas will not bring the promised rest. Tyre’s strength cannot preserve it from the Lord’s purpose.

The closing verses give a limit to its neglect: seventy years, compared with a king’s lifespan. Afterward the city resumes its trade, pictured through the song of a forgotten prostitute seeking attention again. The final surprise is the use of its earnings: they are set apart to the Lord and provide food and clothing for those who live before Him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry, Wesley and Gill read the chapter as bringing down commercial pride. They connect Tyre’s humiliation with its confidence in wealth and its later activity with the return of trade.

The historical sequence receives different explanations. Henry emphasizes the Chaldeans as the instrument of judgment, and Wesley connects the seventy years with the Babylonian captivity. The NABRE notes instead suggest an Assyrian setting for the main warning and understand the seventy years as a conventional long period.

Henry, Wesley and Gill apply the final earnings to wealth devoted to God’s service and the needs of His people. They see a change in what riches are for: resources once tied to pride become useful in worship and care for others.

passages.god_plan_html:
The nations bringing their wealth into God’s service is a theme developed later in Isaiah 60:5–9. There the riches of the sea and the resources of the nations come with praise of the Lord.

Revelation 21:22–27 gives a fuller picture: God and the Lamb are the city’s temple and light, the nations walk by that light, and the kings bring their glory into it. Nothing unclean enters.

This is a connection through the wider theme, rather than a claim that Revelation directly quotes Isaiah 23. The direction is toward the nations’ honor and resources serving God’s glory, instead of being stored up as a monument to human importance.

passages.title: Isaiah 24:1-23
passages.section_title: What can stand when rebellion brings judgment on the earth?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Behold, the LORD lays waste the earth and leaves it in ruins. He will twist its surface and scatter its inhabitants— 2 people and priest alike, servant and master, maid and mistress, buyer and seller, lender and borrower, creditor and debtor. 3 The earth will be utterly laid waste and thoroughly plundered. For the LORD has spoken this word. 4 The earth mourns and withers; the world languishes and fades; the exalted of the earth waste away. 5 The earth is defiled by its people; they have transgressed the laws; they have overstepped the decrees and broken the everlasting covenant. 6 Therefore a curse has consumed the earth, and its inhabitants must bear the guilt; the earth’s dwellers have been burned, and only a few survive. 7 The new wine dries up, the vine withers. All the merrymakers now groan. 8 The joyful tambourines have ceased; the noise of revelers has stopped; the joyful harp is silent. 9 They no longer sing and drink wine; strong drink is bitter to those who consume it. 10 The city of chaos is shattered; every house is closed to entry. 11 In the streets they cry out for wine. passages.context_html:
The view widens from messages about particular nations to a devastated earth. The opening places people of every rank together: priest and people, servant and master, buyer and seller, lender and borrower. Status does not provide an escape.

The reason is stated in verse 5. The inhabitants have defiled the earth by transgressing laws, overstepping decrees and breaking the everlasting covenant. The curse falls on a world marked by rebellion, and only a few remain.

Ordinary celebration disappears. Wine, music and the city’s former activity give way to silence, grief and ruins. A remnant is pictured as the few olives or grapes left after harvest.

Praise nevertheless sounds from the west, the east and the ends of the earth. The song does not make the rest of the warning disappear: the speaker immediately laments treachery, and terror, pit and snare confront the earth’s inhabitants.

The closing scene reaches both the heavenly host and earthly kings. They are confined and await punishment, while the Lord reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem with glory before His elders. The account moves beyond the collapse of human security to the open display of His rule.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley reads the opening land and world language primarily in relation to Canaan and Judah, including the judgments brought through Assyria and Babylon. He also applies the later verses to Christ’s kingdom and to the people gathered under His rule.

Henry places greater emphasis on the wider world’s ruin through sin and the eventual new heavens and new earth. He sees the preserved remnant as people who can rejoice in God even while the surrounding world falls apart.

The readings therefore differ over the reach and sequence of the judgment. They share the emphasis that sin brings ruin, earthly distinctions cannot secure safety, and the Lord preserves people who give Him glory.

passages.god_plan_html:
The movement from judgment to God’s glorious rule has a wider New Testament counterpart in Revelation 20:11–15 and 21:1–5. John describes final judgment, followed by a new heaven and new earth where God dwells with His people (Revelation 21).

The light imagery also has a close parallel. Isaiah’s sun and moon are put to shame before the Lord’s glory; in Revelation 21:22–24, the city needs no sun or moon because God’s glory lights it and the Lamb is its lamp.

These are supported connections between the passages, rather than a detailed timetable supplied by Isaiah 24. The larger hope is that judgment does not leave the world in the hands of its ruined powers: God makes His dwelling with His people and brings His purpose to completion.

passages.title: Isaiah 25:1-12
passages.section_title: What does it mean that God will swallow up death forever?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 O LORD, You are my God! I will exalt You; I will praise Your name. For You have worked wonders— plans formed long ago— in perfect faithfulness. 2 Indeed, You have made the city a heap of rubble, the fortified town a ruin. The fortress of strangers is a city no more; it will never be rebuilt. 3 Therefore, a strong people will honor You. The cities of ruthless nations will revere You. 4 For You have been a refuge for the poor, a stronghold for the needy in distress, a refuge from the storm, a shade from the heat. For the breath of the ruthless is like rain against a wall, 5 like heat in a dry land. You subdue the uproar of foreigners. As the shade of a cloud cools the heat, so the song of the ruthless is silenced. 6 On this mountain the LORD of Hosts will prepare a lavish banquet for all the peoples, a feast of aged wine, of choice meat, of finely aged wine. 7 On this mountain He will swallow up the shroud that enfolds all peoples, the sheet that covers all nations; 8 He will swallow up death forever. The Lord GOD will wipe away the tears from every face and remove the disgrace of His people from the whole earth. For the LORD has spoken. 9 And in that day it will be said, “Surely this is our God; we have waited for Him, and He has saved us. This is the LORD for whom we have waited. Let us rejoice and be glad in His salvation.” 10 For the hand of the LORD will rest on this mountain. But Moab will be trampled in his place as straw is trodden into the dung pile. 11 He will spread out his hands within it, as a swimmer spreads his arms to swim. His pride will be brought low, despite the skill of his hands. 12 The high-walled fortress will be brought down, cast to the ground, into the dust.

passages.context_html:
The chapter answers the preceding judgment with praise. The Lord is exalted for faithfully accomplishing plans formed long ago, bringing down a fortified city and becoming a refuge for the poor and needy.

The images of shade and shelter contrast His care with the harshness of the ruthless. Strong peoples are brought to honor Him, and the noise of their opposition is subdued.

Then the Lord prepares a lavish banquet for all peoples on His mountain. He removes the covering spread over the nations, swallows up death forever and wipes tears from every face. His people’s disgrace is removed, and those who have waited for Him rejoice in His salvation.

The closing warning against Moab keeps judgment beside that promise. Pride and fortified walls are brought down into the dust. The chapter does not present human strength as the way into the feast; its hope rests in the Lord who saves and removes what His people cannot overcome.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley read the feast as the abundance God provides through the gospel for Jews and Gentiles. Henry connects it with the New Testament’s invitations to repentant sinners and sees the promised end of sorrow fully realized in the joy to come.

Gill discusses the gospel’s blessings, the marriage supper of the Lamb and the new Jerusalem as settings for the feast. He reads the defeat of death as including bodily resurrection, appealing to Paul’s use of this verse.

Henry and Wesley understand Moab in the final warning as also representing the enemies of God’s people. Across these readings, the feast and the fall of pride belong together: God comforts His people and ends the power that opposes His rule.

passages.god_plan_html:
First Corinthians 15:50–58 directly applies Isaiah’s promise to resurrection. Paul says the saying about death being swallowed up is fulfilled when the perishable is clothed with the imperishable and the mortal with immortality. He gives thanks for the victory God provides through Jesus Christ.

Revelation 21:1–5 also takes up the promise of tears wiped away, in a world where death, mourning and pain are no more. God dwells with His people and makes all things new.

The New Testament therefore carries this promise into the victory of Christ and the resurrection hope of His people. Death is not merely made easier to bear; its rule is overcome. Paul’s response is practical: remain steadfast and continue in the Lord’s work, knowing that it is not in vain.

passages.title: Isaiah 26:1-21
passages.section_title: Where can God’s people find peace when their own strength fails?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 In that day this song will be sung in the land of Judah: We have a strong city; salvation is established as its walls and ramparts. 2 Open the gates so a righteous nation may enter— one that remains faithful. 3 You will keep in perfect peace the steadfast of mind, because he trusts in You. 4 Trust in the LORD forever, because GOD the LORD is the Rock eternal. 5 For He has humbled those who dwell on high; He lays the lofty city low. He brings it down to the ground; He casts it into the dust. 6 Feet trample it down— the feet of the oppressed, the steps of the poor. 7 The path of the righteous is level; You clear a straight path for the upright. 8 Yes, we wait for You, O LORD; we walk in the path of Your judgments. Your name and renown are the desire of our souls. 9 My soul longs for You in the night; indeed, my spirit seeks You at dawn. For when Your judgments come upon the earth, the people of the world learn righteousness. 10 Though grace is shown to the wicked man, he does not learn righteousness. In the land of righteousness he acts unjustly and fails to see the majesty of the LORD. 11 O LORD, Your hand is upraised, but they do not see it. They will see Your zeal for Your people and be put to shame. The fire set for Your enemies will consume them! 12 O LORD, You will establish peace for us. For all that we have accomplished, You have done for us. 13 O LORD our God, other lords besides You have ruled over us, but Your name alone do we confess. 14 The dead will not live; the departed spirits will not rise. Therefore You have punished and destroyed them; You have wiped out all memory of them. 15 You have enlarged the nation, O LORD; You have enlarged the nation. You have gained glory for Yourself; You have extended all the borders of the land. 16 O LORD, they sought You in their distress; when You disciplined them, they poured out a quiet prayer. 17 As a woman with child about to give birth writhes and cries out in pain, so were we in Your presence, O LORD. 18 We were with child; we writhed in pain; but we gave birth to wind. We have given no salvation to the earth, nor brought any life into the world. 19 Your dead will live; their bodies will rise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust! Hide yourselves a little while until the wrath has passed. 21 For behold, the LORD is coming out of His dwelling to punish the inhabitants of the earth for their iniquity. The earth will reveal her bloodshed and will no longer conceal her slain.

passages.context_html:
The song is to be sung in Judah. Its strong city has salvation for walls, and its gates open to a righteous, faithful people. The Lord keeps those who trust Him in peace, while the lofty city falls beneath the feet of the oppressed.

In verse 3, the Hebrew word שָׁלוֹם, shalom, pronounced shah-LOHM, is repeated twice. Brown–Driver–Briggs explains the word in terms of soundness, well-being and peace. The repetition gives weight to the peace the BSB describes as perfect, grounded here in trust in the Lord.

The song then speaks of waiting for God and longing for Him through the night. His judgments teach righteousness, yet the wicked can resist both His favor and His raised hand. His people acknowledge that He has established their peace and enabled what they have accomplished.

Former rulers have lost their power, while the Lord has enlarged His people. Looking back on distress, the singers compare their efforts to painful labor that produces only wind: they have not brought salvation or life to the world.

The answer is the promise that God’s dead will live and their bodies rise. The chapter closes by calling His people into shelter while His judgment passes. The bloodshed the earth has concealed will be brought to light. Trust and hope are held together with a sober expectation of accountability.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley read the strong city in relation to God’s protection of His people and apply its peace to life under His care. Gill distinguishes the firm foundation of that peace from how fully a believer may feel it at a particular time.

The promise in verse 19 receives two main kinds of explanation. The NABRE notes read it as the restoration of a people whose numbers and national life had been devastated. Henry includes the raising of the church from a low condition, but also applies the words to bodily resurrection. Gill likewise includes bodily resurrection among the promised hopes.

Wesley understands the former rulers in verse 14 as unable to rise again to trouble God’s people. That keeps the line about their not rising within the song’s contrast between broken oppression and renewed life for the people who trust the Lord.

passages.god_plan_html:
The hope of life beyond the grave is developed around the Son in John 5:24–29. Jesus says that those who hear His word and believe the One who sent Him have crossed from death to life. He also speaks of the coming hour when those in their graves hear His voice and rise.

This is a connection through resurrection and God-given life, rather than a claim that Jesus directly quotes Isaiah 26. The song’s confession that human effort cannot produce salvation stands beside the New Testament’s announcement that life and judgment are entrusted to the Son.

The larger hope therefore rests on God doing what His people cannot accomplish for themselves. The Lord who keeps them in peace is also able to bring life where their own labor has reached its limit.

passages.title: Isaiah 27:1-13
passages.section_title: How does God turn a threatened vineyard into a fruitful people?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 In that day the LORD will take His sharp, great, and mighty sword, and bring judgment on Leviathan the fleeing serpent—Leviathan the coiling serpent—and He will slay the dragon of the sea. 2 In that day: “Sing about a fruitful vineyard. 3 I, the LORD, am its keeper; I water it continually. I guard it night and day so no one can disturb it; 4 I am not angry. If only thorns and briers confronted Me, I would march and trample them, I would burn them to the ground. 5 Or let them lay claim to My protection; let them make peace with Me— yes, let them make peace with Me.” 6 In the days to come, Jacob will take root. Israel will bud and blossom and fill the whole world with fruit. 7 Has the LORD struck Israel as He struck her oppressors? Was she killed like those who slayed her? 8 By warfare and exile You contended with her and removed her with a fierce wind, as on the day the east wind blows. 9 Therefore Jacob’s guilt will be atoned for, and the full fruit of the removal of his sin will be this: When he makes all the altar stones like crushed bits of chalk, no Asherah poles or incense altars will remain standing. 10 For the fortified city lies deserted— a homestead abandoned, a wilderness forsaken. There the calves graze, and there they lie down; they strip its branches bare. 11 When its limbs are dry, they are broken off. Women come and use them for kindling; for this is a people without understanding. Therefore their Maker has no compassion on them, and their Creator shows them no favor. 12 In that day the LORD will thresh from the flowing Euphrates to the Wadi of Egypt, and you, O Israelites, will be gathered one by one. 13 And in that day a great ram’s horn will sound, and those who were perishing in Assyria will come forth with those who were exiles in Egypt. And they will worship the LORD on the holy mountain in Jerusalem.

And they will worship the LORD on the holy mountain in Jerusalem.

passages.context_html:
The chapter opens with the Lord judging Leviathan and the dragon of the sea. The Hebrew name לִוְיָתָן, livyathan, pronounced liv-yah-THAHN, is explained by Brown–Driver–Briggs as a serpent, dragon or sea monster in poetic passages. Here the creature’s strength is no match for the Lord’s sword.

The next picture is a fruitful vineyard, guarded and watered by the Lord. This reverses the abandoned vineyard of Isaiah 5. The One who keeps it offers protection and peace, and Jacob takes root until Israel fills the world with fruit.

The middle verses distinguish the Lord’s treatment of Israel from the ruin of its oppressors. Exile and judgment are real, but the removal of guilt is accompanied by the destruction of idolatrous altars. The deserted city shows the severity of the warning against a people without understanding.

The final scene gathers Israelites one by one. A great ram’s horn sounds, and those perishing in Assyria and exiled in Egypt come to worship the Lord in Jerusalem. The chapter moves from defeated hostile power to a people preserved, cleansed and gathered for worship.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads Leviathan in relation to the devil and Christ’s victory over him. Wesley gives a broader explanation: a powerful enemy or enemies of God and His people. Gill includes both oppressive rulers and Satan behind their hostility. These are interpretations of the image, rather than meanings established simply by the creature’s name.

Henry and Wesley read the vineyard as God’s people under His continuing care. They emphasize that correction has a purpose in removing sin, rather than treating Israel exactly like the enemies brought to an end.

Henry connects the closing gathering both with return from captivity and with the gospel gathering people into worship. Gill places particular emphasis on the gospel as the trumpet call, while also allowing a future gathering connected with Jerusalem. The common hope is that scattered people are not beyond the Lord’s care.

passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 11:25–32 draws on Isaiah’s promises of a deliverer and the removal of sins, combining language from Isaiah 59 with Isaiah 27:9. Paul speaks about Israel, the fullness of the Gentiles and God’s mercy, warning his readers against conceit.

The final gathering also has a close parallel in Matthew 24:29–31, where the Son of Man sends angels with a loud trumpet call to gather His elect. This is a parallel in the gathering imagery; the passage does not name every place or settle every question of sequence in Isaiah.

Together these connections place restoration within God’s larger purpose of removing sin, showing mercy and gathering His people. The point is more than survival after a disaster: the gathered people come to worship Him.

passages.title: Isaiah 28:1-13
passages.section_title: What happens when leaders refuse the message that could give them rest?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Woe to the majestic crown of Ephraim’s drunkards, to the fading flower of his glorious splendor, set on the summit above the fertile valley, the pride of those overcome by wine. 2 Behold, the Lord has one who is strong and mighty. Like a hailstorm or destructive tempest, like a driving rain or flooding downpour, he will smash that crown to the ground. 3 The majestic crown of Ephraim’s drunkards will be trampled underfoot. 4 The fading flower of his beautiful splendor, set on the summit above the fertile valley, will be like a ripe fig before the summer harvest: Whoever sees it will take it in his hand and swallow it. 5 On that day the LORD of Hosts will be a crown of glory, a diadem of splendor to the remnant of His people, 6 a spirit of justice to him who sits in judgment, and a strength to those who repel the onslaught at the gate. 7 These also stagger from wine and stumble from strong drink: Priests and prophets reel from strong drink and are befuddled by wine. They stumble because of strong drink, muddled in their visions and stumbling in their judgments. 8 For all their tables are covered with vomit; there is not a place without filth. 9 Whom is He trying to teach? To whom is He explaining His message? To infants just weaned from milk? To babies removed from the breast? 10 For they hear: “Order on order, order on order, line on line, line on line; a little here, a little there.” 11 Indeed, with mocking lips and foreign tongues, He will speak to this people 12 to whom He has said: “This is the place of rest, let the weary rest; this is the place of repose.” But they would not listen. 13 Then the word of the LORD to them will become: “Order on order, order on order, line on line, line on line; a little here, a little there,” so that they will go stumbling backward and will be injured, ensnared, and captured.

7 These also stagger from wine and stumble from strong drink: Priests and prophets reel from strong drink and are befuddled by wine. They stumble because of strong drink, muddled in their visions and stumbling in their judgments. 8 For all their tables are covered with vomit; there is not a place without filth.

9 Whom is He trying to teach? To whom is He explaining His message? To infants just weaned from milk? To babies removed from the breast? 10 For they hear: “Order on order, order on order, line on line, line on line; a little here, a little there.” 11 Indeed, with mocking lips and foreign tongues, He will speak to this people 12 to whom He has said: “This is the place of rest, let the weary rest; this is the place of repose.” But they would not listen. 13 Then the word of the LORD to them will become: “Order on order, order on order, line on line, line on line; a little here, a little there,” so that they will go stumbling backward and will be injured, ensnared, and captured.

passages.context_html:
The warning begins with Ephraim’s proud crown and fading beauty. A strong attacker is pictured as hail, a destructive storm and flooding rain. What appears glorious will be swallowed as quickly as an early ripe fig.

For the surviving people, the Lord Himself becomes the crown of glory, a source of justice and strength. Yet the next scene exposes priests and prophets staggering under strong drink, failing in the very visions and judgments they are supposed to give.

The questions about teaching infants and the repeated lines about order and line show how badly the message is being received. The Lord had offered rest for the weary, but they would not listen.

Foreign lips and tongues will now become part of how He addresses them. The words they would not receive bring no security to their resistance: the passage ends in stumbling, injury, entrapment and capture.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry, Wesley and Gill connect the repeated instruction with people who need to be taught like children but resist learning. They emphasize the contrast between God’s offer of rest and the people’s refusal.

The Cambridge commentary instead reads verses 9–10 as the drunken leaders mocking Isaiah: they resent being addressed like recently weaned children and imitate his repeated instruction. It then reads the foreign speech as the terrible answer to their mockery.

The readings differ over who speaks the repeated words and how they function. Both connect the foreign language with judgment after the people refuse a message they could understand.

passages.god_plan_html:
First Corinthians 14:20–25 directly quotes Isaiah’s warning about foreign tongues and refusal to listen. Paul brings it into his discussion of tongues, prophecy, understanding and the response of unbelievers.

He goes on to describe the danger of an outsider hearing a gathering full of uninterpreted tongues and thinking the believers are out of their minds. By contrast, a message that exposes the heart can lead an unbeliever to fall down and worship God.

The connection keeps the purpose of God’s speech in view. Receiving His message matters more than being impressed by an unusual sound; Paul’s concern is that what happens among believers serves understanding and a right response to God.

passages.title: Isaiah 28:14-22
passages.section_title: What foundation can stand when a refuge of lies is swept away?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 Therefore hear the word of the LORD, O scoffers who rule this people in Jerusalem. 15 For you said, “We have made a covenant with death; we have fashioned an agreement with Sheol. When the overwhelming scourge passes through it will not touch us, because we have made lies our refuge and falsehood our hiding place.” 16 So this is what the Lord GOD says: “See, I lay a stone in Zion, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation; the one who believes will never be shaken. 17 I will make justice the measuring line and righteousness the level. Hail will sweep away your refuge of lies, and water will flood your hiding place. 18 Your covenant with death will be dissolved, and your agreement with Sheol will not stand. When the overwhelming scourge passes through, you will be trampled by it. 19 As often as it passes through, it will carry you away; it will sweep through morning after morning, by day and by night.” The understanding of this message will bring sheer terror. 20 Indeed, the bed is too short to stretch out on, and the blanket too small to wrap around you. 21 For the LORD will rise up as at Mount Perazim. He will rouse Himself as in the Valley of Gibeon, to do His work, His strange work, and to perform His task, His disturbing task. 22 So now, do not mock, or your shackles will become heavier. Indeed, I have heard from the Lord GOD of Hosts a decree of destruction against the whole land.

When the overwhelming scourge passes through, you will be trampled by it. 19 As often as it passes through, it will carry you away; it will sweep through morning after morning, by day and by night.” The understanding of this message will bring sheer terror.

20 Indeed, the bed is too short to stretch out on, and the blanket too small to wrap around you. 21 For the LORD will rise up as at Mount Perazim. He will rouse Himself as in the Valley of Gibeon, to do His work, His strange work, and to perform His task, His disturbing task. 22 So now, do not mock, or your shackles will become heavier. Indeed, I have heard from the Lord GOD of Hosts a decree of destruction against the whole land.

passages.context_html:
The warning now directly addresses the scoffing rulers in Jerusalem. Their claim to have an agreement with death and Sheol expresses confidence that the approaching disaster cannot reach them. The passage exposes their refuge as lies and falsehood.

Against that false security, the Lord lays a tested, precious cornerstone in Zion, a sure foundation for the one who believes. Justice and righteousness become the measuring line and level.

Their claimed protection will be swept away by hail and water. The agreement with death will not stand, and repeated disaster will turn understanding into terror. A bed too short and a blanket too small picture a refuge that cannot provide what it promises.

The Lord’s action is compared with His victories at Perazim and Gibeon, but now the warning is directed at His own people. The closing call is to stop mocking before their shackles become heavier.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill explain the covenant with death as a boast of safety, as though death had agreed to leave the rulers alone. Gill also discusses attempts to identify it with political agreements. These explanations distinguish the claim of security from a literal treaty signed with a person called Death.

Henry, Wesley and Gill identify the stone with the Messiah and the sure foundation He provides. They contrast trusting that foundation with relying on deception or a protection too small to shelter anyone.

For the Lord’s strange work, Wesley and Gill emphasize the reversal: the God who fought against Israel’s enemies now acts against wrongdoing among His own people. Their place in the covenant does not make the warning empty.

passages.god_plan_html:
First Peter 2:4–10 directly quotes Isaiah’s cornerstone promise and applies it to Christ. People who come to Him, the living stone, are themselves built into a spiritual house and holy priesthood.

Peter joins the promise of security for the believer with the warning about stumbling over the stone. He then describes a people called out of darkness to proclaim God’s virtues, a people who have received mercy.

The New Testament therefore makes the foundation personal: the lasting refuge is Christ. Those built upon Him are gathered into a people whose worship and witness show what His mercy has done.

passages.title: Isaiah 28:23-29
passages.section_title: Why does Isaiah end the warning with a farmer’s work?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 23 Listen and hear my voice. Pay attention and hear what I say. 24 Does the plowman plow for planting every day? Does he continuously loosen and harrow the soil? 25 When he has leveled its surface, does he not sow caraway and scatter cumin? He plants wheat in rows and barley in plots, and rye within its border. 26 For his God instructs and teaches him properly. 27 Surely caraway is not threshed with a sledge, and the wheel of a cart is not rolled over the cumin. But caraway is beaten out with a stick, and cumin with a rod. 28 Grain for bread must be ground, but it is not endlessly threshed. Though the wheels of the cart roll over it, the horses do not crush it. 29 This also comes from the LORD of Hosts, who is wonderful in counsel and excellent in wisdom.
paragraphs: 23 Listen and hear my voice. Pay attention and hear what I say. 24 Does the plowman plow for planting every day? Does he continuously loosen and harrow the soil? 25 When he has leveled its surface, does he not sow caraway and scatter cumin? He plants wheat in rows and barley in plots, and rye within its border. 26 For his God instructs and teaches him properly.

27 Surely caraway is not threshed with a sledge, and the wheel of a cart is not rolled over the cumin. But caraway is beaten out with a stick, and cumin with a rod. 28 Grain for bread must be ground, but it is not endlessly threshed. Though the wheels of the cart roll over it, the horses do not crush it. 29 This also comes from the LORD of Hosts, who is wonderful in counsel and excellent in wisdom.

passages.context_html:
The listener is called to pay attention to the ordinary work of farming. A plowman does not keep breaking the ground forever. He prepares it and then plants different crops in their proper places.

Harvesting also calls for judgment. Caraway and cumin do not receive the same treatment as grain for bread. The tools and amount of force must suit what is being worked on; threshing does not continue endlessly.

God is named as the source of the farmer’s instruction. The closing declaration praises the Lord as wonderful in counsel and excellent in wisdom. After the warnings about failed leaders and false security, the farming picture directs attention to purposeful action governed by wisdom.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley read the farming scene as an illustration of God’s wise government. Different tasks have different times, and different crops receive different treatment. His patience is not proof that judgment will never come.

Gill emphasizes care in the threshing: the farmer does not destroy the grain by continuing without limit. Henry similarly applies the picture to correction serving a purpose rather than continuing for its own sake. The comparison concerns the wisdom and purpose of God’s dealings.

passages.god_plan_html:
The purpose of correction is developed for believers in Hebrews 12:1–11. The passage directs them to Jesus, who endured the cross, and describes the Father’s discipline as His treatment of children He loves.

Hebrews says that this discipline is for their good, so they may share His holiness, and that it later yields righteousness and peace. That is a thematic connection with Isaiah’s purposeful farming image, rather than a direct quotation or a way to identify the cause of every individual hardship.

The larger account is of God preparing His people for a life that reflects His character. His wisdom is directed toward fruit, not suffering as an end in itself.

passages.title: Isaiah 29:1-16
passages.section_title: What happens when worship continues but the heart is far from God?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Woe to you, O Ariel, the city of Ariel where David camped! Year upon year let your festivals recur. 2 And I will constrain Ariel, and there will be mourning and lamentation; she will be like an altar hearth before Me. 3 I will camp in a circle around you; I will besiege you with towers and set up siege works against you. 4 You will be brought low, you will speak from the ground, and out of the dust your words will be muffled. Your voice will be like a spirit from the ground; your speech will whisper out of the dust. 5 But your many foes will be like fine dust, the multitude of the ruthless like blowing chaff. Then suddenly, in an instant, 6 you will be visited by the LORD of Hosts with thunder and earthquake and loud noise, with windstorm and tempest and consuming flame of fire. 7 All the many nations going out to battle against Ariel— even all who war against her, laying siege and attacking her— will be like a dream, like a vision in the night, 8 as when a hungry man dreams he is eating, then awakens still hungry; as when a thirsty man dreams he is drinking, then awakens faint and parched. So will it be for all the many nations who go to battle against Mount Zion. 9 Stop and be astonished; blind yourselves and be sightless; be drunk, but not with wine; stagger, but not from strong drink. 10 For the LORD has poured out on you a spirit of deep sleep. He has shut your eyes, O prophets; He has covered your heads, O seers. 11 And the entire vision will be to you like the words sealed in a scroll. If it is handed to someone to read, he will say, “I cannot, because it is sealed.” 12 Or if the scroll is handed to one unable to read, he will say, “I cannot read.” 13 Therefore the Lord said: “These people draw near to Me with their mouths and honor Me with their lips, but their hearts are far from Me. Their worship of Me is but rules taught by men. 14 Therefore I will again confound these people with wonder upon wonder. The wisdom of the wise will vanish, and the intelligence of the intelligent will be hidden.” 15 Woe to those who dig deep to hide their plans from the LORD. In darkness they do their works and say, “Who sees us, and who will know?” 16 You have turned things upside down, as if the potter were regarded as clay. Shall what is formed say to him who formed it, “He did not make me”? Can the pottery say of the potter, “He has no understanding”?

Their worship of Me is but rules taught by men. 14 Therefore I will again confound these people with wonder upon wonder. The wisdom of the wise will vanish, and the intelligence of the intelligent will be hidden.” 15 Woe to those who dig deep to hide their plans from the LORD. In darkness they do their works and say, “Who sees us, and who will know?” 16 You have turned things upside down, as if the potter were regarded as clay. Shall what is formed say to him who formed it, “He did not make me”? Can the pottery say of the potter, “He has no understanding”?

passages.context_html:
Ariel is the name used here for Jerusalem, the city where David camped. Its festivals keep returning, but the Lord announces mourning and a siege. The city will be brought so low that its speech is pictured as a whisper from the dust.

The name itself carries more than one association. The Brown–Driver–Briggs lexicon discusses Ariel, pronounced ah-ree-EL, as a name for Jerusalem and records both a lion-related explanation and an altar-hearth explanation. The passage makes the altar connection explicit in verse 2: the city will become like an altar hearth before God.

The scene then turns to the nations attacking Zion. In the BSB, the foes become like dust and chaff, and their expected satisfaction is compared with a hungry person dreaming of food and waking still hungry. The Lord’s intervention overturns what appears certain.

The deeper trouble is a refusal to see. Prophets and seers are covered in sleep, and God’s message is like a sealed scroll that neither the reader nor the nonreader receives. Religious words continue, but the heart is far away. Those who imagine they can hide their plans from God have reversed the relationship between the potter and the clay.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and the USCCB notes read the sudden change in verses 5–8 as the defeat of Jerusalem’s attackers, with the Assyrian threat in view. Gill instead reads much of the opening as Jerusalem’s destruction by Rome; he takes the dust and chaff to describe the attackers’ numbers and speed. The readings differ over how the siege and the sudden reversal fit together.

For the worship warning, Henry, Wesley and Gill emphasize the gap between outward religious practice and a heart that receives God’s word. Jesus’ own use of verse 13 makes the danger of human rules replacing obedience especially important.

Where traditions differ is in how they distinguish faithful tradition from the human rules condemned here. The Catholic Church, in Catechism 80–83, teaches that Scripture and apostolic Tradition pass on the same revelation and deserve equal reverence. It distinguishes that apostolic inheritance from later local customs, which can change or be abandoned.

The Reformed Westminster Confession 1.6 and the 1689 Baptist Confession 1.6 teach that everything necessary for salvation, faith and life is stated in Scripture or follows from it, and that human traditions must not add to it. Both also allow practical arrangements governed by Scripture’s general rules. These documents explain a difference over authority; none presents a license to replace God’s command with a human preference.
passages.current_position_html: In [Worship as the Early Church Knew It](../studies/worship.html), we read Jesus’ use of this passage as a warning against honoring God in appearance while withholding obedience from the heart. Human tradition cannot make hollow reverence faithful.

passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus directly quotes Isaiah’s warning about lips and hearts in Matthew 15:1–9 and Mark 7:6–13. His example is a tradition that allows people to avoid helping their parents. The problem has visible consequences: religious language is being used to set aside what God commands.

Paul directly quotes the warning about the wisdom of the wise in 1 Corinthians 1:18–25. He explains it through the cross: Christ crucified appears foolish or offensive to human expectations, yet He is God’s power and wisdom for those who are called, both Jews and Greeks.

Romans 11:1–12 also draws on Isaiah’s language about deep sleep. Paul immediately keeps that warning from becoming a claim that God has rejected His people: he points to a remnant, denies that the stumble is beyond recovery, and later describes the hardening as partial. God’s unfolding purpose brings mercy to Gentiles without giving them grounds for pride over Israel.

passages.title: Isaiah 29:17-24
passages.section_title: Can people who refused to listen learn to hear again?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 In a very short time, will not Lebanon become an orchard, and the orchard seem like a forest? 18 On that day the deaf will hear the words of the scroll, and out of the deep darkness the eyes of the blind will see. 19 The humble will increase their joy in the LORD, and the poor among men will rejoice in the Holy One of Israel. 20 For the ruthless will vanish, the mockers will disappear, and all who look for evil will be cut down— 21 those who indict a man with a word, who ensnare the mediator at the gate, and who with false charges deprive the innocent of justice. 22 Therefore the LORD who redeemed Abraham says of the house of Jacob: “No longer will Jacob be ashamed and no more will his face grow pale. 23 For when he sees his children around him, the work of My hands, they will honor My name, they will sanctify the Holy One of Jacob, and they will stand in awe of the God of Israel. 24 Then the wayward in spirit will come to understanding, and those who grumble will accept instruction.”
paragraphs: 17 In a very short time, will not Lebanon become an orchard, and the orchard seem like a forest? 18 On that day the deaf will hear the words of the scroll, and out of the deep darkness the eyes of the blind will see. 19 The humble will increase their joy in the LORD, and the poor among men will rejoice in the Holy One of Israel.

20 For the ruthless will vanish, the mockers will disappear, and all who look for evil will be cut down— 21 those who indict a man with a word, who ensnare the mediator at the gate, and who with false charges deprive the innocent of justice.

22 Therefore the LORD who redeemed Abraham says of the house of Jacob: “No longer will Jacob be ashamed and no more will his face grow pale. 23 For when he sees his children around him, the work of My hands, they will honor My name, they will sanctify the Holy One of Jacob, and they will stand in awe of the God of Israel. 24 Then the wayward in spirit will come to understanding, and those who grumble will accept instruction.”

passages.context_html:
The promise answers the blindness, deafness and confusion of the preceding passage. Lebanon and fruitful land exchange their familiar appearance; the deaf hear the scroll, and the blind see out of darkness. The humble and poor find increasing joy in the Lord.

This restoration reaches public life as well as personal understanding. Ruthless people and mockers disappear. Those who twist words into charges, trap someone seeking justice and deprive the innocent of a fair hearing are cut down.

The Lord speaks to the house of Jacob as the One who redeemed Abraham. Jacob’s shame gives way to seeing children who are the work of God’s hands, honoring His name and standing in awe of Him. The final promise is especially hopeful: the wayward gain understanding, and those who grumbled become willing to learn.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The USCCB notes connect the changed landscape, opened senses and removal of injustice with a reversal of the people’s condition. The promise concerns a community made able to receive God’s instruction and live without its former oppression.

Henry, Wesley and Gill also read the passage through the spread of the gospel. Wesley and Gill connect the fruitful landscape with Gentiles receiving God’s word; Gill also connects the final promise with a future turning of Jewish people to Christ. These are readings of how the promised restoration unfolds, rather than different views of whether God can give understanding.

Across these explanations, the changed hearing and sight belong with changed conduct. Learning God’s word is pictured alongside humility, joy, honest judgment and reverence.

passages.god_plan_html:
When John the Baptist’s disciples ask whether Jesus is the One to come, Jesus points to the blind receiving sight, the deaf hearing and the poor receiving good news in Matthew 11:2–6. These works provide a strong parallel with Isaiah’s promised reversal. Matthew does not identify this answer as a quotation of Isaiah 29 alone.

The connection helps explain what restoration looks like in the ministry of Jesus: people receive sight and hearing, and the poor are welcomed with good news. Isaiah’s wider picture also keeps justice and willingness to learn in view. God’s purpose reaches people’s understanding, their treatment of one another and their joy in Him.

passages.title: Isaiah 30:1-17
passages.section_title: Why can a powerful ally become a refuge that fails?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 “Woe to the rebellious children,” declares the LORD, “to those who carry out a plan that is not Mine, who form an alliance, but against My will, heaping up sin upon sin. 2 They set out to go down to Egypt without asking My advice, to seek shelter under Pharaoh’s protection and take refuge in Egypt’s shade. 3 But Pharaoh’s protection will become your shame, and the refuge of Egypt’s shade your disgrace. 4 For though their princes are at Zoan and their envoys have arrived in Hanes, 5 everyone will be put to shame because of a people useless to them. They bring neither help nor benefit, but only shame and disgrace.” 6 This is the burden against the beasts of the Negev: Through a land of hardship and distress, of lioness and lion, of viper and flying serpent, they carry their wealth on the backs of donkeys and their treasures on the humps of camels, to a people of no profit to them. 7 Egypt’s help is futile and empty; therefore I have called her Rahab Who Sits Still. 8 Go now, write it on a tablet in their presence and inscribe it on a scroll; it will be for the days to come, a witness forever and ever. 9 These are rebellious people, deceitful children, children unwilling to obey the LORD’s instruction. 10 They say to the seers, “Stop seeing visions!” and to the prophets, “Do not prophesy to us the truth! Speak to us pleasant words; prophesy illusions. 11 Get out of the way; turn off the road. Rid us of the Holy One of Israel!” 12 Therefore this is what the Holy One of Israel says: “Because you have rejected this message, trusting in oppression and relying on deceit, 13 this iniquity of yours is like a breach about to fail, a bulge in a high wall, whose collapse will come suddenly— in an instant! 14 It will break in pieces like a potter’s jar, shattered so that no fragment can be found. Not a shard will be found in the dust large enough to scoop the coals from a hearth or to skim the water from a cistern.” 15 For the Lord GOD, the Holy One of Israel, has said: “By repentance and rest you would be saved; your strength would lie in quiet confidence— but you were not willing.” 16 “No,” you say, “we will flee on horses.” Therefore you will flee! “We will ride swift horses,” but your pursuers will be faster. 17 A thousand will flee at the threat of one; at the threat of five you will all flee, until you are left alone like a pole on a mountaintop, like a banner on a hill.

They bring neither help nor benefit, but only shame and disgrace.”

6 This is the burden against the beasts of the Negev: Through a land of hardship and distress, of lioness and lion, of viper and flying serpent, they carry their wealth on the backs of donkeys and their treasures on the humps of camels, to a people of no profit to them. 7 Egypt’s help is futile and empty; therefore I have called her Rahab Who Sits Still.

8 Go now, write it on a tablet in their presence and inscribe it on a scroll; it will be for the days to come, a witness forever and ever. 9 These are rebellious people, deceitful children, children unwilling to obey the LORD’s instruction. 10 They say to the seers, “Stop seeing visions!” and to the prophets, “Do not prophesy to us the truth! Speak to us pleasant words; prophesy illusions. 11 Get out of the way; turn off the road. Rid us of the Holy One of Israel!”

12 Therefore this is what the Holy One of Israel says: “Because you have rejected this message, trusting in oppression and relying on deceit, 13 this iniquity of yours is like a breach about to fail, a bulge in a high wall, whose collapse will come suddenly— in an instant! 14 It will break in pieces like a potter’s jar, shattered so that no fragment can be found. Not a shard will be found in the dust large enough to scoop the coals from a hearth or to skim the water from a cistern.”

15 For the Lord GOD, the Holy One of Israel, has said: “By repentance and rest you would be saved; your strength would lie in quiet confidence— but you were not willing.” 16 “No,” you say, “we will flee on horses.” Therefore you will flee! “We will ride swift horses,” but your pursuers will be faster. 17 A thousand will flee at the threat of one; at the threat of five you will all flee, until you are left alone like a pole on a mountaintop, like a banner on a hill.

passages.context_html:
The rebellious children are carrying out a plan without asking the Lord. They send envoys and wealth to Egypt, seeking Pharaoh’s protection. The journey is difficult and costly, yet the promised help will bring shame instead of safety.

Egypt receives the name Rahab Who Sits Still. Brown–Driver–Briggs identifies Rahab, pronounced RAH-hab, as an emblematic name for Egypt, alongside its use for a poetic sea monster. Here the name exposes the mismatch between impressive power and help that never comes.

The Lord tells Isaiah to record the message as a lasting witness. The people do not merely misunderstand a warning; they ask the seers to stop telling the truth and to give them pleasant words. They want the Holy One of Israel out of the way.

Their apparent security is compared with a bulging wall about to collapse and a jar smashed beyond useful repair. God offers repentance, rest and quiet confidence, but they choose swift horses instead. The answer is a sharp reversal: they will indeed flee, and their pursuers will be swifter.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry, Wesley and Gill read the journey to Egypt as an attempt to obtain security while refusing God’s counsel. Their practical warning is about depending on an arrangement opposed to His word, rather than about the mere existence of human help.

They also connect the demand for pleasant messages with deliberate resistance to correction. The recorded warning exposes the choice the people are making: they prefer reassurance over the truth that could call them back.

Gill discusses older translations of verse 7 that place the emphasis on sitting still in Jerusalem and trusting God. The BSB instead names Egypt as Rahab Who Sits Still. Both readings concern the failure of Egypt to provide the safety Judah expects, but the BSB’s wording directs the nickname at Egypt.

passages.god_plan_html:
The offered rest has a wider connection with the invitation of Jesus in Matthew 11:25–30. He calls the weary to come to Him, take His yoke and learn from Him. Rest is found through receiving His teaching, not through refusing all responsibility.

Hebrews 4:1–11 likewise joins God’s promised rest with hearing His word in faith and refusing to harden the heart. Its direct scriptural discussion is of creation, the wilderness generation and Psalm 95; this is a shared theme with Isaiah, rather than a quotation of Isaiah 30.

These connections place quiet confidence within a life of listening and responding to God. The alternative to frantic self-protection is trust that accepts His direction.

passages.title: Isaiah 30:18-33
passages.section_title: How do mercy, guidance and judgment belong in the same promise?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 Therefore the LORD longs to be gracious to you; therefore He rises to show you compassion, for the LORD is a just God. Blessed are all who wait for Him. 19 O people in Zion who dwell in Jerusalem, you will weep no more. He will surely be gracious when you cry for help; when He hears, He will answer you. 20 The Lord will give you the bread of adversity and the water of affliction, but your Teacher will no longer hide Himself—with your own eyes you will see Him. 21 And whether you turn to the right or to the left, your ears will hear this command behind you: “This is the way. Walk in it.” 22 So you will desecrate your silver-plated idols and your gold-plated images. You will throw them away like menstrual cloths, saying to them, “Be gone!” 23 Then He will send rain for the seed that you have sown in the ground, and the food that comes from your land will be rich and plentiful. Its funeral pyre is deep and wide, with plenty of fire and wood. The breath of the LORD, like a torrent of burning sulfur, sets it ablaze.

passages.context_html:
After the refusal to trust, the Lord still longs to be gracious. The promise pictures Him answering His people’s cry, making their Teacher visible and directing their steps. They respond by throwing away the silver- and gold-covered idols they once treasured.

The scene widens to rain, rich food, open pasture and plentiful water. Even the working animals share in the abundance. Extraordinary moonlight and sunlight accompany the day when the Lord binds up His people’s brokenness and heals the wounds He inflicted.

The final scene brings mercy and judgment together. God’s people sing and go up to His mountain, while His voice and arm strike the oppressor. Assyria is named as the power shattered by His action.

Topheth becomes the image of a funeral pyre made ready for the king and kindled by the Lord’s breath. Elsewhere, Jeremiah 7:30–34 identifies Topheth with the Valley of Ben-hinnom and condemns the burning of children there. Isaiah’s closing picture is a fearful reversal of power, not another source of protection for Assyria.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley connects the return to Jerusalem partly with the return from Babylon and more fully with the gospel. Henry emphasizes restored prayer, instruction, rejection of idols and the comfort of God’s word.

Gill discusses both human teachers and God Himself as explanations of verse 20. The BSB follows the singular reading, Teacher, and speaks of seeing Him. Gill and Henry interpret the greatly increased light as a picture of gospel understanding and joy; Wesley connects the healing with God bringing His people together.

For the closing judgment, Wesley reads the fall of Assyria as an approaching deliverance that gives assurance of greater mercy to come. Henry also treats the terrible fire as pointing beyond that event to final judgment. These explanations differ in how they relate the immediate deliverance to the larger promise.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The combination of God’s light, healed life, worship and the removal of evil reaches its fullest biblical picture in Revelation 21:22–27 and 22:1–5. God and the Lamb give light; the river of life flows from their throne; the tree’s leaves are for the healing of the nations; and God’s servants worship Him.

This is a parallel in the larger biblical account, not a claim that Revelation directly quotes Isaiah 30 or that every detail of the two scenes is identical. Isaiah’s promise already brings together things that can seem separate: God teaches and heals His people, removes what deceives them, and judges the power that threatens them.

The goal is a people who live by His light and gladly worship Him. Mercy does more than interrupt a crisis; it restores the relationship and the life that wrongdoing has damaged.

passages.title: Isaiah 31:1-9
passages.section_title: Who can protect Jerusalem when Egypt’s strength is not enough?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help, who rely on horses, who trust in their abundance of chariots and in their multitude of horsemen. They do not look to the Holy One of Israel; they do not seek the LORD. 2 Yet He too is wise and brings disaster; He does not call back His words. He will rise up against the house of the wicked and against the allies of evildoers. 3 But the Egyptians are men, not God; their horses are flesh, not spirit. When the LORD stretches out His hand, the helper will stumble, and the one he helps will fall; both will perish together. 4 For this is what the LORD has said to me: “Like a lion roaring or a young lion over its prey— and though a band of shepherds is called out against it, it is not terrified by their shouting or subdued by their clamor— so the LORD of Hosts will come down to do battle on Mount Zion and its heights. 5 Like birds hovering overhead, so the LORD of Hosts will protect Jerusalem. He will shield it and deliver it; He will pass over it and preserve it.” 6 Return to the One against whom you have so blatantly rebelled, O children of Israel. 7 For on that day, every one of you will reject the idols of silver and gold that your own hands have sinfully made. 8 “Then Assyria will fall, but not by the sword of man; a sword will devour them, but not one made by mortals. They will flee before the sword, and their young men will be put to forced labor. 9 Their rock will pass away for fear, and their princes will panic at the sight of the battle standard,” declares the LORD, whose fire is in Zion, whose furnace is in Jerusalem.

They will flee before the sword, and their young men will be put to forced labor. 9 Their rock will pass away for fear, and their princes will panic at the sight of the battle standard,” declares the LORD, whose fire is in Zion, whose furnace is in Jerusalem.

passages.context_html:
The warning continues the previous chapter’s concern: Judah looks to Egypt’s horses, chariots and horsemen while failing to seek the Lord. The contrast is between the human help they count and the God whose counsel they disregard. Egyptians are human and their horses are flesh; neither can overrule Him.

Two pictures then describe the Lord’s protection of Jerusalem. Like a lion holding its ground, He will not be frightened off by shouting. Like birds hovering overhead, He will shield and preserve the city. Strength and attentive care belong in the same promise.

The call is to return to the One they have rebelled against and reject their handmade silver and gold idols. Assyria will fall through an action that is not the sword of a human warrior. The Lord’s presence in Zion, pictured as fire and a furnace, becomes the answer to the threat.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry, Wesley and Gill read the chapter against the Assyrian danger to Jerusalem. They connect the sword that is not human with the destruction of the army by the Lord’s angel, later narrated in Isaiah 37.

Henry and Gill explain the lion as an image of power that cannot be intimidated, and the hovering birds as an image of tender protection. Gill also connects the promise of passing over Jerusalem with the Passover in Egypt.

The warning about Egypt is therefore joined to an invitation to return. The Lord does not simply expose an inadequate ally; He calls His people away from idols and toward the protection He has promised.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
The passing-over language gives this promise a clear connection with the earlier rescue from Egypt. The Hebrew verb pasach, pronounced pah-SAKH, is used here and in Exodus 12:23–27; Brown–Driver–Briggs lists both uses under passing over and sparing. Isaiah speaks of preservation through God’s action, as the Passover account does.

The New Testament takes that rescue into the account of Christ: 1 Corinthians 5:6–8 identifies Christ as the Passover lamb who has been sacrificed. Paul then calls believers to leave malice and wickedness for sincerity and truth.

This is a supported connection through Passover, not a statement that Paul directly quotes Isaiah 31. Across the passages, rescue belongs with a changed allegiance: the people spared by God are called to leave behind what dishonors Him.

passages.title: Isaiah 32:1-8
passages.section_title: What would leadership that truly shelters people look like?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Behold, a king will reign in righteousness, and princes will rule with justice. 2 Each will be like a shelter from the wind, a refuge from the storm, like streams of water in a dry land, like the shadow of a great rock in an arid land. 3 Then the eyes of those who see will no longer be closed, and the ears of those who hear will listen. 4 The mind of the rash will know and understand, and the stammering tongue will speak clearly and fluently. 5 No longer will a fool be called noble, nor a scoundrel be respected. 6 For a fool speaks foolishness; his mind plots iniquity. He practices ungodliness and speaks falsely about the LORD; he leaves the hungry empty and deprives the thirsty of drink. 7 The weapons of the scoundrel are destructive; he hatches plots to destroy the poor with lies, even when the plea of the needy is just. 8 But a noble man makes honorable plans; he stands up for worthy causes.
paragraphs: 1 Behold, a king will reign in righteousness, and princes will rule with justice. 2 Each will be like a shelter from the wind, a refuge from the storm, like streams of water in a dry land, like the shadow of a great rock in an arid land. 3 Then the eyes of those who see will no longer be closed, and the ears of those who hear will listen. 4 The mind of the rash will know and understand, and the stammering tongue will speak clearly and fluently.

5 No longer will a fool be called noble, nor a scoundrel be respected. 6 For a fool speaks foolishness; his mind plots iniquity. He practices ungodliness and speaks falsely about the LORD; he leaves the hungry empty and deprives the thirsty of drink. 7 The weapons of the scoundrel are destructive; he hatches plots to destroy the poor with lies, even when the plea of the needy is just. 8 But a noble man makes honorable plans; he stands up for worthy causes.

passages.context_html:
After warnings about leaders who trust the wrong protection, the chapter opens with a king reigning in righteousness and princes ruling with justice. Their rule is compared with shelter in a storm, water in dry country and shade in a weary land. People receive protection rather than being exposed to harm.

The change also reaches understanding and judgment. Eyes and ears become responsive, rash minds understand, and speech becomes clear. A fool will no longer pass for a noble person simply because people give him an honorable name.

The contrast is shown in conduct. The fool speaks falsely about the Lord and leaves the hungry and thirsty without help. The scoundrel uses lies to destroy poor people even when their plea is just. The noble person makes honorable plans and stands up for worthy causes.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley reads the king first as Hezekiah and then as a picture of Christ. He understands the princes as rulers whose conduct protects the people, with the promised change fully realized through Christ.

Henry identifies the righteous king with Christ and connects the shelter and refreshment with His protection. Gill likewise centers the king on Christ, while identifying the princes with ministers who must lead according to His word.

The readings differ over how the reign begins in Judah’s history and how the princes are identified. They share an emphasis on righteous rule that benefits people and exposes the difference between honorable titles and actual conduct.

passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus addresses a similar failure of leadership when His disciples dispute which of them is greatest in Luke 22:24–30. He contrasts rulers who dominate while calling themselves benefactors with His own presence among them as One who serves.

He then speaks of the kingdom His Father has given Him and a place for His disciples at His table. This provides a clear theme alongside Isaiah’s righteous king and just princes: authority under God is meant to serve His purpose and care for people, not to provide an honorable name for self-interest.

The contrast is especially sharp beside Isaiah’s hungry people and falsely accused poor. In the larger biblical picture, the character of the King shapes what leadership among His people should look like.

passages.title: Isaiah 32:9-20
passages.section_title: What can turn complacency and ruined land into lasting peace?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 Stand up, you complacent women; listen to me. Give ear to my word, you overconfident daughters. 10 In a little more than a year you will tremble, O secure ones. For the grape harvest will fail and the fruit harvest will not arrive. 11 Shudder, you ladies of leisure; tremble, you daughters of complacency. Strip yourselves bare and put sackcloth around your waists. 12 Beat your breasts for the pleasant fields, for the fruitful vines, 13 and for the land of my people, overgrown with thorns and briers— even for every house of merriment in this city of revelry. 14 For the palace will be forsaken, the busy city abandoned. The hill and the watchtower will become caves forever— the delight of wild donkeys and a pasture for flocks— 15 until the Spirit is poured out upon us from on high. Then the desert will be an orchard, and the orchard will seem like a forest. 16 Then justice will inhabit the wilderness, and righteousness will dwell in the fertile field. 17 The work of righteousness will be peace; the service of righteousness will be quiet confidence forever. 18 Then my people will dwell in a peaceful place, in safe and secure places of rest. 19 But hail will level the forest, and the city will sink to the depths. 20 Blessed are those who sow beside abundant waters, who let the ox and donkey range freely.

The hill and the watchtower will become caves forever— the delight of wild donkeys and a pasture for flocks—

15 until the Spirit is poured out upon us from on high. Then the desert will be an orchard, and the orchard will seem like a forest. 16 Then justice will inhabit the wilderness, and righteousness will dwell in the fertile field. 17 The work of righteousness will be peace; the service of righteousness will be quiet confidence forever. 18 Then my people will dwell in a peaceful place, in safe and secure places of rest.
19 But hail will level the forest, and the city will sink to the depths. 20 Blessed are those who sow beside abundant waters, who let the ox and donkey range freely.

passages.context_html:
The prophet addresses women who are comfortable and unconcerned, calling them to listen before their security disappears. In a little more than a year the grape and fruit harvest will fail. Fields, vines, joyful houses and the busy city become reasons for mourning.

The abandoned palace and city are pictured as places where animals range. The decisive change comes when the Spirit is poured out from on high. The land becomes fruitful, and justice and righteousness take up residence where ruin had been.

Peace is described as the work of righteousness, with quiet confidence and secure places of rest following it. The closing lines hold blessing and judgment together: the forest is struck by hail and the city brought low, while those sowing beside abundant waters are called blessed.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley connect the warning with complacency that refuses to take coming judgment seriously. Both look to the work of the Spirit for the promised change; Wesley places its full realization in the days of the Messiah.

Gill argues that the outpouring in verse 15 points beyond Pentecost to a future work of the Spirit associated with the turning of Jewish people to Christ and wider fruitfulness among the nations. The difference concerns the timing and reach of the promise, rather than whether the Spirit produces the change.

Wesley emphasizes peace as the outcome of justice and God’s mercy. Gill especially connects the peace with the righteousness Christ provides for His people. Both explanations place the source of lasting confidence in what God does, rather than in the complacency challenged at the beginning.

passages.god_plan_html:
At Pentecost, Peter explains the outpouring of the Spirit in Acts 2:14–21, 32–39. His direct quotation is from Joel, not Isaiah 32. He then declares that the risen and exalted Jesus has poured out the promised Spirit, and calls his hearers to repent.

That makes a strong parallel with Isaiah’s movement from a warning to the Spirit bringing new life. Galatians 5:16–26 develops what that life looks like: the Spirit produces love, joy, peace and other qualities that stand against hostility, rivalry and envy.

The larger purpose is more than a return to comfortable circumstances. God gives His Spirit to form people whose life bears the fruit of His character, including the peace and righteousness Isaiah sets together.

passages.title: Isaiah 33:1-24
passages.section_title: Who can give lasting security when treaties and strength collapse?

versions.label: BSB

When you have finished betraying, you will be betrayed. 2 O LORD, be gracious to us! We wait for You. Be our strength every morning and our salvation in time of trouble. 3 The peoples flee the thunder of Your voice; the nations scatter when You rise. 4 Your spoil, O nations, is gathered as by locusts; like a swarm of locusts men sweep over it. 5 The LORD is exalted, for He dwells on high; He has filled Zion with justice and righteousness. 6 He will be the sure foundation for your times, a storehouse of salvation, wisdom, and knowledge. The fear of the LORD is Zion’s treasure. 7 Behold, their valiant ones cry aloud in the streets; the envoys of peace weep bitterly. 8 The highways are deserted; travel has ceased. The treaty has been broken, the witnesses are despised, and human life is disregarded. 9 The land mourns and languishes; Lebanon is ashamed and decayed. Sharon is like a desert; Bashan and Carmel shake off their leaves. 10 “Now I will arise,” says the LORD. “Now I will lift Myself up. Now I will be exalted. 11 You conceive chaff; you give birth to stubble. Your breath is a fire that will consume you. 12 The peoples will be burned to ashes, like thorns cut down and set ablaze. 13 You who are far off, hear what I have done; you who are near, acknowledge My might.” 14 The sinners in Zion are afraid; trembling grips the ungodly: “Who of us can dwell with a consuming fire? Who of us can dwell with everlasting flames?” 15 He who walks righteously and speaks with sincerity, who refuses gain from extortion, whose hand never takes a bribe, who stops his ears against murderous plots and shuts his eyes tightly against evil— 16 he will dwell on the heights; the mountain fortress will be his refuge; his food will be provided and his water assured. 17 Your eyes will see the King in His beauty and behold a land that stretches afar. 18 Your mind will ponder the former terror: “Where is he who tallies? Where is he who weighs? Where is he who counts the towers?” 19 You will no longer see the insolent, a people whose speech is unintelligible, who stammer in a language you cannot understand. 20 Look upon Zion, the city of our appointed feasts. Your eyes will see Jerusalem, a peaceful pasture, a tent that does not wander; its tent pegs will not be pulled up, nor will any of its cords be broken. 21 But there the Majestic One, our LORD, will be for us a place of rivers and wide canals, where no galley with oars will row, and no majestic vessel will pass. 22 For the LORD is our Judge, the LORD is our lawgiver, the LORD is our King. It is He who will save us.

23 Your ropes are slack; they cannot secure the mast or spread the sail. Then an abundance of spoils will be divided, and even the lame will carry off plunder. 24 And no resident of Zion will say, “I am sick.” The people who dwell there will be forgiven of iniquity.

passages.context_html:
The chapter opens by warning a destroyer and traitor that the treatment given to others will return upon him. A prayer answers the threat: the people ask the Lord for grace, daily strength and salvation in trouble. Justice, righteousness, wisdom and reverence for Him are presented as the real sources of stability.

The suffering is visible. Peace envoys weep, highways are deserted, the treaty is broken and human life is disregarded. The land itself mourns. The Lord announces that He will rise, and the plans of the violent will become fuel for their own destruction.

The sight of His holiness also unsettles sinners within Zion. Their question about living with consuming fire is answered with a portrait of upright conduct: honest speech, refusal of extortion and bribes, and rejection of murderous plans and evil. The promised refuge belongs with a life that turns from wrongdoing.

The closing vision gives eyes something different to see: the King in His beauty, a land no longer hemmed in by terror, and Jerusalem as a secure tent. The Lord is named as Judge, lawgiver and King. The final promises reach beyond military relief to forgiveness of iniquity and the end of the residents’ sickness.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley identifies the destroyer with Sennacherib and connects the broken treaty with the Assyrian threat. Henry also reads the scene through Jerusalem’s distress and the Lord overthrowing a proud, treacherous enemy.

For the King in His beauty, Wesley begins with Hezekiah and then looks to Christ. Henry connects the promise with seeing Christ by faith and ultimately with the life in which sickness and trouble are gone.

Gill gives the secure Zion a wider application to the church, especially its future peace, and relates the final promises to the New Jerusalem. These readings differ over how the historical rescue opens into the larger promise. They do not reduce the last verse to military victory alone: forgiveness is central to the people’s restored life.

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 12:22–29 brings together several of the same themes: Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, God as Judge, an unshakable kingdom and reverent worship before the God who is a consuming fire. This is a thematic connection with Isaiah 33, rather than a claim that Hebrews directly quotes it.

Hebrews places Jesus, the mediator of the new covenant, at the center of that approach to God. The response is gratitude and acceptable worship, together with the warning not to refuse the One who speaks.

Isaiah’s question about safety before a holy God therefore belongs within a larger account of both mercy and holiness. Lasting security is not simply being inside the right city: God saves and forgives His people and calls them into a life that receives His word.

passages.title: Isaiah 34:1-4
passages.section_title: Why are all nations called to hear this warning?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Come near, O nations, to listen; pay attention, O peoples. Let the earth hear, and all that fills it, the world and all that springs from it. 2 The LORD is angry with all the nations and furious with all their armies. He will devote them to destruction; He will give them over to slaughter. 3 Their slain will be left unburied, and the stench of their corpses will rise; the mountains will flow with their blood. 4 All the stars of heaven will be dissolved. The skies will be rolled up like a scroll, and all their stars will fall like withered leaves from the vine, like foliage from the fig tree.
paragraphs: 1 Come near, O nations, to listen; pay attention, O peoples. Let the earth hear, and all that fills it, the world and all that springs from it. 2 The LORD is angry with all the nations and furious with all their armies. He will devote them to destruction; He will give them over to slaughter. 3 Their slain will be left unburied, and the stench of their corpses will rise; the mountains will flow with their blood. 4 All the stars of heaven will be dissolved. The skies will be rolled up like a scroll, and all their stars will fall like withered leaves from the vine, like foliage from the fig tree.

passages.context_html:
The audience expands to the nations, the peoples and the whole inhabited world. The warning concerns the Lord’s anger against their armies. No ruler or military force is outside the reach of His judgment.

The images are deliberately overwhelming: bodies left unburied, mountains flowing with blood, stars dissolving and the sky rolling up like a scroll. The falling stars are compared with withered leaves and foliage dropping from a fig tree.

These opening verses establish the wide scope before the chapter turns specifically to Edom. Read beside chapter 35, they form the dark side of a larger movement from judgment to the restoration of God’s people.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley understand the warning as reaching beyond one attacking army to the enemies of God’s people more broadly. Wesley explains the collapsing sky as the kind of prophetic language used to describe devastating upheaval.

The USCCB notes read chapters 34–35 together as a collection moving from the defeat of Zion’s enemies to Zion’s restoration. Their explanation keeps the worldwide opening connected with the particular judgment on Edom that follows.

These readings emphasize the scale of the warning and its relationship to deliverance. The terrifying language brings earthly strength into perspective before the Lord.
