passages.god_plan_html:
Revelation 6:12–17 takes up the same striking images: stars fall like figs shaken from a tree, and the sky recedes like a rolled scroll. Kings, commanders and people of every station seek shelter from the One on the throne and from the wrath of the Lamb.

This use of Isaiah’s imagery places the warning within the New Testament’s account of judgment. The Lamb is the One whose seal is opened; human rank and power cannot make people secure against Him.

The connection is clear in the images themselves. It does not require assigning a separate modern event to each falling star or leaf. The larger claim is that God’s judgment reaches powers that appear beyond challenge.

passages.title: Isaiah 34:5-17
passages.section_title: What becomes of a land set against God’s people?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 When My sword has drunk its fill in the heavens, then it will come down upon Edom, upon the people I have devoted to destruction. 6 The sword of the LORD is bathed in blood. It drips with fat— with the blood of lambs and goats, with the fat of the kidneys of rams. For the LORD has a sacrifice in Bozrah, a great slaughter in the land of Edom. 7 And the wild oxen will fall with them, the young bulls with the strong ones. Their land will be drenched with blood, and their soil will be soaked with fat. 8 For the LORD has a day of vengeance, a year of recompense for the cause of Zion. 9 Edom’s streams will be turned to tar, and her soil to sulfur; her land will become a blazing pitch. 10 It will not be quenched—day or night. Its smoke will ascend forever. From generation to generation it will lie desolate; no one will ever again pass through it. 11 The desert owl and screech owl will possess it, and the great owl and raven will dwell in it. The LORD will stretch out over Edom a measuring line of chaos and a plumb line of destruction. 12 No nobles will be left to proclaim a king, and all her princes will come to nothing. 13 Her towers will be overgrown with thorns, her fortresses with thistles and briers. She will become a haunt for jackals, an abode for ostriches. 14 The desert creatures will meet with hyenas, and one wild goat will call to another. There the night creature will settle and find her place of repose. 15 There the owl will make her nest; she will lay and hatch her eggs and gather her brood under her shadow. Even there the birds of prey will gather, each with its mate. 16 Search and read the scroll of the LORD: Not one of these will go missing, not one will lack her mate, because He has ordered it by His mouth, and He will gather them by His Spirit. 17 He has allotted their portion; His hand has distributed it by measure. They will possess it forever; they will dwell in it from generation to generation.

There the night creature will settle and find her place of repose. 15 There the owl will make her nest; she will lay and hatch her eggs and gather her brood under her shadow. Even there the birds of prey will gather, each with its mate.

They will possess it forever; they will dwell in it from generation to generation.

passages.context_html:
The judgment now names Edom and Bozrah. A sword and a great sacrifice picture the slaughter, while the reason is stated as the Lord’s day of vengeance for Zion’s cause. The scene presents judgment as His answer to wrong, rather than an uncontrolled contest between equal powers.

Edom’s streams, soil and land are pictured as tar, sulfur and burning pitch. Nobles and princes come to nothing; thorns take over towers and fortresses; and creatures occupy the places where people had lived.

The measuring line and plumb line in verse 11 reverse the usual expectation of building. The Hebrew words tohu, pronounced TOH-hoo, and bohu, pronounced BOH-hoo, are also paired in Genesis 1:2. Brown–Driver–Briggs and its entry for bohu connect their use here with chaos and emptiness. The picture is of an ordered human place being reduced to waste.

The closing command is to search and read the Lord’s scroll. The creatures will have their allotted place because His mouth has commanded and His Spirit gathers them. The ruins are not beyond His rule.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley read Edom as both the named enemy and a picture of opposition to God’s people more broadly. They see its desolation as a warning that attempts to ruin God’s people end in the ruin of the oppressor.

For the night creature in verse 14, Gill discusses a night bird as well as the Jewish association of Lilith with a female demon. The Brown–Driver–Briggs entry and the USCCB note identify the name with that night-demon imagery. The BSB retains the broader wording night creature.

That difference concerns one part of the ruined-land picture. The passage’s main movement is clear: places of human power become uninhabited waste, and the Lord’s announced judgment stands.

passages.god_plan_html:
The language of smoke rising forever appears again in Revelation 14:9–13, in the warning against worshiping the beast, and in Revelation 19:1–4, in praise after the judgment of the great prostitute. The latter passage explicitly joins God’s true and just judgment with His answer to the blood of His servants.

The New Testament thus carries this prophetic language into its larger account of God ending corrupt power and answering violence. Revelation also calls the saints to perseverance and faith in Jesus.

This connection follows the shared judgment imagery; it does not by itself identify Edom’s territory with every place in Revelation. The promise is that oppression does not have the final word before God.

passages.title: Isaiah 35:1-10
passages.section_title: What does God’s promised rescue look like for the weary?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 The wilderness and the dry land will be glad; the desert will rejoice and blossom like a rose. 2 It will bloom profusely and rejoice with joy and singing. The glory of Lebanon will be given to it, the splendor of Carmel and Sharon. They will see the glory of the LORD, the splendor of our God. 3 Strengthen the limp hands and steady the feeble knees! 4 Say to those with anxious hearts: “Be strong, do not fear! Behold, your God will come with vengeance. With divine retribution He will come to save you.” 5 Then the eyes of the blind will be opened and the ears of the deaf unstopped. 6 Then the lame will leap like a deer and the mute tongue will shout for joy. For waters will gush forth in the wilderness, and streams in the desert. 7 The parched ground will become a pool, the thirsty land springs of water. In the haunt where jackals once lay, there will be grass and reeds and papyrus. 8 And there will be a highway called the Way of Holiness. The unclean will not travel it— only those who walk in the Way— and fools will not stray onto it. 9 No lion will be there, and no vicious beast will go up on it. Such will not be found there, but the redeemed will walk upon it. 10 So the redeemed of the LORD will return and enter Zion with singing, crowned with everlasting joy. Gladness and joy will overtake them, and sorrow and sighing will flee.

Behold, your God will come with vengeance. With divine retribution He will come to save you.”

For waters will gush forth in the wilderness, and streams in the desert. 7 The parched ground will become a pool, the thirsty land springs of water. In the haunt where jackals once lay, there will be grass and reeds and papyrus.

8 And there will be a highway called the Way of Holiness. The unclean will not travel it— only those who walk in the Way— and fools will not stray onto it. 9 No lion will be there, and no vicious beast will go up on it. Gladness and joy will overtake them, and sorrow and sighing will flee.

passages.context_html:
The barren landscape of judgment gives way to a desert blooming and singing. The people will see the Lord’s glory, and the weak are called to take courage because God is coming to save them.

The rescue reaches people and land together. Blind eyes open, deaf ears hear, the lame leap and the mute sing. Water breaks out in the wilderness, and thirsty ground becomes a place of springs and growing plants.

A highway called the Way of Holiness leads the redeemed toward Zion. Uncleanness and threatening beasts do not govern this road. The chapter ends with the Lord’s redeemed returning in song, with everlasting joy replacing sorrow and sighing.

The movement is from fear and exhaustion to a secure journey home. The promise is not that the weary must create the way themselves; the God who comes to save is the source of their hope.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry sees the kingdom of Christ as the chapter’s great subject, while also noticing Judah’s historical relief. He connects the opened senses with people made able to receive God’s word and the highway with a life directed toward Him.

Wesley particularly emphasizes peoples receiving God’s grace where there had been spiritual barrenness. Gill includes the actual healings in Jesus’ ministry, changed understanding through the gospel, later restoration and the final joy of God’s redeemed people.

These explanations differ in how they distribute the promises across historical relief, the spread of the gospel and future completion. They share the conviction that the Lord brings restoration, holiness and joy; the images are not merely a call to feel more optimistic.

passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus points to the blind seeing, the deaf hearing and the lame walking when He answers John the Baptist’s question in Matthew 11:2–6. His works give concrete expression to the rescue Isaiah describes and help John’s messengers recognize the One who has come.

Hebrews 12:12–14 also takes up Isaiah’s call to strengthen limp hands and weak knees. It joins that encouragement with making straight paths and pursuing peace and holiness.

Together these uses keep the promise centered on God’s saving work and the life it opens. Jesus brings the promised help, and weary believers are encouraged to continue toward the holiness and joy of life with God.

passages.title: Isaiah 36:1-22
passages.section_title: Can a threatening voice be trusted simply because it sounds convincing?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 In the fourteenth year of Hezekiah’s reign, Sennacherib king of Assyria attacked and captured all the fortified cities of Judah. 2 And the king of Assyria sent the Rabshakeh, with a great army, from Lachish to King Hezekiah at Jerusalem. And he stopped by the aqueduct of the upper pool, on the road to the Launderer’s Field. 3 Then Eliakim son of Hilkiah the palace administrator, Shebna the scribe, and Joah son of Asaph the recorder, went out to him. 4 The Rabshakeh said to them, “Tell Hezekiah that this is what the great king, the king of Assyria, says: What is the basis of this confidence of yours? 5 You claim to have a strategy and strength for war, but these are empty words. In whom are you now trusting, that you have rebelled against me? 6 Look now, you are trusting in Egypt, that splintered reed of a staff that will pierce the hand of anyone who leans on it. Such is Pharaoh king of Egypt to all who trust in him. 7 But if you say to me, ‘We trust in the LORD our God,’ is He not the One whose high places and altars Hezekiah has removed, saying to Judah and Jerusalem, ‘You must worship before this altar’? 8 Now, therefore, make a bargain with my master, the king of Assyria. I will give you two thousand horses—if you can put riders on them! 9 For how can you repel a single officer among the least of my master’s servants when you depend on Egypt for chariots and horsemen? 10 So now, was it apart from the LORD that I have come up against this land to destroy it? The LORD Himself said to me, ‘Go up against this land and destroy it.’” 11 Then Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah said to the Rabshakeh, “Please speak to your servants in Aramaic, since we understand it. Do not speak to us in Hebrew in the hearing of the people on the wall.” 12 But the Rabshakeh replied, “Has my master sent me to speak these words only to you and your master, and not to the men sitting on the wall, who are destined with you to eat their own dung and drink their own urine?” 13 Then the Rabshakeh stood and called out loudly in Hebrew: “Hear the words of the great king, the king of Assyria! 14 This is what the king says: Do not let Hezekiah deceive you, for he cannot deliver you. 15 Do not let Hezekiah persuade you to trust in the LORD when he says, ‘The LORD will surely deliver us; this city will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria.’ 16 Do not listen to Hezekiah, for this is what the king of Assyria says: Make peace with me and come out to me. Then every one of you will eat from his own vine and his own fig tree, and drink water from his own cistern, 17 until I come and take you away to a land like your own—a land of grain and new wine, a land of bread and vineyards. 18 Do not let Hezekiah mislead you when he says, ‘The LORD will deliver us.’ Has the god of any nation ever delivered his land from the hand of the king of Assyria? 19 Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where are the gods of Sepharvaim? Have they delivered Samaria from my hand? 20 Who among all the gods of these lands has delivered his land from my hand? How then can the LORD deliver Jerusalem from my hand?” 21 But the people remained silent and did not answer a word, for Hezekiah had commanded, “Do not answer him.” 22 Then Hilkiah’s son Eliakim the palace administrator, Shebna the scribe, and Asaph’s son Joah the recorder came to Hezekiah with their clothes torn, and they relayed to him the words of the Rabshakeh.

passages.context_html:
The book now tells the story of the Assyrian threat directly. Sennacherib has captured Judah’s fortified cities and sends the Rabshakeh with an army from Lachish to Jerusalem. Eliakim, Shebna and Joah meet him at the upper pool’s aqueduct, on the road to the Launderer’s Field.

This is the same location where Isaiah was sent to meet Ahaz in Isaiah 7:3–9. Once again, Judah faces an intimidating enemy and a question about trust. The Rabshakeh dismisses Egypt’s help, mocks Judah’s military weakness and then attacks confidence in the Lord.

The officials ask him to speak Aramaic, which they understand, instead of Hebrew within hearing of the people on the wall. He refuses to keep the exchange private. Speaking loudly in Hebrew, he threatens the horror of siege and promises food, water and eventual resettlement if the people surrender.

His final appeal treats the Lord as though He were no more able to save than the gods of defeated nations. The people follow Hezekiah’s order and remain silent. The officials return with torn clothes and report the words to the king; the answer to the challenge comes in the next chapter.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Gill reads the speech as an effort to undermine trust and move the people to abandon Hezekiah. He distinguishes its true observation about Egypt’s weakness from its false conclusion that the Lord cannot save.

For the accusation about removed altars, Gill reads Hezekiah’s action as obedience rather than an offense against God. Second Kings 18:3–6 supports that distinction: it praises Hezekiah’s reforms and his trust in the Lord.

Henry’s explanation of the parallel account emphasizes the mixture of pride, deception and blasphemy in the speech, and the wisdom of leaving the matter with God rather than answering every taunt. The silence in this scene follows a particular royal instruction; the narrative continues into prayer and God’s answer.

passages.title: Isaiah 37:1-7
passages.section_title: Where does Hezekiah turn when the threatening words reach him?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 On hearing this report, King Hezekiah tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, and entered the house of the LORD. 2 And he sent Eliakim the palace administrator, Shebna the scribe, and the leading priests, all wearing sackcloth, to the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz 3 to tell him, “This is what Hezekiah says: Today is a day of distress, rebuke, and disgrace; for children have come to the point of birth, but there is no strength to deliver them. 4 Perhaps the LORD your God will hear the words of the Rabshakeh, whom his master the king of Assyria has sent to defy the living God, and He will rebuke him for the words that the LORD your God has heard. Therefore lift up a prayer for the remnant that still survives.” 5 So the servants of King Hezekiah went to Isaiah, 6 who replied, “Tell your master that this is what the LORD says: ‘Do not be afraid of the words you have heard, with which the servants of the king of Assyria have blasphemed Me. 7 Behold, I will put a spirit in him so that he will hear a rumor and return to his own land, where I will cause him to fall by the sword.’”
paragraphs: 1 On hearing this report, King Hezekiah tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, and entered the house of the LORD. 2 And he sent Eliakim the palace administrator, Shebna the scribe, and the leading priests, all wearing sackcloth, to the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz 3 to tell him, “This is what Hezekiah says: Today is a day of distress, rebuke, and disgrace; for children have come to the point of birth, but there is no strength to deliver them. 4 Perhaps the LORD your God will hear the words of the Rabshakeh, whom his master the king of Assyria has sent to defy the living God, and He will rebuke him for the words that the LORD your God has heard. Therefore lift up a prayer for the remnant that still survives.”

5 So the servants of King Hezekiah went to Isaiah, 6 who replied, “Tell your master that this is what the LORD says: ‘Do not be afraid of the words you have heard, with which the servants of the king of Assyria have blasphemed Me. 7 Behold, I will put a spirit in him so that he will hear a rumor and return to his own land, where I will cause him to fall by the sword.’”

passages.context_html:
The Assyrian speech reaches Hezekiah through his officials. He tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth and enters the Lord’s house. He sends the palace officials and leading priests to Isaiah, asking for prayer for the surviving remnant.

His comparison is painfully direct: children have reached the point of birth, but there is no strength to deliver them. It pictures a crisis the people cannot resolve by their own power. He also brings the insult against the living God into the appeal.

Isaiah’s answer begins by telling the king not to fear the words he has heard. The Lord promises to put a spirit in the Assyrian king, who will hear a rumor, return to his own land and fall by the sword there. The threatened people receive a word from God before they see the promised outcome.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry’s explanation of the parallel account emphasizes Hezekiah’s concern for the dishonor done to God and his appeal for the prophet’s prayer. The USCCB notes explain the childbirth comparison as a picture of extreme distress and helplessness.

Gill discusses several explanations of the spirit in verse 7, including fear, an inclination to return, and an angelic action against the king. These are attempts to explain how God brings about the withdrawal; the announced result is the same.

The scene is commonly read as a turn from intimidation toward seeking the Lord. Its assurance rests on the message Isaiah delivers, rather than on Hezekiah discovering that his army is stronger than he thought.

passages.title: Isaiah 37:8-13
passages.section_title: What happens when the threat returns after a word of reassurance?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 When the Rabshakeh heard that the king of Assyria had left Lachish, he withdrew and found the king fighting against Libnah. 9 Now Sennacherib had been warned about Tirhakah king of Cush: “He has set out to fight against you.” On hearing this, Sennacherib sent messengers to Hezekiah, saying, 10 “Give this message to Hezekiah king of Judah: ‘Do not let your God, in whom you trust, deceive you by saying that Jerusalem will not be delivered into the hand of the king of Assyria. 11 Surely you have heard what the kings of Assyria have done to all the other countries, devoting them to destruction. Will you then be spared? 12 Did the gods of the nations destroyed by my fathers rescue those nations—the gods of Gozan, Haran, and Rezeph, and of the people of Eden in Telassar? 13 Where are the kings of Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah?’”

10 “Give this message to Hezekiah king of Judah: ‘Do not let your God, in whom you trust, deceive you by saying that Jerusalem will not be delivered into the hand of the king of Assyria. 11 Surely you have heard what the kings of Assyria have done to all the other countries, devoting them to destruction. Will you then be spared? 12 Did the gods of the nations destroyed by my fathers rescue those nations—the gods of Gozan, Haran, and Rezeph, and of the people of Eden in Telassar? 13 Where are the kings of Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah?’”

passages.context_html:
The Rabshakeh returns and finds Sennacherib fighting at Libnah after leaving Lachish. News arrives that Tirhakah king of Cush has set out against him. Sennacherib then sends another message to Hezekiah.

This time the challenge directly accuses the God Hezekiah trusts of deceiving him. The letter lists defeated lands and asks whether Jerusalem can expect a different outcome. The Assyrian record of conquest is made to sound like proof that no deliverance is possible.

The passage continues the pressure rather than resolving it. Hezekiah has received the Lord’s promise, yet another threatening message still arrives. His response to that letter follows in verses 14–20.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Gill reads the renewed message as an attempt to force a quick surrender while another military concern presses upon Sennacherib. He notes that interpreters differ over which report is meant by the earlier promise that the king would hear a rumor.

Henry’s treatment of the parallel account places this renewed threat beside the prayer it prompts. The enemy’s message becomes the occasion for Hezekiah to bring the matter to God, rather than accept the enemy’s verdict as final.

These explanations follow the movement of the narrative: another danger does not cancel the promise, but it does test how Hezekiah will respond to the words he has received.

passages.title: Isaiah 37:14-20
passages.section_title: What is Hezekiah asking for when he spreads out the letter?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 So Hezekiah received the letter from the messengers, read it, and went up to the house of the LORD and spread it out before the LORD. 15 And Hezekiah prayed to the LORD: 16 “O LORD of Hosts, God of Israel, enthroned above the cherubim, You alone are God over all the kingdoms of the earth. You made the heavens and the earth. 17 Incline Your ear, O LORD, and hear; open Your eyes, O LORD, and see. Listen to all the words that Sennacherib has sent to defy the living God. 18 Truly, O LORD, the kings of Assyria have laid waste all these countries and their lands. 19 They have cast their gods into the fire and destroyed them, for they were not gods, but only wood and stone—the work of human hands. 20 And now, O LORD our God, save us from his hand, so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that You alone, O LORD, are God.”
paragraphs: 14 So Hezekiah received the letter from the messengers, read it, and went up to the house of the LORD and spread it out before the LORD. 15 And Hezekiah prayed to the LORD: 16 “O LORD of Hosts, God of Israel, enthroned above the cherubim, You alone are God over all the kingdoms of the earth. You made the heavens and the earth.

17 Incline Your ear, O LORD, and hear; open Your eyes, O LORD, and see. Listen to all the words that Sennacherib has sent to defy the living God. 18 Truly, O LORD, the kings of Assyria have laid waste all these countries and their lands. 19 They have cast their gods into the fire and destroyed them, for they were not gods, but only wood and stone—the work of human hands. 20 And now, O LORD our God, save us from his hand, so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that You alone, O LORD, are God.”

passages.context_html:
Hezekiah reads the letter, takes it to the house of the Lord and spreads it before Him. His prayer begins by naming God as the Lord of Hosts, the God of Israel and the Creator of heaven and earth. He alone is God over every kingdom.

The prayer does not pretend the Assyrian victories are imaginary. Hezekiah acknowledges the destruction of countries and their gods, then identifies the crucial difference: those gods were human workmanship, wood and stone.

He asks the living God to hear the defiance and save His people. The stated purpose reaches beyond Jerusalem’s relief: all the kingdoms of the earth are to know that the Lord alone is God. The letter is brought into a prayer centered on who God is and the honor of His name.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Gill explains the spread-out letter as a way of presenting the insult and the need before God, rather than supplying information God lacks. He connects the final request with the Lord making Himself known in a way the defeated idols could not.

Henry’s explanation of the parallel prayer emphasizes an appeal grounded in God’s honor. The USCCB note likewise contrasts Assyrian boasting with Hezekiah’s confession that God rules over every kingdom.

These readings make the substance of the prayer central. Spreading out a document expresses the appeal in this scene; the passage does not give the physical action an independent power.

passages.god_plan_html:
The believers’ prayer after Peter and John are threatened in Acts 4:23–31 provides a close parallel. They begin with God as Creator, bring the rulers’ threats before Him, and ask for boldness to speak His word while He acts through Jesus.

The prayers arise in different circumstances: Hezekiah asks for the city’s rescue, while the believers ask to continue their witness. Both bring the threat under the larger truth that human rulers do not stand above God’s purpose.

In Acts, that purpose is made known through Jesus and the Spirit-empowered witness to Him. The connection broadens the meaning of deliverance: prayer seeks more than escape from fear; it seeks the work through which God makes Himself known.

passages.title: Isaiah 37:21-35
passages.section_title: Why can Assyria’s success never make its king greater than God?

versions.label: BSB

Against whom have you raised your voice and lifted your eyes in pride? Against the Holy One of Israel! 24 Through your servants you have taunted the Lord, and you have said: “With my many chariots I have ascended to the heights of the mountains, to the remote peaks of Lebanon. I have cut down its tallest cedars, the finest of its cypresses. I have reached its farthest heights, the densest of its forests. 25 I have dug wells and drunk foreign waters. He will not come before it with a shield or build up a siege ramp against it. 34 He will go back the way he came, and he will not enter this city,’ declares the LORD. 35 ‘I will defend this city and save it for My own sake and for the sake of My servant David.’”

passages.context_html:
Isaiah sends the Lord’s answer because Hezekiah has prayed concerning Sennacherib. The king’s boasts about conquest are exposed as a challenge against the Holy One of Israel. Jerusalem’s threatened people are pictured answering their tormentor with contempt.

The Lord then states what the boast ignores: He planned long ago what has now happened. The fortified cities did not fall because Assyria possessed power independent of Him. He knows the king’s movements and rage, and will turn him back as an animal is controlled by a hook and bit.

A sign of renewed ordinary life is given to Hezekiah. The people will eat what grows on its own for two years, then sow, reap and plant vineyards in the third. The surviving remnant of Judah will take root and bear fruit again.

The final promise is specific. The Assyrian king will not enter Jerusalem or carry the announced attack through there. The Lord will defend the city for His own sake and for the sake of His servant David.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry’s treatment of the parallel passage and Gill emphasize that Assyria’s actions remain under God’s knowledge and government. Military success gives the king no ground to exalt himself against the One who allowed it.

Both connect the harvest sign with recovery after disruption. Henry considers whether a Sabbath year also explains the second year’s produce; Gill discusses that possibility alongside the interruption caused by invasion. The promise itself describes provision and the return of sowing and reaping.

Gill connects the reference to David with God’s promise concerning David’s descendants and, ultimately, the Messiah. Henry likewise places the rescue in God’s purpose and glory, rather than treating it as a reward earned by Jerusalem’s inhabitants.

passages.god_plan_html:
The reference to David reaches back to 2 Samuel 7:12–16, where the Lord promises an enduring house and kingdom. Isaiah’s rescue promise therefore belongs within a history longer than the immediate siege.

Luke 1:30–33 announces that Jesus will receive the throne of His father David and reign over the house of Jacob forever. His kingdom will not end.

This connection follows the promise named in Isaiah and its New Testament continuation. Jerusalem’s rescue is a real event in Judah’s history; the greater hope is the lasting reign God brings through David’s promised Son.

passages.title: Isaiah 37:36-38
passages.section_title: What becomes of the king who said the Lord could not save?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 36 Then the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000 men in the camp of the Assyrians. When the people got up the next morning, there were all the dead bodies! 37 So Sennacherib king of Assyria broke camp and withdrew. He returned to Nineveh and stayed there. 38 One day, while he was worshiping in the temple of his god Nisroch, his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer put him to the sword and escaped to the land of Ararat. And his son Esar-haddon reigned in his place.
paragraphs: 36 Then the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000 men in the camp of the Assyrians. When the people got up the next morning, there were all the dead bodies! 37 So Sennacherib king of Assyria broke camp and withdrew. He returned to Nineveh and stayed there. 38 One day, while he was worshiping in the temple of his god Nisroch, his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer put him to the sword and escaped to the land of Ararat. And his son Esar-haddon reigned in his place.

passages.context_html:
The promised reversal arrives through the angel of the Lord, who strikes down 185,000 in the Assyrian camp. The account presents the dead bodies in the morning as the decisive answer to the threat against Jerusalem.

Sennacherib withdraws to Nineveh. The story then moves to his death while worshiping in the temple of Nisroch: two of his sons kill him and flee to Ararat, and another son, Esar-haddon, succeeds him.

The contrast with the earlier boast is sharp. The king who treated the Lord like the powerless gods of conquered peoples cannot protect his own life in his god’s temple. The withdrawal and death also answer the word announced through Isaiah in verses 6–7.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry’s explanation of the parallel account reads the outcome as the exposure of human strength before God and an encouragement to trust His word. Gill likewise emphasizes the defeat by an angel rather than a victorious Judean army.

Gill records different explanations of the manner of death in the camp, including disease and fire. The biblical account itself names the angel’s action without specifying a medical mechanism.

The story’s emphasis is the fulfillment of God’s announced answer. Sennacherib’s threat does not determine Jerusalem’s fate, and the ruler’s own end stands in contrast with the confidence of his earlier words.

passages.god_plan_html:
Revelation 19:11–21 provides a supported parallel in its picture of rulers and armies unable to overcome the One called Faithful and True, the Word of God and King of kings.

The scenes are not identical: Isaiah describes the Assyrian camp and an angel of the Lord, while Revelation describes the rider and the gathered powers opposing Him. Their shared direction is the overthrow of proud force by God’s action, rather than salvation achieved by a stronger human coalition.

That places Jerusalem’s rescue beside the Bible’s larger hope that the powers opposing God cannot defeat His purpose. It does not require making every detail of the Assyrian campaign a prediction of a separate future event.

passages.title: Isaiah 38:1-8
passages.section_title: How does Hezekiah respond when his own life is threatened?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 In those days Hezekiah became mortally ill. The prophet Isaiah son of Amoz came to him and said, “This is what the LORD says: ‘Put your house in order, for you are about to die; you will not recover.’” 2 Then Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and prayed to the LORD, 3 saying, “Please, O LORD, remember how I have walked before You faithfully and with wholehearted devotion; I have done what is good in Your sight.” And Hezekiah wept bitterly. 4 And the word of the LORD came to Isaiah, saying, 5 “Go and tell Hezekiah that this is what the LORD, the God of your father David, says: ‘I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. Behold, I will add fifteen years to your life. 6 And I will deliver you and this city from the hand of the king of Assyria. I will defend this city. 7 This will be a sign to you from the LORD that He will do what He has promised: 8 I will make the sun’s shadow that falls on the stairway of Ahaz go back ten steps.’” So the sunlight went back the ten steps it had descended.
paragraphs: 1 In those days Hezekiah became mortally ill. The prophet Isaiah son of Amoz came to him and said, “This is what the LORD says: ‘Put your house in order, for you are about to die; you will not recover.’” 2 Then Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and prayed to the LORD, 3 saying, “Please, O LORD, remember how I have walked before You faithfully and with wholehearted devotion; I have done what is good in Your sight.” And Hezekiah wept bitterly.

4 And the word of the LORD came to Isaiah, saying, 5 “Go and tell Hezekiah that this is what the LORD, the God of your father David, says: ‘I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. Behold, I will add fifteen years to your life. 6 And I will deliver you and this city from the hand of the king of Assyria. I will defend this city. 7 This will be a sign to you from the LORD that He will do what He has promised: 8 I will make the sun’s shadow that falls on the stairway of Ahaz go back ten steps.’” So the sunlight went back the ten steps it had descended.

passages.context_html:
The narrative turns from the threatened city to Hezekiah’s serious illness. Isaiah tells him to put his house in order because he will die. The king turns to the wall, prays about his faithful walk before God and weeps bitterly.

The Lord sends Isaiah back with a personal answer: He has heard the prayer and seen the tears, and will add fifteen years to the king’s life. The answer also promises protection for Hezekiah and Jerusalem from Assyria.

The sign concerns the shadow on the stairway of Ahaz, which goes back ten steps. Its purpose is stated plainly: to confirm that the Lord will do what He has promised. The mention of deliverance still to come connects this account with the Assyrian crisis told in the preceding chapters.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry treats the prayer as an encouragement to seek God in illness, while explicitly recognizing that other people may not receive the same answer Hezekiah did. His explanation of 2 Kings 20 also understands the recovery and sign as acts of God’s power.

Gill reads Hezekiah’s reference to a faithful life as an appeal made sincerely before God, rather than a claim that he has earned mercy. He connects the answer’s mention of David with God’s continuing purpose for David’s house.

The USCCB notes place the illness before the siege account, noting the promise of future deliverance. They also discuss the stairway and sundial explanations of the sign. The BSB describes a stairway; the passage does not explain the physical mechanism of the shadow’s reversal.

passages.god_plan_html:
James 5:13–18 places prayer, care for the sick, confession and praise within the life of the church. The sufferer is called to pray, and the sick person to call the elders for prayer in the Lord’s name.

This is a wider biblical theme alongside Hezekiah’s appeal, rather than a direct quotation of Isaiah 38. Need and illness can be brought before God, and His people are to share in that prayer rather than leave the sufferer alone.

The answer to Hezekiah remains a particular promise with a particular sign. The larger connection is the Lord’s attentive mercy and the place of prayer among His people, not a rule that every life will be extended by the same number of years.

passages.title: Isaiah 38:9-22
passages.section_title: What does a restored life give Hezekiah a chance to do?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 This is a writing by Hezekiah king of Judah after his illness and recovery: 10 I said, “In the prime of my life I must go through the gates of Sheol and be deprived of the remainder of my years.” 11 I said, “I will never again see the LORD, even the LORD, in the land of the living; I will no longer look on mankind with those who dwell in this world. 12 My dwelling has been picked up and removed from me like a shepherd’s tent. I have rolled up my life like a weaver; He cuts me off from the loom; from day until night You make an end of me. 13 I composed myself until the morning. Like a lion He breaks all my bones; from day until night You make an end of me. 14 I chirp like a swallow or crane; I moan like a dove. My eyes grow weak as I look upward. O Lord, I am oppressed; be my security.” 15 What can I say? He has spoken to me, and He Himself has done this. I will walk slowly all my years because of the anguish of my soul. 16 O Lord, by such things men live, and in all of them my spirit finds life. You have restored me to health and have let me live. 17 Surely for my own welfare I had such great anguish; but Your love has delivered me from the pit of oblivion, for You have cast all my sins behind Your back. 18 For Sheol cannot thank You; Death cannot praise You. Those who descend to the Pit cannot hope for Your faithfulness. 19 The living, only the living, can thank You, as I do today; fathers will tell their children about Your faithfulness. 20 The LORD will save me; we will play songs on stringed instruments all the days of our lives in the house of the LORD. 21 Now Isaiah had said, “Prepare a lump of pressed figs and apply it to the boil, and he will recover.” 22 And Hezekiah had asked, “What will be the sign that I will go up to the house of the LORD?”

Like a lion He breaks all my bones; from day until night You make an end of me. 14 I chirp like a swallow or crane; I moan like a dove. My eyes grow weak as I look upward. O Lord, I am oppressed; be my security.”

15 What can I say? He has spoken to me, and He Himself has done this. I will walk slowly all my years because of the anguish of my soul. 16 O Lord, by such things men live, and in all of them my spirit finds life. You have restored me to health and have let me live. 17 Surely for my own welfare I had such great anguish; but Your love has delivered me from the pit of oblivion, for You have cast all my sins behind Your back.

18 For Sheol cannot thank You; Death cannot praise You. Those who descend to the Pit cannot hope for Your faithfulness. 19 The living, only the living, can thank You, as I do today; fathers will tell their children about Your faithfulness. 20 The LORD will save me; we will play songs on stringed instruments all the days of our lives in the house of the LORD.
21 Now Isaiah had said, “Prepare a lump of pressed figs and apply it to the boil, and he will recover.” 22 And Hezekiah had asked, “What will be the sign that I will go up to the house of the LORD?”

passages.context_html:
Hezekiah’s writing recalls the distress of expecting an early death. A shepherd’s tent being taken away and a weaver’s cloth being cut from the loom picture a life that seems abruptly ended. His weak cries are compared with birds, and he appeals to the Lord for security.

The song turns toward gratitude for life restored. He speaks of anguish serving his welfare, of God’s love delivering him from the pit, and of his sins being cast behind God’s back.

His reason for valuing continued life includes praise and passing on the Lord’s faithfulness to children. He intends to sing in the Lord’s house throughout his remaining days. The closing notes recall the pressed figs applied to the boil and the king’s question about the sign of returning to worship.

The song holds distress and thanksgiving together. It remembers the fear honestly while describing restored life as an opportunity to honor the One who gave it.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry emphasizes remembering mercy and using restored life to praise God and do good. He also notes that the command to use figs sits alongside the promise of recovery: the account does not set practical means against trust in God.

Wesley explains the statement that the dead cannot praise as referring to praise among people on earth and receiving the promises in the land of the living. Gill similarly distinguishes that earthly activity from his belief that souls praise God in heaven.

For the sins cast behind God’s back, Gill explains the image as forgiveness, not a loss of divine knowledge. The song’s emphasis is on mercy received and the grateful life that follows.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html:
Hezekiah receives more years, but the song’s encounter with death points toward a need beyond a temporary recovery. First Corinthians 15:16–26 names Christ’s resurrection as the beginning of the resurrection of those who belong to Him and death as the last enemy to be destroyed.

Paul ends that chapter by joining the coming victory over death with gratitude and steadfast service in verses 51–58. The hope is not simply a longer version of the same mortal life, but the change from perishability to immortality through the Lord Jesus Christ.

This is a connection in the Bible’s larger account of life and death, not a claim that Hezekiah’s song already explains every detail of resurrection. His renewed chance to praise God is set beside the fuller hope of a life death cannot finally end.

passages.title: Isaiah 39:1-8
passages.section_title: What danger remains after a remarkable rescue?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 At that time Merodach-baladan son of Baladan king of Babylon sent letters and a gift to Hezekiah, for he had heard about Hezekiah’s illness and recovery. 2 And Hezekiah welcomed the envoys gladly and showed them what was in his treasure house—the silver, the gold, the spices, and the precious oil, as well as his entire armory—all that was found in his storehouses. There was nothing in his palace or in all his dominion that Hezekiah did not show them. 3 Then the prophet Isaiah went to King Hezekiah and asked, “Where did those men come from, and what did they say to you?” “They came to me from a distant land,” Hezekiah replied, “from Babylon.” 4 “What have they seen in your palace?” Isaiah asked. “They have seen everything in my palace,” answered Hezekiah. “There is nothing among my treasures that I did not show them.” 5 Then Isaiah said to Hezekiah, “Hear the word of the LORD of Hosts: 6 The time will surely come when everything in your palace and all that your fathers have stored up until this day will be carried off to Babylon. Nothing will be left, says the LORD. 7 And some of your descendants, your own flesh and blood, will be taken away to be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.” 8 But Hezekiah said to Isaiah, “The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good.” For he thought, “At least there will be peace and security in my lifetime.”
paragraphs: 1 At that time Merodach-baladan son of Baladan king of Babylon sent letters and a gift to Hezekiah, for he had heard about Hezekiah’s illness and recovery. 2 And Hezekiah welcomed the envoys gladly and showed them what was in his treasure house—the silver, the gold, the spices, and the precious oil, as well as his entire armory—all that was found in his storehouses. There was nothing in his palace or in all his dominion that Hezekiah did not show them. 3 Then the prophet Isaiah went to King Hezekiah and asked, “Where did those men come from, and what did they say to you?” “They came to me from a distant land,” Hezekiah replied, “from Babylon.” 4 “What have they seen in your palace?” Isaiah asked. “They have seen everything in my palace,” answered Hezekiah. “There is nothing among my treasures that I did not show them.”

5 Then Isaiah said to Hezekiah, “Hear the word of the LORD of Hosts: 6 The time will surely come when everything in your palace and all that your fathers have stored up until this day will be carried off to Babylon. Nothing will be left, says the LORD. 7 And some of your descendants, your own flesh and blood, will be taken away to be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.” 8 But Hezekiah said to Isaiah, “The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good.” For he thought, “At least there will be peace and security in my lifetime.”

passages.context_html:
The king of Babylon sends letters and a gift after hearing of Hezekiah’s illness and recovery. Hezekiah welcomes the envoys and shows them his treasures, supplies and armory. When Isaiah asks what they have seen, the king acknowledges that nothing has been withheld.

The Lord’s answer turns the display of wealth into a warning. Everything accumulated in the palace will one day be carried to Babylon, and some of Hezekiah’s descendants will serve there as eunuchs. The power sending a friendly gift is also the destination named in the coming loss.

Hezekiah calls the Lord’s word good, thinking of peace and security during his lifetime. The chapter closes with relief for the present generation alongside a grave warning about those to come. The earlier rescue from Assyria has not removed the need for faithful trust.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry’s explanation of the parallel account and Gill read the display as pride and confidence in human recognition. Henry connects it with an opportunity to speak of God’s work that was instead occupied by the king’s possessions. Second Chronicles 32:24–31 also links this period with pride, humbling and the test presented by the Babylonian envoys.

For Hezekiah’s final response, Henry, Gill and the Cambridge commentary on verse 8 read it as acceptance of God’s sentence and gratitude that mercy remains in its postponement. Gill explicitly argues that it need not mean indifference to his descendants.

The warning still stands in those readings. A period of peace in Hezekiah’s life does not reverse the announced loss of the palace’s treasures or the exile of his descendants.

passages.god_plan_html:
The move toward Babylon becomes a major part of the history leading to Christ. Matthew 1:11–17 marks the exile as a turning point in Jesus’ genealogy, then continues through the generations after it to Jesus, called Christ.

This is a connection in the unfolding biblical story, not a statement that Matthew directly quotes Isaiah 39. The exile is a real judgment and loss, yet it does not prevent God’s purpose from continuing through the family line.

Beside the Lord’s earlier promise concerning David, the ending leaves the reader looking beyond one king’s lifetime. Lasting hope rests in God’s faithfulness through judgment and restoration, ultimately reaching the promised Christ.

passages.title: Isaiah 40:1-5
passages.section_title: What hope follows the warning about Babylon?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 “Comfort, comfort My people,” says your God. 2 “Speak tenderly to Jerusalem, and proclaim to her that her forced labor has been completed; her iniquity has been pardoned. For she has received from the hand of the LORD double for all her sins.” 3 A voice of one calling: “Prepare the way for the LORD in the wilderness; make a straight highway for our God in the desert. 4 Every valley shall be lifted up, and every mountain and hill made low; the uneven ground will become smooth, and the rugged land a plain. 5 And the glory of the LORD will be revealed, and all humanity together will see it.” For the mouth of the LORD has spoken.
paragraphs: 1 “Comfort, comfort My people,” says your God. 2 “Speak tenderly to Jerusalem, and proclaim to her that her forced labor has been completed; her iniquity has been pardoned. For she has received from the hand of the LORD double for all her sins.”

3 A voice of one calling: “Prepare the way for the LORD in the wilderness; make a straight highway for our God in the desert. 4 Every valley shall be lifted up, and every mountain and hill made low; the uneven ground will become smooth, and the rugged land a plain. 5 And the glory of the LORD will be revealed, and all humanity together will see it.” For the mouth of the LORD has spoken.

passages.context_html:
After chapter 39 announces loss and exile to Babylon, the book turns to words of comfort for God’s people. Jerusalem is to hear that her forced labor has ended and her iniquity has been pardoned. The announcement addresses the suffering without making it the final word.

A voice calls for a highway in the wilderness for the Lord Himself. Valleys rise, mountains and hills are lowered, and rough ground becomes smooth. Every obstacle is pictured giving way before His coming.

The result is the revelation of the Lord’s glory, which all humanity will see together. The final reason for confidence is not the people’s ability to reshape the landscape: the Lord has spoken.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and the USCCB notes connect the comfort and wilderness road with return from Babylon. Wesley also looks principally to redemption through the Messiah, whose coming John the Baptist announces. Henry likewise joins the historical return with the greater comfort made known in Christ.

For double in verse 2, Wesley explains a measure of chastisement sufficient for God’s purpose, rather than punishment beyond what is deserved. Gill discusses both sufficient chastisement and abundant grace, preferring to connect the fullness with Christ’s satisfaction for sin.

The explanations differ over how the language of pardon and double is developed. The shared direction is comfort grounded in God’s action, leading into the announcement of His coming.

passages.god_plan_html:
All four Gospels connect the wilderness voice with John the Baptist preparing for Jesus: Matthew 3:1–3, Mark 1:1–8, Luke 3:1–6 and John 1:19–28. John’s call to repentance is preparation to receive the One coming after him.

Luke includes the valleys, mountains and rough paths, ending with all humanity seeing God’s salvation. John’s own testimony directs attention away from his status and toward the One whose way he prepares.

The New Testament therefore places this promise directly in the announcement of Jesus. Comfort is more than reassurance that difficult circumstances will improve; it is bound to the coming of the Lord and the salvation He brings.

passages.title: Isaiah 40:6-8
passages.section_title: What can be trusted when human strength and beauty fade?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 A voice says, “Cry out!” And I asked, “What should I cry out?” “All flesh is like grass, and all its glory like the flowers of the field. 7 The grass withers and the flowers fall when the breath of the LORD blows on them; indeed, the people are grass. 8 The grass withers and the flowers fall, but the word of our God stands forever.”
paragraphs: 6 A voice says, “Cry out!” And I asked, “What should I cry out?” “All flesh is like grass, and all its glory like the flowers of the field. 7 The grass withers and the flowers fall when the breath of the LORD blows on them; indeed, the people are grass. 8 The grass withers and the flowers fall, but the word of our God stands forever.”

passages.context_html:
Another voice commands a proclamation, and the speaker asks what to announce. The answer compares all flesh and its glory with grass and field flowers. Their beauty is real, but it does not endure.

The Lord’s breath makes the grass wither and the flowers fall. The people themselves are included in the comparison; no human greatness can turn a passing life into something permanent.

The final line gives the contrast on which the surrounding comfort rests: God’s word stands forever. The promise does not depend on human strength lasting long enough to accomplish it.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley read the contrast as an answer to confidence in human status, possessions or accomplishment. What people possess and achieve is fragile beside the word of the One who does not change.

Wesley especially connects the enduring word with the certainty of the promises just announced. Human weakness does not make God’s speech weak or leave its fulfillment dependent on the passing power of a ruler or generation.

passages.god_plan_html:
First Peter 1:22–25 directly quotes the grass, flowers and enduring word. Peter explains that believers have been born again through God’s living and enduring word, and identifies that word with the message proclaimed to them.

The surrounding instruction is to love one another deeply from a pure heart. The enduring word is therefore connected with both new life and the life believers share with one another.

Isaiah’s contrast between passing flesh and lasting speech becomes part of the New Testament’s explanation of hope: God gives life through the good news, and that life is to bear the fruit of sincere love.

passages.title: Isaiah 40:9-31
passages.section_title: Can the God who rules everything overlook His weary people?

passages.context_html:
Zion and Jerusalem are called to announce good news to Judah’s cities: their God is coming. His strength is joined to a shepherd’s care. He gathers lambs close to His heart and gently leads the nursing ewes.

The questions that follow make His greatness plain. Who measures the waters and heavens? Who weighs mountains or teaches the Lord justice? Nations are like a drop or a speck beside Him. Even Lebanon’s resources could not provide an offering equal to His greatness.

The comparison with idols exposes the absurdity of treating a crafted object as His equal. An idol must be made, decorated and secured so it will not fall. The Lord reigns above the earth, brings rulers low and calls the stars by name.

This reaches a very personal complaint: Israel feels its way is hidden and its claim ignored. The answer joins power with care. The everlasting Creator neither tires nor lacks understanding; He gives strength to the faint, and those who wait upon Him receive renewed strength.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley read the questions about creation and rule as grounds for trusting the comfort already announced. God does not need advice, assistance or an image made by human hands in order to act.

For the coming Lord in verse 10, Gill discusses a reading focused on Christ’s second coming, but prefers His first coming in this context because of John’s preparation and the shepherd picture. Henry also connects the shepherd’s tenderness with Christ’s care for His people.

For the final complaint, Wesley and Gill understand hiddenness as the people’s feeling that their suffering and cause are being neglected. The answer is not that their pain is too small to matter, but that the Lord has the understanding and strength to sustain them.

Gill explains waiting as continuing in confidence, prayer and reliance on God, rather than simply standing still. The renewed strength is applied to persevering in faith and obedience through difficulty.

passages.god_plan_html:
Paul directly uses Isaiah’s question about the Lord’s counselor in Romans 11:33–36. It concludes his discussion of God’s mercy to Jews and Gentiles with worship: the wisdom behind His purpose exceeds human ability to trace it.

In 1 Corinthians 2:9–16, Paul again uses the question about knowing or instructing the Lord. He explains that God reveals His gifts through the Spirit and brings the discussion to the mind of Christ. The God who cannot be taught is the One who graciously makes His truth known.

The shepherd picture also has a clear parallel in John 10:11–18. Jesus describes His care through laying down His life for the sheep and gathering them into one flock. Together these connections show divine greatness serving a saving purpose: God reveals, gathers and sustains His people.

passages.title: Isaiah 41:1-20
passages.section_title: Who gives a vulnerable people a reason not to fear?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 “Be silent before Me, O islands, and let the peoples renew their strength. Let them come forward and testify; let us together draw near for judgment. 2 Who has aroused one from the east and called him to his feet in righteousness? He hands nations over to him and subdues kings before him. He turns them to dust with his sword, to windblown chaff with his bow. 3 He pursues them, going on safely, hardly touching the path with his feet. 4 Who has performed this and carried it out, calling forth the generations from the beginning? I, the LORD—the first and the last— I am He.” 5 The islands see and fear; the ends of the earth tremble. They approach and come forward. 6 Each one helps the other and says to his brother, “Be strong!” 7 The craftsman encourages the goldsmith, and he who wields the hammer cheers him who strikes the anvil, saying of the welding, “It is good.” He nails it down so it will not be toppled. 8 “But you, O Israel, My servant, Jacob, whom I have chosen, descendant of Abraham My friend— 9 I brought you from the ends of the earth and called you from its farthest corners. I will turn the desert into a pool of water, and the dry land into flowing springs. 19 I will plant cedars in the wilderness, acacias, myrtles, and olive trees. I will set cypresses in the desert, elms and boxwood together, 20 so that all may see and know, may consider and understand, that the hand of the LORD has done this and the Holy One of Israel has created it.”

passages.context_html:
The islands and peoples are summoned to come forward as in a hearing. The question is who has raised up the victorious figure from the east and directed the generations from the beginning. The Lord answers that He is the first and the last.

The frightened nations encourage one another, but the scene of their work ends with an idol being nailed down so it will not fall. That manufactured support is set beside God’s promise to uphold Israel Himself.

Israel is addressed as the Lord’s chosen servant, Jacob, the descendant of Abraham His friend. The repeated assurance is personal: God is with them, strengthens them and holds their right hand. The small, vulnerable people pictured as a worm will be helped rather than abandoned.

The title Redeemer adds to that promise. The Hebrew form go’el, pronounced goh-EL, comes from a verb that Brown–Driver–Briggs explains as redeeming and acting as a kinsman. The lexicon lists this verse among its uses for God rescuing His people. The One who claims them also takes up their cause.

The closing picture is of the poor and needy receiving water where none could be found. Rivers, springs and trees replace barrenness, so that people see and understand that the Holy One of Israel has done it.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley identifies the victorious figure from the east with Cyrus, and Henry favors Cyrus while also discussing Abraham. They read the success of the figure as evidence that the Lord governs events rather than depending on an idol.

Gill surveys those explanations but offers a different reading centered on Paul’s gospel ministry. He then applies the servant language to believers as Abraham’s spiritual descendants. This is Gill’s own reading, rather than an official statement speaking for all Baptists.

For the assurance to Jacob, Henry and Wesley explain the worm image through weakness and being trampled by proud enemies. Both make God’s help central. Henry also applies the water and fruitfulness to the grace and life God brings through the gospel.

The readings differ over the historical figure and how the promises extend to later believers. The text’s stated foundation for courage is the Lord’s choice, presence and commitment to help His servant.

passages.god_plan_html:
The Redeemer’s care for the vulnerable has a strong connection with Hebrews 2:14–18. It explains that Jesus shares the humanity of those He helps, frees them from slavery through fear of death, and becomes a merciful and faithful high priest.

Hebrews specifically speaks of helping Abraham’s descendants and of Jesus being able to help those who are tempted because He Himself suffered. The connection develops the theme of rescue joined to relationship and attentive care.

This is not a claim that Hebrews directly quotes Isaiah 41 or settles every question about Israel’s future. It shows how God’s saving help is made known through the Son who truly shares human life and acts for His people.

passages.title: Isaiah 41:21-29
passages.section_title: What can an idol actually promise or accomplish?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 “Present your case,” says the LORD. “Submit your arguments,” says the King of Jacob. 22 “Let them come and tell us what will happen. Tell the former things, so that we may reflect on them and know the outcome. Or announce to us what is coming. 23 Tell us the things that are to come, so that we may know that you are gods. Yes, do something good or evil, that we may look on together in dismay. 24 Behold, you are nothing and your work is of no value. Anyone who chooses you is detestable. 25 I have raised up one from the north, and he has come— one from the east who calls on My name. He will march over rulers as if they were mortar, like a potter who treads the clay. 26 Who has declared this from the beginning, so that we may know, and from times past, so that we may say: ‘He was right’? No one announced it, no one foretold it, no one heard your words. 27 I was the first to tell Zion: ‘Look, here they are!’ And I gave to Jerusalem a herald of good news. 28 When I look, there is no one; there is no counselor among them; when I ask them, they have nothing to say. 29 See, they are all a delusion; their works amount to nothing; their images are as empty as the wind.

Tell the former things, so that we may reflect on them and know the outcome. Or announce to us what is coming. 23 Tell us the things that are to come, so that we may know that you are gods. Yes, do something good or evil, that we may look on together in dismay. 24 Behold, you are nothing and your work is of no value. Anyone who chooses you is detestable.

25 I have raised up one from the north, and he has come— one from the east who calls on My name. He will march over rulers as if they were mortar, like a potter who treads the clay. 26 Who has declared this from the beginning, so that we may know, and from times past, so that we may say: ‘He was right’? No one announced it, no one foretold it, no one heard your words. 27 I was the first to tell Zion: ‘Look, here they are!’ And I gave to Jerusalem a herald of good news. 28 When I look, there is no one; there is no counselor among them; when I ask them, they have nothing to say. 29 See, they are all a delusion; their works amount to nothing; their images are as empty as the wind.

passages.context_html:
The hearing turns into a direct challenge. The idols are called to explain former events, announce what is coming or do something that could demonstrate divine power. Their silence exposes the difference between an object of worship and the living God.

The Lord describes raising up a figure who comes from the north and east and marches over rulers like clay. He asks who announced this beforehand. No counselor among the idols can answer, while He gives Jerusalem a herald of good news.

The verdict closes the chapter: the images and their works are empty. The challenge is about reliable speech and effective action together. The Lord does not merely claim knowledge; He brings about the purpose He announces.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley reads the figure from the north and east as Cyrus and connects his calling on the Lord’s name with the proclamation in Ezra 1:1–4. Henry likewise places the chapter’s deliverance against the idols’ inability to know and accomplish God’s purpose.

Gill discusses Cyrus but prefers an application to Constantine and the spread of Christianity. That is a particular commentator’s explanation of the figure, rather than an identification supplied by name in these verses.

Across the explanations, the challenge exposes the idols as unable to give the answer their worshipers need. Henry carries the good news of deliverance forward to the greater rescue made known through Christ.

passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus explains the purpose of telling His disciples what is coming in John 13:18–20: when it happens, they are to believe that He is who He says He is. The Scripture directly quoted there is about the betrayal by one sharing His bread; it is not a quotation of Isaiah 41.

The connection is a shared theme: God’s announced word gives His people grounds for trust when events unfold. In John, the approaching betrayal does not reveal that Jesus has lost control of His mission; He prepares His disciples to recognize Him through it.

Isaiah’s challenge to the silent idols therefore belongs to the wider biblical distinction between powerless assurances and the God who makes Himself known through His word and action. The New Testament centers that trust on Jesus.

passages.title: Isaiah 42:1-9
passages.section_title: How will God’s chosen Servant bring justice?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 “Here is My Servant, whom I uphold, My Chosen One, in whom My soul delights. I will put My Spirit on Him, and He will bring justice to the nations. 2 He will not cry out or raise His voice, nor make His voice heard in the streets. 3 A bruised reed He will not break and a smoldering wick He will not extinguish; He will faithfully bring forth justice. 4 He will not grow weak or discouraged before He has established justice on the earth. In His law the islands will put their hope.” 5 This is what God the LORD says— He who created the heavens and stretched them out, who spread out the earth and its offspring, who gives breath to the people on it and life to those who walk in it: 6 “I, the LORD, have called you for a righteous purpose, and I will take hold of your hand. I will keep you and appoint you to be a covenant for the people and a light to the nations, 7 to open the eyes of the blind, to bring prisoners out of the dungeon and those sitting in darkness out from the prison house. 8 I am the LORD; that is My name! I will not yield My glory to another or My praise to idols. 9 Behold, the former things have happened, and now I declare new things. Before they spring forth I proclaim them to you.”

I will put My Spirit on Him, and He will bring justice to the nations. 2 He will not cry out or raise His voice, nor make His voice heard in the streets. 3 A bruised reed He will not break and a smoldering wick He will not extinguish; He will faithfully bring forth justice. 4 He will not grow weak or discouraged before He has established justice on the earth. In His law the islands will put their hope.”

5 This is what God the LORD says— He who created the heavens and stretched them out, who spread out the earth and its offspring, who gives breath to the people on it and life to those who walk in it: 6 “I, the LORD, have called you for a righteous purpose, and I will take hold of your hand. I will keep you and appoint you to be a covenant for the people and a light to the nations, 7 to open the eyes of the blind, to bring prisoners out of the dungeon and those sitting in darkness out from the prison house. 8 I am the LORD; that is My name! I will not yield My glory to another or My praise to idols. 9 Behold, the former things have happened, and now I declare new things. Before they spring forth I proclaim them to you.”

passages.context_html:
After the challenge to powerless idols, the Lord introduces His chosen Servant. He upholds Him, delights in Him and places His Spirit upon Him. The Servant’s work reaches the nations and establishes justice on the earth.

The manner of that work matters. He does not crush an already bruised reed or extinguish a smoldering wick. His gentleness toward the vulnerable is joined to steadiness: He will not grow weak or discouraged before the work is accomplished.

The Creator commissions Him, takes His hand and appoints Him as a covenant for the people and a light to the nations. Opening blind eyes and bringing prisoners out of darkness belong to His task.

The passage closes with the Lord’s name, His refusal to yield His glory to idols, and His announcement of new things before they happen. The Servant’s mission belongs to the purpose of the living God, in contrast with the images exposed in the previous chapter.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings identify the chosen Servant with Jesus because Matthew 12:15–21 explicitly applies this passage to Him. Henry, Wesley and Gill accordingly connect His gentle treatment of the bruised reed and smoldering wick with His care for weak and wounded people.

They also connect His light and release from darkness with the good news reaching the nations and freeing people from sin. The emphasis is on justice accomplished through the Servant’s faithful work, with tenderness rather than contempt for those who need His help.

passages.god_plan_html:
Matthew places the quotation beside Jesus withdrawing from a plot against Him, healing those who follow and warning them not to make Him known. It explains the character of His ministry, then ends with the nations placing their hope in His name in Matthew 12:14–21.

The promised light also has a strong parallel in Simeon’s words over the infant Jesus in Luke 2:25–32. He recognizes God’s salvation prepared before all people, bringing light to the Gentiles and glory to Israel.

These New Testament connections place the Servant’s work within God’s saving purpose for Israel and the nations together. The One who does not crush the bruised is also the One through whom hope reaches beyond one people.

passages.title: Isaiah 42:10-17
passages.section_title: Why are distant peoples invited to sing a new song?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 Sing to the LORD a new song— His praise from the ends of the earth— you who go down to the sea, and all that is in it, you islands, and all who dwell in them. 11 Let the desert and its cities raise their voices; let the villages of Kedar cry aloud. Let the people of Sela sing for joy; let them cry out from the mountaintops. 12 Let them give glory to the LORD and declare His praise in the islands. 13 The LORD goes forth like a mighty one; He stirs up His zeal like a warrior. He shouts; yes, He roars in triumph over His enemies: 14 “I have kept silent from ages past; I have remained quiet and restrained. But now I will groan like a woman in labor; I will at once gasp and pant. 15 I will lay waste the mountains and hills and dry up all their vegetation. I will turn the rivers into dry land and drain the marshes. 16 I will lead the blind by a way they did not know; I will guide them on unfamiliar paths. I will turn darkness into light before them and rough places into level ground. These things I will do for them, and I will not forsake them. 17 But those who trust in idols and say to molten images, ‘You are our gods!’ will be turned back in utter shame.

Let the people of Sela sing for joy; let them cry out from the mountaintops. 12 Let them give glory to the LORD and declare His praise in the islands. 13 The LORD goes forth like a mighty one; He stirs up His zeal like a warrior. He shouts; yes, He roars in triumph over His enemies:

14 “I have kept silent from ages past; I have remained quiet and restrained. But now I will groan like a woman in labor; I will at once gasp and pant. 15 I will lay waste the mountains and hills and dry up all their vegetation. I will turn the rivers into dry land and drain the marshes. 16 I will lead the blind by a way they did not know; I will guide them on unfamiliar paths. I will turn darkness into light before them and rough places into level ground. These things I will do for them, and I will not forsake them. 17 But those who trust in idols and say to molten images, ‘You are our gods!’ will be turned back in utter shame.

passages.context_html:
The Servant’s introduction is followed by a call for praise from the ends of the earth. Sea travelers, islands, desert settlements, Kedar and Sela are included. The Lord’s glory is to be declared far beyond a single city.

The song celebrates His action against His enemies. A warrior’s shout is followed by the image of a woman in labor after a long silence. Mountains, hills, rivers and marshes all appear in the picture of decisive change.

Within that upheaval, the Lord promises to guide the blind along unfamiliar ways, turn darkness into light and make rough ground level. He will not forsake them. The contrast is with those who trust manufactured images and are finally put to shame.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley connect the song with the good news spreading among the nations. They read the Lord’s victory as removing opposition to His work, and the guidance of the blind as the giving of truth and light.

Gill particularly applies the leading of the blind to Gentiles coming to know God through Christ. He reads the long silence and decisive action through the overthrow of pagan opposition and the spread of the gospel.

These explanations join praise with the Lord’s power to guide people who could not find their own way. The judgment on idols stands beside His commitment not to abandon those He leads.

passages.god_plan_html:
A new song is heard in Revelation 5:9–14, praising the Lamb because His blood has purchased people for God from every tribe, language, people and nation. The song widens into the praise of every creature.

This is a well-supported parallel with Isaiah’s worldwide invitation, rather than a claim that Revelation directly quotes Isaiah 42. The New Testament makes the saving work at the center of that praise explicit: the Lamb was slain and has made a people to serve God.

God’s purpose therefore reaches beyond the defeat of an enemy. People from the world’s many communities are gathered into worship, giving glory to the One who has rescued them.

passages.title: Isaiah 42:18-25
passages.section_title: How can God’s servant see so much and still refuse to listen?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 Listen, you deaf ones; look, you blind ones, that you may see! 19 Who is blind but My servant, or deaf like the messenger I am sending? Who is blind like My covenant partner, or blind like the servant of the LORD? 20 Though seeing many things, you do not keep watch. Though your ears are open, you do not hear.” 21 The LORD was pleased, for the sake of His righteousness, to magnify His law and make it glorious. 22 But this is a people plundered and looted, all trapped in caves or imprisoned in dungeons. They have become plunder with no one to rescue them, and loot with no one to say, “Send them back!” 23 Who among you will pay attention to this? Who will listen and obey hereafter? 24 Who gave Jacob up for spoil, and Israel to the plunderers? Was it not the LORD, against whom we have sinned? They were unwilling to walk in His ways, and they would not obey His law. 25 So He poured out on them His furious anger and the fierceness of battle. It enveloped them in flames, but they did not understand; it consumed them, but they did not take it to heart.

Who is blind like My covenant partner, or blind like the servant of the LORD? 20 Though seeing many things, you do not keep watch. Though your ears are open, you do not hear.” 21 The LORD was pleased, for the sake of His righteousness, to magnify His law and make it glorious.

22 But this is a people plundered and looted, all trapped in caves or imprisoned in dungeons. They have become plunder with no one to rescue them, and loot with no one to say, “Send them back!” 23 Who among you will pay attention to this? Who will listen and obey hereafter? 24 Who gave Jacob up for spoil, and Israel to the plunderers? Was it not the LORD, against whom we have sinned? They were unwilling to walk in His ways, and they would not obey His law. 25 So He poured out on them His furious anger and the fierceness of battle. It enveloped them in flames, but they did not understand; it consumed them, but they did not take it to heart.

passages.context_html:
The servant language now becomes a rebuke. The Lord calls the deaf to hear and the blind to look, then asks who is as unresponsive as His own servant and messenger. This servant has seen many things but does not keep watch, and has open ears without receiving the message.

That failure contrasts with the faithful Servant introduced at the beginning of the chapter. It also contrasts with the Lord’s purpose to magnify His law. The people who should receive and bear His instruction are instead plundered, trapped and imprisoned.

The closing questions identify the cause: Jacob and Israel have been handed over by the Lord against whom they sinned. They would not walk in His ways or obey His law. Even when judgment surrounded them like fire, they failed to take it to heart.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill distinguish this rebuked servant from the faithful Messiah. They connect the blindness with the people and teachers who have received opportunities to hear but resist the message.

Wesley explains the honor of the law through God’s faithfulness and His refusal to treat its violation lightly. Gill discusses that reading and also connects the law’s honor with Christ’s obedience and righteousness.

Henry applies the warning to professing Christians as well: having access to God’s truth is not the same as receiving it. The passage exposes unresponsiveness in a people called to serve, rather than making physical blindness or deafness a measure of a person’s guilt.
