passages.title: Isaiah 43:1-13
passages.section_title: Why does God call a judged people His own?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 But now, this is what the LORD says— He who created you, O Jacob, and He who formed you, O Israel: “Do not fear, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by your name; you are Mine! 2 When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and when you go through the rivers, they will not overwhelm you. When you walk through the fire, you will not be scorched; the flames will not set you ablaze. 3 For I am the LORD your God, the Holy One of Israel, your Savior; I give Egypt for your ransom, Cush and Seba in your place. 4 Because you are precious and honored in My sight, and because I love you, I will give men in exchange for you and nations in place of your life. 5 Do not be afraid, for I am with you; I will bring your offspring from the east and gather you from the west. 6 I will say to the north, ‘Give them up!’ and to the south, ‘Do not hold them back!’ Bring My sons from afar, and My daughters from the ends of the earth— 7 everyone called by My name and created for My glory, whom I have indeed formed and made.” 8 Bring out a people who have eyes but are blind, and who have ears but are deaf. 9 All the nations gather together and the peoples assemble. Who among them can declare this, and proclaim to us the former things? Let them present their witnesses to vindicate them, so that others may hear and say, “It is true.” 10 “You are My witnesses,” declares the LORD, “and My servant whom I have chosen, so that you may consider and believe Me and understand that I am He. Before Me no god was formed, and after Me none will come. 11 I, yes I, am the LORD, and there is no Savior but Me. 12 I alone decreed and saved and proclaimed— I, and not some foreign god among you. So you are My witnesses,” declares the LORD, “that I am God. 13 Even from eternity I am He, and none can deliver out of My hand. When I act, who can reverse it?”

5 Do not be afraid, for I am with you; I will bring your offspring from the east and gather you from the west. 6 I will say to the north, ‘Give them up!’ and to the south, ‘Do not hold them back!’ Bring My sons from afar, and My daughters from the ends of the earth— 7 everyone called by My name and created for My glory, whom I have indeed formed and made.”

So you are My witnesses,” declares the LORD, “that I am God. 13 Even from eternity I am He, and none can deliver out of My hand. When I act, who can reverse it?”

passages.context_html:
The first words turn from the previous rebuke to the Lord’s claim on Jacob and Israel. He created and formed them, redeemed them and called them by name. The repeated assurance is that He is with them as they pass through waters, rivers and fire.

Egypt, Cush and Seba are named in the language of ransom, and the Lord declares His people precious, honored and loved. Sons and daughters are to be brought from every direction, everyone called by His name and created for His glory.

The scene then returns to a hearing before the nations. Witnesses are called to show who can announce and accomplish what happens. The Lord appoints His servant and people to witness that He alone is God and Savior.

The promise and the task belong together. God’s people are not only gathered and preserved; they are to know Him and bear witness to what He has declared and done.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Gill understand the waters and fire as encouragement through affliction. Gill applies the promise to the trials of God’s people, with God’s presence and support sustaining them through what threatens them.

Commentators differ over the historical setting of the named nations given in exchange. Wesley connects it with Assyrian action redirected toward Egypt and nearby lands; the USCCB notes connect it with Persian conquests after Israel’s release. These are proposed explanations of how the ransom language relates to events.

For the witness scene, the USCCB notes emphasize Israel’s calling to testify to the Lord’s announced and accomplished works. Henry and Gill also extend the witness theme to believers making known the grace and faithfulness they have received. The shared emphasis is that the true Savior makes Himself known through His saving action.

passages.god_plan_html:
The relationship between suffering, God’s presence and His glory is developed for Christians in 1 Peter 4:12–19. Peter speaks of a fiery trial, sharing in Christ’s sufferings and the Spirit of glory resting on those insulted for His name.

He calls them to entrust themselves to their faithful Creator and continue doing good. That is a shared theme with Isaiah’s assurance from the Creator who claims His people, rather than a direct quotation of Isaiah 43.

The larger purpose includes a faithful people bearing His name through hardship. His care is not confined to easy circumstances; it gives them reason to remain faithful while looking toward the revelation of Christ’s glory.

passages.title: Isaiah 43:14-21
passages.section_title: Can the God who made a way through the sea make a new way home?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 Thus says the LORD your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel: “For your sake, I will send to Babylon and bring them all as fugitives, even the Chaldeans, in the ships in which they rejoice. 15 I am the LORD, your Holy One, the Creator of Israel, and your King.” 16 Thus says the LORD, who makes a way in the sea and a path through the surging waters, 17 who brings out the chariots and horses, the armies and warriors together, to lie down, never to rise again; to be extinguished, snuffed out like a wick: 18 “Do not call to mind the former things; pay no attention to the things of old. 19 Behold, I am about to do something new; even now it is coming. Do you not see it? Indeed, I will make a way in the wilderness and streams in the desert. 20 The beasts of the field will honor Me, the jackals and the ostriches, because I provide water in the wilderness and rivers in the desert, to give drink to My chosen people. 21 The people I formed for Myself will declare My praise.
paragraphs: 14 Thus says the LORD your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel: “For your sake, I will send to Babylon and bring them all as fugitives, even the Chaldeans, in the ships in which they rejoice. 15 I am the LORD, your Holy One, the Creator of Israel, and your King.” 16 Thus says the LORD, who makes a way in the sea and a path through the surging waters, 17 who brings out the chariots and horses, the armies and warriors together, to lie down, never to rise again; to be extinguished, snuffed out like a wick:

18 “Do not call to mind the former things; pay no attention to the things of old. 19 Behold, I am about to do something new; even now it is coming. Do you not see it? Indeed, I will make a way in the wilderness and streams in the desert. 20 The beasts of the field will honor Me, the jackals and the ostriches, because I provide water in the wilderness and rivers in the desert, to give drink to My chosen people. 21 The people I formed for Myself will declare My praise.

passages.context_html:
The Lord names Himself as Israel’s Redeemer, Holy One, Creator and King, and announces action against Babylon for His people’s sake. Those who rejoiced in their ships will become fugitives.

He recalls making a path through the sea and bringing the chariots, horses and warriors to an end. That memory points back to the exodus, when the sea became both a path of rescue and the place of the pursuing army’s defeat.

The hearers are then told to look for a new thing rather than remain fixed on the former events. The same Lord will make a way in the wilderness and provide streams in the desert. Animals share in the water given for His chosen people.

The closing purpose is worship: the people He formed for Himself will declare His praise. The new rescue displays the same Lord’s faithfulness in circumstances different from the earlier exodus.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and the USCCB notes connect the sea and defeated chariots with Egypt and read the coming rescue as a new exodus from Babylon. The command about former things stresses the greatness of the new act, rather than forbidding grateful remembrance.

Henry sees the Babylonian deliverance opening onto greater redemption through Christ. Gill also reads the former rescue in comparison with the greater saving work of the Messiah.

These readings keep the historical return and the wider hope connected. The Lord who rescued before is not limited to repeating the same event in the same way.

passages.god_plan_html:
The purpose of forming a people to declare God’s praise has a close parallel in 1 Peter 2:9–12. Those who have received mercy are called His people and are to proclaim the virtues of the One who brought them from darkness into light.

Second Corinthians 5:17–21 develops the newness of God’s saving work through Christ: new creation belongs with reconciliation to God and a message entrusted to His people.

These are connections in the larger biblical story, rather than a claim that the wording of Isaiah directly describes every later circumstance. God’s rescue brings people into a renewed relationship with Him and a life that makes His goodness known.

passages.title: Isaiah 43:22-28
passages.section_title: What grounds are left for forgiveness when the people cannot plead innocence?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 But you have not called on Me, O Jacob, because you have grown weary of Me, O Israel. 23 You have not brought Me sheep for burnt offerings, nor honored Me with your sacrifices. I have not burdened you with offerings, nor wearied you with frankincense. 24 You have not bought Me sweet cane with your silver, nor satisfied Me with the fat of your sacrifices. But you have burdened Me with your sins; you have wearied Me with your iniquities. 25 I, yes I, am He who blots out your transgressions for My own sake and remembers your sins no more. 26 Remind Me, let us argue the matter together. State your case, so that you may be vindicated. 27 Your first father sinned, and your spokesmen rebelled against Me. 28 So I will disgrace the princes of your sanctuary, and I will devote Jacob to destruction and Israel to reproach.”
paragraphs: 22 But you have not called on Me, O Jacob, because you have grown weary of Me, O Israel. 23 You have not brought Me sheep for burnt offerings, nor honored Me with your sacrifices. I have not burdened you with offerings, nor wearied you with frankincense. 24 You have not bought Me sweet cane with your silver, nor satisfied Me with the fat of your sacrifices. But you have burdened Me with your sins; you have wearied Me with your iniquities.

25 I, yes I, am He who blots out your transgressions for My own sake and remembers your sins no more. 26 Remind Me, let us argue the matter together. State your case, so that you may be vindicated. 27 Your first father sinned, and your spokesmen rebelled against Me. 28 So I will disgrace the princes of your sanctuary, and I will devote Jacob to destruction and Israel to reproach.”

passages.context_html:
The people formed to praise God have instead grown weary of Him. Their offerings have not honored Him; their sins have become the burden they bring. The contrast is between the service He called them to and the wrongdoing that has replaced it.

Then comes the unexpected declaration: the Lord Himself blots out their transgressions for His own sake and will no longer remember their sins. The initiative is His, in the middle of a charge the people cannot answer with a record of innocence.

The closing invitation to state their case exposes how far the failure reaches. Their first father sinned and their spokesmen rebelled, and judgment falls on sanctuary leaders and people alike. The promise of pardon does not make the history of wrongdoing disappear or turn the warning into an empty threat.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry, Wesley and Gill emphasize that forgiveness rests in God’s mercy rather than the people’s merits. Gill explains remembering sins no more as no longer holding them against His people, rather than God losing knowledge of what happened.

For the first father in verse 27, the USCCB note identifies Jacob. Wesley allows the collective sense of the forefathers, and Gill discusses several named proposals before preferring that collective reading. The point in these explanations is that ancestry and leadership provide no basis for claiming an unbroken history of innocence.

The passage is therefore read as an exposure of self-justification alongside a remarkable offer of pardon. The mercy is God’s action, not a conclusion that the people were right all along.

passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 3:21–26 places the same great needs together: all have sinned, yet people are justified freely by God’s grace through the redemption in Christ Jesus.

Paul explains that God presents Christ as an atoning sacrifice through faith in His blood, demonstrating His righteousness so that He is both just and the One who justifies the person who has faith in Jesus.

This is a theme developed beyond Isaiah’s immediate charge, not a direct quotation of these verses. The New Testament shows how mercy and righteousness meet in Christ: forgiveness is not based on pretending sin never mattered, but on God’s saving provision for those who cannot justify themselves.

passages.title: Isaiah 44:1-20
passages.section_title: Who can give life: the God who formed His people, or an image they form?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 But now listen, O Jacob My servant, Israel, whom I have chosen. 2 This is the word of the LORD, your Maker, who formed you from the womb and who will help you: “Do not be afraid, O Jacob My servant, Jeshurun, whom I have chosen. 3 For I will pour water on the thirsty land, and currents on the dry ground. I will pour out My Spirit on your descendants, and My blessing on your offspring. 4 They will sprout among the grass like willows by flowing streams. 5 One will say, ‘I belong to the LORD,’ another will call himself by the name of Jacob, and still another will write on his hand, ‘The LORD’s,’ and will take the name of Israel.” 6 Thus says the LORD, the King and Redeemer of Israel, the LORD of Hosts: “I am the first and I am the last, and there is no God but Me. 7 Who then is like Me? Let him say so! Let him declare his case before Me, since I established an ancient people. Let him foretell the things to come, and what is to take place. 8 Do not tremble or fear. Have I not told you and declared it long ago? You are My witnesses! Is there any God but Me? There is no other Rock; I know not one.” 9 All makers of idols are nothing, and the things they treasure are worthless. Their witnesses fail to see or comprehend, so they are put to shame. 10 Who fashions a god or casts an idol which profits him nothing? 11 Behold, all his companions will be put to shame, for the craftsmen themselves are only human. Let them all assemble and take their stand; they will all be brought to terror and shame. 12 The blacksmith takes a tool and labors over the coals; he fashions an idol with hammers and forges it with his strong arms. Yet he grows hungry and loses his strength; he fails to drink water and grows faint. 13 The woodworker extends a measuring line; he marks it out with a stylus; he shapes it with chisels and outlines it with a compass. He fashions it in the likeness of man, like man in all his glory, that it may dwell in a shrine. 14 He cuts down cedars or retrieves a cypress or oak. He lets it grow strong among the trees of the forest. He plants a laurel, and the rain makes it grow. 15 It serves as fuel for man. He takes some of it to warm himself, and he kindles a fire and bakes his bread. He also fashions it into a god and worships it; he makes an idol and bows down to it. 16 He burns half of it in the fire, and he roasts meat on that half. He eats the roast and is satisfied. Indeed, he warms himself and says, “Ah! I am warm; I see the fire.” 17 From the rest he makes a god, his graven image. He bows down to it and worships; he prays to it and says, “Save me, for you are my god.” 18 They do not comprehend or discern, for He has shut their eyes so they cannot see and closed their minds so they cannot understand. 19 And no one considers in his heart, no one has the knowledge or insight to say, “I burned half of it in the fire, and I baked bread on its coals; I roasted meat and I ate. Shall I make something detestable with the rest of it? Shall I bow down to a block of wood?” 20 He feeds on ashes. His deluded heart has led him astray, and he cannot deliver himself or say, “Is not this thing in my right hand a lie?”
paragraphs: 1 But now listen, O Jacob My servant, Israel, whom I have chosen. 2 This is the word of the LORD, your Maker, who formed you from the womb and who will help you: “Do not be afraid, O Jacob My servant, Jeshurun, whom I have chosen. 3 For I will pour water on the thirsty land, and currents on the dry ground. I will pour out My Spirit on your descendants, and My blessing on your offspring. 4 They will sprout among the grass like willows by flowing streams. 5 One will say, ‘I belong to the LORD,’ another will call himself by the name of Jacob, and still another will write on his hand, ‘The LORD’s,’ and will take the name of Israel.”

6 Thus says the LORD, the King and Redeemer of Israel, the LORD of Hosts: “I am the first and I am the last, and there is no God but Me. 7 Who then is like Me? Let him say so! Let him declare his case before Me, since I established an ancient people. Let him foretell the things to come, and what is to take place. 8 Do not tremble or fear. Have I not told you and declared it long ago? You are My witnesses! Is there any God but Me? There is no other Rock; I know not one.”

9 All makers of idols are nothing, and the things they treasure are worthless. Their witnesses fail to see or comprehend, so they are put to shame. 10 Who fashions a god or casts an idol which profits him nothing? 11 Behold, all his companions will be put to shame, for the craftsmen themselves are only human. Let them all assemble and take their stand; they will all be brought to terror and shame. 12 The blacksmith takes a tool and labors over the coals; he fashions an idol with hammers and forges it with his strong arms. Yet he grows hungry and loses his strength; he fails to drink water and grows faint. 13 The woodworker extends a measuring line; he marks it out with a stylus; he shapes it with chisels and outlines it with a compass. He fashions it in the likeness of man, like man in all his glory, that it may dwell in a shrine.

14 He cuts down cedars or retrieves a cypress or oak. He lets it grow strong among the trees of the forest. He plants a laurel, and the rain makes it grow. 15 It serves as fuel for man. He takes some of it to warm himself, and he kindles a fire and bakes his bread. He also fashions it into a god and worships it; he makes an idol and bows down to it. 16 He burns half of it in the fire, and he roasts meat on that half. He eats the roast and is satisfied. Indeed, he warms himself and says, “Ah! I am warm; I see the fire.” 17 From the rest he makes a god, his graven image. He bows down to it and worships; he prays to it and says, “Save me, for you are my god.”

18 They do not comprehend or discern, for He has shut their eyes so they cannot see and closed their minds so they cannot understand. 19 And no one considers in his heart, no one has the knowledge or insight to say, “I burned half of it in the fire, and I baked bread on its coals; I roasted meat and I ate. Shall I make something detestable with the rest of it? Shall I bow down to a block of wood?” 20 He feeds on ashes. His deluded heart has led him astray, and he cannot deliver himself or say, “Is not this thing in my right hand a lie?”

passages.context_html:
The Lord again addresses Jacob and Israel as the servant He chose, formed and will help. The opening promises water for thirsty ground, His Spirit for their descendants and a people willing to say that they belong to Him.

The poetic name Jeshurun, pronounced yeh-shoo-ROON, adds a note of intended faithfulness. Brown–Driver–Briggs explains it as upright one, a name for Israel expressing its ideal character. The promise concerns a people shaped by the God who calls them His own.

The Lord declares that He is the first and last and the only God. His people are witnesses to what He has announced. That claim is set beside a detailed picture of craftsmen producing an idol.

The maker grows hungry, thirsty and weak. He depends on wood and rain, shapes the figure and gives it a place to stand. Most sharply, he uses part of the same wood to cook a meal and warm himself, then bows before the rest and asks it to save him.

The problem is deeper than poor workmanship. A deceived heart prevents the worshiper from recognizing the lie he holds. The contrast runs through the whole passage: God forms and gives life to His people, while people form an object that cannot give life back.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry, Wesley and Gill connect the promised water and Spirit with renewed life and belonging to God. Their explanations of the idol scene emphasize human dependence and the inability of a manufactured object to become its maker’s savior.

Where traditions differ is in applying the warning to Christian religious images. The Catholic Church, in Catechism 2129–2132, distinguishes the worship due to God alone from honor directed through an image toward the person represented. It grounds the permitted use of sacred images in the incarnation and the teaching of the Second Council of Nicaea.

The Reformed Westminster Confession 21.1 forbids worshiping God under a visible representation; the Larger Catechism, question 109, also rejects making representations of any person of the Trinity. The 1689 Baptist Confession 22.1 likewise excludes worship under visible representations.

The Methodist Articles of Religion, Article XIV, reject worship and adoration of images. The UMC’s published text also directs readers to its guidance on contemporary interpretation in light of its work toward Christian unity.

These statements explain a real difference over the religious use of images. They should not be turned into a claim that every member of a tradition practices identically, or that Catholic teaching treats a piece of wood as a god that can save.

passages.god_plan_html:
Peter connects the gift of the Spirit with the risen and exalted Jesus in Acts 2:32–39. The promise reaches his hearers, their children and those far away whom God calls. This is a strong parallel with Isaiah’s promised Spirit and renewed people, rather than a claim that Peter directly quotes Isaiah 44.

The turn from idols also appears in 1 Thessalonians 1:8–10: people turn to serve the living God and wait for His risen Son. Colossians 3:1–5 extends the concern beyond carved objects by naming greed as idolatry, within a call to live as people raised with Christ.

Together these connections show the purpose of the change: God gives life and His Spirit so that His people belong to Him and serve Him. Replacing a powerless object is only part of the story; the heart’s allegiance and the life that follows are also changed.

passages.title: Isaiah 44:21-28
passages.section_title: Why does God tell the people He has redeemed to return to Him?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 Remember these things, O Jacob, for you are My servant, O Israel. I have made you, and you are My servant; O Israel, I will never forget you. 22 I have blotted out your transgressions like a cloud, and your sins like a mist. Return to Me, for I have redeemed you. 23 Sing for joy, O heavens, for the LORD has done this; shout aloud, O depths of the earth. Break forth in song, O mountains, you forests and all your trees. For the LORD has redeemed Jacob, and revealed His glory in Israel. 24 Thus says the LORD, your Redeemer who formed you from the womb: “I am the LORD, who has made all things, who alone stretched out the heavens, who by Myself spread out the earth, 25 who foils the signs of false prophets and makes fools of diviners, who confounds the wise and turns their knowledge into nonsense, 26 who confirms the message of His servant and fulfills the counsel of His messengers, who says of Jerusalem, ‘She will be inhabited,’ and of the cities of Judah, ‘They will be rebuilt, and I will restore their ruins,’ 27 who says to the depths of the sea, ‘Be dry, and I will dry up your currents,’ 28 who says of Cyrus, ‘My shepherd will fulfill all that I desire,’ who says of Jerusalem, ‘She will be rebuilt,’ and of the temple, ‘Let its foundation be laid.’”

I have made you, and you are My servant; O Israel, I will never forget you. 22 I have blotted out your transgressions like a cloud, and your sins like a mist. Return to Me, for I have redeemed you. 23 Sing for joy, O heavens, for the LORD has done this; shout aloud, O depths of the earth. Break forth in song, O mountains, you forests and all your trees. For the LORD has redeemed Jacob, and revealed His glory in Israel.

24 Thus says the LORD, your Redeemer who formed you from the womb: “I am the LORD, who has made all things, who alone stretched out the heavens, who by Myself spread out the earth, 25 who foils the signs of false prophets and makes fools of diviners, who confounds the wise and turns their knowledge into nonsense, 26 who confirms the message of His servant and fulfills the counsel of His messengers, who says of Jerusalem, ‘She will be inhabited,’ and of the cities of Judah, ‘They will be rebuilt, and I will restore their ruins,’ 27 who says to the depths of the sea, ‘Be dry, and I will dry up your currents,’ 28 who says of Cyrus, ‘My shepherd will fulfill all that I desire,’ who says of Jerusalem, ‘She will be rebuilt,’ and of the temple, ‘Let its foundation be laid.’”

passages.context_html:
The Lord calls Jacob and Israel to remember the contrast with idols. He formed them as His servant and will not forget them. Their sins are pictured as a cloud and mist He has removed, and His redemption is the reason for the call to return.

The invitation brings a summons to creation itself: heavens, earth, mountains, forest and trees are called to rejoice because the Lord has redeemed Jacob and revealed His glory in Israel.

The Creator then contrasts His action with the failed signs of false prophets and diviners. He confirms His servant’s message, promises that Jerusalem will be inhabited and Judah’s ruined cities rebuilt, and removes the obstacles before that purpose.

The final verse names Cyrus as His shepherd, the one who will carry out His desire concerning Jerusalem and the temple’s foundation. The announcement moves from pardon and praise to a named instrument of restoration.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry, Wesley and Gill understand the cloud and mist as pictures of sins removed through forgiveness. The call to return is grounded in God’s redeeming action and willingness to receive His people.

For Cyrus, Henry and Wesley emphasize the Lord’s power to employ a ruler in the service of His people. Gill connects the shepherd title with leading them out of captivity and making their return possible.

They differ over some details of the dried waters. Wesley stresses God’s power to remove obstacles, while Gill discusses both the Babylonian river explanation and the earlier crossings of the sea and Jordan. The stated outcome is the rebuilding God announces.

passages.god_plan_html:
The restoration begins to take visible form in Ezra 1:1–4, where Cyrus authorizes return and the rebuilding of the Lord’s house. Ezra attributes the proclamation to the Lord stirring the king’s spirit.

The Bible’s larger shepherd theme reaches a greater rescue in John 10:11–18, 27–30. Jesus lays down His life for the sheep, gathers them to hear His voice and gives them eternal life.

This is a connection through the shared theme of God gathering and preserving His people, not an identification of Cyrus with Jesus. The political ruler serves a particular restoration; the saving Shepherd gives His own life and brings a security that reaches beyond that return.

passages.title: Isaiah 45:1-25
passages.section_title: Can God use an unexpected ruler to bring a rescue that reaches the nations?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 This is what the LORD says to Cyrus His anointed, whose right hand I have grasped to subdue nations before him, to disarm kings, to open the doors before him, so that the gates will not be shut: 2 “I will go before you and level the mountains; I will break down the gates of bronze and cut through the bars of iron. 3 I will give you the treasures of darkness and the riches hidden in secret places, so that you may know that I am the LORD, the God of Israel, who calls you by name. 4 For the sake of Jacob My servant and Israel My chosen one, I call you by name; I have given you a title of honor, though you have not known Me. 5 I am the LORD, and there is no other; there is no God but Me. I will equip you for battle, though you have not known Me, 6 so that all may know, from where the sun rises to where it sets, that there is none but Me; I am the LORD, and there is no other. 7 I form the light and create the darkness; I bring prosperity and create calamity. I, the LORD, do all these things. 8 Drip down, O heavens, from above, and let the skies pour down righteousness. Let the earth open up that salvation may sprout and righteousness spring up with it; I, the LORD, have created it. 9 Woe to him who quarrels with his Maker— one clay pot among many. Does the clay ask the potter, ‘What are you making?’ Does your work say, ‘He has no hands’? 10 Woe to him who says to his father, ‘What have you begotten?’ or to his mother, ‘What have you brought forth?’” 11 Thus says the LORD, the Holy One of Israel, and its Maker: “Concerning things to come, do you question Me about My sons, or instruct Me in the work of My hands? 12 It is I who made the earth and created man upon it. It was My hands that stretched out the heavens, and I ordained all their host. 13 I will raise up Cyrus in righteousness, and I will make all his ways straight. He will rebuild My city and set My exiles free, but not for payment or reward, says the LORD of Hosts.” 14 This is what the LORD says: “The products of Egypt and the merchandise of Cush, along with the Sabeans, men of stature, will come over to you and will be yours; they will trudge behind you; they will come over in chains and bow down to you. They will confess to you: ‘God is indeed with you, and there is no other; there is no other God.’” 15 Truly You are a God who hides Himself, O God of Israel, the Savior. 16 They will all be put to shame and humiliated; the makers of idols will depart together in disgrace. 17 But Israel will be saved by the LORD with an everlasting salvation; you will not be put to shame or humiliated, to ages everlasting. 18 For thus says the LORD, who created the heavens—He is God; He formed the earth and fashioned it; He established it; He did not create it to be empty, but formed it to be inhabited: “I am the LORD, and there is no other. 19 I have not spoken in secret, from a place in a land of darkness. I did not say to the descendants of Jacob, ‘Seek Me in a wasteland.’ I, the LORD, speak the truth; I say what is right. 20 Come, gather together, and draw near, you fugitives from the nations. Ignorant are those who carry idols of wood and pray to a god that cannot save. 21 Speak up and present your case— yes, let them take counsel together. Who foretold this long ago? Who announced it from ancient times? Was it not I, the LORD? There is no other God but Me, a righteous God and Savior; there is none but Me. 22 Turn to Me and be saved, all the ends of the earth; for I am God, and there is no other. 23 By Myself I have sworn; truth has gone out from My mouth, a word that will not be revoked: Every knee will bow before Me, every tongue will swear allegiance. 24 Surely they will say of Me, ‘In the LORD alone are righteousness and strength.’” All who rage against Him will come to Him and be put to shame. 25 In the LORD all descendants of Israel will be justified and will exult.

passages.context_html:
The Lord addresses Cyrus as His anointed and promises to take his hand, subdue nations and open what seems securely closed. The purpose is stated twice: for the sake of Jacob and Israel, and so that people everywhere know the Lord alone is God. Cyrus is equipped for the task even though he has not known Him.

Anointed translates the Hebrew mashiach, pronounced mah-SHEE-akh. Brown–Driver–Briggs uses the word for anointed kings and priests and specifically lists Cyrus as commissioned by the Lord here. The title marks an appointment; its use for Cyrus does not identify him as the promised Christ.

The Creator’s rule includes prosperity and calamity. The Hebrew word ra, pronounced rah, has several uses; Brown–Driver–Briggs specifically places Isaiah 45:7 under distress and adversity. Here the contrast concerns what befalls nations, rather than calling moral wrongdoing good.

The potter and clay picture challenges resistance to the Maker’s authority. The Lord promises that Cyrus will rebuild His city and free His exiles without payment. The vision then widens to nations recognizing that God is with His people, while the makers of idols face shame.

The chapter closes with a worldwide invitation to turn to the only God and Savior. His word will not be revoked: every knee will bow and every tongue acknowledge Him. Righteousness, strength, justification and rejoicing are located in the Lord.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry, Wesley and Gill read Cyrus’s appointment as an example of the Lord accomplishing His purpose through a ruler who did not first know Him. The anointing concerns the work assigned to him, rather than a claim that he holds every office of the Messiah.

For the calamity in verse 7, Henry and Gill distinguish the judgment and adversity God brings or governs from the moral evil people commit. Wesley likewise understands the contrast as the comforts and calamities of human life. These readings emphasize God’s rule without making Him a sinner.

For the potter and clay, Wesley focuses on opposition to God’s work through Cyrus, while Gill extends the warning to resistance to God’s way of bringing salvation through Christ. The shared concern is the creature presuming to place the Creator under its direction.

Verse 11 is read differently in older translations. Gill prefers an invitation to ask God concerning His promises, while also discussing the question that challenges anyone who would command Him. Wesley reads it as a challenge to interference with God’s authority. The BSB follows that questioning form.

For the closing promise, Henry, Wesley and Gill look to the nations coming to Christ and the shame of opposition to Him. They connect righteousness and salvation with the Lord, while the New Testament itself takes up the words about every knee.

passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 9:19–24 takes up the potter-and-clay language in discussing God’s mercy and purpose. Paul brings the discussion to people called from both Jews and Gentiles, placing the Creator’s freedom beside the riches of His mercy.

Romans 14:7–12 directly quotes Isaiah’s promise that every knee will bow. Paul uses it to remind believers that each will answer to God and should not belittle a brother. The declaration of God’s rule has consequences for how His people treat one another.

Philippians 2:5–11 uses the same language of every knee and tongue in proclaiming Jesus Christ as Lord, to the glory of God the Father. It places that confession after His willing service and obedience to death on a cross, then calls believers to share His mind.

These connections carry the chapter’s universal horizon into the New Testament. God’s saving purpose reaches the nations through Christ, and acknowledging His lordship belongs with mercy, humility and accountable lives.

passages.title: Isaiah 46:1-13
passages.section_title: Who carries whom: the worshiper and his image, or God and His people?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Bel crouches; Nebo cowers. Their idols weigh down beasts and cattle. The images you carry are burdensome, a load to the weary animal. 2 The gods cower; they crouch together, unable to relieve the burden; but they themselves go into captivity. 3 “Listen to Me, O house of Jacob, all the remnant of the house of Israel, who have been sustained from the womb, carried along since birth. 4 Even to your old age, I will be the same, and I will bear you up when you turn gray. I have made you, and I will carry you; I will sustain you and deliver you. 5 To whom will you liken Me or count Me equal? To whom will you compare Me, that we should be alike? 6 They pour out their bags of gold and weigh out silver on scales; they hire a goldsmith to fashion it into a god, so they can bow down and worship. 7 They lift it to their shoulder and carry it along; they set it in its place, and there it stands, not budging from that spot. They cry out to it, but it does not answer; it saves no one from his troubles. 8 Remember this and be brave; take it to heart, you transgressors! 9 Remember what happened long ago, for I am God, and there is no other; I am God, and there is none like Me. 10 I declare the end from the beginning, and from ancient times what is still to come. I say, ‘My purpose will stand, and all My good pleasure I will accomplish.’ 11 I summon a bird of prey from the east, a man for My purpose from a far-off land. Truly I have spoken, and truly I will bring it to pass. I have planned it, and I will surely do it. 12 Listen to Me, you stubborn people, far removed from righteousness: 13 I am bringing My righteousness near; it is not far away, and My salvation will not be delayed. I will grant salvation to Zion and adorn Israel with My splendor.

passages.context_html:
Bel and Nebo are pictured bowing and cowering while their images become loads for weary animals. The gods cannot relieve the burden; they themselves are taken into captivity. What was carried as a source of security now needs carrying away.

The Lord’s promise to Israel reverses the picture. He has sustained His people from birth and will carry them even when they are old and gray. Their increasing weakness does not turn Him into a burden they must support.

The comparison returns to the expensive image made by a goldsmith. It stays wherever its worshiper places it and cannot answer a cry for help. The living God, by contrast, announces His purpose and brings it about.

The bird of prey from the east and the man from a distant land belong to that announced purpose. The final appeal is to stubborn people far from righteousness: the Lord is bringing His righteousness and salvation near to Zion.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry, Wesley and Gill emphasize the contrast between idols that require human support and the Lord who sustains His people. Wesley reads the carrying from birth through the history of Israel; Henry and Gill also apply the promise to believers needing care in old age.

Wesley and Gill identify the figure from the east with Cyrus, connecting it with the named commission of the previous chapters. Henry likewise emphasizes the Lord’s ability to use people to accomplish His purpose even when they are not seeking to serve Him.

The assurances of power and care belong together. The Lord is unlike the images both in what He can accomplish and in His lasting relationship with the people He made.

passages.god_plan_html:
The picture of carrying those who need rescue has a strong parallel in Jesus’ story of the lost sheep in Luke 15:3–7. The shepherd goes after the lost sheep, puts it on his shoulders and calls others to rejoice when he brings it home.

Jesus explains the story through heaven’s joy over a sinner who repents. The need for rescue becomes an occasion for active care and joy, rather than abandonment.

This is a connection through the shared picture of saving care, not a direct quotation of Isaiah 46. It helps place the promise within the larger biblical account: the God who can carry His people also seeks their return and rejoices in their restoration.

passages.title: Isaiah 47:1-15
passages.section_title: What becomes of power that believes it will never answer to anyone?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 “Go down and sit in the dust, O Virgin Daughter of Babylon. Sit on the ground without a throne, O Daughter of the Chaldeans! For you will no longer be called tender or delicate. 2 Take millstones and grind flour; remove your veil; strip off your skirt, bare your thigh, and wade through the streams. 3 Your nakedness will be uncovered and your shame will be exposed. I will take vengeance; I will spare no one.” 4 Our Redeemer—the LORD of Hosts is His name— is the Holy One of Israel. 5 “Sit in silence and go into darkness, O Daughter of the Chaldeans. For you will no longer be called the queen of kingdoms. 6 I was angry with My people; I profaned My heritage, and I placed them under your control. You showed them no mercy; even on the elderly you laid a most heavy yoke. 7 You said, ‘I will be queen forever.’ You did not take these things to heart or consider their outcome. 8 So now hear this, O lover of luxury who sits securely, who says to herself, ‘I am, and there is none besides me. I will never be a widow or know the loss of children.’ 9 These two things will overtake you in a moment, in a single day: loss of children, and widowhood. They will come upon you in full measure, in spite of your many sorceries and the potency of your spells. 10 You were secure in your wickedness; you said, ‘No one sees me.’ Your wisdom and knowledge led you astray; you told yourself, ‘I am, and there is none besides me.’ 11 But disaster will come upon you; you will not know how to charm it away. A calamity will befall you that you will be unable to ward off. Devastation will happen to you suddenly and unexpectedly. 12 So take your stand with your spells and with your many sorceries, with which you have wearied yourself from your youth. Perhaps you will succeed; perhaps you will inspire terror! 13 You are wearied by your many counselors; let them come forward now and save you— your astrologers who observe the stars, who monthly predict your fate. 14 Surely they are like stubble; the fire will burn them up. They cannot deliver themselves from the power of the flame. There will be no coals to warm them or fire to sit beside. 15 This is what they are to you— those with whom you have labored and traded from youth— each one strays in his own direction; not one of them can save you.
paragraphs: 1 “Go down and sit in the dust, O Virgin Daughter of Babylon. Sit on the ground without a throne, O Daughter of the Chaldeans! For you will no longer be called tender or delicate. 2 Take millstones and grind flour; remove your veil; strip off your skirt, bare your thigh, and wade through the streams. 3 Your nakedness will be uncovered and your shame will be exposed. I will take vengeance; I will spare no one.” 4 Our Redeemer—the LORD of Hosts is His name— is the Holy One of Israel.

5 “Sit in silence and go into darkness, O Daughter of the Chaldeans. For you will no longer be called the queen of kingdoms. 6 I was angry with My people; I profaned My heritage, and I placed them under your control. You showed them no mercy; even on the elderly you laid a most heavy yoke. 7 You said, ‘I will be queen forever.’ You did not take these things to heart or consider their outcome.

8 So now hear this, O lover of luxury who sits securely, who says to herself, ‘I am, and there is none besides me. I will never be a widow or know the loss of children.’ 9 These two things will overtake you in a moment, in a single day: loss of children, and widowhood. They will come upon you in full measure, in spite of your many sorceries and the potency of your spells. 10 You were secure in your wickedness; you said, ‘No one sees me.’ Your wisdom and knowledge led you astray; you told yourself, ‘I am, and there is none besides me.’ 11 But disaster will come upon you; you will not know how to charm it away. A calamity will befall you that you will be unable to ward off. Devastation will happen to you suddenly and unexpectedly.

Perhaps you will succeed; perhaps you will inspire terror! 13 You are wearied by your many counselors; let them come forward now and save you— your astrologers who observe the stars, who monthly predict your fate. 14 Surely they are like stubble; the fire will burn them up. They cannot deliver themselves from the power of the flame. passages.context_html:
Babylon is addressed as a royal daughter brought down from her throne to the dust. The language of grinding flour, wading through streams and exposed shame reverses her former luxury and status.

The reason for judgment is stated clearly. The Lord placed His people under Babylon’s power, but she showed no mercy, laying a heavy yoke even on the elderly. Her authority did not give her freedom to act cruelly without answering for it.

Babylon expects to remain queen forever. She claims unmatched greatness, imagines that no one sees her wrongdoing and assumes she will never know widowhood or the loss of children. Disaster overturns that confidence in a moment.

The final challenge exposes the failure of her spells and counselors. Those who predict by the stars cannot save her or even themselves. The fire that consumes them is no comforting hearth, and the chapter ends with no rescuer found among those she relied upon.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry, Wesley and the USCCB notes read the royal woman as a picture of Babylon’s fall from dominance into humiliation. The contrast is between the status she claimed and the helplessness the coming judgment reveals.

Henry and Wesley emphasize that being used in judgment did not excuse Babylon’s cruelty. The charge concerning the elderly makes the failure of mercy concrete.

They also connect the failed sorcery and counsel with misplaced confidence. Wealth, secrecy and supposed knowledge of the future cannot put Babylon beyond the Lord’s judgment. The warning concerns power that refuses to consider either its conduct or its end.

passages.god_plan_html:
Revelation 18:4–10 takes up Isaiah’s picture directly in its portrayal of Babylon. She claims to sit as a queen, expects no widowhood or grief, and then faces devastating judgment in a single day.

The surrounding call is for God’s people to come out of her and avoid sharing in her sins. Revelation joins the collapse of proud luxury with God’s remembrance of wrongdoing and His power to judge.

This connection shows how the earlier Babylon becomes part of the New Testament’s larger warning about corrupt power. Its security is temporary; belonging to God calls for a different allegiance and a different way of life.

passages.title: Isaiah 48:1-11
passages.section_title: What good is a sacred name when the people will not receive God’s word?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 “Listen to this, O house of Jacob, you who are called by the name of Israel, who have descended from the line of Judah, who swear by the name of the LORD, who invoke the God of Israel— but not in truth or righteousness— 2 who indeed call yourselves after the holy city and lean on the God of Israel; the LORD of Hosts is His name. 3 I foretold the former things long ago; they came out of My mouth and I proclaimed them. Suddenly I acted, and they came to pass. 4 For I knew that you are stubborn; your neck is iron and your forehead is bronze. 5 Therefore I declared it to you long ago; I announced it before it came to pass, so that you could not claim, ‘My idol has done this; my carved image and molten god has ordained it.’ 6 You have heard these things; look at them all. Will you not acknowledge them? From now on I will tell you of new things, hidden things unknown to you. 7 They are created now, and not long ago; you have not heard of them before today. So you cannot claim, ‘I already knew them!’ 8 You have never heard; you have never understood; for a long time your ears have not been open. For I knew how deceitful you are; you have been called a rebel from birth. 9 For the sake of My name I will delay My wrath; for the sake of My praise I will restrain it, so that you will not be cut off. 10 See, I have refined you, but not as silver; I have tested you in the furnace of affliction. 11 For My own sake, My very own sake, I will act; for how can I let Myself be defamed? I will not yield My glory to another.

passages.context_html:
The Lord addresses people who carry Israel’s name, invoke His name and identify with the holy city, yet do not do so in truth or righteousness. Religious identity and language have become separated from faithful response.

He explains why He announced events before they happened: the people were stubborn enough to credit their idols instead. Now He announces new things they cannot claim to have known already. Their resistance is described as long-standing, not a brief failure of information.

Yet the Lord delays His anger for the sake of His name and praise, so that they are not cut off. He describes testing them in the furnace of affliction while refusing to yield His glory to another. Judgment, restraint and His purpose to make Himself known are held together.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley explain the opening as a warning against taking pride in religious descent, a holy place or the right name while failing to live faithfully. The Lord’s announced and fulfilled words leave no basis for giving an idol the credit.

For the furnace, Henry, Wesley and Gill emphasize testing that is accompanied by restraint. They explain the comparison with silver through the severity of a process that would otherwise consume the people.

These readings understand the purpose as exposing false confidence and bringing a people back to the Lord. The honor of His name remains the reason mercy is not exhausted by their failure.

passages.god_plan_html:
The testing of faith is developed for believers in 1 Peter 1:3–9. Peter begins with new birth and living hope through Jesus’ resurrection, then speaks honestly about grief in various trials.

He compares proven faith with gold refined by fire and directs its outcome toward praise, glory and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ. The hope rests in God’s mercy and the coming salvation, rather than in the trial being pleasant.

This is a shared biblical theme, not a direct quotation or an explanation of the cause of every hardship. Testing belongs within the larger purpose of a people whose hope and trust are held by the God who saves them.

passages.title: Isaiah 48:12-22
passages.section_title: What should a redeemed people do with the way God opens for them?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 Listen to Me, O Jacob, and Israel, whom I have called: I am He; I am the first, and I am the last. 13 Surely My own hand founded the earth, and My right hand spread out the heavens; when I summon them, they stand up together. 14 Come together, all of you, and listen: Which of the idols has foretold these things? The LORD’s chosen ally will carry out His desire against Babylon, and His arm will be against the Chaldeans. 15 I, even I, have spoken; yes, I have called him. I have brought him, and he will succeed in his mission. 16 Come near to Me and listen to this: From the beginning I have not spoken in secret; from the time it happened, I was there.” And now the Lord GOD has sent me, accompanied by His Spirit. 17 Thus says the LORD your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel: “I am the LORD your God, who teaches you for your benefit, who directs you in the way you should go. 18 If only you had paid attention to My commandments, your peace would have been like a river, and your righteousness like waves of the sea. 19 Your descendants would have been as countless as the sand, and your offspring as numerous as its grains; their name would never be cut off or eliminated from My presence.” 20 Leave Babylon! Flee from the Chaldeans! Declare it with a shout of joy, proclaim it, let it go out to the ends of the earth, saying, “The LORD has redeemed His servant Jacob!” 21 They did not thirst when He led them through the deserts; He made water flow for them from the rock; He split the rock, and water gushed out. 22 “There is no peace,” says the LORD, “for the wicked.”

20 Leave Babylon! Flee from the Chaldeans! Declare it with a shout of joy, proclaim it, let it go out to the ends of the earth, saying, “The LORD has redeemed His servant Jacob!” 21 They did not thirst when He led them through the deserts; He made water flow for them from the rock; He split the rock, and water gushed out. 22 “There is no peace,” says the LORD, “for the wicked.”

passages.context_html:
The Lord calls Jacob and Israel to listen as the first and last, the One who founded the earth and spread out the heavens. He will bring His chosen ally against Babylon and give success to the mission He announced.

Verse 16 speaks of being sent by the Lord God, accompanied by His Spirit. The passage then names the Lord as Redeemer, teacher and guide. He laments the peace and continuing righteousness His people would have known had they paid attention to His commands.

The command to leave Babylon is to be accompanied by joyful proclamation to the ends of the earth: the Lord has redeemed Jacob. The remembered picture of water coming from a split rock presents Him as the One who provides along the way.

The final warning keeps the promise from becoming a reason for complacency. The rescue calls for receiving the Lord’s direction; the wicked do not find peace simply by sharing the name or outward circumstances of His people.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Commentators differ over the speaker at the end of verse 16. Gill reads the words as Christ speaking of being sent, and connects the passage with the Father, Son and Spirit. Henry also applies the sending to Christ.

Wesley reads the immediate speaker as Isaiah, while also seeing a possible reference through him to Christ. The Cambridge commentary on verse 16 reads a change to the prophet’s voice and understands the Spirit as accompanying his mission. This difference concerns the voice in this verse, rather than a simple division between believing and denying the Trinity.

For the final scene, Henry and Gill connect the rock and water with the exodus account and with Christ’s provision. Wesley reads the account as reassurance for the coming journey from captivity. They join the call to leave with the Lord’s continued guidance and the warning against refusing it.

passages.god_plan_html:
First Corinthians 10:1–13 looks back to the exodus and the wilderness food and drink. Paul explicitly identifies the spiritual rock with Christ, placing God’s provision within the account of Christ’s care for His people.

Paul then warns believers by the example of people who received those gifts but fell into idolatry and other wrongdoing. The history is written for their instruction, so confidence in their standing must go with vigilance and trust in God’s faithfulness.

This connects with Isaiah’s return-from-captivity scene through the earlier exodus, rather than as a direct quotation of Isaiah 48. Rescue and provision lead into a life of listening to God. The purpose is restored people walking in His way, not treating His gifts as a reason to disregard Him.

passages.title: Isaiah 49:1-26
passages.section_title: Can the Servant bring light to the nations and hope to a forgotten city?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Listen to Me, O islands; pay attention, O distant peoples: The LORD called Me from the womb; from the body of My mother He named Me. 2 He made My mouth like a sharp sword; He hid Me in the shadow of His hand. He made Me like a polished arrow; He hid Me in His quiver. 3 He said to Me, “You are My Servant, Israel, in whom I will display My glory.” 4 But I said, “I have labored in vain, I have spent My strength in futility and vanity; yet My vindication is with the LORD, and My reward is with My God.” 5 And now says the LORD, who formed Me from the womb to be His Servant, to bring Jacob back to Him, that Israel might be gathered to Him— for I am honored in the sight of the LORD, and My God is My strength— 6 He says: “It is not enough for You to be My Servant, to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the protected ones of Israel. I will also make You a light for the nations, to bring My salvation to the ends of the earth.” 7 Thus says the LORD, the Redeemer and Holy One of Israel, to Him who was despised and abhorred by the nation, to the Servant of rulers: “Kings will see You and rise, and princes will bow down, because of the LORD, who is faithful, the Holy One of Israel, who has chosen You.” 8 This is what the LORD says: “In the time of favor I will answer You, and in the day of salvation I will help You; I will keep You and appoint You to be a covenant for the people, to restore the land, to apportion its desolate inheritances, 9 to say to the prisoners, ‘Come out,’ and to those in darkness, ‘Show yourselves.’ They will feed along the pathways, and find pasture on every barren hill. 10 They will not hunger or thirst, nor will scorching heat or sun beat down on them. For He who has compassion on them will guide them and lead them beside springs of water. 11 I will turn all My mountains into roads, and My highways will be raised up. 12 Behold, they will come from far away, from the north and from the west, and from the land of Aswan.” 13 Shout for joy, O heavens; rejoice, O earth; break forth in song, O mountains! For the LORD has comforted His people, and He will have compassion on His afflicted ones. 14 But Zion said, “The LORD has forsaken me; the Lord has forgotten me!” 15 “Can a woman forget her nursing child, or lack compassion for the son of her womb? Even if she could forget, I will not forget you! 16 Behold, I have inscribed you on the palms of My hands; your walls are ever before Me. 17 Your builders hasten back; your destroyers and wreckers depart from you. 18 Lift up your eyes and look around. They all gather together; they come to you. As surely as I live,” declares the LORD, “you will wear them all as jewelry and put them on like a bride. 19 For your ruined and desolate places and your ravaged land will now indeed be too small for your people, and those who devoured you will be far away. 20 Yet the children of your bereavement will say in your hearing, ‘This place is too small for us; make room for us to live here.’ 21 Then you will say in your heart, ‘Who has begotten these for me? I was bereaved and barren; I was exiled and rejected. So who has reared them? Look, I was left all alone, so where did they come from?’” 22 This is what the Lord GOD says: “Behold, I will lift up My hand to the nations, and raise My banner to the peoples. They will bring your sons in their arms and carry your daughters on their shoulders. 23 Kings will be your foster fathers, and their queens your nursing mothers. They will bow to you facedown and lick the dust at your feet. Then you will know that I am the LORD; those who hope in Me will never be put to shame.” 24 Can the plunder be snatched from the mighty, or the captives of a tyrant be delivered? 25 Indeed, this is what the LORD says: “Even the captives of the mighty will be taken away, and the plunder of the tyrant will be retrieved; I will contend with those who contend with you, and I will save your children. 26 I will make your oppressors eat their own flesh; they will be drunk on their own blood, as with wine. Then all mankind will know that I, the LORD, am your Savior and your Redeemer, the Mighty One of Jacob.”

passages.context_html:
The islands and distant peoples are called to listen to the Servant. The Lord called and named Him from the womb, made His mouth like a sword and kept Him like a polished arrow ready for use. He is called Israel, the Servant in whom God will display His glory.

The Servant describes labor that appears wasted, yet entrusts His vindication and reward to God. His mission is then stated: to bring Jacob back and gather Israel. It reaches still further, making Him a light to the nations so God’s salvation goes to the ends of the earth.

The Lord promises a time of favor, release for prisoners and people in darkness, and provision along the way. Those He leads will not hunger or thirst or be struck by scorching heat. The announcement calls heaven and earth to rejoice in His compassion.

Zion’s reply is the cry of someone who feels abandoned: the Lord has forgotten her. God answers with the comparison of a mother and her nursing child. Even if a mother could forget, He will not. The image of Zion inscribed on His palms and her walls continually before Him expresses His unbroken attention.

The city’s desolation gives way to children gathering in such numbers that the space seems too small. Nations and rulers help bring sons and daughters home. What seemed an emptied and forsaken place becomes a scene of restoration.

The final question asks whether captives can really be taken from the mighty. The Lord promises to take up their cause and save their children. The outcome will make His identity as Savior and Redeemer known to all humanity.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry, Wesley and Gill read the Servant through Christ and His saving mission. Wesley and Gill explain the name Israel through His relationship to the people and His representative role, while His task of restoring Jacob distinguishes Him from the people He restores.

For Zion’s complaint, these commentators emphasize the Lord’s continuing care despite circumstances that seem to contradict it. Henry and Wesley also apply the enlarged family and help from nations to the gathering and growth of God’s people through the gospel.

The explanations connect the restored city and the Servant’s worldwide work, while differing over how particular details of the gathering unfold. Their central encouragement is that apparent failure and felt abandonment do not cancel the Lord’s promise.

passages.god_plan_html:
The New Testament directly uses three parts of this passage. In Acts 13:44–49, Paul and Barnabas quote the light-to-the-nations promise to explain their mission to Gentiles. The Servant’s worldwide horizon becomes part of the work of carrying the good news outward.

Second Corinthians 6:1–2 quotes the time of favor and day of salvation, then urges people to receive God’s grace now. The promised help calls for a response, rather than merely admiration of a future possibility.

Revelation 7:13–17 takes up the promise of no hunger, thirst or scorching heat and of guidance to springs. The Lamb is their shepherd, and God wipes away their tears.

Together these uses give the chapter a clear place in God’s larger purpose: salvation is proclaimed to the nations, His grace is offered for people to receive, and the redeemed are brought into the care and lasting comfort of the Lamb.

passages.title: Isaiah 50:1-3
passages.section_title: Did captivity mean that God had lost His claim or His power?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 This is what the LORD says: “Where is your mother’s certificate of divorce with which I sent her away? Or to which of My creditors did I sell you? Look, you were sold for your iniquities, and for your transgressions your mother was sent away. 2 Why was no one there when I arrived? Why did no one answer when I called? Is My hand too short to redeem you? Or do I lack the strength to deliver you? Behold, My rebuke dries up the sea; I turn the rivers into a desert; the fish rot for lack of water and die of thirst. 3 I clothe the heavens in black and make sackcloth their covering.”
paragraphs: 1 This is what the LORD says: “Where is your mother’s certificate of divorce with which I sent her away? Or to which of My creditors did I sell you? Look, you were sold for your iniquities, and for your transgressions your mother was sent away. 2 Why was no one there when I arrived? Why did no one answer when I called? Is My hand too short to redeem you? Or do I lack the strength to deliver you? Behold, My rebuke dries up the sea; I turn the rivers into a desert; the fish rot for lack of water and die of thirst. 3 I clothe the heavens in black and make sackcloth their covering.”

passages.context_html:
The Lord challenges the idea that His people’s plight resulted from His debts or a complete abandonment of the relationship. He asks for a certificate of divorce and the name of a creditor to whom He supposedly sold them.

The explanation is given in the same verse: their iniquities and transgressions brought the separation. Their situation is not evidence that another power has purchased authority over the Lord or forced His hand.

The next questions concern His unanswered call and His ability to redeem. The images of sea and rivers drying and heavens clothed in darkness assert His power. The God who calls has not become unable to deliver.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The USCCB notes read the missing certificate as an answer to the complaint of complete abandonment: the bond remains, and the Lord still has power to deliver.

Henry and Wesley emphasize the people’s responsibility in this particular covenant address. The question is not whether God has become powerless, but how the people have answered His call.

The images therefore expose a false explanation of the crisis while leaving room for the promised redemption. The Lord’s right to call and His ability to rescue remain intact.

He awakens Me morning by morning; He awakens My ear to listen as a disciple. 5 The Lord GOD has opened My ears, and I have not been rebellious, nor have I turned back. 6 I offered My back to those who struck Me, and My cheeks to those who tore out My beard. I did not hide My face from scorn and spittle. 7 Because the Lord GOD helps Me, I have not been disgraced; therefore I have set My face like flint, and I know that I will not be put to shame. 8 The One who vindicates Me is near. Let him trust in the name of the LORD; let him lean on his God. 11 Behold, all you who kindle a fire, who array yourselves with firebrands, walk in the light of your fire and of the firebrands you have lit! passages.context_html:
The Servant speaks of receiving the tongue of discipleship so He can sustain the weary with a word. Each morning His ear is awakened to listen. His response is obedience rather than rebellion or retreat.

That obedience continues into suffering. He offers His back to those who strike, His cheeks to those who tear out the beard, and His face to scorn and spitting. The description joins what is done to Him with His refusal to turn away from the task.

His confidence rests in the Lord’s help and approaching vindication. Setting His face like flint pictures resolve; the charges of opponents will not establish the final verdict, and the accusers will wear out.

The closing appeal is to people who fear the Lord and hear His Servant while walking without light. They are to lean on God. The alternative is to trust a fire of their own making, which ends in torment instead of the security they seek.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley understand the faithful, suffering Servant through Christ. Wesley allows that parts may apply to Isaiah, but regards their fullest and clearest realization as belonging to Jesus.

They connect the attentive ear and sustaining word with His faithful teaching, the suffering with His willing submission, and the promised vindication with the Father establishing the righteousness of His Son.

For the darkness in verse 10, both distinguish the distress of a faithful person from a refusal to obey. The contrast with the self-made fire is therefore a contrast in what people trust, rather than a claim that every troubled believer is living wickedly.

passages.god_plan_html:
The Gospel accounts show the blows, humiliation and spitting in Jesus’ suffering in Matthew 26:67–68 and 27:26–31. These scenes provide a close parallel with the Servant’s description. Matthew does not separately narrate every detail, such as the tearing of the beard.

Hebrews 5:7–9 joins Jesus’ prayers and tears with obedience learned through suffering and His becoming the source of eternal salvation. The suffering belongs to His faithful saving work, rather than proving the Father has abandoned His purpose.

Romans 8:31–39 takes up the language of charges, justification and condemnation. It grounds believers’ confidence in Christ’s death, resurrection and intercession, then declares that suffering cannot separate them from God’s love in Him.

The Servant’s vindication thus opens onto assurance for those who belong to Him. The hope is not that faithful people never face distress, but that the One who gave Himself and was raised now acts for them.

passages.title: Isaiah 51:1-16
passages.section_title: What can a frightened people learn from Abraham and Sarah?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 “Listen to Me, you who pursue righteousness, you who seek the LORD: Look to the rock from which you were cut, and to the quarry from which you were hewn. 2 Look to Abraham your father, and to Sarah who gave you birth. When I called him, he was but one; then I blessed him and multiplied him. 3 For the LORD will comfort Zion and will look with compassion on all her ruins; He will make her wilderness like Eden and her desert like the garden of the LORD. Joy and gladness will be found in her, thanksgiving and melodious song. 4 Pay attention to Me, My people, and listen to Me, My nation; for a law will go out from Me, and My justice will become a light to the nations; I will bring it about quickly. 5 My righteousness draws near, My salvation is on the way, and My arms will bring justice to the nations. The islands will look for Me and wait in hope for My arm. 6 Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look at the earth below; for the heavens will vanish like smoke, the earth will wear out like a garment, and its people will die like gnats. But My salvation will last forever, and My righteousness will never fail. 7 Listen to Me, you who know what is right, you people with My law in your hearts: Do not fear the scorn of men; do not be broken by their insults. 8 For the moth will devour them like a garment, and the worm will eat them like wool. But My righteousness will last forever, My salvation through all generations.” 9 Awake, awake, put on strength, O arm of the LORD. Wake up as in days past, as in generations of old. Was it not You who cut Rahab to pieces, who pierced through the dragon? 10 Was it not You who dried up the sea, the waters of the great deep, who made a road in the depths of the sea for the redeemed to cross over? 11 So the redeemed of the LORD will return and enter Zion with singing, crowned with everlasting joy. Gladness and joy will overtake them, and sorrow and sighing will flee. 12 “I, even I, am He who comforts you. Why should you be afraid of mortal man, of a son of man who withers like grass? 13 But you have forgotten the LORD, your Maker, who stretched out the heavens and laid the foundations of the earth. You live in terror all day long because of the fury of the oppressor who is bent on destruction. But where is the fury of the oppressor? 14 The captive will soon be freed; he will not die in the dungeon, and his bread will not be lacking. 15 For I am the LORD your God who stirs up the sea so that its waves roar— the LORD of Hosts is His name. 16 I have put My words in your mouth, and covered you with the shadow of My hand, to establish the heavens, to found the earth, and to say to Zion, ‘You are My people.’”

passages.context_html:
The Lord addresses people who seek Him and pursue righteousness. He tells them to look back to Abraham and Sarah: the family began small, yet He blessed and multiplied it. Their present weakness does not put restoration beyond His reach.

Comfort for Zion is pictured as a wilderness becoming like Eden, filled with joy and thanksgiving. The promise then reaches beyond the city. God’s justice will become a light to the nations, and distant islands will wait for His saving power.

He contrasts what lasts with what wears out. The heavens, earth and human opponents are passing; His righteousness and salvation endure. The people who carry His law in their hearts are therefore told not to let human insults break them.

A plea follows for the Lord to act as He did in the past. The sea made into a road recalls the deliverance from Egypt. The promised return to Zion is marked by singing and an end to sorrow.

The Lord answers as their Maker and comforter. Their oppressors are mortal; He is the One who made heaven and earth and rules the sea. The closing words join His protection and His word with His declaration that Zion belongs to Him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley reads Abraham and Sarah as encouragement for people who cannot see how recovery is possible: the God who multiplied that small beginning can raise His people again. Henry likewise draws attention to dependence on God’s grace.

Both connect the promised light to the nations with the gospel. They read the prayer about the sea as an appeal to the God who has already rescued His people, and the answer as reassurance that human threats cannot overturn His saving purpose.

The chapter does not ask the frightened people to pretend their enemies are harmless. It calls them to remember whose power and promise will outlast those enemies.

passages.god_plan_html:
The appeal to Abraham and Sarah belongs to a larger biblical pattern: God brings about what His promise requires when human strength cannot. Romans 4:16–25 also recalls Abraham’s aged body and Sarah’s inability to bear a child, then explains his confidence that God could do what He had promised.

Paul carries that lesson forward to faith in the God who raised Jesus from the dead. This is a shared theme, rather than a direct quotation of Isaiah 51: hope rests on God’s ability to keep His word, and His saving purpose reaches beyond the limits of the people He calls.

passages.title: Isaiah 51:17-23
passages.section_title: Who can help Jerusalem when her own children cannot?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 Awake, awake! Rise up, O Jerusalem, you who have drunk from the hand of the LORD the cup of His fury; you who have drained the goblet to the dregs— the cup that makes men stagger. 18 Among all the sons she bore, there is no one to guide her; among all the sons she brought up, there is no one to take her hand. 19 These pairs have befallen you: devastation and destruction, famine and sword. Who will grieve for you? Who can comfort you? 20 Your sons have fainted; they lie at the head of every street, like an antelope in a net. They are full of the wrath of the LORD, the rebuke of your God. 21 Therefore now hear this, you afflicted one, drunken, but not with wine. 22 Thus says your Lord, the LORD, even your God, who defends His people: “See, I have removed from your hand the cup of staggering. From that goblet, the cup of My fury, you will never drink again. 23 I will place it in the hands of your tormentors, who told you: ‘Lie down, so we can walk over you,’ so that you made your back like the ground, like a street to be traversed.”

From that goblet, the cup of My fury, you will never drink again. 23 I will place it in the hands of your tormentors, who told you: ‘Lie down, so we can walk over you,’ so that you made your back like the ground, like a street to be traversed.”

passages.context_html:
The call to awake is now addressed to Jerusalem. She is pictured as a woman who has drained a cup that leaves her staggering. The cup represents the Lord’s fury, and the devastation, famine and sword describe the judgment she has experienced.

None of her children can take her hand and guide her. They have collapsed in the streets themselves. The picture makes the depth of her helplessness clear: the people who might have supported her are caught in the same disaster.

The Lord then speaks as the One who defends His people. He promises to remove the cup from her hand and put it into the hands of her tormentors. Those who treated her like a road beneath their feet will face judgment themselves.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley understand the drunkenness as the effect of severe affliction, as the passage itself distinguishes it from drinking wine. The helpless children show that Jerusalem cannot supply her own deliverance.

Both emphasize the reversal: the God whose judgment she has experienced now takes up her cause. Her oppressors do not gain a permanent right to humiliate her. The promise holds together His judgment, His mercy and His defense of the afflicted.

passages.title: Isaiah 52:1-12
passages.section_title: What is the good news that makes Jerusalem sing?

versions.text: 1 Awake, awake, clothe yourself with strength, O Zion! Put on your garments of splendor, O Jerusalem, holy city! For the uncircumcised and unclean will no longer enter you. 2 Shake off your dust! Rise up and sit on your throne, O Jerusalem. Remove the chains from your neck, O captive Daughter of Zion. 3 For this is what the LORD says: “You were sold for nothing, and without money you will be redeemed.” 4 For this is what the Lord GOD says: “At first My people went down to Egypt to live, then Assyria oppressed them without cause. 5 And now what have I here? declares the LORD. For My people have been taken without cause; those who rule them taunt, declares the LORD, and My name is blasphemed continually all day long. 6 Therefore My people will know My name; therefore they will know on that day that I am He who speaks. Here I am!” 7 How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of those who bring good news, who proclaim peace, who bring good tidings, who proclaim salvation, who say to Zion, “Your God reigns!” 8 Listen! Your watchmen lift up their voices, together they shout for joy. For every eye will see when the LORD returns to Zion. 9 Break forth in joy, sing together, O ruins of Jerusalem, for the LORD has comforted His people; He has redeemed Jerusalem. 10 The LORD has bared His holy arm in the sight of all the nations; all the ends of the earth will see the salvation of our God. 11 Depart, depart, go out from there! Touch no unclean thing; come out from it, purify yourselves, you who carry the vessels of the LORD. 12 For you will not leave in a hurry nor flee in haste, for the LORD goes before you, and the God of Israel is your rear guard.
