passages.context_html:
Jerusalem is called to rise from the dust, remove her chains and put on garments of splendor. The opening picture changes her condition from captive humiliation to the dignity of a holy city. Her redemption will not depend on someone raising a purchase price.

The Lord recalls the people’s stay in Egypt and their oppression by Assyria. Now His people are taken away and His name is continually dishonored. He promises that they will know the One who speaks and acts for them.

A messenger announces peace, salvation and the reign of their God. Watchmen lift their voices together, and even the ruined city is called to sing. The Lord has comforted and redeemed His people, and the ends of the earth will see His salvation.

The departure requires purity, especially for those carrying the Lord’s vessels. It will be a secure departure rather than a panicked escape: the Lord goes before them, and the God of Israel guards their rear.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley connects the promised redemption with the return from Babylon and with the Messiah’s fuller saving work. Henry likewise relates the announcement of God’s reign to Christ and to those who carry His good news.

Both read the call to leave uncleanness as part of the freedom God gives. The messengers bring news of His rescue, while the departing people are called to leave the pollutions of captivity behind. His protection accompanies the journey.

passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 10:13–17 directly uses the announcement about beautiful feet to explain the sending of gospel messengers. People need to hear about Christ, and messengers must be sent to tell them. The good news of God’s salvation is carried outward through that work.

Second Corinthians 6:14–18 also takes up the command to come out and touch nothing unclean. Paul applies it to the church’s allegiance to the living God rather than idols. Isaiah’s language therefore serves both the spread of the gospel and the call for God’s people to live faithfully in response.

passages.title: Isaiah 52:13-15
passages.section_title: How can the disfigured Servant be the One God exalts?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 Behold, My Servant will prosper; He will be raised and lifted up and highly exalted. 14 Just as many were appalled at Him— His appearance was disfigured beyond that of any man, and His form was marred beyond human likeness— 15 so He will sprinkle many nations. Kings will shut their mouths because of Him. For they will see what they have not been told, and they will understand what they have not heard.
paragraphs: 13 Behold, My Servant will prosper; He will be raised and lifted up and highly exalted. 14 Just as many were appalled at Him— His appearance was disfigured beyond that of any man, and His form was marred beyond human likeness— 15 so He will sprinkle many nations. Kings will shut their mouths because of Him. For they will see what they have not been told, and they will understand what they have not heard.

passages.context_html:
This begins the account of the Servant that continues through chapter 53. The first announcement is His success and great exaltation. The next line describes an appearance so disfigured that people are appalled.

The contrast is central: the One who suffers such humiliation will affect many nations, and kings will fall silent before Him. People who had never been told will see and understand. The suffering described next must be read alongside this announced outcome.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley identify the Servant with Christ and read the humiliation and exaltation together. His suffering does not mean His mission has failed.

They explain the sprinkling image somewhat differently. Henry connects it with Christ’s blood and its continuing saving power; Wesley connects it with His teaching reaching the nations like water. Both understand the closing words as the revelation of saving truth to people who had not previously received it.

Romans 15:20–21 quotes the closing promise when Paul explains his aim to preach where Christ has not been named. He sees the announcement about those who had not heard as a reason to carry the gospel into new places.

This gives the worldwide reach of the Servant’s work a concrete New Testament connection. The One whose suffering astonishes people becomes the subject of good news carried to nations that had not known Him.

passages.title: Isaiah 53:1-8
passages.section_title: Why does the innocent Servant suffer for people who rejected Him?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Who has believed our message? And to whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed? 2 He grew up before Him like a tender shoot, and like a root out of dry ground. He had no stately form or majesty to attract us, no beauty that we should desire Him. 3 He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief. Like one from whom men hide their faces, He was despised, and we esteemed Him not. 4 Surely He took up our infirmities and carried our sorrows; yet we considered Him stricken, struck down by God, and afflicted. 5 But He was pierced for our transgressions, He was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was upon Him, and by His stripes we are healed. 6 We all like sheep have gone astray, each one has turned to his own way; and the LORD has laid upon Him the iniquity of us all. 7 He was oppressed and afflicted, yet He did not open His mouth. He was led like a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is silent, so He did not open His mouth. 8 By oppression and judgment He was taken away, and who can recount His descendants? For He was cut off from the land of the living; He was stricken for the transgression of My people.

He had no stately form or majesty to attract us, no beauty that we should desire Him. 3 He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief. Like one from whom men hide their faces, He was despised, and we esteemed Him not.

4 Surely He took up our infirmities and carried our sorrows; yet we considered Him stricken, struck down by God, and afflicted. 5 But He was pierced for our transgressions, He was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was upon Him, and by His stripes we are healed. 6 We all like sheep have gone astray, each one has turned to his own way; and the LORD has laid upon Him the iniquity of us all.

7 He was oppressed and afflicted, yet He did not open His mouth. He was led like a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is silent, so He did not open His mouth. 8 By oppression and judgment He was taken away, and who can recount His descendants? For He was cut off from the land of the living; He was stricken for the transgression of My people.

passages.context_html:
The account opens with a question about who has believed the message. The Servant grows like a tender shoot in dry ground. He has none of the outward splendor that would make people naturally desire Him; instead, He is despised and rejected.

The speakers then correct their earlier judgment. They had taken His affliction as evidence that God was striking Him down. Now they describe Him carrying their infirmities and sorrows and suffering because of their transgressions and iniquities. The people are the wandering sheep; He bears what their wandering has brought.

The Hebrew word חֳלִי, choli (kho-LEE), used in the description of infirmities, means sickness or disease. Brown–Driver–Briggs also lists its use for distress pictured as sickness. The passage gives the Servant’s suffering a deeply personal character: He carries the burdens of others.

He does not answer oppression with self-defense. The image is a lamb led to slaughter or a sheep silent before its shearers. The closing lines describe His being taken away through oppression and judgment and cut off from the land of the living for the transgression of the people.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The major Christian traditions read the Servant’s saving suffering through Jesus Christ. The Catholic Catechism, paragraphs 615–616, the Westminster Confession, chapter 8.5 and the Methodist Articles II and XX all teach that His obedient, sacrificial death deals with sin and brings reconciliation with God. That shared reading does not mean their accounts of every aspect of salvation are identical.

Henry and Wesley emphasize the reversal in the speakers’ understanding: the Servant is suffering for their sins, rather than for wrongdoing of His own. They connect the sheep going their own way with humanity’s departure from God and the Servant’s suffering with the peace He secures.

passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 8:26–35 gives an explicit connection. The Ethiopian official is reading the lines about the sheep led to slaughter and the life taken from the earth. Philip begins with that very Scripture and explains the good news about Jesus.

The New Testament also shows two connected uses of the burden-bearing and healing language. Matthew 8:14–17 cites Isaiah when Jesus heals the sick. First Peter 2:21–25 describes Christ bearing sins, enabling people to live righteously, and bringing wandering sheep back to their Shepherd.

These uses keep both His compassion for suffering people and His rescue from sin in view. Matthew describes actual healings in Jesus’ ministry; Peter explains what His suffering means for people who turn from sin to Him. Together they show why this passage is central to the New Testament’s explanation of His saving work.

passages.title: Isaiah 53:9-12
passages.section_title: What does the Servant’s death accomplish?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 He was assigned a grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in His death, although He had done no violence, nor was any deceit in His mouth. 10 Yet it was the LORD’s will to crush Him and to cause Him to suffer; and when His soul is made a guilt offering, He will see His offspring, He will prolong His days, and the good pleasure of the LORD will prosper in His hand. 11 After the anguish of His soul, He will see the light of life and be satisfied. By His knowledge My righteous Servant will justify many, and He will bear their iniquities. 12 Therefore I will allot Him a portion with the great, and He will divide the spoils with the strong, because He has poured out His life unto death, and He was numbered with the transgressors. Yet He bore the sin of many and made intercession for the transgressors.

passages.context_html:
The Servant’s burial is described alongside His innocence: He has done no violence and spoken no deceit. Yet His death belongs to the Lord’s purpose, and His life is made a guilt offering.

The Hebrew word אָשָׁם, asham (ah-SHAHM), can describe guilt or an offering that deals with guilt. Brown–Driver–Briggs specifically lists Isaiah 53:10 under the offering sense. The image explains the purpose of His suffering: His life is given to deal with the wrongdoing of others.

Death is followed by promises of offspring, prolonged days and the Lord’s good pleasure prospering through Him. After His anguish He sees the light of life and is satisfied. The righteous Servant makes many righteous and bears their iniquities.

The final picture is of a victor receiving a share of the spoils. The reason given is His poured-out life: He was counted among transgressors, bore the sin of many and made intercession for transgressors. His innocence, His willing self-giving and the benefit to others belong together.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley read the offering as Christ’s sacrifice for sin and the promised outcome as His living, successful saving work. They understand the offspring as the people brought to God through Him, rather than biological children.

Both connect making many righteous with release from the guilt of sin through Christ. The reward and intercession show the success of His mission: His suffering is followed by the salvation of people for whom He gave Himself. Their reading joins the chapter’s sacrifice language to its promises of life and victory.

passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus explicitly applies the closing passage to Himself in Luke 22:35–38, saying that the Scripture about being numbered with transgressors must be fulfilled in Him. This identification comes from His own explanation of what lies ahead.

First Peter 2:21–25 also uses the description of the Servant’s innocence and connects it with Christ bearing sins. Peter explains the purpose as a changed life: people are to die to sin and live to righteousness.

The burial account in Matthew 27:57–60 provides a further close parallel: the rich disciple Joseph of Arimathea places Jesus’ body in his own new tomb. The Gospel does not explicitly quote Isaiah there, so this is a parallel rather than a stated quotation.

The chapter’s place in God’s purpose is therefore more than an example of enduring pain. Jesus identifies Himself with its condemned Servant, and Peter explains His death as a rescue from sin that brings people back to their Shepherd.

passages.title: Isaiah 54:1-17
passages.section_title: Can the forsaken city become a home overflowing with children?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 “Shout for joy, O barren woman, who bears no children; break forth in song and cry aloud, you who have never travailed; because more are the children of the desolate woman than of her who has a husband,” says the LORD. 2 “Enlarge the site of your tent, stretch out the curtains of your dwellings, do not hold back. Lengthen your ropes and drive your stakes in deep. 3 For you will spread out to the right and left; your descendants will dispossess the nations and inhabit the desolate cities. 4 Do not be afraid, for you will not be put to shame; do not be intimidated, for you will not be humiliated. For you will forget the shame of your youth and will remember no more the reproach of your widowhood. 5 For your husband is your Maker— the LORD of Hosts is His name— the Holy One of Israel is your Redeemer; He is called the God of all the earth. 6 For the LORD has called you back, like a wife deserted and wounded in spirit, like the rejected wife of one’s youth,” says your God. 7 “For a brief moment I forsook you, but with great compassion I will bring you back. 8 In a surge of anger I hid My face from you for a moment, but with everlasting kindness I will have compassion on you,” says the LORD your Redeemer. 9 “For to Me this is like the days of Noah, when I swore that the waters of Noah would never again cover the earth. So I have sworn that I will not be angry with you or rebuke you. 10 Though the mountains may be removed and the hills may be shaken, My loving devotion will not depart from you, and My covenant of peace will not be broken,” says the LORD, who has compassion on you. 11 “O afflicted city, lashed by storms, without solace, surely I will set your stones in antimony and lay your foundations with sapphires. 12 I will make your pinnacles of rubies, your gates of sparkling jewels, and all your walls of precious stones. 13 Then all your sons will be taught by the LORD, and great will be their prosperity. 14 In righteousness you will be established, far from oppression, for you will have no fear. Terror will be far removed, for it will not come near you. 15 If anyone attacks you, it is not from Me; whoever assails you will fall before you. 16 Behold, I have created the craftsman who fans the coals into flame and forges a weapon fit for its task; and I have created the destroyer to wreak havoc. 17 No weapon formed against you shall prosper, and you will refute every tongue that accuses you. This is the heritage of the servants of the LORD, and their vindication is from Me,” declares the LORD.

passages.context_html:
After the Servant’s suffering and promised success, Jerusalem is addressed as a woman who has borne no children. She is told to sing and make her tent larger, because a growing family will fill it. Desolate cities will be inhabited again.

The next picture is of a deserted wife called back by her husband. Her Maker is her husband, the Holy One of Israel her Redeemer, and His rule reaches the whole earth. The Lord contrasts a brief time of anger with the lasting kindness of His promised compassion.

The comparison with Noah emphasizes the reliability of His promise. Even if mountains move and hills shake, His loving devotion and covenant of peace will endure.

The afflicted city is then pictured with precious stones, beautiful gates and secure walls. Her children will be taught by the Lord, and righteousness will replace oppression and terror.

The closing assurance concerns attacks and accusations. The Lord made both those who forge weapons and those who use them; they cannot establish the final outcome against His purpose. He declares that the servants’ vindication comes from Him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The USCCB notes explain the opening picture through Jerusalem receiving returning exiles as children, and recognize Paul’s later use of it in a new setting. The marriage picture emphasizes the tenderness with which the Lord restores His people.

Henry and Wesley give prominent attention to the church and the gathering of Gentiles through the gospel. They connect the enlarged tent with a growing family of believers, and the lasting kindness with God’s faithfulness to those He brings to Himself.

These explanations differ in the setting they emphasize, while treating restoration and God’s dependable mercy as central. The promise to the afflicted city should be read as part of that whole account, rather than as a detached assurance that a person will never experience injury or accusation.

passages.god_plan_html:
Galatians 4:21–31 directly quotes the opening call to the barren woman. Paul uses it in his explanation of the free Jerusalem above and calls believers children of promise, like Isaac. The promised family therefore has an explicit New Testament connection to people brought into freedom through God’s promise.

Jesus also quotes the promise of being taught by God in John 6:41–51. He connects hearing and learning from the Father with coming to Him, believing and receiving eternal life.

The jeweled city provides a further parallel with Revelation 21:18–27, where precious foundations and gates accompany the presence of God and the Lamb. Revelation does not quote this chapter there, but the shared picture carries restoration beyond repaired buildings to a people living in God’s light.

passages.title: Isaiah 55:1-13
passages.section_title: What does God offer to people who cannot pay?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 “Come, all you who are thirsty, come to the waters; and you without money, come, buy, and eat! Come, buy wine and milk without money and without cost! 2 Why spend money on that which is not bread, and your labor on that which does not satisfy? Listen carefully to Me, and eat what is good, and your soul will delight in the richest of foods. 3 Incline your ear and come to Me; listen, so that your soul may live. I will make with you an everlasting covenant— My loving devotion promised to David. 4 Behold, I have made him a witness to the nations, a leader and commander of the peoples. 5 Surely you will summon a nation you do not know, and nations who do not know you will run to you. For the LORD your God, the Holy One of Israel, has bestowed glory on you.” 6 Seek the LORD while He may be found; call on Him while He is near. 7 Let the wicked man forsake his way and the unrighteous man his thoughts; let him return to the LORD, that He may have compassion, and to our God, for He will freely pardon. 8 “For My thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways My ways,” declares the LORD. 9 “For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so My ways are higher than your ways and My thoughts than your thoughts. 10 For just as rain and snow fall from heaven and do not return without watering the earth, making it bud and sprout, and providing seed to sow and food to eat, 11 so My word that proceeds from My mouth will not return to Me empty, but it will accomplish what I please, and it will prosper where I send it. 12 You will indeed go out with joy and be led forth in peace; the mountains and hills will burst into song before you, and all the trees of the field will clap their hands. 13 Instead of the thornbush, the cypress will grow, and instead of the brier, the myrtle will spring up; this will make a name for the LORD, an everlasting sign, never to be destroyed.”

For the LORD your God, the Holy One of Israel, has bestowed glory on you.”

passages.context_html:
The invitation is to thirsty people, including those without money. They are called to receive water, wine, milk and satisfying food without payment. The question about wasted money and labor exposes the pursuit of things that cannot give the life being offered.

The way to receive is to listen and come to the Lord. He promises an everlasting covenant and His loving devotion pledged to David. The horizon includes nations who did not know the one to whom they now run.

The invitation also calls for a response: seek the Lord, call on Him, leave wicked ways and unrighteous thoughts, and return to Him. Compassion and abundant pardon are offered. The declaration that His thoughts and ways are higher follows that promise of mercy.

Rain and snow supply the comparison for His word. They water the earth and produce seed and food; His word likewise accomplishes the purpose for which He sends it. The chapter closes with a joyful departure and a transformed landscape that becomes a lasting sign of His work.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley read the food and drink as the blessings of salvation freely offered through Christ. The invitation contrasts God’s gift with the exhaustion of seeking lasting satisfaction elsewhere.

Both join the promise of pardon with repentance. Returning involves a change of direction and thought, while the scale of God’s mercy exceeds the limited forgiveness people often offer each other.

They understand the effective word as God bringing His saving promises to their intended result. The rain comparison therefore encourages confidence in what He has promised, rather than treating the passage as a guarantee for every plan a person attaches to a Bible verse.

passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 13:32–39 directly quotes the promised blessings of David while explaining the resurrection of Jesus. David died and his body decayed, but the One God raised did not see decay.

Paul then proclaims forgiveness of sins through Jesus and declares that everyone who believes is justified through Him. Isaiah’s covenant promise is thus connected to the risen Son of David and the forgiveness announced in His name.

This gives the invitation a clear place in God’s larger purpose: the dependable mercy He promised is proclaimed through the risen Christ, and people are called to receive what they could not purchase for themselves.

passages.title: Isaiah 56:1-8
passages.section_title: Is there a place for people who fear they will be excluded?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 This is what the LORD says: “Maintain justice and do what is right, for My salvation is coming soon, and My righteousness will be revealed. 2 Blessed is the man who does this, and the son of man who holds it fast, who keeps the Sabbath without profaning it and keeps his hand from doing any evil.” 3 Let no foreigner who has joined himself to the LORD say, “The LORD will utterly exclude me from His people.” And let the eunuch not say, “I am but a dry tree.” 4 For this is what the LORD says: “To the eunuchs who keep My Sabbaths, who choose what pleases Me and hold fast to My covenant— 5 I will give them, in My house and within My walls, a memorial and a name better than that of sons and daughters. I will give them an everlasting name that will not be cut off. 6 And the foreigners who join themselves to the LORD to minister to Him, to love the name of the LORD, and to be His servants— all who keep the Sabbath without profaning it and who hold fast to My covenant— 7 I will bring them to My holy mountain and make them joyful in My house of prayer. Their burnt offerings and sacrifices will be accepted on My altar, for My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations.” 8 Thus declares the Lord GOD, who gathers the dispersed of Israel: “I will gather to them still others besides those already gathered.”

3 Let no foreigner who has joined himself to the LORD say, “The LORD will utterly exclude me from His people.” And let the eunuch not say, “I am but a dry tree.” 4 For this is what the LORD says: “To the eunuchs who keep My Sabbaths, who choose what pleases Me and hold fast to My covenant— 5 I will give them, in My house and within My walls, a memorial and a name better than that of sons and daughters. I will give them an everlasting name that will not be cut off.

Their burnt offerings and sacrifices will be accepted on My altar, for My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations.” 8 Thus declares the Lord GOD, who gathers the dispersed of Israel: “I will gather to them still others besides those already gathered.”

passages.context_html:
The approaching salvation of God calls for justice and right conduct. Keeping the Sabbath and turning away from evil are named as marks of faithfulness.

The Lord then addresses two fears. A foreigner who has joined himself to Him must not assume he will be excluded, and a eunuch must not describe himself as a dry tree with no future. Those who choose what pleases God and hold to His covenant are promised a lasting name in His house, better than sons and daughters.

The foreigners who love and serve the Lord are promised welcome on His holy mountain and joy in His house of prayer. Their offerings will be accepted. His house is to be a house of prayer for all nations.

The One who gathers Israel’s dispersed people declares that He will gather others as well. The repeated emphasis is on belonging to the Lord and receiving a place through His promise.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley emphasize the welcome offered to people who fear that their background or condition leaves them outside. They connect the gathering of foreigners with Gentiles sharing in God’s people.

Their explanations of Sabbath language have different emphases. Henry stresses the duty of keeping a holy day; Wesley treats Sabbath observance here as standing for the worship of God more broadly. Both join the promise of acceptance with faithful service rather than treating belonging as merely a matter of ancestry.

The enduring name answers the eunuch’s fear of having no lasting place. The promise gives a future that does not depend on having biological descendants.

passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus directly quotes the description of a house of prayer for all nations in Mark 11:15–18, as He challenges what is happening in the temple courts. His appeal brings Isaiah’s stated purpose for God’s house into His own teaching and action.

Ephesians 2:11–22 develops the larger theme of welcome: Gentiles once far away are brought near through Christ’s blood. Jewish and Gentile believers have access to the Father by one Spirit and belong to one household.

The Ethiopian eunuch’s baptism in Acts 8:34–40 is a fitting parallel with the promise of welcome. He hears about Jesus from Isaiah, receives baptism and goes on his way rejoicing. Acts does not explicitly quote Isaiah 56 or state that this chapter prompted his question about baptism; the connection is a parallel within the wider story of God gathering people.

passages.title: Isaiah 56:9-12
passages.section_title: What happens when the watchmen care only for themselves?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 Come, all you beasts of the field; eat greedily, all you beasts of the forest. 10 Israel’s watchmen are blind, they are all oblivious; they are all mute dogs, they cannot bark; they are dreamers lying around, loving to slumber. 11 Like ravenous dogs, they are never satisfied. They are shepherds with no discernment; they all turn to their own way, each one seeking his own gain: 12 “Come, let me get the wine, let us imbibe the strong drink, and tomorrow will be like today, only far better!”
paragraphs: 9 Come, all you beasts of the field; eat greedily, all you beasts of the forest. 10 Israel’s watchmen are blind, they are all oblivious; they are all mute dogs, they cannot bark; they are dreamers lying around, loving to slumber. 11 Like ravenous dogs, they are never satisfied. They are shepherds with no discernment; they all turn to their own way, each one seeking his own gain: 12 “Come, let me get the wine, let us imbibe the strong drink, and tomorrow will be like today, only far better!”

passages.context_html:
The welcoming promises give way to a sharp warning. Beasts are invited to devour, while Israel’s watchmen are described as blind, unaware and silent when they should give warning.

The images become increasingly pointed. These guardians are like dogs that cannot bark but remain ravenously hungry. They are also shepherds without discernment, each pursuing his own gain.

Their invitation to drink heavily assumes that tomorrow will simply bring more of the same pleasures. The people charged with vigilance are absorbed in appetite and complacency while danger approaches.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley understand the watchmen and shepherds as leaders and teachers who fail the people entrusted to them. Their neglect, greed and false security belong together.

Henry also applies the warning to leaders in other times and places. The passage exposes what happens when people responsible for warning and care become preoccupied with their own comfort and gain.

passages.title: Isaiah 57:1-2
passages.section_title: What does the careless world miss when the righteous die?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 The righteous perish, and no one takes it to heart; devout men are taken away, while no one considers that the righteous are taken away from the presence of evil. 2 Those who walk uprightly enter into peace; they find rest, lying down in death.
paragraphs: 1 The righteous perish, and no one takes it to heart; devout men are taken away, while no one considers that the righteous are taken away from the presence of evil. 2 Those who walk uprightly enter into peace; they find rest, lying down in death.

passages.context_html:
After the warning about negligent leaders, the death of righteous and devoted people receives little attention. No one takes the loss to heart or considers what their being taken away means.

The passage supplies the perspective others fail to see: they are taken away from the presence of evil and enter peace. Those who walked uprightly find rest in death. The contrast is between the world’s indifference and the peace granted to the departed.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley both understand these verses as the death of righteous people and their release from approaching troubles. Henry distinguishes being spared death from being spared its sting; Wesley explains the beds as graves.

Their reading gives comfort about those who have died while treating the surrounding indifference as a warning. The peace of the righteous does not make the loss of their presence unimportant.

passages.title: Isaiah 57:3-13
passages.section_title: Can the idols people pursue actually rescue them?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 3 “But come here, you sons of a sorceress, you offspring of adulterers and prostitutes! 4 Whom are you mocking? At whom do you sneer and stick out your tongue? Are you not children of transgression, offspring of deceit, 5 who burn with lust among the oaks, under every luxuriant tree, who slaughter your children in the valleys, under the clefts of the rocks? 6 Your portion is among the smooth stones of the valley; indeed, they are your lot. Even to them you have poured out a drink offering and offered a grain offering. Should I relent because of these? 7 On a high and lofty hill you have made your bed, and there you went up to offer sacrifices. 8 Behind the door and doorpost you have set up your memorial. Forsaking Me, you uncovered your bed; you climbed up and opened it wide. And you have made a pact with those whose bed you have loved; you have gazed upon their nakedness. 9 You went to Molech with oil and multiplied your perfumes. You have sent your envoys a great distance; you have descended even to Sheol itself. 10 You are wearied by your many journeys, but you did not say, “There is no hope!” You found renewal of your strength; therefore you did not grow weak. 11 Whom have you dreaded and feared, so that you lied and failed to remember Me or take this to heart? Is it not because I have long been silent that you do not fear Me? 12 I will expose your righteousness and your works, and they will not profit you. 13 When you cry out, let your companies of idols deliver you! Yet the wind will carry off all of them, a breath will take them away. But he who seeks refuge in Me will inherit the land and possess My holy mountain.”

Yet the wind will carry off all of them, a breath will take them away. But he who seeks refuge in Me will inherit the land and possess My holy mountain.”

passages.context_html:
The address turns to people who mock and deceive. Their worship includes passion among the trees, offerings at stones and the slaughter of children. The description is an accusation of serious unfaithfulness, not harmless religious variety.

The language of beds, nakedness and pacts pictures their abandonment of the Lord for other loyalties. Their journeys and gifts continue even when the effort exhausts them. They keep finding strength to pursue a course that does not bring them back to Him.

The Lord asks whom they fear and why they have failed to remember Him. His silence has not made their deeds righteous or profitable. When crisis comes, they are challenged to seek rescue from their collected idols.

The contrast is decisive: the wind can carry those objects away, while the person who takes refuge in the Lord receives the land and His holy mountain. The question is what can truly bear the weight of their trust.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The USCCB notes read the passage as a summons to judgment, with the people’s unfaithfulness described through the image of sexual infidelity. They explain the ending as a contrast between the fate of idols and the inheritance of those who trust God.

Henry and Wesley likewise emphasize misplaced trust and the failure of substitutes for God. Their explanations include false worship and reliance on powers that cannot provide the rescue being sought.

For verse 9, the USCCB notes discuss the possible reference to Molech, the reading used by the BSB. Wesley, commenting on a translation that says king, understands an appeal to Assyria’s king. The explanations differ over that detail while recognizing the larger charge of seeking security away from the Lord.

passages.title: Isaiah 57:14-21
passages.section_title: Why does the holy God draw near to the humble?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 And it will be said, “Build it up, build it up, prepare the way, take every obstacle out of the way of My people.” 15 For thus says the One who is high and lifted up, who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy: “I dwell in a high and holy place, and with the oppressed and humble in spirit, to restore the spirit of the lowly and revive the heart of the contrite. 16 For I will not accuse you forever, nor will I always be angry; for then the spirit of man would grow weak before Me— the breath of life I have made. 17 I was enraged by his sinful greed, so I struck him and hid My face in anger; yet he kept turning back to the desires of his heart. 18 I have seen his ways, but I will heal him; I will guide him and restore comfort to him and his mourners, 19 bringing praise to their lips. Peace, peace to those far and near,” says the LORD, “and I will heal them.” 20 But the wicked are like the storm-tossed sea, for it cannot be still, and its waves churn up mire and muck. 21 “There is no peace,” says my God, “for the wicked.”

Peace, peace to those far and near,” says the LORD, “and I will heal them.”
20 But the wicked are like the storm-tossed sea, for it cannot be still, and its waves churn up mire and muck. 21 “There is no peace,” says my God, “for the wicked.”

passages.context_html:
The way is to be prepared and obstacles removed for God’s people. The One who is high, holy and eternal then declares that He also dwells with the oppressed and humble in spirit. His purpose is to restore and revive them.

He will not keep accusing or remain angry forever, because the people He made would faint under unrelenting judgment. Their sinful greed brought His anger, yet they continued following their own hearts.

The promise of healing comes with His knowledge of those ways. He will lead, restore comfort and bring praise to their lips. Peace is announced to those far away and those near.

The closing contrast prevents the promise from becoming approval of persistent wickedness. The wicked are like a sea that cannot settle and keeps churning up mud. They do not share the peace the Lord gives.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley emphasize God’s mercy toward the humbled and His power to restore people whom judgment alone has not changed. His greatness does not keep Him distant from the lowly.

Both connect peace for the far and near with God’s welcome reaching Gentiles as well as Jews. They understand the restless sea as a picture of life governed by wicked desires, rather than a description of the settled peace God gives.

passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 2:13–22 takes up the announcement of peace to those far away and those near. Christ brings Gentiles near through His blood and reconciles Jewish and Gentile believers to God in one body through the cross.

The result is shared access to the Father by one Spirit and membership in one household. Paul then describes that people as a dwelling place for God in His Spirit. Isaiah’s promise of peace thus connects with Christ gathering people and bringing them into God’s presence.

passages.title: Isaiah 58:1-14
passages.section_title: What kind of fasting does God actually welcome?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 “Cry aloud, do not hold back! Raise your voice like a ram’s horn. Declare to My people their transgression and to the house of Jacob their sins. 2 For day after day they seek Me and delight to know My ways, like a nation that does what is right and does not forsake the justice of their God. They ask Me for righteous judgments; they delight in the nearness of God.” 3 “Why have we fasted, and You have not seen? Why have we humbled ourselves, and You have not noticed?” “Behold, on the day of your fast, you do as you please, and you oppress all your workers. 4 You fast with contention and strife to strike viciously with your fist. You cannot fast as you do today and have your voice be heard on high. 5 Is this the fast I have chosen: a day for a man to deny himself, to bow his head like a reed, and to spread out sackcloth and ashes? Will you call this a fast and a day acceptable to the LORD? 6 Isn’t this the fast that I have chosen: to break the chains of wickedness, to untie the cords of the yoke, to set the oppressed free and tear off every yoke? 7 Isn’t it to share your bread with the hungry, to bring the poor and homeless into your home, to clothe the naked when you see him, and not to turn away from your own flesh and blood? 8 Then your light will break forth like the dawn, and your healing will come quickly. Your righteousness will go before you, and the glory of the LORD will be your rear guard. 9 Then you will call, and the LORD will answer; you will cry out, and He will say, ‘Here I am.’ If you remove the yoke from your midst, the pointing of the finger and malicious talk, 10 and if you give yourself to the hungry and satisfy the afflicted soul, then your light will go forth in the darkness, and your night will be like noonday. 11 The LORD will always guide you; He will satisfy you in a sun-scorched land and strengthen your frame. You will be like a well-watered garden, like a spring whose waters never fail. 12 Your people will rebuild the ancient ruins; you will restore the age-old foundations; you will be called Repairer of the Breach, Restorer of the Streets of Dwelling. 13 If you turn your foot from breaking the Sabbath, from doing as you please on My holy day, if you call the Sabbath a delight, and the LORD’s holy day honorable, if you honor it by not going your own way or seeking your own pleasure or speaking idle words, 14 then you will delight yourself in the LORD, and I will make you ride on the heights of the land and feed you with the heritage of your father Jacob.” For the mouth of the LORD has spoken.

passages.context_html:
The prophet is commanded to declare the people’s sins loudly. They appear eager to seek God, learn His ways and receive just decisions. Yet their complaint reveals a contradiction: they fast and humble themselves outwardly while wondering why He does not notice.

The Lord names what their observance conceals. They pursue their own desires, oppress workers, quarrel and strike one another. Bowed heads, sackcloth and ashes do not make that conduct acceptable.

The fast He chooses is described through freedom and care: break oppressive bonds, release those under the yoke, share bread, shelter the poor and homeless, clothe the naked and stop turning away from family. The promises of light, healing and an answered call accompany the removal of oppression and malicious speech.

The image of a watered garden describes His guidance and renewal, and the rebuilt ruins picture a community restored for people to inhabit. The final appeal concerns the Sabbath: they are to honor His holy day and find delight in Him rather than simply pursuing their own wishes.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley read the chapter as a challenge to religious observance that leaves daily wrongdoing untouched. They emphasize repentance expressed in mercy and justice, rather than outward signs standing in for a changed life.

Both connect the care of those in need with a sincere response to God. They also treat honoring the Sabbath as more than a display: the day is to be set apart with willing delight in Him.

The promises of renewal belong to this call for a restored relationship and community. Fasting is not presented as a way to make God overlook cruelty or to purchase a desired answer.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The same concern appears in Jesus’ teaching on fasting in Matthew 6:16–18. He tells His followers to fast before their Father rather than arrange their appearance to win human notice. This is a parallel in teaching, not an explicit quotation of Isaiah.

Matthew 25:31–46 gives a further connection between devotion to the King and care for people. The acts named include feeding the hungry, welcoming a stranger and clothing the naked; Jesus identifies what is done for the least of His brothers with what is done for Him.

Together these passages show a continuing theme in God’s purpose for His people: worship directed toward Him must reach into how they treat others. The outward act and the life lived around it belong together.

passages.title: Isaiah 59:1-17
passages.section_title: If God can save, why does salvation seem so far away?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Surely the arm of the LORD is not too short to save, nor His ear too dull to hear. 2 But your iniquities have built barriers between you and your God, and your sins have hidden His face from you, so that He does not hear. 3 For your hands are stained with blood, and your fingers with iniquity; your lips have spoken lies, and your tongue mutters injustice. 4 No one calls for justice; no one pleads his case honestly. They rely on empty pleas; they tell lies; they conceive mischief and give birth to iniquity. 5 They hatch the eggs of vipers and weave a spider’s web. Whoever eats their eggs will die; crack one open, and a viper is hatched. 6 Their cobwebs cannot be made into clothing, and they cannot cover themselves with their works. Their deeds are sinful deeds, and acts of violence are in their hands. 7 Their feet run to evil; they are swift to shed innocent blood. Their thoughts are sinful thoughts; ruin and destruction lie in their wake. 8 The way of peace they have not known, and there is no justice in their tracks. They have turned them into crooked paths; no one who treads on them will know peace. 9 Therefore justice is far from us, and righteousness does not reach us. We hope for light, but there is darkness; for brightness, but we walk in gloom. 10 Like the blind, we feel our way along the wall, groping like those without eyes. We stumble at midday as in the twilight; among the vigorous we are like the dead. 11 We all growl like bears and moan like doves. We hope for justice, but find none, for salvation, but it is far from us. 12 For our transgressions are multiplied before You, and our sins testify against us. Our transgressions are indeed with us, and we know our iniquities: 13 rebelling and denying the LORD, turning away from our God, speaking oppression and revolt, conceiving and uttering lies from the heart. 14 So justice is turned away, and righteousness stands at a distance. For truth has stumbled in the public square, and honesty cannot enter. 15 Truth is missing, and whoever turns from evil becomes prey. The LORD looked and was displeased that there was no justice. 16 He saw that there was no man; He was amazed that there was no one to intercede. So His own arm brought salvation, and His own righteousness sustained Him. 17 He put on righteousness like a breastplate, and the helmet of salvation on His head; He put on garments of vengeance and wrapped Himself in a cloak of zeal.

passages.context_html:
The Lord’s inability is ruled out at the start. His arm is not too short to save and His ear is not too dull to hear. The barrier is the people’s iniquity: bloodshed, lies, dishonest claims and injustice mark their dealings.

Vipers’ eggs and cobwebs picture the harm and futility of what they produce. Their plans bring violence without providing a covering. Their paths leave ruin behind them and do not lead to peace.

The voice changes to confession. The people describe groping in darkness, longing for justice and salvation without finding them. They acknowledge that their many sins testify against them: rebellion, denial of the Lord, oppression and lies from the heart.

The picture widens to a public life where truth has fallen and the person who leaves evil becomes prey. The Lord sees the absence of justice and of anyone able to intervene. His own arm brings salvation, and He puts on righteousness and salvation like armor, together with vengeance and zeal.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley emphasize the damage sin does to the people’s relationship with God and to their life together. Their wrongdoing cannot supply the security they seek.

Both see a movement from exposed guilt and acknowledged misery to God’s own intervention. The failure of human justice does not leave Him without power or resolve to act. The armor picture describes the righteousness of His cause and His commitment to rescue and judgment.

passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 3:9–26 uses the description of feet running to bloodshed and paths without peace as part of its account of human sin. Paul’s point includes both Jews and Greeks: everyone is accountable, and righteousness comes through faith in Jesus Christ rather than through works of the law.

Ephesians 6:10–20 takes up the breastplate of righteousness and helmet of salvation in its call to put on God’s armor. Believers are to stand in His strength, armed with truth, faith, His word and prayer.

The change of setting matters. Isaiah describes the Lord acting to rescue and judge; Ephesians calls His people to depend on what He supplies and says their struggle is against spiritual evil, rather than flesh and blood. God’s armor is not permission to carry out private vengeance.

passages.title: Isaiah 59:18-21
passages.section_title: What does the coming Redeemer promise to Jacob?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 So He will repay according to their deeds: fury to His enemies, retribution to His foes, and recompense to the islands. 19 So shall they fear the name of the LORD where the sun sets, and His glory where it rises. For He will come like a raging flood, driven by the breath of the LORD. 20 “The Redeemer will come to Zion, to those in Jacob who turn from transgression,” declares the LORD. 21 “As for Me, this is My covenant with them,” says the LORD. “My Spirit will not depart from you, and My words that I have put in your mouth will not depart from your mouth or from the mouths of your children and grandchildren, from now on and forevermore,” says the LORD.
paragraphs: 18 So He will repay according to their deeds: fury to His enemies, retribution to His foes, and recompense to the islands. 19 So shall they fear the name of the LORD where the sun sets, and His glory where it rises. For He will come like a raging flood, driven by the breath of the LORD.

20 “The Redeemer will come to Zion, to those in Jacob who turn from transgression,” declares the LORD. 21 “As for Me, this is My covenant with them,” says the LORD. “My Spirit will not depart from you, and My words that I have put in your mouth will not depart from your mouth or from the mouths of your children and grandchildren, from now on and forevermore,” says the LORD.

passages.context_html:
The Lord’s intervention brings repayment according to deeds, reaching even the islands. His name will be feared from west to east, and His coming is compared to a raging flood driven by His breath.

A Redeemer is promised to Zion and to those in Jacob who turn from transgression. Rescue is joined to a turning from sin, rather than an assurance that wrongdoing can continue unchanged.

The covenant declaration promises the continuing presence of His Spirit and His words among the people and their descendants. The chapter that began with sin creating a barrier ends with His pledge of an enduring relationship.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley identify the Redeemer with Christ. They connect the promise with His saving work and understand the Spirit and word as essential to the continuing life of His people.

Wesley explicitly points to Paul’s use of the passage in Romans 11. Henry emphasizes that rescue and the Spirit’s work belong together, and that claims about the Spirit must be tested by Scripture. Both read the ending as God securing what human efforts could not supply.

passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 11:25–32 directly draws on the promise of the Deliverer and the removal of ungodliness from Jacob. Paul places it in his discussion of Israel, the Gentiles, God’s covenant and the taking away of sins.

He warns Gentile believers against conceit and speaks of God’s gifts and call as irrevocable. His explanation holds both groups within the story of disobedience and mercy, giving the promised rescue a place in God’s wider saving purpose.

The connection supplied by Paul concerns the Deliverer, the removal of sin and God’s faithfulness. It invites confidence in His mercy rather than superiority over the people whose story Paul is explaining.

passages.title: Isaiah 60:1-22
passages.section_title: What changes when the Lord becomes Zion’s everlasting light?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Arise, shine, for your light has come, and the glory of the LORD rises upon you. 2 For behold, darkness covers the earth, and thick darkness is over the peoples; but the LORD will rise upon you, and His glory will appear over you. 3 Nations will come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your dawn. 4 Lift up your eyes and look around: They all gather and come to you; your sons will come from afar, and your daughters will be carried on the arm. 5 Then you will look and be radiant, and your heart will tremble and swell with joy, because the riches of the sea will be brought to you, and the wealth of the nations will come to you. 6 Caravans of camels will cover your land, young camels of Midian and Ephah, and all from Sheba will come, bearing gold and frankincense and proclaiming the praises of the LORD. 7 All the flocks of Kedar will be gathered to you; the rams of Nebaioth will serve you and go up on My altar with acceptance; I will adorn My glorious house. 8 Who are these who fly like clouds, like doves to their shelters? 9 Surely the islands will wait for Me, with the ships of Tarshish in the lead, to bring your children from afar, with their silver and gold, to the honor of the LORD your God, the Holy One of Israel, for He has glorified you. 10 Foreigners will rebuild your walls, and their kings will serve you. Although I struck you in anger, yet in favor I will show you mercy. 11 Your gates will always stand open; they will never be shut, day or night, so that the wealth of the nations may be brought into you, with their kings being led in procession. 12 For the nation or kingdom that will not serve you will perish; it will be utterly destroyed. 13 The glory of Lebanon will come to you— its cypress, elm, and boxwood together— to adorn the place of My sanctuary, and I will glorify the place of My feet. 14 The sons of your oppressors will come and bow down to you; all who reviled you will fall facedown at your feet and call you the City of the LORD, Zion of the Holy One of Israel. 15 Whereas you have been forsaken and despised, with no one passing through, I will make you an everlasting pride, a joy from age to age. 16 You will drink the milk of nations and nurse at the breasts of royalty; you will know that I, the LORD, am your Savior and your Redeemer, the Mighty One of Jacob. 17 Instead of bronze I will bring you gold; I will bring silver in place of iron, bronze instead of wood, and iron instead of stones. I will appoint peace as your governor and righteousness as your ruler. 18 No longer will violence be heard in your land, nor ruin or destruction within your borders. But you will name your walls Salvation and your gates Praise. 19 No longer will the sun be your light by day, nor the brightness of the moon shine on your night; for the LORD will be your everlasting light, and your God will be your splendor. 20 Your sun will no longer set, and your moon will not wane; for the LORD will be your everlasting light, and the days of your sorrow will cease. 21 Then all your people will be righteous; they will possess the land forever; they are the branch of My planting, the work of My hands, so that I may be glorified. 22 The least of you will become a thousand, and the smallest a mighty nation. I am the LORD; in its time I will accomplish it quickly.

passages.context_html:
Zion is called to rise and shine because the Lord’s glory has appeared over her. Darkness covers the peoples, but nations and kings are drawn to her light. Her scattered children gather, and the sight fills her with joy.

The coming nations bring their wealth and resources, from gold and frankincense to flocks, ships and precious materials. These gifts honor the Lord who has glorified her; the chapter repeatedly identifies Him as the source of the transformation.

Foreigners rebuild the walls, rulers serve, and former oppressors acknowledge the city of the Lord. The gates remain open to receive what is brought. The warning to nations that refuse to serve stands beside the promise that the despised city will become a lasting joy.

Peace and righteousness replace violent rule, and destruction is no longer heard within the borders. Walls are named Salvation and gates Praise. Finally, the Lord Himself is the city’s everlasting light, ending the days of mourning.

The chapter closes with a righteous people settled in the land, described as His planting and handiwork. Even the smallest will become numerous. The Lord will accomplish this in His appointed time.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The USCCB notes emphasize the promises to Zion: returning children, nations bringing wealth, a glorified sanctuary, peace and the Lord’s radiant presence.

Henry reads the chapter principally through a future flourishing and completion of the church. Wesley likewise sees the gathering of nations to Christ in the restoration picture, and connects the promised safety with Christ’s thousand-year reign.

Henry allows the final glory to refer to a future state of the church on earth or its heavenly completion. These explanations differ over how the promised restoration unfolds; they share the conviction that the Lord’s saving presence, rather than the city’s own strength, produces its glory.

passages.god_plan_html:
Revelation 21:22–27 takes up several of this chapter’s images together. God’s glory lights the city, nations walk by that light, kings bring their glory, and the gates remain open. The Lamb is its lamp, and God and the Lamb are its temple.

Revelation 22:1–5 continues the picture: there is no more curse or night, God’s servants see His face, and He shines on them.

These connections carry Isaiah’s hope into the New Testament’s account of God dwelling with His people. The goal is a life illuminated by His presence, with holiness, lasting security and an end to the darkness and sorrow that marked the old condition.

passages.title: Isaiah 61:1-11
passages.section_title: Who brings good news and turns mourning into joy?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 The Spirit of the Lord GOD is on Me, because the LORD has anointed Me to preach good news to the poor. He has sent Me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives and freedom to the prisoners, 2 to proclaim the year of the LORD’s favor and the day of our God’s vengeance, to comfort all who mourn, 3 to console the mourners in Zion— to give them a crown of beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, and a garment of praise for a spirit of despair. So they will be called oaks of righteousness, the planting of the LORD, that He may be glorified. 4 They will rebuild the ancient ruins; they will restore the places long devastated; they will renew the ruined cities, the desolations of many generations. 5 Strangers will stand and feed your flocks, and foreigners will be your plowmen and vinedressers. 6 But you will be called the priests of the LORD; they will speak of you as ministers of our God; you will feed on the wealth of nations, and you will boast in their riches. 7 Instead of shame, My people will have a double portion, and instead of humiliation, they will rejoice in their share; and so they will inherit a double portion in their land, and everlasting joy will be theirs. 8 For I, the LORD, love justice; I hate robbery and iniquity; in My faithfulness I will give them their recompense and make an everlasting covenant with them. 9 Their descendants will be known among the nations, and their offspring among the peoples. All who see them will acknowledge that they are a people the LORD has blessed. 10 I will rejoice greatly in the LORD, my soul will exult in my God; for He has clothed me with garments of salvation and wrapped me in a robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom wears a priestly headdress, as a bride adorns herself with her jewels. 11 For as the earth brings forth its growth, and as a garden enables seed to spring up, so the Lord GOD will cause righteousness and praise to spring up before all the nations.

passages.context_html:
The speaker is sent with the Spirit of the Lord upon Him to bring good news to the poor, bind up the brokenhearted and proclaim freedom. The announcement includes the Lord’s favor, His day of vengeance and comfort for those who mourn.

The Hebrew verb מָשַׁח, mashach (mah-SHAKH), means to anoint. Brown–Driver–Briggs includes setting someone apart for an office and specifically lists Isaiah 61:1. Here the anointing belongs to the speaker’s God-given mission.

For Zion’s mourners, ashes and despair give way to beauty, joy and praise. They become like oaks of righteousness planted by the Lord for His glory. Ruined places are rebuilt, and the people are called His priests and ministers.

Shame is replaced by a double portion and lasting joy. The Lord declares His love of justice and hatred of robbery and iniquity, promising a faithful recompense and an everlasting covenant. Their descendants will be recognized as a people He has blessed.

The chapter ends in rejoicing over garments of salvation and righteousness, pictured through wedding celebration. As a garden brings up its growth, the Lord will cause righteousness and praise to spring up before the nations.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley understand the opening mission chiefly through Christ and His work of freeing and comforting people. Wesley allows a reference to the prophet while emphasizing its fullest application to Christ.

The USCCB notes give attention to the prophet’s commission, the comfort of Zion and the people’s renewed identity and mission. Henry connects the rebuilding promises both with Jews returning from captivity and with lives restored through the gospel.

Henry and Wesley also relate the priestly calling to believers’ service to God. Their explanations emphasize that those who receive rescue are brought into a life that honors Him, and that salvation becomes a reason for joy and praise.

passages.god_plan_html:
Luke 4:16–22 supplies the direct identification. Jesus reads from Isaiah in Nazareth and declares the Scripture fulfilled in His hearers’ presence. The good news, freedom and year of favor belong to His explanation of His own mission.

Luke’s recorded reading ends with the year of favor, before Isaiah’s mention of the day of vengeance. The passage itself connects saving favor and God’s judgment; Luke makes clear that Jesus has come carrying the promised good news.

The calling to serve also has a New Testament parallel in First Peter 2:9–10. Peter describes a royal priesthood and holy people called out of darkness to proclaim God’s virtues. This is a shared priestly theme, rather than an explicit quotation of Isaiah 61.

passages.title: Isaiah 62:1-12
passages.section_title: Will Zion remain forsaken?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 For Zion’s sake I will not keep silent, and for Jerusalem’s sake I will not keep still, until her righteousness shines like a bright light, her salvation like a blazing torch. 2 Nations will see your righteousness, and all kings your glory. You will be called by a new name that the mouth of the LORD will bestow. 3 You will be a crown of glory in the hand of the LORD, a royal diadem in the palm of your God. 4 No longer will you be called Forsaken, nor your land named Desolate; but you will be called Hephzibah, and your land Beulah; for the LORD will take delight in you, and your land will be His bride. 5 For as a young man marries a young woman, so your sons will marry you; and as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so your God will rejoice over you. 6 On your walls, O Jerusalem, I have posted watchmen; they will never be silent day or night. You who call on the LORD shall take no rest for yourselves, 7 nor give Him any rest until He establishes Jerusalem and makes her the praise of the earth. 8 The LORD has sworn by His right hand and by His mighty arm: “Never again will I give your grain to your enemies for food, nor will foreigners drink the new wine for which you have toiled. 9 For those who harvest grain will eat it and praise the LORD, and those who gather grapes will drink the wine in My holy courts.” 10 Go out, go out through the gates; prepare the way for the people! Build it up, build up the highway; clear away the stones; raise a banner for the nations! 11 Behold, the LORD has proclaimed to the ends of the earth, “Say to Daughter Zion: See, your Savior comes! Look, His reward is with Him, and His recompense goes before Him.” 12 And they will be called the Holy People, the Redeemed of The LORD; and you will be called Sought Out, A City Not Forsaken.

passages.context_html:
The opening voice will not be silent until Zion’s righteousness and salvation shine before the nations. Her coming glory is pictured as a crown held in the Lord’s hand, and He will give her a new name.

The names Forsaken and Desolate give way to Hephzibah and Beulah. The explanation in the passage is that the Lord delights in her and her land will be His bride. The marriage picture expresses His joy in the people and the reversal of abandonment.

Watchmen on Jerusalem’s walls will not be silent. Those who call on the Lord are told to persist until He establishes the city as a praise in the earth. His sworn promise is that the people will enjoy their own harvests and praise Him, instead of seeing enemies consume what they worked to produce.

The final summons is to prepare the way, remove stones and raise a banner for the nations. Salvation is announced to Daughter Zion with the coming Savior and His reward. The people are named holy and redeemed, and the city sought out rather than forsaken.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry understands the opening voice as the Son assuring the church of His love and continuing care. Wesley understands it as the prophet’s resolve to keep praying and proclaiming the promised deliverance. They therefore differ over the identity of the first speaker.

Both connect the chapter with the Lord’s faithfulness and the flourishing of His people. The new names express a changed condition and relationship, while the watchmen and repeated calls encourage persistence in prayer.

For Henry, that persistence rests on God’s willingness to receive earnest prayer. Wesley emphasizes a vigilant ministry that keeps the Lord’s promises before the people. Neither explanation treats the command as a need to repair a lapse in God’s memory.

passages.god_plan_html:
The call to Daughter Zion has a close connection with Matthew 21:1–11. Matthew’s account of Jesus entering Jerusalem uses the summons to tell Zion that her King is coming. The entry identifies Jesus as the King received by the crowd, bringing Isaiah’s language of arrival into the Gospel story.

Revelation 22:12–17 takes up the promise of coming with a reward, wording also found earlier in Isaiah 40:10. Jesus identifies Himself as the Root and Offspring of David, and the passage ends with an invitation to receive the water of life freely.

The announced coming and the offered life belong together. God’s people are encouraged to await His promised salvation while hearing and passing on His invitation.

passages.title: Isaiah 63:1-6
passages.section_title: Who is the mighty figure whose garments are stained red?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Who is this coming from Edom, from Bozrah with crimson-stained garments? Who is this robed in splendor, marching in the greatness of His strength? “It is I, proclaiming vindication, mighty to save.” 2 Why are Your clothes red, and Your garments like one who treads the winepress? 3 “I have trodden the winepress alone, and no one from the nations was with Me. I trampled them in My anger and trod them down in My fury; their blood spattered My garments, and all My clothes were stained. 4 For the day of vengeance was in My heart, and the year of My redemption had come. 5 I looked, but there was no one to help; I was appalled that no one assisted. So My arm brought Me salvation, and My own wrath upheld Me. 6 I trampled the nations in My anger; in My wrath I made them drunk and poured out their blood on the ground.”
paragraphs: 1 Who is this coming from Edom, from Bozrah with crimson-stained garments? Who is this robed in splendor, marching in the greatness of His strength? “It is I, proclaiming vindication, mighty to save.” 2 Why are Your clothes red, and Your garments like one who treads the winepress? 3 “I have trodden the winepress alone, and no one from the nations was with Me. I trampled them in My anger and trod them down in My fury; their blood spattered My garments, and all My clothes were stained.

4 For the day of vengeance was in My heart, and the year of My redemption had come. 5 I looked, but there was no one to help; I was appalled that no one assisted. So My arm brought Me salvation, and My own wrath upheld Me. 6 I trampled the nations in My anger; in My wrath I made them drunk and poured out their blood on the ground.”

passages.context_html:
A question introduces a majestic figure coming from Edom and Bozrah in crimson-stained clothing. He identifies Himself as the One who proclaims vindication and is mighty to save. A second question asks why His garments look like those of someone treading a winepress.

The answer turns the winepress into an image of judgment. He has trodden it alone, and the stain is the blood of the nations He has judged. No one from those nations stood with Him.

The day of vengeance and year of redemption have arrived together. When no one supplied help, His own arm brought salvation. The passage connects rescue with His decisive action against those who oppose Him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The USCCB notes identify the approaching figure as the Lord and the winepress as an image of His judgment. Henry and Wesley read the victorious figure through the Messiah, with Edom representing opposition to His people.

Both Henry and Wesley emphasize that the victory comes through His own power. Henry distinguishes the blood He shed in His saving sacrifice from this picture of judgment upon His enemies. The stain here belongs to the explanation supplied by the passage itself.

passages.god_plan_html:
Revelation 19:11–16 takes up the blood-stained robe and the winepress of God’s wrath. The rider judges in righteousness, bears the name Word of God, and is identified as King of kings and Lord of lords.

This gives Isaiah’s victory picture a clear connection with the New Testament’s presentation of Christ as judge. The One whose saving work brings redemption also confronts evil with authority. The action belongs to Him; the passage does not commission readers to take vengeance into their own hands.

passages.title: Isaiah 63:7-14
passages.section_title: What does remembering the exodus reveal about God’s care?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 I will make known the LORD’s loving devotion and His praiseworthy acts, because of all that the LORD has done for us— the many good things for the house of Israel according to His great compassion and loving devotion. 8 For He said, “They are surely My people, sons who will not be disloyal.” So He became their Savior. 9 In all their distress, He too was afflicted, and the Angel of His Presence saved them. In His love and compassion He redeemed them; He lifted them up and carried them all the days of old. 10 But they rebelled and grieved His Holy Spirit. So He turned and became their enemy, and He Himself fought against them. 11 Then His people remembered the days of old, the days of Moses. Where is He who brought them through the sea with the shepherds of His flock? Where is the One who set His Holy Spirit among them, 12 who sent His glorious arm to lead them by the right hand of Moses, who divided the waters before them to gain for Himself everlasting renown, 13 who led them through the depths like a horse in the wilderness, so that they did not stumble? 14 Like cattle going down to the valley, the Spirit of the LORD gave them rest. You led Your people this way to make for Yourself a glorious name.

In His love and compassion He redeemed them; He lifted them up and carried them all the days of old. 10 But they rebelled and grieved His Holy Spirit. So He turned and became their enemy, and He Himself fought against them.

11 Then His people remembered the days of old, the days of Moses. Where is He who brought them through the sea with the shepherds of His flock? Where is the One who set His Holy Spirit among them, 12 who sent His glorious arm to lead them by the right hand of Moses, who divided the waters before them to gain for Himself everlasting renown, 13 who led them through the depths like a horse in the wilderness, so that they did not stumble? 14 Like cattle going down to the valley, the Spirit of the LORD gave them rest. You led Your people this way to make for Yourself a glorious name.

passages.context_html:
The voice changes to praise and remembrance. The speaker recounts the Lord’s compassion and loving devotion toward the house of Israel. He became their Savior, shared their distress, and redeemed and carried them in love.

The Angel of His Presence is named in that rescue. Yet the people rebelled and grieved His Holy Spirit, and the relationship turned into conflict: the One who had saved them fought against them.

The memory then returns to Moses and the journey through the sea. Repeated questions ask where the God who did these things is now. His Spirit had been among them, His glorious arm had led them, and He had made a path through the waters.

The horse moving without stumbling and cattle descending to rest picture the care of His leading. The remembrance acknowledges both His goodness and the people’s rebellion, while recalling that His guidance made His name glorious.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The USCCB notes understand this as the beginning of a community lament that remembers the exodus before asking for help again. Henry and Wesley likewise connect the remembered rescue with the appeal that follows.

Henry and Wesley identify the Angel of His Presence with the Son of God, reading the rescue through His care for the people. They also emphasize the seriousness of rebellion against the Spirit who had guided them.

The remembrance is therefore both praise and an honest account of failure. It recalls the Lord’s faithfulness without making His past kindness an excuse to ignore the people’s response.

passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 4:25–32 takes up the warning about grieving God’s Holy Spirit. Paul addresses people sealed for the day of redemption and calls them to leave falsehood, stealing, destructive speech and malice behind.

The call ends with kindness, compassion and forgiveness patterned on God’s forgiveness in Christ. Isaiah’s memory of rescue and rebellion thus has a direct connection with the life of redeemed people: receiving God’s care calls for conduct that honors His Spirit and serves others.

passages.title: Isaiah 63:15-19
passages.section_title: How can the people call on God when He seems far away?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 Look down from heaven and see, from Your holy and glorious habitation. Where are Your zeal and might? Your yearning and compassion for me are restrained. 16 Yet You are our Father, though Abraham does not know us and Israel does not acknowledge us. You, O LORD, are our Father; our Redeemer from Everlasting is Your name. 17 Why, O LORD, do You make us stray from Your ways and harden our hearts from fearing You? Return, for the sake of Your servants, the tribes of Your heritage. 18 For a short while Your people possessed Your holy place, but our enemies have trampled Your sanctuary. 19 We have become like those You never ruled, like those not called by Your name.
paragraphs: 15 Look down from heaven and see, from Your holy and glorious habitation. Where are Your zeal and might? Your yearning and compassion for me are restrained. 16 Yet You are our Father, though Abraham does not know us and Israel does not acknowledge us. You, O LORD, are our Father; our Redeemer from Everlasting is Your name. 17 Why, O LORD, do You make us stray from Your ways and harden our hearts from fearing You? Return, for the sake of Your servants, the tribes of Your heritage.
18 For a short while Your people possessed Your holy place, but our enemies have trampled Your sanctuary. 19 We have become like those You never ruled, like those not called by Your name.

passages.context_html:
The remembrance becomes an urgent prayer. The people ask the Lord to look down from His holy dwelling and show the zeal, power and compassion they cannot presently see.

They appeal to Him as their Father and ancient Redeemer. Even if Abraham and Israel do not know or acknowledge them, the Lord remains the One to whom they turn. Their deepest appeal is to His relationship with them.

The question about straying and hardened hearts expresses the severity of their condition. They ask Him to return for the sake of His servants and the tribes that belong to Him.

The sanctuary has been trampled, and they feel reduced to the condition of a people He had never ruled or named as His own. The prayer continues into the next chapter with a plea for Him to come down and act.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley read the passage as a plea for renewed mercy grounded in God’s fatherhood and His past redemption. The people bring their condition before Him rather than treating their abandonment as beyond appeal.

Wesley explains the hardening language in terms of God allowing them to stray and their hearts to become hardened. Henry similarly warns of the judgment of being left to one’s own ways. Both understand the request to return as an appeal for God to rescue the people from that condition.

passages.title: Isaiah 64:1-12
passages.section_title: What can people plead when their own righteousness cannot cover them?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 If only You would rend the heavens and come down, so that mountains would quake at Your presence, 2 as fire kindles the brushwood and causes the water to boil, to make Your name known to Your enemies, so that the nations will tremble at Your presence! 3 When You did awesome works that we did not expect, You came down, and the mountains trembled at Your presence. 4 From ancient times no one has heard, no ear has perceived, no eye has seen any God besides You, who acts on behalf of those who wait for Him. 5 You welcome those who gladly do right, who remember Your ways. Surely You were angry, for we sinned. How can we be saved if we remain in our sins? 6 Each of us has become like something unclean, and all our righteous acts are like filthy rags; we all wither like a leaf, and our iniquities carry us away like the wind. 7 No one calls on Your name or strives to take hold of You. For You have hidden Your face from us and delivered us into the hand of our iniquity. 8 But now, O LORD, You are our Father; we are the clay, and You are the potter; we are all the work of Your hand. 9 Do not be angry, O LORD, beyond measure; do not remember our iniquity forever. Oh, look upon us, we pray; we are all Your people! 10 Your holy cities have become a wilderness. Zion has become a wasteland and Jerusalem a desolation. 11 Our holy and beautiful temple, where our fathers praised You, has been burned with fire, and all that was dear to us lies in ruins. 12 After all this, O LORD, will You restrain Yourself? Will You keep silent and afflict us beyond measure?
