paragraphs: 5 This is what the Lord GOD says: ‘This is Jerusalem, which I have set in the center of the nations, with countries all around her. 6 But she has rebelled against My ordinances more wickedly than the nations, and against My statutes worse than the countries around her. For her people have rejected My ordinances and have not walked in My statutes.’ 7 Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘You have been more insubordinate than the nations around you; you have not walked in My statutes or kept My ordinances, nor have you even conformed to the ordinances of the nations around you.’

8 Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Behold, I Myself am against you, Jerusalem, and I will execute judgments among you in the sight of the nations. 9 Because of all your abominations, I will do to you what I have never done before and will never do again. 10 As a result, fathers among you will eat their sons, and sons will eat their fathers. I will execute judgments against you and scatter all your remnant to every wind.’

11 Therefore as surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, because you have defiled My sanctuary with all your detestable idols and abominations, I Myself will withdraw My favor; I will not look upon you with pity, nor will I spare you. 12 A third of your people will die by plague or be consumed by famine within you, a third will fall by the sword outside your walls, and a third I will scatter to every wind and unleash a sword behind them.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord identifies the pictured city: it is Jerusalem, set among the nations with countries surrounding her. Her place and the ordinances she received make the contrast with her conduct especially sharp.

She has rejected His statutes and acted more wickedly than the surrounding nations. The charge is not ignorance of what the Lord required, but refusal to walk in what He had given.

The Lord declares that He Himself is against Jerusalem and will execute judgment in the sight of those nations. The threatened famine is so dreadful that parents and children will turn upon one another for food. Scattering follows the collapse of the city.

The sanctuary’s defilement with idols is named as a cause of His withdrawing favor. The three portions of hair are then explained: a third die by plague or famine within the city, a third by the sword outside, and a third are scattered with a sword pursuing.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley emphasizes Jerusalem’s intended place as a source of light among the nations and the contradiction between that calling and her conduct. Possessing God’s statutes has not produced obedience.

Henry stresses the gravity of the sentence and applies the warning to people and churches who assume that a religious identity will shield them while they reject God’s ways.

Both understand the passage as a judgment in which privilege increases responsibility. The sanctuary does not provide a shelter for the very practices that defile it.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 2:17–24 develops the same concern about receiving God’s law while dishonoring Him through disobedience. Paul asks whether those who teach others also teach themselves, and connects the contradiction with God’s name being dishonored among Gentiles.

A further parallel appears in Luke 19:41–44. Jesus weeps over Jerusalem and warns of enemies surrounding and bringing it down, because it did not recognize the time of God’s visitation.

These passages do not explicitly quote Ezekiel 5. They show the continuing connection between revelation, responsibility and judgment. Jesus’ tears also show how seriously the coming loss is to be regarded, rather than making another’s suffering an occasion for pride.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 5:13-17
passages.section_title: What will the ruined city make known to the nations?

versions.text: 13 And when My anger is spent and I have vented My wrath against them, I will be appeased. And when I have spent My wrath on them, they will know that I, the LORD, in My zeal have spoken. 14 I will make you a ruin and a disgrace among the nations around you, in the sight of all who pass by. 15 So you will be a reproach and a taunt, a warning and a horror to the nations around you, when I execute judgments against you in anger, wrath, and raging fury. I, the LORD, have spoken. 16 When I shower you with the deadly arrows of famine and destruction that I will send to destroy you, I will intensify the famine against you and cut off your supply of food. 17 I will send famine and wild beasts against you, and they will leave you childless. Plague and bloodshed will sweep through you, and I will bring a sword against you. I, the LORD, have spoken.”

And when I have spent My wrath on them, they will know that I, the LORD, in My zeal have spoken. 14 I will make you a ruin and a disgrace among the nations around you, in the sight of all who pass by. 15 So you will be a reproach and a taunt, a warning and a horror to the nations around you, when I execute judgments against you in anger, wrath, and raging fury. I, the LORD, have spoken.

16 When I shower you with the deadly arrows of famine and destruction that I will send to destroy you, I will intensify the famine against you and cut off your supply of food. 17 I will send famine and wild beasts against you, and they will leave you childless. Plague and bloodshed will sweep through you, and I will bring a sword against you. I, the LORD, have spoken.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord declares that His anger and the fulfillment of His word will be recognized through the judgment. The city that stood among the nations will become a warning and an object of horror to them.

The repeated declaration that the Lord has spoken gives the passage its solemn force. The destruction is presented as the outcome of His announced judgment, rather than evidence that His word or rule has failed.

The closing images include the arrows of famine, a cut-off food supply, wild beasts, plague, bloodshed and the sword. They describe a community losing the things that ordinarily sustain and protect life.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry emphasizes that God’s word will prove true, even when people presume they will escape the announced consequences. Wesley connects the city’s condition with a warning visible to other nations.

Their explanations treat the recognition of the Lord as central to the outcome. The calamities expose the seriousness of His rejected word and the failure of the confidence that had ignored it.
passages.god_plan_html:
The same set of judgments appears in Revelation 6:1–8, where the Lamb opens the seals and the fourth rider is given authority involving sword, famine, plague and wild beasts. This is a recurring biblical pattern of judgment, also found elsewhere in Ezekiel, rather than a statement that Revelation quotes only this passage.

The connection places these warnings within the New Testament’s presentation of Christ’s authority as the Lamb. God’s saving purpose includes a real reckoning with evil; the language of rescue does not make His warnings empty.

passages.title: Ezekiel 6:1-7
passages.section_title: Can the high places protect those who worship there?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 And the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 2 “Son of man, set your face against the mountains of Israel and prophesy against them. 3 You are to say: ‘O mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord GOD! This is what the Lord GOD says to the mountains and hills, to the ravines and valleys: I am about to bring a sword against you, and I will destroy your high places. 4 Your altars will be demolished and your incense altars will be smashed; and I will cast down your slain before your idols. 5 I will lay the corpses of the Israelites before their idols and scatter your bones around your altars. 6 Wherever you live, the cities will be laid waste and the high places will be demolished, so that your altars will be laid waste and desecrated, your idols smashed and obliterated, your incense altars cut down, and your works blotted out. 7 The slain will fall among you, and you will know that I am the LORD.

This is what the Lord GOD says to the mountains and hills, to the ravines and valleys: I am about to bring a sword against you, and I will destroy your high places.

4 Your altars will be demolished and your incense altars will be smashed; and I will cast down your slain before your idols. 5 I will lay the corpses of the Israelites before their idols and scatter your bones around your altars. 6 Wherever you live, the cities will be laid waste and the high places will be demolished, so that your altars will be laid waste and desecrated, your idols smashed and obliterated, your incense altars cut down, and your works blotted out. 7 The slain will fall among you, and you will know that I am the LORD.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Ezekiel must turn toward Israel’s mountains and address the mountains, hills, ravines and valleys. The warning reaches across the land because the places of false worship are spread through it.

The Hebrew word בָּמָה, bamah (bah-MAH), means high place. Brown–Driver–Briggs explains its use for worship sites on hills and also on built platforms. Here the surrounding references to idols, altars and incense make the false worship at these sites the focus.

The Lord will bring the sword, demolish the altars and smash the idols. The bodies of worshipers will lie before the objects they trusted, and their bones will be scattered around the altars.

The destruction of cities and shrines ends with the declaration that the people will know He is the Lord. The idols cannot secure their own survival or the safety of their worshipers.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley emphasize the failure of false worship as a source of safety. Wesley connects the bodies before the altars with the exposure of the idols’ inability to help.

Henry points out that God can bring down idolatrous worship even through people who practice idolatry themselves. The passage’s outcome concerns His judgment and the failure of the false gods, rather than the religious faithfulness of the conquering power.
passages.god_plan_html:
First Corinthians 10:14–22 carries the call to undivided worship into the life of believers in Christ. Paul urges them to flee idolatry and explains that sharing the Lord’s cup and table cannot be joined with participation in idol worship.

Paul does not quote Ezekiel 6 there. The shared theme is allegiance to the living God, now explained through participation in Christ and the unity of His body. The Lord’s people are called to honor that relationship in their worship and conduct.

passages.title: Ezekiel 6:8-10
passages.section_title: What hope remains for the people scattered among the nations?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 Yet I will leave a remnant, for some of you will escape the sword when you are scattered among the nations and throughout the lands. 9 Then in the nations to which they have been carried captive, your survivors will remember Me—how I have been grieved by their adulterous hearts that turned away from Me, and by their eyes that lusted after idols. So they will loathe themselves for the evil they have done and for all their abominations. 10 And they will know that I am the LORD; I did not declare in vain that I would bring this calamity upon them.
paragraphs: 8 Yet I will leave a remnant, for some of you will escape the sword when you are scattered among the nations and throughout the lands. 9 Then in the nations to which they have been carried captive, your survivors will remember Me—how I have been grieved by their adulterous hearts that turned away from Me, and by their eyes that lusted after idols. So they will loathe themselves for the evil they have done and for all their abominations. 10 And they will know that I am the LORD; I did not declare in vain that I would bring this calamity upon them.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The announcement of destruction includes a promise that some will escape. They will be scattered among nations, yet a remnant will remain.

In captivity they will remember the Lord and how their unfaithful hearts and desire for idols grieved Him. Their remembrance includes deep remorse for the evil they practiced.

They will recognize Him as the Lord and know that His warning was not spoken in vain. The preserved people do not simply resume their former life; they remember the relationship they had rejected and the truth of His word.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley connect the survivors’ remembrance with repentance. The people recognize both their obligation to the Lord and the seriousness of turning away from Him.

Wesley emphasizes that the Lord Himself preserves the remnant. Henry treats the return to remembering Him as a gracious outcome within the calamity. Both explanations keep the promise of preservation together with the change in how the people regard their sin.
passages.god_plan_html:
The promise follows a pattern already stated in Leviticus 26:39–45: exile and confession appear alongside the Lord’s commitment to remember His covenant and not destroy His people completely.

Romans 11:1–6 develops the wider theme of a remnant preserved by grace. Paul rejects the claim that God has abandoned His people and points to His keeping of a people for Himself.

Romans does not explicitly quote Ezekiel 6 in that discussion. The connection is the continuing faithfulness of God within a history that includes rebellion and judgment. The remnant bears witness to His mercy, rather than to the people’s ability to secure themselves.

passages.title: Ezekiel 6:11-14
passages.section_title: Why is Ezekiel told to clap, stamp and cry out?

versions.label: BSB

So I will vent My fury upon them. 13 Then you will know that I am the LORD, when their slain lie among their idols around their altars, on every high hill, on all the mountaintops, and under every green tree and leafy oak—the places where they offered fragrant incense to all their idols. 14 I will stretch out My hand against them, and wherever they live I will make the land a desolate waste, from the wilderness to Diblah. Then they will know that I am the LORD.’”

Then they will know that I am the LORD.’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Ezekiel must express distress with his hands, feet and voice over the people’s abominations and the coming sword, famine and plague. The warning is to be delivered with visible and audible force.

The different dangers reach those far away, those nearby and those remaining under siege. Distance or another chosen refuge does not make the announced judgment disappear.

The bodies lying among the idols will expose the failure of worship on the hills, under green trees and around the altars. The Lord’s outstretched hand leaves the land desolate.

The repeated ending brings the purpose into focus: they will know that He is the Lord. The chapter has moved from the destruction of false worship, through the promise to preserve some, to a final declaration that His word will be made known.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley read the gestures as an expression of sorrow, indignation and compassion over sin and its consequences. They do not treat the scene as a celebration of suffering.

Both emphasize the reach of the judgment and the failure of the refuges on which the people depended. Henry also urges compassion toward people facing the ruin their wrongdoing brings.

passages.title: Ezekiel 7:1-13
passages.section_title: What happens when the time for warning reaches its end?

The end has come upon the four corners of the land. 3 The end is now upon you, and I will unleash My anger against you. I will judge you according to your ways and repay you for all your abominations. 4 I will not look on you with pity, nor will I spare you, but I will punish you for your ways and for the abominations among you. Then you will know that I am the LORD.’ 5 This is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Disaster! An unprecedented disaster — behold, it is coming! 6 The end has come! The end has come! Then you will know that it is I, the LORD, who strikes the blow. 10 Behold, the day is here! It has come! section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord’s word announces an end to the land of Israel. The repetition makes the message urgent: the time has come, the day is near, and the announced judgment will reach the whole land.

The people will be judged according to their ways and their abominations. The Lord identifies Himself as the One striking the blow, so the approaching disaster cannot be explained as merely the failure of His power to defend them.

Pride and violence are pictured as growth that has reached maturity. What has been allowed to flourish now comes to its dreadful outcome. Wealth and the ordinary structures of life will not remain secure.

The buyer is not to rejoice and the seller not to mourn. The coming upheaval removes the security on which both ordinary expectations depend. The seller will not recover what was sold, and wrongdoing cannot preserve anyone’s life.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley read the repeated announcement as an urgent declaration that the people’s peace and security are ending. Henry emphasizes the force of the repetition; Wesley relates it to the end of the patience that had delayed judgment.

The USCCB notes explain the buyer and seller through the collapse of ordinary affairs in the face of disaster. Wesley similarly emphasizes how little possession will mean when the conqueror overturns the conditions in which property is held.

The shared emphasis is the failure of presumed security. The warning calls the people to take the Lord’s word seriously while showing how completely their usual expectations will be disrupted.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 2:1–16 develops a related theme: God’s patience is meant to lead to repentance, and a stubborn refusal to turn does not make future judgment disappear. Paul also warns people who condemn others while practicing the same wrongs.

Paul places judgment within the gospel’s account of Christ: God will judge human secrets through Jesus Christ. He also insists that God shows no favoritism, addressing both Jew and Gentile.

This is a wider biblical connection, rather than an explicit quotation of Ezekiel 7. The warning belongs within God’s purpose to expose and judge evil truthfully, while His present kindness calls people to turn to Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 7:14-22
passages.section_title: Can weapons, wealth or the sanctuary deliver the city?

Those in the country will die by the sword, and those in the city will be devoured by famine and plague. 16 The survivors will escape and live in the mountains, moaning like doves of the valley, each for his own iniquity. 17 Every hand will go limp, and every knee will turn to water. 18 They will put on sackcloth, and terror will overwhelm them. Shame will cover all their faces, and all their heads will be shaved. 19 They will throw their silver into the streets, and their gold will seem unclean. Their silver and gold cannot save them in the day of the wrath of the LORD. Violent men will enter it, and they will defile it.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The trumpet sounds and preparations are made, but no army goes out to fight. The sword threatens those outside, while plague and famine consume those inside. Even the survivors who reach the mountains mourn over their iniquity.

Limp hands, unsteady knees, sackcloth and shaved heads picture terror and shame. The people are losing the confidence and strength on which they relied.

Silver is thrown into the streets, and gold becomes unclean in their eyes. It cannot deliver them from the Lord’s wrath or fill their empty stomachs. The wealth that had drawn them into wrongdoing proves unable to supply what they most need.

The ornaments used in pride and idolatry become plunder for foreigners. The Lord turns His face away, and violent men enter and defile His treasured place. Wealth and a sacred building cannot shelter the city from the judgment it has been warned about.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley emphasize the failure of riches as a refuge. They connect wealth abused through pride and idolatry with its inability to rescue people in the day of judgment.

Wesley understands the treasured place as the temple and its innermost sanctuary. Henry likewise stresses that possession of the temple will not protect people who refuse to be governed by God.

The passage’s different losses therefore expose the same misplaced confidence. The people cannot use what they possess as a substitute for faithfulness to the Lord.
passages.god_plan_html:
First Peter 1:17–21 develops the contrast between silver and gold and the redemption God provides. Believers were redeemed from an empty way of life through Christ’s precious blood, rather than perishable wealth.

Peter connects that rescue with God’s purpose before the world’s foundation and with His raising and glorifying Jesus. Faith and hope are therefore directed toward God.

Peter does not explicitly quote Ezekiel 7. The shared theme helps distinguish the failure of wealth from the saving provision of God: what people cannot purchase for themselves is supplied through Christ.

passages.title: Ezekiel 7:23-27
passages.section_title: What happens when peace and guidance cannot be found?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 23 Forge the chain, for the land is full of crimes of bloodshed, and the city is full of violence. 24 So I will bring the most wicked of nations to take possession of their houses. I will end the pride of the mighty, and their holy places will be profaned. 25 Anguish is coming! They will seek peace, but find none. 26 Disaster upon disaster will come, and rumor after rumor. Then they will seek a vision from a prophet, but instruction from the priests will perish, as will counsel from the elders. 27 The king will mourn, the prince will be clothed with despair, and the hands of the people of the land will tremble. I will deal with them according to their conduct, and I will judge them by their own standards. Then they will know that I am the LORD.’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The command to forge a chain follows the charge that the land is full of bloodshed and the city full of violence. The coming occupation will take houses, humble the mighty and profane places the people treated as holy.

They will seek peace and find none. Disaster and rumor arrive one after another, and the usual sources of guidance fail: the sought-for vision is absent, priestly instruction perishes, and elders have no counsel to give.

The collapse reaches rulers and ordinary people alike. The king mourns, the prince despairs and the people tremble. The Lord again declares that He will deal with them according to their conduct, and they will know that He is the Lord.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry connects the chain with the consequences of breaking God’s commands: those who refused His rule find themselves bound under judgment. Wesley understands it as the binding of captives.

Both emphasize the complete loss of confidence when God’s judgment arrives. Political position and the offices associated with guidance do not supply the peace that the people seek.

The final recognition of the Lord answers the refusal that brought the chapter to this point. His word, rather than their former confidence, establishes the outcome.

passages.title: Ezekiel 8:1-6
passages.section_title: Why is an idol standing at the Lord’s temple?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 In the sixth year, on the fifth day of the sixth month, I was sitting in my house, and the elders of Judah were sitting before me; and there the hand of the Lord GOD fell upon me. 2 Then I looked and saw a figure like that of a man. From His waist down His appearance was like fire, and from His waist up He was as bright as the gleam of amber. 3 He stretched out what looked like a hand and took me by the hair of my head. Then the Spirit lifted me up between earth and heaven and carried me in visions of God to Jerusalem, to the entrance of the north gate of the inner court, where the idol that provokes jealousy was seated. 4 And there I saw the glory of the God of Israel, like the vision I had seen in the plain. 5 “Son of man,” He said to me, “now lift up your eyes to the north.” So I lifted up my eyes to the north, and in the entrance north of the Altar Gate I saw this idol of jealousy. 6 “Son of man,” He said to me, “do you see what they are doing—the great abominations that the house of Israel is committing—to drive Me far from My sanctuary? Yet you will see even greater abominations.”

5 “Son of man,” He said to me, “now lift up your eyes to the north.” So I lifted up my eyes to the north, and in the entrance north of the Altar Gate I saw this idol of jealousy. 6 “Son of man,” He said to me, “do you see what they are doing—the great abominations that the house of Israel is committing—to drive Me far from My sanctuary? Yet you will see even greater abominations.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Ezekiel is sitting in his house with the elders of Judah when the Lord’s hand comes upon him. The date places this after his first vision. He remains among the exiles, but the Spirit takes him to Jerusalem in a vision.

The fiery brightness recalls the glory he has already seen. At the entrance to the inner court, however, he sees an idol that provokes the Lord’s jealousy. God’s glory and the worship of a rival are being brought together in the place devoted to Him.

The Lord asks Ezekiel to look closely. The question is whether the people’s own conduct is driving Him far from His sanctuary. The temple’s presence cannot make their worship acceptable while they give its space to other gods.

The vision has only begun. Ezekiel is told that still greater offenses will be shown to him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The central reading is that worship of other gods has invaded the Lord’s own sanctuary. Henry and Wesley understand Ezekiel’s journey as a vision, and both connect the temple’s corruption with God’s coming judgment.

Wesley identifies the idol as Baal, but the passage itself gives no name. Its importance here lies in what it does: it places a rival object of worship at the entrance to the Lord’s house. The Lord’s jealousy concerns the people’s broken faithfulness to Him.
passages.god_plan_html:
Second Corinthians 6:14–18 asks what agreement God’s temple can have with idols. Paul applies the temple picture to the people who belong to the living God, drawing on God’s promises to dwell among His people and receive them as His children.

This develops the same larger concern seen in Ezekiel: God intends to dwell with His people, and their worship belongs to Him. Paul’s application goes beyond the fate of Jerusalem’s building to the life of the believing community. He is not explicitly quoting Ezekiel 8.

passages.title: Ezekiel 8:7-13
passages.section_title: What are the elders doing where they think no one sees?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
A hole in a wall leads Ezekiel to a doorway. Inside, the walls are covered with images of crawling creatures, detestable animals and Israel’s idols. Seventy elders stand before the images, each offering incense. Jaazaniah son of Shaphan is named among them.

The scene exposes the conduct of leaders in a place hidden from ordinary view. Their incense rises before images while they say that the Lord does not see and has abandoned the land.

The vision directly challenges that claim. What they do in darkness is being shown to Ezekiel by the very God whose attention they deny. Once again, he is told that there is more to see.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley read this as the exposure of concealed idolatry among Israel’s leaders. Henry emphasizes the contradiction between an outward religious appearance and hidden conduct; Wesley stresses the failure of leaders who should have set an example.

The elders’ claim that God has left them also serves as a reason to seek other objects of worship. The vision answers both parts of their claim: God sees what they are doing, and His coming judgment is a response to their conduct.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 1:18–25 describes people exchanging God’s glory for images of humans, birds, animals and reptiles. Paul explains the underlying exchange: created things are worshiped in place of their Creator.

Paul does not explicitly quote this scene in Ezekiel. His explanation shows why the problem reaches beyond one hidden room or one group of elders. God makes Himself known through His workmanship, yet people can turn that workmanship into a substitute for Him. The gospel addresses this deep refusal to honor the God who made us.

passages.title: Ezekiel 8:14-18
passages.section_title: Why are the worshipers turning their backs on the temple?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 Then He brought me to the entrance of the north gate of the house of the LORD, and I saw women sitting there, weeping for Tammuz. 15 “Son of man,” He said to me, “do you see this? Yet you will see even greater abominations than these.” 16 So He brought me to the inner court of the house of the LORD, and there at the entrance to the temple of the LORD, between the portico and the altar, were about twenty-five men with their backs to the temple of the LORD and their faces toward the east; and they were bowing to the east in worship of the sun. 17 “Son of man,” He said to me, “do you see this? Although they shout loudly in My ears, I will not listen to them.”

Look, they are even putting the branch to their nose! 18 Therefore I will respond with wrath. I will not look on them with pity, nor will I spare them. Although they shout loudly in My ears, I will not listen to them.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
At the north gate, Ezekiel sees women mourning for Tammuz. He is then taken into the inner court, where about twenty-five men stand between the porch and the altar. With their backs toward the Lord’s temple, they face east and worship the sun.

Tammuz is a Mesopotamian deity also known as Dumuzi. Penn Museum’s account of Sumerian stories identifies Dumuzi as a shepherd-god associated with the goddess Inanna. Ezekiel’s point is that mourning for this other god is taking place at the Lord’s house.

The sun worshipers make the rejection visible: they turn their backs on the sanctuary to worship something God made. The Lord also charges the people with filling the land with violence. Wrong worship and wrongdoing toward others stand together in His indictment.

The branch raised to the nose is another act of provocation. The vision ends with the Lord’s announcement that loud cries will not turn away the judgment He has declared.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley understand the scenes as increasingly serious dishonor within the sacred place. They read the men’s turned backs as a visible rejection of the Lord in favor of the sun.

The exact meaning of the branch gesture is less clear. Henry associates it with an idolatrous custom; Wesley proposes a comparison with another form of worship. The Cambridge commentary questions a proposed Persian explanation and notes an alternative understanding as mockery. The surrounding charge is clear even though the specific gesture is uncertain: the people are provoking the Lord while the land is full of violence.

passages.title: Ezekiel 9:1-4
passages.section_title: Who receives the mark before judgment begins?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then I heard Him call out in a loud voice, saying, “Draw near, O executioners of the city, each with a weapon of destruction in hand.” 2 And I saw six men coming from the direction of the Upper Gate, which faces north, each with a weapon of slaughter in his hand. With them was another man clothed in linen who had a writing kit at his side. And they came in and stood beside the bronze altar. 3 Then the glory of the God of Israel rose from above the cherubim, where it had been, and moved to the threshold of the temple. And He called to the man clothed in linen who had the writing kit at his side. 4 “Go throughout the city of Jerusalem,” said the LORD, “and put a mark on the foreheads of the men sighing and groaning over all the abominations committed there.”
paragraphs: 1 Then I heard Him call out in a loud voice, saying, “Draw near, O executioners of the city, each with a weapon of destruction in hand.” 2 And I saw six men coming from the direction of the Upper Gate, which faces north, each with a weapon of slaughter in his hand. With them was another man clothed in linen who had a writing kit at his side. And they came in and stood beside the bronze altar.

3 Then the glory of the God of Israel rose from above the cherubim, where it had been, and moved to the threshold of the temple. And He called to the man clothed in linen who had the writing kit at his side. 4 “Go throughout the city of Jerusalem,” said the LORD, “and put a mark on the foreheads of the men sighing and groaning over all the abominations committed there.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The vision continues at the temple. Six armed figures arrive from the north, accompanied by a man in linen carrying a writing kit. They take their places beside the bronze altar.

The glory of the God of Israel moves from above the cherubim to the temple’s threshold. Before the armed figures are sent through the city, the man in linen receives a different task: mark the foreheads of those who grieve over the wrongdoing in Jerusalem.

The people marked out are distinguished by their response to the evil around them. They have not made peace with it. God sees their grief as clearly as He sees the hidden worship exposed in chapter 8.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The mark identifies people who are to be spared in the judgment shown next. Henry emphasizes God’s care for a faithful remnant and reads the linen-clothed figure in light of Christ’s care for His people. Wesley describes a figure with authority over the others and emphasizes the grief of those marked.

The Hebrew word תָּו, tav (tahv), means a mark here; the Brown–Driver–Briggs entry identifies its use for those exempted from this judgment. The passage does not describe the mark’s shape.

Tertullian, in Against Marcion, book 3, chapter 22, later connected the mark with Christ’s cross by comparing it with the shape of the Greek letter tau and the Latin T. That is an early Christian reading of the sign; Ezekiel does not itself identify the marked shape as a cross or name the man in linen as Christ.
passages.god_plan_html:
Revelation 7:1–4 presents a close parallel: harm is held back until God’s servants have been sealed on their foreheads. Revelation 9:4 likewise distinguishes those who bear God’s seal from those exposed to a particular judgment. Neither passage directly quotes Ezekiel, but the shared picture is striking: God knows His own and marks them out before the announced harm.

Ephesians 1:13–14 explains that those who hear and believe the gospel are sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, the pledge of their inheritance. Paul describes God’s gift to believers rather than a visible forehead mark. Together, these passages show God’s purpose to claim and keep a people for Himself.

passages.title: Ezekiel 9:5-11
passages.section_title: Why does judgment begin at the sanctuary?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The armed figures are ordered to follow the man with the writing kit. They must spare everyone who bears the mark, but the judgment otherwise reaches across the city, without the protection that age, status or closeness to the temple might seem to offer. It begins with the elders at the sanctuary.

This is the execution of judgment within the vision, continuing the exposure of the temple’s corruption. The place intended for worship is filled with the slain. The sanctuary cannot shield the conduct that has been exposed there.

Ezekiel falls facedown and pleads for the remnant of Israel. He is overwhelmed by the prospect of destruction, rather than pleased at the suffering he sees.

The Lord answers by naming the land’s bloodshed and the city’s injustice. The people have claimed that He has abandoned the land and does not see. He declares that their own deeds will come upon them. The man in linen then reports that his task has been completed.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley connect the starting place with the seriousness of sin among those closest to the sanctuary. Religious standing does not cancel responsibility to God. Wesley also makes clear that the killing is being shown in a vision.

Henry joins the warning with an appeal to keep pleading for others. Ezekiel’s response supports that concern: even after seeing the offenses, he asks whether the whole remnant will be destroyed.

The order to spare the marked people belongs to the particular judgment shown here. It does not mean that faithful people never suffer, nor does this account pronounce the eternal destiny of each person depicted in the vision.
passages.god_plan_html:
First Peter 4:12–19 says that judgment begins with God’s household. Peter applies this to Christians facing a fiery trial and calls them to entrust themselves to their faithful Creator while doing good. His words develop the theme of accountability among God’s people; they do not make Christian suffering identical to Jerusalem’s punishment.

Second Peter 2:4–9 recalls earlier judgments and God’s rescue of Noah and Lot. Lot’s distress over the wrongdoing around him also resembles the grief of those marked in Ezekiel’s vision. Peter’s conclusion is that the Lord knows how to rescue the godly and hold the unrighteous for judgment.

These connections hold together the truths the vision presents: God sees wrongdoing, He knows those who belong to Him, and His people can entrust themselves to Him even when judgment is frightening.

passages.title: Ezekiel 10:1-8
passages.section_title: Why is fire taken from among the cherubim?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The temple vision continues. Above the cherubim, Ezekiel sees the likeness of a sapphire throne. The man in linen who marked people for protection now receives another command: take burning coals from beneath the cherubim and scatter them over Jerusalem.

The cherubim stand on the south side of the temple. A cloud fills the inner court, while the Lord’s glory rises to the threshold. Brightness fills the court, and the sound of the wings reaches the outer court.

One of the cherubim uses a hand beneath its wings to place fire into the man’s hands. He receives it and goes out. The same divine presence before which some were marked for preservation now supplies the fire of judgment against the city.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley understand the coals as a sign of the Lord’s judgment on Jerusalem. The city’s coming destruction is presented as something God has commanded, rather than an event that has escaped His control.

Wesley also reads the man in linen as Christ. That identification is an interpretation of the figure; Ezekiel names his clothing, task and obedience without explicitly naming him as the Messiah. The connection between the coals and judgment is clear without settling the figure’s identity.
passages.god_plan_html:
Revelation 8:3–6 presents a related scene: an angel offers incense with the saints’ prayers, then fills a censer with fire from the altar and throws it to the earth before the trumpet judgments.

This is a biblical parallel, rather than an explicit quotation. Both visions connect judgment on the earth with God’s holy presence. Revelation also brings the prayers of God’s people into the scene, showing that the evil they endure has not gone unnoticed by Him.

passages.title: Ezekiel 10:9-17
passages.section_title: Why does Ezekiel describe the living creatures again?

For wherever the head faced, the cherubim would go in that direction, without turning as they moved. 12 Their entire bodies, including their backs, hands, and wings, were full of eyes all around, as were their four wheels. 13 I heard the wheels being called “the whirling wheels.” 14 Each of the cherubim had four faces: the first face was that of a cherub, the second that of a man, the third that of a lion, and the fourth that of an eagle. 15 Then the cherubim rose upward. section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Ezekiel looks again at the wheels and the creatures beside them. Each creature has a wheel, and all four wheels share the same appearance, like a wheel within a wheel. They move in any of four directions without turning.

The creatures and wheels are covered with eyes. Ezekiel hears the wheels called whirling wheels and describes four faces on each creature. Here the first face is called the face of a cherub; chapter 1 described the face of an ox among the four.

The creatures rise, move and stand with the wheels. Their movement is joined because the spirit of the living creatures is in the wheels. Ezekiel explicitly recognizes them as the beings he saw beside the River Kebar.

The repetition ties the Jerusalem vision to his first encounter in exile. The Lord whose glory he saw beside the river is the same Lord now revealing what is happening at the temple.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley read the joined movement as a picture of God directing events toward His purposes. Wesley connects the many eyes with wisdom: events that appear confusing to people remain under God’s direction.

The emphasis is coordinated movement and divine rule. The creatures do not act independently of one another, and the Lord’s glory is not confined to one earthly place. Ezekiel’s recognition of them makes the continuity between the visions explicit.

passages.title: Ezekiel 10:18-22
passages.section_title: Where does the Lord’s glory go next?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 Then the glory of the LORD moved away from the threshold of the temple and stood above the cherubim. 19 As I watched, the cherubim lifted their wings and rose up from the ground, with the wheels beside them as they went. And they stopped at the entrance of the east gate of the house of the LORD, with the glory of the God of Israel above them.

Each creature went straight ahead.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord’s glory moves away from the temple threshold and stands above the cherubim. They lift their wings and rise with the wheels, then stop at the entrance of the temple’s east gate.

The movement carries the vision toward departure. The glory has not simply vanished; Ezekiel is shown it moving from the sanctuary toward the edge of the temple grounds.

He again identifies the creatures as those he saw beneath the God of Israel at the River Kebar. He now knows that they are cherubim. Their faces, wings, hands and straight movement join this scene to the first vision.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley emphasize that the Lord’s withdrawal takes place in stages. They see the pauses as expressing His patience toward a people whose conduct has provoked judgment.

The scene also challenges the assumption that possessing the temple guarantees God’s protection. His glory moves beyond the building while remaining above the cherubim. The God who judged its corruption is free to leave it.
passages.god_plan_html:
John 1:9–18 brings the theme of God dwelling among people to Jesus: the Word becomes flesh, and His witnesses see the Son’s glory. Hebrews 1:1–4 describes the Son as the radiance of God’s glory and the exact representation of His nature.

These passages do not explicitly identify every feature of Ezekiel’s vision with a feature of Jesus’ earthly life. They do explain where the larger theme leads: God makes Himself known through His Son. The departure from a corrupted sanctuary is one part of Scripture’s longer account of God dwelling with His people.

passages.title: Ezekiel 11:1-12
passages.section_title: Can the city protect leaders who reject God’s word?

Among them I saw Jaazaniah son of Azzur and Pelatiah son of Benaiah, who were leaders of the people. 2 And the LORD said to me, “Son of man, these are the men who plot evil and give wicked counsel in this city. 3 They are saying, ‘Is not the time near to build houses? The city is the cooking pot, and we are the meat.’ 4 Therefore prophesy against them; prophesy, O son of man!” 5 And the Spirit of the LORD fell upon me and told me to declare that this is what the LORD says: “That is what you are thinking, O house of Israel; and I know the thoughts that arise in your minds. 6 You have multiplied those you killed in this city and filled its streets with the dead. 7 Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: The slain you have laid within this city are the meat, and the city is the pot; but I will remove you from it. 8 You fear the sword, so I will bring the sword against you, declares the Lord GOD. 9 I will bring you out of the city and deliver you into the hands of foreigners, and I will execute judgments against you. 10 You will fall by the sword, and I will judge you even to the borders of Israel. section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Spirit brings Ezekiel to the east gate, where twenty-five men have gathered. Two leaders are named: Jaazaniah son of Azzur and Pelatiah son of Benaiah. The Lord identifies the group as men who plot evil and give wicked counsel.

In the BSB, their words ask whether the time is near to build houses, then compare the city to a cooking pot and themselves to the meat inside. The picture expresses confidence that they belong safely within the city.

The Lord turns their saying against them. The slain whose deaths they have multiplied are the meat that remains within the city; these leaders will be brought out. The sword they fear will reach them, and judgment will extend to Israel’s borders.

The reason is stated plainly: they have followed the practices of surrounding nations instead of the Lord’s statutes. The protection they imagine cannot cancel their responsibility for what they have done.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads the pot as the leaders’ claim that the city walls will protect them. Wesley likewise understands their counsel as defiance of the announced danger, even though fear is present beneath their confidence.

The wording about building houses is understood differently in translations. The Cambridge commentary on verse 3 discusses both a statement that the time to build is not near and the question reflected in the BSB. Across those readings, the Lord’s answer overturns the claim of safety within the city: the leaders will be brought out to face judgment.

passages.title: Ezekiel 11:13-21
passages.section_title: Has God abandoned the exiles, or will He give them a new heart?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 Now as I was prophesying, Pelatiah son of Benaiah died. Then I fell facedown and cried out in a loud voice, “Oh, Lord GOD, will You bring the remnant of Israel to a complete end?” 14 Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 15 “Son of man, your brothers—your relatives, your fellow exiles, and the whole house of Israel—are those of whom the people of Jerusalem have said, ‘They are far away from the LORD; this land has been given to us as a possession.’ 16 Therefore declare that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Although I sent them far away among the nations and scattered them among the countries, yet for a little while I have been a sanctuary for them in the countries to which they have gone.’ 17 Therefore declare that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘I will gather you from the peoples and assemble you from the countries to which you have been scattered, and I will give back to you the land of Israel.’ 18 When they return to it, they will remove all its detestable things and all its abominations. 19 And I will give them singleness of heart and put a new spirit within them; I will remove their heart of stone and give them a heart of flesh, 20 so that they may follow My statutes, keep My ordinances, and practice them. Then they will be My people, and I will be their God. 21 But as for those whose hearts pursue detestable things and abominations, I will bring their conduct down upon their own heads, declares the Lord GOD.”

17 Therefore declare that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘I will gather you from the peoples and assemble you from the countries to which you have been scattered, and I will give back to you the land of Israel.’ 18 When they return to it, they will remove all its detestable things and all its abominations. 19 And I will give them singleness of heart and put a new spirit within them; I will remove their heart of stone and give them a heart of flesh, 20 so that they may follow My statutes, keep My ordinances, and practice them. Then they will be My people, and I will be their God. 21 But as for those whose hearts pursue detestable things and abominations, I will bring their conduct down upon their own heads, declares the Lord GOD.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
While Ezekiel prophesies, Pelatiah dies. Ezekiel falls facedown and again asks whether the Lord will bring Israel’s remnant to a complete end. The answer turns his attention to those already scattered.

The people remaining in Jerusalem have treated the exiles as far from the Lord and claimed the land for themselves. God answers that, although He sent the exiles away, He has been a sanctuary for them in the countries where they have gone. Distance from the temple has not placed them beyond His care.

He promises to gather them, return the land and remove its detestable worship. The restoration includes something deeper than returning home: He will give them singleness of heart and a new spirit, replacing a heart of stone with a heart of flesh.

The contrast describes a change from stubborn refusal to a heart responsive to God. Its purpose is lived obedience: they will follow His statutes and belong to Him as His people. Those whose hearts continue to pursue the detestable things remain accountable for their conduct.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley connects the promised return and renewed unity with the exiles’ return under Cyrus and the rebuilding of Jerusalem’s worship. Henry emphasizes the inward change God gives, applying the heart of flesh to people made responsive to Him through Christ.

John Walvoord’s account of Israel’s restoration places national restoration and spiritual renewal at Christ’s return. It represents a future fulfillment reading, rather than treating return from Babylon as the completion of Israel’s promised restoration.

The readings differ over the extent and timing of fulfillment. The passage itself joins return, the removal of idols, inward renewal and obedience. Its hope rests on what God promises to give, while its final warning still addresses those who cling to wrongdoing.
passages.god_plan_html:
The heart-and-Spirit promise is developed further in Ezekiel 36:22–28, where God promises cleansing and the gift of His Spirit so His people will walk in His ways.

Romans 8:1–11 explains how God acts through His Son and His indwelling Spirit to free those in Christ from sin and death. Paul is not explicitly quoting Ezekiel 11, but he develops the larger theme of life and obedience made possible by God’s work within His people.

The promise of God’s presence also reaches beyond access to a particular building. Ephesians 2:17–22 describes people once far away gaining access to the Father through Christ and being built together into a dwelling for God by His Spirit. These connections show why restoration involves both belonging to God and a changed life.

passages.title: Ezekiel 11:22-25
passages.section_title: How does the vision of Jerusalem come to an end?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 Then the cherubim, with the wheels beside them, spread their wings, and the glory of the God of Israel was above them. 23 And the glory of the LORD rose up from within the city and stood over the mountain east of the city. 24 And the Spirit lifted me up and carried me back to Chaldea, to the exiles in the vision given by the Spirit of God. After the vision had gone up from me, 25 I told the exiles everything the LORD had shown me.
paragraphs: 22 Then the cherubim, with the wheels beside them, spread their wings, and the glory of the God of Israel was above them. 23 And the glory of the LORD rose up from within the city and stood over the mountain east of the city. 24 And the Spirit lifted me up and carried me back to Chaldea, to the exiles in the vision given by the Spirit of God. After the vision had gone up from me, 25 I told the exiles everything the LORD had shown me.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The cherubim spread their wings with the wheels beside them. The Lord’s glory rises from within Jerusalem and stands over the mountain east of the city.

The movement completes this vision’s account of departure from the temple and city. It follows both the exposure of Jerusalem’s wrongdoing and the promise that the scattered people have not been abandoned.

The Spirit brings Ezekiel back to the exiles in Chaldea, the vision ends, and he tells them everything the Lord has shown him. The people who have been dismissed as far from God are the ones who now receive this report of His judgment and promises.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley identify the eastern mountain as the Mount of Olives. They understand the glory’s movement as the Lord’s withdrawal from the city after its persistent rejection of Him.

Henry also connects the scene with Christ’s ascension from that mountain. That is a Christian reading of the parallel; Ezekiel’s immediate account concerns the glory departing and the prophet returning to report to the exiles.
passages.god_plan_html:
The departure is not the end of Ezekiel’s account of God’s presence. In Ezekiel 43:1–9, he sees the glory coming from the east and entering the temple through the east gate. The earlier departure and later return form a clear connection within the book itself.

Acts 1:9–12 describes Jesus being taken up, a cloud hiding Him from view, and the promise that He will return. The disciples then go back to Jerusalem from the Mount of Olives.

The shared setting and movement provide a meaningful parallel, as Henry notes. Acts does not say that Ezekiel 11 predicts every detail of the ascension, and neither account supplies a timetable for how long the glory remained over the mountain. The wider hope is God’s promised presence with His people, rather than abandonment as the last word.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 12:1-7
passages.section_title: Why does Ezekiel pack his bags and dig through a wall?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 2 “Son of man, you are living in a rebellious house. They have eyes to see but do not see, and ears to hear but do not hear, for they are a rebellious house. 3 Therefore, son of man, pack your bags for exile. In broad daylight, set out from your place and go to another as they watch. Perhaps they will understand, though they are a rebellious house. 4 Bring out your baggage for exile by day, as they watch. Then in the evening, as they watch, go out like those who go into exile. 5 As they watch, dig through the wall and carry your belongings out through it. 6 And as they watch, lift your bags to your shoulder and take them out at dusk; cover your face so that you cannot see the land. For I have made you a sign to the house of Israel.” 7 So I did as I was commanded. I brought out my bags for exile by day, and in the evening I dug through the wall by hand. I took my belongings out at dusk, carrying them on my shoulder as they watched.

They have eyes to see but do not see, and ears to hear but do not hear, for they are a rebellious house. 3 Therefore, son of man, pack your bags for exile. In broad daylight, set out from your place and go to another as they watch. Perhaps they will understand, though they are a rebellious house.

4 Bring out your baggage for exile by day, as they watch. Then in the evening, as they watch, go out like those who go into exile. 5 As they watch, dig through the wall and carry your belongings out through it. 6 And as they watch, lift your bags to your shoulder and take them out at dusk; cover your face so that you cannot see the land. For I have made you a sign to the house of Israel.” 7 So I did as I was commanded. I brought out my bags for exile by day, and in the evening I dug through the wall by hand. I took my belongings out at dusk, carrying them on my shoulder as they watched.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the temple vision, the Lord gives Ezekiel another message to act out. He describes the people as having eyes and ears but refusing to see and hear. Their problem is their rebellion, even after the warnings already given.

Ezekiel must bring out baggage for exile in daylight where people can watch. At dusk, he is to dig through a wall, carry his belongings through it on his shoulder and cover his face so that he cannot see the land.

The Lord makes the purpose clear: Ezekiel is a sign to Israel. Perhaps the people will understand when the warning is placed before their eyes. The prophet reports that he does exactly what he was commanded.

The action comes before the fuller explanation in the next passage. Ezekiel obeys the instruction he has received while the watchers are left asking what it means.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley read the departure as a sign of the captivity still coming upon Jerusalem. It depicts the loss of home and the attempt to leave under threat, rather than an ordinary journey.

Wesley emphasizes that the people are capable of understanding but refuse to do so. The visible sign is another effort to confront that refusal. It gives the warning a form they can watch, even though seeing the action does not guarantee that they will accept its meaning.
passages.god_plan_html:
First Corinthians 4:9–13 describes the apostles being put on public display while enduring weakness, hunger, mistreatment and dishonor. Second Corinthians 6:1–10 likewise connects faithful service with endurance, truthful speech, patience and love amid hardship.

Paul is not identifying the apostles with Ezekiel’s particular sign. The connection is the cost of carrying God’s message: faithfulness may require public discomfort and sacrifice before an audience that does not welcome it. God’s saving work is served through such endurance, rather than through a guarantee of comfort or applause.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 12:8-16
passages.section_title: How can the prince reach Babylon without seeing it?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 And in the morning the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 9 “Son of man, hasn’t the rebellious house of Israel asked you, ‘What are you doing?’ 10 Tell them that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘This burden concerns the prince in Jerusalem and all the house of Israel who are there.’ 11 You are to say, ‘I am a sign to you.’ Just as it happened here, so will it be done to them; they will go into exile as captives. 12 And at dusk the prince among them will lift his bags to his shoulder and go out. They will dig through the wall to bring him out. He will cover his face so he cannot see the land. 13 But I will spread My net over him, and he will be caught in My snare. I will bring him to Babylon, the land of the Chaldeans; yet he will not see it, and there he will die. 14 And I will scatter to every wind all the attendants around him and all his troops, and I will draw a sword to chase after them. 15 And they will know that I am the LORD, when I disperse them among the nations and scatter them throughout the countries. 16 But I will spare a few of them from sword and famine and plague, so that in the nations to which they go, they can recount all their abominations. Then they will know that I am the LORD.”

12 And at dusk the prince among them will lift his bags to his shoulder and go out. They will dig through the wall to bring him out. He will cover his face so he cannot see the land. 13 But I will spread My net over him, and he will be caught in My snare. I will bring him to Babylon, the land of the Chaldeans; yet he will not see it, and there he will die. 14 And I will scatter to every wind all the attendants around him and all his troops, and I will draw a sword to chase after them. 15 And they will know that I am the LORD, when I disperse them among the nations and scatter them throughout the countries. 16 But I will spare a few of them from sword and famine and plague, so that in the nations to which they go, they can recount all their abominations. Then they will know that I am the LORD.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The next morning, the Lord supplies the explanation. The sign concerns the prince in Jerusalem and the people still there: they too will go into exile. The prince will try to leave at dusk, carrying belongings through a wall with his face covered.

His escape will fail. The Lord pictures His capture as a net spread over him. He will be taken to Babylon and die there, yet he will not see it.

Second Kings 25:1–12 explains how those details fit Zedekiah’s fate. After Jerusalem is breached, the king flees by night. He is captured near Jericho and brought to Riblah, where his sons are killed before him and his eyes are put out. He is then taken to Babylon in shackles.

The warning also reaches his attendants and troops, who will be scattered. A few people will be spared from sword, famine and plague so that they can recount their wrongdoing among the nations. Survival is joined to acknowledgment of what brought them there, and to recognition of the Lord.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley identify the prince as Zedekiah and connect the prediction with his capture and blinding. Being brought to Babylon without seeing it is therefore no contradiction: he arrives after losing his sight.

Both also emphasize the survivors’ testimony. They are to acknowledge the sins behind the judgment, rather than treating their survival as proof that nothing was wrong. Wesley sees their scattering becoming an opportunity to honor God among other peoples.

passages.title: Ezekiel 12:17-20
passages.section_title: Why must Ezekiel eat and drink with trembling?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 Moreover, the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 18 “Son of man, eat your bread with trembling, and drink your water with quivering and anxiety. 19 Then tell the people of the land that this is what the Lord GOD says about those living in Jerusalem and in the land of Israel: ‘They will eat their bread with anxiety and drink their water in dread, for their land will be stripped of everything in it because of the violence of all who dwell in it. 20 The inhabited cities will be laid waste, and the land will become desolate. Then you will know that I am the LORD.’”
paragraphs: 17 Moreover, the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 18 “Son of man, eat your bread with trembling, and drink your water with quivering and anxiety. 19 Then tell the people of the land that this is what the Lord GOD says about those living in Jerusalem and in the land of Israel: ‘They will eat their bread with anxiety and drink their water in dread, for their land will be stripped of everything in it because of the violence of all who dwell in it. 20 The inhabited cities will be laid waste, and the land will become desolate. Then you will know that I am the LORD.’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord gives another visible sign. Ezekiel must eat his bread with trembling and drink his water with fear, portraying the experience of those living in Jerusalem and the land of Israel.

Even ordinary meals will be overshadowed by anxiety. The land will be stripped and inhabited cities laid waste because of the violence of their people.

The act brings the coming disaster into daily life. A meal, normally a moment of provision and rest, becomes a picture of the dread that will accompany judgment. Once again, the stated outcome is that the people will know the Lord.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry understands the trembling meal as a portrayal of Jerusalem’s fear during the siege. Wesley connects the land’s desolation with the injustice and oppression practiced among the people.

The sign therefore joins the people’s treatment of one another with the loss of ordinary security. Its message concerns the announced judgment on Jerusalem; it does not diagnose every experience of anxiety as punishment for wrongdoing.

passages.title: Ezekiel 12:21-28
passages.section_title: Does the passing of time mean God’s warning has failed?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 Again the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 22 “Son of man, what is this proverb that you have in the land of Israel: ‘The days go by, and every vision fails’? 23 Therefore tell them that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘I will put an end to this proverb, and in Israel they will no longer recite it.’ But say to them: ‘The days are at hand when every vision will be fulfilled. 24 For there will be no more false visions or flattering divinations within the house of Israel, 25 because I, the LORD, will speak whatever word I speak, and it will be fulfilled without delay. For in your days, O rebellious house, I will speak a message and bring it to pass, declares the Lord GOD.’” 26 Furthermore, the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 27 “Son of man, take note that the house of Israel is saying, ‘The vision that he sees is for many years from now; he prophesies about the distant future.’ 28 Therefore tell them that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘None of My words will be delayed any longer. The message I speak will be fulfilled, declares the Lord GOD.’”

For in your days, O rebellious house, I will speak a message and bring it to pass, declares the Lord GOD.’”

26 Furthermore, the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 27 “Son of man, take note that the house of Israel is saying, ‘The vision that he sees is for many years from now; he prophesies about the distant future.’ 28 Therefore tell them that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘None of My words will be delayed any longer. The message I speak will be fulfilled, declares the Lord GOD.’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord confronts a proverb claiming that the days go by and every vision fails. The saying allows the people to dismiss the warnings: time has passed, so they assume nothing will happen.

He declares that this proverb will end. The time for fulfillment is at hand, and false visions and flattering divination will no longer stand in the way of what He has announced. He will speak and bring His message to pass in the days of the people being addressed.

A second response treats Ezekiel’s visions as true but safely distant. The Lord answers that as well: His words will not be delayed any longer.

The two responses differ, but both remove the need to listen now. One dismisses the warning as a failure; the other pushes it beyond the hearers’ concern. The Lord refuses both evasions.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads the people’s response as a misuse of God’s patience: the time that should have led to repentance has instead hardened them in their conduct. Wesley likewise understands the proverb as dismissing the threatened judgment.

The immediate promise of fulfillment addresses this rebellious generation and the judgment Ezekiel has announced. It is not a rule that every biblical prophecy must happen immediately after it is spoken. The point is that these hearers cannot postpone the Lord’s message to avoid responding to it.
passages.god_plan_html:
Second Peter 3:1–15 describes scoffers asking why Christ has not returned and assuming that everything continues unchanged. Peter answers by recalling God’s past acts and the judgment still to come.

He also explains the place of patience: God is giving opportunity for repentance. The response is to live in holiness and look forward to the promised new heaven and new earth where righteousness dwells.

This is a wider biblical connection, rather than an explicit quotation of Ezekiel 12. In both passages, the passing of time is no reason to dismiss God’s word. Peter adds the hope toward which believers look and calls them to use the present opportunity faithfully.

passages.title: Ezekiel 13:1-9
passages.section_title: What makes a claimed message from God false?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 2 “Son of man, prophesy against the prophets of Israel who are now prophesying. Tell those who prophesy out of their own imagination: Hear the word of the LORD! 3 This is what the Lord GOD says: Woe to the foolish prophets who follow their own spirit yet have seen nothing. 4 Your prophets, O Israel, are like foxes among the ruins. 5 You did not go up to the gaps or restore the wall around the house of Israel so that it would stand in the battle on the Day of the LORD. 6 They see false visions and speak lying divinations. They claim, ‘Thus declares the LORD,’ when the LORD did not send them; yet they wait for the fulfillment of their message. 7 Haven’t you seen a false vision and spoken a lying divination when you proclaim, ‘Thus declares the LORD,’ even though I have not spoken? 8 Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: Because you have uttered vain words and seen false visions, I am against you, declares the Lord GOD. 9 My hand will be against the prophets who see false visions and speak lying divinations. They will not belong to the council of My people or be recorded in the register of the house of Israel, nor will they enter the land of Israel. Then you will know that I am the Lord GOD.
paragraphs: 1 Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 2 “Son of man, prophesy against the prophets of Israel who are now prophesying. Tell those who prophesy out of their own imagination: Hear the word of the LORD! 3 This is what the Lord GOD says: Woe to the foolish prophets who follow their own spirit yet have seen nothing. 4 Your prophets, O Israel, are like foxes among the ruins. 5 You did not go up to the gaps or restore the wall around the house of Israel so that it would stand in the battle on the Day of the LORD.

6 They see false visions and speak lying divinations. They claim, ‘Thus declares the LORD,’ when the LORD did not send them; yet they wait for the fulfillment of their message. 7 Haven’t you seen a false vision and spoken a lying divination when you proclaim, ‘Thus declares the LORD,’ even though I have not spoken? 8 Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: Because you have uttered vain words and seen false visions, I am against you, declares the Lord GOD. 9 My hand will be against the prophets who see false visions and speak lying divinations. They will not belong to the council of My people or be recorded in the register of the house of Israel, nor will they enter the land of Israel. Then you will know that I am the Lord GOD.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord now addresses the false prophets mentioned in chapter 12. Ezekiel must speak against people who claim to prophesy while following their own imagination. They use the Lord’s name, but He has neither sent them nor given them the visions they claim.

They are compared to foxes among ruins. Instead of repairing the gaps and helping Israel stand in the day of battle, they have failed to protect the people. Their confident words do not supply what the people need.

The charge goes beyond mistaken optimism. They present their own words as the Lord’s declaration and wait for a message He never gave to be fulfilled.

God declares Himself against them. They will have no place in His people’s council, no entry in Israel’s register and no return to the land. The authority they claimed in His name cannot protect them from His judgment.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley understand the central failure as speaking without God’s message while encouraging false confidence. Wesley explains repairing the gaps as the work of preserving the people through prayer, instruction and repentance.

Jeremiah 23:16–22 gives a closely related warning. Its false prophets promise peace to people who refuse God’s ways, while a true word from His council would call them away from wrongdoing.

The passage therefore tests the claimed source and effect of the message. Invoking God’s name does not make a message His, and comforting words can harm people when they prevent an honest response to Him.

passages.title: Ezekiel 13:10-16
passages.section_title: Can whitewash make a weak wall safe?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 Because they have led My people astray, saying, ‘Peace,’ when there is no peace, and whitewashing any flimsy wall that is built, 11 tell those whitewashing the wall that it will fall. Rain will come in torrents, I will send hailstones plunging down, and a windstorm will burst forth. 12 Surely when the wall has fallen, you will not be asked, ‘Where is the whitewash with which you covered it?’ 13 Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: In My wrath I will release a windstorm, and in My anger torrents of rain and hail will fall with destructive fury. 14 I will tear down the wall you whitewashed and level it to the ground, so that its foundation is exposed. The city will fall, and you will be destroyed within it. Then you will know that I am the LORD. 15 And after I have vented My wrath against the wall and against those who whitewashed it, I will say to you: ‘The wall is gone, and so are those who whitewashed it— 16 those prophets of Israel who prophesied to Jerusalem and saw a vision of peace for her when there was no peace, declares the Lord GOD.’
