The city will fall, and you will be destroyed within it. Then you will know that I am the LORD. 15 And after I have vented My wrath against the wall and against those who whitewashed it, I will say to you: ‘The wall is gone, and so are those who whitewashed it— 16 those prophets of Israel who prophesied to Jerusalem and saw a vision of peace for her when there was no peace, declares the Lord GOD.’

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The false prophets promise peace when there is no peace. Their assurances are compared to coating a flimsy wall with whitewash: its appearance improves, but its weakness remains.

The Hebrew word תָּפֵל, taphel (tah-FEL), is identified as whitewash in this passage by Brown–Driver–Briggs. The picture is a surface covering that does not make an unsafe wall dependable.

Torrential rain, hail and wind will bring the wall down. The Lord says that He will tear it down to its foundation, and those who covered it will be destroyed with it.

The closing verses return from the wall to the people it pictures: the prophets have announced peace for Jerusalem without a true vision of peace from God. The collapse will expose both the assurance and those who supplied it.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads the wall as a false expectation built by one prophet and made more convincing by others. Wesley similarly emphasizes teaching that encourages people to feel safe in wrongdoing.

The USCCB notes describe the whitewash as concealing the wall’s defects, just as predictions of peace concealed the danger facing the people. These readings share the central point: a reassuring surface cannot change the condition beneath it.
passages.god_plan_html:
Matthew 7:24–27 offers a related building-and-storm picture. Jesus compares hearing and doing His words with building on rock; hearing without acting is like building on sand, where the storm brings collapse.

This is a parallel, rather than an explicit quotation of Ezekiel. Both pictures challenge an appearance of safety that will not survive the test. Jesus brings the response into focus: security rests in receiving His teaching and acting on it, rather than merely hearing it or admiring the building.

passages.title: Ezekiel 13:17-23
passages.section_title: How will God free His people from those who trap them with lies?

versions.label: BSB

Prophesy against them 18 and tell them that this is what the Lord GOD says: Woe to the women who sew magic charms on their wrists and make veils for the heads of people of every height, in order to ensnare their souls. Will you ensnare the souls of My people but preserve your own? 19 You have profaned Me among My people for handfuls of barley and scraps of bread. By lying to My people who would listen, you have killed those who should not have died and spared those who should not have lived. 20 Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: See, I am against the magic charms with which you ensnare souls like birds, and I will tear them from your arms. I will deliver My people from your hands. Then you will know that I am the LORD.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The warning turns to women who likewise prophesy from their own imagination. The BSB describes wrist charms and veils used to ensnare people, with barley and scraps of bread involved in their trade.

The Lord charges them with profaning Him and reversing the response people need. Their lies dishearten the righteous and encourage the wicked to continue in ways that lead to death.

He declares that He will tear away the charms and veils and free the people caught like birds. Those being hunted will no longer be prey in these women’s hands.

The promise is both an end to false visions and a rescue of the people harmed by them. God does not simply expose the deception; He acts against the grip it has on His people.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The objects are understood differently. Henry and Wesley, commenting on older wording about pillows and head coverings, emphasize the false ease and promised success being offered. Wesley treats the pillows as a figure for security.

The Cambridge commentary on verses 18–20 reads the bands and coverings as actual objects used in divination, and the USCCB notes likewise understand them as amulets and veils associated with claims about life and death. That reading is reflected in the BSB’s wording about magic charms.

Both approaches recognize the harm stated at the end: the righteous are discouraged and the wicked are kept from turning back. The precise ritual details remain difficult, but the promise of deliverance from these lies is plain.
passages.god_plan_html:
John 8:31–36 connects continuing in Jesus’ word with knowing the truth and being set free. Jesus explains the deeper slavery as slavery to sin, and identifies the Son as the One who brings true freedom.

John is not explicitly interpreting the charms in Ezekiel. The shared theme is God’s rescue from a bondage that false confidence cannot break. Ezekiel promises release from those who trap people with lies; Jesus explains the freedom He gives and calls His hearers to remain in His word.

passages.title: Ezekiel 14:1-11
passages.section_title: Can people seek God’s counsel while holding on to their idols?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then some of the elders of Israel came and sat down before me. 2 And the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 3 “Son of man, these men have set up idols in their hearts and put wicked stumbling blocks before their faces. Should I consult with them in any way? 4 Therefore speak to them and tell them that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘When any Israelite sets up idols in his heart and puts a wicked stumbling block before his face, and then comes to the prophet, I the LORD will answer him according to his great idolatry, 5 so that I may take hold of the hearts of the people of Israel. For because of their idols, they are all estranged from Me.’ 6 Therefore tell the house of Israel that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Repent and turn away from your idols; turn your faces away from all your abominations. 7 For when any Israelite or any foreigner dwelling in Israel separates himself from Me, sets up idols in his heart, and puts a wicked stumbling block before his face, and then comes to the prophet to inquire of Me, I the LORD will answer him Myself. 8 I will set My face against that man and make him a sign and a proverb; I will cut him off from among My people. Then you will know that I am the LORD. 9 But if the prophet is enticed to speak a message, then it was I the LORD who enticed him, and I will stretch out My hand against him and destroy him from among My people Israel. 10 They will bear their punishment—the punishment of the inquirer will be the same as that of the prophet— 11 in order that the house of Israel may no longer stray from Me and no longer defile themselves with all their transgressions. Then they will be My people and I will be their God, declares the Lord GOD.’”

Then you will know that I am the LORD.

Then they will be My people and I will be their God, declares the Lord GOD.’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Some elders come and sit before Ezekiel. Before their questions are reported, the Lord exposes what is in their hearts: they have given themselves to idols while approaching His prophet for counsel.

The answer will address that idolatry. The Lord intends to take hold of the hearts that have become estranged from Him, and His command is to repent and turn away from the abominations. The warning applies both to Israelites and to foreigners living among them.

Those who insist on separating themselves from Him will face His answer in judgment. A visit to the prophet cannot replace the change of heart and direction He requires.

The warning also reaches the prophet who is enticed into speaking. Both prophet and inquirer will bear punishment. The stated purpose is that Israel should stop straying and defiling itself, and belong to the Lord as His people.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley emphasize that an outward approach to God cannot make an idolatrous heart acceptable. Wesley understands God’s answer as exposing the inquirer’s condition and bringing just judgment.

Verse 9 raises a difficult question: how can the Lord speak of enticing a prophet and also judge him? Wesley explains it as God permitting the false prophet to err or leaving him in his chosen blindness. Calvin’s discussion of verse 9 puts stronger emphasis on God actively judging a people who prefer lies. He compares the scene with the lying spirit in Ahab’s prophets. These are different explanations of God’s part in the deception, while both retain the prophet’s responsibility.

James 1:13–18 states that God does not tempt anyone to evil and traces temptation to a person’s own desires. The difficulty in Ezekiel should be read alongside that teaching. The chapter describes judgment on people committed to idols and false messages, rather than making wrongdoing something they can blame on God.
passages.god_plan_html:
First Corinthians 10:1–22 uses Israel’s earlier experiences to warn Christians against idolatry and false confidence. Sharing in remarkable gifts and experiences did not make disobedience harmless.

Paul calls his readers to flee idolatry and explains their shared participation in Christ through the cup and bread. They cannot treat communion with the Lord and participation in idolatry as compatible.

Paul does not explicitly quote Ezekiel 14. He develops the same larger concern: God calls people into fellowship with Himself, and that relationship demands a response of faithfulness rather than an outward religious act alongside a heart devoted elsewhere.

passages.title: Ezekiel 14:12-20
passages.section_title: Could Noah, Daniel and Job save an unfaithful land?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 And the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 13 “Son of man, if a land sins against Me by acting unfaithfully, and I stretch out My hand against it to cut off its supply of food, to send famine upon it, and to cut off from it both man and beast, 14 then even if these three men—Noah, Daniel, and Job—were in it, their righteousness could deliver only themselves, declares the Lord GOD. 15 Or if I send wild beasts through the land to leave it childless and desolate, with no man passing through it for fear of the beasts, 16 then as surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, even if these three men were in it, they could not deliver their own sons or daughters. They alone would be delivered, but the land would be desolate. 17 Or if I bring a sword against that land and say, ‘Let a sword pass through it,’ so that I cut off from it both man and beast, 18 then as surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, even if these three men were in it, they could not deliver their own sons or daughters. They alone would be delivered. 19 Or if I send a plague into that land and pour out My wrath upon it through bloodshed, cutting off from it both man and beast, 20 then as surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, even if Noah, Daniel, and Job were in it, they could not deliver their own sons or daughters. Their righteousness could deliver only themselves.

They alone would be delivered.

19 Or if I send a plague into that land and pour out My wrath upon it through bloodshed, cutting off from it both man and beast, 20 then as surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, even if Noah, Daniel, and Job were in it, they could not deliver their own sons or daughters. Their righteousness could deliver only themselves.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord asks Ezekiel to consider a land that acts unfaithfully toward Him. Even if Noah, Daniel and Job were present, their righteousness would deliver only themselves.

The point is repeated through four kinds of judgment: famine, wild beasts, sword and plague. In each case, the presence of these righteous men would not secure the land’s release. They could not even deliver their sons or daughters from the judgment being described.

This is a hypothetical picture, not a claim that the three men lived together. Its repetition strips away the hope that association with outstandingly righteous people will shelter a population that refuses God.

The warning prepares for the direct application to Jerusalem in the next passage. The people must answer for their own unfaithfulness; someone else’s presence will not make it disappear.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley read the three men as familiar examples of righteousness and effective prayer. They understand the warning to mean that even such people could not turn aside the judgment now facing this persistently unfaithful land.

There is a difference over the name Daniel. Henry and Wesley identify him with the biblical Daniel associated with Babylon. The USCCB notes instead identify the figure with Danel, a righteous judge known from Ugaritic tradition. That is the study note’s identification, rather than an official church definition of the name.

The force of the warning remains the same in either reading: the reputation and righteousness of exceptional people cannot be treated as automatic protection for others. The passage concerns the judgment of a land; it is not a denial that prayer for other people can matter.

passages.title: Ezekiel 14:21-23
passages.section_title: What will the survivors reveal about Jerusalem’s judgment?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 For this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘How much worse will it be when I send against Jerusalem My four dire judgments—sword, famine, wild beasts, and plague—in order to cut off from it both man and beast? 22 Yet, behold, some survivors will be left in it—sons and daughters who will be brought out. They will come out to you, and when you see their conduct and actions, you will be comforted regarding the disaster I have brought upon Jerusalem—all that I have brought upon it. 23 They will bring you consolation when you see their conduct and actions, and you will know that it was not without cause that I have done all these things within it,’ declares the Lord GOD.”
paragraphs: 21 For this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘How much worse will it be when I send against Jerusalem My four dire judgments—sword, famine, wild beasts, and plague—in order to cut off from it both man and beast? 22 Yet, behold, some survivors will be left in it—sons and daughters who will be brought out. They will come out to you, and when you see their conduct and actions, you will be comforted regarding the disaster I have brought upon Jerusalem—all that I have brought upon it. 23 They will bring you consolation when you see their conduct and actions, and you will know that it was not without cause that I have done all these things within it,’ declares the Lord GOD.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord applies the four judgments directly to Jerusalem: sword, famine, wild beasts and plague. The examples just given show how little basis there is for expecting the city to be spared merely because righteous people belong to it.

Yet some sons and daughters will survive and be brought out. They will join the exiles, who will see their conduct and actions.

The Lord says that this encounter will bring consolation concerning the disaster. What the exiles see will help them understand that His actions against Jerusalem were not without cause. The survivors are evidence to be considered, rather than proof that the city was innocent.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands the survivors’ conduct and punishment as showing why God’s judgment was just. He expects their account to help the exiles recognize both God’s justice and His purpose in what has happened.

Henry also emphasizes mercy in the preservation of some people amid devastation. The USCCB notes focus on the survivors’ continuing corruption as evidence of Jerusalem’s condition.

These emphases address different sides of the ending: some are preserved, and their conduct helps explain the judgment. Survival alone is not presented as a declaration that every survivor was righteous.
passages.god_plan_html:
Revelation 6:7–8 brings together the same four means of death: sword, famine, plague and wild beasts. The Lamb opens the seal before the pale horse appears and the authority described is given.

This close biblical parallel carries the language of judgment beyond Jerusalem’s immediate crisis into Revelation’s vision of God bringing evil to account. It does not make every detail of the two visions identical or establish a timetable from Ezekiel’s list. Both place the threatened devastation under God’s authority rather than outside His rule.

passages.title: Ezekiel 15:1-8
passages.section_title: What does the burned vine show Jerusalem about its condition?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 2 “Son of man, how does the wood of the vine surpass any other branch among the trees in the forest? 3 Can wood be taken from it to make something useful? Or can one make from it a peg on which to hang utensils? 4 No, it is cast into the fire for fuel. The fire devours both ends, and the middle is charred. Can it be useful for anything? 5 Even when it was whole, it could not be made useful. How much less can it ever be useful when the fire has consumed it and charred it! 6 Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Like the wood of the vine among the trees of the forest, which I have given to the fire for fuel, so I will give up the people of Jerusalem. 7 And I will set My face against them. Though they may have escaped the fire, yet another fire will consume them. And when I set My face against them, you will know that I am the LORD. 8 Thus I will make the land desolate, because they have acted unfaithfully,’ declares the Lord GOD.”

Or can one make from it a peg on which to hang utensils? 4 No, it is cast into the fire for fuel. The fire devours both ends, and the middle is charred. Can it be useful for anything? 5 Even when it was whole, it could not be made useful. How much less can it ever be useful when the fire has consumed it and charred it!

6 Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Like the wood of the vine among the trees of the forest, which I have given to the fire for fuel, so I will give up the people of Jerusalem. 7 And I will set My face against them. Though they may have escaped the fire, yet another fire will consume them. And when I set My face against them, you will know that I am the LORD. 8 Thus I will make the land desolate, because they have acted unfaithfully,’ declares the Lord GOD.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord gives Ezekiel a short comparison. Is wood from a vine better than wood from a forest tree? Can it be made into a useful object, even a peg on which to hang utensils?

The picture becomes more pointed when the vine wood is burned at both ends and charred in the middle. If it was unsuitable for the work before, the fire has not improved it.

The Lord applies the image to Jerusalem’s people. As vine wood is given to the fire, they will be given up to judgment. Escaping one fire will not protect them from another.

The final verse gives the reason: they have acted unfaithfully. The warning removes the idea that simply being the Lord’s people makes their conduct unimportant or puts the city beyond His judgment.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley connect the vine’s value with fruitfulness. A vine is valued for its fruit, rather than its usefulness as timber, so its identity alone is no reason to boast.

Both apply the warning to an outward claim of belonging to God that produces no faithful response. Henry also directs readers toward Christ as the source of the fruit they need to bear. Their emphasis is a warning against empty religious confidence, not a statement that a person’s worth depends on social usefulness or achievement.
passages.god_plan_html:
John 15:1–11 uses a related vine-and-branches picture. Jesus identifies Himself as the true vine and calls His disciples to remain in Him, because branches cannot bear fruit by themselves.

The passage includes both pruning that leads to more fruit and the warning of a branch that withers and is burned. Jesus connects remaining in His love with keeping His commandments, and His stated aim includes His disciples’ joy.

John does not explicitly quote Ezekiel 15. The parallel develops the question of fruitfulness by directing attention to Christ: the life that honors the Father depends on remaining in the Son. The warnings should be heard together with that invitation to receive life from Him.

passages.title: Ezekiel 16:1-7
passages.section_title: Why is Jerusalem pictured as an abandoned child?

You were not rubbed with salt or wrapped in cloths. 5 No one cared enough for you to do even one of these things out of compassion for you. Instead, you were thrown out into the open field, because you were despised on the day of your birth.

6 Then I passed by and saw you wallowing in your blood, and as you lay there in your blood I said to you, ‘Live!’ There I said to you, ‘Live!’ 7 I made you thrive like a plant of the field. You grew up and matured and became very beautiful. Your breasts were formed and your hair grew, but you were naked and bare.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord tells Ezekiel to confront Jerusalem with her abominations. He does so through an extended story in which the city is pictured as a person, beginning with a newborn abandoned in an open field.

The child has received none of the care named in the story: the cord has not been cut, the blood has not been washed away, and there are no wrapping cloths. No one has shown compassion.

The Lord passes by and commands the child to live. Under His care she grows and matures, although she is still naked. Her survival begins with His action toward someone who could not rescue herself.

The references to an Amorite father and a Hittite mother challenge Jerusalem’s pride in its beginnings. The story will later return to this family language when comparing the city’s conduct with that of other cities.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads the child’s rescue as a picture of God’s dealings with Israel before its later unfaithfulness. Wesley connects the early stages with God calling Abraham and with Israel’s helpless condition in Egypt.

The Cambridge commentary on verse 3 sees several references coming together: Jerusalem’s Canaanite beginnings, Israel’s beginnings in Canaan and the conduct the prophet condemns. The emphasis is dependence on God’s compassion rather than a claim to inherent greatness.
passages.god_plan_html:
Titus 3:3–8 describes people once enslaved to desires being saved when God’s kindness and love appear. Their rescue rests on His mercy, through new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit, rather than righteous deeds they had already performed.

Titus does not explicitly interpret Ezekiel’s abandoned child. The shared theme is life received through God’s merciful initiative. Titus develops that theme through Jesus Christ and connects the gift of grace with hope and a renewed life devoted to good deeds.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 16:8-14
passages.section_title: Where did Jerusalem’s beauty and honor come from?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 Then I passed by and saw you, and you were indeed old enough for love. So I spread My cloak over you and covered your nakedness. I pledged Myself to you, entered into a covenant with you, and you became Mine, declares the Lord GOD. 9 Then I bathed you with water, rinsed off your blood, and anointed you with oil. 10 I clothed you in embroidered cloth and gave you sandals of fine leather. I wrapped you in fine linen and covered you with silk. 11 I adorned you with jewelry, and I put bracelets on your wrists and a chain around your neck. 12 I put a ring in your nose, earrings on your ears, and a beautiful crown upon your head. 13 So you were adorned with gold and silver, and your clothing was made of fine linen, silk, and embroidered cloth. You ate fine flour, honey, and oil. section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The story moves from rescue to covenant. The Lord spreads His cloak over the young woman, pledges Himself to her and declares that she has become His. He bathes, anoints, clothes and adorns her.

The food, garments and jewelry are gifts. She becomes beautiful, rises to be queen and gains fame among the nations, but the Lord explains the source of that splendor: He bestowed it on her.

The cloak also appears in Ruth 3:6–10, where Ruth asks Boaz to spread his garment over her because he is a kinsman-redeemer. In Ezekiel, the oath and covenant make the marriage picture explicit.

This account of generous provision prepares for the accusation that follows. Jerusalem cannot explain its later success as something achieved independently of the One who rescued and cared for it.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and the Cambridge commentary on verse 8 connect the marriage covenant with Israel’s deliverance from Egypt and covenant at Sinai. Henry’s account of the chapter likewise treats the provision and marriage as God’s generous dealings with His people.

The details build one main picture: the city’s beauty and standing were received. The Lord’s gifts called for a faithful response, rather than pride in possessions or reputation.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 5:25–32 describes Christ loving the church and giving Himself for her, cleansing her and presenting her in glory. The passage uses the marriage picture to explain Christ’s self-giving care.

This is a biblical parallel, rather than an explicit quotation of Ezekiel 16. In both pictures, the beloved’s splendor depends on what the Lord gives. Ephesians develops the theme through Christ’s sacrifice and His purpose to make His people holy, and calls husbands to nourishing, cherishing love.

passages.title: Ezekiel 16:15-22
passages.section_title: How were God’s gifts turned against Him?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 But because of your fame, you trusted in your beauty and played the harlot. You lavished your favors on everyone who passed by, and your beauty was theirs for the asking. 16 You took some of your garments and made colorful high places for yourself, and on them you prostituted yourself. Such things should not have happened; never should they have occurred! 17 You also took the fine jewelry of gold and silver I had given you, and you made male idols with which to prostitute yourself. 18 You took your embroidered garments to cover them, and you set My oil and incense before them. 19 And you set before them as a pleasing aroma the food I had given you—the fine flour, oil, and honey that I had fed you. That is what happened, declares the Lord GOD. 20 You even took the sons and daughters you bore to Me and sacrificed them as food to idols. section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The turning point is trust in the beauty and fame the Lord had given. The story now portrays Jerusalem’s unfaithfulness as prostitution: she offers herself to others instead of remaining faithful to her covenant partner.

The gifts themselves are turned to idolatry. Garments furnish high places and cover images, gold and silver become male idols, and the Lord’s oil, incense and food are offered before them.

The charge then becomes still more severe. Sons and daughters are sacrificed to idols. The Lord calls them His children and describes their deaths as slaughter.

The passage closes by returning to the beginning: Jerusalem has forgotten the days when she lay helpless in her own blood. Forgetting received mercy accompanies the misuse of the gifts that followed it.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads the chapter’s marriage story as an accusation of idolatry. Wesley likewise explains the prostitution as spiritual unfaithfulness and the images as rivals receiving what belonged to the Lord.

The USCCB notes on verse 16 point out how the story moves between the picture of prostitution and the reality of idol worship. The point is the betrayal of the covenant and the harm done with gifts entrusted to Jerusalem. The killing of children is part of the accusation itself, not merely a way of describing a private change of religious opinion.

passages.title: Ezekiel 16:23-34
passages.section_title: Why does Jerusalem pay the very lovers it pursues?

And in addition to all your other wickedness, 24 you built yourself a mound and made yourself a lofty shrine in every public square. 25 At the head of every street you built your lofty shrines and degraded your beauty. With increasing promiscuity, you spread your legs to all who passed by. 26 You prostituted yourself with your lustful neighbors, the Egyptians, and increased your promiscuity to provoke Me to anger. 27 Therefore I stretched out My hand against you and reduced your portion. section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The accusation spreads through the city’s public spaces and outward to Egypt, Assyria and Chaldea. Jerusalem keeps pursuing other partners and remains unsatisfied.

The Lord has already acted against this conduct by reducing Jerusalem’s portion and handing her over to those who hate her. Even the Philistine cities, pictured as daughters, are said to be ashamed of her behavior.

The final comparison exposes how costly and self-defeating the pursuit has become. Instead of receiving gifts from lovers, Jerusalem gives gifts and bribes them to come.

The marriage picture makes the broken loyalty personal. The Lord has provided abundantly, but Jerusalem spends what it has received to secure relationships that displace Him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley emphasizes the wasting of wealth and honor on the very relationships that corrupt Jerusalem’s worship. The Cambridge discussion of the chapter also connects the foreign partners with the influence of surrounding powers and their gods.

The repeated lack of satisfaction is central to the accusation. More partners and greater expense do not repair the estrangement from the Lord. The gifts that should have expressed gratitude are spent sustaining unfaithfulness.
passages.god_plan_html:
James 4:1–10 also uses marital unfaithfulness to describe divided loyalty toward God. James joins that warning with quarrels, coveting and requests driven by the desire to spend on pleasures.

The passage then calls for a return: submit to God, draw near to Him, cleanse hands and purify divided hearts. God opposes pride and gives grace to the humble.

James does not explicitly quote Ezekiel 16. The parallel develops the same concern beyond Jerusalem’s foreign relationships: desires that pull people away from God bring conflict, while His grace calls them back to wholehearted faithfulness.

passages.title: Ezekiel 16:35-43
passages.section_title: What happens when Jerusalem’s lovers turn against it?

I will gather them against you from all around and expose you before them, and they will see you completely naked. 38 And I will sentence you to the punishment of women who commit adultery and those who shed blood; so I will bring upon you the wrath of your bloodshed and jealousy. 39 Then I will deliver you into the hands of your lovers, and they will level your mounds and tear down your lofty shrines. section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord announces judgment for the idolatry and bloodshed just described. The lovers Jerusalem pursued will be gathered against her, and the wealth, clothing and ornaments she received will be taken away.

The marriage story now depicts the city’s defeat through exposure, violence and burning houses. The shrines are torn down, and the city that used its gifts to buy other partners is left bare.

The reason is again tied to memory: Jerusalem has forgotten its helpless beginnings and the Lord’s care. He declares that its own deeds will return upon its head.

The warning concerns the destruction of the city and the end of the practices described. It continues the explanation of why covenant membership has not placed Jerusalem beyond judgment.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry understands the surrounding nations, including those Jerusalem had trusted, as the means of its punishment. The USCCB notes on verse 38 connect the marriage language with the charge of idolatry, while Wesley emphasizes the response to bloodshed and provoked jealousy.

The reversal is the force of the scene: the sought-after partners become attackers, the gifts are stripped away, and public confidence becomes public shame. The Lord’s judgment exposes the failure of the relationships in which Jerusalem placed its trust.
passages.god_plan_html:
Revelation 17:15–18 presents a related judgment picture. The beast and horns turn against the prostitute, leaving her desolate and naked and burning her with fire. The passage states that God is bringing His purpose to completion.

This is a close biblical parallel, rather than a statement that the two cities or every detail are identical. Both scenes show corrupt relationships turning against the city that relied on them. Revelation places the overthrow of such power within the fulfillment of God’s word.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 16:44-52
passages.section_title: Why does Jerusalem make Samaria and Sodom look righteous?

versions.label: BSB

For they appear more righteous than you, because your sins were more vile than theirs. So you too must bear your shame and disgrace, since you have made your sisters appear righteous.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord returns to the family comparison: Jerusalem resembles its mother and sisters in conduct. Samaria is pictured as the older sister to the north, Sodom as the younger to the south, and their surrounding communities as daughters.

The comparison then becomes sharper. Jerusalem has not merely repeated their wrongdoing; its conduct has gone beyond theirs.

Sodom’s arrogance, abundance, complacency and failure to help the poor and needy are named, along with its abominations. Its prosperity supplied no excuse for its neglect of others or its pride.

Jerusalem’s conduct is so much worse that its sisters appear righteous by comparison. That is an accusation against Jerusalem, not a declaration that their own wrongdoing was acceptable. The city must bear the shame it had been ready to place on others.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley explains that the comparison does not make the sisters truly righteous; it shows them to be less guilty than Jerusalem. The USCCB notes on verses 46–47 likewise emphasize how the city’s worse conduct makes the others appear just.

The passage confronts religious superiority that ignores one’s own actions. Jerusalem cannot treat other communities’ failures as a reason to excuse its own, and the named neglect of the needy makes the accusation concrete.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Matthew 11:20–24, Jesus also compares cities facing judgment with Sodom. He warns Capernaum and the other cities because they have seen His mighty works and have not repented.

Matthew does not explicitly quote Ezekiel 16. The shared theme is accountability in light of what has been received. Jesus’ warning brings that responsibility to the response people make to Him: extraordinary opportunity is a reason to turn, rather than a shield against judgment.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 16:53-59
passages.section_title: What does the promise concerning Jerusalem’s sisters mean?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 53 But I will restore Sodom and her daughters from captivity, as well as Samaria and her daughters. And I will restore you along with them. 54 So you will bear your disgrace and be ashamed of all you did to comfort them. 55 And your sisters, Sodom with her daughters and Samaria with her daughters, will return to their former state. You and your daughters will also return to your former state. 56 Did you not treat your sister Sodom as an object of scorn in the day of your pride, 57 before your wickedness was uncovered? Even so, you are now scorned by the daughters of Edom and all those around her, and by the daughters of the Philistines—all those around you who despise you. 58 You will bear the consequences of your lewdness and your abominations, declares the LORD. 59 For this is what the Lord GOD says: I will deal with you according to your deeds, since you have despised the oath by breaking the covenant.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
In the BSB, the Lord promises restoration from captivity for Sodom and its daughters, Samaria and its daughters, and Jerusalem along with them. Jerusalem is not allowed to imagine a future that confirms its former contempt for its neighbors.

The prospect brings shame rather than renewed boasting. The city once treated Sodom as an object of scorn, but its own wrongdoing has now been exposed and surrounding peoples scorn it.

The passage still holds Jerusalem responsible for its conduct. The Lord will deal with the city according to its deeds, because it has despised the oath and broken the covenant.

This prepares for the final promise: the answer to Jerusalem’s failure must come from the Lord’s own covenant faithfulness and provision for its guilt.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The restoration language has been read in different ways. Wesley, working with conditional wording in his translation, understands the comparison as saying that Jerusalem will not regain its former worldly standing any sooner than Sodom and Samaria regain theirs.

The Cambridge commentary on verses 53 and 55 instead reads an actual promise of restoration, as the BSB does. It understands the future as reaching the sister cities alongside Jerusalem, overturning the city’s assumed superiority.

The immediate verses do not describe the mechanism, date or individual eternal destiny of everyone associated with those cities. Their place in the story is to humble Jerusalem and place its own future alongside the very communities it had despised.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 16:60-63
passages.section_title: How can the story end with an everlasting covenant?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 60 But I will remember the covenant I made with you in the days of your youth, and I will establish an everlasting covenant with you. 61 Then you will remember your ways and be ashamed when you receive your older and younger sisters. I will give them to you as daughters, but not because of My covenant with you. 62 So I will establish My covenant with you, and you will know that I am the LORD, 63 so that when I make atonement for all you have done, you will remember and be ashamed and never again open your mouth because of your disgrace, declares the Lord GOD.”
paragraphs: 60 But I will remember the covenant I made with you in the days of your youth, and I will establish an everlasting covenant with you. 61 Then you will remember your ways and be ashamed when you receive your older and younger sisters. I will give them to you as daughters, but not because of My covenant with you. 62 So I will establish My covenant with you, and you will know that I am the LORD, 63 so that when I make atonement for all you have done, you will remember and be ashamed and never again open your mouth because of your disgrace, declares the Lord GOD.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord’s final word turns from Jerusalem’s broken covenant to His own promise. He will remember the covenant made in its youth and establish an everlasting covenant.

Jerusalem will receive its older and younger sisters as daughters, but this will not be something its broken covenant has earned. The Lord Himself will establish the relationship, and the people will know Him.

The ending joins mercy with a changed response. When the Lord makes atonement for all Jerusalem has done, the city remembers, is ashamed and no longer answers with self-justification.

The long story therefore ends with God dealing with the guilt that Jerusalem could not remove. Its future rests on His act of mercy, which leaves no room for the pride that drove its unfaithfulness.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry sees the promise partly fulfilled in the return from Babylon and more fully in the gospel. Wesley traces the covenant promise through Abraham and its renewal after Egypt, then connects the sisters becoming daughters with Gentiles entering the community of God’s people.

The USCCB note on verse 60 emphasizes renewal of the Sinai covenant in a new, Spirit-empowered way. The Cambridge commentary connects the lasting covenant with forgiveness, God’s law within His people and the new heart promised elsewhere in Ezekiel.

These readings emphasize different aspects of the covenant’s continuity and fulfillment. They agree that the ending depends on God’s promised mercy and a renewed relationship with Him, rather than Jerusalem’s past conduct earning its restoration.
passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 8:6–13 identifies Jesus as the mediator of a better covenant and quotes Jeremiah’s promise of God’s law written within His people, their knowing Him and the forgiveness of their sins.

Hebrews 10:10–18 connects that forgiveness with Jesus’ once-for-all offering. After quoting the covenant promise, it explains that where sins are forgiven, another offering for them is no longer needed.

Hebrews is quoting Jeremiah rather than Ezekiel 16. Yet it explains the larger covenant hope found here: God supplies forgiveness through Christ and forms a people who know Him. Mercy answers the guilt exposed by the story and calls forth humility in those who receive it.

passages.title: Ezekiel 17:1-10
passages.section_title: Why does the well-watered vine reach toward another eagle?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 2 “Son of man, pose a riddle; speak a parable to the house of Israel 3 and tell them that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘A great eagle with great wings and long pinions, full of feathers of many colors, came to Lebanon and took away the top of the cedar. 4 He plucked off its topmost shoot, carried it to the land of merchants, and planted it in a city of traders. 5 He took some of the seed of the land and planted it in fertile soil; he placed it by abundant waters and set it out like a willow. 6 It sprouted and became a spreading vine, low in height, with branches turned toward him; yet its roots remained where it stood. So it became a vine and yielded branches and sent out shoots. 7 But there was another great eagle with great wings and many feathers. And behold, this vine bent its roots toward him. It stretched out its branches to him from its planting bed, so that he might water it. 8 It had been planted in good soil by abundant waters in order to yield branches and bear fruit and become a splendid vine.’ 9 So you are to tell them that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Will it flourish? Will it not be uprooted and stripped of its fruit so that it shrivels? All its foliage will wither! It will not take a strong arm or many people to pull it up by its roots. 10 Even if it is transplanted, will it flourish? Will it not completely wither when the east wind strikes? It will wither on the bed where it sprouted.’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord tells Ezekiel to present a riddle and a parable. A great eagle takes the top of a cedar from Lebanon to a city of traders, then plants seed from the land beside abundant water.

The seed becomes a low, spreading vine with its branches turned toward the eagle. It has good soil and enough water to grow and bear fruit.

A second eagle appears, and the vine turns its roots and branches toward this newcomer for water. The story stresses that it was already well provided for where it had been planted.

The Lord asks whether it will flourish. The answer is a warning of uprooting and withering, including the effect of an east wind. The next passage supplies the explanation of the eagles, planting and attempted change of allegiance.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads the eagles as conquering powers whose actions remain under God’s rule. Wesley identifies the first as Nebuchadnezzar and the second as Egypt’s king, following the explanation given later in the chapter.

Both understand the vine’s turning as a misplaced search for security. The issue is not a shortage of provision where it had been planted, but the attempt to gain a different protector through a change of allegiance. The story’s interpretation comes from the Lord’s explanation, rather than requiring a fixed code for every eagle or tree elsewhere in Scripture.

passages.title: Ezekiel 17:11-21
passages.section_title: Why is the king’s broken oath also an offense against God?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 12 “Now say to this rebellious house: ‘Do you not know what these things mean?’ Tell them, ‘Behold, the king of Babylon came to Jerusalem, carried off its king and officials, and brought them back with him to Babylon. 13 He took a member of the royal family and made a covenant with him, putting him under oath. Then he carried away the leading men of the land, 14 so that the kingdom would be brought low, unable to lift itself up, surviving only by keeping his covenant. 15 But this king rebelled against Babylon by sending his envoys to Egypt to ask for horses and a large army. Will he flourish? Will the one who does such things escape? Can he break a covenant and yet escape?’ 16 ‘As surely as I live,’ declares the Lord GOD, ‘he will die in Babylon, in the land of the king who enthroned him, whose oath he despised and whose covenant he broke. 17 Pharaoh with his mighty army and vast horde will not help him in battle, when ramps are built and siege walls constructed to destroy many lives. 18 He despised the oath by breaking the covenant. Seeing that he gave his hand in pledge yet did all these things, he will not escape!’ 19 Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘As surely as I live, I will bring down upon his head My oath that he despised and My covenant that he broke. 20 I will spread My net over him and catch him in My snare. I will bring him to Babylon and execute judgment upon him there for the treason he committed against Me. 21 All his choice troops will fall by the sword, and those who survive will be scattered to every wind. Then you will know that I, the LORD, have spoken.’

Seeing that he gave his hand in pledge yet did all these things, he will not escape!’

I will bring him to Babylon and execute judgment upon him there for the treason he committed against Me. 21 All his choice troops will fall by the sword, and those who survive will be scattered to every wind. Then you will know that I, the LORD, have spoken.’

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord explains the story. Babylon’s king took Jerusalem’s king and officials away, then installed another member of the royal family under an oath. The reduced kingdom could continue by keeping that covenant.

Second Kings 24:10–20 identifies the kings: Jehoiachin was taken to Babylon, and his uncle Mattaniah was made king in his place and renamed Zedekiah.

Zedekiah sought horses and troops from Egypt in rebellion against Babylon. Ezekiel declares that Pharaoh will not deliver him and that he will die in the land of the king who placed him on the throne. Jeremiah 37:4–11 likewise warns that Egypt’s intervention will not prevent Jerusalem’s capture.

The Lord calls the despised oath His own and describes the king’s conduct as treason against Him. Second Chronicles 36:11–14 explains that Nebuchadnezzar had made Zedekiah swear by God. The broken pledge is therefore more than a failed political maneuver: the king has treated an oath made before the Lord as disposable.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry emphasizes that faithfulness is owed even to someone outside one’s own religion. Invoking God as witness while dealing treacherously makes the offense more serious. Wesley similarly reads the judgment as the consequence of perjury and the failure of the hoped-for escape.

The chapter holds the present king responsible for his own choices. Whatever earlier generations did, his own broken oath and refusal of the Lord’s warning give no basis for claiming innocence.
passages.god_plan_html:
Matthew 5:33–37 addresses oaths and calls Jesus’ hearers to truthful speech: their yes and no should be dependable. James 5:12 repeats that instruction and connects it with avoiding judgment.

These passages do not directly interpret Zedekiah’s treaty or settle every later question about formal oaths. They develop the larger concern that words spoken before God cannot be used to disguise an intention to act otherwise. Following Christ includes integrity in ordinary speech as well as in public commitments.

passages.title: Ezekiel 17:22-24
passages.section_title: What will God plant after the royal vine fails?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 This is what the Lord GOD says: ‘I will take a shoot from the lofty top of the cedar, and I will set it out. I will pluck a tender sprig from its topmost shoots, and I will plant it on a high and lofty mountain. 23 I will plant it on the mountain heights of Israel so that it will bear branches; it will yield fruit and become a majestic cedar. Birds of every kind will nest under it, taking shelter in the shade of its branches. 24 Then all the trees of the field will know that I am the LORD. I bring the tall tree down and make the low tree tall. I dry up the green tree and make the withered tree flourish. I, the LORD, have spoken, and I have done it.’”
paragraphs: 22 This is what the Lord GOD says: ‘I will take a shoot from the lofty top of the cedar, and I will set it out. I will pluck a tender sprig from its topmost shoots, and I will plant it on a high and lofty mountain. 23 I will plant it on the mountain heights of Israel so that it will bear branches; it will yield fruit and become a majestic cedar. Birds of every kind will nest under it, taking shelter in the shade of its branches. 24 Then all the trees of the field will know that I am the LORD. I bring the tall tree down and make the low tree tall. I dry up the green tree and make the withered tree flourish. I, the LORD, have spoken, and I have done it.’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord returns to the cedar picture with a promise. This time He Himself takes a tender shoot from its top and plants it on a high mountain in Israel.

The shoot becomes a majestic cedar, bearing branches and fruit, with birds of every kind sheltering beneath it. The failed attempt to secure the kingdom through another eagle is followed by something the Lord establishes Himself.

All the trees will know that He is the Lord. He brings down the tall, raises the low, dries the green and makes the withered flourish. The promise rests on His declared purpose and His power to carry it out.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley read the tender royal shoot as the Messiah. Henry identifies Him as Jesus, David’s Son, whose kingdom is established despite what appears small or contemptible at first.

Wesley connects the sheltering birds with the nations finding peace under that rule. Both place the hope beyond Zedekiah’s failed leadership: the Lord Himself supplies the ruler and kingdom in which His purpose succeeds.
passages.god_plan_html:
Luke 1:30–33 announces that Jesus will receive David’s throne and reign over the house of Jacob forever. His kingdom will have no end. That promise explains the larger royal hope to which Christian readers connect Ezekiel’s planted shoot.

Mark 4:30–34 gives a close picture of kingdom growth: a small mustard seed becomes a great plant with branches where birds nest in the shade.

Mark does not explicitly quote Ezekiel, and mustard and cedar are different plants. The meaningful parallel is the sheltering kingdom brought from a small beginning. Together, the passages direct hope toward God’s action through Jesus, rather than a ruler’s attempt to manufacture security through a broken pledge.

passages.title: Ezekiel 18:1-9
passages.section_title: Is this generation being judged for someone else’s sins?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 2 “What do you people mean by quoting this proverb about the land of Israel: ‘The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the teeth of the children are set on edge’? 3 As surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, you will no longer quote this proverb in Israel. 4 Behold, every soul belongs to Me; both father and son are Mine. The soul who sins is the one who will die. 5 Now suppose a man is righteous and does what is just and right: 6 He does not eat at the mountain or look to the idols of the house of Israel. He does not defile his neighbor’s wife or approach a woman during her period. 7 He does not oppress another, but restores the pledge to the debtor. He does not commit robbery, but gives his bread to the hungry and covers the naked with clothing. 8 He does not engage in usury or take excess interest, but he withholds his hand from iniquity and executes true justice between men. 9 He follows My statutes and faithfully keeps My ordinances. That man is righteous; surely he will live, declares the Lord GOD.

The soul who sins is the one who will die.

5 Now suppose a man is righteous and does what is just and right: 6 He does not eat at the mountain or look to the idols of the house of Israel. He does not defile his neighbor’s wife or approach a woman during her period. 7 He does not oppress another, but restores the pledge to the debtor. He does not commit robbery, but gives his bread to the hungry and covers the naked with clothing. 8 He does not engage in usury or take excess interest, but he withholds his hand from iniquity and executes true justice between men. 9 He follows My statutes and faithfully keeps My ordinances. That man is righteous; surely he will live, declares the Lord GOD.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord confronts a proverb about fathers eating sour grapes and their children feeling the effect in their teeth. The people use it to describe their complaint: an earlier generation sinned, but they are bearing the punishment.

He answers that father and son alike belong to Him. The person who sins is the one accountable for that sin. The complaint cannot be used to avoid looking at the present generation’s own conduct.

The Lord then describes a righteous person in concrete terms. He refuses idolatry and sexual wrongdoing, does not oppress or rob, returns what a debtor has pledged, gives food and clothing to those in need, and practices justice.

This is faithfulness lived out toward both God and neighbor. The warning and promise concern how the person actually responds to the Lord, rather than the reputation of the family from which he comes.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The USCCB notes understand the proverb as a complaint about punishment for ancestors’ sins and read the chapter as an insistence on personal responsibility. Wesley likewise emphasizes that God is equally God of father and son and judges without favoritism.

Readers differ over the full reach of the life-and-death language. Gill’s discussion of verse 9 favors preservation from the immediate calamities, though he also discusses spiritual life. Henry applies the warning beyond outward suffering to final accountability before God. Both retain the chapter’s refusal to substitute family standing for a person’s own response.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 2:1–11 warns people who condemn others while practicing the same wrongs. Paul says that God’s judgment rests on truth and shows no favoritism, and that His kindness is meant to lead to repentance.

Paul is not explicitly quoting Ezekiel 18. He develops the larger theme of personal accountability: neither condemning someone else nor relying on one’s standing removes the need to respond honestly to God. His patience offers an opportunity to turn, rather than permission to continue.

passages.title: Ezekiel 18:10-20
passages.section_title: Can a child break a family’s pattern of wrongdoing?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 Now suppose that man has a violent son, who sheds blood or does any of these things, 11 though the father has done none of them: Indeed, the son eats at the mountain and defiles his neighbor’s wife. 12 He oppresses the poor and needy; he commits robbery and does not restore a pledge. He lifts his eyes to idols; he commits abominations. 13 He engages in usury and takes excess interest. Will this son live? He will not! Since he has committed all these abominations, he will surely die; his blood will be on his own head. 14 Now suppose this son has a son who sees all the sins his father has committed, considers them, and does not do likewise: 15 He does not eat at the mountain or look to the idols of the house of Israel. He does not defile his neighbor’s wife. 16 He does not oppress another, or retain a pledge, or commit robbery. He gives his bread to the hungry and covers the naked with clothing. 17 He withholds his hand from harming the poor and takes no interest or usury. He keeps My ordinances and follows My statutes. Such a man will not die for his father’s iniquity. He will surely live. 18 As for his father, he will die for his own iniquity, because he practiced extortion, robbed his brother, and did what was wrong among his people. 19 Yet you may ask, ‘Why shouldn’t the son bear the iniquity of his father?’ Since the son has done what is just and right, carefully observing all My statutes, he will surely live. 20 The soul who sins is the one who will die. A son will not bear the iniquity of his father, and a father will not bear the iniquity of his son. The righteousness of the righteous man will fall upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked man will fall upon him.

The righteousness of the righteous man will fall upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked man will fall upon him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord considers the righteous man’s son, who chooses a violent and oppressive life. His father’s faithfulness does not make his bloodshed, idolatry and abuse of the poor harmless. He answers for his own actions.

Then comes a third generation. This son sees the wrongdoing of his father, considers it and refuses to follow it. He practices justice and supplies the needs of others. He will not die for his father’s iniquity.

The contrast works in both directions. A righteous parent does not excuse a wicked child, and a wicked parent does not make a child’s faithfulness impossible or meaningless.

The closing statement names the principle again: the righteousness of the righteous belongs to that person, as does the wickedness of the wicked. Each generation is addressed as responsible before God.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley read the examples as a denial that a person’s judgment can simply be transferred to another generation. Henry explains that a faithful son need not share his father’s final fate even when he experiences outward troubles in the same world.

The passage gives real weight to a different choice: the third-generation son sees what happened before him and does otherwise. It does not say that family influence is unreal or that wrongdoing never harms other people; its point is that another person’s conduct does not replace one’s own responsibility to God.

passages.title: Ezekiel 18:21-29
passages.section_title: Does turning back still matter after years of wrongdoing?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 But if the wicked man turns from all the sins he has committed, keeps all My statutes, and does what is just and right, he will surely live; he will not die. 22 None of the transgressions he has committed will be held against him. Because of the righteousness he has practiced, he will live. 23 Do I take any pleasure in the death of the wicked? declares the Lord GOD. Wouldn’t I prefer that he turn from his ways and live? 24 But if a righteous man turns from his righteousness and practices iniquity, committing the same abominations as the wicked, will he live? None of the righteous acts he did will be remembered. Because of the unfaithfulness and sin he has committed, he will die. 25 Yet you say, ‘The way of the Lord is not just.’ Hear now, O house of Israel: Is it My way that is unjust? Is it not your ways that are unjust? 26 If a righteous man turns from his righteousness and practices iniquity, he will die for this. He will die because of the iniquity he has committed. 27 But if a wicked man turns from the wickedness he has committed and does what is just and right, he will save his life. 28 Because he considered and turned from all the transgressions he had committed, he will surely live; he will not die. 29 Yet the house of Israel says, ‘The way of the Lord is not just.’ Are My ways unjust, O house of Israel? Is it not your ways that are unjust?

Is it not your ways that are unjust?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord now considers change within a person’s own life. If a wicked person turns from sin and practices justice, the earlier transgressions will not be held against him. The Lord asks whether He delights in the wicked person’s death, rather than that person turning and living.

The warning also runs the other way. Earlier righteous conduct is no shield for someone who turns to the same abominations as the wicked. The person cannot rely on a former way of life while choosing its opposite.

The people call the Lord’s way unjust. He answers by repeating both examples: the person who turns to wrongdoing answers for it, and the person who considers and turns away from wrongdoing will live.

The call therefore refuses both despair and presumption. A sinful past does not make repentance pointless, and a good past does not make present unfaithfulness safe.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Gill reads the person who abandons righteousness as someone outwardly righteous in human judgment, rather than someone who loses a true saving relationship with Christ. Henry also distinguishes appearing righteous for a time from the faith that continues to the end. These are their explanations of the warning, not words the passage itself adds to its description.

Christians’ wider teachings differ here. The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 17, and the 1689 Baptist Confession, chapter 17, teach that those God truly calls and sanctifies will be preserved to the end. They also teach that serious sin can bring grave harm and discipline.

The Catholic Church teaches that grave sin committed with full knowledge and deliberate consent can result in loss of the state of grace, and calls for repentance and God’s forgiveness; see the Catechism, paragraphs 1857–1861. Methodist Article XII teaches that people may depart from grace after receiving the Holy Spirit and may rise again through God’s grace and repentance.

These documents state broader beliefs about grace and falling away, rather than giving official commentary on every verse of Ezekiel. Across these different explanations, the passage’s demand remains urgent: turn from wrongdoing instead of treating either one’s past sins or past goodness as a reason not to respond.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Luke 15:11–24, Jesus tells of a son who squanders what he received, comes to his senses and returns to his father. The father receives him with compassion and celebrates the return of the one who was lost.

This is a parallel in the call to return and the welcome of mercy, rather than an explicit interpretation of Ezekiel 18. It shows why repentance need not be treated as hopeless: the invitation to turn belongs within God’s purpose to restore people to life with Him.

passages.title: Ezekiel 18:30-32
passages.section_title: Why does God end the warning with an invitation to live?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 30 Therefore, O house of Israel, I will judge you, each according to his ways, declares the Lord GOD. Repent and turn from all your transgressions, so that your iniquity will not become your downfall. 31 Cast away from yourselves all the transgressions you have committed, and fashion for yourselves a new heart and a new spirit. Why should you die, O house of Israel? 32 For I take no pleasure in anyone’s death, declares the Lord GOD. So repent and live!
paragraphs: 30 Therefore, O house of Israel, I will judge you, each according to his ways, declares the Lord GOD. Repent and turn from all your transgressions, so that your iniquity will not become your downfall. 31 Cast away from yourselves all the transgressions you have committed, and fashion for yourselves a new heart and a new spirit. Why should you die, O house of Israel? 32 For I take no pleasure in anyone’s death, declares the Lord GOD. So repent and live!

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord brings the chapter’s examples into a direct appeal. He will judge each person according to that person’s ways, so the people must turn away from their transgressions before iniquity becomes their downfall.

They are called to cast away their offenses and have a new heart and spirit. The final question asks why Israel should die, and the Lord declares that He takes no pleasure in anyone’s death.

The warning serves the invitation: repent and live. They receive an urgent invitation to respond, rather than being left with the claim that their ancestors or past actions have made the future meaningless.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry understands the appeal as a call to use the means God provides and seek from Him the inward change that is needed. Wesley likewise explains the new-heart command as allowing God to do His work within the people.

Gill also notes that the Lord elsewhere promises to give the new heart. He reads the immediate warning in terms of the calamity facing Israel and stresses sincere repentance. These readings connect the required response with God’s provision, rather than imagining that a new heart is created by an outward performance alone.
passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 3:7–14 takes up the danger of a hardened heart and calls believers to encourage one another today, so that sin’s deception does not draw them away from the living God.

Second Peter 3:8–14 explains God’s patience in relation to repentance and the promised new creation. The time before judgment is an opportunity to turn and live faithfully as His people look toward a world where righteousness dwells.

Neither passage explicitly quotes Ezekiel 18. Together they develop the larger purpose behind its invitation: God’s warning calls for a present response, and His patience gives room for repentance rather than making sin harmless.

passages.title: Ezekiel 19:1-9
passages.section_title: Why does Ezekiel sing a lament for the royal lions?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 “As for you, take up a lament for the princes of Israel 2 and say: ‘What was your mother? A lioness among the lions! She lay down among the young lions; she reared her cubs. 3 She brought up one of her cubs, and he became a young lion. After learning to tear his prey, he devoured men. 4 When the nations heard of him, he was trapped in their pit. With hooks they led him away to the land of Egypt. 5 When she saw that she had waited in vain, that her hope was lost, she took another of her cubs and made him a young lion. 6 He prowled among the lions, and became a young lion. After learning to tear his prey, he devoured men. 7 He broke down their strongholds and devastated their cities. The land and everything in it shuddered at the sound of his roaring. 8 Then the nations set out against him from the provinces on every side. They spread their net over him; he was trapped in their pit. 9 With hooks they caged him and brought him to the king of Babylon. They brought him into captivity so that his roar was heard no longer on the mountains of Israel.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Ezekiel is told to take up a lament for Israel’s princes. The royal family is pictured as a lioness raising cubs. One grows into a lion that devours people, until the nations trap it and take it to Egypt.

The lioness raises another cub after her hope for the first is lost. This one also becomes destructive, terrifying the land and its cities. The nations trap it and bring it to Babylon, where its roar will no longer be heard on Israel’s mountains.

The first removal corresponds to Jehoahaz’s fate in Second Kings 23:31–37: Pharaoh Neco deposes him and takes him to Egypt. The later kings’ removals by Babylon are recorded in Second Chronicles 36:1–10.

The poem turns the image of royal strength into a song of loss. The rulers who seemed able to dominate others cannot prevent their own capture.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry understands the lions as Judah’s kings, emphasizing their cruelty and oppression. Wesley identifies the first cub as Jehoahaz and the next as Jehoiakim.

The second cub’s identity is read differently. The USCCB notes report a reading that identifies the two as Jehoahaz and Zedekiah, sons of the same mother. The Cambridge commentary on verse 5 identifies him as Jehoiachin, whose removal to Babylon is recorded in Second Chronicles 36:9–10.

The poem does not supply the second king’s name. Its main force is the downfall of destructive royal power: the nation cannot assume that another ruler of the same kind will rescue it from the judgment being announced.

passages.title: Ezekiel 19:10-14
passages.section_title: What does the ruined vine say about Judah’s kings?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 Your mother was like a vine in your vineyard, planted by the water; it was fruitful and full of branches because of the abundant waters. 11 It had strong branches, fit for a ruler’s scepter. It towered high above the thick branches, conspicuous for its height and for its dense foliage. 12 But it was uprooted in fury, cast down to the ground, and the east wind dried up its fruit. Its strong branches were stripped off and they withered; the fire consumed them. 13 Now it is planted in the wilderness, in a dry and thirsty land. 14 Fire has gone out from its main branch and devoured its fruit; on it no strong branch remains fit for a ruler’s scepter.’ This is a lament and shall be used as a lament.”
paragraphs: 10 Your mother was like a vine in your vineyard, planted by the water; it was fruitful and full of branches because of the abundant waters. 11 It had strong branches, fit for a ruler’s scepter. It towered high above the thick branches, conspicuous for its height and for its dense foliage. 12 But it was uprooted in fury, cast down to the ground, and the east wind dried up its fruit. Its strong branches were stripped off and they withered; the fire consumed them. 13 Now it is planted in the wilderness, in a dry and thirsty land. 14 Fire has gone out from its main branch and devoured its fruit; on it no strong branch remains fit for a ruler’s scepter.’ This is a lament and shall be used as a lament.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The second part of the lament changes the picture from lions to a vine. It was planted beside water, flourished and produced strong branches fit for a ruler’s scepter.

The vine is then uprooted in fury. An east wind dries its fruit, its strong branches wither and fire consumes them. It is left in a dry wilderness instead of its former well-watered place.

The final fire comes from one of its own branches and devours its fruit. No strong branch remains to serve as a ruler’s scepter. The poem ends by insisting that this is a lament and will be used as one.

The loss concerns both the people and the royal rule that had seemed to give them strength. The poem gives the collapse its proper weight instead of offering another easy assurance that the dynasty will recover by its own power.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The USCCB notes identify the vine as Judah and its strong branch as the Davidic king. They read the poem as a lament over the dynasty’s deportation and destruction. Wesley connects the destructive fire from within with Zedekiah’s rebellion.

Henry also sees the nation’s own wickedness feeding its ruin, then points beyond the lament toward Christ as the true and living vine. That Christian connection supplies hope from the larger biblical story, while the immediate poem ends in mourning.
passages.god_plan_html:
Luke 1:30–33 announces a lasting answer to the loss of Davidic rule: Jesus will receive David’s throne, reign over the house of Jacob forever and have a kingdom without end.

Luke does not explicitly interpret Ezekiel 19. The larger connection keeps the lament and promise in their proper places: the failure of Judah’s kings is real, while God’s royal purpose is fulfilled through the Son He gives. Hope rests on His promise, rather than the strength the ruined dynasty once displayed.

passages.title: Ezekiel 20:1-9
passages.section_title: Why does God answer the elders with their people’s history?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 In the seventh year, on the tenth day of the fifth month, some of the elders of Israel came to inquire of the LORD, and they sat down before me. 2 Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 3 “Son of man, speak to the elders of Israel and tell them that this is what the Lord GOD says: Have you come to inquire of Me? As surely as I live, I will not be consulted by you, declares the Lord GOD. 4 Will you judge them, will you judge them, son of man? Confront them with the abominations of their fathers 5 and tell them that this is what the Lord GOD says: On the day I chose Israel, I swore an oath to the descendants of the house of Jacob and made Myself known to them in the land of Egypt. With an uplifted hand I said to them, ‘I am the LORD your God.’ 6 On that day I swore to bring them out of the land of Egypt into a land that I had searched out for them, a land flowing with milk and honey, the glory of all lands. 7 And I said to them: ‘Each of you must throw away the abominations before his eyes, and you must not defile yourselves with the idols of Egypt. I am the LORD your God.’ 8 But they rebelled against Me and refused to listen. None of them cast away the abominations before their eyes, and they did not forsake the idols of Egypt. So I resolved to pour out My wrath upon them and vent My anger against them in the land of Egypt. 9 But I acted for the sake of My name, that it should not be profaned in the eyes of the nations among whom they were living, in whose sight I had revealed Myself to Israel by bringing them out of the land of Egypt.
