section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
In the seventh year, some elders come to consult the Lord through Ezekiel. He refuses their approach and tells the prophet to confront them with the abominations of their fathers.

The account begins in Egypt with God’s initiative. He chose Israel, made Himself known, swore to bring the people into a good land and commanded them to abandon Egypt’s idols.

Their response was rebellion. They refused to listen or put the idols away. The Lord speaks of His resolve to pour out wrath, then explains why He acted otherwise: His name must not be profaned before the nations who had seen Him make Himself known.

The history therefore begins with both unfaithfulness and mercy. The people’s refusal is real, but so is the Lord’s commitment to the name and promise by which He has revealed Himself.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley understand the elders’ approach as inconsistent with their continued rebellion. The history exposes conduct that their present generation is still repeating.

Wesley emphasizes God’s mercy and faithfulness in acting for His name. The point is not that Israel had earned deliverance, but that God remained faithful to His purpose despite its refusal to abandon idols.

passages.title: Ezekiel 20:10-17
passages.section_title: What did Israel receive in the wilderness, and how did it respond?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 So I brought them out of the land of Egypt and led them into the wilderness. 11 And I gave them My statutes and made known to them My ordinances—for the man who does these things will live by them. 12 I also gave them My Sabbaths as a sign between us, so that they would know that I am the LORD who sanctifies them. 13 Yet the house of Israel rebelled against Me in the wilderness. They did not follow My statutes and they rejected My ordinances—though the man who does these things will live by them—and they utterly profaned My Sabbaths. Then I resolved to pour out My wrath upon them and put an end to them in the wilderness. 14 But I acted for the sake of My name, so that it would not be profaned in the eyes of the nations in whose sight I had brought them out. 15 Moreover, with an uplifted hand I swore to them in the wilderness that I would not bring them into the land that I had given them—a land flowing with milk and honey, the glory of all lands— 16 because they kept rejecting My ordinances, refusing to walk in My statutes, and profaning My Sabbaths; for their hearts continually went after their idols. 17 Yet I looked on them with pity and did not destroy them or bring them to an end in the wilderness.

They did not follow My statutes and they rejected My ordinances—though the man who does these things will live by them—and they utterly profaned My Sabbaths. Then I resolved to pour out My wrath upon them and put an end to them in the wilderness.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord brought Israel out of Egypt and into the wilderness. He gave statutes and ordinances associated with life, and Sabbaths as a sign that He was the One making the people holy.

The people rejected the ordinances and profaned the Sabbaths. Their hearts continued to pursue idols, so the gifts meant to identify them with the Lord were met by refusal.

He swore that this rebellious generation would not enter the promised land. Yet He also spared the people from annihilation, acting for His name before the nations.

The account distinguishes judgment from the destruction of the whole people. Israel could neither dismiss its disobedience nor explain its continued existence as something achieved without the Lord’s pity.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry emphasizes the law and Sabbaths as gifts and privileges, followed by the consequences of rejecting them. Wesley understands the Sabbath sign as identifying Israel as God’s particular people.

Wesley also connects the exclusion with the generation that refused to trust God, while its children would enter. The passage joins the seriousness of their failure with the mercy that preserved a future for the people.
passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 4:1–11 develops the wilderness warning through the promise of entering God’s rest. Hearing the message without faith did not bring the earlier generation into that rest.

Hebrews brings together God’s rest on the seventh day, the failure in the wilderness and the continuing invitation to respond today. It says that a Sabbath rest remains for God’s people and warns against repeating the earlier disobedience.

This is a larger biblical connection, rather than an explicit quotation of Ezekiel 20. It shows why received privileges call for faith: God’s purpose is that His people enter the rest He gives, rather than merely possess signs associated with Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

passages.title: Ezekiel 20:18-26
passages.section_title: What does it mean that God gave them over to statutes that were not good?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 In the wilderness I said to their children: ‘Do not walk in the statutes of your fathers or keep their ordinances or defile yourselves with their idols. 19 I am the LORD your God; walk in My statutes, keep My ordinances, and practice them. 20 Keep My Sabbaths holy, that they may be a sign between us, so that you may know that I am the LORD your God.’ 21 But the children rebelled against Me. They did not walk in My statutes or carefully observe My ordinances—though the man who does these things will live by them—and they profaned My Sabbaths. So I resolved to pour out My wrath upon them and vent My anger against them in the wilderness. 22 But I withheld My hand and acted for the sake of My name, so that it would not be profaned in the eyes of the nations in whose sight I had brought them out. 23 However, with an uplifted hand I swore to them in the wilderness that I would scatter them among the nations and disperse them throughout the lands. 24 For they did not practice My ordinances, but they rejected My statutes and profaned My Sabbaths, fixing their eyes on the idols of their fathers. 25 I also gave them over to statutes that were not good and ordinances by which they could not live. 26 And I pronounced them unclean through their gifts—the sacrifice of every firstborn in the fire—so that I might devastate them, in order that they would know that I am the LORD.
paragraphs: 18 In the wilderness I said to their children: ‘Do not walk in the statutes of your fathers or keep their ordinances or defile yourselves with their idols. 19 I am the LORD your God; walk in My statutes, keep My ordinances, and practice them. 20 Keep My Sabbaths holy, that they may be a sign between us, so that you may know that I am the LORD your God.’ 21 But the children rebelled against Me. They did not walk in My statutes or carefully observe My ordinances—though the man who does these things will live by them—and they profaned My Sabbaths. So I resolved to pour out My wrath upon them and vent My anger against them in the wilderness. 22 But I withheld My hand and acted for the sake of My name, so that it would not be profaned in the eyes of the nations in whose sight I had brought them out.

23 However, with an uplifted hand I swore to them in the wilderness that I would scatter them among the nations and disperse them throughout the lands. 24 For they did not practice My ordinances, but they rejected My statutes and profaned My Sabbaths, fixing their eyes on the idols of their fathers. 25 I also gave them over to statutes that were not good and ordinances by which they could not live. 26 And I pronounced them unclean through their gifts—the sacrifice of every firstborn in the fire—so that I might devastate them, in order that they would know that I am the LORD.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord addresses the children in the wilderness and tells them not to repeat their fathers’ ways. They are to follow His statutes and keep His Sabbaths as a sign of belonging to Him.

They too rebel. Once again, He withholds the destruction He had resolved upon, for the sake of His name. But He also swears that they will be scattered among the nations because they reject His ways and fix their attention on inherited idols.

The BSB then says that He gave them over to statutes that were not good, followed by a charge concerning the sacrifice of firstborn children. This stands in sharp contrast with the life-giving ordinances described earlier.

The difficult statement must be read alongside Scripture’s explicit rejection of child sacrifice. Leviticus 18:21 prohibits giving children to Molech, and Jeremiah 7:30–34 says that burning children was something the Lord never commanded.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands the bad statutes as harmful practices God permitted the people to make for themselves after rejecting His good laws. Henry likewise explains judgment through people being given up to their own sinful desires, while denying that God is the author of sin.

The Cambridge discussion of verses 25–26 considers a misuse of the firstborn laws: the requirement concerning offerings was wrongly extended to children, although firstborn sons were to be redeemed. It reads the resulting delusion and destruction as judgment. The USCCB notes likewise connect the words with destructive child sacrifice and discuss the claim that the Lord accepted or required it.

These readings explain the relation between God’s judgment and the people’s practices differently. They do not make the earlier description of His life-giving laws disappear, and the explicit prohibitions prevent treating child sacrifice as an acceptable way to worship Him.
passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 7:37–43 recalls Israel receiving living words through Moses, refusing to obey and turning back toward Egypt in their hearts. Stephen says that God then gave them over to worship the host of heaven.

Acts is not explicitly quoting Ezekiel 20. It develops the same theme of rejected revelation and judgment through being handed over to the worship people choose. The history warns against confusing the possession of God’s word with a faithful response to it.

passages.title: Ezekiel 20:27-32
passages.section_title: Has the present generation left its fathers’ idolatry behind?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 27 Therefore, son of man, speak to the house of Israel, and tell them that this is what the Lord GOD says: In this way also your fathers blasphemed Me by their unfaithfulness against Me. 28 When I brought them into the land that I swore to give them and they saw any high hill or leafy tree, there they offered their sacrifices, presented offerings that provoked Me, sent up their fragrant incense, and poured out their drink offerings. 29 So I asked them: ‘What is this high place to which you go?’ (And to this day it is called Bamah.) 30 Therefore tell the house of Israel that this is what the Lord GOD says: Will you defile yourselves the way your fathers did, prostituting yourselves with their abominations? 31 When you offer your gifts, sacrificing your sons in the fire, you continue to defile yourselves with all your idols to this day. So should I be consulted by you, O house of Israel? As surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, I will not be consulted by you! 32 When you say, ‘Let us be like the nations, like the peoples of the lands, serving wood and stone,’ what you have in mind will never come to pass.

So should I be consulted by you, O house of Israel? section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The account moves into the land the Lord had promised. The people used its hills and leafy trees as places for offerings that provoked Him. Receiving the land had not ended the earlier pattern.

The Lord then addresses the present generation directly. Their gifts and the sacrifice of their sons show that the same defilement continues to this day.

That is why the question of consulting Him returns. They approach His prophet while continuing to dishonor His name through their idols.

He also exposes their desire to become like surrounding nations, serving wood and stone. That plan will not succeed. The next passage explains how He will assert His rule over them.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley understand the passage as exposing continued rebellion after settlement in Canaan. The current generation cannot treat the problem as something belonging only to its ancestors.

Wesley reads the wish to resemble the nations as a hoped-for security through adopting their ways. The answer is that Israel cannot erase its responsibility before the Lord by choosing another religious identity.

passages.title: Ezekiel 20:33-38
passages.section_title: Why does gathering the scattered people include judgment?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 33 As surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, with a strong hand, an outstretched arm, and outpoured wrath I will rule over you. 34 With a strong hand, an outstretched arm, and outpoured wrath I will bring you out from the peoples and gather you from the lands to which you have been scattered. 35 And I will bring you into the wilderness of the nations, where I will enter into judgment with you face to face. 36 Just as I entered into judgment with your fathers in the wilderness of the land of Egypt, so I will enter into judgment with you, declares the Lord GOD. 37 I will make you pass under the rod and will bring you into the bond of the covenant. 38 And I will purge you of those who rebel and transgress against Me. I will bring them out of the land in which they dwell, but they will not enter the land of Israel. Then you will know that I am the LORD.
paragraphs: 33 As surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, with a strong hand, an outstretched arm, and outpoured wrath I will rule over you. 34 With a strong hand, an outstretched arm, and outpoured wrath I will bring you out from the peoples and gather you from the lands to which you have been scattered. 35 And I will bring you into the wilderness of the nations, where I will enter into judgment with you face to face. 36 Just as I entered into judgment with your fathers in the wilderness of the land of Egypt, so I will enter into judgment with you, declares the Lord GOD.

37 I will make you pass under the rod and will bring you into the bond of the covenant. 38 And I will purge you of those who rebel and transgress against Me. I will bring them out of the land in which they dwell, but they will not enter the land of Israel. Then you will know that I am the LORD.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord declares that He will rule over Israel with a strong hand, an outstretched arm and outpoured wrath. He will gather the scattered people and bring them into the wilderness of the nations to meet Him in judgment.

He explicitly compares this encounter with His dealings with their fathers in the wilderness after Egypt. The new gathering does not make rebellion irrelevant any more than the earlier deliverance did.

The people will pass under the rod and be brought into the bond of the covenant. Those who rebel will be purged out and will not enter the land of Israel.

The promised gathering is therefore more than a change of location. The people must come under the rule of the God who gathers them, and they will know that He is the Lord.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley relates the gathering and judgment to the experience of exile, with the obedient brought into covenant and stubborn sinners excluded. The USCCB notes on verses 35–38 emphasize a new exodus and wilderness journey in which rebellion is removed.

John Walvoord’s discussion of Ezekiel 20:33–38 places the judgment in a future gathering of Israel after Christ’s return. He also identifies the covenant with Jeremiah’s promised new covenant. That is his reading of the passage’s fulfillment, rather than a timetable stated in these verses.

The readings differ over the historical setting and fulfillment. The shared point is that the Lord’s gathering involves His authority and a real distinction between faithfulness and rebellion.
passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 8:6–13 explains the new covenant through Jesus as its mediator. God’s promised work includes His law written within His people, their knowing Him and the forgiveness of their sins.

Hebrews quotes Jeremiah rather than Ezekiel 20. Its account develops the larger covenant hope: God forms a people who belong to Him inwardly, through the provision He makes. It adds to the gathering picture by explaining Christ’s work in that renewed relationship, without assigning every feature of Ezekiel’s wilderness scene a date.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 20:39-44
passages.section_title: What will make the restored worship different?

versions.label: BSB

But afterward, you will surely listen to Me, and you will no longer defile My holy name with your gifts and idols. 40 For on My holy mountain, the high mountain of Israel, declares the Lord GOD, there the whole house of Israel, all of them, will serve Me in the land. There I will accept them and will require your offerings and choice gifts, along with all your holy sacrifices. 41 When I bring you from the peoples and gather you from the lands to which you have been scattered, I will accept you as a pleasing aroma. And I will show My holiness through you in the sight of the nations. 42 Then you will know that I am the LORD, when I bring you into the land of Israel, the land that I swore to give your fathers. 43 There you will remember your ways and all the deeds with which you have defiled yourselves, and you will loathe yourselves for all the evils you have done. 44 Then you will know, O house of Israel, that I am the LORD, when I have dealt with you for the sake of My name and not according to your wicked ways and corrupt acts, declares the Lord GOD.”

There I will accept them and will require your offerings and choice gifts, along with all your holy sacrifices. 41 When I bring you from the peoples and gather you from the lands to which you have been scattered, I will accept you as a pleasing aroma. And I will show My holiness through you in the sight of the nations.

42 Then you will know that I am the LORD, when I bring you into the land of Israel, the land that I swore to give your fathers. 43 There you will remember your ways and all the deeds with which you have defiled yourselves, and you will loathe yourselves for all the evils you have done. 44 Then you will know, O house of Israel, that I am the LORD, when I have dealt with you for the sake of My name and not according to your wicked ways and corrupt acts, declares the Lord GOD.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord’s challenge to serve the idols is followed by a promise that this divided worship will not continue. His name will no longer be profaned by gifts offered alongside idolatry.

The whole house of Israel will serve Him on His holy mountain. He will accept the people and their offerings when He gathers them, showing His holiness through them in the sight of the nations.

The people will know Him as the Lord who brings them to the land promised to their fathers. They will remember and recoil from the ways in which they defiled themselves.

The ending explains why their restoration is possible: He deals with them for His name’s sake, rather than according to their wicked conduct. Accepted worship and repentance grow out of His merciful action.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley connects the promise with restored worship in Jerusalem and the people’s sorrow over their former ways. Henry likewise emphasizes repentance produced through God’s kindness and a fuller recognition of His holiness.

The promise is more than the recovery of prosperity. The people’s relation to the Lord and their judgment of their own former conduct have changed. Their future gives the nations a reason to recognize His holiness, rather than to associate His name with their idols.
passages.god_plan_html:
Revelation 7:9–17 presents a multitude from every nation worshiping God and the Lamb. Their robes have been washed in the Lamb’s blood, they serve before God, and the Lamb shepherds them to living water.

Revelation does not explicitly identify that multitude with the whole house of Israel in Ezekiel 20. The shared theme is a people gathered and accepted for worship through God’s saving provision. Revelation develops the wider hope through the Lamb and brings the nations into the picture of life in God’s presence.

passages.title: Ezekiel 20:45-49
passages.section_title: Why does Ezekiel speak of an unquenchable forest fire?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 45 Now the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 46 “Son of man, set your face toward the south, preach against it, and prophesy against the forest of the Negev. 47 Say to the forest of the Negev: Hear the word of the LORD! This is what the Lord GOD says: I am about to ignite in you a fire, and it will devour all your trees, both green and dry. The blazing flame will not be quenched, and by it every face from south to north will be scorched. 48 Then all people will see that I, the LORD, have kindled it; it will not be quenched.” 49 Then I said, “Ah, Lord GOD, they are saying of me, ‘Is he not just telling parables?’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
A new word directs Ezekiel to prophesy against the southern forest of the Negev. The Lord will ignite a fire that consumes green and dry trees alike, scorching the land from south to north.

The fire cannot be quenched, and all people will recognize that the Lord kindled it. The image announces a judgment whose reach and outcome cannot be controlled by the people facing it.

Ezekiel then reports the response he receives: people dismiss him as someone telling parables. The picture has not led them to take the warning seriously.

The following chapter names Jerusalem, its sanctuaries and the land of Israel as the objects of the warning. The forest picture prepares for that more direct explanation.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley understand the forest as the people of Judah and Jerusalem. Wesley takes the green and dry trees as showing that the disaster reaches different conditions and ranks of people.

Henry emphasizes the refusal behind the complaint about parables. The problem is not solved by treating the warning as an interesting story. The Lord’s next words make its application more direct.

passages.title: Ezekiel 21:1-7
passages.section_title: Why must Ezekiel groan over the coming news?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 And the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 2 “Son of man, set your face against Jerusalem and preach against the sanctuaries. Prophesy against the land of Israel 3 and tell her that this is what the LORD says: ‘I am against you, and I will draw My sword from its sheath and cut off from you both the righteous and the wicked. 4 Because I will cut off both the righteous and the wicked, My sword will be unsheathed against everyone from south to north. 5 Then all flesh will know that I, the LORD, have taken My sword from its sheath, not to return it again.’ 6 But you, son of man, groan! Groan before their eyes with a broken heart and bitter grief. 7 And when they ask, ‘Why are you groaning?’ you are to say, ‘Because of the news that is coming. Every heart will melt, and every hand will go limp. Every spirit will faint, and every knee will turn to water.’ Yes, it is coming and it will surely happen, declares the Lord GOD.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The forest-fire warning is now stated directly against Jerusalem, its sanctuaries and the land of Israel. The Lord pictures the judgment as His sword drawn from its sheath.

The calamity reaches both righteous and wicked, from south to north. Its scope prevents anyone from assuming that the collapse of the land will leave ordinary life untouched.

Ezekiel must groan publicly with a broken heart and bitter grief. When people ask why, he is to tell them about the news that is coming: hearts will melt, hands go limp and strength fail.

The prophet’s response makes the warning personal. He does not announce the devastation as a detached observer or treat it as something to celebrate.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads this as the explanation of the preceding chapter’s forest picture. He emphasizes that someone announcing judgment should also grieve for those facing ruin.

Wesley notes that public calamities can involve righteous people along with others. The passage’s sweeping language describes the devastation of the land; being personally faithful does not mean that a person’s community cannot fall into crisis.

passages.title: Ezekiel 21:8-17
passages.section_title: Can a royal scepter stop the sharpened sword?

versions.label: BSB

Should we rejoice in the scepter of My son? The sword despises every such stick. 11 The sword is appointed to be polished, to be grasped in the hand. section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The warning becomes a poem about a sword sharpened for slaughter and polished to flash like lightning. It is prepared for the hand of the one who will wield it.

The princes are threatened along with the people. Ezekiel is called to cry out, strike his thigh and clap his hands as the sword closes in. The repeated images press home the terror and certainty of the coming judgment.

In the BSB, the question about the scepter challenges confidence in royal power. The sword treats the scepter as a stick, and the testing may leave it no longer standing.

The Lord’s own declaration closes the poem. The judgment is presented as His announced act, rather than something a king’s title or the city’s former confidence can prevent.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry emphasizes the seriousness with which the sentence is pronounced and announced. Wesley connects the warning with the threatened end of Judah’s king and kingdom.

The wording about the rod or scepter is difficult, and older translations arrange it differently. The Cambridge discussion of verses 10 and 13 examines both a rod of chastisement and a royal scepter, favoring a connection with the royal house in verse 13. The BSB’s scepter wording places the emphasis on the failure of royal standing to secure the people against judgment.
passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 12:25–29 warns against refusing the God who speaks and describes created things being shaken so that what cannot be shaken remains. Believers are receiving an unshakable kingdom and are called to thankful, reverent worship.

Hebrews is not explicitly quoting Ezekiel 21. It develops the larger contrast between what human confidence treats as secure and the kingdom God gives. The warning against refusal and the promise of that kingdom belong together.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 21:18-24
passages.section_title: Why does Babylon’s choice of road lead to Jerusalem?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 19 “Now you, son of man, mark out two roads for the sword of the king of Babylon to take, both starting from the same land. And make a signpost where the road branches off to each city. 20 Mark out one road for the sword to come against Rabbah of the Ammonites, and another against Judah into fortified Jerusalem. 21 For the king of Babylon stands at the fork in the road, at the junction of the two roads, to seek an omen: He shakes the arrows, he consults the idols, he examines the liver. 22 In his right hand appears the portent for Jerusalem, where he is to set up battering rams, to call for the slaughter, to lift a battle cry, to direct the battering rams against the gates, to build a ramp, and to erect a siege wall. 23 It will seem like a false omen to the eyes of those who have sworn allegiance to him, but it will draw attention to their guilt and take them captive. 24 Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Because you have drawn attention to your guilt, exposing your transgressions, so that your sins are revealed in all your deeds—because you have come to remembrance—you shall be taken in hand.

And make a signpost where the road branches off to each city. 20 Mark out one road for the sword to come against Rabbah of the Ammonites, and another against Judah into fortified Jerusalem. 21 For the king of Babylon stands at the fork in the road, at the junction of the two roads, to seek an omen: He shakes the arrows, he consults the idols, he examines the liver. 22 In his right hand appears the portent for Jerusalem, where he is to set up battering rams, to call for the slaughter, to lift a battle cry, to direct the battering rams against the gates, to build a ramp, and to erect a siege wall.

23 It will seem like a false omen to the eyes of those who have sworn allegiance to him, but it will draw attention to their guilt and take them captive. 24 Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Because you have drawn attention to your guilt, exposing your transgressions, so that your sins are revealed in all your deeds—because you have come to remembrance—you shall be taken in hand.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Ezekiel is to mark two roads for Babylon’s king: one toward Rabbah of the Ammonites and one toward Jerusalem. At the fork, the king seeks an omen through arrows, idols and examination of a liver.

The omen points toward Jerusalem. The scene then shows the practical consequences: battering rams, battle cries, a ramp and a siege wall directed against the city.

Records of liver omens help explain this unfamiliar detail. The Metropolitan Museum’s account of a Mesopotamian liver-omen tablet describes predictions about an army’s success drawn from features of a sacrificial sheep’s liver. That later surviving tablet illustrates the kind of practice described; it is not an artifact from this particular campaign.

Those who have sworn allegiance dismiss the omen as false, but the Lord brings attention to their exposed guilt. Their confidence will not keep them from capture.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry understands Babylon’s decision through divination as still subject to God’s direction of the coming judgment. Wesley connects the sworn allegiance with Zedekiah and his officials’ broken pledge to Babylon.

The scene does not commend the king’s methods as a way for God’s people to seek guidance. Its point is that an apparently favorable reason to dismiss the danger cannot overturn the Lord’s warning or erase the conduct for which Jerusalem is being judged.

passages.title: Ezekiel 21:25-27
passages.section_title: Who has the right to rule when the crown is taken away?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 25 And you, O profane and wicked prince of Israel, the day has come for your final punishment.’ 26 This is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Remove the turban, and take off the crown. Things will not remain as they are: Exalt the lowly and bring low the exalted. 27 A ruin, a ruin, I will make it a ruin! And it will not be restored until the arrival of Him to whom it belongs, to whom I have assigned the right of judgment.’
paragraphs: 25 And you, O profane and wicked prince of Israel, the day has come for your final punishment.’ 26 This is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Remove the turban, and take off the crown. Things will not remain as they are: Exalt the lowly and bring low the exalted. 27 A ruin, a ruin, I will make it a ruin! And it will not be restored until the arrival of Him to whom it belongs, to whom I have assigned the right of judgment.’

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord addresses Israel’s wicked prince as the time for punishment arrives. The turban and crown are to be removed, and the existing order will not continue unchanged.

The lowly are to be raised and the exalted brought low. The repeated declaration of ruin gives the collapse its full weight.

The final line also looks beyond the removal. Restoration waits for the One to whom it belongs, the One assigned the right of judgment. The future depends on God’s appointment, rather than the present prince’s ability to hold his crown.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley identify the prince facing removal as Zedekiah and the coming rightful ruler as the Messiah. Henry sees hope for the Messiah’s kingdom within the warning of overturned governments.

The Cambridge note on verse 27 likewise reads the coming figure as the Messiah. These readings connect the loss of Judah’s royal rule with a future that God gives to His chosen ruler, rather than with an assurance that the present king will escape.
passages.god_plan_html:
Luke 1:30–33 identifies Jesus as the Son who receives David’s throne and whose kingdom has no end. The authority is given by God, matching the larger hope of a ruler appointed by Him.

Revelation 19:11–16 presents the faithful and true King who judges in righteousness. His titles and authority stand above the nations and their rulers.

Neither passage explicitly quotes Ezekiel 21. They explain why Christian readers connect its promise of rightful rule and judgment with Christ: the answer to failed human kingship is the King God appoints.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 21:28-32
passages.section_title: Does Jerusalem’s judgment mean Ammon will escape?

Your blood will stain your own land. You will not be remembered, for I, the LORD, have spoken.’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The warning turns toward the Ammonites and their contempt. A sword is drawn for slaughter, while false visions and lying divinations offer a very different expectation.

The Lord declares that judgment will reach them in their own land. They will be handed over to brutal men skilled in destruction, and the fire picture returns.

The sword’s direction toward Jerusalem earlier in the chapter was therefore no promise of permanent safety for Ammon. The chapter closes with the Lord’s own announcement against another people who have trusted false assurances.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads the false visions as promises of victory that cannot preserve Ammon. Wesley connects the contempt with Ammon’s response to Israel’s affliction and reads the warning as Ammon falling under judgment as well.

The reversal prevents gloating over a neighbor’s disaster. The fact that another community faces judgment is no proof that one’s own conduct or assurances are sound.

passages.title: Ezekiel 22:1-12
passages.section_title: Why does God call Jerusalem a city of bloodshed?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 2 “As for you, son of man, will you judge her? Will you pass judgment on the city of bloodshed? Then confront her with all her abominations 3 and tell her that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘O city who brings her own doom by shedding blood within her walls and making idols to defile herself, 4 you are guilty of the blood you have shed, and you are defiled by the idols you have made. You have brought your days to a close and have come to the end of your years. Therefore I have made you a reproach to the nations and a mockery to all the lands. 5 Those near and far will mock you, O infamous city, full of turmoil. 6 See how every prince of Israel within you has used his power to shed blood. 7 Father and mother are treated with contempt. Within your walls the foreign resident is exploited, the fatherless and the widow are oppressed. 8 You have despised My holy things and profaned My Sabbaths. 9 Among you are slanderous men bent on bloodshed; within you are those who eat on the mountain shrines and commit acts of indecency. 10 In you they have uncovered the nakedness of their fathers; in you they violate women during their menstrual impurity. 11 One man commits an abomination with his neighbor’s wife; another wickedly defiles his daughter-in-law; and yet another violates his sister, his own father’s daughter. 12 In you they take bribes to shed blood. You engage in usury, take excess interest, and extort your neighbors. But Me you have forgotten, declares the Lord GOD.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord directs Ezekiel to confront Jerusalem with its abominations. Bloodshed and idolatry stand at the head of the charge: the city is bringing its own doom near through what it does.

The accusation becomes concrete. Princes use power to shed blood, parents are treated with contempt, and foreign residents, orphans and widows are oppressed. Holy things and Sabbaths are despised, while slander contributes to violence.

Sexual wrongdoing includes adultery and violations within the family. The reference to a father’s nakedness belongs to the language used in Leviticus 18:6–18, which includes dishonoring a father through relations with his wife.

The list ends with bribes for bloodshed, abusive lending and extortion. The Lord names what lies beneath these practices: the people have forgotten Him. The accusation joins worship, family life, public power and treatment of the vulnerable.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley understand the city’s guilt through the actual wrongs listed, including murder, idolatry and oppression. Henry emphasizes forgetting God as the root of the conduct.

The USCCB notes likewise connect bloodshed, oppression of the poor and corrupt worship. These are not separate problems that can be balanced against one another; the charge concerns a life and community that dishonor the Lord in all these ways.
passages.god_plan_html:
James 1:26–27 connects faithful religion with control of the tongue, care for orphans and widows, and freedom from the world’s pollution. James 2:14–17 asks what good a claim to faith does when someone withholds the food and clothing a brother or sister needs.

James does not explicitly quote Ezekiel 22. He develops the larger concern that a claimed relationship with God must shape the treatment of others. The care God desires has visible consequences for people who can easily be ignored or exploited.

passages.title: Ezekiel 22:13-16
passages.section_title: Can dishonest gain give the city strength to endure judgment?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 Now look, I strike My hands together against your unjust gain and against the blood you have shed in your midst. 14 Will your courage endure or your hands be strong in the day I deal with you? I, the LORD, have spoken, and I will act. 15 I will disperse you among the nations and scatter you throughout the lands; I will purge your uncleanness. 16 And when you have defiled yourself in the eyes of the nations, then you will know that I am the LORD.’”

I, the LORD, have spoken, and I will act. 15 I will disperse you among the nations and scatter you throughout the lands; I will purge your uncleanness. 16 And when you have defiled yourself in the eyes of the nations, then you will know that I am the LORD.’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord strikes His hands together against the city’s unjust gain and bloodshed. The wealth accumulated through harm has become part of the accusation against it.

He asks whether the people’s courage and strength will endure when He acts. Their present ability to profit and dominate cannot determine the outcome.

He announces scattering among the nations and the purging of uncleanness. Before the same nations among whom the city will be exposed, the people will come to know that He is the Lord.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry connects the warning with the ruinous outcome of choosing one’s own desires as master. Wesley understands the question about strength as exposing the inability to withstand the evils now coming.

The passage overturns the appearance that successful wrongdoing has made Jerusalem secure. The Lord’s announced action is the answer to that confidence.

passages.title: Ezekiel 22:17-22
passages.section_title: Why is Jerusalem compared to a furnace full of dross?

All of them are copper, tin, iron, and lead inside the furnace; they are but the dross of silver. 19 Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Because all of you have become dross, behold, I will gather you into Jerusalem. 20 Just as one gathers silver, copper, iron, lead, and tin into the furnace to melt with a fiery blast, so I will gather you in My anger and wrath, leave you there, and melt you. 21 Yes, I will gather you together and blow on you with the fire of My wrath, and you will be melted within the city. 22 As silver is melted in a furnace, so you will be melted within the city. Then you will know that I, the LORD, have poured out My wrath upon you.’”
paragraphs: 17 Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 18 “Son of man, the house of Israel has become dross to Me. All of them are copper, tin, iron, and lead inside the furnace; they are but the dross of silver. 19 Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Because all of you have become dross, behold, I will gather you into Jerusalem.

20 Just as one gathers silver, copper, iron, lead, and tin into the furnace to melt with a fiery blast, so I will gather you in My anger and wrath, leave you there, and melt you. 21 Yes, I will gather you together and blow on you with the fire of My wrath, and you will be melted within the city. 22 As silver is melted in a furnace, so you will be melted within the city. Then you will know that I, the LORD, have poured out My wrath upon you.’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord describes the house of Israel as dross, listing copper, tin, iron and lead within a furnace. The comparison concerns a people whose condition has become unacceptable to Him.

The Hebrew term סִיג, sig (seeg), is explained in Brown–Driver–Briggs as dross, the material removed from metal. The image contrasts what is expected from silver with the unwanted material associated with it.

Jerusalem will become the furnace into which the people are gathered. The Lord will blow upon them with the fire of His wrath, and they will be melted within the city.

The repeated announcement leaves the purpose of this immediate warning clear: they will know that He has poured out His wrath. The city that seemed a place of refuge is pictured as the place where judgment concentrates.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley emphasizes the change from a people practicing mercy and justice to a people described as dross. He understands the gathering into Jerusalem as gathering into a furnace where they face destruction.

Henry also describes the degraded condition, then draws on the wider refining picture to emphasize the separation of dross and the purification of good metal. The USCCB notes connect the image with other prophetic descriptions of smelting and purification.

The emphasis differs between the immediate threat and the refining theme drawn from the broader picture. Ezekiel’s repeated words here announce a severe judgment; they do not describe an easy process or guarantee that every individual will respond faithfully.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 22:23-31
passages.section_title: Who will stand in the gap when the leaders and people are corrupt?

versions.label: BSB

They devour the people, seize the treasures and precious things, and multiply the widows within her. 26 Her priests do violence to My law and profane My holy things. They make no distinction between the holy and the common, and they fail to distinguish between the clean and the unclean. They disregard My Sabbaths, so that I am profaned among them. 27 Her officials within her are like wolves tearing their prey, shedding blood, and destroying lives for dishonest gain. 28 Her prophets whitewash these deeds by false visions and lying divinations, saying, ‘This is what the Lord GOD says,’ when the LORD has not spoken. 29 The people of the land have practiced extortion and committed robbery. They have oppressed the poor and needy and have exploited the foreign resident without justice. 30 I searched for a man among them to repair the wall and stand in the gap before Me on behalf of the land, so that I should not destroy it. But I found no one. 31 So I have poured out My indignation upon them and consumed them with the fire of My fury. I have brought their ways down upon their own heads, declares the Lord GOD.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The closing accusation reaches across the community. In the BSB, princes are compared to a roaring lion that devours people and multiplies widows. Priests violate the Lord’s law, blur the distinctions entrusted to them and disregard His Sabbaths.

Officials act like wolves, destroying lives for dishonest gain. Prophets whitewash what is happening through false visions, claiming that the Lord has spoken when He has not.

The people also share in the wrongdoing through robbery, extortion and exploitation of the poor and the foreign resident. Responsibility does not end with the leaders.

The Lord says that He sought someone to repair the wall and stand in the gap before Him on behalf of the land, but found no one. The chapter ends with the announced outpouring of wrath: the people’s own ways return upon their heads.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry understands the passage as the guilt of people across ranks and offices, each abusing the power available to them. Wesley reads standing in the gap as interceding for mercy between the sinful people and the God they have offended.

The picture also recalls Psalm 106:19–23, where Moses stands in the breach when Israel worships the calf. In Ezekiel, the failure to find someone exposes the community’s need for faithful leadership and an effective plea on its behalf.

The statement concerns the situation described in the land. It is not a claim that no faithful person, prophet or prayer existed anywhere in the world; Ezekiel himself is receiving and speaking the Lord’s word.
passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 7:23–28 explains why Jesus’ priesthood supplies a lasting answer to human weakness. He lives forever, intercedes for those who draw near to God through Him, and offered Himself for sin once for all.

Hebrews does not explicitly identify Ezekiel’s missing intercessor as a prediction of Jesus. The wider connection is the need for someone who can truly represent people before God. Where the chapter exposes the failure of human offices and the absence of an effective defender, Hebrews directs hope toward the living Son and His complete saving provision.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 23:1-10
passages.section_title: Who are the two sisters, and why does Samaria fall?

versions.label: BSB

As for their identities, Oholah is Samaria, and Oholibah is Jerusalem. 5 Oholah prostituted herself while she was still Mine. Thus she became a byword among women, and they executed judgment against her.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord tells a story about two sisters, then identifies them: Oholah is Samaria, and Oholibah is Jerusalem. The cities stand for the two kingdoms. Their shared beginnings in Egypt lead into a picture of unfaithfulness to the God to whom they belong.

Oholah is drawn to Assyria’s impressive soldiers and rulers. Verse 7 explains what the sexual picture means: she defiles herself with their idols. The attraction to foreign power carries a betrayal of the Lord.

The power she desired becomes the power that destroys her. The Lord delivers her to the Assyrians, who take her children and put her to the sword. The reversal prepares the warning to Jerusalem: Samaria’s fate is something her sister has already seen.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley read the sisters as the northern and southern kingdoms, and the unfaithfulness as idolatry expressed through their dealings with other nations. The USCCB notes likewise identify the cities and their worship. The story concerns these communities’ relationship with God.

Henry and Wesley also connect the sisters’ names with their sanctuaries: Samaria’s own place of worship and the Lord’s temple in Jerusalem. Cambridge is less certain that the names establish that contrast. The identities supplied in verse 4 are clear even where the full significance of the names is debated.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 23:11-21
passages.section_title: Why does Jerusalem repeat what she saw destroy her sister?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jerusalem sees Samaria’s unfaithfulness and its outcome, yet follows the same path and goes further. The accusation is not that she lacked an example, but that she refused to learn from it.

Assyria’s warriors first attract her. Then images of Babylonian officers stir her desire, and she sends messengers to them. After the Babylonians defile her, she turns away in disgust, while the Lord also turns away from her.

Her changing attachments do not become a return to God. Instead, she remembers Egypt and renews the desire associated with her youth. The deliberately graphic language exposes a consuming appetite beneath the attraction to impressive foreign powers.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry treats the sisters’ story as an exposure of persistent departure from God. Wesley connects Jerusalem’s return to Egypt with renewed idolatry and alliance, after growing weary of the Chaldeans.

The passage portrays the city’s restless pursuit of other sources of security and worship. Its sexual imagery describes that betrayal; it does not establish a general claim about the bodies or character of the peoples it names.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 23:22-35
passages.section_title: What happens when Jerusalem must drink her sister’s cup?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord announces that the former lovers Jerusalem now hates will gather against her. The impressive armies that once attracted her will surround the city and become its enemies.

The threatened losses are severe: mutilation, death, captivity, fire, and the stripping away of clothing and jewelry. The story’s marriage language becomes a picture of the city losing its people, possessions and security.

The cup gathers the warning into one image. Jerusalem will drink the devastation and grief Samaria has already experienced. The final charge explains the relationship behind all of this: she has forgotten the Lord and cast Him behind her back.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands the cup as the sorrow and punishment Jerusalem must endure. The USCCB notes connect it with the wider biblical picture of a cup of divine punishment. The sister’s experience makes the warning concrete: Jerusalem cannot assume she will escape the path she has chosen.

The announced judgment belongs to the Lord’s confrontation with these cities. The passage does not give people permission to mutilate or attack an unfaithful spouse.
passages.god_plan_html:
The cup becomes a powerful picture again when Jesus faces His suffering. In Mark 14:32–42, He asks that the cup might pass from Him, yet submits to the Father’s will. In John 18:1–11, He refuses Peter’s attempt to prevent His arrest and accepts the cup the Father has given Him.

This is a connection in the wider biblical theme, not a statement that Ezekiel’s cup directly predicts Jesus. Jerusalem is facing the consequences of its own unfaithfulness; Jesus willingly goes toward the suffering through which He offers Himself for sins. Hebrews 10:10–18 explains the lasting result of His one offering: forgiveness that removes the need for another offering for sin.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 23:36-49
passages.section_title: Can people harm God’s children and still honor His house?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord brings both sisters together under the accusation. Their idolatry includes the killing of children who belonged to Him. On the same day they slaughter those children, they enter His sanctuary.

The scene then returns to the sisters welcoming visitors, decorating themselves, and preparing a luxurious setting. The Lord’s incense and oil are set before the guests. What belongs to Him has been drawn into their unfaithfulness.

The closing scene announces judgment for adultery and bloodshed. The cities’ houses will burn, their children will be killed, and their conduct will become a warning. The conclusion repeats the purpose of the confrontation: they will know that He is the Lord.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley emphasizes the immediate contradiction between idolatry and murder and then entering the temple. Henry reads the chapter as a call to repentance rather than confidence in one’s own righteousness.

Readings differ over the righteous men in verse 45. The USCCB notes apply the description to the executioners acting as agents of the Lord’s judgment. Cambridge understands righteous judges within the story’s courtroom picture, without identifying them as the nations that carry out the actual destruction. Neither reading turns the invading nations into a model of moral perfection.
passages.god_plan_html:
First Corinthians 10:14–22 brings the issue of divided worship into the life of the church. Paul tells believers to flee idolatry and explains that sharing in the Lord’s table cannot be joined with sharing in the table of demons.

Paul does not explicitly quote this passage. The larger connection is that worship involves belonging and participation, not a ceremony that cancels out another allegiance. Ezekiel exposes people entering God’s sanctuary while persisting in idol worship; Paul calls those who share in Christ to an undivided loyalty to Him.

passages.title: Ezekiel 24:1-14
passages.section_title: Why does Jerusalem become a boiling pot?

Bring it to a boil and cook the bones in it.’ 6 Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Woe to the city of bloodshed, to the pot now rusted, whose rust will not come off! I, too, will pile the kindling high. 10 Pile on the logs and kindle the fire; cook the meat well and mix in the spices; let the bones be burned. 11 Set the empty pot on its coals until it becomes hot and its copper glows. You will not be pure again until My wrath against you has subsided. 14 I, the LORD, have spoken; the time is coming, and I will act. I will not refrain or show pity, nor will I relent. I will judge you according to your ways and deeds,’ declares the Lord GOD.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord tells Ezekiel to record the date because Babylon has laid siege to Jerusalem that very day. Second Kings 25:1–12 records the siege beginning on the same day of the same month in Zedekiah’s ninth year, and describes the later famine, breach and burning of the city.

The Lord gives Ezekiel a parable about a cooking pot filled with choice meat and bones. The pot is Jerusalem. Its persistent rust pictures the uncleanness that remains within the city, while the exposed blood recalls violence that has not been put right.

The fire grows until even the emptied pot is heated. The Lord explains the charge: He sought to cleanse the city, but it would not be purified. This is the point at which the long warning becomes an announced action against its ways and deeds.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley read the pot as the besieged city, with its people gathered inside and its wrongdoing still present. Both connect the image with the failure to turn from sin despite the opportunities already given.

The BSB describes rust that resists removal. Older commentary often uses the language of scum from its Bible translation. The controlling point is the city’s persistent uncleanness and the judgment now coming, rather than an exact description of a metalworking process.
passages.god_plan_html:
A later warning over Jerusalem provides a sobering parallel. In Luke 19:41–44, Jesus weeps over the city and announces that enemies will surround and destroy it because it has not recognized the time of God’s visitation.

These are distinct warnings in different periods, not a single siege or a shared timetable. The parallel shows why a city’s sacred history cannot make refusing God harmless. Jesus’ tears also show that announcing judgment does not mean delighting in the loss it brings.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 24:15-24
passages.section_title: Why is Ezekiel told not to mourn when his wife dies?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 16 “Son of man, behold, I am about to take away the desire of your eyes with a fatal blow. But you must not mourn or weep or let your tears flow. 17 Groan quietly; do not mourn for the dead. Put on your turban and strap your sandals on your feet; do not cover your lips or eat the bread of mourners.” 18 So I spoke to the people in the morning, and in the evening my wife died. And the next morning I did as I had been commanded. 19 Then the people asked me, “Won’t you tell us what these things you are doing mean to us?” 20 So I answered them, “The word of the LORD came to me, saying: 21 Tell the house of Israel that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘I am about to desecrate My sanctuary, the pride of your power, the desire of your eyes, and the delight of your soul. And the sons and daughters you left behind will fall by the sword.’ 22 Then you will do as I have done: You will not cover your lips or eat the bread of mourners. 23 Your turbans will remain on your heads and your sandals on your feet. You will not mourn or weep, but you will waste away because of your sins, and you will groan among yourselves. 24 ‘Thus Ezekiel will be a sign for you; you will do everything that he has done. When this happens, you will know that I am the Lord GOD.’

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord tells Ezekiel that the desire of his eyes will be taken away, and verse 18 identifies the loss as his wife’s death. Ezekiel is commanded to groan quietly while refraining from the mourning actions listed in the passage. His love and loss are not treated as unimportant.

The people ask what his behavior means for them. The Lord answers by naming what they will lose: His sanctuary, which is the desire of their eyes, and the sons and daughters left behind in Jerusalem. Ezekiel’s personal sorrow becomes a sign of the disaster approaching the community.

They too will groan among themselves while wasting away because of their sins. The explanation makes the connection between the sign and the city’s loss; it does not accuse Ezekiel’s wife of a particular sin or tell us her thoughts during her final day.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Cambridge understands the lack of outward mourning as a picture of people stunned by the severity of Jerusalem’s fall. Wesley emphasizes the restrictions of captivity as an explanation for grief that cannot be openly expressed. The passage itself states the sign and the coming behavior without explaining every circumstance that will prevent ordinary mourning.

Henry draws a broader lesson about grief held together with trust in God. This particular command to Ezekiel should not become a rule that faithful people must never cry: John 11:32–36 describes Jesus weeping at the death of Lazarus.

passages.title: Ezekiel 24:25-27
passages.section_title: When will the fugitive’s news open Ezekiel’s mouth?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 25 And you, son of man, know that on the day I take away their stronghold, their pride and joy—the desire of their eyes which uplifted their souls—and their sons and daughters as well, 26 on that day a fugitive will come and tell you the news. 27 On that day your mouth will be opened to him who has escaped; you will speak and no longer be mute. So you will be a sign to them, and they will know that I am the LORD.”
paragraphs: 25 And you, son of man, know that on the day I take away their stronghold, their pride and joy—the desire of their eyes which uplifted their souls—and their sons and daughters as well, 26 on that day a fugitive will come and tell you the news. 27 On that day your mouth will be opened to him who has escaped; you will speak and no longer be mute. So you will be a sign to them, and they will know that I am the LORD.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord closes this message by looking ahead to the loss of Jerusalem’s stronghold, its cherished security and its children. A fugitive will bring the news to Ezekiel, and his mouth will be opened.

The promise answers the restriction on his speech introduced in Ezekiel 3:26–27. His silence and the ending of it belong to his role as a sign through whom the people are confronted with the Lord’s word.

Ezekiel 33:21–22 records the arrival of the fugitive and the opening of Ezekiel’s mouth. It specifically says that his mouth had been opened the evening before the man arrived in the morning. The promise is fulfilled in that setting, without requiring both events to occur at the same instant.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley connects the silence with the period when the following chapters address other nations. Cambridge understands the arrival of the fugitive and the opening of Ezekiel’s mouth together, allowing the expression about that day to describe the period of the great event.

The focus is confirmation of the message and a change in the prophet’s assigned role. The passage supplies no rule that another person’s silence or recovery of speech must have the same prophetic meaning.

passages.title: Ezekiel 25:1-7
passages.section_title: Why does Ammon answer for celebrating Judah’s ruin?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 2 “Son of man, set your face against the Ammonites and prophesy against them. 3 Tell the Ammonites to hear the word of the Lord GOD, for this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Because you exclaimed, “Aha!” when My sanctuary was profaned, when the land of Israel was laid waste, and when the house of Judah went into exile, 4 therefore I will indeed give you as a possession to the people of the East. They will set up their camps and pitch their tents among you. They will eat your fruit and drink your milk. 5 I will make Rabbah a pasture for camels, and Ammon a resting place for sheep. Then you will know that I am the LORD.’ 6 For this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Because you clapped your hands and stomped your feet and rejoiced over the land of Israel with a heart full of contempt, 7 therefore I will indeed stretch out My hand against you and give you as plunder to the nations. I will cut you off from the peoples and exterminate you from the countries. I will destroy you, and you will know that I am the LORD.’

They will set up their camps and pitch their tents among you. They will eat your fruit and drink your milk. 5 I will make Rabbah a pasture for camels, and Ammon a resting place for sheep. Then you will know that I am the LORD.’

6 For this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Because you clapped your hands and stomped your feet and rejoiced over the land of Israel with a heart full of contempt, 7 therefore I will indeed stretch out My hand against you and give you as plunder to the nations. I will cut you off from the peoples and exterminate you from the countries. I will destroy you, and you will know that I am the LORD.’

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The focus turns from Jerusalem to its neighbors. Ammon is accused of rejoicing when the Lord’s sanctuary is profaned, the land is devastated and Judah goes into exile. The clapping and stamping express contempt rather than compassion.

The Lord announces a reversal. Ammon will become plunder, and people from the East will occupy its land and consume its produce. Rabbah will become pasture for camels, and the land a resting place for sheep.

The judgment against Judah does not make delight in its destruction acceptable. The Lord who confronts His own people also holds their neighbors accountable. Ammon too will know that He is the Lord.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley understand the charge as gloating over a calamity that should have prompted pity. The warning does not excuse Judah’s sins; it confronts the contempt of those watching Judah suffer.

The USCCB notes identify the people from the East as desert nomads. Wesley connects Arabian groups with Nebuchadnezzar’s campaign. These explanations fill out the broad description differently; Ezekiel’s announcement itself names people from the East.
passages.god_plan_html:
The wider promise to Abraham includes the Lord’s response to those who curse him, while also looking toward blessing for all families of the earth: Genesis 12:1–3. Deuteronomy 30:1–10 joins Israel’s restoration and changed hearts with judgment on its persecutors.

There is also a promise concerning Ammon itself. After announcing its judgment, Jeremiah 49:1–6 says that the Lord will restore the Ammonites from captivity. Reading the passages together keeps both accountability and mercy in view. Ezekiel’s warning does not supply the whole account of everything God will do for these people.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 25:8-11
passages.section_title: What does Moab miss when it dismisses Judah as just another nation?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 This is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Because Moab and Seir said, “Look, the house of Judah is like all the other nations,” 9 therefore I will indeed expose the flank of Moab beginning with its frontier cities—Beth-jeshimoth, Baal-meon, and Kiriathaim—the glory of the land. 10 I will give it along with the Ammonites as a possession to the people of the East, so that the Ammonites will no longer be remembered among the nations. 11 So I will execute judgments on Moab, and they will know that I am the LORD.’
paragraphs: 8 This is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Because Moab and Seir said, “Look, the house of Judah is like all the other nations,” 9 therefore I will indeed expose the flank of Moab beginning with its frontier cities—Beth-jeshimoth, Baal-meon, and Kiriathaim—the glory of the land. 10 I will give it along with the Ammonites as a possession to the people of the East, so that the Ammonites will no longer be remembered among the nations. 11 So I will execute judgments on Moab, and they will know that I am the LORD.’

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Moab and Seir say that Judah is like all the other nations. In the setting of Judah’s fall, that dismissal denies that its relationship with the Lord makes any difference.

The Lord answers by announcing the exposure of Moab’s flank, beginning with the named frontier cities. The land’s glory will not secure it against judgment.

Moab’s fate is placed beside Ammon’s: the land will be given to the people from the East. The closing purpose answers the original dismissal. Moab will know the Lord through His judgments.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands the taunt as denying that Judah is a people specially chosen by God. Henry emphasizes the danger of relying on defenses other than the Lord’s power and promise.

The passage distinguishes Judah’s relationship with God without denying its guilt. Judah’s defeat is not proof that the Lord has no claim on it or no authority over its neighbors.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jeremiah 48:46–47 also announces captivity for Moab, then promises that the Lord will restore Moab from captivity in the latter days. That promise adds something this short judgment does not state.

The wider picture leaves room for the Lord’s mercy beyond Israel’s borders. Mercy does not erase the wrong being judged, but judgment does not exhaust what the Lord promises.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 25:12-14
passages.section_title: Why does Edom’s vengeance bring judgment on itself?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 This is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Because Edom acted vengefully against the house of Judah, and in so doing incurred grievous guilt, 13 therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: I will stretch out My hand against Edom and cut off from it both man and beast. I will make it a wasteland, and from Teman to Dedan they will fall by the sword. 14 I will take My vengeance on Edom by the hand of My people Israel, and they will deal with Edom according to My anger and wrath. Then they will know My vengeance, declares the Lord GOD.’
paragraphs: 12 This is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Because Edom acted vengefully against the house of Judah, and in so doing incurred grievous guilt, 13 therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: I will stretch out My hand against Edom and cut off from it both man and beast. I will make it a wasteland, and from Teman to Dedan they will fall by the sword. 14 I will take My vengeance on Edom by the hand of My people Israel, and they will deal with Edom according to My anger and wrath. Then they will know My vengeance, declares the Lord GOD.’

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Edom has taken vengeance against Judah and incurred grievous guilt. The Lord’s response addresses the active hostility of a neighbor taking its own revenge.

The announced devastation reaches people and animals, with Teman and Dedan marking the breadth of the threat. The Lord says that His vengeance will be carried out through His people Israel.

The repeated language turns Edom’s conduct back upon it: the people who sought revenge will come to know the Lord’s vengeance. Obadiah 1:10–15 gives a related accusation, describing violence against brother Jacob, gloating, looting and the betrayal of fugitives.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry emphasizes the justice of wrongdoing being answered through those who had suffered it. He also distinguishes trusting God to judge from taking revenge oneself. Wesley identifies Seir with Edom and reads the geographical names as the extent of the threatened devastation.

The passage names the Lord as judge and Israel as the instrument He appoints in this announcement. It does not authorize anyone with an old grievance to claim divine approval for retaliation.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 12:14–21 tells believers how to live while trusting God’s judgment: bless persecutors, refuse repayment of evil with evil, and provide food and drink to an enemy in need. Paul grounds the refusal of personal revenge in the Lord’s right to repay.

Paul does not explicitly quote Ezekiel 25. The wider connection clarifies the response of people who belong to God: confidence that He judges evil frees them from making vengeance their own task. They are called to overcome evil with good.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 25:15-17
passages.section_title: Can ancient hostility make the Philistines’ revenge right?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 This is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Because the Philistines acted in vengeance, taking vengeance with malice of soul to destroy Judah with ancient hostility, 16 therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: Behold, I will stretch out My hand against the Philistines, and I will cut off the Cherethites and destroy the remnant along the coast. 17 I will execute great vengeance against them with furious reproof. Then they will know that I am the LORD, when I lay My vengeance upon them.’”
paragraphs: 15 This is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Because the Philistines acted in vengeance, taking vengeance with malice of soul to destroy Judah with ancient hostility, 16 therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: Behold, I will stretch out My hand against the Philistines, and I will cut off the Cherethites and destroy the remnant along the coast. 17 I will execute great vengeance against them with furious reproof. Then they will know that I am the LORD, when I lay My vengeance upon them.’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The final announcement in the chapter concerns the Philistines. Their old hostility has become a malicious desire to destroy Judah.

The Lord will stretch out His hand against them, cut off the Cherethites and destroy the remnant along the coast. Brown–Driver–Briggs identifies Cherethites as a name for the Philistines or a part of them; the verse is not introducing an unrelated enemy.

The chapter ends as its earlier announcements have: the people will know that He is the Lord when His judgment comes. Longstanding hatred supplies the accusation, not a justification for the revenge.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads stored-up hatred and the search for an opportunity to act on it as accumulating guilt before God. Wesley understands the announcement as directed against Israel’s hostile coastal neighbors.

The chapter has confronted contempt, dismissive pride and revenge. Its closing announcement shows that a grievance carried for generations still answers to the Lord.
