passages.title: Ezekiel 26:1-6
passages.section_title: Why does Tyre’s delight in Jerusalem’s fall bring judgment?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 In the eleventh month of the twelfth year, on the first day of the month, the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 2 “Son of man, because Tyre has said of Jerusalem, ‘Aha! The gate to the nations is broken; it has swung open to me; now that she lies in ruins I will be filled,’ 3 therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Behold, O Tyre, I am against you, and I will raise up many nations against you, as the sea brings up its waves. 4 They will destroy the walls of Tyre and demolish her towers. I will scrape the soil from her and make her a bare rock. 5 She will become a place to spread nets in the sea, for I have spoken, declares the Lord GOD. She will become plunder for the nations, 6 and the villages on her mainland will be slain by the sword. Then they will know that I am the LORD.’

3 therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Behold, O Tyre, I am against you, and I will raise up many nations against you, as the sea brings up its waves. 4 They will destroy the walls of Tyre and demolish her towers. I will scrape the soil from her and make her a bare rock. 5 She will become a place to spread nets in the sea, for I have spoken, declares the Lord GOD. She will become plunder for the nations, 6 and the villages on her mainland will be slain by the sword. Then they will know that I am the LORD.’

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Tyre sees Jerusalem’s ruin as its own opening for gain. The city’s response is an eager expectation that the broken gateway to the nations will now fill its own trade.

The coastal setting matters. UNESCO’s account of Tyre describes a Phoenician maritime center built largely on an island, with settlements on the mainland. Ezekiel’s picture of waves, bare rock, fishing nets and mainland villages speaks directly to that setting.

The Lord turns the expectation around: many nations will rise against Tyre like waves. Its defenses will come down, its wealth will become plunder, and the mainland villages will suffer. Jerusalem’s fall is no guarantee that the neighbor hoping to profit will be safe.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry understands the charge as selfish pleasure in another’s loss when that loss seems likely to benefit oneself. Wesley and the USCCB notes likewise connect the gateway language with trade turning toward Tyre.

The accusation concerns the heart behind that expectation of gain. The city treats another people’s devastation as a welcome business opportunity.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 26:7-14
passages.section_title: How should we understand the destruction and the promise that Tyre will not be rebuilt?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 For this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Behold, I will bring against Tyre from the north Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, king of kings, with horses and chariots, with cavalry and a great company of troops. 8 He will slaughter the villages of your mainland with the sword; he will set up siege works against you, build a ramp to your walls, and raise his shields against you. 9 He will direct the blows of his battering rams against your walls and tear down your towers with his axes. 10 His multitude of horses will cover you in their dust. When he enters your gates as an army entering a breached city, your walls will shake from the noise of cavalry, wagons, and chariots. 11 The hooves of his horses will trample all your streets. He will slaughter your people with the sword, and your mighty pillars will fall to the ground. 12 They will plunder your wealth and pillage your merchandise. They will demolish your walls, tear down your beautiful homes, and throw your stones and timber and soil into the water. 13 So I will silence the sound of your songs, and the music of your lyres will no longer be heard. 14 I will make you a bare rock, and you will become a place to spread the fishing nets. You will never be rebuilt, for I, the LORD, have spoken, declares the Lord GOD.’

He will slaughter your people with the sword, and your mighty pillars will fall to the ground.

12 They will plunder your wealth and pillage your merchandise. They will demolish your walls, tear down your beautiful homes, and throw your stones and timber and soil into the water. 13 So I will silence the sound of your songs, and the music of your lyres will no longer be heard. 14 I will make you a bare rock, and you will become a place to spread the fishing nets. You will never be rebuilt, for I, the LORD, have spoken, declares the Lord GOD.’

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord names Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon as the approaching ruler. The siege picture moves through ramps, battering rams, falling towers, cavalry and slaughter, until the city’s wealth and merchandise are plundered.

The announcement reaches beyond damaged defenses. Homes are demolished, building materials are thrown into the water, and the music of the city is silenced. The place of wealth and celebration becomes bare rock for fishing nets.

The strong statement about never being rebuilt has to be read alongside later biblical references. Ezekiel 29:17–21 says that Nebuchadnezzar’s army labored against Tyre without receiving wages from it. Acts 21:1–6 later describes a ship unloading cargo there and disciples living in the city.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Gill explains that the rebuilding language needs qualification, offering the loss of former grandeur or royal standing among the possible readings. He also reads the materials thrown into the water in connection with Alexander’s later attack. The earlier announcement of many nations helps explain why readers consider more than one campaign.

That later attack is independently documented. Arrian’s account describes Alexander building a causeway with stone and wood toward the island. UNESCO records the causeway and subsequent Greek and Roman construction on the site.

The question is therefore how the announced end of Tyre relates to its later settlement and changed standing. A reading centered on the destruction of its former power is an interpretation of the prophecy, not a claim that the Bible or historical records contain no later city called Tyre.

passages.title: Ezekiel 26:15-18
passages.section_title: Why do the rulers of the sea tremble at Tyre’s fall?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 This is what the Lord GOD says to Tyre: ‘Will not the coastlands quake at the sound of your downfall, when the wounded groan at the slaughter in your midst? 16 All the princes of the sea will descend from their thrones, remove their robes, and strip off their embroidered garments. Clothed with terror, they will sit on the ground, trembling every moment, appalled over you. 17 Then they will lament for you, saying, “How you have perished, O city of renown inhabited by seafaring men— she who was powerful on the sea, along with her people, who imposed terror on all peoples! 18 Now the coastlands tremble on the day of your downfall; the islands in the sea are dismayed by your demise.”’
paragraphs: 15 This is what the Lord GOD says to Tyre: ‘Will not the coastlands quake at the sound of your downfall, when the wounded groan at the slaughter in your midst? 16 All the princes of the sea will descend from their thrones, remove their robes, and strip off their embroidered garments. Clothed with terror, they will sit on the ground, trembling every moment, appalled over you. 17 Then they will lament for you, saying, “How you have perished, O city of renown inhabited by seafaring men— she who was powerful on the sea, along with her people, who imposed terror on all peoples! 18 Now the coastlands tremble on the day of your downfall; the islands in the sea are dismayed by your demise.”’

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The announcement turns from the city’s destruction to the reaction around it. The princes of the sea step down from their thrones, remove their fine clothing and sit trembling.

Their lament remembers Tyre’s reputation and power on the sea. Its fall makes the coastlands and islands afraid: a place that had imposed terror on others has itself become the cause of dismay.

The passage is also a reversal of Tyre’s own response to Jerusalem. Tyre welcomed its neighbor’s ruin; its own fall is met with a funeral song and fear.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley reads the princes as rulers of the islands and understands their trembling as fear for their own concerns. The USCCB notes connect these rulers with the coastal communities commercially linked to Tyre.

Henry draws attention to the collapse of apparently established prosperity. The lament exposes how deeply other rulers had tied their sense of security to this city.
passages.god_plan_html:
A closely supported parallel appears in Revelation 18:7–10. Babylon claims that it will never know grief, but when judgment comes, the kings associated with its luxury stand at a distance in fear and lament its fall.

The parallel carries the exposure of worldly security into Revelation’s account of God’s judgment. It does not require Tyre and Babylon to be the same city. In both scenes, the rulers discover that impressive power and shared prosperity cannot protect the city on which they relied.

passages.title: Ezekiel 26:19-21
passages.section_title: What does Tyre’s descent to the Pit mean?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 For this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘When I make you a desolate city like other deserted cities, and when I raise up the deep against you so that the mighty waters cover you, 20 then I will bring you down with those who descend to the Pit, to the people of antiquity. I will make you dwell in the earth below like the ancient ruins, with those who descend to the Pit, so that you will no longer be inhabited or set in splendor in the land of the living. 21 I will make you an object of horror, and you will be no more. You will be sought, but will never be found,’ declares the Lord GOD.”
paragraphs: 19 For this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘When I make you a desolate city like other deserted cities, and when I raise up the deep against you so that the mighty waters cover you, 20 then I will bring you down with those who descend to the Pit, to the people of antiquity. I will make you dwell in the earth below like the ancient ruins, with those who descend to the Pit, so that you will no longer be inhabited or set in splendor in the land of the living. 21 I will make you an object of horror, and you will be no more. You will be sought, but will never be found,’ declares the Lord GOD.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The final picture is of overwhelming waters and a city descending among the dead. The loss of Tyre is described as the end of a life: it joins those who went down long ago and loses its place in the land of the living.

The Hebrew word בּוֹר, bor (bore), can refer to a pit or cistern. Brown–Driver–Briggs also identifies its use for the grave or the realm of the dead, specifically including this passage. The setting, rather than every possible meaning of the word, explains the picture here.

The Lord’s closing announcement removes the hope that Tyre’s former life can simply be recovered by searching for it. The city that expected to be filled through Jerusalem’s loss is pictured as absent from the living world.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Cambridge understand the descent through the language of death and the grave. The USCCB notes connect the Pit with the dead dwelling in Sheol.

Wesley’s further comment about glory restored to Israel follows the positive wording of his translation at the end of verse 20. The BSB instead continues the negative statement about Tyre no longer being set in splendor among the living. Cambridge discusses both readings. The wording matters when deciding what this particular verse promises.
passages.god_plan_html:
John 5:24–29 moves the larger question of death and judgment toward the Son. Jesus gives eternal life to those who hear and believe, and says that those in the graves will hear His voice and come out to resurrection.

Ezekiel’s description is not an explicit prediction of that teaching. The wider connection is that neither prosperity nor death removes a person from God’s authority. Revelation 20:11–15 pictures the dead, great and small, brought before His judgment, with the sea and Hades giving up their dead. The final word belongs to God, whose Son offers life.

passages.title: Ezekiel 27:1-11
passages.section_title: Why is Tyre pictured as a magnificent ship?

They took a cedar from Lebanon to make a mast for you. 6 Of oaks from Bashan they made your oars; of wood from the coasts of Cyprus they made your deck, inlaid with ivory. 7 Of embroidered fine linen from Egypt they made your sail, which served as your banner. Of blue and purple from the coasts of Elishah they made your awning. 8 The men of Sidon and Arvad were your oarsmen. Your men of skill, O Tyre, were there as your captains. 9 The elders of Gebal were aboard as shipwrights, repairing your leaks. All the ships of the sea and their sailors came alongside to barter for your merchandise. 10 Men of Persia, Lydia, and Put served as warriors in your army. They hung their shields and helmets on your walls; they gave you splendor. 11 Men of Arvad and Helech manned your walls all around, and the men of Gammad were in your towers. They hung their shields around your walls; they perfected your beauty.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord tells Ezekiel to take up a lament for Tyre. The city claims perfect beauty, and the poem develops that claim through the picture of an elaborately built ship.

Timber, ivory, embroidered linen and colored cloth come from many places. Skilled oarsmen, captains and shipwrights contribute their work, while warriors from other peoples add strength and splendor.

The list lets the reader see both the wealth of Tyre and its dependence on others. The city’s beauty has been assembled through materials, skills and protection drawn from far beyond itself. The opening praise prepares for the shipwreck later in the chapter.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry sees the account as a reminder that God’s concern reaches trade and everyday work, as well as worship. He also sees the different resources supplied by different countries as something people can use for one another’s good.

Wesley emphasizes the skilled work and contributions of the people named. The picture recognizes genuine beauty and ability while preparing to expose the danger of treating them as lasting security.
passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 17:24–31 explains the larger place of the nations before their Creator. God gives life and everything else, determines the times and boundaries of peoples, and intends that they should seek Him. Paul concludes by calling all people to repent in view of the judgment entrusted to the risen Jesus.

Paul does not explicitly interpret Ezekiel’s ship. His teaching adds the larger purpose behind gifts, places and opportunities that a prosperous city can mistake for proof of its own greatness: dependence on the Creator should lead people toward Him.

passages.title: Ezekiel 27:12-24
passages.section_title: What does the long list of Tyre’s trading partners show?

They exchanged slaves and bronze utensils for your merchandise. 14 The men of Beth-togarmah exchanged horses, war horses, and mules for your wares. 15 The men of Dedan were your clients; many coastlands were your market; they paid you with ivory tusks and ebony. 16 Aram was your customer because of your many products; they exchanged turquoise, purple, embroidered work, fine linen, coral, and rubies for your wares. 17 Judah and the land of Israel traded with you; they exchanged wheat from Minnith, cakes and honey, oil and balm for your merchandise. 18 Because of your many products and your great wealth of goods, Damascus traded with you wine from Helbon, wool from Zahar, 19 and casks of wine from Izal for your wares. section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The poem widens from the ship and its crew to Tyre’s trading network. Metals, animals, ivory, cloth, jewels, food, wine and spices flow through the marketplace from many peoples.

Judah and Israel are included among the trading partners. The city’s dealings are not limited to a simple division between one friend and one enemy; its wealth is woven into the lives of many neighbors.

The list also names slaves alongside goods. Human lives are part of the merchandise in this rich commercial world. The abundance is impressive, but the account gives readers reason to look beyond the surface of its splendor.

The whole catalogue establishes what is at stake when the ship breaks apart: goods, workers, customers and the people whose lives have become cargo. The coming loss reaches across the network that made Tyre prosperous.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry draws a lesson about conscience in buying and selling, recognizing the usefulness of trade while warning that wealth can make people forget its giver. Cambridge identifies the persons traded in verse 13 as slaves.

Ancient names and some details of the goods are interpreted differently in commentaries. Cambridge notes a particularly difficult text in verse 19. The main point does not depend on locating every place with certainty: the list displays the extraordinary reach and variety of Tyre’s commerce.

passages.title: Ezekiel 27:25-27
passages.section_title: What can the finest ship do when the east wind breaks it?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 25 The ships of Tarshish carried your merchandise. And you were filled with heavy cargo in the heart of the sea. 26 Your oarsmen have brought you onto the high seas, but the east wind will shatter you in the heart of the sea. 27 Your wealth, wares, and merchandise, your sailors, captains, and shipwrights, your merchants and all the warriors within you, with all the other people on board, will sink into the heart of the sea on the day of your downfall.
paragraphs: 25 The ships of Tarshish carried your merchandise. And you were filled with heavy cargo in the heart of the sea. 26 Your oarsmen have brought you onto the high seas, but the east wind will shatter you in the heart of the sea. 27 Your wealth, wares, and merchandise, your sailors, captains, and shipwrights, your merchants and all the warriors within you, with all the other people on board, will sink into the heart of the sea on the day of your downfall.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The trading ships have filled Tyre with heavy cargo. The poem then brings the magnificent vessel onto the high seas, where an east wind shatters it.

Everything gathered into the city falls together: wealth, wares, crew, merchants, warriors and the other people on board. The very fullness that displayed success cannot keep the ship afloat.

The picture concerns Tyre’s overthrow. The poem uses a catastrophe at sea to make the collapse of the city and its supporting world visible.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands the rowers as rulers and advisers, and the east wind as the king of Babylon with his army. Cambridge is more cautious about how far the image identifies particular actions by Tyre’s leaders, emphasizing the force that breaks the vessel beyond human control.

Henry reads the fall as a warning about resting hope in created powers that can themselves collapse. The difference in detail does not alter the poem’s devastating reversal of confidence.
passages.god_plan_html:
The wider biblical answer to fragile security is a foundation God supplies. First Peter 2:4–8 applies Isaiah’s promise of a chosen cornerstone to Christ and describes believers being built into a spiritual house through Him.

This is a connection between themes, not a claim that Tyre’s ship secretly represents the church. Ezekiel exposes confidence that cannot survive the downfall of its object. Peter directs people to the living Christ, the stone chosen by God, in whom those who believe will not be put to shame.

passages.title: Ezekiel 27:28-36
passages.section_title: Why do the sailors and merchants mourn so bitterly for Tyre?

versions.text: 28 The countryside will shake when your sailors cry out. 29 All who handle the oars will abandon their ships. The sailors and all the captains of the sea will stand on the shore. 30 They will raise their voices for you and cry out bitterly. They will throw dust on their heads and roll in ashes. 31 They will shave their heads for you and wrap themselves in sackcloth. They will weep over you with anguish of soul and bitter mourning. 32 As they wail and mourn over you, they will take up a lament for you: ‘Who was ever like Tyre, silenced in the middle of the sea? 33 When your wares went out to sea, you satisfied many nations. You enriched the kings of the earth with your abundant wealth and merchandise. 34 Now you are shattered by the seas in the depths of the waters; your merchandise and the people among you have gone down with you. 35 All the people of the coastlands are appalled over you. Their kings shudder with fear; their faces are contorted. 36 Those who trade among the nations hiss at you; you have come to a horrible end and will be no more.’”

The sailors and all the captains of the sea will stand on the shore. 30 They will raise their voices for you and cry out bitterly. They will throw dust on their heads and roll in ashes. 31 They will shave their heads for you and wrap themselves in sackcloth. They will weep over you with anguish of soul and bitter mourning.

You enriched the kings of the earth with your abundant wealth and merchandise. 34 Now you are shattered by the seas in the depths of the waters; your merchandise and the people among you have gone down with you.

35 All the people of the coastlands are appalled over you. Their kings shudder with fear; their faces are contorted. 36 Those who trade among the nations hiss at you; you have come to a horrible end and will be no more.’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The shipwreck produces an answering cry around the coast. Sailors leave their ships and stand on shore, throwing dust on their heads, rolling in ashes and clothing themselves in sackcloth.

Their lament remembers what Tyre supplied: its wares satisfied nations, and its trade enriched kings. Now merchandise and people have gone down together. The loss reaches those who depended on the city as well as those within it.

The closing reactions mix grief, fear and hissing. The beautiful city of the opening verses has become an object of horror. The long celebration of everything it possessed ends in silence and loss.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley reads the maritime scene as a picture of the city’s fall, with the sea that seemed its protection becoming its grave. Henry draws the lesson toward responsible use of wealth and hope in God.

The lament makes the disaster personal: people are lost with the goods, and those left on shore grieve. Recognizing the judgment does not require treating the suffering as insignificant.
passages.god_plan_html:
The commercial mourning has a closely supported parallel in Revelation 18:11–24. Merchants mourn the end of their market, a long list of cargo includes enslaved human lives, and seafarers stand at a distance lamenting a city whose wealth enriched them.

The parallel carries the critique of a powerful trading center into Revelation’s judgment on Babylon. The issue reaches beyond lost luxury: Revelation names the blood of prophets and saints among the reasons for judgment. The shared pictures call readers to see the human cost and moral character of prosperity, rather than assume that a thriving market proves all is well.

passages.title: Ezekiel 28:1-5
passages.section_title: How does Tyre’s ruler mistake success for being a god?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 And the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 2 “Son of man, tell the ruler of Tyre that this is what the Lord GOD says: Your heart is proud, and you have said, ‘I am a god; I sit in the seat of gods in the heart of the sea.’ Yet you are a man and not a god, though you have regarded your heart as that of a god. 3 Behold, you are wiser than Daniel; no secret is hidden from you! 4 By your wisdom and understanding you have gained your wealth and amassed gold and silver for your treasuries. 5 By your great skill in trading you have increased your wealth, but your heart has grown proud because of it.
paragraphs: 1 And the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 2 “Son of man, tell the ruler of Tyre that this is what the Lord GOD says: Your heart is proud, and you have said, ‘I am a god; I sit in the seat of gods in the heart of the sea.’ Yet you are a man and not a god, though you have regarded your heart as that of a god. 3 Behold, you are wiser than Daniel; no secret is hidden from you!

4 By your wisdom and understanding you have gained your wealth and amassed gold and silver for your treasuries. 5 By your great skill in trading you have increased your wealth, but your heart has grown proud because of it.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord now addresses the ruler of Tyre. The city’s wealth and splendor have become part of its leader’s claim to be a god seated in the heart of the seas.

The reply begins with the limit he has forgotten: he is a man. His wisdom and skill in trade have indeed gained riches, but those riches have made his heart proud.

The reference to being wiser than Daniel exposes the height of the claim. The passage moves from an impressive treasury to the condition of the person who possesses it. Commercial ability cannot settle the question of who he is before God.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley reads the comparison with Daniel as the ruler’s inflated estimate of his own wisdom. Cambridge also understands it as irony, while the USCCB notes describe the confusion of commercial success with divinity.

Henry emphasizes pride’s power to make a person imagine that wealth and ability put him on a level with heaven. The reading recognizes genuine skills while exposing the false conclusion drawn from them.

passages.title: Ezekiel 28:6-10
passages.section_title: Will the ruler still claim to be a god when death comes?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: Because you regard your heart as the heart of a god, 7 behold, I will bring foreigners against you, the most ruthless of nations. They will draw their swords against the beauty of your wisdom and will defile your splendor. 8 They will bring you down to the Pit, and you will die a violent death in the heart of the seas. 9 Will you still say, ‘I am a god,’ in the presence of those who slay you? You will be only a man, not a god, in the hands of those who wound you. 10 You will die the death of the uncircumcised at the hands of foreigners. For I have spoken, declares the Lord GOD.”

They will draw their swords against the beauty of your wisdom and will defile your splendor. 8 They will bring you down to the Pit, and you will die a violent death in the heart of the seas. 9 Will you still say, ‘I am a god,’ in the presence of those who slay you? You will be only a man, not a god, in the hands of those who wound you. 10 You will die the death of the uncircumcised at the hands of foreigners. For I have spoken, declares the Lord GOD.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord’s answer to the ruler’s self-exaltation is the arrival of ruthless foreigners. The beauty associated with his wisdom will be defiled, and he will be brought down to the Pit.

The question becomes painfully direct: will he still say that he is a god in the hands of those who kill him? The approaching death exposes the claim as something he cannot make true.

The death of the uncircumcised completes the picture of humiliation. The ruler’s treasured standing does not give him control over his end. The Lord’s word, rather than the ruler’s estimate of himself, determines the outcome.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The USCCB notes understand the death as a humiliating exposure of the ruler’s claim to divinity. Wesley emphasizes that the ruler remains subject to the troubles and limits of human life.

The point is the defeat of his imagined divine security. The judgment confronts his pride and conduct, rather than making outward circumcision a guarantee that another person will escape death.
passages.god_plan_html:
A useful contrast appears in John 10:14–18. Tyre’s ruler claims a status that cannot protect him when death comes. Jesus says that He lays down His life for the sheep of His own accord and has authority to take it up again.

This is a contrast between the passages, not an identification of Tyre’s ruler as a prediction of Jesus. The Gospel shows why Jesus’ death must not be understood as the collapse of an empty claim: He gives His life in obedience to the Father as the good shepherd.

passages.title: Ezekiel 28:11-19
passages.section_title: Is the lament about Tyre’s king, Satan, or both?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 Again the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 12 “Son of man, take up a lament for the king of Tyre and tell him that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘You were the seal of perfection, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty. 13 You were in Eden, the garden of God. Every kind of precious stone adorned you: ruby, topaz, and diamond, beryl, onyx, and jasper, sapphire, turquoise, and emerald. Your mountings and settings were crafted in gold, prepared on the day of your creation. 14 You were anointed as a guardian cherub, for I had ordained you. You were on the holy mountain of God; you walked among the fiery stones. 15 From the day you were created you were blameless in your ways— until wickedness was found in you. 16 By the vastness of your trade, you were filled with violence, and you sinned. So I drove you in disgrace from the mountain of God, and I banished you, O guardian cherub, from among the fiery stones. 17 Your heart grew proud of your beauty; you corrupted your wisdom because of your splendor; so I cast you to the earth; I made you a spectacle before kings. 18 By the multitude of your iniquities and the dishonesty of your trading you have profaned your sanctuaries. So I made fire come from within you, and it consumed you. I reduced you to ashes on the ground in the eyes of all who saw you. 19 All the nations who know you are appalled over you. You have come to a horrible end and will be no more.’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord introduces a lament for the king of Tyre. Its opening describes extraordinary beauty and wisdom through the language of Eden, precious stones, a guardian cherub and the holy mountain of God.

The turning point is wickedness found in one who had been blameless. Trade is filled with violence, beauty leads to pride, wisdom is corrupted, and dishonest dealings profane sanctuaries. The gifts that marked splendor have become part of the account of ruin.

The king is cast down, consumed by fire and exposed before others as an object of horror. This follows the larger movement of the Tyre chapters: apparent perfection and security give way to judgment. How the Eden and cherub language relates to the human king is the major question in interpreting the passage.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
An early Christian reading appears in Tertullian’s Against Marcion, book II, chapter 10. He sees the devil described through the person of Tyre’s ruler, reasoning that the original goodness, heavenly privilege and subsequent corruption reach beyond an ordinary human king. This is an interpretation with an early history, rather than a view introduced by one recent teacher.

Wesley reads the language as a portrayal of the human ruler’s privilege, self-importance and downfall, with the cherub picture expressing royal dignity and protection. The USCCB notes likewise describe Tyre’s leader through imagery recalling Genesis 2–3. Cambridge develops that reading through the fall and expulsion from the garden.

Where these readings differ is whether the lament reaches behind the human ruler to Satan, or uses the garden and heavenly imagery to expose the ruler himself. The different titles for ruler and king do not settle that question on their own; Cambridge notes their interchangeable use. The passage names the king of Tyre and does not explicitly name Satan.
passages.god_plan_html:
Colossians 1:15–20 places every throne, dominion, ruler and authority under the Son: all were created through Him and for Him. It also places God’s purpose of reconciliation in the peace made through the blood of His cross.

Colossians 2:13–15 joins forgiveness through the cross with the disarming and public defeat of rulers and authorities. This supplies a wider biblical answer to intimidating power, human or spiritual. It does not explicitly interpret Ezekiel 28 or decide the debated identity in the lament. The New Testament directs hope toward Christ’s authority and saving victory.

passages.title: Ezekiel 28:20-24
passages.section_title: How will Sidon come to know the Lord’s holiness?

They will know that I am the LORD when I execute judgments against her and demonstrate My holiness through her. 23 I will send a plague against her and shed blood in her streets; the slain will fall within her, while the sword is against her on every side. Then they will know that I am the LORD. 24 For the people of Israel will no longer face a pricking brier or a painful thorn from all around them who treat them with contempt. Then they will know that I am the Lord GOD.’
paragraphs: 20 Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 21 “Son of man, set your face against Sidon and prophesy against her. 22 And you are to declare that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Behold, I am against you, O Sidon, and I will be glorified within you. They will know that I am the LORD when I execute judgments against her and demonstrate My holiness through her. 23 I will send a plague against her and shed blood in her streets; the slain will fall within her, while the sword is against her on every side. Then they will know that I am the LORD. 24 For the people of Israel will no longer face a pricking brier or a painful thorn from all around them who treat them with contempt. Then they will know that I am the Lord GOD.’

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord directs Ezekiel to speak against Sidon. He announces plague, bloodshed and the sword, saying that His judgments will demonstrate His holiness and make Him known.

The announcement ends by turning toward Israel’s experience among its neighbors. Their contempt has been like a pricking brier or painful thorn. The Lord promises an end to that hostility.

The purpose is repeated through the section: they will know that He is the Lord. The confrontation is not merely a contest between neighboring cities; it concerns His holiness and His people’s life among those who scorn them.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry connects Sidon’s hostility with its corrupting religious influence on Israel. Wesley explains the brier and thorn as the troublesome neighbors named in these judgments.

Wesley also says that the full removal of this threat had not yet been accomplished. The wording looks beyond an isolated military loss toward the security developed in the chapter’s closing promise.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 28:25-26
passages.section_title: What does the Lord promise when He gathers Israel again?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 25 This is what the Lord GOD says: ‘When I gather the house of Israel from the peoples among whom they have been scattered, I will show Myself holy among them in the sight of the nations. Then they will dwell in their own land, which I have given to My servant Jacob. 26 And there they will dwell securely, build houses, and plant vineyards. They will dwell securely when I execute judgments against all those around them who treat them with contempt. Then they will know that I am the LORD their God.’”

Then they will dwell in their own land, which I have given to My servant Jacob. 26 And there they will dwell securely, build houses, and plant vineyards. They will dwell securely when I execute judgments against all those around them who treat them with contempt. Then they will know that I am the LORD their God.’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The chapter closes with a promise to the house of Israel. The Lord will gather His scattered people from the nations and show His holiness among them in the sight of those nations.

The promised life is concrete: dwelling in the land given to Jacob, building houses and planting vineyards. Security means being able to live and work without the contemptuous neighbors continuing to threaten them.

The Lord brings the gathering and the judgments together. The outcome is not simply possession of land but recognition of the One who has acted: they will know Him as the Lord their God.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Jamieson–Fausset–Brown sees a partial fulfillment in the return from Babylon and a fuller future fulfillment for Israel under Christ. Wesley also regards the complete freedom from the hostile neighbors as still awaiting fulfillment.

Henry includes restored safety and prosperity, then carries the full promise toward the heavenly home of all God’s redeemed people. These readings differ in how they describe the final setting and scope, while agreeing that the Lord Himself brings His people into lasting security.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ezekiel 36:22–28 develops the same gathering and display of holiness by adding cleansing from idols, a new heart and the gift of God’s Spirit. The restoration reaches the people’s inner life and their obedience, as well as the land in which they dwell.

Hebrews 8:8–13 quotes the promise of a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, including God’s law within them, knowledge of Him and forgiveness of sins. This wider covenant picture explains why knowing the Lord is more than the relief of surviving a threat: His purpose includes a renewed relationship with His people.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 29:1-7
passages.section_title: Why is Pharaoh pictured as a monster caught in his own river?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 In the tenth year, on the twelfth day of the tenth month, the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 2 “Son of man, set your face against Pharaoh king of Egypt and prophesy against him and against all Egypt. 3 Speak to him and tell him that this is what the Lord GOD says: Behold, I am against you, O Pharaoh king of Egypt, O great monster who lies among his rivers, who says, ‘The Nile is mine; I made it myself.’ 4 But I will put hooks in your jaws and cause the fish of your streams to cling to your scales. I will haul you up out of your rivers, and all the fish of your streams will cling to your scales. 5 I will leave you in the desert, you and all the fish of your streams. You will fall on the open field and will not be taken away or gathered for burial. I have given you as food to the beasts of the earth and the birds of the air. 6 Then all the people of Egypt will know that I am the LORD. For you were only a staff of reeds to the house of Israel. 7 When Israel took hold of you with their hands, you splintered, tearing all their shoulders; when they leaned on you, you broke, and their backs were wrenched.

You will fall on the open field and will not be taken away or gathered for burial. For you were only a staff of reeds to the house of Israel. 7 When Israel took hold of you with their hands, you splintered, tearing all their shoulders; when they leaned on you, you broke, and their backs were wrenched.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord directs Ezekiel against Pharaoh and Egypt. The ruler boasts that the Nile belongs to him and that he made it. The image places him at ease in the very waters he claims as his own creation.

The Hebrew word תַּנִּין, tannin (tah-NEEN), is used for a serpent, dragon or sea creature in Brown–Driver–Briggs. Here the river monster pictures Pharaoh. The Lord will hook its jaws, haul it out with the fish clinging to it, and leave it exposed as food for animals and birds.

The accusation then changes pictures: Egypt has been a staff of reeds for Israel. Instead of supporting those who lean on it, it breaks and injures them. Jeremiah 37:4–11 describes Egypt’s attempted help during Jerusalem’s siege and the Lord’s warning that it would not deliver the city.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley reads the monster as a crocodile and the fish as the people attached to their king. The USCCB notes also explain the Nile crocodile picture while noting the word’s broader associations with a threatening sea monster.

Henry emphasizes pride in possessions and the danger of a false source of security. The two pictures belong together: Egypt claims a power it does not possess and fails the people who depend on it.
passages.god_plan_html:
A supported parallel appears in Revelation 19:11–21, where the rider called the Word of God defeats opposing rulers and armies, and birds feed on the slain. Both passages expose power that cannot protect itself against the Lord.

This shared judgment picture does not establish that every detail in Ezekiel describes the same event or date. Revelation carries the larger theme toward Christ’s victory over the powers gathered against Him. Their rank and strength do not decide the outcome.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 29:8-16
passages.section_title: What do Egypt’s forty years of desolation and its return mean?

versions.text: 8 Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: I will bring a sword against you and cut off from you man and beast. 9 The land of Egypt will become a desolate wasteland. Then they will know that I am the LORD. Because you said, ‘The Nile is mine; I made it,’ 10 therefore I am against you and against your rivers. I will turn the land of Egypt into a ruin, a desolate wasteland from Migdol to Syene, and as far as the border of Cush. 11 No foot of man or beast will pass through, and it will be uninhabited for forty years. 12 I will make the land of Egypt a desolation among desolate lands, and her cities will lie desolate for forty years among the ruined cities. And I will disperse the Egyptians among the nations and scatter them throughout the countries. 13 For this is what the Lord GOD says: At the end of forty years I will gather the Egyptians from the nations to which they were scattered. 14 I will restore Egypt from captivity and bring them back to the land of Pathros, the land of their origin. There they will be a lowly kingdom. 15 Egypt will be the lowliest of kingdoms and will never again exalt itself above the nations. Then they will know that I am the Lord GOD.”

Then they will know that I am the Lord GOD.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord answers Egypt’s claim to have made the Nile with a threat against its land and rivers. The announced devastation reaches from Migdol to Syene and the border of Cush, with neither people nor animals passing through for forty years.

The people will be scattered, but the announcement does not end there. At the end of the forty years, the Lord will gather the Egyptians and restore them to Pathros, the land of their origin.

The restored kingdom will be lowly rather than dominant. Egypt will no longer be Israel’s object of trust, drawing it away from the Lord. The passage therefore holds together a severe humiliation, a return and the ending of a destructive dependence.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley reads the forty years as an actual period during the Babylonian era, ending with Cyrus. Jamieson–Fausset–Brown gives more weight to the picture of a wilderness period of political and social humiliation, rather than requiring that no person or animal literally set foot in the land.

A future fulfillment has also been considered. A Lamb & Lion discussion in The Lamplighter raises that only as a slight possibility connected with a future drought, while favoring an ancient judgment. It does not present a settled future timetable.

These readings differ over the period and how literally to take the description. The text clearly announces the fall of Egypt’s pride, a return after judgment and a reduced kingdom. An exact historical date range should not be treated as established simply because a commentator proposes it.
passages.god_plan_html:
Isaiah 19:19–25 adds a wider promise for Egypt: the Lord will make Himself known, hear its cry, and bring people to worship Him. The picture culminates in Egypt and Assyria sharing blessing with Israel.

Ezekiel’s lowly kingdom and Isaiah’s worshiping people should not be flattened into a single detailed calendar. Together they show that the humbling of a proud nation need not be the end of God’s purposes for its people. The larger biblical horizon includes the Lord healing and receiving those who turn to Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 29:17-21
passages.section_title: Why is Egypt called the wages for Babylon’s labor?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 In the twenty-seventh year, on the first day of the first month, the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 18 “Son of man, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon caused his army to labor strenuously against Tyre. Every head was made bald and every shoulder made raw. But he and his army received no wages from Tyre for the labor they expended on it. 19 Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: I will give the land of Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, who will carry off its wealth, seize its spoil, and remove its plunder. This will be the wages for his army. 20 I have given him the land of Egypt as the reward for his labor, because it was done for Me, declares the Lord GOD. 21 In that day I will cause a horn to sprout for the house of Israel, and I will open your mouth to speak among them. Then they will know that I am the LORD.”

Every head was made bald and every shoulder made raw. But he and his army received no wages from Tyre for the labor they expended on it. 19 Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: I will give the land of Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, who will carry off its wealth, seize its spoil, and remove its plunder. This will be the wages for his army. 20 I have given him the land of Egypt as the reward for his labor, because it was done for Me, declares the Lord GOD. 21 In that day I will cause a horn to sprout for the house of Israel, and I will open your mouth to speak among them. Then they will know that I am the LORD.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
This message is dated to the twenty-seventh year, later than the message at the beginning of the chapter. The arrangement follows the subject of Egypt rather than keeping every announcement in chronological order.

The Lord describes the hard labor of Nebuchadnezzar’s army against Tyre: bald heads, raw shoulders and no wages from the effort. He will give Egypt’s wealth and plunder as the reward for that work, which He says was done for Him.

The message closes by turning toward Israel. The Lord will cause a horn to sprout for His people and open Ezekiel’s mouth among them. Alongside the fall of a false support comes a promise of renewed strength and recognition of the Lord.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry understands the plunder as payment to the ambitious people God employs, while seeing mercy for Israel beyond its adversity. Wesley likewise distinguishes the Lord’s work through Babylon from the intentions of the Babylonians themselves.

The USCCB notes and Cambridge explain the horn as renewed strength for Israel. Cambridge takes it as a general promise of restored prosperity and influence; Jamieson–Fausset–Brown also looks toward the fuller glory associated with the Messiah.
passages.god_plan_html:
The picture of a horn of deliverance appears in Luke 1:67–75. Zechariah praises God for raising a horn of salvation in David’s house, remembering His covenant and granting His people freedom to serve Him in holiness and righteousness.

Luke does not explicitly quote Ezekiel 29, and a horn does not identify the Messiah in every passage. The shared theme is the strength and deliverance God raises for His people. Luke places that hope within the coming salvation through David’s house, with service to God as its purpose.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 30:1-9
passages.section_title: Why does Egypt’s day of judgment shake its allies too?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Again the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 2 “Son of man, prophesy and declare that this is what the Lord GOD says: Wail, ‘Alas for that day!’ 3 For the day is near, the Day of the LORD is near. It will be a day of clouds, a time of doom for the nations. 4 A sword will come against Egypt, and there will be anguish in Cush when the slain fall in Egypt, its wealth is taken away, and its foundations are torn down. 5 Cush, Put, and Lud, and all the various peoples, as well as Libya and the men of the covenant land, will fall with Egypt by the sword. 6 For this is what the LORD says: The allies of Egypt will fall, and her proud strength will collapse. From Migdol to Syene they will fall by the sword within her, declares the Lord GOD. 7 They will be desolate among desolate lands, and their cities will lie among ruined cities. 8 Then they will know that I am the LORD when I set fire to Egypt and all her helpers are shattered. 9 On that day messengers will go out from Me in ships to frighten Cush out of complacency. Anguish will come upon them on the day of Egypt’s doom. For it is indeed coming.

Anguish will come upon them on the day of Egypt’s doom. For it is indeed coming.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The next message opens with a call to wail because the Day of the Lord is near. It is a day of clouds and doom for the nations, beginning with a sword against Egypt and anguish in Cush.

The threat reaches the peoples and allies bound up with Egypt. When its proud strength collapses, the support built around it also fails. Its ruined cities become part of the wider desolation.

Messengers go out in ships to frighten Cush out of complacency. The Lord’s action in one place carries a warning beyond its borders. The repeated outcome is that the people will know Him when Egypt and its helpers are shattered.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads the announced destruction through Babylon and its army, while distinguishing such judgments from the greater wrath from which Jesus delivers His people. Wesley emphasizes Egypt’s allies sharing in the calamity.

Cambridge gives the Day of the Lord a wider reach as the Lord’s decisive judgment and vindication of His cause. Gaebelein, in his discussion of these chapters, also sees earlier national judgments as anticipating the final judgment. These readings connect the immediate setting and the larger horizon differently; the phrase alone does not supply a detailed seven-year schedule.
passages.god_plan_html:
First Thessalonians 5:1–11 carries the Day of the Lord theme into the church’s expectation. Paul contrasts claims of peace and security with sudden destruction, then calls believers to stay awake, sober, faithful and loving.

His purpose is not to give believers a way to date Egypt’s overthrow. He directs them toward the salvation obtained through Jesus Christ, who died so that they might live with Him, and tells them to encourage one another. The larger judgment theme produces watchfulness and hope grounded in Christ.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 30:10-19
passages.section_title: What happens to Egypt’s cities and idols when Babylon comes?

By the hands of foreigners I will bring desolation upon the land and everything in it. section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord names Nebuchadnezzar and his people as the force He will bring against Egypt. The land will be filled with the slain, its streams will dry, and foreigners will possess what it had depended upon.

The announcement moves through the cities and regions of Egypt. Idols and images in Memphis will be destroyed; fear, fire and the sword will reach the places named. Pelusium, the stronghold, cannot secure the land.

Young men fall and cities go into captivity. At Tahpanhes the breaking of Egypt’s yoke is paired with the end of its proud strength. The list leaves no refuge in the prestige of a city, its defenses or its objects of worship.

The closing line states the purpose again: the Lord will execute judgment, and they will know that He is the Lord.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry understands the passage as the breadth of the destruction announced through the Babylonian army. Wesley connects the broken yoke with the ending of Egypt’s oppressive power.

The threatened drying of the rivers is also read in different ways. Wesley suggests the enemy diverting them, while Cambridge emphasizes how devastating the loss of water would be. The Lord’s announcement states the loss; it does not spell out the engineering or maintenance failures by which it occurs.

passages.title: Ezekiel 30:20-26
passages.section_title: Why is Pharaoh’s broken arm contrasted with Babylon’s strengthened arms?

versions.label: BSB

See, it has not been bound up for healing, or splinted for strength to hold the sword. 22 Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: Behold, I am against Pharaoh king of Egypt. I will break his arms, both the strong one and the one already broken, and will make the sword fall from his hand. 23 I will disperse the Egyptians among the nations and scatter them throughout the lands. 24 I will strengthen the arms of Babylon’s king and place My sword in his hand, but I will break the arms of Pharaoh, who will groan before him like a mortally wounded man. 25 I will strengthen the arms of Babylon’s king, but Pharaoh’s arms will fall limp. Then they will know that I am the LORD, when I place My sword in the hand of Babylon’s king, and he wields it against the land of Egypt. 26 I will disperse the Egyptians among the nations and scatter them throughout the lands. Then they will know that I am the LORD.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
This dated message pictures Pharaoh with an already broken arm that has not been bound up to heal or strengthened to hold a sword. The image makes his inability to sustain the fight visible.

The Lord will break both arms, including the one still strong, so that the sword falls from Pharaoh’s hand. In contrast, He will strengthen Babylon’s king and place His sword in that king’s hand.

The movement of power is therefore part of the Lord’s announced action. Pharaoh’s groaning, Egypt’s defeat and the scattering of its people expose the limits of the power on which Israel had leaned.

The repeated promise is that they will know the Lord when these things happen. The final emphasis is not admiration for Babylon’s might, but recognition of the One who gives and removes strength.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands the strong and broken arms as the remaining and already damaged parts of Egypt’s power. Cambridge considers the possibility that the already broken arm refers to Egypt’s failed attempt to relieve Jerusalem, while continuing to treat the arms as a figure for military strength.

Henry reads the contrast as Egypt growing weaker while Babylon grows stronger. The picture explains the rise and fall of these powers without requiring an otherwise unrecorded medical diagnosis of Pharaoh.

passages.title: Ezekiel 31:1-9
passages.section_title: What does the picture of a towering cedar say to Egypt?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 In the eleventh year, on the first day of the third month, the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 2 “Son of man, say to Pharaoh king of Egypt and to his multitude: ‘Who can be compared to your greatness? 3 Look at Assyria, a cedar in Lebanon, with beautiful branches that shaded the forest. It towered on high; its top was among the clouds. 4 The waters made it grow; the deep springs made it tall, directing their streams all around its base and sending their channels to all the trees of the field. 5 Therefore it towered higher than all the trees of the field. Its branches multiplied, and its boughs grew long as it spread them out because of the abundant waters. 6 All the birds of the air nested in its branches, and all the beasts of the field gave birth beneath its boughs; all the great nations lived in its shade. 7 It was beautiful in its greatness, in the length of its limbs, for its roots extended to abundant waters. 8 The cedars in the garden of God could not rival it; the cypresses could not compare with its branches, nor the plane trees match its boughs. No tree in the garden of God could compare with its beauty. 9 I made it beautiful with its many branches, the envy of all the trees of Eden, which were in the garden of God.’

It towered on high; its top was among the clouds. 4 The waters made it grow; the deep springs made it tall, directing their streams all around its base and sending their channels to all the trees of the field.

5 Therefore it towered higher than all the trees of the field. Its branches multiplied, and its boughs grew long as it spread them out because of the abundant waters. 6 All the birds of the air nested in its branches, and all the beasts of the field gave birth beneath its boughs; all the great nations lived in its shade. 7 It was beautiful in its greatness, in the length of its limbs, for its roots extended to abundant waters. 8 The cedars in the garden of God could not rival it; the cypresses could not compare with its branches, nor the plane trees match its boughs. No tree in the garden of God could compare with its beauty. 9 I made it beautiful with its many branches, the envy of all the trees of Eden, which were in the garden of God.’

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord asks Pharaoh and his multitude whom they can be compared with in greatness. The BSB then names Assyria and pictures it as a magnificent cedar in Lebanon, rising above the other trees.

Its growth depends on abundant waters. Birds nest in its branches, animals give birth beneath it, and great nations live in its shade. The tree represents an impressive power that gathers others under its protection.

The beauty is described through the garden of God and the trees of Eden. The Lord says that He made the tree beautiful. The picture prepares a question for Egypt: if such greatness was received rather than self-created, what right does it give a ruler to consider himself secure?
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley read the cedar as Assyria, whose greatness becomes a warning to Egypt. The USCCB notes likewise understand the passage as a comparison with Assyria’s fall.

Cambridge takes a different view of the opening wording, reading it as the name of a tree and understanding the cedar to picture Pharaoh directly. The readings differ over the starting comparison, while agreeing that the magnificent tree portrays a power whose pride and fall must be faced.
passages.god_plan_html:
A supported parallel, with a different outcome, appears in Mark 4:30–34. Jesus compares God’s kingdom to a mustard seed that grows large branches where birds can nest in its shade.

The shared sheltering-tree picture does not make the kingdoms identical. Ezekiel’s great power will collapse through pride; Jesus describes God’s kingdom growing from a small beginning. The comparison turns attention from the size of an earthly empire toward the kingdom God brings.

passages.title: Ezekiel 31:10-14
passages.section_title: Why is the great cedar cut down?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Since it became great in height and set its top among the clouds, and it grew proud on account of its height, 11 I delivered it into the hand of the ruler of the nations, for him to deal with it according to its wickedness. I have banished it. 12 Foreigners, the most ruthless of the nations, cut it down and left it. Its branches have fallen on the mountains and in every valley; its boughs lay broken in all the earth’s ravines. And all the peoples of the earth left its shade and abandoned it. 13 All the birds of the air nested on its fallen trunk, and all the beasts of the field lived among its boughs. 14 This happened so that no other trees by the waters would become great in height and set their tops among the clouds, and no other well-watered trees would reach them in height. For they have all been consigned to death, to the depths of the earth, among the mortals who descend to the Pit.’

For they have all been consigned to death, to the depths of the earth, among the mortals who descend to the Pit.’

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The tree’s height becomes the occasion for pride. Its top among the clouds now expresses the self-exaltation that brings the Lord’s judgment.

The Lord delivers it to the ruler of the nations, and ruthless foreigners cut it down. Branches lie broken across mountains, valleys and ravines, while the peoples once sheltered by it leave its shade.

The fallen tree becomes a place for birds and animals, reversing the scene of life beneath its standing branches. Its downfall warns the other well-watered trees against the same exaltation. Greatness does not exempt them from being brought down among mortals who descend to the Pit.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads the connection as greatness followed by pride and then ruin. The fall warns others against the same course. Wesley likewise takes the announcement as a warning to rulers and flourishing states.

Cambridge emphasizes the violent and dishonorable death pictured here, rather than treating the passage merely as a reminder that everyone eventually dies. The warning concerns what proud power does and the judgment to which that conduct leads.

passages.title: Ezekiel 31:15-18
passages.section_title: Why do the trees of Eden appear among the dead?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 This is what the Lord GOD says: ‘On the day it was brought down to Sheol, I caused mourning. I covered the deep because of it; I held back its rivers; its abundant waters were restrained. I made Lebanon mourn for it, and all the trees of the field fainted because of it. 16 I made the nations quake at the sound of its downfall, when I cast it down to Sheol with those who descend to the Pit. Then all the trees of Eden, the choicest and best of Lebanon, all the well-watered trees, were consoled in the earth below. 17 They too descended with it to Sheol, to those slain by the sword. As its allies they had lived in its shade among the nations. 18 Who then is like you in glory and greatness among the trees of Eden? You also will be brought down to the depths of the earth to be with the trees of Eden. You will lie among the uncircumcised, with those slain by the sword. This is Pharaoh and all his multitude, declares the Lord GOD.’”

I covered the deep because of it; I held back its rivers; its abundant waters were restrained. You also will be brought down to the depths of the earth to be with the trees of Eden. You will lie among the uncircumcised, with those slain by the sword. This is Pharaoh and all his multitude, declares the Lord GOD.’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The fall of the cedar is described as a descent to Sheol. Waters are restrained, Lebanon mourns, and the trees faint. The language gives the collapse a significance that reaches beyond the tree itself.

The Hebrew word שְׁאוֹל, sheol (sheh-OHL), names the realm of the dead in Brown–Driver–Briggs, which specifically includes these verses. The great tree is now among those who have gone down to the Pit.

The trees of Eden in the earth below are consoled at its arrival, and its allies share its descent. The final line turns the warning directly onto Pharaoh and his multitude: impressive glory does not give them a different end.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Cambridge understand the trees as rulers or states. Their consolation belongs to the scene among the dead: another mighty power has shared their humiliation.

Henry emphasizes how many fall when the great fall, and the need to learn humility from their end. The garden picture is being used to describe these powers; it does not require treating each tree as a separately identified angel.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 5:12–21 addresses the wider reign of death through Adam, then sets against it the gift that comes through Jesus Christ. Those who receive God’s abundant grace and gift of righteousness reign in life through Him.

Paul does not explicitly interpret Ezekiel’s trees. His teaching adds the larger answer to the death that earthly greatness cannot escape: God’s saving purpose is not exhausted by bringing proud rulers down. Through Christ, grace brings righteousness and eternal life.

passages.title: Ezekiel 32:1-10
passages.section_title: What happens when the Lord catches Pharaoh in His net?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 In the twelfth year, on the first day of the twelfth month, the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 2 “Son of man, take up a lament for Pharaoh king of Egypt and say to him: ‘You are like a lion among the nations; you are like a monster in the seas. You thrash about in your rivers, churning up the waters with your feet and muddying the streams.’ 3 This is what the Lord GOD says: ‘I will spread My net over you with a company of many peoples, and they will draw you up in My net. 4 I will abandon you on the land and hurl you into the open field. I will cause all the birds of the air to settle upon you, and all the beasts of the earth to eat their fill of you. 5 I will put your flesh on the mountains and fill the valleys with your remains. 6 I will drench the land with the flow of your blood, all the way to the mountains— the ravines will be filled. 7 When I extinguish you, I will cover the heavens and darken their stars. I will cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon will not give its light. 8 All the shining lights in the heavens I will darken over you, and I will bring darkness upon your land,’ declares the Lord GOD. 9 ‘I will trouble the hearts of many peoples, when I bring about your destruction among the nations, in countries you do not know. 10 I will cause many peoples to be appalled over you, and their kings will shudder in horror because of you when I brandish My sword before them. On the day of your downfall each of them will tremble every moment for his life.’

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord commands a lament for Pharaoh. He is pictured as a lion among the nations and a monster thrashing in the waters, churning and muddying the streams.

The Lord will spread a net with a company of peoples and haul the creature onto land. The exposed remains become food for birds and animals, and the land is drenched with blood.

The scene expands to darkened stars, sun and moon. Egypt’s fall shakes the hearts of peoples in lands it has not known, and kings tremble for their own lives. The ruler who spread disturbance now becomes a warning that reaches far beyond his borders.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands the monster’s activity as the harmful effect of Pharaoh’s armies on neighboring peoples. Henry sees the beast picture as exposing an oppressor beneath the appearance of worldly grandeur.

Cambridge reads the darkened heavens as the shock of so great a power’s destruction, using language also associated with the Day of the Lord. Henry also carries the judgment picture toward the defeat of Christ’s enemies. The wider connection should be distinguished from assigning every detail to one exact future calendar.
passages.god_plan_html:
A supported parallel appears in Matthew 24:29–31: darkened sun and moon, shaken heavenly powers, mourning peoples and the coming of the Son of Man. Jesus also speaks there of His angels gathering His elect.

The shared prophetic language connects the humbling of earthly power with the larger display of God’s authority. Matthew does not explicitly identify Ezekiel’s Egyptian judgment as that same event. Its additional emphasis is the Son’s glory and the gathering of His people, alongside the terror associated with judgment.

passages.title: Ezekiel 32:11-16
passages.section_title: Why do Egypt’s busy waters become still?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 For this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘The sword of the king of Babylon will come against you! 12 I will make your hordes fall by the swords of the mighty, the most ruthless of all nations. They will ravage the pride of Egypt and all her multitudes will be destroyed. 13 I will slaughter all her cattle beside the abundant waters. No human foot will muddy them again, and no cattle hooves will disturb them. 14 Then I will let her waters settle and will make her rivers flow like oil,’ declares the Lord GOD. 15 ‘When I make the land of Egypt a desolation and empty it of all that filled it, when I strike down all who live there, then they will know that I am the LORD.’ 16 This is the lament they will chant for her; the daughters of the nations will chant it. Over Egypt and all her multitudes they will chant it, declares the Lord GOD.”

They will ravage the pride of Egypt and all her multitudes will be destroyed. 13 I will slaughter all her cattle beside the abundant waters. No human foot will muddy them again, and no cattle hooves will disturb them. 14 Then I will let her waters settle and will make her rivers flow like oil,’ declares the Lord GOD. 15 ‘When I make the land of Egypt a desolation and empty it of all that filled it, when I strike down all who live there, then they will know that I am the LORD.’ 16 This is the lament they will chant for her; the daughters of the nations will chant it. Over Egypt and all her multitudes they will chant it, declares the Lord GOD.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord names the sword of Babylon’s king as coming against Egypt. Ruthless warriors will ravage its pride and destroy its multitudes.

The cattle beside the waters will be removed, and neither human feet nor cattle hooves will muddy the rivers. The waters settle and flow like oil. The quiet follows the removal of the life and activity that had disturbed them.

The emptied land becomes the subject of a lament chanted by the daughters of the nations. The close repeats that the devastation will bring recognition of the Lord.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Cambridge explains the waters flowing like oil as smooth, clear waters no longer stirred up by people or animals. Henry and Wesley also draw a picture of heaviness and sadness over the nation.

These explanations stay with the comparison: the rivers are said to flow like oil. The verse does not say that the water becomes oil or blood.

passages.title: Ezekiel 32:17-21
passages.section_title: Why must Egypt be laid among the other fallen nations?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 In the twelfth year, on the fifteenth day of the month, the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 18 “Son of man, wail for the multitudes of Egypt, and consign her and the daughters of the mighty nations to the depths of the earth with those who descend to the Pit: 19 Whom do you surpass in beauty? Go down and be placed with the uncircumcised! 20 They will fall among those slain by the sword. The sword is appointed! Let them drag her away along with all her multitudes. 21 Mighty chiefs will speak from the midst of Sheol about Egypt and her allies: ‘They have come down and lie with the uncircumcised, with those slain by the sword.’

Go down and be placed with the uncircumcised! 20 They will fall among those slain by the sword. The sword is appointed! Let them drag her away along with all her multitudes. 21 Mighty chiefs will speak from the midst of Sheol about Egypt and her allies: ‘They have come down and lie with the uncircumcised, with those slain by the sword.’

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
A further dated message tells Ezekiel to wail for Egypt’s multitudes and consign the nation to the depths with those who descend to the Pit. Its beauty is challenged by the same question raised over its greatness.

Egypt will fall among those slain by the sword and be placed with the uncircumcised. Its own standing does not secure a separate, privileged outcome.

The scene pictures mighty chiefs speaking from Sheol about Egypt and its allies. The nation entering the place of the dead finds others already there. The following verses name those whose fate it now shares.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Cambridge reads this as a funeral song in which nations and their leaders are pictured together among the dead. Their ruined communities appear as groups gathered around their graves.

Henry recognizes the destruction of nations as the main picture while also seeing a warning about the judgment of unrepentant people. The public fall of a kingdom and the ultimate question of judgment are connected, without making the poem a detailed map of the unseen world.

passages.title: Ezekiel 32:22-26
passages.section_title: What do Assyria, Elam, Meshech and Tubal have in common?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 Assyria is there with her whole company; her graves are all around her. All of them are slain, fallen by the sword. 23 Her graves are set in the depths of the Pit, and her company is all around her grave. All of them are slain, fallen by the sword— those who once spread terror in the land of the living. 24 Elam is there with all her multitudes around her grave. All of them are slain, fallen by the sword— those who went down uncircumcised to the earth below, who once spread their terror in the land of the living. They bear their disgrace with those who descend to the Pit. 25 Among the slain they prepare a resting place for Elam with all her hordes, with her graves all around her. All of them are uncircumcised, slain by the sword, although their terror was once spread in the land of the living. They bear their disgrace with those who descend to the Pit. They are placed among the slain. 26 Meshech and Tubal are there with all their multitudes, with their graves all around them. All of them are uncircumcised, slain by the sword, because they spread their terror in the land of the living.
