section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The lament names Assyria with its company, Elam with its multitudes, and Meshech and Tubal with their people. Graves surround them, and each group lies among those slain by the sword.

The repeated accusation is that they spread terror in the land of the living. Their power was experienced by others as fear and violence.

Now they bear disgrace with those who descend to the Pit. The repetition makes Egypt’s warning unmistakable: the ability to terrify others does not give a nation immunity from judgment or a lasting place above those it threatened.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands the scene as the disgrace of once-powerful rulers, subjects and allies. Cambridge emphasizes the consequence of lives marked by violence: their dishonor follows them into the scene of death.

The names serve the lament’s repeated warning. The passage does not require turning them into a complete sequence of later world empires in order to understand why Egypt is being shown their graves.

passages.title: Ezekiel 32:27-32
passages.section_title: What comfort can Pharaoh find among the fallen?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 27 They do not lie down with the fallen warriors of old, who went down to Sheol with their weapons of war, whose swords were placed under their heads, whose shields rested on their bones, although the terror of the mighty was once in the land of the living. 28 But you too will be shattered and lie down among the uncircumcised, with those slain by the sword. 29 Edom is there, and all her kings and princes, who despite their might are laid among those slain by the sword. They lie down with the uncircumcised, with those who descend to the Pit. 30 All the leaders of the north and all the Sidonians are there; they went down in disgrace with the slain, despite the terror of their might. They lie uncircumcised with those slain by the sword and bear their shame with those who descend to the Pit. 31 Pharaoh will see them and be comforted over all his multitude— Pharaoh and all his army, slain by the sword, declares the Lord GOD. 32 For I will spread My terror in the land of the living, so that Pharaoh and all his multitude will be laid to rest among the uncircumcised, with those slain by the sword, declares the Lord GOD.”

29 Edom is there, and all her kings and princes, who despite their might are laid among those slain by the sword. They lie down with the uncircumcised, with those who descend to the Pit. 30 All the leaders of the north and all the Sidonians are there; they went down in disgrace with the slain, despite the terror of their might. They lie uncircumcised with those slain by the sword and bear their shame with those who descend to the Pit.

31 Pharaoh will see them and be comforted over all his multitude— Pharaoh and all his army, slain by the sword, declares the Lord GOD. 32 For I will spread My terror in the land of the living, so that Pharaoh and all his multitude will be laid to rest among the uncircumcised, with those slain by the sword, declares the Lord GOD.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The lament refers to warriors who went down with their weapons, then warns its hearer of being shattered among those slain by the sword. Military standing cannot remove the threatened judgment.

Edom’s rulers, the leaders of the north and the Sidonians are also there, despite the terror of their might. The repeated contrast is between what these powers once made others feel and the disgrace they now bear.

Pharaoh will see them and be comforted concerning his own multitude. This is the grim consolation of discovering that other mighty peoples share the same end. It is not a restoration of Egypt’s former power.

The Lord closes by declaring that He will spread His terror in the land of the living. Pharaoh and his multitude will be laid with the fallen. The judgments against the nations end with their inability to place themselves beyond His authority.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley reads verse 27 through a contrast in the honor given to fallen warriors. Cambridge considers the wording difficult and reads the burial scene as another expression of lives and deaths marked by violence. The BSB keeps the distinction between the groups who do not lie together, and refers to shields resting on the warriors’ bones.

Henry and Wesley both regard Pharaoh’s comfort as poor comfort: sharing the humiliation of others is no deliverance from his own. Henry also points beyond the fall of nations toward the resurrection and judgment taught by Christ.
passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 2:14–18 gives a larger answer to the fear of death. The Son shares human flesh and blood, makes atonement as a merciful and faithful high priest, and through His death breaks the devil’s power of death and frees those enslaved by that fear.

Hebrews does not explicitly quote this lament. It adds a hope greater than Pharaoh’s discovery that others have fallen too. The saving help comes from Christ entering human suffering and death on behalf of those He helps, rather than from finding a mightier earthly power in which to hide.

passages.title: Ezekiel 33:1-9
passages.section_title: What is the watchman responsible for?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Again the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 2 “Son of man, speak to your people and tell them: ‘Suppose I bring the sword against a land, and the people of that land choose a man from among them, appointing him as their watchman, 3 and he sees the sword coming against that land and blows the ram’s horn to warn the people. 4 Then if anyone hears the sound of the horn but fails to heed the warning, and the sword comes and takes him away, his blood will be on his own head. 5 Since he heard the sound of the horn but failed to heed the warning, his blood will be on his own head. If he had heeded the warning, he would have saved his life. 6 But if the watchman sees the sword coming and fails to blow the horn to warn the people, and the sword comes and takes away a life, then that one will be taken away in his iniquity, but I will hold the watchman accountable for his blood.’ 7 As for you, O son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel; so hear the word from My mouth and give them the warning from Me. 8 If I say to the wicked, ‘O wicked man, you will surely die,’ but you do not speak out to dissuade him from his way, then that wicked man will die in his iniquity, yet I will hold you accountable for his blood. 9 But if you warn the wicked man to turn from his way, and he does not turn from it, he will die in his iniquity, but you will have saved your life.
paragraphs: 1 Again the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 2 “Son of man, speak to your people and tell them: ‘Suppose I bring the sword against a land, and the people of that land choose a man from among them, appointing him as their watchman, 3 and he sees the sword coming against that land and blows the ram’s horn to warn the people. 4 Then if anyone hears the sound of the horn but fails to heed the warning, and the sword comes and takes him away, his blood will be on his own head. 5 Since he heard the sound of the horn but failed to heed the warning, his blood will be on his own head. If he had heeded the warning, he would have saved his life. 6 But if the watchman sees the sword coming and fails to blow the horn to warn the people, and the sword comes and takes away a life, then that one will be taken away in his iniquity, but I will hold the watchman accountable for his blood.’

7 As for you, O son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel; so hear the word from My mouth and give them the warning from Me. 8 If I say to the wicked, ‘O wicked man, you will surely die,’ but you do not speak out to dissuade him from his way, then that wicked man will die in his iniquity, yet I will hold you accountable for his blood. 9 But if you warn the wicked man to turn from his way, and he does not turn from it, he will die in his iniquity, but you will have saved your life.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord begins with the familiar work of a watchman. When an enemy approaches, he must sound the warning. A person who hears but refuses to respond bears responsibility for that refusal.

If the watchman sees the danger and remains silent, he too is accountable when someone is taken. The failure of one person does not make the other person’s duty disappear.

The Lord applies the picture to Ezekiel, whom He has made a watchman for Israel. His task is to hear the word from the Lord’s mouth and warn the people. He cannot make them turn, but he must not withhold the warning.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads the watchman’s work as a duty to warn rather than reassure people who persist in wrongdoing. Wesley understands the person taken by the sword as still accountable for his own sin.

The USCCB notes connect this commission with Ezekiel’s earlier appointment in chapter 3. The renewal prepares the ministry that will now announce restoration, while keeping the seriousness of hearing and responding.
passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 20:25–32 gives a related pattern in Paul’s farewell to the elders. He says that he is innocent of everyone’s blood because he did not shrink from declaring God’s whole will. He then calls them to watch over the flock and remember his persistent warnings.

Acts does not explicitly quote Ezekiel here. The wider connection is responsibility for faithfully giving God’s word and caring for those entrusted to one’s care. Paul commits the people to God and the word of His grace; faithful warning belongs with that care.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 33:10-20
passages.section_title: Is it too late to turn back when our sins are heavy upon us?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 Now as for you, son of man, tell the house of Israel that this is what they have said: ‘Our transgressions and our sins are heavy upon us, and we are wasting away because of them! How can we live?’ 11 Say to them: ‘As surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, I take no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but rather that the wicked should turn from their ways and live. Turn! Turn from your evil ways! For why should you die, O house of Israel?’ 12 Therefore, son of man, say to your people: ‘The righteousness of the righteous man will not deliver him in the day of his transgression; neither will the wickedness of the wicked man cause him to stumble on the day he turns from his wickedness. Nor will the righteous man be able to survive by his righteousness on the day he sins.’ 13 If I tell the righteous man that he will surely live, but he then trusts in his righteousness and commits iniquity, then none of his righteous works will be remembered; he will die because of the iniquity he has committed. 14 But if I tell the wicked man, ‘You will surely die,’ and he turns from his sin and does what is just and right— 15 if he restores a pledge, makes restitution for what he has stolen, and walks in the statutes of life without practicing iniquity—then he will surely live; he will not die. 16 None of the sins he has committed will be held against him. He has done what is just and right; he will surely live. 17 Yet your people say, ‘The way of the Lord is not just.’ But it is their way that is not just. 18 If a righteous man turns from his righteousness and commits iniquity, he will die for it. 19 But if a wicked man turns from his wickedness and does what is just and right, he will live because of this. 20 Yet you say, ‘The way of the Lord is not just.’ But I will judge each of you according to his ways, O house of Israel.”

He has done what is just and right; he will surely live.

17 Yet your people say, ‘The way of the Lord is not just.’ But it is their way that is not just. 18 If a righteous man turns from his righteousness and commits iniquity, he will die for it. 19 But if a wicked man turns from his wickedness and does what is just and right, he will live because of this. 20 Yet you say, ‘The way of the Lord is not just.’ But I will judge each of you according to his ways, O house of Israel.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The people ask how they can live when their sins are weighing them down. The Lord answers with an appeal to turn: He takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but desires that they turn from their ways and live.

The warning challenges two kinds of confidence. A righteous past cannot be used as protection for present wrongdoing, and a wicked past does not make turning back useless. The Lord describes repentance through concrete actions, including returning a pledge and making restitution for robbery.

The people call His way unjust. He answers that their own way is unjust and that He will judge each according to his ways. The call reaches both the person who despairs of mercy and the person who treats earlier good deeds as permission to sin.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry distinguishes the city’s determined ruin from the final state of individual people, emphasizing God’s willingness to show mercy. Gill reads the failed righteous person as someone trusting his own righteousness, rather than someone made righteous through Christ. Cambridge emphasizes that a sinful past need not make the future hopeless.

Christians differ in their wider teaching about falling from grace. The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 17, and the 1689 Baptist Confession, chapter 17, teach that those God truly calls and sanctifies will be preserved to the end, while serious sin can bring grave harm and discipline.

Methodist Article XII teaches that people may depart from grace after receiving the Holy Spirit and may rise again through grace and repentance. The Catholic Church teaches that grave sin committed with full knowledge and deliberate consent can result in loss of the state of grace; see the Catechism, paragraphs 1857–1861.

Those documents state the traditions’ wider teachings, rather than serving as official commentaries on this passage. The immediate appeal is clear across these disagreements: turn from wrongdoing, seek the Lord’s mercy, and do not rest in self-confidence.
passages.god_plan_html:
Luke 19:1–10 shows the call taking visible shape in Zacchaeus. Welcoming Jesus is followed by a commitment to give to the poor and repay those he has cheated. Jesus announces salvation for his house and says that the Son of Man came to seek and save the lost.

Luke does not explicitly quote Ezekiel 33. The connection is the Lord’s welcome to the lost together with a real change in the way others are treated. Restitution appears as part of that turning, not a reason to imagine that a past full of wrong has put someone beyond the reach of mercy.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 33:21-22
passages.section_title: What changes when the fugitive reports Jerusalem’s fall?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 In the twelfth year of our exile, on the fifth day of the tenth month, a fugitive from Jerusalem came to me and reported, “The city has been taken!” 22 Now the evening before the fugitive arrived, the hand of the LORD was upon me, and He opened my mouth before the man came to me in the morning. So my mouth was opened and I was no longer mute.
paragraphs: 21 In the twelfth year of our exile, on the fifth day of the tenth month, a fugitive from Jerusalem came to me and reported, “The city has been taken!” 22 Now the evening before the fugitive arrived, the hand of the LORD was upon me, and He opened my mouth before the man came to me in the morning. So my mouth was opened and I was no longer mute.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
A fugitive arrives from Jerusalem and reports that the city has been taken. The news confirms the disaster Ezekiel had been announcing.

The Lord’s hand had already been upon Ezekiel the previous evening. His mouth was opened before the fugitive reached him in the morning, and he was no longer mute.

This answers the earlier sign in Ezekiel 24:25–27, which linked the arrival of a survivor with the opening of the prophet’s mouth. The confirmed loss becomes the setting for the messages that now follow.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands the silence as a restriction concerning Israel, rather than an inability to say anything throughout the intervening messages against the nations. The USCCB notes identify the fugitive with the survivor promised in chapter 24.

The passage connects fulfilled warning with a renewed stage of speaking. The evening opening and morning arrival should be kept in the order the text gives.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 33:23-29
passages.section_title: Can those left in the ruins claim Abraham’s promise while rejecting God’s ways?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 23 Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 24 “Son of man, those living in the ruins in the land of Israel are saying, ‘Abraham was only one man, yet he possessed the land. But we are many; surely the land has been given to us as a possession.’ 25 Therefore tell them that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘You eat meat with the blood in it, lift up your eyes to your idols, and shed blood. Should you then possess the land? 26 You have relied on your swords, you have committed detestable acts, and each of you has defiled his neighbor’s wife. Should you then possess the land?’ 27 Tell them that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘As surely as I live, those in the ruins will fall by the sword, those in the open field I will give to be devoured by wild animals, and those in the strongholds and caves will die by plague. 28 I will make the land a desolate waste, and the pride of her strength will come to an end. The mountains of Israel will become desolate, so that no one will pass through. 29 Then they will know that I am the LORD, when I have made the land a desolate waste because of all the abominations they have committed.’

The mountains of Israel will become desolate, so that no one will pass through. 29 Then they will know that I am the LORD, when I have made the land a desolate waste because of all the abominations they have committed.’

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Those living among the ruins reason that Abraham was only one man, yet possessed the land. Since they are many, they conclude that it must surely belong to them.

The Lord answers by naming their conduct: eating meat with blood, idolatry, bloodshed, reliance on the sword, detestable practices and adultery. He repeats the question of whether people living this way should possess the land.

The announcement reaches the ruins, fields, strongholds and caves. The Lord will judge the abominations behind their false confidence and bring the land’s proud strength to an end.

The accusation addresses their claim and their behavior. Jeremiah 39:9–10 also records that Babylon deliberately left some poor people with vineyards and fields; remaining in the land did not by itself explain someone’s faithfulness or wrongdoing.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry understands the claim as presumption: people lay claim to blessings while their conduct contradicts the relationship they claim. Wesley explains their reasoning through descent from Abraham and their presence in the land.

Cambridge sees confidence in the promises without a true knowledge of the Lord whose promises they are. The challenge is not whether Abraham matters, but whether appealing to him can excuse continuing violence and unfaithfulness.

passages.title: Ezekiel 33:30-33
passages.section_title: What is wrong with enjoying God’s word but not doing it?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 30 As for you, son of man, your people are talking about you near the city walls and in the doorways of their houses. One speaks to another, each saying to his brother, ‘Come and hear the message that has come from the LORD!’ 31 So My people come to you as usual, sit before you, and hear your words; but they do not put them into practice. Although they express love with their mouths, their hearts pursue dishonest gain. 32 Indeed, you are to them like a singer of love songs with a beautiful voice, who skillfully plays an instrument. They hear your words but do not put them into practice. 33 So when it comes to pass—and surely it will come—then they will know that a prophet has been among them.”

One speaks to another, each saying to his brother, ‘Come and hear the message that has come from the LORD!’ 31 So My people come to you as usual, sit before you, and hear your words; but they do not put them into practice. Although they express love with their mouths, their hearts pursue dishonest gain. 32 Indeed, you are to them like a singer of love songs with a beautiful voice, who skillfully plays an instrument. They hear your words but do not put them into practice. 33 So when it comes to pass—and surely it will come—then they will know that a prophet has been among them.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The people invite one another to hear Ezekiel’s message. They come, sit before him as the Lord’s people, and listen. The outward attention looks promising.

The Lord identifies the divide beneath it: love is expressed with their mouths, while their hearts pursue dishonest gain. They hear the words but do not put them into practice.

To them Ezekiel is like a skilled singer with a beautiful voice. Enjoying the message has become a substitute for responding to it. When what he announces comes to pass, they will know that a prophet has been among them.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry notes that habit, curiosity and corrupt motives can bring people to hear God’s word. The USCCB notes explain the singer picture as an entertainer enjoyed and then forgotten.

Cambridge connects the desire for gain with self-advancement. The problem is not listening closely or appreciating good teaching; it is the refusal to let what is heard govern what is done.
passages.god_plan_html:
James 1:19–27 warns that hearing without doing becomes self-deception. The response reaches everyday conduct: speech, care for vulnerable people and freedom from the world’s pollution.

Jesus makes the same practical distinction in Luke 6:46–49. Calling Him Lord while refusing His words is like building without a foundation. These passages develop the larger concern exposed in Ezekiel: receiving the word is meant to produce a life that acts on it, rather than leave a listener satisfied with the experience of hearing.

passages.title: Ezekiel 34:1-6
passages.section_title: Why does God accuse Israel’s shepherds of feeding themselves?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 2 “Son of man, prophesy against the shepherds of Israel. Prophesy and tell them that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Woe to the shepherds of Israel, who only feed themselves! Should not the shepherds feed their flock? 3 You eat the fat, wear the wool, and butcher the fattened sheep, but you do not feed the flock. 4 You have not strengthened the weak, healed the sick, bound up the injured, brought back the strays, or searched for the lost. Instead, you have ruled them with violence and cruelty. 5 They were scattered for lack of a shepherd, and when they were scattered they became food for all the wild beasts. 6 My flock went astray on all the mountains and every high hill. They were scattered over the face of all the earth, with no one to search for them or seek them out.’

Prophesy and tell them that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Woe to the shepherds of Israel, who only feed themselves! Should not the shepherds feed their flock? 3 You eat the fat, wear the wool, and butcher the fattened sheep, but you do not feed the flock.

4 You have not strengthened the weak, healed the sick, bound up the injured, brought back the strays, or searched for the lost. Instead, you have ruled them with violence and cruelty. 5 They were scattered for lack of a shepherd, and when they were scattered they became food for all the wild beasts. 6 My flock went astray on all the mountains and every high hill. They were scattered over the face of all the earth, with no one to search for them or seek them out.’

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord turns to Israel’s shepherds, the leaders entrusted with the people’s care. They consume the benefits of the flock—fat, wool and slaughtered sheep—while failing to feed it.

The neglected duties make the accusation specific: strengthen the weak, heal the sick, bind the injured, bring back strays and search for the lost. Instead, the shepherds rule with violence and cruelty.

The scattered flock becomes prey, wandering without anyone to seek it. The Lord repeatedly calls it His flock. Those entrusted with it have been using what belongs to Him for themselves.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley identifies the shepherds broadly as Israel’s rulers, including civil and religious leaders. Cambridge likewise reads the term as rulers. It should not be narrowed automatically to one modern church office.

Henry emphasizes that rank and office do not protect those who neglect their duty and abuse their trust. The picture measures leadership by the care given to people, especially those easily ignored or harmed.
passages.god_plan_html:
First Peter 5:1–4 addresses the elders’ care of God’s flock. Peter opposes greed and domination, calling for willing service and an example others can follow. He places that work under the coming Chief Shepherd.

Peter does not explicitly quote Ezekiel 34. The shared concern takes a concrete form in the church: responsibility for the flock must become care rather than a means of personal gain. The people remain God’s, and those caring for them answer to Christ.

passages.title: Ezekiel 34:7-10
passages.section_title: How will the Lord rescue His flock from its own shepherds?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 Therefore, you shepherds, hear the word of the LORD: 8 ‘As surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, because My flock lacks a shepherd and has become prey and food for every wild beast, and because My shepherds did not search for My flock but fed themselves instead, 9 therefore, you shepherds, hear the word of the LORD!’ 10 This is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Behold, I am against the shepherds, and I will demand from them My flock and remove them from tending the flock, so that they can no longer feed themselves. For I will deliver My flock from their mouths, and it will no longer be food for them.’
paragraphs: 7 Therefore, you shepherds, hear the word of the LORD: 8 ‘As surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, because My flock lacks a shepherd and has become prey and food for every wild beast, and because My shepherds did not search for My flock but fed themselves instead, 9 therefore, you shepherds, hear the word of the LORD!’ 10 This is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Behold, I am against the shepherds, and I will demand from them My flock and remove them from tending the flock, so that they can no longer feed themselves. For I will deliver My flock from their mouths, and it will no longer be food for them.’

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord calls the shepherds to hear His word and states the charge again. They did not search for His flock; they fed themselves while it became prey.

He will oppose the shepherds, demand His flock from them and remove them from tending it. Their position will no longer provide a way to feed themselves at the flock’s expense.

The rescue is pictured as pulling sheep from the shepherds’ mouths. Those appointed to protect have become a threat, and the Lord intervenes on behalf of the people they consume.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads the announcement as mercy toward the scattered flock. Cambridge connects the removal of the cruel shepherds with the care the Lord Himself will undertake in the following verses.

The judgment on the leaders serves the rescue of those under them. The Lord’s concern does not end with condemning the failure; it moves toward restoring care.

passages.title: Ezekiel 34:11-16
passages.section_title: What will the Lord Himself do for His scattered sheep?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 For this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Behold, I Myself will search for My flock and seek them out. 12 As a shepherd looks for his scattered sheep when he is among the flock, so I will look for My flock. I will rescue them from all the places to which they were scattered on a day of clouds and darkness. 13 I will bring them out from the peoples, gather them from the countries, and bring them into their own land. I will feed them on the mountains of Israel, in the ravines, and in all the settlements of the land. 14 I will feed them in good pasture, and the lofty mountains of Israel will be their grazing land. There they will lie down in a good grazing land; they will feed in rich pasture on the mountains of Israel. 15 I will tend My flock and make them lie down, declares the Lord GOD. 16 I will seek the lost, bring back the strays, bind up the broken, and strengthen the weak; but the sleek and strong I will destroy. I will shepherd them with justice.’

I will rescue them from all the places to which they were scattered on a day of clouds and darkness. 13 I will bring them out from the peoples, gather them from the countries, and bring them into their own land. I will feed them on the mountains of Israel, in the ravines, and in all the settlements of the land.

There they will lie down in a good grazing land; they will feed in rich pasture on the mountains of Israel. 15 I will tend My flock and make them lie down, declares the Lord GOD. 16 I will seek the lost, bring back the strays, bind up the broken, and strengthen the weak; but the sleek and strong I will destroy. I will shepherd them with justice.’

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The answer to the failed shepherds begins with the Lord’s own promise: He Himself will search for His flock. He will rescue them from the places to which they were scattered on a day of clouds and darkness.

He will gather them from the peoples and countries, bring them to their land and feed them in good pasture. The picture moves from exposure and hunger to nourishment and rest.

He will seek the lost, bring back strays, bind the broken and strengthen the weak. He will also judge the sleek and strong. His shepherding includes both the rescue of the vulnerable and justice against those who harm them.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry first relates the promise to the restoration of the Jews, then draws out the good Shepherd’s care for His people. Wesley understands the cloudy day as a time of general distress.

Walvoord places the regathering and restored national life within a future earthly reign of Christ. The readings differ over the extent and setting of fulfillment, while recognizing the Lord’s initiative and the faithful care that answers the failed shepherds.
passages.god_plan_html:
A supported connection appears in John 10:1–18. Jesus identifies Himself as the good shepherd, contrasts His care with the thief and the abandoning hired hand, and lays down His life for the sheep. He also speaks of bringing other sheep into one flock under one shepherd.

Luke 15:1–7 pictures a shepherd searching for the lost sheep and rejoicing over its recovery, explaining heaven’s joy over a sinner who repents. These passages show the promised kind of care in Jesus’ ministry and saving work. The connection does not require settling every question about the timing of Israel’s restoration.

passages.title: Ezekiel 34:17-22
passages.section_title: Why does the Lord judge between the sheep themselves?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 This is what the Lord GOD says to you, My flock: ‘I will judge between one sheep and another, between the rams and the goats. 18 Is it not enough for you to feed on the good pasture? Must you also trample the rest of the pasture with your feet? Is it not enough for you to drink the clear waters? Must you also muddy the rest with your feet? 19 Why must My flock feed on what your feet have trampled, and drink what your feet have muddied?’ 20 Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says to them: ‘Behold, I Myself will judge between the fat sheep and the lean sheep. 21 Since you shove with flank and shoulder, butting all the weak ones with your horns until you have scattered them abroad, 22 I will save My flock, and they will no longer be prey. I will judge between one sheep and another.

Must you also trample the rest of the pasture with your feet? Is it not enough for you to drink the clear waters? Must you also muddy the rest with your feet? 19 Why must My flock feed on what your feet have trampled, and drink what your feet have muddied?’

20 Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says to them: ‘Behold, I Myself will judge between the fat sheep and the lean sheep. 21 Since you shove with flank and shoulder, butting all the weak ones with your horns until you have scattered them abroad, 22 I will save My flock, and they will no longer be prey. I will judge between one sheep and another.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord now addresses His flock. The trouble is not limited to appointed shepherds: some of the sheep take the good pasture and clear water, then spoil what remains for others.

The strong shove and butt the weak until they are scattered. The picture exposes conduct that turns another person’s vulnerability into an opportunity to take more.

The Lord will judge between fat and lean sheep and save His flock from being prey. His promise to restore the people includes justice within the community, not only protection against enemies outside it.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Cambridge emphasizes injuries that members of the flock inflict on one another. Wesley connects the contrast with the greater and weaker members of society, including rich people and rulers who must answer for their conduct.

Henry likewise notes that people counted outwardly as one flock can be very different in character. The passage identifies oppression by what the strong do; physical size or poverty alone does not decide the whole moral question.
passages.god_plan_html:
A supported parallel appears in Matthew 25:31–46. The Son of Man separates people like a shepherd dividing sheep from goats, and their response to hunger, thirst, exclusion, sickness and imprisonment is brought before Him.

The scenes should not be treated as identical in every detail. Ezekiel exposes the strong harming the weak within the flock; Jesus describes judgment in which care for the least of His brothers is treated as care for Him. Together they place treatment of other people under the Lord’s searching judgment.

passages.title: Ezekiel 34:23-24
passages.section_title: Who is the one shepherd called God’s servant David?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 23 I will appoint over them one shepherd, My servant David, and he will feed them. He will feed them and be their shepherd. 24 I, the LORD, will be their God, and My servant David will be a prince among them. I, the LORD, have spoken.
paragraphs: 23 I will appoint over them one shepherd, My servant David, and he will feed them. He will feed them and be their shepherd. 24 I, the LORD, will be their God, and My servant David will be a prince among them. I, the LORD, have spoken.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord promises one shepherd in place of the failed shepherds. He names this shepherd His servant David and says that he will feed the people.

The relationship is stated in two parts: the Lord will be their God, and David will be a prince among them. The promise brings faithful leadership together with belonging to the Lord.

How the name David is being used is the main question. The passage makes the promise without explicitly explaining whether the name identifies the earlier king restored to life or the ruler who fulfills the hope associated with David.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley read David here as Christ, the promised ruler from David’s line and the good shepherd. Cambridge also understands the name through the character and rule of the coming Davidic leader rather than David personally returning.

Walvoord favors the resurrected David serving as a prince under Christ, whom he regards as the supreme king. His reasoning distinguishes David from the Son of David and places David among the people who share in Christ’s reign.

The difference concerns the identity of David in this promise, not whether Christ has supreme authority.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 34:25-31
passages.section_title: What kind of life does the covenant of peace promise?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 25 I will make with them a covenant of peace and rid the land of wild animals, so that they may dwell securely in the wilderness and sleep in the forest. 26 I will make them and the places around My hill a blessing. I will send down showers in season—showers of blessing. 27 The trees of the field will give their fruit, and the land will yield its produce; My flock will be secure in their land. Then they will know that I am the LORD, when I have broken the bars of their yoke and delivered them from the hands that enslaved them. 28 They will no longer be prey for the nations, and the beasts of the earth will not consume them. They will dwell securely, and no one will frighten them. 29 And I will raise up for them a garden of renown, and they will no longer be victims of famine in the land or bear the scorn of the nations. 30 Then they will know that I, the LORD their God, am with them, and that they, the house of Israel, are My people,’ declares the Lord GOD. 31 ‘You are My flock, the sheep of My pasture, My people, and I am your God,’ declares the Lord GOD.”

I will send down showers in season—showers of blessing. 27 The trees of the field will give their fruit, and the land will yield its produce; My flock will be secure in their land. Then they will know that I am the LORD, when I have broken the bars of their yoke and delivered them from the hands that enslaved them.

28 They will no longer be prey for the nations, and the beasts of the earth will not consume them. They will dwell securely, and no one will frighten them. 29 And I will raise up for them a garden of renown, and they will no longer be victims of famine in the land or bear the scorn of the nations. 30 Then they will know that I, the LORD their God, am with them, and that they, the house of Israel, are My people,’ declares the Lord GOD. 31 ‘You are My flock, the sheep of My pasture, My people, and I am your God,’ declares the Lord GOD.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord promises a covenant of peace. The people will live securely, free from the beasts and powers that have made them prey. Even wilderness and forest become places where they can rest without fear.

The promise includes rain in season, fruitful trees, a productive land and freedom from famine. The yoke is broken, and the people are delivered from those who enslaved them.

The final assurance goes deeper than comfortable circumstances: they will know that the Lord is with them and that the house of Israel is His people. The flock picture ends by making the relationship plain. They are His people, and He is their God.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry develops the promise through Christ and the flourishing of His church, including the fruit and nourishment of salvation. Cambridge understands the garden of renown in verse 29 as the land’s restored fertility, rather than the name of a single plant.

Walvoord places Israel’s restored national life under Christ’s future earthly rule. These readings give different accounts of the promise’s full expression. The passage itself joins the Lord’s presence, faithful care, freedom from oppression and secure life.
passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 13:20–21 brings together the God of peace, the blood of the eternal covenant, the resurrection of Jesus and His identity as the great Shepherd of the sheep.

Hebrews does not explicitly quote Ezekiel here or provide a calendar for this promised restoration. The shared themes add the New Testament’s saving center: God’s covenant care comes through the living Jesus and equips His people to do His will. Belonging to the Shepherd produces a renewed life in His care.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 35:1-9
passages.section_title: Why does Edom’s old hatred return upon it?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Moreover, the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 2 “Son of man, set your face against Mount Seir and prophesy against it, 3 and declare that this is what the Lord GOD says: Behold, I am against you, O Mount Seir. I will stretch out My hand against you and make you a desolate waste. 4 I will turn your cities into ruins, and you will become a desolation. Then you will know that I am the LORD. 5 Because you harbored an ancient hatred and delivered the Israelites over to the sword in the time of their disaster at the final stage of their punishment, 6 therefore as surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, I will give you over to bloodshed and it will pursue you. Since you did not hate bloodshed, it will pursue you. 7 I will make Mount Seir a desolate waste and will cut off from it those who come and go. 8 I will fill its mountains with the slain; those killed by the sword will fall on your hills, in your valleys, and in all your ravines. 9 I will make you a perpetual desolation, and your cities will not be inhabited. Then you will know that I am the LORD.

I will stretch out My hand against you and make you a desolate waste. 4 I will turn your cities into ruins, and you will become a desolation. Then you will know that I am the LORD.

5 Because you harbored an ancient hatred and delivered the Israelites over to the sword in the time of their disaster at the final stage of their punishment, 6 therefore as surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, I will give you over to bloodshed and it will pursue you. Since you did not hate bloodshed, it will pursue you. 7 I will make Mount Seir a desolate waste and will cut off from it those who come and go. 8 I will fill its mountains with the slain; those killed by the sword will fall on your hills, in your valleys, and in all your ravines. 9 I will make you a perpetual desolation, and your cities will not be inhabited. Then you will know that I am the LORD.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord directs Ezekiel against Mount Seir, identified at the end of the chapter with Edom. The family background reaches back to Esau, whose dwelling in Seir is recorded in Genesis 36:8–9.

The charge is specific: Edom harbored an ancient hatred and handed Israelites over to the sword during their disaster. It chose to deepen the suffering of a people already under judgment.

The Lord announces bloodshed in return for bloodshed. Seir’s cities, hills, valleys and ravines will become places of desolation and death. The repeated outcome is that Edom will know He is the Lord.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands the accusation as delight in bloodshed rather than hatred of it. Cambridge connects the enduring hostility with Edom’s participation in Israel’s calamity and its attempt to seize the land.

Henry emphasizes the seriousness of maintaining hostility toward God and His people. The judgment answers the conduct named in the passage, rather than treating descent from an ancestor as a substitute for examining what these people did.
passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 12:14–17 brings Esau’s story into a warning to pursue peace and holiness, guard against a root of bitterness, and refuse the godlessness that trades away a birthright for a meal.

Hebrews is addressing its own readers, rather than interpreting every detail of Edom’s judgment. The family background gives the passages a meaningful connection: what is received from God must not be treated lightly, and bitterness must not be allowed to grow into harm that spreads to others.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 35:10-13
passages.section_title: Why is Edom’s claim to Israel’s land also a boast against the Lord?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 Because you have said, ‘These two nations and countries will be ours, and we will possess them,’ even though the LORD was there, 11 therefore as surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, I will treat you according to the anger and jealousy you showed in your hatred against them, and I will make Myself known among them when I judge you. 12 Then you will know that I, the LORD, have heard every contemptuous word you uttered against the mountains of Israel when you said, ‘They are desolate; they are given to us to devour!’ 13 You boasted against Me with your mouth and multiplied your words against Me. I heard it Myself!
paragraphs: 10 Because you have said, ‘These two nations and countries will be ours, and we will possess them,’ even though the LORD was there, 11 therefore as surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, I will treat you according to the anger and jealousy you showed in your hatred against them, and I will make Myself known among them when I judge you. 12 Then you will know that I, the LORD, have heard every contemptuous word you uttered against the mountains of Israel when you said, ‘They are desolate; they are given to us to devour!’ 13 You boasted against Me with your mouth and multiplied your words against Me. I heard it Myself!

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Edom claims that the two nations and countries will become its possession. The Lord answers that He was there: the apparent opportunity is not a place outside His concern or authority.

He will deal with Edom according to the anger and jealousy shown in its hatred. What Edom has said about the mountains of Israel is heard by the Lord Himself.

The accusation moves from contempt for Israel’s ruined inheritance to arrogance against God. The people may imagine they are discussing unguarded land, but the Lord holds them accountable for their words and intentions.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands the Lord’s presence in relation to Israel. Cambridge identifies the two nations as Judah and Israel and connects the land with the Lord’s dwelling and claim upon it.

The USCCB notes likewise understand the hostile claim as an attack on the land’s sovereign. Henry draws attention to the words God hears, including those spoken boldly as though no one could call the speaker to account.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 35:14-15
passages.section_title: What becomes of the joy Edom took in Israel’s desolation?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 This is what the Lord GOD says: While the whole earth rejoices, I will make you desolate. 15 As you rejoiced when the inheritance of the house of Israel became desolate, so will I do to you. You will become a desolation, O Mount Seir, and so will all of Edom. Then they will know that I am the LORD.
paragraphs: 14 This is what the Lord GOD says: While the whole earth rejoices, I will make you desolate. 15 As you rejoiced when the inheritance of the house of Israel became desolate, so will I do to you. You will become a desolation, O Mount Seir, and so will all of Edom. Then they will know that I am the LORD.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The closing announcement turns Edom’s celebration around. It rejoiced when Israel’s inheritance became desolate; it will now face desolation itself.

The whole earth’s rejoicing stands beside Edom’s loss, while Mount Seir and all Edom are included in the judgment. The chapter ends by repeating that they will know the Lord.

This prepares the contrast with the mountains of Israel in the next chapter. The neighbor that hoped to gain through Israel’s ruin is judged, and the land it coveted will hear a promise of restoration.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands the rejoicing earth through the surrounding countries enjoying peace and plenty. Cambridge proposes a closer contrast in which the earth rejoices at Edom’s downfall.

The wording is read differently, but the reversal in verse 15 is plain: Edom’s pleasure in another people’s ruin becomes part of the reason for its own judgment.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 36:1-7
passages.section_title: What does the Lord say to the land others have claimed as their own?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 “And you, son of man, prophesy to the mountains of Israel and say: O mountains of Israel, hear the word of the LORD. 2 This is what the Lord GOD says: Because the enemy has said of you, ‘Aha! The ancient heights have become our possession,’ 3 therefore prophesy and declare that this is what the Lord GOD says: Because they have made you desolate and have trampled you on every side, so that you became a possession of the rest of the nations and were taken up in slander by the lips of their talkers, 4 therefore, O mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord GOD. This is what the Lord GOD says to the mountains and hills, to the ravines and valleys, to the desolate ruins and abandoned cities, which have become a spoil and a mockery to the rest of the nations around you. 5 Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: Surely in My burning zeal I have spoken against the rest of the nations, and against all Edom, who took My land as their own possession with wholehearted joy and utter contempt, so that its pastureland became plunder. 6 Therefore, prophesy concerning the land of Israel and tell the mountains and hills, the ravines and valleys, that this is what the Lord GOD says: Behold, I have spoken in My burning zeal because you have endured the reproach of the nations. 7 Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: I have sworn with an uplifted hand that surely the nations around you will endure reproach of their own.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Ezekiel is now told to speak to the mountains of Israel. The enemy has celebrated the ancient heights as a new possession, while the land’s ruins have become spoil and a subject of mockery.

The Lord calls it His land and confronts Edom and the other nations for taking it with joy and contempt. He has heard the reproach directed at the mountains, hills, valleys and abandoned cities.

He swears that the surrounding nations will endure reproach of their own. The desolation does not mean that the Lord has surrendered His claim or forgotten the people for whom the land will bear fruit.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads the promise as the turning back of contempt upon those who inflicted it. Wesley understands the address to the mountains as an address to the land while its inhabitants are in captivity.

The Lord’s response joins His concern for the land with His concern for the people. The following promise will answer the assumption that their ruin is final.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 11:17–32 gives Gentile believers a searching warning about their attitude toward Israel. They must not boast over the branches, because they stand by faith and depend on the root that supports them.

Paul develops the larger place of both Israel and the nations within God’s mercy. This is a fitting response beside Ezekiel’s exposure of contempt: another people’s disobedience gives no ground for arrogance. Those who have received mercy are called to humility before the God whose gifts and calling are irrevocable.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 36:8-15
passages.section_title: How will the ruined land become a home for Israel again?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 But you, O mountains of Israel, will produce branches and bear fruit for My people Israel, for they will soon come home. 9 For behold, I am on your side; I will turn toward you, and you will be tilled and sown. 10 I will multiply the people upon you—the house of Israel in its entirety. The cities will be inhabited and the ruins rebuilt. 11 I will fill you with people and animals, and they will multiply and be fruitful. I will make you as inhabited as you once were, and I will make you prosper more than before. Then you will know that I am the LORD. 12 Yes, I will cause My people Israel to walk upon you; they will possess you, and you will be their inheritance, and you will no longer deprive them of their children. 13 For this is what the Lord GOD says: Because people say to you, ‘You devour men and deprive your nation of its children,’ 14 therefore you will no longer devour men or deprive your nation of its children, declares the Lord GOD. 15 I will no longer allow the taunts of the nations to be heard against you, and you will no longer endure the reproach of the peoples or cause your nation to stumble, declares the Lord GOD.”

The cities will be inhabited and the ruins rebuilt. 11 I will fill you with people and animals, and they will multiply and be fruitful. I will make you as inhabited as you once were, and I will make you prosper more than before. 13 For this is what the Lord GOD says: Because people say to you, ‘You devour men and deprive your nation of its children,’ 14 therefore you will no longer devour men or deprive your nation of its children, declares the Lord GOD. 15 I will no longer allow the taunts of the nations to be heard against you, and you will no longer endure the reproach of the peoples or cause your nation to stumble, declares the Lord GOD.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The mountains will put out branches and bear fruit because the Lord’s people will come home. He declares Himself on the land’s side: it will be tilled and sown again.

The promise includes people and animals multiplying, inhabited cities and rebuilt ruins. The Lord will make the land prosper more than before, and His people will walk upon it and possess it as their inheritance.

The land had been accused of devouring its people and depriving them of their children. The Lord promises an end to that reproach, to the taunts of the nations and to the stumbling associated with the land’s earlier history.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley connects the nearness of the return with the people coming out of Babylon. Henry also recognizes the return to their own border, while seeing a fuller future completion and a picture of the heavenly inheritance of God’s people.

These readings give different weight to the initial return and the promise’s full reach. Both recognize the Lord reversing desolation through a restored people, inhabited land and His renewed favor.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Acts 3:19–26, Peter calls people to turn back so their sins may be wiped away. He speaks of refreshing from the Lord and the restoration announced through the prophets, placing that hope in relation to Jesus.

Peter is not setting out every detail of Ezekiel’s land promise. He shows the larger direction of prophetic hope: God’s promised renewal is bound to His Messiah and the blessing of people being turned from wickedness. Restoration is more than a return to familiar circumstances.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 36:16-21
passages.section_title: How did Israel’s exile profane the Lord’s name?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 Again the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 17 “Son of man, when the people of Israel lived in their land, they defiled it by their own ways and deeds. Their behavior before Me was like the uncleanness of a woman’s impurity. 18 So I poured out My wrath upon them because of the blood they had shed on the land, and because they had defiled it with their idols. 19 I dispersed them among the nations, and they were scattered throughout the lands. I judged them according to their ways and deeds. 20 And wherever they went among the nations, they profaned My holy name, because it was said of them, ‘These are the people of the LORD, yet they had to leave His land.’ 21 But I had concern for My holy name, which the house of Israel had profaned among the nations to which they had gone.
paragraphs: 16 Again the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 17 “Son of man, when the people of Israel lived in their land, they defiled it by their own ways and deeds. Their behavior before Me was like the uncleanness of a woman’s impurity. 18 So I poured out My wrath upon them because of the blood they had shed on the land, and because they had defiled it with their idols. 19 I dispersed them among the nations, and they were scattered throughout the lands. I judged them according to their ways and deeds. 20 And wherever they went among the nations, they profaned My holy name, because it was said of them, ‘These are the people of the LORD, yet they had to leave His land.’ 21 But I had concern for My holy name, which the house of Israel had profaned among the nations to which they had gone.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord explains why Israel was scattered. Their ways and deeds defiled the land through bloodshed and idolatry, and He judged them according to that conduct.

The comparison with a woman’s impurity draws on the language of ritual uncleanness to describe the people’s defilement. The wrongdoing named is their violence and idol worship.

Exile then brought dishonor to the name associated with them. The nations could say that these were the Lord’s people, yet they had been forced out of His land. The Lord declares His concern for His holy name among those nations.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The USCCB notes explain the problem as the impression that God could not protect His people. Cambridge likewise connects the exile with the nations’ misunderstanding of His power and His rule over His own people.

Wesley also emphasizes the people’s wrongdoing and the dishonor it brings. The passage holds together the justice of the exile and the need for the nations to know the Lord truly.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 36:22-23
passages.section_title: Why does the Lord act for His holy name rather than Israel’s merit?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 Therefore tell the house of Israel that this is what the Lord GOD says: It is not for your sake that I will act, O house of Israel, but for My holy name, which you profaned among the nations to which you went. 23 I will show the holiness of My great name, which has been profaned among the nations—the name you have profaned among them. Then the nations will know that I am the LORD, declares the Lord GOD, when I show My holiness in you before their eyes.
paragraphs: 22 Therefore tell the house of Israel that this is what the Lord GOD says: It is not for your sake that I will act, O house of Israel, but for My holy name, which you profaned among the nations to which you went. 23 I will show the holiness of My great name, which has been profaned among the nations—the name you have profaned among them. Then the nations will know that I am the LORD, declares the Lord GOD, when I show My holiness in you before their eyes.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord makes the reason for His action explicit: it is for His holy name, which Israel has profaned among the nations. The coming restoration is not a reward the people have earned.

He will show the holiness of His great name in them before the nations’ eyes. What had become an occasion to misunderstand Him will become a display of who He is.

The aim reaches beyond Israel’s relief. The nations will know that He is the Lord. His concern for His name and His mercy toward His people belong to the same act.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry sees God’s glory as the purpose of the redemption pictured by the restoration. The USCCB notes emphasize God’s initiative rather than the people’s deserving it.

Cambridge explains the display of holiness through the Lord making His character and divine power known. The cleansing and renewal described next show that this involves more than a public display of strength.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus teaches His disciples to pray for the Father’s name to be hallowed, His kingdom to come and His will to be done on earth in Matthew 6:9–13. That prayer brings the concern for God’s name into the life of those who follow Jesus.

Ezekiel describes what the Lord will do; Jesus teaches His people what to desire and ask for. Praying this way means wanting God to be known truthfully through His rule and through lives that honor Him, rather than seeking only relief for ourselves.

passages.title: Ezekiel 36:24-32
passages.section_title: What does God change when He gives a new heart and His Spirit?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 24 For I will take you from among the nations and gather you out of all the countries, and I will bring you back into your own land. 25 I will also sprinkle clean water on you, and you will be clean. I will cleanse you from all your impurities and all your idols. 26 I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you; I will remove your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh. 27 And I will put My Spirit within you and cause you to walk in My statutes and to carefully observe My ordinances. 28 Then you will live in the land that I gave your forefathers; you will be My people, and I will be your God. 29 I will save you from all your uncleanness. I will summon the grain and make it plentiful, and I will not bring famine upon you. 30 I will also make the fruit of the trees and the crops of the field plentiful, so that you will no longer bear reproach among the nations on account of famine. 31 Then you will remember your evil ways and wicked deeds, and you will loathe yourselves for your iniquities and abominations. 32 It is not for your sake that I will act, declares the Lord GOD—let it be known to you. Be ashamed and disgraced for your ways, O house of Israel!

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord will gather His people from the countries and bring them to their land, but His promise goes deeper than changing their location. He will cleanse their impurities and idols.

He will give a new heart and a new spirit, taking away the heart of stone and giving a heart of flesh. The Hebrew word לֵב, lev (lehv), includes the inner person, mind and will in Brown–Driver–Briggs. The promise concerns a change within people who have resisted Him.

He will put His Spirit within them and cause them to walk in His ways. The relationship is restored: they will be His people, and He will be their God.

Plentiful food will replace famine and disgrace. Receiving mercy will not make them proud of their past; they will remember their evil ways with shame. The Lord repeats that His action is not something they have earned.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry, Wesley and the USCCB notes all understand the cleansing, new heart and Spirit as God renewing His people from within, making them responsive to His will. Henry and Wesley also apply the promise to the new covenant life of believers, with the Spirit bringing the change that human self-confidence cannot supply.
passages.god_plan_html:
In John 3:1–12, Jesus tells Nicodemus that entry into God’s kingdom requires birth of water and the Spirit. When Nicodemus struggles to understand, Jesus challenges him as Israel’s teacher. Ezekiel’s promise provides a fitting prophetic background for that need for cleansing and new life.

Titus 3:3–7 makes the saving source explicit: God acts according to mercy, through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit, poured out through Jesus Christ. The shared themes lead toward a life received from God, with grace and the hope of eternal life at its center.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 36:33-38
passages.section_title: Why will people compare the restored land to Eden?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 33 This is what the Lord GOD says: On the day I cleanse you from all your iniquities, I will cause the cities to be resettled and the ruins to be rebuilt. 34 The desolate land will be cultivated instead of lying desolate in the sight of all who pass through. 35 Then they will say, ‘This land that was desolate has become like the garden of Eden. The cities that were once ruined, desolate, and destroyed are now fortified and inhabited.’ 36 Then the nations around you that remain will know that I, the LORD, have rebuilt what was destroyed, and I have replanted what was desolate. I, the LORD, have spoken, and I will do it. 37 This is what the Lord GOD says: Once again I will hear the plea of the house of Israel and do for them this: I will multiply their people like a flock. 38 Like the numerous flocks for sacrifices at Jerusalem during her appointed feasts, so the ruined cities will be filled with flocks of people. Then they will know that I am the LORD.”

Then they will know that I am the LORD.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord joins cleansing from sin with the rebuilding of cities and cultivation of the land. Passersby will see a place once desolate becoming like the garden of Eden.

The nations that remain will recognize the One who has rebuilt and replanted it. The Lord declares that He has spoken and will do it.

He also promises to hear Israel’s plea and multiply its people like a flock. The ruined cities will be filled with people as Jerusalem’s appointed feasts were associated with great flocks for sacrifice. The picture ends with living fullness where there had been emptiness.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry treats the promises as grounds for believers to plead for God’s grace and live in the renewed obedience it gives. Wesley likewise understands the invitation to inquire of the Lord as a call to prayer, rather than a reason to stop asking because a promise has been made.

Cambridge connects the final flock picture with the restoration of the people’s numbers. The Lord’s promised action and His willingness to receive their prayer are presented together.
passages.god_plan_html:
The Eden picture opens onto a larger biblical hope in Revelation 22:1–5: the water of life, the tree of life, healing for the nations and an end to the curse. The throne of God and the Lamb stands at the center, and His servants see His face.

These scenes belong to their own settings, but the connection is clear: God’s purpose answers the ruin brought by sin with life, blessing and His presence. Ezekiel’s rebuilt land is part of that larger movement from desolation toward the life God gives.

passages.title: Ezekiel 37:1-10
passages.section_title: Can these dry bones come to life?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 The hand of the LORD was upon me, and He brought me out by His Spirit and set me down in the middle of the valley, and it was full of bones. 2 He led me all around among them, and I saw a great many bones on the floor of the valley, and indeed, they were very dry. 3 Then He asked me, “Son of man, can these bones come to life?” “O Lord GOD,” I replied, “only You know.” 4 And He said to me, “Prophesy concerning these bones and tell them, ‘Dry bones, hear the word of the LORD! 5 This is what the Lord GOD says to these bones: I will cause breath to enter you, and you will come to life. 6 I will attach tendons to you and make flesh grow upon you and cover you with skin. I will put breath within you so that you will come to life. Then you will know that I am the LORD.’” 7 So I prophesied as I had been commanded. And as I prophesied, there was suddenly a noise, a rattling, and the bones came together, bone to bone. 8 As I looked on, tendons appeared on them, flesh grew, and skin covered them; but there was no breath in them. 9 Then He said to me, “Prophesy to the breath; prophesy, son of man, and tell the breath that this is what the Lord GOD says: Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe into these slain, so that they may live!” 10 So I prophesied as He had commanded me, and the breath entered them, and they came to life and stood on their feet—a vast army.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord’s Spirit sets Ezekiel in a valley full of very dry bones. When asked whether they can live, Ezekiel places the answer with the Lord rather than with what he can see.

He is told to speak the Lord’s word to the bones. They come together, and tendons, flesh and skin cover them, but there is still no breath. A second command brings the breath, and they stand as a vast living company.

The Hebrew word רוּחַ, ruach (ROO-akh), can mean breath, wind or spirit; see Brown–Driver–Briggs. The chapter moves among these related meanings as the Lord’s Spirit brings a vision in which breath enters the dead. The words in English help show different parts of the same life-giving picture.

The explanation follows in verses 11–14. The vision first makes Ezekiel see what the Lord can do where every visible sign suggests that hope has ended.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry and Wesley emphasize that created power cannot accomplish this restoration of life: it is the work of God. The USCCB notes explain the breath, wind and Spirit language as central to the vision’s movement from hopelessness to life.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 37:11-14
passages.section_title: How does the Lord explain the bones and the opened graves?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 Then He said to me, “Son of man, these bones are the whole house of Israel. Look, they are saying, ‘Our bones are dried up, and our hope has perished; we are cut off.’ 12 Therefore prophesy and tell them that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘O My people, I will open your graves and bring you up from them, and I will bring you back to the land of Israel. 13 Then you, My people, will know that I am the LORD, when I open your graves and bring you up from them. 14 I will put My Spirit in you and you will live, and I will settle you in your own land. Then you will know that I, the LORD, have spoken, and I will do it, declares the LORD.’”
