Look, they are saying, ‘Our bones are dried up, and our hope has perished; we are cut off.’ 12 Therefore prophesy and tell them that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘O My people, I will open your graves and bring you up from them, and I will bring you back to the land of Israel. 13 Then you, My people, will know that I am the LORD, when I open your graves and bring you up from them. 14 I will put My Spirit in you and you will live, and I will settle you in your own land. Then you will know that I, the LORD, have spoken, and I will do it, declares the LORD.’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord identifies the bones as the whole house of Israel. Their own words describe the despair behind the vision: their hope has perished, and they feel cut off.

He promises to open their graves, bring His people out and return them to the land of Israel. The movement from the valley to opened graves continues the picture of life restored where there seemed no way forward.

He will put His Spirit in them so that they live and are settled in their land. The repeated assurance is that they will know He has spoken and acted. The promise answers the people’s hopelessness with His own power and faithfulness.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Cambridge and the USCCB notes emphasize the restoration of Israel pictured as resurrection. The people speaking of dried bones are the living exiles describing their shattered national hope; the Lord identifies the subject Himself.

Henry also sees national restoration, while finding an indication of bodily resurrection and a picture of conversion. An early Christian reading in Tertullian’s On the Resurrection of the Flesh, chapters 29–30 insists that the vision also witnesses to God’s raising of bodies, rather than letting national restoration exhaust its meaning.

The distinction is between the immediate explanation about Israel and the wider resurrection meaning Christians have drawn from the image. Recognizing the named people and setting is essential to assessing those further readings.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 8:9–11 brings the Spirit’s life-giving work into the hope of those who belong to Christ. The Spirit of the One who raised Jesus lives in them, and the One who raised Christ will also give life to their mortal bodies.

Ezekiel speaks to Israel’s lost hope and restoration; Paul speaks to people indwelt by Christ’s Spirit. Read together, they show why God’s gift of life reaches beyond an improved situation. Christian resurrection hope rests on the God who raised Jesus and gives His Spirit to His people.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 37:15-23
passages.section_title: What do the two sticks becoming one mean?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 Again the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 16 “And you, son of man, take a single stick and write on it: ‘Belonging to Judah and to the Israelites associated with him.’ Then take another stick and write on it: ‘Belonging to Joseph—the stick of Ephraim—and to all the house of Israel associated with him.’ 17 Then join them together into one stick, so that they become one in your hand. 18 When your people ask you, ‘Won’t you explain to us what you mean by these?’ 19 you are to tell them that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘I will take the stick of Joseph, which is in the hand of Ephraim, and the tribes of Israel associated with him, and I will put them together with the stick of Judah. I will make them into a single stick, and they will become one in My hand.’ 20 When the sticks on which you write are in your hand and in full view of the people, 21 you are to tell them that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘I will take the Israelites out of the nations to which they have gone, and I will gather them from all around and bring them into their own land. 22 I will make them one nation in the land, on the mountains of Israel, and one king will rule over all of them. Then they will no longer be two nations and will never again be divided into two kingdoms. 23 They will no longer defile themselves with their idols or detestable images, or with any of their transgressions. I will save them from all their apostasies by which they sinned, and I will cleanse them. Then they will be My people, and I will be their God.

I will save them from all their apostasies by which they sinned, and I will cleanse them. Then they will be My people, and I will be their God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Ezekiel is told to write on two sticks, identifying one with Judah and its companions and the other with Joseph, Ephraim and its companions. He is to join them so that they become one in his hand.

When the people ask the meaning, the Lord explains it. He will gather the Israelites from the nations and make them one nation in their land, with one king. They will no longer be divided into two kingdoms.

The reunion includes cleansing from idols and rebellion. Becoming one is not simply putting two names on a shared territory; the Lord will save and cleanse the people so that they belong to Him as their God.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry, Wesley and the USCCB notes understand the joining as the uniting of Judah and Israel. Wesley connects their becoming one in God’s hand with His government, care and blessing.

The passage supplies the explanation of the action. The joined sticks point first to the divided people being gathered and made one under the Lord’s rule.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 2:11–22 develops a further work of unity through Christ. Jews and Gentiles are brought near through His blood, reconciled to God in one body, and given access to the Father by one Spirit.

This is a broader connection, not a replacement explanation in which one of Ezekiel’s sticks secretly means the Gentile church. Ezekiel names Judah and Joseph; Paul describes the peace Christ makes across another division. Both direct attention to a people united by God’s saving action and living in His presence.

passages.title: Ezekiel 37:24-28
passages.section_title: What makes the promised peace and God’s dwelling last?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 24 My servant David will be king over them, and there will be one shepherd for all of them. They will follow My ordinances and keep and observe My statutes. 25 They will live in the land that I gave to My servant Jacob, where your fathers lived. They will live there forever with their children and grandchildren, and My servant David will be their prince forever. 26 And I will make a covenant of peace with them; it will be an everlasting covenant. I will establish them and multiply them, and I will set My sanctuary among them forever. 27 My dwelling place will be with them; I will be their God, and they will be My people. 28 Then the nations will know that I the LORD sanctify Israel, when My sanctuary is among them forever.’”

They will live there forever with their children and grandchildren, and My servant David will be their prince forever. 26 And I will make a covenant of peace with them; it will be an everlasting covenant. I will establish them and multiply them, and I will set My sanctuary among them forever. 27 My dwelling place will be with them; I will be their God, and they will be My people. 28 Then the nations will know that I the LORD sanctify Israel, when My sanctuary is among them forever.’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The reunited people will have one shepherd, the Lord’s servant David. They will follow the Lord’s ways and dwell with their descendants in the land given to Jacob.

The Lord will make an everlasting covenant of peace, establish and multiply them, and set His sanctuary among them forever. The promise joins faithful leadership, restored people, secure life and His presence.

The nations will know that He sanctifies Israel when His sanctuary is among them. The closing assurance answers the earlier departure of His glory: His dwelling will be with His people, and He will be their God.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley understand David as Christ, the promised shepherd from David’s line. Walvoord favors the resurrected David serving under Christ. This is the same difference in reading the name found in Ezekiel 34:23–24.

Wesley understands the sanctuary through a spiritual temple and worship brought to completion in heaven. Cambridge emphasizes the temple as the Lord’s dwelling, made holy by His presence. The central promise is His lasting relationship with His people; the fuller account of the sanctuary comes later in Ezekiel.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Second Corinthians 6:14–18, Paul calls believers the temple of the living God and takes up God’s covenant promise to dwell with His people and be their God. That belonging becomes a call to leave uncleanness and live faithfully before Him.

Revelation 21:1–4 carries the dwelling theme to the new creation, where God is with His people and death, sorrow and pain are removed. These New Testament passages show the larger reach of the hope at Ezekiel’s conclusion: peace is bound to God’s presence and to the life He gives His people.

passages.title: Ezekiel 38:1-9
passages.section_title: Who is Gog, and why does he come against Israel?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 And the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 2 “Son of man, set your face against Gog of the land of Magog, the chief prince of Meshech and Tubal. Prophesy against him 3 and declare that this is what the Lord GOD says: Behold, I am against you, O Gog, chief prince of Meshech and Tubal. 4 I will turn you around, put hooks in your jaws, and bring you out with all your army—your horses, your horsemen in full armor, and a great company armed with shields and bucklers, all brandishing their swords. 5 Persia, Cush, and Put will accompany them, all with shields and helmets, 6 as well as Gomer with all its troops, and Beth-togarmah from the far north with all its troops—the many nations with you. 7 Get ready; prepare yourself, you and all your company gathered around you; you will be their guard. 8 After a long time you will be summoned. In the latter years you will enter a land that has recovered from war, whose people were gathered from many nations to the mountains of Israel, which had long been desolate. They had been brought out from the nations, and all now dwell securely. 9 You and all your troops, and many peoples with you will go up, advancing like a thunderstorm; you will be like a cloud covering the land.

Prophesy against him 3 and declare that this is what the Lord GOD says: Behold, I am against you, O Gog, chief prince of Meshech and Tubal. 4 I will turn you around, put hooks in your jaws, and bring you out with all your army—your horses, your horsemen in full armor, and a great company armed with shields and bucklers, all brandishing their swords. 5 Persia, Cush, and Put will accompany them, all with shields and helmets, 6 as well as Gomer with all its troops, and Beth-togarmah from the far north with all its troops—the many nations with you.

7 Get ready; prepare yourself, you and all your company gathered around you; you will be their guard. 8 After a long time you will be summoned. In the latter years you will enter a land that has recovered from war, whose people were gathered from many nations to the mountains of Israel, which had long been desolate. They had been brought out from the nations, and all now dwell securely. 9 You and all your troops, and many peoples with you will go up, advancing like a thunderstorm; you will be like a cloud covering the land.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the promises of restored life, a reunited people and God’s lasting presence, Ezekiel sees a great threat approaching. Gog leads a force drawn from many peoples against Israel, whose people have been gathered from the nations and are living securely.

The Lord names Gog as His opponent. Although Gog commands a huge army, the Lord describes bringing him out with hooks in his jaws. The invader’s strength will not place him beyond God’s reach.

The BSB calls Gog the chief prince of Meshech and Tubal. The Hebrew word רֹאשׁ, rosh (rohsh), can mean head or chief; see Brown–Driver–Briggs. Some translations instead treat Rosh as another name in the list. This difference matters when identifying the places, but neither translation by itself supplies a map of modern countries.

Gog and Magog are names in the prophecy, not a ready-made key to current events. Brown–Driver–Briggs lists Gog as a personal name with an unknown root; its Magog entry discusses a territory with uncertain identification. The passage’s clear emphasis is the gathering of an overwhelming force against a restored people.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads this as an attack in the latter days that God defeats. The USCCB notes understand Gog as a symbolic final enemy whose defeat strengthens Israel’s hope.

Walvoord distinguishes Ezekiel’s invasion from the attack in Revelation 20, placing Ezekiel’s battle before Christ’s thousand-year reign. Other Christian readings connect the two more closely. In The City of God, book 20, chapter 11, Augustine understands Revelation’s Gog and Magog as the final worldwide assault on the church, rather than two particular nations attacking one geographical city.

These are different readings of the scope and timing. They should be tested against both passages, without treating one teacher’s timetable as the shared Christian view.
passages.god_plan_html:
Revelation 20:7–10 explicitly uses the names Gog and Magog for nations deceived by Satan and gathered against God’s people. Fire consumes the attackers, and the devil who deceived them is finally judged.

The connection is clear even though Christians differ over whether John describes the same battle or uses Ezekiel’s names for a later attack. Revelation carries the hope beyond the defeat of a threatening army to the defeat of the deceiver himself. Opposition to God’s people does not have the last word.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 38:10-16
passages.section_title: What does Gog want, and what does the Lord intend?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 This is what the Lord GOD says: On that day, thoughts will arise in your mind, and you will devise an evil plan. 11 You will say, ‘I will go up against a land of unwalled villages; I will come against a quiet people who dwell securely, all of them living without walls or bars or gates— 12 in order to seize the spoil and carry off the plunder, to turn a hand against the desolate places now inhabited and against a people gathered from the nations, who have acquired livestock and possessions and who live at the center of the land.’ 13 Sheba and Dedan and the merchants of Tarshish with all its villages will ask, ‘Have you come to capture the plunder? Have you assembled your hordes to carry away loot, to make off with silver and gold, to take cattle and goods, to seize great spoil?’ 14 Therefore prophesy, son of man, and tell Gog that this is what the Lord GOD says: On that day when My people Israel are dwelling securely, will you not take notice of this? 15 And you will come from your place out of the far north—you and many peoples with you, all riding horses—a mighty horde, a huge army. 16 You will advance against My people Israel like a cloud covering the land. It will happen in the latter days, O Gog, that I will bring you against My land, so that the nations may know Me when I show Myself holy in you before their eyes.

Have you assembled your hordes to carry away loot, to make off with silver and gold, to take cattle and goods, to seize great spoil?’

14 Therefore prophesy, son of man, and tell Gog that this is what the Lord GOD says: On that day when My people Israel are dwelling securely, will you not take notice of this? 15 And you will come from your place out of the far north—you and many peoples with you, all riding horses—a mighty horde, a huge army. 16 You will advance against My people Israel like a cloud covering the land. It will happen in the latter days, O Gog, that I will bring you against My land, so that the nations may know Me when I show Myself holy in you before their eyes.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Gog’s intention is laid bare: he sees a people living securely and plans to seize their wealth. Their unwalled villages appear to offer an easy opportunity for plunder. His target is a people gathered from the nations into land that had been desolate.

Sheba, Dedan and the merchants of Tarshish ask about the spoil. Their questions turn attention to the silver, gold, livestock and goods the invaders want. The text does not describe these merchants mounting a rescue.

Alongside Gog’s evil plan, the Lord states His own purpose. He will bring Gog against His land and show Himself holy before the nations. The same event exposes the invader’s greed and becomes the setting in which the Lord makes Himself known. Gog’s purpose and God’s purpose are not the same.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Cambridge sees the merchants’ interest as the prospect of trading for the spoil; Wesley understands their questions as willingness to help for a share of it. Both readings recognize the appeal of gain rather than an effort to defend Israel.

Wesley describes the Lord’s bringing Gog as permitting him to come. Henry emphasizes the failure of attempts to destroy a people under God’s protection. These explanations distinguish the invader’s hostile intentions from the Lord’s faithful purpose.
passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 2:22–24 gives a further example of evil human action being overtaken by God’s saving purpose. Peter says Jesus was delivered up according to God’s plan, while holding those who killed Him responsible. God then raised Him from the dead.

This is a connection in how God’s purpose prevails, not a claim that Gog’s invasion is a hidden description of the crucifixion. James 1:13–15 also keeps a necessary distinction clear: God does not tempt people to evil; sinful desire draws them toward sin. God’s victory over an evil plan does not turn the evil itself into obedience.

passages.title: Ezekiel 38:17-23
passages.section_title: How does the Lord bring the attack to an end?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 This is what the Lord GOD says: Are you the one of whom I have spoken in former days through My servants, the prophets of Israel, who in those times prophesied for years that I would bring you against them? 18 Now on that day when Gog comes against the land of Israel, declares the Lord GOD, My wrath will flare up. 19 In My zeal and fiery rage I proclaim that on that day there will be a great earthquake in the land of Israel. 20 The fish of the sea, the birds of the air, the beasts of the field, every creature that crawls upon the ground, and all mankind on the face of the earth will tremble at My presence. The mountains will be thrown down, the cliffs will collapse, and every wall will fall to the ground. 21 And I will summon a sword against Gog on all My mountains, declares the Lord GOD, and every man’s sword will be against his brother. 22 I will execute judgment upon him with plague and bloodshed. I will pour out torrents of rain, hailstones, fire, and sulfur on him and on his troops and on the many nations with him. 23 I will magnify and sanctify Myself, and I will reveal Myself in the sight of many nations. Then they will know that I am the LORD.

The mountains will be thrown down, the cliffs will collapse, and every wall will fall to the ground.

21 And I will summon a sword against Gog on all My mountains, declares the Lord GOD, and every man’s sword will be against his brother. 22 I will execute judgment upon him with plague and bloodshed. I will pour out torrents of rain, hailstones, fire, and sulfur on him and on his troops and on the many nations with him. 23 I will magnify and sanctify Myself, and I will reveal Myself in the sight of many nations. Then they will know that I am the LORD.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord places the attack within what He has spoken through Israel’s prophets. The invasion will not catch Him unprepared or overturn His word.

His response is pictured on a vast scale. A great earthquake shakes the land; creatures and people tremble; mountains, cliffs and walls fall. The invaders turn their swords against one another, and the Lord brings plague, bloodshed, torrential rain, hailstones, fire and sulfur.

The account ends with the purpose of the judgment. The Lord will make His greatness and holiness known before many nations. The decisive action belongs to Him, rather than to a stronger army appearing on Israel’s side.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Cambridge understands the earlier prophetic warnings as describing this kind of attack without previously naming Gog. Henry emphasizes that the destruction makes God’s greatness and holiness known.

Wesley describes the great shaking as disturbance and tumult like an earthquake. The more direct reading takes the earthquake and other judgments as events God brings upon the invaders. Both readings place their defeat under His judgment rather than their opponents’ military skill.
passages.god_plan_html:
First Corinthians 15:20–28 places the defeat of God’s enemies within the larger hope secured by Christ’s resurrection. Christ reigns until His enemies are put under His feet, and the last enemy to be destroyed is death.

Ezekiel shows a hostile army brought to nothing. Paul takes the hope further: those who belong to Christ will be raised, and Christ will hand the kingdom to God the Father after every opposing power has been overcome. God’s purpose reaches beyond surviving one invasion to the removal of death itself.

passages.title: Ezekiel 39:1-8
passages.section_title: What will Gog’s defeat make known?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 “As for you, O son of man, prophesy against Gog and declare that this is what the Lord GOD says: Behold, I am against you, O Gog, chief prince of Meshech and Tubal. 2 I will turn you around, drive you along, bring you up from the far north, and send you against the mountains of Israel. 3 Then I will strike the bow from your left hand and dash down the arrows from your right hand. 4 On the mountains of Israel you will fall—you and all your troops and the nations with you. I will give you as food to every kind of ravenous bird and wild beast. 5 You will fall in the open field, for I have spoken, declares the Lord GOD. 6 I will send fire on Magog and on those who dwell securely in the coastlands, and they will know that I am the LORD. 7 So I will make My holy name known among My people Israel and will no longer allow it to be profaned. Then the nations will know that I am the LORD, the Holy One in Israel. 8 Yes, it is coming, and it will surely happen, declares the Lord GOD. This is the day of which I have spoken.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The prophecy returns to Gog’s defeat and begins to describe its aftermath. The Lord brings the invader against Israel’s mountains, strikes the bow and arrows from his hands, and declares that he and his forces will fall.

The army that came to take the land will become food for birds and wild animals. Fire will also reach Magog and those dwelling securely in the coastlands. The judgment is not confined to the soldiers’ immediate position.

The Lord’s holy name is central. He will make it known among His people and before the nations, and will no longer allow it to be profaned. The closing assurance treats His promise as certain: the day He has spoken of will come.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry understands the destruction as a miraculous act by which the Lord makes His name known. Wesley treats the disabled bow as a picture of the failure of the invaders’ weapons generally.

The emphasis is the same: the army’s equipment cannot preserve it when the Lord acts against it. His people’s security rests on His faithfulness.

passages.title: Ezekiel 39:9-16
passages.section_title: Why are the weapons burned and the dead carefully buried?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 Then those who dwell in the cities of Israel will go out, kindle fires, and burn up the weapons—the bucklers and shields, the bows and arrows, the clubs and spears. For seven years they will use them for fuel. 10 They will not gather wood from the countryside or cut it from the forests, for they will use the weapons for fuel. They will loot those who looted them and plunder those who plundered them, declares the Lord GOD. 11 And on that day I will give Gog a burial place in Israel, the Valley of the Travelers, east of the Sea. It will block those who travel through, because Gog and all his hordes will be buried there. So it will be called the Valley of Hamon-gog. 12 For seven months the house of Israel will be burying them in order to cleanse the land. 13 All the people of the land will bury them, and it will bring them renown on the day I display My glory, declares the Lord GOD. 14 And men will be employed to continually pass through the land to cleanse it by burying the invaders who remain on the ground. At the end of the seven months they will begin their search. 15 As they pass through the land, anyone who sees a human bone will set up a pillar next to it, until the gravediggers have buried it in the Valley of Hamon-gog. 16 (Even the city will be named Hamonah.) And so they will cleanse the land.

And so they will cleanse the land.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Those living in Israel’s cities will use the invaders’ weapons as fuel for seven years. Instead of carrying off Israel’s possessions, the attackers leave behind resources for the people they intended to plunder. The reversal is made explicit: the plundered become those who take the spoil.

Gog and his forces receive a burial place in the land they invaded. The people spend seven months burying the dead to cleanse the land, followed by a continuing search for remains. Anyone finding a human bone marks it so that the buriers can collect it.

The concern with cleansing has a background in Numbers 19:11–22, where contact with a corpse, human bone or grave brings ritual uncleanness. Here, even overlooked remains are to be dealt with. The victory includes putting the land in order after the devastation.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Cambridge explains the weapons as fuel and the continuing search as care for remains missed during the first burial work. Wesley draws attention to the reversal: Gog receives a place in Israel, but as a grave rather than a conquered possession.

Henry also draws a lesson about persistent work to remove the reproach left in the land. The readers differ in how far they apply the details as pictures of spiritual renewal, but agree that the aftermath displays the completeness of God’s victory.

The passage gives seven years for burning weapons and seven months for the initial burials. Those details deserve attention when considering a proposed timetable; they do not, by themselves, establish the date of the battle or a particular modern technology.

passages.title: Ezekiel 39:17-20
passages.section_title: Why are birds and wild animals invited to a feast?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 And as for you, son of man, this is what the Lord GOD says: Call out to every kind of bird and to every beast of the field: ‘Assemble and come together from all around to the sacrificial feast that I am preparing for you, a great feast on the mountains of Israel. There you will eat flesh and drink blood. 18 You will eat the flesh of the mighty and drink the blood of the princes of the earth as though they were rams, lambs, goats, and bulls—all the fattened animals of Bashan. 19 At the sacrifice I am preparing, you will eat fat until you are gorged and drink blood until you are drunk. 20 And at My table you will eat your fill of horses and riders, of mighty men and warriors of every kind,’ declares the Lord GOD.
paragraphs: 17 And as for you, son of man, this is what the Lord GOD says: Call out to every kind of bird and to every beast of the field: ‘Assemble and come together from all around to the sacrificial feast that I am preparing for you, a great feast on the mountains of Israel. There you will eat flesh and drink blood. 18 You will eat the flesh of the mighty and drink the blood of the princes of the earth as though they were rams, lambs, goats, and bulls—all the fattened animals of Bashan. 19 At the sacrifice I am preparing, you will eat fat until you are gorged and drink blood until you are drunk. 20 And at My table you will eat your fill of horses and riders, of mighty men and warriors of every kind,’ declares the Lord GOD.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Ezekiel is told to summon birds and wild animals to a great feast on Israel’s mountains. The food is the fallen army, including its mighty men, princes, horses and riders.

The description uses the language of sacrifice and a table prepared by the Lord. Those who came with power and high rank are compared to animals supplied for a feast. Their status cannot protect them from judgment.

This is a summons to scavenging creatures within a prophecy of defeat. It is not an instruction for God’s people to eat human flesh or drink blood. The disturbing picture strips the invading forces of the glory they sought.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads the feast as a picture of God’s judgment on the ambitious and violent. Wesley likewise treats the invitation as a picture whose meaning is the death of the warriors and princes.

The sacrificial language portrays their defeat under God’s judgment. It does not turn their deaths into an offering that forgives the sins of other people.
passages.god_plan_html:
A close parallel appears in Revelation 19:17–21. Birds are summoned to eat the flesh of kings, commanders, mighty men, horses and riders as the forces gathered against Christ are defeated.

The shared picture points to the collapse of earthly power before God. Revelation makes Christ’s victory central: the beast and false prophet are captured, and the armies cannot prevail against the One they oppose. The parallel is strong without requiring every detail in Ezekiel and Revelation to be placed on one agreed timetable.

passages.title: Ezekiel 39:21-24
passages.section_title: What will the nations learn about Israel’s exile?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 I will display My glory among the nations, and all the nations will see the judgment that I execute and the hand that I lay upon them. 22 From that day forward the house of Israel will know that I am the LORD their God. 23 And the nations will know that the house of Israel went into exile for their iniquity, because they were unfaithful to Me. So I hid My face from them and delivered them into the hands of their enemies, so that they all fell by the sword. 24 I dealt with them according to their uncleanness and transgressions, and I hid My face from them.
paragraphs: 21 I will display My glory among the nations, and all the nations will see the judgment that I execute and the hand that I lay upon them. 22 From that day forward the house of Israel will know that I am the LORD their God. 23 And the nations will know that the house of Israel went into exile for their iniquity, because they were unfaithful to Me. So I hid My face from them and delivered them into the hands of their enemies, so that they all fell by the sword. 24 I dealt with them according to their uncleanness and transgressions, and I hid My face from them.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The nations will see the Lord’s judgment and recognize His hand. Israel, too, will know Him as their God. His victory corrects a false conclusion someone might have drawn from the earlier exile.

Israel had not gone into captivity because the Lord lacked power to defend them. The passage identifies their unfaithfulness as the reason He hid His face and delivered them to their enemies.

The explanation holds together His power and His judgment. He was not absent from the history that brought the people low, and their defeat did not mean that another nation’s gods had overcome Him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley emphasize the Lord making Himself known through the defeat of the invaders. The passage itself explains the earlier exile as His response to Israel’s unfaithfulness.

This is an explanation of Israel’s particular covenant history. It does not give a reader grounds to diagnose every person’s suffering as punishment for a particular hidden sin.

passages.title: Ezekiel 39:25-29
passages.section_title: What does the Lord promise beyond captivity and disgrace?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 25 Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: Now I will restore Jacob from captivity and will have compassion on the whole house of Israel, and I will be jealous for My holy name. 26 They will forget their disgrace and all the treachery they committed against Me, when they dwell securely in their land, with no one to frighten them. 27 When I bring them back from the peoples and gather them out of the lands of their enemies, I will show My holiness in them in the sight of many nations. 28 Then they will know that I am the LORD their God, when I regather them to their own land, not leaving any of them behind after their exile among the nations. 29 And I will no longer hide My face from them, for I will pour out My Spirit on the house of Israel, declares the Lord GOD.”
paragraphs: 25 Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: Now I will restore Jacob from captivity and will have compassion on the whole house of Israel, and I will be jealous for My holy name. 26 They will forget their disgrace and all the treachery they committed against Me, when they dwell securely in their land, with no one to frighten them. 27 When I bring them back from the peoples and gather them out of the lands of their enemies, I will show My holiness in them in the sight of many nations. 28 Then they will know that I am the LORD their God, when I regather them to their own land, not leaving any of them behind after their exile among the nations. 29 And I will no longer hide My face from them, for I will pour out My Spirit on the house of Israel, declares the Lord GOD.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord closes with compassion for the whole house of Israel. He will restore Jacob from captivity, gather the people from their enemies’ lands and show His holiness before the nations.

The people will dwell securely, with no one to frighten them. The gathering is described fully: the Lord will not leave them behind among the nations. They will know Him through both the exile and His act of bringing them home.

The final promise reaches beyond a change of location. The Lord will no longer hide His face, and He will pour out His Spirit on the house of Israel. His presence and His gift of the Spirit complete this picture of restoration.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry understands the promise as reaching beyond past returns from exile to Israel turning to Christ; he sees the poured-out Spirit as assurance of God’s continuing favor. Cambridge connects the Spirit here with the renewal described more fully in Ezekiel 36:25–31.

The BSB’s wording in verse 26 speaks of forgetting disgrace and treachery. Cambridge discusses the Hebrew wording behind translations that instead speak of bearing shame. Both readings place the people’s former rebellion against the setting of undeserved restoration, rather than treating it as something to celebrate.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Acts 2:32–39, Peter announces that the risen and exalted Jesus has poured out the promised Holy Spirit. He calls his hearers to repent and receive forgiveness, and speaks of the promise reaching their children and those far off whom God calls.

Peter’s earlier Scripture quotation in that sermon is from Joel. The connection here is the wider biblical promise of God giving His Spirit, rather than a claim that Peter names Ezekiel as his source. Restoration involves people brought into a renewed relationship with God through the work of the risen Christ.

passages.title: Ezekiel 40:1-4
passages.section_title: Why is Ezekiel shown another temple?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 In the twenty-fifth year of our exile, at the beginning of the year, on the tenth day of the month—in the fourteenth year after Jerusalem had been struck down—on that very day the hand of the LORD was upon me, and He took me there. 2 In visions of God He took me to the land of Israel and set me on a very high mountain, on whose southern slope was a structure that resembled a city. 3 So He took me there, and I saw a man whose appearance was like bronze. He was standing in the gateway with a linen cord and a measuring rod in his hand. 4 “Son of man,” he said to me, “look with your eyes, hear with your ears, and pay attention to everything I am going to show you, for that is why you have been brought here. Report to the house of Israel everything you see.”
paragraphs: 1 In the twenty-fifth year of our exile, at the beginning of the year, on the tenth day of the month—in the fourteenth year after Jerusalem had been struck down—on that very day the hand of the LORD was upon me, and He took me there. 2 In visions of God He took me to the land of Israel and set me on a very high mountain, on whose southern slope was a structure that resembled a city. 3 So He took me there, and I saw a man whose appearance was like bronze. He was standing in the gateway with a linen cord and a measuring rod in his hand. 4 “Son of man,” he said to me, “look with your eyes, hear with your ears, and pay attention to everything I am going to show you, for that is why you have been brought here. Report to the house of Israel everything you see.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Fourteen years after Jerusalem was struck down, Ezekiel is taken in visions to the land of Israel. The city’s destruction has not brought the Lord’s purposes to an end. From a very high mountain, the prophet sees a structure resembling a city.

A man with the appearance of bronze stands at the gateway holding a linen cord and a measuring rod. He will guide Ezekiel through a detailed tour of the temple area.

Ezekiel must look, listen, pay attention and report what he sees to Israel. The vision answers the earlier loss of the temple with a picture of ordered worship and, in the chapters that follow, the return of God’s glory.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians differ over how this final vision is fulfilled. Gaebelein reads it as a real temple still to be built when Israel is restored. The USCCB notes understand the arrangement as an ideal picture of restored Israel and God’s holy presence, rather than expecting every detail to become a literal structure. Wesley’s notes on 42:20 apply the temple’s extent to the church and the gathering of Gentiles and Israel.

These are readings offered by the named interpreters, rather than uniform positions held by every member of a denomination. Henry also leaves open whether the guide is the Son of God or a created angel, while Wesley identifies him with Christ. The passage describes his appearance and task without naming him.
passages.god_plan_html:
A close parallel appears in Revelation 21:9–27. John is carried in the Spirit to a high mountain and shown a city, and an angel measures it with a rod. Both visions join careful measurement with the hope of God’s presence.

There is also a striking difference. John sees no temple building in the new Jerusalem because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple. Whatever reading one takes of Ezekiel’s architecture, the larger biblical hope reaches to God and the Lamb dwelling with His people and giving them light.

passages.section_title: What does Ezekiel see at the east gate?

The inner threshold of the gate by the portico facing inward was one rod deep. 8 Then he measured the portico of the gateway inside; 9 it was eight cubits deep, and its jambs were two cubits thick. section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The tour begins at the surrounding wall and the east-facing gateway. The measuring rod is six long cubits, with each cubit described as an ordinary cubit plus a handbreadth. The wall is one rod thick and one rod high.

The gateway is more than a doorway: it contains matching chambers, thresholds, side pillars and an inward-facing covered entrance. Three chambers stand on each side. Windows and carved palm trees are part of the design.

The repeated measurements establish the arrangement of the entrance before Ezekiel moves into the courts. Keeping the measurements in cubits preserves the text’s own scale without depending on an exact conversion into modern units.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Cambridge and the USCCB notes explain the rod as six cubits, each longer by a handbreadth. The USCCB notes emphasize that the east gate receives the fullest description, while the north and south gates share its dimensions.

The immediate task is to follow the layout. The passage supplies no fixed spiritual meaning for each number, chamber or window.

passages.title: Ezekiel 40:17-27
passages.section_title: How is the outer court arranged?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 Then he brought me into the outer court, and there were chambers and a pavement laid out all around the court. Thirty chambers faced the pavement, 18 which flanked the gateways and corresponded to the length of the gates; this was the lower pavement. 19 Then he measured the distance from the front of the lower gateway to the outside of the inner court; it was a hundred cubits on the east side as well as on the north. 20 He also measured the length and width of the gateway of the outer court facing north. 21 Its three gate chambers on each side, its side pillars, and its portico all had the same measurements as the first gate: fifty cubits long and twenty-five cubits wide. 22 Its windows, portico, and palm trees had the same measurements as those of the gate facing east. Seven steps led up to it, with its portico opposite them. 23 There was a gate to the inner court facing the north gate, just as there was on the east. He measured the distance from gateway to gateway to be a hundred cubits. 24 Then he led me to the south side, and I saw a gateway facing south. He measured its side pillars and portico, and they had the same measurements as the others. 25 Both the gateway and its portico had windows all around, like the other windows. It was fifty cubits long and twenty-five cubits wide. 26 Seven steps led up to it, and its portico was opposite them; it had palm trees on its side pillars, one on each side. 27 The inner court also had a gate facing south, and he measured the distance from gateway to gateway toward the south to be a hundred cubits.

Thirty chambers faced the pavement, 18 which flanked the gateways and corresponded to the length of the gates; this was the lower pavement. 19 Then he measured the distance from the front of the lower gateway to the outside of the inner court; it was a hundred cubits on the east side as well as on the north.

20 He also measured the length and width of the gateway of the outer court facing north. 21 Its three gate chambers on each side, its side pillars, and its portico all had the same measurements as the first gate: fifty cubits long and twenty-five cubits wide. 22 Its windows, portico, and palm trees had the same measurements as those of the gate facing east. Seven steps led up to it, with its portico opposite them. 23 There was a gate to the inner court facing the north gate, just as there was on the east. He measured the distance from gateway to gateway to be a hundred cubits.

24 Then he led me to the south side, and I saw a gateway facing south. He measured its side pillars and portico, and they had the same measurements as the others. 25 Both the gateway and its portico had windows all around, like the other windows. It was fifty cubits long and twenty-five cubits wide. 26 Seven steps led up to it, and its portico was opposite them; it had palm trees on its side pillars, one on each side. 27 The inner court also had a gate facing south, and he measured the distance from gateway to gateway toward the south to be a hundred cubits.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Beyond the east gate, Ezekiel enters the outer court. Thirty chambers face a paved area along the sides of the gateways. The guide measures a hundred cubits from the lower gateway toward the inner court.

The north and south gateways follow the east gate’s pattern: the same chambers, windows, covered entrances and palm-tree decorations. Seven steps lead up to each of these outer gates.

Opposite them stand gates leading into the inner court. The tour is preparing the reader for a further movement inward, toward the altar and the temple building.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The USCCB notes distinguish this outer court from the temple’s inner court. Wesley also pays attention to the chambers and the distance between the gates, while drawing a further application to different gifts and callings among God’s people.

That application is a lesson Wesley draws from the arrangement. The passage itself first describes where the chambers, pavement and gates stand.

passages.context_html:
The guide brings Ezekiel into the inner court through the south gate, then measures the east and north gates. Their chambers and overall dimensions follow the earlier pattern.

Two details distinguish these gateways from the outer ones. Their covered entrances face the outer court, and eight steps lead up to them rather than seven. The guide is taking Ezekiel toward the place where the altar stands.

The repetition lets the reader follow an ordered approach: outer gate, outer court, inner gate and inner court. The architecture has direction rather than being a collection of unrelated measurements.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The USCCB notes emphasize the reversed direction of the inner gateways’ covered entrances. Wesley identifies this inner court with the priests’ area next to the temple.

The gates continue the same carefully arranged design as the outer entrances. The text does not explain the eighth step as a hidden code for a particular stage of salvation.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The vision now explains work carried out near the gateways. A chamber is used to wash burnt offerings, and tables provide places for slaughtering burnt offerings, sin offerings and guilt offerings. Other stone tables hold the utensils.

Two chambers in the inner court serve the priests: one for those keeping charge of the temple and another for those keeping charge of the altar. The sons of Zadok are identified as the Levites who may approach the Lord to minister.

The court is a square, a hundred cubits on each side, with the altar in front of the temple. The measurements now give way to purpose: this is a place of worship, priestly responsibility and offerings.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Gaebelein reads the final vision as a future temple with real arrangements for worship. Henry directs Christian readers to Christ as both altar and sacrifice. The USCCB notes understand the vision as a picture of restored holy life rather than a requirement that every architectural detail be built.

These approaches differ over the form of fulfillment. The question of how the offerings relate to Christ’s sacrifice must also be considered; the more detailed instructions come in chapters 43–46.
passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 10:1–18 explains that repeated animal offerings could remind people of sin but could not take it away. Christ’s offering of Himself is once for all, and forgiveness does not require another offering for sin.

This gives an essential New Testament foundation for reading the sacrificial language in Ezekiel. The tables belong to the vision as described, while Hebrews locates the lasting cleansing of God’s people in Christ’s completed offering. A proposed reading of future worship must account for that completed work.

passages.context_html:
After the courts and altar area, the guide brings Ezekiel to the temple’s covered entrance. He measures its side pillars, gateway and sidewalls.

The BSB gives this entrance as twenty cubits wide and twelve cubits deep, reached by ten steps. Columns stand beside the pillars on each side. This short description marks the transition from the courts to the sanctuary rooms measured in the next chapter.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Cambridge discusses the different measurements found in translations of these verses and favors twelve cubits and ten steps, following the Greek text. Those are also the measurements printed in the BSB.

The main movement is clear across those differences: Ezekiel has reached the entrance to the temple itself.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The guide measures the temple’s outer sanctuary, forty cubits long and twenty cubits wide. He then goes inward and measures the entrance and the room identified as the Most Holy Place.

The Most Holy Place is twenty cubits square. The movement from the courts into the sanctuary reaches its innermost room here.

The guide goes into this inner area; Ezekiel is given its measurements and told what it is. The description focuses on the room’s holiness and place within the sanctuary, rather than supplying a new explanation for every dimension.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Cambridge notes that the guide enters the Most Holy Place while Ezekiel does not, and Wesley emphasizes its square shape. Henry draws a lesson from the progress of the tour: attention to what God has already taught prepares people to understand more.

These explanations begin with the distinction between the outer sanctuary and the innermost holy room.
passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 9:1–14, 24–28 explains the earlier sanctuary’s restricted approach to the Most Holy Place and then turns to Christ. He enters by His own blood, securing eternal redemption, and appears for His people in God’s presence.

This is a connection through the sanctuary theme, rather than a claim that Hebrews identifies Ezekiel’s measurements with a heavenly floor plan. The larger purpose is access to God through Christ, whose offering cleanses the conscience so that His people may serve the living God.

passages.context_html:
The guide measures the walls and the side rooms surrounding the temple. The rooms rise in three levels, with thirty rooms on each level. Ledges support them without their supports being fixed into the temple wall itself.

The upper rooms become wider as the wall narrows, and a stairway connects the levels. A raised base, open areas and entrances on the north and south form part of the arrangement.

A separate building stands to the west. The guide then gives the larger measurements of the temple, courtyard and rear building, showing how the parts fit within the whole.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley explains the widening rooms through the changing thickness of the walls and the ledges that support them. His account follows the practical arrangement of the rooms and the ways between them.

The passage provides their structure and location without assigning each level a separate spiritual class or stage of Christian growth.

passages.context_html:
The sanctuary is paneled with wood and decorated with alternating cherubim and palm trees. Each carved cherub has two faces: a human face toward one palm tree and a young lion’s face toward the other.

An altar of wood stands inside, three cubits high and two cubits square. The guide identifies it as the table before the Lord. Double doors with swinging panels also bear cherubim and palm-tree carvings.

The account attends to beauty as well as dimensions. These are carved figures in the sanctuary’s design, distinct from the living creatures Ezekiel described in his earlier visions.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley identifies the wooden altar as an incense altar. Cambridge instead considers it likely to be the table for the bread offered before the Lord. The guide calls it a table, but the passage does not give a fuller description of its use here.

The difference concerns the furnishing’s function. Neither reading requires assigning a hidden meaning to every face or palm-tree carving.

passages.context_html:
The guide takes Ezekiel back into the outer court to inspect a group of chambers beside the temple courtyard. These rooms rise in three levels, with galleries facing one another and a walkway in front.

The upper chambers are smaller because the galleries occupy more of the available space. Entrances connect the rooms with the surrounding court.

A corresponding arrangement stands on the south side. The passage describes matching spaces on either side of the temple before explaining how the priests use them.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry understands this chapter as describing the priests’ chambers, their uses and the surrounding area. Wesley emphasizes the matching arrangement of the northern and southern groups.

The rooms are part of the ordered provision for service near the sanctuary. Their particular use is explained in the next two verses.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.context_html:
The guide explains that these are holy chambers. Priests who approach the Lord will eat the most holy offerings there and place the grain, sin and guilt offerings in this holy area.

The priests must also leave their ministry garments behind before going into the outer court among the people. They put on other clothes for that movement.

The rooms are therefore more than convenient lodging. They provide a proper place for the offerings and garments set apart for service before the Lord.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Cambridge identifies two uses: eating the most holy offerings and setting aside the sacred garments. Wesley likewise understands the rooms as places where holy offerings are kept for their proper use.

The distinction concerns what has been set apart for worship. Ordinary people and ordinary clothing are not described here as morally evil simply because they are outside that particular service.
passages.god_plan_html:
First Peter 2:4–10 describes those who come to Christ as a spiritual house and a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ. They are a people belonging to God, called to proclaim what He has done.

Ezekiel’s priests have particular rooms, offerings and garments; Peter describes the calling of people brought to God through Christ. The wider theme is a life set apart for God’s service. Peter places the acceptance of their worship in Jesus Christ, rather than in their possession of a particular building or outfit.

passages.title: Ezekiel 42:15-20
passages.section_title: What does the wall around the whole area mark?

versions.text: 15 Now when the man had finished measuring the interior of the temple area, he led me out by the gate that faced east, and he measured the area all around: 16 With a measuring rod he measured the east side to be five hundred cubits long. 17 He measured the north side to be five hundred cubits long. 18 He measured the south side to be five hundred cubits long. 19 And he came around and measured the west side to be five hundred cubits long. 20 So he measured the area on all four sides. It had a wall all around, five hundred cubits long and five hundred cubits wide, to separate the holy from the common.

It had a wall all around, five hundred cubits long and five hundred cubits wide, to separate the holy from the common.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After measuring the interior, the guide takes Ezekiel out through the east gate and measures all four sides of the surrounding area. In the BSB, each side measures five hundred cubits.

The enclosing wall has a stated purpose: to separate the holy from the common. The tour ends this stage by returning to the boundary around the whole sanctuary area.

The distinction explains the arrangement the reader has followed through gates, courts, rooms and places of service. Some spaces and tasks are set apart for approaching and serving the Lord.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Cambridge explains the difference between translations that give five hundred reeds and those that give five hundred cubits. It favors cubits in light of the Greek wording and the other measurements in the vision. The BSB also uses cubits.

Wesley follows the larger measurement in his translation and draws a further picture of the church’s worldwide extent. That is his application of the vision; the verse itself states the wall’s purpose as separating the holy from the common. Cambridge explains this distinction in terms of spaces with different degrees of access.

passages.title: Ezekiel 43:1-5
passages.section_title: What changes when the Lord’s glory returns?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then the man brought me back to the gate that faces east, 2 and I saw the glory of the God of Israel coming from the east. His voice was like the roar of many waters, and the earth shone with His glory. 3 The vision I saw was like the vision I had seen when He came to destroy the city and like the visions I had seen by the River Kebar. I fell facedown, 4 and the glory of the LORD entered the temple through the gate facing east. 5 Then the Spirit lifted me up and brought me into the inner court, and the glory of the LORD filled the temple.
paragraphs: 1 Then the man brought me back to the gate that faces east, 2 and I saw the glory of the God of Israel coming from the east. His voice was like the roar of many waters, and the earth shone with His glory. 3 The vision I saw was like the vision I had seen when He came to destroy the city and like the visions I had seen by the River Kebar. I fell facedown, 4 and the glory of the LORD entered the temple through the gate facing east. 5 Then the Spirit lifted me up and brought me into the inner court, and the glory of the LORD filled the temple.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The measured temple is now filled with the presence for which it was prepared. Ezekiel is brought to the east gate and sees the glory of the God of Israel coming from the east. His voice is like the roar of many waters, and His glory lights the earth.

Ezekiel recognizes the appearance from his earlier visions by the River Kebar and of the city’s destruction. He falls facedown. The Spirit then lifts him into the inner court, and he sees the glory filling the temple.

This reverses the movement in chapters 10–11, when the glory departed toward the east. The promise is more than the restoration of a building: the Lord returns to dwell among His people.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley emphasizes the reversal of the departure: the glory that went eastward now returns from the east. Henry sees the vision of God’s glory as leading readers toward the gifts of God through Christ.

The return is the turning point of the temple vision. Measurements and arrangements give way to the Lord’s presence.
passages.god_plan_html:
A close parallel appears in Revelation 1:12–18. The risen Jesus has a voice like many waters, His face shines like the sun, and John falls at His feet. Jesus identifies Himself as the One who died and is alive forever, and reassures John.

Matthew 17:1–8 also shows Jesus shining with glory, the disciples falling facedown and Jesus telling them not to fear. These accounts connect the awe of God’s revealed glory with the glory of Christ. The New Testament adds the assurance that this glorious Lord is the Savior who has overcome death and draws near to His people.

passages.title: Ezekiel 43:6-9
passages.section_title: What must no longer stand beside the Lord’s dwelling?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 While the man was standing beside me, I heard someone speaking to me from inside the temple, 7 and He said to me, “Son of man, this is the place of My throne and the place for the soles of My feet, where I will dwell among the Israelites forever. The house of Israel will never again defile My holy name—neither they nor their kings—by their prostitution and by the funeral offerings for their kings at their deaths. 8 When they placed their threshold next to My threshold and their doorposts beside My doorposts, with only a wall between Me and them, they defiled My holy name by the abominations they committed. Therefore I have consumed them in My anger. 9 Now let them remove far from Me their prostitution and the funeral offerings for their kings, and I will dwell among them forever.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Ezekiel hears a voice from inside the temple while the guide stands beside him. The Lord calls this the place of His throne and the soles of His feet, where He will dwell among the Israelites forever.

The promise also names what must change. The people and their kings had defiled His holy name through prostitution and funeral offerings for their kings. They had placed their thresholds and doorposts beside His, with only a wall between.

The Lord calls for those defiling practices to be removed far from Him. His return does not mean that the earlier wrongdoing was harmless. Lasting fellowship with Him goes together with honoring His holy name.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands the prostitution and neighboring thresholds through the people’s idolatry. Cambridge also connects prostitution with idolatry, but takes the language about dead kings as referring to royal burials near the temple, rather than as another name for idols.

The BSB speaks of funeral offerings for the kings. These explanations differ over the exact practice, while agreeing that royal privilege could not make the defilement of God’s dwelling acceptable.

passages.title: Ezekiel 43:10-12
passages.section_title: Why must the people see the temple’s design?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 As for you, son of man, describe the temple to the people of Israel, so that they may be ashamed of their iniquities. Let them measure the plan, 11 and if they are ashamed of all they have done, then make known to them the design of the temple—its arrangement and its exits and entrances—its whole design along with all its statutes, forms, and laws. Write it down in their sight, so that they may keep its complete design and all its statutes and may carry them out. 12 This is the law of the temple: All its surrounding territory on top of the mountain will be most holy. Yes, this is the law of the temple.
paragraphs: 10 As for you, son of man, describe the temple to the people of Israel, so that they may be ashamed of their iniquities. Let them measure the plan, 11 and if they are ashamed of all they have done, then make known to them the design of the temple—its arrangement and its exits and entrances—its whole design along with all its statutes, forms, and laws. Write it down in their sight, so that they may keep its complete design and all its statutes and may carry them out. 12 This is the law of the temple: All its surrounding territory on top of the mountain will be most holy. Yes, this is the law of the temple.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Ezekiel must describe the temple so that the people become ashamed of their sins. The vision is intended to change their response to the Lord, not simply to satisfy their interest in a building.

If they are ashamed of what they have done, he is to show them the whole arrangement and its laws, writing it down in their sight. They are to keep what they are shown and carry it out.

The central rule is holiness: the surrounding territory on the mountain is to be most holy. The ordered design teaches the people to take the Lord’s presence and instructions seriously.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry connects the showing of God’s gifts through Christ with shame for sin and readiness to understand His redeeming love more fully. Wesley emphasizes the people seeing the glory their wrongdoing had ruined.

Both readings recognize that the vision calls for repentance and a changed life, rather than admiration without obedience.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 2:1–11 explains that God’s kindness, patience and restraint are meant to lead people to repentance. They do not make persistent wrongdoing safe or excuse a person who judges others while doing the same things.

The connection helps explain why a vision of restoration can expose sin so deeply. God’s purpose includes turning people back to Him through His goodness as well as warning them through judgment. Receiving hope is a reason to respond faithfully to Him.

passages.title: Ezekiel 43:13-17
passages.section_title: How is the altar arranged?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 These are the measurements of the altar in long cubits (a cubit and a handbreadth): Its gutter shall be a cubit deep and a cubit wide, with a rim of one span around its edge. And this is the height of the altar: 14 The space from the gutter on the ground to the lower ledge shall be two cubits, and the ledge one cubit wide. The space from the smaller ledge to the larger ledge shall be four cubits, and the ledge one cubit wide. 15 The altar hearth shall be four cubits high, and four horns shall project upward from the hearth. 16 The altar hearth shall be square at its four corners, twelve cubits long and twelve cubits wide. 17 The ledge shall also be square, fourteen cubits long and fourteen cubits wide, with a rim of half a cubit and a gutter of a cubit all around it. The steps of the altar shall face east.”

And this is the height of the altar: 14 The space from the gutter on the ground to the lower ledge shall be two cubits, and the ledge one cubit wide. The space from the smaller ledge to the larger ledge shall be four cubits, and the ledge one cubit wide. 15 The altar hearth shall be four cubits high, and four horns shall project upward from the hearth. 16 The altar hearth shall be square at its four corners, twelve cubits long and twelve cubits wide. 17 The ledge shall also be square, fourteen cubits long and fourteen cubits wide, with a rim of half a cubit and a gutter of a cubit all around it. The steps of the altar shall face east.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord gives the altar’s measurements using the same long cubit described earlier: a cubit plus a handbreadth. The structure rises through ledges to the hearth, with four horns projecting upward.

The hearth is twelve cubits square, and the larger ledge is fourteen cubits square. Rims and a gutter surround the structure, and its steps face east.

The altar stands within the holy area already measured. The next section explains how it is to be cleansed and set apart before regular offerings begin.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley identifies this as the altar for burnt offerings and explains its raised stages. Cambridge also understands it as a structure rising in stages, while differing from the gutter reading in its explanation of the lowest part.

The BSB’s wording describes a gutter. The main arrangement is clear: a substantial altar with ledges, a square hearth, horns and an approach from the east.

passages.title: Ezekiel 43:18-27
passages.section_title: Why must the altar be cleansed before regular offerings begin?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 Then He said to me: “Son of man, this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘These are the statutes for the altar on the day it is constructed, so that burnt offerings may be sacrificed on it and blood may be splattered on it: 19 You are to give a young bull from the herd as a sin offering to the Levitical priests who are of the family of Zadok, who approach Me to minister before Me, declares the Lord GOD. 20 You are to take some of its blood and put it on the four horns of the altar, on the four corners of the ledge, and all around the rim; thus you will cleanse the altar and make atonement for it. 21 Then you are to take away the bull for the sin offering and burn it in the appointed part of the temple area outside the sanctuary. 22 On the second day you are to present an unblemished male goat as a sin offering, and the altar is to be cleansed as it was with the bull. 23 When you have finished the purification, you are to present a young, unblemished bull and an unblemished ram from the flock. 24 You must present them before the LORD; the priests are to sprinkle salt on them and sacrifice them as a burnt offering to the LORD. 25 For seven days you are to provide a male goat daily for a sin offering; you are also to provide a young bull and a ram from the flock, both unblemished. 26 For seven days the priests are to make atonement for the altar and cleanse it; so they shall consecrate it. 27 At the end of these days, from the eighth day on, the priests are to present your burnt offerings and peace offerings on the altar. Then I will accept you, declares the Lord GOD.’”

22 On the second day you are to present an unblemished male goat as a sin offering, and the altar is to be cleansed as it was with the bull. 23 When you have finished the purification, you are to present a young, unblemished bull and an unblemished ram from the flock. 24 You must present them before the LORD; the priests are to sprinkle salt on them and sacrifice them as a burnt offering to the LORD.

25 For seven days you are to provide a male goat daily for a sin offering; you are also to provide a young bull and a ram from the flock, both unblemished. 26 For seven days the priests are to make atonement for the altar and cleanse it; so they shall consecrate it. 27 At the end of these days, from the eighth day on, the priests are to present your burnt offerings and peace offerings on the altar. Then I will accept you, declares the Lord GOD.’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord gives instructions for the altar’s first use. The priests from Zadok’s family receive a bull for a sin offering. Its blood is applied to the horns, corners and rim to cleanse the altar and make atonement for it. The bull is burned in the appointed place outside the sanctuary.

A male goat is presented on the second day, and further unblemished animals are offered. The priests sprinkle salt on the burnt offerings. Seven days are devoted to cleansing and setting the altar apart.

From the eighth day onward, the priests present the people’s burnt offerings and peace offerings, with the Lord’s assurance that He will accept them. The preparation teaches that approaching Him and serving Him are not casual matters.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Cambridge explains the blood applied to the altar as its purification and atonement. Wesley emphasizes God’s acceptance of those who give themselves to Him, through the mediator.

Henry applies the passage to Christian approach to God through Christ’s blood and explicitly rejects the need for new atoning sacrifices now. This differs from reading the final vision as instructions for a future physical sanctuary, while keeping attention on acceptance before God.
passages.god_plan_html:
A related pattern appears in Hebrews 13:10–16. The writer recalls the bodies of sin offerings being burned outside the camp, then connects this with Jesus suffering outside the city gate to sanctify His people by His own blood.

This is a connection through the wider sacrificial pattern; Hebrews does not identify Ezekiel’s altar ceremony as its quoted source. It leads to a further response: going to Jesus despite the disgrace, offering praise through Him, doing good and sharing with others. The goal of being brought near to God includes lives of faithful worship and care for people.

passages.title: Ezekiel 44:1-3
passages.section_title: Why must the east gate remain shut?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 The man then brought me back to the outer gate of the sanctuary that faced east, but it was shut. 2 And the LORD said to me, “This gate is to remain shut. It shall not be opened, and no man shall enter through it, because the LORD, the God of Israel, has entered through it. Therefore it will remain shut. 3 Only the prince himself may sit inside the gateway to eat in the presence of the LORD. He must enter by way of the portico of the gateway and go out the same way.”
paragraphs: 1 The man then brought me back to the outer gate of the sanctuary that faced east, but it was shut. 2 And the LORD said to me, “This gate is to remain shut. It shall not be opened, and no man shall enter through it, because the LORD, the God of Israel, has entered through it. Therefore it will remain shut. 3 Only the prince himself may sit inside the gateway to eat in the presence of the LORD. He must enter by way of the portico of the gateway and go out the same way.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The guide brings Ezekiel back to the outer gate facing east. It is shut, and the Lord says it must remain so because He has entered through it. The gate marks the special honor of His coming to dwell among His people.

The prince may sit within the gateway to eat before the Lord, entering and leaving by its covered entrance. This permission concerns his place inside the gateway rather than opening the closed route for everyone.

The passage names him by his office without naming the individual here. Later instructions describe more of the prince’s worship and responsibilities.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The USCCB notes see the closed gate as a sign that the Lord has entered permanently. Cambridge understands the prince as entering the gateway from the court for a sacrificial meal.

Henry reads the prince as Christ and the gate through Christ’s unique approach to the heavenly sanctuary. Walvoord, discussing the promised prince in Ezekiel 34 and 37, favors the resurrected David serving under Christ. These readings differ over the prince’s identity.

There is also a longstanding reading about Mary. The Catholic Church teaches her continuing virginity in Catechism 499–501. Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae III, question 28, article 3, uses the closed gate as a picture of that belief. A homily published by the Orthodox Patriarchate of Jerusalem likewise reads it as Mary, through whom the Lord came, remaining a virgin.

The teaching about Mary and the use of this particular image should be distinguished: the Catechism states the belief, while Aquinas and the Orthodox homily explain the gate as a picture of it. The immediate scene in Ezekiel remains the temple gate and the prince’s permitted meal.

passages.title: Ezekiel 44:4-9
passages.section_title: What had Israel failed to guard in the sanctuary?
