I looked and saw the glory of the LORD filling His temple, and I fell facedown. 5 The LORD said to me: “Son of man, pay attention; look carefully with your eyes and listen closely with your ears to everything I tell you concerning all the statutes and laws of the house of the LORD. Take careful note of the entrance to the temple, along with all the exits of the sanctuary. 6 Tell the rebellious house of Israel that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘I have had enough of all your abominations, O house of Israel. 7 In addition to all your other abominations, you brought in foreigners uncircumcised in both heart and flesh to occupy My sanctuary; you defiled My temple when you offered My food—the fat and the blood; you broke My covenant. 8 And you have not kept charge of My holy things, but have appointed others to keep charge of My sanctuary for you.’ 9 This is what the Lord GOD says: No foreigner uncircumcised in heart and flesh may enter My sanctuary—not even a foreigner who lives among the Israelites.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
At the north approach, Ezekiel again sees the Lord’s glory filling the temple and falls facedown. He is told to pay careful attention to the laws of the house and to who may enter.

The Lord confronts Israel for handing the care of His holy things to foreigners uncircumcised in both heart and flesh. The people had broken His covenant rather than keeping the responsibilities entrusted to them.

The requirement concerns more than residence: living among Israel did not by itself qualify someone for this service. The reference to the heart also makes clear that an outward connection without faithfulness to the Lord was inadequate.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Cambridge understands the complaint as foreigners being placed in sanctuary service, rather than a ban on foreigners ever presenting offerings to the Lord. It distinguishes people incorporated into Israel’s covenant life from those serving without that commitment.

Wesley similarly emphasizes Israel substituting others for themselves instead of keeping the Lord’s charge. The responsibility for this failure rests with the people who were entrusted with the sanctuary.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 2:11–22 describes Gentiles who were once strangers to the covenants being brought near through Christ’s blood. Jews and Gentiles receive access to the Father by one Spirit and become a dwelling place for God.

The wider story therefore reaches beyond being excluded as an outsider. Christ brings people near and makes them members of God’s household. This does not make Ezekiel’s warning about unfaithful service unimportant; it shows where the New Testament locates the way into belonging and access to God.

passages.title: Ezekiel 44:10-14
passages.section_title: What consequences follow the Levites’ unfaithfulness?

versions.label: BSB

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord addresses Levites who followed Israel into idolatry and helped others stumble. Their position had not protected them from responsibility for leading the people astray.

They will still have work in the temple: caring for its gates, slaughtering offerings for the people and carrying out its service. But they may not approach the Lord as priests or come near the most holy things.

The distinction holds together continued service and real consequences. The work remaining to them does not erase the seriousness of what they had done.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and the USCCB notes understand this as a reduction in priestly responsibility because of earlier wrongdoing. The Levites remain involved in the sanctuary’s work while being restricted from its closest priestly service.

The passage distinguishes responsibilities within the temple. It does not pronounce the eternal destiny of every individual descended from a particular family.

passages.title: Ezekiel 44:15-16
passages.section_title: Why may Zadok’s descendants approach the Lord?

section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The sons of Zadok are set in contrast with those who went astray. They kept charge of the Lord’s sanctuary when the Israelites turned away.

They are permitted to approach Him, present the fat and blood, enter His sanctuary and serve at His table. Their responsibility is described as keeping His charge.

The contrast is about faithfulness in an entrusted calling. Service near the Lord belongs within obedience to Him, rather than being a privilege to use independently of His word.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley emphasizes the honor the Lord gives to those who remain faithful when others draw back. Cambridge understands the passage as reserving priestly service in the new temple to Zadok’s family.

These readings connect their permitted approach with the faithfulness named in the passage itself.
passages.god_plan_html:
First Corinthians 4:1–5 describes Christ’s servants as stewards who must be found faithful. Paul points beyond people’s assessments to the Lord, who will reveal hidden motives and give the praise that is due.

This carries the theme of entrusted service into the life of Christ’s people. Faithfulness matters, and the Lord’s judgment reaches deeper than a public title or reputation. Paul does not supply a chart assigning Ezekiel’s priestly offices to particular Christians.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ezekiel 44:17-19
passages.section_title: Why do the priests wear linen and change before going out?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 When they enter the gates of the inner court, they are to wear linen garments; they must not wear anything made of wool when they minister at the gates of the inner court or inside the temple. 18 They are to wear linen turbans on their heads and linen undergarments around their waists. They must not wear anything that makes them perspire. 19 When they go out to the outer court, to the people, they are to take off the garments in which they have ministered, leave them in the holy chambers, and dress in other clothes so that they do not transmit holiness to the people with their garments.
paragraphs: 17 When they enter the gates of the inner court, they are to wear linen garments; they must not wear anything made of wool when they minister at the gates of the inner court or inside the temple. 18 They are to wear linen turbans on their heads and linen undergarments around their waists. They must not wear anything that makes them perspire. 19 When they go out to the outer court, to the people, they are to take off the garments in which they have ministered, leave them in the holy chambers, and dress in other clothes so that they do not transmit holiness to the people with their garments.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The priests must wear linen when serving in the inner court and temple. Wool is forbidden there, and they must avoid clothing that makes them perspire.

Before going into the outer court among the people, they leave their ministry garments in the holy chambers and put on other clothes. The stated concern is that they not transmit holiness through the garments.

These instructions maintain the distinction between garments set apart for sanctuary service and clothing worn among the people. The passage describes the required practice without saying that the clothing visibly glows.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley explains the concern through contact with things consecrated to holy use. Cambridge likewise understands the changing of clothes as preserving the distinction between the sacred and the common.

The clothing rules belong to the sanctuary service described here. They do not state that ordinary material or ordinary people are morally evil.

passages.title: Ezekiel 44:20-24
passages.section_title: What kind of conduct and teaching does priestly service require?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 20 They must not shave their heads or let their hair grow long, but must carefully trim their hair. 21 No priest may drink wine before he enters the inner court. 22 And they shall not marry a widow or a divorced woman, but must marry a virgin of the descendants of the house of Israel, or a widow of a priest. 23 They are to teach My people the difference between the holy and the common and show them how to discern between the clean and the unclean. 24 In any dispute, they shall officiate as judges and judge according to My ordinances. They must keep My laws and statutes regarding all My appointed feasts, and they must keep My Sabbaths holy.
paragraphs: 20 They must not shave their heads or let their hair grow long, but must carefully trim their hair. 21 No priest may drink wine before he enters the inner court. 22 And they shall not marry a widow or a divorced woman, but must marry a virgin of the descendants of the house of Israel, or a widow of a priest.

23 They are to teach My people the difference between the holy and the common and show them how to discern between the clean and the unclean. 24 In any dispute, they shall officiate as judges and judge according to My ordinances. They must keep My laws and statutes regarding all My appointed feasts, and they must keep My Sabbaths holy.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The priests receive instructions about grooming, wine and marriage. They are to keep their hair trimmed, avoid wine before entering the inner court and marry within the limits stated for their calling.

Their responsibility also includes teaching. They must help the people distinguish the holy from the common and the clean from the unclean.

When disputes arise, the priests must judge according to the Lord’s ordinances. Their authority is tied to His instructions, including the appointed feasts and Sabbaths. Their calling joins personal conduct, sound teaching and fair judgment.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley explains their role in settling disputes according to the Lord’s laws. Cambridge notes the particular marriage restrictions, including permission to marry the widow of a priest.

The rules define duties within this priestly calling. They do not make widowhood or divorce, by themselves, a verdict on a woman’s moral character.
passages.god_plan_html:
First Timothy 3:1–7 also joins spiritual leadership with a trustworthy life. An overseer is to be self-controlled, able to teach, gentle, hospitable and free from the love of money.

The offices and detailed requirements are different, but the shared principle is substantial: caring for God’s people is not separated from character. The New Testament calls for leaders whose conduct supports, rather than undermines, what they teach.

passages.title: Ezekiel 44:25-27
passages.section_title: How do the priests return to service after contact with the dead?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 25 A priest must not defile himself by going near a dead person. However, for a father, a mother, a son, a daughter, a brother, or an unmarried sister, he may do so, 26 and after he is cleansed, he must count off seven days for himself. 27 And on the day he goes into the sanctuary, into the inner court, to minister in the sanctuary, he must present his sin offering, declares the Lord GOD.
paragraphs: 25 A priest must not defile himself by going near a dead person. However, for a father, a mother, a son, a daughter, a brother, or an unmarried sister, he may do so, 26 and after he is cleansed, he must count off seven days for himself. 27 And on the day he goes into the sanctuary, into the inner court, to minister in the sanctuary, he must present his sin offering, declares the Lord GOD.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
A priest is not to go near a dead person in a way that brings ritual defilement, except for the close relatives listed: father, mother, son, daughter, brother or an unmarried sister.

After cleansing, he must count seven days. On returning to minister in the inner court, he must present his sin offering.

The allowance for close family and the preparation for renewed service both belong to the instruction. The passage treats the effects of death with seriousness while providing a way back to the priest’s responsibilities.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Cambridge understands these as rules for necessary contact with the dead and purification before returning to the inner court. Wesley also emphasizes the interval before service resumes.

The uncleanness in view concerns contact with death. The passage does not say that caring about a deceased parent or child is itself an act of moral rebellion.

passages.title: Ezekiel 44:28-31
passages.section_title: How will the priests be provided for?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 28 In regard to their inheritance, I am their inheritance. You are to give them no possession in Israel, for I am their possession. 29 They shall eat the grain offerings, the sin offerings, and the guilt offerings. Everything in Israel devoted to the LORD will belong to them. 30 The best of all the firstfruits and of every contribution from all your offerings will belong to the priests. You are to give your first batch of dough to the priest, so that a blessing may rest upon your homes. 31 The priests may not eat any bird or animal found dead or torn by wild beasts.
paragraphs: 28 In regard to their inheritance, I am their inheritance. You are to give them no possession in Israel, for I am their possession. 29 They shall eat the grain offerings, the sin offerings, and the guilt offerings. Everything in Israel devoted to the LORD will belong to them. 30 The best of all the firstfruits and of every contribution from all your offerings will belong to the priests. You are to give your first batch of dough to the priest, so that a blessing may rest upon your homes. 31 The priests may not eat any bird or animal found dead or torn by wild beasts.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord identifies Himself as the priests’ inheritance and possession. They are not to receive a separate landed possession like the other Israelites.

The offerings, things devoted to the Lord, firstfruits and contributions provide for them. The people are to bring the first of their dough, with a blessing upon their homes.

The priests’ food also remains subject to a limit: they may not eat birds or animals found dead or torn by wild beasts. Provision comes through the people’s worship while remaining under the Lord’s instructions.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Cambridge understands these verses as the priests’ maintenance, with the Lord as their inheritance and offerings supplying their needs. Wesley likewise explains the firstfruits and contributions as provision for them.

The people’s gifts sustain those serving among them; the ministry is not presented as a way to seize someone else’s land.
passages.god_plan_html:
First Corinthians 9:7–18 explicitly draws on those who eat from the temple offerings to explain support for those who preach the gospel. Paul treats material provision for spiritual work as a proper responsibility.

He also says that he did not use that right among the Corinthians, so that nothing would hinder the gospel. The wider lesson includes both generous support and a servant’s willingness to put the gospel before personal advantage.

passages.title: Ezekiel 45:1-8
passages.section_title: Why is land set aside for the sanctuary, the city and the prince?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 “When you divide the land by lot as an inheritance, you are to set aside a portion for the LORD, a holy portion of the land 25,000 cubits long and 20,000 cubits wide. This entire tract of land will be holy. 2 Within this area there is to be a section for the sanctuary 500 cubits square, with 50 cubits around it for open land. 3 From this holy portion, you are to measure off a length of 25,000 cubits and a width of 10,000 cubits, and in it will be the sanctuary, the Most Holy Place. 4 It will be a holy portion of the land to be used by the priests who minister in the sanctuary, who draw near to minister before the LORD. It will be a place for their houses, as well as a holy area for the sanctuary. 5 An adjacent area 25,000 cubits long and 10,000 cubits wide shall belong to the Levites who minister in the temple; it will be their possession for towns in which to live. 6 As the property of the city, you are to set aside an area 5,000 cubits wide and 25,000 cubits long, adjacent to the holy district. It will belong to the whole house of Israel. 7 Now the prince will have the area bordering each side of the area formed by the holy district and the property of the city, extending westward from the western side and eastward from the eastern side, running lengthwise from the western boundary to the eastern boundary and parallel to one of the tribal portions. 8 This land will be his possession in Israel. And My princes will no longer oppress My people, but will give the rest of the land to the house of Israel according to their tribes.

It will be a place for their houses, as well as a holy area for the sanctuary. 5 An adjacent area 25,000 cubits long and 10,000 cubits wide shall belong to the Levites who minister in the temple; it will be their possession for towns in which to live.

It will belong to the whole house of Israel. 7 Now the prince will have the area bordering each side of the area formed by the holy district and the property of the city, extending westward from the western side and eastward from the eastern side, running lengthwise from the western boundary to the eastern boundary and parallel to one of the tribal portions. 8 This land will be his possession in Israel. section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
As the land is divided, a holy portion is set apart for the Lord. Within it are the sanctuary and open space around it, together with places for the priests’ homes. An adjacent area provides for the Levites.

The city also receives a portion belonging to the whole house of Israel. The prince’s land lies on the east and west sides of the holy district and city property.

The closing purpose is practical as well as holy: the princes must no longer oppress the people. Their own provision goes together with the rest of Israel receiving its tribal inheritance.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley explains the arrangement as portions for the sanctuary’s ministers, the city and the ruler on either side. Henry emphasizes provision for worship and ministers alongside just rule and peaceful life for the people.

The arrangement places limits on power. The prince’s position does not entitle him to absorb the people’s inheritance.

passages.title: Ezekiel 45:9-12
passages.section_title: What must replace dishonest and oppressive rule?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 For this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Enough, O princes of Israel! Cease your violence and oppression, and do what is just and right. Stop dispossessing My people, declares the Lord GOD.’ 10 You must use honest scales, a just ephah, and a just bath. 11 The ephah and the bath shall be the same quantity so that the bath will contain a tenth of a homer, and the ephah a tenth of a homer; the homer will be the standard measure for both. 12 The shekel will consist of twenty gerahs. Twenty shekels plus twenty-five shekels plus fifteen shekels will equal one mina.
paragraphs: 9 For this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Enough, O princes of Israel! Cease your violence and oppression, and do what is just and right. Stop dispossessing My people, declares the Lord GOD.’ 10 You must use honest scales, a just ephah, and a just bath. 11 The ephah and the bath shall be the same quantity so that the bath will contain a tenth of a homer, and the ephah a tenth of a homer; the homer will be the standard measure for both. 12 The shekel will consist of twenty gerahs. Twenty shekels plus twenty-five shekels plus fifteen shekels will equal one mina.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord directly commands Israel’s princes to stop violence, oppression and dispossessing His people. They are to do what is just and right.

Honest scales and dependable measures are part of that justice. The ephah and bath must each be a tenth of a homer, and the weights used for the shekel and mina must follow the stated standard.

This brings the vision into everyday dealings. Worship is not separated from the way leaders handle property, payments and the people entrusted to their care.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Cambridge connects the warning with unjustly expelling people from their possessions and with arbitrary demands made possible by unreliable standards. Henry reads just rule as part of the life pictured in the restored order.

The emphasis is straightforward: the Lord’s people must not be prey for those who hold authority over them.
passages.god_plan_html:
Luke 22:24–30 shows Jesus correcting His disciples when they dispute who is greatest. He contrasts rulers who dominate others with leadership that serves, presenting Himself as the One among them who serves.

The connection reaches beyond honest accounting to the purpose of authority. In God’s kingdom, greatness is joined to service rather than using people for personal gain. Jesus’ own conduct gives His followers their pattern.

passages.title: Ezekiel 45:13-17
passages.section_title: What are the people and the prince each responsible to provide?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 This is the contribution you are to offer: a sixth of an ephah from each homer of wheat, and a sixth of an ephah from each homer of barley. 14 The prescribed portion of oil, measured by the bath, is a tenth of a bath from each cor (a cor consists of ten baths or one homer, since ten baths are equivalent to a homer). 15 And one sheep shall be given from each flock of two hundred from the well-watered pastures of Israel. These are for the grain offerings, burnt offerings, and peace offerings, to make atonement for the people, declares the Lord GOD. 16 All the people of the land must participate in this contribution for the prince in Israel. 17 And it shall be the prince’s part to provide the burnt offerings, grain offerings, and drink offerings for the feasts, New Moons, and Sabbaths—for all the appointed feasts of the house of Israel. He will provide the sin offerings, grain offerings, burnt offerings, and peace offerings to make atonement for the house of Israel.

These are for the grain offerings, burnt offerings, and peace offerings, to make atonement for the people, declares the Lord GOD.

16 All the people of the land must participate in this contribution for the prince in Israel. 17 And it shall be the prince’s part to provide the burnt offerings, grain offerings, and drink offerings for the feasts, New Moons, and Sabbaths—for all the appointed feasts of the house of Israel. He will provide the sin offerings, grain offerings, burnt offerings, and peace offerings to make atonement for the house of Israel.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The people must supply measured portions of grain, oil and sheep for the offerings. The grain contribution is a sixth of an ephah from each homer of wheat or barley; one sheep is taken from each two hundred.

All the people participate in the contribution for the prince. In turn, he is responsible to provide the offerings for the feasts, New Moons, Sabbaths and other appointed occasions.

The collection therefore has an assigned purpose. It supports the offerings made for the house of Israel, rather than being described as wealth for the prince to spend without responsibility.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Cambridge explains the grain due as one-sixtieth and the prince’s obligation as providing the public sacrifices in return for the contributions. Henry emphasizes provision for the worship and ministers of God.

The passage gives responsibilities to both the people who contribute and the ruler who receives what is supplied.
passages.god_plan_html:
Second Corinthians 8:12–21 describes a different kind of collection: the churches helping people in need. Paul takes care that the gift is administered honorably before the Lord and before people, and he considers what the givers can actually provide.

The amounts and purpose are different from Ezekiel’s prescribed offerings. The connection is the responsibility that accompanies shared resources. Gifts entrusted for God’s work and people’s needs call for generosity, clear purpose and trustworthy handling.

passages.title: Ezekiel 45:18-20
passages.section_title: Why is the sanctuary cleansed at the beginning of the year?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 This is what the Lord GOD says: ‘On the first day of the first month you are to take a young bull without blemish and purify the sanctuary. 19 And the priest is to take some of the blood from the sin offering and put it on the doorposts of the temple, on the four corners of the ledge of the altar, and on the gateposts of the inner court. 20 You must do the same thing on the seventh day of the month for anyone who strays unintentionally or in ignorance. In this way you will make atonement for the temple.
paragraphs: 18 This is what the Lord GOD says: ‘On the first day of the first month you are to take a young bull without blemish and purify the sanctuary. 19 And the priest is to take some of the blood from the sin offering and put it on the doorposts of the temple, on the four corners of the ledge of the altar, and on the gateposts of the inner court. 20 You must do the same thing on the seventh day of the month for anyone who strays unintentionally or in ignorance. In this way you will make atonement for the temple.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord instructs that an unblemished bull be offered on the first day of the first month to purify the sanctuary. Blood is placed on the temple doorposts, the altar’s ledge and the inner court’s gateposts.

In the BSB, the same is done on the seventh day for those who stray unintentionally or in ignorance. The stated purpose is atonement for the temple.

The provision recognizes that failures among the people affect their common life of worship. The holy place is not to be treated as indifferent to what happens among those who approach it.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Cambridge understands this as cleansing the sanctuary from the people’s defilements. It follows a different reading of the date, placing the second cleansing in the seventh month. The BSB gives the seventh day of the month.

The difference concerns the calendar. Both readings recognize a deliberate provision for purification rather than casual use of the sanctuary.

passages.title: Ezekiel 45:21-25
passages.section_title: What is provided for the Passover and the seventh-month feast?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 On the fourteenth day of the first month you are to observe the Passover, a feast of seven days, during which unleavened bread shall be eaten. 22 On that day the prince shall provide a bull as a sin offering for himself and for all the people of the land. 23 Each day during the seven days of the feast, he shall provide seven bulls and seven rams without blemish as a burnt offering to the LORD, along with a male goat for a sin offering. 24 He shall also provide as a grain offering an ephah for each bull and an ephah for each ram, along with a hin of olive oil for each ephah of grain. 25 During the seven days of the feast that begins on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, he is to make the same provision for sin offerings, burnt offerings, grain offerings, and oil.’
paragraphs: 21 On the fourteenth day of the first month you are to observe the Passover, a feast of seven days, during which unleavened bread shall be eaten. 22 On that day the prince shall provide a bull as a sin offering for himself and for all the people of the land. 23 Each day during the seven days of the feast, he shall provide seven bulls and seven rams without blemish as a burnt offering to the LORD, along with a male goat for a sin offering. 24 He shall also provide as a grain offering an ephah for each bull and an ephah for each ram, along with a hin of olive oil for each ephah of grain.
25 During the seven days of the feast that begins on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, he is to make the same provision for sin offerings, burnt offerings, grain offerings, and oil.’

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Passover is observed on the fourteenth day of the first month, with a seven-day feast and unleavened bread. The prince provides a sin offering for himself and the people, together with the burnt offerings and grain and oil prescribed for the week.

The passage also directs the same provision for the seven-day feast beginning on the fifteenth day of the seventh month. It describes worship in which the ruler bears responsibility along with the people.

The language about an offering for the prince himself matters when considering who he is. The scene includes him among those for whom the offering is provided, rather than treating his office as independent of the Lord’s requirements.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Cambridge identifies the seventh-month feast as the Feast of Tabernacles, also called Booths. Henry reads the Passover through Christ’s sacrifice and the Christian life of sincerity and truth.

The broader difference over the temple vision remains: some readers expect these to be future physical observances, while others understand the restored worship through Christ and His people. The named feasts do not by themselves establish that every unmentioned observance is forbidden.
passages.god_plan_html:
First Corinthians 5:6–8 directly joins Passover and unleavened-bread language to Christ and the church’s life. Christ is the sacrificed Passover lamb, and Paul calls for the removal of malice and wickedness in favor of sincerity and truth.

This connection concerns the Passover pattern across Scripture; Paul does not identify Ezekiel’s festival instructions as his source. It shows the larger purpose moving beyond a calendar observance to a people whose life reflects the deliverance Christ has accomplished.

passages.title: Ezekiel 46:1-8
passages.section_title: When does the inner east gate open for worship?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 “This is what the Lord GOD says: ‘The gate of the inner court that faces east must be kept shut during the six days of work, but on the Sabbath day and on the day of the New Moon it shall be opened. 2 The prince is to enter from the outside through the portico of the gateway and stand by the gatepost, while the priests sacrifice his burnt offerings and peace offerings. He is to bow in worship at the threshold of the gate and then depart, but the gate must not be shut until evening. 3 On the Sabbaths and New Moons the people of the land are also to bow in worship before the LORD at the entrance to that gateway. 4 The burnt offering that the prince presents to the LORD on the Sabbath day shall be six unblemished male lambs and an unblemished ram. 5 The grain offering with the ram shall be one ephah, and the grain offering with the lambs shall be as much as he is able, along with a hin of oil per ephah. 6 On the day of the New Moon he shall offer a young, unblemished bull, six lambs, and a ram without blemish. 7 He is to provide a grain offering of an ephah with the bull, an ephah with the ram, and as much as he is able with the lambs, along with a hin of oil per ephah. 8 When the prince enters, he shall go in through the portico of the gateway, and he shall go out the same way.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The east gate of the inner court remains shut through the six working days but opens on the Sabbath and New Moon. This is a different gate from the permanently closed outer east gate in chapter 44.

The prince stands at the gateway while the priests present his offerings. The people also bow before the Lord at its entrance. The passage distinguishes the prince, the priests and the people without separating them from the shared purpose of worship.

The prince provides the prescribed animals, grain and oil. With some offerings, the amount of grain is described according to what he is able to give. The gate remains open until evening on the appointed days.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Cambridge and the USCCB notes distinguish the prince’s place at the gateway from the priests’ service inside the court. The people worship from outside the inner court, looking through the opened gate.

The account concerns ordered approach and shared worship. It does not say that the worshippers are receiving different kinds of salvation because they stand in different places.
passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 4:1–11 develops the theme of God’s rest beyond a particular day on the calendar. It connects the seventh-day rest, Israel’s failure through unbelief, and the continuing invitation to hear God’s voice and enter His rest.

Ezekiel describes Sabbath worship at the sanctuary; Hebrews calls its hearers to a faithful response to God’s promise. This wider connection shows why rest in God cannot be reduced to attending a ceremony while refusing to trust and obey Him.

passages.title: Ezekiel 46:9-15
passages.section_title: How do the people and prince take part in worship?

No one is to return through the gate by which he entered, but each must go out by the opposite gate. 10 When the people enter, the prince shall go in with them, and when they leave, he shall leave. 11 At the festivals and appointed feasts, the grain offering shall be an ephah with a bull, an ephah with a ram, and as much as one is able to give with the lambs, along with a hin of oil per ephah. 12 When the prince makes a freewill offering to the LORD, whether a burnt offering or a peace offering, the gate facing east must be opened for him. Then he shall go out, and the gate must be closed after he goes out. 13 And you shall provide an unblemished year-old lamb as a daily burnt offering to the LORD; you are to offer it every morning. 14 You are also to provide with it every morning a grain offering of a sixth of an ephah with a third of a hin of oil to moisten the fine flour—a grain offering to the LORD. This is a permanent statute. 15 Thus they shall provide the lamb, the grain offering, and the oil every morning as a regular burnt offering.’

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
At the appointed feasts, worshippers pass through the court rather than returning by the gate they entered. Those coming from the north leave by the south, and those coming from the south leave by the north. The prince goes in and out among the people.

The passage also provides for his voluntary offerings. For these, the east-facing gate opens and is closed after he leaves.

A year-old lamb, grain and oil are to be supplied every morning. Shared festival worship and regular daily offerings both have their place in the life described by the vision.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley suggests that passing through rather than turning back may prevent crowding and confusion. Henry emphasizes daily worship alongside the room left for willing expressions of devotion.

The practical explanation of the route is a suggestion rather than a reason stated by the passage. What is stated is that people and prince come before the Lord within an ordered pattern.
passages.god_plan_html:
First Corinthians 14:26–40 gives instructions for a different gathering, the church coming together. Paul’s concern is that its contributions build people up and that everything be done properly and in order.

This does not transfer Ezekiel’s gateways or sacrificial schedule into a Christian meeting. It carries forward a wider purpose of shared worship: people should be helped to hear, learn and be encouraged, rather than having the gathering overwhelmed by confusion.

passages.title: Ezekiel 46:16-18
passages.section_title: What limits apply to the prince’s gifts and inheritance?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 This is what the Lord GOD says: ‘If the prince gives a gift to any of his sons as an inheritance, it will belong to his descendants. It will become their property by inheritance. 17 But if he gives a gift from his inheritance to one of his servants, it will belong to that servant until the year of freedom; then it will revert to the prince. His inheritance belongs only to his sons; it shall be theirs. 18 The prince must not take any of the inheritance of the people by evicting them from their property. He is to provide an inheritance for his sons from his own property, so that none of My people will be displaced from his property.’”
paragraphs: 16 This is what the Lord GOD says: ‘If the prince gives a gift to any of his sons as an inheritance, it will belong to his descendants. It will become their property by inheritance. 17 But if he gives a gift from his inheritance to one of his servants, it will belong to that servant until the year of freedom; then it will revert to the prince. His inheritance belongs only to his sons; it shall be theirs. 18 The prince must not take any of the inheritance of the people by evicting them from their property. He is to provide an inheritance for his sons from his own property, so that none of My people will be displaced from his property.’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The prince may give property from his own inheritance to his sons, and it becomes theirs. A gift to a servant is held until the year of freedom, when it returns to the prince.

The firm limit is that he must not enlarge his family’s holdings by taking the people’s inheritance. He is to provide for his sons from his own property.

The Lord states the reason: none of His people is to be displaced from his possession. Royal generosity must not be paid for by evicting someone else.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and the USCCB notes understand the year of freedom through the Jubilee. Cambridge also discusses the possibility of the seventh-year release known from Jeremiah.

These readings differ over the release year, while agreeing that the gift to a servant does not permanently remove that property from the prince’s family. The command against taking the people’s land remains explicit.
passages.god_plan_html:
First Timothy 6:6–19 places wealth within a wider call to contentment and trust in God. Those with riches are to do good, be generous and be ready to share, rather than putting their hope in possessions.

Ezekiel restrains a ruler from enriching his family at others’ expense. Paul teaches Christ’s people how to use what they have for good. Together these themes direct attention from acquiring more power over others to responsible care with what God has provided.

passages.title: Ezekiel 46:19-24
passages.section_title: Why are there separate places for preparing the offerings?

Each of the four corner areas had the same dimensions. 23 Around the inside of each of the four courts was a row of masonry with ovens built at the base of the walls on all sides. 24 And he said to me, “These are the kitchens where those who minister at the temple will cook the sacrifices offered by the people.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The guide shows Ezekiel a place at the western end of the priests’ holy chambers. Here they boil the sin and guilt offerings and bake the grain offerings, keeping them from being carried into the outer court and transmitting holiness to the people.

He then shows four enclosed courts, one at each corner of the outer court. Each has masonry with ovens where the temple servants cook the sacrifices offered by the people.

The vision includes these ordinary tasks of preparing food as part of ordered sanctuary life. It distinguishes offerings belonging to the priests’ holy service from preparation for the people.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Cambridge understands the first kitchens as serving the priests’ portions and the corner kitchens as serving the people’s offerings. Wesley likewise explains the smaller courts and the structures used for cooking.

The separation follows the distinction between holy service and common access already stated in chapters 42 and 44. The passage does not describe cooking arrangements as a way of hiding visible supernatural light.

passages.title: Ezekiel 47:1-6
passages.section_title: How does a trickle from the temple become a river?

The water was coming down from under the south side of the temple, south of the altar. 2 Next he brought me out through the north gate and led me around the outside to the outer gate facing east, and there I saw the water trickling out from the south side. 3 As the man went eastward with a measuring line in his hand, he measured off a thousand cubits and led me through ankle-deep water. 4 Then he measured off a thousand cubits and led me through knee-deep water. Again he measured a thousand cubits and led me through waist-deep water. 5 Once again he measured off a thousand cubits, but now it was a river that I could not cross, because the water had risen and was deep enough for swimming—a river that could not be crossed on foot. 6 “Son of man, do you see this?” he asked. Then he led me back to the bank of the river.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Water flows from beneath the temple’s threshold toward the east, passing south of the altar. Ezekiel is taken outside by the north gate and brought around to see it emerging near the closed east gate.

The guide measures successive stretches of a thousand cubits and leads him through the water. First it reaches his ankles, then his knees and waist, and finally it is too deep to cross on foot.

The increasing depth prepares for the explanation that follows: this water carries life and healing from the sanctuary into the land. The guide’s question calls Ezekiel to notice what he has been shown.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads the growing stream as the spread of Christ’s gospel and the life-giving work of the Spirit. He also draws a lesson about the increasing depth of understanding as people attend to God’s word.

Cambridge emphasizes the vision’s restoration of the land as well as its spiritual significance: God’s presence supplies what His people need. The distinction is whether the stream is treated chiefly as a picture of the gospel or as part of the vision’s renewal of the land itself.
passages.god_plan_html:
In John 7:37–39, Jesus invites the thirsty to come to Him and drink, speaking of living water flowing from the believer. John explains that He is speaking about the Spirit whom believers would receive after Jesus was glorified.

This is a connection through the living-water promise, rather than a claim that John identifies Ezekiel’s river as the sole source of Jesus’ words. The wider story shows life coming through Christ and the gift of His Spirit, reaching beyond an outward supply of water.

passages.title: Ezekiel 47:7-12
passages.section_title: What comes to life where the water flows?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 When I arrived, I saw a great number of trees along both banks of the river. 8 And he said to me, “This water flows out to the eastern region and goes down into the Arabah. When it empties into the Dead Sea, the water there becomes fresh. 9 Wherever the river flows, there will be swarms of living creatures and a great number of fish, because it flows there and makes the waters fresh; so wherever the river flows, everything will flourish. 10 Fishermen will stand by the shore; from En-gedi to En-eglaim they will spread their nets to catch fish of many kinds, like the fish of the Great Sea. 11 But the swamps and marshes will not become fresh; they will be left for salt. 12 Along both banks of the river, fruit trees of all kinds will grow. Their leaves will not wither, and their fruit will not fail. Each month they will bear fruit, because the water from the sanctuary flows to them. Their fruit will be used for food and their leaves for healing.”

When it empties into the Dead Sea, the water there becomes fresh. 9 Wherever the river flows, there will be swarms of living creatures and a great number of fish, because it flows there and makes the waters fresh; so wherever the river flows, everything will flourish. 10 Fishermen will stand by the shore; from En-gedi to En-eglaim they will spread their nets to catch fish of many kinds, like the fish of the Great Sea.

Their leaves will not wither, and their fruit will not fail. Each month they will bear fruit, because the water from the sanctuary flows to them. Their fruit will be used for food and their leaves for healing.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Trees line the riverbanks. The guide explains that the water travels into the Arabah and the Dead Sea, making the sea’s waters fresh. Living creatures and many kinds of fish flourish, and fishermen spread their nets along the shore.

The marshes and swamps remain for salt. The picture is not a statement that every part of the region becomes identical.

Along both banks grow fruit trees whose leaves do not wither and whose fruit does not fail. They bear every month because their water comes from the sanctuary. Their fruit provides food and their leaves provide healing: life flows outward from the place of God’s presence.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley uses the healed waters to describe grace renewing what was barren and corrupt. Henry similarly understands the fruit and healing leaves through the nourishing and restoring work of God’s word.

Cambridge emphasizes a renewed creation supplying real human needs, rather than reducing the picture to inward blessings alone. These readings share the importance of God as the source of life while differing over how the earthly details are fulfilled.
passages.god_plan_html:
A close parallel appears in Revelation 22:1–5: a river flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb, the tree of life bears fruit each month, and its leaves are for the healing of the nations.

Revelation takes the hope into the city where the curse is gone, God’s servants see His face and His light replaces the night. The connection reaches beyond restored fishing and fruitful banks to life sustained in God’s presence, free from the curse. It does not provide a medical explanation of how immortal bodies depend on eating particular leaves.

passages.title: Ezekiel 47:13-20
passages.section_title: How are the land’s boundaries and the twelve portions described?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord returns to the division of the land among Israel’s twelve tribes. Joseph receives two portions, and the inheritance is tied to the oath the Lord made to their forefathers.

The boundaries are described by places to the north, the Jordan and Eastern Sea to the east, the southern route through Meribath-kadesh and the Brook of Egypt, and the Great Sea to the west.

The passage places the people’s future life within land the Lord assigns, rather than leaving the exiles’ displacement as their final condition. The following chapter names the tribes and their portions.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands Joseph’s two portions as those of Ephraim and Manasseh. Cambridge likewise explains that these two family portions preserve the count of twelve while Levi has its provision in the holy district.

Individual places along the boundary are not all identified with certainty. The passage can be followed as a description of the inheritance without claiming a fully verified map of present-day national borders.

passages.title: Ezekiel 47:21-23
passages.section_title: What place do resident foreigners have in the inheritance?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 You are to divide this land among yourselves according to the tribes of Israel. 22 You shall allot it as an inheritance for yourselves and for the foreigners who dwell among you and who have children. You are to treat them as native-born Israelites; along with you, they shall be allotted an inheritance among the tribes of Israel. 23 In whatever tribe a foreigner dwells, you are to assign his inheritance there,” declares the Lord GOD.

You are to treat them as native-born Israelites; along with you, they shall be allotted an inheritance among the tribes of Israel. 23 In whatever tribe a foreigner dwells, you are to assign his inheritance there,” declares the Lord GOD.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The division includes foreigners living among Israel who have children there. They are to be treated as native-born Israelites and receive an inheritance among the tribes.

Their portion is to be assigned in the tribe where they dwell. The Lord’s instruction gives them a lasting place in the community’s future rather than leaving them permanently without a share.

This sits alongside the earlier warnings about unauthorized and unfaithful sanctuary service. The vision distinguishes that responsibility from the place of foreigners who share life among the people.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley reads this in the light of Jews and Gentiles becoming one in Christ. Henry likewise sees room for believers united to Christ to share the blessings of the new covenant.

The immediate instruction concerns an inheritance for resident foreigners. Those Christian applications see the welcome here as pointing toward the wider inclusion made known through Christ.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 15:7–13 joins Christ confirming God’s promises to the patriarchs with Gentiles glorifying God for His mercy. Paul calls believers to welcome one another as Christ welcomed them.

This broader connection holds faithfulness to Israel’s promises together with mercy reaching the nations. Paul is not drawing the boundaries of Ezekiel’s tribal lands; he is explaining a shared life of worship and hope made possible through Christ.

passages.section_title: Which tribes receive the northern portions?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The northern allotments are named in order: Dan, Asher, Naphtali, Manasseh, Ephraim, Reuben and Judah. Each portion runs from east to west beside the next.

Manasseh and Ephraim receive separate portions in keeping with Joseph’s double share in 47:13. Genesis 48:3–7 records Jacob receiving Joseph’s two sons as his own, and First Chronicles 5:1–2 distinguishes Joseph’s birthright from the rulership associated with Judah.

The Lord does give the names and arrangement of the tribes. The account moves from the outer boundaries to the people receiving their places within them.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Cambridge reads these as the tribes north of the holy district, beginning with Dan at the northern edge. Henry understands the whole chapter as the ordered portions belonging to the tribes, while also drawing Christian applications from the vision.

The tribal list is part of the restoration picture: the people are assigned an inheritance rather than remaining scattered without a place.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.section_title: What keeps the sanctuary’s portion set apart?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Next to Judah is the district set apart for the Lord, with the sanctuary at its center. A holy portion is assigned to the priests from Zadok’s family, who kept the Lord’s charge.

The Levites have their portion beside the priests. The land set apart for this service may not be sold, exchanged or transferred away, because it is holy to the Lord.

The arrangement carries forward the distinction between the priests and the other Levites described in chapter 44. It also protects the land assigned to worship and service from being treated as ordinary property for sale.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Cambridge explains this section as the priests’ domain and the adjoining Levitical provision. Henry places the assigned portions within the wider picture of restored life before God.

The purpose of setting the land apart is stated directly: it belongs to the Lord’s holy provision. No additional meaning has to be assigned to every dimension to recognize that purpose.

passages.title: Ezekiel 48:15-22
passages.section_title: How do the city, its workers and the prince fit within the district?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The remaining strip is for the city’s common use, including homes and pastureland. The city is square, with open space around it. Land on its east and west provides food for the workers who cultivate it.

Those workers come from all Israel’s tribes. The city serves a shared life among the people rather than belonging exclusively to one tribe.

The whole district, including the holy portions and city property, is twenty-five thousand cubits square. The prince’s land lies on either side, between Judah and Benjamin. Provision is made for worship, work, homes and leadership within the same ordered land.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley explains common use as land not consecrated to the sanctuary and the produce as maintenance for the city’s workers. Cambridge similarly distinguishes the city’s portion from the priests’ and Levites’ areas.

Common does not mean wicked. The vision includes ordinary work and a shared city alongside the areas set apart for sanctuary service.

passages.title: Ezekiel 48:23-29
passages.section_title: Which tribes receive the southern portions?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
South of the special district come Benjamin, Simeon, Issachar, Zebulun and Gad, each with a portion running from east to west.

Gad’s southern boundary follows the route from Tamar through Meribath-kadesh and the Brook of Egypt to the Great Sea. The Lord closes the list by identifying this as the inheritance assigned to Israel’s tribes.

Together with the seven northern portions, these five complete the twelve tribal shares. The holy district stands within a land in which the people themselves have a place.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry treats the chapter as a description of the tribes’ several portions, and Cambridge places the special district between the northern allotments and the remaining tribes.

The arrangement completes the inheritance already announced. It does not explain each tribe’s position through an individual spiritual ranking.

passages.title: Ezekiel 48:30-35
passages.section_title: Why does the book end with the name “The Lord Is There”?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 30 “These will be the exits of the city: Beginning on the north side, which will be 4,500 cubits long, 31 the gates of the city will be named after the tribes of Israel. On the north side there will be three gates: the gate of Reuben, the gate of Judah, and the gate of Levi. 32 On the east side, which will be 4,500 cubits long, there will be three gates: the gate of Joseph, the gate of Benjamin, and the gate of Dan. 33 On the south side, which will be 4,500 cubits long, there will be three gates: the gate of Simeon, the gate of Issachar, and the gate of Zebulun. 34 And on the west side, which will be 4,500 cubits long, there will be three gates: the gate of Gad, the gate of Asher, and the gate of Naphtali. 35 The perimeter of the city will be 18,000 cubits, and from that day on the name of the city will be: THE LORD IS THERE.”

35 The perimeter of the city will be 18,000 cubits, and from that day on the name of the city will be: THE LORD IS THERE.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The city has three gates on each of its four sides. They bear the names of Israel’s tribes, including Levi and Joseph. Here Joseph is named as one tribe rather than divided into Ephraim and Manasseh as in the land portions.

The final measurement gives the city’s perimeter, but its defining feature is its name: the Lord is there. The book that showed His glory departing from a defiled temple ends with His presence among a restored people.

The promise answers the fear that judgment and exile had ended the relationship. The final word is not merely a rebuilt city, an assigned border or a functioning sanctuary. It is the Lord dwelling with His people.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Cambridge understands the name as the fulfillment of the covenant relationship: the Lord is their God and they are His people. Wesley applies the hope both to restored Jerusalem and to the lasting blessing of God’s presence with believers.

Henry likewise reads the closing city through life in Christ’s church and the hope of being with God forever. These readings place the emphasis where the book places it—on the Lord’s presence.
passages.god_plan_html:
A close parallel appears in Revelation 21:1–4, 9–27. The new Jerusalem has twelve gates bearing the tribes’ names, and God’s dwelling is with His people. Death, mourning, crying and pain are removed.

Revelation 22:1–5 adds that His servants see His face and live in His light. These connections carry Ezekiel’s closing hope into the new creation: belonging to God and being with Him are at the heart of the future He gives His people.

passages.title: Daniel 1:1-7
passages.section_title: How do Daniel and his friends come to serve in Babylon?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 In the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim king of Judah, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came to Jerusalem and besieged it. 2 And the Lord delivered into his hand Jehoiakim king of Judah, along with some of the articles from the house of God. He carried these off to the land of Shinar, to the house of his god, where he put them in the treasury of his god. 3 Then the king ordered Ashpenaz, the chief of his court officials, to bring in some Israelites from the royal family and the nobility— 4 young men without blemish, handsome, gifted in all wisdom, knowledgeable, quick to understand, and qualified to serve in the king’s palace—and to teach them the language and literature of the Chaldeans. 5 The king assigned them daily provisions of the royal food and wine. They were to be trained for three years, after which they were to enter the king’s service. 6 Among these young men were some from Judah: Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah. 7 The chief official gave them new names: To Daniel he gave the name Belteshazzar; to Hananiah, Shadrach; to Mishael, Meshach; and to Azariah, Abednego.
paragraphs: 1 In the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim king of Judah, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came to Jerusalem and besieged it. 2 And the Lord delivered into his hand Jehoiakim king of Judah, along with some of the articles from the house of God. He carried these off to the land of Shinar, to the house of his god, where he put them in the treasury of his god.

3 Then the king ordered Ashpenaz, the chief of his court officials, to bring in some Israelites from the royal family and the nobility— 4 young men without blemish, handsome, gifted in all wisdom, knowledgeable, quick to understand, and qualified to serve in the king’s palace—and to teach them the language and literature of the Chaldeans. 5 The king assigned them daily provisions of the royal food and wine. They were to be trained for three years, after which they were to enter the king’s service. 6 Among these young men were some from Judah: Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah. 7 The chief official gave them new names: To Daniel he gave the name Belteshazzar; to Hananiah, Shadrach; to Mishael, Meshach; and to Azariah, Abednego.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Daniel’s story begins with Jerusalem under siege and the king of Judah delivered into Nebuchadnezzar’s hand. Some articles from the temple are carried to the treasury of the Babylonian king’s god. The opening attributes the defeat to the Lord’s action, rather than presenting it as proof that Babylon’s god has overcome Him.

Young men from Israel’s royal and noble families are selected for training in the language and literature of the Chaldeans. They are to receive the king’s food and wine and prepare for three years to enter his service.

Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah are among them. They receive new names—Belteshazzar, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego—and a new setting in which to live faithfully. Exile changes their surroundings and their responsibilities, but does not remove them from the Lord’s care.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry and Wesley understand the education and new names as bringing the young men into the king’s service and Babylon’s religious world. Their reading emphasizes the challenge of remaining faithful to the Lord within that setting.
passages.god_plan_html:
A helpful parallel is the account of Joseph and Moses in Acts 7:9–22. Joseph is sold into Egypt, yet God gives him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh and uses his position when famine threatens his family. Moses is raised by Pharaoh’s daughter and educated in Egyptian wisdom.

These earlier stories do not make captivity good in itself or explain every person’s suffering. They show God’s work reaching into foreign courts and difficult circumstances. Daniel’s training belongs to a similar pattern: displacement does not prevent God from preparing someone to serve His purposes.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 1:8-16
passages.section_title: How does Daniel stay faithful without seeking a confrontation?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 But Daniel made up his mind that he would not defile himself with the king’s food or wine. So he asked the chief official for permission not to defile himself. 9 Now God had granted Daniel favor and compassion from the chief official, 10 but he said to Daniel, “I fear my lord the king, who has assigned your food and drink. For why should he see your faces looking thinner than those of the other young men your age? You would endanger my head before the king!” 11 Then Daniel said to the steward whom the chief official had appointed over Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, 12 “Please test your servants for ten days. Let us be given only vegetables to eat and water to drink. 13 Then compare our appearances with those of the young men who are eating the royal food, and deal with your servants according to what you see.” 14 So he consented to this and tested them for ten days. 15 And at the end of ten days, they looked healthier and better nourished than all the young men who were eating the king’s food. 16 So the steward continued to withhold their choice food and the wine they were to drink, and he gave them vegetables instead.
paragraphs: 8 But Daniel made up his mind that he would not defile himself with the king’s food or wine. So he asked the chief official for permission not to defile himself. 9 Now God had granted Daniel favor and compassion from the chief official, 10 but he said to Daniel, “I fear my lord the king, who has assigned your food and drink. For why should he see your faces looking thinner than those of the other young men your age? You would endanger my head before the king!”

11 Then Daniel said to the steward whom the chief official had appointed over Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, 12 “Please test your servants for ten days. Let us be given only vegetables to eat and water to drink. 13 Then compare our appearances with those of the young men who are eating the royal food, and deal with your servants according to what you see.” 14 So he consented to this and tested them for ten days.

15 And at the end of ten days, they looked healthier and better nourished than all the young men who were eating the king’s food. 16 So the steward continued to withhold their choice food and the wine they were to drink, and he gave them vegetables instead.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Daniel decides that he will not defile himself with the royal food or wine. He first asks permission, and the Lord has already given him favor with the chief official. That official nevertheless fears being held responsible if the young men look poorly nourished.

Daniel proposes a limited test to the steward: vegetables and water for ten days, followed by a comparison. At the end, the four look healthier and better nourished than those receiving the royal food, so the alternative provision continues.

The word translated vegetables covers vegetable food broadly; Brown–Driver–Briggs lists the related forms used in verses 12 and 16, and Cambridge explains that it is not restricted to peas and beans. The passage does not give a detailed menu.

The point is Daniel’s faithfulness and the Lord’s care within a real difficulty. He takes his concern seriously while addressing the officials respectfully and considering the risk they face.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley gives several reasons for Daniel’s concern, including forbidden food and food offered to idols. Cambridge likewise discusses dietary requirements and possible dedication to Babylonian gods. These are explanations of why the royal provisions could defile him; the passage itself does not identify the exact item or preparation at issue.

Henry emphasizes faithfulness and restraint, while Wesley sees the outcome as God’s blessing. The story’s result should be distinguished from a promise that the same menu will always produce the same outcome for every reader.
passages.god_plan_html:
First Peter 2:11–17 calls believers living as foreigners and exiles to honorable conduct, doing good and showing respect for people in authority. In Acts 5:27–32, the apostles also make clear that obedience to God takes priority when authorities forbid their witness to Jesus.

The broader connection holds these responsibilities together. Faithfulness does not require unnecessary hostility, and respect does not require disobeying God. Daniel’s request offers a practical example of seeking peace while keeping the commitment that brought him to ask in the first place.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 1:17-21
passages.section_title: Who gives the wisdom that prepares the four for service?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 To these four young men God gave knowledge and understanding in every kind of literature and wisdom. And Daniel had insight into all kinds of visions and dreams. 18 Now at the end of the time specified by the king, the chief official presented them to Nebuchadnezzar. 19 And the king spoke with them, and among all the young men he found no one equal to Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah. So they entered the king’s service. 20 In every matter of wisdom and understanding about which the king consulted them, he found them ten times better than all the magicians and enchanters in his entire kingdom. 21 And Daniel remained there until the first year of King Cyrus.
paragraphs: 17 To these four young men God gave knowledge and understanding in every kind of literature and wisdom. And Daniel had insight into all kinds of visions and dreams. 18 Now at the end of the time specified by the king, the chief official presented them to Nebuchadnezzar. 19 And the king spoke with them, and among all the young men he found no one equal to Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah. So they entered the king’s service. 20 In every matter of wisdom and understanding about which the king consulted them, he found them ten times better than all the magicians and enchanters in his entire kingdom. 21 And Daniel remained there until the first year of King Cyrus.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The account names God as the source of the four young men’s knowledge and understanding. Daniel also receives insight into visions and dreams, preparing the reader for what follows in the book.

At the end of their training, the king finds none equal to Daniel and his three friends. They enter his service, and he finds them greatly superior to the magicians and enchanters he consults.

The chapter ends by looking ahead to Daniel remaining until the first year of Cyrus. The captive youth’s life of service will extend across the fall of the power that brought him to Babylon. His usefulness and the Lord’s favor coexist with a life spent far from home.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry and Wesley emphasize God giving wisdom and making the four fit for useful service. Cambridge understands the final mention of Cyrus as marking Daniel’s continuance through Babylon’s change of rulers, rather than announcing his death then.
passages.god_plan_html:
James 1:5–8 directs those who lack wisdom to ask God for it. James 3:13–18 then describes wisdom from above by its fruit: humility, peace, gentleness, mercy and sincerity, in contrast with envy and selfish ambition.

Daniel’s gifts prepare him for a particular royal calling; James addresses the life of Christ’s people more widely. The connection shows that wisdom given by God is more than impressive knowledge or success. It should shape the way a person lives and treats others.

passages.title: Daniel 2:1-11
passages.section_title: Why can’t the king’s advisers meet his demand?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 In the second year of his reign, Nebuchadnezzar had dreams that troubled his spirit, and sleep escaped him. 2 So the king gave orders to summon the magicians, enchanters, sorcerers, and astrologers to explain his dreams. When they came and stood before the king, 3 he said to them, “I have had a dream, and my spirit is anxious to understand it.” 4 Then the astrologers answered the king in Aramaic, “O king, may you live forever! Tell your servants the dream, and we will give the interpretation.” 5 The king replied to the astrologers, “My word is final: If you do not tell me the dream and its interpretation, you will be cut into pieces and your houses will be reduced to rubble. 6 But if you tell me the dream and its interpretation, you will receive from me gifts and rewards and great honor. So tell me the dream and its interpretation.” 7 They answered a second time, “Let the king tell the dream to his servants, and we will give the interpretation.” 8 The king replied, “I know for sure that you are stalling for time because you see that my word is final. 9 If you do not tell me the dream, there is only one decree for you. You have conspired to speak before me false and fraudulent words, hoping the situation will change. Therefore tell me the dream, and I will know that you can give me its interpretation.” 10 The astrologers answered the king, “No one on earth can do what the king requests! No king, however great and powerful, has ever asked anything like this of any magician, enchanter, or astrologer. 11 What the king requests is so difficult that no one can tell it to him except the gods, whose dwelling is not with mortals.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Nebuchadnezzar’s dreams leave him troubled and unable to sleep. He summons those expected to explain such matters, but demands more than an interpretation: they must also tell him the dream itself.

The advisers ask him to describe it first. He suspects that they are stalling and preparing a false answer, so he insists that telling the dream will demonstrate their ability to interpret it.

They finally admit that no human being can supply what he asks. In their account, only the gods could know it, and those gods do not dwell with mortals. Their admission prepares for the contrast with the God who will make the mystery known to Daniel.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gaebelein understand the king as having forgotten the dream. Cambridge reads his statement in verse 5 as a firm decree rather than a lost memory. The BSB likewise gives his words as a final decision.

The shared point is the demand for both dream and interpretation. The text does not simply show the advisers failing to explain a dream already supplied to them.

passages.title: Daniel 2:12-18
passages.section_title: How does Daniel respond when the decree threatens his friends?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 This response made the king so angry and furious that he gave orders to destroy all the wise men of Babylon. 13 So the decree went out that the wise men were to be executed, and men went to look for Daniel and his friends to execute them. 14 When Arioch, the commander of the king’s guard, went out to execute the wise men of Babylon, Daniel responded with discretion and tact. 15 “Why is the decree from the king so harsh?” he asked. Then Arioch explained the situation to Daniel. 16 So Daniel went in and asked the king to give him some time, so that he could give him the interpretation. 17 Then Daniel returned to his house and explained the matter to his friends Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, 18 urging them to plead for mercy from the God of heaven concerning this mystery, so that Daniel and his friends would not be killed with the rest of the wise men of Babylon.
