Then Arioch explained the situation to Daniel. 16 So Daniel went in and asked the king to give him some time, so that he could give him the interpretation.

17 Then Daniel returned to his house and explained the matter to his friends Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, 18 urging them to plead for mercy from the God of heaven concerning this mystery, so that Daniel and his friends would not be killed with the rest of the wise men of Babylon.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The king orders the execution of all Babylon’s wise men, placing Daniel and his friends in danger too. Daniel asks Arioch about the harsh decree with discretion and tact, rather than answering recklessly.

He asks the king for time, then explains the situation to Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah. They are to plead for mercy from the God of heaven concerning the mystery.

The response combines practical action and shared prayer. Daniel seeks an opportunity to answer while acknowledging that the knowledge needed to save them must come from God.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry and Gaebelein emphasize the friends seeking God’s mercy together. Henry also draws attention to valuing other people’s prayers and recognizing the answer as a gift, rather than something earned by the petitioners.
passages.god_plan_html:
A similar response appears in Acts 4:23–31. After Peter and John report the authorities’ threats, the believers pray together to the Creator, recognizing opposition to Jesus and asking for boldness to speak God’s word.

The outcomes are not identical: Daniel seeks the knowledge needed to avert executions, while the church asks for courage to continue its witness. Both show threatened people turning together to the God whose purpose is greater than the rulers confronting them.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 2:19-23
passages.section_title: Why does Daniel praise God before returning to the king?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 During the night, the mystery was revealed to Daniel in a vision, and he blessed the God of heaven 20 and declared: “Blessed be the name of God forever and ever, for wisdom and power belong to Him. 21 He changes the times and seasons; He removes kings and establishes them. He gives wisdom to the wise and knowledge to the discerning. 22 He reveals the deep and hidden things; He knows what lies in darkness, and light dwells with Him. 23 To You, O God of my fathers, I give thanks and praise, because You have given me wisdom and power. And now You have made known to me what we have requested, for You have made known to us the dream of the king.”

He gives wisdom to the wise and knowledge to the discerning. 22 He reveals the deep and hidden things; He knows what lies in darkness, and light dwells with Him. 23 To You, O God of my fathers, I give thanks and praise, because You have given me wisdom and power. And now You have made known to me what we have requested, for You have made known to us the dream of the king.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The mystery is revealed to Daniel in a night vision. Before reporting to the king, he blesses the God of heaven and gives thanks for the answer.

His praise reaches beyond his immediate rescue. Wisdom and power belong to God; He changes times and seasons, removes kings and establishes them, and makes hidden things known.

Daniel includes his friends in the thanksgiving by speaking of what they requested and what God made known to them. The answer belongs within God’s care for the petitioners and His authority over history.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry emphasizes Daniel’s gratitude for mercy that saves lives. Cambridge connects the changing of times with the rise and fall of rulers and notes Daniel’s acknowledgment of God as the source of wisdom.

The praise recognizes that the king who appears to control their lives is himself subject to God.
passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 17:24–31 also speaks of the Creator determining nations’ appointed times and boundaries. Paul gives a purpose for this: people are to seek Him, the God who gives life and is near to them.

Paul then announces the call to repentance and the coming judgment through the Man God has appointed, with Jesus’ resurrection as assurance. The larger purpose is more than arranging a succession of rulers. God makes Himself known and calls the nations to respond to Him through Christ.

passages.title: Daniel 2:24-30
passages.section_title: Why does Daniel refuse to take credit for knowing the mystery?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 24 Therefore Daniel went to Arioch, whom the king had appointed to destroy the wise men of Babylon, and said to him, “Do not execute the wise men of Babylon! Bring me before the king, and I will give him the interpretation.” 25 Arioch hastily brought Daniel before the king and said to him, “I have found a man among the exiles from Judah who will tell the king the interpretation.” 26 The king responded to Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar, “Are you able to tell me what I saw in the dream, as well as its interpretation?” 27 Daniel answered the king, “No wise man, enchanter, medium, or magician can explain to the king the mystery of which he inquires. 28 But there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries, and He has made known to King Nebuchadnezzar what will happen in the latter days. Your dream and the visions that came into your mind as you lay on your bed were these: 29 As you lay on your bed, O king, your thoughts turned to the future, and the Revealer of Mysteries made known to you what will happen. 30 And to me this mystery has been revealed, not because I have more wisdom than any man alive, but in order that the interpretation might be made known to the king, and that you may understand the thoughts of your mind.

Bring me before the king, and I will give him the interpretation.” 25 Arioch hastily brought Daniel before the king and said to him, “I have found a man among the exiles from Judah who will tell the king the interpretation.” 26 The king responded to Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar, “Are you able to tell me what I saw in the dream, as well as its interpretation?”

27 Daniel answered the king, “No wise man, enchanter, medium, or magician can explain to the king the mystery of which he inquires. 28 But there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries, and He has made known to King Nebuchadnezzar what will happen in the latter days. Your dream and the visions that came into your mind as you lay on your bed were these: 29 As you lay on your bed, O king, your thoughts turned to the future, and the Revealer of Mysteries made known to you what will happen. 30 And to me this mystery has been revealed, not because I have more wisdom than any man alive, but in order that the interpretation might be made known to the king, and that you may understand the thoughts of your mind.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Daniel asks Arioch to stop the executions and bring him before the king. When asked whether he can tell the dream and its meaning, he first names the limits of human expertise.

There is, however, a God in heaven who reveals mysteries. He has shown the king what will happen, and has given Daniel the explanation so that the king may understand.

The Aramaic word רָז, raz (rahz), means a secret; see Brown–Driver–Briggs. Here the mystery is something hidden that God makes known, rather than something that must remain impossible to understand.

Daniel explicitly denies that the revelation comes because he is wiser than everyone else. His role is to pass on what God has given, not to make himself the source of it.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Gaebelein emphasize Daniel directing honor to God instead of using the occasion to magnify himself. Wesley also sees him preparing the king to recognize the true God.

The explanation will be a witness to the One who reveals, rather than a performance of Daniel’s own power.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 3:1–12 describes another mystery made known by revelation: through the gospel, Gentiles share the inheritance, the body and the promise in Christ Jesus. Paul presents his ministry as a gift of grace serving that revealed purpose.

The mysteries have different contents. Daniel explains a royal dream; Paul announces Gentiles’ shared belonging in Christ. The connection is God making His purpose known through servants, so that others can understand and share what He is doing. Paul carries that purpose to confident access to God through Christ.

passages.title: Daniel 2:31-35
passages.section_title: What does the king’s statue dream show?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 31 As you, O king, were watching, a great statue appeared. A great and dazzling statue stood before you, and its form was awesome. 32 The head of the statue was pure gold, its chest and arms were silver, its belly and thighs were bronze, 33 its legs were iron, and its feet were part iron and part clay. 34 As you watched, a stone was cut out, but not by human hands. It struck the statue on its feet of iron and clay, and crushed them. 35 Then the iron, clay, bronze, silver, and gold were shattered and became like chaff on the threshing floor in summer. The wind carried them away, and not a trace of them could be found. But the stone that had struck the statue became a great mountain and filled the whole earth.
paragraphs: 31 As you, O king, were watching, a great statue appeared. A great and dazzling statue stood before you, and its form was awesome. 32 The head of the statue was pure gold, its chest and arms were silver, its belly and thighs were bronze, 33 its legs were iron, and its feet were part iron and part clay.

34 As you watched, a stone was cut out, but not by human hands. It struck the statue on its feet of iron and clay, and crushed them. 35 Then the iron, clay, bronze, silver, and gold were shattered and became like chaff on the threshing floor in summer. section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Daniel describes a great, dazzling statue: a head of gold, chest and arms of silver, belly and thighs of bronze, legs of iron, and feet combining iron and clay.

A stone cut without human hands strikes its feet and crushes the whole statue. All its materials become like chaff carried away by the wind, leaving no trace.

The stone becomes a great mountain filling the earth. The contrast is between an impressive structure that cannot endure and something brought about without human workmanship that ultimately fills its place. The next verses explain what those images represent.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads the statue as successive earthly kingdoms and the stone as Christ’s kingdom. Cambridge emphasizes the complete disappearance of the statue and the expanding reach of the kingdom represented by the mountain.

The image is explained by the interpretation that follows. It need not be turned into a separate code in which every feature receives a meaning unrelated to that explanation.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 2:36-43
passages.section_title: Which kingdoms do the statue’s materials represent?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 36 This was the dream; now we will tell the king its interpretation. 37 You, O king, are the king of kings, to whom the God of heaven has given sovereignty, power, strength, and glory. 38 Wherever the sons of men or beasts of the field or birds of the air dwell, He has given them into your hand and has made you ruler over them all. You are that head of gold. 39 But after you, there will arise another kingdom, inferior to yours. Next, a third kingdom, one of bronze, will rule the whole earth. 40 Finally, there will be a fourth kingdom as strong as iron; for iron shatters and crushes all things, and like iron that crushes all things, it will shatter and crush all the others. 41 And just as you saw that the feet and toes were made partly of fired clay and partly of iron, so this will be a divided kingdom, yet some of the strength of iron will be in it—just as you saw the iron mixed with clay. 42 And as the toes of the feet were partly iron and partly clay, so this kingdom will be partly strong and partly brittle. 43 As you saw the iron mixed with clay, so the peoples will mix with one another but will not hold together any more than iron mixes with clay.

You are that head of gold.

39 But after you, there will arise another kingdom, inferior to yours. Next, a third kingdom, one of bronze, will rule the whole earth. 40 Finally, there will be a fourth kingdom as strong as iron; for iron shatters and crushes all things, and like iron that crushes all things, it will shatter and crush all the others.

41 And just as you saw that the feet and toes were made partly of fired clay and partly of iron, so this will be a divided kingdom, yet some of the strength of iron will be in it—just as you saw the iron mixed with clay. 42 And as the toes of the feet were partly iron and partly clay, so this kingdom will be partly strong and partly brittle. 43 As you saw the iron mixed with clay, so the peoples will mix with one another but will not hold together any more than iron mixes with clay.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Daniel identifies Nebuchadnezzar as the head of gold and attributes his authority to the God of heaven. Another kingdom will follow, then a third and a fourth.

The fourth has the crushing strength of iron, but its later condition combines strength and brittleness like iron mixed with clay. Its parts do not hold together firmly.

The interpretation names the first kingdom through its ruler but does not give the other kingdoms’ names here. Identifying them involves reading this explanation alongside the book’s later visions and its account of changing rulers.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley give the sequence as Babylon, the combined kingdom of the Medes and Persians, Greece, and Rome. Their reading treats Media and Persia as one kingdom.

Cambridge instead gives Babylon, Media, Persia, and the Greek kingdom established by Alexander. It counts the Median and Persian kingdoms separately, reading the later chapters’ rulers and visions in that way.

The central difference is therefore not the identity of the golden head, but how the next kingdoms are counted. That difference also changes which period is understood through the divided iron-and-clay kingdom.

Wesley understands the attempted mixing in verse 43 as marriage alliances that cannot overcome ambition. Cambridge also reads marriage alliances, specifically among the rulers following Alexander. Both take the image to show a union that does not become lasting harmony.

passages.title: Daniel 2:44-45
passages.section_title: What makes the kingdom God establishes different?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 44 In the days of those kings, the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed, nor will it be left to another people. It will shatter all these kingdoms and bring them to an end, but will itself stand forever. 45 And just as you saw a stone being cut out of the mountain without human hands, and it shattered the iron, bronze, clay, silver, and gold, so the great God has told the king what will happen in the future. The dream is true, and its interpretation is trustworthy.”
paragraphs: 44 In the days of those kings, the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed, nor will it be left to another people. It will shatter all these kingdoms and bring them to an end, but will itself stand forever. 45 And just as you saw a stone being cut out of the mountain without human hands, and it shattered the iron, bronze, clay, silver, and gold, so the great God has told the king what will happen in the future. The dream is true, and its interpretation is trustworthy.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The God of heaven will establish a kingdom that cannot be destroyed or transferred to another people. It will end the preceding kingdoms and stand forever.

This is the meaning of the stone cut from the mountain without human hands. Its origin and lasting victory come from God rather than the workmanship that produced the statue.

Daniel closes with assurance that the dream is true and its interpretation trustworthy. Earthly rulers succeed one another; the kingdom God establishes is not simply another temporary link in that chain.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley read the stone through Christ and His kingdom, beginning in the Roman period and reaching its full victory. Gaebelein places the decisive crushing of the statue at Christ’s future return and the establishment of His earthly kingdom.

Cambridge, following its Greek identification of the fourth kingdom, understands the passage as expecting God’s kingdom after the fall of Antiochus Epiphanes. The difference over the earthly kingdoms therefore carries into the expected timing of this final change.

These are the named interpreters’ readings. The passage’s own emphasis is that God’s kingdom ends the succession of perishable powers and will itself endure.
passages.god_plan_html:
A close parallel appears in Luke 20:17–18, where Jesus speaks of the rejected stone and of those on whom it falls being crushed. This connects the stone’s judgment imagery with Jesus, while the announcement in Luke 1:30–33 identifies Him as the promised ruler whose kingdom will not end.

Revelation 11:15–19 carries the hope to the kingdom of the world becoming that of the Lord and His Christ, with judgment and reward accompanying His reign. Together these passages give the lasting kingdom its New Testament focus in Christ without settling every disputed detail of the statue’s historical sequence.

passages.title: Daniel 2:46-49
passages.section_title: What does the king acknowledge, and what happens to the four friends?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 46 At this, King Nebuchadnezzar fell on his face, paid homage to Daniel, and ordered that an offering and incense be presented to him. 47 The king said to Daniel, “Your God is truly the God of gods and Lord of kings, the Revealer of Mysteries, since you were able to reveal this mystery.” 48 Then the king promoted Daniel and gave him many generous gifts. He made him ruler over the entire province of Babylon and chief administrator over all the wise men of Babylon. 49 And at Daniel’s request, the king appointed Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego to manage the province of Babylon, while Daniel remained in the king’s court.
paragraphs: 46 At this, King Nebuchadnezzar fell on his face, paid homage to Daniel, and ordered that an offering and incense be presented to him. 47 The king said to Daniel, “Your God is truly the God of gods and Lord of kings, the Revealer of Mysteries, since you were able to reveal this mystery.”

48 Then the king promoted Daniel and gave him many generous gifts. He made him ruler over the entire province of Babylon and chief administrator over all the wise men of Babylon. 49 And at Daniel’s request, the king appointed Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego to manage the province of Babylon, while Daniel remained in the king’s court.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The king falls before Daniel and orders an offering and incense for him. He then acknowledges Daniel’s God as God of gods, Lord of kings and the revealer of mysteries.

Daniel receives gifts and authority over the province of Babylon and its wise men. At his request, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego also receive administrative responsibilities, while he remains at the royal court.

The men threatened with execution have been preserved and placed in service. The king’s acknowledgment answers Daniel’s earlier insistence: the knowledge came from God.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley believes Daniel must have prevented the offering, although no refusal is recorded. Cambridge instead understands the homage as honor reaching God through Daniel as His representative. The account itself moves directly from the king’s action to his acknowledgment of Daniel’s God.

Henry cautions that recognizing divine power is not the same as choosing to serve God. The king’s words are significant, but this scene does not by itself give a complete account of his later faithfulness.

passages.title: Daniel 3:1-7
passages.section_title: What does the king demand when the music sounds?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 King Nebuchadnezzar made a golden statue sixty cubits high and six cubits wide, and he set it up on the plain of Dura in the province of Babylon. 2 Then King Nebuchadnezzar sent word to assemble the satraps, prefects, governors, advisers, treasurers, judges, magistrates, and all the other officials of the provinces to attend the dedication of the statue he had set up. 3 So the satraps, prefects, governors, advisers, treasurers, judges, magistrates, and all the rulers of the provinces assembled for the dedication of the statue that King Nebuchadnezzar had set up, and they stood before it. 4 Then the herald loudly proclaimed, “O people of every nation and language, this is what you are commanded: 5 As soon as you hear the sound of the horn, flute, zither, lyre, harp, pipes, and all kinds of music, you must fall down and worship the golden statue that King Nebuchadnezzar has set up. 6 And whoever does not fall down and worship will immediately be thrown into the blazing fiery furnace.” 7 Therefore, as soon as all the people heard the sound of the horn, flute, zither, lyre, harp, and all kinds of music, the people of every nation and language would fall down and worship the golden statue that King Nebuchadnezzar had set up.

4 Then the herald loudly proclaimed, “O people of every nation and language, this is what you are commanded: 5 As soon as you hear the sound of the horn, flute, zither, lyre, harp, pipes, and all kinds of music, you must fall down and worship the golden statue that King Nebuchadnezzar has set up. 6 And whoever does not fall down and worship will immediately be thrown into the blazing fiery furnace.” 7 Therefore, as soon as all the people heard the sound of the horn, flute, zither, lyre, harp, and all kinds of music, the people of every nation and language would fall down and worship the golden statue that King Nebuchadnezzar had set up.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Nebuchadnezzar sets up a golden statue on the plain of Dura and summons the provincial officials to its dedication. Its dimensions—sixty cubits high and six wide—make it an imposing focus for the gathering.

The herald commands people of every nation and language to fall down and worship when the instruments sound. Refusal will mean immediate death in the fiery furnace.

The scene joins royal authority, a public ceremony and a demand for worship. The issue for the faithful is not simply whether to attend an official event, but whether to give the worship the command requires.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry emphasizes the pressure created by public attraction and the threat of punishment. Cambridge notes that the text does not state exactly whom the statue represents, although it considers an image of the king likely.

The demand for worship is clear even where the statue’s precise form is not. The chapter does not state a date or say that the image is a direct copy of the statue in the preceding dream.
passages.god_plan_html:
A close parallel appears in Revelation 13:11–18, where worship of an image is enforced with the threat of death. Power is used to demand allegiance that conflicts with faithfulness to God.

Revelation 14:9–13 places that pressure alongside a call for the saints’ perseverance and the hope of rest for those who die in the Lord. The connection shows the seriousness of faithful worship, without turning every detail of Nebuchadnezzar’s ceremony into a timetable of future events.

passages.title: Daniel 3:8-12
passages.section_title: Why are the three Jewish officials accused?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 At this time some astrologers came forward and maliciously accused the Jews, 9 saying to King Nebuchadnezzar, “O king, may you live forever! 10 You, O king, have issued a decree that everyone who hears the sound of the horn, flute, zither, lyre, harp, pipes, and all kinds of music must fall down and worship the golden statue, 11 and that whoever does not fall down and worship will be thrown into the blazing fiery furnace. 12 But there are some Jews you have appointed to manage the province of Babylon—Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego—who have ignored you, O king, and have refused to serve your gods or worship the golden statue you have set up.”
paragraphs: 8 At this time some astrologers came forward and maliciously accused the Jews, 9 saying to King Nebuchadnezzar, “O king, may you live forever! 10 You, O king, have issued a decree that everyone who hears the sound of the horn, flute, zither, lyre, harp, pipes, and all kinds of music must fall down and worship the golden statue, 11 and that whoever does not fall down and worship will be thrown into the blazing fiery furnace. 12 But there are some Jews you have appointed to manage the province of Babylon—Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego—who have ignored you, O king, and have refused to serve your gods or worship the golden statue you have set up.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Some astrologers bring a malicious accusation against the Jews. They repeat the king’s command and its penalty before naming Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego.

The accusation emphasizes that these are men the king appointed to manage Babylon’s province. Their refusal to serve his gods and worship his statue is presented as disregard for him.

Their official positions do not remove the conflict of loyalty. Service in the king’s government has not made them willing to give the worship he demands.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley read the conflict through the duty to obey God rather than comply with sinful worship. The accusation brings that commitment into a public confrontation with the ruler.

Daniel is not named among the accused. The chapter does not explain his whereabouts, so the three men’s situation should not be filled out with an invented account of what he was doing.

passages.title: Daniel 3:13-18
passages.section_title: Will they remain faithful even if they are not rescued?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 Then Nebuchadnezzar, furious with rage, summoned Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. So these men were brought before the king, 14 and Nebuchadnezzar said to them, “Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, is it true that you do not serve my gods or worship the golden statue I have set up? 15 Now when you hear the sound of the horn, flute, zither, lyre, harp, pipes, and all kinds of music, if you are ready to fall down and worship the statue I have made, very good. But if you refuse to worship, you will be thrown at once into the blazing fiery furnace. Then what god will be able to deliver you from my hands?” 16 Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego replied to the king, “O Nebuchadnezzar, we have no need to answer you in this matter. 17 If the God whom we serve exists, then He is able to deliver us from the blazing fiery furnace and from your hand, O king. 18 But even if He does not, let it be known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden statue you have set up.”
paragraphs: 13 Then Nebuchadnezzar, furious with rage, summoned Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. So these men were brought before the king, 14 and Nebuchadnezzar said to them, “Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, is it true that you do not serve my gods or worship the golden statue I have set up? 15 Now when you hear the sound of the horn, flute, zither, lyre, harp, pipes, and all kinds of music, if you are ready to fall down and worship the statue I have made, very good. But if you refuse to worship, you will be thrown at once into the blazing fiery furnace. Then what god will be able to deliver you from my hands?”

16 Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego replied to the king, “O Nebuchadnezzar, we have no need to answer you in this matter. 17 If the God whom we serve exists, then He is able to deliver us from the blazing fiery furnace and from your hand, O king. 18 But even if He does not, let it be known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden statue you have set up.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The furious king gives the men another opportunity to bow, repeating the threat of the furnace. He ends by challenging whether any god can deliver them from his hand.

They answer by appealing to the God they serve and His power to deliver. Their refusal to worship the statue does not depend on receiving a rescue: even if He does not deliver them, they will not serve the king’s gods.

The answer separates two things often confused. Trusting God’s power is not the same as insisting that He must give the outcome a person wants. Their loyalty is settled before the outcome is known.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands their response as leaving the outcome to God while refusing to sin. The USCCB notes likewise explain their answer as a question of whether God will exercise His saving power, rather than a rejection of His ability.

The BSB phrases verse 17 conditionally, but the men still identify Him as the God they serve. Verse 18 makes their decision unmistakable: deliverance or no deliverance, the statue will not receive their worship.
passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 11:32–40 recalls people whose faith overcame raging fire, alongside others who endured torture and death while hoping for a better resurrection. Both groups are commended for faith.

The wider picture gives weight to the three men’s refusal to make obedience depend on survival. God can rescue His people from a threat, but the hope of those who trust Him also reaches beyond death. The New Testament joins stories of deliverance with the promise of final completion before God.

passages.title: Daniel 3:19-23
passages.section_title: What does the king’s anger accomplish?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 At this, Nebuchadnezzar was filled with rage, and the expression on his face changed toward Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. He gave orders to heat the furnace seven times hotter than usual, 20 and he commanded some mighty men of valor in his army to tie up Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego and throw them into the blazing fiery furnace. 21 So they were tied up, wearing robes, trousers, turbans, and other clothes, and they were thrown into the blazing fiery furnace. 22 The king’s command was so urgent and the furnace so hot that the fiery flames killed the men who carried up Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. 23 And these three men, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, firmly bound, fell into the blazing fiery furnace.
paragraphs: 19 At this, Nebuchadnezzar was filled with rage, and the expression on his face changed toward Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. He gave orders to heat the furnace seven times hotter than usual, 20 and he commanded some mighty men of valor in his army to tie up Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego and throw them into the blazing fiery furnace. 21 So they were tied up, wearing robes, trousers, turbans, and other clothes, and they were thrown into the blazing fiery furnace. 22 The king’s command was so urgent and the furnace so hot that the fiery flames killed the men who carried up Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. 23 And these three men, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, firmly bound, fell into the blazing fiery furnace.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The king orders the furnace heated seven times hotter than usual and commands strong soldiers to bind the men and throw them in. They are cast into the fire fully clothed and firmly bound.

The heat kills the soldiers carrying out the order. The men targeted by the decree fall into the furnace, and the situation appears to leave them no means of escape.

The details establish the severity of the threat before the rescue is described. Neither protective equipment nor an unnoticed avoidance of the fire explains what follows.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley emphasize God’s power to preserve the men when the king has done his worst. The deaths of the soldiers make the danger plain.

The passage states the increased heat and its effect. It does not provide the furnace’s exact construction, a modern temperature reading or a detailed account of the soldiers’ movements.

passages.title: Daniel 3:24-27
passages.section_title: Who is with the men in the fire?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 24 Suddenly King Nebuchadnezzar jumped up in amazement and asked his advisers, “Did we not throw three men, firmly bound, into the fire?” “Certainly, O king,” they replied. 25 “Look!” he exclaimed. “I see four men, unbound and unharmed, walking around in the fire—and the fourth looks like a son of the gods!” 26 Then Nebuchadnezzar approached the door of the blazing fiery furnace and called out, “Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, servants of the Most High God, come out!” So Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego came out of the fire, 27 and when the satraps, prefects, governors, and royal advisers had gathered around, they saw that the fire had no effect on the bodies of these men. Not a hair of their heads was singed, their robes were unaffected, and there was no smell of fire on them.

26 Then Nebuchadnezzar approached the door of the blazing fiery furnace and called out, “Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, servants of the Most High God, come out!” So Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego came out of the fire, 27 and when the satraps, prefects, governors, and royal advisers had gathered around, they saw that the fire had no effect on the bodies of these men. Not a hair of their heads was singed, their robes were unaffected, and there was no smell of fire on them.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The king sees four men walking freely and unharmed where three had been thrown in bound. He describes the fourth as looking like a son of the gods.

He calls Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego servants of the Most High God and tells them to come out. The gathered officials then see that their bodies, hair and clothing have not been damaged, and they do not even smell of fire.

The rescue reverses the king’s challenge about who could deliver them from his hand. The account stresses the completeness of the rescue: they emerge untouched by the fire.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley understand the fourth figure as Christ appearing before His birth as a man. Cambridge understands the description as an angelic being and points to the king’s reference to God sending His angel in verse 28.

The BSB gives the king’s words as a son of the gods, rather than the title the Son of God. Christians who see Christ here draw that identification from a wider reading of His presence with God’s people; the king’s description alone does not name Him as Jesus.
passages.god_plan_html:
First Peter 4:12–19 tells Christians not to be surprised by a fiery trial. Those suffering for Christ are to entrust themselves to their faithful Creator and continue doing good, with the promise that the Spirit of glory and of God rests on them.

This is a wider connection about God’s presence in suffering, rather than a promise that every Christian will emerge physically unharmed as these men did. Peter joins present faithfulness to the coming revelation of Christ’s glory. Suffering for His name does not mean being abandoned by Him.

passages.title: Daniel 3:28-30
passages.section_title: What does the king acknowledge after the rescue?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 28 Nebuchadnezzar declared, “Blessed be the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, who has sent His angel and delivered His servants who trusted in Him. They violated the king’s command and risked their lives rather than serve or worship any god except their own God. 29 Therefore I decree that the people of any nation or language who say anything offensive against the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego will be cut into pieces and their houses reduced to rubble. For there is no other god who can deliver in this way.” 30 Then the king promoted Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego in the province of Babylon.

They violated the king’s command and risked their lives rather than serve or worship any god except their own God. 29 Therefore I decree that the people of any nation or language who say anything offensive against the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego will be cut into pieces and their houses reduced to rubble. For there is no other god who can deliver in this way.” 30 Then the king promoted Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego in the province of Babylon.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Nebuchadnezzar blesses the God who sent His angel and delivered the servants who trusted Him. He recognizes that they risked their lives and disobeyed his command rather than worship another god.

He then issues a decree against speaking offensively about their God and promotes the three within Babylon’s province. The ruler who demanded their death now publicly acknowledges the One who saved them.

His new threat of violent punishment remains the king’s decree. The account records it as part of his response, rather than giving God’s people a command to use the same methods.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry sees the rescue as encouragement for Jews in captivity to remain faithful. He also distinguishes the king’s strong conviction in this moment from a lasting change in his conduct.

The story ends with God’s servants preserved and His power acknowledged. The king’s later life is still to be told.

passages.title: Daniel 4:1-3
passages.section_title: Why does the king announce what God has done for him?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 King Nebuchadnezzar, To the people of every nation and language who dwell in all the earth: May your prosperity be multiplied. 2 I am pleased to declare the signs and wonders that the Most High God has performed for me. 3 How great are His signs, how mighty His wonders! His kingdom is an eternal kingdom; His dominion endures from generation to generation.
paragraphs: 1 King Nebuchadnezzar, To the people of every nation and language who dwell in all the earth: May your prosperity be multiplied. 2 I am pleased to declare the signs and wonders that the Most High God has performed for me. 3 How great are His signs, how mighty His wonders! His kingdom is an eternal kingdom; His dominion endures from generation to generation.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The chapter opens as a proclamation from Nebuchadnezzar to people of every nation and language. He wants them to know the signs and wonders the Most High God has performed for him.

Before telling the experience, he gives its conclusion: God’s kingdom is eternal, and His dominion lasts from generation to generation. The powerful human ruler is about to explain how he learned that his own authority was not ultimate.

The account therefore begins with praise before looking back on warning, humiliation and restoration. Its emphasis is not only what the king suffered, but what he came to acknowledge about God.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry and Wesley read the proclamation as the king making known the mercy and power he experienced. Both connect the opening praise with the changed acknowledgment that closes the chapter.

passages.title: Daniel 4:4-18
passages.section_title: What does the king see in the dream of the great tree?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 4 I, Nebuchadnezzar, was at ease in my house and flourishing in my palace. 5 I had a dream, and it frightened me; while I was in my bed, the images and visions in my mind alarmed me. 6 So I issued a decree that all the wise men of Babylon be brought before me to interpret the dream for me. 7 When the magicians, enchanters, astrologers, and diviners came in, I told them the dream, but they could not interpret it for me. 8 But at last, into my presence came Daniel (whose name is Belteshazzar after the name of my god, and in whom is the spirit of the holy gods). And I told him the dream: 9 “O Belteshazzar, chief of the magicians, I know that the spirit of the holy gods is in you and that no mystery baffles you. So explain to me the visions I saw in my dream, and their interpretation. 10 In these visions of my mind as I was lying in bed, I saw this come to pass: There was a tree in the midst of the land, and its height was great. 11 The tree grew large and strong; its top reached the sky, and it was visible to the ends of the earth. 12 Its leaves were beautiful, its fruit was abundant, and upon it was food for all. Under it the beasts of the field found shelter, in its branches the birds of the air nested, and from it every creature was fed. 13 As I lay on my bed, I also saw in the visions of my mind a watcher, a holy one, coming down from heaven. 14 He called out in a loud voice: ‘Cut down the tree and chop off its branches; strip off its leaves and scatter its fruit. Let the beasts flee from under it, and the birds from its branches. 15 But leave the stump with its roots in the ground, with a band of iron and bronze around it, in the tender grass of the field. Let him be drenched with the dew of heaven and graze with the beasts on the grass of the earth. 16 Let his mind be changed from that of a man, and let him be given the mind of a beast till seven times pass him by. 17 This decision is the decree of the watchers, the verdict declared by the holy ones, so that the living will know that the Most High rules over the kingdom of mankind and gives it to whom He wishes, setting over it the lowliest of men.’ 18 This is the dream that I, King Nebuchadnezzar, saw. Now, Belteshazzar, tell me the interpretation, because none of the wise men of my kingdom can interpret it for me. But you are able, because the spirit of the holy gods is in you.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
While comfortable in his palace, Nebuchadnezzar has another frightening dream. This time he tells it to the wise men, but they cannot explain it. He then turns to Daniel.

The dream shows a vast tree supplying food and shelter to creatures throughout the land. A holy watcher comes down from heaven and commands that it be cut down, leaving the stump and roots bound with iron and bronze.

The description turns from the tree to a man: his mind is to become like a beast’s, and seven times are to pass over him. The stated purpose is that people know the Most High rules over human kingdoms and gives authority to whom He wishes.

The Aramaic word עִיר, ir (eer), means a wakeful one and is used here for an angel; see Brown–Driver–Briggs. The watcher brings a heavenly decree, which Daniel identifies in verse 24 as the decree of the Most High.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands the watcher as an angel carrying out God’s judgment, and Cambridge also explains the term as a wakeful heavenly being. The messenger’s role belongs under the Most High’s rule.

Both Wesley and Cambridge understand the seven times as seven years. The BSB retains times in the passage itself; the interpretation’s central purpose is the humbling of the king until he recognizes who rules.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 4:19-27
passages.section_title: What does Daniel tell the king to change?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 For a time, Daniel, who was also known as Belteshazzar, was perplexed, and his thoughts alarmed him. So the king said, “Belteshazzar, do not let the dream or its interpretation alarm you.” “My lord,” replied Belteshazzar, “may the dream apply to those who hate you, and its interpretation to your enemies! 20 The tree you saw that grew large and strong, whose top reached the sky and was visible to all the earth, 21 whose foliage was beautiful and whose fruit was abundant, providing food for all, under which the beasts of the field lived, and in whose branches the birds of the air nested— 22 you, O king, are that tree! For you have become great and strong; your greatness has grown to reach the sky, and your dominion extends to the ends of the earth. 23 And you, O king, saw a watcher, a holy one, coming down from heaven and saying: ‘Cut down the tree and destroy it, but leave the stump with its roots in the ground, with a band of iron and bronze around it, in the tender grass of the field. Let him be drenched with the dew of heaven, and graze with the beasts of the field till seven times pass him by.’ 24 This is the interpretation, O king, and this is the decree that the Most High has issued against my lord the king: 25 You will be driven away from mankind, and your dwelling will be with the beasts of the field. You will feed on grass like an ox and be drenched with the dew of heaven, and seven times shall pass you by, until you acknowledge that the Most High rules over the kingdom of mankind and gives it to whom He wishes. 26 As for the command to leave the stump of the tree with its roots, your kingdom will be restored to you as soon as you acknowledge that Heaven rules. 27 Therefore, may my advice be pleasing to you, O king. Break away from your sins by doing what is right, and from your iniquities by showing mercy to the oppressed. Perhaps there will be an extension of your prosperity.”

Break away from your sins by doing what is right, and from your iniquities by showing mercy to the oppressed. Perhaps there will be an extension of your prosperity.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Daniel is alarmed by the meaning of the dream and wishes that it applied to the king’s enemies. He nevertheless tells him plainly: the great tree represents the king and his far-reaching dominion.

Nebuchadnezzar will be driven from human society to live and eat like an animal until he acknowledges the Most High’s rule. Leaving the stump means that his kingdom will be restored when he recognizes that Heaven rules.

Daniel ends with an appeal to act now: break away from sin by doing what is right and show mercy to the oppressed. His advice makes the response concrete. Acknowledging God should change the way the king treats those within his power.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry understands Daniel’s advice as repentance that includes both ceasing evil and doing good. Wesley emphasizes the tenderness and plainness of the warning, leaving room for mercy without promising that the king can control the outcome.
passages.god_plan_html:
Luke 19:1–10 gives another picture of a wealthy person’s changed response. When Zacchaeus receives Jesus, he speaks of giving to the poor and restoring what he has taken dishonestly. Jesus announces salvation and His purpose of seeking and saving the lost.

The connection is repentance becoming visible in justice and mercy. God’s saving purpose reaches into the way people handle wealth and the lives of others. A changed relationship with Him has consequences for those a person could otherwise exploit or neglect.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 4:28-33
passages.section_title: What happens when the king takes the glory for himself?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 28 All this happened to King Nebuchadnezzar. 29 Twelve months later, as he was walking on the roof of the royal palace of Babylon, 30 the king exclaimed, “Is this not Babylon the Great, which I myself have built as a royal residence by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty?” 31 While the words were still in the king’s mouth, a voice came from heaven: “It is decreed to you, King Nebuchadnezzar, that the kingdom has departed from you. 32 You will be driven away from mankind to live with the beasts of the field, and you will feed on grass like an ox. And seven times will pass you by, until you acknowledge that the Most High rules over the kingdom of mankind and gives it to whom He wishes.” 33 At that moment the sentence against Nebuchadnezzar was fulfilled. He was driven away from mankind. He ate grass like an ox, and his body was drenched with the dew of heaven, until his hair grew like the feathers of an eagle and his nails like the claws of a bird.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Twelve months later, Nebuchadnezzar walks on the palace roof and boasts that he has built Babylon by his own power and for his own glory.

While he is still speaking, a voice from heaven announces that his kingdom has departed from him. The warning is fulfilled: he is driven away, eats grass like an ox and lives exposed to the dew, his hair and nails growing unkempt.

The story presents the reversal the dream announced. The king who claimed greatness as his own achievement loses the position and ordinary life he took for granted. The experience has an appointed purpose: he must acknowledge the rule of the Most High.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley understand the king’s downfall as judgment on pride and forgetfulness of God. The boast about his own greatness stands immediately before the announcement that he has lost it.

The warning and its fulfillment make the same point: the king’s authority is a gift, and he is accountable to the One who gave it.
passages.god_plan_html:
A related account appears in Acts 12:20–24. Herod receives a crowd’s praise that his voice is divine, fails to give glory to God and is struck down. The account then records God’s word continuing to spread.

The outcomes differ: Nebuchadnezzar is later restored, while Herod dies. Both accounts place a ruler’s apparent greatness under God’s authority. The New Testament also shows that a ruler’s power cannot make the advance of God’s word depend upon him.

passages.title: Daniel 4:34-37
passages.section_title: What does the restored king finally acknowledge?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 34 But at the end of those days I, Nebuchadnezzar, looked up to heaven, and my sanity was restored to me. Then I praised the Most High, and I honored and glorified Him who lives forever: “For His dominion is an everlasting dominion, and His kingdom endures from generation to generation. 35 All the peoples of the earth are counted as nothing, and He does as He pleases with the army of heaven and the peoples of the earth. There is no one who can restrain His hand or say to Him, ‘What have You done?’” 36 At the same time my sanity was restored, my honor and splendor returned to me for the glory of my kingdom. My advisers and nobles sought me out, and I was restored to my throne, and surpassing greatness was added to me. 37 Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and exalt and glorify the King of heaven, for all His works are true and all His ways are just. And He is able to humble those who walk in pride.

Then I praised the Most High, and I honored and glorified Him who lives forever: “For His dominion is an everlasting dominion, and His kingdom endures from generation to generation. 35 All the peoples of the earth are counted as nothing, and He does as He pleases with the army of heaven and the peoples of the earth. There is no one who can restrain His hand or say to Him, ‘What have You done?’”

36 At the same time my sanity was restored, my honor and splendor returned to me for the glory of my kingdom. My advisers and nobles sought me out, and I was restored to my throne, and surpassing greatness was added to me. 37 Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and exalt and glorify the King of heaven, for all His works are true and all His ways are just. And He is able to humble those who walk in pride.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
At the end of the appointed period, Nebuchadnezzar looks toward heaven and his sanity returns. He praises the Most High whose dominion is everlasting and whose rule cannot be restrained by human power.

His advisers and nobles seek him out, and his royal honor is restored. The remaining stump in the dream has its explanation in his return to the throne.

The closing statement answers his earlier boast. He now praises the King of heaven, calls His works true and His ways just, and acknowledges that He can humble those who walk in pride. The king’s own testimony has moved from self-glory to honoring God.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley see the closing praise as evidence of real repentance and a changed heart. Cambridge emphasizes the acknowledgment of God’s sovereignty and the king’s public gratitude after restoration.

The restoration matters, but it is the acknowledgment of the King of heaven that gives the ending its meaning.
passages.god_plan_html:
Philippians 2:3–11 brings humility and exaltation into the revelation of Christ. Jesus willingly takes the servant’s place and obeys to the point of death; God exalts Him, and every knee will bow and every tongue confess Him as Lord, to the Father’s glory.

There is an important difference: Christ does not need to be cured of pride as Nebuchadnezzar does. His willing humility shows the character of the true Lord, while His exaltation brings all people to acknowledge Him. The larger purpose reaches beyond one ruler learning a lesson to creation honoring Christ.

passages.title: Daniel 5:1-4
passages.section_title: What makes the king’s feast an act of defiance?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Later, King Belshazzar held a great feast for a thousand of his nobles, and he drank wine with them. 2 Under the influence of the wine, Belshazzar gave orders to bring in the gold and silver vessels that Nebuchadnezzar his father had taken from the temple in Jerusalem, so that the king could drink from them, along with his nobles, his wives, and his concubines. 3 Thus they brought in the gold vessels that had been taken from the temple, the house of God in Jerusalem, and the king drank from them, along with his nobles, his wives, and his concubines. 4 As they drank the wine, they praised their gods of gold and silver, bronze and iron, wood and stone.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Belshazzar holds a feast for a thousand nobles. Under the influence of wine, he orders the vessels taken from God’s temple in Jerusalem to be brought out. The guests drink from them while praising gods made from metal, wood and stone.

The vessels connect the scene with the beginning of Daniel, when they were carried away from Jerusalem. Here the king turns them into drinking cups for a celebration of other gods. Daniel will later explain why this is defiance against the Lord of heaven.

An inscription by Nabonidus names Belshazzar as his eldest son; see the Nabonidus Cylinder from Ur. Another ancient account says Nabonidus entrusted kingship to his eldest son while he traveled to Tayma; see column II of the Verse Account. These records help explain Belshazzar’s ruling role alongside his father.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley understand the use of the temple vessels as a deliberate insult to God, rather than simply a lavish meal.

Wesley calls Belshazzar Nebuchadnezzar’s grandson. Cambridge treats that family relationship as uncertain, while the USCCB notes identify Nabonidus as his father. The surviving Ur inscription establishes the relationship to Nabonidus; it does not establish a family link to Nebuchadnezzar.

passages.title: Daniel 5:5-9
passages.section_title: Why does the feast turn into terror?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 At that moment the fingers of a human hand appeared and wrote on the plaster of the wall, near the lampstand in the royal palace. As the king watched the hand that was writing, 6 his face grew pale and his thoughts so alarmed him that his hips gave way and his knees knocked together. 7 The king called out for the enchanters, astrologers, and diviners to be brought in, and he said to these wise men of Babylon, “Whoever reads this inscription and tells me its interpretation will be clothed in purple and have a gold chain placed around his neck, and he will be made the third highest ruler in the kingdom.” 8 So all the king’s wise men came in, but they could not read the inscription or interpret it for him. 9 Then King Belshazzar became even more terrified, his face grew even more pale, and his nobles were bewildered.

7 The king called out for the enchanters, astrologers, and diviners to be brought in, and he said to these wise men of Babylon, “Whoever reads this inscription and tells me its interpretation will be clothed in purple and have a gold chain placed around his neck, and he will be made the third highest ruler in the kingdom.” 8 So all the king’s wise men came in, but they could not read the inscription or interpret it for him. 9 Then King Belshazzar became even more terrified, his face grew even more pale, and his nobles were bewildered.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
While the celebration is underway, the fingers of a human hand appear and write on the palace wall near the lampstand. Belshazzar sees the writing, turns pale and begins to shake.

He summons the court’s wise men and offers royal clothing, a gold chain and the kingdom’s third-highest position to whoever can read and explain the inscription. Their inability leaves both the king and his nobles bewildered.

The scene repeats a pattern from Nebuchadnezzar’s court: royal wealth and the assembled experts cannot produce the answer the king needs. The ruler who moments earlier dishonored God now faces a message he cannot control.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry and Wesley see the sudden fear as the collapse of the king’s self-confidence before God. The rewards on offer cannot give the wise men the understanding they lack.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 5:10-16
passages.section_title: Why is Daniel called into the banquet hall?

In the days of your father he was found to have insight, intelligence, and wisdom like that of the gods. Your father, King Nebuchadnezzar, appointed him chief of the magicians, enchanters, astrologers, and diviners. Your own father, the king, 12 did this because Daniel, the one he named Belteshazzar, was found to have an extraordinary spirit, as well as knowledge, understanding, and the ability to interpret dreams, explain riddles, and solve difficult problems. Therefore, if you can read this inscription and give me its interpretation, you will be clothed in purple and have a gold chain placed around your neck, and you will be made the third highest ruler in the kingdom.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The queen hears the disturbance and tells Belshazzar about Daniel’s service under Nebuchadnezzar. She remembers his insight and his ability to explain dreams and difficult problems.

When Daniel arrives, Belshazzar identifies him as one of the exiles from Judah. The king repeats what he has heard about Daniel and offers the same rewards if he can explain the writing.

The queen’s recommendation reconnects the present crisis with what God had already made known in the earlier king’s reign. Daniel is brought in because the wisdom remembered from that time is needed again.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Cambridge understand the queen as a queen mother or senior royal woman, distinguished from the wives already at the feast. Her exact identity is not given in the passage.

Henry emphasizes the contrast between seeking an answer to a frightening mystery and seeking instruction about how to live before God.

passages.title: Daniel 5:17-24
passages.section_title: What had Belshazzar known but refused to learn?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 In response, Daniel said to the king, “You may keep your gifts for yourself and give your rewards to someone else. Nevertheless, I will read the inscription for the king and interpret it for him. 18 As for you, O king, the Most High God gave your father Nebuchadnezzar sovereignty and greatness, glory and honor. 19 Because of the greatness that He bestowed on him, the people of every nation and language trembled in fear before him. He killed whom he wished and kept alive whom he wished; he exalted whom he wished and humbled whom he wished. 20 But when his heart became arrogant and his spirit was hardened with pride, he was deposed from his royal throne, and his glory was taken from him. 21 He was driven away from mankind, and his mind was like that of a beast. He lived with the wild donkeys and ate grass like an ox, and his body was drenched with the dew of heaven until he acknowledged that the Most High God rules over the kingdom of mankind, setting over it whom He wishes. 22 But you his son, O Belshazzar, have not humbled your heart, even though you knew all this. 23 Instead, you have exalted yourself against the Lord of heaven. The vessels from His house were brought to you, and as you drank wine from them with your nobles, wives, and concubines, you praised your gods of silver and gold, bronze and iron, wood and stone, which cannot see or hear or understand. But you have failed to glorify the God who holds in His hand your very breath and all your ways. 24 Therefore He sent the hand that wrote the inscription.
