He lived with the wild donkeys and ate grass like an ox, and his body was drenched with the dew of heaven until he acknowledged that the Most High God rules over the kingdom of mankind, setting over it whom He wishes.

22 But you his son, O Belshazzar, have not humbled your heart, even though you knew all this. 23 Instead, you have exalted yourself against the Lord of heaven. The vessels from His house were brought to you, and as you drank wine from them with your nobles, wives, and concubines, you praised your gods of silver and gold, bronze and iron, wood and stone, which cannot see or hear or understand. But you have failed to glorify the God who holds in His hand your very breath and all your ways. 24 Therefore He sent the hand that wrote the inscription.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Daniel declines the offered gifts but agrees to explain the writing. Before doing so, he reminds the king that Nebuchadnezzar’s power came from the Most High God. When that ruler became proud, he lost his throne and ordinary human life until he acknowledged God’s rule.

Belshazzar knew this history. Daniel’s charge is that he nevertheless refused to humble himself. Instead, he used God’s vessels to honor powerless gods and failed to glorify the One who holds his breath and all his ways in His hand.

That is why the hand appeared. The message on the wall belongs to a moral reckoning: a ruler who had received a warning through another king’s experience chose to defy the God who sustained his own life.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry and Cambridge emphasize Belshazzar’s responsibility for what he already knew. Nebuchadnezzar’s humiliation should have warned him; his own conduct repeats the pride while adding the public dishonoring of God’s vessels.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Acts 17:24–31, Paul tells another audience surrounded by idols that God gives everyone life and breath. Gold, silver and stone cannot represent the One who made and sustains people.

Paul then carries the message forward: God calls everyone to repent and has appointed a day of just judgment through the Man He raised from the dead. Daniel’s confrontation with one king belongs to the wider truth that every person depends on God and is accountable to Him. The gospel identifies the risen Jesus at the center of that coming judgment.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 5:25-28
passages.section_title: What does the writing on the wall mean?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 25 Now this is the inscription that was written: MENE, MENE, TEKEL, PARSIN. 26 And this is the interpretation of the message: MENE means that God has numbered the days of your reign and brought it to an end. 27 TEKEL means that you have been weighed on the scales and found deficient. 28 PERES means that your kingdom has been divided and given over to the Medes and Persians.”
paragraphs: 25 Now this is the inscription that was written: MENE, MENE, TEKEL, PARSIN. 26 And this is the interpretation of the message: MENE means that God has numbered the days of your reign and brought it to an end. 27 TEKEL means that you have been weighed on the scales and found deficient. 28 PERES means that your kingdom has been divided and given over to the Medes and Persians.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Daniel reads the inscription and gives its meaning. God has numbered the king’s reign and brought it to an end; the king has been weighed and found deficient; his kingdom is being given to the Medes and Persians.

The message uses a play on words. The Aramaic terms also belong to the language of weights: מְנֵא, mene (meh-NAY), names a mina, and פְּרֵס, peres (peh-RACE), probably a half-mina; see Brown–Driver–Briggs on mene and peres. Daniel explains the words through numbering, weighing and dividing.

The meaning is therefore much more than a puzzling list. The king’s rule has a limit, his conduct has been judged, and the power he possessed is passing to others.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The USCCB notes and Cambridge explain the weight terms and the play on words in Daniel’s interpretation. Both also note the connection between the final term and the name of the Persians. The explanation in verses 26–28 gives the message its force.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 5:29-31
passages.section_title: What remains of the king’s promises when his kingdom falls?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 29 Then Belshazzar gave the command, and they clothed Daniel in purple, placed a gold chain around his neck, and proclaimed him the third highest ruler in the kingdom. 30 That very night Belshazzar king of the Chaldeans was slain, 31 and Darius the Mede received the kingdom at the age of sixty-two.
paragraphs: 29 Then Belshazzar gave the command, and they clothed Daniel in purple, placed a gold chain around his neck, and proclaimed him the third highest ruler in the kingdom. 30 That very night Belshazzar king of the Chaldeans was slain, 31 and Darius the Mede received the kingdom at the age of sixty-two.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Belshazzar orders the promised honors to be given to Daniel. That same night, the king is killed, and Darius the Mede receives the kingdom at the age of sixty-two.

The contrast is sharp: the king can still announce a promotion, but he cannot preserve the rule in which that promotion has meaning. The judgment Daniel has just explained overtakes him immediately.

The Nabonidus Chronicle, column III independently records Cyrus’s forces entering Babylon without a battle in the city. Daniel brings the focus into the palace and identifies the fall of Belshazzar as the fulfillment of God’s announced judgment.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads the ending as the fulfillment of the sentence Daniel announced. Wesley connects Darius with Cyrus’s conquest.

Cambridge considers the identity of Darius the Mede historically unresolved and regards the portrayal as a historical confusion. Other identifications have been proposed, but the record checked here does not establish one. The passage itself names Darius without explaining his relationship to Cyrus.
passages.god_plan_html:
A broader parallel appears in Revelation 18:1–8. There, Babylon’s luxury and confidence that she will never experience grief give way to sudden judgment. God calls His people to come out of her sins.

Daniel records the fall of a particular ruler, while Revelation presents a larger judgment under the name Babylon. The parallel shows a repeated pattern: power and prosperity cannot make rebellion secure. God’s people are called to faithfulness within a world whose proudest powers remain accountable to Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 6:1-5
passages.section_title: What can Daniel’s opponents find against him?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now it pleased Darius to appoint 120 satraps to rule throughout the kingdom, 2 and over them three administrators, including Daniel, to whom these satraps were accountable so that the king would not suffer loss. 3 Soon, by his extraordinary spirit, Daniel distinguished himself among the administrators and satraps. So the king planned to set him over the whole kingdom. 4 Thus the administrators and satraps sought a charge against Daniel concerning the kingdom, but they could find no charge or corruption, because he was trustworthy, and no negligence or corruption was found in him. 5 Finally these men said, “We will never find any charge against this Daniel unless we find something against him concerning the law of his God.”
paragraphs: 1 Now it pleased Darius to appoint 120 satraps to rule throughout the kingdom, 2 and over them three administrators, including Daniel, to whom these satraps were accountable so that the king would not suffer loss. 3 Soon, by his extraordinary spirit, Daniel distinguished himself among the administrators and satraps. So the king planned to set him over the whole kingdom.

4 Thus the administrators and satraps sought a charge against Daniel concerning the kingdom, but they could find no charge or corruption, because he was trustworthy, and no negligence or corruption was found in him. 5 Finally these men said, “We will never find any charge against this Daniel unless we find something against him concerning the law of his God.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Under the new ruler, Daniel is one of three administrators overseeing the kingdom’s officials. He distinguishes himself so clearly that Darius plans to put him over the whole kingdom.

The other officials search for grounds to accuse him in his work. They find neither corruption nor negligence: Daniel is trustworthy. Their conclusion is that the only way to bring a charge against him is through his loyalty to his God.

The conflict begins with a faithful man doing his ordinary responsibilities well. His opponents decide to make that faithfulness itself the means of trapping him.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry and Wesley emphasize Daniel’s integrity in public service. His opponents’ scrutiny exposes their hostility while showing that they have no genuine charge against his conduct.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Peter 2:11–17 calls believers living as foreigners and exiles to honorable conduct among people who may accuse them of wrongdoing. Their good deeds are meant to lead others to glorify God.

This carries the pattern beyond Daniel’s service in a foreign court. God’s people bear witness through the way they live and serve, even when doing right does not remove hostility. Peter brings together honoring the king and fearing God, placing public responsibility within a greater loyalty to Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 6:6-9
passages.section_title: How do the officials turn prayer into a crime?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 So the administrators and satraps went together to the king and said, “O King Darius, may you live forever! 7 All the royal administrators, prefects, satraps, advisers, and governors have agreed that the king should establish an ordinance and enforce a decree that for thirty days anyone who petitions any god or man except you, O king, will be thrown into the den of lions. 8 Therefore, O king, establish the decree and sign the document so that it cannot be changed—in accordance with the law of the Medes and Persians, which cannot be repealed.” 9 Therefore King Darius signed the written decree.
paragraphs: 6 So the administrators and satraps went together to the king and said, “O King Darius, may you live forever! 7 All the royal administrators, prefects, satraps, advisers, and governors have agreed that the king should establish an ordinance and enforce a decree that for thirty days anyone who petitions any god or man except you, O king, will be thrown into the den of lions. 8 Therefore, O king, establish the decree and sign the document so that it cannot be changed—in accordance with the law of the Medes and Persians, which cannot be repealed.” 9 Therefore King Darius signed the written decree.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The officials ask Darius to make a thirty-day decree: anyone who petitions a god or person other than the king must be thrown into the lions’ den. They present the proposal as having the agreement of the royal administration, though Daniel is plainly not part of their plan.

They also ask for a signed decree that cannot be repealed under the law of the Medes and Persians. Darius signs it.

The trap depends on the king lending legal force to their scheme. They have already decided that Daniel’s devotion to God is the point they will attack; the apparently public measure serves that private purpose.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry reads the decree as persecution disguised as public policy. Cambridge notes the misleading claim of agreement among all the officials, when Daniel himself is an administrator.

The narrative makes the decree’s binding character crucial to what follows: the king will discover that signing it has placed Daniel beyond his own ability to help.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 6:10-15
passages.section_title: What does Daniel do when prayer becomes dangerous?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 Now when Daniel learned that the document had been signed, he went into his house, where the windows of his upper room opened toward Jerusalem, and three times a day he got down on his knees, prayed, and gave thanks to his God, just as he had done before. 11 Then these men went as a group and found Daniel petitioning and imploring his God. 12 So they approached the king and asked about his royal decree: “Did you not sign a decree that for thirty days any man who petitions any god or man except you, O king, will be thrown into the den of lions?” The king replied, “According to the law of the Medes and Persians the order stands, and it cannot be repealed.” 13 Then they told the king, “Daniel, one of the exiles from Judah, shows no regard for you, O king, or for the decree that you have signed. He still makes his petition three times a day.” 14 As soon as the king heard this, he was deeply distressed and set his mind on delivering Daniel, and he labored until sundown to rescue him. 15 Then the men approached the king together and said to him, “Remember, O king, that by the law of the Medes and Persians no decree or ordinance established by the king can be changed.”
paragraphs: 10 Now when Daniel learned that the document had been signed, he went into his house, where the windows of his upper room opened toward Jerusalem, and three times a day he got down on his knees, prayed, and gave thanks to his God, just as he had done before. 11 Then these men went as a group and found Daniel petitioning and imploring his God.

12 So they approached the king and asked about his royal decree: “Did you not sign a decree that for thirty days any man who petitions any god or man except you, O king, will be thrown into the den of lions?” The king replied, “According to the law of the Medes and Persians the order stands, and it cannot be repealed.” 13 Then they told the king, “Daniel, one of the exiles from Judah, shows no regard for you, O king, or for the decree that you have signed. He still makes his petition three times a day.” 14 As soon as the king heard this, he was deeply distressed and set his mind on delivering Daniel, and he labored until sundown to rescue him. 15 Then the men approached the king together and said to him, “Remember, O king, that by the law of the Medes and Persians no decree or ordinance established by the king can be changed.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Knowing the decree has been signed, Daniel continues his established practice. He kneels three times a day in his upper room, prays and gives thanks to God, with the windows open toward Jerusalem.

Praying toward Jerusalem recalls Solomon’s prayer for people taken into exile, especially 1 Kings 8:46–50. Even far from home, they could turn back to God and appeal for Him to hear them.

The officials find Daniel praying and report him to the king as a disloyal exile. Darius is distressed and works until sundown to save him. His advisers insist that the signed decree cannot be changed. Daniel’s continuing worship has brought the conflict between their law and his loyalty to God into the open.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Cambridge emphasize that Daniel continues his usual practice. His prayer is an established commitment, rather than a new display devised to provoke the king.

Henry notes how conduct faithful to God is misrepresented as contempt for civil authority. Darius’s attempt to rescue Daniel shows that he now recognizes the danger created by his decree.
passages.god_plan_html:
The same question of greater loyalty appears in Acts 5:27–32. When ordered to stop teaching about Jesus, the apostles answer that they must obey God rather than men. They continue bearing witness to the Jesus whom God raised and exalted.

Daniel’s prayer and the apostles’ witness are different acts, but both show that human authority cannot take God’s place. In the New Testament, this loyalty serves the spread of the message of repentance and forgiveness through the risen Savior.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 6:16-23
passages.section_title: Who can save Daniel when the king cannot?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 So the king gave the order, and they brought Daniel and threw him into the den of lions. The king said to Daniel, “May your God, whom you serve continually, deliver you!” 17 A stone was brought and placed over the mouth of the den, and the king sealed it with his own signet ring and with the rings of his nobles, so that nothing concerning Daniel could be changed. 18 Then the king went to his palace and spent the night fasting. No entertainment was brought before him, and sleep fled from him. 19 At the first light of dawn, the king got up and hurried to the den of lions. 20 When he reached the den, he cried out in a voice of anguish, “O Daniel, servant of the living God, has your God, whom you serve continually, been able to deliver you from the lions?” 21 Then Daniel replied, “O king, may you live forever! 22 My God sent His angel and shut the mouths of the lions. They have not hurt me, for I was found innocent in His sight, and I have done no wrong against you, O king.” 23 The king was overjoyed and gave orders to lift Daniel out of the den, and when Daniel was lifted out of the den, no wounds whatsoever were found on him, because he had trusted in his God.
paragraphs: 16 So the king gave the order, and they brought Daniel and threw him into the den of lions. The king said to Daniel, “May your God, whom you serve continually, deliver you!” 17 A stone was brought and placed over the mouth of the den, and the king sealed it with his own signet ring and with the rings of his nobles, so that nothing concerning Daniel could be changed. 18 Then the king went to his palace and spent the night fasting. No entertainment was brought before him, and sleep fled from him.

19 At the first light of dawn, the king got up and hurried to the den of lions. 20 When he reached the den, he cried out in a voice of anguish, “O Daniel, servant of the living God, has your God, whom you serve continually, been able to deliver you from the lions?” 21 Then Daniel replied, “O king, may you live forever! 22 My God sent His angel and shut the mouths of the lions. They have not hurt me, for I was found innocent in His sight, and I have done no wrong against you, O king.” 23 The king was overjoyed and gave orders to lift Daniel out of the den, and when Daniel was lifted out of the den, no wounds whatsoever were found on him, because he had trusted in his God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Darius gives the order, and Daniel is thrown into the lions’ den. The king expresses the hope that Daniel’s God will deliver him. A stone closes the opening, sealed with the rings of the king and his nobles.

The king spends a sleepless night and hurries to the den at dawn. He calls out anxiously to ask whether the living God has been able to rescue His servant.

Daniel answers that God sent His angel and shut the lions’ mouths. He has been found innocent before God and has done no wrong against the king. When lifted out, he has no wounds, because he trusted in his God. The ruler who could not prevent the sentence now witnesses a deliverance beyond his own power.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley understand the rescue as God’s protection of His faithful servant. Cambridge connects the closing of the lions’ mouths with Hebrews 11:33.

Daniel’s innocence concerns the accusation against him: his devotion to God was presented as disloyalty to the king. His rescue vindicates him in that conflict.
passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 11:32–40 includes shutting lions’ mouths among the works of faith. The same passage also honors faithful people who were tortured and killed, pointing toward a better resurrection. God’s purpose for His people reaches beyond whether a particular trial ends in escape.

There is also a striking parallel with Jesus’ sealed tomb and the discovery at dawn, continued in Matthew 28:1–10. Both accounts show human efforts to secure a stone giving way to God’s power. The difference matters: Daniel is preserved alive, while Jesus truly dies and rises. Christ’s victory carries the hope of deliverance beyond death itself.

deeper_study.title: Who is The Angel of the Lord?

passages.title: Daniel 6:24
passages.section_title: What happens to the people who accused Daniel?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 24 At the command of the king, the men who had falsely accused Daniel were brought and thrown into the den of lions—they and their children and wives. And before they had reached the bottom of the den, the lions overpowered them and crushed all their bones.
paragraphs: 24 At the command of the king, the men who had falsely accused Daniel were brought and thrown into the den of lions—they and their children and wives. And before they had reached the bottom of the den, the lions overpowered them and crushed all their bones.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Darius orders Daniel’s accusers to be thrown into the den, together with their wives and children. The lions overpower them before they reach the bottom.

The outcome makes the danger Daniel survived unmistakable. His safety was not explained by harmless or uninterested lions. The plot has ended in the destruction of the people who devised it.

The inclusion of their families is a disturbing part of the king’s order. This is Darius’s action; Israel’s own law says that children are not to be executed for their fathers, nor fathers for their children, in Deuteronomy 24:16. The narrative reports the royal punishment rather than giving God’s people an instruction to imitate it.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry emphasizes the reversal: the accusers fall into the danger from which Daniel has been delivered. Cambridge specifically addresses the punishment of their families as part of the harsh royal justice described in the story.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 6:25-28
passages.section_title: What does Darius announce about Daniel’s God?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 25 Then King Darius wrote to the people of every nation and language throughout the land: “May your prosperity abound. 26 I hereby decree that in every part of my kingdom, men are to tremble in fear before the God of Daniel: For He is the living God, and He endures forever; His kingdom will never be destroyed, and His dominion will never end. 27 He delivers and rescues; He performs signs and wonders in the heavens and on the earth, for He has rescued Daniel from the power of the lions.” 28 So Daniel prospered during the reign of Darius and the reign of Cyrus the Persian.
paragraphs: 25 Then King Darius wrote to the people of every nation and language throughout the land: “May your prosperity abound. 26 I hereby decree that in every part of my kingdom, men are to tremble in fear before the God of Daniel: For He is the living God, and He endures forever; His kingdom will never be destroyed, and His dominion will never end. 27 He delivers and rescues; He performs signs and wonders in the heavens and on the earth, for He has rescued Daniel from the power of the lions.”
28 So Daniel prospered during the reign of Darius and the reign of Cyrus the Persian.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Darius writes to people of every nation and language in his dominion. He orders reverence for Daniel’s God and explains why: He is living and enduring, His kingdom cannot be destroyed, and His rule will never end.

The king points to the rescue from the lions as a demonstration of God’s power to deliver and to perform wonders in heaven and on earth. The chapter that began with a decree threatening prayer ends with a proclamation honoring the God to whom Daniel prayed.

Daniel continues to prosper under Darius and Cyrus. The human rulers change, but the testimony at the close centers on the God whose dominion remains.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry takes the proclamation as a public acknowledgment of God’s power while distinguishing an announcement about God from a life of faithfulness to Him. Cambridge emphasizes Daniel’s continuing prosperity after his deliverance.

The conclusion points to the enduring kingdom of the living God, beyond the changing fortunes of His servant or any earthly king.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 7:1-6
passages.section_title: What does Daniel see rising from the troubled sea?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 In the first year of the reign of Belshazzar over Babylon, Daniel had a dream, and visions passed through his mind as he lay on his bed. He wrote down the dream, and this is the summary of his account. 2 Daniel declared: “In my vision in the night I looked, and suddenly the four winds of heaven were churning up the great sea. 3 Then four great beasts came up out of the sea, each one different from the others: 4 The first beast was like a lion, and it had the wings of an eagle. I watched until its wings were torn off and it was lifted up from the ground and made to stand on two feet like a man and given the mind of a man. 5 Suddenly another beast appeared, which looked like a bear. It was raised up on one of its sides, and it had three ribs in its mouth between its teeth. So it was told, ‘Get up and gorge yourself on flesh!’ 6 Next, as I watched, suddenly another beast appeared. It was like a leopard, and on its back it had four wings like those of a bird. The beast also had four heads, and it was given authority to rule.
paragraphs: 1 In the first year of the reign of Belshazzar over Babylon, Daniel had a dream, and visions passed through his mind as he lay on his bed. He wrote down the dream, and this is the summary of his account. 2 Daniel declared: “In my vision in the night I looked, and suddenly the four winds of heaven were churning up the great sea. 3 Then four great beasts came up out of the sea, each one different from the others:

4 The first beast was like a lion, and it had the wings of an eagle. I watched until its wings were torn off and it was lifted up from the ground and made to stand on two feet like a man and given the mind of a man. 5 Suddenly another beast appeared, which looked like a bear. It was raised up on one of its sides, and it had three ribs in its mouth between its teeth. So it was told, ‘Get up and gorge yourself on flesh!’ 6 Next, as I watched, suddenly another beast appeared. It was like a leopard, and on its back it had four wings like those of a bird. The beast also had four heads, and it was given authority to rule.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The account moves back to Belshazzar’s first year, before the feast and fall of Babylon described in chapter 5. Daniel himself now receives a dream and writes down what he sees.

Four winds churn the sea, and four different beasts emerge. The first is a winged lion whose wings are removed; it is made to stand like a man and receives a human mind. The second resembles a bear, raised on one side, with three ribs in its mouth. The third resembles a leopard with four wings and four heads.

The interpretation later identifies the beasts as kings and kingdoms. The vision returns to the subject of chapter 2, but its picture of earthly power is now fierce and unsettling: kingdoms are seen as beasts rather than parts of a magnificent statue.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley reads the kingdoms as Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece and Rome. The USCCB notes read the sequence as Babylon, Media, Persia and Greece. Both connect the four beasts with the four kingdoms of chapter 2, while differing over which empires the symbols represent.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 7:7-8
passages.section_title: What makes the fourth beast especially terrifying?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 After this, as I watched in my vision in the night, suddenly a fourth beast appeared, and it was terrifying—dreadful and extremely strong—with large iron teeth. It devoured and crushed; then it trampled underfoot whatever was left. It was different from all the beasts before it, and it had ten horns. 8 While I was contemplating the horns, suddenly another horn, a little one, came up among them, and three of the first horns were uprooted before it. This horn had eyes like those of a man and a mouth that spoke words of arrogance.
paragraphs: 7 After this, as I watched in my vision in the night, suddenly a fourth beast appeared, and it was terrifying—dreadful and extremely strong—with large iron teeth. It devoured and crushed; then it trampled underfoot whatever was left. It was different from all the beasts before it, and it had ten horns. 8 While I was contemplating the horns, suddenly another horn, a little one, came up among them, and three of the first horns were uprooted before it. This horn had eyes like those of a man and a mouth that spoke words of arrogance.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The fourth beast is dreadful and exceptionally strong. Its iron teeth crush and devour, and its feet trample what remains. Unlike the earlier beasts, it is not compared with a familiar animal.

It has ten horns. As Daniel watches, another, smaller horn rises among them and uproots three. This horn has human-like eyes and a mouth speaking arrogantly.

The later explanation identifies the horns as kings. These opening details draw attention to both the violence of the kingdom and the particular ruler whose boastful speech will become a central concern.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Readings differ over the ruler in view. Henry connects the little horn with papal Rome. Gaebelein expects a future ruler of a revived Roman Empire. The USCCB notes identify the fourth kingdom with the Greek empire and the horn with Antiochus IV, the king who persecuted the Jews.

These are different identifications of the symbols; they should not be treated as one agreed Christian reading.
passages.god_plan_html:
Revelation 13:1–10 takes up Daniel’s imagery: a beast rises from the sea with ten horns and features of a leopard, bear and lion. It speaks against God and wages war on His people.

John places the beast’s authority in opposition to the Lamb and calls the saints to perseverance and faith. The connection carries Daniel’s warning about violent, self-exalting power into the church’s witness to Jesus. The response God seeks from His people is faithful endurance, even when the opposition appears overwhelming.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 7:9-12
passages.section_title: What happens when heaven’s court sits in judgment?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 As I continued to watch, thrones were set in place, and the Ancient of Days took His seat. His clothing was white as snow, and the hair of His head was like pure wool. His throne was flaming with fire, and its wheels were all ablaze. 10 A river of fire was flowing, coming out from His presence. Thousands upon thousands attended Him, and myriads upon myriads stood before Him. The court was convened, and the books were opened. 11 Then I kept watching because of the arrogant words the horn was speaking. As I continued to watch, the beast was slain, and its body was destroyed and thrown into the blazing fire. 12 As for the rest of the beasts, their dominion was removed, but they were granted an extension of life for a season and a time.
paragraphs: 9 As I continued to watch, thrones were set in place, and the Ancient of Days took His seat. His clothing was white as snow, and the hair of His head was like pure wool. His throne was flaming with fire, and its wheels were all ablaze. 10 A river of fire was flowing, coming out from His presence. Thousands upon thousands attended Him, and myriads upon myriads stood before Him. The court was convened, and the books were opened.

11 Then I kept watching because of the arrogant words the horn was speaking. As I continued to watch, the beast was slain, and its body was destroyed and thrown into the blazing fire. 12 As for the rest of the beasts, their dominion was removed, but they were granted an extension of life for a season and a time.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The vision turns from the beasts to a heavenly court. Thrones are set in place, the Ancient of Days takes His seat, and countless attendants stand before Him. Fire surrounds the throne, and the books are opened.

The arrogant horn continues speaking, but its speech cannot prevent judgment. Daniel sees the fourth beast killed and its body destroyed by fire. The other beasts lose their dominion, though they are granted life for a further appointed period.

The court changes the perspective of the vision. What appeared on earth as unchecked power is answerable to a Judge above it. The beasts’ rule has limits, and the decision about its end belongs to heaven.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry connects the scene with the judgment of powers opposed to Christ. Gaebelein places it at Christ’s return before the thousand-year reign, distinguishing it from Revelation’s final judgment.

Cambridge explains the court and opened books as God judging the rulers’ deeds. The common center is divine judgment; the readers differ over how the scene fits into the sequence of later events.
passages.god_plan_html:
A related judgment scene appears in Revelation 20:11–15: a throne, opened books and judgment according to deeds. There the dead themselves stand before the throne, and even Death and Hades are brought to their end.

This is a parallel in the way judgment is pictured, without settling whether the passages describe the same occasion. Revelation extends the horizon beyond the downfall of a kingdom to the final accounting of human life and the end of death’s rule.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 7:13-14
passages.section_title: Who receives the kingdom that will never end?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 In my vision in the night I continued to watch, and I saw One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven. He approached the Ancient of Days and was led into His presence. 14 And He was given dominion, glory, and kingship, that the people of every nation and language should serve Him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion that will not pass away, and His kingdom is one that will never be destroyed.
paragraphs: 13 In my vision in the night I continued to watch, and I saw One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven. He approached the Ancient of Days and was led into His presence. 14 And He was given dominion, glory, and kingship, that the people of every nation and language should serve Him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion that will not pass away, and His kingdom is one that will never be destroyed.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Daniel sees One like the Son of Man coming with heaven’s clouds. He approaches the Ancient of Days and is brought into His presence.

He receives dominion, glory and kingship, so that people of every nation and language serve Him. His kingdom will never be destroyed. The human-like figure stands in contrast to the beasts whose dominion has just been judged.

The direction of movement matters: the figure comes before the Ancient of Days and receives authority. The vision centers on a kingdom granted from heaven, with a reach and permanence beyond any of the earlier powers.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley identifies the figure as the Messiah and connects His reception of authority with Christ’s ascension. Gaebelein emphasizes Christ’s second coming and the kingdom He then receives.

Cambridge understands the figure in the vision as representing God’s glorified people, connecting it with the saints receiving the kingdom later in the chapter. The USCCB notes discuss both individual and collective readings. These questions about the original vision are distinct from the Gospels’ clear application of its language to Jesus.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus directly takes up this language in Mark 14:60–65. Asked whether He is the Christ, He speaks of the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming with heaven’s clouds.

The One being condemned before a human court identifies Himself with the figure who receives heavenly authority. This connection brings Daniel’s everlasting kingdom into the revelation of Jesus Himself: the accused and rejected Messiah is also the One whose authority human judgment cannot remove.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

deeper_study.title: Who is The Angel of the Lord?

passages.title: Daniel 7:15-22
passages.section_title: How can the oppressed saints receive the kingdom?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 I, Daniel, was grieved in my spirit, and the visions in my mind alarmed me. 16 I approached one of those who were standing there, and I asked him the true meaning of all this. So he told me the interpretation of these things: 17 ‘These four great beasts are four kings who will arise from the earth. 18 But the saints of the Most High will receive the kingdom and possess it forever—yes, forever and ever.’ 19 Then I wanted to know the true meaning of the fourth beast, which was different from all the others—extremely terrifying—devouring and crushing with iron teeth and bronze claws, then trampling underfoot whatever was left. 20 I also wanted to know about the ten horns on its head and the other horn that came up, before which three of them fell—the horn whose appearance was more imposing than the others, with eyes and with a mouth that spoke words of arrogance. 21 As I watched, this horn was waging war against the saints and prevailing against them, 22 until the Ancient of Days arrived and pronounced judgment in favor of the saints of the Most High, and the time came for them to possess the kingdom.
paragraphs: 15 I, Daniel, was grieved in my spirit, and the visions in my mind alarmed me. 16 I approached one of those who were standing there, and I asked him the true meaning of all this. So he told me the interpretation of these things: 17 ‘These four great beasts are four kings who will arise from the earth. 18 But the saints of the Most High will receive the kingdom and possess it forever—yes, forever and ever.’

19 Then I wanted to know the true meaning of the fourth beast, which was different from all the others—extremely terrifying—devouring and crushing with iron teeth and bronze claws, then trampling underfoot whatever was left. 20 I also wanted to know about the ten horns on its head and the other horn that came up, before which three of them fell—the horn whose appearance was more imposing than the others, with eyes and with a mouth that spoke words of arrogance. 21 As I watched, this horn was waging war against the saints and prevailing against them, 22 until the Ancient of Days arrived and pronounced judgment in favor of the saints of the Most High, and the time came for them to possess the kingdom.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Daniel is alarmed and asks someone standing nearby to explain the vision. The first answer gives its broad outcome: four kings arise, but the saints of the Most High receive the kingdom forever.

Daniel then asks particularly about the fourth beast and its horns. He adds a troubling detail: the boastful horn wages war against the saints and prevails against them.

That success lasts until the Ancient of Days intervenes and judgment is pronounced in the saints’ favor. Their suffering is real, yet the oppressor’s victories do not determine the final outcome. The kingdom promised to them rests on God’s judgment rather than their present ability to overcome their persecutor.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands the saints as those who reign with Christ. Gaebelein particularly identifies them here as faithful Jews who pass through the final tribulation. Cambridge reads them as God’s holy people Israel.

These readers differ over the people and setting most directly in view, while agreeing that the kingdom comes to God’s people through His intervention.
passages.god_plan_html:
Revelation 20:4–6 brings together thrones, judgment, people persecuted for their witness to Jesus and their reign with Christ. Some have been killed for refusing the beast’s worship, yet they come to life and share in Christ’s reign.

This develops the hope behind Daniel’s reversal. The persecutor’s power to kill cannot cancel God’s purpose for His people. Revelation places their vindication in the life and authority they receive with Christ, carrying the promise beyond temporary survival to victory over death.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 7:23-28
passages.section_title: What limit is placed on the ruler who opposes God?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 23 This is what he said: ‘The fourth beast is a fourth kingdom that will appear on the earth, different from all the other kingdoms, and it will devour the whole earth, trample it down, and crush it. 24 And the ten horns are ten kings who will rise from this kingdom. After them another king, different from the earlier ones, will rise and subdue three kings. 25 He will speak out against the Most High and oppress the saints of the Most High, intending to change the appointed times and laws; and the saints will be given into his hand for a time, and times, and half a time. 26 But the court will convene, and his dominion will be taken away and completely destroyed forever. 27 Then the sovereignty, dominion, and greatness of the kingdoms under all of heaven will be given to the people, the saints of the Most High. His kingdom will be an everlasting kingdom, and all rulers will serve and obey Him.’ 28 Thus ends the matter. As for me, Daniel, my thoughts troubled me greatly, and my face turned pale. But I kept the matter to myself.”
paragraphs: 23 This is what he said: ‘The fourth beast is a fourth kingdom that will appear on the earth, different from all the other kingdoms, and it will devour the whole earth, trample it down, and crush it. 24 And the ten horns are ten kings who will rise from this kingdom. After them another king, different from the earlier ones, will rise and subdue three kings. 25 He will speak out against the Most High and oppress the saints of the Most High, intending to change the appointed times and laws; and the saints will be given into his hand for a time, and times, and half a time.

26 But the court will convene, and his dominion will be taken away and completely destroyed forever. 27 Then the sovereignty, dominion, and greatness of the kingdoms under all of heaven will be given to the people, the saints of the Most High. His kingdom will be an everlasting kingdom, and all rulers will serve and obey Him.’ 28 Thus ends the matter. As for me, Daniel, my thoughts troubled me greatly, and my face turned pale. But I kept the matter to myself.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The explanation identifies the fourth beast as a kingdom and the ten horns as kings. Another king rises after them, puts down three, speaks against the Most High and oppresses His saints. He intends to change the appointed times and laws.

The saints are given into his power for a time, times and half a time. Then the court sits, his dominion is taken away, and the greatness of the kingdoms under heaven is given to the people of the Most High. His kingdom endures, and rulers serve and obey Him.

Daniel closes still pale and troubled, keeping the matter to himself. The vision offers a firm outcome without making the intervening suffering easy. Its final authority belongs to God’s court, and its final kingdom belongs to Him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley connect the persecuting ruler with papal power in their readings. Gaebelein expects a future ruler within a revived Roman Empire. The USCCB notes understand the oppression and changes to worship in relation to Antiochus IV.

The three-and-a-half period is commonly understood as a limited period of persecution. Readings differ over its historical setting and how it relates to later prophecy. The explanation itself ends with the removal of the oppressor and the enduring kingdom of God.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 8:1-4
passages.section_title: What does Daniel see beside the Ulai Canal?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 In the third year of the reign of King Belshazzar, a vision appeared to me, Daniel, subsequent to the one that had appeared to me earlier. 2 And in the vision I saw myself in the citadel of Susa, in the province of Elam. I saw in the vision that I was beside the Ulai Canal. 3 Then I lifted up my eyes and saw a ram with two horns standing beside the canal. The horns were long, but one was longer than the other, and the longer one grew up later. 4 I saw the ram charging toward the west and the north and the south. No animal could stand against him, and there was no deliverance from his power. He did as he pleased and became great.
paragraphs: 1 In the third year of the reign of King Belshazzar, a vision appeared to me, Daniel, subsequent to the one that had appeared to me earlier. 2 And in the vision I saw myself in the citadel of Susa, in the province of Elam. I saw in the vision that I was beside the Ulai Canal. 3 Then I lifted up my eyes and saw a ram with two horns standing beside the canal. The horns were long, but one was longer than the other, and the longer one grew up later. 4 I saw the ram charging toward the west and the north and the south. No animal could stand against him, and there was no deliverance from his power. He did as he pleased and became great.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Daniel receives another vision in Belshazzar’s third year. In it he sees himself at the citadel of Susa in Elam, beside the Ulai Canal.

A ram stands there with two long horns. One grows later but becomes longer than the other. The ram charges west, north and south, and no other animal can withstand it or rescue anyone from its power.

The vision initially presents the picture without naming the kingdom. Gabriel later identifies the ram’s two horns as the kings of Media and Persia. What appears as unstoppable power here will soon meet its own limit.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley and Gaebelein understand the unequal horns as Media and Persia, with Persia becoming the stronger partner. This reading follows the identification Gabriel gives in verse 20.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 8:5-8
passages.section_title: How does the goat overcome the powerful ram?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 As I was contemplating all this, suddenly a goat with a prominent horn between his eyes came out of the west, crossing the surface of the entire earth without touching the ground. 6 He came toward the two-horned ram I had seen standing beside the canal and rushed at him with furious power. 7 I saw him approach the ram in a rage against him, and he struck the ram and shattered his two horns. The ram was powerless to stand against him, and the goat threw him to the ground and trampled him, and no one could deliver the ram from his power. 8 Thus the goat became very great, but at the height of his power, his large horn was broken off, and four prominent horns came up in its place, pointing toward the four winds of heaven.
paragraphs: 5 As I was contemplating all this, suddenly a goat with a prominent horn between his eyes came out of the west, crossing the surface of the entire earth without touching the ground. 6 He came toward the two-horned ram I had seen standing beside the canal and rushed at him with furious power. 7 I saw him approach the ram in a rage against him, and he struck the ram and shattered his two horns. The ram was powerless to stand against him, and the goat threw him to the ground and trampled him, and no one could deliver the ram from his power. 8 Thus the goat became very great, but at the height of his power, his large horn was broken off, and four prominent horns came up in its place, pointing toward the four winds of heaven.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
A goat with a prominent horn comes rapidly from the west, crossing the earth without touching the ground. It attacks the ram furiously, breaks both horns and tramples the ram. Now it is the ram that has no deliverer.

At the height of the goat’s power, its great horn breaks. Four horns replace it, pointing toward the four winds of heaven.

Gabriel’s later explanation identifies the goat with Greece, the great horn with its first king, and the four horns with four kingdoms that rise afterward. The succession shows how quickly the power that overthrows one kingdom can itself be divided.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry and Wesley identify the prominent horn with Alexander the Great and the replacement horns with the divisions of his empire. Both see the breaking of the great horn as the end of the conqueror’s own rule.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 8:9-14
passages.section_title: What happens when the little horn attacks worship?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 From one of these horns a little horn emerged and grew extensively toward the south and the east and toward the Beautiful Land. 10 It grew as high as the host of heaven, and it cast down some of the host and some of the stars to the earth and trampled them. 11 It magnified itself, even to the Prince of the host; it removed His daily sacrifice and overthrew the place of His sanctuary. 12 And in the rebellion, the host and the daily sacrifice were given over to the horn, and it flung truth to the ground and prospered in whatever it did. 13 Then I heard a holy one speaking, and another holy one said to him, “How long until the fulfillment of the vision of the daily sacrifice, the rebellion that causes desolation, and the surrender of the sanctuary and of the host to be trampled?” 14 He said to me, “It will take 2,300 evenings and mornings; then the sanctuary will be properly restored.”
paragraphs: 9 From one of these horns a little horn emerged and grew extensively toward the south and the east and toward the Beautiful Land. 10 It grew as high as the host of heaven, and it cast down some of the host and some of the stars to the earth and trampled them. 11 It magnified itself, even to the Prince of the host; it removed His daily sacrifice and overthrew the place of His sanctuary. 12 And in the rebellion, the host and the daily sacrifice were given over to the horn, and it flung truth to the ground and prospered in whatever it did.

13 Then I heard a holy one speaking, and another holy one said to him, “How long until the fulfillment of the vision of the daily sacrifice, the rebellion that causes desolation, and the surrender of the sanctuary and of the host to be trampled?” 14 He said to me, “It will take 2,300 evenings and mornings; then the sanctuary will be properly restored.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
A little horn grows from one of the four and expands toward the south, east and Beautiful Land. Its assault reaches the host of heaven, the daily sacrifice and God’s sanctuary. Truth is flung to the ground while the horn prospers.

A holy one asks how long the sanctuary and host will be trampled. The answer is 2,300 evenings and mornings, followed by the sanctuary being properly restored. The verb behind restored belongs to צָדַק, tsadaq (tsah-DAHK): Brown–Driver–Briggs explains this form in verse 14 as putting the holy place right or vindicating its cause.

The ancient account in 1 Maccabees 1:41–64 describes Antiochus’s suppression of Jewish sacrifices, profaning of the sanctuary and persecution of those who kept the covenant. It provides historical background for the reading that connects this vision with his rule.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley identifies the horn as Antiochus and understands the trampled stars as God’s people. The USCCB notes also identify Antiochus, while reading the host as heavenly angels.

The period is understood differently. Gaebelein reads 2,300 ordinary days; Cambridge reads 2,300 morning and evening offerings, making 1,150 days. Both connect the period with the sanctuary’s oppression and restoration.

The Seventh-day Adventist Church gives the period a different application. Its official Fundamental Belief 24 connects it with Christ’s heavenly ministry and the beginning of its final phase in 1844. That statement also affirms His once-for-all sacrifice at the cross and His intercession beginning at the ascension.
passages.god_plan_html:
The concern for God’s house and its worship continues in John 2:13–22. Jesus drives trading out of the temple courts and then speaks of a temple that will be raised in three days. John explains that He means His own body.

This is a connection in the wider theme of worship and God’s dwelling, rather than a calculation from Daniel’s 2,300 evenings and mornings. In the gospel, the horizon reaches beyond restoring a damaged sanctuary to Jesus’ own death and resurrection. God’s purpose for His people’s worship comes into focus through His Son.
