passages.title: Daniel 8:15-19
passages.section_title: Why does Daniel need Gabriel to explain the vision?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 While I, Daniel, was watching the vision and trying to understand it, there stood before me one having the appearance of a man. 16 And I heard the voice of a man calling from between the banks of the Ulai: “Gabriel, explain the vision to this man.” 17 As he came near to where I stood, I was terrified and fell facedown. “Son of man,” he said to me, “understand that the vision concerns the time of the end.” 18 While he was speaking with me, I fell into a deep sleep, with my face to the ground. Then he touched me, helped me to my feet, 19 and said, “Behold, I will make known to you what will happen in the latter time of wrath, because it concerns the appointed time of the end.
paragraphs: 15 While I, Daniel, was watching the vision and trying to understand it, there stood before me one having the appearance of a man. 16 And I heard the voice of a man calling from between the banks of the Ulai: “Gabriel, explain the vision to this man.” 17 As he came near to where I stood, I was terrified and fell facedown. “Son of man,” he said to me, “understand that the vision concerns the time of the end.” 18 While he was speaking with me, I fell into a deep sleep, with my face to the ground. Then he touched me, helped me to my feet, 19 and said, “Behold, I will make known to you what will happen in the latter time of wrath, because it concerns the appointed time of the end.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
As Daniel seeks understanding, a figure appears before him and a voice commands Gabriel to explain the vision. Daniel falls facedown in fear as Gabriel approaches.

Gabriel tells him that the vision concerns the time of the end. Daniel falls into a deep sleep, but the messenger touches him and helps him stand. He is to learn what will occur in the latter time of wrath, at the appointed end.

The explanation comes to a man who is overwhelmed by what he has seen. Daniel’s role is to receive and preserve what God makes known, including events that lie beyond his immediate experience.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands the appointed end here in relation to the end of Antiochus’s oppression. Gaebelein sees the language also pointing beyond Antiochus toward a final period of trouble before Christ’s return.

The difference concerns how far the vision reaches. Both readings recognize that the end is appointed by God rather than decided by the persecuting ruler.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 8:20-22
passages.section_title: Which kingdoms does Gabriel identify?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 20 The two-horned ram that you saw represents the kings of Media and Persia. 21 The shaggy goat represents the king of Greece, and the large horn between his eyes is the first king. 22 The four horns that replaced the broken one represent four kingdoms that will rise from that nation but will not have the same power.
paragraphs: 20 The two-horned ram that you saw represents the kings of Media and Persia. 21 The shaggy goat represents the king of Greece, and the large horn between his eyes is the first king. 22 The four horns that replaced the broken one represent four kingdoms that will rise from that nation but will not have the same power.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Gabriel gives direct names for the main symbols. The ram’s two horns are the kings of Media and Persia. The goat represents Greece, and its large horn represents the first king.

The four horns that replace the broken one are four kingdoms that arise from the same nation, though without the first king’s power.

This explanation anchors the vision in a succession of earthly kingdoms. It also shows the limits of their greatness: one power is overcome, and the next ruler’s dominion does not remain intact after him.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry, Wesley and Gaebelein agree on the basic identification: Media and Persia are overcome by the Greek power associated with Alexander, followed by divisions of his empire.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 8:23-27
passages.section_title: What brings the deceitful ruler’s success to an end?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 23 In the latter part of their reign, when the rebellion has reached its full measure, an insolent king, skilled in intrigue, will come to the throne. 24 His power will be great, but it will not be his own. He will cause terrible destruction and succeed in whatever he does. He will destroy the mighty men along with the holy people. 25 Through his craft and by his hand, he will cause deceit to prosper, and in his own mind he will make himself great. In a time of peace he will destroy many, and he will even stand against the Prince of princes. Yet he will be broken off, but not by human hands. 26 The vision of the evenings and the mornings that has been spoken is true. Now you must seal up the vision, for it concerns the distant future.” 27 I, Daniel, was exhausted and lay ill for days. Then I got up and went about the king’s business. I was confounded by the vision; it was beyond understanding.
paragraphs: 23 In the latter part of their reign, when the rebellion has reached its full measure, an insolent king, skilled in intrigue, will come to the throne. 24 His power will be great, but it will not be his own. He will cause terrible destruction and succeed in whatever he does. He will destroy the mighty men along with the holy people. 25 Through his craft and by his hand, he will cause deceit to prosper, and in his own mind he will make himself great. In a time of peace he will destroy many, and he will even stand against the Prince of princes. Yet he will be broken off, but not by human hands.

26 The vision of the evenings and the mornings that has been spoken is true. Now you must seal up the vision, for it concerns the distant future.” 27 I, Daniel, was exhausted and lay ill for days. Then I got up and went about the king’s business. I was confounded by the vision; it was beyond understanding.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The explanation describes an insolent ruler skilled in intrigue. His power brings terrible destruction to the mighty and the holy people. Deceit prospers through him, and he attacks people while they are at peace.

He even stands against the Prince of princes, yet he is broken without human hands. His apparent success does not give him the final word.

Daniel is told that the vision is true and concerns the distant future. He is to seal it up. Exhausted and ill for days, he eventually returns to the king’s business, still overwhelmed by what he has seen. Receiving a true revelation does not mean that he immediately understands everything it contains.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Cambridge understand the ruler as Antiochus, whose end comes through God’s intervention. Gaebelein treats Antiochus’s persecution as a preview of a later attack on Israel near the end.

These readings differ over whether a further ruler is in view. They share the conclusion that arrogant power does not escape God’s appointed limit.
passages.god_plan_html:
A parallel appears in 2 Thessalonians 2:1–12. Paul describes a lawless ruler who exalts himself against God, works through deception and is destroyed by the Lord Jesus at His appearing.

The parallel is the defeat of self-exalting, deceitful power by God’s action, beyond what human strength can achieve. It does not require settling every question about the ruler in Daniel 8. Paul brings the wider hope into focus through Jesus: the power that deceives and oppresses will answer to Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 9:1-3
passages.section_title: Why does reading Jeremiah lead Daniel to pray?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 In the first year of Darius son of Xerxes, a Mede by descent, who was made ruler over the kingdom of the Chaldeans — 2 in the first year of his reign, I, Daniel, understood from the sacred books, according to the word of the LORD to Jeremiah the prophet, that the desolation of Jerusalem would last seventy years. 3 So I turned my attention to the Lord God to seek Him by prayer and petition, with fasting, sackcloth, and ashes.
paragraphs: 1 In the first year of Darius son of Xerxes, a Mede by descent, who was made ruler over the kingdom of the Chaldeans — 2 in the first year of his reign, I, Daniel, understood from the sacred books, according to the word of the LORD to Jeremiah the prophet, that the desolation of Jerusalem would last seventy years. 3 So I turned my attention to the Lord God to seek Him by prayer and petition, with fasting, sackcloth, and ashes.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The setting returns to the first year of Darius, after the fall of Babylon. Reading the sacred books, Daniel understands from Jeremiah that Jerusalem’s desolation is to last seventy years.

Jeremiah 25:8–14 speaks of the nations serving Babylon for seventy years and of Babylon itself being judged afterward. Jeremiah 29:10–14 promises that God will attend to His people, hear them as they seek Him and restore them from captivity.

Daniel responds by turning to God in prayer, fasting, sackcloth and ashes. Learning that God has promised an end to the desolation moves him to seek God earnestly. The rest of the chapter records his confession and the answer that follows.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry and Gaebelein understand God’s promise as the encouragement for Daniel’s prayer. Knowing what God has said gives him reason to appeal to Him, rather than making prayer unnecessary.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 9:4-10
passages.section_title: How does Daniel confess the sins of his people?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 4 And I prayed to the LORD my God and confessed, “O, Lord, the great and awesome God, who keeps His covenant of loving devotion to those who love Him and keep His commandments, 5 we have sinned and done wrong. We have acted wickedly and rebelled. We have turned away from Your commandments and ordinances. 6 We have not listened to Your servants the prophets, who spoke in Your name to our kings, leaders, fathers, and all the people of the land. 7 To You, O Lord, belongs righteousness, but this day we are covered with shame—the men of Judah, the people of Jerusalem, and all Israel near and far, in all the countries to which You have driven us because of our unfaithfulness to You. 8 O LORD, we are covered with shame—our kings, our leaders, and our fathers—because we have sinned against You. 9 To the Lord our God belong compassion and forgiveness, even though we have rebelled against Him 10 and have not obeyed the voice of the LORD our God to walk in His laws, which He set before us through His servants the prophets.
paragraphs: 4 And I prayed to the LORD my God and confessed, “O, Lord, the great and awesome God, who keeps His covenant of loving devotion to those who love Him and keep His commandments, 5 we have sinned and done wrong. We have acted wickedly and rebelled. We have turned away from Your commandments and ordinances. 6 We have not listened to Your servants the prophets, who spoke in Your name to our kings, leaders, fathers, and all the people of the land.

7 To You, O Lord, belongs righteousness, but this day we are covered with shame—the men of Judah, the people of Jerusalem, and all Israel near and far, in all the countries to which You have driven us because of our unfaithfulness to You. 8 O LORD, we are covered with shame—our kings, our leaders, and our fathers—because we have sinned against You. 9 To the Lord our God belong compassion and forgiveness, even though we have rebelled against Him 10 and have not obeyed the voice of the LORD our God to walk in His laws, which He set before us through His servants the prophets.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Daniel begins by honoring the great and awesome God who keeps His covenant and loving devotion. He then confesses rebellion: the people have turned from God’s commands and refused to listen to His prophets.

He speaks as part of the people. Their kings, leaders, fathers and the nation scattered near and far share the shame of unfaithfulness. Daniel does not use his own record of faithfulness as a reason to stand apart from their confession.

At the same time, he attributes righteousness, compassion and forgiveness to God. The prayer holds these together: the people have sinned, God’s judgment is just, and mercy still belongs to the One they have disobeyed.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry emphasizes confession that honestly acknowledges sin and God’s righteousness. Gaebelein particularly notes Daniel’s identification with the people’s failure despite his own faithful service.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 9:11-14
passages.section_title: How does Daniel understand the disaster that came on Jerusalem?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 All Israel has transgressed Your law and turned away, refusing to obey Your voice; so the oath and the curse written in the Law of Moses the servant of God has been poured out on us, because we have sinned against You. 12 You have carried out the words spoken against us and against our rulers by bringing upon us a great disaster. For under all of heaven, nothing has ever been done like what has been done to Jerusalem. 13 Just as it is written in the Law of Moses, all this disaster has come upon us, yet we have not sought the favor of the LORD our God by turning from our iniquities and giving attention to Your truth. 14 Therefore the LORD has kept the calamity in store and brought it upon us. For the LORD our God is righteous in all He does; yet we have not obeyed His voice.
paragraphs: 11 All Israel has transgressed Your law and turned away, refusing to obey Your voice; so the oath and the curse written in the Law of Moses the servant of God has been poured out on us, because we have sinned against You. 12 You have carried out the words spoken against us and against our rulers by bringing upon us a great disaster. For under all of heaven, nothing has ever been done like what has been done to Jerusalem. 13 Just as it is written in the Law of Moses, all this disaster has come upon us, yet we have not sought the favor of the LORD our God by turning from our iniquities and giving attention to Your truth. 14 Therefore the LORD has kept the calamity in store and brought it upon us. For the LORD our God is righteous in all He does; yet we have not obeyed His voice.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Daniel connects the disaster with the oath and curse written in the Law of Moses. The people had turned away from God’s voice, and He had carried out the warnings given to them.

Leviticus 26:31–45 describes ruined cities, a desolate sanctuary, scattering among the nations and the land receiving its neglected rest. It also speaks of humbled hearts, confession and God remembering His covenant.

Daniel acknowledges that even after the disaster, the people have not turned from their iniquity or given attention to God’s truth. His confession therefore concerns the response still needed, as well as the sins that brought them into exile. God has remained righteous in all He has done.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley emphasizes God’s justice in bringing the announced judgment. Cambridge connects the covenant curse with the warnings in Moses’ law and understands attention to God’s truth as a changed response to His revealed will.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 9:15-19
passages.section_title: On what basis does Daniel ask God to restore them?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 Now, O Lord our God, who brought Your people out of the land of Egypt with a mighty hand, and who made for Yourself a name renowned to this day, we have sinned; we have acted wickedly. 16 O Lord, in keeping with all Your righteous acts, I pray that Your anger and wrath may turn away from Your city Jerusalem, Your holy mountain; for because of our sins and the iniquities of our fathers, Jerusalem and Your people are a reproach to all around us. 17 So now, our God, hear the prayers and petitions of Your servant. For Your sake, O Lord, cause Your face to shine upon Your desolate sanctuary. 18 Incline Your ear, O my God, and hear; open Your eyes and see the desolation of the city that bears Your name. For we are not presenting our petitions before You because of our righteous acts, but because of Your great compassion. 19 O Lord, listen! O Lord, forgive! O Lord, hear and act! For Your sake, O my God, do not delay, because Your city and Your people bear Your name.”
paragraphs: 15 Now, O Lord our God, who brought Your people out of the land of Egypt with a mighty hand, and who made for Yourself a name renowned to this day, we have sinned; we have acted wickedly. 16 O Lord, in keeping with all Your righteous acts, I pray that Your anger and wrath may turn away from Your city Jerusalem, Your holy mountain; for because of our sins and the iniquities of our fathers, Jerusalem and Your people are a reproach to all around us. 17 So now, our God, hear the prayers and petitions of Your servant. For Your sake, O Lord, cause Your face to shine upon Your desolate sanctuary.

18 Incline Your ear, O my God, and hear; open Your eyes and see the desolation of the city that bears Your name. For we are not presenting our petitions before You because of our righteous acts, but because of Your great compassion. 19 O Lord, listen! O Lord, forgive! O Lord, hear and act! For Your sake, O my God, do not delay, because Your city and Your people bear Your name.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Daniel recalls the God who brought His people out of Egypt and made His name known. He asks Him to turn His anger from Jerusalem and look with favor on the desolate sanctuary.

He states the ground of the appeal plainly: the people are not presenting their petitions because of their righteous acts, but because of God’s great compassion. Confession leads to a plea for forgiveness and action.

The city and the people bear God’s name. Daniel’s urgent request is therefore for God’s own sake as well as for their relief. Their need is great, but the mercy and honor of God give the prayer its basis.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry and Wesley read the appeal for the Lord’s sake through the Messiah. Cambridge emphasizes God’s own name and honor, consistent with the repeated appeal in verse 19. These readings agree that the plea rests on God rather than the people’s merit.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 2:4–10 describes God as rich in mercy and salvation as His gift through faith. He makes people alive with Christ and creates them for good works.

The chapter then shows Jews and Gentiles brought together through the cross, especially verses 14–22. They have access to the Father and become His household and dwelling place. The wider theme is mercy creating a restored people: the God to whom Daniel appeals makes His grace known through Christ and brings people near to Himself.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 9:20-23
passages.section_title: What answer reaches Daniel while he is still praying?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 20 While I was speaking, praying, confessing my sin and that of my people Israel, and presenting my petition before the LORD my God concerning His holy mountain— 21 while I was still praying, Gabriel, the man I had seen in the earlier vision, came to me in swift flight about the time of the evening sacrifice. 22 He instructed me and spoke with me, saying: “O Daniel, I have come now to give you insight and understanding. 23 At the beginning of your petitions, an answer went out, and I have come to tell you, for you are highly precious. So consider the message and understand the vision:
paragraphs: 20 While I was speaking, praying, confessing my sin and that of my people Israel, and presenting my petition before the LORD my God concerning His holy mountain— 21 while I was still praying, Gabriel, the man I had seen in the earlier vision, came to me in swift flight about the time of the evening sacrifice. 22 He instructed me and spoke with me, saying: “O Daniel, I have come now to give you insight and understanding. 23 At the beginning of your petitions, an answer went out, and I have come to tell you, for you are highly precious. So consider the message and understand the vision:

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Daniel is still confessing his sin and the sin of his people when Gabriel arrives. He recognizes the messenger from the earlier vision. The time is that of the evening sacrifice.

Gabriel says that an answer went out at the beginning of Daniel’s petitions. Daniel is highly precious, and the messenger has come to give him insight and understanding.

The response is more than an announcement that the prayer was heard. Daniel is called to consider a message about his people and Jerusalem that reaches beyond the immediate ruins for which he has been praying.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry sees the answer as opening a larger prospect of redemption. Gaebelein emphasizes that God hears Daniel from the beginning of his prayer. Gabriel’s message supplies understanding that Daniel could not produce for himself.
passages.god_plan_html:
Gabriel appears again in Luke 1:11–20 and 26–38. He tells Zechariah that his prayer has been heard and announces John’s role in preparing people for the Lord. He then tells Mary that Jesus will receive David’s throne and reign without end.

This is a connection through the messenger and the unfolding purpose he announces. In Daniel he brings understanding about Jerusalem’s future; in Luke he announces the birth of the King whose kingdom will never end. God’s answer reaches into a purpose larger than the immediate circumstances of those receiving it.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 9:24
passages.section_title: What is to be accomplished in the seventy weeks?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 24 Seventy weeks are decreed for your people and your holy city to stop their transgression, to put an end to sin, to make atonement for iniquity, to bring in everlasting righteousness, to seal up vision and prophecy, and to anoint the Most Holy Place.
paragraphs: 24 Seventy weeks are decreed for your people and your holy city to stop their transgression, to put an end to sin, to make atonement for iniquity, to bring in everlasting righteousness, to seal up vision and prophecy, and to anoint the Most Holy Place.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Gabriel announces seventy weeks decreed for Daniel’s people and holy city. The stated purposes concern ending transgression and sin, making atonement for iniquity, bringing everlasting righteousness, sealing vision and prophecy, and anointing the Most Holy Place.

The Hebrew שָׁבוּעַ, shabua (shah-BOO-ah), means a period of seven. Brown–Driver–Briggs recognizes periods of seven years in Daniel 9. This is why readers commonly speak of seventy sevens or weeks of years.

The answer moves beyond counting the years of exile. The future of the city is placed within God’s purpose to deal with sin and establish lasting righteousness. How the periods are counted and when all the purposes are fulfilled are questions on which interpretations differ.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry and Wesley connect these purposes with Christ’s redemption. Gaebelein stresses their completion for Israel and Jerusalem at the future kingdom. The USCCB notes read the seventy weeks as a symbolic span of years reaching the crisis under Antiochus rather than an exact calendar calculation.
passages.god_plan_html:
The purpose of dealing with sin finds a clear New Testament expression in Hebrews 9:24–28. Christ appears before God on our behalf and has offered Himself once to take away sin. He will appear again to bring salvation to those awaiting Him.

This connection in theme does not settle every detail of Daniel’s timetable. It shows where the New Testament directs hope for atonement and lasting deliverance: to Christ’s completed offering and His promised appearing. God’s answer to sin reaches further than rebuilding a ruined city.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 9:25-26
passages.section_title: What follows the rebuilding and the cutting off of the Messiah?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 25 Know and understand this: From the issuance of the decree to restore and rebuild Jerusalem until the Messiah, the Prince, there will be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks. It will be rebuilt with streets and a trench, but in times of distress. 26 Then after the sixty-two weeks the Messiah will be cut off and will have nothing. Then the people of the prince who is to come will destroy the city and the sanctuary. The end will come like a flood, and until the end there will be war; desolations have been decreed.
paragraphs: 25 Know and understand this: From the issuance of the decree to restore and rebuild Jerusalem until the Messiah, the Prince, there will be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks. It will be rebuilt with streets and a trench, but in times of distress. 26 Then after the sixty-two weeks the Messiah will be cut off and will have nothing. Then the people of the prince who is to come will destroy the city and the sanctuary. The end will come like a flood, and until the end there will be war; desolations have been decreed.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The message describes a decree to restore and rebuild Jerusalem, a period of seven weeks and sixty-two weeks, and rebuilding under distress. After the sixty-two weeks, the Messiah is cut off and has nothing.

The people of a coming prince then destroy the city and sanctuary. War and decreed desolations follow. The promise of restoration therefore does not mean that Jerusalem will never face further disaster.

The BSB presents the anointed figure as the Messiah, the Prince. Readers differ over the decree from which to count, the relationship of the seven and sixty-two periods, and the people identified in the prophecy. Those differences affect how the sequence is understood.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley identifies the cut-off Messiah as Jesus and the destruction with the Romans under Titus. Gaebelein also sees Jesus’ death and Roman destruction, counting from the decree associated with Nehemiah.

The USCCB notes give a different historical reading: an earlier anointed ruler is Cyrus or the high priest Jeshua, and the later anointed one who is killed is the high priest Onias III. They associate the persecuting leader with Antiochus. This differs from the BSB’s messianic presentation and the readings above.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 9:27
passages.section_title: Who confirms the covenant, and what ends the desolation?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 27 And he will confirm a covenant with many for one week, but in the middle of the week he will put an end to sacrifice and offering. And on the wing of the temple will come the abomination that causes desolation, until the decreed destruction is poured out upon him.”
paragraphs: 27 And he will confirm a covenant with many for one week, but in the middle of the week he will put an end to sacrifice and offering. And on the wing of the temple will come the abomination that causes desolation, until the decreed destruction is poured out upon him.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The final verse describes a covenant confirmed with many for one week. In the middle of the week, sacrifice and offering cease. An abomination brings desolation, until the decreed destruction falls on the desolator.

The identity of the person referred to as he is a central question. So is the relationship between this week and the preceding periods. The verse itself gives the covenant, the interruption of sacrifice and the decreed end of the desolation; readers assemble those details differently.

The conclusion sets a limit even to the desecration. The desolator does not possess authority to decide the final outcome.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands Christ as confirming the new covenant and His death as ending the former sacrificial order. Gaebelein reads a future ruler’s covenant with Jewish people during a final seven-year period, separated from the earlier weeks.

The USCCB notes understand the covenant and interrupted worship within Antiochus’s persecution. These positions differ over the subject, timing and covenant; none should be presented as the uncontested reading.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Matthew 24:15–22, Jesus explicitly directs His hearers to Daniel’s language about the abomination of desolation. He gives practical instructions to flee and speaks of severe trouble whose days are cut short for the elect’s sake.

Jesus therefore treats Daniel’s warning as something His followers need to understand and act upon. The connection does not remove all questions about the seventy weeks. It places watchfulness, prayer and the preservation of God’s people within Jesus’ own teaching, rather than leaving the prophecy only as a disputed calculation.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 10:1-3
passages.section_title: How does Daniel prepare to receive the final vision?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 In the third year of Cyrus king of Persia, a message was revealed to Daniel, who was called Belteshazzar. The message was true, and it concerned a great conflict. And the understanding of the message was given to him in a vision. 2 In those days I, Daniel, was mourning for three full weeks. 3 I ate no rich food, no meat or wine entered my mouth, and I did not anoint myself with oil until the three weeks were completed.
paragraphs: 1 In the third year of Cyrus king of Persia, a message was revealed to Daniel, who was called Belteshazzar. The message was true, and it concerned a great conflict. And the understanding of the message was given to him in a vision. 2 In those days I, Daniel, was mourning for three full weeks. 3 I ate no rich food, no meat or wine entered my mouth, and I did not anoint myself with oil until the three weeks were completed.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The final encounter begins in the third year of Cyrus. Daniel, also called Belteshazzar, receives a true message concerning a great conflict. This encounter continues through the remaining chapters of the book.

He describes three full weeks of mourning. During that time he eats no rich food or meat, drinks no wine and uses no anointing oil. His abstinence expresses the seriousness of his seeking.

The chapter’s opening states that understanding is given to him. What follows explains the encounter through which he is strengthened and prepared to hear about his people’s future.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry and Gaebelein treat the chapter as preparation for the final prophecy. Cambridge connects Daniel’s mourning and self-humbling with his concern to understand the future of his people.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 10:4-9
passages.section_title: What does Daniel see beside the Tigris?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 4 On the twenty-fourth day of the first month, as I was standing on the bank of the great river, the Tigris, 5 I lifted up my eyes, and behold, there was a certain man dressed in linen, with a belt of fine gold from Uphaz around his waist. 6 His body was like beryl, his face like the brilliance of lightning, his eyes like flaming torches, his arms and legs like the gleam of polished bronze, and his voice like the sound of a multitude. 7 Only I, Daniel, saw the vision; the men with me did not see it, but a great terror fell upon them, and they ran and hid themselves. 8 So I was left alone, gazing at this great vision. No strength remained in me; my face grew deathly pale, and I was powerless. 9 I heard the sound of his words, and as I listened, I fell into a deep sleep, with my face to the ground.
paragraphs: 4 On the twenty-fourth day of the first month, as I was standing on the bank of the great river, the Tigris, 5 I lifted up my eyes, and behold, there was a certain man dressed in linen, with a belt of fine gold from Uphaz around his waist. 6 His body was like beryl, his face like the brilliance of lightning, his eyes like flaming torches, his arms and legs like the gleam of polished bronze, and his voice like the sound of a multitude.

7 Only I, Daniel, saw the vision; the men with me did not see it, but a great terror fell upon them, and they ran and hid themselves. 8 So I was left alone, gazing at this great vision. No strength remained in me; my face grew deathly pale, and I was powerless. 9 I heard the sound of his words, and as I listened, I fell into a deep sleep, with my face to the ground.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
On the twenty-fourth day of the first month, Daniel stands beside the Tigris. He sees a man dressed in linen with a belt of fine gold. The figure’s body, face, eyes, limbs and voice are described through brilliant light, fire, polished bronze and the sound of a multitude.

Daniel alone sees the vision, though his companions are terrified and flee. Left alone, he loses his strength and turns pale. As he hears the voice, he falls facedown into a deep sleep.

The description presents an overwhelming heavenly encounter. Before Daniel can receive the explanation, he must be helped to stand and listen.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry, Wesley and Gaebelein understand the radiant figure as Christ appearing before His earthly life. The USCCB notes instead suggest Gabriel. Cambridge emphasizes the heavenly appearance and its similarities to Ezekiel and Revelation.

The identity is interpreted differently; the figure’s radiance and Daniel’s overwhelming response are plain features of the account.
passages.god_plan_html:
Revelation 1:12–18 takes up similar imagery in John’s vision of Jesus: a robe and golden sash, fiery eyes, gleaming feet and a powerful voice. John also falls as though dead and receives reassurance.

The connection does not require treating every detail as proof of the figure’s identity in Daniel. Revelation clearly identifies the risen Jesus as the Living One who holds the keys of Death and Hades. The majesty that overwhelms the witness is joined with words of reassurance and Christ’s victory over death.

passages.title: Daniel 10:10-14
passages.section_title: Had God heard Daniel during the three weeks of waiting?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 Suddenly, a hand touched me and set me trembling on my hands and knees. 11 He said to me, “Daniel, you are a man who is highly precious. Consider carefully the words that I am about to say to you. Stand up, for I have now been sent to you.” And when he had said this to me, I stood up trembling. 12 “Do not be afraid, Daniel,” he said, “for from the first day that you purposed to understand and to humble yourself before your God, your words were heard, and I have come in response to them. 13 However, the prince of the kingdom of Persia opposed me for twenty-one days. Then Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me, for I had been left there with the kings of Persia. 14 Now I have come to explain to you what will happen to your people in the latter days, for the vision concerns those days.”
paragraphs: 10 Suddenly, a hand touched me and set me trembling on my hands and knees. 11 He said to me, “Daniel, you are a man who is highly precious. Consider carefully the words that I am about to say to you. Stand up, for I have now been sent to you.” And when he had said this to me, I stood up trembling. 12 “Do not be afraid, Daniel,” he said, “for from the first day that you purposed to understand and to humble yourself before your God, your words were heard, and I have come in response to them. 13 However, the prince of the kingdom of Persia opposed me for twenty-one days. Then Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me, for I had been left there with the kings of Persia. 14 Now I have come to explain to you what will happen to your people in the latter days, for the vision concerns those days.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
A hand touches Daniel and raises him to his hands and knees. The messenger calls him highly precious and tells him to stand and consider the message.

He then explains that Daniel’s words were heard from the first day he humbled himself and sought understanding. The delay involved opposition from the prince of Persia for twenty-one days, until Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help.

The answer was not delayed because Daniel had been ignored. The account opens a view of conflict beyond what he could see during his mourning. The messenger has come to explain what will happen to Daniel’s people in the latter days.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Gaebelein understands the opposing prince as a spiritual power of darkness associated with Persia. Cambridge and the USCCB notes also understand the princes in relation to heavenly powers connected with nations.

The identity of Michael is read differently: Wesley understands him as Christ, while the USCCB notes describe him as Israel’s patron angel. The passage calls him one of the chief princes and the helper in this conflict.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 6:10–20 tells believers that their struggle is against spiritual evil rather than flesh and blood. The response is to stand in the Lord’s strength, with truth, righteousness, faith, salvation, God’s word and persevering prayer.

Paul also asks for prayer that he may proclaim the gospel boldly. The larger connection is spiritual conflict within God’s work of making Christ known. Believers are directed toward faithful endurance, prayer and the work of making the gospel known.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 10:15-21
passages.section_title: How is Daniel strengthened to hear what comes next?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 While he was speaking these words to me, I set my face toward the ground and became speechless. 16 And suddenly one with the likeness of a man touched my lips, and I opened my mouth and said to the one standing before me, “My lord, because of the vision, I am overcome with anguish, and I have no strength. 17 How can I, your servant, speak with you, my lord? Now I have no strength, nor is any breath left in me.” 18 Again the one with the likeness of a man touched me and strengthened me. 19 “Do not be afraid, you who are highly precious,” he said. “Peace be with you! Be strong now; be very strong!” As he spoke with me, I was strengthened and said, “Speak, my lord, for you have strengthened me.” 20 “Do you know why I have come to you?” he said. “I must return at once to fight against the prince of Persia, and when I have gone forth, behold, the prince of Greece will come. 21 But first I will tell you what is inscribed in the Book of Truth. Yet no one has the courage to support me against these, except Michael your prince.
paragraphs: 15 While he was speaking these words to me, I set my face toward the ground and became speechless. 16 And suddenly one with the likeness of a man touched my lips, and I opened my mouth and said to the one standing before me, “My lord, because of the vision, I am overcome with anguish, and I have no strength. 17 How can I, your servant, speak with you, my lord? Now I have no strength, nor is any breath left in me.” 18 Again the one with the likeness of a man touched me and strengthened me. 19 “Do not be afraid, you who are highly precious,” he said. “Peace be with you! Be strong now; be very strong!” As he spoke with me, I was strengthened and said, “Speak, my lord, for you have strengthened me.”

20 “Do you know why I have come to you?” he said. “I must return at once to fight against the prince of Persia, and when I have gone forth, behold, the prince of Greece will come. 21 But first I will tell you what is inscribed in the Book of Truth. Yet no one has the courage to support me against these, except Michael your prince.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Daniel turns his face toward the ground and cannot speak. One resembling a man touches his lips, and he explains that the vision has left him without strength or breath.

He is touched again and strengthened. The words of reassurance bring peace and courage, and Daniel becomes ready to listen.

The messenger says he must return to the conflict with the prince of Persia, after which the prince of Greece will come. First he will reveal what is written in the Book of Truth. Michael is named as Daniel’s people’s prince and the messenger’s supporter. The coming account of kingdoms is framed by God’s knowledge and care, even amid conflict Daniel cannot fully see.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry emphasizes the assurance of God’s love as a source of strength. Cambridge understands the Book of Truth as the heavenly record of what is to come. The reassurance prepares Daniel to receive the difficult message that follows.
passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 1:1–5 and 13–14 places angelic service within God’s larger purpose. Angels serve those who will inherit salvation, while the Son is above them and has made purification for sins.

Daniel’s experience shows a servant being helped to receive God’s word. Hebrews carries the theme into the full revelation through the Son: God’s care includes ministering servants, but the center of His saving purpose is Christ Himself. The help given in weakness serves that greater hope.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 11:1-4
passages.section_title: What will become of the mighty kings who follow?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 “And I, in the first year of Darius the Mede, stood up to strengthen and protect him. 2 Now then, I will tell you the truth: Three more kings will arise in Persia, and then a fourth, who will be far richer than all the others. By the power of his wealth, he will stir up everyone against the kingdom of Greece. 3 Then a mighty king will arise, who will rule with great authority and do as he pleases. 4 But as soon as he is established, his kingdom will be broken up and parceled out toward the four winds of heaven. It will not go to his descendants, nor will it have the authority with which he ruled, because his kingdom will be uprooted and given to others.
paragraphs: 1 “And I, in the first year of Darius the Mede, stood up to strengthen and protect him. 2 Now then, I will tell you the truth: Three more kings will arise in Persia, and then a fourth, who will be far richer than all the others. By the power of his wealth, he will stir up everyone against the kingdom of Greece. 3 Then a mighty king will arise, who will rule with great authority and do as he pleases. 4 But as soon as he is established, his kingdom will be broken up and parceled out toward the four winds of heaven. It will not go to his descendants, nor will it have the authority with which he ruled, because his kingdom will be uprooted and given to others.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The messenger continues the explanation begun in chapter 10. After recalling his support in Darius’s first year, he speaks of further Persian kings. A wealthy fourth king will stir up opposition to Greece.

A mighty king then rises and rules with great authority. At the height of his establishment, his kingdom is broken and divided toward the four winds. It does not pass to his descendants with the authority he had exercised.

This develops the pattern already shown through the ram and goat in chapter 8. The greatness of a ruler does not secure either the permanence of his kingdom or his family’s possession of it.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley identifies the wealthy Persian king as Xerxes and the mighty king as Alexander. He notes that the passage’s selected Persian kings do not constitute a complete list of everyone who ruled Persia.

passages.title: Daniel 11:5-9
passages.section_title: Why does the royal marriage fail to secure peace?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 The king of the South will grow strong, but one of his commanders will grow even stronger and will rule his own kingdom with great authority. 6 After some years they will form an alliance, and the daughter of the king of the South will go to the king of the North to seal the agreement. But his daughter will not retain her position of power, nor will his strength endure. At that time she will be given up, along with her royal escort and her father and the one who supported her. 7 But one from her family line will rise up in his place, come against the army of the king of the North, and enter his fortress, fighting and prevailing. 8 He will take even their gods captive to Egypt, with their metal images and their precious vessels of silver and gold. For some years he will stay away from the king of the North, 9 who will invade the realm of the king of the South and then return to his own land.

For some years he will stay away from the king of the North, 9 who will invade the realm of the king of the South and then return to his own land.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The explanation turns to kings of the South and North. One ruler’s commander becomes stronger than he is, establishing another powerful kingdom.

After some years, a daughter from the southern royal house is given in marriage to seal an agreement with the northern king. The arrangement collapses, and she and those connected with her are given up.

A member of her family then rises to power, attacks the northern kingdom and carries its valuables and gods to Egypt. Later the northern king invades the South and returns home. The marriage agreement has become another stage in a continuing struggle, rather than an enduring peace.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley connects the rival kingdoms with the Ptolemies and Seleucids. He identifies the daughter as Berenice and the later southern campaign with her brother avenging her fate. The USCCB notes also connect the failed marriage with Berenice and Antiochus II.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 11:10-13
passages.section_title: How long does the southern king’s victory last?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 But his sons will stir up strife and assemble a great army, which will advance forcefully, sweeping through like a flood, and will again carry the battle as far as his fortress. 11 In a rage, the king of the South will march out to fight the king of the North, who will raise a large army, but it will be delivered into the hand of his enemy. 12 When the army is carried off, the king of the South will be proud in heart and will cast down tens of thousands, but he will not triumph. 13 For the king of the North will raise another army, larger than the first, and after some years he will advance with a great army and many supplies.
paragraphs: 10 But his sons will stir up strife and assemble a great army, which will advance forcefully, sweeping through like a flood, and will again carry the battle as far as his fortress. 11 In a rage, the king of the South will march out to fight the king of the North, who will raise a large army, but it will be delivered into the hand of his enemy. 12 When the army is carried off, the king of the South will be proud in heart and will cast down tens of thousands, but he will not triumph. 13 For the king of the North will raise another army, larger than the first, and after some years he will advance with a great army and many supplies.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The northern king’s sons gather forces and renew the conflict. One advances forcefully, prompting the king of the South to fight back.

The South wins a great victory and the king becomes proud. Yet the victory does not secure a lasting triumph. After some years, the North returns with a larger army and more supplies.

The passage follows successive reversals. Numbers, confidence and a moment of military success do not give either kingdom lasting control. The people in the path of these campaigns continue to face the consequences of their rulers’ rivalry.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The USCCB notes connect these campaigns with the battles of Raphia and Paneas. Henry emphasizes the fragile and changing nature of worldly power throughout this part of the chapter.

passages.title: Daniel 11:14-19
passages.section_title: Why do conquest and another marriage fail to secure the king’s plans?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 In those times many will rise up against the king of the South. Violent ones among your own people will exalt themselves in fulfillment of the vision, but they will fail. 15 Then the king of the North will come, build up a siege ramp, and capture a fortified city. The forces of the South will not stand; even their best troops will not be able to resist. 16 The invader will do as he pleases, and no one will stand against him. He will establish himself in the Beautiful Land, with destruction in his hand. 17 He will resolve to come with the strength of his whole kingdom, and will reach an agreement with the king of the South. He will give him a daughter in marriage in order to overthrow the kingdom, but his plan will not succeed or help him. 18 Then he will turn his face to the coastlands and capture many of them. But a commander will put an end to his reproach and will turn it back upon him. 19 After this, he will turn back toward the fortresses of his own land, but he will stumble and fall and be no more.

He will give him a daughter in marriage in order to overthrow the kingdom, but his plan will not succeed or help him. 18 Then he will turn his face to the coastlands and capture many of them. But a commander will put an end to his reproach and will turn it back upon him. 19 After this, he will turn back toward the fortresses of his own land, but he will stumble and fall and be no more.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Many rise against the southern king, including violent people from Daniel’s own nation. Their attempt fails. The northern invader takes a fortified city and establishes himself in the Beautiful Land.

He makes another agreement involving a daughter given in marriage, intending to gain control through it. That plan does not achieve what he intends.

He then turns toward the coastlands, but a commander turns back his aggression. Returning toward his own fortresses, he falls and disappears. The passage follows power that expands through force and marriage arrangements, then meets limits it cannot overcome.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley identifies the northern ruler as Antiochus III and the daughter as Cleopatra, whose loyalty did not serve her father’s design. He connects the reversal in the coastlands with Roman opposition. Henry sees the succession of reversals within God’s knowledge of the nations’ affairs.

passages.title: Daniel 11:20-24
passages.section_title: How does a despised ruler gain power through intrigue?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 20 In his place one will arise who will send out a tax collector for the glory of the kingdom; but within a few days he will be destroyed, though not in anger or in battle. 21 In his place a despicable person will arise; royal honors will not be given to him, but he will come in a time of peace and seize the kingdom by intrigue. 22 Then a flood of forces will be swept away before him and destroyed, along with a prince of the covenant. 23 After an alliance is made with him, he will act deceitfully; for he will rise to power with only a few people. 24 In a time of peace, he will invade the richest provinces and do what his fathers and forefathers never did. He will lavish plunder, loot, and wealth on his followers, and he will plot against the strongholds—but only for a time.

23 After an alliance is made with him, he will act deceitfully; for he will rise to power with only a few people. 24 In a time of peace, he will invade the richest provinces and do what his fathers and forefathers never did. He will lavish plunder, loot, and wealth on his followers, and he will plot against the strongholds—but only for a time.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The next ruler sends out a tax collector, but his own rule ends without battle. He is followed by a despicable person who gains the kingdom through intrigue rather than the expected royal honors.

Opposing forces are swept away, along with a prince of the covenant. The ruler grows stronger through deception, a small following and the distribution of plunder and wealth.

The account is moving from ordinary rivalry between kingdoms toward a ruler whose methods will bring a particular threat to the covenant people. His plotting succeeds, but the passage already places a limit on it: only for a time.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The USCCB notes identify the tax-raising ruler as Seleucus IV and the despised successor as Antiochus IV. They understand the prince of the covenant as the high priest Onias III. Wesley also connects the successor with Antiochus and his rise through flattery and deceit.

passages.title: Daniel 11:25-28
passages.section_title: What happens when two kings speak lies at the same table?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 25 And with a large army he will stir up his power and his courage against the king of the South, who will mobilize a very large and powerful army but will not withstand the plots devised against him. 26 Those who eat from his provisions will seek to destroy him; his army will be swept away, and many will fall slain. 27 And the two kings, with their hearts bent on evil, will speak lies at the same table, but to no avail, for still the end will come at the appointed time. 28 The king of the North will return to his land with great wealth, but his heart will be set against the holy covenant; so he will do damage and return to his own land.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The ruler gathers an army against the South. The southern king raises a powerful force, but plots within his own circle undermine him and many soldiers die.

The two kings then sit at the same table, both intending evil and speaking lies. Their schemes do not determine the final outcome, because the end still comes at the appointed time.

The northern king returns with great wealth, turning his hostility toward the holy covenant along the way. The people’s worship becomes a target within the rulers’ larger contest for power.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley reads the meeting as an appearance of peace covering mutual deception. Henry emphasizes how rulers both deceive and are deceived, while God’s purpose remains beyond their control.

passages.title: Daniel 11:29-31
passages.section_title: How does the renewed campaign become an attack on the sanctuary?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 29 At the appointed time he will invade the South again, but this time will not be like the first. 30 Ships of Kittim will come against him, and he will lose heart. Then he will turn back and rage against the holy covenant and do damage. So he will return and show favor to those who forsake the holy covenant. 31 His forces will rise up and desecrate the temple fortress. They will abolish the daily sacrifice and set up the abomination of desolation.
paragraphs: 29 At the appointed time he will invade the South again, but this time will not be like the first. 30 Ships of Kittim will come against him, and he will lose heart. Then he will turn back and rage against the holy covenant and do damage. So he will return and show favor to those who forsake the holy covenant. 31 His forces will rise up and desecrate the temple fortress. They will abolish the daily sacrifice and set up the abomination of desolation.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The northern ruler returns to the South, but this campaign ends differently. Ships of Kittim oppose him, and he loses heart.

He turns back in anger against the holy covenant, showing favor to those who abandon it. His forces desecrate the temple fortress, stop the daily sacrifice and establish the abomination of desolation.

The attack on worship is central. First Maccabees 1:41–64 provides an ancient account of Antiochus’s suppression of sacrifices, profaning of the sanctuary and punishment of people who remained faithful to the covenant.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley and the USCCB notes connect this persecution with Antiochus IV. Gaebelein also reads it historically, while distinguishing this event from the later desolation warning he understands Jesus to address.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus takes up Daniel’s abomination language in Matthew 24:15–22. He tells those in Judea to flee, urges prayer and warns of great trouble whose duration is limited for the elect’s sake.

Jesus directs His followers to understand Daniel and respond faithfully when worship is threatened by desolating power. His warning gives practical direction for a time of crisis, together with the assurance that even severe trouble has a limit under God’s care.
