passages.title: Daniel 11:32-35
passages.section_title: What does faithfulness look like when the wise are persecuted?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 32 With flattery he will corrupt those who violate the covenant, but the people who know their God will firmly resist him. 33 Those with insight will instruct many, though for a time they will fall by sword or flame, or be captured or plundered. 34 Now when they fall, they will be granted a little help, but many will join them insincerely. 35 Some of the wise will fall so that they may be refined, purified, and made spotless until the time of the end, for it will still come at the appointed time.
paragraphs: 32 With flattery he will corrupt those who violate the covenant, but the people who know their God will firmly resist him. 33 Those with insight will instruct many, though for a time they will fall by sword or flame, or be captured or plundered. 34 Now when they fall, they will be granted a little help, but many will join them insincerely. 35 Some of the wise will fall so that they may be refined, purified, and made spotless until the time of the end, for it will still come at the appointed time.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Flattery draws some away from the covenant, but those who know their God stand firm. People with insight instruct many others.

Their faithfulness does not spare them from suffering. They fall by sword and flame, captivity and plunder. They receive a little help, but some who join them are insincere.

The passage describes testing and purification until the appointed end. Wisdom here involves knowing God, resisting corruption and helping others understand, even when that brings personal cost. The suffering of the teachers does not make their witness a failure.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Cambridge understands the wise as faithful people who hold to God during Antiochus’s persecution and teach others through their example. It reads their suffering as testing the wider people and strengthening the faithful. The USCCB notes connect the little help with the Maccabean resistance.
passages.god_plan_html:
A parallel appears in Revelation 6:9–11. Those killed for God’s word and their testimony ask how long it will be until God judges and answers for their blood. They receive white robes and are told to rest while the appointed course continues.

Both passages place faithful suffering within a purpose that has not yet reached its end. Revelation shows that God has neither forgotten the witnesses nor measured their faithfulness by their survival. Their testimony and their promised answer remain before Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 11:36-39
passages.section_title: What happens when a ruler magnifies himself above every god?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 36 Then the king will do as he pleases and will exalt and magnify himself above every god, and he will speak monstrous things against the God of gods. He will be successful until the time of wrath is completed, for what has been decreed must be accomplished. 37 He will show no regard for the gods of his fathers, nor for the one desired by women, nor for any other god, because he will magnify himself above them all. 38 And in their place, he will honor a god of fortresses—a god his fathers did not know—with gold, silver, precious stones, and riches. 39 He will attack the strongest fortresses with the help of a foreign god and will greatly honor those who acknowledge him, making them rulers over many and distributing the land for a price.
paragraphs: 36 Then the king will do as he pleases and will exalt and magnify himself above every god, and he will speak monstrous things against the God of gods. He will be successful until the time of wrath is completed, for what has been decreed must be accomplished. 37 He will show no regard for the gods of his fathers, nor for the one desired by women, nor for any other god, because he will magnify himself above them all. 38 And in their place, he will honor a god of fortresses—a god his fathers did not know—with gold, silver, precious stones, and riches. 39 He will attack the strongest fortresses with the help of a foreign god and will greatly honor those who acknowledge him, making them rulers over many and distributing the land for a price.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The king acts as he pleases, magnifies himself above every god and speaks against the God of gods. His success continues until the decreed period of wrath is completed.

He disregards inherited gods and the one desired by women, while honoring a god of fortresses with great wealth. He rewards those who acknowledge him with authority and land.

The emphasis falls on self-exaltation supported by force, wealth and patronage. Even this ruler’s apparent freedom remains bounded by what has been decreed.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands Antiochus as the primary subject, with a further application to antichrist. Gaebelein sees a change at verse 36 to a future Antichrist. The USCCB notes retain Antiochus and interpret the one desired by women as Tammuz.

The ruler’s identity and the detailed references are disputed. His opposition to God and his time-limited success are central to the description.
passages.god_plan_html:
2 Thessalonians 2:3–12 presents a clear parallel: a lawless ruler exalts himself above every god or object of worship, uses deception and is destroyed by the Lord Jesus at His appearing.

The shared pattern helps explain the wider warning against power that claims God’s place. Paul names the ultimate answer in Christ’s authority. The hope reaches beyond identifying a dangerous ruler to trusting the Lord who will bring deception to its end.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 11:40-45
passages.section_title: Who can help the conquering ruler when his end comes?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 40 At the time of the end, the king of the South will engage him in battle, but the king of the North will storm out against him with chariots, horsemen, and many ships, invading many countries and sweeping through them like a flood. 41 He will also invade the Beautiful Land, and many countries will fall. But these will be delivered from his hand: Edom, Moab, and the leaders of the Ammonites. 42 He will extend his power over many countries, and not even the land of Egypt will escape. 43 He will gain control of the treasures of gold and silver and over all the riches of Egypt, and the Libyans and Cushites will also submit to him. 44 But news from the east and the north will alarm him, and he will go out with great fury to destroy many and devote them to destruction. 45 He will pitch his royal tents between the sea and the beautiful holy mountain, but he will meet his end with no one to help him.
paragraphs: 40 At the time of the end, the king of the South will engage him in battle, but the king of the North will storm out against him with chariots, horsemen, and many ships, invading many countries and sweeping through them like a flood. 41 He will also invade the Beautiful Land, and many countries will fall. But these will be delivered from his hand: Edom, Moab, and the leaders of the Ammonites. 42 He will extend his power over many countries, and not even the land of Egypt will escape. 43 He will gain control of the treasures of gold and silver and over all the riches of Egypt, and the Libyans and Cushites will also submit to him.

44 But news from the east and the north will alarm him, and he will go out with great fury to destroy many and devote them to destruction. 45 He will pitch his royal tents between the sea and the beautiful holy mountain, but he will meet his end with no one to help him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The closing scene describes renewed conflict involving the kings of the South and North. An invading ruler sweeps through lands, enters the Beautiful Land and gains power over Egypt’s wealth. Edom, Moab and the leading Ammonites escape his hand.

News from the east and north alarms him, and he goes out in fury to destroy many. He pitches his royal tents between the sea and the beautiful holy mountain.

The account ends abruptly: he meets his end, and no one helps him. The ruler who has extended his reach across countries cannot command a deliverer for himself. His conquests do not remove the limit on his own power.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands the ending as God cutting off the ruler. Gaebelein reads future conflicts involving the Antichrist and kings of the North and South.

The USCCB notes understand the closing campaign as an expectation about Antiochus, while acknowledging that it does not match his actual death in Persia. The historical and future readings therefore handle the final campaign differently.
passages.god_plan_html:
A broader parallel appears in Revelation 19:11–21. Kings and armies gather against the rider called the Word of God, but their assembled strength cannot save the beast and false prophet from judgment.

This carries the theme of the conqueror’s limit into the revelation of Christ as King of kings and Lord of lords. The shared theme is the end of power that sets itself against God. In Revelation, that outcome centers on the victory of Jesus, whose authority the gathered kingdoms cannot overthrow.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 12:1-3
passages.section_title: What hope is given beyond the time of great distress?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 “At that time Michael, the great prince who stands watch over your people, will rise up. There will be a time of distress, the likes of which will not have occurred from the beginning of nations until that time. But at that time your people—everyone whose name is found written in the book—will be delivered. 2 And many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life, but others to shame and everlasting contempt. 3 Then the wise will shine like the brightness of the heavens, and those who lead many to righteousness will shine like the stars forever and ever.
paragraphs: 1 “At that time Michael, the great prince who stands watch over your people, will rise up. There will be a time of distress, the likes of which will not have occurred from the beginning of nations until that time. But at that time your people—everyone whose name is found written in the book—will be delivered. 2 And many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life, but others to shame and everlasting contempt. 3 Then the wise will shine like the brightness of the heavens, and those who lead many to righteousness will shine like the stars forever and ever.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The message continues from the conflict at the end of chapter 11. Michael, the great prince who watches over Daniel’s people, rises up during a time of unprecedented distress. Those whose names are written in the book are delivered.

The vision then reaches beyond the present struggle: people sleeping in the earth’s dust awaken, some to everlasting life and others to shame and everlasting contempt.

Those with wisdom, including those who lead many to righteousness, shine like the heavens and the stars. This answers the suffering described in chapter 11, where faithful teachers were persecuted and killed. Their present humiliation does not determine their final place before God.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Henry and Wesley identify Michael with Christ, while Gaebelein understands him as a heavenly prince acting for Israel.

Cambridge reads the awakening as resurrection of individuals, with particular attention to faithful people and their opponents in Israel. Henry includes bodily resurrection alongside figurative awakenings through the gospel. Gaebelein instead reads verse 2 as a picture of Israel’s national restoration, rather than bodily resurrection. These are distinct readings of the awakening language.
passages.god_plan_html:
John 5:24–29 brings the contrast between life and judgment into Jesus’ own teaching. Those in the graves will hear His voice and come out, to the resurrection of life or of judgment. The authority to give life and judge belongs to the Son.

Jesus also speaks of the righteous shining like the sun in their Father’s kingdom, in Matthew 13:40–43, echoing Daniel’s language of future glory. The hope reaches beyond relief from persecution to life under Christ’s authority, where faithfulness that was despised on earth is seen in its true light.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 12:4
passages.section_title: Why is Daniel told to seal the book?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 4 But you, Daniel, shut up these words and seal the book until the time of the end. Many will roam to and fro, and knowledge will increase.”
paragraphs: 4 But you, Daniel, shut up these words and seal the book until the time of the end. Many will roam to and fro, and knowledge will increase.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Daniel is told to shut up the words and seal the book until the time of the end. The message has been entrusted to him, but its appointed fulfillment lies ahead.

The verse then speaks of many roaming to and fro and knowledge increasing. In the setting of a revelation that Daniel has struggled to understand, the relationship between seeking and understanding becomes an important question.

The instruction directs Daniel to preserve what he has received. The truth of the message does not depend on his being able to explain every detail immediately.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley understands the movement to and fro as diligent searching of the prophecies, leading to fuller understanding. Cambridge also presents this as a search within the book for knowledge of God’s purposes.
passages.god_plan_html:
Revelation 22:6–17 deliberately brings a different instruction: John is told not to seal the words because the time is near. The prophecy calls its hearers to keep its words, and Jesus promises His coming and reward.

This contrast links the books through the unfolding of God’s purpose. A message preserved for its appointed time gives way to an urgent call to hear and respond. Revelation closes with the invitation to come and receive the water of life freely, placing prophecy within the hope and invitation centered on Jesus.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 12:5-7
passages.section_title: How is the limit of the time of trouble confirmed?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 Then I, Daniel, looked and saw two others standing there, one on this bank of the river and one on the opposite bank. 6 One of them said to the man dressed in linen, who was above the waters of the river, “How long until the fulfillment of these wonders?” 7 And the man dressed in linen, who was above the waters of the river, raised his right hand and his left hand toward heaven, and I heard him swear by Him who lives forever, saying, “It will be for a time, and times, and half a time. When the power of the holy people has finally been shattered, all these things will be completed.”
paragraphs: 5 Then I, Daniel, looked and saw two others standing there, one on this bank of the river and one on the opposite bank. 6 One of them said to the man dressed in linen, who was above the waters of the river, “How long until the fulfillment of these wonders?” 7 And the man dressed in linen, who was above the waters of the river, raised his right hand and his left hand toward heaven, and I heard him swear by Him who lives forever, saying, “It will be for a time, and times, and half a time. When the power of the holy people has finally been shattered, all these things will be completed.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Daniel sees two others standing on opposite banks of the river. One asks the linen-clothed man above the waters how long it will be until the wonders are fulfilled.

The man raises both hands toward heaven and swears by the One who lives forever. The answer is a time, times and half a time, ending when the power of the holy people has been shattered.

The oath gives solemn assurance that the terrible events have an appointed limit. The question about how long is answered by appeal to the living God, whose authority outlasts the powers causing the distress.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands the period as three and a half years and identifies the man above the river as Christ. Cambridge connects the period with Antiochus’s persecution. Gaebelein places the chapter’s great distress within a future final tribulation.

The readings differ over the setting and speaker’s identity, while treating the oath as confirmation that God has set the limit.
passages.god_plan_html:
Revelation 10:1–11 takes up the raised hand and oath by the One who lives forever. Its mighty angel announces that the mystery of God proclaimed to the prophets will be fulfilled.

The shared language connects Daniel’s question about the appointed end with Revelation’s announcement that God’s purpose is moving toward completion. John is then commissioned to prophesy concerning peoples, nations, languages and kings. What God made known through His prophets remains part of the larger testimony He brings to fulfillment.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 12:8-10
passages.section_title: What is Daniel told when he still does not understand?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 I heard, but I did not understand. So I asked, “My lord, what will be the outcome of these things?” 9 “Go on your way, Daniel,” he replied, “for the words are closed up and sealed until the time of the end. 10 Many will be purified, made spotless, and refined, but the wicked will continue to act wickedly. None of the wicked will understand, but the wise will understand.
paragraphs: 8 I heard, but I did not understand. So I asked, “My lord, what will be the outcome of these things?” 9 “Go on your way, Daniel,” he replied, “for the words are closed up and sealed until the time of the end. 10 Many will be purified, made spotless, and refined, but the wicked will continue to act wickedly. None of the wicked will understand, but the wise will understand.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Daniel hears the answer but does not understand it. He asks what the outcome will be and is told to go on his way: the words remain closed and sealed until the time of the end.

The reply does describe the different responses of people living through the testing. Many will be purified and refined, while the wicked continue in wickedness. The wise will understand.

The passage distinguishes receiving a true message from having immediate understanding of every part. Daniel is called to trust what has been given. The wisdom in view is tied to faithfulness through testing, rather than simply possessing more information than others.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley emphasizes that the events will bring clearer understanding. Cambridge connects the wise with the faithful teachers already described in chapter 11, whose insight shows in the course they choose under pressure. Both connect understanding with a faithful response to God.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Daniel 12:11-13
passages.section_title: What final promise does Daniel receive?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 And from the time the daily sacrifice is abolished and the abomination of desolation set up, there will be 1,290 days. 12 Blessed is he who waits and reaches the end of the 1,335 days. 13 But as for you, go on your way until the end. You will rest, and then you will arise to your inheritance at the end of the days.”
paragraphs: 11 And from the time the daily sacrifice is abolished and the abomination of desolation set up, there will be 1,290 days. 12 Blessed is he who waits and reaches the end of the 1,335 days.
13 But as for you, go on your way until the end. You will rest, and then you will arise to your inheritance at the end of the days.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The closing words give further periods of days: 1,290 from the removal of the daily sacrifice and establishment of the abomination of desolation, followed by a blessing on the one who waits and reaches 1,335 days.

The text does not explain each event within those periods. It ends by addressing Daniel personally: he is to go on his way, rest, and then arise to his inheritance at the end of the days.

This final promise brings the long revelation back to the man who has received it. He will not personally control the history he has been shown, but his own future is held within God’s purpose. The book closes with the assurance of rest and a place in the promised inheritance.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Gaebelein reads the numbers as literal days, including a period beyond the final tribulation before full kingdom blessing. The USCCB notes interpret them as successive calculations of the expected end during the persecution. Cambridge acknowledges uncertainty about the added days.

Wesley reads Daniel’s personal promise as rest in death followed by resurrection and his appointed portion. The assurance given to Daniel is clearer than the disputed details of the calendar.
passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 11:13–16 and 39–40 describes faithful people who died while still looking toward what God had promised. They sought a better country, and God prepared a city for them. His purpose brings them and later believers toward a shared completion.

This is the larger theme of inheritance beyond a faithful person’s lifetime. Daniel can finish his service without seeing everything fulfilled because God’s promise includes his future. Christian hope rests in the God who brings His people into what He has prepared, even when their present part is to wait.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Jonah 1:1-3
passages.section_title: Why does Jonah go the other way when God sends him to Nineveh?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now the word of the LORD came to Jonah son of Amittai, saying, 2 “Get up! Go to the great city of Nineveh and preach against it, because its wickedness has come up before Me.” 3 Jonah, however, got up to flee to Tarshish, away from the presence of the LORD. He went down to Joppa and found a ship bound for Tarshish. So he paid the fare and went aboard to sail for Tarshish, away from the presence of the LORD.
paragraphs: 1 Now the word of the LORD came to Jonah son of Amittai, saying, 2 “Get up! Go to the great city of Nineveh and preach against it, because its wickedness has come up before Me.” 3 Jonah, however, got up to flee to Tarshish, away from the presence of the LORD. He went down to Joppa and found a ship bound for Tarshish. So he paid the fare and went aboard to sail for Tarshish, away from the presence of the LORD.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
God tells Jonah son of Amittai to go to Nineveh and preach against its wickedness. Jonah gets up, but travels to Joppa and boards a ship for Tarshish, fleeing from the Lord’s presence.

2 Kings 14:23–27 also identifies Jonah son of Amittai as a prophet from Gath-hepher during Jeroboam’s reign. Nineveh was an Assyrian city; its remains lie across the Tigris from Mosul’s Old City, as described in Iraq’s heritage submission to UNESCO.

The opening places God’s command beside Jonah’s refusal. Chapter 4 will explain his reason: he knew God was compassionate and feared that Nineveh would receive mercy. For now, the prophet is attempting to leave the work to which God has called him.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry and Wesley read the account as the experience of a prophet who disobeys God. The USCCB introduction discusses the book’s teaching through story, including proposed genres such as parable and satire. These readings differ over the story’s form while recognizing its challenge to narrow views of God’s mercy.
passages.god_plan_html:
Matthew 28:18–20 gives the risen Jesus’ command to make disciples of all nations. His authority and continuing presence support the mission.

Jonah’s commission and the church’s commission belong to different moments, but both confront a reluctance to take God’s word beyond familiar boundaries. God’s saving purpose reaches people His servants might hesitate to approach. In the gospel, that worldwide mission centers on the risen Christ.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Jonah 1:4-6
passages.section_title: Why is the prophet sleeping while the sailors pray?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 4 Then the LORD hurled a great wind upon the sea, and such a violent storm arose that the ship was in danger of breaking apart. 5 The sailors were afraid, and each cried out to his own god. And they threw the ship’s cargo into the sea to lighten the load. But Jonah had gone down to the lowest part of the vessel, where he lay down and fell into a deep sleep. 6 The captain approached him and said, “How can you sleep? Get up and call upon your God. Perhaps this God will consider us, so that we may not perish.”
paragraphs: 4 Then the LORD hurled a great wind upon the sea, and such a violent storm arose that the ship was in danger of breaking apart. 5 The sailors were afraid, and each cried out to his own god. And they threw the ship’s cargo into the sea to lighten the load. But Jonah had gone down to the lowest part of the vessel, where he lay down and fell into a deep sleep. 6 The captain approached him and said, “How can you sleep? Get up and call upon your God. Perhaps this God will consider us, so that we may not perish.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord sends a violent wind, and the ship is in danger of breaking apart. The sailors cry to their own gods and throw cargo overboard to lighten the ship.

Jonah has gone below and fallen into a deep sleep. The captain wakes him and tells him to call on his God, hoping they may be spared.

The contrast is striking. The men who do not yet know Jonah’s God are urgently seeking help, while His prophet is absent from their efforts. The captain’s command to get up recalls the command Jonah received at the beginning, but now it comes from someone caught in the consequences of his flight.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry sees the storm as God pursuing Jonah and his sleep as a picture of spiritual insensitivity. Wesley emphasizes the captain’s hope that Jonah’s God might look on them with pity. Both attend to the contrast between the sailors’ urgency and Jonah’s inactivity.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Jonah 1:7-10
passages.section_title: What does Jonah confess about the God he is fleeing?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 “Come!” said the sailors to one another. “Let us cast lots to find out who is responsible for this calamity that is upon us.” So they cast lots, and the lot fell on Jonah. 8 “Tell us now,” they demanded, “who is to blame for this calamity that is upon us? What is your occupation, and where have you come from? What is your country, and who are your people?” 9 “I am a Hebrew,” replied Jonah. “I worship the LORD, the God of the heavens, who made the sea and the dry land.” 10 Then the men were even more afraid and said to him, “What have you done?” The men knew that he was fleeing from the presence of the LORD, because he had told them.
paragraphs: 7 “Come!” said the sailors to one another. “Let us cast lots to find out who is responsible for this calamity that is upon us.” So they cast lots, and the lot fell on Jonah. 8 “Tell us now,” they demanded, “who is to blame for this calamity that is upon us? What is your occupation, and where have you come from? What is your country, and who are your people?” 9 “I am a Hebrew,” replied Jonah. “I worship the LORD, the God of the heavens, who made the sea and the dry land.” 10 Then the men were even more afraid and said to him, “What have you done?” The men knew that he was fleeing from the presence of the LORD, because he had told them.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The sailors cast lots to find who is responsible for the calamity, and the lot falls on Jonah. They question him about his work, origin and people.

He identifies himself as a Hebrew who worships the Lord, the maker of heaven, sea and dry land. The Hebrew יָרֵא, yare (yah-RAY), can express fear or reverence; Brown–Driver–Briggs includes Jonah 1:9 under reverence for God. The BSB conveys that sense with worship.

The sailors become more afraid when they learn whom he serves and that he is fleeing from His presence. His confession makes the contradiction in his conduct plain: he is trying to escape the maker of the very sea on which he travels.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry and Cambridge emphasize the force of Jonah’s confession before the frightened sailors. Knowing that the Lord made the sea makes his attempt to flee all the more startling.

passages.section_title: How do the sailors respond when Jonah tells them to throw him overboard?

versions.text: 11 Now the sea was growing worse and worse, so they said to Jonah, “What must we do to you to calm this sea for us?” 12 “Pick me up,” he answered, “and cast me into the sea, so it may quiet down for you. Do not charge us with innocent blood! For You, O LORD, have done as You pleased.” 15 Then they picked up Jonah and cast him into the sea, and the raging sea grew calm. 16 Then the men feared the LORD greatly, and they offered a sacrifice to the LORD and made vows to Him.

For You, O LORD, have done as You pleased.” 15 Then they picked up Jonah and cast him into the sea, and the raging sea grew calm. 16 Then the men feared the LORD greatly, and they offered a sacrifice to the LORD and made vows to Him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
As the storm worsens, Jonah tells the sailors to throw him into the sea, acknowledging that it has come because of him.

They first try to row back to dry land. When that fails, they call on the Lord, asking not to be charged with innocent blood. Only then do they throw Jonah overboard, and the sea becomes calm.

The sailors respond with great fear of the Lord, sacrifice and vows. Their concern to spare Jonah’s life stands beside his earlier unwillingness to carry God’s warning to Nineveh. People initially praying to different gods are now calling on the Lord and honoring Him.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry understands Jonah’s admission as accepting responsibility and punishment. Wesley emphasizes the sailors’ efforts to save him and their later acknowledgment of the Lord. The text gives Jonah’s words, without explaining everything he hoped would happen to himself.
passages.god_plan_html:
A strong parallel appears in Mark 4:35–41: a storm, a sleeping figure, terrified companions and sudden calm, followed by deep fear at the power revealed.

The difference brings Jesus into focus. Jonah’s disobedience has endangered the ship; Jesus commands the wind and sea Himself. The disciples are left asking who He is, that creation obeys Him. Read together, the accounts direct attention to God’s rule over the sea and the authority revealed in His Son.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Jonah 1:17
passages.section_title: Why does God appoint a great fish for Jonah?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 Now the LORD had appointed a great fish to swallow Jonah, and Jonah spent three days and three nights in the belly of the fish.
paragraphs: 17 Now the LORD had appointed a great fish to swallow Jonah, and Jonah spent three days and three nights in the belly of the fish.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord appoints a great fish to swallow Jonah, and he remains in its belly for three days and three nights. Being thrown into the sea is not the end of his story.

The fish places him beyond any means of rescuing himself, while becoming the means through which his life is preserved. The next chapter records his prayer from inside it.

The account identifies the creature by its role and size, without naming a species. Its central point is God’s action toward the fleeing prophet: the One who sent the storm also provides what Jonah needs to survive it.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry and Cambridge understand Jonah’s preservation as miraculous and connect it with Jesus’ own use of the sign of Jonah. The emphasis is God’s power and mercy toward His disobedient servant.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus explicitly connects this passage with Himself in Matthew 12:38–41. As Jonah was in the fish for three days and nights, the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth.

The connection is given by Jesus, not supplied merely by a reader noticing a resemblance. Jonah’s descent and return become a sign pointing toward Christ’s death and resurrection. Jesus also identifies Himself as greater than Jonah, calling His hearers to recognize the significance of the One before them.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Jonah 2:1-7
passages.section_title: Can Jonah still call on God from the depths?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 From inside the fish, Jonah prayed to the LORD his God, 2 saying: “In my distress I called to the LORD, and He answered me. From the belly of Sheol I called for help, and You heard my voice. 3 For You cast me into the deep, into the heart of the seas, and the current swirled about me; all Your breakers and waves swept over me. 4 At this, I said, ‘I have been banished from Your sight; yet I will look once more toward Your holy temple.’ 5 The waters engulfed me to take my life; the watery depths closed around me; the seaweed wrapped around my head. 6 To the roots of the mountains I descended; the earth beneath me barred me in forever! But You raised my life from the pit, O LORD my God! 7 As my life was fading away, I remembered the LORD. My prayer went up to You, to Your holy temple.
paragraphs: 1 From inside the fish, Jonah prayed to the LORD his God, 2 saying: “In my distress I called to the LORD, and He answered me. From the belly of Sheol I called for help, and You heard my voice. 3 For You cast me into the deep, into the heart of the seas, and the current swirled about me; all Your breakers and waves swept over me. 4 At this, I said, ‘I have been banished from Your sight; yet I will look once more toward Your holy temple.’

5 The waters engulfed me to take my life; the watery depths closed around me; the seaweed wrapped around my head. 6 To the roots of the mountains I descended; the earth beneath me barred me in forever! But You raised my life from the pit, O LORD my God! 7 As my life was fading away, I remembered the LORD. My prayer went up to You, to Your holy temple.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
From inside the fish, Jonah prays to the Lord his God. He recalls being engulfed by the sea, with weeds around his head and the earth seeming to close him in.

His description uses the language of death and the grave: the belly of Sheol, the roots of the mountains and life brought up from the pit. The prayer conveys how completely he had been beyond his own power to escape.

Yet its refrain is that God heard him. As his life faded, he remembered the Lord, and his prayer reached God’s holy temple. The prophet who fled from God’s presence now turns toward Him and gives thanks for rescue.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry emphasizes that Jonah can pray even from inside the fish. Cambridge relates the death imagery to his peril in the sea and notes the prayer’s resemblance to the Psalms. Wesley reads the language as the experience of someone who seemed shut into the grave yet trusted God for deliverance.
passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 4:14–16 directs people in weakness toward God’s throne of grace, where mercy and help are found through Jesus, the great High Priest.

The wider theme is access to God in need. Jonah’s distance and distress do not prevent God from hearing him; the New Testament gives believers confidence to draw near through the Son who understands their weakness. The reason for hope rests in God’s mercy and Christ’s priestly care.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Jonah 2:8-10
passages.section_title: What does Jonah acknowledge about salvation?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 Those who cling to worthless idols forsake His loving devotion. 9 But I, with the voice of thanksgiving, will sacrifice to You. I will fulfill what I have vowed. Salvation is from the LORD!” 10 And the LORD commanded the fish, and it vomited Jonah onto dry land.
paragraphs: 8 Those who cling to worthless idols forsake His loving devotion. 9 But I, with the voice of thanksgiving, will sacrifice to You. I will fulfill what I have vowed. Salvation is from the LORD!” 10 And the LORD commanded the fish, and it vomited Jonah onto dry land.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jonah contrasts clinging to worthless idols with receiving the Lord’s loving devotion. He promises thanksgiving, sacrifice and fulfillment of his vows, ending with the acknowledgment that salvation comes from the Lord.

The language recalls the sailors, who also turned to the Lord, offered sacrifice and made vows after being rescued. The prophet and the sailors alike depend on mercy they cannot produce for themselves.

God then commands the fish, and it releases Jonah onto dry land. His confession of who saves is followed by the deliverance that makes a renewed response to God possible.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley and Cambridge understand the Lord as the source of the mercy that idols cannot provide. Henry sees the release as a demonstration of God’s command over His creatures and His mercy toward the praying prophet.
passages.god_plan_html:
A parallel in praise appears in Revelation 7:9–12. A multitude from every nation, tribe, people and language gives the credit for salvation to God and the Lamb.

Jonah’s thanksgiving concerns his own rescue. Revelation opens the view to a people gathered from across the world through the Lamb. The shared confession gives salvation’s Author the glory, while the wider scene brings into view the mercy for many peoples that Jonah himself struggles to welcome.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Jonah 3:1-4
passages.section_title: What does Jonah do when God sends him a second time?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then the word of the LORD came to Jonah a second time: 2 “Get up! Go to the great city of Nineveh and proclaim to it the message that I give you.” 3 This time Jonah got up and went to Nineveh, in accordance with the word of the LORD. Now Nineveh was an exceedingly great city, requiring a three-day journey. 4 On the first day of his journey, Jonah set out into the city and proclaimed, “Forty more days and Nineveh will be overturned!”
paragraphs: 1 Then the word of the LORD came to Jonah a second time: 2 “Get up! Go to the great city of Nineveh and proclaim to it the message that I give you.” 3 This time Jonah got up and went to Nineveh, in accordance with the word of the LORD. Now Nineveh was an exceedingly great city, requiring a three-day journey. 4 On the first day of his journey, Jonah set out into the city and proclaimed, “Forty more days and Nineveh will be overturned!”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord’s word comes to Jonah a second time. The command is still to go to Nineveh and proclaim the message God gives him. This time, Jonah goes.

The city is described as exceedingly great, requiring a three-day journey. On his first day there, Jonah announces that Nineveh will be overturned in forty days.

The Hebrew verb הָפַךְ, haphak (hah-FAHK), can mean turn or overturn; Brown–Driver–Briggs identifies its use here as the overthrow of a city. The warning is serious, and the forty days place the hearers under an urgent call to respond. Jonah’s rescue has returned him to the commission he previously refused.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry emphasizes Jonah’s renewed obedience. Wesley and Cambridge understand the threatened destruction in light of the opportunity to repent, which the rest of the chapter brings into view.
passages.god_plan_html:
A parallel of renewed service appears in John 21:15–19. Peter, who had denied Jesus, is addressed by the risen Lord, entrusted with care for His sheep and called again to follow Him.

The failures and commissions differ, but the connection is mercy that leads to renewed obedience and service. God’s purpose includes work done through servants who have themselves needed restoration. In Peter’s case, that renewed service is entrusted directly by the risen Christ.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Jonah 3:5-10
passages.section_title: How do the Ninevites respond to the warning?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 And the Ninevites believed God. They proclaimed a fast and dressed in sackcloth, from the greatest of them to the least. 6 When word reached the king of Nineveh, he got up from his throne, took off his royal robe, covered himself with sackcloth, and sat in ashes. 7 Then he issued a proclamation in Nineveh: “By the decree of the king and his nobles: Let no man or beast, herd or flock, taste anything at all. They must not eat or drink. 8 Furthermore, let both man and beast be covered with sackcloth, and have everyone call out earnestly to God. Let each one turn from his evil ways and from the violence in his hands. 9 Who knows? God may turn and relent; He may turn from His fierce anger, so that we will not perish.” 10 When God saw their actions—that they had turned from their evil ways—He relented from the disaster He had threatened to bring upon them.
paragraphs: 5 And the Ninevites believed God. They proclaimed a fast and dressed in sackcloth, from the greatest of them to the least. 6 When word reached the king of Nineveh, he got up from his throne, took off his royal robe, covered himself with sackcloth, and sat in ashes.

7 Then he issued a proclamation in Nineveh: “By the decree of the king and his nobles: Let no man or beast, herd or flock, taste anything at all. They must not eat or drink. 8 Furthermore, let both man and beast be covered with sackcloth, and have everyone call out earnestly to God. Let each one turn from his evil ways and from the violence in his hands. 9 Who knows? God may turn and relent; He may turn from His fierce anger, so that we will not perish.” 10 When God saw their actions—that they had turned from their evil ways—He relented from the disaster He had threatened to bring upon them.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Ninevites believe God, proclaim a fast and put on sackcloth. The response reaches the king, who leaves his throne, removes his robe and sits in ashes.

His decree includes fasting and sackcloth for people and animals, earnest prayer, and turning from evil and violence. The visible signs of mourning accompany a demand for changed conduct. He hopes God may relent so that they do not perish.

God sees that they have turned from their evil ways and does not bring the threatened disaster. This accords with the principle stated in Jeremiah 18:7–10: when a nation turns from the evil for which it was warned, God may relent from the announced judgment.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry and Cambridge emphasize the change of life, especially the turning from evil. Fasting and sackcloth express repentance, but the account specifically identifies their changed conduct when describing God’s response.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus explicitly returns to this event in Matthew 12:38–42. He says the people of Nineveh will condemn His generation at the judgment because they repented at Jonah’s preaching, while One greater than Jonah stands before His hearers.

The Ninevites’ response becomes a challenge to people receiving a greater revelation through Jesus. God’s warning calls for a real response, and the mercy shown to this foreign city makes continued refusal to listen all the more serious. The connection leads beyond admiration for Nineveh’s repentance to hearing the Son Himself.

passages.title: Jonah 4:1-4
passages.section_title: Why is Jonah angry when God shows mercy?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Jonah, however, was greatly displeased, and he became angry. 2 So he prayed to the LORD, saying, “O LORD, is this not what I said while I was still in my own country? This is why I was so quick to flee toward Tarshish. I knew that You are a gracious and compassionate God, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion—One who relents from sending disaster. 3 And now, O LORD, please take my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live.” 4 But the LORD replied, “Have you any right to be angry?”
paragraphs: 1 Jonah, however, was greatly displeased, and he became angry. 2 So he prayed to the LORD, saying, “O LORD, is this not what I said while I was still in my own country? This is why I was so quick to flee toward Tarshish. I knew that You are a gracious and compassionate God, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion—One who relents from sending disaster. 3 And now, O LORD, please take my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live.” 4 But the LORD replied, “Have you any right to be angry?”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Nineveh has been spared, but Jonah is angry. He now explains why he fled: he knew that God was gracious and compassionate, slow to anger, rich in loving devotion and willing to relent from disaster.

These qualities echo God’s revelation to Moses in Exodus 34:6–7. What gives God’s people reason for hope is the very character Jonah resents when mercy reaches Nineveh.

Jonah asks God to take his life. God responds with a question about whether he has any right to be angry. The prophet has carried out the outward mission, but he is still being challenged to share God’s concern for its recipients.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry emphasizes the contradiction of receiving mercy while resenting it for others. Wesley also sees Jonah’s concern for his reputation when the announced destruction does not occur. The account’s explicit explanation is Jonah’s objection to the mercy he knew God might show.
passages.god_plan_html:
A parallel appears in Luke 15:25–32. The older son is angry when his father celebrates the return of his lost brother. The father comes out to appeal to him and explain why rejoicing is fitting.

Both accounts end with an appeal to someone who resents mercy given to another. Jesus’ parable makes the Father’s joy over the lost being found central to the lesson. Receiving His kindness calls His people to welcome the restoration of others, rather than treating their return as a loss to themselves.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Jonah 4:5-9
passages.section_title: What does God teach Jonah through the shade he gains and loses?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 Then Jonah left the city and sat down east of it, where he made himself a shelter and sat in its shade to see what would happen to the city. 6 So the LORD God appointed a vine, and it grew up to provide shade over Jonah’s head to ease his discomfort, and Jonah was greatly pleased with the plant. 7 When dawn came the next day, God appointed a worm that attacked the plant so that it withered. 8 As the sun was rising, God appointed a scorching east wind, and the sun beat down on Jonah’s head so that he grew faint and wished to die, saying, “It is better for me to die than to live.” 9 Then God asked Jonah, “Have you any right to be angry about the plant?” “I do,” he replied. “I am angry enough to die!”
paragraphs: 5 Then Jonah left the city and sat down east of it, where he made himself a shelter and sat in its shade to see what would happen to the city. 6 So the LORD God appointed a vine, and it grew up to provide shade over Jonah’s head to ease his discomfort, and Jonah was greatly pleased with the plant.

7 When dawn came the next day, God appointed a worm that attacked the plant so that it withered. 8 As the sun was rising, God appointed a scorching east wind, and the sun beat down on Jonah’s head so that he grew faint and wished to die, saying, “It is better for me to die than to live.” 9 Then God asked Jonah, “Have you any right to be angry about the plant?” “I do,” he replied. “I am angry enough to die!”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jonah leaves the city, makes a shelter east of it and waits to see what will happen. God appoints a vine to give him shade, and he is greatly pleased.

The next morning God appoints a worm that attacks the plant, then a scorching east wind. Without the shade, Jonah grows faint and again says he would rather die.

The repeated word appointed belongs to מָנָה, manah (mah-NAH), which in these passages means appoint or assign; see Brown–Driver–Briggs. The fish, plant, worm and wind serve God’s purpose in the story. Through the comfort Jonah welcomes and the loss he resents, God brings his misplaced concern into the open.

Asked whether he has a right to be angry about the plant, Jonah insists that he does. His response prepares the comparison with Nineveh in God’s closing words.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Henry and Wesley understand the plant and its loss as a lesson in the fragility of personal comforts and Jonah’s need for greater mercy. The question about his anger exposes how deeply his own discomfort affects him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Jonah 4:10-11
passages.section_title: Should God not care about the people and animals of Nineveh?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 But the LORD said, “You cared about the plant, which you neither tended nor made grow. It sprang up in a night and perished in a night. 11 So should I not care about the great city of Nineveh, which has more than 120,000 people who cannot tell their right hand from their left, and many cattle as well?”
paragraphs: 10 But the LORD said, “You cared about the plant, which you neither tended nor made grow. It sprang up in a night and perished in a night. 11 So should I not care about the great city of Nineveh, which has more than 120,000 people who cannot tell their right hand from their left, and many cattle as well?”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
God contrasts Jonah’s concern for the short-lived plant with His concern for a great city. Jonah neither tended the plant nor made it grow, yet he grieves its loss.

Nineveh contains more than 120,000 people who cannot tell their right hand from their left, as well as many cattle. God’s closing question asks whether He should not care about them.

The book ends without recording Jonah’s answer. Its question reaches the reader: can someone who has received God’s care begrudge His compassion toward others? The final word belongs to the Lord who sent the warning, heard the city’s response and continued patiently teaching His prophet.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Cambridge understand those unable to distinguish right and left as young children. Both emphasize the force of God’s concern for the city’s vulnerable inhabitants and animals, compared with Jonah’s attachment to the plant.

Henry draws attention to God’s patient mercy toward Jonah himself as part of the same lesson.
passages.god_plan_html:
Matthew 5:43–48 brings this concern into Jesus’ teaching. He calls His followers to love enemies and pray for persecutors, pointing to the Father who gives sunshine and rain to the righteous and unrighteous.

The connection is learning to reflect the Father’s generosity beyond those who already love us. Jonah’s final question challenges a narrow concern for personal comfort; Jesus gives His disciples a positive direction for life within God’s purpose. His people are called to extend love across the boundaries they might otherwise protect.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Malachi 1:1-5
passages.section_title: The LORD’s Love for Israel

Where interpreters differ on details, the immediate setting in Malachi 1 remains the first control on meaning.
passages.current_position_html: No defined position is stated here yet beyond the common interpretations above. As related study develops, this section will be updated where the text warrants a clearer conclusion.

passages.section_title: The Polluted Offerings

passages.context_html: In Malachi 1, this section should be read within the flow of the chapter and the larger movement of Malachi.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Malachi 1:11 became a major proof text in later sacrificial readings of the Lord's Supper, especially once Eucharistic theology was recast in altar-priest-sacrifice terms. That later application carries serious consequences because it shifts the direction of atonement from God's once-for-all provision in Christ toward an ongoing offering made by man back to God.
passages.current_position_html: This site's current position is that Malachi 1 is a condemnation of corrupted priestly worship, not a foundation for reintroducing sacrificial categories into the new-covenant gathering. The chapter exposes contempt for God's name through defiled offerings. For that reason, using Malachi 1:11 to support an ongoing sacrificial offering in Christian worship presses the text in the wrong direction. The once-for-all sufficiency of Christ governs the church's worship, not a revived altar system.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

passages.title: Malachi 2:1-9
passages.section_title: A Warning to the Priests

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Matthew opens by identifying Jesus through two great names in Israel's history: David and Abraham. Before describing the birth, he places Jesus within the family story of promise, kingship, exile, and continuing hope. The genealogy answers a question about who Jesus is, not simply who His ancestors were.

Christ is a title, not a family surname. The Greek word is Χριστός, Christos (khris-TOSS), the anointed one. Thayer's Greek Lexicon explains its use for the expected Messiah. Calling Jesus Christ presents Him as the promised One whose place in the story the following names will show.

The list moves from Abraham to David, from David to the Babylonian exile, and from the exile to Jesus. Matthew deliberately presents three groups of fourteen generations. It is a selected genealogy: comparison with 1 Chronicles 3:10–12 shows kings between Joram and Uzziah who are not individually named here. The arrangement gives the history a clear shape rather than attempting to name every generation.

Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and Uriah's wife also appear in the family record. Their stories bring remembered hardship, unexpected relationships, and people from outside Israel into the line leading to Jesus. The genealogy does not offer a family history free from wrongdoing or painful circumstances.

At the end, the wording changes. Joseph is identified as Mary's husband, and Jesus is born of her. Matthew does not simply repeat the pattern by saying Joseph fathered Jesus. That distinction prepares the next passage's explanation of conception through the Holy Spirit.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read the genealogy as showing Jesus' place in the promises to David and Abraham. Wesley's notes on Matthew 1:1, 6, 16 emphasize both connections. The history reaches through kings and exile to the Messiah rather than ending with the loss of the kingdom.

Christians have offered different explanations when comparing this list with Luke 3:23–38. Wesley's note on Luke 3:23 understands Matthew to trace Joseph's line and Luke to trace Mary's, with Joseph related to Heli as a son-in-law.

An earlier explanation, preserved from Julius Africanus in Eusebius, Church History 1.7.2–10, understands both lists through Joseph: one gives natural descent and the other a legal family line connected with a child raised for a deceased relative. These are attempts to explain the relationship between the accounts. Neither Gospel explicitly supplies all the family details needed to confirm one complete reconstruction.
passages.god_plan_html:
The two opening names point to promises God has been carrying forward. 2 Samuel 7:12–16 speaks of David's enduring house and kingdom, and 2 Timothy 2:8 identifies the risen Jesus as descended from David. The royal family story reaches beyond the exile to the One Matthew calls Christ.

The Abraham connection reaches outward as well. Galatians 3:8, 16 connects the blessing promised to the nations with Christ. Matthew will end with Jesus commissioning disciples among all nations in Matthew 28:18–20. The opening genealogy belongs to that larger movement: God's faithfulness within Israel's history brings a Savior whose blessing reaches beyond one people.

passages.title: Matthew 1:18-25
passages.section_title: The Birth of Jesus Christ

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 This is how the birth of Jesus Christ came about: His mother Mary was pledged in marriage to Joseph, but before they came together, she was found to be with child through the Holy Spirit. 19 Because Joseph her husband was a righteous man and was unwilling to disgrace her publicly, he resolved to divorce her quietly. 20 But after he had pondered these things, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream and said, “Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to embrace Mary as your wife, for the One conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit. 21 She will give birth to a Son, and you are to give Him the name Jesus, because He will save His people from their sins.” 22 All this took place to fulfill what the Lord had said through the prophet: 23 “Behold, the virgin will be with child and will give birth to a son, and they will call Him Immanuel” (which means, “God with us”). 24 When Joseph woke up, he did as the angel of the Lord had commanded him and embraced Mary as his wife. 25 But he had no union with her until she gave birth to a Son. And he gave Him the name Jesus.
paragraphs: 18 This is how the birth of Jesus Christ came about: His mother Mary was pledged in marriage to Joseph, but before they came together, she was found to be with child through the Holy Spirit. 19 Because Joseph her husband was a righteous man and was unwilling to disgrace her publicly, he resolved to divorce her quietly.

20 But after he had pondered these things, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream and said, “Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to embrace Mary as your wife, for the One conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit. 21 She will give birth to a Son, and you are to give Him the name Jesus, because He will save His people from their sins.”

22 All this took place to fulfill what the Lord had said through the prophet: 23 “Behold, the virgin will be with child and will give birth to a son, and they will call Him Immanuel” (which means, “God with us”).
24 When Joseph woke up, he did as the angel of the Lord had commanded him and embraced Mary as his wife. 25 But he had no union with her until she gave birth to a Son. And he gave Him the name Jesus.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Matthew now explains the unusual ending of the genealogy. Mary is pledged to Joseph, but before they come together she is found to be pregnant through the Holy Spirit. The reader is told the child's origin before Joseph receives the explanation.

Their pledge is more binding than a modern engagement. Matthew calls Joseph her husband and describes his proposed action as divorce. The US Catholic bishops' note on Matthew 1:18 explains betrothal as the first part of marriage, before the couple began normal life together. Joseph is described as righteous and unwilling to expose Mary to public disgrace, so he plans to end the bond quietly.

While he considers this, an angel addresses him in a dream as a son of David and tells him not to fear taking Mary as his wife. The child is conceived through the Holy Spirit. Joseph is to name Him Jesus because He will save His people from their sins. The explanation redirects his decision, and his response is to do what he has been told.

The Greek name is Ἰησοῦς, Iēsous (ee-ay-SOOS), the form also used for Joshua. Thayer's Greek Lexicon connects the name with the LORD's saving help and specifically discusses Matthew 1:21. The angel's explanation gives the name its purpose within this account: this child will bring rescue from sin.

Matthew identifies the event as fulfillment of Isaiah's Immanuel promise, explaining Immanuel as God with us. In Isaiah 7:10–17, the sign addresses Ahaz and the house of David amid national danger. Matthew sees the promise fulfilled in this child's birth. Joseph takes Mary as his wife, has no sexual union with her before the birth, and gives the child the commanded name. His obedience joins the child to the Davidic household introduced in the genealogy.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Historic Christian traditions agree that Jesus was conceived through the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary. The Westminster Confession 8.2 describes Him as truly God and truly human, taking His humanity from Mary without sin. The Catholic Catechism, paragraphs 484–486, likewise describes the Son becoming human through the Spirit's work in Mary.

The Catholic Church also teaches that Mary remained a virgin throughout her life, as stated in Catechism paragraphs 499–500. The Orthodox Church in America affirms that same lifelong virginity. This goes beyond the shared affirmation that Jesus was conceived without a human father.

The word until in verse 25 is sometimes treated as deciding what happened after the birth. Wesley's note on Matthew 1:25 cautions that the wording alone does not establish later sexual relations. Baptist commentator John Gill similarly distinguishes what is certain before the birth from what the verse leaves unstated afterward. These comments help keep the verse's clear emphasis on Jesus' conception separate from further conclusions about Mary's later life.
passages.god_plan_html:
Matthew presents more than an unexpected birth. The child will save His people from their sins, and Matthew 26:27–28 later connects Jesus' poured-out blood with forgiveness. The announced rescue at the beginning points toward His self-giving at the end.

The New Testament also connects God's Son entering human life with a new future for His people. Galatians 4:4–7 describes the Son born of a woman to redeem and bring adoption. Romans 5:15–19 contrasts the ruin associated with Adam's disobedience with the life brought through Christ's obedience. Together, these passages present the Son's coming and obedient life as God's answer to sin and death.

Immanuel also introduces a promise of presence that runs through this Gospel. At its close, Matthew 28:18–20 joins the mission to all nations with Jesus' assurance that He is with His disciples. God with us reaches from the birth announcement to the life and mission of the people Jesus sends.

passages.title: Matthew 2:1-12
passages.section_title: The Magi Seek the King

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 After Jesus was born in Bethlehem in Judea, during the time of King Herod, Magi from the east arrived in Jerusalem, 2 asking, “Where is the One who has been born King of the Jews? We saw His star in the east and have come to worship Him.” 3 When King Herod heard this, he was disturbed, and all Jerusalem with him. 4 And when he had assembled all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he asked them where the Christ was to be born. 5 “In Bethlehem in Judea,” they replied, “for this is what the prophet has written: 6 ‘But you, Bethlehem, in the land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah, for out of you will come a ruler who will be the shepherd of My people Israel.’” 7 Then Herod called the Magi secretly and learned from them the exact time the star had appeared. 8 And sending them to Bethlehem, he said: “Go and search carefully for the Child, and when you find Him, report to me, so that I too may go and worship Him.” 9 After they had heard the king, they went on their way, and the star they had seen in the east went ahead of them until it stood over the place where the Child was. 10 When they saw the star, they rejoiced with great delight. 11 On coming to the house, they saw the Child with His mother Mary, and they fell down and worshiped Him. Then they opened their treasures and presented Him with gifts of gold and frankincense and myrrh. 12 And having been warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they withdrew to their country by another route.
paragraphs: 1 After Jesus was born in Bethlehem in Judea, during the time of King Herod, Magi from the east arrived in Jerusalem, 2 asking, “Where is the One who has been born King of the Jews? We saw His star in the east and have come to worship Him.”

3 When King Herod heard this, he was disturbed, and all Jerusalem with him. 4 And when he had assembled all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he asked them where the Christ was to be born. 5 “In Bethlehem in Judea,” they replied, “for this is what the prophet has written: 6 ‘But you, Bethlehem, in the land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah, for out of you will come a ruler who will be the shepherd of My people Israel.’”

7 Then Herod called the Magi secretly and learned from them the exact time the star had appeared. 8 And sending them to Bethlehem, he said: “Go and search carefully for the Child, and when you find Him, report to me, so that I too may go and worship Him.”

9 After they had heard the king, they went on their way, and the star they had seen in the east went ahead of them until it stood over the place where the Child was. 10 When they saw the star, they rejoiced with great delight. 11 On coming to the house, they saw the Child with His mother Mary, and they fell down and worshiped Him. Then they opened their treasures and presented Him with gifts of gold and frankincense and myrrh. 12 And having been warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they withdrew to their country by another route.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the birth account, Matthew introduces visitors from the east looking for the newborn King of the Jews. Their question unsettles Herod and Jerusalem. Herod consults the chief priests and scribes, who identify Bethlehem from the prophetic Scriptures. The king who already holds power and the visitors seeking the child respond very differently to the news.

Magi is the plural of μάγος, magos (MAH-goss). Thayer's Greek Lexicon explains the term's use for eastern wise men and astrologers. Matthew tells us their direction of origin, but gives neither their names nor their number. The three kinds of gifts do not establish that there were three men, and Matthew does not call them kings.

The answer about Bethlehem draws on Micah 5:2–4, where a ruler will come from the small town and shepherd God's people. Matthew's wording also recalls the shepherding language addressed to David in 2 Samuel 5:2. The expected king belongs to the story of God's care for Israel.

Herod secretly asks when the star appeared and requests a report about the child's location, saying he too wants to worship. The following passage exposes his intention to kill Him. The visitors instead rejoice, enter the house, bow before Jesus, and give their treasures. Warned in a dream, they go home without returning to Herod.

The Greek verb translated worshiped is προσκυνέω, proskyneō (pros-koo-NEH-oh). It describes bowing or falling down in reverence. Thayer's Greek Lexicon includes both homage to someone of high rank and worship directed to God. The word's range makes the surrounding account important: these visitors have come seeking the King of the Jews.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly see the visitors as an early sign that Jesus' coming matters beyond Israel. The Catholic Catechism, paragraph 528, describes their adoration of Jesus and the welcome of the nations; Wesley's notes on Matthew 2:1–2 emphasize Gentile visitors paying homage to Israel's king. The Catholic teaching presents the visit within the revelation of Jesus as Son of God and Savior; Wesley's comment on the gesture stresses the honor shown to a monarch.

The gifts have also been read in more than one way. Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.9.2, connects gold with kingship, frankincense with His being God, and myrrh with Jesus' death and burial. Wesley's note on 2:11 instead emphasizes valuable gifts suitable for a person of importance and suggests they provided help for the journey to Egypt. These are interpretations of the gifts' significance; Matthew names the gifts without explaining the visitors' intended meaning.

Early Christian teachers also differed about the star. Chrysostom, Homily 6 on Matthew, section 3, understood it as an invisible power appearing as a star; Origen, Against Celsus 1.58–59, proposed a new heavenly object comparable to a comet. These are teachers' explanations, not a single church definition of the star's physical nature. Matthew focuses on its role in leading the visitors to the child.
passages.god_plan_html:
The visitors from outside Israel anticipate a wider welcome that becomes explicit later in the Gospel. In Matthew 8:10–11, Jesus praises a Gentile centurion's faith and speaks of people coming from east and west to share a banquet with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. At the end He sends His disciples to all nations in Matthew 28:18–20. The newborn Jewish king belongs to God's blessing reaching the nations; the story does not make one people's ancestry the measure of a faithful response.

The gifts also recall older pictures of nations honoring God's king. Psalm 72:10–17 describes distant rulers bringing tribute and nations receiving blessing. Isaiah 60:3–6 describes nations coming to the light and bringing gold and frankincense. These are Scripture-supported parallels to the visit, not proof that the magi themselves ruled kingdoms or understood every later part of Jesus' mission.

The traditional connection between myrrh and Jesus' death also has a later point of comparison: John 19:39–40 records myrrh among the spices used for His burial. Reading the two scenes together can draw our attention from the honored child to the crucified Savior. Matthew does not say that the visitors explained His future death when they gave their gifts.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Worship as the Early Church Knew It understands the magi's action as royal homage: they bow before the child they have come to honor as King of the Jews. It does not read this scene as a statement that they already recognized Him as Savior. The study emphasizes an act of personal submission before the king, rather than a description of a gathered church service.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

passages.title: Matthew 2:11
passages.section_title: The Magi Honor Jesus

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 On coming to the house, they saw the Child with His mother Mary, and they fell down and worshiped Him. Then they opened their treasures and presented Him with gifts of gold and frankincense and myrrh.
paragraphs: 11 On coming to the house, they saw the Child with His mother Mary, and they fell down and worshiped Him. Then they opened their treasures and presented Him with gifts of gold and frankincense and myrrh.

passages.context_html:
This verse is the meeting the magi have been seeking since they arrived in Jerusalem. Herod has asked them to report the child's location, while the star has led them to the house. They see Jesus with Mary, bow before Him, and present gold, frankincense, and myrrh. The next verse sends them home by another route after a warning in a dream.

The Greek verb translated worshiped is προσκυνέω, proskyneō (pros-koo-NEH-oh). It describes bowing or falling down in reverence. Thayer's Greek Lexicon includes both homage to someone of high rank and worship directed to God. The word's range makes the surrounding account important: these visitors have come seeking the King of the Jews.

Matthew describes a house and a child, without giving the child's precise age or the length of the family's stay in Bethlehem. The account names three gifts, not three visitors. Its immediate contrast is between the honor given here and Herod's murderous response in the following passage.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly see the visitors as an early sign that Jesus' coming matters beyond Israel. The Catholic Catechism, paragraph 528, describes their adoration of Jesus and the welcome of the nations; Wesley's notes on Matthew 2:1–2 emphasize Gentile visitors paying homage to Israel's king. The Catholic teaching presents the visit within the revelation of Jesus as Son of God and Savior; Wesley's comment on the gesture stresses the honor shown to a monarch.

The gifts have also been read in more than one way. Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.9.2, connects gold with kingship, frankincense with His being God, and myrrh with Jesus' death and burial. Wesley's note on 2:11 instead emphasizes valuable gifts suitable for a person of importance and suggests they provided help for the journey to Egypt. These are interpretations of the gifts' significance; Matthew names the gifts without explaining the visitors' intended meaning.
