It does not read this scene as a statement that they already recognized Him as Savior. The study emphasizes an act of personal submission before the king, rather than a description of a gathered church service.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The visitors' gifts and bowed posture recall Psalm 72:10–17, where distant rulers bring tribute and the nations receive blessing through the king. Isaiah 60:3–6 similarly pictures nations coming to the light with gold and frankincense. These are parallels that help explain the scene's place in the larger biblical story; they do not establish the visitors' titles or everything they personally understood.

Matthew's Gospel later makes the welcome of people from east and west explicit in Matthew 8:10–11, and ends with the mission to all nations in Matthew 28:18–20. This visit offers an early glimpse of honor coming to Israel's Messiah from beyond Israel.

passages.title: Matthew 2:13-18
passages.section_title: Escape to Egypt and Weeping in Bethlehem

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 When the Magi had gone, an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream. “Get up!” he said. “Take the Child and His mother and flee to Egypt. Stay there until I tell you, for Herod is going to search for the Child to kill Him.” 14 So he got up, took the Child and His mother by night, and withdrew to Egypt, 15 where he stayed until the death of Herod. This fulfilled what the Lord had spoken through the prophet: “Out of Egypt I called My Son.” 16 When Herod saw that he had been outwitted by the Magi, he was filled with rage. Sending orders, he put to death all the boys in Bethlehem and its vicinity who were two years old and under, according to the time he had learned from the Magi. 17 Then what was spoken through the prophet Jeremiah was fulfilled: 18 “A voice is heard in Ramah, weeping and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children and refusing to be comforted, because they are no more.”
paragraphs: 13 When the Magi had gone, an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream. “Get up!” he said. “Take the Child and His mother and flee to Egypt. Stay there until I tell you, for Herod is going to search for the Child to kill Him.” 14 So he got up, took the Child and His mother by night, and withdrew to Egypt, 15 where he stayed until the death of Herod. This fulfilled what the Lord had spoken through the prophet: “Out of Egypt I called My Son.”

16 When Herod saw that he had been outwitted by the Magi, he was filled with rage. Sending orders, he put to death all the boys in Bethlehem and its vicinity who were two years old and under, according to the time he had learned from the Magi. 17 Then what was spoken through the prophet Jeremiah was fulfilled: 18 “A voice is heard in Ramah, weeping and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children and refusing to be comforted, because they are no more.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the magi leave, an angel warns Joseph that Herod intends to kill the child. Joseph acts that night, taking Jesus and Mary to Egypt, where they remain until Herod dies. Matthew then turns from the family's escape to the children Herod has killed in Bethlehem and the surrounding area. The order targets boys two years old and younger, based on the timing Herod learned from the magi.

Matthew connects the escape with Hosea 11:1–4. Hosea is looking back on Israel's childhood as a people: God loved His son and brought him out of Egypt, yet Israel turned to idols. Matthew now applies the words about God's son to Jesus. Understanding Hosea's original reference helps us see the connection Matthew makes; the older passage was not originally a travel report about Joseph's family.

For Bethlehem's grief, Matthew turns to Jeremiah 31:15–17. Rachel, an ancestor of Israel, is pictured weeping for her lost children. In Jeremiah, that grief appears within a promise of return and restoration. Matthew brings the lament into this new scene of bereaved families. He does not give a count of the dead or say that their parents were being punished for personal wrongdoing.

The passage places Joseph's obedience beside Herod's abuse of power. God's warning saves the child, but Matthew still gives space to the other families' devastating loss. The rescue is not presented as a promise that every faithful family will escape violence.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand the Egypt journey as connecting Jesus with Israel's earlier deliverance, and Rachel's weeping as language for the sorrow in Bethlehem. The Catholic Catechism, paragraph 530, connects the account with persecution and a new exodus; Wesley's notes on Matthew 2:15–18 likewise recognize the earlier Israel setting and the application to Jesus and the bereaved.
passages.god_plan_html:
God called Israel His firstborn son in Exodus 4:22–23. By applying Hosea's son-and-Egypt language to Jesus, Matthew places God's Son within the history of the people He has come to save. Jesus shares their danger and displacement, rather than entering the story untouched by human suffering.

There is also a clear parallel with Moses' beginnings. In Exodus 1:15–22 and 2:1–10, a ruler orders Hebrew boys killed, yet the child who will later lead Israel out of slavery is preserved. Herod's attack similarly fails to destroy Jesus. The resemblance supports a comparison between the deliverers; it does not mean every detail of Moses' infancy has a matching event here.

The sorrow is real, and so is the Bible's hope beyond it. Jeremiah's lament is followed by promised restoration, while Revelation 21:3–4 looks toward God dwelling with His people and ending death and mourning. That larger hope does not tell us why each child died or turn Herod's crime into something good. It places the grief within a story whose final word is God's restored life with His people.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 2:19-23
passages.section_title: The Return to Nazareth

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 After Herod died, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt. 20 “Get up!” he said. “Take the Child and His mother and go to the land of Israel, for those seeking the Child’s life are now dead.” 21 So Joseph got up, took the Child and His mother, and went to the land of Israel. 22 But when he learned that Archelaus was reigning in Judea in place of his father Herod, he was afraid to go there. And having been warned in a dream, he withdrew to the district of Galilee, 23 and he went and lived in a town called Nazareth. So was fulfilled what was spoken through the prophets: “He will be called a Nazarene.”
paragraphs: 19 After Herod died, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt. 20 “Get up!” he said. “Take the Child and His mother and go to the land of Israel, for those seeking the Child’s life are now dead.” 21 So Joseph got up, took the Child and His mother, and went to the land of Israel.

22 But when he learned that Archelaus was reigning in Judea in place of his father Herod, he was afraid to go there. And having been warned in a dream, he withdrew to the district of Galilee, 23 and he went and lived in a town called Nazareth. So was fulfilled what was spoken through the prophets: “He will be called a Nazarene.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Herod's death brings another message to Joseph in Egypt: take the child and His mother back to the land of Israel. Joseph obeys, but the news that Archelaus now rules Judea makes him afraid to settle there. A further warning in a dream directs the family toward Galilee, and they make their home in Nazareth.

The repeated pattern is instruction followed by action. Joseph does not know the whole route in advance; he responds to the warning he has received. The danger has changed with Herod's death, but it has not disappeared simply because one ruler is gone.

Matthew ends by connecting Nazareth with the prophets. Unlike the earlier quotations from Micah, Hosea, and Jeremiah, the sentence about being called a Nazarene has no exact matching sentence in the Old Testament. Matthew refers to the prophets in the plural. The US Catholic bishops' note on Matthew 2:23 recognizes the difficulty and discusses possible connections. The wording calls for care rather than inventing a missing verse.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian interpreters agree that Matthew presents the home in Nazareth as part of God's purpose, but differ over the prophetic connection. Jerome, Letter 57, section 7, relates the name to the branch from Jesse in Isaiah 11:1. The Hebrew word is נֵצֶר, netser (NEH-tser), a shoot or sprout, as Brown–Driver–Briggs confirms. The proposed connection is a play on a similar sound, not a claim that the word for branch literally names the town.

Wesley's note on Matthew 2:23 instead understands a summary of the prophets' picture of a rejected Messiah, with Nazareth carrying associations of contempt. John 1:45–46 shows Nathanael questioning whether anything good can come from there. Another historical reading, in Calvin's commentary on 2:23, connects the language with the Nazirite, a person specially dedicated to God. These are identified teachers' explanations, not uniform positions binding every church in their traditions.
passages.god_plan_html:
The return instruction has a close parallel in Exodus 4:19–20: Moses is told to return because those seeking his life are dead, and he sets out with his family. Matthew uses closely corresponding language for Joseph and Jesus. The two accounts invite comparison, while the larger New Testament identifies an important difference: Hebrews 3:1–6 honors Moses as a faithful servant and Christ as the Son over God's house. The parallel points toward Jesus' greater work without making every journey detail a prediction.

Nazareth also leads into the setting of Jesus' public ministry. In Matthew 4:12–16, His move within Galilee is connected with Isaiah's promise of light for people in darkness. This quiet family settlement belongs to the path toward that public announcement. God's purpose moves forward through ordinary places as well as through Jerusalem and its rulers.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 3:1-6
passages.section_title: John Calls Israel to Repent

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 In those days John the Baptist came, preaching in the wilderness of Judea 2 and saying, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near.” 3 This is he who was spoken of through the prophet Isaiah: “A voice of one calling in the wilderness, ‘Prepare the way for the Lord, make straight paths for Him.’” 4 John wore a garment of camel’s hair, with a leather belt around his waist. His food was locusts and wild honey. 5 People went out to him from Jerusalem and all Judea and the whole region around the Jordan. 6 Confessing their sins, they were baptized by him in the Jordan River.
paragraphs: 1 In those days John the Baptist came, preaching in the wilderness of Judea 2 and saying, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near.” 3 This is he who was spoken of through the prophet Isaiah: “A voice of one calling in the wilderness, ‘Prepare the way for the Lord, make straight paths for Him.’”

4 John wore a garment of camel’s hair, with a leather belt around his waist. His food was locusts and wild honey. 5 People went out to him from Jerusalem and all Judea and the whole region around the Jordan. 6 Confessing their sins, they were baptized by him in the Jordan River.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Matthew moves from Jesus' childhood to John preaching in the wilderness of Judea. John's message is urgent: God's kingdom is near, so the people must repent. Matthew identifies him as the voice Isaiah described, preparing the Lord's way. People come from Jerusalem, Judea, and the region around the Jordan, confess their sins, and are baptized.

Repent is translated from μετανοέω, metanoeō (meh-tah-no-EH-oh). Thayer's Greek Lexicon includes a change of mind, but specifically explains this use as a change for the better that turns against past sins. John is calling for more than a different opinion. His demand for the fruit of repentance in the next passage makes the changed direction visible in people's lives.

The kingdom of heaven concerns God's rule, not simply a place people go after death. John's announcement calls his hearers to prepare for God's approaching action. He does not begin by congratulating them on their ancestry or religious standing; he calls them to face their sins.

John's camel-hair clothing and leather belt recall the description of Elijah in 2 Kings 1:7–8. His setting and way of life place him alongside Israel's prophets. Matthew gives these concrete details without telling us how many years he lived in the wilderness or describing a childhood friendship with Jesus.

Baptize comes from βαπτίζω, baptizō (bap-TID-zoh), which Thayer's Greek Lexicon explains in terms of dipping, immersion, and washing. Here the washing accompanies confession and John's message of preparation. Acts 19:1–5 later distinguishes John's baptism from baptism into Jesus' name and explains that John directed people to believe in the One coming after him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand John as preparing people for Jesus through repentance. They differ over what form of baptism the account supports. The Second London Baptist Confession, chapter 29.4, requires immersion and cites Jesus' baptism in Matthew 3:16; the Westminster Confession, chapter 28.3, accepts pouring or sprinkling without requiring immersion. These are distinct confessional positions about Christian baptism, rather than two explicit descriptions supplied by Matthew of John's every action.

The difference also appears in comments on John himself. Baptist commentator John Gill on Matthew 3:6 reads baptism in the river as immersion. Wesley on the same verse instead proposes that John cast water over people standing at the river's edge. These comments draw different conclusions from an account that names the river and the baptism without describing every movement of the washing.
passages.god_plan_html:
John's work belongs to a promise of God's coming help. Isaiah 40:1–5 begins with comfort for God's people and pictures a prepared road in the wilderness before the LORD's glory is revealed. Matthew identifies John with that preparing voice. The call to repentance is part of preparing people to receive the One God is sending.

The Elijah connection is made explicit later by Jesus. Malachi 4:5–6 promises a messenger who turns hearts before the day of the LORD, and Matthew 11:10–14 identifies John with the promised messenger and Elijah who was to come. Matthew 17:10–13 confirms that Jesus is speaking about John. His importance lies in this God-given task: he prepares the way for Jesus rather than gathering people around himself as the final answer.
passages.current_position_html: Our Baptism study understands immersion in water as the intended form of baptism. It connects going down into the water and coming up again with the death-and-resurrection picture developed for believers. That is the study's position on the form and meaning of Christian baptism; it does not make every feature of John's ministry identical to the later practice of the church.

passages.title: Matthew 3:7-12
passages.section_title: Fruit That Shows Repentance

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 But when John saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his place of baptism, he said to them, “You brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the coming wrath? 8 Produce fruit, then, in keeping with repentance. 9 And do not presume to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you that out of these stones God can raise up children for Abraham. 10 The axe lies ready at the root of the trees, and every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire. 11 I baptize you with water for repentance, but after me will come One more powerful than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire. 12 His winnowing fork is in His hand to clear His threshing floor and to gather His wheat into the barn; but He will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.”
paragraphs: 7 But when John saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his place of baptism, he said to them, “You brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the coming wrath? 8 Produce fruit, then, in keeping with repentance. 9 And do not presume to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you that out of these stones God can raise up children for Abraham. 10 The axe lies ready at the root of the trees, and every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.

11 I baptize you with water for repentance, but after me will come One more powerful than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire. 12 His winnowing fork is in His hand to clear His threshing floor and to gather His wheat into the barn; but He will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
John now addresses Pharisees and Sadducees coming to the place of baptism. His severe warning shifts attention from public religious identity to the response God requires. Claiming Abraham as their father cannot take the place of repentance. John insists on fruit: a changed life that fits the change being professed.

The fruit picture becomes practical in Luke 3:10–14. John tells people to share clothing and food, tax collectors not to demand extra, and soldiers not to extort money or use false accusations. Repentance reaches possessions, work, and the treatment of other people. It is not merely a claim to belong to the right family or group.

The axe at the roots makes the warning urgent. John then points away from himself to someone more powerful. His own work involves water and repentance; the coming One will act with the Holy Spirit and fire. John describes himself as unworthy even to carry His sandals.

The final image is a harvest being sorted. A winnowing fork separates the useful grain from the chaff, the unwanted material left from threshing. Thayer's Greek Lexicon identifies the implement as a winnowing shovel. John pictures the wheat brought safely into the barn while the chaff is burned. The One coming after him has authority both to gather and to judge.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read the fruit, axe, and harvest as a call for genuine repentance and a warning of judgment. The fire in verse 11 has more than one established reading.

Wesley's note on Matthew 3:11 understands it as the Spirit kindling love in people's hearts and connects it with the fiery appearance at Pentecost. The Catholic Catechism, paragraph 696, likewise uses John's words when explaining fire as an image of the Spirit's transforming work.

Baptist commentator John Gill on Matthew 3:11 acknowledges the Pentecost reading but favors a judgment reading, pointing to the fire around it in verses 10 and 12. The US Catholic bishops' note on 3:11 also discusses cleansing for the repentant and judgment for the unrepentant. These differences cross church boundaries; the sources do not support assigning one interpretation to every Catholic or every Protestant.
passages.god_plan_html:
John's promise reaches beyond his own work. In Acts 1:4–5, Jesus explicitly contrasts John's water baptism with the coming gift of the Holy Spirit. Acts 2:1–4 then records the Spirit filling the disciples. The messenger can prepare and point ahead, but the promised gift comes through Jesus.

The combination of cleansing and judgment also recalls the prophets. Malachi 3:1–4 describes a messenger preparing the way and the Lord's coming with a refining fire; Malachi 4:1–2 places judgment on evil alongside healing for those who fear God. These are parallels in the Bible's account of God's coming, not grounds for inventing a date or reducing every fire image to exactly the same event.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 3:13-17
passages.section_title: Jesus Is Baptized

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 At that time Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan to be baptized by John. 14 But John tried to prevent Him, saying, “I need to be baptized by You, and do You come to me?” 15 “Let it be so now,” Jesus replied. “It is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness in this way.” Then John permitted Him. 16 As soon as Jesus was baptized, He went up out of the water. Suddenly the heavens were opened, and He saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and resting on Him. 17 And a voice from heaven said, “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased!”
paragraphs: 13 At that time Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan to be baptized by John. 14 But John tried to prevent Him, saying, “I need to be baptized by You, and do You come to me?” 15 “Let it be so now,” Jesus replied. “It is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness in this way.” Then John permitted Him.

16 As soon as Jesus was baptized, He went up out of the water. Suddenly the heavens were opened, and He saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and resting on Him. 17 And a voice from heaven said, “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased!”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus comes from Galilee to the Jordan seeking baptism from John. John objects that he needs baptism from Jesus instead. Jesus answers that this action is fitting to fulfill all righteousness, and John permits it. Matthew presents a deliberate act of obedience, not Jesus confessing a sin He has committed.

The word fitting is πρέπω, prepō (PREH-poh). Thayer's Greek Lexicon explains its use here as being appropriate or becoming. Jesus says that this is the right course for them now. He and John each have a part in carrying out what God requires.

As Jesus comes up from the water, the heavens open, the Spirit descends like a dove and rests on Him, and the heavenly voice declares Him the beloved Son. The scene moves from John's hesitation to God's confirmation. Jesus is the One to whom John's preparatory ministry has been pointing.

John 1:29–34 gives the Baptist's later testimony: the descent and remaining of the Spirit was the sign by which he recognized the One who baptizes with the Holy Spirit. Matthew tells the encounter from its own angle, including John's objection and Jesus' answer. Neither account gives a complete history of what John had understood about Jesus at every earlier stage.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Historic Christian readings understand the baptism as Jesus' willing obedience and the revelation of the Son, with the Father speaking and the Spirit descending. The Catholic Catechism, paragraphs 535–536, and Wesley's notes on Matthew 3:15–17 both emphasize His submission to God's purpose, rather than a need to be cleansed of personal sin.
passages.god_plan_html:
The heavenly declaration recalls the king addressed as God's Son in Psalm 2:6–9. The Spirit resting on the One in whom God delights also recalls Isaiah 42:1–4, where God's servant brings justice to the nations. These are supported connections between the scenes; Matthew later directly applies Isaiah's servant passage to Jesus in Matthew 12:17–21. The beloved Son's mission will display the servant's faithful care and justice.

Jesus enters the water among people being called back to God, and will carry His obedience through to the cross. Philippians 2:5–8 describes His taking the servant's place and becoming obedient to death. The baptism begins the public work that will lead there; the Father’s approval is not a promise that His Son's path will be free of suffering.

The scene also points forward to the mission Jesus gives His followers. Matthew 28:18–20 sends them to make disciples and baptize in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The three named together in that commission are already present here at the opening of Jesus' public work.
passages.current_position_html: Our Baptism study understands immersion in water as the intended form of baptism. It connects going down into the water and coming up again with the death-and-resurrection picture developed for believers. That is the study's position on the form and meaning of Christian baptism; it does not make every feature of John's ministry identical to the later practice of the church.

passages.title: Matthew 4:1-11
passages.section_title: Jesus Resists the Tempter

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. 2 After fasting forty days and forty nights, He was hungry. 3 The tempter came to Him and said, “If You are the Son of God, tell these stones to become bread.” 4 But Jesus answered, “It is written: ‘Man shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God.’” 5 Then the devil took Him to the holy city and set Him on the pinnacle of the temple. 6 “If You are the Son of God,” he said, “throw Yourself down. For it is written: ‘He will command His angels concerning You, and they will lift You up in their hands, so that You will not strike Your foot against a stone.’” 7 Jesus replied, “It is also written: ‘Do not put the Lord your God to the test.’” 8 Again, the devil took Him to a very high mountain and showed Him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory. 9 “All this I will give You,” he said, “if You will fall down and worship me.” 10 “Away from Me, Satan!” Jesus told him. “For it is written: ‘Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only.’” 11 Then the devil left Him, and angels came and ministered to Him.
paragraphs: 1 Then Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. 2 After fasting forty days and forty nights, He was hungry. 3 The tempter came to Him and said, “If You are the Son of God, tell these stones to become bread.” 4 But Jesus answered, “It is written: ‘Man shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God.’”

5 Then the devil took Him to the holy city and set Him on the pinnacle of the temple. 6 “If You are the Son of God,” he said, “throw Yourself down. For it is written: ‘He will command His angels concerning You, and they will lift You up in their hands, so that You will not strike Your foot against a stone.’” 7 Jesus replied, “It is also written: ‘Do not put the Lord your God to the test.’”

8 Again, the devil took Him to a very high mountain and showed Him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory. 9 “All this I will give You,” he said, “if You will fall down and worship me.” 10 “Away from Me, Satan!” Jesus told him. “For it is written: ‘Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only.’” 11 Then the devil left Him, and angels came and ministered to Him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Immediately after the Father's declaration at His baptism, Jesus is led by the Spirit into the wilderness. After forty days and nights of fasting, He is hungry, and the devil challenges Him as the Son of God. The question running through the encounters is how the Son will exercise His calling: in trust and obedience to His Father, or on the tempter's terms.

The Greek verb for being tempted is πειράζω, peirazō (pay-RAH-zoh). Thayer's Greek Lexicon includes testing someone's character and, in this context, enticing someone to sin. Matthew distinguishes the Spirit's leading from the devil's attempts to draw Jesus into disobedience. James 1:13–15 likewise distinguishes God from the enticement to evil.

The first offer targets His hunger: turn stones into bread. Jesus answers from Deuteronomy 8:2–3, where Israel's hunger and manna taught dependence on God's word. His answer places that dependence ahead of the tempter's proposed display of power.

At the temple, the devil quotes the promise of angelic protection in Psalm 91:11–12 and urges Jesus to throw Himself down. Jesus answers with Deuteronomy 6:16, the warning against testing God. A promise of care becomes an invitation to force a demonstration; Jesus keeps the promise within the wider call to trust God.

The last offer is the kingdoms of the world in exchange for bowing before the devil. Jesus again answers from Deuteronomy 6:13–14, directing worship and service to God alone. He rejects the offer, commands Satan to leave, and receives the ministry of angels.

Matthew ends with the kingdoms, while Luke 4:1–13 ends with the temple. The accounts present the same three challenges in different orders. Matthew does not identify the high mountain or give the means by which every kingdom is shown.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand these encounters as Jesus' faithful resistance to temptation and an example of trusting God's word. The Catholic Catechism, paragraphs 538–540, connects His victory with Adam and Israel; Wesley's notes on Matthew 4:4–10 likewise emphasize His obedience to the Father and answers from Scripture.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus' answers deliberately return to Israel's wilderness experience. Deuteronomy 8:2–5 describes forty years of testing, hunger, provision, and God's fatherly care. Matthew's forty-day setting and three Deuteronomy answers form a clear parallel: the Son remains faithful in the very matters where God's people had been tested.

There is also a wider contrast with Adam. Romans 5:15–19 sets Adam's disobedience beside Christ's obedience, and 1 Corinthians 15:45–49 calls Christ the last Adam. Together, they explain why His faithful human life matters beyond the example it gives us. His obedience belongs to God's rescue of humanity from sin and death.

His experience also gives His people confidence to seek help. Hebrews 4:14–16 describes Jesus as tested as we are, yet without sin, and invites us to approach God for mercy and grace. The account leads us to rely on a Savior who knows testing and offers help in our weakness.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Worship as the Early Church Knew It understands the final temptation as a demand for allegiance. Bowing before Satan would acknowledge his authority; Jesus answers that worship and service belong to God alone. The study treats this as personal submission and obedience, rather than a description of a church service.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

passages.title: Matthew 4:9-10
passages.section_title: Worship and Serve God Alone

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 “All this I will give You,” he said, “if You will fall down and worship me.” 10 “Away from Me, Satan!” Jesus told him. “For it is written: ‘Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only.’”
paragraphs: 9 “All this I will give You,” he said, “if You will fall down and worship me.” 10 “Away from Me, Satan!” Jesus told him. “For it is written: ‘Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only.’”

passages.context_html:
These verses conclude the third wilderness temptation in Matthew. The devil has shown Jesus the kingdoms of the world and their glory. The proposed exchange makes the demand explicit: Jesus can have them if He bows before the tempter. Jesus refuses and answers from Deuteronomy 6:13–14, where Israel is called to serve the LORD and refuse other gods.

The verb translated worship is προσκυνέω, proskyneō (pros-koo-NEH-oh). Thayer's Greek Lexicon describes bowing in reverence, including both human homage and worship. Here the demand is for the allegiance that Jesus' answer reserves for God. The wider passage ends with the devil leaving and angels ministering to Jesus.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand Jesus' answer as rejecting idolatry and affirming exclusive devotion to God. Wesley's Matthew 4:9–10 notes and the Catholic Catechism, paragraph 540, place this refusal within His obedience to the Father.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Worship as the Early Church Knew It understands the final temptation as a demand for allegiance. Bowing before Satan would acknowledge his authority; Jesus answers that worship and service belong to God alone. The study treats this as personal submission and obedience, rather than a description of a church service.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The kingdoms offered here contrast with the authority Jesus declares at the close of the Gospel. In Matthew 28:18–20, the risen Jesus has authority in heaven and on earth and sends His disciples to all nations. This is a narrative contrast between the tempter's proposed allegiance and the mission Jesus receives after His faithful life, death, and resurrection.

Philippians 2:8–11 similarly connects Jesus' obedience through death with His exaltation and the acknowledgment of His lordship to the Father's glory. His path brings honor to the Father rather than surrender to the enemy.

passages.title: Matthew 4:10
passages.section_title: Allegiance and Service to God

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 “Away from Me, Satan!” Jesus told him. “For it is written: ‘Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only.’”
paragraphs: 10 “Away from Me, Satan!” Jesus told him. “For it is written: ‘Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only.’”

passages.context_html:
Jesus gives this answer after the devil offers Him the kingdoms of the world in exchange for worship. The refusal directs allegiance and service to God alone. It draws on Deuteronomy 6:13–14, where Israel is warned against following the gods of surrounding peoples.

The command brings Matthew's three temptation scenes to their conclusion. In the next verse the devil leaves Jesus and angels minister to Him. The answer is an act of faithfulness within that encounter, not an isolated slogan about worship.

The study treats this as personal submission and obedience, rather than a description of a church service.

passages.title: Matthew 4:12-17
passages.section_title: Light Dawns in Galilee

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 When Jesus heard that John had been imprisoned, He withdrew to Galilee. 13 Leaving Nazareth, He went and lived in Capernaum, which is by the sea in the region of Zebulun and Naphtali, 14 to fulfill what was spoken through the prophet Isaiah: 15 “Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, the Way of the Sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles— 16 the people living in darkness have seen a great light; on those living in the land of the shadow of death, a light has dawned.” 17 From that time on Jesus began to preach, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near.”
paragraphs: 12 When Jesus heard that John had been imprisoned, He withdrew to Galilee. 13 Leaving Nazareth, He went and lived in Capernaum, which is by the sea in the region of Zebulun and Naphtali, 14 to fulfill what was spoken through the prophet Isaiah: 15 “Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, the Way of the Sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles— 16 the people living in darkness have seen a great light; on those living in the land of the shadow of death, a light has dawned.”
17 From that time on Jesus began to preach, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After John is imprisoned, Jesus withdraws to Galilee and makes His home in Capernaum by the sea. Matthew connects this setting with Isaiah's promise of light in Zebulun and Naphtali. The story has moved from the wilderness testing to Jesus' public preaching among people in need of that light.

The source is Isaiah 8:21–22 and 9:1–7. The darkness described around it belongs to distress and oppression, while the coming light brings joy and the hope of righteous rule. Matthew identifies Jesus' presence and work in Galilee with this promised change.

Jesus begins with the same call heard from John in Matthew 3:2: repentance because the kingdom of heaven is near. The One John announced now proclaims the message Himself. The following scenes show Him gathering disciples, teaching, and healing.

John 3:22–24 records an earlier period when Jesus and His disciples were active before John was imprisoned. Matthew takes us directly to this later stage, when Jesus makes His home in Capernaum and begins the Galilean ministry described here.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the light as the hope and saving work Jesus brings, and the kingdom announcement as a call to respond to God's rule. Wesley's Matthew 4:15–17 notes and the Catholic Catechism, paragraph 541, connect the preaching with God's kingdom taking effect through Jesus, while its full completion still lies ahead.
passages.god_plan_html:
Isaiah's promise reaches from light in the darkened region to the child whose government brings lasting peace and justice on David's throne in Isaiah 9:1–7. Matthew places Jesus' local ministry within that larger royal hope. A move to a lakeside town becomes part of the fulfillment of God's promises.

The reach widens as the Gospel continues. People gather from beyond Galilee in Matthew 4:24–25, and the risen Jesus eventually sends His disciples to all nations in Matthew 28:18–20. Galilee is an important beginning in that movement, rather than the limit of the Messiah's concern.
passages.current_position_html: Our study The Gospel According to Jesus understands repentance as turning away from sin and self-rule toward Jesus as Lord. It treats this response as receiving God's gift through faith, rather than earning entrance into His kingdom by moral achievement.

passages.title: Matthew 4:18-22
passages.section_title: The First Fishermen Follow Jesus

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 As Jesus was walking beside the Sea of Galilee, He saw two brothers, Simon called Peter and his brother Andrew. They were casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen. 19 “Come, follow Me,” Jesus said, “and I will make you fishers of men.” 20 And at once they left their nets and followed Him. 21 Going on from there, He saw two other brothers, James son of Zebedee and his brother John. They were in a boat with their father Zebedee, mending their nets. Jesus called them, 22 and immediately they left the boat and their father and followed Him.
paragraphs: 18 As Jesus was walking beside the Sea of Galilee, He saw two brothers, Simon called Peter and his brother Andrew. They were casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen. 19 “Come, follow Me,” Jesus said, “and I will make you fishers of men.” 20 And at once they left their nets and followed Him.

21 Going on from there, He saw two other brothers, James son of Zebedee and his brother John. They were in a boat with their father Zebedee, mending their nets. Jesus called them, 22 and immediately they left the boat and their father and followed Him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus calls two pairs of brothers beside the Sea of Galilee. Simon Peter and Andrew are casting a net; James and John are mending nets with their father Zebedee. The invitation reaches them during their ordinary work. Matthew emphasizes the prompt response of both pairs: they leave their nets, boat, and former setting to follow Him.

The fishing language gives their future work a familiar picture. Jesus will make them people who gather others. He does not simply tell them to be useful on their own; He calls them to follow Him and promises to shape what they will become.

John 1:35–42 records Andrew meeting Jesus through the Baptist's testimony and bringing Simon to Him. Matthew's lakeside call can therefore be read alongside an earlier introduction.

This scene follows the announcement of the kingdom and comes before the growing public ministry. Following Jesus will involve learning His message and sharing His work. The call changes real relationships and livelihoods, rather than remaining an admiration from a distance.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read the brothers' response as costly discipleship and preparation to share Jesus' mission. The Catholic Catechism, paragraph 551, emphasizes the disciples' participation in His work; Baptist commentator John Gill on Matthew 4:19–20 likewise explains the promise as Jesus equipping them to bring others to faith.
passages.god_plan_html:
The promised work develops later in the Gospel. In Matthew 10:1–8, these men are named among the twelve and sent to proclaim the kingdom and bring help to others. At the end, Matthew 28:18–20 gives the mission its worldwide reach. The call beside the water begins training for that outward work.

The initiative belongs to Jesus. John 15:16 later speaks of His choosing and appointing the disciples to bear lasting fruit. This comparison highlights His purpose and provision: the people He calls must follow, and He prepares them to serve. Their ordinary starting point does not set the limit of what He can do through them.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 4:23-25
passages.section_title: Teaching, Healing, and Growing Crowds

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 23 Jesus went throughout Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every disease and sickness among the people. 24 News about Him spread all over Syria, and people brought to Him all who were ill with various diseases, those suffering acute pain, the demon-possessed, those having seizures, and the paralyzed, and He healed them. 25 Large crowds followed Him, having come from Galilee, the Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea, and beyond the Jordan.
paragraphs: 23 Jesus went throughout Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every disease and sickness among the people.

24 News about Him spread all over Syria, and people brought to Him all who were ill with various diseases, those suffering acute pain, the demon-possessed, those having seizures, and the paralyzed, and He healed them. 25 Large crowds followed Him, having come from Galilee, the Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea, and beyond the Jordan.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Matthew gathers Jesus' early Galilean ministry into three activities: teaching, announcing the good news of the kingdom, and healing. His message and acts of mercy belong together. News spreads, suffering people are brought to Him, and crowds arrive from Galilee and surrounding regions, including Jerusalem, Judea, and beyond the Jordan.

Gospel translates εὐαγγέλιον, euangelion (yoo-ang-GHEL-ee-on), good news. Thayer's Greek Lexicon specifically identifies the kingdom message in Matthew 4:23. Here the good news announces God's coming rule through Jesus; the story has not yet reached His death and resurrection, through which that saving work will unfold.

Synagogues are the Jewish gathering places where He teaches. The name comes from the Greek συναγωγή, synagōgē (soo-nah-go-GAY), an assembly or its meeting place, as Thayer's Greek Lexicon explains. Matthew places Jesus' teaching within the life of Israel, while the report of Him spreads outward.

The list of suffering includes diseases, severe pain, demonic oppression, seizures, and paralysis. Matthew shows the breadth of Jesus' help, without treating all illness as the same condition. The gathering crowds lead directly into Matthew 5:1–2, where Jesus begins the teaching commonly called the Sermon on the Mount.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the healings as acts of compassion and signs of Jesus' authority, joined to the announcement of God's kingdom. The Catholic Catechism, paragraphs 547–550, describes them as signs inviting faith and liberation from evil; Wesley's notes on Matthew 4:23–24 likewise read the proclamation as good news accompanied by help for suffering people.
passages.god_plan_html:
The same pattern returns in Matthew 9:35–38: teaching, kingdom proclamation, healing, and compassion for people like sheep without a shepherd. Jesus then shares this work with His disciples in Matthew 10:1–8. The opening summary therefore leads into a mission that gathers workers as well as crowds.

The works also point beyond immediate relief. In Matthew 11:2–6, Jesus answers John's question about His identity by pointing to what people hear and see: healing, restored life, and good news for the poor. These are signs of the promised rescue taking shape. Their invitation calls for a response; Matthew 11:20–24 later warns towns that saw miracles without repenting.
passages.current_position_html: Our study The Gospel According to Jesus understands the good news as the announcement of Jesus as Savior and King, centered on His death for sins and resurrection. It reads His teaching and acts of mercy as showing the character of the King whose saving work the Gospel announces.

passages.title: Matthew 5:1-12
passages.section_title: The Blessings of the Kingdom

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 When Jesus saw the crowds, He went up on the mountain and sat down. His disciples came to Him, 2 and He began to teach them, saying: 3 “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. 4 Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted. 5 Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth. 6 Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be filled. 7 Blessed are the merciful, for they will be shown mercy. 8 Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God. 9 Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God. 10 Blessed are those who are persecuted because of righteousness, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. 11 Blessed are you when people insult you, persecute you, and falsely say all kinds of evil against you because of Me. 12 Rejoice and be glad, because great is your reward in heaven, for in the same way they persecuted the prophets before you.
paragraphs: 1 When Jesus saw the crowds, He went up on the mountain and sat down. His disciples came to Him, 2 and He began to teach them, saying:

3 “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. 4 Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted. 5 Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth. 6 Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be filled. 7 Blessed are the merciful, for they will be shown mercy. 8 Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God. 9 Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God. 10 Blessed are those who are persecuted because of righteousness, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.

11 Blessed are you when people insult you, persecute you, and falsely say all kinds of evil against you because of Me. 12 Rejoice and be glad, because great is your reward in heaven, for in the same way they persecuted the prophets before you.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The growing crowds at the end of chapter 4 lead into Jesus' teaching on the mountain. He sits down, His disciples come to Him, and He begins the sermon that runs through chapters 5–7. The opening blessings describe people who belong to God's kingdom and the hope held out to them.

Blessed is translated from μακάριος, makarios (mah-KAH-ree-oss), blessed or happy. Thayer's Greek Lexicon specifically includes these sayings. Here the reason for calling someone blessed is the good God promises, even when that person's present circumstances include grief, need, or persecution. The word does not require that the person feel cheerful through everything.

The list joins humble need before God with mercy, purity of heart, peacemaking, and faithfulness under opposition. Jesus specifically describes poverty in spirit and hunger for righteousness. He brings the inner life, relationships, and response to wrongdoing together in one picture.

The promise that the kingdom belongs to them opens the list in verse 3 and returns in verse 10. Both use the present tense, while comfort, satisfaction, seeing God, and the other promises look ahead. The passage holds present belonging and future hope together.

At the end, Jesus addresses His hearers directly about insults, persecution, and false accusations because of Him. The blessing concerns suffering connected with faithfulness to Him, as the prophets had suffered before them. Their hope rests in God's recognition, even when other people reject them.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read these blessings as a picture of the life and hope of people belonging to God's kingdom. The Catholic Catechism, paragraphs 1716–1717, describes the character of Christ reflected in His people and blessings already begun, while Wesley's notes on Matthew 5:3–12 likewise speak of present life with God and future fulfillment.

Wesley's note on Matthew 5:4 understands the mourning as sorrow over one's own sins and the sins of others. In that reading, the promise answers a heart humbled before God, seeking His mercy rather than excusing wrongdoing.

Other Christian readings include the grief of suffering and loss. Calvin's commentary on Matthew 5:4 speaks of calamities and the comfort found in God. In a 2020 address, Pope Francis includes both grief over another person's death or suffering and sorrow for one's own sin. These readings differ over what people are mourning; each looks to God for comfort.
passages.god_plan_html:
The promises reach back into Israel's Scriptures. Psalm 37:7–11 calls for trust rather than angry rivalry and promises the land to the meek. Jesus' blessing of the meek recalls that promise. God's future is received through trust in Him, rather than seized through the violence and self-importance the psalm warns against.

Isaiah 61:1–3 joins good news for the poor with comfort for those who mourn and a renewed life of righteousness. In Luke 4:16–21, Jesus identifies His mission with Isaiah's announcement. That scriptural background helps place the blessings within God's work of rescue and restoration.

The future hope also reaches beyond present hardship. Revelation 7:13–17 pictures people brought through severe suffering, sheltered by God, shepherded by the Lamb, and freed from hunger, thirst, and tears. The picture carries the Beatitudes' hope forward to life with God beyond present suffering.
passages.current_position_html:
Our study The Gospel According to Jesus understands the Beatitudes as the character of people being reshaped by the good news. Jesus is describing what life looks like when His kingdom takes hold of a person. The study does not treat the list as a way to earn salvation; it connects this life with receiving Jesus as Savior and King.

For the mourning in verse 4, our study Who Shepherds the Church? takes the specific reading of sorrow over sin.

passages.title: Matthew 5:4
passages.section_title: Comfort for Those Who Mourn

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 4 Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted.
paragraphs: 4 Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted.

passages.context_html:
This is the second blessing at the opening of the Sermon on the Mount. It follows the blessing of the poor in spirit and comes before the promise to the meek. Jesus speaks of people whose present condition is sorrow, yet promises that they will receive comfort.

The Greek verb is πενθέω, pentheō (pen-THEH-oh), to mourn or lament. Thayer's Greek Lexicon lists Matthew 5:4 among its uses. The word names the grief; it does not by itself specify the particular loss or wrongdoing being mourned. Understanding the surrounding blessings and Scripture's uses of mourning is therefore important.

The promise belongs with the larger hope of the kingdom announced through the list. Jesus is not praising pain for its own sake. He speaks of sorrow that will be answered by God's comfort, rather than left as the final condition of His people.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley's note on Matthew 5:4 understands the mourning as sorrow over one's own sins and the sins of others. In that reading, the promise answers a heart humbled before God, seeking His mercy rather than excusing wrongdoing.

Other Christian readings include the grief of suffering and loss. Calvin's commentary on Matthew 5:4 speaks of calamities and the comfort found in God. In a 2020 address, Pope Francis includes both grief over another person's death or suffering and sorrow for one's own sin. These readings differ over what people are mourning; each looks to God for comfort.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Who Shepherds the Church? understands the mourning here as sorrow over sin. That is the reading it uses in its discussion of the need for careful teaching of this passage.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Isaiah 61:1–3 promises good news, comfort for mourners, and joy in place of ashes. Jesus' identification with Isaiah's mission in Luke 4:16–21 gives this older promise a place in the larger story of His coming. The comparison supports the hope of restoration behind His words here.

Scripture also gives clear examples of sorrow for sin turning toward God. Psalm 51:1–4, 17 seeks mercy with a broken and repentant heart, and 2 Corinthians 7:9–11 describes sorrow that leads to repentance. These passages show what grieving over sin can look like: seeking God's mercy and turning toward Him.

The final picture is one of comfort reaching completion. Revelation 21:3–4 describes God dwelling with His people and ending death, mourning, crying, and pain. The promise reaches beyond a temporary lift in mood to God's restoration of life with Him.

passages.title: Matthew 5:13-16
passages.section_title: Salt and Light

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 You are the salt of the earth. But if the salt loses its savor, how can it be made salty again? It is no longer good for anything, except to be thrown out and trampled by men. 14 You are the light of the world. A city on a hill cannot be hidden. 15 Neither do people light a lamp and put it under a basket. Instead, they set it on a stand, and it gives light to everyone in the house. 16 In the same way, let your light shine before men, that they may see your good deeds and glorify your Father in heaven.
paragraphs: 13 You are the salt of the earth. But if the salt loses its savor, how can it be made salty again? It is no longer good for anything, except to be thrown out and trampled by men.

14 You are the light of the world. A city on a hill cannot be hidden. 15 Neither do people light a lamp and put it under a basket. Instead, they set it on a stand, and it gives light to everyone in the house. 16 In the same way, let your light shine before men, that they may see your good deeds and glorify your Father in heaven.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus now tells the people described in the blessings how their lives should matter to others. They are the salt of the earth and the light of the world. The words follow His warning that faithfulness may bring persecution. His disciples still have a useful and visible place among the people around them.

Salt's flavor and usefulness give force to the warning about losing its savor. It was also used to preserve food: the Roman writer Cato's On Agriculture, section 162, gives an ancient example of curing meat with salt. That wider ancient use helps explain a preserving comparison, alongside the plain idea of flavor.

The verb for losing savor is μωραίνω, mōrainō (moh-RAI-noh). Thayer's Greek Lexicon explains its salt usage as becoming tasteless or losing strength and flavor. The picture warns about failing to serve the purpose for which the salt is useful.

The light pictures make that purpose visible. A city on a hill can be seen, and a lamp belongs on a stand where it gives light to the house. Jesus explains the comparison in verse 16: people should see the disciples' good deeds and give glory to their Father. The attention is meant to reach God through the good their lives bring to others.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand salt and light as a call for Jesus' people to bring good to the world through a visible, faithful life. Wesley on Matthew 5:13–16 applies the words to all who live this way, and the Second Vatican Council's teaching on Christian witness, paragraph 31, likewise describes ordinary life and work as places to make Christ known.
passages.god_plan_html:
The light theme belongs to God's purpose of reaching the nations. Isaiah 49:6 speaks of the servant as light bringing salvation to the ends of the earth. In Acts 13:46–48, Paul and Barnabas apply these words about light for the nations to their work. Jesus' disciples participate in the outward witness of God's saving purpose.

The connection between visible deeds and God's glory appears again in 1 Peter 2:9–12. People brought out of darkness are to live honorably so that others see their good deeds and glorify God, even when they face slander. That is a close parallel with the movement here from persecution to a faithful life before the world.

Ephesians 2:8–10 also holds grace and good works together: salvation is God's gift, and those made new in Christ are prepared to walk in good works. The visible life is part of what His rescue produces.
passages.current_position_html: Our study The Gospel According to Jesus reads the Sermon on the Mount as the character of the King becoming visible in His people. It understands the changed life as growing out of received grace, rather than a way to earn the kingdom. That is the study's framework for the good deeds Jesus calls for here.

passages.title: Matthew 5:17-20
passages.section_title: Fulfilling the Law and the Prophets

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets. I have not come to abolish them, but to fulfill them. 18 For I tell you truly, until heaven and earth pass away, not a single jot, not a stroke of a pen, will disappear from the Law until everything is accomplished. 19 So then, whoever breaks one of the least of these commandments and teaches others to do likewise will be called least in the kingdom of heaven; but whoever practices and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven. 20 For I tell you that unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven.
paragraphs: 17 Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets. I have not come to abolish them, but to fulfill them. 18 For I tell you truly, until heaven and earth pass away, not a single jot, not a stroke of a pen, will disappear from the Law until everything is accomplished.

19 So then, whoever breaks one of the least of these commandments and teaches others to do likewise will be called least in the kingdom of heaven; but whoever practices and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven. 20 For I tell you that unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the blessings and the call to be salt and light, Jesus explains His relationship to the Law and the Prophets. He has come to fulfill them. The following examples about anger, lust, truthfulness, retaliation, and love will show the seriousness of the righteousness He teaches.

The Law and the Prophets point to Israel's Scriptures, not merely the regulations of one religious group. Jesus places His mission within what God has already given. His words prepare the hearers to understand His teaching as bringing that purpose to its fullness.

Fulfill translates πληρόω, plēroō (play-ROH-oh). Thayer's Greek Lexicon explains its use here in terms of God's will being obeyed and His promises receiving fulfillment. The word links what God requires with what He has promised to accomplish.

Jesus then speaks of the smallest written details. The jot points to the small Hebrew letter י, yod (YOHD), as Thayer's entry on the smallest letter explains. The stroke refers to a tiny mark distinguishing letters, according to the entry on that written mark. His emphasis is the lasting seriousness of God's word down to its details.

Practice and teaching belong together in verse 19. Jesus warns against weakening a command and encouraging others to do the same, and honors the one who practices and teaches it. He then says that entrance into the kingdom requires righteousness beyond that of the scribes and Pharisees. The rest of the sermon develops this concern with a life faithful to God from the heart.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Historic Christian readings understand Jesus as fulfilling God's Scriptures, with obedience and grace held together. The Catholic Catechism, paragraphs 577–582, emphasizes His perfect fulfillment and authoritative teaching, while the Westminster Confession, chapter 19.3–7, and Methodist Articles of Religion, article VI, distinguish continuing moral obedience from the older requirements for rituals and sacrifices.
passages.god_plan_html:
After His resurrection, Jesus explicitly describes His suffering, rising, and the proclamation of forgiveness as the fulfillment of Scripture. Luke 24:25–27, 44–47 brings Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms together around that mission. The promise of fulfillment here reaches toward His completed work and its announcement to the nations.

The New Testament also explains how earlier sacrifices point toward Him. Hebrews 10:1–10 calls them a shadow and identifies Jesus' self-offering as the effective act of obedience offered once for all. Colossians 2:16–17 likewise directs attention from shadows to Christ. Fulfillment gives those earlier provisions their place in the story leading to Him.

God's purpose also reaches the lives of those He saves. Romans 3:21–26 describes righteousness through faith in Christ, witnessed by the Law and the Prophets; Romans 8:1–4 connects God's action through His Son with a life directed by the Spirit. These passages hold rescue and renewed obedience together, rather than making outward religious standing sufficient.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Is the Bible the Inerrant Word of God? understands Scripture as God's inspired and trustworthy word. It locates that authority in the original Hebrew and Greek texts and distinguishes them from later translation choices and human interpretations. That is the existing study's position on the authority of Scripture emphasized here.

deeper_study.title: Is the Bible the Inerrant Word of God?

passages.title: Matthew 5:21-26
passages.section_title: Anger and Reconciliation

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 You have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘Do not murder’ and ‘Anyone who murders will be subject to judgment.’ 22 But I tell you that anyone who is angry with his brother will be subject to judgment. Again, anyone who says to his brother, ‘Raca,’ will be subject to the Sanhedrin. But anyone who says, ‘You fool!’ will be subject to the fire of hell. 23 So if you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, 24 leave your gift there before the altar. First go and be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer your gift. 25 Reconcile quickly with your adversary, while you are still on the way to court. Otherwise, he may hand you over to the judge, and the judge may hand you over to the officer, and you may be thrown into prison. 26 Truly I tell you, you will not get out until you have paid the last penny.
paragraphs: 21 You have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘Do not murder’ and ‘Anyone who murders will be subject to judgment.’ 22 But I tell you that anyone who is angry with his brother will be subject to judgment. Again, anyone who says to his brother, ‘Raca,’ will be subject to the Sanhedrin. But anyone who says, ‘You fool!’ will be subject to the fire of hell.

23 So if you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, 24 leave your gift there before the altar. First go and be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer your gift.

25 Reconcile quickly with your adversary, while you are still on the way to court. Otherwise, he may hand you over to the judge, and the judge may hand you over to the officer, and you may be thrown into prison. 26 Truly I tell you, you will not get out until you have paid the last penny.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus now gives the first example of the righteousness He has been describing. The command against murder comes from Exodus 20:13 and Deuteronomy 5:17. His teaching reaches into the anger and contempt that damage a relationship before any physical attack takes place.

Raca represents an Aramaic insult. The Greek text writes it as ῥακά, rhaka (rah-KAH); Thayer's Greek Lexicon explains it as calling someone empty-headed. Jesus names words that treat another person with contempt and places them under the seriousness of God's judgment. The concern is the heart and speech behind the insult, as well as the violence the command forbids. The Sanhedrin is the Jewish council named in the warning; the US Catholic bishops' note on verse 22 explains the sequence of judgments.

This concern also appears in the earlier Law. Leviticus 19:17–18 forbids harboring hatred, seeking revenge, and bearing a grudge, and calls for love of one's neighbor. Jesus' command is rooted in God's concern for how people regard and treat one another.

The first illustration turns the teaching into action. Someone preparing an offering remembers that a brother has a grievance against him. Jesus tells him to seek reconciliation first, then return to the offering. The direction is active: recognizing a broken relationship calls for an effort to put it right.

The second illustration urges the same promptness through a court dispute. A person should settle with the adversary before the case reaches the judge and the consequences become unavoidable. The warning ends with the full debt still owed. It presses the hearer to act while reconciliation remains possible.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly understand this passage as condemning destructive anger and contempt, and as making reconciliation a matter of obedience to God. Wesley's notes on Matthew 5:22–24 emphasize both the treatment of the other person and the importance of putting the relationship right before bringing an offering.

The court illustration has been read in different ways. Baptist commentator John Gill on Matthew 5:25–26 takes it as practical counsel to settle a debt dispute before the case goes to court, rather than reading it as a detailed picture of God's judgment. Wesley on the same verses understands the warning to include the prospect of God's judgment and a debt the sinner cannot finally discharge. Both readings call for a prompt response; they differ over how directly the courtroom picture describes final judgment.
passages.god_plan_html:
Reconciliation belongs to God's saving work as well as to the conduct Jesus requires. 2 Corinthians 5:17–21 describes God reconciling people to Himself through Christ and giving them a message of reconciliation. The peace God brings is meant to shape the relationships of the people He makes new.

Ephesians 4:29–32 connects changed speech, the removal of bitterness, and kindness with the forgiveness God has given in Christ. 1 John 3:11–18 likewise moves from condemning hatred to Jesus laying down His life and His followers showing love in action. These passages show the wider purpose: God's rescue forms people whose words and actions protect one another rather than express contempt.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 5:27-30
passages.section_title: Desire and Faithfulness of Heart

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 27 You have heard that it was said, ‘Do not commit adultery.’ 28 But I tell you that anyone who looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart. 29 If your right eye causes you to sin, gouge it out and throw it away. It is better for you to lose one part of your body than for your whole body to be thrown into hell. 30 And if your right hand causes you to sin, cut it off and throw it away. It is better for you to lose one part of your body than for your whole body to depart into hell.
paragraphs: 27 You have heard that it was said, ‘Do not commit adultery.’ 28 But I tell you that anyone who looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.

29 If your right eye causes you to sin, gouge it out and throw it away. It is better for you to lose one part of your body than for your whole body to be thrown into hell. 30 And if your right hand causes you to sin, cut it off and throw it away. It is better for you to lose one part of your body than for your whole body to depart into hell.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The second example concerns the command against adultery in Exodus 20:14 and Deuteronomy 5:18. As with anger and murder, Jesus brings attention to what is happening within a person before the outward act. He describes looking at a woman in order to lust after her, and calls that adultery in the heart.

The verb for lusting is ἐπιθυμέω, epithymeō (eh-pee-thoo-MEH-oh), to desire or set one's heart on something. Thayer's Greek Lexicon notes its sexual use here and its use for coveting elsewhere. The surrounding words identify the desire at issue. The command against coveting a neighbor's wife in Exodus 20:17 also shows that the Law already addressed desire within the heart.

Jesus then uses the vivid pictures of an eye and a hand causing a person to sin. Losing something precious is presented as better than allowing sin to bring the whole person to ruin. The repeated warning makes the cost of resisting sin smaller than the cost of surrendering to it.

The responsibility remains with the person looking and nurturing the desire. The passage calls for faithfulness within the heart and a serious response to whatever leads a person away from it. The following verses continue the concern for marital faithfulness by addressing divorce.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand the passage as calling for purity of intention and a decisive break with what leads to sin. Chrysostom's Homily 17 on Matthew and Wesley's notes on Matthew 5:29–30 read the eye and hand as forceful pictures of parting with something deeply valued that leads a person into sin, rather than instructions to injure the body.
passages.god_plan_html:
The New Testament places the struggle against sinful desire within the new life God gives in Christ. Colossians 3:5–10 calls for putting sinful practices to death and describes the new self being renewed in the Creator's image. The aim reaches further than avoiding a visible offense: God is renewing the person from within.

Romans 6:12–14 calls people brought from death to life to offer the parts of their bodies to God for righteousness. 1 Corinthians 6:18–20 connects sexual faithfulness with belonging to God and being bought at a price. The body is to honor the One who has redeemed it. That larger purpose gives direction to the costly resistance Jesus describes.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 5:31-32
passages.section_title: Marriage and Faithfulness

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 31 It has also been said, ‘Whoever divorces his wife must give her a certificate of divorce.’ 32 But I tell you that anyone who divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, brings adultery upon her. And he who marries a divorced woman commits adultery.
paragraphs: 31 It has also been said, ‘Whoever divorces his wife must give her a certificate of divorce.’ 32 But I tell you that anyone who divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, brings adultery upon her. And he who marries a divorced woman commits adultery.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus continues His teaching about faithfulness by addressing divorce. The certificate mentioned in verse 31 comes from Deuteronomy 24:1–4. That law describes a woman who is divorced, marries another man, and then loses that second marriage. Its specific prohibition concerns her return to the first husband. It does not command husbands to divorce their wives.

Jesus brings attention to what divorce can do to the marriage relationship. Providing the document does not by itself settle the moral question. His warning connects sending a wife away and marrying a divorced woman with adultery, while including an exception concerning sexual immorality.

The word behind sexual immorality is πορνεία, porneia (por-NAY-ah). Thayer's Greek Lexicon gives the general meaning of unlawful sexual intercourse and includes adultery among its uses. The word identifies a sexual wrong; Christians differ over precisely what situation Jesus means here and how the exception affects divorce and remarriage.

The fuller discussion in Matthew 19:3–9 returns to God's joining husband and wife as one flesh. Jesus describes Moses' permission as a response to human hardness of heart. Mark 10:2–12 also records His teaching about divorce, addressing both husbands and wives. 1 Corinthians 7:10–16 discusses separation, reconciliation, and an unbelieving spouse's departure. These passages are important to the different Christian readings below.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians agree that Jesus treats marriage as a serious, faithful commitment. They differ over when divorce is permitted and whether a later marriage can be recognized.

The Catholic Church teaches that a valid marriage between baptized spouses cannot be ended by human authority once they have had marital relations. Its Catechism, 2382–2386, distinguishes separation or a necessary civil divorce from ending the marriage bond. Civil divorce may be accepted to protect certain rights or children; a new union while the marriage bond remains is regarded as adulterous. The Catechism also distinguishes an unjustly abandoned spouse from the person responsible for destroying the marriage.

In the Reformed tradition, the Westminster Confession, chapter 24.5–6, allows an innocent spouse to divorce and remarry after adultery. It also recognizes deliberate desertion that neither church nor civil authority can remedy as grounds for ending the marriage. This reading brings Matthew's exception together with Paul's discussion of desertion in 1 Corinthians 7.

The Orthodox Church in America's Holy Synod statement on marriage, section F, upholds lifelong marriage while allowing a bishop to consider a later marriage after civil divorce. It describes this as a pastoral response to a broken marriage, with repentance and the possibility of a new beginning, rather than treating divorce as the ideal.

The United Methodist Church's Social Principles, Marriage: Divorce, recognize divorce as sometimes necessary when a relationship has become destructive or cannot be repaired. They state that divorce does not rule out remarriage and that faithfulness does not require remaining in an abusive relationship. This is that church's stated approach; it should not be assumed to describe every Wesleyan church or teacher.
passages.god_plan_html:
Marriage also becomes a way Scripture helps us understand Christ's love. Ephesians 5:25–33 calls husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave Himself for her. Paul repeats the creation account's words about becoming one flesh, then connects this mystery with Christ and the church.

That connection gives marriage a purpose beyond a legal arrangement: it can show faithful, self-giving love. Jesus' return to the Creator's purpose in Matthew 19:4–6 and Paul's description of Christ's care both direct attention to what God intends the relationship to express. The comparison does not supply a separate rule for every divorce situation; it shows why faithfulness and care matter within God's larger work.
