passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 5:33-37
passages.section_title: A Trustworthy Yes and No

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 33 Again, you have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘Do not break your oath, but fulfill your vows to the Lord.’ 34 But I tell you not to swear at all: either by heaven, for it is God’s throne; 35 or by the earth, for it is His footstool; or by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King. 36 Nor should you swear by your head, for you cannot make a single hair white or black. 37 Simply let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes,’ and your ‘No,’ ‘No.’ Anything more comes from the evil one.
paragraphs: 33 Again, you have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘Do not break your oath, but fulfill your vows to the Lord.’ 34 But I tell you not to swear at all: either by heaven, for it is God’s throne; 35 or by the earth, for it is His footstool; or by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King. 36 Nor should you swear by your head, for you cannot make a single hair white or black.
37 Simply let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes,’ and your ‘No,’ ‘No.’ Anything more comes from the evil one.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus moves from marital faithfulness to trustworthiness in speech. Leviticus 19:12 forbids swearing falsely in God's name, and Numbers 30:1–2 requires a person to keep a vow made to the LORD. The concern is whether a person's words can be relied upon.

Jesus names heaven, earth, Jerusalem, and a person's own head as things people might swear by. Each example reaches beyond the speaker's control. Heaven and earth belong to God; Jerusalem is His King's city; even the speaker's life is not something he rules. The throne and footstool imagery appears in Isaiah 66:1–2, and the description of Jerusalem recalls Psalm 48:1–2. Changing the object of an oath does not place the speaker outside God's concern for truth.

The positive direction is simple: a yes should mean yes, and a no should mean no. James 5:12 repeats that instruction. In Matthew 23:16–22, Jesus also rejects distinctions that treat an oath by the temple or altar as less binding than one by its gold or gift. His followers' ordinary words are to be dependable.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the passage as requiring honest speech and rejecting careless or deceptive oaths. They differ over whether Jesus forbids every oath, including one required in court.

The Catholic Church understands Jesus' words to allow an oath for a serious and right purpose, such as truthful testimony in court. Its Catechism, 2153–2155, forbids using God's name for trivial or wrongful purposes. In the Reformed tradition, the Westminster Confession, chapter 22.1–4, likewise permits solemn oaths on just and important occasions. It requires truthfulness and rejects wording intended to mislead.

Mennonite teaching takes the prohibition to include all oaths. Mennonite Church USA's Confession of Faith, article 20, says followers of Jesus should always speak truthfully and use a legal affirmation instead of swearing an oath. An affirmation is a promise to tell the truth without invoking an oath. The difference concerns the use of oaths; both readings require the same honesty in everyday speech.
passages.god_plan_html:
Trustworthy speech reflects the character of the God who keeps His promises. Hebrews 6:13–18 recalls God's promise and oath to Abraham, explaining that His unchanging purpose gives His people strong encouragement. Their hope rests on the One who does not lie.

2 Corinthians 1:18–22 connects God's faithfulness with His promises being fulfilled in Christ. Ephesians 4:25 then calls believers to speak truth because they belong to one another as members of one body. God's dependable word creates a people whose own words should help others trust them. These connections explain the larger purpose of truthful speech without settling the disagreement about whether Christians may take an oath.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 5:38-42
passages.section_title: Mercy Instead of Personal Revenge

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 38 You have heard that it was said, ‘Eye for eye and tooth for tooth.’ 39 But I tell you not to resist an evil person. If someone slaps you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also; 40 if someone wants to sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well; 41 and if someone forces you to go one mile, go with him two miles. 42 Give to the one who asks you, and do not turn away from the one who wants to borrow from you.
paragraphs: 38 You have heard that it was said, ‘Eye for eye and tooth for tooth.’ 39 But I tell you not to resist an evil person. If someone slaps you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also;

40 if someone wants to sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well; 41 and if someone forces you to go one mile, go with him two miles. 42 Give to the one who asks you, and do not turn away from the one who wants to borrow from you.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus next addresses the desire to answer harm with harm. The eye-for-eye rule appears in Exodus 21:22–25, Leviticus 24:19–22, and Deuteronomy 19:18–21. These laws concern proportionate consequences for injury and wrongdoing. Deuteronomy places the decision in the hands of judges investigating a case.

Jesus' examples concern a slap, a lawsuit for clothing, forced service, and requests for help. In each case He directs the hearer away from insisting on personal repayment and toward a response that gives more than the other person demands. The closing words make generosity part of the teaching alongside refusing revenge.

The verb for forcing someone to go a mile is ἀγγαρεύω, angareuō (ang-gar-YOO-oh). Thayer's Greek Lexicon explains it as compelling someone to make a journey, carry a burden, or perform another service. Matthew uses the same verb when Simon is made to carry Jesus' cross in Matthew 27:32. Here Jesus calls for a willing second mile in response to a compelled first one.

The saying about not resisting an evil person raises questions about how far the command extends. The illustrations plainly challenge the impulse to retaliate. Christians differ over how those instructions relate to protecting another person, the work of government, and the use of force.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly reject personal vengeance and call for mercy and generosity. Their differences become clearer when they discuss defense against violence and public responsibility.

Catholic teaching allows proportionate defense of oneself or others and says protecting those in one's care can be a duty; see the Catechism, 2263–2265. The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 23.1–2, permits Christians to serve in government and recognizes a public role in restraining wrongdoing, including war on just and necessary occasions. These teachings distinguish giving up private revenge from rejecting every use of protective or public force.

Mennonite teaching understands following Jesus to require a nonviolent response even to violence and warfare. Mennonite Church USA's Confession of Faith, article 22, rejects military participation and calls believers to resist evil without violence. It also opposes abuse and injustice: this reading seeks an active, peaceful response to wrong rather than simply leaving it unchallenged.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus' own suffering gives the teaching a powerful expression. 1 Peter 2:21–25 describes Him enduring insults and suffering without returning threats, entrusting Himself to the One who judges justly. Peter presents His conduct as an example for His followers and also explains that He bore their sins. The cross is both God's saving work and a pattern of responding to evil without returning it.

Romans 12:17–21 places the same response within trust in God's judgment. Believers are to leave vengeance to God, care for an enemy in need, and overcome evil with good. This gives a larger reason for the costly generosity Jesus describes: His people can act for another person's good because justice does not finally depend on their taking revenge.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 5:43-48
passages.section_title: Loving Beyond Those Who Love Us

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 43 You have heard that it was said, ‘Love your neighbor’ and ‘Hate your enemy.’ 44 But I tell you, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, 45 that you may be sons of your Father in heaven. He causes His sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous. 46 If you love those who love you, what reward will you get? Do not even tax collectors do the same? 47 And if you greet only your brothers, what are you doing more than others? Do not even Gentiles do the same? 48 Be perfect, therefore, as your heavenly Father is perfect.
paragraphs: 43 You have heard that it was said, ‘Love your neighbor’ and ‘Hate your enemy.’ 44 But I tell you, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, 45 that you may be sons of your Father in heaven. He causes His sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous.

46 If you love those who love you, what reward will you get? Do not even tax collectors do the same? 47 And if you greet only your brothers, what are you doing more than others? Do not even Gentiles do the same? 48 Be perfect, therefore, as your heavenly Father is perfect.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
This final example in chapter 5 extends the call to mercy into loving an enemy. The command to love a neighbor comes from Leviticus 19:18. That same chapter also commands love for the foreigner living among Israel in verses 33–34. And Exodus 23:4–5 requires helping an enemy recover a stray animal or lift an animal fallen under its load. God's Law already called for good to reach beyond friendly relationships.

Jesus rejects hatred as the rule for dealing with an enemy. He tells His hearers to love their enemies and pray for their persecutors. This is active concern for another person's good, including someone who has done harm. The Father's example is the reason He gives: God sends sunshine and rain to both the righteous and the unrighteous.

The questions about tax collectors and Gentiles expose the limit of loving only those who return the favor. Jesus calls His people to show more than the kindness that keeps a friendly circle comfortable. Their conduct is to reflect their Father, including toward those outside that circle.

The final command uses τέλειος, teleios (TEH-lay-oss), translated perfect. Thayer's Greek Lexicon describes completeness and, in its use here, integrity of character. The Father is the standard. In this immediate setting, love must reach beyond a favored group; the sentence also gathers up the chapter's wider call to righteousness within the heart and in action. Luke 6:27–36 gives closely related teaching and ends by calling for mercy like the Father's.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the passage as calling for genuine love and prayer for enemies, following the Father's example. The final command also raises a question about how the perfection Jesus describes relates to the believer's present life.

Wesley's note on Matthew 5:48 reads the command as a promise that God can bring about the holiness He requires by changing His people's hearts. He sees it as the conclusion to the holiness described throughout the chapter. In the Reformed tradition, the Westminster Confession, chapter 13, teaches that God's Spirit changes the whole person, while sin remains a continuing struggle in this life. Growth in holiness is real, but remains incomplete.

The Catholic Church's Catechism, 2013–2015, applies this command to all Christians as a call to the fullness of love. It describes a life of service and ongoing growth through Christ's strength, including sacrifice and spiritual struggle. These explanations share the call to become like the Father, while placing different emphasis on the promise and progress of that change.
passages.god_plan_html:
God's kindness toward enemies reaches its fullest expression in Christ. Romans 5:6–11 says Christ died for the ungodly and that people who were God's enemies were reconciled through His Son's death. He acted for their good before they had become His friends. That gives the enemy-love Jesus commands a place within God's own saving work.

The Son also came near to the people He saves. Hebrews 2:9–18 describes Him sharing their humanity, suffering death, and bringing many sons to glory. This is more than a helpful neighbor's gesture: Christ shares human life and bears suffering to rescue His people.

Ephesians 5:1–2 then calls believers to imitate God as His loved children and to walk in the love Christ showed by giving Himself. The family likeness grows out of God's prior love. 1 John 4:9–12,19–21 likewise connects the Son's saving mission with the love His people show. God's purpose includes forming children who make His generous character visible.
passages.current_position_html: Our study The Gospel According to Jesus understands this command as showing the character of the King who died for His enemies. It reads the Sermon on the Mount as the life that grows from receiving the gospel, rather than a way to earn the kingdom.

passages.title: Matthew 6:1-4
passages.section_title: Giving Without Seeking Applause

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 “Be careful not to perform your righteous acts before men to be seen by them. If you do, you will have no reward from your Father in heaven. 2 So when you give to the needy, do not sound a trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and on the streets, to be honored by men. Truly I tell you, they already have their full reward. 3 But when you give to the needy, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing, 4 so that your giving may be in secret. And your Father, who sees what is done in secret, will reward you.
paragraphs: 1 “Be careful not to perform your righteous acts before men to be seen by them. If you do, you will have no reward from your Father in heaven. 2 So when you give to the needy, do not sound a trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and on the streets, to be honored by men. Truly I tell you, they already have their full reward.

3 But when you give to the needy, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing, 4 so that your giving may be in secret. And your Father, who sees what is done in secret, will reward you.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus now addresses the purpose behind acts of righteousness. Chapter 6 begins with giving to the needy, then turns to prayer and fasting. The opening warning concerns doing good in order to be noticed. The action may help someone, yet the giver's aim can still be to win admiration.

The trumpet image makes that desire for attention vivid. Jesus describes people using their giving to gain honor in public, then says they have already received their reward. The praise they sought is the return they have obtained. His contrast is with the Father, who sees what other people do not.

The word for hypocrites is ὑποκριτής, hypokritēs (hoo-poh-kree-TAYS). Thayer's Greek Lexicon lists the earlier use for an actor and explains its biblical use as someone pretending to be what he is not. Here the appearance of generosity conceals a desire for personal honor.

The picture of one hand not knowing what the other is doing presses the opposite response: give quietly, without turning the gift into a display. This fits with Matthew 5:16, where visible good deeds lead people to glorify the Father. In both passages the question is where the attention is meant to go. Jesus calls the giver to trust the Father's knowledge and reward instead of making public recognition the goal.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this passage as a call to sincere generosity, with God's approval taking the place of public admiration. Wesley on Matthew 6:1–3 distinguishes being seen from acting in order to be admired, and understands the hands as a picture of giving as privately as effective help allows. The Catholic Catechism, 1753, likewise uses giving for personal vanity as an example of how a wrong intention can corrupt an outwardly good act.
passages.god_plan_html:
Christian generosity is connected with the grace first received from Christ. 2 Corinthians 8:1–9 describes God's grace producing generous giving even among people in poverty. Paul then points to Jesus, who became poor for their sake so that they could become rich through Him. His self-giving is the foundation for their care for others.

The result of giving is also meant to extend beyond the donor. 2 Corinthians 9:6–15 describes needs being met, thanksgiving rising to God, and relationships strengthened through prayer and affection. God's grace creates a generous people whose service directs gratitude toward Him.

Quiet service is not lost to God. Hebrews 6:10–12 assures believers that He remembers the work and love shown in serving His people. 1 Corinthians 4:5 looks forward to the Lord bringing hidden motives to light. The Father Jesus describes here sees both the gift and the heart behind it.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 6:5-8
passages.section_title: Prayer Before the Father

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 And when you pray, do not be like the hypocrites. For they love to pray standing in the synagogues and on the street corners to be seen by men. Truly I tell you, they already have their full reward. 6 But when you pray, go into your inner room, shut your door, and pray to your Father, who is unseen. And your Father, who sees what is done in secret, will reward you. 7 And when you pray, do not babble on like pagans, for they think that by their many words they will be heard. 8 Do not be like them, for your Father knows what you need before you ask Him.
paragraphs: 5 And when you pray, do not be like the hypocrites. For they love to pray standing in the synagogues and on the street corners to be seen by men. Truly I tell you, they already have their full reward. 6 But when you pray, go into your inner room, shut your door, and pray to your Father, who is unseen. And your Father, who sees what is done in secret, will reward you.
7 And when you pray, do not babble on like pagans, for they think that by their many words they will be heard. 8 Do not be like them, for your Father knows what you need before you ask Him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus applies the warning about seeking public praise to prayer. In the preceding verses, a gift to the needy could become a way to gain honor. Here prayer itself can become a performance. The people Jesus describes want to be seen, and the attention they receive is the reward they have sought.

His alternative is to enter a private room, close the door, and pray to the Father. Without an audience to impress, the person praying can direct attention to God. The Father sees the prayer that others never notice. The point concerns whom the prayer is for, rather than making public prayer wrong: Acts 4:23–31 describes believers praying together and receiving God's help.

The second warning concerns a stream of words treated as a way to secure a hearing. The Greek verb is βαττολογέω, battologeō (bat-toh-loh-GEH-oh). Thayer's Greek Lexicon explains its use here as babbling or using many idle words. Jesus identifies the mistaken expectation: being heard because of the quantity of words.

Repeated words are not automatically empty words. In Matthew 26:39–44, Jesus prays again with the same request while submitting to His Father's will. Luke 18:1–8 also encourages persistence in prayer. The warning here is against relying on a display or a mass of words to make prayer effective.

Verse 8 gives the reason for a different approach: the Father already knows what His children need. Prayer is not the task of bringing a reluctant or uninformed God up to date. The prayer Jesus gives next shows how people who trust their Father can seek His will, ask for provision and forgiveness, and depend on His protection.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand these verses as rejecting prayer offered for show or as an empty stream of words. Wesley on Matthew 6:6–9, the Catholic Catechism, 2700–2704, and the Reformed Westminster Larger Catechism, question 187, all emphasize prayer that is meant from the heart; they allow sincere use of the Lord's Prayer while rejecting words used without understanding or faith.
passages.god_plan_html:
Approaching God as Father belongs to His saving work. Galatians 4:4–7 describes God sending His Son to redeem people and give them the place of children in His family. He also sends the Spirit of His Son into their hearts, enabling them to call on Him as Father. The relationship comes from God's action before it is expressed in their prayer.

Ephesians 2:17–22 describes people once separated being brought into God's household. Through Christ, both groups have access to the Father by one Spirit. This gives the quiet prayer Jesus describes a larger setting: God's rescue brings people near to Him. Their welcome rests on that relationship, rather than on a public display of religious skill.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Prayer and Faith understands prayer as communion with God, submission to His will, and dependence on Christ. It reads Jesus' prayer teaching as a pattern for that relationship, rather than a formula for securing an outcome. Here that directs attention to the Father and the heart of the person praying, rather than to an audience or a word count.

passages.title: Matthew 6:7
passages.section_title: Words That Mean Something

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 And when you pray, do not babble on like pagans, for they think that by their many words they will be heard.
paragraphs: 7 And when you pray, do not babble on like pagans, for they think that by their many words they will be heard.

passages.context_html:
This verse belongs to Jesus' teaching about prayer in Matthew 6:5–13. He has just warned against praying to gain an audience's admiration. He now warns against another mistake: supposing that using many words is what makes God listen.

The verb for babbling is βαττολογέω, battologeō (bat-toh-loh-GEH-oh). Thayer's Greek Lexicon explains it here as using many idle words or repeating things emptily. The end of the verse explains the problem. The speakers trust the amount they say as the reason they will be heard.

Jesus is not setting a maximum prayer length or treating every repeated request as meaningless. In Matthew 26:39–44, He returns to the same request in prayer, always submitting to His Father's will. Luke 18:1–8 calls for persistence. A person can return sincerely to a need without treating repetition as a way to force God's hand.

The next verse says the Father already knows what is needed. The model prayer that follows is direct and purposeful. God's name, kingdom, and will guide the requests; the person praying depends on Him for provision, forgiveness, and protection.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand these verses as rejecting prayer offered for show or as an empty stream of words. Wesley on Matthew 6:6–9, the Catholic Catechism, 2700–2704, and the Reformed Westminster Larger Catechism, question 187, all emphasize prayer that is meant from the heart; they allow sincere use of the Lord's Prayer while rejecting words used without understanding or faith.
passages.current_position_html:
Our study Prayer and Faith rejects treating prayer as a formula for obtaining the result we want. It understands Jesus' model as teaching dependence on God and submission to His will. The warning against mechanical repetition fits that reading: a quantity of words cannot replace trust in the Father.

Our companion study What Does Prayer Look Like? points to Jesus' repeated prayer in Gethsemane and explains that continued asking can remain consistent with surrender. It is the Father's will that must govern the asking.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
God's help in prayer reaches into human weakness. Romans 8:26–27 says people do not know how to pray as they should, yet the Spirit helps and intercedes according to God's will. The passage places their hope in His help, not in an ability to produce impressive speech.

Hebrews 4:14–16 gives another reason for confidence: Jesus is the great High Priest who understands human weakness. Through Him, believers can approach God's grace for mercy and help. God's saving provision opens the way for sincere prayer even when the person praying struggles to find words.

passages.title: Matthew 6:8
passages.section_title: The Father Knows Before We Ask

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 Do not be like them, for your Father knows what you need before you ask Him.
paragraphs: 8 Do not be like them, for your Father knows what you need before you ask Him.

passages.context_html:
Jesus has just described people who expect to be heard because they use many words. Verse 8 gives His followers a different starting point: their Father knows their need before they ask. They do not have to attract His attention by building up a volume of speech.

This does not make prayer unnecessary. Immediately afterward, in Matthew 6:9–13, Jesus teaches His followers how to pray. The Father's prior knowledge is the reason they can approach Him with trust, rather than a reason to remain silent. His name, kingdom, and will shape what they seek.

The same Father-child relationship appears throughout this part of the sermon. The Father sees hidden giving and prayer, and later in Matthew 6:25–34 Jesus returns to His knowledge of their needs. His care gives direction to their response: seek His kingdom instead of being ruled by anxiety.

Wesley's note on Matthew 6:8 understands prayer as exercising dependence on God and preparing the heart to receive His grace. That helps explain why asking still matters when God already knows. The person praying turns toward the Father in a relationship of trust.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand these verses as rejecting prayer offered for show or as an empty stream of words. Wesley on Matthew 6:6–9, the Catholic Catechism, 2700–2704, and the Reformed Westminster Larger Catechism, question 187, all emphasize prayer that is meant from the heart; they allow sincere use of the Lord's Prayer while rejecting words used without understanding or faith.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Prayer and Faith understands prayer as submission to the God who already knows the way ahead. It emphasizes seeking His will and trusting His wisdom, rather than trying to secure a preferred outcome through enough persistence or the right wording. The Father's prior knowledge is part of the study's reason for that trust.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
God takes the initiative in bringing people into His family. Galatians 4:4–7 describes Him sending His Son for redemption and His Spirit into His children's hearts. Their cry to the Father is a response to what He has already done.

Romans 8:14–17,26–27 connects that family relationship with the Spirit's help in prayer. God's children are not left to rely on their own understanding of what to ask. The Father who knows them also provides help in their weakness. His knowledge and care support their dependence; they do not turn prayer into a way to control Him.

passages.title: Matthew 6:9-10
passages.section_title: The Father's Name, Kingdom, and Will

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 So then, this is how you should pray: ‘Our Father in heaven, hallowed be Your name. 10 Your kingdom come, Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven.
paragraphs: 9 So then, this is how you should pray: ‘Our Father in heaven, hallowed be Your name. 10 Your kingdom come, Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven.

passages.context_html:
Jesus has warned against praying to impress others or relying on a large number of words. He now gives a prayer that directs attention to the Father. The opening petitions concern God's name, His kingdom, and His will. What the person praying seeks is shaped by who God is and what He desires.

Hallowed means honored as holy. The verb is ἁγιάζω, hagiazō (hah-gee-AH-zoh). Thayer's Greek Lexicon explains its use here as acknowledging God's name to be holy. The request does not suggest God needs to become morally better. It asks that He be regarded and honored as He truly is.

The request for God's kingdom follows the announcement of the kingdom earlier in Matthew 4:17. It asks for God's reign to come, and the next petition asks that His will be done on earth as in heaven. The prayer reaches beyond the speaker's immediate concerns toward the world being brought under God's good rule.

This orientation continues as the prayer turns to bread, forgiveness, and protection. The word our also places the speaker among others who depend on the same Father. Jesus' own prayer in Matthew 26:39–44 later shows the cost of submitting a real and painful desire to the Father's will.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand these petitions as asking that God be honored, His reign be established, and His will shape life on earth. Wesley's notes on Matthew 6:9–10 and the Reformed Westminster Larger Catechism, questions 189–192, connect the words both with God's work among people now and with the fulfillment of His kingdom; neither treats them as merely an opening phrase before the real requests begin.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Prayer and Faith reads God's will as governing the whole model prayer. The requests that follow are to remain directed toward Him, rather than becoming a way to claim control over events. Our companion study What Does Prayer Look Like? points to Gethsemane as an example of honest asking that yields to the Father's will.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
God's kingdom is part of His work of rescue. Colossians 1:12–14 describes the Father bringing people out of darkness into His Son's kingdom, where they receive redemption and forgiveness. The prayer for His reign concerns the God who is already rescuing and bringing people near.

The purpose also reaches toward a final fulfillment. Ephesians 1:7–10 connects redemption with God's plan to bring all things in heaven and earth together in Christ. 1 Corinthians 15:20–28 describes the risen Christ reigning until His enemies, including death, are overcome. Asking for God's kingdom and will places the person's hope within that larger purpose.

passages.title: Matthew 6:9-13
passages.section_title: The Prayer Jesus Teaches

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 So then, this is how you should pray: ‘Our Father in heaven, hallowed be Your name. 10 Your kingdom come, Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. 11 Give us this day our daily bread. 12 And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors. 13 And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one.’
paragraphs: 9 So then, this is how you should pray: ‘Our Father in heaven, hallowed be Your name. 10 Your kingdom come, Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven.
11 Give us this day our daily bread. 12 And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors. 13 And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one.’

passages.context_html:
After warning against prayer for public attention and empty word counts, Jesus gives His followers a prayer addressed to their Father. Its opening requests seek honor for God's name, the coming of His kingdom, and the doing of His will. Hallowed means honored as holy; see Thayer's explanation of the verb in Matthew 6:9. The Father is approached with both trust and reverence.

The prayer then asks for bread, forgiveness, and protection. These requests remain addressed to the Father whose will has just been sought. The repeated our and us place the speaker among other people who share these needs. Prayer reaches beyond the concerns of one isolated person.

The word translated daily is ἐπιούσιος, epiousios (eh-pee-OO-see-oss). Thayer's Greek Lexicon discusses explanations involving necessary sustenance and the coming day. Its exact formation is debated. The word alone does not settle whether a reader should understand the bread as physical provision, spiritual nourishment, or both; those readings are explained below.

The debts of verse 12 represent sins. Thayer's Greek Lexicon identifies that use of the debt word here, and Luke 11:1–4 gives a related prayer that explicitly asks forgiveness of sins. Jesus connects asking for mercy with forgiving others, then returns to that connection in Matthew 6:14–15.

The final request asks for protection from temptation and the evil one. James 1:12–17 distinguishes enduring a trial from being drawn into sin and says God does not tempt people to evil. In Matthew 26:41, Jesus likewise tells His disciples to watch and pray so that they do not enter into temptation. The request expresses dependence on God for protection and faithfulness.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly use this prayer as a guide to approaching God with trust, reverence, and dependence. Wesley on Matthew 6:9 and the Reformed Westminster Larger Catechism, question 187, also allow its actual words to be prayed sincerely; they distinguish that use from a mechanical formula.

Readers differ in how fully they understand the bread to include spiritual nourishment. The Westminster Larger Catechism, question 193, explains the request as God's provision for the needs of this life. Catholic teaching includes food, God's Word, and Christ received in the Eucharist (the Lord's Supper); see its Compendium, questions 592–593. Wesley on verse 11 likewise includes needs of both body and soul, including the bread of the Lord's Supper and God's grace.

The connection between receiving and extending forgiveness is also understood within different accounts of the Christian life. The Reformed Westminster Confession, 11.5, distinguishes God's continuing acceptance of those He has declared righteous through Christ from His disapproval and the damaged relationship that require repentance. Catholic teaching says mercy cannot enter a heart that refuses forgiveness; see its Compendium, questions 594–595. These readings both take the warning seriously, while explaining the believer's need for renewed forgiveness in different ways.
passages.current_position_html:
Our study Prayer and Faith understands the prayer as a pattern of communion with God and submission to His will. It reads the entire prayer under that purpose, rather than treating the opening petitions as a preface to seeking whatever outcome we prefer.

For the bread petition, the study connects Matthew 6:11 with Jesus as the bread of life in John 6. It understands the request as daily dependence on Christ for continued life in Him, rather than a request for material provision. That is the study's reading of the connection between these passages.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The prayer brings God's purpose and His people's dependence together. Ephesians 1:7–10 places forgiveness through Christ's blood within God's plan to bring all things together in Him. The requests for God's reign and for mercy belong within the same saving purpose.

The Father also makes people His children through the Son and gives them His Spirit. Galatians 4:4–7 describes that work and the resulting cry to God as Father. Romans 8:26–27 adds the Spirit's help when they do not know how to pray. God's rescue creates the relationship expressed in this prayer and provides help for living within it.

passages.title: Matthew 6:11
passages.section_title: Our Daily Bread

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 Give us this day our daily bread.
paragraphs: 11 Give us this day our daily bread.

passages.context_html:
This request follows the petitions for God's name, kingdom, and will in Matthew 6:9–13. The person praying depends on the Father to give what sustains life. The request is for us, drawing others into that dependence, and for this day, rather than claiming control of the whole future.

The word translated daily is ἐπιούσιος, epiousios (eh-pee-OO-see-oss). Thayer's Greek Lexicon discusses necessary sustenance and the coming day among its explanations. The term is unusual, and its formation has been debated. It should not be made to prove a whole interpretation by itself.

The ordinary word for bread can also mean food more broadly. Thayer's entry for bread lists that use in Matthew 6:11 and separately explains Jesus' description of Himself as the bread of life in John 6. Bread therefore has an ordinary use for food and a use as a picture of life in Christ. The context matters in deciding how it is being used.

Luke 11:1–4 places a similar daily request within Jesus' teaching on prayer. Later in Matthew 6, Jesus speaks of the Father's knowledge of food and clothing needs and calls His hearers to seek God's kingdom instead of being ruled by anxiety. Readers bring that surrounding teaching to the different understandings below.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
In the Reformed tradition, the Westminster Larger Catechism, question 193, understands the request as asking God for sufficient provision for this life, with contentment and a right use of what He gives.

Catholic teaching includes bodily nourishment, God's Word, and Christ in the Eucharist (the Lord's Supper); see the Compendium, questions 592–593. Wesley's note on Matthew 6:11 also includes the needs of soul and body, the bread of the Lord's Supper, and God's grace. These readings share dependence on God while differing over how the petition includes spiritual nourishment.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Prayer and Faith connects this petition with Jesus' teaching in John 6 about Himself as the bread of life. It understands daily bread as dependence on Christ for continued life in Him, rather than a request for physical food. In that reading, the request remains centered on seeking Him and living in His will. The study develops the connection with abiding in Christ in John 15.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Bread and dependence have a larger place in Scripture. In Exodus 16:4–5,14–21, God provides manna, and Israel gathers what is needed day by day. That account gives a useful parallel for receiving life and provision from God rather than treating them as independently secured.

In John 6:26–35,47–58, Jesus explicitly compares the wilderness manna with the life He gives. The manna's recipients still died; the life He gives lasts beyond death. This connection moves from God's sustaining people in the wilderness to His Son giving life to the world. This is a comparison with the prayer's theme of dependence; John does not directly explain Matthew 6:11.

passages.title: Matthew 6:14-15
passages.section_title: Receiving and Extending Forgiveness

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 For if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you. 15 But if you do not forgive men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive yours.
paragraphs: 14 For if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you. 15 But if you do not forgive men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive yours.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus returns to the request for forgiveness in the prayer He has just taught. In verse 12 the speaker asks the Father to forgive debts while also forgiving debtors. These two verses explain the seriousness of that connection: receiving mercy and extending mercy cannot be treated as unrelated matters.

The debts in the prayer represent sins, as the related prayer in Luke 11:4 makes explicit. Here Jesus speaks of people's trespasses. The concern here is wrong done against another person.

The warning addresses the person asking for forgiveness. Jesus does not describe mercy as something one may receive while deliberately withholding it from everyone else. He presents both sides of the relationship plainly, including the consequence of refusing to forgive.

A later illustration develops the same concern. In Matthew 18:21–35, a servant is forgiven a huge debt but refuses mercy to a fellow servant. Jesus ends by requiring forgiveness from the heart. Christians agree on the seriousness of that call, while differing over how these warnings relate to a believer's standing before God.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand forgiveness of others as essential to a life that receives God's mercy. They differ in how they describe the consequences of a believer's refusal to forgive.

In the Reformed tradition, the Westminster Confession, 11.5, teaches that those God has declared righteous through Christ do not lose that standing, yet can fall under His disapproval as their Father until they repent, confess, and seek pardon. The Westminster Larger Catechism, question 194, connects asking for pardon with forgiveness of others as a reason for confidence, while grounding pardon in Christ's work and God's grace.

Catholic teaching says God's mercy cannot enter a heart that refuses to forgive; it also directs the person who finds forgiveness difficult to the Holy Spirit's help. See the Compendium, questions 594–595. The call concerns a changed heart, including mercy toward enemies.

The Methodist Articles of Religion, article XII, allow for departing from grace after receiving it and returning through repentance and God's help. This differs from Westminster's teaching that God continues to accept those He has declared righteous through Christ. Wesley's note on Matthew 6:12 asks for forgiveness of sins through Christ's blood while God enables the person praying to forgive others. These are descriptions of the cited teachings, rather than a claim that every member explains the warning in the same way.
passages.god_plan_html:
Forgiving others is connected with the forgiveness God gives through Christ. Ephesians 4:31–32 moves from putting away bitterness and malice to kindness and forgiveness, with God's forgiveness in Christ as the pattern.

Colossians 3:12–15 likewise calls people loved by God to bear with one another and forgive as the Lord forgave them. It places that conduct within the peace and unity of one body. God's mercy restores people to Himself and is meant to reshape their life together. This gives the warning a place within His purpose of forming a people who live by the mercy they have received.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 6:16-18
passages.section_title: Fasting for the Father to See

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 When you fast, do not be somber like the hypocrites, for they disfigure their faces to show men they are fasting. Truly I tell you, they already have their full reward. 17 But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, 18 so that your fasting will not be obvious to men, but only to your Father, who is unseen. And your Father, who sees what is done in secret, will reward you.
paragraphs: 16 When you fast, do not be somber like the hypocrites, for they disfigure their faces to show men they are fasting. Truly I tell you, they already have their full reward. 17 But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, 18 so that your fasting will not be obvious to men, but only to your Father, who is unseen. And your Father, who sees what is done in secret, will reward you.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Fasting is the third example of devotion Jesus addresses after giving and prayer. The same question runs through all three: is the person seeking God or other people's admiration? The fast He describes here has become a public display. A somber, neglected appearance makes sure other people notice the sacrifice.

Jesus says that those who seek this attention already have their reward. He then directs His hearers to anoint their heads and wash their faces, so their fasting will not be obvious. The Father sees what others do not. The value of the devotion is not measured by how much discomfort the person manages to show.

The passage speaks of fasting as a practice His hearers know. Its immediate concern is their purpose and conduct while fasting. It does not give a fasting calendar or specify a number of hours here.

The earlier Scriptures also question a fast that leaves the heart unchanged. In Isaiah 58:3–12, people fast while continuing to oppress and quarrel. God calls for freedom from oppression and practical care for hungry and vulnerable people. Outward self-denial cannot take the place of a life turned toward God and the good of others.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand these verses as calling for fasting directed toward God rather than a display of religious effort. Wesley's notes on Matthew 6:16–17 treat fasting as an established practice and the instructions about appearance as a call to dress normally; the Catholic Catechism, 1430, likewise emphasizes that fasting and other outward acts require a heart turning toward God.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus connects fasting with His own mission in Mark 2:18–20. He compares His presence with His disciples to a bridegroom's presence at a wedding and says they will fast when He is taken from them. Their devotion belongs within their relationship with Him, including the time after His departure.

The early church's fasting also accompanies the work of spreading the gospel. In Acts 13:1–4, worship and fasting surround the Spirit's call to send Barnabas and Saul. In Acts 14:21–23, prayer and fasting accompany the appointment of elders and entrusting the churches to the Lord.

These accounts place fasting within dependence on God as He gathers and strengthens His people. The practice serves that relationship and mission. It is not presented as a performance that purchases God's guidance or forces Him to act.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 6:19-24
passages.section_title: Treasure and an Undivided Heart

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy, and where thieves break in and steal. 20 But store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where moth and rust do not destroy, and where thieves do not break in and steal. 21 For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. 22 The eye is the lamp of the body. If your eyes are good, your whole body will be full of light. 23 But if your eyes are bad, your whole body will be full of darkness. If then the light within you is darkness, how great is that darkness! 24 No one can serve two masters: Either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve both God and money.
paragraphs: 19 Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy, and where thieves break in and steal. 20 But store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where moth and rust do not destroy, and where thieves do not break in and steal. 21 For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.

22 The eye is the lamp of the body. If your eyes are good, your whole body will be full of light. 23 But if your eyes are bad, your whole body will be full of darkness. If then the light within you is darkness, how great is that darkness! 24 No one can serve two masters: Either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve both God and money.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The earlier examples of giving, prayer, and fasting asked whose approval a person seeks. Jesus now addresses what a person treasures. Earthly possessions can be damaged, consumed, or stolen. Treasure kept with God is beyond those losses, and the direction of the heart follows what a person values.

The eye and light picture continues the concern for the whole person. A good eye fills the body with light; a bad eye leaves it in darkness. Placed between the sayings about treasure and two masters, the illustration asks what is guiding a person's life. Something meant to provide light can instead leave the person deeply misdirected.

The final saying presents two masters whose claims cannot both govern the same life. The word translated money is μαμωνᾶς, mamōnas (mah-moh-NAHS). Thayer's Greek Lexicon explains it as wealth or riches and notes its use here as a rival master. Jesus is addressing love, devotion, and service: wealth can claim the loyalty that belongs to God.

The teaching that follows about food, clothing, and worry belongs to this same question of allegiance. If God is the One His followers serve, His knowledge and care are to shape how they face their needs. Their security and purpose are to be directed toward Him.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read the treasure and two-masters sayings as a call to give God first loyalty over wealth. Wesley on Matthew 6:19–24 explains the eye picture as an undivided purpose directed toward God, and the US Catholic bishops' notes on Matthew 6:22–24 connect it with being guided by Jesus' teaching about the passing nature of earthly riches.
passages.god_plan_html:
Faith has often required choosing a future with God over present advantage. Hebrews 11:24–26 describes Moses choosing hardship with God's people over Egypt's treasures, looking ahead to his reward. Hebrews describes that hardship as bearing disgrace for Christ. That provides a concrete example of value being measured by God's future rather than immediate gain.

For those joined to the risen Christ, the future is tied to Him. Colossians 3:1–4 calls believers to seek the things above because their life is hidden with Christ and will be revealed with Him. The reason for a changed focus is the new life He has given.

1 Timothy 6:17–19 makes that hope practical for people who possess wealth: trust God, do good, and share generously. It describes such a life as storing up a foundation for the future. Wealth can be used in service of God's purposes when the heart's hope rests in Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 6:25-34
passages.section_title: Trusting the Father's Care

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 25 Therefore I tell you, do not worry about your life, what you will eat or drink; or about your body, what you will wear. Is not life more than food, and the body more than clothes? 26 Look at the birds of the air: They do not sow or reap or gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not much more valuable than they? 27 Who of you by worrying can add a single hour to his life? 28 And why do you worry about clothes? Consider how the lilies of the field grow: They do not labor or spin. 29 Yet I tell you that not even Solomon in all his glory was adorned like one of these. 30 If that is how God clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the furnace, will He not much more clothe you, O you of little faith? 31 Therefore do not worry, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ or ‘What shall we wear?’ 32 For the Gentiles strive after all these things, and your heavenly Father knows that you need them. 33 But seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things will be added unto you. 34 Therefore do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will worry about itself. Today has enough trouble of its own.
paragraphs: 25 Therefore I tell you, do not worry about your life, what you will eat or drink; or about your body, what you will wear. Is not life more than food, and the body more than clothes? 26 Look at the birds of the air: They do not sow or reap or gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not much more valuable than they? 27 Who of you by worrying can add a single hour to his life?

28 And why do you worry about clothes? Consider how the lilies of the field grow: They do not labor or spin. 29 Yet I tell you that not even Solomon in all his glory was adorned like one of these. 30 If that is how God clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the furnace, will He not much more clothe you, O you of little faith?

31 Therefore do not worry, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ or ‘What shall we wear?’ 32 For the Gentiles strive after all these things, and your heavenly Father knows that you need them. 33 But seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things will be added unto you. 34 Therefore do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will worry about itself. Today has enough trouble of its own.

passages.context_html:
Jesus turns from serving God instead of money to the worries that can make that loyalty difficult. Food, drink, and clothing are real needs. His illustrations begin with the greater gifts already received: life and the body. He then points to the Father's care for birds and the beauty of flowers.

The word for being anxious is μεριμνάω, merimnaō (meh-rim-NAH-oh). Thayer's Greek Lexicon explains its use here as being troubled with cares. The surrounding examples show the concern: attention consumed by sustaining life, clothing the body, and securing tomorrow.

Birds and flowers help His hearers consider the Father's care. Jesus says people matter more to Him than these things do. Worry cannot extend a person's life, and even Solomon's splendor does not equal the flowers' beauty. The questions press His hearers toward trusting the Father who knows them.

Jesus then contrasts a life occupied with securing these things with seeking God's kingdom and righteousness first. The reason He gives is personal: their heavenly Father knows what they need. His rule and what is right before Him are to direct their priorities.

The closing words bring attention back to today. Tomorrow has its own concerns, and today already has trouble to face. Jesus calls His followers to meet the present day in trust, instead of adding the whole imagined weight of the future to it.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this passage as calling for trust in the Father's care and giving His kingdom first place, rather than allowing material needs to dominate life. Wesley's notes on Matthew 6:25–34 and the Catholic Catechism, 305–306, both place the teaching within confidence in God's care; the Catechism also explains that He works through the actions of His creatures.
passages.current_position_html:
Our study Prayer and Faith understands this passage as reordering the whole life toward God's kingdom and will. It places confidence in the Father's knowledge and provision, rather than treating prayer as a method of securing a preferred outcome.

Our companion study What Does Prayer Look Like? makes clear that asking is not itself sinful. Its emphasis is that growing trust releases control of circumstances and gives greater attention to God's purposes. Both studies understand seeking Him as the governing direction of life and prayer.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The Father's care reaches its deepest expression in His gift of the Son. Romans 8:31–39 connects confidence in God's generosity with Christ's death, resurrection, and continuing prayer for His people. God's love has acted decisively for His people.

The same passage names distress, persecution, famine, and danger as hardships that cannot separate them from that love. Paul also describes his own hunger and exposure in 2 Corinthians 11:27. Trust in the Father therefore reaches through hardship; His saving care is larger than the ease of a particular day.

God's care also takes visible shape in the generosity of His people. 2 Corinthians 9:6–15 describes His grace supplying good works, meeting needs, and producing thanksgiving. People who trust the Father are drawn into caring for one another as His saving work creates a generous community.

passages.title: Matthew 6:31-33
passages.section_title: A Different First Priority

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 31 Therefore do not worry, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ or ‘What shall we wear?’ 32 For the Gentiles strive after all these things, and your heavenly Father knows that you need them. 33 But seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things will be added unto you.
paragraphs: 31 Therefore do not worry, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ or ‘What shall we wear?’ 32 For the Gentiles strive after all these things, and your heavenly Father knows that you need them. 33 But seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things will be added unto you.

passages.context_html:
These verses draw together Jesus' teaching about birds, flowers, and the Father's care in Matthew 6:25–34. The repeated questions about food, drink, and clothing express a life taken up with its needs. Jesus directs His followers toward a different first priority.

His comparison turns on knowing the Father. He describes the Gentiles as striving after these things, then reminds His hearers that their Father already knows their need. The contrast asks them to live from that relationship, with His kingdom and righteousness shaping what they pursue.

The promise concerns the needs already named. It is not a blank check for every possession or lifestyle a person might desire. The surrounding chapter has warned against making earthly treasure a master, and verse 34 still speaks of trouble in the present day.

In Luke 12:22–34, the related teaching connects trust, seeking the kingdom, and generosity. The Father's care is meant to free people to follow His purposes and share with others.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this passage as calling for trust in the Father's care and giving His kingdom first place, rather than allowing material needs to dominate life. Wesley's notes on Matthew 6:25–34 and the Catholic Catechism, 305–306, both place the teaching within confidence in God's care; the Catechism also explains that He works through the actions of His creatures.
passages.current_position_html: Our studies Prayer and Faith and What Does Prayer Look Like? understand the central issue as the direction of a person's trust. They call for seeking God and His will, with needs entrusted to His care, rather than making a desired outcome the goal of faith. The companion study distinguishes that surrender from a rule that asking is sinful.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Seeking God's kingdom belongs within His work of bringing people into it. Colossians 1:12–14 describes the Father rescuing people from darkness and bringing them into His Son's kingdom, where they receive redemption and forgiveness. The One they are called to trust is also the One who has acted to rescue them.

The kingdom reaches beyond a person's immediate circumstances. Ephesians 1:7–10 places forgiveness through Christ within God's purpose of bringing all things together in Him. Giving that purpose first place directs a life toward what God is bringing to fulfillment.

passages.title: Matthew 6:33
passages.section_title: Seek His Kingdom First

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 33 But seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things will be added unto you.
paragraphs: 33 But seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things will be added unto you.

passages.context_html:
This verse gives the positive direction at the center of Matthew 6:25–34. Jesus has named the worries of food, drink, and clothing, pointed to God's care in creation, and reminded His hearers that their Father knows their needs. Seeking His kingdom comes within that invitation to trust.

The verb is ζητέω, zēteō (zay-TEH-oh). Thayer's Greek Lexicon explains its use here as aiming at or striving after something. The instruction concerns what directs the life. God's reign and righteousness are to take first place.

All these things refers back to the food, drink, and clothing already discussed. Earlier in the chapter Jesus warned against storing up earthly treasure and trying to serve both God and money. The promise is about the Father's care within a life directed toward Him.

The next verse acknowledges the trouble each day brings. Giving God's kingdom first place provides a direction for facing life, while the Father's knowledge gives a reason for trust.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this verse as calling for God's reign and righteousness to guide life ahead of anxious pursuit of material security. Wesley's note on Matthew 6:33 describes God reigning in the heart and filling the life with righteousness, while the Catholic Catechism, 305, places the words within a child's trust in the Father's care.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Prayer and Faith reads this verse as a call to seek God and His will, rather than demanding outcomes from Him. It understands provision as following the Father's care, not as something owed because a request was worded correctly. Our companion study What Does Prayer Look Like? develops the same emphasis on surrender and trust while recognizing that asking is not itself sinful.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
God's kingdom changes life from within. When discussing disputes about food, Romans 14:17–19 describes its priorities as righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit, then calls believers to pursue peace and build one another up. Seeking His reign has visible consequences in how His people treat each other.

The Father also delights to give His people the kingdom. Luke 12:29–34 connects seeking it with that assurance and with generosity toward the poor. God's care and gift become reasons for an openhanded life, whose hope reaches beyond possessions.

passages.title: Matthew 7:1-5
passages.section_title: Seeing Clearly Before Correcting Others

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 “Do not judge, or you will be judged. 2 For with the same judgment you pronounce, you will be judged, and with the measure you use, it will be measured to you. 3 Why do you look at the speck in your brother’s eye but fail to notice the beam in your own eye? 4 How can you say to your brother, ‘Let me take the speck out of your eye,’ while there is still a beam in your own eye? 5 You hypocrite! First take the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother’s eye.
paragraphs: 1 “Do not judge, or you will be judged. 2 For with the same judgment you pronounce, you will be judged, and with the measure you use, it will be measured to you.

3 Why do you look at the speck in your brother’s eye but fail to notice the beam in your own eye? 4 How can you say to your brother, ‘Let me take the speck out of your eye,’ while there is still a beam in your own eye? 5 You hypocrite! First take the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother’s eye.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus now addresses how His followers regard the faults of other people. The warning begins with judgment and the standard a person uses. Someone who passes judgment is also accountable: the measure used for others will be applied to the person using it.

The verb for judging is κρίνω, krinō (KREE-noh). Thayer's Greek Lexicon gives a range of uses for forming or passing judgment and identifies harsh, unfair faultfinding in this verse. The surrounding illustration shows the problem Jesus is exposing: attending closely to someone else's fault while failing to face one's own.

A tiny speck and a large beam make the contrast vivid. The person offering help cannot see clearly because of the much larger obstruction in his own eye. His claim to help another is hollow while he leaves his own problem untouched. Jesus calls that hypocrisy.

The final instruction gives an order: remove the beam first, then help with the brother's speck. The aim includes genuine help after honest self-examination. Later in this same chapter, Matthew 7:15–20 also calls for recognizing false prophets by their fruit. Wise judgment and humble correction have a place alongside this warning against hypocrisy.

Luke 6:37–42 places a similar warning with forgiveness, generosity, and the same eye illustration. The concern is how people extend mercy and offer help while recognizing their own need.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand these verses as forbidding harsh, hypocritical judgment and requiring honest self-examination before correcting someone else. Wesley's notes on Matthew 7:1–5 stress knowledge and love; the Catholic Catechism, 2477–2478, rejects assuming someone's guilt without sufficient grounds; the Reformed Westminster Larger Catechism, question 145, condemns rash, harsh, and partial judgments.
passages.god_plan_html:
God's mercy changes the way people look at those who have failed. In 1 Timothy 1:12–17, Paul recalls his own violence and unbelief, then explains that Christ showed him mercy. His life becomes an example of Christ's patience for others who will believe. Remembering received mercy gives a reason for humility toward another person's need.

Galatians 6:1–5 brings self-examination and help for another person together. A person caught in sin is to be restored gently, while those helping watch themselves and carry one another's burdens. Paul connects this with fulfilling the law of Christ. His saving mercy forms a people who restore one another with humility.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 7:6
passages.section_title: Treating Holy Things with Care

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 Do not give dogs what is holy; do not throw your pearls before swine. If you do, they may trample them under their feet, and then turn and tear you to pieces.
paragraphs: 6 Do not give dogs what is holy; do not throw your pearls before swine. If you do, they may trample them under their feet, and then turn and tear you to pieces.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
This brief saying follows the warning against hypocritical judgment. It introduces another kind of care: recognizing how something holy and precious may be received. The pictures of dogs and pigs show contempt for what is offered and danger to the person offering it.

Jesus does not identify the holy thing or pearls with a single item in this verse. The images contrast their value with the response of trampling and attack. That leaves readers to consider how the warning applies, rather than treating every person in a broad group as the same kind of hearer.

The preceding instruction still ends with helping a brother after addressing one's own fault. The following teaching turns to asking the Father for good things. This saying calls for wisdom about the response to what is holy within a chapter that also requires humility and generous conduct.

Jesus' ministry includes reaching people known for sin. In Mark 2:15–17, He eats with tax collectors and sinners and explains that He came to call sinners. That account matters when considering the scope of this warning: contemptuous hostility and the mere fact that a person needs God's mercy are different concerns.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings differ over what the holy thing or pearls represent. Wesley's note on Matthew 7:6 applies the warning to sharing deep spiritual teaching with people persisting in sin, or personal spiritual experience with hostile hearers; he still allows appropriate correction of wrongdoing.

An early application concerns sharing the church's bread and cup. The Didache, chapter 9, a Christian teaching manual, cites this saying when limiting participation in its thanksgiving meal to those baptized in the Lord's name. That is a particular early use of the warning, rather than proof that every Christian tradition gives the verse only that meaning.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 7:7-11
passages.section_title: Ask the Father for What Is Good

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and the door will be opened to you. 8 For everyone who asks receives; he who seeks finds; and to him who knocks, the door will be opened. 9 Which of you, if his son asks for bread, will give him a stone? 10 Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a snake? 11 So if you who are evil know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father in heaven give good things to those who ask Him!
paragraphs: 7 Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and the door will be opened to you. 8 For everyone who asks receives; he who seeks finds; and to him who knocks, the door will be opened.

9 Which of you, if his son asks for bread, will give him a stone? 10 Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a snake? 11 So if you who are evil know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father in heaven give good things to those who ask Him!

passages.context_html:
After teaching about judgment and discernment, Jesus encourages His hearers to ask, seek, and knock. Each action is followed by assurance of a response. The picture is of approaching the Father with confidence, and the comparison that follows explains the character of the One being approached.

A child asks for bread or fish. Jesus asks whether the parent would substitute a stone or snake. Even people who share human sinfulness know the difference between feeding a child and giving something harmful. The Father in heaven is more trustworthy still.

The assurance reaches its conclusion in verse 11: the Father gives good things. The promise is understood in relation to His goodness, alongside the earlier prayer for His will in Matthew 6:9–13. The person asking approaches a Father, not a device for making every preference come true.

The related teaching in Luke 11:5–13 places asking, seeking, and knocking after a story about persistence, then names the Holy Spirit as the Father's gift. Matthew's following verse calls for treating others as one wishes to be treated. Trust in the Father and good conduct toward others both belong within the Sermon's call to a life directed toward God.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these verses as encouragement to keep praying with confidence in the Father's goodness. Wesley on Matthew 7:7–11, the Reformed Westminster Larger Catechism, questions 184–185, and the Catholic Compendium, question 575, all direct asking toward God's will and the good He gives, rather than treating Him as a means of obtaining whatever the person wants.
passages.current_position_html:
Our study Prayer and Faith reads this promise alongside Luke 11:13, understanding the Father's highest good gift as His Spirit and the life He forms within His people. It therefore directs asking toward God's will and spiritual growth, rather than treating the passage as a guarantee of every desired outcome.

Our companion study What Does Prayer Look Like? shares that emphasis on surrender and trust. Both studies recognize that asking is not itself sinful; the question is what governs the asking and where the person's confidence rests.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The Father's generosity includes His own Spirit. In the closely related saying in Luke 11:9–13, the Father gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask. That parallel helps place the promise within God's work of bringing people near and helping them live in His ways.

Ephesians 1:13–14 describes the promised Spirit as the pledge of believers' inheritance. The word is ἀρραβών, arrabōn (ar-rah-BOHN). Thayer's Greek Lexicon explains the picture as a deposit assuring the payment to come, and applies it to the Spirit as a foretaste of future blessing. God's gift gives present help and assurance of the future He promises.

passages.title: Matthew 7:11
passages.section_title: The Father's Good Gifts

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 So if you who are evil know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father in heaven give good things to those who ask Him!
paragraphs: 11 So if you who are evil know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father in heaven give good things to those who ask Him!

passages.context_html:
This verse completes the asking, seeking, and knocking teaching in Matthew 7:7–11. Jesus has used bread, fish, a stone, and a snake to compare a parent's response to a child with the Father's response to His people. The comparison directs attention to the giver's goodness.

Jesus describes His hearers as evil while acknowledging that they know how to give good gifts. His reasoning moves from imperfect human parents to the greater goodness of the Father. His character is the reason for confidence in approaching Him.

Matthew describes the Father's gifts as good things. The related saying in Luke 11:9–13 specifically names the Holy Spirit. Both accounts direct the hearer's confidence toward the generous Father.

The Father is also the One whose will Jesus has taught His followers to seek in Matthew 6:9–13. Confidence in His good gifts belongs with that relationship of trust and submission.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these verses as encouragement to keep praying with confidence in the Father's goodness. Wesley on Matthew 7:7–11, the Reformed Westminster Larger Catechism, questions 184–185, and the Catholic Compendium, question 575, all direct asking toward God's will and the good He gives, rather than treating Him as a means of obtaining whatever the person wants.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Prayer and Faith understands the Father's good things in the light of Luke's explicit promise of the Holy Spirit. It reads the passage as directing faith toward God's presence, power, and purposes, rather than guaranteeing a preferred possession or circumstance. Our companion study What Does Prayer Look Like? develops the same focus while distinguishing surrender from a rule that asking is sinful.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The promise of the Spirit in Luke 11:13 points toward the gift that brings God's children into a lived relationship with Him. Romans 8:14–17 describes the Spirit leading them, enabling their cry to the Father, and bearing witness that they belong to His family.

Ephesians 1:13–14 also connects the Spirit with the future inheritance God promises. The Father's good gift reaches beyond a single circumstance: He gives His people His presence and a hope that extends to their final redemption.

passages.title: Matthew 7:12
passages.section_title: Treating Others as We Wish to Be Treated

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 In everything, then, do to others as you would have them do to you. For this is the essence of the Law and the Prophets.
