paragraphs: 12 In everything, then, do to others as you would have them do to you. For this is the essence of the Law and the Prophets.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
This saying draws together Jesus' teaching about life before God and treatment of other people. It follows the assurance that the Father gives good things, and it calls the hearer to act for another person's good. Its reach is broad: Jesus says to apply it in everything.

The direction is active. A person is to consider how he would wish to be treated and then offer that treatment to others. The attention moves beyond noticing another person's faults toward taking responsibility for one's own conduct.

Jesus connects this with the Law and the Prophets. The same expression appeared near the beginning of the Sermon in Matthew 5:17, where He spoke of fulfilling them. Here He describes considerate action toward others as expressing their purpose.

Later, in Matthew 22:34–40, Jesus again brings the Law and the Prophets together under love for God and love for one's neighbor. This saying belongs within that larger call to love.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this saying as a positive call to treat others with the care and consideration one would wish to receive. Wesley on Matthew 7:11–12 connects it with imitating God's love, and the Catholic Catechism, 1789, includes it among the principles that guide moral choices and respect for one's neighbor.
passages.god_plan_html:
The concern for another person's good takes its clearest shape in Christ's own service. Philippians 2:3–8 calls believers to look to others' interests, then points to Jesus taking a servant's place and becoming obedient to death. His saving work supplies the pattern for the life His people share.

Galatians 5:13–14 places loving service within the freedom Christ gives. That freedom is to be used to serve others, and Paul connects such love with the fulfillment of the Law. God's rescue forms a people who use their freedom for one another's good.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 7:13-14
passages.section_title: The Way That Leads to Life

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 Enter through the narrow gate. For wide is the gate and broad is the way that leads to destruction, and many enter through it. 14 But small is the gate and narrow the way that leads to life, and only a few find it.
paragraphs: 13 Enter through the narrow gate. For wide is the gate and broad is the way that leads to destruction, and many enter through it. 14 But small is the gate and narrow the way that leads to life, and only a few find it.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus now calls for a response to His teaching. Two gates and two ways lead to different destinations: destruction or life. The instruction is to enter through the narrow gate. Hearing the Sermon brings a choice about the direction of one's life.

The broad route attracts many, while the way to life is narrow and found by few. The size of the crowd does not remove the need to heed Jesus. His warning makes the destination of the way more important than its ease or popularity.

The description of the narrow way uses a form of θλίβω, thlibō (THLEE-boh), to press or constrain. Thayer's Greek Lexicon explains its use here as a compressed or restricted way. The picture presents a demanding route, rather than an unrestricted path chosen for convenience.

The contrasts that follow continue the call to discern and respond: good and bad fruit, religious claims and doing the Father's will, hearing Jesus' words and acting on them. The two ways introduce that closing appeal.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a serious call to follow the way of Christ rather than drifting with the crowd toward destruction. Wesley's note on Matthew 7:13 connects the narrow way with the holiness taught in the Sermon, and the Catholic Catechism, 1696, applies the two ways to following Christ and the moral choices of a life directed toward Him.
passages.god_plan_html:
Elsewhere Jesus describes Himself as the way to the Father. In John 14:6–7, access to the Father comes through Him. In John 10:7–10, He uses the related picture of a gate through which people enter and receive life. These related pictures place the call to enter within God's larger purpose of rescue through Christ.

Hebrews 10:19–25 explains that Jesus' blood opens a new and living way into God's presence. It joins that welcome with holding to hope, encouraging others, and stirring one another toward love and good deeds. The way God opens through His Son leads into a life of trust and perseverance.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 7:15-20
passages.section_title: Recognizing Teachers by Their Fruit

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 Beware of false prophets. They come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves. 16 By their fruit you will recognize them. Are grapes gathered from thornbushes, or figs from thistles? 17 Likewise, every good tree bears good fruit, but a bad tree bears bad fruit. 18 A good tree cannot bear bad fruit, and a bad tree cannot bear good fruit. 19 Every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. 20 So then, by their fruit you will recognize them.
paragraphs: 15 Beware of false prophets. They come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves. 16 By their fruit you will recognize them. Are grapes gathered from thornbushes, or figs from thistles?

17 Likewise, every good tree bears good fruit, but a bad tree bears bad fruit. 18 A good tree cannot bear bad fruit, and a bad tree cannot bear good fruit. 19 Every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. 20 So then, by their fruit you will recognize them.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After warning about the way that leads to destruction, Jesus warns about people who may lead others there. False prophets appear like members of the flock but are inwardly dangerous. Their outward presentation does not settle whether they can be trusted.

The repeated direction is to recognize them by their fruit. A tree is known by what it produces. Grapes do not come from thornbushes, and figs do not come from thistles. The comparison moves attention from appearance to the actual result of a teacher's life and work.

Jesus also speaks of a fruitless tree being cut down and burned. The warning gives the question weight: the issue is more serious than a teacher's popularity or speaking ability. The following verses show that even striking religious claims cannot take the place of doing the Father's will.

Other New Testament passages also call for testing. 1 John 4:1–3 examines what a message confesses about Jesus, while 1 Thessalonians 5:19–22 calls believers to test what is said and hold to what is good. Such care belongs with the earlier warning against hypocritical judgment.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readers agree that appearances and religious claims are insufficient, while placing different emphasis on what the fruit reveals. Wesley on Matthew 7:15–19 emphasizes the teaching and whether it turns people toward God; he expressly allows that a morally flawed person may sometimes speak true teaching.

The US Catholic bishops' notes on Matthew 7:15–20 emphasize the quality of the prophets' deeds. These explanations place different emphasis on teaching and deeds, while both call for looking beyond an outwardly religious appearance.
passages.god_plan_html:
God's purpose is to produce a changed life through union with Christ. John 15:1–8 uses another fruit picture: Jesus is the vine, the Father tends it, and the branches bear fruit by remaining in Him. Jesus connects that fruit with His Father's glory. This related image directs attention to the source of a fruitful life.

Galatians 5:22–25 describes the Spirit's fruit in qualities such as love, patience, kindness, and self-control. The larger purpose reaches beyond persuasive speech or a successful-looking ministry: God's Spirit forms people whose lives display the character of Christ.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 7:21-23
passages.section_title: More Than Saying Lord

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 Not everyone who says to Me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but only he who does the will of My Father in heaven. 22 Many will say to Me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in Your name, and in Your name drive out demons and perform many miracles?’ 23 Then I will tell them plainly, ‘I never knew you; depart from Me, you workers of lawlessness!’
paragraphs: 21 Not everyone who says to Me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but only he who does the will of My Father in heaven. 22 Many will say to Me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in Your name, and in Your name drive out demons and perform many miracles?’ 23 Then I will tell them plainly, ‘I never knew you; depart from Me, you workers of lawlessness!’

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The warning now reaches beyond outward appearances to claims made before Jesus. The speakers call Him Lord and appeal to prophecy, exorcisms, and miracles performed in His name. Jesus contrasts those claims with doing His Father's will.

The passage reports what the speakers say about their works. Jesus' response centers on His rejection of them and their lawlessness. The account does not separately narrate each claimed miracle or explain the source of its power.

The word for lawlessness is ἀνομία, anomia (ah-noh-MEE-ah). Thayer's Greek Lexicon explains it as disregard for or violation of law, and includes its use here. The contrast with the Father's will makes the moral concern clear: public religious activity can conceal a life of disobedience.

The command to depart echoes Psalm 6:8, where workers of evil are told to go away. Here Jesus Himself gives the final response to those making their appeal. The following house illustration continues the contrast between hearing His words and acting on them.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian traditions commonly understand this as a warning that calling Jesus Lord and claiming impressive deeds do not by themselves establish a right relationship with Him. They describe the relationship between faith and obedience in different ways.

In the Reformed tradition, the Westminster Confession, 16.2 and 16.5, calls good works the fruit and evidence of living faith, while denying that works earn forgiveness or eternal life. Its chapter 18.1 also warns about false confidence in being accepted by God.

The Catholic Catechism, 1815, says faith without hope and love does not fully unite a person to Christ as a living member of His body. Wesley on Matthew 7:21–23 stresses doing the Father's will as taught in the Sermon and applies the warning personally, even to someone whose ministry appears effective.
passages.god_plan_html:
Christ's saving work includes rescue from the lawlessness named here. Titus 2:11–14 describes God's grace training people to leave ungodliness and live rightly while awaiting Christ. It says He gave Himself to redeem people from lawlessness and make them His own, eager to do good.

Ephesians 2:8–10 likewise joins God's gift of salvation with a new life prepared for good works. These passages show the larger purpose: the grace that brings people to Christ is meant to form a life that belongs to Him. The warning against mere claims is understood within that saving and transforming work.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 7:24-27
passages.section_title: Hearing and Building on Jesus’ Words

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 24 Therefore everyone who hears these words of Mine and acts on them is like a wise man who built his house on the rock. 25 The rain fell, the torrents raged, and the winds blew and beat against that house; yet it did not fall, because its foundation was on the rock. 26 But everyone who hears these words of Mine and does not act on them is like a foolish man who built his house on sand. 27 The rain fell, the torrents raged, and the winds blew and beat against that house, and it fell—and great was its collapse!”
paragraphs: 24 Therefore everyone who hears these words of Mine and acts on them is like a wise man who built his house on the rock. 25 The rain fell, the torrents raged, and the winds blew and beat against that house; yet it did not fall, because its foundation was on the rock.

26 But everyone who hears these words of Mine and does not act on them is like a foolish man who built his house on sand. 27 The rain fell, the torrents raged, and the winds blew and beat against that house, and it fell—and great was its collapse!”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus closes the Sermon's instruction with two people who hear the same words. The difference is what they do with them. One acts on His teaching, while the other hears without acting. The houses picture the different results.

Both houses face rain, rising water, and wind. The wise builder's house remains because its foundation is on rock. The foolish builder's house collapses because it rests on sand. The test exposes a difference that may not have been obvious before the storm.

The words to be acted on are Jesus' own words, including the teaching just given. The illustration gathers up the Sermon's call to righteousness in the heart, trust in the Father, mercy toward others, and an obedient response. Its place after the warning about judgment gives the collapse a serious final weight.

Luke 6:46–49 gives a closely related teaching about calling Jesus Lord, hearing Him, and acting on His words. James 1:22–25 likewise warns that hearing without doing can become self-deception.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the rock-and-sand picture as a call to put Jesus' teaching into practice, rather than being satisfied with hearing it. The US Catholic bishops' notes on Matthew 7:24–27 emphasize this contrast between hearing and doing, and the Reformed Westminster Confession, 16.2, similarly describes obedience as the visible fruit of living faith.
passages.god_plan_html:
Putting Jesus' words into practice becomes part of the mission of the risen Christ. In Matthew 28:18–20, He sends His disciples to the nations and tells them to teach people to obey everything He commanded. He also promises His presence. The Sermon's call to act on His words continues within the people He gathers.

Ephesians 2:8–10 places a life of good works within God's work of making people new in Christ. This provides a wider setting for the image: the life built on His words is part of the life His grace creates.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 7:28-29
passages.section_title: The Authority of Jesus’ Teaching

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 28 When Jesus had finished saying these things, the crowds were astonished at His teaching, 29 because He taught as one who had authority, and not as their scribes.
paragraphs: 28 When Jesus had finished saying these things, the crowds were astonished at His teaching, 29 because He taught as one who had authority, and not as their scribes.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Matthew now describes the crowd's response to the Sermon. They are astonished by the authority of Jesus' teaching, which they recognize as different from that of their scribes. The narrative turns from His instructions to their impact on those who hear.

The preceding sayings show the weight of His words. Jesus calls people to enter the way to life, warns of false prophets, speaks of those He will reject, and makes acting on His own words the wise foundation for life. The crowd's response follows those claims.

Earlier in the Sermon, His repeated statements in Matthew 5:21–48 brought His own teaching to bear on anger, desire, faithfulness, truthfulness, retaliation, and love. The closing response highlights the authority with which He has spoken throughout.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the crowd's response as recognizing authority belonging uniquely to Jesus, rather than merely admiration for an engaging speaker. Wesley's note on Matthew 7:29 describes Him as the great Lawgiver, and the Catholic Catechism, 581, connects His authority here with His divine interpretation of God's Law.
passages.god_plan_html:
God's purpose includes sending the One whose words must be heard. Deuteronomy 18:15–19 promises a prophet like Moses who will speak God's words. In Acts 3:19–26, Peter applies that promise to Jesus and connects His mission with blessing the families of the earth. This gives a wider setting for receiving His authoritative teaching.

The same Gospel ends with the risen Jesus declaring authority in heaven and earth and sending disciples to teach the nations to obey His commands in Matthew 28:18–20. The authority heard in the Sermon belongs within His larger mission of gathering a people who follow Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 8:1-4
passages.section_title: Jesus Is Willing to Make Him Clean

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 When Jesus came down from the mountain, large crowds followed Him. 2 Suddenly a leper came and knelt before Him, saying, “Lord, if You are willing, You can make me clean.” 3 Jesus reached out His hand and touched the man. “I am willing,” He said. “Be clean!” And immediately his leprosy was cleansed. 4 Then Jesus instructed him, “See that you don’t tell anyone. But go, show yourself to the priest and offer the gift prescribed by Moses, as a testimony to them.”
paragraphs: 1 When Jesus came down from the mountain, large crowds followed Him. 2 Suddenly a leper came and knelt before Him, saying, “Lord, if You are willing, You can make me clean.”

3 Jesus reached out His hand and touched the man. “I am willing,” He said. “Be clean!” And immediately his leprosy was cleansed. 4 Then Jesus instructed him, “See that you don’t tell anyone. But go, show yourself to the priest and offer the gift prescribed by Moses, as a testimony to them.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the Sermon on the Mount, Matthew shows Jesus' authority in action. Large crowds follow Him down the mountain. A man with leprosy approaches, kneels, and asks to be made clean. His request expresses confidence in Jesus' ability while leaving the decision with Him.

Being clean matters here in more than a medical sense. Leviticus 13:45–46 directs someone declared unclean with this condition to live outside the camp. Leviticus 14:1–20 provides for examination by a priest, cleansing, return to the camp, and offerings after the condition has healed. The healing therefore opens the way to a fuller restoration of the man's life among his people.

Jesus reaches out and touches him, then makes him clean immediately. The Greek verb is καθαρίζω, katharizō (kah-thah-REE-zoh), meaning to make clean or cleanse. Thayer's Greek Lexicon includes the healing of leprosy under this meaning. Here the word describes a real bodily healing within the setting of the Law's cleansing requirements.

Jesus sends him to the priest and tells him to bring Moses' prescribed gift. The priest is to examine a man whom Jesus has already healed; the offering is not what brings about the cure. Jesus calls this a testimony to them. He does not tell the man to set aside the Law's provision for being received as clean.

The command to keep quiet is also part of the encounter. Mark 1:40–45 reports that the man instead spread the news, after which the crowds kept Jesus from entering towns openly. Matthew does not explain every reason for the command, so that related account helps without supplying an invented motive.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a display of Jesus' compassion and power to restore someone who was unclean, joined with the man's humble confidence in Him. The Catholic Catechism, 1503–1505, places Jesus' healings within His care for the whole person and the coming of God's kingdom, while Wesley on Matthew 8:4 also emphasizes the priestly examination as testimony to Jesus' identity.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus later names the cleansing of lepers among the works that answer John's question about whether He is the coming One in Matthew 11:2–6. This healing therefore belongs within the larger revelation of who Jesus is. It is more than an isolated act of kindness, although His kindness is real.

The movement from uncleanness toward restored life also offers a helpful parallel with Christ's saving work. Hebrews 9:11–14 compares the Law's outward purification with the deeper cleansing Christ brings through His own blood: a cleansed conscience and a life of service to God. The same Greek verb for cleansing appears there. This is a comparison between bodily restoration and rescue from sin; Matthew does not say the man's illness resulted from a particular sin, or assign a hidden meaning to every part of the encounter.
passages.current_position_html:
Worship as the Early Church Knew It understands the man's bowing as a personal plea expressed through physical humility. He approaches Jesus in reverent submission and recognizes His divine authority. The focus is his humble appeal to Jesus, rather than the form of a religious service.

That is the study's position on the man's approach in verse 2. It does not provide a separate site position on every detail of the healing or the priestly instructions.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

passages.title: Matthew 8:2
passages.section_title: A Humble Request for Cleansing

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 2 Suddenly a leper came and knelt before Him, saying, “Lord, if You are willing, You can make me clean.”
paragraphs: 2 Suddenly a leper came and knelt before Him, saying, “Lord, if You are willing, You can make me clean.”

passages.context_html:
This request belongs to the healing recorded in Matthew 8:1–4. Jesus has come down from the mountain, and a man with leprosy approaches Him. The man does not question Jesus' ability to make him clean. He asks whether Jesus is willing.

The BSB describes him kneeling before Jesus. The Greek verb is προσκυνέω, proskuneō (pros-koo-NEH-oh). Thayer's Greek Lexicon explains that it can describe kneeling or bowing to show reverence, make a plea, or worship. The setting matters: here a man lowers himself before Jesus while asking for help. The word alone does not tell us everything he understood about Jesus.

The request to be made clean reflects the Law's treatment of this condition. Leviticus 13:45–46 describes exclusion from the camp, and Leviticus 14:1–20 provides for examination and cleansing after healing. In the next two verses Jesus touches the man, cleanses him, and sends him to the priest.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the man's approach as a humble expression of faith in Jesus' power, with the outcome entrusted to His willingness. Wesley's notes on Matthew 8:2–4 place the plea within the healing and priestly testimony that follow, while the Catholic Catechism, 1503–1505, similarly places Jesus' care for the sick within His compassionate mission.
passages.current_position_html:
Worship as the Early Church Knew It understands the man's bowing as a personal plea expressed through physical humility. He approaches Jesus in reverent submission and recognizes His divine authority. The focus is his humble appeal to Jesus, rather than the form of a religious service.

That is the study's position on the man's approach in verse 2. It does not provide a separate site position on every detail of the healing or the priestly instructions.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
This man's approach gives a concrete picture of bringing need to Jesus. The wider invitation becomes explicit in Hebrews 4:14–16: because Jesus the Son of God is the great high priest who understands human weakness, believers may approach God's throne for mercy and help.

That is a supported parallel, rather than a claim that Hebrews is explaining this particular healing. It places the man's humble request beside the larger welcome Christ opens to people in need. The promise in Hebrews is mercy and grace; it does not turn this one healing into a guarantee that every illness will end immediately.

passages.title: Matthew 8:5-13
passages.section_title: Trusting the Authority of Jesus’ Word

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 When Jesus had entered Capernaum, a centurion came and pleaded with Him, 6 “Lord, my servant lies at home, paralyzed and in terrible agony.” 7 “I will go and heal him,” Jesus replied. 8 The centurion answered, “Lord, I am not worthy to have You come under my roof. But just say the word, and my servant will be healed. 9 For I myself am a man under authority, with soldiers under me. I tell one to go, and he goes, and another to come, and he comes. I tell my servant to do something, and he does it.” 10 When Jesus heard this, He marveled and said to those following Him, “Truly I tell you, I have not found anyone in Israel with such great faith. 11 I say to you that many will come from the east and the west to share the banquet with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven. 12 But the sons of the kingdom will be thrown into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” 13 Then Jesus said to the centurion, “Go! As you have believed, so will it be done for you.” And his servant was healed at that very hour.
paragraphs: 5 When Jesus had entered Capernaum, a centurion came and pleaded with Him, 6 “Lord, my servant lies at home, paralyzed and in terrible agony.” 7 “I will go and heal him,” Jesus replied.

8 The centurion answered, “Lord, I am not worthy to have You come under my roof. But just say the word, and my servant will be healed. 9 For I myself am a man under authority, with soldiers under me. I tell one to go, and he goes, and another to come, and he comes. I tell my servant to do something, and he does it.” 10 When Jesus heard this, He marveled and said to those following Him, “Truly I tell you, I have not found anyone in Israel with such great faith.

11 I say to you that many will come from the east and the west to share the banquet with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven. 12 But the sons of the kingdom will be thrown into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” 13 Then Jesus said to the centurion, “Go! As you have believed, so will it be done for you.” And his servant was healed at that very hour.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
In Capernaum, an army officer asks Jesus to heal his servant, who is paralyzed and suffering terribly. The officer is a centurion, with soldiers under his command. Jesus offers to go, but the man says that a word from Him will be enough. His confidence in Jesus' authority is joined with a striking sense of his own unworthiness.

The officer explains through his own experience: he serves under authority and gives orders that others obey. He trusts that Jesus' command can likewise bring the healing about without a visit to the house. Jesus marvels at his faith, contrasts it with what He has found in Israel, and heals the servant at that very hour.

Luke 7:1–10 gives further details. The centurion sends Jewish elders, who speak of his love for their nation and his help in building their synagogue. He then sends friends with the message that he is unworthy and that Jesus need only speak. Matthew presents the exchange directly between the centurion and Jesus; Luke describes the messengers carrying his request. Luke's account makes the different voices clear: the elders appeal to the man's worthiness, while his own message confesses unworthiness.

Jesus' words then widen the scene from one household to the kingdom of heaven. Many will come from east and west to share a banquet with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, while people who expected a place will be shut out. The Gentile officer's faith stands beside a warning that belonging to the people who first received the promises cannot replace responding to Jesus.

The outer darkness, weeping, and gnashing of teeth make that exclusion a grave warning. The passage does not identify every person excluded or lay out a complete timetable for the banquet. Its immediate contrast is between this unexpected faith and confidence that an expected place in the kingdom is already secure.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as an example of humble faith in Jesus' authority, a welcome for people from the nations, and a warning against assuming a place in God's kingdom is already secure. Wesley on Matthew 8:9–12 connects the welcome of distant peoples with Abraham's promised blessing, and the Catholic Catechism, 543, likewise describes the kingdom as first announced to Israel and open to people of all nations who receive Jesus' word.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus names Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob when describing the welcome of people from east and west. Galatians 3:6–14 explains the wider purpose of Abraham's promise: God announced blessing for the nations, and that blessing comes to Gentiles through Christ. Paul connects it with Christ redeeming people from the curse and with receiving the promised Spirit through faith. The centurion's welcome fits that larger movement of blessing beyond Israel.

The banquet also has an earlier scriptural parallel. Isaiah 25:6–9 describes God's feast for all peoples, the removal of disgrace, and the swallowing up of death. Read alongside Jesus' words, it shows how much is at stake in the welcome He describes: God's purpose reaches beyond one restored servant toward a people gathered into His salvation.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 8:14-17
passages.section_title: Healing and the Promise of Isaiah

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 When Jesus arrived at Peter’s house, He saw Peter’s mother-in-law sick in bed with a fever. 15 So He touched her hand, and the fever left her, and she got up and began to serve Him. 16 When evening came, many who were demon-possessed were brought to Jesus, and He drove out the spirits with a word and healed all the sick. 17 This was to fulfill what was spoken through the prophet Isaiah: “He took up our infirmities and carried our diseases.”
paragraphs: 14 When Jesus arrived at Peter’s house, He saw Peter’s mother-in-law sick in bed with a fever. 15 So He touched her hand, and the fever left her, and she got up and began to serve Him.

16 When evening came, many who were demon-possessed were brought to Jesus, and He drove out the spirits with a word and healed all the sick. 17 This was to fulfill what was spoken through the prophet Isaiah: “He took up our infirmities and carried our diseases.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus' healing ministry reaches into Peter's home. His mother-in-law is lying sick with a fever. Jesus touches her hand, the fever leaves, and she rises to serve Him. Matthew moves from this personal encounter to an evening when many sick and demon-possessed people are brought to Him. He heals the sick and drives out the spirits with a word.

Mark 1:29–34 and Luke 4:38–41 describe the household's appeal for her and her immediate return to service. Matthew's brief account keeps the attention on Jesus seeing her need and acting. The woman is restored to active life; the text does not identify the cause of her fever.

Matthew then explains these healings by quoting Isaiah 53:4. This is his own stated connection, rather than a resemblance added by a later reader. The servant described by Isaiah bears the suffering of others, and Matthew sees Jesus' care for sick people as fulfilling that promise.

The Hebrew noun חֳלִי, choli (khoh-LEE), means sickness or disease. Brown–Driver–Briggs includes its use in Isaiah 53:3–4. This helps explain why Matthew applies Isaiah's language to actual bodily suffering. The wider chapter also speaks of sin, forgiveness, and the servant's death; its concern reaches beyond one kind of suffering.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand these healings as signs of Jesus' compassion and His fulfillment of Isaiah's servant passage. Readers place different emphasis on how the healings relate to His saving death and to healing today.

Wesley on Matthew 8:17 sees these bodily healings as one way Isaiah's words come true, while placing the main emphasis on Christ bearing our sins. The Catholic Catechism, 1505, describes the healings as signs announcing the greater victory over sin and death through Christ's death and resurrection.

Among Pentecostal churches, the Assemblies of God explicitly connects bodily healing with Christ's saving sacrifice in its Statement of Fundamental Truths, 12. Its Divine Healing position paper also says that some people are not healed now and that the full restoration of our bodies awaits Christ's return. This should not be confused with a promise that every faithful person will immediately recover.
passages.god_plan_html:
Matthew's quotation places Jesus' healing work within the mission of Isaiah's suffering servant. Isaiah 53:4–12 moves from bearing suffering to bearing sins and giving His life. 1 Peter 2:21–25 explicitly applies that servant language to Jesus' suffering on the cross, His bearing of sins, and the return of wandering people to their Shepherd. The healings and the cross belong within the mission of the same Savior.

That rescue includes a future for the body as well. Romans 8:18–25 describes believers still suffering and waiting for the redemption of their bodies. 1 Corinthians 15:42–55 describes the dead raised beyond decay and death. The hope is larger than repeated temporary relief: Christ's saving work leads toward life in which death itself is defeated.

passages.title: Matthew 8:18-22
passages.section_title: What Following Jesus Will Cost

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 When Jesus saw a large crowd around Him, He gave orders to cross to the other side of the sea. 19 And one of the scribes came to Him and said, “Teacher, I will follow You wherever You go.” 20 Jesus replied, “Foxes have dens and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has no place to lay His head.” 21 Another of His disciples requested, “Lord, first let me go and bury my father.” 22 But Jesus told him, “Follow Me, and let the dead bury their own dead.”
paragraphs: 18 When Jesus saw a large crowd around Him, He gave orders to cross to the other side of the sea. 19 And one of the scribes came to Him and said, “Teacher, I will follow You wherever You go.” 20 Jesus replied, “Foxes have dens and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has no place to lay His head.”
21 Another of His disciples requested, “Lord, first let me go and bury my father.” 22 But Jesus told him, “Follow Me, and let the dead bury their own dead.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
As Jesus prepares to cross the sea, two conversations bring the question of following Him into focus. A scribe offers to go wherever He goes. Jesus answers with a comparison: animals have their shelters, but He has no place to lay His head. The offer to follow must face the unsettled life that following will involve.

Jesus calls Himself the Son of Man. The title will later appear in His teaching about suffering and coming glory, including Matthew 16:24–27. Here it accompanies a statement about His lack of a secure resting place. The person whom disciples follow does not promise them comfort simply through association with Him.

Another disciple asks to bury his father first. Jesus' answer is deliberately striking: the dead are to bury their own dead, while this man is to follow Him. The first use of dead is commonly understood as describing people spiritually unresponsive to God, while the second refers to those who have physically died. The saying sets the call to follow Jesus above the competing claim being made.

Matthew does not say whether the father has already died, whether the request concerns a later burial, or whether the man wishes to remain at home until his father's death. Those possibilities should not be turned into a known biography. Luke 9:57–62 gives related sayings and explicitly joins the call with proclaiming God's kingdom. The point is the urgency and priority of following Jesus.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these sayings as a call to accept the cost of following Jesus and give His call first place. Wesley on Matthew 8:20–22 warns against following for earthly advantage, while the Catholic Catechism, 520, describes Christ's poverty and hardships as part of the example His disciples are called to follow.
passages.god_plan_html:
The cost belongs within Jesus' own path of suffering and glory. In Matthew 16:24–27, He again calls disciples to follow Him, now speaking of taking up a cross, losing life for His sake, and the Son of Man coming in glory. The lack of earthly security in this encounter is not the end of His story or theirs.

There is also a useful parallel with Abraham's life of faith. Hebrews 11:8–16 describes him leaving in obedience, living in tents, and looking toward the city God prepares. Hebrews does not directly explain these two conversations, but the parallel helps show how obedience can involve giving up present security because God's promise reaches further than the present life.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 8:23-27
passages.section_title: Who Can Command the Wind and Sea?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 23 When He got into the boat, His disciples followed Him. 24 Suddenly a violent storm came up on the sea, so that the boat was engulfed by the waves. But Jesus was sleeping. 25 The disciples went and woke Him, saying, “Lord, save us! We are perishing!” 26 “You of little faith,” Jesus replied, “why are you so afraid?” Then He got up and rebuked the winds and the sea, and it was perfectly calm. 27 The men were amazed and asked, “What kind of man is this? Even the winds and the sea obey Him!”
paragraphs: 23 When He got into the boat, His disciples followed Him. 24 Suddenly a violent storm came up on the sea, so that the boat was engulfed by the waves. But Jesus was sleeping. 25 The disciples went and woke Him, saying, “Lord, save us! We are perishing!”

26 “You of little faith,” Jesus replied, “why are you so afraid?” Then He got up and rebuked the winds and the sea, and it was perfectly calm. 27 The men were amazed and asked, “What kind of man is this? Even the winds and the sea obey Him!”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The disciples now do what the preceding conversations have discussed: they follow Jesus, entering the boat after Him. Following does not keep them out of danger. A violent storm engulfs the boat with waves while Jesus sleeps, and they wake Him with a plea to save them.

Jesus addresses their fear and little faith before rebuking the winds and sea. The result is a complete calm. Their attention then turns from the danger to His identity. They have asked for rescue, but the authority they witness still amazes them.

Mark 4:35–41 adds that Jesus is sleeping on a cushion in the stern and that the disciples question whether He cares. It also records His command for the storm to be still. Matthew's account gives special prominence to His challenge to their faith before describing the calm.

The word translated rebuked is ἐπιτιμάω, epitimaō (eh-pee-tee-MAH-oh), to rebuke or address sharply. Thayer's Greek Lexicon includes this verse. Jesus addresses the forces threatening the boat with authority, and they obey. The scene does not describe a technique the disciples must use to control every dangerous circumstance.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the miracle as revealing Jesus' authority over creation while calling His followers to trust Him in danger. The US Catholic bishops' note on Matthew 8:26 connects the calm with the Old Testament picture of God's rule over the waters, and Wesley on Matthew 8:26 draws attention to Jesus addressing the disciples' fear as well as the storm.
passages.god_plan_html:
The scene has a strong scriptural parallel in Psalm 107:23–32. Sailors face overwhelming waves, cry to the LORD, and receive rescue when He stills the storm. Matthew does not quote the psalm here, but the shared pattern gives weight to the disciples' question: Jesus exercises the authority Scripture describes as God's.

The wider promise is greater than escape from one storm. Romans 8:31–39 grounds confidence in God's love in the death, resurrection, and intercession of Christ. It includes danger and even death among the things that cannot separate His people from that love. This carries the lesson beyond an expectation that every crisis will end as the disciples' crisis did: their Savior's care holds even when suffering continues.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 8:28-34
passages.section_title: Jesus Frees the Men at the Tombs

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 28 When Jesus arrived on the other side in the region of the Gadarenes, He was met by two demon-possessed men coming from the tombs. They were so violent that no one could pass that way. 29 “What do You want with us, Son of God?” they shouted. “Have You come here to torture us before the appointed time?” 30 In the distance a large herd of pigs was feeding. 31 So the demons begged Jesus, “If You drive us out, send us into the herd of pigs.” 32 “Go!” He told them. So they came out and went into the pigs, and the whole herd rushed down the steep bank into the sea and died in the waters. 33 Those tending the pigs ran off into the town and reported all this, including the account of the demon-possessed men. 34 Then the whole town went out to meet Jesus. And when they saw Him, they begged Him to leave their region.
paragraphs: 28 When Jesus arrived on the other side in the region of the Gadarenes, He was met by two demon-possessed men coming from the tombs. They were so violent that no one could pass that way. 29 “What do You want with us, Son of God?” they shouted. “Have You come here to torture us before the appointed time?”

30 In the distance a large herd of pigs was feeding. 31 So the demons begged Jesus, “If You drive us out, send us into the herd of pigs.” 32 “Go!” He told them. So they came out and went into the pigs, and the whole herd rushed down the steep bank into the sea and died in the waters.

33 Those tending the pigs ran off into the town and reported all this, including the account of the demon-possessed men. 34 Then the whole town went out to meet Jesus. And when they saw Him, they begged Him to leave their region.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
On the other side of the sea, Jesus meets two demon-possessed men coming from the tombs. Their violence has made the route unsafe. The encounter presents another kind of power that people cannot control, following the storm the disciples could not master.

The demons recognize Jesus as the Son of God and ask about torment before the appointed time. Their recognition is not willing trust or obedience to God. They fear His authority and ask permission to enter a nearby herd of pigs. Jesus gives the command, and they leave the men.

The pigs then rush into the sea and drown. Matthew reports their destruction but does not explain every reason Jesus permits the request or what happens to the demons afterward. Those tending the pigs tell the town about both the herd and the men, and the people ask Jesus to leave.

Mark 5:1–20 and Luke 8:26–39 focus on one man and describe him afterward as clothed and in his right mind. Luke explicitly says the people's request for Jesus to leave arose from great fear. Matthew records two men; he does not tell us why the other accounts focus on one, or allow us to reduce the townspeople's motives to one unrecorded explanation.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the encounter as a real deliverance showing Jesus' authority over evil spirits and His power to restore people beyond human help. The Catholic Catechism, 550, places such deliverances within the defeat of Satan's kingdom, and Wesley on Matthew 8:28–31 likewise emphasizes the spirits' subjection to Jesus and the coming judgment they fear.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus later explains the larger significance of His deliverances in Matthew 12:28–29: driving out demons by God's Spirit shows that God's kingdom has come, and He compares the rescue with overcoming a strong man to take back what he holds. The freedom of these men belongs within that advance of God's kingdom against evil.

Hebrews 2:14–18 takes the purpose further, describing Jesus sharing our humanity and dying to break the devil's power and free those enslaved by fear of death. Matthew's encounter is not a complete account of that victory, but it shows the authority of the One who accomplishes it. The men are freed; evil does not have the final claim over them.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 9:1-8
passages.section_title: Jesus Has Authority to Forgive

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Jesus got into a boat, crossed over, and came to His own town. 2 Just then some men brought to Him a paralytic lying on a mat. When Jesus saw their faith, He said to the paralytic, “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven.” 3 On seeing this, some of the scribes said to themselves, “This man is blaspheming!” 4 But Jesus knew what they were thinking and said, “Why do you harbor evil in your hearts? 5 Which is easier: to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Get up and walk’? 6 But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins...” Then He said to the paralytic, “Get up, pick up your mat, and go home.” 7 And the man got up and went home. 8 When the crowds saw this, they were filled with awe and glorified God, who had given such authority to men.
paragraphs: 1 Jesus got into a boat, crossed over, and came to His own town. 2 Just then some men brought to Him a paralytic lying on a mat. When Jesus saw their faith, He said to the paralytic, “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven.” 3 On seeing this, some of the scribes said to themselves, “This man is blaspheming!”

4 But Jesus knew what they were thinking and said, “Why do you harbor evil in your hearts? 5 Which is easier: to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Get up and walk’? 6 But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins...” Then He said to the paralytic, “Get up, pick up your mat, and go home.”
7 And the man got up and went home. 8 When the crowds saw this, they were filled with awe and glorified God, who had given such authority to men.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the people across the sea ask Jesus to leave, He crosses back to His own town. Matthew 4:13 has already identified Capernaum as His home. Some men bring a paralyzed man on a mat. Jesus sees their faith and begins with an assurance of forgiveness, before saying anything about the man's ability to walk.

Mark 2:1–12 and Luke 5:17–26 describe the crowded house and the men lowering their friend through the roof. They also make the scribes' objection explicit: forgiving sins is God's work. The dispute concerns who Jesus is and what authority He has, rather than whether the man's physical need matters.

The word translated forgiven comes from ἀφίημι, aphiēmi (ah-FEE-ay-mee). Thayer's Greek Lexicon includes both releasing a debt and forgiving sins among its uses, and lists this passage. Jesus announces a release from guilt before God. The word does not identify a particular sin as the cause of the man's paralysis.

Jesus answers the hidden objection with something the witnesses can see. A claim to forgive could be spoken without a visible result, but telling a paralyzed man to stand and walk can be tested immediately. Jesus states the purpose of the healing: they are to know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins. The man rises and goes home, and the crowd glorifies God for giving such authority to men.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the healing as confirming Jesus' authority to forgive sins, with the man's deeper need addressed alongside his bodily need. Wesley on Matthew 9:3–8 sees the healing as evidence of divine power, and the Catholic Catechism, 1441, likewise explains Jesus' forgiveness through His identity as the Son of God.

Readers also consider how the closing reference to authority given to men relates to the Church's later ministry. The US Catholic bishops' note on Matthew 9:8 connects it with the Church's authority to forgive, and the Catholic Catechism, 1441–1442, describes Christ entrusting the forgiveness pronounced in confession to the apostles' ministry.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, 30.2, describes the Church's authority through proclaiming the gospel, exercising discipline, and restoring repentant people to fellowship. These traditions describe that ministry differently, while locating its authority in Christ rather than in a person's independent power to cancel another's offense against God.
passages.god_plan_html:
The forgiveness announced in this house belongs to Jesus' wider saving mission. After His resurrection, in Luke 24:44–49, He explains that the Scriptures point to His suffering and rising, and that repentance and forgiveness will be proclaimed in His name to all nations. What is given to this man reaches far beyond this one room.

His healing is real, but the hope offered here is larger than being able to walk again. Jesus' death and resurrection open the way for the forgiveness that His followers are sent to announce. The episode reveals the authority of the Savior whose mission brings people back to God.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 9:9-13
passages.section_title: Mercy for Those Who Need a Savior

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 As Jesus went on from there, He saw a man named Matthew sitting at the tax booth. “Follow Me,” He told him, and Matthew got up and followed Him. 10 Later, as Jesus was dining at Matthew’s house, many tax collectors and sinners came and ate with Him and His disciples. 11 When the Pharisees saw this, they asked His disciples, “Why does your Teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?” 12 On hearing this, Jesus said, “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick. 13 But go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy, not sacrifice.’ For I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.”
paragraphs: 9 As Jesus went on from there, He saw a man named Matthew sitting at the tax booth. “Follow Me,” He told him, and Matthew got up and followed Him. 10 Later, as Jesus was dining at Matthew’s house, many tax collectors and sinners came and ate with Him and His disciples. 11 When the Pharisees saw this, they asked His disciples, “Why does your Teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?”

12 On hearing this, Jesus said, “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick. 13 But go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy, not sacrifice.’ For I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus calls Matthew from his tax booth, and Matthew gets up and follows. The account then moves to a meal at Matthew's house, where tax collectors and others described as sinners eat with Jesus and His disciples. The Pharisees' question challenges His willingness to share their company.

The related accounts in Mark 2:13–17 and Luke 5:27–32 name the tax collector Levi. Luke says he leaves everything and hosts a large banquet for Jesus.

Jesus answers with the picture of a doctor going to those who are sick. His presence among sinners fits the purpose for which He came. Luke explicitly describes that purpose as calling sinners to repentance. Sharing a meal opens the way for restoration; the account does not describe sin as harmless.

Jesus then sends His questioners back to Hosea 6:4–7. There God contrasts fleeting loyalty with the mercy and knowledge of Him that He desires. The Hebrew word חֶסֶד, ḥesed (KHEH-sed), includes kindness and devotion. Brown–Driver–Briggs explains these uses and notes devotion to God in Hosea 6:6. The contrast challenges outward offerings that are separated from a faithful response to God.

By applying Hosea to this meal, Jesus brings mercy to the center of the question. The people needing help are the very people His mission seeks. His answer calls the questioners to understand God's purpose rather than judge His mission by the company He keeps.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a call to show mercy to sinners and recognize their need for repentance, rather than requiring them to become respectable before Jesus will receive them. Wesley on Matthew 9:13 emphasizes God's preference for mercy over sacrifice, and the Catholic Catechism, 545, describes Jesus welcoming sinners and calling them to conversion; its 1443 paragraph also explains His table fellowship as a sign of restored belonging.
passages.god_plan_html:
The welcome at Matthew's table belongs within the purpose for which Christ came into the world. In 1 Timothy 1:12–17, Paul describes receiving mercy despite his former violence and persecution. He presents that mercy as an example of Christ's patience toward others who will believe and receive eternal life.

Titus 3:3–7 likewise begins with a former life of wrongdoing, then describes God's kindness and salvation through His mercy, new birth, and renewal by the Spirit. God does more than make room at a table: through Christ He gives people a new life and a future with Him. The mercy Jesus shows here is part of that larger rescue.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 9:14-17
passages.section_title: The Bridegroom and the Time to Fast

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 Then John’s disciples came to Jesus and asked, “Why is it that we and the Pharisees fast so often, but Your disciples do not fast?” 15 Jesus replied, “How can the guests of the bridegroom mourn while He is with them? But the time will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them; then they will fast. 16 No one sews a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old garment. For the patch will pull away from the garment, and a worse tear will result. 17 Neither do men pour new wine into old wineskins. If they do, the skins will burst, the wine will spill, and the wineskins will be ruined. Instead, they pour new wine into new wineskins, and both are preserved.”
paragraphs: 14 Then John’s disciples came to Jesus and asked, “Why is it that we and the Pharisees fast so often, but Your disciples do not fast?” 15 Jesus replied, “How can the guests of the bridegroom mourn while He is with them? But the time will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them; then they will fast.

16 No one sews a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old garment. For the patch will pull away from the garment, and a worse tear will result. 17 Neither do men pour new wine into old wineskins. If they do, the skins will burst, the wine will spill, and the wineskins will be ruined. Instead, they pour new wine into new wineskins, and both are preserved.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the meal with tax collectors and sinners, John's disciples ask why Jesus' disciples do not fast as they and the Pharisees do. Jesus answers by turning attention to His presence among them. Wedding guests do not mourn while the bridegroom is with them; His being there calls for joy.

The answer also looks ahead. The bridegroom will be taken from them, and then they will fast. Jesus is not rejecting fasting altogether. Earlier, Matthew 6:16–18 has already described sincere fasting before the Father. Here the question is what response fits the moment and His presence.

The cloth and wineskin pictures continue that concern with what fits. An unshrunk patch pulls away from an old garment, making the tear worse. New wine in old skins bursts them and loses the wine. New wine needs new skins if both are to be preserved.

A wineskin was a leather container. The Greek word is ἀσκός, askos (as-KOSS); Thayer's Greek Lexicon describes a leather bag or bottle used for water or wine. Jesus uses familiar containers to picture the harm caused by forcing together things that do not fit.

Mark 2:18–22 and Luke 5:33–39 give the related exchange. Luke adds the preference of an old-wine drinker for what is familiar.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly see Jesus as the bridegroom whose presence brings joy, while His coming departure explains a future time for fasting. The cloth and wineskin pictures receive different, sometimes overlapping explanations.

Wesley on Matthew 9:15–17 emphasizes both timing and the disciples' readiness for demanding practices. The US Catholic bishops' notes on Matthew 9:16–17 take a broader view: the gospel cannot simply be fitted within the old forms of religious life.

In his Angelus of February 26, 2006, Benedict XVI explains the related passage in Mark through Jesus' identity as bridegroom, His death, and the changed spirit in which Christians fast. These explanations connect fasting with receiving Christ, while placing different emphasis on personal readiness and the newness of His mission.
passages.god_plan_html:
The bridegroom picture also appears in John 3:27–30. John describes his own joy as the bridegroom's friend and directs attention away from himself toward Jesus. That passage provides a clear parallel for the joy Jesus describes here.

The newness of His mission reaches its saving purpose in the new covenant. At the supper before His death, Jesus connects the cup with His blood poured out for His people in Luke 22:14–20. Hebrews 8:6–13 describes Him as the mediator of the promised relationship in which God forgives sins and writes His laws on people's hearts. His coming calls for a response shaped by who He is and what He gives, rather than simply fitting Him into existing expectations.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 9:18-26
passages.section_title: A Daughter Restored and a Woman Healed

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 While Jesus was saying these things, a synagogue leader came and knelt before Him. “My daughter has just died,” he said. “But come and place Your hand on her, and she will live.” 19 So Jesus got up and went with him, along with His disciples. 20 Suddenly a woman who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years came up behind Him and touched the fringe of His cloak. 21 She said to herself, “If only I touch His cloak, I will be healed.” 22 Jesus turned and saw her. “Take courage, daughter,” He said, “your faith has healed you.” And the woman was healed from that very hour. 23 When Jesus entered the house of the synagogue leader, He saw the flute players and the noisy crowd. 24 “Go away,” He told them. “The girl is not dead, but asleep.” And they laughed at Him. 25 After the crowd had been put outside, Jesus went in and took the girl by the hand, and she got up. 26 And the news about this spread throughout that region.
paragraphs: 18 While Jesus was saying these things, a synagogue leader came and knelt before Him. “My daughter has just died,” he said. “But come and place Your hand on her, and she will live.” 19 So Jesus got up and went with him, along with His disciples.

20 Suddenly a woman who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years came up behind Him and touched the fringe of His cloak. 21 She said to herself, “If only I touch His cloak, I will be healed.” 22 Jesus turned and saw her. “Take courage, daughter,” He said, “your faith has healed you.” And the woman was healed from that very hour.

23 When Jesus entered the house of the synagogue leader, He saw the flute players and the noisy crowd. 24 “Go away,” He told them. “The girl is not dead, but asleep.” And they laughed at Him. 25 After the crowd had been put outside, Jesus went in and took the girl by the hand, and she got up. 26 And the news about this spread throughout that region.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
While Jesus is still speaking, a synagogue leader kneels before Him and asks Him to come to his daughter. The man believes that Jesus' touch can bring her life. Jesus goes with him, but the account pauses on the way for another person in need: a woman who has suffered from bleeding for twelve years.

The woman touches the fringe of His cloak, trusting that she will be healed. Jesus turns toward her, calls her daughter, and credits her faith. Leviticus 15:25–30 describes the uncleanness associated with a prolonged discharge of blood and the cleansing that follows its end. Her restoration matters within that setting as well as bringing relief from the illness itself.

Mark 5:21–43 and Luke 8:40–56 name the father Jairus and provide more detail. Matthew presents his plea with the daughter's death already in view. Mark and Luke begin with her dying and report news of her death arriving while Jesus is still speaking to the woman. Jesus tells the father not to fear but to believe. Both accounts also tell us that the girl is about twelve years old.

At the house, Matthew describes flute players and a noisy crowd. Jesus' statement that the girl is asleep is met with laughter, but He takes her hand and she rises. Luke explicitly says the people know she is dead and that her spirit returns when Jesus calls her. The sleep image prepares for her awakening at His word; the account describes life restored, rather than merely an error about whether she had died.

The two encounters bring different forms of helplessness before Jesus. One person approaches after years of suffering; another cannot approach at all, and her father pleads for her. Jesus attends to both. Their place together in the story shows that helping one person does not exhaust His power to help the other.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand these intertwined encounters as revealing Jesus' power to heal and raise the dead, with faith in Him emphasized throughout. Wesley on Matthew 9:22–25 discusses Jesus' encouragement of the woman and the girl's restoration to life, while the Catholic Catechism, 2616, names both Jairus' spoken plea and the woman's silent approach as examples of faith brought to Jesus.
passages.god_plan_html:
The girl's return to life gives a concrete glimpse of the authority Jesus describes in John 5:21–29. The Son gives life, and the dead will hear His voice and rise. John's account states the larger promise; Matthew's encounter shows that death does not place this child beyond Jesus' reach.

Her return to ordinary life is not yet the final defeat of death. 1 Corinthians 15:42–55 describes the resurrection in which the dead are raised beyond decay and mortality. That is the greater hope to which His power points: God's purpose is not only to give temporary relief, but to overcome death through Christ.
passages.current_position_html: On the woman's healing in verses 20–22, Prayer and Faith emphasizes that she reaches toward Jesus in trust without first voicing a request to Him. Jesus credits her faith. The study's position is that the focus belongs on trust in Him, rather than on the wording, frequency, or eloquence of a request.

passages.title: Matthew 9:20-22
passages.section_title: Faith Reaches Out to Jesus

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 20 Suddenly a woman who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years came up behind Him and touched the fringe of His cloak. 21 She said to herself, “If only I touch His cloak, I will be healed.” 22 Jesus turned and saw her. “Take courage, daughter,” He said, “your faith has healed you.” And the woman was healed from that very hour.
paragraphs: 20 Suddenly a woman who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years came up behind Him and touched the fringe of His cloak. 21 She said to herself, “If only I touch His cloak, I will be healed.” 22 Jesus turned and saw her. “Take courage, daughter,” He said, “your faith has healed you.” And the woman was healed from that very hour.

passages.context_html:
This healing takes place while Jesus is on His way to the synagogue leader's daughter in Matthew 9:18–26. A woman with twelve years of bleeding comes up behind Him and touches His cloak. Matthew records what she says to herself, followed by Jesus' assurance that her faith has healed her.

Her condition has a place within the Law's cleansing requirements. Leviticus 15:25–30 describes a prolonged discharge as making a woman unclean until the required cleansing after it ends. This is a statement about her condition under the Law, rather than proof that she has committed a particular sin.

The fringe she touches is described by κράσπεδον, kraspedon (KRAS-peh-don), a garment's edge or tassel. Thayer's Greek Lexicon connects the word here with the tassels prescribed in Numbers 15:37–41, reminders of God's commandments. Matthew says she touches Jesus' garment; he does not describe the clothing as having power apart from Him.

The word translated healed comes from σῴζω, sōzō (SOH-zoh), which can mean rescue, save, or make well. Thayer's Greek Lexicon specifically lists Matthew 9:21–22 under restoration from disease. Here a real bodily healing is in view; the same word can carry a wider saving meaning in other settings.

Mark 5:25–34 and Luke 8:43–48 add that the bleeding stops when she touches Him and that she then tells Him what has happened. Her initial approach contains no spoken request to Jesus. His response is personal: He addresses her as daughter and sends her in peace in those fuller accounts.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the encounter as a response of faith to Jesus' power and mercy, rather than healing produced independently by a garment. The Catholic Catechism, 2616, includes her among those whose faith reaches Jesus without a spoken request, and Wesley on Matthew 9:22 places His encouragement within her fearful approach and cleansing.
passages.current_position_html: On the woman's healing in verses 20–22, Prayer and Faith emphasizes that she reaches toward Jesus in trust without first voicing a request to Him. Jesus credits her faith. The study's position is that the focus belongs on trust in Him, rather than on the wording, frequency, or eloquence of a request.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The peace Jesus gives her in Mark 5:34 belongs alongside a wider theme of welcome through Him. Romans 5:1–2 describes peace with God and access to grace through Jesus Christ, received through faith. Her welcome gives a personal picture beside Paul's wider teaching about peace with God.

Titus 3:3–7 describes God's saving mercy through new birth and renewal by the Spirit, leading to the hope of eternal life. The woman's bodily restoration provides a helpful picture beside that larger rescue: people come in need, and the gift of restored life comes from God.

passages.title: Matthew 9:27-31
passages.section_title: Have Mercy on Us, Son of David

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 27 As Jesus went on from there, two blind men followed Him, crying out, “Have mercy on us, Son of David!” 28 After Jesus had entered the house, the blind men came to Him. “Do you believe that I am able to do this?” He asked. “Yes, Lord,” they answered. 29 Then He touched their eyes and said, “According to your faith will it be done to you.” 30 And their eyes were opened. Jesus warned them sternly, “See that no one finds out about this!” 31 But they went out and spread the news about Him throughout the land.
paragraphs: 27 As Jesus went on from there, two blind men followed Him, crying out, “Have mercy on us, Son of David!” 28 After Jesus had entered the house, the blind men came to Him. “Do you believe that I am able to do this?” He asked. “Yes, Lord,” they answered. 29 Then He touched their eyes and said, “According to your faith will it be done to you.”
30 And their eyes were opened. Jesus warned them sternly, “See that no one finds out about this!” 31 But they went out and spread the news about Him throughout the land.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the girl is restored to life, two blind men follow Jesus and ask Him for mercy. They call Him Son of David, recalling the Gospel's opening identification of Jesus in Matthew 1:1. Their appeal joins a request for help with recognition of the promised King's family line.

The conversation takes place after Jesus enters the house. He asks whether they believe He can do this, and they answer yes. He touches their eyes and speaks of their faith. The account places their confidence in Him at the center of the encounter; it does not describe a technique by which they make themselves see.

Once their eyes are opened, Jesus gives a stern instruction to keep the event quiet. They instead spread the news throughout the land. Matthew leaves the contrast plain: receiving His mercy does not make their response to His instruction an example of obedience.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read the men's appeal as faith in Jesus as David's promised descendant and in His power to heal. The Catholic Catechism, 2616, uses their cry as an example of urgent prayer to Jesus, while the US Catholic bishops' note on Matthew 9:27 identifies Son of David as a title pointing to the Messiah.
passages.god_plan_html:
Their opened eyes belong within Scripture's promise of God's saving arrival. Isaiah 35:4–10 speaks of God coming to save, blind eyes opening, and the redeemed returning with joy. In Matthew 11:2–6, Jesus names sight given to the blind among the works that answer John's question about His identity. This healing fits that wider testimony.

Scripture also uses light and sight to describe coming to know Christ. 2 Corinthians 4:3–6 describes God bringing the light of Christ's glory into people's hearts. That is a related spiritual picture, not an explanation that physical blindness measures someone's faith or moral condition. The larger purpose is that people receive both His mercy and knowledge of who He is.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 9:32-34
passages.section_title: Restoration and an Accusation

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 32 As they were leaving, a demon-possessed man who was mute was brought to Jesus. 33 And when the demon had been driven out, the man began to speak. The crowds were amazed and said, “Nothing like this has ever been seen in Israel!” 34 But the Pharisees said, “It is by the prince of demons that He drives out demons.”
paragraphs: 32 As they were leaving, a demon-possessed man who was mute was brought to Jesus. 33 And when the demon had been driven out, the man began to speak. The crowds were amazed and said, “Nothing like this has ever been seen in Israel!” 34 But the Pharisees said, “It is by the prince of demons that He drives out demons.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
As the healed blind men leave, a man who is mute and demon-possessed is brought to Jesus. The demon is driven out and the man begins to speak. Matthew gives no extended conversation, but turns quickly to the responses of those who witness it.

The crowds express amazement at what they have seen in Israel. The Pharisees give a different explanation: they attribute Jesus' deliverance to the prince of demons. The man's restoration is placed beside opposition to the One who restores him.

The passage identifies a demon in this man's case. It does not give a general explanation for every person's difficulty speaking. Its focus is the freedom Jesus brings and the sharply different responses to His work.

A related accusation appears in Matthew 12:22–29, where Jesus answers it by exposing the contradiction in a divided kingdom and explaining His deliverance as the arrival of God's kingdom. Matthew does not record that fuller answer here.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as a display of Jesus' authority over evil and a sign of the growing opposition to Him. The Catholic Catechism, 550, places His deliverances within the defeat of Satan's kingdom, and the US Catholic bishops' note on Matthew 9:34 highlights the accusation as pointing toward the opposition developed in the following chapters.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus' explanation in Matthew 12:28–29 places deliverance within God's kingdom overcoming the enemy's hold. The man's restored speech is one concrete instance of freedom; it points beyond itself to the greater work of the King who sets people free.

Colossians 2:13–15 joins that victory with the cross, describing God making people alive with Christ, forgiving sins, canceling their debt, and triumphing over hostile powers. The opposition recorded here does not overturn God's saving purpose. The same Jesus who is accused will accomplish His victory through the cross.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 9:35-38
passages.section_title: Compassion and Workers for the Harvest

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 35 Jesus went through all the towns and villages, teaching in their synagogues, preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every disease and sickness. 36 When He saw the crowds, He was moved with compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd. 37 Then He said to His disciples, “The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few. 38 Ask the Lord of the harvest, therefore, to send out workers into His harvest.”
paragraphs: 35 Jesus went through all the towns and villages, teaching in their synagogues, preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every disease and sickness. 36 When He saw the crowds, He was moved with compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd.
37 Then He said to His disciples, “The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few. 38 Ask the Lord of the harvest, therefore, to send out workers into His harvest.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
