Matthew gathers up Jesus' ministry in the towns and villages: teaching, proclaiming the kingdom, and healing. The description recalls Matthew 4:23, which introduced the teaching and healings of these chapters. The summary then leads into His concern for the crowds and the sending of His disciples.

Jesus sees people who are harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd, and responds with compassion. The picture emphasizes their need for care and guidance. He does not turn their need into a reason to keep His distance.

He then changes the picture from a flock to a harvest. There is much work to do, but few workers. His instruction is to ask the Lord of the harvest to send them. The work belongs to God, and the disciples' first response to the need is prayer.

The next passage shows those who pray being drawn into the work. In Matthew 10:1–8, Jesus gives the twelve authority and sends them to the lost sheep of Israel to proclaim the kingdom and bring help. The prayer is therefore closely joined with active service; it is not merely an observation about how much need exists.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as a call to share Jesus' compassion and pray for workers whom God sends to bring His message and care to others. Wesley on Matthew 9:37–38 emphasizes that the Lord sends and equips the workers, and the Catholic Catechism, 2611, likewise connects prayer with readiness to take part in God's purposes.
passages.god_plan_html:
The shepherd picture reaches back into God's care for Israel. In Numbers 27:15–23, Moses asks God to appoint a leader so the people will not be like sheep without a shepherd. In Ezekiel 34:11–16, 23–24, God promises to seek His scattered flock and give them one shepherd, His servant David. Jesus' compassion stands within that larger scriptural pattern of God gathering and caring for His people.

Jesus explains the depth of that care in John 10:11–18. As the good shepherd, He lays down His life, takes it up again, and gathers His sheep into one flock. The workers' service belongs within His saving work. They are sent to care for people who belong to Him, reflecting the compassion of the Shepherd who gives His own life for them.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 10:1-4
passages.section_title: The Twelve Are Called and Sent

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 And calling His twelve disciples to Him, Jesus gave them authority over unclean spirits, so that they could drive them out and heal every disease and sickness. 2 These are the names of the twelve apostles: first Simon, called Peter, and his brother Andrew; James son of Zebedee, and his brother John; 3 Philip and Bartholomew; Thomas and Matthew the tax collector; James son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus; 4 Simon the Zealot, and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed Jesus.
paragraphs: 1 And calling His twelve disciples to Him, Jesus gave them authority over unclean spirits, so that they could drive them out and heal every disease and sickness.

2 These are the names of the twelve apostles: first Simon, called Peter, and his brother Andrew; James son of Zebedee, and his brother John; 3 Philip and Bartholomew; Thomas and Matthew the tax collector; James son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus; 4 Simon the Zealot, and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed Jesus.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus has just told His disciples to ask the Lord of the harvest for workers in Matthew 9:35–38. He now calls the twelve and gives them authority to bring the same kind of help people have received through His ministry. The workers depend on authority He gives, rather than a power they possess independently.

Matthew calls them apostles. The Greek word is ἀπόστολος, apostolos (ah-POS-toh-los), a delegate or messenger sent with a commission. Thayer's Greek Lexicon explains both that general meaning and its particular use for the twelve chosen by Jesus. Here the title prepares for their being sent in the next verses.

Mark 3:13–19 describes their appointment to be with Jesus and to be sent out to preach. Luke 6:12–16 places His choice of the twelve after a night of prayer. Together these accounts show that their mission grows out of being called to Him and learning from Him.

The list names brothers, distinguishes two men named James and two named Simon, and identifies Matthew as the tax collector. Simon Peter heads the list. John 1:40–42 describes Andrew bringing Simon to Jesus and Jesus giving him the name Cephas, translated as Peter. These are people with names and relationships, not simply an unnamed group of messengers.

Judas Iscariot is included, with the betrayal already named. That detail looks ahead to the later Passion account. Matthew does not introduce the twelve as men whose future conduct will always match the responsibility given to them.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the twelve as men specially chosen and authorized by Jesus to share His mission. Wesley on Matthew 10:1 describes them as chosen from His followers, and the Catholic Compendium of the Catechism, 109, likewise describes Jesus choosing the twelve and sharing His mission and authority with them.
passages.god_plan_html:
The number twelve connects this calling with God's purposes for Israel. In Matthew 19:27–30, Jesus explicitly connects His followers' twelve thrones with the twelve tribes in the renewal of all things. The calling here belongs within that larger promise, rather than the creation of an arbitrary group size.

Their role also reaches into the gathering of God's people through Christ. Ephesians 2:19–22 describes people welcomed into God's household, built on the foundation of apostles and prophets, with Jesus Himself as the cornerstone. The apostolic calling therefore reaches beyond a single journey: their witness serves the gathering of God's people around Christ.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 10:5-8
passages.section_title: Sent First to the Lost Sheep of Israel

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 These twelve Jesus sent out with the following instructions: “Do not go onto the road of the Gentiles or enter any town of the Samaritans. 6 Go rather to the lost sheep of Israel. 7 As you go, preach this message: ‘The kingdom of heaven is near.’ 8 Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse the lepers, drive out demons. Freely you have received; freely give.
paragraphs: 5 These twelve Jesus sent out with the following instructions: “Do not go onto the road of the Gentiles or enter any town of the Samaritans. 6 Go rather to the lost sheep of Israel.
7 As you go, preach this message: ‘The kingdom of heaven is near.’ 8 Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse the lepers, drive out demons. Freely you have received; freely give.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus gives the twelve a specific first assignment. They are to go to the lost sheep of Israel rather than Gentile roads or Samaritan towns. This continues His concern for the crowds pictured as sheep without a shepherd in Matthew 9:36. Their message and help are directed first toward His own people.

The message is that the kingdom of heaven is near. It is the message already announced by John in Matthew 3:1–2 and Jesus in Matthew 4:17. The apostles are sent to carry His announcement, rather than invent one of their own.

The word translated preach is κηρύσσω, kērussō (kay-ROOS-soh), to proclaim as a herald. Thayer's Greek Lexicon explains this sense of announcing a message with authority. Here the instruction concerns telling people what God is doing through His King; it is not limited to speaking from a pulpit in a church building.

The works they are to do also continue Jesus' ministry: healing, restoring life, cleansing lepers, and driving out demons. The authority has been given to them by Him. His command to give freely keeps that gift at the center; they are not to turn His help into something people must purchase.

The restriction to Israel belongs to this assignment. The same Gospel later records the risen Jesus sending His followers to all nations in Matthew 28:18–20. The first mission's boundaries therefore should not be made into a permanent exclusion of other peoples.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as an initial mission to Israel, carrying Jesus' kingdom message and freely sharing the help He authorizes. Wesley on Matthew 10:5 distinguishes this restricted commission from the later mission to Gentiles, and the Catholic Catechism, 543, likewise describes the kingdom as first announced to Israel and intended to welcome all nations.
passages.god_plan_html:
The order fits God's faithfulness to His promises. Romans 15:8–12 describes Christ serving Israel to confirm the promises to the patriarchs, so that the nations may glorify God for His mercy. Israel's place and the nations' welcome belong within the same saving purpose.

The free gift also gives the mission its character. 1 Peter 4:10–11 describes God's varied grace being entrusted to His people for service, with God glorified through Jesus Christ. What is received from Him is used for others' good. The apostles' freely given help is part of that larger pattern of grace reaching people through willing servants.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 10:9-15
passages.section_title: Depending on Welcome and Taking Rejection Seriously

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 Do not take along any gold or silver or copper in your belts. 10 Take no bag for the road, or second tunic, or sandals, or staff; for the worker is worthy of his provisions. 11 Whatever town or village you enter, find out who is worthy there and stay at his house until you move on. 12 As you enter the home, greet its occupants. 13 If the home is worthy, let your peace rest on it, but if it is not, let your peace return to you. 14 And if anyone will not welcome you or heed your words, shake the dust off your feet when you leave that home or town. 15 Truly I tell you, it will be more bearable for Sodom and Gomorrah on the day of judgment than for that town.
paragraphs: 9 Do not take along any gold or silver or copper in your belts. 10 Take no bag for the road, or second tunic, or sandals, or staff; for the worker is worthy of his provisions. 11 Whatever town or village you enter, find out who is worthy there and stay at his house until you move on.
12 As you enter the home, greet its occupants. 13 If the home is worthy, let your peace rest on it, but if it is not, let your peace return to you.

14 And if anyone will not welcome you or heed your words, shake the dust off your feet when you leave that home or town. 15 Truly I tell you, it will be more bearable for Sodom and Gomorrah on the day of judgment than for that town.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus now explains how the twelve are to travel and how they are to respond to those they meet. He tells them not to take money or a travel bag, and restricts their clothing and equipment. They are to rely on the hospitality of households that receive them. The worker's right to support is stated alongside that dependence. Giving freely does not mean those who serve have no need for food or shelter.

They are to find a suitable household and stay there until they leave the town. The greeting of peace belongs to their entry into the home. If the house receives them, that peace rests there; if not, it returns to them. Their mission involves a real offer of peace, with a real possibility of refusal.

The related accounts give the travel instructions in different detail. Mark 6:7–13 permits a staff and sandals, while Luke 9:1–6, like Matthew, names a staff among the things not to take. Wesley on Matthew 10:9–10 understands Matthew as forbidding extra preparations rather than discarding what they already have. That is one explanation of the difference; the common emphasis is traveling with simple needs and dependence on the welcome given.

If a home or town refuses both them and their words, they are to leave and shake the dust from their feet. Mark describes this as a testimony against the place, and Acts 13:44–52 later records Paul and Barnabas doing it when driven out. It marks rejection of the message; Jesus does not tell them to force a household to receive it.

The comparison with Sodom and Gomorrah gives that rejection a solemn weight. Jesus speaks of the day of judgment and the responsibility of a town that refuses His messengers. This is a warning about receiving His kingdom announcement, rather than a direction for the apostles to carry out punishment themselves.

The provision instructions address this particular journey. Elsewhere, 1 Corinthians 9:7–14 explains the right of gospel workers to receive material support. In Luke 22:35–36, Jesus Himself refers back to the earlier journey and gives different instructions about a purse and bag. The first commission belongs within that developing story of their service.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand these instructions as teaching trust in God's provision, hospitality toward His messengers, and the seriousness of rejecting their message. Wesley on Matthew 10:9–14 emphasizes dependence and a receptive household, while the US Catholic bishops' notes on Matthew 10:8–14 similarly explain freely given service, support from those who welcome the twelve, and the significance of the peace and dust gestures.
passages.god_plan_html:
The welcome given to Jesus' messengers is connected with receiving Jesus Himself. In the related mission instructions of Luke 10:16, He explains that hearing His messengers means hearing Him, while rejecting them means rejecting Him and the One who sent Him. The importance of the response comes from whose message they bear.

The peace they announce has its fullest expression in Christ's saving work. Ephesians 2:13–18 describes Him making peace through His blood, reconciling people to God through the cross, and bringing those near and far to the Father by one Spirit. The mission's offer of peace belongs within that larger welcome through the Savior.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 10:16-23
passages.section_title: Facing Opposition with Wisdom and Faith

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 Behold, I am sending you out like sheep among wolves; therefore be as shrewd as snakes and as innocent as doves. 17 But beware of men, for they will hand you over to their councils and flog you in their synagogues. 18 On My account you will be brought before governors and kings as witnesses to them and to the Gentiles. 19 But when they hand you over, do not worry about how to respond or what to say. In that hour you will be given what to say. 20 For it will not be you speaking, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you. 21 Brother will betray brother to death, and a father his child; children will rise against their parents and have them put to death. 22 You will be hated by everyone because of My name, but the one who perseveres to the end will be saved. 23 When they persecute you in one town, flee to the next. Truly I tell you, you will not reach all the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes.
paragraphs: 16 Behold, I am sending you out like sheep among wolves; therefore be as shrewd as snakes and as innocent as doves. 17 But beware of men, for they will hand you over to their councils and flog you in their synagogues. 18 On My account you will be brought before governors and kings as witnesses to them and to the Gentiles.

19 But when they hand you over, do not worry about how to respond or what to say. In that hour you will be given what to say. 20 For it will not be you speaking, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you.

21 Brother will betray brother to death, and a father his child; children will rise against their parents and have them put to death. 22 You will be hated by everyone because of My name, but the one who perseveres to the end will be saved. 23 When they persecute you in one town, flee to the next. Truly I tell you, you will not reach all the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus prepares His messengers for opposition. The picture changes from a harvest needing workers to sheep surrounded by wolves. He does not tell them to become like the threat around them. They are to combine practical wisdom with innocence as they carry out His mission.

The word for shrewd is φρόνιμος, phronimos (FROH-nee-mos), prudent or sensible. The word for innocent is ἀκέραιος, akeraios (ah-KEH-rye-os), free from evil or deceit. Thayer's entries for the first word and the second include this verse. The two instructions belong together: care and discernment must be joined with integrity.

The dangers are concrete. Jesus names councils, flogging, governors, kings, and betrayal within families. Yet He also describes those appearances before rulers as opportunities for testimony, even to Gentiles. Their message will reach beyond the setting of the first journey to Israel.

His promise about words to speak addresses being handed over for trial. The Spirit of their Father will help them in that hour. They are not left to carry the witness in their own strength. The promise concerns this moment of pressure; it is not a direction to stop learning His teaching.

The call to persevere comes alongside the warning that witnesses may be put to death. Being saved therefore cannot be reduced to a guarantee that every faithful witness will avoid death. Jesus also tells them to flee to another town when persecuted. Continuing the mission can involve leaving a dangerous place.

He closes with the saying that they will not reach all the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes. Christian interpreters differ over the meaning and timing of that coming, as well as how to explain the promise joined to perseverance.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand this as a call to remain faithful to Jesus under opposition, relying on the Spirit while acting with wisdom and integrity. Traditions differ over whether a believer can finally turn away from Christ.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, 17.1–3, and the 1689 Baptist Confession, 17.1–3, teach that those God has brought into saving faith will not finally be lost: God preserves them, even though they may fall into serious sins for a time.

The Methodist Articles of Religion, XII, say that those who have received the Holy Spirit may depart from grace and fall into sin, yet by God's grace return and change how they live. The Catholic Catechism, 161–162, likewise calls faith a free gift that can be lost and urges believers to keep growing in faith and remain with Christ.

Verse 23 also receives different readings. Wesley on Matthew 10:23 understands the coming as judgment on the temple and nation. C. I. Scofield's 1917 note on 10:16–23 looks ahead to a faithful group in Israel witnessing during a final period of distress before Christ's return. The US Catholic bishops' note on 10:23 considers connections with the risen Jesus' mission or judgment on Jerusalem while acknowledging the difficulty of the saying. These commentators' readings should not be treated as a single view held by everyone in their traditions.
passages.god_plan_html:
Acts shows the promised witness continuing under pressure. In Acts 4:8–13, Peter speaks before the authorities while filled with the Holy Spirit, announcing Jesus' resurrection and the salvation found in Him. The trial becomes a setting for the message of life through Christ.

Acts 8:1–4 describes believers scattered by persecution continuing to proclaim the word. The apostles remain in Jerusalem at that point, while others carry the message into new places. Opposition does not have the final say over God's purpose to make Christ known.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 10:24-33
passages.section_title: Courage Under the Father’s Care

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 24 A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his master. 25 It is enough for a disciple to be like his teacher, and a servant like his master. If the head of the house has been called Beelzebul, how much more the members of his household! 26 So do not be afraid of them. For there is nothing concealed that will not be disclosed, and nothing hidden that will not be made known. 27 What I tell you in the dark, speak in the daylight; what is whispered in your ear, proclaim from the housetops. 28 Do not be afraid of those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Instead, fear the One who can destroy both soul and body in hell. 29 Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? Yet not one of them will fall to the ground apart from the will of your Father. 30 And even the very hairs of your head are all numbered. 31 So do not be afraid; you are worth more than many sparrows. 32 Therefore everyone who confesses Me before men, I will also confess him before My Father in heaven. 33 But whoever denies Me before men, I will also deny him before My Father in heaven.
paragraphs: 24 A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his master. 25 It is enough for a disciple to be like his teacher, and a servant like his master. If the head of the house has been called Beelzebul, how much more the members of his household!

26 So do not be afraid of them. For there is nothing concealed that will not be disclosed, and nothing hidden that will not be made known. 27 What I tell you in the dark, speak in the daylight; what is whispered in your ear, proclaim from the housetops. 28 Do not be afraid of those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Instead, fear the One who can destroy both soul and body in hell.

29 Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? Yet not one of them will fall to the ground apart from the will of your Father. 30 And even the very hairs of your head are all numbered. 31 So do not be afraid; you are worth more than many sparrows.
32 Therefore everyone who confesses Me before men, I will also confess him before My Father in heaven. 33 But whoever denies Me before men, I will also deny him before My Father in heaven.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus explains opposition through the relationship between a disciple and teacher, or a servant and master. His messengers should expect treatment like His own. If He is accused of being aligned with evil, members of His household can expect similar slander. The accusation recalls Matthew 9:34 and is developed further in Matthew 12:24.

He then repeatedly tells them not to fear. The assurance that concealed things will be disclosed leads directly to the command to speak openly what He has taught them. Opposition must not turn His message into something they keep permanently hidden.

The contrast between body and soul puts human threats in perspective. People may kill the body, but their power has a limit. Jesus directs His followers toward reverence for God's final authority over the whole person. The warning about judgment is serious, even as He calls them away from fear of human opponents.

The sparrows and numbered hairs reveal the care of that same Father. His attention reaches what might seem small or easily overlooked, and His disciples matter to Him. This is not a promise that danger will never touch them; the earlier verses have already described it. It is assurance that they are neither forgotten nor worthless to God.

The closing sayings join public allegiance to Jesus with His response before the Father. Acknowledging Him carries a promise; denying Him carries a warning. The related teaching in Luke 12:4–9 likewise brings together human threats, God's judgment, His detailed care, and the Son of Man's response to those who confess or deny Him.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a call to acknowledge Jesus openly, fear God above human opponents, and trust the Father's care. Wesley on Matthew 10:28–32 joins reverence for God with confidence in His care, and the Catholic Catechism, 1816, applies Jesus' confession-and-denial sayings to living faith, public witness, and following Him through persecution.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus' promise before the Father points beyond the present conflict to His saving relationship with His people. Romans 8:31–39 grounds their confidence in God giving His own Son, raising Him, and receiving His intercession on their behalf. Christ's care rests on what He has done and continues to do for them.

Paul includes danger, persecution, and death among the things that cannot separate His people from God's love in Christ. That gives a wider setting for the sparrow picture: God's care is not measured only by whether a threat ends immediately. His saving love holds them through suffering and death.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 10:34-39
passages.section_title: When Following Jesus Divides a Family

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 34 Do not assume that I have come to bring peace to the earth; I have not come to bring peace, but a sword. 35 For I have come to turn ‘a man against his father, a daughter against her mother, a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law. 36 A man’s enemies will be the members of his own household.’ 37 Anyone who loves his father or mother more than Me is not worthy of Me; anyone who loves his son or daughter more than Me is not worthy of Me; 38 and anyone who does not take up his cross and follow Me is not worthy of Me. 39 Whoever finds his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life for My sake will find it.
paragraphs: 34 Do not assume that I have come to bring peace to the earth; I have not come to bring peace, but a sword. 35 For I have come to turn ‘a man against his father, a daughter against her mother, a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law. 36 A man’s enemies will be the members of his own household.’

37 Anyone who loves his father or mother more than Me is not worthy of Me; anyone who loves his son or daughter more than Me is not worthy of Me; 38 and anyone who does not take up his cross and follow Me is not worthy of Me. 39 Whoever finds his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life for My sake will find it.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus now describes the division His coming can bring, even within a household. The sword image explains conflict around allegiance to Him. It belongs with the earlier warning about family betrayal in Matthew 10:21, and should be read alongside His instruction to love enemies in Matthew 5:43–48. The disciples are being prepared to face opposition, rather than commanded to attack their families.

His words about divided households draw from Micah 7:5–7, where betrayal reaches close relationships and the prophet turns in hope to God. Jesus uses that language to describe how deeply the response to Him can divide people.

The issue in verse 37 is loving family more than Him. He names parents and children, the strongest of ordinary bonds, and calls for loyalty to Him even when those claims compete. The saying is not a judgment that family love itself has no value; its force lies in the greater claim He makes.

Taking up a cross deepens the cost. Following Him may mean surrendering security and even life. The final contrast is between trying to preserve life at the cost of allegiance to Him and losing life for His sake. The promise is that life given to Him is not finally lost.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand these sayings as requiring loyalty to Jesus above competing loyalties and willingness to share the cost of following Him. Wesley on Matthew 10:34–39 explains the divisions through opposition to the gospel and the cross through faithfulness when avoiding hardship would mean doing wrong, while the Catholic Catechism, 520, presents Christ's own humility and hardships as the example His disciples follow.
passages.god_plan_html:
The disciple's cross belongs within Jesus' own path. In Matthew 16:21–27, He speaks of His coming suffering, death, and resurrection, then again calls His followers to take up their cross. The call is shaped by the Savior who goes before them.

Philippians 2:5–11 joins His willing service and death on a cross with His exaltation by the Father. God's saving purpose moves through self-giving toward life and glory. Following Jesus means placing one's life with that Savior, whose own suffering was not the end of His story.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 10:40-42
passages.section_title: Welcoming Jesus by Welcoming His People

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 40 He who receives you receives Me, and he who receives Me receives the One who sent Me. 41 Whoever receives a prophet because he is a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward, and whoever receives a righteous man because he is a righteous man will receive a righteous man’s reward. 42 And if anyone gives even a cup of cold water to one of these little ones because he is My disciple, truly I tell you, he will never lose his reward.”
paragraphs: 40 He who receives you receives Me, and he who receives Me receives the One who sent Me. 41 Whoever receives a prophet because he is a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward, and whoever receives a righteous man because he is a righteous man will receive a righteous man’s reward.
42 And if anyone gives even a cup of cold water to one of these little ones because he is My disciple, truly I tell you, he will never lose his reward.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The mission instructions close with welcome and reward. Earlier Jesus warned that some households would refuse the messengers. Here He explains the significance of receiving them: welcoming those He sends means receiving Him and the Father who sent Him.

The welcome is given because of the person's relationship to God and His work. A prophet is received as a prophet, and a righteous person as a righteous person. The host takes part in supporting that service, and Jesus promises a reward.

The last example makes the act very small and concrete: a cup of cold water given to a disciple. Jesus calls the recipient one of these little ones and explicitly identifies him as His disciple. The attention is not limited to celebrated messengers or impressive acts. Ordinary care for someone who belongs to Him matters.

This ending widens the circle of participation. Some carry the message on the road; others welcome them and meet their needs. In the setting of the chapter, hospitality becomes part of receiving the mission Jesus has entrusted to His followers.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand these verses as connecting welcome for Christ's people with welcome for Him, and as assuring helpers that their service matters to God. Wesley on Matthew 10:41–42 applies little ones broadly to the least Christian, while the US Catholic bishops' notes on 10:40–42 understand the descriptions chiefly as referring to the Christian messengers in the mission's setting. Both readings emphasize care given because a person belongs to Jesus, rather than because the person is important in the world's eyes.
passages.god_plan_html:
The welcome fits the larger pattern of the Father sending the Son and the Son sending His followers. After His resurrection, Jesus joins peace with that sending in John 20:19–23. The mission continues from the living Savior, and receiving His messengers is one way others take part in it.

3 John 1:5–8 makes the role of hospitality explicit. Supporting those who travel for Christ's name makes the helpers fellow workers for the truth. A small act like the cup of water belongs within God's larger work of making Christ known; the person giving it has a part to play as well as the person speaking.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 11:1-6
passages.section_title: John’s Question and Jesus’ Answer

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 After Jesus had finished instructing His twelve disciples, He went on from there to teach and preach in their cities. 2 Meanwhile John heard in prison about the works of Christ, and he sent his disciples 3 to ask Him, “Are You the One who was to come, or should we look for someone else?” 4 Jesus replied, “Go back and report to John what you hear and see: 5 The blind receive sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the good news is preached to the poor. 6 Blessed is the one who does not fall away on account of Me.”
paragraphs: 1 After Jesus had finished instructing His twelve disciples, He went on from there to teach and preach in their cities. 2 Meanwhile John heard in prison about the works of Christ, and he sent his disciples 3 to ask Him, “Are You the One who was to come, or should we look for someone else?”

4 Jesus replied, “Go back and report to John what you hear and see: 5 The blind receive sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the good news is preached to the poor. 6 Blessed is the one who does not fall away on account of Me.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After instructing the Twelve, Jesus continues teaching and preaching. John the Baptist hears about His works from prison and sends disciples with a direct question: is Jesus the promised One, or should they expect someone else? Matthew records the question without explaining everything that prompted it.

Jesus answers by pointing to what the messengers can report. People are being healed, the dead are being raised, and the poor are hearing good news. These are the kinds of works Matthew has just described in chapters 8–9. In the related account, Luke 7:18–23, the messengers themselves see Jesus healing people before He sends them back.

His answer also points back to Scripture. Isaiah 35:5–6 describes sight restored, deaf ears opened, and the lame walking; Isaiah 61:1 speaks of good news for the poor. His works and His message belong together as evidence of who He is.

The final blessing calls for receiving Him without turning away because of Him. It gives the question a personal edge: the promised Savior must be received as He reveals Himself. The next verses show Jesus honoring John's ministry after the messengers leave.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readers commonly understand Jesus' works and their connection with Isaiah as His answer about His identity. Interpreters differ over whose uncertainty lies behind the question. Wesley on Matthew 11:2–6 understands John as sending the disciples to strengthen their faith, while the US Catholic bishops' note on 11:3 considers it likely that John himself is struggling with expectations Jesus has not met. These are commentators' readings, rather than separate binding church teachings. Both take the messengers' report as the answer John is to receive.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus connects His mission with Isaiah even more directly in Luke 4:16–21. After reading the promise of good news and release, He declares its fulfillment in the hearing of those present. God's saving purpose is taking shape in a person who teaches, heals, and restores.

The healing here also belongs within the Bible's wider hope of life with God. Revelation 21:1–5 looks ahead to a new creation where death and pain are gone. That is a wider connection, not a claim that every part of that future has already arrived in John's lifetime. The works he hears about give a real glimpse of the restoration God promises.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 11:7-15
passages.section_title: John the Messenger Who Prepared the Way

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 As John’s disciples were leaving, Jesus began to speak to the crowds about John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed swaying in the wind? 8 Otherwise, what did you go out to see? A man dressed in fine clothes? Look, those who wear fine clothing are found in kings’ palaces. 9 What then did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. 10 This is the one about whom it is written: ‘Behold, I will send My messenger ahead of You, who will prepare Your way before You.’ 11 Truly I tell you, among those born of women there has risen no one greater than John the Baptist. Yet even the least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he. 12 From the days of John the Baptist until now, the kingdom of heaven has been subject to violence, and the violent lay claim to it. 13 For all the Prophets and the Law prophesied until John. 14 And if you are willing to accept it, he is the Elijah who was to come. 15 He who has ears, let him hear.
paragraphs: 7 As John’s disciples were leaving, Jesus began to speak to the crowds about John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed swaying in the wind? 8 Otherwise, what did you go out to see? A man dressed in fine clothes? Look, those who wear fine clothing are found in kings’ palaces. 9 What then did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.

10 This is the one about whom it is written: ‘Behold, I will send My messenger ahead of You, who will prepare Your way before You.’ 11 Truly I tell you, among those born of women there has risen no one greater than John the Baptist. Yet even the least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.

12 From the days of John the Baptist until now, the kingdom of heaven has been subject to violence, and the violent lay claim to it. 13 For all the Prophets and the Law prophesied until John. 14 And if you are willing to accept it, he is the Elijah who was to come. 15 He who has ears, let him hear.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Once John's disciples leave, Jesus asks the crowds what drew them into the wilderness. John was no swaying reed or court figure dressed for luxury. The questions lead to a stronger description: he was a prophet, and more than a prophet, because he prepared the way for the One who was coming.

Jesus applies the messenger promise of Malachi 3:1 to John. His greatness is tied to that place in God's work. The saying about the least in the kingdom being greater puts the gift of belonging to God's kingdom above even John's remarkable role. It does not say that John was an enemy of God or that his faithful service counted for nothing.

Verse 12 is difficult. The Greek verb is βιάζω, biazō (bee-AH-zoh), meaning to use force. Thayer's entry explains this saying as people eagerly laying hold of the kingdom, while other interpreters understand hostile force against it. The BSB main text uses the latter kind of wording, and its footnote offers forceful advance as another translation. The different readings are explained below.

The Law and the Prophets pointed forward to what is now unfolding. Jesus identifies John with the promised Elijah of Malachi 4:5–6, and calls the crowd to listen. Luke 1:16–17 describes John's calling in terms of Elijah's spirit and power: turning people back to God and preparing them for the Lord. In Matthew 17:10–13, the disciples again understand Jesus' words about Elijah as referring to John.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly recognize John as the promised messenger who prepared for Jesus. Wesley on Matthew 11:9–11 emphasizes John's closeness to the fulfillment and the fuller knowledge of Christ available after His saving work. The US Catholic bishops' note on 11:11 emphasizes the greater privilege of belonging to the kingdom. These explanations both place John's greatness within the greater gift Jesus brings.

The force language in verse 12 receives different readings. Wesley on 11:12 pictures eager people pressing into the kingdom, like people storming a city. The US Catholic bishops' note on 11:12 instead understands opponents trying to keep people from receiving it. That is a difference between these commentators' explanations; neither note establishes what every Methodist or Catholic believes about the verse. The saying is not a command for the disciples to spread their message through physical attack.
passages.god_plan_html:
John's work is one part of a promise moving toward salvation through Jesus. In Acts 13:23–26, Paul retells that movement: God brings the promised Savior from David's descendants, John prepares the people through a baptism of repentance, and the message of salvation is announced through Jesus.

The same chapter carries the story beyond that first announcement. In Acts 13:46–49, Paul and Barnabas proclaim salvation to Gentiles as well. John prepares the way in Israel, and the Savior he announces becomes the center of good news reaching the nations. The servant's importance lies in helping people receive that Savior.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 11:16-19
passages.section_title: Rejecting Both John and Jesus

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 To what can I compare this generation? They are like children sitting in the marketplaces and calling out to others: 17 ‘We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not mourn.’ 18 For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, ‘He has a demon!’ 19 The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, ‘Look at this glutton and drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ But wisdom is vindicated by her actions.”
paragraphs: 16 To what can I compare this generation? They are like children sitting in the marketplaces and calling out to others: 17 ‘We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not mourn.’

18 For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, ‘He has a demon!’ 19 The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, ‘Look at this glutton and drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ But wisdom is vindicated by her actions.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus compares His generation to children complaining in a marketplace. A joyful tune gets no dance, and a sad song gets no mourning. The picture exposes an unwillingness to respond, whichever kind of approach is offered.

John and Jesus give the example. John's restrained way of life brings an accusation that he has a demon. Jesus eats and drinks with people, and His opponents accuse Him of excess and criticize His friendships. Their contrasting ways of living both become reasons for rejection.

The accusation about Jesus being a glutton and drunkard is what His critics say, not Matthew's judgment about His conduct. His meals with tax collectors and sinners have already raised objections in Matthew 9:9–13, where He explains His mission through mercy and the need of sinners.

The closing saying turns attention from the accusations to wisdom's results. The question is whether the work of God is being recognized in what John and Jesus actually do. A person can keep finding reasons to dismiss the messengers while avoiding the message they bring.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as exposing an unwillingness to receive God's message, despite the different approaches of John and Jesus. Wesley on Matthew 11:16–19 describes people who will not be pleased with either approach; the US Catholic bishops' notes on 11:16–19 likewise connect the illustration with rejecting John's restraint and Jesus' meals with outsiders.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 11:20-24
passages.section_title: When Great Privilege Brings Greater Responsibility

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 20 Then Jesus began to denounce the cities in which most of His miracles had been performed, because they did not repent. 21 “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the miracles that were performed in you had been performed in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes. 22 But I tell you, it will be more bearable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment than for you. 23 And you, Capernaum, will you be lifted up to heaven? No, you will be brought down to Hades! For if the miracles that were performed in you had been performed in Sodom, it would have remained to this day. 24 But I tell you that it will be more bearable for Sodom on the day of judgment than for you.”
paragraphs: 20 Then Jesus began to denounce the cities in which most of His miracles had been performed, because they did not repent. 21 “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the miracles that were performed in you had been performed in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes. 22 But I tell you, it will be more bearable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment than for you.

23 And you, Capernaum, will you be lifted up to heaven? No, you will be brought down to Hades! For if the miracles that were performed in you had been performed in Sodom, it would have remained to this day. 24 But I tell you that it will be more bearable for Sodom on the day of judgment than for you.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus now addresses towns where much of His miraculous work has taken place. Matthew gives the reason for the rebuke: they have not repented. Seeing wonderful things has not led them to turn back to God.

The Greek word is μετανοέω, metanoeō (meh-tah-noh-EH-oh), to repent or change one's mind. Thayer's entry includes turning from past sins and seeking God's pardon, and specifically lists these verses. In this setting, repentance means more than being impressed by a miracle or feeling briefly sorry. It calls for a changed response to God.

The comparison with Tyre, Sidon, and Sodom is deliberately startling. Jesus says those places would have responded differently if they had witnessed the works these towns received. Sackcloth and ashes describe the serious response He says would have followed. Familiarity with His works gives His hearers responsibility, rather than grounds for confidence that they are already safe.

Capernaum receives its own warning about being brought down. The contrast between being lifted to heaven and going down to Hades overturns any expectation of honor based on privilege alone. Jesus repeatedly places the comparison on the day of judgment: these towns must answer for the response they have made to the light they received.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the passage as a warning that greater knowledge of God's work brings greater responsibility. Wesley on Matthew 11:21–24 treats the woes as solemn declarations of coming misery and the comparisons as differences in the severity of judgment. The Reformed Westminster Confession, 33.1–3, likewise teaches a coming judgment through Christ in which people give account, and presents that certainty as a reason to turn from sin and remain watchful.
passages.god_plan_html:
The warning belongs to God's larger purpose of bringing people to repentance and judging with justice. In Acts 17:30–31, Paul announces that God calls people everywhere to repent and has appointed the risen Jesus to judge the world. Judgment is part of the good news's serious claim on human life, alongside the offer of mercy.

Jesus states the principle of responsibility more explicitly in Luke 12:47–48: the servant who knows more is answerable for more. This is a parallel teaching, not a scale by which readers can calculate another person's punishment. God's judgment takes account of what has been entrusted to people and how they respond.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 11:25-27
passages.section_title: The Son Makes the Father Known

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 25 At that time Jesus declared, “I praise You, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because You have hidden these things from the wise and learned, and revealed them to little children. 26 Yes, Father, for this was well-pleasing in Your sight. 27 All things have been entrusted to Me by My Father. No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him.
paragraphs: 25 At that time Jesus declared, “I praise You, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because You have hidden these things from the wise and learned, and revealed them to little children. 26 Yes, Father, for this was well-pleasing in Your sight.
27 All things have been entrusted to Me by My Father. No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After warning the unrepentant towns, Jesus praises the Father. He describes a striking reversal: truths hidden from the wise and learned are revealed to little children. People with little standing can receive what those confident in their own understanding miss.

The child picture points to dependence and receptiveness. In the same prayer, Jesus calls the Father Lord of heaven and earth and gives Him the credit for revealing these things. Knowing God begins with His gift; social importance and learning cannot put Him under anyone's control.

Jesus then speaks of His unique relationship with the Father. Each knows the other, all things have been entrusted to the Son, and the Son makes the Father known. He presents Himself as more than another teacher offering information about God. Access to the Father is bound to Him.

The next words are His invitation for the weary to come to Him. The statements about revelation and the invitation to receive rest belong next to each other. Traditions agree that God's grace is necessary, while explaining differently how that grace brings people to faith.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand these verses as revealing the unique relationship of the Father and Son and our need for God to make Himself known. Traditions differ over how to explain God's choice and the human response.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, 10.1–2, and the 1689 Baptist Confession, 10.1–2, teach that God brings those He has chosen to life through His word and Spirit, renewing their wills so that they freely come to Christ. Their response follows God's work of making them willing.

Wesley on Matthew 11:25–28 reads the hiding as God allowing these things to remain hidden from the self-confident, while revealing them to those with little standing; he connects the following invitation with those who receive revelation. The Methodist Articles of Religion, VIII, affirm that no one can turn to faith through natural strength: God's grace must first enable the response and continue working with the person.

The Catholic Catechism, 1996–2002, likewise says that knowing God depends on His undeserved initiative and that even readiness to receive grace is His work. It joins this with a free human response. Paragraph 1993 explicitly says that a person can reject the Spirit's prompting. This differs from the Reformed account of God's call that brings the chosen person to faith.
passages.god_plan_html:
The reversal between the wise and the little children appears again in 1 Corinthians 1:18–31. Paul describes the message of Christ crucified as God's power and wisdom, though others dismiss it. God brings people to Himself in a way that leaves no room for boasting in status, strength, or intelligence.

That gives a wider setting for Jesus' prayer. God's purpose is to give salvation through His Son, with the glory belonging to Him. Paul includes both Jews and Greeks among those who recognize Christ as God's wisdom. The Father's gift reaches people across the human divisions that so often decide whose voice seems important.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 11:28-30
passages.section_title: Rest with the Gentle Savior

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 28 Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest. 29 Take My yoke upon you and learn from Me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. 30 For My yoke is easy and My burden is light.”
paragraphs: 28 Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest.
29 Take My yoke upon you and learn from Me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. 30 For My yoke is easy and My burden is light.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus follows His words about revealing the Father with a personal invitation: come to Him. He addresses people who are weary and carrying burdens, and promises rest. The invitation brings the reader from hearing about His relationship with the Father to learning from Him.

He describes that learning as taking His yoke. A yoke is equipment used to harness working animals; here it pictures coming under His direction. Jesus explains the image Himself by calling people to learn from Him. Rest and discipleship belong together: the teacher who calls them is gentle and humble in heart.

The word translated easy is χρηστός, chrēstos (khray-STOSS). Thayer's entry gives the sense mild or manageable for the yoke in this verse, in contrast to something harsh or burdensome. The assurance concerns the kind of master Jesus is and the burden He gives. The same Gospel has already described the opposition His disciples may face.

The promise of rest for the soul recalls Jeremiah 6:16, where God calls people to walk in His good way and find rest. Here Jesus directs the weary to Himself. He does not merely point toward relief somewhere else; He offers to give it as they come and learn.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as an invitation to receive rest from Jesus while trusting Him and learning His way. Wesley on Matthew 11:28–30 emphasizes relief from sin's guilt and power, freely given through Christ. The Catholic Catechism, 459, uses the invitation to learn from Jesus in explaining His role as the model for a holy life. These are complementary emphases on His saving gift and the life learned from Him.
passages.god_plan_html:
Rest runs through the Bible's account of God's work. Hebrews 4:1–11 brings together God's rest after creation, Israel's failure to enter through unbelief, and a promise still open after Joshua. It calls people to respond to God's voice in faith today.

That is a Scripture-supported connection with Jesus' invitation, rather than a claim that Hebrews is directly explaining this particular saying. Rest is more than reaching a place or stopping activity for a while; it concerns receiving what God gives and trusting Him. The same chapter then points to Jesus as the great high priest who understands human weakness and welcomes His people to receive mercy and help (Hebrews 4:14–16). His gentleness here fits that larger picture of the Savior through whom people draw near to God.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 12:1-8
passages.section_title: Mercy and the Lord of the Sabbath

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 At that time Jesus went through the grainfields on the Sabbath. His disciples were hungry and began to pick the heads of grain and eat them. 2 When the Pharisees saw this, they said to Him, “Look, Your disciples are doing what is unlawful on the Sabbath.” 3 Jesus replied, “Have you not read what David did when he and his companions were hungry? 4 He entered the house of God, and he and his companions ate the consecrated bread, which was not lawful for them to eat, but only for the priests. 5 Or haven’t you read in the Law that on the Sabbath the priests in the temple break the Sabbath and yet are innocent? 6 But I tell you that One greater than the temple is here. 7 If only you had known the meaning of ‘I desire mercy, not sacrifice,’ you would not have condemned the innocent. 8 For the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.”
paragraphs: 1 At that time Jesus went through the grainfields on the Sabbath. His disciples were hungry and began to pick the heads of grain and eat them. 2 When the Pharisees saw this, they said to Him, “Look, Your disciples are doing what is unlawful on the Sabbath.” 3 Jesus replied, “Have you not read what David did when he and his companions were hungry? 4 He entered the house of God, and he and his companions ate the consecrated bread, which was not lawful for them to eat, but only for the priests.

5 Or haven’t you read in the Law that on the Sabbath the priests in the temple break the Sabbath and yet are innocent? 6 But I tell you that One greater than the temple is here. 7 If only you had known the meaning of ‘I desire mercy, not sacrifice,’ you would not have condemned the innocent. 8 For the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The disciples are hungry and pick grain as they walk through a field. The objection concerns doing this on the Sabbath. Deuteronomy 23:24–25 permits eating from a neighbor's vineyard or plucking grain by hand while forbidding taking a supply away in a basket or harvesting with a sickle. The dispute here concerns the day, rather than simply taking someone else's food.

Jesus answers from Scripture. First He recalls David receiving consecrated bread when he and his companions were hungry (1 Samuel 21:1–6). Jesus explicitly says that this bread was lawful only for priests. Leviticus 24:5–9 assigns it to Aaron and his sons to eat in a holy place. The example asks His hearers to reckon with human need, rather than treating David as an obvious ground for condemnation.

Then He points to priests serving in the temple on the Sabbath. The Law itself requires Sabbath offerings (Numbers 28:9–10). Their service involves work, yet they are innocent. Jesus brings the comparison to Himself: One greater than the temple is present, and the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.

His quotation from Hosea 6:6 puts mercy at the heart of the response. The Greek word is ἔλεος, eleos (EH-leh-oss), mercy or compassion expressed toward people in need. Thayer's entry includes this verse and the readiness to help those in trouble. Knowing what God desires should have kept the critics from condemning the innocent.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as joining Jesus' authority over the Sabbath with God's concern for mercy and human need. Wesley on Matthew 12:3–8 emphasizes need, the priority of mercy, and the disciples serving under Jesus' authority. The Catholic Catechism, 582, teaches that serving God and neighbor does not violate Sabbath rest. The Reformed Westminster Confession, 21.8, also includes duties of necessity and mercy within faithful Sabbath observance. The shared point here is that compassion belongs within honoring God.
passages.god_plan_html:
The claim to be greater than the temple points toward Jesus' central place in bringing people to God. In John 2:18–22, He speaks of the temple being destroyed and raised, and John explains that He means His body. He points to His own death and resurrection as the greater reality behind the temple.

Ephesians 2:18–22 develops that wider picture: through Christ, people have access to the Father by the Spirit, and together become God's dwelling place. This is a connection across the New Testament, rather than a claim that Matthew explains every part of it here. Jesus' authority is bound to the greater work of bringing people near to God.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 12:9-14
passages.section_title: Doing Good on the Sabbath

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 Moving on from there, Jesus entered their synagogue, 10 and a man with a withered hand was there. In order to accuse Jesus, they asked Him, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?” 11 He replied, “If one of you has a sheep and it falls into a pit on the Sabbath, will he not take hold of it and lift it out? 12 How much more valuable is a man than a sheep! Therefore it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath.” 13 Then Jesus said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” So he stretched it out, and it was restored to full use, just like the other. 14 But the Pharisees went out and plotted how they might kill Jesus.
paragraphs: 9 Moving on from there, Jesus entered their synagogue, 10 and a man with a withered hand was there. In order to accuse Jesus, they asked Him, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?” 11 He replied, “If one of you has a sheep and it falls into a pit on the Sabbath, will he not take hold of it and lift it out? 12 How much more valuable is a man than a sheep! Therefore it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath.”

13 Then Jesus said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” So he stretched it out, and it was restored to full use, just like the other. 14 But the Pharisees went out and plotted how they might kill Jesus.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Sabbath dispute continues in a synagogue, where a man has a withered hand. Matthew states the purpose of the question about healing: the questioners want grounds to accuse Jesus. The man's need becomes the setting for another test of His conduct.

Jesus answers with an example of a sheep falling into a pit. Someone would take hold of the animal and lift it out, even on the Sabbath. He then turns attention to the greater value of a human being. The conclusion is direct: doing good on the Sabbath is lawful.

He tells the man to stretch out his hand. The man does so, and it is restored to full use. Matthew describes the action and healing without giving a history of the disability or the man's private thoughts. The focus is on Jesus making the man whole in the very setting where His right to help has been challenged.

The response is a plot to kill Him. That ending sharply contrasts the good He has just done with the harm His opponents intend. In the parallel account, Mark 3:1–6, Jesus' question contrasts doing good with doing evil and saving life with destroying it. The healing and the plot make that contrast concrete.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as showing the rightness of active compassion and the authority of Jesus to restore life. Wesley on Matthew 12:12 follows Jesus' comparison from helping an animal to helping a person. The Catholic Catechism, 582, likewise treats His Sabbath healings as service to God and neighbor. These readings do not make the Sabbath a reason to withhold the good that can be done.
passages.god_plan_html:
The concern for refreshment belongs to the Sabbath command itself. Exodus 23:12 includes workers, foreign residents, and animals in the rest God provides. Jesus' concern for the man fits that wider picture of God's care reaching those who need relief.

The plot also looks ahead to a greater reversal. Acts 2:22–24 recalls Jesus' works of power, His death through human wrongdoing, and God's raising Him to life. Opposition will lead toward the cross, yet God brings salvation through the Savior whom His opponents try to destroy. The healing is part of a ministry whose end will be decided by God, rather than by the plot against Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 12:15-21
passages.section_title: The Gentle Servant and the Hope of the Nations

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 Aware of this, Jesus withdrew from that place. Large crowds followed Him, and He healed them all, 16 warning them not to make Him known. 17 This was to fulfill what was spoken through the prophet Isaiah: 18 “Here is My Servant, whom I have chosen, My beloved, in whom My soul delights. I will put My Spirit on Him, and He will proclaim justice to the nations. 19 He will not quarrel or cry out; no one will hear His voice in the streets. 20 A bruised reed He will not break, and a smoldering wick He will not extinguish, till He leads justice to victory. 21 In His name the nations will put their hope.”
paragraphs: 15 Aware of this, Jesus withdrew from that place. Large crowds followed Him, and He healed them all, 16 warning them not to make Him known. 17 This was to fulfill what was spoken through the prophet Isaiah:

18 “Here is My Servant, whom I have chosen, My beloved, in whom My soul delights. I will put My Spirit on Him, and He will proclaim justice to the nations. 19 He will not quarrel or cry out; no one will hear His voice in the streets. 20 A bruised reed He will not break, and a smoldering wick He will not extinguish, till He leads justice to victory. 21 In His name the nations will put their hope.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Aware of the plot against Him, Jesus withdraws. He continues healing the crowds who follow, while warning them not to make Him known. Withdrawal does not mean that His care for people stops. Matthew places His conduct within the words of Isaiah.

The passage draws from Isaiah 42:1–4: God's chosen Servant receives His Spirit, brings justice, and becomes the hope of the nations. Matthew explicitly identifies what Jesus is doing as fulfillment. The contrast with the preceding plot matters: His mission advances without taking on the character of His opponents.

The bruised reed and smoldering wick picture things already close to breaking or going out. The Servant does not finish their destruction. Gentleness is joined with determination: He will bring justice to victory. Care for the weak and the establishment of what is right belong to the same mission.

The reach of that mission is also clear. The nations will put their hope in Him. The quotation widens the reader's view beyond the immediate dispute, showing that the Father's purpose through Jesus extends far beyond the people gathered around Him on this occasion.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand Matthew as identifying Jesus with Isaiah's Spirit-given Servant, whose gentleness does not weaken His purpose to bring justice. Wesley on Matthew 12:18–21 applies the fragile images to people burdened by sin and those with only a small beginning of hope. The US Catholic bishops' notes on 12:15–21 emphasize Jesus' meekness and the mission reaching Gentiles. These are complementary emphases on the Servant's manner and the people His work reaches.
passages.god_plan_html:
The hope of the nations is part of God's promise before the conflict described here. In Luke 2:25–32, Simeon recognizes the infant Jesus as salvation prepared for all peoples, bringing light to Gentiles and glory to Israel. The wider mission grows from God's announced purpose.

That purpose becomes visible in the apostolic mission. Speaking to the Gentile household of Cornelius, Peter recalls Jesus being anointed with the Holy Spirit, doing good, and freeing people from oppression. He then announces His death, resurrection, and forgiveness for everyone who believes in Him (Acts 10:34–43). The Servant's gentle ministry leads into good news carried across the nations.
