passages.title: Matthew 12:22-30
passages.section_title: The Stronger One Sets People Free

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 Then a demon-possessed man who was blind and mute was brought to Jesus, and He healed the man so that he could speak and see. 23 The crowds were astounded and asked, “Could this be the Son of David?” 24 But when the Pharisees heard this, they said, “Only by Beelzebul, the prince of demons, does this man drive out demons.” 25 Knowing their thoughts, Jesus said to them, “Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste, and every city or household divided against itself will not stand. 26 If Satan drives out Satan, he is divided against himself. How then can his kingdom stand? 27 And if I drive out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons drive them out? So then, they will be your judges. 28 But if I drive out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you. 29 Or again, how can anyone enter a strong man’s house and steal his possessions, unless he first ties up the strong man? Then he can plunder his house. 30 He who is not with Me is against Me, and he who does not gather with Me scatters.
paragraphs: 22 Then a demon-possessed man who was blind and mute was brought to Jesus, and He healed the man so that he could speak and see. 23 The crowds were astounded and asked, “Could this be the Son of David?” 24 But when the Pharisees heard this, they said, “Only by Beelzebul, the prince of demons, does this man drive out demons.”

25 Knowing their thoughts, Jesus said to them, “Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste, and every city or household divided against itself will not stand. 26 If Satan drives out Satan, he is divided against himself. How then can his kingdom stand? 27 And if I drive out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons drive them out? So then, they will be your judges.

28 But if I drive out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you. 29 Or again, how can anyone enter a strong man’s house and steal his possessions, unless he first ties up the strong man? Then he can plunder his house. 30 He who is not with Me is against Me, and he who does not gather with Me scatters.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus heals a man described as demon-possessed, blind, and mute. The man can now speak and see. The crowds ask whether Jesus could be the Son of David, while the Pharisees attribute His work to Beelzebul, whom they call the prince of demons. The disagreement concerns the source and meaning of His power.

Jesus answers the accusation through the picture of a divided kingdom or household. If Satan is driving out Satan, he is undoing his own rule. Jesus also asks His opponents to apply their reasoning to the people among them who drive out demons. Their accusation cannot be treated as a fair standard only when it is used against Him.

His positive explanation is that He acts by God's Spirit and that God's kingdom has come upon them. The Greek verb is φθάνω, phthanō (FTHAH-noh), to reach or arrive. Thayer's entry discusses this verse, including the sense of arrival earlier than expected. Jesus directs attention to God's rule already at work in the release they have witnessed.

The strong man's house gives another picture of what is happening. Someone must first overcome the strong man before taking his possessions. In this setting, Jesus is overcoming Satan's hold and setting people free. Luke 11:20–22 makes the comparison explicit through someone stronger defeating the armed man.

The final saying calls for a response. Being with Jesus means joining His work of gathering; opposing Him means scattering. His opponents have seen release and called it evil. Jesus presses them to recognize what God is doing through Him.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the healing and strong-man picture as evidence that Jesus defeats Satan through God's power. Wesley on Matthew 12:27–30 reads His work as taking people from Satan's rule and calls for allegiance to Him. The Catholic Catechism, 550, similarly connects His freeing people from demons with the arrival of God's kingdom and the victory accomplished through His cross. The shared emphasis is Christ's victory and the response His work calls for.
passages.god_plan_html:
The victory reaches beyond this one healing. Hebrews 2:14–15 says that Jesus shares human life and goes through death to defeat the devil's power and free people enslaved by fear of death. The One who releases the man here will give Himself to bring a deeper freedom.

Colossians 2:13–15 joins forgiveness with Christ's triumph over the powers through the cross. These passages extend the theme of the stronger Savior: His victory includes release from sin's debt and the fear of death, rather than ending with the outward restoration of one person.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 12:31-37
passages.section_title: The Spirit’s Work and the Words of the Heart

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 31 Therefore I tell you, every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven men, but the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven. 32 Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the one to come. 33 Make a tree good and its fruit will be good, or make a tree bad and its fruit will be bad, for a tree is known by its fruit. 34 You brood of vipers, how can you who are evil say anything good? For out of the overflow of the heart the mouth speaks. 35 The good man brings good things out of his good store of treasure, and the evil man brings evil things out of his evil store of treasure. 36 But I tell you that men will give an account on the day of judgment for every careless word they have spoken. 37 For by your words you will be acquitted, and by your words you will be condemned.”
paragraphs: 31 Therefore I tell you, every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven men, but the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven. 32 Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the one to come.

33 Make a tree good and its fruit will be good, or make a tree bad and its fruit will be bad, for a tree is known by its fruit. 34 You brood of vipers, how can you who are evil say anything good? For out of the overflow of the heart the mouth speaks. 35 The good man brings good things out of his good store of treasure, and the evil man brings evil things out of his evil store of treasure.
36 But I tell you that men will give an account on the day of judgment for every careless word they have spoken. 37 For by your words you will be acquitted, and by your words you will be condemned.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The warning follows the accusation that Jesus drives out demons by evil power. He has just identified His work with God's Spirit. His words about blasphemy must be heard within that confrontation: what has brought freedom is being called the work of Satan.

Jesus speaks both of the breadth of forgiveness and of a grave exception concerning speech against the Holy Spirit. He distinguishes it from a word spoken against the Son of Man, and says that it will not be forgiven in this age or the one to come. Mark 3:28–30 directly connects the warning with the accusation that He has an unclean spirit.

The tree and fruit then turn attention to what words reveal. Jesus challenges His hearers about recognizing good and evil, and describes speech as coming from what fills the heart. The accusation is not simply a harmless sound; it gives expression to what is being welcomed or resisted within.

The warning broadens to the day of judgment. The Greek word translated careless is ἀργός, argos (ar-GOSS), idle or unproductive. Thayer's entry applies it here to harmful, unprofitable speech. Jesus treats words as matters for which people must answer. His closing statement belongs with the preceding explanation that speech reveals the heart.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The warning is commonly read in light of the accusation just made against Jesus. Christian teachers differ over how it applies beyond that moment. Wesley on Matthew 12:31–37 identifies the blasphemy with calling the miracles Jesus did by the Holy Spirit the devil's work. He treats words at judgment as evidence of the person's faith and life.

The Reformed teacher John Calvin, on Matthew 12:31–32, understands it as deliberately calling God's revealed work evil, even while knowing its source. He distinguishes this from opposition that comes from ignorance. In his reading, people hardened in this way do not turn back in repentance. The Reformed Westminster Confession, 15.3–4, affirms that forgiveness is God's grace and no sin condemns those who truly repent.

The Catholic Church's Catechism, 1864, explains the warning through deliberately refusing the mercy and forgiveness offered by the Spirit, a hardening that can end in dying without repentance. This differs from Calvin's more specific account of consciously slandering God's revealed work. The readings share the seriousness of rejecting God's grace, while describing the offense in different ways.
passages.god_plan_html:
The heart-and-words connection belongs to a larger biblical need for inward renewal. In Ezekiel 36:25–27, God promises cleansing, a new heart, and His Spirit enabling His people to walk in His ways. The answer to a corrupted heart reaches deeper than improving outward appearances.

Titus 3:3–7 describes God's mercy bringing new birth and renewal through the Holy Spirit, poured out through Jesus Christ. That wider connection shows why the Spirit's work matters so deeply: He is at work bringing the new life people need. The warning here and the promise of renewal belong within the Bible's serious account of sin and God's saving mercy.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 12:38-39
passages.section_title: A Demand for Another Sign

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 38 Then some of the scribes and Pharisees said to Him, “Teacher, we want to see a sign from You.” 39 Jesus replied, “A wicked and adulterous generation demands a sign, but none will be given it except the sign of the prophet Jonah.
paragraphs: 38 Then some of the scribes and Pharisees said to Him, “Teacher, we want to see a sign from You.” 39 Jesus replied, “A wicked and adulterous generation demands a sign, but none will be given it except the sign of the prophet Jonah.

passages.context_html:
This request comes after Jesus has healed people and answered the accusation that His power comes from Satan. Some scribes and Pharisees now ask for a sign. The demand belongs to that setting of resistance to works they have already seen.

The word for demanding a sign is ἐπιζητέω, epizēteō (eh-pee-zay-TEH-oh), to seek after or demand. Thayer's entry explicitly includes this saying. Jesus does not accept the demand as the condition on which His hearers may keep postponing a response.

He names the sign of Jonah. The explanation continues immediately in verses 40–42: His own coming death and resurrection are compared with Jonah's time in the fish, and the response of outsiders is placed beside His hearers' resistance. These two verses introduce that larger answer.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a rebuke to resistant hearers demanding further proof, rather than a rejection of every sincere question about God. Wesley on Matthew 12:38–40 emphasizes the signs already received and understands Jonah as pointing toward Christ. The US Catholic bishops' notes on 12:38–42 likewise connect the demand with refusal to accept Jesus' works and explain the Jonah sign through His death and resurrection.
passages.current_position_html: Should We Seek Signs From God? reads this as a warning against demanding another sign while resisting what God has already revealed. These leaders have already seen Jesus' works; the study distinguishes their demand from sincerely seeking to understand and obey Him.

deeper_study.title: Should We Seek Signs From God?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus' answer points forward to the center of His saving work. In the following verses He connects Jonah's experience with His own coming passage through death. Matthew 16:21 later speaks plainly of His suffering, death, and resurrection on the third day.

The sign will be more than another display requested by opponents. It points to the Savior giving His life and being raised, the events Paul places at the heart of the gospel in 1 Corinthians 15:1–8.

passages.title: Matthew 12:38-42
passages.section_title: The Sign of Jonah and the Greater Savior

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 38 Then some of the scribes and Pharisees said to Him, “Teacher, we want to see a sign from You.” 39 Jesus replied, “A wicked and adulterous generation demands a sign, but none will be given it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. 40 For as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so the Son of Man will be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth. 41 The men of Nineveh will stand at the judgment with this generation and condemn it; for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and now One greater than Jonah is here. 42 The Queen of the South will rise at the judgment with this generation and condemn it; for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and now One greater than Solomon is here.
paragraphs: 38 Then some of the scribes and Pharisees said to Him, “Teacher, we want to see a sign from You.” 39 Jesus replied, “A wicked and adulterous generation demands a sign, but none will be given it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. 40 For as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so the Son of Man will be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.

41 The men of Nineveh will stand at the judgment with this generation and condemn it; for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and now One greater than Jonah is here. 42 The Queen of the South will rise at the judgment with this generation and condemn it; for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and now One greater than Solomon is here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Some scribes and Pharisees ask Jesus for a sign after the healings and confrontation already described. He treats this demand as the response of a wicked and adulterous generation. The problem is not a lack of anything to consider; His works and their meaning have already been before them.

The Greek verb for demanding a sign is ἐπιζητέω, epizēteō (eh-pee-zay-TEH-oh), to seek after or demand. Thayer's entry lists this verse under demanding or clamoring for a sign. Jesus directs them to the sign of Jonah rather than letting a continuing demand for proof determine His mission.

He connects Jonah's three days and nights in the fish with the Son of Man's time in the heart of the earth. Jonah 1:17–2:10 describes the prophet's descent into distress and deliverance; the prayer and release continue in chapter 2. Jesus' own coming death and resurrection give the comparison its greater meaning.

The Ninevites and the Queen of the South provide two more comparisons. Jonah 3:1–10 describes repentance at Jonah's preaching; 1 Kings 10:1–9 describes the queen coming to hear Solomon and recognizing the wisdom God gave him. These outsiders responded to messengers less great than the One now present. Their response exposes the failure to receive Him.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand Jonah's experience here as pointing toward Jesus' death, burial, and resurrection, while the Ninevites and the queen illustrate responsibility to respond to God's revelation. Wesley on Matthew 12:39–42 reads Jonah as a picture of Christ and understands the three-day wording as including parts of days. The Catholic Catechism, 624, emphasizes the reality of Jesus' death and His time in the tomb before the resurrection. The central connection is His passage through death into life.
passages.god_plan_html:
This is a connection Jesus Himself makes: Jonah's experience points ahead to what the Son of Man will undergo. The parallel does not make the prophet and Savior equal. Jesus is greater than Jonah, just as He is greater than Solomon; His own victory will stand at the center of the message.

1 Corinthians 15:1–8 presents that center directly: Christ dies for sins, is buried, is raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, and appears to witnesses. The sign reaches beyond an impressive event to God's saving work. The call is to receive the risen Savior and the good news about Him.
passages.current_position_html: Should We Seek Signs From God? reads this as a warning against demanding another sign while resisting what God has already revealed. These leaders have already seen Jesus' works; the study distinguishes their demand from sincerely seeking to understand and obey Him.

deeper_study.title: Should We Seek Signs From God?

passages.title: Matthew 12:43-45
passages.section_title: The Danger of an Empty House

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 43 When an unclean spirit comes out of a man, it passes through arid places seeking rest and does not find it. 44 Then it says, ‘I will return to the house I left.’ On its return, it finds the house vacant, swept clean, and put in order. 45 Then it goes and brings with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself, and they go in and dwell there. And the final plight of that man is worse than the first. So will it be with this wicked generation.”
paragraphs: 43 When an unclean spirit comes out of a man, it passes through arid places seeking rest and does not find it. 44 Then it says, ‘I will return to the house I left.’ On its return, it finds the house vacant, swept clean, and put in order. 45 Then it goes and brings with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself, and they go in and dwell there. And the final plight of that man is worse than the first. So will it be with this wicked generation.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus describes an unclean spirit leaving a person, finding no rest, and returning to the place it left. The house is vacant, swept, and orderly. Its improved appearance has not made it secure against the returning spirit.

The spirit brings seven others more wicked than itself, and the person's final condition becomes worse than the first. Jesus then applies the picture to the wicked generation He has been addressing. The setting remains the response to His ministry, including the release from evil they have witnessed and the resistance they have shown.

The image warns that a changed outward condition is not the same as receiving God's work through Jesus. Being relieved of one evil does not make continued refusal harmless. In the related sequence in Luke 11:24–28, the returned-spirit saying is followed by Jesus honoring those who hear God's word and obey it. The call concerns a real response to God, rather than satisfaction with appearances.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as a warning against responding inadequately to the good Jesus brings, with a worse outcome possible after an apparent improvement. Wesley on Matthew 12:43–45 applies the empty-house image to a life without God and extends its warning to people who turn away. The US Catholic bishops' note on 12:43–45 emphasizes its application to the generation refusing Jesus. These readings focus on the response to Him, with one stressing its wider application and the other its immediate setting.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 12:46-50
passages.section_title: The Family Gathered Around Jesus

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 46 While Jesus was still speaking to the crowds, His mother and brothers stood outside, wanting to speak to Him. 47 Someone told Him, “Look, Your mother and brothers are standing outside, wanting to speak to You.” 48 But Jesus replied, “Who is My mother, and who are My brothers?” 49 Pointing to His disciples, He said, “Here are My mother and My brothers. 50 For whoever does the will of My Father in heaven is My brother and sister and mother.”
paragraphs: 46 While Jesus was still speaking to the crowds, His mother and brothers stood outside, wanting to speak to Him. 47 Someone told Him, “Look, Your mother and brothers are standing outside, wanting to speak to You.”

48 But Jesus replied, “Who is My mother, and who are My brothers?” 49 Pointing to His disciples, He said, “Here are My mother and My brothers. 50 For whoever does the will of My Father in heaven is My brother and sister and mother.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus is still speaking to the crowds when His mother and brothers arrive outside, wanting to speak to Him. He answers the message by asking who His mother and brothers are, then points to His disciples. The moment becomes a teaching about the family formed around Him.

He names doing His Father's will as the mark of that relationship. The related account in Luke 8:19–21 describes His family as those who hear God's word and carry it out. Nearness to Jesus therefore involves receiving and following God's word; it is not established by a family connection alone.

The Greek word is ἀδελφός, adelphos (ah-del-FOSS), brother. Thayer's entry discusses both family relationships and its use for fellow believers, while arguing that the relatives in this passage are Mary's other children. Jesus deliberately brings family language into His description of disciples. Traditions differ over the precise family relationships of those waiting outside, as explained below.

The saying gives His disciples a remarkable place of belonging. He calls them brother, sister, and mother. His words establish the importance of this relationship with Him; the passage does not require treating ordinary love and care for relatives as worthless.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the central saying as Jesus welcoming those who do the Father's will into His spiritual family. Wesley on Matthew 12:46–50 emphasizes that spiritual relationship, while the Catholic Catechism, 500–501, places the family language within its teaching about Mary and Christ's people.

Traditions differ over the brothers' relationship to Mary. The Catholic Church teaches in Catechism 499–500 that Mary remained a virgin and these brothers are close relatives, not other children of hers. The Orthodox Church in America's life of Joseph presents the Orthodox tradition that they were Joseph's children from an earlier marriage.

An Orthodox Presbyterian Church question-and-answer article reads them as children born to Mary and Joseph after Jesus, and therefore His half-brothers. This is that church resource's explanation, rather than a claim about every Reformed Christian. Protestant interpreters have also differed: Wesley on 12:46 understands them as relatives through Mary's family. The difference over the family tree does not remove Jesus' central call to hear and do His Father's will.
passages.god_plan_html:
The family language reaches into the saving purpose described in Hebrews 2:10–18. God brings many children to glory through Jesus, who shares human life and suffering and is not ashamed to call His people brothers. Their belonging rests on the Savior who comes near enough to help and save them.

That makes this more than a picture of a friendly group. Jesus gathers people into a relationship with Himself and the Father. The disciples He points to anticipate the wider family whose life together will be shaped by hearing God's word and following the Son.

passages.title: Matthew 13:1-9
passages.section_title: The Sower and the Different Soils

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 That same day Jesus went out of the house and sat by the sea. 2 Such large crowds gathered around Him that He got into a boat and sat down, while all the people stood on the shore. 3 And He told them many things in parables, saying, “A farmer went out to sow his seed. 4 And as he was sowing, some seed fell along the path, and the birds came and devoured it. 5 Some fell on rocky ground, where it did not have much soil. It sprang up quickly because the soil was shallow. 6 But when the sun rose, the seedlings were scorched, and they withered because they had no root. 7 Other seed fell among thorns, which grew up and choked the seedlings. 8 Still other seed fell on good soil and produced a crop—a hundredfold, sixtyfold, or thirtyfold. 9 He who has ears, let him hear.”
paragraphs: 1 That same day Jesus went out of the house and sat by the sea. 2 Such large crowds gathered around Him that He got into a boat and sat down, while all the people stood on the shore. 3 And He told them many things in parables, saying, “A farmer went out to sow his seed.

4 And as he was sowing, some seed fell along the path, and the birds came and devoured it. 5 Some fell on rocky ground, where it did not have much soil. It sprang up quickly because the soil was shallow. 6 But when the sun rose, the seedlings were scorched, and they withered because they had no root. 7 Other seed fell among thorns, which grew up and choked the seedlings.
8 Still other seed fell on good soil and produced a crop—a hundredfold, sixtyfold, or thirtyfold. 9 He who has ears, let him hear.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus leaves the house and teaches a large crowd from a boat, with the people standing on the shore. He begins with a farmer scattering seed. The scene turns attention to what happens as the seed reaches different kinds of ground.

The Greek word for parable is παραβολή, parabolē (pah-rah-boh-LAY), a comparison or story that illustrates something. Thayer's entry includes these sayings about God's kingdom. Jesus uses familiar things to invite His hearers to consider a deeper question.

The same sowing has different outcomes. Seed on the path is eaten by birds. Seed on shallow rocky ground grows quickly but withers in the sun. Seed among thorns is choked. Seed on good ground produces a crop, with different amounts of fruit.

Jesus closes by calling people to hear. The story invites more than recognition of a farming scene. His explanation in verses 18–23 will connect the soils with how people receive the message of the kingdom. The question of listening runs through both the story and the conversation that follows.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a picture of different responses to God's message and the importance of fruitful hearing. Wesley on Matthew 13:3–8 emphasizes the obstacles that keep hearers from bearing fruit. The Catholic Catechism, 546, likewise treats the soil image as a question Jesus puts to His hearers about their response to His word. The good harvest matters alongside the warnings about what can prevent it.
passages.god_plan_html:
The seed picture belongs within the Bible's confidence that God's word accomplishes His purpose. Isaiah 55:8–13 compares His word with rain that brings growth and provides seed and food. That is a related picture of God's effective word, rather than a claim that every hearer responds in the same way.

In 1 Corinthians 3:5–9, Paul describes himself and Apollos as servants who plant and water, while God gives the growth. The larger work belongs to God, even as people faithfully take part in it. Different responses do not make the message worthless or put its final outcome entirely in the messenger's hands.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 13:10-17
passages.section_title: Hearing, Understanding, and the Gift of Revelation

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 Then the disciples came to Jesus and asked, “Why do You speak to the people in parables?” 11 He replied, “The knowledge of the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven has been given to you, but not to them. 12 Whoever has will be given more, and he will have an abundance. Whoever does not have, even what he has will be taken away from him. 13 This is why I speak to them in parables: ‘Though seeing, they do not see; though hearing, they do not hear or understand.’ 14 In them the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled: ‘You will be ever hearing but never understanding; you will be ever seeing but never perceiving. 15 For this people’s heart has grown callous; they hardly hear with their ears, and they have closed their eyes. Otherwise they might see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their hearts, and turn, and I would heal them.’ 16 But blessed are your eyes because they see, and your ears because they hear. 17 For truly I tell you, many prophets and righteous men longed to see what you see but did not see it, and to hear what you hear but did not hear it.
paragraphs: 10 Then the disciples came to Jesus and asked, “Why do You speak to the people in parables?” 11 He replied, “The knowledge of the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven has been given to you, but not to them. 12 Whoever has will be given more, and he will have an abundance. Whoever does not have, even what he has will be taken away from him. 13 This is why I speak to them in parables: ‘Though seeing, they do not see; though hearing, they do not hear or understand.’

14 In them the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled: ‘You will be ever hearing but never understanding; you will be ever seeing but never perceiving. 15 For this people’s heart has grown callous; they hardly hear with their ears, and they have closed their eyes. Otherwise they might see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their hearts, and turn, and I would heal them.’

16 But blessed are your eyes because they see, and your ears because they hear. 17 For truly I tell you, many prophets and righteous men longed to see what you see but did not see it, and to hear what you hear but did not hear it.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The disciples ask why Jesus speaks to the crowds in parables. He answers in terms of a gift: knowledge of the kingdom's mysteries has been given to them. He also describes people who see and hear without understanding, and warns that even what they have can be taken away.

The word translated mysteries is μυστήριον, mystērion (moos-TAY-ree-on), something hidden that God makes known. Thayer's entry connects its New Testament use with God's purposes revealed through Christ, and includes this verse. The disciples are receiving understanding of what God is doing through Jesus.

Jesus quotes Isaiah 6:9–10, where hearing and seeing fail to become a real response to God. Matthew's quotation describes calloused hearts and closed eyes. God's gift of understanding and the hearers' resistance both appear in His answer.

He then blesses the disciples for seeing and hearing what earlier prophets and righteous people longed for. Their privilege lies in being present as God's promise unfolds through Him. Receiving that gift carries a call to listen, rather than a reason to take understanding for granted.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings hold together God's gift of understanding and the seriousness of refusing what He reveals, while placing different emphasis on how those relate. Wesley on Matthew 13:11–16 emphasizes people failing to use the light they have received and closing their eyes to it.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, 10.1–2, emphasizes God's word and Spirit renewing the heart and will so that people freely come to Christ. The Catholic Catechism, 546, emphasizes the choice demanded by the parables and becoming a disciple to understand the kingdom. These explanations affirm the need for God's gift, while describing His work and the listener's response in different ways.
passages.god_plan_html:
Isaiah's words also appear in the continuing mission after Jesus' resurrection. In Acts 28:23–28, Paul explains Jesus from the Law and the Prophets. Some are persuaded and others refuse to believe; he then quotes the same warning about hearing without understanding.

Paul goes on to announce that God's salvation has been sent to the Gentiles. The repeated prophecy places these responses within the wider story of the message reaching new hearers. It is a warning to receive God's word, not a reason to assume that every member of a people responds identically.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 13:18-23
passages.section_title: Receiving the Word and Bearing Fruit

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 Consider, then, the parable of the sower: 19 When anyone hears the message of the kingdom but does not understand it, the evil one comes and snatches away what was sown in his heart. This is the seed sown along the path. 20 The seed sown on rocky ground is the one who hears the word and at once receives it with joy. 21 But since he has no root, he remains for only a season. When trouble or persecution comes because of the word, he quickly falls away. 22 The seed sown among the thorns is the one who hears the word, but the worries of this life and the deceitfulness of wealth choke the word, and it becomes unfruitful. 23 But the seed sown on good soil is the one who hears the word and understands it. He indeed bears fruit and produces a crop—a hundredfold, sixtyfold, or thirtyfold.”
paragraphs: 18 Consider, then, the parable of the sower: 19 When anyone hears the message of the kingdom but does not understand it, the evil one comes and snatches away what was sown in his heart. This is the seed sown along the path.

20 The seed sown on rocky ground is the one who hears the word and at once receives it with joy. 21 But since he has no root, he remains for only a season. When trouble or persecution comes because of the word, he quickly falls away. 22 The seed sown among the thorns is the one who hears the word, but the worries of this life and the deceitfulness of wealth choke the word, and it becomes unfruitful.
23 But the seed sown on good soil is the one who hears the word and understands it. He indeed bears fruit and produces a crop—a hundredfold, sixtyfold, or thirtyfold.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus now explains the sower's story. The seed concerns hearing the message of the kingdom. On the path, the hearer does not understand and the evil one snatches away what was sown. The comparison moves from the outward scene into the heart's response.

The rocky-ground hearer receives the message with joy but has no root. Trouble or persecution because of the word brings a quick falling away. Initial excitement does not by itself show the endurance the message calls for.

Among thorns, the message is choked by life's worries and the deceitfulness of wealth. These pressures make it unfruitful. Luke 8:11–15 also names pleasures and describes fruit failing to mature. The warning reaches ordinary desires and concerns that can crowd out a response to God.

Good soil describes the person who hears and understands, then bears fruit. The amounts vary, but fruit is the shared result. Jesus' explanation calls hearers toward a lasting response. Christian traditions explain differently the saving condition of people who initially receive the word and later turn away.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read this as a call to keep trusting and living out the word, beyond the excitement of first hearing it. Traditions differ over whether someone who turns away from Christ once had saving faith.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, 11.2 and 17.1–3, teaches that saving faith is active in love and that God keeps His people to the end, even when they fall into serious sins for a time. The 1689 Baptist Confession, 17.1, likewise teaches that God keeps them to the end.

Wesley on Matthew 13:20–22 warns that worries and riches can gradually choke a person's response to God's word. The Methodist Articles of Religion, XII, allow for departing from grace and falling into sin, with repentance and return possible by grace. The Catholic Catechism, 162, teaches that faith is God's gift, can be lost, and must be nourished. These teachings lead to different explanations of whether a person who turns away ever had saving faith.
passages.god_plan_html:
The connection between hearing and a changed life continues throughout the New Testament. James 1:21–25 calls people to receive the planted word and carry it out, rather than hearing and forgetting. The message is meant to take hold in life.

Colossians 1:5–10 describes the gospel bearing fruit and growing across the world, then speaks of believers bearing fruit in every good work and growing in knowledge of God. That wider picture includes both the spread of the good news and the lives it changes. Fruitfulness cannot be reduced to one visible number or achievement.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 13:24-30
passages.section_title: Waiting for the Harvest

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 24 Jesus put before them another parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like a man who sowed good seed in his field. 25 But while everyone was asleep, his enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat, and slipped away. 26 When the wheat sprouted and bore grain, then the weeds also appeared. 27 The owner’s servants came to him and said, ‘Sir, didn’t you sow good seed in your field? Where then did the weeds come from?’ 28 ‘An enemy did this,’ he replied. So the servants asked him, ‘Do you want us to go and pull them up?’ 29 ‘No,’ he said, ‘if you pull the weeds now, you might uproot the wheat with them. 30 Let both grow together until the harvest. At that time I will tell the harvesters: First collect the weeds and tie them in bundles to be burned; then gather the wheat into my barn.’”
paragraphs: 24 Jesus put before them another parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like a man who sowed good seed in his field. 25 But while everyone was asleep, his enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat, and slipped away. 26 When the wheat sprouted and bore grain, then the weeds also appeared.

27 The owner’s servants came to him and said, ‘Sir, didn’t you sow good seed in your field? Where then did the weeds come from?’ 28 ‘An enemy did this,’ he replied. So the servants asked him, ‘Do you want us to go and pull them up?’ 29 ‘No,’ he said, ‘if you pull the weeds now, you might uproot the wheat with them. 30 Let both grow together until the harvest. At that time I will tell the harvesters: First collect the weeds and tie them in bundles to be burned; then gather the wheat into my barn.’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Another farming story introduces an enemy's work. A landowner sows good seed, but an enemy sows weeds among the wheat while people sleep. When both grow, the servants ask how the unwanted plants appeared and whether they should remove them.

The word for weeds is ζιζάνιον, zizanion (zee-ZAH-nee-on). Thayer's entry identifies it with darnel, a weed that resembles wheat. That resemblance helps explain the difficulty in the picture, while the landowner's stated concern is the risk of uprooting wheat with the weeds.

He names the enemy as the source of the trouble and refuses the proposed immediate removal. Both are to grow until harvest, when the proper separation will take place. Patience does not mean there will never be a judgment; it governs the time before that judgment.

Jesus gives His own explanation in verses 36–43: the field is the world, the enemy is the devil, and the harvest is the end of the age. The story should be read alongside that explanation. The seed imagery is being used differently from the first parable, where the seed represented the message.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a warning against trying to carry out God's final separation ahead of His appointed time. Wesley on Matthew 13:24–28 applies the mixed crop to people who appear to belong to the Christian community and the danger of mistaken removal. The US Catholic bishops' note on 13:24–30 emphasizes patience and the call to repentance before God's judgment. These applications to the community of believers should be kept alongside Jesus' own identification of the field as the world.
passages.god_plan_html:
God's patience before judgment is a wider biblical theme. 2 Peter 3:8–13 joins His patience and desire for repentance with the certainty of a coming day and the promise of a new creation where righteousness dwells. Waiting is not the abandonment of His promise.

Romans 2:3–5 likewise says that His kindness leads toward repentance while warning against a hard heart. The time before the harvest calls for receiving mercy and responding to God. Final judgment belongs to Him, and His present patience has a saving purpose.

passages.title: Matthew 13:31-35
passages.section_title: Small Beginnings and Far-Reaching Growth

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 31 He put before them another parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed that a man took and planted in his field. 32 Although it is the smallest of all seeds, yet it grows into the largest of garden plants and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and nest in its branches.” 33 He told them still another parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven that a woman took and mixed into three measures of flour, until all of it was leavened.” 34 Jesus spoke all these things to the crowds in parables. He did not tell them anything without using a parable. 35 So was fulfilled what was spoken through the prophet: “I will open My mouth in parables; I will utter things hidden since the foundation of the world.”
paragraphs: 31 He put before them another parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed that a man took and planted in his field. 32 Although it is the smallest of all seeds, yet it grows into the largest of garden plants and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and nest in its branches.”

33 He told them still another parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven that a woman took and mixed into three measures of flour, until all of it was leavened.” 34 Jesus spoke all these things to the crowds in parables. He did not tell them anything without using a parable. 35 So was fulfilled what was spoken through the prophet: “I will open My mouth in parables; I will utter things hidden since the foundation of the world.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus gives two short pictures of the kingdom. A tiny mustard seed grows into a large garden plant with birds nesting in its branches. Leaven mixed into flour works through the whole batch. Both pictures contrast an initially small or hidden beginning with a much larger effect.

The seed is described within the picture of sowing and garden growth. Attention falls on the contrast between its size at the beginning and the plant at the end. The leaven picture similarly follows something that is no longer easily seen once mixed in, yet whose effect spreads through the dough.

Interpreters differ over whether every feature pictures good growth or whether some details warn about corruption. Jesus does not provide a separate explanation of these images here as He does for the sower and the weeds. Their place among the kingdom parables matters when considering those readings.

Matthew then connects Jesus' use of parables with Psalm 78:2. The sayings bring hidden things into speech through everyday pictures. His statement that Jesus speaks in parables describes this teaching to the crowds; the chapter itself also records explanations given to the disciples.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley on Matthew 13:31–33 understands the mustard plant and leaven positively, through the gospel spreading and grace working in a person's life. The US Catholic bishops' notes on 13:31–33 likewise emphasize the contrast between the kingdom's small beginning and its great expansion.

C. I. Scofield's 1917 notes on 13:31–33 instead warn about impressive outward growth and false teaching spreading among people who profess Christianity. His leaven reading draws on passages where leaven represents corruption. These are different commentators' positions, not two uniform official church teachings. They differ particularly over what the growth reveals and how the images should be connected with other passages.
passages.god_plan_html:
Matthew's explicit Psalm connection places Jesus' teaching within the story of God making His works known. Psalm 78:1–8 calls the next generation to hear what God has done, trust Him, and avoid the stubbornness of earlier generations. Jesus' words likewise call for hearing that becomes a real response.

A related scriptural picture appears in Ezekiel 17:22–24: God plants a small shoot that becomes a great cedar, with birds finding shelter in its branches. This provides a scriptural parallel of growth and shelter under God's rule.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 13:36-43
passages.section_title: The Son of Man and the Final Harvest

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 36 Then Jesus dismissed the crowds and went into the house. His disciples came to Him and said, “Explain to us the parable of the weeds in the field.” 37 He replied, “The One who sows the good seed is the Son of Man. 38 The field is the world, and the good seed represents the sons of the kingdom. The weeds are the sons of the evil one, 39 and the enemy who sows them is the devil. The harvest is the end of the age, and the harvesters are angels. 40 As the weeds are collected and burned in the fire, so will it be at the end of the age. 41 The Son of Man will send out His angels, and they will weed out of His kingdom every cause of sin and all who practice lawlessness. 42 And they will throw them into the fiery furnace, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. 43 Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. He who has ears, let him hear.
paragraphs: 36 Then Jesus dismissed the crowds and went into the house. His disciples came to Him and said, “Explain to us the parable of the weeds in the field.” 37 He replied, “The One who sows the good seed is the Son of Man. 38 The field is the world, and the good seed represents the sons of the kingdom. The weeds are the sons of the evil one, 39 and the enemy who sows them is the devil. The harvest is the end of the age, and the harvesters are angels.

40 As the weeds are collected and burned in the fire, so will it be at the end of the age. 41 The Son of Man will send out His angels, and they will weed out of His kingdom every cause of sin and all who practice lawlessness. 42 And they will throw them into the fiery furnace, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. 43 Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. He who has ears, let him hear.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After leaving the crowds, Jesus enters the house and answers the disciples' request about the weeds. He identifies the sower as the Son of Man, the field as the world, the good seed as the sons of the kingdom, and the weeds as the sons of the evil one. The enemy is the devil.

He also identifies the harvest and harvesters: the end of the age and the angels. The explanation makes clear that the final separation is His work. The disciples are being taught to understand the present mixture without claiming the angels' final task for themselves.

Jesus describes the removal of causes of sin and those practicing lawlessness, with a serious warning of judgment. He then turns to the future of the righteous, who will shine in their Father's kingdom. The explanation moves from identifying evil to the promise of God's people sharing His kingdom's glory.

The closing call to hear brings the warning and promise to the listener. The story does not end with the enemy controlling the field. The Son of Man sends His angels and brings the harvest to its appointed end.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a promise of final judgment under Christ and the future glory of the righteous. The Reformed Westminster Confession, 33.1–3, teaches that God appoints judgment through Christ and calls His people to watchfulness. The Catholic Catechism, 1038–1041, likewise joins Christ's return, judgment, the disclosure of human lives, and hope in God's justice. The shared point is that Christ will bring the final judgment and fulfill His people's hope.
passages.god_plan_html:
The shining of the righteous recalls Daniel 12:1–3, which joins deliverance, resurrection, judgment, and the brightness of those who lead others toward righteousness. Jesus' promise belongs within that larger hope of life beyond the power of death and evil.

1 Corinthians 15:22–28 carries that hope toward its goal: Christ's people raised, His enemies overcome, death itself defeated, and the kingdom handed to the Father. The harvest is part of God's purpose to set things right through His Son. Evil's present presence is not its final victory.

passages.title: Matthew 13:44-46
passages.section_title: The Treasure and the Pearl of Great Value

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 44 The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field. When a man found it, he hid it again, and in his joy he went and sold all he had and bought that field. 45 Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant in search of fine pearls. 46 When he found one very precious pearl, he went away and sold all he had and bought it.
paragraphs: 44 The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field. When a man found it, he hid it again, and in his joy he went and sold all he had and bought that field.
45 Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant in search of fine pearls. 46 When he found one very precious pearl, he went away and sold all he had and bought it.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus gives two pictures of finding something of extraordinary value. A man discovers treasure in a field and sells what he has to buy the field. A merchant looking for fine pearls finds one especially valuable pearl and sells what he has to obtain it.

The first story explicitly names joy. Giving up possessions follows the recognition of a greater treasure. The second begins with a search and ends with the merchant recognizing the pearl worth everything else. The situations differ, but both involve a discovery that changes what the person is willing to keep or release.

The stories are comparisons about the kingdom, centered on the value recognized and the decisive response.

Unlike the sower and weeds, these parables are not followed by Jesus assigning a separate meaning to every object. Readers therefore differ over whether the buyers primarily picture people receiving the kingdom or Christ giving Himself to obtain His people.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley on Matthew 13:44–45 reads the treasure as God's kingdom received within a person's life and the merchant as someone seeking it. The Catholic Catechism, 546, uses these parables in describing the wholehearted choice Jesus asks of those entering the kingdom. These readings emphasize its surpassing value and the response of a disciple.

C. I. Scofield's 1917 notes on 13:44–46 read the buyer as Christ, the treasure as Israel, and the pearl as the church, obtained through His self-giving. This is his particular interpretation, not a view held by all Protestants. The readings differ over who the buyer represents while both connecting the stories with the worth of what is obtained.
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul gives a related example of value changing a person's priorities in Philippians 3:7–11. He counts former advantages as loss beside knowing Christ and sharing the life that comes through Him. He also explicitly places righteousness in faith in Christ, rather than his own achievement.

Paul describes receiving Christ's righteousness through faith alongside his willingness to release the things he once valued. The greater treasure is bound to the Savior and His resurrection life, which gives a different measure for what is worth keeping.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 13:47-50
passages.section_title: The Net and the Coming Separation

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 47 Once again, the kingdom of heaven is like a net that was cast into the sea and caught all kinds of fish. 48 When it was full, the men pulled it ashore. Then they sat down and sorted the good fish into containers, but threw the bad away. 49 So will it be at the end of the age: The angels will come and separate the wicked from the righteous 50 and throw them into the fiery furnace, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.
paragraphs: 47 Once again, the kingdom of heaven is like a net that was cast into the sea and caught all kinds of fish. 48 When it was full, the men pulled it ashore. Then they sat down and sorted the good fish into containers, but threw the bad away.
49 So will it be at the end of the age: The angels will come and separate the wicked from the righteous 50 and throw them into the fiery furnace, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The final kingdom story returns to the sea. A net gathers fish of many kinds, and the catch is sorted after it is brought ashore. The good fish are kept and the bad discarded. The gathering and the final sorting are distinct moments in the picture.

The Greek word is σαγήνη, sagēnē (sah-GAY-nay), a large fishing net or dragnet. Thayer's entry identifies this use in Matthew 13:47. The image is of a broad catch followed by separation; Jesus does not describe each fish's history.

He then states the point directly. At the end of the age, the angels separate the wicked from the righteous, with a severe warning about the outcome for the wicked. This repeats the final separation of the weeds explanation, using a different everyday scene.

The passage places weight on the coming judgment rather than on impressive totals gathered into the net. The final distinction is real, and it belongs within the Son of Man's authority already described in the chapter.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a warning that gathering people around the kingdom's message is not the same as the final separation of the righteous and wicked. Wesley on Matthew 13:45–50 applies the net to the preached gospel gathering a mixed response and the angels completing the separation. The Catholic Catechism, 1038–1041, likewise emphasizes the reality of final judgment and the call to respond while the time of mercy remains.
passages.god_plan_html:
The reality of judgment becomes a reason to bring God's appeal for reconciliation. In 2 Corinthians 5:10–11, Paul connects giving account before Christ with seeking to persuade people. He then describes the message entrusted to Christ's ambassadors: be reconciled to God through Him (2 Corinthians 5:18–21).

The appeal continues in 2 Corinthians 6:1–2, which calls the present the time of God's favor and salvation. The coming separation therefore gives urgency to receiving and sharing His mercy now. God's plan includes both a just end to evil and a real invitation to life through Christ.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 13:51-52
passages.section_title: Bringing Out Treasures New and Old

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 51 Have you understood all these things?” “Yes,” they answered. 52 Then He told them, “For this reason, every scribe who has been discipled in the kingdom of heaven is like a homeowner who brings out of his storeroom new treasures as well as old.”
paragraphs: 51 Have you understood all these things?” “Yes,” they answered. 52 Then He told them, “For this reason, every scribe who has been discipled in the kingdom of heaven is like a homeowner who brings out of his storeroom new treasures as well as old.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus asks whether the disciples have understood these things, and they answer yes. He follows with a picture of a scribe trained as a disciple of the kingdom: a householder bringing out both new and old treasures from a storeroom.

The picture joins learning with the ability to give something useful to others. Understanding is not treated as private possession alone. A trained teacher has resources to bring out, with both what has long been known and what Jesus is now making clear.

The old and new belong together within the kingdom's teaching. Earlier in this chapter, prophets longed for what the disciples now see, and Jesus explained His work through Isaiah and the Psalms. The new revelation through Him gives greater understanding of the Scriptures already received.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as a call for teachers formed by Jesus to draw on the riches of God's revelation. Wesley on Matthew 13:52 emphasizes a prepared teacher's resources for instruction. The Methodist Articles of Religion, VI, affirm that the Old Testament is not opposed to the New and that both offer life through Christ. The US Catholic bishops' note on 13:52 similarly reads the old as the Law and Prophets and the new as Jesus' teaching, with the former understood through its fulfillment.
passages.god_plan_html:
After His resurrection, Jesus opens the disciples' understanding of the Law, Prophets, and Psalms, connecting them with His suffering, resurrection, and the message of repentance and forgiveness to all nations (Luke 24:44–49). The treasures of Scripture equip people to announce the Savior and His work.

2 Timothy 3:14–17 likewise describes the Scriptures as making a person wise for salvation through faith in Christ and preparing God's servant for every good work. Learning the whole story serves God's purpose of forming people who can live and teach it faithfully.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 13:53-58
passages.section_title: When Familiarity Becomes an Obstacle to Faith

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 53 When Jesus had finished these parables, He withdrew from that place. 54 Coming to His hometown, He taught the people in their synagogue, and they were astonished. “Where did this man get such wisdom and miraculous powers?” they asked. 55 “Isn’t this the carpenter’s son? Isn’t His mother’s name Mary, and aren’t His brothers James, Joseph, Simon, and Judas? 56 Aren’t all His sisters with us as well? Where then did this man get all these things?” 57 And they took offense at Him. But Jesus said to them, “Only in his hometown and in his own household is a prophet without honor.” 58 And He did not do many miracles there, because of their unbelief.
paragraphs: 53 When Jesus had finished these parables, He withdrew from that place. 54 Coming to His hometown, He taught the people in their synagogue, and they were astonished. “Where did this man get such wisdom and miraculous powers?” they asked. 55 “Isn’t this the carpenter’s son? Isn’t His mother’s name Mary, and aren’t His brothers James, Joseph, Simon, and Judas? 56 Aren’t all His sisters with us as well? Where then did this man get all these things?”

57 And they took offense at Him. But Jesus said to them, “Only in his hometown and in his own household is a prophet without honor.” 58 And He did not do many miracles there, because of their unbelief.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The parable teaching ends and Jesus goes to His hometown. The people are astonished at His wisdom and power, but their questions turn toward the family they know. They identify Him as the carpenter's son and name His mother, brothers, and sisters.

The word translated carpenter is τέκτων, tektōn (TEK-tone). Thayer's entry gives woodworker or carpenter. The question places Jesus within a familiar working household. The people struggle to reconcile what they know of His background with the wisdom and power before them.

They take offense, and Jesus speaks of a prophet lacking honor in his own hometown and household. Knowing His family has not become a willingness to receive Him. The ending connects their unbelief with the small number of miracles He does there.

The related account in Mark 6:1–6 says that He heals a few sick people and is amazed at the unbelief. Matthew's statement is not that no healing happens. It describes a rejection within the very place where people might have thought they knew Him best.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read this as a warning that familiarity can become a reason for refusing to honor Jesus. Wesley on Matthew 13:57–58 emphasizes the low standing His neighbors assign Him and their unbelief. The US Catholic bishops' note on 13:54–58 likewise connects their knowledge of His background with their rejection.

The family terms receive different readings. The Catholic Catechism, 500, understands the brothers as close relatives rather than Mary's other children. The Orthodox Church in America's life of Joseph presents them as Joseph's children from an earlier marriage. An Orthodox Presbyterian Church Q&A reads them as Mary's later children by Joseph, while Wesley on 13:55 reads them as relatives through Mary's family.
passages.god_plan_html:
John 1:10–13 places rejection alongside God's gift of belonging: the One who came is not received by His own, yet those who receive Him become God's children. Familiar background and inherited connection do not replace receiving the Son.

The wider story also leaves room for a changed response. John 7:3–5 describes Jesus' brothers as not believing in Him, while Acts 1:12–14 later places His brothers with Mary and the praying disciples. Earlier unbelief is not treated as the whole final story of God's work among those close to Jesus.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 14:1-12
passages.section_title: John the Baptist Is Killed

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 At that time Herod the tetrarch heard the reports about Jesus 2 and said to his servants, “This is John the Baptist; he has risen from the dead! That is why miraculous powers are at work in him.” 3 Now Herod had arrested John and bound him and put him in prison on account of Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife, 4 because John had been telling him, “It is not lawful for you to have her.” 5 Although Herod wanted to kill John, he was afraid of the people, because they regarded John as a prophet. 6 On Herod’s birthday, however, the daughter of Herodias danced before them and pleased Herod 7 so much that he promised with an oath to give to her whatever she asked. 8 Prompted by her mother, she said, “Give me here on a platter the head of John the Baptist.” 9 The king was grieved, but because of his oaths and his guests, he ordered that her wish be granted 10 and sent to have John beheaded in the prison. 11 John’s head was brought in on a platter and presented to the girl, who carried it to her mother. 12 Then John’s disciples came and took his body and buried it. And they went and informed Jesus.
paragraphs: 1 At that time Herod the tetrarch heard the reports about Jesus 2 and said to his servants, “This is John the Baptist; he has risen from the dead! That is why miraculous powers are at work in him.”

3 Now Herod had arrested John and bound him and put him in prison on account of Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife, 4 because John had been telling him, “It is not lawful for you to have her.” 5 Although Herod wanted to kill John, he was afraid of the people, because they regarded John as a prophet.

6 On Herod’s birthday, however, the daughter of Herodias danced before them and pleased Herod 7 so much that he promised with an oath to give to her whatever she asked. 8 Prompted by her mother, she said, “Give me here on a platter the head of John the Baptist.” 9 The king was grieved, but because of his oaths and his guests, he ordered that her wish be granted

10 and sent to have John beheaded in the prison. 11 John’s head was brought in on a platter and presented to the girl, who carried it to her mother. 12 Then John’s disciples came and took his body and buried it. And they went and informed Jesus.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Reports about Jesus reach Herod, who thinks John the Baptist has risen from the dead. Matthew then looks back to explain what happened to John. The story follows the rejection of Jesus in His hometown and shows the danger facing a prophet who speaks unwelcome truth.

John had challenged Herod's marriage to his brother's wife, Herodias. Herod imprisoned him and wanted him dead, but feared the people who regarded John as a prophet. At a birthday celebration, Herod's pleasure in Herodias's daughter's dancing leads him to make a sweeping promise under oath.

Her mother prompts the girl to ask for John's head. Herod is grieved, yet gives the order because of his oaths and his guests. His concern about what others will think ends in an innocent man's death. John's disciples bury him and bring the news to Jesus.

The Jewish historian Josephus, Antiquities 18.5.2, also reports that Herod had John imprisoned and killed. Josephus emphasizes Herod's fear of John's influence over the crowds. Matthew tells the story through John's rebuke of the marriage and the fatal promise at the banquet. The accounts give different emphases rather than identical explanations.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as the death of a faithful prophet and a warning about wrongdoing driven by fear, pride, and a reckless promise. Wesley's note on Matthew 14:9 stresses that keeping a wrongful oath does not make the killing right. The US Catholic bishops' note on 14:1–12 also connects John's death with the suffering Jesus will face.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus Himself makes the connection between John's treatment and His own coming suffering. In Matthew 17:10–13, He says that people failed to recognize the Elijah who had come and did as they wished to him; the disciples understand that He means John. Jesus then says the Son of Man will suffer at their hands as well.

John's role in preparing the way therefore includes rejection as well as proclamation. His death does not mean God's promised work has stopped. It prepares the reader for the Messiah's own suffering, while leaving the cruelty of those responsible fully in view.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 14:13-21
passages.section_title: Jesus Feeds the Crowd

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 When Jesus heard about John, He withdrew by boat privately to a solitary place. But the crowds found out about it and followed Him on foot from the towns. 14 When He stepped ashore and saw a large crowd, He had compassion on them and healed their sick. 15 When evening came, the disciples came to Him and said, “This is a desolate place, and the hour is already late. Dismiss the crowds so they can go to the villages and buy themselves some food.” 16 “They do not need to go away,” Jesus replied. “You give them something to eat.” 17 “We have here only five loaves of bread and two fish,” they answered. 18 “Bring them here to Me,” Jesus said. 19 And He directed the crowds to sit down on the grass. Taking the five loaves and the two fish and looking up to heaven, He spoke a blessing. Then He broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the people. 20 They all ate and were satisfied, and the disciples picked up twelve basketfuls of broken pieces that were left over. 21 About five thousand men were fed, besides women and children.
paragraphs: 13 When Jesus heard about John, He withdrew by boat privately to a solitary place. But the crowds found out about it and followed Him on foot from the towns. 14 When He stepped ashore and saw a large crowd, He had compassion on them and healed their sick.

15 When evening came, the disciples came to Him and said, “This is a desolate place, and the hour is already late. Dismiss the crowds so they can go to the villages and buy themselves some food.” 16 “They do not need to go away,” Jesus replied. “You give them something to eat.” 17 “We have here only five loaves of bread and two fish,” they answered. 18 “Bring them here to Me,” Jesus said.

19 And He directed the crowds to sit down on the grass. Taking the five loaves and the two fish and looking up to heaven, He spoke a blessing. Then He broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the people. 20 They all ate and were satisfied, and the disciples picked up twelve basketfuls of broken pieces that were left over. 21 About five thousand men were fed, besides women and children.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After hearing about John, Jesus withdraws by boat to a solitary place. The crowds follow on foot. When He sees them, He has compassion and heals their sick. Their interruption of His withdrawal becomes an occasion for care.

The word for having compassion is σπλαγχνίζομαι, splagchnizomai (splahng-KHNID-zoh-my), meaning to be deeply moved with compassion. Thayer's entry includes this verse. Matthew shows that concern in what Jesus does for the people, first in healing and then in feeding them.

As evening comes, the disciples want the crowd sent away to buy food. Jesus tells them to feed the people. They have only five loaves and two fish, which He asks them to bring to Him. He blesses and breaks the bread, gives it to the disciples, and they distribute it to the crowd.

Everyone eats and is satisfied, with twelve baskets of pieces left over. The number given is about five thousand men, with women and children in addition. Matthew emphasizes the crowd's real need, the disciples' limited resources, and the abundance Jesus provides. He does not describe the moment-by-moment process by which the food increases.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand this as a miracle showing Jesus' compassion and power to provide, with the disciples serving the people through what He gives them. The story also invites reflection on His place in God's care for His people.

The Catholic Church's Catechism, 1335, additionally sees the feeding as pointing ahead to the abundance of the Eucharist, or Lord's Supper. In this reading, Jesus' generous provision also prepares people to understand the meal He will give His disciples.
passages.god_plan_html:
Mark 6:34–44 describes the same crowd as sheep without a shepherd and has them sit on green grass. This recalls the care pictured in Psalm 23: the Lord shepherds His people, leads them to pasture, and provides a table. This is a scriptural parallel that helps us see both the food and the Shepherd's care behind it.

John 6:1–15, 30–35 places the feeding near Passover and later connects the conversation with the manna in the wilderness. Jesus directs the people beyond the meal to the life the Father gives through Him. God's provision reaches deeper than one day's hunger: the Son Himself gives life to those who come to Him and believe.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 14:22-33
passages.section_title: Jesus Comes to His Disciples on the Sea

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 Immediately Jesus made the disciples get into the boat and go on ahead of Him to the other side, while He dismissed the crowds. 23 After He had dismissed them, He went up on the mountain by Himself to pray. When evening came, He was there alone, 24 but the boat was already far from land, buffeted by the waves because the wind was against it. 25 During the fourth watch of the night, Jesus went out to them, walking on the sea. 26 When the disciples saw Him walking on the sea, they were terrified. “It’s a ghost!” they said, and cried out in fear. 27 But Jesus spoke up at once: “Take courage! It is I. Do not be afraid.” 28 “Lord, if it is You,” Peter replied, “command me to come to You on the water.” 29 “Come,” said Jesus. Then Peter got down out of the boat, walked on the water, and came toward Jesus. 30 But when he saw the strength of the wind, he was afraid and, beginning to sink, cried out, “Lord, save me!” 31 Immediately Jesus reached out His hand and took hold of Peter. “You of little faith,” He said, “why did you doubt?” 32 And when they had climbed back into the boat, the wind died down. 33 Then those who were in the boat worshiped Him, saying, “Truly You are the Son of God!”
paragraphs: 22 Immediately Jesus made the disciples get into the boat and go on ahead of Him to the other side, while He dismissed the crowds. 23 After He had dismissed them, He went up on the mountain by Himself to pray. When evening came, He was there alone, 24 but the boat was already far from land, buffeted by the waves because the wind was against it.

25 During the fourth watch of the night, Jesus went out to them, walking on the sea. 26 When the disciples saw Him walking on the sea, they were terrified. “It’s a ghost!” they said, and cried out in fear. 27 But Jesus spoke up at once: “Take courage! It is I. Do not be afraid.”

28 “Lord, if it is You,” Peter replied, “command me to come to You on the water.” 29 “Come,” said Jesus. Then Peter got down out of the boat, walked on the water, and came toward Jesus. 30 But when he saw the strength of the wind, he was afraid and, beginning to sink, cried out, “Lord, save me!” 31 Immediately Jesus reached out His hand and took hold of Peter. “You of little faith,” He said, “why did you doubt?”
32 And when they had climbed back into the boat, the wind died down. 33 Then those who were in the boat worshiped Him, saying, “Truly You are the Son of God!”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus sends the disciples ahead by boat, dismisses the crowd, and goes up the mountain alone to pray. The boat is far from land, struggling against the wind. During the fourth watch of the night, Jesus comes toward them, walking on the sea.

The disciples are terrified because they think they see a ghost. Jesus immediately reassures them and tells them who He is. Peter asks Him to command him to come on the water, and Jesus tells him to come. Peter gets out and walks toward Him.

When Peter sees the force of the wind, he becomes afraid and starts to sink. He cries to Jesus for rescue, and Jesus immediately takes hold of him. Jesus calls his faith little and asks why he doubted. The account gives us both a real step toward Jesus and a fear that interrupts it.

Once they are in the boat, the wind stops, and those aboard worship Jesus and acknowledge Him as God's Son. The verb is προσκυνέω, proskyneō (prohs-koo-NEH-oh), to bow down or show reverence. Thayer's entry describes its use for homage and worship. Here the act comes with their spoken recognition of who Jesus is.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a revelation of Jesus' authority over the sea and a lesson in trusting Him amid fear.
