Wesley on Matthew 14:28–33 understands Peter as responding to the Jesus he recognizes, then becoming afraid. The US Catholic bishops' notes on 14:22–33 likewise connect the scene with God's power over the waters and the disciples' recognition of Jesus. Peter's faltering and Jesus' immediate rescue belong together in the account.
passages.god_plan_html:
The Old Testament describes mastery over the sea as God's work. Job 9:8 speaks of Him treading on its waves, and Psalm 77:16–20 recalls His path through the waters as He led His people like a flock. Those are strong scriptural parallels for a scene that ends with Jesus acknowledged as God's Son.

The disciples are also learning to recognize the One who provides for them. Mark 6:51–52 connects their astonishment on the sea with their failure to understand the loaves. The feeding and the rescue together reveal more than separate displays of power. They help the disciples come to know Jesus Himself, even while their understanding and trust still need to grow.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

passages.title: Matthew 14:34-36
passages.section_title: Healing at Gennesaret

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 34 When they had crossed over, they landed at Gennesaret. 35 And when the men of that place recognized Jesus, they sent word to all the surrounding region. People brought all the sick to Him 36 and begged Him just to let them touch the fringe of His cloak. And all who touched Him were healed.
paragraphs: 34 When they had crossed over, they landed at Gennesaret. 35 And when the men of that place recognized Jesus, they sent word to all the surrounding region. People brought all the sick to Him 36 and begged Him just to let them touch the fringe of His cloak. And all who touched Him were healed.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After crossing the lake, Jesus and the disciples land at Gennesaret. People recognize Him and send word through the surrounding region. They bring the sick and ask that they might touch even the fringe of His cloak. Matthew closes by saying that all who touch Him are healed.

The Greek word for fringe is κράσπεδον, kraspedon (KRAS-peh-don), an edge, fringe, or tassel on a garment. Thayer's entry connects this usage with the tassels prescribed in Numbers 15:37–41. Those tassels reminded Israel to remember and obey God's commands.

The scene recalls the woman who touches Jesus' garment in Matthew 9:20–22, but now many sick people are brought to Him. The focus remains on Jesus and the healing people receive from Him. Matthew does not record a separate conversation with each person.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as another account of Jesus' healing power and people coming to Him with confidence that He can help. The garment recalls the earlier woman's approach, while the spread of the news brings the need of a whole region into view. Matthew describes the healings without giving a separate explanation of each person's understanding or motives.
passages.god_plan_html:
A possible parallel connects these healings with Malachi 4:2, which pictures healing coming with the rising sun of righteousness. The Hebrew word for wings is כָּנָף, kānāph (kah-NAHF). Brown–Driver–Briggs gives both wing and garment corner among its meanings, while identifying the Malachi image with the sun's wings.

Matthew Poole's commentary on Malachi 4:2 suggests that the verse may also point toward people being healed as they touch Christ's garment. That is a possible parallel, not a connection Matthew explicitly announces. It helps us consider the promised healing alongside what Jesus brings, without assuming the crowd had worked out that connection for themselves.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 15:1-9
passages.section_title: When Tradition Displaces God's Command

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then some Pharisees and scribes came to Jesus from Jerusalem and asked, 2 “Why do Your disciples break the tradition of the elders? They do not wash their hands before they eat.” 3 Jesus replied, “And why do you break the command of God for the sake of your tradition? 4 For God said, ‘Honor your father and mother’ and ‘Anyone who curses his father or mother must be put to death.’ 5 But you say that if anyone says to his father or mother, ‘Whatever you would have received from me is a gift devoted to God,’ 6 he need not honor his father or mother with it. Thus you nullify the word of God for the sake of your tradition. 7 You hypocrites! Isaiah prophesied correctly about you: 8 ‘These people honor Me with their lips, but their hearts are far from Me. 9 They worship Me in vain; they teach as doctrine the precepts of men.’”
paragraphs: 1 Then some Pharisees and scribes came to Jesus from Jerusalem and asked, 2 “Why do Your disciples break the tradition of the elders? They do not wash their hands before they eat.” 3 Jesus replied, “And why do you break the command of God for the sake of your tradition?

4 For God said, ‘Honor your father and mother’ and ‘Anyone who curses his father or mother must be put to death.’ 5 But you say that if anyone says to his father or mother, ‘Whatever you would have received from me is a gift devoted to God,’ 6 he need not honor his father or mother with it. Thus you nullify the word of God for the sake of your tradition.

7 You hypocrites! Isaiah prophesied correctly about you: 8 ‘These people honor Me with their lips, but their hearts are far from Me. 9 They worship Me in vain; they teach as doctrine the precepts of men.’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Pharisees and scribes from Jerusalem question Jesus about His disciples eating without washing their hands. Their complaint concerns the tradition of the elders. Mark 7:1–5 explains that the washing belongs to their practices of ceremonial cleanliness. The dispute is about religious obligation, rather than a lesson about hygiene.

Jesus answers with a question about their own teaching. God commands people to honor their parents, yet they allow a declaration that resources are devoted to God to keep those resources from helping a father or mother. A religious rule is being used to set aside a duty God has given.

Mark calls the declaration Corban. The Greek spelling is κορβᾶν, korban (kor-BAHN), from the Hebrew word for an offering. Thayer's entry explains it as a gift offered, or intended to be offered, to God. In Mark 7:9–13, the problem is that the declaration prevents the help the parents should receive.

Jesus then applies Isaiah's warning about honoring God with words while the heart is far away. The claimed devotion does not excuse the neglected command. His reply asks whether religious teaching leads people to obey God or gives them a way around what He says.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read this as a warning against human teaching that defeats God's commands. Traditions differ over how to distinguish a human custom from teaching received with divine authority.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, 1.6 and 1.10, makes Scripture the final test and rejects additions to God's revealed teaching from human traditions. The 1689 Baptist Confession, 1.6 and 1.10, teaches the same principle. The Methodist Articles of Religion, V, likewise say that a belief cannot be required as necessary for salvation unless it is taught in Scripture or can be proved from it.

The Catholic Church's Catechism, 80–83, distinguishes apostolic Tradition, received from Christ and the apostles, from later customs that can change. It receives Scripture and apostolic Tradition together. Paragraph 86 says the Church's teaching office serves God's word. Catholic teaching therefore does not understand Jesus' rebuke as a rejection of apostolic Tradition. The difference concerns where authoritative teaching is received and how it is recognized.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus explicitly connects this dispute with Isaiah 29:13–14. The warning about lips and hearts shows that the problem reaches deeper than one disputed washing practice. God's people are called to honor Him in truth, including how they treat people entrusted to their care.

That connection continues in James 1:22–27. Hearing God's word must become doing it; an unrestrained tongue can make a person's religious claims empty, while care for vulnerable people belongs to faithful devotion. God's purpose for His word includes a changed life, not simply a religious explanation for avoiding responsibility.
passages.current_position_html: In Worship as the Early Church Knew It, our discussion of Matthew 15:9 identifies the problem as reverence that remains outward while obedience is missing. Religious language cannot make neglected obedience into faithful devotion.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

passages.title: Matthew 15:9
passages.section_title: Empty Worship and Human Commands

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 They worship Me in vain; they teach as doctrine the precepts of men.’”
paragraphs: 9 They worship Me in vain; they teach as doctrine the precepts of men.’”

passages.context_html:
This verse is part of Jesus' quotation of Isaiah in a dispute about the elders' traditions. The immediate example is a teaching that allows resources declared devoted to God to be withheld from needy parents. Jesus has already identified that practice as setting aside God's command.

The word translated worship is σέβομαι, sebomai (SEH-boh-my), meaning to revere or worship. Thayer's entry includes this verse. In the quotation, the claimed reverence is empty because human precepts are being taught as God's doctrine.

The preceding verse supplies the contrast between lips and heart. The issue is not the sincerity of a spoken claim by itself. Jesus measures the teaching against God's command and exposes the disobedience it permits.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand this as a warning against empty religious honor and treating human commands as God's teaching. Wesley on Matthew 15:8–9 emphasizes the missing heart response and human commands being placed alongside or above God's commands.

The wider disagreement concerns which teaching counts as merely human. The Westminster Confession, 1.6 and 1.10, tests church teaching by Scripture as final authority. The Catholic Catechism, 80–83, distinguishes changeable customs from apostolic Tradition, which it receives together with Scripture. Both reject replacing God's word with arbitrary human requirements, while understanding the source of binding teaching differently.
passages.current_position_html: In Worship as the Early Church Knew It, we read this verse as a warning about hollow reverence: people may speak as though they honor God while their teaching permits them to ignore His commands. The study calls for reverence joined to obedience.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
John 4:19–24 places true worship within the work Jesus is bringing: the Father seeks people who worship in spirit and truth. That is a related teaching, rather than a claim that the two conversations address identical customs.

Together, these passages direct attention to a response to God that reaches the heart and follows His truth. The change Jesus brings concerns more than where a person worships or what religious words they use. It reaches the reality of their relationship with the Father.

passages.title: Matthew 15:10-20
passages.section_title: What Makes a Person Unclean?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 Jesus called the crowd to Him and said, “Listen and understand. 11 A man is not defiled by what enters his mouth, but by what comes out of it.” 12 Then the disciples came to Him and said, “Are You aware that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this?” 13 But Jesus replied, “Every plant that My heavenly Father has not planted will be pulled up by its roots. 14 Disregard them! They are blind guides. If a blind man leads a blind man, both will fall into a pit.” 15 Peter said to Him, “Explain this parable to us.” 16 “Do you still not understand?” Jesus asked. 17 “Do you not yet realize that whatever enters the mouth goes into the stomach and then is eliminated? 18 But the things that come out of the mouth come from the heart, and these things defile a man. 19 For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false testimony, and slander. 20 These are what defile a man, but eating with unwashed hands does not defile him.”
paragraphs: 10 Jesus called the crowd to Him and said, “Listen and understand. 11 A man is not defiled by what enters his mouth, but by what comes out of it.”

12 Then the disciples came to Him and said, “Are You aware that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this?” 13 But Jesus replied, “Every plant that My heavenly Father has not planted will be pulled up by its roots. 14 Disregard them! They are blind guides. If a blind man leads a blind man, both will fall into a pit.”

15 Peter said to Him, “Explain this parable to us.” 16 “Do you still not understand?” Jesus asked. 17 “Do you not yet realize that whatever enters the mouth goes into the stomach and then is eliminated?

18 But the things that come out of the mouth come from the heart, and these things defile a man. 19 For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false testimony, and slander. 20 These are what defile a man, but eating with unwashed hands does not defile him.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus calls the crowd to listen and says that what comes out of the mouth defiles a person. The disciples report that the Pharisees are offended. Jesus responds with pictures of an uprooted plant and blind guides, warning against following guidance that leads people into danger.

Peter asks for an explanation. Jesus contrasts the ordinary path of food through the body with words and actions that come from the heart. He names evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false testimony, and slander. The problem He exposes is moral corruption within a person.

The verb for defile is κοινόω, koinoō (koy-NOH-oh), to make unclean or profane. Thayer's entry includes these verses. The discussion begins with unwashed hands, but Jesus uses the language of uncleanness to bring the hearers face to face with the evil expressed in their lives.

He closes by returning to the original complaint: eating with unwashed hands does not defile someone. Mark 7:17–23 gives the related explanation and its implications for food. In Matthew, the list of harmful thoughts and deeds makes clear why outward religious practices cannot substitute for a changed heart.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as teaching that moral uncleanness comes from the heart and appears in a person's thoughts, words, and deeds. Wesley on Matthew 15:19 follows that movement from evil thoughts into the sins Jesus lists. The US Catholic bishops' note on 15:1–20 likewise emphasizes the inner source of defilement and the return to the handwashing question. The warning calls people to examine their lives more deeply than outward observance alone.
passages.god_plan_html:
God's promise of cleansing reaches the heart. In Ezekiel 36:22–28, He promises Israel cleansing, a new heart, and His Spirit enabling obedience. That is a related promise of God addressing what His people cannot repair merely by maintaining appearances.

James 1:21–25 calls people to receive the planted word and put it into practice. God's renewing work is meant to shape what a person does. The larger biblical answer to the heart's corruption includes both His gift of renewal and the life of obedience that grows from it.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 15:21-28
passages.section_title: A Canaanite Woman's Great Faith

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 Leaving that place, Jesus withdrew to the district of Tyre and Sidon. 22 And a Canaanite woman from that region came to Him, crying out, “Lord, Son of David, have mercy on me! My daughter is miserably possessed by a demon.” 23 But Jesus did not answer a word. So His disciples came and urged Him, “Send her away, for she keeps crying out after us.” 24 He answered, “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.” 25 The woman came and knelt before Him. “Lord, help me!” she said. 26 But Jesus replied, “It is not right to take the children’s bread and toss it to the dogs.” 27 “Yes, Lord,” she said, “even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their master’s table.” 28 “O woman,” Jesus answered, “your faith is great! Let it be done for you as you desire.” And her daughter was healed from that very hour.
paragraphs: 21 Leaving that place, Jesus withdrew to the district of Tyre and Sidon. 22 And a Canaanite woman from that region came to Him, crying out, “Lord, Son of David, have mercy on me! My daughter is miserably possessed by a demon.” 23 But Jesus did not answer a word. So His disciples came and urged Him, “Send her away, for she keeps crying out after us.” 24 He answered, “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.”

25 The woman came and knelt before Him. “Lord, help me!” she said. 26 But Jesus replied, “It is not right to take the children’s bread and toss it to the dogs.” 27 “Yes, Lord,” she said, “even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their master’s table.” 28 “O woman,” Jesus answered, “your faith is great! Let it be done for you as you desire.” And her daughter was healed from that very hour.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus withdraws to the district of Tyre and Sidon. A Canaanite woman calls Him Lord and Son of David and asks for mercy for her demon-tormented daughter. Mark 7:24–30 identifies her as a Greek woman of Syrophoenician origin and describes the encounter at a house.

Jesus initially gives no answer, and the disciples ask Him to send her away. He then speaks of His mission to Israel's lost sheep. The woman comes and kneels before Him, continuing to ask for help. The conversation places her need alongside the priority of His mission to Israel.

Jesus uses the picture of children's bread and dogs. The Greek word is κυνάριον, kynarion (koo-NAH-ree-on), a little dog, according to Thayer's entry. The household meal picture gives her reply its force: even the dogs receive crumbs from their master's table. The word's form does not remove the difficult distinction in the exchange.

Her answer asks for mercy within that picture. Jesus praises her great faith and grants her request; her daughter is healed from that hour. The account ends with Jesus praising a Gentile woman's faith and extending His help to her family.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly see persistent trust in Jesus' power and mercy, together with the reach of His help beyond Israel. Wesley on Matthew 15:23–28 reads the delay as a trial of faith and the final praise as recognition of her reliance on God's goodness. The US Catholic bishops' note on 15:28 likewise emphasizes Jesus granting the request in connection with her great faith. The mother's persistence and Jesus' final welcome are central to that reading.
passages.god_plan_html:
The priority of Israel and mercy for the Gentiles belong together in Romans 15:7–13. Paul says Christ confirms God's promises to the patriarchs so that the Gentiles also glorify God for His mercy. He supports that hope from Israel's Scriptures. Mercy reaching this woman fits that larger purpose without requiring Israel's place to be erased.

The mission will become openly worldwide. The risen Jesus sends His disciples to make disciples of all nations in Matthew 28:18–20. Her encounter gives an early glimpse of faith and mercy crossing the boundary that the later commission will tell the disciples to cross.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 15:29-31
passages.section_title: The Crowd Praises the God of Israel

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 29 Moving on from there, Jesus went along the Sea of Galilee. Then He went up on a mountain and sat down. 30 Large crowds came to Him, bringing the lame, the blind, the crippled, the mute, and many others, and laid them at His feet, and He healed them. 31 The crowd was amazed when they saw the mute speaking, the crippled restored, the lame walking, and the blind seeing. And they glorified the God of Israel.
paragraphs: 29 Moving on from there, Jesus went along the Sea of Galilee. Then He went up on a mountain and sat down. 30 Large crowds came to Him, bringing the lame, the blind, the crippled, the mute, and many others, and laid them at His feet, and He healed them. 31 The crowd was amazed when they saw the mute speaking, the crippled restored, the lame walking, and the blind seeing. And they glorified the God of Israel.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus returns to the Sea of Galilee and sits on a mountain. People bring those who are lame, blind, crippled, mute, and suffering in other ways, laying them at His feet. Matthew describes healing that the crowd can see: people speak, walk, and see again.

The crowd's amazement leads to praise of the God of Israel. The account follows the help given to the Canaanite woman and comes before another large feeding. Need, mercy, and recognition of God's work connect the scenes.

Mark 7:31–37 places the related return journey in the region of the Decapolis and describes a deaf man whose speech is restored. That setting helps readers consider the reach of Jesus' work, while Matthew does not identify the background of every person in this crowd.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand these healings as signs of Jesus' mercy and God's saving work, drawing the people toward praise. The US Catholic bishops' reference note on Matthew 15:30 connects the healings with Isaiah 35:5–6. The emphasis is on restored people and the God they glorify, rather than on a separate hidden meaning assigned to each illness.
passages.god_plan_html:
Isaiah 35:3–10 joins God's coming to save with blind eyes opened, the lame leaping, and mute tongues rejoicing. It places those restorations within a wider promise of a renewed creation and God's redeemed people returning with joy. The healings in Matthew form a strong parallel with that promised restoration.

Earlier, Jesus directs John's messengers to the blind seeing and the lame walking as evidence of His work (Matthew 11:2–6). These scenes therefore help answer who Jesus is and what God is bringing through Him. The signs give a glimpse of restoration greater than the needs of one gathering.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 15:32-39
passages.section_title: Jesus Feeds Four Thousand

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 32 Then Jesus called His disciples to Him and said, “I have compassion for this crowd, because they have already been with Me three days and have nothing to eat. I do not want to send them away hungry, or they may faint along the way.” 33 The disciples replied, “Where in this desolate place could we find enough bread to feed such a large crowd?” 34 “How many loaves do you have?” Jesus asked. “Seven,” they replied, “and a few small fish.” 35 And He instructed the crowd to sit down on the ground. 36 Taking the seven loaves and the fish, He gave thanks and broke them. Then He gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the people. 37 They all ate and were satisfied, and the disciples picked up seven basketfuls of broken pieces that were left over. 38 A total of four thousand men were fed, besides women and children. 39 After Jesus had dismissed the crowds, He got into the boat and went to the region of Magadan.
paragraphs: 32 Then Jesus called His disciples to Him and said, “I have compassion for this crowd, because they have already been with Me three days and have nothing to eat. I do not want to send them away hungry, or they may faint along the way.” 33 The disciples replied, “Where in this desolate place could we find enough bread to feed such a large crowd?” 34 “How many loaves do you have?” Jesus asked. “Seven,” they replied, “and a few small fish.”

35 And He instructed the crowd to sit down on the ground. 36 Taking the seven loaves and the fish, He gave thanks and broke them. Then He gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the people. 37 They all ate and were satisfied, and the disciples picked up seven basketfuls of broken pieces that were left over.
38 A total of four thousand men were fed, besides women and children. 39 After Jesus had dismissed the crowds, He got into the boat and went to the region of Magadan.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus tells His disciples that He has compassion for the crowd. They have remained with Him for three days and have nothing to eat. He does not want them sent away hungry and at risk of fainting. Once again, their physical need matters to Him.

The disciples ask where enough bread could be found in such a desolate place. They have seven loaves and a few small fish. Jesus seats the crowd, gives thanks, breaks the food, and gives it to the disciples to distribute. All eat and are satisfied.

Seven baskets of pieces remain. The basket word here is σπυρίς, spyris (spoo-REES), a woven basket or hamper. Thayer's entry includes this verse. Matthew records four thousand men, besides women and children, before Jesus dismisses the crowd and leaves by boat.

The numbers differ from the feeding in chapter 14. Jesus will later recall both feedings distinctly in Matthew 16:9–10. Their similarity invites the disciples to remember what they have already seen and to trust Him as they serve another crowd.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as another account of Jesus' compassionate provision, with His disciples distributing what He gives. Wesley on Matthew 15:32–36 emphasizes the length of the crowd's stay and Jesus' thanksgiving for the food. The repeated provision shows His care continuing, even when the disciples still struggle to see how the people can be fed.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus later uses the two feedings to teach more than confidence that food can be supplied. In Matthew 16:5–12, the disciples think His warning about leaven concerns their missing bread. He reminds them of both crowds and their baskets of leftovers, then directs them to understand His warning about harmful teaching.

The signs are meant to help the disciples recognize who is with them and listen to what He is saying. Mark 8:14–21 likewise connects remembering both meals with their need for understanding. God's provision becomes part of their preparation to serve and teach faithfully, rather than an event to marvel at and then forget.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 16:1
passages.section_title: Testing Jesus with a Request for a Sign

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then the Pharisees and Sadducees came and tested Jesus by asking Him to show them a sign from heaven.
paragraphs: 1 Then the Pharisees and Sadducees came and tested Jesus by asking Him to show them a sign from heaven.

passages.context_html:
This verse opens a new confrontation after the feeding of four thousand. Pharisees and Sadducees come together to ask Jesus for a sign from heaven. Matthew identifies their purpose as testing Him, so the request must be read within that challenge.

Jesus' reply in verses 2–4 exposes their failure to recognize what is already before them and points to the sign of Jonah. The earlier conversation in Matthew 12:38–42 explains that reference through Jonah's experience, the Son of Man's coming death, and the call to respond.

The surrounding Gospel has already described Jesus teaching, healing, and feeding crowds. The question is therefore more than whether He has done anything that calls for attention. It concerns what these challengers will accept and how they are responding to Him.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the request as a challenge to Jesus' authority, with the following refusal exposing the challengers' resistance. Wesley's notes on Matthew 16:1–4 and the US Catholic bishops' notes on 16:1–4 read it within the demand for proof and the failure to recognize the Messiah's work.
passages.current_position_html: In Should We Seek Signs From God?, our discussion of this verse treats the demand for proof as an expression of unbelief in its immediate setting. The leaders are testing Jesus after His works have already given them reason to listen. The study calls us to receive what God has made known rather than build a habit of demanding further signs.

deeper_study.title: Should We Seek Signs From God?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
This demand is answered by pointing toward the death and resurrection that will stand at the center of the gospel (Matthew 12:40; 1 Corinthians 15:1–8). The significance of Jesus' work will be made known through those events and their witnesses.

John 20:30–31 also explains why Jesus' signs are recorded: to lead people to believe who He is and have life in His name. The Bible therefore gives signs a purpose within God's work. The challenge here is refusing that testimony while requiring another sign before responding.

passages.title: Matthew 16:1-4
passages.section_title: The Demand for Another Sign

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then the Pharisees and Sadducees came and tested Jesus by asking Him to show them a sign from heaven. 2 But He replied, “When evening comes, you say, ‘The weather will be fair, for the sky is red,’ 3 and in the morning, ‘Today it will be stormy, for the sky is red and overcast.’ You know how to interpret the appearance of the sky, but not the signs of the times. 4 A wicked and adulterous generation demands a sign, but none will be given it except the sign of Jonah.” Then He left them and went away.
paragraphs: 1 Then the Pharisees and Sadducees came and tested Jesus by asking Him to show them a sign from heaven. 2 But He replied, “When evening comes, you say, ‘The weather will be fair, for the sky is red,’ 3 and in the morning, ‘Today it will be stormy, for the sky is red and overcast.’ You know how to interpret the appearance of the sky, but not the signs of the times.
4 A wicked and adulterous generation demands a sign, but none will be given it except the sign of Jonah.” Then He left them and went away.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After Jesus feeds the four thousand and crosses the lake, Pharisees and Sadducees approach Him together. Matthew says they are testing Him by asking for a sign from heaven. This follows the earlier demand for a sign in chapter 12 and the healings and feedings already described.

The word for sign is σημεῖον, sēmeion (say-MAY-on), a sign or distinguishing mark. Thayer's entry includes its use for miracles that give evidence of a messenger's authority. Here the request asks Jesus to supply another demonstration on the challengers' terms.

Jesus compares their ability to read the sky with their failure to recognize the significance of the time in which they live. BibleHub's BSB footnote notes that several manuscripts omit the weather saying in verses 2–3. The BSB includes it in the text shown here.

He refuses the demand and points again to the sign of Jonah, then leaves them. In Matthew 12:38–42, He had already connected Jonah's experience with the Son of Man's coming passage through death and had called attention to the response His hearers should make.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a rebuke of resistant unbelief demanding more proof, while missing the significance of Jesus' work. Wesley on Matthew 16:3–4 emphasizes the failure to recognize the Messiah, and the US Catholic bishops' notes on 16:2–4 likewise connect the saying with failure to recognize the kingdom's arrival through His deeds and teaching.
passages.god_plan_html:
The sign of Jonah directs attention to the saving work Jesus will accomplish, rather than to an endless series of tests set by His opponents. Matthew 12:40 explicitly draws the connection with His coming death. Later in this chapter, He tells the disciples that He must suffer, be killed, and be raised on the third day (Matthew 16:21).

Paul places those events at the heart of the gospel in 1 Corinthians 15:1–8: Christ dies for sins, is buried, is raised, and appears to witnesses. God's answer reaches deeper than satisfying a demand for a display. The promised Savior gives His life and rises, and that good news is entrusted to people to receive and share.
passages.current_position_html: In Should We Seek Signs From God?, we understand this demand as resistance to believing what Jesus has already made known. The study distinguishes these challengers from someone sincerely seeking God's guidance. Our emphasis is on receiving His revealed truth rather than making faith depend on another demanded sign.

deeper_study.title: Should We Seek Signs From God?

passages.title: Matthew 16:5-12
passages.section_title: Learning to Recognize Harmful Teaching

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 When they crossed to the other side, the disciples forgot to take bread. 6 “Watch out!” Jesus told them. “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.” 7 They discussed this among themselves and concluded, “It is because we did not bring any bread.” 8 Aware of their conversation, Jesus said, “You of little faith, why are you debating among yourselves about having no bread? 9 Do you still not understand? Do you not remember the five loaves for the five thousand, and how many basketfuls you gathered? 10 Or the seven loaves for the four thousand, and how many basketfuls you gathered? 11 How do you not understand that I was not telling you about bread? But beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.” 12 Then they understood that He was not telling them to beware of the leaven used in bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees.
paragraphs: 5 When they crossed to the other side, the disciples forgot to take bread. 6 “Watch out!” Jesus told them. “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.” 7 They discussed this among themselves and concluded, “It is because we did not bring any bread.” 8 Aware of their conversation, Jesus said, “You of little faith, why are you debating among yourselves about having no bread?

9 Do you still not understand? Do you not remember the five loaves for the five thousand, and how many basketfuls you gathered? 10 Or the seven loaves for the four thousand, and how many basketfuls you gathered? 11 How do you not understand that I was not telling you about bread? But beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.” 12 Then they understood that He was not telling them to beware of the leaven used in bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
On the crossing, the disciples have forgotten to take bread. Jesus warns them about the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees, and they assume He is talking about their missing food. Their immediate concern prevents them from understanding the warning.

Leaven is ζύμη, zymē (DZOO-may), the yeast or ferment that works through dough. Thayer's entry explains its figurative use for an influence that spreads. Matthew gives the meaning here in verse 12: Jesus is warning about the groups' teaching.

Jesus calls their faith little and reminds them of both large feedings and the baskets left over. Remembering His provision should help them see that a shortage of bread is not the point of His warning. The events they have witnessed are meant to shape how they listen to Him now.

The passage ends with the disciples understanding. Mark 8:14–21 gives a related conversation that presses the same questions about seeing, hearing, and remembering. Jesus is training His followers to look beyond their immediate worry and recognize what is shaping their understanding.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a warning that harmful teaching can spread and that disciples need to understand Jesus rather than remain absorbed in immediate needs. Wesley on Matthew 16:6–11 explains leaven through the spread of false teaching, and the US Catholic bishops' notes on 16:7–12 likewise emphasize the disciples' misunderstanding and eventual recognition.
passages.god_plan_html:
The work of forming a faithful people includes guarding what they receive as truth. In Galatians 5:1–13, Paul warns about teaching that draws people away from the freedom given through Christ. He uses the same picture of a little leaven spreading through a whole batch.

That is a related use of the image, rather than a claim that Paul is addressing the identical group of teachers. He joins the warning with a positive purpose: faith expressing itself through love, and freedom used to serve others. Sound teaching matters because it shapes trust in Christ and the life His people share.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 16:13-20
passages.section_title: Peter's Confession and Jesus' Promise to Build His Church

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 When Jesus came to the region of Caesarea Philippi, He questioned His disciples: “Who do people say the Son of Man is?” 14 They replied, “Some say John the Baptist; others say Elijah; and still others, Jeremiah or one of the prophets.” 15 “But what about you?” Jesus asked. “Who do you say I am?” 16 Simon Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” 17 Jesus replied, “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah! For this was not revealed to you by flesh and blood, but by My Father in heaven. 18 And I tell you that you are Peter, and on this rock I will build My church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it. 19 I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven.” 20 Then He admonished the disciples not to tell anyone that He was the Christ.
paragraphs: 13 When Jesus came to the region of Caesarea Philippi, He questioned His disciples: “Who do people say the Son of Man is?” 14 They replied, “Some say John the Baptist; others say Elijah; and still others, Jeremiah or one of the prophets.” 15 “But what about you?” Jesus asked. “Who do you say I am?” 16 Simon Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” 17 Jesus replied, “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah! For this was not revealed to you by flesh and blood, but by My Father in heaven.

18 And I tell you that you are Peter, and on this rock I will build My church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it. 19 I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven.” 20 Then He admonished the disciples not to tell anyone that He was the Christ.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
In the region of Caesarea Philippi, Jesus asks what people are saying about the Son of Man. The disciples report several answers, each identifying Him with a prophet. He then asks them directly who they say He is. Peter answers that He is the Christ, the Son of the living God.

Christ is Χριστός, Christos (khris-TOSS), meaning anointed one. Thayer's entry identifies its use here as the title of the promised Messiah. Peter's answer moves beyond naming Jesus as another prophet. Jesus blesses him and identifies the Father as the source of this understanding.

Jesus then speaks of Peter and the rock on which He will build His church. Peter's name, Πέτρος, Petros (PET-ross), and the word πέτρα, petra (PET-rah), both belong to the language of rock or stone. Thayer's Peter entry and rock entry describe the wordplay and the different explanations readers give it. The difference in word forms does not by itself settle who or what the rock represents.

The word for church is ἐκκλησία, ekklēsia (ek-klay-SEE-ah), an assembly or gathered community. Thayer's entry includes its use for Christ's people as a whole in this verse. Jesus promises to build a people who belong to Him. Hades is ᾅδης, hadēs (HAH-days), the realm of the dead; Thayer's entry includes the gates image here. His promise reaches beyond the threats that could destroy an ordinary human gathering.

He gives Peter the keys of the kingdom and speaks of binding and loosing on earth and in heaven. Similar language will appear when He teaches about the community's handling of sin in Matthew 18:15–20. He then tells the disciples to keep His identity as the Christ private. The next passage begins His direct teaching about suffering, death, and resurrection, which Peter still struggles to accept.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians recognize Peter's confession and the promise that Jesus will build His church. They differ over the meaning of the rock, the authority given to Peter, and how that authority continues in the church.

The Catholic Church teaches that Peter, because of the faith he confesses, is the rock on which Christ builds His church. The Catechism, 552–553, connects the keys with governing, teaching, forgiveness, and discipline. Paragraphs 881–882 and the Second Vatican Council's Lumen Gentium, 22, understand Peter's pastoral office as continuing in the Pope, the Bishop of Rome, with the bishops continuing the other apostles' ministry.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, 25.6 and 30.1–2, rejects the Pope as head of the church and places the keys in the ministry and discipline exercised by church leaders under Christ. The 1689 Baptist Confession, 26.4 and 26.7–8, likewise rejects the Pope as head of the church, while emphasizing the authority Christ gives to local congregations and their appointed leaders. Explanations of the rock can still vary within these traditions.

Wesley on Matthew 16:18–19, reads the rock through the faith Peter professes, with Christ as the foundation. He recognizes Peter's early role in preaching to Jews and Gentiles while understanding the keys as shared by the apostles. The Methodist Articles of Religion, XIII and XVI, describe the visible church through its faithful people, preaching of God's word, and baptism and the Lord's Supper. Wesley's explanation of the rock is his commentary; these articles do not define that image.
passages.god_plan_html:
The building picture opens onto God's purpose of forming one people in Christ. 1 Peter 2:4–10 describes believers as living stones being built into a spiritual house, with Christ as the chosen cornerstone. Ephesians 2:11–22 places Jews and Gentiles together in God's household, built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ as the cornerstone. These related pictures show people being brought near to God and joined to one another through Him.

Peter's part in the spread of that message becomes visible in Acts. He preaches in Jerusalem (Acts 2:36–41), joins John among the Samaritans (Acts 8:14–17), and brings the gospel to Cornelius's household (Acts 10:34–48). Later he describes God choosing that the Gentiles should hear the gospel through him and receive the Spirit just as the Jewish believers did (Acts 15:7–11). Those accounts show the important service entrusted to Peter as God's mercy reaches new people.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 16:21
passages.section_title: Jesus Announces His Death and Resurrection

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 From that time on Jesus began to show His disciples that He must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things at the hands of the elders, chief priests, and scribes, and that He must be killed and on the third day be raised to life.
paragraphs: 21 From that time on Jesus began to show His disciples that He must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things at the hands of the elders, chief priests, and scribes, and that He must be killed and on the third day be raised to life.

passages.context_html:
This verse follows Peter's confession that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God. Jesus now begins explaining what lies ahead in Jerusalem: suffering, death, and resurrection on the third day. Matthew presents this as a necessary part of His mission.

The prediction names opposition from the elders, chief priests, and scribes. Peter's protest in the following verses shows how difficult this is for the disciples to accept. They must learn that recognizing the Messiah does not mean His path will match their expectations.

Resurrection is included in the announcement from the beginning. The verse should therefore be read as more than a warning of defeat or a statement about suffering alone. Jesus is preparing His followers for both His death and the life beyond it.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as Jesus plainly teaching that His messianic work includes suffering, death, and resurrection. Wesley on Matthew 16:21 emphasizes this new stage of the disciples' instruction, and the Catholic Catechism, 554, places the same announcement at the turning point after Peter's confession.
passages.current_position_html: In What Does Prayer Look Like?, we draw on this announcement when considering Jesus' later prayer in Gethsemane. He already knows the path before Him, yet its cost is real. The study emphasizes honest prayer governed by surrender to the Father's will. Knowing God's purpose does not make obedience painless.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The events announced here become the heart of the gospel proclaimed after Easter. 1 Corinthians 15:1–8 sets out Christ's death for sins, burial, resurrection on the third day, and appearances to witnesses. His death is saving work, and His resurrection belongs to the same good news.

In Luke 24:44–49, the risen Jesus connects these events with the message of repentance and forgiveness going to all nations, beginning in Jerusalem. The city where He will suffer also becomes the starting place for the message of His victory.

passages.title: Matthew 16:21-23
passages.section_title: The Messiah Must Suffer and Rise

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 From that time on Jesus began to show His disciples that He must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things at the hands of the elders, chief priests, and scribes, and that He must be killed and on the third day be raised to life. 22 Peter took Him aside and began to rebuke Him. “Far be it from You, Lord!” he said. “This shall never happen to You!” 23 But Jesus turned and said to Peter, “Get behind Me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to Me. For you do not have in mind the things of God, but the things of men.”
paragraphs: 21 From that time on Jesus began to show His disciples that He must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things at the hands of the elders, chief priests, and scribes, and that He must be killed and on the third day be raised to life.

22 Peter took Him aside and began to rebuke Him. “Far be it from You, Lord!” he said. “This shall never happen to You!” 23 But Jesus turned and said to Peter, “Get behind Me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to Me. For you do not have in mind the things of God, but the things of men.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Peter has just confessed Jesus as the Christ and heard His promise to build the church. Matthew now marks a new stage: Jesus begins to explain that He must go to Jerusalem, suffer at the hands of the leaders, be killed, and rise on the third day. Understanding His identity must include understanding this path.

Peter takes Him aside and rebukes Him, insisting that this must not happen. Jesus answers with a severe rebuke of His own. He calls Peter Satan and a stumbling block, then explains the problem: Peter is thinking in human terms rather than according to God's purpose.

Stumbling block is σκάνδαλον, skandalon (SKAN-dah-lon), a snare or something that causes a person to stumble. Thayer's entry includes Peter's action in this verse. The disciple who has spoken truly about Jesus is now trying to turn Him away from the road He says He must take.

The contrast is sharp. A correct confession does not mean Peter already understands everything the Messiah will do. Jesus continues teaching and correcting him. The call to deny oneself and follow in the next verses grows directly out of this encounter.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as Jesus preparing His disciples for the necessary suffering and resurrection of the Messiah, with Peter's objection opposing that purpose. Wesley on Matthew 16:21–23 emphasizes the danger of advice that would turn Jesus away from His saving work, while the Catholic Catechism, 554, likewise connects Peter's confession with the difficult revelation of the coming cross.
passages.god_plan_html:
After the resurrection, Jesus explains the same necessity from Scripture. In Luke 24:25–27, 44–49, He connects His suffering and resurrection with the Law, Prophets, and Psalms, then with repentance and forgiveness being proclaimed to all nations. What Peter wants to prevent is central to the saving message the disciples will carry.

Hebrews 2:14–18 explains why the Son shares our humanity and passes through death: He defeats the devil's hold through death, frees people enslaved by its fear, and makes atonement for sins. His suffering also belongs to His help for those who are tempted. God's purpose brings rescue through the costly path Jesus accepts.
passages.current_position_html: In What Does Prayer Look Like?, we draw on this announcement when considering Jesus' later prayer in Gethsemane. He already knows the path before Him, yet its cost is real. The study emphasizes honest prayer governed by surrender to the Father's will. Knowing God's purpose does not make obedience painless.

passages.title: Matthew 16:24-28
passages.section_title: Following Jesus When It Costs Your Life

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 24 Then Jesus told His disciples, “If anyone wants to come after Me, he must deny himself and take up his cross and follow Me. 25 For whoever wants to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for My sake will find it. 26 What will it profit a man if he gains the whole world, yet forfeits his soul? Or what can a man give in exchange for his soul? 27 For the Son of Man will come in His Father’s glory with His angels, and then He will repay each one according to what he has done. 28 Truly I tell you, some who are standing here will not taste death before they see the Son of Man coming in His kingdom.”
paragraphs: 24 Then Jesus told His disciples, “If anyone wants to come after Me, he must deny himself and take up his cross and follow Me. 25 For whoever wants to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for My sake will find it. 26 What will it profit a man if he gains the whole world, yet forfeits his soul? Or what can a man give in exchange for his soul?

27 For the Son of Man will come in His Father’s glory with His angels, and then He will repay each one according to what he has done. 28 Truly I tell you, some who are standing here will not taste death before they see the Son of Man coming in His kingdom.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After correcting Peter's opposition to the cross, Jesus addresses His disciples about following Him. They must deny themselves, take up their cross, and follow. The road He has just announced shapes the life of those who belong to Him.

The call reaches beyond giving up an occasional comfort. Jesus speaks of losing one's life for His sake and asks what the whole world could be worth if a person forfeits the soul. Allegiance to Him changes what is worth protecting and what can be surrendered.

The Greek word ψυχή, psychē (psoo-KHAY), appears in both the life and soul sayings. Thayer's entry includes life, the self, and the soul among its uses, and specifically connects verse 25 with the contrast between present life and life in God's kingdom. The repeated word ties the sayings together; the stakes reach beyond possessions or success.

Jesus then speaks of the Son of Man coming in the Father's glory and repaying each person according to what they have done. He also promises that some standing there will see Him coming in His kingdom before they die. The Greek word βασιλεία, basileia (bah-see-LAY-ah), can describe royal rule as well as a kingdom, according to Thayer's entry. Readers differ over which event shows that royal rule in verse 28.

The next scene, Matthew 17:1–9, comes six days later: Peter, James, and John see Jesus in glory on the mountain. Later the disciples also witness His resurrection and carry His message. The call to costly following is given alongside assurance that His glory and authority are real.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand this as a serious call to follow Jesus even when faithfulness costs deeply. Wesley on Matthew 16:24–27 connects self-denial with doing God's will and treats the warning about life as reaching into eternity. The Catholic Catechism, 618, likewise places the disciple's taking up the cross within sharing the path of Christ's self-giving.

Readers explain verse 28 in different ways. John Chrysostom's Homily 56 on Matthew connects it with the following Transfiguration: the disciples receive a glimpse of the glory Jesus has promised. The US Catholic bishops' note on Matthew 16:28 instead emphasizes His rule becoming visible after the resurrection.

Wesley's note on Matthew 16:28 connects it with the powerful growth of Christ's church and the judgment on Jerusalem. These explanations differ over the event in view, while recognizing a promise that some of Jesus' hearers will witness His kingly authority.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus connects His own self-giving and the disciple's path in John 12:23–28. He compares His coming death with a grain of wheat that dies and bears much fruit, then speaks of losing life in this world, following Him, and the Father's honor for His servant. God's saving work gives the pattern for a life of faithful service.

Hebrews 2:14–18 adds that His victory frees people held in slavery by the fear of death. The call to risk everything for Him rests on more than determination alone. The Savior has entered the danger and brings His people a hope that death cannot finally take away.

In 2 Peter 1:16–19, the mountain vision is remembered as eyewitness testimony to Jesus' majesty and as support for proclaiming His power and coming. His followers are given reason to trust the glory promised beyond suffering. They are called to live by that hope while they follow Him now.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 17:1-9
passages.section_title: Jesus Reveals His Glory on the Mountain

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 After six days Jesus took with Him Peter, James, and John the brother of James, and led them up a high mountain by themselves. 2 There He was transfigured before them. His face shone like the sun, and His clothes became as white as the light. 3 Suddenly Moses and Elijah appeared before them, talking with Jesus. 4 Peter said to Jesus, “Lord, it is good for us to be here. If You wish, I will put up three shelters—one for You, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.” 5 While Peter was still speaking, a bright cloud enveloped them, and a voice from the cloud said, “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to Him!” 6 When the disciples heard this, they fell facedown in terror. 7 Then Jesus came over and touched them. “Get up,” He said. “Do not be afraid.” 8 And when they looked up, they saw no one except Jesus. 9 As they were coming down the mountain, Jesus commanded them, “Do not tell anyone about this vision until the Son of Man has been raised from the dead.”
paragraphs: 1 After six days Jesus took with Him Peter, James, and John the brother of James, and led them up a high mountain by themselves. 2 There He was transfigured before them. His face shone like the sun, and His clothes became as white as the light. 3 Suddenly Moses and Elijah appeared before them, talking with Jesus.

4 Peter said to Jesus, “Lord, it is good for us to be here. If You wish, I will put up three shelters—one for You, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.” 5 While Peter was still speaking, a bright cloud enveloped them, and a voice from the cloud said, “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to Him!”

6 When the disciples heard this, they fell facedown in terror. 7 Then Jesus came over and touched them. “Get up,” He said. “Do not be afraid.” 8 And when they looked up, they saw no one except Jesus. 9 As they were coming down the mountain, Jesus commanded them, “Do not tell anyone about this vision until the Son of Man has been raised from the dead.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Six days after the conversation about His coming suffering and the cost of following Him, Jesus takes Peter, James, and John up a high mountain. His appearance changes before them: His face shines like the sun, and His clothes become white as light. Moses and Elijah appear and speak with Him.

The word translated transfigured is μεταμορφόω, metamorphoō (meh-tah-mor-FOH-oh), to change in form or appearance. Thayer's entry describes its use here for Jesus' appearance shining with divine brightness. The scene reveals His glory to disciples who are struggling to understand His coming death.

Peter offers to make three shelters, one for each of them. While he is still speaking, a bright cloud envelops the scene and the Father's voice identifies Jesus as His beloved Son and commands them to listen to Him. Mark 9:2–8 adds that Peter speaks amid fear, without knowing what else to say.

The disciples fall facedown in terror. Jesus touches them and tells them to get up without fear; when they look again, only He is there. On the descent, He tells them to keep the vision private until His resurrection. Glory and the coming cross remain connected throughout the account.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as a revelation of Jesus' divine glory that confirms His identity and calls the disciples to listen to Him. Wesley on Matthew 17:2–5 emphasizes the witness of Moses, Elijah, and the Father, while the Catholic Catechism, 555, likewise connects the glory with Peter's confession and the necessity of the cross.
passages.god_plan_html:
Luke 9:28–36 tells us what Moses and Elijah discuss: Jesus' departure, to be accomplished at Jerusalem. Departure is ἔξοδος, exodos (EK-soh-doss), according to Thayer's entry. This invites a comparison with God's earlier rescue at the Exodus. Exodus 12:23–28, 41–42 joins Passover deliverance with Israel's departure, and Paul explicitly identifies Christ as the Passover sacrifice in 1 Corinthians 5:7. Jesus' coming death belongs to God's work of rescuing His people.

The mountain, cloud, and glory recall God's meeting with Moses in Exodus 24:12–18. The command to listen also recalls the promised prophet in Deuteronomy 18:15–19, a promise Peter applies to Jesus in Acts 3:19–26. These are scriptural connections that place the disciples' response within the larger call to receive the One God sends.

2 Peter 1:16–19 later recalls the voice on the mountain as eyewitness testimony to Jesus' majesty, supporting the proclamation of His power and coming. The glimpse of glory gives His followers reason to trust Him as they face the difficult road ahead. The coming suffering does not cancel the glory God has revealed.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 17:10-13
passages.section_title: Elijah, John, and the Suffering Messiah

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 The disciples asked Him, “Why then do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?” 11 Jesus replied, “Elijah does indeed come, and he will restore all things. 12 But I tell you that Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him, but have done to him whatever they wished. In the same way, the Son of Man will suffer at their hands.” 13 Then the disciples understood that He was speaking to them about John the Baptist.
paragraphs: 10 The disciples asked Him, “Why then do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?” 11 Jesus replied, “Elijah does indeed come, and he will restore all things. 12 But I tell you that Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him, but have done to him whatever they wished. In the same way, the Son of Man will suffer at their hands.” 13 Then the disciples understood that He was speaking to them about John the Baptist.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After seeing Elijah on the mountain and hearing Jesus speak about resurrection, the disciples ask why the scribes say Elijah must come first. The question recalls Malachi 4:4–6, which promises Elijah before the Day of the Lord and speaks of hearts being turned toward one another.

Jesus affirms the expectation of Elijah and restoration, then says that Elijah has already come and has not been recognized. The disciples understand Him to mean John the Baptist. He also connects the treatment John received with the suffering the Son of Man will face.

Restore is ἀποκαθίστημι, apokathistēmi (ah-poh-kah-THIS-tay-mee), to bring something back to its proper state. Thayer's entry includes the restoration of a disturbed order in this verse. The surrounding Scriptures connect John's preparation with repentance and hearts turning back toward God.

John himself denies being Elijah when questioned in John 1:19–23. Luke 1:13–17 describes him as coming in Elijah's spirit and power to prepare a people for the Lord. Those passages help distinguish the prophetic role from a claim that John is personally Elijah returned.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly recognize Jesus' identification of John as the Elijah-like forerunner. The Catholic Catechism, 718–719, identifies John with the promised Elijah who prepares people for the Lord, and Wesley on Matthew 17:12 likewise understands John as fulfilling the role named by Malachi.

Some Christian writers also expect Elijah himself to return before Christ's coming in glory. Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho, 49, explains John's ministry in Elijah's spirit while also expecting Elijah before Christ's second coming. This shows a further expectation held by an early Christian writer; the shared recognition of John's role does not mean every reader explains the future expectation in the same way.
passages.god_plan_html:
John's task is to lead people toward the Messiah. In John 3:26–30, he distinguishes himself from the Christ and rejoices as people go to Jesus. His place in God's work is fulfilled by directing attention beyond himself. Jesus' words here show that the forerunner's rejection does not make his preparation meaningless.

The link between suffering and glory reaches through the prophetic story. 1 Peter 1:10–13 describes the prophets anticipating the Messiah's sufferings and the glories to follow, now announced in the gospel. Jesus is teaching the disciples to understand His path within that larger purpose, even when the herald has been rejected and the Messiah will suffer.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 17:14-20
passages.section_title: Jesus Rescues the Boy and Teaches About Faith

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 When they came to the crowd, a man came up to Jesus and knelt before Him. 15 “Lord, have mercy on my son,” he said. “He has seizures and is suffering terribly. He often falls into the fire or into the water. 16 I brought him to Your disciples, but they could not heal him.” 17 “O unbelieving and perverse generation!” Jesus replied. “How long must I remain with you? How long must I put up with you? Bring the boy here to Me.” 18 Then Jesus rebuked the demon, and it came out of the boy, and he was healed from that moment. 19 Afterward the disciples came to Jesus privately and asked, “Why couldn’t we drive it out?” 20 “Because you have so little faith,” He answered. “For truly I tell you, if you have faith the size of a mustard seed, you can say to this mountain, ‘Move from here to there,’ and it will move. Nothing will be impossible for you.”
paragraphs: 14 When they came to the crowd, a man came up to Jesus and knelt before Him. 15 “Lord, have mercy on my son,” he said. “He has seizures and is suffering terribly. He often falls into the fire or into the water. 16 I brought him to Your disciples, but they could not heal him.”

17 “O unbelieving and perverse generation!” Jesus replied. “How long must I remain with you? How long must I put up with you? Bring the boy here to Me.” 18 Then Jesus rebuked the demon, and it came out of the boy, and he was healed from that moment.

19 Afterward the disciples came to Jesus privately and asked, “Why couldn’t we drive it out?” 20 “Because you have so little faith,” He answered. “For truly I tell you, if you have faith the size of a mustard seed, you can say to this mountain, ‘Move from here to there,’ and it will move. Nothing will be impossible for you.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Returning to the crowd, Jesus meets a father who kneels and asks for mercy for his son. The boy suffers terribly and repeatedly falls into fire or water. The father has brought him to the disciples, but they have been unable to heal him.

Jesus rebukes the generation's unbelief, calls for the boy, and drives out the demon. The boy is healed at once. Mark 9:14–29 gives more of the conversation: the father acknowledges both belief and unbelief, asks for help, and receives it from Jesus.

The disciples ask privately why they could not drive the demon out. Jesus points to their little faith and speaks of mustard-seed faith moving a mountain. Faith is πίστις, pistis (PIS-tiss), belief or trust. Thayer's entry includes trust in God and confidence in Christ among its uses. The disciples need to rely on the One whose authority they have been given.

The small seed and the mountain put a great contrast before them. What seems beyond their power is within God's power. In Mark's account, Jesus also directs them toward prayer. BibleHub's BSB footnote places the prayer-and-fasting saying numbered verse 21 in the manuscript note rather than the main text; Mark 9:29 includes prayer in its main text.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a lesson in relying on God's power rather than assuming spiritual authority works independently of Him. Wesley on Matthew 17:20 understands the faith in view as confidence that God will work through someone in that moment, and the US Catholic bishops' note on 17:14–20 likewise emphasizes the disciples' need for faith.
passages.god_plan_html:
The Son's authority over evil belongs within the purpose described in 1 John 3:8: He appears to destroy the devil's works. The rescue of this suffering boy is a concrete display of that authority. Jesus brings help where the disciples have been unable to do so.

Luke 10:17–20 places the disciples' service within the same larger struggle. The returning messengers rejoice that demons submit in Jesus' name, but He directs their deepest joy toward belonging to God, with their names recorded in heaven. The purpose of their mission reaches beyond experiencing power to sharing the Savior's work and life with Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 17:22-23
passages.section_title: Jesus Again Announces His Death and Resurrection

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 When they gathered together in Galilee, Jesus told them, “The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men. 23 They will kill Him, and on the third day He will be raised to life.” And the disciples were deeply grieved.
paragraphs: 22 When they gathered together in Galilee, Jesus told them, “The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men. 23 They will kill Him, and on the third day He will be raised to life.” And the disciples were deeply grieved.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Gathered in Galilee, the disciples again hear Jesus say that the Son of Man will be delivered into human hands, killed, and raised on the third day. This follows the announcement in chapter 16 and the mountain conversation about His resurrection. He continues preparing them for what is coming.

The word for delivered is παραδίδωμι, paradidōmi (pah-rah-DID-oh-mee), to hand over or give into another's power. Thayer's entry includes this verse. Jesus describes the danger ahead plainly, while also naming resurrection as part of the same coming events.

Matthew records the disciples' deep grief. The related account in Mark 9:30–32 also describes their lack of understanding and fear of asking Him. Hearing the prediction is not yet the same as understanding how death and resurrection belong within His mission.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as Jesus repeating the necessary preparation for His suffering, death, and resurrection. Wesley on Matthew 16:21 describes the disciples learning that the Messiah enters glory through suffering, while the Catholic Catechism, 554, likewise places that difficult announcement at the heart of their instruction.
passages.god_plan_html:
Peter later proclaims that Jesus' death happened within God's purpose while those who put Him to death were responsible for their actions (Acts 2:22–24). He also announces that God raised Him. The suffering the disciples now grieve over will become central to the message they bring.

Romans 4:23–25 connects Jesus being delivered to death with our sins, and His resurrection with our being put right with God. The prediction is therefore more than advance information about a tragedy. It points toward the saving work through which God brings people to faith and life.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 17:24-27
passages.section_title: The Son Pays the Temple Contribution

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 24 After they had arrived in Capernaum, the collectors of the two-drachma tax came to Peter and asked, “Does your Teacher pay the two drachmas?” 25 “Yes,” he answered. When Peter entered the house, Jesus preempted him. “What do you think, Simon?” He asked. “From whom do the kings of the earth collect customs and taxes: from their own sons, or from others?” 26 “From others,” Peter answered. “Then the sons are exempt,” Jesus said to him. 27 “But so that we may not offend them, go to the sea, cast a hook, and take the first fish you catch. When you open its mouth, you will find a four-drachma coin. Take it and give it to them for My tax and yours.”
paragraphs: 24 After they had arrived in Capernaum, the collectors of the two-drachma tax came to Peter and asked, “Does your Teacher pay the two drachmas?” 25 “Yes,” he answered. When Peter entered the house, Jesus preempted him. “What do you think, Simon?” He asked. “From whom do the kings of the earth collect customs and taxes: from their own sons, or from others?” 26 “From others,” Peter answered. “Then the sons are exempt,” Jesus said to him.

27 “But so that we may not offend them, go to the sea, cast a hook, and take the first fish you catch. When you open its mouth, you will find a four-drachma coin. Take it and give it to them for My tax and yours.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
In Capernaum, collectors ask Peter whether his teacher pays the two-drachma contribution, and Peter says yes. This is the payment associated with the Jerusalem temple. The historian Josephus, Jewish War 7.6.6, later recalls the annual two-drachma amount that had been paid to the temple.

A two-drachma coin is δίδραχμον, didrachmon (dee-DRAKH-mon), according to Thayer's entry. Exodus 30:11–16 provides the earlier half-shekel contribution for the sanctuary in connection with a census. That command gives the scriptural background for the temple contribution.

When Peter enters the house, Jesus speaks first. He asks whether kings collect taxes from their own sons or from others. Peter answers that they collect from others, and Jesus declares the sons free. The family comparison brings His sonship into the question of supporting His Father's house.

Jesus nevertheless chooses to avoid giving offense. He tells Peter to catch a fish and take the coin he will find in its mouth to pay for them both. The coin is a στατήρ, statēr (stah-TARE), which Thayer's entry identifies here with four drachmas, enough for two contributions. The scene ends with Jesus' instruction and promised provision.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly see both Jesus' freedom as the Son and His willingness to pay for the sake of others. Wesley on Matthew 17:26–27 emphasizes the Son's relation to His Father's house and choosing peace and love, while the US Catholic bishops' notes on 17:26–27 likewise connect the freedom of the sons with the decision to avoid offense.
passages.god_plan_html:
The language of the Son and His Father's family belongs within the wider gospel story. Galatians 4:4–7 describes God sending His Son, born under the law, to redeem those under it so that they receive adoption. The Son's work brings others into the family, with His Spirit teaching them to call God Father.

Freedom can also be used to serve. In 1 Corinthians 9:19–23, Paul describes setting aside rights and adapting his conduct for the sake of reaching people with the gospel. That is a related example of freedom shaped by love and God's saving purpose, rather than a demand to insist on every right.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 18:1-5
passages.section_title: Greatness Begins with Humility

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 At that time the disciples came to Jesus and asked, “Who then is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven?” 2 Jesus invited a little child to stand among them. 3 “Truly I tell you,” He said, “unless you change and become like little children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven. 4 Therefore, whoever humbles himself like this little child is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven. 5 And whoever welcomes a little child like this in My name welcomes Me.
paragraphs: 1 At that time the disciples came to Jesus and asked, “Who then is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven?” 2 Jesus invited a little child to stand among them.

3 “Truly I tell you,” He said, “unless you change and become like little children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven. 4 Therefore, whoever humbles himself like this little child is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven. 5 And whoever welcomes a little child like this in My name welcomes Me.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
