section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The disciples ask who is greatest in the kingdom of heaven. Jesus has recently told them that He will be killed and raised, yet they are concerned about greatness. Mark 9:33–37 describes their discussion on the road and Jesus' answer: the person who wants to be first must become a servant to everyone.

Jesus brings a little child among them. Before answering who is greatest, He tells them they must change and become like children even to enter the kingdom. Verse 4 explains the comparison: they must humble themselves. The word is ταπεινόω, tapeinoō (tah-pay-noh-OH), to bring low or humble. Thayer's entry describes its use here as setting aside pride and behaving without self-importance.

Jesus then joins humility to welcome. Receiving a child like this in His name means receiving Him. The disciples' question about their own importance leads to a lesson about how they receive someone else. The warnings that follow show how seriously He takes the treatment of those who believe in Him.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the child as a lesson in humility and dependence on God. Wesley on 18:3–6 emphasizes a humble heart that relies on the Father and welcomes those dear to Christ; the US Catholic bishops' notes on 18:3–5 likewise emphasize dependence and trust.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus will Himself live out the humble service He teaches. Philippians 2:3–11 calls believers to consider others and then points to Christ: He took the form of a servant, humbled Himself to death on a cross, and was exalted by God. His way of bringing salvation also shapes the life of the people He saves.

Hebrews 2:9–11 makes the larger purpose clear. Jesus suffers death by God's grace as He brings many sons to glory, and He calls those He makes holy His brothers. The kingdom's greatness grows out of the Savior's self-giving love. Learning to serve others joins the disciples' daily conduct to His mission.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 18:6-9
passages.section_title: Take Seriously What Leads People into Sin

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 But if anyone causes one of these little ones who believe in Me to stumble, it would be better for him to have a large millstone hung around his neck and to be drowned in the depths of the sea. 7 Woe to the world for the causes of sin. These stumbling blocks must come, but woe to the man through whom they come! 8 If your hand or your foot causes you to sin, cut it off and throw it away. It is better for you to enter life crippled or lame than to have two hands and two feet and be thrown into the eternal fire. 9 And if your eye causes you to sin, gouge it out and throw it away. It is better for you to enter life with one eye than to have two eyes and be thrown into the fire of hell.
paragraphs: 6 But if anyone causes one of these little ones who believe in Me to stumble, it would be better for him to have a large millstone hung around his neck and to be drowned in the depths of the sea. 7 Woe to the world for the causes of sin. These stumbling blocks must come, but woe to the man through whom they come!

8 If your hand or your foot causes you to sin, cut it off and throw it away. It is better for you to enter life crippled or lame than to have two hands and two feet and be thrown into the eternal fire. 9 And if your eye causes you to sin, gouge it out and throw it away. It is better for you to enter life with one eye than to have two eyes and be thrown into the fire of hell.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus has just spoken about welcoming a child in His name. He now warns against causing one of the little ones who believe in Him to stumble. The concern includes His followers, whose faith must be cared for. His picture of a millstone and the sea shows the terrible seriousness of harming them.

The verb is σκανδαλίζω, skandalizō (skan-dah-LEE-zoh). Thayer's entry explains the picture of putting something in another's path that makes them fall, including leading someone into sin. Here the issue reaches deeper than upsetting someone's feelings: their walk with God is being harmed.

Jesus also turns the warning toward what leads the disciples themselves into sin. The hand, foot, and eye make His words personal. Even something as precious or useful as these must be given up if it draws someone away from God. The contrast between entering life and being thrown into fire gives the warning its weight.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these strong pictures as a call to remove what leads into sin, rather than instructions to injure the body. Wesley on 18:5–9 applies them to whatever hinders someone's walk with God, while the US Catholic bishops' notes on 18:6–9 distinguish the harm done to another disciple from the danger of one's own sin.
passages.god_plan_html:
Care for another believer belongs to the work Christ died to accomplish. In Romans 14:13–19, Paul tells Christians to stop placing obstacles in a brother's way and reminds them that Christ died for that person. He then directs them toward peace and helping one another grow.

That gives the disciples' responsibility a larger setting. Someone they might dismiss or lead astray matters to the Savior who gave His life. Life together in God's kingdom calls them to use their influence to help that person continue in faith.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 18:10
passages.section_title: Do Not Look Down on the Little Ones

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 See that you do not look down on any of these little ones. For I tell you that their angels in heaven always see the face of My Father in heaven.
paragraphs: 10 See that you do not look down on any of these little ones. For I tell you that their angels in heaven always see the face of My Father in heaven.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After warning against leading His followers into sin, Jesus warns against looking down on any of them. The little ones belong to the same conversation that began with a child and continued with those who believe in Him. Their apparent importance to other people does not measure their worth before God.

Jesus says their angels in heaven always see His Father's face. His point gives the disciples a reason to treat these people with care: they have heavenly attention even when others overlook them. Hebrews 1:14 also describes angels as spirits sent to serve those who will inherit salvation.

The shepherd's search in verses 12–14 carries this concern forward. BibleHub's BSB footnote places the saying numbered verse 11 about the Son of Man saving the lost in the manuscript note, rather than in the main text. That is why the next passage begins at verse 12.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly see this as a reason to value even the least noticed believer and to trust God's care through His angels. The Catholic Catechism, 336, describes an angel's protection and guidance beside each believer, while Wesley on 18:10 emphasizes the angels' care for even the weakest believer.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 18:12-14
passages.section_title: The Father Cares About the One Who Strays

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 What do you think? If a man has a hundred sheep and one of them goes astray, will he not leave the ninety-nine on the hills and go out to search for the one that is lost? 13 And if he finds it, truly I tell you, he rejoices more over that one sheep than over the ninety-nine that did not go astray. 14 In the same way, your Father in heaven is not willing that any of these little ones should perish.
paragraphs: 12 What do you think? If a man has a hundred sheep and one of them goes astray, will he not leave the ninety-nine on the hills and go out to search for the one that is lost? 13 And if he finds it, truly I tell you, he rejoices more over that one sheep than over the ninety-nine that did not go astray. 14 In the same way, your Father in heaven is not willing that any of these little ones should perish.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus has told His disciples not to look down on any of the little ones. He now asks them to picture a shepherd with a hundred sheep. One wanders, and the shepherd leaves the ninety-nine to search for it. If he finds it, that return brings him particular joy.

Verse 14 explains the comparison through the Father's concern that none of these little ones perish. The one who has wandered still matters. The disciples are being taught to share that concern, and the next passage shows them how to seek the restoration of a brother who sins.

Luke 15:1–7 also tells a lost-sheep parable, in the setting of Jesus welcoming sinners. Here in Matthew, the surrounding teaching especially directs the disciples toward care for one another.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read the shepherd's search as an expression of God's care and a pattern for seeking those who stray. Wesley on 18:14 stresses that the Father does not despise the least of them; the US Catholic bishops' note on 18:10–14 applies the story to bringing wandering disciples back to the community.
passages.god_plan_html:
The searching shepherd is part of a larger biblical picture. In Ezekiel 34:11–16, God promises to search for His scattered flock, rescue them, bring back the strays, and strengthen the weak. The parallel helps explain the Father's concern in Jesus' story: the lost are sought and cared for.

Jesus takes that care further in John 10:11–18, where He calls Himself the good shepherd and says He lays down His life for the sheep. He also speaks of bringing other sheep into one flock under one shepherd. God's saving purpose gathers people to the Shepherd who gives His life for them; the disciples learn to care for the people He gathers.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 18:15-20
passages.section_title: Seeking Restoration Together in Jesus’ Name

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 If your brother sins against you, go and confront him privately. If he listens to you, you have won your brother over. 16 But if he will not listen, take one or two others along, so that ‘every matter may be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses.’ 17 If he refuses to listen to them, tell it to the church. And if he refuses to listen even to the church, regard him as you would a pagan or a tax collector. 18 Truly I tell you, whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven. 19 Again, I tell you truly that if two of you on the earth agree about anything you ask for, it will be done for you by My Father in heaven. 20 For where two or three gather together in My name, there am I with them.”
paragraphs: 15 If your brother sins against you, go and confront him privately. If he listens to you, you have won your brother over. 16 But if he will not listen, take one or two others along, so that ‘every matter may be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses.’ 17 If he refuses to listen to them, tell it to the church. And if he refuses to listen even to the church, regard him as you would a pagan or a tax collector.

18 Truly I tell you, whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven. 19 Again, I tell you truly that if two of you on the earth agree about anything you ask for, it will be done for you by My Father in heaven. 20 For where two or three gather together in My name, there am I with them.”

passages.context_html:
The shepherd's search for a stray is followed by instructions about a brother who sins. Jesus begins with a private conversation, aiming to win the brother over. If he will not listen, one or two others come along; if he still refuses, the matter goes before the church. Continued refusal changes how the community relates to him.

The witnesses come from Deuteronomy 19:15, where a charge must be established by more than one person's testimony. The surrounding law also requires careful investigation of false accusations. Jesus' instructions give a path for addressing sin with the aim of gaining a brother.

Church here is ἐκκλησία, ekklēsia (ek-klay-SEE-ah), an assembly or gathered community. Thayer's entry includes this verse among its uses for a local company of Christ's followers. The matter is brought to people who share life together.

Jesus connects the decisions described as binding and loosing with heaven, then speaks about agreement in asking and His presence among two or three gathered in His name. These sayings follow the steps involving witnesses and the community. Peter's question about forgiveness in verse 21 continues the concern with restoring relationships.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the process as correction that seeks restoration, with exclusion from fellowship as the final step when someone refuses to listen. Traditions differ over how the church exercises the authority Jesus describes.

The Catholic Church connects binding and loosing with the apostles' authority to reconcile sinners with both God and the Church, expressed in the sacrament of Penance and Reconciliation (Catechism, 1440–1449). The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 30, assigns church officers responsibility for correction, suspension, and exclusion, with bringing the person back among its purposes. The 1689 Baptist Confession, 26.7–8, places authority for worship and discipline in each gathered church, with its officers and members.

There is also a difference over the reach of verses 19–20. Some readers keep them closely within the work of correction and restoration. Wesley on 18:18–20 extends them to united prayer and worship more generally, and the US Catholic bishops' notes on 18:19–20 likewise favor a broader prayer setting. These are readings of the passage, rather than a single interpretation shared by every Christian.
passages.current_position_html:
Prayer and Faith reads these verses within Jesus' instructions about church discipline and restoration. The two-or-three language belongs to the witnesses and the gathered community seeking to act faithfully in His name. His presence supports that work.

The study therefore understands verses 19–20 as assurance within that setting. Agreement between people does not turn their wishes into God's will or provide a formula for guaranteed prayer results. The fuller reasoning appears in Prayer and Faith.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The work of restoration continues in the life of the church. Galatians 6:1–2 directs believers to restore someone caught in sin gently, watching themselves and carrying one another's burdens. Helping a brother return requires humility from those doing the helping.

2 Corinthians 2:5–11 shows the other side of correction: Paul urges the community to forgive, comfort, and reaffirm love when punishment has been sufficient, so the person is not overwhelmed by sorrow. Together these passages show how care for the flock includes both taking sin seriously and making room for restoration.

passages.title: Matthew 18:19-20
passages.section_title: Agreement and Jesus’ Presence in the Community

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 Again, I tell you truly that if two of you on the earth agree about anything you ask for, it will be done for you by My Father in heaven. 20 For where two or three gather together in My name, there am I with them.”
paragraphs: 19 Again, I tell you truly that if two of you on the earth agree about anything you ask for, it will be done for you by My Father in heaven. 20 For where two or three gather together in My name, there am I with them.”

passages.context_html:
These words come at the end of Jesus' instructions about a brother who sins. In verses 15–18, He has described private correction, one or two witnesses, bringing the matter to the church, and binding and loosing. The repeated two-or-three language connects this assurance with the community's difficult work of seeking restoration.

Jesus speaks of agreement in what His followers ask and of His presence when they gather in His name. The surrounding teaching joins prayer, responsibility, and care for one another. Peter then asks how often to forgive a brother who sins against him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Readers differ over how closely to limit these sayings to church correction. One reading keeps the two or three with the witnesses and decisions in verses 15–18, seeing Jesus reassure those seeking restoration in His name.

Wesley on 18:18–20 understands the promise to include united prayers beyond intercession for someone being restored, and applies Jesus' presence to worship. The US Catholic bishops' notes on 18:19–20 also favor a broader prayer setting because the language about asking is so general. These sources differ over the immediate scope; neither reading requires Jesus to be absent whenever a believer is alone.
passages.current_position_html:
Prayer and Faith understands this assurance within the correction and restoration described in verses 15–18. Agreement refers to the gathered community's work in that setting, and Jesus is present as it acts faithfully in His name.

The study does not treat agreement as a way to guarantee whatever two people request. Their agreement does not make a request God's will. See Prayer and Faith for the full explanation.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus' presence with His people reaches into the church's whole mission. At the end of Matthew, He sends the disciples to make disciples of all nations and promises to remain with them (Matthew 28:18–20). The community that must undertake difficult restoration is also sent to bring His teaching to others.

Ephesians 2:18–22 describes believers together as God's household and a dwelling for God through His Spirit. His people are being brought into shared life around Christ. Their gathering and care for one another belong within that purpose.

passages.title: Matthew 18:21-35
passages.section_title: Forgive from the Heart

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 Then Peter came to Jesus and asked, “Lord, how many times shall I forgive my brother who sins against me? Up to seven times?” 22 Jesus answered, “I tell you, not just seven times, but seventy-seven times! 23 Because of this, the kingdom of heaven is like a king who wanted to settle accounts with his servants. 24 As he began the settlements, a debtor owing ten thousand talents was brought to him. 25 Since the man was unable to pay, the master ordered that he be sold to pay his debt, along with his wife and children and everything he owned. 26 Then the servant fell on his knees before him. ‘Have patience with me,’ he begged, ‘and I will pay back everything.’ 27 His master had compassion on him, forgave his debt, and released him. 28 But when that servant went out, he found one of his fellow servants who owed him a hundred denarii. He grabbed him and began to choke him, saying, ‘Pay back what you owe me!’ 29 So his fellow servant fell down and begged him, ‘Have patience with me, and I will pay you back.’ 30 But he refused. Instead, he went and had the man thrown into prison until he could pay his debt. 31 When his fellow servants saw what had happened, they were greatly distressed, and they went and recounted all of this to their master. 32 Then the master summoned him and said, ‘You wicked servant! I forgave all your debt because you begged me. 33 Shouldn’t you have had mercy on your fellow servant, just as I had on you?’ 34 In anger his master turned him over to the jailers to be tortured, until he should repay all that he owed. 35 That is how My heavenly Father will treat each of you unless you forgive your brother from your heart.”
paragraphs: 21 Then Peter came to Jesus and asked, “Lord, how many times shall I forgive my brother who sins against me? Up to seven times?” 22 Jesus answered, “I tell you, not just seven times, but seventy-seven times!

23 Because of this, the kingdom of heaven is like a king who wanted to settle accounts with his servants. 24 As he began the settlements, a debtor owing ten thousand talents was brought to him. 25 Since the man was unable to pay, the master ordered that he be sold to pay his debt, along with his wife and children and everything he owned. 26 Then the servant fell on his knees before him. ‘Have patience with me,’ he begged, ‘and I will pay back everything.’ 27 His master had compassion on him, forgave his debt, and released him.

28 But when that servant went out, he found one of his fellow servants who owed him a hundred denarii. He grabbed him and began to choke him, saying, ‘Pay back what you owe me!’ 29 So his fellow servant fell down and begged him, ‘Have patience with me, and I will pay you back.’ 30 But he refused. Instead, he went and had the man thrown into prison until he could pay his debt. 31 When his fellow servants saw what had happened, they were greatly distressed, and they went and recounted all of this to their master.

32 Then the master summoned him and said, ‘You wicked servant! I forgave all your debt because you begged me. 33 Shouldn’t you have had mercy on your fellow servant, just as I had on you?’ 34 In anger his master turned him over to the jailers to be tortured, until he should repay all that he owed. 35 That is how My heavenly Father will treat each of you unless you forgive your brother from your heart.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the instructions about restoring a brother, Peter asks how often he must forgive one who sins against him. He suggests seven times. Jesus answers with seventy-seven in the BSB; its footnote gives seventy times seven as another translation. The story that follows moves the question beyond keeping a count.

A servant owes his king ten thousand talents and cannot pay. The king first orders the sale of the servant, his family, and his possessions, but then responds to his plea with compassion and cancels the debt. The BSB footnotes describe one talent as about twenty years' wages for a laborer and a denarius as a usual day's wage. The difference between this debt and the hundred denarii owed by a fellow servant is enormous.

The forgiven servant seizes and chokes his fellow servant, refuses his plea for patience, and has him imprisoned. When the king hears about it, he calls the servant back. He had received mercy and was expected to show mercy. Instead, the king turns him over to punishment until the debt is paid. Jesus closes with a warning about forgiving a brother from the heart.

Forgive is ἀφίημι, aphiēmi (ah-FEE-ay-mee). Thayer's entry includes releasing a debt and forgiving wrongdoing, using examples from this parable. The canceled debt gives a concrete picture of the mercy the servant received and then refused to extend.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly see the enormous forgiven debt as a picture of God's mercy and the servant's conduct as a warning against withholding mercy from others. The call is to wholehearted forgiveness rather than stopping after a fixed number. Traditions differ over how the closing judgment relates to salvation.

The US Catholic bishops' notes on 18:34–35 understand it as a warning that forgiveness can be withdrawn at final judgment. Catholic teaching also describes grave sin after baptism as a loss of grace that calls for reconciliation (Catechism, 1446). Wesley on 18:34–35 reads the servant's pardon as genuinely withdrawn. The Methodist Articles, XII, likewise allow for departing from grace and affirm restoration through repentance.

Reformed churches following the Westminster Confession, 17.1–3, and Baptists following the 1689 Confession, 17.1–3, understand those truly saved as continuing in faith to the end. They also teach that serious sin brings God's displeasure and judgment in this life. Within that understanding, the warning calls professing believers to repentance and mercy; it does not mean that God finally abandons someone He has truly saved.
passages.god_plan_html:
God's forgiveness comes through the work of Christ. Colossians 2:13–14 describes God making people alive with Christ, forgiving their sins, and canceling the debt that stood against them through the cross. That gives the parable's picture of canceled debt a clear connection with the gospel.

The mercy received is meant to shape the family God is forming. Ephesians 4:31–32 joins the removal of bitterness and malice with forgiving as God forgave in Christ. Colossians 3:12–15 connects the same forgiveness with compassion, patience, love, and peace among members of one body. God's saving mercy bears fruit in how His people live together.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 19:1-9
passages.section_title: Marriage, Divorce, and the Creator’s Purpose

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 When Jesus had finished saying these things, He left Galilee and went into the region of Judea beyond the Jordan. 2 Large crowds followed Him, and He healed them there. 3 Then some Pharisees came and tested Him by asking, “Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any reason?” 4 Jesus answered, “Have you not read that from the beginning the Creator ‘made them male and female,’ 5 and said, ‘For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and the two will become one flesh’? 6 So they are no longer two, but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together, let man not separate.” 7 “Why then,” they asked, “did Moses order a man to give his wife a certificate of divorce and send her away?” 8 Jesus replied, “Moses permitted you to divorce your wives because of your hardness of heart. But it was not this way from the beginning. 9 Now I tell you that whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another woman commits adultery.”
paragraphs: 1 When Jesus had finished saying these things, He left Galilee and went into the region of Judea beyond the Jordan. 2 Large crowds followed Him, and He healed them there. 3 Then some Pharisees came and tested Him by asking, “Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any reason?”

4 Jesus answered, “Have you not read that from the beginning the Creator ‘made them male and female,’ 5 and said, ‘For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and the two will become one flesh’? 6 So they are no longer two, but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together, let man not separate.”

7 “Why then,” they asked, “did Moses order a man to give his wife a certificate of divorce and send her away?” 8 Jesus replied, “Moses permitted you to divorce your wives because of your hardness of heart. But it was not this way from the beginning. 9 Now I tell you that whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another woman commits adultery.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus leaves Galilee and goes to the region beyond the Jordan, followed by crowds whom He heals. Some Pharisees test Him with a question: may a man divorce his wife for any reason? Jesus answers by taking them back to the creation of man and woman and their union as one flesh.

His answer brings together Genesis 1:27 and Genesis 2:24. Marriage belongs within the Creator's purpose. Jesus says that people must not separate what God has joined.

The Pharisees appeal to Moses' certificate of divorce. Deuteronomy 24:1–4 describes a divorced woman who marries again and forbids her first husband from taking her back after that second marriage ends. Jesus distinguishes permission because of hard hearts from God's purpose at the beginning.

The question about any reason also has a background in Jewish discussion of divorce. Mishnah Gittin 9:10 records different readings: the school of Shammai requires sexual indecency, while the school of Hillel allows divorce even over a spoiled meal. Those recorded positions help explain why the grounds for divorce could be disputed.

Jesus' warning about remarriage includes an exception for sexual immorality. The Greek word is πορνεία, porneia (por-NAY-ah). Thayer's entry gives the broad sense of unlawful sexual relations and includes adultery among its uses. Christians differ over the particular situation meant here and how the exception applies.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians agree that Jesus calls for faithfulness in marriage. They differ over the meaning of the exception and the circumstances in which divorce or remarriage can be accepted.

The Catholic Church teaches that a valid marriage between baptized spouses cannot be ended by human power once they have had marital relations. Its Catechism, 2382–2386, distinguishes that bond from separation or a civil divorce needed to protect rights or children. The US Catholic bishops' notes on Matthew 19:9 and 5:31–32 read the exception as concerning an unlawful union, such as a marriage between prohibited relatives, rather than the ending of a lawful marriage.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, 24.5–6, permits an innocent spouse to divorce and remarry after adultery. It also recognizes deliberate desertion that neither church nor civil authority can remedy as grounds for ending the marriage. This reading considers Matthew's exception alongside 1 Corinthians 7:10–16.

The Orthodox Church in America's Holy Synod guidelines, section F, uphold lifelong marriage while allowing a bishop to consider a later marriage after civil divorce, with repentance and care for those affected. The United Methodist Church's Social Principles, Marriage: Divorce, recognize divorce as sometimes necessary when a marriage becomes destructive or cannot be repaired, and do not rule out remarriage. They also state that faithfulness does not require remaining in an abusive relationship. These are the stated approaches of those churches.

Some individual teachers take a stricter reading of remarriage than their own wider tradition. John Piper's personal position paper understands Matthew's exception as sexual unfaithfulness during betrothal, connecting it with Joseph's contemplated divorce in Matthew 1. He distinguishes that reading from his church's official position. This is his personal reading, which differs from other Baptist readings.
passages.god_plan_html:
The one-flesh passage Jesus uses also helps explain Christ's love for His people. In Ephesians 5:25–33, Paul repeats Genesis 2:24 and explicitly connects it with Christ and the church. Christ gives Himself for her, makes her holy, and cares for her as His own body.

Marriage can therefore display the faithful, self-giving care at the heart of God's saving work. Jesus' return to the Creator's purpose asks people to take that relationship seriously. Paul's connection adds depth to its meaning by showing the love with which the Savior gathers and cares for His people.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 19:10-12
passages.section_title: Singleness for the Kingdom

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 His disciples said to Him, “If this is the case between a man and his wife, it is better not to marry.” 11 “Not everyone can accept this word,” He replied, “but only those to whom it has been given. 12 For there are eunuchs who were born that way; others were made that way by men; and still others live like eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. The one who can accept this should accept it.”
paragraphs: 10 His disciples said to Him, “If this is the case between a man and his wife, it is better not to marry.” 11 “Not everyone can accept this word,” He replied, “but only those to whom it has been given. 12 For there are eunuchs who were born that way; others were made that way by men; and still others live like eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. The one who can accept this should accept it.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The disciples respond to Jesus' teaching about marriage by saying that it is better not to marry. Jesus says that not everyone can accept this, but only those to whom it is given. He then describes people who do not enter ordinary married life for different reasons.

The word eunuch is εὐνοῦχος, eunouchos (yoo-NOO-khos). Thayer's entry distinguishes its uses in this verse: a condition from birth, being made a eunuch by others, and voluntarily abstaining from marriage. Jesus includes people who live this way for the kingdom of heaven.

His final invitation is addressed to the person who can accept it. The teaching makes room for a life devoted to the kingdom through singleness alongside the seriousness of marriage He has just explained.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the final example as willingly remaining unmarried to serve God's kingdom. Wesley on 19:11–12 describes a gift for serving God without the distractions of marriage, and the Catholic Catechism, 1618–1620, likewise describes a call to follow Christ in this way while affirming marriage's goodness.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Corinthians 7:7–9, 32–35 explains how different gifts can serve the same Lord. Paul values the freedom an unmarried person has to attend to the Lord's work, while also recognizing marriage. His aim is undivided devotion to God.

God's family includes people whose lives take different forms. Ephesians 2:18–22 describes believers together as His household, built around Christ and joined by the Spirit. A person's place in that family rests in Christ, and both married and unmarried believers share in its life and service.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 19:13-15
passages.section_title: Let the Children Come to Jesus

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 Then little children were brought to Jesus for Him to place His hands on them and pray for them. And the disciples rebuked those who brought them. 14 But Jesus said, “Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them! For the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these.” 15 And after He had placed His hands on them, He went on from there.
paragraphs: 13 Then little children were brought to Jesus for Him to place His hands on them and pray for them. And the disciples rebuked those who brought them. 14 But Jesus said, “Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them! For the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these.” 15 And after He had placed His hands on them, He went on from there.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
People bring little children to Jesus for Him to place His hands on them and pray. The disciples rebuke those who bring them, but Jesus tells them to allow the children to come. He receives them, lays His hands on them, and then goes on His way.

This continues a concern already raised in chapter 18: welcoming a child in Jesus' name, caring for the little ones, and refusing to look down on them. Here that concern is acted out toward actual children who are being brought to Him.

The related accounts add detail. Luke 18:15–17 says people were bringing even babies. Mark 10:13–16 describes Jesus' displeasure with the disciples, His taking the children in His arms, and His blessing them. Mark also records His teaching that the kingdom must be received like a little child.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians agree that Jesus welcomes children and that His followers should help them come to Him. Wesley on 19:13–14 includes both actual children and those who are childlike in faith; the US Catholic bishops' note on 19:13–15 also notes that some Christians connect the passage with infant baptism.

Churches differ over that connection. The Catholic Catechism, 1250–1252, teaches baptism of infants as a gift of new life in Christ. The Reformed Westminster Confession, 28.4, includes the infants of believing parents among those to be baptized, and the Methodist Articles, XVII, also retain baptism of young children. The 1689 Baptist Confession, 29.2, limits baptism to those who personally profess repentance and faith. These differences concern how children are received into the church; this particular scene describes Jesus' prayer and blessing rather than a baptism.
passages.god_plan_html:
God's saving purpose reaches people others may overlook. In 1 Corinthians 1:26–31, Paul reminds believers that few were powerful or highly placed when called. God chooses the weak and lowly, and Christ becomes their righteousness, holiness, and redemption. Human importance gives no one a privileged claim on Him.

The welcome Jesus gives also shapes the care His people offer. James 1:27 describes care for orphans and widows in their distress as part of faithful life before God. The disciples are learning to notice and receive the very people they might otherwise push aside.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 19:16-22
passages.section_title: The Rich Young Man Is Called to Follow Jesus

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 Just then a man came up to Jesus and inquired, “Teacher, what good thing must I do to obtain eternal life?” 17 “Why do you ask Me about what is good?” Jesus replied. “There is only One who is good. If you want to enter life, keep the commandments.” 18 “Which ones?” the man asked. Jesus answered, “‘Do not murder, do not commit adultery, do not steal, do not bear false witness, 19 honor your father and mother, and love your neighbor as yourself.’” 20 “All these I have kept,” said the young man. “What do I still lack?” 21 Jesus told him, “If you want to be perfect, go, sell your possessions and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. Then come, follow Me.” 22 When the young man heard this, he went away in sorrow, because he had great wealth.
paragraphs: 16 Just then a man came up to Jesus and inquired, “Teacher, what good thing must I do to obtain eternal life?” 17 “Why do you ask Me about what is good?” Jesus replied. “There is only One who is good. If you want to enter life, keep the commandments.” 18 “Which ones?” the man asked. Jesus answered, “‘Do not murder, do not commit adultery, do not steal, do not bear false witness, 19 honor your father and mother, and love your neighbor as yourself.’”

20 “All these I have kept,” said the young man. “What do I still lack?” 21 Jesus told him, “If you want to be perfect, go, sell your possessions and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. Then come, follow Me.” 22 When the young man heard this, he went away in sorrow, because he had great wealth.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
A man asks Jesus what good thing he must do to obtain eternal life. Jesus directs him toward the One who is good and tells him to keep the commandments. When he asks which ones, Jesus names commands about his treatment of others, including love for his neighbor.

The young man says he has kept them and asks what he still lacks. Jesus tells him to sell his possessions, give to the poor, and follow Him. He promises treasure in heaven. The man's sorrowful departure reveals the weight of the choice: he has great wealth.

Perfect is τέλειος, teleios (TEH-lay-oss). Thayer's entry gives the sense of completeness and includes Matthew 19:21 among uses concerning a person's character. Jesus brings the question about what is lacking to the concrete choice of generosity and following Him.

The conversation continues in verses 23–26 with the difficulty wealth presents and God's power to save. Mark 10:17–22 records Jesus' love for the man, while Luke 18:18–23 calls him a ruler. Matthew emphasizes that he is young and owns much.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly see the man's wealth as an obstacle to following Jesus. Wesley on 19:17–21 understands obedience as flowing from loving faith and the command to sell as a particular requirement for this man. The US Catholic bishops' notes on 19:16–22 likewise stress the hold of possessions and do not treat selling everything as a command addressed to every Christian.

There is a broader difference over particular ways of pursuing holiness. Catholic teaching distinguishes commands given to everyone from invitations to give up things that can hinder growth in love, practiced according to each person's calling (Catechism, 1973–1974). The command to love God and neighbor remains for all.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, 16.2–5, describes good works as the fruit of faith and denies that anyone can do more than God requires or earn eternal life by those works. The Methodist Articles, X–XI, likewise affirm good works flowing from faith while rejecting the claim to perform extra works beyond one's duty to God. These differences should not obscure the passage's direct question: will this man follow Jesus when doing so costs him what he holds dear?
passages.god_plan_html:
God brings people to Himself through Christ. 2 Corinthians 5:18–21 describes Him reconciling the world to Himself in Christ and making the sinless One to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become God's righteousness. The Savior who calls the man to follow Him will give His own life for sinners.

Ephesians 2:8–10 joins salvation by grace through faith with a life created for good works. God's gift brings people into a new way of living. The call to generosity and following Jesus belongs within that larger purpose of receiving life in Christ and learning to walk with Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 19:23-26
passages.section_title: What Is Impossible for People Is Possible with God

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 23 Then Jesus said to His disciples, “Truly I tell you, it is hard for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven. 24 Again I tell you, it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God.” 25 When the disciples heard this, they were greatly astonished and asked, “Who then can be saved?” 26 Jesus looked at them and said, “With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.”
paragraphs: 23 Then Jesus said to His disciples, “Truly I tell you, it is hard for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven. 24 Again I tell you, it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God.”

25 When the disciples heard this, they were greatly astonished and asked, “Who then can be saved?” 26 Jesus looked at them and said, “With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the rich young man leaves in sorrow, Jesus tells the disciples how hard it is for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven. He sets before them the picture of a camel passing through the eye of a needle. The enormous contrast shows a difficulty beyond human ability.

The disciples are astonished and ask who can be saved. Jesus' answer turns their attention to God: what is impossible with people is possible with Him. The question in this conversation is salvation, arising from the man's attachment to his wealth and the call to follow Jesus.

Peter's next question asks what will become of those who have left everything to follow Him. The chapter moves from the wealth someone cannot bear to leave toward the inheritance Jesus promises His followers.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as exposing both the danger of wealth and the need for God's saving power. Wesley on 19:24–26 takes the camel and needle as a picture of human impossibility, and the US Catholic bishops' notes on 19:23–26 likewise understand riches as an obstacle overcome by God's power.
passages.god_plan_html:
God's mercy supplies what people cannot produce for themselves. Titus 3:3–7 describes people once enslaved to their desires being saved through God's kindness, mercy, and renewal by the Holy Spirit, poured out through Jesus Christ. By His grace they become heirs of eternal life.

That purpose also changes how wealth is used. 1 Timothy 6:17–19 tells believers who are rich to put their hope in God and to be generous and ready to share. Following Christ gives possessions a place in serving others while directing hope toward the life He gives.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 19:27-30
passages.section_title: Following Jesus and the Renewal of All Things

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 27 “Look,” Peter replied, “we have left everything to follow You. What then will there be for us?” 28 Jesus said to them, “Truly I tell you, in the renewal of all things, when the Son of Man sits on His glorious throne, you who have followed Me will also sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. 29 And everyone who has left houses or brothers or sisters or father or mother or wife or children or fields for the sake of My name will receive a hundredfold and will inherit eternal life. 30 But many who are first will be last, and the last will be first.
paragraphs: 27 “Look,” Peter replied, “we have left everything to follow You. What then will there be for us?” 28 Jesus said to them, “Truly I tell you, in the renewal of all things, when the Son of Man sits on His glorious throne, you who have followed Me will also sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.

29 And everyone who has left houses or brothers or sisters or father or mother or wife or children or fields for the sake of My name will receive a hundredfold and will inherit eternal life. 30 But many who are first will be last, and the last will be first.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Peter responds to the rich man's encounter by pointing out that the disciples have left everything and followed Jesus. He asks what there will be for them. Jesus answers with a promise reaching beyond what they have lost: the Son of Man on His glorious throne, the disciples sharing in judgment, and eternal life for those who have sacrificed for His name.

The word for renewal is παλιγγενεσία, palingenesia (pah-lin-ghen-eh-SEE-ah). Thayer's entry gives the ideas of new birth, renewal, and restoration, and understands this use as the great renewal of the world. Jesus places the disciples' service within that coming change.

He also promises a hundredfold to those who have left family, homes, or fields for His sake. Mark 10:28–31 speaks of receiving a new abundance of homes and family in the present age, along with persecutions, and eternal life in the age to come. The promise holds care and costly discipleship together.

The final saying about first and last leads directly into the vineyard workers in Matthew 20:1–16. There the first workers resent the owner's generosity toward those hired last. That next story matters when considering how Jesus' promises should shape the disciples' expectations.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand Jesus to be assuring His followers that their sacrifices are not forgotten and that they share in His coming kingdom. Wesley on 19:28–29 places the thrones in the final renewal and judgment and also recognizes present help for those who have given things up. The US Catholic bishops' note on 19:28 likewise favors a connection with the final judgment.

Readers differ over the emphasis of first and last. Wesley on 19:30 sees people called earlier receiving a lower reward than some called later. The US Catholic bishops' note on 19:30 points toward the following parable and the kingdom's benefits as God's gift to all who answer His call. Both readings ask the disciples to reassess greatness and reward in light of God's purposes.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus' promise belongs within Scripture's hope of restoration. Acts 3:19–21 connects repentance, Christ's return, and the restoration God announced through His prophets. In Luke 22:28–30, Jesus again promises His faithful disciples a place at His table and thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.

The wider hope comes into view in Revelation 21:1–5: a new heaven and earth, God dwelling with His people, and the end of death and sorrow. The disciples' losses are set beside God's work of making all things new and bringing His people into life with Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 20:1-16
passages.section_title: The Generous Owner and the Vineyard Workers

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 “For the kingdom of heaven is like a landowner who went out early in the morning to hire workers for his vineyard. 2 He agreed to pay them a denarius for the day and sent them into his vineyard. 3 About the third hour he went out and saw others standing in the marketplace doing nothing. 4 ‘You also go into my vineyard,’ he said, ‘and I will pay you whatever is right.’ 5 So they went. He went out again about the sixth hour and the ninth hour and did the same thing. 6 About the eleventh hour he went out and found still others standing around. ‘Why have you been standing here all day long doing nothing?’ he asked. 7 ‘Because no one has hired us,’ they answered. So he told them, ‘You also go into my vineyard.’ 8 When evening came, the owner of the vineyard said to his foreman, ‘Call the workers and pay them their wages, starting with the last ones hired and moving on to the first.’ 9 The workers who were hired about the eleventh hour came and each received a denarius. 10 So when the original workers came, they assumed they would receive more. But each of them also received a denarius. 11 On receiving their pay, they began to grumble against the landowner. 12 ‘These men who were hired last worked only one hour,’ they said, ‘and you have made them equal to us who have borne the burden and the scorching heat of the day.’ 13 But he answered one of them, ‘Friend, I am not being unfair to you. Did you not agree with me on one denarius? 14 Take your pay and go. I want to give this last man the same as I gave you. 15 Do I not have the right to do as I please with what is mine? Or are you envious because I am generous?’ 16 So the last will be first, and the first will be last.”

So he told them, ‘You also go into my vineyard.’
