But each of them also received a denarius. 11 On receiving their pay, they began to grumble against the landowner. 12 ‘These men who were hired last worked only one hour,’ they said, ‘and you have made them equal to us who have borne the burden and the scorching heat of the day.’

13 But he answered one of them, ‘Friend, I am not being unfair to you. Did you not agree with me on one denarius? 14 Take your pay and go. I want to give this last man the same as I gave you. 15 Do I not have the right to do as I please with what is mine? Or are you envious because I am generous?’ 16 So the last will be first, and the first will be last.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus has just promised that those who sacrifice for His name will inherit eternal life, then warned that many who are first will be last. This story follows that promise and ends with the same reversal. It helps the disciples think about God's generosity as they consider what they will receive.

A landowner hires workers early in the morning, then returns at the third, sixth, ninth, and eleventh hours. The first workers agree to a denarius for the day; those hired later trust him to pay what is right. The BSB footnotes identify a denarius as a customary day's wage and the later hiring times as roughly nine, noon, three, and five.

At evening, the workers hired last are paid first and receive a denarius. Those who worked all day expect more, but receive the amount they agreed to. They object because the last group worked only one hour. The owner answers that he has kept his agreement and has chosen to be generous to the others.

The closing question brings their envy into the open. Their complaint arises when they compare what they received with the kindness shown to someone else. Jesus again tells the disciples that the last will be first and the first last.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly see the owner as a picture of God's generosity and the first workers' complaint as a warning against envy. Readers differ over what the different hiring times and equal payment especially represent.

The US Catholic bishops' notes on 20:1–16 emphasize all disciples sharing the gift of eternal life, including those who come late. Wesley on 20:1–16 applies the different calling times both to Jewish and Gentile believers and to people who come to faith at different stages of life. He also sees a reversal in which some called later receive greater honor. Both readings direct attention to God's generosity rather than a claim that longer service gives someone control over His gifts.
passages.god_plan_html:
God's promised inheritance comes through Christ. Ephesians 1:11–14 describes believers hearing and trusting the gospel, receiving the Holy Spirit, and looking toward their inheritance with His Spirit as its pledge. 1 Peter 1:3–5 connects that inheritance with God's mercy and Jesus' resurrection. The future He gives rests on His saving work.

The welcome of people called later also has a clear example in the church's life. In Acts 15:7–11, Peter says that God gave Gentile believers the Holy Spirit just as He did Jewish believers and cleansed their hearts by faith. Both are saved through the grace of Jesus. That is a related example of sharing God's gift without treating an earlier calling as a reason to resent another person's welcome.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 20:17-19
passages.section_title: Jesus Announces the Cross and Resurrection Again

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 As Jesus was going up to Jerusalem, He took the twelve disciples aside and said, 18 “Look, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and scribes. They will condemn Him to death 19 and will deliver Him over to the Gentiles to be mocked and flogged and crucified. And on the third day He will be raised to life.”
paragraphs: 17 As Jesus was going up to Jerusalem, He took the twelve disciples aside and said, 18 “Look, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and scribes. They will condemn Him to death 19 and will deliver Him over to the Gentiles to be mocked and flogged and crucified. And on the third day He will be raised to life.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
On the way up to Jerusalem, Jesus takes the Twelve aside and tells them what is coming. The Son of Man will be handed over to the chief priests and scribes, condemned, delivered to the Gentiles, mocked, flogged, and crucified. The announcement ends with His being raised on the third day.

This follows His earlier announcements in Matthew 16:21 and 17:22–23, now with more detail about the suffering. The disciples have been hearing about the kingdom and its rewards; Jesus keeps bringing them back to the path He will take to Jerusalem.

Luke 18:31–34 records the same prediction and says the disciples did not understand it. The request for places of honor that follows in Matthew shows how much they still need to learn about greatness and Jesus' mission.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as Jesus preparing His disciples for His death and resurrection. The US Catholic bishops' note on 20:17–19 identifies it as the third and most detailed prediction, while the related Catholic Catechism, 557, describes His deliberate journey toward Jerusalem with knowledge of what awaits Him.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus' suffering belongs within the saving purpose He later explains from Scripture. After His resurrection, He opens the disciples' understanding and connects His death and resurrection with the message of repentance and forgiveness going to all nations (Luke 24:44–49). What they struggle to understand on the road will become the message they are sent to proclaim.

Peter's preaching in Acts 2:22–24 brings those events together: Jesus was delivered up within God's purpose, people were responsible for putting Him to death, and God raised Him. The cross and resurrection stand at the heart of the gospel the disciples will carry.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 20:20-28
passages.section_title: Greatness Through Service and the Son’s Ransom

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 20 Then the mother of Zebedee’s sons came to Jesus with her sons and knelt down to make a request of Him. 21 “What do you want?” He inquired. She answered, “Declare that in Your kingdom one of these two sons of mine may sit at Your right hand, and the other at Your left.” 22 “You do not know what you are asking,” Jesus replied. “Can you drink the cup I am going to drink?” “We can,” the brothers answered. 23 “You will indeed drink My cup,” Jesus said. “But to sit at My right or left is not Mine to grant. These seats belong to those for whom My Father has prepared them.” 24 When the ten heard about this, they were indignant with the two brothers. 25 But Jesus called them aside and said, “You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their superiors exercise authority over them. 26 It shall not be this way among you. Instead, whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant, 27 and whoever wants to be first among you must be your slave— 28 just as the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many.”
paragraphs: 20 Then the mother of Zebedee’s sons came to Jesus with her sons and knelt down to make a request of Him. 21 “What do you want?” He inquired. She answered, “Declare that in Your kingdom one of these two sons of mine may sit at Your right hand, and the other at Your left.” 22 “You do not know what you are asking,” Jesus replied. “Can you drink the cup I am going to drink?” “We can,” the brothers answered. 23 “You will indeed drink My cup,” Jesus said. “But to sit at My right or left is not Mine to grant. These seats belong to those for whom My Father has prepared them.” 24 When the ten heard about this, they were indignant with the two brothers.

25 But Jesus called them aside and said, “You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their superiors exercise authority over them. 26 It shall not be this way among you. Instead, whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant, 27 and whoever wants to be first among you must be your slave— 28 just as the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Immediately after Jesus describes His coming suffering, the mother of Zebedee's sons asks for her sons to sit at His right and left in the kingdom. The brothers say they can drink His cup. Jesus tells them they will share that cup, but the places of honor belong to those for whom His Father has prepared them. The other ten are indignant.

Mark 10:35–45 names the brothers as James and John and records their request directly. Both accounts connect the request with Jesus' coming suffering and His teaching about service.

Jesus contrasts rulers who dominate others with the life He expects among His followers. Servant is διάκονος, diakonos (dee-AH-koh-noss), someone who serves or attends to another. Thayer's entry includes this verse and the related saying in Mark. Slave is δοῦλος, doulos (DOOH-loss); Thayer explains its use here as devoting oneself to another's good. Greatness is expressed in giving oneself to serve.

Jesus then gives His own mission as the example. He came to serve and give His life as a ransom for many. Ransom is λύτρον, lytron (LOOH-tron), the price of release. Thayer's entry connects this use with freeing people from the misery and penalty of sin. The coming death He has announced is also His act of service for others.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the cup as suffering and Jesus' instruction as a call to humble service. The US Catholic bishops' notes on 20:20–28 place His saving death at the height of that service; Wesley on 20:22–26 likewise connects the cup with suffering and greatness with serving.

Christians differ over whom Jesus means by many. The Catholic Church teaches that many here contrasts the one Redeemer with humanity as a whole, and that Christ died for everyone without exception (Catechism, 605). The Methodist Articles, XX, also describe His sacrifice as being for the sins of the whole world.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, 8.5 and 8.8, and 1689 Baptist Confession, 8.5 and 8.8, teach that Christ's death secures salvation for the people the Father has chosen and given Him. Christ brings them to faith and obedience and gives them the lasting inheritance He won for them. The shared conviction across these traditions is that His self-giving death brings rescue from sin.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus' language has a strong connection with Isaiah 53:10–12. There the Servant gives His life, bears the sins of many, and brings them into a right relationship with God. That is a strong scriptural parallel to the service Jesus describes in giving His life for others. 1 Timothy 2:3–6 also joins His role as the mediator between God and people with His giving Himself as a ransom.

His saving service also shapes the community He gathers. Philippians 2:3–11 calls believers to consider others and points to Christ's humility and obedience to death. 1 Peter 5:1–4 calls church leaders to care for the flock willingly, by example, as they look toward the Chief Shepherd's appearing. The One who gives His life teaches His people how to care for one another.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 20:29-34
passages.section_title: The Son of David Gives Sight and Mercy

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 29 As they were leaving Jericho, a large crowd followed Him. 30 And there were two blind men sitting beside the road. When they heard that Jesus was passing by, they cried out, “Lord, Son of David, have mercy on us!” 31 The crowd admonished them to be silent, but they cried out all the louder, “Lord, Son of David, have mercy on us!” 32 Jesus stopped and called them. “What do you want Me to do for you?” He asked. 33 “Lord,” they answered, “let our eyes be opened.” 34 Moved with compassion, Jesus touched their eyes, and at once they received their sight and followed Him.
paragraphs: 29 As they were leaving Jericho, a large crowd followed Him. 30 And there were two blind men sitting beside the road. When they heard that Jesus was passing by, they cried out, “Lord, Son of David, have mercy on us!” 31 The crowd admonished them to be silent, but they cried out all the louder, “Lord, Son of David, have mercy on us!”

32 Jesus stopped and called them. “What do you want Me to do for you?” He asked. 33 “Lord,” they answered, “let our eyes be opened.” 34 Moved with compassion, Jesus touched their eyes, and at once they received their sight and followed Him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
As Jesus and the crowd leave Jericho, two blind men beside the road hear that He is passing. They call to Him as Lord and Son of David, asking for mercy. The crowd tells them to be quiet, but they cry out even more loudly.

Jesus stops and asks what they want Him to do. They ask for their eyes to be opened. Moved with compassion, He touches their eyes; they receive sight at once and follow Him. The scene shows the service He has just taught: He gives His attention to people the crowd tries to silence.

Mark 10:46–52 gives an account of a blind beggar named Bartimaeus calling for mercy near Jericho and following Jesus after receiving sight. Matthew tells the scene with two men. The title Son of David connects their appeal with the royal line introduced in Matthew 1:1, just before Jesus' entry into Jerusalem in the next chapter.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a display of Jesus' mercy and a call to turn to Him with trust. Wesley on 20:30–31 emphasizes the men's persistent appeal despite the crowd's opposition; receiving sight leads them to follow Jesus.
passages.god_plan_html:
The gift of sight belongs within the promised work of God's salvation. Isaiah 35:4–6 describes God coming to save and blind eyes being opened. When John the Baptist's messengers ask whether Jesus is the One to come, Jesus points them to what they have seen: blind people receiving sight and the good news reaching the poor (Luke 7:18–23).

The mercy beside the road is therefore part of a larger picture. The Son of David brings help to those calling on Him as He travels toward Jerusalem and the self-giving death He has just announced. Those whose eyes He opens join Him on the road.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 21:1-11
passages.section_title: The Humble King Enters Jerusalem

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 As they approached Jerusalem and came to Bethphage on the Mount of Olives, Jesus sent out two disciples, 2 saying to them, “Go into the village ahead of you, and at once you will find a donkey tied there, with her colt beside her. Untie them and bring them to Me. 3 If anyone questions you, tell him that the Lord needs them, and he will send them right away.” 4 This took place to fulfill what was spoken through the prophet: 5 “Say to the Daughter of Zion, ‘See, your King comes to you, gentle and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.’” 6 So the disciples went and did as Jesus had directed them. 7 They brought the donkey and the colt and laid their cloaks on them, and Jesus sat on them. 8 A massive crowd spread their cloaks on the road, while others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road. 9 The crowds that went ahead of Him and those that followed were shouting: “Hosanna to the Son of David!” “Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord!” “Hosanna in the highest!” 10 When Jesus had entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred and asked, “Who is this?” 11 The crowds replied, “This is Jesus, the prophet from Nazareth in Galilee.”
paragraphs: 1 As they approached Jerusalem and came to Bethphage on the Mount of Olives, Jesus sent out two disciples, 2 saying to them, “Go into the village ahead of you, and at once you will find a donkey tied there, with her colt beside her. Untie them and bring them to Me. 3 If anyone questions you, tell him that the Lord needs them, and he will send them right away.” 4 This took place to fulfill what was spoken through the prophet: 5 “Say to the Daughter of Zion, ‘See, your King comes to you, gentle and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.’”

6 So the disciples went and did as Jesus had directed them. 7 They brought the donkey and the colt and laid their cloaks on them, and Jesus sat on them. 8 A massive crowd spread their cloaks on the road, while others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road. 9 The crowds that went ahead of Him and those that followed were shouting: “Hosanna to the Son of David!” “Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord!” “Hosanna in the highest!”
10 When Jesus had entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred and asked, “Who is this?” 11 The crowds replied, “This is Jesus, the prophet from Nazareth in Galilee.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus approaches Jerusalem after telling the disciples that He will suffer, die, and be raised there. At Bethphage on the Mount of Olives, He sends two disciples to bring a donkey and her colt. They follow His directions, bring the animals, and lay their cloaks on them. John 12:14–16 also describes His riding a young donkey.

Matthew explains the scene through prophecy. The King comes gently, riding on a donkey, as Zechariah 9:9 had said. The opening call to the Daughter of Zion also echoes Isaiah 62:11. Jerusalem is being called to recognize the One who comes to her.

The crowd spreads cloaks and branches on the road and greets Jesus as the Son of David. Hosanna is ὡσαννά, hōsanna (hoh-sahn-NAH), a word carried from Hebrew into Greek. Thayer's entry traces it to a plea for salvation. Psalm 118:25–26 joins that plea with blessing the one who comes in the Lord's name; here it becomes a shout of welcome and praise.

The city is stirred and asks who this is. The crowd identifies Jesus as the prophet from Nazareth in Galilee. The scene brings royal welcome and questions about His identity together as He enters the place where His announced suffering will unfold.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as Jesus openly entering Jerusalem as the promised King, with humility marking His arrival. Wesley on 21:5 emphasizes that humility, and the Catholic Catechism, 559–560, likewise connects His arrival as the promised King with the saving work of His death and resurrection.
passages.god_plan_html:
The prophecy reaches beyond the procession. Zechariah 9:9–10 joins the humble King's arrival with peace proclaimed to the nations and rule extending to the ends of the earth. Jesus' entry belongs within that larger hope of God's King bringing salvation and peace.

The coming Passover also gives His journey a deeper setting. Exodus 12:3–7 describes the unblemished Passover lamb, and 1 Corinthians 5:7–8 explicitly identifies Christ as the Passover lamb who has been sacrificed. That provides a supported parallel for approaching His final days: the King who enters the city will give His life to bring deliverance.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 21:12-17
passages.section_title: A House of Prayer, Healing, and Praise

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 Then Jesus entered the temple courts and drove out all who were buying and selling there. He overturned the tables of the money changers and the seats of those selling doves. 13 And He declared to them, “It is written: ‘My house will be called a house of prayer.’ But you are making it ‘a den of robbers.’” 14 The blind and the lame came to Him at the temple, and He healed them. 15 But the chief priests and scribes were indignant when they saw the wonders He performed and the children shouting in the temple courts, “Hosanna to the Son of David!” 16 “Do You hear what these children are saying?” they asked. “Yes,” Jesus answered. “Have you never read: ‘From the mouths of children and infants You have ordained praise’?” 17 Then He left them and went out of the city to Bethany, where He spent the night.
paragraphs: 12 Then Jesus entered the temple courts and drove out all who were buying and selling there. He overturned the tables of the money changers and the seats of those selling doves. 13 And He declared to them, “It is written: ‘My house will be called a house of prayer.’ But you are making it ‘a den of robbers.’”

14 The blind and the lame came to Him at the temple, and He healed them. 15 But the chief priests and scribes were indignant when they saw the wonders He performed and the children shouting in the temple courts, “Hosanna to the Son of David!” 16 “Do You hear what these children are saying?” they asked. “Yes,” Jesus answered. “Have you never read: ‘From the mouths of children and infants You have ordained praise’?” 17 Then He left them and went out of the city to Bethany, where He spent the night.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the entry into Jerusalem, Matthew brings us into the temple courts. Jesus drives out those buying and selling, overturns the money changers' tables, and removes the seats of the dove sellers. He explains His action through God's words about the purpose of His house.

His words bring together Isaiah 56:7, where God's house welcomes people in prayer, and Jeremiah 7:3–11, where God confronts people who practice injustice and then treat the temple as a place of safety. The phrase about robbers carries that serious warning into the scene.

The blind and lame then come to Jesus in the temple, and He heals them. Children continue the praise heard on the road, calling Him Son of David. The chief priests and scribes object, but Jesus answers with Psalm 8:2, which speaks of praise from children and infants. He then leaves for Bethany for the night.

The scene holds together His challenge to the temple's misuse and His welcome of those who come for help. His authority is shown through both the correction and the healing, while the children's praise brings the question of His identity before the leaders.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand Jesus to be defending God's house as a place of prayer and displaying His authority through His actions and the praise He accepts. Wesley on 21:12–16 connects the warning with Isaiah and Jeremiah, while the US Catholic bishops' notes on 21:12–17 emphasize the challenge His actions and healings present to the temple authorities.
passages.god_plan_html:
The wider promise in Isaiah 56:3–8 includes foreigners and others who might fear exclusion. God promises to gather people and make them joyful in His house of prayer. The words Jesus uses belong within that purpose of bringing people into worship before Him.

The New Testament develops the temple theme around Christ. In John 2:19–22, in another temple scene, Jesus speaks about His body being raised. Ephesians 2:18–22 describes Jewish and Gentile believers having access to the Father through Him and becoming His household, a dwelling for God through the Spirit. God's gathering work builds a people around the risen Christ.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 21:18-22
passages.section_title: The Fruitless Fig Tree and Trusting Prayer

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 In the morning, as Jesus was returning to the city, He was hungry. 19 Seeing a fig tree by the road, He went up to it but found nothing on it except leaves. “May you never bear fruit again!” He said. And immediately the tree withered. 20 When the disciples saw this, they marveled and asked, “How did the fig tree wither so quickly?” 21 “Truly I tell you,” Jesus replied, “if you have faith and do not doubt, not only will you do what was done to the fig tree, but even if you say to this mountain, ‘Be lifted up and thrown into the sea,’ it will happen. 22 If you believe, you will receive whatever you ask for in prayer.”
paragraphs: 18 In the morning, as Jesus was returning to the city, He was hungry. 19 Seeing a fig tree by the road, He went up to it but found nothing on it except leaves. “May you never bear fruit again!” He said. And immediately the tree withered.

20 When the disciples saw this, they marveled and asked, “How did the fig tree wither so quickly?” 21 “Truly I tell you,” Jesus replied, “if you have faith and do not doubt, not only will you do what was done to the fig tree, but even if you say to this mountain, ‘Be lifted up and thrown into the sea,’ it will happen. 22 If you believe, you will receive whatever you ask for in prayer.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Returning to the city in the morning, Jesus is hungry. He approaches a fig tree but finds only leaves. He declares that it will never bear fruit again, and it withers. The disciples are amazed and ask how this happened so quickly.

Jesus responds by teaching about faith without doubt, a mountain being lifted into the sea, and believing prayer. The disciples' attention to the tree's sudden withering becomes an opportunity to teach them about trusting God's power.

The surrounding chapter repeatedly raises the question of fruit: the tree has none, one son actually goes to work, and the vineyard's tenants refuse the owner his harvest. Mark 11:12–25 gives the related fig-tree account around the temple scene, with the disciples seeing the withered tree the next morning. In Mark, Jesus expressly directs their faith toward God.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read the fruitless tree as a warning about a life that does not bear the fruit God seeks, alongside a lesson in trusting Him in prayer. Wesley on 21:20–21 draws out both fruitfulness and faith; the US Catholic bishops' note on 21:18–22 understands the act as a warning of judgment on fruitlessness and an example of the power of believing prayer.
passages.god_plan_html:
The fruit God seeks comes through a living relationship with Christ. John 15:1–8 describes Him as the vine and His followers as branches. Remaining in Him leads to fruit that glorifies the Father. The warning about barrenness belongs beside that positive purpose: God forms people whose lives bear fruit through His Son.

Prayer is part of that relationship. John 15 joins remaining in Jesus and His words with asking, and 1 John 5:14–15 describes confidence in asking according to God's will. The larger picture brings faith, prayer, and fruitful life together around Him.
passages.current_position_html:
Prayer and Faith discusses Mark's account of this same fig-tree event. It reads the act as a warning that Israel's outward religious life was not bearing the fruit God sought, and that judgment was coming. The study understands the mountain-moving teaching as faith working in line with God's purposes.

The study therefore reads believing prayer as trust in God and what He purposes to do. It does not treat confidence in a desired result as a way to make that result happen. Its fuller explanation appears in Prayer and Faith.

passages.title: Matthew 21:23-27
passages.section_title: The Leaders Question Jesus’ Authority

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 23 When Jesus returned to the temple courts and began to teach, the chief priests and elders of the people came up to Him. “By what authority are You doing these things?” they asked. “And who gave You this authority?” 24 “I will also ask you one question,” Jesus replied, “and if you answer Me, I will tell you by what authority I am doing these things. 25 What was the source of John’s baptism? Was it from heaven or from men?” They deliberated among themselves and said, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ He will ask, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’ 26 But if we say, ‘From men,’ we are afraid of the people, for they all regard John as a prophet.” 27 So they answered, “We do not know.” And Jesus replied, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I am doing these things.
paragraphs: 23 When Jesus returned to the temple courts and began to teach, the chief priests and elders of the people came up to Him. “By what authority are You doing these things?” they asked. “And who gave You this authority?” 24 “I will also ask you one question,” Jesus replied, “and if you answer Me, I will tell you by what authority I am doing these things. 25 What was the source of John’s baptism? Was it from heaven or from men?” They deliberated among themselves and said, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ He will ask, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’ 26 But if we say, ‘From men,’ we are afraid of the people, for they all regard John as a prophet.” 27 So they answered, “We do not know.” And Jesus replied, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I am doing these things.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
While Jesus teaches in the temple courts, the chief priests and elders ask what authority He has and who gave it to Him. The question follows His entry, His actions in the temple, and His healings. His right to do these things is being challenged.

Jesus answers with a question about John's baptism: did it come from heaven or from people? The leaders discuss the consequences of either answer. If they acknowledge that John's ministry came from God, they must explain why they did not believe him. If they deny it, they fear the people, who regard John as a prophet.

They answer that they do not know, and Jesus declines to answer their original question. The next parable returns directly to their response to John. This exchange is therefore about more than the wording of a difficult question: it exposes their refusal to respond to a ministry calling them to repentance.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand Jesus' question to expose the leaders' unwillingness to acknowledge God's work through John. Wesley on 21:24–27 connects John's ministry with his testimony to Jesus, and the US Catholic bishops' note on 21:27 emphasizes how their embarrassment and fear shape their refusal to answer.
passages.god_plan_html:
John's ministry belongs within God's witness to His Son. In John 1:29–34, John explains that his baptizing ministry served to reveal Jesus to Israel, and he testifies to the Spirit resting on Him. The question about John therefore reaches into the preparation for recognizing Jesus.

Jesus also speaks of the Father's witness in John 5:36–40. His works and the Scriptures testify to Him, yet His hearers refuse to come to Him for life. The dispute in the temple belongs within that larger issue of how people respond to the One the Father has sent.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 21:28-32
passages.section_title: The Son Who Changes His Mind and Obeys

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 28 But what do you think? There was a man who had two sons. He went to the first one and said, ‘Son, go and work today in the vineyard.’ 29 ‘I will not,’ he replied. But later he changed his mind and went. 30 Then the man went to the second son and told him the same thing. ‘I will, sir,’ he said. But he did not go. 31 Which of the two did the will of his father?” “The first,” they answered. Jesus said to them, “Truly I tell you, the tax collectors and prostitutes are entering the kingdom of God before you. 32 For John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him, but the tax collectors and prostitutes did. And even after you saw this, you did not repent and believe him.
paragraphs: 28 But what do you think? There was a man who had two sons. He went to the first one and said, ‘Son, go and work today in the vineyard.’ 29 ‘I will not,’ he replied. But later he changed his mind and went. 30 Then the man went to the second son and told him the same thing. ‘I will, sir,’ he said. But he did not go.

31 Which of the two did the will of his father?” “The first,” they answered. Jesus said to them, “Truly I tell you, the tax collectors and prostitutes are entering the kingdom of God before you. 32 For John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him, but the tax collectors and prostitutes did. And even after you saw this, you did not repent and believe him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus continues speaking to the leaders with a story about two sons. A father asks each to work in his vineyard. The first refuses, then changes his mind and goes. The second agrees respectfully, but never goes. When Jesus asks which did the father's will, the answer is the first.

The word for changing his mind is μεταμέλομαι, metamelomai (meh-tah-MEH-loh-my). Thayer's entry gives the sense of repenting or feeling regret and lists both verses 29 and 32. In the story, the change becomes visible when the son goes to the vineyard.

Jesus applies the contrast to the response to John. Tax collectors and prostitutes believed him, while the leaders did not. Even seeing those changed lives did not bring the leaders to repent and believe. The father's question brings the difference between saying we will obey and actually responding to God's call into view.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the first son as a picture of people who turn from their earlier refusal and respond to God, while the second pictures a profession of obedience that is not lived out. Wesley on 21:30–32 and the US Catholic bishops' notes on 21:28–32 both connect this contrast with the religious leaders and those who responded to John's call to repentance.
passages.god_plan_html:
God's call to turn and live runs through Scripture. In Ezekiel 18:21–23, He speaks of a wicked person turning from sin and asks whether He takes pleasure in the person's death rather than their turning and living. The first son's changed response fits that wider call to return to God.

Jesus describes His own mission in similar terms in Luke 5:29–32. Eating with tax collectors, He explains that He has come to call sinners to repentance. The people who respond to John are the kind of people the Savior has come to seek, bringing them into a changed life with God.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 21:33-46
passages.section_title: The Rejected Son and the Cornerstone

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 33 Listen to another parable: There was a landowner who planted a vineyard. He put a wall around it, dug a winepress in it, and built a tower. Then he rented it out to some tenants and went away on a journey. 34 When the harvest time drew near, he sent his servants to the tenants to collect his share of the fruit. 35 But the tenants seized his servants. They beat one, killed another, and stoned a third. 36 Again, he sent other servants, more than the first group. But the tenants did the same to them. 37 Finally, he sent his son to them. ‘They will respect my son,’ he said. 38 But when the tenants saw the son, they said to one another, ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him and take his inheritance.’ 39 So they seized him and threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. 40 Therefore, when the owner of the vineyard returns, what will he do to those tenants?” 41 “He will bring those wretches to a wretched end,” they replied, “and will rent out the vineyard to other tenants who will give him his share of the fruit at harvest time.” 42 Jesus said to them, “Have you never read in the Scriptures: ‘The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. This is from the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes’? 43 Therefore I tell you that the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a people who will produce its fruit. 44 He who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces, but he on whom it falls will be crushed.” 45 When the chief priests and Pharisees heard His parables, they knew that Jesus was speaking about them. 46 Although they wanted to arrest Him, they were afraid of the crowds, because the people regarded Him as a prophet.

Then he rented it out to some tenants and went away on a journey. 34 When the harvest time drew near, he sent his servants to the tenants to collect his share of the fruit. 35 But the tenants seized his servants. They beat one, killed another, and stoned a third. 36 Again, he sent other servants, more than the first group. But the tenants did the same to them. 37 Finally, he sent his son to them. ‘They will respect my son,’ he said. 38 But when the tenants saw the son, they said to one another, ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him and take his inheritance.’ 39 So they seized him and threw him out of the vineyard and killed him.

40 Therefore, when the owner of the vineyard returns, what will he do to those tenants?” 41 “He will bring those wretches to a wretched end,” they replied, “and will rent out the vineyard to other tenants who will give him his share of the fruit at harvest time.” 42 Jesus said to them, “Have you never read in the Scriptures: ‘The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. This is from the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes’?

43 Therefore I tell you that the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a people who will produce its fruit. 44 He who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces, but he on whom it falls will be crushed.” 45 When the chief priests and Pharisees heard His parables, they knew that Jesus was speaking about them. 46 Although they wanted to arrest Him, they were afraid of the crowds, because the people regarded Him as a prophet.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus tells the leaders another vineyard story. Its planting, wall, winepress, and tower recall Isaiah 5:1–7, where Israel is God's vineyard and He seeks justice and righteousness. Here the owner entrusts the vineyard to tenants and sends servants to collect his share of the fruit.

The tenants attack the servants and finally kill the owner's son, hoping to take his inheritance. Jesus asks what the owner will do, and His hearers answer that he will judge the tenants and entrust the vineyard to others who give him its fruit.

Jesus then quotes Psalm 118:22–23: the rejected stone becomes the cornerstone through the Lord's doing. The warning about rejecting the son is followed by a promise that rejection will not have the last word. God gives the rejected stone its place.

The people who receive the kingdom are described by their fruit. People is ἔθνος, ethnos (ETH-noss), a people or nation. Thayer's entry lists uses for the Jewish people as well as other nations. Here the emphasis is on a people producing what God seeks.

The stone also carries a warning of judgment, with both falling on it and its falling on someone described as destructive. By the end, the chief priests and Pharisees understand that Jesus is speaking about them. They want to arrest Him but fear the crowds.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the owner as God, the servants as His messengers, and the son as Jesus, with judgment falling on those who reject Him. Wesley on 21:33–44 connects the cornerstone with the church gathered around Christ, while the US Catholic bishops' note on 21:43 identifies the fruit-bearing people as believing Israelites and Gentiles.
passages.god_plan_html:
The New Testament directly identifies the rejected cornerstone with Jesus. In Acts 4:10–12, Peter proclaims His resurrection, applies the same psalm to Him, and announces salvation in His name. The rejection described in the parable leads into the saving work God brings through His risen Son.

1 Peter 2:4–10 develops the building picture further. Those who come to Christ, the living stone, are themselves built into a spiritual house and become a people who proclaim God's goodness. Ephesians 2:19–22 likewise places Christ at the foundation of God's household as its cornerstone. God gathers His people around the One others rejected, so that their shared life bears witness to Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 22:1-14
passages.section_title: The Invitation to the Wedding Feast

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Once again, Jesus spoke to them in parables: 2 “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who prepared a wedding banquet for his son. 3 He sent his servants to call those he had invited to the banquet, but they refused to come. 4 Again, he sent other servants and said, ‘Tell those who have been invited that I have prepared my dinner. My oxen and fattened cattle have been killed, and everything is ready. Come to the wedding banquet.’ 5 But they paid no attention and went away, one to his field, another to his business. 6 The rest seized his servants, mistreated them, and killed them. 7 The king was enraged, and he sent his troops to destroy those murderers and burn their city. 8 Then he said to his servants, ‘The wedding banquet is ready, but those I invited were not worthy. 9 Go therefore to the crossroads and invite to the banquet as many as you can find.’ 10 So the servants went out into the streets and gathered everyone they could find, both evil and good, and the wedding hall was filled with guests. 11 But when the king came in to see the guests, he spotted a man who was not dressed in wedding clothes. 12 ‘Friend,’ he asked, ‘how did you get in here without wedding clothes?’ But the man was speechless. 13 Then the king told the servants, ‘Tie him hand and foot, and throw him into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.’ 14 For many are called, but few are chosen.”
paragraphs: 1 Once again, Jesus spoke to them in parables: 2 “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who prepared a wedding banquet for his son. 3 He sent his servants to call those he had invited to the banquet, but they refused to come. 4 Again, he sent other servants and said, ‘Tell those who have been invited that I have prepared my dinner. My oxen and fattened cattle have been killed, and everything is ready. Come to the wedding banquet.’

5 But they paid no attention and went away, one to his field, another to his business. 6 The rest seized his servants, mistreated them, and killed them. 7 The king was enraged, and he sent his troops to destroy those murderers and burn their city. 8 Then he said to his servants, ‘The wedding banquet is ready, but those I invited were not worthy. 9 Go therefore to the crossroads and invite to the banquet as many as you can find.’ 10 So the servants went out into the streets and gathered everyone they could find, both evil and good, and the wedding hall was filled with guests.

11 But when the king came in to see the guests, he spotted a man who was not dressed in wedding clothes. 12 ‘Friend,’ he asked, ‘how did you get in here without wedding clothes?’ But the man was speechless. 13 Then the king told the servants, ‘Tie him hand and foot, and throw him into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.’ 14 For many are called, but few are chosen.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus continues speaking in parables after the vineyard tenants have rejected the owner's son. Now He describes a king preparing a wedding feast for his son. Those already invited refuse to come. Some turn to their ordinary work; others mistreat and kill the servants. The king judges the murderers and sends servants to invite people from the roads.

The hall fills with guests, both evil and good. Yet the story does not end with their arrival. The king finds a guest without wedding clothes, questions him, and has him removed. Jesus closes with a warning about the difference between being called and being chosen.

The invitation is generous, and rejecting it is serious. The final scene also challenges those who have come: being among the guests does not put someone beyond the king's judgment. The story itself does not say who supplied the clothes or explain how the man came to be without them.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the feast as God's invitation into His kingdom through His Son, with a warning against both rejecting the invitation and assuming that outward membership is enough. Readers differ over what the clothing and the closing words emphasize.

The Catholic Church's Catechism, 546, says the kingdom's invitation calls for a changed life. The US Catholic bishops' note on 22:11 understands the garment as repentance continued in good deeds. Wesley on 22:12–14 describes Christ's righteousness both credited to believers and taking shape within them; hearing the invitation is different from believing it.

Reformed churches following the Westminster Confession, chapter 10, and Baptists following the 1689 Confession, chapter 10, distinguish the invitation people hear from God's inward work that brings His chosen people freely to faith. In this reading, the closing distinction points to more than an outward response.

Wesley's emphasis is that many hear but few believe. The Methodist Articles of Religion, VIII–X, teach that God's grace must first enable a response, that people are accepted through Christ by faith, and that good works follow living faith. Catholic teaching likewise makes grace God's free initiative while affirming a person's free response (Catechism, 1996–2002). These traditions explain the relationship between God's choice and the hearer's response differently; none of these statements treats salvation as earned by attending a gathering.
passages.god_plan_html:
The feast belongs within a larger biblical picture of salvation shared with God's people. Isaiah 25:6–9 describes the LORD preparing a banquet for all peoples, swallowing up death, and wiping away tears. The wedding feast provides a parallel to that hope: God's purpose brings people into the joy of His saving work.

Revelation 19:6–9 uses the picture of the Lamb's wedding and blesses those invited to His supper. Its bride receives fine linen, which the passage identifies with the saints' righteous acts. This is a related picture of salvation, readiness, and joy; it does not make every detail of the two scenes identical.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 22:15-22
passages.section_title: What Belongs to Caesar and What Belongs to God?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 Then the Pharisees went out and conspired to trap Jesus in His words. 16 They sent their disciples to Him along with the Herodians. “Teacher,” they said, “we know that You are honest and that You teach the way of God in accordance with the truth. You seek favor from no one, because You pay no attention to external appearance. 17 So tell us what You think: Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar or not?” 18 But Jesus knew their evil intent and said, “You hypocrites, why are you testing Me? 19 Show Me the coin used for the tax.” And they brought Him a denarius. 20 “Whose image is this,” He asked, “and whose inscription?” 21 “Caesar’s,” they answered. So Jesus told them, “Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.” 22 And when they heard this, they were amazed. So they left Him and went away.
paragraphs: 15 Then the Pharisees went out and conspired to trap Jesus in His words. 16 They sent their disciples to Him along with the Herodians. “Teacher,” they said, “we know that You are honest and that You teach the way of God in accordance with the truth. You seek favor from no one, because You pay no attention to external appearance. 17 So tell us what You think: Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar or not?”

18 But Jesus knew their evil intent and said, “You hypocrites, why are you testing Me? 19 Show Me the coin used for the tax.” And they brought Him a denarius. 20 “Whose image is this,” He asked, “and whose inscription?” 21 “Caesar’s,” they answered. So Jesus told them, “Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.” 22 And when they heard this, they were amazed. So they left Him and went away.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the parable, the Pharisees plan to trap Jesus through His words. Their disciples come with the Herodians, praise His honesty and impartiality, and ask whether God's law permits paying taxes to Caesar. Matthew tells us their purpose before recording the question, so their praise must be read in light of the trap.

Jesus recognizes their intent and asks for the tax coin. They bring a denarius. He asks whose image and inscription it bears, and they answer that it is Caesar's. His reply joins giving Caesar his due with giving God His due. They are amazed and leave.

The verb behind give is ἀποδίδωμι, apodidōmi (ah-poh-DID-oh-mee), which can mean to repay or give what is owed. Thayer's entry places this verse among payments due to government. Jesus moves beyond the choice His questioners have set before Him and brings their duty to God into the answer.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as recognizing duties to civil government while preserving the higher claim of God. Wesley on 22:17–21 explains the trap and both obligations; the Catholic Catechism, 2240–2242, joins the duty to pay taxes with the duty to refuse commands contrary to God's demands.
passages.god_plan_html:
The coin's image can be placed beside a wider biblical truth: human beings bear God's image (Genesis 1:26–28). This is a parallel, rather than something Jesus spells out in this scene. It helps bring the closing words home: our obligation to God reaches into who we are and how we live.

Romans 12:1–2 calls believers to offer their lives to God in response to His mercy. Romans 13:1–7 then describes responsible conduct toward governing authorities, including taxes. Acts 5:27–32 shows the apostles obeying God when authorities forbid their witness to Jesus. God's people are called to serve Him faithfully within society, with their whole lives belonging to Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 22:23-33
passages.section_title: The God of the Living and the Resurrection

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 23 That same day the Sadducees, who say there is no resurrection, came to Jesus and questioned Him. 24 “Teacher,” they said, “Moses declared that if a man dies without having children, his brother is to marry the widow and raise up offspring for him. 25 Now there were seven brothers among us. The first one married and died without having children. So he left his wife to his brother. 26 The same thing happened to the second and third brothers, down to the seventh. 27 And last of all, the woman died. 28 In the resurrection, then, whose wife will she be of the seven? For all of them were married to her.” 29 Jesus answered, “You are mistaken because you do not know the Scriptures or the power of God. 30 In the resurrection, people will neither marry nor be given in marriage. Instead, they will be like the angels in heaven. 31 But concerning the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what God said to you: 32 ‘I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’? He is not the God of the dead, but of the living.” 33 When the crowds heard this, they were astonished at His teaching.
paragraphs: 23 That same day the Sadducees, who say there is no resurrection, came to Jesus and questioned Him. 24 “Teacher,” they said, “Moses declared that if a man dies without having children, his brother is to marry the widow and raise up offspring for him. 25 Now there were seven brothers among us. The first one married and died without having children. So he left his wife to his brother. 26 The same thing happened to the second and third brothers, down to the seventh. 27 And last of all, the woman died. 28 In the resurrection, then, whose wife will she be of the seven? For all of them were married to her.”

29 Jesus answered, “You are mistaken because you do not know the Scriptures or the power of God. 30 In the resurrection, people will neither marry nor be given in marriage. Instead, they will be like the angels in heaven. 31 But concerning the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what God said to you: 32 ‘I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’? He is not the God of the dead, but of the living.” 33 When the crowds heard this, they were astonished at His teaching.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Sadducees approach Jesus that same day. Matthew identifies them as people who deny resurrection. They draw on the marriage provision in Deuteronomy 25:5–10, which preserved a dead brother's family line, and present a case in which seven brothers successively marry the same childless widow. Their question assumes those marriages must compete in the resurrection.

Jesus challenges their understanding of Scripture and God's power. Resurrected life does not repeat marriage as they know it: people neither marry nor are given in marriage but are like the angels in heaven. Being like angels here describes the comparison Jesus makes; He does not say that people become angels.

Resurrection is ἀνάστασις, anastasis (ah-NAH-stah-siss), a rising from the dead. Thayer's entry includes this passage among its uses. The issue is God's power to raise the dead, rather than a way to resolve the proposed marriages.

Jesus then turns to Exodus 3:6. God identifies Himself to Moses as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, although their earthly lives had ended. Jesus grounds His answer in God's continuing relationship with them: He is God of the living. Luke 20:34–38 gives the related answer and explains that those raised to that life can no longer die.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Catholic and Protestant readings commonly understand Jesus to affirm resurrection while correcting the assumption that marriage continues as in this life. Wesley on 22:29–32 emphasizes God's power and the patriarchs' continuing life before Him; the US Catholic bishops' notes on 22:23–33 likewise explain a life transformed by God's power.

A different reading appears in the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints' student manual on Matthew 22:23–30. It distinguishes marriages performed after resurrection from marriages already joined by the church's sealing ceremony. It teaches that a marriage sealed by the required authority can endure beyond death, drawing on Doctrine and Covenants 132 as well as its reading of Jesus' answer.
passages.god_plan_html:
God's promises reach beyond the limits of a human lifetime. Genesis 17:7–8 joins His covenant with Abraham's descendants, their promised inheritance, and His commitment to be their God. Hebrews 11:8–19 describes Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob living by faith before receiving all they hoped for, looking toward God's prepared city. It also describes Abraham trusting God's power to raise the dead. These passages help place Jesus' answer within God's faithfulness to His people, without supplying a detailed timetable for the resurrection.

The New Testament places that hope firmly in Christ. 1 Corinthians 15:12–26 connects His resurrection with the future raising of those who belong to Him and the final defeat of death. The power the Sadducees failed to recognize is central to God's purpose through His Son.
passages.current_position_html: Our existing study, Who is The Angel of the Lord?, identifies the One who appears and speaks from the burning bush in Exodus 3 as the Son before His human birth. It notes that Jesus quotes this very scene when answering the Sadducees. That is the study's conclusion about the Exodus passage; Jesus' immediate point here is God's relationship with the living and the reality of resurrection.

deeper_study.title: Who is The Angel of the Lord?

passages.title: Matthew 22:32
passages.section_title: God Has Not Abandoned Those Who Have Died

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 32 ‘I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’? He is not the God of the dead, but of the living.”
paragraphs: 32 ‘I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’? He is not the God of the dead, but of the living.”

passages.context_html:
This verse belongs to Jesus' answer to the Sadducees in Matthew 22:23–33. They deny resurrection and propose a woman whose seven successive marriages would create a problem if raised life simply continued those marriages. Jesus first corrects that assumption, then points them to God's words at the burning bush.

In Exodus 3:1–8, the God who calls Moses identifies Himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and promises to rescue His people. Those patriarchs had died, yet God still identifies Himself in relation to them. Jesus brings that continuing relationship into His answer about resurrection.

The surrounding verses keep the subject clear: Jesus is teaching about God's power to raise the dead. In the related account, Luke 20:37–38 explicitly connects Moses' burning-bush passage with their being raised and alive to God.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this verse to affirm God's continuing relationship with His people beyond death, within Jesus' defense of resurrection. Wesley on 22:32 draws out their continuing life before God, while the US Catholic bishops' note on 22:31–32 keeps that relationship within the passage's hope of bodily resurrection.
passages.current_position_html: Our existing study, Who is The Angel of the Lord?, identifies the One who appears and speaks from the burning bush in Exodus 3 as the Son before His human birth. It notes that Jesus quotes this very scene when answering the Sadducees. That is the study's conclusion about the Exodus passage; Jesus' immediate point here is God's relationship with the living and the reality of resurrection.

deeper_study.title: Who is The Angel of the Lord?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The God who remembers His covenant does not lose His people when their earthly lives end. Hebrews 11:8–16 describes the patriarchs dying in faith while looking toward the home God prepares, and says He is not ashamed to be called their God. The passage brings the same relationship into view alongside a hope that reaches beyond death.

1 Corinthians 15:20–26 connects the resurrection of those who belong to Christ with His victory over death itself. God's relationship with His people belongs within that larger purpose of bringing them into life through His risen Son.

passages.title: Matthew 22:34-40
passages.section_title: Love God and Love Your Neighbor

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 34 And when the Pharisees heard that Jesus had silenced the Sadducees, they themselves gathered together. 35 One of them, an expert in the law, tested Him with a question: 36 “Teacher, which commandment is the greatest in the Law?” 37 Jesus declared, “‘Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind.’ 38 This is the first and greatest commandment. 39 And the second is like it: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’ 40 All the Law and the Prophets hang on these two commandments.”
paragraphs: 34 And when the Pharisees heard that Jesus had silenced the Sadducees, they themselves gathered together. 35 One of them, an expert in the law, tested Him with a question: 36 “Teacher, which commandment is the greatest in the Law?”

37 Jesus declared, “‘Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind.’ 38 This is the first and greatest commandment. 39 And the second is like it: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’ 40 All the Law and the Prophets hang on these two commandments.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After Jesus silences the Sadducees, the Pharisees gather and an expert in the law asks Him which commandment is greatest. Matthew describes this as a test. Jesus answers from Deuteronomy 6:4–9, where Israel is called to love the LORD wholeheartedly and carry His words into daily life.

Jesus adds a second commandment from Leviticus 19:18: love for one's neighbor. Its setting includes honest dealings, care for the poor, fair judgment, and refusing hatred and revenge. Love has practical content in the very passage from which Jesus draws it.

All the Law and the Prophets depend on these two commandments. They bring devotion to God and our treatment of others together. Mark 12:28–34 records the scribe agreeing that such love is greater than burnt offerings and sacrifices, and Jesus commending his wise answer. That fuller account helps us hear the exchange without inventing a hidden motive for every word.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand these two commands as holding together wholehearted love for God and active love for other people. The Catholic Catechism, 2055, reads the commandments in that light; the US Catholic bishops' notes on 22:37–40 and Wesley's references on 22:37–39 likewise connect Jesus' answer with Deuteronomy and Leviticus.
passages.god_plan_html:
God's purpose is to form people whose lives reflect His love. 1 John 4:7–21 begins with His love shown in sending His Son so that we might live through Him. It then connects receiving that love with loving one another: love for God cannot be separated from how we treat a brother or sister.

Galatians 5:13–25 calls believers to serve one another in love and names love among the fruit of the Spirit. The commands Jesus names fit within that larger work of God: through His Son and Spirit, He brings people into a shared life marked by love.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 22:41-46
passages.section_title: How Can the Messiah Be David's Son and David's Lord?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 41 While the Pharisees were assembled, Jesus questioned them: 42 “What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is He?” “David’s,” they answered. 43 Jesus said to them, “How then does David in the Spirit call Him ‘Lord’? For he says: 44 ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at My right hand until I put Your enemies under Your feet.”’ 45 So if David calls Him ‘Lord,’ how can He be David’s son?” 46 No one was able to answer a word, and from that day on no one dared to question Him any further.
paragraphs: 41 While the Pharisees were assembled, Jesus questioned them: 42 “What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is He?” “David’s,” they answered. 43 Jesus said to them, “How then does David in the Spirit call Him ‘Lord’? For he says:

44 ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at My right hand until I put Your enemies under Your feet.”’ 45 So if David calls Him ‘Lord,’ how can He be David’s son?” 46 No one was able to answer a word, and from that day on no one dared to question Him any further.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus now asks the assembled Pharisees a question: whose son is the Christ? They answer that He is David's son. Matthew has introduced Jesus as the Son of David from the beginning of the Gospel, so the question takes up a central part of His identity.

Jesus points to Psalm 110:1, where David speaks by the Spirit and calls the one seated at God's right hand his Lord. How can the Messiah be David's descendant and also the one David acknowledges above himself? The question asks them to think further about who the promised King is.

The leaders cannot answer, and their questioning comes to an end. The passage leads into Jesus' warning to the crowds and disciples about the scribes and Pharisees in chapter 23. The One they have been testing has exposed the limits of their answer about the Messiah.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the question to show that the Messiah is greater than an ordinary descendant of David: He is also David's Lord. Wesley on 22:43–44 emphasizes His heavenly authority, and the US Catholic bishops' note on 22:45 explains that His greater identity does not cancel His place in David's family.
passages.god_plan_html:
God's promise to establish David's house and throne in 2 Samuel 7:12–16 provides the background. Luke 1:30–33 identifies Jesus as the Son who receives David's throne and reigns forever. The promised descendant belongs within a purpose that reaches beyond David's own lifetime.

The New Testament directly applies Psalm 110 to Jesus after His resurrection. In Acts 2:29–36, Peter connects David's promise, Jesus' resurrection, His exaltation, and the gift of the Spirit. Hebrews 1:1–13 likewise places the Son at God's right hand after His saving work and quotes the same psalm. The question in the temple points toward the risen and exalted King through whom God carries out His purpose.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

deeper_study.title: Who is The Angel of the Lord?

passages.title: Matthew 23:1-12
passages.section_title: Leadership That Serves Instead of Seeking Honor

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then Jesus spoke to the crowds and to His disciples: 2 “The scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses’ seat. 3 So practice and observe everything they tell you. But do not do what they do, for they do not practice what they preach. 4 They tie up heavy, burdensome loads and lay them on men’s shoulders, but they themselves are not willing to lift a finger to move them. 5 All their deeds are done for men to see. They broaden their phylacteries and lengthen their tassels. 6 They love the places of honor at banquets, the chief seats in the synagogues, 7 the greetings in the marketplaces, and the title of ‘Rabbi’ by which they are addressed. 8 But you are not to be called ‘Rabbi,’ for you have one Teacher, and you are all brothers. 9 And do not call anyone on earth your father, for you have one Father, who is in heaven. 10 Nor are you to be called instructors, for you have one Instructor, the Christ. 11 The greatest among you shall be your servant. 12 For whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.
paragraphs: 1 Then Jesus spoke to the crowds and to His disciples: 2 “The scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses’ seat. 3 So practice and observe everything they tell you. But do not do what they do, for they do not practice what they preach. 4 They tie up heavy, burdensome loads and lay them on men’s shoulders, but they themselves are not willing to lift a finger to move them.

5 All their deeds are done for men to see. They broaden their phylacteries and lengthen their tassels. 6 They love the places of honor at banquets, the chief seats in the synagogues, 7 the greetings in the marketplaces, and the title of ‘Rabbi’ by which they are addressed.

8 But you are not to be called ‘Rabbi,’ for you have one Teacher, and you are all brothers. 9 And do not call anyone on earth your father, for you have one Father, who is in heaven. 10 Nor are you to be called instructors, for you have one Instructor, the Christ. 11 The greatest among you shall be your servant. 12 For whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After answering the leaders' questions, Jesus speaks to the crowds and His disciples about the scribes and Pharisees. They occupy Moses' seat, a position associated with teaching his law. Jesus tells His hearers to practice what they are taught while refusing the example of teachers whose actions contradict their words.

He describes burdens placed on others without help, religious deeds performed for attention, and a love of honored seats, greetings, and titles. The phylacteries were small cases containing passages of Scripture, worn on the forehead and arm; Thayer's entry explains that practice. Tassels reminded Israel to remember and obey God's commands (Numbers 15:37–41). Here the widening and lengthening make the outward signs more noticeable.

Jesus turns to His disciples and places their relationships under one Teacher, one Father, and one Instructor, the Christ. They are brothers, and greatness among them takes the form of service. His warning reaches beyond whether people admire a leader: it asks what the leader seeks and how the people are treated.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand this as a warning against hypocrisy, pride, and spiritual domination. In his Angelus of November 5, 2017, Pope Francis applies it to Christian leaders: teaching must be matched by example, and authority must serve rather than oppress.

Readers differ over the use of religious titles. Wesley on 23:8–10 understands Jesus to forbid giving teachers the unquestioning reverence that belongs to God. Some Christians therefore avoid titles that place a leader above other believers. The Catholic Church describes priests as spiritual fathers who care for the faithful in Lumen Gentium, 28. Its explanation in Call No Man Father, a tract approved for publication by a Catholic bishop, permits calling a priest father as a recognition of spiritual care. It points to Paul's description of becoming the Corinthians' father through the gospel in 1 Corinthians 4:14–17, while maintaining God's unique fatherhood. These readings differ over which uses of a title express the superiority Jesus rejects.
passages.god_plan_html:
The warning continues a long concern for God's flock. Ezekiel 34:1–16 condemns shepherds who feed themselves while neglecting the weak, then promises that God will seek and care for His sheep. In John 10:11–18, Jesus identifies Himself as the good shepherd who gives His life for them. The contrast helps place humble leadership within God's care for His people.

1 Peter 5:1–6 carries that pattern into the church: elders care for God's flock through example, willingly and without greed or domination, under the Chief Shepherd. Philippians 2:3–11 grounds humility in Christ's own service, obedience, and exaltation. He forms a people whose leaders reflect the care He has shown them.
passages.current_position_html: Our existing study, Who Shepherds the Church?, argues for qualified elders serving among believers, with leadership recognized by character, teaching, and care rather than a title that raises someone into a separate class. It also emphasizes that rejecting a titled hierarchy does not mean rejecting responsible, qualified teaching. That developed conclusion supplies our position on the leadership question raised here.

passages.title: Matthew 23:13
passages.section_title: When Religious Guides Block the Way

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, you hypocrites! You shut the kingdom of heaven in men’s faces. You yourselves do not enter, nor will you let in those who wish to enter.
paragraphs: 13 Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, you hypocrites! You shut the kingdom of heaven in men’s faces. You yourselves do not enter, nor will you let in those who wish to enter.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus has warned His disciples against seeking honor and placing burdens on others. He now addresses the scribes and Pharisees directly with a series of woes. The first charges them with shutting the kingdom against people: they do not enter, and they obstruct others who want to enter.

Woe is οὐαί, ouai (oo-EYE), an expression of grief or denunciation. Thayer's entry includes the warnings in this chapter. Here the word introduces a grave charge about the damage religious leaders do to those they guide. Luke 11:52 gives a related warning about taking away the key to knowledge and hindering those entering.

The BSB places the words numbered 23:14 in some translations in a footnote. Its main text moves from verse 13 to verse 15. That note points to the warning about exploiting widows and making long prayers in Mark 12:40 and Luke 20:47; this page follows the BSB's main-text numbering.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a warning that religious teaching can become an obstacle to entering God's kingdom. Wesley on 23:13 connects the barrier with a refusal of humility; the US Catholic bishops' note emphasizes authority used to obstruct entry.
passages.god_plan_html: Jesus' purpose is to bring people into life. In John 10:7–10, He describes Himself as the gate through whom people enter and are saved, contrasting His life-giving work with destruction. Ephesians 2:13–22 describes people brought near through His death, sharing access to the Father and a place in God's household. Leadership that closes the way stands against that gathering purpose.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 23:15
passages.section_title: What Kind of Disciple Are We Making?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, you hypocrites! You traverse land and sea to win a single convert, and when he becomes one, you make him twice as much a son of hell as you are.
paragraphs: 15 Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, you hypocrites! You traverse land and sea to win a single convert, and when he becomes one, you make him twice as much a son of hell as you are.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The next woe follows the warning about shutting the kingdom against others. Jesus describes leaders traveling over land and sea to win a convert, then making that person even more deserving of judgment than themselves. Great effort and a growing following do not by themselves show that someone is guiding people rightly.

The charge is about what the convert becomes under their guidance. The leaders reproduce the very wrongdoing Jesus is exposing throughout the chapter. The question is therefore deeper than whether they have persuaded someone: where has their teaching led that person?
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as a warning against spreading a religious allegiance that forms people in the teacher's wrongdoing. The US Catholic bishops' note on 23:15 understands the convert's greater zeal as one possible reason for the stronger condemnation; Jesus' criticism concerns the harmful result of that conversion.
passages.god_plan_html: Jesus later gives His followers a different mission in Matthew 28:18–20: to make disciples of all nations, baptizing them and teaching them to obey Him. The aim is a life shaped by His teaching under His authority, with His presence among them. That purpose provides a clear contrast to winning a convert only to reproduce the leader's wrongdoing.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 23:16-22
passages.section_title: Promises Cannot Be Separated from God

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 Woe to you, blind guides! You say, ‘If anyone swears by the temple, it means nothing; but if anyone swears by the gold of the temple, he is bound by his oath.’ 17 You blind fools! Which is greater: the gold, or the temple that makes it sacred? 18 And you say, ‘If anyone swears by the altar, it means nothing; but if anyone swears by the gift on it, he is bound by his oath.’ 19 You blind men!
