Which is greater: the gift, or the altar that makes it sacred? 20 So then, he who swears by the altar swears by it and by everything on it. 21 And he who swears by the temple swears by it and by the One who dwells in it. 22 And he who swears by heaven swears by God’s throne and by the One who sits on it.
paragraphs: 16 Woe to you, blind guides! You say, ‘If anyone swears by the temple, it means nothing; but if anyone swears by the gold of the temple, he is bound by his oath.’ 17 You blind fools! Which is greater: the gold, or the temple that makes it sacred? 18 And you say, ‘If anyone swears by the altar, it means nothing; but if anyone swears by the gift on it, he is bound by his oath.’ 19 You blind men! Which is greater: the gift, or the altar that makes it sacred?

20 So then, he who swears by the altar swears by it and by everything on it. 21 And he who swears by the temple swears by it and by the One who dwells in it. 22 And he who swears by heaven swears by God’s throne and by the One who sits on it.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus next calls the leaders blind guides and examines their rules about oaths. They treat swearing by the temple as nonbinding but swearing by its gold as binding. They make a similar distinction between the altar and the gift placed on it.

Jesus asks what makes the gold and the gift sacred. The temple and altar give them their setting before God; placing greater weight on the gold or gift reverses that relationship. Exodus 29:36–37 describes the altar's consecration and the holiness associated with it.

Jesus then traces the oaths back to God. An oath by the altar includes what is on it; an oath by the temple involves the One who dwells there; an oath by heaven involves God's throne. These distinctions do not create a way to speak as though God is involved while escaping responsibility to Him. The law already called people to keep the promises they made (Numbers 30:1–2; Deuteronomy 23:21–23).
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as exposing false distinctions that make some promises appear binding while excusing others. Wesley on 23:20 emphasizes that an oath involving sacred things appeals to God; the US Catholic bishops' note on 23:16–22 stresses the reversal of what has greater value.
passages.god_plan_html: God forms a people whose words can be trusted. Jesus' teaching in Matthew 5:33–37 also challenges oath-making and calls for honest speech. Ephesians 4:20–25 connects putting away falsehood with the new life learned in Christ. Truthfulness matters because believers belong to one another; honest speech serves the shared life God is building.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 23:23-24
passages.section_title: Careful with the Small Things, Neglecting What Matters Most

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 23 Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, you hypocrites! You pay tithes of mint, dill, and cumin. But you have disregarded the weightier matters of the law: justice, mercy, and faithfulness. You should have practiced the latter, without neglecting the former. 24 You blind guides! You strain out a gnat but swallow a camel.
paragraphs: 23 Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, you hypocrites! You pay tithes of mint, dill, and cumin. But you have disregarded the weightier matters of the law: justice, mercy, and faithfulness. You should have practiced the latter, without neglecting the former. 24 You blind guides! You strain out a gnat but swallow a camel.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus turns from oaths to tithing. The leaders carefully give a tenth of small garden herbs while neglecting justice, mercy, and faithfulness. He says they should practice the weightier matters without neglecting the others. His correction brings their priorities into view rather than declaring that small acts of obedience are worthless.

Faithfulness is πίστις, pistis (PISS-tiss), a word that can describe faith or trust, and also the reliability of someone who can be depended on. Thayer's entry specifically places Matthew 23:23 under that latter meaning. The charge includes a failure to live faithfully, alongside failures of justice and mercy.

The gnat and camel make the mismatch vivid. Leviticus 11:4, 41–45 places the camel and small crawling creatures among prohibited foods. Jesus pictures careful removal of something tiny alongside swallowing something enormous. Their scruples in small matters have not stopped a much greater wrong.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as a warning against meticulous religious observance that neglects justice, mercy, and trustworthy conduct. Wesley on 23:23–24 explains the practical meaning of faithfulness; the US Catholic bishops' note on 23:23 likewise places the criticism on neglected priorities.
passages.god_plan_html:
The prophets had already joined worship with the life God seeks. Micah 6:6–8 answers questions about offerings with a call to justice, mercy, and humility. Hosea 6:4–6 places mercy and knowing God above empty sacrifice. Jesus' warning continues that concern for a faithful people.

The New Testament also connects God's saving mercy with changed conduct. Titus 3:3–8 describes salvation through His mercy and the Spirit's renewal, then calls believers to devote themselves to good deeds. God does not merely create an outwardly careful religious community; His work bears fruit in how people live and care for others.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 23:25-28
passages.section_title: A Clean Appearance Cannot Hide What Is Inside

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 25 Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, you hypocrites! You clean the outside of the cup and dish, but inside they are full of greed and self-indulgence. 26 Blind Pharisee! First clean the inside of the cup and dish, so that the outside may become clean as well. 27 Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, you hypocrites! You are like whitewashed tombs, which look beautiful on the outside but on the inside are full of dead men’s bones and every kind of impurity. 28 In the same way, on the outside you appear to be righteous, but on the inside you are full of hypocrisy and wickedness.
paragraphs: 25 Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, you hypocrites! You clean the outside of the cup and dish, but inside they are full of greed and self-indulgence. 26 Blind Pharisee! First clean the inside of the cup and dish, so that the outside may become clean as well.

27 Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, you hypocrites! You are like whitewashed tombs, which look beautiful on the outside but on the inside are full of dead men’s bones and every kind of impurity. 28 In the same way, on the outside you appear to be righteous, but on the inside you are full of hypocrisy and wickedness.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Two woes develop the difference between appearance and reality. First, Jesus compares the leaders to a cup and dish cleaned outside but filled inside with greed and self-indulgence. He calls for the inside to be cleaned first, so that the outside becomes clean as well.

Then He compares them to whitewashed tombs: attractive outside, but containing bones and uncleanness within. Numbers 19:11–16 explains the uncleanness associated with contact with a corpse or grave. A later Jewish text, Mishnah Shekalim 1:1, records the marking of graves in Adar. That supplies background for making graves visible; Matthew's own emphasis is the contrast between the tomb's appearance and its contents.

Jesus states the comparison plainly: outward righteousness conceals hypocrisy and wickedness. The two pictures expose a religious life concerned with how it appears while its inner character remains corrupt. Cleaning the outside cannot settle what is wrong within.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand these pictures as a call for inner character to agree with outward conduct. Wesley on 23:25 connects the inner corruption with unjust gain and uncontrolled desires; the US Catholic bishops' notes on 23:25–28 emphasize appearances hiding impurity.
passages.god_plan_html:
Scripture gives a positive answer to the need for inward cleansing. Psalm 51:6–12 asks God for a clean heart and a willing spirit. In Ezekiel 36:24–28, He promises cleansing, a new heart, and His Spirit leading His people into obedience.

Titus 3:4–8 describes God's mercy bringing new birth and renewal through the Holy Spirit, poured out through Jesus Christ. It then calls those who believe to do good. The larger purpose reaches from the inward change God gives into the visible life of His people.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 23:29-36
passages.section_title: Honoring Past Prophets While Rejecting Those God Sends

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 29 Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, you hypocrites! You build tombs for the prophets and decorate the monuments of the righteous. 30 And you say, ‘If we had lived in the days of our fathers, we would not have been partners with them in shedding the blood of the prophets.’ 31 So you testify against yourselves that you are the sons of those who murdered the prophets. 32 Fill up, then, the measure of the sin of your fathers. 33 You snakes! You brood of vipers! How will you escape the sentence of hell? 34 Because of this, I am sending you prophets and wise men and teachers. Some of them you will kill and crucify, and others you will flog in your synagogues and persecute from town to town. 35 And so upon you will come all the righteous blood shed on earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Berechiah, whom you murdered between the temple and the altar. 36 Truly I tell you, all these things will come upon this generation.
paragraphs: 29 Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, you hypocrites! You build tombs for the prophets and decorate the monuments of the righteous. 30 And you say, ‘If we had lived in the days of our fathers, we would not have been partners with them in shedding the blood of the prophets.’ 31 So you testify against yourselves that you are the sons of those who murdered the prophets. 32 Fill up, then, the measure of the sin of your fathers. 33 You snakes! You brood of vipers! How will you escape the sentence of hell?

34 Because of this, I am sending you prophets and wise men and teachers. Some of them you will kill and crucify, and others you will flog in your synagogues and persecute from town to town. 35 And so upon you will come all the righteous blood shed on earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Berechiah, whom you murdered between the temple and the altar. 36 Truly I tell you, all these things will come upon this generation.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The final woe challenges the leaders' claim that they would never have joined their ancestors in killing the prophets. They build and decorate the prophets' tombs, yet Jesus says their conduct continues the same pattern. Their treatment of the messengers He sends will reveal the gap between honoring faithful people of the past and receiving God's word in the present.

Jesus warns that some of His messengers will be killed, flogged, or pursued from town to town. The warning recalls what He told the disciples in Matthew 10:16–23. He then speaks of the righteous blood shed from Abel to Zechariah and says these things will come upon this generation. The charge concerns participation in a repeated course of wrongdoing; it gives no license to assign inherited guilt to every later person of the same ancestry.

Abel's murder is recorded in Genesis 4:8–12. A prophet named Zechariah is killed in the temple courtyard in 2 Chronicles 24:20–22, but that account calls him the son of Jehoiada, while Matthew names the son of Berechiah. Zechariah 1:1 names the prophet Zechariah as Berechiah's son without describing his death. Those details should remain visible rather than being silently treated as identical.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read the warning as exposing people who honor earlier messengers while rejecting those God sends to them. Wesley on 23:29–35 connects their present conduct with their ancestors' violence; the US Catholic bishops' notes on 23:29–36 likewise emphasize that continuing pattern.
passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 7:51–60 shows the pattern continuing when Stephen charges his hearers with resisting God's messengers and is then killed. Yet his final prayer asks that the sin not be held against them. The witness to Jesus includes both the cost of faithfulness and mercy toward persecutors.

The reference to Abel also opens a striking New Testament connection. Hebrews 12:22–24 brings believers to Jesus, the mediator of the new covenant, and His sprinkled blood, which speaks a better word than Abel's. Alongside the warning about bloodshed stands God's saving work through the One whose death brings people near to Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 23:37-39
passages.section_title: The King Who Longs to Gather Jerusalem's Children

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 37 O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those sent to her, how often I have longed to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you were unwilling! 38 Look, your house is left to you desolate. 39 For I tell you that you will not see Me again until you say, ‘Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord.’”
paragraphs: 37 O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those sent to her, how often I have longed to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you were unwilling! 38 Look, your house is left to you desolate. 39 For I tell you that you will not see Me again until you say, ‘Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord.’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The sharp warnings end in a lament over Jerusalem. Jesus speaks of its killing God's messengers, yet also of His repeated desire to gather its children as a hen gathers her chicks. The refusal is set beside His longing, so the judgment is heard together with grief over those He would shelter.

The image recalls the shelter of God's wings in Psalm 91:1–4. Jesus then announces desolation and speaks of a future recognition using Psalm 118:26, the blessing already heard at His entry into Jerusalem.

The next scene shows Jesus leaving the temple and predicting its destruction (Matthew 24:1–2). The house left desolate therefore leads directly into the disciples' questions about what is coming. Jesus' lament holds His desire to gather, their unwillingness, and the approaching judgment together.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly hear both grief over rejection and a warning of judgment. Readers differ over the future welcome in the closing verse. Wesley on 23:39 expects a later joyful reception of Jesus. The US Catholic bishops' note on 23:37–39 records two readings: eventual acceptance, or recognition of Him when He comes as judge. The words themselves do not give a complete timetable.
passages.god_plan_html:
God's purpose includes His faithfulness and mercy toward those to whom He made promises. Romans 11:1–6 rejects the claim that God has simply cast off His people and points to a remnant chosen by grace. Romans 11:25–32 then warns Gentile believers against pride, describes a hardening in part, and places Israel's future within God's continuing call and mercy.

That larger passage guards against treating the lament as permission to despise Jewish people or declare God's faithfulness finished. Jesus' desire to gather and His warning of desolation belong within the wider scriptural story of God's judgment, promises, and mercy. The connection does not require assigning a date or a complete end-times sequence to these three verses.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 24:1-3
passages.section_title: The Temple's Future and the Disciples' Questions

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 As Jesus left the temple and was walking away, His disciples came up to Him to point out its buildings. 2 “Do you see all these things?” He replied. “Truly I tell you, not one stone here will be left on another; every one will be thrown down.” 3 While Jesus was sitting on the Mount of Olives, the disciples came to Him privately. “Tell us,” they said, “when will these things happen, and what will be the sign of Your coming and of the end of the age?”
paragraphs: 1 As Jesus left the temple and was walking away, His disciples came up to Him to point out its buildings. 2 “Do you see all these things?” He replied. “Truly I tell you, not one stone here will be left on another; every one will be thrown down.”

3 While Jesus was sitting on the Mount of Olives, the disciples came to Him privately. “Tell us,” they said, “when will these things happen, and what will be the sign of Your coming and of the end of the age?”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus has ended His lament over Jerusalem by announcing that its house is left desolate. As He leaves the temple, the disciples draw attention to the buildings. His answer is startling: the stones they admire will be thrown down. The warning about the house now becomes a direct prediction about the temple before them.

Later, on the Mount of Olives, the disciples ask Him privately when these things will happen and what will signal His coming and the end of the age. Their questions set up the teaching that continues through chapters 24 and 25. Keeping the questions in view helps us follow the warnings, promises, and calls to faithfulness that follow.

Coming is παρουσία, parousia (pah-roo-SEE-ah), which can mean presence or arrival. Thayer's entry includes this verse among references to Jesus' return. The word names what the disciples ask about; it does not by itself provide a date or settle how every later part of His answer fits together.

Mark 13:1–4 records the admiration of the temple's stones and names Peter, James, John, and Andrew as the private questioners. Luke 21:5–7 also records the temple prediction and their question about its signs. Each account helps us see the setting without replacing Matthew's own wording.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand Jesus to predict the temple's destruction and to answer questions that also concern His return and the end of the age. Wesley on 24:3 distinguishes those subjects, and the US Catholic bishops' notes on 24:2–3 likewise connect the temple warning with the preceding lament while distinguishing it from the final coming. Readers differ over how the later details relate to those questions.
passages.god_plan_html:
The temple warning does not leave God's people without hope of His presence. In another temple scene, John 2:19–22 explains that Jesus' words about raising the temple concerned His body and resurrection. Ephesians 2:13–22 then describes people brought near through Him and built together as God's dwelling through the Spirit. Those passages develop the wider temple theme around the risen Christ.

After His resurrection, Jesus again hears a question about the timing of the kingdom in Acts 1:6–11. He places the times under the Father's authority and directs the disciples to their Spirit-empowered witness; His return is also promised. Learning about God's future work belongs together with faithful participation in the work He gives His people now.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 24:4-8
passages.section_title: Do Not Be Deceived or Overcome by Fear

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 4 Jesus answered, “See to it that no one deceives you. 5 For many will come in My name, claiming, ‘I am the Christ,’ and will deceive many. 6 You will hear of wars and rumors of wars, but see to it that you are not alarmed. These things must happen, but the end is still to come. 7 Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. There will be famines and earthquakes in various places. 8 All these are the beginning of birth pains.
paragraphs: 4 Jesus answered, “See to it that no one deceives you. 5 For many will come in My name, claiming, ‘I am the Christ,’ and will deceive many. 6 You will hear of wars and rumors of wars, but see to it that you are not alarmed. These things must happen, but the end is still to come.
7 Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. There will be famines and earthquakes in various places. 8 All these are the beginning of birth pains.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus begins His answer with a warning about deception. Many will claim to be the Christ and lead people astray. His disciples need to test those claims rather than follow someone simply because that person speaks in His name.

He then addresses wars and rumors of wars. His instruction is not to be alarmed, because these things must happen while the end is still to come. He goes on to speak of nations and kingdoms in conflict, famines, and earthquakes in various places, calling them the beginning of birth pains. The movement of His answer matters: suffering is real, yet its appearance is not permission to announce that the end has arrived.

The birth-pain picture describes distress before what is coming. These verses do not give a start date, a calendar, or a method for calculating the end from reports of disasters. Luke 21:8–11 gives a related warning against people announcing that the time is near and against being terrified by conflict. Jesus prepares His followers to remain discerning and steady.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand these verses as warnings against false messiahs and fearful conclusions drawn from conflict and calamity. They differ over how the events relate to Jerusalem's fall and the period before Christ's final return.

Wesley on 24:4–6 begins with events surrounding Jerusalem's destruction while allowing that some words reach further into the future. The US Catholic bishops' notes on 24:4–8 place the calamities within the suffering that precedes the end of the age. Neither explanation makes every report of war an announcement that the end has already come.
passages.god_plan_html:
The image of birth pains has a hopeful parallel in Romans 8:18–25. Paul describes creation groaning while awaiting freedom from decay, and believers waiting for the redemption of their bodies. This is a related picture of suffering before God's promised renewal, rather than a timetable identifying every event in Matthew.

1 Peter 1:3–9 grounds living hope in Jesus' resurrection even while believers grieve through trials. 1 Thessalonians 4:13–18 likewise offers encouragement through the promise that those who belong to Christ will be with Him. The larger hope rests in His saving work and promised future, giving His people reason to remain faithful through uncertainty and suffering.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 24:9-14
passages.section_title: Faithful Witness Through Persecution

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 Then they will deliver you over to be persecuted and killed, and you will be hated by all nations because of My name. 10 At that time many will fall away and will betray and hate one another, 11 and many false prophets will arise and deceive many. 12 Because of the multiplication of wickedness, the love of most will grow cold. 13 But the one who perseveres to the end will be saved. 14 And this gospel of the kingdom will be preached in all the world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come.
paragraphs: 9 Then they will deliver you over to be persecuted and killed, and you will be hated by all nations because of My name. 10 At that time many will fall away and will betray and hate one another, 11 and many false prophets will arise and deceive many. 12 Because of the multiplication of wickedness, the love of most will grow cold.
13 But the one who perseveres to the end will be saved. 14 And this gospel of the kingdom will be preached in all the world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After speaking about deception, war, famine, and earthquakes, Jesus turns to what His followers will face because they bear His name. They will be handed over, persecuted, and killed. The danger also reaches inside their relationships: many will fall away, betray one another, and hate one another.

Fall away is σκανδαλίζω, skandalizō (skahn-dah-LEE-zoh). Thayer's entry explains that the word can describe stumbling into sin or turning away from someone a person should trust; it specifically includes Matthew 24:10 in that latter use. The warning involves a serious failure of loyalty, seen here alongside betrayal and hatred.

False prophets add deception to the pressure, and increasing wickedness chills love. Jesus then promises salvation to the one who perseveres. The verb is ὑπομένω, hypomenō (hoo-poh-MEH-noh), which Thayer's entry explains here as holding fast to faith in Christ under trials. His call is to remain faithful through the pressure He has described.

The passage ends with the gospel of the kingdom being proclaimed throughout the world as a testimony to all nations, followed by the end. Persecution and betrayal do not cancel that witness. The promise stands beside the warning: Jesus prepares His followers for costly faithfulness while speaking of the message reaching beyond them.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly hear a call to faithfulness through persecution and a promise that God's good news will be proclaimed among the nations. They differ over the period in view and how the warning about falling away relates to salvation.

On timing, Wesley's notes on 24:9–14 connect the passage first with the early church and Jerusalem's destruction. He understands the worldwide proclamation in light of the apostles' mission. The US Catholic bishops' note on 24:4–14 describes suffering that continues until the gospel reaches the nations and the end comes.

Christians also differ over whether the church will pass through the final tribulation. The Catholic Church teaches that it will face a final trial before Christ's return (Catechism, 675–677). Dallas Theological Seminary's statement of belief, XVIII–XX, expects Christ to gather the church into heaven before a future period of tribulation. These are different frameworks for reading the larger discourse; the seminary's statement is its own teaching, rather than a belief shared by all Protestants.

On enduring faith, Reformed churches following the Westminster Confession, 17, and Baptists following the 1689 Confession, 17, teach that God keeps those truly brought to faith so that they finally persevere, even though they may fall into serious sin for a time. Endurance is the outcome of His keeping them, rather than a way of earning salvation.

Catholic teaching says that faith is God's free gift and can be lost, and calls believers to nourish it and persevere (Catechism, 162). The Methodist Articles of Religion, XII, likewise allow that a person may depart from grace, while affirming repentance and restoration through God's grace. These readings take the danger of falling away seriously without treating every failure as beyond forgiveness.
passages.god_plan_html:
The New Testament shows witness continuing under pressure. In Acts 4:23–31, believers respond to threats by praying for boldness, and the Spirit enables them to speak God's word. 1 Peter 4:12–19 calls those suffering for Christ to entrust themselves to their faithful Creator and continue doing good. God's purpose includes forming faithful witnesses whose conduct reflects Him even when they are opposed.

Revelation 7:9–17 gives a hopeful picture of a multitude from every nation, standing before God and the Lamb after great tribulation. Their salvation is attributed to God and the Lamb, who shepherds them and wipes away their tears. This provides a supported connection between witness among the nations, suffering, and God's saving care; it does not by itself settle every question about the timetable in Matthew.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 24:15-22
passages.section_title: An Urgent Warning to Flee from Danger

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 So when you see standing in the holy place ‘the abomination of desolation,’ spoken of by the prophet Daniel (let the reader understand), 16 then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains. 17 Let no one on the housetop come down to retrieve anything from his house. 18 And let no one in the field return for his cloak. 19 How miserable those days will be for pregnant and nursing mothers! 20 Pray that your flight will not occur in the winter or on the Sabbath. 21 For at that time there will be great tribulation, unseen from the beginning of the world until now, and never to be seen again. 22 If those days had not been cut short, nobody would be saved. But for the sake of the elect, those days will be cut short.
paragraphs: 15 So when you see standing in the holy place ‘the abomination of desolation,’ spoken of by the prophet Daniel (let the reader understand), 16 then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains. 17 Let no one on the housetop come down to retrieve anything from his house. 18 And let no one in the field return for his cloak.

19 How miserable those days will be for pregnant and nursing mothers! 20 Pray that your flight will not occur in the winter or on the Sabbath. 21 For at that time there will be great tribulation, unseen from the beginning of the world until now, and never to be seen again. 22 If those days had not been cut short, nobody would be saved. But for the sake of the elect, those days will be cut short.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus has described persecution, betrayal, and the gospel's proclamation among the nations. He now gives a warning tied to a particular place: when those in Judea see the desolating abomination standing in the holy place, they must flee to the mountains. He expressly directs the reader to Daniel.

Abomination is βδέλυγμα, bdelygma (BDEH-loog-mah), something detestable. Thayer's entry explains its frequent association with idolatry. Daniel 11:31 and 12:11 connect the expression with the stopping of regular sacrifice and the defiling of the sanctuary; Daniel 9:27 also joins sacrifice, abomination, and desolation. The picture is of a holy place violated and laid waste, with grave danger for those nearby.

The flight must be immediate. People are not to return for possessions or even a cloak. Jesus names the hardship for pregnant and nursing mothers and tells His hearers to pray about winter and the Sabbath. His instructions take the difficulty of escaping seriously.

The distress will be unlike anything before or after it. Yet the warning ends with a limit: the days are cut short for the sake of God's chosen people. Mark 13:14–20 gives the related warning. Luke 21:20–24 speaks of Jerusalem surrounded by armies and likewise tells people in Judea to flee. These related accounts help frame the different readings of the event.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians agree that Jesus gives a serious warning rather than a reason to remain in danger. They differ over the desecration and the period He describes.

Wesley on 24:15–22 connects the warning first with the Roman attack on Jerusalem, while allowing that the words may reach further. Calvin on 24:15–22 likewise applies it to the temple's loss and Jerusalem's calamity. The US Catholic bishops' notes on 24:15–22 connect the desecration with the Romans. These are the commentators' readings, rather than a claim that every member of their traditions resolves every detail alike.

A future reading appears in John Walvoord's explanation of 24:15–25. He expects a future temple desecration before Christ's return, connecting Daniel's final week with a seven-year period and its latter half with the great tribulation. The Dallas Theological Seminary statement, XIX, also teaches a future period of tribulation and cites Matthew 24:15–21. That timetable comes from reading these passages together; it is not a date or duration stated in Matthew's warning itself.
passages.god_plan_html:
Daniel's vision does not end with distress. Daniel 12:1–3 speaks of deliverance for God's people, resurrection, and those who lead others to righteousness. Jesus' use of Daniel places this warning beside a larger hope: God's purposes reach beyond the calamity and beyond death.

Another New Testament passage describes evil's limit in relation to Christ. 2 Thessalonians 2:1–12 warns about deception and a lawless opponent who exalts himself in God's temple, then announces his destruction at the Lord's coming. This is a supported connection with the themes of defilement, deception, and Christ's victory, without treating every question about the two passages' timing as settled.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 24:23-28
passages.section_title: Do Not Chase Claims of a Hidden Christ

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 23 At that time, if anyone says to you, ‘Look, here is the Christ!’ or ‘There He is!’ do not believe it. 24 For false Christs and false prophets will appear and perform great signs and wonders to deceive even the elect, if that were possible. 25 See, I have told you in advance. 26 So if they tell you, ‘There He is, in the wilderness,’ do not go out, or, ‘Here He is, in the inner rooms,’ do not believe it. 27 For just as the lightning comes from the east and flashes as far as the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. 28 Wherever there is a carcass, there the vultures will gather.
paragraphs: 23 At that time, if anyone says to you, ‘Look, here is the Christ!’ or ‘There He is!’ do not believe it. 24 For false Christs and false prophets will appear and perform great signs and wonders to deceive even the elect, if that were possible. 25 See, I have told you in advance.

26 So if they tell you, ‘There He is, in the wilderness,’ do not go out, or, ‘Here He is, in the inner rooms,’ do not believe it. 27 For just as the lightning comes from the east and flashes as far as the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. 28 Wherever there is a carcass, there the vultures will gather.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus follows the warning about great distress with another warning about deception. Reports that the Christ is here or there must not draw His followers away. False christs and false prophets will offer great signs and wonders, with deception so powerful that even God's chosen people are named as its target, if that were possible.

Jesus emphasizes that He has warned them beforehand. Claims about the wilderness or hidden rooms are to be refused. His comparison with lightning then points in another direction: the coming of the Son of Man will not depend on someone's private report of a concealed savior.

The passage ends with the picture of vultures gathering where a carcass lies. A carcass is a dead body; the picture is stark, and readers differ over exactly how it completes the warning. Luke 17:23–24, 37 also contains the warning against chasing reports, the lightning comparison, and the carcass saying. Those connections matter more than turning the birds into an unverified code for a modern event.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the warning to mean that impressive wonders do not by themselves establish a claimant as Christ. Readers differ over the final picture.

The US Catholic bishops' note on 24:26–28 links the vultures with the clear, recognizable character of the coming. Wesley on 24:28 sees a warning of judgment on Jerusalem, associating the birds with Rome's eagles. Calvin on 24:28 takes the gathering as a comparison calling scattered believers to remain united to Christ, while Walvoord's explanation sees judgment following corruption as naturally as vultures gather at a dead body. These are different explanations of the picture; none requires accepting a private claim that Jesus has appeared in a hidden place.
passages.god_plan_html:
The New Testament places deceptive wonders beside the final defeat of evil. 2 Thessalonians 2:8–12 describes powerful deception and the lawless one's destruction through Christ's appearing. God's purpose is not overturned by the strength of a false claim or the spectacle attached to it.

The birds gathering around the dead also have a parallel in Revelation 19:17–21, where the defeat of the beast and false prophet is followed by birds consuming those killed in judgment. 2 Thessalonians 1:6–10 likewise joins Christ's appearing with judgment on evil and relief for His afflicted people. These are related pictures of His victory, rather than proof that only one reading of Matthew's saying is possible.

The true Christ is also the center of God's gathering purpose. Ephesians 1:7–10 connects forgiveness through His blood with God's plan to bring all things in heaven and on earth together in Him. That wider purpose gives the warning its positive direction: His people belong to the Savior through whom God brings His work to completion.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 24:29-31
passages.section_title: The Son of Man Comes in Glory and Gathers His People

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 29 Immediately after the tribulation of those days: ‘The sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light; the stars will fall from the sky, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken.’ 30 At that time the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven, and all the tribes of the earth will mourn. They will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory. 31 And He will send out His angels with a loud trumpet call, and they will gather His elect from the four winds, from one end of the heavens to the other.
paragraphs: 29 Immediately after the tribulation of those days: ‘The sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light; the stars will fall from the sky, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken.’

30 At that time the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven, and all the tribes of the earth will mourn. They will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory. 31 And He will send out His angels with a loud trumpet call, and they will gather His elect from the four winds, from one end of the heavens to the other.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus now speaks of what follows the distress: the darkening of sun and moon, falling stars, and the shaking of heavenly powers. The language recalls Isaiah 13:6–13 and 34:1–8, where upheaval in the heavens accompanies God's judgment. The prophets provide the setting for hearing these words.

The Son of Man appears with power and great glory, and the tribes of the earth mourn. Daniel 7:9–14 describes one like a son of man coming with heaven's clouds and receiving enduring dominion. The mourning also recalls Zechariah 12:10–14, where Jerusalem's people and clans mourn over the one pierced. Zechariah describes mourning among Jerusalem's people and clans, providing a concrete background for the scene.

Jesus then sends angels with a great trumpet call to gather His chosen people from the four winds. Isaiah 27:12–13 joins a great trumpet with the gathering of Israel's scattered people to worship the LORD. Mark 13:24–27 gives the related account of the Son of Man and the gathering. The warning about false private appearances is followed by a scene of His power and His care for those who belong to Him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read this as a promise of Christ's glorious coming and the gathering of His people. They differ over the preceding period of distress and how the gathering relates to other promises of His return.

Calvin on 24:29–31 understands the distress to encompass the church's trials through its earthly life, ending in Christ's final appearing and the gathering of His scattered church. Wesley on 24:29–31 likewise reads these verses as His final coming and identifies the gathered people as those who have endured in faith.

Walvoord on 24:26–31 places the scene after a future great tribulation and distinguishes it from an earlier gathering of the church into heaven. He understands the elect here broadly as the saints of all ages, while acknowledging another view that gives special emphasis to Israel. His own explanation shows that readers who expect a future tribulation do not all identify the gathered people in exactly the same way.
passages.god_plan_html:
God's purpose brings His people to their King. Daniel 7:13–14 gives the Son of Man a kingdom served by people of every nation and language, with a rule that will not pass away. Revelation 1:5–7 joins Jesus' saving blood, His people made a kingdom, and His coming with the clouds. It explicitly says every eye will see Him and repeats the mourning of the tribes.

The trumpet also has a hopeful New Testament connection. 1 Corinthians 15:50–57 speaks of the dead being raised and believers being changed at the trumpet, with death overcome through Jesus Christ. This is a related promise of resurrection and victory, rather than proof that every detail of the two passages describes an identical sequence. The future held before God's people is life with the victorious Son, whose rule defeats even death (1 Corinthians 15:20–28).
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 24:32-35
passages.section_title: Recognizing the Season and Trusting Jesus' Words

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 32 Now learn this lesson from the fig tree: As soon as its branches become tender and sprout leaves, you know that summer is near. 33 So also, when you see all these things, you will know that He is near, right at the door. 34 Truly I tell you, this generation will not pass away until all these things have happened. 35 Heaven and earth will pass away, but My words will never pass away.
paragraphs: 32 Now learn this lesson from the fig tree: As soon as its branches become tender and sprout leaves, you know that summer is near. 33 So also, when you see all these things, you will know that He is near, right at the door.
34 Truly I tell you, this generation will not pass away until all these things have happened. 35 Heaven and earth will pass away, but My words will never pass away.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After describing the Son of Man's coming and the gathering of His people, Jesus turns to a familiar seasonal lesson. Tender branches and new leaves tell people that summer is near. In the same way, His hearers are to recognize the nearness indicated by the things He has described.

The comparison itself explains the tree's role: people recognize a season from what they see. Luke 21:29–33 gives the related lesson with the fig tree and all the trees, then speaks of knowing that God's kingdom is near. The tree in this illustration should be read within that comparison before another symbolic meaning is assigned to it.

Jesus then says that this generation will not pass away before all these things happen. Generation is γενεά, genea (geh-neh-AH). Thayer's entry includes family descent, people sharing a character, and people living at the same time; it lists Matthew 24:34 under that last sense. Readers' different understandings of the events and the people in view are set out below.

The closing assurance gives the passage its firm foundation: heaven and earth will pass away, but Jesus' words will never pass away. The next verse warns that the day and hour are unknown. The lesson joins recognition and confidence in His words with a limit on what His followers are told about timing.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians agree that Jesus calls His followers to recognize what He has described and trust His words. They differ over the generation in view and how all these things relate to the temple's destruction and His coming.

Wesley on 24:32–35 connects this generation with people then living and the destruction of Jerusalem. Calvin on 24:34 likewise says the disciples' generation would experience the foretold troubles, while later generations would continue to face such suffering. The US Catholic bishops' note on 24:34 offers the generation of Matthew and his community as another explanation.

A future reading understands the generation as those alive when the final signs occur. Walvoord's discussion of 24:32–36 includes this among the possible explanations and applies the tree's seasonal lesson to those who see the coming tribulation. He treats the tree as an illustration of recognizing a season, rather than a direct identification of modern Israel.

A different reading in Scofield's note on 24:34 takes generation in the sense of the people of Israel. It understands the promise to mean that Israel will be preserved until the foretold events are fulfilled. These are distinct readings of the passage; the dictionary's range of meanings does not by itself settle the choice between them.
passages.god_plan_html:
The permanence of Jesus' words belongs within a wider promise about God's word. Isaiah 40:6–8 contrasts human life's passing glory with the word that endures. 1 Peter 1:22–25 applies that promise to the good news believers have received and connects it with their new birth and love for one another. The word that announces God's future also brings people into a changed life now.

Hebrews 12:25–29 describes created things being shaken while God's people receive an unshakable kingdom. 2 Peter 3:8–14 joins the coming passing of the present order with God's promise of a new heaven and earth, calling believers to holy and peaceful lives as they wait. Trust in His enduring promise is meant to shape how His people live, rather than merely satisfy curiosity about a date.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

deeper_study.title: Is the Bible the Inerrant Word of God?

passages.title: Matthew 24:36-39
passages.section_title: An Unknown Day and the Lesson of Noah

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 36 No one knows about that day or hour, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father. 37 As it was in the days of Noah, so will it be at the coming of the Son of Man. 38 For in the days before the flood, people were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, up to the day Noah entered the ark. 39 And they were oblivious until the flood came and swept them all away. So will it be at the coming of the Son of Man.
paragraphs: 36 No one knows about that day or hour, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father.

37 As it was in the days of Noah, so will it be at the coming of the Son of Man. 38 For in the days before the flood, people were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, up to the day Noah entered the ark. 39 And they were oblivious until the flood came and swept them all away. So will it be at the coming of the Son of Man.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus has assured His followers that His words will not pass away. He now sets a limit on their knowledge: the day and hour are known only to the Father, not to the angels or the Son. Mark 13:32–37 gives the same statement and follows it with repeated calls to keep watch.

Jesus compares the coming of the Son of Man with Noah's day. People continued eating, drinking, and marrying until Noah entered the ark. They were unaware until the flood swept them away. His point is how people can continue ordinary life without taking approaching judgment seriously; the passage does not make eating or marriage sinful in themselves.

Genesis 7:1–16 describes Noah following God's instruction, entering the ark with his family, and being shut in by the LORD. Jesus' comparison brings the contrast between preparation and unpreparedness into His teaching about the coming day. He is preparing His hearers to live ready rather than giving them its date.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly understand Noah's story here as a warning against being unprepared, alongside the clear limit on knowing the time. Calvin on 24:37–39 emphasizes people treating ordinary life as though it could never change; the US Catholic bishops' note on 24:37–39 likewise stresses the flood's unexpected arrival for the unprepared.

The Son's statement about not knowing has also required careful explanation. Calvin on 24:36 understands it as a limitation in Jesus' human knowledge while He carries out His mission, without denying His divine nature. The Catholic Catechism, 472–474, describes His human knowledge within real human conditions, while emphasizing that what He admitted not knowing concerned what He was not sent to reveal. These explanations seek to hold His real human life together with His identity as God's Son.
passages.god_plan_html:
The New Testament itself develops Noah's story as a lesson about faith and God's saving care. Hebrews 11:7 describes Noah trusting God's warning and preparing the ark for his family's preservation. 2 Peter 2:4–9 joins Noah's preservation with God's knowledge of how to rescue the godly and judge wrongdoing. These connections support hope in God's care without turning every detail of the ark into an end-times calendar.

2 Peter 3:3–14 returns to the flood when answering people who dismiss the promise of Christ's coming. It explains God's patience in relation to repentance and calls His people to holy lives as they await what He has promised. Preparation therefore includes responding to Him now and living in light of His future.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 24:40-44
passages.section_title: One Taken, One Left: Be Ready for Your Lord

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 40 Two men will be in the field: one will be taken and the other left. 41 Two women will be grinding at the mill: one will be taken and the other left. 42 Therefore keep watch, because you do not know the day on which your Lord will come. 43 But understand this: If the homeowner had known in which watch of the night the thief was coming, he would have kept watch and would not have let his house be broken into. 44 For this reason, you also must be ready, because the Son of Man will come at an hour you do not expect.
paragraphs: 40 Two men will be in the field: one will be taken and the other left. 41 Two women will be grinding at the mill: one will be taken and the other left. 42 Therefore keep watch, because you do not know the day on which your Lord will come.

43 But understand this: If the homeowner had known in which watch of the night the thief was coming, he would have kept watch and would not have let his house be broken into. 44 For this reason, you also must be ready, because the Son of Man will come at an hour you do not expect.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus continues with two scenes of ordinary work: two men in a field and two women grinding at a mill. In each pair, one is taken and the other left. He immediately draws the practical conclusion that His followers must keep watch because they do not know the day their Lord will come.

Taken comes from παραλαμβάνω, paralambanō (pah-rah-lahm-BAH-noh), to take someone with oneself or receive someone. Thayer's entry includes both companions and people taken as prisoners. The word alone does not tell us whether being taken here means rescue or judgment; that question depends on how the surrounding comparison is read.

Keep watch is γρηγορέω, grēgoreō (gray-gor-EH-oh). Thayer's entry explains its use here as staying attentive and active. Jesus illustrates the need through a homeowner who would have guarded his house if he had known when the thief was coming. The comparison concerns an unexpected arrival and the need to be ready.

The coming of the Son of Man will be at an hour they do not expect. Jesus then moves directly to a servant carrying out his master's work. That next picture makes the kind of readiness He seeks concrete: faithful conduct while waiting.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Readers differ over which person is taken. Both main readings recognize a decisive separation and the call to be ready.

Wesley on 24:40–41 understands the taken person to enter God's protection, while the other remains exposed to calamity. The US Catholic bishops' note on 24:40–41 similarly proposes being taken into the kingdom and being left for destruction. In this reading, being taken is the hopeful side of the contrast.

Walvoord on 24:40–41 reads it the other way: as the flood swept away the unprepared, the person taken is taken in judgment, while the one left enters the kingdom. He distinguishes this scene from the earlier gathering of the church that he expects before the tribulation. The different outcomes attached to the same words show why the context must be considered alongside the Greek verb.
passages.god_plan_html:
The wider promise to Christ's people is that they will be with Him. In John 14:1–6, Jesus speaks of preparing a place and welcoming His followers into His presence. 1 Thessalonians 4:13–18 joins His coming with resurrection, His people gathered to Him, and encouragement rooted in being with Him always. These promises supply hope without making the disputed meaning of taken here certain.

1 Thessalonians 5:1–11 likewise uses the thief comparison, then calls believers to remain awake, live in faith and love, hold the hope of salvation, and build one another up. God's purpose gives readiness a positive shape: a community living faithfully together as it waits for its Lord.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 24:45-51
passages.section_title: The Master Returns to Find How His Servants Have Lived

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 45 Who then is the faithful and wise servant, whom the master has put in charge of his household, to give the others their food at the proper time? 46 Blessed is that servant whose master finds him doing so when he returns. 47 Truly I tell you, he will put him in charge of all his possessions. 48 But suppose that servant is wicked and says in his heart, ‘My master will be away a long time.’ 49 And he begins to beat his fellow servants and to eat and drink with drunkards. 50 The master of that servant will come on a day he does not expect and at an hour he does not anticipate. 51 Then he will cut him to pieces and assign him a place with the hypocrites, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.
paragraphs: 45 Who then is the faithful and wise servant, whom the master has put in charge of his household, to give the others their food at the proper time? 46 Blessed is that servant whose master finds him doing so when he returns. 47 Truly I tell you, he will put him in charge of all his possessions.

48 But suppose that servant is wicked and says in his heart, ‘My master will be away a long time.’ 49 And he begins to beat his fellow servants and to eat and drink with drunkards. 50 The master of that servant will come on a day he does not expect and at an hour he does not anticipate. 51 Then he will cut him to pieces and assign him a place with the hypocrites, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus answers the call to readiness with a household scene. A master places a servant in charge of providing food for the others at the proper time. The faithful and wise servant is blessed when the master returns and finds him doing that work, and he receives greater responsibility.

The other possibility is a servant who assumes the master will be away a long time. He begins beating his fellow servants and eating and drinking with drunkards. The delay becomes an excuse to abuse those placed in his care and live for himself.

The master returns unexpectedly and brings severe judgment, assigning the wicked servant a place with the hypocrites, with weeping and gnashing of teeth. Jesus ends this part of the teaching with both a blessing for faithful care and a warning against using His apparent absence as permission for wrongdoing.

Luke 12:35–48 gives a related teaching about servants, the returning master, and responsibility for what has been entrusted to them. The illustrations that follow in Matthew 25 continue the concern with readiness and accountability.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand readiness here as faithful service rather than merely watching for a date. Calvin on 24:45–51 particularly emphasizes the responsibility of those caring for others, and the US Catholic bishops' notes on 24:45–51 likewise connect watchfulness with carrying out the assigned duty.

Readers differ over how to describe the wicked servant's earlier relationship with the master. Churches following the Westminster Confession, 17, or the 1689 Baptist Confession, 17, hold that those truly brought to saving faith will finally persevere. Within that understanding, a final rejection is distinguished from a true believer's temporary fall into sin.

Wesley on 24:48–51 describes a servant who has put away faith and a good conscience. The Methodist Articles of Religion, XII, allow departure from grace and restoration through repentance; Catholic teaching also warns that faith can be lost (Catechism, 162). These readings differ about falling away, while retaining the seriousness of the warning against abuse and unfaithfulness.
passages.god_plan_html:
God's purpose includes care for His household and an honest reckoning of those entrusted with it. 1 Corinthians 4:1–5 calls Christ's servants to faithfulness and looks toward His coming, when hidden things and motives are brought to light. 1 Corinthians 3:5–15 places the servants' different tasks within God's work: He gives the growth, and each person's labor is tested. Faithful service matters even when it attracts little public attention.

1 Peter 5:1–4 applies this care directly to elders, calling them to serve God's flock willingly, through example and without greed or domination, as they await the Chief Shepherd. The returning Lord seeks a people cared for in His name, with their leaders reflecting His character. Waiting for Him belongs together with serving the people He has entrusted to us.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 25:1-13
passages.section_title: The Ten Virgins: Ready When the Bridegroom Comes

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 “At that time the kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom. 2 Five of them were foolish, and five were wise. 3 The foolish ones took their lamps but did not take along any extra oil. 4 But the wise ones took oil in flasks along with their lamps. 5 When the bridegroom was delayed, they all became drowsy and fell asleep. 6 At midnight the cry rang out: ‘Here is the bridegroom! Come out to meet him!’ 7 Then all the virgins woke up and trimmed their lamps. 8 The foolish ones said to the wise, ‘Give us some of your oil; our lamps are going out.’ 9 ‘No,’ said the wise ones, ‘or there may not be enough for both us and you. Instead, go to those who sell oil and buy some for yourselves.’ 10 But while they were on their way to buy it, the bridegroom arrived. Those who were ready went in with him to the wedding banquet, and the door was shut. 11 Later the other virgins arrived and said, ‘Lord, lord, open the door for us!’ 12 But he replied, ‘Truly I tell you, I do not know you.’ 13 Therefore keep watch, because you do not know the day or the hour.
paragraphs: 1 “At that time the kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom. 2 Five of them were foolish, and five were wise. 3 The foolish ones took their lamps but did not take along any extra oil. 4 But the wise ones took oil in flasks along with their lamps. 5 When the bridegroom was delayed, they all became drowsy and fell asleep.

6 At midnight the cry rang out: ‘Here is the bridegroom! Come out to meet him!’ 7 Then all the virgins woke up and trimmed their lamps. 8 The foolish ones said to the wise, ‘Give us some of your oil; our lamps are going out.’ 9 ‘No,’ said the wise ones, ‘or there may not be enough for both us and you. Instead, go to those who sell oil and buy some for yourselves.’ 10 But while they were on their way to buy it, the bridegroom arrived. Those who were ready went in with him to the wedding banquet, and the door was shut.

11 Later the other virgins arrived and said, ‘Lord, lord, open the door for us!’ 12 But he replied, ‘Truly I tell you, I do not know you.’ 13 Therefore keep watch, because you do not know the day or the hour.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus continues His teaching about being ready for His coming. Ten virgins go out with lamps to meet a bridegroom. Five bring extra oil and five do not. The delay affects everyone: all ten become drowsy and sleep. The difference is whether they have prepared for the wait.

When the announcement comes at midnight, all ten wake and prepare their lamps. The foolish ones discover that their lamps are going out. The others cannot provide enough oil for both groups, and while the unprepared women go to buy it, the bridegroom arrives. Those who are ready enter the wedding banquet, and the door is shut.

The late arrivals call for the door to be opened, but the bridegroom says he does not know them. Jesus closes by calling His hearers to keep watch because they do not know the day or hour. Since even the wise women slept, the story directs attention to lasting readiness rather than going without physical sleep.

The warning follows the faithful and wicked servants in Matthew 24:45–51 and leads into another story about a master returning after a long absence. Together, these scenes ask what it means to be prepared when the wait is longer than expected.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readers commonly see the bridegroom as Christ and the closed door as a serious warning about being unprepared for His coming. They differ over how much meaning to assign to the oil and other details.

Calvin on 25:1–13 emphasizes continuing in faith through the whole wait and cautions against giving every object a separate hidden meaning. Wesley on 25:3–4 understands the lamp as faith and the oil as love that keeps faith alive. The US Catholic bishops' note on 25:2–4 suggests that the oil may represent good deeds, connecting the wise and foolish women with the people who hear and either practice or neglect Jesus' teaching in Matthew 7:24–27.

Walvoord on 25:1–13 proposes the Holy Spirit and His saving work as the meaning of the oil. He places the scene at Christ's return to earth after an earlier gathering of the church, while applying its warning to Christians now as well. That timing is his reading; the different explanations share the call to genuine readiness rather than reliance on outward appearance.
passages.god_plan_html:
The wedding picture belongs to a wider biblical promise of joyful life with the Lord. Revelation 19:6–9 describes the marriage of the Lamb, the bride made ready, and the blessing of those invited to the marriage supper. This is a supported parallel to the wedding banquet here, without requiring each woman, flask, or moment in the story to match a separate future event.

In Luke 12:35–40, Jesus also describes servants with lamps burning as they wait for their master. He adds the striking promise that the master will serve the servants he finds ready. The larger hope is a welcome into His presence. Readiness is a response to the Lord whose coming His people await, and it cannot be replaced simply by being near others who know Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 25:14-30
passages.section_title: The Talents: What Will We Do with What We Have Been Given?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 For it is just like a man going on a journey, who called his servants and entrusted them with his possessions. 15 To one he gave five talents, to another two talents, and to another one talent—each according to his own ability. And he went on his journey. 16 The servant who had received the five talents went at once and put them to work and gained five more. 17 Likewise, the one with the two talents gained two more. 18 But the servant who had received the one talent went off, dug a hole in the ground, and hid his master’s money. 19 After a long time the master of those servants returned and settled accounts with them. 20 The servant who had received the five talents came and presented five more. ‘Master,’ he said, ‘you entrusted me with five talents. See, I have gained five more.’ 21 His master replied, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant! You have been faithful with a few things; I will put you in charge of many things. Enter into the joy of your master!’ 22 The servant who had received the two talents also came and said, ‘Master, you entrusted me with two talents. See, I have gained two more.’ 23 His master replied, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant! You have been faithful with a few things; I will put you in charge of many things. Enter into the joy of your master!’ 24 Finally, the servant who had received the one talent came and said, ‘Master, I knew that you are a hard man, reaping where you have not sown and gathering where you have not scattered seed. 25 So I was afraid and went out and hid your talent in the ground. But the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away from him. 30 And throw that worthless servant into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.’

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
A man going on a journey entrusts his possessions to three servants, giving five talents, two, and one according to their abilities. Two put the money to work and double it. The third buries his master's money. After a long time, the master returns and asks them to account for it.

Talent here is τάλαντον, talanton (TAH-lahn-ton). Thayer's lexicon explains it as a weight and then a sum of money measured by that weight, with its value varying by place and time. The story concerns entrusted money; applying it to abilities or opportunities is an explanation of the story, rather than the Greek word's meaning here.

The servants who began with five and two receive the same words of approval, greater responsibility, and a welcome into their master's joy. Their starting amounts and final totals differ, but both have been faithful with what they received.

The third servant describes his master as harsh and says fear led him to hide the money. The master calls him wicked and lazy: even on the servant's own description, he should have done something with what was entrusted to him. The money is taken away, and he is thrown into the outer darkness. The story makes readiness active: the wait is a time for faithful service, and neglect carries serious consequences.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly understand the entrusted wealth as a picture of responsibilities and resources to be used in God's service. The equal praise for the first two servants emphasizes faithfulness with what each received, rather than comparison with someone else's larger assignment.

Readers explain the rejected servant in different ways. Walvoord on 25:14–30 understands him as someone who never truly believed, with his inactivity revealing that lack of faith. The Westminster Confession, chapters 16–17, likewise distinguishes works as the fruit of true faith and teaches that those truly brought to saving faith will finally persevere; it does not offer a detailed explanation of every part of this parable.

Wesley on 25:14–30 stresses the warning to someone who treats merely doing no harm as enough while leaving good undone. The Catholic Catechism, 1036, applies the warnings about the wedding feast and the lazy servant to the responsibility of remaining ready through one's earthly life. These explanations retain the severity of exclusion, while differing in how they describe the person's faith and response to God.
passages.god_plan_html:
God equips His people to serve one another. 1 Peter 4:7–11 connects awareness of the approaching end with prayer, love, hospitality, and using the gifts received from God. It also says that service draws on the strength God supplies. The larger purpose is that God is glorified through Jesus Christ, rather than that one person looks more impressive than another.

Colossians 3:22–24 speaks to people doing ordinary work under earthly masters and directs them to serve Christ wholeheartedly, with the promise of an inheritance from Him. That connection brings the lesson into daily life: faithful service can involve work, money, time, and care that receives little public notice. These promises give reason to serve without specifying exactly what each future responsibility or reward will be.

passages.title: Matthew 25:31-46
passages.section_title: The Sheep and the Goats: How Have We Treated the Least?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 31 When the Son of Man comes in His glory, and all the angels with Him, He will sit on His glorious throne. 32 All the nations will be gathered before Him, and He will separate the people one from another, as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats. 33 He will place the sheep on His right and the goats on His left. 34 Then the King will say to those on His right, ‘Come, you who are blessed by My Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. 35 For I was hungry and you gave Me something to eat, I was thirsty and you gave Me something to drink, I was a stranger and you took Me in, 36 I was naked and you clothed Me, I was sick and you looked after Me, I was in prison and you visited Me.’ 37 Then the righteous will answer Him, ‘Lord, when did we see You hungry and feed You, or thirsty and give You something to drink? 38 When did we see You a stranger and take You in, or naked and clothe You? 39 When did we see You sick or in prison and visit You?’ 40 And the King will reply, ‘Truly I tell you, whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers of Mine, you did for Me.’ 41 Then He will say to those on His left, ‘Depart from Me, you who are cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. 42 For I was hungry and you gave Me nothing to eat, I was thirsty and you gave Me nothing to drink, 43 I was a stranger and you did not take Me in, I was naked and you did not clothe Me, I was sick and in prison and you did not look after Me.’ 44 And they too will reply, ‘Lord, when did we see You hungry or thirsty or a stranger or naked or sick or in prison, and did not minister to You?’ 45 Then the King will answer, ‘Truly I tell you, whatever you did not do for one of the least of these, you did not do for Me.’ 46 And they will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.”
