section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus ends this teaching with the Son of Man coming in glory, accompanied by angels and seated on His throne. All nations gather before Him. He separates people as a shepherd separates sheep from goats, placing the sheep on His right and the goats on His left.

The King welcomes those on His right to inherit the kingdom prepared for them from the foundation of the world. He recounts their care for Him when hungry, thirsty, a stranger, unclothed, sick, and imprisoned. They are surprised: when did they see Him in those conditions? His answer identifies what they did for the least of His brothers as service to Him.

Those on His left are likewise surprised, but their neglect of those in need was neglect of Him. He sends them away into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. The passage ends with eternal punishment and eternal life. Jesus presents both His authority to judge and the weight of everyday actions toward people who could easily be overlooked.

The point is more searching than whether someone recognized the King in person. Both groups ask when they saw Him. His judgment exposes the significance of the care they gave or withheld, and the next chapter moves from His teaching about judgment to the events leading to His own death.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Readers differ about who the least of His brothers are and how this judgment fits with other passages about Christ's return.

The Catholic Catechism, 1033, applies the passage as a warning against neglecting the serious needs of the poor and the little ones who are Christ's brothers. The US Catholic bishops' note on 25:31–46 acknowledges different readings and favors a focus on suffering Christians, probably missionaries, in Matthew's use of the passage. It connects receiving them with receiving Jesus in Matthew 10:40. This illustrates a difference of explanation within Catholic sources rather than a single reading held by every Catholic.

Wesley on 25:34–40 emphasizes faith working through love, care for fellow believers, and doing good to everyone. Calvin on 25:34–40 understands the promised inheritance as God's gracious gift and the deeds of mercy as the life that follows His grace. The Westminster Confession, chapters 16 and 33, similarly holds together good works as the fruit of faith and a judgment of all people (text).

Walvoord on 25:31–46 instead places this judgment of living Gentiles before Christ's thousand-year reign and identifies the brothers as Jewish people helped during the preceding time of persecution. He takes that costly care as evidence of faith, rather than as earning salvation. This differs from the final judgment of all people described by Wesley, Calvin, and the bishops' notes. The passage's demand to take mercy seriously remains central across these readings.
passages.god_plan_html:
The shepherd who judges also belongs to Scripture's promise of rescue for the vulnerable. In Ezekiel 34:11–24, God promises to seek His scattered flock, strengthen the weak, judge between members of the flock, and establish one shepherd from David's line. This is a supported parallel: the King's judgment in Matthew concerns the treatment of people who need protection and care.

The invitation to inherit the kingdom also reaches beyond a reward for a single kind action. Romans 8:14–23 describes God's children as heirs with Christ, sharing His sufferings and awaiting glory and the freeing of creation from decay. Ephesians 1:3–14 places adoption, redemption, and the promised inheritance within God's purpose to bring all things together in Christ. The kingdom prepared by the Father belongs to that larger hope.

James 2:1–17 brings this hope into the life of a congregation: the poor can be heirs of the promised kingdom, favoritism dishonors them, and words of concern do not feed or clothe a person in need. God's future purpose gives present care lasting significance. Service to Christ can take place in the needs immediately before us, even when we do not recognize how He values it.

passages.title: Matthew 26:1-5
passages.section_title: Jesus Announces His Death While the Leaders Make Their Plans

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 When Jesus had finished saying all these things, He told His disciples, 2 “You know that the Passover is two days away, and the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified.” 3 At that time the chief priests and elders of the people assembled in the courtyard of the high priest, whose name was Caiaphas, 4 and they conspired to arrest Jesus covertly and kill Him. 5 “But not during the feast,” they said, “or there may be a riot among the people.”
paragraphs: 1 When Jesus had finished saying all these things, He told His disciples, 2 “You know that the Passover is two days away, and the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified.”

3 At that time the chief priests and elders of the people assembled in the courtyard of the high priest, whose name was Caiaphas, 4 and they conspired to arrest Jesus covertly and kill Him. 5 “But not during the feast,” they said, “or there may be a riot among the people.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus has finished teaching about His return and judgment. He now brings His disciples back to what lies immediately ahead: Passover is two days away, and He will be handed over for crucifixion. The final chapters of Matthew follow His suffering, death, and resurrection.

At the same time, the chief priests and elders gather at the home of Caiaphas, the high priest. They plan to arrest Jesus secretly and kill Him, but fear that acting during the feast could provoke a riot. Matthew places their planning beside Jesus' announcement, so the reader sees what the disciples are being told and what His opponents are arranging.

Handed over comes from παραδίδωμι, paradidōmi (pah-rah-DEE-doh-mee). Thayer's entry explains its use for giving someone into another's power, including custody or execution. The same verb is used for Judas' betrayal later in the chapter. It links Jesus' announcement with the acts that will lead to His death, without making those acts morally innocent.

The leaders hope to control the circumstances. Jesus already speaks of His approaching death. Judas' offer in verses 14–16 will give them an opportunity to act despite their concern about the crowd.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see a contrast between Jesus' knowledge of His approaching death and the leaders' secret planning. Wesley on 26:1–5 and Walvoord on 26:1–5 both emphasize that their plans do not prevent the death Jesus has announced.
passages.god_plan_html:
The New Testament explicitly connects Christ with Passover. Exodus 12:1–14 describes Israel's deliverance from Egypt and the blood marking the households spared from judgment. 1 Corinthians 5:6–8 identifies Christ as the sacrificed Passover lamb and calls His people to leave behind malice and wickedness. The setting of Jesus' death therefore belongs to a connection the New Testament itself makes, rather than a resemblance we have to invent.

Acts 2:22–24 also holds together God's purpose and human responsibility: Jesus was handed over according to God's plan, those who killed Him acted lawlessly, and God raised Him from death. The conspiracy does not place His death outside God's saving work, and God's purpose does not excuse the conspiracy.

passages.title: Matthew 26:6-13
passages.section_title: A Costly Gift That Jesus Calls Beautiful

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 While Jesus was in Bethany in the home of Simon the Leper, 7 a woman came to Him with an alabaster jar of expensive perfume, which she poured on His head as He reclined at the table. 8 When the disciples saw this, they were indignant and asked, “Why this waste? 9 This perfume could have been sold at a high price, and the money given to the poor.” 10 Aware of this, Jesus asked, “Why are you bothering this woman? She has done a beautiful deed to Me. 11 The poor you will always have with you, but you will not always have Me. 12 By pouring this perfume on Me, she has prepared My body for burial. 13 Truly I tell you, wherever this gospel is preached in all the world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her.”
paragraphs: 6 While Jesus was in Bethany in the home of Simon the Leper, 7 a woman came to Him with an alabaster jar of expensive perfume, which she poured on His head as He reclined at the table. 8 When the disciples saw this, they were indignant and asked, “Why this waste? 9 This perfume could have been sold at a high price, and the money given to the poor.”

10 Aware of this, Jesus asked, “Why are you bothering this woman? She has done a beautiful deed to Me. 11 The poor you will always have with you, but you will not always have Me. 12 By pouring this perfume on Me, she has prepared My body for burial. 13 Truly I tell you, wherever this gospel is preached in all the world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
In Bethany, at the home of Simon the Leper, a woman pours expensive perfume on Jesus' head while He reclines at the table. The disciples object that it could have been sold and the money given to the poor. Jesus defends her and connects her act with preparing His body for burial.

John 12:1–8 describes an anointing at Bethany by Mary, with Martha serving and Lazarus at the table. John describes Jesus' feet being anointed and identifies Judas as the person objecting, adding that he stole from the money bag. Matthew leaves the woman unnamed and describes the disciples' objection. Mark 14:3–9 also records the perfume poured on His head and Jesus' defense of the woman.

Jesus' statement about always having the poor echoes Deuteronomy 15:7–11, which commands openhanded care for those in need. In Mark's account, He also says they can help the poor whenever they want. The approaching end of His bodily presence gives this act its particular moment; His words do not cancel their responsibility to the poor.

Jesus promises that her deed will be remembered wherever the gospel is proclaimed. Between the plot against Him and Judas' agreement to betray Him, Matthew records someone honoring Him at great cost. What the disciples call waste, Jesus receives as a beautiful deed.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readers commonly understand the gift as costly devotion and Jesus' words as pointing toward His burial. Walvoord on 26:6–13 reads Matthew, Mark, and John as accounts of the same anointing, with John supplying Mary's name and further details.

Readers differ about how fully the woman herself understood what she was doing. Wesley on 26:12 says Jesus gave the act its burial meaning rather than that this was her own intention. Walvoord proposes that Mary had grasped at least something of His approaching death. Matthew clearly gives Jesus' explanation, but does not describe the woman's private thoughts. Both readings recognize the honor Jesus gives her.
passages.god_plan_html:
This gift points toward the burial that will follow Jesus' death, and He Himself connects its remembrance with the worldwide proclamation of the gospel. The act is personal and local, yet Jesus places it within a message that will travel far beyond Bethany. Someone whose action others dismissed becomes part of how His story is told.

There is also a useful parallel with the response to God's mercy in Romans 12:1–2: offering our lives to God rather than letting the world set our values. The woman's costly honor illustrates that kind of response; it is not a command that every believer must make her exact gift. Philippians 2:5–11 grounds the wider call to humility in Christ's own willing obedience through death. His self-giving gives depth to the question of what we value and how we respond to Him.

passages.title: Matthew 26:14-16
passages.section_title: Judas Agrees to Hand Jesus Over for Silver

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 Then one of the Twelve, the one called Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests 15 and asked, “What are you willing to give me if I hand Him over to you?” And they set out for him thirty pieces of silver. 16 So from then on Judas looked for an opportunity to betray Jesus.
paragraphs: 14 Then one of the Twelve, the one called Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests 15 and asked, “What are you willing to give me if I hand Him over to you?” And they set out for him thirty pieces of silver. 16 So from then on Judas looked for an opportunity to betray Jesus.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Judas, one of the Twelve, goes to the chief priests and asks what they will give him to hand Jesus over. They set out thirty pieces of silver, and he begins looking for an opportunity. Matthew follows the costly gift at Bethany with a sharply different use of money: an agreement to betray the One who received it.

The phrase one of the Twelve makes the betrayal especially painful. This is someone within Jesus' close circle. Luke 22:1–6 adds that Satan entered Judas and that he sought an opportunity away from the crowd, connecting his offer with the leaders' fear of public reaction.

John 12:4–6 has already described Judas stealing from the shared money bag. That supplies a further picture of his conduct, but neither account gives us a complete account of every thought behind his decision. Here, Matthew states the offer, the payment, and the search for a moment to act.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand this as a deliberate betrayal, with Matthew bringing the payment into focus. Wesley on 26:15 and the US Catholic bishops' note on 26:15 both connect the thirty pieces with the compensation for a slave killed by an ox in Exodus 21:32; the bishops also connect it with the rejected shepherd's payment in Zechariah 11:12–13.
passages.god_plan_html:
The price becomes part of a larger scriptural connection. In Zechariah 11:10–13, a rejected shepherd receives thirty pieces of silver, which are then thrown in the house of the LORD. Matthew 27:3–10 returns to Judas' silver, the temple, and the purchase of the potter's field, explicitly describing the events in relation to prophetic fulfillment. Matthew's later account cites Jeremiah; the wording also recalls Zechariah. The fuller explanation belongs with that later passage rather than treating the payment here as an isolated coincidence.

The New Testament's wider account does not let betrayal have the final word. Acts 2:22–24 proclaims the crucified Jesus raised by God while still calling His killing lawless. God's saving purpose works through this history without turning Judas' bargain into an act of faithfulness.

passages.title: Matthew 26:17-19
passages.section_title: The Disciples Prepare the Passover

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 On the first day of the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the disciples came to Jesus and asked, “Where do You want us to prepare for You to eat the Passover?” 18 He answered, “Go into the city to a certain man and tell him that the Teacher says, ‘My time is near. I will keep the Passover with My disciples at your house.’” 19 So the disciples did as Jesus had directed them and prepared the Passover.
paragraphs: 17 On the first day of the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the disciples came to Jesus and asked, “Where do You want us to prepare for You to eat the Passover?” 18 He answered, “Go into the city to a certain man and tell him that the Teacher says, ‘My time is near. I will keep the Passover with My disciples at your house.’” 19 So the disciples did as Jesus had directed them and prepared the Passover.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The disciples ask Jesus where He wants them to prepare the Passover meal. He directs them into the city with a message for a certain man: His time is near, and He will keep the Passover with His disciples at the man's house. They follow His directions and prepare the meal.

Matthew tells the preparations briefly. Mark 14:12–16 describes two disciples following a man carrying a jug of water to a furnished upper room. Luke 22:7–13 names the two as Peter and John. These accounts give fuller instructions, but none names the owner or tells us what had led him to have the room ready.

The meal belongs to Israel's remembrance of deliverance. Exodus 12:1–20 describes the lamb, the meal with unleavened bread, and the continuing memorial of God's rescue from Egypt. Luke 22:1 also calls the Feast of Unleavened Bread the Passover, showing how the two names are used together in the Gospel setting.

Jesus' approaching time shapes the scene. He will share the meal with His disciples before His arrest and death, and will explain the bread and cup in relation to His own body and blood. The preparation in these verses makes room for that final meal.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see the disciples carrying out Jesus' directions as His suffering approaches. Calvin on 26:18 emphasizes His knowledge and willing approach to what lies ahead; the US Catholic bishops' note on 26:18 likewise stresses the weight of His declaration that His appointed time is near.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus Himself connects this Passover with the coming kingdom. In Luke 22:14–16, He expresses His desire to eat it with the disciples before His suffering and looks toward its fulfillment in God's kingdom. The meal remembers a past rescue while His words direct their hope forward.

1 Corinthians 5:6–8 then connects the Passover sacrifice with Christ and calls the gathered believers to a changed life marked by sincerity and truth. The preparations here lead toward a meal whose meaning Jesus will explain through His death, and whose significance reaches into the life of His people.

passages.title: Matthew 26:20-25
passages.section_title: One at the Table Will Betray Him

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 20 When evening came, Jesus was reclining with the twelve disciples. 21 And while they were eating, He said to them, “Truly I tell you, one of you will betray Me.” 22 They were deeply grieved and began to ask Him one after another, “Surely not I, Lord?” 23 Jesus answered, “The one who has dipped his hand into the bowl with Me will betray Me. 24 The Son of Man will go just as it is written about Him, but woe to that man by whom He is betrayed. It would be better for him if he had not been born.” 25 Then Judas, who would betray Him, said, “Surely not I, Rabbi?” Jesus answered, “You have said it yourself.”
paragraphs: 20 When evening came, Jesus was reclining with the twelve disciples. 21 And while they were eating, He said to them, “Truly I tell you, one of you will betray Me.” 22 They were deeply grieved and began to ask Him one after another, “Surely not I, Lord?”

23 Jesus answered, “The one who has dipped his hand into the bowl with Me will betray Me. 24 The Son of Man will go just as it is written about Him, but woe to that man by whom He is betrayed. It would be better for him if he had not been born.” 25 Then Judas, who would betray Him, said, “Surely not I, Rabbi?” Jesus answered, “You have said it yourself.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus reclines at the meal with the Twelve and announces that one of them will betray Him. The disciples are deeply grieved and each asks whether he could be the one. The betrayal is not coming only from an openly hostile group outside; it reaches into the company sharing His table.

Jesus identifies His betrayer as one who has dipped his hand into the bowl with Him. He then holds together two truths: the Son of Man will go as Scripture has said, and the man who betrays Him bears terrible responsibility. God's purpose does not make betrayal an innocent act.

Judas also asks whether Jesus means him, addressing Him as Rabbi. Jesus answers that Judas has said it himself. Matthew has already told the reader about the agreement for thirty pieces of silver, so his question is heard against that knowledge.

John 13:18–30 gives further details: the disciple beside Jesus asks who it is, Jesus gives Judas a dipped morsel, and Judas goes out into the night. John also says the others do not understand why Jesus has told him to act quickly. Matthew's shorter account does not supply a complete seating plan or describe Judas' departure.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see the shared bowl as making the betrayal especially grievous, and Jesus' warning as affirming Judas' responsibility despite Scripture's fulfillment. Wesley on 26:24–25 and Walvoord on 26:20–25 both retain that distinction between God's purpose and the betrayer's wrongdoing.
passages.god_plan_html:
John explicitly connects the shared meal and betrayal with Scripture. Psalm 41:9 describes the pain of betrayal by a trusted companion who shared bread. In John 13:18–20, Jesus applies that passage to what is happening and says He is telling His disciples beforehand so that they will believe when it happens. The betrayal will wound them, but it does not mean their Lord has been taken by surprise.

The same account moves from betrayal to the disciples' continuing mission: receiving the person Jesus sends is receiving Him and the One who sent Him. Human treachery does not bring God's work to an end. The meal that reveals betrayal also leads toward the self-giving through which Jesus will bring forgiveness.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 26:26-30
passages.section_title: The Bread, the Cup, and the Promise of the Kingdom

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 26 While they were eating, Jesus took bread, spoke a blessing and broke it, and gave it to the disciples, saying, “Take and eat; this is My body.” 27 Then He took the cup, gave thanks, and gave it to them, saying, “Drink from it, all of you. 28 This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins. 29 I tell you, I will not drink of this fruit of the vine from now on until that day when I drink it anew with you in My Father’s kingdom.” 30 And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.
paragraphs: 26 While they were eating, Jesus took bread, spoke a blessing and broke it, and gave it to the disciples, saying, “Take and eat; this is My body.” 27 Then He took the cup, gave thanks, and gave it to them, saying, “Drink from it, all of you. 28 This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.

29 I tell you, I will not drink of this fruit of the vine from now on until that day when I drink it anew with you in My Father’s kingdom.” 30 And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
During the meal Jesus takes bread, blesses and breaks it, and gives it to the disciples in relation to His body. He then takes a cup, gives thanks, and tells them all to drink. He explains the cup in relation to His covenant blood, poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.

The meal looks toward His approaching death, but also beyond it. Jesus promises a future sharing of the fruit of the vine with them in His Father's kingdom. After singing a hymn, they leave for the Mount of Olives. Matthew does not name the hymn or number the cups.

Luke 22:19–20 and 1 Corinthians 11:23–26 also record the bread and cup, with the command to remember Him. Paul explains that repeating the meal proclaims the Lord's death until He comes. That is why this final meal remains central to Christian gatherings.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians agree that Jesus connects the bread and cup with His body, His death, and forgiveness. They differ over how He is present as the meal is celebrated.

The Catholic Church teaches that the bread and wine become Christ's body and blood while their outward appearances remain. Its name for this change is transubstantiation. The Catechism, 1362–1367 and 1374–1377, also describes the Eucharist as making His one sacrifice present, rather than Christ being killed again.

Luther's Small Catechism, The Sacrament of the Altar, teaches that Christ's true body and blood are received under the bread and wine. It connects His words and the believer's trust in His promise with the forgiveness given in the meal. This is more than treating the bread and wine as reminders alone.

The Westminster Confession, 29, and the 1689 Baptist Confession, 30, teach that the bread and wine remain bread and wine while believers truly receive Christ and the benefits of His death spiritually through faith. These confessions describe more than a bare act of recollection. The Methodist Articles of Religion, XVIII, likewise describes receiving Christ in a heavenly and spiritual manner through faith.

A reading focused on the bread and cup as symbols and remembrance is set out by Walvoord on 26:26–30; Wesley on 26:26–28 also explains Jesus' language about the bread and cup as signs of His body and blood. Churches and teachers differ in how they explain this remembrance and participation, so a single Protestant label does not settle the question.
passages.god_plan_html:
The covenant language reaches back to Exodus 24:3–8, where Moses presents the covenant's words and uses sacrificial blood in its confirmation. Jeremiah 31:31–34 then promises a new covenant, God's law within His people, and forgiveness of sins. In Luke 22:20 and 1 Corinthians 11:25, Jesus' cup is expressly connected with the new covenant in His blood. His death belongs to God's work of bringing His people into a forgiven relationship with Him.

Paul also brings that meaning into the way Christians treat one another. In 1 Corinthians 11:17–34, he rebukes gatherings where some go hungry while others eat and drink without regard for them. Remembering the Lord who gave Himself calls for a shared life that honors His people. The meal looks back to His death, shapes the gathering now, and looks forward to His coming and the kingdom He promises.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 26:31-35
passages.section_title: The Shepherd Will Be Struck, but He Will Meet Them Again

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 31 Then Jesus said to them, “This very night you will all fall away on account of Me. For it is written: ‘I will strike the Shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.’ 32 But after I have risen, I will go ahead of you into Galilee.” 33 Peter said to Him, “Even if all fall away on account of You, I never will.” 34 “Truly I tell you,” Jesus declared, “this very night, before the rooster crows, you will deny Me three times.” 35 Peter replied, “Even if I have to die with You, I will never deny You.” And all the other disciples said the same thing.
paragraphs: 31 Then Jesus said to them, “This very night you will all fall away on account of Me. For it is written: ‘I will strike the Shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.’ 32 But after I have risen, I will go ahead of you into Galilee.”

33 Peter said to Him, “Even if all fall away on account of You, I never will.” 34 “Truly I tell you,” Jesus declared, “this very night, before the rooster crows, you will deny Me three times.” 35 Peter replied, “Even if I have to die with You, I will never deny You.” And all the other disciples said the same thing.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
On the way to the Mount of Olives, Jesus tells His disciples that they will all fall away because of Him that very night. He supports the warning with Zechariah's picture of a shepherd struck and sheep scattered. He then immediately promises that after His resurrection He will go ahead of them into Galilee.

Peter insists that even if everyone else falls away, he never will. Jesus answers with a specific warning: before the rooster crows that night, Peter will deny Him three times. Peter replies that he would die with Jesus rather than deny Him, and the other disciples say the same.

Matthew will show the disciples fleeing at the arrest and Peter denying Jesus in the courtyard. Their declarations of loyalty are sincere-sounding, but do not show how they will act under pressure. Jesus knows the coming failure and speaks of a meeting beyond it.

Luke 22:28–34 adds Jesus' prayer for Peter's faith and His instruction that, after turning back, Peter should strengthen his brothers. This supplies another side of the warning: Jesus addresses both the danger and the return.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readers commonly see a warning against overconfidence together with hope in Jesus' promised meeting after the resurrection. Wesley on 26:31–32 stresses that their forsaking Him will not make Him forsake them.

Churches differ in how they relate a believer's serious failure to salvation. The Westminster Confession, 17, and 1689 Baptist Confession, 17, teach that believers may fall into grievous sins but will finally persevere through God's preserving grace. Peter's promised return fits that understanding of failure followed by restoration.

The Methodist Articles of Religion, XII, allow departure from grace and restoration through repentance. Catholic teaching also says faith can be lost and urges perseverance (Catechism, 162). These traditions also recognize forgiveness and restoration; they do not teach that every lapse leaves a person beyond mercy. The different explanations should not obscure what Jesus promises these disciples here.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus explicitly applies Zechariah 13:7 to the coming scattering. The shepherd's suffering does not end with a permanently abandoned flock: He also announces His resurrection and their meeting in Galilee. God's purpose includes bringing the scattered disciples back together after the cross.

That hope takes personal shape in John 21:15–19, where the risen Jesus calls Peter to care for His sheep and follow Him. 1 Peter 1:3–9 later describes new birth into a living hope through Jesus' resurrection, an enduring inheritance, and God's protection through faith amid real trials. These connections retain the comfort of Christ's care while taking both failure and faithful response seriously.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 26:36-46
passages.section_title: Gethsemane: Honest Sorrow and the Father’s Will

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 36 Then Jesus went with His disciples to a place called Gethsemane, and He told them, “Sit here while I go over there and pray.” 37 He took with Him Peter and the two sons of Zebedee and began to be sorrowful and deeply distressed. 38 Then He said to them, “My soul is consumed with sorrow to the point of death. Stay here and keep watch with Me.” 39 Going a little farther, He fell facedown and prayed, “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me. Yet not as I will, but as You will.” 40 Then Jesus returned to the disciples and found them sleeping. “Were you not able to keep watch with Me for one hour?” He asked Peter. 41 “Watch and pray so that you will not enter into temptation. For the spirit is willing, but the body is weak.” 42 A second time He went away and prayed, “My Father, if this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, may Your will be done.” 43 And again Jesus returned and found them sleeping, for their eyes were heavy. 44 So He left them and went away once more and prayed a third time, saying the same thing. 45 Then He returned to the disciples and said, “Are you still sleeping and resting? Look, the hour is near, and the Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners. 46 Rise, let us go! See, My betrayer is approaching!”
paragraphs: 36 Then Jesus went with His disciples to a place called Gethsemane, and He told them, “Sit here while I go over there and pray.” 37 He took with Him Peter and the two sons of Zebedee and began to be sorrowful and deeply distressed. 38 Then He said to them, “My soul is consumed with sorrow to the point of death. Stay here and keep watch with Me.” 39 Going a little farther, He fell facedown and prayed, “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me. Yet not as I will, but as You will.”

40 Then Jesus returned to the disciples and found them sleeping. “Were you not able to keep watch with Me for one hour?” He asked Peter. 41 “Watch and pray so that you will not enter into temptation. For the spirit is willing, but the body is weak.” 42 A second time He went away and prayed, “My Father, if this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, may Your will be done.” 43 And again Jesus returned and found them sleeping, for their eyes were heavy. 44 So He left them and went away once more and prayed a third time, saying the same thing.

45 Then He returned to the disciples and said, “Are you still sleeping and resting? Look, the hour is near, and the Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners. 46 Rise, let us go! See, My betrayer is approaching!”

passages.context_html:
After warning that His disciples will scatter, Jesus brings them to Gethsemane. He leaves some sitting while He goes to pray, taking Peter and the two sons of Zebedee with Him. He tells the three that His sorrow reaches to the point of death and asks them to remain and keep watch with Him.

Jesus goes farther, falls facedown, and asks the Father whether the cup can pass from Him. In the same prayer He submits His will to the Father's. Cup is ποτήριον, potērion (poh-TAY-ree-on), a drinking vessel also used as a picture of what someone must undergo. Thayer's entry specifically places this verse among uses referring to Christ's suffering. In John 18:11, Jesus likewise describes accepting the cup the Father has given Him.

The disciples repeatedly fall asleep. Jesus calls them to watch and pray so they will not enter temptation, acknowledging both their willing spirit and their bodily weakness. This follows their strong promises of loyalty and comes just before the arrest that will test them.

Jesus prays a second and third time. The second prayer accepts that if the cup cannot pass without His drinking it, the Father's will is to be done. Matthew says the third repeats the same thing. He then announces the approaching betrayal and rises to meet it. His anguish is real, and so is His willing movement toward what lies ahead.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as real human anguish joined with Jesus' willing obedience, rather than either pretend suffering or sinful rebellion. The Catholic Catechism, 612, and the Westminster Confession, 8.4, both affirm His willing acceptance of suffering for our salvation.
passages.current_position_html:
What Does Prayer Look Like? reads Gethsemane as a model of honest surrender. Jesus brings the real cost of His suffering before the Father and places the outcome entirely in His hands. Expressing grief is not treated as a failure of faith.

The study also emphasizes that Jesus prays three times. Continued asking can belong with surrender when the Father's will governs it. Prayer and Faith likewise reads this scene as prayer rooted in trust and submission to God, rather than a way to secure the outcome we choose. These studies supply our position on prayer here; they do not make every detail of Jesus' suffering a claim about what a believer will experience.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The cup belongs to Scripture's larger account of judgment and rescue. Psalm 75:7–8 pictures the wicked drinking from the LORD's cup, while Isaiah 53:4–6 describes the servant bearing others' iniquities and the punishment that brings peace. 1 Peter 2:20–25 explicitly applies the sin-bearing servant's suffering to Christ, who entrusts Himself to the righteous Judge. This supports the connection between His suffering and salvation without making the Greek word cup alone carry the whole explanation.

Hebrews 5:7–10 speaks of Jesus' prayers with cries and tears, His obedience through suffering, and His becoming the source of eternal salvation. Hebrews 4:14–16 then gives comfort to people who struggle: their high priest understands weakness, has remained without sin, and invites them to seek mercy and help. Gethsemane belongs to the saving obedience of the Son who also understands the people He helps.

passages.title: Matthew 26:39
passages.section_title: Not as I Will, but as You Will
passages.note: Gethsemane and surrendered faith: not as I will, but as You will.

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 39 Going a little farther, He fell facedown and prayed, “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me. Yet not as I will, but as You will.”
paragraphs: 39 Going a little farther, He fell facedown and prayed, “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me. Yet not as I will, but as You will.”

passages.context_html:
This verse belongs inside Jesus' prayer in Gethsemane, after He has spoken of His overwhelming sorrow and before His arrest. Matthew 26:36–46 gives the full scene, including the disciples' sleep and Jesus' three periods of prayer.

Falling facedown, Jesus addresses the Father and asks whether the cup can pass from Him. He immediately places that desire under the Father's will. The prayer expresses both the reality of the suffering He faces and the obedience with which He faces it.

Cup is ποτήριον, potērion (poh-TAY-ree-on). Thayer's lexicon explains its figurative use here as the suffering Christ must undergo. John 18:11 returns to the same picture when Jesus speaks of drinking the cup given by the Father.

The surrounding verses matter: Jesus prays again and again, always accepting the Father's will, then rises to meet His betrayer. This one sentence is not a promise that the right wording will remove every trial, or a rebuke to someone who feels genuine fear or grief.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as real human anguish joined with Jesus' willing obedience, rather than either pretend suffering or sinful rebellion. The Catholic Catechism, 612, and the Westminster Confession, 8.4, both affirm His willing acceptance of suffering for our salvation.
passages.current_position_html:
What Does Prayer Look Like? reads Gethsemane as a model of honest surrender. Jesus brings the real cost of His suffering before the Father and places the outcome entirely in His hands. Expressing grief is not treated as a failure of faith.

The study also emphasizes that Jesus prays three times. Continued asking can belong with surrender when the Father's will governs it. Prayer and Faith likewise reads this scene as prayer rooted in trust and submission to God, rather than a way to secure the outcome we choose. These studies supply our position on prayer here; they do not make every detail of Jesus' suffering a claim about what a believer will experience.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 5:7–10 connects Jesus' earthly prayers, suffering, obedience, and saving work. His tears are part of His real human life, and the passage presents Him as the source of eternal salvation. The cross that He approaches is more than an example of courage; it belongs to what He does for those He saves.

That saving work also opens a way for weak people to approach God. Hebrews 4:14–16 describes Jesus as the high priest who understands weakness without sin and directs His people to seek mercy and grace in their need. His surrender in suffering stands alongside His continuing care for those who come through Him.

passages.title: Matthew 26:47-56
passages.section_title: The Arrest: Jesus Puts Away the Sword and Accepts the Cup

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 47 While Jesus was still speaking, Judas, one of the Twelve, arrived, accompanied by a large crowd armed with swords and clubs, sent from the chief priests and elders of the people. 48 Now the betrayer had arranged a signal with them: “The One I kiss is the man; arrest Him.” 49 Going directly to Jesus, he said, “Greetings, Rabbi!” and kissed Him. 50 “Friend,” Jesus replied, “do what you came for.” Then the men stepped forward, seized Jesus, and arrested Him. 51 At this, one of Jesus’ companions drew his sword and struck the servant of the high priest, cutting off his ear. 52 “Put your sword back in its place,” Jesus said to him. “For all who draw the sword will die by the sword. 53 Are you not aware that I can call on My Father, and He will at once put at My disposal more than twelve legions of angels? 54 But how then would the Scriptures be fulfilled that say it must happen this way?” 55 At that time Jesus said to the crowd, “Have you come out with swords and clubs to arrest Me as you would an outlaw? Every day I sat teaching in the temple courts, and you did not arrest Me. 56 But this has all happened so that the writings of the prophets would be fulfilled.” Then all the disciples deserted Him and fled.
paragraphs: 47 While Jesus was still speaking, Judas, one of the Twelve, arrived, accompanied by a large crowd armed with swords and clubs, sent from the chief priests and elders of the people. 48 Now the betrayer had arranged a signal with them: “The One I kiss is the man; arrest Him.” 49 Going directly to Jesus, he said, “Greetings, Rabbi!” and kissed Him. 50 “Friend,” Jesus replied, “do what you came for.” Then the men stepped forward, seized Jesus, and arrested Him.

51 At this, one of Jesus’ companions drew his sword and struck the servant of the high priest, cutting off his ear. 52 “Put your sword back in its place,” Jesus said to him. “For all who draw the sword will die by the sword. 53 Are you not aware that I can call on My Father, and He will at once put at My disposal more than twelve legions of angels? 54 But how then would the Scriptures be fulfilled that say it must happen this way?”

55 At that time Jesus said to the crowd, “Have you come out with swords and clubs to arrest Me as you would an outlaw? Every day I sat teaching in the temple courts, and you did not arrest Me. 56 But this has all happened so that the writings of the prophets would be fulfilled.” Then all the disciples deserted Him and fled.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Judas arrives with an armed crowd sent by the chief priests and elders. He has arranged a kiss as the signal identifying Jesus. The familiar greeting becomes an act of betrayal, and the men seize Him.

One of Jesus' companions draws a sword and cuts off the high priest's servant's ear. Matthew leaves both men unnamed; John 18:1–12 identifies them as Peter and Malchus. Luke 22:47–53 adds that Jesus stops the violence and heals the injured man.

Jesus orders the sword put away and warns about the outcome of taking up the sword. He says He could appeal to the Father for more than twelve legions of angels. His acceptance of arrest is therefore not presented as a lack of help or power: He connects it with the fulfillment of Scripture.

He also challenges the crowd's manner of arresting Him. He had taught openly in the temple courts, yet they have come armed as though He were an outlaw. Again He points to the prophets' writings being fulfilled. The disciples then desert Him and flee, just as He has warned them.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly recognize that Jesus refuses an armed attempt to prevent His arrest and willingly accepts the path toward the cross. Churches differ over how this example relates to all uses of force by Christians.

Mennonite Church USA's Confession of Faith, article 22, directly cites Matthew 26:52–53 in teaching that followers of Jesus should resist evil without violence, including when facing warfare. It joins this with love of enemies, reconciliation, and active peacemaking.

The Catholic Catechism, 2263–2265, distinguishes wrongful killing from proportionate defense of oneself or those entrusted to one's care. This is a wider teaching about defense rather than permission to stop Jesus' saving work by force. The traditions differ about the reach of nonviolence, while both treat this particular attack as contrary to Jesus' direction.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus' words here fit His explanation of His mission in John 10:14–18: the shepherd knows His sheep and lays down His life willingly, with authority to take it up again. The arrest leads toward that self-giving rather than defeating it. Hebrews 2:14–18 explains the larger victory: through sharing human life and undergoing death, He breaks the devil's power and frees people held by fear of death.

The refusal of retaliation also has a place in the life of His people. Romans 12:17–21 calls believers to seek peace, leave vengeance to God, and answer an enemy's need with practical care. In Luke's account, Jesus' healing of the man wounded during His arrest supplies a concrete example of doing good amid hostility. His saving purpose and His treatment of an enemy belong together.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 26:57-68
passages.section_title: Before Caiaphas: False Witnesses and the Son of Man’s Answer

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 57 Those who had arrested Jesus led Him away to the house of Caiaphas the high priest, where the scribes and elders had gathered. 58 But Peter followed Him at a distance, right up to the courtyard of the high priest. And he went in and sat down with the guards to see the outcome. 59 Now the chief priests and the whole Sanhedrin were seeking false testimony against Jesus in order to put Him to death. 60 But they did not find any, though many false witnesses came forward. Finally two came forward 61 and declared, “This man said, ‘I am able to destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days.’” 62 So the high priest stood up and asked Him, “Have You no answer? What are these men testifying against You?” 63 But Jesus remained silent. Then the high priest said to Him, “I charge You under oath by the living God: Tell us if You are the Christ, the Son of God.” 64 “You have said it yourself,” Jesus answered. “But I say to all of you, from now on you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven.” 65 At this, the high priest tore his clothes and declared, “He has blasphemed! Why do we need any more witnesses? Look, now you have heard the blasphemy. 66 What do you think?” “He deserves to die,” they answered. 67 Then they spit in His face and struck Him. Others slapped Him 68 and said, “Prophesy to us, Christ! Who hit You?”
paragraphs: 57 Those who had arrested Jesus led Him away to the house of Caiaphas the high priest, where the scribes and elders had gathered. 58 But Peter followed Him at a distance, right up to the courtyard of the high priest. And he went in and sat down with the guards to see the outcome. 59 Now the chief priests and the whole Sanhedrin were seeking false testimony against Jesus in order to put Him to death. 60 But they did not find any, though many false witnesses came forward. Finally two came forward 61 and declared, “This man said, ‘I am able to destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days.’”

62 So the high priest stood up and asked Him, “Have You no answer? What are these men testifying against You?” 63 But Jesus remained silent. Then the high priest said to Him, “I charge You under oath by the living God: Tell us if You are the Christ, the Son of God.” 64 “You have said it yourself,” Jesus answered. “But I say to all of you, from now on you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven.”

65 At this, the high priest tore his clothes and declared, “He has blasphemed! Why do we need any more witnesses? Look, now you have heard the blasphemy. 66 What do you think?” “He deserves to die,” they answered. 67 Then they spit in His face and struck Him. Others slapped Him 68 and said, “Prophesy to us, Christ! Who hit You?”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus is brought to Caiaphas, where the scribes and elders are assembled. Peter follows at a distance and sits with the guards in the courtyard to see what will happen. Matthew then moves between Jesus inside the hearing and Peter outside.

The chief priests and the council seek false testimony that can lead to Jesus' death. After many witnesses, two accuse Him of saying He can destroy God's temple and rebuild it in three days. John 2:18–22 records Jesus' temple saying and explains that He spoke about His body and resurrection. Matthew reports the accusation here without treating the witnesses' version as Jesus' own explanation.

Jesus remains silent before the testimony. When the high priest charges Him under oath to say whether He is the Christ, God's Son, He answers and speaks of the Son of Man at the right hand of Power and coming on heaven's clouds. His reply directs attention beyond their judgment of Him to His own coming authority.

The high priest tears his clothes and calls the answer blasphemy. The others declare that Jesus deserves death, and He is spat on, struck, slapped, and mocked with a demand to identify who hit Him. The scene brings false accusation, a claim of authority, and humiliation together as the account moves toward the cross.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand Jesus' answer as affirming His identity and pointing toward His vindication and authority, rather than confessing wrongdoing. The US Catholic bishops' note on 26:64 and Walvoord on 26:57–68 both connect His words with Psalm 110:1 and Daniel 7:13.
passages.god_plan_html:
Psalm 110:1 pictures the Lord seated at God's right hand, while Daniel 7:13–14 describes the Son of Man receiving enduring dominion and the service of all peoples. Jesus brings these pictures into His answer at the moment when His hearers are preparing to condemn Him. The One being judged claims a place in God's lasting rule.

The suffering also recalls Isaiah 50:5–9, where the servant endures blows and spitting while trusting the Lord who vindicates him. This is a supported parallel, not a reason to add unrecorded details to Matthew's scene. Hebrews 12:1–3 explicitly places Jesus' endurance of the cross and shame beside His seat at God's right hand, encouraging His people not to lose heart. Humiliation does not have the final word in God's purpose.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 26:69-75
passages.section_title: Peter Denies Jesus and Remembers His Words

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 69 Meanwhile, Peter was sitting out in the courtyard, and a servant girl came up to him. “You also were with Jesus the Galilean,” she said. 70 But he denied it before them all: “I do not know what you are talking about.” 71 When Peter had gone out to the gateway, another servant girl saw him and said to the people there, “This man was with Jesus of Nazareth.” 72 And again he denied it with an oath: “I do not know the man!” 73 After a little while, those standing nearby came up to Peter. “Surely you are one of them,” they said, “for your accent gives you away.” 74 At that he began to curse and swear to them, “I do not know the man!” And immediately a rooster crowed. 75 Then Peter remembered the word that Jesus had spoken: “Before the rooster crows, you will deny Me three times.” And he went outside and wept bitterly.
paragraphs: 69 Meanwhile, Peter was sitting out in the courtyard, and a servant girl came up to him. “You also were with Jesus the Galilean,” she said. 70 But he denied it before them all: “I do not know what you are talking about.” 71 When Peter had gone out to the gateway, another servant girl saw him and said to the people there, “This man was with Jesus of Nazareth.” 72 And again he denied it with an oath: “I do not know the man!”

73 After a little while, those standing nearby came up to Peter. “Surely you are one of them,” they said, “for your accent gives you away.” 74 At that he began to curse and swear to them, “I do not know the man!” And immediately a rooster crowed. 75 Then Peter remembered the word that Jesus had spoken: “Before the rooster crows, you will deny Me three times.” And he went outside and wept bitterly.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
While Jesus faces the hearing, Peter sits outside in the courtyard. A servant girl identifies him as someone who was with Jesus the Galilean, and he denies understanding her. At the gateway another servant girl identifies him, and this time he denies knowing Jesus with an oath.

The bystanders then say his accent gives him away. Peter responds with cursing and swearing that he does not know the man. A rooster crows, and he remembers Jesus' prediction of three denials before its crowing. He goes outside and weeps bitterly.

The movement of the story answers Peter's earlier promise in verses 33–35 that he would die rather than deny Jesus. His confidence in his own loyalty has not held. Matthew records the failure and its grief rather than hiding them.

Luke 22:54–62 adds Jesus turning to look at Peter when the rooster crows, and places about an hour before the last accusation. The denials should therefore not be compressed into a few seconds simply because Matthew tells them briefly. The fuller setting joins Peter's failure with the Lord whose words he remembers.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read Peter's denials as a serious failure followed by grief and repentance, with his later restoration showing that the failure does not end his service to Christ. The US Catholic bishops' note on 26:70 emphasizes repentance, while Walvoord on 26:69–75 emphasizes Peter facing the truth of his failure; the related questions about perseverance are discussed with Matthew 26:31–35.
passages.god_plan_html:
The risen Jesus later calls Peter to care for His sheep and follow Him in John 21:15–19. The man who denied knowing Him is given work that serves others. This does not excuse the denial, but shows how Jesus' care reaches beyond a disciple's failure.

That restored service becomes visible in Acts 4:8–13, where Peter speaks openly about Jesus before rulers, and Acts 5:27–32, where the apostles continue their witness under pressure. 1 Peter 3:13–17 likewise calls believers to answer for their hope with gentleness and respect, even amid suffering. God's work can turn a story of fear and failure into service that strengthens others.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 27:1-2
passages.section_title: Jesus Is Handed Over to Pilate

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 When morning came, all the chief priests and elders of the people conspired against Jesus to put Him to death. 2 They bound Him, led Him away, and handed Him over to Pilate the governor.
paragraphs: 1 When morning came, all the chief priests and elders of the people conspired against Jesus to put Him to death. 2 They bound Him, led Him away, and handed Him over to Pilate the governor.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Morning comes after Jesus' hearing before Caiaphas and Peter's denials. The chief priests and elders confer about putting Jesus to death, bind Him, and hand Him over to Pilate, the governor. The account now moves from the religious leaders' hearing to the governor's examination.

John 18:28–32 gives a fuller account of this handover. The leaders say they are not permitted to execute anyone, and John connects what follows with Jesus' words about the kind of death He would die. Matthew briefly interrupts the scene with Judas' response before returning to Pilate's questions.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand this as the step that brings Jesus before the governor for the death His opponents seek. Walvoord on 27:1–2 and the US Catholic bishops' note on 27:1 both relate the handover to the leaders' inability to carry out the execution themselves, as stated in John 18:31.
passages.god_plan_html:
The New Testament later looks back on these events as human opposition taken up within God's saving purpose. In Acts 4:23–31, believers pray about rulers gathering against the Lord and His Anointed, then name Herod, Pilate, Gentiles, and the people of Israel in what happened to Jesus. They also affirm that God's purpose was being carried out.

Their response is to ask for boldness to continue speaking His word. The handover leads toward the cross, yet the risen Jesus' mission continues through witnesses who themselves face pressure. God's purpose does not make the wrongdoing good; it gives His people confidence that opposition cannot finally defeat His work.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 27:3-10
passages.section_title: Judas Returns the Silver, and the Potter’s Field Is Bought

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 3 When Judas, who had betrayed Him, saw that Jesus was condemned, he was filled with remorse and returned the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders. 4 “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood,” he said. “What is that to us?” they replied. “You bear the responsibility.” 5 So Judas threw the silver into the temple and left. Then he went away and hanged himself. 6 The chief priests picked up the pieces of silver and said, “It is unlawful to put this into the treasury, since it is blood money.” 7 After conferring together, they used the money to buy the potter’s field as a burial place for foreigners. 8 That is why it has been called the Field of Blood to this day. 9 Then what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet was fulfilled: “They took the thirty pieces of silver, the price set on Him by the people of Israel, 10 and they gave them for the potter’s field, as the Lord had commanded me.”
paragraphs: 3 When Judas, who had betrayed Him, saw that Jesus was condemned, he was filled with remorse and returned the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders. 4 “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood,” he said. “What is that to us?” they replied. “You bear the responsibility.” 5 So Judas threw the silver into the temple and left. Then he went away and hanged himself.

6 The chief priests picked up the pieces of silver and said, “It is unlawful to put this into the treasury, since it is blood money.” 7 After conferring together, they used the money to buy the potter’s field as a burial place for foreigners. 8 That is why it has been called the Field of Blood to this day.

9 Then what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet was fulfilled: “They took the thirty pieces of silver, the price set on Him by the people of Israel, 10 and they gave them for the potter’s field, as the Lord had commanded me.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
When Judas sees that Jesus has been condemned, he returns the thirty pieces of silver and acknowledges that he has sinned by betraying innocent blood. The chief priests and elders refuse responsibility. He throws the money into the temple, leaves, and takes his own life.

The word translated filled with remorse comes from μεταμέλομαι, metamelomai (meh-tah-MEH-loh-my), to regret or change one's mind afterward. Thayer's entry includes this verse as well as Matthew 21:29 and 32, where a change of mind can lead to a right response. It cautions against an absolute word-based division between emotional regret and real repentance. Judas' response must therefore be understood from the account as a whole, rather than decided by the Greek word alone.

The chief priests call the money blood money and say it cannot go into the treasury. They use it to buy a potter's field for burying foreigners, which Matthew says became known as the Field of Blood. Their concern about the money's proper use stands beside Judas' acknowledgment that an innocent man has been betrayed.

Matthew explicitly relates the silver and field to prophetic fulfillment, naming Jeremiah. The thirty pieces and silver thrown in the temple closely recall Zechariah 11:12–13. The naming of Jeremiah requires explanation; it should neither be silently changed to Zechariah nor passed over as though the wording raised no question.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly see both the tragedy of Judas' guilt and the leaders' refusal to face their own wrongdoing. Calvin on 27:3 distinguishes Judas' distress from a return to God, while Wesley on 27:4–7 emphasizes the contrast between the leaders' concern about the treasury and their treatment of innocent blood.

Readers differ over the reference to Jeremiah. The US Catholic bishops' note on 27:9–10 describes an explanation in which Matthew combines Zechariah's silver with Jeremiah's potter, field, and burial-place passages. Calvin on 27:9 instead thought Jeremiah's name had been written by mistake in place of Zechariah's. These are explanations offered by particular sources; the text quoted above retains Jeremiah as the BSB gives it.

Readers also compare Matthew's hanging and the priests' purchase of the field with the fatal fall and Judas' acquisition of a field in Acts 1:18–19. Walvoord on 27:3–10 treats Acts as adding details to the death Matthew describes; the US Catholic bishops' note on 27:5–8 treats them as different traditions about his death. Neither account states that a rope broke, so that familiar reconstruction should be recognized as a proposed way of joining the accounts rather than a recorded event.
passages.god_plan_html:
The connection to the prophets brings Jesus' rejection into a larger pattern of refusing God's shepherding care. Zechariah 11:10–13 portrays the shepherd's work met with a contemptuous payment, while Jeremiah 19:1–13 joins a potter's vessel, innocent blood, judgment, and burial. These provide supported connections, rather than a reason to make every detail of Judas' story a prediction with only one possible explanation.

Acts 1:15–20 also relates Judas, the field, and the loss of his place among the apostles to Scripture. The disciples must face the betrayal within their own circle as they prepare to continue the work entrusted to them. Human failure is taken seriously without making it the end of God's mission.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 27:11-14
passages.section_title: The King Stands Silent before His Accusers

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 Meanwhile Jesus stood before the governor, who questioned Him: “Are You the King of the Jews?” “You have said so,” Jesus replied. 12 And when He was accused by the chief priests and elders, He gave no answer. 13 Then Pilate asked Him, “Do You not hear how many charges they are bringing against You?” 14 But Jesus gave no answer, not even to a single charge, much to the governor’s amazement.
paragraphs: 11 Meanwhile Jesus stood before the governor, who questioned Him: “Are You the King of the Jews?” “You have said so,” Jesus replied. 12 And when He was accused by the chief priests and elders, He gave no answer. 13 Then Pilate asked Him, “Do You not hear how many charges they are bringing against You?” 14 But Jesus gave no answer, not even to a single charge, much to the governor’s amazement.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Matthew returns to Jesus standing before Pilate. The governor asks whether He is the King of the Jews, and Jesus replies that Pilate has said so. When the chief priests and elders bring accusations, He gives no answer. Pilate is amazed that He does not respond to the charges.

The question about kingship connects the hearing with the identity that has run through Matthew. His opening chapters introduced the search for the newborn King; now the governor questions a prisoner about that title. The following scenes will return to it in the crowd's choice, the soldiers' mockery, and the inscription at the cross.

John 18:33–38 gives a longer conversation about Jesus' kingdom and His witness to the truth. Jesus explains that His kingdom does not come from this world, pointing out that His servants would otherwise have fought against His arrest. Matthew focuses on His brief answer about kingship and His silence toward the accusations.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand Jesus as affirming His kingship without accepting the assumptions of a rival political claimant, and His silence as a willing approach to suffering. Wesley on 27:11 stresses that His silence is not fear, while the US Catholic bishops' notes on 27:11–14 distinguish His kingship from Pilate's expectations and connect His silence with Isaiah's suffering servant.
passages.god_plan_html:
Isaiah 53:7–12 describes the servant's silence under oppression, His unjust treatment, and His bearing others' sins. Acts 8:30–35 explicitly uses that Scripture to explain the good news about Jesus. This is a connection the New Testament itself makes, giving His silence a place within His saving work rather than treating it merely as a refusal to cooperate.

The kingdom He describes in John 18:36–37 is bound to His witness to the truth, not to His followers fighting to prevent His death. The apparent weakness of the prisoner does not settle the truth of His claim. His way toward the cross is part of the work through which the King brings salvation.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 27:15-26
passages.section_title: Barabbas Is Released, and Jesus Is Condemned

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 Now it was the governor’s custom at the feast to release to the crowd a prisoner of their choosing. 16 At that time they were holding a notorious prisoner named Barabbas. 17 So when the crowd had assembled, Pilate asked them, “Which one do you want me to release to you: Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ?” 18 For he knew it was out of envy that they had handed Jesus over to him. 19 While Pilate was sitting on the judgment seat, his wife sent him this message: “Have nothing to do with that innocent man, for I have suffered terribly in a dream today because of Him.” 20 But the chief priests and elders persuaded the crowds to ask for Barabbas and to have Jesus put to death. 21 “Which of the two do you want me to release to you?” asked the governor. “Barabbas,” they replied. 22 “What then should I do with Jesus who is called Christ?” Pilate asked. They all answered, “Crucify Him!” 23 “Why?” asked Pilate. “What evil has He done?” But they shouted all the louder, “Crucify Him!” 24 When Pilate saw that he was accomplishing nothing, but that instead a riot was breaking out, he took water and washed his hands before the crowd. “I am innocent of this man’s blood,” he said. “You bear the responsibility.” 25 All the people answered, “His blood be on us and on our children!” 26 So Pilate released Barabbas to them. But he had Jesus flogged, and handed Him over to be crucified.
paragraphs: 15 Now it was the governor’s custom at the feast to release to the crowd a prisoner of their choosing. 16 At that time they were holding a notorious prisoner named Barabbas. 17 So when the crowd had assembled, Pilate asked them, “Which one do you want me to release to you: Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ?” 18 For he knew it was out of envy that they had handed Jesus over to him. 19 While Pilate was sitting on the judgment seat, his wife sent him this message: “Have nothing to do with that innocent man, for I have suffered terribly in a dream today because of Him.”

20 But the chief priests and elders persuaded the crowds to ask for Barabbas and to have Jesus put to death. 21 “Which of the two do you want me to release to you?” asked the governor. “Barabbas,” they replied. 22 “What then should I do with Jesus who is called Christ?” Pilate asked. They all answered, “Crucify Him!” 23 “Why?” asked Pilate. “What evil has He done?” But they shouted all the louder, “Crucify Him!”

24 When Pilate saw that he was accomplishing nothing, but that instead a riot was breaking out, he took water and washed his hands before the crowd. “I am innocent of this man’s blood,” he said. “You bear the responsibility.” 25 All the people answered, “His blood be on us and on our children!” 26 So Pilate released Barabbas to them. But he had Jesus flogged, and handed Him over to be crucified.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Pilate offers the crowd a choice between Barabbas and Jesus, following the governor's custom of releasing a prisoner at the feast. Matthew calls Barabbas notorious and says Pilate knows envy has motivated Jesus' accusers. Mark 15:6–15 and Luke 23:18–25 connect Barabbas with insurrection and murder.

While Pilate sits on the judgment seat, his wife sends a message calling Jesus innocent and warning him against involvement, after suffering because of Him in a dream. Matthew does not tell us her name, describe the dream, or say what later became of her. Her warning adds another acknowledgment of Jesus' innocence within the account.

The chief priests and elders persuade the crowds to ask for Barabbas and Jesus' death. Pilate asks what he should do with Jesus and what evil He has done. The crowd answers with louder demands for crucifixion. Their insistence does not supply evidence that the charges are true.

Seeing a riot developing, Pilate washes his hands and declares himself innocent of Jesus' blood. The people accept the blood on themselves and their children. Matthew then records what Pilate actually does: he releases Barabbas, has Jesus flogged, and hands Him over for crucifixion. His declaration and the crowd's words do not remove his part in that decision.

The scene concerns the people acting in it. Deuteronomy 24:16 states the principle that children are not to be executed for their fathers' sins. The crowd's statement must not be turned into permission to blame or harm Jewish people in other times and places.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly see the release of a guilty prisoner alongside the condemnation of the innocent Jesus, and Pilate's handwashing as an unsuccessful attempt to shift responsibility. Readers have differed over how far to extend the crowd's words about their children.

Wesley on 27:25 connects those words with Jerusalem's later destruction and subsequent calamities among Jewish people. That is his historical commentary, rather than a statement of what every Methodist today believes.

The Catholic Church expressly rejects assigning the guilt of the Passion to all Jews then living or to Jewish people today. Nostra Aetate, 4, and the Catechism, 597–598, also reject presenting Jewish people as rejected or cursed by God on the basis of these events. The Catechism places Christ's suffering within the larger reality of human sin, including Christians' own sin.
passages.god_plan_html:
Barabbas' release supplies a striking, supported parallel to the wider saving purpose of Jesus' death: a guilty person goes free while the innocent One is condemned. 2 Corinthians 5:14–21 explains Christ's death in relation to reconciliation and the sinless One acting on behalf of sinners. The parallel does not tell us that Barabbas himself came to faith; it helps us see the contrast between the guilt of those being rescued and the innocence of their Savior.

The New Testament also brings responsibility and mercy together. In Acts 3:13–19, Peter recalls the choice of a murderer over Jesus, declares that God raised Jesus, and calls his hearers to turn back so that their sins may be wiped away. His message confronts wrongdoing and offers forgiveness.

Romans 11:1–6, 17–32 then gives the wider setting for God's dealings with Israel and the nations. Paul denies that God has rejected His people, warns Gentile believers against arrogance, speaks of Israel's partial hardening and promised salvation, and emphasizes God's mercy and enduring call. That larger purpose gives no ground for inherited ethnic guilt or pride toward the people through whom the promises came.

passages.title: Matthew 27:27-31
passages.section_title: The Soldiers Mock the King

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 27 Then the governor’s soldiers took Jesus into the Praetorium and gathered the whole company around Him. 28 They stripped Him and put a scarlet robe on Him. 29 And they twisted together a crown of thorns and set it on His head. They put a staff in His right hand, knelt down before Him, and mocked Him, saying, “Hail, King of the Jews!” 30 Then they spit on Him and took the staff and struck Him on the head repeatedly. 31 After they had mocked Him, they removed the robe and put His own clothes back on Him. Then they led Him away to crucify Him.
paragraphs: 27 Then the governor’s soldiers took Jesus into the Praetorium and gathered the whole company around Him. 28 They stripped Him and put a scarlet robe on Him. 29 And they twisted together a crown of thorns and set it on His head. They put a staff in His right hand, knelt down before Him, and mocked Him, saying, “Hail, King of the Jews!”

30 Then they spit on Him and took the staff and struck Him on the head repeatedly. 31 After they had mocked Him, they removed the robe and put His own clothes back on Him. Then they led Him away to crucify Him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After Pilate has Jesus flogged and hands Him over for crucifixion, the governor's soldiers gather around Him. Matthew brings the title King of the Jews into a scene of deliberate mockery: they dress Him in scarlet, put a crown of thorns on His head and a staff in His hand, and kneel with an insulting royal greeting.

The Praetorium is πραιτώριον, praitōrion (prai-TOH-ree-on), a term borrowed from Latin. Thayer's entry explains its use here as the governor's residence. It identifies the setting without requiring us to decide between proposed locations for Pilate's headquarters in Jerusalem.

The soldiers then spit on Jesus and use the staff to strike His head. The objects that imitate royal honor become instruments of humiliation and violence. Afterward they remove the robe, put His own clothes back on Him, and lead Him away to crucify Him.

Mark 15:16–20 and John 19:1–5 also describe the crown, robe, and mock greeting. Matthew's account keeps the reader facing the contrast between the King's identity and the treatment He receives on the way to His death.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a cruel imitation of royal honor, in which the soldiers mock the very identity Matthew presents as true. The US Catholic bishops' notes on 27:27–30 explain the robe, crown, and staff in relation to this mockery and connect the spitting with the suffering servant in Isaiah 50:6.
passages.god_plan_html:
The crown brings to mind the beginning of Scripture's story of sin and rescue. Genesis 3:17–19 names thorns among the consequences of the ground's curse after human disobedience. Here, a crown made from thorns is placed on Jesus as He approaches His death. This is a parallel with Genesis; Matthew does not directly explain the crown in those terms.

The New Testament does explicitly teach that Christ bears a curse for others. Galatians 3:10–14 speaks specifically of redemption from the curse of the Law, so that Abraham's promised blessing and the Spirit reach the nations through faith. Paul is speaking about the Law here; he does not directly explain the soldiers' crown.

Romans 3:21–26 places Christ's death within God's demonstration of righteousness and His gracious gift to those who believe. Hebrews 12:1–3 then directs believers to Jesus' endurance of the cross and shame as they seek to leave sin behind and keep going. The public humiliation of the King belongs to the costly saving work that shapes His people's hope and way of life.
