passages.title: Matthew 27:32-36
passages.section_title: Simon Carries the Cross, and the Soldiers Divide Jesus’ Clothes

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 32 Along the way they found a man from Cyrene, named Simon, and they forced him to carry the cross of Jesus. 33 And when they came to a place called Golgotha, which means The Place of the Skull, 34 they offered Him wine to drink, mixed with gall; but after tasting it, He refused to drink it. 35 When they had crucified Him, they divided up His garments by casting lots. 36 And sitting down, they kept watch over Him there.
paragraphs: 32 Along the way they found a man from Cyrene, named Simon, and they forced him to carry the cross of Jesus. 33 And when they came to a place called Golgotha, which means The Place of the Skull, 34 they offered Him wine to drink, mixed with gall; but after tasting it, He refused to drink it.
35 When they had crucified Him, they divided up His garments by casting lots. 36 And sitting down, they kept watch over Him there.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
On the way to the execution, the soldiers compel Simon of Cyrene to carry Jesus' cross. Cyrene was in what is now Libya (UNESCO's site record). Matthew identifies Simon by name and origin, but does not tell us how he understood the experience or whether he had already become a follower of Jesus.

Forced to serve comes from ἀγγαρεύω, angareuō (ahn-gah-REH-oo-oh). Thayer's entry explains its use for compelling someone to make a journey, carry a burden, or perform another service. It is also the verb in Matthew 5:41, where Jesus teaches about being compelled to go a mile. Simon is pressed into the task rather than described as volunteering.

They reach Golgotha, which Matthew translates as The Place of the Skull. Jesus tastes wine mixed with gall but refuses to drink it. Mark 15:21–24 describes wine mixed with myrrh. Matthew does not explain Jesus' reason for refusing the drink.

The crucifixion itself is stated briefly. The soldiers divide His garments by casting lots and sit down to watch Him. John 19:16–24 adds that Jesus went out carrying His cross and describes the soldiers dividing the clothing while leaving the seamless tunic to be awarded by lot. The Gospel accounts supply different details without telling us exactly when Simon took over or that Jesus fell.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readers commonly see Simon's burden beside Jesus' suffering and the division of clothing as part of the humiliation of the crucifixion. John 19:24 explicitly connects the clothing with Psalm 22:18.

Readers differ in how they explain the drink. Wesley on 27:34 regards Matthew's gall mixture as mockery and distinguishes it from the myrrh mixture in Mark. The US Catholic bishops' note on 27:34 relates Matthew's wording to Mark's account and to Psalm 69:21. The accounts record the offered drink and refusal; identifying its exact contents, purpose, and sequence requires more than the word gall by itself.
passages.god_plan_html:
Simon carrying the cross behind Jesus, as Luke 23:26 describes it, provides a visible parallel to Jesus' call in Luke 9:23–26 to take up one's cross and follow Him. That comparison helps make the cost of following concrete, without telling us Simon's private thoughts or making his forced service proof of conversion.

The soldiers' actions also belong to a connection the New Testament directly makes. Psalm 22:11–18 describes a sufferer surrounded by enemies, exposed to their gaze, with his clothing divided by lot. John 19:23–24 specifically identifies the division of Jesus' garments with that Scripture. What looks like the soldiers' small gain is placed within the story Scripture has prepared us to recognize.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 27:37-44
passages.section_title: The King Is Mocked for Refusing to Save Himself

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 37 Above His head they posted the written charge against Him: THIS IS JESUS, THE KING OF THE JEWS. 38 Two robbers were crucified with Him, one on His right and the other on His left. 39 And those who passed by heaped abuse on Him, shaking their heads 40 and saying, “You who are going to destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days, save Yourself! If You are the Son of God, come down from the cross!” 41 In the same way, the chief priests, scribes, and elders mocked Him, saying, 42 “He saved others, but He cannot save Himself. He is the King of Israel! Let Him come down now from the cross, and we will believe in Him. 43 He trusts in God. Let God deliver Him now if He wants Him. For He said, ‘I am the Son of God.’ ” 44 In the same way, even the robbers who were crucified with Him berated Him.
paragraphs: 37 Above His head they posted the written charge against Him: THIS IS JESUS, THE KING OF THE JEWS. 38 Two robbers were crucified with Him, one on His right and the other on His left. 39 And those who passed by heaped abuse on Him, shaking their heads 40 and saying, “You who are going to destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days, save Yourself! If You are the Son of God, come down from the cross!”

41 In the same way, the chief priests, scribes, and elders mocked Him, saying, 42 “He saved others, but He cannot save Himself. He is the King of Israel! Let Him come down now from the cross, and we will believe in Him. 43 He trusts in God. Let God deliver Him now if He wants Him. For He said, ‘I am the Son of God.’ ” 44 In the same way, even the robbers who were crucified with Him berated Him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The written charge above Jesus identifies Him as King of the Jews. Two robbers are crucified beside Him. The title that Pilate has questioned and the soldiers have mocked now stands over His cross as passersby and religious leaders challenge His identity.

Robber is λῃστής, lēstēs (lays-TACE). Thayer's entry describes a robber or plunderer, distinguishing it from someone who steals secretly. Matthew uses the word for the two men, but does not identify them as Barabbas' associates or give their individual charges.

Those passing by repeat the accusation about destroying and rebuilding the temple, and demand that Jesus save Himself by coming down. The chief priests, scribes, and elders likewise say they will believe if He comes down. They also question whether God will rescue the One who has claimed to be His Son.

Their challenge echoes the language of the earlier temptation in Matthew 4:3–7: if He is God's Son, He should demonstrate it on the challenger's terms. In Matthew's account the men crucified beside Him also join the insults. Luke 23:39–43 records a different response from one of them: acknowledging Jesus' innocence and asking to be remembered in His kingdom.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readers commonly see irony in the demand that Jesus save Himself: His willing death is central to the salvation He brings to others. Walvoord on 27:37–44 emphasizes His obedience to the Father rather than a lack of power, while Calvin on 27:43 warns against assuming God's love is absent whenever help does not arrive immediately.

Readers differ over how to relate Matthew's plural description of the robbers to Luke's repentant criminal. Chrysostom, Homily 87 on Matthew, understands both men as mocking at first, with one later changing his response. Augustine, Harmony of the Gospels, III.16, and Calvin on 27:44 understand the plural as a general description that can refer to the conduct of one member of the pair. These are ways of reading the accounts together. The Gospels do not give a detailed timetable for these responses.
passages.god_plan_html:
The mockery closely recalls Psalm 22:6–8: a despised sufferer, heads shaken at him, and a challenge for God to rescue the one who trusts Him. Jesus will soon pray the opening words of this same psalm. The connection lets Scripture's earlier account of suffering and trust help us recognize what the crowd's insults fail to understand.

His place among condemned men also fits Isaiah 53:12. Jesus explicitly applies the servant's being counted among transgressors to Himself in Luke 22:37. The servant pours out His life and bears others' sins; the humiliation is part of the saving work, rather than proof that His mission has failed.

Luke's account then gives a personal glimpse of mercy within that suffering. In Luke 23:39–43, the condemned man acknowledges his own guilt and Jesus' innocence, appeals to Him, and receives a promise of being with Him in Paradise. John 6:35–40 likewise joins coming to Jesus with His welcome and the promise of life. The King who will not escape His own cross still receives someone who turns to Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 27:45-50
passages.section_title: Darkness, the Cry from the Cross, and Jesus’ Death

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 45 From the sixth hour until the ninth hour darkness came over all the land. 46 About the ninth hour Jesus cried out in a loud voice, “Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani?” which means, “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?” 47 When some of those standing there heard this, they said, “He is calling Elijah.” 48 One of them quickly ran and brought a sponge. He filled it with sour wine, put it on a reed, and held it up for Jesus to drink. 49 But the others said, “Leave Him alone. Let us see if Elijah comes to save Him.” 50 When Jesus had cried out again in a loud voice, He yielded up His spirit.
paragraphs: 45 From the sixth hour until the ninth hour darkness came over all the land. 46 About the ninth hour Jesus cried out in a loud voice, “Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani?” which means, “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”

47 When some of those standing there heard this, they said, “He is calling Elijah.” 48 One of them quickly ran and brought a sponge. He filled it with sour wine, put it on a reed, and held it up for Jesus to drink. 49 But the others said, “Leave Him alone. Let us see if Elijah comes to save Him.” 50 When Jesus had cried out again in a loud voice, He yielded up His spirit.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Darkness covers the land from the sixth to the ninth hour, which the BSB note identifies as noon to three in the afternoon. About the ninth hour Jesus cries out with the opening words of Psalm 22:1. Matthew preserves the sound of the cry and then gives its meaning: a prayer asking why God has forsaken Him.

Forsaken comes from ἐγκαταλείπω, enkataleipō (eng-kah-tah-LAY-poh). Thayer's entry explains its use here as abandoning someone in distress or leaving someone helpless. The word conveys the depth of the cry; it does not by itself explain every aspect of the relationship between the Father and the Son.

Some standing nearby speak of Elijah. One runs for a sponge, fills it with sour wine, and holds it up for Jesus, while the others say to wait and see whether Elijah will rescue Him. Matthew then records another loud cry and Jesus yielding up His spirit. The next verses describe the torn temple veil and other events surrounding His death.

John 19:28–30 also records the sour wine and Jesus' declaration that His work is finished. Luke 23:44–46 records His final entrusting of His spirit to the Father. Reading these accounts together keeps both the anguish and the willing self-giving in view.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly recognize the words of Psalm 22:1 in Jesus' cry and understand His suffering and death as part of His saving work. They differ in how they explain His experience of being forsaken.

Calvin on 27:46 understands Jesus as bearing the judgment due to sinners in both body and soul, while His trust in God remains firm through the anguish. Wesley on 27:46 likewise emphasizes both trust and the terrible loss of the felt comfort of God's presence. The Westminster Confession, 8.4–5, teaches His willing suffering in soul and body and His sacrifice for reconciliation.

The Catholic Catechism, 603–604, emphasizes that Jesus did not become a sinner rejected by God: He remains united to the Father in redeeming love while taking our condition upon Himself and speaking in our name. This explanation preserves both His real anguish and the Father's continuing love. These sources give the cry serious weight without treating it as playacting or a failure of faith.
passages.god_plan_html:
Psalm 22 moves from a sufferer's cry to praise, God's hearing of the afflicted, and the nations turning to the LORD (Psalm 22:22–31). The New Testament itself carries this connection further: Hebrews 2:10–13 quotes the psalm's declaration of God's name among brothers when describing Jesus bringing many children to glory. The cry belongs within a larger scriptural story that reaches beyond the suffering to a people gathered in praise.

Romans 5:6–11 explicitly describes reconciliation through the death of God's Son and presents that death as the demonstration of God's love for sinners. 1 Corinthians 15:20–22 then places Christ's resurrection beside the death that came through Adam. His death and resurrection belong together in the saving purpose that brings reconciliation and life.
passages.current_position_html: On Jesus' cry in verse 46, What Does Prayer Look Like? emphasizes honest prayer within suffering. Jesus brings the weight of His experience before the Father without pretending that the anguish is less than it is. The study takes this as a model for bringing grief to God without treating such honesty as unfaithfulness. This supplies our position on the prayer; it does not decide every explanation of the darkness or of how Jesus' suffering accomplishes salvation.

passages.title: Matthew 27:46
passages.section_title: My God, My God, Why Have You Forsaken Me?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 46 About the ninth hour Jesus cried out in a loud voice, “Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani?” which means, “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”
paragraphs: 46 About the ninth hour Jesus cried out in a loud voice, “Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani?” which means, “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”

passages.context_html:
This cry comes near the end of the darkness while Jesus hangs on the cross. Matthew 27:45–50 gives the surrounding account, including the hearers' reference to Elijah, the offered sour wine, and His death.

Jesus uses the opening words of Psalm 22:1. It is a direct prayer to God from within profound distress. The psalm itself begins with the question of abandonment and continues through suffering toward God's hearing and praise.

Forsaken is ἐγκαταλείπω, enkataleipō (eng-kah-tah-LAY-poh). Thayer's lexicon describes abandoning someone in distress. The force of the word should be taken seriously, while the fuller explanation of His suffering must also consider His words and the surrounding Scriptures.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly recognize the words of Psalm 22:1 in Jesus' cry and understand His suffering and death as part of His saving work. They differ in how they explain His experience of being forsaken.

Calvin on 27:46 understands Jesus as bearing the judgment due to sinners in both body and soul, while His trust in God remains firm through the anguish. Wesley on 27:46 likewise emphasizes both trust and the terrible loss of the felt comfort of God's presence. The Westminster Confession, 8.4–5, teaches His willing suffering in soul and body and His sacrifice for reconciliation.

The Catholic Catechism, 603–604, emphasizes that Jesus did not become a sinner rejected by God: He remains united to the Father in redeeming love while taking our condition upon Himself and speaking in our name. This explanation preserves both His real anguish and the Father's continuing love. These sources give the cry serious weight without treating it as playacting or a failure of faith.

Jesus brings the weight of His experience before the Father without pretending that the anguish is less than it is. The study takes this as a model for bringing grief to God without treating such honesty as unfaithfulness. This supplies our position on the prayer; it does not decide every explanation of the darkness or of how Jesus' suffering accomplishes salvation.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The prayer's scriptural setting reaches beyond its opening question. Psalm 22:22–31 speaks of the afflicted person's cry being heard, praise in the assembly, and the nations turning to the LORD. This does not make the opening anguish unreal; it shows where the psalm's whole movement leads.

Hebrews 2:10–13 explicitly applies the psalm's words about proclaiming God's name among brothers to Jesus, in the context of bringing many children to glory through His suffering. The One who cries from the cross also gathers a family who share in His saving work. That is a connection the New Testament makes, rather than a reason to explain away His pain.

passages.title: Matthew 27:51-54
passages.section_title: The Torn Curtain, Opened Tombs, and the Soldiers’ Confession

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 51 At that moment the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom. The earth quaked, and the rocks were split. 52 The tombs broke open, and the bodies of many saints who had fallen asleep were raised. 53 After Jesus’ resurrection, when they had come out of the tombs, they entered the holy city and appeared to many people. 54 When the centurion and those with him who were guarding Jesus saw the earthquake and all that had happened, they were terrified and said, “Truly this was the Son of God.”
paragraphs: 51 At that moment the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom. The earth quaked, and the rocks were split. 52 The tombs broke open, and the bodies of many saints who had fallen asleep were raised. 53 After Jesus’ resurrection, when they had come out of the tombs, they entered the holy city and appeared to many people.
54 When the centurion and those with him who were guarding Jesus saw the earthquake and all that had happened, they were terrified and said, “Truly this was the Son of God.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Immediately after Jesus dies, Matthew describes the temple curtain tearing from top to bottom, an earthquake, and rocks splitting. Tombs open and many of God's people are raised. Verse 53 places their coming out of the tombs and appearing in Jerusalem after Jesus' resurrection. Matthew brings these events together around His death, while also looking ahead to His rising.

The curtain belongs to the temple sanctuary. Josephus, Jewish War 5.5.4–5, describes both a curtain at the entrance and another before the innermost room. The Greek word καταπέτασμα, katapetasma (kah-tah-PEH-tahs-mah), means a curtain or veil. Thayer's lexicon identifies this Gospel reference with the inner curtain, which separated the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place. Hebrews 9:1–7 explains the restricted access behind that curtain under the former arrangement for worship.

The centurion and the soldiers guarding Jesus see the earthquake and what has happened, become terrified, and acknowledge Him as God's Son. Their words stand in sharp contrast to the mockery just before His death. Matthew does not name the raised people or tell us what happened to them afterward.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly see these events as signs that Jesus' death brings a decisive change in humanity's relationship with God and breaks death's power. Calvin on 27:51–53 and Wesley on 27:51–52 connect the curtain with access to God through Christ and the raised saints with the hope of resurrection.

The US Catholic bishops' notes on 27:51–53 also describe access to God's presence as a reading of the torn curtain, while allowing another emphasis: the exposed sanctuary points toward the temple's coming destruction. These are explanatory notes, rather than a rule that every Catholic must choose one explanation.

Readers also differ over how far the soldiers' confession goes. The bishops' note on 27:54 calls it a Christian confession of faith by Gentiles. Calvin on 27:54 instead understands the centurion's response as a brief recognition prompted by fear, without a lasting conversion. Matthew records their fear and words, but gives no account of their later lives.
passages.god_plan_html:
The torn curtain fits a connection the New Testament develops at length. Hebrews 9:11–15, 24 describes Jesus as the High Priest who enters God's presence on our behalf through His own sacrifice. Hebrews 10:19–25 then invites believers to draw near through Him, hold to their hope, and encourage one another in love. Access to God remains through Jesus; the invitation is to approach with confidence because of Him.

This also gives believers a life of service. 1 Peter 2:4–10 describes them as a priesthood offering spiritual sacrifices through Jesus and making God's goodness known. Romans 12:1–2 brings that worship into ordinary life: offering ourselves to God and letting Him change how we think and live. These passages help explain why Christ's saving work leads to more than relief from judgment; it gives His people a purpose.

The opened tombs also look toward the defeat of death. 1 Corinthians 15:20–26 calls the risen Christ the firstfruits—the beginning of a harvest that includes those who belong to Him. Matthew does not explain the later lives of these particular saints, but the larger promise is clear: death will not have the final word.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 27:55-56
passages.section_title: The Women Who Remained Near the Cross

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 55 And many women were there, watching from a distance. They had followed Jesus from Galilee to minister to Him. 56 Among them were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joseph, and the mother of Zebedee’s sons.
paragraphs: 55 And many women were there, watching from a distance. They had followed Jesus from Galilee to minister to Him. 56 Among them were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joseph, and the mother of Zebedee’s sons.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After describing the soldiers' response, Matthew turns to women watching from a distance. They had followed Jesus from Galilee and served Him. He names Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joseph, and the mother of Zebedee's sons. These are followers whose service began before the crucifixion.

Luke 8:1–3 gives a wider picture of women who accompanied Jesus and supported His ministry from their own resources. Matthew's account here leads into their continued presence: Mary Magdalene and the other Mary watch the burial in 27:61 and return to the tomb in 28:1. They connect the account of His death with what happens at His tomb.

Matthew's list is not a statement that no other follower was nearby. Luke 23:49 mentions those who knew Him standing at a distance, and John 19:25–27 describes Jesus' mother and the disciple He loved near the cross.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly recognize these women as faithful followers whose presence matters to the account of Jesus' death, burial, and empty tomb. Calvin on 27:55 emphasizes their devotion and witness, while the US Catholic bishops' note on 27:55–56 highlights the same women's appearance at the burial and the tomb afterward; no denominational breakdown is needed here.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 27:57-61
passages.section_title: Joseph Places Jesus in His Own Tomb

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 57 When it was evening, there came a rich man from Arimathea named Joseph, who himself was a disciple of Jesus. 58 He went to Pilate to ask for the body of Jesus, and Pilate ordered that it be given to him. 59 So Joseph took the body, wrapped it in a clean linen cloth, 60 and placed it in his own new tomb that he had cut into the rock. Then he rolled a great stone across the entrance to the tomb and went away. 61 Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were sitting there opposite the tomb.
paragraphs: 57 When it was evening, there came a rich man from Arimathea named Joseph, who himself was a disciple of Jesus. 58 He went to Pilate to ask for the body of Jesus, and Pilate ordered that it be given to him.

59 So Joseph took the body, wrapped it in a clean linen cloth, 60 and placed it in his own new tomb that he had cut into the rock. Then he rolled a great stone across the entrance to the tomb and went away. 61 Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were sitting there opposite the tomb.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
As evening comes, Joseph of Arimathea, a wealthy disciple, asks Pilate for Jesus' body. Pilate grants the request. Joseph wraps the body in clean linen, places it in his own new tomb cut into the rock, and rolls a large stone across its entrance. Mary Magdalene and the other Mary sit opposite the tomb.

The other Gospels add details without making Joseph's private thoughts known. Luke 23:50–56 calls him a good and righteous Council member who had not agreed with its decision and action. John 19:38–42 says he had followed Jesus secretly because of fear, and that Nicodemus helped with the burial, bringing myrrh and aloes. John explicitly says they wrapped the body with spices; Matthew's shorter account does not mean none were used.

John also explains that the tomb was nearby and the day was Preparation Day. Luke says the Sabbath was beginning. These details explain the urgency. The women see the burial place rather than hearing about it later, which matters when Matthew returns to them at the start of chapter 28.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the burial as the burial of someone who truly died, leading to the proclamation that this same Jesus rose. The Catholic Catechism, 624–627, and the Reformed Westminster Confession, 8.4, both affirm His real death, burial, and resurrection; Joseph's care gives concrete detail to that shared confession.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Corinthians 15:3–5 includes Jesus' burial among the central events of the gospel, between His death for sins and His resurrection. Burial is part of the story of His saving work, not an interruption of it. Acts 13:27–39 likewise moves from His condemnation and burial to God's raising Him and the announcement of forgiveness.

Joseph's wealth and his gift of a tomb also recall Isaiah 53:9, where the suffering servant is associated with a rich man in death. Matthew does not introduce this detail with a quotation, so the connection should be recognized as a scriptural parallel. The New Testament explicitly connects Isaiah's servant with Jesus in Acts 8:30–35.

There is also a moving picture here: Jesus is placed in a disciple's own tomb. That can bring to mind His taking the place of sinners, as Romans 5:6–11 explains. It is a parallel for reflection, rather than a claim that Matthew assigns a special meaning to Joseph's ownership or tells us what Joseph thought about it.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 27:62-66
passages.section_title: The Tomb Is Sealed and Guarded

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 62 The next day, the one after Preparation Day, the chief priests and Pharisees assembled before Pilate. 63 “Sir,” they said, “we remember that while He was alive that deceiver said, ‘After three days I will rise again.’ 64 So give the order that the tomb be secured until the third day. Otherwise, His disciples may come and steal Him away and tell the people He has risen from the dead. And this last deception would be worse than the first.” 65 “You have a guard,” Pilate said. “Go, make the tomb as secure as you know how.” 66 So they went and secured the tomb by sealing the stone and posting the guard.
paragraphs: 62 The next day, the one after Preparation Day, the chief priests and Pharisees assembled before Pilate. 63 “Sir,” they said, “we remember that while He was alive that deceiver said, ‘After three days I will rise again.’ 64 So give the order that the tomb be secured until the third day. Otherwise, His disciples may come and steal Him away and tell the people He has risen from the dead. And this last deception would be worse than the first.”
65 “You have a guard,” Pilate said. “Go, make the tomb as secure as you know how.” 66 So they went and secured the tomb by sealing the stone and posting the guard.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
On the day after Preparation Day, the chief priests and Pharisees ask Pilate to secure the tomb until the third day. They remember Jesus speaking about rising after three days, but call Him a deceiver and fear that His disciples will steal the body and announce a resurrection.

Pilate tells them they have a guard and to make the tomb as secure as they know how. They seal the stone and post the guard. Matthew does not describe the seal's design or give the number of guards.

This scene prepares for Matthew 28:11–15, where guards report what has happened and are paid to spread the claim that the disciples stole the body while they slept. Reading the two scenes together shows why Matthew includes the precautions taken at the tomb.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly understand the guard and seal as precautions intended to prevent a stolen-body claim, which later become part of Matthew's account of the empty tomb. Calvin on 27:62–66 and Wesley on 27:66 both emphasize the irony that efforts to suppress Jesus' resurrection end up strengthening the testimony to it.

There is a smaller question about whose guard Pilate meant. The US Catholic bishops' note on 27:65 explains that the wording can refer to Roman soldiers granted by Pilate or to the authorities being told to use their own guards. This uncertainty about their identity does not change their role in the account: the tomb is deliberately secured.
passages.god_plan_html:
The leaders remember Jesus' prediction while trying to prevent what they regard as a deception. Readers have already heard Him say that He must suffer, be killed, and rise on the third day (Matthew 16:21). The secured tomb sets human precautions beside the promise He has made.

Acts 13:27–39 looks back on the same larger story: Jesus is condemned and buried, but God raises Him, fulfills His promises, and announces forgiveness through Him. The burial is real, and the guards are real obstacles to removing a body; neither determines what God can do. Matthew's next chapter tells how His promise is fulfilled.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 28:1-10
passages.section_title: The Empty Tomb and the Risen Jesus

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 After the Sabbath, at dawn on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary went to see the tomb. 2 Suddenly there was a great earthquake, for an angel of the Lord descended from heaven, rolled away the stone, and sat on it. 3 His appearance was like lightning, and his clothes were white as snow. 4 The guards trembled in fear of him and became like dead men. 5 But the angel said to the women, “Do not be afraid, for I know that you are looking for Jesus, who was crucified. 6 He is not here; He has risen, just as He said! Come, see the place where He lay. 7 Then go quickly and tell His disciples, ‘He has risen from the dead and is going ahead of you into Galilee. There you will see Him.’ See, I have told you.” 8 So they hurried away from the tomb in fear and great joy, and ran to tell His disciples. 9 Suddenly Jesus met them and said, “Greetings!” They came to Him, grasped His feet, and worshiped Him. 10 “Do not be afraid,” said Jesus. “Go and tell My brothers to go to Galilee. There they will see Me.”
paragraphs: 1 After the Sabbath, at dawn on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary went to see the tomb. 2 Suddenly there was a great earthquake, for an angel of the Lord descended from heaven, rolled away the stone, and sat on it. 3 His appearance was like lightning, and his clothes were white as snow. 4 The guards trembled in fear of him and became like dead men.

5 But the angel said to the women, “Do not be afraid, for I know that you are looking for Jesus, who was crucified. 6 He is not here; He has risen, just as He said! Come, see the place where He lay. 7 Then go quickly and tell His disciples, ‘He has risen from the dead and is going ahead of you into Galilee. There you will see Him.’ See, I have told you.” 8 So they hurried away from the tomb in fear and great joy, and ran to tell His disciples.

9 Suddenly Jesus met them and said, “Greetings!” They came to Him, grasped His feet, and worshiped Him. 10 “Do not be afraid,” said Jesus. “Go and tell My brothers to go to Galilee. There they will see Me.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the Sabbath, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary go to the tomb at dawn on the first day of the week. They are the women Matthew has already placed opposite Jesus' tomb in 27:61. The account of their visit follows the sealing of the tomb and posting of a guard.

An angel descends, the earth shakes, and the stone is rolled away. The guards tremble and become like dead men. The angel tells the women not to fear: Jesus, who was crucified, has risen as He said. They are invited to see where He lay and told to carry the news to His disciples, with the promise that they will see Him in Galilee.

As they hurry away in fear and joy, Jesus Himself meets them. They grasp His feet and worship Him. He repeats the reassurance and calls His disciples His brothers, sending the women to tell them to go to Galilee. The passage moves from an empty tomb and an angel's message to an encounter with Jesus Himself.

John 20:11–18 gives a more personal account of Mary Magdalene meeting Him. The Gospels select different details; Matthew does not give a minute-by-minute account of every visit or describe what happened inside the tomb as Jesus rose.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The major Christian traditions understand this as Jesus truly rising from the dead, rather than His followers merely keeping His memory alive. The Catholic Catechism, 639–646, the Reformed Westminster Confession, 8.4, and the Methodist Articles of Religion, Article III, all affirm His real resurrection; the women touching His feet belongs to that witness to the living Jesus.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Corinthians 15:12–22 explains why the resurrection is central to Christian hope: if Christ has not been raised, faith is empty and sin still holds its claim. Because He has been raised, His people can look toward life beyond death. Paul connects the death that came through Adam with the resurrection that comes through Christ.

That hope concerns the whole person. 1 Corinthians 15:35–44 describes the body raised beyond its present weakness and decay. Matthew's women meet and touch Jesus; they are not told to settle for a comforting idea about Him. The risen Lord also gives them a message to carry, so the announcement of life begins moving outward.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 28:11-15
passages.section_title: The Guards Are Paid to Tell a Different Story

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 While the women were on their way, some of the guards went into the city and reported to the chief priests all that had happened. 12 And after the chief priests had met with the elders and formed a plan, they gave the soldiers a large sum of money 13 and instructed them: “You are to say, ‘His disciples came by night and stole Him away while we were asleep.’ 14 If this report reaches the governor, we will satisfy him and keep you out of trouble.” 15 So the guards took the money and did as they were instructed. And this account has been circulated among the Jews to this very day.
paragraphs: 11 While the women were on their way, some of the guards went into the city and reported to the chief priests all that had happened. 12 And after the chief priests had met with the elders and formed a plan, they gave the soldiers a large sum of money 13 and instructed them: “You are to say, ‘His disciples came by night and stole Him away while we were asleep.’ 14 If this report reaches the governor, we will satisfy him and keep you out of trouble.” 15 So the guards took the money and did as they were instructed. And this account has been circulated among the Jews to this very day.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
While the women go to tell the disciples, some guards enter the city and report to the chief priests. The priests meet with the elders, pay the soldiers a large sum, and give them a story to repeat: the disciples stole Jesus' body while they slept. They promise to deal with the governor if the report reaches him.

This follows the deliberate securing of the tomb in Matthew 27:62–66. The people who asked for protection against a stolen-body claim now pay the guards to spread that very claim. Matthew contrasts it with the women's encounter with Jesus and says the account was still circulating when he wrote.

The passage describes these officials and soldiers making this arrangement. It does not assign their actions or motives to every Jewish person, either then or in later generations. Jesus, His disciples, and the women bringing the resurrection news were themselves Jewish.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand this as Matthew's account of an organized attempt to explain away the empty tomb. Wesley on 28:13 points to the problem of sleeping guards claiming to know who took the body, while the US Catholic bishops' note on 28:11–15 describes the dispute as being over why the tomb was empty; no denominational breakdown is needed for that shared reading.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Matthew 28:16-20
passages.section_title: Jesus Sends His Disciples to All Nations

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 Meanwhile, the eleven disciples went to Galilee, to the mountain Jesus had designated. 17 When they saw Him, they worshiped Him, but some doubted. 18 Then Jesus came to them and said, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me. 19 Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, 20 and teaching them to obey all that I have commanded you. And surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age.”

19 Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, 20 and teaching them to obey all that I have commanded you. And surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The eleven disciples go to the mountain in Galilee that Jesus designated. They worship Him, yet Matthew also reports that some doubt. Jesus comes to them and speaks of His authority, their mission, and His continuing presence.

The word for doubting is διστάζω, distazō (dis-TAH-zoh). Thayer's lexicon gives the sense of doubting or wavering and also lists Peter's hesitation in Matthew 14:31. Matthew does not say exactly what each disciple was thinking. The commission is addressed to people who still need His reassurance.

Jesus commands them to make disciples of all nations, baptizing in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit and teaching obedience to His commands. Making disciples comes from μαθητεύω, mathēteuō (mah-thay-TYOO-oh), which Thayer explains here as making a disciple, teaching, or instructing. The goal is a people learning to follow Him, with baptism and continued teaching belonging to that work.

The Gospel ends with His promise to be with them until the end of the age. Matthew does not narrate the ascension here. He closes by setting the mission within Jesus' authority and presence.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Catholic, Reformed, Baptist, Wesleyan, and Lutheran readings share the command to make disciples, baptize in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and teach obedience to Jesus. They differ over who should receive baptism, what God gives through it, and how it should be administered.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, 28.1–6, includes believers and their children, calls baptism a sign and seal of God's promise of grace, and permits pouring or sprinkling. It does not teach that every baptized person is necessarily born again or that God's grace is confined to the moment of baptism. The 1689 Baptist Confession, 29.1–4, instead limits baptism to people who profess repentance and faith, and requires immersion. It describes baptism as a sign of fellowship with Christ in His death and resurrection and a commitment to new life.

The Catholic Catechism, 1247–1255, describes preparation in faith for adults and baptism of infants, who are to grow in the faith of the Church with help from parents and godparents. It understands baptism as the beginning of new life in Christ. The Lutheran Augsburg Confession, Article IX, likewise affirms infant baptism and emphasizes that God offers His saving grace through baptism.

The Methodist Articles of Religion, Article XVII, call baptism both a mark of Christian profession and a sign of new birth, and retain the baptism of young children. Wesley's note on 28:19 explains that adults are taught before baptism, while children are baptized and then taught. These documents identify particular traditions' teachings; individual congregations and members do not all explain every detail in the same way.

The mission to all nations belongs to a promise running through Scripture. God tells Abraham that the families of the earth will be blessed through him (Genesis 12:1–3); Galatians 3:6–9 explicitly connects that promise with the good news reaching the Gentiles through faith. The commission carries that worldwide purpose forward.

Jesus' authority also recalls Daniel 7:13–14, where one like the Son of Man receives enduring rule and peoples of every nation serve Him. This is a scriptural parallel, not a quotation introduced by Matthew. The Gospel's closing promise of His presence also recalls its opening description of Immanuel, God with us (Matthew 1:22–23). The disciples are sent under His authority and with His presence, rather than left to carry the mission alone.
passages.current_position_html:
I Am a Disciple and The True Church According to Jesus understand disciple-making as helping people become lifelong learners and followers of Jesus. It includes knowing His teaching, practicing it, loving others, and bearing witness in ordinary life. The mission belongs to Christ's people across generations and reaches beyond a single event or a program run by a few leaders.

Baptism supplies our position on that part of the commission: baptism is commanded and is a meaningful response of faith in Christ, while salvation is received by grace through faith. The study prefers immersion because it pictures burial and new life with Him, while recognizing that Scripture does not explicitly declare every other mode invalid. These points come from those existing studies.

passages.title: Mark 1:1-3
passages.section_title: The Good News and the Promised Messenger

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 This is the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God. 2 As it is written in Isaiah the prophet: “Behold, I will send My messenger ahead of You, who will prepare Your way.” 3 “A voice of one calling in the wilderness, ‘Prepare the way for the Lord, make straight paths for Him.’”
paragraphs: 1 This is the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God.

2 As it is written in Isaiah the prophet: “Behold, I will send My messenger ahead of You, who will prepare Your way.” 3 “A voice of one calling in the wilderness, ‘Prepare the way for the Lord, make straight paths for Him.’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Mark opens by identifying the subject of his account: the good news of Jesus Christ, the Son of God. He begins with the promised messenger who will prepare the way, before describing John the Baptist in the wilderness. Unlike Matthew and Luke, he does not begin with Jesus' birth.

Gospel translates εὐαγγέλιον, euangelion (yoo-ang-GHEL-ee-on), meaning good news or glad tidings. Thayer's lexicon explains its New Testament use as the good news of God's kingdom and salvation through Christ. Mark is introducing what God is doing through Jesus, rather than using a word that simply means a religious book.

The quotation brings together Malachi 3:1 and Isaiah 40:3, with wording also recalling the messenger sent ahead in Exodus 23:20. The BSB's notes identify Malachi and Isaiah as the quoted passages. Isaiah's name heads the combined quotation, whose wilderness voice leads into John's appearance.

The BSB retains the words identifying Jesus as the Son of God in verse 1 and notes that some textual editions omit them there. The same identification is made clearly later in this chapter, when the voice from heaven addresses Jesus at His baptism (Mark 1:9–11).
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand John as the promised messenger preparing people for Jesus, and the opening as announcing the good news of salvation through Him. Wesley on 1:1–3 and the US Catholic bishops' notes on 1:1–3 share that basic reading; no denominational breakdown is needed here.
passages.god_plan_html:
Mark himself links Jesus' arrival with God's earlier promises. In Isaiah 40:1–11, the wilderness announcement belongs to a message of comfort for Jerusalem: God is coming to rule, gather His people, and care for them as a shepherd. Mark applies the preparation of the Lord's way to the coming of Jesus. The good news grows from that long story of God's faithfulness.

Malachi 3:1–4 also places a messenger before the coming Lord and speaks of cleansing His people. John is not presented as the destination of their hope. His place is to prepare them for the One who follows. As Mark's account unfolds, the good news will include Jesus' service, suffering, and victory over death—the central events Paul summarizes in 1 Corinthians 15:1–5.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 1:4-8
passages.section_title: John Calls for Repentance and Points to Jesus

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 4 John the Baptist appeared in the wilderness, preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. 5 People went out to him from all of Jerusalem and the countryside of Judea. Confessing their sins, they were baptized by him in the Jordan River. 6 John was clothed in camel’s hair, with a leather belt around his waist. His food was locusts and wild honey. 7 And he proclaimed: “After me will come One more powerful than I, the straps of whose sandals I am not worthy to stoop down and untie. 8 I baptize you with water, but He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit.”
paragraphs: 4 John the Baptist appeared in the wilderness, preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. 5 People went out to him from all of Jerusalem and the countryside of Judea. Confessing their sins, they were baptized by him in the Jordan River. 6 John was clothed in camel’s hair, with a leather belt around his waist. His food was locusts and wild honey.

7 And he proclaimed: “After me will come One more powerful than I, the straps of whose sandals I am not worthy to stoop down and untie. 8 I baptize you with water, but He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
John appears in the wilderness, preaching a baptism of repentance for forgiveness. People come from Jerusalem and the Judean countryside, confess their sins, and are baptized in the Jordan. This is the messenger's work introduced in the opening verses: preparing people for the Lord.

Repentance translates μετάνοια, metanoia (meh-TAH-noy-ah). Thayer's entry describes recognizing one's sins and changing course, with a changed life as its result. Luke 3:10–14 shows the practical force of John's message: share with people in need, collect honestly, and stop using power to take from others.

John's camel-hair clothing and leather belt recall Elijah's appearance in 2 Kings 1:7–8. Mark names his food as locusts and wild honey. Yet John directs attention away from himself: the One coming after him is so much greater that he is unworthy even to stoop down and untie His sandals.

John then sets his baptism with water beside the coming One's baptism with the Holy Spirit. Mark does not add the words about fire found in Matthew and Luke. The immediate emphasis is on what Jesus can give that John cannot.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly see a call to genuine repentance and a clear declaration that Jesus is greater than John. They differ in explaining how John's baptism relates to Christian baptism.

The Catholic Catechism, 717–720, treats John as the Spirit-filled forerunner and distinguishes his baptism of repentance from the new birth associated with baptism in water and the Spirit. His work prepares for what Christ brings.

In his Reformed commentary on the parallel account, Calvin instead stresses continuity between John's baptism and Christian baptism. He understands the main contrast as the difference between a servant administering the outward sign and Christ giving its spiritual reality. That is Calvin's explanation, rather than a claim that every Reformed Christian interprets every detail alike. Wesley on Mark 1:4 describes John's baptism as a sign and means of repentance.
passages.god_plan_html:
The promise of the Spirit reaches beyond John getting people ready. Ezekiel 36:22–28, spoken to Israel, joins God's cleansing with His gift of a new heart and His Spirit enabling His people to walk in His ways. That is a theme parallel to John's announcement: God's purpose involves changing people from within, not simply washing their bodies.

The New Testament makes the connection with John's words explicit in Acts 1:4–8. Jesus recalls John's baptism with water, promises baptism with the Holy Spirit, and tells His followers they will receive power to bear witness to Him beyond Jerusalem. The preparation in the wilderness looks ahead to a people empowered to carry His message.

Acts 19:1–7 also explains that John's baptism pointed people toward faith in the coming Jesus. John's humility fits his place in that purpose: he prepares the way, while the life-giving gift belongs to the One he announces.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 1:9-11
passages.section_title: Jesus Is Baptized and the Father Speaks

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 In those days Jesus came from Nazareth in Galilee and was baptized by John in the Jordan. 10 As soon as Jesus came up out of the water, He saw the heavens breaking open and the Spirit descending on Him like a dove. 11 And a voice came from heaven: “You are My beloved Son; in You I am well pleased.”
paragraphs: 9 In those days Jesus came from Nazareth in Galilee and was baptized by John in the Jordan. 10 As soon as Jesus came up out of the water, He saw the heavens breaking open and the Spirit descending on Him like a dove. 11 And a voice came from heaven: “You are My beloved Son; in You I am well pleased.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The One John has been announcing now arrives from Nazareth in Galilee and is baptized in the Jordan. As Jesus comes up from the water, He sees the heavens breaking open, the Spirit descending on Him like a dove, and hears the voice identifying Him as the beloved Son in whom God delights.

Breaking open comes from σχίζω, schizō (SKHEE-zoh), meaning to tear or split apart. Thayer's entry explicitly lists the heavens in this verse. Mark uses vivid language for God's disclosure of His Son.

Mark keeps the scene brief. Matthew 3:13–17 also records John's hesitation and Jesus' answer about fulfilling righteousness. John 1:29–34 explains that the Spirit descending and remaining was the sign John had been given to recognize the One who baptizes with the Holy Spirit.

The Father speaks, the Son is baptized, and the Spirit descends. The scene follows John's promise of the coming One's greater work and comes immediately before Jesus' testing in the wilderness.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The major Christian traditions understand this as the public revelation of Jesus as God's beloved Son and the beginning of His ministry, rather than His admission of personal sin. The Catholic Catechism, 535–536, and Calvin on the parallel Matthew 3:13–17, both emphasize His willing obedience to the Father and His action for others; no denominational breakdown is needed for that shared understanding.
passages.god_plan_html:
The Father's words bring together themes found in Psalm 2:6–9, where God speaks of His royal Son, and Isaiah 42:1–7, where He delights in His servant and places His Spirit on Him. These are scriptural parallels: Mark does not introduce the voice as a direct quotation of either passage. Together they help us see the coming ministry as both the work of God's King and the service of the One He has chosen.

John's testimony in John 1:29–34 joins this identification with Jesus' work as the Lamb who takes away the world's sin. He comes among those receiving John's baptism, while His own calling is to deal with their sin. The scene points forward to the saving work of the Son whom the Father loves, not to Jesus becoming God's Son for the first time.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 1:12-13
passages.section_title: Jesus Is Tested in the Wilderness

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 At once the Spirit drove Jesus into the wilderness, 13 and He was there for forty days, being tempted by Satan. He was with the wild animals, and the angels ministered to Him.
paragraphs: 12 At once the Spirit drove Jesus into the wilderness, 13 and He was there for forty days, being tempted by Satan. He was with the wild animals, and the angels ministered to Him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Immediately after His baptism, the Spirit drives Jesus into the wilderness. He remains there for forty days, is tempted by Satan, is with the wild animals, and is served by angels. Mark places this testing directly after the Father's declaration of love and before Jesus begins preaching in Galilee.

Tempted comes from πειράζω, peirazō (pay-RAH-zoh). Thayer's lexicon explains the word's range of testing and tempting, and identifies Satan's use here as an enticement to sin. The Spirit's leading and Satan's temptation have different purposes. James 1:13–15 explains that God does not entice people to evil.

Matthew 4:1–11 and Luke 4:1–13 give the exchanges that Mark leaves unreported. They describe Jesus' hunger and His answers from Scripture. Mark concentrates on the wilderness conflict and God's care through the angels, without describing the animals' behavior or naming particular temptations.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian traditions commonly understand this as real testing in which Jesus remains faithful, showing His obedience and His ability to help people who are tempted. The Catholic Catechism, 538–540, and Calvin on the parallel Matthew 4:1, both relate the wilderness trial to His saving mission.

The US Catholic bishops' note on Mark 1:12–13 offers two possible emphases for the wild animals: the wilderness's danger, or a picture recalling creation at peace. These are possibilities in explanatory notes, rather than an official requirement to read the animals one way. Mark says they were there; he does not say whether they threatened Jesus or lived peaceably around Him.
passages.god_plan_html:
The forty days invite comparison with Israel's wilderness story. Exodus 4:22–23 calls Israel God's son, and Deuteronomy 8:1–6 recalls forty years of testing, hunger, and learning to trust His word. Jesus has just been declared God's Son and now enters the wilderness. This is a scriptural parallel, strengthened by His use of Deuteronomy in Matthew 4:1–11. He remains faithful where Israel had struggled.

The connection reaches people facing temptation now. Hebrews 2:14–18 says that Jesus shares our humanity and, because He suffered when tempted, is able to help those being tempted. Hebrews 4:14–16 joins His sinlessness with His understanding of our weakness and invites us to seek mercy and help from Him. His testing is part of His work for us, not simply a lesson in willpower.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 1:14-15
passages.section_title: The Kingdom Is Near: Repent and Believe

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 After the arrest of John, Jesus went into Galilee and proclaimed the gospel of God. 15 “The time is fulfilled,” He said, “and the kingdom of God is near. Repent and believe in the gospel!”
paragraphs: 14 After the arrest of John, Jesus went into Galilee and proclaimed the gospel of God. 15 “The time is fulfilled,” He said, “and the kingdom of God is near. Repent and believe in the gospel!”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After John's arrest, Jesus comes into Galilee and announces the good news of God. Mark has moved from the messenger's preparation and Jesus' baptism and testing into His public preaching. He will explain John's imprisonment more fully in Mark 6:17–29.

Jesus' message joins an announcement with a response: the time has been fulfilled, God's kingdom has drawn near, and people are called to repent and believe. Time is καιρός, kairos (kye-ROSS). Thayer's lexicon gives its range as a definite time, season, or appointed occasion. In this sentence, fulfilled makes the point that the awaited moment has arrived.

Kingdom concerns God's rule. Thayer's entry for βασιλεία, basileia (bah-see-LAY-ah), includes kingship, dominion, and a kingdom. Here the announcement is connected with Jesus' arrival and work. The next scenes begin showing what responding to Him looks like, as people leave their former work to follow Him.

Repentance and faith belong together: turning from sin and placing trust in the good news. Mark's account is still at the beginning of the ministry, before Jesus' death and resurrection. Readers will learn what the good news involves as His story unfolds.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as the arrival of the promised time and a call to respond to God's rule through Jesus with repentance and faith. The Catholic Catechism, 541–545, Calvin on Mark 1:14–15, and Wesley on 1:15 share that basic reading.
passages.god_plan_html:
The opening of Mark has already joined Jesus' arrival with the prophets' promises. Romans 1:1–6 later uses the same expression, the gospel of God, for the good news promised in Scripture concerning His Son, including His resurrection. Jesus' first announcement belongs within that unfolding work of salvation.

God's rule also changes how people live together. Romans 14:17–19 connects His kingdom with righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit, and calls believers to pursue peace and build one another up. The announcement looks toward a people whose life together is shaped by the King they receive.
passages.current_position_html: The Gospel According to Jesus understands repentance as turning away from sin and self-rule toward Jesus as Lord, joined with faith in Him. The study treats salvation as God's gift received through faith. The changed life that follows expresses His rule rather than earning a place in His kingdom.

passages.title: Mark 1:16-20
passages.section_title: Four Fishermen Follow Jesus

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 As Jesus was walking beside the Sea of Galilee, He saw Simon and his brother Andrew. They were casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen. 17 “Come, follow Me,” Jesus said, “and I will make you fishers of men.” 18 And at once they left their nets and followed Him. 19 Going on a little farther, He saw James son of Zebedee and his brother John. They were in a boat, mending their nets. 20 Immediately Jesus called them, and they left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired men and followed Him.
paragraphs: 16 As Jesus was walking beside the Sea of Galilee, He saw Simon and his brother Andrew. They were casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen. 17 “Come, follow Me,” Jesus said, “and I will make you fishers of men.” 18 And at once they left their nets and followed Him.

19 Going on a little farther, He saw James son of Zebedee and his brother John. They were in a boat, mending their nets. 20 Immediately Jesus called them, and they left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired men and followed Him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Walking beside the Sea of Galilee, Jesus calls two sets of brothers during their work. Simon and Andrew are casting a net. James and John are mending nets in a boat with their father Zebedee. Both pairs respond promptly, leaving their former setting to follow Him.

Jesus uses their familiar work as a picture of what He will make them: people who gather others. The promise puts their future service in His hands. He calls them to follow, learn from Him, and become able to share His work.

Mark includes the hired men who remain in Zebedee's boat. That is a concrete detail about what the brothers leave behind, rather than a statement that every disciple must abandon every trade or leave family members without support.

John 1:35–42 records Andrew following Jesus after the Baptist's testimony and bringing Simon to Him. Luke 5:1–11 tells the call alongside a remarkable catch of fish. These accounts can be read together, while Mark's own emphasis stays on Jesus' summons and their response.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see costly discipleship and preparation for sharing Jesus' mission. The Catholic Catechism, 551, emphasizes participation in His work, while Wesley on Mark 1:18 stresses their prompt response; no denominational breakdown is needed for that shared understanding.
passages.god_plan_html:
The promise begins to take shape within Mark's own story. In Mark 3:13–19, these men are among the twelve appointed to be with Jesus and to be sent out to preach. In Mark 6:7–13, He sends them in pairs, and they call people to repent and bring help to those in need. Learning at His side becomes service to others.

John 15:16 also speaks of Jesus choosing and appointing His disciples to bear lasting fruit. This is a connection with His wider teaching, not a claim that Mark records everything the fishermen already understood. Their beginning in ordinary work does not set the limit of what He can make of them.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 1:21-28
passages.section_title: Jesus Teaches and Commands an Unclean Spirit

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 Then Jesus and His companions went to Capernaum, and right away Jesus entered the synagogue on the Sabbath and began to teach. 22 The people were astonished at His teaching, because He taught as one who had authority, and not as the scribes. 23 Suddenly a man with an unclean spirit cried out in the synagogue: 24 “What do You want with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have You come to destroy us? I know who You are—the Holy One of God!” 25 But Jesus rebuked the spirit. “Be silent!” He said. “Come out of him!” 26 At this, the unclean spirit threw the man into convulsions and came out with a loud shriek. 27 All the people were amazed and began to ask one another, “What is this? A new teaching with authority! He commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey Him!” 28 And the news about Jesus spread quickly through the whole region of Galilee.
paragraphs: 21 Then Jesus and His companions went to Capernaum, and right away Jesus entered the synagogue on the Sabbath and began to teach. 22 The people were astonished at His teaching, because He taught as one who had authority, and not as the scribes.

23 Suddenly a man with an unclean spirit cried out in the synagogue: 24 “What do You want with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have You come to destroy us? I know who You are—the Holy One of God!” 25 But Jesus rebuked the spirit. “Be silent!” He said. “Come out of him!” 26 At this, the unclean spirit threw the man into convulsions and came out with a loud shriek.

27 All the people were amazed and began to ask one another, “What is this? A new teaching with authority! He commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey Him!” 28 And the news about Jesus spread quickly through the whole region of Galilee.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus and His companions enter Capernaum, and He teaches in the synagogue on the Sabbath. The people are astonished by His authority. Mark then shows that authority in action: an unclean spirit recognizes Him, fears destruction, and must obey His command to leave the man.

Authority is ἐξουσία, exousia (ex-oo-SEE-ah). Thayer's entry includes the power and weight of Jesus' teaching in verses 22 and 27. The crowd's response joins His words and His action: He teaches with authority, and the spirits obey Him.

The spirit calls Him the Holy One of God. Jesus silences it and orders it out. The man is thrown into convulsions, the spirit departs with a cry, and the news spreads through Galilee. Mark describes a personal confrontation and release, rather than merely reporting an impressive lecture.

This follows Jesus' announcement that God's kingdom is near and His call of the fishermen. They now accompany Him as His teaching and power become known. The account will move from this public setting to care for someone in Simon and Andrew's home.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand this as Jesus demonstrating authority over evil spirits, with His action confirming the authority heard in His teaching. Wesley on Mark 1:26–34 distinguishes the spirits from disease, and the Catholic Catechism, 550, describes Jesus' freeing people from demons as a sign of God's kingdom overcoming Satan's power.
passages.god_plan_html:
The connection between this release and God's kingdom is made explicit in Jesus' later teaching. In Luke 11:14–23, He says that His driving out demons by God's power shows the kingdom has come upon His hearers. In Mark 3:22–27, He describes overpowering a strong man before taking what he holds. The rescue in the synagogue gives an early picture of that victory.

1 John 3:7–10 says that the Son of God was revealed to destroy the devil's works, in a passage calling God's children toward righteousness and love. Jesus' authority is directed toward freeing people from evil and restoring a life that belongs to God. The scene belongs within that larger saving purpose.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 1:29-34
passages.section_title: Healing in a Home and Help for the Crowds

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 29 As soon as Jesus and His companions had left the synagogue, they went with James and John to the home of Simon and Andrew. 30 Simon’s mother-in-law was sick in bed with a fever, and they promptly told Jesus about her. 31 So He went to her, took her by the hand, and helped her up. The fever left her, and she began to serve them. 32 That evening, after sunset, people brought to Jesus all the sick and demon-possessed, 33 and the whole town gathered at the door. 34 And He healed many who were ill with various diseases and drove out many demons. But He would not allow the demons to speak, because they knew who He was.
paragraphs: 29 As soon as Jesus and His companions had left the synagogue, they went with James and John to the home of Simon and Andrew. 30 Simon’s mother-in-law was sick in bed with a fever, and they promptly told Jesus about her. 31 So He went to her, took her by the hand, and helped her up. The fever left her, and she began to serve them.

32 That evening, after sunset, people brought to Jesus all the sick and demon-possessed, 33 and the whole town gathered at the door. 34 And He healed many who were ill with various diseases and drove out many demons. But He would not allow the demons to speak, because they knew who He was.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After leaving the synagogue, Jesus goes with James and John to Simon and Andrew's home. Simon's mother-in-law is in bed with a fever. They tell Him about her, and He takes her hand and helps her up. The fever leaves, and she begins serving them.

Serve is διακονέω, diakoneō (dee-ah-koh-NEH-oh). Thayer's entry explains its use here as waiting on people, including providing food and drink. Her return to ordinary service shows the change in her condition. The word does not make this an appointment to a church office.

That evening, after sunset, the scene widens. People bring the sick and those troubled by demons, and a large crowd gathers at the door. Jesus heals many and drives out many demons. Mark distinguishes the illnesses from the spirits; the passage does not identify every sickness as possession.

Jesus again refuses to let the demons speak because they know who He is. The movement from the synagogue to a family home and then the crowded doorway shows His care reaching people in both public and personal settings.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly see Jesus' compassion and authority in these healings, with the woman's restored ability to serve showing how fully she has been helped. Calvin on Mark 1:29–34 emphasizes the personal experience of His grace and the further requests for help, while the Catholic Catechism, 1503–1505, connects His care for the sick with the saving work of God's kingdom.

On the silencing of the demons, Calvin on 1:34 suggests both the timing of the fuller revelation and Jesus' refusal to use evil spirits as His witnesses. Wesley on 1:26 likewise emphasizes that He does not seek their endorsement. Mark states that they knew Him, while leaving their silencing's fuller purpose for readers to consider as His story continues.
passages.god_plan_html:
The New Testament directly connects these healings with the suffering servant. Matthew 8:14–17 recounts the same woman's healing and the evening help for others, then applies Isaiah 53:4 to Jesus bearing people's infirmities. The care shown in this home belongs within His larger work against the suffering and sin that burden humanity.

There is also a simple pattern worth noticing: she receives help and then helps others. Later Jesus teaches that greatness among His followers means serving, and explains that He Himself came to serve and give His life for many (Mark 10:42–45). Her response is an early picture of that kind of life, without making recovery from sickness a condition for being useful to God.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 1:35-39
passages.section_title: Jesus Prays and Takes the Message to Other Towns

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 35 Early in the morning, while it was still dark, Jesus got up and went out to a solitary place to pray. 36 Simon and his companions went to look for Him, 37 and when they found Him, they said, “Everyone is looking for You!” 38 But Jesus answered, “Let us go on to the neighboring towns so I can preach there as well, for that is why I have come.” 39 So He went throughout Galilee, preaching in their synagogues and driving out demons.
paragraphs: 35 Early in the morning, while it was still dark, Jesus got up and went out to a solitary place to pray. 36 Simon and his companions went to look for Him, 37 and when they found Him, they said, “Everyone is looking for You!”

38 But Jesus answered, “Let us go on to the neighboring towns so I can preach there as well, for that is why I have come.” 39 So He went throughout Galilee, preaching in their synagogues and driving out demons.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the crowded evening at Simon's home, Jesus rises before daylight and goes to a solitary place to pray. Simon and his companions find Him and tell Him that everyone is looking for Him. Jesus answers that they should go to the nearby towns so He can preach there too.

The word for their search is καταδιώκω, katadiōkō (kah-tah-dee-OH-koh). Thayer's lexicon gives the sense of following after or seeking someone, and specifically treats this verse as a search in a good sense. The word alone does not tell us that Simon is angry with Jesus.

The contrast is between the crowd's desire for His return and His purpose to take the message farther. He continues through Galilee, preaching in synagogues and driving out demons. Mark puts prayer and active service beside each other within that work.

Luke 4:42–44 gives a related account in which the crowds try to keep Him from leaving and He explains that He has been sent to proclaim God's kingdom to other towns. Neither account gives us the words of this particular prayer.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as Jesus praying amid the demands of His ministry and remaining faithful to the purpose for which He came. Calvin on Mark 1:38 and the parallel Luke 4:43 emphasizes the Father's calling and the need to spread the message, while Wesley on Mark 1:35 notes His sustained service; no denominational breakdown is needed here.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus' prayer belongs to His life of obedience to the Father. John 5:19–20 describes the Son's work in unity with the Father, and Hebrews 5:7–9 places His earthly prayers and obedience within His saving mission. Mark's brief scene lets us see that ministry is rooted in that relationship, even while people press for His attention.

Taking the message to other towns also looks beyond one place's response. Romans 10:14–17 later explains the connection between sending, preaching, hearing, and faith. Jesus' movement through Galilee begins showing why the good news must be carried to people who have not yet heard it.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 1:40-45
passages.section_title: Jesus Makes a Man Clean and Sends Him to the Priest

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 40 Then a leper came to Jesus, begging on his knees: “If You are willing, You can make me clean.” 41 Moved with compassion, Jesus reached out His hand and touched the man. “I am willing,” He said. “Be clean!” 42 And immediately the leprosy left him, and the man was cleansed. 43 Jesus promptly sent him away with a stern warning: 44 “See that you don’t tell anyone. But go, show yourself to the priest and present the offering Moses prescribed for your cleansing, as a testimony to them.” 45 But the man went out and openly began to proclaim and spread the news.
