Consequently, Jesus could no longer enter a town in plain view, but He stayed out in solitary places. Yet people came to Him from every quarter.
paragraphs: 40 Then a leper came to Jesus, begging on his knees: “If You are willing, You can make me clean.” 41 Moved with compassion, Jesus reached out His hand and touched the man. “I am willing,” He said. “Be clean!” 42 And immediately the leprosy left him, and the man was cleansed.

43 Jesus promptly sent him away with a stern warning: 44 “See that you don’t tell anyone. But go, show yourself to the priest and present the offering Moses prescribed for your cleansing, as a testimony to them.” 45 But the man went out and openly began to proclaim and spread the news. Consequently, Jesus could no longer enter a town in plain view, but He stayed out in solitary places. Yet people came to Him from every quarter.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
A man with a skin disease comes to Jesus, kneels, and asks to be made clean if Jesus is willing. He expresses confidence in Jesus' ability while leaving the decision with Him. Jesus reaches out, touches him, and makes him clean immediately.

The BSB uses leper and notes that the term refers to a skin disease. Under Leviticus 13:45–46, a person declared unclean with such a condition lived outside the camp. Leviticus 14:1–20 provides for priestly examination, cleansing, and offerings after healing. Restoring this man therefore concerns his place among his people as well as his body.

The BSB describes Jesus as moved with compassion. The word behind that reading is σπλαγχνίζομαι, splagchnizomai (splangkh-NEE-zoh-my), meaning to be moved with pity or compassion (Thayer's entry). Some translations use anger here because they follow a different Greek reading, as the BSB footnote notes. That is a difference in the underlying wording, rather than compassion itself meaning anger.

Jesus tells the healed man to keep quiet, go to the priest, and bring what Moses commanded as testimony. The priest is to examine someone already healed; the ceremony does not cause the cure. The man instead spreads the news widely, and Jesus can no longer enter towns openly. People continue coming to Him in the solitary places.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly see Jesus' power to restore someone who was unclean and the man's humble trust in His willingness to help. Calvin on the parallel Matthew 8:2–4 treats the conditional request as compatible with real faith, while the US Catholic bishops' note on Mark 1:40 emphasizes the priest's role in receiving the healed man back into the community.

This encounter is often read alongside the wider question of faith and healing. The Catholic Catechism, 1505–1508, and the Pentecostal Assemblies of God's official Divine Healing paper, sections III–IV, both affirm God's healing work while recognizing that not everyone is healed now. The Assemblies of God specifically rejects using Jesus' name as a formula to compel God; its position should not be confused with every individual healing teacher's claims.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus later includes the cleansing of lepers among the works that answer John's question about whether He is the coming One (Matthew 11:2–6). This restoration is part of how His identity and saving purpose become known.

The Law's cleansing also provides a parallel with a deeper need. Hebrews 9:11–14 compares outward purification with Christ cleansing the conscience through His own sacrifice, so that people can serve the living God. The man's bodily cleansing helps us picture restoration, without making his disease proof of a particular personal sin.

There is a striking change at the end: the man is helped, but his spreading the news leaves Jesus staying outside the towns. This can also bring to mind the cost of bearing another person's burden. It is a parallel for reflection, not a claim that Jesus became a leper. His saving work goes farther: Romans 5:8–11 describes Him giving His life to reconcile sinners to God.
passages.current_position_html: On the same man's approach in Matthew 8:2, Worship as the Early Church Knew It understands his bowing as a personal appeal made with physical humility and recognition of Jesus' divine authority. Mark likewise describes him kneeling and making his request. This supplies our position on his humble approach, while leaving a fuller position on the healing and priestly instructions open.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

passages.title: Mark 2:1-12
passages.section_title: The Man Lowered Through the Roof: Forgiveness and Healing

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 A few days later Jesus went back to Capernaum. And when the people heard that He was home, 2 they gathered in such large numbers that there was no more room, not even outside the door, as Jesus spoke the word to them. 3 Then a paralytic was brought to Him, carried by four men. 4 Since they were unable to get to Jesus through the crowd, they uncovered the roof above Him, made an opening, and lowered the paralytic on his mat. 5 When Jesus saw their faith, He said to the paralytic, “Son, your sins are forgiven.” 6 But some of the scribes were sitting there and thinking in their hearts, 7 “Why does this man speak like this? He is blaspheming! Who can forgive sins but God alone?” 8 At once Jesus knew in His spirit that they were thinking this way within themselves. “Why are you thinking these things in your hearts?” He asked. 9 “Which is easier: to say to a paralytic, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Get up, pick up your mat, and walk’? 10 But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins...” He said to the paralytic, 11 “I tell you, get up, pick up your mat, and go home.” 12 And immediately the man got up, picked up his mat, and walked out in front of them all. As a result, they were all astounded and glorified God, saying, “We have never seen anything like this!”
paragraphs: 1 A few days later Jesus went back to Capernaum. And when the people heard that He was home, 2 they gathered in such large numbers that there was no more room, not even outside the door, as Jesus spoke the word to them. 3 Then a paralytic was brought to Him, carried by four men. 4 Since they were unable to get to Jesus through the crowd, they uncovered the roof above Him, made an opening, and lowered the paralytic on his mat.

5 When Jesus saw their faith, He said to the paralytic, “Son, your sins are forgiven.” 6 But some of the scribes were sitting there and thinking in their hearts, 7 “Why does this man speak like this? He is blaspheming! Who can forgive sins but God alone?” 8 At once Jesus knew in His spirit that they were thinking this way within themselves. “Why are you thinking these things in your hearts?” He asked. 9 “Which is easier: to say to a paralytic, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Get up, pick up your mat, and walk’?

10 But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins...” He said to the paralytic, 11 “I tell you, get up, pick up your mat, and go home.” 12 And immediately the man got up, picked up his mat, and walked out in front of them all. As a result, they were all astounded and glorified God, saying, “We have never seen anything like this!”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus returns to Capernaum after some days, and people crowd the house where He is teaching. Four men bring a paralyzed man but cannot reach Him through the crowd. They uncover the roof, make an opening, and lower him on his mat. Mark does not name the house's owner or the men carrying him.

Jesus sees their faith and first tells the man that his sins are forgiven. Forgive comes from ἀφίημι, aphiēmi (ah-FEE-ay-mee). Thayer's lexicon includes releasing or remitting a debt and forgiving sins, explicitly listing this passage. Jesus is making a claim about the man's standing before God, before his physical condition changes.

Some scribes silently object that only God can forgive sins. Jesus knows their thoughts and asks which is easier to say: that the sins are forgiven, or that the man should rise and walk. He then heals him to show that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive. What the crowd can see supports the claim they cannot inspect in the same way.

The man gets up, carries his mat, and walks out before them all. Their amazement turns to praise of God. The story joins the man's bodily restoration with the greater question of Jesus' authority, rather than using the healing only to display power.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly understand the visible healing as confirming Jesus' authority to forgive sins. Calvin on the parallel Matthew 9:2–6 and the US Catholic bishops' note on Mark 2:5 also include the man's own faith alongside that of those bringing him, rather than making another person's faith an automatic substitute for his.

There is a smaller difference over how to read verse 10. Calvin reads the claim about the Son of Man as part of Jesus' spoken response. The bishops' note on 2:10 suggests that Mark pauses the scene to explain its meaning to Christian readers. That is a view in their explanatory notes, rather than a teaching every Catholic must hold; both readings see the miracle as revealing Jesus' authority.
passages.god_plan_html:
The scribes' question concerns something God claims for Himself. In Isaiah 43:24–25, He declares that He blots out His people's transgressions. Jesus' answer brings His own identity into view. The title Son of Man also recalls the figure receiving enduring authority in Daniel 7:13–14. This is a scriptural parallel; later in Mark Jesus explicitly joins that title with coming on heaven's clouds (Mark 14:61–62).

Forgiveness also belongs to God's promised new covenant in Jeremiah 31:31–34. Hebrews 10:10–18 connects that promise with Christ's once-for-all offering and the forgiveness it brings. In Mark 14:22–25, Jesus will speak of His own blood and the covenant. The authority shown in this house points forward to His giving Himself for the people He forgives.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 2:13-17
passages.section_title: Jesus Calls Levi and Eats with Sinners

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 Once again Jesus went out beside the sea. All the people came to Him, and He taught them there. 14 As He was walking along, He saw Levi son of Alphaeus sitting at the tax booth. “Follow Me,” He told him, and Levi got up and followed Him. 15 While Jesus was dining at Levi’s house, many tax collectors and sinners were eating with Him and His disciples—for there were many who followed Him. 16 When the scribes who were Pharisees saw Jesus eating with these people, they asked His disciples, “Why does He eat with tax collectors and sinners?” 17 On hearing this, Jesus told them, “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick. I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.”
paragraphs: 13 Once again Jesus went out beside the sea. All the people came to Him, and He taught them there. 14 As He was walking along, He saw Levi son of Alphaeus sitting at the tax booth. “Follow Me,” He told him, and Levi got up and followed Him.

15 While Jesus was dining at Levi’s house, many tax collectors and sinners were eating with Him and His disciples—for there were many who followed Him. 16 When the scribes who were Pharisees saw Jesus eating with these people, they asked His disciples, “Why does He eat with tax collectors and sinners?” 17 On hearing this, Jesus told them, “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick. I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus teaches beside the sea, then calls Levi son of Alphaeus from his tax booth. Levi gets up and follows Him. In the parallel account, Matthew 9:9–13, the tax collector is called Matthew; Christians have traditionally understood these as two names for the same man. Mark does not describe a change of name.

The next scene brings Jesus and His disciples to a meal with many tax collectors and sinners. Luke 5:27–32 explains that Levi hosts the banquet at his own house. Some scribes who are Pharisees question why Jesus eats with these people. Their objection brings the purpose of His ministry into focus: whom has He come to call?

Jesus answers with the picture of a doctor going to sick people. Their need is the reason for His presence. Eating with sinners does not mean declaring their conduct harmless: Luke's account explicitly says He calls them to repentance. Levi's response gives the scene a concrete example of that change—he gets up to follow Jesus.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand Jesus' meal as mercy toward sinners and a call to change, rather than approval of sin. Calvin on Matthew 9:12–13 and the US Catholic bishops' note on Mark 2:17 understand the healthy people in His comparison as those who consider themselves righteous, rather than a separate group with no need of God's help.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Matthew 9:13, Jesus explains this same meal by pointing to Hosea 6:6, where God puts mercy and knowing Him ahead of empty religious observance. Jesus' welcome does not abandon God's earlier purpose; it shows that purpose at work among people others want to keep at a distance.

The need reaches beyond the people around this table. Romans 3:9–26 includes both Jews and Gentiles under sin, then describes the grace and redemption God gives through Jesus Christ. The doctor picture helps us see why Jesus' saving work is needed by everyone, including people with a respectable religious life.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 2:18-22
passages.section_title: The Bridegroom, the Patch, and the Wineskins

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 Now John’s disciples and the Pharisees were often fasting. So people came to Jesus and asked, “Why don’t Your disciples fast like John’s disciples and those of the Pharisees?” 19 Jesus replied, “How can the guests of the bridegroom fast while He is with them? As long as He is with them, they cannot fast. 20 But the time will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them; then they will fast. 21 No one sews a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old garment. If he does, the new piece will pull away from the old, and a worse tear will result. 22 And no one pours new wine into old wineskins. If he does, the wine will burst the skins, and both the wine and the wineskins will be ruined. Instead, new wine is poured into new wineskins.”
paragraphs: 18 Now John’s disciples and the Pharisees were often fasting. So people came to Jesus and asked, “Why don’t Your disciples fast like John’s disciples and those of the Pharisees?” 19 Jesus replied, “How can the guests of the bridegroom fast while He is with them? As long as He is with them, they cannot fast. 20 But the time will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them; then they will fast.

21 No one sews a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old garment. If he does, the new piece will pull away from the old, and a worse tear will result. 22 And no one pours new wine into old wineskins. If he does, the wine will burst the skins, and both the wine and the wineskins will be ruined. Instead, new wine is poured into new wineskins.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
People ask why Jesus' disciples do not fast as John's disciples and the Pharisees do. Jesus answers with a wedding picture. Guests celebrate while the bridegroom is with them. His presence makes this a time for joy, though He also speaks of a coming time when He will be taken away and His disciples will fast.

He follows with two pictures of things that do not fit together: an unshrunk patch on an old garment, and new wine in old wineskins. The Greek word ἄγναφος, agnaphos (AG-nah-foss), describes cloth that has not been finished or fulled, according to Thayer's lexicon. It has not yet gone through the treatment that prepares cloth for use. The wineskins are leather containers (Thayer). Jesus describes the damage when the patch pulls away or the wine bursts its container.

These pictures answer the question about fasting. Following Jesus requires attention to what His presence means, rather than simply requiring His disciples to copy another group's practices. He anticipates fasting after His departure, so the passage does not do away with fasting altogether.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings generally see Jesus as the bridegroom and His coming removal as pointing toward His death. They differ over the patch and wineskins. The US Catholic bishops' notes on Mark 2:18–22 emphasize the new relationship and joyful time Jesus brings, which cannot simply fit earlier practices.

Calvin, explaining Matthew 9:16–17, instead sees Jesus protecting His still-weak disciples from a discipline they are not yet ready to bear. On this reading, the pictures concern patient training. These are readings offered by the bishops' notes and a historical Reformed teacher; neither speaks for every member of those churches.
passages.god_plan_html:
The bridegroom picture belongs to a larger scriptural theme. In Isaiah 62:4–5, God rejoices over His restored people as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride. In John 3:27–30, John the Baptist describes his own joy as that of the bridegroom's friend. These connections help explain why Jesus' presence is cause for celebration, not merely a break in a fasting schedule.

Revelation 19:6–9 carries the theme forward to the marriage supper of the Lamb. Mark's picture thus opens onto a larger hope: the bridegroom's removal is not the end of God's purpose for His people. Later, Jesus speaks of His covenant blood and of drinking anew in God's kingdom (Mark 14:22–25).
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 2:23-28
passages.section_title: The Sabbath Was Made for People

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 23 One Sabbath Jesus was passing through the grainfields, and His disciples began to pick the heads of grain as they walked along. 24 So the Pharisees said to Him, “Look, why are they doing what is unlawful on the Sabbath?” 25 Jesus replied, “Have you never read what David did when he and his companions were hungry and in need? 26 During the high priesthood of Abiathar, he entered the house of God and ate the consecrated bread, which was lawful only for the priests. And he gave some to his companions as well.” 27 Then Jesus declared, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. 28 Therefore, the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath.”
paragraphs: 23 One Sabbath Jesus was passing through the grainfields, and His disciples began to pick the heads of grain as they walked along. 24 So the Pharisees said to Him, “Look, why are they doing what is unlawful on the Sabbath?” 25 Jesus replied, “Have you never read what David did when he and his companions were hungry and in need? 26 During the high priesthood of Abiathar, he entered the house of God and ate the consecrated bread, which was lawful only for the priests. And he gave some to his companions as well.”
27 Then Jesus declared, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. 28 Therefore, the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
As Jesus and His disciples walk through grainfields on the Sabbath, the disciples pick heads of grain. The Pharisees challenge this as unlawful on the Sabbath. Deuteronomy 23:25 permits taking a neighbor's grain by hand, while forbidding the use of a sickle. The dispute here concerns the Sabbath, rather than simply taking grain from another person's field.

Jesus directs them to David's need for food in 1 Samuel 21:1–6. The priest gives David consecrated bread, which Leviticus 24:5–9 reserves for the priests. Jesus brings human need into the discussion, then explains that the Sabbath was made for people. He ends by declaring His own authority as Lord of the Sabbath.

There is a question about the priest's name: Mark names Abiathar, while 1 Samuel names Ahimelech. Wesley's note on Mark 2:26 understands the reference as the time of Abiathar, who became high priest afterward. That is one proposed explanation; the names in the two accounts should remain visible rather than silently changing either text.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand this passage as defending care for human need and affirming Jesus' authority over the Sabbath. Calvin on the parallel Matthew 12:1–8 and the US Catholic bishops' note on Mark 2:27–28 both emphasize the Sabbath's purpose for people's good. This scene does not by itself settle every later question about Christian worship days.
passages.god_plan_html:
The Sabbath command already carries a story of God's care. Exodus 20:8–11 links it to God's rest after creation. Deuteronomy 5:12–15 links it to Israel's rescue from slavery and specifically includes rest for servants and animals. Jesus' concern for people fits that purpose: God's gift of rest was never meant to become an excuse to disregard their needs.

The Bible also looks beyond a weekly pause. Hebrews 4:1–11 draws together creation's seventh day, Israel's journey, faith, and the continuing promise of entering God's rest. It then points to Jesus as the great high priest through whom we approach God for mercy and help (4:14–16). In Matthew 11:28–30, Jesus personally invites the weary to come to Him for rest.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 3:1-6
passages.section_title: Doing Good on the Sabbath

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Once again Jesus entered the synagogue, and a man with a withered hand was there. 2 In order to accuse Jesus, they were watching to see if He would heal on the Sabbath. 3 Then Jesus said to the man with the withered hand, “Stand up among us.” 4 And He asked them, “Which is lawful on the Sabbath: to do good or to do evil, to save life or to destroy it?” But they were silent. 5 Jesus looked around at them with anger and sorrow at their hardness of heart. Then He said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” So he stretched it out, and it was restored. 6 At this, the Pharisees went out and began plotting with the Herodians how they might kill Jesus.
paragraphs: 1 Once again Jesus entered the synagogue, and a man with a withered hand was there. 2 In order to accuse Jesus, they were watching to see if He would heal on the Sabbath. 3 Then Jesus said to the man with the withered hand, “Stand up among us.”

4 And He asked them, “Which is lawful on the Sabbath: to do good or to do evil, to save life or to destroy it?” But they were silent. 5 Jesus looked around at them with anger and sorrow at their hardness of heart. Then He said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” So he stretched it out, and it was restored. 6 At this, the Pharisees went out and began plotting with the Herodians how they might kill Jesus.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Sabbath dispute continues in a synagogue, where a man has a withered hand. Some people watch Jesus to see whether He will heal him so that they can accuse Him. Luke 6:6–11 identifies the observers as scribes and Pharisees and says Jesus knows their thoughts. Mark does not say they brought the man there as a trap.

Jesus brings the man before everyone and asks whether the Sabbath calls for doing good or evil, saving life or destroying it. His question makes the man's need central. In Matthew 12:9–14, He also asks whether they would rescue a sheep from a pit on the Sabbath, then points to the greater value of a person.

Their silence is followed by Jesus' anger and sorrow at their hardness of heart. The word πώρωσις, pōrōsis (POH-roh-sis), can describe stubbornness or dulled understanding; Thayer's lexicon specifically lists this verse. The problem is their resistance to what is good, rather than lack of information. His anger appears alongside grief over them.

Jesus tells the man to stretch out his hand, and it is restored. The Pharisees then leave and begin planning with the Herodians to kill Him. The ending sharpens His earlier question: He has done good and restored a man, while they turn toward taking a life.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see the healing as showing that care for a person belongs within the Sabbath's purpose. Calvin on Mark 3:5 and Wesley's note on the same verse also read Jesus' anger together with His grief, rather than as careless or selfish rage.
passages.god_plan_html:
God's earlier call in Micah 6:8 joins justice, mercy, and humble life with Him. Jesus puts that concern into action here. Knowing religious requirements while refusing mercy misses what those requirements are meant to serve. James 4:17 likewise warns that knowing the good we should do and failing to do it is sin.

The plot also points ahead to the cost of Jesus' saving work. He will explain that He came to serve and give His life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:42–45). Acts 4:24–30 later places the rulers' conspiracy against Him within God's larger purpose, while John 10:17–18 makes clear that He lays down His life willingly. This early threat belongs to the road toward that self-giving; His death is more than His enemies' success.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 3:7-12
passages.section_title: The Crowds by the Sea and the Son of God

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 So Jesus withdrew with His disciples to the sea, accompanied by a large crowd from Galilee, Judea, 8 Jerusalem, Idumea, the region beyond the Jordan, and the vicinity of Tyre and Sidon. The large crowd came to Him when they heard what great things He was doing. 9 Jesus asked His disciples to have a boat ready for Him so that the crowd would not crush Him. 10 For He had healed so many that all who had diseases were pressing forward to touch Him. 11 And when the unclean spirits saw Him, they fell down before Him and cried out, “You are the Son of God!” 12 But He warned them sternly not to make Him known.
paragraphs: 7 So Jesus withdrew with His disciples to the sea, accompanied by a large crowd from Galilee, Judea, 8 Jerusalem, Idumea, the region beyond the Jordan, and the vicinity of Tyre and Sidon. The large crowd came to Him when they heard what great things He was doing. 9 Jesus asked His disciples to have a boat ready for Him so that the crowd would not crush Him. 10 For He had healed so many that all who had diseases were pressing forward to touch Him.
11 And when the unclean spirits saw Him, they fell down before Him and cried out, “You are the Son of God!” 12 But He warned them sternly not to make Him known.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the plot against Him, Jesus withdraws with His disciples to the sea. People come from Galilee, Judea, Jerusalem, Idumea, beyond the Jordan, and the area of Tyre and Sidon. The list shows how widely news of His works has spread. Mark identifies their home regions without telling us every person's background or reason for coming.

The crowd's needs create real physical pressure. Jesus asks His disciples to keep a boat ready so He will not be crushed, because people with diseases press forward to touch Him. The Greek verb θλίβω, thlibō (THLEE-boh), means to press hard upon; Thayer's lexicon lists Mark 3:9 as a literal use. The scene describes more than a large audience watching from a distance.

Unclean spirits fall before Jesus and identify Him as the Son of God. He sternly forbids them to make Him known. Their recognition shows His authority over them, but it is not the trusting response of a disciple; James 2:19 likewise distinguishes the demons' belief from faith that follows God. Mark leaves their testimony under Jesus' command rather than allowing them to direct how His identity is made known.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see these scenes as showing Jesus' healing power and authority over unclean spirits, while distinguishing the spirits' recognition from faithful discipleship. Calvin on the parallel Matthew 12:16 and Wesley on Mark 3:12 explain the silence in terms of unsuitable witnesses and the timing of His public disclosure.
passages.god_plan_html:
Matthew 12:15–21 connects Jesus' withdrawal, healings, and command for silence with God's servant in Isaiah 42:1–4. The servant brings justice to the nations and deals gently with the bruised reed and smoldering wick. These pictures speak of care for what is damaged and vulnerable. Jesus' ministry joins power with that gentleness.

Matthew explicitly extends the hope to the nations. Mark's list of places is not a complete account of who has believed, but it fits the growing reach of Jesus' work beyond one town. Hebrews 1:1–3 identifies the Son as the One through whom God speaks and who provides purification for sins. What begins here with people seeking relief belongs to His larger saving mission.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 3:13-19
passages.section_title: Jesus Appoints the Twelve

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 Then Jesus went up on the mountain and called for those He wanted, and they came to Him. 14 He appointed twelve of them, whom He designated as apostles, to accompany Him, to be sent out to preach, 15 and to have authority to drive out demons. 16 These are the twelve He appointed: Simon (whom He named Peter), 17 James son of Zebedee and his brother John (whom He named Boanerges, meaning “Sons of Thunder”), 18 Andrew, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Thomas, James son of Alphaeus, Thaddaeus, Simon the Zealot, 19 and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed Jesus.
paragraphs: 13 Then Jesus went up on the mountain and called for those He wanted, and they came to Him. 14 He appointed twelve of them, whom He designated as apostles, to accompany Him, to be sent out to preach, 15 and to have authority to drive out demons.

16 These are the twelve He appointed: Simon (whom He named Peter), 17 James son of Zebedee and his brother John (whom He named Boanerges, meaning “Sons of Thunder”), 18 Andrew, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Thomas, James son of Alphaeus, Thaddaeus, Simon the Zealot, 19 and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed Jesus.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus goes up the mountain and calls those He wants, and they come to Him. Luke 6:12–16 adds that He spends the preceding night in prayer and chooses the Twelve from His disciples. Mark emphasizes Jesus' initiative without describing the content of that prayer.

The appointment has a clear purpose: they are to accompany Him, preach, and exercise authority over demons. Being with Jesus belongs alongside being sent by Him. The Greek word ἀπόστολος, apostolos (ah-POSS-toh-loss), means a messenger or delegate sent with a commission. Thayer's lexicon distinguishes its special use for the Twelve from its broader use for other messengers.

The list includes Simon, whom Jesus names Peter, and James and John, whom He calls Sons of Thunder. It also includes Judas Iscariot, whose later betrayal Mark names immediately. Being appointed to this group is therefore not presented as a guarantee that every member will remain faithful.

The sending described here will be carried out in Mark 6:7–13, when Jesus sends the Twelve in pairs. They proclaim repentance, drive out demons, and heal. Their work extends His ministry under His authority.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand this as Jesus choosing and preparing the Twelve for a particular mission, with companionship preceding their later sending. Calvin on Mark 3:13–14 and the US Catholic bishops' notes on 3:14–15 both connect the appointment with their later work on His behalf.
passages.god_plan_html:
The number twelve connects this group with Israel. Jesus Himself makes the link in Matthew 19:28, speaking of twelve thrones and the twelve tribes. Revelation 21:12–14 places the tribes' names on the holy city's gates and the names of the Lamb's twelve apostles on its foundations. Their appointment belongs within God's continuing purpose for His people.

Ephesians 2:19–22 describes God's household as built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Himself as the cornerstone. Jesus is preparing witnesses whose message will serve a community much larger than the circle on the mountain. The lasting foundation remains centered on Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 3:20-21
passages.section_title: The Crowds and His Family’s Concern

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 20 Then Jesus went home, and once again a crowd gathered, so that He and His disciples could not even eat. 21 When His family heard about this, they went out to take custody of Him, saying, “He is out of His mind.”
paragraphs: 20 Then Jesus went home, and once again a crowd gathered, so that He and His disciples could not even eat. 21 When His family heard about this, they went out to take custody of Him, saying, “He is out of His mind.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus returns home, and the crowd gathers so densely that He and His disciples cannot even eat. The pressure of ministry now reaches into the ordinary need for a meal. Mark does not identify the house's owner in these verses.

His family hears about it and sets out to take custody of Him, saying that He is out of His mind. This is their judgment of Him, not Mark's judgment. The account shows that people close to Jesus can misunderstand what He is doing.

Their journey introduces a story that resumes in Mark 3:31–35, when His mother and brothers arrive. Between those moments Mark tells of the scribes' accusation and Jesus' reply. Both scenes concern responses to Jesus, though the family concern and the claim that His power comes from Satan are different responses.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian interpreters commonly connect this family scene with the relatives' arrival in verses 31–35 and with the question of truly understanding Jesus. Calvin on Mark 3:20–21 and the US Catholic bishops' note on 3:20–35 read the passage as misunderstanding among His relatives; the text does not separately report every family member's thoughts.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 3:22-30
passages.section_title: The Strong Man and the Warning About the Spirit

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 And the scribes who had come down from Jerusalem were saying, “He is possessed by Beelzebul,” and, “By the prince of the demons He drives out demons.” 23 So Jesus called them together and began to speak to them in parables: “How can Satan drive out Satan? 24 If a kingdom is divided against itself, it cannot stand. 25 If a house is divided against itself, it cannot stand. 26 And if Satan is divided and rises against himself, he cannot stand; his end has come. 27 Indeed, no one can enter a strong man’s house to steal his possessions unless he first ties up the strong man. Then he can plunder his house. 28 Truly I tell you, the sons of men will be forgiven all sins and blasphemies, as many as they utter. 29 But whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will never be forgiven; he is guilty of eternal sin.” 30 Jesus made this statement because they were saying, “He has an unclean spirit.”
paragraphs: 22 And the scribes who had come down from Jerusalem were saying, “He is possessed by Beelzebul,” and, “By the prince of the demons He drives out demons.” 23 So Jesus called them together and began to speak to them in parables: “How can Satan drive out Satan?

24 If a kingdom is divided against itself, it cannot stand. 25 If a house is divided against itself, it cannot stand. 26 And if Satan is divided and rises against himself, he cannot stand; his end has come. 27 Indeed, no one can enter a strong man’s house to steal his possessions unless he first ties up the strong man. Then he can plunder his house.

28 Truly I tell you, the sons of men will be forgiven all sins and blasphemies, as many as they utter. 29 But whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will never be forgiven; he is guilty of eternal sin.” 30 Jesus made this statement because they were saying, “He has an unclean spirit.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Scribes from Jerusalem explain Jesus' authority over demons by claiming He is possessed and works through the ruler of demons. Jesus answers their charge directly. If Satan is driving out Satan, his kingdom is working against itself and cannot stand.

Jesus then gives a different explanation through the picture of a strong man's house. Someone must first overpower the strong man before taking his possessions. In the surrounding discussion, the picture describes Jesus defeating Satan's hold over people, rather than cooperating with him. Matthew 12:22–29 explicitly identifies these works with God's Spirit and the arrival of God's kingdom.

Jesus speaks of the wide reach of forgiveness, then gives a grave warning about blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. Blasphemy comes from βλασφημία, blasphēmia (blas-fay-MEE-ah), speech that slanders or reviles; Thayer's lexicon includes speech dishonoring God. Here Mark supplies the setting for the warning: they are calling the work before them the work of an unclean spirit.

Verse 30 keeps the warning tied to that accusation. Jesus is not discussing an accidental choice of words or a sincere request to understand Him. The passage describes people responding to His freeing work by naming its source evil. Christians differ over how this warning applies beyond that confrontation, as explained below.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly recognize Jesus as the one stronger than Satan. On the Spirit warning, Wesley's note on Mark 3:30 emphasizes attributing to the devil the miracles Jesus works by the Holy Spirit.

The Reformed teacher Calvin, on the parallel Matthew 12:31–32, understands the offense as knowingly and maliciously calling God's revealed work evil. He distinguishes this from ignorance and holds that someone hardened in this way does not return in repentance. The Reformed Westminster Confession, 15.3–4, teaches that pardon is God's grace and that those who truly repent are not condemned by the greatness of their sin; it does not give a verse-by-verse definition here.

The Catholic Church teaches in Catechism 1864 that deliberately refusing the mercy and salvation offered by the Spirit can harden a person into dying without repentance. This puts the emphasis on refusing God's mercy, while Calvin gives a more specific account of knowingly slandering His revealed work. Neither explanation makes God's willingness to show mercy the problem.
passages.god_plan_html:
The strong-man picture opens onto the larger freedom Jesus brings. Colossians 2:13–15 joins forgiveness with Christ's victory over hostile powers through the cross. Hebrews 2:14–15 says He shares human life and dies to break the devil's power and free people held by fear of death. The deliverances in Mark are signs of a saving work that reaches further than relief in one encounter.

The warning belongs alongside Scripture's account of real mercy. In 1 Timothy 1:12–16, Paul recalls that he had been a blasphemer and persecutor, yet received mercy after acting in ignorance and unbelief. He presents Christ's patience toward him as an example for others who will believe. That testimony shows why serious past opposition should not be turned into a blanket declaration that a person is beyond the reach of grace.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 3:31-35
passages.section_title: Who Belongs to Jesus’ Family?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 31 Then Jesus’ mother and brothers came and stood outside. They sent someone in to summon Him, 32 and a crowd was sitting around Him. “Look,” He was told, “Your mother and brothers are outside, asking for You.” 33 But Jesus replied, “Who are My mother and My brothers?” 34 Looking at those seated in a circle around Him, He said, “Here are My mother and My brothers! 35 For whoever does the will of God is My brother and sister and mother.”
paragraphs: 31 Then Jesus’ mother and brothers came and stood outside. They sent someone in to summon Him, 32 and a crowd was sitting around Him. “Look,” He was told, “Your mother and brothers are outside, asking for You.”

33 But Jesus replied, “Who are My mother and My brothers?” 34 Looking at those seated in a circle around Him, He said, “Here are My mother and My brothers! 35 For whoever does the will of God is My brother and sister and mother.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus' mother and brothers arrive and send for Him from outside. Their arrival resumes the family story introduced in verses 20–21. A crowd sits around Him, and He uses the message about His relatives to ask who belongs to His family.

Looking at those around Him, He calls the person who does God's will His brother, sister, and mother. Luke 8:19–21 describes that response as hearing God's word and carrying it out. Jesus offers a place of belonging that reaches beyond birth and ancestry.

The saying does not make ordinary care for relatives worthless. Its point is that a family connection to Jesus cannot replace responding to God. Nor does Mark tell us everything Mary or each brother privately believes at this moment. The emphasis falls on the open invitation to do God's will.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand Jesus' central saying as describing His spiritual family. They differ over the relationship of the brothers standing outside. The Catholic Church teaches in Catechism 499–500 that Mary remained a virgin and these brothers are close relatives, rather than other children of hers.

The Orthodox Church in America's account of Joseph presents the Orthodox tradition that they are Joseph's children from an earlier marriage. An Orthodox Presbyterian Church answer instead reads them as children born to Mary and Joseph after Jesus, and therefore His half-brothers. That is the explanation in this church resource, not a view held by every Protestant interpreter. These different family trees leave the central saying clear: Jesus welcomes those who do God's will.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus' family language points toward the relationship His saving work brings. Hebrews 2:10–18 says that He shares our humanity, brings God's children to glory, and is not ashamed to call them brothers. He comes close enough to suffer, make atonement, and help those who are tempted.

This family also crosses divisions between peoples. Ephesians 2:11–22 describes Jews and Gentiles brought near through Christ's blood, reconciled through the cross, and welcomed into God's household with access to the Father by one Spirit. The belonging Jesus describes grows into a people united through Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 4:1-9
passages.section_title: One Sowing, Four Kinds of Ground

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Once again Jesus began to teach beside the sea, and such a large crowd gathered around Him that He got into a boat and sat in it, while all the people crowded along the shore. 2 And He taught them many things in parables, and in His teaching He said, 3 “Listen! A farmer went out to sow his seed. 4 And as he was sowing, some seed fell along the path, and the birds came and devoured it. 5 Some fell on rocky ground, where it did not have much soil. It sprang up quickly because the soil was shallow. 6 But when the sun rose, the seedlings were scorched, and they withered because they had no root. 7 Other seed fell among thorns, which grew up and choked the seedlings, and they yielded no crop. 8 Still other seed fell on good soil, where it sprouted, grew up, and produced a crop—one bearing thirtyfold, another sixtyfold, and another a hundredfold.” 9 Then Jesus said, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”
paragraphs: 1 Once again Jesus began to teach beside the sea, and such a large crowd gathered around Him that He got into a boat and sat in it, while all the people crowded along the shore. 2 And He taught them many things in parables, and in His teaching He said, 3 “Listen! A farmer went out to sow his seed. 4 And as he was sowing, some seed fell along the path, and the birds came and devoured it.

5 Some fell on rocky ground, where it did not have much soil. It sprang up quickly because the soil was shallow. 6 But when the sun rose, the seedlings were scorched, and they withered because they had no root. 7 Other seed fell among thorns, which grew up and choked the seedlings, and they yielded no crop.

8 Still other seed fell on good soil, where it sprouted, grew up, and produced a crop—one bearing thirtyfold, another sixtyfold, and another a hundredfold.” 9 Then Jesus said, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus teaches beside the sea again. This time Mark says He gets into a boat and sits while the crowd stays on shore. He tells a story about seed scattered on four kinds of ground: the path, rocky ground, thorny ground, and good soil.

The outcomes differ. Birds eat the seed on the path. Seed in shallow soil springs up quickly but withers in the sun because it has no root. Thorns choke other seedlings so they produce no crop. The good soil receives seed that grows and produces a harvest, though the amounts vary.

Jesus begins by calling the crowd to listen and ends by calling those with ears to hear. The story asks for more than noticing familiar pictures. His own explanation in Mark 4:13–20 identifies the seed with the word and the different ground with ways people respond to it. His explanation gives us the starting point for understanding it.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see the different soils as different responses to God's word, with lasting fruitfulness as the good outcome. The US Catholic bishops' note on Mark 4:1–34 and Calvin on the parallel Matthew 13:1–9 both follow the story into Jesus' own explanation.
passages.god_plan_html:
The word-and-growth picture has an earlier parallel in Isaiah 55:10–13. Rain waters the earth and brings seed and food; God's word accomplishes the purpose for which He sends it. This is a scriptural parallel, rather than a statement that Isaiah describes these four soils or promises that every individual hearer responds alike.

The message is also meant to be shared. Romans 10:14–17 connects sending, preaching, hearing, and faith, while acknowledging that not everyone welcomes the good news. Jesus' story prepares His followers to understand both the importance of spreading the word and the different responses it meets.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 4:10-12
passages.section_title: Why Does Jesus Teach in Parables?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 As soon as Jesus was alone with the Twelve and those around Him, they asked Him about the parable. 11 He replied, “The mystery of the kingdom of God has been given to you, but to those on the outside everything is expressed in parables, 12 so that, ‘they may be ever seeing but never perceiving, and ever hearing but never understanding; otherwise they might turn and be forgiven.’”
paragraphs: 10 As soon as Jesus was alone with the Twelve and those around Him, they asked Him about the parable. 11 He replied, “The mystery of the kingdom of God has been given to you, but to those on the outside everything is expressed in parables, 12 so that, ‘they may be ever seeing but never perceiving, and ever hearing but never understanding; otherwise they might turn and be forgiven.’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
When Jesus is apart from the crowd, the Twelve and others around Him ask about the parable. The group receiving His explanation is therefore larger than the Twelve alone. Their question also shows that being close to Him does not mean they already understand everything.

Jesus describes knowledge of God's kingdom as something given to them. The word μυστήριον, mystērion (moos-TAY-ree-on), can describe a hidden purpose God makes known; Thayer's lexicon specifically includes this verse. Mystery here concerns what God reveals, rather than a puzzle people solve by being clever enough.

His words about seeing without perceiving and hearing without understanding recall Isaiah 6:9–10. In Isaiah's commission, the people encounter God's message yet remain hardened. Mark has already described opposition to Jesus and the accusation against His works in chapter 3. Against that background, this is a serious statement about revelation, resistance, and judgment—not simply a claim that stories make teaching easier.

The passage holds together the gift of understanding and the danger of failing to receive what Jesus says. He continues by explaining the parable to those asking Him. Christian interpreters differ in how they describe God's action and the hearers' responsibility in the contrast.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin on the parallel Matthew 13:11–15 emphasizes God's gracious choice in revealing His kingdom, while also holding resistant hearers responsible for their blindness. Wesley's notes on Mark 4:11–12 emphasize judgment on people who had already chosen not to see: God gives them over to the blindness they have resisted leaving.

These are different emphases in the two teachers' explanations, rather than a reason to say either denies God's grace or human responsibility. Both treat the saying as a warning about persistent resistance, while recognizing that understanding is God's gift.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus explicitly brings Isaiah's commission into His own ministry. The same word can be heard without being welcomed, and being present when God speaks is not the same as receiving Him. This connection places the parables within Scripture's longer account of God addressing His people.

Hiddenness is not the last word about God's purpose. Romans 16:25–27 describes the mystery once concealed and now made known through the prophetic writings, leading the nations toward the obedience of faith. 1 Corinthians 2:7–14 describes God's Spirit revealing what human wisdom could not uncover. The larger purpose is the saving truth made known in Christ, not secrecy for its own sake.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 4:13-20
passages.section_title: Hearing the Word and Bearing Fruit

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 Then Jesus said to them, “Do you not understand this parable? Then how will you understand any of the parables? 14 The farmer sows the word. 15 Some are like the seeds along the path, where the word is sown. As soon as they hear it, Satan comes and takes away the word that was sown in them. 16 Some are like the seeds sown on rocky ground. They hear the word and at once receive it with joy. 17 But they themselves have no root, and they remain for only a season. When trouble or persecution comes because of the word, they quickly fall away. 18 Others are like the seeds sown among the thorns. They hear the word, 19 but the worries of this life, the deceitfulness of wealth, and the desire for other things come in and choke the word, and it becomes unfruitful. 20 Still others are like the seeds sown on good soil. They hear the word, receive it, and produce a crop—thirtyfold, sixtyfold, or a hundredfold.”
paragraphs: 13 Then Jesus said to them, “Do you not understand this parable? Then how will you understand any of the parables? 14 The farmer sows the word. 15 Some are like the seeds along the path, where the word is sown. As soon as they hear it, Satan comes and takes away the word that was sown in them.

16 Some are like the seeds sown on rocky ground. They hear the word and at once receive it with joy. 17 But they themselves have no root, and they remain for only a season. When trouble or persecution comes because of the word, they quickly fall away. 18 Others are like the seeds sown among the thorns. They hear the word, 19 but the worries of this life, the deceitfulness of wealth, and the desire for other things come in and choke the word, and it becomes unfruitful.
20 Still others are like the seeds sown on good soil. They hear the word, receive it, and produce a crop—thirtyfold, sixtyfold, or a hundredfold.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus explains that the farmer sows the word. On the path, Satan takes away what people hear. On rocky ground, people receive the word with joy but have no root; trouble or persecution because of the word brings a quick falling away. A promising first response is not the end of the story.

The thorny ground describes people in whom life's worries, wealth's deceitfulness, and desire for other things choke the word. The verb συμπνίγω, sympnigō (soom-PNEE-goh), means to choke or press so closely as to suffocate (Thayer's lexicon). The picture shows competing concerns crowding out the word's fruitfulness. Jesus names ordinary pressures and desires as well as open persecution.

The good-soil hearers receive the word and produce a crop. The yields vary, but all are fruitful. Luke 8:11–15 adds the language of holding to the word and producing a crop through perseverance. Jesus calls for a response that continues into life, beyond hearing or initial excitement.

Traditions differ over whether someone who later turns away had saving faith before that departure. The readings below explain that difference.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read this as a call to receive the word and continue in it. Reformed teaching in the Westminster Confession, 17.1–3, holds that God keeps those He has brought to saving faith to the end, though they can fall into serious sin for a time. The 1689 Baptist Confession, 17.1–3, teaches the same preservation. Calvin on Matthew 13:20–21 consequently distinguishes the rocky-ground response from faith rooted in new birth.

The Methodist Articles of Religion, XII, teach that a person can depart from grace and fall into sin, with repentance and return possible by God's grace. The Catholic Church teaches in Catechism 162 that faith is God's gift, can be lost, and must be nourished. These teachings lead to different accounts of what has happened when a person who welcomed the word later abandons it.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jeremiah 4:1–4 also uses ground and thorns to address the heart. God calls Judah and Jerusalem to return to Him and break up their unplowed ground. This is a scriptural parallel: outward religious life cannot replace a heart responsive to God.

Colossians 1:5–10 describes the gospel bearing fruit and growing throughout the world, then speaks of believers bearing fruit in every good work and growing in their knowledge of God. This expands the picture beyond a single harvest number. God's message spreads among people and shapes how they live.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 4:21-25
passages.section_title: The Lamp and the Way We Listen

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 Jesus also said to them, “Does anyone bring in a lamp to put it under a basket or under a bed? Doesn’t he set it on a stand? 22 For there is nothing hidden that will not be disclosed, and nothing concealed that will not be brought to light. 23 If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear.” 24 He went on to say, “Pay attention to what you hear. With the measure you use, it will be measured to you, and even more will be added to you. 25 For whoever has will be given more. But whoever does not have, even what he has will be taken away from him.”
paragraphs: 21 Jesus also said to them, “Does anyone bring in a lamp to put it under a basket or under a bed? Doesn’t he set it on a stand? 22 For there is nothing hidden that will not be disclosed, and nothing concealed that will not be brought to light. 23 If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear.”

24 He went on to say, “Pay attention to what you hear. With the measure you use, it will be measured to you, and even more will be added to you. 25 For whoever has will be given more. But whoever does not have, even what he has will be taken away from him.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus moves from seed to light. A lamp belongs on a stand, where it can give light, rather than beneath a basket or bed. He adds that what is hidden will be disclosed. Following His words about the kingdom's mystery, this points toward truth being brought into the open.

He again calls people to hear, then tells them to pay attention to what they hear. The measure saying places responsibility on the listener: what is received matters, and more can be given. The warning about losing even what one has makes careless hearing a serious concern.

Luke 8:16–18 places the same lamp and listening sayings after the soils and speaks of losing even what someone thinks he has. The concern is how people respond to what God makes known.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly connect the lamp with truth meant to be made known and the measure with responsible hearing. Wesley's notes on Mark 4:21–25 emphasize both sharing received light with others and allowing Jesus' teaching to shape one's life.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Matthew 10:26–27, Jesus joins a similar hidden-and-revealed saying with His followers' public witness: what they hear from Him is to be proclaimed openly. The private instruction of disciples serves a purpose larger than their private understanding.

2 Corinthians 4:1–7 likewise joins God's light in the heart with openly proclaiming Jesus Christ as Lord. The knowledge of God's glory comes through Christ and is carried by ordinary, fragile people. Light received from God becomes a message His people are entrusted to share.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 4:26-29
passages.section_title: The Seed Grows While the Farmer Sleeps

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 26 Jesus also said, “The kingdom of God is like a man who scatters seed on the ground. 27 Night and day he sleeps and wakes, and the seed sprouts and grows, though he knows not how. 28 All by itself the earth produces a crop—first the stalk, then the head, then grain that ripens within. 29 And as soon as the grain is ripe, he swings the sickle, because the harvest has come.”
paragraphs: 26 Jesus also said, “The kingdom of God is like a man who scatters seed on the ground. 27 Night and day he sleeps and wakes, and the seed sprouts and grows, though he knows not how. 28 All by itself the earth produces a crop—first the stalk, then the head, then grain that ripens within. 29 And as soon as the grain is ripe, he swings the sickle, because the harvest has come.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus gives another seed picture for God's kingdom. A man scatters seed, then goes through his ordinary nights and days. The seed sprouts and grows, though he does not know how. The story turns our attention from the different soils to growth the farmer cannot make happen by command.

The earth produces the crop in stages: stalk, head, and ripe grain. The phrase all by itself uses αὐτόματος, automatos (ow-TOH-mah-toss). Thayer's lexicon includes plants growing without human cultivation and specifically names this verse. The point is the growth beyond the farmer's direct control, not a claim that God has no part in it.

The farmer still has work to do. He sows, and when the grain is ripe he harvests. The picture holds patient trust together with action at the proper time. The growth has a goal: a harvest rather than endless waiting.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly emphasize growth that the person sowing cannot produce or control. Calvin on Mark 4:26 applies this to teachers who need patience when results are not immediately visible, while the US Catholic bishops' note on 4:26–29 emphasizes God's kingdom growing toward its final establishment and judgment.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Corinthians 3:5–9 gives a closely related picture. Paul plants and Apollos waters, but God gives the growth. Their service matters, yet neither servant is the source of life. The parable encourages trust in God's work beyond what a teacher can see or manage.

Harvest also appears in Scripture's account of God's final judgment. Joel 3:12–14 joins the ripe harvest and sickle with the nations brought before Him. This is a scriptural parallel rather than a separate explanation Jesus supplies here. It helps us see why the story ends with completion: God's kingdom moves toward a purpose He will bring about.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 4:30-32
passages.section_title: The Mustard Seed and the Growing Kingdom

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 30 Then He asked, “To what can we compare the kingdom of God? With what parable shall we present it? 31 It is like a mustard seed, which is the smallest of all seeds sown upon the earth. 32 But after it is planted, it grows to be the largest of all garden plants and puts forth great branches, so that the birds of the air nest in its shade.”
paragraphs: 30 Then He asked, “To what can we compare the kingdom of God? With what parable shall we present it? 31 It is like a mustard seed, which is the smallest of all seeds sown upon the earth. 32 But after it is planted, it grows to be the largest of all garden plants and puts forth great branches, so that the birds of the air nest in its shade.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus asks what picture can describe God's kingdom and chooses a mustard seed. The contrast runs from a tiny beginning to a plant with large branches and shade where birds can nest. The smallness at the start does not reveal the whole outcome.

This follows the stories about sowing, hearing, and growth. The kingdom Jesus announces may appear unimpressive beside the size of the surrounding world, yet its beginning is not the measure of what God will do. Mark's picture includes both growth and shelter.

The birds lead to different readings. Earlier in the chapter, birds taking seed from the path represent Satan taking away the word. Here they nest in the branches. Interpreters differ over whether that earlier meaning should control this different scene, or whether the shelter recalls the wider reach of God's kingdom.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin on the parallel Matthew 13:31–32 reads the mustard seed as encouragement about the gospel's small beginning and surprising growth. The US Catholic bishops' note on Mark 4:32 sees the birds as pointing toward the kingdom's reach among the nations.

C. I. Scofield's 1917 note on Matthew 13:31 instead warns about impressive outward growth that lacks lasting substance. He connects the birds' shelter with Nebuchadnezzar's tree in Daniel 4, which comes under judgment. These are commentators' readings, rather than two uniform official church positions; they differ over whether the expanded shelter is chiefly encouragement or warning.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ezekiel 17:22–24 offers a related picture: God plants a tender shoot that becomes a great cedar, with birds of every kind sheltering beneath it. The passage declares His power to bring down the tall tree and raise the low one. This is a supported parallel of God bringing growth and shelter from a small beginning.

Tree-and-bird pictures also occur in Daniel 4:10–26 and Ezekiel 31:1–9, where great kingdoms provide shelter but remain answerable to God. The wider theme places power and its outcome in His hands. Mark gives a kingdom comparison, rather than an invitation to judge God's work only by present size.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 4:33-34
passages.section_title: Parables for the Crowds, Explanation for the Disciples

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 33 With many such parables Jesus spoke the word to them, to the extent that they could understand. 34 He did not tell them anything without using a parable. But privately He explained everything to His own disciples.
paragraphs: 33 With many such parables Jesus spoke the word to them, to the extent that they could understand. 34 He did not tell them anything without using a parable. But privately He explained everything to His own disciples.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Mark summarizes the teaching just described. Jesus speaks the word through many parables, to the extent His hearers can understand, and explains them privately to His disciples. The public stories and the private explanations belong together.

This brings us back to the question in verses 10–12. The disciples need Jesus' help to understand; they are learners receiving instruction. The summary describes His teaching in this setting and prepares for the new scene that evening, when they cross the sea.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly distinguish the crowd's hearing of the stories from the fuller explanation Jesus gives His disciples. Wesley's note on Mark 4:33 emphasizes teaching suited to hearers' capacity, while Calvin on the parallel Matthew 13:34 emphasizes knowledge Jesus develops privately before its fuller public disclosure.
passages.god_plan_html:
Matthew 13:34–35 explicitly connects Jesus' parable teaching with Psalm 78:1–8. The psalm opens by calling God's people to listen, then tells of making His works known to the next generation so they will trust Him and keep His commands.

That connection places Jesus' teaching within God's continuing work of making Himself known. The disciples' understanding is meant to become more than a private advantage: the truth they receive prepares them to teach others. The concern is a people who remember God's works and respond faithfully to Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 4:35-41
passages.section_title: Who Is This, That Even the Sea Obeys Him?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 35 When that evening came, He said to His disciples, “Let us cross to the other side.” 36 After they had dismissed the crowd, they took Jesus with them, since He was already in the boat. And there were other boats with Him. 37 Soon a violent windstorm came up, and the waves were breaking over the boat, so that it was being swamped. 38 But Jesus was in the stern, sleeping on the cushion. So they woke Him and said, “Teacher, don’t You care that we are perishing?” 39 Then Jesus got up and rebuked the wind and the sea. “Silence!” He commanded. “Be still!” And the wind died down, and it was perfectly calm. 40 “Why are you so afraid?” He asked. “Do you still have no faith?” 41 Overwhelmed with fear, they asked one another, “Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?”
paragraphs: 35 When that evening came, He said to His disciples, “Let us cross to the other side.” 36 After they had dismissed the crowd, they took Jesus with them, since He was already in the boat. And there were other boats with Him. 37 Soon a violent windstorm came up, and the waves were breaking over the boat, so that it was being swamped. 38 But Jesus was in the stern, sleeping on the cushion. So they woke Him and said, “Teacher, don’t You care that we are perishing?”

39 Then Jesus got up and rebuked the wind and the sea. “Silence!” He commanded. “Be still!” And the wind died down, and it was perfectly calm. 40 “Why are you so afraid?” He asked. “Do you still have no faith?” 41 Overwhelmed with fear, they asked one another, “Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
That evening Jesus tells His disciples to cross to the other side. They leave the crowd and take Him in the boat where He has been teaching; other boats accompany them. A violent storm rises, and waves begin swamping the boat while Jesus sleeps in the stern.

The disciples wake Him with a question about whether He cares that they are perishing. The danger is real. Jesus responds by commanding the wind and sea, and the storm gives way to complete calm. The Greek verb φιμόω, phimoō (fee-MOH-oh), can mean to muzzle or silence; Thayer's lexicon lists this command. Mark shows the force of His word over what threatens them.

Jesus then asks about their fear and faith. They have seen His power for others, yet need to learn what trusting Him means in danger themselves. Their final question turns attention from the storm to His identity: who is this person whom even wind and water obey?

Matthew 8:23–27 and Luke 8:22–25 recount the same rescue. Mark's account lets us hear the disciples' fear that He does not care, alongside the authority of the One they have called upon.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand this as a display of Jesus' authority over creation and a call to trust Him in danger. Calvin on Matthew 8:25–26 distinguishes the fear that overwhelms trust from every ordinary experience of fear, while the US Catholic bishops' note on Mark 4:41 also sees encouragement about Jesus' saving presence amid threats to His people.
passages.god_plan_html:
Psalm 107:23–32 describes sailors overwhelmed by waves, crying to the LORD, and seeing Him still the storm. This is a striking scriptural parallel to Mark's scene. The power Scripture attributes to the LORD is displayed in Jesus' command, giving weight to the disciples' question about who He is.

There is also a parallel with Jonah 1:4–16: a storm, a sleeping figure, frightened sailors, and calm that leads to great fear of the LORD. The difference matters. Jonah is fleeing God's commission and is thrown into the sea; Jesus commands the sea Himself. The shared details make the difference stand out: Jonah needs God's rescue, while Jesus speaks and the storm obeys.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 5:1-20
passages.section_title: Restored and Sent Home to Tell of God’s Mercy

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 On the other side of the sea, they arrived in the region of the Gerasenes. 2 As soon as Jesus got out of the boat, He was met by a man with an unclean spirit, who was coming from the tombs. 3 This man had been living in the tombs and could no longer be restrained, even with chains. 4 Though he was often bound with chains and shackles, he had broken the chains and shattered the shackles. Now there was no one with the strength to subdue him. 5 Night and day in the tombs and in the mountains he kept crying out and cutting himself with stones. 6 When the man saw Jesus from a distance, he ran and fell on his knees before Him. 7 And he shouted in a loud voice, “What do You want with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg You before God not to torture me!” 8 For Jesus had already declared, “Come out of this man, you unclean spirit!” 9 “What is your name?” Jesus asked. “My name is Legion,” he replied, “for we are many.” 10 And he begged Jesus repeatedly not to send them out of that region. 11 There on the nearby hillside a large herd of pigs was feeding. 12 So the demons begged Jesus, “Send us to the pigs, so that we may enter them.” 13 He gave them permission, and the unclean spirits came out and went into the pigs, and the herd of about two thousand rushed down the steep bank into the sea and drowned in the water. 14 Those tending the pigs ran off and reported this in the town and countryside, and the people went out to see what had happened. 15 When they came to Jesus, they saw the man who had been possessed by the legion of demons sitting there, clothed and in his right mind; and they were afraid. 16 Those who had seen it described what had happened to the demon-possessed man and also to the pigs. 17 And the people began to beg Jesus to leave their region. 18 As He was getting into the boat, the man who had been possessed by the demons begged to go with Him. 19 But Jesus would not allow him. “Go home to your own people,” He said, “and tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and what mercy He has shown you.” 20 So the man went away and began to proclaim throughout the Decapolis how much Jesus had done for him. And everyone was amazed.
