I beg You before God not to torture me!” 8 For Jesus had already declared, “Come out of this man, you unclean spirit!” 9 “What is your name?” Jesus asked. “My name is Legion,” he replied, “for we are many.” 10 And he begged Jesus repeatedly not to send them out of that region.

11 There on the nearby hillside a large herd of pigs was feeding. 12 So the demons begged Jesus, “Send us to the pigs, so that we may enter them.” 13 He gave them permission, and the unclean spirits came out and went into the pigs, and the herd of about two thousand rushed down the steep bank into the sea and drowned in the water.

14 Those tending the pigs ran off and reported this in the town and countryside, and the people went out to see what had happened. 15 When they came to Jesus, they saw the man who had been possessed by the legion of demons sitting there, clothed and in his right mind; and they were afraid. 16 Those who had seen it described what had happened to the demon-possessed man and also to the pigs. 17 And the people began to beg Jesus to leave their region.

18 As He was getting into the boat, the man who had been possessed by the demons begged to go with Him. 19 But Jesus would not allow him. “Go home to your own people,” He said, “and tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and what mercy He has shown you.” 20 So the man went away and began to proclaim throughout the Decapolis how much Jesus had done for him. And everyone was amazed.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the crossing, Jesus arrives in the region of the Gerasenes and meets a man living among the tombs. Mark describes his suffering and isolation: no one can restrain him, and he cries out and cuts himself with stones. The encounter begins where other people's efforts have failed.

The voice addressing Jesus identifies Him as the Son of the Most High God and begs not to be tormented. Asked his name, the reply is Legion, because they are many. The Greek λεγιών, legiōn (leh-gee-OHN), is a borrowed military word for a body of soldiers; Thayer's lexicon notes that its size varied. Mark's explanation emphasizes many spirits, rather than giving an exact count of six thousand.

The spirits ask to enter a herd of pigs. Jesus permits it, and the herd of about two thousand rushes down the bank and drowns. The spirits act under His permission. Mark reports what happens without explaining every reason Jesus allows the herd's destruction.

Those tending the pigs report the event. The people find the man sitting, clothed, and in his right mind, yet ask Jesus to leave. Luke 8:35–37 explicitly connects their request with great fear. The text tells us about the loss of the pigs, but does not reduce every person's response to a calculation about money.

The restored man wants to accompany Jesus. Instead, Jesus sends him home to tell his own people of the Lord's mercy. Mark then describes him announcing what Jesus has done throughout the Decapolis. His changed life becomes a message for the people around him. The parallel Matthew 8:28–34 describes two men; Mark follows the story of this one in detail.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see Jesus' authority over evil spirits and His mercy restoring a person to life among others. Calvin on Mark 5:9 and Luke 8:38–39 and the US Catholic bishops' notes on Mark 5:9,19 emphasize the many spirits overcome and the restored man's task of making God's kindness known.
passages.god_plan_html:
Earlier, Jesus describes overcoming a strong man before taking what he holds (Mark 3:22–27). This encounter shows that freeing work in a person's life. 1 John 3:8 states the larger purpose directly: the Son of God appeared to destroy the devil's works. The man's restoration belongs to that conflict and victory.

God's mercy also produces a witness. Psalm 66:16–20 calls others to hear what God has done for the speaker. Jesus gives this man a similarly personal message: tell what the Lord has done and the mercy He has shown. Mark's movement from the Lord's work in verse 19 to Jesus' work in verse 20 draws attention to God's saving action through Him.

The man is sent back to people who have asked Jesus to depart. Even there, the account does not end with silence. The person they knew in suffering can now speak to them about the mercy he has received.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 5:21-43
passages.section_title: A Daughter Restored and a Woman Made Well

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 When Jesus had again crossed by boat to the other side, a large crowd gathered around Him beside the sea. 22 A synagogue leader named Jairus arrived, and seeing Jesus, he fell at His feet 23 and pleaded with Him urgently, “My little daughter is near death. Please come and place Your hands on her, so that she will be healed and live.” 24 So Jesus went with him, and a large crowd followed and pressed around Him. 25 And a woman was there who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years. 26 She had borne much agony under the care of many physicians and had spent all she had, but to no avail. Instead, her condition had only grown worse. 27 When the woman heard about Jesus, she came up through the crowd behind Him and touched His cloak. 28 For she kept saying, “If only I touch His garments, I will be healed.” 29 Immediately her bleeding stopped, and she sensed in her body that she was healed of her affliction. 30 At once Jesus was aware that power had gone out from Him. Turning to the crowd, He asked, “Who touched My garments?” 31 His disciples answered, “You can see the crowd pressing in on You, and yet You ask, ‘Who touched Me?’ ” 32 But He kept looking around to see who had done this. 33 Then the woman, knowing what had happened to her, came and fell down before Him trembling in fear, and she told Him the whole truth. 34 “Daughter,” said Jesus, “your faith has healed you. Go in peace and be free of your affliction.” 35 While He was still speaking, messengers from the house of Jairus arrived and said, “Your daughter is dead; why bother the Teacher anymore?” 36 But Jesus overheard their conversation and said to Jairus, “Do not be afraid; just believe.” 37 And He did not allow anyone to accompany Him except Peter, James, and John the brother of James. 38 When they arrived at the house of the synagogue leader, Jesus saw the commotion and the people weeping and wailing loudly. 39 He went inside and asked, “Why all this commotion and weeping? The child is not dead, but asleep.” 40 And they laughed at Him. After He had put them all outside, He took the child’s father and mother and His own companions, and went in to see the child. 41 Taking her by the hand, Jesus said, “Talitha koum!” which means, “Little girl, I say to you, get up!” 42 Immediately the girl got up and began to walk around (she was twelve years old). And at once they were utterly astounded. 43 Then Jesus gave strict orders that no one should know about this, and He told them to give her something to eat.

Go in peace and be free of your affliction.”

The child is not dead, but asleep.” 40 And they laughed at Him. After He had put them all outside, He took the child’s father and mother and His own companions, and went in to see the child.

41 Taking her by the hand, Jesus said, “Talitha koum!” which means, “Little girl, I say to you, get up!” 42 Immediately the girl got up and began to walk around (she was twelve years old). And at once they were utterly astounded. 43 Then Jesus gave strict orders that no one should know about this, and He told them to give her something to eat.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Back across the sea, Jairus, a synagogue leader, asks Jesus to save his dying daughter. Jesus goes with him, but another person's need interrupts the journey. Mark places the woman's healing inside the daughter's story, letting us follow Jairus through a delay before the outcome at his home.

The woman has bled for twelve years, spent everything seeking treatment, and grown worse. After hearing about Jesus, she comes through the crowd and touches His cloak. Leviticus 15:19,25–30 describes the ritual uncleanness connected with ongoing bleeding, which helps explain the wider burden of her condition. That law does not tell us she caused her illness through a particular personal sin.

Her bleeding stops. Jesus knows power has gone out from Him and asks who touched His garments. The woman comes forward in fear and tells Him the truth; He addresses her as daughter, credits her faith, and sends her in peace. The verb σῴζω, sōzō (SOH-zoh), can mean to save or rescue, and here to heal. Thayer's lexicon specifically includes her healing and Jairus's request. The word's wider range does not make the bodily cure less real.

While Jesus speaks, messengers announce the girl's death. Jesus tells Jairus not to fear but to believe. At the house He admits the parents and Peter, James, and John, takes the child by the hand, and tells her to rise. Mark preserves His words, Talitha koum, and immediately supplies their meaning. The girl gets up and walks, and Jesus asks that she be given food.

Calling her asleep is not the narrator denying the reported death. Luke 8:49–55 says the people know she is dead and describes her spirit returning. Jesus treats as temporary a condition the messengers regard as the end of hope. The girl is twelve, matching the length of the woman's suffering; Mark draws the stories together without explaining the number as a hidden code.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see the two stories as calls to trust Jesus and as displays of His authority to heal and restore life. Calvin on Matthew 9:20–22 and Mark 5:39–41 and the US Catholic bishops' notes on Mark 5:28,35,39 connect the healings with faith and understand the girl's sleep language in relation to death from which Jesus raises her, rather than an ordinary nap.
passages.god_plan_html:
Both stories bring Jesus close to conditions Israel's law associates with uncleanness: ongoing bleeding in Leviticus 15 and contact with the dead in Numbers 19:11–16. The focus of the encounter is restoration. The woman is healed, and the child is alive and eating.

The New Testament carries cleansing into a deeper saving purpose. Hebrews 9:11–14 compares the earlier cleansing rites with Christ's own offering, which purifies the conscience for serving God. Romans 5:6–11 describes His death and life bringing reconciliation when people were powerless and estranged. These are wider scriptural connections, not claims that every detail of the two miracles predicts a separate event.

The girl's restoration also points us toward the larger hope beyond death. 1 Corinthians 15:20–23,50–57 grounds that hope in Christ's resurrection and promises an imperishable life to those who belong to Him. Jairus's daughter returns to ordinary life here; the final victory over death reaches beyond this one rescue.
passages.current_position_html: For the woman's healing, we draw from Prayer and Faith, which uses the parallel Matthew 9:20–22 to emphasize faith in Jesus over the wording of a request. She reaches out to Him before making a spoken request for healing. Mark also records her later conversation with Him, so this does not mean she remains silent throughout the encounter. Our point here is the trust Jesus credits, not a formula for producing a miracle. We have not developed a separate position on Jairus's part of the passage.

passages.title: Mark 6:1-6
passages.section_title: A Prophet Without Honor at Home

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Jesus went on from there and came to His hometown, accompanied by His disciples. 2 When the Sabbath came, He began to teach in the synagogue, and many who heard Him were astonished. “Where did this man get these ideas?” they asked. “What is this wisdom He has been given? And how can He perform such miracles? 3 Isn’t this the carpenter, the son of Mary and the brother of James, Joses, Judas, and Simon? Aren’t His sisters here with us as well?” And they took offense at Him. 4 Then Jesus said to them, “Only in his hometown, among his relatives, and in his own household is a prophet without honor.” 5 So He could not perform any miracles there, except to lay His hands on a few of the sick and heal them. 6 And He was amazed at their unbelief. And He went around from village to village, teaching the people.
paragraphs: 1 Jesus went on from there and came to His hometown, accompanied by His disciples. 2 When the Sabbath came, He began to teach in the synagogue, and many who heard Him were astonished. “Where did this man get these ideas?” they asked. “What is this wisdom He has been given? And how can He perform such miracles? 3 Isn’t this the carpenter, the son of Mary and the brother of James, Joses, Judas, and Simon? Aren’t His sisters here with us as well?” And they took offense at Him. 4 Then Jesus said to them, “Only in his hometown, among his relatives, and in his own household is a prophet without honor.”

5 So He could not perform any miracles there, except to lay His hands on a few of the sick and heal them. 6 And He was amazed at their unbelief. And He went around from village to village, teaching the people.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus comes to His hometown with His disciples and teaches in the synagogue on the Sabbath. The hometown is Nazareth, where He grew up (Luke 4:16). His listeners are astonished by His wisdom and mighty works, yet their questions move toward offense rather than trust.

They know His work and family: the carpenter, Mary's son, with brothers and sisters among them. What is familiar becomes a reason to doubt what they are hearing and seeing. Mark records their response without saying every relative has exactly the same thoughts.

Jesus answers with the saying about a prophet lacking honor in his hometown, among relatives, and in his own household. The people closest to a messenger can resist the message. This continues the earlier family and rejection themes, though the disciples still accompany Him.

Mark then says He could not perform miracles there, except that He heals a few sick people by laying His hands on them. The account keeps those healings alongside the strong statement about unbelief. Jesus is amazed at their unbelief and continues teaching in the surrounding villages. Their rejection does not end His mission.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly see familiarity becoming an obstacle to receiving Jesus. On the statement that He could not perform miracles there, Wesley on Mark 6:5 understands the restraint in relation to Jesus' wisdom and goodness, while the US Catholic bishops' note on 6:5 emphasizes unbelief preventing His power from taking effect.

Traditions also differ over the brothers' relationship to Mary. The Catholic Church teaches in Catechism 499–500 that Mary remained a virgin and these are close relatives, rather than other children of hers. The Orthodox Church in America's account of Joseph presents the Orthodox tradition that they are his children from an earlier marriage.

An Orthodox Presbyterian Church answer reads them as children born to Mary and Joseph after Jesus. Protestant readings also vary: Calvin on Matthew 13:55 understands brothers as wider relatives. These differences about the family tree should be distinguished from the passage's central account of rejecting Jesus despite hearing His wisdom.
passages.god_plan_html:
Luke 4:16–30 gives a related Nazareth rejection scene. There Jesus points to Elijah sent to the widow in Sidon and Elisha's cleansing of Naaman the Syrian. Familiarity and ancestry do not give people control over God's mercy. This is a connection between the accounts; Mark does not identify the Scripture read or repeat all of Luke's dialogue.

John 1:10–13 places rejection and reception within a larger purpose. The One through whom the world was made is not recognized, yet those who receive Him and believe in His name are given the right to become God's children. Nearness by hometown or family is different from receiving the Son God has sent.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 6:7-13
passages.section_title: The Twelve Are Sent to Preach and Heal

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 Then Jesus called the Twelve to Him and began to send them out two by two, giving them authority over unclean spirits. 8 He instructed them to take nothing but a staff for the journey—no bread, no bag, no money in their belts— 9 and to wear sandals, but not a second tunic. 10 And He told them, “When you enter a house, stay there until you leave that area. 11 If anyone will not welcome you or listen to you, shake the dust off your feet when you leave that place, as a testimony against them.” 12 So they set out and preached that the people should repent. 13 They also drove out many demons and healed many of the sick, anointing them with oil.
paragraphs: 7 Then Jesus called the Twelve to Him and began to send them out two by two, giving them authority over unclean spirits. 8 He instructed them to take nothing but a staff for the journey—no bread, no bag, no money in their belts— 9 and to wear sandals, but not a second tunic.

10 And He told them, “When you enter a house, stay there until you leave that area. 11 If anyone will not welcome you or listen to you, shake the dust off your feet when you leave that place, as a testimony against them.”
12 So they set out and preached that the people should repent. 13 They also drove out many demons and healed many of the sick, anointing them with oil.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus now sends the Twelve out in pairs and gives them authority over unclean spirits. Their earlier appointment in Mark 3:13–19 included being with Him and being sent. They now carry out the mission for which He has been preparing them.

The instructions require traveling light and receiving hospitality. Mark permits a staff and sandals, but no bread, bag, money, or spare tunic. They are to remain in the house that receives them until they leave the area. If people will neither welcome nor listen to them, they are to leave and shake off the dust as a testimony against that place.

They preach repentance, cast out demons, and heal sick people while anointing them with oil. Repent comes from μετανοέω, metanoeō (meh-tah-noh-EH-oh). Thayer's lexicon includes a changed mind joined with turning from past sins, and specifically lists Mark 6:12. Their message calls for a changed response to God, beyond admiring a new teacher.

Matthew 10:5–15 and Luke 9:1–6 give related instructions, with differences about travel equipment. Mark's wording should remain visible as we consider those accounts. The central picture is a mission carried out under Jesus' authority, with dependence on provision and readiness for both welcome and rejection.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly understand the journey as Jesus preparing His chosen messengers to preach and serve under His authority. They differ in explaining some details. Wesley on Mark 6:8–9 understands the staff allowance as taking what they already have rather than acquiring new equipment. The US Catholic bishops' note on 6:8–9 suggests that the instructions were adjusted for different settings in which the message was being preached. These are explanatory readings, not uniform church rulings about the wording.

The oil anointing also has different church applications. The Catholic Church identifies this passage as pointing toward the sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick (Catechism 1511). Reformed teaching in the Westminster Confession, 27.4, recognizes baptism and the Lord's Supper as the two sacraments and does not count this anointing among them.
passages.god_plan_html:
The mission answers a need Jesus Himself identifies. In Matthew 9:35–38, His compassion for people like sheep without a shepherd leads to a call for prayer that the Lord of the harvest send workers. The next chapter describes His sending the Twelve. God meets people's need through messengers He calls and equips.

The early journey also prepares them for later service. In Luke 22:35, Jesus asks whether they lacked anything when He sent them without provisions; they answer that they lacked nothing. The following instructions change as their circumstances change. Dependence on Him continues through different circumstances.

After the resurrection, the mission reaches all nations under His authority (Matthew 28:18–20). Acts 13:48–52 shows Paul and Barnabas meeting both welcome and rejection, shaking off dust, and continuing their work. This first sending belongs to the larger movement of God's good news through His people.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 6:14-29
passages.section_title: John’s Death and Herod’s Fear

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 Now King Herod heard about this, for Jesus’ name had become well known, and people were saying, “John the Baptist has risen from the dead! That is why miraculous powers are at work in him.” 15 Others were saying, “He is Elijah,” and still others, “He is a prophet, like one of the prophets of old.” 16 But when Herod heard this, he said, “John, whom I beheaded, has risen from the dead!” 17 For Herod himself had ordered that John be arrested and bound and imprisoned, on account of his brother Philip’s wife Herodias, whom Herod had married. 18 For John had been telling Herod, “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife!” 19 So Herodias held a grudge against John and wanted to kill him. But she had been unable, 20 because Herod feared John and protected him, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man. When he heard John’s words, he was greatly perplexed; yet he listened to him gladly. 21 On Herod’s birthday, her opportunity arose. Herod held a banquet for his nobles and military commanders and the leading men of Galilee. 22 When the daughter of Herodias came and danced, she pleased Herod and his guests, and the king said to the girl, “Ask me for whatever you wish, and I will give it to you.” 23 And he swore to her, “Whatever you ask of me, I will give you, up to half my kingdom!” 24 Then she went out and asked her mother, “What should I request?” And her mother answered, “The head of John the Baptist.” 25 At once the girl hurried back to the king with her request: “I want you to give me the head of John the Baptist on a platter immediately.” 26 The king was consumed with sorrow, but because of his oaths and his guests, he did not want to refuse her. 27 So without delay, the king commanded that John’s head be brought in. He sent an executioner, who went and beheaded him in the prison. 28 The man brought John’s head on a platter and presented it to the girl, who gave it to her mother. 29 When John’s disciples heard about this, they came and took his body and placed it in a tomb.

But she had been unable, 20 because Herod feared John and protected him, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man. When he heard John’s words, he was greatly perplexed; yet he listened to him gladly.

21 On Herod’s birthday, her opportunity arose. Herod held a banquet for his nobles and military commanders and the leading men of Galilee. 22 When the daughter of Herodias came and danced, she pleased Herod and his guests, and the king said to the girl, “Ask me for whatever you wish, and I will give it to you.” 23 And he swore to her, “Whatever you ask of me, I will give you, up to half my kingdom!” 24 Then she went out and asked her mother, “What should I request?” And her mother answered, “The head of John the Baptist.” 25 At once the girl hurried back to the king with her request: “I want you to give me the head of John the Baptist on a platter immediately.”

26 The king was consumed with sorrow, but because of his oaths and his guests, he did not want to refuse her. 27 So without delay, the king commanded that John’s head be brought in. He sent an executioner, who went and beheaded him in the prison. 28 The man brought John’s head on a platter and presented it to the girl, who gave it to her mother. 29 When John’s disciples heard about this, they came and took his body and placed it in a tomb.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
News of Jesus reaches Herod, and people offer different explanations of His identity: John raised from the dead, Elijah, or a prophet like those of old. Herod settles on John, the man he had beheaded. These are the speakers' conclusions about Jesus, not Mark saying that John has actually returned to life.

Mark then looks back to explain John's death. John had challenged Herod's marriage to his brother Philip's wife, Herodias. Leviticus 18:16 and 20:21 give the scriptural background to his protest. Herodias wants John dead, while Herod recognizes him as righteous and holy, protects him for a time, and listens gladly despite being perplexed.

The Herod in this account is Antipas. The historian Josephus, Antiquities 18.5.1–2, also reports his imprisonment and execution of John, emphasizing Herod's fear that John's influence over crowds could lead to unrest. Mark follows the marriage protest and the events at the birthday banquet.

Herodias's daughter dances before Herod and his guests. He promises her whatever she asks, even up to half his kingdom. After consulting her mother, she requests John's head. Herod is deeply grieved, yet chooses to honor his public promise rather than refuse the killing. Mark places his oaths and his guests directly in the explanation of his decision.

John is executed in prison, his head is brought to the banquet, and his disciples take his body for burial. Herod's respect for John has not become obedience to the truth John spoke. The story also interrupts the account of the Twelve's mission: their sending in verses 7–13 is followed by their return in verse 30. The danger faced by a faithful messenger stands between those two scenes.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see John's faithful witness contrasted with Herod's refusal to act on what he recognizes as right. Calvin on Matthew 14:9 and Mark 6:26 and Wesley on Mark 6:26 emphasize the failure of an honor that keeps a rash promise at the cost of innocent life; sorrow over the outcome does not excuse the decision.
passages.god_plan_html:
John's suffering points ahead to the suffering of the One whose way he prepares. In Mark 9:11–13, Jesus joins the discussion of Elijah's coming with the Son of Man's rejection. The parallel Matthew 17:10–13 explicitly identifies John as the person in view and connects his mistreatment with what Jesus will suffer. This is a connection Jesus Himself draws.

There are further parallels in Mark 15:9–15,42–47: a ruler yields to pressure, an innocent man is killed, and someone who cares for Him seeks His body for burial. The parallel prepares us for the cost of Jesus' mission. His death also has a saving purpose He states directly: He gives His life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). The Gospel leads beyond the silencing of a messenger to the Savior's own self-giving.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 6:30-44
passages.section_title: Jesus Feeds the Five Thousand

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 30 Meanwhile, the apostles gathered around Jesus and brought Him news of all they had done and taught. 31 And He said to them, “Come with Me privately to a solitary place, and let us rest for a while.” For many people were coming and going, and they did not even have time to eat. 32 So they went away in a boat by themselves to a solitary place. 33 But many people saw them leaving and recognized them. They ran together on foot from all the towns and arrived before them. 34 When Jesus stepped ashore and saw a large crowd, He had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd. And He began to teach them many things. 35 By now the hour was already late. So the disciples came to Jesus and said, “This is a desolate place, and the hour is already late. 36 Dismiss the crowd so they can go to the surrounding countryside and villages and buy themselves something to eat.” 37 But Jesus told them, “You give them something to eat.” They asked Him, “Should we go out and spend two hundred denarii to give all of them bread to eat?” 38 “Go and see how many loaves you have,” He told them. And after checking, they said, “Five—and two fish.” 39 Then Jesus directed them to have the people sit in groups on the green grass. 40 So they sat down in groups of hundreds and fifties. 41 Taking the five loaves and the two fish and looking up to heaven, Jesus spoke a blessing and broke the loaves. Then He gave them to His disciples to set before the people. And He divided the two fish among them all. 42 They all ate and were satisfied, 43 and the disciples picked up twelve basketfuls of broken pieces of bread and fish. 44 And there were five thousand men who had eaten the loaves.

They ran together on foot from all the towns and arrived before them. 34 When Jesus stepped ashore and saw a large crowd, He had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd. And He began to teach them many things.

35 By now the hour was already late. So the disciples came to Jesus and said, “This is a desolate place, and the hour is already late. 36 Dismiss the crowd so they can go to the surrounding countryside and villages and buy themselves something to eat.” 37 But Jesus told them, “You give them something to eat.” They asked Him, “Should we go out and spend two hundred denarii to give all of them bread to eat?” 38 “Go and see how many loaves you have,” He told them. And after checking, they said, “Five—and two fish.”

39 Then Jesus directed them to have the people sit in groups on the green grass. 40 So they sat down in groups of hundreds and fifties. 41 Taking the five loaves and the two fish and looking up to heaven, Jesus spoke a blessing and broke the loaves. Then He gave them to His disciples to set before the people. And He divided the two fish among them all. 42 They all ate and were satisfied, 43 and the disciples picked up twelve basketfuls of broken pieces of bread and fish. 44 And there were five thousand men who had eaten the loaves.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Twelve return and tell Jesus what they have done and taught. He calls them away to rest because the crowds have left them no time even to eat. Their need for rest is real, yet the people recognize them and reach the destination ahead of the boat.

Jesus responds to the crowd with compassion. The Greek verb σπλαγχνίζομαι (splagchnizomai, splangkh-NEE-zoh-my) describes being deeply moved with pity. Here that concern becomes action: He teaches people who need a shepherd and then provides their meal.

Late in the day, the disciples suggest sending the people to buy food. Jesus tells the disciples to feed them. Their reply about two hundred denarii shows the size of the problem. A denarius is the day's pay agreed with workers in Matthew 20:1–2, so they are speaking about a substantial cost, not a small purchase.

There are five loaves and two fish. Jesus seats the people in groups, looks to heaven, blesses the food, and gives it through the disciples. Everyone eats enough, and twelve baskets of bread and fish remain. Mark counts five thousand men; Matthew 14:21 adds that women and children were also present, without giving a total for them.

The parallel account in John 6:4–15 places this near Passover, identifies a boy with barley loaves, and says Jesus was testing Philip. Those details come from John. Mark emphasizes Jesus' compassion, the disciples' involvement, and a provision far beyond what they could supply.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand this as Jesus' miraculous provision for the crowd and a lesson in depending on Him while serving others. Calvin's discussion of Mark 6:30–44 emphasizes His care for both people's teaching and their bodily needs; the USCCB notes likewise describe Him as the faithful shepherd who feeds His people.
passages.god_plan_html:
The shepherd language has a history. In Numbers 27:15–18, Moses asks for a leader so God's people will not be sheep without a shepherd. In Ezekiel 34:1–16,23–24, God condemns leaders who feed themselves, promises to care for His flock, and promises one shepherd from David's line. Jesus' teaching and feeding provide a strong parallel to that promised care. The green grass also recalls the restful provision of Psalm 23; Mark does not announce a direct quotation of the psalm.

There is another clear parallel in 2 Kings 4:42–44: Elisha tells a servant to feed people with an apparently inadequate amount of bread, and food remains after they eat. Here Jesus feeds a much larger crowd from much less. The comparison helps us see the scale of His provision.

John 6:26–35 then takes the meal beyond full stomachs. Jesus directs people toward the life the Father gives through Him and identifies Himself as the bread of life. The gift points people to the Giver, whose purpose reaches beyond one day's hunger.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 6:45-52
passages.section_title: Jesus Comes Across the Sea

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 45 Immediately Jesus made His disciples get into the boat and go on ahead of Him to Bethsaida, while He dismissed the crowd. 46 After bidding them farewell, He went up on the mountain to pray. 47 When evening came, the boat was in the middle of the sea, and Jesus was alone on land. 48 He could see that the disciples were straining to row, because the wind was against them. About the fourth watch of the night, Jesus went out to them, walking on the sea. He intended to pass by them, 49 but when they saw Him walking on the sea, they cried out, thinking He was a ghost— 50 for they all saw Him and were terrified. But Jesus spoke up at once: “Take courage! It is I. Do not be afraid.” 51 Then He climbed into the boat with them, and the wind died down. And the disciples were utterly astounded, 52 for they had not understood about the loaves, but their hearts had been hardened.
paragraphs: 45 Immediately Jesus made His disciples get into the boat and go on ahead of Him to Bethsaida, while He dismissed the crowd. 46 After bidding them farewell, He went up on the mountain to pray. 47 When evening came, the boat was in the middle of the sea, and Jesus was alone on land. 48 He could see that the disciples were straining to row, because the wind was against them. About the fourth watch of the night, Jesus went out to them, walking on the sea. He intended to pass by them,

49 but when they saw Him walking on the sea, they cried out, thinking He was a ghost— 50 for they all saw Him and were terrified. But Jesus spoke up at once: “Take courage! It is I. Do not be afraid.” 51 Then He climbed into the boat with them, and the wind died down. And the disciples were utterly astounded, 52 for they had not understood about the loaves, but their hearts had been hardened.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the meal, Jesus sends the disciples ahead by boat toward Bethsaida, dismisses the crowd, and goes up the mountain to pray. John 6:14–15 adds that the people wanted to make Him king by force. Mark does not tell us that the disciples joined that attempt or give the content of Jesus' prayer.

Jesus is alone on land while the disciples struggle to row against the wind. He sees their difficulty and comes toward them on the sea in the fourth watch, the period the BSB footnote identifies as between three and six in the morning. Mark does not specify the exact hour or how many hours they have been rowing.

He intends to pass by them, but they see Him and cry out, thinking He is a ghost. Jesus speaks reassurance, identifies Himself, and tells them not to fear. He climbs into the boat and the wind dies down. Their terror gives way to astonishment.

Mark then explains their surprise by connecting this scene with the loaves: they have not understood what that earlier work showed them. The Greek verb πωρόω (poroo, poh-ROH-oh), translated as hearts being hardened, can describe becoming dull or unable to understand. It is a serious failure to grasp what Jesus is showing them; this verse does not announce that the disciples can never learn.

Matthew 14:28–33 also tells of Peter coming onto the water and the disciples worshiping Jesus. Mark leaves Peter's part out and concentrates on the whole group's failure to understand the loaves and recognize Jesus.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see Jesus revealing His authority over the sea while teaching His frightened disciples to trust Him. Calvin on this account connects their failure with forgetting the power shown in the loaves, and Wesley on verse 52 understands their hardened hearts here as slowness to understand rather than a declaration of final rejection.
passages.god_plan_html:
The sea scene recalls things Scripture says about God. Job 9:8–11 describes Him treading on the waves and passing by beyond Job's perception. In Exodus 33:18–23 and 34:5–8, God passes before Moses as He makes Himself known. These are meaningful parallels to Jesus walking on the sea and passing by His disciples. Mark does not explicitly name those passages as quotations.

The USCCB note on Mark 6:50 also sees a possible echo of God's self-revelation in Jesus' words of reassurance. The Greek wording can simply identify the speaker, as Thayer's entry for εἰμί explains for this verse; the case for the larger connection rests on the whole scene, including His authority over the water. Mark brings us back to the question the loaves already raised: who is this One who provides for His people and comes to them with power they cannot explain?
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 6:53-56
passages.section_title: Healing at Gennesaret

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 53 When they had crossed over, they landed at Gennesaret and moored the boat. 54 As soon as they got out of the boat, the people recognized Jesus 55 and ran through that whole region, carrying the sick on mats to wherever they heard He was. 56 And wherever He went—villages and towns and countrysides—they laid the sick in the marketplaces and begged Him just to let them touch the fringe of His cloak. And all who touched Him were healed.
paragraphs: 53 When they had crossed over, they landed at Gennesaret and moored the boat. 54 As soon as they got out of the boat, the people recognized Jesus 55 and ran through that whole region, carrying the sick on mats to wherever they heard He was. 56 And wherever He went—villages and towns and countrysides—they laid the sick in the marketplaces and begged Him just to let them touch the fringe of His cloak. And all who touched Him were healed.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The boat lands at Gennesaret. People recognize Jesus and spread the news through the region, carrying the sick on mats to wherever they hear He is. Mark describes activity across villages, towns, and countryside rather than one isolated healing.

People lay the sick in marketplaces and ask that they be allowed to touch even the fringe of His cloak. All who touch Him are healed. The scene recalls the woman who touched His clothing in Mark 5:25–34, but Mark does not tell each person's story or explain what everyone understands about Jesus.

This summary follows the disciples' struggle to recognize what His works mean. The crowds recognize Jesus and seek His help; recognition and a desire for healing are not, by themselves, a full account of their faith or their later response to His teaching. Mark gives us the healings without supplying those missing details.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see these healings as evidence of Jesus' compassionate power and the eagerness of people to bring others to Him. Calvin on Matthew 14:34–36 and Mark 6:53–56 emphasizes the many public witnesses to His works and the need to seek in Him more than bodily relief.
passages.god_plan_html:
The healings belong to a larger scriptural picture of God's rescue. Isaiah 35:4–6 joins God's coming to save with restored sight, hearing, and movement. When asked whether He is the expected One, Jesus points to works of this kind in Matthew 11:2–6. Gennesaret provides another scene in that wider pattern; Mark does not label this summary a separate fulfillment quotation.

Scripture's promised end reaches beyond these local recoveries. Revelation 21:1–5 describes God dwelling with His people and the removal of death, mourning, and pain. These healings offer a glimpse of His restoring power, while that final renewal remains more than a promise that every illness will disappear immediately in the present.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 7:1-13
passages.section_title: When Tradition Overrides God's Command

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then the Pharisees and some of the scribes who had come from Jerusalem gathered around Jesus, 2 and they saw some of His disciples eating with hands that were defiled—that is, unwashed. 3 Now in holding to the tradition of the elders, the Pharisees and all the Jews do not eat until they wash their hands ceremonially. 4 And on returning from the market, they do not eat unless they wash. And there are many other traditions for them to observe, including the washing of cups, pitchers, kettles, and couches for dining. 5 So the Pharisees and scribes questioned Jesus: “Why do Your disciples not walk according to the tradition of the elders? Instead, they eat with defiled hands.” 6 Jesus answered them, “Isaiah prophesied correctly about you hypocrites, as it is written: ‘These people honor Me with their lips, but their hearts are far from Me. 7 They worship Me in vain; they teach as doctrine the precepts of men.’ 8 You have disregarded the commandment of God to keep the tradition of men.” 9 He went on to say, “You neatly set aside the command of God to maintain your own tradition. 10 For Moses said, ‘Honor your father and your mother’ and ‘Anyone who curses his father or mother must be put to death.’ 11 But you say that if a man says to his father or mother, ‘Whatever you would have received from me is Corban’ (that is, a gift devoted to God), 12 he is no longer permitted to do anything for his father or mother. 13 Thus you nullify the word of God by the tradition you have handed down. And you do so in many such matters.”

And there are many other traditions for them to observe, including the washing of cups, pitchers, kettles, and couches for dining. 5 So the Pharisees and scribes questioned Jesus: “Why do Your disciples not walk according to the tradition of the elders? Instead, they eat with defiled hands.”

6 Jesus answered them, “Isaiah prophesied correctly about you hypocrites, as it is written: ‘These people honor Me with their lips, but their hearts are far from Me. 7 They worship Me in vain; they teach as doctrine the precepts of men.’ 8 You have disregarded the commandment of God to keep the tradition of men.” 9 He went on to say, “You neatly set aside the command of God to maintain your own tradition.

10 For Moses said, ‘Honor your father and your mother’ and ‘Anyone who curses his father or mother must be put to death.’ 11 But you say that if a man says to his father or mother, ‘Whatever you would have received from me is Corban’ (that is, a gift devoted to God), 12 he is no longer permitted to do anything for his father or mother. 13 Thus you nullify the word of God by the tradition you have handed down. And you do so in many such matters.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Pharisees and some scribes from Jerusalem gather around Jesus and notice some disciples eating without ceremonially washing their hands. The question is why they do not follow the tradition of the elders. Mark explains the washing practices for his readers; the dispute concerns religious obligation and purity.

The distinction between written law and inherited practices was a real point of disagreement within Judaism. Josephus, Antiquities 13.10.6, reports that Pharisees passed down observances not written in Moses' law, while Sadducees rejected those as binding. That background helps explain the issue without treating every Jewish group as holding the same position.

Jesus answers from Isaiah 29:13: people can honor God with words while their hearts remain far away. He then gives a concrete example. God commands people to honor their parents (Exodus 20:12) and treats cursing them as a grave offense (Exodus 21:17). Yet their rule permits a religious declaration to prevent the help a parent should receive.

Mark explains the declaration as Corban, a gift devoted to God. The Greek spelling κορβᾶν (korban, kor-BAHN) represents the Hebrew word for an offering; Thayer describes a gift offered or intended to be offered to God. Here the declaration is being used to keep resources from helping a father or mother.

The example brings Jesus' charge into focus: a rule defended as devotion to God has become a reason to neglect what He commands. The problem is more than failing to carry out a washing custom. Religious teaching is being used to excuse a failure of care, and Jesus says this happens in many such matters.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand Jesus to be condemning human rules that set aside God's commands. The difference between traditions concerns how to recognize teaching received with divine authority, rather than whether disobeying God is acceptable.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, 1.6 and 1.10, and the 1689 Baptist Confession, 1.6 and 1.10, make Scripture the final test for church teaching and reject additions from human traditions. They also allow practical arrangements for church life under Scripture's guidance. The Methodist Articles of Religion, V and XXII, say that nothing can be required as necessary for salvation unless taught or proved from Scripture, while allowing church customs that do not contradict God's word.

The Catholic Church distinguishes apostolic Tradition, received from Christ and the apostles, from later customs that can change. Its Catechism, 80–83, receives Scripture and apostolic Tradition together; paragraph 86 says the Church's teaching office serves God's word. Catholic teaching therefore reads Jesus' rebuke as a condemnation of corrupt human practices, rather than a rejection of apostolic Tradition.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus explicitly applies Isaiah 29:13–14 to this dispute. The warning reaches beyond a single custom: speaking honorably about God cannot replace a heart and life that respond to Him. A teaching's religious appearance does not settle whether it honors His purpose.

James 1:21–27 develops the same larger concern. Receiving God's word must lead to doing it, and faithful devotion includes care for vulnerable people. The Corban example shows what goes wrong when a religious explanation protects people from that responsibility instead of moving them toward it.
passages.current_position_html: In The Berean Standard, our discussion of Mark 7:8–9 identifies the danger as tradition becoming the authority and displacing what God actually says. Useful customs are not the problem in themselves; they must remain open to examination against Scripture.

passages.title: Mark 7:8-9
passages.section_title: God's Command and Human Tradition

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 You have disregarded the commandment of God to keep the tradition of men.” 9 He went on to say, “You neatly set aside the command of God to maintain your own tradition.
paragraphs: 8 You have disregarded the commandment of God to keep the tradition of men.” 9 He went on to say, “You neatly set aside the command of God to maintain your own tradition.

passages.context_html:
These words belong to Jesus' reply about the disciples eating without ceremonially washing their hands. The leaders appeal to the tradition of the elders; Jesus has just applied Isaiah's warning about lips honoring God while hearts remain far away.

He immediately explains His charge through the Corban example in Mark 7:10–13. A declaration that resources are devoted to God is used to prevent help for a parent, although God commands children to honor their parents. The tradition's effect on actual obedience is the issue.

The contrast is therefore a practical one: does the rule help people do what God says, or provide a way around it? This short reference should be read with the full exchange in verses 1–13.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, 1.6 and 1.10, and the 1689 Baptist Confession, 1.6 and 1.10, make Scripture the final test for church teaching and reject additions from human traditions. They also allow practical arrangements for church life under Scripture's guidance. Its Catechism, 80–83, receives Scripture and apostolic Tradition together; paragraph 86 says the Church's teaching office serves God's word. Catholic teaching therefore reads Jesus' rebuke as a condemnation of corrupt human practices, rather than a rejection of apostolic Tradition.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html: The wider exchange explicitly reaches back to Isaiah 29:13. God's concern includes the heart behind worship and the obedience it produces. James 1:22–27 carries that concern forward by joining hearing the word with doing it, including care for people in need. Religious practice is meant to express a response to God rather than shelter us from His commands.

passages.title: Mark 7:14-23
passages.section_title: What Makes a Person Unclean?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 Once again Jesus called the crowd to Him and said, “All of you, listen to Me and understand: 15 Nothing that enters a man from the outside can defile him; but the things that come out of a man, these are what defile him.” 17 After Jesus had left the crowd and gone into the house, His disciples inquired about the parable. 18 “Are you still so dull?” He asked. “Do you not understand? Nothing that enters a man from the outside can defile him, 19 because it does not enter his heart, but it goes into the stomach and then is eliminated.” (Thus all foods are clean.) 20 He continued: “What comes out of a man, that is what defiles him. 21 For from within the hearts of men come evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, 22 greed, wickedness, deceit, debauchery, envy, slander, arrogance, and foolishness. 23 All these evils come from within, and these are what defile a man.”
paragraphs: 14 Once again Jesus called the crowd to Him and said, “All of you, listen to Me and understand: 15 Nothing that enters a man from the outside can defile him; but the things that come out of a man, these are what defile him.”

17 After Jesus had left the crowd and gone into the house, His disciples inquired about the parable. 18 “Are you still so dull?” He asked. “Do you not understand? Nothing that enters a man from the outside can defile him, 19 because it does not enter his heart, but it goes into the stomach and then is eliminated.” (Thus all foods are clean.)

20 He continued: “What comes out of a man, that is what defiles him. 21 For from within the hearts of men come evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, 22 greed, wickedness, deceit, debauchery, envy, slander, arrogance, and foolishness. 23 All these evils come from within, and these are what defile a man.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus turns from the leaders' complaint about unwashed hands to the crowd, then explains His teaching privately to the disciples. The question is what makes a person unclean before God. His answer moves attention from food entering the body to evil coming from the heart.

The verb κοινόω (koinoo, koy-NOH-oh) means to make unclean or defile. It links the discussion of ceremonial uncleanness with Jesus' deeper point about moral corruption. Food passes through the stomach and is eliminated; evil thoughts and actions arise from within the person.

The BSB ends verse 19 with a comment that all foods are clean. Its main text does not include the sentence traditionally numbered verse 16; that sentence is noted in the BibleHub BSB footnote. The passage above follows the BSB's main text and verse numbering.

Jesus' list includes both actions and attitudes: sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, greed, wickedness, deceit, debauchery, envy, slander, arrogance, and foolishness. The issue reaches beyond the words a person says. What goes wrong within can become harmful conduct toward others.

This explanation follows the Corban example, where a religious rule was being used to withhold help from parents. Ceremonial attention did not prevent a failure of obedience and care. Jesus now identifies the source of such evil instead of treating outward washing as its cure.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand Jesus to locate moral defilement in the heart rather than in food. Calvin's discussion of this passage and Wesley's notes on Mark 7:15 both stress that sinful attitudes and conduct come from the person; the Catholic Catechism, 582, likewise connects Jesus' teaching about clean food with what comes from the heart.
passages.god_plan_html:
The problem of an unclean heart belongs to a larger story of God's cleansing work. In Ezekiel 36:22–28, God promises Israel cleansing, a new heart, and His Spirit leading people into obedience. That is a supported connection in theme: the need Jesus exposes calls for more than improving an outward appearance.

Hebrews 9:11–15 explains how Christ's self-offering reaches the conscience and enables service to the living God. Galatians 5:16–25 describes the contrasting fruit of life by the Spirit, including love, patience, and self-control. Scripture carries us from recognizing the inner source of evil to God's work of cleansing and a changed life.

The clean-and-unclean language also matters when the gospel reaches Gentiles. In Acts 10:9–20,28,34–48, Peter's vision uses food, and Peter explicitly applies what God shows him to people: he must not call a person impure or unclean. He then witnesses Gentiles receiving the Holy Spirit. This later account shows the wider reach of God's welcome; it is a connection between the accounts, not a claim that Jesus names Cornelius in this passage.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 7:24-30
passages.section_title: The Woman Who Asked for Crumbs

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 24 Jesus left that place and went to the region of Tyre. Not wanting anyone to know He was there, He entered a house, but was unable to escape their notice. 25 Instead, a woman whose little daughter had an unclean spirit soon heard about Jesus, and she came and fell at His feet. 26 Now she was a Greek woman of Syrophoenician origin, and she kept asking Jesus to drive the demon out of her daughter. 27 “First let the children have their fill,” He said. “For it is not right to take the children’s bread and toss it to the dogs.” 28 “Yes, Lord,” she replied, “even the dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs.” 29 Then Jesus told her, “Because of this answer, you may go. The demon has left your daughter.” 30 And she went home and found her child lying on the bed, and the demon was gone.
paragraphs: 24 Jesus left that place and went to the region of Tyre. Not wanting anyone to know He was there, He entered a house, but was unable to escape their notice. 25 Instead, a woman whose little daughter had an unclean spirit soon heard about Jesus, and she came and fell at His feet. 26 Now she was a Greek woman of Syrophoenician origin, and she kept asking Jesus to drive the demon out of her daughter.

27 “First let the children have their fill,” He said. “For it is not right to take the children’s bread and toss it to the dogs.” 28 “Yes, Lord,” she replied, “even the dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs.” 29 Then Jesus told her, “Because of this answer, you may go. The demon has left your daughter.” 30 And she went home and found her child lying on the bed, and the demon was gone.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus goes to the region of Tyre and enters a house, seeking privacy. A woman hears He is there, comes to Him, and keeps asking Him to drive an unclean spirit from her daughter. Mark identifies her as Greek and Syrophoenician by origin, placing this encounter beyond Jesus' own Jewish community.

Jesus answers with a household picture: the children should eat first, and their bread should not be taken and given to the dogs. The parallel Matthew 15:21–28 makes the reference to Israel clear by recording His statement about being sent to Israel's lost sheep. Mark's word first is important: the picture describes a priority.

The Greek noun κυνάριον (kynarion, koo-NAH-ree-on) means a little dog. The setting is a household table, with dogs underneath it. The word helps explain the picture, but cannot by itself tell us Jesus' tone of voice or make the distinction between children and dogs disappear.

The woman accepts the picture and replies from within it: even the dogs receive crumbs under the table. She does not ask for the children to lose their meal. She asks for help that can reach her daughter too.

Jesus responds to her answer by telling her that the demon has left. She goes home and finds her child on the bed, free from it. Matthew explicitly praises her great faith; Mark emphasizes her answer and the help Jesus gives without going to the child's bedside.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see the woman's persistent faith and Jesus' mercy reaching a Gentile alongside His mission to Israel. Calvin on Mark 7:24–30 emphasizes her faith through the difficult exchange, while the USCCB notes on verses 27–28 explain Israel's priority and Jesus' response to her faith.
passages.god_plan_html:
Mercy reaching beyond Israel fits promises already present in Scripture. Isaiah 49:5–6 describes the Servant restoring Israel and bringing God's salvation to the nations. Romans 15:7–13 joins Christ's confirmation of the patriarchs' promises with Gentiles glorifying God for mercy. The woman's receiving help fits that wider pattern of promise and welcome.

Ephesians 2:11–22 describes the larger result through Christ's blood and cross: those once far away are brought near, and Jews and Gentiles have access to the Father by one Spirit. They become members of God's household. The future opened by Christ reaches beyond receiving crumbs outside a privileged group to sharing life together in Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 7:31-37
passages.section_title: Jesus Opens Ears and Restores Speech

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 31 Then Jesus left the region of Tyre and went through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee and into the region of the Decapolis. 32 Some people brought to Him a man who was deaf and hardly able to speak, and they begged Jesus to place His hand on him. 33 So Jesus took him aside privately, away from the crowd, and put His fingers into the man’s ears. Then He spit and touched the man’s tongue. 34 And looking up to heaven, He sighed deeply and said to him, “Ephphatha!” (which means, “Be opened!” ). 35 Immediately the man’s ears were opened and his tongue was released, and he began to speak plainly. 36 Jesus ordered them not to tell anyone. But the more He ordered them, the more widely they proclaimed it. 37 The people were utterly astonished and said, “He has done all things well! He makes even the deaf hear and the mute speak!”
paragraphs: 31 Then Jesus left the region of Tyre and went through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee and into the region of the Decapolis. 32 Some people brought to Him a man who was deaf and hardly able to speak, and they begged Jesus to place His hand on him. 33 So Jesus took him aside privately, away from the crowd, and put His fingers into the man’s ears. Then He spit and touched the man’s tongue. 34 And looking up to heaven, He sighed deeply and said to him, “Ephphatha!” (which means, “Be opened!” ). 35 Immediately the man’s ears were opened and his tongue was released, and he began to speak plainly.

36 Jesus ordered them not to tell anyone. But the more He ordered them, the more widely they proclaimed it. 37 The people were utterly astonished and said, “He has done all things well! He makes even the deaf hear and the mute speak!”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus travels from the region of Tyre through Sidon toward the Sea of Galilee and the Decapolis. Some people bring Him a man who is deaf and has difficulty speaking, asking Jesus to place His hand on him. Mark does not identify the man's nationality or say how long he has had these difficulties.

Jesus takes him away from the crowd and deals with him personally. He puts His fingers into the man's ears, spits, and touches his tongue. Looking to heaven, He sighs deeply and speaks. Mark records these actions without prescribing them as a method everyone must repeat.

The word ἐφφαθά (ephphatha, ef-fah-THAH) preserves an Aramaic command, which Mark translates for his readers as be opened. The man's hearing is restored immediately and he speaks plainly. The account focuses on the change Jesus brings about.

Jesus orders them not to tell anyone, but they keep spreading the news. Their amazement is understandable, yet the contrast remains between His instruction and their response. The crowd's praise brings the scene to its close: they recognize the good He has done in restoring hearing and speech.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see Jesus' compassion and authority in this personal healing. Calvin on Mark 7:32–36 understands His actions as outward signs through which He makes His help known, while Wesley on verse 33 cautions against requiring Jesus to heal by the method people expect.
passages.god_plan_html:
The language of restored hearing and speech closely recalls Isaiah 35:4–6, where God's coming to save is accompanied by opened ears and a voice restored to joy. There is even a word connection: Thayer's entry for μογιλάλος (mogilalos, moh-gee-LAH-los), meaning speaking with difficulty, identifies its use in Mark 7:32 and the ancient Greek translation of Isaiah 35:6. This is a strong scriptural parallel to what Jesus does here.

Jesus Himself points to restored sight, hearing, and life when answering whether He is the expected One (Matthew 11:2–6). The healing therefore belongs to the larger question of His identity and God's saving work. Isaiah's picture goes on to people returning with lasting joy, with sorrow fleeing away; the individual restoration is part of a much larger hope.
