passages.title: Mark 8:1-10
passages.section_title: Jesus Feeds the Four Thousand

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 In those days the crowd once again became very large, and they had nothing to eat. Jesus called the disciples to Him and said, 2 “I have compassion for this crowd, because they have already been with Me three days and have nothing to eat. 3 If I send them home hungry, they will faint along the way. For some of them have come a great distance.” 4 His disciples replied, “Where in this desolate place could anyone find enough bread to feed all these people?” 5 “How many loaves do you have?” Jesus asked. “Seven,” they replied. 6 And He instructed the crowd to sit down on the ground. Then He took the seven loaves, gave thanks and broke them, and gave them to His disciples to set before the people. And they distributed them to the crowd. 7 They also had a few small fish, and Jesus blessed them and ordered that these be set before them as well. 8 The people ate and were satisfied, and the disciples picked up seven basketfuls of broken pieces that were left over. 9 And about four thousand men were present. And when Jesus had dismissed the crowd, 10 He immediately got into the boat with His disciples and went to the district of Dalmanutha.
paragraphs: 1 In those days the crowd once again became very large, and they had nothing to eat. Jesus called the disciples to Him and said, 2 “I have compassion for this crowd, because they have already been with Me three days and have nothing to eat. 3 If I send them home hungry, they will faint along the way. For some of them have come a great distance.” 4 His disciples replied, “Where in this desolate place could anyone find enough bread to feed all these people?” 5 “How many loaves do you have?” Jesus asked. “Seven,” they replied.

6 And He instructed the crowd to sit down on the ground. Then He took the seven loaves, gave thanks and broke them, and gave them to His disciples to set before the people. And they distributed them to the crowd. 7 They also had a few small fish, and Jesus blessed them and ordered that these be set before them as well. 8 The people ate and were satisfied, and the disciples picked up seven basketfuls of broken pieces that were left over. 9 And about four thousand men were present. And when Jesus had dismissed the crowd, 10 He immediately got into the boat with His disciples and went to the district of Dalmanutha.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Another large crowd has been with Jesus for three days and has nothing to eat. He takes the initiative, telling the disciples that He has compassion for them and does not want them to collapse on their way home. Some have traveled a great distance.

The disciples ask where enough food could be found in this desolate place. Jesus asks how many loaves they have: seven. He gives thanks, breaks the bread, and has the disciples distribute it, along with a few small fish. About four thousand men eat and are satisfied, with seven baskets of leftovers.

This follows Jesus' travel through the Decapolis in Mark 7:31. That setting helps explain why readers connect the meal with His help reaching beyond His own people, although Mark does not identify every person in the crowd as Gentile.

The basket word here is σπυρίς (spyris, spoo-REES), a woven basket or hamper. Mark uses a different basket word in the earlier feeding. The change is a real detail in the accounts, but the word itself does not establish the crowd's ethnicity or explain the meaning of the number seven.

Mark presents this separately from the feeding of the five thousand. Jesus later recalls both meals and their different quantities in Mark 8:19–20. After dismissing this crowd, He and the disciples travel by boat to Dalmanutha.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly see Jesus' compassion, His power to provide, and the disciples' continuing need to depend on Him. Wesley on Mark 8:8 also connects the provision of bread with the life people receive from Christ.

Commentators differ over how the two feeding accounts arose. Calvin's discussion of the second feeding treats it as a further miracle; the USCCB note on Mark 8:1–10 reports the view that the accounts developed from two traditions about one event. That is a discussion of the accounts' history in an explanatory note, not a binding Catholic ruling on how many feedings occurred.
passages.god_plan_html:
The generous meal fits a wider picture of God's provision and welcome. Isaiah 25:6–9 describes a banquet for all peoples and God's victory over death and tears. Jesus later speaks of people coming from every direction to the table in God's kingdom (Luke 13:28–30). These provide a supported parallel to a meal that meets the needs of a crowd beyond Jesus' usual Galilean setting; Mark does not declare every detail of Isaiah's vision completed here.

The broader purpose is stated plainly in Romans 15:7–13: Christ confirms God's promises to Israel, and Gentiles glorify God for mercy. Reading this meal after the Syrophoenician woman's request and the Decapolis healing helps us follow that growing picture of His generosity. His mission reaches people the disciples must learn to welcome and serve.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 8:11-13
passages.section_title: The Demand for a Sign

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 Then the Pharisees came and began to argue with Jesus, testing Him by demanding from Him a sign from heaven. 12 Jesus sighed deeply in His spirit and said, “Why does this generation demand a sign? Truly I tell you, no sign will be given to this generation.” 13 And He left them, got back into the boat, and crossed to the other side.
paragraphs: 11 Then the Pharisees came and began to argue with Jesus, testing Him by demanding from Him a sign from heaven. 12 Jesus sighed deeply in His spirit and said, “Why does this generation demand a sign? Truly I tell you, no sign will be given to this generation.” 13 And He left them, got back into the boat, and crossed to the other side.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the feeding, Pharisees approach Jesus and demand a sign from heaven to test Him. Mark describes a confrontation rather than a request from someone simply seeking help. The works already narrated give this demand its setting.

Jesus sighs deeply and refuses the demand. He asks why this generation seeks a sign, states that none will be given to it, and leaves by boat. Mark does not name a particular heavenly spectacle they want Him to perform.

The parallel Matthew 16:1–4 includes Sadducees and records an exception concerning the sign of Jonah. Mark's account contains the refusal without that exception. Keeping each account's wording visible helps us hear Mark's emphasis rather than silently adding Matthew's sentences to it.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand Jesus to be refusing a hostile test, rather than condemning every honest question or denying that His works reveal who He is. Calvin on Mark 8:11–13 emphasizes resistance despite what has already been shown, while the USCCB note explains that a sign on the challengers' terms will not be supplied.
passages.god_plan_html:
The wider Gospel accounts point the sign question toward Jesus' death and resurrection. In Matthew 16:4, the parallel refusal names Jonah; Matthew 12:38–42 records Jesus connecting Jonah's three days with what the Son of Man will undergo. The call is also to respond to the One greater than Jonah. This connection comes from Jesus' teaching in Matthew, while Mark leaves the demand here with a refusal.

Within Mark itself, the chapter soon moves toward Jesus' declaration that He must suffer, die, and rise again (Mark 8:31). God's saving purpose unfolds through that path, rather than through Jesus performing whatever proof His opponents demand.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 8:14-21
passages.section_title: Remembering the Bread, Missing the Meaning

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 Now the disciples had forgotten to take bread, except for one loaf they had with them in the boat. 15 “Watch out!” He cautioned them. “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod.” 16 So they began to discuss with one another the fact that they had no bread. 17 Aware of their conversation, Jesus asked them, “Why are you debating about having no bread? Do you still not see or understand? Do you have such hard hearts? 18 ‘Having eyes, do you not see? And having ears, do you not hear?’ And do you not remember? 19 When I broke the five loaves for the five thousand, how many basketfuls of broken pieces did you collect?” “Twelve,” they answered. 20 “And when I broke the seven loaves for the four thousand, how many basketfuls of broken pieces did you collect?” “Seven,” they said. 21 Then He asked them, “Do you still not understand?”
paragraphs: 14 Now the disciples had forgotten to take bread, except for one loaf they had with them in the boat. 15 “Watch out!” He cautioned them. “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod.” 16 So they began to discuss with one another the fact that they had no bread. 17 Aware of their conversation, Jesus asked them, “Why are you debating about having no bread? Do you still not see or understand? Do you have such hard hearts? 18 ‘Having eyes, do you not see? And having ears, do you not hear?’ And do you not remember?

19 When I broke the five loaves for the five thousand, how many basketfuls of broken pieces did you collect?” “Twelve,” they answered. 20 “And when I broke the seven loaves for the four thousand, how many basketfuls of broken pieces did you collect?” “Seven,” they said. 21 Then He asked them, “Do you still not understand?”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
In the boat, the disciples have only one loaf because they forgot to bring bread. Jesus warns them about the leaven of the Pharisees and Herod, but their discussion stays on their lack of food. They hear a warning and mistake its subject.

Leaven is the small amount worked into dough that affects the batch. The Greek word ζύμη (zyme, DZOO-may) can describe an influence spreading through something; the context determines whether the picture is good or bad. Here Jesus warns against an influence they need to resist.

The surrounding accounts help explain the danger. The Pharisees have just demanded a sign to test Jesus. Herod's treatment of John in Mark 6:17–29 shows respect for a righteous man giving way to pressure and a deadly decision. Jesus is warning His own disciples, so they should not assume that being near Him makes them immune to wrong responses.

He presses them with questions about understanding, hardened hearts, seeing, hearing, and remembering. They can recall twelve baskets from the first feeding and seven from the second. Yet correct answers about the quantities have not become a clear grasp of what His works mean.

Matthew 16:5–12 explicitly identifies the leaven there as teaching. Luke 12:1, in another setting, identifies the Pharisees' leaven as hypocrisy. These passages help explain the picture; Mark's exchange ends with Jesus' unanswered question about whether the disciples understand.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly take the leaven as a warning about corrupting influence, rather than a prohibition about the bread the disciples may eat. Calvin on this passage connects it with teaching that draws people away from God's word; Wesley on verses 17–18 stresses that the disciples' present failure to understand does not by itself declare them finally rejected.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus' words about eyes and ears recall the warnings in Jeremiah 5:20–25 and Ezekiel 12:1–3. God's people can have the ability to see and hear while resisting what He shows them. This scriptural parallel gives weight to the disciples' failure: receiving evidence is meant to lead to a response, not merely to remembering details.

The leaven picture also appears in 1 Corinthians 5:6–8. Paul connects Christ's sacrifice as the Passover lamb with a shared life of sincerity and truth rather than malice and wickedness. The parallel extends Jesus' warning beyond the boat to the life of a community shaped by what Christ has done.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 8:22-26
passages.section_title: From Blurred Sight to Seeing Clearly

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 When they arrived at Bethsaida, some people brought a blind man and begged Jesus to touch him. 23 So He took the blind man by the hand and led him out of the village. Then He spit on the man’s eyes and placed His hands on him. “Can you see anything?” He asked. 24 The man looked up and said, “I can see the people, but they look like trees walking around.” 25 Once again Jesus placed His hands on the man’s eyes, and when he opened them his sight was restored, and he could see everything clearly. 26 Jesus sent him home and said, “Do not go back into the village.”
paragraphs: 22 When they arrived at Bethsaida, some people brought a blind man and begged Jesus to touch him. 23 So He took the blind man by the hand and led him out of the village. Then He spit on the man’s eyes and placed His hands on him. “Can you see anything?” He asked. 24 The man looked up and said, “I can see the people, but they look like trees walking around.” 25 Once again Jesus placed His hands on the man’s eyes, and when he opened them his sight was restored, and he could see everything clearly. 26 Jesus sent him home and said, “Do not go back into the village.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
At Bethsaida, people bring a blind man to Jesus and ask Him to touch him. Jesus takes him by the hand and leads him out of the village. As in the healing of the man with hearing and speech difficulties, He gives personal attention away from the crowd.

After Jesus spits on his eyes and places His hands on him, the man can see people but cannot see them clearly: they look like trees walking around. Jesus places His hands on his eyes again, and his sight becomes clear. Mark deliberately records both stages of the recovery rather than describing an immediate complete cure.

Jesus sends him home with an instruction not to return to the village. The passage does not state why He chooses this setting or this manner of healing. The BSB footnote records a longer instruction in other manuscripts; the Scripture above follows the BSB's main text.

The setting in the chapter matters. Just before this, Jesus asks disciples who have eyes why they do not see. Just after it, Peter identifies Him as the Christ but resists His teaching about suffering and death (Mark 8:27–33). That sequence helps explain why readers connect the man's growing sight with the disciples' growing understanding.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings recognize the unusual two-stage healing while differing in emphasis about its purpose. Calvin on Mark 8:22–26 emphasizes Jesus' freedom to heal in different ways; the USCCB note reports a reading in which the gradual recovery pictures the disciples' gradual recognition of His identity. These are explanations of the narrative, not a fixed medical or spiritual procedure the passage commands.
passages.god_plan_html:
Restored sight recalls Isaiah 35:4–6, where God's coming to save includes opened eyes. Jesus points to restored sight among the works that answer the question of whether He is the expected One (Matthew 11:2–6). This healing belongs to that wider picture of His saving work.

The disciples' understanding also has a future. After His resurrection, Jesus opens their minds to understand Scripture and explains His suffering, resurrection, and the proclamation of repentance and forgiveness to the nations (Luke 24:44–49). That later account gives a supported parallel to movement from partial sight toward clarity. It does not turn each touch here into a required stage that every person's faith must follow.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 8:27-30
passages.section_title: Who Do You Say Jesus Is?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 27 Then Jesus and His disciples went on to the villages around Caesarea Philippi. On the way, He questioned His disciples: “Who do people say I am?” 28 They replied, “Some say John the Baptist; others say Elijah; and still others, one of the prophets.” 29 “But what about you?” Jesus asked. “Who do you say I am?” Peter answered, “You are the Christ.” 30 And Jesus warned them not to tell anyone about Him.
paragraphs: 27 Then Jesus and His disciples went on to the villages around Caesarea Philippi. On the way, He questioned His disciples: “Who do people say I am?” 28 They replied, “Some say John the Baptist; others say Elijah; and still others, one of the prophets.” 29 “But what about you?” Jesus asked. “Who do you say I am?” Peter answered, “You are the Christ.” 30 And Jesus warned them not to tell anyone about Him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
On the way to the villages around Caesarea Philippi, Jesus asks His disciples what people are saying about Him. They repeat explanations already heard in Mark 6:14–16: John the Baptist, Elijah, or one of the prophets. Those answers recognize something remarkable but do not reach Peter's confession.

Jesus then puts the question directly to the disciples. Peter identifies Him as the Christ. The title χριστός (Christos, khris-TOSS) means anointed and is used for the promised Messiah. Peter is naming who Jesus is, not supplying a family surname.

Jesus warns them not to tell anyone about Him. The following verses immediately show why the title still needs explanation: Peter resists the announcement that this Messiah must suffer, be killed, and rise again. Correctly naming Jesus has not yet brought full understanding of His mission.

Matthew 16:13–20 records a fuller confession and Jesus' reply about the Father's revelation, Peter, and the church. Mark concentrates on the direct question, Peter's answer, and the instruction to keep silent. The debate about Matthew's rock saying belongs with that fuller passage.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand Peter's confession as a turning point: Jesus is the promised Messiah, and the disciples must now learn what His mission involves. Calvin on this confession emphasizes what the title includes in God's saving work; the USCCB note on Mark 8:27–30 likewise treats this as a turning point whose meaning must be understood beyond popular expectations.
passages.god_plan_html:
The identity confessed here will be joined to Jesus' suffering and glory. When later asked whether He is the Christ, Jesus answers by speaking of the Son of Man at God's right hand and coming with the clouds (Mark 14:61–62). That language draws on the figure receiving lasting dominion in Daniel 7:13–14. Mark's story develops what the confession means through Jesus' own words and the path He takes.

After the resurrection, Peter announces that the crucified Jesus has been raised and exalted and is Lord and Christ (Acts 2:32–36). The early confession leads toward that fuller public witness. Jesus' identity cannot be separated from His death, resurrection, and reign.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 8:31-33
passages.section_title: The Messiah Must Suffer and Rise

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 31 Then He began to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders, chief priests, and scribes, and that He must be killed and after three days rise again. 32 He spoke this message quite frankly, and Peter took Him aside and began to rebuke Him. 33 But Jesus, turning and looking at His disciples, rebuked Peter and said, “Get behind Me, Satan! For you do not have in mind the things of God, but the things of men.”
paragraphs: 31 Then He began to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders, chief priests, and scribes, and that He must be killed and after three days rise again. 32 He spoke this message quite frankly, and Peter took Him aside and began to rebuke Him. 33 But Jesus, turning and looking at His disciples, rebuked Peter and said, “Get behind Me, Satan! For you do not have in mind the things of God, but the things of men.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Immediately after Peter's confession, Jesus begins to explain His coming suffering. He names rejection by elders, chief priests, and scribes, His death, and His rising after three days. Mark says He speaks frankly. The announcement includes both the cost and what follows it.

Peter takes Jesus aside and rebukes Him. Jesus then turns, looks at His disciples, and rebukes Peter in return. The person who has just named Him as the Christ now opposes the path He says He must take.

Jesus addresses Peter as Satan and gives the reason: Peter has human concerns in mind rather than God's. The rebuke exposes how Peter's response stands against Jesus' mission. The passage does not diagnose Peter as possessed or say that he has literally become Satan.

This is the first of several plain announcements of suffering and resurrection in Mark. It also prepares for Jesus' next words to the crowd about denying oneself, taking up a cross, and following Him. The disciple's path is being explained in relation to the Messiah's own.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see Peter's rebuke as resistance to a suffering Messiah and Jesus' answer as a forceful rejection of that resistance. Calvin on Mark 8:31–33 explains that even zeal for Jesus can oppose His calling when it refuses the cross; Wesley's note on verse 32 emphasizes how directly Jesus now states what He will undergo.
passages.god_plan_html:
The suffering has a saving purpose. Isaiah 53:10–12 describes the Servant pouring out His life and bearing the sins of many. 1 Peter 2:21–25 applies the language of that passage to Christ, who bears sins in His body and brings people back to their Shepherd. Jesus later states His purpose in Mark as giving His life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). His death is part of His mission, not its defeat.

Acts 2:22–24 holds together God's set purpose, the responsibility of those who kill Jesus, and God's raising Him from death. That wider account helps explain the necessity announced here without excusing the rejection or leaving the story at the cross.
passages.current_position_html: In What Does Prayer Look Like?, we draw on the parallel announcement in Matthew 16:21 when considering Jesus' later prayer in Gethsemane. He already knows the path before Him, yet its cost remains real. The study emphasizes honest prayer governed by surrender to the Father's will. Knowing God's purpose does not make obedience painless.

passages.title: Mark 8:34-38
passages.section_title: Following Jesus When It Costs

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 34 Then Jesus called the crowd to Him along with His disciples, and He told them, “If anyone wants to come after Me, he must deny himself and take up his cross and follow Me. 35 For whoever wants to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for My sake and for the gospel will save it. 36 What does it profit a man to gain the whole world, yet forfeit his soul? 37 Or what can a man give in exchange for his soul? 38 If anyone is ashamed of Me and My words in this adulterous and sinful generation, the Son of Man will also be ashamed of him when He comes in His Father’s glory with the holy angels.”
paragraphs: 34 Then Jesus called the crowd to Him along with His disciples, and He told them, “If anyone wants to come after Me, he must deny himself and take up his cross and follow Me. 35 For whoever wants to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for My sake and for the gospel will save it.

36 What does it profit a man to gain the whole world, yet forfeit his soul? 37 Or what can a man give in exchange for his soul? 38 If anyone is ashamed of Me and My words in this adulterous and sinful generation, the Son of Man will also be ashamed of him when He comes in His Father’s glory with the holy angels.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus calls the crowd alongside His disciples, so this teaching reaches beyond Peter or the Twelve. It follows His announcement of suffering, death, and resurrection. He now describes what it means for someone to come after Him: deny oneself, take up a cross, and follow.

The cross is a severe image. Mark 15:21–24 later narrates a cross being carried on the way to Jesus' crucifixion. In this call, loyalty to Jesus and the gospel can cost security, standing, and even life. The issue is how a person responds when following Him carries a price.

Jesus then turns ordinary ideas of gain and loss upside down. A person can preserve what seems most valuable now and lose what matters most, or lose life for His sake and the gospel and save it. Possessing the whole world cannot pay for the life forfeited in the exchange.

The same Greek noun, ψυχή (psyche, psoo-KHAY), appears where the BSB uses life in verse 35 and soul in verses 36–37. Its range includes life and the person or soul; the connection makes Jesus' questions one joined warning. The word alone does not settle every dispute about salvation and rewards.

The final warning looks toward the Son of Man's coming in His Father's glory with the angels. Shame about Jesus and His words is set against His response then. The teaching asks hearers to weigh present acceptance against their relationship to Him and the future He announces.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians agree that this is a serious call to costly loyalty. They differ over how the warning about saving or losing life relates to salvation and rewards.

In Reformed teaching, the Westminster Confession, 11.2, and the 1689 Baptist Confession, 11.2, teach that a person is put right with God through faith alone, and that this is a living faith that works through love. Calvin's reading of this passage connects losing earthly life for Christ with eternal life. Those confessions do not present obedience as the price paid to earn acceptance by God.

The Catholic Catechism, 1816, says disciples must live their faith, confess Christ, and follow the way of the cross. It describes service and witness to faith as necessary for salvation. The Catholic USCCB note on Mark 8:34–35 reads loyalty to Christ, even through death, in relation to fullness of life, and life spent denying Him in relation to destruction.

Wesley on Mark 8:34 describes self-denial as continually yielding to God's will, including when it is painful. The Methodist Articles of Religion, XII, teach that believers can depart from grace and, through God's grace, return. This framework differs from readings that hold salvation secure while addressing a believer's future rewards.

Some Free Grace teachers make a different distinction. In the Grace Evangelical Society's discussion of Mark 8:34–38, the warning concerns believers' discipleship, future reward, and honor rather than obtaining or losing eternal salvation. This is an identifiable reading within that movement, not a position shared by every evangelical or Baptist.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus' call follows the pattern of His own self-giving. Philippians 2:5–11 calls believers to His way of thinking, then describes His humility, obedience to death on a cross, and exaltation by God. The connection between suffering and glory gives a larger setting for the cost and future Jesus places before His hearers.

2 Timothy 1:8–12 joins the same themes: do not be ashamed, share in suffering for the gospel, and trust the Savior who has defeated death. It also describes salvation as God's purpose and grace rather than the result of our works. Paul's willingness to count loss for the sake of knowing Christ in Philippians 3:7–11 shows that this call became part of the lived witness of the early church.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 9:1-8
passages.section_title: The Son Revealed in Glory

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then Jesus said to them, “Truly I tell you, there are some standing here who will not taste death before they see the kingdom of God arrive with power.” 2 After six days Jesus took with Him Peter, James, and John, and led them up a high mountain by themselves. There He was transfigured before them. 3 His clothes became radiantly white, brighter than any launderer on earth could bleach them. 4 And Elijah and Moses appeared before them, talking with Jesus. 5 Peter said to Jesus, “Rabbi, it is good for us to be here. Let us put up three shelters—one for You, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.” 6 For they were all so terrified that Peter did not know what else to say. 7 Then a cloud appeared and enveloped them, and a voice came from the cloud: “This is My beloved Son. Listen to Him!” 8 Suddenly, when they looked around, they saw no one with them except Jesus.
paragraphs: 1 Then Jesus said to them, “Truly I tell you, there are some standing here who will not taste death before they see the kingdom of God arrive with power.” 2 After six days Jesus took with Him Peter, James, and John, and led them up a high mountain by themselves. There He was transfigured before them. 3 His clothes became radiantly white, brighter than any launderer on earth could bleach them.

4 And Elijah and Moses appeared before them, talking with Jesus. 5 Peter said to Jesus, “Rabbi, it is good for us to be here. Let us put up three shelters—one for You, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.” 6 For they were all so terrified that Peter did not know what else to say. 7 Then a cloud appeared and enveloped them, and a voice came from the cloud: “This is My beloved Son. Listen to Him!” 8 Suddenly, when they looked around, they saw no one with them except Jesus.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
This scene follows Jesus' announcement of suffering and His call to follow Him at real cost. He promises that some standing there will see God's kingdom arrive with power. Six days later He takes Peter, James, and John up a high mountain, where His appearance changes before them.

His clothes become brilliantly white, beyond anything an earthly launderer could produce. Moses and Elijah appear and speak with Him. Mark names the men but does not identify the mountain or explain how the disciples recognize them.

Peter proposes three shelters, one for each of them. Mark explains that the disciples are terrified and Peter does not know what to say. The text gives us that explanation without revealing a detailed plan Peter has worked out about a feast or the kingdom's timing.

A cloud envelops them, and the heavenly voice identifies Jesus as the beloved Son and commands them to listen to Him. Then they see Jesus alone. The direction to listen matters especially after Peter has resisted what Jesus said about suffering and death.

The parallel Luke 9:28–36 adds that Jesus is praying and that Moses and Elijah discuss His departure at Jerusalem. Matthew 17:1–8 also describes His shining face and His reassuring the terrified disciples. Those fuller details belong to the parallel accounts.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly see the transfiguration as a revelation of the Son's glory, joined to the suffering He has announced. The Catholic Compendium of the Catechism, 110, describes glory coming through the cross and a preview of His resurrection and glorious return.

Interpreters differ over the particular event promised in verse 1. Scofield's note on Mark 9:1, with its reference to Matthew 17:2, connects it with the mountain scene as a preview of the kingdom. Wesley on Mark 9:1 points to the kingdom's power at Pentecost.

The USCCB note on verse 1 reports both the Church's establishment in power and an expectation of Jesus' near return, favoring the latter as an explanation of the saying. These are differing commentary readings of the promise; that note is not a binding Catholic ruling that excludes every other interpretation.
passages.god_plan_html:
Luke's account makes the connection with Jesus' mission explicit: Moses and Elijah speak about His departure, to be accomplished at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31). The word is ἔξοδος (exodos, EK-soh-dos), meaning departure and used here for the end He will meet. With Moses present, it invites a parallel with Israel's departure from Egypt in Exodus 12:31–42. The parallel is supported by Paul's explicit identification of Christ as the Passover lamb in 1 Corinthians 5:7; the word by itself does not explain every part of the scene.

The command to listen also recalls Deuteronomy 18:15–19, where Moses speaks of the coming prophet whom God's people must hear. Acts 3:18–26 applies that promise to Jesus. Hebrews 1:1–3 joins God's earlier speech through prophets with His final speech through the Son, who reveals His glory and provides purification for sins.

2 Peter 1:16–18 directly recalls the mountain and the heavenly voice when speaking of Jesus' majesty and coming. This is the New Testament's own connection: the disciples' glimpse of glory belongs to the witness about the One who suffers, rises, and will come in power.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 9:9-13
passages.section_title: Elijah, John, and the Suffering Messiah

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 As they were coming down the mountain, Jesus admonished them not to tell anyone what they had seen until the Son of Man had risen from the dead. 10 So they kept this matter to themselves, discussing what it meant to rise from the dead. 11 And they asked Jesus, “Why do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?” 12 He replied, “Elijah does indeed come first, and he restores all things. Why then is it written that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected? 13 But I tell you that Elijah has indeed come, and they have done to him whatever they wished, just as it is written about him.”
paragraphs: 9 As they were coming down the mountain, Jesus admonished them not to tell anyone what they had seen until the Son of Man had risen from the dead. 10 So they kept this matter to themselves, discussing what it meant to rise from the dead.

11 And they asked Jesus, “Why do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?” 12 He replied, “Elijah does indeed come first, and he restores all things. Why then is it written that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected? 13 But I tell you that Elijah has indeed come, and they have done to him whatever they wished, just as it is written about him.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
As they descend the mountain, Jesus tells the three disciples to keep what they have seen private until the Son of Man has risen from the dead. They obey but discuss among themselves what rising from the dead means. Seeing His glory has not yet removed their difficulty with the path He describes.

They ask about the scribes' teaching that Elijah must come first. The expectation has a scriptural basis in Malachi 4:5–6, which promises Elijah before the great Day of the LORD, turning hearts within God's people. They have also just seen Elijah on the mountain.

Jesus affirms Elijah's coming and restoring work, then asks how Scripture also speaks of the Son of Man's suffering and rejection. He says Elijah has already come and been treated as people wished. The parallel Matthew 17:9–13 explicitly says the disciples understand Him to mean John the Baptist.

Luke 1:13–17 describes John coming in Elijah's spirit and power to prepare people for the Lord. John 1:19–23 also records John's denial that he is Elijah. Those statements distinguish a shared prophetic role from John being the same person returned to earth.

The treatment of John has already been narrated in Mark 6:17–29. Jesus brings that rejected messenger into the discussion of His own coming suffering. Restoration and glory must be understood alongside what God's messengers, and the Son Himself, undergo.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian interpreters recognize the connection between John and Elijah while differing over whether another personal coming of Elijah is still expected. Calvin on Mark 9:9–13 understands Malachi's promise as fulfilled in John's preparing work; the USCCB note likewise explains Elijah's coming here through John the Baptist.

In the dispensational Scofield notes on Matthew 17:10–13, John fulfills an Elijah-like ministry before Jesus' first coming, while a future ministry of Elijah remains expected. This is a particular prophetic reading, rather than something every Protestant, evangelical, or Baptist teaches. The shared identification of John in the present exchange should be distinguished from that further question about the future.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus makes the larger connection Himself: the promise of restoration does not remove what Scripture says about the Son of Man's suffering. John prepares His way and suffers rejection; Jesus then takes the path He has announced. The glory witnessed on the mountain cannot be separated from that mission.

After His resurrection, Jesus again joins Moses and the Prophets with the necessity of the Christ's suffering and His entrance into glory (Luke 24:25–27). 1 Peter 1:10–12 describes the prophets searching into the sufferings of Christ and the glories to follow, now announced through the gospel. The disciples' question sits within that wider movement from promise toward understanding what God accomplishes through His Son.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 9:14-29
passages.section_title: Help My Unbelief

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 When they returned to the other disciples, they saw a large crowd around them, and scribes arguing with them. 15 As soon as all the people saw Jesus, they were filled with awe and ran to greet Him. 16 “What are you disputing with them?” He asked. 17 Someone in the crowd replied, “Teacher, I brought You my son, who has a spirit that makes him mute. 18 Whenever it seizes him, it throws him to the ground. He foams at the mouth, gnashes his teeth, and becomes rigid. I asked Your disciples to drive it out, but they were unable.” 19 “O unbelieving generation!” Jesus replied. “How long must I remain with you? How long must I put up with you? Bring the boy to Me.” 20 So they brought him, and seeing Jesus, the spirit immediately threw the boy into a convulsion. He fell to the ground and rolled around, foaming at the mouth. 21 Jesus asked the boy’s father, “How long has this been with him?” “From childhood,” he said. 22 “It often throws him into the fire or into the water, trying to kill him. But if You can do anything, have compassion on us and help us.” 23 “If You can?” echoed Jesus. “All things are possible to him who believes!” 24 Immediately the boy’s father cried out, “I do believe; help my unbelief!” 25 When Jesus saw that a crowd had come running, He rebuked the unclean spirit. “You deaf and mute spirit,” He said, “I command you to come out and never enter him again.” 26 After shrieking and convulsing him violently, the spirit came out. The boy became like a corpse, so that many said, “He is dead.” 27 But Jesus took him by the hand and helped him to his feet, and he stood up. 28 After Jesus had gone into the house, His disciples asked Him privately, “Why couldn’t we drive it out?” 29 Jesus answered, “This kind cannot come out, except by prayer.”

He foams at the mouth, gnashes his teeth, and becomes rigid. I asked Your disciples to drive it out, but they were unable.” 19 “O unbelieving generation!” Jesus replied. “How long must I remain with you? How long must I put up with you? Bring the boy to Me.”

20 So they brought him, and seeing Jesus, the spirit immediately threw the boy into a convulsion. He fell to the ground and rolled around, foaming at the mouth. 21 Jesus asked the boy’s father, “How long has this been with him?” “From childhood,” he said. 22 “It often throws him into the fire or into the water, trying to kill him. But if You can do anything, have compassion on us and help us.” 23 “If You can?” echoed Jesus. “All things are possible to him who believes!” 24 Immediately the boy’s father cried out, “I do believe; help my unbelief!”

25 When Jesus saw that a crowd had come running, He rebuked the unclean spirit. “You deaf and mute spirit,” He said, “I command you to come out and never enter him again.” 26 After shrieking and convulsing him violently, the spirit came out. The boy became like a corpse, so that many said, “He is dead.” 27 But Jesus took him by the hand and helped him to his feet, and he stood up. 28 After Jesus had gone into the house, His disciples asked Him privately, “Why couldn’t we drive it out?” 29 Jesus answered, “This kind cannot come out, except by prayer.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus and the three return to find a crowd and scribes disputing with the other disciples. A father explains that he brought his son, who is tormented by a spirit that makes him unable to speak. The disciples have been unable to drive it out, although they had previously been given authority over unclean spirits in Mark 6:7–13.

When the boy is brought to Jesus, the spirit throws him into a convulsion. His father says this has happened since childhood and describes repeated attempts to destroy him in fire or water. The father's request includes doubt about what Jesus can do. Jesus answers that doubt, and the father openly asks for help with his unbelief.

Jesus commands the spirit to leave and never return. After a violent departure, the boy lies so still that many think he is dead. Jesus takes his hand and helps him stand. Mark reports what the onlookers say, without declaring that the boy actually died.

In private, the disciples ask why they could not drive the spirit out. Jesus directs them to prayer. Their earlier experience does not remove their need to depend on God now. The father also comes with dependence rather than a claim to flawless confidence: he asks for the help he needs, including help with his faith.

The BSB footnote to verse 29 records manuscripts that add fasting. The Scripture above follows its main text, which names prayer. The passage does not give a detailed ranking of spirits or a set of ritual steps for readers to reproduce.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly emphasize reliance on Jesus and God rather than confidence in the disciples' own ability. Calvin on Mark 9:24 recognizes real faith alongside remaining unbelief, while the USCCB notes on verses 14–29 explain prayer as conscious reliance on God's power.
passages.god_plan_html: This deliverance belongs to the wider work of the Son against what destroys people. 1 John 3:8 states that He was revealed to destroy the devil's works. Hebrews 2:14–18 carries that purpose through His own humanity, suffering, and death: He breaks the devil's hold and frees people enslaved by fear of death. The rescue of this child offers a concrete picture of His power to help, while the larger victory comes through the mission He has just announced.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 9:30-32
passages.section_title: The Disciples Still Do Not Understand

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 30 Going on from there, they passed through Galilee. But Jesus did not want anyone to know, 31 because He was teaching His disciples. He told them, “The Son of Man will be delivered into the hands of men. They will kill Him, and after three days He will rise.” 32 But they did not understand this statement, and they were afraid to ask Him about it.
paragraphs: 30 Going on from there, they passed through Galilee. But Jesus did not want anyone to know, 31 because He was teaching His disciples. He told them, “The Son of Man will be delivered into the hands of men. They will kill Him, and after three days He will rise.” 32 But they did not understand this statement, and they were afraid to ask Him about it.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus and His disciples pass through Galilee, and He seeks privacy because He is teaching them. He repeats what He said after Peter's confession: the Son of Man will be handed over, killed, and raised after three days. The coming death continues to shape the instruction He gives them.

The expression about being delivered uses παραδίδωμι (paradidomi, pah-rah-DEE-doh-mee), meaning to hand over or give into another's power. The word can describe betrayal or delivery into custody; its meaning alone does not identify every person involved or explain all of God's purpose in the event.

The disciples do not understand and are afraid to ask. Mark tells us both things but does not state exactly why they are afraid. This leaves a striking contrast between Jesus' clear announcement and their difficulty receiving it.

The announcement is the second of three concentrated predictions in this part of Mark: 8:31, here, and 10:33–34. The next scene, in which the disciples dispute their greatness, further exposes the distance between His path and their concerns.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand this as Jesus preparing the disciples for His death and resurrection while their understanding remains incomplete. Calvin's discussion of this announcement and Wesley on Mark 9:32 connect their difficulty with expectations that do not yet make room for His suffering.
passages.god_plan_html:
The handing over, death, and resurrection become part of the church's explanation of God's saving love. Romans 8:31–34 says that the Father gives His Son for us, and that the Christ who dies is raised, exalted, and intercedes for His people. That is a later, fuller explanation of the mission being announced here; the Greek verb alone is not proof of all those connections.

Paul then speaks of confidence in Christ's love even amid trouble, persecution, and death (Romans 8:35–39). The announcement that frightens the disciples leads toward hope grounded in what God does through His Son. The suffering is real, but it does not have the last word.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 9:33-37
passages.section_title: Greatness That Serves

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 33 Then they came to Capernaum. While Jesus was in the house, He asked them, “What were you discussing on the way?” 34 But they were silent, for on the way they had been arguing about which of them was the greatest. 35 Sitting down, Jesus called the Twelve and said, “If anyone wants to be first, he must be the last of all and the servant of all.” 36 Then He had a little child stand among them. Taking the child in His arms, He said to them, 37 “Whoever welcomes one of these little children in My name welcomes Me, and whoever welcomes Me welcomes not only Me, but the One who sent Me.”
paragraphs: 33 Then they came to Capernaum. While Jesus was in the house, He asked them, “What were you discussing on the way?” 34 But they were silent, for on the way they had been arguing about which of them was the greatest. 35 Sitting down, Jesus called the Twelve and said, “If anyone wants to be first, he must be the last of all and the servant of all.”

36 Then He had a little child stand among them. Taking the child in His arms, He said to them, 37 “Whoever welcomes one of these little children in My name welcomes Me, and whoever welcomes Me welcomes not only Me, but the One who sent Me.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
In a house at Capernaum, Jesus asks what the disciples discussed along the road. They are silent because they have been disputing which of them is greatest. Their concern with standing comes immediately after His announcement that He will be handed over and killed.

Jesus sits down, calls the Twelve, and reverses the terms of their discussion: anyone wanting to be first must become last and servant of all. The word διάκονος (diakonos, dee-AH-koh-nos) describes a servant or attendant, someone who attends to another's needs. Here the emphasis is service, rather than claiming a superior place.

He then places a little child among them and takes the child into His arms. The example makes the teaching concrete: welcoming a child in His name is a way of welcoming Him, and welcoming Him reaches to the Father who sent Him.

The child is someone to receive and care for, rather than a competitor in the disciples' contest. Jesus brings their attention to a person before them. Mark does not identify whose child this is or give a complete social history of children to explain the scene.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand Jesus to redirect ambition toward humility and service. Calvin on this exchange emphasizes setting aside the desire to outrank others, while the USCCB note on Mark 9:33–37 emphasizes service to the poor and lowly illustrated through receiving the child.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus' call to serve follows His own mission. In Mark 10:42–45, He again contrasts the pursuit of power with service and explains that He gives His own life as a ransom for many. The teaching about greatness belongs with the self-giving through which He rescues people.

Philippians 2:1–11 draws that pattern into the community's life: put aside selfish ambition, attend to others' interests, and take the attitude shown by Christ in His humility and obedience to the cross. The goal reaches beyond individual modesty to people learning to live and serve together in a way shaped by Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 9:38-41
passages.section_title: Serving Beyond Our Own Circle

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 38 John said to Him, “Teacher, we saw someone else driving out demons in Your name, and we tried to stop him, because he does not accompany us.” 39 “Do not stop him,” Jesus replied. “For no one who performs a miracle in My name can turn around and speak evil of Me. 40 For whoever is not against us is for us. 41 Indeed, if anyone gives you even a cup of water because you bear the name of Christ, truly I tell you, he will never lose his reward.
paragraphs: 38 John said to Him, “Teacher, we saw someone else driving out demons in Your name, and we tried to stop him, because he does not accompany us.” 39 “Do not stop him,” Jesus replied. “For no one who performs a miracle in My name can turn around and speak evil of Me. 40 For whoever is not against us is for us. 41 Indeed, if anyone gives you even a cup of water because you bear the name of Christ, truly I tell you, he will never lose his reward.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
John tells Jesus that the disciples tried to stop someone driving out demons in His name because the man was not accompanying them. This follows the dispute about greatness and Jesus' call to welcome a child. Once again, the disciples must learn that service in His name reaches beyond their own standing.

Jesus tells them to stop interfering. Someone doing a mighty work in His name is not likely to turn around immediately and speak against Him. He then widens the picture from a dramatic deliverance to an ordinary kindness: even a cup of water given because someone belongs to Christ will be remembered by God.

The reason John gives is that the man does not accompany their group. Mark does not identify him, explain how he came to know Jesus, or describe his whole ministry. The correction addresses the disciples' attempt to exclude him on that basis.

The cup of water also brings the teaching within reach of people who have no prominent role. The act matters because it expresses care for someone who belongs to Christ. Jesus does not provide a formula for calculating rewards.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand this as a correction of jealousy and a warning against treating one's own circle as the limit of Christ's work. Wesley on Mark 9:38–40 applies it to cooperation despite differences that do not overturn the heart of the faith; the USCCB notes on this scene likewise emphasize openness toward people serving outside the disciples' group. Neither reading requires treating every belief or claimed miracle as trustworthy.
passages.god_plan_html:
A close parallel appears in Numbers 11:24–29. Eldad and Medad receive the Spirit and prophesy in the camp. They are among the registered elders, but have not gone out to the tent. Joshua asks Moses to stop them; Moses instead welcomes God's work and wishes the Spirit rested on all the LORD's people. The situations are not identical, but both expose the mistake of protecting a leader's circle at the expense of what God is doing.

1 Corinthians 12:4–27 develops the wider purpose for the church: the same Spirit gives different gifts for the common good, and the members of Christ's body need one another. God's work makes people fellow servants with different contributions. This gives the disciples' small dispute a much larger setting: learning to welcome genuine service is part of learning to live as a people gathered around Christ.

passages.title: Mark 9:42-48
passages.section_title: Taking Sin and Its Harm Seriously

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 42 But if anyone causes one of these little ones who believe in Me to stumble, it would be better for him to have a large millstone hung around his neck and to be thrown into the sea. 43 If your hand causes you to sin, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life crippled than to have two hands and go into hell, into the unquenchable fire. 45 If your foot causes you to sin, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life lame than to have two feet and be thrown into hell. 47 And if your eye causes you to sin, pluck it out. It is better for you to enter the kingdom of God with one eye than to have two eyes and be thrown into hell, 48 where ‘their worm never dies, and the fire is never quenched.’
paragraphs: 42 But if anyone causes one of these little ones who believe in Me to stumble, it would be better for him to have a large millstone hung around his neck and to be thrown into the sea. 43 If your hand causes you to sin, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life crippled than to have two hands and go into hell, into the unquenchable fire.

45 If your foot causes you to sin, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life lame than to have two feet and be thrown into hell. 47 And if your eye causes you to sin, pluck it out. It is better for you to enter the kingdom of God with one eye than to have two eyes and be thrown into hell, 48 where ‘their worm never dies, and the fire is never quenched.’

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus moves from rewarding a small kindness to warning against great harm: leading one of the little ones who believe in Him into sin. The child He welcomed and the man the disciples tried to stop remain part of the surrounding conversation. His warning protects people whom others may dismiss or hinder.

The Greek word σκανδαλίζω (skandalizo, skan-dah-LEE-zoh) means to cause someone to stumble or fall into sin. Here the concern is deeper than upsetting someone or disagreeing with them: it is helping turn them away from faithful obedience to God.

Jesus uses the terrible image of drowning under a large millstone to show how seriously He takes that harm. He then turns the warning toward the hearer's own conduct. Hand, foot, and eye describe things a person uses, pursues, or treasures that can become involved in sin. His comparisons demand decisive action, even when giving something up is painful.

The images are commonly read as forceful pictures rather than instructions to injure the body. Jesus has already located the source of evil in the heart in Mark 7:20–23. Removing a body part would not remove that source. His repeated contrast is between entering life and facing God's judgment.

The word translated hell is γέεννα (Gehenna, geh-EN-nah), a name connected with the Valley of Hinnom and used for future punishment. The valley's association with child sacrifice appears in 2 Kings 23:10. Verse 48 draws its language about worm and fire directly from Isaiah 66:24.

The BSB footnotes explain the gaps in numbering above: some manuscripts repeat the words of verse 48 as verses 44 and 46. This page follows the BSB main text, which gives the saying once at verse 48.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings generally agree that Jesus warns against leading others into sin and calls for costly action against sin in one's own life. Calvin's discussion stresses care for believers whom the world despises, while Wesley's notes apply the cutting-off imagery to relationships and things that draw a person away from God.

Where traditions differ is in how they understand the judgment described and how the warning relates to salvation. The Catholic Church teaches the reality of hell and lasting separation from God for those who die refusing repentance (Catechism 1033–1037). Reformed churches following Westminster 33.2, and Baptists following the 1689 Confession 32.2, likewise teach everlasting punishment. These statements describe the teaching of those documents, rather than every person carrying a denominational label.

Seventh-day Adventists understand the final fire as bringing the wicked to an end. Their official Fundamental Beliefs 26–27 say immortality is God's gift to the redeemed and that fire consumes the wicked. This differs from the continuing punishment described in the confessions above.

On the warning's relation to believers, Westminster 17 teaches that those truly saved will persevere, while recognizing serious sin, harm to others, and God's discipline along the way. The Catholic teaching above warns against persisting in grave sin without repentance. Within Free Grace teaching, Charlie Bing's GraceLife study of this passage reads Jesus as contrasting a disciple's costly self-denial with the unbeliever's destiny, rather than threatening a believer with losing salvation. That is an individual teacher's reading, not a statement representing all evangelicals.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus' reference reaches back to the closing vision of Isaiah 66:18–24. There God gathers people from the nations to see His glory, promises enduring new heavens and a new earth, and exposes the outcome of rebellion. Jesus places the choice between life in God's kingdom and judgment within that larger picture. The promise of restoration does not make evil or its harm unimportant.

The concern for the little ones also reappears in the church's life. In 1 Corinthians 8:9–13, Paul tells knowledgeable believers to give up a freedom rather than encourage a weaker believer into sin. His reason reaches to the cross: this is a brother for whom Christ died, and harming that brother is a sin against Christ. What Jesus warns about here becomes a concrete way of caring for people He gave His life to rescue.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 9:49-50
passages.section_title: Salt, Fire, and Peace with One Another

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 49 For everyone will be salted with fire. 50 Salt is good, but if the salt loses its saltiness, with what will you season it? Have salt among yourselves, and be at peace with one another.”
paragraphs: 49 For everyone will be salted with fire. 50 Salt is good, but if the salt loses its saltiness, with what will you season it? Have salt among yourselves, and be at peace with one another.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus closes the conversation with a short saying about everyone being salted with fire, followed by a warning about salt losing its saltiness. He ends with a direct command to have salt among themselves and live at peace with one another. This brings the conversation back to the disciples' dispute over greatness and their attempt to stop someone outside their circle.

The two images come together in Israel's offerings. Leviticus 2:1–16 describes burning a portion of the grain offering on the altar and requires salt with the offerings. Verse 13 calls it the salt of God's covenant. This provides a biblical background for reading Jesus' saying in terms of lives offered to God, although He does not explain each detail of the comparison here.

The BSB footnote to verse 49 records manuscripts that add an explicit statement about salting every sacrifice. The quotation above follows the shorter main text. The connection with Leviticus can be explored without adding the longer wording to it.

The final instruction is clear even where the imagery is debated: the disciples must retain the quality Jesus calls for and live together in peace. In the immediate setting, ambition and competition are the problems needing correction. The salt image should lead back to changed conduct toward one another, rather than becoming a puzzle detached from that concern.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
There are different readings of the fire. Calvin on Mark 9:49–50 connects the saying with offerings in Leviticus and understands believers as people purified and devoted to God through the gospel. The USCCB note on verse 49 likewise emphasizes purification and preservation in the disciples' spiritual life.

Wesley takes the first fire as the continuing judgment just described, contrasting it with the grace that prepares believers as acceptable offerings. Within Free Grace teaching, Charlie Bing instead connects the fire with judgment of everyone's works, with different outcomes for believers and unbelievers. These are commentary readings, rather than official rulings binding every member of a tradition. Despite their differences, they bring verse 50 back to lives shaped by God and peace within the community.
passages.god_plan_html:
The offering background has a wider parallel in Romans 12:1–5. Because of God's mercy, believers are to offer their bodies as living sacrifices, let their minds be renewed, put pride aside, and recognize that they belong to one another in Christ. This does not settle every detail of Mark's fire image, but it shows how devotion to God and life together belong to the same calling.

Another biblical comparison is 1 Peter 1:3–9: people given new birth through Christ's resurrection may suffer trials in which faith is tested like gold by fire. That is a supported parallel for the refining reading of this saying, rather than a claim that Peter is explaining Mark 9:49 directly.

Jesus later makes love for one another a mark by which His disciples will be recognized (John 13:34–35). The peace urged here serves that larger purpose: people shaped by His self-giving love are to make that love visible in their life together.

passages.title: Mark 10:1-12
passages.section_title: Marriage and the Creator’s Purpose

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then Jesus left that place and went into the region of Judea, beyond the Jordan. Again the crowds came to Him and He taught them, as was His custom. 2 Some Pharisees came to test Him. “Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife?” they inquired. 3 “What did Moses command you?” He replied. 4 They answered, “Moses permitted a man to write his wife a certificate of divorce and send her away.” 5 But Jesus told them, “Moses wrote this commandment for you because of your hardness of heart. 6 However, from the beginning of creation, ‘God made them male and female.’ 7 ‘For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, 8 and the two will become one flesh.’ So they are no longer two, but one flesh. 9 Therefore what God has joined together, let man not separate.” 10 When they were back inside the house, the disciples asked Jesus about this matter. 11 So He told them, “Whoever divorces his wife and marries another woman commits adultery against her. 12 And if a woman divorces her husband and marries another man, she commits adultery.”
paragraphs: 1 Then Jesus left that place and went into the region of Judea, beyond the Jordan. Again the crowds came to Him and He taught them, as was His custom. 2 Some Pharisees came to test Him. “Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife?” they inquired. 3 “What did Moses command you?” He replied. 4 They answered, “Moses permitted a man to write his wife a certificate of divorce and send her away.” 5 But Jesus told them, “Moses wrote this commandment for you because of your hardness of heart.

6 However, from the beginning of creation, ‘God made them male and female.’ 7 ‘For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, 8 and the two will become one flesh.’ So they are no longer two, but one flesh. 9 Therefore what God has joined together, let man not separate.”

10 When they were back inside the house, the disciples asked Jesus about this matter. 11 So He told them, “Whoever divorces his wife and marries another woman commits adultery against her. 12 And if a woman divorces her husband and marries another man, she commits adultery.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus leaves the previous setting and teaches the crowds in the region of Judea beyond the Jordan. Some Pharisees test Him by asking whether a man may divorce his wife. Jesus asks them what Moses commanded, and they answer by referring to permission to give a certificate of divorce.

Deuteronomy 24:1–4 describes a divorce followed by another marriage and forbids the first husband from taking the woman back after that second marriage ends. Jesus explains the permission in relation to hard hearts, then takes His hearers further back to creation. The permission does not describe everything God intended marriage to be.

Jewish discussion of the grounds for divorce is recorded in Mishnah Gittin 9:10. It preserves a stricter reading associated with Shammai's school and a broader one associated with Hillel's, even including a spoiled meal. That recorded debate helps explain the subject's contested nature, without telling us the private motives of each person questioning Jesus here.

Jesus brings together Genesis 1:27 and 2:24: God made man and woman, and the two become one flesh. He grounds His answer in a union God establishes, rather than in ways to dismiss a spouse. His command not to separate that union expresses the seriousness of the bond.

In private, He tells the disciples that divorce followed by another marriage involves adultery against the spouse. Mark records the warning about both a husband and a wife. The account does not include Matthew's exception for sexual immorality, so that exception has not been inserted into the quotation above. Christians consider this passage alongside Matthew 19:1–9 and 1 Corinthians 7:10–16 when asking how the teaching applies.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian traditions commonly read this as a call to lasting faithfulness in marriage. They differ over how Mark's unqualified warning relates to other passages and the circumstances in which a later marriage can be accepted.

The Catholic Church teaches that a valid marriage between baptized spouses, once consummated, cannot be dissolved by human power. Its Catechism 2382–2386 distinguishes that bond from legitimate separation or a civil divorce needed to protect rights, children, or inheritance. It also distinguishes an unjustly abandoned spouse from one responsible for breaking the marriage.

Reformed churches following the Westminster Confession 24.5–6 allow an innocent spouse to divorce and remarry after adultery, and recognize deliberate desertion that cannot be remedied as another ground for ending the marriage. This reading considers Matthew's exception and Paul's teaching about an unbelieving spouse's departure alongside Mark.

The Orthodox Church in America's guidelines, section F, uphold lifelong marriage while allowing a bishop to consider remarriage after divorce with repentance and attention to the people involved. The United Methodist Social Principles, Marriage: Divorce, recognize that divorce can become necessary when a marriage is destructive or beyond repair, and do not rule out remarriage. These are the stated approaches of those churches; they do not imply that every member or other church shares every detail.
passages.god_plan_html:
The creation text Jesus uses becomes an explicit picture of Christ's relationship with His people. In Ephesians 5:25–33, Paul repeats Genesis 2:24 and connects the one-flesh union with Christ and the church. Christ gives Himself for her, makes her holy, and nourishes and cares for her as His own body. The larger purpose reaches beyond defending an institution: marriage is called to reflect faithful, self-giving love.

A related picture appears in Hosea 3:1–5, where the prophet's renewed love for an unfaithful wife is explicitly compared with the LORD's love for Israel despite their turning to other gods. That is a parallel about God's faithfulness, rather than a separate rule settling every divorce case. Together these passages show why covenant faithfulness matters within the Bible's account of God's work to reclaim His people.
