passages.title: Mark 10:13-16
passages.section_title: Receiving the Kingdom Like a Child

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 Now people were bringing the little children to Jesus for Him to place His hands on them, and the disciples rebuked those who brought them. 14 But when Jesus saw this, He was indignant and told them, “Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them! For the kingdom of God belongs to such as these. 15 Truly I tell you, anyone who does not receive the kingdom of God like a little child will never enter it.” 16 And He took the children in His arms, placed His hands on them, and blessed them.
paragraphs: 13 Now people were bringing the little children to Jesus for Him to place His hands on them, and the disciples rebuked those who brought them. 14 But when Jesus saw this, He was indignant and told them, “Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them! For the kingdom of God belongs to such as these. 15 Truly I tell you, anyone who does not receive the kingdom of God like a little child will never enter it.” 16 And He took the children in His arms, placed His hands on them, and blessed them.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
People bring little children to Jesus for Him to lay His hands on them. The disciples rebuke those who bring them, but Jesus is indignant and tells them to let the children come. He then takes the children in His arms, lays His hands on them, and blesses them.

His indignation is more than mild disappointment. The Greek verb ἀγανακτέω (aganakteo, ah-gah-nak-TEH-oh) describes strong displeasure. The disciples are hindering the very people He wants to receive. This repeats a lesson from Mark 9:33–37, where He welcomed a child after their dispute about greatness.

Jesus speaks both about the children before Him and about anyone who would enter God's kingdom. The kingdom must be received like a little child. The focus is receiving what God gives rather than claiming a place through importance or achievement; the next account, about a wealthy man seeking eternal life, brings that contrast into sharper view.

Luke 18:15–17 says people were bringing even babies. Neither account identifies all those bringing them or gives their exact ages. Mark describes a blessing, not a baptism, and does not describe each child's inner response. The welcome is concrete: Jesus receives the children the disciples were turning away.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly see both a welcome for actual children and a call to receive God's kingdom with humble dependence. Wesley on Mark 10:14–15 emphasizes receiving without a claim to personal worthiness; the USCCB note on verse 15 likewise stresses dependence and obedience to the gospel.

Traditions differ over the connection with infant baptism. Calvin's discussion of this scene sees Christ's welcome as support for including infants in baptism. The Catholic Catechism 1250–1252 teaches infant baptism as a gift of new life. The Reformed Westminster Confession 28.4 includes infants of believing parents, and the Methodist Articles XVII also retain baptism of young children. By contrast, the 1689 Baptist Confession 29.2 limits baptism to those who personally profess repentance and faith. These documents explain different practices; the scene itself narrates Jesus' welcome and blessing.
passages.god_plan_html:
The welcome fits a pattern that becomes clear in the church's life. 1 Corinthians 1:26–31 says God calls people without giving human status, power, or impressive ancestry the final say. He chooses the weak and lowly so that no one can boast before Him; Christ becomes their righteousness, holiness, and redemption. Receiving the kingdom like a child belongs within that larger story of receiving what God provides.

That purpose also shapes how His people treat others. James 1:27 places care for orphans and widows within faithful life before God. The connection does not make every child in this scene an orphan. It carries the lesson forward: a community gathered by God's grace is to make room for people who can offer it little status or advantage. Jesus' embrace teaches the disciples what that welcome looks like.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 10:17-22
passages.section_title: The Man Who Could Not Let Go

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 As Jesus started on His way, a man ran up and knelt before Him. “Good Teacher,” he asked, “what must I do to inherit eternal life?” 18 “Why do you call Me good?” Jesus replied. “No one is good except God alone. 19 You know the commandments: ‘Do not murder, do not commit adultery, do not steal, do not bear false witness, do not cheat others, honor your father and mother.’” 20 “Teacher,” he replied, “all these I have kept from my youth.” 21 Jesus looked at him, loved him, and said to him, “There is one thing you lack: Go, sell everything you own and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. Then come, follow Me.” 22 But the man was saddened by these words and went away in sorrow, because he had great wealth.
paragraphs: 17 As Jesus started on His way, a man ran up and knelt before Him. “Good Teacher,” he asked, “what must I do to inherit eternal life?” 18 “Why do you call Me good?” Jesus replied. “No one is good except God alone. 19 You know the commandments: ‘Do not murder, do not commit adultery, do not steal, do not bear false witness, do not cheat others, honor your father and mother.’” 20 “Teacher,” he replied, “all these I have kept from my youth.”

21 Jesus looked at him, loved him, and said to him, “There is one thing you lack: Go, sell everything you own and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. Then come, follow Me.” 22 But the man was saddened by these words and went away in sorrow, because he had great wealth.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
A man runs to Jesus, kneels, and asks what he must do to inherit eternal life. The encounter follows Jesus' teaching about receiving the kingdom like a child. Here someone comes with an account of commandments he has kept, yet still has a question about life with God.

Jesus asks why he calls Him good and directs attention to God as the measure of goodness. He then names commands concerning other people, including the prohibition of cheating them. The man says he has kept these from his youth. Mark reports that claim without saying that it proves a complete, sinless life.

Jesus looks at him and loves him. The costly instruction that follows belongs within that love: sell what he owns, give to the poor, receive treasure in heaven, and follow Him. The invitation reaches beyond adding another achievement to the man's record. It asks him to release what he holds and entrust his future to Jesus.

He goes away sorrowful because he has great wealth. Mark tells us his response at this encounter, not the story of everything that happens to him afterward. The next paragraph will develop the danger wealth presents and the need for God's saving power.

The familiar description of him as a rich young ruler brings together details from the related accounts. Matthew 19:16–22 calls him young; Luke 18:18–23 calls him a ruler. Neither description by itself identifies him as a member of the Sanhedrin.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly see the encounter as exposing an attachment that stands in the way of following Jesus. Wesley on Mark 10:21 connects the command with the man's love of riches and his need to love God. Jesus' love for him and the seriousness of His call belong together.

Traditions differ over how the command to sell everything relates to Christian life more generally. The Catholic Catechism 2053 connects this scene with following Christ and His call to poverty. Its account of commands and counsels, 1973–1974, distinguishes what love requires of everyone from particular ways of giving oneself more fully according to one's calling. It does not require every Christian to follow every counsel in the same form.

Reformed churches following Westminster 16.1–5 reject the idea that anyone can do more than God requires and place good works within obedience that depends on Christ's Spirit. This reading treats the man's surrender as a response to God's claim on him, rather than an extra level of obedience through which eternal life could be earned. These are differences between the cited teachings, not descriptions of every individual Catholic or Protestant.
passages.god_plan_html:
The invitation to follow Jesus leads toward the saving work He is going to accomplish in Jerusalem. 2 Corinthians 5:14–21 explains that Christ dies and rises so that people may live for Him, and that God reconciles people to Himself through Him. Becoming right with God rests on what God does through Christ, and brings a changed direction for life.

Ephesians 2:4–10 holds the same two things together: salvation is God's gift, received through faith rather than earned by works, and those made alive in Christ are created for good works. The man's question and Jesus' costly call belong within that wider account of grace creating a new life. Generosity and following Jesus are not reduced to the price of admission.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 10:23-27
passages.section_title: What Only God Can Do

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 23 Then Jesus looked around and said to His disciples, “How hard it is for the rich to enter the kingdom of God!” 24 And the disciples were amazed at His words. But Jesus said to them again, “Children, how hard it is to enter the kingdom of God! 25 It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God.” 26 They were even more astonished and said to one another, “Who then can be saved?” 27 Jesus looked at them and said, “With man this is impossible, but not with God. For all things are possible with God.”
paragraphs: 23 Then Jesus looked around and said to His disciples, “How hard it is for the rich to enter the kingdom of God!” 24 And the disciples were amazed at His words. But Jesus said to them again, “Children, how hard it is to enter the kingdom of God! 25 It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God.”

26 They were even more astonished and said to one another, “Who then can be saved?” 27 Jesus looked at them and said, “With man this is impossible, but not with God. For all things are possible with God.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the wealthy man leaves, Jesus tells the disciples how hard it is for the rich to enter God's kingdom. They are astonished, and He repeats the difficulty before describing a camel passing through the eye of a needle. Their next question shows the subject: who can be saved?

The word for needle is ῥαφίς (rhaphis, hrah-FEES), a sewing needle. The image sets a large animal against a tiny opening. Jesus brings the hearers to a human impossibility and then directs their hope to what God can do.

Verse 24 in the BSB main text speaks of the difficulty of entering God's kingdom without adding a qualification about trusting in riches. The BSB footnote records that longer wording in other manuscripts. The passage as a whole begins with wealth and reaches a question about salvation more broadly.

Jesus' answer is about God's ability to save. Its setting gives meaning to the statement that all things are possible with God. The disciples are being led beyond confidence in a person's resources to dependence on God for the life they cannot secure for themselves.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand the camel-and-needle comparison as showing that human resources cannot bring salvation and that hope must rest in God. Wesley's notes on Mark 10:24–25 emphasize the hold of trusting in riches; the USCCB notes on verses 23–27 emphasize the false security of wealth, power, and merit and God's saving gift.
passages.god_plan_html:
Titus 3:3–8 explains how God's saving ability meets human need: His kindness appears, He saves according to His mercy, and the Holy Spirit brings new birth and renewal through Jesus Christ. The result is people made right with God by grace and given the hope of eternal life. That gives substance to the hope Jesus sets before the astonished disciples.

The wider New Testament also shows what this means for wealthy believers. 1 Timothy 6:17–19 tells them to put their hope in God, become generous, and share readily. Wealth is to become a means of serving others within the life God gives. Neither having money nor giving it away can take God's place as the source of salvation.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 10:28-31
passages.section_title: A New Family, Persecution, and Life to Come

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 28 Peter began to say to Him, “Look, we have left everything and followed You.” 29 “Truly I tell you,” Jesus replied, “no one who has left home or brothers or sisters or mother or father or children or fields for My sake and for the gospel 30 will fail to receive a hundredfold in the present age—houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children and fields, along with persecutions—and in the age to come, eternal life. 31 But many who are first will be last, and the last will be first.”
paragraphs: 28 Peter began to say to Him, “Look, we have left everything and followed You.” 29 “Truly I tell you,” Jesus replied, “no one who has left home or brothers or sisters or mother or father or children or fields for My sake and for the gospel 30 will fail to receive a hundredfold in the present age—houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children and fields, along with persecutions—and in the age to come, eternal life. 31 But many who are first will be last, and the last will be first.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Peter responds that the disciples have left everything and followed Jesus. His statement stands beside the wealthy man's unwillingness to let go. Jesus answers with a promise to those who lose home, family ties, or fields for His sake and for the gospel.

The promise has two time settings. In the present age, Jesus describes multiplied homes, family relationships, and provision, together with persecutions. In the age to come, He promises eternal life. Keeping both settings in view prevents the present care and the future hope from being confused.

The family language recalls Mark 3:31–35, where Jesus identifies those who do God's will as His brother, sister, and mother. The promise makes sense within a new community that opens its homes and shares what it has, even while its members may face rejection and suffering.

The final saying about first and last challenges ordinary judgments about importance and advantage. It also keeps the disciples' own sacrifices from becoming a claim to superior standing. Following Jesus changes where they look for security and how they regard one another.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see both the cost of following Jesus and His assurance that those losses are not overlooked. Wesley on Mark 10:30 understands the multiplied return in terms of greater value and happiness, rather than an identical replacement of every possession, and keeps the accompanying persecutions in view. The promise is commonly read as abundant care and future life, rather than a guaranteed financial return for a gift or a risk-free life.
passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 2:41–47 shows a concrete expression of the new community: people gathered through the gospel devote themselves to teaching, fellowship, meals, and prayer, open their homes, and share possessions with those in need. This is a supported connection with Jesus' family-and-provision promise. God supplies care through people who learn to treat one another as belonging together.

The future promise has the same foundation as the present community. 1 Peter 1:3–9 joins new birth through Jesus' resurrection with an enduring inheritance, while acknowledging painful trials now. The disciples are learning to measure loss and gain within that larger hope: Christ's resurrection opens a future that persecution and the loss of earthly security cannot finally take away.

passages.title: Mark 10:32-34
passages.section_title: Jesus Leads the Way to Jerusalem

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 32 As they were going up the road to Jerusalem, Jesus was walking ahead of them. The disciples were amazed, but those who followed were afraid. Again Jesus took the Twelve aside and began to tell them what was going to happen to Him: 33 “Look, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and scribes. They will condemn Him to death and will deliver Him over to the Gentiles, 34 who will mock Him and spit on Him and flog Him and kill Him. And after three days He will rise again.”
paragraphs: 32 As they were going up the road to Jerusalem, Jesus was walking ahead of them. The disciples were amazed, but those who followed were afraid. Again Jesus took the Twelve aside and began to tell them what was going to happen to Him: 33 “Look, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and scribes. They will condemn Him to death and will deliver Him over to the Gentiles, 34 who will mock Him and spit on Him and flog Him and kill Him. And after three days He will rise again.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus walks ahead as the group travels toward Jerusalem. The disciples are amazed and those following are afraid. Mark reports their reactions without describing the exact thought behind each one. Jesus takes the Twelve aside and again explains what will happen to Him.

This announcement adds detail to those in Mark 8:31 and 9:30–32. Jerusalem is named, as are condemnation by the chief priests and scribes, delivery to the Gentiles, mockery, spitting, flogging, killing, and resurrection after three days.

The prediction places humiliation and death alongside resurrection. Jesus is leading them toward a mission whose cost He knows. The request for positions of glory in the next scene will again show how hard the disciples find it to take in the path He describes.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand this as Jesus deliberately preparing the disciples for His suffering and resurrection. Wesley on Mark 10:32 emphasizes His courage in going forward and His care in telling them more fully what lies ahead.
passages.god_plan_html:
After the resurrection, Jesus explains in Luke 24:25–27 that the Christ's suffering and entrance into glory belong to what the prophets announced. The detailed warning here is part of that larger purpose, even before the disciples can understand it.

The church's proclamation in Acts 2:22–24 holds together God's purpose, the responsibility of those who put Jesus to death, and God's raising Him. His announcement is not simply advance notice of tragedy. It prepares for the saving work that leads through death to resurrection and becomes the heart of the gospel.

passages.title: Mark 10:35-45
passages.section_title: The King Who Gives His Life to Serve

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 35 Then James and John, the sons of Zebedee, came to Jesus and declared, “Teacher, we want You to do for us whatever we ask.” 36 “What do you want Me to do for you?” He inquired. 37 They answered, “Grant that one of us may sit at Your right hand and the other at Your left in Your glory.” 38 “You do not know what you are asking,” Jesus replied. “Can you drink the cup I will drink, or be baptized with the baptism I will undergo?” 39 “We can,” the brothers answered. “You will drink the cup that I drink,” Jesus said, “and you will be baptized with the baptism that I undergo. 40 But to sit at My right or left is not Mine to grant. These seats belong to those for whom they have been prepared.” 41 When the ten heard about this, they became indignant with James and John. 42 So Jesus called them together and said, “You know that those regarded as rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their superiors exercise authority over them. 43 But it shall not be this way among you. Instead, whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant, 44 and whoever wants to be first must be the slave of all. 45 For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many.”
paragraphs: 35 Then James and John, the sons of Zebedee, came to Jesus and declared, “Teacher, we want You to do for us whatever we ask.” 36 “What do you want Me to do for you?” He inquired. 37 They answered, “Grant that one of us may sit at Your right hand and the other at Your left in Your glory.” 38 “You do not know what you are asking,” Jesus replied. “Can you drink the cup I will drink, or be baptized with the baptism I will undergo?” 39 “We can,” the brothers answered. “You will drink the cup that I drink,” Jesus said, “and you will be baptized with the baptism that I undergo. 40 But to sit at My right or left is not Mine to grant. These seats belong to those for whom they have been prepared.”

41 When the ten heard about this, they became indignant with James and John. 42 So Jesus called them together and said, “You know that those regarded as rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their superiors exercise authority over them. 43 But it shall not be this way among you. Instead, whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant, 44 and whoever wants to be first must be the slave of all. 45 For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
James and John ask for the places at Jesus' right and left in His glory, immediately after His announcement of suffering. He answers by asking about the cup He will drink and the baptism He will undergo. They say they can share them; He tells them they will, while refusing to promise the seats they request.

The cup and baptism describe suffering that lies ahead. Jesus will use the cup image again when He prays in Mark 14:32–36. Here the brothers seek the honor without understanding its cost. The prediction of their sharing suffering does not mean that their deaths will do the same saving work as His.

The other ten become indignant. Jesus gathers them all and contrasts the domination associated with rulers with the service He expects among His followers. Anyone seeking greatness must serve, and anyone wanting to be first must become the slave of all. The correction reaches the whole group, rather than leaving the ten as judges of the two.

He grounds this calling in His own mission: the Son of Man gives His life as a ransom for many. The Greek noun λύτρον (lytron, LOO-tron) means a price of release. Here His life is given to free others from the misery and penalty of sin. His death is both saving service and the pattern that confronts their ambition.

Matthew 20:20–28 includes the brothers' mother in the request and explicitly names the Father as the one who prepares the places. Mark gives the brothers' request directly. These added details need not be turned into a claim that a known family relationship with Jesus explains their motives.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the cup and baptism as suffering, and the instruction about greatness as a call to humble service. The USCCB notes on Mark 10:38–45 connect that service with Jesus' death for others; Wesley on verses 38–45 likewise connects suffering, glory, and the giving of His life.

Traditions differ over the scope of the ransom. The Catholic Church teaches that Christ died for everyone without exception, taking many as a contrast between the one Redeemer and humanity as a whole (Catechism 605). The Methodist Articles XX also describe His sacrifice as being for the sins of the whole world.

Reformed churches following Westminster 8.5 and 8.8, and Baptists following the 1689 Confession 8.5 and 8.8, teach that His death secures redemption for those the Father has given Him, and that He brings them to faith and gives them the inheritance He has won. These are the cited confessions' teachings, rather than every Baptist's or Protestant's position. The shared conviction is that His self-giving death rescues people from sin.
passages.god_plan_html:
The language strongly parallels Isaiah 53:10–12: the Servant gives His life, bears the sins of many, and brings others into a right relationship with God. Jesus' promised death belongs within that picture of one serving by giving Himself for others. The cost He asks the disciples to face grows out of the rescue He accomplishes, not a competition to outrank one another.

Philippians 2:3–13 brings the same pattern into the church's life. Believers are to put selfish ambition aside and attend to others, taking the attitude of Christ in His humility, obedience to the cross, and exaltation. God is at work in them to shape both their willing and doing.

Sharing Christ's sufferings also becomes part of the church's experience. Acts 12:1–2 records James' death, and 1 Peter 4:12–19 encourages those suffering as Christians to entrust themselves to their faithful Creator and continue doing good. Their calling is faithful service in the face of cost, while Christ remains the One whose life brings the ransom.

passages.title: Mark 10:46-52
passages.section_title: Bartimaeus Receives Sight and Follows

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 46 Next, they came to Jericho. And as Jesus and His disciples were leaving Jericho with a large crowd, a blind beggar named Bartimaeus, the son of Timaeus, was sitting beside the road. 47 When he heard that it was Jesus of Nazareth, he began to cry out, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” 48 Many people admonished him to be silent, but he cried out all the louder, “Son of David, have mercy on me!” 49 Jesus stopped and said, “Call him.” So they called the blind man. “Take courage!” they said. “Get up! He is calling for you.” 50 Throwing off his cloak, Bartimaeus jumped up and came to Jesus. 51 “What do you want Me to do for you?” Jesus asked. “Rabboni,” said the blind man, “let me see again.” 52 “Go,” said Jesus, “your faith has healed you.” And immediately he received his sight and followed Jesus along the road.
paragraphs: 46 Next, they came to Jericho. And as Jesus and His disciples were leaving Jericho with a large crowd, a blind beggar named Bartimaeus, the son of Timaeus, was sitting beside the road. 47 When he heard that it was Jesus of Nazareth, he began to cry out, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” 48 Many people admonished him to be silent, but he cried out all the louder, “Son of David, have mercy on me!” 49 Jesus stopped and said, “Call him.” So they called the blind man. “Take courage!” they said. “Get up! He is calling for you.” 50 Throwing off his cloak, Bartimaeus jumped up and came to Jesus.

51 “What do you want Me to do for you?” Jesus asked. “Rabboni,” said the blind man, “let me see again.” 52 “Go,” said Jesus, “your faith has healed you.” And immediately he received his sight and followed Jesus along the road.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
As Jesus leaves Jericho with His disciples and a large crowd, a blind beggar named Bartimaeus hears that He is passing. He calls out to Jesus as the Son of David and asks for mercy. Many try to silence him, but he calls all the more. Jesus stops and asks for him to be brought.

The crowd's words change from rebuke to encouragement. Bartimaeus throws off his cloak, gets up, and comes to Jesus. Mark gives these movements without saying that the cloak was his only possession or that he never retrieved it.

Jesus asks what he wants Him to do, echoing His question to James and John in verse 36. Their request concerned places of honor; Bartimaeus asks to see again. Jesus credits his faith, and he immediately receives sight and follows Him along the road. The response brings healing and following together.

The title preserved in verse 51 is ῥαββουνί (rabbouni, rah-boo-NEE), an Aramaic form of respectful address for a teacher, written here in Greek. Bartimaeus approaches Jesus with trust and a plainly stated need.

The related accounts present details differently: Matthew 20:29–34 names two blind men as Jesus leaves Jericho, while Luke 18:35–43 describes a blind man as He approaches Jericho. Mark concentrates on the named Bartimaeus. These observations can be acknowledged without claiming that a particular reconstruction of the route has been proved.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly emphasize persistent trust in Jesus, His mercy, and the healed man's response in following Him. Calvin on Mark 10:52 understands the faith in relation to Bartimaeus recognizing the promised Messiah, rather than confidence in a healing technique. He also reads the rescue as reaching beyond bodily sight to the man's relationship with God.
passages.god_plan_html:
The cry to the Son of David places the encounter within Israel's hope. Jeremiah 23:5–6 promises a righteous king from David's line, and Romans 1:1–4 identifies the gospel's promised Son as David's descendant, revealed in resurrection power. The man the crowd tries to silence addresses Jesus with a title that reaches into that larger promise.

The restored sight also fits the prophetic picture of God's rescue in Isaiah 35:4–10, where blind eyes are opened and the redeemed return with joy. Jesus explicitly includes recovery of sight in His mission in Luke 4:16–21. This healing is a concrete work of the promised Savior as He goes toward the death and resurrection through which He brings His saving mission to fulfillment.

Bartimaeus then joins Him on the road. His response offers a narrative contrast with the wealthy man's sorrowful departure earlier in the chapter. The connection concerns responding to Jesus; it does not make physical blindness a measure of a person's spiritual condition.
passages.current_position_html: In Prayer and Faith, section 5, we use Mark 10:51–52 to distinguish the need Bartimaeus speaks from the faith Jesus credits. He asks plainly for sight in response to Jesus' question, and Jesus names his faith when healing him. Our point is that trust rests in Jesus, rather than in finding a particular form of words. The account includes both a spoken request and faith; it should be allowed to show both.

passages.title: Mark 10:51-52
passages.section_title: A Plain Request and Faith in Jesus

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 51 “What do you want Me to do for you?” Jesus asked. “Rabboni,” said the blind man, “let me see again.” 52 “Go,” said Jesus, “your faith has healed you.” And immediately he received his sight and followed Jesus along the road.
paragraphs: 51 “What do you want Me to do for you?” Jesus asked. “Rabboni,” said the blind man, “let me see again.” 52 “Go,” said Jesus, “your faith has healed you.” And immediately he received his sight and followed Jesus along the road.

passages.context_html:
These verses close the encounter with Bartimaeus beside the road at Jericho. He has called on Jesus for mercy despite people trying to silence him. Jesus stops, calls him forward, and asks what he wants Him to do.

Bartimaeus answers with a specific request to see again. Jesus credits his faith, and he immediately receives sight and follows Him. Mark records neither a required prayer formula nor an elaborate test of how he phrases the request.

The question recalls Jesus' earlier question to James and John in Mark 10:35–40. The brothers ask for places of glory; Bartimaeus asks for sight. His response at the end is to follow Jesus along the road.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly connect the healing with trust in Jesus and the man's grateful following. Calvin on Mark 10:52 understands his faith as recognition of the promised Messiah, and reads the rescue as including more than physical recovery. The narrated result remains clear: his sight is restored, and he follows Jesus.
passages.current_position_html: In Prayer and Faith, section 5, we draw on this exchange because it contains a specific request and Jesus' explicit recognition of faith. Bartimaeus speaks his need when Jesus asks, and Jesus credits his trust. The study's point here is that faith rests in Christ rather than in a formula of words. We retain the spoken request as part of what the passage actually says.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The restoration of sight belongs with Jesus' announced mission in Luke 4:16–21, where He includes recovery of sight in proclaiming God's favor. This makes the exchange part of the Savior's work, rather than an isolated lesson in how to obtain a desired result.

The healed man's following also has a wider parallel in Philippians 3:7–11. Paul describes knowing Christ, receiving righteousness through faith, and sharing in His sufferings and resurrection hope as greater than what he once counted gain. Bartimaeus' story does not supply Paul's whole teaching, but it gives a concrete picture of turning toward Jesus and going with Him.

passages.title: Mark 11:1-11
passages.section_title: The Humble King Enters Jerusalem

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 As they approached Jerusalem and came to Bethphage and Bethany at the Mount of Olives, Jesus sent out two of His disciples 2 and said to them, “Go into the village ahead of you, and as soon as you enter it, you will find a colt tied there, on which no one has ever sat. Untie it and bring it here. 3 If anyone asks, ‘Why are you doing this?’ tell him, ‘The Lord needs it and will return it shortly.’” 4 So they went and found the colt outside in the street, tied at a doorway. They untied it, 5 and some who were standing there asked, “Why are you untying the colt?” 6 The disciples answered as Jesus had instructed them, and the people gave them permission. 7 Then they led the colt to Jesus and threw their cloaks over it, and He sat on it. 8 Many in the crowd spread their cloaks on the road, while others spread branches they had cut from the fields. 9 The ones who went ahead and those who followed were shouting: “Hosanna!” “Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord!” 10 “Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David!” “Hosanna in the highest!” 11 Then Jesus entered Jerusalem and went into the temple courts. He looked around at everything, but since it was already late, He went out to Bethany with the Twelve.
paragraphs: 1 As they approached Jerusalem and came to Bethphage and Bethany at the Mount of Olives, Jesus sent out two of His disciples 2 and said to them, “Go into the village ahead of you, and as soon as you enter it, you will find a colt tied there, on which no one has ever sat. Untie it and bring it here. 3 If anyone asks, ‘Why are you doing this?’ tell him, ‘The Lord needs it and will return it shortly.’” 4 So they went and found the colt outside in the street, tied at a doorway. They untied it, 5 and some who were standing there asked, “Why are you untying the colt?” 6 The disciples answered as Jesus had instructed them, and the people gave them permission.

7 Then they led the colt to Jesus and threw their cloaks over it, and He sat on it. 8 Many in the crowd spread their cloaks on the road, while others spread branches they had cut from the fields. 9 The ones who went ahead and those who followed were shouting: “Hosanna!” “Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord!” 10 “Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David!” “Hosanna in the highest!” 11 Then Jesus entered Jerusalem and went into the temple courts. He looked around at everything, but since it was already late, He went out to Bethany with the Twelve.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
As Jesus approaches Jerusalem near Bethphage and Bethany at the Mount of Olives, He sends two disciples to fetch a colt on which no one has sat. They find it as He described, answer the people's question with His instructions, and receive permission to take it. They put their cloaks on it, and Jesus rides toward the city.

People spread cloaks and branches on the road. Their shouts use the blessing from Psalm 118:25–26 and celebrate the coming kingdom of David. ὡσαννά (hosanna, hoh-ZAN-ah) carries a Hebrew plea meaning save, we pray. The BSB footnote explains how it also became a shout of praise.

The way Jesus enters recalls the king in Zechariah 9:9, humble and riding on a donkey's colt. John 12:12–16 explicitly connects the entry with that prophecy and says the disciples understood the connection after Jesus was glorified.

Jesus then enters the temple courts and looks around. Since it is late, He leaves for Bethany with the Twelve. Mark gives this visit its own place before the following day's action in the temple. The arrival celebrated by the crowd leads toward the suffering He has just announced.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly understand the entry as a public sign of Jesus' kingship, with His humble arrival shaped by Zechariah's prophecy. Calvin's discussion emphasizes both the royal claim and its difference from displays of worldly splendor.

Readers differ over how much the crowd's words reveal about their understanding. Calvin describes an acknowledgment of Jesus as king; the USCCB note on Mark 11:1–11 reads Mark's particular wording as greeting a prophet of the coming kingdom, stopping short of an explicit declaration that Jesus is Messiah. These are readings of the narrative, not competing official church definitions of who Christ is.
passages.god_plan_html:
The coming kingdom reaches back to God's promise that David's house and throne would endure (2 Samuel 7:12–16). Yet the king pictured in Zechariah 9:9–10 comes humbly, brings an end to instruments of war, and proclaims peace to the nations. Jesus' entry belongs within that larger promise, while His coming death shows the cost of the rescue He brings.

A later picture offers a striking parallel: in Revelation 7:9–17, people from every nation stand with palm branches and praise God and the Lamb for salvation. They have been made clean through the Lamb's blood, and He shepherds them into lasting comfort. This is not a claim that Mark's crowd already understood that whole vision. It is a wider biblical picture of the King whose victory gathers people through His self-giving life.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 11:12-14
passages.section_title: Looking for Fruit Beyond the Leaves

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 The next day, when they had left Bethany, Jesus was hungry. 13 Seeing in the distance a fig tree in leaf, He went to see if there was any fruit on it. But when He reached it, He found nothing on it except leaves, since it was not the season for figs. 14 Then He said to the tree, “May no one ever eat of your fruit again.” And His disciples heard this statement.
paragraphs: 12 The next day, when they had left Bethany, Jesus was hungry. 13 Seeing in the distance a fig tree in leaf, He went to see if there was any fruit on it. But when He reached it, He found nothing on it except leaves, since it was not the season for figs. 14 Then He said to the tree, “May no one ever eat of your fruit again.” And His disciples heard this statement.

passages.context_html:
The morning after the entry into Jerusalem, Jesus leaves Bethany hungry. He sees a fig tree in leaf and goes to see whether it has fruit, but finds only leaves. Mark explicitly says it is not the season for figs. Jesus declares that no one will eat its fruit again, and the disciples hear Him.

The brief scene is the first part of a larger sequence. Jesus next confronts the activity in the temple courts; the following morning, the disciples see the tree withered from its roots (Mark 11:15–21). Mark places the temple action between the word spoken to the tree and the discovery of its condition.

That arrangement encourages readers to consider the scenes together. The tree has leaves but no fruit; the temple has busy religious activity, yet Jesus challenges what it has become. The account works as a visible warning about the difference between outward appearance and a life that answers God's call.

The detail about the season should remain part of the reading. Mark does not explain a precise timetable for buds or identify this tree's variety. The wider prophetic setting helps make sense of the act without requiring a botanical reconstruction to be treated as established fact.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Many Christian readings understand the tree as a prophetic act of judgment rather than a lesson about a gardener's expectations. The USCCB note on Mark 11:12–14 connects it with the prophets' fig-tree imagery and Jerusalem's failure to receive Jesus' teaching; Wesley on verse 13 likewise reads it as a warning about unfruitfulness.
passages.current_position_html: In Prayer and Faith, in the discussion of Mark 11:24, we read the fig tree as a deliberate prophetic warning about Israel's spiritual condition and coming judgment. We consider the tree, the temple confrontation, and the later teaching on faith together. The study's conclusion here is that Jesus acts within God's purpose; this is not an example of using faith to produce whatever personal outcome one prefers.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The prophets already use fruit and fig trees to describe a people's response to God. Hosea 9:10,16 moves from Israel pictured as early figs to a withered root that cannot bear fruit. Micah 7:1–7 compares the absence of faithful people with searching for fruit and finding none, then turns toward hope in the God who saves. These are supported parallels for reading the tree as more than a passing incident.

The larger concern is the fruitful life God desires. In John 15:1–8, Jesus teaches His followers to remain in Him because they cannot bear fruit apart from Him. Fruit brings glory to the Father. The warning about empty appearance therefore belongs beside the positive calling to a life sustained by Christ, rather than becoming a reason to condemn a people from a distance.

passages.title: Mark 11:15-19
passages.section_title: A House of Prayer for All Nations

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 When they arrived in Jerusalem, Jesus entered the temple courts and began to drive out those who were buying and selling there. He overturned the tables of the money changers and the seats of those selling doves. 16 And He would not allow anyone to carry merchandise through the temple courts. 17 Then Jesus began to teach them, and He declared, “Is it not written: ‘My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations’? But you have made it ‘a den of robbers.’” 18 When the chief priests and scribes heard this, they looked for a way to kill Him. For they were afraid of Him, because the whole crowd was astonished at His teaching. 19 And when evening came, Jesus and His disciples went out of the city.
paragraphs: 15 When they arrived in Jerusalem, Jesus entered the temple courts and began to drive out those who were buying and selling there. He overturned the tables of the money changers and the seats of those selling doves. 16 And He would not allow anyone to carry merchandise through the temple courts. 17 Then Jesus began to teach them, and He declared, “Is it not written: ‘My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations’? But you have made it ‘a den of robbers.’”

18 When the chief priests and scribes heard this, they looked for a way to kill Him. For they were afraid of Him, because the whole crowd was astonished at His teaching. 19 And when evening came, Jesus and His disciples went out of the city.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus enters the temple courts and drives out buyers and sellers, overturning the money changers' tables and the seats of those selling doves. He also stops people carrying merchandise through the courts. He then teaches about the purpose of God's house.

His explanation joins Isaiah 56:7, about a house of prayer for all nations, with Jeremiah 7:11, about a den of robbers. Isaiah speaks of foreigners welcomed by God. Jeremiah challenges people who practice injustice and then treat the temple as a place that makes them safe from judgment.

The temple complex had different courts and access restrictions. Josephus, Jewish War 5.5.2, describes a stone barrier with notices forbidding foreigners from entering the inner sanctuary. This helps illuminate the importance of Jesus' words about all nations, while Mark identifies the setting broadly as the temple courts.

Jesus' accusation therefore reaches beyond the fact that goods change hands. Jeremiah's background brings the conduct of worshipers and their treatment of others into view. Mark does not provide a price list or say that every transaction involved a particular fraudulent fee.

The chief priests and scribes seek a way to kill Him. They fear Him because the crowd is astonished at His teaching. Jesus and the disciples leave the city that evening. The confrontation sits within the fig-tree sequence and leads into further challenges about His authority.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand this as Jesus defending the holiness and purpose of God's house and exposing its misuse. Wesley on Mark 11:16–18 emphasizes the regard due to a place dedicated to God. Reading Jesus' two prophetic references together also keeps prayer, justice, and the welcome of the nations within view.
passages.god_plan_html:
The promise Jesus cites is larger than the removal of a market. In Isaiah 56:3–8, God welcomes foreigners who join themselves to Him and promises to gather still others beside those already gathered. His house is a place where people once afraid of exclusion can find a name, belonging, and joyful worship.

Ephesians 2:11–22 explains how people once far away are brought near through Christ's blood. Jew and Gentile are reconciled to God through the cross, have access to the Father by one Spirit, and are built together into a dwelling for God. This is a wider connection with the purpose Jesus defends: His saving work gathers people into shared access to God, rather than leaving worship as a privilege to be guarded for one's own advantage.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

deeper_study.title: The True Church According to Jesus

passages.title: Mark 11:20-25
passages.section_title: Faith, Prayer, and Forgiveness

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 20 As they were walking back in the morning, they saw the fig tree withered from its roots. 21 Peter remembered it and said, “Look, Rabbi! The fig tree You cursed has withered.” 22 “Have faith in God,” Jesus said to them. 23 “Truly I tell you that if anyone says to this mountain, ‘Be lifted up and thrown into the sea,’ and has no doubt in his heart but believes that it will happen, it will be done for him. 24 Therefore I tell you, whatever you ask for in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours. 25 And when you stand to pray, if you hold anything against another, forgive it, so that your Father in heaven will forgive your trespasses as well.”
paragraphs: 20 As they were walking back in the morning, they saw the fig tree withered from its roots. 21 Peter remembered it and said, “Look, Rabbi! The fig tree You cursed has withered.” 22 “Have faith in God,” Jesus said to them. 23 “Truly I tell you that if anyone says to this mountain, ‘Be lifted up and thrown into the sea,’ and has no doubt in his heart but believes that it will happen, it will be done for him. 24 Therefore I tell you, whatever you ask for in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours.
25 And when you stand to pray, if you hold anything against another, forgive it, so that your Father in heaven will forgive your trespasses as well.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The next morning, the disciples see the fig tree withered from its roots. Peter draws Jesus' attention to it, and Jesus directs them to faith in God. The tree's condition closes the sequence that has placed His temple confrontation between the warning to the tree and its visible result.

Faith here is πίστις (pistis, PIS-tis), trust or confidence. Thayer specifically explains Mark 11:22 as trusting in God. Jesus' opening instruction identifies the One on whom that confidence rests.

The mountain thrown into the sea is a striking picture of what is beyond human ability. Jesus calls for undivided trust and confidence in prayer. The words about believing one has received are strong; the following instruction about forgiveness is part of the same teaching, rather than an unrelated addition.

Jesus then tells people praying to forgive what they hold against another, connecting their conduct with receiving the Father's forgiveness. Prayer is presented within relationship with God and with other people. Confidence before the Father belongs alongside a willingness to release grievances.

Other passages help readers consider the promise within the wider teaching on prayer. 1 John 5:14–15 joins confidence with asking according to God's will, while James 4:1–3 warns about requests driven by selfish motives. Mark 14:32–36 later shows Jesus making an honest request while surrendering to His Father's will.

Verse 26 appears in the BSB footnotes, where some manuscripts add a further warning about refusing to forgive. The quotation above follows the main text and ends this group at verse 25.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly take this as a strong invitation to confident prayer and a serious call to forgive. They differ over how confidently a believer may claim a particular outcome before it occurs and what role spoken declarations play.

The Catholic Catechism 2610–2611 directly uses this promise to encourage bold faith while placing the praying heart within the Father's will. Its discussion of trust in prayer, 2734–2741, stresses trust in the Father, the transformation of the person praying, and perseverance when the expected result is delayed. Reformed Westminster 21.3 and the 1689 Baptist Confession 22.3 likewise place faithful prayer in Christ's name, with the Spirit's help, according to God's will.

Within Word of Faith teaching, Kenneth Copeland Ministries' explanation of this passage puts particular emphasis on speaking the desired result, believing it received, and acting on the promise before circumstances change, including in matters of healing or prosperity. The ministry also says prayer should agree with God's Word. This is that ministry's stated approach, not the position of every Pentecostal or charismatic Christian.
passages.god_plan_html:
Prayer belongs within the relationship God gives through His Son and Spirit. Romans 8:14–17,26–27 describes believers receiving the Spirit of adoption and calling God Father. That same Spirit helps them when they do not know how to pray and intercedes according to God's will. The wider picture is people brought into God's family and helped in their weakness, not left to make prayer depend on their own ability.

The call to forgive also flows from what God accomplishes in Christ. Ephesians 4:29–32 connects life in the Spirit with putting bitterness and malice aside and forgiving one another as God has forgiven in Christ. The faith Jesus calls for is to shape a community whose relationships show the mercy it has received.
passages.current_position_html: In Prayer and Faith, in the discussion of Mark 11:24, we read the promise within the fig-tree and temple setting and alongside Scripture's teaching about God's will. Our conclusion is that Jesus calls for trust in God's purpose, rather than confidence that personal desire can determine the result. The study compares this promise with Jesus' surrender in Gethsemane and Paul's prayer about his thorn. We retain both the invitation to ask and the call to rest in God.

passages.title: Mark 11:24
passages.section_title: Trusting God When We Pray

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 24 Therefore I tell you, whatever you ask for in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours.
paragraphs: 24 Therefore I tell you, whatever you ask for in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours.

passages.context_html:
This promise is part of Jesus' answer after the disciples find the fig tree withered. He begins by directing them to faith in God, describes a mountain being moved, and calls them to pray with confidence. The following verse tells them to forgive what they hold against others.

Read on its own, verse 24 can sound detached from that relationship and setting. The full Mark 11:20–25 keeps God's power, faith, prayer, and forgiveness together. The tree and temple scenes also place the conversation within Jesus' public challenge to unfruitful religion.

The language about believing one has received expresses strong confidence. It should also be considered alongside 1 John 5:14–15, which speaks of asking according to God's will, and Jesus' own prayer in Mark 14:36. The different readings of that relationship are part of the passage's interpretation.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The Catholic Catechism 2610–2611 uses the promise to encourage bold faith and a heart ready to do the Father's will. Reformed Westminster 21.3 and the 1689 Baptist Confession 22.3 likewise teach faithful prayer according to God's will.

A different emphasis appears in Kenneth Copeland Ministries' Word of Faith teaching, which directs people to speak the desired result, believe it received, and act on the promise before circumstances change. It also calls for agreement with God's Word. The difference concerns how a promised answer is applied to particular circumstances, rather than whether prayer should involve faith. This ministry's approach does not represent every Pentecostal or charismatic church.
passages.current_position_html: In Prayer and Faith, in the discussion of this verse, we conclude that faith rests in God's purpose rather than using prayer to produce an outcome of one's own choosing. The study reads the promise within the fig-tree setting and tests it alongside Jesus' prayer in Gethsemane and Paul's request about his thorn. Our emphasis is surrendered trust in the Father, while preserving Jesus' actual invitation to pray and ask.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
John 14:12–17 places asking in Jesus' name within His departure to the Father, the Father's glory through the Son, and the gift of the Spirit. Prayer participates in God's continuing work among His people as they live in relationship with Christ.

Romans 8:26–27 adds that the Spirit helps in weakness and intercedes according to God's will when believers do not know how to pray. The larger story gives prayer a secure foundation in God's own help, even where the person praying does not possess a complete understanding of the situation.

passages.title: Mark 11:27-33
passages.section_title: Where Does Jesus’ Authority Come From?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 27 After their return to Jerusalem, Jesus was walking in the temple courts, and the chief priests, scribes, and elders came up to Him. 28 “By what authority are You doing these things?” they asked. “And who gave You the authority to do them?” 29 “I will ask you one question,” Jesus replied, “and if you answer Me, I will tell you by what authority I am doing these things. 30 John’s baptism—was it from heaven or from men? Answer Me!” 31 They deliberated among themselves what they should answer: “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ He will ask, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’ 32 But if we say, ‘From men’...” they were afraid of the people, for they all held that John truly was a prophet. 33 So they answered, “We do not know.” And Jesus replied, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I am doing these things.”
paragraphs: 27 After their return to Jerusalem, Jesus was walking in the temple courts, and the chief priests, scribes, and elders came up to Him. 28 “By what authority are You doing these things?” they asked. “And who gave You the authority to do them?” 29 “I will ask you one question,” Jesus replied, “and if you answer Me, I will tell you by what authority I am doing these things. 30 John’s baptism—was it from heaven or from men? Answer Me!”

31 They deliberated among themselves what they should answer: “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ He will ask, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’ 32 But if we say, ‘From men’...” they were afraid of the people, for they all held that John truly was a prophet. 33 So they answered, “We do not know.” And Jesus replied, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I am doing these things.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Back in Jerusalem, Jesus walks in the temple courts. The chief priests, scribes, and elders ask by what authority He acts and who gave it to Him. Their question follows His disruption of the temple trade and His teaching about God's house.

Jesus responds with a question about John's baptism: was it from heaven or from human beings? The issue reaches beyond the act of washing to the source of John's ministry. Mark 1:2–11 has already introduced John as the messenger preparing the Lord's way and placed Jesus' baptism within the Father's declaration about His Son.

The leaders consider the consequences of each answer. If they say John's ministry came from heaven, Jesus can ask why they did not believe him. If they say it came from people, they fear the crowd, who regard John as a prophet. They answer that they do not know, and Jesus declines to answer their question directly.

Mark lets us hear their discussion. Their concern with the cost of answering explains the stalemate. The account does not give a detailed first-century licensing system for rabbis or identify each speaker's school; its focus is their response to God's messenger and their challenge to Jesus.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand Jesus' question as exposing the leaders' unwillingness to face the implications of John's ministry. Calvin on this exchange connects recognizing John with recognizing the One he announced; the USCCB note on Mark 11:27–33 places the challenge within the mounting rejection of God's messengers.
passages.god_plan_html:
John 1:6–13,29–34 explains that the Baptizer was sent from God to bear witness to the Light. He identifies Jesus as the Lamb who takes away the world's sin and testifies that He is the Son of God. The question about where John's authority came from therefore reaches into God's work of making His Son known so that people may believe and become His children.

Acts 13:23–33 later gathers John's preparation, Jesus as the promised Savior, His rejection and death, and His resurrection into one proclamation of salvation. The disagreement in the temple is part of that larger story: human resistance does not prevent God from fulfilling His promise, but the question of how people respond to His witness remains real.

passages.title: Mark 12:1-12
passages.section_title: The Rejected Son and the Cornerstone

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then Jesus began to speak to them in parables: “A man planted a vineyard. He put a wall around it, dug a wine vat, and built a watchtower. Then he rented it out to some tenants and went away on a journey. 2 At harvest time, he sent a servant to the tenants to collect his share of the fruit of the vineyard. 3 But they seized the servant, beat him, and sent him away empty-handed. 4 Then he sent them another servant, and they struck him over the head and treated him shamefully. 5 He sent still another, and this one they killed. He sent many others; some they beat and others they killed. 6 Finally, having one beloved son, he sent him to them. ‘They will respect my son,’ he said. 7 But the tenants said to one another, ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.’ 8 So they seized the son, killed him, and threw him out of the vineyard. 9 What then will the owner of the vineyard do? He will come and kill those tenants and give the vineyard to others. 10 Have you never read this Scripture: ‘The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. 11 This is from the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes’?” 12 At this, the leaders sought to arrest Jesus, for they knew that He had spoken this parable against them. But fearing the crowd, they left Him and went away.
paragraphs: 1 Then Jesus began to speak to them in parables: “A man planted a vineyard. He put a wall around it, dug a wine vat, and built a watchtower. Then he rented it out to some tenants and went away on a journey. 2 At harvest time, he sent a servant to the tenants to collect his share of the fruit of the vineyard. 3 But they seized the servant, beat him, and sent him away empty-handed. 4 Then he sent them another servant, and they struck him over the head and treated him shamefully. 5 He sent still another, and this one they killed. He sent many others; some they beat and others they killed.

6 Finally, having one beloved son, he sent him to them. ‘They will respect my son,’ he said. 7 But the tenants said to one another, ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.’ 8 So they seized the son, killed him, and threw him out of the vineyard. 9 What then will the owner of the vineyard do? He will come and kill those tenants and give the vineyard to others.

10 Have you never read this Scripture: ‘The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. 11 This is from the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes’?” 12 At this, the leaders sought to arrest Jesus, for they knew that He had spoken this parable against them. But fearing the crowd, they left Him and went away.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the leaders challenge His authority, Jesus tells a story about a vineyard owner and the people entrusted with its care. The owner prepares the vineyard, rents it out, and sends servants to collect his share at harvest. The tenants beat, humiliate, or kill the messengers instead of giving what is due.

The vineyard's wall, wine vat, and tower recall Isaiah 5:1–7. There God identifies the vineyard as Israel and looks for justice and righteousness, but finds bloodshed and distress. Jesus' story places particular attention on the tenants' refusal to honor the owner.

Finally the owner sends his beloved son. The tenants recognize him as the heir, kill him, and throw him out of the vineyard. Jesus asks what the owner will do and answers with judgment on those tenants and the vineyard being given to others. The son stands apart from the earlier messengers: he is the beloved heir.

Jesus then quotes Psalm 118:22–23, moving from the murdered son to the rejected stone that God makes the cornerstone. The rejection does not give the builders the last word. God's action gives the rejected one the central place.

The leaders understand that the parable is directed against them. They want to arrest Jesus but fear the crowd. Mark gives their recognition explicitly, so the warning should not be turned into an accusation against every Jewish person. The people opposing Jesus, His disciples, and the prophets whose words He uses all belong within Israel's story.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand the owner as God, the servants as His messengers, and the beloved son as Jesus. The USCCB notes on Mark 12:1–12 identify the tenants with Israel's religious leaders and the new recipients with the people of the new Israel; Calvin's discussion likewise emphasizes leaders' responsibility as stewards rather than owners and the judgment their rejection brings.
passages.god_plan_html:
The prophets' concern for faithful leadership forms part of this larger picture. Ezekiel 34:1–6 condemns shepherds who feed themselves while neglecting the weak, injured, and scattered flock. The vineyard parable similarly exposes the misuse of a responsibility received from God, reaching its climax in the rejection of His Son.

The New Testament explicitly applies the cornerstone passage to Jesus' resurrection and saving work. In Acts 4:8–12, Peter identifies the rejected stone as the Jesus whom God raised and proclaims salvation in His name. The opposition pictured here becomes part of the story through which God brings rescue, rather than defeating His purpose.

1 Peter 2:4–10 carries the picture into the community gathered around Him. Christ is the living stone; those who come to Him are built into a spiritual house and become a people who proclaim God's goodness. The larger outcome is a people shaped around the Son others rejected, called to bear witness to the mercy they have received.
