passages.title: Mark 12:13-17
passages.section_title: What Belongs to Caesar and What Belongs to God?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 Later, they sent some of the Pharisees and Herodians to catch Jesus in His words. 14 “Teacher,” they said, “we know that You are honest and seek favor from no one. Indeed, You are impartial and teach the way of God in accordance with the truth. Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar or not? Should we pay them or not?” 15 But Jesus saw through their hypocrisy and said, “Why are you testing Me? Bring Me a denarius to inspect.” 16 So they brought it, and He asked them, “Whose image is this? And whose inscription?” “Caesar’s,” they answered. 17 Then Jesus told them, “Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.” And they marveled at Him.
paragraphs: 13 Later, they sent some of the Pharisees and Herodians to catch Jesus in His words. 14 “Teacher,” they said, “we know that You are honest and seek favor from no one. Indeed, You are impartial and teach the way of God in accordance with the truth. Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar or not? Should we pay them or not?” 15 But Jesus saw through their hypocrisy and said, “Why are you testing Me? Bring Me a denarius to inspect.” 16 So they brought it, and He asked them, “Whose image is this? And whose inscription?” “Caesar’s,” they answered. 17 Then Jesus told them, “Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.” And they marveled at Him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Some Pharisees and Herodians are sent to catch Jesus in His words. They begin by praising His honesty and impartiality, then ask whether it is lawful to pay taxes to Caesar. Mark identifies their purpose and says Jesus recognizes their hypocrisy; the flattering introduction does not describe an honest search for instruction.

Jesus asks for a denarius and directs attention to its image and inscription. They identify Caesar, and He tells them to give Caesar what belongs to Caesar and God what belongs to God. His answer refuses to let the tax question erase the more searching question of what they owe God.

The verb translated give is ἀποδίδωμι (apodidomi, ah-poh-DEE-doh-mee), which can mean to give back or pay what is due. Thayer specifically includes this passage's payment of government dues. The wording concerns an obligation, while the second half of the answer preserves God's claim.

Mark does not identify the person who supplies the coin or transcribe its inscription. The account gives enough for Jesus' question and answer without requiring us to name a particular surviving coin as the one He held. Those questioning Him are left marveling at His reply.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand the answer as recognizing responsibilities to civil government while preserving God's higher claim. The Catholic Catechism 2240–2242 joins paying taxes with refusing commands that contradict God's demands; Westminster 23.4 likewise calls for obedience to lawful commands. Calvin on this answer explains that civil obligations do not displace the supreme authority of God.
passages.god_plan_html:
The coin's image has a wider biblical parallel in Genesis 1:26–28: human beings bear God's image. Jesus does not spell out that comparison in this scene, so it should be identified as a parallel. It gives depth to the closing obligation: what belongs to God reaches beyond a payment into the whole person.

Romans 12:1–2 calls believers to offer their lives to God in response to His mercy, and Romans 13:1–7 places duties to governing authorities, including taxes, within that life. 1 Peter 2:13–17 likewise brings doing good, serving God, and honoring the ruler together.

The distinction remains important in Acts 5:27–32, where the apostles obey God when authorities forbid their witness to the risen Jesus. God's saving work forms people who serve faithfully within society while giving Him their ultimate loyalty. The passage's larger lesson is not exhausted by deciding who receives a coin.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 12:18-27
passages.section_title: The God of the Living

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 Then the Sadducees, who say there is no resurrection, came to Jesus and questioned Him: 19 “Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man’s brother dies and leaves a wife but no children, the man is to marry his brother’s widow and raise up offspring for him. 20 Now there were seven brothers. The first one married and died, leaving no children. 21 Then the second one married the widow, but he also died and left no children. And the third did likewise. 22 In this way, none of the seven left any children. And last of all, the woman died. 23 In the resurrection, then, whose wife will she be? For all seven were married to her.” 24 Jesus said to them, “Aren’t you mistaken, because you do not know the Scriptures or the power of God? 25 When the dead rise, they will neither marry nor be given in marriage. Instead, they will be like the angels in heaven. 26 But concerning the dead rising, have you not read about the burning bush in the Book of Moses, how God told him, ‘I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’? 27 He is not the God of the dead, but of the living. You are badly mistaken!”
paragraphs: 18 Then the Sadducees, who say there is no resurrection, came to Jesus and questioned Him: 19 “Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man’s brother dies and leaves a wife but no children, the man is to marry his brother’s widow and raise up offspring for him. 20 Now there were seven brothers. The first one married and died, leaving no children. 21 Then the second one married the widow, but he also died and left no children. And the third did likewise. 22 In this way, none of the seven left any children. And last of all, the woman died. 23 In the resurrection, then, whose wife will she be? For all seven were married to her.”

24 Jesus said to them, “Aren’t you mistaken, because you do not know the Scriptures or the power of God? 25 When the dead rise, they will neither marry nor be given in marriage. Instead, they will be like the angels in heaven. 26 But concerning the dead rising, have you not read about the burning bush in the Book of Moses, how God told him, ‘I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’? 27 He is not the God of the dead, but of the living. You are badly mistaken!”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Sadducees, whom Mark identifies as denying resurrection, present a case involving seven brothers. One after another marries the same widow and dies without children; finally she dies. They ask whose wife she will be when the dead rise.

Their case draws on Deuteronomy 25:5–10, where a brother has a duty toward his deceased brother's childless widow so the dead man's name will continue. The question assumes that resurrection life must preserve the same marriage arrangement and therefore creates a conflict about which husband she belongs to.

Jesus says they fail to understand both Scripture and God's power. Those raised do not marry or enter marriage as people do now; in this respect they are like the angels in heaven. He says they are like angels, not that human beings become angels.

He then turns to Exodus 3:2–6, where God speaks to Moses from the burning bush and identifies Himself in relationship with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Jesus uses that continuing relationship to affirm life before God and the reality of resurrection. The God who binds Himself to His people is not defeated by their death.

The answer does more than solve the marriage puzzle. It challenges the limits the questioners place on what God can do. The passage gives an assurance about life with God; it does not provide a complete description of every relationship or feature of the resurrection world.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Catholic and Protestant readings commonly understand Jesus to affirm resurrection while correcting the assumption that marriage continues as in this life. Wesley on Mark 12:25–27 connects God's enduring relationship with the patriarchs to the hope of bodily resurrection. The USCCB notes on the parallel Matthew 22:23–33 likewise explain a life transformed by God's power.

A different reading is taught by the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Its student manual on the parallel Matthew account distinguishes new marriages being performed after resurrection from marriages already joined through the church's authorized sealing. It teaches that a marriage sealed according to its requirements can endure beyond death, drawing on Doctrine and Covenants 132 as well as its interpretation of Jesus' answer. This is that church's stated teaching, rather than the general Christian reading above.
passages.god_plan_html:
God's commitment to be the God of Abraham and his descendants is part of His covenant promise in Genesis 17:7–8. Hebrews 11:8–19 describes Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob living by faith before receiving all they hoped for and looking toward the city God prepares. It also describes Abraham reasoning that God could raise the dead. These connections place Jesus' answer within God's faithfulness across generations and beyond a person's lifetime.

That hope reaches its decisive foundation in Christ. 1 Corinthians 15:12–28 connects His resurrection with the future raising of those who belong to Him and the final destruction of death. John 6:37–40 likewise joins the Father's will, faith in the Son, eternal life, and the Son's promise to raise His people. Resurrection belongs at the heart of God's saving purpose.

Paul's description in 1 Corinthians 15:42–58 adds that the raised body is no longer perishable or subject to death. This is the power the Sadducees' scenario leaves out: God brings a transformed life whose future cannot be measured only by the conditions of the present one.
passages.current_position_html: In Who is The Angel of the Lord?, in the section on Exodus 3:2–6, we identify the One who appears and speaks from the burning bush as the Son before His human birth. The study explicitly relates that scene to Jesus' answer to the Sadducees in the parallel Matthew account. That is our conclusion about the speaker in Exodus; Jesus' immediate point in this exchange is the reality of resurrection and God's relationship with the living.

deeper_study.title: Who is The Angel of the Lord?

passages.title: Mark 12:28-34
passages.section_title: What matters most to God?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 28 Now one of the scribes had come up and heard their debate. Noticing how well Jesus had answered them, he asked Him, “Which commandment is the most important of all?” 29 Jesus replied, “This is the most important: ‘Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is One. 30 Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength.’ 31 The second is this: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’ No other commandment is greater than these.” 32 “Right, Teacher,” the scribe replied. “You have stated correctly that God is One and there is no other but Him, 33 and to love Him with all your heart and with all your understanding and with all your strength, and to love your neighbor as yourself. This is more important than all burnt offerings and sacrifices.” 34 When Jesus saw that the man had answered wisely, He said, “You are not far from the kingdom of God.” And no one dared to question Him any further.
paragraphs: 28 Now one of the scribes had come up and heard their debate. Noticing how well Jesus had answered them, he asked Him, “Which commandment is the most important of all?” 29 Jesus replied, “This is the most important: ‘Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is One. 30 Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength.’ 31 The second is this: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’ No other commandment is greater than these.”

32 “Right, Teacher,” the scribe replied. “You have stated correctly that God is One and there is no other but Him, 33 and to love Him with all your heart and with all your understanding and with all your strength, and to love your neighbor as yourself. This is more important than all burnt offerings and sacrifices.” 34 When Jesus saw that the man had answered wisely, He said, “You are not far from the kingdom of God.” And no one dared to question Him any further.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
A scribe hears Jesus answer the Sadducees and recognizes that He has answered well. His question brings the discussion back to the heart of the law: which commandment matters most? Mark presents a thoughtful exchange, ending with Jesus recognizing the man’s understanding. We should let that description stand rather than assume that every questioner has the same motive.

Jesus begins with Deuteronomy 6:4–5 and adds Leviticus 19:18. The first passage calls Israel to love the one God with its whole life; the second requires love for one’s neighbor. The opening Hebrew word in Deuteronomy is שְׁמַע (shema, shuh-MAH), meaning hear or listen. That is where the familiar name Shema comes from. The command calls for attention that reaches beyond words into the way a person lives. (Deuteronomy 6:4–9; Leviticus 19:18, 33–34; Brown–Driver–Briggs, שמע)

The scribe sees that love matters more than sacrifices. This agrees with the earlier warning that religious offerings cannot replace obedience. Jesus tells him he is near God’s kingdom, but Mark does not tell us what he does afterward. Understanding the right answer is important; the passage leaves his next response untold. (1 Samuel 15:22–23)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Across the major Christian traditions, these commands are understood as calling for wholehearted love for God and practical care for other people. Wesley explains them as embracing the person’s whole capacity to love and serve, with love taking priority over even costly sacrifices. (Wesley, notes on Mark 12:28–34)
passages.god_plan_html:
The contrast with sacrifices points toward a larger question: how will God bring people into a faithful relationship with Him? Hebrews explains that repeated animal sacrifices could not finally remove sin, and that Jesus came to do God’s will through the offering of His own body. His obedience accomplishes what repeated offerings could not. (Hebrews 10:1–10)

The New Testament also shows where love for others begins: God loved us and sent His Son while we were still sinners. Those who receive that love are called to share it. The commands here therefore belong within God’s work of reconciling people to Himself and forming a people who care for one another. (Romans 5:6–11; 1 John 4:7–21)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 12:35-37
passages.section_title: How can the Messiah be David’s son and David’s Lord?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 35 While Jesus was teaching in the temple courts, He asked, “How can the scribes say that the Christ is the Son of David? 36 Speaking by the Holy Spirit, David himself declared: ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at My right hand until I put Your enemies under Your feet.”’ 37 David himself calls Him ‘Lord.’ So how can He be David’s son?” And the large crowd listened to Him with delight.
paragraphs: 35 While Jesus was teaching in the temple courts, He asked, “How can the scribes say that the Christ is the Son of David? 36 Speaking by the Holy Spirit, David himself declared: ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at My right hand until I put Your enemies under Your feet.”’ 37 David himself calls Him ‘Lord.’ So how can He be David’s son?” And the large crowd listened to Him with delight.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After answering the questions put to Him, Jesus raises a question of His own while teaching in the temple. People expect the Christ—the Messiah, God’s promised king—to come from David’s family. Jesus asks them to consider what David himself says about that king.

He quotes Psalm 110:1, where David describes the LORD speaking to someone David calls his Lord. The place at God’s right hand expresses extraordinary honor and authority. Jesus’ question asks how the promised descendant can also hold that higher place. It presses beyond a family tree to the identity and authority of the Messiah. (Psalm 110:1–7)

Mark says that David spoke by the Holy Spirit. Jesus treats the psalm as a word that deserves their attention, and the large crowd listens gladly. He does not resolve the question with another exchange here; later New Testament passages explicitly connect the psalm with His resurrection and exaltation.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The major Christian traditions understand Jesus as truly belonging to David’s family and also being greater than David: He is God’s Son and David’s Lord. Both the Catholic study notes and Calvin read Jesus’ question as showing that Davidic descent alone does not fully explain who the Messiah is. (USCCB, note on Mark 12:35–37; Calvin, Mark 12:35–37)
passages.god_plan_html:
Peter directly uses this same psalm when announcing Jesus’ resurrection. David died, but God raised Jesus and exalted Him at His right hand; the risen Lord then poured out the promised Holy Spirit. What sounds like an unanswered question in the temple becomes part of the apostles’ explanation of what God has done through Jesus. (Acts 2:29–36)

Colossians brings the wider purpose into view: the Son through whom all things were created is also the One through whom God makes peace by the blood of His cross. His greatness and His saving work belong together. God’s promised king brings forgiveness, reconciliation, and a people gathered under His care. (Colossians 1:13–22)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 12:38-40
passages.section_title: What can religious appearances hide?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 38 In His teaching Jesus also said, “Watch out for the scribes. They like to walk around in long robes, to receive greetings in the marketplaces, 39 and to have the chief seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at banquets. 40 They defraud widows of their houses, and for a show make lengthy prayers. These men will receive greater condemnation.”
paragraphs: 38 In His teaching Jesus also said, “Watch out for the scribes. They like to walk around in long robes, to receive greetings in the marketplaces, 39 and to have the chief seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at banquets. 40 They defraud widows of their houses, and for a show make lengthy prayers. These men will receive greater condemnation.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus warns His hearers about scribes who enjoy public recognition, honored seats, and impressive religious appearances while taking advantage of widows. The warning follows an exchange with a scribe whose understanding Jesus praised. Mark therefore gives us reason to distinguish a person’s conduct from the title or group to which he belongs.

The charge about consuming widows’ homes is serious: religious standing is being used alongside exploitation of people who need protection. Mark does not explain the exact financial arrangement. We can understand the wrongdoing without inventing a particular legal scheme.

The long prayers are offered for show. Jesus’ warning concerns the use of devotion as a cover for wrongdoing, and He says the judgment will be greater. The next scene draws our attention to a poor widow giving at the temple, making His warning especially important to remember as we read on.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readers broadly understand this as a warning against religious pride, hypocrisy, and the abuse of vulnerable people. Calvin distinguishes the appearance of devoted prayer from the corrupt purpose it can conceal; the length of a prayer alone is not the problem. (Calvin, Mark 12:40)
passages.god_plan_html:
God’s purpose for His people includes protecting those whom others overlook. James carries this concern into the church: honoring the well-dressed rich person while humiliating the poor contradicts love for one’s neighbor, and words of concern do little for someone who lacks food or clothing unless help follows. The church is called to make God’s care visible in its shared life. (James 2:1–17)

That responsibility also reaches its teachers. James warns that teachers face stricter judgment. Public influence is an opportunity to serve people faithfully, and it brings accountability for how those people are treated. (James 3:1–2)

passages.title: Mark 12:41-44
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus draw attention to the widow’s gift?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 41 As Jesus was sitting opposite the treasury, He watched the crowd putting money into it. And many rich people put in large amounts. 42 Then one poor widow came and put in two small copper coins, which amounted to a small fraction of a denarius. 43 Jesus called His disciples to Him and said, “Truly I tell you, this poor widow has put more than all the others into the treasury. 44 For they all contributed out of their surplus, but she out of her poverty has put in all she had to live on.”
paragraphs: 41 As Jesus was sitting opposite the treasury, He watched the crowd putting money into it. And many rich people put in large amounts. 42 Then one poor widow came and put in two small copper coins, which amounted to a small fraction of a denarius. 43 Jesus called His disciples to Him and said, “Truly I tell you, this poor widow has put more than all the others into the treasury. 44 For they all contributed out of their surplus, but she out of her poverty has put in all she had to live on.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus sits opposite the temple treasury and watches people give. Many wealthy people contribute large amounts. A poor widow gives two small copper coins. Jesus calls the disciples over because the small amount would not tell them what her gift had cost her.

His comparison rests on what remains after the giving. The wealthy contribute from their surplus, while the widow gives everything she has to live on. Mark does not tell us her private thoughts or what happens to her afterward. The contrast is already striking without adding those details.

The surrounding scenes matter too. Jesus has just condemned the exploitation of widows, and as He leaves the temple He will announce its destruction. Readers need to hear His words about this woman within that setting, alongside His recognition of the extent of her gift. (Mark 12:38–40; Mark 13:1–2)
passages.common_interpretations_html:
A long-standing reading sees the widow as an example of wholehearted giving: God values devotion and sacrifice rather than the size of a donation. Calvin explains the passage this way, emphasizing her willingness to give from very limited means. (Calvin, Mark 12:41–44)

Other readers emphasize the tragedy of a poor woman surrendering her last means of support within a religious system Jesus is judging. Sung Soo Hong makes this case by connecting the scene with the warning about exploiting widows and the coming destruction of the temple. This is an individual scholar’s reading, not an official position shared by every church. The difference concerns whether Jesus is chiefly holding up her gift as an example or exposing what has happened to someone who should have been protected. (Hong, commentary on Mark 12:38–44)
passages.god_plan_html:
There is a useful parallel between the widow’s costly gift and Jesus’ giving of Himself, though Mark does not explicitly call her an advance picture of His death. Paul makes Christ’s generosity the foundation for Christian giving: the Lord accepted poverty for our sake so that we could receive the riches of His grace. That connects generosity with God’s saving gift through His Son. (2 Corinthians 8:8–9)

Paul also explains how that generosity should shape a community. Gifts are welcomed according to what people have, the aim is to meet needs without leaving others burdened, and giving is to be freely chosen. Together these passages show a people sharing what God provides and caring for those in need. The widow’s story should be read alongside that care when considering what Christian giving means. (2 Corinthians 8:10–15; 2 Corinthians 9:6–12)

passages.title: Mark 13:1-4
passages.section_title: What will happen to the temple?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 As Jesus was leaving the temple, one of His disciples said to Him, “Teacher, look at the magnificent stones and buildings!” 2 “Do you see all these great buildings?” Jesus replied. “Not one stone here will be left on another; every one will be thrown down.” 3 While Jesus was sitting on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple, Peter, James, John, and Andrew asked Him privately, 4 “Tell us, when will these things happen? And what will be the sign that they are about to be fulfilled?”
paragraphs: 1 As Jesus was leaving the temple, one of His disciples said to Him, “Teacher, look at the magnificent stones and buildings!” 2 “Do you see all these great buildings?” Jesus replied. “Not one stone here will be left on another; every one will be thrown down.”

3 While Jesus was sitting on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple, Peter, James, John, and Andrew asked Him privately, 4 “Tell us, when will these things happen? And what will be the sign that they are about to be fulfilled?”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
As Jesus leaves the temple, a disciple admires its impressive stones and buildings. Jesus announces that these buildings will be torn down. The contrast is unsettling: the place that looks so solid will not endure. This follows His confrontations with the leaders and His warning about the exploitation of widows.

Later, seated on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple, Jesus hears a private question from Peter, James, John, and Andrew. They ask when these things will happen and what sign will announce their fulfillment. Their question introduces the warnings and promises that fill the rest of the chapter.

The Romans destroyed Jerusalem’s temple in AD 70. Josephus describes orders to demolish the temple and city, while also identifying parts of the city’s defenses that were left standing. Jesus’ words here concern the temple buildings before Him; they do not require us to claim that every stone anywhere in Jerusalem disappeared. (USCCB, note on Mark 13:1–2; Josephus, Jewish War 7.1.1)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readers commonly understand this as a prediction of the temple’s destruction, with the disciples’ questions introducing teaching that also concerns Christ’s coming. Wesley distinguishes those subjects, while readers differ over how the later parts of Jesus’ answer fit them together. (Wesley, notes on Mark 13:1–4)
passages.god_plan_html:
The loss of a building does not end God’s purpose to dwell with His people. In John’s Gospel, Jesus speaks about a temple being raised in three days, and John explains that He means His body. The disciples understand after His resurrection. This is a separate saying, but it helps us see why the story’s hope rests on Jesus rather than on the survival of Jerusalem’s buildings. (John 2:13–22)

Ephesians develops that hope further: people brought together in Christ become God’s household, with Jesus as the cornerstone and the Spirit dwelling among them. The connection concerns God’s presence with His people through Christ; it does not require assigning a hidden meaning to every feature of the temple’s destruction. (Ephesians 2:19–22)

passages.title: Mark 13:5-8
passages.section_title: How should we respond to alarming events?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 Jesus began by telling them, “See to it that no one deceives you. 6 Many will come in My name, claiming, ‘I am He,’ and will deceive many. 7 When you hear of wars and rumors of wars, do not be alarmed. These things must happen, but the end is still to come. 8 Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. There will be earthquakes in various places, as well as famines. These are the beginning of birth pains.
paragraphs: 5 Jesus began by telling them, “See to it that no one deceives you. 6 Many will come in My name, claiming, ‘I am He,’ and will deceive many. 7 When you hear of wars and rumors of wars, do not be alarmed. These things must happen, but the end is still to come. 8 Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. There will be earthquakes in various places, as well as famines. These are the beginning of birth pains.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The disciples ask about timing and signs. Jesus begins by teaching them how to respond: they must resist deception and refuse to let reports of war overwhelm them. Many will claim His identity and mislead people. An alarming claim does not become reliable simply because it comes during frightening events.

The Greek verb βλέπω (blepō, BLEH-poh) ordinarily means to see or look, and it can also mean to take care or pay close attention. Here it introduces a warning to watch against deception. Jesus is calling for discernment, not merely for people to notice events around them. (Thayer, βλέπω)

Wars, earthquakes, and famines will occur, but Jesus describes these as the beginning of birth pains. He explicitly says that the end is still to come. The childbirth picture distinguishes suffering along the way from the completion ahead; these verses give neither a date nor a method for calculating one.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Readers differ over the period chiefly in view. Calvin treats the warning as preparation for troubles and deception throughout the church’s life before Christ’s return. In that reading, distress does not mean that God’s promises have failed or that believers can skip the long work of faithfulness. (Calvin, Mark 13:1–8)

John Walvoord also recognizes recurring troubles throughout the age, but expects them to intensify toward a future period of great tribulation. His explanation of the parallel in Matthew distinguishes these general troubles from more specific signs later in the discourse. These are different ways of arranging the events, rather than official timelines held by every member of a denomination. (Walvoord, Matthew 24:4–14)
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul also uses the picture of childbirth when describing creation’s suffering and hope. Creation groans under decay while awaiting the freedom that accompanies the revealing of God’s children. Believers share that longing as they await the redemption of their bodies. This is a related picture, not a statement that every detail in Romans and Mark belongs to the same timetable. (Romans 8:18–25)

The connection gives the suffering world a future beyond its present troubles. God’s purpose includes resurrection and freedom from decay, so His people can wait with hope without treating each disaster as a new prediction of the date.

passages.title: Mark 13:9-13
passages.section_title: How will the gospel move forward through opposition?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 So be on your guard. You will be delivered over to the councils and beaten in the synagogues. On My account you will stand before governors and kings as witnesses to them. 10 And the gospel must first be proclaimed to all the nations. 11 But when they arrest you and hand you over, do not worry beforehand what to say. Instead, speak whatever you are given at that time, for it will not be you speaking, but the Holy Spirit. 12 Brother will betray brother to death, and a father his child. Children will rise against their parents and have them put to death. 13 You will be hated by everyone because of My name, but the one who perseveres to the end will be saved.
paragraphs: 9 So be on your guard. You will be delivered over to the councils and beaten in the synagogues. On My account you will stand before governors and kings as witnesses to them. 10 And the gospel must first be proclaimed to all the nations. 11 But when they arrest you and hand you over, do not worry beforehand what to say. Instead, speak whatever you are given at that time, for it will not be you speaking, but the Holy Spirit.

12 Brother will betray brother to death, and a father his child. Children will rise against their parents and have them put to death. 13 You will be hated by everyone because of My name, but the one who perseveres to the end will be saved.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus turns from public upheavals to the opposition His followers will face personally. Religious councils, beatings, governors, and kings will become part of their experience. Even family relationships may break under the pressure. He prepares them for costly loyalty rather than promising an easy mission.

Yet these threats do not stop the gospel. The hearings become opportunities to bear witness, and the Holy Spirit will supply what they need to say. This promise addresses their defense when arrested; it does not make study, preparation, or responsible teaching unnecessary. Acts later records Peter speaking before the authorities while filled with the Spirit, and apostles continuing to preach after being flogged. (Acts 4:5–13; Acts 5:40–42)

The closing promise joins perseverance with being saved. The Greek verb σῴζω (sōzō, SOH-zoh) can describe rescue from danger or salvation through Christ. The word’s range alone cannot decide which is foremost here; the warning, the promised outcome, and the wider teaching must be considered together. (Thayer, σῴζω)
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Many Christians understand the closing promise as final salvation for those who remain faithful to Christ. They differ over how that continuing faith relates to God’s preserving grace. The Reformed position in Westminster says that those truly brought to Christ will finally persevere because God keeps them, even though they may fall into serious sin for a time. (Westminster Confession 17)

The Catholic Church teaches that faith is God’s gift but can be lost, and calls believers to nourish it and persevere. Methodist teaching likewise says that people who have received grace can depart from it and, through God’s grace, repent and return. These readings treat continued faith as a real responsibility; they should not be reduced to the claim that people earn salvation by their own strength. (Catechism 162; Methodist Articles VIII–XII)

Another reading takes being saved here chiefly as physical rescue at Christ’s return for believers who survive the coming tribulation. Walvoord explains the matching promise in Matthew this way and distinguishes those survivors from believers who are killed yet still belong to Christ. This is that teacher’s explanation, not a position shared by all Protestants. (Walvoord, Matthew 24:13)
passages.god_plan_html:
The warning includes a promise about God’s larger purpose: the gospel will be proclaimed to all nations. Opposition can become part of that advance. Paul describes his imprisonment as opening opportunities for the message and encouraging others to speak more boldly. The suffering is real, but it does not put God’s mission beyond reach. (Philippians 1:12–14)

Revelation shows the destination of that worldwide gathering: a vast people from every nation before God and the Lamb, brought through suffering and cared for by Him. Their hope rests in the Lamb’s saving work, and the One they follow becomes their shepherd. This supplies the wider hope behind costly witness without requiring a verdict here on every disputed stage of the timeline. (Revelation 7:9–17)

passages.title: Mark 13:14-23
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus tell people to flee?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 So when you see the abomination of desolation standing where it should not be (let the reader understand), then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains. 15 Let no one on the housetop go back inside to retrieve anything from his house. 16 And let no one in the field return for his cloak. 17 How miserable those days will be for pregnant and nursing mothers! 18 Pray that this will not occur in the winter. 19 For those will be days of tribulation unseen from the beginning of God’s creation until now, and never to be seen again. 20 If the Lord had not cut short those days, nobody would be saved. But for the sake of the elect, whom He has chosen, He has cut them short. 21 At that time if anyone says to you, ‘Look, here is the Christ!’ or ‘There He is!’ do not believe it. 22 For false Christs and false prophets will appear and perform signs and wonders to deceive even the elect, if that were possible. 23 So be on your guard; I have told you everything in advance.
paragraphs: 14 So when you see the abomination of desolation standing where it should not be (let the reader understand), then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains. 15 Let no one on the housetop go back inside to retrieve anything from his house. 16 And let no one in the field return for his cloak. 17 How miserable those days will be for pregnant and nursing mothers! 18 Pray that this will not occur in the winter.

19 For those will be days of tribulation unseen from the beginning of God’s creation until now, and never to be seen again. 20 If the Lord had not cut short those days, nobody would be saved. But for the sake of the elect, whom He has chosen, He has cut them short.

21 At that time if anyone says to you, ‘Look, here is the Christ!’ or ‘There He is!’ do not believe it. 22 For false Christs and false prophets will appear and perform signs and wonders to deceive even the elect, if that were possible. 23 So be on your guard; I have told you everything in advance.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus describes a desecration so serious that people in Judea must flee immediately. Someone on a roof must not go inside for belongings, and someone in a field must not return for a cloak. His concern for pregnant and nursing mothers, and His instruction to pray about winter, draw attention to the human cost of escape.

The expression about an abomination that brings desolation comes from Daniel, where it concerns the profaning of worship and the interruption of sacrifice. Mark urges the reader to understand but does not spell out every detail of the event’s identity here. The command to flee is clear even where readers differ over its fulfillment. (Daniel 9:26–27; Daniel 11:31–35)

The distress will be severe, yet the Lord limits it for the sake of His chosen people. Jesus then warns against false messiahs and prophets whose signs appear convincing. A display of power cannot overturn what He has already told His followers. His advance warning is meant to help them remain alert rather than chase another claimed rescuer.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
One reading connects the desecration and flight with Rome’s assault on Jerusalem and its temple. The US Catholic bishops’ study notes identify the profaning power as Roman and read the instructions as a warning to flee rather than defend the city through a mistaken expectation of deliverance. These are study notes, not a requirement that every Catholic interpret each detail identically. (USCCB, note on Mark 13:3–37)

Another reading places the central crisis in a future period of tribulation before Christ’s return. Dallas Theological Seminary’s statement connects Daniel’s final week with judgment on the earth and its latter half with the great tribulation, after an earlier gathering of the church into heaven. This is the seminary’s stated position; it does not represent every Protestant church. (Dallas Theological Seminary, Articles XVIII–XIX)
passages.god_plan_html:
Daniel joins extraordinary distress with God’s deliverance and the hope of resurrection. That wider setting keeps the warning from ending in despair: the people’s future rests with God, whose power reaches beyond death. Mark’s account will likewise move from distress to the Son of Man gathering His people. (Daniel 12:1–3; Mark 13:24–27)

Paul also warns about deceptive signs and a figure who exalts himself in God’s temple, but says that Jesus will bring that figure’s power to an end. This is a supported connection between passages about false worship and Christ’s victory. It does not require adding a location for every image or assigning a date that these verses do not provide. (2 Thessalonians 2:1–12)

passages.title: Mark 13:24-27
passages.section_title: What will the Son of Man do?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 24 But in those days, after that tribulation: ‘The sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light; 25 the stars will fall from the sky, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken.’ 26 At that time they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds with great power and glory. 27 And He will send out the angels to gather His elect from the four winds, from the ends of the earth to the ends of heaven.
paragraphs: 24 But in those days, after that tribulation: ‘The sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light; 25 the stars will fall from the sky, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken.’ 26 At that time they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds with great power and glory. 27 And He will send out the angels to gather His elect from the four winds, from the ends of the earth to the ends of heaven.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After warning about false messiahs and misleading signs, Jesus describes the Son of Man coming with power and glory. He places this scene after the tribulation just described. The focus moves from frightening claims on earth to His own authority and the gathering of His people.

The darkened sun and moon and the falling stars recall the prophets’ descriptions of God’s judgment. Isaiah uses such language when announcing judgment on Babylon and on the nations. These scriptural connections help us hear the gravity of the scene without turning the passage into a scientific explanation of how the heavens will change. (Isaiah 13:9–13; Isaiah 34:1–4)

The Son of Man coming with the clouds recalls Daniel’s vision of One receiving lasting dominion from God. Jesus then sends angels to gather His elect from every direction. The scene emphasizes His authority and their being gathered to Him; Mark does not describe the fate of every other person in these four verses. (Daniel 7:9–14)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians broadly read this as an announcement of Christ’s coming in divine power and the gathering of His people. The US Catholic bishops’ note links the Son of Man with Daniel’s heavenly figure; Dallas Theological Seminary describes Christ’s glorious return after the tribulation within its expectation of a future reign on earth. The timing and arrangement of these events differ among readers, as the surrounding passage discussions explain. (USCCB, note on Mark 13:26; Dallas Theological Seminary, Article XX)
passages.god_plan_html:
The gathering belongs to a much older promise of God restoring His scattered people. Isaiah pictures Israelites gathered one by one from distant places to worship the Lord. Jesus’ words echo that hope on a sweeping scale, with His messengers gathering from the ends of earth and heaven. The connection is the promised gathering; it need not make every detail of Isaiah and Mark identical. (Isaiah 27:12–13)

Paul sets Christ’s coming within God’s purpose to defeat every enemy, including death. Those who belong to Christ are raised, and His reign brings the destruction of hostile powers. The hope is therefore larger than escape from a crisis: God’s victorious king brings His people into the life secured by His resurrection. (1 Corinthians 15:20–28)

passages.title: Mark 13:28-31
passages.section_title: What should the fig tree teach us?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 28 Now learn this lesson from the fig tree: As soon as its branches become tender and sprout leaves, you know that summer is near. 29 So also, when you see these things happening, know that He is near, right at the door. 30 Truly I tell you, this generation will not pass away until all these things have happened. 31 Heaven and earth will pass away, but My words will never pass away.
paragraphs: 28 Now learn this lesson from the fig tree: As soon as its branches become tender and sprout leaves, you know that summer is near. 29 So also, when you see these things happening, know that He is near, right at the door. 30 Truly I tell you, this generation will not pass away until all these things have happened. 31 Heaven and earth will pass away, but My words will never pass away.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus turns to an ordinary seasonal observation. When a fig tree’s branches become tender and put out leaves, people recognize that summer is near. In the same way, those who see the events He has described are to recognize their significance. The illustration concerns learning from what can be observed.

The statement about this generation raises a question about which people and events Jesus means. The Greek word γενεά (genea, geh-neh-AH) can refer to people living at the same time; Thayer lists this verse under that sense. The central disagreement is how that group relates to the events in Jesus’ answer, rather than whether the word supplies a fixed forty-year countdown. (Thayer, γενεά)

Jesus finishes by contrasting the passing of heaven and earth with the permanence of His words. The next paragraph states that the day and hour are unknown. We need to keep the certainty of His promise together with that limit on knowing its timing.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley takes the events in the generation saying to concern the temple and city, placing that part of the promise within the first hearers’ lifetime. (Wesley, note on Mark 13:30)

A future reading takes the generation as those alive when the final signs occur; Walvoord includes this explanation in his discussion of the matching saying. (Walvoord, Matthew 24:34)

Scofield offers another reading: the family or people of Israel will continue until the promised events are fulfilled. His note appeals to the word’s family sense. These interpretations differ over the group being described and how much of the preceding discourse is included; none turns the saying into a date Jesus names. (Scofield, note on Matthew 24:34)
passages.god_plan_html:
The enduring word is also the means by which God gives His people new life. Peter contrasts human life, which fades like grass, with God’s word, which remains, and identifies that word with the good news preached to his readers. Jesus’ assurance belongs within a larger biblical confidence that God’s promises outlast the world’s apparent permanence. (1 Peter 1:22–25)

Peter also connects the passing of the present heavens and earth with the promise of a new heaven and a new earth where righteousness dwells. God’s future calls for faithful living now, and His patience leaves room for repentance. The promise’s purpose extends beyond satisfying curiosity about dates. (2 Peter 3:8–15)

passages.title: Mark 13:32-37
passages.section_title: What does it mean to stay ready?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 32 No one knows about that day or hour, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father. 33 Be on your guard and stay alert! For you do not know when the appointed time will come. 34 It is like a man going on a journey who left his house, put each servant in charge of his own task, and instructed the doorkeeper to keep watch. 35 Therefore keep watch, because you do not know when the master of the house will return—whether in the evening, at midnight, when the rooster crows, or in the morning. 36 Otherwise, he may arrive without notice and find you sleeping. 37 And what I say to you, I say to everyone: Keep watch!”
paragraphs: 32 No one knows about that day or hour, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father. 33 Be on your guard and stay alert! For you do not know when the appointed time will come.

34 It is like a man going on a journey who left his house, put each servant in charge of his own task, and instructed the doorkeeper to keep watch. 35 Therefore keep watch, because you do not know when the master of the house will return—whether in the evening, at midnight, when the rooster crows, or in the morning. 36 Otherwise, he may arrive without notice and find you sleeping. 37 And what I say to you, I say to everyone: Keep watch!”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus states that no one knows the day or hour except the Father—not the angels and not the Son. He then repeats the practical consequence: His hearers must remain alert because the appointed time is unknown. The point is to live ready, not to solve a hidden calendar.

His illustration gives that readiness a daily shape. A man leaves his household, puts the servants in charge of their work, and tells the doorkeeper to watch. The servants have responsibilities during his absence. Waiting faithfully means attending to those responsibilities rather than abandoning them to speculate about his arrival.

The master may return at any part of the night. Jesus closes by extending the warning to everyone. The language of waking and sleeping concerns readiness for Him; it is not an instruction to stay physically awake every night.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readers commonly understand the household picture as a call to faithful service and readiness for Christ. Wesley applies the assigned responsibilities to His servants and extends the lesson beyond ministers to all people. (Wesley, notes on Mark 13:33–37)

The Son’s statement about not knowing receives different explanations within belief that He is both truly God and truly human. Wesley relates it to His human knowledge while affirming His divine knowledge. The Catholic Catechism describes His real human knowledge and its union with divine wisdom, explaining the admitted lack of knowledge in relation to what He was not sent to reveal. These accounts seek to take His human life and His identity as God’s Son seriously. (Wesley, note on Mark 13:32; Catechism 472–474)
passages.god_plan_html:
The Son’s obedience to the Father belongs within His saving mission. Philippians describes Him taking a servant’s place and obeying even to death on a cross, followed by His exaltation and the confession of His lordship. That gives the wider setting for His life of humble service; it does not settle every question about His knowledge by itself. (Philippians 2:5–11)

Paul uses the call to wake from sleep when urging believers to put aside wrongdoing and live in a way that reflects Christ. Readiness therefore has moral substance: honesty in how we live, freedom from rivalry and destructive desires, and active loyalty to the Lord we await. God’s promised future shapes the work and choices of the present. (Romans 13:11–14)

passages.title: Mark 14:1-2
passages.section_title: Why are the leaders looking for a secret arrest?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now the Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread were two days away, and the chief priests and scribes were looking for a covert way to arrest Jesus and kill Him. 2 “But not during the feast,” they said, “or there may be a riot among the people.”
paragraphs: 1 Now the Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread were two days away, and the chief priests and scribes were looking for a covert way to arrest Jesus and kill Him. 2 “But not during the feast,” they said, “or there may be a riot among the people.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After Jesus’ teaching on the Mount of Olives, Mark brings us to the approach of Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread. These feasts remember God’s deliverance of Israel from Egypt. Against that setting of remembered rescue, the chief priests and scribes seek a covert way to arrest and kill Jesus. (Exodus 12:1–20)

Their concern is the crowd’s reaction. They want to avoid a riot during the feast. The next scenes show a woman honoring Jesus and Judas offering the leaders a way to reach Him. Mark places those responses side by side as the plot moves toward His arrest.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readers commonly understand these verses as the opening of the final plot against Jesus, with the leaders’ fear of the crowd shaping their plans. The Catholic study notes connect their intention with earlier attempts that had also been restrained by fear of the people. (USCCB, note on Mark 14:1)
passages.god_plan_html:
The first Christians later prayed about the opposition to Jesus in light of Psalm 2. Acts names Herod, Pilate, Gentiles, and Israelites among those who gathered against Him, yet also places the outcome within God’s saving purpose. Human plans to silence Jesus did not take His death and resurrection outside God’s care. (Acts 4:24–30)

That connection leads to a practical response in Acts: the believers ask for boldness to continue speaking God’s word. Their confidence does not deny the danger; it rests on the God whose purpose was carried forward even through opposition to His Son.

passages.title: Mark 14:3-9
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus call this costly gift beautiful?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 3 While Jesus was in Bethany reclining at the table in the home of Simon the Leper, a woman came with an alabaster jar of expensive perfume, made of pure nard. She broke open the jar and poured it on Jesus’ head. 4 Some of those present, however, expressed their indignation to one another: “Why this waste of perfume? 5 It could have been sold for over three hundred denarii and the money given to the poor.” And they scolded her. 6 But Jesus said, “Leave her alone; why are you bothering her? She has done a beautiful deed to Me. 7 The poor you will always have with you, and you can help them whenever you want. But you will not always have Me. 8 She has done what she could to anoint My body in advance of My burial. 9 And truly I tell you, wherever the gospel is preached in all the world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her.”
paragraphs: 3 While Jesus was in Bethany reclining at the table in the home of Simon the Leper, a woman came with an alabaster jar of expensive perfume, made of pure nard. She broke open the jar and poured it on Jesus’ head. 4 Some of those present, however, expressed their indignation to one another: “Why this waste of perfume? 5 It could have been sold for over three hundred denarii and the money given to the poor.” And they scolded her.

6 But Jesus said, “Leave her alone; why are you bothering her? She has done a beautiful deed to Me. 7 The poor you will always have with you, and you can help them whenever you want. But you will not always have Me. 8 She has done what she could to anoint My body in advance of My burial. 9 And truly I tell you, wherever the gospel is preached in all the world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Between the leaders’ plot and Judas’s agreement with them, Mark tells of a meal in Bethany at Simon the Leper’s home. A woman pours expensive perfume on Jesus’ head. Some present call it wasteful because it could have been sold for a large amount and the proceeds given to the poor. Jesus defends her and relates her act to His coming burial.

Mark leaves the woman unnamed. John describes an anointing at Bethany involving Mary, Lazarus’s sister, and identifies Judas as the person objecting to the cost. Reading the accounts together helps explain why the woman here is commonly identified as Mary, while keeping each account’s own details visible. Luke’s earlier account concerns a sinful woman at a Pharisee’s home; Luke does not name her Mary or call her a prostitute. (John 12:1–8; Luke 7:36–50)

Jesus’ words about the poor do not cancel care for them: He says His followers can help them whenever they want. Deuteronomy similarly joins the continued presence of poverty with a command to give generously. What is unique here is the approaching end of His life among them and this woman’s opportunity to honor Him before His burial. Mark does not tell us the full extent of her understanding. (Deuteronomy 15:7–11)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readers broadly understand this as costly devotion that Jesus accepts in view of His death and burial. The Catholic study notes emphasize His defense of the woman and His promise that her deed will be remembered wherever the gospel is proclaimed. (USCCB, note on Mark 14:3)
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus explicitly places the woman’s act alongside the future worldwide proclamation of the gospel. Paul’s summary of that gospel centers on Christ dying for our sins, being buried, and being raised. The burial she anticipates belongs to the saving events that will be announced far beyond this room. (1 Corinthians 15:1–8)

The contrast with the surrounding plot is striking: as some prepare to hand Him over, she gives something precious to honor Him. That is a contrast Mark’s arrangement invites us to notice, rather than a claim that her gift purchases forgiveness or explains every detail of the cross.

passages.title: Mark 14:10-11
passages.section_title: How does betrayal enter the circle of the Twelve?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 Then Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve, went to the chief priests to betray Jesus to them. 11 They were delighted to hear this, and they promised to give him money. So Judas began to look for an opportunity to betray Jesus.
paragraphs: 10 Then Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve, went to the chief priests to betray Jesus to them. 11 They were delighted to hear this, and they promised to give him money. So Judas began to look for an opportunity to betray Jesus.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Judas goes to the chief priests and offers to betray Jesus. Mark stresses that he belongs to the Twelve: the opening comes from someone within Jesus’ own circle. The leaders welcome his approach, promise money, and gain a person looking for a suitable opportunity.

The agreement follows the woman’s costly gift. The neighboring scenes contrast giving something valuable to honor Jesus with receiving money to hand Him over. Mark records the agreement without explaining every thought that led Judas to it. John’s account gives further information about his dishonesty with the group’s money. (John 12:4–6)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians generally read this as a real betrayal by a close disciple, with the promised payment showing how the leaders and Judas come to cooperate. Calvin emphasizes the destructive part played by greed, drawing on John’s account of Judas’s theft. (Calvin, Mark 14:10–11 and Matthew 26:14)
passages.god_plan_html:
At the meal, Jesus Himself connects the betrayal with Scripture about a trusted companion who shared bread and then turned against the speaker. John explicitly applies that saying to the betrayal in Jesus’ circle. This connection comes from the Gospel itself, rather than from assigning a hidden meaning to Judas’s name or the payment. (Psalm 41:9; John 13:18–30)

Jesus says He is telling His followers beforehand so that the event will strengthen their belief in Him when it happens. The betrayal will be grievous, but it will not show that He was unaware of what was coming or that His mission had escaped His Father’s purpose. (John 13:19)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 14:12-21
passages.section_title: What does Jesus reveal at the Passover meal?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 On the first day of the Feast of Unleavened Bread, when the Passover lamb was to be sacrificed, Jesus’ disciples asked Him, “Where do You want us to prepare for You to eat the Passover?” 13 So He sent two of His disciples and told them, “Go into the city, and a man carrying a jug of water will meet you. Follow him, 14 and whichever house he enters, say to the owner, ‘The Teacher asks: Where is My guest room, where I may eat the Passover with My disciples?’ 15 And he will show you a large upper room, furnished and ready. Make preparations for us there.” 16 So the disciples left and went into the city, where they found everything as Jesus had described. And they prepared the Passover. 17 When evening came, Jesus arrived with the Twelve. 18 And while they were reclining and eating, Jesus said, “Truly I tell you, one of you who is eating with Me will betray Me.” 19 They began to be grieved and to ask Him one after another, “Surely not I?” 20 He answered, “It is one of the Twelve—the one who is dipping his hand into the bowl with Me. 21 The Son of Man will go just as it is written about Him, but woe to that man by whom He is betrayed! It would be better for him if he had not been born.”
paragraphs: 12 On the first day of the Feast of Unleavened Bread, when the Passover lamb was to be sacrificed, Jesus’ disciples asked Him, “Where do You want us to prepare for You to eat the Passover?” 13 So He sent two of His disciples and told them, “Go into the city, and a man carrying a jug of water will meet you. Follow him, 14 and whichever house he enters, say to the owner, ‘The Teacher asks: Where is My guest room, where I may eat the Passover with My disciples?’ 15 And he will show you a large upper room, furnished and ready. Make preparations for us there.” 16 So the disciples left and went into the city, where they found everything as Jesus had described. And they prepared the Passover.

17 When evening came, Jesus arrived with the Twelve. 18 And while they were reclining and eating, Jesus said, “Truly I tell you, one of you who is eating with Me will betray Me.” 19 They began to be grieved and to ask Him one after another, “Surely not I?” 20 He answered, “It is one of the Twelve—the one who is dipping his hand into the bowl with Me. 21 The Son of Man will go just as it is written about Him, but woe to that man by whom He is betrayed! It would be better for him if he had not been born.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The disciples ask where to prepare the Passover. Jesus sends two of them with instructions that lead to a furnished upper room, and they find things as He described. Luke names the two as Peter and John. Mark does not name the householder or explain whether the meeting had been arranged in advance. (Luke 22:7–13)

The Greek word πάσχα (pascha, PAHS-khah) can refer to the Passover lamb, the meal, or the festival. Those related uses help explain the language here: a lamb is sacrificed, a meal is prepared, and the disciples gather during the feast. The word itself does not resolve every question about the Gospel accounts’ calendars. (Thayer, πάσχα)

At the meal, Jesus says that one eating with Him will betray Him. The disciples grieve and question themselves. Sharing the table makes the betrayal especially painful. Jesus then holds two truths together: the Son of Man’s death accords with Scripture, and the betrayer bears grave responsibility. A place among the Twelve and at the table does not excuse what he is doing.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readers commonly see Jesus’ preparation and warning as showing that the betrayal does not take Him by surprise. The Catholic study notes emphasize the contrast between sharing the Passover table and betraying the One who shares it; Wesley sees the fulfilled instructions as evidence of Jesus’ knowledge and authority. (USCCB, notes on Mark 14:18–21; Wesley, note on Mark 14:13)
passages.god_plan_html:
Passover remembers God rescuing His people from bondage and judgment. Paul explicitly identifies Christ with the sacrificed Passover lamb and calls the church to live with sincerity and truth in light of that sacrifice. The meal’s setting therefore belongs to a scriptural story of deliverance that reaches its fulfillment through Jesus. (Exodus 12:1–14; 1 Corinthians 5:6–8)

Peter’s preaching likewise holds God’s purpose and human responsibility together: Jesus was handed over according to God’s plan, people put Him to death, and God raised Him. The warning to the betrayer does not disappear because God brings salvation through the cross. The saving outcome is God’s victory over sin and death, not approval of the betrayal. (Acts 2:22–24)

passages.title: Mark 14:22-26
passages.section_title: What do the bread and cup mean?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 While they were eating, Jesus took bread, spoke a blessing and broke it, and gave it to the disciples, saying, “Take it; this is My body.” 23 Then He took the cup, gave thanks, and gave it to them, and they all drank from it. 24 He said to them, “This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many. 25 Truly I tell you, I will no longer drink of the fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it anew in the kingdom of God.” 26 And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.
paragraphs: 22 While they were eating, Jesus took bread, spoke a blessing and broke it, and gave it to the disciples, saying, “Take it; this is My body.” 23 Then He took the cup, gave thanks, and gave it to them, and they all drank from it. 24 He said to them, “This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many. 25 Truly I tell you, I will no longer drink of the fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it anew in the kingdom of God.”
26 And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
During the Passover meal, Jesus takes bread, blesses and breaks it, and gives it to the disciples in relation to His body. He gives them a cup and explains it in relation to His covenant blood, poured out for many. With His death approaching, He gives them a way to understand what He is about to give for them.

The language recalls the covenant made at Sinai, where Moses presented the blood of the covenant to the people. Jesus now speaks about His own blood. His words also look ahead: He will drink the fruit of the vine anew in God’s kingdom. The scene holds His coming death and the promised future together. (Exodus 24:3–8)

After a hymn, they leave for the Mount of Olives. Mark does not name the hymn or number the cups. Paul’s account adds the instruction to remember Jesus and explains that sharing the meal proclaims His death until He comes. (1 Corinthians 11:23–29)
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians agree that Jesus connects the meal with His body and blood and His saving death. They differ over how He is present when believers share it.

The Catholic Church teaches that the bread and wine become Christ’s body and blood while their outward appearance remains. It calls this change transubstantiation. The Mass makes His one sacrifice present; Catholic teaching does not describe Jesus as being killed again. (Catechism 1362–1367, 1374–1377)

Lutheran teaching also affirms receiving Christ’s true body and blood, under the bread and wine. Luther’s Small Catechism ties the gift of forgiveness to Christ’s promise and calls for faith in His words. The meal is more than thinking back to an absent event. (Small Catechism, Sacrament of the Altar)

The Orthodox Church in America’s teaching guide likewise affirms genuine communion with Christ’s body and blood through the Holy Spirit. It stresses that this is a mystery and that its use of symbolic language does not mean the meal is merely an act of mental recollection. (OCA, Holy Eucharist)

The Westminster and 1689 Baptist confessions say that the bread and wine remain bread and wine while believers truly receive Christ and the benefits of His death spiritually, through faith. Methodist teaching similarly describes receiving Him in a heavenly and spiritual manner through faith. These teachings describe participation in Christ, with important differences from the explanations above. (Westminster 29.5–7; 1689 Baptist Confession 30.5–7; Methodist Articles XVIII)

Other explanations emphasize the bread and cup as signs that remember His death. Wesley’s note on Mark calls the cup a continuing sign and memorial of the blood establishing the covenant. His wording should be read alongside Methodist teaching about spiritual participation, rather than used to make every Protestant view identical. (Wesley, note on Mark 14:24)
passages.god_plan_html:
Jeremiah’s promise of a new covenant includes God’s instruction written within His people and forgiveness of their sins. Hebrews connects that promise with Jesus’ once-for-all offering and describes Him as the mediator of the new covenant. His death brings cleansing and access to God that repeated animal sacrifices could not secure. (Jeremiah 31:31–34; Hebrews 9:11–15; Hebrews 10:10–18)

The meal also keeps the church looking forward. Paul says it proclaims the Lord’s death until His coming, while Jesus promises future sharing in the kingdom. Remembering the cross and awaiting the kingdom belong together in the life of the people He gathers. (1 Corinthians 11:23–26)
