passages.title: Mark 14:27-31
passages.section_title: What does Jesus promise before the disciples fail?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 27 Then Jesus said to them, “You will all fall away, for it is written: ‘I will strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.’ 28 But after I have risen, I will go ahead of you into Galilee.” 29 Peter declared, “Even if all fall away, I never will.” 30 “Truly I tell you,” Jesus replied, “this very night, before the rooster crows twice, you will deny Me three times.” 31 But Peter kept insisting, “Even if I have to die with You, I will never deny You.” And all the others said the same thing.
paragraphs: 27 Then Jesus said to them, “You will all fall away, for it is written: ‘I will strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.’ 28 But after I have risen, I will go ahead of you into Galilee.”

29 Peter declared, “Even if all fall away, I never will.” 30 “Truly I tell you,” Jesus replied, “this very night, before the rooster crows twice, you will deny Me three times.” 31 But Peter kept insisting, “Even if I have to die with You, I will never deny You.” And all the others said the same thing.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
On the way to the Mount of Olives, Jesus tells the disciples that they will all fall away. He quotes Zechariah’s picture of a struck shepherd and scattered sheep. Yet He immediately gives a promise beyond their failure: after rising, He will go ahead of them to Galilee. (Zechariah 13:7–9)

Peter insists that he will remain loyal even if everyone else fails. Jesus makes the warning personal and precise: before the rooster crows twice that night, Peter will deny Him three times. Peter keeps protesting, and the others make the same promise of loyalty.

The passage places their confidence beside Jesus’ knowledge of what is coming. Their intentions are not enough to carry them through the trial. The scene that follows, where they struggle to remain awake and pray, will make that weakness visible before the arrest even begins.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readers commonly see both a warning against self-confidence and a promise of restoration after the disciples’ failure. The Catholic study notes emphasize that Jesus reassures those who will abandon Him that He will gather them again in Galilee after His resurrection. (USCCB, note on Mark 14:27–31)
passages.god_plan_html:
Luke’s account adds that Jesus has prayed for Peter and tells him to strengthen his brothers when he turns back. After the resurrection, John shows Jesus entrusting Peter with care for His sheep. These passages develop the hope already present in the Galilee promise: the risen Shepherd restores failed disciples for service. (Luke 22:28–34; John 21:15–19)

Paul later learns that Christ’s power is displayed in weakness rather than in impressive personal strength. This is a related lesson, not a claim that Paul’s thorn and Peter’s denial are the same kind of event. God’s work through His people depends on the grace of Christ, who sustains them as they serve. (2 Corinthians 12:7–10)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 14:32-42
passages.section_title: How does Jesus pray when obedience costs Him everything?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 32 Then they came to a place called Gethsemane, and Jesus told His disciples, “Sit here while I pray.” 33 He took with Him Peter, James, and John, and began to be deeply troubled and distressed. 34 Then He said to them, “My soul is consumed with sorrow to the point of death. Stay here and keep watch.” 35 Going a little farther, He fell to the ground and prayed that, if it were possible, the hour would pass from Him. 36 “Abba, Father,” He said, “all things are possible for You. Take this cup from Me. Yet not what I will, but what You will.” 37 Then Jesus returned and found them sleeping. “Simon, are you asleep?” He asked. “Were you not able to keep watch for one hour? 38 Watch and pray so that you will not enter into temptation. For the spirit is willing, but the body is weak.” 39 Again He went away and prayed, saying the same thing. 40 And again Jesus returned and found them sleeping, for their eyes were heavy. And they did not know what to answer Him. 41 When Jesus returned the third time, He said, “Are you still sleeping and resting? That is enough! The hour has come. Look, the Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners. 42 Rise, let us go. See, My betrayer is approaching!”
paragraphs: 32 Then they came to a place called Gethsemane, and Jesus told His disciples, “Sit here while I pray.” 33 He took with Him Peter, James, and John, and began to be deeply troubled and distressed. 34 Then He said to them, “My soul is consumed with sorrow to the point of death. Stay here and keep watch.” 35 Going a little farther, He fell to the ground and prayed that, if it were possible, the hour would pass from Him. 36 “Abba, Father,” He said, “all things are possible for You. Take this cup from Me. Yet not what I will, but what You will.”

37 Then Jesus returned and found them sleeping. “Simon, are you asleep?” He asked. “Were you not able to keep watch for one hour? 38 Watch and pray so that you will not enter into temptation. For the spirit is willing, but the body is weak.” 39 Again He went away and prayed, saying the same thing. 40 And again Jesus returned and found them sleeping, for their eyes were heavy. And they did not know what to answer Him.

41 When Jesus returned the third time, He said, “Are you still sleeping and resting? That is enough! The hour has come. Look, the Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners. 42 Rise, let us go. See, My betrayer is approaching!”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
At Gethsemane, Jesus takes Peter, James, and John with Him and speaks openly about His overwhelming sorrow. These are the three who witnessed His glory at the transfiguration. Now they are asked to remain with Him and keep watch as He faces what is coming.

Jesus addresses God as Abba, the Aramaic אַבָּא (abba, AHB-bah), meaning Father. Mark supplies the translation. His prayer combines trust in His Father’s power, an honest request for the cup to be removed, and submission to His Father’s will. We should hear all three parts together. (Thayer, Ἀββᾶ)

The disciples repeatedly sleep, and Jesus tells them to watch and pray against temptation. Their willing intentions meet the weakness of their bodies. Jesus, meanwhile, returns to prayer and then rises to meet the approaching betrayal. His surrender does not make the sorrow unreal; it governs His response through it.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Across the major Christian traditions, this prayer is understood as showing Jesus’ real human anguish and His willing obedience to the Father. The Catholic study notes emphasize that obedience while connecting it with His call for the disciples to pray amid their own weakness; Wesley likewise draws attention to the depth of His distress and Mark’s explanation of Abba as Father. (USCCB, notes on Mark 14:32–38; Wesley, notes on Mark 14:33–36)
passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews places Jesus’ prayers and suffering within His saving work as high priest. He is able to sympathize with human weakness, and His people can approach God for mercy and help. The One who prays in anguish here becomes the source of eternal salvation through His obedient suffering. (Hebrews 4:14–16; Hebrews 5:7–10)

The address Abba also appears in Paul’s explanation of believers’ adoption. God sent His Son to redeem people and the Spirit of His Son into their hearts, enabling them to call God Father. That does not make our suffering identical to Jesus’ saving sacrifice. It shows the family relationship His mission opens to those who belong to Him. (Romans 8:14–17; Galatians 4:4–7)
passages.current_position_html: What Does Prayer Look Like? reads Gethsemane as a model of honest surrender: Jesus expresses the real cost of His suffering and places the outcome in His Father’s hands. The study emphasizes that His repeated prayer is compatible with surrender when the Father’s will governs it. Prayer and Faith likewise understands this scene as trust in God rather than a method for securing the outcome we choose. These studies supply our position on prayer here.

passages.title: Mark 14:43-52
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus face arrest while everyone else flees?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 43 While Jesus was still speaking, Judas, one of the Twelve, arrived, accompanied by a crowd armed with swords and clubs, sent from the chief priests, scribes, and elders. 44 Now the betrayer had arranged a signal with them: “The One I kiss is the man; arrest Him and lead Him away securely.” 45 Going directly to Jesus, he said, “Rabbi!” and kissed Him. 46 Then the men seized Jesus and arrested Him. 47 And one of the bystanders drew his sword and struck the servant of the high priest, cutting off his ear. 48 Jesus asked the crowd, “Have you come out with swords and clubs to arrest Me as you would an outlaw? 49 Every day I was with you, teaching in the temple courts, and you did not arrest Me. But this has happened that the Scriptures would be fulfilled.” 50 Then everyone deserted Him and fled. 51 One young man who had been following Jesus was wearing a linen cloth around his body. They caught hold of him, 52 but he pulled free of the linen cloth and ran away naked.
paragraphs: 43 While Jesus was still speaking, Judas, one of the Twelve, arrived, accompanied by a crowd armed with swords and clubs, sent from the chief priests, scribes, and elders. 44 Now the betrayer had arranged a signal with them: “The One I kiss is the man; arrest Him and lead Him away securely.” 45 Going directly to Jesus, he said, “Rabbi!” and kissed Him. 46 Then the men seized Jesus and arrested Him. 47 And one of the bystanders drew his sword and struck the servant of the high priest, cutting off his ear.

48 Jesus asked the crowd, “Have you come out with swords and clubs to arrest Me as you would an outlaw? 49 Every day I was with you, teaching in the temple courts, and you did not arrest Me. But this has happened that the Scriptures would be fulfilled.” 50 Then everyone deserted Him and fled. 51 One young man who had been following Jesus was wearing a linen cloth around his body. They caught hold of him, 52 but he pulled free of the linen cloth and ran away naked.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
While Jesus is still speaking about the approaching betrayal, Judas arrives with an armed crowd sent by the religious authorities. He has arranged a kiss as the signal identifying Jesus. A greeting that would ordinarily express closeness becomes the means of handing Him over.

The Greek verb for the kiss is καταφιλέω (kataphileō, kah-tah-fee-LEH-oh), which can mean to kiss warmly or repeatedly. The word makes the use of affection as a sign of betrayal especially painful, but it does not tell us how long the kiss lasted. (Thayer, καταφιλέω)

Someone nearby draws a sword and cuts off the high priest’s servant’s ear. John identifies the attacker as Peter and the servant as Malchus, while Luke records Jesus healing the injury. Mark emphasizes Jesus’ question: why arrest Him like an outlaw when He has taught openly in the temple? He then places what is happening within the fulfillment of Scripture. (John 18:1–11; Luke 22:47–53)

Everyone deserts Him. Even a young man who has been following escapes only by leaving his linen covering behind. Mark does not name him. The scene leaves Jesus in custody as the others flee, bringing the earlier warning about their failure into view.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readers commonly see Jesus willingly facing the suffering ahead while His followers fail to remain with Him. The young man’s identity remains uncertain; Calvin rejects confident identification and takes his seizure as further evidence of the crowd’s violence. (Calvin, Mark 14:51)
passages.god_plan_html:
Isaiah’s suffering servant is rejected and led like a lamb to slaughter, yet bears the sins of others. Peter explicitly applies that servant language to Christ: He does not retaliate under abuse and carries sins in His body so that His people may live rightly. Jesus’ submission here belongs to that saving path, not to a lack of authority to resist. (Isaiah 53:4–12; 1 Peter 2:21–25)

Peter also describes Jesus as the Shepherd to whom wandering people return. That supplies the wider hope behind this scene of abandonment: the One left alone goes on to give His life for people who need to be brought back to God. (1 Peter 2:24–25)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 14:53-65
passages.section_title: Who is really standing before the council?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 53 They led Jesus away to the high priest, and all the chief priests, elders, and scribes assembled. 54 Peter followed Him at a distance, right into the courtyard of the high priest. And he sat with the officers and warmed himself by the fire. 55 Now the chief priests and the whole Sanhedrin were seeking testimony against Jesus to put Him to death, but they did not find any. 56 For many bore false witness against Jesus, but their testimony was inconsistent. 57 Then some men stood up and testified falsely against Him: 58 “We heard Him say, ‘I will destroy this man-made temple, and in three days I will build another that is made without hands.’” 59 But even their testimony was inconsistent. 60 So the high priest stood up before them and questioned Jesus, “Have You no answer? What are these men testifying against You?” 61 But Jesus remained silent and made no reply. Again the high priest questioned Him, “Are You the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One?” 62 “I am,” said Jesus, “and you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven.” 63 At this, the high priest tore his clothes and declared, “Why do we need any more witnesses? 64 You have heard the blasphemy. What is your verdict?” And they all condemned Him as deserving of death. 65 Then some of them began to spit on Him. They blindfolded Him, struck Him with their fists, and said to Him, “Prophesy!” And the officers received Him with slaps in His face.
paragraphs: 53 They led Jesus away to the high priest, and all the chief priests, elders, and scribes assembled. 54 Peter followed Him at a distance, right into the courtyard of the high priest. And he sat with the officers and warmed himself by the fire. 55 Now the chief priests and the whole Sanhedrin were seeking testimony against Jesus to put Him to death, but they did not find any. 56 For many bore false witness against Jesus, but their testimony was inconsistent. 57 Then some men stood up and testified falsely against Him: 58 “We heard Him say, ‘I will destroy this man-made temple, and in three days I will build another that is made without hands.’” 59 But even their testimony was inconsistent.

60 So the high priest stood up before them and questioned Jesus, “Have You no answer? What are these men testifying against You?” 61 But Jesus remained silent and made no reply. Again the high priest questioned Him, “Are You the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One?” 62 “I am,” said Jesus, “and you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven.”

63 At this, the high priest tore his clothes and declared, “Why do we need any more witnesses? 64 You have heard the blasphemy. What is your verdict?” And they all condemned Him as deserving of death. 65 Then some of them began to spit on Him. They blindfolded Him, struck Him with their fists, and said to Him, “Prophesy!” And the officers received Him with slaps in His face.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus is taken to the high priest, where the chief priests, elders, and scribes assemble. Peter follows at a distance and sits near the fire in the courtyard. Mark will return to his experience after showing what happens to Jesus inside.

The council seeks testimony that will support a death sentence, but the witnesses do not agree. Even the testimony about destroying and rebuilding the temple is inconsistent. Deuteronomy requires a matter to be established by more than one witness and warns against false accusation. Mark’s own description shows the failure of the evidence without requiring us to reconstruct every later courtroom rule. (Deuteronomy 19:15–21)

Jesus remains silent before the accusations, but answers when asked whether He is the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One. He affirms it and combines the language of God’s right hand with the Son of Man coming on the clouds. The high priest treats His answer as blasphemy, and the council condemns Him. The scene then turns to spitting, blindfolding, blows, and mockery. (Psalm 110:1; Daniel 7:13–14)
passages.common_interpretations_html: The major Christian traditions understand Jesus’ answer as affirming His identity and God-given authority, while the council rejects that claim. The Catholic study notes connect His words with Psalm 110 and Daniel 7, emphasizing His coming glory and authority as judge. (USCCB, note on Mark 14:61–62)
passages.god_plan_html:
The contrast reaches beyond a courtroom verdict: the man being condemned speaks of the authority God gives Him. Daniel’s Son of Man receives an everlasting kingdom, and Psalm 110 places the Lord at God’s right hand. Hebrews connects Jesus’ endurance of the cross and its shame with His being seated at God’s right hand. The rejected One is the One God exalts. (Daniel 7:9–14; Psalm 110:1–4; Hebrews 12:1–3)

Isaiah also pictures the Lord’s servant accepting blows and spitting while trusting God’s vindication. This is a supported parallel with the abuse Jesus receives here. His suffering belongs to the path by which He serves and saves, while those who trust Him are called to endure without returning abuse for abuse. (Isaiah 50:4–9; 1 Peter 2:21–25)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 14:66-72
passages.section_title: What happens when Peter’s confidence gives way?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 66 While Peter was in the courtyard below, one of the servant girls of the high priest came down 67 and saw him warming himself there. She looked at Peter and said, “You also were with Jesus the Nazarene.” 68 But he denied it. “I do not know or even understand what you are talking about,” he said. Then he went out to the gateway, and the rooster crowed. 69 There the servant girl saw him and again said to those standing nearby, “This man is one of them.” 70 But he denied it again. After a little while, those standing nearby said once more to Peter, “Surely you are one of them, for you too are a Galilean.” 71 But he began to curse and swear, “I do not know this man of whom you speak!” 72 And immediately the rooster crowed a second time. Then Peter remembered the word that Jesus had spoken to him: “Before the rooster crows twice, you will deny Me three times.” And he broke down and wept.
paragraphs: 66 While Peter was in the courtyard below, one of the servant girls of the high priest came down 67 and saw him warming himself there. She looked at Peter and said, “You also were with Jesus the Nazarene.” 68 But he denied it. “I do not know or even understand what you are talking about,” he said. Then he went out to the gateway, and the rooster crowed.

69 There the servant girl saw him and again said to those standing nearby, “This man is one of them.” 70 But he denied it again. After a little while, those standing nearby said once more to Peter, “Surely you are one of them, for you too are a Galilean.” 71 But he began to curse and swear, “I do not know this man of whom you speak!” 72 And immediately the rooster crowed a second time. Then Peter remembered the word that Jesus had spoken to him: “Before the rooster crows twice, you will deny Me three times.” And he broke down and wept.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Mark returns to Peter in the courtyard while Jesus is being questioned. A servant girl identifies him as someone who was with Jesus. He denies understanding what she means and moves toward the gateway. She repeats the identification to others, and he denies it again.

When bystanders press him about being a Galilean, Peter begins to curse and swear that he does not know the man they mean. At the rooster’s second crow, he remembers Jesus’ prediction and breaks down in tears. The one who promised to die with Jesus has now denied even knowing Him.

The two scenes belong together: Jesus acknowledges who He is before those condemning Him, while Peter denies his connection with Him in the courtyard. Luke adds that Jesus turns and looks at Peter before he leaves weeping. Neither account tells us every thought behind that look or every feeling Peter experiences. (Luke 22:54–62)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand Peter’s denial as a serious failure that exposes the weakness of his earlier confidence, with his tears showing recognition of what he has done. The Gospels also place this failure within a story that includes his return and restoration; it is not the final scene of his life with Christ. (Luke 22:31–34; John 21:15–19)
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus has already promised to meet His followers after His resurrection. John later shows Him giving Peter responsibility to care for His sheep. Acts then shows Peter publicly announcing Jesus’ resurrection and, filled with the Holy Spirit, speaking before the authorities. The man who denies Jesus here becomes a witness through the risen Lord’s restoring work. (John 21:15–19; Acts 2:14–24, 37–41; Acts 4:8–13)

First Peter later joins humility, dependence on God, and vigilance against temptation with the promise that God strengthens His suffering people. That is a fitting connection to this scene: confidence in God’s grace belongs together with taking weakness and temptation seriously. (1 Peter 5:6–10)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 15:1-5
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus give so little answer to Pilate?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Early in the morning, the chief priests, elders, scribes, and the whole Sanhedrin devised a plan. They bound Jesus, led Him away, and handed Him over to Pilate. 2 So Pilate questioned Him, “Are You the King of the Jews?” “You have said so,” Jesus replied. 3 And the chief priests began to accuse Him of many things. 4 Then Pilate questioned Him again, “Have You no answer? Look how many charges they are bringing against You!” 5 But to Pilate’s amazement, Jesus made no further reply.
paragraphs: 1 Early in the morning, the chief priests, elders, scribes, and the whole Sanhedrin devised a plan. They bound Jesus, led Him away, and handed Him over to Pilate. 2 So Pilate questioned Him, “Are You the King of the Jews?” “You have said so,” Jesus replied.

3 And the chief priests began to accuse Him of many things. 4 Then Pilate questioned Him again, “Have You no answer? Look how many charges they are bringing against You!” 5 But to Pilate’s amazement, Jesus made no further reply.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
At daybreak the council brings Jesus bound to Pilate. The hearing now moves from the religious leaders to the governor. Pilate asks whether He is the King of the Jews, bringing the question of His kingship into the setting of Roman judgment. (Matthew 27:1–2)

Jesus answers Pilate’s question, but gives no further reply to the many accusations from the chief priests. His silence amazes the governor. Mark does not say that Jesus has nothing to say about His identity; he has just recorded His answer and will repeatedly bring the title of king before us.

The other Gospels give more of the surrounding exchange. Luke reports accusations about subverting the nation, taxes, and kingship. John records Jesus explaining that His kingdom does not come from this world and is not defended by His servants fighting to prevent His arrest. Those passages help us understand why the word king could mean something different to Pilate from what Jesus meant. (Luke 23:1–5; John 18:28–38)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand Jesus as innocent and willingly facing the suffering ahead, rather than as unable to answer His accusers. The Reformed Heidelberg Catechism makes His condemnation under Pilate part of its explanation of the innocent Christ suffering to deliver others from judgment. (Heidelberg Catechism, question 38)
passages.god_plan_html:
The kingdom question reaches beyond Pilate’s courtroom. Jesus tells Pilate that He came to bear witness to the truth, while Philippians describes His obedience through death followed by His exaltation. The One standing bound before a governor will be acknowledged as Lord, to the Father’s glory. (John 18:36–37; Philippians 2:5–11)

This is the pattern of a king whose saving work passes through humble obedience. His silence in the face of accusation belongs within that willing path to the cross; it does not make the accusations true or give earthly rulers the final word about Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 15:6-15
passages.section_title: Why is Barabbas released while Jesus is condemned?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 Now it was Pilate’s custom at the feast to release to the people a prisoner of their choosing. 7 And a man named Barabbas was imprisoned with the rebels who had committed murder during the insurrection. 8 So the crowd went up and began asking Pilate to keep his custom. 9 “Do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?” Pilate asked. 10 For he knew it was out of envy that the chief priests had handed Jesus over. 11 But the chief priests stirred up the crowd to have him release Barabbas to them instead. 12 So Pilate asked them again, “What then do you want me to do with the One you call the King of the Jews?” 13 And they shouted back, “Crucify Him!” 14 “Why?” asked Pilate. “What evil has He done?” But they shouted all the louder, “Crucify Him!” 15 And wishing to satisfy the crowd, Pilate released Barabbas to them. But he had Jesus flogged, and handed Him over to be crucified.
paragraphs: 6 Now it was Pilate’s custom at the feast to release to the people a prisoner of their choosing. 7 And a man named Barabbas was imprisoned with the rebels who had committed murder during the insurrection. 8 So the crowd went up and began asking Pilate to keep his custom. 9 “Do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?” Pilate asked. 10 For he knew it was out of envy that the chief priests had handed Jesus over. 11 But the chief priests stirred up the crowd to have him release Barabbas to them instead.

12 So Pilate asked them again, “What then do you want me to do with the One you call the King of the Jews?” 13 And they shouted back, “Crucify Him!” 14 “Why?” asked Pilate. “What evil has He done?” But they shouted all the louder, “Crucify Him!” 15 And wishing to satisfy the crowd, Pilate released Barabbas to them. But he had Jesus flogged, and handed Him over to be crucified.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Mark describes Pilate’s custom of releasing a prisoner at the feast. Barabbas is held with rebels involved in murder during an insurrection. The crowd asks for the customary release, and Pilate puts Jesus before them as the King of the Jews.

Pilate recognizes envy in the chief priests’ actions, but they stir the crowd to ask for Barabbas instead. When Pilate asks what Jesus has done wrong, the response is a louder demand for crucifixion. Mark gives the governor’s reason for yielding: he wants to satisfy the crowd. Barabbas is released, and Jesus is flogged and handed over for execution.

The responsibility in this scene is specific: the leaders stir the crowd, those present demand crucifixion, and Pilate orders the outcome. Mark does not identify every person in the crowd or say they are all the same people who welcomed Jesus into Jerusalem. The passage does not transfer their actions to every Jewish person.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readers generally see an unjust exchange: a prisoner associated with violent rebellion is freed while Jesus is sent to death. Wesley stresses Pilate’s failure to uphold justice under public pressure; recognizing the wrong does not prevent the governor from authorizing it. (Wesley, notes on Mark 15:7–9)
passages.god_plan_html:
The release of Barabbas offers a striking parallel with Christ’s saving work: a guilty man goes free while the innocent Jesus faces death. Mark does not tell us that Barabbas became a believer or explain him as a detailed picture of every sinner. The wider connection is stated clearly in 1 Peter: Christ, the righteous One, suffered for the unrighteous to bring them to God. (1 Peter 3:18)

Paul develops the same saving purpose through reconciliation and new life. The sinless Christ bears what belongs to sinners so that people may be made right with God in Him; those who receive that life are called to live for the One who died and rose for them. The purpose extends beyond release from a human sentence to restored relationship with God and a changed life. (2 Corinthians 5:14–21)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 15:16-21
passages.section_title: What does the soldiers’ mock coronation reveal?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 Then the soldiers led Jesus away into the palace (that is, the Praetorium) and called the whole company together. 17 They dressed Him in a purple robe, twisted together a crown of thorns, and set it on His head. 18 And they began to salute Him: “Hail, King of the Jews!” 19 They kept striking His head with a staff and spitting on Him. And they knelt down and bowed before Him. 20 After they had mocked Him, they removed the purple robe and put His own clothes back on Him. Then they led Him out to crucify Him. 21 Now Simon of Cyrene, the father of Alexander and Rufus, was passing by on his way in from the country, and the soldiers forced him to carry the cross of Jesus.
paragraphs: 16 Then the soldiers led Jesus away into the palace (that is, the Praetorium) and called the whole company together. 17 They dressed Him in a purple robe, twisted together a crown of thorns, and set it on His head. 18 And they began to salute Him: “Hail, King of the Jews!” 19 They kept striking His head with a staff and spitting on Him. And they knelt down and bowed before Him. 20 After they had mocked Him, they removed the purple robe and put His own clothes back on Him. Then they led Him out to crucify Him.
21 Now Simon of Cyrene, the father of Alexander and Rufus, was passing by on his way in from the country, and the soldiers forced him to carry the cross of Jesus.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The soldiers bring Jesus inside the palace and turn His kingship into a cruel performance. They put a purple robe and a crown of thorns on Him, salute Him as king, bow before Him, strike Him, and spit on Him. The gestures that imitate honor accompany real abuse.

When the mockery ends, they put His own clothes back on Him and lead Him away to crucifixion. They compel a passerby, Simon of Cyrene, to carry His cross. Mark names Simon’s sons, Alexander and Rufus, but does not tell us when they came to faith or identify Rufus with the man later greeted in Romans. (Romans 16:13)

John records Jesus setting out carrying His cross, while Luke describes Simon carrying it behind Him. The accounts give us those details without recording the familiar later picture of Jesus falling three times or telling us the exact point at which Simon was brought in. (John 19:17; Luke 23:26)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readers commonly understand the robe, crown, greeting, and bowing as mock royal honors directed at Jesus. The Catholic study notes on the parallel scene explain the royal parody, while Mark’s wider story presents the king being mocked as the One whose authority will be revealed. (USCCB, notes on Matthew 27:28–30; Mark 14:62)
passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews describes Jesus as crowned with glory and honor because He suffered death, and connects that suffering with bringing God’s children to glory. The contrast with the soldiers’ crown is a useful parallel: human mockery does not determine the honor God gives His Son. His suffering serves the salvation of others. (Hebrews 2:9–13)

The same passage explains that He shared human flesh and blood to break death’s power and free those enslaved by fear of death. He becomes a merciful high priest able to help the tempted. The abuse on this road belongs within that saving mission, and His people receive both help and an example of faithfulness in suffering. (Hebrews 2:14–18; 1 Peter 2:21–25)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 15:22-32
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus remain on the cross?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 They brought Jesus to a place called Golgotha, which means The Place of the Skull. 23 There they offered Him wine mixed with myrrh, but He did not take it. 24 And they crucified Him. They also divided His garments by casting lots to decide what each of them would take. 25 It was the third hour when they crucified Him. 26 And the charge inscribed against Him read: THE KING OF THE JEWS. 27 Along with Jesus, they crucified two robbers, one on His right and one on His left. 29 And those who passed by heaped abuse on Him, shaking their heads and saying, “Aha! You who are going to destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days, 30 come down from the cross and save Yourself!” 31 In the same way, the chief priests and scribes mocked Him among themselves, saying, “He saved others, but He cannot save Himself! 32 Let the Christ, the King of Israel, come down now from the cross, so that we may see and believe!” And even those who were crucified with Him berated Him.
paragraphs: 22 They brought Jesus to a place called Golgotha, which means The Place of the Skull. 23 There they offered Him wine mixed with myrrh, but He did not take it. 24 And they crucified Him. They also divided His garments by casting lots to decide what each of them would take. 25 It was the third hour when they crucified Him. 26 And the charge inscribed against Him read: THE KING OF THE JEWS. 27 Along with Jesus, they crucified two robbers, one on His right and one on His left.

29 And those who passed by heaped abuse on Him, shaking their heads and saying, “Aha! You who are going to destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days, 30 come down from the cross and save Yourself!” 31 In the same way, the chief priests and scribes mocked Him among themselves, saying, “He saved others, but He cannot save Himself! 32 Let the Christ, the King of Israel, come down now from the cross, so that we may see and believe!” And even those who were crucified with Him berated Him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
At Golgotha, which Mark translates as the Place of the Skull, Jesus refuses wine mixed with myrrh and is crucified. The soldiers divide His clothes by casting lots. Mark gives the time as the third hour and records the charge placed above Him: the King of the Jews.

Two robbers are crucified beside Him. Passersby mock His words about the temple and call for Him to save Himself. The chief priests and scribes join the mockery, demanding that the Christ, the King of Israel, come down so that they may see and believe. Even the men crucified alongside Him insult Him.

The demand misunderstands the mission Jesus has already explained: He came to give His life as a ransom for others. Mark’s scene is full of people interpreting the cross as failure while the story is moving toward the saving death He foretold. (Mark 10:32–45)

Luke also records a criminal asking Jesus to remember him and receiving His promise of being with Him in Paradise. That later response adds to the picture without telling us every step of the man’s change of heart. (Luke 23:39–43)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians broadly understand Jesus’ remaining on the cross as willing suffering for the sake of others. The Heidelberg Catechism, for example, describes the innocent Christ enduring condemnation to deliver those who need God’s grace, rather than treating His suffering as proof that He has no saving power. (Heidelberg Catechism, questions 37–39)
passages.god_plan_html:
The mockery and the dividing of clothing recall Psalm 22, where a suffering man is surrounded by people who shake their heads and demand that God rescue him. John explicitly connects the soldiers’ casting lots with that psalm. The story of the cross is being told within Scripture’s account of suffering and God’s faithfulness. (Psalm 22:6–18; John 19:23–24)

Colossians then explains what appearances hide: through the cross God cancels the debt standing against His people and defeats hostile powers. The scene that looks like the humiliation of a powerless prisoner becomes the place of forgiveness and victory. That is why the gospel’s hope rests in what Jesus accomplishes through the cross, rather than His coming down to satisfy the mockers. (Colossians 2:9–15)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 15:33-39
passages.section_title: What does Jesus’ death reveal?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 33 From the sixth hour until the ninth hour darkness came over all the land. 34 At the ninth hour, Jesus cried out in a loud voice, “Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?” which means, “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?” 35 When some of those standing nearby heard this, they said, “Behold, He is calling Elijah.” 36 And someone ran and filled a sponge with sour wine. He put it on a reed and held it up for Jesus to drink, saying, “Leave Him alone. Let us see if Elijah comes to take Him down.” 37 But Jesus let out a loud cry and breathed His last. 38 And the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom. 39 When the centurion standing there in front of Jesus saw how He had breathed His last, he said, “Truly this man was the Son of God!”
paragraphs: 33 From the sixth hour until the ninth hour darkness came over all the land. 34 At the ninth hour, Jesus cried out in a loud voice, “Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?” which means, “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?” 35 When some of those standing nearby heard this, they said, “Behold, He is calling Elijah.” 36 And someone ran and filled a sponge with sour wine. He put it on a reed and held it up for Jesus to drink, saying, “Leave Him alone. Let us see if Elijah comes to take Him down.” 37 But Jesus let out a loud cry and breathed His last.

38 And the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom. 39 When the centurion standing there in front of Jesus saw how He had breathed His last, he said, “Truly this man was the Son of God!”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Darkness covers the land from the sixth hour to the ninth. Jesus cries out in the opening words of Psalm 22, and Mark translates the cry for his readers. The psalm gives voice to deep suffering and the question of why God seems far away; it also continues toward an answer and praise among the nations. We should hear the real anguish of the opening without forgetting the rest of the psalm. (Psalm 22:1–5, 19–31)

Some bystanders interpret the cry as a call for Elijah. Someone offers sour wine, and the scene continues with talk of waiting to see whether Elijah will take Him down. Jesus gives a loud cry and dies. Mark then records the temple curtain tearing from top to bottom and a centurion recognizing Him as the Son of God.

The centurion’s words answer the question running through the Gospel: who is Jesus? Mark connects his response with the way Jesus dies. It does not say that the officer can see the temple curtain from his place at the cross or give the full story of his later faith.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian traditions generally hear genuine anguish in this prayer and connect Jesus’ suffering with salvation. The Reformed Heidelberg Catechism emphasizes suffering that delivers others from judgment, while the Catholic Catechism explains that He bears sinners’ distance from God without ceasing to be united with His Father in love. (Heidelberg Catechism, question 44; Catechism 603)

The torn curtain is often understood as marking access to God through Jesus’ death. The Catholic study notes on the parallel scene also consider a warning of judgment on the temple; they acknowledge uncertainty about the curtain’s identity rather than making the architecture certain. (USCCB, note on Matthew 27:51–53)
passages.god_plan_html:
A striking parallel joins the beginning and end of Mark’s account. At Jesus’ baptism, the heavens break open and the Father identifies His Son; at His death, the curtain tears and a Roman officer identifies Him as God’s Son. Mark uses the same Greek verb, σχίζω (schizō, SKHEE-zoh), meaning split or tear, in both scenes. The repeated wording and declarations help frame the story around the identity of the Son who gives His life. (Mark 1:9–11; Thayer, σχίζω)

Hebrews explains the wider saving result through the language of access: Jesus’ blood opens a new and living way into God’s presence. Those who belong to Him are called to draw near, hold firmly to hope, and encourage one another in love and good deeds. His death forms a people who can approach God together through their great priest. (Hebrews 9:1–10; Hebrews 10:19–25)
passages.current_position_html: What Does Prayer Look Like? reads Jesus’ cry as honest prayer in the midst of suffering. He brings the full weight of His experience before God without pretending that the anguish is less than it is. The study takes this as a model for bringing grief to God without treating such honesty as unfaithfulness. This supplies our position on the prayer; it does not decide every explanation of the darkness, the curtain, or how His suffering accomplishes salvation.

deeper_study.title: The True Church According to Jesus

passages.title: Mark 15:40-47
passages.section_title: Who stays to witness Jesus’ burial?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 40 And there were also women watching from a distance. Among them were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome. 41 These women had followed Jesus and ministered to Him while He was in Galilee, and there were many other women who had come up to Jerusalem with Him. 42 Now it was already evening. Since it was Preparation Day (that is, the day before the Sabbath), 43 Joseph of Arimathea, a prominent Council member who himself was waiting for the kingdom of God, boldly went to Pilate to ask for the body of Jesus. 44 Pilate was surprised to hear that Jesus was already dead, so he summoned the centurion to ask if this was so. 45 When Pilate had confirmed it with the centurion, he granted the body to Joseph. 46 So Joseph bought a linen cloth, took down the body of Jesus, wrapped it in the cloth, and placed it in a tomb that had been cut out of the rock. Then he rolled a stone against the entrance to the tomb. 47 Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joseph saw where His body was placed.

Among them were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome. 41 These women had followed Jesus and ministered to Him while He was in Galilee, and there were many other women who had come up to Jerusalem with Him.

42 Now it was already evening. Since it was Preparation Day (that is, the day before the Sabbath), 43 Joseph of Arimathea, a prominent Council member who himself was waiting for the kingdom of God, boldly went to Pilate to ask for the body of Jesus. 44 Pilate was surprised to hear that Jesus was already dead, so he summoned the centurion to ask if this was so. 45 When Pilate had confirmed it with the centurion, he granted the body to Joseph. 46 So Joseph bought a linen cloth, took down the body of Jesus, wrapped it in the cloth, and placed it in a tomb that had been cut out of the rock. Then he rolled a stone against the entrance to the tomb. 47 Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joseph saw where His body was placed.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Mark names women who watch from a distance and explains that they had followed and served Jesus in Galilee. Their presence carries the story from His death to His burial and, in the next chapter, to the visit to the tomb. They see where His body is placed.

With the Sabbath approaching, Joseph of Arimathea boldly asks Pilate for Jesus’ body. He is a prominent council member waiting for God’s kingdom. Luke adds that he had not agreed with the council’s decision and action. His conduct reminds us to distinguish people within the council rather than assume every member acted alike. (Luke 23:50–56)

Pilate checks with the centurion that Jesus is dead before granting the body. Joseph wraps it in linen, lays it in a rock-cut tomb, and rolls a stone across the entrance. Matthew identifies the tomb as Joseph’s own new tomb; John adds that Nicodemus helps with the burial preparations. (Matthew 27:57–61; John 19:38–42)

The pressure of time belongs to the account’s stated setting: this is the day before the Sabbath. Deuteronomy calls for an executed person’s body not to remain hanging overnight, and John records the concern about leaving bodies on crosses during the Sabbath. These passages explain the urgency without requiring a reconstruction of every detail of the funeral. (Deuteronomy 21:22–23; John 19:31)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian traditions commonly regard the burial as testimony that Jesus truly died, with the named witnesses connecting His death and tomb. The Heidelberg Catechism explicitly explains the burial as confirmation of His real death; the Gospel accounts also draw attention to the care given to His body. (Heidelberg Catechism, question 41)
passages.god_plan_html:
The burial belongs to the gospel Paul received and proclaimed: Christ died for sins, was buried, and was raised. Isaiah’s servant passage also speaks of a grave associated with the wicked and a rich man in death, a supported connection with the Gospel’s account of Joseph’s tomb. The story moves toward resurrection through a real death and burial. (1 Corinthians 15:3–8; Isaiah 53:9; Matthew 27:57–60)

Paul also connects believers’ baptism with burial and resurrection with Christ. The intended outcome is a new way of life grounded in His resurrection. The burial is therefore part of the saving story in which His people come to share, not simply an interval to pass over on the way to the empty tomb. (Romans 6:3–5)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 16:1-8
passages.section_title: What do the women find at the tomb?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 When the Sabbath was over, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought spices so they could go and anoint the body of Jesus. 2 Very early on the first day of the week, just after sunrise, they went to the tomb. 3 They were asking one another, “Who will roll away the stone from the entrance of the tomb?” 4 But when they looked up, they saw that the stone had been rolled away, even though it was extremely large. 5 When they entered the tomb, they saw a young man dressed in a white robe sitting on the right side, and they were alarmed. 6 But he said to them, “Do not be alarmed. You are looking for Jesus the Nazarene, who was crucified. He has risen! He is not here! See the place where they put Him. 7 But go, tell His disciples and Peter, ‘He is going ahead of you into Galilee. There you will see Him, just as He told you.’” 8 So the women left the tomb and ran away, trembling and bewildered. And in their fear they did not say a word to anyone.
paragraphs: 1 When the Sabbath was over, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought spices so they could go and anoint the body of Jesus. 2 Very early on the first day of the week, just after sunrise, they went to the tomb. 3 They were asking one another, “Who will roll away the stone from the entrance of the tomb?” 4 But when they looked up, they saw that the stone had been rolled away, even though it was extremely large.

5 When they entered the tomb, they saw a young man dressed in a white robe sitting on the right side, and they were alarmed. 6 But he said to them, “Do not be alarmed. You are looking for Jesus the Nazarene, who was crucified. He has risen! He is not here! See the place where they put Him. 7 But go, tell His disciples and Peter, ‘He is going ahead of you into Galilee. There you will see Him, just as He told you.’” 8 So the women left the tomb and ran away, trembling and bewildered. And in their fear they did not say a word to anyone.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The women who watched Jesus’ burial now return with spices to anoint His body. Their concern is practical: the stone is too large for them to move. When they arrive just after sunrise on the first day of the week, it has already been rolled away. The place where they saw His body laid is empty.

Inside, a young man in white tells them that the crucified Jesus has risen. He directs them to tell the disciples and Peter to meet Jesus in Galilee. This returns to Jesus’ promise before His arrest: He would go ahead of them after being raised. Peter is named even after his denial. The promise of reunion reaches disciples who failed Him. (Mark 14:27–31)

The women flee in trembling and fear, saying nothing to anyone. This is how verse 8 leaves the scene. Other Gospel accounts describe their reports and encounters with Jesus; Mark’s sentence should first be allowed to convey its own shock and fear. (Matthew 28:8–10; Luke 24:9–12)

There is also an important note about what follows. Some early manuscripts end the Gospel here, while others continue with verses 9–20 or another short ending. The BSB explains this in its footnote to verse 8. Whether verse 8 was Mark’s intended ending or an ending was lost is a separate question from the passage’s clear announcement that Jesus has risen.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian traditions commonly understand the empty tomb and the messenger’s announcement as testimony that the crucified Jesus has truly risen. The message recalls His promise, includes His failing disciples, and calls for the news to be carried to them. (Methodist Article III; USCCB notes on Mark 16:1–8)
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul explains why this changes more than the disciples’ immediate grief. Christ’s resurrection is the beginning of the resurrection promised to His people, and His reign leads toward the defeat of death itself. The empty tomb opens onto a future in which death no longer has the last word. (1 Corinthians 15:12–28, 42–57)

Peter connects Jesus’ resurrection with new birth into a living hope and an inheritance that cannot perish. That hope sustains people who still suffer. The same chapter speaks of believers who love Jesus without having seen Him: the good news at the tomb reaches beyond the first witnesses to those who receive their testimony. (1 Peter 1:3–9)

passages.title: Mark 16:9-14
passages.section_title: Why do the disciples struggle to believe?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 Early on the first day of the week, after Jesus had risen, He appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom He had driven out seven demons. 10 She went and told those who had been with Him, who were mourning and weeping. 11 And when they heard that Jesus was alive and she had seen Him, they did not believe it. 12 After this, Jesus appeared in a different form to two of them as they walked along in the country. 13 And they went back and reported it to the rest, but they did not believe them either. 14 Later, as they were eating, Jesus appeared to the Eleven and rebuked them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they did not believe those who had seen Him after He had risen.
paragraphs: 9 Early on the first day of the week, after Jesus had risen, He appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom He had driven out seven demons. 10 She went and told those who had been with Him, who were mourning and weeping. 11 And when they heard that Jesus was alive and she had seen Him, they did not believe it.

12 After this, Jesus appeared in a different form to two of them as they walked along in the country. 13 And they went back and reported it to the rest, but they did not believe them either. 14 Later, as they were eating, Jesus appeared to the Eleven and rebuked them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they did not believe those who had seen Him after He had risen.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Some early manuscripts end Mark at verse 8; others include these final verses. The BSB prints verses 9–20 and explains the difference in its chapter footnote. The question is whether these verses belonged to Mark’s original ending; the resurrection itself is already announced in verse 6 and is also described in the other Gospels.

This passage moves from appearances of Jesus to reports that the disciples refuse to believe. Mary Magdalene tells the grieving group that He is alive. Two disciples also report an encounter with Him. At last Jesus appears to the Eleven and confronts their refusal to believe those who saw Him.

John gives the fuller account of Mary meeting Jesus, and Luke describes two disciples recognizing Him on the road to Emmaus and at a meal. Mark’s brief account resembles these events, but does not supply every detail or settle the exact order of all the appearances. Luke says the travelers were kept from recognizing Jesus; Mark’s different-form wording does not itself explain how His appearance changed. (John 20:11–18; Luke 24:13–35)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these appearances as testimony to Jesus’ real resurrection and the disciples’ difficulty accepting it. Jesus’ rebuke addresses their refusal to receive the witnesses’ reports; it does not portray the disciples as people who expected a resurrection and immediately accepted every report. (Wesley on Mark 16:9–14; USCCB notes)
passages.god_plan_html:
The witnesses’ struggle becomes part of the story through which later readers hear the good news. In John’s account, Thomas moves from demanding to see Jesus to confessing Him as Lord and God. Jesus then speaks of blessing for those who believe without seeing, and John explains that his written account is meant to lead readers to faith and life. Faith after the first generation receives testimony about Jesus rather than requiring everyone to repeat the first witnesses’ experience. (John 20:24–31)

Luke also shows Jesus opening the Scriptures to explain why the Christ had to suffer and enter His glory. Resurrection faith is rooted in what God has done and what Scripture says about it. The witnesses are then sent to proclaim repentance and forgiveness to the nations. (Luke 24:25–27, 44–49)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Mark 16:9-20
passages.section_title: What does Mark’s longer ending tell us?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 Early on the first day of the week, after Jesus had risen, He appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom He had driven out seven demons. 10 She went and told those who had been with Him, who were mourning and weeping. 11 And when they heard that Jesus was alive and she had seen Him, they did not believe it. 12 After this, Jesus appeared in a different form to two of them as they walked along in the country. 13 And they went back and reported it to the rest, but they did not believe them either. 14 Later, as they were eating, Jesus appeared to the Eleven and rebuked them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they did not believe those who had seen Him after He had risen. 15 And He said to them, “Go into all the world and preach the gospel to every creature. 16 Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned. 17 And these signs will accompany those who believe: In My name they will drive out demons; they will speak in new tongues; 18 they will pick up snakes with their hands, and if they drink any deadly poison, it will not harm them; they will lay their hands on the sick, and they will be made well.” 19 After the Lord Jesus had spoken to them, He was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God. 20 And they went out and preached everywhere, and the Lord worked through them, confirming His word by the signs that accompanied it.

15 And He said to them, “Go into all the world and preach the gospel to every creature. 16 Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned. 17 And these signs will accompany those who believe: In My name they will drive out demons; they will speak in new tongues; 18 they will pick up snakes with their hands, and if they drink any deadly poison, it will not harm them; they will lay their hands on the sick, and they will be made well.”

19 After the Lord Jesus had spoken to them, He was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God. 20 And they went out and preached everywhere, and the Lord worked through them, confirming His word by the signs that accompanied it.

passages.context_html:
Some early manuscripts end Mark at verse 8; others include these final verses. The BSB prints verses 9–20 and explains the difference in its chapter footnote. The question is whether these verses belonged to Mark’s original ending; the resurrection itself is already announced in verse 6 and is also described in the other Gospels.

These verses move from resurrection appearances and the disciples’ unbelief to worldwide preaching, signs, and Jesus’ ascension. The One they struggle to believe is alive becomes the Lord who sends them and works through their message. For closer reading, see the appearance passage and the commission passage.

The manuscript question is old. Irenaeus cites verse 19 as part of Mark near the close of his Gospel, showing that this ending was known early in Christian history. Eusebius later discusses copies ending at verse 8 and also explains how a reader accepting the longer text might understand it. Their testimony shows an early history of both use and discussion, rather than a concern first invented by modern Bible translators. (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.10.5; Eusebius, To Marinus 1, translated pages 97–99)
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The Catholic bishops’ notes recognize the longer ending as received Scripture while discussing evidence that someone other than Mark wrote it. These are distinct questions: a passage’s place in a church’s Bible and who first wrote it. The BSB’s note records manuscripts with different endings, allowing readers to see the textual question while reading the verses. (USCCB notes on Mark 16:9–20; BSB footnote)

Within the passage, the main differences concern baptism and the continuing place of miraculous signs. Catholic and Lutheran teaching connect baptism with God giving saving grace; Reformed and Baptist confessions explain its relation to faith in different ways, and Wesley emphasizes belief with baptism as its outward expression. The verse 16 page explains these readings from their own documents.

On signs, Dallas Theological Seminary emphasizes their role in establishing the apostles’ authority, while the Assemblies of God expects the Spirit to continue empowering mission with signs. Both affirm God’s power; they differ about how the promises apply across the church’s history. The commission passage explains these positions and their sources. (Dallas, Article XVI; Assemblies of God, section 10)
passages.current_position_html: Baptism examines this verse directly. The study observes that the promise joins belief and baptism, while the warning names unbelief as the reason for condemnation. Its conclusion is that baptism is the expected response of genuine faith, rather than a separate condition that earns salvation. The study treats baptism as commanded and meaningful. This supplies our position on verse 16; it does not settle the original ending of Mark or whether particular miraculous gifts continue today.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The movement from uncertain disciples to witnesses belongs to the New Testament’s account of God spreading the gospel. Luke describes Jesus opening their minds to understand His suffering and resurrection, then sending them to proclaim repentance and forgiveness among the nations. Acts connects that witness with the Spirit’s power. Their mission depends on the risen Lord. (Luke 24:44–49; Acts 1:1–11)

The resurrection also promises more than the survival of a message. Paul connects Christ’s resurrection with His people’s future resurrection and the final defeat of death. The Lord who sends witnesses is bringing His saving work toward that promised completion. (1 Corinthians 15:20–28, 50–58)

passages.title: Mark 16:15-20
passages.section_title: How does the risen Lord send His witnesses?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 And He said to them, “Go into all the world and preach the gospel to every creature. 16 Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned. 17 And these signs will accompany those who believe: In My name they will drive out demons; they will speak in new tongues; 18 they will pick up snakes with their hands, and if they drink any deadly poison, it will not harm them; they will lay their hands on the sick, and they will be made well.” 19 After the Lord Jesus had spoken to them, He was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God. 20 And they went out and preached everywhere, and the Lord worked through them, confirming His word by the signs that accompanied it.

19 After the Lord Jesus had spoken to them, He was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God. 20 And they went out and preached everywhere, and the Lord worked through them, confirming His word by the signs that accompanied it.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Some early manuscripts end Mark at verse 8; others include these final verses. The BSB prints verses 9–20 and explains the difference in its chapter footnote. The question is whether these verses belonged to Mark’s original ending; the resurrection itself is already announced in verse 6 and is also described in the other Gospels.

After confronting the Eleven’s unbelief, Jesus sends them to proclaim the gospel throughout the world. Belief and baptism are joined in the promise of salvation; unbelief is named in the warning of condemnation. Signs accompany believers, and the closing sentence describes the Lord confirming the message through those signs.

The ending brings together Jesus’ return to heaven, His place at God’s right hand, and the witnesses’ work on earth. His departure does not mean He has stopped acting: the final verse describes Him working through those who preach. Acts gives a fuller account of His instruction, ascension, and promise of the Spirit’s power. (Acts 1:1–11)
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians agree that Jesus calls people to believe the gospel and that baptism belongs to Christian life. They differ over how baptism relates to receiving salvation.

The Catholic Church teaches that baptism is necessary for those who hear the gospel and can receive it. It also teaches that God can save beyond the ordinary reception of the sacrament, including through martyrdom or a sincere desire for baptism. This is a claim about God giving grace through baptism, not about someone earning salvation by performing a ceremony. (Catechism 1257–1261)

Luther’s Small Catechism cites this verse to teach that baptism gives forgiveness and salvation to those who believe God’s promise. The saving gift rests on God’s word and promise. (Small Catechism, Holy Baptism)

The Reformed Westminster Confession calls baptism a sign and seal of God’s grace, while explicitly denying that everyone baptized is saved or that no one can be saved without baptism. The 1689 Baptist Confession describes baptism as a sign of sharing Christ’s death and resurrection and cites this verse when limiting baptism to people who profess repentance and faith. (Westminster 28.1, 5–6; Baptist Confession 29.1–2)

Wesley explains baptism here as the outward expression of belief, and says unbelief condemns whether a person has been baptized or not. Methodist teaching also gives baptism a greater place than a public badge: its Articles describe the sacraments as ways God strengthens faith and baptism as a sign of new birth. (Wesley on Mark 16:16; Methodist Articles XVI–XVII)

Christians also differ over whether these signs describe gifts that continue throughout the church’s life or signs with a special place in its beginning. Dallas Theological Seminary teaches that the signs establishing the apostles’ authority ended with that foundational period, while affirming that God can still work miracles. The Assemblies of God teaches that the Spirit continues to empower the church’s mission with signs, including tongues and healing. These are these organizations’ stated positions; neither represents every Protestant believer. (Dallas statement, Article XVI; Assemblies of God, sections 7–8, 10 and 12)

The signs are read alongside the rest of the New Testament. Acts records Paul surviving an unexpected snakebite and praying for the sick; it does not describe him arranging a dangerous test of faith. Wesley likewise explains the poison statement as protection if it happens, not permission to experiment. Jesus’ refusal to test God also matters here. (Acts 28:1–9; Wesley on Mark 16:18; Matthew 4:5–7)
passages.god_plan_html:
The mission belongs to the larger purpose of bringing the news of repentance and forgiveness to the nations. Luke records that purpose in the risen Jesus’ teaching, and Acts shows the witnesses receiving power for it. The strength for the task comes from God rather than from the disciples’ earlier courage or understanding. (Luke 24:44–49; Acts 1:8)

Jesus’ place at God’s right hand also looks beyond the immediate mission. Ephesians describes Him as raised above every power and made head over everything for the church. Hebrews connects signs and gifts with God’s confirmation of the salvation first announced by the Lord. Together these passages keep the focus on the risen King, the saving message, and God’s work through His people. (Ephesians 1:19–23; Hebrews 2:1–4)

Its conclusion is that baptism is the expected response of genuine faith, rather than a separate condition that earns salvation. The study treats baptism as commanded and meaningful. This supplies our position on verse 16; it does not settle the original ending of Mark or whether particular miraculous gifts continue today.

passages.title: Mark 16:16
passages.section_title: How do belief and baptism belong together?

versions.label: BSB
