passages.god_plan_html: The wider New Testament connects baptism with belonging to the crucified and risen Christ. Romans describes burial with Him through baptism and a life made new through His resurrection. The passage calls Christians to live out that new life, refusing sin’s rule and offering themselves to God. The discussion of baptism should therefore lead beyond the ceremony to the life it points toward. (Romans 6:3–14)

passages.title: Luke 1:1-4
passages.section_title: Why has Luke written this account?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Many have undertaken to compose an account of the things that have been fulfilled among us, 2 just as they were handed down to us by the initial eyewitnesses and servants of the word. 3 Therefore, having carefully investigated everything from the beginning, it seemed good also to me to write an orderly account for you, most excellent Theophilus, 4 so that you may know the certainty of the things you have been taught.
paragraphs: 1 Many have undertaken to compose an account of the things that have been fulfilled among us, 2 just as they were handed down to us by the initial eyewitnesses and servants of the word. 3 Therefore, having carefully investigated everything from the beginning, it seemed good also to me to write an orderly account for you, most excellent Theophilus, 4 so that you may know the certainty of the things you have been taught.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Luke begins by explaining what he is doing and why. Others have already written about the events fulfilled among them. Those events were passed on by people who saw them from the beginning and served in spreading the message. Luke has investigated carefully and now writes for Theophilus, who has already received instruction.

The aim is confidence grounded in a careful account. Luke points to events, eyewitnesses, teaching, and investigation. The opening gives readers a reason to pay attention to what follows and examine how the account supports what they have been taught.

The Greek word behind orderly is καθεξῆς, kathexēs (kath-ex-ACE), meaning in order or in sequence. Luke promises a connected account readers can follow. The word itself does not settle whether every smaller episode is arranged in strict time order; that must be considered as the account unfolds. (Thayer’s lexicon)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readers commonly understand this opening as Luke’s explanation of his careful work and his desire to strengthen confidence in the message about Jesus. Wesley and the Catholic bishops’ study notes both emphasize investigation, an orderly account, and the reader’s assurance. (Wesley on Luke 1:1–4; USCCB notes on Luke 1:1–4)
passages.god_plan_html:
Luke begins with things fulfilled, and near the Gospel’s end Jesus explains His suffering and resurrection through the Law, Prophets, and Psalms. The story is moving toward the fulfillment of God’s promises and the proclamation of repentance and forgiveness to the nations. Reading the whole account lets us see that purpose develop. (Luke 24:44–49)

Acts continues the account for Theophilus, describing the risen Jesus and the witnesses sent in the Spirit’s power. Luke’s writing helps carry testimony about these events beyond the people who first saw them. John states a related purpose for his own written Gospel: that readers may believe in Jesus and have life in His name. (Acts 1:1–8; John 20:30–31)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 1:5-17
passages.section_title: Why is John’s birth announced before Jesus’?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 In the time of Herod king of Judea there was a priest named Zechariah, who belonged to the priestly division of Abijah, and whose wife Elizabeth was a descendant of Aaron. 6 Both of them were righteous in the sight of God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and decrees of the Lord. 7 But they had no children, because Elizabeth was barren, and they were both well along in years. 8 One day while Zechariah’s division was on duty and he was serving as priest before God, 9 he was chosen by lot, according to the custom of the priesthood, to enter the temple of the Lord and burn incense. 10 And at the hour of the incense offering, the whole congregation was praying outside. 11 Just then an angel of the Lord appeared to Zechariah, standing at the right side of the altar of incense. 12 When Zechariah saw him, he was startled and gripped with fear. 13 But the angel said to him, “Do not be afraid, Zechariah, because your prayer has been heard. Your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you are to give him the name John. 14 He will be a joy and delight to you, and many will rejoice at his birth, 15 for he will be great in the sight of the Lord. He shall never take wine or strong drink, and he will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb. 16 Many of the sons of Israel he will turn back to the Lord their God. 17 And he will go on before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to their children and the disobedient to the wisdom of the righteous—to make ready a people prepared for the Lord.”
paragraphs: 5 In the time of Herod king of Judea there was a priest named Zechariah, who belonged to the priestly division of Abijah, and whose wife Elizabeth was a descendant of Aaron. 6 Both of them were righteous in the sight of God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and decrees of the Lord. 7 But they had no children, because Elizabeth was barren, and they were both well along in years.

8 One day while Zechariah’s division was on duty and he was serving as priest before God, 9 he was chosen by lot, according to the custom of the priesthood, to enter the temple of the Lord and burn incense. 10 And at the hour of the incense offering, the whole congregation was praying outside. 11 Just then an angel of the Lord appeared to Zechariah, standing at the right side of the altar of incense. 12 When Zechariah saw him, he was startled and gripped with fear.

13 But the angel said to him, “Do not be afraid, Zechariah, because your prayer has been heard. Your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you are to give him the name John. 14 He will be a joy and delight to you, and many will rejoice at his birth, 15 for he will be great in the sight of the Lord. He shall never take wine or strong drink, and he will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb. 16 Many of the sons of Israel he will turn back to the Lord their God. 17 And he will go on before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to their children and the disobedient to the wisdom of the righteous—to make ready a people prepared for the Lord.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Luke moves from his introduction into the time of Herod, king of Judea. Zechariah serves as a priest in the division of Abijah, and Elizabeth also comes from Aaron’s family. The divisions belong to the priestly order described in 1 Chronicles, where Abijah is named among the twenty-four groups. (1 Chronicles 24:1–19)

The couple are described as righteous and faithful to God’s commands, yet they have no child and are well along in years. Luke puts their faithfulness and their sorrow together. Their childlessness is not presented as proof that they have failed to please God.

While the congregation prays outside, Zechariah is chosen by lot to burn incense inside the temple. An angel appears and tells him that his prayer has been heard: Elizabeth will bear a son named John. The promised joy will reach beyond their household because John has a work to do among the people of Israel.

John will be set apart for God’s service, filled with the Holy Spirit from his mother’s womb, and sent to turn people back to the Lord. His work is described in terms of Elijah’s spirit and power, including reconciliation within families and a turning from disobedience. The announcement reaches back to Malachi’s promise of a messenger preparing the Lord’s way. (Malachi 3:1; Malachi 4)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian traditions commonly read John as the promised forerunner who prepares people for Jesus, serving with the kind of Spirit-given power associated with Elijah. Calvin, Wesley, and the Catholic bishops’ notes connect his work with Malachi’s promise and the call to return to God. (Calvin on Luke 1:16–17; Wesley on Luke 1:16–17; USCCB notes on Luke 1:17)
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus later identifies John as the messenger who prepares His way and explains his connection with Elijah. John himself denies being Elijah in person and directs attention to the One coming after him. Luke’s description of spirit and power helps us understand the connection as a God-given role and work, rather than the same person living another life. (Matthew 11:7–15; Matthew 17:9–13; John 1:19–34)

Later in the chapter, Zechariah connects these events with God remembering His covenant with Abraham. He describes John’s task as giving people knowledge of salvation through forgiveness of sins. The family’s joy is part of that wider mercy: God is preparing people to receive the Savior He promised. Paul’s account of Israel’s story in Acts likewise places John’s call to repentance immediately before the arrival of Jesus. (Luke 1:67–79; Acts 13:16–26)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 1:18-25
passages.section_title: What happens when Zechariah doubts the promise?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 “How can I be sure of this?” Zechariah asked the angel. “I am an old man, and my wife is well along in years.” 19 “I am Gabriel,” replied the angel. “I stand in the presence of God, and I have been sent to speak to you and to bring you this good news. 20 And now you will be silent and unable to speak until the day this comes to pass, because you did not believe my words, which will be fulfilled at their proper time.” 21 Meanwhile, the people were waiting for Zechariah and wondering why he took so long in the temple. 22 When he came out and was unable to speak to them, they realized he had seen a vision in the temple. He kept making signs to them but remained unable to speak. 23 And when the days of his service were complete, he returned home. 24 After these days, his wife Elizabeth became pregnant and for five months remained in seclusion. She declared, 25 “The Lord has done this for me. In these days He has shown me favor and taken away my disgrace among the people.”
paragraphs: 18 “How can I be sure of this?” Zechariah asked the angel. “I am an old man, and my wife is well along in years.” 19 “I am Gabriel,” replied the angel. “I stand in the presence of God, and I have been sent to speak to you and to bring you this good news. 20 And now you will be silent and unable to speak until the day this comes to pass, because you did not believe my words, which will be fulfilled at their proper time.”

21 Meanwhile, the people were waiting for Zechariah and wondering why he took so long in the temple. 22 When he came out and was unable to speak to them, they realized he had seen a vision in the temple. He kept making signs to them but remained unable to speak. 23 And when the days of his service were complete, he returned home. 24 After these days, his wife Elizabeth became pregnant and for five months remained in seclusion. She declared, 25 “The Lord has done this for me. In these days He has shown me favor and taken away my disgrace among the people.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Zechariah asks how he can be sure of the announcement, pointing to his own age and Elizabeth’s. The angel identifies himself as Gabriel, sent from God to bring this good news. He also gives the reason for Zechariah’s coming silence: he has not believed the message.

The silence is both a consequence and a sign. Zechariah will be unable to speak until the promised events happen. His disbelief does not cancel the promise: Gabriel says the words will be fulfilled at their proper time. The waiting people realize he has seen a vision when he emerges unable to speak.

After finishing his service, Zechariah goes home. Elizabeth becomes pregnant and remains in seclusion for five months. Luke records her gratitude but does not explain why she withdraws. She understands the pregnancy as God’s favor taking away her disgrace among the people. Her own words tell us what the change means to her.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readers commonly understand Zechariah’s silence as a response to his unbelief, with the promised pregnancy displaying God’s faithfulness and mercy. The account holds together a real failure of trust and a promise that God still brings to fulfillment. (Wesley on Luke 1:18–25; USCCB notes on Luke 1:20)
passages.god_plan_html:
There is a supported parallel with earlier births in Israel’s story. Sarah receives the promise of a son when she and Abraham are old; Hannah brings her grief over childlessness to God and later bears Samuel. In each account a particular child has a place in the unfolding story of God’s people. Elizabeth’s pregnancy belongs to that pattern of God giving life and preparing His servants. The parallel does not turn their particular promises into a promise that every childless couple will conceive. (Genesis 18:9–15; 1 Samuel 1:1–20)

The story also moves toward restored praise. When John is born and named, Zechariah will speak again and praise God’s mercy and faithfulness. His temporary silence is part of a story that ends with testimony about the God who keeps His word. Elizabeth’s gratitude and Zechariah’s later praise draw attention to Him. (Luke 1:57–79)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 1:26-38
passages.section_title: Who is the child promised to Mary?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 26 In the sixth month, God sent the angel Gabriel to a town in Galilee called Nazareth, 27 to a virgin pledged in marriage to a man named Joseph, who was of the house of David. And the virgin’s name was Mary. 28 The angel appeared to her and said, “Greetings, you who are highly favored! The Lord is with you.” 29 Mary was greatly troubled at his words and wondered what kind of greeting this might be. 30 So the angel told her, “Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God. 31 Behold, you will conceive and give birth to a son, and you are to give Him the name Jesus. 32 He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. The Lord God will give Him the throne of His father David, 33 and He will reign over the house of Jacob forever. His kingdom will never end!” 34 “How can this be,” Mary asked the angel, “since I am a virgin?” 35 The angel replied, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Six months into Elizabeth’s pregnancy, Gabriel is sent to Mary in Nazareth. She is a virgin pledged to Joseph, a descendant of David. The announcement resembles the one given to Zechariah, but now the promised child is the Son of the Most High who will reign forever.

Mary is troubled by the greeting and asks how she can have a child while she is a virgin. Gabriel answers by describing the work of the Holy Spirit and the power of God. He also tells her about Elizabeth’s pregnancy. Mary responds by offering herself as the Lord’s servant and accepting His word.

The word behind highly favored comes from χαριτόω, charitoō (khar-ee-TOH-oh), meaning to show favor or bestow grace. Mary is the recipient of God’s favor. The word helps us hear the gift in the greeting; its meaning alone does not settle every later belief about Mary. (Thayer’s lexicon)

The promise about David’s throne recalls God’s covenant with David. The child’s identity brings the two announcements into focus: John prepares people for the Lord, while Jesus is the Son whose kingdom has no end. (2 Samuel 7:8–16)
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian traditions share the central confession that Jesus is conceived through the Holy Spirit and born of the virgin Mary. Catholic and Reformed teaching both affirm that He truly receives human nature from her; He is truly human and remains the eternal Son of God. (Catechism 484–496; Westminster 8.2)

Traditions differ over how the greeting relates to Mary’s own life. The Catholic Church connects her being filled with grace with its teaching that she was preserved from original sin from her conception. It explicitly describes this as salvation given through Christ’s merits, not independence from a Savior. Calvin and Wesley read the greeting as God freely favoring Mary; their explanations do not draw that further conclusion from it. The Reformed confession describes inherited sin as belonging to Adam’s descendants born in the ordinary way. (Catechism 490–494; Calvin on Luke 1:28; Wesley on Luke 1:28; Westminster 6.3)

Readers also differ over how David’s kingdom promise unfolds. Wesley explains the throne as Christ’s spiritual kingdom and includes all true believers within the house of Jacob. Dallas Theological Seminary’s statement expects Christ’s return to include Israel’s restoration and the fulfillment of God’s covenant promises to that nation. Both affirm His kingship; they place different emphasis on how the promise reaches its fulfillment. (Wesley on Luke 1:32–33; Dallas statement, Article XX)
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul describes the Son’s coming as happening when the time had fully come: He is born of a woman and born under the law to redeem and bring people into God’s family. The announcement is part of that movement from promise to the Son’s coming, and from His coming to the gift of adoption and the Spirit. (Galatians 4:4–7)

The wider New Testament also connects Jesus’ true humanity with His saving work. Romans contrasts Adam’s disobedience with Christ’s obedience, and Hebrews explains that the Son shares our flesh and blood to defeat death’s power and become a merciful priest for His people. These are explicit New Testament connections. His coming joins Him to the people He came to save, and His obedience opens the way to life. (Romans 5:12–21; Hebrews 2:9–18)

passages.title: Luke 1:39-45
passages.section_title: What does Elizabeth recognize when Mary arrives?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 39 In those days Mary got ready and hurried to a town in the hill country of Judah, 40 where she entered the home of Zechariah and greeted Elizabeth. 41 When Elizabeth heard Mary’s greeting, the baby leaped in her womb, and Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit. 42 In a loud voice she exclaimed, “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb! 43 And why am I so honored, that the mother of my Lord should come to me? 44 For as soon as the sound of your greeting reached my ears, the baby in my womb leaped for joy. 45 Blessed is she who has believed that the Lord’s word to her will be fulfilled.”
paragraphs: 39 In those days Mary got ready and hurried to a town in the hill country of Judah, 40 where she entered the home of Zechariah and greeted Elizabeth. 41 When Elizabeth heard Mary’s greeting, the baby leaped in her womb, and Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit.

42 In a loud voice she exclaimed, “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb! 43 And why am I so honored, that the mother of my Lord should come to me? 44 For as soon as the sound of your greeting reached my ears, the baby in my womb leaped for joy. 45 Blessed is she who has believed that the Lord’s word to her will be fulfilled.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Mary hurries to the hill country of Judah and enters Zechariah’s home. When she greets Elizabeth, the baby leaps in Elizabeth’s womb and Elizabeth is filled with the Holy Spirit. The two birth announcements now meet in one household.

Elizabeth blesses Mary and her child, identifies Mary as the mother of her Lord, and describes the baby’s movement as joy. Her words direct attention to who Mary’s child is. Jesus is acknowledged as Lord before His birth.

Elizabeth also blesses Mary for believing that God’s word will be fulfilled. This follows Zechariah’s earlier failure to believe Gabriel. The difference appears in the story itself: Mary receives assurance and offers herself as a servant; Zechariah’s silence is expressly connected with his disbelief. Luke presents faith in God’s promise as something to celebrate. (Luke 1:18–20, 34–38)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly see this meeting as Spirit-given recognition of Jesus and encouragement for Mary’s faith: Catholic teaching connects Elizabeth’s words with calling Mary the Mother of God, meaning that the Son she bears is truly God become human; Calvin also explains mother of my Lord through Jesus being both God and man in one person. The title concerns who Jesus is and does not mean that Mary is the source of God’s eternal existence or the mother of the Father and the Spirit. (Catechism 495; Calvin on Luke 1:43; Westminster 8.2)
passages.god_plan_html:
John’s promised work is to prepare people for the Lord, and even this meeting draws attention to Jesus. It is a fitting early sign of the direction his ministry will take. Later John explains that his baptism serves to reveal Jesus to Israel and testifies that Jesus is the Son of God. The connection is about the purpose of John’s witness, without claiming that Luke explains everything the unborn child understands. (Luke 1:15–17; John 1:29–34)

The Spirit’s work here also belongs to a wider pattern of making Jesus known. Jesus later teaches that the Spirit will glorify Him and lead His witnesses into truth. The household’s joy anticipates a witness that will reach beyond the family, through people empowered to speak about the risen Lord. (John 16:7–15; Acts 1:8)

passages.title: Luke 1:46-56
passages.section_title: Why does Mary praise God for lifting up the humble?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 46 Then Mary said: “My soul magnifies the Lord, 47 and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior! 48 For He has looked with favor on the humble state of His servant. From now on all generations will call me blessed. 49 For the Mighty One has done great things for me. Holy is His name. 50 His mercy extends to those who fear Him, from generation to generation. 51 He has performed mighty deeds with His arm; He has scattered those who are proud in the thoughts of their hearts. 52 He has brought down rulers from their thrones, but has exalted the humble. 53 He has filled the hungry with good things, but has sent the rich away empty. 54 He has helped His servant Israel, remembering to be merciful, 55 as He promised to our fathers, to Abraham and his descendants forever.” 56 Mary stayed with Elizabeth for about three months and then returned home.

From now on all generations will call me blessed. 49 For the Mighty One has done great things for me. Holy is His name. 50 His mercy extends to those who fear Him, from generation to generation.

51 He has performed mighty deeds with His arm; He has scattered those who are proud in the thoughts of their hearts. 52 He has brought down rulers from their thrones, but has exalted the humble. 53 He has filled the hungry with good things, but has sent the rich away empty. 54 He has helped His servant Israel, remembering to be merciful, 55 as He promised to our fathers, to Abraham and his descendants forever.” 56 Mary stayed with Elizabeth for about three months and then returned home.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Mary answers Elizabeth’s blessing with praise directed to God. She rejoices in Him as her Savior and acknowledges what He has done for His lowly servant. The reason future generations will call her blessed is the Mighty One’s work for her.

Her praise then reaches beyond her own experience. She speaks of mercy across generations, the proud being scattered, rulers brought down, the humble lifted up, and the hungry filled. The song takes ordinary measures of importance—power, rank, and wealth—and places them under God’s judgment and mercy.

The final lines identify God’s help for Israel with His promise to Abraham and his descendants. This is praise for the God who remembers His word. Mary stays with Elizabeth about three months and then returns home; Luke does not explicitly say whether she remains for John’s birth.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian traditions commonly hear a song of gratitude for God’s mercy, His care for the humble, and His faithfulness to Israel. Mary’s own blessing belongs within that larger praise, rather than making her the source of the saving work. (Calvin on Luke 1:46–49; USCCB notes on Luke 1:46–55)

Her description of God as her Savior enters a real difference about Mary. Wesley understands her as sharing the same need for rescue from sin as other believers. Catholic teaching also affirms her need for Christ as Savior, while explaining her salvation as His grace preserving her from original sin from the start. Both readings call her saved by God; they differ over how that salvation applies to her. (Wesley on Luke 1:47; Catechism 491–492)
passages.god_plan_html:
There is a strong scriptural parallel with Hannah’s song after Samuel’s birth. Hannah likewise praises God’s holiness and salvation, the breaking of human pride, and His lifting of the poor. The resemblance places Mary’s praise within Israel’s long story of God working through people whom the powerful overlook. Her words about mercy for those who fear Him also echo Psalm 103. These are supported connections between the songs, not a claim that every detail is identical. (1 Samuel 2:1–10; Psalm 103:1–18)

Paul later explains how the blessing promised to Abraham reaches the nations through Christ. Those who belong to Christ become heirs of the promise, receiving the Spirit through faith. Mary’s praise for God remembering Abraham thus belongs to a saving purpose that reaches beyond one household to people from the nations. (Galatians 3:6–14, 26–29)

passages.title: Luke 1:57-66
passages.section_title: Why is the child named John?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 57 When the time came for Elizabeth to have her child, she gave birth to a son. 58 Her neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had shown her great mercy, and they rejoiced with her. 59 On the eighth day, when they came to circumcise the child, they were going to name him after his father Zechariah. 60 But his mother replied, “No! He shall be called John.” 61 They said to her, “There is no one among your relatives who bears this name.” 62 So they made signs to his father to find out what he wanted to name the child. 63 Zechariah asked for a tablet and wrote, “His name is John.” And they were all amazed. 64 Immediately Zechariah’s mouth was opened and his tongue was released, and he began to speak, praising God. 65 All their neighbors were filled with awe, and people throughout the hill country of Judea were talking about these events. 66 And all who heard this wondered in their hearts and asked, “What then will this child become?” For the Lord’s hand was with him.

He shall be called John.”

61 They said to her, “There is no one among your relatives who bears this name.” 62 So they made signs to his father to find out what he wanted to name the child. 63 Zechariah asked for a tablet and wrote, “His name is John.” And they were all amazed. 64 Immediately Zechariah’s mouth was opened and his tongue was released, and he began to speak, praising God. 65 All their neighbors were filled with awe, and people throughout the hill country of Judea were talking about these events. 66 And all who heard this wondered in their hearts and asked, “What then will this child become?” For the Lord’s hand was with him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Elizabeth gives birth to the son Gabriel promised. Her neighbors and relatives share her joy because they recognize the Lord’s mercy toward her. The account moves from a promise given privately in the temple to events known throughout the surrounding community.

On the eighth day, the child is circumcised. The family expects him to be called Zechariah, but Elizabeth insists on John. When they ask his father, Zechariah writes that John is his name. He accepts the name God gave through Gabriel, and his speech is immediately restored. (Luke 1:13, 20)

The first use Luke records of his restored voice is praise to God. The neighbors respond with awe and wonder about the child’s future. Their question prepares for Zechariah’s prophecy, which explains John’s part in God’s saving work.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian traditions commonly read the naming and restored speech as fulfillment of Gabriel’s announcement, with Zechariah now acting on the word he had doubted. The community’s joy and awe draw attention to God’s mercy and the work ahead for this child. (Wesley on Luke 1:60–66; USCCB notes on Luke 1:57–66)
passages.god_plan_html:
John’s circumcision places him within Israel’s covenant story. God had given Abraham circumcision as the covenant sign, including the instruction about the eighth day. The forerunner of Jesus comes from within the people who received those promises; his birth does not begin an unrelated story. (Genesis 17:9–14)

The neighbors wonder what John will become. Later, John will describe his own calling as going ahead of Christ, comparing his joy to that of a bridegroom’s friend. The extraordinary attention surrounding his birth leads toward a ministry that directs attention to Jesus. (John 3:22–30)

passages.title: Luke 1:67-80
passages.section_title: What salvation does Zechariah celebrate?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 67 Then his father Zechariah was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied: 68 “Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, because He has visited and redeemed His people. 69 He has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of His servant David, 70 as He spoke through His holy prophets, those of ages past, 71 salvation from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us, 72 to show mercy to our fathers and to remember His holy covenant, 73 the oath He swore to our father Abraham, to grant us 74 deliverance from hostile hands, that we may serve Him without fear, 75 in holiness and righteousness before Him all the days of our lives. 76 And you, child, will be called a prophet of the Most High; for you will go on before the Lord to prepare the way for Him, 77 to give to His people the knowledge of salvation through the forgiveness of their sins, 78 because of the tender mercy of our God, by which the Dawn will visit us from on high, 79 to shine on those who live in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the path of peace.” 80 And the child grew and became strong in spirit; and he lived in the wilderness until the time of his public appearance to Israel.

76 And you, child, will be called a prophet of the Most High; for you will go on before the Lord to prepare the way for Him, 77 to give to His people the knowledge of salvation through the forgiveness of their sins, 78 because of the tender mercy of our God, by which the Dawn will visit us from on high, 79 to shine on those who live in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the path of peace.” 80 And the child grew and became strong in spirit; and he lived in the wilderness until the time of his public appearance to Israel.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Filled with the Holy Spirit, Zechariah praises the God of Israel for visiting and redeeming His people. His words begin with the promised Savior from David’s house, rather than with his own son. John’s family belongs to Aaron’s line; the coming child announced to Mary is the King linked with David. (Luke 1:5, 27, 32–33)

The image of a horn of salvation speaks of strength to rescue. The Greek word is κέρας, keras (KEH-ras), a horn, used here as a picture of a mighty deliverer. Psalm 18 uses the same image when praising God as protector and rescuer. Zechariah is celebrating God’s saving power. (Thayer’s lexicon; Psalm 18:1–3)

The prophecy connects rescue with God’s covenant and oath to Abraham. Its purpose includes a changed life: serving God without fear, in holiness and righteousness. Then Zechariah addresses John as the prophet who will prepare the Lord’s way by making salvation known through forgiveness of sins.

The closing picture is dawn bringing light to people in darkness and the shadow of death, guiding them toward peace. The chapter ends with John growing strong in spirit and living in the wilderness until his public appearance. The promised ministry lies ahead.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian traditions commonly understand the song as praise for God’s promised salvation through Christ, with John preparing His way. The references to David, Abraham, forgiveness, and holy service place the child’s future work within God’s faithfulness to His people. (USCCB notes on Luke 1:68–79; Wesley on Luke 1:67–78)

Readings differ over how the promises of rescue and restoration unfold. Wesley emphasizes deliverance from Satan and sin so that people can love and serve God in holiness. Dallas Theological Seminary also expects a future restoration of Israel and fulfillment of the nation’s covenant promises at Christ’s return. These emphases affect how readers connect the song’s present gift of forgiveness with the promised future. (Wesley on Luke 1:74–75; Dallas statement, Article XX)
passages.god_plan_html:
The oath to Abraham included blessing reaching all nations through his offspring. Paul explicitly connects the promised offspring with Christ and explains that people who belong to Him share in the inheritance. Zechariah’s praise for remembered mercy therefore belongs to a purpose whose reach extends to the nations. (Genesis 22:15–18; Galatians 3:6–18, 26–29)

The dawn picture has a supported connection with Isaiah’s promise of light for people in darkness and the shadow of death. Matthew explicitly applies that prophecy to Jesus’ ministry in Galilee. This is a related prophetic picture, not a claim that every detail in Zechariah’s song comes from that single passage. (Isaiah 9:1–7; Matthew 4:12–17)

God’s mercy also forms a people who live differently. Ephesians describes salvation by grace leading into good works, and Jews and Gentiles brought near to God together through Christ. Its account of peace and shared access to the Father shows how rescue can lead into the holy service and life with God celebrated here. (Ephesians 2:1–22)

passages.title: Luke 2:1-7
passages.section_title: Why is Jesus born in Bethlehem?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now in those days a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that a census should be taken of the whole empire. 2 This was the first census to take place while Quirinius was governor of Syria. 3 And everyone went to his own town to register. 4 So Joseph also went up from Nazareth in Galilee to Judea, to the city of David called Bethlehem, since he was from the house and line of David. 5 He went there to register with Mary, who was pledged to him in marriage and was expecting a child. 6 While they were there, the time came for her Child to be born. 7 And she gave birth to her firstborn, a Son. She wrapped Him in swaddling cloths and laid Him in a manger, because there was no room for them in the inn.
paragraphs: 1 Now in those days a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that a census should be taken of the whole empire. 2 This was the first census to take place while Quirinius was governor of Syria. 3 And everyone went to his own town to register. 4 So Joseph also went up from Nazareth in Galilee to Judea, to the city of David called Bethlehem, since he was from the house and line of David. 5 He went there to register with Mary, who was pledged to him in marriage and was expecting a child.

6 While they were there, the time came for her Child to be born. 7 And she gave birth to her firstborn, a Son. She wrapped Him in swaddling cloths and laid Him in a manger, because there was no room for them in the inn.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Luke places the birth within the rule of Caesar Augustus and a registration connected with Quirinius. Joseph travels from Nazareth to Bethlehem because he belongs to David’s house and line. Mary, pledged to him and expecting a child, goes with him.

While they are there, Mary gives birth, wraps her Son in cloths, and lays Him in a manger—a feeding trough. Luke tells us there is no room in the lodging place. He does not give the time of night, say the birth happens immediately on their arrival, or describe an innkeeper refusing them.

The Greek word translated inn is κατάλυμα, kataluma (kat-AL-oo-mah), meaning a lodging place or room. Luke uses the same word for the guest room where Jesus will eat the Passover. This helps explain why readers picture different settings for the birth; the word does not by itself identify a particular building or household. (Thayer’s lexicon; Luke 22:11)
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian traditions commonly understand this as the birth of the promised Savior in humble circumstances, with His connection to David important to the account. The Catholic Catechism and Wesley both emphasize the lowly setting rather than worldly rank or comfort. (Catechism 525–526; Wesley on Luke 2:6–7)

The census date is harder to establish. Josephus describes Quirinius’s registration after the removal of Archelaus, later than Herod the Great’s reign, while Luke opens his birth narrative during Herod’s time. The BSB offers an alternative reading of verse 2 that places this census before Quirinius’s governorship. The USCCB’s study notes suggest Luke may have combined events from different times; researcher David Armitage examines ways Luke and Josephus might fit together, while acknowledging that no proposed solution can be proved. These are explanations under discussion, not an agreed date supplied by the surviving records. (Josephus, Antiquities 18.1.1; Luke 1:5; BSB verse 2 footnote; USCCB notes; David Armitage on the census)
passages.god_plan_html:
Bethlehem connects the birth with the promised ruler from David’s people. Matthew explicitly links Jesus’ birthplace with Micah’s prophecy of a ruler who will shepherd Israel. Luke’s account of the journey places Jesus in that same town of promise, even as the story unfolds amid the decisions of earthly rulers. (Micah 5:2–4; Matthew 2:1–6)

The humble arrival also has a supported connection with Paul’s description of Christ taking a servant’s place and becoming obedient to death before His exaltation. Paul gives that account to call believers away from selfish ambition and toward caring for others. The birth’s lowliness belongs to a life of self-giving whose meaning reaches into the way His people live together. (Philippians 2:1–11)

Paul makes a related connection when he speaks of Christ becoming poor for others’ sake while encouraging generous care for people in need. The response to His grace includes practical generosity, not simply admiration for a humble birth scene. (2 Corinthians 8:8–15)

passages.title: Luke 2:8-14
passages.section_title: What good news do the shepherds hear?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 And there were shepherds residing in the fields nearby, keeping watch over their flocks by night. 9 Just then an angel of the Lord stood before them, and the glory of the Lord shone around them, and they were terrified. 10 But the angel said to them, “Do not be afraid! For behold, I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people: 11 Today in the city of David a Savior has been born to you. He is Christ the Lord! 12 And this will be a sign to you: You will find a baby wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger.” 13 And suddenly there appeared with the angel a great multitude of the heavenly host, praising God and saying: 14 “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men on whom His favor rests!”
paragraphs: 8 And there were shepherds residing in the fields nearby, keeping watch over their flocks by night. 9 Just then an angel of the Lord stood before them, and the glory of the Lord shone around them, and they were terrified. 10 But the angel said to them, “Do not be afraid! For behold, I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people: 11 Today in the city of David a Savior has been born to you. He is Christ the Lord! 12 And this will be a sign to you: You will find a baby wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger.”
13 And suddenly there appeared with the angel a great multitude of the heavenly host, praising God and saying: 14 “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men on whom His favor rests!”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The scene moves from the birth to shepherds watching their flocks at night. An angel appears, God’s glory shines around them, and they are afraid. The angel tells them not to fear and announces a birth that brings great joy.

The child is identified as Savior, Christ, and Lord. Christ is a title: Χριστός, Christos (khris-TOSS), means Anointed One. The announcement identifies the baby as the promised Messiah, not merely another child born in David’s town. (Thayer’s lexicon)

The sign is concrete and unexpected: a baby wrapped in cloths and lying in a feeding trough. A multitude of the heavenly host then praises God. Luke places the greatness of the child’s identity beside the ordinary, lowly circumstances in which the shepherds will find Him.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian traditions commonly understand the announcement as good news of God’s promised Savior, with heavenly praise declaring God’s glory and the peace His favor brings. The shepherds receive the news of a King whose arrival is marked by a manger, showing God’s attention to people outside the centers of power. (USCCB notes on Luke 2:8–14; Wesley on Luke 2:11–14)
passages.god_plan_html:
The peace announced here reaches its saving depth in Jesus’ work. Paul connects peace with God to being made right with Him through faith, and explains reconciliation through the Son’s death and life. The birth begins the earthly story of the Savior through whom that peace comes. (Romans 5:1–11)

Ephesians also describes Christ making peace between Jews and Gentiles and bringing both near to the Father through the cross and the Spirit. The good news gathers people into a shared household with God. This develops the promise of peace beyond an expectation that every conflict on earth immediately ends at the birth. (Ephesians 2:11–22)

passages.title: Luke 2:15-20
passages.section_title: How do the shepherds respond to the news?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 When the angels had left them and gone into heaven, the shepherds said to one another, “Let us go to Bethlehem and see this thing that has happened, which the Lord has made known to us.” 16 So they hurried off and found Mary and Joseph and the Baby, who was lying in the manger. 17 After they had seen the Child, they spread the message they had received about Him. 18 And all who heard it were amazed at what the shepherds said to them. 19 But Mary treasured up all these things and pondered them in her heart. 20 The shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all they had heard and seen, which was just as the angel had told them.
paragraphs: 15 When the angels had left them and gone into heaven, the shepherds said to one another, “Let us go to Bethlehem and see this thing that has happened, which the Lord has made known to us.” 16 So they hurried off and found Mary and Joseph and the Baby, who was lying in the manger. 17 After they had seen the Child, they spread the message they had received about Him. 18 And all who heard it were amazed at what the shepherds said to them.

19 But Mary treasured up all these things and pondered them in her heart. 20 The shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all they had heard and seen, which was just as the angel had told them.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the angels leave, the shepherds decide to go to Bethlehem. They treat the announcement as something the Lord has made known and hurry to see what has happened. They find Mary, Joseph, and the baby in the manger, just as they were told.

Seeing leads to speaking: they spread the message about the child, and those who hear are amazed. Mary treasures the events and considers them in her heart. Luke distinguishes the public response of wonder from her continuing reflection without claiming that she already understands everything.

The shepherds return to their ordinary setting praising God for what they have heard and seen. The passage moves from receiving the message to finding it confirmed, sharing it, and giving God glory. Luke describes no star leading these shepherds; Matthew’s star belongs to his account of the Magi. (Matthew 2:1–12)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian traditions commonly see the shepherds as responding to God’s message with action, testimony, and praise, while Mary remembers and reflects on what is unfolding. Their response keeps attention on the child and the Lord who has made Him known. (Wesley on Luke 2:20; USCCB notes on Luke 2:8–20)
passages.god_plan_html:
The movement from hearing to sharing belongs to the wider way the gospel reaches people. Paul explains that people hear because someone brings the message, and faith comes through hearing the word of Christ. The shepherds’ report is an early example of news about Jesus being carried from those who have received it to others. (Romans 10:14–17)

Later in Luke, Jesus describes His family in terms of hearing God’s word and carrying it out. When a woman blesses His mother, He likewise directs attention to those who hear and obey God’s word. Mary’s receiving, remembering, and believing belong within this larger call to a life that responds to God, a call that reaches beyond family status to all who hear Him. (Luke 8:19–21; Luke 11:27–28)

passages.title: Luke 2:21-24
passages.section_title: Why is Jesus presented to the Lord?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 When the eight days before His circumcision had passed, He was named Jesus, the name the angel had given Him before He was conceived. 22 And when the time of purification according to the Law of Moses was complete, His parents brought Him to Jerusalem to present Him to the Lord 23 (as it is written in the Law of the Lord: “Every firstborn male shall be consecrated to the Lord”), 24 and to offer the sacrifice specified in the Law of the Lord: “A pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons.”
paragraphs: 21 When the eight days before His circumcision had passed, He was named Jesus, the name the angel had given Him before He was conceived. 22 And when the time of purification according to the Law of Moses was complete, His parents brought Him to Jerusalem to present Him to the Lord 23 (as it is written in the Law of the Lord: “Every firstborn male shall be consecrated to the Lord”), 24 and to offer the sacrifice specified in the Law of the Lord: “A pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus is circumcised and receives the name announced before His conception. As with John’s naming, the family follows the word given through the angel. The child’s name belongs to the promise already unfolding. (Luke 1:31)

The family then goes to Jerusalem for the requirements of the Law. Luke brings together the mother’s purification, the firstborn belonging to the Lord, and the offering of two birds. Exodus calls for the firstborn to be dedicated to God, and Leviticus gives the purification instructions after childbirth. (Exodus 13:1–2; Leviticus 12:1–8)

Leviticus allows two birds when a family cannot afford a lamb. That is the provision Luke records them using. Its language of ceremonial cleansing after childbirth should be read within those instructions; the passage does not accuse Mary of committing a moral offense by giving birth.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian traditions commonly understand the presentation as showing Jesus’ place within Israel’s covenant life and His family’s faithfulness to God’s Law. The child who will fulfill God’s saving promises enters the ordinary practices of the people to whom those promises were given. (Catechism 527–529; Wesley on Luke 2:21–24)
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul explains that God sent His Son, born of a woman and under the Law, to redeem and bring people into His family. These early acts of obedience belong to the earthly life through which the Son carries out that saving purpose. (Galatians 4:4–7)

The temple offering also looks toward a wider New Testament distinction. Hebrews explains that the Law’s repeated sacrifices could not complete the cleansing people needed, and that Christ came in a real human body to do God’s will through His own once-for-all offering. The family’s obedience is part of Israel’s worshiping life; the child Himself will bring the saving work to its fulfillment. (Hebrews 10:1–10)

passages.title: Luke 2:25-35
passages.section_title: What does Simeon see in this child?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 25 Now there was a man in Jerusalem named Simeon, who was righteous and devout. He was waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was upon him. 26 The Holy Spirit had revealed to him that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ. 27 Led by the Spirit, he went into the temple courts. And when the parents brought in the child Jesus to do for Him what was customary under the Law, 28 Simeon took Him in his arms and blessed God, saying: 29 “Sovereign Lord, as You have promised, You now dismiss Your servant in peace. 30 For my eyes have seen Your salvation, 31 which You have prepared in the sight of all people, 32 a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to Your people Israel.” 33 The Child’s father and mother were amazed at what was spoken about Him. 34 Then Simeon blessed them and said to His mother Mary: “Behold, this Child is appointed to cause the rise and fall of many in Israel, and to be a sign that will be spoken against, 35 so that the thoughts of many hearts will be revealed— and a sword will pierce your soul as well.”
paragraphs: 25 Now there was a man in Jerusalem named Simeon, who was righteous and devout. He was waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was upon him. 26 The Holy Spirit had revealed to him that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ. 27 Led by the Spirit, he went into the temple courts. And when the parents brought in the child Jesus to do for Him what was customary under the Law, 28 Simeon took Him in his arms and blessed God, saying:

29 “Sovereign Lord, as You have promised, You now dismiss Your servant in peace. 30 For my eyes have seen Your salvation, 31 which You have prepared in the sight of all people, 32 a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to Your people Israel.”

33 The Child’s father and mother were amazed at what was spoken about Him. 34 Then Simeon blessed them and said to His mother Mary: “Behold, this Child is appointed to cause the rise and fall of many in Israel, and to be a sign that will be spoken against, 35 so that the thoughts of many hearts will be revealed— and a sword will pierce your soul as well.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Simeon is a righteous and devout man waiting for God to bring comfort and deliverance to Israel. The Spirit has promised that he will see the Lord’s Christ before he dies and leads him into the temple courts. He takes Jesus in his arms and blesses God for keeping that promise.

His praise names the child as God’s salvation, prepared openly for the peoples: light for the Gentiles and glory for Israel. The comfort he has awaited is not confined to his own final years or to one household. God’s mercy reaches Israel and the nations.

His words to Mary also include opposition and pain. The child will cause rising and falling, will be spoken against, and will reveal hearts. A sword will pierce Mary’s own soul. The promise of salvation does not mean Jesus and His mother will be spared suffering.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian traditions commonly read Simeon as recognizing the promised Messiah and foretelling both salvation and opposition. The sorrow predicted for Mary is commonly connected with Jesus’ suffering and death, where John records His mother standing near the cross. (Catechism 529; Wesley on Luke 2:30–35; John 19:25–27)
passages.god_plan_html:
Isaiah describes God’s servant as restoring Israel and bringing light and salvation to the nations. Acts explicitly applies that light-for-the-nations promise to the spread of the gospel. Simeon’s words belong within that scriptural purpose: Israel’s Messiah brings salvation whose reach extends to the ends of the earth. (Isaiah 49:5–7; Acts 13:44–49)

The image of people responding differently to Christ also has a supported connection with Peter’s account of the living stone. Christ is precious to those who believe and a stumbling stone to those who disobey; those receiving mercy are formed into a people called to proclaim God’s goodness. This develops the theme of a response to Jesus revealing the heart. (1 Peter 2:4–10)

Paul’s fuller discussion of Israel and the nations keeps this subject centered on mercy. He affirms a faithful remnant, warns Gentile believers against boasting, and speaks of hope for those who have stumbled. Simeon says many in Israel, and Luke has already shown faithful Israelites welcoming Jesus. The wider picture should be read with that care rather than turned into a blanket accusation against a people. (Romans 11:1–36)

passages.title: Luke 2:36-40
passages.section_title: How does Anna respond to the promised redemption?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 36 There was also a prophetess named Anna, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher, who was well along in years. She had been married for seven years, 37 and then was a widow to the age of eighty-four. She never left the temple, but worshiped night and day, fasting and praying. 38 Coming forward at that moment, she gave thanks to God and spoke about the Child to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem. 39 When Jesus’ parents had done everything required by the Law of the Lord, they returned to Galilee, to their own town of Nazareth. 40 And the Child grew and became strong. He was filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was upon Him.
paragraphs: 36 There was also a prophetess named Anna, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher, who was well along in years. She had been married for seven years, 37 and then was a widow to the age of eighty-four. She never left the temple, but worshiped night and day, fasting and praying. 38 Coming forward at that moment, she gave thanks to God and spoke about the Child to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem.

39 When Jesus’ parents had done everything required by the Law of the Lord, they returned to Galilee, to their own town of Nazareth. 40 And the Child grew and became strong. He was filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was upon Him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Anna is introduced as a prophetess, a woman who speaks for God, from the tribe of Asher and well along in years. Luke describes her life of worship, fasting, and prayer at the temple. Her devotion places her among the people waiting for God’s promised help.

She comes forward, thanks God, and speaks about the child to those waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem. Alongside Simeon, she gives public testimony that this child belongs to the hope they have been awaiting.

After the family completes the Law’s requirements, Luke takes the account back to Nazareth. He summarizes Jesus’ growth in strength and wisdom under God’s grace. His story includes both the remarkable recognition at the temple and an ordinary human childhood.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian traditions commonly see Anna as a faithful witness who responds to the coming of the Messiah with thanks and testimony. The return to Nazareth and the child’s growth continue Luke’s presentation of Jesus as truly sharing human life. (USCCB notes on Luke 2:36–40; Catechism 531)
passages.god_plan_html:
Anna belongs to the scriptural pattern of women bearing witness to God’s work. At Pentecost, Peter explains the Spirit’s outpouring through Joel’s promise that sons and daughters will prophesy. Anna’s earlier witness does not depend on being part of the later Pentecost event; the connection is the broader purpose of God making His work known through people He calls. (Acts 2:16–18)

There is also a helpful parallel in faithful waiting. Anna looks for Jerusalem’s redemption, while Paul describes believers waiting with hope and patience for the redemption of their bodies. These are distinct moments in the saving story, but both direct hope toward what God has promised rather than treating the waiting as empty time. (Romans 8:22–25)

passages.title: Luke 2:41-52
passages.section_title: What does Jesus reveal about His Father?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 41 Every year His parents went to Jerusalem for the Feast of the Passover. 42 And when He was twelve years old, they went up according to the custom of the Feast. 43 When those days were over and they were returning home, the boy Jesus remained behind in Jerusalem, but His parents were unaware He had stayed. 44 Assuming He was in their company, they traveled on for a day before they began to look for Him among their relatives and friends. 45 When they could not find Him, they returned to Jerusalem to search for Him. 46 Finally, after three days they found Him in the temple courts, sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions. 47 And all who heard Him were astounded at His understanding and His answers. 48 When His parents saw Him, they were astonished. “Child, why have You done this to us?” His mother asked. “Your father and I have been anxiously searching for You.” 49 “Why were you looking for Me?” He asked. “Did you not know that I had to be in My Father’s house?” 50 But they did not understand the statement He was making to them. 51 Then He went down to Nazareth with them and was obedient to them. But His mother treasured up all these things in her heart. 52 And Jesus grew in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and man.
paragraphs: 41 Every year His parents went to Jerusalem for the Feast of the Passover. 42 And when He was twelve years old, they went up according to the custom of the Feast. 43 When those days were over and they were returning home, the boy Jesus remained behind in Jerusalem, but His parents were unaware He had stayed. 44 Assuming He was in their company, they traveled on for a day before they began to look for Him among their relatives and friends. 45 When they could not find Him, they returned to Jerusalem to search for Him.

46 Finally, after three days they found Him in the temple courts, sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions. 47 And all who heard Him were astounded at His understanding and His answers. 48 When His parents saw Him, they were astonished. “Child, why have You done this to us?” His mother asked. “Your father and I have been anxiously searching for You.” 49 “Why were you looking for Me?” He asked. “Did you not know that I had to be in My Father’s house?” 50 But they did not understand the statement He was making to them.
51 Then He went down to Nazareth with them and was obedient to them. But His mother treasured up all these things in her heart. 52 And Jesus grew in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and man.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus’ parents go to Jerusalem each year for Passover. When He is twelve, He stays behind as their traveling company leaves. His parents assume He is with the group, search among relatives and friends, and return to Jerusalem when they cannot find Him.

After three days they find Him among the teachers in the temple courts, listening and asking questions. Those who hear Him are amazed at His understanding and answers. Luke describes His exceptional understanding without giving the teachers’ names or saying that every question is a test meant to expose them.

Mary speaks of their anxious search. Jesus answers by pointing to His Father’s house. The BSB footnote also allows the sense of being about His Father’s business. His special relationship and obligation to His Father are central in either wording. (BSB footnote to verse 49)

His parents do not understand the statement. He nevertheless goes home with them and remains obedient, while Mary keeps these things in her heart. Luke closes by recording growth in wisdom, stature, and favor. The claim about His Father stands alongside genuine human growth and family life.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian traditions commonly understand this scene as revealing Jesus’ unique relationship with His Father while affirming His real humanity and obedience at home. Catholic teaching explicitly connects His growth with genuine human knowledge and experience, and the Reformed confession likewise affirms that the eternal Son takes a complete human nature without ceasing to be God. (Catechism 472–474; Catechism 531–534; Westminster 8.2)
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus’ relationship to His Father’s house continues in His adult ministry. John records Him calling the temple His Father’s house, then speaking of His own body as the temple that will be raised after death. That later account explicitly connects His words with resurrection and the disciples’ growing understanding. The childhood scene introduces a relationship and purpose that will unfold through the rest of His life. (John 2:13–22)

His true humanity also belongs to His work as the Son who helps His people. Hebrews describes Him as a high priest able to sympathize with human weakness, yet without sin, and calls believers to approach God confidently for mercy and help. The Gospel’s account of His human life helps us understand the Savior who knows the life of those He serves. (Hebrews 4:14–16)

passages.title: Luke 3:1-6
passages.section_title: How does John prepare the Lord’s way?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, while Pontius Pilate was governor of Judea, Herod tetrarch of Galilee, his brother Philip tetrarch of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene, 2 during the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas, the word of God came to John son of Zechariah in the wilderness. 3 He went into all the region around the Jordan, preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins, 4 as it is written in the book of the words of Isaiah the prophet: “A voice of one calling in the wilderness, ‘Prepare the way for the Lord, make straight paths for Him. 5 Every valley shall be filled in, and every mountain and hill made low. The crooked ways shall be made straight, and the rough ways smooth. 6 And all humanity will see God’s salvation.’”
paragraphs: 1 In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, while Pontius Pilate was governor of Judea, Herod tetrarch of Galilee, his brother Philip tetrarch of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene, 2 during the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas, the word of God came to John son of Zechariah in the wilderness. 3 He went into all the region around the Jordan, preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins,

4 as it is written in the book of the words of Isaiah the prophet: “A voice of one calling in the wilderness, ‘Prepare the way for the Lord, make straight paths for Him. 5 Every valley shall be filled in, and every mountain and hill made low. The crooked ways shall be made straight, and the rough ways smooth. 6 And all humanity will see God’s salvation.’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Luke places John’s public ministry within the reign of Tiberius and names the civil and religious leaders of the time. Then the focus moves to John, Zechariah’s son, receiving God’s word in the wilderness. The child promised in the opening chapter now begins his work.

John travels through the region around the Jordan, preaching a baptism of repentance for forgiveness of sins. Repentance is μετάνοια, metanoia (met-ah-NOY-ah): a change of mind that turns away from sin toward a changed life. John’s next words will make that change practical through the fruit it produces. (Thayer’s lexicon)

Luke identifies this ministry through Isaiah’s picture of preparing a road for the Lord: valleys filled, heights lowered, crooked places straightened, and rough ways made smooth. The picture belongs to the announcement of God’s coming salvation. John prepares people to receive the One who is coming, rather than organizing a road-building project. (Isaiah 40:1–11)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian traditions commonly understand John as the promised messenger calling people to repentance and preparing them for the Lord. His baptism belongs to that call and points forward to Jesus, as Paul later explains to people who had received John’s baptism. (Catechism 718–720; Wesley on Luke 3:4–6; Acts 19:1–7)
passages.god_plan_html:
Isaiah’s road picture comes within a larger message of comfort, forgiveness, and the Lord coming to care for His flock. Luke carries the quotation through its announcement that humanity will see God’s salvation. This continues the reach already heard in Simeon’s praise: light for the nations and glory for Israel. (Isaiah 40:1–11; Luke 2:29–32)

The same chapter of Isaiah contrasts human life’s frailty with God’s enduring word. Peter explicitly connects that enduring word with the gospel through which people receive new life. John’s call belongs to this movement from God’s promise to the good news of what He brings about in Christ. (Isaiah 40:6–8; 1 Peter 1:23–25)

passages.title: Luke 3:7-14
passages.section_title: What does genuine repentance look like?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 Then John said to the crowds coming out to be baptized by him, “You brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the coming wrath? 8 Produce fruit, then, in keeping with repentance. And do not begin to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you that out of these stones God can raise up children for Abraham. 9 The axe lies ready at the root of the trees, and every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.” 10 The crowds asked him, “What then should we do?” 11 John replied, “Whoever has two tunics should share with him who has none, and whoever has food should do the same.” 12 Even tax collectors came to be baptized. “Teacher,” they asked, “what should we do?” 13 “Collect no more than you are authorized,” he answered. 14 Then some soldiers asked him, “And what should we do?” “Do not take money by force or false accusation,” he said. “Be content with your wages.”
paragraphs: 7 Then John said to the crowds coming out to be baptized by him, “You brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the coming wrath? 8 Produce fruit, then, in keeping with repentance. And do not begin to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you that out of these stones God can raise up children for Abraham. 9 The axe lies ready at the root of the trees, and every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.”

10 The crowds asked him, “What then should we do?” 11 John replied, “Whoever has two tunics should share with him who has none, and whoever has food should do the same.” 12 Even tax collectors came to be baptized. “Teacher,” they asked, “what should we do?” 13 “Collect no more than you are authorized,” he answered. 14 Then some soldiers asked him, “And what should we do?” “Do not take money by force or false accusation,” he said. “Be content with your wages.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
John confronts the crowds with a warning about coming judgment. They must produce fruit that fits repentance rather than rely on being Abraham’s descendants. Their family connection does not remove the need to respond to God.

The warning uses a tree ready to be cut down if it bears no good fruit. When the crowds ask what to do, John answers with ordinary actions: share clothing and food, collect only what is authorized, refuse extortion and false accusations, and be content with wages.

His answers address people in their actual responsibilities. Tax collectors and soldiers are called to change the way they treat others. John does not let religious interest or participation in baptism stand in place of honesty, generosity, and justice.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian traditions commonly read these instructions as the visible fruit of a genuine turning to God, with outward privilege unable to substitute for a changed heart and life. Wesley summarizes the response as turning from evil to doing good, while the Catholic bishops’ notes likewise emphasize the practical reform John calls for. (Wesley on Luke 3:8–14; USCCB notes on Luke 3:7–18)
passages.god_plan_html:
The practical care John calls for has a supported parallel in Isaiah’s criticism of fasting that leaves oppression and hunger untouched. God’s people are called to share bread, clothe people in need, and break oppressive bonds. John’s message continues that scriptural concern for a life in which worship and treatment of neighbors belong together. (Isaiah 58:5–12)

The New Testament develops both parts of his warning. Paul describes Abraham’s family through faith and belonging to Christ, while John explains that Christ’s self-giving love should lead believers to help those in material need. The intended fruit is a people whose life reflects God’s mercy in concrete action. (Galatians 3:6–14, 26–29; 1 John 3:16–18)

passages.title: Luke 3:15-20
passages.section_title: Who is coming after John?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 The people were waiting expectantly and were all wondering in their hearts if John could be the Christ. 16 John answered all of them: “I baptize you with water, but One more powerful than I will come, the straps of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire. 17 His winnowing fork is in His hand to clear His threshing floor and to gather the wheat into His barn; but He will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.” 18 With these and many other exhortations, John proclaimed the good news to the people. 19 But when he rebuked Herod the tetrarch regarding his brother’s wife Herodias and all the evils he had done, 20 Herod added this to them all: He locked John up in prison.

He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire. 17 His winnowing fork is in His hand to clear His threshing floor and to gather the wheat into His barn; but He will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.”

18 With these and many other exhortations, John proclaimed the good news to the people. 19 But when he rebuked Herod the tetrarch regarding his brother’s wife Herodias and all the evils he had done, 20 Herod added this to them all: He locked John up in prison.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The people wonder whether John might be the Christ. He directs them to One far greater, saying he is unworthy even to untie His sandals. John baptizes with water; the coming One will baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire.

The next picture is a harvest being sorted: wheat gathered safely and chaff burned. The message brings together salvation and the seriousness of judgment. Luke calls John’s many exhortations good news, without removing the warnings from that message.

Luke then records John confronting Herod over Herodias and the ruler’s other evils. Herod responds by imprisoning him. This closes the summary of John’s public ministry before Luke turns to Jesus’ baptism; it need not mean John was already in prison when he baptized Jesus. Wesley likewise treats the imprisonment as an event placed here to complete the account of John’s work. (Wesley on Luke 3:20; Matthew 3:13–17)
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand John as directing attention away from himself to Jesus, whose work goes beyond John’s water baptism. The gathering and burning picture gives the announcement a serious warning as well as a promise.

They differ over the fire in the baptism promise. The Catholic Catechism connects it with the Spirit’s transforming power, including the fire-like tongues at Pentecost; the USCCB notes also draw on the prophets’ images of cleansing and refining. John Walvoord instead reads it as a distinct future judgment, reasoning from the surrounding warning and the burning chaff. His is one teacher’s explanation, not the position of every Protestant. (Catechism 696; USCCB notes on Luke 3:16; John Walvoord on baptism with fire)
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus later recalls the distinction between John’s water baptism and the coming gift of the Holy Spirit, then promises power for witness to the ends of the earth. John’s preparatory ministry leads toward the risen Lord giving His people what they need to carry the message. (Acts 1:4–8)

Paul describes that wider task as a ministry of reconciliation: God brings people to Himself through Christ and entrusts His people with the message. Those who receive new life are called to live for the One who died and rose for them. The appeal directs attention to Christ’s love and the mercy His people are entrusted to share. (2 Corinthians 5:11–21)
