passages.title: Luke 3:21-22
passages.section_title: What is revealed as Jesus is baptized?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 When all the people were being baptized, Jesus was baptized too. And as He was praying, heaven was opened, 22 and the Holy Spirit descended on Him in a bodily form like a dove. And a voice came from heaven: “You are My beloved Son; in You I am well pleased.”
paragraphs: 21 When all the people were being baptized, Jesus was baptized too. And as He was praying, heaven was opened, 22 and the Holy Spirit descended on Him in a bodily form like a dove. And a voice came from heaven: “You are My beloved Son; in You I am well pleased.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus is baptized among the people, and Luke draws attention to His praying. Heaven opens, the Spirit descends in a bodily form like a dove, and the voice from heaven identifies Him as the beloved Son in whom the Father delights.

The Father’s words confirm the identity announced before His birth. The child promised to Mary as the Son of God now stands at the beginning of His public ministry. Luke will next trace His family line and then describe His testing in the wilderness. (Luke 1:31–35)

The other Gospels add details that help explain the event. Matthew records John’s hesitation and Jesus’ answer about fulfilling righteousness; John explains that the Spirit descending and remaining was the sign given to identify the One who baptizes with the Holy Spirit. These accounts help us understand the baptism as an act of obedience and a revelation of His identity. (Matthew 3:13–17; John 1:29–34)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian traditions commonly understand the baptism as revealing Jesus as the beloved Son and marking the beginning of His mission, with the Father speaking and the Spirit descending upon Him. Catholic and Reformed teaching recognize the Father, Son, and Spirit as distinct persons of the one God; the scene is read within that confession and Jesus’ willing obedience to the Father. (Catechism 535–536; Westminster 2.3)
passages.god_plan_html:
The Father’s declaration has supported scriptural parallels with the royal Son in Psalm 2 and the servant in Isaiah 42, in whom God delights and upon whom He puts His Spirit. Luke does not introduce the voice as a formal quotation of either passage. Together these themes help explain the coming ministry as the work of God’s King and His chosen servant, bringing justice and light to the nations. (Psalm 2:6–9; Isaiah 42:1–7)

The connection becomes explicit in the accounts of Jesus’ ministry. At Nazareth He identifies His work through Isaiah’s announcement of the Spirit’s anointing for good news and release. Peter later summarizes His ministry as God anointing Him with the Holy Spirit and power, leading into His death, resurrection, and the proclamation of forgiveness to those who believe. The baptism opens onto that saving mission. (Luke 4:16–21; Acts 10:34–43)

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Luke places the family list after the Father’s declaration about Jesus and before the wilderness testing. Jesus is about thirty when He begins His ministry. The account identifies Him as regarded as Joseph’s son while preserving what it has already said about His conception through the Holy Spirit. (Luke 1:26–35)

The list moves backward through David and Abraham, then beyond Israel’s founding family to Adam and God. It roots Jesus within Israel’s story and also within the wider human family. The scope fits the salvation for Israel and the nations already announced in Luke.

Matthew’s list begins with Abraham and moves toward Jesus. The names between Joseph and David differ: Matthew follows David’s son Solomon, while Luke follows Nathan. The difference is visible in the texts themselves and should be acknowledged when the lists are read together. (Matthew 1:1–17)
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the family lists as connecting Jesus with God’s promises to David and Abraham and affirming His place in real human history. They differ over how the two lists fit together.

Wesley explains Luke as tracing Mary’s family, with Heli understood as Joseph’s father-in-law, while Matthew traces Joseph’s line. An early Christian writer, Julius Africanus, offered another explanation: both lists trace Joseph, one through birth and the other through a family’s legal line after a childless relative’s death. These are proposed explanations; Luke does not spell out either reconstruction. (Wesley on Luke 3:23; Africanus preserved in Eusebius, Church History 1.7)
passages.god_plan_html:
Tracing the line to Adam has a supported connection with Paul’s explicit comparison of Adam and Christ. Romans describes sin and death entering through Adam, then contrasts that with the grace and life that come through Christ’s obedience. Jesus’ place in the human story matters to His work of bringing life to people caught under sin and death. (Romans 5:12–21)

Paul also calls Christ the last Adam and connects His resurrection with the future resurrection of His people. The one who shares our humanity brings a new future beyond the death inherited in Adam. Luke’s family list does not explain every part of that teaching, but its reach back to Adam gives a fitting setting for the Son’s obedient life and saving work. (1 Corinthians 15:20–28, 42–49)

passages.title: Luke 4:1-13
passages.section_title: How does Jesus remain faithful under testing?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit into the wilderness, 2 where for forty days He was tempted by the devil. He ate nothing during those days, and when they had ended, He was hungry. 3 The devil said to Him, “If You are the Son of God, tell this stone to become bread.” 4 But Jesus answered, “It is written: ‘Man shall not live on bread alone.’” 5 Then the devil led Him up to a high place and showed Him in an instant all the kingdoms of the world. 6 “I will give You authority over all these kingdoms and all their glory,” he said. “For it has been relinquished to me, and I can give it to anyone I wish. 7 So if You worship me, it will all be Yours.” 8 But Jesus answered, “It is written: ‘Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only.’” 9 Then the devil led Him to Jerusalem and set Him on the pinnacle of the temple. “If You are the Son of God,” he said, “throw Yourself down from here. 10 For it is written: ‘He will command His angels concerning You to guard You carefully, 11 and they will lift You up in their hands, so that You will not strike Your foot against a stone.’” 12 But Jesus answered, “It also says, ‘Do not put the Lord your God to the test.’” 13 When the devil had finished every temptation, he left Him until an opportune time.
paragraphs: 1 Then Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit into the wilderness, 2 where for forty days He was tempted by the devil. He ate nothing during those days, and when they had ended, He was hungry. 3 The devil said to Him, “If You are the Son of God, tell this stone to become bread.” 4 But Jesus answered, “It is written: ‘Man shall not live on bread alone.’”

5 Then the devil led Him up to a high place and showed Him in an instant all the kingdoms of the world. 6 “I will give You authority over all these kingdoms and all their glory,” he said. “For it has been relinquished to me, and I can give it to anyone I wish. 7 So if You worship me, it will all be Yours.” 8 But Jesus answered, “It is written: ‘Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only.’”

9 Then the devil led Him to Jerusalem and set Him on the pinnacle of the temple. “If You are the Son of God,” he said, “throw Yourself down from here. 10 For it is written: ‘He will command His angels concerning You to guard You carefully, 11 and they will lift You up in their hands, so that You will not strike Your foot against a stone.’” 12 But Jesus answered, “It also says, ‘Do not put the Lord your God to the test.’” 13 When the devil had finished every temptation, he left Him until an opportune time.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After His baptism, Jesus enters the wilderness full of the Holy Spirit. He is tempted by the devil during forty days without food. The testing follows the Father’s declaration that He is the beloved Son, and the devil’s challenges press on what it means for Him to live as that Son.

The first challenge concerns hunger and the use of His power to make bread. Next comes an offer of the world’s kingdoms in exchange for worship. Luke’s final scene moves to Jerusalem, where the devil quotes Scripture to urge Jesus to throw Himself from the temple and demand God’s protection.

Jesus answers each challenge from Deuteronomy. His responses concern dependence on God, worship and service owed to God alone, and refusing to put God to the test. The devil’s use of Psalm 91 shows why quoting Scripture is not enough: a proposed action must be read against what God actually commands. (Deuteronomy 8:1–5; Deuteronomy 6:10–18; Psalm 91)

The Greek word translated worship is προσκυνέω, proskyneō (pros-kooh-NEH-oh), meaning to bow down in homage or worship. Here the proposed act is bound to allegiance: the devil offers authority in return for Jesus acknowledging him. Jesus’ answer joins worship with serving God alone. (Thayer’s lexicon)

The Spirit leads Jesus into the wilderness, while the devil urges disobedience. James likewise distinguishes endurance under trial from the claim that God entices someone to sin. The passage ends with the devil withdrawing until another opportunity; the testing belongs to Jesus’ continuing mission. (James 1:12–18)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian traditions commonly understand this as the obedient Son resisting the devil and remaining faithful to His Father through real testing. The Catholic Catechism explicitly connects His victory with Adam and Israel, while the Reformed confession affirms the Son’s real humanity and sinless obedience. (Catechism 538–540; Westminster 8.2–4)
passages.god_plan_html:
The wilderness and Jesus’ answers form a supported parallel with Israel’s testing. Deuteronomy recalls forty years in which Israel learned dependence through hunger and God’s provision. Its warning against testing God points back to Massah, where the people questioned whether the Lord was with them. Jesus remains faithful in the very matters to which these passages speak. (Deuteronomy 8:1–5; Deuteronomy 6:16; Exodus 17:1–7)

The wider connection with Adam is explicit in Paul’s teaching: Adam’s disobedience brought sin and death, while Christ’s obedience brings grace and life. Luke has just traced Jesus’ human family back to Adam. His faithful response to testing belongs within the saving life of the Son who comes to rescue humanity. (Romans 5:12–21; 1 Corinthians 15:45–49)

This also reaches His people’s need for help. Hebrews describes Jesus as tested yet without sin and able to help those being tested, then invites believers to approach God confidently for mercy and grace. Paul also uses Israel’s wilderness failures as warnings and points to God’s faithfulness in providing a way to endure temptation. The account leads to reliance on this faithful Savior and attentive obedience. (Hebrews 2:14–18; Hebrews 4:14–16; 1 Corinthians 10:1–13)
passages.current_position_html: Worship as the Early Church Knew It examines the demand to bow to Satan in Matthew’s account of the same testing. The study understands the act as allegiance: bowing would acknowledge his authority, and Jesus answers that worship and service belong to God alone. This supplies our position on the demand for worship and Jesus’ response; the passage’s other questions remain open for further study.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

passages.title: Luke 4:14-30
passages.section_title: What does Jesus announce in His hometown?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 Jesus returned to Galilee in the power of the Spirit, and the news about Him spread throughout the surrounding region. 15 He taught in their synagogues and was glorified by everyone. 16 Then Jesus came to Nazareth, where He had been brought up. As was His custom, He entered the synagogue on the Sabbath. And when He stood up to read, 17 the scroll of the prophet Isaiah was handed to Him. Unrolling it, He found the place where it was written: 18 “The Spirit of the Lord is on Me, because He has anointed Me to preach good news to the poor. He has sent Me to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind, to release the oppressed, 19 to proclaim the year of the Lord’s favor.” 20 Then He rolled up the scroll, returned it to the attendant, and sat down. The eyes of everyone in the synagogue were fixed on Him, 21 and He began by saying, “Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing.” 22 All spoke well of Him and marveled at the gracious words that came from His lips. “Isn’t this the son of Joseph?” they asked. 23 Jesus said to them, “Surely you will quote this proverb to Me: ‘Physician, heal yourself! Do here in Your hometown what we have heard that You did in Capernaum.’” 24 Then He added, “Truly I tell you, no prophet is accepted in his hometown. 25 But I tell you truthfully that there were many widows in Israel in the time of Elijah, when the sky was shut for three and a half years and great famine swept over all the land. 26 Yet Elijah was not sent to any of them, but to the widow of Zarephath in Sidon. 27 And there were many lepers in Israel in the time of Elisha the prophet. Yet not one of them was cleansed—only Naaman the Syrian.” 28 On hearing this, all the people in the synagogue were enraged. 29 They got up, drove Him out of the town, and led Him to the brow of the hill on which the town was built, in order to throw Him over the cliff. 30 But Jesus passed through the crowd and went on His way.

The eyes of everyone in the synagogue were fixed on Him, 21 and He began by saying, “Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing.”

22 All spoke well of Him and marveled at the gracious words that came from His lips. “Isn’t this the son of Joseph?” they asked. 23 Jesus said to them, “Surely you will quote this proverb to Me: ‘Physician, heal yourself! section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus returns to Galilee in the Spirit’s power and teaches in the synagogues. At Nazareth, where He grew up, He follows His custom of attending on the Sabbath. He stands to read from Isaiah, then sits and declares that the Scripture is being fulfilled in their hearing.

The setting is a local Jewish gathering for reading and teaching Scripture. An ancient synagogue inscription from Jerusalem likewise names reading the Law and teaching the commandments among its purposes. Luke shows those practices in action without giving a complete order of service. (Jerusalem synagogue inscription)

The reading announces the Spirit’s anointing for good news to the poor, release for captives, sight for the blind, freedom for the oppressed, and the Lord’s favor. Its language comes from Isaiah 61 and also recalls Isaiah 58’s call to set the oppressed free. Jesus identifies His own ministry with this promised work. (Isaiah 61:1–3; Isaiah 58:6)

The word for release is ἄφεσις, aphesis (AH-feh-sis). It can describe freedom from captivity or the forgiveness of sins; Luke also uses it in John’s preaching about forgiveness. Both uses help us hear the saving mercy in Jesus’ announcement. (Thayer’s lexicon; Luke 3:3)

The listeners initially marvel at His gracious words but question Him as Joseph’s son. Jesus addresses their expectation that the reports from Capernaum should be repeated at home. He then recalls Elijah helping a widow in Sidon and Elisha’s part in Naaman the Syrian’s healing. God’s mercy in these accounts reaches beyond Israel’s borders and is not something His hometown can claim as its own privilege.

Their response turns to rage, and they try to throw Him from the hill. Jesus passes through the crowd and goes on His way. Luke does not explain how He does so. The announcement of grace is followed immediately by opposition.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian traditions commonly read this as Jesus announcing the fulfillment of God’s promised saving work, with good news for the poor and mercy reaching beyond hometown privilege. Wesley explicitly includes both material and spiritual need in the good news to the poor, while the Catholic Catechism likewise connects His kingdom with the lowly, active care for the poor, and mercy for sinners. (Wesley on Luke 4:18–28; Catechism 544–545)
passages.god_plan_html:
There is a supported connection with the Jubilee instructions in Leviticus. That year proclaimed liberty and restored Israelite family land, with release for Israelites serving because of poverty. Jesus’ announcement of the Lord’s favor belongs to this scriptural picture of God bringing freedom and restoration. John’s Gospel also records Jesus explaining the freedom He gives from slavery to sin. (Leviticus 25:8–17, 39–43; John 8:31–36)

Jesus Himself connects His ministry with the earlier prophets’ work among foreigners. The widow’s story records both provision and the restoration of her son’s life; Naaman’s story includes initial resistance followed by obedience and healing. Their accounts show God’s mercy reaching people outside Israel without portraying those people as having no struggles or questions. (1 Kings 17:8–24; 2 Kings 5:1–19)

That reach continues in the mission after Jesus’ resurrection. When Peter speaks to Cornelius’s household, he recognizes that God does not show favoritism and proclaims Jesus’ Spirit-anointed ministry, death, resurrection, and forgiveness for everyone who believes. The hometown scene thus fits a saving purpose that reaches the nations while remaining rooted in God’s promises to Israel. (Acts 10:34–43)

passages.title: Luke 4:31-37
passages.section_title: Why do the unclean spirits obey Jesus?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 31 Then He went down to Capernaum, a town in Galilee, and on the Sabbath He began to teach the people. 32 They were astonished at His teaching, because His message had authority. 33 In the synagogue there was a man possessed by the spirit of an unclean demon. He cried out in a loud voice, 34 “Ha! What do You want with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have You come to destroy us? I know who You are—the Holy One of God!” 35 But Jesus rebuked the demon. “Be silent!” He said. “Come out of him!” At this, the demon threw the man down before them all and came out without harming him. 36 All the people were overcome with amazement and asked one another, “What is this message? With authority and power He commands the unclean spirits, and they come out!” 37 And the news about Jesus spread throughout the surrounding region.

He cried out in a loud voice, 34 “Ha! What do You want with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have You come to destroy us? I know who You are—the Holy One of God!”

With authority and power He commands the unclean spirits, and they come out!” 37 And the news about Jesus spread throughout the surrounding region.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus teaches in Capernaum on the Sabbath, and the people are struck by the authority of His message. The account then shows that authority in action when an unclean spirit speaks through a man in the synagogue.

The spirit recognizes Jesus as the Holy One of God and asks whether He has come to destroy them. Jesus silences it and commands it to leave. It throws the man down but comes out without harming him. The man’s release shows the effect of Jesus’ command.

The people’s response joins His message with His authority and power: His words bring about what He commands. News spreads through the surrounding region. This continues the ministry of release announced in Nazareth, now seen in a particular person’s rescue. (Luke 4:18–21)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian traditions commonly read this as Jesus exercising authority over a real evil spirit and freeing the man from its power. The Catholic Catechism connects such acts with the coming of God’s kingdom and the defeat of Satan, while the Gospel itself emphasizes the authority of Jesus’ command. (Catechism 547–550; Mark 1:21–28)
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus later explicitly connects driving out demons with God’s kingdom coming upon people. He describes the victory through the picture of someone stronger overcoming an armed man. The release in Capernaum belongs within that wider work of overcoming evil’s hold. (Luke 11:14–23)

The New Testament carries this purpose toward the cross. John says the Son of God was revealed to destroy the devil’s works, and Paul describes the powers and authorities being disarmed through Christ’s cross. The command in the synagogue is an early expression of the authority of the Savior whose victory reaches beyond this one encounter. (1 John 3:8; Colossians 2:9–15)

passages.title: Luke 4:38-41
passages.section_title: How does Jesus care for the sick in Capernaum?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 38 After Jesus had left the synagogue, He went to the home of Simon, whose mother-in-law was suffering from a high fever. So they appealed to Jesus on her behalf, 39 and He stood over her and rebuked the fever, and it left her. And she got up at once and began to serve them. 40 At sunset, all who were ill with various diseases were brought to Jesus, and laying His hands on each one, He healed them. 41 Demons also came out of many people, shouting, “You are the Son of God!” But He rebuked the demons and would not allow them to speak, because they knew He was the Christ.
paragraphs: 38 After Jesus had left the synagogue, He went to the home of Simon, whose mother-in-law was suffering from a high fever. So they appealed to Jesus on her behalf, 39 and He stood over her and rebuked the fever, and it left her. And she got up at once and began to serve them.

40 At sunset, all who were ill with various diseases were brought to Jesus, and laying His hands on each one, He healed them. 41 Demons also came out of many people, shouting, “You are the Son of God!” But He rebuked the demons and would not allow them to speak, because they knew He was the Christ.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After leaving the synagogue, Jesus enters Simon’s home. Simon’s mother-in-law has a high fever, and the people appeal to Him on her behalf. He stands over her, rebukes the fever, and it leaves her.

She gets up at once and serves them. The action shows how immediate and complete her recovery is. Luke shows her returning to ordinary activity right away. He tells us she had a fever without identifying a particular disease.

At sunset, people bring others with various illnesses. Jesus lays His hands on each one and heals them. Demons also come out of many, identifying Him as the Son of God, but He silences them. The account distinguishes illness and demonic oppression while showing His authority over both. (Mark 1:29–34)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian traditions commonly see these healings as expressions of Jesus’ compassion and authority, with Simon’s mother-in-law’s immediate activity showing her restoration. They also understand His works as signs of the saving mission He has begun. (Catechism 547–549; Matthew 8:14–17)
passages.god_plan_html:
Matthew explicitly connects the healings in this same scene with Isaiah’s servant carrying infirmities and diseases. The help given to these suffering people belongs to the promised servant’s saving work. It also fits Peter’s later description of Jesus going about doing good and healing in the power of the Spirit. (Matthew 8:14–17; Acts 10:34–43)

The Bible’s wider hope reaches toward the complete removal of suffering. Revelation describes God dwelling with His people, wiping away tears, and bringing an end to death and pain in the new creation. These particular acts of restoration give a glimpse of the goodness of the Savior whose work leads toward that promised future. (Revelation 21:1–5)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 4:42-44
passages.section_title: Why must Jesus go to other towns?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 42 At daybreak, Jesus went out to a solitary place, and the crowds were looking for Him. They came to Him and tried to keep Him from leaving. 43 But Jesus told them, “I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well, because that is why I was sent.” 44 And He continued to preach in the synagogues of Judea.
paragraphs: 42 At daybreak, Jesus went out to a solitary place, and the crowds were looking for Him. They came to Him and tried to keep Him from leaving. 43 But Jesus told them, “I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well, because that is why I was sent.” 44 And He continued to preach in the synagogues of Judea.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
At daybreak Jesus goes to a solitary place. The crowds find Him and try to keep Him from leaving. After the previous evening’s healings, their desire for Him to remain is understandable, but He explains that His commission also concerns other towns.

He must proclaim the good news of God’s kingdom because that is why He was sent. Luke places the authority and compassion shown in Capernaum within this wider purpose. Jesus continues preaching in the synagogues.

Mark’s parallel account explicitly describes Jesus praying in the solitary place and gives the same reason for moving on to the neighboring towns. Luke’s account emphasizes His being sent and the need to carry the message onward. (Mark 1:35–39)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian traditions commonly understand this as Jesus allowing His God-given mission to determine His work, bringing the good news beyond a single community. The proclamation of the kingdom and His works of mercy belong together in that mission. (Mark 1:35–39; Catechism 547–550)
passages.god_plan_html:
The movement to other towns is an early part of a mission whose reach becomes clearer by the Gospel’s end. The risen Jesus explains that His suffering and resurrection lead into the proclamation of repentance and forgiveness among all nations. The good news Capernaum has received is meant to reach others. (Luke 24:44–49)

Acts continues that purpose through the witnesses who receive the Holy Spirit’s power and are sent outward from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth. The Lord’s own movement beyond one place prepares readers for the wider witness of His people. (Acts 1:4–8)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 5:1-11
passages.section_title: Why do the fishermen leave everything to follow Jesus?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 On one occasion, while Jesus was standing by the Lake of Gennesaret with the crowd pressing in on Him to hear the word of God, 2 He saw two boats at the edge of the lake. The fishermen had left them and were washing their nets. 3 Jesus got into the boat belonging to Simon and asked him to put out a little from shore. And sitting down, He taught the people from the boat. 4 When Jesus had finished speaking, He said to Simon, “Put out into deep water and let down your nets for a catch.” 5 “Master,” Simon replied, “we have worked hard all night without catching anything. But because You say so, I will let down the nets.” 6 When they had done so, they caught such a large number of fish that their nets began to tear. 7 So they signaled to their partners in the other boat to come and help them, and they came and filled both boats so full that they began to sink. 8 When Simon Peter saw this, he fell at Jesus’ knees. “Go away from me, Lord,” he said, “for I am a sinful man.” 9 For he and his companions were astonished at the catch of fish they had taken, 10 and so were his partners James and John, the sons of Zebedee. “Do not be afraid,” Jesus said to Simon. “From now on you will catch men.” 11 And when they had brought their boats ashore, they left everything and followed Him.
paragraphs: 1 On one occasion, while Jesus was standing by the Lake of Gennesaret with the crowd pressing in on Him to hear the word of God, 2 He saw two boats at the edge of the lake. The fishermen had left them and were washing their nets. 3 Jesus got into the boat belonging to Simon and asked him to put out a little from shore. And sitting down, He taught the people from the boat.

4 When Jesus had finished speaking, He said to Simon, “Put out into deep water and let down your nets for a catch.” 5 “Master,” Simon replied, “we have worked hard all night without catching anything. But because You say so, I will let down the nets.” 6 When they had done so, they caught such a large number of fish that their nets began to tear. 7 So they signaled to their partners in the other boat to come and help them, and they came and filled both boats so full that they began to sink.

8 When Simon Peter saw this, he fell at Jesus’ knees. “Go away from me, Lord,” he said, “for I am a sinful man.” 9 For he and his companions were astonished at the catch of fish they had taken, 10 and so were his partners James and John, the sons of Zebedee. “Do not be afraid,” Jesus said to Simon. “From now on you will catch men.” 11 And when they had brought their boats ashore, they left everything and followed Him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The crowd is pressing around Jesus to hear God’s word. He steps into Simon’s boat, asks him to move a little from shore, and teaches from there. Simon is already known to the reader: Jesus has visited his home and healed his mother-in-law. (Luke 4:38–39)

After teaching, Jesus tells Simon to go into deep water and let down the nets. Simon explains that they have worked all night without a catch, but he acts on Jesus’ word. The catch is so large that the nets begin to tear and both boats begin to sink as the partners help bring it in.

Simon’s response turns attention from the fish to the One before him. He falls at Jesus’ knees and confesses his sinfulness. Jesus answers his fear with a new calling. James and John are named among the astonished partners, and the account ends with the fishermen leaving everything to follow Him.

The Greek verb behind catching people is ζωγρέω, zōgreō (dzoh-GREH-oh). It can mean to take alive; Thayer explains its use here as winning people for God’s kingdom through teaching. The fishing picture now points toward people being gathered through the message Jesus will send His followers to carry. (Thayer, G2221)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand the catch as revealing Jesus’ power and the fishermen’s response as trust that changes the direction of their lives. The call prepares them to bring others to Him; Calvin also distinguishes this particular call to leave their work from a command that every believer must abandon an occupation. (Calvin on Luke 5:1–11; Wesley on Luke 5:8–11)
passages.god_plan_html:
There is a helpful parallel with Isaiah’s call. Faced with God’s holiness, Isaiah confesses his unclean lips; after receiving cleansing, he is sent to speak. Peter likewise recognizes his sinfulness in Jesus’ presence, then receives reassurance and a calling. Luke does not say Isaiah predicted this fishing scene, but the parallel shows God calling people who know their need for His mercy. (Isaiah 6:1–9)

Acts shows the outward reach of this calling. Peter proclaims the risen Jesus, calls his hearers to repent, and about three thousand receive the message and are added to the believers. The promised work of gathering people is taking shape through the gospel. A later catch in John also forms a striking parallel: after another empty night, Jesus provides fish and renews Peter’s calling to care for His people. These are distinct scenes, joined by dependence on Jesus and a commission to serve others. (Acts 2:37–42; John 21:1–19)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 5:12-16
passages.section_title: What happens when a man asks Jesus to make him clean?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 While Jesus was in one of the towns, a man came along who was covered with leprosy. When he saw Jesus, he fell facedown and begged Him, “Lord, if You are willing, You can make me clean.” 13 Jesus reached out His hand and touched the man. “I am willing,” He said. “Be clean!” And immediately the leprosy left him. 14 “Do not tell anyone,” Jesus instructed him. “But go, show yourself to the priest and present the offering Moses prescribed for your cleansing, as a testimony to them.” 15 But the news about Jesus spread all the more, and great crowds came to hear Him and to be healed of their sicknesses. 16 Yet He frequently withdrew to the wilderness to pray.
paragraphs: 12 While Jesus was in one of the towns, a man came along who was covered with leprosy. When he saw Jesus, he fell facedown and begged Him, “Lord, if You are willing, You can make me clean.” 13 Jesus reached out His hand and touched the man. “I am willing,” He said. “Be clean!” And immediately the leprosy left him. 14 “Do not tell anyone,” Jesus instructed him. “But go, show yourself to the priest and present the offering Moses prescribed for your cleansing, as a testimony to them.”
15 But the news about Jesus spread all the more, and great crowds came to hear Him and to be healed of their sicknesses. 16 Yet He frequently withdrew to the wilderness to pray.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
A man covered with leprosy falls facedown before Jesus and asks to be made clean. He trusts Jesus’ ability while placing the request in His hands. Jesus touches him, declares His willingness, and the disease immediately leaves.

The language of cleansing has a place in the Law of Moses. Leviticus gives priests responsibility for examining certain skin conditions and describes the cleansing process for a person who has recovered. Jesus directs the man to the priest and the prescribed offering as a testimony. The healing has already happened; the priest’s examination does not cause it. (Leviticus 13:45–46; Leviticus 14:1–9)

News continues to spread, and crowds gather both to hear Jesus and to seek healing. Luke closes the scene by telling us that Jesus frequently withdraws to pray. His growing public ministry includes time away from the crowds with the Father.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see both the man’s humble trust and Jesus’ willingness and power to restore him. The priestly instructions are read in connection with the Law’s provision for cleansing, while the wider Christian teaching on healing recognizes that earnest prayer does not always bring recovery from every illness now. (Calvin on the parallel Matthew 8:2–4; Catechism 1505–1508)
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus later includes the cleansing of lepers among the works His messengers should report when John asks whether He is the One who was to come. This healing therefore belongs to the evidence Jesus Himself gives about His mission. It brings real help to a suffering person while showing the promised restoration arriving through Him. (Matthew 11:2–6)

Isaiah describes God coming to save, with the blind seeing, the lame restored, and the redeemed returning in joy. This man’s cleansing is part of that wider pattern of restoration. The connection concerns God’s saving work; it does not require treating every detail of the man’s disease as a hidden symbol for sin. (Isaiah 35:3–10)
passages.current_position_html: Worship as the Early Church Knew It discusses this man’s approach in Matthew 8:2 as a personal plea expressed through physical humility and recognition of Jesus’ divine authority. Luke likewise describes him falling facedown before making his request. This is our position on his humble approach; a fuller position on the healing and the priestly instructions remains open.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

passages.title: Luke 5:17-26
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus forgive the man before telling him to walk?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 One day Jesus was teaching, and the Pharisees and teachers of the law were sitting there. People had come from Jerusalem and from every village of Galilee and Judea, and the power of the Lord was present for Him to heal the sick. 18 Just then some men came carrying a paralyzed man on a mat. They tried to bring him inside to set him before Jesus, 19 but they could not find a way through the crowd. So they went up on the roof and lowered him on his mat through the tiles into the middle of the crowd, right in front of Jesus. 20 When Jesus saw their faith, He said, “Friend, your sins are forgiven.” 21 But the scribes and Pharisees began thinking to themselves, “Who is this man who speaks blasphemy? Who can forgive sins but God alone?” 22 Knowing what they were thinking, Jesus replied, “Why are you thinking these things in your hearts? 23 Which is easier: to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Get up and walk’? 24 But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on the earth to forgive sins…” He said to the paralytic, “I tell you, get up, pick up your mat, and go home.” 25 And immediately the man stood up before them, took what he had been lying on, and went home glorifying God. 26 Everyone was taken with amazement and glorified God. They were filled with awe and said, “We have seen remarkable things today.”
paragraphs: 17 One day Jesus was teaching, and the Pharisees and teachers of the law were sitting there. People had come from Jerusalem and from every village of Galilee and Judea, and the power of the Lord was present for Him to heal the sick. 18 Just then some men came carrying a paralyzed man on a mat. They tried to bring him inside to set him before Jesus, 19 but they could not find a way through the crowd. So they went up on the roof and lowered him on his mat through the tiles into the middle of the crowd, right in front of Jesus. 20 When Jesus saw their faith, He said, “Friend, your sins are forgiven.”

21 But the scribes and Pharisees began thinking to themselves, “Who is this man who speaks blasphemy? Who can forgive sins but God alone?” 22 Knowing what they were thinking, Jesus replied, “Why are you thinking these things in your hearts? 23 Which is easier: to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Get up and walk’? 24 But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on the earth to forgive sins…” He said to the paralytic, “I tell you, get up, pick up your mat, and go home.”

25 And immediately the man stood up before them, took what he had been lying on, and went home glorifying God. 26 Everyone was taken with amazement and glorified God. They were filled with awe and said, “We have seen remarkable things today.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus is teaching with Pharisees and teachers of the law present. Some men bring a paralyzed man, but the crowd prevents them from reaching Him. They go onto the roof and lower the man through the tiles, placing him before Jesus. Their persistence brings him within reach of Jesus.

Jesus sees their faith and tells the man that his sins are forgiven. The scribes and Pharisees recognize the weight of that claim: forgiveness belongs to God. Jesus knows their thoughts and asks which is easier to say—an announcement of forgiveness or a command to get up and walk.

He then explains the purpose of the visible healing: they are to know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins. The man immediately stands, carries his mat home, and glorifies God. The crowd’s amazement also becomes praise.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand the visible healing as confirming Jesus’ authority to forgive sins, with the men’s actions showing their faith in Him. The scene directs attention to who Jesus is and what He can give, rather than establishing that one person’s faith automatically secures another person’s forgiveness. (Calvin on the parallel Matthew 9:2–6; Mark 2:1–12)
passages.god_plan_html:
Isaiah’s picture of God coming to save includes the lame being restored. Here the man’s restored movement accompanies the announcement of forgiveness, bringing physical restoration and the deeper need for mercy together in one encounter. This is a supported parallel with the promised restoration, while Jesus Himself states that this particular healing demonstrates His authority to forgive. (Isaiah 35:3–6)

By the end of Luke, Jesus explains how that forgiveness will reach beyond the people gathered in this house. His suffering and resurrection lead into the proclamation of repentance and forgiveness in His name to all nations. The authority made known here belongs to the Savior whose death and resurrection stand at the center of that message. (Luke 24:44–49)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 5:27-32
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus eat with tax collectors and sinners?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 27 After this, Jesus went out and saw a tax collector named Levi sitting at the tax booth. “Follow Me,” He told him, 28 and Levi got up, left everything, and followed Him. 29 Then Levi hosted a great banquet for Jesus at his house. A large crowd of tax collectors was there, along with others who were eating with them. 30 But the Pharisees and their scribes complained to Jesus’ disciples, “Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?” 31 Jesus answered, “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick. 32 I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners, to repentance.”
paragraphs: 27 After this, Jesus went out and saw a tax collector named Levi sitting at the tax booth. “Follow Me,” He told him, 28 and Levi got up, left everything, and followed Him. 29 Then Levi hosted a great banquet for Jesus at his house. A large crowd of tax collectors was there, along with others who were eating with them.

30 But the Pharisees and their scribes complained to Jesus’ disciples, “Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?” 31 Jesus answered, “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick. 32 I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners, to repentance.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus calls Levi from his tax booth, and Levi gets up, leaves everything, and follows Him. Levi then hosts a large banquet for Jesus, with many tax collectors and others at the table. The call leads both to a changed direction for Levi and to a gathering where others meet Jesus.

The Pharisees and their scribes object to the disciples eating and drinking with tax collectors and sinners. Jesus answers with the picture of a doctor attending the sick. His mission is to call sinners to repentance, so being among people who need that help fits the work He has come to do.

Levi’s response gives this gathering its setting: a man whom Jesus has called now welcomes Him among his companions. Matthew’s parallel account names the tax collector Matthew and includes Jesus’ appeal to Hosea’s call for mercy. (Matthew 9:9–13)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand Jesus’ welcome as mercy that calls people to a changed life, rather than approval of their sin. In the doctor comparison, Calvin reads the healthy people as those who think themselves righteous, while Jesus’ stated purpose is to reach sinners in need of repentance. (Calvin on Matthew 9:12–13; Luke 5:31–32)
passages.god_plan_html:
Luke returns to this same complaint when tax collectors and sinners gather to hear Jesus. His pictures of a lost sheep and a lost coin explain the joy over a sinner’s repentance. Levi’s banquet belongs within that larger purpose of seeking people who need to be brought back. (Luke 15:1–10)

At the Gospel’s end, repentance and forgiveness in Jesus’ name are to be proclaimed to all nations. The welcome at this table is an early example of that outward-reaching mercy: Jesus approaches sinners and calls them to turn toward Him. (Luke 24:44–49)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 5:33-39
passages.section_title: Why do Jesus’ disciples feast while others fast?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 33 Then they said to Him, “John’s disciples and those of the Pharisees frequently fast and pray, but Yours keep on eating and drinking.” 34 Jesus replied, “Can you make the guests of the bridegroom fast while He is with them? 35 But the time will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them; then they will fast.” 36 He also told them a parable: “No one tears a piece of cloth from a new garment and sews it on an old one. If he does, he will tear the new garment as well, and the patch from the new will not match the old. 37 And no one pours new wine into old wineskins. If he does, the new wine will burst the skins, the wine will spill, and the wineskins will be ruined. 38 Instead, new wine is poured into new wineskins. 39 And no one after drinking old wine wants new, for he says, ‘The old is better.’”
paragraphs: 33 Then they said to Him, “John’s disciples and those of the Pharisees frequently fast and pray, but Yours keep on eating and drinking.” 34 Jesus replied, “Can you make the guests of the bridegroom fast while He is with them? 35 But the time will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them; then they will fast.”

36 He also told them a parable: “No one tears a piece of cloth from a new garment and sews it on an old one. If he does, he will tear the new garment as well, and the patch from the new will not match the old. 37 And no one pours new wine into old wineskins. If he does, the new wine will burst the skins, the wine will spill, and the wineskins will be ruined. 38 Instead, new wine is poured into new wineskins. 39 And no one after drinking old wine wants new, for he says, ‘The old is better.’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The question about fasting follows the meal at Levi’s house. The questioners contrast the fasting and prayers of John’s disciples and the Pharisees’ disciples with the eating and drinking of Jesus’ followers.

Jesus compares His presence with a bridegroom’s presence at a wedding. That is a reason for joy; a time for fasting will come when the bridegroom is taken away. He does not make fasting meaningless. He explains why the disciples’ present circumstances matter.

He then gives two pictures of things that do not fit together: a piece torn from a new garment to patch an old one, and new wine poured into old wineskins. Luke adds the saying about someone who has drunk old wine preferring it to new. These pictures continue the discussion about how people receive what Jesus brings; they should be read within that setting.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly recognize Jesus as the bridegroom and connect His being taken away with His coming death. The pictures of clothing and wineskins receive different explanations.

The Catholic bishops’ notes on the parallel Matthew passage emphasize the newness of Jesus’ teaching and the gospel’s reach beyond the existing forms of religious life. Calvin, a historical Reformed teacher, instead reads the pictures as Jesus protecting His still-weak disciples from a demanding discipline they are not ready to bear. These are interpretations in explanatory notes and a teacher’s commentary, rather than a claim that every Catholic or Reformed Christian holds one reading. (USCCB notes on Matthew 9:15–17; Calvin on Matthew 9:16–17 and Luke 5:39)

On the final saying, Wesley explains the preference for old wine as the difficulty of letting go of accustomed ideas. The bishops’ note on Luke likewise sees satisfaction with the familiar as a reason some resist what Jesus offers. (Wesley on Luke 5:39; USCCB note on Luke 5:39)
passages.god_plan_html:
The bridegroom’s coming removal points forward to the suffering that Luke will later narrate. At the final Passover meal, Jesus speaks of His coming suffering and gives the cup as the new covenant in His blood. That later scene states plainly how His death will bring the promised covenant into effect. (Luke 22:14–20)

Hebrews describes Jesus as the mediator of the better covenant and recalls God’s promise to write His laws on His people’s hearts and forgive their sins. This helps place the newness Jesus brings within the Bible’s larger story. The promised change includes inward renewal and forgiveness, rather than freedom to disregard what pleases God. (Hebrews 8:6–13)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 6:1-5
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus defend His disciples eating grain on the Sabbath?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 One Sabbath Jesus was passing through the grainfields, and His disciples began to pick the heads of grain, rub them in their hands, and eat them. 2 But some of the Pharisees asked, “Why are you doing what is unlawful on the Sabbath?” 3 Jesus replied, “Have you not read what David did when he and his companions were hungry? 4 He entered the house of God, took the consecrated bread and gave it to his companions, and ate what is lawful only for the priests to eat.” 5 Then Jesus declared, “The Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.”
paragraphs: 1 One Sabbath Jesus was passing through the grainfields, and His disciples began to pick the heads of grain, rub them in their hands, and eat them. 2 But some of the Pharisees asked, “Why are you doing what is unlawful on the Sabbath?”

3 Jesus replied, “Have you not read what David did when he and his companions were hungry? 4 He entered the house of God, took the consecrated bread and gave it to his companions, and ate what is lawful only for the priests to eat.” 5 Then Jesus declared, “The Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
As Jesus and His disciples pass through grainfields on a Sabbath, the disciples pick heads of grain, rub them in their hands, and eat. Some Pharisees object that this is unlawful on the Sabbath. The immediate question concerns Sabbath observance; the Law already permits someone to pluck grain by hand in a neighbor’s field. (Deuteronomy 23:24–25)

Jesus answers with David’s hunger and the consecrated bread given to him by the priest. Leviticus assigns that bread to Aaron and his sons, and Jesus Himself acknowledges the restriction to priests. He brings the account of David’s need into the present discussion and then declares His authority as Lord of the Sabbath. (1 Samuel 21:1–6; Leviticus 24:5–9)

The answer asks His hearers to consider the Scriptural example and the identity of the One standing before them. The dispute continues on another Sabbath in the following scene, where the question of doing good becomes explicit.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly connect this defense of the disciples with concern for human need and Jesus’ authority over the Sabbath. The Catholic Catechism expresses the shared principle that serving God and neighbor belongs within honoring Sabbath rest. (Catechism 582; USCCB note on Luke 6:1–11)
passages.god_plan_html: Paul later places Sabbath observance within the larger relationship between the things that point ahead and Christ, to whom they point. His teaching helps readers see why Jesus’ identity matters in this encounter: the discussion concerns the Lord to whom the sacred day ultimately points. This is a later New Testament connection, not a claim that Luke’s five verses answer every question about Christian worship days. (Colossians 2:16–19)

passages.title: Luke 6:6-11
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus heal the man’s hand on the Sabbath?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 On another Sabbath Jesus entered the synagogue and was teaching, and a man was there whose right hand was withered. 7 Looking for a reason to accuse Jesus, the scribes and Pharisees were watching Him closely to see if He would heal on the Sabbath. 8 But Jesus knew their thoughts and said to the man with the withered hand, “Get up and stand among us.” So he got up and stood there. 9 Then Jesus said to them, “I ask you, which is lawful on the Sabbath: to do good or to do evil, to save life or to destroy it?” 10 And after looking around at all of them, He said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” He did so, and it was restored. 11 But the scribes and Pharisees were filled with rage and began to discuss with one another what they might do to Jesus.
paragraphs: 6 On another Sabbath Jesus entered the synagogue and was teaching, and a man was there whose right hand was withered. 7 Looking for a reason to accuse Jesus, the scribes and Pharisees were watching Him closely to see if He would heal on the Sabbath. 8 But Jesus knew their thoughts and said to the man with the withered hand, “Get up and stand among us.” So he got up and stood there.

9 Then Jesus said to them, “I ask you, which is lawful on the Sabbath: to do good or to do evil, to save life or to destroy it?” 10 And after looking around at all of them, He said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” He did so, and it was restored. 11 But the scribes and Pharisees were filled with rage and began to discuss with one another what they might do to Jesus.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
On another Sabbath, Jesus teaches in a synagogue where a man has a withered right hand. The scribes and Pharisees watch for a healing so they can accuse Him. Jesus knows their thoughts and brings the man into the open.

He asks whether doing good or doing evil, saving life or destroying it, is lawful on the Sabbath. His question puts the person’s need at the center of the discussion. He tells the man to stretch out his hand, and it is restored.

The healing brings an angry response from the watchers, who begin discussing what they might do to Jesus. Luke places their response beside the good He has just done. The episode continues the previous Sabbath encounter, moving from the disciples’ need for food to a man’s need for restoration.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand Jesus as showing that mercy and care for a person fit the purpose of honoring God on the Sabbath. The healing reveals His authority while His question exposes the failure to welcome the good being done. (Catechism 582; USCCB note on Luke 6:1–11)
passages.god_plan_html:
The concern for doing good belongs to the Bible’s larger call to love one’s neighbor. James joins the command to love with a warning against withholding mercy, then gives the example of meeting a person’s need for food and clothing. That is a thematic connection: faith is to become visible in care for people. Jesus’ action here shows such care in the face of opposition. (James 2:8–17)

Peter later summarizes Jesus’ ministry as going about doing good and healing those oppressed by the devil, with God’s presence and the Spirit’s power. The restoration of this hand is one particular act within that saving ministry of goodness and mercy. (Acts 10:38)

passages.title: Luke 6:12-16
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus choose twelve apostles?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 In those days Jesus went out to the mountain to pray, and He spent the night in prayer to God. 13 When daylight came, He called His disciples to Him and chose twelve of them, whom He also designated as apostles: 14 Simon, whom He named Peter, and his brother Andrew; James and John; Philip and Bartholomew; 15 Matthew and Thomas; James son of Alphaeus and Simon called the Zealot; 16 Judas son of James, and Judas Iscariot, who became a traitor.
paragraphs: 12 In those days Jesus went out to the mountain to pray, and He spent the night in prayer to God. 13 When daylight came, He called His disciples to Him and chose twelve of them, whom He also designated as apostles:

14 Simon, whom He named Peter, and his brother Andrew; James and John; Philip and Bartholomew; 15 Matthew and Thomas; James son of Alphaeus and Simon called the Zealot; 16 Judas son of James, and Judas Iscariot, who became a traitor.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus spends the night on the mountain in prayer to God. At daylight He calls His disciples and chooses twelve from among them. Luke places the choice within His life of prayer, then gives the names of those chosen.

These twelve come from the larger group of disciples. The Greek word ἀπόστολος, apostolos (ah-POS-toh-loss), means a messenger or someone sent with a commission. Here it names the twelve Jesus selects for a particular role alongside Him. (Thayer, G652)

The list begins with Simon, whom Jesus named Peter, and ends with Judas Iscariot, identified as the one who became a traitor. Luke introduces these men before the teaching that follows, allowing readers to see both their appointment and the instruction through which Jesus prepares them.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see the choice as Jesus appointing a particular group to share in His mission and later bear witness to Him. The number twelve is connected with Israel’s twelve tribes, a connection Jesus later makes explicit when speaking of their place in His kingdom. (USCCB note on Luke 6:13; Luke 22:28–30)
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus later speaks to these disciples about His kingdom and the twelve tribes of Israel. The choice of twelve therefore belongs within His purposes for God’s people, with a connection to Israel that Scripture itself makes. At the same meal, He teaches that leadership among them must take the form of service, following His own example. (Luke 22:24–30)

Paul describes God’s household as built on the foundation of apostles and prophets, with Christ as the cornerstone. Revelation’s picture of the holy city joins gates bearing the tribes’ names with foundations bearing the apostles’ names. Together these passages show the appointment reaching into the building of God’s people around Christ. (Ephesians 2:17–22; Revelation 21:9–14)

passages.title: Luke 6:17-26
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus call the poor and the rejected blessed?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 Then Jesus came down with them and stood on a level place. A large crowd of His disciples was there, along with a great number of people from all over Judea, Jerusalem, and the seacoast of Tyre and Sidon. 18 They had come to hear Him and to be healed of their diseases, and those troubled by unclean spirits were healed. 19 The entire crowd was trying to touch Him, because power was coming from Him and healing them all. 20 Looking up at His disciples, Jesus said: “Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God. 21 Blessed are you who hunger now, for you will be filled. Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh. 22 Blessed are you when people hate you, and when they exclude you and insult you and reject your name as evil because of the Son of Man. 23 Rejoice in that day and leap for joy, because great is your reward in heaven. For their fathers treated the prophets in the same way. 24 But woe to you who are rich, for you have already received your comfort. 25 Woe to you who are well fed now, for you will hunger. Woe to you who laugh now, for you will mourn and weep. 26 Woe to you when all men speak well of you, for their fathers treated the false prophets in the same way.
paragraphs: 17 Then Jesus came down with them and stood on a level place. A large crowd of His disciples was there, along with a great number of people from all over Judea, Jerusalem, and the seacoast of Tyre and Sidon. 18 They had come to hear Him and to be healed of their diseases, and those troubled by unclean spirits were healed. 19 The entire crowd was trying to touch Him, because power was coming from Him and healing them all.

20 Looking up at His disciples, Jesus said: “Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God. 21 Blessed are you who hunger now, for you will be filled. Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh. 22 Blessed are you when people hate you, and when they exclude you and insult you and reject your name as evil because of the Son of Man. 23 Rejoice in that day and leap for joy, because great is your reward in heaven. For their fathers treated the prophets in the same way.

24 But woe to you who are rich, for you have already received your comfort. 25 Woe to you who are well fed now, for you will hunger. Woe to you who laugh now, for you will mourn and weep. 26 Woe to you when all men speak well of you, for their fathers treated the false prophets in the same way.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus comes down with the twelve and stands on a level place. Disciples and people from a wide region gather to hear Him and seek healing. He then looks toward His disciples and begins teaching them about the kingdom.

Four blessings are followed by four warnings. Poverty is set beside riches, hunger beside being well fed, weeping beside laughter, and rejection because of the Son of Man beside universal praise. The repeated contrast between now and what is to come directs attention beyond present circumstances.

The word translated blessed is μακάριος, makarios (mah-KAH-ree-oss), meaning blessed or happy. Here Jesus explains the reason for that blessing through God’s kingdom and promised future, even when a person is suffering now. (Thayer, G3107)

The rejection He describes has a stated cause: allegiance to the Son of Man. Jesus places those who suffer this way alongside the prophets, while warning that praise can also be given to false prophets. His teaching asks the disciples to consider whose approval and whose promised future they are living for.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian interpreters place different emphasis on the relationship between outward hardship and inward dependence on God. The Catholic bishops’ notes stress Luke’s direct concern with actual poverty, hunger and social rejection; Wesley also takes the poor here literally, particularly disciples who have left things behind. (USCCB note on Luke 6:20–26; Wesley on Luke 6:20–26)

Calvin reads Luke alongside Matthew’s poverty of spirit: hardship is joined with humility and reliance on God. On the warnings, he emphasizes the danger of making present wealth and pleasure one’s whole comfort. These emphases can overlap. The Catholic Catechism likewise joins detachment from wealth with humility and trust in the Father; the bishops’ notes should not be taken to mean Catholic teaching ignores the heart. (Calvin on Matthew 5:3 and Luke 6:24–26; Catechism 2544–2547)
passages.god_plan_html:
Mary’s earlier song describes God bringing down the mighty, lifting the humble, filling the hungry and sending the rich away empty. Jesus’ blessings and warnings continue that theme of God overturning the security people find in present status. The link is a shared theme within Luke, not a claim that every poor or wealthy person has the same relationship with God. (Luke 1:51–55)

The New Testament also develops the promised comfort. Revelation describes people shepherded by the Lamb, no longer hungry or thirsty, with their tears wiped away. Peter connects suffering for Christ’s name with blessing and future joy at His appearing. These passages carry the teaching toward God’s final restoration and the hope that sustains His people before it arrives. (Revelation 7:15–17; 1 Peter 4:12–16)

passages.title: Luke 6:27-36
passages.section_title: What does it mean to love people who mistreat us?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 27 But to those of you who will listen, I say: Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, 28 bless those who curse you, pray for those who mistreat you. 29 If someone strikes you on one cheek, turn to him the other also. And if someone takes your cloak, do not withhold your tunic as well. 30 Give to everyone who asks you, and if anyone takes what is yours, do not demand it back. 31 Do to others as you would have them do to you. 32 If you love those who love you, what credit is that to you? Even sinners love those who love them. 33 If you do good to those who do good to you, what credit is that to you? Even sinners do the same. 34 And if you lend to those from whom you expect repayment, what credit is that to you? Even sinners lend to sinners, expecting to be repaid in full. 35 But love your enemies, do good to them, and lend to them, expecting nothing in return. Then your reward will be great, and you will be sons of the Most High; for He is kind to the ungrateful and wicked. 36 Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful.
paragraphs: 27 But to those of you who will listen, I say: Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, 28 bless those who curse you, pray for those who mistreat you. 29 If someone strikes you on one cheek, turn to him the other also. And if someone takes your cloak, do not withhold your tunic as well. 30 Give to everyone who asks you, and if anyone takes what is yours, do not demand it back. 31 Do to others as you would have them do to you.

32 If you love those who love you, what credit is that to you? Even sinners love those who love them. 33 If you do good to those who do good to you, what credit is that to you? Even sinners do the same. 34 And if you lend to those from whom you expect repayment, what credit is that to you? Even sinners lend to sinners, expecting to be repaid in full. 35 But love your enemies, do good to them, and lend to them, expecting nothing in return. Then your reward will be great, and you will be sons of the Most High; for He is kind to the ungrateful and wicked. 36 Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After speaking about rejection because of the Son of Man, Jesus tells His hearers how to respond to enemies. Love is expressed in action: doing good, blessing, praying and giving. His examples concern people who cause harm or take advantage, making the instruction demanding and concrete.

The direction to treat others as we would want to be treated applies even when they have treated us badly. Jesus then asks what distinguishes His followers if they love, help or lend only when they expect the same in return.

The Father’s kindness supplies the reason for a different response. He is kind to the ungrateful and wicked, and His children are to show the family likeness through mercy. The passage reaches its summary in the call to be merciful as their Father is merciful.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian traditions commonly call for love of enemies, prayer for those who mistreat us and the surrender of personal revenge. They differ over what that requires when violence and protection of others are involved.

The Catholic Church permits proportionate defense and teaches that protecting someone entrusted to one’s care can be a duty. Reformed teaching in the Westminster Confession permits a public role for Christians in restraining wrongdoing, including force on just and necessary occasions. These readings distinguish personal vengeance from protective or public responsibility. (Catechism 2263–2265; Westminster Confession 23.1–2)

Mennonite Church USA’s confession instead calls believers to resist evil without violence, including in the face of warfare, and rejects military participation. Its position also opposes abuse and injustice and calls for active peacemaking. This reading understands nonviolence as a way of pursuing justice and reconciliation. (Confession of Faith, article 22)
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul explains God’s mercy through Christ’s death for people who were still sinners and enemies. The love Jesus commands reflects the love through which God brings enemies into reconciliation with Himself. The cross gives the larger saving setting for the Father’s kindness described here. (Romans 5:6–11)

Romans also carries this teaching into the life of believers: bless persecutors, give food and drink to an enemy in need, leave vengeance with God, and overcome evil with good. Mercy becomes a visible response to the mercy already received. (Romans 12:14–21)

passages.title: Luke 6:37-42
passages.section_title: How can we help others without overlooking our own faults?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 37 Do not judge, and you will not be judged. Do not condemn, and you will not be condemned. Forgive, and you will be forgiven. 38 Give, and it will be given to you. A good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over will be poured into your lap. For with the measure you use, it will be measured back to you.” 39 Jesus also told them a parable: “Can a blind man lead a blind man? Will they not both fall into a pit? 40 A disciple is not above his teacher, but everyone who is fully trained will be like his teacher. 41 Why do you look at the speck in your brother’s eye but fail to notice the beam in your own eye? 42 How can you say, ‘Brother, let me take the speck out of your eye,’ while you yourself fail to see the beam in your own eye? You hypocrite! First take the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother’s eye.
paragraphs: 37 Do not judge, and you will not be judged. Do not condemn, and you will not be condemned. Forgive, and you will be forgiven. 38 Give, and it will be given to you. A good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over will be poured into your lap. For with the measure you use, it will be measured back to you.”

39 Jesus also told them a parable: “Can a blind man lead a blind man? Will they not both fall into a pit? 40 A disciple is not above his teacher, but everyone who is fully trained will be like his teacher.

41 Why do you look at the speck in your brother’s eye but fail to notice the beam in your own eye? 42 How can you say, ‘Brother, let me take the speck out of your eye,’ while you yourself fail to see the beam in your own eye? You hypocrite! First take the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother’s eye.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The call to be merciful continues in instructions about judging, condemning, forgiving and giving. Jesus describes a generous measure that is filled beyond the brim, then says the measure people use will be measured back to them. The saying belongs within this discussion of mercy and how we treat others.

He follows with pictures about sight and learning. A blind guide puts both himself and his follower in danger. A disciple who is fully trained becomes like the teacher. These sayings ask His hearers to consider the guidance they receive and the people they are becoming.

The speck and beam make the danger of hypocrisy easy to see. Someone is trying to correct a small fault while overlooking a much larger obstruction in himself. Jesus tells him to deal with his own obstruction first, so he can then see clearly enough to help his brother.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand the warning as a call to merciful, honest self-examination when dealing with others’ faults. Calvin reads it as correcting harsh condemnation and hypocrisy, while the instruction to remove one’s own beam leaves a place for clear-sighted help afterward. (Calvin on Matthew 7:1–5 and Luke 6:37–42; Luke 6:41–42)
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul gives a closely related pattern for the life of Christ’s people: restore someone caught in wrongdoing with gentleness, watch yourself, and carry one another’s burdens. This is a thematic connection with the sight Jesus calls for here. Help for another person and honest attention to oneself belong together. (Galatians 6:1–5)

James likewise joins mercy with the command to love one’s neighbor and warns against judgment without mercy. Across these teachings, the community God is forming is to reflect His mercy in the way its members deal with need and failure. (James 2:8–17)
