passages.title: Luke 6:43-45
passages.section_title: What do our words reveal about our hearts?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 43 No good tree bears bad fruit, nor does a bad tree bear good fruit. 44 For each tree is known by its own fruit. Indeed, figs are not gathered from thornbushes, nor grapes from brambles. 45 The good man brings good things out of the good treasure of his heart, and the evil man brings evil things out of the evil treasure of his heart. For out of the overflow of the heart the mouth speaks.
paragraphs: 43 No good tree bears bad fruit, nor does a bad tree bear good fruit. 44 For each tree is known by its own fruit. Indeed, figs are not gathered from thornbushes, nor grapes from brambles. 45 The good man brings good things out of the good treasure of his heart, and the evil man brings evil things out of the evil treasure of his heart. For out of the overflow of the heart the mouth speaks.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus turns from the eye to the tree. A tree is recognized by the fruit it produces, and different kinds of plants bear different fruit. The comparison follows His warnings about guidance and hypocrisy.

He then explains the human connection: good and evil come from what is stored in the heart, and speech flows from what fills it. The teaching reaches beneath an outward impression to the source from which a person’s words and actions come.

This prepares for His final question about calling Him Lord without doing what He says. Speech matters, but the kind of heart it reveals and the life that accompanies it also matter.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand the fruit as revealing a person’s inward character, with speech showing what fills the heart. The instruction applies to those receiving the teaching as well as to the teachers whose guidance they follow. (Luke 6:39–45; USCCB notes on Luke 6:43–46 and the Matthew parallels)
passages.god_plan_html:
God’s promise through Ezekiel reaches the source of a changed life: He will cleanse His people, give them a new heart, put His Spirit within them and lead them into obedience. This is a Bible-wide connection with the importance of the heart here; Luke does not label the tree saying as a direct quotation of Ezekiel. (Ezekiel 36:25–27)

Jesus later uses a different plant picture to explain fruitful life through dependence on Him. As branches remain in the vine, His disciples are to remain in Him; their fruit glorifies the Father. The sayings together direct attention to both inward change and an ongoing life with Christ. (John 15:1–8)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 6:46-49
passages.section_title: What gives a life a foundation that will hold?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 46 Why do you call Me ‘Lord, Lord,’ but do not do what I say? 47 I will show you what he is like who comes to Me and hears My words and acts on them: 48 He is like a man building a house, who dug down deep and laid his foundation on the rock. When the flood came, the torrent crashed against that house but could not shake it, because it was well built. 49 But the one who hears My words and does not act on them is like a man who built his house on ground without a foundation. The torrent crashed against that house, and immediately it fell—and great was its destruction!”
paragraphs: 46 Why do you call Me ‘Lord, Lord,’ but do not do what I say? 47 I will show you what he is like who comes to Me and hears My words and acts on them: 48 He is like a man building a house, who dug down deep and laid his foundation on the rock. When the flood came, the torrent crashed against that house but could not shake it, because it was well built.

49 But the one who hears My words and does not act on them is like a man who built his house on ground without a foundation. The torrent crashed against that house, and immediately it fell—and great was its destruction!”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus closes His teaching by asking why people call Him Lord while failing to do what He says. The question brings the whole discourse toward a personal response.

Both builders hear His words. The difference is what they do with them. The person who comes to Jesus, hears and acts is like someone who digs deep and lays a foundation on rock. When floodwater strikes, the house stands because it is well built.

The person who hears without acting is like someone who builds directly on the ground without a foundation. The flood exposes that weakness and the house collapses. Jesus’ picture connects a durable foundation with receiving His words in a way that shapes life.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand the houses as contrasting lived response to Jesus with hearing or profession that produces no obedience. Calvin emphasizes the difference becoming visible under testing, while the Catholic bishops’ notes on the parallel Matthew passage likewise identify hearing and doing as the central contrast. (Calvin on Matthew 7:24–27 and Luke 6:47–49; USCCB note on Matthew 7:24–27)
passages.god_plan_html:
James gives another picture of the same danger: a person hears the word but does not carry it out, like someone who looks in a mirror and then forgets what he has seen. He calls for a continuing response that becomes visible in action, including care for vulnerable people and restraint in speech. This is a thematic parallel to the life built on Jesus’ words. (James 1:19–27)

The connection brings the discourse into the wider purpose of forming a people who live by what God says. Jesus has described mercy, generosity, honesty and inward goodness; the closing picture calls His hearers to put that teaching into practice.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 7:1-10
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus marvel at the centurion’s faith?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 When Jesus had concluded His discourse in the hearing of the people, He went to Capernaum. 2 There a highly valued servant of a centurion was sick and about to die. 3 When the centurion heard about Jesus, he sent some Jewish elders to ask Him to come and heal his servant. 4 They came to Jesus and pleaded with Him earnestly, “This man is worthy to have You grant this, 5 for he loves our nation and has built our synagogue.” 6 So Jesus went with them. But when He was not far from the house, the centurion sent friends with the message: “Lord, do not trouble Yourself, for I am not worthy to have You come under my roof. 7 That is why I did not consider myself worthy to come to You. But just say the word, and my servant will be healed. 8 For I myself am a man under authority, with soldiers under me. I tell one to go, and he goes, and another to come, and he comes. I tell my servant to do something, and he does it.” 9 When Jesus heard this, He marveled at the centurion. Turning to the crowd following Him, He said, “I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such great faith.” 10 And when the messengers returned to the house, they found the servant in good health.
paragraphs: 1 When Jesus had concluded His discourse in the hearing of the people, He went to Capernaum. 2 There a highly valued servant of a centurion was sick and about to die. 3 When the centurion heard about Jesus, he sent some Jewish elders to ask Him to come and heal his servant. 4 They came to Jesus and pleaded with Him earnestly, “This man is worthy to have You grant this, 5 for he loves our nation and has built our synagogue.”

6 So Jesus went with them. But when He was not far from the house, the centurion sent friends with the message: “Lord, do not trouble Yourself, for I am not worthy to have You come under my roof. 7 That is why I did not consider myself worthy to come to You. But just say the word, and my servant will be healed. 8 For I myself am a man under authority, with soldiers under me. I tell one to go, and he goes, and another to come, and he comes. I tell my servant to do something, and he does it.”

9 When Jesus heard this, He marveled at the centurion. Turning to the crowd following Him, He said, “I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such great faith.” 10 And when the messengers returned to the house, they found the servant in good health.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After finishing His teaching, Jesus enters Capernaum. A centurion, an officer with soldiers under him, has a highly valued servant who is close to death. He sends Jewish elders to ask Jesus for help. They speak warmly of his love for their nation and his building of their synagogue.

As Jesus approaches the house, the centurion sends friends with a second message. The elders have called him worthy of help, but he describes himself as unworthy to receive Jesus under his roof or even to come to Him personally. He nevertheless trusts that Jesus can heal by a word.

His explanation comes from his own experience of authority. He receives orders and gives orders, and those under his command obey. He believes that Jesus’ authority can likewise accomplish what He commands without requiring His physical presence beside the sick man.

Jesus marvels and commends the faith He has found, saying He has not found such great faith even in Israel. The messengers return and find the servant well. Luke places the centurion’s trust in Jesus’ word at the center of the account.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see humble trust in Jesus’ authority and a welcome reaching beyond Israel. The centurion’s faith, his care for his servant and the Jewish elders’ appeal are all part of the scene; the Catholic bishops’ notes also connect it with the later account of Cornelius in Acts. (USCCB note on Luke 7:1–10; Matthew 8:5–13)
passages.god_plan_html:
Matthew’s parallel includes Jesus speaking of people coming from east and west to share the kingdom with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. The faith of this man from outside Israel belongs within the larger welcome of the nations into God’s promised blessing. (Matthew 8:10–12)

Acts gives a related scene involving another centurion, Cornelius. Peter enters his household and explains that God does not show favoritism, but welcomes people from every nation. This is a later parallel, not the same officer or the same event. The two accounts show the good news reaching across a boundary that could otherwise keep people apart. (Acts 10:24–36)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 7:11-17
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus stop the funeral at Nain?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 Soon afterward, Jesus went to a town called Nain. His disciples went with Him, accompanied by a large crowd. 12 As He approached the town gate, He saw a dead man being carried out, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow. And a large crowd from the town was with her. 13 When the Lord saw her, He had compassion on her and said, “Do not weep.” 14 Then He went up and touched the coffin, and those carrying it stood still. “Young man,” He said, “I tell you, get up!” 15 And the dead man sat up and began to speak! Then Jesus gave him back to his mother. 16 A sense of awe swept over all of them, and they glorified God. “A great prophet has appeared among us!” they said. “God has visited His people!” 17 And the news about Jesus spread throughout Judea and all the surrounding region.
paragraphs: 11 Soon afterward, Jesus went to a town called Nain. His disciples went with Him, accompanied by a large crowd. 12 As He approached the town gate, He saw a dead man being carried out, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow. And a large crowd from the town was with her. 13 When the Lord saw her, He had compassion on her and said, “Do not weep.”

14 Then He went up and touched the coffin, and those carrying it stood still. “Young man,” He said, “I tell you, get up!” 15 And the dead man sat up and began to speak! Then Jesus gave him back to his mother. 16 A sense of awe swept over all of them, and they glorified God. “A great prophet has appeared among us!” they said. “God has visited His people!” 17 And the news about Jesus spread throughout Judea and all the surrounding region.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
As Jesus approaches Nain with His disciples and a crowd, another crowd is leaving with a funeral. The dead man is his mother’s only son, and she is a widow. Luke draws attention to her loss before describing what Jesus does.

Jesus sees her and has compassion. He tells her not to weep, touches the coffin and speaks to the young man. Luke records no request for a miracle from the mother and sets no test of her faith before Jesus acts.

The word translated coffin is σορός, soros (soh-ROSS). Thayer identifies its use here as the funeral bier or couch used to carry the dead. It helps us picture the bearers stopping when Jesus reaches out. (Thayer, G4673)

The man sits up and speaks, and Jesus gives him back to his mother. The crowd responds with awe and praise, recognizing a great prophet and God’s visitation among His people. The report spreads through Judea and the surrounding region.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand this as a real restoration to life that reveals Jesus’ power and His compassion for the bereaved mother. The Catholic bishops’ notes highlight its echo of Elijah restoring a widow’s son and its preparation for Jesus’ later answer that the dead are raised. (USCCB note on Luke 7:11–17; Luke 7:22)
passages.god_plan_html:
The parallel with Elijah is especially close: a widow loses her son, the son lives again, and he is returned to his mother. In Kings, Elijah cries to the Lord and the Lord restores the child’s life; here Jesus commands the young man to get up. Elisha’s restoration of the Shunammite woman’s son gives another related Old Testament scene. These are supported parallels that help explain the crowd’s recognition of a prophet. (1 Kings 17:17–24; 2 Kings 4:32–37)

The New Testament carries the hope beyond this return to ordinary life. Jesus speaks of a coming hour when those in their graves will hear His voice and come out. The event at Nain displays the authority of the One whose voice Scripture places at the center of the future resurrection. (John 5:24–29)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 7:18-23
passages.section_title: How does Jesus answer John’s question about who He is?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 Then John’s disciples informed him about all these things. 19 So John called two of his disciples and sent them to ask the Lord, “Are You the One who was to come, or should we look for someone else?” 20 When the men came to Jesus, they said, “John the Baptist sent us to ask, ‘Are You the One who was to come, or should we look for someone else?’” 21 At that very hour Jesus healed many people of their diseases, afflictions, and evil spirits, and He gave sight to many who were blind. 22 So He replied, “Go back and report to John what you have seen and heard: The blind receive sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the good news is preached to the poor. 23 Blessed is the one who does not fall away on account of Me.”
paragraphs: 18 Then John’s disciples informed him about all these things. 19 So John called two of his disciples and sent them to ask the Lord, “Are You the One who was to come, or should we look for someone else?” 20 When the men came to Jesus, they said, “John the Baptist sent us to ask, ‘Are You the One who was to come, or should we look for someone else?’”

21 At that very hour Jesus healed many people of their diseases, afflictions, and evil spirits, and He gave sight to many who were blind. 22 So He replied, “Go back and report to John what you have seen and heard: The blind receive sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the good news is preached to the poor. 23 Blessed is the one who does not fall away on account of Me.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
John’s disciples bring him reports about Jesus. John then sends two of them to ask whether Jesus is the One who was to come or whether they should expect someone else. The question follows the accounts of healing and the restoration of the widow’s son.

At that time Jesus heals people with diseases, afflictions and evil spirits, and gives sight to the blind. He tells the messengers to report what they have seen and heard, including restored sight and hearing, the lame walking, lepers cleansed, the dead raised and good news reaching the poor.

His answer joins what is happening before them with the promises of Scripture. He ends with a blessing for the person who does not fall away because of Him. The messengers are given something definite to carry back: His works and His message.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly understand Jesus’ works and the echoes of Isaiah as His answer about His identity. Interpreters differ over whose uncertainty the question is intended to address.

Wesley reads John as sending the disciples for their own assurance, and understands Jesus’ later praise of John as guarding against the idea that John had abandoned his testimony. The Catholic bishops’ note on the parallel Matthew passage considers it likely that John himself is struggling because Jesus’ mission differs from his expectations of judgment. These are commentators’ explanations, not separate binding doctrines for all members of their traditions. (Wesley on Luke 7:18–24; USCCB notes on Matthew 11:3–6)
passages.god_plan_html:
Isaiah describes God coming to save, with blind eyes opened, deaf ears unstopped and the lame restored. Another passage describes the Lord’s anointed bringing good news to the afflicted and release to captives—the passage Jesus had read at Nazareth. His reply points the messengers toward that promised work now taking place. (Isaiah 35:4–6; Isaiah 61:1–3; Luke 4:16–21)

This connection helps explain the shape of His ministry: mercy, restoration and the announcement of good news make known who has come. The answer invites John and his disciples to recognize God’s promised work in Jesus, even where His actions challenge their expectations.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 7:24-30
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus call John more than a prophet?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 24 After John’s messengers had left, Jesus began to speak to the crowds about John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed swaying in the wind? 25 Otherwise, what did you go out to see? A man dressed in fine clothes? Look, those who wear elegant clothing and live in luxury are found in palaces. 26 What then did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. 27 This is the one about whom it is written: ‘Behold, I will send My messenger ahead of You, who will prepare Your way before You.’ 28 I tell you, among those born of women there is no one greater than John, yet even the least in the kingdom of God is greater than he.” 29 All the people who heard this, even the tax collectors, acknowledged God’s justice. For they had received the baptism of John. 30 But the Pharisees and experts in the law rejected God’s purpose for themselves, because they had not been baptized by John.
paragraphs: 24 After John’s messengers had left, Jesus began to speak to the crowds about John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed swaying in the wind? 25 Otherwise, what did you go out to see? A man dressed in fine clothes? Look, those who wear elegant clothing and live in luxury are found in palaces. 26 What then did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. 27 This is the one about whom it is written: ‘Behold, I will send My messenger ahead of You, who will prepare Your way before You.’ 28 I tell you, among those born of women there is no one greater than John, yet even the least in the kingdom of God is greater than he.”

29 All the people who heard this, even the tax collectors, acknowledged God’s justice. For they had received the baptism of John. 30 But the Pharisees and experts in the law rejected God’s purpose for themselves, because they had not been baptized by John.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After John’s messengers leave, Jesus speaks to the crowd about John himself. His questions set the wilderness messenger apart from a reed that bends with the wind and from someone living in palace luxury. He directs attention to John’s prophetic calling.

John is more than a prophet because he is the messenger sent ahead to prepare the way. Jesus then gives John extraordinary praise while saying that even the least in God’s kingdom is greater than he. The statement draws attention to the significance of the kingdom John has announced.

The passage closes with contrasting responses. People who had received John’s baptism, including tax collectors, acknowledge God’s justice. The Pharisees and experts in the law described here had refused that baptism and rejected God’s purpose for themselves. Their response to John’s call is part of their response to the work Jesus is now making known.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly recognize John as the promised forerunner whose importance comes from preparing the way for Jesus. The comparison with the least in the kingdom receives different explanations.

The Catholic bishops’ note on the parallel Matthew passage emphasizes the great privilege of belonging to the kingdom John announced. Wesley takes the least here more specifically as the least teacher Jesus sends out. These are explanations of the comparison in a set of notes and a commentator’s work; they do not mean John is simply being dismissed as unfaithful. (USCCB note on Matthew 11:11; Wesley on Luke 7:28)
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus explicitly identifies John with the messenger promised in Scripture. Malachi describes a messenger preparing the way before the Lord’s coming; Jesus applies that preparing role to John. This places their ministries within the promised approach of God to His people. (Malachi 3:1; Luke 7:27)

John’s own testimony in the fourth Gospel gives a related picture. He is sent ahead of the Christ and rejoices as the bridegroom’s friend when the bridegroom arrives. The point of his ministry is to direct people toward Jesus, and his joy is bound up with Jesus becoming greater. (John 3:25–30)

passages.title: Luke 7:31-35
passages.section_title: Why do people reject both John and Jesus?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 31 “To what, then, can I compare the men of this generation? What are they like? 32 They are like children sitting in the marketplace and calling out to one another: ‘We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not weep.’ 33 For John the Baptist came neither eating bread nor drinking wine, and you say, ‘He has a demon!’ 34 The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and you say, ‘Look at this glutton and drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ 35 But wisdom is vindicated by all her children.”
paragraphs: 31 “To what, then, can I compare the men of this generation? What are they like? 32 They are like children sitting in the marketplace and calling out to one another: ‘We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not weep.’ 33 For John the Baptist came neither eating bread nor drinking wine, and you say, ‘He has a demon!’ 34 The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and you say, ‘Look at this glutton and drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ 35 But wisdom is vindicated by all her children.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus compares this generation with children complaining that others will neither dance to their flute nor mourn with their sad song. The picture introduces two different ways of living that have both met with criticism.

John’s abstaining is met with the charge that he has a demon. Jesus’ eating and drinking is met with charges of gluttony and drunkenness and criticism of His friendship with tax collectors and sinners. Those are accusations Jesus reports, not the narrator’s description of His conduct.

The contrasting objections reveal a refusal to receive either messenger. Jesus closes by saying that wisdom is vindicated by all her children. The focus turns from the critics’ demands to the people in whom God’s wisdom is being received and shown.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see a refusal to respond to God despite the different manner of John’s and Jesus’ ministries. Wesley understands wisdom’s children as those who recognize and welcome God’s wisdom in His ways of calling people to repentance. (Wesley on Luke 7:31–35; USCCB notes on Luke 7:31–35)
passages.god_plan_html:
The difference between rejecting God’s work and recognizing His wisdom continues in the preaching of the cross. Paul describes the crucified Christ as a stumbling block to some and foolishness to others, yet God’s power and wisdom to those who are called. God’s saving work can meet resistance precisely where people expect it to take a different form. (1 Corinthians 1:18–25)

This is a shared theme, not a claim that Jesus’ picture of the children predicts each detail of Paul’s ministry. Both passages direct attention toward receiving the wisdom God makes known through Christ instead of judging it only by human expectations.

passages.title: Luke 7:36-50
passages.section_title: What does the woman’s love reveal about forgiveness?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 36 Then one of the Pharisees invited Jesus to eat with him, and He entered the Pharisee’s house and reclined at the table. 37 When a sinful woman from that town learned that Jesus was dining there, she brought an alabaster jar of perfume. 38 As she stood behind Him at His feet weeping, she began to wet His feet with her tears and wipe them with her hair. Then she kissed His feet and anointed them with the perfume. 39 When the Pharisee who had invited Jesus saw this, he said to himself, “If this man were a prophet, He would know who this is and what kind of woman is touching Him—for she is a sinner!” 40 But Jesus answered him, “Simon, I have something to tell you.” “Tell me, Teacher,” he said. 41 “Two men were debtors to a certain moneylender. One owed him five hundred denarii, and the other fifty. 42 When they were unable to repay him, he forgave both of them. Which one, then, will love him more?” 43 “I suppose the one who was forgiven more,” Simon replied. “You have judged correctly,” Jesus said. 44 And turning toward the woman, He said to Simon, “Do you see this woman? When I entered your house, you did not give Me water for My feet, but she wet My feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair. 45 You did not greet Me with a kiss, but she has not stopped kissing My feet since I arrived. 46 You did not anoint My head with oil, but she has anointed My feet with perfume. 47 Therefore I tell you, her many sins have been forgiven, for she has loved much. But he who has been forgiven little loves little.” 48 Then Jesus said to her, “Your sins are forgiven.” 49 But those at the table began to say to themselves, “Who is this who even forgives sins?” 50 And Jesus told the woman, “Your faith has saved you; go in peace.”

One owed him five hundred denarii, and the other fifty. 42 When they were unable to repay him, he forgave both of them. Which one, then, will love him more?” 43 “I suppose the one who was forgiven more,” Simon replied. “You have judged correctly,” Jesus said.

44 And turning toward the woman, He said to Simon, “Do you see this woman? When I entered your house, you did not give Me water for My feet, but she wet My feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair. 45 You did not greet Me with a kiss, but she has not stopped kissing My feet since I arrived. 46 You did not anoint My head with oil, but she has anointed My feet with perfume. 47 Therefore I tell you, her many sins have been forgiven, for she has loved much. But he who has been forgiven little loves little.”

48 Then Jesus said to her, “Your sins are forgiven.” 49 But those at the table began to say to themselves, “Who is this who even forgives sins?” 50 And Jesus told the woman, “Your faith has saved you; go in peace.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
A Pharisee named Simon invites Jesus to eat with him. A woman known in the town as sinful comes with perfume, weeps at Jesus’ feet, wipes them with her hair, kisses them and anoints them. Luke does not give her name or identify the particular sins behind her reputation.

Simon privately questions whether Jesus can be a prophet if He allows such a woman to touch Him. Jesus answers with a story about two debtors who cannot repay what they owe. The lender forgives both debts, and Simon agrees that the one forgiven more will love more.

Jesus then contrasts the woman’s care with Simon’s reception of Him: she has offered tears, kisses and perfume where Simon supplied no water, kiss or oil. The comparison makes her love visible and challenges the way Simon has assessed her.

Jesus declares her sins forgiven and ends by telling her that her faith has saved her and that she may go in peace. The other guests question who can forgive sins. As in the earlier healing of the paralyzed man, the encounter brings Jesus’ authority to forgive into view. (Luke 5:17–26)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand the woman’s great love as the response to, and evidence of, forgiveness. Wesley and the Catholic bishops’ notes both read the debtors’ story in that direction, joining the gift of forgiveness with the faith and love shown in her response. (Wesley on Luke 7:43–50; USCCB notes on Luke 7:36–50, especially 47)
passages.god_plan_html:
The wider New Testament explains the cost and source of the forgiveness Jesus gives. Paul describes redemption and forgiveness through Christ’s blood as the riches of God’s grace. The mercy shown in this house belongs within the saving work that leads toward His death and resurrection. (Ephesians 1:7–10)

That mercy also shapes the life of those who receive it. Ephesians calls believers to forgive each other as God has forgiven them in Christ and to walk in the love shown by Christ’s self-giving. The connection carries the lesson beyond the meal: received forgiveness is to bear fruit in love toward others. (Ephesians 4:31–32; Ephesians 5:1–2)

passages.title: Luke 8:1-3
passages.section_title: Who helps support Jesus’ traveling ministry?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Soon afterward, Jesus traveled from one town and village to another, preaching and proclaiming the good news of the kingdom of God. The Twelve were with Him, 2 as well as some women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out, 3 Joanna the wife of Herod’s household manager Chuza, Susanna, and many others. These women were ministering to them out of their own means.
paragraphs: 1 Soon afterward, Jesus traveled from one town and village to another, preaching and proclaiming the good news of the kingdom of God. The Twelve were with Him, 2 as well as some women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out, 3 Joanna the wife of Herod’s household manager Chuza, Susanna, and many others. These women were ministering to them out of their own means.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus continues from town to town proclaiming the good news of God’s kingdom. The twelve accompany Him, and Luke also names women who travel with the group and support the ministry from their own resources.

Mary Magdalene had been freed from seven demons. Joanna is identified through her marriage to Chuza, Herod’s household manager. Susanna is named without further explanation, and many others also contribute. Luke gives these women a visible place in the account of how the ministry is sustained.

The support is a practical response within a traveling ministry. These women have received help from Jesus and now use what they have in serving the group. The short passage draws attention to people whose participation could be missed if readers noticed only the twelve.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see these women as active participants in the ministry, offering practical support from their resources. The Catholic bishops’ notes also trace their presence forward to the witnesses of Jesus’ death and resurrection. (USCCB note on Luke 8:1–3; Luke 24:1–10)
passages.god_plan_html:
Luke later names Mary Magdalene and Joanna among the women who report the empty tomb to the apostles. The people supporting the ministry here become witnesses who carry news of the resurrection. Their place in the story reaches from ordinary provision during the journey to the announcement at its decisive turning point. (Luke 24:1–12)

Paul describes those who belong to Christ as children of God and heirs of the promise, including both men and women. That is a wider connection with the people Jesus gathers around Himself: women share in the promised inheritance and participate in the life formed around Him. (Galatians 3:26–29)

passages.title: Luke 8:4-15
passages.section_title: Why does the same word produce different responses?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 4 While a large crowd was gathering and people were coming to Jesus from town after town, He told them this parable: 5 “A farmer went out to sow his seed. And as he was sowing, some seed fell along the path, where it was trampled, and the birds of the air devoured it. 6 Some fell on rocky ground, and when it came up, the seedlings withered because they had no moisture. 7 Other seed fell among thorns, which grew up with it and choked the seedlings. 8 Still other seed fell on good soil, where it sprang up and produced a crop—a hundredfold.” As Jesus said this, He called out, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.” 9 Then His disciples asked Him what this parable meant. 10 He replied, “The knowledge of the mysteries of the kingdom of God has been given to you, but to others I speak in parables, so that, ‘though seeing, they may not see; though hearing, they may not understand.’ 11 Now this is the meaning of the parable: The seed is the word of God. 12 The seeds along the path are those who hear, but the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts, so that they may not believe and be saved. 13 The seeds on rocky ground are those who hear the word and receive it with joy, but they have no root. They believe for a season, but in the time of testing, they fall away. 14 The seeds that fell among the thorns are those who hear, but as they go on their way, they are choked by the worries, riches, and pleasures of this life, and their fruit does not mature. 15 But the seeds on good soil are those with a noble and good heart, who hear the word, cling to it, and by persevering produce a crop.
paragraphs: 4 While a large crowd was gathering and people were coming to Jesus from town after town, He told them this parable: 5 “A farmer went out to sow his seed. And as he was sowing, some seed fell along the path, where it was trampled, and the birds of the air devoured it. 6 Some fell on rocky ground, and when it came up, the seedlings withered because they had no moisture. 7 Other seed fell among thorns, which grew up with it and choked the seedlings. 8 Still other seed fell on good soil, where it sprang up and produced a crop—a hundredfold.” As Jesus said this, He called out, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”

9 Then His disciples asked Him what this parable meant. 10 He replied, “The knowledge of the mysteries of the kingdom of God has been given to you, but to others I speak in parables, so that, ‘though seeing, they may not see; though hearing, they may not understand.’

11 Now this is the meaning of the parable: The seed is the word of God. 12 The seeds along the path are those who hear, but the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts, so that they may not believe and be saved. 13 The seeds on rocky ground are those who hear the word and receive it with joy, but they have no root. They believe for a season, but in the time of testing, they fall away. 14 The seeds that fell among the thorns are those who hear, but as they go on their way, they are choked by the worries, riches, and pleasures of this life, and their fruit does not mature. 15 But the seeds on good soil are those with a noble and good heart, who hear the word, cling to it, and by persevering produce a crop.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
People come to Jesus from many towns, and He tells a story about a farmer sowing seed. Some falls on a path, some on rocky ground, some among thorns and some on good soil. The outcomes differ: the seed is eaten, the seedlings wither, the growth is choked, or a crop is produced.

When the disciples ask what the story means, Jesus says that knowledge of the kingdom’s mysteries has been given to them. His words about seeing without seeing and hearing without understanding echo Isaiah’s commission. The parable involves both the gift of understanding and a serious warning about hearing. (Isaiah 6:9–10)

Jesus identifies the seed as God’s word and explains the different responses. The devil takes away the word from the first hearers. The rocky-ground hearers receive it joyfully but have no root; they believe for a time and fall away under testing. Worries, riches and pleasures choke the response of others so that their fruit does not mature.

The good-soil hearers keep hold of the word and produce a crop through perseverance. The explanation asks more than whether someone has heard a message or welcomed it at first. It draws attention to what happens to that word over time.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly see different responses to God’s word and a call to lasting, fruitful hearing. Traditions differ over how God’s gift of understanding relates to the hearer’s response, and over what happens when someone who believed later turns away.

Reformed teaching in Westminster emphasizes God renewing the heart and will so that people freely come to Christ. Wesley’s notes on the Matthew parallel emphasize people refusing to use the light already given and closing their eyes to it. The Catholic Catechism describes the parables as confronting hearers with a choice and calls them to become disciples who receive the kingdom’s meaning. These emphases all recognize the need for God’s grace. (Westminster Confession 10.1–2; Wesley on Matthew 13:11–16; Catechism 546)

On continuing in faith, the Westminster Confession and the 1689 Baptist Confession teach that God keeps those He has brought to saving faith to the end, though they can fall into serious sin for a time. This gives Reformed Christians and Baptists who follow that confession a way of distinguishing temporary response from saving faith that endures. (Westminster Confession 17.1–3; 1689 Baptist Confession 17.1–3)

The Methodist Articles allow for departing from grace and falling into sin after receiving the Holy Spirit, with repentance and return possible by grace. The Catholic Church teaches that faith is God’s free gift, that it can be lost and that it must be nourished. These teachings lead to different explanations of whether someone who abandons faith once had saving faith. (Methodist Articles of Religion, XII; Catechism 162)
passages.god_plan_html:
The Isaiah passage Jesus echoes also appears near the end of Acts. Paul speaks about Jesus and God’s kingdom; some are convinced and others refuse to believe. He then cites Isaiah and announces that God’s salvation has been sent to the nations. The repeated connection places the mixed response to the word within the gospel’s widening journey. (Acts 28:23–28)

Peter uses the picture of seed to describe new birth through God’s living and enduring word, then identifies that word with the good news proclaimed to his readers. This is a related picture, not a second code for assigning each soil to a group. It connects the message Jesus describes here with the life God brings through the gospel. (1 Peter 1:22–25)

passages.title: Luke 8:16-18
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus tell us to pay attention to how we listen?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 No one lights a lamp and covers it with a jar or puts it under a bed. Instead, he sets it on a stand, so those who enter can see the light. 17 For there is nothing hidden that will not be disclosed, and nothing concealed that will not be made known and brought to light. 18 Pay attention, therefore, to how you listen. Whoever has will be given more, but whoever does not have, even what he thinks he has will be taken away from him.”
paragraphs: 16 No one lights a lamp and covers it with a jar or puts it under a bed. Instead, he sets it on a stand, so those who enter can see the light. 17 For there is nothing hidden that will not be disclosed, and nothing concealed that will not be made known and brought to light. 18 Pay attention, therefore, to how you listen. Whoever has will be given more, but whoever does not have, even what he thinks he has will be taken away from him.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus follows the sower’s explanation with a lamp. A person lights it and places it where those entering can see. Covering it would defeat its purpose.

He adds that hidden things will be disclosed, then tells His hearers to pay attention to how they listen. The warning includes both receiving more and losing even what someone thinks he has. Within this sequence, hearing God’s word carries responsibility for what is received.

The lamp picture directs attention outward: what is given is to become visible. The warning directs attention inward: the hearer must consider the reality of his response. The following scene about Jesus’ family will return once more to hearing and doing.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly connect the lamp with making the received word visible in life and witness, and the warning with a serious, continuing response. Wesley and the Catholic bishops’ notes both follow that connection between hearing, fruitfulness and light for others. (Wesley on Luke 8:16–18; USCCB note on Luke 8:16–18)
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul calls believers light in the Lord and tells them to live as children of light, bearing fruit in goodness, righteousness and truth. This is a wider thematic connection with the lamp: God’s work in His people is to become visible in the way they live. (Ephesians 5:8–14)

The disclosure of what is hidden also has a place in the New Testament’s future hope and accountability. Paul says that when the Lord comes He will bring hidden things to light and expose the motives of hearts. The connection adds weight to Jesus’ warning about the difference between what a hearer really has and what he merely thinks he has. (1 Corinthians 4:1–5)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 8:19-21
passages.section_title: Who does Jesus call His family?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 Then Jesus’ mother and brothers came to see Him, but they were unable to reach Him because of the crowd. 20 He was told, “Your mother and brothers are standing outside, wanting to see You.” 21 But He replied, “My mother and brothers are those who hear the word of God and carry it out.”
paragraphs: 19 Then Jesus’ mother and brothers came to see Him, but they were unable to reach Him because of the crowd. 20 He was told, “Your mother and brothers are standing outside, wanting to see You.” 21 But He replied, “My mother and brothers are those who hear the word of God and carry it out.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus’ mother and brothers come to see Him but cannot reach Him because of the crowd. Someone tells Him they are standing outside and want to see Him.

His answer describes His family as those who hear God’s word and carry it out. It gathers up the theme of the preceding scenes: hearing becomes a continuing response that shapes life.

Luke has already shown Mary receiving God’s message and accepting the part entrusted to her. Jesus’ saying therefore gives a description of belonging that readers have already seen her live out. It places receiving and doing God’s word at the center of the family He is gathering. (Luke 1:38)
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the central saying as describing a family joined through response to God. They differ over the relationship of the brothers standing outside.

The Catholic Church teaches that Mary remained a virgin and understands these brothers as close relatives. The Orthodox Church in America presents the tradition that they are Joseph’s children from an earlier marriage. An Orthodox Presbyterian Church answer instead reads them as children born to Mary and Joseph after Jesus, and thus His half-brothers. That church answer represents one Protestant reading, not every Protestant interpreter. (Catechism 499–500; OCA account of Joseph; OPC answer on Jesus’ brothers)

These different accounts of the family relationship leave the stated invitation clear: Jesus includes those who hear God’s word and live by it.
passages.god_plan_html:
John’s Gospel describes those who receive Christ and believe in His name as given the right to become God’s children. Their birth into that family comes from God. This is a related explanation of the larger belonging Jesus announces here. (John 1:10–13)

Paul describes the Spirit’s work in God’s children through adoption, calling God Father and sharing the inheritance with Christ. The family Jesus gathers reaches beyond the relatives seeking Him at this moment into that wider life with the Father. (Romans 8:14–17)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 8:22-25
passages.section_title: Who is Jesus, that even the wind and water obey Him?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 One day Jesus said to His disciples, “Let us cross to the other side of the lake.” So He got into a boat with them and set out. 23 As they sailed, He fell asleep, and a windstorm came down on the lake, so that the boat was being swamped, and they were in great danger. 24 The disciples went and woke Him, saying, “Master, Master, we are perishing!” Then Jesus got up and rebuked the wind and the raging waters, and they subsided, and all was calm. 25 “Where is your faith?” He asked. Frightened and amazed, they asked one another, “Who is this? He commands even the winds and the water, and they obey Him!”
paragraphs: 22 One day Jesus said to His disciples, “Let us cross to the other side of the lake.” So He got into a boat with them and set out. 23 As they sailed, He fell asleep, and a windstorm came down on the lake, so that the boat was being swamped, and they were in great danger. 24 The disciples went and woke Him, saying, “Master, Master, we are perishing!” Then Jesus got up and rebuked the wind and the raging waters, and they subsided, and all was calm. 25 “Where is your faith?” He asked. Frightened and amazed, they asked one another, “Who is this? He commands even the winds and the water, and they obey Him!”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus tells the disciples to cross the lake, and they set out together. He falls asleep during the journey. A windstorm comes down on the lake, the boat is swamped, and Luke describes them as being in great danger.

The disciples wake Him with their fear that they are perishing. Jesus gets up and rebukes the wind and raging water. They subside, and the lake becomes calm.

He then asks where their faith is. The disciples’ fear is joined by amazement at His authority, and they ask who He is that the wind and water obey Him. Following the teaching about hearing God’s word, the account shows the power of His word in a situation they cannot control.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see Jesus’ authority over creation and a call to trust Him in danger. Calvin distinguishes the fear that overwhelms trust from every ordinary experience of fear, keeping the encounter from becoming a claim that faithful people never feel alarm. (Calvin on Matthew 8:25–26 and Luke 8:22–25; Luke 8:24–25)
passages.god_plan_html:
Psalm 107 gives a close Scriptural parallel: sailors face a storm, cry to the Lord, and are brought into calm as He stills the waves. Luke’s account places that kind of authority in Jesus’ command. The parallel helps readers understand the weight of the disciples’ question about who He is. (Psalm 107:23–32)

The Bible’s larger hope includes creation itself being set free from its bondage to decay as God’s children receive their promised glory. The Lord whose word commands the waters belongs at the center of that wider hope of restoration. His people still face suffering while they wait for it. (Romans 8:18–23)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 8:26-39
passages.section_title: What changes when Jesus frees the man among the tombs?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 26 Then they sailed to the region of the Gerasenes, across the lake from Galilee. 27 When Jesus stepped ashore, He was met by a demon-possessed man from the town. For a long time this man had not worn clothing or lived in a house, but he stayed in the tombs. 28 When the man saw Jesus, he cried out and fell down before Him, shouting in a loud voice, “What do You want with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg You not to torture me!” 29 For Jesus had commanded the unclean spirit to come out of the man. Many times it had seized him, and though he was bound with chains and shackles, he had broken the chains and been driven by the demon into solitary places. 30 “What is your name?” Jesus asked. “Legion,” he replied, because many demons had gone into him. 31 And the demons kept begging Jesus not to order them to go into the Abyss. 32 There on the hillside a large herd of pigs was feeding. So the demons begged Jesus to let them enter the pigs, and He gave them permission. 33 Then the demons came out of the man and went into the pigs, and the herd rushed down the steep bank into the lake and was drowned. 34 When those tending the pigs saw what had happened, they ran off and reported this in the town and countryside. 35 So the people went out to see what had happened. They came to Jesus and found the man whom the demons had left, sitting at Jesus’ feet, clothed and in his right mind; and they were afraid. 36 Meanwhile, those who had seen it reported how the demon-possessed man had been healed. 37 Then all the people of the region of the Gerasenes asked Jesus to depart from them, because great fear had taken hold of them. So He got into the boat and started back. 38 The man whom the demons had left begged to go with Jesus. But He sent him away, saying, 39 “Return home and describe how much God has done for you.” So the man went away and proclaimed all over the town how much Jesus had done for him.

I beg You not to torture me!” 29 For Jesus had commanded the unclean spirit to come out of the man. Many times it had seized him, and though he was bound with chains and shackles, he had broken the chains and been driven by the demon into solitary places. 30 “What is your name?” Jesus asked. “Legion,” he replied, because many demons had gone into him. 31 And the demons kept begging Jesus not to order them to go into the Abyss.

32 There on the hillside a large herd of pigs was feeding. So the demons begged Jesus to let them enter the pigs, and He gave them permission. 33 Then the demons came out of the man and went into the pigs, and the herd rushed down the steep bank into the lake and was drowned. 34 When those tending the pigs saw what had happened, they ran off and reported this in the town and countryside. 35 So the people went out to see what had happened. They came to Jesus and found the man whom the demons had left, sitting at Jesus’ feet, clothed and in his right mind; and they were afraid. 36 Meanwhile, those who had seen it reported how the demon-possessed man had been healed.

37 Then all the people of the region of the Gerasenes asked Jesus to depart from them, because great fear had taken hold of them. So He got into the boat and started back. 38 The man whom the demons had left begged to go with Jesus. But He sent him away, saying, 39 “Return home and describe how much God has done for you.” So the man went away and proclaimed all over the town how much Jesus had done for him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Across the lake, Jesus meets a man whose life has been dominated by demons. He has lived among the tombs without clothing, broken restraints and been driven into solitary places. The encounter shows a man cut off from ordinary life with other people.

The spirits recognize Jesus as the Son of the Most High God. The answer Legion is explained in the text by the many demons in the man. They beg not to be sent into the Abyss and ask permission to enter a herd of pigs.

The word Abyss comes from ἄβυσσος, abussos (ah-BOOS-soss), a term for an immeasurable depth or pit. Thayer identifies its use here with the dwelling of demons. Their plea shows their fear of Jesus’ authority to send them there. (Thayer, G12)

After the spirits enter the pigs and the herd drowns, the people find the man clothed, in his right mind and sitting at Jesus’ feet. They ask Jesus to leave because they are afraid. The restored man wants to accompany Him, but Jesus sends him home to tell what God has done. He responds by telling the town what Jesus has done for him.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand the scene as Jesus exercising authority over evil spirits and restoring the man to life among others. His commission to speak of God’s help turns the deliverance into a witness within his own community. (Catechism 550; Calvin on Luke 8:38–39)
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul describes Christ’s cross as a victory in which the powers and authorities are disarmed. The release of this man belongs within the larger saving work that overcomes evil’s hold, a work carried through the death and resurrection of Jesus. (Colossians 2:13–15)

Revelation also describes evil being confined and finally judged. It distinguishes the Abyss, where Satan is bound for a period, from the lake of fire that marks his final judgment. These passages place the spirits’ fear here within the larger biblical certainty that evil remains subject to God and will not rule forever. (Revelation 20:1–3, 10)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 8:40-56
passages.section_title: What do the woman and Jairus learn about trusting Jesus?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 40 When Jesus returned, the crowd welcomed Him, for they had all been waiting for Him. 41 Just then a synagogue leader named Jairus came and fell at Jesus’ feet. He begged Him to come to his house, 42 because his only daughter, who was about twelve, was dying. As Jesus went with him, the crowds pressed around Him, 43 including a woman who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years. She had spent all her money on physicians, but no one was able to heal her. 44 She came up behind Jesus and touched the fringe of His cloak, and immediately her bleeding stopped. 45 “Who touched Me?” Jesus asked. But they all denied it. “Master,” said Peter, “the people are crowding and pressing against You.” 46 But Jesus declared, “Someone touched Me, for I know that power has gone out from Me.” 47 Then the woman, seeing that she could not escape notice, came trembling and fell down before Him. In the presence of all the people, she explained why she had touched Him and how she had immediately been healed. 48 “Daughter,” said Jesus, “your faith has healed you. Go in peace.” 49 While He was still speaking, someone arrived from the house of the synagogue leader. “Your daughter is dead,” he told Jairus. “Do not bother the Teacher anymore.” 50 But Jesus overheard them and said to Jairus, “Do not be afraid; just believe, and she will be healed.” 51 When He entered the house, He did not allow anyone to go in with Him except Peter, John, James, and the child’s father and mother. 52 Meanwhile, everyone was weeping and mourning for her. But Jesus said, “Stop weeping; she is not dead but asleep.” 53 And they laughed at Him, knowing that she was dead. 54 But Jesus took her by the hand and called out, “Child, get up!” 55 Her spirit returned, and at once she got up. And He directed that she be given something to eat. 56 Her parents were astounded, but Jesus ordered them not to tell anyone what had happened.

In the presence of all the people, she explained why she had touched Him and how she had immediately been healed. 48 “Daughter,” said Jesus, “your faith has healed you. Go in peace.”

49 While He was still speaking, someone arrived from the house of the synagogue leader. “Your daughter is dead,” he told Jairus. “Do not bother the Teacher anymore.” 50 But Jesus overheard them and said to Jairus, “Do not be afraid; just believe, and she will be healed.”

51 When He entered the house, He did not allow anyone to go in with Him except Peter, John, James, and the child’s father and mother. 52 Meanwhile, everyone was weeping and mourning for her. But Jesus said, “Stop weeping; she is not dead but asleep.” 53 And they laughed at Him, knowing that she was dead. 54 But Jesus took her by the hand and called out, “Child, get up!” 55 Her spirit returned, and at once she got up. And He directed that she be given something to eat. 56 Her parents were astounded, but Jesus ordered them not to tell anyone what had happened.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jairus, a synagogue leader, asks Jesus to come because his only daughter, about twelve years old, is dying. As Jesus goes with him through the crowd, another person in desperate need approaches from behind: a woman who has suffered bleeding for twelve years.

She touches the fringe of His cloak, and her bleeding immediately stops. The Law’s instructions about prolonged bleeding help explain the significance of being made clean, as well as the burden this condition could carry. Luke focuses on her healing and her encounter with Jesus. (Leviticus 15:25–30)

Jesus asks who touched Him and says He knows power has gone out from Him. The woman comes forward trembling and publicly explains what happened. He addresses her as daughter, credits her faith and sends her in peace.

During this exchange, news arrives that Jairus’ daughter has died. Jesus tells Jairus to believe and continues to the house. He takes the girl’s hand, calls her to get up, and her spirit returns. The instruction to give her food shows His care continuing after the extraordinary act.

Jesus’ description of death as sleep is also found in John’s account of Lazarus, where the Gospel explicitly explains that He is speaking about death. Here, too, the girl’s return to life displays His authority over what has happened. (John 11:11–15)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see the two intertwined encounters as displays of Jesus’ power to heal and restore life, with trust in Him central to both. The Catholic Catechism includes Jairus’ spoken plea and the woman’s silent approach as expressions of faith brought to Jesus, while Luke shows Him answering fear with reassurance and restoration. (Catechism 2616; USCCB note on Luke 8:40–56)
passages.god_plan_html:
When Jesus speaks with Martha about her brother’s death, He identifies Himself as the resurrection and the life and promises life to those who believe in Him. The restoration of Jairus’ daughter is an early display of that authority. It directs attention to the person in whom the hope of life is found. (John 11:25–27)

The final hope goes beyond these particular recoveries. Revelation describes God dwelling with His people and bringing an end to death, mourning and pain. Jesus’ care for the woman and the child gives a glimpse of the restoration His saving work leads toward. (Revelation 21:1–5)
passages.current_position_html: For the woman’s healing, Prayer and Faith draws from the parallel Matthew 9:20–22 to emphasize trust in Jesus over the wording of a request. She reaches out before making a spoken request for healing, and Jesus credits her faith. Luke also records her later explanation to Him, so the point concerns how she approaches Him for healing. We have not developed a separate position on Jairus’ part of the passage.

passages.title: Luke 9:1-6
passages.section_title: How does Jesus send the twelve out to serve?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then Jesus called the Twelve together and gave them power and authority over all demons, and power to cure diseases. 2 And He sent them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal the sick. 3 “Take nothing for the journey,” He told them, “no staff, no bag, no bread, no money, no second tunic. 4 Whatever house you enter, stay there until you leave that area. 5 If anyone does not welcome you, shake the dust off your feet when you leave that town, as a testimony against them.” 6 So they set out and went from village to village, preaching the gospel and healing people everywhere.
paragraphs: 1 Then Jesus called the Twelve together and gave them power and authority over all demons, and power to cure diseases. 2 And He sent them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal the sick.

3 “Take nothing for the journey,” He told them, “no staff, no bag, no bread, no money, no second tunic. 4 Whatever house you enter, stay there until you leave that area. 5 If anyone does not welcome you, shake the dust off your feet when you leave that town, as a testimony against them.” 6 So they set out and went from village to village, preaching the gospel and healing people everywhere.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus gathers the twelve and gives them power and authority over demons and disease. He then sends them to proclaim God’s kingdom and heal the sick. Their work extends the preaching and restoration readers have already seen in His own ministry.

The Greek words bring out what He gives: δύναμις, dunamis (DOO-nah-miss), is power or ability; ἐξουσία, exousia (ek-soo-SEE-ah), includes authority or the right to act. Both are supplied by Jesus for this mission. (Thayer, G1411; G1849)

They are to travel without provisions of their own and remain in the house that receives them. If a town refuses them, shaking the dust from their feet is to serve as a testimony against it. The instructions combine dependence on hospitality with the seriousness of the message they carry.

Later Jesus recalls how they lacked nothing on this journey, then gives different instructions for the circumstances ahead. Reading the two scenes together keeps this first mission within the course of His preparation of the disciples. (Luke 22:35–38)
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly see Jesus preparing His chosen messengers to preach and serve under His authority, relying on God’s provision. The Catholic bishops’ note on Luke describes the mission as continuing the work Jesus has been doing. (USCCB note on Luke 9:1–6)

Interpreters explain the differing travel instructions in the Gospel accounts in more than one way. Wesley reads Mark’s allowance of a staff as permission to take one already owned, while the Catholic bishops’ notes on Mark suggest adaptation to different settings of ministry. These are explanations in commentaries and notes, not uniform rulings held by every member of their churches. (Wesley on Mark 6:8–9; USCCB note on Mark 6:8–9)
passages.god_plan_html:
At the end of Luke, the risen Jesus sends His witnesses to proclaim repentance and forgiveness to all nations and promises power from on high. Acts continues with the promise of the Holy Spirit and witness to the ends of the earth. This earlier journey is part of the preparation of those who will carry that message. (Luke 24:44–49; Acts 1:4–8)

The mission is therefore larger than learning a travel routine. Jesus is forming people who receive from Him and bring His message and care to others, a purpose that will continue through the suffering, resurrection and outward witness that follow.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 9:7-9
passages.section_title: Why is Herod puzzled by the reports about Jesus?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 When Herod the tetrarch heard about all that was happening, he was perplexed. For some were saying that John had risen from the dead, 8 others that Elijah had appeared, and still others that a prophet of old had arisen. 9 “I beheaded John,” Herod said, “but who is this man I hear such things about?” And he kept trying to see Jesus.
paragraphs: 7 When Herod the tetrarch heard about all that was happening, he was perplexed. For some were saying that John had risen from the dead, 8 others that Elijah had appeared, and still others that a prophet of old had arisen. 9 “I beheaded John,” Herod said, “but who is this man I hear such things about?” And he kept trying to see Jesus.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Reports about Jesus reach Herod the tetrarch, the ruler already connected with John’s imprisonment in Luke. Different explanations are circulating: John has risen, Elijah has appeared, or a prophet from long ago has returned. (Luke 3:19–20)

Herod knows that he had John beheaded, and he asks who this man can be. His desire to see Jesus introduces the question of Jesus’ identity from the viewpoint of a ruler hearing reports at a distance.

The following scenes give readers more to consider: Jesus provides food for a great crowd, Peter names Him as God’s Christ, and Jesus explains that He must suffer and rise again. Herod’s question sits within this developing account of who Jesus is.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand Herod’s uncertainty as part of the question of Jesus’ identity that runs through this chapter. The Catholic bishops’ notes also connect his wish to see Jesus with their later meeting during the proceedings before the crucifixion. (USCCB notes on Luke 9:7–9; Luke 23:6–12)
passages.god_plan_html:
Herod later does see Jesus, hoping to watch a miracle. That encounter becomes part of the rejection and humiliation Jesus endures on the way to the cross. The curiosity recorded here reaches into the Gospel’s account of His suffering. (Luke 23:6–12)

In Acts, the believers name Herod and Pilate among those who gathered against Jesus, while recognizing that God’s saving purpose was being carried out. Their prayer holds human opposition and God’s purpose together. Herod’s place in the story belongs within that larger account of the rejected Messiah through whom God brings salvation. (Acts 4:24–30)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 9:10-17
passages.section_title: How does Jesus provide for the crowd?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 Then the apostles returned and reported to Jesus all that they had done. Taking them away privately, He withdrew to a town called Bethsaida. 11 But the crowds found out and followed Him. He welcomed them and spoke to them about the kingdom of God, and He healed those who needed healing. 12 As the day neared its end, the Twelve came to Jesus and said, “Dismiss the crowd so they can go to the surrounding villages and countryside for lodging and provisions. For we are in a desolate place here.” 13 But Jesus told them, “You give them something to eat.” “We have only five loaves of bread and two fish,” they answered, “unless we go and buy food for all these people.” 14 (There were about five thousand men.) He told His disciples, “Have them sit down in groups of about fifty each.” 15 They did so, and everyone was seated. 16 Taking the five loaves and the two fish and looking up to heaven, Jesus spoke a blessing and broke them. Then He gave them to the disciples to set before the people. 17 They all ate and were satisfied, and the disciples picked up twelve basketfuls of broken pieces that were left over.
paragraphs: 10 Then the apostles returned and reported to Jesus all that they had done. Taking them away privately, He withdrew to a town called Bethsaida. 11 But the crowds found out and followed Him. He welcomed them and spoke to them about the kingdom of God, and He healed those who needed healing. 12 As the day neared its end, the Twelve came to Jesus and said, “Dismiss the crowd so they can go to the surrounding villages and countryside for lodging and provisions. For we are in a desolate place here.”

13 But Jesus told them, “You give them something to eat.” “We have only five loaves of bread and two fish,” they answered, “unless we go and buy food for all these people.” 14 (There were about five thousand men.) He told His disciples, “Have them sit down in groups of about fifty each.” 15 They did so, and everyone was seated.

16 Taking the five loaves and the two fish and looking up to heaven, Jesus spoke a blessing and broke them. Then He gave them to the disciples to set before the people. 17 They all ate and were satisfied, and the disciples picked up twelve basketfuls of broken pieces that were left over.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The apostles return and report to Jesus. He takes them away toward Bethsaida, but the crowds follow. He welcomes the people, teaches them about God’s kingdom and heals those who need healing.

As evening approaches, the twelve suggest sending the crowd to nearby villages for food and lodging. Jesus tells them to give the people something to eat. They have five loaves and two fish, with about five thousand men present.

Jesus has the people sit in groups. He looks toward heaven, speaks a blessing, breaks the food and gives it to the disciples to serve. Everyone eats and is satisfied, and twelve baskets of pieces remain.

The disciples take part in caring for the crowd through what Jesus supplies. Their lack of food has become the setting for a provision that exceeds what they could have offered on their own.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand this as Jesus’ miraculous provision and care for the crowd, with the disciples serving through what He gives. The Catholic Church also sees the multiplied loaves as pointing ahead to the abundance of the Eucharist, or Lord’s Supper; the bishops’ note draws attention to the similar actions at the later meal. (Catechism 1335; USCCB note on Luke 9:16)
passages.god_plan_html:
Elisha’s feeding of a hundred people supplies an earlier Scriptural parallel. A small quantity of barley bread seems inadequate, yet the Lord’s word promises that the people will eat and have some left over. Luke’s scene shows a far larger crowd receiving abundant food through Jesus. The parallel belongs to the wider story of God providing for His people. (2 Kings 4:42–44)

John’s account carries the meaning beyond the meal. After this feeding, Jesus directs people toward food that endures to eternal life and identifies Himself as the bread of life. The provision points toward the One the Father sends to give life to the world. (John 6:26–35)
