passages.title: Luke 9:18-22
passages.section_title: Why does Peter’s confession lead into Jesus’ coming suffering?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 One day as Jesus was praying in private and the disciples were with Him, He questioned them: “Who do the crowds say I am?” 19 They replied, “Some say John the Baptist; others say Elijah; and still others, that a prophet of old has arisen.” 20 “But what about you?” Jesus asked. “Who do you say I am?” Peter answered, “The Christ of God.” 21 Jesus strictly warned them not to tell this to anyone. 22 “The Son of Man must suffer many things,” He said. “He must be rejected by the elders, chief priests, and scribes, and He must be killed and on the third day be raised to life.”
paragraphs: 18 One day as Jesus was praying in private and the disciples were with Him, He questioned them: “Who do the crowds say I am?” 19 They replied, “Some say John the Baptist; others say Elijah; and still others, that a prophet of old has arisen.” 20 “But what about you?” Jesus asked. “Who do you say I am?” Peter answered, “The Christ of God.”

21 Jesus strictly warned them not to tell this to anyone. 22 “The Son of Man must suffer many things,” He said. “He must be rejected by the elders, chief priests, and scribes, and He must be killed and on the third day be raised to life.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
While Jesus is praying in private with His disciples present, He asks who the crowds say He is. They repeat the reports about John, Elijah and a prophet from long ago. He then asks what they themselves say.

Peter answers that Jesus is the Christ of God. Jesus strictly warns them not to spread this and immediately explains the path ahead: the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected by the elders, chief priests and scribes, be killed and be raised on the third day.

The explanation gives the disciples something essential to hear alongside the confession. Recognizing Him as God’s Christ includes learning that His mission will pass through rejection and death into resurrection. The next teaching will address what following Him will mean for them.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand the confession and the announcement together: Jesus is God’s Messiah, and His mission includes suffering, death and resurrection. The Catholic Catechism places this announcement at the turning point after Peter’s confession, while the Gospel itself makes the coming suffering explicit. (Catechism 554–555; Luke 9:20–22)
passages.god_plan_html:
Isaiah’s servant suffers despite His innocence, bears the sins of others and brings them peace. The announcement here prepares the disciples to recognize that God’s saving work includes such suffering. This is a Scriptural connection with the servant’s mission, not an assumption that rejection means God’s purpose has failed. (Isaiah 53:4–12)

After the resurrection, Peter proclaims that Jesus was handed over according to God’s purpose, put to death through human actions and raised by God. Acts holds those truths together. The death and resurrection Jesus announces here stand within God’s saving purpose while those involved in killing Him remain responsible for their acts. (Acts 2:22–24)
passages.current_position_html: What Does Prayer Look Like? draws on the parallel announcement in Matthew 16:21 when discussing Jesus’ prayer in Gethsemane. He already knows the path ahead, yet its cost remains real. The study emphasizes honest prayer governed by surrender to the Father’s will: knowing God’s purpose does not make obedience painless. This supplies our position on His awareness of the coming suffering, while a fuller position on the whole passage remains open.

passages.title: Luke 9:23-27
passages.section_title: Why does following Jesus mean taking up a cross?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 23 Then Jesus said to all of them, “If anyone wants to come after Me, he must deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow Me. 24 For whoever wants to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for My sake will save it. 25 What does it profit a man to gain the whole world, yet lose or forfeit his very self? 26 If anyone is ashamed of Me and My words, the Son of Man will be ashamed of him when He comes in His glory and in the glory of the Father and of the holy angels. 27 But I tell you truly, some who are standing here will not taste death before they see the kingdom of God.”
paragraphs: 23 Then Jesus said to all of them, “If anyone wants to come after Me, he must deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow Me. 24 For whoever wants to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for My sake will save it. 25 What does it profit a man to gain the whole world, yet lose or forfeit his very self?

26 If anyone is ashamed of Me and My words, the Son of Man will be ashamed of him when He comes in His glory and in the glory of the Father and of the holy angels. 27 But I tell you truly, some who are standing here will not taste death before they see the kingdom of God.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus has just announced His coming suffering, death and resurrection. He now describes what following Him means: denying oneself, taking up a cross daily and coming after Him. The call concerns the direction of a whole life.

The comparison between saving and losing life presses the question of what is worth holding onto. Gaining the world cannot compensate for forfeiting oneself. Allegiance to Jesus and His words matters more than the security or approval a person can preserve by turning away from Him.

Jesus places the decision within the prospect of His coming glory, with the Father and the holy angels. He then promises that some standing there will see God’s kingdom before they die. Luke follows that promise with the account of three disciples seeing His glory on the mountain.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly understand this as a serious call to follow Jesus even when faithfulness costs deeply. Wesley connects self-denial with doing God’s will in both the great and the daily demands of life. (Wesley on Matthew 16:24–27)

The promise about seeing the kingdom receives different explanations. John Chrysostom connects it with the following Transfiguration, where the disciples glimpse the glory Jesus has promised. Calvin emphasizes the display of Christ’s rule beginning with His resurrection and the sending of the Spirit. Wesley connects it with the powerful growth of the church and judgment on Jerusalem. These are the readings of particular teachers, not a claim that every member of their traditions chooses the same event. (Chrysostom, Homily 56 on Matthew; Calvin on Matthew 16:28 and Luke 9:27; Wesley on Matthew 16:28)
passages.god_plan_html:
Peter later describes Christ’s suffering as a pattern for those who follow His steps. Jesus entrusts Himself to the just Judge while bearing sins and bringing people back to their Shepherd. The call to follow a costly path belongs within the life shaped by the Savior who first gives Himself for His people. (1 Peter 2:21–25)

Paul also connects sharing Christ’s sufferings with sharing His glory. Present suffering is placed beside the coming freedom and restoration God promises His children. That wider hope helps explain why the cost of following Jesus is measured against more than what can be gained in the present world. (Romans 8:17–23)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 9:28-36
passages.section_title: Why do Moses and Elijah appear with Jesus?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 28 About eight days after Jesus had said these things, He took with Him Peter, John, and James, and went up on a mountain to pray. 29 And as He was praying, the appearance of His face changed, and His clothes became radiantly white. 30 Suddenly two men, Moses and Elijah, began talking with Jesus. 31 They appeared in glory and spoke about His departure, which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem. 32 Meanwhile Peter and his companions were overcome by sleep, but when they awoke, they saw Jesus’ glory and the two men standing with Him. 33 As Moses and Elijah were leaving, Peter said to Jesus, “Master, it is good for us to be here. Let us put up three shelters—one for You, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.” (He did not know what he was saying.) 34 While Peter was speaking, a cloud appeared and enveloped them, and they were afraid as they entered the cloud. 35 And a voice came from the cloud, saying, “This is My Son, whom I have chosen. Listen to Him!” 36 After the voice had spoken, only Jesus was present with them. The disciples kept this to themselves, and in those days they did not tell anyone what they had seen.
paragraphs: 28 About eight days after Jesus had said these things, He took with Him Peter, John, and James, and went up on a mountain to pray. 29 And as He was praying, the appearance of His face changed, and His clothes became radiantly white. 30 Suddenly two men, Moses and Elijah, began talking with Jesus. 31 They appeared in glory and spoke about His departure, which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.

32 Meanwhile Peter and his companions were overcome by sleep, but when they awoke, they saw Jesus’ glory and the two men standing with Him. 33 As Moses and Elijah were leaving, Peter said to Jesus, “Master, it is good for us to be here. Let us put up three shelters—one for You, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.” (He did not know what he was saying.)

34 While Peter was speaking, a cloud appeared and enveloped them, and they were afraid as they entered the cloud. 35 And a voice came from the cloud, saying, “This is My Son, whom I have chosen. Listen to Him!” 36 After the voice had spoken, only Jesus was present with them. The disciples kept this to themselves, and in those days they did not tell anyone what they had seen.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
About eight days after the sayings about suffering and glory, Jesus takes Peter, John and James up a mountain to pray. As He prays, His appearance changes and His clothing becomes radiantly white. Moses and Elijah appear in glory and speak with Him.

Their conversation concerns His departure, which He is about to accomplish at Jerusalem. The Greek word is ἔξοδος, exodos (EK-soh-doss), meaning an exit or departure; it can also describe a person’s death. With Moses present, the word invites attention to the saving journey Jesus is approaching. (Thayer, G1841)

The disciples see His glory. As Moses and Elijah are leaving, Peter offers to make three shelters. Luke tells us that he does not know what he is saying. A cloud envelops them, and the voice from it identifies Jesus as the chosen Son and tells them to listen to Him.

Afterward Jesus is alone with them, and they remain silent about what they have seen. The scene sets His coming suffering beside His revealed glory and the Father’s affirmation of who He is.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see the event as a revelation of Jesus’ glory that confirms His identity while preparing the disciples for His coming suffering. The Catholic Catechism and the bishops’ notes connect Moses and Elijah with the Law and the Prophets, directing attention to their witness to Christ and to the command to listen to the Son. (Catechism 554–556; USCCB notes on Luke 9:28–35)
passages.god_plan_html:
There is a meaningful parallel between the earlier Exodus and the departure Jesus will accomplish at Jerusalem. God brought Israel out of slavery; Hebrews describes Jesus’ death as freeing people held in slavery through fear of death. Luke’s word and Moses’ presence bring that saving pattern into view, while the details of the two journeys remain distinct. (Exodus 12:40–42; Hebrews 2:14–18)

The command to listen also recalls Moses’ promise of a prophet whom God’s people must hear. Acts explicitly applies that promise to Jesus and connects Him with the blessing promised through Abraham’s offspring. The Son’s mission carries forward the purposes announced in the Scriptures. (Deuteronomy 18:15–19; Acts 3:19–26)

Peter’s later account directly recalls the glory and the voice on the mountain as eyewitness testimony concerning Jesus’ majesty. What the three see here becomes part of the witness through which others are called to trust the Lord and His promised coming. (2 Peter 1:16–21)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 9:37-45
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus speak of being handed over after freeing the boy?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 37 The next day, when they came down from the mountain, Jesus was met by a large crowd. 38 Suddenly a man in the crowd cried out, “Teacher, I beg You to look at my son, for he is my only child. 39 A spirit keeps seizing him, and he screams abruptly. It throws him into convulsions so that he foams at the mouth. It keeps mauling him and rarely departs from him. 40 I begged Your disciples to drive it out, but they were unable.” 41 “O unbelieving and perverse generation!” Jesus replied. “How long must I remain with you and put up with you? Bring your son here.” 42 Even while the boy was approaching, the demon slammed him to the ground in a convulsion. But Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit, healed the boy, and gave him back to his father. 43 And they were all astonished at the greatness of God. While everyone was marveling at all that Jesus was doing, He said to His disciples, 44 “Let these words sink into your ears: The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men.” 45 But they did not understand this statement. It was veiled from them so that they could not comprehend it, and they were afraid to ask Him about it.
paragraphs: 37 The next day, when they came down from the mountain, Jesus was met by a large crowd. 38 Suddenly a man in the crowd cried out, “Teacher, I beg You to look at my son, for he is my only child. 39 A spirit keeps seizing him, and he screams abruptly. It throws him into convulsions so that he foams at the mouth. It keeps mauling him and rarely departs from him. 40 I begged Your disciples to drive it out, but they were unable.”

41 “O unbelieving and perverse generation!” Jesus replied. “How long must I remain with you and put up with you? Bring your son here.” 42 Even while the boy was approaching, the demon slammed him to the ground in a convulsion. But Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit, healed the boy, and gave him back to his father. 43 And they were all astonished at the greatness of God. While everyone was marveling at all that Jesus was doing, He said to His disciples,

44 “Let these words sink into your ears: The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men.” 45 But they did not understand this statement. It was veiled from them so that they could not comprehend it, and they were afraid to ask Him about it.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The day after the mountain scene, a father brings his only child’s distress before Jesus. An evil spirit has repeatedly seized and injured the boy, and the disciples have been unable to drive it out.

Jesus rebukes the unbelief around Him and has the boy brought forward. Even as the spirit throws the child down again, Jesus rebukes it, heals the boy and returns him to his father. The crowd is astonished at God’s greatness.

While they marvel, Jesus tells the disciples to pay close attention: the Son of Man is about to be delivered into human hands. They do not understand, the meaning remains veiled from them, and they are afraid to ask.

The two parts belong together in Luke’s account. The One who has just shown such authority also announces His coming surrender. The disciples still need to understand how His power and His path toward suffering belong within the same mission.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly recognize Jesus’ authority to restore the child and the disciples’ continuing need to understand His mission. Wesley highlights how the announcement of the cross is placed amid the crowd’s admiration, keeping the coming suffering in view alongside the display of power. (Wesley on Luke 9:44; Luke 9:42–45)
passages.god_plan_html:
Colossians describes the cross itself as the place of Christ’s triumph over the powers and authorities. The release of the boy and the coming handing over of Jesus can therefore be read within the larger victory God accomplishes through Him. His suffering will not mean that evil has become the final ruler of the story. (Colossians 2:13–15)

After the resurrection, Jesus opens the disciples’ minds to understand the Scriptures and explains how His suffering and resurrection lead into the proclamation of forgiveness to the nations. Luke brings their present lack of understanding toward that later clarity and commission. (Luke 24:44–49)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 9:46-48
passages.section_title: Who is great in the family Jesus is forming?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 46 Then an argument started among the disciples as to which of them would be the greatest. 47 But Jesus, knowing the thoughts of their hearts, had a little child stand beside Him. 48 And He said to them, “Whoever welcomes this little child in My name welcomes Me, and whoever welcomes Me welcomes the One who sent Me. For whoever is the least among all of you, he is the greatest.”
paragraphs: 46 Then an argument started among the disciples as to which of them would be the greatest. 47 But Jesus, knowing the thoughts of their hearts, had a little child stand beside Him. 48 And He said to them, “Whoever welcomes this little child in My name welcomes Me, and whoever welcomes Me welcomes the One who sent Me. For whoever is the least among all of you, he is the greatest.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The disciples begin disputing which of them is greatest. Jesus knows their thoughts and places a little child beside Him.

He describes welcoming the child in His name as welcoming Himself, and welcoming Him as welcoming the One who sent Him. Then He identifies the least among them as the great one.

The answer moves the disciples away from comparing their standing and toward receiving someone in Jesus’ name. Greatness is shown in the kind of welcome they give, with Jesus and the Father at the center of that act.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see Jesus correcting rivalry and teaching humble service through the child’s welcome. Wesley emphasizes becoming humble in the work one is willing to do, while the Catholic bishops’ notes identify the rivalry as an attitude opposed to discipleship. (Wesley on Luke 9:48; USCCB note on Luke 9:46–50)
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus returns to the issue of greatness at the final meal. He tells the disciples that leadership among them must take the form of service and points to Himself as the One serving them. The child’s welcome belongs within that preparation for a community whose leaders follow His example. (Luke 22:24–27)

Paul likewise tells the Corinthians to consider God’s calling of people whom the world does not regard as powerful or important. God’s work leaves room for boasting in the Lord, not in personal standing. This is a shared theme with the reversal of greatness Jesus teaches here. (1 Corinthians 1:26–31)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 9:49-50
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus tell John not to stop the other man?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 49 “Master,” said John, “we saw someone driving out demons in Your name, and we tried to stop him, because he does not accompany us.” 50 “Do not stop him,” Jesus replied, “for whoever is not against you is for you.”
paragraphs: 49 “Master,” said John, “we saw someone driving out demons in Your name, and we tried to stop him, because he does not accompany us.” 50 “Do not stop him,” Jesus replied, “for whoever is not against you is for you.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
John reports that the disciples saw someone driving out demons in Jesus’ name and tried to stop him. Their stated reason is that he does not accompany their group.

Jesus tells them not to stop him and says that whoever is not against them is for them. The correction follows the dispute about greatness and continues to challenge the way the disciples draw boundaries around themselves.

The encounter concerns a particular man doing this work in Jesus’ name. Jesus directs the disciples to receive that work without making membership in their immediate circle the deciding question.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand Jesus as correcting an attempt to exclude someone simply because he is outside the disciples’ immediate group. The Catholic bishops’ notes place the incident alongside the preceding rivalry as another lesson in the attitudes of discipleship. (USCCB note on Luke 9:46–50; Luke 9:49–50)
passages.god_plan_html:
Numbers gives a close parallel. When Eldad and Medad prophesy in the camp, Joshua asks Moses to stop them. Moses answers by rejecting jealousy for his own position and expressing the wish that all the Lord’s people might receive His Spirit. In both scenes, a leader corrects resistance to God’s work beyond the expected gathering. (Numbers 11:24–30)

Paul later describes different gifts, ministries and ways of working under the same Spirit, Lord and God, given for the common good. That is a wider connection with receiving genuine service as part of God’s work rather than treating one’s own circle as its whole extent. (1 Corinthians 12:4–7)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 9:51-56
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus refuse the call for fire on the Samaritan village?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 51 As the day of His ascension approached, Jesus resolutely set out for Jerusalem. 52 He sent messengers on ahead, who went into a village of the Samaritans to make arrangements for Him. 53 But the people there refused to welcome Him, because He was heading for Jerusalem. 54 When the disciples James and John saw this, they asked, “Lord, do You want us to call down fire from heaven to consume them?” 55 But Jesus turned and rebuked them. 56 And He and His disciples went on to another village.
paragraphs: 51 As the day of His ascension approached, Jesus resolutely set out for Jerusalem. 52 He sent messengers on ahead, who went into a village of the Samaritans to make arrangements for Him. 53 But the people there refused to welcome Him, because He was heading for Jerusalem.

54 When the disciples James and John saw this, they asked, “Lord, do You want us to call down fire from heaven to consume them?” 55 But Jesus turned and rebuked them. 56 And He and His disciples went on to another village.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Luke marks a turning point: as the time of His ascension approaches, Jesus sets out resolutely for Jerusalem. He sends messengers ahead to make arrangements in a Samaritan village.

The people refuse to welcome Him because He is heading for Jerusalem. John’s Gospel records a Samaritan woman describing the disagreement over worship on her people’s mountain or in Jerusalem, which helps readers understand the significance of the destination. (John 4:19–24)

James and John ask whether they should call down fire to consume the village. Jesus turns and rebukes them, and the group goes to another village. His determined movement toward Jerusalem is accompanied by a refusal to let the disciples answer this rejection with destruction.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see Jesus correcting the disciples’ desire to punish those who refuse Him. The Catholic bishops’ notes emphasize His rejection of that response, while Wesley places His determined journey within the suffering and glory ahead. (USCCB notes on Luke 9:51–55; Wesley on Luke 9:51)
passages.god_plan_html:
The journey is directed toward the saving events that culminate in Jesus’ death, resurrection and ascension. At the Gospel’s end, He explains that repentance and forgiveness will be proclaimed in His name to the nations. Rejection in this village does not change the purpose of His mission. (Luke 24:44–49)

Acts later provides a striking contrast with the request for fire. Samaritans receive Philip’s proclamation of Christ, and Peter and John go to them and pray for them to receive the Holy Spirit. John, who asked about destroying a Samaritan village in the Gospel, now prays for Samaritan believers. The larger witness Jesus commissions explicitly includes Samaria. (Acts 8:4–17; Acts 1:8)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 9:57-62
passages.section_title: What can stand in the way of following Jesus?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 57 As they were walking along the road, someone said to Jesus, “I will follow You wherever You go.” 58 Jesus replied, “Foxes have dens and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has no place to lay His head.” 59 Then He said to another man, “Follow Me.” The man replied, “Lord, first let me go and bury my father.” 60 But Jesus told him, “Let the dead bury their own dead. You, however, go and proclaim the kingdom of God.” 61 Still another said, “I will follow You, Lord; but first let me bid farewell to my family.” 62 Then Jesus declared, “No one who puts his hand to the plow and then looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.”
paragraphs: 57 As they were walking along the road, someone said to Jesus, “I will follow You wherever You go.” 58 Jesus replied, “Foxes have dens and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has no place to lay His head.”

59 Then He said to another man, “Follow Me.” The man replied, “Lord, first let me go and bury my father.” 60 But Jesus told him, “Let the dead bury their own dead. You, however, go and proclaim the kingdom of God.”

61 Still another said, “I will follow You, Lord; but first let me bid farewell to my family.” 62 Then Jesus declared, “No one who puts his hand to the plow and then looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
As Jesus travels, three exchanges bring the cost of following Him into focus. One person offers to follow wherever He goes. Jesus answers by describing His lack of a place to lay His head, putting the promise beside the insecurity of His own journey.

Another receives the call to follow but asks first to bury his father. Jesus answers with the command to go and proclaim God’s kingdom. The exchange places the urgency of that call beside a deeply important family obligation.

A third offers to follow after saying goodbye at home. Jesus responds with the picture of someone taking hold of a plow and looking back. The three encounters ask what claim on a person’s life is allowed to govern the response to Him.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand the exchanges as a demanding call to wholehearted discipleship, with the kingdom’s claim reaching beyond comfort and competing obligations. The Catholic bishops’ notes emphasize its urgency, and Wesley points to the need to understand the terms of following and the earlier scene of Elisha’s call from the plow. (USCCB notes on Luke 9:57–62; Wesley on Luke 9:58–62)
passages.god_plan_html:
Elisha’s call supplies a close Scriptural parallel. Elijah finds him plowing; Elisha asks to say goodbye to his parents, then leaves his former work and follows. Jesus’ image recalls that kind of decisive response while pressing His own hearers to attend to the kingdom before them. (1 Kings 19:19–21)

Hebrews describes people of faith as seeking the better home God prepares, then calls believers to run with endurance while fixing their eyes on Jesus. He Himself endures the cross for the joy ahead. The forward-looking call here belongs within that larger journey of faith toward what God promises. (Hebrews 11:13–16; Hebrews 12:1–3)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 10:1-12
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus send more workers ahead of Him?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 After this, the Lord appointed seventy-two others and sent them two by two ahead of Him to every town and place He was about to visit. 2 And He told them, “The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few. Ask the Lord of the harvest, therefore, to send out workers into His harvest. 3 Go! I am sending you out like lambs among wolves. 4 Carry no purse or bag or sandals. Do not greet anyone along the road. 5 Whatever house you enter, begin by saying, ‘Peace to this house.’ 6 If a man of peace is there, your peace will rest on him; if not, it will return to you. 7 Stay at the same house, eating and drinking whatever you are offered. For the worker is worthy of his wages. Do not move around from house to house. 8 If you enter a town and they welcome you, eat whatever is set before you. 9 Heal the sick who are there and tell them, ‘The kingdom of God is near you.’ 10 But if you enter a town and they do not welcome you, go into the streets and declare, 11 ‘Even the dust of your town that clings to our feet, we wipe off as a testimony against you. Yet be sure of this: The kingdom of God is near.’ 12 I tell you, it will be more bearable on that day for Sodom than for that town.
paragraphs: 1 After this, the Lord appointed seventy-two others and sent them two by two ahead of Him to every town and place He was about to visit. 2 And He told them, “The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few. Ask the Lord of the harvest, therefore, to send out workers into His harvest. 3 Go! I am sending you out like lambs among wolves. 4 Carry no purse or bag or sandals. Do not greet anyone along the road.

5 Whatever house you enter, begin by saying, ‘Peace to this house.’ 6 If a man of peace is there, your peace will rest on him; if not, it will return to you. 7 Stay at the same house, eating and drinking whatever you are offered. For the worker is worthy of his wages. Do not move around from house to house. 8 If you enter a town and they welcome you, eat whatever is set before you. 9 Heal the sick who are there and tell them, ‘The kingdom of God is near you.’

10 But if you enter a town and they do not welcome you, go into the streets and declare, 11 ‘Even the dust of your town that clings to our feet, we wipe off as a testimony against you. Yet be sure of this: The kingdom of God is near.’ 12 I tell you, it will be more bearable on that day for Sodom than for that town.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus appoints seventy-two others and sends them ahead in pairs to the places He intends to visit. This work reaches beyond the Twelve. He describes a harvest with too few workers and tells them to ask its Lord to send more.

Their task joins care for the sick with the announcement that God’s kingdom is near. They are to travel without the supplies that would normally support them, accept a household’s hospitality and remain there rather than move from house to house. The instructions call for dependence, focus and contentment with what they receive.

They begin by offering peace. Where a town refuses them, they are to leave a public warning, wiping off its dust while still announcing the kingdom’s nearness. Jesus ends with a sober comparison to Sodom: refusing this visit has consequences.

Some Bible translations say seventy rather than seventy-two because the manuscripts differ. The BSB uses seventy-two here and when the group returns in verse 17. (BibleHub BSB footnote on Luke 10:1)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see an urgent mission carried out in dependence on God and through the hospitality of those who receive the message. Wesley stresses God’s role in supplying workers, while the Catholic bishops’ notes emphasize the focus required of those Jesus sends. (Wesley on Luke 10:2; USCCB notes on Luke 10:1–12)
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus also uses the harvest picture in John, where the work of different people comes together in gathering a crop for eternal life. Some have labored before others arrive, and both can share the joy. This helps place the seventy-two within a work larger than any one group’s contribution. (John 4:35–38)

Paul later describes himself and Apollos as servants with different tasks in God’s field. One plants, another waters, and God gives the growth. The need for workers remains, but the harvest belongs to God. (1 Corinthians 3:5–9)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 10:13-16
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus warn the towns that saw His miracles?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the miracles that were performed in you had been performed in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes. 14 But it will be more bearable for Tyre and Sidon at the judgment than for you. 15 And you, Capernaum, will you be lifted up to heaven? No, you will be brought down to Hades! 16 Whoever listens to you listens to Me; whoever rejects you rejects Me; and whoever rejects Me rejects the One who sent Me.”
paragraphs: 13 Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the miracles that were performed in you had been performed in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes. 14 But it will be more bearable for Tyre and Sidon at the judgment than for you. 15 And you, Capernaum, will you be lifted up to heaven? No, you will be brought down to Hades!
16 Whoever listens to you listens to Me; whoever rejects you rejects Me; and whoever rejects Me rejects the One who sent Me.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The warning to towns that refuse the messengers leads into Jesus’ words about Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum. These places have received evidence of His work, yet His comparison with Tyre and Sidon exposes their failure to repent.

Jesus says the judgment will be more bearable for Tyre and Sidon. Capernaum’s imagined rise to heaven is answered with a descent to Hades. The contrast overturns any confidence that witnessing His works makes a town secure regardless of its response.

Then Jesus explains the seriousness of receiving or refusing the people He sends. Their message comes from Him, and He comes from the Father. In this commission, refusing the messenger means refusing the One whose message the messenger carries.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand these warnings as a call to repentance and an account of the responsibility that comes with receiving Jesus’ message. The Catholic bishops’ notes connect the towns’ judgment with the rejection of His mission. (USCCB note on Luke 10:13–16; Luke 10:13–16)
passages.god_plan_html:
In John, Jesus again connects His words with the Father who sent Him. He comes to save, yet warns that the word a person rejects will judge that person on the last day. The warnings here belong within that same account of salvation offered through the Son and accountability for the response. (John 12:44–50)

Acts shows the mission continuing through rejection. When opposition drives Paul and Barnabas from a district, they shake off its dust and move on; others have received the message with joy, and the word continues to spread. Rejection is serious, but it does not bring God’s work to an end. (Acts 13:44–52)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 10:17-20
passages.section_title: What should bring the returning disciples their greatest joy?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 The seventy-two returned with joy and said, “Lord, even the demons submit to us in Your name.” 18 So He told them, “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven. 19 Behold, I have given you authority to tread on snakes and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy. Nothing will harm you. 20 Nevertheless, do not rejoice that the spirits submit to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.”
paragraphs: 17 The seventy-two returned with joy and said, “Lord, even the demons submit to us in Your name.” 18 So He told them, “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven. 19 Behold, I have given you authority to tread on snakes and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy. Nothing will harm you.
20 Nevertheless, do not rejoice that the spirits submit to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The seventy-two return delighted that even demons submit to them in Jesus’ name. Jesus responds with the picture of Satan falling like lightning and speaks of the authority He has given them over the enemy’s power.

The authority comes from Jesus. The disciples’ report concerns what happens in His name, rather than an ability they possess independently. His words about snakes, scorpions and protection are spoken to these people in the setting of their commission.

Jesus then directs their joy toward something greater than the powers they have exercised: their names are written in heaven. Their place with God is the reason for celebration He puts first.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley, Calvin and the Catholic bishops’ notes connect Satan’s fall here with the defeat of his power through Jesus’ mission. They also recognize the movement from rejoicing over extraordinary works to rejoicing over belonging to God. This reading follows the setting of the disciples’ return without making the verse a complete account of Satan’s history. (Wesley on Luke 10:18–20; Calvin on Luke 10:18–20; USCCB note on Luke 10:18)
passages.god_plan_html:
Revelation also pictures Satan being thrown down and describes believers overcoming him through the Lamb’s blood and their faithful testimony. This is a related picture of victory through Christ; the connection does not require treating the two scenes as a single event on a settled timeline. (Revelation 12:7–12)

Hebrews describes believers coming to the heavenly city, to a people enrolled in heaven and to Jesus, who brings the new covenant. That wider picture helps explain why having one’s name in heaven is a joy greater than any particular work a disciple performs. (Hebrews 12:22–24)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 10:21-24
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus rejoice over what His disciples have received?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 At that time Jesus rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and declared, “I praise You, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because You have hidden these things from the wise and learned, and revealed them to little children. Yes, Father, for this was well-pleasing in Your sight. 22 All things have been entrusted to Me by My Father. No one knows who the Son is except the Father, and no one knows who the Father is except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him.” 23 Then Jesus turned to the disciples and said privately, “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see. 24 For I tell you that many prophets and kings desired to see what you see but did not see it, and to hear what you hear but did not hear it.”
paragraphs: 21 At that time Jesus rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and declared, “I praise You, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because You have hidden these things from the wise and learned, and revealed them to little children. Yes, Father, for this was well-pleasing in Your sight. 22 All things have been entrusted to Me by My Father. No one knows who the Son is except the Father, and no one knows who the Father is except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him.”

23 Then Jesus turned to the disciples and said privately, “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see. 24 For I tell you that many prophets and kings desired to see what you see but did not see it, and to hear what you hear but did not hear it.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
At this moment Jesus rejoices in the Holy Spirit and thanks the Father, Lord of heaven and earth. What is hidden from the wise and learned has been revealed to little children. His thanksgiving places the Father’s generous revelation at the center of the disciples’ privilege.

Jesus then speaks of the unique knowledge shared by Father and Son. Those who come to know the Father receive what the Son reveals to them. The passage directs attention to Jesus Himself as the One through whom the Father becomes known.

Turning privately to the disciples, He tells them how blessed they are to see and hear what is unfolding before them. Prophets and kings desired this sight, but the disciples are living in the time of its arrival.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly emphasize the gift of knowing God through the Son and the humble reception of that gift. The Catholic Catechism describes this prayer as thanksgiving and loving agreement with the Father’s will; Wesley likewise emphasizes God’s grace rather than human pride as the reason for Jesus’ joy. (Catechism §2603; Wesley on Luke 10:21–22)
passages.god_plan_html:
First Peter describes the prophets searching into the salvation they foretold, including Christ’s sufferings and the glory that would follow. Their service looked ahead to the gospel later announced through the Holy Spirit. The disciples’ privilege here belongs to that movement from promise toward fulfillment. (1 Peter 1:10–12)

John states the same central truth about knowing the Father: the Son, who is at His side, has made Him known. God’s purpose is being disclosed through the person of Jesus, not simply through information about Him. (John 1:18)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 10:25-37
passages.section_title: What does it mean to become a neighbor to someone in need?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 25 One day an expert in the law stood up to test Him. “Teacher,” he asked, “what must I do to inherit eternal life?” 26 “What is written in the Law?” Jesus replied. “How do you read it?” 27 He answered, “‘Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength and with all your mind’ and ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’” 28 “You have answered correctly,” Jesus said. “Do this and you will live.” 29 But wanting to justify himself, he asked Jesus, “And who is my neighbor?” 30 Jesus took up this question and said, “A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho when he fell into the hands of robbers. They stripped him, beat him, and went away, leaving him half dead. 31 Now by chance a priest was going down the same road, but when he saw him, he passed by on the other side. 32 So too, when a Levite came to that spot and saw him, he passed by on the other side. 33 But a Samaritan on a journey came upon him, and when he saw him, he had compassion. 34 He went to him and bandaged his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. Then he put him on his own animal, brought him to an inn, and took care of him. 35 The next day he took out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper. ‘Take care of him,’ he said, ‘and on my return I will repay you for any additional expense.’ 36 Which of these three do you think was a neighbor to the man who fell into the hands of robbers?” 37 “The one who showed him mercy,” replied the expert in the law. Then Jesus told him, “Go and do likewise.”
paragraphs: 25 One day an expert in the law stood up to test Him. “Teacher,” he asked, “what must I do to inherit eternal life?” 26 “What is written in the Law?” Jesus replied. “How do you read it?” 27 He answered, “‘Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength and with all your mind’ and ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’” 28 “You have answered correctly,” Jesus said. “Do this and you will live.” 29 But wanting to justify himself, he asked Jesus, “And who is my neighbor?”

30 Jesus took up this question and said, “A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho when he fell into the hands of robbers. They stripped him, beat him, and went away, leaving him half dead. 31 Now by chance a priest was going down the same road, but when he saw him, he passed by on the other side. 32 So too, when a Levite came to that spot and saw him, he passed by on the other side. 33 But a Samaritan on a journey came upon him, and when he saw him, he had compassion. 34 He went to him and bandaged his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. Then he put him on his own animal, brought him to an inn, and took care of him. 35 The next day he took out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper. ‘Take care of him,’ he said, ‘and on my return I will repay you for any additional expense.’

36 Which of these three do you think was a neighbor to the man who fell into the hands of robbers?” 37 “The one who showed him mercy,” replied the expert in the law. Then Jesus told him, “Go and do likewise.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
An expert in the law tests Jesus with a question about inheriting eternal life. Jesus directs him to the Law, and the man answers with love for God and love for one’s neighbor. These commands come from Deuteronomy 6:5 and Leviticus 19:18. Jesus approves the answer and tells him to live it out. (Deuteronomy 6:5; Leviticus 19:18)

The man then asks who counts as his neighbor, wanting to justify himself. Jesus answers with a story: robbers leave a traveler half dead on the road from Jerusalem to Jericho. A priest and a Levite see him but pass by. A Samaritan sees him and has compassion.

The Samaritan’s compassion becomes action. He tends the wounds, provides transport and lodging, pays for care and promises to cover further expense. Jesus asks which person became a neighbor to the injured man. The answer is the one who showed mercy, and Jesus tells the questioner to do the same.

The choice of a Samaritan matters: John’s Gospel records the division between Jews and Samaritans. Here, the person across that divide gives the example of mercy. The story does not identify the injured man’s ethnicity or explain the private motives of those who pass him by. (John 4:9)
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly recognize a demand for practical mercy that reaches beyond familiar boundaries. Wesley emphasizes helping the person who needs assistance, and the Catholic bishops’ notes emphasize the Samaritan’s unexpected place as the example. (Wesley on Luke 10:36–37; USCCB notes on Luke 10:25–37)

Teachers also place different emphasis on the earlier exchange about eternal life. Calvin explains that the Law’s demand is righteous but that human failure makes freely given justification necessary. Wesley stresses the seriousness of Jesus’ command to love God and neighbor. These are the teachers’ explanations of how the exchange fits salvation; neither removes Jesus’ concluding call to show mercy. (Calvin on Luke 10:28; Wesley on Luke 10:28)
passages.god_plan_html:
The command to love was already part of God’s instruction to Israel. Leviticus also commands love for the foreigner living among them. Jesus’ story draws the questioner toward the active, generous love that the Law calls for, rather than a search for reasons to withhold it. (Leviticus 19:18, 33–34)

Paul later explains that love fulfills the Law because it does no wrong to a neighbor. First John places self-giving love under the example of Jesus laying down His life, then asks how God’s love can remain in someone who has resources but shuts off compassion toward a brother in need. The Samaritan’s concrete care belongs within this wider Scriptural call for love expressed in action. (Romans 13:8–10; 1 John 3:16–18)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 10:38-42
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus defend Mary’s choice to listen?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 38 As they traveled along, Jesus entered a village where a woman named Martha welcomed Him into her home. 39 She had a sister named Mary, who sat at the Lord’s feet listening to His message. 40 But Martha was distracted by all the preparations to be made. She came to Jesus and said, “Lord, do You not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her to help me!” 41 “Martha, Martha,” the Lord replied, “you are worried and upset about many things. 42 But only one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion, and it will not be taken away from her.”
paragraphs: 38 As they traveled along, Jesus entered a village where a woman named Martha welcomed Him into her home. 39 She had a sister named Mary, who sat at the Lord’s feet listening to His message. 40 But Martha was distracted by all the preparations to be made. She came to Jesus and said, “Lord, do You not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her to help me!”
41 “Martha, Martha,” the Lord replied, “you are worried and upset about many things. 42 But only one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion, and it will not be taken away from her.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Martha welcomes Jesus into her home, while her sister Mary sits at His feet and listens to His message. Martha becomes distracted by the preparations and asks Jesus to tell Mary to help her.

Jesus answers Martha directly and acknowledges her worry over many things. He identifies one necessary thing and defends the good portion Mary has chosen. Her opportunity to listen will not be taken from her.

The scene follows a story in which mercy takes the form of costly service. Read together, the passages call for both attention to Jesus and care for others. Martha’s hospitality provides the setting, but her many tasks have become a distraction from the One she has welcomed.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see Jesus giving priority to receiving His teaching. Calvin explains that other responsibilities still have their place, while hearing Jesus must remain central; the Catholic bishops’ notes likewise emphasize listening to the Lord. (Calvin on Luke 10:42; USCCB notes on Luke 10:38–42)
passages.god_plan_html:
Deuteronomy describes Israel learning through the manna that life depends on every word from God’s mouth. Mary’s attention to Jesus can be read alongside that larger theme: receiving God’s word is necessary nourishment, not an optional extra after every other task is finished. This is a connection between the passages, rather than an explicit identification made by Luke. (Deuteronomy 8:3)

James brings hearing and action together. God’s word is to be welcomed and then practiced, including care for people in distress. Listening and serving therefore belong together in the life God forms; hearing His word gives direction to the care His people offer. (James 1:19–27)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 11:1-4
passages.section_title: How does Jesus teach His disciples to pray?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 One day in a place where Jesus had just finished praying, one of His disciples requested, “Lord, teach us to pray, just as John taught his disciples.” 2 So Jesus told them, “When you pray, say: ‘Father, hallowed be Your name. Your kingdom come. 3 Give us each day our daily bread. 4 And forgive us our sins, for we also forgive everyone who sins against us. And lead us not into temptation.’”
paragraphs: 1 One day in a place where Jesus had just finished praying, one of His disciples requested, “Lord, teach us to pray, just as John taught his disciples.”

2 So Jesus told them, “When you pray, say: ‘Father, hallowed be Your name. Your kingdom come. 3 Give us each day our daily bread. 4 And forgive us our sins, for we also forgive everyone who sins against us. And lead us not into temptation.’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After Jesus finishes praying, a disciple asks Him to teach them, as John taught his own disciples. Jesus responds with words they can bring to the Father. Luke’s account is shorter than the prayer in Matthew; the passage text here follows Luke without adding Matthew’s phrases.

The prayer begins with God’s name and kingdom, then brings daily bread, forgiveness and protection from temptation before Him. Its repeated language of us and our includes others in these requests.

To hallow God’s name is to honor it as holy. The Greek verb is ἁγιάζω, hagiazō (hah-gee-AH-zoh), which Thayer’s lexicon explains here as acknowledging or treating as holy. The request asks that God receive the honor due Him. (Thayer, Greek 37)

Forgiveness received and forgiveness extended belong together in the prayer. The final petition brings human weakness before the Father rather than treating resistance to temptation as something the disciples can manage alone.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian traditions broadly receive this prayer as instruction in approaching God as Father, honoring Him and depending on Him. They commonly use it both to shape other prayers and as words that can themselves be prayed sincerely: the Westminster Larger Catechism explicitly allows both, as does Wesley’s note on Luke 11:2. (Westminster Larger Catechism 186–190; Wesley on Luke 11:1–2)

There are differences in how the bread petition is explained. The Reformed Westminster Larger Catechism emphasizes the material provision needed for life, received with contentment. The Catholic Church’s Compendium includes that need and also hunger for God’s word, the Holy Spirit and Christ received in the Lord’s Supper. These descriptions need not mean that every member of either tradition places the same emphasis on each part. (Westminster Larger Catechism 193; Catholic Compendium 592–593)

The Greek word behind daily, ἐπιούσιος, epiousios (eh-pee-OO-see-os), has a debated formation. Thayer discusses readings involving needed sustenance or food for the coming day. The word alone does not settle every theological meaning Christians find in the petition. (Thayer, Greek 1967)
passages.god_plan_html:
Galatians connects calling God Father with His saving work: He sends His Son to redeem and bring people into His family, then sends the Spirit of His Son into their hearts. The relationship expressed in this prayer belongs within that work of redemption and adoption. (Galatians 4:4–7)

Romans adds that the Spirit helps believers in their weakness and intercedes according to God’s will when they do not know how to pray. God’s people depend on Him even in learning to address Him. (Romans 8:26–27)
passages.current_position_html: Prayer and Faith understands this prayer as a pattern of dependence on God, with His purposes governing the requests. It reads daily bread as dependence on Christ, the living bread, drawing that connection from John 6. That is the study’s interpretation, rather than a meaning proved by the Greek word alone. What Does Prayer Look Like? also emphasizes honest prayer governed by surrender to the Father’s will.

passages.title: Luke 11:5-13
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus tell His disciples to keep asking?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 Then Jesus said to them, “Suppose one of you goes to his friend at midnight and says, ‘Friend, lend me three loaves of bread, 6 because a friend of mine has come to me on a journey, and I have nothing to set before him.’ 7 And suppose the one inside answers, ‘Do not bother me. My door is already shut, and my children and I are in bed. I cannot get up to give you anything.’ 8 I tell you, even though he will not get up to provide for him because of his friendship, yet because of the man’s persistence, he will get up and give him as much as he needs. 9 So I tell you: Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and the door will be opened to you. 10 For everyone who asks receives; he who seeks finds; and to him who knocks, the door will be opened. 11 What father among you, if his son asks for a fish, will give him a snake instead? 12 Or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion? 13 So if you who are evil know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him!”
paragraphs: 5 Then Jesus said to them, “Suppose one of you goes to his friend at midnight and says, ‘Friend, lend me three loaves of bread, 6 because a friend of mine has come to me on a journey, and I have nothing to set before him.’ 7 And suppose the one inside answers, ‘Do not bother me. My door is already shut, and my children and I are in bed. I cannot get up to give you anything.’ 8 I tell you, even though he will not get up to provide for him because of his friendship, yet because of the man’s persistence, he will get up and give him as much as he needs.

9 So I tell you: Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and the door will be opened to you. 10 For everyone who asks receives; he who seeks finds; and to him who knocks, the door will be opened.

11 What father among you, if his son asks for a fish, will give him a snake instead? 12 Or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion? 13 So if you who are evil know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him!”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus continues His teaching with a midnight request for bread. A traveler has arrived, and the host has nothing to offer him. His friend initially refuses to get out of bed, but the request succeeds because of the man’s persistence.

The Greek word in verse 8 is ἀναίδεια, anaideia (ah-NYE-day-ah). Thayer gives the sense of shamelessness or impudence and applies it here to someone pressing his request. The picture is of someone willing to ask boldly despite the inconvenience. (Thayer, Greek 335)

Jesus then tells the disciples to ask, seek and knock. He follows the story with a second comparison: fathers who are themselves sinful still know how to give their children good gifts rather than something harmful.

The argument moves from these imperfect human responses to the Father’s goodness. Jesus ends by naming the Holy Spirit as the gift the Father gives to those who ask. The reluctant friend is part of the comparison; the Father’s generous care is where the teaching leads.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand this passage as encouragement to persevere in prayer and trust the Father’s goodness. The Catholic bishops’ notes identify persistence and the effectiveness of prayer across these episodes, while Wesley emphasizes the Holy Spirit as the gift that brings God’s other gifts with it. (USCCB notes on Luke 11:1–13; Wesley on Luke 11:13)
passages.god_plan_html:
In Acts, the risen Jesus calls the Holy Spirit the Father’s promised gift and connects that gift with witness reaching to the ends of the earth. At Pentecost, the gathered disciples receive the Spirit; Peter explains the outpouring through the risen and exalted Jesus. The Father’s generosity serves His purpose of making Christ known. (Acts 1:4–8; Acts 2:1–4, 32–39)

Later, threatened believers pray for boldness and for God’s healing work, and they are filled with the Spirit to speak His word. Luke’s second volume gives a concrete picture of a praying people receiving help for the mission God has entrusted to them. (Acts 4:23–31)
passages.current_position_html: Prayer and Faith and What Does Prayer Look Like? both draw attention to the gift Jesus names here: the Holy Spirit. Their emphasis is on prayer that seeks God’s purposes and His work within us, rather than treating asking as a way to secure a chosen outcome. What Does Prayer Look Like? also recognizes that continued petition can be governed by real surrender; repetition by itself does not establish a lack of faith.

passages.title: Luke 11:13
passages.section_title: What gift does Jesus name when He speaks of the Father’s goodness?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 So if you who are evil know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him!”
paragraphs: 13 So if you who are evil know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him!”

passages.context_html:
This verse concludes Jesus’ teaching about prayer in Luke 11:1–13. After giving the disciples a prayer and the midnight-friend story, Jesus compares the Father’s giving with the ordinary care of earthly parents.

Even sinful people can recognize a child’s need and give something good. Jesus directs the disciples’ confidence toward their Father in heaven, whose goodness is greater, and identifies the Holy Spirit as His gift.

The verse is best read with the whole exchange, including the call to ask, seek and knock. Read Luke 11:5–13.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly recognize the Father’s generous care and the importance of the Holy Spirit as His gift to those who ask. Wesley emphasizes the greatness of that gift, and the Catholic bishops’ note likewise places the gift of the Spirit at the conclusion of Jesus’ teaching on prayer. (Wesley on Luke 11:13; USCCB note on Luke 11:13)
passages.current_position_html: Prayer and Faith and What Does Prayer Look Like? use this verse to emphasize what Jesus names as the Father’s gift: the Holy Spirit. They understand mature prayer as seeking God’s purposes, His presence and His work of forming us, with trust in His goodness governing what we ask.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html: Galatians describes the Father sending His Son to redeem and then sending the Spirit of His Son into the hearts of His children. Romans likewise connects the Spirit with belonging to God’s family. The gift named here is part of God bringing people into a life of relationship with Him through Christ. (Galatians 4:4–7; Romans 8:14–17)

passages.title: Luke 11:14-23
passages.section_title: What does Jesus’ victory over evil reveal about His kingdom?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 One day Jesus was driving out a demon that was mute. And when the demon was gone, the man who had been mute spoke. The crowds were amazed, 15 but some of them said, “It is by Beelzebul, the prince of the demons, that He drives out demons.” 16 And others tested Him by demanding a sign from heaven. 17 Knowing their thoughts, Jesus said to them, “Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste, and a house divided against a house will fall. 18 If Satan is divided against himself, how can his kingdom stand? After all, you say that I drive out demons by Beelzebul. 19 And if I drive out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons drive them out? So then, they will be your judges. 20 But if I drive out demons by the finger of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you. 21 When a strong man, fully armed, guards his house, his possessions are secure. 22 But when someone stronger attacks and overpowers him, he takes away the armor in which the man trusted, and then he divides up his plunder. 23 He who is not with Me is against Me, and he who does not gather with Me scatters.
paragraphs: 14 One day Jesus was driving out a demon that was mute. And when the demon was gone, the man who had been mute spoke. The crowds were amazed, 15 but some of them said, “It is by Beelzebul, the prince of the demons, that He drives out demons.” 16 And others tested Him by demanding a sign from heaven.

17 Knowing their thoughts, Jesus said to them, “Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste, and a house divided against a house will fall. 18 If Satan is divided against himself, how can his kingdom stand? After all, you say that I drive out demons by Beelzebul. 19 And if I drive out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons drive them out? So then, they will be your judges. 20 But if I drive out demons by the finger of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you.

21 When a strong man, fully armed, guards his house, his possessions are secure. 22 But when someone stronger attacks and overpowers him, he takes away the armor in which the man trusted, and then he divides up his plunder. 23 He who is not with Me is against Me, and he who does not gather with Me scatters.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus drives out a demon, and the man who had been mute speaks. Some in the amazed crowd attribute the work to Beelzebul, the prince of demons. Others test Jesus by demanding a sign from heaven.

Jesus answers that a kingdom torn against itself cannot stand. If His work is defeating Satan’s power, attributing it to Satan makes no sense. He also asks what the same accusation would mean for the work of their own people who drive out demons.

Then He states the alternative: if He drives out demons by God’s power, God’s kingdom has come upon them. The healing is part of that arrival, rather than evidence of an alliance with the enemy.

The picture of a stronger man overcoming an armed guard explains the release. Jesus’ work takes from the enemy what the enemy could not keep secure against Him. His concluding words call for a response to Himself: being against Him and scattering are the opposite of gathering with Him.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand Jesus as the stronger One who defeats the enemy and brings God’s kingdom. Wesley identifies the strong guard with the devil, while the Catholic Catechism places these releases within Christ’s victory over Satan. (Wesley on Luke 11:20–21; Catechism §550)
passages.god_plan_html:
The phrase about God’s finger recalls Exodus, where Pharaoh’s magicians recognize God’s power in a plague they cannot reproduce, yet Pharaoh remains hardened. This is a parallel between the accounts: an act of deliverance reveals God’s power and calls for a response. (Exodus 8:16–19)

Hebrews explains that Jesus shares our humanity and, through His death, defeats the devil’s power and frees those enslaved by fear of death. Colossians describes God rescuing people from darkness and bringing them into His Son’s kingdom. The release before the crowd belongs within this larger purpose of rescue through Christ. (Hebrews 2:14–15; Colossians 1:13–14)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 11:24-26
passages.section_title: Why is a swept house not the end of the story?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 24 When an unclean spirit comes out of a man, it passes through arid places seeking rest and does not find it. Then it says, ‘I will return to the house I left.’ 25 On its return, it finds the house swept clean and put in order. 26 Then it goes and brings seven other spirits more wicked than itself, and they go in and dwell there. And the final plight of that man is worse than the first.”
paragraphs: 24 When an unclean spirit comes out of a man, it passes through arid places seeking rest and does not find it. Then it says, ‘I will return to the house I left.’ 25 On its return, it finds the house swept clean and put in order. 26 Then it goes and brings seven other spirits more wicked than itself, and they go in and dwell there. And the final plight of that man is worse than the first.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After describing the defeat of the strong guard, Jesus tells of an unclean spirit leaving a man and later returning. It finds the house swept clean and in order, then brings seven spirits more wicked than itself. The man’s final condition is worse than his first.

The warning follows a healing that some people have refused to recognize as God’s work. A welcome change in someone’s condition is not presented as the whole answer to evil; the story ends with a return and a worse captivity.

Matthew’s parallel account explicitly applies the warning to the wicked generation Jesus is addressing. Luke gives the picture here in the continuing exchange about His authority, the arrival of God’s kingdom and the need to respond to Him. (Matthew 12:43–45)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly recognize a warning about a worse condition after an earlier release or improvement. Calvin emphasizes the danger of rejecting the grace offered through Christ, while Wesley applies the warning to rejection and a final turning away from faith. Their explanations share the seriousness of the response without making this short picture a complete account of every question about salvation. (Calvin on the unclean spirit; Wesley on Luke 11:26)
passages.god_plan_html:
Second Peter gives a related warning: people can escape corruption through knowledge of Jesus Christ and then become entangled again, ending in a worse condition. The shared theme is the seriousness of turning back after receiving something of God’s rescue and instruction. This is a parallel warning, rather than a claim that the two passages describe the same individuals. (2 Peter 2:20–22)

Placed beside the preceding announcement of God’s kingdom, the story presses beyond an outwardly improved situation toward the question of receiving Jesus. God’s rescue brings people into His Son’s kingdom; a cleaned house by itself is not the same description as that relationship. (Luke 11:20–26; Colossians 1:13–14)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 11:27-28
passages.section_title: Who does Jesus call blessed?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 27 As Jesus was saying these things, a woman in the crowd raised her voice and said, “Blessed is the womb that bore You, and blessed are the breasts that nursed You!” 28 But He replied, “Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it.”
paragraphs: 27 As Jesus was saying these things, a woman in the crowd raised her voice and said, “Blessed is the womb that bore You, and blessed are the breasts that nursed You!” 28 But He replied, “Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
A woman in the crowd praises the mother who bore and nursed Jesus. He answers by directing attention to people who hear God’s word and obey it.

The brief exchange continues the question of how people respond to Him. Admiration of Jesus and His family leads into a call that reaches everyone listening: receive God’s word and live by it.

Luke has already described Mary accepting God’s message and Elizabeth blessing her for believing it. Hearing and believing are therefore part of Mary’s own story, not a reason to place her outside the blessing Jesus describes. (Luke 1:38, 45)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly emphasize hearing God’s word and putting it into practice. The Catholic bishops’ notes explain that the saying does not reject Jesus’ mother, while Wesley likewise makes hearing and keeping the word central even for her. (USCCB note on Luke 11:27–28; Wesley on Luke 11:27–28)
passages.god_plan_html:
Galatians describes people becoming God’s children through faith in Christ and sharing the inheritance promised to Abraham. The blessing reaches across differences of ancestry and standing because they belong to Christ. Jesus’ invitation to hear and obey fits this wider gathering of a family around Him. (Galatians 3:26–29)

James similarly joins hearing with doing and describes the blessing of persevering in God’s word. The response Jesus calls for becomes a way of life, rather than admiration that never reaches action. (James 1:22–25)
