passages.title: Luke 11:29-32
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus point to Jonah and the Queen of the South?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 29 As the crowds were increasing, Jesus said, “This is a wicked generation. It demands a sign, but none will be given it except the sign of Jonah. 30 For as Jonah was a sign to the Ninevites, so the Son of Man will be a sign to this generation. 31 The Queen of the South will rise at the judgment with the men of this generation and condemn them; for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and now One greater than Solomon is here. 32 The men of Nineveh will stand at the judgment with this generation and condemn it; for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and now One greater than Jonah is here.
paragraphs: 29 As the crowds were increasing, Jesus said, “This is a wicked generation. It demands a sign, but none will be given it except the sign of Jonah. 30 For as Jonah was a sign to the Ninevites, so the Son of Man will be a sign to this generation.

31 The Queen of the South will rise at the judgment with the men of this generation and condemn them; for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and now One greater than Solomon is here. 32 The men of Nineveh will stand at the judgment with this generation and condemn it; for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and now One greater than Jonah is here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
As the crowd grows, Jesus addresses its demand for a sign. He calls the generation wicked and says that the sign it will receive is the sign of Jonah. Just as Jonah became a sign to the Ninevites, the Son of Man will be a sign to this generation.

Jesus then names two responses from Scripture. The Queen of the South traveled to hear Solomon’s wisdom, and Nineveh repented at Jonah’s preaching. Their responses will expose the failure of the people now receiving someone greater.

Jonah’s account says that the Ninevites believed God and turned from their evil ways after hearing his proclamation. First Kings describes the queen’s encounter with Solomon’s wisdom and her praise of the Lord. Jesus uses those accounts to challenge the response to what is present in Him. (Jonah 3:1–10; 1 Kings 10:1–9)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand Jesus as calling for repentance and a response to His greater wisdom and authority. The Catholic bishops’ notes emphasize Jonah’s preaching in Luke, while pointing out that Matthew explicitly connects Jonah’s time in the fish with the Son of Man’s time in the earth. Those are distinct emphases in the two Gospel accounts. (USCCB note on Luke 11:29–32; Matthew 12:38–42)
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus Himself makes the larger connection: Jonah and Solomon point beyond their own ministries toward the greater One now before the crowd. The response of people outside Israel also becomes a witness at the judgment. These are connections stated by Jesus, rather than hidden meanings assigned to details by a later teacher. (Luke 11:29–32)

Matthew’s account adds the explicit comparison between Jonah’s three days and nights in the fish and the Son of Man’s time in the heart of the earth. Read alongside Luke’s emphasis on repentance, the comparison places the sign within Jesus’ coming death and resurrection. (Matthew 12:39–42)
passages.current_position_html: Should We Seek Signs From God? examines the parallel demand in Matthew 12 and understands it as resistance to what God has already made known. The study distinguishes that demand from every sincere request for guidance: the issue here is making trust conditional on another sign despite the witness already received.

deeper_study.title: Should We Seek Signs From God?

passages.title: Luke 11:33-36
passages.section_title: How can the light someone thinks they have be darkness?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 33 No one lights a lamp and puts it in a cellar or under a basket. Instead, he sets it on a stand, so those who enter can see the light. 34 Your eye is the lamp of your body. When your eyes are good, your whole body also is full of light. But when they are bad, your body is full of darkness. 35 Be careful, then, that the light within you is not darkness. 36 So if your whole body is full of light, with no part of it in darkness, you will be radiant, as though a lamp were shining on you.”
paragraphs: 33 No one lights a lamp and puts it in a cellar or under a basket. Instead, he sets it on a stand, so those who enter can see the light. 34 Your eye is the lamp of your body. When your eyes are good, your whole body also is full of light. But when they are bad, your body is full of darkness. 35 Be careful, then, that the light within you is not darkness. 36 So if your whole body is full of light, with no part of it in darkness, you will be radiant, as though a lamp were shining on you.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus follows the warning about demanding signs with the picture of a lamp placed where people entering can see it. The light is meant to be visible.

Then He describes the eye as the body’s lamp. A good eye brings light; a bad one leaves the body in darkness. He warns the hearer to examine whether what seems to be inward light is actually darkness.

The Greek word describing the good eye is ἁπλοῦς, haplous (hah-PLOOS). Thayer describes an eye that is sound and fulfills its purpose, while noting discussion of the word’s moral sense. Jesus uses the picture to address the hearer’s inward condition, rather than to diagnose physical eyesight. (Thayer, Greek 573)

The passage ends with the whole person illuminated. In the surrounding conversation, the warning asks people who have seen Jesus’ work to consider how they are receiving its light.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand the lamp and eye as pictures of receiving God’s truth and the need for an undivided response. Wesley explains the passage in terms of directing one’s aim toward pleasing God and allowing His light to reach the whole life. (Wesley on Luke 11:33–36; Luke 11:33–36)
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul connects God’s original command for light with His act of shining into human hearts through the knowledge of His glory in Jesus Christ. The larger Scriptural theme is God overcoming darkness so people can know Him through His Son. (2 Corinthians 4:4–6)

Ephesians then describes the changed life of people who are light in the Lord: goodness, righteousness and truth become its fruit, and they are to test what pleases Him. The light God gives is meant to reach the way His people live. (Ephesians 5:8–14)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 11:37-44
passages.section_title: What does an outwardly clean cup reveal about the heart?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 37 As Jesus was speaking, a Pharisee invited Him to dine with him; so He went in and reclined at the table. 38 But the Pharisee was surprised to see that Jesus did not first wash before the meal. 39 Then the Lord said, “Now you Pharisees clean the outside of the cup and dish, but inside you are full of greed and wickedness. 40 You fools! Did not the One who made the outside make the inside as well? 41 But give as alms the things that are within you, and behold, everything will be clean for you. 42 Woe to you Pharisees! For you pay tithes of mint, rue, and every herb, but you disregard justice and the love of God. You should have practiced the latter without neglecting the former. 43 Woe to you Pharisees! For you love the chief seats in the synagogues and the greetings in the marketplaces. 44 Woe to you! For you are like unmarked graves, which men walk over without even noticing.”
paragraphs: 37 As Jesus was speaking, a Pharisee invited Him to dine with him; so He went in and reclined at the table. 38 But the Pharisee was surprised to see that Jesus did not first wash before the meal. 39 Then the Lord said, “Now you Pharisees clean the outside of the cup and dish, but inside you are full of greed and wickedness. 40 You fools! Did not the One who made the outside make the inside as well? 41 But give as alms the things that are within you, and behold, everything will be clean for you.

42 Woe to you Pharisees! For you pay tithes of mint, rue, and every herb, but you disregard justice and the love of God. You should have practiced the latter without neglecting the former. 43 Woe to you Pharisees! For you love the chief seats in the synagogues and the greetings in the marketplaces. 44 Woe to you! For you are like unmarked graves, which men walk over without even noticing.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
A Pharisee invites Jesus to a meal and is surprised when He does not first wash. Mark’s account of a similar dispute explains the ceremonial handwashing as a tradition of the elders. Luke’s scene turns from that concern with washing toward what is happening inside the people at the table. (Mark 7:1–8)

Jesus compares their attention to appearances with cleaning a cup’s outside while leaving its inside dirty. He names greed and wickedness, reminds them that God made both inside and outside, and calls for giving to those in need.

Three warnings follow. They carefully tithe garden herbs while disregarding justice and love for God; they seek honored seats and public greetings; and they are like unmarked graves. Jesus does not say that care over the tithe excuses neglecting the weightier responsibilities. He says they should have practiced those responsibilities without neglecting the others.

The grave picture carries a warning about harmful influence that goes unnoticed. Numbers identifies contact with a grave as a source of ceremonial uncleanness, supplying the background to the image. (Numbers 19:16)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand Jesus as exposing the gap between outward religious care and inward greed, while calling for justice, love and generosity. Calvin explains the giving in verse 41 through practical help for the poor, and Wesley likewise connects it with a change contrary to greed and wickedness. (Calvin on Luke 11:39–41; Wesley on Luke 11:39–44)
passages.god_plan_html:
Micah had already placed justice, mercy and humble life with God at the center of what He requires. Jesus’ warnings continue this Scriptural insistence that religious activity cannot replace the life God calls His people to live. (Micah 6:6–8)

Jeremiah describes God’s promised covenant in terms of His law written on people’s hearts, knowing Him and receiving forgiveness. Paul later describes people in Christ as a new creation, reconciled to God through Him. These passages provide the larger setting for inward change: God’s purpose reaches the person, rather than merely the appearance presented to others. (Jeremiah 31:31–34; 2 Corinthians 5:17–21)

passages.title: Luke 11:45-54
passages.section_title: How can teachers stand in the way of the truth they teach?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 45 One of the experts in the law told Him, “Teacher, when You say these things, You insult us as well.” 46 “Woe to you as well, experts in the law!” He replied. “For you weigh men down with heavy burdens, but you yourselves will not lift a finger to lighten their load. 47 Woe to you! For you build tombs for the prophets, but it was your fathers who killed them. 48 So you are witnesses consenting to the deeds of your fathers: They killed the prophets, and you build their tombs. 49 Because of this, the wisdom of God said, ‘I will send them prophets and apostles; some of them they will kill and others they will persecute.’ 50 As a result, this generation will be charged with the blood of all the prophets that has been shed since the foundation of the world, 51 from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, who was killed between the altar and the sanctuary. Yes, I tell you, all of it will be charged to this generation. 52 Woe to you experts in the law! For you have taken away the key to knowledge. You yourselves have not entered, and you have hindered those who were entering.” 53 As Jesus went on from there, the scribes and Pharisees began to oppose Him bitterly and to ply Him with questions about many things, 54 waiting to catch Him in something He might say.
paragraphs: 45 One of the experts in the law told Him, “Teacher, when You say these things, You insult us as well.” 46 “Woe to you as well, experts in the law!” He replied. “For you weigh men down with heavy burdens, but you yourselves will not lift a finger to lighten their load. 47 Woe to you! For you build tombs for the prophets, but it was your fathers who killed them. 48 So you are witnesses consenting to the deeds of your fathers: They killed the prophets, and you build their tombs.

49 Because of this, the wisdom of God said, ‘I will send them prophets and apostles; some of them they will kill and others they will persecute.’ 50 As a result, this generation will be charged with the blood of all the prophets that has been shed since the foundation of the world, 51 from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, who was killed between the altar and the sanctuary. Yes, I tell you, all of it will be charged to this generation. 52 Woe to you experts in the law! For you have taken away the key to knowledge. You yourselves have not entered, and you have hindered those who were entering.”
53 As Jesus went on from there, the scribes and Pharisees began to oppose Him bitterly and to ply Him with questions about many things, 54 waiting to catch Him in something He might say.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
An expert in the law objects that Jesus’ words insult his group too. Jesus responds with three further warnings directed to these experts.

First, they place heavy burdens on people without helping to carry them. Second, they build tombs for prophets whom their ancestors killed. Jesus exposes a continuing pattern: people may honor the memory of God’s messengers while resisting those He sends in their own time.

He speaks of prophets and apostles being sent, killed and persecuted, and of this generation’s accountability for the blood of the prophets, from Abel to Zechariah. The warning joins the present response to a long history of resistance to God’s word.

The final charge concerns the key to knowledge. The experts have failed to enter and have hindered others who were entering. The chapter closes with scribes and Pharisees questioning Jesus bitterly and trying to catch Him in something He says. Their response continues the resistance He has just described.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see a warning about teachers who burden others, resist God’s messengers and obstruct understanding. Wesley connects the key to knowledge with knowing the Messiah, while the Catholic bishops’ notes connect the sending of prophets and apostles with the continuing mission and its opposition. (Wesley on Luke 11:46–52; USCCB notes on Luke 11:45–52)
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus explicitly joins the sending of prophets and apostles in this warning. Hebrews describes God speaking through the prophets and then through His Son. The present encounter therefore belongs within the larger question of how people receive God’s message as it reaches them through Christ. (Luke 11:49–52; Hebrews 1:1–3)

Acts gives a later example in Stephen’s testimony. He recalls the persecution of the prophets and confronts his hearers’ resistance to the Holy Spirit; they then kill him. Even while being stoned, he prays to Jesus and asks that the sin not be held against them. The witness continues amid the very opposition Jesus describes. (Acts 7:51–60)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 12:1-3
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus warn His disciples about hypocrisy?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 In the meantime, a crowd of many thousands had gathered, so that they were trampling one another. Jesus began to speak first to His disciples: “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy. 2 There is nothing concealed that will not be disclosed, and nothing hidden that will not be made known. 3 What you have spoken in the dark will be heard in the daylight, and what you have whispered in the inner rooms will be proclaimed from the housetops.
paragraphs: 1 In the meantime, a crowd of many thousands had gathered, so that they were trampling one another. Jesus began to speak first to His disciples: “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy. 2 There is nothing concealed that will not be disclosed, and nothing hidden that will not be made known. 3 What you have spoken in the dark will be heard in the daylight, and what you have whispered in the inner rooms will be proclaimed from the housetops.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The chapter begins with a crowd so large that people are trampling one another. Jesus speaks first to His disciples, immediately after the confrontation with religious leaders at the end of chapter 11.

He warns them about the leaven of the Pharisees and identifies what He means: hypocrisy. In this setting, the concern is the gap between the religious appearance someone presents and the reality concealed beneath it.

The warning reaches the disciples themselves. Jesus says that what is hidden will be disclosed and what is whispered privately will become publicly known. They cannot build their life with Him on the assumption that appearances will hide the truth forever.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand the passage as a call to honesty before God and courage in public witness. Wesley connects the following sayings with resisting the pressure to conceal what Jesus has commissioned the disciples to make known, while the Catholic bishops’ notes place them within fearless acknowledgment of His mission. (Wesley on Luke 12:1–4; USCCB note on Luke 12:2–9)
passages.god_plan_html:
Galatians later gives a concrete example of hypocrisy spreading through a community. Peter withdraws from eating with Gentile believers out of fear of another group, and even Barnabas is carried along. Paul confronts the behavior because it does not match the truth of the gospel. The warning Jesus gives can therefore speak to His own followers, rather than leaving them to inspect only someone else’s failures. (Galatians 2:11–14)

Paul also describes the Lord’s coming as the time when hidden things and the motives of hearts will be exposed. Faithful service is lived before that final judgment, not merely the judgment of an audience in the present. (1 Corinthians 4:1–5)

passages.title: Luke 12:4-7
passages.section_title: How can fearing God help His friends face human threats?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 4 I tell you, My friends, do not be afraid of those who kill the body and after that can do no more. 5 But I will show you whom you should fear: Fear the One who, after you have been killed, has authority to throw you into hell. Yes, I tell you, fear Him! 6 Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies? Yet not one of them is forgotten by God. 7 And even the very hairs of your head are all numbered. So do not be afraid; you are worth more than many sparrows.
paragraphs: 4 I tell you, My friends, do not be afraid of those who kill the body and after that can do no more. 5 But I will show you whom you should fear: Fear the One who, after you have been killed, has authority to throw you into hell. Yes, I tell you, fear Him!

6 Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies? Yet not one of them is forgotten by God. 7 And even the very hairs of your head are all numbered. So do not be afraid; you are worth more than many sparrows.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus addresses His hearers as friends and tells them not to be ruled by fear of people who can kill the body. He directs their fear toward the One whose authority reaches beyond death and into final judgment.

Then He turns to sparrows sold for a small price. God forgets none of them, and even the hairs on the disciples’ heads are numbered. The warning about God’s authority stands beside the assurance of His detailed care.

The passage does not deny the possibility of human violence; Jesus names it directly. He gives His friends a reason to remain faithful under its threat: people do not have the final word, and God does not lose sight of them.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly hold together reverence for God’s authority and trust in His care. Wesley explicitly joins fear with trust in his notes on these verses, and the Catholic bishops’ notes understand the sayings as encouragement for followers facing persecution. (Wesley on Luke 12:4–7; USCCB note on Luke 12:2–9)
passages.god_plan_html: Romans gives the wider ground for this confidence: God has given His Son, raised Him, and Christ intercedes for His people. Paul names persecution, danger and death, yet declares that none can separate them from God’s love in Christ. The care Jesus describes reaches beyond being spared every immediate harm to belonging to God through whatever comes. (Romans 8:31–39)

passages.title: Luke 12:8-12
passages.section_title: What does Jesus promise those who must speak for Him under pressure?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 I tell you, everyone who confesses Me before men, the Son of Man will also confess him before the angels of God. 9 But whoever denies Me before men will be denied before the angels of God. 10 And everyone who speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven. 11 When you are brought before synagogues, rulers, and authorities, do not worry about how to defend yourselves or what to say. 12 For at that time the Holy Spirit will teach you what you should say.”
paragraphs: 8 I tell you, everyone who confesses Me before men, the Son of Man will also confess him before the angels of God. 9 But whoever denies Me before men will be denied before the angels of God. 10 And everyone who speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven.

11 When you are brought before synagogues, rulers, and authorities, do not worry about how to defend yourselves or what to say. 12 For at that time the Holy Spirit will teach you what you should say.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus connects acknowledging Him before people with being acknowledged by the Son of Man before God’s angels. He also warns about denial. The public response to Him has a significance beyond the immediate audience.

He then distinguishes a word spoken against the Son of Man, which can be forgiven, from blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, which will not be forgiven. The warning treats the response to God’s work with the utmost seriousness.

The teaching ends with help for the disciples who are brought before synagogues, rulers and authorities. They are not to be consumed by anxiety about how to defend themselves or what to say: the Holy Spirit will teach them at that time.

These words concern pressured witness before authorities. The promise gives confidence in God’s help in that setting rather than declaring that learning, preparation or careful teaching is unnecessary.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly see both a call to acknowledge Christ and a promise of the Spirit’s help under persecution. The Catholic bishops’ notes connect that help with the Spirit’s guidance of the mission in Acts. (USCCB notes on Luke 12:2–12)

Teachers explain the warning about the Spirit in different ways. Wesley distinguishes a denial from which a person can repent from blasphemy against the Spirit, which he regards as a condition from which the person will not return to repentance. The Catholic Church teaches that deliberately refusing the mercy and salvation offered by the Spirit can harden a person into dying without repentance. These explanations focus on a grave rejection of God, rather than making His willingness to forgive the problem. (Wesley on Luke 12:10; Catechism §1864)
passages.god_plan_html:
Acts shows Peter brought before rulers and speaking while filled with the Holy Spirit. He bears witness to Jesus’ death and resurrection and names Him as the source of salvation. This is a concrete continuation of the mission and help Jesus describes. (Acts 4:5–13)

Second Timothy joins faithful endurance with the risen Christ and repeats the seriousness of denying Him. Even imprisonment does not chain God’s word. The disciples’ witness under pressure belongs within a mission whose reach is greater than the limits imposed on its messengers. (2 Timothy 2:8–13)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 12:13-21
passages.section_title: Why can a person with full barns still be a fool?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 Someone in the crowd said to Him, “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.” 14 But Jesus replied, “Man, who appointed Me judge or executor between you?” 15 And He said to them, “Watch out! Guard yourselves against every form of greed, for one’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions.” 16 Then He told them a parable: “The ground of a certain rich man produced an abundance. 17 So he thought to himself, ‘What shall I do, since I have nowhere to store my crops?’ 18 Then he said, ‘This is what I will do: I will tear down my barns and will build bigger ones, and there I will store up all my grain and my goods. 19 Then I will say to myself, “You have plenty of good things laid up for many years. Take it easy. Eat, drink, and be merry!”’ 20 But God said to him, ‘You fool! This very night your life will be required of you. Then who will own what you have accumulated?’ 21 This is how it will be for anyone who stores up treasure for himself but is not rich toward God.”
paragraphs: 13 Someone in the crowd said to Him, “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.” 14 But Jesus replied, “Man, who appointed Me judge or executor between you?” 15 And He said to them, “Watch out! Guard yourselves against every form of greed, for one’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions.”

16 Then He told them a parable: “The ground of a certain rich man produced an abundance. 17 So he thought to himself, ‘What shall I do, since I have nowhere to store my crops?’ 18 Then he said, ‘This is what I will do: I will tear down my barns and will build bigger ones, and there I will store up all my grain and my goods. 19 Then I will say to myself, “You have plenty of good things laid up for many years. Take it easy. Eat, drink, and be merry!”’

20 But God said to him, ‘You fool! This very night your life will be required of you. Then who will own what you have accumulated?’ 21 This is how it will be for anyone who stores up treasure for himself but is not rich toward God.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
A man in the crowd asks Jesus to tell his brother to divide an inheritance. Jesus declines to act as their judge or executor and turns to a warning about greed: a person’s life is more than the amount he possesses.

The Greek word for greed is πλεονεξία, pleonexia (pleh-oh-nek-SEE-ah). Thayer describes a greedy desire to have more. The warning concerns the desire that governs a person, rather than simply the size of an estate. (Thayer, Greek 4124)

Jesus tells of a rich man whose land produces abundantly. The man plans larger barns and imagines many years of ease from what he has stored. But God tells him that his life is required that very night. The goods he has accumulated cannot keep him alive or guarantee who will own them afterward.

The story ends by contrasting storing treasure for oneself with being rich toward God. The man has counted his crops and future comforts while leaving the most important part of his future out of account.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand the parable as a warning against treating wealth as lasting security and neglecting God. Wesley explains being rich toward God through faith, love and good works, while the Catholic bishops’ notes contrast self-reliance in possessions with dependence on God. (Wesley on Luke 12:20–21; USCCB notes on Luke 12:13–34)
passages.god_plan_html:
James gives a related warning to people announcing their future business profits as if they controlled tomorrow. Life is brief, and their plans depend on the Lord’s will. This is a parallel to the farmer’s confidence in years he cannot secure. (James 4:13–17)

First Timothy directs wealthy believers toward a different use of what they have: hope in God, generosity and readiness to share, with treasure that reaches beyond the present age. God’s purpose redirects wealth toward good for others and a life whose future rests with Him. (1 Timothy 6:17–19)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 12:22-31
passages.section_title: What does Jesus ask His disciples to seek instead of worrying?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 Then Jesus said to His disciples, “Therefore I tell you, do not worry about your life, what you will eat, or about your body, what you will wear. 23 For life is more than food, and the body more than clothes. 24 Consider the ravens: They do not sow or reap, they have no storehouse or barn; yet God feeds them. How much more valuable you are than the birds! 25 Who of you by worrying can add a single hour to his life? 26 So if you cannot do such a small thing, why do you worry about the rest? 27 Consider how the lilies grow: They do not labor or spin. Yet I tell you, not even Solomon in all his glory was adorned like one of these. 28 If that is how God clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the furnace, how much more will He clothe you, O you of little faith! 29 And do not be concerned about what you will eat or drink. Do not worry about it. 30 For the Gentiles of the world strive after all these things, and your Father knows that you need them. 31 But seek His kingdom, and these things will be added unto you.
paragraphs: 22 Then Jesus said to His disciples, “Therefore I tell you, do not worry about your life, what you will eat, or about your body, what you will wear. 23 For life is more than food, and the body more than clothes. 24 Consider the ravens: They do not sow or reap, they have no storehouse or barn; yet God feeds them. How much more valuable you are than the birds! 25 Who of you by worrying can add a single hour to his life? 26 So if you cannot do such a small thing, why do you worry about the rest?

27 Consider how the lilies grow: They do not labor or spin. Yet I tell you, not even Solomon in all his glory was adorned like one of these. 28 If that is how God clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the furnace, how much more will He clothe you, O you of little faith! 29 And do not be concerned about what you will eat or drink. Do not worry about it. 30 For the Gentiles of the world strive after all these things, and your Father knows that you need them. 31 But seek His kingdom, and these things will be added unto you.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus turns to the disciples and applies the warning about possessions to worry over daily life. Food and clothing matter, but life and the body are greater than the things that sustain and cover them.

He points to ravens fed by God without barns and to flowers clothed more beautifully than Solomon without making their own garments. The comparisons direct attention toward God’s care and the disciples’ value to Him.

Worry cannot add even an hour to a person’s life. Jesus asks why they should let it govern the rest of their needs. Their Father already knows what they need; He calls them to seek His kingdom, with provision entrusted to Him.

The teaching moves from the farmer’s stored-up security to the disciple’s daily trust. The question is what will command their attention and direct their lives.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see a call to trust the Father and give His kingdom priority over anxious pursuit of provision. Calvin distinguishes this from abandoning every ordinary responsibility, while Wesley points to the greater inheritance the Father gives His people. (Calvin on Luke 12:22–32; Wesley on Luke 12:22–32)
passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews joins freedom from the love of money and contentment with God’s promise not to abandon His people. The larger ground for trust is His presence and faithfulness. (Hebrews 13:5–6)

Philippians gives a practical picture of that care. Paul has learned contentment in both hunger and plenty, while the Philippians share in his need through their gifts. He acknowledges their generosity and God’s provision together. Trust in the Father can take shape through His people caring for one another, rather than requiring that every faithful person escape all hardship. (Philippians 4:10–19)
passages.current_position_html: Prayer and Faith develops the parallel teaching in Matthew 6:25–34 as a reordering of what a person seeks: God’s kingdom rather than provision as life’s controlling pursuit. The study emphasizes trust in the Father’s knowledge and care, with surrender governing prayer and the direction of life. This is its developed application of the parallel, rather than a new rule here about every occupation or financial decision.

passages.title: Luke 12:32-34
passages.section_title: How does the Father’s gift change the way His people use possessions?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 32 Do not be afraid, little flock, for your Father is pleased to give you the kingdom. 33 Sell your possessions and give to the poor. Provide yourselves with purses that will not wear out, an inexhaustible treasure in heaven, where no thief approaches and no moth destroys. 34 For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.
paragraphs: 32 Do not be afraid, little flock, for your Father is pleased to give you the kingdom. 33 Sell your possessions and give to the poor. Provide yourselves with purses that will not wear out, an inexhaustible treasure in heaven, where no thief approaches and no moth destroys. 34 For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus reassures the disciples as a little flock: their Father is pleased to give them the kingdom. His generosity stands before the instruction about their own giving.

They are to sell possessions and give to the poor, turning toward treasure in heaven that cannot be exhausted, stolen or destroyed. The contrast reaches beyond deciding how best to preserve earthly goods.

Jesus connects treasure with the heart. What they value and where they place it are part of the same question. The Father’s promised gift invites them to release possessions for the good of others instead of treating them as their final security.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly emphasize generosity and freedom from being controlled by wealth. The Catholic Church teaches that Christ’s followers must place Him above riches and keep their attachment to possessions from obstructing love. Wesley likewise stresses the greater inheritance of the kingdom, while reading the particular sale instruction as addressed to these disciples rather than a universal rule that every Christian must sell everything. (Catechism §§2544–2547; Wesley on Luke 12:32–33)
passages.god_plan_html:
Acts shows believers selling possessions and sharing with those in need as part of their common life of teaching, meals and prayer. The generosity Jesus calls for becomes visible in the community gathered around His message. (Acts 2:42–47)

Paul grounds another collection for needy believers in Christ’s own grace: though rich, He became poor for their sake. Giving is then described according to what people have, with one community’s surplus helping another’s need. This places generosity within God’s work of forming a people who receive grace and share with one another. (2 Corinthians 8:9–15)

passages.title: Luke 12:35-40
passages.section_title: What does it mean to be ready for the Master’s return?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 35 Be dressed for service and keep your lamps burning. 36 Then you will be like servants waiting for their master to return from the wedding banquet, so that when he comes and knocks, they can open the door for him at once. 37 Blessed are those servants whom the master finds on watch when he returns. Truly I tell you, he will dress himself to serve and will have them recline at the table, and he himself will come and wait on them. 38 Even if he comes in the second or third watch of the night and finds them alert, those servants will be blessed. 39 But understand this: If the homeowner had known at what hour the thief was coming, he would not have let his house be broken into. 40 You also must be ready, because the Son of Man will come at an hour you do not expect.”
paragraphs: 35 Be dressed for service and keep your lamps burning. 36 Then you will be like servants waiting for their master to return from the wedding banquet, so that when he comes and knocks, they can open the door for him at once. 37 Blessed are those servants whom the master finds on watch when he returns. Truly I tell you, he will dress himself to serve and will have them recline at the table, and he himself will come and wait on them. 38 Even if he comes in the second or third watch of the night and finds them alert, those servants will be blessed.

39 But understand this: If the homeowner had known at what hour the thief was coming, he would not have let his house be broken into. 40 You also must be ready, because the Son of Man will come at an hour you do not expect.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus moves from treasure and the heart to readiness. The disciples are to be dressed for service with lamps burning, like servants waiting for their master to return from a wedding banquet.

The watchful servants are ready to open when he knocks, even late in the night. Jesus describes a remarkable welcome in return: the master himself prepares to serve and waits on them at the table.

The picture then changes to a homeowner who does not know when a thief will arrive. The shared point is the need for readiness when the time is unknown. Jesus states the application directly: the Son of Man will come at an hour they do not expect.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand these pictures as a call to remain faithful while awaiting Christ, with a gracious welcome for those He finds ready. Wesley emphasizes the love expressed when the master serves, and the Catholic bishops’ notes connect readiness with faithfulness to Jesus’ instructions while awaiting His return. (Wesley on Luke 12:35–38; USCCB note on Luke 12:35–48)
passages.god_plan_html:
At the final meal in Luke, Jesus describes Himself as the One who serves and promises His disciples a place at His table in His kingdom. The master serving here can be read alongside that combination of present service and future welcome. (Luke 22:24–30)

John gives a further parallel when Jesus wraps a towel around Himself and washes His disciples’ feet. The Lord takes the servant’s place and calls them to follow His example. These connections locate readiness within a relationship shaped by His own generous service, rather than a timetable the disciples can calculate. (John 13:3–5, 12–17)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 12:41-48
passages.section_title: What responsibility comes with being entrusted to care for others?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 41 “Lord,” said Peter, “are You addressing this parable to us, or to everyone else as well?” 42 And the Lord answered, “Who then is the faithful and wise manager, whom the master puts in charge of his servants to give them their portion at the proper time? 43 Blessed is that servant whose master finds him doing so when he returns. 44 Truly I tell you, he will put him in charge of all his possessions. 45 But suppose that servant says in his heart, ‘My master will be a long time in coming,’ and he begins to beat the menservants and maidservants, and to eat and drink and get drunk. 46 The master of that servant will come on a day he does not expect and at an hour he does not anticipate. Then he will cut him to pieces and assign him a place with the unbelievers. 47 That servant who knows his master’s will but does not get ready or follow his instructions will be beaten with many blows. 48 But the one who unknowingly does things worthy of punishment will be beaten with few blows. From everyone who has been given much, much will be required; and from him who has been entrusted with much, even more will be demanded.
paragraphs: 41 “Lord,” said Peter, “are You addressing this parable to us, or to everyone else as well?” 42 And the Lord answered, “Who then is the faithful and wise manager, whom the master puts in charge of his servants to give them their portion at the proper time? 43 Blessed is that servant whose master finds him doing so when he returns. 44 Truly I tell you, he will put him in charge of all his possessions.

45 But suppose that servant says in his heart, ‘My master will be a long time in coming,’ and he begins to beat the menservants and maidservants, and to eat and drink and get drunk. 46 The master of that servant will come on a day he does not expect and at an hour he does not anticipate. Then he will cut him to pieces and assign him a place with the unbelievers.

47 That servant who knows his master’s will but does not get ready or follow his instructions will be beaten with many blows. 48 But the one who unknowingly does things worthy of punishment will be beaten with few blows. From everyone who has been given much, much will be required; and from him who has been entrusted with much, even more will be demanded.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Peter asks whether the preceding parable is addressed to the disciples or to everyone. Jesus answers with a manager entrusted to give the household its food at the proper time. Faithfulness means continuing that care until the master returns.

The opposite response is to assume the master is delayed, abuse the other servants and indulge in eating, drinking and drunkenness. The master’s unexpected arrival exposes that behavior and brings judgment.

Jesus then distinguishes a servant who knew the master’s will from one who acted wrongly without knowing. Greater knowledge brings greater accountability. The closing principle extends the responsibility: much is required from those who have received much.

The question is therefore larger than whether a person has a title or privileged place in the household. What has been entrusted to someone must shape how that person treats others and responds to the master.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly see a warning about faithful care, abusive leadership and accountability in proportion to what has been received. Wesley especially applies the manager picture to those who minister God’s word, and the Catholic bishops’ notes emphasize faithfulness during the wait for Jesus’ return. (Wesley on Luke 12:41–48; USCCB note on Luke 12:35–48)

There is a real difference over whether saving faith can finally be lost. Wesley reads the servant’s fate as a warning that someone once faithful can fall and perish. The Catholic Church likewise teaches that faith is a gift that can be lost and must be nourished. In contrast, the Reformed Westminster Confession teaches that people truly accepted in Christ will persevere to the end, even though they can fall into serious sin. The Catechism and Confession state those broader teachings rather than explaining each detail of this parable. (Wesley on Luke 12:43–46; Catechism §162; Westminster Confession 17)
passages.god_plan_html:
First Peter calls elders to shepherd God’s people willingly, without greed or domination, and points ahead to the Chief Shepherd’s appearing. The responsibility and future reckoning Jesus describes find a close parallel in that instruction to the church’s leaders. (1 Peter 5:1–4)

James similarly warns that teachers will be judged more strictly. Greater opportunity to shape others is not a reason to feel beyond correction; it brings responsibility for how that opportunity is used. God’s purpose for His people includes care that reflects the Lord they await. (James 3:1–2)

passages.title: Luke 12:49-53
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus speak of fire, suffering and divided households?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 49 I have come to ignite a fire on the earth, and how I wish it were already kindled! 50 But I have a baptism to undergo, and how distressed I am until it is accomplished! 51 Do you think that I have come to bring peace to the earth? No, I tell you, but division. 52 From now on, five in one household will be divided, three against two and two against three. 53 They will be divided, father against son and son against father, mother against daughter and daughter against mother, mother-in-law against daughter-in-law and daughter-in-law against mother-in-law.”
paragraphs: 49 I have come to ignite a fire on the earth, and how I wish it were already kindled! 50 But I have a baptism to undergo, and how distressed I am until it is accomplished!

51 Do you think that I have come to bring peace to the earth? No, I tell you, but division. 52 From now on, five in one household will be divided, three against two and two against three. 53 They will be divided, father against son and son against father, mother against daughter and daughter against mother, mother-in-law against daughter-in-law and daughter-in-law against mother-in-law.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus speaks of bringing fire to the earth and of a baptism He has yet to undergo. His distress continues until that baptism is accomplished. The words look ahead to a costly part of His mission rather than describing His earlier baptism in the Jordan.

He then challenges the expectation that His arrival will bring immediate peace among everyone. His coming brings division, reaching even into the closest family relationships.

The household picture makes the cost personal. People bound together by family can find themselves divided over Him. The passage describes that conflict as a consequence of His mission; it does not instruct disciples to mistreat their relatives.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly connect the coming baptism with Jesus’ suffering and death, while recognizing that response to Him can divide households. The Catholic bishops’ notes make both connections. (USCCB notes on Luke 12:49–53)

Teachers explain the fire image with different emphases. Wesley describes the spread of heavenly love; Calvin describes the gospel’s power to unsettle and change the world; the Catholic bishops’ notes speak of the kingdom’s refining and purifying work. These are explanations offered in the sources, rather than a single meaning unanimously assigned to every detail. (Wesley on Luke 12:49; Calvin on Luke 12:49; USCCB note on Luke 12:49–53)
passages.god_plan_html:
The divided-family language recalls Micah’s description of broken trust within households. Micah turns from that distress toward waiting for the God who saves. The parallel places the cost of faithfulness within the wider Scriptural experience of looking to God when close relationships become painful. (Micah 7:5–7)

The New Testament also explains the peace Jesus brings: peace with God through faith, and reconciliation of divided people through His cross. Those gifts do not mean that every person will welcome Him or that all households will immediately agree. His suffering makes reconciliation possible even while response to Him exposes division. (Romans 5:1–2; Ephesians 2:13–18)

passages.title: Luke 12:54-59
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus tell the crowd to recognize the time and make peace now?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 54 Then Jesus said to the crowds, “As soon as you see a cloud rising in the west, you say, ‘A shower is coming,’ and that is what happens. 55 And when the south wind blows, you say, ‘It will be hot,’ and it is. 56 You hypocrites! You know how to interpret the appearance of the earth and sky. Why don’t you know how to interpret the present time? 57 And why don’t you judge for yourselves what is right? 58 Make every effort to reconcile with your adversary while you are on your way to the magistrate. Otherwise, he may drag you off to the judge, and the judge may hand you over to the officer, and the officer may throw you into prison. 59 I tell you, you will not get out until you have paid the very last penny.”
paragraphs: 54 Then Jesus said to the crowds, “As soon as you see a cloud rising in the west, you say, ‘A shower is coming,’ and that is what happens. 55 And when the south wind blows, you say, ‘It will be hot,’ and it is. 56 You hypocrites! You know how to interpret the appearance of the earth and sky. Why don’t you know how to interpret the present time?

57 And why don’t you judge for yourselves what is right? 58 Make every effort to reconcile with your adversary while you are on your way to the magistrate. Otherwise, he may drag you off to the judge, and the judge may hand you over to the officer, and the officer may throw you into prison. 59 I tell you, you will not get out until you have paid the very last penny.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus turns to the crowds. They can recognize a coming shower from a cloud in the west and heat from a south wind, yet they fail to interpret the time in which they are living.

The contrast follows His teaching about His own mission, the coming reckoning and the response He requires. He challenges people who can draw conclusions from ordinary observations to consider what is happening before them.

Then He asks why they do not judge what is right and gives a picture of urgency: make peace with an adversary while on the way to the magistrate. Once judgment and imprisonment follow, the debt must be paid to the last penny.

The scene gives weight to the present opportunity to act. Recognizing the situation should lead to a response before the opportunity is gone.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand this conclusion as an urgent call to recognize Jesus’ mission and respond before judgment. Wesley connects discerning the time with the Messiah’s coming and reads the journey toward the judge as a warning that there is no time to waste. (Wesley on Luke 12:54–59; Luke 12:54–59)
passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews repeatedly brings the response to God into the present: while it is called today, His people are to encourage one another and guard against hardened unbelief. Hearing His voice calls for an answer rather than indefinite postponement. This is a shared theme with Jesus’ warning to the crowd. (Hebrews 3:12–15)

Paul likewise urges his hearers not to receive God’s grace in vain and identifies the present as the day of salvation. God’s saving invitation makes the time for response significant; the opportunity is a gift to receive now. (2 Corinthians 6:1–2)

deeper_study.title: Should We Seek Signs From God?

passages.title: Luke 13:1-5
passages.section_title: Does tragedy prove that its victims were worse sinners?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 At that time some of those present told Jesus about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mixed with their sacrifices. 2 To this He replied, “Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered this way? 3 No, I tell you. But unless you repent, you too will all perish. 4 Or those eighteen who were killed when the tower of Siloam collapsed on them: Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem? 5 No, I tell you. But unless you repent, you too will all perish.”
paragraphs: 1 At that time some of those present told Jesus about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mixed with their sacrifices. 2 To this He replied, “Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered this way? 3 No, I tell you. But unless you repent, you too will all perish.

4 Or those eighteen who were killed when the tower of Siloam collapsed on them: Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem? 5 No, I tell you. But unless you repent, you too will all perish.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Some people report to Jesus that Pilate has mixed the blood of Galileans with their sacrifices. Jesus responds by asking whether the way they suffered proves they were worse sinners than other Galileans. His answer is no.

He brings up another tragedy: eighteen people died when the tower of Siloam fell. Again, He rejects the conclusion that those who died were more sinful than everyone else in Jerusalem.

Both examples lead to the same warning for the hearers: they too must repent or perish. Jesus moves attention from ranking the victims to the response each listener needs to make before God.

The passage gives these events as reported here without supplying a fuller account of the killings or the tower’s collapse. Its emphasis is on what the hearers should and should not conclude from them.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand Jesus as rejecting the assumption that exceptional suffering proves exceptional guilt. The Catholic bishops’ notes explain the tragedies as reminders of everyone’s need to repent, rather than a reason to single out the victims as worse sinners. (USCCB note on Luke 13:1–5; Luke 13:1–5)
passages.god_plan_html:
John records a related encounter in which the disciples connect a man’s blindness with his sin or his parents’ sin. Jesus redirects them toward the work of God that will be displayed in him, then heals him. This is a parallel correction of an attempt to read a person’s standing before God directly from his suffering. (John 9:1–7)

Romans warns people who judge others not to imagine themselves beyond judgment. God’s kindness and patience are meant to lead them to repentance. The call Jesus gives here fits that wider purpose: the opportunity to turn to God is something to receive, rather than use to feel superior to someone else. (Romans 2:1–5)

passages.title: Luke 13:6-9
passages.section_title: What is the extra time for the fig tree meant to accomplish?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 Then Jesus told this parable: “A man had a fig tree that was planted in his vineyard. He went to look for fruit on it but did not find any. 7 So he said to the keeper of the vineyard, ‘Look, for the past three years I have come to search for fruit on this fig tree and haven’t found any. Therefore cut it down! Why should it use up the soil?’ 8 ‘Sir,’ the man replied, ‘leave it alone again this year, until I dig around it and fertilize it. 9 If it bears fruit next year, fine. But if not, you can cut it down.’”
paragraphs: 6 Then Jesus told this parable: “A man had a fig tree that was planted in his vineyard. He went to look for fruit on it but did not find any. 7 So he said to the keeper of the vineyard, ‘Look, for the past three years I have come to search for fruit on this fig tree and haven’t found any. Therefore cut it down! Why should it use up the soil?’ 8 ‘Sir,’ the man replied, ‘leave it alone again this year, until I dig around it and fertilize it. 9 If it bears fruit next year, fine. But if not, you can cut it down.’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus follows the call to repentance with a story about a fig tree planted in a vineyard. Its owner has looked for fruit for three years without finding any and tells the keeper to cut it down.

The keeper asks for another year in which to dig around the tree and fertilize it. More care and more time offer an opportunity for fruit, but the possibility of cutting it down remains if it continues to bear none.

The story holds patience and accountability together. In its setting, the extra time is an opportunity to respond to the call Jesus has just given. The passage ends without telling us what the tree eventually produces.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand the parable as a picture of God’s patience and the seriousness of responding to it. Calvin emphasizes that delayed judgment does not mean God approves of continued refusal, and the Catholic bishops’ notes connect the expected fruit with evidence of repentance. (Calvin on Luke 13:6–9; USCCB note on Luke 13:6–9)
passages.god_plan_html:
Isaiah gives an earlier vineyard picture in which God has carefully tended His people but finds the opposite of the justice and righteousness He seeks. The vineyard is explicitly identified there with Israel and Judah. This is a Scriptural parallel to care that rightly looks for a response. (Isaiah 5:1–7)

Second Peter likewise explains patience as an opportunity for repentance while insisting that the day of the Lord will come. Colossians describes the positive purpose of life with God as bearing fruit in good works and growing in knowing Him. God’s patience makes room for that response; it is not an invitation to postpone it forever. (2 Peter 3:8–10; Colossians 1:9–14)

passages.title: Luke 13:10-17
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus call the Sabbath a fitting day to set this woman free?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 One Sabbath Jesus was teaching in one of the synagogues, 11 and a woman there had been disabled by a spirit for eighteen years. She was hunched over and could not stand up straight. 12 When Jesus saw her, He called her over and said, “Woman, you are set free from your disability.” 13 Then He placed His hands on her, and immediately she straightened up and began to glorify God. 14 But the synagogue leader was indignant that Jesus had healed on the Sabbath. “There are six days for work,” he told the crowd. “So come and be healed on those days and not on the Sabbath.” 15 “You hypocrites!” the Lord replied. “Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or donkey from the stall and lead it to water? 16 Then should not this daughter of Abraham, whom Satan has kept bound for eighteen long years, be released from her bondage on the Sabbath day?” 17 When Jesus said this, all His adversaries were humiliated. And the whole crowd rejoiced at all the glorious things He was doing.
paragraphs: 10 One Sabbath Jesus was teaching in one of the synagogues, 11 and a woman there had been disabled by a spirit for eighteen years. She was hunched over and could not stand up straight. 12 When Jesus saw her, He called her over and said, “Woman, you are set free from your disability.” 13 Then He placed His hands on her, and immediately she straightened up and began to glorify God.

14 But the synagogue leader was indignant that Jesus had healed on the Sabbath. “There are six days for work,” he told the crowd. “So come and be healed on those days and not on the Sabbath.” 15 “You hypocrites!” the Lord replied. “Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or donkey from the stall and lead it to water? 16 Then should not this daughter of Abraham, whom Satan has kept bound for eighteen long years, be released from her bondage on the Sabbath day?” 17 When Jesus said this, all His adversaries were humiliated. And the whole crowd rejoiced at all the glorious things He was doing.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
While teaching in a synagogue on the Sabbath, Jesus sees a woman who has been disabled by a spirit for eighteen years. She is bent over and cannot stand straight. He calls her forward, announces her release and places His hands on her. She immediately straightens and glorifies God.

The synagogue leader objects to healing on the Sabbath and tells the crowd to come on the other six days. Jesus answers by pointing to an ordinary act they allow: untying an ox or donkey to lead it to water.

His comparison moves from care for an animal to the release of this daughter of Abraham. Satan has bound her for eighteen years; the Sabbath is an appropriate day for her freedom. His adversaries are humiliated, while the crowd rejoices.

The Greek verb λύω, lyō (LOO-oh), links the comparison: it can mean to untie what is fastened or release someone who is bound. Thayer specifically lists both the animal’s untying in verse 15 and the woman’s release in verse 16. The word helps show the connection Jesus makes between their accepted care and the healing they object to. (Thayer, Greek 3089)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand Jesus as exposing a double standard and defending the woman’s release as fitting the Sabbath. The Catholic bishops’ notes emphasize the movement from untying animals to freeing her, while Wesley stresses her greater worth as a person and a daughter of Abraham. (USCCB notes on Luke 13:15–16; Wesley on Luke 13:16)
passages.god_plan_html:
Isaiah joins the loosening of oppressive bonds and care for people in need with honoring the Sabbath. That combination offers a wider Scriptural parallel to the freedom and mercy Jesus defends here. The Sabbath is not set against the good of the person God sees. (Isaiah 58:6–14)

Colossians describes God rescuing people from the dominion of darkness and bringing them into His Son’s kingdom. Jesus explicitly describes this woman’s condition as Satan’s bondage and His healing as release. Her restoration is a concrete instance of the deliverance His mission brings, without making every illness the result of a particular person’s sin. (Luke 13:16; Colossians 1:13–14)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 13:18-21
passages.section_title: How can such small beginnings lead to a kingdom?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 Then Jesus asked, “What is the kingdom of God like? To what can I compare it? 19 It is like a mustard seed that a man tossed into his garden. It grew and became a tree, and the birds of the air nested in its branches.” 20 Again He asked, “To what can I compare the kingdom of God? 21 It is like leaven that a woman took and mixed into three measures of flour, until all of it was leavened.”
paragraphs: 18 Then Jesus asked, “What is the kingdom of God like? To what can I compare it? 19 It is like a mustard seed that a man tossed into his garden. It grew and became a tree, and the birds of the air nested in its branches.”
20 Again He asked, “To what can I compare the kingdom of God? 21 It is like leaven that a woman took and mixed into three measures of flour, until all of it was leavened.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the woman’s healing and the crowd’s rejoicing, Jesus asks what God’s kingdom is like. He gives two everyday pictures of a beginning whose outcome is much larger.

A mustard seed grows into a tree where birds nest. A woman mixes leaven into flour until all of it is leavened. Each comparison draws attention from an initially small or hidden presence toward its far-reaching result.

These pictures describe the kingdom Jesus is announcing through His teaching and works. What is before the crowd does not have to look impressive at its beginning to accomplish what God intends.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see the kingdom’s growth from small beginnings in these two comparisons. Calvin emphasizes God’s power beyond the unimpressive first appearance, and the Catholic bishops’ notes connect the beginning with Jesus’ preaching and healing ministry. (Calvin on the mustard seed and leaven; USCCB note on Luke 13:18–21)
passages.god_plan_html:
Ezekiel gives a related picture: God plants a tender shoot that becomes a great cedar, with birds of every kind finding shelter in its branches. He declares His power to make the low tree tall. This is a supported parallel to God bringing a great outcome from what begins small. (Ezekiel 17:22–24)

Acts traces the message outward. Jesus commissions witness from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth, and the book closes with Paul in Rome welcoming people and proclaiming God’s kingdom. The story shows the message reaching far beyond the places where Jesus first taught it. (Acts 1:8; Acts 28:30–31)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 13:22-30
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus turn a question about numbers into a call to enter?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 Then Jesus traveled throughout the towns and villages, teaching as He made His way toward Jerusalem. 23 “Lord,” someone asked Him, “will only a few people be saved?” Jesus answered, 24 “Make every effort to enter through the narrow door. For many, I tell you, will try to enter and will not be able. 25 After the master of the house gets up and shuts the door, you will stand outside knocking and saying, ‘Lord, open the door for us.’ But he will reply, ‘I do not know where you are from.’ 26 Then you will say, ‘We ate and drank with you, and you taught in our streets.’ 27 And he will answer, ‘I tell you, I do not know where you are from. Depart from me, all you evildoers.’ 28 There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth when you see Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and all the prophets in the kingdom of God, but you yourselves are thrown out. 29 People will come from east and west and north and south, and will recline at the table in the kingdom of God. 30 And indeed, some who are last will be first, and some who are first will be last.”
paragraphs: 22 Then Jesus traveled throughout the towns and villages, teaching as He made His way toward Jerusalem. 23 “Lord,” someone asked Him, “will only a few people be saved?” Jesus answered, 24 “Make every effort to enter through the narrow door. For many, I tell you, will try to enter and will not be able.

25 After the master of the house gets up and shuts the door, you will stand outside knocking and saying, ‘Lord, open the door for us.’ But he will reply, ‘I do not know where you are from.’ 26 Then you will say, ‘We ate and drank with you, and you taught in our streets.’ 27 And he will answer, ‘I tell you, I do not know where you are from. Depart from me, all you evildoers.’

28 There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth when you see Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and all the prophets in the kingdom of God, but you yourselves are thrown out. 29 People will come from east and west and north and south, and will recline at the table in the kingdom of God. 30 And indeed, some who are last will be first, and some who are first will be last.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus continues teaching through towns and villages on His way to Jerusalem. Someone asks whether only a few will be saved. He answers by calling His hearers to make every effort to enter through the narrow door.

The picture becomes urgent when the householder closes the door. Those outside appeal to their familiarity with him: they ate and drank with him and heard him teach. But they are not received. Nearness to the activity is not presented as the same thing as a right response to the master.

Jesus describes Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and the prophets in the kingdom, while some who expect to belong find themselves outside. People from every direction come to its table. His final reversal unsettles assumptions about who is first and who is last.

The passage directs the question toward the hearer’s own response and the time available to make it. It does not supply a count of the final number saved.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly hear an urgent call to respond to Jesus rather than rely on familiarity or assumed privilege. Calvin emphasizes turning from curiosity about the number saved to the hearer’s own response; Wesley stresses the need to respond before the door closes through faith, prayer and a life directed toward God. (Calvin on Luke 13:23–24; Wesley on Luke 13:24–25)
passages.god_plan_html:
Isaiah describes the Lord preparing a banquet for all peoples and overcoming death and tears. Jesus’ picture of people gathering from every direction around the kingdom’s table shares that wider hope of God’s saving welcome. This is a connection between the pictures, not a claim that every detail is being explained here. (Isaiah 25:6–9)

In John, Jesus explicitly identifies Himself as the gate through whom people enter and are saved. That gives a wider New Testament connection with the call to enter here: the welcome and life God offers are found through Him. (John 10:7–10)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 13:31-35
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus continue toward the city He longs to gather?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 31 At that very hour, some Pharisees came to Jesus and told Him, “Leave this place and get away, because Herod wants to kill You.” 32 But Jesus replied, “Go tell that fox, ‘Look, I will keep driving out demons and healing people today and tomorrow, and on the third day I will reach My goal.’ 33 Nevertheless, I must keep going today and tomorrow and the next day, for it is not admissible for a prophet to perish outside of Jerusalem. 34 O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those sent to her, how often I have longed to gather your children together as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you were unwilling! 35 Look, your house is left to you desolate. And I tell you that you will not see Me again until you say, ‘Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord.’”
paragraphs: 31 At that very hour, some Pharisees came to Jesus and told Him, “Leave this place and get away, because Herod wants to kill You.” 32 But Jesus replied, “Go tell that fox, ‘Look, I will keep driving out demons and healing people today and tomorrow, and on the third day I will reach My goal.’ 33 Nevertheless, I must keep going today and tomorrow and the next day, for it is not admissible for a prophet to perish outside of Jerusalem.

34 O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those sent to her, how often I have longed to gather your children together as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you were unwilling! 35 Look, your house is left to you desolate. And I tell you that you will not see Me again until you say, ‘Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord.’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Some Pharisees warn Jesus to leave because Herod wants to kill Him. Jesus answers with a message for Herod: His work of driving out demons and healing will continue toward its goal.

He describes His necessary journey toward Jerusalem in the language of the city’s resistance to prophets. The threat does not redirect His mission.

Then the words turn to lament. Jesus longs to gather Jerusalem’s children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but they are unwilling. The image of shelter stands beside the warning that their house is left desolate.

He ends with words from Psalm 118: they will not see Him again until they speak the blessing over the One who comes in the Lord’s name. The saying places their response to Him alongside both His departure and the recognition He names. (Psalm 118:25–29)
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly recognize Jesus’ determination to complete His mission, His grief over rejection and His desire to gather the city’s children. The Catholic bishops’ notes emphasize that Herod’s threat cannot overturn His work or the journey to Jerusalem. (USCCB notes on Luke 13:32–33; Luke 13:31–35)

The final saying is explained in different ways. Wesley reads it as people brought by calamity to long for the Messiah, without taking it as a promise that they will then see Jesus. Calvin, discussing the parallel in Matthew, emphasizes that those who reject Him as Redeemer will encounter Him as Judge, and does not treat until as a guarantee of their later welcome. These are the individual teachers’ readings. (Wesley on Luke 13:35; Calvin on Matthew 23:39)

The Catholic Church teaches more broadly that Christ’s glorious coming is connected with Israel’s recognition of Him and the full inclusion of the Jews in His salvation. Catechism §674 develops that future hope from the wider New Testament, rather than explaining every detail of Luke’s sentence. These accounts should not be reduced to one unanimous timetable. (Catechism §674)
passages.god_plan_html:
The sheltering wings recall the Psalm’s picture of refuge under God’s protection. Jesus’ lament brings that desire for gathering and safety into the encounter with a resistant city. This is a Scriptural parallel, while the hen and chicks are the image Jesus Himself uses. (Psalm 91:1–4)

Romans warns against concluding that God has simply rejected His people. Paul speaks of a remnant by grace, partial hardening, God’s enduring call and His purpose of mercy. Those statements keep the wider picture of God’s faithfulness in view alongside Jerusalem’s real refusal and the warning Jesus gives. (Romans 11:1–6, 25–32)
