passages.title: Luke 14:1-6
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus ask about rescue on the Sabbath?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 One Sabbath, Jesus went to eat in the home of a leading Pharisee, and those in attendance were watching Him closely. 2 Right there before Him was a man with dropsy. 3 So Jesus asked the experts in the law and the Pharisees, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath or not?” 4 But they remained silent. Then Jesus took hold of the man, healed him, and sent him on his way. 5 And He asked them, “Which of you whose son or ox falls into a pit on the Sabbath day will not immediately pull him out?” 6 And they were unable to answer these questions.
paragraphs: 1 One Sabbath, Jesus went to eat in the home of a leading Pharisee, and those in attendance were watching Him closely. 2 Right there before Him was a man with dropsy. 3 So Jesus asked the experts in the law and the Pharisees, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath or not?” 4 But they remained silent. Then Jesus took hold of the man, healed him, and sent him on his way.
5 And He asked them, “Which of you whose son or ox falls into a pit on the Sabbath day will not immediately pull him out?” 6 And they were unable to answer these questions.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
One Sabbath, Jesus goes to eat at the home of a leading Pharisee, where the guests watch Him closely. A man with dropsy is there before Him. Dropsy is another name for edema, swelling caused by fluid in the body’s tissues. Luke does not name the underlying cause in this man’s case. (MedlinePlus: edema)

Jesus asks the experts in the law and the Pharisees whether healing on the Sabbath is lawful. They remain silent. He takes hold of the man, heals him and sends him on his way.

Then He asks whether they would immediately rescue a son or an ox that had fallen into a pit on the Sabbath. They cannot answer. The question places His act of healing alongside the urgent rescue they would recognize in their own lives.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand Jesus as defending mercy and rescue as fitting the Sabbath. The Catholic bishops’ notes connect this scene with the preceding healing of the woman, where care for an animal exposes the inconsistency of objecting to a person’s release. (USCCB notes on Luke 14:1–6 and Luke 13:15–16; Luke 13:10–17)
passages.god_plan_html:
Colossians describes the Sabbath and other observances as a shadow whose reality belongs to Christ. Read alongside Jesus’ healing, that connection places the day within God’s purpose that comes into view through Him. (Colossians 2:16–17)

Hebrews speaks of the rest that remains for God’s people and calls them to enter it faithfully. The rescue in this meal scene can be read within that larger theme of the good God intends for His people, rather than setting His command against His mercy. (Hebrews 4:9–11)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 14:7-11
passages.section_title: Why should a guest leave the place of honor to the host?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 When Jesus noticed how the guests chose the places of honor, He told them a parable: 8 “When you are invited to a wedding banquet, do not sit in the place of honor, in case someone more distinguished than you has been invited. 9 Then the host who invited both of you will come and tell you, ‘Give this man your seat.’ And in humiliation, you will have to take the last place. 10 But when you are invited, go and sit in the last place, so that your host will come and tell you, ‘Friend, move up to a better place.’ Then you will be honored in front of everyone at the table with you. 11 For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and the one who humbles himself will be exalted.”
paragraphs: 7 When Jesus noticed how the guests chose the places of honor, He told them a parable: 8 “When you are invited to a wedding banquet, do not sit in the place of honor, in case someone more distinguished than you has been invited. 9 Then the host who invited both of you will come and tell you, ‘Give this man your seat.’ And in humiliation, you will have to take the last place. 10 But when you are invited, go and sit in the last place, so that your host will come and tell you, ‘Friend, move up to a better place.’ Then you will be honored in front of everyone at the table with you. 11 For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and the one who humbles himself will be exalted.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus notices guests choosing the places of honor and tells them a parable about being invited to a wedding banquet. Taking the highest place risks the humiliation of being moved when a more distinguished guest arrives.

Instead, the guest is to take the last place and let the host invite him higher. The honor comes from the host’s welcome rather than the guest’s claim about himself.

Jesus states the principle beyond the seating arrangement: those who exalt themselves will be humbled, and those who humble themselves will be exalted. His words reach the desire for status that the guests’ choices reveal.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand this as instruction in humility that reaches beyond table manners. Wesley applies the principle across life, and Calvin emphasizes the inward posture before God rather than an outward performance of modesty. (Wesley on Luke 14:7–11; Calvin on Luke 14:7–11)
passages.god_plan_html:
Proverbs offers a close parallel: do not put yourself among the great, because being invited higher is better than being publicly moved down. Jesus’ banquet picture continues that Scriptural wisdom about receiving honor rather than claiming it. (Proverbs 25:6–7)

Philippians places humility under Christ’s own example. He takes the servant’s place and becomes obedient to death, and God exalts Him. First Peter likewise calls believers to humble themselves under God’s hand and trust Him for the time of lifting them up. Humility belongs within following the Lord who first walked that path. (Philippians 2:3–11; 1 Peter 5:5–6)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 14:12-14
passages.section_title: Who should receive a welcome when they cannot repay it?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 Then Jesus said to the man who had invited Him, “When you host a dinner or a banquet, do not invite your friends or brothers or relatives or rich neighbors. Otherwise, they may invite you in return, and you will be repaid. 13 But when you host a banquet, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind, 14 and you will be blessed. Since they cannot repay you, you will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous.”
paragraphs: 12 Then Jesus said to the man who had invited Him, “When you host a dinner or a banquet, do not invite your friends or brothers or relatives or rich neighbors. Otherwise, they may invite you in return, and you will be repaid. 13 But when you host a banquet, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind, 14 and you will be blessed. Since they cannot repay you, you will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus then speaks to the host. An invitation can remain within a circle of friends, relatives and wealthy neighbors who can return the favor. He calls the man to welcome people who cannot offer that kind of repayment.

The poor and people with disabilities are to be invited to the banquet. Their inability to repay does not diminish the worth of welcoming them; it is central to the generosity Jesus describes.

The promised repayment is at the resurrection of the righteous. The host is directed toward God’s future rather than the social return another invitation might bring.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see a call to generosity beyond the expectation of return. Wesley understands it as a higher duty toward those in need rather than a ban on every meal with friends, and Calvin emphasizes giving that looks to God instead of personal advantage or popularity. (Wesley on Luke 14:12; Calvin on Luke 14:14)
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul asks the Corinthians to consider how God has called many whom the world would not regard as wise, powerful or important. Their life in Christ leaves them boasting in the Lord rather than their standing. That wider pattern helps explain a community whose welcome is not determined by what a guest can offer in return. (1 Corinthians 1:26–31)

James warns against giving the rich a place of honor while humiliating the poor, connecting that behavior with the command to love one’s neighbor. Acts gives a positive picture: as the apostles testify to Jesus’ resurrection, believers share so that others’ needs are met. God’s work forms a people whose care and welcome reflect the grace they have received. (James 2:1–9; Acts 4:32–35)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 14:15-24
passages.section_title: What happens when invited guests keep making excuses?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 When one of those reclining with Him heard this, he said to Jesus, “Blessed is everyone who will eat at the feast in the kingdom of God.” 16 But Jesus replied, “A certain man prepared a great banquet and invited many guests. 17 When it was time for the banquet, he sent his servant to tell those who had been invited, ‘Come, for everything is now ready.’ 18 But one after another they all began to make excuses. The first one said, ‘I have bought a field, and I need to go see it. Please excuse me.’ 19 Another said, ‘I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I am going to try them out. Please excuse me.’ 20 Still another said, ‘I have married a wife, so I cannot come.’ 21 The servant returned and reported all this to his master. Then the owner of the house became angry and said to his servant, ‘Go out quickly into the streets and alleys of the city, and bring in the poor, the crippled, the blind, and the lame.’ 22 ‘Sir,’ the servant replied, ‘what you ordered has been done, and there is still room.’ 23 So the master told his servant, ‘Go out to the highways and hedges and compel them to come in, so that my house will be full. 24 For I tell you, not one of those men who were invited will taste my banquet.’”
paragraphs: 15 When one of those reclining with Him heard this, he said to Jesus, “Blessed is everyone who will eat at the feast in the kingdom of God.” 16 But Jesus replied, “A certain man prepared a great banquet and invited many guests. 17 When it was time for the banquet, he sent his servant to tell those who had been invited, ‘Come, for everything is now ready.’ 18 But one after another they all began to make excuses. The first one said, ‘I have bought a field, and I need to go see it. Please excuse me.’ 19 Another said, ‘I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I am going to try them out. Please excuse me.’ 20 Still another said, ‘I have married a wife, so I cannot come.’

21 The servant returned and reported all this to his master. Then the owner of the house became angry and said to his servant, ‘Go out quickly into the streets and alleys of the city, and bring in the poor, the crippled, the blind, and the lame.’ 22 ‘Sir,’ the servant replied, ‘what you ordered has been done, and there is still room.’ 23 So the master told his servant, ‘Go out to the highways and hedges and compel them to come in, so that my house will be full. 24 For I tell you, not one of those men who were invited will taste my banquet.’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
A guest responds to Jesus’ words about resurrection by praising the blessing of eating in God’s kingdom. Jesus answers with a story about a great banquet whose invited guests refuse to come when everything is ready.

Their excuses concern a field, oxen and a marriage. Each turns from the prepared meal toward another concern. The host then sends his servant into the city to bring in the poor and people with disabilities.

There is still room, so the invitation goes farther, to the highways and hedges. The host wants his house filled, yet warns that those who refused will not taste his banquet.

The story follows Jesus’ instruction to welcome people who cannot repay an invitation. It now places that generous welcome beside the seriousness of refusing the host’s call.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly recognize both the warning against refusing God’s invitation and His welcome reaching beyond those who assume their place is secure. The Catholic bishops’ notes read the city’s new guests as Israel’s needy hearers and the further invitation as reaching Gentiles. Wesley emphasizes how ordinary, lawful activities can become excuses for refusing. (USCCB note on Luke 14:15–24; Wesley on Luke 14:18)

The command to compel people has received differing applications. Wesley understands it as an urgent appeal through love and God’s word. Calvin emphasizes earnest appeals too, but also approved civil laws compelling religious worship. That is his historical position, not a statement that every Reformed church teaches it. (Wesley on Luke 14:23; Calvin on Luke 14:23)

The Westminster Confession as published by the Orthodox Presbyterian Church says civil rulers must not interfere in matters of faith and must protect people from religious violence. The Catholic Church’s Declaration on Religious Freedom likewise rejects forcing people to act against their religious beliefs. These official statements distinguish those churches’ teaching from Calvin’s historical application. (Westminster Confession 23.3; Declaration on Religious Freedom §2)
passages.god_plan_html:
Isaiah pictures the Lord preparing a banquet for all peoples and bringing death and tears to an end. That promise supplies a wider Scriptural setting for the kingdom feast the guest praises and Jesus’ parable describes. (Isaiah 25:6–9)

Ephesians describes people once far away being brought near through Christ and made members of God’s household. Romans likewise connects salvation reaching Gentiles with mercy that still holds hope for Israel. The widening invitation can be read alongside this gathering through Christ, without turning the story into a claim that God has abandoned His people. (Ephesians 2:11–22; Romans 11:11–15)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 14:25-33
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus tell the crowd to count the cost of following Him?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 25 Now large crowds were traveling with Jesus, and He turned and said to them, 26 “If anyone comes to Me and does not hate his father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters—yes, even his own life—he cannot be My disciple. 27 And whoever does not carry his cross and follow Me cannot be My disciple. 28 Which of you, wishing to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost to see if he has the resources to complete it? 29 Otherwise, if he lays the foundation and is unable to finish the work, everyone who sees it will ridicule him, 30 saying, ‘This man could not finish what he started to build.’ 31 Or what king on his way to war with another king will not first sit down and consider whether he can engage with ten thousand men the one coming against him with twenty thousand? 32 And if he is unable, he will send a delegation while the other king is still far off, to ask for terms of peace. 33 In the same way, any one of you who does not give up everything he has cannot be My disciple.
paragraphs: 25 Now large crowds were traveling with Jesus, and He turned and said to them, 26 “If anyone comes to Me and does not hate his father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters—yes, even his own life—he cannot be My disciple. 27 And whoever does not carry his cross and follow Me cannot be My disciple.

28 Which of you, wishing to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost to see if he has the resources to complete it? 29 Otherwise, if he lays the foundation and is unable to finish the work, everyone who sees it will ridicule him, 30 saying, ‘This man could not finish what he started to build.’

31 Or what king on his way to war with another king will not first sit down and consider whether he can engage with ten thousand men the one coming against him with twenty thousand? 32 And if he is unable, he will send a delegation while the other king is still far off, to ask for terms of peace. 33 In the same way, any one of you who does not give up everything he has cannot be My disciple.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Large crowds are traveling with Jesus when He turns and speaks about the demands of following Him. His words reach family relationships, one’s own life, carrying the cross and giving up possessions.

Two pictures call for honest consideration. A builder must know whether he can finish a tower before laying its foundation. A king must consider whether his army can face a greater force and seek terms if it cannot.

Jesus ends by applying the point to the hearers: someone who does not give up everything he has cannot be His disciple. The demand is not left at admiring His teaching from within a crowd. It reaches the claims and attachments that could stand above Him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly understand the passage as a call to put Christ above every competing attachment. Wesley reads the family language by comparison with loyalty to Christ, and the Catholic bishops’ notes likewise understand family and possessions as unable to displace the commitment He requires. (Wesley on Luke 14:26–33; USCCB notes on Luke 14:25–33)

Luke uses the strong Greek verb μισέω, miseō (mih-SEH-oh), meaning to hate. Matthew gives the parallel demand in terms of loving family more than Jesus. The readings above understand Luke’s language through that comparison while retaining the real cost of putting Him first. (Thayer, Greek 3404; Matthew 10:37–39)
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul describes counting former gains as loss for the sake of knowing Christ, sharing His sufferings and pressing toward the hope of resurrection. His own account gives a concrete example of a life whose values have been reordered around the Lord. (Philippians 3:7–14)

Hebrews calls believers to lay aside what entangles them and run with endurance while looking to Jesus. He endured the cross for the joy before Him. The cost of following belongs within His own path through suffering toward glory, rather than being an isolated test of determination. (Hebrews 12:1–3)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 14:34-35
passages.section_title: What is the warning in salt that no longer serves its purpose?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 34 Salt is good, but if the salt loses its savor, with what will it be seasoned? 35 It is fit neither for the soil nor for the manure pile, and it is thrown out. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”
paragraphs: 34 Salt is good, but if the salt loses its savor, with what will it be seasoned? 35 It is fit neither for the soil nor for the manure pile, and it is thrown out. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus closes the teaching about discipleship with the picture of salt. Salt is good, but salt that has lost its savor is no longer useful, even for the soil or the manure pile. It is thrown out.

The image follows the call to count the cost and give Him priority. It presses the question of what a follower’s life is actually doing, rather than whether someone merely travels with the crowd.

Jesus ends by calling those with ears to hear. The warning asks for attention and a response to the teaching that has just been given.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand the salt as a picture of discipleship that must retain its purpose. The Catholic bishops’ notes connect it with the wholehearted commitment of the preceding sayings, while Wesley applies it to Christians and especially those who minister. (USCCB note on Luke 14:34–35; Wesley on Luke 14:34)
passages.god_plan_html:
Matthew records Jesus calling His disciples the salt of the earth and the light of the world, with good deeds that lead others to glorify the Father. That parallel gives the wider direction of a useful life: witness that makes God known. (Matthew 5:13–16)

Colossians uses salt in another picture of that outward-facing life: wise conduct toward outsiders and gracious speech suited to each person. The images are related, without requiring that salt always carry one fixed meaning in every passage. (Colossians 4:5–6)

passages.title: Luke 15:1-7
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus describe finding a lost sheep as a reason to celebrate?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now all the tax collectors and sinners were gathering around to listen to Jesus. 2 So the Pharisees and scribes began to grumble: “This man welcomes sinners and eats with them.” 3 Then Jesus told them this parable: 4 “What man among you, if he has a hundred sheep and loses one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the pasture and go after the one that is lost, until he finds it? 5 And when he finds it, he joyfully puts it on his shoulders, 6 comes home, and calls together his friends and neighbors to tell them, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found my lost sheep!’ 7 I tell you that in the same way there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous ones who do not need to repent.
paragraphs: 1 Now all the tax collectors and sinners were gathering around to listen to Jesus. 2 So the Pharisees and scribes began to grumble: “This man welcomes sinners and eats with them.” 3 Then Jesus told them this parable:

4 “What man among you, if he has a hundred sheep and loses one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the pasture and go after the one that is lost, until he finds it? 5 And when he finds it, he joyfully puts it on his shoulders, 6 comes home, and calls together his friends and neighbors to tell them, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found my lost sheep!’ 7 I tell you that in the same way there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous ones who do not need to repent.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Tax collectors and sinners gather to listen to Jesus. The Pharisees and scribes grumble that He welcomes sinners and eats with them. That complaint supplies the setting for all three stories in this chapter.

Jesus asks them to imagine losing one sheep from a flock of a hundred. The shepherd goes after the lost one, carries it home on his shoulders and calls others to share his joy.

He applies the picture to heaven’s joy over a sinner who repents. The answer to the complaint is an invitation to see the welcome from God’s side: recovering the lost calls for celebration.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly recognize God’s concern for the lost and His joy over repentance. The Catholic bishops’ notes place this story alongside the coin and the two sons as Jesus’ response to resistance against that welcome. (USCCB note on Luke 15:1–32)

Calvin and Wesley explain the contrast with the ninety-nine through the special joy of a dramatic return from a lost way of life. Calvin explicitly adds that believers still need repentance throughout life. That explanation does not require the ninety-nine to be people who have never sinned. (Calvin on Luke 15:7; Wesley on Luke 15:7)
passages.god_plan_html:
Ezekiel describes God Himself seeking His scattered flock, finding the lost, bringing back strays and caring for the injured. The shepherd’s search belongs within that larger Scriptural picture of God acting to restore His people. (Ezekiel 34:11–16)

In John, Jesus identifies Himself as the good shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep and gathers them into one flock. The wider purpose is more than retrieving something misplaced: God’s saving care comes through Christ’s own self-giving and the people He gathers around Himself. (John 10:11–16)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 15:8-10
passages.section_title: Why does finding one coin become shared joy?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 Or what woman who has ten silver coins and loses one of them does not light a lamp, sweep her house, and search carefully until she finds it? 9 And when she finds it, she calls together her friends and neighbors to say, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found my lost coin.’ 10 In the same way, I tell you, there is joy in the presence of God’s angels over one sinner who repents.”
paragraphs: 8 Or what woman who has ten silver coins and loses one of them does not light a lamp, sweep her house, and search carefully until she finds it? 9 And when she finds it, she calls together her friends and neighbors to say, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found my lost coin.’ 10 In the same way, I tell you, there is joy in the presence of God’s angels over one sinner who repents.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus follows the sheep with another lost-and-found picture. A woman with ten silver coins loses one, lights a lamp, sweeps the house and searches carefully until she finds it.

The recovered coin leads her to call friends and neighbors to rejoice with her. Jesus again connects finding what was lost with joy over a sinner who repents, this time naming the joy in the presence of God’s angels.

The setting remains the complaint that He receives sinners. The second story reinforces the first: a person’s recovery is worthy of care, effort and shared gladness.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see the coin reinforcing God’s care for those who are lost and His joy when a sinner returns. Wesley explicitly treats the sheep, coin and son as three pictures of how God receives sinners, and the Catholic bishops’ notes recognize the same shared theme. (Wesley on Luke 15:3; USCCB note on Luke 15:1–32)
passages.god_plan_html:
Zephaniah describes the Lord present among His people as the One who saves and rejoices over them. That is a related Scriptural picture of salvation bringing gladness to God as well as to those He restores. (Zephaniah 3:14–17)

Later in Luke, Jesus explains His mission after entering Zacchaeus’ home: the Son of Man came to seek and save the lost. The search and celebration here fit that stated purpose, expressed through His welcome of the very people others criticize Him for receiving. (Luke 19:9–10)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 15:11-32
passages.section_title: Will both sons share their father’s joy?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 Then Jesus said, “There was a man who had two sons. 12 The younger son said to him, ‘Father, give me my share of the estate.’ So he divided his property between them. 13 After a few days, the younger son got everything together and journeyed to a distant country, where he squandered his wealth in wild living. 14 After he had spent all he had, a severe famine swept through that country, and he began to be in need. 15 So he went and hired himself out to a citizen of that country, who sent him into his fields to feed the pigs. 16 He longed to fill his belly with the pods the pigs were eating, but no one would give him a thing. 17 Finally he came to his senses and said, ‘How many of my father’s hired servants have plenty of food, but here I am, starving to death! 18 I will get up and go back to my father and say to him, “Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. 19 I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me like one of your hired servants.”’ 20 So he got up and went to his father. But while he was still in the distance, his father saw him and was filled with compassion. He ran to his son, embraced him, and kissed him. 21 The son declared, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’ 22 But the father said to his servants, ‘Quick! Bring the best robe and put it on him. Put a ring on his finger and sandals on his feet. 23 Bring the fattened calf and kill it. Let us feast and celebrate. 24 For this son of mine was dead and is alive again! He was lost and is found!’ So they began to celebrate. 25 Meanwhile the older son was in the field, and as he approached the house, he heard music and dancing. 26 So he called one of the servants and asked what was going on. 27 ‘Your brother has returned,’ he said, ‘and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has him back safe and sound.’ 28 The older son became angry and refused to go in. So his father came out and pleaded with him. 29 But he answered his father, ‘Look, all these years I have served you and never disobeyed a commandment of yours. Yet you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends. 30 But when this son of yours returns from squandering your wealth with prostitutes, you kill the fattened calf for him!’ 31 ‘Son, you are always with me,’ the father said, ‘and all that is mine is yours. 32 But it was fitting to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.’”

So his father came out and pleaded with him. 29 But he answered his father, ‘Look, all these years I have served you and never disobeyed a commandment of yours. Yet you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends. 30 But when this son of yours returns from squandering your wealth with prostitutes, you kill the fattened calf for him!’ 31 ‘Son, you are always with me,’ the father said, ‘and all that is mine is yours. 32 But it was fitting to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus’ third story begins with a father and two sons. The younger asks for his share of the estate, and the father divides his property between them. The son leaves for a distant country and wastes what he has received.

When his money is gone, a famine leaves him in need. He takes work feeding pigs and becomes desperately hungry. Remembering that his father’s hired servants have food, he decides to return, confess his sin and ask to be received as a hired servant.

While he is still far away, his father sees him, runs to meet him and embraces him. The son confesses. The father calls for a robe, a ring, sandals and a feast, describing the return as a son dead and now alive, lost and now found.

The older son comes from the field, hears the celebration and learns what has happened. He becomes angry and refuses to enter. The father comes out and pleads with him too.

The older son appeals to his years of service and complains about the generosity shown to his brother. The father assures him of their continuing relationship and what is his, then explains why they must rejoice: this is his brother, restored to them.

The story ends without telling us whether the older son goes inside. Both sons matter in the setting of the chapter. The welcome of the returning son answers the complaint about Jesus receiving sinners, while the older son’s resistance brings the question of shared joy back to those who grumble.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly recognize a picture of repentance, the Father’s merciful welcome and the challenge of receiving a restored brother. The Catholic Catechism makes the merciful father central to its account of conversion and describes the welcome and feast as signs of renewed life in God’s family. (Catechism §1439)

Calvin emphasizes God’s generous readiness to receive the returning sinner and the older brother’s resistance to that mercy. Wesley likewise connects the elder son with the Pharisees and scribes of the opening scene. These readings keep the story’s ending connected to the complaint that prompted it. (Calvin on Luke 15:20, 25–32; Wesley on Luke 15:25–32)
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans places the human story within the contrast between Adam’s disobedience, which brings sin and death, and Christ’s obedience, which brings righteousness and life. The son’s movement from estrangement to restoration can be read alongside that larger movement of God’s saving purpose. This is a parallel between the stories, rather than an identification of the younger son as Adam. (Romans 5:12–19)

Paul also explains that God reconciles people to Himself through Christ and entrusts them with a message of reconciliation. In Romans, that love is shown while people are still sinners, through the death and life of the Son. The father’s welcome belongs with this wider account of mercy that restores a broken relationship. (2 Corinthians 5:17–21; Romans 5:6–11)

Ephesians uses the language of being dead and made alive to describe God’s mercy in Christ. It identifies salvation as His gift and the new life as a life directed toward good works. That is a related New Testament picture of the life and welcome God gives, rather than a reward someone can demand by comparing himself with a brother. (Ephesians 2:1–10)

passages.title: Luke 16:1-9
passages.section_title: What can a dishonest manager teach about using a passing opportunity?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Jesus also said to His disciples, “There was a rich man whose manager was accused of wasting his possessions. 2 So he called him in to ask, ‘What is this I hear about you? Turn in an account of your management, for you cannot be manager any longer.’ 3 The manager said to himself, ‘What shall I do, now that my master is taking away my position? I am too weak to dig and too ashamed to beg. 4 I know what I will do so that after my removal from management, people will welcome me into their homes.’ 5 And he called in each one of his master’s debtors. ‘How much do you owe my master?’ he asked the first. 6 ‘A hundred measures of olive oil,’ he answered. ‘Take your bill,’ said the manager, ‘sit down quickly, and write fifty.’ 7 Then he asked another, ‘And how much do you owe?’ ‘A hundred measures of wheat,’ he replied. ‘Take your bill and write eighty,’ he told him. 8 The master commended the dishonest manager because he had acted shrewdly. For the sons of this age are more shrewd in dealing with their own kind than are the sons of light. 9 I tell you, use worldly wealth to make friends for yourselves so that when it is gone, they will welcome you into eternal dwellings.
paragraphs: 1 Jesus also said to His disciples, “There was a rich man whose manager was accused of wasting his possessions. 2 So he called him in to ask, ‘What is this I hear about you? Turn in an account of your management, for you cannot be manager any longer.’ 3 The manager said to himself, ‘What shall I do, now that my master is taking away my position? I am too weak to dig and too ashamed to beg. 4 I know what I will do so that after my removal from management, people will welcome me into their homes.’

5 And he called in each one of his master’s debtors. ‘How much do you owe my master?’ he asked the first. 6 ‘A hundred measures of olive oil,’ he answered. ‘Take your bill,’ said the manager, ‘sit down quickly, and write fifty.’ 7 Then he asked another, ‘And how much do you owe?’ ‘A hundred measures of wheat,’ he replied. ‘Take your bill and write eighty,’ he told him.

8 The master commended the dishonest manager because he had acted shrewdly. For the sons of this age are more shrewd in dealing with their own kind than are the sons of light. 9 I tell you, use worldly wealth to make friends for yourselves so that when it is gone, they will welcome you into eternal dwellings.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus tells His disciples about a rich man’s manager who is accused of wasting the property under his care. The owner demands an account and announces that the manager can no longer keep his position.

Facing that loss, the manager considers his future. He is too weak to dig and ashamed to beg, so he reduces the bills of his master’s debtors in the hope that they will welcome him afterward.

The master commends him for acting shrewdly, while the story still calls him dishonest. Jesus compares the foresight of people concerned with this age with that of the children of light, then directs His disciples to use passing wealth with eternal welcome in view.

The comparison uses the Greek word φρόνιμος, phronimos (FROH-nih-moss). Thayer gives the sense of being prudent or mindful of one’s interests and lists the comparison in verse 8. The manager has recognized that his opportunity is running out and acted with his future in mind. (Thayer, Greek 5429)
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly distinguish the manager’s foresight from his dishonesty and hear a call to use present resources with the future in view. Wesley explicitly makes that distinction in his explanation of the commendation. (Wesley on Luke 16:8–9)

One explanation of the bill reductions appears in the Catholic bishops’ notes: the manager gives up his own commission, leaving the amount actually owed to the master. Luke does not identify the reductions as commissions, so this remains an explanation of the story rather than a detail stated in it. The notes connect the parable’s point with using material goods wisely in light of the coming crisis. (USCCB note on Luke 16:1–8)
passages.god_plan_html:
First Timothy calls wealthy believers to put hope in God, be generous and ready to share, and store up a foundation for the future. This gives a wider New Testament connection with using what cannot last for the sake of what truly does. (1 Timothy 6:17–19)

Paul’s account of a collection for believers in need shows how that use of resources serves God’s purpose. Needs are met, thanksgiving grows and people glorify God for the generosity that expresses the gospel. Money becomes a means of care and shared praise rather than the final object of trust. (2 Corinthians 9:6–15)

passages.title: Luke 16:10-13
passages.section_title: Why does faithfulness with money matter beyond money itself?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 Whoever is faithful with very little will also be faithful with much, and whoever is dishonest with very little will also be dishonest with much. 11 So if you have not been faithful with worldly wealth, who will entrust you with true riches? 12 And if you have not been faithful with the belongings of another, who will give you belongings of your own? 13 No servant can serve two masters. Either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve both God and money.”
paragraphs: 10 Whoever is faithful with very little will also be faithful with much, and whoever is dishonest with very little will also be dishonest with much. 11 So if you have not been faithful with worldly wealth, who will entrust you with true riches? 12 And if you have not been faithful with the belongings of another, who will give you belongings of your own?
13 No servant can serve two masters. Either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve both God and money.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus follows the manager’s story with sayings about faithfulness. The way someone handles a little reveals something about how that person will handle much; the same is true of dishonesty.

He distinguishes worldly wealth from true riches and asks about faithfulness with another’s belongings. What has been entrusted to someone is a responsibility, rather than something whose use has no significance beyond the present.

The final saying brings the issue to loyalty. A servant cannot be devoted to two competing masters. Jesus names the choice plainly: God and money cannot both be the master of a person’s life.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand these sayings as a call to integrity in entrusted responsibilities and undivided service to God. Wesley emphasizes faithfulness as well as wisdom, while the Catholic bishops’ notes connect responsibility with the incompatibility of trusting wealth as a master while serving God. (Wesley on Luke 16:10–13; USCCB notes on Luke 16:10–13)
passages.god_plan_html:
First Peter describes believers as stewards of God’s varied grace, each using a received gift to serve others with the strength God supplies. The purpose is that God be glorified through Jesus Christ. Faithfulness with money fits within that larger life of receiving from God and serving with what He gives. (1 Peter 4:7–11)

Hebrews joins freedom from the love of money and contentment with God’s promise to remain with His people. Loyalty to Him is grounded in His faithfulness, not in money’s ability to make life secure. (Hebrews 13:5–6)

passages.title: Luke 16:14-17
passages.section_title: What changes with the kingdom’s announcement, and what does not fail?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 The Pharisees, who were lovers of money, heard all of this and were scoffing at Jesus. 15 So He said to them, “You are the ones who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts. For what is prized among men is detestable before God. 16 The Law and the Prophets were proclaimed until John. Since that time, the gospel of the kingdom of God is being preached, and everyone is forcing his way into it. 17 But it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for a single stroke of a pen to drop out of the Law.
paragraphs: 14 The Pharisees, who were lovers of money, heard all of this and were scoffing at Jesus. 15 So He said to them, “You are the ones who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts. For what is prized among men is detestable before God.

16 The Law and the Prophets were proclaimed until John. Since that time, the gospel of the kingdom of God is being preached, and everyone is forcing his way into it. 17 But it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for a single stroke of a pen to drop out of the Law.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Pharisees hear Jesus’ teaching about money and scoff. Luke identifies them as lovers of money, and Jesus answers that God knows the hearts beneath the righteousness they present to other people.

He then speaks about the Law and the Prophets being proclaimed until John, followed by the preaching of God’s kingdom and people forcing their way into it. John marks a turning point in the announcement.

The next sentence guards against treating that turning point as the failure of God’s word. Jesus says it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for a single stroke to drop out of the Law. The new proclamation stands beside confidence in what God has already spoken.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly recognize both a turning point with John and the continuing reliability of God’s word. The Catholic bishops’ notes describe the movement from promise toward fulfillment, while Wesley says the gospel does not destroy the Law and understands the entry language as people receiving the message with great earnestness. (USCCB note on Luke 16:16; Wesley on Luke 16:16–17)
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans describes God’s righteousness being revealed through faith in Jesus Christ, while the Law and the Prophets bear witness to it. What God is accomplishing through Christ is therefore presented as the fulfillment toward which His earlier revelation points. (Romans 3:21–26)

After the resurrection, Jesus explains the Scriptures concerning Himself, including His suffering, resurrection and the proclamation of repentance and forgiveness to the nations. Luke’s account moves from the kingdom’s announcement here toward that fuller understanding of what God has promised and brought about. (Luke 24:25–27, 44–47)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 16:18
passages.section_title: What does Jesus’ warning say about faithfulness in marriage?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 Anyone who divorces his wife and marries another woman commits adultery, and he who marries a divorced woman commits adultery.
paragraphs: 18 Anyone who divorces his wife and marries another woman commits adultery, and he who marries a divorced woman commits adultery.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Immediately after affirming the durability of the Law, Jesus speaks of divorce and remarriage as adultery. Luke records the warning both for the man who divorces and marries another and for the man who marries a divorced woman.

This saying contains no exception clause. Christians consider it alongside Jesus’ fuller discussion in Matthew and Paul’s instructions about separation, reconciliation and an unbelieving spouse’s departure. Those passages are central to the differences described below. (Matthew 19:3–9; 1 Corinthians 7:10–16)
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian traditions commonly understand Jesus as defending lasting faithfulness in marriage. They differ over how this warning relates to other passages and the circumstances in which a later marriage can be accepted.

The Catholic Church teaches that a valid, consummated marriage between baptized spouses cannot be dissolved by human power. Its Catechism distinguishes that bond from legitimate separation or a civil divorce needed to protect rights, children or inheritance, and distinguishes an unjustly abandoned spouse from the person responsible for breaking the marriage. (Catechism §§2382–2386)

Reformed churches following the Westminster Confession permit an innocent spouse to divorce and remarry after adultery, and also recognize deliberate desertion that cannot be remedied as grounds for ending the marriage. They read Matthew’s exception and Paul’s teaching alongside this warning. (Westminster Confession 24.5–6)

The Orthodox Church in America upholds lifelong marriage while allowing a bishop to consider remarriage after divorce with repentance and attention to the people involved. The United Methodist Church recognizes that divorce can become necessary when a marriage is destructive or beyond repair and does not rule out remarriage. These are statements of those churches, rather than a claim that every Orthodox or Methodist church or member has the same approach. (OCA guidelines, section F; United Methodist Social Principles, Marriage: Divorce)
passages.god_plan_html: Genesis describes husband and wife becoming one flesh. Ephesians repeats that passage and explicitly connects marriage with Christ and the church, calling husbands to the self-giving love shown by Christ. Faithfulness in marriage belongs within that larger picture of a relationship marked by love, care and commitment. (Genesis 2:21–24; Ephesians 5:25–33)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 16:19-31
passages.section_title: What should the rich man and his brothers have heard already?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 Now there was a rich man dressed in purple and fine linen, who lived each day in joyous splendor. 20 And a beggar named Lazarus lay at his gate, covered with sores 21 and longing to be fed with the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table. Even the dogs came and licked his sores. 22 One day the beggar died and was carried by the angels to Abraham’s side. And the rich man also died and was buried. 23 In Hades, where he was in torment, he looked up and saw Abraham from afar, with Lazarus by his side. 24 So he cried out, ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue. For I am in agony in this fire.’ 25 But Abraham answered, ‘Child, remember that during your lifetime you received your good things, while Lazarus received bad things. But now he is comforted here, while you are in agony. 26 And besides all this, a great chasm has been fixed between us and you, so that even those who wish cannot cross from here to you, nor can anyone cross from there to us.’ 27 ‘Then I beg you, father,’ he said, ‘send Lazarus to my father’s house, 28 for I have five brothers. Let him warn them, so that they will not also end up in this place of torment.’ 29 But Abraham replied, ‘They have Moses and the Prophets; let your brothers listen to them.’ 30 ‘No, father Abraham,’ he said, ‘but if someone is sent to them from the dead, they will repent.’ 31 Then Abraham said to him, ‘If they do not listen to Moses and the Prophets, they will not be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead.’”
paragraphs: 19 Now there was a rich man dressed in purple and fine linen, who lived each day in joyous splendor. 20 And a beggar named Lazarus lay at his gate, covered with sores 21 and longing to be fed with the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table. Even the dogs came and licked his sores.

22 One day the beggar died and was carried by the angels to Abraham’s side. And the rich man also died and was buried. 23 In Hades, where he was in torment, he looked up and saw Abraham from afar, with Lazarus by his side. 24 So he cried out, ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue. For I am in agony in this fire.’ 25 But Abraham answered, ‘Child, remember that during your lifetime you received your good things, while Lazarus received bad things. But now he is comforted here, while you are in agony. 26 And besides all this, a great chasm has been fixed between us and you, so that even those who wish cannot cross from here to you, nor can anyone cross from there to us.’

27 ‘Then I beg you, father,’ he said, ‘send Lazarus to my father’s house, 28 for I have five brothers. Let him warn them, so that they will not also end up in this place of torment.’ 29 But Abraham replied, ‘They have Moses and the Prophets; let your brothers listen to them.’ 30 ‘No, father Abraham,’ he said, ‘but if someone is sent to them from the dead, they will repent.’ 31 Then Abraham said to him, ‘If they do not listen to Moses and the Prophets, they will not be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead.’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus describes a rich man living in daily splendor while Lazarus lies hungry and covered with sores at his gate. Their closeness makes the contrast immediate: abundance is on one side of the gate, need on the other.

Both die, and their conditions are reversed. Lazarus is comforted at Abraham’s side, while the rich man is in torment and asks for relief. Abraham describes the reversal and the fixed chasm that cannot be crossed.

The BSB calls the place of the rich man’s torment Hades. The Greek word is Ἅδης, Hadēs (HAY-deez), which Thayer describes as the realm of the dead. The story presents the rich man’s suffering and Lazarus’ comfort without giving a complete description of every question about life after death. (Thayer, Greek 86)

The rich man then asks that Lazarus be sent to warn his five brothers. Abraham directs them to Moses and the Prophets. When the man insists that someone returning from the dead would bring repentance, Abraham says that those who refuse that existing witness will not be persuaded even by a resurrection.

The ending brings the warning back to people still living. The opportunity before the brothers is to hear God’s word and respond while they can.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly recognize a warning about neglected need, the use of wealth and judgment, together with the call to listen to God’s word. The Catholic bishops’ notes emphasize the reversal of the men’s conditions and the ending’s connection with rejection even after resurrection; Wesley connects the rich man’s fate with making worldly goods his happiness and stresses the power of God’s word to bring repentance. (USCCB notes on Luke 16:19–31; Wesley on Luke 16:25–31)
passages.god_plan_html:
The Law already commands an open hand toward the poor rather than a hardened heart. James later connects living faith with meeting a brother’s or sister’s need for food and clothing. The care missing at the rich man’s gate belongs within a Scriptural call for God’s people to make mercy visible in their common life. (Deuteronomy 15:7–11; James 2:14–17)

John records a resurrection sign that leads many to believe, while some leaders respond by plotting Jesus’ death. That is a concrete parallel to the warning that an extraordinary sign does not guarantee a willing response from every person who receives its witness. (John 11:43–53)

At Luke’s conclusion, the risen Jesus explains what Moses and the Prophets say about Him and commissions the proclamation of repentance and forgiveness. The witness Abraham tells the brothers to hear belongs within the larger revelation fulfilled in Christ and carried to the nations. (Luke 24:25–27, 44–47)

deeper_study.title: Should We Seek Signs From God?

passages.title: Luke 17:1-4
passages.section_title: How should we respond to harm and repentance?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Jesus said to His disciples, “It is inevitable that stumbling blocks will come, but woe to the one through whom they come! 2 It would be better for him to have a millstone hung around his neck and to be thrown into the sea than to cause one of these little ones to stumble. 3 Watch yourselves. If your brother sins, rebuke him; and if he repents, forgive him. 4 Even if he sins against you seven times in a day, and seven times returns to say, ‘I repent,’ you must forgive him.”
paragraphs: 1 Jesus said to His disciples, “It is inevitable that stumbling blocks will come, but woe to the one through whom they come! 2 It would be better for him to have a millstone hung around his neck and to be thrown into the sea than to cause one of these little ones to stumble.

3 Watch yourselves. If your brother sins, rebuke him; and if he repents, forgive him. 4 Even if he sins against you seven times in a day, and seven times returns to say, ‘I repent,’ you must forgive him.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus now speaks to His disciples. He warns that stumbling blocks will come, but that causing another person to stumble carries grave responsibility. The image of a millstone and the sea makes the warning especially forceful: His little ones must not be treated as expendable.

He then tells the disciples to watch themselves, confront a brother’s sin and forgive when he repents. Correction and forgiveness belong together. Jesus does not tell them to pretend that no wrong occurred, and repeated wrongdoing does not give them permission to refuse repeated repentance.

The Greek word behind rebuke is ἐπιτιμάω, epitimaō (eh-pee-tee-MAH-oh), meaning to rebuke or speak a firm correction. The word does not itself mean removing someone from a teaching office; the instruction concerns a brother who sins. (Thayer, Greek 2008)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see these sayings as a call to take the harm of sin seriously, correct a fellow believer and extend forgiveness rather than keep a limit on mercy. Wesley applies the warning to weaker believers and reads the repeated forgiveness as a response to genuine repentance, while also calling for goodwill toward those who have not repented. (Wesley on Luke 17:1–4)
passages.god_plan_html: Ephesians describes a people whose shared life reflects the forgiveness they have received in Christ. Truthful speech, kindness and care for one another replace bitterness and destructive words. That wider picture helps explain why Jesus joins responsibility for others with a readiness to forgive: the people God is bringing together are to make His mercy visible in their relationships. (Ephesians 4:25–32)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 17:5-6
passages.section_title: How can faith as small as a seed meet such a demanding call?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 The apostles said to the Lord, “Increase our faith!” 6 And the Lord answered, “If you have faith the size of a mustard seed, you can say to this mulberry tree, ‘Be uprooted and planted in the sea,’ and it will obey you.
paragraphs: 5 The apostles said to the Lord, “Increase our faith!” 6 And the Lord answered, “If you have faith the size of a mustard seed, you can say to this mulberry tree, ‘Be uprooted and planted in the sea,’ and it will obey you.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the command to forgive repeatedly, the apostles ask the Lord to increase their faith. Jesus answers with a mustard seed and an extraordinary image: a mulberry tree uprooted and planted in the sea.

The contrast is between something very small and something beyond ordinary human ability. In this setting, the apostles’ sense of inadequacy meets Jesus’ call to trust Him. The saying does not describe a technique for measuring faith or give a procedure for transplanting trees.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley reads even a small measure of true faith as sufficient for duties that otherwise seem too hard. Calvin likewise understands the tree-and-mountain imagery as emphasizing God’s power, while cautioning that faith seeks what God promises rather than every wish a person can imagine. These readings emphasize dependence on God, without treating the saying as an unrestricted promise that any desired outcome must occur. (Wesley on Luke 17:5–6; Calvin on Luke 17:5–6 and the Matthew parallel)
passages.god_plan_html: Philippians calls believers to live in obedience because God is at work in both their willing and their doing. That is a supported connection with the apostles’ difficulty here: obedience to God need not rest on confidence in our own strength. The same letter points to His work within His people as they pursue His good purpose. (Philippians 2:12–13)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 17:7-10
passages.section_title: Does doing our duty put God in our debt?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 Which of you whose servant comes in from plowing or shepherding in the field will say to him, ‘Come at once and sit down to eat’? 8 Instead, won’t he tell him, ‘Prepare my meal and dress yourself to serve me while I eat and drink, and afterward you may eat and drink’? 9 Does he thank the servant because he did what he was told? 10 So you also, when you have done everything commanded of you, should say, ‘We are unworthy servants; we have only done our duty.’”
paragraphs: 7 Which of you whose servant comes in from plowing or shepherding in the field will say to him, ‘Come at once and sit down to eat’? 8 Instead, won’t he tell him, ‘Prepare my meal and dress yourself to serve me while I eat and drink, and afterward you may eat and drink’? 9 Does he thank the servant because he did what he was told?
10 So you also, when you have done everything commanded of you, should say, ‘We are unworthy servants; we have only done our duty.’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus continues His answer with a servant who returns from field work and still has a meal to prepare. The master does not treat the servant’s required work as an extraordinary favor that places him under an obligation.

Jesus applies the picture to His disciples: even after doing everything commanded, they have done their duty. Obedience is not a way to make God owe them something.

The BSB’s unworthy servants translates ἀχρεῖος, achreios (ah-KHRAY-oss). Thayer explains its use here as the servant’s humble acknowledgment that he has done only what was required. The emphasis is on having no claim to special credit, rather than a statement that people have no value to God. (Thayer, Greek 888)
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly see a call to humility: obedience cannot turn God’s generosity into a debt. Traditions differ in how they explain the place of good works and reward within that shared emphasis.

Reformed churches following the Westminster Confession explicitly use this saying to teach that even our best works cannot earn forgiveness or eternal life. They also teach that God accepts believers’ sincere works through Christ and graciously rewards them. (Westminster Confession 16.5–6)

The Catholic Church teaches that no one has an independent claim on God or can earn the initial grace of forgiveness. It also teaches that, after God’s gracious initiative, actions done in Christ’s love can have merit: God grants them a real share in His promised reward, including eternal life. The Catechism attributes this to His grace rather than unaided human achievement. (Catechism §§2007–2011)

Wesley similarly stresses that service gives God no benefit He needs, yet says God graciously gives good works value and rewards them according to His promise. (Wesley on Luke 17:9–10)
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians places good works after God’s merciful rescue: people are saved by grace and made alive with Christ, then created in Him for a life of good works. Paul also asks the Corinthians what they possess that they did not receive. Together these passages describe fruitful service as a response to God’s generosity, with no room for boasting over others. (Ephesians 2:1–10; 1 Corinthians 4:6–7)

The servant image does not exhaust what Jesus says about God’s generosity. Earlier in Luke, He pictures a master who himself serves the servants he finds ready. Read together, these sayings preserve both the disciple’s humble duty and the surprising generosity of the Lord. (Luke 12:35–38)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 17:11-19
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus draw attention to the man who returns?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 While Jesus was on His way to Jerusalem, He was passing between Samaria and Galilee. 12 As He entered one of the villages, He was met by ten lepers. They stood at a distance 13 and raised their voices, shouting, “Jesus, Master, have mercy on us!” 14 When Jesus saw them, He said, “Go, show yourselves to the priests.” And as they were on their way, they were cleansed. 15 When one of them saw that he was healed, he came back, praising God in a loud voice. 16 He fell facedown at Jesus’ feet in thanksgiving to Him—and he was a Samaritan. 17 “Were not all ten cleansed?” Jesus asked. “Where then are the other nine? 18 Was no one found except this foreigner to return and give glory to God?” 19 Then Jesus said to him, “Rise and go; your faith has made you well!”
paragraphs: 11 While Jesus was on His way to Jerusalem, He was passing between Samaria and Galilee. 12 As He entered one of the villages, He was met by ten lepers. They stood at a distance 13 and raised their voices, shouting, “Jesus, Master, have mercy on us!” 14 When Jesus saw them, He said, “Go, show yourselves to the priests.” And as they were on their way, they were cleansed.

15 When one of them saw that he was healed, he came back, praising God in a loud voice. 16 He fell facedown at Jesus’ feet in thanksgiving to Him—and he was a Samaritan. 17 “Were not all ten cleansed?” Jesus asked. “Where then are the other nine? 18 Was no one found except this foreigner to return and give glory to God?” 19 Then Jesus said to him, “Rise and go; your faith has made you well!”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
On His way to Jerusalem, Jesus meets ten men with leprosy between Samaria and Galilee. They stand at a distance and ask for mercy. The BSB’s footnote explains that leper refers to someone with a skin disease; the passage does not identify a modern medical diagnosis.

Jesus tells them to show themselves to the priests, and they are cleansed as they go. Leviticus required separation while such a disease made someone unclean and assigned priests the examination and cleansing process. Jesus’ instruction fits that Scriptural setting. (Leviticus 13:45–46; Leviticus 14:1–11)

One man returns, praises God and falls at Jesus’ feet in thanks. Luke then identifies him as a Samaritan. Jesus asks about the other nine and draws attention to this foreigner who has returned to give God glory.

Jesus’ final words link the man’s faith with being made well. The Greek verb is σῴζω, sōzō (SOH-zoh), which can mean save, rescue or heal. Thayer includes this verse among its uses for healing; the BSB footnote also offers has saved you. The word’s range is useful, but does not by itself settle every question about the other men. (Thayer, Greek 4982)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly emphasize thanksgiving, faith and the surprising example set by the Samaritan. The Catholic bishops’ notes understand the final saying as pointing to salvation through faith, beyond the cleansing all ten received. That reading gives weight both to the shared healing and to Jesus’ particular response to the man who returns. (USCCB notes on Luke 17:11–19)
passages.god_plan_html:
Earlier in Luke, Jesus recalls Naaman, the Syrian whom Elisha healed. The grateful Samaritan provides a further example of God’s mercy being received by someone described as an outsider. This is a parallel within Luke’s account, rather than a claim that the two men are identical figures or that every person in Israel rejects Jesus. (Luke 4:24–27)

Psalm 107 calls those God has rescued and gathered from different lands to give Him thanks. The Samaritan’s return fits that larger response to mercy: the person helped by God openly praises Him. As Luke’s story continues into Acts, the witness to Jesus is commissioned to reach Samaria and the ends of the earth. (Psalm 107:1–3; Acts 1:6–8)
