deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

passages.title: Luke 17:20-21
passages.section_title: Is God’s kingdom only something still to arrive?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 20 When asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God would come, Jesus replied, “The kingdom of God will not come with observable signs. 21 Nor will people say, ‘Look, here it is,’ or ‘There it is.’ For you see, the kingdom of God is in your midst.”
paragraphs: 20 When asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God would come, Jesus replied, “The kingdom of God will not come with observable signs. 21 Nor will people say, ‘Look, here it is,’ or ‘There it is.’ For you see, the kingdom of God is in your midst.”

passages.context_html:
The Pharisees ask when God’s kingdom will come. Jesus answers that it will not arrive in a way they can locate by announcing that it is over here or over there. His answer directs their attention to the kingdom already in their midst.

The Greek expression uses ἐντός, entos (en-TOSS), meaning within or inside. Thayer recognizes that the wording can describe an inward reality, but understands this context as in your midst. The BSB uses that wording and gives within you as a footnote alternative. Because Jesus is addressing Pharisees, readers must consider who is being addressed as well as the word’s possible meanings. (Thayer, Greek 1787)

Jesus next turns to the disciples and speaks about the coming day of the Son of Man. Keeping those next verses in view prevents the present kingdom from being used to erase everything He says about what is still ahead. (Luke 17:22–37)
passages.common_interpretations_html: The difference here concerns how the kingdom is present, rather than whether God reigns. The Catholic bishops’ notes prefer among you, pointing to Jesus’ preaching and healing ministry. Wesley allows within or among, then emphasizes the inward reign of God in a true believer. These are identifiable readings in those sources, rather than a rule that every Catholic or Methodist explains the phrase in exactly the same way. (USCCB notes on Luke 17:20–21; Wesley on Luke 17:20–21)
passages.current_position_html: What Is the True Church?, in its section The Kingdom is Within Us, understands this passage as a call to live under Christ’s rule from the heart. The study emphasizes surrender, obedience, mercy and faithfulness as expressions of that reign, rather than measuring the kingdom by a religious organization’s size, influence or outward display.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html: Colossians describes believers as already rescued from darkness and brought into the kingdom of God’s Son. Acts also records the risen Jesus directing His followers away from knowledge of the Father’s timetable and toward Spirit-empowered witness, while promising His return. These passages hold together belonging to Christ now, a task to carry out, and a future still in God’s hands. (Colossians 1:12–14; Acts 1:6–11)

passages.title: Luke 17:22-37
passages.section_title: How should we live while waiting for the Son of Man?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 Then He said to the disciples, “The time is coming when you will long to see one of the days of the Son of Man, but you will not see it. 23 People will tell you, ‘Look, there He is!’ or ‘Look, here He is!’ Do not go out or chase after them. 24 For just as the lightning flashes and lights up the sky from one end to the other, so will be the Son of Man in His day. 25 But first He must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation. 26 Just as it was in the days of Noah, so also will it be in the days of the Son of Man: 27 People were eating and drinking, marrying and being given in marriage, up to the day Noah entered the ark. Then the flood came and destroyed them all. 28 It was the same in the days of Lot: People were eating and drinking, buying and selling, planting and building. 29 But on the day Lot left Sodom, fire and sulfur rained down from heaven and destroyed them all. 30 It will be just like that on the day the Son of Man is revealed. 31 On that day, let no one on the housetop come down to retrieve his possessions. Likewise, let no one in the field return for anything he has left behind. 32 Remember Lot’s wife! 33 Whoever tries to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life will preserve it. 34 I tell you, on that night two people will be in one bed: one will be taken and the other left. 35 Two women will be grinding grain together: one will be taken and the other left.” 37 “Where, Lord?” they asked. Jesus answered, “Wherever there is a carcass, there the vultures will gather.”
paragraphs: 22 Then He said to the disciples, “The time is coming when you will long to see one of the days of the Son of Man, but you will not see it. 23 People will tell you, ‘Look, there He is!’ or ‘Look, here He is!’ Do not go out or chase after them. 24 For just as the lightning flashes and lights up the sky from one end to the other, so will be the Son of Man in His day. 25 But first He must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation.

26 Just as it was in the days of Noah, so also will it be in the days of the Son of Man: 27 People were eating and drinking, marrying and being given in marriage, up to the day Noah entered the ark. Then the flood came and destroyed them all. 28 It was the same in the days of Lot: People were eating and drinking, buying and selling, planting and building. 29 But on the day Lot left Sodom, fire and sulfur rained down from heaven and destroyed them all. 30 It will be just like that on the day the Son of Man is revealed.

31 On that day, let no one on the housetop come down to retrieve his possessions. Likewise, let no one in the field return for anything he has left behind. 32 Remember Lot’s wife! 33 Whoever tries to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life will preserve it.

34 I tell you, on that night two people will be in one bed: one will be taken and the other left. 35 Two women will be grinding grain together: one will be taken and the other left.” 37 “Where, Lord?” they asked. Jesus answered, “Wherever there is a carcass, there the vultures will gather.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus turns from the Pharisees to His disciples. They will long to see one of the days of the Son of Man, but must not chase reports that He is here or there. His day is compared with lightning lighting the sky. First, however, He must suffer and be rejected by this generation.

He then recalls Noah and Lot. People carry on eating, marrying, trading, planting and building until judgment interrupts ordinary life. The warning is that everyday activity can continue right up to the moment that changes everything.

The commands about possessions and the reminder of Lot’s wife reinforce the urgency. Genesis records her looking back after the command to flee without doing so. Jesus joins that reminder with a saying about losing or preserving one’s life. (Genesis 19:16–17, 24–26)

Finally, people sharing a bed or grinding grain are separated: one is taken and the other left. When the disciples ask where, Jesus answers with the image of a carcass and gathering vultures. How these images relate is one of the interpretive questions described below.

The BSB moves from verse 35 to verse 37. Its footnote records the additional field saying found in the later Greek text used by some translations; that wording is not part of the BSB main text reproduced here.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly recognize a call to readiness and a warning that judgment will not wait for ordinary life to stop. The Catholic bishops’ notes emphasize the unexpected day of the Son of Man. Wesley also relates the warning about flight to Jerusalem’s danger as a picture of the final day. (USCCB notes on Luke 17:20–37; Wesley on Luke 17:22–33)

Readers differ over whether the person taken is rescued or taken to judgment. The NET study notes identify both readings: Noah and Lot’s rescue supports the first, while the closing image is read there as a scene of judgment. The notes stress the sudden separation rather than treating the images as a complete timetable. (NET notes on Luke 17:34–37)

Calvin reads the separation as a warning not to let earthly ties delay faithful obedience. He takes the final gathering image as the gathering of God’s people to Christ, which differs from the NET notes’ judgment reading of that image. These are differences between commentators; neither reading should be presented as the official explanation of every member of a church tradition. (Calvin on Luke 17:26–37 and Matthew 24:37–42)
passages.god_plan_html:
Second Peter explicitly returns to Noah and Lot, drawing from their stories both God’s judgment and His ability to rescue the godly. That is a direct New Testament connection for the examples Jesus gives. It supports confidence in God’s care without supplying every step or interval of an end-times schedule. (2 Peter 2:4–9)

Paul likewise describes the Day of the Lord arriving unexpectedly, then calls believers to wakefulness, faith, love, hope and mutual encouragement because salvation is through Jesus Christ. The larger picture gives the waiting community something to practice now, rather than a date to calculate. (1 Thessalonians 5:1–11)

Revelation’s vision of the faithful and true rider presents Christ’s judgment and royal authority openly. It is a supported parallel to the public revealing described here, rather than proof that Luke has supplied the full sequence of Revelation’s visions. (Revelation 19:11–16)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

deeper_study.title: Should We Seek Signs From God?

passages.title: Luke 18:1-8
passages.section_title: Why keep praying when justice seems delayed?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then Jesus told them a parable about their need to pray at all times and not lose heart: 2 “In a certain town there was a judge who neither feared God nor respected men. 3 And there was a widow in that town who kept appealing to him, ‘Give me justice against my adversary.’ 4 For a while he refused, but later he said to himself, ‘Though I neither fear God nor respect men, 5 yet because this widow keeps pestering me, I will give her justice. Otherwise, she will wear me out with her perpetual requests.’” 6 And the Lord said, “Listen to the words of the unjust judge. 7 Will not God bring about justice for His elect who cry out to Him day and night? Will He delay in helping them? 8 I tell you, He will promptly carry out justice on their behalf. Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will He find faith on earth?”
paragraphs: 1 Then Jesus told them a parable about their need to pray at all times and not lose heart: 2 “In a certain town there was a judge who neither feared God nor respected men. 3 And there was a widow in that town who kept appealing to him, ‘Give me justice against my adversary.’ 4 For a while he refused, but later he said to himself, ‘Though I neither fear God nor respect men, 5 yet because this widow keeps pestering me, I will give her justice. Otherwise, she will wear me out with her perpetual requests.’”

6 And the Lord said, “Listen to the words of the unjust judge. 7 Will not God bring about justice for His elect who cry out to Him day and night? Will He delay in helping them? 8 I tell you, He will promptly carry out justice on their behalf. Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will He find faith on earth?”

passages.context_html:
Luke tells us why Jesus gives this parable: His followers need to keep praying and not lose heart. It follows the teaching about the day of the Son of Man, and its closing question returns to His coming.

A widow repeatedly asks a judge for justice against an adversary. The judge neither fears God nor respects people. He eventually acts because he wants to be free of her repeated requests.

The Greek verb behind the widow’s appeal is ἐκδικέω, ekdikeō (ek-dee-KEH-oh), meaning here to do someone justice or defend them against another person. Her request concerns justice, rather than a list of things she would like to have. Luke does not give the details of her legal dispute. (Thayer, Greek 1556)

Jesus draws attention to what this unjust judge says, then asks about God’s justice for His people who cry to Him day and night. The story moves from the judge’s reluctant action to confidence in God’s response. The final question asks whether faith will be found when the Son of Man comes.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand this as encouragement to persist in prayer and trust God through waiting and suffering. The Catholic bishops’ notes connect persistent prayer with remaining faithful; Wesley emphasizes God’s justice even while wrongs and suffering continue for a time. (USCCB notes on Luke 18:1–8; Wesley on Luke 18:1, 7–8)
passages.current_position_html: Prayer and Faith directly addresses this parable in its section Luke 18:1–8 — The Persistent Widow. The study understands it as a call to keep trusting God and seeking His justice through prolonged suffering. The judge acts after being worn down, but God’s character is different: persistent prayer does not make an unwilling God become generous. The study emphasizes enduring faith and continued prayer for His purposes while the answer is still awaited.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Psalm 146 presents God as the faithful judge who gives justice to the oppressed and sustains the widow. That Scriptural picture makes the difference between God and the indifferent judge especially clear: the one to whom His people appeal already cares about those being wronged. (Psalm 146:5–9)

Revelation portrays people killed for their witness crying to God for judgment and being told to rest a little longer. This is a supported parallel to faithful prayer during delay. Their appeal is heard even while they await the completion of God’s justice; waiting does not mean He has forgotten them. (Revelation 6:9–11)

passages.title: Luke 18:9-14
passages.section_title: What changes when we ask for mercy instead of comparing ourselves?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 To some who trusted in their own righteousness and viewed others with contempt, He also told this parable: 10 “Two men went up to the temple to pray. One was a Pharisee and the other a tax collector. 11 The Pharisee stood by himself and prayed, ‘God, I thank You that I am not like other men—swindlers, evildoers, adulterers—or even like this tax collector. 12 I fast twice a week and pay tithes of all that I acquire.’ 13 But the tax collector stood at a distance, unwilling even to lift up his eyes to heaven. Instead, he beat his breast and said, ‘God, have mercy on me, a sinner!’ 14 I tell you, this man, rather than the Pharisee, went home justified. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted.”
paragraphs: 9 To some who trusted in their own righteousness and viewed others with contempt, He also told this parable: 10 “Two men went up to the temple to pray. One was a Pharisee and the other a tax collector. 11 The Pharisee stood by himself and prayed, ‘God, I thank You that I am not like other men—swindlers, evildoers, adulterers—or even like this tax collector. 12 I fast twice a week and pay tithes of all that I acquire.’

13 But the tax collector stood at a distance, unwilling even to lift up his eyes to heaven. Instead, he beat his breast and said, ‘God, have mercy on me, a sinner!’ 14 I tell you, this man, rather than the Pharisee, went home justified. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Luke again explains the audience and purpose before the story begins. Jesus speaks to people who trust in their own righteousness and look on others with contempt. The two men go to the temple to pray, but their prayers reveal very different ways of approaching God.

The Pharisee names other people’s wrongs and lists his own fasting and tithing. The tax collector stands at a distance, lowers his eyes, beats his breast and asks God for mercy. The contrast concerns where their confidence rests and how they regard themselves before God.

The tax collector’s request uses ἱλάσκομαι, hilaskomai (hee-LAHS-koh-my). Thayer explains the form used here as asking God to be gracious or merciful. The man appeals for mercy rather than offering a list of achievements. (Thayer, Greek 2433)

Jesus says that the tax collector, rather than the Pharisee, goes home justified. He concludes with the reversal that those who exalt themselves will be humbled, while those who humble themselves will be exalted.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand this parable as a warning against self-righteousness and contempt, and a call to acknowledge sin and depend on God’s mercy. The Catholic bishops’ notes emphasize complete dependence on His grace; Wesley likewise understands the tax collector, rather than the man relying on his own righteousness, as the one who is justified. (USCCB notes on Luke 18:9–14; Wesley on Luke 18:9–14)
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans describes all people as falling short of God’s glory and being justified freely by grace through the redemption in Jesus Christ. It then excludes boasting. This supplies the wider account of salvation in Christ within which the tax collector’s appeal to mercy can be understood. (Romans 3:21–28)

James applies the same reversal of pride and humility to the life of believers, calling them to draw near to God, repent and humble themselves before Him. Receiving mercy continues to shape how God’s people live and approach Him. (James 4:6–10)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 18:15-17
passages.section_title: What does receiving God’s kingdom like a child look like?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 Now people were even bringing their babies to Jesus for Him to place His hands on them. And when the disciples saw this, they rebuked those who brought them. 16 But Jesus called the children to Him and said, “Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them! For the kingdom of God belongs to such as these. 17 Truly I tell you, anyone who does not receive the kingdom of God like a little child will never enter it.”
paragraphs: 15 Now people were even bringing their babies to Jesus for Him to place His hands on them. And when the disciples saw this, they rebuked those who brought them. 16 But Jesus called the children to Him and said, “Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them! For the kingdom of God belongs to such as these. 17 Truly I tell you, anyone who does not receive the kingdom of God like a little child will never enter it.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
People bring even babies to Jesus for His touch, but the disciples rebuke those bringing them. Jesus calls the children to Him, tells the disciples to stop hindering them and says that God’s kingdom belongs to such as these.

Luke’s word for babies is βρέφος, brephos (BREH-foss), which Thayer identifies here as an infant. The scene includes actual very young children; Jesus then makes their reception of the kingdom a lesson for everyone. (Thayer, Greek 1025)

Placed after the Pharisee and tax collector and before the wealthy ruler, the saying continues the question of how people approach God. Jesus speaks of receiving the kingdom, with a child as the example.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly emphasize Jesus’ welcome of children and the trust and dependence involved in receiving God’s kingdom. The Catholic bishops’ notes connect that dependence with the surrounding warnings against relying on personal merit. (USCCB notes on Luke 18:15–17)

Churches differ over the connection with baptism. Calvin explicitly uses this scene to support infant baptism. The Catholic Church teaches infant baptism as a gift of new life, Reformed churches following Westminster include infants of believing parents, and the Methodist Articles retain baptism of young children. (Calvin on Luke 18:15–17 and its parallels; Catechism §§1250–1252; Westminster Confession 28.4; Methodist Articles XVII)

The 1689 Baptist Confession limits baptism to those who personally profess repentance, faith and obedience to Christ. That distinguishes the Baptist practice from the others described above. Luke’s scene itself describes children being brought for Jesus’ touch and His welcome of them. (1689 Baptist Confession 29.2)
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul reminds the Corinthians that God’s calling is not measured by worldly wisdom, power or noble birth. Their life in Christ leaves them with reason to praise God rather than boast about their standing. That is a broader connection with receiving the kingdom in dependence rather than approaching it as a personal achievement. (1 Corinthians 1:26–31)

Galatians describes God sending His Son so that people could receive adoption and the Spirit could lead them to call God Father. It is a supported connection with the wider picture of receiving life as God’s children, rather than a claim that Luke’s brief scene settles every question about baptism or the salvation of infants. (Galatians 4:4–7)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 18:18-30
passages.section_title: What can wealth give us, and what can only God give?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 Then a certain ruler asked Him, “Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?” 19 “Why do you call Me good?” Jesus replied. “No one is good except God alone. 20 You know the commandments: ‘Do not commit adultery, do not murder, do not steal, do not bear false witness, honor your father and mother.’” 21 “All these I have kept from my youth,” he said. 22 On hearing this, Jesus told him, “You still lack one thing: Sell everything you own and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. Then come, follow Me.” 23 But when the ruler heard this, he became very sad, because he was extremely wealthy. 24 Seeing the man’s sadness, Jesus said, “How hard it is for the rich to enter the kingdom of God! 25 Indeed, it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God.” 26 Those who heard this asked, “Who then can be saved?” 27 But Jesus said, “What is impossible with man is possible with God.” 28 “Look,” said Peter, “we have left all we had to follow You.” 29 “Truly I tell you,” Jesus replied, “no one who has left home or wife or brothers or parents or children for the sake of the kingdom of God 30 will fail to receive many times more in this age—and in the age to come, eternal life.”
paragraphs: 18 Then a certain ruler asked Him, “Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?” 19 “Why do you call Me good?” Jesus replied. “No one is good except God alone. 20 You know the commandments: ‘Do not commit adultery, do not murder, do not steal, do not bear false witness, honor your father and mother.’” 21 “All these I have kept from my youth,” he said.

22 On hearing this, Jesus told him, “You still lack one thing: Sell everything you own and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. Then come, follow Me.” 23 But when the ruler heard this, he became very sad, because he was extremely wealthy.

24 Seeing the man’s sadness, Jesus said, “How hard it is for the rich to enter the kingdom of God! 25 Indeed, it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God.” 26 Those who heard this asked, “Who then can be saved?” 27 But Jesus said, “What is impossible with man is possible with God.”

28 “Look,” said Peter, “we have left all we had to follow You.” 29 “Truly I tell you,” Jesus replied, “no one who has left home or wife or brothers or parents or children for the sake of the kingdom of God 30 will fail to receive many times more in this age—and in the age to come, eternal life.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
A ruler asks what he must do to inherit eternal life. Jesus first questions his use of good and points to God’s goodness, then names commandments concerning how people treat others. The ruler says he has kept them from his youth.

Jesus tells him to sell everything, give to the poor and follow Him. Luke records his deep sadness and explains that he is extremely wealthy. The demand brings his possessions and Jesus’ invitation together at a point of decision.

Jesus then compares a rich person’s entrance into the kingdom with a camel passing through a needle’s eye. The hearers ask who can be saved. His answer places the possibility with God where human ability fails.

Peter responds that the disciples have left their possessions and followed Jesus. Jesus assures them that loss for the kingdom’s sake will be met with far more in this age and eternal life in the age to come. This assurance belongs with the costly invitation and the warning about wealth, rather than being a separate promise of effortless prosperity.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly see wealth as a serious obstacle when it holds a person’s allegiance, and salvation as something that depends on God. Wesley takes the command to sell everything as the particular remedy for this ruler’s love of wealth, while directing other believers to use their possessions for God’s glory. (Wesley on Luke 18:22)

The Catholic Catechism likewise teaches that disciples must prefer Christ to everything and be detached from riches. The emphasis is on the claim possessions make on the heart and the need to put Christ first. These sources do not treat having money as a substitute for faithfulness or giving it away as an automatic purchase of salvation. (Catechism §§2544–2547)
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul makes Christ’s own self-giving the reason for generosity: He became poor for the sake of others. Paul then describes one community’s abundance meeting another’s need, and Acts records believers sharing possessions so that people among them did not lack what they needed. This is a supported connection with both the call to give and the wider family life of those who follow Jesus. (2 Corinthians 8:8–15; Acts 4:32–35)

First Timothy tells wealthy believers to put their hope in God, do good and be ready to share, laying up treasure for the future. That instruction shows the wider response the gospel calls for: present resources serve others, while lasting hope rests with God. (1 Timothy 6:17–19)

passages.title: Luke 18:31-34
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus speak of suffering on the way to Jerusalem?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 31 Then Jesus took the Twelve aside and said to them, “Look, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything the prophets have written about the Son of Man will be fulfilled. 32 He will be delivered over to the Gentiles and will be mocked and insulted and spit upon. 33 They will flog Him and kill Him, and on the third day He will rise again.” 34 But the disciples did not understand any of these things. The meaning was hidden from them, and they did not comprehend what He was saying.
paragraphs: 31 Then Jesus took the Twelve aside and said to them, “Look, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything the prophets have written about the Son of Man will be fulfilled. 32 He will be delivered over to the Gentiles and will be mocked and insulted and spit upon. 33 They will flog Him and kill Him, and on the third day He will rise again.” 34 But the disciples did not understand any of these things. The meaning was hidden from them, and they did not comprehend what He was saying.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus takes the Twelve aside as they approach Jerusalem. He tells them that what the prophets have written about the Son of Man will be fulfilled, then describes being handed over to the Gentiles, mocked, insulted, spit upon, flogged and killed. He also says that He will rise on the third day.

Luke emphasizes the disciples’ lack of understanding: they do not grasp these things, and the meaning is hidden from them. The announcement gives the reader a clear view of where Jesus’ journey leads even while His closest followers do not yet understand it.

The saying belongs alongside the earlier predictions of His suffering in Luke 9. Here the details become more explicit, and resurrection is included in the outcome He announces. (Luke 9:22, 43–45)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand this as Jesus’ deliberate announcement of His suffering, death and resurrection in fulfillment of Scripture. The Catholic bishops’ notes emphasize prophetic fulfillment; Wesley connects the disciples’ confusion with their expectations of the Messiah’s kingdom. (USCCB notes on Luke 18:31–34; Wesley on Luke 18:34)
passages.god_plan_html:
After the resurrection, Luke records Jesus opening the disciples’ understanding of Scripture and explaining His suffering, resurrection and the proclamation of repentance and forgiveness to all nations. That later scene directly addresses the lack of understanding recorded here and shows how the journey to Jerusalem belongs within the worldwide announcement of salvation. (Luke 24:44–48)

Peter later declares that God fulfilled the prophets’ witness to the Messiah’s suffering. Paul places Christ’s death for sins, burial and third-day resurrection at the center of the gospel he received and passed on. The events predicted here become the message the apostles proclaim. (Acts 3:17–19; 1 Corinthians 15:1–8)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 18:35-43
passages.section_title: What happens when the man beside the road calls to Jesus?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 35 As Jesus drew near to Jericho, a blind man was sitting beside the road, begging. 36 When he heard the crowd going by, he asked what was happening. 37 “Jesus of Nazareth is passing by,” they told him. 38 So he called out, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” 39 Those who led the way admonished him to be silent, but he cried out all the louder, “Son of David, have mercy on me!” 40 Jesus stopped and directed that the man be brought to Him. When he had come near, Jesus asked him, 41 “What do you want Me to do for you?” “Lord,” he said, “let me see again.” 42 “Receive your sight!” Jesus replied. “Your faith has healed you.” 43 Immediately he received his sight and followed Jesus, glorifying God. And all the people, when they saw it, gave praise to God.
paragraphs: 35 As Jesus drew near to Jericho, a blind man was sitting beside the road, begging. 36 When he heard the crowd going by, he asked what was happening. 37 “Jesus of Nazareth is passing by,” they told him. 38 So he called out, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” 39 Those who led the way admonished him to be silent, but he cried out all the louder, “Son of David, have mercy on me!”

40 Jesus stopped and directed that the man be brought to Him. When he had come near, Jesus asked him, 41 “What do you want Me to do for you?” “Lord,” he said, “let me see again.” 42 “Receive your sight!” Jesus replied. “Your faith has healed you.” 43 Immediately he received his sight and followed Jesus, glorifying God. And all the people, when they saw it, gave praise to God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
As Jesus draws near to Jericho, a blind man hears the passing crowd and asks what is happening. When told that Jesus of Nazareth is passing by, he calls to Him as Son of David and asks for mercy.

People leading the way try to silence him, but he continues calling. Jesus stops, has him brought near and asks what he wants. The man asks to see again. Jesus grants his sight and connects the healing with his faith.

The response extends beyond the healing itself. The man follows Jesus and glorifies God, and the people who witness it also praise God. Coming after the disciples’ lack of understanding, the account provides a striking narrative contrast: this man at the roadside calls to Jesus, receives sight and follows Him.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly recognize a real act of healing, an appeal of faith and the man’s response in following Jesus and praising God. The Catholic bishops’ notes understand Son of David as a title connected with Jesus’ role as Messiah and link the healing with the salvation He brings. (USCCB notes on Luke 18:38–42)
passages.god_plan_html:
At the beginning of Luke, Gabriel promises that Jesus will receive David’s throne and reign in an unending kingdom. The man’s appeal to the Son of David connects this roadside scene with that larger royal promise. (Luke 1:31–33)

Isaiah pictures God coming to save, with blind eyes opened and other afflictions relieved. This healing is a supported parallel to that picture of restoration. The account also shows how mercy becomes a witness: the person restored follows Jesus, and those who see what happened give praise to God. (Isaiah 35:4–6)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 19:1-10
passages.section_title: What changes when Jesus comes to Zacchaeus’ house?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then Jesus entered Jericho and was passing through. 2 And there was a man named Zacchaeus, a chief tax collector, who was very wealthy. 3 He was trying to see who Jesus was, but could not see over the crowd because he was small in stature. 4 So he ran on ahead and climbed a sycamore tree to see Him, since Jesus was about to pass that way. 5 When Jesus came to that place, He looked up and said, “Zacchaeus, hurry down, for I must stay at your house today.” 6 So Zacchaeus hurried down and welcomed Him joyfully. 7 And all who saw this began to grumble, saying, “He has gone to be the guest of a sinful man!” 8 But Zacchaeus stood up and said to the Lord, “Look, Lord, half of my possessions I give to the poor, and if I have cheated anyone, I will repay it fourfold.” 9 Jesus said to him, “Today salvation has come to this house, because this man too is a son of Abraham. 10 For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.”
paragraphs: 1 Then Jesus entered Jericho and was passing through. 2 And there was a man named Zacchaeus, a chief tax collector, who was very wealthy. 3 He was trying to see who Jesus was, but could not see over the crowd because he was small in stature. 4 So he ran on ahead and climbed a sycamore tree to see Him, since Jesus was about to pass that way.

5 When Jesus came to that place, He looked up and said, “Zacchaeus, hurry down, for I must stay at your house today.” 6 So Zacchaeus hurried down and welcomed Him joyfully. 7 And all who saw this began to grumble, saying, “He has gone to be the guest of a sinful man!”

8 But Zacchaeus stood up and said to the Lord, “Look, Lord, half of my possessions I give to the poor, and if I have cheated anyone, I will repay it fourfold.” 9 Jesus said to him, “Today salvation has come to this house, because this man too is a son of Abraham. 10 For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus enters Jericho after the roadside healing. Zacchaeus is a wealthy chief tax collector who wants to see Him, but his height and the crowd prevent it. He runs ahead and climbs a sycamore tree.

Jesus calls him by name and says He must stay at his house that day. Zacchaeus comes down quickly and receives Him with joy. The people who see it grumble that Jesus has become the guest of a sinful man.

Zacchaeus publicly speaks of giving half his possessions to the poor and repaying four times anything he has taken by cheating. His response brings the use of his wealth and his treatment of other people into view.

The Law provides different kinds of restitution for different wrongs. Exodus requires four sheep for a sheep stolen and sold or slaughtered, but gives other amounts in other cases. Leviticus requires returning property obtained by fraud or extortion with an added fifth. Zacchaeus’ fourfold commitment should not be described as the universal minimum for every theft. (Exodus 22:1–4; Leviticus 6:1–7)

Jesus announces salvation for this house, identifies Zacchaeus too as a son of Abraham and describes the Son of Man’s mission as seeking and saving the lost. The encounter follows the wealthy ruler’s sadness in the previous chapter and supplies a different response from another man with substantial possessions.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly recognize repentance, generosity and a changed use of wealth in Zacchaeus’ response. The Catholic bishops’ notes contrast him with the ruler who was unable to part with his possessions; Calvin stresses faith and understands the changed conduct as evidence of God’s saving work. (USCCB notes on Luke 19:1–10; Calvin on Luke 19:9)

The description son of Abraham receives different emphases. Wesley points to Zacchaeus’ Jewish identity and his place among those first offered salvation. Calvin emphasizes Abraham’s faith, while the Catholic bishops’ notes describe the repentant Zacchaeus as an heir of God’s promises. These are the explanations given by those sources, rather than a single official interpretation shared by all their readers. (Wesley on Luke 19:9; Calvin on Luke 19:9; USCCB note on Luke 19:9)
passages.god_plan_html:
Ezekiel describes God searching for His scattered flock, seeking the lost and appointing one shepherd from David’s line. Jesus’ description of His mission here is a supported connection with that shepherd picture: God’s saving care reaches a person whom the crowd regards as an unsuitable guest. (Ezekiel 34:11–16, 23–24)

Galatians identifies people of faith as Abraham’s children and explains that the promised blessing reaches the nations through Christ. Romans likewise speaks of Abraham as father of believers, both circumcised and uncircumcised. These passages place Abraham’s family within God’s larger purpose of bringing people into the blessing through faith, without erasing Zacchaeus’ own Jewish identity. (Galatians 3:7–9, 26–29; Romans 4:9–12)

passages.title: Luke 19:11-27
passages.section_title: What does faithfulness look like while the king is away?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 While the people were listening to this, Jesus proceeded to tell them a parable, because He was near Jerusalem and they thought the kingdom of God would appear imminently. 12 So He said, “A man of noble birth went to a distant country to lay claim to his kingship and then return. 13 Beforehand, he called ten of his servants and gave them ten minas. ‘Conduct business with this until I return,’ he said. 14 But his subjects hated him and sent a delegation after him to say, ‘We do not want this man to rule over us.’ 15 When he returned from procuring his kingship, he summoned the servants to whom he had given the money, to find out what each one had earned. 16 The first servant came forward and said, ‘Master, your mina has produced ten more minas.’ 17 His master replied, ‘Well done, good servant! Because you have been faithful in a very small matter, you shall have authority over ten cities.’ 18 The second servant came and said, ‘Master, your mina has made five minas.’ 19 And to this one he said, ‘You shall have authority over five cities.’ 20 Then another servant came and said, ‘Master, here is your mina, which I have laid away in a piece of cloth. 21 For I was afraid of you, because you are a harsh man. You withdraw what you did not deposit and reap what you did not sow.’ 22 His master replied, ‘You wicked servant, I will judge you by your own words. So you knew that I am a harsh man, withdrawing what I did not deposit and reaping what I did not sow? 23 Why then did you not deposit my money in the bank, and upon my return I could have collected it with interest?’ 24 Then he told those standing by, ‘Take the mina from him and give it to the one who has ten minas.’ 25 ‘Master,’ they said, ‘he already has ten!’ 26 He replied, ‘I tell you that everyone who has will be given more; but the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away from him. 27 And these enemies of mine who were unwilling for me to rule over them, bring them here and slay them in front of me.’”

Because you have been faithful in a very small matter, you shall have authority over ten cities.’ 18 The second servant came and said, ‘Master, your mina has made five minas.’ 19 And to this one he said, ‘You shall have authority over five cities.’

20 Then another servant came and said, ‘Master, here is your mina, which I have laid away in a piece of cloth. 21 For I was afraid of you, because you are a harsh man. You withdraw what you did not deposit and reap what you did not sow.’ 22 His master replied, ‘You wicked servant, I will judge you by your own words. So you knew that I am a harsh man, withdrawing what I did not deposit and reaping what I did not sow? 23 Why then did you not deposit my money in the bank, and upon my return I could have collected it with interest?’

24 Then he told those standing by, ‘Take the mina from him and give it to the one who has ten minas.’ 25 ‘Master,’ they said, ‘he already has ten!’ 26 He replied, ‘I tell you that everyone who has will be given more; but the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away from him. 27 And these enemies of mine who were unwilling for me to rule over them, bring them here and slay them in front of me.’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Luke gives the reason for this parable: Jesus is near Jerusalem, and the people expect God’s kingdom to appear immediately. The story instead describes a nobleman who leaves to receive kingship and later returns.

Before leaving, he entrusts ten minas to ten servants and tells them to conduct business. A mina is a sum of money; the Greek word is μνᾶ, mnā (mnah). Thayer identifies the amount in this passage with one hundred drachmas. The story gives the servants something entrusted to them and an instruction to use it during the master’s absence. (Thayer, Greek 3414)

The journey to receive rule and the opposing delegation have a recognizable historical parallel. Josephus records Archelaus appearing before Caesar in Rome while a Jewish delegation opposes rule by Herod’s family. Caesar grants Archelaus regional authority without immediately making him king. This provides a possible background for the story, rather than making every action of its ruler an exact description of Jesus. (Josephus, Antiquities 17.11.1–4)

When the ruler returns, two servants report gains and receive authority over cities. Another has kept the money wrapped in cloth, explaining that he feared his harsh master. The master judges him by his own stated reasoning and takes the mina away.

The story also includes people who reject the ruler’s authority. Their opposition ends in judgment. The servants’ responsibility and the subjects’ rejection belong to the same warning about what it means to wait for this king’s return.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly connect the absent ruler with Christ and understand the servants’ work as a call to faithful service while His kingdom’s full appearing is awaited. The Catholic bishops’ notes emphasize the correction of an immediate-kingdom expectation and the coming reward and judgment. Calvin likewise emphasizes patience during the delay and the active use of what God entrusts to His people. (USCCB notes on Luke 19:11–27; Calvin on Luke 19:11–13)
passages.god_plan_html:
First Peter calls believers to use the gifts they have received in service to one another, relying on the strength God supplies so that He receives glory through Christ. That gives a wider picture of what faithful use of entrusted resources can look like in the life of His people. (1 Peter 4:7–11)

Paul describes ministry built on Christ’s foundation being tested, with reward for work that lasts and loss for work that does not. He also says that all must appear before Christ’s judgment seat. These are supported connections with responsibility, reward and accountability; they do not by themselves identify every servant’s spiritual condition or turn the cities in the parable into a complete schedule of future appointments. (1 Corinthians 3:5–15; 2 Corinthians 5:6–10)

passages.title: Luke 19:28-40
passages.section_title: Why do the disciples welcome Jesus as King?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 28 After Jesus had said this, He went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem. 29 As He approached Bethphage and Bethany at the Mount of Olives, He sent out two of His disciples, 30 saying, “Go into the village ahead of you, and as you enter it, you will find a colt tied there, on which no one has ever sat. Untie it and bring it here. 31 If anyone asks, ‘Why are you untying it?’ tell him, ‘The Lord needs it.’” 32 So those who were sent went out and found it just as Jesus had told them. 33 As they were untying the colt, its owners asked, “Why are you untying the colt?” 34 “The Lord needs it,” they answered. 35 Then they led the colt to Jesus, threw their cloaks over it, and put Jesus on it. 36 As He rode along, the people spread their cloaks on the road. 37 And as He approached the descent from the Mount of Olives, the whole multitude of disciples began to praise God joyfully in a loud voice for all the miracles they had seen: 38 “Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord!” “Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!” 39 But some of the Pharisees in the crowd said to Him, “Teacher, rebuke Your disciples!” 40 “I tell you,” He answered, “if they remain silent, the very stones will cry out.”

Untie it and bring it here. 31 If anyone asks, ‘Why are you untying it?’ tell him, ‘The Lord needs it.’” 32 So those who were sent went out and found it just as Jesus had told them. 33 As they were untying the colt, its owners asked, “Why are you untying the colt?” 34 “The Lord needs it,” they answered.

35 Then they led the colt to Jesus, threw their cloaks over it, and put Jesus on it. 36 As He rode along, the people spread their cloaks on the road. 37 And as He approached the descent from the Mount of Olives, the whole multitude of disciples began to praise God joyfully in a loud voice for all the miracles they had seen: 38 “Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord!” “Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!”
39 But some of the Pharisees in the crowd said to Him, “Teacher, rebuke Your disciples!” 40 “I tell you,” He answered, “if they remain silent, the very stones will cry out.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the parable about the ruler’s absence and return, Jesus continues toward Jerusalem. Near Bethphage and Bethany, He sends two disciples to bring a colt that has never been ridden. They find it as He described and answer its owners with the words He supplied.

The disciples place their cloaks on the colt and help Jesus onto it. Others spread cloaks along the road. Near the descent of the Mount of Olives, the multitude of disciples praises God for the miracles they have seen and welcomes the King who comes in the Lord’s name.

The words of welcome draw on Psalm 118. Luke also records their praise of peace in heaven and glory in the highest. When some Pharisees ask Jesus to rebuke them, He answers that if they are silent, the stones will cry out. (Psalm 118:22–26)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand this as Jesus’ royal welcome on His approach to Jerusalem. The Catholic bishops’ notes emphasize the acclamation of Him as King and the peace associated with His saving work; Wesley understands the answer about stones as declaring that God will find a way for His praise to be heard. (USCCB notes on Luke 19:28–40; Wesley on Luke 19:38–40)
passages.god_plan_html:
Zechariah describes Zion’s righteous, humble King arriving on a donkey, followed by a picture of peace reaching the nations. John explicitly connects Jesus’ entry with that prophecy and says the disciples understood the connection after He was glorified. John explicitly identifies the Scriptural connection. (Zechariah 9:9–10; John 12:12–16)

An earlier Scriptural scene also gives a useful royal parallel: Solomon rides David’s mule to his anointing and is greeted with public rejoicing. The animals and circumstances differ, but Scripture itself provides a picture of an arriving king riding a mount and receiving acclaim. (1 Kings 1:32–40)

Jesus’ journey also leads toward the Passover. Exodus describes the unblemished lamb and the blood associated with deliverance, and Paul explicitly calls Christ the sacrificed Passover lamb. That larger connection places this welcome on the way to His saving death. (Exodus 12:3–7; 1 Corinthians 5:6–8)

passages.title: Luke 19:41-44
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus weep as He approaches Jerusalem?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 41 As Jesus approached Jerusalem and saw the city, He wept over it 42 and said, “If only you had known on this day what would bring you peace! But now it is hidden from your eyes. 43 For the days will come upon you when your enemies will barricade you and surround you and hem you in on every side. 44 They will level you to the ground—you and the children within your walls. They will not leave one stone on another, because you did not recognize the time of your visitation from God.”
paragraphs: 41 As Jesus approached Jerusalem and saw the city, He wept over it 42 and said, “If only you had known on this day what would bring you peace! But now it is hidden from your eyes. 43 For the days will come upon you when your enemies will barricade you and surround you and hem you in on every side. 44 They will level you to the ground—you and the children within your walls. They will not leave one stone on another, because you did not recognize the time of your visitation from God.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The joyful approach is followed by Jesus’ tears over Jerusalem. He speaks of the peace the city has failed to recognize and describes a coming siege: enemies surrounding it, its people hemmed in and devastating destruction.

Jesus connects this warning with the city’s failure to recognize the time of God’s visitation. The Greek word is ἐπισκοπή, episkopē (eh-pih-skoh-PAY), meaning a visitation or inspection. Thayer explains its use here as God graciously offering salvation through Christ. The word therefore points to an opportunity to receive God’s help, not merely the arrival of an army. (Thayer, Greek 1984)

The tears matter alongside the warning. Jesus’ announcement of judgment is spoken with grief over what the city has missed.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly connect the warning with Jerusalem’s destruction under the Romans. The Catholic bishops’ notes identify the disaster of AD 70 as its historical setting; Wesley likewise connects the siege with Titus, while Calvin emphasizes Christ’s compassion as He grieves over the city’s coming ruin. (USCCB notes on Luke 19:41–44; Wesley on Luke 19:42–44; Calvin on Luke 19:41–42)

Josephus independently describes Roman siege works, the capture of Jerusalem and the burning of its neighborhoods. That is checkable historical background for this reading, rather than an added description of every person’s individual guilt. (Josephus, Jewish War 6.8.1–5)
passages.god_plan_html:
Luke’s account does not end with this warning. After the resurrection, Jesus commissions repentance and forgiveness to be proclaimed to the nations beginning at Jerusalem. The city over which He weeps is also the starting place of the announced mission of forgiveness. (Luke 24:44–48)

Romans holds warning and mercy together: Paul says God has not rejected His people, warns Gentile believers against boasting over broken branches and speaks of God’s enduring call and purpose of mercy. That wider teaching keeps this lament within a Scriptural account of judgment and mercy, rather than making it a reason for contempt toward Jewish people. (Romans 11:1–2, 17–22, 28–32)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 19:45-48
passages.section_title: What has happened to God’s house of prayer?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 45 Then Jesus entered the temple courts and began to drive out those who were selling there. 46 He declared to them, “It is written: ‘My house will be a house of prayer.’ But you have made it ‘a den of robbers.’” 47 Jesus was teaching at the temple every day, but the chief priests, scribes, and leaders of the people were intent on killing Him. 48 Yet they could not find a way to do so, because all the people hung on His words.
paragraphs: 45 Then Jesus entered the temple courts and began to drive out those who were selling there. 46 He declared to them, “It is written: ‘My house will be a house of prayer.’ But you have made it ‘a den of robbers.’”

47 Jesus was teaching at the temple every day, but the chief priests, scribes, and leaders of the people were intent on killing Him. 48 Yet they could not find a way to do so, because all the people hung on His words.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus enters the temple courts and drives out those selling there. He explains His action with two passages of Scripture: the house of prayer from Isaiah and the den of robbers from Jeremiah.

Isaiah’s setting includes foreigners joining themselves to the Lord and being welcomed in His house of prayer. Jeremiah confronts people who oppress others and commit wrong, then treat the temple as a place where they can claim safety while continuing unchanged. These passages give Jesus’ action a setting deeper than disruption in a busy marketplace. (Isaiah 56:6–8; Jeremiah 7:3–14)

Jesus then teaches in the temple every day. The chief priests, scribes and leading people want to kill Him, but cannot find a way because the people are listening intently. The next chapter opens with a challenge to His authority in this same setting.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand this action as a defense of God’s purpose for His house and a confrontation with its misuse. The Catholic bishops’ notes also emphasize Jesus’ authority and the temple becoming the setting for His teaching in Jerusalem. (USCCB notes on Luke 19:45–48)
passages.god_plan_html:
John’s temple account connects Jesus’ challenge to the temple’s misuse with a saying about raising the temple again in three days. John explicitly explains that Jesus means His body, and that the disciples understand after His resurrection. This is a connection supplied by another Gospel, rather than an extra saying inserted into Luke’s scene. (John 2:13–22)

Ephesians describes people once separated being brought near through Christ, with access to the Father by one Spirit. Together they become a holy temple and a dwelling place for God. This wider picture carries the purpose of fellowship with God into the shared life of His people, with Christ as their cornerstone. (Ephesians 2:13–22)

passages.title: Luke 20:1-8
passages.section_title: What does John’s baptism have to do with Jesus’ authority?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 One day as Jesus was teaching the people in the temple courts and proclaiming the gospel, the chief priests and scribes, together with the elders, came up to Him. 2 “Tell us,” they said, “by what authority are You doing these things, and who gave You this authority?” 3 “I will also ask you a question,” Jesus replied. “Tell Me: 4 John’s baptism—was it from heaven, or from men?” 5 They deliberated among themselves and said, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ He will ask, ‘Why did you not believe him?’ 6 But if we say, ‘From men,’ all the people will stone us, for they are convinced that John was a prophet.” 7 So they answered that they did not know where it was from. 8 And Jesus replied, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I am doing these things.”
paragraphs: 1 One day as Jesus was teaching the people in the temple courts and proclaiming the gospel, the chief priests and scribes, together with the elders, came up to Him. 2 “Tell us,” they said, “by what authority are You doing these things, and who gave You this authority?” 3 “I will also ask you a question,” Jesus replied. “Tell Me: 4 John’s baptism—was it from heaven, or from men?”

5 They deliberated among themselves and said, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ He will ask, ‘Why did you not believe him?’ 6 But if we say, ‘From men,’ all the people will stone us, for they are convinced that John was a prophet.” 7 So they answered that they did not know where it was from. 8 And Jesus replied, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I am doing these things.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus is teaching and proclaiming the gospel in the temple courts when chief priests, scribes and elders challenge Him. They ask both what authority He has and who gave it to Him. The question follows His action in the temple and His continued teaching there.

Jesus asks whether John’s baptism came from heaven or from people. The leaders discuss what each answer would cost them: acknowledging a heavenly source would expose their failure to believe John, while denying it would bring them into conflict with people convinced he was a prophet.

They answer that they do not know. Jesus then refuses to tell them by what authority He acts. Luke shows a conversation shaped by their calculations about credibility and the crowd, rather than a straightforward examination of John’s message.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand Jesus’ question as exposing the leaders’ failure to respond to John’s witness. Calvin explains that John had been sent ahead of Christ and had identified Him, so the question is directly relevant to the challenge about Jesus’ authority. The Catholic bishops’ notes place this encounter among the leaders’ attempts to discredit Jesus. (Calvin on Luke 20:1–8 and Matthew 21:23–27; USCCB notes on Luke 20)
passages.god_plan_html:
John’s Gospel records the Baptist identifying Jesus as the Lamb of God, testifying to the Spirit’s descent and declaring Him to be God’s Son. John’s ministry is therefore part of the witness directing people to Jesus and His saving work. (John 1:29–34)

Acts later records Paul explaining that John’s baptism of repentance directed people to believe in the One coming after him, Jesus. This is an explicit New Testament account of how John’s preparatory ministry fits within the announcement of Christ. (Acts 19:1–5)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 20:9-19
passages.section_title: What happens when the tenants reject the owner’s son?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 Then He proceeded to tell the people this parable: “A man planted a vineyard, rented it out to some tenants, and went away for a long time. 10 At harvest time, he sent a servant to the tenants to collect his share of the fruit of the vineyard. But the tenants beat the servant and sent him away empty-handed. 11 So he sent another servant, but they beat him and treated him shamefully, sending him away empty-handed. 12 Then he sent a third, but they wounded him and threw him out. 13 ‘What shall I do?’ asked the owner of the vineyard. ‘I will send my beloved son. Perhaps they will respect him.’ 14 But when the tenants saw the son, they discussed it among themselves and said, ‘This is the heir. Let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.’ 15 So they threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. What then will the owner of the vineyard do to them? 16 He will come and kill those tenants and give the vineyard to others.” And when the people heard this, they said, “May such a thing never happen!” 17 But Jesus looked directly at them and said, “Then what is the meaning of that which is written: ‘The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone’? 18 Everyone who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces, but he on whom it falls will be crushed.” 19 When the scribes and chief priests realized that Jesus had spoken this parable against them, they sought to arrest Him that very hour. But they were afraid of the people.
paragraphs: 9 Then He proceeded to tell the people this parable: “A man planted a vineyard, rented it out to some tenants, and went away for a long time. 10 At harvest time, he sent a servant to the tenants to collect his share of the fruit of the vineyard. But the tenants beat the servant and sent him away empty-handed. 11 So he sent another servant, but they beat him and treated him shamefully, sending him away empty-handed. 12 Then he sent a third, but they wounded him and threw him out.

13 ‘What shall I do?’ asked the owner of the vineyard. ‘I will send my beloved son. Perhaps they will respect him.’ 14 But when the tenants saw the son, they discussed it among themselves and said, ‘This is the heir. Let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.’ 15 So they threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. What then will the owner of the vineyard do to them? 16 He will come and kill those tenants and give the vineyard to others.” And when the people heard this, they said, “May such a thing never happen!”

17 But Jesus looked directly at them and said, “Then what is the meaning of that which is written: ‘The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone’? 18 Everyone who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces, but he on whom it falls will be crushed.” 19 When the scribes and chief priests realized that Jesus had spoken this parable against them, they sought to arrest Him that very hour. But they were afraid of the people.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus tells the people about a vineyard owner who goes away and sends servants to collect his share of the harvest. The tenants beat and shame them, then wound the third servant and throw him out. The conflict concerns their refusal to recognize the owner’s claim.

The owner sends his beloved son, but the tenants plot to kill him and take the inheritance. They throw him out and kill him. Jesus asks what the owner will do, then describes judgment on the tenants and the vineyard being given to others.

Isaiah’s vineyard song provides a Scriptural background: God tends His vineyard and looks for justice, but finds bloodshed and distress. Jesus’ story places particular attention on the tenants, and Luke explicitly says the scribes and chief priests understand the parable as directed against them. (Isaiah 5:1–7)

Jesus then cites the rejected stone that becomes the cornerstone and warns of being broken or crushed by that stone. The leaders want to arrest Him, but fear the people. Their reaction keeps the parable’s warning tied to the confrontation unfolding around Him. (Psalm 118:22–23)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand God as the owner, the rejected servants as His messengers and the son as Jesus. Calvin emphasizes the history of rejecting God’s prophets and the coming rejection of His Son. The Catholic bishops’ notes identify the tenants with the religious leadership that rejects Jesus’ teaching. (Calvin on Luke 20:9–19 and Matthew 21:33–46; USCCB notes on Luke 20:9–19)
passages.god_plan_html:
The son is described as beloved. The Greek word is ἀγαπητός, agapētos (ah-gah-pay-TOSS), meaning dearly loved or cherished. Luke has already used the same word when the Father identifies Jesus as His beloved Son at His baptism. That repetition provides a supported connection with the identity of the son in the parable. (Thayer, Greek 27; Luke 3:21–22)

Hebrews describes God speaking through the prophets and then through His Son, the appointed heir who provides purification for sins and sits at God’s right hand. This broader witness gives depth to the movement from messengers to Son and heir. (Hebrews 1:1–4)

Acts explicitly identifies the rejected cornerstone as the crucified and risen Jesus, through whom salvation comes. First Peter uses the same Scripture to describe people being built around Him into a spiritual house and called to proclaim God’s goodness. Rejection does not prevent Him from becoming the foundation of the people God is gathering. (Acts 4:8–12; 1 Peter 2:4–10)

passages.title: Luke 20:20-26
passages.section_title: What do we owe Caesar, and what do we owe God?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 20 So they watched Him closely and sent spies who pretended to be sincere. They were hoping to catch Him in His words in order to hand Him over to the rule and authority of the governor. 21 “Teacher,” they inquired, “we know that You speak and teach correctly. You show no partiality but teach the way of God in accordance with the truth. 22 Is it lawful for us to pay taxes to Caesar or not?” 23 But Jesus saw through their duplicity and said to them, 24 “Show Me a denarius. Whose image and inscription are on it?” “Caesar’s,” they answered. 25 So Jesus told them, “Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.” 26 And they were unable to trap Him in His words before the people. And amazed at His answer, they fell silent.

You show no partiality but teach the way of God in accordance with the truth. 22 Is it lawful for us to pay taxes to Caesar or not?”

23 But Jesus saw through their duplicity and said to them, 24 “Show Me a denarius. Whose image and inscription are on it?” “Caesar’s,” they answered. 25 So Jesus told them, “Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.” 26 And they were unable to trap Him in His words before the people. And amazed at His answer, they fell silent.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The leaders now send spies who pretend to be sincere. Luke states their purpose: to catch Jesus in something He says and hand Him over to the governor’s authority. Their flattering introduction leads to a question about paying taxes to Caesar.

Jesus recognizes the deception and asks to see a denarius. The question about its image and inscription brings Caesar’s claim into view. Jesus then tells them to give Caesar what belongs to Caesar and God what belongs to God.

The Greek verb behind give is ἀποδίδωμι, apodidōmi (ah-poh-DEE-doh-mee). Thayer explains its use here as paying or discharging what is due, including taxes. It can also mean give back, but that meaning does not make this a refusal to pay what is owed. (Thayer, Greek 591)

The spies cannot trap Him before the people. They are amazed and fall silent. His answer addresses both the civil obligation they have raised and the obligation to God that their question has left aside.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly recognize a real duty toward civil authority while keeping God’s claim above human authority. The Catholic Catechism teaches paying taxes and refusing directives contrary to God’s moral order; the Westminster Confession likewise requires tribute and obedience to lawful commands. (Catechism §§2240–2242; Westminster Confession 23.4)
passages.god_plan_html:
Genesis supplies a useful Scriptural parallel to the image on the coin: human beings bear God’s image. Romans then calls believers to offer their whole lives to Him in response to His mercy. Read together, these passages point to a claim that reaches beyond money to the people we are and the lives we live. (Genesis 1:26–27; Romans 12:1–2)

The apostles later teach both paying what is due to governing authorities and obeying God when a human command conflicts with His commission. These texts show how service to God shapes life within civil society without making earthly rulers the highest authority. (Romans 13:1–7; Acts 5:27–29)
