passages.title: Luke 20:27-40
passages.section_title: Can God’s promise to His people end at death?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 27 Then some of the Sadducees, who say there is no resurrection, came to question Him. 28 “Teacher,” they said, “Moses wrote for us that if a man’s brother dies and leaves a wife but no children, the man is to marry his brother’s widow and raise up offspring for him. 29 Now there were seven brothers. The first one married a wife but died childless. 30 Then the second 31 and the third married the widow, and in the same way all seven died, leaving no children. 32 And last of all, the woman died. 33 So then, in the resurrection, whose wife will she be? For all seven were married to her.” 34 Jesus answered, “The sons of this age marry and are given in marriage. 35 But those who are considered worthy to share in the age to come and in the resurrection from the dead will neither marry nor be given in marriage. 36 In fact, they can no longer die, because they are like the angels. And since they are sons of the resurrection, they are sons of God. 37 Even Moses demonstrates that the dead are raised, in the passage about the burning bush. For he calls the Lord ‘the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.’ 38 He is not the God of the dead, but of the living, for to Him all are alive.” 39 Some of the scribes answered, “Teacher, You have spoken well!” 40 And they did not dare to question Him any further.
paragraphs: 27 Then some of the Sadducees, who say there is no resurrection, came to question Him. 28 “Teacher,” they said, “Moses wrote for us that if a man’s brother dies and leaves a wife but no children, the man is to marry his brother’s widow and raise up offspring for him. 29 Now there were seven brothers. The first one married a wife but died childless. 30 Then the second 31 and the third married the widow, and in the same way all seven died, leaving no children. 32 And last of all, the woman died. 33 So then, in the resurrection, whose wife will she be? For all seven were married to her.”

34 Jesus answered, “The sons of this age marry and are given in marriage. 35 But those who are considered worthy to share in the age to come and in the resurrection from the dead will neither marry nor be given in marriage. 36 In fact, they can no longer die, because they are like the angels. And since they are sons of the resurrection, they are sons of God.

37 Even Moses demonstrates that the dead are raised, in the passage about the burning bush. For he calls the Lord ‘the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.’ 38 He is not the God of the dead, but of the living, for to Him all are alive.” 39 Some of the scribes answered, “Teacher, You have spoken well!” 40 And they did not dare to question Him any further.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Sadducees, whom Luke identifies as denying resurrection, propose a case involving seven brothers and one woman. Each brother marries her after the previous one dies without children. They ask whose wife she will be in the resurrection.

The question draws on the instruction that a surviving brother should preserve his deceased brother’s line through marriage to the widow. Deuteronomy explains that family obligation; the Sadducees use an extreme case to challenge resurrection. (Deuteronomy 25:5–10)

Jesus distinguishes this age from the resurrection. Those who share in that age neither marry nor are given in marriage, and they can no longer die. His comparison with angels belongs within that explanation of life beyond death.

He then points to Moses’ account of the burning bush, where God identifies Himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Jesus makes that relationship with the living the basis of His answer about resurrection. Some scribes praise His response, and the questioning stops. (Exodus 3:2–6, 15–17)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand this as affirming resurrection and a life that is changed from the conditions of the present age. The Catholic bishops’ notes emphasize Jesus’ correction of the Sadducees’ assumptions and His appeal to Moses; Wesley connects God’s enduring relationship with His people to their continued life and resurrection. (USCCB notes on Luke 20:27–40; Wesley on Luke 20:34–38)
passages.god_plan_html:
In Exodus, the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob also promises to bring their descendants out of oppression. His identity is tied to faithful care and promises that stretch across generations. Hebrews describes the patriarchs dying in faith while still awaiting what was promised, and looking toward the city God prepared. Death does not make His faithfulness or their hope meaningless. (Exodus 3:15–17; Hebrews 11:13–16, 39–40)

Paul explicitly places the resurrection of those who belong to Christ within the victory begun by Christ’s own resurrection. His reign leads to the destruction of death itself. That supplies the wider gospel setting for Jesus’ answer here. (1 Corinthians 15:20–26)

Paul also describes the body being raised from weakness and perishability into power and lasting life, using the seed and the body God gives it as his illustration. The resurrection hope is larger than an endless repetition of present conditions. (1 Corinthians 15:35–49)
passages.current_position_html: Who is The Angel of the Lord?, in its section on Exodus 3:2–6, identifies the One who appears and speaks from the burning bush as the Son before His human birth. The study explicitly connects that passage with Jesus’ answer to the Sadducees in Matthew’s parallel account. This is the study’s conclusion about the speaker in Exodus; Jesus’ immediate point here concerns resurrection and God’s relationship with the living.

deeper_study.title: Who is The Angel of the Lord?

passages.title: Luke 20:41-44
passages.section_title: How can David’s son also be David’s Lord?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 41 Then Jesus declared, “How can it be said that the Christ is the Son of David? 42 For David himself says in the book of Psalms: ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at My right hand 43 until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet.”’ 44 Thus David calls Him ‘Lord.’ So how can He be David’s son?”
paragraphs: 41 Then Jesus declared, “How can it be said that the Christ is the Son of David? 42 For David himself says in the book of Psalms: ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at My right hand 43 until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet.”’ 44 Thus David calls Him ‘Lord.’ So how can He be David’s son?”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus now poses a question of His own. He asks how the Christ can be called David’s son when David himself calls Him Lord in Psalm 110. The quoted saying places this Lord at God’s right hand until His enemies are put beneath His feet. (Psalm 110:1–4)

The question brings ancestry and authority together. Being descended from David does not exhaust what the Psalm says about the Messiah. David’s own words require attention to the greater standing of the One he calls Lord.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand the Messiah as David’s promised descendant whose authority also surpasses David’s. Calvin reads the question as pointing to Christ’s humanity and divinity, a confession also stated in the Westminster Confession and Methodist Articles. (Calvin on Luke 20:41–44 and Matthew 22:41–46; Westminster Confession 8.2; Methodist Articles II)
passages.god_plan_html:
At Pentecost, Peter explicitly connects this Psalm with Jesus’ resurrection and exaltation. David died, but God raised Jesus, seated Him at His right hand and gave Him the promised Spirit to pour out. Peter uses that connection to proclaim Jesus as Lord and Christ. (Acts 2:29–36)

Paul also describes Christ reigning until His enemies are under His feet, with death the last enemy to be destroyed. The royal authority raised in Jesus’ question therefore belongs within the New Testament’s hope of resurrection and God’s final victory. (1 Corinthians 15:20–26)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 20:45-47
passages.section_title: What should make us cautious about a religious leader?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 45 In the hearing of all the people, Jesus said to His disciples, 46 “Beware of the scribes. They like to walk around in long robes, and they love the greetings in the marketplaces, the chief seats in the synagogues, and the places of honor at banquets. 47 They defraud widows of their houses, and for a show make lengthy prayers. These men will receive greater condemnation.”
paragraphs: 45 In the hearing of all the people, Jesus said to His disciples, 46 “Beware of the scribes. They like to walk around in long robes, and they love the greetings in the marketplaces, the chief seats in the synagogues, and the places of honor at banquets. 47 They defraud widows of their houses, and for a show make lengthy prayers. These men will receive greater condemnation.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
With everyone listening, Jesus turns to His disciples and warns them about scribes who seek public honor. He lists impressive clothing, prominent greetings and preferred places in synagogues and at banquets.

The warning then moves from the honor they seek to the harm they do: widows lose their homes through their wrongdoing, while lengthy prayers become a public show. Religious standing and visible devotion are being used alongside exploitation.

Jesus says these men will receive greater condemnation. The warning concerns how people entrusted with religious influence behave toward God and toward those vulnerable to their power.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly recognize a warning against pride, exploitation and using religion to impress others. Jesus’ description tests outward standing against actual conduct, especially the treatment of widows; the warning follows the chapter’s confrontations with leaders who have resisted His teaching. (Luke 20:45–47; USCCB notes on Luke 20)
passages.god_plan_html:
James describes care for widows and orphans in distress as part of pure religion before God. That gives the wider positive picture behind this warning: devotion to Him should be visible in care for the people being harmed here. (James 1:26–27)

First Peter calls elders to care for God’s flock willingly, without greed or domination, and to lead by example as they await the Chief Shepherd. This is a supported connection with the kind of leadership Jesus’ followers are to practice instead of the pattern He condemns. (1 Peter 5:1–4)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 21:1-4
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus say the widow has given more?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then Jesus looked up and saw the rich putting their gifts into the treasury, 2 and He saw a poor widow put in two small copper coins. 3 “Truly I tell you,” He said, “this poor widow has put in more than all the others. 4 For they all contributed out of their surplus, but she out of her poverty has put in all she had to live on.”
paragraphs: 1 Then Jesus looked up and saw the rich putting their gifts into the treasury, 2 and He saw a poor widow put in two small copper coins. 3 “Truly I tell you,” He said, “this poor widow has put in more than all the others. 4 For they all contributed out of their surplus, but she out of her poverty has put in all she had to live on.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Immediately after warning about scribes who defraud widows, Jesus watches people putting gifts into the temple treasury. He sees wealthy people contributing and a poor widow giving two small copper coins.

The Greek word for one of these small coins is λεπτόν, lepton (lep-TON). Thayer describes it as a very small brass coin. The point of the comparison does not depend on a modern currency estimate: Jesus explains the difference in terms of what the gift costs its giver. (Thayer, Greek 3016)

The others give from their surplus, while she gives all she has to live on. Jesus calls her gift greater even though its monetary amount is small. The placement beside the warning about exploited widows also keeps her vulnerability before the reader.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand Jesus as recognizing the depth of the widow’s giving rather than judging the gift by its size. Calvin emphasizes the heart and the giver’s means; the Catholic bishops’ notes emphasize her dependence on God and the contrast with the scribes’ outward display. (Calvin on Luke 21:1–4 and Mark 12:41–44; USCCB notes on Luke 21:1–4)
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul describes poor Macedonian believers giving generously and first giving themselves to the Lord. He then grounds Christian generosity in Christ’s own self-giving and explains that willingness is measured according to what a person has. That is a supported parallel to the costly gift Jesus notices here. (2 Corinthians 8:1–5, 9, 12–14)

The larger picture of self-giving reaches its center in Christ’s death for people who were powerless and sinful. The widow’s gift provides a parallel of costly giving as Luke moves toward Jesus’ suffering and death, while Romans explicitly identifies Christ’s death as the demonstration of God’s saving love. (Romans 5:6–8)

passages.title: Luke 21:5-11
passages.section_title: What should we do when people say the end is near?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 As some of the disciples were remarking how the temple was adorned with beautiful stones and consecrated gifts, Jesus said, 6 “As for what you see here, the time will come when not one stone will be left on another; every one will be thrown down.” 7 “Teacher,” they asked, “when will these things happen? And what will be the sign that they are about to take place?” 8 Jesus answered, “See to it that you are not deceived. For many will come in My name, claiming, ‘I am He,’ and, ‘The time is near.’ Do not follow them. 9 When you hear of wars and rebellions, do not be alarmed. These things must happen first, but the end is not imminent.” 10 Then He told them, “Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. 11 There will be great earthquakes, famines, and pestilences in various places, along with fearful sights and great signs from heaven.
paragraphs: 5 As some of the disciples were remarking how the temple was adorned with beautiful stones and consecrated gifts, Jesus said, 6 “As for what you see here, the time will come when not one stone will be left on another; every one will be thrown down.” 7 “Teacher,” they asked, “when will these things happen? And what will be the sign that they are about to take place?”

8 Jesus answered, “See to it that you are not deceived. For many will come in My name, claiming, ‘I am He,’ and, ‘The time is near.’ Do not follow them. 9 When you hear of wars and rebellions, do not be alarmed. These things must happen first, but the end is not imminent.” 10 Then He told them, “Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. 11 There will be great earthquakes, famines, and pestilences in various places, along with fearful sights and great signs from heaven.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Some disciples admire the temple’s beautiful stones and dedicated gifts. Jesus answers with a warning that the structure they are looking at will be thrown down. They ask when this will happen and what sign will announce it.

Jesus begins by warning them against deception. People will come in His name, claiming His identity and announcing that the time is near. He tells His followers not to follow them.

He also tells them not to be alarmed by wars and rebellions, since these things happen first and do not mean that the end has immediately arrived. He then speaks of conflict between nations and kingdoms, earthquakes, famine, disease and signs from heaven.

This is the opening of a longer teaching. The following sections address persecution, Jerusalem’s danger, the Son of Man and watchfulness; those parts belong together when considering the questions the disciples ask.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly recognize a warning against deception and panic while taking Jesus’ announcement of the temple’s destruction seriously. The Catholic bishops’ notes distinguish the chapter’s historical events from the later signs surrounding the Son of Man; Wesley connects the earlier fearful signs with events described by Josephus. Those sources do not make a fresh claim of immediate fulfillment every time a war or disaster occurs. (USCCB notes on Luke 21:5–36; Wesley on Luke 21:8–11)
passages.god_plan_html:
Second Thessalonians also warns believers against being shaken or alarmed by messages claiming that the Day of the Lord has already arrived. The concern for a community that stays faithful without being swept away by alarming claims continues beyond this conversation. (2 Thessalonians 2:1–3)

Hebrews describes created things being shaken while God’s people receive a kingdom that cannot be shaken. Its response is gratitude, reverence and worship. This provides a wider Scriptural connection with the loss of even impressive earthly structures and the enduring hope God gives His people. (Hebrews 12:25–29)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

deeper_study.title: Should We Seek Signs From God?

passages.title: Luke 21:12-19
passages.section_title: How can persecution become an opportunity to bear witness?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 But before all this, they will seize you and persecute you. On account of My name they will deliver you to the synagogues and prisons, and they will bring you before kings and governors. 13 This will be your opportunity to serve as witnesses. 14 So make up your mind not to worry beforehand how to defend yourselves. 15 For I will give you speech and wisdom that none of your adversaries will be able to resist or contradict. 16 You will be betrayed even by parents and brothers and relatives and friends, and some of you will be put to death. 17 And you will be hated by everyone because of My name. 18 Yet not even a hair of your head will perish. 19 By your patient endurance you will gain your souls.
paragraphs: 12 But before all this, they will seize you and persecute you. On account of My name they will deliver you to the synagogues and prisons, and they will bring you before kings and governors. 13 This will be your opportunity to serve as witnesses. 14 So make up your mind not to worry beforehand how to defend yourselves. 15 For I will give you speech and wisdom that none of your adversaries will be able to resist or contradict.

16 You will be betrayed even by parents and brothers and relatives and friends, and some of you will be put to death. 17 And you will be hated by everyone because of My name. 18 Yet not even a hair of your head will perish. 19 By your patient endurance you will gain your souls.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus now says that before these things, His followers will be seized, brought before religious authorities and imprisoned, and made to appear before kings and governors because of His name. He describes these experiences as opportunities to bear witness.

He tells them not to worry beforehand about their defense and promises to give them speech and wisdom their opponents cannot withstand. This instruction concerns their response when brought before hostile authorities.

The warning reaches close to home: relatives and friends will betray them, they will face hatred, and some will be killed. Alongside that warning, Jesus promises that not even a hair will perish and calls them to patient endurance. The promise must be heard together with His explicit warning that some will die.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see a call to enduring trust in God through suffering, with Christ’s help for the testimony His followers must give. Wesley relates the promise about their hair to God’s care and reward, while Calvin describes entrusting one’s life to God even while facing death. These readings keep the promise together with the warning of martyrdom. (Wesley on Luke 21:18–19; Calvin on Luke 21:19)
passages.god_plan_html:
Acts gives concrete examples of the promised witness. Peter speaks before rulers while filled with the Holy Spirit, and Stephen’s opponents cannot withstand the wisdom and Spirit with which he speaks. Stephen is nevertheless killed, praying that Jesus will receive his spirit. God’s help in bearing witness and the reality of suffering appear together in Luke’s continuing account. (Acts 4:8–13; Acts 6:8–12; Acts 7:54–60)

Paul later stands before Agrippa and testifies to the suffering and resurrection of Christ and the light reaching Israel and the Gentiles. He wants those hearing him to share his faith. The forced appearance before rulers becomes an occasion for the saving message to reach people who might otherwise never have heard that witness. (Acts 26:19–29)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 21:20-24
passages.section_title: What does Jesus tell people to do when Jerusalem is surrounded?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 20 But when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, you will know that her desolation is near. 21 Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains, let those in the city get out, and let those in the country stay out of the city. 22 For these are the days of vengeance, to fulfill all that is written. 23 How miserable those days will be for pregnant and nursing mothers! For there will be great distress upon the land and wrath against this people. 24 They will fall by the edge of the sword and be led captive into all the nations. And Jerusalem will be trodden down by the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled.
paragraphs: 20 But when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, you will know that her desolation is near. 21 Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains, let those in the city get out, and let those in the country stay out of the city. 22 For these are the days of vengeance, to fulfill all that is written. 23 How miserable those days will be for pregnant and nursing mothers! For there will be great distress upon the land and wrath against this people. 24 They will fall by the edge of the sword and be led captive into all the nations. And Jerusalem will be trodden down by the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus now names Jerusalem and the armies surrounding it. He gives practical instructions: people in Judea are to flee to the mountains, those in the city are to leave, and those outside are to stay out.

He describes days of judgment, great distress and particular hardship for pregnant and nursing women. Death by the sword and captivity follow. The warning concerns people facing the destruction of the place they know, rather than an abstract discussion of history.

The section ends with Jerusalem being trampled by the Gentiles until their appointed times are fulfilled. The word until leaves a boundary to that period, though Jesus does not provide its length here.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly connect these verses with Jerusalem’s fall to Rome. The Catholic bishops’ notes place the times of the Gentiles between that destruction and the later signs surrounding the Son of Man. Wesley links their completion with the Gentiles’ conversion. (USCCB notes on Luke 21:20–24; Wesley on Luke 21:24)

John Walvoord gives a wider timeline, reading the period as Gentile domination beginning with Babylon and continuing until Christ returns. These are different readings of the period’s extent and ending, rather than one detailed timetable agreed by every Christian tradition. (Walvoord, The Return of the Lord, chapter 11)
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans also places Israel and the Gentiles within a larger purpose of mercy. Paul speaks of Israel’s partial hardening, the coming in of the Gentiles and Israel’s salvation, while insisting that God’s gifts and calling remain in place. That is a supported connection with the question raised here about how Jerusalem’s distress fits within God’s continuing purposes. (Romans 11:25–32)

Luke later records the risen Jesus commissioning repentance and forgiveness to be announced to all nations, beginning at Jerusalem. The warning of destruction therefore belongs alongside a mission in which mercy is proclaimed from this same city. (Luke 24:44–48)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 21:25-28
passages.section_title: Why can Jesus’ followers lift their heads when others are afraid?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 25 There will be signs in the sun and moon and stars, and on the earth dismay among the nations, bewildered by the roaring of the sea and the surging of the waves. 26 Men will faint from fear and anxiety over what is coming upon the earth, for the powers of the heavens will be shaken. 27 At that time they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory. 28 When these things begin to happen, stand up and lift up your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.”
paragraphs: 25 There will be signs in the sun and moon and stars, and on the earth dismay among the nations, bewildered by the roaring of the sea and the surging of the waves. 26 Men will faint from fear and anxiety over what is coming upon the earth, for the powers of the heavens will be shaken. 27 At that time they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory. 28 When these things begin to happen, stand up and lift up your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The description widens from Jerusalem’s danger to signs in the heavens and distress among the nations. People are overwhelmed by fear as the powers of the heavens are shaken.

Jesus then describes the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory. He tells His followers to stand up and lift their heads because their redemption is drawing near. The same scene that brings widespread fear brings them a reason for hope.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand this coming as a moment of Christ’s power and His people’s deliverance. The Catholic bishops’ notes distinguish it from the earlier destruction of Jerusalem; Calvin emphasizes the contrast between the world’s distress and believers’ hope in the salvation Christ brings. (USCCB notes on Luke 21:24–28; Calvin on Luke 21:28)
passages.god_plan_html:
Daniel sees a figure like a son of man coming with heaven’s clouds to the Ancient of Days and receiving enduring dominion over all nations. Jesus draws on that royal picture here. Revelation likewise announces Christ’s coming with clouds and describes Him as the risen ruler who has freed His people from sin by His blood. (Daniel 7:13–14; Revelation 1:5–7)

Romans describes believers awaiting the redemption of their bodies while creation itself groans for freedom from decay. That wider hope gives depth to the redemption Jesus announces: His people await the completion of a rescue that reaches beyond immediate relief from fear. (Romans 8:18–25)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 21:29-33
passages.section_title: What does the lesson of the trees tell us to trust?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 29 Then Jesus told them a parable: “Look at the fig tree and all the trees. 30 When they sprout leaves, you can see for yourselves and know that summer is near. 31 So also, when you see these things happening, know that the kingdom of God is near. 32 Truly I tell you, this generation will not pass away until all these things have happened. 33 Heaven and earth will pass away, but My words will never pass away.
paragraphs: 29 Then Jesus told them a parable: “Look at the fig tree and all the trees. 30 When they sprout leaves, you can see for yourselves and know that summer is near. 31 So also, when you see these things happening, know that the kingdom of God is near. 32 Truly I tell you, this generation will not pass away until all these things have happened. 33 Heaven and earth will pass away, but My words will never pass away.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus points to the fig tree and all the trees. New leaves tell observers that summer is near. In the same way, the events He describes are to make His followers recognize the nearness of God’s kingdom.

He then says that this generation will not pass away until all these things have happened and that His words will outlast heaven and earth. Which generation is meant and how the events fit together are important questions in the readings below.

The Greek word is γενεά, genea (geh-neh-AH), translated generation. Thayer includes the people living at the same time among its meanings. The word helps identify the question, but its meaning alone does not decide which group or time Jesus is referring to in this teaching. (Thayer, Greek 1074)
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Readers differ over this generation. Wesley understands the statement in relation to the destruction of Jerusalem and the earlier events in the discourse. The NET study notes describe another reading in which it is the generation that sees the final signs, with the remaining events following within that generation. The notes also discuss other possibilities, so neither source should be treated as proof that there is only one Christian reading. (Wesley on Luke 21:32; NET notes on Luke 21:32)

The tree illustration itself concerns recognizing a season from visible growth, and Luke includes all the trees alongside the fig tree. The certainty of Jesus’ words remains part of the saying across these different readings.
passages.god_plan_html: Isaiah contrasts human life and splendor with God’s word, which stands forever. First Peter repeats that Scripture and applies it to the enduring word through which believers have received new birth and heard the good news. This gives a broader Scriptural setting for Jesus’ assurance that His words will not pass away: God’s people receive life and hope from a message that remains when human strength and visible glory fade. (Isaiah 40:6–11; 1 Peter 1:22–25)

deeper_study.title: Should We Seek Signs From God?

passages.title: Luke 21:34-38
passages.section_title: How does Jesus tell us to stay ready?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 34 But watch yourselves, or your hearts will be weighed down by dissipation, drunkenness, and the worries of life—and that day will spring upon you suddenly like a snare. 35 For it will come upon all who dwell on the face of all the earth. 36 So keep watch at all times, and pray that you may have the strength to escape all that is about to happen and to stand before the Son of Man.” 37 Every day Jesus taught at the temple, but every evening He went out to spend the night on the Mount of Olives. 38 And early in the morning all the people would come to hear Him at the temple.
paragraphs: 34 But watch yourselves, or your hearts will be weighed down by dissipation, drunkenness, and the worries of life—and that day will spring upon you suddenly like a snare. 35 For it will come upon all who dwell on the face of all the earth. 36 So keep watch at all times, and pray that you may have the strength to escape all that is about to happen and to stand before the Son of Man.”
37 Every day Jesus taught at the temple, but every evening He went out to spend the night on the Mount of Olives. 38 And early in the morning all the people would come to hear Him at the temple.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus concludes by calling His followers to watch themselves. He names excess, drunkenness and the worries of life as things that weigh down the heart, leaving people unprepared when the day arrives.

His response is watchfulness and prayer for strength to escape what is coming and stand before the Son of Man. The teaching directs His followers toward a way of living and depending on God while they wait.

Luke closes the chapter by describing Jesus’ pattern: teaching in the temple during the day, spending the night on the Mount of Olives and being heard by people who come early in the morning. The final teaching takes place within His continuing ministry as the Passover approaches.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand these verses as a call to spiritual alertness, prayer and a life that is ready to meet the Lord. Wesley takes the warning seriously even for established believers and describes watchfulness as the conclusion of the teaching; the following summary emphasizes listening to Jesus’ instruction. (Wesley on Luke 21:34–38)
passages.god_plan_html:
First Thessalonians connects wakefulness and sobriety with faith, love and hope, grounding that hope in Christ’s death so that His people may live with Him. The waiting community is called to encourage and build up one another. (1 Thessalonians 5:4–11)

First Peter likewise joins sober prayer to deep love, hospitality and using God-given abilities to serve others. These passages show the shared life that grows from readiness: dependence on God becomes care for people, with God glorified through Jesus Christ. (1 Peter 4:7–11)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 22:1-6
passages.section_title: How does the plan to arrest Jesus take shape?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now the Feast of Unleavened Bread, called the Passover, was approaching, 2 and the chief priests and scribes were looking for a way to put Jesus to death, for they feared the people. 3 Then Satan entered Judas Iscariot, who was one of the Twelve. 4 And Judas went to discuss with the chief priests and temple officers how he might betray Jesus to them. 5 They were delighted and agreed to give him money. 6 Judas consented, and began to look for an opportunity to betray Jesus to them in the absence of a crowd.
paragraphs: 1 Now the Feast of Unleavened Bread, called the Passover, was approaching, 2 and the chief priests and scribes were looking for a way to put Jesus to death, for they feared the people.

3 Then Satan entered Judas Iscariot, who was one of the Twelve. 4 And Judas went to discuss with the chief priests and temple officers how he might betray Jesus to them. 5 They were delighted and agreed to give him money. 6 Judas consented, and began to look for an opportunity to betray Jesus to them in the absence of a crowd.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Luke moves from Jesus’ public teaching to preparations for His death as the Feast of Unleavened Bread, called Passover, approaches. Leviticus distinguishes the Passover observance from the following seven-day feast; Luke uses the closely connected festival names together. (Leviticus 23:4–8)

The chief priests and scribes want to kill Jesus but fear the people. Judas, one of the Twelve, then approaches the leaders and temple officers. Luke says that Satan enters him, and also describes Judas agreeing to payment and looking for an opportunity away from the crowd.

The Greek verb behind betray is παραδίδωμι, paradidōmi (pah-rah-DEE-doh-mee), meaning to hand someone over. Thayer specifically includes Judas’ betrayal in Luke 22:4 and 6: he is arranging to deliver Jesus into the power of those who want to seize Him. (Thayer, Greek 3860)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly recognize both the evil at work in the betrayal and Judas’ willing involvement. Wesley emphasizes Satan’s action in a heart turned toward wrongdoing; the Catholic bishops’ notes place this scene within Luke’s account of Jesus facing the powers of evil as He goes toward His death. (Wesley on Luke 22:3; USCCB introduction to Luke 22–23)
passages.god_plan_html:
John records Jesus identifying the betrayal as a fulfillment of Scripture and telling His disciples beforehand so that what happens will strengthen their faith in Him. The betrayal is a real act of treachery within a story Jesus understands before it unfolds. (John 13:18–21, 26–27)

Acts later places Jesus’ death within God’s plan and foreknowledge while still describing those who kill Him as acting lawlessly. Its prayer names Herod, Pilate, Gentiles and people of Israel together, then speaks of God’s purpose being carried out. The larger picture holds human wrongdoing and God’s saving purpose together, ending in the resurrection the conspirators could not prevent. (Acts 2:22–24; Acts 4:27–28)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 22:7-13
passages.section_title: How is the Passover meal prepared?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 Then came the day of Unleavened Bread on which the Passover lamb was to be sacrificed. 8 Jesus sent Peter and John, saying, “Go and make preparations for us to eat the Passover.” 9 “Where do You want us to prepare it?” they asked. 10 He answered, “When you enter the city, a man carrying a jug of water will meet you. Follow him to the house he enters, 11 and say to the owner of that house, ‘The Teacher asks: Where is the guest room, where I may eat the Passover with My disciples?’ 12 And he will show you a large upper room, already furnished. Make preparations there.” 13 So they went and found it just as Jesus had told them. And they prepared the Passover.
paragraphs: 7 Then came the day of Unleavened Bread on which the Passover lamb was to be sacrificed. 8 Jesus sent Peter and John, saying, “Go and make preparations for us to eat the Passover.” 9 “Where do You want us to prepare it?” they asked.

10 He answered, “When you enter the city, a man carrying a jug of water will meet you. Follow him to the house he enters, 11 and say to the owner of that house, ‘The Teacher asks: Where is the guest room, where I may eat the Passover with My disciples?’ 12 And he will show you a large upper room, already furnished. Make preparations there.” 13 So they went and found it just as Jesus had told them. And they prepared the Passover.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The day arrives for the Passover sacrifice, and Jesus sends Peter and John to prepare the meal. They ask where He wants it made ready.

He gives them a sequence to follow: meet a man carrying a water jug, follow him to a house and ask its owner for the guest room where the Teacher may eat with His disciples. The owner will show them a large, furnished upper room.

They go, find things as Jesus has described and prepare the Passover. Luke’s focus falls on Jesus’ directions and their fulfillment as the meal is made ready.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see Jesus deliberately preparing for the meal and the suffering that follows. Calvin understands the detailed directions as a sign of His knowledge and willing action, and emphasizes the disciples’ readiness to follow His instruction. (Calvin on Luke 22:7–13 and Matthew 26:18–19)
passages.god_plan_html:
Exodus makes the Passover a memorial of God’s deliverance, with the blood as a sign of protection and the feast carried forward through the generations. Preparing this meal places Jesus and His disciples within that remembrance of rescue from Egypt. (Exodus 12:12–17)

Paul explicitly identifies Christ as the sacrificed Passover lamb and uses the removal of leaven to call believers away from malice and wickedness toward sincerity and truth. That gives a New Testament connection between the remembered deliverance, Jesus’ saving death and the life His people are to live in response. (1 Corinthians 5:6–8)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 22:14-23
passages.section_title: How does Jesus explain His coming death at this meal?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 When the hour had come, Jesus reclined at the table with His apostles. 15 And He said to them, “I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you before My suffering. 16 For I tell you that I will not eat it again until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God.” 17 After taking the cup, He gave thanks and said, “Take this and divide it among yourselves. 18 For I tell you that I will not drink of the fruit of the vine from now on until the kingdom of God comes.” 19 And He took the bread, gave thanks and broke it, and gave it to them, saying, “This is My body, given for you; do this in remembrance of Me.” 20 In the same way, after supper He took the cup, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in My blood, which is poured out for you. 21 Look! The hand of My betrayer is with Mine on the table. 22 Indeed, the Son of Man will go as it has been determined, but woe to that man who betrays Him.” 23 Then they began to question among themselves which of them was going to do this.
paragraphs: 14 When the hour had come, Jesus reclined at the table with His apostles. 15 And He said to them, “I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you before My suffering. 16 For I tell you that I will not eat it again until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God.” 17 After taking the cup, He gave thanks and said, “Take this and divide it among yourselves. 18 For I tell you that I will not drink of the fruit of the vine from now on until the kingdom of God comes.”

19 And He took the bread, gave thanks and broke it, and gave it to them, saying, “This is My body, given for you; do this in remembrance of Me.” 20 In the same way, after supper He took the cup, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in My blood, which is poured out for you.

21 Look! The hand of My betrayer is with Mine on the table. 22 Indeed, the Son of Man will go as it has been determined, but woe to that man who betrays Him.” 23 Then they began to question among themselves which of them was going to do this.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus reclines with the apostles and speaks of His eager desire to share this Passover before He suffers. He also looks toward its fulfillment in God’s kingdom. The coming suffering and the kingdom’s hope frame the meal.

Luke records Jesus sharing a cup, then giving bread with thanks and describing it as His body given for them. He tells them to do this in remembrance of Him. The cup after supper is identified with the new covenant in His blood, poured out for them.

Jesus also says that His betrayer’s hand is at the table. He holds together the path determined for the Son of Man and the warning of woe to the person who betrays Him. The disciples question among themselves who will do it.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians agree that Jesus connects the bread and cup with His body, blood and saving death. They differ over how Christ is present in the meal and how His sacrifice is remembered and shared.

The Catholic Church teaches that the bread and wine become Christ’s body and blood while their outward appearances remain. It also teaches that the Mass makes His one sacrifice present, rather than Jesus being killed again. (Catechism §§1362–1367, 1374–1377)

Lutheran teaching in the Small Catechism says that Christ’s true body and blood are received under the bread and wine. It connects forgiveness, life and salvation with His promise and calls the recipient to trust His words. (Small Catechism, Sacrament of the Altar)

The Orthodox Church in America’s teaching guide also affirms genuine communion with Christ’s body and blood through the Holy Spirit. It describes this as a mystery, and explains that symbolic language does not reduce the meal to thinking about an absent event. (OCA, Holy Eucharist)

Reformed churches following Westminster and Baptists following the 1689 Confession teach that the bread and wine remain bread and wine while believers truly receive Christ and the benefits of His death spiritually, through faith. These confessions describe real participation, beyond simply recalling information about the past. (Westminster Confession 29.5–7; 1689 Baptist Confession 30.5–7)

The Methodist Articles likewise describe receiving Christ spiritually through faith. Wesley’s notes on this passage explain the bread and cup as signs of His body and the blood establishing the covenant; those notes belong alongside the Articles’ teaching about participation. (Methodist Articles XVIII; Wesley on Luke 22:19–20)

Walvoord emphasizes the bread and cup as figures pointing to Christ and stresses the believer’s real union with Him rather than a physical change in the elements. This is a commentator’s reading, rather than a definition of what every Protestant church teaches. (Walvoord on Matthew’s parallel, 26:26–30)
passages.god_plan_html:
Jeremiah promises a new covenant with Israel and Judah, with God’s law written on hearts and sins forgiven. Hebrews repeats that promise and identifies Jesus as the One who brings this better covenant to His people. Jesus’ words over the cup therefore belong within God’s announced purpose to bring His people into a forgiven relationship with Him. (Jeremiah 31:31–34; Hebrews 8:6–13)

Hebrews also explains Christ’s own blood as securing redemption and His death as opening the promised inheritance under the new covenant. It describes His self-offering as once for all. That gives the larger meaning of His body given and blood poured out: His death brings cleansing, forgiveness and access to God. (Hebrews 9:11–15, 24–28; Hebrews 10:10–18)

Paul passes on the meal’s words to the church and says that sharing it proclaims the Lord’s death until He comes. He also connects the one loaf with the many believers forming one body. The remembrance shapes a people who share in Christ, care for one another and wait for His return. (1 Corinthians 11:23–34; 1 Corinthians 10:16–17)

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

passages.title: Luke 22:24-30
passages.section_title: What does greatness look like at Jesus’ table?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 24 A dispute also arose among the disciples as to which of them should be considered the greatest. 25 So Jesus declared, “The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those in authority over them call themselves benefactors. 26 But you shall not be like them. Instead, the greatest among you should be like the youngest, and the one who leads like the one who serves. 27 For who is greater, the one who reclines at the table or the one who serves? Is it not the one who reclines? But I am among you as one who serves. 28 You are the ones who have stood by Me in My trials. 29 And I bestow on you a kingdom, just as My Father has bestowed one on Me, 30 so that you may eat and drink at My table in My kingdom and sit on thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.
paragraphs: 24 A dispute also arose among the disciples as to which of them should be considered the greatest. 25 So Jesus declared, “The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those in authority over them call themselves benefactors. 26 But you shall not be like them. Instead, the greatest among you should be like the youngest, and the one who leads like the one who serves. 27 For who is greater, the one who reclines at the table or the one who serves? Is it not the one who reclines? But I am among you as one who serves.

28 You are the ones who have stood by Me in My trials. 29 And I bestow on you a kingdom, just as My Father has bestowed one on Me, 30 so that you may eat and drink at My table in My kingdom and sit on thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The disciples also dispute which of them should be considered greatest. Jesus contrasts their way of life with rulers who exercise mastery over others while calling themselves benefactors.

The Greek word is εὐεργέτης, euergetēs (yoo-er-GEH-tays). A benefactor is someone who helps others; Thayer also notes its use as a title of honor for rulers. Jesus contrasts the honored title with the example He gives: the greatest is to become like the youngest, and the leader like the person serving. (Thayer, Greek 2110)

He places Himself at the center of the lesson as the One serving among them. He then acknowledges those who have stood by Him in His trials and promises a place at His table and a share in the kingdom, including judging the twelve tribes of Israel.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand Jesus’ own service as the pattern for greatness among His followers. Wesley emphasizes doing good through service rather than domination, and reads the table and kingdom promises as the honor and joy Christ gives His faithful disciples, with a particular application to the apostles. (Wesley on Luke 22:25–30)
passages.god_plan_html:
John records Jesus washing His disciples’ feet and explicitly presenting His action as an example for them. Philippians places the same pattern within His whole saving work: He takes the servant’s place, humbles Himself to death on the cross and is exalted by God. The service He calls for reflects who the King is and how He gives Himself for His people. (John 13:1–17; Philippians 2:5–11)

Paul speaks of the saints judging the world, and Revelation describes people redeemed from every people and nation becoming a kingdom and priests who reign. These are supported connections with the shared future Jesus promises to His people. (1 Corinthians 6:1–3; Revelation 5:9–10)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 22:31-34
passages.section_title: What does Jesus promise before Peter fails?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 31 Simon, Simon, Satan has asked to sift all of you like wheat. 32 But I have prayed for you, Simon, that your faith will not fail. And when you have turned back, strengthen your brothers.” 33 “Lord,” said Peter, “I am ready to go with You even to prison and to death.” 34 But Jesus replied, “I tell you, Peter, the rooster will not crow today until you have denied three times that you know Me.”
paragraphs: 31 Simon, Simon, Satan has asked to sift all of you like wheat. 32 But I have prayed for you, Simon, that your faith will not fail. And when you have turned back, strengthen your brothers.”

33 “Lord,” said Peter, “I am ready to go with You even to prison and to death.” 34 But Jesus replied, “I tell you, Peter, the rooster will not crow today until you have denied three times that you know Me.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus addresses Simon Peter immediately after promising the disciples a place in His kingdom. That promise does not mean the coming hours will be easy. Satan has asked to shake their faith, and Peter will discover how little he understands his own weakness.

The first warning concerns all the disciples: the BSB makes this clear by translating all of you. Jesus then speaks personally to Simon about His prayer for him and the help he is to give his brothers after turning back. The move from the whole group to Peter is also noted in the USCCB’s explanation of the Greek pronouns. (Luke 22:31–32 notes)

Peter declares himself ready for prison and death. Jesus answers with a specific warning: before the rooster crows, Peter will deny three times that he knows Him. Jesus’ prayer and the command to strengthen others come before Peter’s failure, rather than after Peter has proved himself strong.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readers commonly see both a warning against self-confidence and hope for a disciple who fails. Wesley reads Jesus’ prayer as preserving Peter’s faith from complete collapse, and his return as preparing him to help others whose faith is weak. (Wesley on Luke 22:31–34)

Traditions differ over whether this commission also supports a continuing office of authority in the church. The Catholic Church applies the command to strengthen the brothers to the pope’s role as Peter’s successor. Vatican II cites this verse when explaining protection from error in definitive teaching on faith or morals by the pope as shepherd of the whole church. That defined teaching role is distinct from a claim that every personal remark or action is without error. (Lumen Gentium 25 and note 166)

Wesley’s notes focus instead on Peter returning from his failure and strengthening fellow believers. His reading does not draw the same conclusion about a continuing papal office. This is Wesley’s interpretation, rather than a claim that every Protestant explains every detail identically. (Wesley on Luke 22:32)
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus’ prayer for a disciple facing failure belongs within the wider New Testament teaching about His care for His people. Hebrews says that He lives to intercede for those who draw near to God through Him, and Romans describes the risen Christ speaking on their behalf at God’s right hand. Peter’s hope rests on the One praying for him, beyond Peter’s confidence in his own loyalty. (Hebrews 7:23–28; Romans 8:31–34)

After the resurrection, John records Jesus entrusting His sheep to Peter’s care. This is a supported connection with the task of strengthening his brothers: the disciple who will deny Jesus is still called to follow Him and care for His people. Failure is taken seriously, and restoration leads back into service. (John 21:15–19)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 22:35-38
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus warn His disciples to prepare for danger?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 35 Then Jesus asked them, “When I sent you out without purse or bag or sandals, did you lack anything?” “Nothing,” they answered. 36 “Now, however,” He told them, “the one with a purse should take it, and likewise a bag; and the one without a sword should sell his cloak and buy one. 37 For I tell you that this Scripture must be fulfilled in Me: ‘And He was numbered with the transgressors.’ For what is written about Me is reaching its fulfillment.” 38 So they said, “Look, Lord, here are two swords.” “That is enough,” He answered.
paragraphs: 35 Then Jesus asked them, “When I sent you out without purse or bag or sandals, did you lack anything?” “Nothing,” they answered. 36 “Now, however,” He told them, “the one with a purse should take it, and likewise a bag; and the one without a sword should sell his cloak and buy one.

37 For I tell you that this Scripture must be fulfilled in Me: ‘And He was numbered with the transgressors.’ For what is written about Me is reaching its fulfillment.” 38 So they said, “Look, Lord, here are two swords.” “That is enough,” He answered.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus asks the disciples to remember their earlier mission. When He sent them without purse, bag or sandals, they lacked nothing. He then warns of changed circumstances, speaking of taking supplies and buying a sword even at the cost of a cloak.

The reason He gives centers on His own coming suffering. Isaiah’s description of the Servant being counted among wrongdoers must be fulfilled in Him. His followers need to understand the danger ahead as their Teacher is treated as a criminal.

The disciples respond by pointing to two swords, and Jesus ends the exchange. Later in this same chapter, when a disciple uses a sword during His arrest, Jesus stops the violence and heals the injured man. The warning must be read alongside that action. (Luke 22:49–51)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Calvin and Wesley both read the sword language as a forceful warning of approaching danger, rather than an instruction to spread Jesus’ message by armed force. Calvin emphasizes the severe trials ahead; Wesley says the saying is not a literal requirement for each disciple to obtain a weapon. The USCCB’s notes likewise explain the exchange as preparing the disciples for hostility and regard their reply about two swords as taking the image literally. These sources broadly agree on that point, so a separate denominational breakdown would overstate their differences. (Calvin on Luke 22:35–38; Wesley on Luke 22:35–38; USCCB notes on Luke 22:36, 38)
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus Himself makes the connection with God’s announced purpose by applying Isaiah 53:12 to His coming suffering. In Isaiah, the Servant is counted with wrongdoers while bearing the sins of others and pleading for them. Being treated as a criminal does not mean Jesus has abandoned His mission; He identifies that rejection as part of what Scripture said He would face. (Isaiah 53:4–12)

Paul later uses the picture of armor and a sword to describe believers standing firm through truth, faith, God’s word and prayer. He also distinguishes the church’s struggle from warfare with ordinary weapons. This is a useful parallel for spiritual readiness, rather than proof that every object Jesus mentions here has a hidden meaning. His followers face opposition while depending on God to remain faithful. (Ephesians 6:10–20; 2 Corinthians 10:3–5)
