passages.title: Luke 22:39-46
passages.section_title: How does Jesus pray when obedience brings suffering?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 39 Jesus went out as usual to the Mount of Olives, and the disciples followed Him. 40 When He came to the place, He told them, “Pray that you will not enter into temptation.” 41 And He withdrew about a stone’s throw beyond them, where He knelt down and prayed, 42 “Father, if You are willing, take this cup from Me. Yet not My will, but Yours be done.” 43 Then an angel from heaven appeared to Him and strengthened Him. 44 And in His anguish, He prayed more earnestly, and His sweat became like drops of blood falling to the ground. 45 When Jesus rose from prayer and returned to the disciples, He found them asleep, exhausted from sorrow. 46 “Why are you sleeping?” He asked. “Get up and pray so that you will not enter into temptation.”
paragraphs: 39 Jesus went out as usual to the Mount of Olives, and the disciples followed Him. 40 When He came to the place, He told them, “Pray that you will not enter into temptation.” 41 And He withdrew about a stone’s throw beyond them, where He knelt down and prayed, 42 “Father, if You are willing, take this cup from Me. Yet not My will, but Yours be done.”

43 Then an angel from heaven appeared to Him and strengthened Him. 44 And in His anguish, He prayed more earnestly, and His sweat became like drops of blood falling to the ground. 45 When Jesus rose from prayer and returned to the disciples, He found them asleep, exhausted from sorrow. 46 “Why are you sleeping?” He asked. “Get up and pray so that you will not enter into temptation.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus goes to the Mount of Olives as He usually does, and His disciples follow. Before withdrawing to pray, He tells them to pray that they will not enter into temptation. That same instruction returns at the end of the scene.

He kneels and asks the Father to take the cup from Him if the Father is willing, while yielding His own will to the Father’s. An angel strengthens Him, and His prayer becomes more earnest in His anguish. The Greek word ἀγωνία, agōnia (ah-go-NEE-ah), describes severe inner struggle or anguish. His willing obedience carries a real cost. (Thayer, Greek 74)

Luke describes His sweat becoming like drops of blood falling to the ground. He then returns to disciples who are asleep from sorrow and again calls them to get up and pray. The BSB includes verses 43–44 in the main text and notes that some manuscripts omit them. (BSB text and footnote)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand this prayer as showing Jesus’ real human distress and willing obedience to the Father. The Catholic Catechism describes Him accepting His saving death in His human will; Wesley’s notes likewise take the anguish seriously and connect it with the weight of the suffering ahead. These readings share the central point that His obedience is willing and costly. (Catechism §612; Wesley on Luke 22:43–44)
passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews describes Jesus praying with cries and tears and learning obedience through suffering, before calling Him the source of eternal salvation. Philippians similarly traces His obedience to death on the cross and His exaltation by God. His prayer in the garden belongs within that willing obedience through which He carries out His saving work. (Hebrews 5:7–10; Philippians 2:5–11)

The cup also has a wider scriptural background. Isaiah uses a cup to describe God’s judgment, while John records Jesus describing His coming suffering as the cup the Father has given Him. Isaiah’s image helps explain why the cup is so weighty; John makes the connection with the Father’s will explicit. The comparison is supported by these passages, without assigning a hidden meaning to every detail in the garden. (Isaiah 51:17–23; John 18:10–11)

Hebrews also says that because Jesus Himself suffered when tempted, He is able to help those who are tempted. His call to the disciples to pray therefore sits alongside the assurance that their Savior understands suffering and can help them endure it. (Hebrews 2:17–18)
passages.current_position_html: Our study What Does Prayer Look Like? draws this lesson from Matthew’s account of the same prayer: bring fear and grief honestly to the Father, while surrendering the outcome to His will. Asking is not treated as wrong; what matters is that surrender governs the request. Repeated prayer can still be faithful when it continues in that surrender. Luke’s account shows the same combination of an honest request and willing obedience.

passages.title: Luke 22:47-53
passages.section_title: How does Jesus respond when betrayal turns into arrest?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 47 While He was still speaking, a crowd arrived, led by the man called Judas, one of the Twelve. He approached Jesus to kiss Him. 48 But Jesus asked him, “Judas, are you betraying the Son of Man with a kiss?” 49 Those around Jesus saw what was about to happen and said, “Lord, should we strike with our swords?” 50 And one of them struck the servant of the high priest, cutting off his right ear. 51 But Jesus answered, “No more of this!” And He touched the man’s ear and healed him. 52 Then Jesus said to the chief priests, temple officers, and elders who had come for Him, “Have you come out with swords and clubs as you would against an outlaw? 53 Every day I was with you in the temple courts, and you did not lay a hand on Me. But this hour belongs to you and to the power of darkness.”
paragraphs: 47 While He was still speaking, a crowd arrived, led by the man called Judas, one of the Twelve. He approached Jesus to kiss Him. 48 But Jesus asked him, “Judas, are you betraying the Son of Man with a kiss?”

49 Those around Jesus saw what was about to happen and said, “Lord, should we strike with our swords?” 50 And one of them struck the servant of the high priest, cutting off his right ear. 51 But Jesus answered, “No more of this!” And He touched the man’s ear and healed him.

52 Then Jesus said to the chief priests, temple officers, and elders who had come for Him, “Have you come out with swords and clubs as you would against an outlaw? 53 Every day I was with you in the temple courts, and you did not lay a hand on Me. But this hour belongs to you and to the power of darkness.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
A crowd arrives while Jesus is still speaking. Judas, one of the Twelve, leads them and approaches with a kiss. Jesus exposes the contradiction between that familiar gesture and the betrayal it is being used to carry out.

The disciples ask whether they should strike with their swords, and one cuts off the right ear of the high priest’s servant. Jesus stops the violence and heals him. John’s account identifies the disciple as Peter and the servant as Malchus. (John 18:10–11)

Jesus then addresses the chief priests, temple officers and elders who have come against Him. They bring swords and clubs as if He were leading a rebellion, although He taught openly in the temple without being seized. He identifies this moment as their hour and the power of darkness.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see Jesus refusing an armed rescue while continuing in willing obedience to the Father. His healing of the injured servant shows mercy even during His arrest. The Catholic Catechism describes His self-offering as freely given, and Wesley’s notes on this scene emphasize the final act of mercy and the limited hour granted to the powers opposing Him. (Catechism §614; Wesley on Luke 22:51–53)
passages.god_plan_html:
John’s account makes the connection with the garden prayer clear: Jesus tells Peter to put away his sword and accepts the cup the Father has given Him. His arrest begins the path He has already said fulfills Isaiah’s picture of the Servant counted among wrongdoers. The injustice done to Him and His willing obedience are both present. (John 18:10–11; Luke 22:37; Isaiah 53:7–12)

The wider New Testament shows where the apparent victory of darkness leads. Hebrews says that through death Jesus breaks the devil’s power over those held by fear of death. Colossians describes believers being rescued from the dominion of darkness into the Son’s kingdom, where there is redemption and forgiveness. These passages supply the larger connection: the darkness surrounding His arrest does not have the final word over His saving work. (Hebrews 2:14–15; Colossians 1:12–14)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 22:54-62
passages.section_title: What happens when Peter’s confidence gives way?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 54 Then they seized Jesus, led Him away, and took Him into the house of the high priest. And Peter followed at a distance. 55 When those present had kindled a fire in the middle of the courtyard and sat down together, Peter sat down among them. 56 A servant girl saw him seated in the firelight and looked intently at him. “This man also was with Him,” she said. 57 But Peter denied it. “Woman, I do not know Him,” he said. 58 A short time later, someone else saw him and said, “You also are one of them.” But Peter said, “Man, I am not.” 59 About an hour later, another man insisted, “Certainly this man was with Him, for he too is a Galilean.” 60 “Man, I do not know what you are talking about,” Peter replied. And immediately, while he was still speaking, the rooster crowed. 61 And the Lord turned and looked at Peter. Then Peter remembered the word that the Lord had spoken to him: “Before the rooster crows today, you will deny Me three times.” 62 And he went outside and wept bitterly.
paragraphs: 54 Then they seized Jesus, led Him away, and took Him into the house of the high priest. And Peter followed at a distance. 55 When those present had kindled a fire in the middle of the courtyard and sat down together, Peter sat down among them. 56 A servant girl saw him seated in the firelight and looked intently at him. “This man also was with Him,” she said. 57 But Peter denied it. “Woman, I do not know Him,” he said.

58 A short time later, someone else saw him and said, “You also are one of them.” But Peter said, “Man, I am not.” 59 About an hour later, another man insisted, “Certainly this man was with Him, for he too is a Galilean.” 60 “Man, I do not know what you are talking about,” Peter replied. And immediately, while he was still speaking, the rooster crowed.

61 And the Lord turned and looked at Peter. Then Peter remembered the word that the Lord had spoken to him: “Before the rooster crows today, you will deny Me three times.” 62 And he went outside and wept bitterly.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus is taken to the high priest’s house, and Peter follows at a distance. He joins people gathered around a courtyard fire. The disciple who said he was ready for prison and death now faces questions about whether he belongs to Jesus.

A servant girl identifies him as someone who was with Jesus. Another person says he belongs to the group, and about an hour later a man insists that his Galilean identity points to the same connection. Peter denies knowing Jesus or understanding the accusation.

The rooster crows while Peter is still speaking. Jesus turns and looks at him; Peter remembers the warning that he would deny Him three times. He goes outside and weeps bitterly. Luke brings the prediction and its fulfillment together through that remembered word.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see the scene as exposing the gap between Peter’s confident promise and his weakness under pressure. His tears express the grief that follows remembering Jesus’ warning. The USCCB’s note emphasizes the connection between Jesus’ look and Peter’s weeping, while Wesley notices the time that passed without Peter coming to his senses. (USCCB note on Luke 22:61; Wesley on Luke 22:59)
passages.god_plan_html:
Peter’s failure must be read alongside Jesus’ earlier prayer and command that he strengthen his brothers after returning. John later records Jesus calling Peter to care for His sheep, and Acts shows him publicly witnessing to Jesus’ resurrection. Those connections show a larger purpose beyond exposing Peter’s weakness: the disciple who denies Jesus is restored to serving His people. (Luke 22:31–34; John 21:15–19; Acts 2:22–36)

The contrast is especially clear in Acts. Peter, who denies knowing Jesus here, later declares openly that God raised Him from the dead and made Him Lord and Christ. The risen Jesus remains the center of that message; Peter’s failure does not become the final account of his relationship with Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 22:63-65
passages.section_title: What does the mockery of Jesus reveal?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 63 The men who were holding Jesus began to mock Him and beat Him. 64 They blindfolded Him and kept demanding, “Prophesy! Who hit You?” 65 And they said many other blasphemous things against Him.
paragraphs: 63 The men who were holding Jesus began to mock Him and beat Him. 64 They blindfolded Him and kept demanding, “Prophesy! Who hit You?” 65 And they said many other blasphemous things against Him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The men holding Jesus mock and beat Him. After blindfolding Him, they demand that He identify who struck Him. Their challenge turns the language of prophecy into a means of humiliation.

Luke describes their other words as blasphemous. The Greek verb is βλασφημέω, blasphēmeō (blas-fay-MEH-oh). Thayer explains it as speaking abusively or reviling, and also as speech that dishonors God or sacred things; Luke 22:65 is specifically listed. Here the speech accompanies the physical abuse of Jesus. (Thayer, Greek 987)

Luke places this abuse between Peter’s denial and the council gathering at daybreak. The short account keeps attention on what the captive Jesus suffers, without supplying the private thoughts of either Him or His captors.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readers commonly understand this scene as part of the innocent suffering and humiliation Jesus endures. Wesley also notices the irony: those who reject His identity dishonor Him with their own words, which Luke calls blasphemous. The passage exposes the conduct of these men without extending guilt to every member of their people. (Wesley on Luke 22:64–65)
passages.god_plan_html:
Isaiah’s obedient Servant offers His back to those who strike Him and does not hide His face from contempt. That is a supported scriptural parallel with the abuse Jesus suffers here. Isaiah also looks to God for help and vindication, so the suffering is not the whole story. (Isaiah 50:4–9)

Peter later describes Christ enduring abuse without retaliation and entrusting Himself to the One who judges justly. He connects that suffering both with Christ bearing our sins and with an example for His followers. The humiliation therefore belongs within His saving self-giving and the pattern of faithful endurance He leaves His people. (1 Peter 2:21–25)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 22:66-71
passages.section_title: Who does Jesus say He is before the council?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 66 At daybreak the council of the elders of the people, both the chief priests and scribes, met together. They led Jesus into their Sanhedrin and said, 67 “If You are the Christ, tell us.” Jesus answered, “If I tell you, you will not believe. 68 And if I ask you a question, you will not answer. 69 But from now on the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God.” 70 So they all asked, “Are You then the Son of God?” He replied, “You say that I am.” 71 “Why do we need any more testimony?” they declared. “We have heard it for ourselves from His own lips.”
paragraphs: 66 At daybreak the council of the elders of the people, both the chief priests and scribes, met together. They led Jesus into their Sanhedrin and said, 67 “If You are the Christ, tell us.” Jesus answered, “If I tell you, you will not believe. 68 And if I ask you a question, you will not answer. 69 But from now on the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God.”
70 So they all asked, “Are You then the Son of God?” He replied, “You say that I am.” 71 “Why do we need any more testimony?” they declared. “We have heard it for ourselves from His own lips.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
At daybreak the elders, chief priests and scribes gather and bring Jesus before their council. They ask Him to say whether He is the Christ. He answers that they will not believe His answer or respond to His question.

Jesus then declares that the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of God’s power. That moves the scene beyond the authority of the people questioning Him: the captive standing before them speaks of the place He will hold beside God.

They ask whether He is therefore the Son of God. He replies that they say He is, and they treat His own words as sufficient testimony. Luke closes the chapter with their response; the next chapter follows them taking Him to Pilate.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian traditions commonly read Jesus’ words about God’s right hand as a claim to heavenly honor and authority, fulfilled in His exaltation. The Catholic Catechism connects that place with the Son’s divine glory and the Messiah’s kingdom; the Westminster Confession likewise describes the risen Jesus ascending to the Father’s right hand. Those documents share this central reading, without settling every question about the kingdom’s timing in the same way. (Catechism §§663–664; Westminster Confession 8.4)
passages.god_plan_html:
The place at God’s right hand points to Psalm 110, where David’s Lord is invited to sit beside God until His enemies are subdued. The title Son of Man also recalls Daniel’s vision of One who approaches the Ancient of Days and receives an everlasting kingdom embracing every people and language. These passages explain the authority claimed by the One standing before the council. (Psalm 110:1–2; Daniel 7:13–14)

Acts makes the first connection explicit. Peter applies Psalm 110 to the risen and exalted Jesus, and Stephen later sees the Son of Man at God’s right hand. Luke’s account of Jesus’ hearing thus looks ahead to the witness His followers will bear after His resurrection. (Acts 2:32–36; Acts 7:54–60)

Hebrews joins that exaltation to His saving work: after providing cleansing for sins, the Son sits at the right hand of God’s majesty. The leaders’ rejection is therefore held within the larger story of the Son who brings cleansing and reigns in honor beside the Father. (Hebrews 1:1–4)

deeper_study.title: Who is The Angel of the Lord?

passages.title: Luke 23:1-5
passages.section_title: What accusation is brought before Pilate?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then the whole council rose and led Jesus away to Pilate. 2 And they began to accuse Him, saying, “We found this man subverting our nation, forbidding payment of taxes to Caesar, and proclaiming Himself to be Christ, a King.” 3 So Pilate asked Him, “Are You the King of the Jews?” “You have said so,” Jesus replied. 4 Then Pilate said to the chief priests and the crowds, “I find no basis for a charge against this man.” 5 But they kept insisting, “He stirs up the people all over Judea with His teaching. He began in Galilee and has come all the way here.”
paragraphs: 1 Then the whole council rose and led Jesus away to Pilate. 2 And they began to accuse Him, saying, “We found this man subverting our nation, forbidding payment of taxes to Caesar, and proclaiming Himself to be Christ, a King.” 3 So Pilate asked Him, “Are You the King of the Jews?” “You have said so,” Jesus replied.

4 Then Pilate said to the chief priests and the crowds, “I find no basis for a charge against this man.” 5 But they kept insisting, “He stirs up the people all over Judea with His teaching. He began in Galilee and has come all the way here.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The council takes Jesus to Pilate and presents accusations that concern Roman rule: stirring up the nation, opposing taxes to Caesar and claiming to be Christ, a king. The charge about taxes conflicts with Jesus’ earlier instruction to give Caesar what belongs to Caesar. (Luke 20:20–26)

Pilate is the Roman governor of Judea. Josephus independently places him in the succession of Roman officials governing the region, after Valerius Gratus. The hearing therefore moves from the council’s questions about Jesus’ identity to accusations before the governing Roman authority. (Josephus, Antiquities 18.2.2)

Pilate asks whether Jesus is the King of the Jews. Jesus answers that Pilate has said so. Pilate then says he finds no basis for a charge against Him. The accusers persist, emphasizing the reach of His teaching from Galilee into Judea.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see Luke emphasizing Jesus’ innocence before the Roman authority. The USCCB’s notes trace that emphasis across Pilate’s repeated declarations, while Wesley explains that Pilate finds no attempt against Caesar in Jesus’ defense. The accusations and the governor’s finding are kept distinct. (USCCB note on Luke 23:1–5, 13–25; Wesley on Luke 23:4)
passages.god_plan_html:
John’s account gives more of Jesus’ answer about kingship. He explains that His kingdom does not come from this world and that His servants are not fighting to prevent His arrest. He also says that He came to bear witness to the truth. The King stands before a governor, yet the source and purpose of His kingdom extend beyond the political threat His accusers describe. (John 18:33–38)

Paul later points specifically to Jesus’ testimony before Pontius Pilate when charging Timothy to remain faithful until Christ appears. This hearing becomes an example of faithful witness for those who follow Him. God’s purpose advances through the King’s truthful testimony even while human authorities judge Him. (1 Timothy 6:11–16)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 23:6-12
passages.section_title: What does Herod want from Jesus?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 When Pilate heard this, he asked if the man was a Galilean. 7 And learning that Jesus was under Herod’s jurisdiction, he sent Him to Herod, who himself was in Jerusalem at that time. 8 When Herod saw Jesus, he was greatly pleased. He had wanted to see Him for a long time, because he had heard about Him and was hoping to see Him perform a miracle. 9 Herod questioned Jesus at great length, but He gave no answer. 10 Meanwhile, the chief priests and scribes stood there, vehemently accusing Him. 11 And even Herod and his soldiers ridiculed and mocked Him. Dressing Him in a fine robe, they sent Him back to Pilate. 12 That day Herod and Pilate became friends; before this time they had been enemies.
paragraphs: 6 When Pilate heard this, he asked if the man was a Galilean. 7 And learning that Jesus was under Herod’s jurisdiction, he sent Him to Herod, who himself was in Jerusalem at that time.

8 When Herod saw Jesus, he was greatly pleased. He had wanted to see Him for a long time, because he had heard about Him and was hoping to see Him perform a miracle. 9 Herod questioned Jesus at great length, but He gave no answer. 10 Meanwhile, the chief priests and scribes stood there, vehemently accusing Him.

11 And even Herod and his soldiers ridiculed and mocked Him. Dressing Him in a fine robe, they sent Him back to Pilate. 12 That day Herod and Pilate became friends; before this time they had been enemies.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The mention of Galilee leads Pilate to ask whether Jesus is a Galilean. Learning that He falls under Herod’s jurisdiction, Pilate sends Him to Herod, who is also in Jerusalem. This is Herod Antipas, the ruler of Galilee already introduced in Luke. Josephus likewise describes the Galilean tetrarch and his city of Tiberias. (Luke 3:1; Josephus, Antiquities 18.2.3)

Herod is pleased because he has long wanted to see Jesus perform a miracle. He questions Him at length, but Jesus gives no answer. The chief priests and scribes continue their accusations.

Herod and his soldiers then mock Jesus, dress Him in a fine robe and send Him back to Pilate. Luke says that the two rulers become friends that day, having previously been enemies. The account tells us that their relationship changes, while leaving the earlier cause of their hostility unexplained.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readers commonly distinguish Herod’s curiosity about miracles from trust in Jesus. The USCCB’s notes make that distinction explicitly, and Wesley describes Herod’s interest as curiosity rather than a response of faith. The scene also shows Jesus enduring ridicule without providing the spectacle Herod wants. (USCCB note on Luke 23:6–12; Wesley on Luke 23:8–11)
passages.god_plan_html:
Acts directly names Herod and Pontius Pilate when the church prays about the opposition Jesus faced. The believers connect the rulers’ actions with Psalm 2, which describes rulers gathering against the Lord and His Anointed. They also say that these actions took place within God’s saving purpose. The friendship formed over Jesus’ humiliation does not put His mission outside God’s care. (Acts 4:23–28)

The church then asks for boldness to speak God’s word amid continuing threats. Its response carries the connection forward: remembering what happened to Jesus strengthens His followers to bear witness, rather than requiring every ruler to welcome them first. (Acts 4:29–31)

deeper_study.title: Should We Seek Signs From God?

passages.title: Luke 23:13-25
passages.section_title: Why is Barabbas released while Jesus is condemned?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 Then Pilate called together the chief priests, the rulers, and the people, 14 and said to them, “You brought me this man as one who was inciting the people to rebellion. I have examined Him here in your presence and found Him not guilty of your charges against Him. 15 Neither has Herod, for he sent Him back to us. As you can see, He has done nothing deserving of death. 16 Therefore I will punish Him and release Him.” 18 But they all cried out in unison: “Away with this man! Release Barabbas to us!” 19 (Barabbas had been imprisoned for an insurrection in the city, and for murder.) 20 Wanting to release Jesus, Pilate addressed them again, 21 but they kept shouting, “Crucify Him! Crucify Him!” 22 A third time he said to them, “What evil has this man done? I have found in Him no offense worthy of death. So after I punish Him, I will release Him.” 23 But they were insistent, demanding with loud voices for Jesus to be crucified. And their clamor prevailed. 24 So Pilate sentenced that their demand be met. 25 As they had requested, he released the one imprisoned for insurrection and murder, and he handed Jesus over to their will.
paragraphs: 13 Then Pilate called together the chief priests, the rulers, and the people, 14 and said to them, “You brought me this man as one who was inciting the people to rebellion. I have examined Him here in your presence and found Him not guilty of your charges against Him. 15 Neither has Herod, for he sent Him back to us. As you can see, He has done nothing deserving of death. 16 Therefore I will punish Him and release Him.”

18 But they all cried out in unison: “Away with this man! Release Barabbas to us!” 19 (Barabbas had been imprisoned for an insurrection in the city, and for murder.) 20 Wanting to release Jesus, Pilate addressed them again, 21 but they kept shouting, “Crucify Him! Crucify Him!” 22 A third time he said to them, “What evil has this man done? I have found in Him no offense worthy of death. So after I punish Him, I will release Him.”

23 But they were insistent, demanding with loud voices for Jesus to be crucified. And their clamor prevailed. 24 So Pilate sentenced that their demand be met. 25 As they had requested, he released the one imprisoned for insurrection and murder, and he handed Jesus over to their will.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Pilate gathers the leaders and people and again states that he has found Jesus innocent of the charges. He also points to Herod returning Him without a finding that deserves death. Yet Pilate proposes to punish Jesus before releasing Him, even while declaring Him innocent.

The crowd demands Barabbas instead. Luke identifies him as a prisoner involved in insurrection and murder. Pilate wants to release Jesus and speaks again, but the demand for crucifixion continues. His third declaration that Jesus has done nothing deserving death does not stop the pressure.

Pilate finally grants their demand, releases Barabbas and hands Jesus over. Luke’s contrast is direct: the man imprisoned for rebellion and murder goes free, while the man declared innocent is delivered to death. Pilate makes the decision; his statements about innocence do not remove his part in the outcome.

The BSB places verse 17, about releasing a prisoner at the feast, in a footnote rather than its main text. The numbering here follows that text. (BSB footnote)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see both Jesus’ innocence and the injustice of the decision. Wesley highlights Pilate’s three declarations that Jesus is innocent, and the USCCB’s notes likewise identify this repeated finding as a major feature of Luke’s account. The scene does not present the released prisoner’s later beliefs or actions. (Wesley on Luke 23:16–22; USCCB note on Luke 23:1–5, 13–25)
passages.god_plan_html:
Peter later recalls this very contrast: Jesus was rejected before Pilate and a murderer was requested in His place. He then proclaims that God raised the Author of life from the dead and calls his hearers to repent so their sins may be wiped away. The injustice is named honestly, and the message still opens the way to forgiveness. (Acts 3:13–21)

The innocent Jesus condemned while a guilty prisoner goes free also provides a striking parallel with Peter’s teaching that Christ suffered for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring people to God. That wider teaching explains His saving purpose. The parallel does not tell us whether Barabbas personally came to faith; Luke does not answer that question. (1 Peter 3:17–18)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 23:26-31
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus tell the women to weep for themselves?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 26 As the soldiers led Him away, they seized Simon of Cyrene on his way in from the country, and they put the cross on him to carry behind Jesus. 27 A great number of people followed Him, including women who kept mourning and wailing for Him. 28 But Jesus turned to them and said, “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for Me, but weep for yourselves and for your children. 29 Look, the days are coming when people will say, ‘Blessed are the barren women, the wombs that never bore, and breasts that never nursed!’ 30 At that time ‘they will say to the mountains, “Fall on us!” and to the hills, “Cover us!”’ 31 For if men do these things while the tree is green, what will happen when it is dry?”
paragraphs: 26 As the soldiers led Him away, they seized Simon of Cyrene on his way in from the country, and they put the cross on him to carry behind Jesus. 27 A great number of people followed Him, including women who kept mourning and wailing for Him.

28 But Jesus turned to them and said, “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for Me, but weep for yourselves and for your children. 29 Look, the days are coming when people will say, ‘Blessed are the barren women, the wombs that never bore, and breasts that never nursed!’ 30 At that time ‘they will say to the mountains, “Fall on us!” and to the hills, “Cover us!”’ 31 For if men do these things while the tree is green, what will happen when it is dry?”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Simon of Cyrene is seized on his way in from the country and made to carry the cross behind Jesus. A large crowd follows, including women mourning for Him.

Jesus turns to the women of Jerusalem and directs their concern toward themselves and their children. He warns of coming days so terrible that having no children will be considered a blessing. Their present grief points toward a greater distress still ahead.

He uses Hosea’s language of people asking the mountains and hills to cover them, then adds the picture of green and dry wood. The question presses the seriousness of what is coming: if this is happening now, what will happen under conditions represented by the dry wood?
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly take Jesus’ words as a warning that reaches beyond His immediate suffering to coming judgment. Wesley explains the green wood in relation to the innocent Jesus and the dry wood in relation to those facing judgment; the USCCB’s notes connect this warning with Jesus’ earlier grief over Jerusalem. These readings agree on the warning’s seriousness. (Wesley on Luke 23:30–31; USCCB notes on Luke 23:26–32 and cross references)
passages.god_plan_html:
Simon carrying the cross behind Jesus gives a visible parallel with Jesus’ earlier call for disciples to take up their cross and follow Him. Luke does not tell us whether Simon had already chosen discipleship, so the connection concerns the picture of following, rather than a claim about his conversion. (Luke 9:23–26)

Hosea’s original warning concerns Israel’s false worship, guilt and coming devastation, including exile to Assyria. Jesus uses its language to warn Jerusalem about approaching distress. Revelation later uses the same picture of people seeking shelter beneath mountains in the face of judgment. These are supported connections in the Bible’s wider warning that human power and hiding places cannot finally shield people from God’s judgment. (Hosea 10:1–15; Revelation 6:12–17)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 23:32-38
passages.section_title: What kind of King remains on the cross?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 32 Two others, who were criminals, were also led away to be executed with Jesus. 33 When they came to the place called The Skull, they crucified Him there, along with the criminals, one on His right and the other on His left. 34 Then Jesus said, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” And they divided up His garments by casting lots. 35 The people stood watching, and the rulers sneered at Him, saying, “He saved others; let Him save Himself if He is the Christ of God, the Chosen One.” 36 The soldiers also mocked Him and came up to offer Him sour wine. 37 “If You are the King of the Jews,” they said, “save Yourself!” 38 Above Him was posted an inscription: THIS IS THE KING OF THE JEWS.
paragraphs: 32 Two others, who were criminals, were also led away to be executed with Jesus. 33 When they came to the place called The Skull, they crucified Him there, along with the criminals, one on His right and the other on His left. 34 Then Jesus said, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” And they divided up His garments by casting lots.

35 The people stood watching, and the rulers sneered at Him, saying, “He saved others; let Him save Himself if He is the Christ of God, the Chosen One.” 36 The soldiers also mocked Him and came up to offer Him sour wine. 37 “If You are the King of the Jews,” they said, “save Yourself!” 38 Above Him was posted an inscription: THIS IS THE KING OF THE JEWS.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus is led away with two criminals and crucified between them at the place called The Skull. The Greek word κρανίον, kranion (krah-NEE-on), means skull. Thayer lists its use here and in the other Gospel accounts of this place. (Thayer, Greek 2898)

He asks the Father to forgive those acting in ignorance while His garments are divided by casting lots. The BSB includes this prayer and notes that some manuscripts omit it. (BSB text and footnotes)

The rulers and soldiers challenge Him to save Himself if He is God’s Christ or the King of the Jews. Above Him, the inscription identifies Him as that King. Their challenge measures His identity by escape from the cross, while the account presents Him enduring it.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see the contrast between Jesus’ mercy and the mockery surrounding Him. Wesley notices that the rulers ridicule His claim as Messiah while the soldiers ridicule His kingship; His prayer seeks the good of the people doing Him harm. (Wesley on Luke 23:34–38)
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus has already applied Isaiah’s description of the Servant counted among wrongdoers to His own coming suffering. Now He is executed between criminals. Isaiah also describes the Servant bearing others’ sins and interceding for wrongdoers, which provides a supported connection with the prayer offered here. (Luke 22:37; Isaiah 53:11–12)

The dividing of His garments recalls the suffering speaker in Psalm 22, whose clothing is divided by lot and whose trust in God is mocked. The psalm moves from distress toward God’s deliverance and worship among the nations. That larger movement helps place the humiliation within the hope of God’s saving work. (Psalm 22:7–8, 18, 22–31)

Hebrews explicitly connects Jesus’ suffering outside the city gate with the sin-offering bodies burned outside Israel’s camp. Leviticus distinguishes those sacrificed animals from the live goat that carries away the people’s sins. Both images help readers see the cost of cleansing and the removal of sin, while Hebrews itself makes the outside-the-gate connection. It then calls believers to go to Jesus and share His disgrace. (Hebrews 13:10–16; Leviticus 16:20–28)
passages.current_position_html: Our study What Does Prayer Look Like? reads Jesus’ prayer for forgiveness as intercession entrusted to the Father. Jesus brings those responsible for His death before God in mercy. The lesson we draw is to pray for others while leaving the outcome with the Father. This position concerns the prayer in verse 34; it does not supply a separate conclusion on every detail of the crucifixion scene.

passages.title: Luke 23:34
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus pray for forgiveness from the cross?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 34 Then Jesus said, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” And they divided up His garments by casting lots.
paragraphs: 34 Then Jesus said, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” And they divided up His garments by casting lots.

passages.context_html:
This verse belongs to the crucifixion account in Luke 23:32–38. Jesus has been placed between two criminals, and His garments are being divided. He addresses the Father in a prayer for the forgiveness of those who do not know what they are doing. (Read the surrounding passage)

Their ignorance does not turn the crucifixion into a good act. It is the condition Jesus brings before the Father as He seeks mercy for them. The verse places His prayer beside the dividing of His clothing, holding His intercession and their actions together.

The BSB includes the prayer in its main text and notes that some manuscripts omit it. The whole verse is retained here, including the dividing of the garments. (BSB text and footnote)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand the prayer as mercy toward those responsible for Jesus’ suffering. Wesley emphasizes His concern for their salvation, and the Catholic Catechism connects His prayer and the people’s ignorance while rejecting collective blame against Jews as a whole or in later generations. (Wesley on Luke 23:34; Catechism §597)
passages.current_position_html: Our study What Does Prayer Look Like? reads Jesus’ prayer for forgiveness as intercession entrusted to the Father. Jesus brings those responsible for His death before God in mercy. The lesson we draw is to pray for others while leaving the outcome with the Father.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Isaiah’s Servant bears the sin of many and intercedes for wrongdoers. Jesus’ prayer is a supported parallel with that description: His saving work includes seeking mercy for people who are doing wrong, rather than only displaying their guilt. (Isaiah 53:11–12)

Jesus has also taught His followers to love their enemies and pray for those who mistreat them. Acts records Stephen praying that the sin of his killers not be held against them. Stephen’s prayer is a clear parallel with Jesus’ example, showing how the mercy seen at the cross shapes the people who follow Him. (Luke 6:27–36; Acts 7:54–60)

passages.title: Luke 23:39-43
passages.section_title: What hope does Jesus give the criminal beside Him?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 39 One of the criminals who hung there heaped abuse on Him. “Are You not the Christ?” he said. “Save Yourself and us!” 40 But the other one rebuked him, saying, “Do you not even fear God, since you are under the same judgment? 41 We are punished justly, for we are receiving what our actions deserve. But this man has done nothing wrong.” 42 Then he said, “Jesus, remember me when You come into Your kingdom!” 43 And Jesus said to him, “Truly I tell you, today you will be with Me in Paradise.”
paragraphs: 39 One of the criminals who hung there heaped abuse on Him. “Are You not the Christ?” he said. “Save Yourself and us!” 40 But the other one rebuked him, saying, “Do you not even fear God, since you are under the same judgment? 41 We are punished justly, for we are receiving what our actions deserve. But this man has done nothing wrong.”
42 Then he said, “Jesus, remember me when You come into Your kingdom!” 43 And Jesus said to him, “Truly I tell you, today you will be with Me in Paradise.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
One of the criminals joins the abuse directed at Jesus and calls on Him to save Himself and them. The other challenges him, acknowledges that their own punishment is deserved and declares that Jesus has done nothing wrong.

He then asks Jesus to remember him when He comes into His kingdom. Jesus answers with the promise that he will be with Him in Paradise. Even while facing death, Jesus speaks as the One who can welcome this man into life with Him.

The Greek word is παράδεισος, paradeisos (pah-RAH-day-soss). Thayer traces its use from a garden or park to the blessed dwelling of God’s people. Its other New Testament uses are Paul’s account of being caught up to Paradise and Jesus’ promise of the tree of life in God’s Paradise. (Thayer, Greek 3857; 2 Corinthians 12:2–4; Revelation 2:7)
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly see repentance, faith and Jesus’ mercy in this exchange. Wesley emphasizes the man’s acknowledgment of sin, defense of Jesus and trust in His kingdom. (Wesley on Luke 23:39–43)

Traditions differ over the timing of the promised life with Christ. The Catholic Catechism cites Jesus’ words to this man when teaching about a person’s destiny immediately after death. Reformed teaching in Westminster likewise holds that the righteous are with God after death while awaiting bodily resurrection. Wesley reads Jesus as promising the man a place with Him that very day. (Catechism §§1021–1022; Westminster Confession 32.1; Wesley on Luke 23:43)

Seventh-day Adventist teaching holds that the dead are unconscious until resurrection. An explanation published by its Biblical Research Institute reads the reference to today as emphasizing when Jesus gives the promise, with life in Paradise fulfilled after resurrection. That is the author’s explanation within the church’s stated teaching about death. The BSB text printed above retains its own wording and punctuation. (Adventist Belief 26; Biblical Research Institute, What Jesus Told the Thief)
passages.god_plan_html:
The promise of Paradise reaches into the Bible’s larger story of life with God. Genesis describes humanity losing access to the tree of life after sin. Revelation promises the tree of life in God’s Paradise and finally pictures God’s people seeing His face, with the curse removed. These passages form a supported connection between the hope Jesus gives this dying man and God’s purpose to restore His people to life in His presence. (Genesis 3:22–24; Revelation 2:7; Revelation 22:1–5)

The center of Jesus’ promise is being with Him. The criminal asks to be remembered in the kingdom, and Jesus gives personal assurance of belonging with its King. His saving work reaches a guilty man who turns to Him while both are facing death.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 23:44-49
passages.section_title: How does Jesus entrust Himself to the Father as He dies?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 44 It was now about the sixth hour, and darkness came over all the land until the ninth hour. 45 The sun was darkened, and the veil of the temple was torn down the middle. 46 Then Jesus called out in a loud voice, “Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit.” And when He had said this, He breathed His last. 47 When the centurion saw what had happened, he gave glory to God, saying, “Surely this was a righteous man.” 48 And when all the people who had gathered for this spectacle saw what had happened, they returned home beating their breasts. 49 But all those who knew Jesus, including the women who had followed Him from Galilee, stood at a distance watching these things.
paragraphs: 44 It was now about the sixth hour, and darkness came over all the land until the ninth hour. 45 The sun was darkened, and the veil of the temple was torn down the middle. 46 Then Jesus called out in a loud voice, “Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit.” And when He had said this, He breathed His last.

47 When the centurion saw what had happened, he gave glory to God, saying, “Surely this was a righteous man.” 48 And when all the people who had gathered for this spectacle saw what had happened, they returned home beating their breasts. 49 But all those who knew Jesus, including the women who had followed Him from Galilee, stood at a distance watching these things.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Darkness covers the land from about noon until three in the afternoon, and the temple curtain is torn down the middle. These signs frame Jesus’ final prayer and death. The BSB’s footnote explains the sixth and ninth hours using those times. (BSB text and footnotes)

Jesus calls out loudly and entrusts His Spirit to the Father, using the words of Psalm 31:5. After saying this, He breathes His last. His final address continues the trust expressed in His prayer in the garden. (Psalm 31:1–5)

The centurion gives glory to God and declares Jesus righteous. The crowd leaves beating their breasts, while those who knew Him, including the women from Galilee, watch from a distance. Luke closes the scene with these differing responses to His death.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand this as the real death of the innocent Jesus, who entrusts Himself to the Father. Wesley points to the Father receiving His Spirit, and the Westminster Confession includes His suffering, death and burial in its account of His saving work. (Wesley on Luke 23:46–47; Westminster Confession 8.4)
passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews explains that Jesus’ blood opens the way for His people to draw near to God, using the image of a way through the curtain of His body. That is the New Testament’s own connection between His self-offering and access to God. The torn curtain at His death can be read alongside that teaching about cleansing, a great priest and confidence to approach the Father. (Hebrews 10:19–25)

His final prayer also stands within the scriptural pattern of entrusting life to God: Psalm 31 addresses God as refuge and Redeemer. Acts later records Stephen entrusting his spirit to the risen Lord Jesus as he dies. That is a supported parallel showing Christ’s followers depending on Him in the way His own prayer expresses trust in the Father. (Psalm 31:1–5; Acts 7:59–60)
passages.current_position_html: Our study What Does Prayer Look Like? understands Jesus’ final prayer as surrender of Himself into the Father’s care. He entrusts His Spirit to the Father at the moment of death. The lesson concerns trust carried through suffering to the end. This is our position on the prayer in verse 46; it does not settle every detail of the surrounding signs.

passages.title: Luke 23:46
passages.section_title: What does Jesus’ final prayer show about trust?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 46 Then Jesus called out in a loud voice, “Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit.” And when He had said this, He breathed His last.
paragraphs: 46 Then Jesus called out in a loud voice, “Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit.” And when He had said this, He breathed His last.

passages.context_html:
This verse is part of Luke 23:44–49, after the darkness and tearing of the temple curtain. Jesus calls out loudly to the Father, commits His Spirit into His hands and breathes His last. (Read the surrounding passage)

His words draw from Psalm 31:5, a prayer to the Lord as refuge, deliverer and faithful God. Luke records Jesus continuing to address God as Father at the point of death. (Psalm 31:1–5)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readers commonly understand the words as an expression of willing trust in the Father at death. Wesley connects the Father receiving Jesus’ Spirit with Jesus Himself receiving the spirits of His faithful people. (Wesley on Luke 23:46)
passages.current_position_html: Our study What Does Prayer Look Like? understands Jesus’ final prayer as surrender of Himself into the Father’s care. He entrusts His Spirit to the Father at the moment of death. The lesson concerns trust carried through suffering to the end.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The prayer brings the trust of Psalm 31 into Jesus’ own suffering. The psalm calls on God as a secure refuge and places life in His hands. Jesus draws on that prayer as He carries His obedience through death. (Psalm 31:1–5)

Acts records Stephen entrusting his spirit to the Lord Jesus while he is being killed. This is a clear parallel with Jesus’ final prayer: those who belong to Him can place themselves in His care as they face death. The One who entrusted Himself to the Father is now addressed as the risen Lord who receives His servant. (Acts 7:54–60)

passages.title: Luke 23:50-56
passages.section_title: Who cares for Jesus’ body after His death?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 50 Now there was a Council member named Joseph, a good and righteous man, 51 who had not consented to their decision or action. He was from the Judean town of Arimathea and was waiting for the kingdom of God. 52 He went to Pilate to ask for the body of Jesus. 53 Then he took it down, wrapped it in a linen cloth, and placed it in a tomb cut into the rock, where no one had yet been laid. 54 It was Preparation Day, and the Sabbath was beginning. 55 The women who had come with Jesus from Galilee followed, and they saw the tomb and how His body was placed. 56 Then they returned to prepare spices and perfumes. And they rested on the Sabbath, according to the commandment.
paragraphs: 50 Now there was a Council member named Joseph, a good and righteous man, 51 who had not consented to their decision or action. He was from the Judean town of Arimathea and was waiting for the kingdom of God. 52 He went to Pilate to ask for the body of Jesus. 53 Then he took it down, wrapped it in a linen cloth, and placed it in a tomb cut into the rock, where no one had yet been laid.

54 It was Preparation Day, and the Sabbath was beginning. 55 The women who had come with Jesus from Galilee followed, and they saw the tomb and how His body was placed. 56 Then they returned to prepare spices and perfumes. And they rested on the Sabbath, according to the commandment.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Joseph of Arimathea is a member of the council, but Luke carefully distinguishes him from its decision and action against Jesus. He describes him as good and righteous, waiting for God’s kingdom.

Joseph asks Pilate for Jesus’ body, takes it down, wraps it in linen and places it in a tomb cut into rock where no one has yet been laid. The burial takes place on Preparation Day as the Sabbath is beginning.

The women from Galilee follow and see the tomb and how His body is placed. They prepare spices and perfumes, then rest on the Sabbath according to the commandment. Their observation connects this burial directly with the tomb they will visit in the next chapter.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand this as Jesus’ actual burial following His actual death, and as the setting for the resurrection account that follows. The Westminster Confession includes burial between death and resurrection, affirming that He rises in the same body in which He suffered. (Westminster Confession 8.4)
passages.god_plan_html:
Isaiah describes the Servant being assigned a grave with the wicked and being with a rich man in His death. Matthew identifies Joseph as a rich disciple and says he places Jesus in his own new tomb. Together, these passages provide a supported connection between this burial and Isaiah’s picture of the suffering Servant. (Isaiah 53:9; Matthew 27:57–61)

Paul includes Christ’s burial within the message he received and passed on: Christ died for sins, was buried and was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures. The care taken with Jesus’ body therefore belongs within the gospel’s account of death overcome through resurrection. (1 Corinthians 15:3–8)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 24:1-12
passages.section_title: Why is Jesus’ tomb empty?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 On the first day of the week, very early in the morning, the women came to the tomb, bringing the spices they had prepared. 2 They found the stone rolled away from the tomb, 3 but when they entered, they did not find the body of the Lord Jesus. 4 While they were puzzling over this, suddenly two men in radiant apparel stood beside them. 5 As the women bowed their faces to the ground in terror, the two men asked them, “Why do you look for the living among the dead? 6 He is not here; He has risen! Remember how He told you while He was still in Galilee: 7 ‘The Son of Man must be delivered into the hands of sinful men, and be crucified, and on the third day rise again.’ ” 8 Then they remembered His words. 9 And when they returned from the tomb, they reported all these things to the Eleven and to all the others. 10 It was Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Mary the mother of James, and the other women with them who told this to the apostles. 11 But their words seemed like nonsense to them, and they did not believe the women. 12 Peter, however, got up and ran to the tomb. And after bending down and seeing only the linen cloths, he went away, wondering to himself what had happened.
paragraphs: 1 On the first day of the week, very early in the morning, the women came to the tomb, bringing the spices they had prepared. 2 They found the stone rolled away from the tomb, 3 but when they entered, they did not find the body of the Lord Jesus. 4 While they were puzzling over this, suddenly two men in radiant apparel stood beside them. 5 As the women bowed their faces to the ground in terror, the two men asked them, “Why do you look for the living among the dead?

6 He is not here; He has risen! Remember how He told you while He was still in Galilee: 7 ‘The Son of Man must be delivered into the hands of sinful men, and be crucified, and on the third day rise again.’ ” 8 Then they remembered His words. 9 And when they returned from the tomb, they reported all these things to the Eleven and to all the others.

10 It was Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Mary the mother of James, and the other women with them who told this to the apostles. 11 But their words seemed like nonsense to them, and they did not believe the women. 12 Peter, however, got up and ran to the tomb. And after bending down and seeing only the linen cloths, he went away, wondering to himself what had happened.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
On the first day of the week, the women return with the spices they prepared. These are the women who saw the tomb and how Jesus’ body was placed there. They find the stone rolled away and the body gone.

Two men in radiant clothing stand beside them and ask why they are looking for the living among the dead. They announce that Jesus has risen and remind the women that He had foretold His betrayal, crucifixion and resurrection on the third day.

The women remember His words and report what happened to the Eleven and the others. Luke names Mary Magdalene, Joanna and Mary the mother of James, along with other women. The apostles initially dismiss their report as nonsense.

Peter runs to the tomb, sees only the linen cloths and leaves wondering. Luke records the empty tomb, the announcement, the remembered promise and the first responses to the news; fuller recognition follows in the rest of the chapter.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian traditions commonly understand the empty tomb within the announcement that Jesus truly rose from the dead. The Catholic Catechism describes it as an essential sign leading toward recognition of the resurrection, and Westminster affirms His rising in the same body in which He suffered. (Catechism §§639–641; Westminster Confession 8.4)
passages.god_plan_html:
The announcement calls the women back to Jesus’ own promise, including the suffering they had just witnessed. Acts later presents His burial and resurrection as the fulfillment of God’s promises, applying the promise that God’s Holy One would not see decay to Jesus. It joins that proclamation with forgiveness through Him. (Luke 9:22; Luke 18:31–33; Acts 13:29–39)

Paul also explains Christ’s resurrection as the beginning of the promised harvest: those who belong to Him will be raised at His coming. Romans connects being united with His death and resurrection with walking in newness of life now. The empty tomb therefore stands within both the hope of resurrection and the new life His people are called to live. (1 Corinthians 15:20–23; Romans 6:3–11)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 24:13-35
passages.section_title: How does Jesus help the travelers to Emmaus understand?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 That same day two of them were going to a village called Emmaus, about seven miles from Jerusalem. 14 They were talking with each other about everything that had happened. 15 And as they talked and deliberated, Jesus Himself came up and walked along with them. 16 But their eyes were kept from recognizing Him. 17 He asked them, “What are you discussing so intently as you walk along?” They stood still, with sadness on their faces. 18 One of them, named Cleopas, asked Him, “Are You the only visitor to Jerusalem who does not know the things that have happened there in recent days?” 19 “What things?” He asked. “The events involving Jesus of Nazareth,” they answered. “This man was a prophet, powerful in speech and action before God and all the people. 20 Our chief priests and rulers delivered Him up to the sentence of death, and they crucified Him. 21 But we were hoping He was the One who would redeem Israel. And besides all this, it is the third day since these things took place. 22 Furthermore, some of our women astounded us. They were at the tomb early this morning, 23 but they did not find His body. They came and told us they had seen a vision of angels, who said that Jesus was alive. 24 Then some of our companions went to the tomb and found it just as the women had described. But Him they did not see.” 25 Then Jesus said to them, “O foolish ones, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! 26 Was it not necessary for the Christ to suffer these things and then to enter His glory?” 27 And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, He explained to them what was written in all the Scriptures about Himself. 28 As they approached the village where they were headed, He seemed to be going farther. 29 But they pleaded with Him, “Stay with us, for it is nearly evening and the day is almost over.” So He went in to stay with them. 30 While He was reclining at the table with them, He took bread, spoke a blessing and broke it, and gave it to them. 31 Then their eyes were opened and they recognized Jesus—and He disappeared from their sight. 32 They asked each other, “Were not our hearts burning within us as He spoke with us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?” 33 And they got up that very hour and returned to Jerusalem. There they found the Eleven and those with them, gathered together 34 and saying, “The Lord has indeed risen and has appeared to Simon!” 35 Then the two told what had happened on the road, and how they had recognized Jesus in the breaking of the bread.

But Him they did not see.”

25 Then Jesus said to them, “O foolish ones, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! 26 Was it not necessary for the Christ to suffer these things and then to enter His glory?” 27 And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, He explained to them what was written in all the Scriptures about Himself.

33 And they got up that very hour and returned to Jerusalem. There they found the Eleven and those with them, gathered together 34 and saying, “The Lord has indeed risen and has appeared to Simon!” 35 Then the two told what had happened on the road, and how they had recognized Jesus in the breaking of the bread.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Two followers leave Jerusalem for Emmaus that same day, discussing what has happened. Jesus joins them, but they are kept from recognizing Him. One is named Cleopas; Luke does not identify the other.

They describe Jesus as a prophet powerful in word and deed and explain their disappointed hope that He would redeem Israel. The Greek verb is λυτρόω, lytroō (loo-TROH-oh), meaning to redeem or deliver, with a background of release by ransom. Thayer includes this verse among its uses for deliverance. The word carries the hope of rescue, while Jesus’ explanation will show how His suffering belongs within that hope. (Thayer, Greek 3084)

They know about the women’s report and the empty tomb, but have not seen Jesus. He challenges their slowness to believe the prophets and explains that the Christ had to suffer before entering His glory. Beginning with Moses and the Prophets, He explains what Scripture says about Him.

Near the village they urge Him to stay. At the table He takes bread, blesses it, breaks it and gives it to them. Their eyes open, they recognize Him and He disappears from their sight. They then recall how their hearts burned as He opened the Scriptures on the road.

They return to Jerusalem that very hour. The gathered believers tell them that the Lord has risen and appeared to Simon; the two add their own account of the road and the breaking of bread. Scripture, recognition and shared witness come together in the scene.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readers commonly understand the encounter as Jesus helping His followers see that His suffering belongs within God’s promised work, rather than proving that their hope has failed. Wesley emphasizes that the sufferings which troubled them were part of the promised Messiah’s work. (Wesley on Luke 24:25–27)

Readers differ over the meal’s relation to the Lord’s Supper. The Catholic Catechism uses the movement from Scripture explained on the road to bread shared at the table to explain the unity of the Eucharistic celebration. Wesley explicitly identifies the breaking of bread here with the Lord’s Supper. (Catechism §§1346–1347; Wesley on Luke 24:30–35)

Calvin instead understands it as an ordinary meal at which Jesus gives thanks in His familiar manner. His explanation differs from the meal being the Lord’s Supper. This is his commentary’s reading, rather than a claim that every Reformed Christian interprets the scene identically. (Calvin on Luke 24:30)
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus Himself makes the central connection: suffering and glory belong together in the work of the Christ promised in Scripture. Peter later describes the prophets searching into the sufferings of Christ and the glories to follow. Isaiah’s Servant bearing sin and the promise applied to Jesus in Acts that He would not see decay are examples of this scriptural pattern. Luke does not list every passage Jesus used on the road. (1 Peter 1:10–12; Isaiah 53:4–12; Acts 13:32–39)

Their hope for Israel’s redemption also has deep roots. Psalm 130 calls Israel to hope in the Lord who redeems from iniquity. At the chapter’s close, Jesus explains that His suffering and resurrection lead into repentance and forgiveness being proclaimed in His name to all nations, beginning in Jerusalem. The story carries their disappointed hope toward the redemption He is actually accomplishing. (Psalm 130:6–8; Luke 24:44–49)

passages.title: Luke 24:36-43
passages.section_title: How does Jesus show His followers that He is alive?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 36 While they were describing these events, Jesus Himself stood among them and said, “Peace be with you.” 37 But they were startled and frightened, thinking they had seen a spirit. 38 “Why are you troubled,” Jesus asked, “and why do doubts arise in your hearts? 39 Look at My hands and My feet. It is I Myself. Touch Me and see—for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see I have.” 40 And when He had said this, He showed them His hands and feet. 41 While they were still in disbelief because of their joy and amazement, He asked them, “Do you have anything here to eat?” 42 So they gave Him a piece of broiled fish, 43 and He took it and ate it in front of them.
paragraphs: 36 While they were describing these events, Jesus Himself stood among them and said, “Peace be with you.” 37 But they were startled and frightened, thinking they had seen a spirit. 38 “Why are you troubled,” Jesus asked, “and why do doubts arise in your hearts? 39 Look at My hands and My feet. It is I Myself. Touch Me and see—for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see I have.” 40 And when He had said this, He showed them His hands and feet.

41 While they were still in disbelief because of their joy and amazement, He asked them, “Do you have anything here to eat?” 42 So they gave Him a piece of broiled fish, 43 and He took it and ate it in front of them.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
While the two travelers are describing their encounter, Jesus stands among the gathered followers and speaks peace to them. They are frightened because they think they are seeing a spirit.

He addresses their doubts by pointing to His hands and feet and inviting them to touch Him. He explains that a spirit does not have flesh and bones as they see He has. His identity is continuous with the Jesus who suffered, and His presence is bodily.

Their joy and amazement still make the moment difficult to take in. Jesus asks for food, receives a piece of broiled fish and eats it in front of them. Luke records His words and these concrete actions together.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian traditions commonly understand the touching and eating as affirming Jesus’ real bodily resurrection. The Catholic Catechism describes His risen body as the same body that suffered, now glorified; Westminster likewise affirms His rising in the same body in which He suffered. (Catechism §§645–646; Westminster Confession 8.4)
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul describes the resurrection body as raised imperishable and in glory, contrasting the weakness of mortal life with what God gives through Christ. The risen Jesus is central to that hope. Romans likewise promises that the Spirit who raised Him will give life to His people’s mortal bodies. His bodily appearance therefore belongs within God’s purpose to overcome death for those who belong to Him. (1 Corinthians 15:42–49; Romans 8:10–11)

Acts begins by recalling that Jesus presented Himself alive with many convincing proofs before commissioning His witnesses. This scene forms part of the foundation for the message they carry: they testify to the Lord who suffered and is truly alive. (Acts 1:1–8)

passages.title: Luke 24:44-49
passages.section_title: What mission does Jesus give His witnesses?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 44 Jesus said to them, “These are the words I spoke to you while I was still with you: Everything must be fulfilled that is written about Me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms.” 45 Then He opened their minds to understand the Scriptures. 46 And He told them, “This is what is written: The Christ will suffer and rise from the dead on the third day, 47 and in His name repentance and forgiveness of sins will be proclaimed to all nations, beginning in Jerusalem. 48 You are witnesses of these things. 49 And behold, I am sending the promise of My Father upon you. But remain in the city until you have been clothed with power from on high.”
paragraphs: 44 Jesus said to them, “These are the words I spoke to you while I was still with you: Everything must be fulfilled that is written about Me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms.” 45 Then He opened their minds to understand the Scriptures. 46 And He told them, “This is what is written: The Christ will suffer and rise from the dead on the third day, 47 and in His name repentance and forgiveness of sins will be proclaimed to all nations, beginning in Jerusalem.
48 You are witnesses of these things. 49 And behold, I am sending the promise of My Father upon you. But remain in the city until you have been clothed with power from on high.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus brings His followers back to what He had told them before His death. What was written about Him in the Law of Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled. He opens their minds to understand the Scriptures.

He gathers the message around His suffering, resurrection on the third day, and the proclamation of repentance and forgiveness in His name. That message is to reach all nations, beginning in Jerusalem.

He identifies them as witnesses and promises the Father’s gift. They are to remain in the city until they receive power from on high. Acts identifies this promised gift as the Holy Spirit and carries the same instruction forward. (Acts 1:4–8)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand these words as a commission to proclaim Christ and the forgiveness He brings, depending on the Holy Spirit. Wesley emphasizes the mercy of beginning at Jerusalem, where even those responsible for Jesus’ death are called to repentance, and identifies the Father’s promise with the Spirit. (Wesley on Luke 24:44–49)
passages.god_plan_html:
Isaiah presents the Servant’s task as reaching beyond restoring Israel to bringing God’s salvation to the ends of the earth. Acts explicitly applies that passage to the mission among the nations. Jesus’ commission carries forward this scriptural purpose already announced. (Isaiah 49:5–6; Acts 13:46–48)

Acts also shows the promised power arriving at Pentecost: the followers are filled with the Holy Spirit, and people from many nations hear them speaking in their own languages. Peter connects that gift with the exalted Jesus pouring out what the Father promised. The message about Christ moves outward through the power He gives His witnesses. (Acts 2:1–8, 32–36)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Luke 24:50-53
passages.section_title: Why do Jesus’ followers return with joy after He leaves?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 50 When Jesus had led them out as far as Bethany, He lifted up His hands and blessed them. 51 While He was blessing them, He left them and was carried up into heaven. 52 And they worshiped Him and returned to Jerusalem with great joy, 53 praising God continually in the temple.
paragraphs: 50 When Jesus had led them out as far as Bethany, He lifted up His hands and blessed them. 51 While He was blessing them, He left them and was carried up into heaven. 52 And they worshiped Him and returned to Jerusalem with great joy, 53 praising God continually in the temple.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus leads His followers out toward Bethany, raises His hands and blesses them. While He is blessing them, He is carried up into heaven. Their response is worship and great joy as they return to Jerusalem.

Luke ends with them continually praising God in the temple. The followers who were frightened and doubtful are now worshiping the risen Lord and waiting as He instructed.

This is a compact closing account. Acts supplies the fuller time frame of appearances over forty days, followed by the ascension, the promise of His return and the followers gathering in prayer. (Acts 1:1–14)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian traditions commonly understand the ascension as Jesus being exalted into heavenly glory, with His risen humanity retained. The Catholic Catechism explains His place at the Father’s right hand in terms of divine honor and the Messiah’s kingdom; Westminster describes Him ascending in the same body in which He rose. (Catechism §§659–664; Westminster Confession 8.4)
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus’ heavenly presence is connected with continuing care for His people. Hebrews describes Him as the great high priest who has passed through the heavens and invites believers to draw near for mercy and help. It also says that He lives to intercede for those who come to God through Him. His departure belongs within that ongoing ministry on their behalf. (Hebrews 4:14–16; Hebrews 7:23–28)

Acts joins the ascension with both mission and hope: the witnesses will receive the Spirit’s power, and the same Jesus will return. Their joyful worship and prayer prepare for the next stage of the story, in which His work continues through the people He sends. (Acts 1:6–14)
