passages.title: John 1:1
passages.section_title: Why is Jesus called the Word?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
paragraphs: 1 In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.

passages.context_html:
This is the opening verse of John 1:1–5, which describes the Word as already present at the beginning and as the One through whom everything is made. The verse holds together His relationship with God and His divine identity. (Read the surrounding passage)

Word translates λόγος, logos (LOH-goss), a Greek word used for a word or what someone says. The surrounding passage presents the Word as Someone who gives life, and verse 14 says He became flesh. This is the Son who makes the Father known. (Thayer, Greek 3056; John 1:3–4, 14–18)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Historic Christian readings understand the Word as the eternal Son, truly God while distinct from the Father. Catholic, Reformed and Methodist primary teaching shares that point; this verse is read alongside the account of the Son becoming human. (Catechism §§464–469; Westminster Confession 8.2; Methodist Articles I–II)
passages.current_position_html: Our study Prayer and Faith identifies the Word in John 1:1, 14 with Jesus Christ. It uses that identification when explaining the relationship between Jesus as the Word and His teaching about the bread of life.

deeper_study.title: Who is The Angel of the Lord?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html: The opening recalls the beginning of Genesis, where God creates and speaks light into darkness. The following verses identify the Word with the making of all things. Colossians likewise identifies the Son as the One through whom and for whom creation exists, then connects Him with reconciliation through the cross. This verse therefore introduces the Savior within the whole story of creation and redemption. (Genesis 1:1–5; John 1:2–5; Colossians 1:15–20)

passages.title: John 1:1-5
passages.section_title: Who is the Word at the beginning?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. 2 He was with God in the beginning. 3 Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made. 4 In Him was life, and that life was the light of men. 5 The Light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it.
paragraphs: 1 In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. 2 He was with God in the beginning. 3 Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made.
4 In Him was life, and that life was the light of men. 5 The Light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Gospel opens before the story of Jesus’ public ministry, at the beginning of creation itself. The Word already exists, is with God and is God. Everything that comes into being is made through Him.

The Greek word is λόγος, logos (LOH-goss). In ordinary use it can mean a word or what someone says. Here the Gospel speaks of Someone who is with God and through whom all things are made. The opening later identifies Him as the Son who becomes flesh and makes the Father known. (Thayer, Greek 3056; John 1:14–18)

Life is in Him, and that life is the light of humanity. The BSB describes the Light shining in darkness and the darkness failing to overcome it. These images introduce the life, revelation and opposition that will unfold through the Gospel.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Historic Christian readings understand the Word as the eternal Son, truly God and distinct from the Father. The Catholic Catechism, Westminster and Methodist Articles share that central understanding of the Son’s divine identity. (Catechism §§464–469; Westminster Confession 8.2; Methodist Articles I–II)
passages.god_plan_html:
Genesis opens with God creating the heavens and earth and calling light into darkness. The opening of John deliberately brings creation, life and light together around the Word. Paul makes a related connection explicit when he describes the God who called light out of darkness shining in people’s hearts so they know His glory in the face of Jesus Christ. This is a supported connection between creation and the new life and knowledge God gives through Christ. (Genesis 1:1–5; 2 Corinthians 4:3–6)

Colossians also holds together the Son’s work in creation and His saving work: all things are created through Him and for Him, and reconciliation comes through the blood of His cross. The One who gives life to creation is central to God’s purpose to bring His creation back into peace with Him. (Colossians 1:15–20)
passages.current_position_html: Our study Prayer and Faith identifies the Word in John 1:1, 14 with Jesus Christ. It uses that identification when explaining the relationship between Jesus as the Word and His teaching about the bread of life.

passages.title: John 1:6-13
passages.section_title: How do people become God’s children?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 There came a man who was sent from God. His name was John. 7 He came as a witness to testify about the Light, so that through him everyone might believe. 8 He himself was not the Light, but he came to testify about the Light. 9 The true Light, who gives light to everyone, was coming into the world. 10 He was in the world, and though the world was made through Him, the world did not recognize Him. 11 He came to His own, and His own did not receive Him. 12 But to all who did receive Him, to those who believed in His name, He gave the right to become children of God— 13 children born not of blood, nor of the desire or will of man, but born of God.
paragraphs: 6 There came a man who was sent from God. His name was John. 7 He came as a witness to testify about the Light, so that through him everyone might believe. 8 He himself was not the Light, but he came to testify about the Light.

9 The true Light, who gives light to everyone, was coming into the world. 10 He was in the world, and though the world was made through Him, the world did not recognize Him. 11 He came to His own, and His own did not receive Him.
12 But to all who did receive Him, to those who believed in His name, He gave the right to become children of God— 13 children born not of blood, nor of the desire or will of man, but born of God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Gospel introduces John the Baptist as a man sent by God to bear witness to the Light. He is the witness whose testimony points people toward the One in whom they are to believe.

The true Light comes into the world He made, but the world does not recognize Him and His own do not receive Him. The account then turns toward those who do receive Him and believe in His name: they are given the right to become God’s children.

Their birth comes from God. Human ancestry, desire and will are not its source. The passage places receiving Christ and believing in His name alongside God’s action in giving this new life.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian traditions commonly agree that becoming God’s child depends on God’s grace and cannot be secured by ancestry or human effort alone. They differ in how they explain God’s initiative, the response of faith and the gift of new birth.

Reformed churches following Westminster and Baptists following the 1689 Confession teach that God renews and draws those He has chosen so they freely come to Christ. Their ability to respond follows the Spirit giving life and renewing their wills. (Westminster Confession 10.1–2; 1689 Baptist Confession 10.1–2)

The Catholic Church likewise teaches that grace is an undeserved gift and that even preparation to receive it is already God’s work. It connects new life with baptism and teaches that God’s initiative calls for a free response and cooperation made possible by His grace. (Catechism §§1996–2002)

The Methodist Articles teach that fallen people cannot turn to God by their own strength: grace comes first, enabling a good will and then working with it. Wesley describes this prior grace as given to everyone, while people may resist its light. This is his explanation of how God enables a response, alongside the Articles’ teaching about grace. (Methodist Articles VIII; Wesley, On Working Out Our Own Salvation, II.1 and III.3–5)
passages.god_plan_html:
Galatians explains God sending His Son to redeem those under the law so that they receive adoption as His children. The Spirit of the Son then enables them to address God as Father. Romans likewise connects the Spirit, belonging in God’s family and sharing in Christ’s inheritance. These passages show the larger purpose of the new life described here: being brought into the Father’s family through the Son. (Galatians 4:4–7; Romans 8:14–17)

Peter links God’s mercy in giving new birth with a living hope through Jesus’ resurrection and an inheritance kept for His people. Birth from God therefore reaches beyond a change of label; it belongs to the life and future He gives through Christ. (1 Peter 1:3–5)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: John 1:14-18
passages.section_title: What does it mean that the Word became flesh?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us. We have seen His glory, the glory of the one and only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth. 15 John testified concerning Him. He cried out, saying, “This is He of whom I said, ‘He who comes after me has surpassed me because He was before me.’” 16 From His fullness we have all received grace upon grace. 17 For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. 18 No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father’s side, has made Him known.
paragraphs: 14 The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us. We have seen His glory, the glory of the one and only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth. 15 John testified concerning Him. He cried out, saying, “This is He of whom I said, ‘He who comes after me has surpassed me because He was before me.’”

16 From His fullness we have all received grace upon grace. 17 For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. 18 No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father’s side, has made Him known.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Word introduced at the beginning becomes flesh and lives among people. The testimony centers on His glory as the Father’s one and only Son, full of grace and truth. John the Baptist points to His greatness, saying that the One coming after him was before him.

The Greek verb for making His dwelling is σκηνόω, skēnoō (skay-NOH-oh). Thayer explains it as living in a tent or dwelling among others. Its use here gives the passage a connection with the tabernacle, the tent associated with God’s presence among Israel. (Thayer, Greek 4637; Exodus 40:34–38)

The account speaks of receiving from His fullness and places Moses’ giving of the law alongside grace and truth coming through Jesus Christ. It ends by saying that no one has seen God, but the Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father’s side, has made Him known.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian traditions commonly understand becoming flesh as the eternal Son truly becoming human while remaining truly God. The Catholic Catechism, Westminster and Methodist Articles affirm one Christ who is fully divine and fully human. (Catechism §§461–469; Westminster Confession 8.2; Methodist Articles II)
passages.god_plan_html:
Exodus describes God’s glory filling the tabernacle among Israel. Here the Word dwells among people and His glory is seen. Jesus later identifies His body with the temple, and Revelation finally describes God dwelling with His people in a world freed from death and mourning. These are supported connections in the Bible’s larger story of God making His presence known among the people He redeems. (Exodus 40:34–38; John 2:19–21; Revelation 21:1–4)

Hebrews also connects God’s earlier speech through the prophets with His final revelation through the Son, through whom He made the universe. It identifies the Son with God’s glory, His nature and the cleansing of sins. The Word becoming flesh brings together the themes of creation, God made known and salvation. (Hebrews 1:1–4)
passages.current_position_html: Our study Who is The Angel of the Lord? reads John 1:18 as an anchor for understanding God’s visible appearances in the Old Testament. It concludes that the eternal Son made the unseen Father known in those encounters before becoming human. That is the study’s developed conclusion from this verse.

deeper_study.title: Who is The Angel of the Lord?

passages.title: John 1:18
passages.section_title: How does the Son make the Father known?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father’s side, has made Him known.
paragraphs: 18 No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father’s side, has made Him known.

passages.context_html:
This verse concludes John 1:14–18, where the Word becomes flesh and His glory is seen. It first says that no one has ever seen God, then identifies the Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father’s side, as the One who makes Him known. (Read the surrounding passage)

The verb behind made Him known is ἐξηγέομαι, exēgeomai (ex-ay-GEH-oh-my). Thayer gives the sense of unfolding or declaring and specifically lists this verse. The Son makes God known through the unique relationship described here. (Thayer, Greek 1834)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readers commonly understand the verse as the Son uniquely making the unseen God known. Wesley connects the Son’s place beside the Father with their closest unity and the Son’s intimate knowledge of Him. (Wesley on John 1:18)
passages.current_position_html: Our study Who is The Angel of the Lord? reads John 1:18 as an anchor for understanding God’s visible appearances in the Old Testament. It concludes that the eternal Son made the unseen Father known in those encounters before becoming human. That is the study’s developed conclusion from this verse.

deeper_study.title: Who is The Angel of the Lord?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html: Jesus later tells Philip that seeing Him is seeing the Father and explains that His words and works express the Father’s presence in Him. Hebrews similarly identifies the Son as the radiance of God’s glory and the exact expression of His nature. These passages develop the larger purpose stated here: God makes Himself known through His Son, whose work also brings cleansing from sins. (John 14:8–11; Hebrews 1:1–4)

passages.title: John 1:19-28
passages.section_title: Who does John say he is?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 And this was John’s testimony when the Jews of Jerusalem sent priests and Levites to ask him, “Who are you?” 20 He did not refuse to confess, but openly declared, “I am not the Christ.” 21 “Then who are you?” they inquired. “Are you Elijah?” He said, “I am not.” “Are you the Prophet?” He answered, “No.” 22 So they said to him, “Who are you? We need an answer for those who sent us. What do you say about yourself?” 23 John replied in the words of Isaiah the prophet: “I am a voice of one calling in the wilderness, ‘Make straight the way for the Lord.’” 24 Then the Pharisees who had been sent 25 asked him, “Why then do you baptize, if you are not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet?” 26 “I baptize with water,” John replied, “but among you stands One you do not know. 27 He is the One who comes after me, the straps of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie.” 28 All this happened at Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing.
paragraphs: 19 And this was John’s testimony when the Jews of Jerusalem sent priests and Levites to ask him, “Who are you?” 20 He did not refuse to confess, but openly declared, “I am not the Christ.” 21 “Then who are you?” they inquired. “Are you Elijah?” He said, “I am not.” “Are you the Prophet?” He answered, “No.” 22 So they said to him, “Who are you? We need an answer for those who sent us. What do you say about yourself?” 23 John replied in the words of Isaiah the prophet: “I am a voice of one calling in the wilderness, ‘Make straight the way for the Lord.’”

24 Then the Pharisees who had been sent 25 asked him, “Why then do you baptize, if you are not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet?” 26 “I baptize with water,” John replied, “but among you stands One you do not know. 27 He is the One who comes after me, the straps of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie.” 28 All this happened at Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
A delegation from Jerusalem questions John about his identity and authority to baptize. He openly denies being the Christ. When asked whether he is Elijah or the Prophet, he denies those identities as well.

The questions draw on promises in Scripture. Malachi speaks of Elijah before the Day of the Lord, and Moses speaks of a prophet like himself whom the people must hear. John answers by identifying his task with Isaiah’s voice preparing the Lord’s way. (Malachi 4:5–6; Deuteronomy 18:15–19; Isaiah 40:3–5)

He then points beyond his own water baptism to One already among them whom they do not know. John describes himself as unworthy even to untie His sandal straps. The scene takes place at Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John is baptizing.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly distinguish John’s denial of being Elijah himself from the Elijah-like role described in Luke: preparing a people in Elijah’s spirit and power. Wesley likewise reads the denial as John saying he is not the same man as Elijah, while identifying his mission with Isaiah’s promised voice. (Luke 1:13–17; Wesley on John 1:21–23)
passages.god_plan_html:
Isaiah’s call to prepare the Lord’s way belongs to a passage announcing that His glory will be revealed. John explicitly identifies himself with that preparatory voice, and the next scene identifies Jesus as the One he is announcing. His ministry therefore stands within Scripture’s expectation of God coming to make Himself known to His people. (Isaiah 40:3–5; John 1:29–34)

The expectation of the Prophet also finds its larger answer in Jesus. Acts applies Moses’ promise of a prophet like himself to Christ and joins it with God’s purpose to bless people by turning them from wickedness. John’s answer directs attention toward the One who fulfills the promises, rather than claiming their place for himself. (Deuteronomy 18:15–19; Acts 3:20–26)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: John 1:29-34
passages.section_title: Why does John call Jesus the Lamb of God?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 29 The next day John saw Jesus coming toward him and said, “Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world! 30 This is He of whom I said, ‘A man who comes after me has surpassed me because He was before me.’ 31 I myself did not know Him, but the reason I came baptizing with water was that He might be revealed to Israel.” 32 Then John testified, “I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove and resting on Him. 33 I myself did not know Him, but the One who sent me to baptize with water told me, ‘The man on whom you see the Spirit descend and rest is He who will baptize with the Holy Spirit.’ 34 I have seen and testified that this is the Son of God.”
paragraphs: 29 The next day John saw Jesus coming toward him and said, “Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world! 30 This is He of whom I said, ‘A man who comes after me has surpassed me because He was before me.’ 31 I myself did not know Him, but the reason I came baptizing with water was that He might be revealed to Israel.”

32 Then John testified, “I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove and resting on Him. 33 I myself did not know Him, but the One who sent me to baptize with water told me, ‘The man on whom you see the Spirit descend and rest is He who will baptize with the Holy Spirit.’ 34 I have seen and testified that this is the Son of God.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The next day John sees Jesus approaching and identifies Him as the Lamb of God who takes away the world’s sin. He repeats that the One coming after him ranks above him because He was before him.

John explains that his water baptism serves the purpose of revealing Jesus to Israel. He testifies that he saw the Spirit descend from heaven like a dove and remain on Him.

This was the sign given by the One who sent John: the man on whom the Spirit descended and remained would baptize with the Holy Spirit. John’s testimony ends with his declaration that Jesus is the Son of God. The Gospel reports his witness to the sign and its meaning.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand the Lamb as pointing to Jesus’ saving death and removal of sin. The Catholic Catechism connects the title with Isaiah’s suffering Servant and the Passover lamb; Wesley and Calvin likewise explain it through sacrifice, sin-bearing and reconciliation with God. (Catechism §608; Wesley on John 1:29; Calvin on John 1:29)
passages.god_plan_html:
Isaiah describes the Servant led like a lamb to slaughter and bearing the sins of others. Exodus describes the Passover blood marking the houses spared in judgment, and Paul explicitly calls Christ the sacrificed Passover lamb. These are supported connections behind the sacrificial title John gives Jesus. Revelation carries the picture forward with the slain Lamb whose blood purchases people from every tribe and nation. (Isaiah 53:7–12; Exodus 12:5–14; 1 Corinthians 5:7–8; Revelation 5:6–10)

The promise of baptism with the Holy Spirit also reaches beyond this first testimony in Israel. Peter later recalls the Lord’s contrast between John’s water baptism and baptism with the Spirit when the same gift is given to Gentiles. The church recognizes that God has granted them repentance leading to life. The One announced here gathers people into God’s saving work and gives the Spirit. (Acts 11:15–18)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: John 1:35-42
passages.section_title: How do the first followers begin bringing others to Jesus?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 35 The next day John was there again with two of his disciples. 36 When he saw Jesus walking by, he said, “Look, the Lamb of God!” 37 And when the two disciples heard him say this, they followed Jesus. 38 Jesus turned and saw them following. “What do you want?” He asked. They said to Him, “Rabbi” (which means Teacher), “where are You staying?” 39 “Come and see,” He replied. So they went and saw where He was staying, and spent that day with Him. It was about the tenth hour. 40 Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, was one of the two who heard John’s testimony and followed Jesus. 41 He first found his brother Simon and told him, “We have found the Messiah” (which is translated as Christ). 42 Andrew brought him to Jesus, who looked at him and said, “You are Simon son of John. You will be called Cephas” (which is translated as Peter).
paragraphs: 35 The next day John was there again with two of his disciples. 36 When he saw Jesus walking by, he said, “Look, the Lamb of God!” 37 And when the two disciples heard him say this, they followed Jesus. 38 Jesus turned and saw them following. “What do you want?” He asked. They said to Him, “Rabbi” (which means Teacher), “where are You staying?” 39 “Come and see,” He replied. So they went and saw where He was staying, and spent that day with Him. It was about the tenth hour.

40 Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, was one of the two who heard John’s testimony and followed Jesus. 41 He first found his brother Simon and told him, “We have found the Messiah” (which is translated as Christ). 42 Andrew brought him to Jesus, who looked at him and said, “You are Simon son of John. You will be called Cephas” (which is translated as Peter).

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
John again identifies Jesus as the Lamb of God, and two of his disciples begin following Jesus. When He asks what they want, they address Him as Rabbi and ask where He is staying. The Gospel explains Rabbi as Teacher.

Jesus invites them to come and see, and they spend that day with Him. Andrew is named as one of the two. He then finds his brother Simon and announces that they have found the Messiah, which the Gospel translates as Christ.

Andrew brings Simon to Jesus. Jesus identifies him as Simon son of John and says he will be called Cephas, translated as Peter. Cephas comes from the Aramaic word כֵּיפָא, kepha (kay-FAH), meaning rock. Thayer confirms the connection between the Aramaic name and its Greek counterpart. (Thayer, Greek 2786)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly see John’s testimony leading people to Jesus, followed by Andrew sharing his discovery with his brother. Jesus’ naming of Simon is understood as looking ahead to the place he will have among His followers; Wesley likewise explains Cephas and Peter as the corresponding names meaning rock. (Wesley on John 1:37–42)
passages.god_plan_html:
Scripture records other names given alongside a calling: Abram becomes Abraham in the promise concerning many nations, and Jacob becomes Israel. Those are supported parallels with Jesus giving Simon a new name, though each person has a distinct place in God’s work. The shared pattern is a future shaped by God’s calling. (Genesis 17:4–8; Genesis 32:27–30)

The personal witness beginning here also looks toward the public witness of the apostles. Acts later records Peter proclaiming Jesus’ resurrection and exaltation. Andrew’s act of bringing his brother belongs within the beginning of that wider gathering of witnesses through whom the message about Christ will go out. (Acts 2:32–36)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: John 1:43-51
passages.section_title: What greater things does Jesus promise Nathanael?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 43 The next day Jesus decided to set out for Galilee. Finding Philip, He told him, “Follow Me.” 44 Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the same town as Andrew and Peter. 45 Philip found Nathanael and told him, “We have found the One Moses wrote about in the Law, the One the prophets foretold—Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph.” 46 “Can anything good come from Nazareth?” Nathanael asked. “Come and see,” said Philip. 47 When Jesus saw Nathanael approaching, He said of him, “Here is a true Israelite, in whom there is no deceit.” 48 “How do You know me?” Nathanael asked. Jesus replied, “Before Philip called you, I saw you under the fig tree.” 49 “Rabbi,” Nathanael answered, “You are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!” 50 Jesus said to him, “Do you believe just because I told you I saw you under the fig tree? You will see greater things than these.” 51 Then He declared, “Truly, truly, I tell you, you will all see heaven open and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.”
paragraphs: 43 The next day Jesus decided to set out for Galilee. Finding Philip, He told him, “Follow Me.” 44 Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the same town as Andrew and Peter. 45 Philip found Nathanael and told him, “We have found the One Moses wrote about in the Law, the One the prophets foretold—Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph.” 46 “Can anything good come from Nazareth?” Nathanael asked. “Come and see,” said Philip.

47 When Jesus saw Nathanael approaching, He said of him, “Here is a true Israelite, in whom there is no deceit.” 48 “How do You know me?” Nathanael asked. Jesus replied, “Before Philip called you, I saw you under the fig tree.” 49 “Rabbi,” Nathanael answered, “You are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!”

50 Jesus said to him, “Do you believe just because I told you I saw you under the fig tree? You will see greater things than these.” 51 Then He declared, “Truly, truly, I tell you, you will all see heaven open and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus decides to go to Galilee, finds Philip and calls him to follow. Philip finds Nathanael and identifies Jesus of Nazareth as the One Moses and the Prophets wrote about. Nathanael questions whether anything good can come from Nazareth, and Philip invites him to come and see.

Jesus describes Nathanael as a true Israelite without deceit. When Nathanael asks how He knows him, Jesus says He saw him under the fig tree before Philip called him. Nathanael responds by confessing Him as the Son of God and King of Israel.

Jesus promises greater things. His final words widen the promise beyond Nathanael: they will see heaven opened and God’s angels ascending and descending on the Son of Man. The BSB expresses the plural address as you will all see. (John 1:51)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly connect the opened heaven and ascending and descending angels with Jacob’s dream and the revelation Jesus brings. Calvin emphasizes continuing access to God through Christ, while Wesley emphasizes the coming display of His glory and also allows a reference to the ascension. These are the commentators’ emphases rather than separate official positions for every member of their traditions. (Calvin on John 1:51; Wesley on John 1:51)
passages.god_plan_html:
Jacob dreams of a ladder reaching from earth to heaven with angels ascending and descending, and hears God’s promise to remain with him and bless the families of the earth through his offspring. Jesus’ words clearly echo that scene while placing the Son of Man at its center. The connection points to God making His presence and access to heaven known through Him. (Genesis 28:10–17)

The wider New Testament identifies Jesus as the one mediator between God and humanity, giving Himself as a ransom, and records His own claim to be the way to the Father. Those passages help explain the larger significance of the picture: the relationship between heaven and earth is centered on the Son who brings people to God. (1 Timothy 2:3–6; John 14:6)

passages.title: John 2:1-12
passages.section_title: What does the first sign reveal about Jesus?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 On the third day a wedding took place at Cana in Galilee. Jesus’ mother was there, 2 and Jesus and His disciples had also been invited to the wedding. 3 When the wine ran out, Jesus’ mother said to Him, “They have no more wine.” 4 “Woman, what is that to you and to Me?” Jesus replied. “My hour has not yet come.” 5 His mother said to the servants, “Do whatever He tells you.” 6 Now six stone water jars had been set there for the Jewish rites of purification. Each could hold from twenty to thirty gallons. 7 Jesus told the servants, “Fill the jars with water.” So they filled them to the brim. 8 “Now draw some out,” He said, “and take it to the master of the banquet.” They did so, 9 and the master of the banquet tasted the water that had been turned into wine. He did not know where it was from, but the servants who had drawn the water knew. Then he called the bridegroom aside 10 and said, “Everyone serves the fine wine first, and then the cheap wine after the guests are drunk. But you have saved the fine wine until now!” 11 Jesus performed this, the first of His signs, at Cana in Galilee. He thus revealed His glory, and His disciples believed in Him. 12 After this, He went down to Capernaum with His mother and brothers and His disciples, and they stayed there a few days.
paragraphs: 1 On the third day a wedding took place at Cana in Galilee. Jesus’ mother was there, 2 and Jesus and His disciples had also been invited to the wedding. 3 When the wine ran out, Jesus’ mother said to Him, “They have no more wine.” 4 “Woman, what is that to you and to Me?” Jesus replied. “My hour has not yet come.” 5 His mother said to the servants, “Do whatever He tells you.”

6 Now six stone water jars had been set there for the Jewish rites of purification. Each could hold from twenty to thirty gallons. 7 Jesus told the servants, “Fill the jars with water.” So they filled them to the brim. 8 “Now draw some out,” He said, “and take it to the master of the banquet.” They did so, 9 and the master of the banquet tasted the water that had been turned into wine. He did not know where it was from, but the servants who had drawn the water knew. Then he called the bridegroom aside 10 and said, “Everyone serves the fine wine first, and then the cheap wine after the guests are drunk. But you have saved the fine wine until now!”

11 Jesus performed this, the first of His signs, at Cana in Galilee. He thus revealed His glory, and His disciples believed in Him. 12 After this, He went down to Capernaum with His mother and brothers and His disciples, and they stayed there a few days.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus, His disciples and His mother are at a wedding in Cana. When the wine runs out, His mother tells Him about the need. He replies that His hour has not yet come, and she tells the servants to do whatever He says.

Six stone jars are there for Jewish washing rites, each holding twenty to thirty gallons. Jesus tells the servants to fill them with water and take some to the master of the banquet. The water has become wine, and the master praises its quality without knowing where it came from.

The servants know what happened, and the Gospel identifies this as Jesus’ first sign: He reveals His glory and His disciples believe in Him. The account then follows Jesus, His family and His disciples to Capernaum for a short stay.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readers commonly understand the sign as revealing Jesus’ glory and strengthening His disciples’ faith. Readers differ over how to understand His exchange with His mother.

The Catholic Catechism presents Mary’s request as intercession offered in faith for the needs of the wedding feast. It also sees that feast as pointing toward the wedding of the Lamb. (Catechism §2618)

Wesley reads Jesus’ reply as a gentle correction of an untimely intervention. Calvin values Mary’s concern for others but thinks she goes beyond her proper place in trying to direct Jesus’ work. These are their interpretations of the exchange; both keep Jesus’ authority over His own work at the center. (Wesley on John 2:3–5; Calvin on John 2:4)
passages.god_plan_html:
Isaiah pictures God’s salvation as a lavish feast for all peoples, with fine wine, death swallowed up and tears wiped away. Revelation pictures the joy of the marriage supper of the Lamb. The wedding and abundance at Cana form a supported parallel with this wider scriptural hope of joy in God’s saving work. The sign reveals the glory of the One through whom that hope is brought to fulfillment. (Isaiah 25:6–9; Revelation 19:6–9)

The mention of His hour also looks ahead within the Gospel. Jesus later announces that the hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified, and connects it with His approaching death and its fruit. The glory first revealed at Cana belongs within the larger story of the Son giving Himself so that others may have life. (John 12:23–32)

passages.title: John 2:13-22
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus speak of His body as the temple?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 When the Jewish Passover was near, Jesus went up to Jerusalem. 14 In the temple courts He found men selling cattle, sheep, and doves, and money changers seated at their tables. 15 So He made a whip out of cords and drove all from the temple courts, both sheep and cattle. He poured out the coins of the money changers and overturned their tables. 16 To those selling doves He said, “Get these out of here! How dare you turn My Father’s house into a marketplace!” 17 His disciples remembered that it is written: “Zeal for Your house will consume Me.” 18 On account of this, the Jews demanded, “What sign can You show us to prove Your authority to do these things?” 19 Jesus answered, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again.” 20 “This temple took forty-six years to build,” the Jews replied, “and You are going to raise it up in three days?” 21 But Jesus was speaking about the temple of His body. 22 After He was raised from the dead, His disciples remembered that He had said this. Then they believed the Scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken.
paragraphs: 13 When the Jewish Passover was near, Jesus went up to Jerusalem. 14 In the temple courts He found men selling cattle, sheep, and doves, and money changers seated at their tables. 15 So He made a whip out of cords and drove all from the temple courts, both sheep and cattle. He poured out the coins of the money changers and overturned their tables. 16 To those selling doves He said, “Get these out of here! How dare you turn My Father’s house into a marketplace!” 17 His disciples remembered that it is written: “Zeal for Your house will consume Me.”

18 On account of this, the Jews demanded, “What sign can You show us to prove Your authority to do these things?” 19 Jesus answered, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again.” 20 “This temple took forty-six years to build,” the Jews replied, “and You are going to raise it up in three days?” 21 But Jesus was speaking about the temple of His body. 22 After He was raised from the dead, His disciples remembered that He had said this. Then they believed the Scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
At Passover Jesus goes to Jerusalem and finds sellers of cattle, sheep and doves, along with money changers, in the temple courts. With a whip of cords He drives out the sheep and cattle, pours out the coins and overturns the tables. He tells the dove sellers to remove their goods and stop turning His Father’s house into a marketplace.

His disciples remember the words of Psalm 69 about zeal for God’s house. The people challenging His authority ask for a sign. Jesus answers that if they destroy this temple, He will raise it up in three days. (Psalm 69:6–9)

They understand Him to mean the building and point to its forty-six years of construction. The Gospel explains that He means His own body. After His resurrection, His disciples remember His words and believe the Scripture and what He had said.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand Jesus as acting out of devotion to His Father’s house, with the saying about His body pointing toward His death and resurrection. The Catholic Catechism and Wesley’s notes reflect that central reading. (Catechism §§584–586; Wesley on John 2:19–22)
passages.god_plan_html:
The psalm remembered by the disciples joins zeal for God’s house with the suffering of someone who bears reproach for God’s sake. Paul applies the same verse’s language about bearing insults to Christ. Jesus’ devotion to the Father belongs within the wider scriptural pattern of the faithful sufferer who bears the cost of His mission. (Psalm 69:6–9; Romans 15:3)

The temple theme also reaches forward into the people Christ brings near to God. Ephesians describes Jews and Gentiles reconciled through the cross, with access to the Father by one Spirit, becoming a holy temple and God’s dwelling. Paul likewise calls the gathered believers God’s temple because His Spirit lives in them. These passages connect Jesus’ saving work with God making His home among a people He has brought together. (Ephesians 2:13–22; 1 Corinthians 3:16–17)

passages.title: John 2:23-25
passages.section_title: What does Jesus know beyond people’s first response?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 23 While He was in Jerusalem at the Passover Feast, many people saw the signs He was doing and believed in His name. 24 But Jesus did not entrust Himself to them, for He knew them all. 25 He did not need any testimony about man, for He knew what was in a man.
paragraphs: 23 While He was in Jerusalem at the Passover Feast, many people saw the signs He was doing and believed in His name. 24 But Jesus did not entrust Himself to them, for He knew them all. 25 He did not need any testimony about man, for He knew what was in a man.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
During the Passover feast, many people see Jesus’ signs and believe in His name. Yet He does not entrust Himself to them, because He knows them all and knows what is within a person.

The Greek verb πιστεύω, pisteuō (pis-TYOO-oh), appears on both sides of that exchange. It is translated as believing when describing the people, and entrusting when describing Jesus. Thayer specifically lists John 2:24 under the meaning of entrusting something to someone. The word connection draws attention to the difference between their response and His knowledge of them. (Thayer, Greek 4100)

This leads into the next chapter, where a man who recognizes the signs comes to Jesus and is told about new birth. The Gospel is beginning to explore what lies beneath people’s responses to Him.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readers commonly understand this as Jesus discerning more than outward enthusiasm. Calvin reads the response as incomplete belief that might develop further, while Wesley emphasizes Jesus’ knowledge of the human heart and His caution about entrusting Himself to people. (Calvin on John 2:23–25; Wesley on John 2:23–25)
passages.god_plan_html:
Knowing the heart belongs within Scripture’s account of God’s own knowledge and judgment. Jeremiah describes the Lord searching the heart and examining the mind; Revelation records the risen Jesus saying that He searches minds and hearts and repays according to people’s deeds. His knowledge here belongs within that larger picture of the Lord who knows people truthfully. (Jeremiah 17:9–10; Revelation 2:23)

The Gospel also states its purpose plainly: the signs are written so that people may believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life in His name. This scene should be read alongside that purpose. Signs can lead toward faith; the goal is life-giving trust in the Son whose identity they reveal. (John 20:30–31)

passages.title: John 3:1-8
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus say we must be born again?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a leader of the Jews. 2 He came to Jesus at night and said, “Rabbi, we know that You are a teacher who has come from God. For no one could perform the signs You are doing if God were not with him.” 3 Jesus replied, “Truly, truly, I tell you, no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again.” 4 “How can a man be born when he is old?” Nicodemus asked. “Can he enter his mother’s womb a second time to be born?” 5 Jesus answered, “Truly, truly, I tell you, no one can enter the kingdom of God unless he is born of water and the Spirit. 6 Flesh is born of flesh, but spirit is born of the Spirit. 7 Do not be amazed that I said, ‘You must be born again.’ 8 The wind blows where it wishes. You hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it is going. So it is with everyone born of the Spirit.”
paragraphs: 1 Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a leader of the Jews. 2 He came to Jesus at night and said, “Rabbi, we know that You are a teacher who has come from God. For no one could perform the signs You are doing if God were not with him.” 3 Jesus replied, “Truly, truly, I tell you, no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again.”

4 “How can a man be born when he is old?” Nicodemus asked. “Can he enter his mother’s womb a second time to be born?” 5 Jesus answered, “Truly, truly, I tell you, no one can enter the kingdom of God unless he is born of water and the Spirit. 6 Flesh is born of flesh, but spirit is born of the Spirit. 7 Do not be amazed that I said, ‘You must be born again.’ 8 The wind blows where it wishes. You hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it is going. So it is with everyone born of the Spirit.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Nicodemus is a Pharisee and a Jewish ruler. He comes to Jesus at night and says that His signs show that God is with Him. Jesus turns the conversation toward what Nicodemus needs: new birth in order to see God’s kingdom. The account tells us when he came, but does not state why he chose the night.

Nicodemus asks how an old person could be born a second time. The Greek word ἄνωθεν, anōthen (AN-oh-then), can mean again or from above. Thayer records both meanings and the differing readings of this passage. Nicodemus thinks about another physical birth; Jesus explains a birth brought about by the Spirit. (Thayer, Greek 509)

Jesus speaks of birth through water and the Spirit, distinguishes human birth from birth through the Spirit, and uses the wind as a comparison. We hear the wind without directing its movement or knowing its whole course. In the same way, the Spirit’s work is real even though we cannot control or fully explain it.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian traditions agree that Jesus calls for a new life given by God’s Spirit. Where traditions differ is the meaning of water and its connection with baptism.

The Catholic Church identifies this birth with baptism, through which God gives new life. Lutheran teaching likewise presents baptism as God’s saving work, with its gift received through faith. Neither account presents it as a human achievement that earns salvation. (Catechism §1215; Large Catechism, Baptism §§10, 28–37)

Wesley reads the words as an inward change through the Spirit together with baptism, where baptism is available, as its outward sign and means. Reformed teaching also connects baptism with new birth, but the Westminster Confession says that salvation is not inseparable from the rite and that its effect is not tied to the moment it is administered. Calvin’s own reading of this verse takes water as a picture of the Spirit’s inward cleansing. His interpretation of the wording should be distinguished from the confession’s broader teaching about baptism. (Wesley on John 3:5; Westminster Confession 28.1, 5–6; Calvin on John 3:5)

The Baptist Confession describes baptism as a sign of belonging to Christ and of the new life, and reserves it for those who profess repentance and faith. That establishes its teaching about baptism without settling every Baptist reader’s interpretation of water here. (Baptist Confession 29.1–2)

Another reading takes water as referring to ordinary physical birth, followed by the needed spiritual birth. Chuck Smith favors this reading because verse 6 contrasts flesh and Spirit, while acknowledging the baptism reading as another possibility. This is an individual teacher’s reading, rather than an official statement for all evangelical Christians. (Smith’s teaching on John 3, pages 2–3)
passages.god_plan_html:
Ezekiel records God’s promise to cleanse His people, give them a new heart and put His Spirit within them. That gives a scriptural background for Jesus’ words about cleansing and Spirit-given life. The connection is a parallel with God’s promise, rather than an explicit quotation in this conversation. (Ezekiel 36:25–28)

Titus later joins new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit with God’s mercy, the Spirit poured out through Jesus, and the hope of eternal life. The wider purpose is God making people heirs of life through His gracious work. (Titus 3:4–7)

passages.title: John 3:9-15
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus compare Himself with the lifted snake?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 “How can this be?” Nicodemus asked. 10 “You are Israel’s teacher,” said Jesus, “and you do not understand these things? 11 Truly, truly, I tell you, we speak of what we know, and we testify to what we have seen, and yet you people do not accept our testimony. 12 If I have told you about earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you about heavenly things? 13 No one has ascended into heaven except the One who descended from heaven—the Son of Man. 14 Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, 15 that everyone who believes in Him may have eternal life.
paragraphs: 9 “How can this be?” Nicodemus asked. 10 “You are Israel’s teacher,” said Jesus, “and you do not understand these things? 11 Truly, truly, I tell you, we speak of what we know, and we testify to what we have seen, and yet you people do not accept our testimony. 12 If I have told you about earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you about heavenly things?

13 No one has ascended into heaven except the One who descended from heaven—the Son of Man. 14 Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, 15 that everyone who believes in Him may have eternal life.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Nicodemus asks how this new birth can happen. Jesus challenges him as a teacher of Israel who has not understood, and speaks of testimony that has not been received. The conversation moves from the Spirit’s work to the authority of the Son of Man, who has come from heaven.

Jesus then recalls a wilderness event. After the Israelites sinned and were bitten by deadly snakes, God told Moses to mount a bronze snake on a pole. Those who were bitten could look at it and live. Jesus says the Son of Man must likewise be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in Him may have eternal life. (Numbers 21:4–9)

The comparison concerns God’s provision of life for people facing death. The text does not ask us to assign a separate hidden meaning to every detail of the pole, the metal or the snake.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The familiar Christian reading connects being lifted up with Jesus’ crucifixion: people receive life by trusting the One God provides. Wesley explains the wilderness event as a comparison between looking at the snake and looking to Christ in faith. Later in this Gospel, being lifted up is explicitly connected with the way Jesus would die. (Wesley on John 3:14–15; John 12:32–33)

Calvin takes the emphasis here differently: he reads the lifting up as Christ being set before everyone through the preaching of the gospel. This is a difference between commentators over the comparison’s immediate emphasis, rather than a church-wide division over whether Jesus died for salvation. (Calvin on John 3:14)
passages.god_plan_html:
This connection is made by Jesus Himself. The wilderness rescue points beyond survival from snakebite to eternal life through the Son of Man. God provides the means of rescue in both accounts, and those in danger are called to respond to what He provides. (Numbers 21:8–9; John 3:14–15)

The later explanation of Jesus being lifted up places His death within that saving purpose. The Gospel joins the cross with His being glorified and drawing people to Himself; the apparent defeat of His death belongs to His work of bringing life. (John 12:23–33)

passages.title: John 3:16
passages.section_title: What does God give because He loves the world?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 For God so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son, that everyone who believes in Him shall not perish but have eternal life.
paragraphs: 16 For God so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son, that everyone who believes in Him shall not perish but have eternal life.

passages.context_html:
This verse belongs to Jesus’ conversation with Nicodemus about new birth and the Son of Man being lifted up. It explains the love behind the gift of the Son and promises eternal life to everyone who believes in Him.

The next verses explain that the Son comes to save, while unbelief leaves people under condemnation. Reading the verse in that setting keeps God’s love, the gift of His Son and the response of faith together. Read John 3:16–21 in context.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian traditions share the central reading that salvation begins in God’s love, comes through His Son and is received through faith. The passage holds together the promise of life and the seriousness of rejecting the Son.

Where traditions differ is how they explain the reach of Christ’s saving work and why people come to faith. The Catholic Church teaches that Christ died for every human being without exception. Wesley likewise reads world as all people, including those who reject God’s love. (Catechism §§604–605; Wesley on John 3:16)

The Westminster Confession describes Christ’s saving work as securing redemption for those God has chosen. Calvin’s commentary nevertheless reads this verse as an invitation to everyone without exception, while saying that God opens the eyes of those He has chosen to believe. Reformed readers therefore should not all be described as replacing world with only the chosen in this verse. (Westminster Confession 3.6; 8.5, 8; Calvin on John 3:16)
passages.current_position_html: Our study The Gospel According to Jesus reads John 3:16 as a summary of the good news: God acts out of love, gives His Son and promises life to everyone who believes in Him. The study calls people to turn from sin and trust Jesus as Lord.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Paul describes the same movement from God’s love toward people who need rescue: Christ dies for the ungodly while they are still sinners, bringing reconciliation and the hope of being saved through His life. God’s love acts toward people before they have made themselves worthy. (Romans 5:6–11)

Ephesians places forgiveness through Christ’s blood within God’s stated purpose to bring all things in heaven and on earth together in Christ. The gift of the Son belongs within that wider purpose of restoration under Him. That wider hope should be read alongside this passage’s own distinction between faith and unbelief. (Ephesians 1:7–10)

passages.section_title: What does God’s love ask us to face?

passages.context_html:

The passage also speaks plainly about judgment. The believer is not condemned; the unbeliever is already under condemnation. Light has come, but people love darkness because their deeds are evil. Coming to the light means facing the truth about what we do and recognizing the work of God.

The Greek word κόσμος, kosmos (KOS-moss), translated world, has several uses. Thayer includes both the created world and humanity, depending on the context. Here the surrounding references to believing, evil deeds and coming to the light concern people. The word itself does not mean only the physical planet. (Thayer, Greek 2889)

passages.title: John 3:22-30
passages.section_title: Why is John glad when people go to Jesus?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 After this, Jesus and His disciples went into the Judean countryside, where He spent some time with them and baptized. 23 Now John was also baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because the water was plentiful there, and people kept coming to be baptized. 24 (For John had not yet been thrown into prison.) 25 Then a dispute arose between John’s disciples and a certain Jew over the issue of ceremonial washing. 26 So John’s disciples came to him and said, “Look, Rabbi, the One who was with you beyond the Jordan, the One you testified about—He is baptizing, and everyone is going to Him.” 27 John replied, “A man can receive only what is given him from heaven. 28 You yourselves can testify that I said, ‘I am not the Christ, but am sent ahead of Him.’ 29 The bride belongs to the bridegroom. The friend of the bridegroom stands and listens for him, and is overjoyed to hear the bridegroom’s voice. That joy is mine, and it is now complete. 30 He must increase; I must decrease.
paragraphs: 22 After this, Jesus and His disciples went into the Judean countryside, where He spent some time with them and baptized. 23 Now John was also baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because the water was plentiful there, and people kept coming to be baptized. 24 (For John had not yet been thrown into prison.)

25 Then a dispute arose between John’s disciples and a certain Jew over the issue of ceremonial washing. 26 So John’s disciples came to him and said, “Look, Rabbi, the One who was with you beyond the Jordan, the One you testified about—He is baptizing, and everyone is going to Him.” 27 John replied, “A man can receive only what is given him from heaven. 28 You yourselves can testify that I said, ‘I am not the Christ, but am sent ahead of Him.’ 29 The bride belongs to the bridegroom. The friend of the bridegroom stands and listens for him, and is overjoyed to hear the bridegroom’s voice. That joy is mine, and it is now complete. 30 He must increase; I must decrease.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus and His disciples spend time in the Judean countryside while John continues baptizing at Aenon near Salim. The Gospel notes that John has not yet been imprisoned. The next chapter clarifies that Jesus’ disciples carry out the baptizing. Aenon’s plentiful water is given as the reason for John’s activity there; this does not locate Jesus at that same spring. (John 4:1–2)

After a discussion about ceremonial washing, John’s disciples report that people are going to Jesus. John answers that a person receives only what heaven gives. He reminds them that he has always said he is sent ahead of the Christ, rather than being the Christ himself.

John compares his joy to that of a bridegroom’s friend who is delighted to hear the groom. His mission succeeds as attention turns toward Jesus. The account records his disciples’ concern; it does not tell us that every one of them is an unbelieving person seeking a career.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readers understand this as a period when John’s work and Jesus’ growing ministry overlap, with John gladly directing attention to the Christ. The plentiful water also enters discussions about how baptism should be performed.

Where traditions differ is whether immersion is required. The Baptist Confession requires immersion for the proper administration of baptism. The Westminster Confession permits pouring or sprinkling, while the Catholic Catechism calls triple immersion the most expressive form and also recognizes pouring. These documents explain their traditions’ broader teachings; the single detail about plentiful water does not state every part of those teachings. (Baptist Confession 29.4; Westminster Confession 28.3; Catechism §1239) Wesley and Calvin both understand the wedding comparison as John welcoming Christ’s rightful place rather than treating Him as a rival. Calvin applies the distinction to teachers who serve Christ without claiming the people as their own. (Wesley on John 3:27–30; Calvin on John 3:29)
passages.god_plan_html:
The wedding comparison belongs within a wider scriptural picture of Christ’s love for His people. Ephesians describes Christ loving the church, giving Himself for her and preparing her to stand before Him. John’s joy as the bridegroom’s friend is a parallel with that larger picture: the people belong to Christ, and His servants rejoice in their being brought to Him. (Ephesians 5:25–32)

Paul later addresses rivalry around teachers by calling himself and Apollos servants with different tasks, while God gives the growth. That provides another scriptural parallel to John’s acceptance of his assigned work. God’s purpose brings people to Christ through servants who work together. (1 Corinthians 3:4–9)
passages.current_position_html: Our study Baptism reads the plentiful water in John 3:23 as support for immersion as the intended, normal practice. Its conclusion also recognizes that Scripture does not explicitly declare every other mode invalid and allows for pouring when immersion is unavailable.

passages.title: John 3:23
passages.section_title: Why does the Gospel mention plentiful water?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 23 Now John was also baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because the water was plentiful there, and people kept coming to be baptized.
paragraphs: 23 Now John was also baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because the water was plentiful there, and people kept coming to be baptized.

passages.context_html:
John is baptizing at Aenon near Salim because there is plentiful water and people keep coming. This happens while Jesus’ ministry is growing and before John is imprisoned. The Gospel later clarifies that Jesus’ disciples perform the baptisms associated with His ministry. (John 4:1–2)

This detail belongs within John’s continuing witness to Christ. When his disciples report Jesus’ growing following, John welcomes it and says that Jesus must increase while he decreases. Read John 3:22–30 in context.

(Baptist Confession 29.4; Westminster Confession 28.3; Catechism §1239)

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
John’s work prepares people to recognize the One who takes away sin and gives the Holy Spirit. His baptism belongs within that forward-looking witness. The Gospel has already distinguished his baptism with water from the work of the One he announces. (John 1:29–34)

Later, Paul explains Christian baptism in relation to sharing in Christ’s death and walking in new life through His resurrection. That later explanation gives the wider picture of the new life baptism expresses; it should not erase the distinction between John’s preparatory work and the risen Christ’s completed work. (Romans 6:3–11)

passages.title: John 3:31-36
passages.section_title: Why does our response to the Son matter so much?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 31 The One who comes from above is above all. The one who is from the earth belongs to the earth and speaks as one from the earth. The One who comes from heaven is above all. 32 He testifies to what He has seen and heard, yet no one accepts His testimony. 33 Whoever accepts His testimony has certified that God is truthful. 34 For the One whom God has sent speaks the words of God, for God gives the Spirit without limit. 35 The Father loves the Son and has placed all things in His hands. 36 Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life. Whoever rejects the Son will not see life. Instead, the wrath of God remains on him.”
paragraphs: 31 The One who comes from above is above all. The one who is from the earth belongs to the earth and speaks as one from the earth. The One who comes from heaven is above all. 32 He testifies to what He has seen and heard, yet no one accepts His testimony. 33 Whoever accepts His testimony has certified that God is truthful. 34 For the One whom God has sent speaks the words of God, for God gives the Spirit without limit. 35 The Father loves the Son and has placed all things in His hands. 36 Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life. Whoever rejects the Son will not see life. Instead, the wrath of God remains on him.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The chapter closes by contrasting the One who comes from heaven with those who belong to the earth. The Son speaks from what He has seen and heard, speaks God’s words, and receives all things from the Father who loves Him.

The passage speaks of people not accepting His testimony, then immediately describes the person who does accept it. The sweeping statement about rejection should be read with that following sentence: it is not a claim that no one at all can ever receive Him.

The closing verse holds together present life through believing in the Son and the judgment that remains on the person who rejects Him. It returns to the same choice described earlier in the chapter.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings agree that the Son has authority from the Father and that receiving Him is a matter of life and judgment. Calvin and Wesley both read these words as placing Jesus above merely human teachers and calling for faith in Him. (Calvin on John 3:31–36; Wesley on John 3:31–36)

Readers differ about whose words close the chapter. Calvin treats them as the Baptist’s continuing testimony; Wesley thinks they may be the Gospel writer’s reflection. The USCCB’s notes also identify uncertainty about the speaker. That is a question about the passage’s presentation, rather than a different claim about the Son’s authority. (Calvin on John 3:31–32; Wesley on John 3:31; USCCB note on John 3:31–36)
passages.god_plan_html:
Colossians gives a wider account of the Son’s place: all things are created through Him and for Him, He holds them together, and He is head of the church. The Father’s placing all things in His hands here fits that larger scriptural account of His authority. (Colossians 1:15–18)

That authority serves a saving purpose. Colossians goes on to connect God’s fullness in Christ with reconciliation through the blood of His cross. The One whose testimony calls for faith is also the One through whom God makes peace. (Colossians 1:19–20)

passages.title: John 4:1-15
passages.section_title: What is the living water Jesus offers?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 When Jesus realized that the Pharisees were aware He was gaining and baptizing more disciples than John 2 (although it was not Jesus who baptized, but His disciples), 3 He left Judea and returned to Galilee. 4 Now He had to pass through Samaria. 5 So He came to a town of Samaria called Sychar, near the plot of ground that Jacob had given to his son Joseph. 6 Since Jacob’s well was there, Jesus, weary from His journey, sat down by the well. It was about the sixth hour. 7 When a Samaritan woman came to draw water, Jesus said to her, “Give Me a drink.” 8 (His disciples had gone into the town to buy food.) 9 “You are a Jew,” said the woman. “How can You ask for a drink from me, a Samaritan woman?” (For Jews do not associate with Samaritans.) 10 Jesus answered, “If you knew the gift of God and who is asking you for a drink, you would have asked Him, and He would have given you living water.” 11 “Sir,” the woman replied, “You have nothing to draw with and the well is deep. Where then will You get this living water? 12 Are You greater than our father Jacob, who gave us this well and drank from it himself, as did his sons and his livestock?” 13 Jesus said to her, “Everyone who drinks this water will be thirsty again. 14 But whoever drinks the water I give him will never thirst. Indeed, the water I give him will become in him a fount of water springing up to eternal life.” 15 The woman said to Him, “Sir, give me this water so that I will not get thirsty and have to keep coming here to draw water.”

It was about the sixth hour.

7 When a Samaritan woman came to draw water, Jesus said to her, “Give Me a drink.” 8 (His disciples had gone into the town to buy food.) 9 “You are a Jew,” said the woman. “How can You ask for a drink from me, a Samaritan woman?” (For Jews do not associate with Samaritans.) 10 Jesus answered, “If you knew the gift of God and who is asking you for a drink, you would have asked Him, and He would have given you living water.” 11 “Sir,” the woman replied, “You have nothing to draw with and the well is deep. Where then will You get this living water? 12 Are You greater than our father Jacob, who gave us this well and drank from it himself, as did his sons and his livestock?”

13 Jesus said to her, “Everyone who drinks this water will be thirsty again. 14 But whoever drinks the water I give him will never thirst. Indeed, the water I give him will become in him a fount of water springing up to eternal life.” 15 The woman said to Him, “Sir, give me this water so that I will not get thirsty and have to keep coming here to draw water.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus leaves Judea for Galilee and travels through Samaria. He sits, tired from the journey, at Jacob’s well near Sychar while His disciples buy food. A Samaritan woman comes to draw water, and He asks her for a drink.

She is surprised that a Jewish man would ask a Samaritan woman for water. The Gospel names the separation between their communities. Jesus responds by speaking about God’s gift and the living water He could give her.

The Greek expression ὕδωρ ζῶν, hydōr zōn (HOO-dor zohn), means living water and can describe water bubbling up or flowing from a spring. Thayer explains its figurative use here for God’s Spirit and truth meeting the soul’s need. That helps explain the woman’s question about where Jesus could get water without drawing equipment. (Thayer, Greek 2198)

Jesus contrasts water that must be drawn again with His gift becoming a spring within a person, leading to eternal life. She asks for this water so that she will not have to keep returning to the well. Her question keeps the conversation moving toward the identity of the One offering it.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly understand living water as the life God gives through Christ and His Spirit. Later in the Gospel, Jesus’ invitation to thirsty people is explicitly explained as referring to the Spirit. (John 7:37–39)

Calvin and Wesley differ in how they explain the promise of never thirsting. Calvin emphasizes the Spirit as an enduring source that will not finally run dry, even while believers desire more grace. Wesley emphasizes continuing to drink from that source. Both locate the life in God’s gift; their difference concerns how the promise relates to continuing faith. These are their own readings of the passage. (Calvin on John 4:13–14; Wesley on John 4:14)
passages.god_plan_html:
Jeremiah describes the Lord as the fountain of living water, whom His people have forsaken for broken cisterns. Ezekiel pictures water flowing from God’s sanctuary, bringing life where it goes, with fruit for food and leaves for healing. Jesus’ offer belongs alongside this larger scriptural theme of life flowing from God. These are supported parallels, rather than an explicit quotation of either prophet in this conversation. (Jeremiah 2:11–13; Ezekiel 47:1–12)

Revelation carries that picture into the final hope: the river of the water of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb, beside the tree whose leaves are for the healing of the nations. The gift Jesus offers points toward lasting life in God’s presence. (Revelation 22:1–5)

passages.title: John 4:16-26
passages.section_title: What kind of worship does the Father seek?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 Jesus told her, “Go, call your husband and come back.” 17 “I have no husband,” the woman replied. Jesus said to her, “You are correct to say that you have no husband. 18 In fact, you have had five husbands, and the man you now have is not your husband. You have spoken truthfully.” 19 “Sir,” the woman said, “I see that You are a prophet. 20 Our fathers worshiped on this mountain, but you Jews say that the place where one must worship is in Jerusalem.” 21 “Believe Me, woman,” Jesus replied, “a time is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem. 22 You worship what you do not know; we worship what we do know, for salvation is from the Jews. 23 But a time is coming and has now come when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and in truth, for the Father is seeking such as these to worship Him. 24 God is Spirit, and His worshipers must worship Him in spirit and in truth.” 25 The woman said, “I know that Messiah” (called Christ) “is coming. When He comes, He will explain everything to us.” 26 Jesus answered, “I who speak to you am He.”
paragraphs: 16 Jesus told her, “Go, call your husband and come back.” 17 “I have no husband,” the woman replied. Jesus said to her, “You are correct to say that you have no husband. 18 In fact, you have had five husbands, and the man you now have is not your husband. You have spoken truthfully.” 19 “Sir,” the woman said, “I see that You are a prophet. 20 Our fathers worshiped on this mountain, but you Jews say that the place where one must worship is in Jerusalem.”

21 “Believe Me, woman,” Jesus replied, “a time is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem. 22 You worship what you do not know; we worship what we do know, for salvation is from the Jews. 23 But a time is coming and has now come when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and in truth, for the Father is seeking such as these to worship Him. 24 God is Spirit, and His worshipers must worship Him in spirit and in truth.”
25 The woman said, “I know that Messiah” (called Christ) “is coming. When He comes, He will explain everything to us.” 26 Jesus answered, “I who speak to you am He.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus asks the woman to call her husband. When she says she has no husband, He acknowledges her truthful answer and tells her that He knows about her five husbands and the man who is not her husband. The account does not explain how the earlier marriages ended or give a complete history of her present circumstances.

She recognizes Him as a prophet and raises the question of the proper place to worship. The mountain associated with Samaritan worship is Gerizim, where an ancient Samaritan sacred precinct has been excavated. Jerusalem is the rival place named in her question. (Mount Gerizim, archaeological site description)

Jesus announces a time, already arriving, when worship of the Father will not be bound to either location. He also affirms that salvation comes from the Jews and says that the Father seeks worshipers in spirit and truth. When the woman speaks of the coming Messiah, Jesus identifies Himself as that One.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian traditions commonly read these verses as opening worship of the Father beyond the rival claims of Gerizim and Jerusalem, through the Spirit and the truth God reveals. The Catholic Catechism and Westminster Confession both affirm that worship is no longer tied to one exclusive location, while continuing to recognize gathered worship. (Catechism §§1179–1180; Westminster Confession 21.6)
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus says that salvation comes from the Jews. Paul later identifies Israel’s covenants, promises and patriarchs, and the Messiah’s human descent from Israel. The welcome extended to the Samaritan woman belongs within God’s faithfulness to those promises. (Romans 9:4–5)

Ephesians describes people once far apart being reconciled through Christ’s cross, with access to the Father by one Spirit. Together they become God’s dwelling. Hebrews likewise invites believers to draw near through the way Jesus opens by His blood. These passages give the wider picture of the access to the Father Jesus announces here. (Ephesians 2:13–22; Hebrews 10:19–22)
passages.current_position_html: Our studies Worship as the Early Church Knew It and What Is the True Church? read John 4:21–24 as ending the requirement to approach God at one sacred location. They understand true worship as a life turned toward the Father, led by His Spirit and aligned with His revealed truth. The passage addresses that relationship and access to God, rather than prescribing the format of a Christian gathering.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

passages.title: John 4:21
passages.section_title: Must we go to one sacred place to reach the Father?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 “Believe Me, woman,” Jesus replied, “a time is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem.
paragraphs: 21 “Believe Me, woman,” Jesus replied, “a time is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem.

passages.context_html:

The following verses explain His answer through worship in spirit and truth, and His identity as the Messiah. This verse should be read with that explanation. Read John 4:16–26 in context.
