Ephesians describes people once far apart being reconciled through Christ’s cross, with access to the Father by one Spirit. Together they become God’s dwelling. Hebrews likewise invites believers to draw near through the way Jesus opens by His blood. These passages give the wider picture of the access to the Father Jesus announces here. (Ephesians 2:13–22; Hebrews 10:19–22)

passages.title: John 4:21-24
passages.section_title: Why is worship no longer bound to one place?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 “Believe Me, woman,” Jesus replied, “a time is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem. 22 You worship what you do not know; we worship what we do know, for salvation is from the Jews. 23 But a time is coming and has now come when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and in truth, for the Father is seeking such as these to worship Him. 24 God is Spirit, and His worshipers must worship Him in spirit and in truth.”
paragraphs: 21 “Believe Me, woman,” Jesus replied, “a time is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem. 22 You worship what you do not know; we worship what we do know, for salvation is from the Jews. 23 But a time is coming and has now come when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and in truth, for the Father is seeking such as these to worship Him. 24 God is Spirit, and His worshipers must worship Him in spirit and in truth.”

passages.context_html:
The Samaritan woman has asked whether worship belongs on her community’s mountain or in Jerusalem. Jesus answers that the Father is seeking people who worship in spirit and truth, and that the time for this is already coming.

His answer holds two things together: salvation comes from the Jews, and access to the Father will not remain confined to the rival locations. The conversation then leads to His identifying Himself as the Messiah. Read John 4:16–26 in context.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian traditions commonly read these verses as opening worship of the Father beyond the rival claims of Gerizim and Jerusalem, through the Spirit and the truth God reveals. The Catholic Catechism and Westminster Confession both affirm that worship is no longer tied to one exclusive location, while continuing to recognize gathered worship. (Catechism §§1179–1180; Westminster Confession 21.6)
passages.current_position_html: Our studies Worship as the Early Church Knew It and What Is the True Church? read John 4:21–24 as ending the requirement to approach God at one sacred location. They understand true worship as a life turned toward the Father, led by His Spirit and aligned with His revealed truth. The passage addresses that relationship and access to God, rather than prescribing the format of a Christian gathering.

passages.title: John 4:27-38
passages.section_title: What harvest does Jesus want His disciples to see?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 27 Just then His disciples returned and were surprised that He was speaking with a woman. But no one asked Him, “What do You want from her?” or “Why are You talking with her?” 28 Then the woman left her water jar, went back into the town, and said to the people, 29 “Come, see a man who told me everything I ever did. Could this be the Christ?” 30 So they left the town and made their way toward Jesus. 31 Meanwhile the disciples urged Him, “Rabbi, eat something.” 32 But He told them, “I have food to eat that you know nothing about.” 33 So the disciples asked one another, “Could someone have brought Him food?” 34 Jesus explained, “My food is to do the will of Him who sent Me and to finish His work. 35 Do you not say, ‘There are still four months until the harvest’? I tell you, lift up your eyes and look at the fields, for they are ripe for harvest. 36 Already the reaper draws his wages and gathers a crop for eternal life, so that the sower and the reaper may rejoice together. 37 For in this case the saying ‘One sows and another reaps’ is true. 38 I sent you to reap what you have not worked for; others have done the hard work, and now you have taken up their labor.”

But no one asked Him, “What do You want from her?” or “Why are You talking with her?” 28 Then the woman left her water jar, went back into the town, and said to the people, 29 “Come, see a man who told me everything I ever did. Could this be the Christ?” 30 So they left the town and made their way toward Jesus.

31 Meanwhile the disciples urged Him, “Rabbi, eat something.” 32 But He told them, “I have food to eat that you know nothing about.” 33 So the disciples asked one another, “Could someone have brought Him food?” 34 Jesus explained, “My food is to do the will of Him who sent Me and to finish His work.

35 Do you not say, ‘There are still four months until the harvest’? I tell you, lift up your eyes and look at the fields, for they are ripe for harvest. 36 Already the reaper draws his wages and gathers a crop for eternal life, so that the sower and the reaper may rejoice together. 37 For in this case the saying ‘One sows and another reaps’ is true. 38 I sent you to reap what you have not worked for; others have done the hard work, and now you have taken up their labor.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The disciples return and are surprised to find Jesus speaking with the woman, but do not question Him. She leaves her water jar, returns to town and invites the people to come and consider whether He is the Christ. They start toward Him.

Meanwhile, the disciples urge Jesus to eat. He tells them that doing the will of the One who sent Him and finishing His work is His food. As with the earlier conversation about water, an everyday need becomes the starting point for explaining His mission.

Jesus then speaks of fields ready for harvest, workers gathering a crop for eternal life, and sowers and reapers rejoicing together. His disciples are entering work others have already begun. The approaching townspeople put the call to notice the harvest within the immediate scene.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readers commonly understand the food as Jesus’ devotion to His Father’s work and the harvest as people being brought to life through His message. Calvin and Wesley both read the different workers as sharing in that mission and its joy, with the disciples benefiting from work done before them. (Calvin on John 4:34–36; Wesley on John 4:34–38)
passages.god_plan_html:
The work Jesus comes to finish reaches beyond this encounter. Hebrews describes Christ coming to do God’s will and connects that obedience with the offering of His body. His dedication to the Father’s work here is a parallel with the obedience through which His saving mission is completed. (Hebrews 10:5–10)

The harvest also becomes a picture for His followers’ mission. In Luke, Jesus sends workers ahead of Him and tells them to ask the Lord of the harvest for more workers. Paul describes different servants planting and watering while God gives growth. Together these passages show God drawing people to Christ through shared work that no servant owns alone. (Luke 10:1–3; 1 Corinthians 3:4–9)

passages.title: John 4:39-42
passages.section_title: How does one person’s witness lead others to Jesus?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 39 Many of the Samaritans from that town believed in Jesus because of the woman’s testimony, “He told me everything I ever did.” 40 So when the Samaritans came to Him, they asked Him to stay with them, and He stayed two days. 41 And many more believed because of His message. 42 They said to the woman, “We now believe not only because of your words; we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this man truly is the Savior of the world.”
paragraphs: 39 Many of the Samaritans from that town believed in Jesus because of the woman’s testimony, “He told me everything I ever did.” 40 So when the Samaritans came to Him, they asked Him to stay with them, and He stayed two days. 41 And many more believed because of His message. 42 They said to the woman, “We now believe not only because of your words; we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this man truly is the Savior of the world.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Many people from the Samaritan town believe because of the woman’s testimony about Jesus knowing her life. When they come to Him, they ask Him to stay, and He remains for two days.

More people believe as they hear His own message. They tell the woman that their faith now rests on having heard for themselves, and they recognize Him as the Savior of the world. Her witness brings them to Jesus; His message deepens their own recognition of Him.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readers commonly see the woman’s witness and Jesus’ own teaching working together to bring people to faith. The confession that He is the Savior of the world recognizes a salvation reaching beyond one people, as Wesley also emphasizes in his note on verse 42. (Wesley on John 4:42)
passages.god_plan_html:
After His resurrection, Jesus names Samaria among the places where His followers will bear witness in the Spirit’s power. Acts later records Philip proclaiming Christ in a Samaritan city, with people listening and great joy following. The welcome in this chapter is a parallel with the wider mission that carries His message beyond its first Jewish setting. (Acts 1:8; Acts 8:4–8)

Paul describes the same connection between being sent, speaking, hearing and believing. God uses the witness of others so that people can hear Christ’s message for themselves. The woman’s part in this encounter gives a concrete example of that larger pattern. (Romans 10:13–17)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: John 4:43-54
passages.section_title: Can the official trust Jesus before seeing the result?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 43 After two days, Jesus left for Galilee. 44 Now He Himself had testified that a prophet has no honor in his own hometown. 45 Yet when He arrived, the Galileans welcomed Him. They had seen all the great things He had done in Jerusalem at the feast, for they had gone there as well. 46 So once again He came to Cana in Galilee, where He had turned the water into wine. And there was a royal official whose son lay sick at Capernaum. 47 When he heard that Jesus had come from Judea to Galilee, he went and begged Him to come down and heal his son, who was about to die. 48 Jesus said to him, “Unless you people see signs and wonders, you will never believe.” 49 “Sir,” the official said, “come down before my child dies.” 50 “Go,” said Jesus. “Your son will live.” The man took Jesus at His word and departed. 51 And while he was still on the way, his servants met him with the news that his boy was alive. 52 So he inquired as to the hour when his son had recovered, and they told him, “The fever left him yesterday at the seventh hour.” 53 Then the father realized that this was the very hour in which Jesus had told him, “Your son will live.” And he and all his household believed. 54 This was now the second sign that Jesus performed after coming from Judea into Galilee.
paragraphs: 43 After two days, Jesus left for Galilee. 44 Now He Himself had testified that a prophet has no honor in his own hometown. 45 Yet when He arrived, the Galileans welcomed Him. They had seen all the great things He had done in Jerusalem at the feast, for they had gone there as well. 46 So once again He came to Cana in Galilee, where He had turned the water into wine. And there was a royal official whose son lay sick at Capernaum. 47 When he heard that Jesus had come from Judea to Galilee, he went and begged Him to come down and heal his son, who was about to die. 48 Jesus said to him, “Unless you people see signs and wonders, you will never believe.”

49 “Sir,” the official said, “come down before my child dies.” 50 “Go,” said Jesus. “Your son will live.” The man took Jesus at His word and departed. 51 And while he was still on the way, his servants met him with the news that his boy was alive. 52 So he inquired as to the hour when his son had recovered, and they told him, “The fever left him yesterday at the seventh hour.” 53 Then the father realized that this was the very hour in which Jesus had told him, “Your son will live.” And he and all his household believed. 54 This was now the second sign that Jesus performed after coming from Judea into Galilee.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus returns to Galilee after two days in Samaria. The Gospel recalls His saying about a prophet lacking honor in his hometown, then tells how the Galileans welcome Him because they have seen His works in Jerusalem. He comes again to Cana, where He had turned water into wine.

A royal official whose son is near death in Capernaum begs Jesus to come and heal him. Jesus speaks about people needing signs and wonders before believing. The father presses his request, and Jesus tells him to go because his son will live. The man takes Him at His word and leaves.

On the way, his servants report the recovery. The father learns that the fever left at the same hour Jesus spoke, and he and his household believe. The Gospel calls this the second sign after Jesus’ return from Judea, linking it with the earlier sign at Cana. It has also mentioned other signs in Jerusalem, so this is not a claim that Jesus has performed only two miracles in total. (John 2:23)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand this as Jesus giving life through His word across a distance, and the father responding in trust before receiving confirmation. Calvin emphasizes Jesus’ patience with the man’s growing faith, while Wesley notes how examining the timing strengthens faith; neither point makes the father’s initial need for help a reason to withhold mercy. (Calvin on John 4:50; Wesley on John 4:52)
passages.god_plan_html:
The healing prepares for the Gospel’s wider account of the Son giving life. In the next chapter Jesus speaks of those who hear His word passing from death to life, and of the dead hearing His voice and rising. The child’s recovery is a sign alongside that greater promise of life through the Son. (John 5:24–29)

The Gospel later states why its signs are recorded: so that readers may believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life in His name. This sign serves that purpose. Its place in the story gives grounds for trusting Him without turning one child’s recovery into a promise that every illness will be healed immediately. (John 20:30–31)

passages.title: John 5:1-9
passages.section_title: How does Jesus help the man who cannot reach the water?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Some time later there was a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. 2 Now there is in Jerusalem near the Sheep Gate a pool with five covered colonnades, which in Hebrew is called Bethesda. 3 On these walkways lay a great number of the sick, the blind, the lame, and the paralyzed. 5 One man there had been an invalid for thirty-eight years. 6 When Jesus saw him lying there and realized that he had spent a long time in this condition, He asked him, “Do you want to get well?” 7 “Sir,” the invalid replied, “I have no one to help me into the pool when the water is stirred. While I am on my way, someone else goes in before me.” 8 Then Jesus told him, “Get up, pick up your mat, and walk.” 9 Immediately the man was made well, and he picked up his mat and began to walk. Now this happened on the Sabbath day,
paragraphs: 1 Some time later there was a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. 2 Now there is in Jerusalem near the Sheep Gate a pool with five covered colonnades, which in Hebrew is called Bethesda. 3 On these walkways lay a great number of the sick, the blind, the lame, and the paralyzed.

5 One man there had been an invalid for thirty-eight years. 6 When Jesus saw him lying there and realized that he had spent a long time in this condition, He asked him, “Do you want to get well?” 7 “Sir,” the invalid replied, “I have no one to help me into the pool when the water is stirred. While I am on my way, someone else goes in before me.” 8 Then Jesus told him, “Get up, pick up your mat, and walk.” 9 Immediately the man was made well, and he picked up his mat and began to walk. Now this happened on the Sabbath day,

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus goes to Jerusalem for a Jewish feast, which this account does not name. Near the Sheep Gate is the pool called Bethesda, with five covered colonnades where many sick people lie. One man has been ill for thirty-eight years. That describes the length of his illness; it does not say he has spent all those years beside the pool.

Excavations near St. Anne’s Church uncovered a double-pool complex. Archaeologist E. Jerry Vardaman describes how a covered walkway between the pools, together with those around the outside, explains the five-colonnade arrangement. This gives useful physical background to the scene. (Vardaman, The Pool of Bethesda, pages 27–28)

When Jesus asks whether he wants to get well, the man explains that no one helps him into the water before someone else gets there. Jesus tells him to get up, carry his mat and walk. He is made well immediately, and the Gospel notes that this happens on the Sabbath.

If you notice the verse numbers moving from 3 to 5, this follows the BSB’s text. Its footnote records the additional words found in some manuscripts about an angel stirring the water. The main account still records the man’s expectation about the water in verse 7. (BSB footnote on John 5:3–4)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readers commonly see Jesus giving the man help that he cannot obtain by reaching the pool. His recovery comes through Jesus’ command, and the Sabbath setting prepares for the dispute that follows. (John 5:6–16)
passages.god_plan_html:
Isaiah pictures God coming to save, with weak hands strengthened, blind eyes opened and the lame leaping for joy. The man walking at Jesus’ word is a supported parallel with that promised restoration. It shows His life-giving work within the wider hope of God coming to rescue and restore His people. (Isaiah 35:3–10)

The chapter goes on to connect this act with the Son’s power to give life, including the promise that the dead will hear His voice. The healing introduces that larger claim; it is more than an isolated display of power. (John 5:19–29)

passages.title: John 5:10-18
passages.section_title: Why does the Sabbath healing lead to a dispute about God?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 so the Jews said to the man who had been healed, “This is the Sabbath! It is unlawful for you to carry your mat.” 11 But he answered, “The man who made me well told me, ‘Pick up your mat and walk.’ ” 12 “Who is this man who told you to pick it up and walk?” they asked. 13 But the man who was healed did not know who it was, for Jesus had slipped away while the crowd was there. 14 Afterward, Jesus found the man at the temple and said to him, “See, you have been made well. Stop sinning, or something worse may happen to you.” 15 And the man went away and told the Jews that it was Jesus who had made him well. 16 Now because Jesus was doing these things on the Sabbath, the Jews began to persecute Him. 17 But Jesus answered them, “To this very day My Father is at His work, and I too am working.” 18 Because of this, the Jews tried all the harder to kill Him. Not only was He breaking the Sabbath, but He was even calling God His own Father, making Himself equal with God.
paragraphs: 10 so the Jews said to the man who had been healed, “This is the Sabbath! It is unlawful for you to carry your mat.” 11 But he answered, “The man who made me well told me, ‘Pick up your mat and walk.’ ” 12 “Who is this man who told you to pick it up and walk?” they asked. 13 But the man who was healed did not know who it was, for Jesus had slipped away while the crowd was there. 14 Afterward, Jesus found the man at the temple and said to him, “See, you have been made well. Stop sinning, or something worse may happen to you.” 15 And the man went away and told the Jews that it was Jesus who had made him well.

16 Now because Jesus was doing these things on the Sabbath, the Jews began to persecute Him. 17 But Jesus answered them, “To this very day My Father is at His work, and I too am working.” 18 Because of this, the Jews tried all the harder to kill Him. Not only was He breaking the Sabbath, but He was even calling God His own Father, making Himself equal with God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The people challenging the healed man say that carrying his mat violates the Sabbath. He explains that the person who healed him told him to carry it, but he does not yet know Jesus’ identity. Later Jesus finds him at the temple and warns him to stop sinning, lest something worse happen.

After the man identifies Jesus, the opposition turns toward Him for doing these things on the Sabbath. Jesus answers by speaking of His Father’s continuing work and His own work. The Gospel says the conflict intensifies because He calls God His own Father, making Himself equal with God.

The question about carrying a load has a scriptural background: Jeremiah warns against bringing loads through Jerusalem’s gates on the Sabbath. The dispute concerns the application of Sabbath obligations to this healed man and Jesus’ authority; it should not be explained by claiming that Scripture never mentions carrying loads. (Jeremiah 17:19–23)
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly understand Jesus’ answer as claiming a unique relationship with the Father and authority to share in His work. Wesley reads the following discourse as confirming, rather than withdrawing, that claim. (Wesley on John 5:17–19)

Readers differ over what the warning about sin tells us about this man’s illness. Wesley thinks it suggests that his earlier illness was connected with sin. The USCCB’s note cautions against turning such a connection into a rule for all suffering, pointing to Jesus’ refusal to blame the blind man’s condition on his or his parents’ sin. The account here does not name the healed man’s earlier sin or give us grounds to diagnose someone else’s illness. (Wesley on John 5:14; USCCB note on John 5:14; John 9:1–3)
passages.god_plan_html:
Genesis records God resting after His completed work of creation. Hebrews also describes the Son continually upholding all things by His powerful word. Scripture therefore speaks both of completed creation and of God’s continuing care for what He has made. Jesus’ work of restoring the man fits within that larger account of divine care. (Genesis 2:1–3; Hebrews 1:1–4)

Hebrews carries the theme of rest beyond a single healing, calling people to hear God’s voice in faith and enter His rest. That provides a wider scriptural parallel to the restoration seen here, without making this dispute settle every question about which day Christians observe. (Hebrews 4:1–11)

passages.title: John 5:19-29
passages.section_title: What does the Son’s voice bring: life or judgment?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 So Jesus replied, “Truly, truly, I tell you, the Son can do nothing by Himself, unless He sees the Father doing it. For whatever the Father does, the Son also does. 20 The Father loves the Son and shows Him all He does. And to your amazement, He will show Him even greater works than these. 21 For just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom He wishes. 22 Furthermore, the Father judges no one, but has assigned all judgment to the Son, 23 so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father. Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent Him. 24 Truly, truly, I tell you, whoever hears My word and believes Him who sent Me has eternal life and will not come under judgment. Indeed, he has crossed over from death to life. 25 Truly, truly, I tell you, the hour is coming and has now come when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live. 26 For as the Father has life in Himself, so also He has granted the Son to have life in Himself. 27 And He has given Him authority to execute judgment, because He is the Son of Man. 28 Do not be amazed at this, for the hour is coming when all who are in their graves will hear His voice 29 and come out—those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment.
paragraphs: 19 So Jesus replied, “Truly, truly, I tell you, the Son can do nothing by Himself, unless He sees the Father doing it. For whatever the Father does, the Son also does. 20 The Father loves the Son and shows Him all He does. And to your amazement, He will show Him even greater works than these. 21 For just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom He wishes. 22 Furthermore, the Father judges no one, but has assigned all judgment to the Son, 23 so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father. Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent Him.

24 Truly, truly, I tell you, whoever hears My word and believes Him who sent Me has eternal life and will not come under judgment. Indeed, he has crossed over from death to life. 25 Truly, truly, I tell you, the hour is coming and has now come when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live. 26 For as the Father has life in Himself, so also He has granted the Son to have life in Himself. 27 And He has given Him authority to execute judgment, because He is the Son of Man.

28 Do not be amazed at this, for the hour is coming when all who are in their graves will hear His voice 29 and come out—those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus explains His work in relation to the Father who loves Him. The Son acts in complete unity with the Father, gives life and receives authority to judge. Honoring the Son is inseparable from honoring the Father who sent Him.

He promises that the person who hears His word and believes the One who sent Him has eternal life and has crossed from death to life. He speaks both of an hour already arriving when the dead hear His voice and of a coming hour when everyone in the graves will come out.

The final distinction is between resurrection to life for those who have done good and resurrection to judgment for those who have done evil. The passage keeps present life through faith and future resurrection and judgment together.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian traditions commonly read the Son’s unity with the Father as consistent with His divine authority, rather than His being a separate, competing god. They also affirm a future resurrection and judgment: the Catholic Catechism and Westminster Confession both teach that people will answer to Christ for their lives. (Wesley on John 5:19–23; Catechism §§1038–1040; Westminster Confession 33.1–2)

Readers differ over how the promise of life relates to continuing faith. Reformed teaching in the Westminster Confession says that those truly received by God will be kept to the end, despite serious failures. Wesley reads verse 24’s assurance with the condition that a person does not abandon faith. Both locate life in Christ, while differing over whether a believer can finally fall away. (Westminster Confession 17.1–3; Wesley on John 5:24)

Calvin reads the good works in verse 29 as the fruit that identifies believers, while insisting that their acceptance rests on God’s mercy. This is his explanation of how that verse relates to the promise of life through faith. (Calvin on John 5:29)
passages.god_plan_html:
Daniel sees one like a son of man receiving enduring authority, glory and a kingdom whose rule reaches every people. Jesus’ words about the Son of Man’s authority to judge belong alongside that scriptural picture. This is a supported connection between the passages; John does not quote Daniel’s vision here. (Daniel 7:13–14)

Philippians describes the Son’s humble obedience through death and His exaltation, when every knee bows and every tongue confesses Him as Lord to the Father’s glory. Honoring the Son and honoring the Father belong together within God’s purpose. (Philippians 2:5–11)

passages.title: John 5:30-47
passages.section_title: What do the witnesses and the Scriptures say about Jesus?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 30 I can do nothing by Myself; I judge only as I hear. And My judgment is just, because I do not seek My own will, but the will of Him who sent Me. 31 If I testify about Myself, My testimony is not valid. 32 There is another who testifies about Me, and I know that His testimony about Me is valid. 33 You have sent to John, and he has testified to the truth. 34 Even though I do not accept human testimony, I say these things so that you may be saved. 35 John was a lamp that burned and gave light, and you were willing for a season to bask in his light. 36 But I have testimony more substantial than that of John. For the works that the Father has given Me to accomplish—the very works I am doing—testify about Me that the Father has sent Me. 37 And the Father who sent Me has Himself testified about Me. You have never heard His voice nor seen His form, 38 nor does His word abide in you, because you do not believe the One He sent. 39 You pore over the Scriptures because you presume that by them you possess eternal life. These are the very words that testify about Me, 40 yet you refuse to come to Me to have life. 41 I do not accept glory from men, 42 but I know you, that you do not have the love of God within you. 43 I have come in My Father’s name, and you have not received Me; but if someone else comes in his own name, you will receive him. 44 How can you believe if you accept glory from one another, yet do not seek the glory that comes from the only God? 45 Do not think that I will accuse you before the Father. Your accuser is Moses, in whom you have put your hope. 46 If you had believed Moses, you would believe Me, because he wrote about Me. 47 But since you do not believe what he wrote, how will you believe what I say?”
paragraphs: 30 I can do nothing by Myself; I judge only as I hear. And My judgment is just, because I do not seek My own will, but the will of Him who sent Me. 31 If I testify about Myself, My testimony is not valid. 32 There is another who testifies about Me, and I know that His testimony about Me is valid. 33 You have sent to John, and he has testified to the truth. 34 Even though I do not accept human testimony, I say these things so that you may be saved. 35 John was a lamp that burned and gave light, and you were willing for a season to bask in his light.

36 But I have testimony more substantial than that of John. For the works that the Father has given Me to accomplish—the very works I am doing—testify about Me that the Father has sent Me. 37 And the Father who sent Me has Himself testified about Me. You have never heard His voice nor seen His form, 38 nor does His word abide in you, because you do not believe the One He sent. 39 You pore over the Scriptures because you presume that by them you possess eternal life. These are the very words that testify about Me, 40 yet you refuse to come to Me to have life.

41 I do not accept glory from men, 42 but I know you, that you do not have the love of God within you. 43 I have come in My Father’s name, and you have not received Me; but if someone else comes in his own name, you will receive him. 44 How can you believe if you accept glory from one another, yet do not seek the glory that comes from the only God? 45 Do not think that I will accuse you before the Father. Your accuser is Moses, in whom you have put your hope. 46 If you had believed Moses, you would believe Me, because he wrote about Me. 47 But since you do not believe what he wrote, how will you believe what I say?”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus continues by saying that His judgment is just because He seeks the will of the One who sent Him. He then turns to the testimony supporting His mission: John’s witness, the works the Father gives Him, the Father’s own testimony and the Scriptures.

His opponents have searched the Scriptures expecting life, yet refuse to come to the One to whom those Scriptures point. He also challenges their willingness to receive approval from one another while failing to seek God’s approval.

The chapter closes with Moses. They place their hope in him, but Jesus says that Moses wrote about Him. Their response to Jesus exposes a failure to receive what they claim to honor in Moses’ writings.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readers commonly understand this as Jesus pointing to converging testimony about His identity, with Scripture study meant to lead people to receive Him. Calvin and Wesley both emphasize that refusing Christ misses the purpose of those writings. (Calvin on John 5:39–40; Wesley on John 5:39–40)

Wesley reads verse 39 as an instruction to search the Scriptures. The BSB presents it as a statement that His hearers already pore over them. Either way, the surrounding rebuke concerns their refusal to come to the One the Scriptures reveal; it does not make careful reading itself the problem. (Wesley on John 5:39; John 5:39–40 BSB)
passages.god_plan_html:
Moses promises a prophet through whom God will speak and whom the people must hear. In Acts, Peter directly applies that promise to Jesus and calls his hearers to turn back to God. This gives a specific New Testament connection between Moses’ writings and the mission of Christ. (Deuteronomy 18:15–19; Acts 3:18–23)

Peter also places that mission within God’s promise to Abraham that all families of the earth will be blessed, describing the blessing as God’s Servant turning people from wickedness. The goal of the testimony is therefore life with God and a changed direction, extending beyond the first hearers. (Acts 3:24–26)

passages.title: John 6:1-15
passages.section_title: What does the feeding reveal about Jesus?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 After this, Jesus crossed to the other side of the Sea of Galilee (that is, the Sea of Tiberias). 2 A large crowd followed Him because they saw the signs He was performing on the sick. 3 Then Jesus went up on the mountain and sat down with His disciples. 4 Now the Jewish Feast of the Passover was near. 5 When Jesus looked up and saw a large crowd coming toward Him, He said to Philip, “Where can we buy bread for these people to eat?” 6 But He was asking this to test him, for He knew what He was about to do. 7 Philip answered, “Two hundred denarii would not buy enough bread for each of them to have a small piece.” 8 One of His disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, said to Him, 9 “Here is a boy with five barley loaves and two small fish. But what difference will these make among so many?” 10 “Have the people sit down,” Jesus said. Now there was plenty of grass in that place, so the men sat down, about five thousand of them. 11 Then Jesus took the loaves and the fish, gave thanks, and distributed to those who were seated as much as they wanted. 12 And when everyone was full, He said to His disciples, “Gather the pieces that are left over, so that nothing will be wasted.” 13 So they collected them and filled twelve baskets with the pieces of the five barley loaves left over by those who had eaten. 14 When the people saw the sign that Jesus had performed, they began to say, “Truly this is the Prophet who is to come into the world.” 15 Then Jesus, realizing that they were about to come and make Him king by force, withdrew again to a mountain by Himself.

But what difference will these make among so many?” 10 “Have the people sit down,” Jesus said. Now there was plenty of grass in that place, so the men sat down, about five thousand of them. 11 Then Jesus took the loaves and the fish, gave thanks, and distributed to those who were seated as much as they wanted. 12 And when everyone was full, He said to His disciples, “Gather the pieces that are left over, so that nothing will be wasted.” 13 So they collected them and filled twelve baskets with the pieces of the five barley loaves left over by those who had eaten.

14 When the people saw the sign that Jesus had performed, they began to say, “Truly this is the Prophet who is to come into the world.” 15 Then Jesus, realizing that they were about to come and make Him king by force, withdrew again to a mountain by Himself.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
A large crowd follows Jesus across the Sea of Galilee because of His signs among the sick. He sits on a mountainside with His disciples, and the Gospel notes that Passover is near.

Jesus asks Philip where they can buy bread for the people. This is a test; He already knows what He will do. Philip sees that even a large sum would not buy everyone a little. Andrew points to a boy with five barley loaves and two small fish, while asking what such a small amount could accomplish.

Jesus has the people sit on the grass, gives thanks and distributes the food. Everyone has as much as they want, and twelve baskets of pieces remain. About five thousand men are seated; the account does not give the exact total of everyone present.

The people recognize a sign and call Jesus the Prophet who is to come. When He realizes they intend to make Him king by force, He withdraws alone. Their response raises the question of whether they understand what kind of mission He has come to carry out.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readers commonly understand this as Jesus truly feeding the crowd and revealing His identity through the sign. Calvin also emphasizes the difference between recognizing something about Him and trying to take control of His kingship, as the crowd attempts to do. (Calvin on John 6:14–15)
passages.god_plan_html:
The Passover setting places this feeding beside Israel’s memory of deliverance and God’s provision of bread in the wilderness. Later in this chapter, the crowd explicitly raises the manna account, and Jesus points to the Father’s gift of the true bread that gives life. The connection is therefore part of the Gospel’s own explanation, rather than only a similarity noticed by later readers. (Exodus 16:1–15; John 6:31–35)

Another supported parallel is Elisha’s feeding of a hundred people with twenty barley loaves. His servant questions the small supply, yet the people eat and have some left over according to the Lord’s word. Jesus’ provision for the much larger crowd belongs alongside that earlier sign of God’s abundance. (2 Kings 4:42–44)

The grass and the satisfying meal also recall the shepherd’s care in Psalm 23: God leads His flock to pasture and provides for them. That is a parallel with Jesus’ care here, not a claim that John quotes the psalm. The scene holds together the crowd’s actual hunger and the greater life-giving purpose that Jesus will explain. (Psalm 23:1–5)

passages.title: John 6:16-21
passages.section_title: Why can the disciples take courage on the sea?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 When evening came, His disciples went down to the sea, 17 got into a boat, and started across the sea to Capernaum. It was already dark, and Jesus had not yet gone out to them. 18 A strong wind was blowing, and the sea grew agitated. 19 When they had rowed about three or four miles, they saw Jesus approaching the boat, walking on the sea—and they were terrified. 20 But Jesus spoke up: “It is I; do not be afraid.” 21 Then they were willing to take Him into the boat, and at once the boat reached the shore where they were heading.
paragraphs: 16 When evening came, His disciples went down to the sea, 17 got into a boat, and started across the sea to Capernaum. It was already dark, and Jesus had not yet gone out to them. 18 A strong wind was blowing, and the sea grew agitated. 19 When they had rowed about three or four miles, they saw Jesus approaching the boat, walking on the sea—and they were terrified. 20 But Jesus spoke up: “It is I; do not be afraid.” 21 Then they were willing to take Him into the boat, and at once the boat reached the shore where they were heading.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
At evening, the disciples set out by boat toward Capernaum while Jesus is still apart from them. Darkness falls, a strong wind blows and the sea grows rough. They have rowed about three or four miles when they see Him walking toward them on the water.

They are terrified, but Jesus identifies Himself and tells them not to be afraid. They are willing to receive Him into the boat, and the account says the boat reaches the shore at once. John gives that arrival without explaining a physical mechanism.

This follows the feeding and leads into the crowd finding Jesus on the other side. The two signs place His care for people alongside His authority over the natural world.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readers commonly understand the scene as a real display of Jesus’ authority and His reassuring presence with the disciples. Calvin emphasizes the confidence His words give them, while the USCCB’s notes connect His walking on the sea with Scripture’s portrayal of God’s power. (Calvin on John 6:20; USCCB notes on John 6:16–21)
passages.god_plan_html:
Job describes God as the One who treads on the waves of the sea. Psalm 77 pictures God making a path through mighty waters and leading His people like a flock through Moses and Aaron. Jesus walking on the sea forms a supported parallel with those accounts of God’s authority and saving guidance. (Job 9:8–10; Psalm 77:16–20)

The shepherd’s promise of presence in Psalm 23 also helps explain why reassurance matters. The psalmist faces danger without being abandoned, because the Lord is with him. Jesus’ words to the frightened disciples belong alongside that scriptural hope of the Lord present with His people in danger. This is a connection about His presence and care, rather than a promise that believers will never face rough waters. (Psalm 23:1–4)

passages.title: John 6:22-34
passages.section_title: What bread should the crowd be seeking?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 The next day, the crowd that had remained on the other side of the sea realized that only one boat had been there, and that Jesus had not boarded it with His disciples, but they had gone away alone. 23 However, some boats from Tiberias landed near the place where the people had eaten the bread after the Lord had given thanks. 24 So when the crowd saw that neither Jesus nor His disciples were there, they got into the boats and went to Capernaum to look for Him. 25 When they found Him on the other side of the sea, they asked Him, “Rabbi, when did You get here?” 26 Jesus replied, “Truly, truly, I tell you, it is not because you saw these signs that you are looking for Me, but because you ate the loaves and had your fill. 27 Do not work for food that perishes, but for food that endures to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give you. For on Him God the Father has placed His seal of approval.” 28 Then they inquired, “What must we do to perform the works of God?” 29 Jesus replied, “The work of God is this: to believe in the One He has sent.” 30 So they asked Him, “What sign then will You perform, so that we may see it and believe You? What will You do? 31 Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, as it is written: ‘He gave them bread from heaven to eat.’” 32 Jesus said to them, “Truly, truly, I tell you, it was not Moses who gave you the bread from heaven, but it is My Father who gives you the true bread from heaven. 33 For the bread of God is He who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.” 34 “Sir,” they said, “give us this bread at all times.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The day after the feeding, the crowd realizes Jesus did not leave in the disciples’ boat. Other boats arrive, and the people go to Capernaum to find Him. They ask when He got there.

Jesus addresses why they are looking for Him: they ate and were filled. He directs them toward the food that endures to eternal life, which the Son of Man gives. When they ask what God requires them to do, He calls them to believe in the One God has sent.

They ask for a sign and recall their ancestors receiving manna. Jesus corrects the focus on Moses: the Father gives the true bread from heaven, the One who gives life to the world. Their request for that bread leads into His explanation that He Himself is the bread of life.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand Jesus as turning the crowd’s attention from another meal toward faith in the One sent by God. Calvin and Wesley both read the work named in verse 29 as believing in Christ, with that faith directing the rest of life rather than making a list of achievements the basis for receiving Him. (Calvin on John 6:29; Wesley on John 6:27–29)
passages.god_plan_html:
Deuteronomy explains that manna taught Israel to depend on every word from God, rather than bread alone. Jesus quotes that teaching during His own wilderness temptation. The movement from food toward trusting God’s word therefore has a clear scriptural background, including Jesus’ own use of it. (Deuteronomy 8:2–3; Matthew 4:1–4)

Paul also reads Israel’s wilderness experience in relation to Christ. He describes their spiritual food and drink and identifies the accompanying rock with Christ. That gives a further New Testament connection between God’s earlier provision and the One who now offers lasting life. (1 Corinthians 10:1–4)
passages.current_position_html: Our study Prayer and Faith reads the true bread from heaven as Christ Himself, whom the Father gives for life. It connects this passage with daily dependence on Him as the source of lasting life, rather than treating bread only as material provision.

The crowd has asked Jesus for a sign and pointed to the manna eaten by their ancestors. Jesus places the credit for that provision with His Father and directs them toward the true bread that gives life to the world.

He identifies that bread as Himself in the following verses. The statement belongs within His call to believe in the One sent by God. Read John 6:22–34 in context.

passages.title: John 6:32-58
passages.section_title: How does Jesus explain the bread that gives lasting life?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 32 Jesus said to them, “Truly, truly, I tell you, it was not Moses who gave you the bread from heaven, but it is My Father who gives you the true bread from heaven. 33 For the bread of God is He who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.” 34 “Sir,” they said, “give us this bread at all times.” 35 Jesus answered, “I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to Me will never hunger, and whoever believes in Me will never thirst. 36 But as I stated, you have seen Me and still you do not believe. 37 Everyone the Father gives Me will come to Me, and the one who comes to Me I will never drive away. 38 For I have come down from heaven, not to do My own will, but to do the will of Him who sent Me. 39 And this is the will of Him who sent Me, that I shall lose none of those He has given Me, but raise them up at the last day. 40 For it is My Father’s will that everyone who looks to the Son and believes in Him shall have eternal life, and I will raise him up at the last day.” 41 At this, the Jews began to grumble about Jesus because He had said, “I am the bread that came down from heaven.” 42 They were asking, “Is this not Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? passages.context_html:
This extended passage belongs to the conversation after the feeding. Jesus points beyond the manna associated with Moses to the Father’s true bread, identifies Himself as that bread, and promises life and resurrection to those who come in faith.

He answers objections to His heavenly origin by speaking of the Father’s drawing and teaching. He then names His flesh as the gift for the world’s life and develops the language of receiving His flesh and blood and remaining in Him.

The connected sequence helps keep the Father’s initiative, faith, Jesus’ self-giving and His promise of resurrection together. The next section records how His hearers respond to the teaching.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian traditions agree that Jesus is the bread giving life and that people need God’s grace to come to Him. They differ over the Father’s drawing, continuing faith and how the eating language relates to Communion.

Reformed teaching describes God bringing those He has chosen willingly to Christ and preserving them to the end. Wesley reads the Father’s drawing as grace that can be resisted and the promises as calling for continuing faith. Catholic teaching also begins with God’s undeserved initiative while affirming a free response and the possibility of losing faith. (Westminster Confession 10, 17; Wesley on John 6:37–44; Catechism §§1996–2002; Catechism §162)

The Catholic Church reads the discourse as an announcement of the Eucharist and teaches that the bread and wine become Christ’s body and blood, with the whole Christ truly present. (Catechism §1336; Catechism §§1374–1376)

The Lutheran Formula of Concord explains John 6 as receiving Christ through faith, which happens through hearing the gospel and also in Communion. Lutheran teaching separately affirms that Christ’s true body and blood are received in and under the bread and wine. (Formula of Concord VII.61–65; Large Catechism, Altar §§8–14)

Calvin reads John 6 as receiving Christ continually through faith, rather than as referring directly to the Communion rite. The Westminster and Baptist confessions nevertheless teach that believers truly receive spiritual nourishment from Christ in the meal; their account is more than simply recalling a distant event. (Calvin on John 6:53; Westminster Confession 29.5–7; Baptist Confession 30.1, 7)

Wesley connects the words directly with Christ’s suffering and receiving Him through faith, and only remotely, if at all, with the Lord’s Supper. This is his interpretation of the passage, rather than a denial that Christians should share the meal. (Wesley on John 6:51–53)
passages.current_position_html: Our study Prayer and Faith reads Jesus as the living bread to whom the manna pointed. The manna sustained life for a time; Christ Himself gives lasting life. The study connects receiving that life with faith and continued dependence on Him. Our study also identifies the Father’s stated will here as life and resurrection for those who believe in the Son.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Deuteronomy says that manna taught dependence on God’s word, and Jesus draws on that lesson in His wilderness temptation. The bread theme belongs within that larger call to live by what God gives and says. (Deuteronomy 8:2–3; Matthew 4:1–4)

Hebrews connects Christ’s self-offering with redemption and a cleansed conscience for serving God. Paul connects the shared bread and cup with a people joined to Christ and one another, proclaiming His death until He returns. These passages place the gift of life within His sacrifice and the community formed through it. (Hebrews 9:11–14; 1 Corinthians 10:16–17; 1 Corinthians 11:23–26)

The promised resurrection also belongs within the victory begun by Christ’s own resurrection and ending in death’s defeat. (1 Corinthians 15:20–28)

passages.title: John 6:35
passages.section_title: What does it mean to come to the bread of life?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 35 Jesus answered, “I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to Me will never hunger, and whoever believes in Me will never thirst.
paragraphs: 35 Jesus answered, “I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to Me will never hunger, and whoever believes in Me will never thirst.

passages.context_html:
After the crowd asks for the true bread from heaven, Jesus identifies Himself as the bread of life. Coming to Him and believing in Him appear together as the response to His gift.

The surrounding promise leads toward eternal life and resurrection, rather than a claim that believers never again need ordinary food or drink. Read John 6:35–40 in context.

passages.title: John 6:41-51
passages.section_title: How does the Father draw people to the living bread?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 41 At this, the Jews began to grumble about Jesus because He had said, “I am the bread that came down from heaven.” 42 They were asking, “Is this not Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How then can He say, ‘I have come down from heaven’ ?” 43 “Stop grumbling among yourselves,” Jesus replied. 44 “No one can come to Me unless the Father who sent Me draws him, and I will raise him up at the last day. 45 It is written in the Prophets: ‘And they will all be taught by God.’ Everyone who has heard the Father and learned from Him comes to Me— 46 not that anyone has seen the Father except the One who is from God; only He has seen the Father. 47 Truly, truly, I tell you, he who believes has eternal life. 48 I am the bread of life. 49 Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, yet they died. 50 This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that anyone may eat of it and not die. 51 I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. And this bread, which I will give for the life of the world, is My flesh.”
paragraphs: 41 At this, the Jews began to grumble about Jesus because He had said, “I am the bread that came down from heaven.” 42 They were asking, “Is this not Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How then can He say, ‘I have come down from heaven’ ?” 43 “Stop grumbling among yourselves,” Jesus replied. 44 “No one can come to Me unless the Father who sent Me draws him, and I will raise him up at the last day. 45 It is written in the Prophets: ‘And they will all be taught by God.’ Everyone who has heard the Father and learned from Him comes to Me— 46 not that anyone has seen the Father except the One who is from God; only He has seen the Father.

47 Truly, truly, I tell you, he who believes has eternal life. 48 I am the bread of life. 49 Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, yet they died. 50 This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that anyone may eat of it and not die. 51 I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. And this bread, which I will give for the life of the world, is My flesh.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Some of Jesus’ hearers grumble because He says He has come from heaven. They think they know His family, so His claim does not fit what they assume about Him. Jesus answers by speaking of the Father drawing people to Him and teaching them.

The Greek verb behind drawing is ἕλκω, helkō (HEL-koh). Thayer lists physical pulling or hauling among its uses, and also lists the inward leading described here. That figurative use helps explain why Jesus immediately speaks about hearing and learning from the Father. (Thayer, Greek 1670)

Jesus quotes the promise that people will be taught by God, then distinguishes His own knowledge of the Father from theirs. He repeats that the believer has eternal life and contrasts the manna eaten by ancestors who died with the living bread He gives. He identifies that gift with His flesh given for the life of the world.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian traditions agree that coming to Christ depends on God’s grace. Where traditions differ is how His drawing works in a person’s response.

Reformed teaching in the Westminster Confession says that God changes the hearts of those He calls so that they freely and willingly come to Christ. Calvin likewise reads this as an inward work that brings about the response, rather than external force against a person who remains unwilling. (Westminster Confession 10.1–2; Calvin on John 6:44)

Wesley teaches that God first gives the ability and desire to respond, while allowing that this grace can be resisted. The Catholic Catechism also places the beginning entirely in God’s undeserved initiative, while teaching that His initiative calls for a free human response. These readings differ from saying that a person can come to Christ without God first acting. (Wesley on John 6:44; Catechism §§1996–2002)
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus explicitly connects His teaching with Isaiah’s promise that the children of God’s restored people will be taught by the Lord. Isaiah places that promise alongside God’s enduring love and covenant of peace. The Father’s teaching here belongs within that scriptural hope of a people restored and taught by Him. (Isaiah 54:10–14; John 6:45)

Ephesians describes God’s purpose in Christ as bringing people into His family, making them holy, and giving forgiveness through the Son. That provides a wider account of what His gracious initiative is for: life with Him as His children, to the praise of His grace. (Ephesians 1:3–10)
passages.current_position_html: Our study Prayer and Faith reads Jesus as the living bread to whom the manna pointed. The manna sustained life for a time; Christ Himself gives lasting life. The study connects receiving that life with faith and continued dependence on Him.

passages.title: John 6:48-51
passages.section_title: How is the living bread different from manna?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 48 I am the bread of life. 49 Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, yet they died. 50 This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that anyone may eat of it and not die. 51 I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. And this bread, which I will give for the life of the world, is My flesh.”
paragraphs: 48 I am the bread of life. 49 Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, yet they died. 50 This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that anyone may eat of it and not die. 51 I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. And this bread, which I will give for the life of the world, is My flesh.”

passages.context_html:
Jesus has spoken of the Father drawing and teaching people, and has promised eternal life to the believer. He now contrasts Himself as living bread with the manna eaten in the wilderness.

Those ancestors died despite the food they received. Jesus promises lasting life through Himself and names His flesh as the bread given for the life of the world. The following verses develop the language of receiving His flesh and blood. Read John 6:41–51 in context.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readers understand these words as a call to receive life from Christ through His self-giving. Where traditions differ is how the language of eating and drinking relates to Communion, also called the Lord’s Supper or Eucharist.

The Catholic Church reads the discourse as an announcement of the Eucharist and teaches that the bread and wine become Christ’s body and blood, with the whole Christ truly present. (Catechism §1336; Catechism §§1374–1376)

The Lutheran Formula of Concord explains John 6 as receiving Christ through faith, which happens through hearing the gospel and also in Communion. Lutheran teaching separately affirms that Christ’s true body and blood are received in and under the bread and wine. (Formula of Concord VII.61–65; Large Catechism, Altar §§8–14)

Calvin reads John 6 as receiving Christ continually through faith, rather than as referring directly to the Communion rite. The Westminster and Baptist confessions nevertheless teach that believers truly receive spiritual nourishment from Christ in the meal; their account is more than simply recalling a distant event. (Calvin on John 6:53; Westminster Confession 29.5–7; Baptist Confession 30.1, 7)

Wesley connects the words directly with Christ’s suffering and receiving Him through faith, and only remotely, if at all, with the Lord’s Supper. This is his interpretation of the passage, rather than a denial that Christians should share the meal. (Wesley on John 6:51–53)

Hebrews describes Christ entering God’s presence by His own blood, securing redemption and cleansing the conscience so that people may serve the living God. His flesh and blood given for life belong alongside that wider account of His self-offering. (Hebrews 9:11–14)

Paul connects the shared cup and bread with participation in Christ and with many believers becoming one body. He also says that the meal proclaims the Lord’s death until He comes. The gift of life through Christ therefore reaches into a people joined to Him and to one another, remembering His death while awaiting His return. (1 Corinthians 10:16–17; 1 Corinthians 11:23–26)

passages.title: John 6:58
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus promise a life that manna could not give?

passages.title: John 6:60-71
passages.section_title: Where else would the disciples find words of eternal life?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 60 On hearing it, many of His disciples said, “This is a difficult teaching. Who can accept it?” 61 Aware that His disciples were grumbling about this teaching, Jesus asked them, “Does this offend you? 62 Then what will happen if you see the Son of Man ascend to where He was before? 63 The Spirit gives life; the flesh profits nothing. The words I have spoken to you are spirit and they are life. 64 However, there are some of you who do not believe.” (For Jesus had known from the beginning which of them did not believe and who would betray Him.) 65 Then Jesus said, “This is why I told you that no one can come to Me unless the Father has granted it to him.” 66 From that time on many of His disciples turned back and no longer walked with Him. 67 So Jesus asked the Twelve, “Do you want to leave too?” 68 Simon Peter replied, “Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life. 69 We believe and know that You are the Holy One of God.” 70 Jesus answered them, “Have I not chosen you, the Twelve? Yet one of you is a devil!” 71 He was speaking about Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot. For although Judas was one of the Twelve, he was later to betray Jesus.

Who can accept it?” 61 Aware that His disciples were grumbling about this teaching, Jesus asked them, “Does this offend you? 62 Then what will happen if you see the Son of Man ascend to where He was before? 63 The Spirit gives life; the flesh profits nothing. The words I have spoken to you are spirit and they are life. 64 However, there are some of you who do not believe.” (For Jesus had known from the beginning which of them did not believe and who would betray Him.) 65 Then Jesus said, “This is why I told you that no one can come to Me unless the Father has granted it to him.”

66 From that time on many of His disciples turned back and no longer walked with Him. 67 So Jesus asked the Twelve, “Do you want to leave too?” 68 Simon Peter replied, “Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life. 69 We believe and know that You are the Holy One of God.” 70 Jesus answered them, “Have I not chosen you, the Twelve? Yet one of you is a devil!” 71 He was speaking about Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot. For although Judas was one of the Twelve, he was later to betray Jesus.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Many disciples find the teaching difficult to accept. Jesus asks whether it offends them, speaks of the Son of Man ascending to where He was before, and says that the Spirit gives life. He also says that some do not believe, and the Gospel notes His knowledge of unbelief and the coming betrayal.

When many turn back, Jesus asks the Twelve whether they also want to leave. Peter answers that Jesus has the words of eternal life and confesses Him as the Holy One of God.

Jesus then reminds them that He has chosen the Twelve while warning that one of them is a devil. The Gospel identifies the coming betrayer as Judas. Being among the closest followers does not make that warning unnecessary.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readers commonly understand Peter’s answer as a confession of trust in Jesus, set beside the departure of others and the warning about Judas. Calvin and Wesley both treat the answer as a confession of faith, while distinguishing membership among the Twelve from a guarantee of faithfulness. (Calvin on John 6:68–70; Wesley on John 6:68–70)
passages.god_plan_html:
First Peter describes new birth through God’s living and enduring word, the message proclaimed in the gospel. That is a scriptural parallel to Jesus’ words giving life through the Spirit: God brings people to life through a message that outlasts human weakness. (1 Peter 1:22–25)

The warning about betrayal also looks toward the cross. In Acts, Peter describes Jesus being handed over according to God’s purpose and foreknowledge, while holding those who killed Him responsible, and then announces God raising Him from death. Betrayal and opposition do not overturn the saving purpose fulfilled through the crucified and risen Son. (Acts 2:22–24)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: John 7:1-13
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus go to the feast in His own time?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 After this, Jesus traveled throughout Galilee. He did not want to travel in Judea, because the Jews there were trying to kill Him. 2 However, the Jewish Feast of Tabernacles was near. 3 So Jesus’ brothers said to Him, “Leave here and go to Judea, so that Your disciples there may see the works You are doing. 4 For no one who wants to be known publicly acts in secret. Since You are doing these things, show Yourself to the world.” 5 For even His own brothers did not believe in Him. 6 Therefore Jesus told them, “Although your time is always at hand, My time has not yet come. 7 The world cannot hate you, but it hates Me, because I testify that its works are evil. 8 Go up to the feast on your own. I am not going up to this feast, because My time has not yet come.” 9 Having said this, Jesus remained in Galilee. 10 But after His brothers had gone up to the feast, He also went—not publicly, but in secret. 11 So the Jews were looking for Him at the feast and asking, “Where is He?” 12 Many in the crowds were whispering about Him. Some said, “He is a good man.” But others replied, “No, He deceives the people.” 13 Yet no one would speak publicly about Him for fear of the Jews.
paragraphs: 1 After this, Jesus traveled throughout Galilee. He did not want to travel in Judea, because the Jews there were trying to kill Him. 2 However, the Jewish Feast of Tabernacles was near. 3 So Jesus’ brothers said to Him, “Leave here and go to Judea, so that Your disciples there may see the works You are doing. 4 For no one who wants to be known publicly acts in secret. Since You are doing these things, show Yourself to the world.” 5 For even His own brothers did not believe in Him.

6 Therefore Jesus told them, “Although your time is always at hand, My time has not yet come. 7 The world cannot hate you, but it hates Me, because I testify that its works are evil. 8 Go up to the feast on your own. I am not going up to this feast, because My time has not yet come.” 9 Having said this, Jesus remained in Galilee. 10 But after His brothers had gone up to the feast, He also went—not publicly, but in secret.

11 So the Jews were looking for Him at the feast and asking, “Where is He?” 12 Many in the crowds were whispering about Him. Some said, “He is a good man.” But others replied, “No, He deceives the people.” 13 Yet no one would speak publicly about Him for fear of the Jews.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus remains active in Galilee while facing a threat to His life in Judea. As the Feast of Tabernacles approaches, His brothers urge Him to go where His works will be seen publicly. The Gospel says that they do not yet believe in Him.

The feast is also called the Feast of Booths. Leviticus describes the people living in temporary shelters to remember how God made Israel dwell in booths after bringing them out of Egypt. It is also a joyful harvest celebration. (Leviticus 23:33–43; Deuteronomy 16:13–17)

Jesus says that His time has not come. The BSB’s main text says He is not going up to this feast; its footnote records the reading not yet in other manuscripts. The account then shows Him remaining behind and later going privately, after His brothers have left. (BSB footnote on John 7:8)

At the feast, people are divided about Him. Some call Him good and others say He misleads people. Fear of the authorities keeps the discussion quiet. The scene presents different responses within a Jewish setting, rather than one view held by every Jewish person.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readers commonly understand Jesus as refusing to let others set His course. Commentators differ over the emphasis of His time: Calvin understands the immediate reference as when to begin the journey, while the USCCB’s note connects it with the larger theme of His death and resurrection. (Calvin on John 7:6; USCCB note on John 7:6)

Readers also differ over the family relationship meant by His brothers. The Catholic Church teaches that these are close relatives, rather than other children of Mary. The Orthodox tradition reflected in the Orthodox Church in America’s life of Joseph understands them as Joseph’s children from a previous marriage. (Catechism §§499–500; OCA, Joseph the Betrothed)

A published Orthodox Presbyterian Church answer reads them as Mary and Joseph’s later children, making them Jesus’ half-brothers. Protestant readers do not all agree: Wesley identifies cousins here, and Calvin understands the term as including wider relatives. The OPC answer is a church-published explanation, while Wesley and Calvin give their own interpretations. (OPC Q&A; Wesley on John 7:3; Calvin on John 7:3)
passages.god_plan_html:
The feast’s memory of life in temporary shelters can be read alongside the wider scriptural theme of God making His home with His people. This Gospel has already said that the Word becomes flesh and dwells among us. Jesus’ presence at the feast belongs within that larger story of God coming near through the Son. This is a thematic parallel, rather than a claim that John assigns a hidden meaning to every feast detail. (John 1:14)

Revelation carries the hope forward to God dwelling with His people, wiping away tears and ending death. The purpose reaches beyond one journey to a feast: life with God in the renewed creation. (Revelation 21:1–4)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: John 7:14-24
passages.section_title: How should people judge Jesus’ teaching and healing?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 About halfway through the feast, Jesus went up to the temple courts and began to teach. 15 The Jews were amazed and asked, “How did this man attain such learning without having studied?” 16 “My teaching is not My own,” Jesus replied. “It comes from Him who sent Me. 17 If anyone desires to do His will, he will know whether My teaching is from God or whether I speak on My own. 18 He who speaks on his own authority seeks his own glory, but He who seeks the glory of the One who sent Him is a man of truth; in Him there is no falsehood. 19 Has not Moses given you the law? Yet not one of you keeps it. Why are you trying to kill Me?” 20 “You have a demon,” the crowd replied. “Who is trying to kill You?” 21 Jesus answered them, “I did one miracle, and you are all amazed. 22 But because Moses gave you circumcision, you circumcise a boy on the Sabbath (not that it is from Moses, but from the patriarchs.) 23 If a boy can be circumcised on the Sabbath so that the law of Moses will not be broken, why are you angry with Me for making the whole man well on the Sabbath? 24 Stop judging by outward appearances, and start judging justly.”
paragraphs: 14 About halfway through the feast, Jesus went up to the temple courts and began to teach. 15 The Jews were amazed and asked, “How did this man attain such learning without having studied?” 16 “My teaching is not My own,” Jesus replied. “It comes from Him who sent Me. 17 If anyone desires to do His will, he will know whether My teaching is from God or whether I speak on My own. 18 He who speaks on his own authority seeks his own glory, but He who seeks the glory of the One who sent Him is a man of truth; in Him there is no falsehood.

19 Has not Moses given you the law? Yet not one of you keeps it. Why are you trying to kill Me?” 20 “You have a demon,” the crowd replied. “Who is trying to kill You?” 21 Jesus answered them, “I did one miracle, and you are all amazed. 22 But because Moses gave you circumcision, you circumcise a boy on the Sabbath (not that it is from Moses, but from the patriarchs.) 23 If a boy can be circumcised on the Sabbath so that the law of Moses will not be broken, why are you angry with Me for making the whole man well on the Sabbath? 24 Stop judging by outward appearances, and start judging justly.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
About halfway through the feast, Jesus teaches in the temple courts. His hearers wonder how He has acquired such learning without the study they expect. He points to the One who sent Him as the source of His teaching and connects recognizing that teaching with a willingness to do God’s will.

The discussion turns to the effort to kill Him and His earlier Sabbath healing. Some in the crowd deny knowing about a threat against Him. Jesus compares their objection to making a whole person well with their acceptance of circumcision on the Sabbath.

The eighth-day command reaches back to Abraham and is repeated in the law given through Moses. Jesus reasons from that accepted command and practice, then calls for just judgment that looks beyond appearances. (Genesis 17:9–14; Leviticus 12:1–3)
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readers commonly understand Jesus as calling for a judgment shaped by God’s will and the truth of His work, rather than by prejudice or appearances. Calvin and Wesley both read the circumcision comparison as exposing an inconsistent objection to the Sabbath healing. (Calvin on John 7:17–24; Wesley on John 7:17–22)
passages.god_plan_html:
The covenant sign also belongs within a wider promise about the heart. Deuteronomy speaks of God circumcising His people’s hearts so that they love Him and live. The concern for doing God’s will here can be read beside that promise of inward renewal. This is a scriptural parallel, rather than an explanation Jesus explicitly adds to His comparison. (Deuteronomy 30:5–6)

Colossians connects a circumcision performed by Christ with sharing in His death and resurrection, forgiveness and the cancellation of sin’s debt. It gives the broader picture of the life Christ brings, beyond a dispute over an outward act. (Colossians 2:11–14)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: John 7:25-36
passages.section_title: Do the people know where Jesus comes from and where He is going?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 25 Then some of the people of Jerusalem began to say, “Isn’t this the man they are trying to kill? 26 Yet here He is, speaking publicly, and they are not saying anything to Him. Have the rulers truly recognized that this is the Christ? 27 But we know where this man is from. When the Christ comes, no one will know where He is from.” 28 Then Jesus, still teaching in the temple courts, cried out, “You know Me, and you know where I am from. I have not come of My own accord, but He who sent Me is true. You do not know Him, 29 but I know Him, because I am from Him and He sent Me.” 30 So they tried to seize Him, but no one laid a hand on Him, because His hour had not yet come. 31 Many in the crowd, however, believed in Him and said, “When the Christ comes, will He perform more signs than this man?” 32 When the Pharisees heard the crowd whispering these things about Jesus, they and the chief priests sent officers to arrest Him. 33 So Jesus said, “I am with you only a little while longer, and then I am going to the One who sent Me. 34 You will look for Me, but you will not find Me; and where I am, you cannot come.” 35 At this, the Jews said to one another, “Where does He intend to go that we will not find Him? Will He go where the Jews are dispersed among the Greeks, and teach the Greeks? 36 What does He mean by saying, ‘You will look for Me, but you will not find Me,’ and, ‘Where I am, you cannot come’ ?”
