Have the rulers truly recognized that this is the Christ? 27 But we know where this man is from. When the Christ comes, no one will know where He is from.” 28 Then Jesus, still teaching in the temple courts, cried out, “You know Me, and you know where I am from. I have not come of My own accord, but He who sent Me is true. You do not know Him, 29 but I know Him, because I am from Him and He sent Me.” 30 So they tried to seize Him, but no one laid a hand on Him, because His hour had not yet come. 31 Many in the crowd, however, believed in Him and said, “When the Christ comes, will He perform more signs than this man?”

32 When the Pharisees heard the crowd whispering these things about Jesus, they and the chief priests sent officers to arrest Him. 33 So Jesus said, “I am with you only a little while longer, and then I am going to the One who sent Me. 34 You will look for Me, but you will not find Me; and where I am, you cannot come.” 35 At this, the Jews said to one another, “Where does He intend to go that we will not find Him? Will He go where the Jews are dispersed among the Greeks, and teach the Greeks? 36 What does He mean by saying, ‘You will look for Me, but you will not find Me,’ and, ‘Where I am, you cannot come’ ?”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Some people in Jerusalem know of the threat against Jesus and wonder why He is teaching openly without being stopped. They also question His claim because they think they know where He comes from. Jesus directs them toward the One who sent Him, whom He knows.

An attempt to seize Him fails because His hour has not yet come. Many in the crowd nevertheless believe, asking what greater signs the Christ could perform. The chief priests and Pharisees then send officers to arrest Him.

Jesus says He will remain only a little longer before going to the One who sent Him. His hearers puzzle over whether He means traveling to Jewish communities among the Greeks, or teaching the Greeks themselves. Their geographical questions miss His statement about returning to the Father.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly understand Jesus’ departure as pointing toward His return to the Father through death and resurrection. Calvin reads it as assurance that His opponents cannot prevent the mission’s completion, while Wesley contrasts their earthly guesses with His heavenly destination. (Calvin on John 7:33; Wesley on John 7:33–35)
passages.god_plan_html:
Later in the Gospel, Jesus states the whole movement plainly: He comes from the Father into the world and returns to the Father. He also speaks of completing the work given to Him and sharing again in the glory He had before the world existed. His destination here belongs within that larger mission. (John 16:28; John 17:1–5)

Acts records His ascension alongside the promise of the Spirit and a mission reaching the ends of the earth. Returning to the Father leads into the wider witness carried by His followers. The people’s question about Greeks is not itself a prediction of a journey He will make to Greece; the wider purpose is made clear in these later passages. (Acts 1:8–11)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: John 7:37-44
passages.section_title: What is the living water Jesus promises?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 37 On the last and greatest day of the feast, Jesus stood up and called out in a loud voice, “If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink. 38 Whoever believes in Me, as the Scripture has said: ‘Streams of living water will flow from within him.’” 39 He was speaking about the Spirit, whom those who believed in Him were later to receive. For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified. 40 On hearing these words, some of the people said, “This is truly the Prophet.” 41 Others declared, “This is the Christ.” But still others asked, “How can the Christ come from Galilee? 42 Doesn’t the Scripture say that the Christ will come from the line of David and from Bethlehem, the village where David lived?” 43 So there was division in the crowd because of Jesus. 44 Some of them wanted to seize Him, but no one laid a hand on Him.
paragraphs: 37 On the last and greatest day of the feast, Jesus stood up and called out in a loud voice, “If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink. 38 Whoever believes in Me, as the Scripture has said: ‘Streams of living water will flow from within him.’” 39 He was speaking about the Spirit, whom those who believed in Him were later to receive. For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified.

40 On hearing these words, some of the people said, “This is truly the Prophet.” 41 Others declared, “This is the Christ.” But still others asked, “How can the Christ come from Galilee? 42 Doesn’t the Scripture say that the Christ will come from the line of David and from Bethlehem, the village where David lived?” 43 So there was division in the crowd because of Jesus. 44 Some of them wanted to seize Him, but no one laid a hand on Him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
On the last and greatest day of the feast, Jesus calls thirsty people to come to Him and drink. He speaks of streams of living water flowing from within the believer. The Gospel explains that He means the Spirit, to be received after Jesus is glorified. That points ahead to His death, resurrection and return to the Father.

The Greek word κοιλία, koilia (koy-LEE-ah), can describe the belly and can also refer to the inner person. Thayer lists John 7:38 under this figurative meaning: the heart or inward life. That helps explain the picture of life flowing from within. (Thayer, Greek 2836)

The Mishnah, a collection of Jewish teachings, describes water being brought from the pool of Siloam and poured at the altar during the feast. This gives background for the invitation, though the Gospel does not narrate each part of that ceremony or identify the exact moment when Jesus speaks. (Mishnah Sukkah 4:9)

The crowd remains divided. Some identify Jesus as the Prophet or the Christ, while others question how He could qualify if He comes from Galilee. They appeal to the Messiah’s Davidic descent and Bethlehem. Some want to seize Him, but no one lays a hand on Him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readers agree on the Gospel’s own explanation that the living water concerns the Spirit. The wording also leads to different readings of how that life flows.

Wesley reads the streams as God’s life filling believers and flowing onward to others. Calvin also reads the water as flowing within believers, with the main emphasis on an enduring supply of spiritual life. (Wesley on John 7:38; Calvin on John 7:38)

The USCCB’s notes also record a reading in which Jesus Himself is the source from whom the water flows, alongside the reading centered on the believer. The BSB’s wording follows the latter, as does the main reading in those notes. These are interpretations of the image within the shared account of the Spirit’s gift. (USCCB note on John 7:38)
passages.god_plan_html:
Isaiah invites the thirsty to come to God’s provision without payment and pictures joyful water drawn from the springs of salvation. Zechariah pictures living water flowing from Jerusalem alongside the Lord’s rule over all the earth. Jesus’ invitation belongs alongside these scriptural promises of life from God. The connections are supported parallels; the words here are not an exact quotation of one single verse. (Isaiah 12:1–6; Isaiah 55:1–3; Zechariah 14:8–9)

Acts supplies the later connection between Jesus’ glorification and the Spirit being poured out. Peter announces that God has raised Jesus and exalted Him, and that He has received the promised Spirit from the Father and poured out what the people see and hear. The invitation at the feast looks ahead within that larger saving mission. (Acts 2:32–33)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: John 7:45-52
passages.section_title: Will Jesus be heard before He is judged?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 45 Then the officers returned to the chief priests and Pharisees, who asked them, “Why didn’t you bring Him in?” 46 “Never has anyone spoken like this man!” the officers answered. 47 “Have you also been deceived?” replied the Pharisees. 48 “Have any of the rulers or Pharisees believed in Him? 49 But this crowd that does not know the law—they are under a curse.” 50 Nicodemus, who had gone to Jesus earlier and who himself was one of them, asked, 51 “Does our law convict a man without first hearing from him to determine what he has done?” 52 “Aren’t you also from Galilee?” they replied. “Look into it, and you will see that no prophet comes out of Galilee.”
paragraphs: 45 Then the officers returned to the chief priests and Pharisees, who asked them, “Why didn’t you bring Him in?” 46 “Never has anyone spoken like this man!” the officers answered. 47 “Have you also been deceived?” replied the Pharisees. 48 “Have any of the rulers or Pharisees believed in Him? 49 But this crowd that does not know the law—they are under a curse.” 50 Nicodemus, who had gone to Jesus earlier and who himself was one of them, asked, 51 “Does our law convict a man without first hearing from him to determine what he has done?” 52 “Aren’t you also from Galilee?” they replied. “Look into it, and you will see that no prophet comes out of Galilee.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The officers return without arresting Jesus. Asked why, they say that no one has spoken as He does. The chief priests and Pharisees challenge whether they have been misled, appeal to the response of the rulers, and dismiss the crowd as ignorant of the law.

Nicodemus, who previously visited Jesus, asks whether their law judges someone without first hearing him and learning what he has done. Deuteronomy calls judges to hear fairly and without partiality, including both the small and the great. (Deuteronomy 1:16–17)

The reply questions whether Nicodemus is also from Galilee and asserts that no prophet comes from there. It does not answer his request for a hearing. The episode records his intervention without giving a complete account of his faith or his private motives at this moment.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readers commonly understand the scene as showing the need to hear Jesus fairly, rather than deciding about Him through status or pressure to agree with others. Wesley emphasizes that Nicodemus asks the authorities to apply the law they claim to know. (Wesley on John 7:50–52)
passages.god_plan_html:
The Gospel later brings Nicodemus back into the story after Jesus’ death. He joins Joseph of Arimathea in caring for Jesus’ body and preparing it for burial. His question here is therefore one part of an unfolding account that eventually places him at the burial of the One being opposed. (John 19:38–42)

Paul includes Christ’s death for sins, burial and resurrection among the central truths of the good news. The growing opposition in this chapter leads toward those saving events, while the Gospel also shows people within the leadership acting differently from one another. God’s purpose cannot be reduced to a single reaction from an entire group. (1 Corinthians 15:3–4)
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: John 7:53-8:11
passages.section_title: How does Jesus meet accusation with mercy and a call to change?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7:53 Then each went to his own home. 8:1 But Jesus went to the Mount of Olives. 8:2 Early in the morning He went back into the temple courts. All the people came to Him, and He sat down to teach them. 8:3 The scribes and Pharisees, however, brought to Him a woman caught in adultery. They made her stand before them 8:4 and said, “Teacher, this woman was caught in the act of adultery. 8:5 In the Law Moses commanded us to stone such a woman. So what do You say?” 8:6 They said this to test Him, in order to have a basis for accusing Him. But Jesus bent down and began to write on the ground with His finger. 8:7 When they continued to question Him, He straightened up and said to them, “Let him who is without sin among you be the first to cast a stone at her.” 8:8 And again He bent down and wrote on the ground. 8:9 When they heard this, they began to go away one by one, beginning with the older ones, until only Jesus was left, with the woman standing there. 8:10 Then Jesus straightened up and asked her, “Woman, where are your accusers? Has no one condemned you?” 8:11 “No one, Lord,” she answered. “Then neither do I condemn you,” Jesus declared. “Now go and sin no more.”
paragraphs: 7:53 Then each went to his own home.
8:1 But Jesus went to the Mount of Olives. 8:2 Early in the morning He went back into the temple courts. All the people came to Him, and He sat down to teach them.

8:3 The scribes and Pharisees, however, brought to Him a woman caught in adultery. They made her stand before them 8:4 and said, “Teacher, this woman was caught in the act of adultery. 8:5 In the Law Moses commanded us to stone such a woman. So what do You say?” 8:6 They said this to test Him, in order to have a basis for accusing Him. But Jesus bent down and began to write on the ground with His finger.

8:7 When they continued to question Him, He straightened up and said to them, “Let him who is without sin among you be the first to cast a stone at her.” 8:8 And again He bent down and wrote on the ground. 8:9 When they heard this, they began to go away one by one, beginning with the older ones, until only Jesus was left, with the woman standing there. 8:10 Then Jesus straightened up and asked her, “Woman, where are your accusers? Has no one condemned you?” 8:11 “No one, Lord,” she answered. “Then neither do I condemn you,” Jesus declared. “Now go and sin no more.”

passages.context_html:
The BSB includes this account and notes that some early manuscripts do not contain John 7:53–8:11. That manuscript difference is worth knowing about as we read the passage. (BSB note on John 7:52)

After the people return home, Jesus goes to the Mount of Olives and returns to teach in the temple courts the next morning. Scribes and Pharisees bring a woman accused of adultery and ask Him to rule on stoning her. The account explicitly says they are testing Him to find grounds for an accusation.

Moses’ law names both the man and the woman as liable for adultery; only the woman is brought here, and the account does not explain what happened to the man. Deuteronomy also gives a death-penalty instruction requiring witnesses and placing their hands first in carrying it out. These details help explain the setting of the challenge. (Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:22–24; Deuteronomy 17:6–7)

Jesus bends down and writes on the ground; the account does not tell us what He writes. When pressed, He challenges the person without sin to cast the first stone. The accusers leave, beginning with the older ones. He tells the woman that He does not condemn her and calls her to leave sin behind.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings commonly hold together Jesus’ mercy and His call to turn from sin. Pope Francis’s letter on mercy, Wesley’s notes and Calvin’s commentary all connect the woman’s release with the possibility and responsibility of a changed life. (Misericordia et misera §1; Wesley on John 8:11; Calvin on John 8:11)

Commentators differ over the precise force of the challenge to the accusers. Wesley focuses on a witness being guilty of the same or a closely related sin. Calvin reads it as a broader challenge to hypocritical accusers to examine themselves, while saying it does not abolish every duty to judge wrongdoing. These are their explanations of the scene, rather than a single official rule held by every Christian tradition. (Wesley on John 8:7; Calvin on John 8:7)
passages.current_position_html: Our study Is There a Source of Truth? identifies this passage as one of the places where manuscript copies differ. It argues that readers should know about the difference, while recognizing that Scripture’s teaching about grace toward sinners is clearly established elsewhere.

deeper_study.title: Is There a Source of Truth?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Romans places mercy within God’s wider rescue of sinners: all have sinned, and God freely puts people right through the redemption in Jesus. Christ’s self-giving shows God’s righteousness while opening forgiveness to those who trust Him. The mercy in this scene belongs alongside that larger scriptural account of grace. (Romans 3:21–26)

Ephesians connects forgiveness through Christ’s blood with God’s purpose to bring all things together in Him. Mercy aims toward restored life with God under Christ, giving the call to leave sin its place within that larger hope. (Ephesians 1:7–10)

passages.title: John 8:12-20
passages.section_title: What does it mean to follow the light of the world?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 Once again, Jesus spoke to the people and said, “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows Me will never walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life.” 13 So the Pharisees said to Him, “You are testifying about Yourself; Your testimony is not valid.” 14 Jesus replied, “Even if I testify about Myself, My testimony is valid, because I know where I came from and where I am going. But you do not know where I came from or where I am going. 15 You judge according to the flesh; I judge no one. 16 But even if I do judge, My judgment is true, because I am not alone; I am with the Father who sent Me. 17 Even in your own Law it is written that the testimony of two men is valid. 18 I am One who testifies about Myself, and the Father, who sent Me, also testifies about Me.” 19 “Where is Your Father?” they asked Him. “You do not know Me or My Father,” Jesus answered. “If you knew Me, you would know My Father as well.” 20 He spoke these words while teaching in the temple courts, near the treasury. Yet no one seized Him, because His hour had not yet come.
paragraphs: 12 Once again, Jesus spoke to the people and said, “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows Me will never walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life.”

13 So the Pharisees said to Him, “You are testifying about Yourself; Your testimony is not valid.” 14 Jesus replied, “Even if I testify about Myself, My testimony is valid, because I know where I came from and where I am going. But you do not know where I came from or where I am going. 15 You judge according to the flesh; I judge no one. 16 But even if I do judge, My judgment is true, because I am not alone; I am with the Father who sent Me. 17 Even in your own Law it is written that the testimony of two men is valid. 18 I am One who testifies about Myself, and the Father, who sent Me, also testifies about Me.”

19 “Where is Your Father?” they asked Him. “You do not know Me or My Father,” Jesus answered. “If you knew Me, you would know My Father as well.” 20 He spoke these words while teaching in the temple courts, near the treasury. Yet no one seized Him, because His hour had not yet come.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus is still teaching publicly in the temple. The discussion turns from the woman brought before Him to His own identity: He offers the light of life to those who follow Him. Verse 20 places this teaching near the treasury and explains why He is not arrested: His hour has not yet come. John does not give a new date for this exchange.

The setting gives the picture of light added depth. The Feast of Tabernacles has framed the visit since John 7, and Mishnah Sukkah 5:2 describes large golden lamps in the temple courtyard during the celebration. That is useful background, but John does not say that Jesus spoke while lamps were being lit or after they had gone dark. His claim reaches beyond a festival display: He offers a way out of darkness and into life.

The Pharisees challenge the validity of His testimony because He is speaking about Himself. The Law required more than one witness to establish a charge (Deuteronomy 19:15). Jesus answers that He knows His own origin and destination, and that the Father also testifies about Him. His earlier teaching identifies His works and the Scriptures as witnesses to the Father’s sending Him (John 5:31–40). The issue is not simply how many voices can be counted, but whether His listeners recognize the One who sent Him.

Jesus also contrasts their judgment according to the flesh with His relationship to the Father. Read verses 15 and 16 together: His statement that He judges no one is immediately followed by His assurance that any judgment He makes is true. This passage does not cancel His authority to judge, which John has already described in John 5:22–30. Knowing the Father and recognizing the Son belong together.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the light as the life and truth Jesus brings, calling for people to follow Him rather than merely admire His teaching. John Wesley’s notes on verse 12 and John Calvin’s commentary on verse 12 both connect His light with rescue from spiritual darkness.

The main difference here concerns how to explain verse 15. Wesley relates it to the saving purpose of Jesus’ first coming. Calvin focuses on this encounter, where Jesus teaches rather than taking the role of judge against His accusers. The Catholic bishops’ Bible note on verse 15 emphasizes that His judgment does not follow outward, human standards. These are differences of emphasis in the cited explanations; none requires treating verse 15 as a denial of His authority in verse 16.
passages.god_plan_html:
Light has already marked God’s guidance and saving purpose. In Exodus 13:21–22, the LORD leads Israel with a pillar of fire by night. That is a helpful parallel to following Jesus out of darkness, though John does not explicitly identify this saying as a fulfillment of the pillar of fire.

The scope also widens beyond one people or one place. Isaiah 49:6 describes God’s Servant bringing His salvation to the nations, and Revelation 21:22–27 pictures the nations walking by the light of God’s glory, with the Lamb as the city’s lamp. These passages trace a larger theme: God brings people into His light through Christ. The promise here begins with following Him now and points toward life in God’s presence.

passages.title: John 8:21-30
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus point His listeners toward the cross?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 Again He said to them, “I am going away, and you will look for Me, but you will die in your sin. Where I am going, you cannot come.” 22 So the Jews began to ask, “Will He kill Himself, since He says, ‘Where I am going, you cannot come’ ?” 23 Then He told them, “You are from below; I am from above. You are of this world; I am not of this world. 24 That is why I told you that you would die in your sins. For unless you believe that I am He, you will die in your sins.” 25 “Who are You?” they asked. “Just what I have been telling you from the beginning,” Jesus replied. 26 “I have much to say about you and much to judge. But the One who sent Me is truthful, and what I have heard from Him, I tell the world.” 27 They did not understand that He was telling them about the Father. 28 So Jesus said, “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am He, and that I do nothing on My own, but speak exactly what the Father has taught Me. 29 He who sent Me is with Me. He has not left Me alone, because I always do what pleases Him.” 30 As Jesus spoke these things, many believed in Him.

Where I am going, you cannot come.” 22 So the Jews began to ask, “Will He kill Himself, since He says, ‘Where I am going, you cannot come’ ?” 23 Then He told them, “You are from below; I am from above. You are of this world; I am not of this world. 24 That is why I told you that you would die in your sins. For unless you believe that I am He, you will die in your sins.”

25 “Who are You?” they asked. “Just what I have been telling you from the beginning,” Jesus replied. 26 “I have much to say about you and much to judge. But the One who sent Me is truthful, and what I have heard from Him, I tell the world.” 27 They did not understand that He was telling them about the Father.

28 So Jesus said, “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am He, and that I do nothing on My own, but speak exactly what the Father has taught Me. 29 He who sent Me is with Me. He has not left Me alone, because I always do what pleases Him.” 30 As Jesus spoke these things, many believed in Him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus continues speaking about where He comes from and where He is going. His listeners wonder whether His departure means suicide. He redirects them to the real danger: dying in their sins through unbelief. His contrast between above and below is about His origin with the Father and their outlook in a world estranged from God, not a claim that some people are worth less than others.

When they ask who He is, Jesus refers them back to what He has been telling them. The BSB renders His reply as a reminder of His earlier teaching. Verse 27 then says they did not understand that He was speaking about the Father. We should not fill in a complete picture of their understanding or motives when John himself describes their misunderstanding.

The turning point is His coming death. He says they will know who He is when they lift up the Son of Man. Later, John 12:32–33 explicitly explains lifting up as a reference to the kind of death Jesus would die. The cross is therefore central to this exchange, even though His listeners do not yet grasp it. His obedience to the Father continues through what lies ahead; He does not speak or act as an independent rival to the Father.

John ends this part by saying that many believed in Him. The next paragraph turns to continuing in His word. Keeping those statements together helps us hear both the response to His teaching and the call to a life shaped by it, without assuming that we know the final spiritual condition of every person present.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings share the central warning: sin is not overcome by rejecting Jesus, and faith in Him matters for life with God. They also connect His being lifted up with the cross. The details of His self-identification and the recognition He promises are explained in more than one way.

The words translated “I am He” receive different emphasis. John Wesley’s notes on verses 24 and 28 see a claim to the divine name. The Catholic bishops’ Bible note on these verses connects them with God’s self-identification in Isaiah 43:10. John Calvin’s commentary on verses 24 and 28 instead stresses recognizing Jesus as the promised Messiah and the One carrying out the Father’s saving work. This describes their readings of these particular verses; it does not mean Calvin denies Christ’s deity.

They also differ over the knowledge promised in verse 28. Wesley includes people coming to recognize and believe in Jesus through His crucifixion. Calvin emphasizes opponents being forced to recognize the authority they rejected, which does not necessarily mean repentance. Neither reading makes the cross a defeat of the Father’s purpose.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus places the cross within His obedience to the Father. What His opponents will do to Him does not turn His mission into a failed attempt at rescue. In John 12:27–33, He describes His coming hour as the purpose for which He came, asks that the Father be glorified, and connects His death with drawing people to Himself.

This gives the warning about sin a wider setting: the One warning His listeners is also going to the cross. God’s purpose in Christ includes redemption and forgiveness, as Ephesians 1:7–10 explains. The passage holds together the seriousness of refusing Him and the saving work He has come to complete.

passages.title: John 8:31-47
passages.section_title: What kind of freedom does Jesus give?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 31 So He said to the Jews who had believed Him, “If you continue in My word, you are truly My disciples. 32 Then you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.” 33 “We are Abraham’s descendants,” they answered. “We have never been slaves to anyone. How can You say we will be set free?” 34 Jesus replied, “Truly, truly, I tell you, everyone who sins is a slave to sin. 35 A slave does not remain in the house forever, but a son remains forever. 36 So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed. 37 I know you are Abraham’s descendants, but you are trying to kill Me because My word has no place within you. 38 I speak of what I have seen in the presence of the Father, and you do what you have heard from your father.” 39 “Abraham is our father,” they replied. “If you were children of Abraham,” said Jesus, “you would do the works of Abraham. 40 But now you are trying to kill Me, a man who has told you the truth that I heard from God. Abraham never did such a thing. 41 You are doing the works of your father.” “We are not illegitimate children,” they declared. “Our only Father is God Himself.” 42 Jesus said to them, “If God were your Father, you would love Me, for I have come here from God. I have not come on My own, but He sent Me. 43 Why do you not understand what I am saying? It is because you are unable to accept My message. 44 You belong to your father, the devil, and you want to carry out his desires. He was a murderer from the beginning, refusing to uphold the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he lies, he speaks his native language, because he is a liar and the father of lies. 45 But because I speak the truth, you do not believe Me! 46 Which of you can prove Me guilty of sin? If I speak the truth, why do you not believe Me? 47 Whoever belongs to God hears the words of God. The reason you do not hear is that you do not belong to God.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus tells those who have believed Him to continue in His word. Following Him means letting His teaching shape life over time. The Greek word μένω, menō (MEN-oh), means to remain or stay; Thayer’s lexicon specifically connects its use in verse 31 with holding firmly to something. This is more than hearing a message once and moving on.

The promise of freedom brings an objection from people who appeal to their descent from Abraham. Jesus explains the slavery He means: being ruled by sin. Their claim about never having been slaves does not answer that problem. In the picture of a household, a slave has no lasting place, while a son remains. The lasting freedom they need comes from the Son.

Jesus acknowledges their physical descent from Abraham in verse 37, then asks whether their conduct resembles Abraham’s. They seek to kill a man who has told them God’s truth. Abraham did not respond that way. The question becomes whether their actions match the spiritual relationship they claim, first with Abraham and then with God.

The words about the devil are severe, and Jesus gives His reason: His opponents want to carry out murderous desires and reject the truth. The charge concerns their response to Him and the desires they follow. It is not a claim that their ancestry is literally from the devil; Jesus has just acknowledged their descent from Abraham. Jesus and His own disciples are also Jewish.

By verse 47, the issue is hearing God’s words in the sense of accepting them, not simply having functioning ears. The passage asks whether a claimed relationship with God shows itself in receiving the One He sent. It also brings the promise of freedom back to its source: the Son, whose word they are resisting.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the promised freedom as deliverance from sin through Christ, rather than merely political independence or freedom to do whatever one wants. Calvin’s commentary on verses 34–36 and Wesley’s notes on verses 32–37 both connect it with the Son’s saving work and a changed relationship with God.

One question concerns who is speaking as the exchange becomes hostile. Wesley identifies the reply in verse 33 with other people nearby, rather than those who believed. Calvin says the identification is uncertain, but favors a reply from opponents within a mixed crowd. The Catholic bishops’ Bible note on verse 31 instead points to a difficult transition in the way the account is presented. These explanations caution against assuming that every person mentioned in this scene has the same faith or motives; the demand to continue in Jesus’ word remains clear.
passages.god_plan_html:
The promise to Abraham is not set aside when Jesus challenges His opponents’ appeal to ancestry. Galatians 3:6–9 explains that the promise of blessing for the nations looked ahead to God justifying people by faith. Verses 26–29 then connect belonging to Christ with being God’s children and heirs of Abraham’s promise. The larger purpose is a family gathered through Christ, crossing the boundaries of ancestry and social status.

The freedom Jesus offers is also freedom for a changed life. Romans 6:16–23 describes release from slavery to sin leading to service to God and eternal life in Christ. This adds a needed direction to the word freedom: God rescues people from sin’s mastery so that they can live in relationship with Him.

passages.title: John 8:48-59
passages.section_title: How can Jesus be greater than Abraham?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 48 The Jews answered Him, “Are we not right to say that You are a Samaritan and You have a demon?” 49 “I do not have a demon,” Jesus replied, “but I honor My Father, and you dishonor Me. 50 I do not seek My own glory. There is One who seeks it, and He is the Judge. 51 Truly, truly, I tell you, if anyone keeps My word, he will never see death.” 52 “Now we know that You have a demon!” declared the Jews. “Abraham died, and so did the prophets, yet You say that anyone who keeps Your word will never taste death. 53 Are You greater than our father Abraham? He died, as did the prophets. Who do You claim to be?” 54 Jesus answered, “If I glorify Myself, My glory means nothing. The One who glorifies Me is My Father, of whom you say, ‘He is our God.’ 55 You do not know Him, but I know Him. If I said I did not know Him, I would be a liar like you. But I do know Him, and I keep His word. 56 Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see My day. He saw it and was glad.” 57 Then the Jews said to Him, “You are not yet fifty years old, and You have seen Abraham?” 58 “Truly, truly, I tell you,” Jesus declared, “before Abraham was born, I am!” 59 At this, they picked up stones to throw at Him. But Jesus was hidden and went out of the temple area.
paragraphs: 48 The Jews answered Him, “Are we not right to say that You are a Samaritan and You have a demon?” 49 “I do not have a demon,” Jesus replied, “but I honor My Father, and you dishonor Me. 50 I do not seek My own glory. There is One who seeks it, and He is the Judge. 51 Truly, truly, I tell you, if anyone keeps My word, he will never see death.”

52 “Now we know that You have a demon!” declared the Jews. “Abraham died, and so did the prophets, yet You say that anyone who keeps Your word will never taste death. 53 Are You greater than our father Abraham? He died, as did the prophets. Who do You claim to be?” 54 Jesus answered, “If I glorify Myself, My glory means nothing. The One who glorifies Me is My Father, of whom you say, ‘He is our God.’ 55 You do not know Him, but I know Him. If I said I did not know Him, I would be a liar like you. But I do know Him, and I keep His word. 56 Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see My day. He saw it and was glad.”

57 Then the Jews said to Him, “You are not yet fifty years old, and You have seen Abraham?” 58 “Truly, truly, I tell you,” Jesus declared, “before Abraham was born, I am!” 59 At this, they picked up stones to throw at Him. But Jesus was hidden and went out of the temple area.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The reply to Jesus now becomes a personal attack: His opponents call Him a Samaritan and accuse Him of having a demon. He denies the charge of a demon and returns to His relationship with the Father. He honors the Father rather than seeking glory on His own terms, and He leaves judgment with the One who knows the truth.

His promise that the person who keeps His word will never see death sounds impossible to His listeners. Abraham and the prophets died; how can He promise something greater? They are thinking of bodily death. Elsewhere Jesus makes clear that His followers may die physically yet receive life that death cannot finally destroy (John 11:25–26). Keeping His word is a response of faith and obedience, not a promise of immunity from physical death.

Jesus says Abraham rejoiced to see His day. The statement places His mission within the hope of God’s earlier promises, rather than in competition with Abraham. The passage does not describe exactly when or how Abraham saw that day. The question about Jesus being under fifty does not establish His precise age or prove that He looked unusually old.

The exchange reaches its height in verse 58. Jesus contrasts Abraham’s beginning with His own existence: He does not simply say that He lived a little earlier. The Greek verbs checked in Thayer’s lexicon distinguish Abraham coming into existence from Jesus’ statement that He is. His listeners take up stones, and He leaves the temple. John does not describe how He was hidden, so we need not add a detailed escape or a claim that He became invisible.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The major Christian traditions read verse 58 as a testimony to the Son’s existence before Abraham and His divine identity. The Catholic Catechism, paragraph 590, Calvin on verse 58 and Wesley on verse 58 agree on that central point.

Explanations of Abraham seeing Jesus’ day emphasize different parts of his story. Calvin describes Abraham looking forward by faith to Christ’s coming. Wesley points to promises and earlier encounters with God, including Genesis 18. The Catholic bishops’ note on verse 56 points particularly to Isaac’s birth as the beginning of the promised blessing. The Gospel itself states Abraham’s joy without identifying one specific event.
passages.god_plan_html:
God’s saving work in Jesus belongs to the same story as His promises to Abraham. Galatians 3:8–9 says that the promise of blessing for all nations announced the gospel to Abraham in advance. Hebrews 11:8–19 describes Abraham living by faith in promises whose full outcome he had not yet received.

Jesus therefore presents His coming as the fulfillment of an earlier hope, while making a claim greater than that of another prophet in the sequence. John 1:1–14 has already introduced the Word who existed with God before creation and then became flesh. His saving work does not begin with His birth, and His promise of life rests on who He is.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Who is The Angel of the Lord? understands John 8:58 as Jesus identifying Himself as the eternal Son who existed before Abraham. Drawing on John 1:18 and Genesis 18, it also concludes that the Son was the One who appeared to Abraham and made the Father known. This is the study’s conclusion about the earlier appearance, not a detail John 8:56 explicitly spells out.

deeper_study.title: Who is The Angel of the Lord?

passages.title: John 8:58
passages.section_title: What does Jesus claim by saying He existed before Abraham?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 58 “Truly, truly, I tell you,” Jesus declared, “before Abraham was born, I am!”
paragraphs: 58 “Truly, truly, I tell you,” Jesus declared, “before Abraham was born, I am!”

passages.context_html:
This verse answers the question raised by the whole discussion in John 8:48–59: how can Jesus speak of Abraham seeing His day when He is not yet fifty years old? Jesus is not claiming an unusually long human lifespan. He places His existence before Abraham’s beginning.

The wording matters. Thayer’s entry for the verb meaning to come into existence directly cites Abraham in this verse, while the entry for the verb meaning to be cites Jesus’ statement. The contrast supports reading more here than the memory of an ordinary man. The connection with God’s self-revelation in Exodus 3:13–15 also helps explain why Christians have read this saying as a claim to divine identity.

In the next verse His opponents pick up stones. John records Jesus leaving the temple rather than submitting to their attack at this point. The verse should be read in that setting, alongside the Father’s sending of Jesus and His promise of life, rather than as an isolated puzzle about grammar.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The major Christian traditions understand this saying as testimony to the Son’s existence before Abraham and His divine identity. This shared reading appears in the Catholic Catechism, paragraph 590, Calvin’s commentary and Wesley’s notes.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Who is The Angel of the Lord? reads this verse as Jesus identifying Himself as the eternal Son, personally present before Abraham. The study connects that claim with Genesis 18 and John 1:18 and concludes that the Son was the One who appeared to Abraham and made the Father known. That identification is the study’s developed conclusion; this verse itself does not name a particular earlier encounter.

deeper_study.title: Who is The Angel of the Lord?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html: The One who comes to fulfill God’s promises is not a late arrival in God’s purpose. John 1:1–14 describes the eternal Word becoming flesh, and Galatians 3:8–9 connects the gospel with the blessing promised to Abraham. Jesus’ coming brings that long-promised saving purpose into view. His identity explains how Abraham’s hope and the life Jesus offers belong to one story.

passages.title: John 9:1-12
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus give sight to a man born blind?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now as Jesus was passing by, He saw a man blind from birth, 2 and His disciples asked Him, “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?” 3 Jesus answered, “Neither this man nor his parents sinned, but this happened so that the works of God would be displayed in him. 4 While it is daytime, we must do the works of Him who sent Me. Night is coming, when no one can work. 5 While I am in the world, I am the light of the world.” 6 When Jesus had said this, He spit on the ground, made some mud, and applied it to the man’s eyes. 7 Then He told him, “Go, wash in the Pool of Siloam” (which means “Sent”). So the man went and washed, and came back seeing. 8 At this, his neighbors and those who had formerly seen him begging began to ask, “Isn’t this the man who used to sit and beg?” 9 Some claimed that he was, but others said, “No, he just looks like him.” But the man kept saying, “I am the one.” 10 “How then were your eyes opened?” they asked. 11 He answered, “The man they call Jesus made some mud and anointed my eyes, and He told me to go to Siloam and wash. So I went and washed and received my sight.” 12 “Where is He?” they asked. “I do not know,” he answered.

Night is coming, when no one can work. 5 While I am in the world, I am the light of the world.”

6 When Jesus had said this, He spit on the ground, made some mud, and applied it to the man’s eyes. 7 Then He told him, “Go, wash in the Pool of Siloam” (which means “Sent”). So the man went and washed, and came back seeing.

8 At this, his neighbors and those who had formerly seen him begging began to ask, “Isn’t this the man who used to sit and beg?” 9 Some claimed that he was, but others said, “No, he just looks like him.” But the man kept saying, “I am the one.” 10 “How then were your eyes opened?” they asked. 11 He answered, “The man they call Jesus made some mud and anointed my eyes, and He told me to go to Siloam and wash. So I went and washed and received my sight.” 12 “Where is He?” they asked. “I do not know,” he answered.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The disciples see a man blind from birth and ask whose sin caused his blindness. Their question offers two explanations, both built around blame. Jesus rejects those explanations for this man’s condition and directs them instead to what God is about to do. He is not declaring that the man and his parents have never sinned; He is answering the question about why he was born blind.

Jesus again identifies Himself as the light of the world and speaks of doing the Father’s work while there is opportunity. He makes mud, puts it on the man’s eyes and sends him to wash in Siloam. John translates the pool’s name as Sent. That wording sits alongside Jesus’ reference to the Father who sent Him, but the account does not explain a hidden meaning for every part of the healing.

The man goes, washes and returns able to see. John does not tell us that his eyes were already healed underneath the mud or describe the exact moment his sight returned. The emphasis is on Jesus’ action and the man doing what He tells him. We should not turn this particular way of healing into a technique that every sick person must repeat.

The neighbors’ questions establish that the change is real and surprising. Some doubt that he is the same man, but he keeps identifying himself and tells them what happened. His knowledge is still limited: he knows Jesus’ name and what He did, but does not know where He is. The rest of the chapter will follow his growing understanding.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand Jesus’ answer as rejecting a direct link between this man’s blindness and a particular sin by him or his parents, while showing God’s work through his healing. Calvin on verse 3, Wesley on verse 3 and the Catholic bishops’ note on verse 2 agree on that central point.

The details have also invited symbolic readings. Augustine, Tractate 44, section 2, connects the mud with the Word becoming flesh and the washing with baptism in Christ. Calvin, in his explanation of verse 7, declines the mud-as-incarnation reading and emphasizes Christ’s power to work through physical things. These are the named teachers’ explanations; the text itself directly records the healing and John’s translation of Siloam.
passages.god_plan_html:
Isaiah 35:4–6 places the opening of blind eyes within the hope of God coming to save His people. This healing fits that larger picture of restoration: God’s work reaches an actual person whose need has been present from birth.

Jesus Himself gives the story a further meaning in John 9:39–41, where seeing and blindness also describe people’s response to Him. The physical healing is real; it also helps us understand His work of bringing people into the light. The man who begins by receiving sight will come to confess faith in the One who healed him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: John 9:13-23
passages.section_title: Why does a healing lead to questioning and fear?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 They brought to the Pharisees the man who had been blind. 14 Now the day on which Jesus had made the mud and opened his eyes was a Sabbath. 15 So the Pharisees also asked him how he had received his sight. The man answered, “He put mud on my eyes, and I washed, and now I can see.” 16 Because of this, some of the Pharisees said, “This man is not from God, for He does not keep the Sabbath.” But others said, “How can a sinful man perform such signs?” And there was division among them. 17 So once again they asked the man who had been blind, “What do you say about Him, since it was your eyes He opened?” “He is a prophet,” the man replied. 18 The Jews still did not believe that the man had been blind and had received his sight until they summoned his parents 19 and asked, “Is this your son, the one you say was born blind? So how is it that he can now see?” 20 His parents answered, “We know he is our son, and we know he was born blind. 21 But how he can now see or who opened his eyes, we do not know. Ask him. He is old enough to speak for himself.” 22 His parents said this because they were afraid of the Jews. For the Jews had already determined that anyone who confessed Jesus as the Christ would be put out of the synagogue. 23 That was why his parents said, “He is old enough. Ask him.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The man is brought to the Pharisees, and John now tells us that the healing happened on a Sabbath. The question becomes not only what happened but what it reveals about Jesus. Some conclude that He cannot be from God because He does not keep the Sabbath; others ask how a sinful man could perform such a sign. John explicitly records division among them, rather than one response shared by every Pharisee.

The dispute concerns what counts as Sabbath work. Mishnah Shabbat 7:2 lists kneading among prohibited kinds of work, giving background to the objection over making mud. That list does not by itself tell us everything each person in this encounter believed, and John does not provide a full legal hearing. The man answers the question put to him by calling Jesus a prophet.

His parents confirm two important facts: he is their son, and he was born blind. They do not explain how he now sees. Instead they direct the questioners back to their adult son. John tells us why they hold back: they fear being put out of the synagogue if they confess Jesus as the Christ. We do not need an invented account of their private conversation or their final beliefs to understand that pressure.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this scene as showing how an evident work of mercy can be resisted when it challenges an existing judgment about Jesus. Calvin’s explanation of verses 16–18 and Wesley’s notes on verses 16–22 emphasize the questions about His authority and the cost of acknowledging Him.
passages.god_plan_html:
This is an early example of a cost Jesus later prepares His disciples to face. In John 16:1–4, He warns that people will put them out of synagogues and may even think persecution serves God. That later warning is a clear parallel to the fear described here.

The larger story is not only about receiving a miracle. It is about recognizing the One sent by the Father when doing so brings pressure. The man’s response will develop through that pressure, and Jesus will seek him out after he is rejected. Human exclusion does not place him beyond the reach of Christ.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: John 9:24-34
passages.section_title: How does the healed man answer pressure to deny what happened?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 24 So a second time they called for the man who had been blind and said, “Give glory to God! We know that this man is a sinner.” 25 He answered, “Whether He is a sinner I do not know. There is one thing I do know: I was blind, but now I see!” 26 “What did He do to you?” they asked. “How did He open your eyes?” 27 He replied, “I already told you, and you did not listen. Why do you want to hear it again? Do you also want to become His disciples?” 28 Then they heaped insults on him and said, “You are His disciple; we are disciples of Moses. 29 We know that God spoke to Moses, but we do not know where this man is from.” 30 “That is remarkable indeed!” the man said. “You do not know where He is from, and yet He opened my eyes. 31 We know that God does not listen to sinners, but He does listen to the one who worships Him and does His will. 32 Never before has anyone heard of opening the eyes of a man born blind. 33 If this man were not from God, He could do no such thing.” 34 They replied, “You were born in utter sin, and you are instructing us?” And they threw him out.
paragraphs: 24 So a second time they called for the man who had been blind and said, “Give glory to God! We know that this man is a sinner.” 25 He answered, “Whether He is a sinner I do not know. There is one thing I do know: I was blind, but now I see!” 26 “What did He do to you?” they asked. “How did He open your eyes?” 27 He replied, “I already told you, and you did not listen. Why do you want to hear it again? Do you also want to become His disciples?” 28 Then they heaped insults on him and said, “You are His disciple; we are disciples of Moses. 29 We know that God spoke to Moses, but we do not know where this man is from.”

30 “That is remarkable indeed!” the man said. “You do not know where He is from, and yet He opened my eyes. 31 We know that God does not listen to sinners, but He does listen to the one who worships Him and does His will. 32 Never before has anyone heard of opening the eyes of a man born blind. 33 If this man were not from God, He could do no such thing.” 34 They replied, “You were born in utter sin, and you are instructing us?” And they threw him out.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The questioners call the man back and urge him to give glory to God while declaring that Jesus is a sinner. The phrase is a serious call to tell the truth, not simply an invitation to sing praise. Joshua 7:19–21 uses the same appeal when Joshua asks Achan to confess what he has done. Here the pressure is to accept the questioners’ conclusion about Jesus.

The man keeps returning to the fact he knows: he was blind and now sees. When they ask him to repeat the details, he challenges whether they have listened and asks whether they also want to become Jesus’ disciples. They answer with insults and appeal to Moses. Their claimed knowledge of Jesus’ supposed sinfulness sits beside their admission that they do not know where He comes from.

The man reasons that such a healing points to God’s work through Jesus. Verse 31 is part of that reasoning: God listens to the person who honors Him and does His will. It should be read within this discussion of whether Jesus is acting against God, rather than made into a rule that God never hears a sinner asking for mercy. Jesus’ own account of the repentant tax collector in Luke 18:9–14 shows why that broader conclusion would be mistaken.

They end by accusing the man of having been born in utter sin and throwing him out. The accusation returns to the kind of blame Jesus rejected at the beginning. Their action removes the witness from their presence, but it does not undo his sight or answer his testimony.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian readings commonly emphasize the man’s courage in holding to what Jesus has done and the questioners’ refusal to receive his testimony. On verse 31, Wesley specifically distinguishes unrepentant sinners and this kind of answered prayer, while Calvin stresses sincere prayer offered in faith; neither treats sinful behavior as an obstacle that people can never turn from.
passages.god_plan_html:
The man’s testimony anticipates a pattern seen as the gospel spreads. In Acts 4:13–20, Peter and John stand before authorities after a healing, face an order to stop speaking about Jesus, and hold to what they have seen and heard. This is a parallel, not a claim that the two encounters are identical.

God’s work is made known through witnesses who do not control the response to their message. Here a man with growing knowledge of Jesus can still speak truthfully about what he has received. His testimony leads the story toward a fuller encounter with Christ, rather than ending with the authorities’ verdict.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: John 9:35-41
passages.section_title: What does Jesus help the healed man see next?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 35 When Jesus heard that they had thrown him out, He found the man and said, “Do you believe in the Son of Man?” 36 “Who is He, Sir?” he replied. “Tell me so that I may believe in Him.” 37 “You have already seen Him,” Jesus answered. “He is the One speaking with you.” 38 “Lord, I believe,” he said. And he worshiped Jesus. 39 Then Jesus declared, “For judgment I have come into this world, so that the blind may see and those who see may become blind.” 40 Some of the Pharisees who were with Him heard this, and they asked Him, “Are we blind too?” 41 “If you were blind,” Jesus replied, “you would not be guilty of sin. But since you claim you can see, your guilt remains.”
paragraphs: 35 When Jesus heard that they had thrown him out, He found the man and said, “Do you believe in the Son of Man?” 36 “Who is He, Sir?” he replied. “Tell me so that I may believe in Him.” 37 “You have already seen Him,” Jesus answered. “He is the One speaking with you.” 38 “Lord, I believe,” he said. And he worshiped Jesus.

39 Then Jesus declared, “For judgment I have come into this world, so that the blind may see and those who see may become blind.” 40 Some of the Pharisees who were with Him heard this, and they asked Him, “Are we blind too?” 41 “If you were blind,” Jesus replied, “you would not be guilty of sin. But since you claim you can see, your guilt remains.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus hears that the man has been thrown out and finds him. The healing is not the end of His care. He asks about faith in the Son of Man, identifies Himself, and receives the man’s confession and worship. The BSB reads Son of Man in verse 35; its footnote records Son of God in other manuscripts. Older commentaries using the latter wording should not silently replace the BSB text.

The word translated worshiped is προσκυνέω, proskyneō (pros-koo-NEH-oh). Thayer’s lexicon describes bowing or showing deep honor, with the setting determining whom the person honors and what the act means. Here it follows Jesus making Himself known and the man confessing belief. John describes a personal response to Jesus, rather than giving the order of a worship service.

Jesus then explains a deeper division revealed by His coming. The man who lacked physical sight now receives Jesus, while people confident in their own sight resist Him. Some Pharisees hear the words and ask whether they are blind too. His reply directs attention to their claimed knowledge and continuing guilt. He is not saying that a physical disability makes someone sinful or that every person who knows little is automatically free of sin.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly see the man’s response as faith and honor directed toward Jesus, with the final sayings contrasting receiving His light and resisting it. Wesley’s notes on verses 35–41 emphasize teachability and the greater responsibility that comes with opportunities to know.

Commentators differ over how fully the man understands Jesus’ identity at this moment. John Chrysostom, Homily 59, sees his worship as an acknowledgment of Jesus’ divine power. Calvin on verse 38 sees honor beyond that given to an ordinary man or prophet, while allowing that his understanding of Christ’s deity is still incomplete. Their difference concerns the man’s understanding, not whether Christ is divine.
passages.god_plan_html:
The healing and this meeting belong together. Isaiah 42:5–9 connects God’s Servant with light, opened eyes and release from darkness. John’s account shows restoration reaching beyond a physical change to a person recognizing and trusting Jesus.

The rejected man is found by Christ. The story then leads directly into Jesus’ teaching about the shepherd who knows and cares for his sheep in John 10. That connection helps us see the direction of the chapter: Jesus does not merely perform a sign and leave; He makes Himself known to the person who received it.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Worship as the Early Church Knew It uses John 9:38 to describe a personal act of reverent honor rooted in faith. The man responds to Jesus making Himself known by bowing in acknowledgment of Him. The study does not treat this scene as a description of a scheduled service or a set of required meeting practices.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

passages.title: John 9:38
passages.section_title: How does the man respond when Jesus makes Himself known?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 38 “Lord, I believe,” he said. And he worshiped Jesus.
paragraphs: 38 “Lord, I believe,” he said. And he worshiped Jesus.

passages.context_html:
This response comes after Jesus finds the man who has been thrown out. Asked about believing in the Son of Man, he wants to know who that is. Jesus identifies Himself, and the man answers with belief and worship. The full exchange in John 9:35–41 shows that his response grows out of Jesus making Himself known.

The Greek verb προσκυνέω, proskyneō (pros-koo-NEH-oh), can describe bowing or showing deep honor; Thayer’s lexicon includes this verse among its examples. Its use here joins what the man says with his response to Jesus. The scene does not describe music, a timetable or the conduct of a gathered service.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christian interpreters read this as faith expressed in honor toward Jesus, while differing over how much the man yet understands. Chrysostom’s Homily 59 emphasizes acknowledgment of divine power, while Calvin’s commentary on verse 38 allows for genuine reverence accompanied by an understanding of Christ that is still growing.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Worship as the Early Church Knew It reads this verse as a personal act of reverent acknowledgment: the man believes Jesus and bows in honor before Him. It describes a spontaneous response rooted in faith, rather than a prescribed ceremony or the format of a church service.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html: The chapter begins with a man receiving sight and reaches a fuller response when he recognizes and trusts the One who healed him. Jesus’ explanation in John 9:39–41 shows that the account also concerns receiving His light. The confession here gives that theme a human face: a person whom others rejected is found by Jesus and responds to Him in faith.

passages.title: John 10:1-10
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus describe Himself as the gate?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 “Truly, truly, I tell you, whoever does not enter the sheepfold by the gate, but climbs in some other way, is a thief and a robber. 2 But the one who enters by the gate is the shepherd of the sheep. 3 The gatekeeper opens the gate for him, and the sheep listen for his voice. He calls his own sheep by name and leads them out. 4 When he has brought out all his own, he goes on ahead of them, and his sheep follow him because they know his voice. 5 But they will never follow a stranger; in fact, they will flee from him because they do not recognize his voice.” 6 Jesus spoke to them using this illustration, but they did not understand what He was telling them. 7 So He said to them again, “Truly, truly, I tell you, I am the gate for the sheep. 8 All who came before Me were thieves and robbers, but the sheep did not listen to them. 9 I am the gate. If anyone enters through Me, he will be saved. He will come in and go out and find pasture. 10 The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. I have come that they may have life, and have it in all its fullness.

He calls his own sheep by name and leads them out. 4 When he has brought out all his own, he goes on ahead of them, and his sheep follow him because they know his voice. 5 But they will never follow a stranger; in fact, they will flee from him because they do not recognize his voice.” 6 Jesus spoke to them using this illustration, but they did not understand what He was telling them.

7 So He said to them again, “Truly, truly, I tell you, I am the gate for the sheep. 8 All who came before Me were thieves and robbers, but the sheep did not listen to them. 9 I am the gate. If anyone enters through Me, he will be saved. He will come in and go out and find pasture. 10 The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. I have come that they may have life, and have it in all its fullness.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
This teaching continues the conversation at the end of John 9. Jesus has found the man who was thrown out, received his faith, and challenged the confidence of those who claim to see. He now uses a picture of sheep, a shepherd, strangers and a gate to explain the difference between care that brings life and leadership that harms the people it claims to serve.

In the first part, the shepherd enters properly, calls his sheep by name and leads them. Strangers try another way in and do not receive the same response from the sheep. The picture emphasizes recognition and a relationship of trust. John then says that the listeners do not understand the illustration, so Jesus explains further.

Jesus identifies Himself as the gate through whom the sheep enter and find safety and pasture. The images serve His teaching; we need not assign an unrecorded identity to every detail. He can speak of Himself as the gate here and as the shepherd in the next paragraph without either picture losing its purpose.

The thieves and robbers are contrasted with the life He gives. His statement about those who came before Him should be read alongside His earlier affirmation that Moses wrote about Him (John 5:45–47). It is not a rejection of every messenger God sent before His birth. Likewise, the fullness of life He offers is more than a promise of comfortable circumstances: the man in John 9 has received His care while facing rejection.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the gate as Jesus Himself, through whom people receive salvation and care. Calvin on verses 7–9 and Wesley on verses 7–10 both emphasize coming through Him rather than following claims of authority that lead people away from Him.

The gatekeeper in verse 3 has been explained in different ways. Wesley identifies the gatekeeper with the Father; Calvin allows a reference to God while focusing on His approval of true shepherds. Jesus does not explicitly identify the gatekeeper, so the main point need not depend on settling that detail. The recognition of the shepherd’s voice and the life Jesus gives remain central.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ezekiel 34:1–16 describes leaders who feed themselves while leaving God’s people scattered, then promises that God Himself will seek, rescue and feed His sheep. That is a strong background to Jesus’ contrast between destructive intruders and His own care.

The story of the man born blind has already given this contrast a human face: he is rejected by those questioning him, and Jesus finds him. The gate illustration points toward God gathering and sustaining His people through Christ. Life comes from receiving His care and following Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: John 10:11-21
passages.section_title: What makes Jesus the good shepherd?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep. 12 The hired hand is not the shepherd, and the sheep are not his own. When he sees the wolf coming, he abandons the sheep and runs away. Then the wolf pounces on them and scatters the flock. 13 The man runs away because he is a hired servant and is unconcerned for the sheep. 14 I am the good shepherd. I know My sheep and My sheep know Me, 15 just as the Father knows Me and I know the Father. And I lay down My life for the sheep. 16 I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them in as well, and they will listen to My voice. Then there will be one flock and one shepherd. 17 The reason the Father loves Me is that I lay down My life in order to take it up again. 18 No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of My own accord. I have authority to lay it down and authority to take it up again. This charge I have received from My Father.” 19 Again there was division among the Jews because of Jesus’ message. 20 Many of them said, “He is demon-possessed and insane. Why would you listen to Him?” 21 But others replied, “These are not the words of a man possessed by a demon. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?”
