When he sees the wolf coming, he abandons the sheep and runs away. Then the wolf pounces on them and scatters the flock. 13 The man runs away because he is a hired servant and is unconcerned for the sheep.

14 I am the good shepherd. I know My sheep and My sheep know Me, 15 just as the Father knows Me and I know the Father. And I lay down My life for the sheep. 16 I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them in as well, and they will listen to My voice. Then there will be one flock and one shepherd. 17 The reason the Father loves Me is that I lay down My life in order to take it up again. 18 No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of My own accord. I have authority to lay it down and authority to take it up again. This charge I have received from My Father.”

19 Again there was division among the Jews because of Jesus’ message. 20 Many of them said, “He is demon-possessed and insane. Why would you listen to Him?” 21 But others replied, “These are not the words of a man possessed by a demon. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus explains His care through a contrast with a hired hand who abandons the sheep when danger comes. The difference appears in what each does for the flock: Jesus lays down His life. The picture is about love and costly faithfulness, not proof that every worker who receives wages is untrustworthy.

He knows His sheep, and they know Him. He also speaks of other sheep whom He must bring, so that there will be one flock under one shepherd. The Greek word ποίμνη, poimnē (POYM-nay), means a flock; Thayer’s lexicon directly connects its use here with people following Christ. The emphasis is on a people gathered around Him, rather than a requirement that everyone occupy one physical enclosure.

His coming death is voluntary and belongs with His resurrection. He has authority to lay down His life and take it up again, in obedience to the Father’s command. This does not remove the part played by those who crucify Him. Acts 2:23–24 holds human responsibility together with God’s purpose and His raising Jesus from death.

The teaching again divides the listeners. Some repeat the accusation that He has a demon; others return to the evidence of the opened eyes. The healing in John 9 remains part of the question before them: does Jesus’ work reveal the Father who sent Him?
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians agree that the shepherd’s laying down His life points to Jesus’ saving death, joined here to His resurrection. Calvin on verses 16–18 and Wesley on those verses also identify the other sheep with Gentiles being gathered into one people with Jewish believers.

Traditions differ over how His death for the sheep relates to His saving purpose for humanity. The Reformed Westminster Confession, 8.5 and 8.8, teaches that Christ purchases redemption for those given to Him by the Father and certainly brings that redemption to them. This reading emphasizes a saving work that achieves its purpose for His people.

The Catholic Church teaches that Christ died for every human being without exception (Catechism 605). The Methodist Article XX likewise describes His one offering as the complete sacrifice for the sins of the whole world, and Wesley’s note on verse 18 speaks of His ransom for the whole world. These readings do not take the mention of the sheep to restrict everyone for whom He died. They also do not mean that everyone is automatically saved.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ezekiel 34:23–24 promises one shepherd from David’s line to care for God’s people. Jesus’ self-giving care fits that hope, and Hebrews 13:20–21 explicitly calls the risen Jesus the great Shepherd of the sheep. His death and resurrection are central to how He brings His people into life with God.

The gathering reaches beyond one people. Ephesians 2:11–22 describes Jews and Gentiles reconciled to God in one body through the cross, with shared access to the Father by one Spirit. That gives the promise of one flock a wider setting: Christ brings people who were far apart into one household under His care.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: John 10:22-30
passages.section_title: What does Jesus promise the sheep in His care?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 At that time the Feast of Dedication took place in Jerusalem. It was winter, 23 and Jesus was walking in the temple courts in Solomon’s Colonnade. 24 So the Jews gathered around Him and demanded, “How long will You keep us in suspense? If You are the Christ, tell us plainly.” 25 “I already told you,” Jesus replied, “but you did not believe. The works I do in My Father’s name testify on My behalf. 26 But because you are not My sheep, you refuse to believe. 27 My sheep listen to My voice; I know them, and they follow Me. 28 I give them eternal life, and they will never perish. No one can snatch them out of My hand. 29 My Father who has given them to Me is greater than all. No one can snatch them out of My Father’s hand. 30 I and the Father are one.”
paragraphs: 22 At that time the Feast of Dedication took place in Jerusalem. It was winter, 23 and Jesus was walking in the temple courts in Solomon’s Colonnade. 24 So the Jews gathered around Him and demanded, “How long will You keep us in suspense? If You are the Christ, tell us plainly.” 25 “I already told you,” Jesus replied, “but you did not believe. The works I do in My Father’s name testify on My behalf. 26 But because you are not My sheep, you refuse to believe.

27 My sheep listen to My voice; I know them, and they follow Me. 28 I give them eternal life, and they will never perish. No one can snatch them out of My hand. 29 My Father who has given them to Me is greater than all. No one can snatch them out of My Father’s hand. 30 I and the Father are one.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
John now gives a new setting: the Feast of Dedication in Jerusalem, in winter. This is Hanukkah, commemorating the temple’s rededication after its desecration. Josephus, Antiquities 12.7.6–7, describes the restored sacrifices and the annual eight-day celebration. John places Jesus in Solomon’s Colonnade, where people press Him to say plainly whether He is the Christ.

Jesus points to what He has already said and to the works He does in the Father’s name. He then contrasts His questioners with His sheep. His sheep listen to His voice, are known by Him and follow Him. The discussion therefore concerns both His identity and the response to Him, rather than information about Him alone.

His promise is strong: He gives His sheep eternal life, and no one can snatch them from His hand or the Father’s. The Greek verb ἁρπάζω, harpazō (har-PAH-zoh), means to seize or carry away by force; Thayer’s lexicon directly cites verses 28–29. The assurance rests on the power and care of the Father and Son. Questions about how this relates to continuing faith need the wider teaching of Scripture, not just a dictionary definition.

Jesus closes by saying that He and the Father are one. In this setting, their united care for the sheep is unmistakable. The words also lead directly into the next exchange about His relationship with God, where His opponents accuse Him of making Himself God. We should read the promise and that response together.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians read these verses as a strong assurance of Christ’s care, but differ over how His sheep come to believe and whether a believer can finally fall away.

Reformed churches following the Westminster Confession, chapters 10 and 17, understand God’s call as bringing those He has chosen to faith, freely and willingly through His grace. Those truly called and renewed will be preserved to the end, even though they may fall into serious sin. Calvin’s explanation of verses 26–28 reads the passage in that way.

Wesley’s notes on verses 26–29 emphasize the refusal to follow Jesus and understand His promise in connection with continuing to believe, love and follow Him. Methodist Article XII allows falling from grace and being restored by grace. The Catholic Church teaches that grace begins with God and calls for a free response (Catechism 1996–2002); it also teaches that the gift of faith can be lost (Catechism 162). These positions affirm dependence on God’s grace while differing from the Reformed account of final preservation.

On verse 30, Wesley and the Catholic Catechism, paragraph 590, connect the saying with Christ’s divine identity. Calvin focuses its immediate meaning on the Father and Son acting together in power and protection. That is a difference over this saying’s emphasis; Calvin also affirms Christ’s deity in his explanation of verse 36.
passages.god_plan_html:
The shepherd’s care belongs within God’s larger purpose to bring His people into lasting life with Him. Ezekiel 37:21–28 joins the promise of one shepherd with peace and God dwelling among His people. Jesus’ promise reaches beyond surviving a single threat to receiving eternal life in His care.

Romans 8:31–39 gives another view of that assurance: Christ has died, has been raised and intercedes for His people, and no created power can separate them from God’s love in Him. The security of the flock rests on the saving work of the One who holds them, rather than on their ability to overpower every enemy.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: John 10:31-42
passages.section_title: Why do some seek to stone Jesus while others believe?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 31 At this, the Jews again picked up stones to stone Him. 32 But Jesus responded, “I have shown you many good works from the Father. For which of these do you stone Me?” 33 “We are not stoning You for any good work,” said the Jews, “but for blasphemy, because You, who are a man, make Yourself out to be God.” 34 Jesus replied, “Is it not written in your Law: ‘I have said you are gods’? 35 If he called them gods to whom the word of God came—and the Scripture cannot be broken— 36 then what about the One whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world? How then can you accuse Me of blasphemy for stating that I am the Son of God? 37 If I am not doing the works of My Father, then do not believe Me. 38 But if I am doing them, even though you do not believe Me, believe the works themselves, so that you may know and understand that the Father is in Me, and I am in the Father.” 39 At this, they tried again to seize Him, but He escaped their grasp. 40 Then Jesus went back across the Jordan to the place where John had first been baptizing, and He stayed there. 41 Many came to Him and said, “Although John never performed a sign, everything he said about this man was true.” 42 And many in that place believed in Jesus.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After Jesus says that He and the Father are one, His opponents take up stones. He asks which of His good works has brought this response. They say the issue is blasphemy: in their judgment, He is a man claiming to be God. Their accusation makes the question of His identity explicit.

Jesus answers from Psalm 82, where God addresses others as gods while judging their injustice. He points out that Scripture uses the term for those to whom God’s word came, then directs attention to the One the Father has set apart and sent into the world. His reply challenges their immediate accusation; it does not withdraw His claim to be the Son of God.

He again asks them to consider His works. They reveal the Father at work in Him and His own unity with the Father. Whatever questions His words raise, He does not ask them to ignore the evidence of what He has done. They attempt to seize Him, but He escapes; John does not describe the method.

The closing scene moves across the Jordan, to the place associated with John’s earlier baptizing. People remember that John performed no sign, but recognize that his testimony about Jesus was true. Many believe there. The contrast is between responses to Jesus and His witness, rather than a claim that one location or social group makes faith automatic.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian interpreters commonly understand Jesus’ reply as defending His claim through Scripture and the Father’s works. Calvin on verses 34–38 and Wesley on verses 35–38 both distinguish His unique identity and mission from the lesser use of the title in the psalm.

There are different readings of the figures addressed in Psalm 82. Calvin identifies them as earthly kings and judges entrusted with authority. The Catholic bishops’ note on Psalm 82 instead understands the scene as God judging subordinate heavenly beings. These are interpretations of the psalm, not uniform positions held by every member of those traditions. John’s account states Jesus’ central point without resolving every question about the psalm’s setting: Scripture uses this language, and His claim must be considered in light of the Father who sent Him and the works He does.
passages.god_plan_html:
Psalm 82 ends by calling on God to judge the earth and affirming His claim over all nations. Jesus’ earlier teaching in John 5:22–23 says that the Father has entrusted judgment to the Son. Read together, these passages place the question of Jesus’ identity within God’s wider rule and His purpose to be known and honored through the Son.

The belief across the Jordan also brings the witness of John the Baptist back into view. His role was to point people toward Christ, not to replace Him. John 20:30–31 explains the Gospel’s own purpose in the same direction: its recorded signs lead readers to believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and to receive life in His name.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: John 11:1-16
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus wait before going to Lazarus?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 At this time a man named Lazarus was sick. He lived in Bethany, the village of Mary and her sister Martha. 2 (Mary, whose brother Lazarus was sick, was to anoint the Lord with perfume and wipe His feet with her hair.) 3 So the sisters sent word to Jesus, “Lord, the one You love is sick.” 4 When Jesus heard this, He said, “This sickness will not end in death. No, it is for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it.” 5 Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus. 6 So on hearing that Lazarus was sick, He stayed where He was for two days, 7 and then He said to the disciples, “Let us go back to Judea.” 8 “Rabbi,” they replied, “the Jews just tried to stone You, and You are going back there?” 9 Jesus answered, “Are there not twelve hours of daylight? If anyone walks in the daytime, he will not stumble, because he sees by the light of this world. 10 But if anyone walks at night, he will stumble, because he has no light.” 11 After He had said this, He told them, “Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I am going there to wake him up.” 12 His disciples replied, “Lord, if he is sleeping, he will get better.” 13 They thought that Jesus was talking about actual sleep, but He was speaking about the death of Lazarus. 14 So Jesus told them plainly, “Lazarus is dead, 15 and for your sake I am glad I was not there, so that you may believe. But let us go to him.” 16 Then Thomas called Didymus said to his fellow disciples, “Let us also go, so that we may die with Him.”

But let us go to him.” 16 Then Thomas called Didymus said to his fellow disciples, “Let us also go, so that we may die with Him.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Lazarus is ill in Bethany, the village of Mary and Martha. The sisters send word to Jesus, appealing to His love for their brother. John identifies Mary by looking ahead to her anointing of Jesus, which he records in John 12:1–8. This account does not name her as the unnamed woman who anoints Jesus in Luke 7.

Jesus says the illness will not end in death but will show the glory of God and His Son. Lazarus does die, as verse 14 makes explicit. The promise concerns the outcome Jesus intends to bring, rather than a statement that His friend will never enter the grave.

John places Jesus’ love for the family directly alongside His decision to remain where He is for two more days. The delay is part of the story, but it is not explained as indifference. Nor does John give enough information here to reconstruct the hour of Lazarus’s death or the messenger’s whole journey.

Returning to Judea brings danger back into view. The disciples remember the attempted stoning. Jesus answers with the picture of walking in daylight, continuing the Gospel’s theme of light and the work given Him by the Father. He then speaks of Lazarus sleeping. When they take that as ordinary sleep and hope of recovery, He plainly tells them Lazarus is dead.

Jesus says that what follows will serve their faith and announces that He will go to Lazarus. Thomas urges the others to go and die with Him. His words acknowledge the danger and express willingness to accompany Jesus; the text does not give a complete account of his motives. The disciples are being led toward seeing more of Jesus’ power than they yet understand.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the delay as part of Jesus’ purpose to reveal God’s glory and strengthen faith, rather than a failure of love. Calvin on verses 4–5 and 15 and Wesley on verses 4 and 11 connect the promise with the life Jesus will bring from death.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus knowingly returns toward danger to bring life to His friend. As the chapter unfolds, the raising of Lazarus leads to a decision to kill Jesus (John 11:45–53). The sign of life therefore becomes part of the road to His own death.

This anticipates a larger saving purpose. Hebrews 2:14–18 describes the Son sharing our humanity, entering death and freeing people from its fear. Lazarus’s story gives a preview of His authority over death; the cross and resurrection will reveal the greater work through which He brings His people into life.

passages.title: John 11:17-27
passages.section_title: How does Jesus give hope in the face of death?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 When Jesus arrived, He found that Lazarus had already spent four days in the tomb. 18 Now Bethany was near Jerusalem, a little less than two miles away, 19 and many of the Jews had come to Martha and Mary to console them in the loss of their brother. 20 So when Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went out to meet Him, but Mary stayed at home. 21 Martha said to Jesus, “Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died. 22 But even now I know that God will give You whatever You ask of Him.” 23 “Your brother will rise again,” Jesus told her. 24 Martha replied, “I know that he will rise again in the resurrection at the last day.” 25 Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in Me will live, even though he dies. 26 And everyone who lives and believes in Me will never die. Do you believe this?” 27 “Yes, Lord,” she answered, “I believe that You are the Christ, the Son of God, who was to come into the world.”
paragraphs: 17 When Jesus arrived, He found that Lazarus had already spent four days in the tomb. 18 Now Bethany was near Jerusalem, a little less than two miles away, 19 and many of the Jews had come to Martha and Mary to console them in the loss of their brother. 20 So when Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went out to meet Him, but Mary stayed at home. 21 Martha said to Jesus, “Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died. 22 But even now I know that God will give You whatever You ask of Him.”

23 “Your brother will rise again,” Jesus told her. 24 Martha replied, “I know that he will rise again in the resurrection at the last day.” 25 Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in Me will live, even though he dies. 26 And everyone who lives and believes in Me will never die. Do you believe this?” 27 “Yes, Lord,” she answered, “I believe that You are the Christ, the Son of God, who was to come into the world.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
When Jesus arrives, Lazarus has been in the tomb four days. John locates Bethany near Jerusalem, a little less than two miles away, and tells us that many people have come to console the sisters. Martha goes to meet Jesus, while Mary remains at home. The loss is real and already being mourned.

Martha speaks both her grief and her confidence in Jesus. She believes His presence could have prevented her brother’s death and still trusts His relationship with God. When He promises that Lazarus will rise, she answers with her hope of resurrection on the last day. Jesus then directs that hope toward Himself: resurrection and life come through Him.

His words hold together two truths that can seem difficult to place side by side. A believer may die physically and yet live through Him; the life He gives is not finally overcome by death. This is why the promise does not mean that faithful people are guaranteed to avoid a grave.

Jesus asks Martha whether she believes, and she confesses Him as the Christ, the Son of God, the One coming into the world. The conversation moves beyond whether an event called resurrection will happen someday to whether she trusts the One who gives life. Her confession is important in its own right; it need not be turned into a formula that forces God to perform the same miracle in every bereavement.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand Jesus as the source of resurrection and eternal life, with faith in Him reaching beyond bodily death. The Catholic Catechism, paragraph 994, Wesley on verse 25 and Calvin on verses 25–26 all place that hope in Christ Himself.
passages.god_plan_html:
The promise reaches beyond Lazarus receiving life again in this story. 1 Corinthians 15:20–26 connects the resurrection of those who belong to Christ with His own resurrection and describes death as the last enemy to be destroyed.

Verses 42–49 describe the future risen body as imperishable and glorious. God’s purpose is therefore more than postponing loss for a few years: through Christ He brings His people into a life that death will not keep taking away. Martha’s hope of the last day finds its foundation in the person standing before her.

passages.title: John 11:28-37
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus weep when He knows what He will do?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 28 After Martha had said this, she went back and called her sister Mary aside to tell her, “The Teacher is here and is asking for you.” 29 And when Mary heard this, she got up quickly and went to Him. 30 Now Jesus had not yet entered the village, but was still at the place where Martha had met Him. 31 When the Jews who were in the house consoling Mary saw how quickly she got up and went out, they followed her, supposing she was going to the tomb to mourn there. 32 When Mary came to Jesus and saw Him, she fell at His feet and said, “Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died.” 33 When Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her also weeping, He was deeply moved in spirit and troubled. 34 “Where have you put him?” He asked. “Come and see, Lord,” they answered. 35 Jesus wept. 36 Then the Jews said, “See how He loved him!” 37 But some of them asked, “Could not this man who opened the eyes of the blind also have kept Lazarus from dying?”
paragraphs: 28 After Martha had said this, she went back and called her sister Mary aside to tell her, “The Teacher is here and is asking for you.” 29 And when Mary heard this, she got up quickly and went to Him. 30 Now Jesus had not yet entered the village, but was still at the place where Martha had met Him. 31 When the Jews who were in the house consoling Mary saw how quickly she got up and went out, they followed her, supposing she was going to the tomb to mourn there. 32 When Mary came to Jesus and saw Him, she fell at His feet and said, “Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died.”

33 When Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her also weeping, He was deeply moved in spirit and troubled. 34 “Where have you put him?” He asked. “Come and see, Lord,” they answered. 35 Jesus wept. 36 Then the Jews said, “See how He loved him!” 37 But some of them asked, “Could not this man who opened the eyes of the blind also have kept Lazarus from dying?”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Martha returns and privately tells Mary that the Teacher is asking for her. Mary goes quickly. The people consoling her follow because they think she is going to the tomb, but she goes to Jesus, who is still outside the village. She falls at His feet and speaks the same words Martha used about His presence and her brother’s death.

Jesus sees her weeping and the others weeping with her. John describes Him as deeply moved and troubled, then records His tears. His knowledge of the coming raising does not make Him distant from the grief before Him. The story holds His power and His love together.

The Greek word behind deeply moved is ἐμβριμάομαι, embrimaomai (em-brim-AH-oh-my). Thayer’s lexicon describes strong indignation and directly cites this scene. The word for troubled can describe deep inward distress or sorrow. These words show the force of His response; they do not, by themselves, identify one exact object of anger or rule out compassion.

The observers respond in different ways. Some recognize His love for Lazarus; others ask why the One who opened the blind man’s eyes did not prevent this death. Their question brings the earlier sign into the present loss. John records it without giving us every questioner’s private motive or the full content of Jesus’ thoughts.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly see Jesus’ tears as showing real compassion and His sharing in human sorrow. Wesley on verse 35 and Calvin on verse 33 connect His response both with the mourners before Him and with the wider misery of humanity.

The stronger wording also leads some interpreters to emphasize His response to death itself. The Catholic bishops’ note on verse 33 suggests anger at evil’s presence in death. That is an interpretation of the scene; the text shows His profound response without stating every reason for it.
passages.god_plan_html: Hebrews 4:14–16 describes Jesus as the great high priest who can sympathize with our weakness and through whom we approach God for mercy. His tears here help us see that sympathy in a particular human loss. The One who brings life does not do so as a distant observer: He enters our suffering and brings His care to the people He has come to save.

passages.title: John 11:38-44
passages.section_title: What does Jesus reveal when He calls Lazarus out?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 38 Jesus, once again deeply moved, came to the tomb. It was a cave with a stone laid across the entrance. 39 “Take away the stone,” Jesus said. “Lord, by now he stinks,” said Martha, the sister of the dead man. “It has already been four days.” 40 Jesus replied, “Did I not tell you that if you believed, you would see the glory of God?” 41 So they took away the stone. Then Jesus lifted His eyes upward and said, “Father, I thank You that You have heard Me. 42 I knew that You always hear Me, but I say this for the benefit of the people standing here, so they may believe that You sent Me.” 43 After Jesus had said this, He called out in a loud voice, “Lazarus, come out!” 44 The man who had been dead came out with his hands and feet bound in strips of linen, and his face wrapped in a cloth. “Unwrap him and let him go,” Jesus told them.
paragraphs: 38 Jesus, once again deeply moved, came to the tomb. It was a cave with a stone laid across the entrance. 39 “Take away the stone,” Jesus said. “Lord, by now he stinks,” said Martha, the sister of the dead man. “It has already been four days.” 40 Jesus replied, “Did I not tell you that if you believed, you would see the glory of God?”

41 So they took away the stone. Then Jesus lifted His eyes upward and said, “Father, I thank You that You have heard Me. 42 I knew that You always hear Me, but I say this for the benefit of the people standing here, so they may believe that You sent Me.” 43 After Jesus had said this, He called out in a loud voice, “Lazarus, come out!” 44 The man who had been dead came out with his hands and feet bound in strips of linen, and his face wrapped in a cloth. “Unwrap him and let him go,” Jesus told them.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus comes to the tomb still deeply moved. John describes a cave with a stone at the entrance. When Jesus orders the stone removed, Martha objects because Lazarus has been dead four days. Her concern makes clear that this is a body in a grave, not a person recovering from an ordinary sleep.

Jesus directs her back to belief and the glory of God. After the stone is removed, He lifts His eyes and thanks the Father for hearing Him. He also explains the purpose of speaking for the witnesses: they are to believe that the Father sent Him. The prayer presents the Father and Son acting together, rather than Jesus working against an unwilling Father.

He calls Lazarus by name and commands him to come out. Lazarus emerges with his hands and feet bound and his face wrapped in a cloth. Jesus tells those present to unwrap him and let him go. John gives these concrete details without describing every movement of his body or a complete set of burial customs.

The sign shows the life Jesus gives in a way the witnesses can see. It does not report where Lazarus was during the four days, what he remembered, or what he later thought about returning. The next chapter does show him alive at a meal with Jesus (John 12:1–2).
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the raising as a real sign of Jesus’ power to give life, with His prayer making clear His relationship with the Father. The Catholic Catechism, paragraph 2604, Calvin on verses 41–43 and Wesley on verses 41–43 all emphasize the thanksgiving, the Father’s hearing Him and the life given through His word.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus has already said that the dead will hear His voice and that those in the tombs will come out (John 5:25–29). Lazarus’s raising is a striking preview of that authority, not an account of the final resurrection of everyone.

1 Corinthians 15:20–26 places the resurrection of Christ’s people within His victory over death. The sign here directs attention to the One who will enter death Himself and rise as the source of their lasting life. What Jesus gives to Lazarus points beyond this one family to God’s purpose to overcome death through His Son.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Prayer and Faith reads verses 41–42 as thanksgiving spoken in settled trust in the Father, before Lazarus comes out of the tomb. The recorded words express the Son’s confidence that He is heard, and Jesus says He speaks for the witnesses so that they may believe the Father sent Him. The study treats this prayer as an expression of that trust, rather than a technique that makes the miracle happen.

passages.title: John 11:41-42
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus thank the Father before Lazarus comes out?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 41 So they took away the stone. Then Jesus lifted His eyes upward and said, “Father, I thank You that You have heard Me. 42 I knew that You always hear Me, but I say this for the benefit of the people standing here, so they may believe that You sent Me.”
paragraphs: 41 So they took away the stone. Then Jesus lifted His eyes upward and said, “Father, I thank You that You have heard Me. 42 I knew that You always hear Me, but I say this for the benefit of the people standing here, so they may believe that You sent Me.”

passages.context_html:
The stone has been removed from Lazarus’s tomb, but Jesus has not yet called him out. His first recorded words here are thanks to the Father for hearing Him. He says He already knows that the Father always hears Him, and explains why He speaks before the people standing there.

The purpose is stated plainly: the witnesses are to believe that the Father sent Him. Read these words within John 11:38–44, where thanksgiving is followed by the command that brings Lazarus out. The account reveals the Son’s confidence and His relationship with the Father; it does not supply the words or timing of any earlier private prayer.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly see thanksgiving and testimony joined in these words: Jesus is heard by the Father, and the witnesses are directed toward recognizing who sent Him. The Catholic Catechism, paragraph 2604, Calvin on verses 41–42 and Wesley on verse 41 all connect His thanksgiving before the event with His confidence in the Father.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Prayer and Faith identifies this as thanksgiving rooted in the Son’s settled trust in the Father. Jesus is not using the recorded words to press the Father into acting; He thanks Him for being heard and speaks for the benefit of the witnesses. The study understands the prayer as expressing confidence in the Father’s purpose before its visible outcome.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html: Jesus explicitly gives the saving direction of the sign: belief in the One sent by the Father. John 20:30–31 states the Gospel’s wider purpose in the same terms—its recorded signs lead to believing that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and to life in His name. The prayer helps the witnesses see whose work is being revealed, beyond the extraordinary event itself.

passages.title: John 11:45-57
passages.section_title: How does the plan to kill Jesus reveal a greater purpose?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 45 Therefore many of the Jews who had come to Mary, and had seen what Jesus did, believed in Him. 46 But some of them went to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done. 47 Then the chief priests and Pharisees convened the Sanhedrin and said, “What are we to do? This man is performing many signs. 48 If we let Him go on like this, everyone will believe in Him, and then the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation.” 49 But one of them, named Caiaphas, who was high priest that year, said to them, “You know nothing at all! 50 You do not realize that it is better for you that one man die for the people than that the whole nation perish.” 51 Caiaphas did not say this on his own. Instead, as high priest that year, he was prophesying that Jesus would die for the nation, 52 and not only for the nation, but also for the scattered children of God, to gather them together into one. 53 So from that day on they plotted to kill Him. 54 As a result, Jesus no longer went about publicly among the Jews, but He withdrew to a town called Ephraim in an area near the wilderness. And He stayed there with the disciples. 55 Now the Jewish Passover was near, and many people went up from the country to Jerusalem to purify themselves before the Passover. 56 They kept looking for Jesus and asking one another as they stood in the temple courts, “What do you think? Will He come to the feast at all?” 57 But the chief priests and Pharisees had given orders that anyone who knew where He was must report it, so that they could arrest Him.

This man is performing many signs. 48 If we let Him go on like this, everyone will believe in Him, and then the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation.”

Instead, as high priest that year, he was prophesying that Jesus would die for the nation, 52 and not only for the nation, but also for the scattered children of God, to gather them together into one. 53 So from that day on they plotted to kill Him.

54 As a result, Jesus no longer went about publicly among the Jews, but He withdrew to a town called Ephraim in an area near the wilderness. And He stayed there with the disciples. 55 Now the Jewish Passover was near, and many people went up from the country to Jerusalem to purify themselves before the Passover. 56 They kept looking for Jesus and asking one another as they stood in the temple courts, “What do you think? Will He come to the feast at all?” 57 But the chief priests and Pharisees had given orders that anyone who knew where He was must report it, so that they could arrest Him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The raising of Lazarus brings different responses. Many of those who came to Mary believe in Jesus; others report what happened to the Pharisees. The chief priests and Pharisees convene the council and acknowledge His many signs. Their stated concern is that growing belief in Him will bring Roman intervention and the loss of their place and nation.

Caiaphas, the high priest, proposes that one man die rather than the nation perish. Within the council’s discussion, this is a decision to remove Jesus for what they consider the people’s advantage. John then explains a meaning beyond that calculation: as high priest, Caiaphas has prophesied that Jesus will die for the nation and gather God’s scattered children into one.

Those two purposes must be distinguished. John does not present the decision to kill Jesus as a good act merely because God brings His saving purpose through it. The council plots His death, while the Gospel describes that death as reaching farther than the council intends.

Jesus withdraws to Ephraim near the wilderness and remains with His disciples. As Passover approaches, people go to Jerusalem to purify themselves and wonder whether He will come. The authorities order anyone who knows His whereabouts to report Him for arrest. The story has moved from a public sign of life toward the events of His death.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read Caiaphas’s words as having a meaning beyond his own plan: God uses them to announce Christ’s saving death and the gathering of His people. Calvin on verses 51–52 and Wesley on verses 50–52 distinguish that larger purpose from the high priest’s decision against Jesus.
passages.god_plan_html:
John explicitly extends the purpose of Jesus’ death beyond one nation. This gathering belongs with the promise of one flock in John 10:14–18. The shepherd lays down His life and brings people who were outside the first fold into His care.

Ephesians 2:13–18 explains how the cross brings Jews and Gentiles near to God, reconciles them in one body and gives both access to the Father by one Spirit. The plot to preserve one threatened place therefore stands within a much wider story: through Christ’s death, God gathers a people into shared life with Him.

passages.title: John 12:1-11
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus connect Mary’s gift with His burial?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Six days before the Passover, Jesus came to Bethany, the hometown of Lazarus, whom He had raised from the dead. 2 So they hosted a dinner for Jesus there. Martha served, and Lazarus was among those reclining at the table with Him. 3 Then Mary took about a pint of expensive perfume, made of pure nard, and she anointed Jesus’ feet and wiped them with her hair. And the house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume. 4 But one of His disciples, Judas Iscariot, who was going to betray Him, asked, 5 “Why wasn’t this perfume sold for three hundred denarii and the money given to the poor?” 6 Judas did not say this because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief. As keeper of the money bag, he used to take from what was put into it. 7 “Leave her alone,” Jesus replied. “She has kept this perfume in preparation for the day of My burial. 8 The poor you will always have with you, but you will not always have Me.” 9 Meanwhile a large crowd of Jews learned that Jesus was there. And they came not only because of Him, but also to see Lazarus, whom He had raised from the dead. 10 So the chief priests made plans to kill Lazarus as well, 11 for on account of him many of the Jews were deserting them and believing in Jesus.

And the house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume.

4 But one of His disciples, Judas Iscariot, who was going to betray Him, asked, 5 “Why wasn’t this perfume sold for three hundred denarii and the money given to the poor?” 6 Judas did not say this because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief. As keeper of the money bag, he used to take from what was put into it. 7 “Leave her alone,” Jesus replied. “She has kept this perfume in preparation for the day of My burial. 8 The poor you will always have with you, but you will not always have Me.”

9 Meanwhile a large crowd of Jews learned that Jesus was there. And they came not only because of Him, but also to see Lazarus, whom He had raised from the dead. 10 So the chief priests made plans to kill Lazarus as well, 11 for on account of him many of the Jews were deserting them and believing in Jesus.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus returns to Bethany six days before Passover. At the dinner, Martha serves and Lazarus sits with Him. Mary pours costly perfume on Jesus’ feet and wipes them with her hair. The man who had been in the tomb is now at the table, while Jesus speaks about His own approaching burial.

Judas objects that the perfume could have been sold for three hundred denarii and the money given to the poor. The amount signals its value: in Matthew 20:1–2, a worker agrees to one denarius for a day’s labor. John tells us why Judas raises the objection: he has been stealing from the group’s money bag. This is a motive the Gospel explicitly supplies, not a reason to assume every concern for poor people is dishonest.

Jesus defends Mary and connects the perfume with His burial. His words about always having the poor do not cancel the call to help them. Deuteronomy 15:7–11 joins the continuing presence of poverty with a command to be generous. Jesus draws attention to the particular opportunity before Mary and the limited time remaining before His death.

The scene ends with another response to Lazarus’s raising. People come to see both him and Jesus, and many believe in Jesus because of him. The chief priests therefore plan to kill Lazarus as well. His restored life has become a public witness that they want to remove.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand Mary’s act as honoring Jesus and anticipating His burial, as Wesley’s note on verse 7 explains. His words about the poor preserve the duty of generosity; that continuing duty is affirmed in Calvin’s explanation of verse 8 and the Catholic Catechism, paragraph 2449.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus interprets the gift in light of the death that is drawing near. The dinner places restored life and coming burial in the same scene, helping us see that His mission has moved toward its decisive cost.

1 Corinthians 15:3–4 places Christ’s death for sins, His burial and His resurrection together at the heart of the gospel. Mary’s act belongs to the approach to that burial. The One who has brought Lazarus out of a grave will Himself enter death and rise, bringing a hope greater than a temporary return to ordinary life.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: John 12:12-19
passages.section_title: What kind of king enters Jerusalem on a donkey?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 The next day the great crowd that had come to the feast heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem. 13 They took palm branches and went out to meet Him, shouting: “Hosanna!” “Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord!” “Blessed is the King of Israel!” 14 Finding a young donkey, Jesus sat on it, as it is written: 15 “Do not be afraid, O Daughter of Zion. See, your King is coming, seated on the colt of a donkey.” 16 At first His disciples did not understand these things, but after Jesus was glorified they remembered what had been done to Him, and they realized that these very things had also been written about Him. 17 Meanwhile, many people who had been with Jesus when He called Lazarus from the tomb and raised him from the dead continued to testify. 18 That is also why the crowd went out to meet Him, because they heard that He had performed this sign. 19 Then the Pharisees said to one another, “You can see that this is doing you no good. Look how the whole world has gone after Him!”

See, your King is coming, seated on the colt of a donkey.” 16 At first His disciples did not understand these things, but after Jesus was glorified they remembered what had been done to Him, and they realized that these very things had also been written about Him.

17 Meanwhile, many people who had been with Jesus when He called Lazarus from the tomb and raised him from the dead continued to testify. 18 That is also why the crowd went out to meet Him, because they heard that He had performed this sign. 19 Then the Pharisees said to one another, “You can see that this is doing you no good. Look how the whole world has gone after Him!”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The next day, people who have come for the feast hear that Jesus is approaching Jerusalem. They take palm branches to meet Him and greet Him as the King of Israel. The testimony about Lazarus’s raising helps explain their response: some have witnessed the sign, and others have heard about it.

The cry ὡσαννά, hōsanna (hoh-zan-NAH), preserves a Hebrew plea for salvation. Thayer’s lexicon connects it with the prayer in Psalm 118:25–26. Here the crowd uses it while welcoming Jesus as King. Their words are more than a general cheer for a popular teacher.

Jesus rides a young donkey, and John directly connects this with what was written about Zion’s coming king. Zechariah 9:9–10 describes a humble king arriving on a donkey and goes on to speak of peace for the nations. This is a royal arrival with a character different from conquest by war.

The disciples do not understand the meaning at first. After Jesus is glorified, they remember the Scripture and recognize how it relates to what happened. The story therefore distinguishes taking part in an event from grasping its full meaning. The Pharisees’ final complaint that the whole world has gone after Him expresses their alarm; it is not a count of every person’s faith.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read the entry as Jesus presenting Himself as the promised King in humility, with the Scripture becoming clearer to His disciples afterward. The Catholic Catechism, paragraphs 559–560, Calvin on verses 12–16 and Wesley on verses 15–16 share that central understanding.
passages.god_plan_html:
John identifies the arrival with Scripture’s promised king, but the path ahead leads to the cross. A few verses later Jesus describes His coming death as the way much fruit will be produced and people will be drawn to Him (John 12:23–33). His kingship and His self-giving belong together.

Zechariah’s vision also reaches beyond Jerusalem to peace among the nations. Ephesians 2:13–18 explains how Christ makes peace through His cross and brings Jews and Gentiles into shared access to the Father. The humble arrival belongs within that wider saving purpose, rather than ending with the crowd’s immediate welcome.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: John 12:20-26
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus compare His death with a seed?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 20 Now there were some Greeks among those who went up to worship at the feast. 21 They came to Philip, who was from Bethsaida in Galilee, and requested of him, “Sir, we want to see Jesus.” 22 Philip relayed this appeal to Andrew, and both of them went and told Jesus. 23 But Jesus replied, “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified. 24 Truly, truly, I tell you, unless a kernel of wheat falls to the ground and dies, it remains only a seed. But if it dies, it bears much fruit. 25 Whoever loves his life will lose it, but whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life. 26 If anyone serves Me, he must follow Me; and where I am, My servant will be as well. If anyone serves Me, the Father will honor him.
paragraphs: 20 Now there were some Greeks among those who went up to worship at the feast. 21 They came to Philip, who was from Bethsaida in Galilee, and requested of him, “Sir, we want to see Jesus.” 22 Philip relayed this appeal to Andrew, and both of them went and told Jesus. 23 But Jesus replied, “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.

24 Truly, truly, I tell you, unless a kernel of wheat falls to the ground and dies, it remains only a seed. But if it dies, it bears much fruit. 25 Whoever loves his life will lose it, but whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life. 26 If anyone serves Me, he must follow Me; and where I am, My servant will be as well. If anyone serves Me, the Father will honor him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Some people John calls Greeks have come to worship at the feast and ask Philip to help them see Jesus. Philip tells Andrew, and they bring the request to Him. John does not record the visitors’ later conversation with Jesus. Instead, he gives Jesus’ announcement that the hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.

The picture of a kernel of wheat explains why death lies on that path. A seed kept alone does not produce a crop; in the picture Jesus uses, its death leads to much fruit. He is preparing His listeners to understand His death through what it will bring, rather than see it only as the loss of a teacher.

He then speaks to those who would serve Him. Loving or hating one’s life is about what has first place: clinging to life on one’s own terms or following Him. The contrast calls for a loyalty that can be costly. It does not mean that life has no value; the promise itself is eternal life.

The servant is called to follow where Jesus leads and is promised the Father’s honor. This joins the coming self-giving of Jesus with the life of His followers. They are not asked to produce His saving work, but to belong to Him and follow Him through the cost of serving.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read the seed as a picture of Jesus’ death bringing life to others, with His followers called to costly faithfulness. Calvin on verses 24–26 and Wesley on those verses share that central reading.

Commentators differ over the visitors’ background. Wesley understands them as Gentiles seeking Israel’s God. The Catholic bishops’ note on verse 20 considers them probably Gentile converts to Judaism. Calvin instead takes them as Jews living among Greek-speaking peoples. These are interpretations of the group John calls Greeks; the passage does not supply a fuller biography.
passages.god_plan_html:
A helpful parallel appears in Isaiah 53:10–12: the Servant gives His life, bears others’ sins and sees the outcome of His suffering. Jesus’ picture likewise looks beyond His death to the people who will receive life through Him.

1 Corinthians 15:35–38 uses the image of a seed when explaining the future resurrection body. The two passages use the picture for distinct but connected purposes: Jesus gives His life so that others may live, and God will bring His people into risen life. Death does not have the final word in either picture.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: John 12:27-36
passages.section_title: How does the cross reveal God’s glory?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 27 Now My soul is troubled, and what shall I say? ‘Father, save Me from this hour’? No, it is for this purpose that I have come to this hour. 28 Father, glorify Your name!” Then a voice came from heaven: “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.” 29 The crowd standing there heard it and said that it had thundered. Others said that an angel had spoken to Him. 30 In response, Jesus said, “This voice was not for My benefit, but yours. 31 Now judgment is upon this world; now the prince of this world will be cast out. 32 And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw everyone to Myself.” 33 He said this to indicate the kind of death He was going to die. 34 The crowd replied, “We have heard from the Law that the Christ will remain forever. So how can You say that the Son of Man must be lifted up? Who is this Son of Man?” 35 Then Jesus told them, “For a little while longer, the Light will be among you. Walk while you have the Light, so that darkness will not overtake you. The one who walks in the darkness does not know where he is going. 36 While you have the Light, believe in the Light, so that you may become sons of light.” After Jesus had spoken these things, He went away and was hidden from them.

No, it is for this purpose that I have come to this hour. 28 Father, glorify Your name!” Then a voice came from heaven: “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.” 29 The crowd standing there heard it and said that it had thundered. Others said that an angel had spoken to Him. 30 In response, Jesus said, “This voice was not for My benefit, but yours.

31 Now judgment is upon this world; now the prince of this world will be cast out. 32 And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw everyone to Myself.” 33 He said this to indicate the kind of death He was going to die.

34 The crowd replied, “We have heard from the Law that the Christ will remain forever. So how can You say that the Son of Man must be lifted up? Who is this Son of Man?” 35 Then Jesus told them, “For a little while longer, the Light will be among you. Walk while you have the Light, so that darkness will not overtake you. The one who walks in the darkness does not know where he is going. 36 While you have the Light, believe in the Light, so that you may become sons of light.” After Jesus had spoken these things, He went away and was hidden from them.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus is troubled as the hour approaches, yet He asks the Father to glorify His name. His distress and His obedience appear together. John does not portray the suffering as easy for Him, or as a reason for abandoning the purpose for which He came.

The voice from heaven answers that the Father has glorified His name and will do so again. The people offer different explanations of what they heard: thunder or an angel’s voice. Jesus says the voice came for their benefit. The witness is meant to direct them toward the Father’s work through Him.

Jesus then speaks of judgment, the defeat of the ruler of this world and His own being lifted up. John explicitly explains that lifting up refers to the kind of death He would die. The cross is therefore presented as the place of victory and of drawing people to Himself, even though it will appear to His opponents as their success.

The crowd asks how this can fit with a Christ who remains forever. Jesus calls them to walk in the light and believe while the opportunity is before them. He then withdraws. The passage records both the explanation of His coming death and the urgent invitation to receive Him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly connect Jesus’ being lifted up with the cross and understand His death as bringing victory over sin and evil. The main difference concerns how to understand the promise of drawing everyone to Himself.

Calvin’s commentary on verse 32 understands everyone as God’s people gathered from both Jews and Gentiles. In the Reformed Westminster Confession, 8.8, Christ certainly brings those for whom He has purchased redemption into its benefits. This reading emphasizes a saving work that brings His people to Him.

Wesley’s note on verse 32 also includes Jews and Gentiles, while distinguishing those who follow His drawing. The Catholic Church teaches that Christ died for all without exception (Catechism 605) and that God’s grace calls for a free response (Catechism 2002). These teachings describe the wider reach of His saving work without treating the verse as a promise that every person is automatically saved.
passages.god_plan_html:
The obedience of Jesus answers a much older story. Romans 5:12–19 contrasts Adam’s disobedience, through which sin and death entered, with Christ’s obedience, through which righteousness and life come. His resolve here belongs to that reversal: the Son carries out the Father’s saving purpose in a world marked by Adam’s sin.

The cross also confronts the powers that hold people in bondage. Colossians 2:13–15 joins forgiveness and canceled debt with God’s triumph over the powers through the cross. This helps explain why Jesus speaks of judgment and victory while moving toward His death. What appears to be defeat becomes the means of rescue.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: John 12:37-43
passages.section_title: Why do signs not lead everyone to believe?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 37 Although Jesus had performed so many signs in their presence, they still did not believe in Him. 38 This was to fulfill the word of Isaiah the prophet: “Lord, who has believed our message? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” 39 For this reason they were unable to believe. For again, Isaiah says: 40 “He has blinded their eyes and hardened their hearts, so that they cannot see with their eyes, and understand with their hearts, and turn, and I would heal them.” 41 Isaiah said these things because he saw Jesus’ glory and spoke about Him. 42 Nevertheless, many of the leaders believed in Him. But because of the Pharisees they did not confess Him, for fear that they would be put out of the synagogue. 43 For they loved praise from men more than praise from God.
paragraphs: 37 Although Jesus had performed so many signs in their presence, they still did not believe in Him. 38 This was to fulfill the word of Isaiah the prophet: “Lord, who has believed our message? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” 39 For this reason they were unable to believe. For again, Isaiah says: 40 “He has blinded their eyes and hardened their hearts, so that they cannot see with their eyes, and understand with their hearts, and turn, and I would heal them.” 41 Isaiah said these things because he saw Jesus’ glory and spoke about Him.

42 Nevertheless, many of the leaders believed in Him. But because of the Pharisees they did not confess Him, for fear that they would be put out of the synagogue. 43 For they loved praise from men more than praise from God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
John reflects on the response to Jesus’ public ministry. Many signs have been performed, yet unbelief remains. He connects this with Isaiah 53:1, where the prophet asks who has believed the message and received the revelation of the LORD’s power.

He then quotes the warning of blinded eyes and hardened hearts from Isaiah 6:9–10. John describes this as judgment, using the severe language that they were unable to believe. The signs do not turn faith into an automatic response. The words must be heard alongside the Gospel’s repeated calls to believe and its accounts of refusing the light.

John also says that Isaiah saw Jesus’ glory and spoke about Him. In Isaiah 6, the prophet sees the Lord enthroned in holiness and receives a difficult commission. John places that vision and warning within his account of Christ, connecting Jesus with the glory Isaiah saw.

The next words prevent us from treating every leader as having one response. Many believed, but fear of being put out of the synagogue kept them from confessing Him. John rebukes their preference for human praise over God’s praise. He records both their belief and their failure to acknowledge Him openly, without giving the later history of each person.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the hardening as a warning about persistent unbelief and God’s judgment. Calvin on verses 39–40, Wesley on verse 39 and the Catholic bishops’ note on verses 38–41 hold the warning together with people’s response to God.
passages.god_plan_html:
The same warning from Isaiah appears in Acts 28:23–28, where some hearers receive Paul’s testimony about Jesus and others resist. Paul then speaks of God’s salvation reaching the Gentiles. This shows the warning within the wider movement of the gospel beyond one people.

That movement must not be confused with God abandoning His people. Romans 11:1–6 explicitly denies that conclusion and points to a people preserved by grace. Judgment, continuing mercy and the gathering of people from the nations all belong in the biblical picture.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: John 12:44-50
passages.section_title: Why does receiving Jesus mean receiving the Father?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 44 Then Jesus cried out, “Whoever believes in Me does not believe in Me alone, but in the One who sent Me. 45 And whoever sees Me sees the One who sent Me. 46 I have come into the world as a light, so that no one who believes in Me should remain in darkness. 47 As for anyone who hears My words and does not keep them, I do not judge him. For I have not come to judge the world, but to save the world. 48 There is a judge for the one who rejects Me and does not receive My words: The word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day. 49 I have not spoken on My own, but the Father who sent Me has commanded Me what to say and how to say it. 50 And I know that His command leads to eternal life. So I speak exactly what the Father has told Me to say.”
paragraphs: 44 Then Jesus cried out, “Whoever believes in Me does not believe in Me alone, but in the One who sent Me. 45 And whoever sees Me sees the One who sent Me. 46 I have come into the world as a light, so that no one who believes in Me should remain in darkness.

47 As for anyone who hears My words and does not keep them, I do not judge him. For I have not come to judge the world, but to save the world. 48 There is a judge for the one who rejects Me and does not receive My words: The word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day. 49 I have not spoken on My own, but the Father who sent Me has commanded Me what to say and how to say it. 50 And I know that His command leads to eternal life. So I speak exactly what the Father has told Me to say.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
John brings this section of Jesus’ public teaching to its close with a call to believe. The words gather themes heard throughout the Gospel: the Father has sent the Son, Jesus brings light, and His message leads to life. John does not give a new date or location for this declaration.

Jesus directs belief in Himself toward the Father who sent Him. To see Him is to see the Father made known through Him. The point is not simply that He is one teacher with a message worth considering, but that His words and work reveal the One who sent Him.

He says that He has come to save the world, then warns that rejecting His words has consequences on the last day. Read verses 47 and 48 together: the saving purpose of His coming does not cancel judgment. The word being offered as life will also expose the refusal to receive Him.

The passage ends where it began, with the Father and Son together in this mission. Jesus speaks what the Father has commanded, and that command leads to eternal life. The invitation is therefore to receive the life God makes known through His Son.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly distinguish the saving purpose of Jesus’ coming from the judgment faced by those who reject His words. Calvin on verses 47–48 and Wesley on verses 44–50 read the message as an invitation to life that also carries responsibility for the response.
passages.god_plan_html:
The Gospel began by describing the Word who was with God, became flesh and made the Father known (John 1:1–18). This closing call shows the purpose of that coming in direct terms: through the Son, people are brought out of darkness and into life with God.

Ephesians 1:9–10 describes God’s purpose to bring all things together in Christ. Jesus’ message belongs to that larger work of making the Father known and gathering people into life with Him.

passages.title: John 13:1-17
passages.section_title: Why does the Lord wash His disciples’ feet?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 It was now just before the Passover Feast, and Jesus knew that His hour had come to leave this world and return to the Father. Having loved His own who were in the world, He loved them to the very end. 2 The evening meal was underway, and the devil had already put into the heart of Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot, to betray Jesus. 3 Jesus knew that the Father had delivered all things into His hands, and that He had come from God and was returning to God. 4 So He got up from the supper, laid aside His outer garments, and wrapped a towel around His waist. 5 After that, He poured water into a basin and began to wash the disciples’ feet and dry them with the towel that was around Him. 6 He came to Simon Peter, who asked Him, “Lord, are You going to wash my feet?” 7 Jesus replied, “You do not realize now what I am doing, but later you will understand.” 8 “Never shall You wash my feet!” Peter told Him. Jesus answered, “Unless I wash you, you have no part with Me.” 9 “Then, Lord,” Simon Peter replied, “not only my feet, but my hands and my head as well!” 10 Jesus told him, “Whoever has already bathed needs only to wash his feet, and he will be completely clean. And you are clean, though not all of you.” 11 For He knew who would betray Him. That is why He said, “Not all of you are clean.” 12 When Jesus had washed their feet and put on His outer garments, He reclined with them again and asked, “Do you know what I have done for you? 13 You call Me Teacher and Lord, and rightly so, because I am. 14 So if I, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also should wash one another’s feet. 15 I have set you an example so that you should do as I have done for you. 16 Truly, truly, I tell you, no servant is greater than his master, nor is a messenger greater than the one who sent him. 17 If you know these things, you will be blessed if you do them.

Jesus answered, “Unless I wash you, you have no part with Me.” 9 “Then, Lord,” Simon Peter replied, “not only my feet, but my hands and my head as well!” 10 Jesus told him, “Whoever has already bathed needs only to wash his feet, and he will be completely clean. And you are clean, though not all of you.” 11 For He knew who would betray Him. That is why He said, “Not all of you are clean.”

12 When Jesus had washed their feet and put on His outer garments, He reclined with them again and asked, “Do you know what I have done for you? 13 You call Me Teacher and Lord, and rightly so, because I am. 14 So if I, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also should wash one another’s feet. 15 I have set you an example so that you should do as I have done for you. 16 Truly, truly, I tell you, no servant is greater than his master, nor is a messenger greater than the one who sent him. 17 If you know these things, you will be blessed if you do them.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus knows that His hour has come and that He will return to the Father. John introduces the meal by speaking of His enduring love for His own. Knowing that the Father has placed all things in His hands, Jesus takes a towel and basin and washes the disciples’ feet. His authority is expressed through service.

Peter objects to receiving this service from his Lord. When Jesus tells him that receiving His washing is necessary to having a part with Him, Peter asks for his hands and head to be washed too. Jesus answers with the difference between someone who has bathed and the washing of the feet.

The word for bathed is λούω, louō (LOO-oh). Thayer’s lexicon distinguishes bathing the whole body from the word used here for washing a part of it. This helps us follow the conversation, but the vocabulary alone does not settle every question about the cleansing Jesus gives. John makes clear that more than bodily dirt is involved: the exception to being clean concerns the betrayer.

Jesus then explains the example. They rightly call Him Teacher and Lord; His service shows how they are to treat one another. The servant is not greater than the master, and knowing what He has done is to lead to doing it. The scene joins receiving His care with learning to give humble care to others.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the act as both humble service and a sign of the cleansing received from Jesus. Wesley on verses 8–10 emphasizes receiving His cleansing and walking in holiness; Calvin on verse 10 emphasizes the continuing renewal of His followers. The Catholic bishops’ note on verse 10 also notes a possible connection with baptism.

Traditions differ over how to practice the example. The Catholic Church’s 2016 decree on washing feet describes a rite at the Mass of the Lord’s Supper on Holy Thursday that represents Christ’s humility and love. It does not replace the continuing call to serve.

Mennonite Church USA’s Confession of Faith, Article 13, encourages washing one another’s feet when it meaningfully expresses service and love. The document explicitly acknowledges that some congregations practice it and others do not.

Wesley’s note on verse 14 understands the command as every kind of lowly service, rather than a requirement to repeat the particular action. Calvin, in verses 14–15, likewise emphasizes continuing service and objects to treating a ceremony alone as fulfillment of the example. These are the named teachers’ explanations, not a claim that every Methodist or Reformed congregation follows one practice.
passages.god_plan_html:
The towel and basin fit the larger shape of Christ’s mission. Philippians 2:5–11 describes the One equal with God taking the form of a servant and humbling Himself even to death on a cross. His service here gives the disciples a concrete example of that self-giving love.

The cleansing also points beyond washing skin. Hebrews 9:11–14 describes Christ’s offering of Himself as cleansing the conscience so that people may serve the living God. Jesus brings people into a relationship in which they receive His cleansing and learn His way of service.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: John 13:18-30
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus speak about betrayal before it happens?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 I am not speaking about all of you; I know whom I have chosen. But this is to fulfill the Scripture: ‘The one who shares My bread has lifted up his heel against Me.’ 19 I am telling you now before it happens, so that when it comes to pass, you will believe that I am He. 20 Truly, truly, I tell you, whoever receives the one I send receives Me, and whoever receives Me receives the One who sent Me.” 21 After Jesus had said this, He became troubled in spirit and testified, “Truly, truly, I tell you, one of you will betray Me.” 22 The disciples looked at one another, perplexed as to which of them He meant. 23 One of His disciples, the one whom Jesus loved, was reclining at His side. 24 So Simon Peter motioned to him to ask Jesus which one He was talking about. 25 Leaning back against Jesus, he asked, “Lord, who is it?” 26 Jesus answered, “It is the one to whom I give this morsel after I have dipped it.” Then He dipped the morsel and gave it to Judas son of Simon Iscariot. 27 And when Judas had taken the morsel, Satan entered into him. Then Jesus said to Judas, “What you are about to do, do quickly.” 28 But no one at the table knew why Jesus had said this to him. 29 Since Judas kept the money bag, some thought that Jesus was telling him to buy what was needed for the feast, or to give something to the poor. 30 As soon as he had received the morsel, Judas went out into the night.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus distinguishes His words to the disciples from the response of the betrayer. He quotes Psalm 41:9, where a close companion who shares bread turns against the speaker. He explains why He tells them beforehand: when it happens, they are to believe in who He is. The betrayal will not mean that His mission has taken Him by surprise.

He is troubled as He announces that one of them will betray Him. The disciples are perplexed. Peter motions to the disciple described as the one Jesus loved, who is reclining near Him, to ask whom He means. Jesus gives a dipped morsel to Judas as the identifying sign. The Gospel does not provide a complete seating plan or identify everyone’s age.

John says that Satan enters Judas, and Jesus tells him to act quickly. The others do not understand why He says this; some think Judas is being sent to buy supplies or give money to the poor because he keeps the money bag. Judas leaves, and John closes the scene by noting that it is night.

The account presents real evil and real responsibility. Luke 22:21–22 holds together the Son of Man’s determined path and the warning against the man who betrays Him. The fact that God knows what Judas will do does not make his betrayal innocent.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read the prediction as showing Jesus’ knowledge of what is coming and preparing the disciples to keep trusting Him. The place of Judas within the chosen group is explained in different ways.

Calvin on verse 18 connects the choosing with God’s saving purpose and the preservation of those who truly belong to Christ. Wesley on verse 18 refers to Jesus choosing the Twelve, one of whom will betray Him. Both acknowledge the warning and the fulfillment of Scripture; they place different emphasis on what the choosing means in this saying.
passages.god_plan_html:
The appeal to Psalm 41 places the betrayal within the Scripture Jesus is fulfilling. It is a painful part of His road to the cross, not the end of the Father’s purpose. Acts 2:23–24 later describes His death as occurring within God’s plan while also holding those who killed Him responsible.

The movement toward death will overturn the enemy’s work. Hebrews 2:14–15 describes Jesus sharing our humanity so that through death He defeats the one who holds its power and frees people from its fear. The darkness of this scene belongs to the approach to that victory.
