passages.title: John 13:31-35
passages.section_title: What will identify Jesus’ disciples after He leaves?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 31 When Judas had gone out, Jesus said, “Now the Son of Man is glorified, and God is glorified in Him. 32 If God is glorified in Him, God will also glorify the Son in Himself—and will glorify Him at once. 33 Little children, I am with you only a little while longer. You will look for Me, and as I said to the Jews, so now I say to you: ‘Where I am going, you cannot come.’ 34 A new commandment I give you: Love one another. As I have loved you, so you also must love one another. 35 By this everyone will know that you are My disciples, if you love one another.”
paragraphs: 31 When Judas had gone out, Jesus said, “Now the Son of Man is glorified, and God is glorified in Him. 32 If God is glorified in Him, God will also glorify the Son in Himself—and will glorify Him at once. 33 Little children, I am with you only a little while longer. You will look for Me, and as I said to the Jews, so now I say to you: ‘Where I am going, you cannot come.’
34 A new commandment I give you: Love one another. As I have loved you, so you also must love one another. 35 By this everyone will know that you are My disciples, if you love one another.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After Judas leaves, Jesus speaks of the Son of Man being glorified and of God being glorified in Him. The betrayal has set the road to the cross in motion. In this Gospel, that approaching death is bound up with His glory: John 12:23–33 has already connected His hour, His death and the drawing of people to Himself.

Jesus addresses the disciples tenderly as children and tells them that He will be with them only a little longer. They cannot follow Him where He is going now. Into that approaching separation He gives a command for their life together: they are to love one another as He has loved them.

The standard is personal and concrete. They have just received His humble service at the basin, and they will soon see the cost of His love at the cross. Their love for one another is to make their connection with Him recognizable to others. Jesus does not describe a badge or a slogan; He describes how His followers will treat one another.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand this command as a defining mark of following Jesus: His followers are to love one another in a way shaped by His own love. The command is not an invitation to claim superiority over other people; it calls disciples to make His love visible in their life together.

Calling the command new does not mean that God had never required love before. Leviticus 19:18, 34 already commands love for the neighbor and the foreigner. Here Jesus makes His own love the pattern for the disciples. Calvin on verse 34 emphasizes the renewed force of a command that must remain before them; Wesley on verse 34 emphasizes loving to the degree and in the manner Jesus has loved. The Catholic Church’s Catechism, paragraphs 1823–1827, likewise describes Christ’s love as the source and pattern of Christian love. These explanations share the central point rather than presenting opposing commands.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus is preparing a community whose life will bear witness after His departure. In John 17:20–23, He prays for later believers to be one so that the world may believe that the Father sent Him. The love commanded here belongs to that public witness.

1 John 3:16–18 makes the connection practical: Christ’s laying down His life teaches His people what love is, and love responds when a brother has material needs. God’s purpose takes shape in people who pass on the care they have received.
passages.current_position_html: Our studies What Is the True Church? and I Am a Disciple identify love for one another as a visible mark of belonging to Jesus. This means patient, forgiving, self-giving care in practice. A claim to follow Him is meant to be recognizable in how we treat people, not simply in the name we use for ourselves.

passages.title: John 13:34-35
passages.section_title: What makes this command to love new?
passages.note: Love as the identifying mark of the true Church.

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 34 A new commandment I give you: Love one another. As I have loved you, so you also must love one another. 35 By this everyone will know that you are My disciples, if you love one another.”
paragraphs: 34 A new commandment I give you: Love one another. As I have loved you, so you also must love one another. 35 By this everyone will know that you are My disciples, if you love one another.”

passages.context_html:
This command comes during Jesus’ final meal with His disciples, after He washes their feet and Judas leaves. Jesus has just told them that He will soon depart. He now tells them how they are to live with one another when He is no longer present with them in the same way.

They are to love as He has loved them. The measure is the care they have received from Him, shown in His service and brought to its fullest expression in His coming death. Their relationship with Jesus is to become visible in their relationships with each other.

The command concerns love within the company of disciples. It does not cancel love for neighbors or enemies: Leviticus 19:18, 34 commands care for neighbor and foreigner, and Luke 6:27–36 records Jesus’ teaching to love enemies. Here He stresses the witness of a community learning His way of love.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
In John 15:9–13, Jesus connects the Father’s love for Him, His love for the disciples and their love for one another. He then speaks of the greatest love as laying down one’s life for one’s friends. Their care is a response to God’s love, not an attempt to invent it.

Jesus’ later prayer in John 17:20–23 also connects the unity of believers with the world recognizing that the Father sent Him. The command prepares His followers to bear that witness together.

passages.title: John 13:35
passages.section_title: How will people recognize Jesus’ disciples?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 35 By this everyone will know that you are My disciples, if you love one another.”
paragraphs: 35 By this everyone will know that you are My disciples, if you love one another.”

passages.context_html:
This verse gives the result of the command immediately before it. Jesus has told the disciples to love one another as He has loved them. Their love is to identify them publicly as His followers.

The setting matters. Jesus has served them by washing their feet and has told them that His departure is near. They will carry His teaching into a world that cannot see Him at their table. Their treatment of one another is to bear witness to the Teacher they follow.

This is a call to visible care, not merely warm words. 1 John 3:16–18 develops that same connection between Christ’s self-giving love and meeting a brother’s need. The verse does not say that a convincing religious label can take the place of love.

The command is not an invitation to claim superiority over other people; it calls disciples to make His love visible in their life together.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html: The connection between community life and witness appears again in John 17:20–23. Jesus prays for those who will believe through the apostles’ message and asks that their unity help the world recognize the Father’s sending of the Son. Love among disciples serves a purpose beyond the group itself: it makes something of God’s love visible to others.

passages.title: John 13:36-38
passages.section_title: Why can Peter not follow Jesus yet?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 36 “Lord, where are You going?” Simon Peter asked. Jesus answered, “Where I am going, you cannot follow Me now, but you will follow later.” 37 “Lord,” said Peter, “why can’t I follow You now? I will lay down my life for You.” 38 “Will you lay down your life for Me?” Jesus replied. “Truly, truly, I tell you, before the rooster crows, you will deny Me three times.
paragraphs: 36 “Lord, where are You going?” Simon Peter asked. Jesus answered, “Where I am going, you cannot follow Me now, but you will follow later.” 37 “Lord,” said Peter, “why can’t I follow You now? I will lay down my life for You.” 38 “Will you lay down your life for Me?” Jesus replied. “Truly, truly, I tell you, before the rooster crows, you will deny Me three times.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Peter returns to the question raised by Jesus’ departure: where is He going? Jesus says that Peter cannot follow now but will follow later. Peter responds with a promise to lay down his life for Him.

Jesus answers by telling Peter that he will deny Him three times before the rooster crows. The contrast is sharp. Peter is ready to promise his life, but Jesus knows the failure that is approaching. The passage does not require us to guess every feeling or motive behind Peter’s words.

The promise of following later remains alongside the warning. The denial will be real, but Jesus has not described it as the last word about Peter. John 18:15–27 records the denial, and John 21:15–19 returns to Peter’s calling after the resurrection.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this exchange as a warning about relying on our own promises of loyalty. Peter’s confidence does not equip him to carry out what he promises at this moment. Calvin on verses 36–38 and Wesley on verses 36–38 both connect the warning with Peter’s weakness and his later following of Jesus.
passages.god_plan_html:
Luke 22:31–34 supplies another part of the picture. Jesus tells Peter that He has prayed for him and instructs him to strengthen his brothers after he turns back. Failure will call for repentance, and Jesus prepares for Peter’s renewed service.

In John 21:15–19, the risen Jesus entrusts His sheep to Peter, speaks of the death by which Peter will glorify God and calls him to follow. That later scene gives weight to the promise here: Peter’s failure does not end the calling Jesus will renew.

passages.title: John 14:1-7
passages.section_title: How can the disciples trust Jesus when He is leaving?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 “Do not let your hearts be troubled. You believe in God; believe in Me as well. 2 In My Father’s house are many rooms. If it were not so, would I have told you that I am going there to prepare a place for you? 3 And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come back and welcome you into My presence, so that you also may be where I am. 4 You know the way to the place where I am going.” 5 “Lord,” said Thomas, “we do not know where You are going, so how can we know the way?” 6 Jesus answered, “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me. 7 If you had known Me, you would know My Father as well. From now on you do know Him and have seen Him.”
paragraphs: 1 “Do not let your hearts be troubled. You believe in God; believe in Me as well. 2 In My Father’s house are many rooms. If it were not so, would I have told you that I am going there to prepare a place for you? 3 And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come back and welcome you into My presence, so that you also may be where I am. 4 You know the way to the place where I am going.”

5 “Lord,” said Thomas, “we do not know where You are going, so how can we know the way?” 6 Jesus answered, “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me. 7 If you had known Me, you would know My Father as well. From now on you do know Him and have seen Him.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus has just spoken about His departure and Peter’s coming denial. He now calls the disciples to trust Him rather than be overcome by the trouble ahead. He does not promise that the coming hours will be painless. He gives them a reason to keep trusting through them.

His departure will not mean that He has abandoned them. He speaks of preparing a place in His Father’s house and returning to welcome them into His presence. The point of the promise is being with Him. The rooms are not described as rewards for different levels of wealth or achievement.

The Greek word translated rooms is μονή, monē (mo-NAY). Thayer’s lexicon gives the sense of a dwelling or abode and identifies its other use in John 14:23, where the Father and Son make their home with the believer. The word itself does not describe the size or luxury of a building.

Thomas asks how they can know the way when they do not know where Jesus is going. Jesus answers by directing Thomas to Himself: access to the Father is through Him. Knowing Him means coming to know the Father He reveals. This is an invitation to trust a Person, not a set of directions that could be followed apart from Him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the passage as assurance that Jesus brings His followers into life with the Father and that He Himself is the way to that life. Wesley on verses 1–7 emphasizes trust and the sufficiency of Christ. The Catholic Church’s Catechism, paragraphs 1025–1027, describes heaven as life with Christ and teaches that His death and resurrection open it to His people.

Readings differ over how the promised return fits with the other passages about His coming. Calvin on verses 2–3 places the gathering of His people at the final resurrection and judgment.

A different reading is stated in Dallas Theological Seminary’s doctrinal statement, Articles XVIII–XX. It cites John 14:1–3 for Christ’s gathering His people to Himself in heaven and places that gathering before the tribulation and His later return to earth. This is that institution’s stated teaching, not the position of every Protestant or Baptist. The disagreement concerns the sequence of events; both readings understand Jesus to promise that His people will be with Him.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus’ promise belongs to the larger hope of His people living with Him. In John 17:24, He asks that those the Father has given Him may be with Him and see His glory. 1 Thessalonians 4:13–18 likewise comforts believers facing death with the promise that they will always be with the Lord.

The way to the Father runs through what Jesus is about to accomplish. Hebrews 10:19–23 describes a new and living way opened through His body and calls believers to draw near with confidence. His departure through death is part of bringing people near to God, not a retreat from that purpose.

passages.title: John 14:8-11
passages.section_title: What does seeing Jesus show us about the Father?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 Philip said to Him, “Lord, show us the Father, and that will be enough for us.” 9 Jesus replied, “Philip, I have been with you all this time, and still you do not know Me? Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father. How can you say, ‘Show us the Father’? 10 Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in Me? The words I say to you, I do not speak on My own. Instead, it is the Father dwelling in Me, performing His works. 11 Believe Me that I am in the Father and the Father is in Me—or at least believe on account of the works themselves.
paragraphs: 8 Philip said to Him, “Lord, show us the Father, and that will be enough for us.” 9 Jesus replied, “Philip, I have been with you all this time, and still you do not know Me? Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father. How can you say, ‘Show us the Father’?

10 Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in Me? The words I say to you, I do not speak on My own. Instead, it is the Father dwelling in Me, performing His works. 11 Believe Me that I am in the Father and the Father is in Me—or at least believe on account of the works themselves.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Philip asks Jesus to show them the Father. The request follows Jesus’ statement that knowing Him means knowing the Father. Jesus answers by pointing Philip back to the years they have spent together: His presence has already been making the Father known.

He explains this through His relationship with the Father. The Father is in Him, and He is in the Father. His words and works are not a separate mission carried out on His own authority. The Father dwelling in Him is at work.

The conversation still distinguishes Jesus from the Father: Jesus speaks about the Father who dwells in Him. At the same time, it does not reduce Him to an unrelated messenger. His words and works reveal the Father in a way that calls for trust in Him. He urges them to believe what He says, or at least to consider the works that bear witness to it.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as Jesus making the Father known through His own person, words and works. Wesley on verses 10–11 emphasizes His unity with the Father in being and action. Calvin on verse 10 concentrates on how the Father is revealed in Him, while also affirming that the passage supports Christ’s deity. Their emphases differ without making the Father and Son the same person.
passages.god_plan_html:
This is part of the New Testament’s larger account of God making Himself known through His Son. Hebrews 1:1–3 moves from God speaking through the prophets to speaking through the Son, who perfectly represents His nature.

The revelation also belongs to the work of bringing people back to God. Colossians 1:15–20 describes the Son as the image of the invisible God and connects His fullness with reconciliation through the blood of His cross. The One who makes the Father known is the One through whom peace is made.

passages.title: John 14:12-14
passages.section_title: How will Jesus continue His work through His followers?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 Truly, truly, I tell you, whoever believes in Me will also do the works that I am doing. He will do even greater things than these, because I am going to the Father. 13 And I will do whatever you ask in My name, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son. 14 If you ask Me for anything in My name, I will do it.
paragraphs: 12 Truly, truly, I tell you, whoever believes in Me will also do the works that I am doing. He will do even greater things than these, because I am going to the Father.
13 And I will do whatever you ask in My name, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son. 14 If you ask Me for anything in My name, I will do it.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus has appealed to His works as evidence of the Father’s presence in Him. He now tells the disciples that believing in Him will lead to their continuing His work, even to greater things, because He is going to the Father. His departure will extend His work through His followers rather than bring it to an end.

The book of Acts shows what follows. The risen Jesus pours out the Holy Spirit, and the apostles bear witness to Him. Acts 2:32–41 records Peter’s proclamation of the risen Lord and the addition of about three thousand people. The work depends on Jesus’ exaltation and gift of the Spirit.

Jesus then joins their work with asking in His name. He promises that He will act, and He states the purpose: the Father’s glory in the Son. The promise belongs within that relationship and mission. It is not a transfer of control from Jesus to whoever makes a request.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the greater works as depending on the risen Christ’s power, not on disciples becoming greater than their Lord. Calvin on verse 12 emphasizes the spread of faith after Jesus’ ascension. Wesley on verse 12 mentions apostolic miracles and regards the conversion of a sinner as greater still. Their explanations connect the promise with what follows Jesus’ return to the Father.

Christians commonly understand asking in Jesus’ name as approaching God through Him, rather than treating His name as a formula that guarantees any desired result. The Reformed Westminster Larger Catechism, questions 180–181, describes confidence in Christ and His mediation, explicitly distinguishing this from merely mentioning His name. The Catholic Church’s Catechism, paragraphs 2614–2615, likewise connects prayer in His name with faith, love, keeping His word and communion with the Father through Him.
passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 2:32–41 connects Jesus’ exaltation, the pouring out of the Spirit and the growth of the believing community. It shows how His going to the Father advances the work described here.

The prayer promise serves the same purpose. 1 John 5:14–15 describes confidence in asking according to God’s will. Jesus’ followers participate in His work by depending on Him and seeking what serves the Father’s purposes.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Prayer and Faith understands asking in Jesus’ name as asking in keeping with His character, authority and purposes. Adding His name to the end of a request does not turn it into a promise that our preferred outcome must happen. The study draws attention to the purpose stated here: the Father being glorified in the Son.

passages.title: John 14:13
passages.section_title: What does it mean to ask in Jesus’ name?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 And I will do whatever you ask in My name, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son.
paragraphs: 13 And I will do whatever you ask in My name, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son.

passages.context_html:
This promise follows Jesus’ statement that His followers will continue His works because He is going to the Father. Read in that setting, asking in His name belongs to their dependence on Him as they carry out His work.

Jesus identifies both the One who acts and the purpose of His action. He will do what is asked in His name so that the Father may be glorified in the Son. The final purpose is not simply the satisfaction of the person asking.

The wider teaching on prayer helps keep the promise in view. 1 John 5:14–15 connects confidence in prayer with asking according to God’s will. Jesus’ name is bound to who He is and what He is doing.

The Reformed Westminster Larger Catechism, questions 180–181, describes confidence in Christ and His mediation, explicitly distinguishing this from merely mentioning His name. The Catholic Church’s Catechism, paragraphs 2614–2615, likewise connects prayer in His name with faith, love, keeping His word and communion with the Father through Him.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Prayer and Faith understands asking in Jesus’ name as asking in keeping with His character, authority and purposes. Adding His name to the end of a request does not turn it into a promise that our preferred outcome must happen. The study draws attention to the purpose stated here: the Father being glorified in the Son.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html: The purpose of prayer here reaches into the relationship between the Father and Son: the Son’s action brings glory to the Father. Philippians 2:9–11 likewise describes the confession of Jesus as Lord bringing glory to God the Father. Praying through Jesus belongs to a life directed toward that glory.

passages.title: John 14:13-14
passages.section_title: Why is the promise tied to Jesus’ name?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 And I will do whatever you ask in My name, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son. 14 If you ask Me for anything in My name, I will do it.
paragraphs: 13 And I will do whatever you ask in My name, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son. 14 If you ask Me for anything in My name, I will do it.

passages.context_html:
Jesus speaks these words while preparing the disciples for His departure. He has just promised that His work will continue through those who believe in Him. Asking in His name is part of that continuing dependence on Him.

The repetition gives the disciples strong assurance that He will act. It also repeats the connection with His name. Verse 13 states the purpose that governs the promise: the Father’s glory in the Son. The two verses should be read together, rather than separating anything from the relationship and purpose Jesus names.

John 15:7 later joins asking with remaining in Jesus and His words remaining in the disciples. 1 John 5:14–15 connects confidence in prayer with God’s will. Those passages help explain how the promise fits the life He is calling them to live.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand asking in Jesus’ name as approaching God through Him, rather than treating His name as a formula that guarantees any desired result. The Reformed Westminster Larger Catechism, questions 180–181, describes confidence in Christ and His mediation, explicitly distinguishing this from merely mentioning His name. The Catholic Church’s Catechism, paragraphs 2614–2615, likewise connects prayer in His name with faith, love, keeping His word and communion with the Father through Him.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Prayer and Faith understands asking in Jesus’ name as asking in keeping with His character, authority and purposes. Adding His name to the end of a request does not turn it into a promise that our preferred outcome must happen. The study draws attention to the purpose stated here: the Father being glorified in the Son.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html: Jesus’ departure will not cut His followers off from His work. In Acts 2:32–41, the exalted Jesus pours out the Spirit and people come to faith through the apostles’ witness. The promise of His action belongs to that continuing mission, directed toward the Father’s glory.

passages.title: John 14:15-24
passages.section_title: How will Jesus remain with the people who love Him?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 If you love Me, you will keep My commandments. 16 And I will ask the Father, and He will give you another Advocate to be with you forever— 17 the Spirit of truth. The world cannot receive Him, because it neither sees Him nor knows Him. But you do know Him, for He abides with you and will be in you. 18 I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you. 19 In a little while the world will see Me no more, but you will see Me. Because I live, you also will live. 20 On that day you will know that I am in My Father, and you are in Me, and I am in you. 21 Whoever has My commandments and keeps them is the one who loves Me. The one who loves Me will be loved by My Father, and I will love him and reveal Myself to him.” 22 Judas (not Iscariot) asked Him, “Lord, why are You going to reveal Yourself to us and not to the world?” 23 Jesus replied, “If anyone loves Me, he will keep My word. My Father will love him, and We will come to him and make Our home with him. 24 Whoever does not love Me does not keep My words. The word that you hear is not My own, but it is from the Father who sent Me.

The one who loves Me will be loved by My Father, and I will love him and reveal Myself to him.”

My Father will love him, and We will come to him and make Our home with him. 24 Whoever does not love Me does not keep My words. The word that you hear is not My own, but it is from the Father who sent Me.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus connects love for Him with keeping His commandments. He then promises the disciples another Advocate, the Spirit of truth, who will remain with them forever. His approaching departure will not leave them without help.

The word Advocate is παράκλητος, paraklētos (pah-rah-KLAY-toss). Thayer’s lexicon describes someone called to another’s aid and explains its use here as a helper who strengthens the disciples and leads them into a deeper understanding of the truth. The role includes more than making them feel better.

Jesus promises not to leave them as orphans. Their life will be bound to His life, and they will come to know His presence with them. Judas, explicitly distinguished from Iscariot, asks why Jesus will reveal Himself to them rather than to the world. Jesus answers by returning to love, obedience and the Father and Son making their home with the believer.

The scene holds together the Father who gives, the Son who asks and the Spirit who comes. It also holds together the promise of God’s presence and a practical response to Jesus’ words. The disciples are being prepared for a life of receiving His help and following His teaching.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the promised Spirit as God’s continuing presence and help for Jesus’ followers, with love for Jesus expressed in obedience. Wesley on verses 15–20 connects the promise with the disciples’ life after the resurrection and, especially, Pentecost. Calvin on verses 16–20 emphasizes Christ’s presence by the Spirit and the continuing life His people receive from Him. These readings see the promise reaching beyond the hours of the meal.

Obedience is closely joined to love here; it is not presented as an isolated achievement. Calvin’s note on verse 21 also warns against concluding that people first earn God’s love, appealing to God’s prior love in Romans 5:10 and 1 John 4:10.
passages.god_plan_html:
The promise of the Spirit continues a biblical theme of God changing His people from within. Ezekiel 36:25–27 speaks of cleansing, a new heart and God’s Spirit enabling obedience. This is a supported connection with the promise here, not a claim that every detail of Ezekiel’s setting disappears.

Romans 8:9–17 develops life by the indwelling Spirit as belonging to Christ and living as God’s children. Jesus’ promise not to leave His disciples as orphans fits that larger purpose: His people receive His presence and learn to live as children of the Father.

passages.title: John 14:25-31
passages.section_title: What peace does Jesus give as the cross approaches?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 25 All this I have spoken to you while I am still with you. 26 But the Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in My name, will teach you all things and will remind you of everything I have told you. 27 Peace I leave with you; My peace I give to you. I do not give to you as the world gives. Do not let your hearts be troubled; do not be afraid. 28 You heard Me say, ‘I am going away, and I am coming back to you.’ If you loved Me, you would rejoice that I am going to the Father, because the Father is greater than I. 29 And now I have told you before it happens, so that when it does happen, you will believe. 30 I will not speak with you much longer, for the prince of this world is coming, and he has no claim on Me. 31 But I do exactly what the Father has commanded Me, so that the world may know that I love the Father. Get up! Let us go on from here.
paragraphs: 25 All this I have spoken to you while I am still with you. 26 But the Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in My name, will teach you all things and will remind you of everything I have told you. 27 Peace I leave with you; My peace I give to you. I do not give to you as the world gives. Do not let your hearts be troubled; do not be afraid.

28 You heard Me say, ‘I am going away, and I am coming back to you.’ If you loved Me, you would rejoice that I am going to the Father, because the Father is greater than I. 29 And now I have told you before it happens, so that when it does happen, you will believe. 30 I will not speak with you much longer, for the prince of this world is coming, and he has no claim on Me. 31 But I do exactly what the Father has commanded Me, so that the world may know that I love the Father. Get up! Let us go on from here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus promises that the Holy Spirit will teach the disciples and bring His words to their remembrance. The immediate hearers are the people who have been with Him and heard His teaching. Their understanding and witness will not depend on unaided memory.

He gives them His peace as the danger approaches. The promise does not remove the coming betrayal, arrest or cross. It gives them a reason to trust Him through what is coming, and He repeats His call not to be troubled or afraid.

He says that they would rejoice in His going to the Father if they understood His departure rightly. His statement that the Father is greater than He is belongs within this account of His mission and return. It must be read alongside His words in John 14:8–11, where His words and works reveal the Father.

The prince of this world is approaching, but Jesus says that the enemy has no claim on Him. What follows will show His love for the Father and His obedience to the Father’s command. John presents Him going toward the cross willingly, not surrendering His mission to the enemy.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the Spirit’s teaching and Jesus’ peace as gifts that sustain His followers through His departure. Wesley on verses 26–31 emphasizes the Spirit’s teaching, peace with God and Christ’s willing obedience. Calvin on verses 27–31 likewise connects peace with His continuing presence and understands His death within the Father’s purpose.

The statement that the Father is greater has different explanations within readings that affirm Jesus’ deity. Wesley’s note on verse 28 refers it to Jesus’ humanity. Calvin’s note emphasizes His humbled condition and return to the Father’s glory. The Catholic Church’s Catechism, paragraphs 464–469, provides the wider doctrinal setting: Jesus remains truly God while becoming truly human. These explanations do not treat Him as a lesser created god.
passages.god_plan_html:
The peace Jesus gives belongs to the reconciliation He accomplishes. Ephesians 2:13–18 describes His cross bringing near those who were far away, making peace between divided peoples and giving access to the Father through one Spirit.

The Spirit’s presence also points ahead. Ephesians 1:13–14 describes the promised Holy Spirit as the pledge of the inheritance God will complete. The disciples face real trouble, but Jesus’ departure serves a purpose that the approaching enemy will not overthrow.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: John 15:1-11
passages.section_title: What does it mean to remain in the true vine?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 “I am the true vine, and My Father is the keeper of the vineyard. 2 He cuts off every branch in Me that bears no fruit, and every branch that does bear fruit, He prunes to make it even more fruitful. 3 You are already clean because of the word I have spoken to you. 4 Remain in Me, and I will remain in you. Just as no branch can bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, neither can you bear fruit unless you remain in Me. 5 I am the vine and you are the branches. The one who remains in Me, and I in him, will bear much fruit. For apart from Me you can do nothing. 6 If anyone does not remain in Me, he is like a branch that is thrown away and withers. Such branches are gathered up, thrown into the fire, and burned. 7 If you remain in Me and My words remain in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you. 8 This is to My Father’s glory, that you bear much fruit, proving yourselves to be My disciples. 9 As the Father has loved Me, so have I loved you. Remain in My love. 10 If you keep My commandments, you will remain in My love, just as I have kept My Father’s commandments and remain in His love. 11 I have told you these things so that My joy may be in you and your joy may be complete.
