4 Remain in Me, and I will remain in you. Just as no branch can bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, neither can you bear fruit unless you remain in Me. 5 I am the vine and you are the branches. The one who remains in Me, and I in him, will bear much fruit. For apart from Me you can do nothing. 6 If anyone does not remain in Me, he is like a branch that is thrown away and withers. Such branches are gathered up, thrown into the fire, and burned.

7 If you remain in Me and My words remain in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you. 8 This is to My Father’s glory, that you bear much fruit, proving yourselves to be My disciples. 9 As the Father has loved Me, so have I loved you. Remain in My love. 10 If you keep My commandments, you will remain in My love, just as I have kept My Father’s commandments and remain in His love. 11 I have told you these things so that My joy may be in you and your joy may be complete.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus continues preparing the disciples for His departure with the picture of a vine and its branches. He is the true vine, the Father tends the vineyard, and the disciples are the branches. The picture centers on their dependence on Him for a fruitful life.

The Father removes fruitless branches and prunes fruitful ones for greater fruitfulness. Jesus also tells the disciples that they are already clean because of His word. The word translated prunes is καθαίρω, kathairō (kah-THY-roh). Thayer’s lexicon explains its use for cleansing a vine by pruning. The picture brings together the Father’s care, Jesus’ word and the growth He seeks.

The command to remain is μένω, menō (MEH-noh): to remain or abide. Thayer’s entry connects its use here with continuing fellowship with Christ. Jesus fills out that relationship in the passage: His words remain in the disciples, they keep His commandments and they remain in His love.

The warning about a branch that withers and is burned is serious. It stands beside the promise of fruitfulness and the assurance that Jesus wants His joy to be in them. The chapter calls for a continuing life with Him, not a moment of enthusiasm followed by independence.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians agree that fruitful life depends on Christ. They differ over whom the fruitless branches represent and what their removal and burning mean.

In a Reformed reading, Calvin on verses 2 and 6 understands the removed branches as people whose outward association never had a living root in Christ. The Westminster Confession, chapter 17, and the 1689 Baptist Confession, chapter 17, teach that those truly saved will be kept by God and finally persevere, while acknowledging that they may fall into serious sin for a time. These confessions provide the wider setting for that reading; they do not speak for every Baptist.

In Wesley’s notes on verses 4–6 and 9, the branches are people united to Christ by living faith who must continue in that faith. He reads the warning as a real possibility of departing from that life. The Methodist Articles of Religion, Article XII, teach that people may depart from grace after receiving the Spirit and may, by God’s grace, repent and return.

The Catholic Church likewise teaches a real possibility of losing the state of grace through mortal sin. Its Catechism, paragraphs 1855–1861, distinguishes this from every lesser fault: mortal sin involves grave matter, full knowledge and deliberate consent, and calls for repentance and God’s forgiveness. This is the doctrinal setting of the warning, not a claim that every failure means a person is cut off.

A further reading appears in Thomas Constable’s notes on verses 2–6. He understands the branches as believers and the warning as loss of usefulness or service, without loss of eternal salvation. He favors lifting up in verse 2. The Greek verb can have both lifting and removing senses, but Thayer’s entry assigns John 15:2 to cutting away. Vocabulary alone does not settle the whole passage, and the BSB’s wording is retained here. Constable’s explanation is an individual reading, not the teaching of all churches that affirm eternal security.
passages.god_plan_html:
The vineyard picture has a long biblical background. Isaiah 5:1–7 describes God’s vineyard, identified as Israel, and His search for justice and righteousness. Jesus’ description of Himself as the true vine provides a meaningful parallel: the fruitful life He calls for depends on remaining in Him. This connection does not by itself settle every question about Israel and the church.

Galatians 5:22–25 describes the Spirit’s fruit in qualities such as love, patience and self-control. Colossians 1:9–14 joins knowing God’s will, good works, endurance and thanksgiving with His rescue into the Son’s kingdom. These passages help us see the kind of life God is growing, beyond a simple measure of visible success.
passages.current_position_html: On abiding and prayer, our study Prayer and Faith describes remaining in Christ as living in keeping with His teaching and example. Dependence on Him shapes how we live and what we desire; it is more than adding religious words to plans we have already decided to pursue. In its discussion of John 15:7, the study understands asking as being shaped by His word and will. This position concerns that connection; it does not settle the disputed identity of the removed branches.

passages.title: John 15:4-5
passages.section_title: Why must the branches remain in the vine?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 4 Remain in Me, and I will remain in you. Just as no branch can bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, neither can you bear fruit unless you remain in Me. 5 I am the vine and you are the branches. The one who remains in Me, and I in him, will bear much fruit. For apart from Me you can do nothing.
paragraphs: 4 Remain in Me, and I will remain in you. Just as no branch can bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, neither can you bear fruit unless you remain in Me. 5 I am the vine and you are the branches. The one who remains in Me, and I in him, will bear much fruit. For apart from Me you can do nothing.

passages.context_html:
Jesus has identified Himself as the true vine and the Father as the keeper of the vineyard. He now identifies the disciples as the branches. A branch draws its life from the vine; it cannot produce grapes on its own.

The command to remain in Him calls for continuing dependence. The Greek word is μένω, menō (MEH-noh), meaning to remain or abide. Thayer’s lexicon describes its use here in terms of continuing fellowship. The following verses explain that life through Jesus’ words, commandments and love.

The promise of much fruit is tied to His presence and supply. Jesus is speaking about the life and work that come from belonging to Him. This is more than a call to try harder: the branch needs what the vine gives.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand these verses as teaching ongoing dependence on Christ for a fruitful life. The Catholic Church’s Catechism, paragraph 2011, describes Christ’s love and grace as the source of good actions. The Methodist Articles of Religion, Article VIII, likewise teach that people cannot do what is pleasing to God without His grace at work in them. The shared point is that spiritual fruit does not arise from self-sufficiency.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Prayer and Faith describes remaining in Christ as living in keeping with His teaching and example. Dependence on Him shapes how we live and what we desire; it is more than adding religious words to plans we have already decided to pursue.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html: Colossians 1:9–14 describes God’s people growing in the knowledge of His will, bearing fruit in good works and being strengthened with His power. It places that life within His rescue into the kingdom of His Son. Remaining in Christ serves that larger purpose of a people learning to live in His strength.

passages.title: John 15:5
passages.section_title: Where does a fruitful life come from?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 I am the vine and you are the branches. The one who remains in Me, and I in him, will bear much fruit. For apart from Me you can do nothing.
paragraphs: 5 I am the vine and you are the branches. The one who remains in Me, and I in him, will bear much fruit. For apart from Me you can do nothing.

passages.context_html:
The vine-and-branches picture makes the relationship clear. Jesus is the source of life, and His disciples depend on Him. The promise of much fruit is joined to remaining in Him and His remaining in them.

The surrounding passage explains what this dependence involves: His words remain in them, they keep His commandments and they remain in His love. The image describes a continuing relationship that shapes their life and work.

The final statement about doing nothing apart from Him concerns the fruit of that life. It is not a denial that people can perform everyday tasks; it presses the disciples to recognize the source of the life He is calling them to live.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a call to rely on Christ for spiritual life and fruitfulness. Calvin on verse 5 emphasizes that the power for such fruit comes from Him. The Catholic Church’s Catechism, paragraph 2011, also teaches that Christ’s love and grace are the source of good actions. The shared dependence should not be obscured by treating Christians as though they generally believe they can produce this life alone.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Prayer and Faith describes remaining in Christ as living in keeping with His teaching and example. Dependence on Him shapes how we live and what we desire; it is more than adding religious words to plans we have already decided to pursue.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html: Galatians 5:22–25 describes love, joy, patience and the other fruit of the Spirit, and calls those who live by the Spirit to walk in step with Him. This gives practical shape to the fruitful life Jesus describes: God forms His people’s character as they live in dependence on Him.

passages.title: John 15:7
passages.section_title: How does remaining in Jesus shape what we ask?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 If you remain in Me and My words remain in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you.
paragraphs: 7 If you remain in Me and My words remain in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you.

passages.context_html:
The promise comes within the vine-and-branches teaching. Jesus has called the disciples to remain in Him because a branch cannot produce fruit apart from the vine. He now connects asking with that relationship.

There are two linked conditions: the disciples remain in Him, and His words remain in them. Their asking grows within a life being shaped by what He has taught. The promise is followed by the Father’s glory in their fruitfulness.

This continues the connection between prayer and His mission in John 14:12–14. Jesus’ action and the Father’s glory belong together. Remaining in Him concerns the whole direction of their life, including their requests.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the promise in connection with its stated conditions. Calvin on verse 7 explains that Jesus’ words shape the desires of those who remain in Him, rather than approving every passing wish. Wesley on verse 7 describes prayer as both fruit of faith and a means of further fruitfulness. These explanations place asking within an ongoing life of faith.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Prayer and Faith understands this promise through its stated conditions: remaining in Christ and His words remaining in us. As His teaching shapes our life, it also shapes our desires and our asking. The study connects this with asking according to God’s will in 1 John 5:14–15, rather than treating the verse as a guarantee for plans formed independently of Him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html: Colossians 1:9–12 provides a related pattern: Paul asks for believers to know God’s will so that they may live worthily, bear fruit, grow in knowledge and give thanks. Prayer serves the growth of people whose life reflects the God they belong to.

passages.title: John 15:12-17
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus call His disciples friends?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 This is My commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you. 13 Greater love has no one than this, that he lay down his life for his friends. 14 You are My friends if you do what I command you. 15 No longer do I call you servants, for a servant does not understand what his master is doing. But I have called you friends, because everything I have learned from My Father I have made known to you. 16 You did not choose Me, but I chose you. And I appointed you to go and bear fruit—fruit that will remain—so that whatever you ask the Father in My name, He will give you. 17 This is My command to you: Love one another.
paragraphs: 12 This is My commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you. 13 Greater love has no one than this, that he lay down his life for his friends. 14 You are My friends if you do what I command you.

15 No longer do I call you servants, for a servant does not understand what his master is doing. But I have called you friends, because everything I have learned from My Father I have made known to you. 16 You did not choose Me, but I chose you. And I appointed you to go and bear fruit—fruit that will remain—so that whatever you ask the Father in My name, He will give you. 17 This is My command to you: Love one another.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus returns to the command to love one another. The measure is His own love, and He speaks of laying down one’s life for one’s friends as the greatest expression of it. The approaching cross gives His words their immediate weight.

He calls the disciples friends because He has made known to them what He has heard from the Father. They are being brought into an understanding of His work. Friendship does not make His teaching optional: He connects it with doing what He commands.

Jesus also reminds them that He chose and appointed them to go and bear lasting fruit. Their calling begins with His initiative and leads into service, dependence and prayer in His name. The paragraph ends where it began, with the command to love one another.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the passage as joining Christ’s self-giving love, His disclosure of the Father’s purposes and the disciples’ calling to serve. Calvin on verses 12–15 emphasizes Jesus’ example and the sharing of His teaching with friends. Wesley on verses 12–16 likewise connects friendship with obedience and the apostles’ mission.

The choosing in verse 16 is sometimes drawn into wider discussions of salvation. Both Calvin and Wesley identify the immediate setting as Jesus’ appointment of the apostles. Calvin also draws a wider lesson about God’s gracious initiative. Recognizing the particular calling in view helps keep a larger doctrinal discussion from replacing the passage’s direct call to fruitful service and love.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus’ coming sacrifice is both the source and pattern of His people’s love. Ephesians 5:1–2 calls believers to walk in love because Christ loved them and gave Himself for them. Romans 5:8–10 adds that He died for people who were still sinners and enemies, showing the depth of the love that brings them near.

Friendship with God also has a place in the earlier biblical story: James 2:21–23 recalls Abraham’s faith expressed in action and calls him God’s friend. Here Jesus brings His disciples into the knowledge of the Father’s work and sends them to bear lasting fruit. This is a connection in the theme of relationship with God, not a claim that Abraham’s story predicts every detail of this meal.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: John 15:18-27
passages.section_title: How will the disciples bear witness when they face hatred?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 If the world hates you, understand that it hated Me first. 19 If you were of the world, it would love you as its own. Instead, the world hates you, because you are not of the world, but I have chosen you out of the world. 20 Remember the word that I spoke to you: ‘No servant is greater than his master.’ If they persecuted Me, they will persecute you as well; if they kept My word, they will keep yours as well. 21 But they will treat you like this because of My name, since they do not know the One who sent Me. 22 If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not be guilty of sin. Now, however, they have no excuse for their sin. 23 Whoever hates Me hates My Father as well. 24 If I had not done among them the works that no one else did, they would not be guilty of sin; but now they have seen and hated both Me and My Father. 25 But this is to fulfill what is written in their Law: ‘They hated Me without reason.’ 26 When the Advocate comes, whom I will send to you from the Father—the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father—He will testify about Me. 27 And you also must testify, because you have been with Me from the beginning.
paragraphs: 18 If the world hates you, understand that it hated Me first. 19 If you were of the world, it would love you as its own. Instead, the world hates you, because you are not of the world, but I have chosen you out of the world. 20 Remember the word that I spoke to you: ‘No servant is greater than his master.’ If they persecuted Me, they will persecute you as well; if they kept My word, they will keep yours as well. 21 But they will treat you like this because of My name, since they do not know the One who sent Me.

22 If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not be guilty of sin. Now, however, they have no excuse for their sin. 23 Whoever hates Me hates My Father as well. 24 If I had not done among them the works that no one else did, they would not be guilty of sin; but now they have seen and hated both Me and My Father. 25 But this is to fulfill what is written in their Law: ‘They hated Me without reason.’

26 When the Advocate comes, whom I will send to you from the Father—the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father—He will testify about Me. 27 And you also must testify, because you have been with Me from the beginning.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The command to love one another is followed by a warning about the hatred the disciples will face. Their connection with Jesus will bring them into the opposition He has already encountered. A servant cannot assume exemption from the treatment given to his master.

Jesus connects the rejection of His words and works with rejection of the Father who sent Him. His statement about their guilt concerns the responsibility of those who have received this witness and rejected it. It does not mean that no one had sinned before He came.

He describes this hatred as fulfilling Scripture. The words have a parallel in Psalm 69:4, where the speaker suffers hostility without cause. The opposition will not put the disciples’ mission outside God’s purpose.

The answer to that opposition includes witness. The Spirit of truth will testify about Jesus, and the disciples must testify because they have been with Him from the beginning. Their firsthand knowledge of Him matters, and their testimony will be supported by the Spirit He sends from the Father.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read the warning as preparation for opposition to Christ’s witness. Calvin on verses 20–22 and Wesley on verses 21–22 connect the rejection with ignorance of God and responsibility for rejecting Jesus’ revelation. The warning is not permission to treat every personal dispute as persecution. 1 Peter 4:14–16 distinguishes suffering for Christ from suffering for wrongdoing.

Traditions differ over the Spirit’s eternal relationship to the Father and Son. The Orthodox Church in America’s teaching on the Holy Spirit identifies the Father as the Spirit’s eternal source and rejects adding “and the Son” to that statement in the creed. Its account of spiritual life also affirms that the Spirit is sent into the world through Christ.

The Catholic Church’s Catechism, paragraphs 243–248, teaches that the Spirit is eternally from the Father and Son as one source, while still recognizing the Father as the first origin. The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 2.3, and Methodist Articles of Religion, Article IV, also confess the Spirit’s eternal relation to the Father and Son.

This disagreement concerns the Spirit’s eternal relationship within God, which is distinct from His being sent to the disciples in history. These traditions all affirm that the Spirit is divine and bears witness to Jesus. Neither reading treats Him as a creature or denies the sending described in this passage.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus’ appeal to Scripture places the rejection He faces within the biblical story of unjust hostility. The promised Spirit means that rejection will not end the witness to Him.

After the resurrection, Acts 1:6–8 connects the coming of the Spirit with the disciples becoming Jesus’ witnesses from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth. The mission grows beyond the room even as it encounters resistance. The Spirit and the witnesses serve the same purpose: making Jesus known.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: John 16:1-6
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus warn the disciples about persecution?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 “I have told you these things so that you will not fall away. 2 They will put you out of the synagogues. In fact, a time is coming when anyone who kills you will think he is offering a service to God. 3 They will do these things because they have not known the Father or Me. 4 But I have told you these things so that when their hour comes, you will remember that I told you about them. I did not tell you these things from the beginning, because I was with you. 5 Now, however, I am going to Him who sent Me; yet none of you asks Me, ‘Where are You going?’ 6 Instead, your hearts are filled with sorrow because I have told you these things.
paragraphs: 1 “I have told you these things so that you will not fall away. 2 They will put you out of the synagogues. In fact, a time is coming when anyone who kills you will think he is offering a service to God. 3 They will do these things because they have not known the Father or Me. 4 But I have told you these things so that when their hour comes, you will remember that I told you about them. I did not tell you these things from the beginning, because I was with you.
5 Now, however, I am going to Him who sent Me; yet none of you asks Me, ‘Where are You going?’ 6 Instead, your hearts are filled with sorrow because I have told you these things.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus explains why He has warned the disciples about hatred: He wants them to be prepared rather than fall away when it comes. He names rejection from the synagogues and even killing carried out by people who believe they are serving God. Religious confidence is not the same as knowing the Father and Son.

The warning is meant to be remembered when the events occur. Jesus is preparing them for His departure, when they will face these things without His bodily presence beside them. Their grief is real, and He names it directly.

His statement that none of them asks where He is going concerns this moment of sorrow. Peter has already asked that question in John 13:36, and Thomas has spoken about not knowing the way in John 14:5. Here Jesus turns their attention from the pain of His leaving toward what His return to the Father will accomplish.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this warning as preparation for faithful witness under opposition. Calvin on verses 1–5 emphasizes remembering Jesus’ words when trials arrive. Wesley on verses 3–5 connects persecution with not knowing God and notes that Peter had asked about Jesus’ destination earlier. The passage gives the disciples reason to persevere; it does not make religious violence acceptable.
passages.god_plan_html:
The warning belongs to the mission Jesus is giving His followers. Acts 1:8 connects their witness with the power of the Spirit, so opposition is faced with God’s help rather than by their own strength alone.

God’s saving purpose can also reach persecutors. In 1 Timothy 1:12–16, Paul describes his former violence and the mercy Christ showed him as an example of His patience. This does not lessen the evil of persecution; it shows why a warning about enemies need not end in giving up hope for them.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: John 16:7-15
passages.section_title: Why is Jesus’ departure for the disciples’ good?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 But I tell you the truth, it is for your benefit that I am going away. Unless I go away, the Advocate will not come to you; but if I go, I will send Him to you. 8 And when He comes, He will convict the world in regard to sin and righteousness and judgment: 9 in regard to sin, because they do not believe in Me; 10 in regard to righteousness, because I am going to the Father and you will no longer see Me; 11 and in regard to judgment, because the prince of this world has been condemned. 12 I still have much to tell you, but you cannot yet bear to hear it. 13 However, when the Spirit of truth comes, He will guide you into all truth. For He will not speak on His own, but He will speak what He hears, and He will declare to you what is to come. 14 He will glorify Me by taking from what is Mine and disclosing it to you. 15 Everything that belongs to the Father is Mine. That is why I said that the Spirit will take from what is Mine and disclose it to you.
paragraphs: 7 But I tell you the truth, it is for your benefit that I am going away. Unless I go away, the Advocate will not come to you; but if I go, I will send Him to you. 8 And when He comes, He will convict the world in regard to sin and righteousness and judgment: 9 in regard to sin, because they do not believe in Me; 10 in regard to righteousness, because I am going to the Father and you will no longer see Me; 11 and in regard to judgment, because the prince of this world has been condemned.

12 I still have much to tell you, but you cannot yet bear to hear it. 13 However, when the Spirit of truth comes, He will guide you into all truth. For He will not speak on His own, but He will speak what He hears, and He will declare to you what is to come. 14 He will glorify Me by taking from what is Mine and disclosing it to you. 15 Everything that belongs to the Father is Mine. That is why I said that the Spirit will take from what is Mine and disclose it to you.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus tells the grieving disciples that His departure will bring a benefit: He will send the Advocate to them. The promised Spirit will continue the work of making Him known and will expose the world’s error about sin, righteousness and judgment.

The word translated convict is ἐλέγχω, elenchō (eh-LENG-khoh). Thayer’s lexicon explains it as bringing fault or error to light and identifies this use in verse 8. The point is more than creating a bad feeling: the Spirit shows what is wrong and what is true.

Jesus gives a reason for each part of that work. Sin is connected with unbelief in Him; righteousness with His going to the Father; judgment with the condemnation of the prince of this world. These statements direct attention to who Jesus is and what His departure accomplishes.

The Spirit will also guide the disciples into truth they cannot yet bear. His work will glorify Jesus, taking what belongs to Him and making it known. The Father, Son and Spirit work together in this revelation. The disciples are being promised the help they need to understand and bear witness.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the Spirit’s work here as exposing error and making the truth about Jesus known. The details of righteousness and judgment receive different emphases. Wesley on verses 10–11 emphasizes the vindication of Jesus’ righteousness in His return to the Father and the defeat of the world’s ruler. Calvin on verses 10–11 emphasizes the righteousness received through Christ and the order restored by His victory over Satan. These are the named teachers’ explanations.

Christians also differ over how the Spirit’s promised guidance relates to the church’s teaching after the apostles. The Catholic Church’s Catechism, paragraphs 889–892, teaches that the Spirit preserves the church in the apostolic faith through its teaching office. It identifies particular definitive teaching on faith and morals by the pope or bishops united with him as protected from error. This does not mean that every statement by a church leader is infallible.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 1.6 and 1.10, recognizes the Spirit’s help in understanding Scripture and identifies the Spirit speaking in Scripture as the final judge of doctrine. It rejects adding new revelations or human traditions to what God has given there.

The Catholic account also distinguishes growth in understanding from new public revelation: Catechism paragraphs 65–67 teach that Christ’s revelation is complete. The disagreement concerns the authority by which that faith is preserved and explained, rather than whether the Spirit should lead people away from Jesus.
passages.god_plan_html:
The promised benefit becomes visible in Acts 2:32–41: the exalted Jesus pours out the Spirit, the apostles announce His resurrection and hearers are moved to repentance. His departure advances the witness instead of ending it.

The judgment of the world’s ruler also fits the victory accomplished through the cross. Colossians 2:13–15 joins forgiveness and the cancellation of sin’s debt with Christ’s triumph over hostile powers. The Spirit makes known a victory grounded in Jesus’ work.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: John 16:16-24
passages.section_title: How will the disciples’ sorrow turn to joy?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 In a little while you will see Me no more, and then after a little while you will see Me.” 17 Then some of His disciples asked one another, “Why is He telling us, ‘In a little while you will not see Me, and then after a little while you will see Me’ and ‘Because I am going to the Father’ ?” 18 They kept asking, “Why is He saying, ‘a little while’ ? We do not understand what He is saying.” 19 Aware that they wanted to question Him, Jesus said to them, “Are you asking one another why I said, ‘In a little while you will not see Me, and then after a little while you will see Me’? 20 Truly, truly, I tell you, you will weep and wail while the world rejoices. You will grieve, but your grief will turn to joy. 21 A woman has pain in childbirth because her time has come; but when she brings forth her child, she forgets her anguish because of her joy that a child has been born into the world. 22 So also you have sorrow now, but I will see you again and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take away your joy. 23 In that day you will no longer ask Me anything. Truly, truly, I tell you, whatever you ask the Father in My name, He will give you. 24 Until now you have not asked for anything in My name. Ask and you will receive, so that your joy may be complete.
paragraphs: 16 In a little while you will see Me no more, and then after a little while you will see Me.” 17 Then some of His disciples asked one another, “Why is He telling us, ‘In a little while you will not see Me, and then after a little while you will see Me’ and ‘Because I am going to the Father’ ?” 18 They kept asking, “Why is He saying, ‘a little while’ ? We do not understand what He is saying.” 19 Aware that they wanted to question Him, Jesus said to them, “Are you asking one another why I said, ‘In a little while you will not see Me, and then after a little while you will see Me’?

20 Truly, truly, I tell you, you will weep and wail while the world rejoices. You will grieve, but your grief will turn to joy. 21 A woman has pain in childbirth because her time has come; but when she brings forth her child, she forgets her anguish because of her joy that a child has been born into the world. 22 So also you have sorrow now, but I will see you again and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take away your joy.

23 In that day you will no longer ask Me anything. Truly, truly, I tell you, whatever you ask the Father in My name, He will give you. 24 Until now you have not asked for anything in My name. Ask and you will receive, so that your joy may be complete.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The disciples are puzzled by Jesus’ words about a little while without seeing Him and then seeing Him again. They discuss the question among themselves, and Jesus responds to what they want to ask.

He does not deny the grief ahead. They will weep while the world rejoices, but their sorrow will turn to joy. He compares that change with the pain of childbirth giving way to the joy of a child’s birth. The image explains a painful passage into joy; it does not make their sorrow imaginary.

Jesus promises that He will see them again and that their joy will endure. John 20:19–20 later records the disciples rejoicing when they see the risen Lord. The death that will grieve them will not end His life or their relationship with Him.

He then speaks of asking the Father in His name. Their present confusion will give way to a new understanding and confidence before the Father. The promise of receiving is tied to His name and to the complete joy He is describing, within the larger teaching about His departure and return.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley on verses 16–22 connects the little while with Jesus’ death and resurrection. Calvin on verses 16, 20 and 22 places special emphasis on His continuing presence through the Spirit and the joy that follows the Spirit’s coming. These readings share the promise of renewed life with Jesus while emphasizing different parts of its fulfillment.

The prayer promise is commonly read within that relationship. The Catholic Church’s Catechism, paragraphs 2614–2615, connects asking in Jesus’ name with faith, love, His word and the Spirit. The Reformed Westminster Larger Catechism, question 180, likewise describes confidence in Christ rather than merely mentioning His name.
passages.god_plan_html:
The promised joy has a direct narrative fulfillment when the disciples see the risen Jesus in John 20:19–22. He brings peace, shows His wounds and sends them into His continuing mission.

That resurrection also becomes the ground of hope for later believers. 1 Peter 1:3–9 describes new birth into a living hope through Jesus’ resurrection and joy that persists amid trials. God’s purpose reaches beyond ending one evening of grief: He gives His people a hope that suffering cannot finally undo.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Prayer and Faith understands asking in Jesus’ name as asking in keeping with His character, authority and purposes. It reads the promise of complete joy within Jesus’ teaching about His resurrection, the Spirit’s coming and life with Him. The promise directs us toward that life, rather than making His name a formula for obtaining whatever we already wanted.

passages.title: John 16:23-24
passages.section_title: What kind of asking belongs to the joy Jesus promises?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 23 In that day you will no longer ask Me anything. Truly, truly, I tell you, whatever you ask the Father in My name, He will give you. 24 Until now you have not asked for anything in My name. Ask and you will receive, so that your joy may be complete.
paragraphs: 23 In that day you will no longer ask Me anything. Truly, truly, I tell you, whatever you ask the Father in My name, He will give you. 24 Until now you have not asked for anything in My name. Ask and you will receive, so that your joy may be complete.

passages.context_html:
These words follow Jesus’ promise that the disciples’ sorrow will turn to joy when they see Him again. Their questions about His departure belong to an understanding that is still incomplete. He points them toward life after His death and resurrection.

He directs them to ask the Father in His name. The promise continues what He has already taught about prayer in John 14:12–14 and remaining in Him in John 15:7. Asking belongs within their relationship with Him and the work He is giving them.

The complete joy is part of this same conversation about renewed life with Jesus. It should be read beside His promise to see them again, rather than separated into a guarantee that any desired possession or outcome will produce lasting joy.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly connect prayer in Jesus’ name with trust in Him and access to the Father through Him. The Reformed Westminster Larger Catechism, question 180, distinguishes that confidence from bare mention of His name. The Catholic Church’s Catechism, paragraphs 2614–2615, places this prayer within faith, love and life in the Spirit.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Prayer and Faith understands asking in Jesus’ name as asking in keeping with His character, authority and purposes. It reads the promise of complete joy within Jesus’ teaching about His resurrection, the Spirit’s coming and life with Him. The promise directs us toward that life, rather than making His name a formula for obtaining whatever we already wanted.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html: John 20:19–22 connects the disciples’ renewed joy with the risen Jesus, His peace and His sending of them. Ephesians 2:18 describes access to the Father through Christ by one Spirit. The prayer promise belongs to this life of being brought near to God.

passages.title: John 16:25-33
passages.section_title: How can Jesus promise peace when His disciples will scatter?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 25 I have spoken these things to you in figures of speech. An hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you this way, but will tell you plainly about the Father. 26 In that day you will ask in My name. I am not saying that I will ask the Father on your behalf. 27 For the Father Himself loves you, because you have loved Me and have believed that I came from God. 28 I came from the Father and entered the world. In turn, I will leave the world and go to the Father.” 29 His disciples said, “See, now You are speaking plainly and without figures of speech. 30 Now we understand that You know all things and that You have no need for anyone to question You. Because of this, we believe that You came from God.” 31 “Do you finally believe?” Jesus replied. 32 “Look, an hour is coming and has already come when you will be scattered, each to his own home, and you will leave Me all alone. Yet I am not alone, because the Father is with Me. 33 I have told you these things so that in Me you may have peace. In the world you will have tribulation. But take courage; I have overcome the world!”
paragraphs: 25 I have spoken these things to you in figures of speech. An hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you this way, but will tell you plainly about the Father. 26 In that day you will ask in My name. I am not saying that I will ask the Father on your behalf. 27 For the Father Himself loves you, because you have loved Me and have believed that I came from God. 28 I came from the Father and entered the world. In turn, I will leave the world and go to the Father.”

29 His disciples said, “See, now You are speaking plainly and without figures of speech. 30 Now we understand that You know all things and that You have no need for anyone to question You. Because of this, we believe that You came from God.” 31 “Do you finally believe?” Jesus replied. 32 “Look, an hour is coming and has already come when you will be scattered, each to his own home, and you will leave Me all alone. Yet I am not alone, because the Father is with Me. 33 I have told you these things so that in Me you may have peace. In the world you will have tribulation. But take courage; I have overcome the world!”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus promises clearer understanding of the Father and speaks of the Father’s own love for the disciples. Their asking in His name is not an effort to persuade an unwilling Father to care for them. They have believed that Jesus came from God, and He is returning to the Father.

The disciples now profess that they understand and believe. Jesus answers by warning that they will soon scatter and leave Him. Their confidence has not yet been tested by the arrest that is approaching. He nevertheless says that He is not alone, because the Father is with Him.

The final promise holds together peace in Him and trouble in the world. Jesus does not promise the absence of suffering. He gives the reason for courage: He has overcome the world. Their weakness and the coming opposition will not overturn His mission.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley on verse 26 and Calvin on verse 26 both explain that Jesus is emphasizing the Father’s love, rather than denying His continuing intercession. Hebrews 7:23–25 explicitly describes His lasting work on behalf of those who draw near to God through Him.

Christians commonly understand the promise of peace as grounded in Jesus’ victory amid real affliction. Calvin’s note on verse 33 emphasizes courage drawn from that victory. The disciples’ coming failure does not make His words empty, and the promise does not turn every trial into an easy experience.
passages.god_plan_html:
Colossians 2:13–15 describes Christ’s triumph through the cross, joining His victory with forgiveness. The suffering now approaching belongs to the work through which He overcomes, rather than showing that His mission has failed.

His return to the Father also leads into continuing help for His people. Hebrews 7:23–25 describes His permanent priesthood and intercession. The disciples are being prepared to depend on a living Lord whose care continues after His departure.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: John 17:1-5
passages.section_title: What does Jesus ask as His hour arrives?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 When Jesus had spoken these things, He lifted up His eyes to heaven and said, “Father, the hour has come. Glorify Your Son, that Your Son may glorify You. 2 For You granted Him authority over all people, so that He may give eternal life to all those You have given Him. 3 Now this is eternal life, that they may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom You have sent. 4 I have glorified You on earth by accomplishing the work You gave Me to do. 5 And now, Father, glorify Me in Your presence with the glory I had with You before the world existed.
paragraphs: 1 When Jesus had spoken these things, He lifted up His eyes to heaven and said, “Father, the hour has come. Glorify Your Son, that Your Son may glorify You. 2 For You granted Him authority over all people, so that He may give eternal life to all those You have given Him. 3 Now this is eternal life, that they may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom You have sent.
4 I have glorified You on earth by accomplishing the work You gave Me to do. 5 And now, Father, glorify Me in Your presence with the glory I had with You before the world existed.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After speaking to the disciples about His departure, the Spirit, trouble and peace, Jesus lifts His eyes to heaven and prays. He begins with the hour that has arrived. His request for the Son’s glory has a stated purpose: that the Son may glorify the Father.

The authority given to Him is directed toward giving eternal life to those the Father has given Him. He describes that life in terms of knowing the Father and Jesus Christ, whom the Father sent. Eternal life is more than a length of time; it is life in relationship with God through the Son.

Jesus speaks of the work the Father gave Him as accomplished while the cross is immediately ahead. The prayer stands at the completion of that mission, not at an escape from it. He asks to be glorified in the Father’s presence with the glory He had before the world existed.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the prayer as joining the Father’s glory, the Son’s saving mission and the gift of eternal life. Calvin on verses 3–5 and Wesley on verses 3–5 understand knowing God as a life of faith, and the glory before creation as belonging to the eternal Son. Neither reads the reference to the only true God as excluding the Son from divine life.

They explain those given to Jesus differently. Calvin’s note on verse 2 refers to God’s chosen people, whose faith follows His gracious choice. Wesley’s note identifies them as believers and emphasizes Christ’s saving provision for all. These are distinct explanations of the gift, while both direct the reader to life received through Christ.
passages.god_plan_html:
The movement through suffering into glory is developed in Hebrews 2:9–11. Jesus suffers death and is crowned with glory and honor as He brings many children to glory. His request belongs to that saving work.

The Son who makes the Father known is also the One through whom God made the universe. Hebrews 1:1–3 joins His revelation of God with creation, the cleansing of sins and His place at God’s right hand. The prayer gathers His mission into the glory He shares with the Father.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: John 17:6-12
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus ask the Father to keep His disciples?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 I have revealed Your name to those You have given Me out of the world. They were Yours; You gave them to Me, and they have kept Your word. 7 Now they know that everything You have given Me comes from You. 8 For I have given them the words You gave Me, and they have received them. They knew with certainty that I came from You, and they believed that You sent Me. 9 I ask on their behalf. I do not ask on behalf of the world, but on behalf of those You have given Me; for they are Yours. 10 All I have is Yours, and all You have is Mine; and in them I have been glorified. 11 I will no longer be in the world, but they are in the world, and I am coming to You. Holy Father, protect them by Your name, the name You gave Me, so that they may be one as We are one. 12 While I was with them, I protected and preserved them by Your name, the name You gave Me. Not one of them has been lost, except the son of destruction, so that the Scripture would be fulfilled.
paragraphs: 6 I have revealed Your name to those You have given Me out of the world. They were Yours; You gave them to Me, and they have kept Your word. 7 Now they know that everything You have given Me comes from You. 8 For I have given them the words You gave Me, and they have received them. They knew with certainty that I came from You, and they believed that You sent Me.

9 I ask on their behalf. I do not ask on behalf of the world, but on behalf of those You have given Me; for they are Yours. 10 All I have is Yours, and all You have is Mine; and in them I have been glorified. 11 I will no longer be in the world, but they are in the world, and I am coming to You. Holy Father, protect them by Your name, the name You gave Me, so that they may be one as We are one. 12 While I was with them, I protected and preserved them by Your name, the name You gave Me. Not one of them has been lost, except the son of destruction, so that the Scripture would be fulfilled.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus now speaks about the people who have received the Father’s words through Him. They have believed that He came from the Father and have kept the word entrusted to them. He places their life and calling within what the Father has given.

His prayer is directed toward their coming situation. He is returning to the Father, and they will remain in the world. He asks the Holy Father to protect them by His name so that they may be one. The unity He desires is grounded in the relationship between the Father and Son.

He also speaks of His care for them and of the loss of the son of destruction, the betrayer. The reference recalls Judas’s departure and betrayal in John 13:18–30. The prayer names the loss and the fulfillment of Scripture without treating the betrayal as a surprise that overturns Jesus’ work.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the prayer as expressing Jesus’ care for His followers as He departs. The reference to Judas raises a real difference about his place among those given to Jesus.

Calvin on verse 12 understands Judas as outwardly sharing the appointed role of an apostle, without belonging to God’s truly chosen flock. Wesley on verse 12 reads the exception as one of those given to Jesus being lost. The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 17, teaches final perseverance for those truly saved; the Methodist Articles of Religion, Article XII, allow for departing from grace and returning through repentance. These documents supply the broader doctrinal setting, while the individual notes address Judas directly.

The focus on the disciples in verse 9 should not be turned into a command never to pray for anyone else. 1 Timothy 2:1–4 explicitly calls for prayer for all people. Here Jesus is asking for what His followers need in the calling He has given them.
passages.god_plan_html:
The disciples’ preservation serves the mission they will carry forward. In John 18:8–9, Jesus asks that His companions be allowed to go, and John connects their release with His word that He has not lost those given to Him. The narrative shows His care as the arrest approaches.

His continuing care is also described in Hebrews 7:23–25, where His permanent priesthood and intercession belong to His saving work. The disciples will lose His visible presence at their table, but they are not being left without His concern.
passages.current_position_html: Our study What Does Prayer Look Like? treats Jesus’ request that His followers be kept in the Father’s name and united as a pattern for praying for others. It directs our attention to their life with God and faithful formation. Here the priority is that they remain His people and carry out their calling together, rather than making easier circumstances the main goal.

passages.title: John 17:13-19
passages.section_title: What does Jesus ask for people sent into a hostile world?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 But now I am coming to You; and I am saying these things while I am in the world, so that they may have My joy fulfilled within them. 14 I have given them Your word and the world has hated them. For they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world. 15 I am not asking that You take them out of the world, but that You keep them from the evil one. 16 They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world. 17 Sanctify them by the truth; Your word is truth. 18 As You sent Me into the world, I have also sent them into the world. 19 For them I sanctify Myself, so that they too may be sanctified by the truth.
paragraphs: 13 But now I am coming to You; and I am saying these things while I am in the world, so that they may have My joy fulfilled within them. 14 I have given them Your word and the world has hated them. For they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world. 15 I am not asking that You take them out of the world, but that You keep them from the evil one. 16 They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world.

17 Sanctify them by the truth; Your word is truth. 18 As You sent Me into the world, I have also sent them into the world. 19 For them I sanctify Myself, so that they too may be sanctified by the truth.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus speaks of His joy being fulfilled in the disciples even as they face the world’s hatred. He has given them the Father’s word, and their life is now shaped by belonging to Him. He asks that they be kept from the evil one while remaining in the world.

He then asks the Father to sanctify them by the truth and identifies the Father’s word as truth. The word sanctify is ἁγιάζω, hagiazō (hah-gee-AH-zoh). Thayer’s lexicon explains its senses of dedicating someone to God and making holy, with direct references to verses 17 and 19. Here their dedication and holiness belong to the mission Jesus is giving them.

Jesus says that He sanctifies Himself for their sake. This does not describe His becoming free of a sin He previously had. The same lexical entry identifies His self-dedication through death in verse 19. He is committing Himself to the Father’s work so that His followers may be set apart in truth.

The movement is outward: as the Father sent Him, He sends them into the world. Their holiness is not a reason to abandon the people they are sent to reach. It is part of being equipped to represent Him faithfully.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the prayer as asking for protection and holiness within the disciples’ mission. Wesley on verses 15–19 joins their dedication to service with growth in holiness and understands Jesus’ self-dedication in relation to His sacrifice. Calvin on verses 17–19 likewise connects their renewal through the word with Christ’s dedication of Himself for them. The central point is shared: God’s truth shapes the people He sends.
passages.god_plan_html:
The connection between Jesus’ self-offering and His people’s holiness is explicit in Hebrews 10:5–10. He comes to do God’s will, and His people are sanctified through the offering of His body. Their dedication rests on His saving work.

The sending continues after the resurrection. In John 20:21–22, Jesus again speaks of sending the disciples as the Father sent Him and gives them the Holy Spirit. The prayer prepares people who will make Him known in the world.
passages.current_position_html: Our study What Does Prayer Look Like? draws attention to Jesus’ requests for His followers to be kept from the evil one and made holy in truth. It takes these as a pattern for interceding for people: seek their faithful formation and life with God, rather than making the removal of hardship the main purpose of prayer. Jesus’ request here concerns people who will remain in the world to serve Him.

passages.title: John 17:20-26
passages.section_title: What does Jesus ask for those who will believe later?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 20 I am not asking on behalf of them alone, but also on behalf of those who will believe in Me through their message, 21 that all of them may be one, as You, Father, are in Me, and I am in You. May they also be in Us, so that the world may believe that You sent Me. 22 I have given them the glory You gave Me, so that they may be one as We are one— 23 I in them and You in Me—that they may be perfectly united, so that the world may know that You sent Me and have loved them just as You have loved Me. 24 Father, I want those You have given Me to be with Me where I am, that they may see the glory You gave Me because You loved Me before the foundation of the world. 25 Righteous Father, although the world has not known You, I know You, and they know that You sent Me. 26 And I have made Your name known to them and will continue to make it known, so that the love You have for Me may be in them, and I in them.”
paragraphs: 20 I am not asking on behalf of them alone, but also on behalf of those who will believe in Me through their message, 21 that all of them may be one, as You, Father, are in Me, and I am in You. May they also be in Us, so that the world may believe that You sent Me. 22 I have given them the glory You gave Me, so that they may be one as We are one— 23 I in them and You in Me—that they may be perfectly united, so that the world may know that You sent Me and have loved them just as You have loved Me.

24 Father, I want those You have given Me to be with Me where I am, that they may see the glory You gave Me because You loved Me before the foundation of the world. 25 Righteous Father, although the world has not known You, I know You, and they know that You sent Me. 26 And I have made Your name known to them and will continue to make it known, so that the love You have for Me may be in them, and I in them.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus’ prayer reaches beyond the disciples present with Him to those who will believe through their message. He asks that they may be one, grounding their unity in the shared life of the Father and Son and in His presence with them.

He connects this unity with witness: the world is to recognize that the Father sent Him and loves His people. The prayer does not treat their life together as an unimportant detail alongside the message. Their unity is part of how that message is made visible.

He also asks that those given to Him may be with Him and see His glory. He speaks of the Father’s love for Him before the foundation of the world and of making the Father’s name known so that this love may be in His followers. The prayer joins their present shared life with the hope of being in His presence.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand this as a prayer for the unity and future life of Jesus’ people. They differ over how the one church and its visible unity should be understood.

The Catholic Church’s Catechism, paragraphs 813–819, grounds unity in the Trinity and also identifies shared faith, sacraments and ministry handed down from the apostles as visible bonds. It locates the fullness of that communion in the Catholic Church under the pope and bishops united with him, while recognizing other baptized Christians as brothers and acknowledging gifts of truth and grace outside its visible boundaries.

The Orthodox Church in America’s account of the Church likewise understands unity as a gift from God and affirms the fullness of church life in the historic Orthodox Church, with its teaching received from the apostles, ministry and sacraments. It does not accept papal authority as the bond that establishes this unity.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 25, distinguishes the whole company of God’s people united under Christ from the visible church professing the faith throughout the world. It recognizes particular churches with differing degrees of purity and identifies Christ alone as the church’s head. This does not make visible teaching, worship or fellowship unimportant; the confession names them as part of the church’s life.

These differences concern real beliefs about the church. They should not be reduced to the claim that one group values unity and the others do not, or that every disagreement is only a matter of style.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 4:1–6 describes one body, one Spirit, one Lord, one faith and one God and Father. It calls believers to preserve that unity through humility, patience and love. This gives practical shape to the shared life for which Jesus prays.

The hope of seeing Him also has a clear place in the larger promise. 1 John 3:1–3 joins being God’s children with seeing Christ as He is. Philippians 3:20–21 describes His transforming His people’s bodies to be like His glorious body. The prayer reaches toward the completion of life with Him.
passages.current_position_html: Our study What Does Prayer Look Like? treats Jesus’ request that His followers be brought to see His glory as a model for praying for others. Together with His requests that they be kept and made holy, it directs prayer toward their life with God and its completion in His presence. This gives a priority for intercession here; it does not settle the disputed church structures described above.

passages.title: John 18:1-11
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus step forward to meet the people arresting Him?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 After Jesus had spoken these words, He went out with His disciples across the Kidron Valley, where they entered a garden. 2 Now Judas His betrayer also knew the place, because Jesus had often met there with His disciples. 3 So Judas brought a band of soldiers and officers from the chief priests and Pharisees. They arrived at the garden carrying lanterns, torches, and weapons. 4 Jesus, knowing all that was coming upon Him, stepped forward and asked them, “Whom are you seeking?” 5 “Jesus of Nazareth,” they answered. Jesus said, “I am He.” And Judas His betrayer was standing there with them. 6 When Jesus said, “I am He,” they drew back and fell to the ground. 7 So He asked them again, “Whom are you seeking?” “Jesus of Nazareth,” they answered. 8 “I told you that I am He,” Jesus replied. “So if you are looking for Me, let these men go.” 9 This was to fulfill the word He had spoken: “I have not lost one of those You have given Me.” 10 Then Simon Peter drew his sword and struck the servant of the high priest, cutting off his right ear. The servant’s name was Malchus. 11 “Put your sword back in its sheath!” Jesus said to Peter. “Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given Me?”
paragraphs: 1 After Jesus had spoken these words, He went out with His disciples across the Kidron Valley, where they entered a garden. 2 Now Judas His betrayer also knew the place, because Jesus had often met there with His disciples. 3 So Judas brought a band of soldiers and officers from the chief priests and Pharisees. They arrived at the garden carrying lanterns, torches, and weapons.

4 Jesus, knowing all that was coming upon Him, stepped forward and asked them, “Whom are you seeking?” 5 “Jesus of Nazareth,” they answered. Jesus said, “I am He.” And Judas His betrayer was standing there with them. 6 When Jesus said, “I am He,” they drew back and fell to the ground. 7 So He asked them again, “Whom are you seeking?” “Jesus of Nazareth,” they answered. 8 “I told you that I am He,” Jesus replied. “So if you are looking for Me, let these men go.” 9 This was to fulfill the word He had spoken: “I have not lost one of those You have given Me.”

10 Then Simon Peter drew his sword and struck the servant of the high priest, cutting off his right ear. The servant’s name was Malchus. 11 “Put your sword back in its sheath!” Jesus said to Peter. “Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given Me?”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After His prayer, Jesus crosses the Kidron Valley with His disciples and enters a garden they have visited before. Judas knows the place and brings soldiers and officers from the chief priests and Pharisees. John describes their weapons and lights without giving an exact number of men.

Jesus knows what is coming and steps forward to ask whom they seek. When He identifies Himself, they draw back and fall to the ground. He then repeats the question and asks that His disciples be allowed to go. John explicitly connects this with His word about not losing those given to Him.

Peter draws a sword and cuts off the right ear of Malchus, the high priest’s servant. Jesus commands him to put it away and speaks of drinking the cup the Father has given Him. The action Peter begins is stopped by the One he is trying to defend.

The account keeps Jesus’ willingness in view. He is not unaware of the danger, and His concern for the disciples continues as the arrest takes place. His acceptance of what the Father has given Him explains why He does not allow Peter to fight His way out of it.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read the scene as showing Jesus’ authority and willing submission together. Calvin on verses 4–9 and Wesley on verses 6–9 understand the arresting party’s fall and the disciples’ release as displays of His power and care. His rebuke of Peter directs attention to the mission He has accepted, rather than a rescue by the sword.
passages.god_plan_html:
This is the Good Shepherd acting in keeping with what He has taught. John 10:11, 17–18 describes His laying down His life for the sheep willingly. In the garden, He steps forward and seeks His followers’ release while accepting what lies ahead.

Hebrews 10:5–10 connects Christ’s coming to do God’s will with the offering of His body. His words about the Father’s cup belong to that willing offering. The arrest is part of the road to His sacrifice, not the collapse of His calling.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: John 18:12-27
passages.section_title: What happens as Jesus is questioned and Peter denies Him?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 Then the band of soldiers, with its commander and the officers of the Jews, arrested Jesus and bound Him. 13 They brought Him first to Annas, who was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, the high priest that year. 14 Caiaphas was the one who had advised the Jews that it would be better if one man died for the people. 15 Now Simon Peter and another disciple were following Jesus. Since that disciple was known to the high priest, he also went with Jesus into the courtyard of the high priest. 16 But Peter stood outside at the door. Then the disciple who was known to the high priest went out and spoke to the doorkeeper, and brought Peter in. 17 At this, the servant girl watching the door said to Peter, “Aren’t you also one of this man’s disciples?” “I am not,” he answered. 18 Because it was cold, the servants and officers were standing around a charcoal fire they had made to keep warm. And Peter was also standing with them, warming himself. 19 Meanwhile, the high priest questioned Jesus about His disciples and His teaching. 20 “I have spoken openly to the world,” Jesus answered. “I always taught in the synagogues and at the temple, where all the Jews come together. I said nothing in secret. 21 Why are you asking Me? Ask those who heard My message. Surely they know what I said.” 22 When Jesus had said this, one of the officers standing nearby slapped Him in the face and said, “Is this how You answer the high priest?” 23 Jesus replied, “If I said something wrong, testify as to what was wrong. But if I spoke correctly, why did you strike Me?” 24 Then Annas sent Him, still bound, to Caiaphas the high priest. 25 Simon Peter was still standing and warming himself. So they asked him, “Aren’t you also one of His disciples?” He denied it and said, “I am not.” 26 One of the high priest’s servants, a relative of the man whose ear Peter had cut off, asked, “Didn’t I see you with Him in the garden?” 27 Peter denied it once more, and immediately a rooster crowed.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus is bound and brought first to Annas, the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who is high priest that year. John recalls Caiaphas’s earlier advice that one man should die for the people. The questioning takes place within the leadership already involved in the decision against Jesus.

Annas had himself held the high priesthood. Josephus, Antiquities 18.2.2, records a Roman official removing him and later appointing Caiaphas after other appointments. This gives independent background to the older high priest’s place in the account, alongside the family relationship John names.

Peter and another disciple follow. The other disciple is known to the high priest and helps Peter gain entry to the courtyard. John does not identify this disciple here. Peter denies being one of Jesus’ disciples and stands warming himself by the charcoal fire.

When questioned about His disciples and teaching, Jesus points to His public message and to people who heard Him. An officer slaps Him, and He asks for evidence of wrongdoing rather than responding with violence. John also records Annas sending Him bound to Caiaphas.

The account returns to Peter. He denies Jesus twice more, and a rooster crows, recalling the warning in John 13:36–38. John places Jesus’ open witness beside His disciple’s repeated denial.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read the contrast as exposing the weakness of Peter’s earlier confidence while showing Jesus’ faithfulness under questioning. Jesus’ appeal to His public teaching concerns the message He has proclaimed; it does not mean that He never taught the disciples privately.

Readers differ over where the questioning belongs in the sequence. The Catholic bishops’ note on verse 13 understands an inquiry before Annas. Calvin on verse 24 and Wesley on verse 24 read the sending to Caiaphas as having already occurred, so they place the questioning there. The BSB’s wording is retained as given. These are explanations of the narrative’s order, not separate church doctrines about Jesus.
passages.god_plan_html:
The contrast fits the New Testament’s description of a faithful High Priest who can help weak people. Hebrews 4:14–16 describes Jesus as tested yet without sin and invites His people to seek mercy and help through Him. Peter’s weakness does not make Jesus’ faithfulness disappear.

Peter’s story also continues beyond the denial. In John 21:15–19, the risen Jesus again calls him to follow and entrusts His sheep to him. His failure is real, and so is the grace through which Jesus renews his service.

passages.title: John 18:28-40
passages.section_title: What kind of king stands before Pilate?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 28 Then they led Jesus away from Caiaphas into the Praetorium. By now it was early morning, and the Jews did not enter the Praetorium, to avoid being defiled and unable to eat the Passover. 29 So Pilate went out to them and asked, “What accusation are you bringing against this man?” 30 “If He were not a criminal,” they replied, “we would not have handed Him over to you.” 31 “You take Him and judge Him by your own law,” Pilate told them. “We are not permitted to execute anyone,” the Jews replied. 32 This was to fulfill the word that Jesus had spoken to indicate the kind of death He was going to die. 33 Pilate went back into the Praetorium, summoned Jesus, and asked Him, “Are You the King of the Jews?” 34 “Are you saying this on your own,” Jesus asked, “or did others tell you about Me?” 35 “Am I a Jew?” Pilate replied. “Your own people and chief priests handed You over to me. What have You done?” 36 Jesus answered, “My kingdom is not of this world; if it were, My servants would fight to prevent My arrest by the Jews. But now My kingdom is not of this realm.” 37 “Then You are a king!” Pilate said. “You say that I am a king,” Jesus answered. “For this reason I was born and have come into the world, to testify to the truth. Everyone who belongs to the truth listens to My voice.” 38 “What is truth?” Pilate asked. And having said this, he went out again to the Jews and told them, “I find no basis for a charge against Him. 39 But it is your custom that I release to you one prisoner at the Passover. So then, do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?” 40 “Not this man,” they shouted, “but Barabbas!” (Now Barabbas was an insurrectionist.)
