section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The leaders bring Jesus from Caiaphas to Pilate’s headquarters early in the morning. They remain outside because of their concern about ritual defilement and eating the Passover. Pilate goes out to ask for the charge against Him. John records their statement that they are not permitted to execute anyone and connects the proceedings with Jesus’ prediction of the kind of death He would die.

Inside, Pilate asks whether Jesus is the King of the Jews. Jesus answers that His kingdom is not of this world and points to the fact that His servants are not fighting to prevent His arrest. His kingship does not depend on the means by which worldly rulers hold power.

Jesus speaks of coming into the world to testify to the truth and of those who belong to the truth listening to His voice. Pilate asks what truth is and then goes out again, declaring that he finds no basis for a charge against Jesus.

Pilate offers to release Him under the Passover custom, but the people calling for a release ask for Barabbas instead. The BSB identifies Barabbas as an insurrectionist. The episode places the man declared innocent beside a prisoner associated with the kind of violence Jesus has refused.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand Jesus to affirm His kingship while distinguishing it from a revolt for worldly power. Wesley on verses 36–37 emphasizes its spiritual character and witness to truth. Calvin on verse 36 likewise emphasizes its heavenly character and explicitly distinguishes not being of this world from having no presence in it. Their central point is shared; this passage should not be made to settle every later question about governments or force.
passages.god_plan_html:
John explicitly connects the movement toward Roman execution with Jesus’ prediction. John 12:32–33 had connected His being lifted up with the manner of His death. His witness before Pilate is also remembered in 1 Timothy 6:13–16, where it becomes part of the call to faithful service while awaiting His appearing.

The kingship belongs to God’s larger purpose. Daniel 7:13–14 describes the Son of Man receiving lasting dominion over all peoples. Jesus standing before a governor is therefore not the whole measure of His authority.

The choice of Barabbas provides another meaningful contrast. Mark 15:6–15 explicitly records the guilty prisoner being released and Jesus being handed over. This is a narrative parallel to the exchange described in 2 Corinthians 5:18–21: the sinless Christ bears sin on behalf of others so that they may be reconciled to God. The parallel concerns undeserved release at His cost; it is not a claim that the text records Barabbas’s conversion.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: John 19:1-16
passages.section_title: Why is an innocent man handed over to be crucified?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then Pilate took Jesus and had Him flogged. 2 The soldiers twisted together a crown of thorns, set it on His head, and dressed Him in a purple robe. 3 And they went up to Him again and again, saying, “Hail, King of the Jews!” and slapping Him in the face. 4 Once again Pilate came out and said to the Jews, “Look, I am bringing Him out to you to let you know that I find no basis for a charge against Him.” 5 When Jesus came out wearing the crown of thorns and the purple robe, Pilate said to them, “Here is the man!” 6 As soon as the chief priests and officers saw Him, they shouted, “Crucify Him! Crucify Him!” “You take Him and crucify Him,” Pilate replied, “for I find no basis for a charge against Him.” 7 “We have a law,” answered the Jews, “and according to that law He must die, because He declared Himself to be the Son of God.” 8 When Pilate heard this statement, he was even more afraid, 9 and he went back into the Praetorium. “Where are You from?” he asked. But Jesus gave no answer. 10 So Pilate said to Him, “Do You refuse to speak to me? Do You not know that I have authority to release You and authority to crucify You?” 11 Jesus answered, “You would have no authority over Me if it were not given to you from above. Therefore the one who handed Me over to you is guilty of greater sin.” 12 From then on, Pilate tried to release Him, but the Jews kept shouting, “If you release this man, you are no friend of Caesar. Anyone who declares himself a king is defying Caesar.” 13 When Pilate heard these words, he brought Jesus out and sat on the judgment seat at a place called the Stone Pavement, which in Hebrew is Gabbatha. 14 It was the day of Preparation for the Passover, about the sixth hour. And Pilate said to the Jews, “Here is your King!” 15 At this, they shouted, “Away with Him! Away with Him! Crucify Him!” “Shall I crucify your King?” Pilate asked. “We have no king but Caesar,” replied the chief priests. 16 Then Pilate handed Jesus over to be crucified, and the soldiers took Him away.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Pilate has Jesus flogged, and the soldiers mock Him with a crown of thorns, a purple robe and a royal greeting. Pilate then presents Him while again declaring that he finds no basis for a charge. The declaration of innocence stands beside the abuse he has authorized.

The chief priests and officers demand crucifixion and appeal to their law concerning Jesus’ claim to be the Son of God. Pilate becomes more afraid and questions Jesus again. When he speaks of his authority to release or crucify Him, Jesus answers that this authority is given from above.

Jesus also speaks of greater sin in the one who handed Him over. The words do not make Pilate innocent. They hold authority and responsibility together: receiving power from God is not permission to use it unjustly.

The pressure then turns to Pilate’s loyalty to Caesar. He brings Jesus to the judgment seat, and the chief priests answer his question about their king by declaring allegiance to Caesar. Pilate finally hands Jesus over to be crucified. John records these particular leaders and officials; the scene does not assign guilt to every Jewish person.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read the scene as showing Jesus’ innocence, willing submission and authority above that claimed by Pilate. The greater sin has been understood in relation to those who delivered Him for judgment. Wesley on verse 11 names Caiaphas; Calvin on verse 11 emphasizes the guilt of pressuring a judge to misuse his office against an innocent person. Neither explanation removes Pilate’s responsibility.
passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 4:27–28 later names Herod, Pilate, Gentiles and people of Israel acting against Jesus within God’s saving purpose. That connection holds together the reality of human wrongdoing and the purpose accomplished through Christ’s suffering.

The thorns also allow a thematic parallel with the larger biblical story. Genesis 3:17–19 associates thorns with the ground’s curse after sin; here the mocked King wears them. John does not identify this as a direct prediction of the crown. Alongside it, Romans 8:19–23 looks toward creation’s freedom from decay and the redemption of God’s children. The suffering of this King belongs within that wider hope.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: John 19:17-27
passages.section_title: What does John show us as Jesus hangs on the cross?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 Carrying His own cross, He went out to The Place of the Skull, which in Hebrew is called Golgotha. 18 There they crucified Him, and with Him two others, one on each side, with Jesus in the middle. 19 Pilate also had a notice posted on the cross. It read: JESUS OF NAZARETH, THE KING OF THE JEWS. 20 Many of the Jews read this sign, because the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city, and it was written in Hebrew, Latin, and Greek. 21 So the chief priests of the Jews said to Pilate, “Do not write, ‘The King of the Jews,’ but only that He said, ‘I am the King of the Jews.’” 22 Pilate answered, “What I have written, I have written.” 23 When the soldiers had crucified Jesus, they divided His garments into four parts, one for each soldier, with the tunic remaining. It was seamless, woven in one piece from top to bottom. 24 So they said to one another, “Let us not tear it. Instead, let us cast lots to see who will get it.” This was to fulfill the Scripture: “They divided My garments among them, and cast lots for My clothing.” So that is what the soldiers did. 25 Near the cross of Jesus stood His mother and her sister, as well as Mary the wife of Clopas and Mary Magdalene. 26 When Jesus saw His mother and the disciple whom He loved standing nearby, He said to His mother, “Woman, here is your son.” 27 Then He said to the disciple, “Here is your mother.” So from that hour, this disciple took her into his home.

It read: JESUS OF NAZARETH, THE KING OF THE JEWS. 20 Many of the Jews read this sign, because the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city, and it was written in Hebrew, Latin, and Greek. 21 So the chief priests of the Jews said to Pilate, “Do not write, ‘The King of the Jews,’ but only that He said, ‘I am the King of the Jews.’” 22 Pilate answered, “What I have written, I have written.”

23 When the soldiers had crucified Jesus, they divided His garments into four parts, one for each soldier, with the tunic remaining. It was seamless, woven in one piece from top to bottom. 24 So they said to one another, “Let us not tear it. Instead, let us cast lots to see who will get it.” This was to fulfill the Scripture: “They divided My garments among them, and cast lots for My clothing.” So that is what the soldiers did.

25 Near the cross of Jesus stood His mother and her sister, as well as Mary the wife of Clopas and Mary Magdalene. 26 When Jesus saw His mother and the disciple whom He loved standing nearby, He said to His mother, “Woman, here is your son.” 27 Then He said to the disciple, “Here is your mother.” So from that hour, this disciple took her into his home.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus carries His cross to the Place of the Skull and is crucified between two others. Pilate’s notice identifies Him as Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews. It is written in Hebrew, Latin and Greek and is read by many because the place is near the city.

The chief priests object to the title being stated as fact rather than as Jesus’ claim. Pilate refuses to change it. Within the scene of humiliation, the title of King remains publicly displayed.

The soldiers divide His garments and cast lots for the seamless tunic. John expressly connects this with Psalm 22:18. The details are part of his account of Scripture being fulfilled, not an invitation to reconstruct every item of clothing or every dimension of the cross.

Near Him stand His mother, other women and the disciple whom He loved. Jesus entrusts His mother and that disciple to one another, and the disciple takes her into his home. His concern for her is expressed in a practical provision even as He is dying.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly recognize Jesus’ care for His mother in this exchange. Calvin on verses 26–27 emphasizes the disciple taking the place of a son in caring for her; Wesley on verse 27 reads the same practical charge.

The Catholic Church also reads the scene in relation to Mary’s motherhood toward the church. Its Catechism, paragraphs 963–964, connects her union with Christ at the cross and His words to the disciple with that wider role. This adds a spiritual reading to the care expressed in the scene; it should not be confused with a claim that Jesus was unconcerned about her home and support.
passages.god_plan_html:
The casting of lots directly places the suffering of Jesus within the language of Psalm 22. The King is humiliated, yet the events unfold within the Scripture John is presenting as fulfilled.

The place of His suffering also belongs to a wider connection. Hebrews 13:11–14 compares Jesus suffering outside the city gate with the bodies of sin offerings burned outside the camp. It then calls His people to go to Him bearing His disgrace, looking toward the city to come. The cross becomes a calling to faithful identification with Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: John 19:28-37
passages.section_title: What is finished when Jesus dies?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 28 After this, knowing that everything had now been accomplished, and to fulfill the Scripture, Jesus said, “I am thirsty.” 29 A jar of sour wine was sitting there. So they soaked a sponge in the wine, put it on a stalk of hyssop, and lifted it to His mouth. 30 When Jesus had received the sour wine, He said, “It is finished.” And bowing His head, He yielded up His spirit. 31 It was the day of Preparation, and the next day was a High Sabbath. In order that the bodies would not remain on the cross during the Sabbath, the Jews asked Pilate to have the legs broken and the bodies removed. 32 So the soldiers came and broke the legs of the first man who had been crucified with Jesus, and those of the other. 33 But when they came to Jesus and saw that He was already dead, they did not break His legs. 34 Instead, one of the soldiers pierced His side with a spear, and immediately blood and water flowed out. 35 The one who saw it has testified to this, and his testimony is true. He knows that he is telling the truth, so that you also may believe. 36 Now these things happened so that the Scripture would be fulfilled: “Not one of His bones will be broken.” 37 And, as another Scripture says: “They will look on the One they have pierced.”
paragraphs: 28 After this, knowing that everything had now been accomplished, and to fulfill the Scripture, Jesus said, “I am thirsty.” 29 A jar of sour wine was sitting there. So they soaked a sponge in the wine, put it on a stalk of hyssop, and lifted it to His mouth. 30 When Jesus had received the sour wine, He said, “It is finished.” And bowing His head, He yielded up His spirit.

31 It was the day of Preparation, and the next day was a High Sabbath. In order that the bodies would not remain on the cross during the Sabbath, the Jews asked Pilate to have the legs broken and the bodies removed. 32 So the soldiers came and broke the legs of the first man who had been crucified with Jesus, and those of the other. 33 But when they came to Jesus and saw that He was already dead, they did not break His legs. 34 Instead, one of the soldiers pierced His side with a spear, and immediately blood and water flowed out.

35 The one who saw it has testified to this, and his testimony is true. He knows that he is telling the truth, so that you also may believe. 36 Now these things happened so that the Scripture would be fulfilled: “Not one of His bones will be broken.” 37 And, as another Scripture says: “They will look on the One they have pierced.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus speaks of thirst as Scripture is being fulfilled. He receives sour wine and declares that His work is finished before yielding up His spirit. Psalm 69:21 supplies the scriptural language of thirst answered with vinegar.

The word translated it is finished is τετέλεσται, tetelestai (teh-TEH-les-tie), a form of the verb meaning to complete or accomplish. Thayer’s lexicon specifically connects John 19:30 with completing what the Father has appointed Him to do and bear. The word directs attention to the fulfillment of His work.

Because the Sabbath is approaching, the authorities ask for the bodies to be removed. The soldiers break the legs of the other two men, but they see that Jesus is already dead. They do not break His legs. One soldier pierces His side with a spear, and blood and water flow out.

John stresses the truth of the eyewitness testimony and its purpose: that the reader may believe. He also connects the unbroken bones and the piercing with Scripture. The account presents His real death within the fulfillment of God’s word.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the declaration of completion in connection with Christ’s saving work. Wesley on verse 30 speaks of His suffering and the accomplishment of redemption. Calvin on verse 30 likewise locates the fullness of salvation in Him, while keeping His death and resurrection together.

The blood and water receive further explanations. Wesley’s note on verse 34 treats the event as miraculous. Calvin’s note does not require that explanation; it emphasizes the saving meaning of atonement and cleansing, and also accepts a connection with baptism and the Lord’s Supper. These are the commentators’ readings, rather than a medical diagnosis supplied by the passage.

The Catholic Church’s Catechism, paragraph 766, sees the blood and water as signs of the church’s life arising from Christ’s total self-giving. These readings recognize meaning beyond the physical detail, with different emphases. None needs to replace John’s explicit concern with the reality of the death and the truth of the testimony.
passages.god_plan_html:
The unbroken bones recall the Passover requirement in Exodus 12:46, alongside the protection of the righteous sufferer in Psalm 34:19–20. 1 Corinthians 5:7 explicitly identifies Christ as the sacrificed Passover lamb. His death accomplishes the deliverance to which that earlier feast pointed.

The pierced One is also connected with Zechariah 12:10, a passage of grace, prayer and mourning. Revelation 1:7 takes up the language of seeing the pierced One at Christ’s coming. The death John witnesses is joined to a hope extending beyond the cross.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: John 19:38-42
passages.section_title: How is Jesus buried?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 38 Afterward, Joseph of Arimathea, who was a disciple of Jesus (but secretly for fear of the Jews), asked Pilate to let him remove the body of Jesus. Pilate gave him permission, so he came and removed His body. 39 Nicodemus, who had previously come to Jesus at night, also brought a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about seventy-five pounds. 40 So they took the body of Jesus and wrapped it in linen cloths with the spices, according to the Jewish burial custom. 41 Now there was a garden in the place where Jesus was crucified, and in the garden a new tomb in which no one had yet been laid. 42 And because it was the Jewish day of Preparation and the tomb was nearby, they placed Jesus there.
paragraphs: 38 Afterward, Joseph of Arimathea, who was a disciple of Jesus (but secretly for fear of the Jews), asked Pilate to let him remove the body of Jesus. Pilate gave him permission, so he came and removed His body. 39 Nicodemus, who had previously come to Jesus at night, also brought a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about seventy-five pounds. 40 So they took the body of Jesus and wrapped it in linen cloths with the spices, according to the Jewish burial custom.

41 Now there was a garden in the place where Jesus was crucified, and in the garden a new tomb in which no one had yet been laid. 42 And because it was the Jewish day of Preparation and the tomb was nearby, they placed Jesus there.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Joseph of Arimathea, whom John identifies as a secret disciple because of fear, asks Pilate for Jesus’ body and receives permission. Nicodemus joins him with myrrh and aloes. John recalls that Nicodemus first came to Jesus at night, linking this act with the earlier conversation in John 3.

They wrap the body in linen with the spices according to the burial custom John describes. The account concerns a body taken down and prepared for burial. It does not describe Jesus merely recovering from His injuries.

A new tomb stands in a nearby garden, and no one has yet been laid in it. Because it is the day of Preparation and the tomb is close, they place Him there. These details establish the setting in which the next chapter’s empty-tomb account begins.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the burial as confirming the reality of Jesus’ death and preparing for the account of His resurrection. Wesley on verses 38–42 also emphasizes Joseph and Nicodemus stepping forward to identify themselves with Him. Their action is significant without requiring a later legend about their travels or an imagined account of what happened to their careers.
passages.god_plan_html:
The burial has a connection with Isaiah 53:9, which places the innocent sufferer with a rich man in death. Matthew 27:57–60 identifies Joseph as wealthy and describes his placing Jesus in his own new tomb. This is a supported parallel in the Gospel accounts.

The burial also belongs to the central Gospel message. 1 Corinthians 15:3–4 places Christ’s death for sins, His burial and His resurrection together. The tomb is part of the story of real death overcome by the life of the risen Lord.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: John 20:1-10
passages.section_title: What do the disciples find at the empty tomb?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Early on the first day of the week, while it was still dark, Mary Magdalene went to the tomb and saw that the stone had been removed from the entrance. 2 So she came running to Simon Peter and the other disciple, the one whom Jesus loved. “They have taken the Lord out of the tomb,” she said, “and we do not know where they have put Him!” 3 Then Peter and the other disciple set out for the tomb. 4 The two were running together, but the other disciple outran Peter and reached the tomb first. 5 He bent down and looked in at the linen cloths lying there, but he did not go in. 6 Simon Peter arrived just after him. He entered the tomb and saw the linen cloths lying there. 7 The cloth that had been around Jesus’ head was rolled up, lying separate from the linen cloths. 8 Then the other disciple, who had reached the tomb first, also went in. And he saw and believed. 9 For they still did not understand from the Scripture that Jesus had to rise from the dead. 10 Then the disciples returned to their homes.
paragraphs: 1 Early on the first day of the week, while it was still dark, Mary Magdalene went to the tomb and saw that the stone had been removed from the entrance. 2 So she came running to Simon Peter and the other disciple, the one whom Jesus loved. “They have taken the Lord out of the tomb,” she said, “and we do not know where they have put Him!”

3 Then Peter and the other disciple set out for the tomb. 4 The two were running together, but the other disciple outran Peter and reached the tomb first. 5 He bent down and looked in at the linen cloths lying there, but he did not go in. 6 Simon Peter arrived just after him. He entered the tomb and saw the linen cloths lying there. 7 The cloth that had been around Jesus’ head was rolled up, lying separate from the linen cloths.

8 Then the other disciple, who had reached the tomb first, also went in. And he saw and believed. 9 For they still did not understand from the Scripture that Jesus had to rise from the dead. 10 Then the disciples returned to their homes.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
John has just described Jesus’s burial in a nearby, unused tomb. Early on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene finds the entrance open. Her first explanation is that someone has moved His body. An empty tomb does not immediately lead her to expect a resurrection.

Peter and the disciple Jesus loved run to investigate. They find the burial cloths, with the head cloth lying separately. John does not explain exactly how the body left the cloths, and the cloths do not supply a detailed account of how resurrection works.

The other disciple enters, sees and believes. Verse 9 adds that they still do not understand from Scripture that Jesus must rise. John allows us to see their understanding develop rather than presenting them as people who had everything worked out in advance.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read the empty tomb alongside the appearances that follow as testimony to Jesus’s bodily resurrection. The disciples’ initial confusion is part of the account.

Commentators differ over what the other disciple believes in verse 8. Calvin’s note on verses 8–9 understands a beginning of resurrection faith before a fuller grasp of Scripture. Wesley’s note on verse 8 understands belief in Mary’s report that the body has been taken. These are two readings of the disciples’ developing understanding; neither changes the resurrection announced in the rest of the chapter.
passages.god_plan_html: Jesus’s resurrection belongs to the fulfillment of Scripture, even while the disciples are still learning to recognize it. In Acts 2:25–32, Peter explains David’s words about God’s Holy One not seeing decay and applies them to the risen Jesus. The same Peter who now examines an empty tomb will later announce publicly what God has done.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

deeper_study.title: Should We Seek Signs From God?

passages.title: John 20:11-18
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus send Mary to His disciples?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 But Mary stood outside the tomb weeping. And as she wept, she bent down to look into the tomb, 12 and she saw two angels in white sitting where the body of Jesus had lain, one at the head and the other at the feet. 13 “Woman, why are you weeping?” they asked. “Because they have taken my Lord away,” she said, “and I do not know where they have put Him.” 14 When she had said this, she turned around and saw Jesus standing there. But she did not recognize that it was Jesus. 15 “Woman, why are you weeping?” Jesus asked. “Whom are you seeking?” Thinking He was the gardener, she said, “Sir, if you have carried Him off, tell me where you have put Him, and I will get Him.” 16 Jesus said to her, “Mary.” She turned and said to Him in Hebrew, “Rabboni!” (which means “Teacher”). 17 “Do not cling to Me,” Jesus said, “for I have not yet ascended to the Father. But go and tell My brothers, ‘I am ascending to My Father and your Father, to My God and your God.’” 18 Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, “I have seen the Lord!” And she told them what He had said to her.
paragraphs: 11 But Mary stood outside the tomb weeping. And as she wept, she bent down to look into the tomb, 12 and she saw two angels in white sitting where the body of Jesus had lain, one at the head and the other at the feet. 13 “Woman, why are you weeping?” they asked. “Because they have taken my Lord away,” she said, “and I do not know where they have put Him.” 14 When she had said this, she turned around and saw Jesus standing there. But she did not recognize that it was Jesus. 15 “Woman, why are you weeping?” Jesus asked. “Whom are you seeking?” Thinking He was the gardener, she said, “Sir, if you have carried Him off, tell me where you have put Him, and I will get Him.”

16 Jesus said to her, “Mary.” She turned and said to Him in Hebrew, “Rabboni!” (which means “Teacher”). 17 “Do not cling to Me,” Jesus said, “for I have not yet ascended to the Father. But go and tell My brothers, ‘I am ascending to My Father and your Father, to My God and your God.’” 18 Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, “I have seen the Lord!” And she told them what He had said to her.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Mary remains outside the tomb crying. Even when she sees angels, she is still looking for a body someone has moved. She sees Jesus but mistakes Him for the gardener. Recognition comes when He addresses her by name.

Jesus tells her not to cling to Him and sends her to His brothers with a message about His return to the Father. The Greek verb ἅπτομαι, haptomai (HAP-toh-my), can mean to touch or hold on to someone; Thayer’s lexicon lists that range. The word alone does not explain every part of Jesus’s instruction.

Mary’s task is to tell the disciples that she has seen the Lord and to pass on His words. Jesus speaks of His Father and their Father, His God and their God. He welcomes them as His brothers while still speaking of His own relationship with the Father distinctly.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand this as a real encounter with the risen Jesus and a commission to report the news. Mary is a witness, rather than someone who has merely reached a comforting conclusion about His death.

Wesley on verse 17 reads the instruction as not holding on to Jesus or detaining Him. Calvin on verse 17 likewise emphasizes that Mary must not try to keep His earthly presence as before; His return to the Father matters. Their emphasis is on the changed relationship and her task, rather than a rule that the risen body cannot be touched. The command to Thomas later in this chapter also needs to be heard alongside these words.
passages.god_plan_html: Calling the disciples His brothers brings the resurrection into the story of God welcoming people into His family. Hebrews 2:10–12 speaks of God bringing many sons to glory and of Jesus not being ashamed to call His people brothers. This is a connection between the passages, not a claim that Mary or the disciples become divine. The risen Son brings His people into a relationship with His Father.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: John 20:19-23
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus give the Spirit and send His disciples?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 It was the first day of the week, and that very evening, while the disciples were together with the doors locked for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood among them. “Peace be with you!” He said to them. 20 After He had said this, He showed them His hands and His side. The disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord. 21 Again Jesus said to them, “Peace be with you. As the Father has sent Me, so also I am sending you.” 22 When He had said this, He breathed on them and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit. 23 If you forgive anyone his sins, they are forgiven; if you withhold forgiveness from anyone, it is withheld.”
paragraphs: 19 It was the first day of the week, and that very evening, while the disciples were together with the doors locked for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood among them. “Peace be with you!” He said to them. 20 After He had said this, He showed them His hands and His side. The disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord.

21 Again Jesus said to them, “Peace be with you. As the Father has sent Me, so also I am sending you.” 22 When He had said this, He breathed on them and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit. 23 If you forgive anyone his sins, they are forgiven; if you withhold forgiveness from anyone, it is withheld.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
That evening the disciples are behind locked doors because they are afraid. Jesus stands among them, speaks peace, and shows them His hands and side. The risen Lord is the same Jesus who was crucified. Their fear gives way to joy.

Jesus then sends them as the Father sent Him. He breathes on them and tells them to receive the Holy Spirit. Their task is joined to His authority and His gift; it is not something they are expected to carry out by confidence or ability alone.

The words about forgiving and withholding sins belong within that sending. Jesus is commissioning His disciples to serve His work of reconciliation. The passage does not describe permission to grant or refuse forgiveness on a personal whim.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians agree that Jesus gives the Spirit and entrusts His followers with a mission involving forgiveness. They differ over how this authority is exercised in the church.

The Catholic Church teaches that God alone forgives sins and that Christ entrusted the ministry of absolution to the apostles. In its Catechism, paragraphs 1441–1449, this authority continues through bishops and priests in the sacrament of reconciliation: forgiveness of sins and restoration of communion with the church.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 30, connects the church’s keys with the ministry of the gospel and church discipline. The kingdom is opened to repentant sinners through the gospel and release from church censure, and shut against the unrepentant through the Word and discipline. This describes a real responsibility entrusted to church officers, with God’s Word governing its exercise.

The Lutheran Small Catechism’s explanation of the Office of the Keys emphasizes that Christ’s called ministers forgive repentant sinners and withhold forgiveness from the unrepentant by His command. A repentant person can receive that spoken forgiveness as Christ’s own assurance, rather than merely a pastor’s personal opinion.

The relationship to Pentecost also needs care. Wesley on verse 22 describes a gift anticipating Pentecost, and Calvin on verse 22 describes an initial gift before the fuller empowering in Acts 2. These commentators do not take the later Pentecost account to mean that Jesus gives His disciples nothing here.
passages.god_plan_html:
The breathing recalls the biblical theme of God giving life: Genesis 2:7 describes God breathing life into the first man, and Ezekiel 37:9–14 joins breath, God’s Spirit and the restoration of Israel. This is a parallel between the passages. John does not explicitly call this scene a fulfillment of either one, and Ezekiel’s promise should still be read in its own setting.

Here the risen Jesus gives His Spirit and sends His disciples to carry the message of forgiveness. New life leads outward into service: His peace is something they receive, and His mission is something they are sent to continue.

passages.title: John 20:24-29
passages.section_title: What does Jesus teach Thomas about believing?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 24 Now Thomas called Didymus, one of the Twelve, was not with the disciples when Jesus came. 25 So the other disciples told him, “We have seen the Lord!” But he replied, “Unless I see the nail marks in His hands, and put my finger where the nails have been, and put my hand into His side, I will never believe.” 26 Eight days later, His disciples were once again inside with the doors locked, and Thomas was with them. Jesus came and stood among them and said, “Peace be with you.” 27 Then Jesus said to Thomas, “Put your finger here and look at My hands. Reach out your hand and put it into My side. Stop doubting and believe.” 28 Thomas replied, “My Lord and my God!” 29 Jesus said to him, “Because you have seen Me, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.”
paragraphs: 24 Now Thomas called Didymus, one of the Twelve, was not with the disciples when Jesus came. 25 So the other disciples told him, “We have seen the Lord!” But he replied, “Unless I see the nail marks in His hands, and put my finger where the nails have been, and put my hand into His side, I will never believe.”

26 Eight days later, His disciples were once again inside with the doors locked, and Thomas was with them. Jesus came and stood among them and said, “Peace be with you.” 27 Then Jesus said to Thomas, “Put your finger here and look at My hands. Reach out your hand and put it into My side. Stop doubting and believe.” 28 Thomas replied, “My Lord and my God!” 29 Jesus said to him, “Because you have seen Me, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Thomas was absent when Jesus appeared to the gathered disciples. He refuses their report unless he can personally see the nail marks and touch Jesus’s wounds. His demand sets the scene for the next appearance.

Eight days later, Jesus comes again while Thomas is present. He addresses the very conditions Thomas had named and calls him to believe. Thomas answers Jesus as his Lord and his God. John does not say whether Thomas actually touches the wounds.

Jesus then blesses those who believe without seeing Him. That includes readers who will encounter the testimony in this Gospel rather than standing in the room with Thomas. The next two verses explain why John has written these signs down.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read Thomas’s response as a confession addressed to the risen Jesus, and Jesus’s blessing as encouragement for later believers. Wesley on verse 28 identifies the confession of Jesus as God; Calvin on verse 29 emphasizes trusting God’s word without requiring personal sight of the risen Lord. John’s written testimony gives later readers something definite to hear and consider.
passages.god_plan_html:
The Gospel began by identifying the Word as God in John 1:1–5. Near its close, Thomas addresses the risen Jesus as his God. The opening announcement and this personal confession belong together.

1 Peter 1:8–9 describes believers who love Jesus without having seen Him and rejoice as they receive the goal of their faith. The blessing here reaches beyond the first witnesses to the people who will believe their testimony.
passages.current_position_html: Should We Seek Signs From God? uses this exchange to explain that ordinary Christian faith rests on what God has revealed, without needing repeated personal signs to keep believing. Thomas’s demand to see and touch is not a requirement every believer must meet. John also supplies written testimony in verses 30–31, so this does not mean refusing evidence or discouraging honest questions.

deeper_study.title: Should We Seek Signs From God?

passages.title: John 20:27-29
passages.section_title: Why are those who believe without seeing blessed?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 27 Then Jesus said to Thomas, “Put your finger here and look at My hands. Reach out your hand and put it into My side. Stop doubting and believe.” 28 Thomas replied, “My Lord and my God!” 29 Jesus said to him, “Because you have seen Me, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.”
paragraphs: 27 Then Jesus said to Thomas, “Put your finger here and look at My hands. Reach out your hand and put it into My side. Stop doubting and believe.” 28 Thomas replied, “My Lord and my God!” 29 Jesus said to him, “Because you have seen Me, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.”

passages.context_html:
Thomas was absent when Jesus appeared to the gathered disciples. He refuses their report unless he can personally see the nail marks and touch Jesus’s wounds. His demand sets the scene for the next appearance.

Eight days later, Jesus comes again while Thomas is present. He addresses the very conditions Thomas had named and calls him to believe. Thomas answers Jesus as his Lord and his God. John does not say whether Thomas actually touches the wounds.

Jesus then blesses those who believe without seeing Him. That includes readers who will encounter the testimony in this Gospel rather than standing in the room with Thomas. The next two verses explain why John has written these signs down.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read Thomas’s response as a confession addressed to the risen Jesus, and Jesus’s blessing as encouragement for later believers. Wesley on verse 28 identifies the confession of Jesus as God; Calvin on verse 29 emphasizes trusting God’s word without requiring personal sight of the risen Lord. John’s written testimony gives later readers something definite to hear and consider.
passages.current_position_html: Should We Seek Signs From God? uses this exchange to explain that ordinary Christian faith rests on what God has revealed, without needing repeated personal signs to keep believing. Thomas’s demand to see and touch is not a requirement every believer must meet. John also supplies written testimony in verses 30–31, so this does not mean refusing evidence or discouraging honest questions.

deeper_study.title: Should We Seek Signs From God?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The Gospel began by identifying the Word as God in John 1:1–5. Near its close, Thomas addresses the risen Jesus as his God. The opening announcement and this personal confession belong together.

1 Peter 1:8–9 describes believers who love Jesus without having seen Him and rejoice as they receive the goal of their faith. The blessing here reaches beyond the first witnesses to the people who will believe their testimony.

passages.title: John 20:30-31
passages.section_title: Why has John written this Gospel?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 30 Jesus performed many other signs in the presence of His disciples, which are not written in this book. 31 But these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in His name.
paragraphs: 30 Jesus performed many other signs in the presence of His disciples, which are not written in this book. 31 But these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in His name.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After Thomas’s encounter with the risen Jesus, John turns directly to the purpose of the written account. Jesus did more signs than this book records. John has chosen what to include for a reason.

The purpose is belief that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and life in His name. Christ identifies Him as the promised Messiah. The signs are not collected simply to impress readers; they direct attention to who Jesus is and the life found in Him.

These verses help explain the whole Gospel. Its encounters, teachings and signs are testimony meant to lead the reader to Jesus. The reader who has not seen Him personally is still being invited to believe.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand these verses as John’s stated purpose: the testimony points to Jesus as Messiah and Son of God, and to life through believing in Him. Calvin on verse 31 explains that the signs support faith and direct people toward Christ’s word. The USCCB’s note on verses 30–31 also identifies these verses as an explanation of the Gospel’s purpose. Differences over other doctrines should not obscure that straightforward point.
passages.god_plan_html: God’s purpose includes bringing people who were not present into the life revealed through His Son. 1 John 1:1–4 follows the same movement: what the witnesses saw and heard is proclaimed so others may share fellowship with the Father and His Son. Written testimony carries the news beyond the first generation of witnesses.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: John 21:1-14
passages.section_title: What happens when Jesus meets the disciples by the lake?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Later, by the Sea of Tiberias, Jesus again revealed Himself to the disciples. He made Himself known in this way: 2 Simon Peter, Thomas called Didymus, Nathanael from Cana in Galilee, the sons of Zebedee, and two other disciples were together. 3 Simon Peter told them, “I am going fishing.” “We will go with you,” they said. So they went out and got into the boat, but caught nothing that night. 4 Early in the morning, Jesus stood on the shore, but the disciples did not recognize that it was Jesus. 5 So He called out to them, “Children, do you have any fish?” “No,” they answered. 6 He told them, “Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some.” So they cast it there, and they were unable to haul it in because of the great number of fish. 7 Then the disciple whom Jesus loved said to Peter, “It is the Lord!” As soon as Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he put on his outer garment (for he had removed it) and jumped into the sea. 8 The other disciples came ashore in the boat. They dragged in the net full of fish, for they were not far from land, only about a hundred yards. 9 When they landed, they saw a charcoal fire there with fish on it, and some bread. 10 Jesus told them, “Bring some of the fish you have just caught.” 11 So Simon Peter went aboard and dragged the net ashore. It was full of large fish, 153, but even with so many, the net was not torn. 12 “Come, have breakfast,” Jesus said to them. None of the disciples dared to ask Him, “Who are You?” They knew it was the Lord. 13 Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and He did the same with the fish. 14 This was now the third time that Jesus appeared to the disciples after He was raised from the dead.

They dragged in the net full of fish, for they were not far from land, only about a hundred yards. 9 When they landed, they saw a charcoal fire there with fish on it, and some bread. 10 Jesus told them, “Bring some of the fish you have just caught.” 11 So Simon Peter went aboard and dragged the net ashore. It was full of large fish, 153, but even with so many, the net was not torn.

None of the disciples dared to ask Him, “Who are You?” They knew it was the Lord. 13 Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and He did the same with the fish. 14 This was now the third time that Jesus appeared to the disciples after He was raised from the dead.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the appearances in Jerusalem, John describes another meeting with the risen Jesus, this time by the Sea of Tiberias. Seven disciples go fishing together. They work through the night and catch nothing.

At daybreak Jesus stands on the shore, though they do not yet recognize Him. At His instruction they cast the net on the right side of the boat and make a large catch. The disciple Jesus loved recognizes Him, and Peter jumps into the water to reach Him.

Jesus has a charcoal fire, fish and bread ready. He invites them to breakfast and also asks them to bring some of their catch. The account gives a precise count of 153 fish, but it does not explain the number as a code. The emphasis is on the Lord who meets, directs and provides for His disciples.

The third appearance in verse 14 refers to Jesus appearing to the gathered disciples. It should not be read as a denial of the individual encounters already described, including Mary’s meeting with Him in the previous chapter.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read this as another encounter with the bodily risen Jesus, showing His care and the disciples’ dependence on Him. Wesley on verse 6 sees both practical provision and a picture of the work ahead as fishers of people.

Going fishing is sometimes understood as slipping back into an old life. The passage does not expressly rebuke them for fishing, however. Calvin on verse 3 does not regard it as inconsistent with their calling while they await the power needed for their public work. The miraculous catch shows their need for Jesus without requiring us to decide that their night’s work was itself disobedience.
passages.god_plan_html:
The scene recalls the earlier catch in Luke 5:1–11. There too Peter and his companions work without success, follow Jesus’s direction, and receive an overwhelming catch. In that earlier account Jesus explicitly calls Peter to a mission involving people.

This is a parallel between the two scenes, rather than an explanation John gives of every fish or movement of the net. The Lord who first called them is still with them after His resurrection. Their work depends on Him, and His care for them accompanies His call to serve.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: John 21:15-19
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus ask Peter three times about his love?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 When they had finished eating, Jesus asked Simon Peter, “Simon son of John, do you love Me more than these?” “Yes, Lord,” he answered, “You know I love You.” Jesus replied, “Feed My lambs.” 16 Jesus asked a second time, “Simon son of John, do you love Me?” “Yes, Lord,” he answered, “You know I love You.” Jesus told him, “Shepherd My sheep.” 17 Jesus asked a third time, “Simon son of John, do you love Me?” Peter was deeply hurt that Jesus had asked him a third time, “Do you love Me?” “Lord, You know all things,” he replied. “You know I love You.” Jesus said to him, “Feed My sheep. 18 Truly, truly, I tell you, when you were young, you dressed yourself and walked where you wanted; but when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and someone else will dress you and lead you where you do not want to go.” 19 Jesus said this to indicate the kind of death by which Peter would glorify God. And after He had said this, He told him, “Follow Me.”
paragraphs: 15 When they had finished eating, Jesus asked Simon Peter, “Simon son of John, do you love Me more than these?” “Yes, Lord,” he answered, “You know I love You.” Jesus replied, “Feed My lambs.” 16 Jesus asked a second time, “Simon son of John, do you love Me?” “Yes, Lord,” he answered, “You know I love You.” Jesus told him, “Shepherd My sheep.” 17 Jesus asked a third time, “Simon son of John, do you love Me?” Peter was deeply hurt that Jesus had asked him a third time, “Do you love Me?” “Lord, You know all things,” he replied. “You know I love You.” Jesus said to him, “Feed My sheep.

18 Truly, truly, I tell you, when you were young, you dressed yourself and walked where you wanted; but when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and someone else will dress you and lead you where you do not want to go.” 19 Jesus said this to indicate the kind of death by which Peter would glorify God. And after He had said this, He told him, “Follow Me.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After breakfast, Jesus asks Peter three times whether he loves Him. Peter had denied knowing Jesus three times before the crucifixion. Now, in front of the other disciples, Jesus entrusts him with caring for His lambs and sheep. Peter’s failure has not brought this relationship or calling to an end.

Peter is hurt by the repeated question, and he appeals to what Jesus knows. Each response receives a task: feed or shepherd the flock. Love for Jesus is joined to the care of people who belong to Jesus.

The Greek uses two verbs for love: ἀγαπάω, agapaō (ah-gah-PAH-oh), and φιλέω, phileō (fee-LEH-oh). Thayer’s entries for agapaō and phileō describe love with different shades of goodwill and affection. These are not simply labels for genuine love and inadequate love. The second word is also used of the Father’s love for the Son in John 5:20. The repeated question and repeated commission remain clear even where readers differ over the word choice.

Jesus also tells Peter that following Him will involve a death that glorifies God. John explicitly explains the prediction in that way. The renewed call to follow is serious: Peter is being entrusted with service, not promised an easy life.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly connect the three questions with Peter’s three denials and understand the scene as his restoration and commission to care for Christ’s people. Wesley on verse 15 makes that connection, and Calvin on verse 15 describes his restoration to ministry.

The Catholic Church also understands the passage as establishing Peter’s role as shepherd of the whole flock. Its Catechism, paragraphs 880–882, connects this pastoral responsibility with Peter’s primacy and its continuation through the bishops under the pope.

The Reformed reading differs on that further conclusion. Calvin’s discussion of verse 15 understands the commission as pastoral service under Christ, shared in substance by other ministers, rather than proof of universal papal authority. The Westminster Confession, chapter 25, identifies Christ as the church’s head and rejects the pope’s claim to that role.

Commentators also differ over more than these in verse 15. Wesley understands it as asking whether Peter loves Jesus more than the other disciples do, recalling Peter’s earlier confidence. The USCCB’s note on verse 15 prefers that reading while noting alternatives involving love for the other disciples or for fishing. The wording does not identify its comparison as explicitly as we might wish.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus has already described Himself as the good shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep in John 10:11–21. Peter’s task is to care for that same flock; Jesus continues to call the sheep His own.

In 1 Peter 5:1–4, Peter later urges fellow elders to shepherd God’s flock willingly, without greed or domination, under the Chief Shepherd. The care entrusted to him here belongs within that wider pattern of leadership through service.

passages.title: John 21:20-25
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus tell Peter to keep following Him?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 20 Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following them. He was the one who had leaned back against Jesus at the supper to ask, “Lord, who is going to betray You?” 21 When Peter saw him, he asked, “Lord, what about him?” 22 Jesus answered, “If I want him to remain until I return, what is that to you? You follow Me!” 23 Because of this, the rumor spread among the brothers that this disciple would not die. However, Jesus did not say that he would not die, but only, “If I want him to remain until I return, what is that to you?” 24 This is the disciple who testifies to these things and who has written them down. And we know that his testimony is true. 25 There are many more things that Jesus did. If all of them were written down, I suppose that not even the world itself would have space for the books that would be written.
paragraphs: 20 Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following them. He was the one who had leaned back against Jesus at the supper to ask, “Lord, who is going to betray You?” 21 When Peter saw him, he asked, “Lord, what about him?” 22 Jesus answered, “If I want him to remain until I return, what is that to you? You follow Me!” 23 Because of this, the rumor spread among the brothers that this disciple would not die. However, Jesus did not say that he would not die, but only, “If I want him to remain until I return, what is that to you?”

24 This is the disciple who testifies to these things and who has written them down. And we know that his testimony is true. 25 There are many more things that Jesus did. If all of them were written down, I suppose that not even the world itself would have space for the books that would be written.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After hearing about his own future, Peter asks about the disciple Jesus loved. Jesus directs him back to his own calling. The other disciple’s future is in the Lord’s hands; Peter is to follow Jesus.

A rumor spreads that this disciple will not die. John carefully corrects it: Jesus did not make that promise. He spoke conditionally about what He might choose. The difference between what was said and what people assumed matters, even among the first believers.

The closing verses identify this disciple as the witness behind the written account and affirm that his testimony is true. They also acknowledge that the book records only part of what Jesus did. The Gospel ends with confidence in its testimony and wonder at a life larger than any single written account.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand Jesus’s answer as a call to faithful discipleship without making another person’s future the condition for one’s own obedience. Calvin on verse 22 distinguishes proper care for others from curiosity that distracts a person from their calling.

The correction in verse 23 is generally read as a warning against turning Jesus’s conditional words into a definite prediction. His return remains part of the hope in the saying, but the verse does not promise that the beloved disciple will survive until then. The closing statement about the world and its books expresses the greatness of Jesus’s works, rather than asking readers to calculate literal shelf space.
passages.god_plan_html:
This ending returns to the purpose stated in John 20:30–31. The account is selective, yet its testimony points readers to life through believing in Jesus. God’s work is greater than the book’s contents, while what has been written gives readers a real witness to trust.

The corrected rumor also shows why faithful expectation of Christ’s return must attend carefully to His words. Hope in His purposes and obedience to His call belong together; neither requires knowing the timetable or another disciple’s whole future.

passages.title: Acts 1:1-5
passages.section_title: What does Jesus tell His apostles to wait for?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 In my first book, O Theophilus, I wrote about all that Jesus began to do and to teach, 2 until the day He was taken up to heaven, after giving instructions through the Holy Spirit to the apostles He had chosen. 3 After His suffering, He presented Himself to them with many convincing proofs that He was alive. He appeared to them over a span of forty days and spoke about the kingdom of God. 4 And while they were gathered together, He commanded them: “Do not leave Jerusalem, but wait for the gift the Father promised, which you have heard Me discuss. 5 For John baptized with water, but in a few days you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.”
paragraphs: 1 In my first book, O Theophilus, I wrote about all that Jesus began to do and to teach, 2 until the day He was taken up to heaven, after giving instructions through the Holy Spirit to the apostles He had chosen. 3 After His suffering, He presented Himself to them with many convincing proofs that He was alive. He appeared to them over a span of forty days and spoke about the kingdom of God.

4 And while they were gathered together, He commanded them: “Do not leave Jerusalem, but wait for the gift the Father promised, which you have heard Me discuss. 5 For John baptized with water, but in a few days you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Acts opens by addressing Theophilus, the same person addressed at the beginning of Luke’s Gospel. The first account told what Jesus began to do and teach up to His being taken into heaven. This second account follows the work forward through His chosen witnesses.

The risen Jesus presents Himself alive with many convincing proofs. Over forty days He appears to the apostles and teaches about God’s kingdom. Their coming witness is grounded in encounters with the Lord who suffered and rose, rather than a message they developed on their own.

Before they begin, Jesus tells them to remain in Jerusalem for the Father’s promised gift. He contrasts John’s baptism with water and the baptism with the Holy Spirit they will shortly receive. Waiting is part of obedience: the mission must begin with what God gives.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this opening as the bridge between Luke’s account of Jesus and the spread of the gospel in Acts. The promised Spirit will equip the apostles for the work Jesus entrusts to them. Wesley on verses 1–5 emphasizes both that continuity and the promised gift, including the extraordinary empowering of these witnesses.
passages.god_plan_html: Luke 24:44–49 brings together Scripture’s fulfillment, the Messiah’s suffering and resurrection, the proclamation of forgiveness to all nations, and the promise of power from God. Acts begins where that commission leads. The Spirit’s coming belongs to the way the risen Jesus carries His message beyond the first disciples.

passages.title: Acts 1:6-11
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus turn their attention from timing to witness?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 So when they came together, they asked Him, “Lord, will You at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?” 7 Jesus replied, “It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by His own authority. 8 But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be My witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.” 9 After He had said this, they watched as He was taken up, and a cloud hid Him from their sight. 10 They were looking intently into the sky as He was going, when suddenly two men dressed in white stood beside them. 11 “Men of Galilee,” they said, “why do you stand here looking into the sky? This same Jesus, who has been taken from you into heaven, will come back in the same way you have seen Him go into heaven.”
paragraphs: 6 So when they came together, they asked Him, “Lord, will You at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?” 7 Jesus replied, “It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by His own authority. 8 But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be My witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.”

9 After He had said this, they watched as He was taken up, and a cloud hid Him from their sight. 10 They were looking intently into the sky as He was going, when suddenly two men dressed in white stood beside them. 11 “Men of Galilee,” they said, “why do you stand here looking into the sky? This same Jesus, who has been taken from you into heaven, will come back in the same way you have seen Him go into heaven.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The disciples ask whether Jesus will now restore the kingdom to Israel. They have heard Him teach about the kingdom and promise the Spirit. His answer directs their attention away from the Father’s timetable and toward the work they will receive power to do.

They will be His witnesses in Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria and to the ends of the earth. The Greek word μάρτυς, martys (MAR-toos), means a witness: someone who can testify to what they have seen, heard or know. Thayer’s lexicon specifically includes Acts 1:8 and 1:22. Here the emphasis is on their testimony about Jesus.

Jesus is then taken up, and a cloud hides Him from their sight. Two men in white announce that this same Jesus will return. His departure does not cancel His mission or make His return something the disciples can schedule.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians agree that the passage commissions Spirit-enabled witness and promises Jesus’s return. They differ over how the question about Israel’s kingdom fits that promise.

Calvin on verse 6 understands the disciples as still expecting an earthly kingdom too narrowly centered on Israel. Wesley on verse 6 similarly sees expectations of outward national dominion needing correction. These are their readings of the question and Jesus’s response, rather than a statement that every Reformed or Wesleyan reader explains the details identically.

Thomas Constable’s notes on verses 6–7 give a different reading: Jesus leaves a future earthly restoration to Israel in view while correcting the expectation that its timing can be known or that it must begin immediately. His account distinguishes that future kingdom from the church’s present mission. It is one commentator’s reading, rather than a summary of all Christians who expect a future kingdom.

In either reading, the instruction Jesus actually gives is clear: the Father holds the times under His authority, and the disciples are to receive the Spirit and bear witness.
passages.god_plan_html:
The movement toward the ends of the earth belongs to the wider promise of salvation reaching the nations. Isaiah 49:6 joins the Servant’s work for Israel with being a light for the nations. The commission here carries the message of the risen Jesus outward, without requiring us to settle every question about the kingdom’s timetable.

The cloud also recalls the royal vision in Daniel 7:13–14, where One like the Son of Man comes with the clouds before the Ancient of Days and receives enduring dominion. This is a parallel of exaltation and kingship; Daniel’s movement into God’s presence should not simply be rewritten as a descent to earth. Acts itself supplies the separate assurance that Jesus will return.

passages.title: Acts 1:12-14
passages.section_title: How do the disciples wait together?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 Then they returned to Jerusalem from the Mount of Olives, which is near the city, a Sabbath day’s journey away. 13 When they arrived, they went to the upper room where they were staying: Peter and John, James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James son of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Judas son of James. 14 With one accord they all continued in prayer, along with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with His brothers.
paragraphs: 12 Then they returned to Jerusalem from the Mount of Olives, which is near the city, a Sabbath day’s journey away. 13 When they arrived, they went to the upper room where they were staying: Peter and John, James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James son of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Judas son of James. 14 With one accord they all continued in prayer, along with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with His brothers.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The disciples return from the Mount of Olives to Jerusalem, as Jesus instructed. They gather in the upper room where they are staying. The list names eleven apostles; Judas Iscariot is absent, and the following passage will address that vacancy.

They continue in prayer with one accord. The gathering includes the women, Mary the mother of Jesus, and His brothers. Luke shows a community waiting together on God rather than scattering after Jesus’s departure.

The passage describes shared devotion without recording the words of their prayers. It does not identify the room as certainly the room of the Last Supper or give us a complete schedule of their days.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as the apostles and other followers responding to Jesus’s command with obedience and united prayer. The inclusion of Mary and the other women makes clear that the waiting community is wider than the eleven apostles alone. Wesley’s notes on verses 12–15 place the gathering and prayer within that continuing community.
passages.god_plan_html: Luke 24:50–53 closes with Jesus blessing His followers, their return to Jerusalem, and their praise of God. Acts continues that response in a gathering devoted to prayer. Praise, waiting and witness belong to the same unfolding work: the community that will carry the message first receives the Lord’s direction and promise.

passages.title: Acts 1:15-26
passages.section_title: Why is Matthias chosen to join the eleven?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 In those days Peter stood up among the brothers (a gathering of about a hundred and twenty) and said, 16 “Brothers, the Scripture had to be fulfilled that the Holy Spirit foretold through the mouth of David concerning Judas, who became a guide for those who arrested Jesus. 17 He was one of our number and shared in this ministry.” 18 (Now with the reward for his wickedness Judas bought a field; there he fell headlong and burst open in the middle, and all his intestines spilled out. 19 This became known to all who lived in Jerusalem, so they called that field in their own language Akeldama, that is, Field of Blood.) 20 “For it is written in the book of Psalms: ‘May his place be deserted; let there be no one to dwell in it,’ and, ‘May another take his position.’ 21 Therefore it is necessary to choose one of the men who have accompanied us the whole time the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, 22 beginning from John’s baptism until the day Jesus was taken up from us. For one of these must become a witness with us of His resurrection.” 23 So they proposed two men: Joseph called Barsabbas (also known as Justus) and Matthias. 24 And they prayed, “Lord, You know everyone’s heart. Show us which of these two You have chosen 25 to take up this ministry and apostleship, which Judas abandoned to go to his rightful place.” 26 Then they cast lots, and the lot fell to Matthias. So he was added to the eleven apostles.
paragraphs: 15 In those days Peter stood up among the brothers (a gathering of about a hundred and twenty) and said, 16 “Brothers, the Scripture had to be fulfilled that the Holy Spirit foretold through the mouth of David concerning Judas, who became a guide for those who arrested Jesus. 17 He was one of our number and shared in this ministry.” 18 (Now with the reward for his wickedness Judas bought a field; there he fell headlong and burst open in the middle, and all his intestines spilled out. 19 This became known to all who lived in Jerusalem, so they called that field in their own language Akeldama, that is, Field of Blood.) 20 “For it is written in the book of Psalms: ‘May his place be deserted; let there be no one to dwell in it,’ and, ‘May another take his position.’

21 Therefore it is necessary to choose one of the men who have accompanied us the whole time the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, 22 beginning from John’s baptism until the day Jesus was taken up from us. For one of these must become a witness with us of His resurrection.” 23 So they proposed two men: Joseph called Barsabbas (also known as Justus) and Matthias.

24 And they prayed, “Lord, You know everyone’s heart. Show us which of these two You have chosen 25 to take up this ministry and apostleship, which Judas abandoned to go to his rightful place.” 26 Then they cast lots, and the lot fell to Matthias. So he was added to the eleven apostles.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Peter stands among about 120 believers and addresses the place left by Judas. Judas had shared the apostles’ ministry but became a guide to those who arrested Jesus. Peter reads his betrayal and the need for a replacement in the light of the Psalms.

Luke also describes Judas’s death and the Field of Blood. Matthew 27:3–10 tells of his hanging and of the priests buying a field with the returned betrayal money. Acts emphasizes the money connected with his wickedness and his terrible death. Neither account supplies every step connecting those details.

The replacement is to be someone who accompanied the disciples from John’s baptism to Jesus’s ascension and can join them as a witness to His resurrection. They propose Joseph called Barsabbas and Matthias, pray for the Lord to make His choice known, and cast lots. Matthias is added to the eleven.

These are the stated requirements for filling this place among the Twelve. The passage should not be turned into a claim that every later use of the word apostle must describe someone who meets these exact conditions.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the choosing of Matthias as restoring the number of the Twelve and maintaining the witness to Jesus’s ministry and resurrection. Wesley on verses 21–23 emphasizes the witnesses’ qualifications and their appeal to God where their own decision reaches its limit. Calvin on verse 24 emphasizes God’s knowledge of the heart and the need for prayer in choosing people for ministry.

Explanations of Judas’s death differ. Wesley’s note on verse 18 proposes a broken rope to connect the fall with the hanging. The USCCB’s note on verse 18 instead describes the accounts as differing traditions. A reconstruction such as a broken rope is a proposed explanation, not an additional event stated in either passage.
passages.god_plan_html:
Peter directly connects this moment with Psalm 69:25 and Psalm 109:8: the betrayer’s place is left desolate, and another takes his position. The betrayal does not bring God’s purposes or the apostles’ witness to an end.

The prayer also places the decision in the hands of the Lord who knows hearts. The next stage of the mission begins with witnesses to the resurrection, Scripture guiding their understanding, and dependence on God rather than confidence that they can see everything about a candidate.

passages.title: Acts 2:1-13
passages.section_title: What happens when the Holy Spirit comes at Pentecost?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 When the day of Pentecost came, they were all together in one place. 2 Suddenly a sound like a mighty rushing wind came from heaven and filled the whole house where they were sitting. 3 They saw tongues like flames of fire that separated and came to rest on each of them. 4 And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues as the Spirit enabled them. 5 Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem God-fearing Jews from every nation under heaven. 6 And when this sound rang out, a crowd came together in bewilderment, because each one heard them speaking his own language. 7 Astounded and amazed, they asked, “Are not all these who are speaking Galileans? 8 How is it then that each of us hears them in his own native language? 9 Parthians, Medes, and Elamites; residents of Mesopotamia, Judea and Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, 10 Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the parts of Libya near Cyrene; visitors from Rome, 11 both Jews and converts to Judaism; Cretans and Arabs—we hear them declaring the wonders of God in our own tongues!” 12 Astounded and perplexed, they asked one another, “What does this mean?” 13 But others mocked them and said, “They are drunk on new wine!”
