5 Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem God-fearing Jews from every nation under heaven. 6 And when this sound rang out, a crowd came together in bewilderment, because each one heard them speaking his own language. 7 Astounded and amazed, they asked, “Are not all these who are speaking Galileans? 8 How is it then that each of us hears them in his own native language? 9 Parthians, Medes, and Elamites; residents of Mesopotamia, Judea and Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, 10 Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the parts of Libya near Cyrene; visitors from Rome, 11 both Jews and converts to Judaism; Cretans and Arabs—we hear them declaring the wonders of God in our own tongues!”
12 Astounded and perplexed, they asked one another, “What does this mean?” 13 But others mocked them and said, “They are drunk on new wine!”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The disciples have been waiting in Jerusalem for the gift Jesus promised. On Pentecost they are together when a sound like a mighty wind fills the house. They see tongues like flames of fire resting on each person, and they are filled with the Holy Spirit. Luke describes a sound like wind and an appearance like fire; he does not say the room is being blown apart or the people are being burned.

Pentecost falls within Israel’s festival calendar. Leviticus 23:15–21 describes counting seven weeks and then fifty days, bringing a new-grain offering and holding a sacred assembly. Acts places the promised gift within that setting of worship and gathering.

The Spirit enables the believers to speak in other tongues. The Greek word γλῶσσα, glōssa (GLOHS-sah), can mean the physical tongue or a language. Thayer’s lexicon specifically identifies the use in Acts 2:4 with speaking foreign languages. The surrounding verses make the point concrete: listeners recognize their own native languages.

The crowd includes God-fearing Jews from many regions and converts to Judaism. They hear the wonders of God and are amazed, but they do not all reach the same conclusion. Some ask what it means; others mock. Peter’s explanation in the following passage answers that question.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand Pentecost as the fulfillment of Jesus’s promise to send the Spirit and equip His witnesses. They differ over how this event relates to each believer’s experience.

The Catholic Church’s Catechism, paragraphs 731–732, describes the outpouring as the fulfillment of Christ’s Passover and the beginning of the church’s life in the last days. Its emphasis here is on the gift of the divine Person and communion with God.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 13, describes the Spirit dwelling in believers and forming holiness in their lives. A more specific Reformed explanation appears in the 1978 Orthodox Presbyterian committee report, section I: every believer shares in baptism with the Spirit through union with Christ at conversion, rather than through a separate later experience. The report distinguishes this from repeated filling with the Spirit. It is a committee’s explanation, rather than a confessional document binding every Reformed church.

The Assemblies of God teaches a distinct experience of baptism in the Holy Spirit after the new birth, bringing power for service. Its Statement of Fundamental Truths, sections 7–8, identifies speaking in tongues as the initial physical evidence and distinguishes that initial purpose from the public use of the gift. This represents that Pentecostal body’s teaching; it should not be assigned to every church that believes spiritual gifts continue today.

For the language miracle itself, Calvin on verse 4 and Wesley on verse 4 both emphasize the speakers being enabled to speak other languages. The recognizable languages in this scene give a clear starting point without settling every question about tongues elsewhere.
passages.god_plan_html:
The scene offers a meaningful contrast with Genesis 11:1–9. At Babel, confused language accompanies people’s scattering; here, people with different languages hear the same wonders of God. This is a parallel between the passages, not an explicit statement by Luke that every part of Babel has now been reversed. The listeners do not lose their languages or become one nationality.

The wider direction is toward a people brought together through God’s Spirit. Ephesians 2:18–22 describes Jews and Gentiles having access to the Father through one Spirit and being built into God’s dwelling. Acts 2 begins with Jews and converts gathered in Jerusalem; the narrative will later describe the message reaching other communities. Pentecost opens the way outward without compressing that whole story into a single morning.

passages.title: Acts 2:14-21
passages.section_title: Why does Peter turn to the prophet Joel?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 Then Peter stood up with the Eleven, lifted up his voice, and addressed the crowd: “Men of Judea and all who dwell in Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and listen carefully to my words. 15 These men are not drunk, as you suppose. It is only the third hour of the day! 16 No, this is what was spoken by the prophet Joel: 17 ‘In the last days, God says, I will pour out My Spirit on all people. Your sons and daughters will prophesy, your young men will see visions, your old men will dream dreams. 18 Even on My menservants and maidservants I will pour out My Spirit in those days, and they will prophesy. 19 I will show wonders in the heavens above and signs on the earth below, blood and fire and billows of smoke. 20 The sun will be turned to darkness, and the moon to blood, before the coming of the great and glorious Day of the Lord. 21 And everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.’

It is only the third hour of the day! 16 No, this is what was spoken by the prophet Joel:

17 ‘In the last days, God says, I will pour out My Spirit on all people. Your sons and daughters will prophesy, your young men will see visions, your old men will dream dreams. 18 Even on My menservants and maidservants I will pour out My Spirit in those days, and they will prophesy. 19 I will show wonders in the heavens above and signs on the earth below, blood and fire and billows of smoke. 20 The sun will be turned to darkness, and the moon to blood, before the coming of the great and glorious Day of the Lord. 21 And everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.’

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Peter stands with the eleven and answers the crowd’s accusation of drunkenness. It is only the third hour of the day. His main explanation comes from Scripture: what they are seeing is connected with the Spirit’s promised outpouring in Joel.

The quotation names sons and daughters, young and old, male and female servants. The gift is not described as the preserve of one age, sex or social rank. It also speaks of signs before the Day of the Lord and ends with the promise of salvation for everyone who calls on His name.

The quotation reaches beyond the immediate sound and languages that drew the crowd. Peter places the event within God’s promises and prepares his listeners for the announcement of Jesus as Lord in the rest of the sermon.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians agree that Peter uses Joel to explain the work of God’s Spirit. Commentators differ over how much of Joel’s prophecy is being fulfilled at Pentecost and how the remaining signs relate to later events.

Calvin’s discussion of verses 14–17 understands the Spirit’s outpouring as evidence that the Messiah has come and that the promised renewal has begun. Wesley on verse 17 likewise understands the last days as the time of the Messiah, while his notes on verses 19–20 connect the signs with judgments reaching beyond that morning.

Thomas Constable’s notes on verses 16–21 give a different explanation. He understands Peter as pointing to a similar work of the Spirit, with Joel’s complete fulfillment still associated with a future outpouring on Israel. These are the commentators’ own readings. Neither the signs nor the words about the last days should be silently dropped when considering the whole quotation.
passages.god_plan_html: The closing promise connects this event with God’s purpose to bring salvation beyond one people. Romans 10:9–13 also uses Joel’s promise while explaining that the same Lord is Lord of Jew and Greek. Peter’s sermon begins in Jerusalem, and the wider New Testament shows the invitation extending to all who call on the Lord.
passages.current_position_html: Should We Seek Signs From God? specifically recognizes Peter’s use of Joel as a passage Christians cite when discussing dreams and visions today. That study leaves the broader question open while insisting that claims of divine communication must be tested. This passage should not be used to treat every dream, impression or secondhand report as a message from God.

deeper_study.title: Should We Seek Signs From God?

passages.title: Acts 2:22-36
passages.section_title: How does Peter explain Jesus’s death and resurrection?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 Men of Israel, listen to this message: Jesus of Nazareth was a man certified by God to you by miracles, wonders, and signs, which God did among you through Him, as you yourselves know. 23 He was delivered up by God’s set plan and foreknowledge, and you, by the hands of the lawless, put Him to death by nailing Him to the cross. 24 But God raised Him from the dead, releasing Him from the agony of death, because it was impossible for death to keep Him in its grip. 25 David says about Him: ‘I saw the Lord always before me; because He is at my right hand, I will not be shaken. 26 Therefore my heart is glad and my tongue rejoices; my body also will dwell in hope, 27 because You will not abandon my soul to Hades, nor will You let Your Holy One see decay. 28 You have made known to me the paths of life; You will fill me with joy in Your presence.’ 29 Brothers, I can tell you with confidence that the patriarch David died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day. 30 But he was a prophet and knew that God had promised him on oath that He would place one of his descendants on his throne. 31 Foreseeing this, David spoke about the resurrection of the Christ, that He was not abandoned to Hades, nor did His body see decay. 32 God has raised this Jesus to life, to which we are all witnesses. 33 Exalted, then, to the right hand of God, He has received from the Father the promised Holy Spirit and has poured out what you now see and hear. 34 For David did not ascend into heaven, but he himself says: ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at My right hand 35 until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet.”’ 36 Therefore let all Israel know with certainty that God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ!”

29 Brothers, I can tell you with confidence that the patriarch David died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day. 30 But he was a prophet and knew that God had promised him on oath that He would place one of his descendants on his throne. 31 Foreseeing this, David spoke about the resurrection of the Christ, that He was not abandoned to Hades, nor did His body see decay. 32 God has raised this Jesus to life, to which we are all witnesses. 33 Exalted, then, to the right hand of God, He has received from the Father the promised Holy Spirit and has poured out what you now see and hear.

34 For David did not ascend into heaven, but he himself says: ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at My right hand 35 until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet.”’ 36 Therefore let all Israel know with certainty that God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ!”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Peter now identifies the Jesus whom the crowd needs to understand. His ministry was accompanied by God’s signs, He was put to death, and God raised Him. Peter holds together God’s purpose and the responsibility of those involved in the crucifixion. The plan does not make their actions innocent.

Peter quotes David’s words in Psalm 16 and explains why they point beyond David’s own experience. David died and was buried, but he spoke as a prophet of the Messiah’s resurrection. The apostles present themselves as witnesses that God has raised Jesus.

The sermon then joins resurrection, exaltation and the gift of the Spirit. The Jesus who has been raised and exalted has poured out what the crowd sees and hears. Psalm 110 supplies the royal language of sitting at God’s right hand while awaiting the defeat of His enemies.

The conclusion calls Israel to recognize this crucified Jesus as Lord and Christ. Peter is announcing the authority of the risen Messiah, rather than leaving the crowd to admire an unexplained miracle.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a central statement of the apostolic gospel: Jesus’s death belongs within God’s purpose, His resurrection fulfills Scripture, and His exaltation explains the outpouring of the Spirit. Wesley on verses 23–35 follows those connections between Christ’s saving death, David’s promises and the risen Lord’s authority. The passage gives no basis for assigning responsibility for the crucifixion indiscriminately to Jewish people of later generations.
passages.god_plan_html:
Peter directly applies Psalm 16:8–11 and Psalm 110:1 to the Messiah’s resurrection and exaltation. The promises are not left as distant hopes; the witnesses announce that God has acted in Jesus.

Hebrews 10:12–14 also joins Christ’s place at God’s right hand with His completed sacrifice and the future defeat of His enemies. The risen Lord’s present reign and the expectation of what God will yet bring to completion belong together.

passages.title: Acts 2:37-41
passages.section_title: How does Peter call the crowd to respond?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 37 When the people heard this, they were cut to the heart and asked Peter and the other apostles, “Brothers, what shall we do?” 38 Peter replied, “Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. 39 This promise belongs to you and your children and to all who are far off—to all whom the Lord our God will call to Himself.” 40 With many other words he testified, and he urged them, “Be saved from this corrupt generation.” 41 Those who embraced his message were baptized, and about three thousand were added to the believers that day.
paragraphs: 37 When the people heard this, they were cut to the heart and asked Peter and the other apostles, “Brothers, what shall we do?” 38 Peter replied, “Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. 39 This promise belongs to you and your children and to all who are far off—to all whom the Lord our God will call to Himself.”

40 With many other words he testified, and he urged them, “Be saved from this corrupt generation.” 41 Those who embraced his message were baptized, and about three thousand were added to the believers that day.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The message about the crucified and risen Jesus cuts the listeners to the heart. They ask Peter and the other apostles what they should do. Peter calls them to repent and be baptized in Jesus Christ’s name, speaks of forgiveness, and promises the gift of the Holy Spirit.

The promise reaches the listeners, their children and those far off, all whom the Lord calls. Peter continues to warn and urge them. Luke’s summary is brief; it is not a transcript of every word spoken that day.

Those who receive the message are baptized, and about three thousand people are added. The response becomes a shared life, described in the next passage. The crowd is being called to turn toward the Jesus Peter has proclaimed, not simply to have an emotional reaction to the signs.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians agree that repentance, baptism, forgiveness and the Spirit belong closely together in this response. They differ over how baptism brings God’s grace and who should receive it.

The Catholic Church’s Catechism, paragraphs 1226–1228, directly cites Peter’s words and describes baptism as a life-giving sacrament joined to faith, purification and communion with Christ’s death and resurrection. Paragraphs 1257–1259 also recognize that God is not bound by the sacraments and discuss baptism of blood and the desire for baptism. This teaching should not be reduced to a claim that water works independently of God or faith.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 28, calls baptism a sign and seal of God’s covenant, including forgiveness of sins. It teaches that the Spirit truly confers the promised grace according to God’s purpose, while denying that every baptized person is necessarily given new life or that salvation is inseparably tied to the time of the water rite. It includes the infants of believers among those to be baptized.

The 1689 Baptist Confession, chapter 29, also describes baptism as a sign of fellowship with Christ, forgiveness of sins and new life. It limits those baptized to people who profess repentance, faith and obedience, and requires immersion. That differs from Westminster’s inclusion of believers’ infants and its acceptance of pouring or sprinkling.

Wesley on verse 38 emphasizes repentance, belief in Jesus and the Spirit’s continuing fruits. He does not identify the promised gift here simply with everyone receiving the power to speak in tongues. The different readings need to keep the whole call to respond in view, rather than treating one word as if it supplied the entire teaching by itself.
passages.god_plan_html:
Peter’s invitation carries forward the promise at the end of the Joel quotation: the Lord calls people to salvation, and they are to respond to Him. The address includes children and those far away without giving us a complete timetable for every community that will later hear.

Acts 10:44–48 will show Gentiles receiving the Spirit and then being baptized. That later event belongs to the same expanding story of God’s gift. Reading the accounts together helps us hear the continuing mission without assuming every conversion scene must follow an identical sequence.
passages.current_position_html: Baptism reads Acts 2:38 as describing the whole response to the gospel: repentance, forgiveness, baptism and the Spirit belong together. It rejects a fixed formula in which nothing spiritual can happen before the water rite, pointing to the Gentiles receiving the Spirit before baptism in Acts 10. Baptism is the expected response of faith; this conclusion does not make it something to neglect.

passages.section_title: What does Peter mean by repent and be baptized?

passages.title: Acts 2:42-47
passages.section_title: What does life together look like after Pentecost?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 42 They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and to the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer. 43 A sense of awe came over everyone, and the apostles performed many wonders and signs. 44 All the believers were together and had everything in common. 45 Selling their possessions and goods, they shared with anyone who was in need. 46 With one accord they continued to meet daily in the temple courts and to break bread from house to house, sharing their meals with gladness and sincerity of heart, 47 praising God and enjoying the favor of all the people. And the Lord added to their number daily those who were being saved.
paragraphs: 42 They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and to the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer. 43 A sense of awe came over everyone, and the apostles performed many wonders and signs.

44 All the believers were together and had everything in common. 45 Selling their possessions and goods, they shared with anyone who was in need. 46 With one accord they continued to meet daily in the temple courts and to break bread from house to house, sharing their meals with gladness and sincerity of heart, 47 praising God and enjoying the favor of all the people. And the Lord added to their number daily those who were being saved.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Luke turns from the large response to Peter’s message to the community’s continuing life. The believers devote themselves to the apostles’ teaching, fellowship, breaking bread and prayer. Their commitment continues beyond the excitement of one day.

The verb translated devoted themselves is προσκαρτερέω, proskartereō (prohs-kar-teh-REH-oh). Thayer’s lexicon explains it as continuing steadfastly or giving constant attention, specifically including Acts 2:42. This describes sustained devotion rather than an occasional interest.

Luke describes awe at the apostles’ signs, practical sharing with those in need, daily gathering in the temple courts, meals in homes and praise of God. The Lord continues adding those being saved. Teaching, prayer and care for people appear as parts of the same shared life.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand this passage as a picture of the early believers’ devotion and mutual care. Calvin on verse 42 emphasizes all four practices, including fellowship expressed in practical help. Wesley on verse 45 sees the sharing as an expression of love that should continue to matter for the church.

The breaking of bread receives more than one explanation. Calvin understands verse 42 as referring to the Lord’s Supper, while reading verse 46 as ordinary meals together. Wesley connects the breaking of bread in both places with the Lord’s Supper, while also recognizing their shared meals. The text places worship and everyday fellowship close together.

The sharing also raises questions about possessions. The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 26, requires believers to help one another according to their abilities and needs while affirming that fellowship does not abolish each person’s ownership of goods. Wesley’s emphasis is that the measure of love shown here should continue. Neither explanation makes indifference to a neighbor’s need the point of the passage.
passages.god_plan_html:
The Spirit’s gift is followed by people learning, praying, praising God and caring for one another. The new community is more than an audience for miracles. Its shared life makes the message visible in ordinary relationships.

Hebrews 13:15–16 similarly joins praise of God with doing good and sharing, describing both as sacrifices pleasing to Him. That wider connection helps us see the temple gatherings and home life here as parts of a life offered to God, rather than unrelated religious and practical activities.

passages.title: Acts 3:1-10
passages.section_title: What happens to the man at the Beautiful Gate?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 One afternoon Peter and John were going up to the temple at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour. 2 And a man who was lame from birth was being carried to the temple gate called Beautiful, where he was put every day to beg from those entering the temple courts. 3 When he saw Peter and John about to enter, he asked them for money. 4 Peter looked directly at him, as did John. “Look at us!” said Peter. 5 So the man gave them his attention, expecting to receive something from them. 6 But Peter said, “Silver or gold I do not have, but what I have I give you: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, get up and walk!” 7 Taking him by the right hand, Peter helped him up, and at once the man’s feet and ankles were made strong. 8 He sprang to his feet and began to walk. Then he went with them into the temple courts, walking and leaping and praising God. 9 When all the people saw him walking and praising God, 10 they recognized him as the man who used to sit begging at the Beautiful Gate of the temple, and they were filled with wonder and amazement at what had happened to him.
paragraphs: 1 One afternoon Peter and John were going up to the temple at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour. 2 And a man who was lame from birth was being carried to the temple gate called Beautiful, where he was put every day to beg from those entering the temple courts. 3 When he saw Peter and John about to enter, he asked them for money. 4 Peter looked directly at him, as did John. “Look at us!” said Peter. 5 So the man gave them his attention, expecting to receive something from them.

6 But Peter said, “Silver or gold I do not have, but what I have I give you: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, get up and walk!” 7 Taking him by the right hand, Peter helped him up, and at once the man’s feet and ankles were made strong. 8 He sprang to his feet and began to walk. Then he went with them into the temple courts, walking and leaping and praising God. 9 When all the people saw him walking and praising God, 10 they recognized him as the man who used to sit begging at the Beautiful Gate of the temple, and they were filled with wonder and amazement at what had happened to him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Peter and John are going to the temple at the afternoon hour of prayer. A man unable to walk from birth is brought each day to the gate called Beautiful to ask for money. He is a familiar presence to the people entering the temple courts.

He asks the apostles for money, but Peter tells him that he has something different to give. In Jesus Christ’s name, he commands him to get up and walk. Peter takes his hand, his feet and ankles become strong, and he begins walking, leaping and praising God.

The crowd recognizes the man. Their amazement rests on the change in someone they know, rather than an anonymous story about a distant event. The next passage gives Peter’s explanation of whose power has brought the healing.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a real healing performed in Jesus’s name and a sign of His continuing saving power. The USCCB’s note on verses 6–10 connects it with the message Peter will proclaim. The account’s attention to the man’s lifelong condition, immediate strength and public recognition gives the sign its force.
passages.god_plan_html:
The man’s leaping and praise recall Isaiah 35:4–6, where God’s coming to save is accompanied by opened eyes, hearing and the lame leaping. This is a parallel between the passages; Acts does not introduce the healing with an explicit quotation of Isaiah.

The sign points beyond the apostles to the risen Jesus and draws people toward hearing about Him. It gives a visible glimpse of restoration without turning this event into a promise that every person will receive the same healing on demand.

deeper_study.title: Should We Seek Signs From God?

passages.title: Acts 3:11-16
passages.section_title: Why does Peter turn the crowd’s attention toward Jesus?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 While the man clung to Peter and John, all the people were astonished and ran to them in the walkway called Solomon’s Colonnade. 12 And when Peter saw this, he addressed the people: “Men of Israel, why are you surprised by this? Why do you stare at us as if by our own power or godliness we had made this man walk? 13 The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the God of our fathers, has glorified His servant Jesus. You handed Him over and rejected Him before Pilate, even though he had decided to release Him. 14 You rejected the Holy and Righteous One and asked that a murderer be released to you. 15 You killed the Author of life, but God raised Him from the dead, and we are witnesses of this fact. 16 By faith in the name of Jesus, this man whom you see and know has been made strong. It is Jesus’ name and the faith that comes through Him that has given him this complete healing in your presence.
paragraphs: 11 While the man clung to Peter and John, all the people were astonished and ran to them in the walkway called Solomon’s Colonnade. 12 And when Peter saw this, he addressed the people: “Men of Israel, why are you surprised by this? Why do you stare at us as if by our own power or godliness we had made this man walk? 13 The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the God of our fathers, has glorified His servant Jesus. You handed Him over and rejected Him before Pilate, even though he had decided to release Him.

14 You rejected the Holy and Righteous One and asked that a murderer be released to you. 15 You killed the Author of life, but God raised Him from the dead, and we are witnesses of this fact. 16 By faith in the name of Jesus, this man whom you see and know has been made strong. It is Jesus’ name and the faith that comes through Him that has given him this complete healing in your presence.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The healed man stays close to Peter and John, and the crowd gathers in Solomon’s Colonnade. Peter immediately rejects the idea that their own power or godliness made the man walk. The healing is not an invitation to make the apostles the center of attention.

Peter speaks of the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob glorifying His servant Jesus. The word servant is παῖς, pais (pice). Thayer’s lexicon lists child and servant among its meanings and specifically identifies the servant usage for Jesus in Acts 3:13 and 3:26. Here it draws attention to the One who carries out God’s purposes.

The sermon sets the rejection of the Holy and Righteous One alongside the release of a murderer. The Author of life was killed, but God raised Him, and the apostles testify as witnesses. Peter is not saying the whole crowd saw the risen Jesus; he identifies the apostles as the witnesses.

The healing is then explained through Jesus’s name and faith that comes through Him. The name points to Jesus Himself and His authority. Peter gives Him the credit for the complete healing the crowd can see.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand Peter as directing faith and praise toward Jesus rather than toward the apostles. Calvin on verse 16 emphasizes Christ’s power and faith grounded in Him. He notes that the faith mentioned can be considered in relation to the healed man or the apostles, without making that question the center of the account. Wesley on verse 16 likewise directs attention to Jesus as both the giver and the object of faith.
passages.god_plan_html:
Peter’s language joins Israel’s God, the glorified Servant and the risen Jesus. Isaiah 52:13–15 describes God’s Servant being raised and exalted despite His disfigured appearance. This is a connection in the language and pattern, rather than an explicit quotation Peter announces here.

The healing belongs to the same message as the resurrection: the Jesus who was rejected is alive and at work. God’s saving purpose continues through Him, and the witnesses serve that purpose by pointing people toward Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Acts 3:17-26
passages.section_title: How does Peter connect repentance with God’s promises?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 And now, brothers, I know that you acted in ignorance, as did your leaders. 18 But in this way God has fulfilled what He foretold through all the prophets, saying that His Christ would suffer. 19 Repent, then, and turn back, so that your sins may be wiped away, 20 that times of refreshing may come from the presence of the Lord, and that He may send Jesus, the Christ, who has been appointed for you. 21 Heaven must take Him in until the time comes for the restoration of all things, which God announced long ago through His holy prophets. 22 For Moses said, ‘The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers. You must listen to Him in everything He tells you. 23 Everyone who does not listen to Him will be completely cut off from among his people.’ 24 Indeed, all the prophets from Samuel on, as many as have spoken, have proclaimed these days. 25 And you are sons of the prophets and of the covenant God made with your fathers when He said to Abraham, ‘Through your offspring all the families of the earth will be blessed.’ 26 When God raised up His Servant, He sent Him first to you to bless you by turning each of you from your wicked ways.”
paragraphs: 17 And now, brothers, I know that you acted in ignorance, as did your leaders. 18 But in this way God has fulfilled what He foretold through all the prophets, saying that His Christ would suffer. 19 Repent, then, and turn back, so that your sins may be wiped away, 20 that times of refreshing may come from the presence of the Lord, and that He may send Jesus, the Christ, who has been appointed for you. 21 Heaven must take Him in until the time comes for the restoration of all things, which God announced long ago through His holy prophets.

22 For Moses said, ‘The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers. You must listen to Him in everything He tells you. 23 Everyone who does not listen to Him will be completely cut off from among his people.’ 24 Indeed, all the prophets from Samuel on, as many as have spoken, have proclaimed these days. 25 And you are sons of the prophets and of the covenant God made with your fathers when He said to Abraham, ‘Through your offspring all the families of the earth will be blessed.’ 26 When God raised up His Servant, He sent Him first to you to bless you by turning each of you from your wicked ways.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Peter acknowledges that the people and their leaders acted in ignorance. He does not treat that as a reason they need no forgiveness. He calls them to repent and turn back, placing the invitation alongside what God has fulfilled through the Messiah’s suffering.

He speaks of sins being wiped away, times of refreshing, and Jesus’s return in connection with the restoration God promised through the prophets. The Greek noun ἀποκατάστασις, apokatastasis (ah-poh-kah-TAH-stah-sis), means restoration. Thayer’s lexicon discusses Acts 3:21 in relation to the restoration of God’s order, including the physical creation. The word gives the idea of things being put right; it does not by itself settle every detail of the future.

Peter then appeals to Moses’s promise of a prophet the people must hear, and to God’s covenant with Abraham. He identifies the listeners as heirs of those promises and describes the blessing as turning people away from their wicked ways. The promises call for a response to Jesus, not merely pride in possessing a religious heritage.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read the passage as a call to repentance and forgiveness, grounded in the promises God fulfills through Jesus. They differ over the scope and timing of the refreshing and restoration.

Calvin on verse 21 understands Christ’s death as securing restoration, with its effects already unfolding and its fullness awaiting His return. Wesley on verses 19–21 likewise places the promises within the course of the New Testament and its coming completion.

Thomas Constable’s notes on verses 19–21 emphasize Israel accepting its Messiah before the beginning of His earthly kingdom. That reading sees a national dimension alongside the individual call to forgiveness. These explanations should be recognized as the commentators’ readings, while retaining Peter’s explicit call to turn back and listen to Jesus.
passages.god_plan_html:
Peter applies Deuteronomy 18:15–19 to the call to hear Jesus. God’s people are to listen to the prophet He raises up, rather than reject Him while claiming loyalty to Moses.

The promise to bless the families of the earth through Abraham’s offspring appears in Genesis 22:18. Galatians 3:7–9 also explains the blessing of the nations in connection with faith. Peter’s address begins with his own people, yet the promise he quotes reaches the families of the earth. The blessing includes the changed direction of people’s lives through God’s Servant.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Acts 4:1-12
passages.section_title: What does Peter tell the council about Jesus?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 While Peter and John were speaking to the people, the priests and the captain of the temple guard and the Sadducees came up to them, 2 greatly disturbed that they were teaching the people and proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection of the dead. 3 They seized Peter and John, and because it was evening, they put them in custody until the next day. 4 But many who heard the message believed, and the number of men grew to about five thousand. 5 The next day the rulers, elders, and scribes assembled in Jerusalem, 6 along with Annas the high priest, Caiaphas, John, Alexander, and many others from the high priest’s family. 7 They had Peter and John brought in and began to question them: “By what power or what name did you do this?” 8 Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them, “Rulers and elders of the people! 9 If we are being examined today about a kind service to a man who was lame, to determine how he was healed, 10 then let this be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel: It is by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified but whom God raised from the dead, that this man stands before you healed. 11 This Jesus is ‘the stone you builders rejected, which has become the cornerstone.’ 12 Salvation exists in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved.”
paragraphs: 1 While Peter and John were speaking to the people, the priests and the captain of the temple guard and the Sadducees came up to them, 2 greatly disturbed that they were teaching the people and proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection of the dead. 3 They seized Peter and John, and because it was evening, they put them in custody until the next day. 4 But many who heard the message believed, and the number of men grew to about five thousand.

5 The next day the rulers, elders, and scribes assembled in Jerusalem, 6 along with Annas the high priest, Caiaphas, John, Alexander, and many others from the high priest’s family. 7 They had Peter and John brought in and began to question them: “By what power or what name did you do this?”

8 Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them, “Rulers and elders of the people! 9 If we are being examined today about a kind service to a man who was lame, to determine how he was healed, 10 then let this be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel: It is by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified but whom God raised from the dead, that this man stands before you healed. 11 This Jesus is ‘the stone you builders rejected, which has become the cornerstone.’ 12 Salvation exists in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Peter and John are still speaking after the man’s healing when the temple authorities intervene. They are disturbed by the teaching and the proclamation of resurrection in Jesus. Acts 23:8 expressly notes the Sadducees’ rejection of resurrection, which helps explain their objection here.

The apostles are held until the next day, but the arrest does not prevent people from believing the message. Luke says the number of men grows to about five thousand. He does not say another five thousand were added on this occasion.

The council asks by what power or name they acted. Filled with the Spirit, Peter names Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom they crucified and God raised. The man standing healed before them is evidence of His power.

Peter then applies the image of the rejected cornerstone to Jesus. The answer moves from one man’s healing to salvation itself: the rejected Jesus is the One through whom God saves.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand Peter’s declaration as identifying Jesus as the unique source of salvation, rather than crediting the apostles with a saving power of their own. Calvin on verse 12 and Wesley on verse 12 both follow the movement from the man’s physical healing to the greater salvation found in Christ.
passages.god_plan_html:
Peter directly applies Psalm 118:22–23 to Jesus: the stone rejected by the builders becomes the cornerstone. Rejection by powerful people does not overturn the place God gives Him.

The setting also recalls Jesus’s promise in Luke 12:11–12 that the Spirit would teach His followers what to say when brought before rulers and authorities. The Spirit’s help equips Peter to name Jesus publicly in the very place where he is being questioned.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Acts 4:13-22
passages.section_title: Why do Peter and John refuse to stop speaking?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 When they saw the boldness of Peter and John and realized that they were unschooled, ordinary men, they marveled and took note that these men had been with Jesus. 14 And seeing the man who had been healed standing there with them, they had nothing to say in response. 15 So they ordered them to leave the Sanhedrin and then conferred together. 16 “What shall we do with these men?” they asked. “It is clear to everyone living in Jerusalem that a remarkable miracle has occurred through them, and we cannot deny it. 17 But to keep this message from spreading any further among the people, we must warn them not to speak to anyone in this name.” 18 Then they called them in again and commanded them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus. 19 But Peter and John replied, “Judge for yourselves whether it is right in God’s sight to listen to you rather than God. 20 For we cannot stop speaking about what we have seen and heard.” 21 After further threats they let them go. They could not find a way to punish them, because all the people were glorifying God for what had happened. 22 For the man who was miraculously healed was over forty years old.
paragraphs: 13 When they saw the boldness of Peter and John and realized that they were unschooled, ordinary men, they marveled and took note that these men had been with Jesus. 14 And seeing the man who had been healed standing there with them, they had nothing to say in response. 15 So they ordered them to leave the Sanhedrin and then conferred together. 16 “What shall we do with these men?” they asked. “It is clear to everyone living in Jerusalem that a remarkable miracle has occurred through them, and we cannot deny it. 17 But to keep this message from spreading any further among the people, we must warn them not to speak to anyone in this name.”

They could not find a way to punish them, because all the people were glorifying God for what had happened. 22 For the man who was miraculously healed was over forty years old.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The council sees the apostles’ boldness and recognizes them as ordinary, unschooled men who have been with Jesus. The healed man is standing beside them. The leaders cannot deny that a remarkable miracle has occurred.

Their response is to try to stop the message spreading. They order Peter and John not to speak or teach in Jesus’s name. The apostles answer by placing the command alongside their responsibility to God and to what they have seen and heard.

The leaders threaten them again but let them go because of the people, who are praising God. Luke adds that the healed man is over forty years old. His long-standing condition gives weight to the public recognition described in the preceding chapter.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the refusal as obedience to God’s commission when a human command directly forbids it. Calvin on verse 19 emphasizes God’s authority over conflicting human decrees, while Wesley on verse 13 observes that God works through ordinary people without making lack of learning a requirement for service.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Luke 21:12–15, Jesus says that arrest and questioning will become opportunities to bear witness. The command to remain silent becomes just such an occasion: Peter and John explain why they must continue speaking about Him.

The mission’s progress is therefore not measured only by whether its messengers avoid opposition. Their task is to testify faithfully, with the help Jesus promised, even when those hearing them try to prevent the message from going further.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Acts 4:23-31
passages.section_title: What do the believers pray for after the threats?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 23 On their release, Peter and John returned to their own people and reported everything that the chief priests and elders had said to them. 24 When the believers heard this, they lifted up their voices to God with one accord. “Sovereign Lord,” they said, “You made the heaven and the earth and the sea and everything in them. 25 You spoke by the Holy Spirit through the mouth of Your servant, our father David: ‘Why do the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain? 26 The kings of the earth take their stand and the rulers gather together against the Lord and against His Anointed One.’ 27 In fact, this is the very city where Herod and Pontius Pilate conspired with the Gentiles and the people of Israel against Your holy servant Jesus, whom You anointed. 28 They carried out what Your hand and will had decided beforehand would happen. 29 And now, Lord, consider their threats, and enable Your servants to speak Your word with complete boldness, 30 as You stretch out Your hand to heal and perform signs and wonders through the name of Your holy servant Jesus.” 31 After they had prayed, their meeting place was shaken, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke the word of God boldly.
paragraphs: 23 On their release, Peter and John returned to their own people and reported everything that the chief priests and elders had said to them. 24 When the believers heard this, they lifted up their voices to God with one accord. “Sovereign Lord,” they said, “You made the heaven and the earth and the sea and everything in them. 25 You spoke by the Holy Spirit through the mouth of Your servant, our father David: ‘Why do the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain? 26 The kings of the earth take their stand and the rulers gather together against the Lord and against His Anointed One.’ 27 In fact, this is the very city where Herod and Pontius Pilate conspired with the Gentiles and the people of Israel against Your holy servant Jesus, whom You anointed. 28 They carried out what Your hand and will had decided beforehand would happen.

29 And now, Lord, consider their threats, and enable Your servants to speak Your word with complete boldness, 30 as You stretch out Your hand to heal and perform signs and wonders through the name of Your holy servant Jesus.” 31 After they had prayed, their meeting place was shaken, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke the word of God boldly.

passages.context_html:
After their release, Peter and John report the threats to the other believers. The community turns to God together, addressing Him as the sovereign Creator. Their prayer begins with who God is and what He has spoken.

They quote Psalm 2 and connect its opposition to the Lord’s Anointed with the actions of Herod, Pilate, Gentiles and people of Israel against Jesus. Those actions were real opposition, yet God’s purpose was not defeated.

The prayer then names the present threats and asks for boldness to speak God’s word, alongside healing and signs through Jesus’s name. The meeting place is shaken, the believers are filled with the Spirit, and they speak boldly. Luke connects their request with the answer he records.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a prayer for God’s work to continue through threatened witnesses, with the Spirit giving fresh boldness. Wesley on verse 31 describes them as filled afresh, and Calvin on verse 31 emphasizes both the sign of God’s presence and the practical answer of strengthened witness.
passages.current_position_html: Prayer and Faith reads this as a specific request aimed at God’s purpose: boldness to proclaim His word and His power at work through Jesus’s name. What Does Prayer Look Like? also emphasizes the believers’ desire to remain faithful under pressure. The account records God strengthening them for the witness they have asked to continue.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The believers explicitly apply Psalm 2:1–2 to the opposition against Jesus. The wider psalm places the nations’ hostility alongside God’s established King and His purpose for the nations. Their prayer rests on that larger view of whose purposes will stand.

Ephesians 6:18–20 gives a later echo: Paul asks believers to pray that he will proclaim the gospel fearlessly while in chains. Prayer supports the witness of God’s people through hardship as the mission continues.

passages.section_title: How does God answer the prayer for boldness?

passages.title: Acts 4:32-37
passages.section_title: How does the believers’ unity become practical help?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 32 The multitude of believers was one in heart and soul. No one claimed that any of his possessions was his own, but they shared everything they owned. 33 With great power the apostles continued to give their testimony about the resurrection of the Lord Jesus. And abundant grace was upon them all. 34 There were no needy ones among them, because those who owned lands or houses would sell their property, bring the proceeds from the sales, 35 and lay them at the apostles’ feet for distribution to anyone as he had need. 36 Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus, whom the apostles called Barnabas (meaning Son of Encouragement), 37 sold a field he owned, brought the money, and laid it at the apostles’ feet.
paragraphs: 32 The multitude of believers was one in heart and soul. No one claimed that any of his possessions was his own, but they shared everything they owned. 33 With great power the apostles continued to give their testimony about the resurrection of the Lord Jesus. And abundant grace was upon them all. 34 There were no needy ones among them, because those who owned lands or houses would sell their property, bring the proceeds from the sales, 35 and lay them at the apostles’ feet for distribution to anyone as he had need.
36 Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus, whom the apostles called Barnabas (meaning Son of Encouragement), 37 sold a field he owned, brought the money, and laid it at the apostles’ feet.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Luke follows the prayer and bold witness with another account of the community’s life together. The believers are united in heart and soul. They hold their possessions open to one another’s needs, while the apostles continue to testify to Jesus’s resurrection.

People who own property sell it and bring proceeds to the apostles for distribution according to need. The result Luke describes is concrete: no one among them is left needy. The account focuses on people being provided for, rather than simply celebrating a large sum of money.

Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus whom the apostles call Barnabas, gives a particular example. He sells a field and brings the money. This introduction prepares for his later part in Acts and for the contrasting account of dishonest giving that follows.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the sharing as an expression of the believers’ unity and love, with goods directed toward actual needs. Calvin on verse 34 understands the sales as proportionate to those needs rather than every person necessarily selling everything, while Wesley on verse 34 emphasizes generosity arising from love rather than a particular command to sell.
passages.god_plan_html:
The absence of needy people recalls the concern of Deuteronomy 15:4–11: God’s people are to open their hands rather than harden their hearts toward a poor neighbor. This is a parallel in the pattern of care, rather than an explicit quotation by Luke.

1 John 3:16–18 connects Jesus’s self-giving love with sharing material help when a brother is in need. The resurrection message in Acts is accompanied by a community learning to put love into action.

passages.title: Acts 5:1-11
passages.section_title: Why is the deception of Ananias and Sapphira so serious?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now a man named Ananias, together with his wife Sapphira, also sold a piece of property. 2 With his wife’s full knowledge, he kept back some of the proceeds for himself, but brought a portion and laid it at the apostles’ feet. 3 Then Peter said, “Ananias, how is it that Satan has filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and withhold some of the proceeds from the land? 4 Did it not belong to you before it was sold? And after it was sold, was it not at your disposal? How could you conceive such a deed in your heart? You have not lied to men, but to God!” 5 On hearing these words, Ananias fell down and died. And great fear came over all who heard what had happened. 6 Then the young men stepped forward, wrapped up his body, and carried him out and buried him. 7 About three hours later his wife also came in, unaware of what had happened. 8 “Tell me,” said Peter, “is this the price you and your husband got for the land?” “Yes,” she answered, “that is the price.” 9 “How could you agree to test the Spirit of the Lord?” Peter replied. “Look, the feet of the men who buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out also.” 10 At that instant she fell down at his feet and died. Then the young men came in and, finding her dead, carried her out and buried her beside her husband. 11 And great fear came over the whole church and all who heard about these events.

And after it was sold, was it not at your disposal? How could you conceive such a deed in your heart? You have not lied to men, but to God!” 5 On hearing these words, Ananias fell down and died. And great fear came over all who heard what had happened. 6 Then the young men stepped forward, wrapped up his body, and carried him out and buried him.

7 About three hours later his wife also came in, unaware of what had happened. 8 “Tell me,” said Peter, “is this the price you and your husband got for the land?” “Yes,” she answered, “that is the price.” 9 “How could you agree to test the Spirit of the Lord?” Peter replied. “Look, the feet of the men who buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out also.” 10 At that instant she fell down at his feet and died. Then the young men came in and, finding her dead, carried her out and buried her beside her husband. 11 And great fear came over the whole church and all who heard about these events.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After Barnabas’s example of generosity, Luke describes a contrasting gift. Ananias sells property, keeps some of the proceeds with his wife’s knowledge, and presents a portion to the apostles. Peter exposes the deception and identifies it as lying to the Holy Spirit and to God.

The verb used for keeping back is νοσφίζω, nosphizō (NOHS-fee-zoh). Thayer’s lexicon explains the use as secretly setting something apart for oneself, and lists Acts 5:2–3. The concealment matters. Peter expressly says the property and its proceeds had been at Ananias’s disposal.

Ananias falls down and dies. About three hours later, Sapphira arrives without knowing what has happened. Peter asks about the price, and she confirms the false account. He describes their action as an agreement to test the Spirit of the Lord; she also falls down and dies.

The result is great fear within the church and among those who hear. The account presents the deception as something done in God’s presence, rather than a private financial arrangement that has no bearing on the community.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
A common reading locates the offense in deception rather than simply in giving less than the full sale price. Calvin on verse 4 emphasizes the freedom to keep the property or money, and the USCCB’s note on verses 1–11 likewise distinguishes withholding money from deceiving the community.

Commentators differ about the couple’s standing. Wesley on verse 1 takes Ananias to be an unbeliever. Thomas Constable’s discussion following verse 11 understands the couple as believers receiving severe judgment. Those conclusions go beyond a direct statement about their eternal fate in Luke’s account.

The identification of lying to the Spirit with lying to God is also important. Calvin’s note on verse 4 and Wesley’s note on that verse both understand it as testimony to the Holy Spirit’s deity.
passages.god_plan_html:
The account recalls the hidden wrongdoing and judgment within God’s people in Joshua 7:1, 10–12, 19–26. Thayer’s entry also notes the same verb in the Greek version of Joshua 7:1. This is a parallel of concealed wrongdoing, not a claim that Ananias’s privately owned field was subject to the same command as the goods at Jericho.

1 Corinthians 11:27–32 also describes serious judgment within the church, while distinguishing the Lord’s discipline from condemnation with the world. Together these passages show that belonging to a community shaped by grace does not make dishonesty or disregard for God harmless. That wider comparison does not decide the couple’s individual eternal fate.

passages.title: Acts 5:12-16
passages.section_title: How do the signs affect the growing community?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 The apostles performed many signs and wonders among the people, and with one accord the believers gathered together in Solomon’s Colonnade. 13 Although the people regarded them highly, no one else dared to join them. 14 Yet more and more believers were brought to the Lord—large numbers of both men and women. 15 As a result, people brought the sick into the streets and laid them on cots and mats, so that at least Peter’s shadow might fall on some of them as he passed by. 16 Crowds also gathered from the towns around Jerusalem, bringing the sick and those tormented by unclean spirits, and all of them were healed.
paragraphs: 12 The apostles performed many signs and wonders among the people, and with one accord the believers gathered together in Solomon’s Colonnade. 13 Although the people regarded them highly, no one else dared to join them. 14 Yet more and more believers were brought to the Lord—large numbers of both men and women.

15 As a result, people brought the sick into the streets and laid them on cots and mats, so that at least Peter’s shadow might fall on some of them as he passed by. 16 Crowds also gathered from the towns around Jerusalem, bringing the sick and those tormented by unclean spirits, and all of them were healed.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Luke returns to the apostles’ signs and the believers’ life together in Solomon’s Colonnade. The community is held in high regard, yet people also hesitate to associate with it. The recent judgment helps explain why joining is not presented as a casual matter.

At the same time, more men and women come to believe in the Lord. Luke holds the hesitation and the growth together. Respect, fear and genuine faith are not all the same response.

People bring the sick into the streets, hoping even Peter’s shadow will fall on them. Crowds also come from surrounding towns with the sick and people tormented by unclean spirits. Luke reports that all those brought in this scene are healed.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this summary as a display of God’s power through the apostles, accompanying the spread of the message. Calvin on verse 15 sees God’s power at work even through Peter’s shadow in support of the gospel, rather than treating Peter as a source of power independent of God.
passages.god_plan_html:
The gathering of sick and troubled people recalls Luke 6:17–19, where crowds come to Jesus to hear Him and receive healing, including those troubled by unclean spirits. This is a parallel between the scenes: the work now associated with His witnesses points back to the Lord they proclaim.

The movement also reaches beyond Jerusalem as people come from nearby towns. The gift promised to the witnesses is making its effects known more widely, while the message remains centered on the Lord rather than the reputation of an individual apostle.

passages.title: Acts 5:17-26
passages.section_title: Why are the apostles sent back to the temple after their release?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 Then the high priest and all his associates, who belonged to the party of the Sadducees, were filled with jealousy. They went out 18 and arrested the apostles and put them in the public jail. 19 But during the night an angel of the Lord opened the doors of the jail and brought them out, saying, 20 “Go, stand in the temple courts and tell the people the full message of this new life.” 21 At daybreak the apostles entered the temple courts as they had been told and began to teach the people. When the high priest and his associates arrived, they convened the Sanhedrin—the full assembly of the elders of Israel—and sent to the jail for the apostles. 22 But on arriving at the jail, the officers did not find them there. So they returned with the report: 23 “We found the jail securely locked, with the guards posted at the doors; but when we opened them, we found no one inside.” 24 When the captain of the temple guard and the chief priests heard this account, they were perplexed as to what was happening. 25 Then someone came in and announced, “Look, the men you put in jail are standing in the temple courts teaching the people!” 26 At that point, the captain went with the officers and brought the apostles—but not by force, for fear the people would stone them.

They went out 18 and arrested the apostles and put them in the public jail. 19 But during the night an angel of the Lord opened the doors of the jail and brought them out, saying, 20 “Go, stand in the temple courts and tell the people the full message of this new life.” 21 At daybreak the apostles entered the temple courts as they had been told and began to teach the people. When the high priest and his associates arrived, they convened the Sanhedrin—the full assembly of the elders of Israel—and sent to the jail for the apostles.

22 But on arriving at the jail, the officers did not find them there. So they returned with the report: 23 “We found the jail securely locked, with the guards posted at the doors; but when we opened them, we found no one inside.” 24 When the captain of the temple guard and the chief priests heard this account, they were perplexed as to what was happening. 25 Then someone came in and announced, “Look, the men you put in jail are standing in the temple courts teaching the people!” 26 At that point, the captain went with the officers and brought the apostles—but not by force, for fear the people would stone them.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The high priest and his Sadducee associates react with jealousy and have the apostles arrested. During the night an angel opens the prison doors and brings them out. The release comes with an instruction: return to the temple courts and tell the people the full message of this new life.

The apostles obey at daybreak. When the council sends for them, the officers find the prison locked and guarded but empty. The missing prisoners are then reported to be teaching openly in the temple.

The captain and officers bring them back without force because they fear the people’s reaction. Luke’s account contrasts the attempt to confine the messengers with their return to the very work they had been forbidden to do.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the release as God’s intervention in support of the apostles’ mission, with obedience to the renewed command following immediately. Wesley on verse 20 understands the message of this life as the words that show the way to eternal life.
passages.god_plan_html:
Later, Acts 12:7–10 will describe another angelic release, this time of Peter. These events show God preserving witnesses for the work before them; they do not make imprisonment or death impossible for His servants.

2 Timothy 2:8–9 expresses the wider point from a prisoner’s circumstances: Paul is chained, but God’s word is not. Here the attempt to stop the message is followed by the apostles teaching it in public again.

passages.title: Acts 5:27-32
passages.section_title: What does obedience to God require of the apostles?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 27 They brought them in and made them stand before the Sanhedrin, where the high priest interrogated them. 28 “We gave you strict orders not to teach in this name,” he said. “Yet you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching and are determined to make us responsible for this man’s blood.” 29 But Peter and the other apostles replied, “We must obey God rather than men. 30 The God of our fathers raised up Jesus, whom you had killed by hanging Him on a tree. 31 God exalted Him to His right hand as Prince and Savior, in order to grant repentance and forgiveness of sins to Israel. 32 We are witnesses of these things, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey Him.”
paragraphs: 27 They brought them in and made them stand before the Sanhedrin, where the high priest interrogated them. 28 “We gave you strict orders not to teach in this name,” he said. “Yet you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching and are determined to make us responsible for this man’s blood.” 29 But Peter and the other apostles replied, “We must obey God rather than men.

30 The God of our fathers raised up Jesus, whom you had killed by hanging Him on a tree. 31 God exalted Him to His right hand as Prince and Savior, in order to grant repentance and forgiveness of sins to Israel. 32 We are witnesses of these things, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey Him.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The high priest confronts the apostles with the council’s earlier prohibition and with the spread of their teaching throughout Jerusalem. He also objects that they are holding the authorities responsible for Jesus’s death.

Peter and the apostles answer that they must obey God rather than men. This is the same conflict seen in the preceding chapter: a command to stop proclaiming Jesus stands against the commission they received from Him.

Their answer becomes another announcement of the gospel. God raised the Jesus who was killed by hanging on a tree and exalted Him as Prince and Savior, bringing repentance and forgiveness to Israel. The apostles identify themselves and the Holy Spirit as witnesses. Their defense continues the message rather than retreating from it.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the apostles as giving God’s command priority when it directly conflicts with the council’s prohibition. Calvin on verse 29 distinguishes that conflict from situations in which authorities are properly carrying out their responsibilities.

Commentators emphasize different aspects of repentance as a gift. Calvin’s note on verse 31 connects it with Christ’s inward renewal through the Spirit. Wesley on verse 31 expressly includes the person’s cooperation in repentance while affirming that God alone forgives sins. These are their explanations of how people respond to the saving work of the exalted Jesus.
passages.god_plan_html:
The language of hanging on a tree also appears in Galatians 3:13–14, where Paul explains Christ bearing the law’s curse so that Abraham’s blessing reaches the Gentiles and the promised Spirit is received through faith. Peter’s address here is to Israel’s leaders; the wider New Testament shows the saving work reaching the nations.

The Jesus who was put to death is now proclaimed as Savior, offering repentance and forgiveness even in a setting of hostility. His exaltation serves God’s saving purpose, rather than merely reversing who holds power.

passages.title: Acts 5:33-42
passages.section_title: Why do the apostles leave the council rejoicing?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 33 When the Council members heard this, they were enraged, and they resolved to put the apostles to death. 34 But a Pharisee named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law who was honored by all the people, stood up in the Sanhedrin and ordered that the men be put outside for a short time. 35 “Men of Israel,” he said, “consider carefully what you are about to do to these men. 36 Some time ago Theudas rose up, claiming to be somebody, and about four hundred men joined him. He was killed, all his followers were dispersed, and it all came to nothing. 37 After him, Judas the Galilean appeared in the days of the census and drew away people after him. He too perished, and all his followers were scattered. 38 So in the present case I advise you: Leave these men alone. Let them go! For if their purpose or endeavor is of human origin, it will fail. 39 But if it is from God, you will not be able to stop them. You may even find yourselves fighting against God.” 40 At this, they yielded to Gamaliel. They called the apostles in and had them flogged. Then they ordered them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and released them. 41 The apostles left the Sanhedrin, rejoicing that they had been counted worthy of suffering disgrace for the Name. 42 Every day, in the temple courts and from house to house, they did not stop teaching and proclaiming the good news that Jesus is the Christ.

He was killed, all his followers were dispersed, and it all came to nothing. 37 After him, Judas the Galilean appeared in the days of the census and drew away people after him. He too perished, and all his followers were scattered. 38 So in the present case I advise you: Leave these men alone. Let them go! For if their purpose or endeavor is of human origin, it will fail. 39 But if it is from God, you will not be able to stop them. You may even find yourselves fighting against God.”

40 At this, they yielded to Gamaliel. They called the apostles in and had them flogged. Then they ordered them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and released them. 41 The apostles left the Sanhedrin, rejoicing that they had been counted worthy of suffering disgrace for the Name. 42 Every day, in the temple courts and from house to house, they did not stop teaching and proclaiming the good news that Jesus is the Christ.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The council reacts with anger and considers killing the apostles. Gamaliel, a respected Pharisee and teacher of the law, has them taken outside while he counsels caution. He recalls movements that collapsed after their leaders died and warns that the council may find itself fighting God.

The council follows his advice in allowing the apostles to live, yet still has them flogged and repeats the ban on speaking in Jesus’s name. The outcome is a release with real suffering, rather than an acceptance of their message.

The apostles leave rejoicing that they have been counted worthy to suffer disgrace for Jesus’s name. They continue teaching in the temple and in homes, announcing that Jesus is the Christ. The council’s repeated prohibition has not brought the mission to an end.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley on verse 38 understands Gamaliel’s caution as useful in an unclear case, while distinguishing it from the need to respond to what is already plainly good or evil. His advice is being considered as counsel in this situation, rather than a complete test of whether every successful movement comes from God.

Christians commonly understand the apostles’ rejoicing as joy in belonging to Christ through persecution. Calvin on verse 41 emphasizes that this joy does not mean they are unable to feel pain or shame; their confidence in the cause they serve gives them strength to continue.
passages.god_plan_html:
The response recalls Matthew 5:10–12, where Jesus blesses those persecuted for righteousness and for His sake, and calls them to rejoice. Their disgrace before the council is understood in the light of belonging to Him.

1 Peter 4:12–16 later joins suffering for Christ’s name with blessing and the Spirit’s presence. It also distinguishes suffering as a Christian from suffering for wrongdoing. The apostles’ joy here belongs to faithful witness, rather than to pain for its own sake.
