passages.title: Acts 6:1-6
passages.section_title: Why are seven people appointed to care for the distribution?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 In those days when the disciples were increasing in number, the Grecian Jews among them began to grumble against the Hebraic Jews because their widows were being overlooked in the daily distribution of food. 2 So the Twelve summoned all the disciples and said, “It is unacceptable for us to neglect the word of God in order to wait on tables. 3 Therefore, brothers, select from among you seven men confirmed to be full of the Spirit and wisdom. We will assign this responsibility to them 4 and will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word.” 5 This proposal pleased the whole group. They chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, as well as Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolas from Antioch, a convert to Judaism. 6 They presented these seven to the apostles, who prayed and laid their hands on them.
paragraphs: 1 In those days when the disciples were increasing in number, the Grecian Jews among them began to grumble against the Hebraic Jews because their widows were being overlooked in the daily distribution of food. 2 So the Twelve summoned all the disciples and said, “It is unacceptable for us to neglect the word of God in order to wait on tables. 3 Therefore, brothers, select from among you seven men confirmed to be full of the Spirit and wisdom. We will assign this responsibility to them 4 and will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word.”

5 This proposal pleased the whole group. They chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, as well as Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolas from Antioch, a convert to Judaism. 6 They presented these seven to the apostles, who prayed and laid their hands on them.

passages.context_html:
The growing community faces a problem within its own life. Greek-speaking Jewish believers complain that their widows are being overlooked in the daily distribution of food. The contrast is with the Hebraic Jews. Thayer’s entry for Hellenist explains the term in relation to Greek-speaking Jews, including those who have become followers of Jesus.

The Twelve gather the disciples and propose appointing seven men of proven character, full of the Spirit and wisdom, to take responsibility. They intend to continue devoting themselves to prayer and the ministry of the word. The response provides care for the widows while protecting the work the apostles have been entrusted to do.

The Greek noun διακονία, diakonia (dee-ah-koh-NEE-ah), means service or ministry. Thayer’s lexicon identifies it both with the distribution in verse 1 and with the ministry of the word in verse 4. The work differs, but both are described as service.

The group chooses the Seven and presents them to the apostles, who pray and lay hands on them. Luke then reports continuing growth, including many priests coming to faith. The account does not identify which person caused the earlier neglect or say that caring for widows can be left undone.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly see the Seven as an important beginning or pattern for recognized service in the church. Calvin on verses 3 and 6 understands the appointment in connection with deacons caring for the poor; Wesley on verses 2–4 also emphasizes that care and the spiritual qualities needed for it. Churches develop the office differently.

The Catholic Church’s Catechism, paragraphs 1569–1571, describes deacons as ordained for ministry rather than priesthood, serving in connection with the bishop. Their work includes worship, proclaiming the gospel and charity, within the church’s ordered leadership.

The Reformed Orthodox Presbyterian Church’s Form of Government, chapter XI, describes a distinct ministry of mercy and care for people in need, carried out under the supervision of the congregation’s council of elders. The 1689 Baptist Confession, chapter 26, paragraphs 8–10, names elders and deacons as the church’s officers and appeals directly to Acts 6 in describing the church’s choice and the setting apart of deacons through prayer and laying on of hands.

The narrative itself describes the work and the appointment without using the noun deacon as a title for the Seven. Its account of Stephen in the following verses also shows that a person chosen for this responsibility can be active in speaking God’s word.
passages.current_position_html: Who Shepherds the Church? directly uses Acts 6:1–6 to describe deacon service as different in kind, rather than a lower rung in a ladder of spiritual rank. The study understands recognized leadership through its responsibilities for people. Here the practical need receives capable, spiritually qualified servants, while the apostles continue in prayer and the ministry of the word.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Care for the overlooked fits the character of the God described in Deuteronomy 10:17–19: He shows no partiality and cares for widows, the fatherless and foreigners. The dispute here is not solved by ignoring one group’s need; the community makes provision for that need.

1 Corinthians 12:4–7 later describes different gifts and ministries from the same Spirit and Lord, given for the common good. Acts shows differing responsibilities serving that shared purpose. Prayer, teaching and practical care need people fitted to do them faithfully.

passages.title: Acts 6:8-15
passages.section_title: Why is Stephen brought before the council?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 Now Stephen, who was full of grace and power, was performing great wonders and signs among the people. 9 But resistance arose from what was called the Synagogue of the Freedmen, including Cyrenians, Alexandrians, and men from the provinces of Cilicia and Asia. They disputed with Stephen, 10 but they could not stand up to his wisdom or the Spirit by whom he spoke. 11 Then they prompted some men to say, “We heard Stephen speak words of blasphemy against Moses and against God.” 12 So they stirred up the people, elders, and scribes and confronted Stephen. They seized him and brought him before the Sanhedrin, 13 where they presented false witnesses who said, “This man never stops speaking against this holy place and against the law. 14 For we have heard him say that Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and change the customs that Moses handed down to us.” 15 All who were sitting in the Sanhedrin looked intently at Stephen, and they saw that his face was like the face of an angel.

They disputed with Stephen, 10 but they could not stand up to his wisdom or the Spirit by whom he spoke.

11 Then they prompted some men to say, “We heard Stephen speak words of blasphemy against Moses and against God.” 12 So they stirred up the people, elders, and scribes and confronted Stephen. They seized him and brought him before the Sanhedrin, 13 where they presented false witnesses who said, “This man never stops speaking against this holy place and against the law. 14 For we have heard him say that Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and change the customs that Moses handed down to us.” 15 All who were sitting in the Sanhedrin looked intently at Stephen, and they saw that his face was like the face of an angel.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Stephen, one of the Seven, now appears as a public witness full of grace and power. He performs signs, and opposition arises from people associated with the Synagogue of the Freedmen and several named regions. They dispute with him but cannot withstand his wisdom or the Spirit by whom he speaks.

The opposition then moves to accusations. Men are prompted to claim that he speaks against Moses and God. He is seized and brought before the council, where false witnesses accuse him of speaking against the temple and the law, and of saying that Jesus will destroy the place and change the customs handed down by Moses.

Luke calls them false witnesses. Their charges should therefore be read as accusations to examine, rather than a complete and reliable summary of Stephen’s teaching. The chapter ends with the council looking at him and seeing his face like an angel’s. His answer begins in the next chapter.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read the passage as the beginning of Stephen’s witness before the council, with the Spirit’s wisdom standing against false testimony. His defense and its consequences belong to the following chapter and help explain the charges more fully.

Commentators explain the face comparison differently. Wesley on verse 15 understands supernatural brightness like the glory seen on Moses. Calvin on verse 15 understands a present dignity and composure, contrasting with the fear commonly seen in someone on trial. Both explanations see something striking in Stephen’s appearance before his accusers; Luke gives the comparison without describing every physical detail.
passages.god_plan_html:
The Spirit-given wisdom recalls Jesus’s promise in Luke 21:12–15 that opposition and questioning would become opportunities for witness, with speech and wisdom the adversaries could not withstand. Stephen’s witness shows that the Spirit’s work in the expanding community reaches beyond the Twelve.

The accusations also recall the false witnesses against Jesus in Matthew 26:59–61, including the charge about destroying the temple. This is a parallel between the narratives. The follower faces a pattern of opposition already seen against the Lord he serves.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Acts 7:1-8
passages.section_title: Why does Stephen begin his answer with Abraham?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then the high priest asked Stephen, “Are these charges true?” 2 And Stephen declared: “Brothers and fathers, listen to me! The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham while he was still in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran, 3 and told him, ‘Leave your country and your kindred and go to the land I will show you.’ 4 So Abraham left the land of the Chaldeans and settled in Haran. After his father died, God brought him out of that place and into this land where you are now living. 5 He gave him no inheritance here, not even a foot of ground. But God promised to give possession of the land to Abraham and his descendants, even though he did not yet have a child. 6 God told him that his descendants would be foreigners in a strange land, and that they would be enslaved and mistreated four hundred years. 7 ‘But I will punish the nation that enslaves them,’ God said, ‘and afterward they will come forth and worship Me in this place.’ 8 Then God gave Abraham the covenant of circumcision, and Abraham became the father of Isaac and circumcised him on the eighth day. And Isaac became the father of Jacob, and Jacob of the twelve patriarchs.

The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham while he was still in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran, 3 and told him, ‘Leave your country and your kindred and go to the land I will show you.’ 4 So Abraham left the land of the Chaldeans and settled in Haran. After his father died, God brought him out of that place and into this land where you are now living. 5 He gave him no inheritance here, not even a foot of ground. But God promised to give possession of the land to Abraham and his descendants, even though he did not yet have a child.

6 God told him that his descendants would be foreigners in a strange land, and that they would be enslaved and mistreated four hundred years. 7 ‘But I will punish the nation that enslaves them,’ God said, ‘and afterward they will come forth and worship Me in this place.’ 8 Then God gave Abraham the covenant of circumcision, and Abraham became the father of Isaac and circumcised him on the eighth day. And Isaac became the father of Jacob, and Jacob of the twelve patriarchs.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The high priest asks whether the charges against Stephen are true. Stephen answers by recounting God’s dealings with Israel, beginning with Abraham. He addresses the council respectfully and speaks of the God of glory who took the initiative to call their father.

God’s appearance comes in Mesopotamia, before Abraham settles in Haran or enters the promised land. The promise of land and descendants comes before Abraham has a child, and its fulfillment is still ahead. Stephen’s opening makes God’s work larger than one location or one moment in Israel’s history.

The account includes the promised descendants’ suffering, God’s judgment of their oppressor, their future worship, and the covenant of circumcision. Isaac, Jacob and the twelve patriarchs belong to the story of God keeping His word through generations.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the opening as a respectful account of God’s promises that also prepares Stephen’s answer about the temple and the law. Wesley’s discussion of verse 2 emphasizes the sequence: God was at work before the law was given or the temple built, and His presence was not confined to the place where the council now sits.
passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 11:8–16 also describes Abraham and his family living by faith while the fullness of the promise remains ahead. Their life as strangers is joined to hope in the city God prepares. The delay in receiving everything promised does not mean God has forgotten His word.

Galatians 3:16, 29 connects the promise to Abraham’s offspring with Christ and with those who belong to Him. Stephen begins with a family story whose reach the wider New Testament explains through the promised Messiah.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Acts 7:9-16
passages.section_title: What does Joseph’s rejection show about God’s purposes?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 Because the patriarchs were jealous of Joseph, they sold him as a slave into Egypt. But God was with him 10 and rescued him from all his troubles. He granted Joseph favor and wisdom in the sight of Pharaoh king of Egypt, who appointed him ruler over Egypt and all his household. 11 Then famine and great suffering swept across Egypt and Canaan, and our fathers could not find food. 12 When Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent our fathers on their first visit. 13 On their second visit, Joseph revealed his identity to his brothers, and his family became known to Pharaoh. 14 Then Joseph sent for his father Jacob and all his relatives, seventy-five in all. 15 So Jacob went down to Egypt, where he and our fathers died. 16 Their bones were carried back to Shechem and placed in the tomb that Abraham had bought from the sons of Hamor at Shechem for a price he paid in silver.
paragraphs: 9 Because the patriarchs were jealous of Joseph, they sold him as a slave into Egypt. But God was with him 10 and rescued him from all his troubles. He granted Joseph favor and wisdom in the sight of Pharaoh king of Egypt, who appointed him ruler over Egypt and all his household.

11 Then famine and great suffering swept across Egypt and Canaan, and our fathers could not find food. 12 When Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent our fathers on their first visit. 13 On their second visit, Joseph revealed his identity to his brothers, and his family became known to Pharaoh. 14 Then Joseph sent for his father Jacob and all his relatives, seventy-five in all. 15 So Jacob went down to Egypt, where he and our fathers died. 16 Their bones were carried back to Shechem and placed in the tomb that Abraham had bought from the sons of Hamor at Shechem for a price he paid in silver.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Stephen turns from the patriarchs as recipients of God’s promise to their jealousy of Joseph. They sell their brother into Egypt, yet God is with him. Rejection by his own family does not prevent God from giving him favor, wisdom and responsibility.

The famine then brings the brothers to the man they had rejected. Joseph makes himself known on their second visit and sends for Jacob and the family. God’s work outside the land preserves the family through which His promises will continue.

The account closes this part of the story with the move to Egypt and a reference to the family’s later burial in the land. Some details invite comparison with Genesis and Joshua, especially the number of people and the burial purchases.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand Joseph’s story here as an example of God working through a person his own people first reject. The repeated contrast between rejection and God’s choice prepares for Stephen’s later charge concerning Jesus.

The family count is seventy-five in Acts, while Genesis 46:27 in the BSB gives seventy. Seventy-five also appears in the Greek Genesis text shown in the Apostolic Bible Polyglot, Genesis 46:27. Stephen’s number is therefore attested in the Greek form of the earlier account; readers should notice which text they are comparing.

The burial reference raises a different question. Genesis 23:16–20 describes Abraham buying the burial site near Hebron from Ephron, and Genesis 50:12–13 places Jacob’s burial there. Joshua 24:32 places Joseph’s bones at Shechem, on land Jacob bought from Hamor’s sons. Acts 7:16 instead names Abraham in its reference to the Shechem purchase.

Wesley on verse 16 proposes that Stephen compresses the two burial accounts into one brief summary. Calvin on verse 16 instead thinks the name Abraham should read Jacob. These are proposed explanations of the difficulty; the places and purchasers in the earlier accounts should still be compared carefully.
passages.god_plan_html:
Genesis 50:20 gives Joseph’s own explanation of the family’s history: their evil intent was met by God’s purpose to preserve many lives. Stephen’s account highlights that pattern of human rejection within a larger saving purpose.

The pattern prepares for the speech’s conclusion in Acts 7:52, where Stephen names the betrayal of the Righteous One. Joseph’s rejection and later role in preserving his people provide a meaningful comparison with Jesus. The passage does not require assigning a separate prediction to every visit or detail of Joseph’s story.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Acts 7:17-29
passages.section_title: How does Moses’s story continue the pattern of rejection?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 As the time drew near for God to fulfill His promise to Abraham, our people in Egypt increased greatly in number. 18 Then another king, who knew nothing of Joseph, arose over Egypt. 19 He exploited our people and oppressed our fathers, forcing them to abandon their infants so they would die. 20 At that time Moses was born, and he was beautiful in the sight of God. For three months he was nurtured in his father’s house. 21 When he was set outside, Pharaoh’s daughter took him and brought him up as her own son. 22 So Moses was educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians and was powerful in speech and action. 23 When Moses was forty years old, he decided to visit his brothers, the children of Israel. 24 And when he saw one of them being mistreated, Moses went to his defense and avenged him by striking down the Egyptian who was oppressing him. 25 He assumed his brothers would understand that God was using him to deliver them, but they did not. 26 The next day he came upon two Israelites who were fighting, and he tried to reconcile them, saying, ‘Men, you are brothers. Why are you mistreating each other?’ 27 But the man who was abusing his neighbor pushed Moses aside and said, ‘Who made you ruler and judge over us? 28 Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?’ 29 At this remark, Moses fled to the land of Midian, where he lived as a foreigner and had two sons.

Why are you mistreating each other?’ 27 But the man who was abusing his neighbor pushed Moses aside and said, ‘Who made you ruler and judge over us? 28 Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?’ 29 At this remark, Moses fled to the land of Midian, where he lived as a foreigner and had two sons.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The promise to Abraham remains in view as the people multiply in Egypt. A new king oppresses them and threatens their children. Moses is born under that threat, is cared for in his father’s house, and is then brought up by Pharaoh’s daughter.

Stephen describes his Egyptian education and ability before turning to his concern for his own people. At forty, Moses intervenes when he sees an Israelite mistreated. He expects his brothers to understand that God is using him for their deliverance, but they do not.

The next day his attempt to reconcile two Israelites is rejected with a challenge to his authority. Moses flees to Midian and becomes a foreign resident with a family of his own. The following passage will show God sending back the man whose leadership had been refused.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this section as preparation for Moses’s calling and as another instance of God’s chosen servant being misunderstood or rejected. Wesley’s notes on verses 20–29 follow the movement from his preservation and upbringing to his rejected intervention and flight; the speech will return explicitly to that rejection in verse 35.
passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 11:23–26 also places Moses’s preservation and identification with God’s people within the story of faith. It connects his choice to share their mistreatment with valuing disgrace for Christ above Egypt’s treasures. The New Testament itself brings Moses’s costly identification with his people into the story centered on Christ.

In Stephen’s speech, the early rejection does not end Moses’s part in God’s purpose. God will send him as a deliverer in the next section. That repeated contrast helps prepare the council to consider its own response to the One God has sent.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Acts 7:30-43
passages.section_title: What does Stephen show about Moses and the people’s response?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 30 After forty years had passed, an angel appeared to Moses in the flames of a burning bush in the desert near Mount Sinai. 31 When Moses saw it, he marveled at the sight. As he approached to look more closely, the voice of the Lord came to him: 32 ‘I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.’ Moses trembled with fear and did not dare to look. 33 Then the Lord said to him, ‘Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy ground. 34 I have indeed seen the oppression of My people in Egypt. I have heard their groaning and have come down to deliver them. Now come, I will send you back to Egypt.’ 35 This Moses, whom they had rejected with the words, ‘Who made you ruler and judge?’ is the one whom God sent to be their ruler and redeemer through the angel who appeared to him in the bush. 36 He led them out and performed wonders and signs in the land of Egypt, at the Red Sea, and for forty years in the wilderness. 37 This is the same Moses who told the Israelites, ‘God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers.’ 38 He was in the assembly in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him on Mount Sinai, and with our fathers. And he received living words to pass on to us. 39 But our fathers refused to obey him. Instead, they rejected him and in their hearts turned back to Egypt. 40 They said to Aaron, ‘Make us gods who will go before us! As for this Moses who led us out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has happened to him.’ 41 At that time they made a calf and offered a sacrifice to the idol, rejoicing in the works of their hands. 42 But God turned away from them and gave them over to the worship of the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets: ‘Did you bring Me sacrifices and offerings forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel? 43 You have taken along the tabernacle of Molech and the star of your god Rephan, the idols you made to worship. Therefore I will send you into exile beyond Babylon.’

And he received living words to pass on to us.

39 But our fathers refused to obey him. Instead, they rejected him and in their hearts turned back to Egypt. 40 They said to Aaron, ‘Make us gods who will go before us! As for this Moses who led us out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has happened to him.’ 41 At that time they made a calf and offered a sacrifice to the idol, rejoicing in the works of their hands. 42 But God turned away from them and gave them over to the worship of the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets: ‘Did you bring Me sacrifices and offerings forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel? 43 You have taken along the tabernacle of Molech and the star of your god Rephan, the idols you made to worship. Therefore I will send you into exile beyond Babylon.’

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After Moses’s years in Midian, God calls him from the burning bush and sends him back to Egypt. Stephen stresses the reversal: the man rejected as ruler and judge is the man God sends as ruler and redeemer. The earlier rejection does not determine God’s choice.

Moses leads the people out, receives living words to pass on, and promises a prophet whom God will raise up. Stephen speaks respectfully of Moses and of what God gave through him. His criticism is directed at the refusal to obey.

The word translated assembly in verse 38 is ἐκκλησία, ekklēsia (ek-klay-SEE-ah). Thayer’s lexicon lists its use for Israel’s assembly and specifically cites this verse. It is a word for a gathered people; its use here should be understood in the wilderness setting.

The people turn back toward Egypt in their hearts, make the calf, and rejoice in what their hands have made. Stephen closes this section with the prophetic warning about false worship and exile, drawing on Amos 5:25–27. Possessing the law has not guaranteed obedience to the God who gave it.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read the section as defending Moses’s place in God’s work while exposing the people’s resistance. Wesley on verses 35–43 emphasizes that the rejected Moses was sent by God and that the people nevertheless turned toward idols.

The identity of the angel at the bush receives different explanations. Calvin’s discussion of verse 30 and Wesley’s notes on verses 30 and 35 identify the messenger with the Son of God before His human birth.

Augustine, On the Trinity, book II, chapter 13, allows the reading that the Savior is appearing, but also considers a created angel representing God. He does not treat the identity of the divine Person represented as fully settled. These are the interpreters’ own readings; the passage itself speaks of an angel and the voice of the Lord.
passages.god_plan_html:
The burning-bush account in Exodus 3:2–12 joins God’s awareness of His people’s suffering with His sending a deliverer. Stephen highlights that the deliverer is someone the people had rejected. The pattern prepares for his accusation concerning the rejection of Jesus at the end of the speech.

Verse 37 also repeats Moses’s promise of a coming prophet, already applied to Jesus in Acts 3:22. Hearing Moses faithfully therefore includes listening to the One he announced. Stephen presents the story as part of God’s continuing purpose, rather than a reason to set Moses against Jesus.
passages.current_position_html: Who is The Angel of the Lord? identifies the messenger in the burning bush with the Son appearing before His human birth. Its discussion of Exodus 3 emphasizes that the messenger appears, the LORD speaks, and the speaker identifies Himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. That is the existing study’s reading of the event Stephen recounts here; Acts 7 does not separately name the angel as Jesus.

deeper_study.title: Who is The Angel of the Lord?

passages.title: Acts 7:44-53
passages.section_title: Why does Stephen say God cannot be contained in a house?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 44 Our fathers had the tabernacle of the Testimony with them in the wilderness. It was constructed exactly as God had directed Moses, according to the pattern he had seen. 45 And our fathers who received it brought it in with Joshua when they dispossessed the nations God drove out before them. It remained until the time of David, 46 who found favor in the sight of God and asked to provide a dwelling place for the God of Jacob. 47 But it was Solomon who built the house for Him. 48 However, the Most High does not dwell in houses made by human hands. As the prophet says: 49 ‘Heaven is My throne and the earth is My footstool. What kind of house will you build for Me, says the Lord, or where will My place of repose be? 50 Has not My hand made all these things?’ 51 You stiff-necked people with uncircumcised hearts and ears! You always resist the Holy Spirit, just as your fathers did. 52 Which of the prophets did your fathers fail to persecute? They even killed those who foretold the coming of the Righteous One. And now you are His betrayers and murderers— 53 you who received the law ordained by angels, yet have not kept it.”

It was constructed exactly as God had directed Moses, according to the pattern he had seen. 45 And our fathers who received it brought it in with Joshua when they dispossessed the nations God drove out before them. It remained until the time of David, 46 who found favor in the sight of God and asked to provide a dwelling place for the God of Jacob. 47 But it was Solomon who built the house for Him.

48 However, the Most High does not dwell in houses made by human hands. As the prophet says: 49 ‘Heaven is My throne and the earth is My footstool. What kind of house will you build for Me, says the Lord, or where will My place of repose be? 50 Has not My hand made all these things?’

51 You stiff-necked people with uncircumcised hearts and ears! You always resist the Holy Spirit, just as your fathers did. 52 Which of the prophets did your fathers fail to persecute? They even killed those who foretold the coming of the Righteous One. And now you are His betrayers and murderers— 53 you who received the law ordained by angels, yet have not kept it.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Stephen recounts the tabernacle made according to God’s pattern, its arrival in the land, David’s desire for a dwelling place, and Solomon’s building of the temple. He recognizes that history before making the point that the Most High does not dwell in houses made by human hands.

The quotation from Isaiah places the building alongside the God who made heaven and earth. The Creator is greater than what people can construct. The speech then turns directly to the council’s response to God: resistance to the Spirit, persecution of the prophets and betrayal of the Righteous One.

The language of uncircumcised hearts and ears contrasts an outward religious mark with a refusal to listen. Deuteronomy 10:16 already joined circumcision of the heart with ceasing to be stiff-necked. Stephen applies a familiar scriptural challenge to people who claim to defend the law while failing to keep it.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand Stephen as rejecting the idea that a building can contain God or guarantee the faithfulness of those who use it. Wesley on verse 48 connects the point with Solomon’s own acknowledgment that even heaven cannot contain God.

Traditions explain the place of church buildings differently. The Catholic Church’s Catechism, paragraphs 1179–1181, says new-covenant worship is not tied exclusively to one place while describing church buildings as visible signs of the church and places where the Lord’s Supper is celebrated and Christ’s real presence in that sacrament is honored.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 21, paragraph 6, says worship is not made more acceptable by a location, while requiring care for the gathered public worship of the church. Both recognize that God is greater than a building, while understanding the significance of church buildings and worship within them differently.
passages.god_plan_html:
Isaiah 66:1–2, the passage Stephen quotes, goes on to describe the person God regards: humble, sorry for sin and responsive to His word. The challenge is therefore about the worshipper’s response as well as the limits of the building.

Ephesians 2:19–22 describes God’s people being built together on Christ the cornerstone into His dwelling by the Spirit. The wider New Testament develops the theme of God’s presence through Christ and His people, rather than confining it within what human hands construct.
passages.current_position_html: Worship as the Early Church Knew It directly uses Acts 7:48–50 to challenge an understanding of God’s dwelling centered on a building. The study connects this with the gathered people as God’s temple through His Spirit. Its emphasis is reverence for God’s presence among His people and a faithful response to His word, rather than treating a place as a substitute for that life.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

passages.god_plan_html:
Isaiah 66:1–2, the passage Stephen quotes, goes on to describe the person God regards: humble, sorry for sin and responsive to His word. The challenge is therefore about the worshipper’s response as well as the limits of the building.

Ephesians 2:19–22 describes God’s people being built together on Christ the cornerstone into His dwelling by the Spirit. The wider New Testament develops the theme of God’s presence through Christ and His people, rather than confining it within what human hands construct.

passages.title: Acts 7:54-60
passages.section_title: What does Stephen see and pray as he is killed?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 54 On hearing this, the members of the Sanhedrin were enraged, and they gnashed their teeth at him. 55 But Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, looked intently into heaven and saw the glory of God and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. 56 “Look,” he said, “I see heaven open and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.” 57 At this they covered their ears, cried out in a loud voice, and rushed together at him. 58 They dragged him out of the city and began to stone him. Meanwhile the witnesses laid their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul. 59 While they were stoning him, Stephen appealed, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” 60 Falling on his knees, he cried out in a loud voice, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” And when he had said this, he fell asleep.

57 At this they covered their ears, cried out in a loud voice, and rushed together at him. 58 They dragged him out of the city and began to stone him. Meanwhile the witnesses laid their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul. 59 While they were stoning him, Stephen appealed, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” 60 Falling on his knees, he cried out in a loud voice, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” And when he had said this, he fell asleep.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The council responds to Stephen’s accusation with fury. Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, sees God’s glory and Jesus standing at God’s right hand. He describes the Son of Man in that place of authority.

The people cover their ears, rush at him and drag him outside the city to stone him. The witnesses leave their garments with a young man named Saul. It is a brief introduction to someone who will have a much larger part in the story.

Stephen’s final words are prayers. He asks the Lord Jesus to receive his spirit and asks that this sin not be held against those killing him. Luke describes his death as falling asleep. His witness ends in trust and a prayer for his enemies rather than a demand that they suffer with him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read the vision as confirmation of Jesus’s authority with God and Stephen’s confidence in Him at death. Commentators explain the standing differently: Wesley on verse 56 sees Jesus ready to receive him, while Calvin on verse 56 understands both standing and sitting at God’s right hand as expressions of Christ’s power and kingdom.

Wesley’s note on verse 59 also understands the prayer directed to Jesus as worship of Him. Calvin’s discussion of that verse emphasizes Stephen’s faith in entrusting his spirit to Christ and his love in praying for his enemies. Neither emphasis requires imagining that Stephen feels no pain or that Luke has supplied every detail of his thoughts.
passages.god_plan_html:
At His own hearing, Jesus speaks of the Son of Man at God’s right hand in Luke 22:69. Stephen’s vision presents the rejected Jesus in that place of authority. The verdict of the people killing the witness does not overturn the Lord’s place before God.

Stephen’s entrusting of his spirit recalls Jesus’s prayer to the Father in Luke 23:46. His prayer for his attackers also follows Jesus’s instruction in Matthew 5:44 to love enemies and pray for persecutors. The witness follows his Lord in both trust and mercy at the point of death.

passages.title: Acts 8:1-8
passages.section_title: How does persecution carry the message beyond Jerusalem?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 And Saul was there, giving approval to Stephen’s death. On that day a great persecution broke out against the church in Jerusalem, and all except the apostles were scattered throughout Judea and Samaria. 2 God-fearing men buried Stephen and mourned deeply over him. 3 But Saul began to destroy the church. Going from house to house, he dragged off men and women and put them in prison. 4 Those who had been scattered preached the word wherever they went. 5 Philip went down to a city in Samaria and proclaimed the Christ to them. 6 The crowds all paid close attention to Philip’s message and to the signs they saw him perform. 7 With loud shrieks, unclean spirits came out of many who were possessed, and many of the paralyzed and lame were healed. 8 So there was great joy in that city.

On that day a great persecution broke out against the church in Jerusalem, and all except the apostles were scattered throughout Judea and Samaria. 2 God-fearing men buried Stephen and mourned deeply over him. 3 But Saul began to destroy the church. Going from house to house, he dragged off men and women and put them in prison.

4 Those who had been scattered preached the word wherever they went. 5 Philip went down to a city in Samaria and proclaimed the Christ to them. 6 The crowds all paid close attention to Philip’s message and to the signs they saw him perform. 7 With loud shrieks, unclean spirits came out of many who were possessed, and many of the paralyzed and lame were healed. 8 So there was great joy in that city.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Saul approves of Stephen’s death, and severe persecution breaks out against the Jerusalem church. Believers scatter through Judea and Samaria, while the apostles remain. God-fearing men bury Stephen and mourn him, while Saul enters homes and imprisons both men and women.

Those who scatter continue proclaiming the word. Their departure is more than a change of address: the message goes with them. Philip travels to a city in Samaria and proclaims the Christ. Acts 21:8 later identifies this Philip as the evangelist who was one of the Seven.

The crowds attend to his message and the signs that accompany it. People troubled by unclean spirits are delivered, and people who were paralyzed or lame are healed. The scene ends with great joy in the city, following the grief and violence described at its beginning.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the scattering as a major step in the message’s movement beyond Jerusalem, through believers who continue speaking about Jesus. Wesley on verse 4 connects this account with the later continuation of the scattered believers’ witness in Acts 11:19.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus named Judea and Samaria in the commission recorded in Acts 1:8. Those are the very regions named in the scattering here. Opposition to the witnesses becomes part of the circumstances through which the message reaches the next places.

The suffering remains real: Stephen is mourned, and men and women are imprisoned. The spread of the word does not make that violence good. It shows that the attempt to silence the message has not brought God’s purpose to an end.

passages.title: Acts 8:9-25
passages.section_title: Why does Peter rebuke Simon’s offer of money?

versions.text: 9 Prior to that time, a man named Simon had practiced sorcery in the city and astounded the people of Samaria. He claimed to be someone great, 10 and all the people, from the least to the greatest, heeded his words and said, “This man is the divine power called the Great Power.” 11 They paid close attention to him because he had astounded them for a long time with his sorcery. 12 But when they believed Philip as he preached the gospel of the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women. 13 Even Simon himself believed and was baptized. He followed Philip closely and was astounded by the great signs and miracles he observed. 14 When the apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them. 15 On their arrival, they prayed for them to receive the Holy Spirit. 16 For the Holy Spirit had not yet fallen upon any of them; they had simply been baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus. 17 Then Peter and John laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit. 18 When Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money. 19 “Give me this power as well,” he said, “so that everyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit.” 20 But Peter replied, “May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could buy the gift of God with money! 21 You have no part or share in our ministry, because your heart is not right before God. 22 Repent, therefore, of your wickedness, and pray to the Lord. section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Simon has long impressed the people through sorcery and his claim to greatness. Philip’s message directs them toward God’s kingdom and Jesus Christ. Men and women believe and are baptized. Luke says Simon also believes and is baptized, then follows Philip in amazement at the signs.

When the apostles in Jerusalem hear that Samaria has received God’s word, they send Peter and John. The two pray and lay hands on the baptized believers, who receive the Holy Spirit. Luke explicitly describes that order here; it needs to be read alongside the other accounts of receiving the Spirit.

Simon sees what happens and offers money for the authority to give the Spirit through his own hands. Peter rebukes the attempt to buy God’s gift, exposes the condition of his heart, and calls him to repent and pray for forgiveness. Simon asks the apostles to pray for him. Luke does not describe the rest of his life.

The visit ends with Peter and John speaking God’s word and preaching in Samaritan villages on their return journey. The message is spreading through Philip and through the apostles who have joined the work.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians agree that God’s gift cannot be bought. They differ over how the Samaritans’ reception of the Spirit relates to baptism and to the experience of other believers.

The Catholic Church’s Catechism, paragraphs 1315–1316, directly cites Acts 8:14–17 in teaching about confirmation. Paragraph 1288 understands the apostolic laying on of hands as its origin: a gift of the Spirit that completes and strengthens the grace God gives in baptism.

Reformed explanations also vary. Calvin on verse 16 understands the later reception as extraordinary gifts given to people in whom the Spirit was already at work giving new life. The 1978 Orthodox Presbyterian committee report, section I, places Samaria within the historical stages of the Spirit’s coming to the church, while teaching that every believer shares in baptism with the Spirit through belonging to Christ from the time they come to faith. That report is a committee’s explanation rather than an official confession of faith.

The Assemblies of God’s Statement of Fundamental Truths, sections 7–8, cites the Samaritan account in teaching a baptism in the Spirit distinct from and following the beginning of Christian life, giving power for service. It identifies tongues as the initial physical evidence of that experience. Luke does not explicitly name tongues in this scene.

Simon’s belief is another question. Calvin’s note on verse 13 understands a real conviction that the message is true, but without the new life and wholehearted response he distinguishes from that conviction. Thomas Constable on verse 13 instead understands Simon as a genuine believer who falls into serious sin. These are different readings of his condition, not different judgments about whether his offer needs repentance.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus had already been welcomed by Samaritans who confessed Him as Savior of the world in John 4:39–42. Now the risen Lord’s message brings baptized believers and the apostles into a shared work in Samaria. Their place in the story is not an afterthought to His mission.

John’s participation also provides a striking comparison with Luke 9:52–55. There, James and John wanted fire called down on an unwelcoming Samaritan village, and Jesus rebuked them. Here John prays for Samaritans to receive the Spirit and joins in proclaiming the good news among them. This comparison highlights the change in his service without claiming to know every motive behind his journey.

passages.title: Acts 8:26-40
passages.section_title: How does Philip help the Ethiopian official understand Jesus?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 26 Now an angel of the Lord said to Philip, “Get up and go south to the desert road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza.” 27 So he started out, and on his way he met an Ethiopian eunuch, a court official in charge of the entire treasury of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians. He had gone to Jerusalem to worship, 28 and on his return was sitting in his chariot reading Isaiah the prophet. 29 The Spirit said to Philip, “Go over to that chariot and stay by it.” 30 So Philip ran up and heard the man reading Isaiah the prophet. “Do you understand what you are reading?” Philip asked. 31 “How can I,” he said, “unless someone guides me?” And he invited Philip to come up and sit with him. 32 The eunuch was reading this passage of Scripture: “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and as a lamb before the shearer is silent, so He did not open His mouth. 33 In His humiliation He was deprived of justice. Who can recount His descendants? For His life was removed from the earth.” 34 “Tell me,” said the eunuch, “who is the prophet talking about, himself or someone else?” 35 Then Philip began with this very Scripture and told him the good news about Jesus. 36 As they traveled along the road and came to some water, the eunuch said, “Look, here is water! What is there to prevent me from being baptized?” 38 And he gave orders to stop the chariot. Then both Philip and the eunuch went down into the water, and Philip baptized him. 39 When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord carried Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more, but went on his way rejoicing. 40 But Philip appeared at Azotus and traveled through that region, preaching the gospel in all the towns until he came to Caesarea.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
An angel directs Philip to the desert road from Jerusalem toward Gaza. There he meets an Ethiopian royal official returning from worship in Jerusalem and reading Isaiah. The Spirit directs Philip to join him, and a question about understanding the text becomes an invitation to sit alongside him.

Luke calls the man a eunuch and says he manages the queen’s treasury. Eunuchs were men unable to father children, often through castration, and could hold important court responsibilities; Thayer’s entry explains the connection. Candace is a form of the royal title kandake, associated with Nubia south of Egypt. The Met’s account of Nubia describes the title for a ruling queen mother in that region.

The official is reading about the suffering servant and asks whether Isaiah is speaking about himself or someone else. Philip begins with that Scripture and tells him the good news about Jesus. Luke gives the starting point and the subject, rather than a full transcript of Philip’s explanation.

When they come to water, the official asks about baptism. Philip baptizes him, the Spirit carries Philip away, and the official continues rejoicing. Philip continues preaching as he travels toward Caesarea. The meeting joins God’s direction, careful attention to Scripture and a personal response to the message.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand Philip’s explanation as identifying the suffering servant of Isaiah 53 with Jesus and leading the official to baptism. Traditions differ over how baptism should be performed and over how much this particular account establishes about it.

The Catholic Church’s Catechism, paragraph 1239, calls immersion—being put fully under the water—the most expressive way of performing baptism while also allowing pouring. The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 28, paragraph 3, says immersion is not necessary and accepts pouring or sprinkling. The 1689 Baptist Confession, chapter 29, paragraph 4, requires immersion for proper administration.

Commentators also differ about the descent into the water. Calvin on verse 38 understands it as the ancient practice of immersing the body, while allowing other ways of baptizing. Wesley on verse 38 does not regard the account of going down as establishing immersion by itself.

Some Bible editions include a confession of faith at verse 37. The BSB places it in a footnote, so its main text goes from verse 36 to verse 38. The USCCB’s note on verse 37 explains its absence from the earliest manuscripts. The official’s question, baptism and rejoicing remain in the account.
passages.god_plan_html:
Isaiah 53:7–12 moves from the servant’s suffering and death to bearing the sins of many and bringing them righteousness. Acts explicitly shows Philip beginning with that passage to announce Jesus. Scripture’s suffering servant is central to the good news, not an obstacle that has to be explained away.

Isaiah 56:3–7 also promises welcome and a lasting name for faithful foreigners and eunuchs, joining their hope to God’s house of prayer for all nations. Luke does not explicitly quote that passage here. It provides a meaningful biblical parallel to the welcome and joy of a foreign eunuch responding to Jesus.
passages.current_position_html: Baptism uses the official’s question and baptism as a direct example of responding to the gospel with obedience. The study also reads going down into and coming up from the water alongside the wider biblical picture as supporting immersion as the normal practice. It does not treat every other way of baptizing as automatically invalid in every circumstance. The emphasis is faith expressed in baptism, rather than delaying the response without reason.

He approached the high priest 2 and requested letters to the synagogues in Damascus, so that if he found any men or women belonging to the Way, he could bring them as prisoners to Jerusalem. 3 As Saul drew near to Damascus on his journey, suddenly a light from heaven flashed around him. 4 He fell to the ground and heard a voice say to him, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?” 5 “Who are You, Lord?” Saul asked. “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting,” He replied. 6 “Now get up and go into the city, and you will be told what you must do.” 7 The men traveling with Saul stood there speechless. Saul is still threatening the disciples when he requests letters to the synagogues in Damascus. His aim is to arrest men and women belonging to the Way and bring them to Jerusalem. The Way is a name for the followers of Jesus; the people Saul seeks are the same community he has been attacking.

Near Damascus, a light from heaven interrupts the journey. Saul falls to the ground and hears Jesus identify Himself as the One Saul is persecuting. Saul has been attacking disciples, yet Jesus speaks of those attacks as directed against Himself. He orders Saul into the city to await further instructions.

The man who came to take others away as prisoners now has to be led by the hand. For three days he cannot see and takes neither food nor drink. Luke describes an encounter with the risen Jesus, followed by helplessness and waiting, before introducing Ananias.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians read this as an act of mercy initiated by Jesus, who confronts a persecutor rather than waiting for him to become friendly to the faith. They differ over how this striking account relates to God’s grace and human response in conversion more generally.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 10, paragraphs 1–2, teaches that God renews the will of those He has chosen and brings them to Christ, so that they come freely because His grace makes them willing. Calvin on verse 3 emphasizes the reversal of Saul’s hostile purpose.

The Methodist Articles of Religion, Article VIII, teach that people cannot turn to faith by their own natural strength: God’s grace goes before them and works with their response. Wesley on verse 15 distinguishes God’s unconditional selection of particular people for particular work from the broader questions readers may ask about salvation.

The Catholic Church’s Catechism, paragraphs 153–155, likewise calls faith God’s gift while describing believing as a human act in which the mind and will cooperate with grace. These statements give different frameworks for understanding God’s action; none makes Saul the person who first sought this meeting with Jesus.

The later accounts add details. Acts 22:9, in the BSB, says the companions could not understand the voice, while verse 7 here says they heard it. Acts 26:13–14 describes the light and says they all fell. Luke’s accounts should be compared rather than filling this scene with details it does not give, such as a horse.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus’ identification with the people Saul attacks is a powerful part of the encounter. A related connection appears in 1 Corinthians 12:12–27, where Paul describes believers as Christ’s body and explains that one member’s suffering concerns the others. This is a biblical connection, not a claim that this scene contains every later detail of Paul’s teaching about the church.

Paul later explains the mercy shown to him in 1 Timothy 1:12–16: his former violence becomes the background against which Christ’s patience is displayed for others who will believe. His past is not denied or excused. It does not prevent Christ from showing mercy and appointing him to service.
passages.current_position_html: Returning to the Word draws on the name “the Way” in this passage to describe a life rooted in Jesus and grounded in what God has said. Following Him involves a way of living, not simply adopting a religious label. This is the study’s developed point about the name; it does not settle the separate questions about how every conversion takes place.

passages.title: Acts 9:10-19
passages.section_title: Why does Jesus send Ananias to Saul?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 In Damascus there was a disciple named Ananias. The Lord spoke to him in a vision, “Ananias!” “Here I am, Lord,” he answered. 11 “Get up!” the Lord told him. “Go to the house of Judas on Straight Street and ask for a man from Tarsus named Saul, for he is praying. 12 In a vision he has seen a man named Ananias come and place his hands on him to restore his sight.” 13 But Ananias answered, “Lord, many people have told me about this man and all the harm he has done to Your saints in Jerusalem. 14 And now he is here with authority from the chief priests to arrest all who call on Your name.” 15 “Go!” said the Lord. “This man is My chosen instrument to carry My name before the Gentiles and their kings, and before the people of Israel. 16 I will show him how much he must suffer for My name.” 17 So Ananias went to the house, and when he arrived, he placed his hands on Saul. “Brother Saul,” he said, “the Lord Jesus, who appeared to you on the road as you were coming here, has sent me so that you may see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit.” 18 At that instant, something like scales fell from Saul’s eyes, and his sight was restored. He got up and was baptized, 19 and after taking some food, he regained his strength. And he spent several days with the disciples in Damascus.
paragraphs: 10 In Damascus there was a disciple named Ananias. The Lord spoke to him in a vision, “Ananias!” “Here I am, Lord,” he answered. 11 “Get up!” the Lord told him. “Go to the house of Judas on Straight Street and ask for a man from Tarsus named Saul, for he is praying. 12 In a vision he has seen a man named Ananias come and place his hands on him to restore his sight.” 13 But Ananias answered, “Lord, many people have told me about this man and all the harm he has done to Your saints in Jerusalem. 14 And now he is here with authority from the chief priests to arrest all who call on Your name.” 15 “Go!” said the Lord. “This man is My chosen instrument to carry My name before the Gentiles and their kings, and before the people of Israel. 16 I will show him how much he must suffer for My name.”

17 So Ananias went to the house, and when he arrived, he placed his hands on Saul. “Brother Saul,” he said, “the Lord Jesus, who appeared to you on the road as you were coming here, has sent me so that you may see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit.” 18 At that instant, something like scales fell from Saul’s eyes, and his sight was restored. He got up and was baptized, 19 and after taking some food, he regained his strength. And he spent several days with the disciples in Damascus.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lord speaks to Ananias, a disciple in Damascus, and gives him an address and a person to find. Saul is praying and has seen a vision of Ananias laying hands on him so that he may see again. God is preparing both men for a meeting neither has arranged.

Ananias knows about Saul’s violence and the authority behind his visit. His concern is specific and understandable. Jesus repeats the command to go and identifies Saul as His chosen instrument to carry His name before Gentiles, kings and Israel. The calling includes suffering; it is not a promise of an easy life.

Ananias goes, lays hands on Saul and addresses him as a brother. He says Jesus has sent him for the restoration of Saul’s sight and his filling with the Holy Spirit. Something like scales falls from Saul’s eyes, he sees again and is baptized. Food restores his strength, and he spends several days with the Damascus disciples. The community he came to imprison now receives him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly see Ananias as an obedient disciple through whom Jesus restores and welcomes Saul. They differ over how baptism relates to the forgiveness and new life involved in his response.

The Catholic Church’s Catechism, paragraph 1213, teaches that through baptism people are freed from sin, born into God’s family and joined to Christ and the church. The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 28, paragraphs 5–6, teaches that God truly gives the grace baptism promises, while denying that salvation is inseparably tied to receiving it or that its effect must occur at the moment it is performed.

The later retelling in Acts 22:12–16 includes Ananias’s call to baptism, washing away sins and calling on Jesus’ name. The two accounts belong together. Here Luke gives the sequence of restoration, baptism and food without stopping to define the exact instant at which every part of Saul’s response takes place.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus names a purpose that reaches beyond Saul’s own recovery: witness before the nations, rulers and Israel. Galatians 1:15–16 gives Paul’s own account of being called by grace so that he might proclaim God’s Son among the Gentiles. This is an explicit explanation of his calling, rather than a hidden meaning assigned to his blindness.

Jesus also brings Saul into contact with a disciple who has reason to fear him. The commission comes from the Lord, yet its outworking includes prayer, an obedient visit and the help of the people Saul has harmed. God’s larger purpose does not make those personal acts of care unimportant.
passages.current_position_html: Baptism addresses this same encounter through Ananias’s words in Acts 22:16. The study connects the washing away of sins with calling on Jesus in genuine faith and rejects the idea that the water acts independently of faith. Saul’s baptism belongs to his response to Jesus; the study does not treat the physical water as having saving power of its own.

passages.title: Acts 9:20-31
passages.section_title: How does Saul become a witness among people who fear him?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 20 Saul promptly began to proclaim Jesus in the synagogues, declaring, “He is the Son of God.” 21 All who heard him were astounded and asked, “Isn’t this the man who wreaked havoc in Jerusalem on those who call on this name? And hasn’t he come here to take them as prisoners to the chief priests?” 22 But Saul was empowered all the more, and he confounded the Jews living in Damascus by proving that Jesus is the Christ. 23 After many days had passed, the Jews conspired to kill him, 24 but Saul learned of their plot. Day and night they watched the city gates in order to kill him. 25 One night, however, his disciples took him and lowered him in a basket through a window in the wall. 26 When Saul arrived in Jerusalem, he tried to join the disciples, but they were all afraid of him, not believing that he was a disciple. 27 Then Barnabas brought him to the apostles and described how Saul had seen the Lord, who had spoken to him on the road to Damascus, and how Saul had spoken boldly in that city in the name of Jesus. 28 So Saul stayed with them, moving about freely in Jerusalem and speaking boldly in the name of the Lord. 29 He talked and debated with the Grecian Jews, but they tried to kill him. 30 When the brothers learned of this, they took him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus. 31 Then the church throughout Judea, Galilee, and Samaria experienced a time of peace. It grew in strength and numbers, living in the fear of the Lord and the encouragement of the Holy Spirit.

And hasn’t he come here to take them as prisoners to the chief priests?” 22 But Saul was empowered all the more, and he confounded the Jews living in Damascus by proving that Jesus is the Christ. 23 After many days had passed, the Jews conspired to kill him, 24 but Saul learned of their plot. Day and night they watched the city gates in order to kill him. 25 One night, however, his disciples took him and lowered him in a basket through a window in the wall.

26 When Saul arrived in Jerusalem, he tried to join the disciples, but they were all afraid of him, not believing that he was a disciple. 27 Then Barnabas brought him to the apostles and described how Saul had seen the Lord, who had spoken to him on the road to Damascus, and how Saul had spoken boldly in that city in the name of Jesus. 28 So Saul stayed with them, moving about freely in Jerusalem and speaking boldly in the name of the Lord. 29 He talked and debated with the Grecian Jews, but they tried to kill him. 30 When the brothers learned of this, they took him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus. 31 Then the church throughout Judea, Galilee, and Samaria experienced a time of peace. It grew in strength and numbers, living in the fear of the Lord and the encouragement of the Holy Spirit.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Saul promptly begins proclaiming Jesus as God’s Son in the Damascus synagogues. The hearers recognize the man who had come to arrest believers. His message astonishes them, and he grows stronger in showing that Jesus is the Christ.

After many days, a plot against his life leads his disciples to lower him through a window in the wall in a basket. Luke’s brief account does not supply every journey during this period. Galatians 1:17–19 records a journey to Arabia, a return to Damascus and a Jerusalem visit after three years. 2 Corinthians 11:32–33 also describes the escape and identifies a governor under King Aretas as seeking Saul’s arrest.

In Jerusalem, the disciples fear Saul and do not believe he is a disciple. Barnabas brings him to the apostles and describes his encounter with Jesus and his bold witness in Damascus. Saul is then able to move among them and speak openly about the Lord.

When another attempt is made to kill him, the brothers take him to Caesarea and send him to Tarsus. Luke closes with the church throughout Judea, Galilee and Samaria enjoying peace, growing stronger and increasing in numbers through reverence for the Lord and the Spirit’s encouragement.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as the visible reversal of Saul’s former work and an account of the church learning to receive him through Barnabas’s help. Wesley on verses 26–27 connects the Jerusalem visit with Galatians 1 and treats evidence of Saul’s changed life as relevant to the disciples’ concerns.
passages.god_plan_html:
Galatians 1:23–24 explains how other believers heard that their former persecutor was now proclaiming the faith he had tried to destroy, and glorified God because of him. The changed life points beyond Saul’s abilities to God’s mercy.

The threatened violence also begins to show the cost named in Acts 9:16. Saul’s rescue depends on other disciples, a basket and a night escape. Being chosen for a significant work does not make him self-sufficient or exempt him from danger.

passages.title: Acts 9:32-35
passages.section_title: Who does Peter say is healing Aeneas?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 32 As Peter traveled throughout the area, he went to visit the saints in Lydda. 33 There he found a man named Aeneas who had been paralyzed and bedridden for eight years. 34 “Aeneas,” Peter said to him, “Jesus Christ heals you! Get up and put away your mat.” Immediately Aeneas got up, 35 and all who lived in Lydda and Sharon saw him and turned to the Lord.
paragraphs: 32 As Peter traveled throughout the area, he went to visit the saints in Lydda. 33 There he found a man named Aeneas who had been paralyzed and bedridden for eight years. 34 “Aeneas,” Peter said to him, “Jesus Christ heals you! Get up and put away your mat.” Immediately Aeneas got up, 35 and all who lived in Lydda and Sharon saw him and turned to the Lord.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Luke turns from Saul to Peter’s visits among the believers. In Lydda he finds Aeneas, who has been paralyzed and bedridden for eight years. Peter names Jesus Christ as the One healing him and tells him to get up and put away his mat.

Aeneas rises immediately. The people in Lydda and Sharon see him and turn to the Lord. The result Luke stresses is not only a change in one man’s condition, but a response to the Lord among those who see him.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the healing as Christ’s work through Peter, with the apostle directing attention to Jesus rather than claiming independent power. The event leads its witnesses to the Lord.
passages.god_plan_html: This continues the pattern already visible in Acts 3:12–16: Peter refuses personal credit for a healing and directs people to the risen Jesus. Acts shows Jesus’ work continuing through His witnesses after His ascension, with the healing serving the spread of the message.

passages.title: Acts 9:36-43
passages.section_title: What does Tabitha’s return to life show?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 36 In Joppa there was a disciple named Tabitha (which is translated as Dorcas), who was always occupied with works of kindness and charity. 37 At that time, however, she became sick and died, and her body was washed and placed in an upper room. 38 Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to urge him, “Come to us without delay.” 39 So Peter got up and went with them. On his arrival, they took him to the upper room. All the widows stood around him, weeping and showing him the tunics and other clothing that Dorcas had made while she was still with them. 40 Then Peter sent them all out of the room. He knelt down and prayed, and turning toward her body, he said, “Tabitha, get up!” She opened her eyes, and seeing Peter, she sat up. 41 Peter took her by the hand and helped her up. Then he called the saints and widows and presented her to them alive. 42 This became known all over Joppa, and many people believed in the Lord. 43 And Peter stayed for several days in Joppa with a tanner named Simon.

On his arrival, they took him to the upper room. All the widows stood around him, weeping and showing him the tunics and other clothing that Dorcas had made while she was still with them.

40 Then Peter sent them all out of the room. He knelt down and prayed, and turning toward her body, he said, “Tabitha, get up!” She opened her eyes, and seeing Peter, she sat up. 41 Peter took her by the hand and helped her up. Then he called the saints and widows and presented her to them alive. 42 This became known all over Joppa, and many people believed in the Lord. 43 And Peter stayed for several days in Joppa with a tanner named Simon.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Tabitha is a disciple in Joppa known for kindness and help for others. Luke gives Dorcas as the translation of her name. The Greek name Δορκάς (Dorkas, dor-KAHS) means gazelle; Thayer’s entry explains the name. Her work has a personal effect: the widows show Peter clothing she made while she was with them.

She becomes sick and dies. Her body is washed and placed in an upstairs room, and the disciples urgently send for Peter in nearby Lydda. Luke reports the request without telling us everything they expect him to do.

Peter sends the others out, kneels and prays. Then he tells Tabitha to get up. She opens her eyes, sits up and is presented alive to the believers and widows. News spreads through Joppa, and many believe in the Lord. Peter remains with Simon, a tanner, setting the location for the next account.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a real restoration to life through God’s power, with Peter’s prayer showing his dependence on God. Tabitha’s kindness and the community’s grief are part of the account, but Luke does not say that good works earned her return to life.
passages.god_plan_html:
The scene has clear biblical parallels. In Mark 5:35–43, Peter is present when Jesus raises Jairus’s daughter. Here he again encounters a grieving household and a command to rise. The important distinction remains: Peter kneels in prayer; he is serving the Lord whose power restores life.

1 Kings 17:17–24 provides another parallel: Elijah prays, a dead child lives and the restored child is returned to a grieving person. These are comparisons Scripture supports, not predictions that every detail in one scene must match another. In Acts, the result is that many people in Joppa believe in the Lord.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Acts 10:1-16
passages.section_title: Why does God prepare both Cornelius and Peter?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 At Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius, a centurion in what was called the Italian Regiment. 2 He and all his household were devout and God-fearing. He gave generously to the people and prayed to God regularly. 3 One day at about the ninth hour, he had a clear vision of an angel of God who came to him and said, “Cornelius!” 4 Cornelius stared at him in fear and asked, “What is it, Lord?” The angel answered, “Your prayers and gifts to the poor have ascended as a memorial offering before God. 5 Now send men to Joppa to call for a man named Simon who is called Peter. 6 He is staying with Simon the tanner, whose house is by the sea.” 7 When the angel who spoke to him had gone, Cornelius called two of his servants and a devout soldier from among his attendants. 8 He explained what had happened and sent them to Joppa. 9 The next day at about the sixth hour, as the men were approaching the city on their journey, Peter went up on the roof to pray. 10 He became hungry and wanted something to eat, but while the meal was being prepared, he fell into a trance. 11 He saw heaven open and something like a large sheet being let down to earth by its four corners. 12 It contained all kinds of four-footed animals and reptiles of the earth, as well as birds of the air. 13 Then a voice said to him: “Get up, Peter, kill and eat!” 14 “No, Lord!” Peter answered. “I have never eaten anything impure or unclean.” 15 The voice spoke to him a second time: “Do not call anything impure that God has made clean.” 16 This happened three times, and all at once the sheet was taken back up into heaven.
