9 The next day at about the sixth hour, as the men were approaching the city on their journey, Peter went up on the roof to pray. 10 He became hungry and wanted something to eat, but while the meal was being prepared, he fell into a trance. 11 He saw heaven open and something like a large sheet being let down to earth by its four corners. 12 It contained all kinds of four-footed animals and reptiles of the earth, as well as birds of the air. 13 Then a voice said to him: “Get up, Peter, kill and eat!” 14 “No, Lord!” Peter answered. “I have never eaten anything impure or unclean.” 15 The voice spoke to him a second time: “Do not call anything impure that God has made clean.” 16 This happened three times, and all at once the sheet was taken back up into heaven.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Cornelius is a centurion in Caesarea. Luke describes him and his household as devout and God-fearing, and specifically mentions his generosity and regular prayer. An angel tells him that his prayers and gifts have been remembered before God and directs him to send for Peter in Joppa.

Cornelius obeys by sending two servants and a devout soldier. Meanwhile, Peter goes to the roof to pray. He becomes hungry while food is being prepared and sees a vision of a sheet containing animals, reptiles and birds.

The command to kill and eat meets Peter’s objection that he has never eaten anything impure or unclean. The voice tells him not to call impure what God has made clean. The event happens three times. Peter does not yet understand its full meaning; the next encounter will bring the vision and the people sent by Cornelius together.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand these visions as God preparing a Gentile household and a Jewish apostle for the same meeting. Peter’s explanation in verse 28 and his retelling in Acts 11:1–18 make the welcome of Gentiles central to their meaning.
passages.god_plan_html:
The events are coordinated, but not through a plan either man has made. One receives instructions to send, while the other is being prepared to go. God’s purpose includes a real encounter in which people hear the message about Jesus.

In Acts 11:13–18, Peter explains that Cornelius was promised a message through which his household would be saved. The church’s eventual conclusion is that God has granted Gentiles repentance leading to life. That later explanation supplies the larger purpose of these unusual events.
passages.current_position_html: Should We Seek Signs From God? includes Cornelius in Acts 10 among the specific biblical accounts of God communicating through visions at important points in His larger purpose. The study distinguishes these recorded events from treating every present-day dream, impression or secondhand story as a dependable message from God. It leaves the broader debate about continuing visions open while insisting that claims must be tested.

deeper_study.title: Should We Seek Signs From God?

passages.title: Acts 10:17-33
passages.section_title: What helps Peter understand the vision?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 While Peter was puzzling over the meaning of the vision, the men sent by Cornelius found Simon’s house and approached the gate. 18 They called out to ask if Simon called Peter was staying there. 19 As Peter continued to reflect on the vision, the Spirit said to him, “Behold, three men are looking for you. 20 So get up! Go downstairs and accompany them without hesitation, because I have sent them.” 21 So Peter went down to the men and said, “Here am I, the one you are looking for. Why have you come?” 22 “Cornelius the centurion has sent us,” they said. “He is a righteous and God-fearing man with a good reputation among the whole Jewish nation. A holy angel instructed him to request your presence in his home so he could hear a message from you.” 23 So Peter invited them in as his guests. And the next day he got ready and went with them, accompanied by some of the brothers from Joppa. 24 The following day he arrived in Caesarea, where Cornelius was expecting them and had called together his relatives and close friends. 25 As Peter was about to enter, Cornelius met him and fell at his feet to worship him. 26 But Peter helped him up. “Stand up,” he said, “I am only a man myself.” 27 As Peter talked with him, he went inside and found many people gathered together. 28 He said to them, “You know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with a foreigner or visit him. But God has shown me that I should not call any man impure or unclean. 29 So when I was invited, I came without objection. I ask, then, why have you sent for me?” 30 Cornelius answered: “Four days ago I was in my house praying at this, the ninth hour. Suddenly a man in radiant clothing stood before me 31 and said, ‘Cornelius, your prayer has been heard, and your gifts to the poor have been remembered before God. 32 Therefore send to Joppa for Simon, who is called Peter. He is a guest in the home of Simon the tanner, by the sea.’ 33 So I sent for you immediately, and you were kind enough to come. Now then, we are all here in the presence of God to listen to everything the Lord has instructed you to tell us.”
paragraphs: 17 While Peter was puzzling over the meaning of the vision, the men sent by Cornelius found Simon’s house and approached the gate. 18 They called out to ask if Simon called Peter was staying there. 19 As Peter continued to reflect on the vision, the Spirit said to him, “Behold, three men are looking for you. 20 So get up! Go downstairs and accompany them without hesitation, because I have sent them.” 21 So Peter went down to the men and said, “Here am I, the one you are looking for. Why have you come?” 22 “Cornelius the centurion has sent us,” they said. “He is a righteous and God-fearing man with a good reputation among the whole Jewish nation. A holy angel instructed him to request your presence in his home so he could hear a message from you.” 23 So Peter invited them in as his guests. And the next day he got ready and went with them, accompanied by some of the brothers from Joppa.

24 The following day he arrived in Caesarea, where Cornelius was expecting them and had called together his relatives and close friends. 25 As Peter was about to enter, Cornelius met him and fell at his feet to worship him. 26 But Peter helped him up. “Stand up,” he said, “I am only a man myself.” 27 As Peter talked with him, he went inside and found many people gathered together. 28 He said to them, “You know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with a foreigner or visit him. But God has shown me that I should not call any man impure or unclean. 29 So when I was invited, I came without objection. I ask, then, why have you sent for me?”

30 Cornelius answered: “Four days ago I was in my house praying at this, the ninth hour. Suddenly a man in radiant clothing stood before me 31 and said, ‘Cornelius, your prayer has been heard, and your gifts to the poor have been remembered before God. 32 Therefore send to Joppa for Simon, who is called Peter. He is a guest in the home of Simon the tanner, by the sea.’ 33 So I sent for you immediately, and you were kind enough to come. Now then, we are all here in the presence of God to listen to everything the Lord has instructed you to tell us.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Peter is still puzzling over the vision when the messengers arrive. The Spirit directs him to accompany them without hesitation, saying He has sent them. Their account of Cornelius’s vision explains why they have come, and Peter welcomes them as guests.

The next day Peter travels with them and some believers from Joppa. Cornelius has gathered relatives and close friends to hear him. When Cornelius falls at his feet in worship, Peter helps him up and identifies himself as another human being.

Peter then gives the vision’s application to the people before him: God has shown him not to call any person impure or unclean. He has come despite the barrier he describes between a Jew and a foreigner. Luke reports Peter’s explanation without spelling out every legal or customary detail behind it.

Cornelius retells what happened while he was praying and thanks Peter for coming. The gathering is ready to hear what the Lord has instructed him to say. The story now moves from the visions and travel to the message they have brought people together to hear.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand Peter’s welcome and visit as the practical outworking of the vision: he enters a Gentile home to speak about Jesus. His refusal of worship keeps the distinction clear between God and the human messenger.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 2:11–22 describes Gentiles who were far away being brought near through Christ, with both groups having access to the Father through one Spirit. Peter’s visit is a concrete episode in this larger biblical movement toward a shared household of God.

The connection does not mean that every cultural difference disappears or that Peter now understands every consequence. In this scene, the instruction becomes an actual welcome, a journey and a willingness to speak to people he had held apart.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Acts 10:34-43
passages.section_title: What good news does Peter announce to the household?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 34 Then Peter began to speak: “I now truly understand that God does not show favoritism, 35 but welcomes those from every nation who fear Him and do what is right. 36 He has sent this message to the people of Israel, proclaiming the gospel of peace through Jesus Christ, who is Lord of all. 37 You yourselves know what has happened throughout Judea, beginning in Galilee with the baptism that John proclaimed: 38 how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power, and how Jesus went around doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, because God was with Him. 39 We are witnesses of all that He did, both in the land of the Jews and in Jerusalem. And although they put Him to death by hanging Him on a tree, 40 God raised Him up on the third day and caused Him to be seen— 41 not by all the people, but by the witnesses God had chosen beforehand, by us who ate and drank with Him after He rose from the dead. 42 And He commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that He is the One appointed by God to judge the living and the dead. 43 All the prophets testify about Him that everyone who believes in Him receives forgiveness of sins through His name.”

39 We are witnesses of all that He did, both in the land of the Jews and in Jerusalem. And although they put Him to death by hanging Him on a tree, 40 God raised Him up on the third day and caused Him to be seen— 41 not by all the people, but by the witnesses God had chosen beforehand, by us who ate and drank with Him after He rose from the dead. 42 And He commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that He is the One appointed by God to judge the living and the dead. 43 All the prophets testify about Him that everyone who believes in Him receives forgiveness of sins through His name.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Peter begins with what he now understands: God does not show favoritism toward one nation over another. He welcomes those who fear Him and do what is right. Peter immediately directs the gathered household to Jesus Christ, whom he identifies as Lord of all.

The message follows Jesus’ ministry, His death and His resurrection. Peter speaks as a witness to His work and to the risen Jesus, with whom the chosen witnesses ate and drank. Jesus’ appointment as judge of the living and the dead gives the message weight for everyone hearing it.

The speech ends with forgiveness through Jesus’ name for everyone who believes in Him. The absence of national favoritism does not make the message about Jesus unnecessary: it is the message Peter has been sent to announce to this Gentile gathering.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read the speech as announcing the same Lord and forgiveness to Gentiles as to Jews. Readers differ over the wider implications of verse 35 for people who have not yet heard about Christ.

Wesley on verse 35 understands acceptance through Christ as possible even where a person does not yet know Him, while treating the fuller knowledge brought by Peter as a great blessing. The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 10, paragraph 4, rejects salvation by another way for people who do not profess the Christian faith; its broader teaching places salvation in Christ’s call and grace.

The Catholic Church’s Catechism, paragraphs 847–848, teaches that those ignorant of the gospel through no fault of their own may attain salvation when moved by grace to seek and obey God. It also insists that the church must still proclaim the gospel. These are different accounts of how Christ’s salvation reaches people, rather than a shared claim that Jesus is unnecessary.
passages.god_plan_html:
Deuteronomy 10:17–19 already describes God as showing no partiality and loving the foreigner. Peter’s realization does not introduce a previously unloving God who has now changed His character. The news about Jesus reaches across the national boundary in keeping with God’s justice and care.

Peter later refers to this Gentile hearing in Acts 15:7–11. He says God made no distinction between the groups, cleansing their hearts by faith, and places their salvation together in the grace of Jesus. That is the New Testament’s own explanation of this episode’s importance.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Acts 10:44-48
passages.section_title: Why can Peter no longer withhold baptism from these Gentiles?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 44 While Peter was still speaking these words, the Holy Spirit fell upon all who heard his message. 45 All the circumcised believers who had accompanied Peter were astounded that the gift of the Holy Spirit had been poured out even on the Gentiles. 46 For they heard them speaking in tongues and exalting God. Then Peter said, 47 “Can anyone withhold the water to baptize these people? They have received the Holy Spirit just as we have!” 48 So he ordered that they be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to stay for a few days.
paragraphs: 44 While Peter was still speaking these words, the Holy Spirit fell upon all who heard his message. 45 All the circumcised believers who had accompanied Peter were astounded that the gift of the Holy Spirit had been poured out even on the Gentiles. 46 For they heard them speaking in tongues and exalting God. Then Peter said, 47 “Can anyone withhold the water to baptize these people? They have received the Holy Spirit just as we have!” 48 So he ordered that they be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to stay for a few days.

passages.context_html:
The Holy Spirit comes upon the hearers while Peter is still speaking. The circumcised believers who have come with him are astonished that the gift has been poured out on Gentiles. They hear them speaking in tongues and exalting God.

Peter draws a practical conclusion from what God has done: these people have received the Spirit just as the Jewish believers have, so water cannot be withheld from them. He orders their baptism in Jesus Christ’s name. They then ask him to remain with them for a few days.

The sequence matters. The Spirit is given before water baptism in this account, and baptism still follows as a command to obey. The Gentile believers are not asked to become Jews first.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians agree that the gift of the Spirit here precedes water baptism and that Peter nevertheless commands baptism. They explain the relationship between this event, baptism and other believers’ experiences in different ways.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 28, paragraphs 5–6, denies that salvation is inseparably tied to receiving water baptism or that the grace it promises must be given at that precise moment. The Catholic Church’s Catechism, paragraph 1257, teaches the necessity of baptism while explicitly saying God Himself is not bound by the sacraments.

The Assemblies of God’s Statement of Fundamental Truths, sections 7–8, places speaking in tongues within its teaching about baptism in the Spirit, distinct from the beginning of Christian life and giving power for service. In this account, Luke specifically names tongues and gives the Jewish witnesses’ astonishment at the Gentiles’ reception of the same gift.
passages.current_position_html: Baptism directly examines Cornelius and his household receiving the Holy Spirit before water baptism. The study therefore rejects a fixed sequence in which nothing spiritual can happen until the water is applied. It also keeps Peter’s command in view: receiving the Spirit is a reason to proceed with baptism, rather than a reason to leave it out.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 11:15–18 explains how Peter later defends the event. He remembers Jesus’ promise of baptism in the Holy Spirit and asks who he was to hinder God. The others then glorify God for granting Gentiles repentance leading to life.

The significance reaches beyond a private experience for Cornelius. The same divine gift provides public grounds for welcoming Gentiles into the community. Acts 15:8–11 returns to this evidence when the church faces the question of what must be required of Gentile believers.

passages.title: Acts 11:1-18
passages.section_title: How does Peter explain welcoming the Gentiles?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 The apostles and brothers throughout Judea soon heard that the Gentiles also had received the word of God. 2 So when Peter went up to Jerusalem, the circumcised believers took issue with him 3 and said, “You visited uncircumcised men and ate with them.” 4 But Peter began and explained to them the whole sequence of events: 5 “I was in the city of Joppa praying, and in a trance I saw a vision of something like a large sheet being let down from heaven by its four corners, and it came right down to me. 6 I looked at it closely and saw four-footed animals of the earth, wild beasts, reptiles, and birds of the air. 7 Then I heard a voice saying to me, ‘Get up, Peter, kill and eat.’ 8 ‘No, Lord,’ I said, ‘for nothing impure or unclean has ever entered my mouth.’ 9 But the voice spoke from heaven a second time, ‘Do not call anything impure that God has made clean.’ 10 This happened three times, and everything was drawn back up into heaven. 11 Just then three men sent to me from Caesarea stopped at the house where I was staying. 12 The Spirit told me to accompany them without hesitation. These six brothers also went with me, and we entered the man’s home. 13 He told us how he had seen an angel standing in his house and saying, ‘Send to Joppa for Simon who is called Peter. 14 He will convey to you a message by which you and all your household will be saved.’ 15 As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell upon them, just as He had fallen upon us at the beginning. 16 Then I remembered the word of the Lord, how He said, ‘John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.’ 17 So if God gave them the same gift He gave us who believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I to hinder the work of God?” 18 When they heard this, they had no further objections, and they glorified God, saying, “So then, God has granted even the Gentiles repentance unto life.”

These six brothers also went with me, and we entered the man’s home. 13 He told us how he had seen an angel standing in his house and saying, ‘Send to Joppa for Simon who is called Peter. 14 He will convey to you a message by which you and all your household will be saved.’

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
News that Gentiles have received God’s word reaches the apostles and believers in Judea. When Peter returns to Jerusalem, circumcised believers challenge him about visiting and eating with uncircumcised people. Luke identifies the objection without saying that every apostle joined in it.

Peter responds by explaining the sequence of events. He recounts the vision, the Spirit’s direction to accompany the messengers and the six brothers who went with him. Cornelius had also received instructions, including the promise of a message through which his household would be saved.

The decisive point is the gift of the Holy Spirit. Peter connects what happened to Jesus’ promise and to the gift received at the beginning. He asks how he could hinder God after God had given the same gift to these believers.

The hearers withdraw their objections and glorify God. The scene ends with recognition that God has granted Gentiles repentance leading to life. An uncomfortable question about eating together leads to a shared acknowledgment of God’s work.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand Peter’s explanation as grounds for welcoming Gentile believers on the basis of what God has done. Calvin on verse 18 highlights the hearers’ willingness to change their judgment and give God glory when the events are explained.
passages.god_plan_html:
Peter explicitly connects the event with Jesus’ promise of baptism in the Holy Spirit in Acts 1:5. He does not treat the Gentiles’ reception as a lesser gift that leaves them outside the people of God.

Acts 15:7–11 later returns to this same event when Peter explains that God made no distinction between the groups and cleansed their hearts by faith. The inclusion at stake here will matter again when the church discusses what may be required of Gentile believers.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Acts 11:19-26
passages.section_title: How does the growing church in Antioch learn to follow Jesus?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 Meanwhile those scattered by the persecution that began with Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch, speaking the message only to Jews. 20 But some of them, men from Cyprus and Cyrene, went to Antioch and began speaking to the Greeks as well, proclaiming the good news about the Lord Jesus. 21 The hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number of people believed and turned to the Lord. 22 When news of this reached the ears of the church in Jerusalem, they sent Barnabas to Antioch. 23 When he arrived and saw the grace of God, he rejoiced and encouraged them all to abide in the Lord with all their hearts. 24 Barnabas was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and faith, and a great number of people were brought to the Lord. 25 Then Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for Saul, 26 and when he found him, he brought him back to Antioch. So for a full year they met together with the church and taught large numbers of people. The disciples were first called Christians at Antioch.
paragraphs: 19 Meanwhile those scattered by the persecution that began with Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch, speaking the message only to Jews. 20 But some of them, men from Cyprus and Cyrene, went to Antioch and began speaking to the Greeks as well, proclaiming the good news about the Lord Jesus. 21 The hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number of people believed and turned to the Lord. 22 When news of this reached the ears of the church in Jerusalem, they sent Barnabas to Antioch. 23 When he arrived and saw the grace of God, he rejoiced and encouraged them all to abide in the Lord with all their hearts. 24 Barnabas was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and faith, and a great number of people were brought to the Lord.

25 Then Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for Saul, 26 and when he found him, he brought him back to Antioch. So for a full year they met together with the church and taught large numbers of people. The disciples were first called Christians at Antioch.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Luke returns to the believers scattered by the persecution associated with Stephen. They have carried the message to Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, speaking to Jews. Others from Cyprus and Cyrene also proclaim the Lord Jesus to Greeks in Antioch, and many believe and turn to the Lord.

The church in Jerusalem sends Barnabas when it hears the news. He sees God’s grace at work and rejoices. His encouragement is to remain with the Lord wholeheartedly, and Luke describes him as good, full of the Holy Spirit and faith.

Barnabas then seeks Saul in Tarsus and brings him to Antioch. Together they meet with the church and teach large numbers for a full year. The account gives room to the continuing work of teaching after people first believe.

The disciples are first called Christians in Antioch. The Greek word Χριστιανός (Christianos, khrees-tee-ah-NOS) means a follower of Christ; Thayer’s entry explains the term. Luke records where the name is first used without identifying the individual who coined it or the exact tone in which it was first spoken.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read Barnabas’s joy, encouragement and partnership with Saul as support for a growing community’s continuing life in Christ. Calvin on verse 23 emphasizes rejoicing in God’s work through other people and helping believers continue in the teaching they have received.
passages.god_plan_html:
Galatians 3:26–29 describes people of different backgrounds as one in Christ through faith and as heirs of the promise to Abraham. The mixed community in Antioch belongs within that larger biblical picture of belonging to Christ together.

This shared identity takes practical shape through encouragement and sustained teaching. Luke does not stop with the report of new believers; he shows Barnabas seeking a coworker and both men investing a year in helping the community learn.
passages.current_position_html: Worship as the Early Church Knew It uses Acts 11:26 to emphasize that the church is the gathered people, rather than the building where they meet. Barnabas and Saul meet with an assembly of believers and teach them. The study’s point here is the community’s identity, not a new rule against using a particular kind of meeting place.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

passages.title: Acts 11:26
passages.section_title: What are Barnabas and Saul doing with the church in Antioch?

passages.title: Acts 11:27-30
passages.section_title: How do the Antioch believers respond to the coming famine?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 27 In those days some prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch. 28 One of them named Agabus stood up and predicted through the Spirit that a great famine would sweep across the whole world. (This happened under Claudius.) 29 So the disciples, each according to his ability, decided to send relief to the brothers living in Judea. 30 This they did, sending their gifts to the elders with Barnabas and Saul.
paragraphs: 27 In those days some prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch. 28 One of them named Agabus stood up and predicted through the Spirit that a great famine would sweep across the whole world. (This happened under Claudius.) 29 So the disciples, each according to his ability, decided to send relief to the brothers living in Judea. 30 This they did, sending their gifts to the elders with Barnabas and Saul.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Prophets come from Jerusalem to Antioch, and Agabus predicts through the Spirit that a great famine is coming. Luke adds that it happened under Claudius. The BSB footnote gives the entire Roman world as an alternative rendering of the scope of the warning.

An independent ancient account also describes severe hunger in Judea. Josephus, Antiquities 20.2.5 and 20.5.2, records famine relief supplied by Queen Helena and her son. That provides historical context for Judea’s need; it does not establish a simultaneous shortage in every part of the globe.

The disciples decide to help according to what each can provide. Their concern becomes an actual contribution for the believers in Judea, entrusted to Barnabas and Saul for delivery to the elders. Luke puts the emphasis on the response to the warning, not on a detailed explanation of how Agabus received it.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as practical care for fellow believers: a warning about hardship leads to generous action according to each person’s means. Wesley on verses 28–29 emphasizes the disciples’ response to the distress the Judean believers would face.
passages.god_plan_html:
The welcome of Gentile believers is becoming a relationship of shared responsibility. The Antioch community is not merely receiving news and teaching from Judea; it sends material help back to believers there.

A similar principle appears in a later, different collection described in Romans 15:25–27. Paul connects Gentile participation in spiritual blessings with care for the material needs of believers in Jerusalem. That later explanation provides a useful biblical connection without identifying the two collections as the same event.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

passages.title: Acts 12:1-5
passages.section_title: How does the church respond when Herod attacks its members?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 About that time, King Herod reached out to harm some who belonged to the church. 2 He had James, the brother of John, put to death with the sword. 3 And seeing that this pleased the Jews, Herod proceeded to seize Peter during the Feast of Unleavened Bread. 4 He arrested him and put him in prison, handing him over to be guarded by four squads of four soldiers each. Herod intended to bring him out to the people after the Passover. 5 So Peter was kept in prison, but the church was fervently praying to God for him.
paragraphs: 1 About that time, King Herod reached out to harm some who belonged to the church. 2 He had James, the brother of John, put to death with the sword. 3 And seeing that this pleased the Jews, Herod proceeded to seize Peter during the Feast of Unleavened Bread. 4 He arrested him and put him in prison, handing him over to be guarded by four squads of four soldiers each. Herod intended to bring him out to the people after the Passover. 5 So Peter was kept in prison, but the church was fervently praying to God for him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the report of growth and relief for Judea, Luke describes renewed persecution. Herod has James, the brother of John, killed with the sword. This is one of the sons of Zebedee who followed Jesus, not the James Peter will mention later in the chapter.

Herod sees that this pleases the Jews and arrests Peter as well. The arrest takes place during the Feast of Unleavened Bread. Peter is guarded by four squads of four soldiers each, and Herod plans to bring him before the people after Passover.

The church’s response is fervent prayer to God for Peter. Luke sets that prayer beside the king’s confinement of him. James has died, Peter remains in danger, and the believers are appealing to God in circumstances they cannot control.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read the church’s prayer as active concern for a fellow believer under persecution. Calvin on verse 5 emphasizes sharing the burden of those suffering for the gospel rather than abandoning them.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Mark 10:35–40, James and John ask for places of honor, and Jesus tells them they will share His cup of suffering. James’s death belongs within that costly pattern of following Jesus, rather than proving that his discipleship has failed.

Luke does not explain James’s death by comparing the quality of his faith with Peter’s. The wider story of witness includes both lives given in service and dramatic deliverances; this chapter does not provide a formula for predicting which outcome any believer will receive.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Acts 12:6-19
passages.section_title: How does Peter reach the people who are praying for him?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 On the night before Herod was to bring him to trial, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, with sentries standing guard at the entrance to the prison. 7 Suddenly an angel of the Lord appeared and a light shone in the cell. He tapped Peter on the side and woke him up, saying, “Get up quickly.” And the chains fell off his wrists. 8 “Get dressed and put on your sandals,” said the angel. Peter did so, and the angel told him, “Wrap your cloak around you and follow me.” 9 So Peter followed him out, but he was unaware that what the angel was doing was real. He thought he was only seeing a vision. 10 They passed the first and second guards and came to the iron gate leading to the city, which opened for them by itself. When they had gone outside and walked the length of one block, the angel suddenly left him. 11 Then Peter came to himself and said, “Now I know for sure that the Lord has sent His angel and rescued me from Herod’s grasp and from everything the Jewish people were anticipating.” 12 And when he had realized this, he went to the house of Mary the mother of John, also called Mark, where many people had gathered together and were praying. 13 He knocked at the outer gate, and a servant girl named Rhoda came to answer it. 14 When she recognized Peter’s voice, she was so overjoyed that she forgot to open the gate, but ran inside and announced, “Peter is standing at the gate!” 15 “You are out of your mind,” they told her. But when she kept insisting it was so, they said, “It must be his angel.” 16 But Peter kept on knocking, and when they opened the door and saw him, they were astounded. 17 Peter motioned with his hand for silence, and he described how the Lord had brought him out of the prison. “Send word to James and to the brothers,” he said, and he left for another place. 18 At daybreak there was no small commotion among the soldiers as to what had become of Peter. 19 After Herod had searched for him unsuccessfully, he examined the guards and ordered that they be executed. Then he went down from Judea to Caesarea and spent some time there.

He tapped Peter on the side and woke him up, saying, “Get up quickly.” And the chains fell off his wrists. 8 “Get dressed and put on your sandals,” said the angel. Peter did so, and the angel told him, “Wrap your cloak around you and follow me.” 9 So Peter followed him out, but he was unaware that what the angel was doing was real. But when she kept insisting it was so, they said, “It must be his angel.” 16 But Peter kept on knocking, and when they opened the door and saw him, they were astounded. 17 Peter motioned with his hand for silence, and he described how the Lord had brought him out of the prison. “Send word to James and to the brothers,” he said, and he left for another place.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Peter is asleep between two soldiers when an angel wakes him. His chains fall, he dresses and follows the angel past the guards and through the iron gate. At first he thinks he is seeing a vision. Once outside, he realizes that the Lord has actually rescued him.

He goes to Mary’s house, where many people are praying. Rhoda recognizes his voice at the gate, but her joy sends her running inside before she lets him in. The others initially reject her report. Peter keeps knocking until they open the gate and see him.

Peter quiets them and explains how the Lord brought him out. He asks them to tell James and the other believers, then leaves for another place. Luke does not identify his destination. This James is distinct from the brother of John killed earlier.

At daybreak, Herod searches for Peter, questions the guards and orders their execution. The rescue is followed by further violence from the king. Luke then places Herod in Caesarea, preparing for the next scene.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the release as God’s action rather than Peter’s skill in escaping. The praying community’s surprise does not erase its prayer; Calvin on verse 15 does not treat their inability to believe Rhoda as proof that they had prayed without faith.

The words about Peter’s angel also raise a question about angelic care. The Catholic Church’s Catechism, paragraph 336, teaches that an angel stands beside each believer as a protector. Calvin’s comment on verse 15 instead says this scene does not establish a particular angel assigned to every individual, while affirming God’s protection through angels. These are a church’s teaching and an individual Reformed commentator’s reading, respectively.

Luke reports what the people say, then shows them discovering Peter himself at the gate. Their remark is not an explanation that angels must look or sound exactly like the people they protect.
passages.god_plan_html:
Peter’s rescue continues his service, but it does not mean he will never face death for following Jesus. In John 21:18–19, Jesus had already spoken about the death by which Peter would glorify God and called him to follow.

That connection keeps the deliverance in proportion. Being brought out of prison is a real gift, while faithful service can still include suffering. The story gives grounds for trust in the Lord without making escape from every danger the measure of His care.

passages.title: Acts 12:20-25
passages.section_title: What happens to Herod while God’s word continues to spread?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 20 Now Herod was in a furious dispute with the people of Tyre and Sidon, and they convened before him. Having secured the support of Blastus, the king’s chamberlain, they asked for peace, because their region depended on the king’s country for food. 21 On the appointed day, Herod donned his royal robes, sat on his throne, and addressed the people. 22 And they began to shout, “This is the voice of a god, not a man!” 23 Immediately, because Herod did not give glory to God, an angel of the Lord struck him down, and he was eaten by worms and died. 24 But the word of God continued to spread and multiply. 25 When Barnabas and Saul had fulfilled their mission to Jerusalem, they returned, bringing with them John, also called Mark.

Having secured the support of Blastus, the king’s chamberlain, they asked for peace, because their region depended on the king’s country for food. 21 On the appointed day, Herod donned his royal robes, sat on his throne, and addressed the people. 22 And they began to shout, “This is the voice of a god, not a man!” 23 Immediately, because Herod did not give glory to God, an angel of the Lord struck him down, and he was eaten by worms and died.
24 But the word of God continued to spread and multiply. 25 When Barnabas and Saul had fulfilled their mission to Jerusalem, they returned, bringing with them John, also called Mark.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Herod is in a dispute with Tyre and Sidon. Their region depends on his country for food, so representatives gain the support of Blastus, a royal official, and ask for peace. Luke does not explain every step of the dispute or say exactly how they secure his support.

On the appointed day, Herod addresses the people in royal clothing. They acclaim his voice as divine, and he does not give glory to God. Luke describes an angel striking him, his being eaten by worms and his death.

Josephus, Antiquities 19.8.2, independently describes Agrippa receiving divine acclaim at Caesarea, not rejecting it, becoming severely ill and dying after five days. His account adds the silver garment and abdominal pain; it does not supply Luke’s statement about worms. The two accounts have points of contact without being identical.

Luke then returns attention to God’s word, which continues to spread and multiply. Barnabas and Saul complete their mission and return with John Mark. The king who harmed the church has died, while the message and the work continue.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read Herod’s death as judgment upon accepting glory that belongs to God. The contrast with the continuing spread of the word shows the limits of the king’s power without requiring a medical diagnosis of his illness.
passages.god_plan_html:
Daniel 4:28–37 provides a biblical parallel in the humbling of a ruler who takes glory to himself. The outcomes differ: Nebuchadnezzar is restored and praises God, while Herod dies. The comparison concerns the limits of human rule under God, not a claim that every detail or outcome must match.

The closing report about the word carries that theme into the church’s witness. A ruler’s opposition can bring real harm, as James’s death has shown, but the ruler does not control the future of God’s message.

passages.title: Acts 13:1-3
passages.section_title: How are Barnabas and Saul sent into their next work?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now in the church at Antioch there were prophets and teachers: Barnabas, Simeon called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen (who had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch), and Saul. 2 While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, “Set apart for Me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.” 3 And after they had fasted and prayed, they laid their hands on them and sent them off.
paragraphs: 1 Now in the church at Antioch there were prophets and teachers: Barnabas, Simeon called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen (who had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch), and Saul. 2 While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, “Set apart for Me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.” 3 And after they had fasted and prayed, they laid their hands on them and sent them off.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Luke names prophets and teachers in the Antioch church: Barnabas, Simeon called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen and Saul. He notes that Manaen had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch. The list shows several people serving together without specifying that their order establishes a ranking.

While they are worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit directs them to set apart Barnabas and Saul for work to which He has already called them. The initiative comes from the Spirit, and the community responds through fasting, prayer, laying on hands and sending.

The word translated worshiping is λειτουργέω (leitourgeō, lay-toor-GEH-oh). Thayer’s entry describes service rendered to the Lord, including prayer, teaching and other service. Luke names fasting and prayer here but does not give a complete order of worship or identify every activity taking place.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly see the Spirit initiating the mission and the church responding through prayer and a public sending. Wesley on verse 2 understands this as commissioning people for their appointed work, rather than Saul first becoming an apostle at this moment.
passages.god_plan_html:
This sending moves forward the calling already described in Acts 9:15–16. Saul was chosen to carry Jesus’ name before Gentiles, rulers and Israel; the next account will show that witness reaching another place and another hearer.

Galatians 1:15–16 describes Paul’s calling by grace to proclaim God’s Son among the Gentiles. Acts places that personal calling within the praying life and practical support of a community. God’s direction and the help of fellow believers are working together in the mission.
passages.current_position_html: Worship as the Early Church Knew It directly examines the word used in Acts 13:2 as sacred service directed toward the Lord. The study emphasizes active service rather than treating believers as spectators. Here that service is connected with fasting, prayer and responding to the Spirit’s call; Luke does not supply a full list of everything the gathering included.

passages.title: Acts 13:4-12
passages.section_title: What happens when Elymas tries to turn a hearer from the message?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 4 So Barnabas and Saul, sent forth by the Holy Spirit, went down to Seleucia and sailed from there to Cyprus. 5 When they arrived at Salamis, they proclaimed the word of God in the Jewish synagogues. And John was with them as their helper. 6 They traveled through the whole island as far as Paphos, where they found a Jewish sorcerer and false prophet named Bar-Jesus, 7 an attendant of the proconsul, Sergius Paulus. The proconsul, a man of intelligence, summoned Barnabas and Saul because he wanted to hear the word of God. 8 But Elymas the sorcerer (for that is what his name means) opposed them and tried to turn the proconsul from the faith. 9 Then Saul, who was also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, looked directly at Elymas 10 and said, “O child of the devil and enemy of all righteousness, you are full of all kinds of deceit and trickery! Will you never stop perverting the straight ways of the Lord? 11 Now look, the hand of the Lord is against you, and for a time you will be blind and unable to see the light of the sun.” Immediately mist and darkness came over him, and he groped about, seeking someone to lead him by the hand. 12 When the proconsul saw what had happened, he believed, for he was astonished at the teaching about the Lord.
paragraphs: 4 So Barnabas and Saul, sent forth by the Holy Spirit, went down to Seleucia and sailed from there to Cyprus. 5 When they arrived at Salamis, they proclaimed the word of God in the Jewish synagogues. And John was with them as their helper. 6 They traveled through the whole island as far as Paphos, where they found a Jewish sorcerer and false prophet named Bar-Jesus, 7 an attendant of the proconsul, Sergius Paulus. The proconsul, a man of intelligence, summoned Barnabas and Saul because he wanted to hear the word of God. 8 But Elymas the sorcerer (for that is what his name means) opposed them and tried to turn the proconsul from the faith.

9 Then Saul, who was also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, looked directly at Elymas 10 and said, “O child of the devil and enemy of all righteousness, you are full of all kinds of deceit and trickery! Will you never stop perverting the straight ways of the Lord? 11 Now look, the hand of the Lord is against you, and for a time you will be blind and unable to see the light of the sun.” Immediately mist and darkness came over him, and he groped about, seeking someone to lead him by the hand. 12 When the proconsul saw what had happened, he believed, for he was astonished at the teaching about the Lord.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Barnabas and Saul, sent by the Holy Spirit, travel through Seleucia to Cyprus. They proclaim God’s word in the Jewish synagogues at Salamis, with John as their helper, and continue across the island to Paphos.

There Sergius Paulus, the proconsul, asks to hear God’s word. A sorcerer and false prophet named Bar-Jesus, also called Elymas, opposes the messengers and tries to turn the proconsul from the faith. Luke presents a hearer seeking the message and another person trying to obstruct his hearing.

Saul, whom Luke also identifies as Paul, confronts Elymas while filled with the Holy Spirit. He exposes his deceit and announces temporary blindness. Elymas immediately needs someone to lead him by the hand. The proconsul believes, astonished at the teaching about the Lord.

Luke’s wording introduces Paul as another name Saul already has; it does not describe a new name given at his conversion. The USCCB’s note on verse 9 likewise distinguishes the double name from a conversion-related renaming.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read the blindness as judgment on deliberate obstruction of the message, with the result directing the proconsul to the Lord’s teaching. Calvin on verse 12 connects the sign with the hearer taking that teaching seriously, rather than treating the miracle as a substitute for it.
passages.god_plan_html:
There is a notable parallel with Acts 9:1–19. Saul had opposed Jesus’ people, become blind and needed to be led by the hand; now Elymas meets temporary blindness while opposing the message. The resemblance is clear, but Luke does not say that Elymas afterward comes to faith as Saul did.

The journey also shows the witness moving among different hearers: people in Jewish synagogues and a Roman official who wants to hear. The message remains God’s word about the Lord, even as the setting changes and opposition takes another form.

passages.title: Acts 13:13-25
passages.section_title: Why does Paul begin with Israel’s history?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 After setting sail from Paphos, Paul and his companions came to Perga in Pamphylia, where John left them to return to Jerusalem. 14 And from Perga, they traveled inland to Pisidian Antioch, where they entered the synagogue on the Sabbath and sat down. 15 After the reading from the Law and the Prophets, the synagogue leaders sent word to them: “Brothers, if you have a word of encouragement for the people, please speak.” 16 Paul stood up, motioned with his hand, and began to speak: “Men of Israel and you Gentiles who fear God, listen to me! 17 The God of the people of Israel chose our fathers. He made them into a great people during their stay in Egypt, and with an uplifted arm He led them out of that land. 18 He endured their conduct for about forty years in the wilderness. 19 And having vanquished seven nations in Canaan, He gave their land to His people as an inheritance. 20 All this took about 450 years. After this, God gave them judges until the time of Samuel the prophet. 21 Then the people asked for a king, and God gave them Saul son of Kish, from the tribe of Benjamin, who ruled forty years. 22 After removing Saul, He raised up David as their king and testified about him: ‘I have found David son of Jesse a man after My own heart; he will carry out My will in its entirety.’ 23 From the descendants of this man, God has brought to Israel the Savior Jesus, as He promised. 24 Before the arrival of Jesus, John preached a baptism of repentance to all the people of Israel. 25 As John was completing his course, he said, ‘Who do you suppose I am? I am not that One. But there is One coming after me whose sandals I am not worthy to untie.’

17 The God of the people of Israel chose our fathers. He made them into a great people during their stay in Egypt, and with an uplifted arm He led them out of that land. 18 He endured their conduct for about forty years in the wilderness. 19 And having vanquished seven nations in Canaan, He gave their land to His people as an inheritance. 20 All this took about 450 years. After this, God gave them judges until the time of Samuel the prophet. 21 Then the people asked for a king, and God gave them Saul son of Kish, from the tribe of Benjamin, who ruled forty years. 22 After removing Saul, He raised up David as their king and testified about him: ‘I have found David son of Jesse a man after My own heart; he will carry out My will in its entirety.’

23 From the descendants of this man, God has brought to Israel the Savior Jesus, as He promised. 24 Before the arrival of Jesus, John preached a baptism of repentance to all the people of Israel. 25 As John was completing his course, he said, ‘Who do you suppose I am? I am not that One. But there is One coming after me whose sandals I am not worthy to untie.’

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul and his companions sail from Paphos to Perga, where John leaves them and returns to Jerusalem. Luke does not give the reason for his departure here. The others continue to Pisidian Antioch, a different Antioch from the community that sent them.

In the synagogue, the leaders invite them to speak after the reading from the Law and the Prophets. Paul addresses both Israelites and Gentiles who fear God. He begins with what God has done: choosing the fathers, bringing the people out of Egypt, bearing with them in the wilderness and giving them the land.

The account moves through the judges and Samuel to Saul and David. The reference to David becomes the bridge to Jesus: God has brought Israel the promised Savior from David’s descendants. Paul also recalls John’s call to repentance and his refusal to claim the place of the One coming after him.

The historical summary is directed toward a person, rather than being a complete timeline for its own sake. The events prepare the hearers to understand Paul’s announcement about Jesus in the next part of the speech.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this opening as presenting Jesus within the history of God’s promises to Israel. The reference to David’s descendants leads directly to Jesus as Savior, while John’s testimony directs attention away from himself toward the One to come.
passages.god_plan_html:
God’s promise to David includes an enduring house and kingdom in 2 Samuel 7:12–16. Luke 1:31–33 explicitly connects Jesus with David’s throne and a kingdom without end. Paul’s announcement in verse 23 belongs within that stated biblical connection.

Neither the failures of Israel’s leaders nor the passing of earlier generations has brought the promise to an end. Paul is announcing that the Savior has come in keeping with God’s promise, not asking the synagogue to forget the story it has been reading.

passages.title: Acts 13:26-41
passages.section_title: How does Jesus’ resurrection fulfill the promised good news?

They are now His witnesses to our people. 32 And now we proclaim to you the good news: What God promised our fathers 33 He has fulfilled for us, their children, by raising up Jesus. As it is written in the second Psalm: ‘You are My Son; today I have become Your Father.’ 34 In fact, God raised Him from the dead, never to see decay. As He has said: ‘I will give you the holy and sure blessings promised to David.’ 35 So also, He says in another Psalm: ‘You will not let Your Holy One see decay.’ 36 For when David had served God’s purpose in his own generation, he fell asleep. For I am doing a work in your days that you would never believe, even if someone told you.’”

For I am doing a work in your days that you would never believe, even if someone told you.’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul tells the hearers that this message of salvation has been sent to them. He describes Jesus’ condemnation, death and burial, then announces God’s reversal: Jesus has been raised, and witnesses have seen Him alive.

He explains the resurrection through the promised Son in Psalm 2, the sure blessings promised to David in Isaiah 55 and the Holy One who does not see decay in Psalm 16. David served God in his generation and died; Jesus, whom God raised, did not remain in decay.

Paul then announces forgiveness through Jesus and says that everyone who believes is justified through Him from what the law of Moses could not provide. To be justified concerns being put right with God. The message is offered to the people listening, not merely explained as something that happened elsewhere.

The closing warning draws on Habakkuk: the hearers must not dismiss God’s work as unbelievable. Paul’s speech joins promise, resurrection, forgiveness and a call to take what they have heard seriously.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the resurrection as revealing the Son’s identity and fulfilling God’s promise, rather than making Jesus begin to exist. Wesley on verse 33 and the Catholic Catechism, paragraph 445, both describe His sonship being made known through the resurrection.

Traditions differ over how to explain being put right with God through faith. The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 11, paragraphs 1–2, describes God pardoning sinners and counting them righteous by counting Christ’s obedience as theirs, received through faith alone. It distinguishes this acceptance from God’s inward renewal of their lives, while insisting that living faith works through love.

The Catholic Church’s Catechism, paragraphs 1989–1993, includes forgiveness and inward renewal in being put right with God. It locates the gift in Christ’s saving work, received through faith and given in baptism, with the person’s response itself enabled by grace.

The Methodist Articles of Religion, Article IX, teach that people are counted righteous only because of what Christ has done, received through faith, rather than their own works or deserving. These explanations share dependence on Christ while differing over how forgiveness, renewal, faith and baptism relate.
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul himself makes the connections to Psalm 2:7, Isaiah 55:3 and Psalm 16:10. The resurrection is not an isolated marvel added to the story; he presents it as central to God keeping His promise and giving the blessings announced through David.

The warning in Habakkuk 1:5–11 originally concerns God’s unexpected work in raising up the Chaldeans. Paul applies its warning against unbelieving dismissal to his hearers’ response to the good news. This is his stated use of the prophetic warning, not a claim that every detail of the earlier crisis is repeated here.

passages.title: Acts 13:42-52
passages.section_title: How do the hearers respond when the message reaches the city?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 42 As Paul and Barnabas were leaving the synagogue, the people urged them to continue this message on the next Sabbath. 43 After the synagogue was dismissed, many of the Jews and devout converts to Judaism followed Paul and Barnabas, who spoke to them and urged them to continue in the grace of God. 44 On the following Sabbath, nearly the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord. 45 But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy, and they blasphemously contradicted what Paul was saying. 46 Then Paul and Barnabas answered them boldly: “It was necessary to speak the word of God to you first. But since you reject it and do not consider yourselves worthy of eternal life, we now turn to the Gentiles. 47 For this is what the Lord has commanded us: ‘I have made you a light for the Gentiles, to bring salvation to the ends of the earth.’” 48 When the Gentiles heard this, they rejoiced and glorified the word of the Lord, and all who were appointed for eternal life believed. 49 And the word of the Lord spread throughout that region. 50 The Jews, however, incited the religious women of prominence and the leading men of the city. They stirred up persecution against Paul and Barnabas and drove them out of their district. 51 So they shook the dust off their feet in protest against them and went to Iconium. 52 And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.
paragraphs: 42 As Paul and Barnabas were leaving the synagogue, the people urged them to continue this message on the next Sabbath. 43 After the synagogue was dismissed, many of the Jews and devout converts to Judaism followed Paul and Barnabas, who spoke to them and urged them to continue in the grace of God.

44 On the following Sabbath, nearly the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord. 45 But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy, and they blasphemously contradicted what Paul was saying. 46 Then Paul and Barnabas answered them boldly: “It was necessary to speak the word of God to you first. But since you reject it and do not consider yourselves worthy of eternal life, we now turn to the Gentiles. 47 For this is what the Lord has commanded us: ‘I have made you a light for the Gentiles, to bring salvation to the ends of the earth.’” 48 When the Gentiles heard this, they rejoiced and glorified the word of the Lord, and all who were appointed for eternal life believed. 49 And the word of the Lord spread throughout that region.

50 The Jews, however, incited the religious women of prominence and the leading men of the city. They stirred up persecution against Paul and Barnabas and drove them out of their district. 51 So they shook the dust off their feet in protest against them and went to Iconium. 52 And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The first response includes a request to hear more on the next Sabbath. Many Jews and devout converts to Judaism follow Paul and Barnabas, who encourage them to continue in God’s grace. Luke therefore describes a positive response among Jewish hearers before describing opposition.

The word behind devout comes from σέβομαι (sebomai, SEH-boh-my), meaning to show deep respect or worship. Thayer’s entry specifically includes the devout converts in verse 43. The description concerns their reverence for God; it does not by itself tell us everything about each person’s response to Jesus.

On the next Sabbath, nearly the whole city comes to hear. Opponents among the Jewish hearers react with jealousy and contradict Paul. He and Barnabas explain why the word came to them first and announce their turn toward the Gentiles, citing the command to bring salvation to the ends of the earth.

The Gentiles rejoice, those appointed for eternal life believe, and the word spreads through the region. Opposition then draws in prominent religious women and leading men, and the messengers are driven out. They go to Iconium, while the disciples are filled with joy and the Holy Spirit.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The description of those appointed for eternal life in verse 48 is read differently within Christianity. The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 3, paragraphs 5–6, and the 1689 Baptist Confession, chapter 3, paragraphs 5–6, teach God’s gracious choice before the world’s foundation, with faith among the means by which that choice is fulfilled. Calvin on verse 48 reads the verse in those terms.

Wesley on verse 48 instead emphasizes God’s present work of grace enabling faith as the message is heard. He does not understand this verse as a statement about a fixed choice from eternity, and distinguishes the hearers who receive grace from those who reject the message. His reading still places God’s grace behind the response.

The Catholic Church’s Catechism, paragraph 1037, explicitly rejects the idea that God decides beforehand that anyone will go to hell, connecting final loss with a persistent, willful turning away. That is a relevant boundary in its broader teaching, rather than a detailed commentary on this verse.

The account also records real human responses: a request for more teaching, belief, rejoicing, jealousy and rejection. The opposition described here is not a verdict that every Jewish person everywhere rejects Jesus.
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul and Barnabas explicitly apply Isaiah 49:6 to the mission: God’s salvation is to reach the ends of the earth. In Isaiah, the servant’s work includes restoring Israel and being a light for the nations. The Gentile welcome is therefore presented as part of God’s declared purpose, not a last-minute substitute invented because one meeting became hostile.

The continuing spread of the word and the disciples’ joy also show that expulsion does not end the work. This community has received teaching and encouragement to continue in grace, and its life in the Spirit carries on after the messengers leave.
passages.current_position_html: Worship as the Early Church Knew It directly examines the devout converts in verse 43 as people marked by reverence for God. The study emphasizes their continuing response to grace as they follow Paul and Barnabas and receive encouragement. Its developed point here concerns reverence and continuing in grace.

passages.title: Acts 14:1-7
passages.section_title: Why do Paul and Barnabas stay, and then flee?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 At Iconium, Paul and Barnabas went as usual into the Jewish synagogue, where they spoke so well that a great number of Jews and Greeks believed. 2 But the unbelieving Jews stirred up the Gentiles and poisoned their minds against the brothers. 3 So Paul and Barnabas spent considerable time there, speaking boldly for the Lord, who affirmed the message of His grace by enabling them to perform signs and wonders. 4 The people of the city were divided. Some sided with the Jews, and others with the apostles. 5 But when the Gentiles and Jews, together with their rulers, set out to mistreat and stone them, 6 they found out about it and fled to the Lycaonian cities of Lystra and Derbe and to the surrounding region, 7 where they continued to preach the gospel.
paragraphs: 1 At Iconium, Paul and Barnabas went as usual into the Jewish synagogue, where they spoke so well that a great number of Jews and Greeks believed. 2 But the unbelieving Jews stirred up the Gentiles and poisoned their minds against the brothers. 3 So Paul and Barnabas spent considerable time there, speaking boldly for the Lord, who affirmed the message of His grace by enabling them to perform signs and wonders.

4 The people of the city were divided. Some sided with the Jews, and others with the apostles. 5 But when the Gentiles and Jews, together with their rulers, set out to mistreat and stone them, 6 they found out about it and fled to the Lycaonian cities of Lystra and Derbe and to the surrounding region, 7 where they continued to preach the gospel.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
In Iconium, Paul and Barnabas again speak in the synagogue, and a great number of Jews and Greeks believe. Opposition also develops: unbelieving Jews turn Gentiles against the believers. Luke records both belief and resistance within the same setting.

The messengers remain for a considerable time, speaking boldly for the Lord. The signs and wonders are described as the Lord’s confirmation of the message of His grace. Their confidence rests in Him, rather than in the absence of opposition.

When an attempt develops to mistreat and stone them, they learn of it and flee to Lystra, Derbe and the surrounding region. They continue preaching there. Staying through resistance and leaving when a violent plot is uncovered are both part of the account.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly see perseverance and prudent escape together here: opposition does not immediately silence the witness, and leaving a place of danger does not end it. Calvin on verse 3 emphasizes the messengers’ courage through the Lord’s help rather than their own strength.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus had prepared His messengers for opposition and, in Matthew 10:16–23, told them to flee to another town when persecuted. Paul and Barnabas’s movement provides a supported parallel to that instruction, while continuing the spread of the message.

The new believers and the prolonged witness remain important even though the city is divided. The mission’s progress cannot be measured only by whether the messengers are welcomed by everyone or remain permanently in one place.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Acts 14:8-18
passages.section_title: Why do the messengers stop the crowd from honoring them as gods?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 In Lystra there sat a man crippled in his feet, who was lame from birth and had never walked. 9 This man was listening to the words of Paul, who looked intently at him and saw that he had faith to be healed. 10 In a loud voice Paul called out, “Stand up on your feet!” And the man jumped up and began to walk. 11 When the crowds saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voices in the Lycaonian language: “The gods have come down to us in human form!” 12 Barnabas they called Zeus, and Paul they called Hermes, because he was the chief speaker. 13 The priest of Zeus, whose temple was just outside the city, brought bulls and wreaths to the city gates, hoping to offer a sacrifice along with the crowds. 14 But when the apostles Barnabas and Paul found out about this, they tore their clothes and rushed into the crowd, shouting, 15 “Men, why are you doing this? We too are only men, human like you. We are bringing you good news that you should turn from these worthless things to the living God, who made heaven and earth and sea and everything in them. 16 In past generations, He let all nations go their own way. 17 Yet He has not left Himself without testimony to His goodness: He gives you rain from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling your hearts with food and gladness.” 18 Even with these words, Paul and Barnabas could hardly stop the crowds from sacrificing to them.
paragraphs: 8 In Lystra there sat a man crippled in his feet, who was lame from birth and had never walked. 9 This man was listening to the words of Paul, who looked intently at him and saw that he had faith to be healed. 10 In a loud voice Paul called out, “Stand up on your feet!” And the man jumped up and began to walk. 11 When the crowds saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voices in the Lycaonian language: “The gods have come down to us in human form!” 12 Barnabas they called Zeus, and Paul they called Hermes, because he was the chief speaker. 13 The priest of Zeus, whose temple was just outside the city, brought bulls and wreaths to the city gates, hoping to offer a sacrifice along with the crowds.

14 But when the apostles Barnabas and Paul found out about this, they tore their clothes and rushed into the crowd, shouting, 15 “Men, why are you doing this? We too are only men, human like you. We are bringing you good news that you should turn from these worthless things to the living God, who made heaven and earth and sea and everything in them. 16 In past generations, He let all nations go their own way. 17 Yet He has not left Himself without testimony to His goodness: He gives you rain from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling your hearts with food and gladness.” 18 Even with these words, Paul and Barnabas could hardly stop the crowds from sacrificing to them.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
In Lystra, Paul sees that a man who has never walked has faith to be healed and calls him to stand. The man gets up and walks. The crowd interprets the healing through its belief that gods can appear in human form.

They call Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes, identifying Paul as the chief speaker. A priest brings bulls and wreaths for sacrifice. Luke gives the reason for the identification of Paul; he does not infer either man’s height or appearance from these names.

When Barnabas and Paul realize what is happening, they tear their clothes and urgently protest. They are human beings like the hearers. Their good news calls people away from these objects of worship toward the living God who made heaven, earth and sea.

They point to God’s generosity in rain, fruitful seasons, food and gladness as testimony to His goodness. Even after that explanation, they can barely stop the crowd from offering sacrifice. A real healing has not automatically produced a right understanding of its source.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the protest as directing worship to the Creator rather than His human servants. The healing is God’s work, while the message corrects the crowd’s mistaken explanation of it.
passages.god_plan_html:
The Creator described here is the God already praised in Psalm 146:5–10: Maker of heaven, earth and sea, giver of food and helper of the afflicted. The rain and harvest point to the living God’s care rather than to several competing gods with separate powers.

Paul later makes a related appeal in Acts 17:24–31, identifying the Creator as the giver of life and calling people to repentance. These are related biblical appeals to Gentile hearers, not identical speeches. The witness of creation becomes a reason to turn toward God.
