passages.title: Acts 14:19-28
passages.section_title: How are the new churches strengthened before the messengers return home?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 Then some Jews arrived from Antioch and Iconium and won over the crowds. They stoned Paul and dragged him outside the city, presuming he was dead. 20 But after the disciples had gathered around him, he got up and went back into the city. And the next day he left with Barnabas for Derbe. 21 They preached the gospel to that city and made many disciples. Then they returned to Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch, 22 strengthening the souls of the disciples and encouraging them to continue in the faith. “We must endure many hardships to enter the kingdom of God,” they said. 23 Paul and Barnabas appointed elders for them in each church, praying and fasting as they entrusted them to the Lord, in whom they had believed. 24 After passing through Pisidia, they came to Pamphylia. 25 And when they had spoken the word in Perga, they went down to Attalia. 26 From Attalia they sailed to Antioch, where they had been commended to the grace of God for the work they had just completed. 27 When they arrived, they gathered the church together and reported all that God had done through them, and how He had opened the door of faith to the Gentiles. 28 And they spent a long time there with the disciples.
paragraphs: 19 Then some Jews arrived from Antioch and Iconium and won over the crowds. They stoned Paul and dragged him outside the city, presuming he was dead. 20 But after the disciples had gathered around him, he got up and went back into the city. And the next day he left with Barnabas for Derbe. 21 They preached the gospel to that city and made many disciples. Then they returned to Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch, 22 strengthening the souls of the disciples and encouraging them to continue in the faith. “We must endure many hardships to enter the kingdom of God,” they said. 23 Paul and Barnabas appointed elders for them in each church, praying and fasting as they entrusted them to the Lord, in whom they had believed.

24 After passing through Pisidia, they came to Pamphylia. 25 And when they had spoken the word in Perga, they went down to Attalia. 26 From Attalia they sailed to Antioch, where they had been commended to the grace of God for the work they had just completed. 27 When they arrived, they gathered the church together and reported all that God had done through them, and how He had opened the door of faith to the Gentiles. 28 And they spent a long time there with the disciples.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Opponents arrive from Antioch and Iconium, win over the crowd and stone Paul. They drag him outside Lystra, presuming him dead. After the disciples gather around him, he gets up and returns to the city, then leaves with Barnabas for Derbe the next day. Luke describes the attackers’ assumption without stating that Paul had actually died.

After making many disciples in Derbe, the two return through the places where they had faced danger. They strengthen the believers and encourage them to continue in the faith, explaining that entering God’s kingdom involves many hardships. The new communities need ongoing care after their first response.

Paul and Barnabas appoint elders in each church, with prayer and fasting, and entrust the believers to the Lord. The word translated appointed is χειροτονέω (cheirotoneō, khay-roh-toh-NEH-oh). Thayer’s entry includes choosing by a raised-hand vote and the broader sense of appointing; it places this verse under that broader use. Luke identifies the messengers as appointing the elders but does not describe every step by which the people are selected.

They continue through Pisidia and Pamphylia, speak in Perga and sail from Attalia to the Antioch that sent them. The gathered church hears what God has done through them and how He has opened faith to Gentiles. They remain with the disciples for a considerable time.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly see the appointment of elders as provision for continuing care and teaching. Traditions differ over how this relates to the selection, ordination and authority of church leaders.

The Catholic Church’s Catechism, paragraphs 1562–1567, describes priests, also called presbyters, as sharing in the bishop’s mission and serve in communion with him and under his authority.

The Reformed Orthodox Presbyterian Church’s Form of Government, chapter XXV, requires a congregation to elect qualified elders who share in its oversight and calls for them to be formally set apart for that work. The 1689 Baptist Confession, chapter 26, paragraph 9, directly cites Acts 14:23 for choosing an elder by the congregation’s vote, with fasting, prayer and the laying on of elders’ hands.

Within the Wesleyan tradition, the United Methodist Church’s Book of Discipline, paragraph 304.3, places authorization with the ordained members of the annual conference, a regional church body, and ordination with the bishop. These are distinct church arrangements, rather than a claim that the Greek word alone sets out each complete system.
passages.god_plan_html:
The work continues beyond the arrival of new believers. Ephesians 4:11–16 explains the purpose of Christ’s gifts of ministry: equipping His people and helping the whole body grow toward maturity in Him. Teaching, encouragement and local care here fit that wider purpose.

Titus 1:5–9 also describes appointing elders and connects their qualifications with faithful teaching and care. The prayer and entrusting in Acts keep that responsibility dependent on the Lord, rather than treating leadership as a substitute for His keeping of the church.
passages.current_position_html: Who Shepherds the Church? cites Acts 14:23 alongside Titus 1:5 as a clear example of appointing elders. The study emphasizes shared responsibility among elders who teach and care for the people, rather than building a ladder of ranks above them. Its point here is recognized care shared among elders within each community.

passages.title: Acts 15:1-11
passages.section_title: Must Gentile believers become Jews to be saved?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then some men came down from Judea and were teaching the brothers, “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved.” 2 And after engaging these men in sharp debate, Paul and Barnabas were appointed, along with some other believers, to go up to Jerusalem to see the apostles and elders about this question. 3 Sent on their way by the church, they passed through Phoenicia and Samaria, recounting the conversion of the Gentiles and bringing great joy to all the brothers. 4 On their arrival in Jerusalem, they were welcomed by the church and apostles and elders, to whom they reported all that God had done through them. 5 But some believers from the party of the Pharisees stood up and declared, “The Gentiles must be circumcised and required to obey the law of Moses.” 6 So the apostles and elders met to look into this matter. 7 After much discussion, Peter got up and said to them, “Brothers, you know that in the early days God made a choice among you that the Gentiles would hear from my lips the message of the gospel and believe. 8 And God, who knows the heart, showed His approval by giving the Holy Spirit to them, just as He did to us. 9 He made no distinction between us and them, for He cleansed their hearts by faith. 10 Now then, why do you test God by placing on the necks of the disciples a yoke that neither we nor our fathers have been able to bear? 11 On the contrary, we believe it is through the grace of the Lord Jesus that we are saved, just as they are.”

6 So the apostles and elders met to look into this matter. 7 After much discussion, Peter got up and said to them, “Brothers, you know that in the early days God made a choice among you that the Gentiles would hear from my lips the message of the gospel and believe. 8 And God, who knows the heart, showed His approval by giving the Holy Spirit to them, just as He did to us. 9 He made no distinction between us and them, for He cleansed their hearts by faith. 10 Now then, why do you test God by placing on the necks of the disciples a yoke that neither we nor our fathers have been able to bear? 11 On the contrary, we believe it is through the grace of the Lord Jesus that we are saved, just as they are.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Some men from Judea teach the believers in Antioch that circumcision according to Moses is necessary for salvation. Paul and Barnabas strongly oppose this teaching. The church sends them and others to Jerusalem to discuss the question with the apostles and elders.

The journey brings encouragement to believers in Phoenicia and Samaria as they hear about Gentile conversions. In Jerusalem, the visitors are welcomed and report God’s work. Some believers from the Pharisees’ party then insist that the Gentiles must be circumcised and obey the law of Moses.

After much discussion, Peter points back to what God has already done among the Gentiles. God gave them the Holy Spirit and cleansed their hearts by faith, making no distinction between them and Jewish believers. Peter calls the added requirement a yoke, a burden that neither their ancestors nor they have been able to bear.

He concludes by placing both groups on the same ground: salvation through the grace of the Lord Jesus. Luke describes a serious question within the believing community, not merely a dispute between Christians and outsiders.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand Peter’s conclusion as rejecting circumcision and adoption of the Mosaic law as conditions Gentiles must meet to be saved. Jews and Gentiles alike depend on Jesus’ grace, rather than one group entering through a superior national standing.
passages.god_plan_html:
Peter himself connects this decision with the gift of the Spirit in Acts 10:44–48. The church must reckon with the fact that God has already received Gentiles; its decision is not what first makes God willing to receive them.

Galatians 2:15–16 expresses the related point that both Jewish and Gentile believers are put right with God through faith in Christ rather than works of the law. That connection concerns the gospel itself, without requiring every detail of the visits described in the two books to be fitted into one proposed chronology.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Acts 15:12-21
passages.section_title: How does James connect the Gentile welcome with Scripture?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 The whole assembly fell silent as they listened to Barnabas and Paul describing the signs and wonders God had done among the Gentiles through them. 13 When they had finished speaking, James declared, “Brothers, listen to me! 14 Simon has told us how God first visited the Gentiles to take from them a people to be His own. 15 The words of the prophets agree with this, as it is written: 16 ‘After this I will return and rebuild the fallen tent of David. section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The assembly listens while Barnabas and Paul describe God’s work among Gentiles. James then recalls Peter’s account of God taking a people for His name from among the nations. He brings the discussion to the words of the prophets, quoting Amos about the restoration of David’s fallen tent and Gentiles who bear God’s name.

The quotation’s wording differs from the BSB’s main text of Amos 9:11–12, which speaks of the remnant of Edom. The BSB footnote in Acts points to the connection with the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament. James’s stated point is that the Gentile welcome agrees with Scripture.

His judgment is that Gentiles turning to God should not be troubled with the demand under discussion. He proposes a letter directing them to abstain from food polluted by idols, sexual immorality, strangled meat and blood. He also mentions the longstanding reading of Moses in the synagogues.

The speech connects a clear welcome with instructions about the communities’ life together. The letter in the next passage will communicate the decision, rather than leaving Antioch dependent on an uncertain report of the meeting.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly see James using Scripture to support the Gentile welcome. They differ over how the restoration of David’s fallen tent relates to the present church and the future.

Calvin on verse 16 reads the prophecy as bringing Jews and Gentiles into one family under David’s kingdom. Wesley on verse 16 connects the restored tent with Christ’s enduring spiritual kingdom. Both find the present Gentile welcome within that promised work.

Thomas Constable on verses 15–17 instead understands Amos as describing a future restoration under the Messiah and James as showing that the current Gentile welcome is consistent with it. These are different commentators’ readings of the prophecy, rather than a claim that every member of a tradition gives the same explanation.

Church leadership is another point of difference. The Catholic Church’s Catechism, paragraphs 880–882, teaches that Peter heads the apostles as a united body and that his office continues in the pope alongside the bishops. The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 31, paragraphs 2–3, receives council decisions according to their agreement with Scripture and says councils after the apostles can err. Wesley on verse 23 reads the shared decision and letter as evidence against Peter being the sole chief judge. These differences concern how the council’s example relates to authority in the church.
passages.god_plan_html:
James explicitly brings the Gentile response into conversation with Amos 9:11–12. The nations called by God’s name are not outside His announced purpose. That is the connection James uses in deciding how to receive them.

The appeal also joins what God is doing with what He has said. Reports of signs and conversions are heard, and the prophets are brought into the discussion. The larger purpose is a people belonging to God, rather than Gentiles having to erase their national origin before they may turn to Him.
passages.current_position_html: Who Shepherds the Church? directly examines James’s judgment in verse 19 alongside the decision and letter in verses 22–23. The study recognizes his real standing while emphasizing the shared action of the apostles, elders and whole church. It understands his role here as recognized leadership within that body of elders, rather than an office of supreme rank passed on above them.

passages.title: Acts 15:22
passages.section_title: Who shares in choosing the messengers?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 Then the apostles and elders, with the whole church, decided to select men from among them to send to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas. They chose Judas called Barsabbas and Silas, two leaders among the brothers,
paragraphs: 22 Then the apostles and elders, with the whole church, decided to select men from among them to send to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas. They chose Judas called Barsabbas and Silas, two leaders among the brothers,

passages.context_html:
The apostles and elders, with the whole church, choose Judas Barsabbas and Silas to accompany Barnabas and Paul. Their letter addresses Gentile believers in Antioch, Syria and Cilicia. It explains that the unsettling teachers had gone out without the senders’ authorization.

The BSB’s main text moves from verse 33 to verse 35. Its footnote records a reading about Silas remaining that some manuscripts include as verse 34. That wording is not part of the main quotation on this page.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read the choice of messengers as a shared action that helps communicate and confirm the council’s decision. Wesley on verse 22 explicitly notices the whole church’s participation.
passages.current_position_html: Who Shepherds the Church? points to the whole church sharing in the decision in verse 22 and to the apostles and elders sending the letter in verse 23. It reads these as shared responsibility among recognized leaders and the community. The study therefore describes James’s contribution as part of that common work, rather than the whole decision being his solitary act.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 4:1–6 calls believers to preserve the Spirit’s unity in peace, grounded in one body and one Lord. The council’s decision takes practical form through a letter, trusted messengers, teaching and the removal of an unauthorized burden.

That unity concerns people who are now addressed as brothers across the Jewish and Gentile boundary. The response in Antioch is joy and encouragement: clarity about the gospel helps the community continue its life and witness together.

passages.title: Acts 15:22-35
passages.section_title: How does the council’s letter bring clarity and encouragement?

They chose Judas called Barsabbas and Silas, two leaders among the brothers, 23 and sent them with this letter: The apostles and the elders, your brothers, To the brothers among the Gentiles in Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia: Greetings. 24 It has come to our attention that some went out from us without our authorization and unsettled you, troubling your minds by what they said. 25 So we all agreed to choose men to send to you along with our beloved Barnabas and Paul, 26 men who have risked their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. 27 Therefore we are sending Judas and Silas to tell you in person the same things we are writing. 28 It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us not to burden you with anything beyond these essential requirements: 29 You must abstain from food sacrificed to idols, from blood, from the meat of strangled animals, and from sexual immorality. section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The apostles and elders, with the whole church, choose Judas Barsabbas and Silas to accompany Barnabas and Paul. Their letter addresses Gentile believers in Antioch, Syria and Cilicia. It explains that the unsettling teachers had gone out without the senders’ authorization.

passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians agree that the letter rejects the demand for circumcision and calls the Gentile believers to a faithful life. They differ over whether the food restrictions are continuing rules or directions especially suited to that setting.

The Catholic Church’s Council of Florence, session 11, explains the restrictions on sacrificial food, blood and strangled meat as serving fellowship between Jews and Gentiles in that period, with their force ending when the reason for them ceased. Calvin on verses 19–20 likewise treats the food restrictions as measures to avoid offense and protect fellowship.

Wesley on verse 29 takes the prohibition on eating blood as continuing, connecting it with the command to Noah. The Orthodox canonical tradition also retains a prohibition: the Council in Trullo, canon 67, forbids eating animal blood. The Orthodox Church in America’s account of that council explains its recognized place in Orthodox church law.

The food question should be distinguished from permission to commit sexual immorality. 1 Corinthians 6:18–20 separately commands believers to flee it. The different readings of the food instructions do not turn that command into a temporary social courtesy.

passages.title: Acts 15:36-41
passages.section_title: What happens when Paul and Barnabas disagree about Mark?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 36 Some time later Paul said to Barnabas, “Let us go back and visit the brothers in every town where we proclaimed the word of the Lord, to see how they are doing.” 37 Barnabas wanted to take John, also called Mark. 38 But Paul thought it best not to take him, because he had deserted them in Pamphylia and had not accompanied them in the work. 39 Their disagreement was so sharp that they parted company. Barnabas took Mark and sailed for Cyprus, 40 but Paul chose Silas and left, commended by the brothers to the grace of the Lord. 41 And he traveled through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches.
paragraphs: 36 Some time later Paul said to Barnabas, “Let us go back and visit the brothers in every town where we proclaimed the word of the Lord, to see how they are doing.” 37 Barnabas wanted to take John, also called Mark. 38 But Paul thought it best not to take him, because he had deserted them in Pamphylia and had not accompanied them in the work. 39 Their disagreement was so sharp that they parted company. Barnabas took Mark and sailed for Cyprus, 40 but Paul chose Silas and left, commended by the brothers to the grace of the Lord. 41 And he traveled through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul proposes revisiting the believers in the towns where they have preached. Barnabas wants to take John Mark, but Paul objects because Mark had left them in Pamphylia and not continued in the work. Luke identifies the earlier departure as the issue between them.

The disagreement becomes sharp enough for them to separate. Barnabas takes Mark to Cyprus; Paul chooses Silas and leaves with the brothers’ commendation to the Lord’s grace. He travels through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches.

The account does not describe a disagreement about the gospel they have just defended together. It records a painful division over who should accompany the work. Both routes continue outward, though Luke now follows Paul and Silas.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Commentators differ over how to assess the conduct of the two men. Wesley on verse 39 regards Paul as right and places the sharpness chiefly with Barnabas. Calvin’s discussion of Barnabas’s proposal also takes Paul’s concern seriously, but allows that both men may have gone too far and that a reasonable accommodation was possible.

Luke states the reason for Paul’s objection and the resulting separation without giving a full judgment on every motive or emotion. These assessments belong to the commentators, rather than a unanimous Christian verdict that one partner’s entire ministry is discredited.
passages.god_plan_html:
Mark’s earlier departure and this disagreement are not the end of his service. Philemon 24 lists Mark among Paul’s coworkers, and 2 Timothy 4:11 records Paul asking for him because he is useful in ministry.

The later references show room for renewed service after a damaged partnership. They do not make the painful separation harmless, but they keep this incident from becoming the final word on Mark or the work God continues through His servants.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Acts 16:1-5
passages.section_title: Why is Timothy circumcised after the council’s decision?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Paul came to Derbe and then to Lystra, where he found a disciple named Timothy, the son of a believing Jewish woman and a Greek father. 2 The brothers in Lystra and Iconium spoke well of him. 3 Paul wanted Timothy to accompany him, so he took him and circumcised him on account of the Jews in that area, for they all knew that his father was a Greek. 4 As they went from town to town, they delivered the decisions handed down by the apostles and elders in Jerusalem for the people to obey. 5 So the churches were strengthened in the faith and grew daily in numbers.
paragraphs: 1 Paul came to Derbe and then to Lystra, where he found a disciple named Timothy, the son of a believing Jewish woman and a Greek father. 2 The brothers in Lystra and Iconium spoke well of him. 3 Paul wanted Timothy to accompany him, so he took him and circumcised him on account of the Jews in that area, for they all knew that his father was a Greek. 4 As they went from town to town, they delivered the decisions handed down by the apostles and elders in Jerusalem for the people to obey. 5 So the churches were strengthened in the faith and grew daily in numbers.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul returns to Derbe and Lystra and finds Timothy, a disciple with a believing Jewish mother and a Greek father. Believers in Lystra and Iconium speak well of him. Paul wants him to join the work and circumcises him because the local Jews know his father was Greek.

This happens while the travelers are carrying the Jerusalem council’s decisions for the churches to obey. Luke places the two actions alongside one another: Timothy is prepared to accompany the mission, and the council’s judgment about Gentile believers is being delivered.

The churches become stronger in faith and increase in number. Timothy is joining work that includes teaching and strengthening existing communities as well as carrying the message farther.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly distinguish Timothy’s circumcision for the sake of the Jewish hearers from requiring circumcision for salvation. Calvin on verse 3 treats the action as avoiding an obstacle to the mission rather than restoring circumcision as a condition of being accepted by God.
passages.god_plan_html:
In 1 Corinthians 9:19–23, Paul explains his willingness to adapt for the sake of reaching people while remaining under Christ’s authority. Timothy’s preparation provides a concrete connection with that concern.

The contrast with Titus in Galatians 2:1–5 is useful: Titus was not compelled to be circumcised when the freedom of Gentile believers was at stake. A voluntary step for a particular mission is different from making that step a requirement of salvation.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Acts 16:6-10
passages.section_title: How is the journey directed toward Macedonia?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 After the Holy Spirit had prevented them from speaking the word in the province of Asia, they traveled through the region of Phrygia and Galatia. 7 And when they came to the border of Mysia, they tried to enter Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus would not permit them. 8 So they passed by Mysia and went down to Troas. 9 During the night, Paul had a vision of a man of Macedonia standing and pleading with him, “Come over to Macedonia and help us.” 10 As soon as Paul had seen the vision, we got ready to leave for Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them.
paragraphs: 6 After the Holy Spirit had prevented them from speaking the word in the province of Asia, they traveled through the region of Phrygia and Galatia. 7 And when they came to the border of Mysia, they tried to enter Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus would not permit them. 8 So they passed by Mysia and went down to Troas. 9 During the night, Paul had a vision of a man of Macedonia standing and pleading with him, “Come over to Macedonia and help us.” 10 As soon as Paul had seen the vision, we got ready to leave for Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Holy Spirit prevents the travelers from speaking in the province of Asia, and the Spirit of Jesus does not permit their intended entry into Bithynia. They continue to Troas. Luke records the prohibitions without explaining exactly how they are communicated.

Paul then sees a nighttime vision of a Macedonian man asking for help. The group gets ready to cross to Macedonia, concluding that God has called them to preach there. Luke begins using we in describing the preparations, placing the narrator with the travelers.

The direction concerns a particular journey and the spread of the gospel. The passage does not say that Asia is permanently excluded from hearing, or that every later change of plan will carry the same kind of revelation.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the journey as directed by God toward a new place of witness. The text names the Spirit’s prohibitions and Paul’s vision but does not reduce either to a general method of interpreting feelings or inconvenient circumstances.
passages.god_plan_html:
The response to the vision is a plan to preach, not merely to travel. The help sought from Macedonia is understood in connection with the good news about Jesus, and the next scenes will show that message reaching actual people and households.

This continues the outward witness described in Acts 1:8. The commission reaches beyond the places already visited, while the route unfolds through direction the messengers have not planned for themselves.
passages.current_position_html: Should We Seek Signs From God? names Paul’s experience in Acts 16 as a specific biblical account of God directing His servants through a vision. The study distinguishes such recorded events from treating every dream, impression or coincidence as reliable divine communication. It calls for testing claims while leaving the broader question of continuing visions open.

deeper_study.title: Should We Seek Signs From God?

passages.title: Acts 16:11-15
passages.section_title: What happens when Lydia hears the message beside the river?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 We sailed from Troas straight to Samothrace, and the following day on to Neapolis. 12 From there we went to the Roman colony of Philippi, the leading city of that district of Macedonia. And we stayed there several days. 13 On the Sabbath we went outside the city gate along the river, where it was customary to find a place of prayer. After sitting down, we spoke to the women who had gathered there. 14 Among those listening was a woman named Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth from the city of Thyatira, who was a worshiper of God. The Lord opened her heart to respond to Paul’s message. 15 And when she and her household had been baptized, she urged us, “If you consider me a believer in the Lord, come and stay at my house.” And she persuaded us.
paragraphs: 11 We sailed from Troas straight to Samothrace, and the following day on to Neapolis. 12 From there we went to the Roman colony of Philippi, the leading city of that district of Macedonia. And we stayed there several days. 13 On the Sabbath we went outside the city gate along the river, where it was customary to find a place of prayer. After sitting down, we spoke to the women who had gathered there. 14 Among those listening was a woman named Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth from the city of Thyatira, who was a worshiper of God. The Lord opened her heart to respond to Paul’s message. 15 And when she and her household had been baptized, she urged us, “If you consider me a believer in the Lord, come and stay at my house.” And she persuaded us.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The travelers cross from Troas through Samothrace and Neapolis to Philippi, which Luke identifies as a Roman colony. On the Sabbath they go outside the gate to a place of prayer by the river and speak to the women gathered there.

Lydia is a dealer in purple cloth from Thyatira and a worshiper of God. The word behind worshiper comes from σέβομαι (sebomai, SEH-boh-my), meaning to show deep respect or worship; Thayer’s entry includes this verse. Luke says the Lord opens her heart to respond to Paul’s message.

She and her household are baptized, and she urges the travelers to stay in her house. Her response includes hospitality as well as hearing the message. Luke does not describe the ages or relationships of everyone in the household.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians agree that the Lord opens Lydia’s heart as she hears Paul’s message. They explain the relationship between God’s grace and the person’s response in different ways.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 10, paragraphs 1–2, teaches that God renews the will and brings those He has chosen to Christ, making them willing so that they come freely. Calvin on verse 14 connects Lydia’s response with that gracious inward work alongside Paul’s spoken message.

The Catholic Church’s Catechism, paragraphs 153–155, describes faith as God’s gift and a human act in which the mind and will cooperate with grace. The Methodist Articles of Religion, Article VIII, likewise teach that grace goes before a person’s good will and works with the response. These readings all recognize God’s initiative while explaining its relation to the response differently.

Household baptism is also read differently. The Catholic Catechism, paragraph 1252, notes the possibility that infants were included in apostolic household baptisms. The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 28, paragraph 4, includes the children of believers among those to be baptized. The 1689 Baptist Confession, chapter 29, paragraph 2, limits baptism to those who profess repentance, faith and obedience. Luke does not identify the ages of the household members in this account.
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul later thanks God for the Philippians’ partnership in the gospel from the first day in Philippians 1:3–6. Lydia’s welcome offers a concrete beginning to the shared life surrounding the mission in this city.

Philippians 4:15–18 describes the community’s later material support for Paul. That later generosity is not attributed to Lydia alone; it shows how the gospel’s arrival can grow into an ongoing partnership of service and care.

The study emphasizes reverence, a heart turned toward God, rather than treating worship merely as participation in a ceremony. The account gives the Lord the credit for opening her heart.

passages.title: Acts 16:14
passages.section_title: What does it mean that the Lord opens Lydia’s heart?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 Among those listening was a woman named Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth from the city of Thyatira, who was a worshiper of God. The Lord opened her heart to respond to Paul’s message.
paragraphs: 14 Among those listening was a woman named Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth from the city of Thyatira, who was a worshiper of God. The Lord opened her heart to respond to Paul’s message.

passages.context_html:
The travelers cross from Troas through Samothrace and Neapolis to Philippi, which Luke identifies as a Roman colony. On the Sabbath they go outside the gate to a place of prayer by the river and speak to the women gathered there.

Lydia is a dealer in purple cloth from Thyatira and a worshiper of God. The word behind worshiper comes from σέβομαι (sebomai, SEH-boh-my), meaning to show deep respect or worship; Thayer’s entry includes this verse. Luke says the Lord opens her heart to respond to Paul’s message.

She and her household are baptized, and she urges the travelers to stay in her house. Her response includes hospitality as well as hearing the message. Luke does not describe the ages or relationships of everyone in the household.

passages.title: Acts 16:16-24
passages.section_title: Why does the girl’s release lead to the messengers’ imprisonment?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 One day as we were going to the place of prayer, we were met by a slave girl with a spirit of divination, who earned a large income for her masters by fortune-telling. 17 This girl followed Paul and the rest of us, shouting, “These men are servants of the Most High God, who are proclaiming to you the way of salvation!” 18 She continued this for many days. Eventually Paul grew so aggravated that he turned and said to the spirit, “In the name of Jesus Christ I command you to come out of her!” And the spirit left her at that very moment. 19 When the girl’s owners saw that their hope of making money was gone, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them before the authorities in the marketplace. 20 They brought them to the magistrates and said, “These men are Jews and are throwing our city into turmoil 21 by promoting customs that are unlawful for us Romans to adopt or practice.” 22 The crowd joined in the attack against Paul and Silas, and the magistrates ordered that they be stripped and beaten with rods. 23 And after striking them with many blows, they threw them into prison and ordered the jailer to guard them securely. 24 On receiving this order, he placed them in the inner cell and fastened their feet in the stocks.
paragraphs: 16 One day as we were going to the place of prayer, we were met by a slave girl with a spirit of divination, who earned a large income for her masters by fortune-telling. 17 This girl followed Paul and the rest of us, shouting, “These men are servants of the Most High God, who are proclaiming to you the way of salvation!” 18 She continued this for many days. Eventually Paul grew so aggravated that he turned and said to the spirit, “In the name of Jesus Christ I command you to come out of her!” And the spirit left her at that very moment.

19 When the girl’s owners saw that their hope of making money was gone, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them before the authorities in the marketplace. 20 They brought them to the magistrates and said, “These men are Jews and are throwing our city into turmoil 21 by promoting customs that are unlawful for us Romans to adopt or practice.” 22 The crowd joined in the attack against Paul and Silas, and the magistrates ordered that they be stripped and beaten with rods. 23 And after striking them with many blows, they threw them into prison and ordered the jailer to guard them securely. 24 On receiving this order, he placed them in the inner cell and fastened their feet in the stocks.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
A slave girl with a spirit of divination follows the group and repeatedly announces that they proclaim the way of salvation. Her fortune-telling provides a large income for her owners. After many days, Paul commands the spirit to leave in Jesus Christ’s name, and it leaves immediately.

The owners react when their hope of income disappears. They seize Paul and Silas and bring them to the authorities. Their accusation stresses that the men are Jews and claims they are promoting customs Romans may not adopt.

The crowd joins the attack, the magistrates order a beating and Paul and Silas are imprisoned. The jailer places them in an inner cell with their feet in stocks. Luke makes the lost income visible before reporting the public accusation; the case is not presented as a disinterested concern for religious truth.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read the spirit’s departure as an act of Jesus’ authority through Paul, followed by opposition from those whose profits have been disrupted. The girl’s announcement does not make the source of her power an approved partner in the gospel.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Mark 1:23–28, an unclean spirit recognizes Jesus, yet Jesus commands it to be silent and leave. Here the release is commanded in His name. The connection concerns His authority over the spirit, rather than every supernatural announcement being a trustworthy guide.

The account also exposes a conflict between a person’s release and other people’s financial interests. The message’s arrival confronts exploitation as well as mistaken worship, and faithful service can bring suffering rather than immediate public approval.

passages.title: Acts 16:25-34
passages.section_title: How does a night in prison become a household’s hearing of the gospel?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 25 About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the other prisoners were listening to them. 26 Suddenly a strong earthquake shook the foundations of the prison. At once all the doors flew open and everyone’s chains came loose. 27 When the jailer woke up and saw the prison doors open, he drew his sword and was about to kill himself, presuming that the prisoners had escaped. 28 But Paul called out in a loud voice, “Do not harm yourself! We are all here!” 29 Calling for lights, the jailer rushed in and fell trembling before Paul and Silas. 30 Then he brought them out and asked, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” 31 They replied, “Believe in the Lord Jesus and you will be saved, you and your household.” 32 Then Paul and Silas spoke the word of the Lord to him and to everyone in his house. 33 At that hour of the night, the jailer took them and washed their wounds. And without delay, he and all his household were baptized. 34 Then he brought them into his home and set a meal before them. So he and all his household rejoiced that they had come to believe in God.
paragraphs: 25 About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the other prisoners were listening to them. 26 Suddenly a strong earthquake shook the foundations of the prison. At once all the doors flew open and everyone’s chains came loose. 27 When the jailer woke up and saw the prison doors open, he drew his sword and was about to kill himself, presuming that the prisoners had escaped. 28 But Paul called out in a loud voice, “Do not harm yourself! We are all here!”

29 Calling for lights, the jailer rushed in and fell trembling before Paul and Silas. 30 Then he brought them out and asked, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” 31 They replied, “Believe in the Lord Jesus and you will be saved, you and your household.” 32 Then Paul and Silas spoke the word of the Lord to him and to everyone in his house. 33 At that hour of the night, the jailer took them and washed their wounds. And without delay, he and all his household were baptized. 34 Then he brought them into his home and set a meal before them. So he and all his household rejoiced that they had come to believe in God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul and Silas pray and sing hymns while the other prisoners listen. An earthquake opens the doors and loosens the chains. The jailer wakes, assumes the prisoners have escaped and prepares to kill himself, but Paul calls out that everyone is still there.

The jailer asks what he must do to be saved. Paul and Silas direct him to believe in the Lord Jesus and then speak the word of the Lord to him and everyone in his house. The promise to the household is followed by the household’s hearing; it is not presented as one person’s faith automatically replacing every other person’s response.

The jailer washes their wounds, and he and his household are baptized without delay. He brings them food, and the household rejoices in believing God. The man who had secured them in confinement is now caring for their injuries and welcoming them at his table.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the answer to the jailer as directing him to Jesus rather than to an achievement that earns salvation. Wesley on verse 31 reads the household’s salvation in connection with believing, and Calvin on verse 31 emphasizes that Paul and Silas also teach the message about the One in whom they are to believe.

Household baptism is also read differently. The Catholic Catechism, paragraph 1252, notes the possibility that infants were included in apostolic household baptisms. The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 28, paragraph 4, includes the children of believers among those to be baptized. The 1689 Baptist Confession, chapter 29, paragraph 2, limits baptism to those who profess repentance, faith and obedience. Luke does not identify the ages of the household members in this account.
passages.god_plan_html:
In a later imprisonment, Paul tells the Philippians that his circumstances have served the gospel’s progress in Philippians 1:12–14. This earlier scene offers a related pattern: real suffering becomes the setting in which others hear about the Lord.

Philippians 4:4–7 joins joy in the Lord with prayer and God’s peace. The prison scene puts prayer and praise alongside pain, rather than making them depend on comfortable circumstances. Luke’s account still names the wounds and the care they need.

passages.title: Acts 16:35-40
passages.section_title: Why does Paul ask for a public release?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 35 When daylight came, the magistrates sent their officers with the order: “Release those men.” 36 The jailer informed Paul: “The magistrates have sent orders to release you. Now you may go on your way in peace.” 37 But Paul said to the officers, “They beat us publicly without a trial and threw us into prison, even though we are Roman citizens. And now do they want to send us away secretly? Absolutely not! Let them come themselves and escort us out!” 38 So the officers relayed this message to the magistrates, who were alarmed to hear that Paul and Silas were Roman citizens. 39 They came to appease them and led them out, requesting that they leave the city. 40 After Paul and Silas came out of the prison, they went to Lydia’s house to see the brothers and encourage them. Then they left the city.
paragraphs: 35 When daylight came, the magistrates sent their officers with the order: “Release those men.” 36 The jailer informed Paul: “The magistrates have sent orders to release you. Now you may go on your way in peace.” 37 But Paul said to the officers, “They beat us publicly without a trial and threw us into prison, even though we are Roman citizens. And now do they want to send us away secretly? Absolutely not! Let them come themselves and escort us out!” 38 So the officers relayed this message to the magistrates, who were alarmed to hear that Paul and Silas were Roman citizens. 39 They came to appease them and led them out, requesting that they leave the city. 40 After Paul and Silas came out of the prison, they went to Lydia’s house to see the brothers and encourage them. Then they left the city.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The next morning, the magistrates send orders to release Paul and Silas. Paul objects to being quietly dismissed after a public beating and imprisonment without trial. He identifies both men as Roman citizens and asks the magistrates to come themselves.

Roman citizenship gives the objection weight. In an earlier Roman speech, Cicero, Against Verres 2.5.162–170, condemns the beating of a Roman citizen as an abuse of citizens’ rights. That earlier complaint helps explain the alarm when these magistrates learn the men are citizens.

They come to appease the men, escort them out and ask them to leave the city. Before departing, Paul and Silas visit Lydia’s house and encourage the believers. The chapter closes with attention to the community, as well as to the messengers’ release.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand Paul’s response as an appeal to his citizenship after unjust treatment. Wesley on verse 37 reads the concern as protecting the witness from the public suspicion the treatment could create, rather than simply seeking personal revenge.
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul later urges these believers to stand together for the gospel in Philippians 1:27–30, referring to the struggle they had seen in him. His suffering belongs to the shared history from which he encourages their own perseverance.

The return to Lydia’s house fits that continuing concern. The journey will move on, but the believers who remain need encouragement to live and witness together. The mission includes strengthening those people, not only securing the travelers’ next destination.

passages.title: Acts 17:1-9
passages.section_title: Why does the message about Jesus divide the hearers in Thessalonica?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 When they had passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where there was a Jewish synagogue. 2 As was his custom, Paul went into the synagogue, and on three Sabbaths he reasoned with them from the Scriptures, 3 explaining and proving that the Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead. “This Jesus I am proclaiming to you is the Christ,” he declared. 4 Some of the Jews were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas, along with a large number of God-fearing Greeks and quite a few leading women. 5 The Jews, however, became jealous. So they brought in some troublemakers from the marketplace, formed a mob, and sent the city into an uproar. They raided Jason’s house in search of Paul and Silas, hoping to bring them out to the people. 6 But when they could not find them, they dragged Jason and some other brothers before the city officials, shouting, “These men who have turned the world upside down have now come here, 7 and Jason has welcomed them into his home. They are all defying Caesar’s decrees, saying that there is another king, named Jesus!” 8 On hearing this, the crowd and city officials were greatly disturbed. 9 And they collected bond from Jason and the others and then released them.
paragraphs: 1 When they had passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where there was a Jewish synagogue. 2 As was his custom, Paul went into the synagogue, and on three Sabbaths he reasoned with them from the Scriptures, 3 explaining and proving that the Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead. “This Jesus I am proclaiming to you is the Christ,” he declared. 4 Some of the Jews were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas, along with a large number of God-fearing Greeks and quite a few leading women.

5 The Jews, however, became jealous. So they brought in some troublemakers from the marketplace, formed a mob, and sent the city into an uproar. They raided Jason’s house in search of Paul and Silas, hoping to bring them out to the people. 6 But when they could not find them, they dragged Jason and some other brothers before the city officials, shouting, “These men who have turned the world upside down have now come here, 7 and Jason has welcomed them into his home. They are all defying Caesar’s decrees, saying that there is another king, named Jesus!” 8 On hearing this, the crowd and city officials were greatly disturbed. 9 And they collected bond from Jason and the others and then released them.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After passing through Amphipolis and Apollonia, Paul and Silas arrive in Thessalonica. Paul goes to the synagogue, as is his custom, and reasons from Scripture on three Sabbaths. His explanation centers on the Messiah’s necessary suffering and resurrection, identifying Jesus as that Messiah.

Some Jewish hearers are persuaded, along with many God-fearing Greeks and leading women. Luke records this response before describing the jealous opposition. The account does not divide everyone neatly into believing Gentiles and unbelieving Jews.

Troublemakers are gathered from the marketplace, a mob forms and Jason’s house is raided in search of Paul and Silas. When they cannot be found, Jason and other believers are brought before the city officials. The accusation turns the proclamation of Jesus as king into a charge of defying Caesar.

The crowd and officials are disturbed, and bond is collected from Jason and the others before they are released. Luke does not specify the exact amount or all the conditions attached to it. The hospitality Jason has offered now exposes him to the conflict surrounding his guests.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read Paul’s reasoning as an explanation of why the crucified and risen Jesus fulfills the hope of the Messiah. The political charge is the opponents’ accusation, not a statement that the message is a plan to overthrow the city by force.
passages.god_plan_html:
In 1 Thessalonians 2:1–2, Paul recalls the mistreatment in Philippi and the courage God gave to speak in Thessalonica despite strong opposition. The letter connects the suffering in the previous city with the continuing witness here.

1 Thessalonians 1:5–10 describes the wider result: people who turn to the living God become an example, and the message sounds out from them. The trouble described by Luke is not the whole story of what God brings from the visit.

passages.title: Acts 17:10-15
passages.section_title: How do the Bereans receive the message and test it?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 As soon as night had fallen, the brothers sent Paul and Silas away to Berea. On arriving there, they went into the Jewish synagogue. 11 Now the Bereans were more noble-minded than the Thessalonians, for they received the message with great eagerness and examined the Scriptures every day to see if these teachings were true. 12 As a result, many of them believed, along with quite a few prominent Greek women and men. 13 But when the Jews from Thessalonica learned that Paul was also proclaiming the word of God in Berea, they went there themselves to incite and agitate the crowds. 14 The brothers immediately sent Paul to the coast, but Silas and Timothy remained in Berea. 15 Those who escorted Paul brought him to Athens and then returned with instructions for Silas and Timothy to join him as soon as possible.
paragraphs: 10 As soon as night had fallen, the brothers sent Paul and Silas away to Berea. On arriving there, they went into the Jewish synagogue. 11 Now the Bereans were more noble-minded than the Thessalonians, for they received the message with great eagerness and examined the Scriptures every day to see if these teachings were true. 12 As a result, many of them believed, along with quite a few prominent Greek women and men.

13 But when the Jews from Thessalonica learned that Paul was also proclaiming the word of God in Berea, they went there themselves to incite and agitate the crowds. 14 The brothers immediately sent Paul to the coast, but Silas and Timothy remained in Berea. 15 Those who escorted Paul brought him to Athens and then returned with instructions for Silas and Timothy to join him as soon as possible.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The believers send Paul and Silas to Berea at night, where they again enter a Jewish synagogue. Luke commends the hearers’ eagerness to receive the message and their daily examination of Scripture to see whether the teaching is true. Many believe, including prominent Greek women and men.

The description noble-minded comes from εὐγενής (eugenēs, yoo-geh-NAYS). Thayer’s entry distinguishes noble birth from the noble-minded sense used here. Luke explains the commendation through the hearers’ response to the message and their examination of Scripture.

Opponents from Thessalonica come to stir up the crowds when they learn that Paul is teaching in Berea. The believers send him toward the coast, while Silas and Timothy remain. His escorts take him to Athens and return with instructions for the others to join him soon.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly commend the combination of eager hearing and careful examination in this account. Traditions differ over how Scripture, the church’s teaching and authoritative interpretation relate when readers apply that example.

The Catholic Church’s Catechism, paragraphs 85–87, entrusts authoritative interpretation to the bishops in communion with the pope. It expressly describes that teaching office as serving God’s word, not standing above it.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 1, paragraph 10, identifies the Holy Spirit speaking in Scripture as the final judge by which councils, teachers and religious claims are examined. The Methodist Articles of Religion, Article V, teach that nothing absent from Scripture or unable to be proved from it may be required as necessary to salvation.

Wesley on verse 11 stresses that being teachable and carefully searching for truth belong together. The Bereans’ examination is not portrayed as a refusal ever to believe; Luke connects it with the belief that follows.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Luke 24:25–27, the risen Jesus explains from Moses and the prophets why the Messiah must suffer and enter His glory. Paul’s message and the Bereans’ examination belong within that connection between Jesus and the Scriptures that point to Him.

The result is more than winning a debate. People come to faith, and a community remains to be cared for after Paul is sent away. Careful attention to what God has said serves the receiving of the good news and the continuing life of His people.
passages.current_position_html: The Berean Standard directly develops this passage as the site’s method of hearing and testing teaching. It calls for eagerness to learn, daily attention to the whole passage and a willingness to let Scripture correct what we already believe. That includes testing the teaching on this site: confidence in a teacher is a reason to listen carefully, while the text remains the measure of the claim.

passages.title: Acts 17:16-21
passages.section_title: Why does Paul speak in both the synagogue and the marketplace?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 While Paul was waiting for them in Athens, he was deeply disturbed in his spirit to see that the city was full of idols. 17 So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and God-fearing Gentiles, and in the marketplace with those he met each day. 18 Some Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also began to debate with him. Some of them asked, “What is this babbler trying to say?” Others said, “He seems to be advocating foreign gods.” They said this because Paul was proclaiming the good news of Jesus and the resurrection. 19 So they took Paul and brought him to the Areopagus, where they asked him, “May we know what this new teaching is that you are presenting? 20 For you are bringing some strange notions to our ears, and we want to know what they mean.” 21 Now all the Athenians and foreigners who lived there spent their time doing nothing more than hearing and articulating new ideas.
paragraphs: 16 While Paul was waiting for them in Athens, he was deeply disturbed in his spirit to see that the city was full of idols. 17 So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and God-fearing Gentiles, and in the marketplace with those he met each day. 18 Some Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also began to debate with him. Some of them asked, “What is this babbler trying to say?” Others said, “He seems to be advocating foreign gods.” They said this because Paul was proclaiming the good news of Jesus and the resurrection.

19 So they took Paul and brought him to the Areopagus, where they asked him, “May we know what this new teaching is that you are presenting? 20 For you are bringing some strange notions to our ears, and we want to know what they mean.” 21 Now all the Athenians and foreigners who lived there spent their time doing nothing more than hearing and articulating new ideas.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul is waiting in Athens for Silas and Timothy when the city’s many idols deeply trouble him. He speaks in the synagogue with Jewish hearers and God-fearing Gentiles, and in the marketplace with the people he meets each day. His concern leads to conversation in both settings.

Epicureans and Stoics represent different approaches to life. Epicurus describes happiness in terms of freedom from bodily pain and inner distress, rather than endless indulgence; see his Letter to Menoeceus. A later Stoic teacher, Epictetus, describes reverence for gods who govern with goodness and justice, and a willingness to accept what lies beyond our control; see The Enchiridion, section 31. These writings help explain the schools without telling us exactly what each person listening to Paul believed.

Some philosophers dismiss him as a babbler. The Greek word σπερμολόγος (spermologos, sper-moh-LOH-goss) originally describes picking up seeds and is used as an insult for an empty talker. Thayer’s lexicon identifies that insulting sense here. This is their judgment of Paul, not Luke’s assessment of his message.

Others think he is promoting foreign gods because he is preaching Jesus and the resurrection. They take him to the Areopagus and ask him to explain. Luke highlights their appetite for new ideas, while the speech that follows asks for something more demanding than curiosity: a changed response to God.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this scene as an example of bringing the message about Jesus into everyday conversation as well as a place of religious gathering. Paul’s distress over idols does not stop him from reasoning with people who disagree with him; their interest in a new idea does not yet mean they believe his message.
passages.god_plan_html: The witness promised in Acts 1:8 keeps reaching new people and settings. Here the message enters a conversation with people whose starting point is Greek philosophy rather than Israel’s Scriptures. The next speech begins with the Creator they do not know and leads to the risen Man appointed to judge the world. The setting changes, while the witness remains centered on Jesus and the resurrection.
passages.current_position_html: Worship as the Early Church Knew It discusses the God-fearing Gentiles in Acts 17:17 as people already marked by reverence for Israel’s God. That reverence is a setting in which they hear Paul’s message. It is not a claim that every religious response is already directed toward the truth, or that reverence makes further teaching unnecessary.

passages.title: Acts 17:17
passages.section_title: Who hears Paul in Athens?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and God-fearing Gentiles, and in the marketplace with those he met each day.
paragraphs: 17 So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and God-fearing Gentiles, and in the marketplace with those he met each day.

passages.context_html:
This verse sits between Paul’s distress at the idols of Athens and the philosophers’ response to his preaching. He speaks with Jewish hearers and God-fearing Gentiles in the synagogue, and with people he meets in the marketplace each day. Luke describes sustained conversation, not only a single public speech.

The God-fearing Gentiles are connected with reverence for Israel’s God. Their presence should not be confused with the city’s idol worship as though all the people Paul meets begin with the same beliefs.

passages.title: Acts 17:22-34
passages.section_title: How does Paul lead the Athenians from an unknown god to the risen Jesus?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 Then Paul stood up in the meeting of the Areopagus and said, “Men of Athens, I see that in every way you are very religious. 23 For as I walked around and examined your objects of worship, I even found an altar with this inscription: TO AN UNKNOWN GOD. Therefore what you worship as something unknown, I now proclaim to you. 24 The God who made the world and everything in it is the Lord of heaven and earth and does not live in temples made by human hands. 25 Nor is He served by human hands, as if He needed anything, because He Himself gives everyone life and breath and everything else. 26 From one man He made every nation of men, that they should inhabit the whole earth; and He determined their appointed times and the boundaries of their lands. 27 God intended that they would seek Him and perhaps reach out for Him and find Him, though He is not far from each one of us. 28 ‘For in Him we live and move and have our being.’ As some of your own poets have said, ‘We are His offspring.’ 29 Therefore, being offspring of God, we should not think that the Divine Being is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by man’s skill and imagination. 30 Although God overlooked the ignorance of earlier times, He now commands all people everywhere to repent. 31 For He has set a day when He will judge the world with justice by the Man He has appointed. He has given proof of this to everyone by raising Him from the dead.” 32 When they heard about the resurrection of the dead, some began to mock him, but others said, “We want to hear you again on this topic.” 33 At that, Paul left the Areopagus. 34 But some joined him and believed, including Dionysius the Areopagite, a woman named Damaris, and others who were with them.
paragraphs: 22 Then Paul stood up in the meeting of the Areopagus and said, “Men of Athens, I see that in every way you are very religious. 23 For as I walked around and examined your objects of worship, I even found an altar with this inscription: TO AN UNKNOWN GOD. Therefore what you worship as something unknown, I now proclaim to you. 24 The God who made the world and everything in it is the Lord of heaven and earth and does not live in temples made by human hands. 25 Nor is He served by human hands, as if He needed anything, because He Himself gives everyone life and breath and everything else.

26 From one man He made every nation of men, that they should inhabit the whole earth; and He determined their appointed times and the boundaries of their lands. 27 God intended that they would seek Him and perhaps reach out for Him and find Him, though He is not far from each one of us. 28 ‘For in Him we live and move and have our being.’ As some of your own poets have said, ‘We are His offspring.’ 29 Therefore, being offspring of God, we should not think that the Divine Being is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by man’s skill and imagination.

30 Although God overlooked the ignorance of earlier times, He now commands all people everywhere to repent. 31 For He has set a day when He will judge the world with justice by the Man He has appointed. He has given proof of this to everyone by raising Him from the dead.” 32 When they heard about the resurrection of the dead, some began to mock him, but others said, “We want to hear you again on this topic.” 33 At that, Paul left the Areopagus. 34 But some joined him and believed, including Dionysius the Areopagite, a woman named Damaris, and others who were with them.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul starts with something his hearers recognize: the city’s religious activity and an altar dedicated to an unknown god. He uses their acknowledged lack of knowledge as an opening to proclaim the Creator. He does not tell them that all their gods are simply different names for the same God.

The description very religious uses δεισιδαίμων (deisidaimōn, day-see-DYE-mohn). Thayer’s lexicon records both a respectful sense, religious or devout, and a negative sense, superstitious. Paul’s opening recognizes their religious concern, but the rest of his speech challenges what they believe about God.

The Creator is Lord of heaven and earth. He does not depend on a human building for a home or on human service for support. Every person depends on Him for life and breath. All nations share one human origin, and their histories unfold under His rule; no people has a different kind of human beginning from the rest.

Paul draws on words familiar from their poets to explain that human life depends on God. In this setting, being God’s offspring describes our origin and dependence. The point is that the living Creator cannot be reduced to an object fashioned by the creatures He made. It does not say everyone is already reconciled to Him.

The speech then moves from ignorance to responsibility. God commands all people everywhere to repent—to turn from their wrong ways toward Him—because He has appointed a day of judgment and raised the appointed Judge from the dead. Some mock, others ask to hear more, and some join Paul and believe. Luke names Dionysius and Damaris among those who believe; he does not describe the whole visit as a failure.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians broadly read this speech as a proclamation of one Creator who sustains all people, calls them to repent and will judge through the risen Jesus. Human dependence on God is not treated as proof that all beliefs lead to Him or that repentance is unnecessary.

Traditions differ over how the rejection of man-made images relates to images used by Christians. The Catholic Church’s Catechism, paragraphs 2129–2132, rejects idols while permitting sacred images in light of the Son of God becoming human. It distinguishes respect shown through an image to the person portrayed from the adoration owed to God alone. The Reformed Westminster Confession 21:1 instead rejects worshiping God under any visible representation. These are different accounts of permitted religious images; neither teaching describes God as a manufactured object dependent on its makers.
passages.god_plan_html:
The speech joins creation, the nations and the risen Jesus in one account of God’s purposes. Genesis 1:1, 26–27 presents God as Creator and humanity as His creation. Paul takes his hearers back to that shared dependence before speaking about what God now commands them to do. The many nations are not outside the Creator’s concern.

The appointed Judge is the same risen Jesus whom Paul has been proclaiming. Acts 10:42–43 explicitly connects Jesus’ appointment as Judge with forgiveness through faith in Him. Athens therefore belongs to the wider witness to all peoples: the One on whom everyone depends is calling people everywhere to respond, and the resurrection makes that call urgent.
passages.current_position_html: Worship as the Early Church Knew It directly discusses Acts 17:23 and 25. Its position is that sincere devotion needs to be directed toward the true God, and that our religious acts do not supply something He lacks. Paul redirects his hearers toward the One who gives them life. This position does not turn the passage into a verdict on every disputed use of Christian art or every form of gathered worship.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

passages.title: Acts 17:23
passages.section_title: Does Paul approve of worship directed toward an unknown god?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 23 For as I walked around and examined your objects of worship, I even found an altar with this inscription: TO AN UNKNOWN GOD. Therefore what you worship as something unknown, I now proclaim to you.
paragraphs: 23 For as I walked around and examined your objects of worship, I even found an altar with this inscription: TO AN UNKNOWN GOD. Therefore what you worship as something unknown, I now proclaim to you.

passages.context_html:
Paul has been invited to explain the message he was preaching in Athens. He points to an altar whose inscription acknowledges an unknown god. That gives him an opening to tell his hearers about the Creator; it does not mean he accepts the surrounding idol worship as an adequate knowledge of Him.

The rest of the speech explains who this God is: Creator and giver of life, unlike an image made by human skill. Paul concludes by calling for repentance in view of the coming judgment and the resurrection. The opening should be read with that conclusion, not detached as approval of every form of devotion.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the altar as Paul’s starting point for explaining the God his hearers do not know. The invitation to listen leads toward a change of belief and life, rather than an assurance that religious sincerity by itself is enough.
passages.current_position_html: Worship as the Early Church Knew It reads Acts 17:23 as sincere devotion needing to be redirected toward the truth. Paul recognizes the Athenians’ religious activity while explaining the God they do not know. Reverence matters, but it must be directed toward the true God.

The appointed Judge is the same risen Jesus whom Paul has been proclaiming. Acts 10:42–43 explicitly connects Jesus’ appointment as Judge with forgiveness through faith in Him.
