passages.title: Acts 17:25
passages.section_title: Why does God need nothing from human hands?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 25 Nor is He served by human hands, as if He needed anything, because He Himself gives everyone life and breath and everything else.
paragraphs: 25 Nor is He served by human hands, as if He needed anything, because He Himself gives everyone life and breath and everything else.

passages.context_html:
Paul has just described God as the Maker and Lord of the world, who does not live in temples made by human hands. He now explains why God does not need people to sustain Him: the direction of dependence runs the other way. He gives everyone life, breath and everything else.

The word served comes from θεραπεύω (therapeuō, theh-rah-PYOO-oh). Thayer’s lexicon lists serving or doing service as its meaning in Acts 17:25. Elsewhere the word often describes healing, but Paul is not saying God needs medical care. The qualifying phrase about needing anything explains the kind of mistaken dependence he is rejecting.

This does not make obedience, generosity or service to others pointless. Paul is correcting the idea that the Creator relies on His creatures to meet a lack in Himself. The following verses explain our dependence on Him and His call for us to repent.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this verse as teaching that God sustains creation without needing creation to sustain Him. Serving God is therefore not a way of supplying something missing from His life or making Him dependent on our gifts.
passages.current_position_html: Worship as the Early Church Knew It directly uses Acts 17:25 to explain that our acts of devotion do not sustain God or add something He lacks. He gives life; we receive it. The study calls for reverence grounded in that truth, rather than treating religious activity as a way to maintain or impress a needy deity.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html: The giver of life to everyone is also the One who calls everyone to repent in Acts 17:30–31. Creation and judgment belong together: people remain accountable to the God on whom they depend. Acts 10:42–43 connects the risen Jesus’ role as Judge with forgiveness for those who believe in Him. God’s freedom from need does not mean indifference toward the people He made.

passages.title: Acts 18:1-5
passages.section_title: How do shared work and returning companions support Paul in Corinth?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 After this, Paul left Athens and went to Corinth. 2 There he found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, who had recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla because Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome. Paul went to visit them, 3 and he stayed and worked with them because they were tentmakers by trade, just as he was. 4 Every Sabbath he reasoned in the synagogue, trying to persuade Jews and Greeks alike. 5 And when Silas and Timothy came down from Macedonia, Paul devoted himself fully to the word, testifying to the Jews that Jesus is the Christ.
paragraphs: 1 After this, Paul left Athens and went to Corinth. 2 There he found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, who had recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla because Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome. Paul went to visit them, 3 and he stayed and worked with them because they were tentmakers by trade, just as he was.

4 Every Sabbath he reasoned in the synagogue, trying to persuade Jews and Greeks alike. 5 And when Silas and Timothy came down from Macedonia, Paul devoted himself fully to the word, testifying to the Jews that Jesus is the Christ.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul leaves Athens for Corinth, where he meets Aquila and Priscilla. They have recently come from Italy because Claudius ordered the Jews to leave Rome. Paul stays and works with them because they share the trade of tentmaking. Luke does not tell us precisely when the couple first believed in Jesus.

The Roman writer Suetonius, Claudius 25.4, also records an expulsion of Jews from Rome, connecting it with disturbances associated with someone he calls Chrestus. This supports the historical setting of the expulsion without settling every detail of the dispute or exactly what Suetonius understood about it.

Paul reasons in the synagogue each Sabbath, seeking to persuade Jewish and Greek hearers. When Silas and Timothy arrive from Macedonia, he devotes himself fully to proclaiming the word and testifying that Jesus is the Christ—the promised Messiah.

The description of his devotion uses συνέχω (synechō, soo-NEH-khoh). Thayer’s entry gives the sense of being closely occupied with a task in Acts 18:5. Paul’s concentration on teaching increases; the word itself does not tell us every detail of his working hours or finances.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly see practical work, hospitality and fellow workers supporting the preaching in this account. Paul works with his hands and teaches; neither activity makes the other unimportant. His example here does not by itself require every Christian teacher to follow one identical pattern of employment.
passages.god_plan_html: In 2 Corinthians 11:7–9, Paul recalls receiving help from other churches and having his needs supplied by brothers arriving from Macedonia while he was serving the Corinthians. Together with Luke’s account, this shows how one community’s generosity helps the message reach another. God’s work includes the people who welcome, work alongside and support the messenger.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Acts 18:6-11
passages.section_title: Why does Paul keep speaking after opposition in Corinth?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 But when they opposed and insulted him, he shook out his garments and told them, “Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent of it. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.” 7 So Paul left the synagogue and went next door to the house of Titus Justus, a worshiper of God. 8 Crispus, the synagogue leader, and his whole household believed in the Lord. And many of the Corinthians who heard the message believed and were baptized. 9 One night the Lord spoke to Paul in a vision: “Do not be afraid; keep on speaking; do not be silent. 10 For I am with you and no one will lay a hand on you, because I have many people in this city.” 11 So Paul stayed for a year and a half, teaching the word of God among the Corinthians.
paragraphs: 6 But when they opposed and insulted him, he shook out his garments and told them, “Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent of it. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.” 7 So Paul left the synagogue and went next door to the house of Titus Justus, a worshiper of God. 8 Crispus, the synagogue leader, and his whole household believed in the Lord. And many of the Corinthians who heard the message believed and were baptized.

9 One night the Lord spoke to Paul in a vision: “Do not be afraid; keep on speaking; do not be silent. 10 For I am with you and no one will lay a hand on you, because I have many people in this city.” 11 So Paul stayed for a year and a half, teaching the word of God among the Corinthians.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
When opponents resist and insult him, Paul shakes out his garments and declares that they bear responsibility for rejecting his testimony. He turns his attention toward the Gentiles and moves the teaching next door, to the house of Titus Justus, a worshiper of God.

This is not a rejection of every Jewish person. Crispus, the synagogue leader, believes with his household, and many Corinthians hear, believe and are baptized. Later Paul recalls personally baptizing Crispus in 1 Corinthians 1:14–17.

The Lord speaks to Paul in a night vision, telling him not to fear or fall silent. The promise is personal and specific: the Lord is with him, will protect him here and has many people in this city. Paul remains for a year and a half, teaching God’s word.

Paul later describes coming to Corinth in weakness, fear and trembling in 1 Corinthians 2:1–5. His need for encouragement does not mean Luke is accusing him of faithlessness or a failed preaching technique.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read the vision as reassurance that Paul should continue the work despite opposition. The promise that God has many people in the city gives him reason to keep speaking and teaching. It is a promise in this particular mission, not an assurance that every believer in every place will escape physical harm.
passages.god_plan_html: In 1 Corinthians 2:1–5, Paul explains that the Corinthians’ faith should rest on God’s power rather than a speaker’s impressive skill. The frightened messenger is sustained, people believe and a community is taught. God’s purposes advance through a servant who needs help, not through a hero who has no weakness.
passages.current_position_html: Worship as the Early Church Knew It discusses Titus Justus in Acts 18:7 as a person whose reverence for God matters more than the kind of building in which believers meet. His home becomes a place for the message and fellowship. The study places the emphasis on people who honor God, rather than a structure imagined to be sacred in itself.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

passages.title: Acts 18:7
passages.section_title: What makes Titus Justus’s home a place for the message?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 So Paul left the synagogue and went next door to the house of Titus Justus, a worshiper of God.
paragraphs: 7 So Paul left the synagogue and went next door to the house of Titus Justus, a worshiper of God.

passages.context_html:
After opposition in the synagogue, Paul moves next door to the house of Titus Justus, described as a worshiper of God. The location changes, but the teaching continues. The following verse reports belief by Crispus and his household and by many Corinthians.

Justus’s description points to reverence for God. The account makes a private home part of the setting in which people hear the message; it does not describe a special construction or ceremony that turns the building into a dwelling God needs.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this move as the opening of another place for teaching after synagogue opposition. Hospitality and reverence help make room for the message; the passage does not require that all believers meet in the same kind of building.
passages.current_position_html: Worship as the Early Church Knew It directly discusses Acts 18:7. It emphasizes Justus’s reverence for God and the way his home becomes a setting for Christian fellowship. The focus is on people who honor God, rather than on a building regarded as sacred in itself.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html: The house next door becomes part of the continuing witness in Corinth. The following vision promises the Lord’s presence and further work in the city, and Paul remains to teach. 1 Corinthians 3:5–9 later describes the Corinthians themselves as God’s field and building: the lasting work concerns the people He brings to faith and helps to grow.

passages.title: Acts 18:12-17
passages.section_title: What happens when Paul is brought before Gallio?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 While Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews coordinated an attack on Paul and brought him before the judgment seat. 13 “This man is persuading the people to worship God in ways contrary to the law,” they said. 14 But just as Paul was about to speak, Gallio told the Jews, “If this matter involved a wrongdoing or vicious crime, O Jews, it would be reasonable for me to hear your complaint. 15 But since it is a dispute about words and names and your own law, settle it yourselves. I refuse to be a judge of such things.” 16 And he drove them away from the judgment seat. 17 At this, the crowd seized Sosthenes the synagogue leader and beat him in front of the judgment seat. But none of this was of concern to Gallio.
paragraphs: 12 While Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews coordinated an attack on Paul and brought him before the judgment seat. 13 “This man is persuading the people to worship God in ways contrary to the law,” they said. 14 But just as Paul was about to speak, Gallio told the Jews, “If this matter involved a wrongdoing or vicious crime, O Jews, it would be reasonable for me to hear your complaint. 15 But since it is a dispute about words and names and your own law, settle it yourselves. I refuse to be a judge of such things.” 16 And he drove them away from the judgment seat.
17 At this, the crowd seized Sosthenes the synagogue leader and beat him in front of the judgment seat. But none of this was of concern to Gallio.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul’s opponents bring him before Gallio, the proconsul, or Roman governor, of Achaia. They charge him with persuading people to worship God contrary to the law. Before Paul can answer, Gallio refuses the case: he regards it as a dispute about words, names and their own law rather than a wrongdoing or serious crime that requires his judgment.

Gallio drives the accusers away from the judgment seat. The crowd then seizes Sosthenes, the synagogue leader, and beats him there. Gallio shows no concern. Paul escapes the threatened proceedings, but the scene also includes violence against someone else and an official’s indifference.

Luke does not explain all the crowd’s motives or settle Sosthenes’ later history. The refusal to hear this case should not be expanded into a declaration that Rome has permanently legalized Christian preaching everywhere.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly connect Paul’s preservation here with the Lord’s promise in the preceding vision. Gallio’s refusal leaves Paul free to continue, while his indifference to Sosthenes’ beating is reported without being held up as a model of justice.
passages.god_plan_html: The promise of Acts 18:9–10 takes concrete shape as the attempted prosecution fails to stop Paul’s work in Corinth. God preserves an opportunity for sustained teaching. The surrounding story matters: this is protection for a particular task, not a promise that God’s servants will never suffer. Sosthenes’ beating also keeps us from treating the scene as a simple celebration of everything the governor does.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Acts 18:18-23
passages.section_title: How does Paul leave room for God’s will while continuing the work?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 Paul remained in Corinth for quite some time before saying goodbye to the brothers. He had his head shaved in Cenchrea to keep a vow he had made, and then he sailed for Syria, accompanied by Priscilla and Aquila. 19 When they reached Ephesus, Paul left Priscilla and Aquila. He himself went into the synagogue there and reasoned with the Jews. 20 When they asked him to stay for a while longer, he declined. 21 But as he left, he said, “I will come back to you if God is willing.” And he set sail from Ephesus. 22 When Paul had landed at Caesarea, he went up and greeted the church at Jerusalem. Then he went down to Antioch. 23 After Paul had spent some time in Antioch, he traveled from place to place throughout the region of Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples.
paragraphs: 18 Paul remained in Corinth for quite some time before saying goodbye to the brothers. He had his head shaved in Cenchrea to keep a vow he had made, and then he sailed for Syria, accompanied by Priscilla and Aquila. 19 When they reached Ephesus, Paul left Priscilla and Aquila. He himself went into the synagogue there and reasoned with the Jews. 20 When they asked him to stay for a while longer, he declined. 21 But as he left, he said, “I will come back to you if God is willing.” And he set sail from Ephesus.

22 When Paul had landed at Caesarea, he went up and greeted the church at Jerusalem. Then he went down to Antioch. 23 After Paul had spent some time in Antioch, he traveled from place to place throughout the region of Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After remaining in Corinth for some time, Paul leaves with Priscilla and Aquila. At Cenchrea he has his head shaved because of a vow he has made—a promise or commitment to God. Luke records the act without explaining the vow’s exact words, purpose or duration.

Numbers 6:1–8, 13–21 gives the background of a Nazirite commitment, including allowing the hair to grow and cutting it when the period is complete. That background helps explain why readers connect Paul’s haircut with such a vow. Acts does not supply enough detail to reconstruct every part of the ceremony.

At Ephesus, Paul reasons in the synagogue. When asked to stay, he declines but says he will return if God is willing. Priscilla and Aquila remain there. Paul continues by sea to Caesarea, greets the church at Jerusalem and returns to Antioch.

After some time, he travels again through Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening the disciples. Luke’s brief travel account links the return from one period of work with the beginning of another; helping existing believers grow remains part of the mission.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read Paul’s promise to return as a plan held subject to God’s will, and his later travels as continuing care for the disciples. His vow is often understood against the Jewish background of Numbers 6. The text does not say that making such a vow is necessary for salvation or required of all Christians.
passages.god_plan_html: The pattern of returning to strengthen disciples continues the care seen in Acts 14:21–23. The mission includes both reaching new hearers and helping believers remain steady. Ephesus also connects the journeys: the couple who traveled with Paul will help another teacher there in the next passage.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Acts 18:24-28
passages.section_title: How does a gifted teacher grow through further instruction?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 24 Meanwhile a Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, came to Ephesus. He was an eloquent man, well versed in the Scriptures. 25 He had been instructed in the way of the Lord and was fervent in spirit. He spoke and taught accurately about Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John. 26 And he began to speak boldly in the synagogue. When Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately. 27 When Apollos resolved to cross over to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples there to welcome him. On his arrival, he was a great help to those who by grace had believed. 28 For he powerfully refuted the Jews in public debate, proving from the Scriptures that Jesus is the Christ.
paragraphs: 24 Meanwhile a Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, came to Ephesus. He was an eloquent man, well versed in the Scriptures. 25 He had been instructed in the way of the Lord and was fervent in spirit. He spoke and taught accurately about Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John. 26 And he began to speak boldly in the synagogue. When Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately.

27 When Apollos resolved to cross over to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples there to welcome him. On his arrival, he was a great help to those who by grace had believed. 28 For he powerfully refuted the Jews in public debate, proving from the Scriptures that Jesus is the Christ.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Apollos, a Jewish man from Alexandria, comes to Ephesus with ability as a speaker and a strong knowledge of Scripture. He teaches accurately about Jesus and is fervent in spirit, yet he knows only John’s baptism. Luke gives him real commendation while also identifying a limit in his understanding.

Priscilla and Aquila hear him speaking boldly in the synagogue. They take him aside and explain God’s way more accurately. Both are named in this work of instruction. Luke does not provide their full conversation or a list of every point they clarify.

When Apollos wants to go to Achaia, the believers encourage him and write to the disciples there to welcome him. He greatly helps those who have believed through grace and uses Scripture to demonstrate publicly that Jesus is the Christ.

The account does not record Apollos being baptized again, nor does it say he personally baptized the people Paul meets in the next chapter. His knowledge of John’s baptism is a real limitation; it does not give us a complete account of everything he knew or of where he learned it.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly see a lesson in teachability: a capable and enthusiastic teacher can still need a fuller understanding, and patient instruction can make his service more useful. Readers differ over how much Apollos knew before this conversation. Calvin’s comments on verses 24–26 commend his faith while describing the need for further teaching; Wesley’s notes on verses 25–26 understand him as knowing John’s preparation for the coming Messiah. These are individual interpreters’ readings, not official rulings binding every member of their traditions.
passages.god_plan_html: Paul later describes their shared work in 1 Corinthians 3:5–9: Paul plants, Apollos waters and God gives the growth. Acts shows part of how that partnership develops. A husband and wife help a teacher grow; believers commend him to another community; his gifts then strengthen people there. God builds His people through contributions that belong together, rather than through loyalty to one impressive teacher.

passages.title: Acts 19:1-7
passages.section_title: What do these disciples need to understand about Jesus and the Holy Spirit?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 While Apollos was at Corinth, Paul passed through the interior and came to Ephesus. There he found some disciples 2 and asked them, “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you became believers?” “No,” they answered, “we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.” 3 “Into what, then, were you baptized?” Paul asked. “The baptism of John,” they replied. 4 Paul explained: “John’s baptism was a baptism of repentance. He told the people to believe in the One coming after him, that is, in Jesus.” 5 On hearing this, they were baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus. 6 And when Paul laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied. 7 There were about twelve men in all.
paragraphs: 1 While Apollos was at Corinth, Paul passed through the interior and came to Ephesus. There he found some disciples 2 and asked them, “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you became believers?” “No,” they answered, “we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.” 3 “Into what, then, were you baptized?” Paul asked. “The baptism of John,” they replied. 4 Paul explained: “John’s baptism was a baptism of repentance. He told the people to believe in the One coming after him, that is, in Jesus.”

5 On hearing this, they were baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus. 6 And when Paul laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied. 7 There were about twelve men in all.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
While Apollos is in Corinth, Paul reaches Ephesus and meets some disciples. His questions uncover a gap in their understanding: they know John’s baptism but say they have not heard that there is a Holy Spirit. Paul explains that John called people to repentance and directed them to believe in the One coming after him, Jesus.

On hearing this, they are baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus. Paul lays his hands on them, the Holy Spirit comes upon them, and they speak in tongues and prophesy. Luke gives their number as about twelve. He does not say that Apollos taught or baptized them, nor describe a command for everyone to reproduce each step in exactly this order.

The word disciples tells us they are learners or followers, but the questions and explanation matter for understanding whom they follow and what they know. The account moves from John’s preparation for the Messiah to an explicit response to Jesus and the gift of the Spirit.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians agree that John points beyond himself to Jesus. They differ over the disciples’ earlier spiritual condition and how this sequence relates to Christian life today.

The Catholic Church’s Catechism, paragraph 1288, understands the apostles’ laying on of hands as the origin of confirmation, which strengthens and completes the grace given in baptism. Its summary in 1315–1316 explicitly uses the related account in Acts 8.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 12, says those God receives as His children receive the Spirit. A 1978 Orthodox Presbyterian committee report, section I, reads Ephesus as one stage in the Spirit’s coming to the church, involving previously unreached disciples of John. It says every believer shares in baptism with the Spirit through belonging to Christ from the time they come to faith. The report explains a Reformed reading; it is not itself a confession binding all Reformed churches.

The Pentecostal Assemblies of God’s Fundamental Truths 7–8 teach baptism in the Holy Spirit as an empowering experience distinct from and following the beginning of Christian life, with speaking in tongues as its first outward evidence. That teaching distinguishes this experience from salvation; it does not say a person earns salvation by producing a sign.

Individual interpreters also differ about verse 5. Calvin understands it as baptism with the Spirit rather than another water baptism. Wesley’s note on verse 5 understands a new baptism in water, distinct from John’s. Neither individual reading should be assigned automatically to every member of a denomination.
passages.god_plan_html:
John’s ministry was preparation for Jesus, and the promised gift of the Spirit belongs to the risen Lord’s work. The speaking in tongues and prophecy here recalls Acts 2:1–4 and 10:44–48. This is a supported parallel in Luke’s account, not a claim that these twelve men replace the twelve apostles.

1 Corinthians 12:4–13 connects the Spirit’s varied gifts with the common good and one body made up of different people. The wider purpose is a people belonging to Christ and equipped to serve together, rather than a contest over who has the most impressive experience.

passages.title: Acts 19:8-10
passages.section_title: How does daily teaching in Ephesus reach beyond the city?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 Then Paul went into the synagogue and spoke boldly there for three months, arguing persuasively about the kingdom of God. 9 But when some of them stubbornly refused to believe and publicly maligned the Way, Paul took his disciples and left the synagogue to conduct daily discussions in the lecture hall of Tyrannus. 10 This continued for two years, so that everyone who lived in the province of Asia, Jews and Greeks alike, heard the word of the Lord.
paragraphs: 8 Then Paul went into the synagogue and spoke boldly there for three months, arguing persuasively about the kingdom of God. 9 But when some of them stubbornly refused to believe and publicly maligned the Way, Paul took his disciples and left the synagogue to conduct daily discussions in the lecture hall of Tyrannus. 10 This continued for two years, so that everyone who lived in the province of Asia, Jews and Greeks alike, heard the word of the Lord.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul speaks boldly in the synagogue for three months, explaining and seeking to persuade his hearers about God’s kingdom. When some refuse to believe and publicly speak against the Way, he leaves with the disciples and continues daily discussions in the lecture hall of Tyrannus.

The teaching continues for two years, with the result that Jewish and Greek people throughout the province of Asia hear the Lord’s word. Asia here is a Roman province, rather than the whole modern continent. Luke describes the wide reach of the message without listing every journey or naming the founder of every church.

The move changes the place of instruction without ending the work. The regular teaching matters alongside the remarkable events that follow. Luke does not tell us the hall’s precise schedule or every detail of how it was made available.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as persistent teaching that adapts when opposition closes one setting. The account values sustained explanation and the spread of the message through a wider region; it does not make a particular kind of meeting building essential to the mission.
passages.god_plan_html: Paul had earlier been prevented from speaking the word in Asia in Acts 16:6. Now the same region hears it widely. The earlier restraint was not a permanent rejection of its people. In the larger movement promised in Acts 1:8, God opens opportunities at different times, and steady teaching becomes a means by which the witness reaches beyond one gathering.

passages.title: Acts 19:11-20
passages.section_title: What separates God’s power from using Jesus’ name as a formula?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 God did extraordinary miracles through the hands of Paul, 12 so that even handkerchiefs and aprons that had touched him were taken to the sick, and the diseases and evil spirits left them. 13 Now there were some itinerant Jewish exorcists who tried to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those with evil spirits. They would say, “I command you by Jesus, whom Paul proclaims.” 14 Seven sons of Sceva, a Jewish chief priest, were doing this. 15 But one day the evil spirit responded, “Jesus I know, and I know about Paul, but who are you?” 16 Then the man with the evil spirit jumped on them and overpowered them all. The attack was so violent that they ran out of the house naked and wounded. 17 This became known to all the Jews and Greeks living in Ephesus, and fear came over all of them. So the name of the Lord Jesus was held in high honor. 18 Many who had believed now came forward, confessing and disclosing their deeds. 19 And a number of those who had practiced magic arts brought their books and burned them in front of everyone. When the value of the books was calculated, the total came to fifty thousand drachmas. 20 So the word of the Lord powerfully continued to spread and prevail.
paragraphs: 11 God did extraordinary miracles through the hands of Paul, 12 so that even handkerchiefs and aprons that had touched him were taken to the sick, and the diseases and evil spirits left them.

13 Now there were some itinerant Jewish exorcists who tried to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those with evil spirits. They would say, “I command you by Jesus, whom Paul proclaims.” 14 Seven sons of Sceva, a Jewish chief priest, were doing this. 15 But one day the evil spirit responded, “Jesus I know, and I know about Paul, but who are you?” 16 Then the man with the evil spirit jumped on them and overpowered them all. The attack was so violent that they ran out of the house naked and wounded.

17 This became known to all the Jews and Greeks living in Ephesus, and fear came over all of them. So the name of the Lord Jesus was held in high honor. 18 Many who had believed now came forward, confessing and disclosing their deeds. 19 And a number of those who had practiced magic arts brought their books and burned them in front of everyone. When the value of the books was calculated, the total came to fifty thousand drachmas. 20 So the word of the Lord powerfully continued to spread and prevail.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Luke identifies God as the One doing extraordinary miracles through Paul. Even cloths that have touched Paul are carried to sick people, and diseases and evil spirits leave them. The account credits God; it does not describe a power the cloths possess independently of Him.

Some traveling Jewish exorcists try to invoke Jesus’ name by referring to the Jesus Paul proclaims. An exorcist is someone who attempts to drive out an evil spirit. Thayer’s entry for ἐξορκιστής (exorkistēs, ex-or-kis-TAYS) describes someone using a spoken formula for that purpose. The word does not identify an ethnic group of travelers or prove every such person has the same motives.

Seven sons of Sceva, described as a Jewish chief priest, are involved. The evil spirit recognizes Jesus and knows about Paul, but challenges them; the afflicted man attacks and overpowers them. They flee wounded and naked. Luke does not give us Sceva’s full history or explain what every demon knows about every Christian.

The event becomes widely known, and Jesus’ name is held in honor. Many believers confess their deeds, and people who have practiced magic bring their books to be burned. Luke gives their value as fifty thousand drachmas, a large sum. The account describes people giving up their own practices and possessions, not an order to seize everyone else’s books.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians broadly distinguish these God-given miracles from attempts to control spiritual power through a borrowed name or technique. The confession and costly abandonment of magic show a changed way of life, rather than simply a more effective spell.

Traditions differ over the related question of honoring relics—remains or objects associated with saints. The Catholic Church’s Council of Trent, session 25, affirms honoring saints’ relics while requiring superstition and financial abuse to be removed. Its Catechism 2111 rejects treating religious practices as effective merely through their external performance.

The Reformed Westminster Confession 21:1–2 limits worship to what God has revealed and to God alone. Applying that concern here, Calvin’s comment on verse 11 rejects using Paul’s cloths to justify devotion to relics, understanding the miracles as confirming the apostolic message. This is his explicit application of the passage, not evidence that Catholics officially teach magic or that every Protestant has an identical view of physical objects.
passages.god_plan_html:
The healing recalls the sick being brought to the apostles in Acts 5:12–16. This is a parallel between God’s work through Peter and the apostles in Jerusalem and through Paul in Ephesus; the connection does not make either man an independent source of divine power.

The result reaches beyond physical relief. Jesus is honored, hidden practices are confessed and people leave costly attachments behind. Luke’s conclusion centers on the Lord’s word spreading and prevailing. The power serves the witness to Christ and a changed people, rather than becoming a possession someone can purchase or manipulate.

passages.title: Acts 19:21-22
passages.section_title: Why does Paul begin looking toward Jerusalem and Rome?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 After these things had happened, Paul resolved in the Spirit to go to Jerusalem, passing through Macedonia and Achaia. “After I have been there,” he said, “I must see Rome as well.” 22 He sent two of his helpers, Timothy and Erastus, to Macedonia, while he stayed for a time in the province of Asia.
paragraphs: 21 After these things had happened, Paul resolved in the Spirit to go to Jerusalem, passing through Macedonia and Achaia. “After I have been there,” he said, “I must see Rome as well.” 22 He sent two of his helpers, Timothy and Erastus, to Macedonia, while he stayed for a time in the province of Asia.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the events in Ephesus, Paul resolves in the Spirit to travel through Macedonia and Achaia to Jerusalem, then to see Rome. He sends Timothy and Erastus ahead to Macedonia while remaining for a time in Asia. These two verses turn our attention from the long work in Ephesus toward the next stage of the journey.

Paul’s later account in Romans 15:22–29 explains a journey to Jerusalem with help from Macedonia and Achaia for poor believers there, along with his desire to visit Rome. This gives a wider view of his concerns without supplying a complete timetable for every plan in Acts.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these plans as continuing mission and care for the churches, directed toward Jerusalem and beyond it. Paul makes practical arrangements and sends helpers; dependence on the Spirit is not presented as the absence of planning or shared responsibility.
passages.god_plan_html:
Rome now becomes an explicit destination in the narrative. In Acts 23:11, the Lord will tell Paul that he must testify there as he has in Jerusalem. The later promise connects this intention with God’s continuing purpose, even though the route will include arrest and hardship.

Romans 15:25–27 also shows Gentile churches sharing material help with believers in Jerusalem. The expanding mission does not discard earlier communities: people who have received spiritual blessings express their unity through practical care.

passages.title: Acts 19:23-27
passages.section_title: Why does the message about God threaten the idol trade?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 23 About that time there arose a great disturbance about the Way. 24 It began with a silversmith named Demetrius who made silver shrines of Artemis, bringing much business to the craftsmen. 25 Demetrius assembled the craftsmen, along with the workmen in related trades. “Men,” he said, “you know that this business is our source of prosperity. 26 And you can see and hear that not only in Ephesus, but in nearly the whole province of Asia, this Paul has persuaded a great number of people to turn away. He says that man-made gods are no gods at all. 27 There is danger not only that our business will fall into disrepute, but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis will be discredited and her majesty deposed—she who is worshiped by all the province of Asia and the whole world.”
paragraphs: 23 About that time there arose a great disturbance about the Way. 24 It began with a silversmith named Demetrius who made silver shrines of Artemis, bringing much business to the craftsmen. 25 Demetrius assembled the craftsmen, along with the workmen in related trades. “Men,” he said, “you know that this business is our source of prosperity. 26 And you can see and hear that not only in Ephesus, but in nearly the whole province of Asia, this Paul has persuaded a great number of people to turn away. He says that man-made gods are no gods at all. 27 There is danger not only that our business will fall into disrepute, but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis will be discredited and her majesty deposed—she who is worshiped by all the province of Asia and the whole world.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Demetrius makes silver shrines of Artemis, and the business supports other craftsmen and related workers. He gathers them and begins with the issue of their prosperity. Paul’s message that man-made gods are not gods has persuaded many people to turn away, threatening the trade.

He then appeals to the honor of Artemis and her temple. Luke lets us hear how economic anxiety and religious loyalty are joined in the appeal. The claim that the whole world worships her is part of Demetrius’s speech, not Luke’s announcement that every person in every nation does so.

The account identifies a real trade interest without telling us that Demetrius holds formal authority over every worker or that all the city’s religious concern is knowingly dishonest. The disturbance grows out of what he says to this gathering.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as an example of opposition arising when a change of worship affects livelihoods and social loyalties. Demetrius’s own speech joins concern for income with concern for the goddess. The narrative does not command believers to provoke riots as proof that their witness is effective.
passages.god_plan_html: Jesus’ warning in Luke 16:13 that a servant cannot serve both God and money helps explain the larger question of loyalty. Turning to the living God can unsettle arrangements built around another object of devotion. God’s purposes reach into work, spending and the things people protect, as well as what they say they believe.

passages.title: Acts 19:28-41
passages.section_title: How is the confused crowd prevented from turning its anger into further violence?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 28 When the men heard this, they were enraged and began shouting, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” 29 Soon the whole city was in disarray. They rushed together into the theatre, dragging with them Gaius and Aristarchus, Paul’s traveling companions from Macedonia. 30 Paul wanted to go before the assembly, but the disciples would not allow him. 31 Even some of Paul’s friends who were officials of the province of Asia sent word to him, begging him not to venture into the theatre. 32 Meanwhile the assembly was in turmoil. section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The craftsmen’s anger spreads into the city. Gaius and Aristarchus, Paul’s companions from Macedonia, are dragged into the theatre. Paul wants to enter, but the disciples stop him, and friends among the provincial officials also urge him to stay away. Luke does not present accepting their warning as cowardice.

The gathering is confused: people shout different things, and most do not know why they have come. Alexander is pushed forward by Jews in the crowd to make a defense. When the crowd recognizes that he is Jewish, it drowns him out with a chant honoring Artemis for about two hours. Luke does not identify him as the Alexander named in Paul’s later letters or tell us the speech he would have made.

The city clerk finally quiets the crowd. He appeals to their confidence in the city’s religious standing, says the men brought before them have neither robbed the temple nor blasphemed their goddess, and directs complaints to the courts and a lawful assembly. He warns that they risk being charged with rioting without a justification.

When the clerk speaks about an image falling from heaven, Luke is reporting his appeal to the crowd’s beliefs. The account does not ask readers to accept that claim as the truth about the image’s origin. The official dismisses the gathering, bringing the immediate danger to an end.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly see the value of wise restraint and lawful resolution in this account. Paul accepts the protection of fellow believers and friends, and an official ends the uproar. The clerk’s useful intervention does not mean his belief about Artemis has become Christian teaching.
passages.god_plan_html:
Here the witness is preserved through warnings, friendship and civic action, rather than another extraordinary miracle. Romans 13:3–4 describes governing authority as serving the good and restraining wrongdoing. The clerk’s effort to end a groundless riot provides a concrete parallel to that purpose.

This does not make every official action just. Earlier in Acts 5:29, the apostles insist on obeying God when commanded to stop their witness. The larger story includes both protection through authorities and faithfulness under unjust pressure. Here, the restraint gives the work room to continue.

passages.title: Acts 20:1-6
passages.section_title: Why does Paul revisit the disciples and change his route?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 When the uproar had ended, Paul sent for the disciples. And after encouraging them, he said goodbye to them and left for Macedonia. 2 After traveling through that area and speaking many words of encouragement, he arrived in Greece, 3 where he stayed three months. And when the Jews formed a plot against him as he was about to sail for Syria, he decided to go back through Macedonia. 4 Paul was accompanied by Sopater son of Pyrrhus from Berea, Aristarchus and Secundus from Thessalonica, Gaius from Derbe, Timothy, and Tychicus and Trophimus from the province of Asia. 5 These men went on ahead and waited for us in Troas. 6 And after the Feast of Unleavened Bread, we sailed from Philippi, and five days later we rejoined them in Troas, where we stayed seven days.
paragraphs: 1 When the uproar had ended, Paul sent for the disciples. And after encouraging them, he said goodbye to them and left for Macedonia. 2 After traveling through that area and speaking many words of encouragement, he arrived in Greece, 3 where he stayed three months. And when the Jews formed a plot against him as he was about to sail for Syria, he decided to go back through Macedonia.

4 Paul was accompanied by Sopater son of Pyrrhus from Berea, Aristarchus and Secundus from Thessalonica, Gaius from Derbe, Timothy, and Tychicus and Trophimus from the province of Asia. 5 These men went on ahead and waited for us in Troas. 6 And after the Feast of Unleavened Bread, we sailed from Philippi, and five days later we rejoined them in Troas, where we stayed seven days.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the uproar in Ephesus ends, Paul encourages the disciples and leaves for Macedonia. He gives much encouragement as he travels, then spends three months in Greece. A plot against him changes his intended voyage to Syria: he returns through Macedonia instead.

Luke names companions from Berea, Thessalonica, Derbe and the province of Asia, as well as Timothy. Some go ahead to Troas, while the narrator again uses we for the journey from Philippi after the Feast of Unleavened Bread. They rejoin the others in Troas after five days and stay for seven.

The plot is real, but Luke does not describe its exact method or say that Paul was to be thrown overboard. The list of companions shows a mission involving people from different places; it does not supply every person’s assignment or the complete reason each travels.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly see continuing care for believers and practical wisdom in this account. Paul strengthens communities he has already visited and changes his travel arrangements when danger becomes known. Perseverance in the mission does not require ignoring a threat or refusing an available safer route.
passages.god_plan_html: Romans 15:25–27 explains Paul’s journey to Jerusalem with material help from Macedonia and Achaia for poor believers there. Alongside the travel account, this shows the expanding mission joining communities in practical care. The work is not only a growing list of places visited: people who share in Christ’s blessings learn to support one another.

passages.title: Acts 20:7-12
passages.section_title: How does a frightening fall become a source of comfort at Troas?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 On the first day of the week we came together to break bread. Since Paul was ready to leave the next day, he talked to them and kept on speaking until midnight. 8 Now there were many lamps in the upper room where we were gathered. 9 And a certain young man named Eutychus, seated in the window, was sinking into a deep sleep as Paul talked on and on. When he was sound asleep, he fell from the third story and was picked up dead. 10 But Paul went down, threw himself on the young man, and embraced him. “Do not be alarmed!” he said. “He is still alive!” 11 Then Paul went back upstairs, broke bread, and ate. And after speaking until daybreak, he departed. 12 And the people were greatly relieved to take the boy home alive.
paragraphs: 7 On the first day of the week we came together to break bread. Since Paul was ready to leave the next day, he talked to them and kept on speaking until midnight. 8 Now there were many lamps in the upper room where we were gathered. 9 And a certain young man named Eutychus, seated in the window, was sinking into a deep sleep as Paul talked on and on. When he was sound asleep, he fell from the third story and was picked up dead.

10 But Paul went down, threw himself on the young man, and embraced him. “Do not be alarmed!” he said. “He is still alive!” 11 Then Paul went back upstairs, broke bread, and ate. And after speaking until daybreak, he departed. 12 And the people were greatly relieved to take the boy home alive.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The believers gather to break bread on the first day of the week. Paul is leaving the next day and continues speaking until midnight. Many lamps light the upper room. Eutychus, a young man sitting in a window, falls deeply asleep and drops from the third story; Luke says he is picked up dead.

Paul goes down, throws himself on him and embraces him, then tells the others not to be alarmed because the young man is alive. After returning upstairs, Paul breaks bread, eats and continues speaking until daybreak. The people take Eutychus home alive and are greatly relieved.

The account moves from death to restored life and comfort. It does not blame the young man’s character, prescribe a required sermon length or explain a medical mechanism for what happens. The description of breaking bread is commonly understood as including the Lord’s Supper in the gathered meal.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read Eutychus’s restoration as God giving life and comfort through Paul. The gathering on the first day of the week also matters in discussions of Christian worship, but traditions draw different conclusions about weekly observance.

The Catholic Church’s Catechism 2174–2177 connects Sunday with Christ’s resurrection, describes its celebration as fulfilling the spiritual truth of the Sabbath and teaches the obligation of the Sunday celebration.

The Reformed Westminster Confession 21:7–8 and the Reformed Baptist 1689 Confession 22:7–8 describe the first day as the Christian Sabbath, continuing a weekly command to set apart a day for worship and rest.

The Lutheran Augsburg Confession 28:53–60 supports an orderly common day for gathering while rejecting the idea that observance of Sunday or another day is necessary to obtain salvation. Its account emphasizes Christian freedom and consideration for the church’s order.

Seventh-day Adventists’ Fundamental Belief 20 instead affirms the continuing seventh-day Sabbath as the day of rest, worship and ministry. They do not understand this first-day gathering as a command changing the Sabbath to Sunday. These positions concern how this passage relates to Scripture as a whole, rather than a disagreement that Luke reports a gathering on the first day.
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul’s action recalls the restoration of children through Elijah in 1 Kings 17:17–24 and Elisha in 2 Kings 4:32–37. These are supported parallels: a child dies, God’s servant draws near and the child is returned alive. They do not make Paul’s embrace a technique anyone can use to command life.

The comfort at Troas belongs to the wider witness of God’s power over death. It also shows His care for a particular person and a frightened community in the middle of the mission’s travels. Eutychus is more than an illustration attached to a sermon; he is brought home alive.

passages.title: Acts 20:13-16
passages.section_title: Why does Paul sail past Ephesus on the way to Jerusalem?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 We went on ahead to the ship and sailed to Assos, where we were to take Paul aboard. He had arranged this because he was going there on foot. 14 And when he met us at Assos, we took him aboard and went on to Mitylene. 15 Sailing on from there, we arrived the next day opposite Chios. The day after that we arrived at Samos, and on the following day we came to Miletus. 16 Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus to avoid spending time in the province of Asia, because he was in a hurry to reach Jerusalem, if possible, by the day of Pentecost.
paragraphs: 13 We went on ahead to the ship and sailed to Assos, where we were to take Paul aboard. He had arranged this because he was going there on foot. 14 And when he met us at Assos, we took him aboard and went on to Mitylene. 15 Sailing on from there, we arrived the next day opposite Chios. The day after that we arrived at Samos, and on the following day we came to Miletus. 16 Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus to avoid spending time in the province of Asia, because he was in a hurry to reach Jerusalem, if possible, by the day of Pentecost.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul arranges to go on foot to Assos while his companions travel there by ship. They take him aboard and continue by Mitylene, Chios and Samos to Miletus. Luke records the stages of the journey without explaining why Paul chooses to walk that part of the route.

He sails past Ephesus because he does not want to spend time in Asia while hurrying to reach Jerusalem, if possible, for Pentecost. The next passage shows that this does not mean he has stopped caring about the Ephesian believers: he sends for their elders to meet him at Miletus.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as practical travel planning in view of Paul’s intended arrival at Jerusalem. Luke states his goal and the choice to pass Ephesus; the account does not require an additional hidden meaning for each port or route.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Acts 20:17
passages.section_title: Whom does Paul call to meet him at Miletus?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 From Miletus, Paul sent to Ephesus for the elders of the church.
paragraphs: 17 From Miletus, Paul sent to Ephesus for the elders of the church.

passages.context_html:
Paul has sailed past Ephesus while trying to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost. From Miletus he sends for the church’s elders. The speech that follows reminds them of his ministry and prepares them to care for the believers after his departure.

In verse 28, Paul describes these same elders as overseers and tells them to shepherd the church. Reading the invitation with that instruction keeps the focus on the people entrusted with care, rather than treating three descriptions as automatically three separate levels of rank.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the elders as responsible for caring for the community and guarding its teaching. Traditions differ over how this group relates to later forms of church leadership.

The Catholic Church’s Catechism, paragraphs 1562–1567, describes priests, also called presbyters or elders, as coworkers who share in the bishop’s mission and serve in communion with him and under his authority. In this account, their shared work does not erase the distinction between bishop and priest.

The Reformed Baptist 1689 Confession 26:8–9 names bishops or elders as the same local office, alongside deacons, and expressly cites Acts 20:17 and 28. It describes qualified leaders chosen by the congregation and set apart with prayer. That is the teaching of this confession, not a claim that every Baptist congregation has an identical arrangement.
passages.current_position_html: Who Shepherds the Church? directly compares Acts 20:17 and 28. The people Paul calls elders are the same people described as overseers and told to shepherd the church. The study understands these as descriptions of shared, qualified care, rather than separate ranks of elder, bishop and pastor. It calls for several capable leaders who teach, correct and serve among the people.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

passages.god_plan_html: The same pattern of care appears in 1 Peter 5:1–4, where elders shepherd the flock under Christ, the Chief Shepherd. Paul’s meeting helps prepare the community for faithful care after his departure. Its continuing life is centered on the Lord and His word, rather than on the permanent presence of one apostle.

passages.title: Acts 20:17-27
passages.section_title: What does Paul want the Ephesian elders to remember about his ministry?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 From Miletus, Paul sent to Ephesus for the elders of the church. 18 When they came to him, he said, “You know how I lived the whole time I was with you, from the first day I arrived in the province of Asia. 19 I served the Lord with great humility and with tears, especially in the trials that came upon me through the plots of the Jews. 20 I did not shrink back from declaring anything that was helpful to you as I taught you publicly and from house to house, 21 testifying to Jews and Greeks alike about repentance to God and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ. 22 And now, compelled by the Spirit, I am going to Jerusalem, not knowing what will happen to me there. 23 I only know that in town after town the Holy Spirit warns me that chains and afflictions await me. 24 But I consider my life of no value to me, if only I may finish my course and complete the ministry I have received from the Lord Jesus—the ministry of testifying to the good news of God’s grace. 25 Now I know that none of you among whom I have preached the kingdom will see my face again. 26 Therefore I testify to you this day that I am innocent of the blood of all men. 27 For I did not shrink back from declaring to you the whole will of God.

22 And now, compelled by the Spirit, I am going to Jerusalem, not knowing what will happen to me there. 23 I only know that in town after town the Holy Spirit warns me that chains and afflictions await me. 24 But I consider my life of no value to me, if only I may finish my course and complete the ministry I have received from the Lord Jesus—the ministry of testifying to the good news of God’s grace.

25 Now I know that none of you among whom I have preached the kingdom will see my face again. 26 Therefore I testify to you this day that I am innocent of the blood of all men. 27 For I did not shrink back from declaring to you the whole will of God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
From Miletus, Paul calls the Ephesian elders to meet him. He reminds them of a life they have seen: service with humility, tears and trials, and teaching both publicly and from house to house. His message to Jewish and Greek hearers alike has been repentance toward God and faith in Jesus.

He is now compelled by the Spirit to go to Jerusalem, where the Spirit has warned that chains and suffering await him. He does not know every detail of what will happen. His concern is to finish the work received from the Lord Jesus, testifying to the good news of God’s grace.

Paul tells them they will not see him again. He declares that he has not held back God’s whole will from them and is therefore innocent of their blood. In context, he is speaking about faithful delivery of the message entrusted to him, not claiming personal sinlessness or the power to make every listener believe.

The farewell prepares the elders for the responsibility described in the following verses. Paul’s example is meant to shape their care when he is no longer with them; it does not make their faith depend on keeping him physically present.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the elders as responsible for caring for the community and guarding its teaching. Traditions differ over how this group relates to later forms of church leadership.

The Catholic Church’s Catechism, paragraphs 1562–1567, describes priests, also called presbyters or elders, as coworkers who share in the bishop’s mission and serve in communion with him and under his authority. In this account, their shared work does not erase the distinction between bishop and priest.

The Reformed Baptist 1689 Confession 26:8–9 names bishops or elders as the same local office, alongside deacons, and expressly cites Acts 20:17 and 28. It describes qualified leaders chosen by the congregation and set apart with prayer. That is the teaching of this confession, not a claim that every Baptist congregation has an identical arrangement.
passages.god_plan_html:
The language about responsibility for others’ blood recalls the watchman in Ezekiel 33:7–9, who must deliver God’s warning rather than withhold it. This is a supported parallel in the responsibility to speak faithfully; it does not transfer every detail of Ezekiel’s commission to every church member.

Paul’s desire to finish the course also connects with 2 Timothy 4:6–8, where he looks back on a completed race and forward to the Lord’s judgment and promised reward. The larger aim is faithfulness to Christ through the whole course, including suffering, rather than securing an easy ending.

The study understands these as descriptions of shared, qualified care, rather than separate ranks of elder, bishop and pastor. It calls for several capable leaders who teach, correct and serve among the people.

passages.title: Acts 20:28-38
passages.section_title: How should shepherds care for the church after Paul leaves?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 28 Keep watch over yourselves and the entire flock of which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers. Be shepherds of the church of God, which He purchased with His own blood. 29 I know that after my departure, savage wolves will come in among you and will not spare the flock. 30 Even from your own number, men will rise up and distort the truth to draw away disciples after them. 31 Therefore be alert and remember that for three years I never stopped warning each of you night and day with tears. 32 And now I commit you to God and to the word of His grace, which can build you up and give you an inheritance among all who are sanctified. 33 I have not coveted anyone’s silver or gold or clothing. 34 You yourselves know that these hands of mine have ministered to my own needs and those of my companions. 35 In everything, I showed you that by this kind of hard work we must help the weak, remembering the words of the Lord Jesus Himself: ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’ ” 36 When Paul had said this, he knelt down with all of them and prayed. 37 They all wept openly as they embraced Paul and kissed him. 38 They were especially grieved by his statement that they would never see his face again. Then they accompanied him to the ship.

Be shepherds of the church of God, which He purchased with His own blood. 29 I know that after my departure, savage wolves will come in among you and will not spare the flock. 30 Even from your own number, men will rise up and distort the truth to draw away disciples after them. 31 Therefore be alert and remember that for three years I never stopped warning each of you night and day with tears.

32 And now I commit you to God and to the word of His grace, which can build you up and give you an inheritance among all who are sanctified. 33 I have not coveted anyone’s silver or gold or clothing. 34 You yourselves know that these hands of mine have ministered to my own needs and those of my companions. 35 In everything, I showed you that by this kind of hard work we must help the weak, remembering the words of the Lord Jesus Himself: ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’ ”

36 When Paul had said this, he knelt down with all of them and prayed. 37 They all wept openly as they embraced Paul and kissed him. 38 They were especially grieved by his statement that they would never see his face again. Then they accompanied him to the ship.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul tells the elders to watch themselves as well as the whole flock. The Holy Spirit has made them overseers, and they are to shepherd the church God has purchased at the cost of Christ’s blood. The people belong to God, not to the leaders who care for them.

The word overseers comes from ἐπίσκοπος (episkopos, eh-PEE-skoh-poss), a person charged with watching over and caring for others. Thayer’s entry identifies its use here for oversight of a Christian church. The same people called elders in verse 17 now receive this description and the task of shepherding.

The danger comes both from outside and from their own number. Paul warns of people who distort the truth to draw disciples after themselves. His own care has included repeated warnings with tears. He now entrusts them to God and the word of His grace, which can build them up and give them an inheritance among His people.

Paul also reminds them that he has not coveted their possessions. His work has supported his own needs and those of companions, showing the duty to help the weak and the blessing of giving. He quotes a saying of Jesus that Acts preserves even though it is not recorded in the four Gospels.

They kneel and pray together, then weep, embrace and accompany him to the ship. Their grief centers on his words that they will not see him again. The warning and instruction are delivered within a relationship of deep affection.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the elders as responsible for caring for the community and guarding its teaching. Traditions differ over how this group relates to later forms of church leadership.

The Catholic Church’s Catechism, paragraphs 1562–1567, describes priests, also called presbyters or elders, as coworkers who share in the bishop’s mission and serve in communion with him and under his authority. In this account, their shared work does not erase the distinction between bishop and priest.

The Reformed Baptist 1689 Confession 26:8–9 names bishops or elders as the same local office, alongside deacons, and expressly cites Acts 20:17 and 28. It describes qualified leaders chosen by the congregation and set apart with prayer. That is the teaching of this confession, not a claim that every Baptist congregation has an identical arrangement.

Across these different accounts of leadership, Christians commonly recognize the duties to guard the teaching, care for people and avoid greed. Paul’s own work is an example of generosity; it does not erase his teaching elsewhere that churches can support those who serve them. The 1689 Confession 26:10, for example, expressly calls for such support.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Peter 5:1–4 gives elders a closely related charge: shepherd willingly, without greed or domination, and live as examples. It identifies Christ as the Chief Shepherd. The wider purpose is care under His authority, with the people’s growth in view, rather than the building of a leader’s personal following.

Paul’s departure does not leave the church without its Lord. He entrusts the elders to God and the word of grace, and the promised inheritance looks beyond this painful farewell. The ministry serves a people whose future rests with God, even as human workers come and go.

passages.title: Acts 21:1-6
passages.section_title: Why do the believers at Tyre urge Paul not to continue to Jerusalem?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 After we had torn ourselves away from them, we sailed directly to Cos, and the next day on to Rhodes, and from there to Patara. 2 Finding a ship crossing over to Phoenicia, we boarded it and set sail. 3 After sighting Cyprus and passing south of it, we sailed on to Syria and landed at Tyre, where the ship was to unload its cargo. 4 We sought out the disciples in Tyre and stayed with them seven days. Through the Spirit they kept telling Paul not to go up to Jerusalem. 5 But when our time there had ended, we set out on our journey. All the disciples, with their wives and children, accompanied us out of the city and knelt down on the beach to pray with us. 6 And after we had said our farewells, we went aboard the ship, and they returned home.
paragraphs: 1 After we had torn ourselves away from them, we sailed directly to Cos, and the next day on to Rhodes, and from there to Patara. 2 Finding a ship crossing over to Phoenicia, we boarded it and set sail. 3 After sighting Cyprus and passing south of it, we sailed on to Syria and landed at Tyre, where the ship was to unload its cargo. 4 We sought out the disciples in Tyre and stayed with them seven days. Through the Spirit they kept telling Paul not to go up to Jerusalem.

5 But when our time there had ended, we set out on our journey. All the disciples, with their wives and children, accompanied us out of the city and knelt down on the beach to pray with us. 6 And after we had said our farewells, we went aboard the ship, and they returned home.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the painful farewell at Miletus, Paul and his companions sail by Cos, Rhodes and Patara, then find a ship bound for Phoenicia. They pass Cyprus and land at Tyre, where the ship unloads its cargo. They seek out the disciples and stay seven days.

Luke says the disciples keep telling Paul through the Spirit not to go to Jerusalem. This needs to be read alongside Paul’s statement in Acts 20:22–23 that he is compelled by the Spirit to go there and has been warned of chains and suffering. The account presents both statements; it does not explain the whole tension in a single word.

When the travelers leave, the disciples accompany them out of the city with their wives and children. They kneel and pray on the beach, say farewell and part. The appeal against continuing comes within a relationship of care, not hostility toward Paul or his work.
passages.common_interpretations_html: A common reading distinguishes the Spirit’s warning of danger from the believers’ wish that Paul avoid it. Calvin on verse 4 and Wesley on verse 4 understand the danger as revealed by the Spirit and the advice against going as the disciples’ response to it. This reading brings the warning together with Paul’s earlier sense of obligation; it is an explanation of the wider account, not something proved by contrasting the English words through and by.
passages.god_plan_html: Acts 11:19 describes the word reaching Phoenicia after the persecution connected with Stephen. Now a community in the Phoenician port of Tyre welcomes and prays with Paul. Luke does not identify its founders here, but the connection shows the wider fruit of the mission: people in different places become a family who share one another’s concerns.

passages.title: Acts 21:7-14
passages.section_title: How do Paul and his companions respond to the warning about his arrest?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 When we had finished our voyage from Tyre, we landed at Ptolemais, where we greeted the brothers and stayed with them for a day. 8 Leaving the next day, we went on to Caesarea and stayed at the home of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the Seven. 9 He had four unmarried daughters who prophesied. 10 After we had been there several days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea. 11 Coming over to us, he took Paul’s belt, bound his own feet and hands, and said, “The Holy Spirit says: ‘In this way the Jews of Jerusalem will bind the owner of this belt and hand him over to the Gentiles.’” 12 When we heard this, we and the people there pleaded with Paul not to go up to Jerusalem. 13 Then Paul answered, “Why are you weeping and breaking my heart? I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.” 14 When he would not be dissuaded, we quieted down and said, “The Lord’s will be done.”
paragraphs: 7 When we had finished our voyage from Tyre, we landed at Ptolemais, where we greeted the brothers and stayed with them for a day. 8 Leaving the next day, we went on to Caesarea and stayed at the home of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the Seven. 9 He had four unmarried daughters who prophesied. 10 After we had been there several days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea. 11 Coming over to us, he took Paul’s belt, bound his own feet and hands, and said, “The Holy Spirit says: ‘In this way the Jews of Jerusalem will bind the owner of this belt and hand him over to the Gentiles.’”

12 When we heard this, we and the people there pleaded with Paul not to go up to Jerusalem. 13 Then Paul answered, “Why are you weeping and breaking my heart? I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.” 14 When he would not be dissuaded, we quieted down and said, “The Lord’s will be done.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After greeting believers at Ptolemais, the travelers reach Caesarea and stay with Philip the evangelist, one of the Seven introduced in Acts 6. Luke notes that Philip has four unmarried daughters who prophesy, without giving their messages here. Their mention does not explain the later warning as a message from them.

Agabus comes from Judea, takes Paul’s belt and binds his own hands and feet with it. He announces that the Holy Spirit says the owner will be bound in Jerusalem and handed over to Gentiles. His action gives the coming danger a visible form.

Paul’s companions and the local believers plead with him not to go. He tells them their weeping is breaking his heart, but says he is ready to be imprisoned and even to die for Jesus’ name. They stop trying to persuade him and entrust the outcome to the Lord’s will.

Agabus’s quoted message predicts what will happen; it does not contain an explicit command to abandon the journey. That observation matters when comparing this scene with the wording at Tyre. It does not mean a warning from God should simply be ignored or that seeking safety is always wrong.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a costly decision made amid affection, grief and a warning of suffering. Wesley on verses 13–14 understands Paul’s determination as Christian resolve rather than stubbornness. The companions’ final response expresses trust in the Lord’s will; the text does not call their love for Paul selfish or say that all concern for physical safety is unbelief.
passages.god_plan_html:
The prayerful acceptance of the Lord’s will recalls Jesus’ prayer in Luke 22:42. This is a parallel in surrender to God under the prospect of suffering. Paul’s suffering is service to Jesus, not another sacrifice that saves people as Jesus’ death does.

Acts 9:15–16 had already connected Paul’s calling to bear Jesus’ name with suffering for that name. The warnings prepare him and the communities around him for a mission that continues through hardship, rather than promising an untroubled journey.

passages.title: Acts 21:15-26
passages.section_title: Why does Paul join the purification after meeting James and the elders?
