section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The travelers go up to Jerusalem and are welcomed by the believers. On the next day Paul meets James with all the elders present. He recounts what God has done among the Gentiles through his ministry, and they glorify God.

The leaders then explain a concern among many Jewish believers who remain zealous for the law. They have heard that Paul tells Jews living among the Gentiles to abandon Moses, circumcision and their customs. Luke reports the concern as something people have been told, not as a complete and settled summary of Paul’s teaching.

The leaders advise Paul to join four men who have made a vow, undergo purification with them and pay their expenses so they can shave their heads. They intend this public action to counter the reports about him. They also restate the earlier decision concerning Gentile believers. Paul follows the advice and enters the temple to give notice of when the purification and offerings will be complete.

Numbers 6:13–21 provides the background for offerings and cutting the hair at the completion of a Nazirite vow. It includes several kinds of offering, including a sin offering. Acts does not spell out every ritual detail or say that Paul himself takes a new vow and shaves his own head.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly recognize the leaders’ aim of preserving fellowship and answering damaging reports. Interpreters differ over whether the chosen action is a wise use of freedom or a concession that obscures it.

The Catholic USCCB notes on 21:17–26 understand Acts as allowing Jewish Christians to retain these practices while Gentile believers remain under the earlier agreed requirements. These are the published notes’ explanation of the scene, rather than an instruction that Christians today must perform its temple rites.

Calvin on verse 26 rejects the claim that Paul’s later trouble proves God is punishing him for hypocrisy. He sees a voluntary accommodation for the good of others, although he questions aspects of the leaders’ advice. Wesley on verses 23–26 is more critical: he thinks Paul yields too far and risks appearing to treat the Mosaic law as still binding. Those are individual teachers’ judgments of the event, not official verdicts that every Reformed or Wesleyan Christian must share.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 15:7–9 calls believers to welcome one another and connects Christ’s service to Israel’s promises with the Gentiles glorifying God for mercy. That larger purpose helps explain why fellowship between Jewish and Gentile believers matters so deeply here.

In 1 Corinthians 9:19–23, Paul explains his willingness to adapt in order to reach others, while distinguishing that service from being outside God’s authority. This provides a relevant framework for the question of accommodation. It does not by itself settle every disputed judgment about the particular action in Jerusalem.
passages.current_position_html: Who Shepherds the Church? directly discusses Acts 21:18 alongside the earlier Jerusalem meeting. Its position is that James has recognized personal standing while the elders continue to function together. Paul visits James with all the elders present; the study does not read this as a scene in which one man has replaced their shared responsibility.

passages.title: Acts 21:18
passages.section_title: Why does Luke mention James and all the elders together?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 The next day Paul went in with us to see James, and all the elders were present.
paragraphs: 18 The next day Paul went in with us to see James, and all the elders were present.

passages.context_html:
Paul has arrived in Jerusalem and received a warm welcome. The next day he meets James, and all the elders are present. He reports what God has done among the Gentiles, and the gathered leaders glorify God before discussing the concerns about his teaching.

The verse names James without removing the elders from the scene. The advice that follows is presented within this gathered leadership. Reading only James’s name and leaving out the rest of the verse would give an incomplete picture of the meeting.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly recognize James’s prominence in Jerusalem and the presence of a group of elders. Traditions differ over how this relates to later church offices. The Catholic Catechism 1562–1567 describes bishops with priests as their coworkers. The Reformed Baptist 1689 Confession 26:8–9 describes bishops or elders as the same local office. These wider accounts of leadership shape how readers understand James’s standing; this single verse does not describe every later arrangement.
passages.current_position_html: Who Shepherds the Church? directly discusses Acts 21:18 alongside the earlier Jerusalem meeting. Its position is that James has recognized personal standing while the elders continue to function together. Paul visits James with all the elders present; the study does not read this as a scene in which one man has replaced their shared responsibility.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html: Paul’s report brings the Gentile mission before the Jerusalem believers, who respond by glorifying God. Romans 15:7–9 connects welcome between believers with God’s promises to Israel and mercy shown among the Gentiles. Their shared praise belongs to that larger concern for one people welcoming those God has received.

passages.title: Acts 21:27-36
passages.section_title: How does an assumption about Trophimus lead to violence against Paul?

Then he asked who he was and what he had done. 34 Some in the crowd were shouting one thing, and some another. And since the commander could not get at the truth because of the uproar, he ordered that Paul be brought into the barracks. 35 When Paul reached the steps, he had to be carried by the soldiers because of the violence of the mob. 36 For the crowd that followed him kept shouting, “Away with him!”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
As the seven days near their end, some Jews from Asia see Paul in the temple and stir up the crowd. They accuse him of teaching against the people, the law and the temple, and of bringing Greeks into the holy place. Luke explains the basis of the last accusation: they had seen Trophimus with Paul in the city and assumed Paul had brought him into the temple.

A surviving temple warning helps explain the seriousness of that accusation. The University of Michigan’s record of the Greek inscription describes a notice warning non-Jews not to pass the restricted entrance, on pain of death. This supplies background for the charge, not evidence that Trophimus actually crossed the boundary.

The crowd seizes Paul, drags him out and tries to kill him. Roman soldiers arrive, and the beating stops. The commander arrests Paul and orders two chains, but cannot establish the facts amid contradictory shouting. The soldiers have to carry Paul because of the crowd’s violence as they bring him toward the barracks.

The accusations must remain distinct from the narrator’s explanation. Seeing two people together in the city did not establish that one had taken the other into a restricted temple area. Nor does the arrest itself prove the crowd’s charges true.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a violent attack driven by accusation and an untested assumption. The Roman intervention preserves Paul’s life while also placing him in custody. The text does not present the crowd’s anger as a reliable judgment about his guilt.
passages.god_plan_html:
The charges about the law and the holy place recall those brought against Stephen in Acts 6:13–14. This is a supported parallel in how the witness is opposed, not proof that every detail of the two events is identical.

Paul once took part in the persecution surrounding Stephen’s death; he is now the one suffering for Jesus’ name. Acts 9:15–16 joins his commission with that suffering. His arrest becomes part of the continuing witness rather than the end of the calling, though Luke does not ask us to call the violence good or the accusations true.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Acts 21:37-40
passages.section_title: Why does Paul ask to speak to the crowd after being rescued?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.context_html:
As Paul is about to enter the barracks, he asks the commander in Greek for permission to speak. The commander’s response reveals another mistaken identification: he wonders whether Paul is the Egyptian connected with an earlier rebellion and four thousand members of the Assassins.

Paul answers by identifying himself as a Jew from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of a notable city, and asks to address the people. The commander allows it. Paul stands on the steps, signals for quiet and begins speaking in Hebrew.

The scene ends at the opening of the speech continued in Acts 22. Paul has corrected the officer’s assumption and gained a hearing from the crowd. Luke does not say that the officer now believes Paul’s message or that everyone in the crowd has been persuaded.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly see courage and respectful use of an available opportunity here. Paul clarifies who he is and requests permission to speak, rather than accepting either the crowd’s accusation or the commander’s mistaken identity as the last word.
passages.god_plan_html: Acts 9:15–16 describes Paul’s calling to bear Jesus’ name before Gentiles, rulers and the people of Israel, alongside suffering for that name. Here he stands between a Roman officer and a Jewish crowd, under arrest yet still seeking a hearing. The speech that follows will make his testimony part of the very situation intended to silence him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Acts 22:1-5
passages.section_title: Why does Paul begin his defense with his former zeal and persecution?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 “Brothers and fathers, listen now to my defense before you.” 2 When they heard him speak to them in Hebrew, they became even more quiet. Then Paul declared, 3 “I am a Jew, born in Tarsus of Cilicia, but raised in this city. I was educated at the feet of Gamaliel in strict conformity to the law of our fathers. I was just as zealous for God as any of you are today. 4 I persecuted this Way even to the death, detaining both men and women and throwing them into prison, 5 as the high priest and the whole Council can testify about me. I even obtained letters from them to their brothers in Damascus, and I was on my way to apprehend these people and bring them to Jerusalem to be punished.

Then Paul declared, 3 “I am a Jew, born in Tarsus of Cilicia, but raised in this city. I was educated at the feet of Gamaliel in strict conformity to the law of our fathers. I was just as zealous for God as any of you are today. 4 I persecuted this Way even to the death, detaining both men and women and throwing them into prison, 5 as the high priest and the whole Council can testify about me. I even obtained letters from them to their brothers in Damascus, and I was on my way to apprehend these people and bring them to Jerusalem to be punished.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul stands on the steps under Roman protection, addressing the crowd that has just tried to kill him. He asks them to hear his defense and speaks in Hebrew. He identifies himself as a Jew born in Tarsus but raised in Jerusalem, taught under Gamaliel and deeply committed to the ancestral law.

His opening establishes something he has shared with his hearers: zeal for God. He also admits that his zeal once drove him to persecute the Way, imprisoning men and women and pursuing believers to Damascus. His former authority can be checked with the high priest and council.

This is not a claim that his violence was right because he was sincere. It prepares the hearers to understand how sharply his encounter with Jesus changed his direction. The story begins with the former persecutor acknowledging what he had done.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read the opening as a respectful appeal to shared background followed by an honest account of serious wrongdoing. Religious knowledge and zeal do not by themselves prove that a person is serving God rightly. Paul’s earlier conduct becomes part of his testimony to mercy rather than a record that earns him approval.
passages.god_plan_html: 1 Timothy 1:12–16 explicitly describes the former persecutor receiving mercy and becoming an example of Christ’s patience toward future believers. Paul’s past is not hidden, but neither is it the final word about him. His service displays God’s ability to turn an enemy of the message into its witness.

passages.title: Acts 22:6-11
passages.section_title: How does meeting Jesus change the direction of Paul’s journey?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 About noon as I was approaching Damascus, suddenly a bright light from heaven flashed around me. 7 I fell to the ground and heard a voice say to me, ‘Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?’ 8 ‘Who are You, Lord?’ I asked. ‘I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting,’ He replied. 9 My companions saw the light, but they could not understand the voice of the One speaking to me. 10 Then I asked, ‘What should I do, Lord?’ ‘Get up and go into Damascus,’ He told me. ‘There you will be told all that you have been appointed to do.’ 11 Because the brilliance of the light had blinded me, my companions led me by the hand into Damascus.

10 Then I asked, ‘What should I do, Lord?’ ‘Get up and go into Damascus,’ He told me. ‘There you will be told all that you have been appointed to do.’ 11 Because the brilliance of the light had blinded me, my companions led me by the hand into Damascus.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul recalls traveling toward Damascus around noon when a bright light from heaven flashes around him. He falls and hears Jesus of Nazareth ask why he is persecuting Him. The people Paul has been attacking belong to Jesus; his actions against them have been directed against their Lord.

His companions see the light but do not understand the voice. This explains an important distinction when reading the account alongside Acts 9:7, where they hear the sound. They witness something happening without receiving the message in the way Paul does.

Paul asks what he should do, and Jesus tells him to enter Damascus, where he will learn what has been appointed for him. Blinded by the light, he has to be led by the hand. He approaches the city in dependence on others, rather than arriving simply to exercise his former power against believers.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as the risen Jesus confronting and redirecting Paul. Calvin’s comment on verse 9 and Wesley’s note on verse 9 distinguish hearing a sound from understanding the message when comparing the accounts. Neither account makes the companions witnesses to every word and experience in precisely the same way as Paul.
passages.god_plan_html: Galatians 1:13–16 connects Paul’s former persecution with God’s gracious calling and the revelation of His Son for the purpose of preaching among the Gentiles. The encounter is therefore more than an individual change of mind. It redirects a life toward the wider mission that Paul will describe to this crowd.

passages.title: Acts 22:12-16
passages.section_title: What does Ananias call Paul to receive and do?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 There a man named Ananias, a devout observer of the law who was highly regarded by all the Jews living there, 13 came and stood beside me. ‘Brother Saul,’ he said, ‘receive your sight.’ And at that moment I could see him. 14 Then he said, ‘The God of our fathers has appointed you to know His will and to see the Righteous One and to hear His voice. 15 You will be His witness to everyone of what you have seen and heard. 16 And now what are you waiting for? Get up, be baptized, and wash your sins away, calling on His name.’
paragraphs: 12 There a man named Ananias, a devout observer of the law who was highly regarded by all the Jews living there, 13 came and stood beside me. ‘Brother Saul,’ he said, ‘receive your sight.’ And at that moment I could see him. 14 Then he said, ‘The God of our fathers has appointed you to know His will and to see the Righteous One and to hear His voice. 15 You will be His witness to everyone of what you have seen and heard. 16 And now what are you waiting for? Get up, be baptized, and wash your sins away, calling on His name.’

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul describes Ananias as a devout observer of the law, respected by the Jewish people living in Damascus. This helps his Jerusalem hearers understand that the person who received him was not presented as an enemy of their people. Ananias addresses him as a brother, and his sight returns.

Ananias tells him that the God of their fathers has appointed him to know His will, see the Righteous One and hear His voice. Paul is to witness to what he has seen and heard. The response now urged is immediate: be baptized, wash away sins and call on His name.

The washing word is ἀπολούω (apolouō, ah-poh-LOO-oh), to wash off or away. Thayer’s entry identifies the figurative cleansing from sins in this verse. Restored eyesight is not the whole change being described; the language concerns Paul’s standing before God and the life he is now called to live.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians agree that Ananias calls Paul to be baptized and to call on the Lord. They differ over how baptism’s washing relates to forgiveness and faith.

The Catholic Church’s Catechism 1213 teaches that through baptism God frees people from sin and gives new life. The Lutheran Large Catechism, Baptism 14–17, 28–31 and 41, likewise presents forgiveness as a gift brought in baptism. It joins the water with God’s word and promise, received through faith, rather than attributing the gift to water’s natural qualities.

The Reformed Westminster Confession 28:5–6 says the Holy Spirit truly gives the promised grace to those for whom it is intended, in God’s appointed time. It rejects both the claim that salvation is impossible without baptism and the claim that every baptized person has certainly received new life. It also says baptism’s effect is not tied to the precise moment of the ceremony.

The Reformed Baptist 1689 Confession 29:1–2 describes baptism as a sign of fellowship with Christ in His death and resurrection, forgiveness of sins and a new life given to God. It expressly cites Acts 22:16 and identifies those who profess repentance and faith as its recipients.

The Methodist Articles XVI–XVII describe the sacraments as signs through which God works and baptism as a sign of the new life He gives. Wesley’s note on verse 16 describes baptism for people who have truly turned to God as both a means and a seal of pardon. That is his explanation of the verse; the Articles do not prescribe every detail of one reading of its grammar.
passages.god_plan_html:
Titus 3:4–7 connects salvation with God’s kindness, mercy, washing and renewal by the Holy Spirit, leading to the hope of eternal life. The cleansing language belongs within that larger work of God, rather than being detached as a human achievement that earns His favor.

Paul is being prepared to witness to what he has seen and heard. Restored sight and cleansing lead into a changed life of service. 1 Timothy 1:12–16 later holds up the mercy shown to this former persecutor as an example of Christ’s patience toward those who will believe.
passages.current_position_html: Baptism directly discusses Acts 22:16. The study distinguishes forgiveness received through faith from the washing of the believer in baptism, and joins that washing with calling on Jesus’ name. It therefore treats baptism as a commanded response of genuine faith, not as water acting independently of faith or the Lord.

passages.title: Acts 22:16
passages.section_title: Why are baptism, washing and calling on the Lord joined here?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 And now what are you waiting for? Get up, be baptized, and wash your sins away, calling on His name.’
paragraphs: 16 And now what are you waiting for? Get up, be baptized, and wash your sins away, calling on His name.’

Ananias has just told Paul that God appointed him to know His will, see the Righteous One and become a witness. passages.title: Acts 22:17-21
passages.section_title: Why does Paul say he was sent away from Jerusalem to the Gentiles?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 Later, when I had returned to Jerusalem and was praying at the temple, I fell into a trance 18 and saw the Lord saying to me, ‘Hurry! Leave Jerusalem quickly, because the people here will not accept your testimony about Me.’ 19 ‘Lord,’ I answered, ‘they know very well that in one synagogue after another I imprisoned and beat those who believed in You. 20 And when the blood of Your witness Stephen was shed, I stood there giving my approval and watching over the garments of those who killed him.’ 21 Then He said to me, ‘Go! I will send you far away to the Gentiles.’ ”
paragraphs: 17 Later, when I had returned to Jerusalem and was praying at the temple, I fell into a trance 18 and saw the Lord saying to me, ‘Hurry! Leave Jerusalem quickly, because the people here will not accept your testimony about Me.’ 19 ‘Lord,’ I answered, ‘they know very well that in one synagogue after another I imprisoned and beat those who believed in You. 20 And when the blood of Your witness Stephen was shed, I stood there giving my approval and watching over the garments of those who killed him.’ 21 Then He said to me, ‘Go! I will send you far away to the Gentiles.’ ”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul recalls a later visit to Jerusalem when he was praying in the temple and saw the Lord in a trance. The Lord told him to leave quickly because people there would not accept his testimony. The setting matters for the present defense: Paul’s account includes prayer in the temple he has been accused of opposing.

Paul points to his former imprisonment and beating of believers and his approval when Stephen was killed. His hearers knew that past. But the Lord directs him to go, sending him far away to the Gentiles. His mission is presented as a commission from the Lord, not a private decision to abandon the people among whom he was raised.

The passage gives the substance of this exchange without telling us every thought Paul had about persuading his former associates. It should not be turned into a claim that he thought his own reputation could control everyone’s response.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read the Gentile mission here as a calling from Jesus that Paul is explaining to his Jewish hearers. His remembered involvement in Stephen’s death shows how far his life has changed. The command to go beyond Jerusalem does not mean every Jewish person is rejected by God.
passages.god_plan_html:
Isaiah 49:6 sets the Servant’s work in relation to both Israel and the nations. Acts 13:46–47 explicitly uses that promise when Paul and Barnabas explain the mission to the Gentiles. The direction Paul receives here belongs to that wider purpose of bringing God’s salvation to the nations.

His encounter and commission do not end with private assurance. What he has seen and heard becomes testimony for people beyond his former circle. The crowd’s reaction in the next verses makes clear that this wider mercy is also a point of conflict.

passages.title: Acts 22:22-30
passages.section_title: How does Paul’s citizenship stop the threatened flogging?

Then he brought Paul down and had him stand before them.
paragraphs: 22 The crowd listened to Paul until he made this statement. Then they lifted up their voices and shouted, “Rid the earth of him! He is not fit to live!” 23 As they were shouting and throwing off their cloaks and tossing dust into the air, 24 the commander ordered that Paul be brought into the barracks. He directed that Paul be flogged and interrogated to determine the reason for this outcry against him. 25 But as they stretched him out to strap him down, Paul said to the centurion standing there, “Is it lawful for you to flog a Roman citizen without a trial?”

26 On hearing this, the centurion went and reported it to the commander. “What are you going to do?” he said. “This man is a Roman citizen.” 27 The commander went to Paul and asked, “Tell me, are you a Roman citizen?” “Yes,” he answered. 28 “I paid a high price for my citizenship,” said the commander. “But I was born a citizen,” Paul replied. 29 At once those who were about to interrogate Paul stepped back, and the commander himself was alarmed when he realized that he had put a Roman citizen in chains. 30 The next day the commander, wanting to learn the real reason Paul was accused by the Jews, released him and ordered the chief priests and the whole Sanhedrin to assemble. Then he brought Paul down and had him stand before them.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The crowd listens until Paul speaks of being sent to the Gentiles, then calls for him to be removed from the earth. Shouting, cloaks thrown off and dust tossed into the air accompany the anger. The commander orders Paul brought inside and interrogated by flogging to discover why the crowd is shouting against him.

As Paul is being strapped down, he asks whether it is lawful to flog a Roman citizen without a trial. The centurion reports his citizenship, and the commander questions him directly. The officer says he paid a large sum for his citizenship; Paul says he was born a citizen.

Those preparing the interrogation step back, and the commander is alarmed that he has put a citizen in chains. An earlier Roman speech, Cicero, Against Verres 2.5.162–170, condemns the beating of a Roman citizen as an abuse of citizenship. That background helps explain the weight of Paul’s question without supplying a complete legal code for every form of Roman custody.

The next day the commander brings Paul before the chief priests and the whole Sanhedrin, the Jewish council, to discover the real accusation. Citizenship has stopped the threatened flogging; it has not ended the dispute or brought every proceeding to a close.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read Paul’s appeal as a legitimate use of available protection while he continues his witness. Readiness to suffer for Jesus does not require accepting an unlawful punishment in silence. Luke reports the crowd’s reaction without making it the attitude of every Jewish person toward Gentiles.
passages.god_plan_html: The later promise in Acts 23:11 connects Paul’s witness in Jerusalem with the witness he must give in Rome. This episode shows the mission continuing through opposition, custody and an appeal to citizenship. God’s preservation of a witness can work through an ordinary question and a public responsibility, alongside the extraordinary encounters Paul has just described.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Acts 23:1-5
passages.section_title: How does Paul respond when the high priest orders him to be struck?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Paul looked directly at the Sanhedrin and said, “Brothers, I have conducted myself before God in all good conscience to this day.” 2 At this, the high priest Ananias ordered those standing near Paul to strike him on the mouth. 3 Then Paul said to him, “God will strike you, you whitewashed wall! You sit here to judge me according to the law, yet you yourself violate the law by commanding that I be struck.” 4 But those standing nearby said, “How dare you insult the high priest of God!” 5 “Brothers,” Paul replied, “I was not aware that he was the high priest, for it is written: ‘Do not speak evil about the ruler of your people.’”
paragraphs: 1 Paul looked directly at the Sanhedrin and said, “Brothers, I have conducted myself before God in all good conscience to this day.” 2 At this, the high priest Ananias ordered those standing near Paul to strike him on the mouth. 3 Then Paul said to him, “God will strike you, you whitewashed wall! You sit here to judge me according to the law, yet you yourself violate the law by commanding that I be struck.” 4 But those standing nearby said, “How dare you insult the high priest of God!” 5 “Brothers,” Paul replied, “I was not aware that he was the high priest, for it is written: ‘Do not speak evil about the ruler of your people.’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul stands before the Sanhedrin, the Jewish council, and says he has conducted himself before God in good conscience. This does not erase his own account of persecuting believers in the preceding chapter. A claim about his conscience is not a claim that every action in his past was right.

The high priest Ananias orders him struck on the mouth. Paul calls him a whitewashed wall and challenges the contradiction of judging according to the law while ordering an unlawful blow. When others object that he has insulted the high priest, Paul says he was not aware the man was high priest and recalls the command not to speak evil of the ruler of the people.

The command comes from Exodus 22:28. Luke reports Paul’s answer without explaining exactly why he says he did not know. The account does not supply a diagnosis of his eyesight, details about the priest’s clothing or a full history of who held the office.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly recognize both the injustice of the blow and the importance of Paul’s appeal to Scripture about speaking of a ruler. Interpreters differ over the intention of his reply.

The Catholic USCCB note on verse 5 understands Paul as withdrawing the accusation in reverence for the law when told Ananias is high priest. Calvin’s comment on verse 5 instead reads an ironic rebuke: Paul recognizes nothing in the man’s conduct worthy of the priestly calling. These are explanations offered in commentaries, not official church rulings that settle Paul’s precise intention for every reader.
passages.god_plan_html:
The scene recalls John 18:19–23, where Jesus is struck during questioning and asks why He was struck if He spoke rightly. This is a supported parallel in the unjust treatment of a witness and a challenge to it; the words and responses are not identical.

1 Peter 2:19–23 identifies Jesus as the example for His people under unjust suffering, entrusting Himself to the One who judges justly. That wider teaching keeps the focus on following Christ, rather than using a disputed detail of Paul’s response as permission for every angry reaction.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Acts 23:6-11
passages.section_title: Why does Paul speak about resurrection, and how is he reassured afterward?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 Then Paul, knowing that some of them were Sadducees and the others Pharisees, called out in the Sanhedrin, “Brothers, I am a Pharisee, the son of a Pharisee. It is because of my hope in the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial.” 7 As soon as he had said this, a dispute broke out between the Pharisees and Sadducees, and the assembly was divided. 8 For the Sadducees say that there is neither a resurrection nor angels nor spirits, but the Pharisees acknowledge them all. 9 A great clamor arose, and some scribes from the party of the Pharisees got up and contended sharply, “We find nothing wrong with this man. What if a spirit or an angel has spoken to him?” 10 The dispute grew so violent that the commander was afraid they would tear Paul to pieces. He ordered the soldiers to go down and remove him by force and bring him into the barracks. 11 The following night the Lord stood near Paul and said, “Take courage! As you have testified about Me in Jerusalem, so also you must testify in Rome.”
paragraphs: 6 Then Paul, knowing that some of them were Sadducees and the others Pharisees, called out in the Sanhedrin, “Brothers, I am a Pharisee, the son of a Pharisee. It is because of my hope in the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial.” 7 As soon as he had said this, a dispute broke out between the Pharisees and Sadducees, and the assembly was divided. 8 For the Sadducees say that there is neither a resurrection nor angels nor spirits, but the Pharisees acknowledge them all. 9 A great clamor arose, and some scribes from the party of the Pharisees got up and contended sharply, “We find nothing wrong with this man. What if a spirit or an angel has spoken to him?”

10 The dispute grew so violent that the commander was afraid they would tear Paul to pieces. He ordered the soldiers to go down and remove him by force and bring him into the barracks. 11 The following night the Lord stood near Paul and said, “Take courage! As you have testified about Me in Jerusalem, so also you must testify in Rome.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul knows the council includes Pharisees and Sadducees. He identifies his Pharisaic background and says he is on trial because of his hope in the resurrection of the dead. Luke explains the division: the Sadducees deny resurrection, angels and spirits, while the Pharisees acknowledge them.

The council divides, and some Pharisaic scribes say they find nothing wrong with him, asking whether a spirit or angel may have spoken to him. That is not the same as all of them confessing faith in the risen Jesus. Their response exposes a disagreement within the council.

The dispute becomes so violent that the commander fears Paul will be torn apart and orders soldiers to remove him. The following night the Lord stands near Paul, tells him to take courage and says he must testify in Rome as he has in Jerusalem. The assurance concerns the continuation of his witness, not an immediate end to all trouble.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand resurrection as a real issue in Paul’s message, even though the immediate accusations also concern the law, the people and the temple. Calvin on verse 6 acknowledges the tactical effect while maintaining that Paul’s statement is true. The Lord’s reassurance then turns attention from the council’s division to the work still entrusted to Paul.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Corinthians 15:12–23 explains why resurrection is central: without Christ raised, the preaching and faith would be empty; because He is raised, those who belong to Him have a future beyond death. Paul’s hope is therefore more than a point useful for dividing his judges.

The Lord explicitly joins Jerusalem and Rome in Paul’s continuing witness. What Paul had intended in Acts 19:21 is now confirmed by a direct promise. The journey ahead remains difficult, but its purpose has not disappeared in the violence of the hearing.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Acts 23:12-22
passages.section_title: How does a report from Paul’s nephew expose the ambush?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 When daylight came, the Jews formed a conspiracy and bound themselves with an oath not to eat or drink until they had killed Paul. 13 More than forty of them were involved in this plot. 14 They went to the chief priests and elders and said, “We have bound ourselves with a solemn oath not to eat anything until we have killed Paul. 15 Now then, you and the Sanhedrin petition the commander to bring him down to you on the pretext of examining his case more carefully. We are ready to kill him on the way.” 16 But when the son of Paul’s sister heard about the plot, he went into the barracks and told Paul. 17 Then Paul called one of the centurions and said, “Take this young man to the commander; he has something to tell him.” 18 So the centurion took him to the commander and said, “Paul the prisoner sent and asked me to bring this young man to you. He has something to tell you.” 19 The commander took the young man by the hand, drew him aside, and asked, “What do you need to tell me?” 20 He answered, “The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul to the Sanhedrin tomorrow on the pretext of acquiring more information about him. 21 Do not let them persuade you, because more than forty men are waiting to ambush him. They have bound themselves with an oath not to eat or drink until they have killed him; they are ready now, awaiting your consent.” 22 So the commander dismissed the young man and instructed him, “Do not tell anyone that you have reported this to me.”

We are ready to kill him on the way.”

16 But when the son of Paul’s sister heard about the plot, he went into the barracks and told Paul. 17 Then Paul called one of the centurions and said, “Take this young man to the commander; he has something to tell him.” 18 So the centurion took him to the commander and said, “Paul the prisoner sent and asked me to bring this young man to you. He has something to tell you.” 19 The commander took the young man by the hand, drew him aside, and asked, “What do you need to tell me?” 20 He answered, “The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul to the Sanhedrin tomorrow on the pretext of acquiring more information about him. 21 Do not let them persuade you, because more than forty men are waiting to ambush him. They have bound themselves with an oath not to eat or drink until they have killed him; they are ready now, awaiting your consent.” 22 So the commander dismissed the young man and instructed him, “Do not tell anyone that you have reported this to me.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
More than forty men bind themselves with an oath not to eat or drink until they have killed Paul. They approach the chief priests and elders with a plan: the council should request another hearing as a pretext for a more thorough inquiry, while they wait to kill him on the way.

The oath uses ἀναθεματίζω (anathematizō, ah-nah-theh-mah-TEE-zoh), to bind oneself under a curse. Thayer’s entry identifies that sense in Acts 23:12, 14 and 21. The men are invoking severe consequences on themselves, not merely making a casual promise. Luke does not tell us what becomes of the oath after the plot fails.

Paul’s sister’s son hears of the plot and tells him. Paul calls a centurion and has the young man taken to the commander, who draws him aside and listens privately. The nephew explains the false request and waiting ambush. The commander dismisses him with instructions not to disclose that he has reported it.

The young man’s report matters, but Luke does not tell us his exact age, where he heard the plan or whether his mother had been Paul’s host. His actions and the officials’ responses are enough to explain how the immediate threat becomes known.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as the exposure of a deliberate murder plot, not a legitimate conclusion to the hearing. The conspirators’ religiously serious oath does not make the intended killing just. The account also gives practical action a place: Paul passes on information rather than treating the Lord’s promise as a reason to do nothing.
passages.god_plan_html:
The promise of witness in Rome comes immediately before this new attempt to kill Paul. Its protection now unfolds through a relative hearing the danger, Paul taking the report seriously and a commander listening. The narrative shows ordinary people and responsible action serving the continuation of the mission.

People who do not carry the public preaching role can still play an essential part in the work. The young man who brings information and the officer who listens help preserve the messenger for the task the Lord has given him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Acts 23:23-35
passages.section_title: Why is Paul transferred under guard to Caesarea?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 23 Then he called two of his centurions and said, “Prepare two hundred soldiers, seventy horsemen, and two hundred spearmen to go to Caesarea in the third hour of the night. 24 Provide mounts for Paul to take him safely to Governor Felix.” 25 And he wrote the following letter: 26 Claudius Lysias, To His Excellency, Governor Felix: Greetings. 27 This man was seized by the Jews, and they were about to kill him when I came with my troops to rescue him. For I had learned that he is a Roman citizen, 28 and since I wanted to understand their charges against him, I brought him down to their Sanhedrin. 29 I found that the accusation involved questions about their own law, but there was no charge worthy of death or imprisonment. 30 When I was informed that there was a plot against the man, I sent him to you at once. I also instructed his accusers to present their case against him before you. 31 So the soldiers followed their orders and brought Paul by night to Antipatris. 32 The next day they returned to the barracks and let the horsemen go on with him. 33 When the horsemen arrived in Caesarea, they delivered the letter to the governor and presented Paul to him. 34 The governor read the letter and asked what province Paul was from. Learning that he was from Cilicia, 35 he said, “I will hear your case when your accusers arrive.” Then he ordered that Paul be kept under guard in Herod’s Praetorium.

25 And he wrote the following letter: 26 Claudius Lysias, To His Excellency, Governor Felix: Greetings. 27 This man was seized by the Jews, and they were about to kill him when I came with my troops to rescue him. For I had learned that he is a Roman citizen, 28 and since I wanted to understand their charges against him, I brought him down to their Sanhedrin. 29 I found that the accusation involved questions about their own law, but there was no charge worthy of death or imprisonment. 30 When I was informed that there was a plot against the man, I sent him to you at once. I also instructed his accusers to present their case against him before you.

31 So the soldiers followed their orders and brought Paul by night to Antipatris. 32 The next day they returned to the barracks and let the horsemen go on with him. 33 When the horsemen arrived in Caesarea, they delivered the letter to the governor and presented Paul to him. 34 The governor read the letter and asked what province Paul was from. Learning that he was from Cilicia, 35 he said, “I will hear your case when your accusers arrive.” Then he ordered that Paul be kept under guard in Herod’s Praetorium.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The commander orders a substantial escort ready for a night journey to Caesarea: two hundred soldiers, seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen, with mounts for Paul. He is to be delivered safely to Governor Felix. The response removes Paul from the known ambush while keeping him in Roman custody.

The accompanying letter identifies the commander as Claudius Lysias. He reports the rescue, the council hearing and the plot, saying the accusation concerns questions of Jewish law rather than a charge deserving death or imprisonment.

The letter places knowledge of Paul’s citizenship alongside the initial rescue. Luke’s earlier account in Acts 21:31–33 and 22:25–29 showed the commander learning that fact later, when Paul was threatened with flogging. The official report does not include every detail of how the encounter unfolded.

The soldiers bring Paul by night to Antipatris. The next day the horsemen continue with him to Caesarea while the others return. Felix reads the letter, asks Paul’s province and agrees to hear the case when the accusers arrive. He orders Paul kept under guard in Herod’s Praetorium, the governor’s residence.

The transfer is protection from a murder attempt, not an acquittal or a release. Luke reports the next step of the case without explaining a complete rule of jurisdiction for every Roman province.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly see the guarded transfer as preserving Paul for further testimony while the accusations remain unresolved. The commander’s letter presents a favorable assessment of his legal position; Felix still waits to hear the accusers. Neither custody nor an official report should be confused with a final judgment on the case.
passages.god_plan_html:
The move to Caesarea is one stage in the continuing witness promised in Acts 23:11. Paul has not reached Rome, and he remains a prisoner, but the effort to kill him has not ended his commission. Human arrangements—an escort, a letter and a governor’s decision to hear the case—become part of the route by which the witness continues.

God’s care for Paul accompanies an unfinished and costly task. The following hearings will give the prisoner further opportunities to speak about the hope for which he is held.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Acts 24:1-9
passages.section_title: What accusations does Tertullus bring against Paul?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Five days later the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and a lawyer named Tertullus, who presented to the governor their case against Paul. 2 When Paul had been called in, Tertullus opened the prosecution: “Because of you, we have enjoyed a lasting peace, and your foresight has brought improvements to this nation. 3 In every way and everywhere, most excellent Felix, we acknowledge this with all gratitude. 4 But in order not to delay you any further, I beg your indulgence to hear us briefly. 5 We have found this man to be a pestilence, stirring up dissension among the Jews all over the world. He is a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes, 6 and he even tried to desecrate the temple; so we seized him. 8 By examining him yourself, you will be able to learn the truth about all our charges against him.” 9 The Jews concurred, asserting that these charges were true.
paragraphs: 1 Five days later the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and a lawyer named Tertullus, who presented to the governor their case against Paul. 2 When Paul had been called in, Tertullus opened the prosecution: “Because of you, we have enjoyed a lasting peace, and your foresight has brought improvements to this nation. 3 In every way and everywhere, most excellent Felix, we acknowledge this with all gratitude. 4 But in order not to delay you any further, I beg your indulgence to hear us briefly.

5 We have found this man to be a pestilence, stirring up dissension among the Jews all over the world. He is a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes, 6 and he even tried to desecrate the temple; so we seized him. 8 By examining him yourself, you will be able to learn the truth about all our charges against him.” 9 The Jews concurred, asserting that these charges were true.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Five days after Paul’s transfer to Caesarea, the high priest Ananias arrives with some elders and Tertullus, a lawyer presenting their case. Tertullus begins by praising Felix for peace and improvements, then asks for a brief hearing. Luke records the speech as an appeal to the governor; it is not a separate endorsement of every claim about Felix’s government.

The charges portray Paul as a plague to society, a source of unrest among Jews across the world, a leader of the Nazarenes and someone who attempted to desecrate the temple. The accompanying accusers affirm the charges. Calling him a pestilence is an insult, not a claim that he carries a literal disease.

The word sect is αἵρεσις (hairesis, HAI-reh-sis). Thayer’s entry includes a party or school and lists its use for Sadducees, Pharisees and the followers of Jesus. Here the label is used against Paul. The word alone does not establish whether the accusations are true.

The BSB’s main text moves from verse 6 to verse 8. Its footnote preserves a longer wording found in some Bibles, including verse 7, about Lysias taking Paul from his accusers. That difference explains the verse-number gap; Acts 21 gives the fuller account of the arrest.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read the speech as a prosecution that seeks to turn disputes about Paul’s message and the temple into a case requiring the governor’s action. The charges must be distinguished from what has been demonstrated. The defense in the following verses challenges both the description of his conduct and the lack of the original accusers.
passages.god_plan_html: In Luke 21:12–13, Jesus describes His followers being brought before governors and rulers, with these situations becoming opportunities to testify. Paul’s appearance before Felix fits that pattern. An accusation meant to stop the messenger brings the message before another audience.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Acts 24:10-21
passages.section_title: How does Paul join his defense with his hope in God?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 When the governor motioned for Paul to speak, he began his response: “Knowing that you have been a judge over this nation for many years, I gladly make my defense. 11 You can verify for yourself that no more than twelve days ago I went up to Jerusalem to worship. 12 Yet my accusers did not find me debating with anyone in the temple or riling up a crowd in the synagogues or in the city. 13 Nor can they prove to you any of their charges against me. 14 I do confess to you, however, that I worship the God of our fathers according to the Way, which they call a sect. I believe everything that is laid down by the Law and written in the Prophets, 15 and I have the same hope in God that they themselves cherish, that there will be a resurrection of both the righteous and the wicked. 16 In this hope, I strive always to maintain a clear conscience before God and man. 17 After several years, then, I returned to Jerusalem to bring alms to my people and to present offerings. 18 At the time they found me in the temple, I was ceremonially clean and was not inciting a crowd or an uproar. But there are some Jews from the province of Asia 19 who ought to appear before you and bring charges, if they have anything against me. 20 Otherwise, let these men state for themselves any crime they found in me when I stood before the Sanhedrin, 21 unless it was this one thing I called out as I stood in their presence: ‘It is concerning the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial before you today.’”

14 I do confess to you, however, that I worship the God of our fathers according to the Way, which they call a sect. I believe everything that is laid down by the Law and written in the Prophets, 15 and I have the same hope in God that they themselves cherish, that there will be a resurrection of both the righteous and the wicked. 16 In this hope, I strive always to maintain a clear conscience before God and man.

17 After several years, then, I returned to Jerusalem to bring alms to my people and to present offerings. 18 At the time they found me in the temple, I was ceremonially clean and was not inciting a crowd or an uproar. But there are some Jews from the province of Asia 19 who ought to appear before you and bring charges, if they have anything against me. 20 Otherwise, let these men state for themselves any crime they found in me when I stood before the Sanhedrin, 21 unless it was this one thing I called out as I stood in their presence: ‘It is concerning the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial before you today.’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul points to the short interval since he went to Jerusalem and denies that his accusers found him stirring up crowds in the temple, synagogues or city. He challenges them to prove their charges. His defense addresses conduct that can be examined, not only his opinion of himself.

He freely acknowledges following the Way, while insisting that he worships the God of his fathers and believes what is laid down in the Law and written in the Prophets. He holds the hope of a resurrection of both the righteous and the wicked and seeks a clear conscience before God and people.

The worship word is λατρεύω (latreuō, lah-TREH-oo-oh), to render religious service or worship. Thayer’s entry includes Acts 24:14 in its broad use for serving God. Paul’s declaration concerns his allegiance and service, in a defense that also speaks of his beliefs, hope and conduct.

He explains that he came with help for his people and offerings, and was found in the temple purified, without a crowd or uproar. The people from Asia who first accused him are not present to state their case. He asks those who are present to name the wrongdoing found at the council, apart from his declaration about resurrection.

Acts 21:27–29 has already explained that the charge about Trophimus grew from seeing him with Paul in the city and assuming he entered the temple. That context helps explain Paul’s demand that the original accusers appear and state their case.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand Paul as confessing faithfulness to Israel’s God and Scriptures while rejecting the claim that following Jesus makes him a criminal. The resurrection of both righteous and wicked brings accountability before God into the defense. This passage affirms that hope without setting out a detailed timetable of every event at the end.
passages.god_plan_html:
John 5:28–29 speaks of the dead hearing the Son’s voice and coming out to resurrection, with both life and judgment in view. Paul’s hope concerns God’s final dealing with people, not simply success or vindication in the present hearing.

In 2 Corinthians 5:9–11, Paul connects the coming judgment with seeking to please Christ and persuading others. That helps explain why the hope of resurrection shapes his conscience here. The future God promises has consequences for how he serves and lives now.
passages.current_position_html: Worship as the Early Church Knew It directly discusses Acts 24:14 as Paul’s declaration of loyal service to God, expressed through his obedience and ministry. Returning to the Word also uses this verse in explaining the early name the Way and the site’s emphasis on following Christ through a life grounded in Scripture. Together, these studies place the emphasis on faithful service and a lived response to God’s word, rather than a label by itself.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

passages.title: Acts 24:14
passages.section_title: What does Paul mean by worshiping God according to the Way?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 I do confess to you, however, that I worship the God of our fathers according to the Way, which they call a sect. I believe everything that is laid down by the Law and written in the Prophets,
paragraphs: 14 I do confess to you, however, that I worship the God of our fathers according to the Way, which they call a sect. I believe everything that is laid down by the Law and written in the Prophets,

passages.context_html:
Paul is answering charges before Felix, including the accusation that he leads the sect of the Nazarenes. He admits following the Way but denies that this means rejecting the God of his fathers or the Scriptures. His confession is followed by the hope of resurrection and a concern for a clear conscience.

The worship word λατρεύω (latreuō, lah-TREH-oo-oh) describes religious service or worship; Thayer’s entry specifically includes this verse. Here Paul is declaring whom he serves and what he believes. The statement is broader than describing one activity at a gathering.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read the verse as a confession of continuity with the God revealed in Israel’s Scriptures. Paul accepts the name the Way while refusing to let the accusers’ label settle the truth about his faith or conduct.
passages.current_position_html: Worship as the Early Church Knew It directly discusses Acts 24:14 as Paul’s declaration of loyal service to God, expressed through his obedience and ministry. Returning to the Word also uses this verse in explaining the early name the Way and the site’s emphasis on following Christ through a life grounded in Scripture. Together, these studies place the emphasis on faithful service and a lived response to God’s word, rather than a label by itself.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
John 5:28–29 speaks of the dead hearing the Son’s voice and coming out to resurrection, with both life and judgment in view. Paul’s hope concerns God’s final dealing with people, not simply success or vindication in the present hearing.

In 2 Corinthians 5:9–11, Paul connects the coming judgment with seeking to please Christ and persuading others. That helps explain why the hope of resurrection shapes his conscience here. The future God promises has consequences for how he serves and lives now.

passages.title: Acts 24:22-27
passages.section_title: Why does Felix keep listening yet leave Paul in prison?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 Then Felix, who was well informed about the Way, adjourned the hearing and said, “When Lysias the commander comes, I will decide your case.” 23 He ordered the centurion to keep Paul under guard, but to allow him some freedom and permit his friends to minister to his needs. 24 After several days, Felix returned with his wife Drusilla, who was a Jewess. He sent for Paul and listened to him speak about faith in Christ Jesus. 25 As Paul expounded on righteousness, self-control, and the coming judgment, Felix became frightened and said, “You may go for now. When I find the time, I will call for you.” 26 At the same time, he was hoping that Paul would offer him a bribe. So he sent for Paul frequently and talked with him. 27 After two years had passed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus. And wishing to do the Jews a favor, Felix left Paul in prison.
paragraphs: 22 Then Felix, who was well informed about the Way, adjourned the hearing and said, “When Lysias the commander comes, I will decide your case.” 23 He ordered the centurion to keep Paul under guard, but to allow him some freedom and permit his friends to minister to his needs.

24 After several days, Felix returned with his wife Drusilla, who was a Jewess. He sent for Paul and listened to him speak about faith in Christ Jesus. 25 As Paul expounded on righteousness, self-control, and the coming judgment, Felix became frightened and said, “You may go for now. When I find the time, I will call for you.” 26 At the same time, he was hoping that Paul would offer him a bribe. So he sent for Paul frequently and talked with him. 27 After two years had passed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus. And wishing to do the Jews a favor, Felix left Paul in prison.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Felix is already well informed about the Way, but postpones a decision until Lysias comes. He orders Paul kept under guard with some freedom and allows his friends to attend to his needs. Luke does not report Lysias arriving during this part of the account.

Later Felix and his Jewish wife Drusilla hear Paul speak about faith in Christ Jesus. Paul discusses righteousness, self-control and the coming judgment. Felix becomes frightened and sends him away, saying he will call for him when he has time.

Luke then tells us another reason for the repeated conversations: Felix hopes Paul will offer a bribe. After two years, Porcius Festus succeeds him, and Felix leaves Paul imprisoned to gain favor with the Jews. The delay is therefore connected with money and political advantage, not presented as a verdict proving Paul guilty.

The ruler has authority over the prisoner’s circumstances, but the prisoner speaks about matters for which the ruler must answer to God. Hearing frequently and feeling fear are not described here as the same thing as responding in faith and obedience.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly see a warning in Felix’s response: interest in the message and fear of judgment can coexist with an unwillingness to do what is right. Luke reports the hope of a bribe and the decision to leave Paul imprisoned. He does not give a complete account of Felix’s later life or ask readers to determine his final standing before God.
passages.god_plan_html:
A related theme appears in Jesus’ teaching in John 16:8–11: the Spirit confronts the world concerning sin, righteousness and judgment. Paul’s message brings these questions before a ruler whose authority over others does not place him above accountability to God.

Titus 2:11–14 joins God’s saving grace with learning to reject ungodliness, live uprightly and await Jesus. Paul’s witness before Felix likewise reaches into how a person lives and uses power. The Lord’s work concerns a changed people, not simply an audience willing to hear religious ideas.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Acts 25:1-12
passages.section_title: Why does Paul appeal to Caesar rather than return to Jerusalem?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Three days after his arrival in the province, Festus went up from Caesarea to Jerusalem, 2 where the chief priests and Jewish leaders presented their case against Paul. They urged Festus 3 to grant them a concession against Paul by summoning him to Jerusalem, because they were preparing an ambush to kill him along the way. 4 But Festus replied, “Paul is being held in Caesarea, and I myself am going there soon. 5 So if this man has done anything wrong, let some of your leaders come down with me and accuse him there.” 6 After spending no more than eight or ten days with them, Festus went down to Caesarea. The next day he sat on the judgment seat and ordered that Paul be brought in. 7 When Paul arrived, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing many serious charges that they could not prove. 8 Then Paul made his defense: “I have committed no offense against the law of the Jews or against the temple or against Caesar.” 9 But Festus, wishing to do the Jews a favor, said to Paul, “Are you willing to go up to Jerusalem to stand trial before me on these charges?” 10 Paul replied, “I am standing before the judgment seat of Caesar, where I ought to be tried. I have done nothing wrong to the Jews, as you yourself know very well. 11 If, however, I am guilty of anything worthy of death, I do not refuse to die. But if there is no truth to their accusations against me, no one has the right to hand me over to them. I appeal to Caesar!” 12 Then Festus conferred with his council and replied, “You have appealed to Caesar. To Caesar you will go!”
