They urged Festus 3 to grant them a concession against Paul by summoning him to Jerusalem, because they were preparing an ambush to kill him along the way. 4 But Festus replied, “Paul is being held in Caesarea, and I myself am going there soon. 5 So if this man has done anything wrong, let some of your leaders come down with me and accuse him there.”

6 After spending no more than eight or ten days with them, Festus went down to Caesarea. The next day he sat on the judgment seat and ordered that Paul be brought in. 7 When Paul arrived, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing many serious charges that they could not prove. 8 Then Paul made his defense: “I have committed no offense against the law of the Jews or against the temple or against Caesar.” 9 But Festus, wishing to do the Jews a favor, said to Paul, “Are you willing to go up to Jerusalem to stand trial before me on these charges?”

10 Paul replied, “I am standing before the judgment seat of Caesar, where I ought to be tried. I have done nothing wrong to the Jews, as you yourself know very well. 11 If, however, I am guilty of anything worthy of death, I do not refuse to die. But if there is no truth to their accusations against me, no one has the right to hand me over to them. I appeal to Caesar!” 12 Then Festus conferred with his council and replied, “You have appealed to Caesar. To Caesar you will go!”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Felix has left Paul imprisoned after two years, and Festus now takes charge. Three days after arriving in the province, the new governor goes to Jerusalem. The chief priests and leaders ask him to bring Paul there, while planning an ambush to kill him on the way. Luke explains the danger behind the request.

Festus first keeps the case in Caesarea and invites the accusers to come there. At the hearing, they bring serious charges they cannot prove. Paul denies wrongdoing against the Jewish law, the temple or Caesar. Festus then asks whether he is willing to be tried before him in Jerusalem, wishing to do the Jewish leaders a favor.

Paul says he is already before Caesar’s judgment seat, where he ought to be tried. He is willing to face a proper judgment if guilty of a capital offense, but refuses to be handed over on accusations he denies are true. He appeals to Caesar. After consulting his council, Festus accepts the appeal and says he will go to Caesar.

The scene identifies both a continued threat and a practical response. It does not tell us exactly why Paul had not appealed earlier or provide a complete history of the Roman right of appeal. His willingness to accept a valid judgment is not a confession that the present charges are true.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read the appeal as a lawful means of protection that serves Paul’s continuing witness. Calvin’s comment on verse 11 explicitly treats the use of courts and legal protection as compatible with trust in God. Readiness to suffer and willingness to use an available remedy can belong together.
passages.god_plan_html:
The Lord’s promise in Acts 23:11 is that Paul will testify in Rome as he has in Jerusalem. The two years of delay have not erased that purpose. The appeal now sets the case toward the destination already named, through an ordinary public proceeding rather than an escape from all custody.

The episode keeps both parts of the story in view: there are human attempts to kill or retain control of Paul, and there is a commission that continues through them. The promise supports his courage without making every official choice wise or just.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

deeper_study.title: Should We Seek Signs From God?

passages.title: Acts 25:13-22
passages.section_title: Why does Festus bring Paul’s case to Agrippa?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 After several days had passed, King Agrippa and Bernice came down to Caesarea to pay their respects to Festus. 14 Since they were staying several days, Festus laid out Paul’s case before the king: “There is a certain man whom Felix left in prison. 15 While I was in Jerusalem, the chief priests and elders of the Jews presented their case and requested a judgment against him. 16 I told them that it is not the Roman custom to hand a man over before he has had an opportunity to face his accusers and defend himself against their charges. 17 So when they came here with me, I did not delay. The next day I sat on the judgment seat and ordered that the man be brought in. 18 But when his accusers rose to speak, they did not charge him with any of the crimes I had expected. 19 They only had some contentions with him regarding their own religion and a certain Jesus who had died, but whom Paul affirmed to be alive. 20 Since I was at a loss as to how to investigate these matters, I asked if he was willing to go to Jerusalem and be tried there on these charges. 21 But when Paul appealed to be held over for the decision of the Emperor, I ordered that he be held until I could send him to Caesar.” 22 Then Agrippa said to Festus, “I would like to hear this man myself.” “Tomorrow you will hear him,” Festus declared.
paragraphs: 13 After several days had passed, King Agrippa and Bernice came down to Caesarea to pay their respects to Festus. 14 Since they were staying several days, Festus laid out Paul’s case before the king: “There is a certain man whom Felix left in prison. 15 While I was in Jerusalem, the chief priests and elders of the Jews presented their case and requested a judgment against him. 16 I told them that it is not the Roman custom to hand a man over before he has had an opportunity to face his accusers and defend himself against their charges. 17 So when they came here with me, I did not delay. The next day I sat on the judgment seat and ordered that the man be brought in. 18 But when his accusers rose to speak, they did not charge him with any of the crimes I had expected.

19 They only had some contentions with him regarding their own religion and a certain Jesus who had died, but whom Paul affirmed to be alive. 20 Since I was at a loss as to how to investigate these matters, I asked if he was willing to go to Jerusalem and be tried there on these charges. 21 But when Paul appealed to be held over for the decision of the Emperor, I ordered that he be held until I could send him to Caesar.” 22 Then Agrippa said to Festus, “I would like to hear this man myself.” “Tomorrow you will hear him,” Festus declared.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
King Agrippa and Bernice come to Caesarea to pay their respects to Festus. During their stay, he explains the unresolved case inherited from Felix. He recounts the request for judgment against Paul and his own insistence that an accused person face the accusers and have an opportunity to answer.

Festus says the charges were different from the crimes he expected. He summarizes the dispute as questions about religion and about Jesus, who had died but whom Paul affirmed to be alive. This is his report of the issue, not Luke’s attempt to reduce the resurrection to an unimportant curiosity.

He also describes asking whether Paul would go to Jerusalem and Paul’s appeal to the Emperor. His retelling stresses uncertainty about investigating the matters; the earlier narrative in verse 9 also told us he wished to do the accusers a favor. Reading both together gives a fuller view of his proposed change of venue.

Agrippa asks to hear Paul himself, and Festus arranges it for the next day. The meeting prepares another audience for the testimony, while the accepted appeal remains in place. Luke does not describe a new conviction or a settled charge at this point.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly notice that even Festus’s brief summary identifies the central Christian claim: Jesus died and is alive. His uncertainty about how to handle the case does not settle that claim. The following hearing gives Paul space to explain what it means and why he testifies to it.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Corinthians 15:12–23 explains the weight of the issue Festus names. If Christ were not raised, Paul’s preaching and the believers’ faith would be empty; because He is raised, those who belong to Him have hope beyond death. The question about Jesus is at the heart of the witness being carried through these proceedings.

The mission is therefore reaching people who initially see a religious dispute or an administrative problem. They are being brought into contact with the announcement of the risen Lord, whose significance is greater than the immediate dispute over the prisoner.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Acts 25:23-27
passages.section_title: Why is a prisoner brought before such a prominent gathering?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 23 The next day Agrippa and Bernice came with great pomp and entered the auditorium, along with the commanders and leading men of the city. And Festus ordered that Paul be brought in. 24 Then Festus said, “King Agrippa and all who are present with us, you see this man. The whole Jewish community has petitioned me about him, both here and in Jerusalem, crying out that he ought not to live any longer. 25 But I found he had done nothing worthy of death, and since he has now appealed to the Emperor, I decided to send him. 26 I have nothing definite to write to our sovereign about him. Therefore I have brought him before all of you, and especially before you, King Agrippa, so that after this inquiry I may have something to write. 27 For it seems unreasonable to me to send on a prisoner without specifying the charges against him.”
paragraphs: 23 The next day Agrippa and Bernice came with great pomp and entered the auditorium, along with the commanders and leading men of the city. And Festus ordered that Paul be brought in. 24 Then Festus said, “King Agrippa and all who are present with us, you see this man. The whole Jewish community has petitioned me about him, both here and in Jerusalem, crying out that he ought not to live any longer. 25 But I found he had done nothing worthy of death, and since he has now appealed to the Emperor, I decided to send him. 26 I have nothing definite to write to our sovereign about him. Therefore I have brought him before all of you, and especially before you, King Agrippa, so that after this inquiry I may have something to write. 27 For it seems unreasonable to me to send on a prisoner without specifying the charges against him.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Agrippa and Bernice enter the auditorium with great ceremony, accompanied by military commanders and leading people of the city. Paul is brought in at Festus’s order. The scene places one prisoner before an audience of people who hold public influence.

Festus explains that demands for Paul’s death have come from the Jewish community in Jerusalem and Caesarea, yet he has found nothing deserving death. Paul has appealed to the Emperor, but Festus has nothing definite to write about him. He hopes the inquiry, especially Agrippa’s examination, will help him specify the case.

The governor’s report should remain distinct from a completed verdict or an exhaustive legal rule. He acknowledges the weakness of the case while continuing the process. The chapter ends with the reason for the audience assembled to hear the defense that follows in Acts 26.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly see a striking reversal of outward importance: the prisoner is about to give testimony before a king, a governor and influential listeners. The ceremony does not make their understanding complete, and Paul’s chains do not make his message false. The hearing must still be assessed by what is said and whether it is true.
passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 9:15–16 describes Paul’s calling to bear Jesus’ name before Gentiles, kings and the people of Israel, alongside suffering for that name. This gathering gives that commission a concrete setting. Custody has brought the witness before a king and other public figures.

The pattern also recalls Jesus’ words in Luke 21:12–13, where appearances before kings and governors become opportunities for testimony. Paul’s next speech will use the opportunity to explain the risen Jesus and appeal to the people listening, not simply to display skill before a prestigious audience.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Acts 26:1-11
passages.section_title: Why does Paul connect Israel’s hope with his own history of persecution?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Agrippa said to Paul, “You have permission to speak for yourself.” Then Paul stretched out his hand and began his defense: 2 “King Agrippa, I consider myself fortunate to stand before you today to defend myself against all the accusations of the Jews, 3 especially since you are acquainted with all the Jewish customs and controversies. I beg you, therefore, to listen to me patiently. 4 Surely all the Jews know how I have lived from my earliest childhood among my own people, and also in Jerusalem. 5 They have known me for a long time and can testify, if they are willing, that I lived as a Pharisee, adhering to the strictest sect of our religion. 6 And now I stand on trial because of my hope in the promise that God made to our fathers, 7 the promise our twelve tribes are hoping to see fulfilled as they earnestly serve God day and night. It is because of this hope, O king, that I am accused by the Jews. 8 Why would any of you consider it incredible that God raises the dead? 9 So then, I too was convinced that I ought to do all I could to oppose the name of Jesus of Nazareth. 10 And that is what I did in Jerusalem. With authority from the chief priests I put many of the saints in prison, and when they were condemned to death, I cast my vote against them. 11 I frequently had them punished in the synagogues, and I tried to make them blaspheme. In my raging fury against them, I even went to foreign cities to persecute them.

I beg you, therefore, to listen to me patiently. 4 Surely all the Jews know how I have lived from my earliest childhood among my own people, and also in Jerusalem. 5 They have known me for a long time and can testify, if they are willing, that I lived as a Pharisee, adhering to the strictest sect of our religion.

6 And now I stand on trial because of my hope in the promise that God made to our fathers, 7 the promise our twelve tribes are hoping to see fulfilled as they earnestly serve God day and night. It is because of this hope, O king, that I am accused by the Jews. 8 Why would any of you consider it incredible that God raises the dead?

9 So then, I too was convinced that I ought to do all I could to oppose the name of Jesus of Nazareth. 10 And that is what I did in Jerusalem. With authority from the chief priests I put many of the saints in prison, and when they were condemned to death, I cast my vote against them. 11 I frequently had them punished in the synagogues, and I tried to make them blaspheme. In my raging fury against them, I even went to foreign cities to persecute them.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Agrippa gives Paul permission to speak. Paul welcomes the opportunity because the king knows Jewish customs and disputes, and asks him to listen patiently. He describes his upbringing among his own people and in Jerusalem, and his life as a Pharisee.

He places the case in relation to God’s promises to Israel and the hope of resurrection. His appeal to the twelve tribes presents the hope of the people as a whole; it is not a claim that no Jewish group has ever disagreed about resurrection. Luke has already described the Sadducean disagreement in Acts 23.

Paul then admits how fiercely he once opposed Jesus’ name. With authority from the chief priests, he imprisoned believers, approved their condemnation to death, punished them and tried to make them blaspheme. He even pursued them beyond the country. His account gives no excuse that his sincerity made the violence right.

His reference to casting a vote expresses his part in their condemnation. He recalls supporting the persecution, not simply observing it from a distance. His testimony emphasizes how deeply he opposed the people he now serves.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read Paul’s past as evidence of a profound change brought by encountering Jesus. Knowledge and religious zeal can be turned against the very One a person claims to serve. His former persecution prepares the hearers to understand the mercy and calling described next.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Timothy 1:12–16 explicitly presents the mercy shown to Paul as an example of Christ’s patience toward those who will believe. The former opponent is appointed to service. His story demonstrates the reach of that mercy rather than treating a violent past as beyond God’s ability to change.

The resurrection hope also connects his personal story with God’s promises. In Luke 24:44–47, Jesus joins the fulfillment of Scripture, His suffering and resurrection, and the proclamation of repentance and forgiveness to the nations. Paul’s defense is moving toward that same larger account.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Acts 26:12-18
passages.section_title: What is Paul sent to do after Jesus confronts him?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 In this pursuit I was on my way to Damascus with the authority and commission of the chief priests. 13 About noon, O king, as I was on the road, I saw a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, shining around me and my companions. 14 We all fell to the ground, and I heard a voice say to me in Hebrew, ‘Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads.’ 15 ‘Who are You, Lord?’ I asked. ‘I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting,’ the Lord replied. 16 ‘But get up and stand on your feet. For I have appeared to you to appoint you as a servant and as a witness of what you have seen from Me and what I will show you. 17 I will rescue you from your own people and from the Gentiles. I am sending you to them 18 to open their eyes, so that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins and an inheritance among those sanctified by faith in Me.’
paragraphs: 12 In this pursuit I was on my way to Damascus with the authority and commission of the chief priests. 13 About noon, O king, as I was on the road, I saw a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, shining around me and my companions. 14 We all fell to the ground, and I heard a voice say to me in Hebrew, ‘Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads.’ 15 ‘Who are You, Lord?’ I asked. ‘I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting,’ the Lord replied.

16 ‘But get up and stand on your feet. For I have appeared to you to appoint you as a servant and as a witness of what you have seen from Me and what I will show you. 17 I will rescue you from your own people and from the Gentiles. I am sending you to them 18 to open their eyes, so that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins and an inheritance among those sanctified by faith in Me.’

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul recalls traveling to Damascus with authority from the chief priests when a light brighter than the midday sun surrounds him and his companions. They fall to the ground, and he hears Jesus ask why he is persecuting Him.

The saying about kicking against the goads uses an image from handling working animals. κέντρον (kentron, KEN-tron) can mean an iron goad used to urge an animal onward; Thayer’s entry explains the saying as dangerous and futile resistance. An animal kicking against the point injures itself. Jesus is confronting Paul’s resistance and the harm it is doing.

Jesus appoints him as a servant and witness, with further things to be shown to him. The mission reaches both his own people and the Gentiles. Its aim is to open eyes, turn people from darkness to light and from Satan’s power to God, and bring forgiveness and a share among those who belong to Him through faith in Jesus.

The word sanctified describes being made holy and brought near to God. Thayer’s entry for the word specifically includes Acts 26:18 in that setting. Paul is being sent to people who need this change; his testimony credits Jesus with the authority and purpose of the mission.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the commission as a work of salvation and changed allegiance, not simply a transfer of information. Paul bears witness, while the forgiveness and belonging offered through faith are God’s gifts. The promised rescue does not mean he will avoid every arrest or period of suffering; he is recounting it while in chains.
passages.god_plan_html:
Colossians 1:12–14 gives a closely related account: the Father brings people into the inheritance of His people in the light, rescues them from darkness and brings them into the kingdom of His Son, in whom there is forgiveness. The mission entrusted to Paul serves that movement into life under Christ.

Ephesians 1:7–14 joins forgiveness, God’s purpose to bring all things together in Christ, and the inheritance secured by the promised Spirit. The horizon is larger than one encounter on a road: God is gathering a people in Christ who share the future He promises.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

deeper_study.title: Should We Seek Signs From God?

passages.title: Acts 26:19-23
passages.section_title: How does Paul describe obedience to the calling he received?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 So then, King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision. 20 First to those in Damascus and Jerusalem, then to everyone in the region of Judea, and then to the Gentiles, I declared that they should repent and turn to God, performing deeds worthy of their repentance. 21 For this reason the Jews seized me in the temple courts and tried to kill me. 22 But I have had God’s help to this day, and I stand here to testify to small and great alike. I am saying nothing beyond what the prophets and Moses said would happen: 23 that the Christ would suffer, and as the first to rise from the dead, would proclaim light to our people and to the Gentiles.”
paragraphs: 19 So then, King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision. 20 First to those in Damascus and Jerusalem, then to everyone in the region of Judea, and then to the Gentiles, I declared that they should repent and turn to God, performing deeds worthy of their repentance. 21 For this reason the Jews seized me in the temple courts and tried to kill me. 22 But I have had God’s help to this day, and I stand here to testify to small and great alike. I am saying nothing beyond what the prophets and Moses said would happen: 23 that the Christ would suffer, and as the first to rise from the dead, would proclaim light to our people and to the Gentiles.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul tells Agrippa that he did not disobey the heavenly vision. He preached in Damascus, Jerusalem, Judea and among the Gentiles, calling people to repent, turn to God and do things consistent with that repentance. Turning to God is expected to take shape in a changed life.

He says this witness led to his seizure in the temple and the attempt to kill him. Yet God has helped him, and he is still testifying to people of every standing. He is saying what Moses and the prophets foretold: the Messiah’s suffering, resurrection and light for both Israel and the Gentiles.

His claim about the first to rise should be read with the wider New Testament witness to Christ’s resurrection. Earlier people restored to life, such as Eutychus in Acts 20, do not remove the distinctive hope in the risen Christ. 1 Corinthians 15:20–23 identifies Him as the beginning of the resurrection promised to those who belong to Him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly recognize that repentance should be shown in how a person lives. They differ in their wider accounts of how God’s grace brings about the willing response Paul describes.

The Reformed Westminster Confession 10:1–2 describes God’s effective call as renewing the will and drawing people to Christ so that they come freely, made willing by grace. It credits that response to God’s work rather than to an independent ability to produce faith.

The Methodist Article VIII likewise teaches that God’s grace must come before and enable a good will, and continue to work with it. Wesley’s note on verse 19 understands Paul as receiving power to obey and then using it, and takes the verse to show that grace can be resisted. This is his application of the passage within that wider account of grace.

Both explanations acknowledge Paul’s dependence on God. The passage itself credits God’s help and describes a response of obedience, preaching and changed conduct.
passages.god_plan_html:
The content Paul gives here closely matches Luke 24:25–27, 44–47: the Messiah suffers and rises, Scripture is fulfilled, and repentance and forgiveness are proclaimed to the nations. It is the same good news that Jesus commissioned His followers to proclaim.

The inclusion of both Israel and the Gentiles is part of the purpose announced in Scripture. Paul’s work, his endurance and the changed lives he calls for belong to that mission. His survival matters here because the witness is continuing, not because mere survival is treated as its final goal.

passages.title: Acts 26:24-32
passages.section_title: What does Paul want for the people who have heard his defense?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 24 At this stage of Paul’s defense, Festus exclaimed in a loud voice, “You are insane, Paul! Your great learning is driving you to madness!” 25 But Paul answered, “I am not insane, most excellent Festus; I am speaking words of truth and sobriety. 26 For the king knows about these matters, and I can speak freely to him. I am confident that none of this has escaped his notice, because it was not done in a corner. 27 King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know you do.” 28 Then Agrippa said to Paul, “Can you persuade me in such a short time to become a Christian?” 29 “Short time or long,” Paul replied, “I wish to God that not only you but all who hear me this day may become what I am, except for these chains.” 30 Then the king and the governor rose, along with Bernice and those seated with them. 31 On their way out, they said to one another, “This man has done nothing worthy of death or imprisonment.” 32 And Agrippa said to Festus, “This man could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar.”

Your great learning is driving you to madness!” 25 But Paul answered, “I am not insane, most excellent Festus; I am speaking words of truth and sobriety. 26 For the king knows about these matters, and I can speak freely to him. I am confident that none of this has escaped his notice, because it was not done in a corner. 27 King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know you do.” 28 Then Agrippa said to Paul, “Can you persuade me in such a short time to become a Christian?” 29 “Short time or long,” Paul replied, “I wish to God that not only you but all who hear me this day may become what I am, except for these chains.”

30 Then the king and the governor rose, along with Bernice and those seated with them. 31 On their way out, they said to one another, “This man has done nothing worthy of death or imprisonment.” 32 And Agrippa said to Festus, “This man could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Festus interrupts, accusing Paul of being driven mad by learning. Paul answers respectfully that he is speaking truth with a clear mind. He turns to Agrippa’s knowledge of the events and asks about his belief in the prophets. The question presses the relationship between the Scriptures and the testimony Agrippa has heard.

Agrippa asks whether Paul can persuade him to become a Christian in such a short time. Paul’s answer embraces both short and long: he wishes that everyone listening might become what he is, apart from his chains. His desire is for their faith and freedom, not merely a favorable opinion of his defense.

The king, governor, Bernice and others leave the gathering and say Paul has done nothing deserving death or imprisonment. Agrippa tells Festus that he could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar. Luke records this assessment while the appeal and the journey it will entail remain in place.

The scene does not report Agrippa becoming a Christian. It ends with a judgment about Paul’s legal position, which is different from the personal response to Jesus Paul desires for his hearers.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly see Paul’s answer as an appeal for the good of all his listeners, including people who hold power over him. Readers differ over Agrippa’s tone and how to understand his question.

Calvin on verse 28 allows a reading about being persuaded nearly or in a short time; Wesley’s note on verse 28 emphasizes being almost persuaded. Thayer’s entry for the phrase offers the sense of persuading with little effort, while the BSB presents a question about shortness of time. These differences do not establish a certain account of Agrippa’s inner state. Luke reports the reply and Paul’s wish for everyone, without recording a conversion.
passages.god_plan_html:
The calling described in Acts 9:15–16 has brought Paul before a king with the message of Jesus, and his answer shows the purpose of that witness: he wants the hearers themselves to share in the life he has received. The audience is not merely a means of obtaining a release.

The contrast between his chains and his desire for their good shows a mission that continues under restraint. Their favorable legal opinion does not complete the task he longs to see fulfilled. The testimony points beyond the prisoner’s case to a response to the risen Lord.

passages.title: Acts 27:1-13
passages.section_title: Why does the voyage become dangerous before the storm begins?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 When it was decided that we would sail for Italy, Paul and some other prisoners were handed over to a centurion named Julius, who belonged to the Imperial Regiment. 2 We boarded an Adramyttian ship about to sail for ports along the coast of Asia, and we put out to sea. Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica, was with us. 3 The next day we landed at Sidon, and Julius treated Paul with consideration, allowing him to visit his friends and receive their care. 4 After putting out from there, we sailed to the lee of Cyprus because the winds were against us. 5 And when we had sailed across the open sea off the coast of Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came to Myra in Lycia. 6 There the centurion found an Alexandrian ship sailing for Italy and put us on board. 7 After sailing slowly for many days, we arrived off Cnidus. When the wind impeded us, we sailed to the lee of Crete, opposite Salmone. 8 After we had moved along the coast with difficulty, we came to a place called Fair Havens, near the town of Lasea. 9 By now much time had passed, and the voyage had already become dangerous because it was after the Fast. So Paul advised them, 10 “Men, I can see that our voyage will be filled with disaster and great loss, not only to ship and cargo, but to our own lives as well.” 11 But contrary to Paul’s advice, the centurion was persuaded by the pilot and by the owner of the ship. 12 Since the harbor was unsuitable to winter in, the majority decided to sail on, hoping that somehow they could reach Phoenix to winter there. Phoenix was a harbor in Crete facing both southwest and northwest. 13 When a gentle south wind began to blow, they thought they had their opportunity. So they weighed anchor and sailed along, hugging the coast of Crete.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul and other prisoners are placed under Julius, a centurion of the Imperial Regiment, for the voyage to Italy. Aristarchus accompanies the travelers, and the narrator again speaks as one of the company. At Sidon, Julius treats Paul kindly and allows friends to care for him.

Contrary winds slow the journey. The ships sail along the sheltered sides of islands—the lee, away from the wind—and the party changes to an Alexandrian vessel at Myra. They eventually reach Fair Havens on Crete with difficulty.

The Day of Atonement fast has already passed, and Luke says sailing has become dangerous. Paul warns of serious loss to the cargo, ship and lives. The centurion gives more weight to the pilot and owner. Since the harbor is unsuitable for wintering, the majority hopes to reach Phoenix, another Cretan harbor, rather than remain where they are.

A gentle south wind seems to offer the chance they want, and they set out close to the coast. The decision is not described as an attempt to cross the whole sea immediately. Paul’s first warning is also not introduced as an angel’s announcement; the explicit message from God comes later.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The first warning is often understood as Paul’s assessment of a dangerous voyage, distinct from the later promise that no life will be lost. Calvin on verse 21 thinks the Spirit guided his counsel while acknowledging that Luke records no special revelation at that earlier point. The account clearly identifies the source of the later assurance in verses 23–24.
passages.god_plan_html:
The promise that Paul will testify in Rome, given in Acts 23:11, continues through a journey that includes delay, difficult weather and dependence on others. Julius’s consideration and the friends’ care are part of how the messenger is supported.

2 Corinthians 11:25–27 places danger at sea, shipwreck and exposure among the hardships of Paul’s service. The mission does not take him outside ordinary human vulnerability. God’s purpose is carried forward through a life that still needs practical care and wise decisions.

passages.title: Acts 27:14-26
passages.section_title: Where does Paul find hope when everyone expects the ship to be lost?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 But it was not long before a cyclone called the Northeaster swept down across the island. 15 Unable to head into the wind, the ship was caught up. So we gave way and let ourselves be driven along. 16 Passing to the lee of a small island called Cauda, we barely managed to secure the lifeboat. 17 After hoisting it up, the crew used ropes to undergird the ship. And fearing that they would run aground on the sandbars of Syrtis, they lowered the sea anchor and were driven along. 18 We were tossed so violently that the next day the men began to jettison the cargo. 19 On the third day, they threw the ship’s tackle overboard with their own hands. 20 When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days and the great storm continued to batter us, we abandoned all hope of being saved. 21 After the men had gone a long time without food, Paul stood up among them and said, “Men, you should have followed my advice not to sail from Crete. Then you would have averted this disaster and loss. 22 But now I urge you to keep up your courage, because you will not experience any loss of life, but only of the ship. 23 For just last night an angel of the God to whom I belong and whom I serve stood beside me 24 and said, ‘Do not be afraid, Paul; you must stand before Caesar. And look, God has granted you the lives of all who sail with you.’ 25 So take courage, men, for I believe God that it will happen just as He told me. 26 However, we must run aground on some island.”

And look, God has granted you the lives of all who sail with you.’ 25 So take courage, men, for I believe God that it will happen just as He told me. 26 However, we must run aground on some island.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
A violent Northeaster catches the ship, preventing it from holding its course. The crew secures the lifeboat, braces the ship with ropes and takes measures to control the drift. As the storm continues, cargo and equipment are thrown overboard. With neither sun nor stars visible for days, hope of rescue disappears.

After a long period without food, Paul reminds them of his earlier advice and then gives a new assurance. No life will be lost, though the ship will be. He explains why: an angel of the God to whom he belongs and whom he serves has told him that he must stand before Caesar and that God has granted the lives of those sailing with him.

Paul urges courage because he trusts that God will do what He has said. He also says they must run aground on an island. His confidence does not depend on the storm having ended or on the ship remaining intact. The promise names both preservation and loss.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as confidence grounded in a particular word from God amid otherwise desperate circumstances. It concerns the lives of this ship’s company and Paul’s continuing commission. The account does not report that all aboard have become believers or make Paul the source of the power that preserves them.
passages.god_plan_html:
There is a useful parallel with Jonah 1:1–16: a servant of God is at sea among endangered sailors, cargo is thrown overboard, and the servant speaks about the God he serves. Jonah 3:1–10 also places that servant within God’s purpose of bringing a message to a Gentile city.

The difference matters. Jonah initially flees his commission; Paul is continuing toward the witness promised in Rome. This is a comparison between the accounts, not a claim that Luke identifies Paul as a new Jonah or that every storm detail has a hidden counterpart. In both stories, God’s purpose reaches beyond the messenger’s own people and circumstances.

passages.title: Acts 27:27-38
passages.section_title: Why must the sailors stay, and why does Paul urge everyone to eat?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 27 On the fourteenth night we were still being driven across the Adriatic Sea. About midnight the sailors sensed they were approaching land. 28 They took soundings and found that the water was twenty fathoms deep. Going a little farther, they took another set of soundings that read fifteen fathoms. 29 Fearing that we would run aground on the rocks, they dropped four anchors from the stern and prayed for daybreak. 30 Meanwhile, the sailors attempted to escape from the ship. Pretending to lower anchors from the bow, they let the lifeboat down into the sea. 31 But Paul said to the centurion and the soldiers, “Unless these men remain with the ship, you cannot be saved.” 32 So the soldiers cut the ropes to the lifeboat and set it adrift. 33 Right up to daybreak, Paul kept urging them all to eat: “Today is your fourteenth day in constant suspense, without taking any food. 34 So for your own preservation, I urge you to eat something, because not a single hair of your head will be lost.” 35 After he had said this, Paul took bread and gave thanks to God in front of them all. Then he broke it and began to eat. 36 They were all encouraged and took some food themselves. 37 In all, there were 276 of us on board. 38 After the men had eaten their fill, they lightened the ship by throwing the grain into the sea.

Then he broke it and began to eat. 36 They were all encouraged and took some food themselves. 37 In all, there were 276 of us on board. 38 After the men had eaten their fill, they lightened the ship by throwing the grain into the sea.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
On the fourteenth night, the sailors sense land is near. Their depth measurements show shallower water, and they drop anchors, fearing rocks. Some then try to escape in the lifeboat, pretending to put out more anchors. Paul tells the centurion and soldiers that the men must remain with the ship for the company to be saved. The soldiers cut the lifeboat loose.

Paul then urges everyone to eat after the prolonged strain and lack of food. He reassures them that their lives will be preserved, takes bread, thanks God publicly, breaks it and begins eating. The others take courage and eat as well.

Luke gives the number aboard as 276. After eating, they lighten the ship further by throwing grain into the sea. The promise of preservation is accompanied by concrete action: keeping the crew aboard, taking food and preparing for the landing.

Here being saved means surviving the danger and reaching land alive. Luke records the preservation of the whole company; he does not describe a response of faith by every person aboard.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read the promise and the warning together: trust in God includes responding to the instruction given and taking practical steps. Paul’s encouragement strengthens people to act rather than leaving them passive.

The Catholic USCCB note on verse 35 notices language associated with the Eucharist, or Lord’s Supper, in taking bread, giving thanks and breaking it. Calvin on verse 35 explains Paul’s example and thanksgiving in eating a meal that encourages the frightened company. These readings differ in the emphasis given to the meal’s language; neither requires us to invent a conversion account for all 276 people.
passages.god_plan_html:
God’s promise in verses 23–24 grants Paul not only his own continuing life but the lives of the people with him. The concern reaches the entire company. Paul helps preserve their strength through food and hope, and the crew’s remaining aboard is part of the rescue that follows.

The scene shows God’s purpose being served through words, decisions and care for bodies under strain. Public thanksgiving also acknowledges the Giver of life before the danger is over. The mission to Rome proceeds with people being cared for along the way.

passages.title: Acts 27:39-44
passages.section_title: How does everyone reach shore when the ship breaks apart?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 39 When daylight came, they did not recognize the land, but they sighted a bay with a sandy beach, where they decided to run the ship aground if they could. 40 Cutting away the anchors, they left them in the sea as they loosened the ropes that held the rudders. Then they hoisted the foresail to the wind and made for the beach. 41 But the ship struck a sandbar and ran aground. The bow stuck fast and would not move, and the stern was being broken up by the pounding of the waves. 42 The soldiers planned to kill the prisoners so none of them could swim to freedom. 43 But the centurion, wanting to spare Paul’s life, thwarted their plan. He commanded those who could swim to jump overboard first and get to land. 44 The rest were to follow on planks and various parts of the ship. In this way everyone was brought safely to land.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
At daylight the crew sees an unfamiliar bay with a sandy beach and tries to run the ship onto it. They abandon the anchors, free the rudders and raise the foresail. But the ship strikes a sandbar: its bow sticks fast, and the waves begin breaking the stern apart.

The soldiers plan to kill the prisoners to prevent any escaping. Julius, wanting to spare Paul’s life, stops that plan. He orders those who can swim to go first, with the others following on planks and pieces of the ship. Everyone reaches land safely.

The rescue includes both threatened dangers: the sea and the soldiers’ proposed action. Luke reports the centurion’s desire to preserve Paul, but does not say that Julius has become a Christian or give the final destination and sentence of each prisoner.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read the outcome as the fulfillment of the assurance that no life would be lost even though the ship would be. Human decisions remain part of that outcome: the crew’s effort, Julius’s intervention, swimming and floating on wreckage all belong to the account of everyone reaching shore.
passages.god_plan_html:
The preservation promised in Acts 27:22–26 has now taken a concrete form: the ship is lost, and the people live. This keeps Paul on the way toward the testimony in Rome promised in Acts 23:11. The wreck has not ended that commission.

The next chapter identifies the island as Malta and describes hospitality and healing there. The route to one destination opens another setting for God’s care along the way. The story’s value is greater than a successful arrival for one traveler; the lives of the people around him also matter.

passages.title: Acts 28:1-10
passages.section_title: What do the people of Malta learn from Paul’s survival and care?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Once we were safely ashore, we learned that the island was called Malta. 2 The islanders showed us extraordinary kindness. They kindled a fire and welcomed all of us because it was raining and cold. 3 Paul gathered a bundle of sticks, and as he laid them on the fire, a viper, driven out by the heat, fastened itself to his hand. 4 When the islanders saw the creature hanging from his hand, they said to one another, “Surely this man is a murderer. Although he was saved from the sea, Justice has not allowed him to live.” 5 But Paul shook the creature off into the fire and suffered no ill effects. 6 The islanders were expecting him to swell up or suddenly drop dead. But after waiting a long time and seeing nothing unusual happen to him, they changed their minds and said he was a god. 7 Nearby stood an estate belonging to Publius, the chief official of the island. He welcomed us and entertained us hospitably for three days. 8 The father of Publius was sick in bed, suffering from fever and dysentery. Paul went in to see him, and after praying and placing his hands on him, he healed the man. 9 After this had happened, the rest of the sick on the island came and were cured as well. 10 The islanders honored us in many ways and supplied our needs when we were ready to sail.

But after waiting a long time and seeing nothing unusual happen to him, they changed their minds and said he was a god.

7 Nearby stood an estate belonging to Publius, the chief official of the island. He welcomed us and entertained us hospitably for three days. 8 The father of Publius was sick in bed, suffering from fever and dysentery. Paul went in to see him, and after praying and placing his hands on him, he healed the man. 9 After this had happened, the rest of the sick on the island came and were cured as well. 10 The islanders honored us in many ways and supplied our needs when we were ready to sail.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The survivors learn that the island is Malta. Its people welcome them with a fire against the rain and cold. Paul helps gather wood, and a viper fastens onto his hand. The onlookers first decide he must be a murderer whom Justice will not allow to live. When he suffers no harm, they change their minds and call him a god.

Here Justice refers to the islanders’ idea of a divine power that punishes wrongdoing. The Greek word, dikē (DEE-kay), can mean justice or punishment; Thayer’s entry explains its use here for the goddess Justice. Luke reports the people’s changing conclusions without endorsing either one. They have not discovered Paul’s guilt or his identity by watching the snake.

Publius, the island’s chief official, welcomes the travelers for three days. His father is sick with fever and dysentery. Paul visits him, prays, lays hands on him and heals him. Other sick people come and are cured as well. The islanders honor the travelers and provide supplies when they leave. Luke records generous hospitality and healing, without telling us that every islander becomes a believer.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as God preserving His servant and extending care to the people who welcome the survivors. The onlookers’ reversal also exposes how quickly people can mistake an accident or an escape for proof of someone’s guilt or greatness. Paul’s prayer directs attention beyond himself.
passages.god_plan_html:
The promise that Paul will bear witness in Rome, given in Acts 23:11, continues through an unexpected stay where other people receive help. The islanders care for the shipwrecked company, and Paul becomes a means of care for their sick. The delay is part of a story that concerns more than Paul’s arrival.

There is a limited parallel with Acts 14:8–18, where healing leads people to mistake Paul and Barnabas for gods. There the apostles explicitly turn the crowd toward the living God. Malta’s story is shorter and does not record the same speech. Both scenes help us distinguish God’s work through a person from the mistaken conclusion that the person is a god.

passages.title: Acts 28:11-16
passages.section_title: How do fellow believers strengthen Paul as he reaches Rome?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 After three months we set sail in an Alexandrian ship that had wintered in the island. It had the Twin Brothers as a figurehead. 12 Putting in at Syracuse, we stayed there three days. 13 From there we weighed anchor and came to Rhegium. After one day, a south wind came up, and on the second day we arrived at Puteoli. 14 There we found some brothers who invited us to spend the week with them. And so we came to Rome. 15 The brothers there had heard about us and traveled as far as the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns to meet us. When Paul saw them, he was encouraged and gave thanks to God. 16 When we arrived in Rome, Paul was permitted to stay by himself, with a soldier to guard him.
