section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After three months, the travelers leave on an Alexandrian ship that has wintered at Malta. Its figurehead bears the Twin Brothers, Castor and Pollux. Ancient sailors associated these figures with protection at sea: Homeric Hymn 33 describes them as rescuers of ships in storms. This explains the image’s background; Luke does not say that the travelers are protected by these figures.

They sail through Syracuse and Rhegium to Puteoli, where believers invite them to stay a week. News of their arrival reaches Rome, and believers come as far as the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns to meet them. Paul sees them, thanks God and takes courage.

In Rome Paul is allowed to live in private quarters, with a soldier guarding him. He has reached the city, but he is still a prisoner. The welcome does not amount to an acquittal or tell us the outcome of his appeal.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly see the believers’ welcome as practical fellowship that gives Paul courage for what lies ahead. The account presents a messenger who needs encouragement as well as giving it. His arrival fulfills the promised journey to Rome while leaving his legal situation unresolved.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Romans 1:11–12, Paul expresses his desire to see the Roman believers so that they may strengthen one another through their faith. Here their welcome strengthens him before Luke describes his teaching in the city. Encouragement runs both ways.

The arrival also brings the promise of Acts 23:11 into view: Paul will testify in Rome. The story will show that witness taking place under guard. Luke does not go on to narrate the appearance before Caesar mentioned in Acts 27:24.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Acts 28:17-22
passages.section_title: Why does Paul begin in Rome by speaking of Israel’s hope?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 After three days, he called together the leaders of the Jews. When they had gathered, he said to them, “Brothers, although I have done nothing against our people or the customs of our fathers, I was taken prisoner in Jerusalem and handed over to the Romans. 18 They examined me and wanted to release me, because there was no basis for a death sentence against me. 19 But when the Jews objected, I was compelled to appeal to Caesar, even though I have no charge to bring against my nation. 20 So for this reason I have called to see you and speak with you. It is because of the hope of Israel that I am bound with this chain.” 21 The leaders replied, “We have not received any letters about you from Judea, nor have any of the brothers from there reported or even mentioned anything bad about you. 22 But we consider your views worth hearing, because we know that people everywhere are speaking against this sect.”
paragraphs: 17 After three days, he called together the leaders of the Jews. When they had gathered, he said to them, “Brothers, although I have done nothing against our people or the customs of our fathers, I was taken prisoner in Jerusalem and handed over to the Romans. 18 They examined me and wanted to release me, because there was no basis for a death sentence against me. 19 But when the Jews objected, I was compelled to appeal to Caesar, even though I have no charge to bring against my nation. 20 So for this reason I have called to see you and speak with you. It is because of the hope of Israel that I am bound with this chain.” 21 The leaders replied, “We have not received any letters about you from Judea, nor have any of the brothers from there reported or even mentioned anything bad about you. 22 But we consider your views worth hearing, because we know that people everywhere are speaking against this sect.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Three days after arriving, Paul calls together the local Jewish leaders. He explains that he has done nothing against his people or their ancestral customs, yet was handed over as a prisoner. The Romans wished to release him because they found no offense deserving death, but opposition led him to appeal to Caesar. He adds that his appeal is not an accusation against his nation.

Paul says he is bound because of the hope of Israel. This continues the explanation he has given in earlier hearings: his message about Jesus and the resurrection grows out of the hope found in Israel’s Scriptures.

The leaders say they have received no letters about Paul from Judea and no visiting report against him. They want to hear his thinking because they know this movement is spoken against. Their answer opens a conversation; it does not tell us that every legal accusation has been withdrawn.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read Paul’s explanation as a claim of continuity with Israel’s hope, rather than a rejection of Israel or its Scriptures. The leaders have not yet heard his full presentation, and their willingness to hear should be distinguished from the mixed response that follows.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 15:7–9 brings together God’s faithfulness to His promises to the fathers and His mercy toward the Gentiles. Paul’s message in Rome belongs within that same purpose. The welcome of the nations does not make God’s promises to Israel a mistake.

The conversation begins with the hope of Israel and will lead to testimony about Jesus from Moses and the Prophets. The wider invitation grows from that scriptural story, rather than requiring Paul to abandon it.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Acts 28:23-29
passages.section_title: Why do some believe Paul’s message while others turn away?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 23 So they set a day to meet with Paul, and many people came to the place he was staying. He expounded to them from morning to evening, testifying about the kingdom of God and persuading them about Jesus from the Law of Moses and the Prophets. 24 Some of them were convinced by what he said, but others refused to believe. 25 They disagreed among themselves and began to leave after Paul had made this final statement: “The Holy Spirit was right when He spoke to your fathers through Isaiah the prophet: 26 ‘Go to this people and say, “You will be ever hearing but never understanding; you will be ever seeing but never perceiving.” 27 For this people’s heart has grown callous; they hardly hear with their ears, and they have closed their eyes. Otherwise they might see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their hearts, and turn, and I would heal them.’ 28 Be advised, therefore, that God’s salvation has been sent to the Gentiles, and they will listen!”
paragraphs: 23 So they set a day to meet with Paul, and many people came to the place he was staying. He expounded to them from morning to evening, testifying about the kingdom of God and persuading them about Jesus from the Law of Moses and the Prophets. 24 Some of them were convinced by what he said, but others refused to believe.

25 They disagreed among themselves and began to leave after Paul had made this final statement: “The Holy Spirit was right when He spoke to your fathers through Isaiah the prophet: 26 ‘Go to this people and say, “You will be ever hearing but never understanding; you will be ever seeing but never perceiving.” 27 For this people’s heart has grown callous; they hardly hear with their ears, and they have closed their eyes. Otherwise they might see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their hearts, and turn, and I would heal them.’ 28 Be advised, therefore, that God’s salvation has been sent to the Gentiles, and they will listen!”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
On the appointed day, many people come to Paul’s lodging. From morning until evening he explains the kingdom of God and tries to persuade them about Jesus from the Law of Moses and the Prophets. Some are convinced; others refuse to believe. Luke records a divided response, not a rejection by every Jewish hearer.

As they leave in disagreement, Paul quotes the Holy Spirit’s words through Isaiah about people who hear without understanding and see without perceiving. The warning includes hearts that have grown callous and eyes that have been closed. Paul then declares that God’s salvation has been sent to the Gentiles, who will listen.

This continues a mission already visible throughout Acts. It is not the first invitation to Gentiles, and it does not mean that every Gentile will believe. The passage contrasts responses to the message without giving a verdict on every member of either people.

The BSB places verse 29 in a footnote because it occurs in some manuscript traditions. The Scripture text above therefore runs from verse 28 to the next passage at verse 30.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read Isaiah’s warning here as a serious call to hear and respond, alongside the continuing offer of salvation beyond Israel. Calvin on verse 28 also distinguishes the Gentiles’ reception of the message from a claim that all Gentiles will believe. The mixed response in verse 24 must remain part of the reading.
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul explicitly connects the response he encounters with Isaiah 6:9–10. A messenger can speak God’s word faithfully while hearers resist it. The warning exposes the seriousness of that response; it does not erase the people who do believe.

Romans 11:1–2 guards against turning this scene into a claim that God has rejected His people: Paul himself is an Israelite. Together with the movement toward the nations in Acts 1:8, these passages keep both the widening witness and God’s faithfulness in view. They do not settle every question about Israel and the church.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Acts 28:30-31
passages.section_title: Why does Acts end with the message still being heard?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 30 Paul stayed there two full years in his own rented house, welcoming all who came to visit him. 31 Boldly and freely he proclaimed the kingdom of God and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ.
paragraphs: 30 Paul stayed there two full years in his own rented house, welcoming all who came to visit him. 31 Boldly and freely he proclaimed the kingdom of God and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Luke closes with two years in Paul’s rented house. Paul welcomes everyone who comes to him and teaches about the kingdom of God and the Lord Jesus Christ boldly and freely. The soldier’s guard, mentioned in verse 16, has not prevented people from hearing the message.

The word translated freely is akōlytōs (ah-koh-LOO-tohs), ἀκωλύτως, meaning without hindrance; see Thayer’s entry. The emphasis is on the freedom to proclaim and teach. It does not say that Paul has been acquitted or released.

Acts does not narrate the outcome of the appeal, Paul’s later movements or his death. Its closing picture is of people being welcomed and Jesus being proclaimed while the messenger’s circumstances remain restricted.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this ending as an emphasis on the continuing spread of the message. Luke ends with the kingdom of God and Jesus being taught openly in Rome, rather than completing a biography of Paul or reporting his final court verdict.
passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 1:8 announces witness to Jesus moving outward from Jerusalem. The closing scene places that witness in Rome and leaves the teaching continuing. Reaching Rome is a major stage in the story, not a statement that every nation has now heard.

The distinction between a restricted messenger and a message that keeps going also appears in 2 Timothy 2:8–10. Paul speaks there of suffering in chains while God’s word cannot be chained. Acts ends with that same encouragement made visible: confinement has not stopped people from hearing about the risen Lord.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 1:1-7
passages.section_title: How does Paul introduce himself and the good news about Jesus?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus, called to be an apostle, and set apart for the gospel of God— 2 the gospel He promised beforehand through His prophets in the Holy Scriptures, 3 regarding His Son, who was a descendant of David according to the flesh, 4 and who through the Spirit of holiness was declared with power to be the Son of God by His resurrection from the dead: Jesus Christ our Lord. 5 Through Him and on behalf of His name, we received grace and apostleship to call all those among the Gentiles to the obedience that comes from faith. 6 And you also are among those who are called to belong to Jesus Christ. 7 To all in Rome who are loved by God and called to be saints: Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
paragraphs: 1 Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus, called to be an apostle, and set apart for the gospel of God— 2 the gospel He promised beforehand through His prophets in the Holy Scriptures, 3 regarding His Son, who was a descendant of David according to the flesh, 4 and who through the Spirit of holiness was declared with power to be the Son of God by His resurrection from the dead: Jesus Christ our Lord.

5 Through Him and on behalf of His name, we received grace and apostleship to call all those among the Gentiles to the obedience that comes from faith. 6 And you also are among those who are called to belong to Jesus Christ. 7 To all in Rome who are loved by God and called to be saints: Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul introduces himself as belonging to Christ Jesus, called to be an apostle and set apart for God’s gospel. Before saying much about his own plans, he explains whose message this is and whom it concerns: God’s Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.

The word translated servant is doulos (DOO-loss), δοῦλος. It can mean a slave, and here expresses Paul’s service under Christ’s authority; see Thayer’s entry. Paul’s title is therefore both humble and weighty: he serves another, and his calling to speak comes from the Lord he serves.

The gospel was promised beforehand through the prophets. Jesus belongs to David’s family in His human ancestry, and His resurrection declares Him with power to be the Son of God. Paul already calls Him God’s Son before mentioning the resurrection; he is not introducing an ordinary man who only became God’s Son after death.

Through Jesus, Paul has received grace and a commission that reaches the Gentiles. Its aim is the obedience that comes from faith. The Roman believers belong within this calling: they are loved by God, called to belong to Jesus and called to be saints. Paul addresses the believing community this way, then greets them with grace and peace from the Father and the Lord Jesus.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this greeting as a summary of the message Paul will explain: the promised Son has come, has risen, and calls people from the nations to faith and a life of obedience. The description of Jesus’ ancestry and resurrection holds His human life and divine sonship together; the resurrection makes His identity known in power.
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul himself places the gospel within God’s earlier promises. The reference to David’s family recalls the promise of an enduring royal house in 2 Samuel 7:12–16. Romans identifies Jesus, the risen Lord, as the Son at the center of this good news.

The letter’s ending returns to the same purpose: Romans 16:25–27 connects the prophetic writings, the proclamation of Jesus and the obedience that comes from faith among all nations. The opening and closing belong to one story: God keeps His promises and makes His salvation known beyond Israel.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 1:8-15
passages.section_title: Why does Paul want to visit believers who already have faith?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 First, I thank my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because your faith is being proclaimed all over the world. 9 God, whom I serve with my spirit in preaching the gospel of His Son, is my witness how constantly I remember you 10 in my prayers at all times, asking that now at last by God’s will I may succeed in coming to you. 11 For I long to see you so that I may impart to you some spiritual gift to strengthen you, 12 that is, that you and I may be mutually encouraged by each other’s faith. 13 I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, how often I planned to come to you (but have been prevented from visiting until now), in order that I might have a harvest among you, just as I have had among the other Gentiles. 14 I am obligated both to Greeks and non-Greeks, both to the wise and the foolish. 15 That is why I am so eager to preach the gospel also to you who are in Rome.
paragraphs: 8 First, I thank my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because your faith is being proclaimed all over the world. 9 God, whom I serve with my spirit in preaching the gospel of His Son, is my witness how constantly I remember you 10 in my prayers at all times, asking that now at last by God’s will I may succeed in coming to you. 11 For I long to see you so that I may impart to you some spiritual gift to strengthen you, 12 that is, that you and I may be mutually encouraged by each other’s faith.

13 I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, how often I planned to come to you (but have been prevented from visiting until now), in order that I might have a harvest among you, just as I have had among the other Gentiles. 14 I am obligated both to Greeks and non-Greeks, both to the wise and the foolish. 15 That is why I am so eager to preach the gospel also to you who are in Rome.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul thanks God through Jesus Christ because the Roman believers’ faith is widely known. He constantly remembers them in prayer and asks that, by God’s will, he may finally visit. This is a relationship he values before meeting the whole community in person.

He wants to share a spiritual gift that will strengthen them, then immediately describes the benefit as mutual: their faith will encourage him, and his will encourage them. His authority as an apostle does not remove his need for the faith and company of other believers.

Paul has often planned a visit but has been prevented. Later, Romans 15:18–24 explains that his work of taking the gospel to places where Christ was not known has delayed the journey. The letter does not tell us that the Romans resent him or that his thanksgiving is an attempt to repair an insult.

His obligation reaches Greeks and non-Greeks, the wise and the foolish. He is eager to preach in Rome as well. Their existing faith is a reason to strengthen them, not a reason to regard the gospel as something they have outgrown.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read these verses as an example of prayerful planning, care for fellow believers and encouragement that flows both ways. Paul’s desired visit serves their growth as well as his continuing mission.

Commentators differ over the spiritual gift he hopes to share. Calvin on verse 11 includes teaching, encouragement and prophecy among the gifts Paul could use for them. Wesley on verse 11 places greater emphasis on gifts associated with an apostle’s personal ministry and laying on of hands. These are individual explanations; both must be read with Paul’s own emphasis on mutual encouragement in verse 12.
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul’s obligation to people across cultural and educational boundaries fits the commission to the nations in verses 5–6. The gospel is not reserved for people with a particular background or level of learning. His travel plans serve that wider calling.

Acts 28:14–16 later shows Roman believers coming out to meet Paul. He thanks God and takes courage at the sight of them. His arrival is under guard, yet the encouragement he desires in this letter becomes visible through their welcome. God’s work through an apostle includes the support he receives from others.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 1:16
passages.section_title: What gives the gospel its power to save?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 I am not ashamed of the gospel, because it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, first to the Jew, then to the Greek.
paragraphs: 16 I am not ashamed of the gospel, because it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, first to the Jew, then to the Greek.

passages.context_html:
Paul has just said he is eager to preach in Rome. He now explains why he is unashamed: the gospel is God’s power for salvation to everyone who believes. His confidence rests in God’s saving work, rather than the prestige of the messenger or the city receiving him.

The invitation reaches the Jew first and also the Greek. The order preserves the connection with God’s promises to Israel while making clear that the saving message reaches beyond Israel. Verse 17 continues the thought by connecting God’s righteousness and faith. Read the full movement in Romans 1:16–17.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this verse as confidence in God’s saving power through the gospel, offered to people across the distinction between Jew and Gentile. The statement identifies believers as those who receive salvation; it does not say that hearing the message automatically saves every hearer.
passages.current_position_html: The Gospel According to Jesus uses Romans 1:16 to explain that the gospel announces Jesus’ death for sins and His resurrection, through which God brings salvation to those who believe. Our position is that this salvation is God’s gift through faith in Christ, rather than something earned by religious effort or moral improvement.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html: The same movement appears in Acts 13:46–48, where Paul and Barnabas speak first to Jewish hearers and then turn to Gentiles, citing God’s purpose of salvation reaching the ends of the earth. Romans presents the gospel’s wide invitation as part of God’s purpose, rather than a message restricted to one ancestry.

passages.title: Romans 1:16-17
passages.section_title: Why is Paul unashamed of the gospel?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 I am not ashamed of the gospel, because it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, first to the Jew, then to the Greek. 17 For the gospel reveals the righteousness of God that comes by faith from start to finish, just as it is written: “The righteous will live by faith.”
paragraphs: 16 I am not ashamed of the gospel, because it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, first to the Jew, then to the Greek. 17 For the gospel reveals the righteousness of God that comes by faith from start to finish, just as it is written: “The righteous will live by faith.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul moves from his eagerness to preach in Rome to the reason for his confidence: the gospel is God’s power for salvation to everyone who believes. It reaches the Jew first and also the Greek. The message he serves is not confined to one people.

Verse 17 explains that the gospel reveals the righteousness of God. This concerns God’s rightness and the way people are brought into a right relationship with Him, a subject Paul will develop throughout the letter. The BSB renders the phrase about faith as by faith from start to finish; its footnote gives the more literal from faith to faith.

Paul supports his statement from Habakkuk rather than presenting faith as a new idea unrelated to Israel’s Scriptures. The question of how people stand right before God will now shape his account of sin, grace and the work of Christ.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand these verses as a central statement of Romans: salvation comes through God’s action in Christ and is received through faith. They differ over how to describe being made right with God, often called justification.

Where traditions differ, the Reformed Westminster Confession 11.1–2 and the 1689 Baptist Confession 11.1–2 describe God pardoning sins and counting believers righteous because of Christ’s obedience, received through faith alone. They distinguish this acceptance from the inward growth in holiness that accompanies it. These confessions represent churches that receive them, rather than every Presbyterian or Baptist’s personal account.

The Catholic Church teaches that justification includes forgiveness and inward renewal, given through Christ’s grace and conferred in baptism. The Catechism, paragraphs 1987–1993, describes faith and a response made possible by grace; it does not describe people making themselves right with God unaided.

The Methodist Articles IX–X say people are counted righteous through faith because of Christ, rather than because of their own works. Good works follow as the fruit of living faith. Wesley’s note on verse 17 describes the whole benefit God gives through Christ for a sinner’s salvation. These accounts share the need for grace while differing in how they relate forgiveness, faith and a renewed life.
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul explicitly draws on Habakkuk 2:1–4, where God calls for trust in His word while the promised fulfillment is awaited. The contrast with pride places life in dependence on God rather than self-confidence. Paul brings that scriptural witness into his explanation of the gospel.

The invitation to Jew and Greek also carries forward the opening promise of a message for the nations. God’s faithfulness to His earlier word and His welcome of people beyond Israel belong together. The gospel’s reach does not require a different Savior or a different source of salvation for each people.
passages.current_position_html: The Gospel According to Jesus draws on Romans 1:16 to identify the gospel as God’s saving announcement about Jesus, centered on His death for sins and His resurrection. Our position here is that salvation is God’s gift, received through faith in Christ, rather than an achievement earned by religious effort or moral improvement. This states that study’s conclusion; it does not settle every difference about justification described above.

passages.title: Romans 1:18-23
passages.section_title: What happens when people refuse to honor the God creation reveals?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 The wrath of God is being revealed from heaven against all the godlessness and wickedness of men who suppress the truth by their wickedness. 19 For what may be known about God is plain to them, because God has made it plain to them. 20 For since the creation of the world God’s invisible qualities, His eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly seen, being understood from His workmanship, so that men are without excuse. 21 For although they knew God, they neither glorified Him as God nor gave thanks to Him, but they became futile in their thinking and darkened in their foolish hearts. 22 Although they claimed to be wise, they became fools, 23 and exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images of mortal man and birds and animals and reptiles.
paragraphs: 18 The wrath of God is being revealed from heaven against all the godlessness and wickedness of men who suppress the truth by their wickedness. 19 For what may be known about God is plain to them, because God has made it plain to them. 20 For since the creation of the world God’s invisible qualities, His eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly seen, being understood from His workmanship, so that men are without excuse.

21 For although they knew God, they neither glorified Him as God nor gave thanks to Him, but they became futile in their thinking and darkened in their foolish hearts. 22 Although they claimed to be wise, they became fools, 23 and exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images of mortal man and birds and animals and reptiles.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After announcing God’s saving power in the gospel, Paul describes the problem that makes salvation necessary. God’s wrath is His judgment against godlessness and wrongdoing. Paul speaks of it as being revealed, rather than describing only a distant event that has no bearing on the present.

The charge is that people suppress truth God has made plain. The verb behind suppress is katechō (kah-TEH-khoh), κατέχω. It can mean holding something back or restraining it; Thayer’s entry identifies that use in verse 18. Paul’s concern here is a refusal of what God has shown, not simply the absence of information.

Creation makes God’s eternal power and divine nature known through what He has made. Yet knowledge is not met with honor and thanks. Thinking becomes futile, hearts become darkened, and claims to wisdom lead to exchanging God’s glory for images of created beings.

This passage begins the account of sin that continues through chapter 3. The next chapter turns toward the person who condemns others while doing wrong as well. Paul is not giving that reader a place above the people being described.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this passage as teaching that creation bears witness to its Maker and that people are accountable for refusing to honor Him. This is often called natural revelation: knowledge of God made available through the world He created. It should be distinguished from the gospel about Jesus that Paul has just introduced.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Acts 17:24–31, Paul likewise points people to the Creator who gives life and is not represented by objects people make. That speech leads toward repentance, judgment and the risen Jesus. The witness of creation belongs within a larger invitation to turn toward the living God.

The exchange of God’s glory for an image also recalls Psalm 106:19–23, which describes Israel’s worship of the calf. This is a parallel in the Scriptures, not a claim that Paul explicitly quotes that psalm here. It shows that this failure is not confined to people outside Israel. God’s people also need the mercy and correction the biblical story describes.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 1:24-27
passages.section_title: What does Paul mean when he says God gave people over?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 24 Therefore God gave them over in the desires of their hearts to impurity for the dishonoring of their bodies with one another. 25 They exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is forever worthy of praise! Amen. 26 For this reason God gave them over to dishonorable passions. Even their women exchanged natural relations for unnatural ones. 27 Likewise, the men abandoned natural relations with women and burned with lust for one another. Men committed indecent acts with other men and received in themselves the due penalty for their error.
paragraphs: 24 Therefore God gave them over in the desires of their hearts to impurity for the dishonoring of their bodies with one another. 25 They exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is forever worthy of praise! Amen.

26 For this reason God gave them over to dishonorable passions. Even their women exchanged natural relations for unnatural ones. 27 Likewise, the men abandoned natural relations with women and burned with lust for one another. Men committed indecent acts with other men and received in themselves the due penalty for their error.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul connects the exchange of the Creator for created things with a further handing over: God gives people over to the desires that dishonor their bodies. The phrase appears again in verse 26 and will appear a third time in verse 28. The repeated pattern presents wrongdoing and judgment as connected.

Verse 25 keeps worship at the center of the passage. People have exchanged God’s truth for a lie and served the creature rather than the Creator. Paul interrupts the description with praise to the Creator, whose worth does not change when people refuse Him.

He then describes women exchanging natural relations for unnatural ones and men leaving relations with women to desire one another. Paul calls these passions dishonorable and the acts indecent. Christians differ over how the scope and setting of this description apply to same-sex relationships today, as the readings below explain.

The passage does not name a particular disease as the penalty in verse 27. Nor does it end the account of wrongdoing with sexual behavior. Paul immediately continues with a broad list that includes greed, deceit, arrogance, gossip and mercilessness.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly connect God’s giving people over with judgment in the midst of human wrongdoing. Wesley on verse 24 describes a withdrawal of restraining grace: God ceases to hold people back from the course they pursue. That is his explanation of the action, rather than wording Paul supplies about every step of the process.

Where traditions differ, the Catholic Church reads the passage as part of the scriptural basis for rejecting same-sex sexual acts. The Catechism, paragraphs 2357–2359, also requires respect, compassion and sensitivity toward people with same-sex attraction and rejects unjust discrimination. The teaching distinguishes its judgment about acts from its obligation to care for people.

A traditional Reformed reading likewise understands the acts as contrary to God’s created order. Calvin on verse 26 takes this approach; the Westminster Confession 24.1 defines marriage as between one man and one woman. Calvin’s explanation and the confession’s marriage teaching are related sources, rather than identical kinds of authority.

An affirming Protestant reading places greater weight on the setting of idolatry, excessive desire and ancient expectations of male and female roles. In an essay published by the United Methodist Church, John C. Holbert understands Paul’s description within that first-century framework and does not apply it as a universal rejection of faithful same-sex relationships today. This is a named teacher’s reading, not a claim that all Methodists interpret the passage alike. The disagreement concerns the reach of Paul’s description, not whether verses 26–27 contain a negative judgment.
passages.god_plan_html:
The attention to bodies has a place in the letter’s wider story. Romans 8:18–25 looks toward creation’s freedom from decay and the redemption of believers’ bodies. God’s saving purpose concerns embodied life and the creation He made, not only thoughts or an escape from the physical world.

This is a connection across the letter rather than a separate ruling on the disputed applications above. The Creator who is refused in chapter 1 remains the source of the hope described in chapter 8.

passages.title: Romans 1:28-32
passages.section_title: Why does Paul end with so many kinds of wrongdoing?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 28 Furthermore, since they did not see fit to acknowledge God, He gave them up to a depraved mind, to do what ought not to be done. 29 They have become filled with every kind of wickedness, evil, greed, and depravity. They are full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, and malice. They are gossips, 30 slanderers, God-haters, insolent, arrogant, and boastful. They invent new forms of evil; they disobey their parents. 31 They are senseless, faithless, heartless, merciless. 32 Although they know God’s righteous decree that those who do such things are worthy of death, they not only continue to do these things, but also approve of those who practice them.
paragraphs: 28 Furthermore, since they did not see fit to acknowledge God, He gave them up to a depraved mind, to do what ought not to be done. 29 They have become filled with every kind of wickedness, evil, greed, and depravity. They are full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, and malice. They are gossips, 30 slanderers, God-haters, insolent, arrogant, and boastful. They invent new forms of evil; they disobey their parents. 31 They are senseless, faithless, heartless, merciless.
32 Although they know God’s righteous decree that those who do such things are worthy of death, they not only continue to do these things, but also approve of those who practice them.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul describes a third giving over: because people have not seen fit to acknowledge God, He gives them up to a depraved mind, a way of thinking that approves what ought not to be done. The description moves from false worship and disordered desires into the harm people do to one another.

The list is deliberately broad. It includes greed, envy, murder, deceit, malice, gossip, slander, arrogance, disobedience to parents, faithlessness and lack of mercy. Sexual behavior is not the only subject of Paul’s account, and the list does not say that every person has committed every deed named.

The final verse adds approval of wrongdoing to the practice of it. Paul describes people who know God’s judgment and nevertheless encourage what comes under that judgment. The concern reaches what a community celebrates as well as what individuals do.

The next sentence, Romans 2:1, turns directly toward the judging reader. Condemning another person does not excuse someone who also practices wrongdoing. The chapter division should not hide that turn.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this list as a picture of the wide damage caused by refusing God, including familiar social sins as well as more publicly condemned acts. The movement into chapter 2 prevents the passage from becoming a way for the reader to claim innocence simply by condemning someone else.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 3:9–24 states where this developing account leads: Jews and Greeks alike are under sin, and God’s righteousness is made known through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe. The exposure of wrongdoing prepares for the announcement of grace; it does not establish one group’s right to look down on another.

The same Creator who holds people accountable provides redemption in Christ. That wider purpose gives the list its place in the letter: it helps explain the need shared by those who read it, rather than giving them only a catalog of other people’s failures.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 2:1-5
passages.section_title: Why does Paul turn from their wrongdoing to the person judging them?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 You, therefore, have no excuse, you who pass judgment on another. For on whatever grounds you judge the other, you are condemning yourself, because you who pass judgment do the same things. 2 And we know that God’s judgment against those who do such things is based on truth. 3 So when you, O man, pass judgment on others, yet do the same things, do you think you will escape God’s judgment? 4 Or do you disregard the riches of His kindness, tolerance, and patience, not realizing that God’s kindness leads you to repentance? 5 But because of your hard and unrepentant heart, you are storing up wrath against yourself for the day of wrath, when God’s righteous judgment will be revealed.
paragraphs: 1 You, therefore, have no excuse, you who pass judgment on another. For on whatever grounds you judge the other, you are condemning yourself, because you who pass judgment do the same things. 2 And we know that God’s judgment against those who do such things is based on truth. 3 So when you, O man, pass judgment on others, yet do the same things, do you think you will escape God’s judgment?

4 Or do you disregard the riches of His kindness, tolerance, and patience, not realizing that God’s kindness leads you to repentance? 5 But because of your hard and unrepentant heart, you are storing up wrath against yourself for the day of wrath, when God’s righteous judgment will be revealed.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The opening therefore connects this passage to the end of chapter 1. Paul now addresses the person who passes judgment on others while also practicing wrongdoing. Recognizing another person’s sin does not establish the judge’s innocence.

God’s judgment is based on truth. Paul challenges the assumption that someone who condemns the same behavior in others will escape that judgment. The issue is hypocrisy, not a declaration that there is no such thing as right or wrong.

He then asks what the reader makes of God’s kindness, tolerance and patience. A delay in judgment is an opportunity to repent, to turn from wrongdoing toward God. Treating that kindness as permission to continue only stores up wrath for the day when God’s righteous judgment is revealed.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these verses as a warning against condemning others while excusing oneself. God’s patience calls for a changed response; it is not proof that He approves of whatever someone is doing. The passage challenges a self-satisfied reader rather than allowing that reader to remain outside Paul’s account of sin.
passages.god_plan_html:
2 Peter 3:8–10 also connects God’s patience with repentance while maintaining the reality of coming judgment. The delay serves mercy without making wrongdoing harmless.

This helps explain the place of Paul’s warning within the gospel he has introduced. God’s kindness is meant to draw the reader toward Him. The reader who sees only other people’s need for repentance has missed the invitation being extended to them as well.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 2:6-11
passages.section_title: What does God look at when He judges?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 God “will repay each one according to his deeds.” 7 To those who by perseverance in doing good seek glory, honor, and immortality, He will give eternal life. 8 But for those who are self-seeking and who reject the truth and follow wickedness, there will be wrath and anger. 9 There will be trouble and distress for every human being who does evil, first for the Jew, then for the Greek; 10 but glory, honor, and peace for everyone who does good, first for the Jew, then for the Greek. 11 For God does not show favoritism.
paragraphs: 6 God “will repay each one according to his deeds.” 7 To those who by perseverance in doing good seek glory, honor, and immortality, He will give eternal life. 8 But for those who are self-seeking and who reject the truth and follow wickedness, there will be wrath and anger.

9 There will be trouble and distress for every human being who does evil, first for the Jew, then for the Greek; 10 but glory, honor, and peace for everyone who does good, first for the Jew, then for the Greek. 11 For God does not show favoritism.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul states that God will repay each person according to their deeds. He contrasts perseverance in doing good, seeking glory, honor and immortality, with self-seeking, refusal of truth and the pursuit of wickedness. The outcomes are eternal life on one side and wrath, trouble and distress on the other.

The same pattern applies to Jew and Greek. Being first in receiving God’s message does not create immunity from His judgment, and being a Gentile does not make someone unworthy of the good He gives. God does not show favoritism.

These verses must be read alongside the letter’s account of sin and grace. Paul will say that all have sinned and that people are justified freely through Christ in Romans 3:21–24. Christians differ over how to explain the relationship between that gift and the judgment according to deeds described here.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the passage to affirm a real judgment that takes people’s lives seriously, without favoring a religious name or ancestry. Where traditions differ is in how they describe good works in relation to grace and eternal life.

The Reformed Westminster Confession 16.2–6 describes good works as the fruit and evidence of living faith, enabled by the Spirit. They cannot earn forgiveness or eternal life, yet God accepts and rewards them through Christ. Calvin on verses 6–7 reads Paul’s promised reward in that setting of grace, rather than treating the works as a payment God owes.

The Catholic Church teaches that no one can earn the initial grace of forgiveness and justification. It also teaches that works made possible by grace and love have a real part in growth toward eternal life. The Catechism, paragraphs 2007–2011, places God’s initiative first and describes the believer’s good actions as gifts of His grace.

The Methodist Articles IX–X distinguish being counted righteous through faith because of Christ from good works that follow as the fruit of faith. Those works cannot remove sin, but they are pleasing to God. None of these documents describes unaided human effort as the source of salvation, though they differ over how acceptance, renewal and reward fit together.
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul draws the language of repayment from Psalm 62:11–12, where God’s power and loving devotion stand beside His judgment according to deeds. Judgment and faithful love belong to the same God.

Deuteronomy 10:17–19 likewise describes God as showing no partiality and accepting no bribe, then speaks of His justice for the fatherless and widow and His love for the foreigner. Paul’s insistence on an impartial judgment continues that scriptural account of God’s character; it is not a new standard invented for Gentiles.

passages.title: Romans 2:12-16
passages.section_title: How can people be accountable without having the Law of Moses?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 All who sin apart from the law will also perish apart from the law, and all who sin under the law will be judged by the law. 13 For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but it is the doers of the law who will be declared righteous. 14 Indeed, when Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature what the law requires, they are a law to themselves, even though they do not have the law. 15 So they show that the work of the law is written on their hearts, their consciences also bearing witness, and their thoughts either accusing or defending them 16 on the day when God will judge men’s secrets through Christ Jesus, as proclaimed by my gospel.
paragraphs: 12 All who sin apart from the law will also perish apart from the law, and all who sin under the law will be judged by the law. 13 For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but it is the doers of the law who will be declared righteous.

14 Indeed, when Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature what the law requires, they are a law to themselves, even though they do not have the law. 15 So they show that the work of the law is written on their hearts, their consciences also bearing witness, and their thoughts either accusing or defending them 16 on the day when God will judge men’s secrets through Christ Jesus, as proclaimed by my gospel.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul distinguishes those who sin without the law from those who sin under it. Having heard the law is not the same as obeying it. The issue is what people do with what they have, rather than the prestige of possessing the written teaching.

He points to Gentiles who do not have the law yet sometimes do what it requires. Their actions show the work of the law written on their hearts. Their consciences bear witness, and their thoughts accuse or defend them.

The Greek word for conscience is syneidēsis (soo-NAY-day-sis), συνείδησις. Thayer’s entry describes an awareness that distinguishes moral good and bad, approving or condemning a person’s actions. In Paul’s picture, conscience is a witness to accountability; it is not a claim that every inner feeling is an infallible message from God.

The passage looks toward the day when God judges people’s secrets through Christ Jesus. Public reputation and outward religious knowledge cannot hide the inward life. Paul includes this judgment within the gospel he proclaims.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read these verses as denying that possession of the law gives someone an automatic advantage over a person who has not received it. Readers differ over how verse 13’s promise to the doers of the law fits the letter’s teaching about faith.

The Reformed commentator Calvin on verse 13 understands Paul as stating what the law requires: someone seeking righteousness on that basis must fulfill it, which exposes the need for another source of righteousness. The Wesleyan founder John Wesley on verses 13–14 emphasizes final acquittal and reward for those who do it, while describing even the Gentiles’ response as made possible by God’s prior grace. These are distinct explanations by named commentators, rather than a claim that every member of either tradition speaks identically.
passages.god_plan_html:
The judgment through Christ belongs with the announcement in Acts 17:30–31: God calls people everywhere to repent and has appointed a man through whom He will judge the world, giving assurance through the resurrection.

That connection places conscience and accountability within a purpose reaching all nations. The judge is the risen Jesus proclaimed in the gospel, and the invitation to turn toward God is wider than the people who possess the written law.

passages.title: Romans 2:17-24
passages.section_title: What happens when someone teaches God’s law but does not live it?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 Now you, if you call yourself a Jew; if you rely on the law and boast in God; 18 if you know His will and approve of what is superior because you are instructed by the law; 19 if you are convinced that you are a guide for the blind, a light for those in darkness, 20 an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of infants, because you have in the law the embodiment of knowledge and truth— 21 you, then, who teach others, do you not teach yourself? You who preach against stealing, do you steal? 22 You who forbid adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you rob temples? 23 You who boast in the law, do you dishonor God by breaking the law? 24 As it is written: “God’s name is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you.”
paragraphs: 17 Now you, if you call yourself a Jew; if you rely on the law and boast in God; 18 if you know His will and approve of what is superior because you are instructed by the law; 19 if you are convinced that you are a guide for the blind, a light for those in darkness, 20 an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of infants, because you have in the law the embodiment of knowledge and truth—

21 you, then, who teach others, do you not teach yourself? You who preach against stealing, do you steal? 22 You who forbid adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you rob temples? 23 You who boast in the law, do you dishonor God by breaking the law? 24 As it is written: “God’s name is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul now explicitly addresses the person who calls himself a Jew, relies on the law and boasts in God. He describes the confidence of someone instructed in God’s will who sees himself as a guide and teacher for others.

The questions then turn that teaching back on the teacher. Does the person who preaches against stealing steal? Does the person who forbids adultery commit it? Does the person who rejects idols rob temples? Claiming to teach what is right cannot excuse violating it.

Paul turns the teacher’s own teaching into a test of his life. Breaking the law dishonors the God in whom he boasts. The questions address hypocrisy in the person making these claims; they are not a description of every Jewish person.

He concludes with Scripture about God’s name being blasphemed among the Gentiles. Here blasphemed means spoken against or dishonored. The failure has a consequence beyond the teacher’s reputation: it affects how others speak of God.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a warning that religious knowledge and the work of teaching increase responsibility rather than cancel it. The questions confront hypocrisy in the person making the claims; they should not become a stereotype about an entire people. Christian teachers must also hear the challenge they apply to others.
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul explicitly uses Isaiah 52:5. In that setting, God’s name is blasphemed amid His people’s humiliation and their rulers’ taunts. Paul applies the language of dishonor to people who claim God’s law while breaking it. The connection is real, though the two settings are not identical.

Ezekiel 36:20–27 joins concern for God’s name among the nations with His promise to cleanse His people, give them a new heart and put His Spirit within them. The larger answer to dishonor is more than protecting a religious reputation: it includes the inward renewal God promises to bring.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 2:25-29
passages.section_title: Why does Paul speak of circumcision of the heart?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 25 Circumcision has value if you observe the law, but if you break the law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision. 26 If a man who is not circumcised keeps the requirements of the law, will not his uncircumcision be regarded as circumcision? 27 The one who is physically uncircumcised yet keeps the law will condemn you who, even though you have the written code and circumcision, are a lawbreaker. 28 A man is not a Jew because he is one outwardly, nor is circumcision only outward and physical. 29 No, a man is a Jew because he is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the written code. Such a man’s praise does not come from men, but from God.
paragraphs: 25 Circumcision has value if you observe the law, but if you break the law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision. 26 If a man who is not circumcised keeps the requirements of the law, will not his uncircumcision be regarded as circumcision? 27 The one who is physically uncircumcised yet keeps the law will condemn you who, even though you have the written code and circumcision, are a lawbreaker.

28 A man is not a Jew because he is one outwardly, nor is circumcision only outward and physical. 29 No, a man is a Jew because he is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the written code. Such a man’s praise does not come from men, but from God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Circumcision is the physical covenant sign given to Abraham and his descendants in Genesis 17. Paul says the sign has value in connection with observing the law. It does not shield a lawbreaker from the consequences of disobedience.

He then reverses the assumed advantage. A physically uncircumcised person who keeps the law exposes the failure of someone who has both the written code and circumcision yet breaks the law. The outward sign cannot do the work of an obedient heart.

Paul’s conclusion moves inward: circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit. He is describing an inward work, rather than a physical procedure on the heart. The approval that matters comes from God, who sees what outward observers cannot.

This prepares the next question in chapter 3 about the advantage of being Jewish. Paul’s warning against relying on outward identity should therefore be read within the argument he continues to develop, rather than treated as the last sentence he will say about Israel.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these verses as a contrast between outward religious identity and the inward response God seeks. The sign is not condemned simply for being physical; the confidence placed in it apart from obedience is challenged. The emphasis on the Spirit and God’s approval also prevents the inward response from becoming merely another way to impress other people.
passages.god_plan_html:
The heart language is already present in Israel’s Scriptures. Deuteronomy 10:16 calls the people to circumcise their hearts and stop being stubborn. Deuteronomy 30:6 promises that God will circumcise their hearts so that they love Him and live. Paul’s inward emphasis continues that concern.

Colossians 2:11–13 also describes a circumcision performed by Christ rather than human hands, connecting it with being made alive in Him. These passages direct attention to God’s work in people, beyond the possession of an outward mark. That connection does not by itself settle every later question about Israel and the church.

passages.title: Romans 3:1-8
passages.section_title: Does human unfaithfulness mean God has failed His people?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 What, then, is the advantage of being a Jew? Or what is the value of circumcision? 2 Much in every way. First of all, they have been entrusted with the very words of God. 3 What if some did not have faith? Will their lack of faith nullify God’s faithfulness? 4 Certainly not! Let God be true and every man a liar. As it is written: “So that You may be proved right when You speak and victorious when You judge.” 5 But if our unrighteousness highlights the righteousness of God, what shall we say? That God is unjust to inflict His wrath on us? I am speaking in human terms. 6 Certainly not! In that case, how could God judge the world? 7 However, if my falsehood accentuates God’s truthfulness, to the increase of His glory, why am I still condemned as a sinner? 8 Why not say, as some slanderously claim that we say, “Let us do evil that good may result”? Their condemnation is deserved!
paragraphs: 1 What, then, is the advantage of being a Jew? Or what is the value of circumcision? 2 Much in every way. First of all, they have been entrusted with the very words of God. 3 What if some did not have faith? Will their lack of faith nullify God’s faithfulness? 4 Certainly not! Let God be true and every man a liar. As it is written: “So that You may be proved right when You speak and victorious when You judge.”

5 But if our unrighteousness highlights the righteousness of God, what shall we say? That God is unjust to inflict His wrath on us? I am speaking in human terms. 6 Certainly not! In that case, how could God judge the world? 7 However, if my falsehood accentuates God’s truthfulness, to the increase of His glory, why am I still condemned as a sinner? 8 Why not say, as some slanderously claim that we say, “Let us do evil that good may result”? Their condemnation is deserved!

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul has challenged confidence in outward identity and circumcision. He now raises the natural question: is there any advantage to being Jewish? His answer is yes. Israel has been entrusted with God’s words. The warning against hypocrisy does not erase that gift.

The next question concerns God’s faithfulness. If some did not have faith, does their failure cancel His faithfulness? Paul firmly denies it and appeals to Scripture about God being proved right when He speaks and judges. God’s truth does not depend on people always responding truthfully.

Paul then voices an objection he rejects: if human wrongdoing makes God’s righteousness clearer, would God be unjust to punish it? That reasoning would undermine His judgment of the world. A related claim would excuse a lie because it brought attention to God’s truth.

The conclusion would be that people should do evil so good may result. Paul says some have falsely accused him of teaching this, and he condemns the claim. He is describing the reasoning to reject it, not recommending wrongdoing as a way to serve God.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this passage as holding together God’s faithfulness, the real value of His words entrusted to Israel and human accountability. Neither covenant privilege nor a good result turns wrongdoing into obedience. Paul’s teaching about grace does not authorize doing evil.
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul explicitly appeals to Psalm 51:4. In that prayer, confession of sin goes together with acknowledging that God speaks and judges rightly. The same prayer asks for mercy and cleansing in verses 1–2.

That connection keeps judgment and mercy within the story of God’s faithfulness. God does not become unfaithful by exposing His people’s sin, and their need for forgiveness does not mean His word has failed. The gospel Paul is explaining will address wrongdoing rather than require God to pretend it never mattered.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 3:9-20
passages.section_title: Why does Paul bring everyone under the same charge of sin?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 What then? Are we any better? Not at all. For we have already made the charge that Jews and Greeks alike are all under sin. 10 As it is written: “There is no one righteous, not even one. 11 There is no one who understands, no one who seeks God. 12 All have turned away, they have together become worthless; there is no one who does good, not even one.” 13 “Their throats are open graves; their tongues practice deceit.” “The venom of vipers is on their lips.” 14 “Their mouths are full of cursing and bitterness.” 15 “Their feet are swift to shed blood; 16 ruin and misery lie in their wake, 17 and the way of peace they have not known.” 18 “There is no fear of God before their eyes.” 19 Now we know that whatever the law says, it says to those who are under the law, so that every mouth may be silenced and the whole world held accountable to God. 20 Therefore no one will be justified in His sight by works of the law. For the law merely brings awareness of sin.
paragraphs: 9 What then? Are we any better? Not at all. For we have already made the charge that Jews and Greeks alike are all under sin. 10 As it is written: “There is no one righteous, not even one. 11 There is no one who understands, no one who seeks God. 12 All have turned away, they have together become worthless; there is no one who does good, not even one.”

13 “Their throats are open graves; their tongues practice deceit.” “The venom of vipers is on their lips.” 14 “Their mouths are full of cursing and bitterness.” 15 “Their feet are swift to shed blood; 16 ruin and misery lie in their wake, 17 and the way of peace they have not known.” 18 “There is no fear of God before their eyes.”

19 Now we know that whatever the law says, it says to those who are under the law, so that every mouth may be silenced and the whole world held accountable to God. 20 Therefore no one will be justified in His sight by works of the law. For the law merely brings awareness of sin.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul returns to the question of superiority. Jews and Greeks alike are under sin. The gifts entrusted to Israel do not establish a separate standard of innocence for those who receive them.

He brings together passages from the Psalms and Isaiah. The sequence describes failure to seek God, destructive speech, violence, the absence of peace and a lack of reverence for Him. Psalm 14:1–3 and Isaiah 59:7–8 are among the sources identified in the BSB footnotes.

The references to throats, tongues, lips, mouths, feet and eyes make the spread of wrongdoing concrete. Sin affects how people think, speak, act and treat one another. Paul is not allowing the reader to stand outside the charge by finding someone with a worse record.

He then says that the law speaks to those under it, silencing every mouth and holding the whole world accountable. Here the scriptural testimony includes the Psalms and Prophets he has just cited. Works of the law cannot establish a person’s righteousness before God; the law brings awareness of sin. The next passage announces what God has done in response.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this passage as establishing the shared need for God’s grace: neither Jew nor Gentile can claim a righteousness that makes Christ unnecessary. The scriptural charges expose sin rather than provide a ladder on which one people can climb above another.
passages.god_plan_html:
Israel’s own Scriptures supply the testimony that silences boasting. The law and prophets do not merely identify failures among outsiders; they also speak to the people who receive them. That prepares for Paul’s announcement that God’s righteousness is available through faith in Christ without distinction.

Ephesians 2:1–10 follows a related movement from sin and death to God’s mercy, life with Christ and salvation as a gift. It ends with people created in Christ for good works. Exposing sin serves the larger announcement of a life God gives and renews.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 3:21-26
passages.section_title: How can God put sinners right while remaining just?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 But now, apart from the law, the righteousness of God has been revealed, as attested by the Law and the Prophets. 22 And this righteousness from God comes through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe. There is no distinction, 23 for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, 24 and are justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. 25 God presented Him as an atoning sacrifice in His blood through faith, in order to demonstrate His righteousness, because in His forbearance He had passed over the sins committed beforehand. 26 He did this to demonstrate His righteousness at the present time, so as to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus.
paragraphs: 21 But now, apart from the law, the righteousness of God has been revealed, as attested by the Law and the Prophets. 22 And this righteousness from God comes through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe. There is no distinction, 23 for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, 24 and are justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.

25 God presented Him as an atoning sacrifice in His blood through faith, in order to demonstrate His righteousness, because in His forbearance He had passed over the sins committed beforehand. 26 He did this to demonstrate His righteousness at the present time, so as to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
But now marks the turn from the exposure of sin to God’s answer. His righteousness has been revealed apart from the law, yet the Law and the Prophets bear witness to it. Paul is not announcing a rescue unrelated to the Scriptures he has been using.

All have sinned and fall short of God’s glory. The answer comes through faith in Jesus Christ: people are justified freely by grace through the redemption in Him. Justified concerns being put right before God; redemption describes a costly release. The emphasis is on what God gives through Christ, rather than a record of achievement people bring.

God presents Christ as an atoning sacrifice in His blood, received through faith. Atonement means dealing with sin so that people can be reconciled to God. Paul connects this with God’s patience toward sins previously committed and with the demonstration of His righteousness now.

The Greek word behind atoning sacrifice is hilastērion (hee-lahs-TAY-ree-on), ἱλαστήριον. Thayer’s entry discusses both an atoning sacrifice and the mercy seat, the cover of the ark of the covenant associated with atonement. These meanings help explain the sacrificial background without requiring a reader to know Greek.

The final statement holds two truths together: God is just, and He puts right the person who has faith in Jesus. Forgiveness is presented through Christ’s death, rather than as indifference toward evil.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand these verses as a central account of salvation through Christ, given by grace and received through faith. Where traditions differ is in how they describe justification and the effect of Christ’s sacrifice.

The Reformed Westminster Confession 11.1–2 and 1689 Baptist Confession 11.1–2 describe God pardoning sins and counting believers righteous because of Christ’s obedience, received through faith alone. Their inward renewal accompanies this acceptance but is distinguished from its basis.

The Catholic Church teaches that justification includes forgiveness and inward renewal through Christ’s grace, conferred in baptism. The Catechism, paragraphs 1987–1993, makes God’s initiative the source of the person’s response. The Methodist Article IX describes being counted righteous through faith because of Christ, rather than one’s own works.

There are also different emphases in explaining the sacrifice. The Catholic USCCB note on verse 25 favors wording that emphasizes the removal of sin. Wesley on verses 25–26 emphasizes God’s judgment against sin being answered through Christ’s death. These are explanations from a commentary and a named teacher; they should not be mistaken for complete statements of every Catholic or Wesleyan’s understanding.
passages.god_plan_html:
The mercy-seat meaning invites comparison with Exodus 25:17–22, where the cover of the ark is the place above which God promises to meet with Moses. The same word is used for the mercy seat in Hebrews 9:5. This is a supported connection in the sacrificial language, rather than a claim that every interpreter translates Romans 3:25 identically.

Hebrews 9:7–15 makes the larger connection explicit. It moves from the high priest’s entry with sacrificial blood to Christ’s entry by His own blood, securing eternal redemption and cleansing the conscience. Christ’s death also redeems transgressions under the first covenant. That helps show how the mercy announced now belongs with God’s earlier dealings, rather than making the earlier story irrelevant.
passages.current_position_html: The Gospel According to Jesus draws on Romans 3:23 to explain that everyone needs salvation and cannot earn it through moral effort or religious activity. Our position here is that God gives salvation through Jesus’ death for sins and resurrection, received through faith in Him. That study supplies this conclusion; it does not settle every difference about justification or the language of atonement described above.

passages.title: Romans 3:23
passages.section_title: Who needs the salvation God gives?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 23 for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God,
paragraphs: 23 for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God,

passages.context_html:
Paul has placed Jews and Greeks alike under sin. He now says that there is no distinction in the righteousness offered through faith in Christ, because all have sinned and fall short of God’s glory.

The sentence continues into the gift of being justified by grace through Christ’s redemption. Read Romans 3:21–26 to keep the statement of need together with God’s answer. Paul does not leave his readers with the verdict of failure alone.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this verse as declaring humanity’s shared need for God’s saving grace. Neither ancestry, religious knowledge nor comparison with someone else supplies a ground for claiming that Christ’s salvation is unnecessary.
passages.current_position_html: The Gospel According to Jesus uses Romans 3:23 to explain that every person needs salvation. Our position is that salvation is received through faith in Jesus Christ rather than inherited from family, earned through moral effort or secured by religious activity. The need named here leads directly into the gift God provides through Christ.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html: The verse belongs within Paul’s announcement of one saving gift for Jew and Gentile. Romans 3:24–26 immediately connects the shared need with grace, redemption and faith in Jesus. Its place in the story is to explain why that gift is needed by the people who receive it.

passages.title: Romans 3:27-31
passages.section_title: Why does faith leave no room for boasting?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 27 Where, then, is boasting? It is excluded. On what principle? On that of works? No, but on that of faith. 28 For we maintain that a man is justified by faith apart from works of the law. 29 Is God the God of Jews only? Is He not the God of Gentiles too? Yes, of Gentiles too, 30 since there is only one God, who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through that same faith. 31 Do we, then, nullify the law by this faith? Certainly not! Instead, we uphold the law.
paragraphs: 27 Where, then, is boasting? It is excluded. On what principle? On that of works? No, but on that of faith. 28 For we maintain that a man is justified by faith apart from works of the law.

29 Is God the God of Jews only? Is He not the God of Gentiles too? Yes, of Gentiles too, 30 since there is only one God, who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through that same faith. 31 Do we, then, nullify the law by this faith? Certainly not! Instead, we uphold the law.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul draws out the consequence of the rescue he has described: boasting is excluded. A person is justified by faith apart from works of the law. There is no achievement that allows the rescued person to claim the place of the rescuer.

He connects this directly with the nations. God is the God of Gentiles as well as Jews. Since there is one God, circumcised and uncircumcised people are put right through the same faith. Paul does not offer one route for Israel and another for everyone else.

The last question anticipates a misunderstanding: does faith make the law void? Paul answers that faith upholds it. He has already said that the Law and the Prophets bear witness to God’s righteousness. The gospel does not require treating that testimony as false or worthless, and the next chapter will turn to Abraham as a scriptural example.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these verses as excluding pride in human achievement and affirming one God’s saving invitation to both Jew and Gentile. Paul’s final answer also prevents faith from being presented as permission to disregard everything God has taught. The differences over justification explained in the preceding passage do not remove these shared concerns.
passages.god_plan_html:
