Galatians 3:6–14 explicitly connects Abraham’s faith, the promise of blessing to the nations and Christ’s redemption. Paul describes the Gentiles’ justification by faith as part of the good news announced beforehand to Abraham.

That places the shared faith of Jew and Gentile within God’s earlier promise. The widening invitation is not an improvised second plan. It carries forward the purpose witnessed by the Scriptures while removing grounds for one group to boast over another.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 4:1-5
passages.section_title: What did Abraham receive by believing God?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 What then shall we say that Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh, has discovered? 2 If Abraham was indeed justified by works, he had something to boast about, but not before God. 3 For what does the Scripture say? “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness.” 4 Now the wages of the worker are not credited as a gift, but as an obligation. 5 However, to the one who does not work, but believes in Him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is credited as righteousness.
paragraphs: 1 What then shall we say that Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh, has discovered? 2 If Abraham was indeed justified by works, he had something to boast about, but not before God. 3 For what does the Scripture say? “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness.”

4 Now the wages of the worker are not credited as a gift, but as an obligation. 5 However, to the one who does not work, but believes in Him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is credited as righteousness.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul turns to Abraham to show that the message he has announced is witnessed by Scripture. If Abraham had been justified by works, he could boast in his achievement. Instead, Genesis says that he believed God and that this was credited to him as righteousness.

The setting is Genesis 15:1–6. Abram has no child to be his heir, and God promises an heir from his own body and descendants as numerous as the stars. Abram trusts the Lord who gives the promise.

The word behind credited is logizomai (loh-GID-zoh-my), λογίζομαι, meaning to reckon, count or take into account; see Thayer’s entry. Paul uses the same word when speaking of wages in verse 4. The difference between wages and a gift comes from the situation he describes, rather than from the word credited by itself.

A worker receives wages as something owed. Paul contrasts that with trusting the God who justifies the ungodly. The person comes with a need for God’s mercy, rather than a claim that God owes them a favorable verdict.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read Abraham’s example as showing that a right relationship with God begins in His grace and is received through faith, rather than earned as wages. Abraham’s trust rests on the One who promises, not on a record that makes mercy unnecessary.
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul reaches back to Genesis to show that faith is not a late replacement for an earlier way of earning God’s acceptance. The promise and Abram’s response are already part of the scriptural story the gospel fulfills.

Hebrews 11:8–12 also describes Abraham and Sarah living by trust in the God who promises. That trust leads to action and endurance. The contrast with earning wages does not make faith a life of doing nothing; it identifies the One on whom the life depends.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 4:6-8
passages.section_title: Why does David call the forgiven person blessed?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 And David speaks likewise of the blessedness of the man to whom God credits righteousness apart from works: 7 “Blessed are they whose lawless acts are forgiven, whose sins are covered. 8 Blessed is the man whose sin the Lord will never count against him.”
paragraphs: 6 And David speaks likewise of the blessedness of the man to whom God credits righteousness apart from works: 7 “Blessed are they whose lawless acts are forgiven, whose sins are covered. 8 Blessed is the man whose sin the Lord will never count against him.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul adds David’s voice to Abraham’s example. He introduces the words as describing the person to whom God credits righteousness apart from works, then quotes the opening of Psalm 32.

The blessing is forgiveness: lawless acts forgiven, sins covered and sin not counted against the person. The person is blessed because God deals mercifully with real wrongdoing, rather than because the wrong never happened.

Psalm 32:3–5 continues with the burden of concealed sin, confession and God’s forgiveness. Paul’s quotation belongs to a prayer about coming honestly before God, not making wrongdoing into a reason for pride.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand these words as celebrating forgiveness given by God to people who need it. David’s testimony supports Paul’s distinction between a gift of mercy and acceptance claimed as something owed for one’s achievements.
passages.god_plan_html:
Abraham’s story and David’s prayer speak from different points in Israel’s history, yet Paul brings them together as witnesses to God’s gift. The Scriptures that expose sin also teach people to seek forgiveness and trust His mercy.

This prepares the reader to understand the redemption just described in Romans 3:24–26. The announcement about Christ answers the need expressed in the psalm; it does not begin with the claim that people have no sins to forgive.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 4:9-12
passages.section_title: Why does the timing of Abraham’s circumcision matter?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 Is this blessing only on the circumcised, or also on the uncircumcised? We have been saying that Abraham’s faith was credited to him as righteousness. 10 In what context was it credited? Was it after his circumcision, or before? It was not after, but before. 11 And he received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised. So then, he is the father of all who believe but are not circumcised, in order that righteousness might be credited to them. 12 And he is also the father of the circumcised who not only are circumcised, but who also walk in the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had before he was circumcised.
paragraphs: 9 Is this blessing only on the circumcised, or also on the uncircumcised? We have been saying that Abraham’s faith was credited to him as righteousness. 10 In what context was it credited? Was it after his circumcision, or before? It was not after, but before.

11 And he received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised. So then, he is the father of all who believe but are not circumcised, in order that righteousness might be credited to them. 12 And he is also the father of the circumcised who not only are circumcised, but who also walk in the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had before he was circumcised.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul asks whether the blessing of forgiveness belongs only to the circumcised. He answers by asking when Abraham’s faith was credited as righteousness. The answer is before circumcision, not after it.

The order appears in Genesis itself: faith is credited in Genesis 15:6, while the command and sign of circumcision appear in Genesis 17:9–14. Paul calls the sign a seal of the righteousness Abraham already had by faith.

This makes Abraham the father of uncircumcised believers as well as of circumcised people who follow his faith. Physical descent and possession of the sign do not replace the trust Paul is describing. People from outside Israel’s physical family are included without first receiving that mark.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this sequence as showing that circumcision did not create Abraham’s right standing before God. The sign confirms a relationship already received through faith, and Paul uses that order to explain the inclusion of uncircumcised believers.
passages.god_plan_html:
The timing of events in Genesis serves the invitation to the nations that Paul has been explaining. Abraham’s story contains room for people who share his faith without sharing his physical mark.

Galatians 3:7–9 states the connection explicitly: people of faith share the blessing with Abraham, and the promise of blessing to all nations anticipates God’s justification of Gentiles by faith. The family gathered through that promise reaches beyond one ancestry.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 4:13-17
passages.section_title: Why does the promise rest on grace rather than law?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 For the promise to Abraham and his offspring that he would be heir of the world was not given through the law, but through the righteousness that comes by faith. 14 For if those who live by the law are heirs, faith is useless and the promise is worthless, 15 because the law brings wrath. And where there is no law, there is no transgression. 16 Therefore, the promise comes by faith, so that it may rest on grace and may be guaranteed to all Abraham’s offspring—not only to those who are of the law, but also to those who are of the faith of Abraham. He is the father of us all. 17 As it is written: “I have made you a father of many nations.” He is our father in the presence of God, in whom he believed, the God who gives life to the dead and calls into being what does not yet exist.
paragraphs: 13 For the promise to Abraham and his offspring that he would be heir of the world was not given through the law, but through the righteousness that comes by faith. 14 For if those who live by the law are heirs, faith is useless and the promise is worthless, 15 because the law brings wrath. And where there is no law, there is no transgression.

16 Therefore, the promise comes by faith, so that it may rest on grace and may be guaranteed to all Abraham’s offspring—not only to those who are of the law, but also to those who are of the faith of Abraham. He is the father of us all. 17 As it is written: “I have made you a father of many nations.” He is our father in the presence of God, in whom he believed, the God who gives life to the dead and calls into being what does not yet exist.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul describes the promise to Abraham and his offspring in terms of inheriting the world. It came through the righteousness of faith, rather than through the law. Making inheritance depend on the law would empty faith and the promise of their force.

The law identifies transgression and brings wrath against it. Paul’s statement that there is no transgression where there is no law concerns the breaking of a command; it does not reverse his earlier account of human accountability without possession of the Law of Moses.

The promise therefore comes by faith so that it rests on grace and is assured to Abraham’s family of faith. Paul includes those associated with the law and those who share Abraham’s faith beyond that setting. The father of many nations belongs within this wider invitation.

The God Abraham believes gives life to the dead and calls into being what does not yet exist. This leads into the account of the promised child and, by the chapter’s ending, faith in the God who raised Jesus.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand Paul as grounding confidence in God’s gracious promise, rather than treating inheritance as wages earned through keeping the law. The promise opens a shared future for people who trust Him across the distinction between Jew and Gentile.
passages.god_plan_html:
Galatians 3:15–18 makes a closely related point: the law that came later does not cancel the earlier promise. God’s faithfulness is not dependent on changing that promise into a different kind of arrangement.

The promise of many nations in Genesis 17:4–6 is part of the connection Paul draws. His point here concerns inheritance through faith and grace. It should not be made to settle every later question about the land, Israel and the church that these verses do not explain in detail.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 4:18-25
passages.section_title: How does Abraham’s hope point us toward the resurrection?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 Against all hope, Abraham in hope believed and so became the father of many nations, just as he had been told, “So shall your offspring be.” 19 Without weakening in his faith, he acknowledged the decrepitness of his body (since he was about a hundred years old) and the lifelessness of Sarah’s womb. 20 Yet he did not waver through disbelief in the promise of God, but was strengthened in his faith and gave glory to God, 21 being fully persuaded that God was able to do what He had promised. 22 This is why “it was credited to him as righteousness.” 23 Now the words “it was credited to him” were written not only for Abraham, 24 but also for us, to whom righteousness will be credited—for us who believe in Him who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead. 25 He was delivered over to death for our trespasses and was raised to life for our justification.
paragraphs: 18 Against all hope, Abraham in hope believed and so became the father of many nations, just as he had been told, “So shall your offspring be.” 19 Without weakening in his faith, he acknowledged the decrepitness of his body (since he was about a hundred years old) and the lifelessness of Sarah’s womb. 20 Yet he did not waver through disbelief in the promise of God, but was strengthened in his faith and gave glory to God, 21 being fully persuaded that God was able to do what He had promised. 22 This is why “it was credited to him as righteousness.”

23 Now the words “it was credited to him” were written not only for Abraham, 24 but also for us, to whom righteousness will be credited—for us who believe in Him who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead. 25 He was delivered over to death for our trespasses and was raised to life for our justification.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Abraham trusts God’s promise of descendants when ordinary expectations give him no reason to hope for a child. He recognizes the condition of his own aged body and Sarah’s womb. His faith does not require pretending those limits are absent.

Paul emphasizes Abraham’s confidence that God can do what He has promised. Genesis also records questions, laughter and missteps along the journey, including Abraham’s questions in Genesis 17:17–18. Paul’s emphasis on faith should be read with that fuller story, rather than turned into a claim that Abraham never faced difficulty or acted wrongly.

The words about righteousness being credited were written for others as well. Paul applies them to those who believe in the God who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead. Jesus was delivered over to death for our trespasses and raised for our justification, our being put right before God.

The connection is trust in the God who gives life. Paul does not give a general promise that every outcome a person strongly wants will happen. Abraham’s confidence answers a promise God actually made.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as faith resting on God’s ability to keep His word even where human resources fail. The USCCB note on verse 20 describes doubts resolved in commitment to the promise; Calvin on verse 20 likewise distinguishes Abraham’s astonished questions from rejecting what God says. These comments allow the strength of Paul’s emphasis to stand alongside the struggles Genesis records.
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul makes the connection to Christ explicit: the same God who fulfilled His promise in the face of Abraham and Sarah’s inability raised Jesus from the dead. The story of Abraham’s faith is written for those who will trust Him in that greater announcement.

Hebrews 11:17–19 adds another connection from Abraham’s life. When tested with Isaac, he reasons that God can raise the dead, and he receives Isaac back in a figurative sense. That is a scripturally stated comparison, not a claim that Isaac literally died. Across these accounts, hope rests in the God for whom death cannot defeat His promise.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 5:1-5
passages.section_title: How can peace with God belong alongside suffering?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Therefore, since we have been justified through faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, 2 through whom we have gained access by faith into this grace in which we stand. And we rejoice in the hope of the glory of God. 3 Not only that, but we also rejoice in our sufferings, because we know that suffering produces perseverance; 4 perseverance, character; and character, hope. 5 And hope does not disappoint us, because God has poured out His love into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, whom He has given us.
paragraphs: 1 Therefore, since we have been justified through faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, 2 through whom we have gained access by faith into this grace in which we stand. And we rejoice in the hope of the glory of God.

3 Not only that, but we also rejoice in our sufferings, because we know that suffering produces perseverance; 4 perseverance, character; and character, hope. 5 And hope does not disappoint us, because God has poured out His love into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, whom He has given us.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul now describes what follows from being justified through faith: peace with God through Jesus Christ, access to grace and hope of sharing God’s glory. These gifts rest on the relationship Christ has opened.

Peace with God does not mean that life has become free of trouble. Paul immediately speaks of suffering, endurance, character and hope. The peace concerns the relationship with God; it should not be reduced to a test of whether someone feels calm every moment.

Hope is grounded in God’s love poured into believers’ hearts through the Holy Spirit. Paul does not ask them to manufacture confidence from their own strength. He points to the God who has given Himself to them and continues His work amid hardship.

The BSB follows the reading we have peace in verse 1 and notes let us have as an alternative found in the manuscript tradition. The passage still places this peace through Jesus, not in human achievement.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these verses as encouragement that suffering does not by itself mean God has rejected a believer. Calvin on verse 3 explicitly distinguishes hope amid trouble from feeling no grief or bitterness. Endurance can grow within real distress; rejoicing does not require pretending pain is pleasant.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 2:13–18 connects Christ’s blood, peace, reconciliation and access to the Father through one Spirit. It also places Jewish and Gentile believers together within that access. Peace with God belongs to a larger work of bringing people near and together in Christ.

The hope ahead is described in Romans 8:18–25, where present suffering stands beside the coming glory, creation’s freedom and the redemption of believers’ bodies. Present trouble has not canceled that future.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 5:6-11
passages.section_title: How does Christ’s death show God’s love before people deserve it?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 For at just the right time, while we were still powerless, Christ died for the ungodly. 7 Very rarely will anyone die for a righteous man, though for a good man someone might possibly dare to die. 8 But God proves His love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us. 9 Therefore, since we have now been justified by His blood, how much more shall we be saved from wrath through Him! 10 For if, when we were enemies of God, we were reconciled to Him through the death of His Son, how much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved through His life! 11 Not only that, but we also rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation.
paragraphs: 6 For at just the right time, while we were still powerless, Christ died for the ungodly. 7 Very rarely will anyone die for a righteous man, though for a good man someone might possibly dare to die. 8 But God proves His love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.

9 Therefore, since we have now been justified by His blood, how much more shall we be saved from wrath through Him! 10 For if, when we were enemies of God, we were reconciled to Him through the death of His Son, how much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved through His life! 11 Not only that, but we also rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul grounds confidence in what God has already done. Christ died for the ungodly while they were still powerless. Human beings may sometimes give their lives for someone they regard as good, but God demonstrates His love through Christ’s death for sinners.

The reasoning then moves from what God did for enemies to what believers can expect as people reconciled to Him. If reconciliation came through His Son’s death, Paul says, how much more will they be saved through His life. Hope rests in the living Christ as well as His death.

Reconciliation means a broken relationship being restored. The Greek word katallagē (kah-tah-lah-GAY), καταλλαγή, carries that sense of reconciliation or restoration to favor; see Thayer’s entry. Paul presents it as something received through Jesus, rather than a relationship repaired by making oneself worthy first.

This leads to rejoicing in God Himself. The account is not of a reluctant God whom people finally persuade to love them. His love is already at work toward them while they are sinners.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand these verses as a strong statement of God’s initiative in salvation and a foundation for trust in His continuing care. Christ’s death precedes the sinner’s claim to worthiness, and His risen life grounds the hope that follows reconciliation.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 8:31–34 returns to this reasoning: God gave His Son, God justifies, and the Christ who died and rose intercedes for His people. The saving work is carried forward by the living Lord, rather than ending with His death.

This also reveals the character of the love believers are called to reflect. The Gospel According to Jesus connects Romans 5:8 with Jesus’ command to love enemies: the King gives Himself for people while they are still His enemies. The command grows from the character already displayed in His saving work.
passages.current_position_html: The Gospel According to Jesus uses Romans 5:8 to explain that God did not wait for people to become worthy before Christ died for them. Our position is that salvation begins in God’s love and mercy toward sinners, and that Jesus’ command to love enemies reflects the character He has already shown in giving Himself for them.

passages.title: Romans 5:8
passages.section_title: When did God show His love for sinners?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 But God proves His love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
paragraphs: 8 But God proves His love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.

passages.context_html:
Paul has described Christ dying for the ungodly while they were still powerless. This verse identifies that death as the demonstration of God’s love. People do not first make themselves worthy and then become the objects of His concern.

The following verses connect Christ’s death with reconciliation and His life with the hope of salvation. Read Romans 5:6–11 to follow the whole movement from enemies to reconciliation and rejoicing in God.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this verse as a direct statement of God’s initiating love, displayed in Christ’s self-giving for people who are still sinners. It grounds hope in what He has done, rather than a claim that the recipients had already become worthy of His gift.
passages.current_position_html: The Gospel According to Jesus uses Romans 5:8 to explain that God’s love toward sinners precedes their worthiness. Our position is that Christ died for sinners and that salvation is a gift of mercy, rather than a reward for making oneself acceptable first. His self-giving also reveals the love behind His command to love enemies.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html: The verse shows the character of the God who provides the rescue. Romans 5:9–11 carries that love into reconciliation and confidence through the living Christ. The gift addresses hostility by bringing people into a restored relationship, rather than waiting for them to repair it unaided.

passages.title: Romans 5:12-14
passages.section_title: Why does Paul turn from Jesus to Adam?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 Therefore, just as sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin, so also death was passed on to all men, because all sinned. 13 For sin was in the world before the law was given; but sin is not taken into account when there is no law. 14 Nevertheless, death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those who did not sin in the way that Adam transgressed. He is a pattern of the One to come.
paragraphs: 12 Therefore, just as sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin, so also death was passed on to all men, because all sinned. 13 For sin was in the world before the law was given; but sin is not taken into account when there is no law. 14 Nevertheless, death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those who did not sin in the way that Adam transgressed. He is a pattern of the One to come.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul begins a comparison that will explain the reach of Christ’s work. Through one man sin entered the world, and death through sin. Death then spread to all because all sinned. Adam’s act belongs to the story of the human condition, not only to a private failure without consequences for others.

Sin and death were present before the Law of Moses. Even people who did not transgress in the same way Adam did were under death’s reign. Paul is explaining why the arrival of the law did not create the need for rescue.

He explicitly calls Adam a pattern of the One to come, Christ. The next verses will develop both the comparison and the difference. The damage associated with one man prepares the reader to consider the far greater gift through another.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand Paul as connecting humanity’s plight with Adam’s sin and its rescue with Christ. Where traditions differ is how they describe what people inherit from Adam.

The Reformed Westminster Confession 6.2–4 and 1689 Baptist Confession 6.2–3 teach that Adam’s guilt is counted to his descendants and a corrupted nature is passed on. This is often described as Adam representing humanity: his act has consequences for those he represents.

The Catholic Church describes original sin as an inherited fallen state, deprived of original holiness, rather than an act personally committed by each descendant. The Catechism, paragraphs 404–405, says it does not have the character of a personal fault in Adam’s descendants, while affirming the need for Christ’s healing grace.

The Methodist Article VII describes a corrupted human nature inclined toward evil. Wesley’s note on verse 12 also understands humanity as having sinned in Adam. His account should be distinguished from treating original sin as only the bad example of someone long ago.

The Orthodox Church in America’s explanation emphasizes inherited consequences, especially death, while distinguishing them from Adam and Eve’s own guilt. This presents an Orthodox account in its own terms; the traditions should not be reduced to a claim that some recognize human sin and others do not.
passages.god_plan_html:
The connection between Adam and Christ is Paul’s own, explicitly stated in verse 14. 1 Corinthians 15:20–28 develops it through the resurrection: death comes through a man, resurrection comes through a man, and death itself is named as an enemy to be destroyed.

In 1 Corinthians 15:45–49 Paul also contrasts the first Adam with the last Adam, Christ. The promise reaches beyond changing a verdict to the life and likeness of the risen Lord. This is a connection the New Testament makes, rather than a hidden parallel supplied by a later teacher.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 5:15-21
passages.section_title: How does the gift through Christ exceed the damage through Adam?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 But the gift is not like the trespass. For if the many died by the trespass of the one man, how much more did God’s grace and the gift that came by the grace of the one man, Jesus Christ, abound to the many! 16 Again, the gift is not like the result of the one man’s sin: The judgment that followed one sin brought condemnation, but the gift that followed many trespasses brought justification. 17 For if, by the trespass of the one man, death reigned through that one man, how much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness reign in life through the one man, Jesus Christ! 18 So then, just as one trespass brought condemnation for all men, so also one act of righteousness brought justification and life for all men. 19 For just as through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous. 20 The law came in so that the trespass would increase; but where sin increased, grace increased all the more, 21 so that, just as sin reigned in death, so also grace might reign through righteousness to bring eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.
paragraphs: 15 But the gift is not like the trespass. For if the many died by the trespass of the one man, how much more did God’s grace and the gift that came by the grace of the one man, Jesus Christ, abound to the many! 16 Again, the gift is not like the result of the one man’s sin: The judgment that followed one sin brought condemnation, but the gift that followed many trespasses brought justification. 17 For if, by the trespass of the one man, death reigned through that one man, how much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness reign in life through the one man, Jesus Christ!

18 So then, just as one trespass brought condemnation for all men, so also one act of righteousness brought justification and life for all men. 19 For just as through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous. 20 The law came in so that the trespass would increase; but where sin increased, grace increased all the more, 21 so that, just as sin reigned in death, so also grace might reign through righteousness to bring eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul now emphasizes that the gift is not simply a matching opposite of the trespass. One sin brought judgment, but the gift answers many trespasses. Where death reigned through one man, those receiving the abundance of grace and the gift of righteousness reign in life through Jesus Christ.

He sets condemnation and justification, disobedience and obedience, alongside one another. The language of all in verse 18 and many in verse 19 stresses the great reach of both Adam’s act and Christ’s work. Christians differ over how to understand the final scope of the life announced here.

The law’s arrival exposes and increases transgression, but sin does not have the final word. Grace abounds beyond it. Paul ends with grace reigning through righteousness to eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.

This does not turn sin into a goal. The next chapter will directly reject continuing in sin so that grace may increase. The greatness of the gift is a reason to receive and live from it, rather than manufacture more wrongdoing.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand this as a declaration that Christ’s saving work exceeds the ruin sin brings. Where readers differ is how the all of verse 18 relates to receiving the gift in verse 17.

The Reformed commentator Calvin on verse 18 understands the gift as offered to all, while distinguishing that offer from all people actually receiving Christ. Wesley on verse 19 likewise identifies those made righteous as all who believe. These readings retain the wide offer while connecting its saving benefit with faith.

The Christian Universalist Association’s statement of belief cites Romans 5:18 in support of the eventual restoration of every person through Christ. Its reading takes the reach of Christ’s work as finally extending to everyone affected by Adam. This is the association’s stated view, rather than a position shared by all Christian churches or a conclusion supplied here as our own.
passages.god_plan_html:
The movement from sin reigning in death to grace bringing eternal life belongs to the Bible’s wider story of restoration. Genesis 3 describes the curse, human death and exclusion from the tree of life. Revelation 22:1–5 pictures the tree of life, the removal of the curse and God’s servants living in His presence.

This is a thematic connection between the beginning and the promised restoration, not a claim that Romans 5 directly quotes Revelation. Christ’s obedience answers the story’s ruin with a gift greater than what sin has brought. The comparison concerns God’s victory over sin and death; it should not erase the differences of interpretation about the passage’s scope.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 6:1-4
passages.section_title: Why does grace call us into a new life rather than more sin?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 What then shall we say? Shall we continue in sin so that grace may increase? 2 Certainly not! How can we who died to sin live in it any longer? 3 Or aren’t you aware that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into His death? 4 We were therefore buried with Him through baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too may walk in newness of life.
paragraphs: 1 What then shall we say? Shall we continue in sin so that grace may increase? 2 Certainly not! How can we who died to sin live in it any longer? 3 Or aren’t you aware that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into His death? 4 We were therefore buried with Him through baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too may walk in newness of life.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul has said that grace abounds where sin increases. He now rejects the conclusion that people should continue in sin to make grace greater. His answer begins with their changed relationship to sin: they have died to it.

He brings baptism into the explanation. Those baptized into Christ Jesus have been baptized into His death and buried with Him, so that they may walk in newness of life as Christ was raised. Death and resurrection are connected with the life believers are now called to live.

The verb baptize comes from baptizō (bap-TID-zoh), βαπτίζω. Thayer’s entry includes dipping, immersion and washing, and explains the use here in terms of fellowship with Christ and His death. The word and the passage’s burial imagery matter, while the differences over baptism’s mode and effect require more than a bare word definition.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly see union with Christ’s death and resurrection as the foundation of the new life Paul describes. Where traditions differ is how they explain baptism’s part in that union.

The Catholic Church teaches that baptism brings forgiveness of sins and new birth in the Holy Spirit; see the Catechism, paragraphs 1262–1266. This is a work of God’s grace through the sacrament, rather than a claim that water has independent power.

The Reformed Westminster Confession 28.1–6 calls baptism a sign and seal of grace, incorporation into Christ and new life. It allows pouring or sprinkling and baptism of believers’ children, while denying that every baptized person is necessarily regenerated or that grace is tied to the exact moment of administration.

The 1689 Baptist Confession 29.1–4 describes a sign of fellowship with Christ in His death and resurrection, remission of sins and walking in new life. It limits baptism to those professing repentance and faith, and requires immersion. This represents churches that receive that confession, rather than every Baptist’s personal explanation.

The Methodist Articles XVI–XVII describe sacraments as signs through which God works to strengthen faith, and baptism as a sign of new birth as well as profession. They retain infant baptism. Wesley on verse 3 speaks of being joined to Christ in baptism through faith. These readings share the call to new life while differing over recipients, mode and the relation between the sign and God’s work.
passages.god_plan_html:
Colossians 2:11–13 likewise connects being buried with Christ in baptism and raised through faith in God’s power. The One who raised Jesus brings people from death to life. The connection comes from the New Testament itself.

Galatians 3:26–29 joins faith, being clothed with Christ in baptism and belonging to one family in Him. The new life is more than a private improvement project: it belongs to God’s work of gathering people into Christ across former divisions.
passages.current_position_html: The Baptism study understands this passage as death and resurrection with Christ enacted in the believer’s baptism. Our position favors immersion because it expresses burial and rising, and treats baptism as a real, faith-filled act of obedience rather than an empty performance. The study also distinguishes this act from earning salvation: forgiveness and the gift of the Spirit come through faith, and the water has no power apart from Christ.

passages.title: Romans 6:3-4
passages.section_title: How does baptism connect us with Christ’s death and resurrection?
passages.note: The theological heart of baptism: buried and raised with Christ.

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 3 Or aren’t you aware that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into His death? 4 We were therefore buried with Him through baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too may walk in newness of life.
paragraphs: 3 Or aren’t you aware that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into His death? 4 We were therefore buried with Him through baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too may walk in newness of life.

passages.context_html:
Paul is answering the suggestion that grace should lead to more sin. He appeals to baptism into Christ’s death and burial with Him, directing the reader toward walking in newness of life.

The full discussion in Romans 6:1–4 explains the question Paul is answering and the different traditions’ accounts of baptism. These verses connect baptism with belonging to Christ and the life that follows His resurrection.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians share the connection between baptism, Christ’s death and resurrection, and the call to a changed life. They differ over how baptism brings or signifies that participation. The Catholic Catechism 1262–1266 teaches forgiveness and new birth through baptism; the Reformed Westminster Confession 28.1–6 describes a sign and seal whose effect is not tied to the moment of administration.

The 1689 Baptist Confession 29 describes the sign of fellowship with Christ for professing believers and requires immersion. The Methodist Articles XVI–XVII describe God working through sacramental signs and retain infant baptism. These distinctions concern the act’s recipients, mode and relation to God’s grace, rather than disagreement that the passage calls for new life.
passages.current_position_html: The Baptism study understands this passage as death and resurrection with Christ enacted in the believer’s baptism. Our position favors immersion because it expresses burial and rising, and treats baptism as a real, faith-filled act of obedience rather than an empty performance. The study also distinguishes this act from earning salvation: forgiveness and the gift of the Spirit come through faith, and the water has no power apart from Christ.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html: Colossians 2:12–13 also connects burial with Christ in baptism and being raised through faith in the God who raised Him. Paul places the new life of believers within the same saving work that raises Jesus, rather than presenting baptism as an isolated religious performance.

passages.title: Romans 6:5-11
passages.section_title: What does it mean to count ourselves alive to God?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 For if we have been united with Him like this in His death, we will certainly also be united with Him in His resurrection. 6 We know that our old self was crucified with Him so that the body of sin might be rendered powerless, that we should no longer be slaves to sin. 7 For anyone who has died has been freed from sin. 8 Now if we died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with Him. 9 For we know that since Christ was raised from the dead, He cannot die again; death no longer has dominion over Him. 10 The death He died, He died to sin once for all; but the life He lives, He lives to God. 11 So you too must count yourselves dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus.
paragraphs: 5 For if we have been united with Him like this in His death, we will certainly also be united with Him in His resurrection. 6 We know that our old self was crucified with Him so that the body of sin might be rendered powerless, that we should no longer be slaves to sin. 7 For anyone who has died has been freed from sin.

8 Now if we died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with Him. 9 For we know that since Christ was raised from the dead, He cannot die again; death no longer has dominion over Him. 10 The death He died, He died to sin once for all; but the life He lives, He lives to God. 11 So you too must count yourselves dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul continues the connection between Christ’s death and the believer’s life. Union with His death points toward union with His resurrection. The old self is crucified with Him so that sin’s mastery is broken and the person no longer serves it as a slave.

Christ’s resurrection is decisive: He will not die again, and death no longer rules over Him. His death was once for all, and He lives to God. Paul calls believers to reckon with what their belonging to Him means.

To count oneself dead to sin and alive to God is to live from that changed allegiance. It does not mean pretending that temptation is absent. The commands that follow call for concrete choices about how people use their bodies and conduct their lives.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this passage as connecting freedom from sin’s rule with participation in Christ’s death and life. Calvin on verse 6 distinguishes that freedom from an immediate end to every sinful act; Wesley on verse 6 likewise describes the old nature being put to death through union with Christ. Both connect what Christ has done with an ongoing changed life.
passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 2:14–18 connects Jesus’ sharing our humanity, His death, freedom from slavery to the fear of death and His help for those being tempted. Rescue and continuing help belong to the same Lord.

The future also matters. Romans 8:23–25 describes believers waiting for the redemption of their bodies. New life now and the hope of resurrection belong together; Paul does not limit God’s saving work to an inward feeling or abandon the body’s future.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 6:12-14
passages.section_title: How do we offer our bodies to God instead of sin?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 Therefore do not let sin reign in your mortal body so that you obey its desires. 13 Do not present the parts of your body to sin as instruments of wickedness, but present yourselves to God as those who have been brought from death to life; and present the parts of your body to Him as instruments of righteousness. 14 For sin shall not be your master, because you are not under law, but under grace.
paragraphs: 12 Therefore do not let sin reign in your mortal body so that you obey its desires. 13 Do not present the parts of your body to sin as instruments of wickedness, but present yourselves to God as those who have been brought from death to life; and present the parts of your body to Him as instruments of righteousness. 14 For sin shall not be your master, because you are not under law, but under grace.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The therefore applies the preceding account of death and life with Christ. Believers must not let sin reign in their mortal bodies or offer their bodily powers to wrongdoing. Instead, they are to offer themselves to God as people brought from death to life.

The body is part of that offering. Paul speaks of its parts becoming instruments of righteousness. Hands, speech, movement and the ways people act can serve the new life God gives.

The promise that sin will not be their master is connected with being under grace rather than law. Paul immediately follows it with another rejection of sin in verse 15. Grace is the setting for freedom and obedience, not a reason to return to sin’s rule.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a call to active obedience grounded in grace. The person freed by Christ offers the whole life to God, including bodily action. Freedom from sin’s mastery does not make the choices Paul commands unnecessary.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 12:1–2 returns to this bodily offering: because of God’s mercy, believers offer their bodies as living sacrifices and are transformed through the renewal of their minds. The response involves the person’s practical life, not only a religious label.

The same letter that announces grace therefore develops worship as an embodied response to mercy. God’s rescue makes room for people to live for Him in the ordinary actions of their days.
passages.current_position_html: What Is the True Church? draws on Romans 6:14 to explain holiness as the fruit of grace. Our position is that grace both pardons and transforms, empowering believers to turn from sin and live in obedience to Christ. Obedience grows from His work in them rather than serving as a way to earn salvation.

passages.title: Romans 6:14
passages.section_title: Why does being under grace change sin’s mastery?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 For sin shall not be your master, because you are not under law, but under grace.
paragraphs: 14 For sin shall not be your master, because you are not under law, but under grace.

passages.context_html:
Paul has just called believers to offer themselves and their bodies to God as instruments of righteousness. This verse grounds that call in the promise that sin will not be their master, because they are under grace.

The next verse explicitly rejects using grace as permission to sin. Read Romans 6:12–14 with Romans 6:15–23 to follow freedom, obedience and the gift of life together.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this verse as encouragement that God’s grace frees people for a new allegiance and life. It should be read with Paul’s commands to offer oneself to God and his rejection of returning to sin, rather than isolated as permission for disobedience.
passages.current_position_html: What Is the True Church? draws on Romans 6:14 to explain holiness as the fruit of grace. Our position is that grace both pardons and transforms, empowering believers to turn from sin and live in obedience to Christ. Obedience grows from His work in them rather than serving as a way to earn salvation.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html: Romans 12:1–2 develops the response to God’s mercy as the offering of one’s body and renewal of one’s mind. Grace leads into a life made available to God’s purposes, which is already the concern of the verses around this promise.

passages.title: Romans 6:15-23
passages.section_title: What kind of freedom leads to holiness and life?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 What then? Shall we sin because we are not under law, but under grace? Certainly not! 16 Do you not know that when you offer yourselves as obedient slaves, you are slaves to the one you obey, whether you are slaves to sin leading to death, or to obedience leading to righteousness? 17 But thanks be to God that, though you once were slaves to sin, you wholeheartedly obeyed the form of teaching to which you were committed. 18 You have been set free from sin and have become slaves to righteousness. 19 I am speaking in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. Just as you used to offer the parts of your body in slavery to impurity and to escalating wickedness, so now offer them in slavery to righteousness leading to holiness. 20 For when you were slaves to sin, you were free of obligation to righteousness. 21 What fruit did you reap at that time from the things of which you are now ashamed? The outcome of those things is death. 22 But now that you have been set free from sin and have become slaves to God, the fruit you reap leads to holiness, and the outcome is eternal life. 23 For the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.
paragraphs: 15 What then? Shall we sin because we are not under law, but under grace? Certainly not! 16 Do you not know that when you offer yourselves as obedient slaves, you are slaves to the one you obey, whether you are slaves to sin leading to death, or to obedience leading to righteousness? 17 But thanks be to God that, though you once were slaves to sin, you wholeheartedly obeyed the form of teaching to which you were committed. 18 You have been set free from sin and have become slaves to righteousness.

19 I am speaking in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. Just as you used to offer the parts of your body in slavery to impurity and to escalating wickedness, so now offer them in slavery to righteousness leading to holiness. 20 For when you were slaves to sin, you were free of obligation to righteousness. 21 What fruit did you reap at that time from the things of which you are now ashamed? The outcome of those things is death. 22 But now that you have been set free from sin and have become slaves to God, the fruit you reap leads to holiness, and the outcome is eternal life. 23 For the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul again rejects the idea that being under grace permits sin. He uses the relationship between a slave and master to explain allegiance: what people obey shapes the life they serve. Sin leads toward death; obedience leads toward righteousness.

He thanks God that the believers have obeyed from the heart the teaching entrusted to them. Their change is described as release from sin and service to righteousness. Paul acknowledges that he is using human terms to make the point understandable.

The fruit of the former life was shame and death. The fruit of belonging to God is holiness, with eternal life as the outcome. Holiness means a life increasingly given to God and shaped by what is right.

The final contrast keeps the gift clear. Death is the wage sin pays; eternal life is God’s gift in Christ Jesus. Paul’s call to serve God does not turn that gift into a wage people earn. The gift changes the life they are called to live.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the passage as freedom from one master for a new allegiance to God, rather than freedom to serve every desire. The contrast between wages and gift keeps grace central, while the account of obedience and holiness keeps the changed life in view.
passages.god_plan_html:
John 8:31–36 likewise speaks of slavery to sin and the Son who sets people free. Freedom is connected with continuing in Jesus’ word, rather than merely claiming a privileged ancestry.

Ephesians 2:8–10 puts the gift of salvation beside being created in Christ for good works. That connection helps hold Paul’s two emphases together: God gives life freely, and the people He makes alive are called into a life that serves His purposes.
passages.current_position_html: The Gospel According to Jesus uses Romans 6:23 to distinguish the wages sin earns from the gift God gives. Our position is that eternal life comes through Jesus Christ as a gift received in faith, rather than a wage for religious effort or moral achievement. The life He gives also calls the believer into repentance and following Him.

passages.title: Romans 6:23
passages.section_title: Why is eternal life called a gift rather than wages?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 23 For the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.
paragraphs: 23 For the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.

passages.context_html:
This verse closes Paul’s contrast between service to sin and belonging to God. The former ends in death; the latter bears the fruit of holiness. The final words identify eternal life as God’s gift in Christ Jesus our Lord.

The contrast between wages and gift matters. Sin pays what it produces, while life comes from God’s generosity in Christ. Read Romans 6:15–23 to keep the gift together with the new life Paul describes.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this verse as contrasting sin’s deadly outcome with the life God gives through Christ. The gift is received from Him; the surrounding call to holiness describes the life of those who belong to Him, rather than a price that purchases it.
passages.current_position_html: The Gospel According to Jesus uses Romans 6:23 to distinguish the wages sin earns from the gift God gives. Our position is that eternal life comes through Jesus Christ as a gift received in faith, rather than a wage for religious effort or moral achievement. The life He gives also calls the believer into repentance and following Him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html: Ephesians 2:8–10 likewise connects salvation as a gift with the good works for which believers are created in Christ. God’s giving and the changed life that follows are held together without turning eternal life into earned wages.

passages.title: Romans 7:1-6
passages.section_title: How does belonging to the risen Christ change the way we serve God?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Do you not know, brothers (for I am speaking to those who know the law), that the law has authority over a man only as long as he lives? 2 For instance, a married woman is bound by law to her husband as long as he lives. But if her husband dies, she is released from the law of marriage. 3 So then, if she is joined to another man while her husband is still alive, she is called an adulteress; but if her husband dies, she is free from that law and is not an adulteress if she marries another man. 4 Therefore, my brothers, you also died to the law through the body of Christ, that you might belong to another, to Him who was raised from the dead, in order that we might bear fruit to God. 5 For when we lived according to the flesh, the sinful passions aroused by the law were at work in our bodies, bearing fruit for death. 6 But now, having died to what bound us, we have been released from the law, so that we serve in the new way of the Spirit, and not in the old way of the written code.
paragraphs: 1 Do you not know, brothers (for I am speaking to those who know the law), that the law has authority over a man only as long as he lives? 2 For instance, a married woman is bound by law to her husband as long as he lives. But if her husband dies, she is released from the law of marriage. 3 So then, if she is joined to another man while her husband is still alive, she is called an adulteress; but if her husband dies, she is free from that law and is not an adulteress if she marries another man.

4 Therefore, my brothers, you also died to the law through the body of Christ, that you might belong to another, to Him who was raised from the dead, in order that we might bear fruit to God. 5 For when we lived according to the flesh, the sinful passions aroused by the law were at work in our bodies, bearing fruit for death. 6 But now, having died to what bound us, we have been released from the law, so that we serve in the new way of the Spirit, and not in the old way of the written code.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul continues the discussion of being under grace rather than law. Speaking to people who know the law, he uses marriage to illustrate how death ends a binding relationship. A widow is released from the bond that held while her husband lived.

He then applies the image through Christ’s death: the believers have died to the law through His body so that they may belong to the risen Christ and bear fruit for God. The point of the release is a new belonging and fruitful service.

The word translated released in verse 6 is katargeō (kah-tar-GEH-oh), καταργέω. In this setting Thayer’s entry gives the sense of being discharged or loosed from a relationship. Paul uses the same word in the marriage illustration in verse 2. The imagery explains release from a binding claim, rather than freedom without any new allegiance.

Paul contrasts the former life, where sinful passions bore fruit for death, with service in the new way of the Spirit. He will next defend the law as holy and good. The problem he addresses is not solved simply by calling God’s instruction evil.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the passage as describing a changed relationship through Christ that leads to service in the Spirit. The marriage image serves that explanation: release leads to belonging to the risen Lord and bearing fruit, rather than permission to disregard God.
passages.god_plan_html:
2 Corinthians 3:4–18 also contrasts the written code with the life-giving work of the Spirit in the new covenant. Paul describes freedom and transformation into the Lord’s image as gifts from Him.

The connection shows what the new service is for. God’s saving work does more than remove a former bond; it brings people into a life where the Spirit forms them for His purposes. The fruitfulness of belonging to Christ is part of that wider renewal.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 7:7-13
passages.section_title: If the law is good, why does it expose so much sin?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 What then shall we say? Is the law sin? Certainly not! Indeed, I would not have been mindful of sin if not for the law. For I would not have been aware of coveting if the law had not said, “Do not covet.” 8 But sin, seizing its opportunity through the commandment, produced in me every kind of covetous desire. For apart from the law, sin is dead. 9 Once I was alive apart from the law; but when the commandment came, sin sprang to life and I died. 10 So I discovered that the very commandment that was meant to bring life actually brought death. 11 For sin, seizing its opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through the commandment put me to death. 12 So then, the law is holy, and the commandment is holy, righteous, and good. 13 Did that which is good, then, become death to me? Certainly not! But in order that sin might be exposed as sin, it produced death in me through what was good, so that through the commandment sin might become utterly sinful.
paragraphs: 7 What then shall we say? Is the law sin? Certainly not! Indeed, I would not have been mindful of sin if not for the law. For I would not have been aware of coveting if the law had not said, “Do not covet.” 8 But sin, seizing its opportunity through the commandment, produced in me every kind of covetous desire. For apart from the law, sin is dead. 9 Once I was alive apart from the law; but when the commandment came, sin sprang to life and I died. 10 So I discovered that the very commandment that was meant to bring life actually brought death. 11 For sin, seizing its opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through the commandment put me to death.

12 So then, the law is holy, and the commandment is holy, righteous, and good. 13 Did that which is good, then, become death to me? Certainly not! But in order that sin might be exposed as sin, it produced death in me through what was good, so that through the commandment sin might become utterly sinful.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul anticipates an objection to what he has said about release from the law: is the law itself sin? He firmly rejects that conclusion. The commandment makes wrongdoing known, as the prohibition against coveting makes sinful desire visible.

The example comes from Exodus 20:17. It reaches beyond a public act into what a person wants. Sin seizes the commandment as an opportunity and produces the very desire it forbids.

Paul describes this in the first person: the commandment comes, sin springs to life, and what should point toward life exposes death. Christians discuss the identity and experience of this speaker in different ways, especially in the next passage. The conclusion here is clear: the law is holy, righteous and good.

It is sin that deceives and brings death through what is good. The commandment exposes how serious sin is, including its ability to turn good instruction into an occasion for disobedience.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these verses as a defense of God’s law and an exposure of sin’s power. The law makes wrongdoing known but does not, by that knowledge alone, supply the power to overcome it. Blaming the good commandment would miss Paul’s distinction between the instruction and the sin that exploits it.
passages.god_plan_html:
Galatians 3:19–24 asks a related question about the law’s purpose. It explains that the law does not oppose God’s promise, yet cannot itself impart life. Its role leads toward Christ and the promise received through faith.

This places the exposure of sin within God’s larger saving purpose. The instruction that makes the need known is not the enemy of the rescue. Paul’s story moves toward the One who can give the life the law itself cannot supply.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 7:14-25
passages.section_title: Who is speaking about wanting the good but doing the wrong?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 We know that the law is spiritual; but I am unspiritual, sold as a slave to sin. 15 I do not understand what I do. For what I want to do, I do not do. But what I hate, I do. 16 And if I do what I do not want to do, I admit that the law is good. 17 In that case, it is no longer I who do it, but it is sin living in me that does it. 18 I know that nothing good lives in me, that is, in my flesh; for I have the desire to do what is good, but I cannot carry it out. 19 For I do not do the good I want to do. Instead, I keep on doing the evil I do not want to do. 20 And if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but it is sin living in me that does it. 21 So this is the principle I have discovered: When I want to do good, evil is right there with me. 22 For in my inner being I delight in God’s law. 23 But I see another law at work in my body, warring against the law of my mind and holding me captive to the law of sin that dwells within me. 24 What a wretched man I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death? 25 Thanks be to God, through Jesus Christ our Lord! So then, with my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin.
