But what I hate, I do. 16 And if I do what I do not want to do, I admit that the law is good. 17 In that case, it is no longer I who do it, but it is sin living in me that does it. 18 I know that nothing good lives in me, that is, in my flesh; for I have the desire to do what is good, but I cannot carry it out. 19 For I do not do the good I want to do. Instead, I keep on doing the evil I do not want to do. 20 And if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but it is sin living in me that does it.

21 So this is the principle I have discovered: When I want to do good, evil is right there with me. 22 For in my inner being I delight in God’s law. 23 But I see another law at work in my body, warring against the law of my mind and holding me captive to the law of sin that dwells within me. 24 What a wretched man I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death? 25 Thanks be to God, through Jesus Christ our Lord! So then, with my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul now gives a vivid first-person account of conflict. The speaker recognizes the goodness of God’s law and wants to do good, yet repeatedly does what he hates. Desire for the right and the ability to carry it out do not match.

The language distinguishes that desire from sin living within the person. It describes sin’s grip and the distress of being drawn against what one approves. It does not turn the wrongdoing into something harmless; the cry for rescue shows how serious the condition is.

The contrast between mind, flesh and the law at work in the body makes the conflict concrete. Paul has just called for bodily life to be offered to God in chapter 6. These words should be read within that account of freedom and obedience, rather than taken as a simple declaration that the physical body is evil.

The passage reaches a cry for deliverance from the body of death, then thanksgiving to God through Jesus Christ. The last sentence still acknowledges the conflict. The next chapter continues into life and freedom through the Spirit, so the cry is not the end of the story.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians differ over whose experience the first-person voice represents. The main readings agree that knowledge of the good is insufficient on its own and that rescue comes through Christ, but they place the conflict at different points in a person’s life.

The Reformed commentator Calvin on verses 14–17 reads the speaker as someone already renewed by God who still struggles with remaining sin. The desire to obey reflects the Spirit’s work, while the conflict shows the continuing need for grace. Calvin also rejects using sin living within as an excuse that makes the person blameless.

The Wesleyan founder John Wesley on verses 7, 14 and 25 understands Paul as assuming the voice of someone under the law, sincerely striving but not yet experiencing the freedom described in chapter 8. He therefore does not treat the bondage as the defining condition of a person living in Christ’s liberating grace.

The Catholic USCCB notes on verses 7–25 describe a voice used for the sake of the explanation. They apply the failure both to people without justifying grace and to Christians who return to reliance on law as the basis of their relationship with God. These are identified commentary readings, rather than a claim that every member of a tradition gives the same account of the speaker.
passages.god_plan_html:
The thanksgiving through Jesus leads into Romans 8:1–4. There Paul announces no condemnation in Christ and describes God doing through His Son what the law, weakened by the flesh, could not do. The Spirit’s life supplies the direction in which the argument moves.

Whatever reading is taken of the speaker’s stage of life, the passage directs hope beyond self-rescue. God’s purpose is not merely to make people aware of a conflict but to bring them into life through Christ and the Spirit. The different readings above should not obscure that movement in the letter.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 8:1-4
passages.section_title: What has God done that the law could not do?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Therefore, there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. 2 For in Christ Jesus the law of the Spirit of life set you free from the law of sin and death. 3 For what the law was powerless to do in that it was weakened by the flesh, God did by sending His own Son in the likeness of sinful man, as an offering for sin. He thus condemned sin in the flesh, 4 so that the righteous standard of the law might be fulfilled in us, who do not walk according to the flesh but according to the Spirit.
paragraphs: 1 Therefore, there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. 2 For in Christ Jesus the law of the Spirit of life set you free from the law of sin and death. 3 For what the law was powerless to do in that it was weakened by the flesh, God did by sending His own Son in the likeness of sinful man, as an offering for sin. He thus condemned sin in the flesh, 4 so that the righteous standard of the law might be fulfilled in us, who do not walk according to the flesh but according to the Spirit.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul moves from the cry for rescue in chapter 7 to the announcement that there is now no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus. The answer is found in belonging to Him, not in finally producing a flawless record through one’s own strength.

The Spirit’s life in Christ brings freedom from the rule of sin and death. The law could identify what was right but could not overcome the weakness of sinful human nature. God acts by sending His own Son as an offering for sin and condemning sin in His flesh.

The purpose includes a changed life: the righteous standard of the law is fulfilled in people who walk according to the Spirit. Paul places release from condemnation beside the Spirit’s work in the way people live. The gift does not make God’s concern for righteousness disappear.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand these verses as a strong assurance centered on Christ and the Spirit, joined to a call to new life. The law’s inability to rescue does not mean it is evil; God supplies through His Son and Spirit what sinful people cannot achieve by knowing the command alone.
passages.god_plan_html: Ezekiel 36:25–27 promises cleansing, a new heart and God’s Spirit within His people, causing them to walk in His ways. That promise provides a wider scriptural setting for the life Paul describes: God brings the inward renewal that makes obedience possible. This is a connection in the theme of God-given renewal, rather than a claim that Paul directly quotes Ezekiel here.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 8:5-11
passages.section_title: How does the Spirit bring life to people who still face death?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 Those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh; but those who live according to the Spirit set their minds on the things of the Spirit. 6 The mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace, 7 because the mind of the flesh is hostile to God: It does not submit to God’s law, nor can it do so. 8 Those controlled by the flesh cannot please God. 9 You, however, are controlled not by the flesh, but by the Spirit, if the Spirit of God lives in you. And if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to Christ. 10 But if Christ is in you, your body is dead because of sin, yet your spirit is alive because of righteousness. 11 And if the Spirit of Him who raised Jesus from the dead is living in you, He who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through His Spirit, who lives in you.
paragraphs: 5 Those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh; but those who live according to the Spirit set their minds on the things of the Spirit. 6 The mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace, 7 because the mind of the flesh is hostile to God: It does not submit to God’s law, nor can it do so. 8 Those controlled by the flesh cannot please God.

9 You, however, are controlled not by the flesh, but by the Spirit, if the Spirit of God lives in you. And if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to Christ. 10 But if Christ is in you, your body is dead because of sin, yet your spirit is alive because of righteousness. 11 And if the Spirit of Him who raised Jesus from the dead is living in you, He who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through His Spirit, who lives in you.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul contrasts two ways of life. A mind governed by the flesh is hostile to God and leads toward death; a mind governed by the Spirit is life and peace. The contrast concerns what rules and directs the person.

The Spirit’s presence marks belonging to Christ. Paul speaks of the Spirit of God, the Spirit of Christ and Christ dwelling within believers. Life with God depends on His presence and work, rather than an outward claim of religious identity.

Believers still face bodily death because of sin. Yet Paul promises that the God who raised Jesus will give life to their mortal bodies through His Spirit who lives in them. The future he describes includes the body’s renewal, not simply leaving embodied life behind.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these verses as connecting belonging to Christ, the Spirit living within believers and the hope of resurrection. Present weakness and mortality do not cancel the life God has begun. The direction is toward His renewal of the whole person.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Corinthians 15:42–49 develops the promised change from a perishable body to an imperishable one and connects the life to come with the risen Christ. The Spirit’s work now and the body’s future belong within the same saving purpose.

This also clarifies the contrast with the flesh. Paul is not declaring created bodies beyond God’s concern. He looks toward God giving life to the very mortal bodies that presently experience weakness and death.

passages.title: Romans 8:12-17
passages.section_title: What does it mean to live as God’s adopted children?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 Therefore, brothers, we have an obligation, but it is not to the flesh, to live according to it. 13 For if you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live. 14 For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God. 15 For you did not receive a spirit of slavery that returns you to fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption to sonship, by whom we cry, “Abba! Father!” 16 The Spirit Himself testifies with our spirit that we are God’s children. 17 And if we are children, then we are heirs: heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ—if indeed we suffer with Him, so that we may also be glorified with Him.
paragraphs: 12 Therefore, brothers, we have an obligation, but it is not to the flesh, to live according to it. 13 For if you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live. 14 For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God.

15 For you did not receive a spirit of slavery that returns you to fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption to sonship, by whom we cry, “Abba! Father!” 16 The Spirit Himself testifies with our spirit that we are God’s children. 17 And if we are children, then we are heirs: heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ—if indeed we suffer with Him, so that we may also be glorified with Him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul draws out the obligation that follows the Spirit’s life. Believers do not owe obedience to the flesh. He warns of death through living according to it and calls them, by the Spirit, to put sinful deeds to death. New belonging calls for a new way of life.

He then speaks of being led by God’s Spirit and receiving adoption rather than returning to fearful slavery. Adoption translates huiothesia (hwee-oh-theh-SEE-ah), υἱοθεσία, the receiving of the standing of sons; see Thayer’s entry. Paul is describing a family relationship with God and a share in what belongs to Christ.

The Spirit enables the cry Abba, Father and testifies with believers’ spirits that they are God’s children. The emphasis is on the relationship God gives, rather than a title people claim for themselves.

Children are also heirs with Christ. Paul includes sharing His sufferings on the way to sharing His glory. Being welcomed into the family does not mean present hardship proves someone has been excluded from it.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the passage as joining the Spirit’s work in holiness with the assurance of belonging to God’s family. The call to put sinful deeds to death is held together with the freedom to approach God as Father, and the hope of glory is held together with present suffering.
passages.god_plan_html: Galatians 4:4–7 gives the same movement in a compact form: God sends His Son to redeem, grants adoption and sends the Spirit of His Son into believers’ hearts, crying Abba, Father. The invitation into God’s family grows from the work of the Son and Spirit, bringing people from slavery into the standing of children and heirs.

passages.title: Romans 8:18-25
passages.section_title: What are we waiting for while creation groans?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 I consider that our present sufferings are not comparable to the glory that will be revealed in us. 19 The creation waits in eager expectation for the revelation of the sons of God. 20 For the creation was subjected to futility, not by its own will, but because of the One who subjected it, in hope 21 that the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to decay and brought into the glorious freedom of the children of God. 22 We know that the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until the present time. 23 Not only that, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for our adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies. 24 For in this hope we were saved; but hope that is seen is no hope at all. Who hopes for what he can already see? 25 But if we hope for what we do not yet see, we wait for it patiently.
paragraphs: 18 I consider that our present sufferings are not comparable to the glory that will be revealed in us. 19 The creation waits in eager expectation for the revelation of the sons of God. 20 For the creation was subjected to futility, not by its own will, but because of the One who subjected it, in hope 21 that the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to decay and brought into the glorious freedom of the children of God. 22 We know that the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until the present time.

23 Not only that, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for our adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies. 24 For in this hope we were saved; but hope that is seen is no hope at all. Who hopes for what he can already see? 25 But if we hope for what we do not yet see, we wait for it patiently.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul has just connected being God’s children with sharing Christ’s suffering and glory. He now looks beyond present suffering to what God will reveal. He does not deny the pain; he sets it beside a future great enough to change how believers wait.

Creation itself shares in the waiting. Paul pictures it as subjected to frustration and decay, yet looking toward freedom when God’s children are revealed. His image of childbirth brings pain and expectation together: the groaning belongs to a world awaiting what it cannot bring about for itself.

Believers groan too. Having the Spirit does not mean they have already received everything God promises. They await the redemption of their bodies. The Spirit is the firstfruits—the beginning of the gift that points toward its completion. Hope concerns what is still unseen, so waiting calls for patience.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a promise that God’s saving work reaches beyond present inward comfort to bodily resurrection and creation’s freedom from decay. Groaning and faith can exist together. Suffering does not prove that the Spirit is absent, and hope does not require pretending that life is painless.
passages.god_plan_html:
Genesis 3:17–19 connects human sin with a cursed ground, painful labor and return to dust. Paul’s picture looks toward release from the decay that now marks created life.

Revelation 21:1–5 carries that hope into the picture of a new heaven and earth, God dwelling with His people, and the end of death and mourning. These passages share the wider promise of God renewing life with His people. Romans gives hope in that renewal without supplying a schedule for every event.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 8:26
passages.section_title: Can we come to God without knowing what to say?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 26 In the same way, the Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know how we ought to pray, but the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groans too deep for words.
paragraphs: 26 In the same way, the Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know how we ought to pray, but the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groans too deep for words.

passages.context_html:
Paul has described believers waiting for the redemption of their bodies, sharing in creation’s groaning. He now speaks of another kind of help during that wait: the Spirit meets them in their weakness, including not knowing how to pray.

Intercedes means acts on their behalf. The next verse explains that this help agrees with God’s will. The point is not that believers must discover a special prayer technique, but that their limited understanding does not exhaust the help God provides.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this verse as comfort for people whose prayer is marked by weakness or an inability to find words. The assurance rests in the Spirit’s help, rather than in an impressive or carefully managed performance of prayer. Reading verse 26 together with verse 27 keeps that help connected to God’s will.
passages.current_position_html: Our studies Prayer and Faith and What Does Prayer Look Like? understand these verses as an invitation to bring our weakness honestly before God. Prayer does not depend on perfectly formed requests. The Spirit helps where our understanding and words fall short, according to God’s will. We can trust Him without treating prayer as a way to secure a particular outcome.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html: Paul also says in Romans 8:34 that the risen Christ intercedes for believers. Read together, the statements show God providing help through both the Son and the Spirit. The family relationship described earlier in the chapter includes help in the weakness of those who belong to Him.

passages.title: Romans 8:26-27
passages.section_title: What happens when we do not know how to pray?
passages.note: When words fail, the Spirit intercedes according to the will of God.

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 26 In the same way, the Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know how we ought to pray, but the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groans too deep for words. 27 And He who searches our hearts knows the mind of the Spirit, because the Spirit intercedes for the saints according to the will of God.
paragraphs: 26 In the same way, the Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know how we ought to pray, but the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groans too deep for words. 27 And He who searches our hearts knows the mind of the Spirit, because the Spirit intercedes for the saints according to the will of God.

passages.context_html:
Creation groans, believers groan, and now Paul speaks of the Spirit’s help in their weakness. The setting is the long wait for bodily redemption. Not knowing how to pray belongs within that experience of limited understanding and hope.

The Spirit intercedes—He acts on believers’ behalf. God, who searches hearts, knows the Spirit’s mind, and the Spirit’s intercession agrees with God’s will. Paul locates the assurance in God’s knowledge and help, rather than in a person’s ability to find exactly the right words.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand these verses as reassurance that weakness in prayer does not leave believers without God’s help. Both Calvin’s comments on verses 26–27 and Wesley’s notes on those verses connect the Spirit’s help with prayer directed toward God’s will. Their explanations differ in emphasis, but both place confidence in the Spirit’s work.
passages.current_position_html: Our studies Prayer and Faith and What Does Prayer Look Like? understand these verses as an invitation to bring our weakness honestly before God. Prayer does not depend on perfectly formed requests. The Spirit helps where our understanding and words fall short, according to God’s will. We can trust Him without treating prayer as a way to secure a particular outcome.

section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

The family relationship described earlier in the chapter includes help in the weakness of those who belong to Him.

passages.title: Romans 8:27
passages.section_title: How can God understand what we cannot put into words?

paragraphs: 27 And He who searches our hearts knows the mind of the Spirit, because the Spirit intercedes for the saints according to the will of God.

passages.context_html:
This verse completes Paul’s explanation of the Spirit’s help in prayer. Verse 26 describes weakness and wordless groaning; verse 27 says that the God who searches hearts knows the Spirit’s mind.

The Spirit intercedes for the saints—God’s people—according to God’s will. The reason for confidence is the agreement between the Spirit’s work and God’s will, even when the person praying cannot see what should happen next.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as assurance that God understands the Spirit’s intercession and that it accords with His will. The passage directs trust toward God’s understanding. It does not identify every desired outcome as something the Spirit must be requesting.
passages.current_position_html: Our studies Prayer and Faith and What Does Prayer Look Like? understand these verses as an invitation to bring our weakness honestly before God. Prayer does not depend on perfectly formed requests. The Spirit helps where our understanding and words fall short, according to God’s will. We can trust Him without treating prayer as a way to secure a particular outcome.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html: Paul also says in Romans 8:34 that the risen Christ intercedes for believers. Read together, the statements show God providing help through both the Son and the Spirit. The family relationship described earlier in the chapter includes help in the weakness of those who belong to Him.

passages.title: Romans 8:28-30
passages.section_title: What is the good God is working toward?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 28 And we know that God works all things together for the good of those who love Him, who are called according to His purpose. 29 For those God foreknew, He also predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son, so that He would be the firstborn among many brothers. 30 And those He predestined, He also called; those He called, He also justified; those He justified, He also glorified.
paragraphs: 28 And we know that God works all things together for the good of those who love Him, who are called according to His purpose. 29 For those God foreknew, He also predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son, so that He would be the firstborn among many brothers. 30 And those He predestined, He also called; those He called, He also justified; those He justified, He also glorified.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul continues speaking to people who suffer, wait and need help praying. The promise is addressed to those who love God and are called according to His purpose. It does not call every event good. It says God works through all things toward the good He intends for His people.

Verse 29 names that purpose: being made like His Son, who is firstborn among many brothers. The good in view reaches further than immediate comfort or a preferred outcome. It concerns belonging to Christ’s family and sharing His likeness and glory.

Paul links God’s foreknowledge, purpose, calling, justification and glory. The Greek word translated predestined is proorizō (proh-or-ID-zoh), προορίζω, meaning to decide or determine beforehand; see Thayer’s entry. The word identifies a prior purpose. How that purpose relates to human response is part of the difference between Christian readings below.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians broadly agree that God’s grace comes first and that His purpose is to bring His people into Christ’s likeness. Traditions differ over how election and the believer’s continuing response fit together.

Reformed churches following the Westminster Confession, chapter 3, teach that God’s choice of those brought to salvation is fixed and rests on His grace rather than foreseen faith or perseverance. The 1689 Baptist Confession, chapter 3, paragraphs 4–6, gives the same account of election. This reading understands the sequence as assurance that God brings those He chooses through to glory.

Wesley’s note on verse 30 reads the sequence as the way God leads people toward glory while allowing that a believer may turn away before its completion. This reflects the Wesleyan emphasis on continuing in God’s grace; it does not make grace unnecessary or faith a way of earning salvation.

The Catholic Church teaches that God’s eternal plan includes each person’s free response to grace (Catechism 600) and that God predestines no one to hell (Catechism 1037). These teachings set boundaries for a Catholic reading without settling every question about how foreknowledge and election work.
passages.god_plan_html: Ephesians 1:3–14 places adoption, redemption and the promised inheritance within God’s purpose in Christ. Verses 9–10 describe His purpose to bring together all things in heaven and on earth in Christ. Romans adds the personal dimension: the people God calls are to become like His Son. The goal is larger than arranging convenient circumstances; it is a renewed people whose life is centered on Christ.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 8:31-39
passages.section_title: Can suffering separate us from God’s love?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 31 What then shall we say in response to these things? If God is for us, who can be against us? 32 He who did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all, how will He not also, along with Him, freely give us all things? 33 Who will bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies. 34 Who is there to condemn us? For Christ Jesus, who died, and more than that was raised to life, is at the right hand of God—and He is interceding for us. 35 Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall trouble or distress or persecution or famine or nakedness or danger or sword? 36 As it is written: “For Your sake we face death all day long; we are considered as sheep to be slaughtered.” 37 No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through Him who loved us. 38 For I am convinced that neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities, neither the present nor the future, nor any powers, 39 neither height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.
paragraphs: 31 What then shall we say in response to these things? If God is for us, who can be against us? 32 He who did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all, how will He not also, along with Him, freely give us all things? 33 Who will bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies. 34 Who is there to condemn us? For Christ Jesus, who died, and more than that was raised to life, is at the right hand of God—and He is interceding for us.

35 Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall trouble or distress or persecution or famine or nakedness or danger or sword? 36 As it is written: “For Your sake we face death all day long; we are considered as sheep to be slaughtered.” 37 No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through Him who loved us.

38 For I am convinced that neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities, neither the present nor the future, nor any powers, 39 neither height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul brings the chapter’s account of life, adoption and hope to a series of questions. If God is for His people, what opponent can overturn His purpose? The gift of His own Son is the reason for confidence that He will provide what is needed to complete His saving work.

The questions then move into a courtroom picture. God is the one who justifies, and Christ has died, risen and taken His place at God’s right hand. He also intercedes for believers. Their assurance rests in what God has done through Christ and what Christ continues to do for them.

Paul names real threats: distress, persecution, hunger, exposure, danger and violent death. He quotes Psalm 44, where faithful people suffer and cry out for help. These hardships can happen to God’s people. The promise is that they cannot sever the love of Christ.

The closing list stretches across death and life, spiritual powers, present and future, height and depth, and the rest of creation. Paul’s confidence reaches beyond any single circumstance: God’s love is found in Christ Jesus our Lord.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read these verses as deep reassurance that suffering and hostile powers cannot defeat God’s love in Christ. Victory through Him does not require escaping every hardship named in the passage.

Traditions differ over whether a believer can finally turn away. Reformed churches following the Westminster Confession, chapter 17, teach that those God truly calls and sanctifies will certainly remain His to the end. They may fall into serious sin, with painful consequences, but will not finally fall from grace.

Wesley’s notes on verses 30 and 38–39 affirm God’s protecting love while retaining the possibility that a believer may turn away. On this reading, no hostile power can tear believers from Christ, but continuing faith still matters.

The Catholic Church also distinguishes the strength of God’s love from a person’s ability to reject grace. It teaches that mortal sin—a grave wrong committed with full knowledge and deliberate consent—can result in the loss of grace and requires repentance and God’s forgiveness (Catechism 1857–1861). This is not the claim that every failure or anxious thought means someone has lost salvation.
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul explicitly brings Psalm 44:17–26 into his account of life in Christ. The psalm’s speakers say they have not abandoned God’s covenant, yet they face defeat and death. They appeal to His loving devotion for rescue.

That connection places Christian suffering within the longer experience of God’s people, who have cried out while waiting for His help. Paul answers the fear of abandonment by pointing to the Son whom God gave, raised and seated at His right hand. The love revealed in Christ is the ground of hope even when present circumstances remain painful.

passages.title: Romans 9:1-5
passages.section_title: Why does Paul speak about Israel with such grief?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 I speak the truth in Christ; I am not lying, as confirmed by my conscience in the Holy Spirit. 2 I have deep sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart. 3 For I could wish that I myself were cursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my own flesh and blood, 4 the people of Israel. Theirs is the adoption as sons; theirs the divine glory and the covenants; theirs the giving of the law, the temple worship, and the promises. 5 Theirs are the patriarchs, and from them proceeds the human descent of Christ, who is God over all, forever worthy of praise! Amen.
paragraphs: 1 I speak the truth in Christ; I am not lying, as confirmed by my conscience in the Holy Spirit. 2 I have deep sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart. 3 For I could wish that I myself were cursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my own flesh and blood,

4 the people of Israel. Theirs is the adoption as sons; theirs the divine glory and the covenants; theirs the giving of the law, the temple worship, and the promises. 5 Theirs are the patriarchs, and from them proceeds the human descent of Christ, who is God over all, forever worthy of praise! Amen.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After celebrating God’s love in Christ, Paul turns to a painful question: what about his own people, Israel? He insists that his grief is genuine. His concern is so deep that he describes wishing he could be cut off from Christ for their sake.

He then lists Israel’s gifts: adoption, divine glory, covenants, the law, worship, promises and the patriarchs. These gifts matter to the discussion that follows. Paul is asking how Israel’s present situation relates to what God has promised.

The list reaches its high point in Christ, whose human descent comes from Israel. In the BSB wording, Paul also identifies Him as God over all. The passage holds together Christ’s Jewish ancestry and His divine identity.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand these verses as an expression of Paul’s love for his people and his recognition of Israel’s place in God’s work. His wish communicates the depth of his grief; it does not establish that someone can exchange their salvation for another person’s.
passages.god_plan_html:
God’s promise to Abraham included blessing for all the families of the earth (Genesis 12:1–3). Paul’s account of Christ coming from Israel places the saving work of Jesus within that long history of promise.

The same chapter will speak of God calling people from both Jews and Gentiles (verse 24). The movement toward the nations grows from the history Paul honors here. It gives no reason to treat the Jewish people with contempt.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 9:6-13
passages.section_title: Has God’s promise failed?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 It is not as though God’s word has failed. For not all who are descended from Israel are Israel. 7 Nor because they are Abraham’s descendants are they all his children. On the contrary, “Through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned.” 8 So it is not the children of the flesh who are God’s children, but it is the children of the promise who are regarded as offspring. 9 For this is what the promise stated: “At the appointed time I will return, and Sarah will have a son.” 10 Not only that, but Rebecca’s children were conceived by one man, our father Isaac. 11 Yet before the twins were born or had done anything good or bad, in order that God’s plan of election might stand, 12 not by works but by Him who calls, she was told, “The older will serve the younger.” 13 So it is written: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.”
paragraphs: 6 It is not as though God’s word has failed. For not all who are descended from Israel are Israel. 7 Nor because they are Abraham’s descendants are they all his children. On the contrary, “Through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned.” 8 So it is not the children of the flesh who are God’s children, but it is the children of the promise who are regarded as offspring. 9 For this is what the promise stated: “At the appointed time I will return, and Sarah will have a son.”

10 Not only that, but Rebecca’s children were conceived by one man, our father Isaac. 11 Yet before the twins were born or had done anything good or bad, in order that God’s plan of election might stand, 12 not by works but by Him who calls, she was told, “The older will serve the younger.” 13 So it is written: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul denies that God’s word has failed. He distinguishes physical descent from sharing in the promise, beginning with Abraham’s family: the promised line runs through Isaac. He then points to Jacob and Esau, twins whose different roles were announced before either had done good or bad.

The quotations come from different settings. Genesis 25:19–26 speaks of two nations arising from Rebekah’s children. Malachi 1:1–5 addresses Israel and contrasts God’s treatment of Jacob’s people with judgment on Edom, Esau’s people. Paul brings these family and national histories into his explanation of God’s purpose.

His stated contrast is between works and the One who calls. The promise does not become a debt owed simply because of ancestry or achievement. How this relates to the salvation of particular people is one of the main differences in readings of the chapter.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Traditions differ over how far these examples describe the eternal destiny of individuals. Reformed churches following the Westminster Confession, chapter 3, understand election as God’s free choice of individuals for salvation, by grace rather than foreseen faith or works.

Wesley’s notes on verses 6–13 emphasize the promised family line and the brothers’ nations. He does not take these examples as declarations of either man’s eternal destiny. The readings differ over what the examples establish about individual election.
passages.god_plan_html:
The younger child receiving the promised role fits a wider scriptural pattern in which God’s work overturns expected grounds for boasting. In 1 Corinthians 1:26–31, Paul points to God calling the weak and overlooked, with Christ becoming their righteousness and redemption.

This is a parallel in how God’s grace removes boasting, rather than a claim that every younger sibling has the same calling as Jacob. God’s purpose advances through His gift and calling, beyond the status people would normally prize.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 9:14-18
passages.section_title: How does Paul answer the question of God’s fairness?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 What then shall we say? Is God unjust? Certainly not! 15 For He says to Moses: “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.” 16 So then, it does not depend on man’s desire or effort, but on God’s mercy. 17 For the Scripture says to Pharaoh: “I raised you up for this very purpose, that I might display My power in you, and that My name might be proclaimed in all the earth.” 18 Therefore God has mercy on whom He wants to have mercy, and He hardens whom He wants to harden.
paragraphs: 14 What then shall we say? Is God unjust? Certainly not! 15 For He says to Moses: “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.” 16 So then, it does not depend on man’s desire or effort, but on God’s mercy.

17 For the Scripture says to Pharaoh: “I raised you up for this very purpose, that I might display My power in you, and that My name might be proclaimed in all the earth.” 18 Therefore God has mercy on whom He wants to have mercy, and He hardens whom He wants to harden.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul anticipates the question raised by God’s choice: does this make God unjust? He answers emphatically that it does not. He turns to God’s words to Moses about mercy and compassion, then says that mercy does not depend on human desire or effort.

The second example is Pharaoh. God’s dealings with him display divine power and make God’s name known beyond Egypt. Paul concludes with God’s freedom to show mercy and to harden.

The Exodus account includes both God hardening Pharaoh’s heart and Pharaoh hardening his own heart (Exodus 9:12, 27–35). Pharaoh’s resistance and God’s action both belong to the account. The different readings below concern how those actions relate.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Reformed readers such as Calvin, commenting on verses 16–18, understand this as God determining whom He brings to saving faith. Calvin reads hardening as an act of divine judgment, beyond merely allowing resistance.

Wesley’s notes on verses 14–18 also deny that mercy is earned. He understands God as establishing the way mercy is received through faith, and hardening as leaving persistent unbelievers in their chosen resistance. The difference concerns God’s initiative and human response.
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul’s two Exodus quotations concern God making Himself known. In Exodus 33:12–23, Moses seeks God’s presence and asks to see His glory; God answers by proclaiming His goodness, name and freedom to show mercy.

In Exodus 9:13–17, God says His power will be displayed and His name proclaimed throughout the earth. Paul places his discussion of mercy within that larger purpose of revealing who God is, beyond the immediate contest with Pharaoh.

passages.title: Romans 9:19-24
passages.section_title: What does the picture of the potter and clay explain?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 One of you will say to me, “Then why does God still find fault? For who can resist His will?” 20 But who are you, O man, to talk back to God? Shall what is formed say to Him who formed it, “Why did You make me like this?” 21 Does not the potter have the right to make from the same lump of clay one vessel for special occasions and another for common use? 22 What if God, intending to show His wrath and make His power known, bore with great patience the vessels of His wrath, prepared for destruction? 23 What if He did this to make the riches of His glory known to the vessels of His mercy, whom He prepared in advance for glory— 24 including us, whom He has called not only from the Jews, but also from the Gentiles?
paragraphs: 19 One of you will say to me, “Then why does God still find fault? For who can resist His will?” 20 But who are you, O man, to talk back to God? Shall what is formed say to Him who formed it, “Why did You make me like this?” 21 Does not the potter have the right to make from the same lump of clay one vessel for special occasions and another for common use?

22 What if God, intending to show His wrath and make His power known, bore with great patience the vessels of His wrath, prepared for destruction? 23 What if He did this to make the riches of His glory known to the vessels of His mercy, whom He prepared in advance for glory— 24 including us, whom He has called not only from the Jews, but also from the Gentiles?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul voices a further objection: if no one can resist God’s will, why does God still find fault? His response uses the picture of a maker and what he makes. Clay cannot place the potter under its authority; the Creator has rights over His creation.

He then asks readers to consider God bearing patiently with vessels of wrath and making known the riches of His glory to vessels of mercy. The language includes judgment, patience and mercy. Verse 23 explicitly says God prepared the vessels of mercy beforehand for glory.

Verse 24 identifies the people Paul has in view: those God has called from both Jews and Gentiles. That brings the discussion back to the question running through the chapter—how God’s purpose is unfolding among Israel and the nations.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Readings differ over what determines the two groups. Calvin’s comments on verses 22–23 connect both their outcomes with God’s prior decision, while distinguishing mercy from deserved judgment. This fits the Reformed emphasis on God’s choice described in the Westminster Confession, chapter 3.

Wesley’s notes on verses 21–24 identify the groups through faith and persistent unbelief. He reads preparation for destruction in terms of continued refusal of mercy, while affirming that God prepares believers for glory by grace. The readings differ over the place of human response.
passages.god_plan_html:
The potter picture draws on Isaiah 29:15–16 and Isaiah 45:9–13, where people are warned against treating their Maker as though He lacks understanding or authority. Isaiah 45 also places the image beside God’s purpose to restore His exiles.

Paul uses that familiar picture while describing a people called from both Jews and Gentiles. His explanation of mercy has a wider horizon than any one person’s status: God is forming a people who receive and display the riches of His mercy.

passages.title: Romans 9:25-29
passages.section_title: Why does Paul bring Hosea and Isaiah into this discussion?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 25 As He says in Hosea: “I will call them ‘My People’ who are not My people, and I will call her ‘My Beloved’ who is not My beloved,” 26 and, “It will happen that in the very place where it was said to them, ‘You are not My people,’ they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’” 27 Isaiah cries out concerning Israel: “Though the number of the Israelites is like the sand of the sea, only the remnant will be saved. 28 For the Lord will carry out His sentence on the earth thoroughly and decisively.” 29 It is just as Isaiah foretold: “Unless the Lord of Hosts had left us descendants, we would have become like Sodom, we would have resembled Gomorrah.”
paragraphs: 25 As He says in Hosea: “I will call them ‘My People’ who are not My people, and I will call her ‘My Beloved’ who is not My beloved,” 26 and, “It will happen that in the very place where it was said to them, ‘You are not My people,’ they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’”

27 Isaiah cries out concerning Israel: “Though the number of the Israelites is like the sand of the sea, only the remnant will be saved. 28 For the Lord will carry out His sentence on the earth thoroughly and decisively.” 29 It is just as Isaiah foretold: “Unless the Lord of Hosts had left us descendants, we would have become like Sodom, we would have resembled Gomorrah.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul supports the calling of people from Jews and Gentiles with words from the prophets. Hosea supplies the language of people once rejected being called God’s people and His children. Isaiah speaks of a remnant—a surviving part of Israel—rather than the nation’s size guaranteeing its safety.

The original setting matters. Hosea 1:6–11 and 2:14–23 concern judgment on Israel followed by promised restoration. Paul brings that language into his account of God’s calling. He also uses Isaiah’s warnings of judgment and assurance that God preserves survivors.

The final comparison with Sodom and Gomorrah emphasizes dependence on God’s mercy. Without the survivors God leaves, destruction would be complete. The point is preservation by God, rather than an entitlement created by numbers or ancestry.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly see these quotations as showing that judgment does not bring God’s purpose to an end: He preserves a remnant and calls people into a restored relationship with Him. Explanations differ over the reach of Hosea’s words here.

Calvin’s comment on verse 25 recognizes Hosea’s original reference to Israel and reads Paul’s use as extending to the Gentiles. Wesley’s notes on verses 25–26 emphasize Israel’s final restoration. These are differences between these teachers’ explanations; neither should be treated as the only reading within his wider tradition.
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul explicitly joins the prophets’ language to the calling of people from both Jews and Gentiles in verse 24. Hosea 2:19–23 pictures renewed belonging through God’s faithfulness and compassion. Isaiah 10:20–23 describes a remnant returning to rely on the Lord, and Isaiah 1:9 credits Him with preserving survivors.

These passages bring judgment and hope together. God’s people owe their continued life and belonging to His mercy. Paul uses that history to explain the people God is calling, rather than treating the arrival of Gentiles as proof that His earlier word failed.

passages.title: Romans 9:30-33
passages.section_title: How can people seeking righteousness miss it?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 30 What then will we say? That the Gentiles, who did not pursue righteousness, have obtained it, a righteousness that is by faith; 31 but Israel, who pursued a law of righteousness, has not attained it. 32 Why not? Because their pursuit was not by faith, but as if it were by works. They stumbled over the stumbling stone, 33 as it is written: “See, I lay in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense; and the one who believes in Him will never be put to shame.”
paragraphs: 30 What then will we say? That the Gentiles, who did not pursue righteousness, have obtained it, a righteousness that is by faith; 31 but Israel, who pursued a law of righteousness, has not attained it. 32 Why not? Because their pursuit was not by faith, but as if it were by works. They stumbled over the stumbling stone, 33 as it is written: “See, I lay in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense; and the one who believes in Him will never be put to shame.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul closes the chapter with a striking contrast. Gentiles who had not pursued righteousness have received righteousness by faith, while Israel’s pursuit of a law of righteousness has not reached its goal.

He gives the reason in verse 32: the pursuit was treated as a matter of works rather than faith. The stumbling stone is Christ, the very One in whom righteousness is received. Religious effort can miss its aim when it becomes a basis for confidence instead of leading to trust in Him.

This is Paul’s explanation of the situation he is addressing, not a claim that every Jewish person rejected Christ or that Jewish Scripture contains no teaching about faith and mercy. Paul himself is a Jewish believer, and he has just described a remnant. The warning also confronts anyone who treats religious achievement as a substitute for trust.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the passage as a warning against relying on works to obtain the righteousness God gives through faith. The closing promise directs attention to the One trusted, rather than the amount of effort invested.

The wider disagreement about election also affects how readers connect these verses with the earlier chapter. Calvin’s comment on verse 30 places unbelief beneath God’s prior decision; Wesley’s note on verse 32 treats failure to believe as Paul’s explanation rather than a decree preventing faith. Both identify faith in Christ as essential.
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul combines the stone imagery of Isaiah 8:13–15 and Isaiah 28:14–18. In the first, the Lord is both a sanctuary and a stone over which people stumble. In the second, God lays a sure foundation in Zion and promises security to the one who trusts.

Paul applies that contrast to Christ. The same One who is rejected is God’s provision for those who believe. That connection places the call to faith within the prophets’ account of finding safety in what God provides, rather than in the refuges people devise for themselves.
