passages.title: Romans 10:1-4
passages.section_title: Why does sincere zeal still need the truth?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Brothers, my heart’s desire and prayer to God for the Israelites is for their salvation. 2 For I testify about them that they are zealous for God, but not on the basis of knowledge. 3 Because they were ignorant of God’s righteousness and sought to establish their own, they did not submit to God’s righteousness. 4 For Christ is the end of the law, to bring righteousness to everyone who believes.
paragraphs: 1 Brothers, my heart’s desire and prayer to God for the Israelites is for their salvation. 2 For I testify about them that they are zealous for God, but not on the basis of knowledge. 3 Because they were ignorant of God’s righteousness and sought to establish their own, they did not submit to God’s righteousness. 4 For Christ is the end of the law, to bring righteousness to everyone who believes.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul continues the concern for Israel expressed at the start of chapter 9. He prays for their salvation and acknowledges their zeal for God. His criticism is not that they care too little, but that their pursuit does not recognize the righteousness God gives.

He describes an effort to establish their own righteousness instead of submitting to God’s. Verse 4 places Christ at the center: He is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes. The promise is directed to the believer, rather than to a particular ancestry.

The Greek word for end is telos (TEH-loss), τέλος. Its range includes an ending and an aim or goal; see Thayer’s entry. The word’s range helps explain the readings below, but the dictionary alone cannot decide how all of God’s law relates to Christian life.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read the passage as directing confidence toward Christ rather than one’s own religious achievement. Readers differ over the emphasis of end in verse 4.

Wesley’s note on verse 4 emphasizes Christ as the law’s goal. Calvin’s comment similarly speaks of completion and the law leading people to righteousness in Christ. The Catholic bishops’ Bible notes emphasize the end of the Mosaic law as the basis for a right relationship with God, while also recognizing the goal reading and the possibility of both meanings. These are explanations of the verse, rather than a simple division in which every denomination has only one view.
passages.god_plan_html:
Galatians 3:23–29 gives a related explanation: the law served as a guardian leading to Christ, and those who belong to Christ are heirs of the promise to Abraham. Paul connects the arrival of faith with a new standing as God’s children.

This places the question of righteousness within the larger movement from promise to its fulfillment in Christ. The same passage joins Jews and Greeks in belonging to Him, matching the invitation to everyone who believes in Romans 10.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 10:5-13
passages.section_title: What does it mean to believe and call on the Lord?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 For concerning the righteousness that is by the law, Moses writes: “The man who does these things will live by them.” 6 But the righteousness that is by faith says: “Do not say in your heart, ‘Who will ascend into heaven?’ (that is, to bring Christ down) 7 or, ‘Who will descend into the Abyss?’ (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead).” 8 But what does it say? “The word is near you; it is in your mouth and in your heart,” that is, the word of faith we are proclaiming: 9 that if you confess with your mouth, “Jesus is Lord,” and believe in your heart that God raised Him from the dead, you will be saved. 10 For with your heart you believe and are justified, and with your mouth you confess and are saved. 11 It is just as the Scripture says: “Anyone who believes in Him will never be put to shame.” 12 For there is no difference between Jew and Greek: The same Lord is Lord of all, and gives richly to all who call on Him, 13 for, “Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.”
paragraphs: 5 For concerning the righteousness that is by the law, Moses writes: “The man who does these things will live by them.” 6 But the righteousness that is by faith says: “Do not say in your heart, ‘Who will ascend into heaven?’ (that is, to bring Christ down) 7 or, ‘Who will descend into the Abyss?’ (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead).” 8 But what does it say? “The word is near you; it is in your mouth and in your heart,” that is, the word of faith we are proclaiming:

9 that if you confess with your mouth, “Jesus is Lord,” and believe in your heart that God raised Him from the dead, you will be saved. 10 For with your heart you believe and are justified, and with your mouth you confess and are saved. 11 It is just as the Scripture says: “Anyone who believes in Him will never be put to shame.” 12 For there is no difference between Jew and Greek: The same Lord is Lord of all, and gives richly to all who call on Him, 13 for, “Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul draws on Moses’ words to contrast righteousness approached through doing the law with righteousness received by faith. He applies the picture of a word near the mouth and heart to the message about Christ that he proclaims.

No one needs to bring Christ down from heaven or raise Him from the dead. God has already acted. Paul joins belief in the heart with confession of Jesus as Lord, centering that belief on God raising Him from the dead.

The invitation reaches both Jew and Greek. The same Lord gives richly to all who call on Him. Paul ends with Joel’s promise of salvation to everyone who calls on the Lord’s name. The emphasis is on whom people trust and confess, rather than on religious ancestry or a difficult journey to find Him.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand these verses as joining genuine faith in the risen Jesus with openly acknowledging Him as Lord. Heart and mouth belong together: confession is more than repeating words, and faith is more than knowing that a claim exists. The invitation includes both Jews and Gentiles.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Deuteronomy 30:11–20, Moses describes God’s command as near, calling Israel to love the Lord, listen and hold fast to Him. Paul draws on that language and applies it to the proclaimed message about Christ. He is making a connection within the history of God addressing His people, rather than quoting a statement that originally named Jesus.

Joel 2:28–32 places calling on the Lord within a promise of the Spirit’s outpouring and deliverance. Paul uses its invitation while naming Jesus as Lord and affirming that the same Lord is Lord of both Jew and Greek. The good news he proclaims grows from promises already present in Scripture.
passages.current_position_html: The Gospel According to Jesus understands these verses as a call to turn to Jesus in faith, confess Him as Lord and call on Him. Salvation is received through Him, not earned through moral effort or religious activity. The study emphasizes that there is no special wording that saves; the response is trust in the risen Lord and a turning of the heart toward Him.

passages.title: Romans 10:9
passages.section_title: What does confessing Jesus as Lord mean?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 that if you confess with your mouth, “Jesus is Lord,” and believe in your heart that God raised Him from the dead, you will be saved.
paragraphs: 9 that if you confess with your mouth, “Jesus is Lord,” and believe in your heart that God raised Him from the dead, you will be saved.

passages.context_html:
Paul is explaining the message of faith through Moses’ picture of the word being near the mouth and heart. In this verse, confession and belief focus on Jesus as Lord and on God raising Him from the dead.

The surrounding verses keep the statement within a wide invitation: the same Lord is Lord of Jew and Greek, and everyone who calls on Him is invited to salvation. Verse 10 joins the heart’s belief with the mouth’s confession.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as a call to genuine faith in the risen Jesus and acknowledgment of Him as Lord. The words express who is trusted. They are not a verbal technique that works independently of the heart’s response.
passages.current_position_html: The Gospel According to Jesus and I Am a Disciple connect confession of Jesus as Lord with faith in His resurrection as the foundation of a life following Him. The Gospel study emphasizes trust and a turning of the heart, rather than a saving formula. Baptism also cites this verse in teaching that forgiveness is received through faith in Christ and is not withheld until water baptism.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html: In verses 12–13 Paul connects this confession with Joel 2:32, the promise that everyone calling on the Lord’s name will be saved. The confession of Jesus belongs within the scriptural promise of deliverance and Paul’s insistence that the same Lord is Lord of Jew and Greek.

passages.title: Romans 10:9-10
passages.section_title: How do belief and confession belong together?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 that if you confess with your mouth, “Jesus is Lord,” and believe in your heart that God raised Him from the dead, you will be saved. 10 For with your heart you believe and are justified, and with your mouth you confess and are saved.
paragraphs: 9 that if you confess with your mouth, “Jesus is Lord,” and believe in your heart that God raised Him from the dead, you will be saved. 10 For with your heart you believe and are justified, and with your mouth you confess and are saved.

passages.context_html:
Paul describes the response to the message of faith: confessing Jesus as Lord and believing that God raised Him from the dead. Verse 9 moves from mouth to heart; verse 10 moves from heart to mouth, connecting belief with justification and confession with salvation.

The two verses belong to Paul’s use of Deuteronomy’s language about the word being near, in the mouth and heart. He is explaining a response to the risen Jesus, not giving people a way to produce His saving work by their own effort.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read belief and confession here as belonging together in a real response to Christ. Faith involves trusting the risen Lord, and confession acknowledges Him. Repeating a statement without that trust does not capture the relationship between heart and mouth that Paul describes.
passages.current_position_html: The Gospel According to Jesus and I Am a Disciple understand belief in the risen Jesus and confession of Him as Lord as the foundation of responding to the gospel and following Him. The Gospel study describes that response as turning toward Jesus and entrusting oneself to Him, with no special wording that works as a saving formula.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html: In verses 12–13 Paul connects this confession with Joel 2:32, the promise that everyone calling on the Lord’s name will be saved. The confession of Jesus belongs within the scriptural promise of deliverance and Paul’s insistence that the same Lord is Lord of Jew and Greek.

passages.title: Romans 10:13
passages.section_title: Who is invited to call on the Lord?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 for, “Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.”
paragraphs: 13 for, “Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.”

passages.context_html:
Paul quotes Joel after saying that there is no difference between Jew and Greek: the same Lord is Lord of all and gives richly to those who call on Him. Everyone in this promise makes its welcome clear.

The surrounding verses connect calling with believing in Christ and hearing the good news. Calling on the Lord is an expression of reliance on Him, within the message Paul has just described through belief and confession.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this verse as an invitation that crosses the distinction between Jew and Gentile. No ancestry gives someone a separate Lord or a different source of salvation. The verse calls people to trust Him; it does not say that salvation occurs without any response to Him.
passages.current_position_html: The Gospel According to Jesus uses this verse to invite people to turn to Jesus in faith and call on Him. The study emphasizes a response of the heart rather than a formula: trusting the Lord who saves, instead of trying to secure salvation through ancestry, moral achievement or religious activity.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html: Joel 2:28–32 places this promise within the outpouring of God’s Spirit and deliverance associated with the day of the Lord. Paul brings that promise into his announcement of the risen Jesus and the shared welcome to Jews and Gentiles. Calling on the Lord belongs to God’s promised rescue, reaching beyond inherited religious standing.

passages.title: Romans 10:14-17
passages.section_title: Why does sharing the good news matter?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 How then can they call on the One in whom they have not believed? And how can they believe in the One of whom they have not heard? And how can they hear without someone to preach? 15 And how can they preach unless they are sent? As it is written: “How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news!” 16 But not all of them welcomed the good news. For Isaiah says, “Lord, who has believed our message?” 17 Consequently, faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of Christ.
paragraphs: 14 How then can they call on the One in whom they have not believed? And how can they believe in the One of whom they have not heard? And how can they hear without someone to preach? 15 And how can they preach unless they are sent? As it is written: “How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news!” 16 But not all of them welcomed the good news. For Isaiah says, “Lord, who has believed our message?” 17 Consequently, faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of Christ.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul follows the promise about calling on the Lord with a chain of questions. Calling depends on believing; believing involves hearing; hearing requires a messenger; and the messenger must be sent. Proclaiming the good news belongs within the way people come to faith.

He quotes Isaiah’s welcome for a bearer of good news, then Isaiah’s question about who has believed the report. Sending and hearing do not mean everyone welcomes what is announced. Paul holds the need for proclamation beside the reality of unbelief.

Verse 17 connects faith with hearing and hearing with the word of Christ. The focus is the message about Him, rather than the messenger’s status or ability to impress an audience.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a strong reason to proclaim the gospel: people need to hear the message of Christ in order to respond in faith. The passage also recognizes that hearing a message and welcoming it are different. It does not promise that every presentation will produce an immediate conversion.
passages.god_plan_html:
Isaiah 52:7–10 pictures good news arriving in Zion: God reigns, comforts His people and makes His salvation known to the nations. Paul brings that messenger picture into the proclamation of Christ.

He also draws on Isaiah 53:1–3, where the report meets disbelief and the servant is despised. The two quotations hold together the greatness of God’s saving news and the painful possibility of its rejection. Faithful proclamation belongs to God’s work even when its reception is difficult.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 10:18-21
passages.section_title: What if the message has been heard but refused?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 But I ask, did they not hear? Indeed they did: “Their voice has gone out into all the earth, their words to the ends of the world.” 19 I ask instead, did Israel not understand? First, Moses says: “I will make you jealous by those who are not a nation; I will make you angry by a nation without understanding.” 20 And Isaiah boldly says: “I was found by those who did not seek Me; I revealed Myself to those who did not ask for Me.” 21 But as for Israel he says: “All day long I have held out My hands to a disobedient and obstinate people.”
paragraphs: 18 But I ask, did they not hear? Indeed they did: “Their voice has gone out into all the earth, their words to the ends of the world.” 19 I ask instead, did Israel not understand? First, Moses says: “I will make you jealous by those who are not a nation; I will make you angry by a nation without understanding.” 20 And Isaiah boldly says: “I was found by those who did not seek Me; I revealed Myself to those who did not ask for Me.” 21 But as for Israel he says: “All day long I have held out My hands to a disobedient and obstinate people.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul asks whether the problem has been a failure to hear or understand. He answers by drawing on the Psalms, Moses and Isaiah. The argument belongs to his continuing concern for Israel and the place of Gentiles in God’s purpose.

He uses the worldwide language of Psalm 19, then Moses’ warning that God would provoke jealousy through a people outside Israel’s covenant life. Isaiah supplies the contrast between God being found by those who had not sought Him and God continually holding out His hands to a resistant people.

The final picture is an extended invitation met by resistance. Paul does not end with permission to despise Israel. His own prayer for their salvation opened the chapter, and the question of God’s faithfulness continues in chapter 11.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Readers differ over the immediate reference of the hearing question. Calvin’s comment on verse 18 connects it with God making Himself known to the Gentiles. Wesley’s note and the Catholic bishops’ notes on verses 14–21 emphasize Israel’s opportunity to hear. Both approaches place the discussion within God’s communication and the response it receives.

The quotations are commonly read as showing that the arrival of Gentiles and Israel’s resistance do not take God by surprise. They should not be turned into a judgment about the motives or knowledge of every Jewish person in every time and place.
passages.god_plan_html:
Deuteronomy 32:15–22 sets the jealousy warning within Israel’s turning to other gods. Paul uses it alongside Isaiah 65:1–2, where God makes Himself known and reaches out to a disobedient people.

These connections show the tension between God’s initiative and human resistance running through the earlier Scriptures as well as Paul’s day. The outstretched hands keep God’s invitation visible. His dealings with Israel and the nations are part of the same continuing question of mercy and faithfulness, rather than evidence that His promises have been forgotten.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 11:1-6
passages.section_title: Has God rejected His people?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 I ask then, did God reject His people? Certainly not! I am an Israelite myself, a descendant of Abraham, from the tribe of Benjamin. 2 God did not reject His people, whom He foreknew. Do you not know what the Scripture says about Elijah, how he appealed to God against Israel: 3 “Lord, they have killed Your prophets and torn down Your altars. I am the only one left, and they are seeking my life as well”? 4 And what was the divine reply to him? “I have reserved for Myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal.” 5 In the same way, at the present time there is a remnant chosen by grace. 6 And if it is by grace, then it is no longer by works. Otherwise, grace would no longer be grace.
paragraphs: 1 I ask then, did God reject His people? Certainly not! I am an Israelite myself, a descendant of Abraham, from the tribe of Benjamin. 2 God did not reject His people, whom He foreknew. Do you not know what the Scripture says about Elijah, how he appealed to God against Israel: 3 “Lord, they have killed Your prophets and torn down Your altars. I am the only one left, and they are seeking my life as well”? 4 And what was the divine reply to him? “I have reserved for Myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal.”
5 In the same way, at the present time there is a remnant chosen by grace. 6 And if it is by grace, then it is no longer by works. Otherwise, grace would no longer be grace.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul answers the question directly: God has not rejected His people. He points to himself as an Israelite descended from Abraham and belonging to Benjamin. His faith is a present example that Jewish people have not been excluded from God’s saving work.

He then recalls Elijah, who believed he was the only faithful person left. God’s answer revealed a preserved remnant of seven thousand who had not bowed to Baal. Elijah’s knowledge of the situation did not cover everything God was doing.

Paul applies that example to his own day: there is a remnant chosen by grace. He contrasts grace with works, because a gift of mercy cannot at the same time be a payment earned. The remnant is evidence of God’s faithfulness, rather than a reason for its members to boast.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a clear denial that God has abandoned Israel altogether. Paul and other Jewish believers show that His work continues. The Elijah example also warns against assuming that what one person can see is the whole extent of God’s faithfulness.
passages.god_plan_html:
In the fuller account of 1 Kings 19:1–18, God provides for a fearful, exhausted Elijah and gives him further work, including a successor. The preserved remnant belongs within that continuing work, beyond what the discouraged prophet knew.

Paul explicitly brings this history into his explanation of Israel’s present situation. A moment when God’s work seems near its end can still be part of His provision for its continuation. The connection rests on Paul’s use of Elijah’s story, rather than an invented prediction that every difficult situation will unfold the same way.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 11:7-10
passages.section_title: What does Paul mean by the others being hardened?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 What then? What Israel was seeking, it failed to obtain, but the elect did. The others were hardened, 8 as it is written: “God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that could not see, and ears that could not hear, to this very day.” 9 And David says: “May their table become a snare and a trap, a stumbling block and a retribution to them. 10 May their eyes be darkened so they cannot see, and their backs be bent forever.”
paragraphs: 7 What then? What Israel was seeking, it failed to obtain, but the elect did. The others were hardened, 8 as it is written: “God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that could not see, and ears that could not hear, to this very day.” 9 And David says: “May their table become a snare and a trap, a stumbling block and a retribution to them. 10 May their eyes be darkened so they cannot see, and their backs be bent forever.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul contrasts the elect, who have obtained what Israel sought, with others who were hardened. This continues the earlier discussion of righteousness, grace and unbelief. It does not describe every Israelite as unbelieving; the preceding verses have expressly identified a remnant.

He draws on Moses and Isaiah for the picture of people seeing and hearing without understanding. He then quotes David’s prayer that his opponents’ table become a trap and their eyes be darkened. These are serious words of judgment, placed within a chapter that also speaks of God’s ability to bring people back.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The main difference follows the discussion of mercy and hardening in chapter 9. Calvin’s comment on verse 7 emphasizes God’s election as the reason for the distinction. Wesley’s notes on verses 7–8 emphasize persistent resistance followed by God giving people over to it. Both take hardening seriously as judgment; they differ over how God’s choice and human response relate.
passages.god_plan_html:
Deuteronomy 29:2–6 distinguishes witnessing God’s acts from truly understanding them. Isaiah 29:9–14 places spiritual blindness alongside worship that honors God with words while the heart remains far away.

Yet Isaiah’s chapter also looks toward a day when the deaf hear, the blind see and the humble rejoice in God (verses 18–19). That wider setting keeps judgment beside the possibility of God’s restoring work. Romans 11 likewise goes on to speak of renewed faith and being grafted in again; this passage should be read within that larger movement.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 11:11-16
passages.section_title: Can Israel’s stumbling be the end of the story?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 I ask then, did they stumble so as to fall beyond recovery? Certainly not! However, because of their trespass, salvation has come to the Gentiles to make Israel jealous. 12 But if their trespass means riches for the world, and their failure means riches for the Gentiles, how much greater riches will their fullness bring! 13 I am speaking to you Gentiles. Inasmuch as I am the apostle to the Gentiles, I magnify my ministry 14 in the hope that I may provoke my own people to jealousy and save some of them. 15 For if their rejection is the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance be but life from the dead? 16 If the first part of the dough is holy, so is the whole batch; if the root is holy, so are the branches.
paragraphs: 11 I ask then, did they stumble so as to fall beyond recovery? Certainly not! However, because of their trespass, salvation has come to the Gentiles to make Israel jealous. 12 But if their trespass means riches for the world, and their failure means riches for the Gentiles, how much greater riches will their fullness bring!

13 I am speaking to you Gentiles. Inasmuch as I am the apostle to the Gentiles, I magnify my ministry 14 in the hope that I may provoke my own people to jealousy and save some of them. 15 For if their rejection is the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance be but life from the dead? 16 If the first part of the dough is holy, so is the whole batch; if the root is holy, so are the branches.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul denies that Israel has stumbled beyond recovery. Salvation reaching the Gentiles is part of the story, but he also anticipates riches through Israel’s fullness and acceptance. He describes God’s work with one group as reaching toward the good of the other.

He speaks directly to Gentiles about his ministry among them. Even that ministry carries a desire for his own people: he hopes to provoke them to jealousy and save some. His purpose includes their coming to faith, rather than merely keeping a general interest in a Messiah alive.

The pictures of a holy first portion of dough and a holy root point toward the continuing significance of Israel’s beginning. The verses prepare for the olive-tree picture that follows. Paul’s confidence concerns God’s faithfulness, not an assertion that ancestry makes every individual righteous.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand Paul as refusing despair about Israel while explaining the arrival of salvation among the Gentiles. Readers differ about the precise scope and timing of the future acceptance he anticipates, but his desire that some of his own people be saved is explicit. Their present unbelief is not a reason for indifference to them.
passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 13:44–48 provides a narrated parallel: opposition to Paul’s message is followed by his turning to the Gentiles, who rejoice in the word. That episode illustrates the movement Paul describes here; it does not prove that every Jewish hearer in every city responded alike.

In Romans, the movement outward remains joined to hope for Israel. God’s work among the nations and His faithfulness to the people from whom the promises came are held together, rather than made into rival reasons for celebration.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 11:17-24
passages.section_title: Why must the grafted branches stay humble?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 Now if some branches have been broken off, and you, a wild olive shoot, have been grafted in among the others to share in the nourishment of the olive root, 18 do not boast over those branches. If you do, remember this: You do not support the root, but the root supports you. 19 You will say then, “Branches were broken off so that I could be grafted in.” 20 That is correct: They were broken off because of unbelief, but you stand by faith. Do not be arrogant, but be afraid. 21 For if God did not spare the natural branches, He will certainly not spare you either. 22 Take notice, therefore, of the kindness and severity of God: severity to those who fell, but kindness to you, if you continue in His kindness. Otherwise you also will be cut off. 23 And if they do not persist in unbelief, they will be grafted in, for God is able to graft them in again. 24 For if you were cut from a wild olive tree, and contrary to nature were grafted into one that is cultivated, how much more readily will these, the natural branches, be grafted into their own olive tree!
paragraphs: 17 Now if some branches have been broken off, and you, a wild olive shoot, have been grafted in among the others to share in the nourishment of the olive root, 18 do not boast over those branches. If you do, remember this: You do not support the root, but the root supports you. 19 You will say then, “Branches were broken off so that I could be grafted in.” 20 That is correct: They were broken off because of unbelief, but you stand by faith. Do not be arrogant, but be afraid. 21 For if God did not spare the natural branches, He will certainly not spare you either.

22 Take notice, therefore, of the kindness and severity of God: severity to those who fell, but kindness to you, if you continue in His kindness. Otherwise you also will be cut off. 23 And if they do not persist in unbelief, they will be grafted in, for God is able to graft them in again. 24 For if you were cut from a wild olive tree, and contrary to nature were grafted into one that is cultivated, how much more readily will these, the natural branches, be grafted into their own olive tree!

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul pictures Gentile believers as a wild olive shoot grafted into a cultivated tree. Some natural branches have been broken off, while the newcomers share the root’s nourishment among the others. The picture contains a continuing tree and shared dependence.

He directly forbids boasting over the branches. The root supports the grafted shoot, not the other way around. Broken branches are connected with unbelief, while the Gentile hearers stand by faith. Their proper response is humility and reverence.

The warning includes continuing in God’s kindness and the possibility of being cut off. The hope includes God’s ability to graft natural branches in again if they do not persist in unbelief. Both warning and hope belong to the picture.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly recognize the warning against Gentile arrogance and the dependence of all believers on God’s grace. Readings differ over how the warning about being cut off applies.

In Calvin’s comments on verse 22, Paul addresses the Gentile community’s privileged standing; Calvin also treats the warning as necessary for humbling believers. He does not read it as the final loss of those God has elected to salvation. This agrees with the Westminster Confession’s teaching on perseverance, chapter 17.

Wesley’s notes on verses 20–22 take continued faith as a real condition and the warning as including a believer’s final falling away. Both readings retain the call to humility; they differ over whether a true believer can finally lose that standing.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 2:11–22 gives a related picture of Gentiles once far from the covenants of promise being brought near through Christ. Jews and Gentiles are reconciled to God in one body through the cross and share access to the Father by the Spirit.

The pictures are different, but the shared theme is clear: welcome into God’s people removes grounds for hostility and pride. In Romans, the grafted branch depends on the root; in Ephesians, those brought near become members of God’s household through Christ’s work.

passages.title: Romans 11:25-27
passages.section_title: What does Paul mean by all Israel being saved?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 25 I do not want you to be ignorant of this mystery, brothers, so that you will not be conceited: A hardening in part has come to Israel, until the full number of the Gentiles has come in. 26 And so all Israel will be saved, as it is written: “The Deliverer will come from Zion; He will remove godlessness from Jacob. 27 And this is My covenant with them when I take away their sins.”
paragraphs: 25 I do not want you to be ignorant of this mystery, brothers, so that you will not be conceited: A hardening in part has come to Israel, until the full number of the Gentiles has come in. 26 And so all Israel will be saved, as it is written: “The Deliverer will come from Zion; He will remove godlessness from Jacob. 27 And this is My covenant with them when I take away their sins.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul explains a mystery so that Gentile believers will not become conceited. Israel’s hardening is in part, and he relates it to the full number of the Gentiles coming in. He then says that all Israel will be saved.

His scriptural explanation focuses on a Deliverer, the removal of godlessness from Jacob, and God taking away sins in keeping with His covenant. The promised rescue concerns God’s work of deliverance and forgiveness. The verses do not provide a date or a complete schedule for future events.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians differ over who all Israel includes and how this salvation unfolds. Wesley’s note on verse 26 anticipates Israel’s coming to faith. The Catholic Church’s Catechism 674 also connects the full inclusion of the Jews in the Messiah’s salvation with Christ’s return.

Dispensational teaching, represented by Dallas Theological Seminary’s doctrinal statement, Article XX, places Israel’s restoration to its land and the fulfillment of its covenant promises within Christ’s future reign on earth. The statement itself cites Romans 11:25–27. That fuller timeline is a particular theological reading, rather than detail spelled out in these three verses.

Calvin’s comment on verse 26 understands all Israel as the completed people of God gathered from Jews and Gentiles, while also expecting Jewish people to return to faith. Reformed interpreters are not all bound to this particular explanation. These readings share confidence in God’s saving faithfulness but differ over the expression’s scope and the events it describes.
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul explicitly draws on Isaiah 59:15–21 and the removal of Jacob’s sin described in Isaiah 27:6–9. In Isaiah 59, God acts to bring salvation when no human rescuer is found, and His covenant promise includes His Spirit and word.

The connection directs attention to the Deliverer’s work: dealing with godlessness and taking away sin. Whatever timeline a reader adopts, Paul explains the promised salvation through God’s covenant faithfulness and cleansing, rather than ancestry saving people apart from His action.

passages.title: Romans 11:28-32
passages.section_title: How do disobedience and mercy meet in God’s purpose?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 28 Regarding the gospel, they are enemies on your account; but regarding election, they are loved on account of the patriarchs. 29 For God’s gifts and His call are irrevocable. 30 Just as you who formerly disobeyed God have now received mercy through their disobedience, 31 so they too have now disobeyed, in order that they too may now receive mercy through the mercy shown to you. 32 For God has consigned everyone to disobedience so that He may have mercy on everyone.
paragraphs: 28 Regarding the gospel, they are enemies on your account; but regarding election, they are loved on account of the patriarchs. 29 For God’s gifts and His call are irrevocable.

30 Just as you who formerly disobeyed God have now received mercy through their disobedience, 31 so they too have now disobeyed, in order that they too may now receive mercy through the mercy shown to you. 32 For God has consigned everyone to disobedience so that He may have mercy on everyone.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul describes Israel from two perspectives: opposition in relation to the gospel, yet being loved in relation to election on account of the patriarchs. God’s gifts and call are irrevocable. The history of promise remains important to understanding the present.

He then places Gentiles and Israel beside one another in disobedience and mercy. Gentile believers formerly disobeyed and have now received mercy; Israel’s disobedience is also set within the prospect of mercy. Neither group has a ground for treating itself as morally self-sufficient.

The concluding statement brings everyone under disobedience and points toward mercy for everyone. Paul moves toward praise of God’s wisdom, rather than giving either group a basis for superiority.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read this as an affirmation of God’s faithfulness and the shared need of Jews and Gentiles for mercy. The Catholic Church’s Nostra Aetate, section 4, draws on this chapter in refusing to present Jewish people as rejected or cursed by God.

Christians differ over the final reach of mercy. Calvin’s comment on verse 32 understands everyone in terms of both Jews and Gentiles, not a promise that every individual will be saved. Christian universalists, represented by the Christian Universalist Association’s beliefs, teach that every person will ultimately be reconciled to God through Christ. That is a distinct account of salvation, not agreement across Christian traditions.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 2:1–10 similarly places people’s former disobedience beside God’s rich mercy. God makes them alive with Christ and intends to display the riches of His grace and kindness in the coming ages.

That wider setting gives mercy a purpose beyond one group gaining an advantage over another. God’s grace produces a people whose life displays His kindness and whose good works follow His gift. Paul’s account of Israel and the nations leads toward praise of that mercy.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 11:33-36
passages.section_title: Why does Paul end this discussion with praise?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 33 O, the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are His judgments, and untraceable His ways! 34 “Who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been His counselor?” 35 “Who has first given to God, that God should repay him?” 36 For from Him and through Him and to Him are all things. To Him be the glory forever! Amen.
paragraphs: 33 O, the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are His judgments, and untraceable His ways! 34 “Who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been His counselor?” 35 “Who has first given to God, that God should repay him?” 36 For from Him and through Him and to Him are all things. To Him be the glory forever! Amen.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After tracing disobedience, judgment and mercy among Jews and Gentiles, Paul responds with wonder at God’s wisdom and knowledge. He has explained much, yet he does not claim to have mastered God’s ways.

His questions deny that God depends on a human counselor or owes repayment to someone who first supplied His needs. The final statement gathers everything around Him as its source, the One through whom it exists, and its goal. Paul ends by giving God glory.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand these verses as praise offered in response to God’s saving wisdom and mercy. Humility follows from recognizing the limits of human understanding and the freedom of God’s gifts. The praise concludes a sustained explanation; it does not suggest that careful study or honest questions have no place.
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul draws on Isaiah 40:12–17, where the Creator needs no counselor, and Job 41:10–11, where everything under heaven already belongs to God. The saving purpose discussed in Romans belongs to the same God who sustains creation.

In Acts 17:24–28, Paul tells the people of Athens that God gives life and breath to all and has ordered the nations’ lives so that they might seek Him. That wider proclamation helps explain the fitting end to Romans 11: the God whose mercy reaches Jews and Gentiles is the source of the life of all peoples.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 12:1
passages.section_title: What is a living sacrifice?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Therefore I urge you, brothers, on account of God’s mercy, to offer your bodies as living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God, which is your spiritual service of worship.
paragraphs: 1 Therefore I urge you, brothers, on account of God’s mercy, to offer your bodies as living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God, which is your spiritual service of worship.

passages.context_html:
Paul appeals to believers on account of God’s mercy. The instruction to offer their bodies follows his account of God’s saving work; it describes a response to mercy, rather than a way to make God owe it to them.

The sacrifice is living: people place their embodied lives at God’s service. Verse 2 continues the thought with renewal of the mind, and the rest of the chapter makes the service concrete through humility, using gifts, sincere love and kindness even to enemies.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the living sacrifice as the dedication of the person’s life to God. The imagery brings worship and daily conduct together. It does not restrict service to a religious event or require bodily harm as a way of offering oneself.
passages.current_position_html: Worship as the Early Church Knew It reads the living sacrifice as a life offered in service to God. Its emphasis is on worship expressed through obedience and sacrificial service throughout life. The study places this beside Christ’s sacrifice and the New Testament description of believers as a priestly people.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html: Hebrews 13:15–16 uses sacrifice language for praise, doing good and sharing with others. 1 Peter 2:5 describes God’s people offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable through Jesus Christ. Paul’s living sacrifice belongs within that wider picture of a people whose service grows from Christ’s work.

passages.title: Romans 12:1-2
passages.section_title: What does worship look like in everyday life?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Therefore I urge you, brothers, on account of God’s mercy, to offer your bodies as living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God, which is your spiritual service of worship. 2 Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind. Then you will be able to test and approve what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God.
paragraphs: 1 Therefore I urge you, brothers, on account of God’s mercy, to offer your bodies as living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God, which is your spiritual service of worship. 2 Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind. Then you will be able to test and approve what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul turns from his explanation of God’s mercy to the life that responds to it. His appeal begins with what God has given, then calls believers to offer their bodies as living sacrifices. Daily, embodied life belongs within their service to God.

The word translated service of worship is latreia (lah-TRAY-ah), λατρεία. It concerns service or worship of God; see Thayer’s entry. Paul uses the language of sacrifice for people offering themselves while alive. Worship here reaches into what they do with their lives.

The next verse joins that offering to a changed way of thinking. Believers are not to take their shape from the surrounding world’s patterns, but to be transformed through renewal of the mind. That renewal enables them to recognize and approve what pleases God. The call reaches inward to judgment and desires as well as outward to conduct.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand these verses as a call to wholehearted service in response to God’s mercy. Worship includes the way people live, and transformation includes the renewal of how they think. The appeal is grounded in God’s gift rather than a claim that an impressive sacrifice can place Him in someone’s debt.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Peter 2:4–10 describes believers as a spiritual house and holy priesthood, offering sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ. Their new belonging grows from receiving mercy. This provides a wider setting for Paul’s picture of people offering themselves in response to God.

Hebrews 13:15–16 names praise, doing good and sharing as sacrifices pleasing to God through Jesus. Together, these passages show sacrificial language reaching into the life of God’s people—their words, care for others and service—because of Christ’s work.
passages.current_position_html: Worship as the Early Church Knew It understands this passage as calling believers to offer their lives in service to God. Worship reaches beyond a gathering or a song into obedience, sacrifice and care for others. The study connects the believer’s living sacrifice with the wider New Testament picture of God’s people serving Him through Christ.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

passages.title: Romans 12:3-8
passages.section_title: How do different gifts serve one body?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 3 For by the grace given me I say to every one of you: Do not think of yourself more highly than you ought, but think of yourself with sober judgment, according to the measure of faith God has given you. 4 Just as each of us has one body with many members, and not all members have the same function, 5 so in Christ we who are many are one body, and each member belongs to one another. 6 We have different gifts according to the grace given us. If one’s gift is prophecy, let him use it in proportion to his faith; 7 if it is serving, let him serve; if it is teaching, let him teach; 8 if it is encouraging, let him encourage; if it is giving, let him give generously; if it is leading, let him lead with diligence; if it is showing mercy, let him do it cheerfully.
paragraphs: 3 For by the grace given me I say to every one of you: Do not think of yourself more highly than you ought, but think of yourself with sober judgment, according to the measure of faith God has given you. 4 Just as each of us has one body with many members, and not all members have the same function, 5 so in Christ we who are many are one body, and each member belongs to one another.

6 We have different gifts according to the grace given us. If one’s gift is prophecy, let him use it in proportion to his faith; 7 if it is serving, let him serve; if it is teaching, let him teach; 8 if it is encouraging, let him encourage; if it is giving, let him give generously; if it is leading, let him lead with diligence; if it is showing mercy, let him do it cheerfully.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul makes the call to a renewed mind practical by addressing how believers see themselves. They are to avoid an inflated sense of importance and think with sound judgment, recognizing what God has given.

The body picture explains why differences need not create rivalry. Many members have different functions, yet they belong to one body in Christ and to one another. A gift is part of shared life, rather than a reason to imagine one can do without the rest.

Paul names prophecy, serving, teaching, encouraging, giving, leading and showing mercy. He joins the gifts to the manner of their use: generosity, diligence and cheerfulness matter. The emphasis is on putting God’s grace to work for others, rather than collecting titles or comparing status.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read this as a call to humble, active service in a community whose members need one another. Traditions differ over how the gift of prophecy operates.

Calvin’s comment on verse 6 and Wesley’s note understand prophecy here chiefly as explaining Scripture and God’s will faithfully. These are their readings of this passage, rather than a claim that all Reformed or Wesleyan Christians explain the gift identically.

The Assemblies of God affirms prophecy as a continuing gift through which the Spirit strengthens the Church. Its position paper on modern-day prophecy requires messages to be judged by Scripture and the believing community; it does not give present prophecies Scripture’s authority.

The Catholic Church also recognizes gifts of the Spirit, including extraordinary gifts, for the Church’s common good. Its Catechism 2003–2004 places them at the service of love and cites this passage’s gifts of ministry. Across these differences, the gifts are directed toward building up others.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Corinthians 12:12–27 develops the same body picture. No part can dismiss another as unnecessary, and members share in one another’s suffering and honor. Difference serves mutual care rather than superiority.

Ephesians 4:7–16 connects Christ’s gifts with equipping His people and bringing the body toward maturity in Him. Together these passages place each person’s service within Christ’s purpose for a people growing in unity, truth and love.

passages.title: Romans 12:9-13
passages.section_title: What makes love more than a good appearance?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 Love must be sincere. Detest what is evil; cling to what is good. 10 Be devoted to one another in brotherly love. Outdo yourselves in honoring one another. 11 Do not let your zeal subside; keep your spiritual fervor, serving the Lord. 12 Be joyful in hope, patient in affliction, persistent in prayer. 13 Share with the saints who are in need. Practice hospitality.
paragraphs: 9 Love must be sincere. Detest what is evil; cling to what is good. 10 Be devoted to one another in brotherly love. Outdo yourselves in honoring one another. 11 Do not let your zeal subside; keep your spiritual fervor, serving the Lord. 12 Be joyful in hope, patient in affliction, persistent in prayer. 13 Share with the saints who are in need. Practice hospitality.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul moves from particular gifts to qualities that should shape the whole community. Love must be sincere. It belongs beside rejecting evil and holding to good, so kindness is not the same as pretending that harmful conduct does not matter.

He calls believers to family affection and to taking the lead in honoring one another. Zeal, spiritual fervor and serving the Lord give that love energy and direction. Other people’s good matters more than gaining recognition for oneself.

Hope, patience in trouble and persistent prayer belong together. These are ways to continue with God through changing circumstances, not a demand to feel cheerful about every loss. Sharing with those in need and practicing hospitality make the community’s care tangible.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand these commands as a picture of sincere, practical love. They join affection and honor with moral seriousness, perseverance, prayer and material care. Hospitality and generosity are expressions of service to the Lord, rather than ways to gain status in the community.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus gives love for one another a public significance in John 13:34–35: it identifies His disciples. The life Paul describes gives concrete shape to that shared belonging.

Acts 2:42–47 provides a lived example of believers committed to prayer, fellowship and meeting needs. This is a parallel in the life of the early community, not a claim that Romans requires one particular financial arrangement. God’s people make His mercy visible as they care for one another.

passages.title: Romans 12:14-21
passages.section_title: How can good overcome evil?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 Bless those who persecute you. Bless and do not curse. 15 Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep. 16 Live in harmony with one another. Do not be proud, but associate with the lowly. Do not be conceited. 17 Do not repay anyone evil for evil. Carefully consider what is right in the eyes of everybody. 18 If it is possible on your part, live at peace with everyone. 19 Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God’s wrath. For it is written: “Vengeance is Mine; I will repay, says the Lord.” 20 On the contrary, “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him a drink. For in so doing, you will heap burning coals on his head.” 21 Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.
paragraphs: 14 Bless those who persecute you. Bless and do not curse. 15 Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep. 16 Live in harmony with one another. Do not be proud, but associate with the lowly. Do not be conceited.

17 Do not repay anyone evil for evil. Carefully consider what is right in the eyes of everybody. 18 If it is possible on your part, live at peace with everyone. 19 Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God’s wrath. For it is written: “Vengeance is Mine; I will repay, says the Lord.” 20 On the contrary, “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him a drink. For in so doing, you will heap burning coals on his head.” 21 Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul extends the call to sincere love into difficult relationships. Believers are to bless persecutors, share in others’ joy and grief, live in harmony and associate with the lowly. Humility changes whose company they seek and how they respond to others’ lives.

He then forbids repaying evil with evil and calls for peace wherever it is possible on their part. That qualification recognizes that one person cannot control everyone else’s conduct. The responsibility is to pursue what is good without making retaliation the answer to harm.

The final commands put revenge in God’s hands and replace it with concrete kindness: feed a hungry enemy and give a thirsty enemy a drink. Paul draws on Deuteronomy and Proverbs before gathering the passage into the call to overcome evil with good. His instruction concerns how believers act, even when the other person remains hostile.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the passage as rejecting personal revenge and calling for active kindness toward enemies. Seeking peace and showing compassion belong together with trusting God to judge rightly.

The burning-coals image receives different explanations. Calvin’s comment on verse 20 understands kindness as either softening an enemy or troubling the enemy’s conscience. Wesley’s notes on verses 20–21 also emphasize overcoming opposition through kindness. These explanations keep attention on doing good; the passage does not promise that every enemy will respond in the same way.
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul’s instruction shares the pattern of Jesus’ teaching in Matthew 5:43–48: love enemies and pray for persecutors, reflecting the Father’s generosity toward the righteous and unrighteous. Luke 6:27–36 likewise connects kindness to enemies with being merciful as the Father is merciful.

The Old Testament quotations already place justice and kindness together: vengeance belongs to God (Deuteronomy 32:35–36), while the enemy’s hunger calls for a meal (Proverbs 25:21–22). Life shaped by God’s mercy does not need to copy the evil it encounters. It can entrust judgment to Him and seek another person’s good.

passages.title: Romans 13:1-7
passages.section_title: How should believers relate to governing authorities?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Everyone must submit himself to the governing authorities, for there is no authority except that which is from God. The authorities that exist have been appointed by God. 2 Consequently, whoever resists authority is opposing what God has set in place, and those who do so will bring judgment on themselves. 3 For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad. Do you want to be unafraid of the one in authority? Then do what is right, and you will have his approval. 4 For he is God’s servant for your good. But if you do wrong, be afraid, for he does not carry the sword in vain. He is God’s servant, an agent of retribution to the wrongdoer. 5 Therefore it is necessary to submit to authority, not only to avoid punishment, but also as a matter of conscience. 6 This is also why you pay taxes. For the authorities are God’s servants, who devote themselves to their work. 7 Pay everyone what you owe him: taxes to whom taxes are due, revenue to whom revenue is due, respect to whom respect is due, honor to whom honor is due.
paragraphs: 1 Everyone must submit himself to the governing authorities, for there is no authority except that which is from God. The authorities that exist have been appointed by God. 2 Consequently, whoever resists authority is opposing what God has set in place, and those who do so will bring judgment on themselves. 3 For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad. Do you want to be unafraid of the one in authority? Then do what is right, and you will have his approval. 4 For he is God’s servant for your good. But if you do wrong, be afraid, for he does not carry the sword in vain. He is God’s servant, an agent of retribution to the wrongdoer.

5 Therefore it is necessary to submit to authority, not only to avoid punishment, but also as a matter of conscience. 6 This is also why you pay taxes. For the authorities are God’s servants, who devote themselves to their work. 7 Pay everyone what you owe him: taxes to whom taxes are due, revenue to whom revenue is due, respect to whom respect is due, honor to whom honor is due.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After forbidding personal revenge, Paul describes the role of governing authorities. He places their authority under God and presents their purpose as serving the public good by restraining wrongdoing. The sword belongs to that picture of authority carrying out punishment.

He calls for submission as a matter of conscience, not simply a way to avoid penalties. Taxes, revenue, respect and honor are included among what people owe. Faith in Christ is not treated as an exemption from responsibilities in society.

The description also gives rulers a standard: their service is for good and against wrongdoing. The passage should be read alongside Scripture’s accounts of authorities acting unjustly and of people remaining faithful to God when rulers oppose Him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly recognize civil authority as having a God-given responsibility for public order and justice. Traditions differ over the forms of participation open to Christians and the use of force.

Reformed churches following the Westminster Confession, chapter 23, teach obedience to lawful commands and allow Christians to hold civil office. They also allow war on just and necessary occasions. The authority of rulers is understood as a responsibility under God, rather than an unlimited personal right.

The Catholic Church teaches civic duties while also requiring refusal of directives contrary to the moral order, fundamental human rights or the gospel (Catechism 2238–2242). Respect for authority includes responsibility toward the common good and the ability to voice just criticism.

Mennonite Church USA’s confession likewise recognizes government’s role in maintaining order, while limiting participation by loyalty to Christ (Article 23). Its Article 22 calls Christians to nonviolent resistance to evil and excludes participation in war. This differs from readings that permit Christians to exercise the state’s coercive authority.
passages.god_plan_html:
Before Pilate, Jesus says that the governor’s authority has been given from above, while still speaking of guilt in the events leading to His death (John 19:10–11). God’s authority over events does not turn human wrongdoing into innocence.

In Acts 5:27–32, the apostles refuse an order to stop proclaiming Jesus because obedience to God comes first. Read together, these passages place human rule within a larger purpose and under a higher authority. Romans’ call to civic responsibility belongs within that scriptural setting.

passages.title: Romans 13:8-10
passages.section_title: Why is love a debt that remains?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 Be indebted to no one, except to one another in love. For he who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law. 9 The commandments “Do not commit adultery,” “Do not murder,” “Do not steal,” “Do not covet,” and any other commandments, are summed up in this one decree: “Love your neighbor as yourself.” 10 Love does no wrong to its neighbor. Therefore love is the fulfillment of the law.
paragraphs: 8 Be indebted to no one, except to one another in love. For he who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law. 9 The commandments “Do not commit adultery,” “Do not murder,” “Do not steal,” “Do not covet,” and any other commandments, are summed up in this one decree: “Love your neighbor as yourself.” 10 Love does no wrong to its neighbor. Therefore love is the fulfillment of the law.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul moves from paying what is owed in society to the continuing obligation to love one another. A bill can be settled; the call to seek another person’s good does not reach a point where it has been paid off for the rest of life.

He names commandments concerning adultery, murder, theft and coveting, then gathers them under the command to love one’s neighbor as oneself. The summary gives love concrete moral content: love does not wrong the neighbor.

Calling love the fulfillment of the law therefore does not make the neighbor’s life, marriage or possessions unimportant. Love seeks the good those commands protect, rather than using religious language to excuse harm.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand love here as an ongoing obligation expressed in how people treat their neighbors. It is more than affection or a general good intention: it refuses to harm another person and actively seeks their good. Paul’s summary connects moral conduct with the purpose of the commandments.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus places love for God and love for the neighbor at the center of the Law and Prophets in Matthew 22:34–40. Paul’s summary follows that same concern for the purpose running through God’s commands.

Galatians 5:13–15 joins Christian freedom to serving one another in love and repeats the command to love one’s neighbor. Freedom in Christ is directed toward the good of others, rather than becoming permission for desires and rivalry to injure them.
