passages.title: Romans 13:11-14
passages.section_title: How should the coming day change life now?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 And do this, understanding the occasion. The hour has come for you to wake up from your slumber, for our salvation is nearer now than when we first believed. 12 The night is nearly over; the day has drawn near. So let us lay aside the deeds of darkness and put on the armor of light. 13 Let us behave decently, as in the daytime, not in carousing and drunkenness, not in sexual immorality and debauchery, not in dissension and jealousy. 14 Instead, clothe yourselves with the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the desires of the flesh.
paragraphs: 11 And do this, understanding the occasion. The hour has come for you to wake up from your slumber, for our salvation is nearer now than when we first believed. 12 The night is nearly over; the day has drawn near. So let us lay aside the deeds of darkness and put on the armor of light. 13 Let us behave decently, as in the daytime, not in carousing and drunkenness, not in sexual immorality and debauchery, not in dissension and jealousy. 14 Instead, clothe yourselves with the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the desires of the flesh.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul gives urgency to the life of love he has described. Salvation is nearer than when his readers first believed, and he pictures the night nearing its end and the day drawing close. Hope for what God will complete becomes a reason to wake up and live differently now.

The change includes putting aside the deeds of darkness and putting on the armor of light. His examples cover drunken excess, sexual wrongdoing, conflict and jealousy. The warning reaches both outward indulgence and the resentments that damage relationships.

He gathers the response into being clothed with the Lord Jesus Christ and making no provision for sinful desires. The clothing picture concerns a life shaped by belonging to Him. Believers are to stop arranging their lives around satisfying the desires they are called to leave behind.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a call to alert, faithful living in light of the salvation God will complete. Readiness is expressed through present conduct, not through calculating a date. Being clothed with Christ connects the way people live with the Lord to whom they belong.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Thessalonians 5:1–11 develops the same pattern of night, day, wakefulness and armor. Paul names faith and love as a breastplate and the hope of salvation as a helmet, then directs believers to encourage and build one another up.

That connection shows what expectation of the coming day is meant to produce: a people living with faith, love and hope, helping one another remain ready. The future promise gives direction to daily life while its timing remains outside the schedule supplied in these verses.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 14:1-4
passages.section_title: How can believers disagree without rejecting one another?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Accept him whose faith is weak, without passing judgment on his opinions. 2 For one person has faith to eat all things, while another, who is weak, eats only vegetables. 3 The one who eats everything must not belittle the one who does not, and the one who does not eat everything must not judge the one who does, for God has accepted him. 4 Who are you to judge someone else’s servant? To his own master he stands or falls. And he will stand, for the Lord is able to make him stand.
paragraphs: 1 Accept him whose faith is weak, without passing judgment on his opinions. 2 For one person has faith to eat all things, while another, who is weak, eats only vegetables. 3 The one who eats everything must not belittle the one who does not, and the one who does not eat everything must not judge the one who does, for God has accepted him. 4 Who are you to judge someone else’s servant? To his own master he stands or falls. And he will stand, for the Lord is able to make him stand.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul addresses a community divided over food. One believer feels free to eat everything, while another eats only vegetables. He tells them to welcome the person whose faith is weak without turning that welcome into an opportunity to pass judgment.

Both sides have a temptation: the eater may look down on the abstainer, while the abstainer may condemn the eater. Paul counters both by pointing to God’s welcome. The other person is a servant of the Lord, rather than someone whose standing belongs to a fellow believer to decide.

The weakness concerns the convictions being discussed. Paul is speaking about people who belong to God, not describing the abstainer as an unbeliever. He ends with confidence in the Lord’s ability to make His servant stand.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a call to receive fellow believers despite differences in food convictions. Freedom does not justify contempt, and restraint does not justify condemning someone God has welcomed. The instruction concerns the disputed practices in view, rather than making every moral question a matter of personal preference.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Acts 15:8–11, Peter points to God receiving Gentiles, giving them the Spirit and cleansing their hearts by faith. That history places the welcome of believers within God’s wider work of gathering a people through grace.

The situations are not identical, and Romans does not identify every abstainer’s background. The shared point is that God’s welcome must shape how believers receive one another. Fellowship cannot be reduced to requiring everyone to have the same cultural habits.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 14:5-9
passages.section_title: How can different practices be offered to the same Lord?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 One person regards a certain day above the others, while someone else considers every day alike. Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind. 6 He who observes a special day does so to the Lord; he who eats does so to the Lord, for he gives thanks to God; and he who abstains does so to the Lord and gives thanks to God. 7 For none of us lives to himself alone, and none of us dies to himself alone. 8 If we live, we live to the Lord, and if we die, we die to the Lord. So whether we live or die, we belong to the Lord. 9 For this reason Christ died and returned to life, that He might be the Lord of both the dead and the living.
paragraphs: 5 One person regards a certain day above the others, while someone else considers every day alike. Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind. 6 He who observes a special day does so to the Lord; he who eats does so to the Lord, for he gives thanks to God; and he who abstains does so to the Lord and gives thanks to God.

7 For none of us lives to himself alone, and none of us dies to himself alone. 8 If we live, we live to the Lord, and if we die, we die to the Lord. So whether we live or die, we belong to the Lord. 9 For this reason Christ died and returned to life, that He might be the Lord of both the dead and the living.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul adds the example of days: one person gives a particular day special regard, while another regards them alike. He calls each person to be convinced in their own mind and describes both eating and abstaining as accompanied by thanksgiving to God.

The question reaches beyond the meal or calendar. Believers live and die belonging to the Lord. Paul grounds that belonging in Christ’s death and return to life, so that He is Lord of both the dead and the living. The practices are to express service to Him, rather than become a way of ruling one another.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly recognize the call to act for the Lord with gratitude and a clear conscience. They differ over how this relates to a weekly day of rest and worship. Wesley’s note on verse 5 identifies the disputed days as Jewish festivals.

An official Grace Communion International teaching article reads Romans 14:5–6 as allowing Christians to observe a day or treat it like others, without requiring a particular weekly Sabbath.

Reformed churches following the Westminster Confession, chapter 21, paragraphs 7–8, retain Sunday as the Christian Sabbath. The Catholic Church requires Sunday worship centered on the Eucharist (Catechism 2174–2177). These traditions do not understand freedom over disputed days as removing every obligation of weekly worship.

The Seventh-day Adventist Church instead teaches observance of the seventh-day Sabbath as a continuing command (Fundamental Belief 20). These differences should be represented in their own terms while retaining Paul’s direct instruction to serve the Lord and avoid contempt.
passages.god_plan_html:
2 Corinthians 5:14–15 gives a related reason for a changed life: Christ died and was raised so that those who live would live for Him. His saving work creates a new center for their decisions.

This helps explain the movement in Romans from food and days to life and death. God’s purpose is larger than getting everyone to adopt one person’s habits. Those who belong to the risen Lord are called to direct their lives toward Him, including the ordinary choices through which they give thanks.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 14:10-12
passages.section_title: Who will give the final account of our lives?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 Why, then, do you judge your brother? Or why do you belittle your brother? For we will all stand before God’s judgment seat. 11 It is written: “As surely as I live, says the Lord, every knee will bow before Me; every tongue will confess to God.” 12 So then, each of us will give an account of himself to God.
paragraphs: 10 Why, then, do you judge your brother? Or why do you belittle your brother? For we will all stand before God’s judgment seat. 11 It is written: “As surely as I live, says the Lord, every knee will bow before Me; every tongue will confess to God.” 12 So then, each of us will give an account of himself to God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul confronts both condemning and belittling a fellow believer. The reason is shared accountability: all will stand before God’s judgment seat. No one in the dispute occupies a place above the others as their final judge.

He quotes Isaiah’s picture of every knee bowing and every tongue acknowledging God. Each person will give an account of themselves. That prospect turns attention toward responsibility before God, rather than confidence in one’s ability to assess everyone else.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a warning against taking God’s place when judging another believer’s disputed practices. Accountability is personal and universal. The teaching calls for humility about oneself, rather than indifference to right and wrong.
passages.god_plan_html:
Isaiah 45:22–25 places every knee bowing within God’s call for the ends of the earth to turn to Him for salvation. The universal acknowledgment belongs to His rule as the only God.

Philippians 2:9–11 uses the same picture in describing the exalted Jesus, confessed as Lord to the Father’s glory. Romans brings that wide horizon into a local disagreement: people who will acknowledge God together should not treat one another with contempt now.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 14:13-18
passages.section_title: When does using our freedom stop being loving?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 Therefore let us stop judging one another. Instead, make up your mind not to put any stumbling block or obstacle in your brother’s way. 14 I am convinced and fully persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself. But if anyone regards something as unclean, then for him it is unclean. 15 If your brother is distressed by what you eat, you are no longer acting in love. Do not by your eating destroy your brother, for whom Christ died. 16 Do not allow what you consider good, then, to be spoken of as evil. 17 For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking, but of righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. 18 For whoever serves Christ in this way is pleasing to God and approved by men.
paragraphs: 13 Therefore let us stop judging one another. Instead, make up your mind not to put any stumbling block or obstacle in your brother’s way. 14 I am convinced and fully persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself. But if anyone regards something as unclean, then for him it is unclean. 15 If your brother is distressed by what you eat, you are no longer acting in love. Do not by your eating destroy your brother, for whom Christ died.

16 Do not allow what you consider good, then, to be spoken of as evil. 17 For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking, but of righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. 18 For whoever serves Christ in this way is pleasing to God and approved by men.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul redirects judgment toward a practical decision: do not put an obstacle in another believer’s way. He is persuaded that food is not unclean in itself, yet recognizes the seriousness of someone eating what they believe to be wrong.

The freedom to eat does not excuse harming another person’s faith. Paul makes the value of that person clear by naming Christ’s death for them. A meal is too small a thing to set above someone for whom Christ gave His life.

The kingdom of God is characterized by righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit. Paul changes the measure of success from whether a preferred food is served to whether the community’s life serves Christ and reflects those qualities.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the passage as placing love above displaying one’s freedom. The warning concerns serious harm to another’s faith, rather than winning a disagreement about food.

The warning also touches a wider disagreement about perseverance. Wesley’s note on verse 15 understands it as a real possibility of destruction for one for whom Christ died. Reformed churches following the Westminster Confession, chapter 17, teach that those God truly calls will not finally fall from grace. That doctrinal difference does not remove the passage’s direct demand to protect another person rather than use liberty carelessly.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Corinthians 8:7–13 gives a close parallel. Paul again describes a weak conscience, a freedom that can become a stumbling block, and a brother for whom Christ died. He connects wounding that person with sinning against Christ.

The value of the person is measured by Christ’s saving work. Care for another believer is therefore part of honoring the Lord who gave Himself for them. The connection turns knowledge and freedom toward the preservation and good of God’s people.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 14:19-23
passages.section_title: How can we build up another person’s faith?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 So then, let us pursue what leads to peace and to mutual edification. 20 Do not destroy the work of God for the sake of food. All food is clean, but it is wrong for a man to let his eating be a stumbling block. 21 It is better not to eat meat or drink wine or to do anything to cause your brother to stumble. 22 Keep your belief about such matters between yourself and God. Blessed is the one who does not condemn himself by what he approves. 23 But the one who has doubts is condemned if he eats, because his eating is not from faith; and everything that is not from faith is sin.
paragraphs: 19 So then, let us pursue what leads to peace and to mutual edification. 20 Do not destroy the work of God for the sake of food. All food is clean, but it is wrong for a man to let his eating be a stumbling block. 21 It is better not to eat meat or drink wine or to do anything to cause your brother to stumble.

22 Keep your belief about such matters between yourself and God. Blessed is the one who does not condemn himself by what he approves. 23 But the one who has doubts is condemned if he eats, because his eating is not from faith; and everything that is not from faith is sin.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul tells believers to pursue peace and the building up of one another. He repeats the disproportion in tearing down God’s work for the sake of food. Giving up meat or wine is preferable to using them in a way that causes another person to stumble.

Conviction about these matters can be held before God without being made a public test for others. The person with doubts must not borrow someone else’s confidence and act against their own belief about what is right.

The final statement about what is not from faith belongs to this discussion of conduct and conscience. Paul is warning about choosing to do what one believes displeases God. The emphasis is honest obedience, rather than treating private certainty as permission to do anything.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a call to use freedom with concern for another person’s conscience and growth. Building up faith matters more than proving how much freedom someone has. Both careless pressure and acting against one’s own conviction can turn an otherwise permitted practice into an occasion of sin.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Corinthians 10:23–33 similarly distinguishes what is permitted from what benefits and builds up others. Paul discusses eating with thanksgiving, taking another person’s conscience seriously and seeking the good of others.

That passage brings eating and drinking under the wider aim of God’s glory and the good of many. The ordinary meal becomes a place where love takes concrete form: knowledge is used to help people, and freedom can be set aside so that another person is strengthened.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 15:1-6
passages.section_title: What is strength for?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 We who are strong ought to bear with the shortcomings of the weak and not to please ourselves. 2 Each of us should please his neighbor for his good, to build him up. 3 For even Christ did not please Himself, but as it is written: “The insults of those who insult You have fallen on Me.” 4 For everything that was written in the past was written for our instruction, so that through endurance and the encouragement of the Scriptures, we might have hope. 5 Now may the God who gives endurance and encouragement grant you harmony with one another in Christ Jesus, 6 so that with one mind and one voice you may glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.
paragraphs: 1 We who are strong ought to bear with the shortcomings of the weak and not to please ourselves. 2 Each of us should please his neighbor for his good, to build him up. 3 For even Christ did not please Himself, but as it is written: “The insults of those who insult You have fallen on Me.”

4 For everything that was written in the past was written for our instruction, so that through endurance and the encouragement of the Scriptures, we might have hope. 5 Now may the God who gives endurance and encouragement grant you harmony with one another in Christ Jesus, 6 so that with one mind and one voice you may glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul continues the discussion of food, conscience and life together. Those who are strong are to bear with the weak, directing their concern toward the neighbor’s good and growth rather than their own satisfaction.

Christ supplies the pattern. Paul recalls that He did not please Himself and applies the words of Psalm 69 about bearing insults directed at God. The call to bear with others grows from what Christ has done, rather than from an expectation that differences will never be inconvenient.

Paul then speaks of Scripture giving instruction, endurance, encouragement and hope. He asks God to grant harmony in Christ so that the community can glorify the Father with one voice. Scripture and prayer serve a shared life shaped by Christ.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as a call for strength to be used in service of others. Bearing with someone aims at their good and growth. The model is Christ’s self-giving, and the goal is a community united in honoring God.
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul explicitly applies Psalm 69:7–13 to Christ. The psalm joins suffering for God’s sake, zeal for His house and prayer for His faithful help. Paul draws from that history a pattern for people whose Lord bore reproach.

The movement from Christ’s suffering to the community’s shared praise shows how His work is to shape the people He gathers. God gives endurance and encouragement so that people with different strengths can live together and honor Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 15:7-13
passages.section_title: Why does welcoming one another belong to God’s larger purpose?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 Accept one another, then, just as Christ accepted you, in order to bring glory to God. 8 For I tell you that Christ has become a servant of the circumcised on behalf of God’s truth, to confirm the promises made to the patriarchs, 9 so that the Gentiles may glorify God for His mercy. As it is written: “Therefore I will praise You among the Gentiles; I will sing hymns to Your name.” 10 Again, it says: “Rejoice, O Gentiles, with His people.” 11 And again: “Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles, and extol Him, all you peoples.” 12 And once more, Isaiah says: “The Root of Jesse will appear, One who will arise to rule over the Gentiles; in Him the Gentiles will put their hope.” 13 Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace as you believe in Him, so that you may overflow with hope by the power of the Holy Spirit.
paragraphs: 7 Accept one another, then, just as Christ accepted you, in order to bring glory to God. 8 For I tell you that Christ has become a servant of the circumcised on behalf of God’s truth, to confirm the promises made to the patriarchs, 9 so that the Gentiles may glorify God for His mercy. As it is written: “Therefore I will praise You among the Gentiles; I will sing hymns to Your name.”

10 Again, it says: “Rejoice, O Gentiles, with His people.” 11 And again: “Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles, and extol Him, all you peoples.” 12 And once more, Isaiah says: “The Root of Jesse will appear, One who will arise to rule over the Gentiles; in Him the Gentiles will put their hope.” 13 Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace as you believe in Him, so that you may overflow with hope by the power of the Holy Spirit.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul gives the standard for welcome: receive one another as Christ has received them, bringing glory to God. He then connects Christ’s service to the circumcised with God’s faithfulness to the patriarchs and the Gentiles’ praise for His mercy.

The quotations bring Israel and the nations into the same horizon of praise. Paul is explaining why fellowship across their differences belongs within what God has promised and accomplished through Christ.

He ends by asking the God of hope to fill them with joy and peace as they believe, so that hope overflows through the Spirit’s power. These gifts are sought from God for a community learning to live out its shared welcome.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as joining mutual acceptance with God’s faithfulness and mercy in Christ. Jews and Gentiles are brought into praise of the same God. The prayer for joy, peace and hope keeps their life together dependent on His work, rather than merely on their ability to avoid disagreement.
passages.god_plan_html:
The sequence of quotations makes the wider purpose explicit. Psalm 18:46–50 speaks of praising God among the nations; Deuteronomy 32:43 calls the nations to rejoice with His people; and Psalm 117 summons all peoples to praise Him for His love and faithfulness.

Isaiah 11:1–10 describes the Spirit-endowed ruler from Jesse’s line, His righteous rule and the nations seeking Him. Paul places Gentile hope in Christ within that promise. A community welcoming both Jews and Gentiles gives local expression to the wide praise these Scriptures anticipate.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 15:14-21
passages.section_title: What does Paul hope his ministry will offer to God?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 I myself am convinced, my brothers, that you yourselves are full of goodness, brimming with knowledge, and able to instruct one another. 15 However, I have written you a bold reminder on some points, because of the grace God has given me 16 to be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles in the priestly service of the gospel of God, so that the Gentiles might become an offering acceptable to God, sanctified by the Holy Spirit. 17 Therefore I exult in Christ Jesus in my service to God. 18 I will not presume to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me in leading the Gentiles to obedience by word and deed, 19 by the power of signs and wonders, and by the power of the Spirit of God. So from Jerusalem all the way around to Illyricum, I have fully proclaimed the gospel of Christ. 20 In this way I have aspired to preach the gospel where Christ was not known, so that I would not be building on someone else’s foundation. 21 Rather, as it is written: “Those who were not told about Him will see, and those who have not heard will understand.”
paragraphs: 14 I myself am convinced, my brothers, that you yourselves are full of goodness, brimming with knowledge, and able to instruct one another. 15 However, I have written you a bold reminder on some points, because of the grace God has given me 16 to be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles in the priestly service of the gospel of God, so that the Gentiles might become an offering acceptable to God, sanctified by the Holy Spirit.

17 Therefore I exult in Christ Jesus in my service to God. 18 I will not presume to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me in leading the Gentiles to obedience by word and deed, 19 by the power of signs and wonders, and by the power of the Spirit of God. So from Jerusalem all the way around to Illyricum, I have fully proclaimed the gospel of Christ. 20 In this way I have aspired to preach the gospel where Christ was not known, so that I would not be building on someone else’s foundation. 21 Rather, as it is written: “Those who were not told about Him will see, and those who have not heard will understand.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul affirms the Roman believers’ goodness, knowledge and ability to instruct one another, then explains why he has written boldly. His reminder belongs to the grace God has given him for ministry among the Gentiles.

He describes that ministry in priestly language. The verb is hierourgeō (hee-eh-roor-GEH-oh), ἱερουργέω, to carry out priestly service; see Thayer’s entry. The Gentiles are pictured as an offering made acceptable to God through the Holy Spirit’s sanctifying work.

Paul’s confidence is in what Christ has accomplished through him by word, deed and the Spirit’s power. His account reaches from Jerusalem toward Illyricum and explains his aim of announcing Christ where He was not yet known. He describes his particular mission rather than setting up a rivalry with workers in established churches.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as Paul explaining his calling and giving credit to Christ for its fruit. The priestly picture focuses on people brought to God through the gospel and sanctified by the Spirit. His desire to reach new places is a mission priority, not a claim that teaching and supporting existing believers have no value.
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul explicitly quotes Isaiah 52:13–15, where God’s servant is exalted and nations encounter what they had not previously been told or understood. Paul sees his proclamation of Christ among new hearers within that scriptural horizon.

The aim is larger than covering territory. People from the nations come to belong to God, with the Spirit making them an acceptable offering. The ministry serves God’s purpose of making Christ known and forming a people who respond to Him in faith and obedience.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 15:22-29
passages.section_title: How do travel plans and a collection belong to the same mission?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 That is why I have often been hindered from coming to you. 23 But now that there are no further opportunities for me in these regions, and since I have longed for many years to visit you, 24 I hope to see you on my way to Spain. And after I have enjoyed your company for a while, you can equip me for my journey. 25 Now, however, I am on my way to Jerusalem to serve the saints there. 26 For Macedonia and Achaia were pleased to make a contribution for the poor among the saints in Jerusalem. 27 They were pleased to do it, and indeed they owe it to them. For if the Gentiles have shared in their spiritual blessings, they are obligated to minister to them with material blessings. 28 So after I have completed this service and have safely delivered this bounty to them, I will set off to Spain by way of you. 29 I know that when I come to you, I will come in the fullness of the blessing of Christ.
paragraphs: 22 That is why I have often been hindered from coming to you. 23 But now that there are no further opportunities for me in these regions, and since I have longed for many years to visit you, 24 I hope to see you on my way to Spain. And after I have enjoyed your company for a while, you can equip me for my journey.

25 Now, however, I am on my way to Jerusalem to serve the saints there. 26 For Macedonia and Achaia were pleased to make a contribution for the poor among the saints in Jerusalem. 27 They were pleased to do it, and indeed they owe it to them. For if the Gentiles have shared in their spiritual blessings, they are obligated to minister to them with material blessings. 28 So after I have completed this service and have safely delivered this bounty to them, I will set off to Spain by way of you. 29 I know that when I come to you, I will come in the fullness of the blessing of Christ.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul explains that his work in other regions has delayed his visit to Rome. He hopes to see the believers there on his way to Spain, enjoy their company and receive their help for the journey.

First, he is going to Jerusalem with a contribution for poor believers. Macedonia and Achaia have shared willingly, and Paul describes their material help in relation to the spiritual blessings Gentiles have received.

The plans join fellowship, relief and the spread of the gospel. The Gentile churches’ gift gives practical expression to a relationship that crosses distance and background. Paul expects his visit to Rome to carry Christ’s blessing, while still speaking of plans yet to unfold.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a picture of partnership in mission and care for fellow believers. Material support expresses gratitude and shared belonging. Paul’s intended journey to Spain is clear; this passage itself does not record its completion.
passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 11:27–30 gives an earlier example of believers in Antioch sending relief to brothers in Judea, according to what each could give. It is a parallel in practical care across communities, rather than the same collection Paul describes here.

Romans connects such care with the spiritual blessings Gentiles have received. The unity explained throughout the letter takes material form: people who belong to Christ bear responsibility for one another’s needs as well as for making the gospel known.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 15:30-32
passages.section_title: What is Paul asking the church to pray for?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 30 Now I urge you, brothers, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the love of the Spirit, to join me in my struggle by praying to God for me. 31 Pray that I may be delivered from the unbelievers in Judea, and that my service in Jerusalem may be acceptable to the saints there, 32 so that by God’s will I may come to you with joy and together with you be refreshed.
paragraphs: 30 Now I urge you, brothers, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the love of the Spirit, to join me in my struggle by praying to God for me. 31 Pray that I may be delivered from the unbelievers in Judea, and that my service in Jerusalem may be acceptable to the saints there, 32 so that by God’s will I may come to you with joy and together with you be refreshed.

passages.context_html:
Paul is preparing to take a collection to Jerusalem before his hoped-for visit to Rome. He asks the church to share his struggle in prayer for safety, the acceptance of his service and a joyful visit that brings mutual refreshment.

The words by God’s will belong to the request itself. Prayer is presented as partnership with Paul’s work, while the outcome remains in God’s hands.

Acts records a difficult journey that includes rescue from a violent crowd, Roman custody and encouragement from believers who meet him near Rome (Acts 21:31–36; 28:15–16). Those details help readers assess the requests without reducing the entire story to comfort or to failure.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as an appeal for earnest prayer and partnership in the gospel. Specific requests and submission to God’s will appear together. The request is not a guarantee that the journey will be comfortable or that events will follow Paul’s preferred route.
passages.current_position_html: Prayer and Faith emphasizes entrusting the outcome to God. It applies this passage as a warning against treating prayer as a way to secure personal comfort or control the route ahead. The call is to trust God’s will and seek His purposes even when the path includes hardship.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
In Acts 23:11, the Lord assures Paul that he will testify in Rome as he has in Jerusalem. Acts 28:15–16, 30–31 shows that witness continuing through a journey and circumstances that include Roman custody.

The connection places the prayer request within God’s purpose of making Christ known. Danger and confinement do not bring that purpose to an end. The narrative also keeps room for genuine encouragement and help along a difficult route.

passages.section_title: How can prayer join someone else’s struggle?

passages.context_html:
Paul asks the Roman believers to join his struggle through prayer. His requests concern deliverance from opponents in Judea, the acceptance of his service in Jerusalem and a visit to Rome with joy and mutual refreshment.

He places the hoped-for visit under God’s will. The appeal makes prayer part of their shared ministry before they can meet in person. Paul names what he hopes for while acknowledging that the journey belongs to God.

Acts later records both danger and help: soldiers rescue him from a violent crowd, and he reaches Rome under guard. When believers come to meet him, he is encouraged and thanks God (Acts 21:31–36; 28:15–16). That fuller account includes hardship, deliverance and encouragement, so it should be consulted when considering how the requests unfolded.

passages.title: Romans 16:1-2
passages.section_title: Why does Paul ask the church to welcome Phoebe?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 I commend to you our sister Phoebe, a servant of the church in Cenchrea. 2 Welcome her in the Lord in a manner worthy of the saints, and assist her with anything she may need from you. For she has been a great help to many people, including me.
paragraphs: 1 I commend to you our sister Phoebe, a servant of the church in Cenchrea. 2 Welcome her in the Lord in a manner worthy of the saints, and assist her with anything she may need from you. For she has been a great help to many people, including me.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul commends Phoebe as a sister and a servant of the church in Cenchrea. He asks the Roman believers to receive her in a way worthy of God’s people and to help her with whatever she needs.

The word translated servant is diakonos (dee-AH-koh-noss), διάκονος. Its range includes servant, minister and deacon; see Thayer’s entry. Paul identifies her service with a particular church and honors the help she has given to many, including himself.

The request makes mutual care practical. Someone who has supported others is now to receive support from another community. Paul’s commendation calls the church to recognize her service and act on that recognition.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly recognize this as a commendation of Phoebe’s important service and a call to welcome and assist her. Wesley’s note on verse 1 understands her role as that of a deaconess, and Calvin’s comment also treats it as recognized service in the church. The passage identifies her work and the response it deserves without describing an appointment ceremony or a complete set of duties.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Peter 4:10–11 calls each believer to use God’s gifts in service to others, with the strength He provides and for His glory through Christ. Phoebe’s commendation gives a concrete example of service being recognized and supported within God’s people.

The movement between communities also matters: care is not confined to people already familiar to the receiving church. Shared belonging in the Lord becomes a reason to welcome and help a sister whose work has benefited others.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 16:3-5
passages.section_title: Why does Paul thank Prisca and Aquila?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 3 Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus, 4 who have risked their lives for me. Not only I but all the churches of the Gentiles are grateful to them. 5 Greet also the church that meets at their house. Greet my beloved Epenetus, who was the first convert to Christ in the province of Asia.
paragraphs: 3 Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus, 4 who have risked their lives for me. Not only I but all the churches of the Gentiles are grateful to them. 5 Greet also the church that meets at their house. Greet my beloved Epenetus, who was the first convert to Christ in the province of Asia.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul greets Prisca and Aquila as fellow workers in Christ who risked their lives for him. His gratitude is shared by the Gentile churches. Their service has mattered beyond a private friendship.

He also greets the church meeting at their house and Epenetus, the first convert to Christ in Asia. The word church is ekklēsia (ek-klay-SEE-ah), ἐκκλησία, an assembly or community; see Thayer’s entry. Here Paul distinguishes the gathered people from the house where they meet.

Prisca is also called Priscilla in Acts. Acts 18:24–26 describes the couple helping Apollos understand God’s way more accurately. Their household and their work provide support for both people and the message they share.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these greetings as honoring a couple’s costly partnership and a community gathering in their home. Paul gives thanks for service that includes risk, hospitality and work alongside others. The church at their house is a body of people to be greeted, not simply an address.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Corinthians 16:19 also sends greetings from Aquila, Prisca and the church at their house. Their hospitality belongs to a wider pattern of homes supporting the life and work of believers.

Ephesians 2:19–22 develops the larger picture of believers as God’s household and a dwelling place for Him by the Spirit, with Christ as the cornerstone. A house provides a meeting place; God is forming the people who gather into a shared life in Him.
passages.current_position_html: Worship as the Early Church Knew It understands the church here as the community of believers, distinct from the building in which they meet. The house provides a place for the assembly; the people are the church. The study uses this passage to emphasize shared spiritual life and service rather than identifying the church with an address.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

passages.title: Romans 16:5
passages.section_title: Who is the church that meets in their house?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 Greet also the church that meets at their house. Greet my beloved Epenetus, who was the first convert to Christ in the province of Asia.
paragraphs: 5 Greet also the church that meets at their house. Greet my beloved Epenetus, who was the first convert to Christ in the province of Asia.

passages.context_html:
Paul is greeting Prisca and Aquila, fellow workers who have risked their lives for him. He includes the church meeting in their house and then Epenetus, the first convert to Christ in Asia.

The greeting distinguishes the community from its meeting place. A household has opened space for believers to gather, and Paul greets those people as part of the church’s shared life.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as a local gathering of believers meeting in a home. The house gives the setting, while the church consists of the people Paul greets. The verse shows the practical contribution hospitality makes to the community.

The house provides a place for the assembly; the people are the church. The study uses this passage to emphasize shared spiritual life and service rather than identifying the church with an address.

passages.title: Romans 16:6-16
passages.section_title: Why does Paul honor so many people by name?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 Greet Mary, who has worked very hard for you. 7 Greet Andronicus and Junia, my fellow countrymen and fellow prisoners. They are outstanding among the apostles, and they were in Christ before I was. 8 Greet Ampliatus, my beloved in the Lord. 9 Greet Urbanus, our fellow worker in Christ, and my beloved Stachys. 10 Greet Apelles, who is approved in Christ. Greet those who belong to the household of Aristobulus. 11 Greet Herodion, my fellow countryman. Greet those from the household of Narcissus who are in the Lord. 12 Greet Tryphena and Tryphosa, women who have worked hard in the Lord. Greet my beloved Persis, who has worked very hard in the Lord. 13 Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother, who has been a mother to me as well. 14 Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers with them. 15 Greet Philologus and Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas and all the saints with them. 16 Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the churches of Christ send you greetings.

11 Greet Herodion, my fellow countryman. Greet those from the household of Narcissus who are in the Lord. 12 Greet Tryphena and Tryphosa, women who have worked hard in the Lord. Greet my beloved Persis, who has worked very hard in the Lord. 13 Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother, who has been a mother to me as well. 14 Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers with them. 15 Greet Philologus and Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas and all the saints with them. 16 Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the churches of Christ send you greetings.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The greetings honor many forms of faithful life: hard work, shared imprisonment, service with Paul, endurance and care. Men and women are named, along with people belonging to households and groups of believers.

Andronicus and Junia were in Christ before Paul and shared imprisonment with him. Mary, Tryphena, Tryphosa and Persis are remembered for their work. Rufus’s mother is honored for having been a mother to Paul as well. The details give the community a human shape beyond a list of teachings.

Paul ends with a call to greet one another with a holy kiss and passes on the greetings of the churches of Christ. Affection and recognition reach beyond those he names individually, linking the believers with a wider fellowship.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly recognize the greetings as evidence of shared labor and belonging across a network of believers. The description of Andronicus and Junia receives differing explanations.

The BSB presents them as outstanding among the apostles. In his homily on this passage, John Chrysostom explicitly identifies Junia as a woman and praises her as worthy of being called an apostle. Calvin’s comment on verse 7 understands apostles here more widely than the Twelve, including traveling workers who plant churches.

The ESV’s translation of verse 7 instead takes the description as people known and respected by the apostles. That difference concerns their relation to the group. Their early faith and costly service are clear; the phrase is not a complete account of every modern church office.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus describes those who do God’s will as His brother, sister and mother in Mark 3:31–35. This provides a wider New Testament setting for the family language and practical care running through Paul’s greetings.

Paul’s description of Rufus’s mother as a mother to him gives that belonging a personal form. Alongside the workers and fellow prisoners, she is remembered for care. God’s gathered people are connected through the ordinary and costly ways they serve one another.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 16:17-20
passages.section_title: How should the church respond to teaching that harms it?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 Now I urge you, brothers, to watch out for those who create divisions and obstacles that are contrary to the teaching you have learned. Turn away from them. 18 For such people are not serving our Lord Christ, but their own appetites. By smooth talk and flattery they deceive the hearts of the naive. 19 Everyone has heard about your obedience, so I rejoice over you. But I want you to be wise about what is good and innocent about what is evil. 20 The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.
paragraphs: 17 Now I urge you, brothers, to watch out for those who create divisions and obstacles that are contrary to the teaching you have learned. Turn away from them. 18 For such people are not serving our Lord Christ, but their own appetites. By smooth talk and flattery they deceive the hearts of the naive. 19 Everyone has heard about your obedience, so I rejoice over you. But I want you to be wise about what is good and innocent about what is evil. 20 The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul interrupts the greetings with a warning about people creating divisions and obstacles contrary to the teaching the believers have learned. He tells them to watch for these people and turn away from them.

The danger includes self-serving motives hidden by smooth speech and flattery. Paul connects their discernment with the obedience he already rejoices over: they are to be wise about good and innocent about evil.

The warning ends in hope. The God of peace will crush Satan under their feet, and Paul speaks the grace of Jesus over them. Their vigilance belongs within confidence in God’s victory, rather than confidence in their own ability to outmaneuver every deceiver.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as a call to discern and resist destructive teaching. Paul’s standard concerns what is contrary to the teaching received and the harm caused through deception. The warning belongs alongside his earlier call for patience in disputed practices, so disagreement itself is not enough to identify someone as a deceiver.
passages.god_plan_html:
The defeat of the serpent in Genesis 3:15 provides a biblical parallel to the promise of Satan’s defeat here. The shared theme is God overcoming the evil that threatens His people.

Hebrews 2:14–18 connects deliverance from the devil’s power with Christ sharing our humanity and dying for us. Romans assures a community facing deception that the God of peace will prevail. The promise rests in His work, giving them reason to remain faithful while resisting evil.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Romans 16:21-23
passages.section_title: Who joins Paul in sending these greetings?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 Timothy, my fellow worker, sends you greetings, as do Lucius, Jason, and Sosipater, my fellow countrymen. 22 I, Tertius, who wrote down this letter, greet you in the Lord. 23 Gaius, who has hosted me and all the church, sends you greetings. Erastus, the city treasurer, sends you greetings, as does our brother Quartus.
paragraphs: 21 Timothy, my fellow worker, sends you greetings, as do Lucius, Jason, and Sosipater, my fellow countrymen. 22 I, Tertius, who wrote down this letter, greet you in the Lord. 23 Gaius, who has hosted me and all the church, sends you greetings. Erastus, the city treasurer, sends you greetings, as does our brother Quartus.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The greetings now come from people with Paul. Timothy is named as a fellow worker, followed by Lucius, Jason and Sosipater. Tertius then identifies himself as the person who wrote down the letter and adds his greeting in the Lord.

Gaius is remembered as host to Paul and the church. Erastus, the city treasurer, and Quartus also send greetings. Writing, hospitality, shared work and personal relationships all appear in the final exchanges.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a glimpse of the people supporting and sharing Paul’s ministry. Tertius’s part in writing down the letter and Gaius’s hospitality show practical contributions alongside the work of those more widely known. The names should not be assigned detailed biographies beyond what can be established.

passages.title: Romans 16:25-27
passages.section_title: What does God make known through the gospel?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 25 Now to Him who is able to strengthen you by my gospel and by the proclamation of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery concealed for ages past 26 but now revealed and made known through the writings of the prophets by the command of the eternal God, in order to lead all nations to the obedience that comes from faith — 27 to the only wise God be glory forever through Jesus Christ! Amen.
paragraphs: 25 Now to Him who is able to strengthen you by my gospel and by the proclamation of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery concealed for ages past 26 but now revealed and made known through the writings of the prophets by the command of the eternal God, in order to lead all nations to the obedience that comes from faith — 27 to the only wise God be glory forever through Jesus Christ! Amen.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The letter closes by praising the God who can strengthen believers through the gospel and the proclamation of Jesus Christ. The emphasis returns to God’s power and the message on which their faith rests.

The mystery once concealed is now revealed and made known through the prophetic writings by God’s command. Its reach is all nations, and its purpose is the obedience that comes from faith.

These themes recall the letter’s opening: gospel, Jesus Christ, the Scriptures, the nations and the response of faith. Paul’s argument ends in glory to the only wise God through Jesus Christ.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as praise for God making His saving purpose known in Christ and strengthening His people through that message. Revelation moves toward a response of faith and obedience among the nations. The ending gathers the letter’s teaching into worship of the God whose wisdom and mercy it has described.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 3:4–6 gives an explicit explanation of the revealed mystery in Christ: through the gospel, Gentiles share the inheritance, the body and the promise with God’s people. What was hidden is now made known by the Spirit.

That connection brings Romans’ long discussion of Jews and Gentiles into its closing purpose. God makes Christ known so that people from the nations belong to Him in faith. The letter ends where its mission points: a people strengthened by His gospel, responding to Him and giving Him glory through Jesus.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 1:1-3
passages.section_title: Who does Paul say these believers are?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Paul, called to be an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and our brother Sosthenes, 2 To the church of God in Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus and called to be holy, together with all those everywhere who call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, their Lord and ours: 3 Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
paragraphs: 1 Paul, called to be an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and our brother Sosthenes, 2 To the church of God in Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus and called to be holy, together with all those everywhere who call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, their Lord and ours: 3 Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul opens with his calling as an apostle of Christ Jesus and names Sosthenes alongside him as a brother. He addresses the church as belonging to God. Before correcting its divisions and misconduct, he reminds its members who has called them and whom they belong to.

To be sanctified is to be made holy and devoted to God. The Greek verb is hagiazō (hah-gee-AH-zoh), ἁγιάζω; Thayer’s entry includes dedication to God and inward cleansing. Paul locates their holiness in Christ Jesus and calls them to a holy life. His later corrections show that this greeting does not mean their conduct is already faultless.

The greeting also reaches beyond Corinth to everyone everywhere who calls on Jesus Christ. He is their Lord and ours. The believers about to be corrected belong to a people much larger than their own congregation, and Paul begins by wishing them grace and peace from the Father and the Son.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this greeting as grounding the church’s identity in God’s call and its relationship with Christ, with holiness as both a gift and a calling. The words about believers everywhere also place the local congregation within the wider people who belong to the same Lord.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Peter 2:4–10 describes believers coming to Christ as living stones being built into a spiritual house. It calls them a holy people whose purpose includes declaring the goodness of the One who brought them out of darkness.

That wider picture helps explain why the church’s identity matters before Paul addresses its problems. God is forming a people who belong to Him and make His goodness known; the way they live together should reflect that calling.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 1:4-9
passages.section_title: Why does Paul give thanks before correcting them?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 4 I always thank my God for you because of the grace He has given you in Christ Jesus. 5 For in Him you have been enriched in every way, in all speech and all knowledge, 6 because our testimony about Christ was confirmed in you. 7 Therefore you do not lack any spiritual gift as you eagerly await the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ. 8 He will sustain you to the end, so that you will be blameless on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. 9 God, who has called you into fellowship with His Son Jesus Christ our Lord, is faithful.
paragraphs: 4 I always thank my God for you because of the grace He has given you in Christ Jesus. 5 For in Him you have been enriched in every way, in all speech and all knowledge, 6 because our testimony about Christ was confirmed in you.

7 Therefore you do not lack any spiritual gift as you eagerly await the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ. 8 He will sustain you to the end, so that you will be blameless on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. 9 God, who has called you into fellowship with His Son Jesus Christ our Lord, is faithful.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul gives thanks for grace God has already given the Corinthians in Christ. Their ability to speak and their knowledge are gifts, rather than achievements that make one group better than another. His gratitude prepares the ground for corrections about how they use those gifts.

The church does not lack spiritual gifts while it waits for Christ to be revealed. Paul is addressing the community; he is not saying every member has every gift. Later, in 1 Corinthians 12:12–27, he explains how different members contribute to one body.

Paul directs their hope to the One who sustains them and to God’s faithfulness. The coming day of Christ gives their present life a destination. God has called them into fellowship with His Son, so their confidence has a deeper basis than their abilities, personalities or current level of maturity.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians recognize these verses as strong encouragement to rely on God’s faithfulness while awaiting Christ. Where traditions differ is whether someone truly brought into grace can finally turn away from it.

The Reformed teaching in Westminster Confession 17.1–3 holds that those God has truly accepted in Christ will be preserved to the end, although they can fall into serious sin. The Methodist Articles, Article XII, allow that a believer can depart from grace and can be restored through God’s grace. Wesley’s note on verse 8 reads Paul’s assurance with the need to continue relying on God. These readings agree that perseverance depends on His help; they differ over whether final falling away remains possible.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 1:9–14 places believers’ hope within God’s purpose to bring all things in heaven and on earth together in Christ. The promised Spirit is a pledge of the inheritance still to come.

The Corinthians’ waiting therefore belongs to something larger than the improvement of their own congregation. God’s present gifts sustain His people as they look toward the fulfillment of His purposes in Christ.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 1:10-17
passages.section_title: Why is following a favorite teacher dividing the church?

versions.label: BSB

Was Paul crucified for you? Were you baptized into the name of Paul? 14 I thank God that I did not baptize any of you except Crispus and Gaius, 15 so no one can say that you were baptized into my name. 16 Yes, I also baptized the household of Stephanas; beyond that I do not remember if I baptized anyone else. 17 For Christ did not send me to baptize, but to preach the gospel, not with words of wisdom, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power.
paragraphs: 10 I appeal to you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that all of you agree together, so that there may be no divisions among you and that you may be united in mind and conviction. 11 My brothers, some from Chloe’s household have informed me that there are quarrels among you. 12 What I mean is this: Individuals among you are saying, “I follow Paul,” “I follow Apollos,” “I follow Cephas,” or “I follow Christ.” 13 Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Were you baptized into the name of Paul?

14 I thank God that I did not baptize any of you except Crispus and Gaius, 15 so no one can say that you were baptized into my name. 16 Yes, I also baptized the household of Stephanas; beyond that I do not remember if I baptized anyone else. 17 For Christ did not send me to baptize, but to preach the gospel, not with words of wisdom, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
People from Chloe’s household have reported quarrels. Some believers identify themselves by Paul, Apollos or Cephas, who is Peter; another slogan claims Christ. Paul calls them back to agreement in the name of their shared Lord rather than allowing these names to become rival loyalties.

His questions put the issue plainly. Christ cannot be divided among competing groups. Paul did not die for them, and they were not baptized into his name. Gratitude for a teacher is different from treating that person as the source of salvation or the basis for looking down on other believers.

Paul recalls baptizing Crispus, Gaius and the household of Stephanas, then says he does not remember others. His central commission was to preach the gospel. Because he actually baptized people, the contrast in verse 17 does not mean baptism was forbidden to him. It brings the focus back to Christ’s cross rather than the reputation of the person speaking or baptizing.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand Paul to be correcting rival loyalties that damage the church’s unity, while distinguishing his main preaching assignment from the work of baptizing. Calvin’s comment on verse 17 and Wesley’s note both read the contrast as a matter of his principal task, rather than a rejection of baptism.
passages.god_plan_html:
In John 17:20–23, Jesus prays for those who will believe through His disciples’ message to be one. He connects their unity with the world recognizing that the Father sent Him.

That prayer adds a purpose beyond avoiding unpleasant quarrels. The church’s shared life should bear witness to Christ. Turning His servants into competing centers of loyalty obscures the One whose message they carry.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 1:18-25
passages.section_title: How can the cross reveal God’s wisdom and power?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 For the message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God. 19 For it is written: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise; the intelligence of the intelligent I will frustrate.” 20 Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the philosopher of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world? 21 For since in the wisdom of God the world through its wisdom did not know Him, God was pleased through the foolishness of what was preached to save those who believe. 22 Jews demand signs and Greeks search for wisdom, 23 but we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles, 24 but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. 25 For the foolishness of God is wiser than man’s wisdom, and the weakness of God is stronger than man’s strength.
paragraphs: 18 For the message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God. 19 For it is written: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise; the intelligence of the intelligent I will frustrate.” 20 Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the philosopher of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world? 21 For since in the wisdom of God the world through its wisdom did not know Him, God was pleased through the foolishness of what was preached to save those who believe.

22 Jews demand signs and Greeks search for wisdom, 23 but we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles, 24 but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. 25 For the foolishness of God is wiser than man’s wisdom, and the weakness of God is stronger than man’s strength.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul turns from impressive messengers to the message itself. The cross is dismissed as foolishness by those who are perishing, but believers encounter God’s saving power in it. The point is not that the gospel is actually foolish. God’s way of saving overturns the standards by which people expect to recognize wisdom and strength.

He quotes Isaiah 29:14, where God frustrates human wisdom. People have not come to know Him through the world’s wisdom, yet He saves those who believe through the message being preached.

Paul describes demands for signs and searches for wisdom, then announces Christ crucified. The crucified Messiah confronts both expectations, yet Christ is God’s wisdom and power for those called from among Jews and Greeks. Paul is describing responses to the message, not claiming that every Jewish or Gentile person reacts in the same way; verse 24 explicitly includes believers from both.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians share the central reading that salvation comes through the crucified Christ rather than human brilliance or strength. Where traditions differ is how God’s call brings a person to faith.

The Reformed Westminster Confession 10.1–2 teaches that God renews those He has chosen so that they willingly come to Christ. In a Wesleyan reading, God’s grace first enables a response: the Methodist Articles, Article VIII, deny that people can turn to Him by their own unaided strength. Wesley’s note on verse 24 describes the called as those who obey the heavenly call. Neither reading makes intelligence or social standing the reason someone is saved; they differ over how grace and the human response relate.
passages.god_plan_html:
After His resurrection, Jesus explains in Luke 24:25–27, 44–47 that the Messiah’s suffering and resurrection belong to the fulfillment of Scripture. Repentance for the forgiveness of sins is then to be proclaimed in His name to all nations.

The cross, which can look like the collapse of hope, belongs to the way God fulfills His saving purpose. Paul’s preaching of the crucified Christ to Jews and Gentiles fits that worldwide mission. The shame of the death does not cancel the purpose Jesus explains.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 1:26-31
passages.section_title: Why does Paul ask them to remember who they were?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 26 Brothers, consider the time of your calling: Not many of you were wise by human standards; not many were powerful; not many were of noble birth. 27 But God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise; God chose the weak things of the world to shame the strong. 28 He chose the lowly and despised things of the world, and the things that are not, to nullify the things that are, 29 so that no one may boast in His presence. 30 It is because of Him that you are in Christ Jesus, who has become for us wisdom from God: our righteousness, holiness, and redemption. 31 Therefore, as it is written: “Let him who boasts boast in the Lord.”
paragraphs: 26 Brothers, consider the time of your calling: Not many of you were wise by human standards; not many were powerful; not many were of noble birth. 27 But God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise; God chose the weak things of the world to shame the strong. 28 He chose the lowly and despised things of the world, and the things that are not, to nullify the things that are, 29 so that no one may boast in His presence.

30 It is because of Him that you are in Christ Jesus, who has become for us wisdom from God: our righteousness, holiness, and redemption. 31 Therefore, as it is written: “Let him who boasts boast in the Lord.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul asks the Corinthians to look at their own calling. Not many were considered wise, influential or well born. He says not many, rather than none: his point does not exclude educated, powerful or wealthy people from faith.

God has chosen people the world overlooks and treats as insignificant, exposing the limits of its judgments. That leaves no basis for claiming a superior place before Him. It also undercuts the church’s effort to gain status through attachment to a preferred teacher.

Their life in Christ comes from God. Christ is their wisdom, righteousness, holiness and redemption: what they need to be put right with God, made holy and freed comes through Him. Paul closes with Jeremiah 9:23–24, where knowing the Lord replaces boasting in wisdom, strength or riches.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these verses as removing human grounds for boasting and directing gratitude to God for life in Christ. Christ’s gifts include both being put right with God and being made holy; Wesley’s note on verse 30 treats holiness as a present work of grace as well as looking ahead to complete deliverance.
passages.god_plan_html:
A useful parallel appears in 1 Samuel 16:6–13. Samuel first judges by appearance, but God directs him to David, the youngest son who was tending sheep. This is a parallel in how God overturns human expectations, rather than a claim that Paul is quoting that event.

Paul later describes God’s power working through his own weakness in 2 Corinthians 12:7–10. Together these passages show why the people God uses need not match the world’s measures of importance. Dependence on Him makes His work visible rather than turning the person serving into the source of glory.
