passages.title: 1 Corinthians 2:1-5
passages.section_title: What did Paul want their faith to rest on?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 When I came to you, brothers, I did not come with eloquence or wisdom as I proclaimed to you the testimony about God. 2 For I resolved to know nothing while I was with you except Jesus Christ and Him crucified. 3 I came to you in weakness and fear, and with much trembling. 4 My message and my preaching were not with persuasive words of wisdom, but with a demonstration of the Spirit’s power, 5 so that your faith would not rest on men’s wisdom, but on God’s power.
paragraphs: 1 When I came to you, brothers, I did not come with eloquence or wisdom as I proclaimed to you the testimony about God. 2 For I resolved to know nothing while I was with you except Jesus Christ and Him crucified. 3 I came to you in weakness and fear, and with much trembling. 4 My message and my preaching were not with persuasive words of wisdom, but with a demonstration of the Spirit’s power, 5 so that your faith would not rest on men’s wisdom, but on God’s power.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul asks the Corinthians to remember how he first came to them. He did not make an impressive performance the foundation of his message. Jesus Christ and His crucifixion were at its center, and Paul himself came in weakness, fear and trembling.

That focus does not mean he taught nothing about Jesus’ life, resurrection or commands. It identifies the center around which his preaching belongs. The message should direct people to the crucified Christ rather than make them dependent on admiration for the messenger.

Paul contrasts persuasive words of wisdom with the Spirit’s power. His stated purpose is that their faith should rest on God’s power. A teacher’s confidence, skill or reputation cannot take that place. Paul’s own weakness helps expose the difference between the messenger and the source of saving power.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these verses as placing confidence in God rather than the preacher’s ability to impress. On the Spirit’s demonstration, Calvin’s comment on verse 4 includes God’s powerful work throughout Paul’s ministry, rather than limiting it to miracles; Wesley’s note emphasizes the Spirit’s convincing work on the conscience. These explanations do not turn the passage into a ban on clear reasoning or careful teaching.
passages.god_plan_html:
2 Corinthians 4:5–12 develops this pattern through the picture of treasure carried in jars of clay. The servants are vulnerable, but the power belongs to God. Paul connects their suffering with Jesus’ death and with His life being made visible through them.

Weakness is therefore not automatically a sign that God’s work has failed. His saving message can reach others through people who depend on Him in the middle of hardship. The servant does not have to become the source of strength in order for God to work.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 2:6-9
passages.section_title: What wisdom had the rulers failed to recognize?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 Among the mature, however, we speak a message of wisdom—but not the wisdom of this age or of the rulers of this age, who are coming to nothing. 7 No, we speak of the mysterious and hidden wisdom of God, which He destined for our glory before time began. 8 None of the rulers of this age understood it. For if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. 9 Rather, as it is written: “No eye has seen, no ear has heard, no heart has imagined, what God has prepared for those who love Him.”
paragraphs: 6 Among the mature, however, we speak a message of wisdom—but not the wisdom of this age or of the rulers of this age, who are coming to nothing. 7 No, we speak of the mysterious and hidden wisdom of God, which He destined for our glory before time began. 8 None of the rulers of this age understood it. For if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. 9 Rather, as it is written: “No eye has seen, no ear has heard, no heart has imagined, what God has prepared for those who love Him.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul does speak wisdom, but it is different from the wisdom associated with the present age and its passing rulers. The word translated mature is teleios (TEH-lay-oss), τέλειος. Thayer’s entry includes full-grown or mature and applies it here in contrast with infants in Christ. Paul is describing growth in understanding, rather than a secret class of believers who no longer need correction.

God’s wisdom was hidden and destined for His people’s glory before time began. The rulers failed to recognize it and crucified the Lord of glory. Their judgment about Jesus did not reveal the true value of the One they rejected.

Paul then draws on Isaiah 64:4, which speaks of the God who acts for those who wait for Him. The next verse is essential to Paul’s point: God has revealed these things by His Spirit. This is not simply a statement that nothing God has prepared can ever be known.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as God’s saving wisdom being hidden from the world’s rulers and made known through the Spirit. Readers differ over the scope of the rulers: Wesley’s notes on verses 6–8 discuss Jewish and Gentile rulers, while the USCCB note on verse 8 sees human rulers with spiritual powers behind them. Both readings recognize the crucifixion as a failure to understand who Christ is.
passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 4:27–28 names Herod, Pilate, Gentiles and people of Israel in the opposition to Jesus, while placing what happened within God’s purpose. Human rejection did not take Him outside God’s saving plan.

Jesus’ own explanation in Luke 24:26–27, 44–47 connects His suffering with glory, resurrection and the worldwide proclamation of forgiveness. Paul’s contrast between the rejected Lord and God’s hidden wisdom belongs within that larger story.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 2:10-13
passages.section_title: How does God make His gifts known?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 But God has revealed it to us by the Spirit. The Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God. 11 For who among men knows the thoughts of man except his own spirit within him? So too, no one knows the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God. 12 We have not received the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God, that we may understand what God has freely given us. 13 And this is what we speak, not in words taught us by human wisdom, but in words taught by the Spirit, expressing spiritual truths in spiritual words.
paragraphs: 10 But God has revealed it to us by the Spirit. The Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God. 11 For who among men knows the thoughts of man except his own spirit within him? So too, no one knows the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God. 12 We have not received the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God, that we may understand what God has freely given us. 13 And this is what we speak, not in words taught us by human wisdom, but in words taught by the Spirit, expressing spiritual truths in spiritual words.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
God has revealed what human observation could not uncover on its own. The Spirit knows even the deep things of God. Paul compares this with a person’s own spirit knowing that person’s thoughts; his point is the Spirit’s intimate knowledge of God, rather than a promise that believers become all-knowing.

Those who have received the Spirit can understand what God has freely given. Understanding is itself part of the gift. The Corinthians should not credit their social standing or their favorite teacher with opening a way into God’s wisdom.

Paul also identifies the source of the message he and his fellow messengers speak. It is taught by the Spirit, rather than produced by human wisdom. The closing phrase is rendered in the BSB as spiritual truths in spiritual words; its footnote also allows the sense of explaining them to spiritual people. In either case, the message and its understanding depend on the Spirit.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these verses as identifying the Spirit as the source of revealed truth and of the understanding needed to receive it. Wesley’s notes on verses 10–13 emphasize both the Spirit’s knowledge of God and His teaching of the message; the two possible senses of verse 13 are also acknowledged in the USCCB note.
passages.god_plan_html:
In John 14:26, Jesus promises His disciples that the Spirit will teach them and bring His words to mind. John 16:13–15 adds that the Spirit will make known what belongs to Christ and glorify Him. These promises give a setting for the Spirit-taught witness Paul describes.

Ephesians 3:4–6 gives a concrete example of what God has revealed by the Spirit: Gentiles share the inheritance, body and promise in Christ through the gospel. Revelation makes God’s saving purpose known and gathers people into a shared life; it is more than private spiritual insight.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 2:14-16
passages.section_title: What does it mean to have the mind of Christ?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 The natural man does not accept the things that come from the Spirit of God. For they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them, because they are spiritually discerned. 15 The spiritual man judges all things, but he himself is not subject to anyone’s judgment. 16 “For who has known the mind of the Lord, so as to instruct Him?” But we have the mind of Christ.
paragraphs: 14 The natural man does not accept the things that come from the Spirit of God. For they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them, because they are spiritually discerned. 15 The spiritual man judges all things, but he himself is not subject to anyone’s judgment. 16 “For who has known the mind of the Lord, so as to instruct Him?” But we have the mind of Christ.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul contrasts the person who does not receive the things of God’s Spirit with the person whose judgment is shaped by the Spirit. The message dismissed as foolish cannot be rightly received simply by applying the world’s standards of wisdom and importance.

The spiritual person’s judgment comes from the Spirit’s help. That does not make every personal opinion correct or every criticism invalid. Paul is writing to correct this church, and immediately afterward he calls its jealous and quarrelsome members infants in Christ. Possessing the Spirit does not make growth and correction unnecessary.

Paul draws on Isaiah 40:13, where no one can instruct the Lord, then says that we have the mind of Christ. God’s people receive understanding from Him. They are not His counselors, and the point is not that each believer now knows everything God knows.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these verses as teaching dependence on the Spirit to receive God’s truth. Calvin’s comment on verse 15 explicitly denies that spiritual people are free from every error, and Wesley’s note on verse 16 relates the mind of Christ to understanding God’s saving purpose. The passage gives no individual a license to place personal claims beyond examination.
passages.god_plan_html:
Philippians 2:1–11 connects shared life in the Spirit with a concrete call to share Christ’s way of thinking: humility, care for others and service. Christ’s own example leads through obedience and the cross to His exaltation.

This is a helpful connection, rather than a claim that the two passages address exactly the same question. Together they show why receiving understanding from Christ should lead away from self-importance. God forms a people who learn His truth and whose life together reflects His Son.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 3:1-4
passages.section_title: What shows that the Corinthians still need to grow?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Brothers, I could not address you as spiritual, but as worldly—as infants in Christ. 2 I gave you milk, not solid food, for you were not yet ready for solid food. In fact, you are still not ready, 3 for you are still worldly. For since there is jealousy and dissension among you, are you not worldly? Are you not walking in the way of man? 4 For when one of you says, “I follow Paul,” and another, “I follow Apollos,” are you not mere men?
paragraphs: 1 Brothers, I could not address you as spiritual, but as worldly—as infants in Christ. 2 I gave you milk, not solid food, for you were not yet ready for solid food. In fact, you are still not ready, 3 for you are still worldly. For since there is jealousy and dissension among you, are you not worldly? Are you not walking in the way of man? 4 For when one of you says, “I follow Paul,” and another, “I follow Apollos,” are you not mere men?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul has just spoken about receiving understanding through the Spirit. He now tells the Corinthians that he could not address them as spiritually mature. They are brothers and infants in Christ, yet their conduct still follows the world’s pattern.

Milk and solid food picture teaching suited to different stages of growth. Paul gave them what they were ready to receive, but their continuing unreadiness is now a problem. Having received gifts and knowledge has not automatically produced a mature way of living.

His evidence is concrete: jealousy, quarrels and rival claims to Paul or Apollos. Spiritual growth should affect how they treat one another. The issue is not merely whether they can discuss difficult subjects, but whether their shared life reflects what they have received from Christ.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a rebuke of believers whose jealousy and divisions reveal immaturity. Wesley’s notes on verses 1–4 distinguish having gifts from growing in grace, while treating Paul’s teaching as adapted to what his hearers can receive.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 4:11–16 describes Christ giving servants to equip His people so that the whole body grows toward maturity. Speaking the truth in love and each part contributing belong to that growth.

God’s purpose for teaching therefore reaches beyond increasing someone’s knowledge. He is building a people who grow together in Christ. Rival loyalties work against the shared maturity for which His gifts are given.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 3:5-9
passages.section_title: Who makes the church grow?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 What then is Apollos? And what is Paul? They are servants through whom you believed, as the Lord has assigned to each his role. 6 I planted the seed and Apollos watered it, but God made it grow. 7 So neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but only God, who makes things grow. 8 He who plants and he who waters are one in purpose, and each will be rewarded according to his own labor. 9 For we are God’s fellow workers; you are God’s field, God’s building.
paragraphs: 5 What then is Apollos? And what is Paul? They are servants through whom you believed, as the Lord has assigned to each his role. 6 I planted the seed and Apollos watered it, but God made it grow. 7 So neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but only God, who makes things grow. 8 He who plants and he who waters are one in purpose, and each will be rewarded according to his own labor. 9 For we are God’s fellow workers; you are God’s field, God’s building.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul and Apollos are servants through whom the Corinthians believed, each carrying out a role the Lord assigned. Paul pictures himself planting and Apollos watering. Their work differs, but the growth comes from God.

This does not make their labor pointless. Paul immediately speaks of each worker receiving a reward according to that worker’s labor. Dependence on God leaves room for diligent service while removing the claim that the servant is the source of life.

The two workers share one purpose rather than competing for ownership of the crop. The believers are God’s field and God’s building. These pictures prepare for Paul’s next warning about the responsibility of those who build, and they remind the church whose people they are.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand planting and watering as complementary service, with God giving the growth. Wesley’s note on verse 8 emphasizes faithful labor rather than apparent success as the measure of the worker’s reward; the servants’ different tasks are no reason to divide the community.
passages.god_plan_html:
In John 4:35–38, Jesus describes sowing and reaping as work in which different people contribute and rejoice together. His disciples enter a harvest for which others have labored.

This is a helpful parallel to Paul’s picture. God’s work is larger than one person’s contribution or one stage of ministry. A servant can work faithfully without claiming the whole harvest, and can value the work of someone whose task is different.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 3:10-15
passages.section_title: What happens when the work is tested?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 By the grace God has given me, I laid a foundation as an expert builder, and someone else is building on it. But each one must be careful how he builds. 11 For no one can lay a foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ. 12 If anyone builds on this foundation using gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, or straw, 13 his workmanship will be evident, because the Day will bring it to light. It will be revealed with fire, and the fire will prove the quality of each man’s work. 14 If what he has built survives, he will receive a reward. 15 If it is burned up, he will suffer loss. He himself will be saved, but only as if through the flames.
paragraphs: 10 By the grace God has given me, I laid a foundation as an expert builder, and someone else is building on it. But each one must be careful how he builds. 11 For no one can lay a foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ.

12 If anyone builds on this foundation using gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, or straw, 13 his workmanship will be evident, because the Day will bring it to light. It will be revealed with fire, and the fire will prove the quality of each man’s work. 14 If what he has built survives, he will receive a reward. 15 If it is burned up, he will suffer loss. He himself will be saved, but only as if through the flames.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul develops the building picture. By God’s grace he laid the foundation, Jesus Christ, and others are building on it. The warning is to take care how they build. The community is not a project in which every method or teaching is equally sound.

Gold, silver and precious stones are contrasted with wood, hay and straw. The materials picture work whose quality will be exposed. The coming Day will reveal what the builders have done, rather than leaving the judgment to the church’s present admiration for a teacher.

Work that survives receives a reward; work that burns brings loss. Paul says the builder in verse 15 is saved, but as someone escaping through flames. The passage distinguishes the fate of that builder from the fate of the work. This is a serious warning about wasted or harmful contributions, not a reason to treat service as unimportant.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians recognize a warning that God will judge the quality of work built on Christ. Where traditions differ is how this fire relates to purification after death.

The Catholic Church teaches a final purification for those who die in God’s grace but are not yet completely purified. Catechism 1030–1031 and footnote 605 cite verse 15 among the scriptural references for cleansing fire. This concerns people assured of salvation, rather than a second opportunity to choose salvation after death. Catholic interpretation of this particular passage is not uniform: the USCCB note on verse 15 says its immediate subject is not purgatory.

The Reformed Westminster Confession 32.1 instead teaches that righteous souls are made perfect in holiness and received into heaven at death. Wesley’s notes on verses 13–15 read the fire as the testing of teaching at the day of judgment and the loss as loss of reward. These readings distinguish testing what someone has built from a period of purification after death.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Matthew 24:45–47, Jesus describes a servant entrusted with care for the household while the master is away. The master’s return reveals whether that responsibility has been carried out faithfully.

This is a parallel in accountability, rather than a claim that every detail of the two pictures corresponds. The people entrusted to a servant’s care belong to the Master. Work that truly serves them matters to Him even when public recognition gives an unreliable picture.
passages.current_position_html: Our study What Is the True Church? identifies Christ Himself as the church’s foundation. A teacher, institution or system must serve Him rather than take His place. This is the study’s conclusion about the foundation in verse 11; it does not establish a site conclusion about every detail of the fire and reward in these verses.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 3:11
passages.section_title: Who is the church’s foundation?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 For no one can lay a foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ.
paragraphs: 11 For no one can lay a foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ.

passages.context_html:
This verse stands within Paul’s picture of building God’s community. He laid the foundation through his preaching; others must take care how they build on it. That foundation is Jesus Christ, rather than Paul himself.

The surrounding verses test the quality of what is built. Teachers and members are accountable for their contribution, but no one is free to replace Christ with a rival foundation. The statement answers the church’s tendency to make a human leader the basis of its identity.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this verse as making Jesus Christ the indispensable foundation of the church. The surrounding building picture calls those who teach and serve to build faithfully on Him.
passages.current_position_html: Our study What Is the True Church? identifies the living person of Christ as the church’s foundation. No teaching, title, institution or admired personality can take His place. Those who lead and teach must help people remain faithful to Him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 2:19–22 uses a related building picture, naming the apostles and prophets in the foundation and Christ as the cornerstone. Their witness belongs to the structure whose unity and growth depend on Him.

Paul’s pictures give different details, but both direct the community to Christ. God is forming a household and dwelling by the Spirit, rather than rival groups whose ultimate identity rests on the servants who taught them.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 3:16
passages.section_title: Where does God’s Spirit dwell?
passages.note: A core church passage: the people of God are His temple.

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 Do you not know that you yourselves are God’s temple, and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?
paragraphs: 16 Do you not know that you yourselves are God’s temple, and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?

passages.context_html:
Paul has called the Corinthians God’s field and building. He now tells them that they themselves are God’s temple because His Spirit dwells among them. The immediate concern is the community being built up or harmed by its members and teachers.

The word for temple, naos (nah-OSS), ναός, is used for a sanctuary. Thayer’s entry applies it here to the community in which God’s Spirit dwells. Their holiness comes from belonging to Him, rather than from the importance of a place or a human leader.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand Paul to be describing the believers together as God’s temple. Calvin’s comment on verse 16 explicitly reads the community collectively as one temple, a reading that fits the chapter’s concern with building up the church.
passages.current_position_html: Our study What Is the True Church? draws on this verse to locate God’s dwelling in His people. It calls for reverence expressed through daily conduct and relationships, rather than treating a building as the source of God’s presence.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 2:19–22 describes people once separated being built together in Christ as a dwelling for God by the Spirit. 1 Peter 2:4–10 similarly calls believers living stones and a holy people who declare God’s goodness.

The temple picture gives a purpose to life together. God forms a people who belong to Him and make Him known. How they treat one another should reflect the presence of the One who dwells among them.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 3:16-17
passages.section_title: Why is harming this community so serious?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 Do you not know that you yourselves are God’s temple, and that God’s Spirit dwells in you? 17 If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him; for God’s temple is holy, and you are that temple.
paragraphs: 16 Do you not know that you yourselves are God’s temple, and that God’s Spirit dwells in you? 17 If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him; for God’s temple is holy, and you are that temple.

passages.context_html:
God’s building is now called His temple. Paul is addressing the gathered community: they themselves are God’s temple because His Spirit dwells among them. The warning belongs to his concern about what teachers and members are doing to that community.

The Greek word for temple is naos (nah-OSS), ναός, used for a sanctuary. Thayer’s entry identifies its use here for a community in which God’s Spirit dwells. Paul gives ordinary believers the dignity and responsibility of belonging to God’s holy dwelling.

The warning about destroying the temple is stronger than the earlier picture of work burning up. God takes the harm done to His people seriously. Divisions and teaching that corrupt the community cannot be treated as harmless competition among personalities.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as identifying the community as God’s holy dwelling and warning against corrupting it. Calvin’s comment on verse 16 explicitly treats the believers collectively as one temple; Wesley’s note on verse 17 reads destruction as a warning of judgment, distinct from the builder who is saved in verse 15.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Worship as the Early Church Knew It reads these verses as describing God’s people together as His temple. The Spirit’s presence calls for reverence in how we treat the community and live before God. A meeting place must not displace the people themselves as the focus of that responsibility.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 2:19–22 describes people brought together in Christ as a holy temple and a dwelling for God by the Spirit. The picture belongs to God making one household from those once separated.

Revelation 21:22–27 carries the theme of God’s presence to its final setting: the city has no temple because God and the Lamb are its temple, and the nations walk by its light. Caring for God’s people now belongs within His larger purpose to dwell with them in holiness.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 3:18-23
passages.section_title: Why stop boasting in people when all things are yours?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 Let no one deceive himself. If any of you thinks he is wise in this age, he should become a fool, so that he may become wise. 19 For the wisdom of this world is foolishness in God’s sight. As it is written: “He catches the wise in their craftiness.” 20 And again, “The Lord knows that the thoughts of the wise are futile.” 21 Therefore, stop boasting in men. All things are yours, 22 whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas or the world or life or death or the present or the future. All of them belong to you, 23 and you belong to Christ, and Christ belongs to God.
paragraphs: 18 Let no one deceive himself. If any of you thinks he is wise in this age, he should become a fool, so that he may become wise. 19 For the wisdom of this world is foolishness in God’s sight. As it is written: “He catches the wise in their craftiness.” 20 And again, “The Lord knows that the thoughts of the wise are futile.”

21 Therefore, stop boasting in men. All things are yours, 22 whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas or the world or life or death or the present or the future. All of them belong to you, 23 and you belong to Christ, and Christ belongs to God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul warns against self-deception. Anyone who thinks himself wise by this age’s standards must be willing to be regarded as foolish in order to receive God’s wisdom. The challenge is to pride and misplaced confidence, rather than a command to stop thinking or learning.

He draws on Job 5:13 and Psalm 94:11 to show how God exposes human cleverness and knows the limits of human thoughts. Those sources turn attention from our ability to outsmart others toward the God who knows and judges.

Paul then reverses the Corinthians’ way of relating to their teachers. Instead of belonging to rival leaders, they receive the service of Paul, Apollos and Cephas as shared gifts. Even life, death, the present and the future are included in the assurance. They belong to Christ, and Christ belongs to God; their security and identity do not depend on winning a contest between human groups.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these verses as ending the appeal to abandon pride in human leaders and recognize shared belonging to Christ. Wesley’s notes on verses 21–23 understand the teachers as serving the believers, with present and future circumstances under God’s care, rather than granting permission to possess anything someone wants.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 8:31–39 gives a closely related assurance: God’s love in Christ holds His people through death, life, present circumstances and what is to come. Neither danger nor death can make Christ cease to love them.

This connection shows how far the answer to pride in rival groups reaches. Belonging to Christ gives a hope larger than a teacher’s reputation or a congregation’s present status. Shared gratitude and trust can replace the effort to secure importance through a preferred human name.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 4:1-5
passages.section_title: How should the church judge its teachers?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 So then, men ought to regard us as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. 2 Now it is required of stewards that they be found faithful. 3 I care very little, however, if I am judged by you or by any human court. In fact, I do not even judge myself. 4 My conscience is clear, but that does not vindicate me. It is the Lord who judges me. 5 Therefore judge nothing before the appointed time; wait until the Lord comes. He will bring to light what is hidden in darkness and will expose the motives of men’s hearts. At that time each will receive his praise from God.
paragraphs: 1 So then, men ought to regard us as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. 2 Now it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.

3 I care very little, however, if I am judged by you or by any human court. In fact, I do not even judge myself. 4 My conscience is clear, but that does not vindicate me. It is the Lord who judges me. 5 Therefore judge nothing before the appointed time; wait until the Lord comes. He will bring to light what is hidden in darkness and will expose the motives of men’s hearts. At that time each will receive his praise from God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul asks the church to regard him and his fellow workers as servants of Christ, entrusted with making God’s revealed purposes known. They are not competing masters who own the people they teach.

A steward manages something entrusted by another. The Greek word is oikonomos (oy-koh-NOH-moss), οἰκονόμος; Thayer’s entry includes a household manager and applies the picture here to teachers entrusted with God’s message. Faithfulness to that trust matters more than popularity.

Paul does not let the Corinthians’ verdict, a human court or even his own clear conscience become the final judgment on his service. The Lord knows what people cannot yet see, including motives. Waiting for His coming means refusing to assign a final value to servants on the basis of partial knowledge. It does not prevent the correction and examination Paul himself carries out in this letter.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a call to faithful service and humility about judging another person’s hidden motives or final standing. Calvin’s comment on verse 5 distinguishes premature judgments from every kind of judgment, while Wesley’s notes on verses 3–5 place the final verdict with the Lord.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Luke 12:42–48, Jesus pictures a manager entrusted with care of a household. Faithful care matters when the master returns, and greater responsibility brings greater accountability.

This is a direct parallel in the role of a steward, rather than a claim that each detail of the two passages is identical. God entrusts people with work for the good of His household. Their service looks toward His judgment, which gives both a reason for diligence and a reason to resist the search for human applause.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 4:6-13
passages.section_title: Why does Paul contrast their pride with the apostles’ suffering?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 Brothers, I have applied these things to myself and Apollos for your benefit, so that you may learn from us not to go beyond what is written. Then you will not take pride in one man over another. 7 For who makes you so superior? What do you have that you did not receive? And if you did receive it, why do you boast as though you did not? 8 Already you have all you want. Already you have become rich. Without us, you have become kings. How I wish you really were kings, so that we might be kings with you! 9 For it seems to me that God has displayed us apostles at the end of the procession, like prisoners appointed for death. We have become a spectacle to the whole world, to angels as well as to men. 10 We are fools for Christ, but you are wise in Christ. We are weak, but you are strong. You are honored, but we are dishonored. 11 To this very hour we are hungry and thirsty, we are poorly clothed, we are brutally treated, we are homeless. 12 We work hard with our own hands. When we are vilified, we bless; when we are persecuted, we endure it; 13 when we are slandered, we answer gently. Up to this moment we have become the scum of the earth, the refuse of the world.
paragraphs: 6 Brothers, I have applied these things to myself and Apollos for your benefit, so that you may learn from us not to go beyond what is written. Then you will not take pride in one man over another. 7 For who makes you so superior? What do you have that you did not receive? And if you did receive it, why do you boast as though you did not? 8 Already you have all you want. Already you have become rich. Without us, you have become kings. How I wish you really were kings, so that we might be kings with you!

9 For it seems to me that God has displayed us apostles at the end of the procession, like prisoners appointed for death. We have become a spectacle to the whole world, to angels as well as to men. 10 We are fools for Christ, but you are wise in Christ. We are weak, but you are strong. You are honored, but we are dishonored. 11 To this very hour we are hungry and thirsty, we are poorly clothed, we are brutally treated, we are homeless. 12 We work hard with our own hands. When we are vilified, we bless; when we are persecuted, we endure it; 13 when we are slandered, we answer gently. Up to this moment we have become the scum of the earth, the refuse of the world.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul has used himself and Apollos to teach the Corinthians not to go beyond what is written or take pride in one person over another. His question cuts through their claims to superiority: whatever they have was received. Gifts cannot honestly become a reason to act as though they made themselves important.

His words about being satisfied, rich and kings are pointed irony. They are behaving as though they have already arrived, while the apostles who brought them the message experience weakness and public dishonor. Paul wishes they really had reached the fullness they imagine, so that the apostles could share it.

He then describes hunger, thirst, poor clothing, mistreatment, homelessness and hard manual work. The apostles respond to abuse with blessing, endurance and gentle answers. Their hardship does not prove the message has failed, and outward comfort does not prove spiritual maturity. The contrast exposes how unreliable the church’s measures of importance have become.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand Paul’s contrast as exposing pride in gifts and outward status. Wesley’s notes on verses 7–13 read the Corinthians’ self-satisfaction against the apostles’ costly service, while recognizing blessing and endurance as their response to mistreatment.
passages.god_plan_html:
In John 15:18–21, Jesus tells His disciples that the world’s hostility toward Him will also affect His servants. Sharing His mission does not guarantee public honor or an easy life.

Matthew 5:10–12 likewise places suffering for righteousness and for Jesus within the hope of the kingdom and God’s reward. These connections explain why present hardship cannot be the church’s test for whether someone belongs to God or serves Him faithfully.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 4:14-17
passages.section_title: Why does Paul call them his children and ask them to imitate him?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 I am not writing this to shame you, but to warn you as my beloved children. 15 Even if you have ten thousand guardians in Christ, you do not have many fathers; for in Christ Jesus I became your father through the gospel. 16 Therefore I urge you to imitate me. 17 That is why I have sent you Timothy, my beloved and faithful child in the Lord. He will remind you of my way of life in Christ Jesus, which is exactly what I teach everywhere in every church.
paragraphs: 14 I am not writing this to shame you, but to warn you as my beloved children. 15 Even if you have ten thousand guardians in Christ, you do not have many fathers; for in Christ Jesus I became your father through the gospel. 16 Therefore I urge you to imitate me. 17 That is why I have sent you Timothy, my beloved and faithful child in the Lord. He will remind you of my way of life in Christ Jesus, which is exactly what I teach everywhere in every church.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After strong correction, Paul explains his purpose: he is warning beloved children rather than trying to humiliate them. He describes the relationship formed when he brought them the gospel as becoming their father in Christ Jesus.

This language concerns care and responsibility, not a claim that he is the source of their salvation. Earlier he called himself a servant and said God gave the growth. His appeal to imitate him is therefore an appeal to a life shaped by Christ, rather than another competing loyalty to Paul’s name.

Timothy will remind them of that way of life. Paul’s teaching and example belong together, and he describes them as consistent with what he teaches in every church. The Corinthians need more than another impressive speaker; they need to live out the message they have received.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a fatherly appeal grounded in Paul’s role in bringing the gospel and continuing to care for the church. Wesley’s notes on verses 14–17 emphasize affection and imitation through both teaching and example; Calvin’s comment on verse 15 also connects this relationship with their life in Christ through the gospel.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Thessalonians 2:7–12 uses both a mother’s care and a father’s encouragement to describe gospel ministry. Paul shares not only the message but his life, urging believers to walk in a way worthy of the God who calls them into His kingdom and glory.

This is a parallel in parental care, rather than an equation between every leader’s wishes and God’s will. The purpose of such care is to help people live faithfully before God. Teaching, example, encouragement and correction serve that larger calling.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 4:18-21
passages.section_title: What does Paul mean by power rather than talk?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 Some of you have become arrogant, as if I were not coming to you. 19 But I will come to you shortly, if the Lord is willing, and then I will find out not only what these arrogant people are saying, but what power they have. 20 For the kingdom of God is not a matter of talk but of power. 21 Which do you prefer? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and with a gentle spirit?
paragraphs: 18 Some of you have become arrogant, as if I were not coming to you. 19 But I will come to you shortly, if the Lord is willing, and then I will find out not only what these arrogant people are saying, but what power they have. 20 For the kingdom of God is not a matter of talk but of power. 21 Which do you prefer? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and with a gentle spirit?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Some in Corinth are acting as though Paul will never return. He says he intends to come soon, subject to the Lord’s will. His absence has not made the church’s pride or its need for correction unimportant.

Paul will look beyond what the arrogant people say to the power behind their claims. The kingdom of God is not established by impressive talk. The letter has already located saving power in the message of the cross and the work of the Spirit, rather than human brilliance.

His final question offers a choice between firm correction and a visit marked by love and gentleness. The image of a rod continues the father-and-children language. He wants a response that allows him to come gently, rather than having to confront continued arrogance. The passage does not specify every form that the threatened correction would take.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a warning that empty claims will be exposed and that Paul is prepared to correct the church. Wesley’s note on verse 20 emphasizes God’s power ruling the heart; Calvin’s comment likewise points to the Spirit’s effective work rather than outward skill in speaking.
passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 12:5–11 explains God’s discipline through the relationship of a father and children. Its purpose is their good: sharing His holiness and learning a life that bears righteousness and peace.

That larger purpose helps explain why loving care can include difficult correction. This is a connection in purpose, not a claim that a human leader’s every action carries God’s approval. Paul’s own stated aim is to help the community turn from pride and live faithfully in Christ.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 5:1-5
passages.section_title: Why does Paul tell the church to act?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and of a kind that is intolerable even among pagans: A man has his father’s wife. 2 And you are proud! Shouldn’t you rather have been stricken with grief and have removed from your fellowship the man who did this? 3 Although I am absent from you in body, I am present with you in spirit, and I have already pronounced judgment on the one who did this, just as if I were present. 4 When you are assembled in the name of our Lord Jesus and I am with you in spirit, along with the power of the Lord Jesus, 5 hand this man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved on the Day of the Lord.
paragraphs: 1 It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and of a kind that is intolerable even among pagans: A man has his father’s wife. 2 And you are proud! Shouldn’t you rather have been stricken with grief and have removed from your fellowship the man who did this?

3 Although I am absent from you in body, I am present with you in spirit, and I have already pronounced judgment on the one who did this, just as if I were present. 4 When you are assembled in the name of our Lord Jesus and I am with you in spirit, along with the power of the Lord Jesus, 5 hand this man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved on the Day of the Lord.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul has received a report of a man having a sexual relationship with his father’s wife. He describes the behavior as intolerable even among pagans. Yet the church has responded with pride rather than grief, and has failed to remove the man from its fellowship.

The correction is directed at the community as well as the offender. Paul has already reached a judgment about the reported conduct. He calls for the church to act when assembled in the name and power of the Lord Jesus, rather than leaving the matter as a private disagreement between individuals.

Handing the man over to Satan is severe language for the action Paul requires. The stated goal reaches beyond immediate punishment: that his spirit may be saved on the Day of the Lord. The passage calls for a response to serious wrongdoing while keeping the person’s ultimate good in view. It does not report what later happened to him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read this as serious church discipline aimed at the offender’s good and the community’s holiness. The Reformed Westminster Confession 30.3–4, for example, describes correction and exclusion as serving the recovery of offenders as well as protecting the church.

Interpreters differ over the destruction of the flesh. Wesley’s note on verse 5 understands bodily pain or sickness, with repentance able to avert the threatened destruction. Calvin’s comment instead emphasizes exclusion from the church and a severe but temporary judgment intended for salvation. These are their readings of the warning, rather than a single detailed explanation held by all Christians.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Timothy 1:18–20 also speaks of handing people over to Satan, there with the stated purpose of teaching them not to blaspheme. The parallel shows correction directed toward a changed response to God.

In 2 Corinthians 2:5–11, Paul urges forgiveness, comfort and reaffirmed love when a punishment has been sufficient. That passage does not name its offender, so it need not be treated as a certain account of this man’s later history. It does show why discipline must keep restoration in view rather than become a reason to prolong someone’s despair.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 5:6-8
passages.section_title: Why does Paul connect their conduct with Passover?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 Your boasting is not good. Do you not know that a little leaven works through the whole batch of dough? 7 Get rid of the old leaven, that you may be a new unleavened batch, as you really are. For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed. 8 Therefore let us keep the feast, not with the old bread, leavened with malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and of truth.
paragraphs: 6 Your boasting is not good. Do you not know that a little leaven works through the whole batch of dough? 7 Get rid of the old leaven, that you may be a new unleavened batch, as you really are. For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed. 8 Therefore let us keep the feast, not with the old bread, leavened with malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and of truth.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul returns to the church’s boasting and uses leaven to explain the danger. A little works through a whole batch of dough. In this setting, tolerated wrongdoing can shape the life and expectations of the community rather than remaining one person’s isolated matter.

The picture draws on Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread. Exodus 12:14–20 commands Israel to remove leaven and eat unleavened bread in remembering its deliverance. Paul applies the image to a community whose life has been changed by Christ’s sacrifice.

He identifies Christ as their Passover lamb and calls them to leave behind malice and wickedness for sincerity and truth. His appeal joins identity with conduct: live as the people you have become. Grace is not a reason to celebrate what harms the community.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the old leaven as a picture of sin to be put away because of Christ’s sacrifice. Wesley’s note on verse 8 especially connects keeping the feast with the Lord’s Supper; the USCCB notes on verses 7–8 emphasize the community’s continuing life of purity and integrity. Both explanations connect celebration of Christ with the way His people live.
passages.god_plan_html:
Exodus 12:11–20 places the Passover meal, the blood marking the houses and the removal of leaven within Israel’s deliverance from Egypt. Paul’s identification of Christ as the Passover lamb makes the connection to God’s saving work explicit, rather than leaving it as a resemblance suggested by a teacher.

At the Passover meal in Luke 22:14–20, Jesus speaks of His body given for His disciples and the new covenant in His blood. These passages give the church’s call to sincerity and truth a deeper setting: its shared life follows a deliverance received through Christ, and should reflect the One who gave Himself for His people.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 5:9-13
passages.section_title: Who is the church responsible for correcting?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 I wrote you in my letter not to associate with sexually immoral people. 10 I was not including the sexually immoral of this world, or the greedy and swindlers, or idolaters. In that case you would have to leave this world. 11 But now I am writing you not to associate with anyone who claims to be a brother but is sexually immoral or greedy, an idolater or a verbal abuser, a drunkard or a swindler. With such a man do not even eat. 12 What business of mine is it to judge those outside the church? Are you not to judge those inside? 13 God will judge those outside. “Expel the wicked man from among you.”

In that case you would have to leave this world. 11 But now I am writing you not to associate with anyone who claims to be a brother but is sexually immoral or greedy, an idolater or a verbal abuser, a drunkard or a swindler. With such a man do not even eat.
12 What business of mine is it to judge those outside the church? Are you not to judge those inside? 13 God will judge those outside. “Expel the wicked man from among you.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul clarifies an instruction from an earlier letter. He did not mean the Corinthians should cut off all contact with sexually immoral people, the greedy, swindlers or idolaters in the world. Doing that would require leaving the world altogether.

His instruction concerns someone who claims to be a brother while persisting in conduct incompatible with that claim. The list includes sexual immorality, greed, idolatry, verbal abuse, drunkenness and swindling. The concern is wider than one kind of sexual sin, and Paul says the community must not continue ordinary fellowship as though nothing is wrong.

Paul distinguishes the church’s responsibility for those inside from God’s judgment of those outside. He closes with language used in Deuteronomy 17:7 about removing evil from the community. The action he commands here is removal from fellowship, not the civil penalty described in that earlier setting.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as distinguishing accountability within the church from withdrawal from everyone outside it. Calvin’s comment on verse 12 specifically treats the issue as the church’s responsibility to exercise discipline, while Wesley’s notes on verses 10–13 retain ordinary contact with outsiders and distinguish it from fellowship with a professing member living in the conduct Paul names.
passages.god_plan_html:
In John 17:14–18, Jesus prays for His disciples to be kept from evil while being sent into the world. He does not ask the Father to take them out of it.

That connection places the church’s distinct way of life alongside its mission. God’s people need not choose between tolerating serious wrongdoing within their fellowship and avoiding everyone who does not share their faith. Their calling includes both faithfulness to Christ and presence among the people to whom He sends them.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 6:1-8
passages.section_title: Why are their lawsuits already a defeat?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 If any of you has a grievance against another, how dare he go to law before the unrighteous instead of before the saints! 2 Do you not know that the saints will judge the world? And if you are to judge the world, are you not competent to judge trivial cases? 3 Do you not know that we will judge angels? How much more the things of this life! 4 So if you need to settle everyday matters, do you appoint as judges those of no standing in the church? 5 I say this to your shame. Is there really no one among you wise enough to arbitrate between his brothers? 6 Instead, one brother goes to law against another, and this in front of unbelievers! 7 The very fact that you have lawsuits among you means that you are thoroughly defeated already. Why not rather be wronged? Why not rather be cheated? 8 Instead, you yourselves cheat and do wrong, even against your own brothers!
paragraphs: 1 If any of you has a grievance against another, how dare he go to law before the unrighteous instead of before the saints! 2 Do you not know that the saints will judge the world? And if you are to judge the world, are you not competent to judge trivial cases? 3 Do you not know that we will judge angels? How much more the things of this life!

4 So if you need to settle everyday matters, do you appoint as judges those of no standing in the church? 5 I say this to your shame. Is there really no one among you wise enough to arbitrate between his brothers? 6 Instead, one brother goes to law against another, and this in front of unbelievers!

7 The very fact that you have lawsuits among you means that you are thoroughly defeated already. Why not rather be wronged? Why not rather be cheated? 8 Instead, you yourselves cheat and do wrong, even against your own brothers!

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul is addressing disputes in which believers take one another before outside judges. He asks why a community destined to share in God’s judgment cannot find someone wise enough to settle its everyday disagreements.

The failure runs deeper than the choice of a courtroom. The Corinthians are cheating and wronging their own brothers. Paul challenges their determination to win against one another, even asking why they would not rather accept a loss than continue the conflict. The person causing the loss is also directly rebuked, not excused.

The immediate subject is everyday disputes between members of the church. Paul’s own appeal to legal protection in Acts 25:10–12 shows that he recognizes a place for civil authority. Here his concern is the church’s failure to act with wisdom and justice toward its own members.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a rebuke of destructive litigation and wrongdoing among believers, with a call to wise settlement and willingness to bear loss. Calvin’s comment on verse 1 distinguishes avoidable lawsuits used to harass a brother from appearing and defending a case when summoned; his reading does not make every involvement in a civil court the same situation Paul condemns.
passages.god_plan_html:
Daniel 7:18–27 describes God overturning oppressive rule and giving the kingdom to His holy people. Jesus also promises His disciples a share in judgment in Matthew 19:28. These passages give a wider setting for Paul’s reminder about the saints’ future role.

Paul uses that future responsibility to challenge present conduct. People called to share in God’s just rule should learn to deal justly with one another now. He does not explain here every detail of judging the world or angels, and the practical appeal does not depend on supplying a complete timetable.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 6:9-11
passages.section_title: What has changed for people who belong to Christ?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 Do you not know that the wicked will not inherit the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived: Neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor men who submit to or perform homosexual acts, 10 nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor verbal abusers, nor swindlers, will inherit the kingdom of God. 11 And that is what some of you were. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.
paragraphs: 9 Do you not know that the wicked will not inherit the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived: Neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor men who submit to or perform homosexual acts, 10 nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor verbal abusers, nor swindlers, will inherit the kingdom of God. 11 And that is what some of you were. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The warning about inheriting God’s kingdom follows Paul’s rebuke of believers who cheat one another. His list includes sexual wrongdoing alongside idolatry, greed, theft, drunkenness, verbal abuse and swindling. Reading only one part of that list would miss its force against the community’s own misconduct.

Paul then reminds them of a change: some of them once lived in these ways, but they were washed, made holy and put right with God in Jesus’ name and by the Spirit. Their past is not a reason to deny the possibility of renewal, and their new identity is not permission to return to what Paul condemns.

Two terms behind the BSB’s wording about homosexual acts are malakos (mah-lah-KOSS), μαλακός, and arsenokoitēs (ar-seh-noh-KOY-tays), ἀρσενοκοίτης. Thayer’s entry for the first includes the ordinary meaning soft and a sexual sense here; the second entry describes a man having intercourse with a male. How broadly to apply these terms is part of the difference between readings below. A dictionary entry alone does not settle every question about modern relationships.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians recognize both the warning against wrongdoing and the hope of a changed life through Christ and the Spirit. Traditions differ over how being put right with God relates to inward renewal and baptism. The Catholic Church’s Catechism 1987–1992 includes forgiveness and inward renewal in justification and teaches that it is conferred in baptism. The Reformed Westminster Confession 11.1–2 defines justification as God’s pardon and acceptance through Christ, received by faith, while insisting that this faith is accompanied by other graces and works through love.

There are also differences in reading and applying the sexual terms. The USCCB note on verse 9 discusses boys used in prostitution and the adult males involved with them. That note’s explanation of the ancient setting should be distinguished from the Catholic Church’s wider teaching: Catechism 2357–2359 rejects homosexual acts, calls people experiencing same-sex attraction to chastity, and requires respect, compassion and avoidance of unjust discrimination. The Reformed Westminster Confession 24.1 defines marriage as between one man and one woman.

The United Methodist Church’s current Social Principles on marriage affirm a lifelong covenant that can unite two consenting adults of the same sex. One explanation of an affirming reading is offered by United Methodist minister John Holbert, who suggests that Paul’s terms concern sexual or economic exploitation rather than a blanket rejection of same-sex relationships. That is his interpretation, rather than a word-for-word explanation supplied by the Social Principles, and it should not be attributed to every Methodist or Wesleyan.
passages.god_plan_html:
Titus 3:3–8 describes a similar movement from harmful desires and hatred to new birth and renewal through the Spirit. It places salvation in God’s mercy, rather than righteous deeds people had already performed, and looks ahead to inheritance and eternal life.

The passage then calls believers to devote themselves to good deeds. This gives a wider purpose to the change Paul recalls: God’s mercy gathers people into a new life whose conduct benefits others. Hope for those with a sinful past and seriousness about present behavior belong together.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 6:12-17
passages.section_title: Why does freedom not make the body unimportant?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 “Everything is permissible for me,” but not everything is beneficial. “Everything is permissible for me,” but I will not be mastered by anything. 13 “Food for the stomach and the stomach for food,” but God will destroy them both. The body is not intended for sexual immorality, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body. 14 By His power God raised the Lord from the dead, and He will raise us also. 15 Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I then take the members of Christ and unite them with a prostitute? Never! 16 Or don’t you know that he who unites himself with a prostitute is one with her in body? For it is said, “The two will become one flesh.” 17 But he who unites himself with the Lord is one with Him in spirit.
paragraphs: 12 “Everything is permissible for me,” but not everything is beneficial. “Everything is permissible for me,” but I will not be mastered by anything. 13 “Food for the stomach and the stomach for food,” but God will destroy them both. The body is not intended for sexual immorality, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body. 14 By His power God raised the Lord from the dead, and He will raise us also.

15 Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I then take the members of Christ and unite them with a prostitute? Never! 16 Or don’t you know that he who unites himself with a prostitute is one with her in body? For it is said, “The two will become one flesh.” 17 But he who unites himself with the Lord is one with Him in spirit.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul qualifies the claim that everything is permissible: not everything is beneficial, and he will not be mastered by anything. Freedom cannot simply mean giving every appetite control. The comparison between food and the stomach does not turn sexual behavior into a matter of indifference.

The body belongs to the Lord, and God’s raising of Jesus points toward believers’ own resurrection. What happens in bodily life therefore matters to Him. The body is not a disposable part of a person whose choices have no bearing on belonging to Christ.

Paul applies that belonging to sex with a prostitute. He draws on Genesis 2:24 to describe bodily union, then contrasts it with union with the Lord. Taking members of Christ into such a relationship contradicts the relationship they already have with Him. The text says prostitute without identifying a particular temple or religious ceremony.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these verses as rejecting the use of freedom to excuse sexual immorality and affirming the body’s importance to the Lord. Calvin’s comment on verse 12 recognizes an appeal to liberty being misused, while Wesley’s note on verse 13 connects the body’s purpose with the Lord who will raise it.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 5:25–32 also draws on Genesis 2:24, there connecting the love and care of husband and wife with Christ’s love for the church. It explicitly relates the one-flesh picture to Christ and His people.

That connection adds a positive purpose beyond the warning against prostitution. Bodily relationships can express faithful love and care; they are not merely outlets for appetite. The church belongs to the Christ who gave Himself for her and works for her holiness.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 6:18-20
passages.section_title: What does it mean to glorify God with your body?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 Flee from sexual immorality. Every other sin a man can commit is outside his body, but he who sins sexually sins against his own body. 19 Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have received from God? You are not your own; 20 you were bought at a price. Therefore glorify God with your body.
paragraphs: 18 Flee from sexual immorality. Every other sin a man can commit is outside his body, but he who sins sexually sins against his own body. 19 Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have received from God? You are not your own; 20 you were bought at a price. Therefore glorify God with your body.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul’s instruction is to flee sexual immorality. His description of sin against one’s own body follows the discussion of joining the body to a prostitute. It emphasizes the seriousness of that union rather than suggesting that other sins never harm bodies or relationships.

He calls the body a temple of the Holy Spirit, received from God. Earlier he used temple language for the community together; here the argument concerns what believers do with their bodies. Both uses place life under the claim of the God who dwells with His people.

They are not their own because they were bought at a price. The conclusion is positive as well as corrective: honor God through bodily life. Paul does not describe sexual wrongdoing as beyond forgiveness, and the earlier reminder that they were washed and made holy keeps the call to turn away from sin within the hope of renewal.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand these verses as calling believers to honor God through sexual conduct because their bodies belong to Him and receive His Spirit. Calvin’s comments on verses 18–19 recognize that other sins also dishonor the body, while preserving Paul’s particular warning about sexual sin.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 8:9–11 connects the Spirit’s presence with belonging to Christ and with God giving life to mortal bodies. Redemption is not a plan to discard bodily life as worthless.

Romans 12:1–2 then calls believers to offer their bodies as a living sacrifice in response to God’s mercy. Together these passages place the call to glorify God with the body within a life of worship, renewed thinking and future resurrection.
