passages.title: 1 Corinthians 7:1-7
passages.section_title: How should married believers care for one another?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now for the matters you wrote about: It is good to abstain from sexual relations. 2 But because there is so much sexual immorality, each man should have his own wife, and each woman her own husband. 3 The husband should fulfill his marital duty to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband. 4 The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife. 5 Do not deprive each other, except by mutual consent and for a time, so you may devote yourselves to prayer. Then come together again, so that Satan will not tempt you through your lack of self-control. 6 I say this as a concession, not as a command. 7 I wish that all men were as I am. But each man has his own gift from God; one has this gift, another has that.
paragraphs: 1 Now for the matters you wrote about: It is good to abstain from sexual relations. 2 But because there is so much sexual immorality, each man should have his own wife, and each woman her own husband. 3 The husband should fulfill his marital duty to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband. 4 The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife.

5 Do not deprive each other, except by mutual consent and for a time, so you may devote yourselves to prayer. Then come together again, so that Satan will not tempt you through your lack of self-control. 6 I say this as a concession, not as a command. 7 I wish that all men were as I am. But each man has his own gift from God; one has this gift, another has that.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul now answers matters the Corinthians wrote about. He begins with abstaining from sexual relations, then explains the place of marriage and the responsibilities of both spouses. He does not treat intimacy within marriage as something unclean that a more spiritual couple must abandon.

The duties are reciprocal: the husband owes care to his wife, and the wife to her husband. Paul speaks about each person’s body in relation to the other and then requires mutual consent for a temporary interruption of intimacy for prayer. His instructions direct both spouses away from acting only for themselves.

After a time set aside for prayer, they are to come together again. Paul recognizes temptation and the limits of self-control. He also distinguishes a concession from a command and acknowledges that people receive different gifts from God. His own unmarried way of life is not a pattern everyone can simply be required to copy.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these verses as honoring marital intimacy and mutual responsibility, with temporary abstinence by agreement rather than as a requirement for every married couple. Wesley’s notes on verses 3–7 emphasize that married people should not treat living as though unmarried as a higher form of purity, and that the gift of remaining unmarried is not given to everyone.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 5:25–30 connects a husband’s care for his wife with Christ’s self-giving love and care for the church. The body of the other person is a reason for faithful care, not simply a means of personal satisfaction.

That larger picture gives the practical instructions here a purpose beyond avoiding temptation. Life together should reflect the love of the Christ to whom both spouses belong. Attention to a spouse’s needs, shared decisions and prayer can become expressions of serving Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 7:8-9
passages.section_title: Should an unmarried believer seek marriage?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 Now to the unmarried and widows I say this: It is good for them to remain unmarried, as I am. 9 But if they cannot control themselves, let them marry. For it is better to marry than to burn with passion.
paragraphs: 8 Now to the unmarried and widows I say this: It is good for them to remain unmarried, as I am. 9 But if they cannot control themselves, let them marry. For it is better to marry than to burn with passion.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul addresses the unmarried and widows, commending remaining unmarried as he is. He also tells those who cannot exercise self-control to marry. Marriage is a permitted and good response, rather than a spiritual failure.

The counsel continues his recognition of different gifts. He is asking people to be honest about their circumstances and capacity, rather than trying to prove their devotion by adopting a way of life that leaves them struggling with temptation. These verses establish that Paul was unmarried when writing; they do not give a complete account of his earlier marital history.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this counsel as valuing unmarried service to God while permitting marriage and recognizing different gifts. The Catholic Catechism 1618–1620 honors both marriage and virginity for the kingdom as gifts from the Lord; Wesley’s note on verse 7 likewise connects remaining unmarried with a gift not given to everyone.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Matthew 19:10–12, Jesus describes some people choosing to forgo marriage for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. He also says this is something only those given the capacity can receive.

This connection places voluntary singleness within service to God’s kingdom, rather than making it simply the absence of a spouse. Paul’s permission to marry also matters within that purpose: the call is to faithful service with the gifts one has received, rather than a single required household arrangement for every believer.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 7:10-11
passages.section_title: Why does Paul call separated spouses toward reconciliation?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 To the married I give this command (not I, but the Lord): A wife must not separate from her husband. 11 But if she does, she must remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her husband. And a husband must not divorce his wife.
paragraphs: 10 To the married I give this command (not I, but the Lord): A wife must not separate from her husband. 11 But if she does, she must remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her husband. And a husband must not divorce his wife.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul distinguishes this instruction from the concessions he has just discussed: he appeals to the Lord’s command. A wife must not separate from her husband, and a husband must not divorce his wife. If separation occurs, he directs the wife to remain unmarried or be reconciled.

The words not I, but the Lord point to teaching Jesus had given. Mark 10:6–12 places His teaching about divorce within God’s joining husband and wife together. Paul is applying that seriousness to the marriages he addresses.

The chapter will next discuss marriages in which only one spouse believes. These two verses should therefore be read within Paul’s whole discussion and alongside Jesus’ teaching, rather than treated as a complete description of every difficult circumstance. They make reconciliation and faithfulness the aim rather than an easy exchange of one marriage for another.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians agree that marriage calls for lasting faithfulness, but traditions differ over when a separation or divorce permits another marriage.

The Catholic Church teaches that a ratified and consummated marriage between baptized spouses cannot be dissolved except by death. It allows separation while the bond remains and can tolerate civil divorce where needed to protect rights or children; see Catechism 2382–2386. The Reformed Westminster Confession 24.5–6 recognizes adultery and irremediable willful desertion as grounds for dissolving a marriage, and explicitly permits the innocent party to remarry after divorce for adultery.

The United Methodist Church’s current Social Principles on divorce recognize that divorce can become necessary when a relationship becomes destructive or beyond repair. They do not require remaining in an abusive relationship and allow remarriage after divorce. These differences concern how the wider biblical teaching is applied; they should not be collapsed into a claim that every Christian tradition treats every separation in the same way.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus directs His hearers back to creation in Mark 10:6–9: the union of husband and wife belongs to what God joins together. Marriage is therefore more than an arrangement kept only while it is convenient.

Ephesians 5:25–32 adds a positive picture of the love such a bond should express, connecting it with Christ’s giving Himself for the church and caring for her. The larger purpose includes faithful, self-giving care, rather than merely retaining a relationship’s outward form. This connection does not by itself settle every disputed question about divorce.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 7:12-14
passages.section_title: Does a difference in faith make an existing marriage unholy?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 To the rest I say this (I, not the Lord): If a brother has an unbelieving wife and she is willing to live with him, he must not divorce her. 13 And if a woman has an unbelieving husband and he is willing to live with her, she must not divorce him. 14 For the unbelieving husband is sanctified through his believing wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified through her believing husband. Otherwise your children would be unclean, but now they are holy.
paragraphs: 12 To the rest I say this (I, not the Lord): If a brother has an unbelieving wife and she is willing to live with him, he must not divorce her. 13 And if a woman has an unbelieving husband and he is willing to live with her, she must not divorce him. 14 For the unbelieving husband is sanctified through his believing wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified through her believing husband. Otherwise your children would be unclean, but now they are holy.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul now addresses a marriage in which one spouse believes and the other does not. If the unbelieving spouse is willing to continue living together, the believer must not end the marriage because of that difference.

His words I, not the Lord distinguish this situation from the teaching of Jesus he has just recalled. Paul is giving direction for a question the church now faces, rather than dismissing his own instruction as unimportant.

The language of being sanctified and holy answers concern about the household’s standing. Paul still calls the spouse unbelieving, so he is not saying the marriage automatically gives that person faith or salvation. The believer need not treat the marriage or its children as defiled simply because only one spouse has come to Christ.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read this as a reason to preserve an existing marriage with a willing unbelieving spouse. They differ over the holiness of the children and how it relates to baptism.

Calvin’s comment on verse 14 connects their holiness with the blessing of God’s covenant and supports giving them baptism. The Reformed Westminster Confession 28.4–5 calls for baptism of infants with one or both parents believing, while denying that everyone baptized is necessarily born anew.

The Baptist 1689 Confession 29.2 limits baptism to those who profess repentance, faith and obedience to Christ. Baptist commentator John Gill’s note on verse 14 reads the holiness language here as affirming the marriage and the children’s legitimacy, rather than establishing infant baptism. That is his explanation of the verse, not a single interpretation required of every Baptist.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Peter 3:1–6 also addresses wives whose husbands do not believe the word. It describes how reverent conduct and a gentle spirit can bear witness within a household.

This connection shows a purpose beyond simply keeping a marriage intact. Faith can become visible through daily life among people close to the believer. It gives reason for hope without making one person responsible for producing another person’s faith or promising that every spouse will be converted.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 7:15-16
passages.section_title: What if the unbelieving spouse leaves?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 But if the unbeliever leaves, let him go. The believing brother or sister is not bound in such cases. God has called you to live in peace. 16 How do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?
paragraphs: 15 But if the unbeliever leaves, let him go. The believing brother or sister is not bound in such cases. God has called you to live in peace. 16 How do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
If the unbelieving spouse leaves, Paul says to let that person go. The believing brother or sister is not bound in such cases, and God has called His people to peace. This follows the instruction to continue a marriage when the unbelieving spouse is willing to remain.

The question about saving a spouse recognizes something the believer cannot know or control. Hope for a spouse’s salvation matters, but it is not a guarantee that the marriage will continue or that the other person will believe. Paul does not tell the believer to preserve cohabitation at any cost.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians recognize Paul’s permission to let the departing unbeliever go, but differ over the scope of the resulting freedom and when another marriage is permitted.

The Catholic Church’s canons 1143–1147 describe the Pauline privilege: a marriage initially entered by two unbaptized people can be dissolved in favor of the faith when one receives baptism and the other departs or refuses peaceful life together under the stated conditions. This can permit a new marriage through the church’s prescribed process; it is a different case from a consummated sacramental marriage between baptized spouses.

The Reformed Westminster Confession 24.6 recognizes willful desertion that cannot be remedied by the church or civil authorities as a ground for dissolving a marriage. In his own reading of verse 15, Baptist commentator John Gill permits remarriage after efforts at reconciliation have failed in the circumstances he describes. These explanations should not be reduced to a rule that any disagreement or departure automatically authorizes another marriage.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 7:17-24
passages.section_title: Must coming to Christ change a person’s social position?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 Regardless, each one should lead the life that the Lord has assigned to him and to which God has called him. This is what I prescribe in all the churches. 18 Was a man already circumcised when he was called? He should not become uncircumcised. Was a man still uncircumcised when called? He should not be circumcised. 19 Circumcision is nothing and uncircumcision is nothing. Keeping God’s commandments is what counts. 20 Each one should remain in the situation he was in when he was called. 21 Were you a slave when you were called? Do not let it concern you—but if you can gain your freedom, take the opportunity. 22 For he who was a slave when he was called by the Lord is the Lord’s freedman. Conversely, he who was a free man when he was called is Christ’s slave. 23 You were bought at a price; do not become slaves of men. 24 Brothers, each one should remain in the situation he was in when God called him.
paragraphs: 17 Regardless, each one should lead the life that the Lord has assigned to him and to which God has called him. This is what I prescribe in all the churches. 18 Was a man already circumcised when he was called? He should not become uncircumcised. Was a man still uncircumcised when called? He should not be circumcised. 19 Circumcision is nothing and uncircumcision is nothing. Keeping God’s commandments is what counts. 20 Each one should remain in the situation he was in when he was called.

21 Were you a slave when you were called? Do not let it concern you—but if you can gain your freedom, take the opportunity. 22 For he who was a slave when he was called by the Lord is the Lord’s freedman. Conversely, he who was a free man when he was called is Christ’s slave. 23 You were bought at a price; do not become slaves of men. 24 Brothers, each one should remain in the situation he was in when God called him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul broadens the discussion beyond marriage: live faithfully in the circumstances in which God called you. He uses circumcision and slavery as examples of outward conditions that do not determine whether someone can belong to Christ and serve Him.

The circumcised person need not undo that condition, and the uncircumcised person need not acquire it. What matters is obedience to God. Paul is rejecting a requirement to gain a different religious or social identity before one can live faithfully.

To the enslaved person, he gives assurance that this condition does not exclude the Lord’s call, while the BSB explicitly encourages taking an opportunity for freedom. The free person also belongs to Christ. Both are reminded that they were bought at a price, so human status cannot become their ultimate master.

Remaining with God is the thread holding the examples together. This does not require refusing every opportunity for change: verse 21 itself allows movement into freedom. The call is to live before God, rather than assuming that another outward condition is what makes faithfulness possible.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as directing attention from outward status to faithful life with God. Calvin’s comment on verse 21 and Wesley’s note both recognize freedom as preferable when it becomes available, rather than treating remaining in slavery as the condition for serving Christ.
passages.god_plan_html:
Galatians 3:26–29 describes people united in Christ across the distinctions of Jew and Greek, slave and free, male and female. Those who belong to Christ share in the promise given to Abraham.

Philemon 15–17 gives a concrete example of a changed relationship: Paul asks that Onesimus be received as a beloved brother and as Paul himself would be received. God’s call reaches people within unequal circumstances while bringing them into a shared belonging that changes how they should treat one another.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 7:25-28
passages.section_title: Why does Paul advise remaining as they are?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 25 Now about virgins, I have no command from the Lord, but I give a judgment as one who by the Lord’s mercy is trustworthy. 26 Because of the present crisis, I think it is good for a man to remain as he is. 27 Are you committed to a wife? Do not seek to be released. Are you free of commitment? Do not look for a wife. 28 But if you do marry, you have not sinned. And if a virgin marries, she has not sinned. But those who marry will face troubles in this life, and I want to spare you this.
paragraphs: 25 Now about virgins, I have no command from the Lord, but I give a judgment as one who by the Lord’s mercy is trustworthy. 26 Because of the present crisis, I think it is good for a man to remain as he is. 27 Are you committed to a wife? Do not seek to be released. Are you free of commitment? Do not look for a wife. 28 But if you do marry, you have not sinned. And if a virgin marries, she has not sinned. But those who marry will face troubles in this life, and I want to spare you this.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul turns to the unmarried and gives his judgment as someone made trustworthy by the Lord’s mercy. He does not present a direct command Jesus had given about this situation. He offers counsel in view of the present crisis and the troubles marriage can bring.

The advice fits his recurring call not to assume that faith requires a change of outward condition. Those committed to a wife should not seek release, and those free of commitment should consider remaining that way. Yet he explicitly says that marrying is not a sin.

Paul is trying to spare his hearers added difficulty. Paul does not name the crisis in these verses. His counsel takes real pressures into account while preserving the permission to marry.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly distinguish this pastoral recommendation from a universal prohibition of marriage. Wesley’s notes on verses 26–28 focus on persecution, while Calvin’s comment on verse 26 takes a broader view of pressures Christians face throughout life; both preserve the distinction between recommending singleness and declaring marriage sinful.
passages.god_plan_html:
2 Timothy 2:3–13 places disciplined service and hardship within the hope of life and reign with the risen Christ. Its pictures of a soldier, athlete and farmer direct attention to faithful service and what lies ahead.

This is a parallel in purpose, rather than a command that all servants must have the same household arrangements. Paul’s practical advice belongs within a life directed toward Christ’s purposes and the hope He gives. Decisions about marriage can be considered honestly in that setting without treating marriage itself as a failure of devotion.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 7:29-35
passages.section_title: What should remain at the center when life is passing away?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 29 What I am saying, brothers, is that the time is short. From now on those who have wives should live as if they had none; 30 those who weep, as if they did not; those who are joyful, as if they were not; those who make a purchase, as if they had nothing; 31 and those who use the things of this world, as if not dependent on them. For this world in its present form is passing away. 32 I want you to be free from concern. The unmarried man is concerned about the work of the Lord, how he can please the Lord. 33 But the married man is concerned about the affairs of this world, how he can please his wife, 34 and his interests are divided. The unmarried woman or virgin is concerned about the work of the Lord, how she can be holy in both body and spirit. But the married woman is concerned about the affairs of this world, how she can please her husband. 35 I am saying this for your own good, not to restrict you, but in order to promote proper decorum and undivided devotion to the Lord.
paragraphs: 29 What I am saying, brothers, is that the time is short. From now on those who have wives should live as if they had none; 30 those who weep, as if they did not; those who are joyful, as if they were not; those who make a purchase, as if they had nothing; 31 and those who use the things of this world, as if not dependent on them. For this world in its present form is passing away.

32 I want you to be free from concern. The unmarried man is concerned about the work of the Lord, how he can please the Lord. 33 But the married man is concerned about the affairs of this world, how he can please his wife, 34 and his interests are divided. The unmarried woman or virgin is concerned about the work of the Lord, how she can be holy in both body and spirit. But the married woman is concerned about the affairs of this world, how she can please her husband. 35 I am saying this for your own good, not to restrict you, but in order to promote proper decorum and undivided devotion to the Lord.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul places marriage, grief, joy, possessions and use of the world within a short time and a world whose present form is passing away. None should become the final center of a believer’s life. The words about living as though without a wife must be read alongside his earlier commands to honor marital responsibilities, rather than as an instruction to abandon them.

He describes the attention marriage requires: a husband thinks about pleasing his wife, and a wife about pleasing her husband. The unmarried person can have a freedom of attention for serving the Lord. Paul is identifying different responsibilities, not claiming every unmarried person automatically uses time faithfully or that caring for a spouse is wrong.

His purpose is stated in verse 35: their good and undivided devotion to the Lord, rather than placing a restraint on them. The advice invites them to order their lives around Him while being honest about what their commitments require.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these verses as a call to give the Lord first place while recognizing the practical demands of marriage. Wesley’s note on verse 33 explicitly treats provision and care for one’s family as a duty, and Calvin’s comment on verse 35 commends singleness for undistracted devotion while refusing to impose it on everyone.
passages.god_plan_html:
A useful parallel appears in Luke 10:38–42, where Mary listens at Jesus’ feet while Martha is distracted by many concerns. Jesus directs attention to what is needed. This is a parallel about attention to Him, not a statement about either woman’s marital status.

In Matthew 6:19–21, Jesus connects lasting treasure with the direction of the heart. Together these passages place Paul’s counsel within a wider call to give one’s life to what endures with God. Present responsibilities matter, but they should be carried out with a heart centered on Him rather than ruled by passing circumstances.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 7:36-38
passages.section_title: Is choosing to marry a failure to follow Paul’s counsel?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 36 However, if someone thinks he is acting inappropriately toward his betrothed, and if she is beyond her youth and they ought to marry, let him do as he wishes; he is not sinning; they should get married. 37 But the man who is firmly established in his heart and under no constraint, with control over his will and resolve in his heart not to marry the virgin, he will do well. 38 So then, he who marries the virgin does well, but he who does not marry her does even better.
paragraphs: 36 However, if someone thinks he is acting inappropriately toward his betrothed, and if she is beyond her youth and they ought to marry, let him do as he wishes; he is not sinning; they should get married. 37 But the man who is firmly established in his heart and under no constraint, with control over his will and resolve in his heart not to marry the virgin, he will do well. 38 So then, he who marries the virgin does well, but he who does not marry her does even better.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
In the BSB, Paul describes a man considering his responsibility toward his betrothed. If marriage is appropriate, they should marry; he is not sinning. If the man is settled in his decision, under no pressure and able to remain unmarried, Paul says he does well.

The comparison between doing well and doing better continues the chapter’s counsel about circumstances, gifts and freedom to serve. Paul does not turn his preference into a declaration that marriage is disobedience. This particular decision must be made honestly rather than as a way of appearing more spiritual.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Readers differ over the relationship Paul describes. The BSB presents an engaged couple, while Wesley’s notes on verses 36–38 and Calvin’s comment on verse 36 understand a father considering his unmarried daughter’s marriage. The USCCB note acknowledges both possibilities. Both approaches preserve the central reassurance that choosing marriage is not a sin, while Paul continues to commend the advantages of remaining unmarried.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 7:39-40
passages.section_title: What freedom does Paul give to a widow?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 39 A wife is bound to her husband as long as he lives. But if her husband dies, she is free to marry anyone she wishes, as long as he belongs to the Lord. 40 In my judgment, however, she is happier if she remains as she is. And I think that I too have the Spirit of God.
paragraphs: 39 A wife is bound to her husband as long as he lives. But if her husband dies, she is free to marry anyone she wishes, as long as he belongs to the Lord. 40 In my judgment, however, she is happier if she remains as she is. And I think that I too have the Spirit of God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul ends with a wife whose husband has died. While he lives she is bound to him; after his death she is free to marry someone she chooses, provided he belongs to the Lord. He allows a widow to marry again.

Paul again recommends remaining unmarried, but gives that as his judgment rather than withdrawing the freedom he has just stated. He also affirms the Spirit’s part in his counsel. The chapter closes with both a serious recommendation and a permitted choice, rather than requiring every widow to make the same decision.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly recognize a widow’s freedom to remarry and Paul’s recommendation of remaining unmarried. Wesley’s notes on verses 39–40 read only in the Lord as marriage within the Christian faith and regard Paul’s reference to the Spirit as confidence in his counsel.

Traditions differ in their rules for marriage across differences of faith. The Reformed Westminster Confession 24.3 requires Christians to marry in the Lord. Catholic canons 1086 and 1124–1125 allow permission for marriage with another baptized Christian outside the Catholic Church, and a special exception can permit marriage with an unbaptized person. The stated conditions include safeguarding the Catholic spouse’s faith and commitments about raising children in that faith.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 7:1–6 uses the ending of a marriage bond at death as an illustration within a larger explanation of life in Christ. Paul says believers have died to the law through Christ’s body so that they may belong to the risen Christ and bear fruit for God.

The two passages address different questions, but the explicit marriage illustration connects the household rule with God’s purpose of bringing people into fruitful life with His Son. That larger purpose helps keep the choices discussed here directed toward belonging to the Lord and serving Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 8:1-3
passages.section_title: Can knowing the right answer still leave something missing?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now about food sacrificed to idols: We know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up. 2 The one who thinks he knows something does not yet know as he ought to know. 3 But the one who loves God is known by God.
paragraphs: 1 Now about food sacrificed to idols: We know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up. 2 The one who thinks he knows something does not yet know as he ought to know. 3 But the one who loves God is known by God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul begins another subject raised by the Corinthians: food sacrificed to idols. Before answering the food question, he challenges the way knowledge is being used. Knowing something can become a reason for pride, while love works to build other people up.

The correction is not a rejection of learning. Paul will explain what believers know about God and idols. His concern is confidence that becomes self-important and careless about other people. The person who thinks he has mastered the matter still needs humility about what he knows and how he acts on it.

The closing sentence shifts attention from how much a person knows to being known by God as someone who loves Him. A relationship with God is not an intellectual contest in which having the best answer gives someone permission to disregard another believer.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a warning against knowledge separated from love. Calvin’s comment on verse 1 and Wesley’s note both preserve the distinction between learning that serves others and knowledge used to feed pride.
passages.god_plan_html:
In John 13:34–35, Jesus makes love shaped by His own love the distinguishing mark of His disciples. Their life together should help others recognize whom they follow.

1 Corinthians 13:1–7 develops the point further: even impressive knowledge, gifts and sacrifice are empty without love. God’s work among His people is directed toward a life that reflects Christ, rather than merely a community able to display correct information.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 8:4-6
passages.section_title: What do believers know about God and idols?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 4 So about eating food sacrificed to idols: We know that an idol is nothing at all in the world, and that there is no God but one. 5 For even if there are so-called gods, whether in heaven or on earth (as there are many so-called gods and lords), 6 yet for us there is but one God, the Father, from whom all things came and for whom we exist. And there is but one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things came and through whom we exist.
paragraphs: 4 So about eating food sacrificed to idols: We know that an idol is nothing at all in the world, and that there is no God but one. 5 For even if there are so-called gods, whether in heaven or on earth (as there are many so-called gods and lords), 6 yet for us there is but one God, the Father, from whom all things came and for whom we exist. And there is but one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things came and through whom we exist.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
An idol may exist as an object people worship, but it is not another true god. Paul contrasts the many so-called gods and lords with the one God to whom believers belong. The existence of many religious claims does not make all their objects divine.

He names the Father as the source of all things and the One for whom we exist. He also names Jesus Christ as the one Lord through whom all things came and through whom we exist. The confession places both creation and the believer’s life in relation to the Father and the Son.

This knowledge will matter to the food question, but it is not the whole answer. Paul will next address believers whose past connection with idols still affects their conscience. The truth about God must be joined with care for those learning to live by it.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these verses as a confession of the one God and one Lord Jesus Christ in contrast with idols. Wesley’s note on verse 6 explicitly understands the contrast as excluding idols, rather than treating Jesus as a lesser god or placing Him outside the worship due to God.
passages.god_plan_html:
Colossians 1:15–20 likewise describes all things being created through the Son and for Him, then connects His place in creation with His headship of the church and reconciliation through the blood of His cross.

That passage makes the larger purpose clear: the One through whom creation exists is also central to God’s work of reconciliation. Belonging to Christ directs life toward the Father’s purpose for creation, rather than leaving faith as one more religious attachment alongside competing gods.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 8:7-13
passages.section_title: When should love change how someone uses freedom?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 But not everyone has this knowledge. Some people are still so accustomed to idols that they eat such food as if it were sacrificed to an idol. And since their conscience is weak, it is defiled. 8 But food does not bring us closer to God: We are no worse if we do not eat, and no better if we do. 9 Be careful, however, that your freedom does not become a stumbling block to the weak. 10 For if someone with a weak conscience sees you who are well informed eating in an idol’s temple, will he not be encouraged to eat food sacrificed to idols? 11 So this weak brother, for whom Christ died, is destroyed by your knowledge. 12 By sinning against your brothers in this way and wounding their weak conscience, you sin against Christ. 13 Therefore, if what I eat causes my brother to stumble, I will never eat meat again, so that I will not cause him to stumble.
paragraphs: 7 But not everyone has this knowledge. Some people are still so accustomed to idols that they eat such food as if it were sacrificed to an idol. And since their conscience is weak, it is defiled. 8 But food does not bring us closer to God: We are no worse if we do not eat, and no better if we do. 9 Be careful, however, that your freedom does not become a stumbling block to the weak.

10 For if someone with a weak conscience sees you who are well informed eating in an idol’s temple, will he not be encouraged to eat food sacrificed to idols? 11 So this weak brother, for whom Christ died, is destroyed by your knowledge. 12 By sinning against your brothers in this way and wounding their weak conscience, you sin against Christ. 13 Therefore, if what I eat causes my brother to stumble, I will never eat meat again, so that I will not cause him to stumble.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Not everyone has left old associations with idols behind in the same way. Some eat the food as though still participating in its worship, and their conscience is wounded. Paul says food itself does not bring someone closer to God, but the effect on another person still matters.

He pictures a believer seen eating in an idol’s temple. Archaeologists have found dining rooms and cooking facilities at Corinth’s sanctuary of Demeter and Kore; see the excavation summary. This illustrates the connection between sanctuaries and meals without identifying that sanctuary as the place Paul means.

The danger is that a person with a troubled conscience may follow the example into conduct he still understands as involvement with idols. This is more than someone disliking another person’s food choice. Paul treats leading a brother into sin as an offense against that brother and against Christ, who died for him.

Paul would therefore give up meat rather than cause that harm. The discussion continues through chapter 10, where 1 Corinthians 10:14–22 explicitly forbids participation in idolatry. Concern for conscience is not a declaration that joining pagan worship becomes harmless whenever someone feels free to do it.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly recognize the call to put a brother or sister’s good above the enjoyment of a freedom. The warning about the brother being destroyed is taken seriously, though traditions differ over whether someone truly brought into grace can finally be lost.

Wesley’s note on verse 11 reads it as a real possibility that someone for whom Christ died may perish. The Methodist Articles, Article XII, likewise allow departure from grace and restoration through God’s grace. Catholic Catechism 1857–1861 teaches that grave sin committed with full knowledge and deliberate consent can bring loss of God’s saving grace, with repentance and God’s forgiveness necessary for restoration.

The Reformed Westminster Confession 17.1–3 instead affirms that those God truly accepts in Christ will not finally fall away, even though they can fall into serious sin. These broader differences affect how readers understand the warning’s final outcome; they do not remove Paul’s demand to avoid harming a fellow believer.
passages.god_plan_html:
A useful parallel appears in Matthew 18:10–14, where Jesus describes a shepherd seeking one sheep that has wandered and the Father’s concern that His little ones should not perish. The point of comparison is care for the person in danger, rather than an assumption that every detail names exactly the same situation.

Paul’s reminder that Christ died for the weak brother gives that care its weight here. The person affected by a meal is someone Christ has loved at great cost. In God’s purpose of gathering and caring for His people, that person’s good matters more than another believer’s opportunity to demonstrate freedom.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 9:1-6
passages.section_title: Why does Paul defend rights he has chosen not to use?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord? Are you yourselves not my workmanship in the Lord? 2 Even if I am not an apostle to others, surely I am to you. For you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord. 3 This is my defense to those who scrutinize me: 4 Have we no right to food and to drink? 5 Have we no right to take along a believing wife, as do the other apostles and the Lord’s brothers and Cephas? 6 Or are Barnabas and I the only apostles who must work for a living?
paragraphs: 1 Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord? Are you yourselves not my workmanship in the Lord? 2 Even if I am not an apostle to others, surely I am to you. For you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord. 3 This is my defense to those who scrutinize me:

4 Have we no right to food and to drink? 5 Have we no right to take along a believing wife, as do the other apostles and the Lord’s brothers and Cephas? 6 Or are Barnabas and I the only apostles who must work for a living?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul has just said he would give up meat rather than harm another believer. He now uses his own ministry to show how someone can have a real right and still choose to set it aside for others’ good.

He defends his apostleship by pointing to having seen Jesus and to the Corinthians themselves as the work of his service in the Lord. His decision to work for a living does not mean that he lacks the rights enjoyed by other apostles.

Those rights include food and drink and taking a believing wife along, as other apostles, the Lord’s brothers and Cephas do. Cephas is Peter. Paul also names Barnabas when asking whether only they must earn their own support. The point is that declining a right does not prove someone never had it.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand Paul to be defending his apostolic calling and right to support, including the needs of a wife accompanying him. His reference to married apostles is also relevant to differences in churches’ rules for ministers.

The Catholic Catechism 1579–1580 describes Latin-rite priests as normally chosen from men committed to celibacy, while recognizing married men being ordained as priests in the Eastern churches. Bishops there are chosen from celibate men, and men already ordained do not subsequently marry.

The Methodist Articles, Article XXI, teach that Christ’s ministers are not commanded by God’s law to vow singleness or abstain from marriage. These are differences in how churches order ministry; Paul’s immediate case concerns a right he can hold without exercising it.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Acts 9:15–16, the Lord identifies Paul as His chosen instrument to carry His name before Gentiles, kings and the people of Israel. His calling includes both witness and costly service.

The community in Corinth belongs within that wider mission. Paul’s work is directed toward people coming to know Christ, rather than toward proving his importance through visible privileges. His freedom can be used to serve the people God is gathering.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 9:7-14
passages.section_title: Why should those who receive ministry help support it?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 Who serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Who tends a flock and does not drink of its milk? 8 Do I say this from a human perspective? Doesn’t the Law say the same thing? 9 For it is written in the Law of Moses: “Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain.” Is it about oxen that God is concerned? 10 Isn’t He actually speaking on our behalf? Indeed, this was written for us, because when the plowman plows and the thresher threshes, they should also expect to share in the harvest. 11 If we have sown spiritual seed among you, is it too much for us to reap a material harvest from you? 12 If others have this right to your support, shouldn’t we have it all the more? But we did not exercise this right. Instead, we put up with anything rather than hinder the gospel of Christ. 13 Do you not know that those who work in the temple eat of its food, and those who serve at the altar partake of its offerings? 14 In the same way, the Lord has prescribed that those who preach the gospel should receive their living from the gospel.
paragraphs: 7 Who serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Who tends a flock and does not drink of its milk? 8 Do I say this from a human perspective? Doesn’t the Law say the same thing? 9 For it is written in the Law of Moses: “Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain.” Is it about oxen that God is concerned? 10 Isn’t He actually speaking on our behalf? Indeed, this was written for us, because when the plowman plows and the thresher threshes, they should also expect to share in the harvest. 11 If we have sown spiritual seed among you, is it too much for us to reap a material harvest from you?

12 If others have this right to your support, shouldn’t we have it all the more? But we did not exercise this right. Instead, we put up with anything rather than hinder the gospel of Christ. 13 Do you not know that those who work in the temple eat of its food, and those who serve at the altar partake of its offerings? 14 In the same way, the Lord has prescribed that those who preach the gospel should receive their living from the gospel.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul gives three ordinary examples: a soldier, someone tending a vineyard, and a shepherd. Workers receive provision connected with their labor. He then turns to the law of Moses about not muzzling an ox while it treads out grain, drawing a principle of sharing in the benefit of work.

His application is to the spiritual work he has done among the Corinthians and the material support he has a right to receive. He also recalls the support received by those serving at the temple and says that the Lord has appointed provision for those who preach the gospel.

Yet Paul has not exercised that right among them. He is willing to endure difficulty rather than hinder the gospel. That voluntary choice does not cancel the right to support. It shows that the good of the message and its hearers can take precedence over claiming what one is entitled to receive.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these verses as establishing a right to material support for gospel ministry while recognizing Paul’s freedom to waive it. Paul presents declining that provision as a choice made for the gospel’s sake.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Luke 10:1–9, Jesus sends workers to announce the kingdom and receive hospitality, explaining that a worker deserves wages. The mission involves both those sent and those who welcome and provide for them.

1 Timothy 5:17–18 again combines the law about the ox with the worker’s right to wages when discussing elders who labor in preaching and teaching. These connections place practical provision within shared responsibility for God’s work. Supporting a servant and serving without taking support can both be directed toward the good of the gospel.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 9:15-18
passages.section_title: What does Paul value about offering the gospel without charge?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 But I have not used any of these rights. And I am not writing this to suggest that something be done for me. Indeed, I would rather die than let anyone nullify my boast. 16 Yet when I preach the gospel, I have no reason to boast, because I am obligated to preach. Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel! 17 If my preaching is voluntary, I have a reward. But if it is not voluntary, I am still entrusted with a responsibility. 18 What then is my reward? That in preaching the gospel I may offer it free of charge, and so not use up my rights in preaching it.
paragraphs: 15 But I have not used any of these rights. And I am not writing this to suggest that something be done for me. Indeed, I would rather die than let anyone nullify my boast. 16 Yet when I preach the gospel, I have no reason to boast, because I am obligated to preach. Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel! 17 If my preaching is voluntary, I have a reward. But if it is not voluntary, I am still entrusted with a responsibility. 18 What then is my reward? That in preaching the gospel I may offer it free of charge, and so not use up my rights in preaching it.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul makes clear that explaining his rights is not a request to start paying him. He wants to preserve the freedom to offer the gospel without charge, and speaks strongly about the value he places on doing so.

He cannot treat preaching itself as a special favor he has chosen to do for God. A responsibility has been entrusted to him, and he is obligated to carry it out. His question about reward leads to the particular choice he can make within that responsibility: preaching without using his full right to support.

This continues the chapter’s distinction between holding a right and choosing to exercise it. Paul is explaining his own service among the Corinthians. The explanation does not withdraw the right to support he has just defended for those who preach.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these verses as explaining Paul’s personal choice to offer the gospel without charge. Wesley’s note on verse 17 recognizes that another preacher could serve willingly while receiving support; Calvin’s comment emphasizes Paul’s readiness to do what benefits the church rather than serving grudgingly.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Matthew 10:7–10, Jesus sends His disciples to announce the kingdom, give freely from what they have received, and receive provision as workers. Generosity and practical support belong together in that mission.

This is a connection in the purpose of service, rather than a requirement that every worker make exactly Paul’s financial choice. God’s gift is to reach people through servants who give themselves to His work. Paul’s decision removes a possible obstacle to that message among the people he serves.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 9:19-23
passages.section_title: What does becoming all things to all people mean?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 Though I am free of obligation to anyone, I make myself a slave to everyone, to win as many as possible. 20 To the Jews I became like a Jew, to win the Jews. To those under the law I became like one under the law (though I myself am not under the law), to win those under the law. 21 To those without the law I became like one without the law (though I am not outside the law of God but am under the law of Christ), to win those without the law. 22 To the weak I became weak, to win the weak. I have become all things to all people so that by all possible means I might save some. 23 I do all this for the sake of the gospel, so that I may share in its blessings.
paragraphs: 19 Though I am free of obligation to anyone, I make myself a slave to everyone, to win as many as possible. 20 To the Jews I became like a Jew, to win the Jews. To those under the law I became like one under the law (though I myself am not under the law), to win those under the law. 21 To those without the law I became like one without the law (though I am not outside the law of God but am under the law of Christ), to win those without the law.

22 To the weak I became weak, to win the weak. I have become all things to all people so that by all possible means I might save some. 23 I do all this for the sake of the gospel, so that I may share in its blessings.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Though free from obligation to people, Paul makes himself their servant in order to win them. He describes adapting his conduct among Jews, people under the law, those without the law and the weak. His freedom can be used to make room for others rather than require them to begin where he is.

The adaptation has a clear boundary: he is not outside God’s law, but under the law of Christ. He does not make pleasing an audience the final test of right and wrong. His aim is to bring people to the gospel while remaining faithful to the Lord he proclaims.

The repeated purpose is to win or save some. Paul does not claim that everyone will respond, or that he can produce salvation by technique. He gives up personal advantages and adjusts what he can for the gospel’s sake, seeking to share in its blessings.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as adapting to people for their good while remaining faithful to Christ. Wesley’s notes on verses 20–22 describe accommodation consistent with truth, and Calvin’s comment on verse 21 emphasizes that freedom from the Mosaic law does not remove obedience to Christ.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 2:11–22 describes Christ bringing people once separated into one body, giving both Jews and Gentiles access to the Father through the Spirit. God’s household is gathered across a division that had marked their lives.

Paul’s willingness to serve different people fits that larger purpose. He is not trying to make his own social position the condition for receiving the message. The people he approaches are being called to belong to Christ and share in the household God is building.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 9:24-27
passages.section_title: Why is Paul so concerned about finishing well?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 24 Do you not know that in a race all the runners run, but only one receives the prize? Run in such a way as to take the prize. 25 Everyone who competes in the games trains with strict discipline. They do it for a crown that is perishable, but we do it for a crown that is imperishable. 26 Therefore I do not run aimlessly; I do not fight like I am beating the air. 27 No, I discipline my body and make it my slave, so that after I have preached to others, I myself will not be disqualified.
paragraphs: 24 Do you not know that in a race all the runners run, but only one receives the prize? Run in such a way as to take the prize. 25 Everyone who competes in the games trains with strict discipline. They do it for a crown that is perishable, but we do it for a crown that is imperishable. 26 Therefore I do not run aimlessly; I do not fight like I am beating the air. 27 No, I discipline my body and make it my slave, so that after I have preached to others, I myself will not be disqualified.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul turns to runners and athletes who train seriously for a prize. Their crown will perish; the goal he sets before believers will not. The comparison calls for purpose and self-control, rather than suggesting that only one Christian can receive God’s approval.

He applies the pictures to himself: he does not run without a goal or box at empty air. His own desires and habits must serve the work entrusted to him. Teaching other people does not remove his need to live faithfully.

The word translated disqualified is adokimos (ah-DOH-kee-moss), ἀδόκιμος, meaning not approved or failing the test; see Thayer’s entry. The word makes the warning serious, but does not by itself settle whether the loss in view is ministry approval, reward or final salvation. That question requires reading the whole argument.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read the athletic picture as a call to disciplined, faithful living. They differ over what Paul means by the possibility of being disqualified.

The USCCB note on verse 27 connects Paul’s discipline with his own salvation, and Wesley’s note treats rejection as a real possibility even for someone already called to faith. The Catholic Catechism 1861 and the Methodist Articles, Article XII, provide the wider teaching that grace can be lost and restoration is possible.

The Reformed Westminster Confession 17.1–3 holds that those God truly accepts in Christ will be preserved to the end. In his own discussion of this verse, Sam Storms favors a warning about losing approval and rewards in apostolic service, while also considering a warning about perseverance in faith. This is his explanation, not a single reading required of every Reformed Christian. In each case, Paul’s self-discipline is taken seriously rather than treated as unnecessary.
passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 12:1–3 also describes the life of faith as a race, directing believers to Jesus, who endured the cross and is seated at God’s right hand. Their endurance looks to Him rather than resting only on determination.

2 Timothy 4:6–8 returns to the picture near the end of Paul’s life: finishing the race, keeping the faith and looking to the Lord’s award. The promised crown is also for all who long for Christ’s appearing. God’s purpose calls His people toward lasting life with Christ, not a contest in which another believer’s faithfulness takes away their opportunity.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 10:1-5
passages.section_title: Why does Paul bring up Israel’s journey through the wilderness?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that our forefathers were all under the cloud, and that they all passed through the sea. 2 They were all baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea. 3 They all ate the same spiritual food 4 and drank the same spiritual drink; for they drank from the spiritual rock that accompanied them, and that rock was Christ. 5 Nevertheless, God was not pleased with most of them, for they were struck down in the wilderness.
paragraphs: 1 I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that our forefathers were all under the cloud, and that they all passed through the sea. 2 They were all baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea. 3 They all ate the same spiritual food 4 and drank the same spiritual drink; for they drank from the spiritual rock that accompanied them, and that rock was Christ. 5 Nevertheless, God was not pleased with most of them, for they were struck down in the wilderness.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul has just described his own need for self-control. Now he turns to Israel’s history to show why the Corinthians should take that need seriously. An impressive beginning and shared blessings did not keep Israel from becoming unfaithful.

The repeated word all matters. The people shared God’s protection in the cloud, passage through the sea, food and water. Exodus 14:19–31, 16:12–18 and 17:1–7 describe those gifts. Being baptized into Moses connects the people’s passage through the cloud and sea with their shared relationship to the leader God had appointed. Paul is drawing a comparison, rather than saying Exodus describes a Christian baptism ceremony.

Calling the food and drink spiritual does not mean they were imaginary. The people really ate and drank; God supplied what they could not supply for themselves. Paul then identifies Christ with the spiritual rock that accompanied them. His emphasis is on the source of their provision. The Exodus account describes water coming from a rock, but does not say that a physical rock traveled behind the people.

Yet most of that generation did not enter the promised land. Numbers 14:26–35 connects their deaths in the wilderness with their rebellion. That is Paul’s warning to a church tempted to treat its privileges as protection from the consequences of disobedience.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand Israel’s experience here as a warning against relying on outward privileges while disregarding God. Wesley’s notes on verses 1–5 and the USCCB notes also connect the sea and the spiritual food and drink with Christian baptism and the Lord’s Supper. That shared comparison does not settle the differences between churches over what those practices accomplish.
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul himself makes the connection to Christ: Israel’s life-giving provision was not separate from Him. The connection reaches back before His earthly ministry and places the wilderness story within the work of the same Lord whom the Corinthians now confess.

In John 6:31–35, Jesus moves from the manna given in the wilderness to the lasting life He gives as the bread of life. God’s purpose reaches beyond keeping people alive for another day: He calls them to receive life through His Son. The earlier provision helps readers understand the gift; it also makes refusing the Giver all the more serious.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 10:6-13
passages.section_title: What can Israel’s failures teach us about temptation?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 These things took place as examples to keep us from craving evil things as they did. 7 Do not be idolaters, as some of them were. As it is written: “The people sat down to eat and drink and got up to indulge in revelry.” 8 We should not commit sexual immorality, as some of them did, and in one day twenty-three thousand of them died. 9 We should not test Christ, as some of them did, and were killed by snakes. 10 And do not complain, as some of them did, and were killed by the destroying angel. 11 Now these things happened to them as examples and were written down as warnings for us, on whom the fulfillment of the ages has come. 12 So the one who thinks he is standing firm should be careful not to fall. 13 No temptation has seized you except what is common to man. And God is faithful; He will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear. But when you are tempted, He will also provide an escape, so that you can stand up under it.
paragraphs: 6 These things took place as examples to keep us from craving evil things as they did. 7 Do not be idolaters, as some of them were. As it is written: “The people sat down to eat and drink and got up to indulge in revelry.” 8 We should not commit sexual immorality, as some of them did, and in one day twenty-three thousand of them died. 9 We should not test Christ, as some of them did, and were killed by snakes. 10 And do not complain, as some of them did, and were killed by the destroying angel.

11 Now these things happened to them as examples and were written down as warnings for us, on whom the fulfillment of the ages has come. 12 So the one who thinks he is standing firm should be careful not to fall. 13 No temptation has seized you except what is common to man. And God is faithful; He will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear. But when you are tempted, He will also provide an escape, so that you can stand up under it.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
These events were recorded for the church’s instruction. Paul names cravings for evil, idol worship, sexual immorality, testing Christ and complaining. His examples make the warning concrete: people who had received God’s help still chose conduct that brought judgment.

The meal and revelry recall the golden calf in Exodus 32:1–8. Numbers 25:1–9 connects sexual immorality with joining the worship of other gods; Numbers 21:4–9 describes complaints followed by deadly snakes. Paul is preparing the Corinthians to recognize the danger of idol worship in their own setting, not inviting them to look down on Israel.

His warning about confidence applies to anyone who thinks falling is someone else’s problem. But the next verse gives encouragement: temptation is not unique to them, and God remains faithful. He provides a way to endure without giving in. The promise calls for trusting Him and taking the way He provides; the very next instruction is to flee idolatry.

The Greek word peirasmos (pie-rahs-MOSS), πειρασμός, can refer to a test or a temptation; Thayer’s entry explains both uses. Here the surrounding examples concern temptation to sin. Paul is not promising that every grief or hardship will feel manageable. He elsewhere describes suffering beyond his own ability to endure, which taught him to depend on God rather than himself (2 Corinthians 1:8–10).
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this passage as both a serious warning and reassurance of God’s faithfulness. Wesley’s notes on verses 12–13 and the USCCB notes hold those together: confidence in one’s own safety is misplaced, while God’s help gives a reason to resist temptation rather than surrender to it.
passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 3:7–19 also brings Israel’s wilderness history directly to believers in Christ. It warns against a heart that turns away from God and calls people to encourage one another daily, so that sin does not harden them.

That gives these warnings a place in the life of God’s people together. Remembering the past is meant to help a community remain faithful now. The goal is sharing in Christ and holding firmly to Him; helping another person resist temptation belongs to that purpose, alongside taking our own choices seriously.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 10:14-22
passages.section_title: Why can’t believers share in both kinds of worship?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry. 15 I speak to reasonable people; judge for yourselves what I say. 16 Is not the cup of blessing that we bless a participation in the blood of Christ? And is not the bread that we break a participation in the body of Christ? 17 Because there is one loaf, we who are many are one body; for we all partake of the one loaf. 18 Consider the people of Israel: Are not those who eat the sacrifices fellow partakers in the altar? 19 Am I suggesting, then, that food sacrificed to an idol is anything, or that an idol is anything? 20 No, but the sacrifices of pagans are offered to demons, not to God. And I do not want you to be participants with demons. 21 You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons too; you cannot partake in the table of the Lord and the table of demons too. 22 Are we trying to provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than He?
paragraphs: 14 Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry. 15 I speak to reasonable people; judge for yourselves what I say. 16 Is not the cup of blessing that we bless a participation in the blood of Christ? And is not the bread that we break a participation in the body of Christ? 17 Because there is one loaf, we who are many are one body; for we all partake of the one loaf. 18 Consider the people of Israel: Are not those who eat the sacrifices fellow partakers in the altar?

19 Am I suggesting, then, that food sacrificed to an idol is anything, or that an idol is anything? 20 No, but the sacrifices of pagans are offered to demons, not to God. And I do not want you to be participants with demons. 21 You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons too; you cannot partake in the table of the Lord and the table of demons too. 22 Are we trying to provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than He?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul’s instruction is direct: flee idolatry. Knowing that an idol is not a real god does not make joining its worship harmless. He asks the Corinthians to consider what sharing a religious meal means.

The cup and bread of the Lord’s Supper express participation in Christ’s blood and body. The one loaf also expresses the unity of the many people who share it. Paul then points to Israel’s sacrifices: those who eat share in the altar. His concern reaches beyond what food is made of to the relationship in which people participate.

He is not taking back his teaching that an idol has no divine power. He is saying that pagan sacrifices involve demons rather than God, and he does not want believers to participate with them. Deuteronomy 32:16–21 already connects sacrifices to demons with provoking God’s jealousy.

This gives a clear boundary to Christian freedom. A meal that joins people in idol worship is different from buying food at a market or accepting an ordinary invitation, which Paul addresses next. Belonging to Christ cannot be treated as compatible with sharing the worship of His rivals.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read this as forbidding participation in idol worship. They differ over how believers participate in Christ’s body and blood in the Lord’s Supper.

The Catholic Church teaches that Christ is truly present and that the bread and wine become His body and blood; see Catechism 1374–1377. Lutheran teaching likewise affirms receiving Christ’s actual body and blood under the bread and wine; see Luther’s Small Catechism. That statement does not make the two churches’ explanations identical.

The Reformed Westminster Confession 29.5–7 and the 1689 Baptist Confession 30.5–7 teach that the elements remain bread and wine while believers truly receive Christ and the benefits of His death spiritually through faith. The Methodist Articles, Article XVIII, also describe receiving Christ spiritually through faith. These teachings go beyond remembering an absent person; they should not be reduced to the claim that nothing is received.

These are the stated positions of those documents. Individual Christians and congregations may explain the meal differently. The disagreement does not remove Paul’s shared demand for undivided loyalty to Christ.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Luke 22:19–20, Jesus gives the bread and cup in connection with His coming death and the new covenant in His blood. Paul’s description of one body formed from many people shows the communal reach of that covenant: the gift binds people to Christ and to one another.

The Lord’s table therefore belongs within God’s work of gathering a people through His Son’s death. Its meaning is not exhausted by a private moment between an individual and God. Sharing that table calls the gathered people to live as those who belong to the same Lord.
