passages.title: 1 Corinthians 10:23-30
passages.section_title: When should freedom give way to concern for someone else?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 23 “Everything is permissible,” but not everything is beneficial. “Everything is permissible,” but not everything is edifying. 24 No one should seek his own good, but the good of others. 25 Eat anything sold in the meat market without raising questions of conscience, 26 for, “The earth is the Lord’s, and the fullness thereof.” 27 If an unbeliever invites you to a meal and you want to go, eat anything set before you without raising questions of conscience. 28 But if someone tells you, “This food was offered to idols,” then do not eat it, for the sake of the one who told you and for the sake of conscience— 29 the other one’s conscience, I mean, not your own. For why should my freedom be determined by someone else’s conscience? 30 If I partake in the meal with thankfulness, why am I denounced because of that for which I give thanks?
paragraphs: 23 “Everything is permissible,” but not everything is beneficial. “Everything is permissible,” but not everything is edifying. 24 No one should seek his own good, but the good of others. 25 Eat anything sold in the meat market without raising questions of conscience, 26 for, “The earth is the Lord’s, and the fullness thereof.” 27 If an unbeliever invites you to a meal and you want to go, eat anything set before you without raising questions of conscience.

28 But if someone tells you, “This food was offered to idols,” then do not eat it, for the sake of the one who told you and for the sake of conscience— 29 the other one’s conscience, I mean, not your own. For why should my freedom be determined by someone else’s conscience? 30 If I partake in the meal with thankfulness, why am I denounced because of that for which I give thanks?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul returns to the claim that everything is permissible and asks two further questions: is it helpful, and does it build others up? Seeking another person’s good changes how freedom is used. The preceding ban on idol worship still stands; this is not permission to do whatever someone can defend.

His practical instructions distinguish ordinary food from participation in worship. Buy what is sold at the meat market without investigating its history. If an unbeliever invites you to eat and you want to go, accept the food without raising questions of conscience. The earth belongs to the Lord, so an idol does not own part of His creation.

The situation changes when someone specifically identifies the food as having been offered to idols. Paul says not to eat for that person’s sake. The food has not become a different substance; the meaning of eating it in front of this person has changed. Paul does not identify the person closely enough to turn the example into a detailed story about a particular host, shopkeeper or fellow Christian.

The final questions preserve a distinction: someone else’s conscience does not determine the truth about my freedom, yet I can willingly limit my conduct for that person’s good. Thankfulness for God’s gifts belongs alongside care for people. Freedom is something to use lovingly, rather than a right that must always be exercised.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly distinguish the food itself from the effect of eating it in a particular situation. Wesley’s notes on verses 25–30 explain both permission to eat without investigation and restraint for another person’s conscience. His note on verse 29 also recognizes that another person’s conviction does not become the standard that decides the believer’s freedom.
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul grounds ordinary eating in Psalm 24:1–2: the earth and its fullness belong to its Creator. Food does not become an idol’s property because people have used it in false worship.

1 Timothy 4:1–5 likewise sets God’s good creation against religious teaching that forbids receiving His gifts. Those gifts are to be received with thanksgiving. Together, these passages show how ordinary life can acknowledge the Creator: receive what He gives gratefully, and use that freedom with concern for the people He has placed around us.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 10:31-33
passages.section_title: What should guide even the ordinary choices of life?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 31 So whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do it all to the glory of God. 32 Do not become a stumbling block, whether to Jews or Greeks or the church of God— 33 as I also try to please everyone in all I do. For I am not seeking my own good, but the good of many, that they may be saved.
paragraphs: 31 So whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do it all to the glory of God. 32 Do not become a stumbling block, whether to Jews or Greeks or the church of God— 33 as I also try to please everyone in all I do. For I am not seeking my own good, but the good of many, that they may be saved.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul closes the discussion with a principle that reaches beyond disputed food: eating, drinking and everything else should be done for God’s glory. Even an ordinary meal offers an opportunity to honor Him through the way we treat people.

He names Jews, Greeks and the church of God, extending the concern beyond those already inside the congregation. Avoiding a stumbling block means taking care not to put an obstacle in the way of their response to God. It cannot mean agreeing with every opinion or never saying anything someone dislikes; Paul has just given a firm instruction against idolatry.

Paul presents his own practice as an example. His aim in pleasing others is their good and, ultimately, their salvation. This brings the discussion back to the gospel’s purpose. Personal advantage is not the measure of a good decision when another person’s spiritual good is at stake.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand these verses as calling every part of life into service to God and the good of others. Wesley’s note on verse 31 applies the instruction to ordinary daily activities as well as explicitly religious ones; his notes on verses 32–33 recognize the concern to avoid needless offense as far as possible.
passages.god_plan_html:
In John 17:15–23, Jesus prays for His people to remain in the world, be kept from evil, be made holy in the truth, and be united so that the world may believe the Father sent Him. Their shared life is part of their witness.

Paul’s concern for everyday conduct fits that purpose. A community can honor God in the way its members use freedom, make room for one another and meet those who do not yet believe. The goal reaches beyond maintaining a good reputation: people are being invited to know the Father through His Son.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 11:1-2
passages.section_title: What kind of example and teaching should the church follow?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 You are to imitate me, just as I imitate Christ. 2 Now I commend you for remembering me in everything and for maintaining the traditions, just as I passed them on to you.
paragraphs: 1 You are to imitate me, just as I imitate Christ. 2 Now I commend you for remembering me in everything and for maintaining the traditions, just as I passed them on to you.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul’s invitation to imitate him finishes the thought at the end of chapter 10. He has described setting aside personal advantage for the good of others and their salvation. Christ is the standard behind that example: Paul asks people to follow him as he follows Christ.

He then commends the Corinthians for remembering him and maintaining what he passed on. This praise introduces a discussion of practices in their worship, some of which will need correction. It does not mean every part of their life together already has Paul’s approval.

The word traditions translates paradosis (pah-RAH-doh-sis), παράδοσις: teaching or instruction handed on; see Thayer’s entry. The word itself does not mean an empty custom or a human addition to God’s commands. Here Paul is speaking positively about instruction he delivered. What was handed on, and whether it is faithful, matter more than simply labeling something traditional.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand Paul’s example as accountable to Christ and his instruction as something the church should preserve. Calvin’s comment on verse 1 identifies the verse with the preceding discussion and stresses Christ as the pattern. Wesley’s note on verse 2 recognizes the genuine praise without treating it as approval of everyone’s conduct.
passages.god_plan_html:
In John 13:12–17, Jesus washes His disciples’ feet and gives them an example of serving one another. His authority as Lord leads them into service, not into competing for importance.

Paul’s imitation of Christ belongs within that same calling. The teaching passed from one generation of believers to another is meant to shape a people whose life reflects their Lord. A leader’s example helps only as it leads people toward Him.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 11:3-6
passages.section_title: Why does Paul connect head coverings with honor?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 3 But I want you to understand that the head of every man is Christ, and the head of the woman is man, and the head of Christ is God. 4 Every man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonors his head. 5 And every woman who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonors her head, for it is just as if her head were shaved. 6 If a woman does not cover her head, she should have her hair cut off. And if it is shameful for a woman to have her hair cut or shaved off, she should cover her head.
paragraphs: 3 But I want you to understand that the head of every man is Christ, and the head of the woman is man, and the head of Christ is God. 4 Every man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonors his head. 5 And every woman who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonors her head, for it is just as if her head were shaved. 6 If a woman does not cover her head, she should have her hair cut off. And if it is shameful for a woman to have her hair cut or shaved off, she should cover her head.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul begins with relationships: Christ and man, man and woman, and God and Christ. He then speaks about men and women praying or prophesying and whether their heads are covered. The word head moves between a person’s physical head and a relationship that can be honored or dishonored.

The passage assumes that women pray and prophesy; the immediate correction concerns how that is done. Paul compares an uncovered woman’s head with having her hair cut or shaved off, treating both as shameful in the situation he addresses. He is pressing the seriousness of dishonor, rather than giving a separate instruction that women should shave their heads.

The Greek words translated man and woman can also mean husband and wife; see Thayer’s entry for man and woman. A word’s possible meanings do not by themselves decide whether Paul is speaking only about married couples here. His discussion of prayer, prophecy and the churches must also be considered.

The text gives enough to see that the Corinthians’ conduct carries meaning beyond personal preference. It does not explain every local custom or give the private motives of the women involved. Those gaps should not be filled by confidently retelling a story Paul did not record.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin’s comment on verse 3 and Wesley’s notes read headship in terms of authority and understand the covering as expressing the woman’s relationship to man. They explain God’s headship of Christ in relation to the Son’s work as mediator, rather than as proof that He has a lesser divine nature.

Other interpreters emphasize connection and mutual dependence. In her own CBE International article, Juliann Bullock reads the head-and-body picture as describing an inseparable relationship, and understands the passage as protecting women’s honor and participation. This is an individual scholar’s reading, not the official position of an entire denomination.

The readings differ over the relationships Paul is describing, as well as how his instruction applies today. Neither the English word head nor one dictionary entry settles every part of that discussion.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 11:7-12
passages.section_title: How does creation shape this discussion without making either sex independent?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 A man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God; but the woman is the glory of man. 8 For man did not come from woman, but woman from man. 9 Neither was man created for woman, but woman for man. 10 For this reason a woman ought to have a sign of authority on her head, because of the angels. 11 In the Lord, however, woman is not independent of man, nor is man independent of woman. 12 For just as woman came from man, so also man is born of woman. But everything comes from God.
paragraphs: 7 A man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God; but the woman is the glory of man. 8 For man did not come from woman, but woman from man. 9 Neither was man created for woman, but woman for man. 10 For this reason a woman ought to have a sign of authority on her head, because of the angels.
11 In the Lord, however, woman is not independent of man, nor is man independent of woman. 12 For just as woman came from man, so also man is born of woman. But everything comes from God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul brings the creation of man and woman into his explanation of covering and honor. His references to woman coming from man and being created for him recall Genesis 2:18–24. That account begins with the man’s need for a suitable helper, not with his being complete without her.

His description of man as God’s image must also be read with Genesis 1:26–28, which explicitly includes both male and female in God’s image. Paul does not say women lack that image.

Verse 10 refers to authority on the woman’s head and gives a further reason: the angels. The BSB footnote also allows the wording have authority over. Paul does not explain the angels’ role here, so an interpretation of that phrase should be identified as an interpretation.

The final two verses prevent the creation reference from becoming a claim that men have no need of women. In the Lord, neither is independent of the other. Woman came from man at creation; men are born through women; and everything comes from God. Both their relationship and their dependence on Him belong in the reading.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin’s comment on verse 10 understands the covering as a sign of being under a husband’s authority and sees angels as witnesses to conduct in worship. Wesley’s note also connects the angels with the gathered assembly.

Juliann Bullock instead understands the authority as the woman’s authority concerning her own head, and reads verses 11–12 as emphasizing mutual dependence. The BSB’s alternative wording makes the translation question visible, but does not settle the full interpretation. The brief reference to angels remains a point on which explanations should be held with care.
passages.god_plan_html:
The creation account gives both man and woman a place in the human calling to bear God’s image and care for His world (Genesis 1:26–28). Neither can claim to be the source of the other’s ultimate worth.

Galatians 3:26–29 brings male and female alike into the promise through belonging to Christ. Their shared inheritance is not reserved for one sex. Whatever conclusions readers reach about roles or coverings, those conclusions must account for the place both have among God’s children and heirs.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 11:13-16
passages.section_title: Does Paul’s instruction about coverings still apply today?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 Judge for yourselves: Is it proper for a woman to pray to God with her head uncovered? 14 Doesn’t nature itself teach you that if a man has long hair, it is a disgrace to him, 15 but that if a woman has long hair, it is her glory? For long hair is given to her as a covering. 16 If anyone is inclined to dispute this, we have no other practice, nor do the churches of God.
paragraphs: 13 Judge for yourselves: Is it proper for a woman to pray to God with her head uncovered? 14 Doesn’t nature itself teach you that if a man has long hair, it is a disgrace to him, 15 but that if a woman has long hair, it is her glory? For long hair is given to her as a covering. 16 If anyone is inclined to dispute this, we have no other practice, nor do the churches of God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul asks the Corinthians to judge what is proper and appeals to the way they understand long hair on men and women. A woman’s long hair is described as her glory and as a covering. Readers differ over how this relates to the covering discussed earlier in the passage.

The wording does not give a required hair length in inches or identify one hairstyle that every culture must share. Paul is asking his readers to recognize a distinction that supports his appeal about honor in prayer.

He closes by addressing the person inclined to dispute the matter and appeals to the practice of the churches. The discussion has a shared setting: their choices affect the worshiping community. Applying that instruction today requires considering both his stated reasons and what the covering communicates.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Some Christians understand the covering as an instruction still binding in worship. The Head Covering Movement’s explanation grounds that reading in Paul’s appeal to creation, seeing the covering as a Christian sign rather than a custom that expires when local clothing changes. The movement is an advocate for this reading, not a voice for all Protestants.

Others distinguish an enduring concern for fitting conduct from a requirement to keep the same garment. The Catholic declaration Inter Insigniores, section 4, explicitly treats the requirement for women to wear a veil in this passage as a disciplinary practice that no longer binds.

The disagreement is therefore not simply whether to take Scripture seriously. It concerns how Paul’s reasons, his appeal to the churches and the meaning of the practice determine its continuing application.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 11:17-22
passages.section_title: How can a church gathering do more harm than good?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 In the following instructions I have no praise to offer, because your gatherings do more harm than good. 18 First of all, I hear that when you come together as a church, there are divisions among you, and in part I believe it. 19 And indeed, there must be differences among you to show which of you are approved. 20 Now then, when you come together, it is not the Lord’s Supper you eat. 21 For as you eat, each of you goes ahead without sharing his meal. While one remains hungry, another gets drunk. 22 Don’t you have your own homes in which to eat and drink? Or do you despise the church of God and humiliate those who have nothing? What can I say to you? Shall I praise you for this? No, I will not!
paragraphs: 17 In the following instructions I have no praise to offer, because your gatherings do more harm than good. 18 First of all, I hear that when you come together as a church, there are divisions among you, and in part I believe it. 19 And indeed, there must be differences among you to show which of you are approved. 20 Now then, when you come together, it is not the Lord’s Supper you eat. 21 For as you eat, each of you goes ahead without sharing his meal. While one remains hungry, another gets drunk. 22 Don’t you have your own homes in which to eat and drink? Or do you despise the church of God and humiliate those who have nothing? What can I say to you? Shall I praise you for this? No, I will not!

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul’s earlier praise gives way to a direct rebuke. The Corinthians gather as a church, but the way they eat divides and humiliates people instead of expressing the fellowship of the Lord’s Supper.

The failure is concrete: one person goes hungry while another gets drunk. Some go ahead with their own meal without sharing. Paul asks whether they despise God’s church and shame those who have nothing. He is exposing behavior that contradicts the meaning of the meal, rather than objecting simply to people eating together.

His statement that differences reveal who is approved does not authorize creating factions. The divisions expose the character of the people involved. The surrounding rebuke makes clear that humiliating the poor is no mark of God’s approval.

The passage shows unequal access to food and a failure to wait or share. It does not describe the building’s floor plan, assign every person a social rank, or explain exactly how the problem began. The wrongdoing is clear without turning a possible reconstruction into recorded history.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand these verses as condemning a gathering that humiliates poorer members while others indulge themselves. Wesley’s notes on verses 20–22 emphasize the failure to share, and the USCCB introduction to verses 17–34 connects the abuse with neglect of the Lord’s Supper’s meaning.
passages.god_plan_html:
James 2:1–9 similarly rejects honoring the rich while pushing the poor aside in the assembly. It connects the treatment of people with faith in Jesus and with the kingdom promised to those who love God. Wealth does not determine a person’s place among His people.

2 Corinthians 8:9 places generosity in the setting of Christ’s own grace: He gave Himself for others’ good. The shared meal belongs to a people being shaped by that gift. Treating another believer as an unwanted guest contradicts the welcome they themselves have received through Him.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 11:23-26
passages.section_title: What is the Lord’s Supper meant to proclaim?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 23 For I received from the Lord what I also passed on to you: The Lord Jesus, on the night He was betrayed, took bread, 24 and when He had given thanks, He broke it and said, “This is My body, which is for you; do this in remembrance of Me.” 25 In the same way, after supper He took the cup, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in My blood; do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of Me.” 26 For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until He comes.
paragraphs: 23 For I received from the Lord what I also passed on to you: The Lord Jesus, on the night He was betrayed, took bread, 24 and when He had given thanks, He broke it and said, “This is My body, which is for you; do this in remembrance of Me.” 25 In the same way, after supper He took the cup, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in My blood; do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of Me.” 26 For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until He comes.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
To correct the Corinthians, Paul returns to what he received from the Lord and passed on to them. He places the meal on the night Jesus was betrayed. The church’s practice is accountable to Jesus’ gift and instruction, not to whichever social habits its members prefer.

Jesus takes bread, gives thanks, and identifies it with His body given for them. He gives the cup in connection with the new covenant in His blood. Both actions are to be repeated in remembrance of Him. The people’s attention is directed toward His self-giving, making their selfish meals especially out of place.

The meal looks backward and forward: it proclaims the Lord’s death until He comes. Remembrance is therefore more than recalling a sad event. The church confesses the significance of His death while awaiting the living Lord’s return.

Paul speaks of eating and drinking repeatedly without setting a calendar in these verses. He gives the meal’s meaning and purpose; this passage alone does not prescribe a weekly, monthly or annual schedule.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the bread and cup as instituted by Jesus to remember and proclaim His saving death while awaiting His return. They differ over how He is present and received in the meal.

The Catholic Catechism 1374–1377 teaches that Christ is truly present and the bread and wine become His body and blood. Luther’s Small Catechism affirms receiving His true body and blood under the bread and wine. Their explanations should not be treated as identical.

The Reformed Westminster Confession 29.5–7, 1689 Baptist Confession 30.5–7 and Methodist Article XVIII describe receiving Christ spiritually through faith rather than a change of the elements into His body and blood. Those documents teach more than simply remembering; they do not represent every individual Protestant interpretation.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jeremiah 31:31–34 promises a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, marked by God’s law written within, knowing Him, and forgiveness. Jesus explicitly connects the cup with the new covenant in His blood.

Hebrews 8:6–13 quotes Jeremiah’s promise and identifies Jesus as the mediator of the better covenant. Paul’s account of the meal therefore points beyond a gathering’s immediate needs to God’s promised work of bringing people into a forgiven relationship with Himself. Its future horizon remains Christ’s coming.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 11:27-34
passages.section_title: What does it mean to examine ourselves before sharing the meal?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 27 Therefore, whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty of sinning against the body and blood of the Lord. 28 Each one must examine himself before he eats of the bread and drinks of the cup. 29 For anyone who eats and drinks without recognizing the body eats and drinks judgment on himself. 30 That is why many among you are weak and sick, and a number of you have fallen asleep. 31 Now if we judged ourselves properly, we would not come under judgment. 32 But when we are judged by the Lord, we are being disciplined so that we will not be condemned with the world. 33 So, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another. 34 If anyone is hungry, he should eat at home, so that when you come together it will not result in judgment. And when I come, I will give instructions about the remaining matters.
paragraphs: 27 Therefore, whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty of sinning against the body and blood of the Lord. 28 Each one must examine himself before he eats of the bread and drinks of the cup. 29 For anyone who eats and drinks without recognizing the body eats and drinks judgment on himself.

30 That is why many among you are weak and sick, and a number of you have fallen asleep. 31 Now if we judged ourselves properly, we would not come under judgment. 32 But when we are judged by the Lord, we are being disciplined so that we will not be condemned with the world. 33 So, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another. 34 If anyone is hungry, he should eat at home, so that when you come together it will not result in judgment. And when I come, I will give instructions about the remaining matters.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The seriousness of the meal leads Paul to warn against eating or drinking in an unworthy manner. The warning concerns the way people participate. In this chapter, that includes selfishness, drunkenness, humiliation of the poor and failure to wait for one another.

Each person is to examine himself and then eat and drink. The instruction is a call to take part rightly, rather than to search for a sinless person who deserves Christ’s gift. Recognizing the body must be read with both the bread given in remembrance of Christ’s body and the divided people who are supposed to share as one body.

Paul identifies weakness, sickness and deaths among them as consequences of this wrongdoing. He distinguishes the Lord’s discipline from condemnation with the world: the correction has a purpose beyond punishment. The warning is serious without making the word judgment automatically mean final condemnation in every use.

His practical remedy returns to the problem: wait for one another, and satisfy hunger at home rather than turn the gathering into a selfish meal. Other matters can be addressed when he comes. This passage identifies a particular situation in Corinth; it does not give readers grounds to label every sick person as guilty of the same offense. John 9:1–3 also warns against assuming someone’s suffering proves a particular person’s sin.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand self-examination as necessary to honor Christ and participate responsibly. They place different emphasis on recognizing the body. Wesley’s notes on verses 27–29 emphasize treating the meal’s sacred signs according to their purpose; Calvin’s comment on verse 29 likewise stresses recognizing Christ’s body as holy.

The USCCB note on verse 28 connects recognizing Jesus’ self-giving with the unity it requires among those who share the meal. The emphases can overlap: honoring Christ’s death and caring for the people joined to Him both speak directly to the conduct Paul is correcting.
passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 12:5–11 describes the Lord’s discipline as a Father’s care for His children, intended to bring them to share His holiness and bear the fruit of righteousness and peace. Paul’s distinction between correction and condemnation fits that stated purpose.

The goal is not a community frightened away from the table, but a people whose conduct is being changed by the Lord they confess. His saving work calls for a shared life consistent with His gift, including honest self-examination and practical care for one another.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 12:1-3
passages.section_title: How can we recognize the Spirit’s work?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now about spiritual gifts, brothers, I do not want you to be uninformed. 2 You know that when you were pagans, you were influenced and led astray to mute idols. 3 Therefore I inform you that no one who is speaking by the Spirit of God says, “Jesus be cursed,” and no one can say, “Jesus is Lord,” except by the Holy Spirit.
paragraphs: 1 Now about spiritual gifts, brothers, I do not want you to be uninformed. 2 You know that when you were pagans, you were influenced and led astray to mute idols. 3 Therefore I inform you that no one who is speaking by the Spirit of God says, “Jesus be cursed,” and no one can say, “Jesus is Lord,” except by the Holy Spirit.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul introduces the subject of spiritual gifts, which continues through chapters 13 and 14. Before discussing particular gifts, he reminds the Corinthians of the difference between their former worship of idols and their present confession of Jesus.

Being led toward mute idols had not brought them to the truth. Paul now gives a clear test of speech attributed to God’s Spirit: the Spirit does not lead someone to curse Jesus. A genuine confession of Jesus as Lord, by contrast, depends on the Holy Spirit.

The point is not that an unbeliever’s mouth cannot form the words, or that quoting a curse while explaining the passage is itself evidence of evil. Paul is speaking about what people truly confess and the Spirit behind it. The direction of their allegiance to Jesus matters more than how impressive their speech sounds.

This prepares the church to assess gifts without confusing spiritual display with faithfulness to Christ. The following discussion will ask how those gifts serve His people, rather than treating a striking experience as sufficient proof of its source.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as directing attention to Jesus rather than trusting every claim of spiritual inspiration. Wesley’s note on verse 3 understands the confession as truly receiving Jesus as Lord, and the USCCB note on verses 2–3 explains that the Spirit’s work cannot contradict allegiance to Him.
passages.god_plan_html:
In John 16:12–15, Jesus tells His disciples that the Spirit of truth will guide them and glorify Him. The Spirit’s work continues the revelation of the Son, rather than drawing people away from Him.

Paul’s test belongs within that purpose. Spiritual gifts are part of a life turned toward the Lord whom the Spirit makes known. Before asking what an experience can do for us, the passage asks whether it honors the Jesus at the center of God’s saving work.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 12:4-7
passages.section_title: Why does God give different gifts to different people?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 4 There are different gifts, but the same Spirit. 5 There are different ministries, but the same Lord. 6 There are different ways of working, but the same God works all things in all people. 7 Now to each one the manifestation of the Spirit is given for the common good.
paragraphs: 4 There are different gifts, but the same Spirit. 5 There are different ministries, but the same Lord. 6 There are different ways of working, but the same God works all things in all people. 7 Now to each one the manifestation of the Spirit is given for the common good.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul repeats the contrast between variety and a common source. There are different gifts, ministries and ways of working, but the same Spirit, Lord and God. Differences in service do not require a divided church or competing spiritual loyalties.

The word for gift is charisma (KHAH-ris-mah), χάρισμα, a gift of grace; see Thayer’s entry. Paul’s language directs attention to what God gives, rather than to an achievement that makes its recipient superior to someone else.

Verse 7 states the purpose: what the Spirit makes evident through each person is given for the common good. A gift is not simply private property or a badge of importance. How it helps other people belongs to understanding what it is for.

These verses establish the source and purpose of the variety before Paul lists examples. They do not require every believer to perform the same task, or make a person with a conspicuous gift more valuable than someone serving less visibly.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the variety of gifts as serving the good of one community under God. Wesley’s notes on verses 4–7 distinguish gifts, service and the effects God produces, while the USCCB note on verses 4–6 connects all three with God’s gracious work. Their shared purpose is more than personal spiritual distinction.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 4:7–16 connects the giving of gifts with the ascended Christ and the building up of His body. People are equipped for service so the community grows toward unity, maturity and the knowledge of the Son of God.

That gives the gifts a direction beyond accomplishing isolated tasks. God is forming a people who grow in truth and love under Christ, with each part contributing to the whole. The differences are meant to help the body mature together, rather than keep some members permanently dependent on a few gifted people.
passages.current_position_html: In What Is the True Church?, we understand the Spirit’s gifts as given for the common good, with every believer sharing responsibility to serve. We therefore read this passage as calling the whole community to use what God gives for one another’s benefit. This statement does not settle which particular gifts continue today or how each should be practiced.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 12:8-11
passages.section_title: Who decides which gifts each person receives?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 To one there is given through the Spirit the message of wisdom, to another the message of knowledge by the same Spirit, 9 to another faith by the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing by that one Spirit, 10 to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another distinguishing between spirits, to another speaking in various tongues, and to still another the interpretation of tongues. 11 All these are the work of one and the same Spirit, who apportions them to each one as He determines.
paragraphs: 8 To one there is given through the Spirit the message of wisdom, to another the message of knowledge by the same Spirit, 9 to another faith by the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing by that one Spirit, 10 to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another distinguishing between spirits, to another speaking in various tongues, and to still another the interpretation of tongues. 11 All these are the work of one and the same Spirit, who apportions them to each one as He determines.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul gives examples of the variety he has just described: messages of wisdom and knowledge, faith, healing, miracles, prophecy, distinguishing between spirits, tongues and their interpretation. He repeatedly names the same Spirit as their source, then states that the Spirit distributes them as He determines.

The faith listed as one person’s gift cannot simply mean that only some members believe in Christ. It points to a particular exercise of trust within a community of believers. The list likewise distinguishes speaking in tongues from interpreting them. Not everyone is given the same contribution.

Paul does not define every gift in detail here. He will discuss prophecy and tongues more fully in chapter 14. Wisdom and knowledge should not be assigned rigid modern job descriptions from these verses alone, and this list should be read alongside the different examples later in the chapter and in Romans 12:6–8.

The point is the Spirit’s purposeful giving for the common good. These abilities do not become personal possessions to control at will, or grounds for deciding that one recipient matters more than another.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians agree that the gifts Paul describes come from God and serve His people. They differ over which continue in the same form today.

The Assemblies of God affirms prophecy for the church today, with every claim tested and no modern prophecy carrying Scripture’s authority; see its 2025 position paper. The Catholic Catechism 799–801 likewise recognizes extraordinary as well as ordinary gifts, requiring discernment and their use in love under the church’s shepherds.

The Reformed Westminster Confession 1.1 teaches that the former ways of revealing God’s will have ceased now that it has been committed to Scripture. That statement should not be expanded into a claim that God can no longer perform a miracle. Dallas Theological Seminary’s statement, Article XVI, more specifically holds that certain revelatory signs belonged to the apostolic period, while explicitly allowing that God performs miracles in every age. This is that institution’s teaching, not the position of every evangelical Christian.

Even descriptions of individual gifts vary. Wesley’s note on verse 9 allows healing to work alongside natural remedies. It would therefore be inaccurate to describe every Christian reading as requiring the same account of how healing occurs.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Acts 4:29–31, the church asks God for boldness to speak His word and for healing and signs through Jesus’ name. The gifts are placed alongside the mission of bearing witness to Him, rather than attracting attention to the people who receive them.

That setting helps explain their larger purpose. The Spirit equips people so Christ is made known and His people are helped. Whatever conclusions readers reach about gifts today, Paul’s emphasis challenges the use of spiritual ability as a measure of personal importance.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 12:12-13
passages.section_title: What makes very different people one body?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 The body is a unit, though it is composed of many parts. And although its parts are many, they all form one body. So it is with Christ. 13 For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, slave or free, and we were all given one Spirit to drink.
paragraphs: 12 The body is a unit, though it is composed of many parts. And although its parts are many, they all form one body. So it is with Christ. 13 For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, slave or free, and we were all given one Spirit to drink.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul compares the church with a human body: many parts belong to one whole. The comparison explains both unity and difference. To belong together, the members do not have to become identical.

He connects that shared life with the one Spirit and one body into which all were baptized. Jews and Greeks, slaves and free people are included. Their backgrounds and social positions do not give them separate kinds of membership in Christ.

The repeated all matters to the discussion of gifts. Paul is describing what the whole community shares before explaining the different work of its members. No particular gift becomes the condition for counting someone as part of the body in these verses.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand Paul to describe the Spirit bringing believers into one people, but they differ over the relationship between this baptism and water baptism.

The Catholic Catechism 1267–1269 explicitly cites this verse for baptism making people members of Christ’s body. Wesley’s note on verse 13 also connects receiving the Spirit and the community’s baptism. Calvin’s comment speaks of baptism joining believers to Christ while insisting that its effective power belongs to the Spirit, rather than the outward sign alone.

Other evangelical readers distinguish the Spirit’s act of joining believers to Christ from the water ceremony. Dallas Theological Seminary’s Articles XII–XIV describe the Spirit baptizing all believers into one body and water baptism as testimony. The Assemblies of God’s position paper likewise reads this verse as incorporation into Christ at conversion, while distinguishing a further experience of empowerment that it calls baptism in the Holy Spirit. It does not teach that a believer without that further experience is outside Christ’s body.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 2:11–22 describes people once divided as Jews and Gentiles brought near through Christ’s blood. Both have access to the Father through one Spirit and become members of one household.

Paul’s one-body description fits that stated purpose of reconciliation. God is gathering people who do not share the same history or standing into a common life through His Son. Their unity is rooted in what He has done, and is meant to change how they receive one another.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 12:14-20
passages.section_title: What if I feel less useful than someone else?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 For the body does not consist of one part, but of many. 15 If the foot should say, “Because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body,” that would not make it any less a part of the body. 16 And if the ear should say, “Because I am not an eye, I do not belong to the body,” that would not make it any less a part of the body. 17 If the whole body were an eye, where would the sense of hearing be? If the whole body were an ear, where would the sense of smell be? 18 But in fact, God has arranged the members of the body, every one of them, according to His design. 19 If they were all one part, where would the body be? 20 As it is, there are many parts, but one body.
paragraphs: 14 For the body does not consist of one part, but of many. 15 If the foot should say, “Because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body,” that would not make it any less a part of the body. 16 And if the ear should say, “Because I am not an eye, I do not belong to the body,” that would not make it any less a part of the body. 17 If the whole body were an eye, where would the sense of hearing be? If the whole body were an ear, where would the sense of smell be?

18 But in fact, God has arranged the members of the body, every one of them, according to His design. 19 If they were all one part, where would the body be? 20 As it is, there are many parts, but one body.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul imagines a foot comparing itself with a hand, and an ear comparing itself with an eye. Each might conclude that being different means not belonging. Paul rejects that conclusion: saying it does not make it true.

The body would fail if every part tried to be an eye or an ear. Its ability to function depends on differences. Paul is not asking one member to copy another before being accepted; he is explaining why the variety matters.

God has arranged the members according to His design. In the discussion of gifts, that gives a reason to resist envy and the feeling that only the most visible work counts. A person’s place cannot be measured simply by resemblance to someone whose contribution attracts attention.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the body picture as correcting comparison and discouragement over different gifts. Wesley’s notes on verses 15–20 emphasize that the parts need one another, while the USCCB note on verses 12–26 explains that diversity of function belongs within the body’s unity.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Peter 4:8–11 also calls each person to use the gift received in service to others, describing that service as stewardship of God’s varied grace. Both speaking and serving depend on what God supplies.

The purpose reaches beyond finding a task that makes us feel useful: God is to be glorified through Jesus Christ. His grace is displayed in different forms of service working together. A quieter contribution can belong fully to that calling.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 12:21-26
passages.section_title: Why can’t stronger members dismiss those who seem weaker?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 The eye cannot say to the hand, “I do not need you.” Nor can the head say to the feet, “I do not need you.” 22 On the contrary, the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable, 23 and the parts we consider less honorable, we treat with greater honor. And our unpresentable parts are treated with special modesty, 24 whereas our presentable parts have no such need. But God has composed the body and has given greater honor to the parts that lacked it, 25 so that there should be no division in the body, but that its members should have mutual concern for one another. 26 If one part suffers, every part suffers with it; if one part is honored, every part rejoices with it.
paragraphs: 21 The eye cannot say to the hand, “I do not need you.” Nor can the head say to the feet, “I do not need you.” 22 On the contrary, the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable, 23 and the parts we consider less honorable, we treat with greater honor. And our unpresentable parts are treated with special modesty, 24 whereas our presentable parts have no such need. But God has composed the body and has given greater honor to the parts that lacked it,

25 so that there should be no division in the body, but that its members should have mutual concern for one another. 26 If one part suffers, every part suffers with it; if one part is honored, every part rejoices with it.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The picture now addresses the opposite mistake. The eye cannot tell the hand it is unnecessary, and the head cannot dismiss the feet. Having a conspicuous or respected part does not make someone self-sufficient.

Paul goes further: the parts that seem weaker are indispensable. The body’s less presentable parts receive particular care and covering. The comparison challenges the way a community assigns honor, rather than inviting it to identify people as permanently embarrassing or inferior.

God’s arrangement aims at mutual care instead of division. Paul describes sharing both suffering and honor: another member’s pain is not irrelevant to the rest, and another’s recognition is a reason for joy rather than resentment.

The passage does not require an exact church role for every physical organ. Its practical force is clear without that chart. Members who can offer help still need others, and those needing care are people to honor, rather than burdens whose absence would improve the church.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as a call to reject contempt and care for members who might otherwise be overlooked. Wesley’s notes on verses 21–24 connect Paul’s comparison with the special care given to vulnerable parts of a body. The emphasis falls on belonging and mutual concern, not ranking people by usefulness.
passages.god_plan_html:
Philippians 2:1–11 connects concern for others with the mind of Christ. He takes the form of a servant, humbles Himself in obedience, and is exalted by God. The community’s pattern of honor is shaped by Him.

That connection gives mutual care a deeper setting than practical teamwork. God’s people are being formed to reflect the Lord who gave Himself for others. Making room for the vulnerable and sharing another’s suffering are part of a life shaped by His humility and love.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 12:27-31
passages.section_title: How should a church value its different gifts?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 27 Now you are the body of Christ, and each of you is a member of it. 28 And in the church God has appointed first of all apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then workers of miracles, and those with gifts of healing, helping, administration, and various tongues. 29 Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Do all work miracles? 30 Do all have gifts of healing? Do all speak in tongues? Do all interpret? 31 But eagerly desire the greater gifts. And now I will show you the most excellent way.
paragraphs: 27 Now you are the body of Christ, and each of you is a member of it. 28 And in the church God has appointed first of all apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then workers of miracles, and those with gifts of healing, helping, administration, and various tongues. 29 Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Do all work miracles? 30 Do all have gifts of healing? Do all speak in tongues? Do all interpret? 31 But eagerly desire the greater gifts. And now I will show you the most excellent way.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul applies the body picture directly to the Corinthians: together they are Christ’s body, and each person belongs as a member. He then names different appointments and gifts within the church, beginning with apostles, prophets and teachers.

The repeated questions expect a negative answer. Not everyone is an apostle, prophet, teacher, miracle worker, healer, speaker in tongues or interpreter. Diversity is part of God’s arrangement, rather than a problem to be solved by making every member do the same thing.

Paul’s ordering shows that the gifts are not interchangeable, even though the people who receive them must not be treated as disposable. His appeal to desire the greater gifts needs to be read with the common good already stated in verse 7 and the concern for building up the church developed in chapter 14.

The last sentence opens the next chapter: Paul will show a still better way. The answer to rivalry over gifts is not simply a different ranking. Love must govern the way every gift is valued and used.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand this passage to distinguish the gifts and work given to different members. Calvin’s comment on verse 31 emphasizes valuing what most builds up the church rather than pursuing a display.

The questions about tongues raise a further difference in application. Dallas Theological Seminary’s Article XVI rejects tongues as a necessary sign of the Spirit’s baptism or filling. The Assemblies of God’s Statement of Fundamental Truths, section 8, teaches tongues as the initial sign of baptism in the Spirit while distinguishing that use from the congregational gift in this chapter. The disagreement concerns that distinction; it should not be described as the Assemblies of God overlooking Paul’s questions.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 2:19–22 describes God’s household as built on the foundation of apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus as the cornerstone. It gives those ministries a place within God’s work of forming a people in whom He dwells by the Spirit.

That foundation serves the whole household. The picture directs attention beyond personal rank to the people being built together under Christ. Paul’s turn to love fits a community whose members belong to that shared work.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 13:1-3
passages.section_title: Why aren’t impressive gifts and sacrifices enough?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am only a ringing gong or a clanging cymbal. 2 If I have the gift of prophecy and can fathom all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have absolute faith so as to move mountains, but have not love, I am nothing. 3 If I give all I possess to the poor and exult in the surrender of my body, but have not love, I gain nothing.
paragraphs: 1 If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am only a ringing gong or a clanging cymbal. 2 If I have the gift of prophecy and can fathom all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have absolute faith so as to move mountains, but have not love, I am nothing. 3 If I give all I possess to the poor and exult in the surrender of my body, but have not love, I gain nothing.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul’s description of love continues his correction of the church’s use of gifts. He imagines speech of the greatest possible reach, prophecy and knowledge of the widest possible scope, extraordinary faith, and extreme generosity or bodily sacrifice. None supplies what is missing if love is absent.

The repeated result is devastating: impressive speech becomes noise, the gifted person is nothing, and the giver gains nothing. Paul is not denying the value of speaking, knowing, believing or giving. He is exposing the failure of those activities when separated from love.

The BSB’s wording in verse 3 refers to exulting in the surrender of one’s body—taking pride in that surrender. Its footnote records the alternative reading about being burned. The main warning is plain in either case: even an extraordinary sacrifice does not make love unnecessary.

This section therefore asks a question that external results alone cannot answer: are other people being loved? Gifts and costly actions can attract admiration while leaving that central requirement unmet.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand Paul’s examples as showing the necessity of love, rather than dismissing service or gifts. They differ over the reference to the tongues of angels.

Calvin’s comment on verse 1 treats it as deliberately heightened language: even the most extraordinary speech would be worthless without love. The Assemblies of God’s paper on baptism in the Holy Spirit allows that Spirit-inspired speech may include heavenly or angelic language. That question does not change Paul’s stated test: love remains necessary.
passages.god_plan_html:
In John 13:34–35, Jesus gives His disciples the command to love one another as He has loved them. Their love will identify them as His disciples.

Paul’s warning belongs within that purpose. The church is to make its Lord known through a shared life shaped by His love. Spectacular ability or sacrifice cannot substitute for the very quality Jesus says will mark His people.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 13:4-7
passages.section_title: What does love look like in the way we treat people?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 4 Love is patient, love is kind. It does not envy, it does not boast, it is not proud. 5 It is not rude, it is not self-seeking, it is not easily angered, it keeps no account of wrongs. 6 Love takes no pleasure in evil, but rejoices in the truth. 7 It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.
paragraphs: 4 Love is patient, love is kind. It does not envy, it does not boast, it is not proud. 5 It is not rude, it is not self-seeking, it is not easily angered, it keeps no account of wrongs. 6 Love takes no pleasure in evil, but rejoices in the truth. 7 It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul makes love visible through conduct. It is patient and kind; it refuses envy, boasting and pride. In a church divided over status and gifts, those qualities answer the behavior he has been correcting throughout the letter.

Love does not behave rudely or make its own interests the center. It is not easily angered and does not keep a running account of wrongs to use against someone. These are choices in a relationship, rather than simply a feeling we either happen to have or lack.

Love also rejoices with the truth and takes no pleasure in evil. That matters for reading the sweeping statements that follow. Believing, hoping and enduring do not require calling a lie true, celebrating harm or refusing to confront wrongdoing. Paul has already required the church to address serious misconduct in chapter 5.

The final four expressions describe love’s persistence. It does not become cynical, abandon hope or discard a person as soon as care becomes costly. Truth and perseverance belong together in that commitment.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand these verses as describing love through action and character. Calvin’s comment on verse 4 connects the description with preserving the church’s unity and correcting the Corinthians’ faults. Wesley’s notes on verses 5–7 likewise distinguish refusing baseless suspicion from being unable to recognize evil.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 5:1–2 calls God’s beloved children to imitate Him and walk in love, connecting that life directly with Christ loving them and giving Himself for them.

Paul’s description is therefore part of more than a general call to be agreeable. God’s children are being formed to reflect the love they have received through His Son. Patience, kindness, truth and endurance give that love a recognizable shape in everyday life.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 13:8-13
passages.section_title: Why is love greater than gifts that will pass away?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 Love never fails. But where there are prophecies, they will cease; where there are tongues, they will be restrained; where there is knowledge, it will be dismissed. 9 For we know in part and we prophesy in part, 10 but when the perfect comes, the partial passes away. 11 When I was a child, I talked like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child. When I became a man, I set aside childish ways. 12 Now we see but a dim reflection as in a mirror; then we shall see face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I am fully known. 13 And now these three remain: faith, hope, and love; but the greatest of these is love.
paragraphs: 8 Love never fails. But where there are prophecies, they will cease; where there are tongues, they will be restrained; where there is knowledge, it will be dismissed. 9 For we know in part and we prophesy in part, 10 but when the perfect comes, the partial passes away.

11 When I was a child, I talked like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child. When I became a man, I set aside childish ways. 12 Now we see but a dim reflection as in a mirror; then we shall see face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I am fully known. 13 And now these three remain: faith, hope, and love; but the greatest of these is love.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul adds a further reason to make love central: love lasts. Prophecy, tongues and the knowledge he has been discussing do not have the same lasting role. They serve people whose present understanding is incomplete.

The word translated perfect is teleios (tell-AY-oss), τέλειος, which can mean complete or fully mature; see Thayer’s entry. Paul contrasts the partial with what brings that partial state to an end. The word’s meaning helps identify the contrast, but a dictionary definition alone does not settle when that happens.

He illustrates the change with growing from childhood to adulthood, then with seeing an indirect reflection rather than face to face. The Greek word for mirror really does mean a mirror (Thayer). The picture emphasizes the limits of present understanding and the greater clarity to come; it does not promise that a human being will become all-knowing as God is.

Faith, hope and love remain central, with love called the greatest. This completes Paul’s correction of a church tempted to make gifts its chief measure of importance. Whatever their usefulness now, they cannot replace the love that gives their use its proper character.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Many Christians understand the perfect as the fullness of life with God, rather than the completion of a book. Calvin’s comment on verse 10 looks toward perfection fully manifested at the day of judgment; Wesley’s notes on verses 8–12 likewise read the contrast in the light of life beyond the present age.

A different reading identifies the perfect with completed New Testament revelation. In an article published by La Vista Church of Christ, Dylan Steward reasons that the partial revelations give way to the complete revelation, and understands the mirror as God’s word making people known to themselves. This is that author’s reading, not a position that can be assigned to every Church of Christ congregation.

Belief that some gifts have ceased does not always depend on that second reading. The Grace Community Church statement on tongues understands the perfect as the eternal state, while arguing separately that tongues ceased earlier. The timing of the perfect and the timing of every individual gift are therefore distinct questions within the discussion. The shared point is that gifts do not have love’s lasting place.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 John 3:1–3 connects the Father’s love with the future of His children: when Christ appears, they will be like Him and see Him as He is. That hope is meant to lead them toward purity now.

Romans 8:18–30 also places present weakness and waiting within God’s purpose to bring His children to glory and conform them to His Son. The lasting love Paul describes belongs within that larger goal. Learning to love faithfully now is consistent with the life God is preparing for His people, beyond the limits and needs of the present.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 14:1-5
passages.section_title: Which use of a gift actually helps the church?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Earnestly pursue love and eagerly desire spiritual gifts, especially the gift of prophecy. 2 For he who speaks in a tongue does not speak to men, but to God. Indeed, no one understands him; he utters mysteries in the Spirit. 3 But he who prophesies speaks to men for their edification, encouragement, and comfort. 4 The one who speaks in a tongue edifies himself, but the one who prophesies edifies the church. 5 I wish that all of you could speak in tongues, but I would rather have you prophesy. He who prophesies is greater than one who speaks in tongues, unless he interprets so that the church may be edified.
paragraphs: 1 Earnestly pursue love and eagerly desire spiritual gifts, especially the gift of prophecy. 2 For he who speaks in a tongue does not speak to men, but to God. Indeed, no one understands him; he utters mysteries in the Spirit. 3 But he who prophesies speaks to men for their edification, encouragement, and comfort. 4 The one who speaks in a tongue edifies himself, but the one who prophesies edifies the church. 5 I wish that all of you could speak in tongues, but I would rather have you prophesy. He who prophesies is greater than one who speaks in tongues, unless he interprets so that the church may be edified.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul brings the discussion of love directly into the practice of gifts. Love is to be pursued, and gifts are to be desired, with particular attention to prophecy. His reason is the benefit people receive when they can understand what is said.

The repeated word edification means building people up. Its Greek word, oikodomē (oy-koh-doh-MAY), οἰκοδομή, comes from the language of building and is used for helping people grow in faith and godly life; see Thayer’s entry. Paul is asking what strengthens the community, rather than what produces the most striking display.

An uninterpreted tongue is directed to God and benefits the speaker, while prophecy strengthens, encourages and comforts other people. Paul does not simply condemn tongues: he expresses a desire that the Corinthians speak in them. But he would rather they prophesy because others can be helped.

The exception at the end matters: if the tongue is interpreted so the church is built up, the comparison changes. The deciding concern is not how unusual the speech sounds, but whether other people receive something that helps them.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly recognize the priority of building up the congregation, while differing over the kind of speech involved. The Grace Community Church statement on tongues understands the gift as an unlearned human language. The Assemblies of God’s baptism paper also allows speech that may be heavenly rather than an identifiable human language. These are the positions of the named church and denomination, not of all their broader traditions.

There are also differences in explaining prophecy. Wesley’s note on verse 1 emphasizes opening and applying Scripture. The Assemblies of God’s 2025 prophecy paper affirms Spirit-given messages for the church today, subject to testing and without Scripture’s authority. Both accounts direct attention to helping the people who hear, rather than giving a speaker personal importance.
passages.god_plan_html:
At Pentecost, people from many nations hear God’s mighty works in their own languages (Acts 2:1–11). The Spirit’s gift serves God’s purpose of making His work known beyond one language group.

That event gives the discussion a wider setting: the Spirit’s work serves God’s people and His witness in the world. Paul’s concern for understandable communication is consistent with that purpose. A message that can be received can strengthen, encourage and comfort the people God is gathering.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 14:6-12
passages.section_title: Why does understanding matter more than impressive sound?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 Now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, how will I benefit you, unless I bring you some revelation or knowledge or prophecy or teaching? 7 Even in the case of lifeless instruments, such as the flute or harp, how will anyone recognize the tune they are playing unless the notes are distinct? 8 Again, if the trumpet sounds a muffled call, who will prepare for battle? 9 So it is with you. Unless you speak intelligible words with your tongue, how will anyone know what you are saying? You will just be speaking into the air. 10 Assuredly, there are many different languages in the world, yet none of them is without meaning. 11 If, then, I do not know the meaning of someone’s language, I am a foreigner to the speaker, and he is a foreigner to me. 12 It is the same with you. Since you are eager to have spiritual gifts, strive to excel in gifts that build up the church.
paragraphs: 6 Now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, how will I benefit you, unless I bring you some revelation or knowledge or prophecy or teaching? 7 Even in the case of lifeless instruments, such as the flute or harp, how will anyone recognize the tune they are playing unless the notes are distinct? 8 Again, if the trumpet sounds a muffled call, who will prepare for battle? 9 So it is with you. Unless you speak intelligible words with your tongue, how will anyone know what you are saying? You will just be speaking into the air.

10 Assuredly, there are many different languages in the world, yet none of them is without meaning. 11 If, then, I do not know the meaning of someone’s language, I am a foreigner to the speaker, and he is a foreigner to me. 12 It is the same with you. Since you are eager to have spiritual gifts, strive to excel in gifts that build up the church.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul asks what benefit his visit would bring if he spoke in tongues without communicating revelation, knowledge, prophecy or teaching. He puts the same test to his own ministry: others must receive something they can understand and use.

He illustrates the point with music and a trumpet call. Distinct notes make a tune recognizable; a clear call lets people know how to respond. Noise alone does not accomplish the purpose for which an instrument is used.

The comparison with ordinary language makes the point personal. If speaker and listener do not know one another’s language, each is a foreigner to the other. The BSB uses foreigner here; its footnote records the literal term barbarian. Paul is describing a communication barrier, rather than giving one language group greater human worth.

His conclusion channels their eagerness: strive to excel in gifts that build up the church. The desire for spiritual things must become concern for the people beside them. Merely filling the room with sound does not meet that aim.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand these comparisons as establishing the need for understandable communication in the gathering. Wesley’s notes on verses 6–11 and the USCCB note on verses 6–12 both connect the examples from music and language with the benefit others should receive.
passages.god_plan_html:
An earlier parallel appears in Nehemiah 8:7–12. God’s Law is read and explained so the people understand. Their response includes joy and sending food to people who have none prepared.

This is a shared biblical pattern, not a claim that Nehemiah predicts Corinth’s gifts. God’s word forms a people as it is heard and understood, leading to a response in their lives together. Paul’s concern belongs within that larger purpose of instruction that reaches people and bears fruit.
