passages.title: 1 Corinthians 14:13-19
passages.section_title: How can others join in prayer and thanksgiving?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 Therefore, the one who speaks in a tongue should pray that he may interpret. 14 For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is unfruitful. 15 What then shall I do? I will pray with my spirit, but I will also pray with my mind. I will sing with my spirit, but I will also sing with my mind. 16 Otherwise, if you speak a blessing in spirit, how can someone who is uninstructed say “Amen” to your thanksgiving, since he does not know what you are saying? 17 You may be giving thanks well enough, but the other one is not edified. 18 I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you. 19 But in the church, I would rather speak five coherent words to instruct others than ten thousand words in a tongue.
paragraphs: 13 Therefore, the one who speaks in a tongue should pray that he may interpret. 14 For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is unfruitful. 15 What then shall I do? I will pray with my spirit, but I will also pray with my mind. I will sing with my spirit, but I will also sing with my mind.

16 Otherwise, if you speak a blessing in spirit, how can someone who is uninstructed say “Amen” to your thanksgiving, since he does not know what you are saying? 17 You may be giving thanks well enough, but the other one is not edified. 18 I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you. 19 But in the church, I would rather speak five coherent words to instruct others than ten thousand words in a tongue.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul tells the person speaking in a tongue to pray for interpretation. He does not respond to the lack of understanding by abandoning prayer or song. He wants to pray and sing with both spirit and mind.

The person listening also matters. Someone who cannot understand the thanksgiving cannot knowingly add an Amen. The speaker may be giving thanks well, but the other person is not being built up. Sincerity toward God does not make the listener’s need disappear.

Paul’s own example prevents the correction from sounding like resentment of a gift he lacks. He thanks God that he speaks in tongues more than they do, yet in church he prefers five coherent words that instruct others to ten thousand words in a tongue.

The setting of that preference is explicit: in the church. Paul is directing the shared gathering toward understandable instruction and participation. His aim is not a contest between having a spiritual experience and using one’s mind, but service in which others can receive and join what is offered.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly agree that Paul wants the congregation to understand and benefit. Readers differ over what he means by his mind being unfruitful.

Wesley’s note on verse 14 understands the speaker as knowing the words through the Spirit while that knowledge remains unfruitful for others. The USCCB note on verses 14–15 instead emphasizes prayer in tongues taking place without ordinary understanding. Both readings must account for Paul’s instruction to involve the mind and enable the hearer’s response.
passages.god_plan_html:
Colossians 3:12–17 places teaching, songs and gratitude within the life of one body, clothed in compassion and love. Christ’s word is to dwell richly among them as they teach and encourage one another.

That gives shared prayer and singing a purpose that includes both God and the people present. Thanksgiving is offered to the Father through Jesus, while the community is strengthened by the truth it receives. Paul’s concern for the hearer serves that life together.
passages.current_position_html: In Worship as the Early Church Knew It, we understand the gathered assembly as a place where believers build one another up. The study specifically uses 1 Corinthians 14:19 to show that words must be understandable if they are to instruct others. We therefore value shared prayer, singing and teaching by how they help people grow in truth, faith and love, rather than mainly by the emotional response they produce.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 14:19
passages.section_title: Why would Paul prefer five clear words?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 But in the church, I would rather speak five coherent words to instruct others than ten thousand words in a tongue.
paragraphs: 19 But in the church, I would rather speak five coherent words to instruct others than ten thousand words in a tongue.

passages.context_html:
This sentence summarizes Paul’s discussion of prayer, interpretation and the listener’s need to understand. It belongs within 1 Corinthians 14:13–19, where he wants prayer and singing to involve both spirit and mind.

Paul is not rejecting tongues out of personal dislike: the previous verse thanks God that he speaks in tongues more than the Corinthians. His comparison is about what serves a church gathering. Five words that instruct others accomplish something that ten thousand words they cannot understand do not.

The numbers make a strong contrast, rather than setting a five-word limit on teaching. The test is whether people can receive the meaning and be helped.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as giving understandable instruction priority over uninterpreted speech in church. Wesley’s note on verse 19 stresses both understanding oneself and being understood by others. The USCCB note on verses 13–19 likewise emphasizes interpretation as the way a tongue can benefit the congregation.
passages.current_position_html: In Worship as the Early Church Knew It, we use this verse as a standard for understandable speech in the gathered church. A contribution should help other people grow in knowledge, faith or love. Its value cannot be measured mainly by the speaker’s performance or the intensity of the feelings it produces.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Colossians 3:16–17 describes Christ’s word dwelling richly among His people through teaching, songs and thanksgiving to the Father through Jesus. Their shared life includes receiving truth from one another.

Paul’s preference serves that purpose. Clear words give another person something to understand, respond to and live by, helping a community grow together under Christ.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 14:20-25
passages.section_title: What might an outsider encounter in the gathering?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 20 Brothers, stop thinking like children. In regard to evil be infants, but in your thinking be mature. 21 It is written in the Law: “By strange tongues and foreign lips I will speak to this people, but even then they will not listen to Me, says the Lord.” 22 Tongues, then, are a sign, not for believers, but for unbelievers. Prophecy, however, is for believers, not for unbelievers. 23 So if the whole church comes together and everyone speaks in tongues, and some who are uninstructed or some unbelievers come in, will they not say that you are out of your minds? 24 But if an unbeliever or uninstructed person comes in while everyone is prophesying, he will be convicted and called to account by all, 25 and the secrets of his heart will be made known. So he will fall facedown and worship God, proclaiming, “God is truly among you!”
paragraphs: 20 Brothers, stop thinking like children. In regard to evil be infants, but in your thinking be mature. 21 It is written in the Law: “By strange tongues and foreign lips I will speak to this people, but even then they will not listen to Me, says the Lord.” 22 Tongues, then, are a sign, not for believers, but for unbelievers. Prophecy, however, is for believers, not for unbelievers.

23 So if the whole church comes together and everyone speaks in tongues, and some who are uninstructed or some unbelievers come in, will they not say that you are out of your minds? 24 But if an unbeliever or uninstructed person comes in while everyone is prophesying, he will be convicted and called to account by all, 25 and the secrets of his heart will be made known. So he will fall facedown and worship God, proclaiming, “God is truly among you!”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul calls for mature thinking while remaining innocent of evil. His quotation comes from Isaiah 28:11–12, where people who would not listen to God hear foreign speech instead. In its setting, that speech belongs to a warning of judgment. A striking sign is not automatically a mark of God’s approval.

The next comparison shows why the effect on listeners matters. If the whole church speaks in tongues and outsiders cannot understand, they may conclude the people are out of their minds. A sign can confront someone without bringing that person to understanding or faith.

By contrast, understandable prophetic speech can expose a visitor’s heart, bring conviction and lead to worship of God. Calling prophecy a gift for believers does not mean an unbeliever can never benefit from hearing it; Paul immediately describes that very possibility.

These are contrasting situations meant to guide the church’s choices. They do not promise that every visitor will respond identically, or give a speaker permission to invent private information about someone. The desired outcome is recognition of God’s presence, rather than amazement at a person’s performance.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly recognize the contrast between an outsider’s confusion and being brought to conviction. They explain the sign language in different ways.

Calvin’s comment on verse 22 considers both a warning of judgment connected with Isaiah and a miraculous sign directed toward unbelievers. Wesley’s note emphasizes the sign drawing unbelievers’ attention to God’s message. The USCCB note on verses 20–22 emphasizes Isaiah’s warning against unbelief, distinguishing the faithless people addressed there from the outside visitors in verses 23–25.

These readings give different weight to the sign’s warning and witness. All must account for Paul’s practical conclusion: speech in the assembly should help people hear and respond to God, rather than leave them unable to understand.
passages.god_plan_html:
An earlier parallel appears in Zechariah 8:20–23: people from different nations seek the Lord because they have heard that God is with His people. Paul’s picture of a visitor acknowledging God among the Corinthians has that same theme of God’s presence drawing people to worship.

This is a parallel in the response to God’s presence, not a claim that every detail of Zechariah’s promise is exhausted in Corinth. The larger purpose includes people coming to know the Lord. The way a congregation uses its gifts should serve that purpose.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 14:26
passages.section_title: What should every contribution to a gathering accomplish?
passages.note: Let all things be done for edification: a closing standard for the whole project.

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 26 What then shall we say, brothers? When you come together, everyone has a psalm or a teaching, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation. All of these must be done to build up the church.
paragraphs: 26 What then shall we say, brothers? When you come together, everyone has a psalm or a teaching, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation. All of these must be done to build up the church.

passages.context_html:
This verse moves Paul’s discussion from the value of understandable speech to the practical conduct of a gathering. Different people have different contributions, but all are directed toward building up the church.

The following instructions in 1 Corinthians 14:26–33 show that participation includes taking turns, interpretation, testing and knowing when to be silent. Having something to offer does not mean insisting on offering it in any manner one chooses.

The list is not a requirement that every person perform each activity at every meeting. Paul’s concern is that the variety of what is brought should help the gathered people grow.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read the verse as directing the church’s different contributions toward a shared benefit. Calvin’s note on verse 26 stresses using each gift for everyone’s good, while the USCCB note on verses 26–33 identifies building up as the governing test.
passages.current_position_html: In Worship as the Early Church Knew It, we understand this verse as the framework for mutual participation in the assembly. Believers bring what God has given them to build one another up in Christ. The purpose is shared growth, rather than a gathering evaluated mainly as a performance or a personal emotional experience.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
1 Peter 4:8–11 similarly calls each person to use what has been received to serve others as a steward of God’s varied grace. Speaking and serving are to depend on what God supplies so He is glorified through Jesus Christ.

That places the gathering within a life of shared service. A contribution matters because it helps people and honors the God whose grace made it possible.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 14:26-33
passages.section_title: How can many people contribute without the gathering becoming disorderly?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 26 What then shall we say, brothers? When you come together, everyone has a psalm or a teaching, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation. All of these must be done to build up the church. 27 If anyone speaks in a tongue, two, or at most three, should speak in turn, and someone must interpret. 28 But if there is no interpreter, he should remain silent in the church and speak only to himself and God. 29 Two or three prophets should speak, and the others should weigh carefully what is said. 30 And if a revelation comes to someone who is seated, the first speaker should stop. 31 For you can all prophesy in turn so that everyone may be instructed and encouraged. 32 The spirits of prophets are subject to prophets. 33 For God is not a God of disorder, but of peace—as in all the churches of the saints.
paragraphs: 26 What then shall we say, brothers? When you come together, everyone has a psalm or a teaching, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation. All of these must be done to build up the church. 27 If anyone speaks in a tongue, two, or at most three, should speak in turn, and someone must interpret. 28 But if there is no interpreter, he should remain silent in the church and speak only to himself and God.

29 Two or three prophets should speak, and the others should weigh carefully what is said. 30 And if a revelation comes to someone who is seated, the first speaker should stop. 31 For you can all prophesy in turn so that everyone may be instructed and encouraged. 32 The spirits of prophets are subject to prophets. 33 For God is not a God of disorder, but of peace—as in all the churches of the saints.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul names a range of contributions—psalm, teaching, revelation, tongue and interpretation—and gives the test that governs them: build up the church. The variety belongs within a shared purpose, rather than a competition for the floor.

He then gives concrete limits. Two, or at most three, should speak in tongues, taking turns, and someone must interpret. Without an interpreter, that person is to be silent in the gathering and speak to himself and God. Having a gift does not remove responsibility for how it affects others.

Prophecy is also subject to order and testing. Two or three prophets speak, and others weigh what is said. A person already speaking must make room when a revelation comes to someone seated. The aim is that people learn and are encouraged.

The spirits of prophets are subject to prophets: inspiration does not excuse refusing to stop or listen. Paul grounds this order in God’s character as the God of peace. A contribution is to serve the gathered people, with room for discernment and mutual consideration.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand Paul to require understandable, orderly contributions directed toward the good of the congregation. Calvin’s comment on verse 26 emphasizes each gift serving the advantage of all. Wesley’s notes on verses 27–32 likewise stress taking turns, interpretation and the speaker’s self-control.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 4:11–16 describes Christ equipping His people for service so His body grows toward unity and maturity. The goal is a community growing in truth and love through the contribution of its different parts.

The order Paul describes serves that larger purpose. It makes space for people to receive, weigh and learn, rather than letting a few voices overwhelm the rest. God’s gifts are being used to form a people together under Christ.
passages.current_position_html: In Worship as the Early Church Knew It, we understand 1 Corinthians 14:26 as making mutual edification the purpose of the gathered assembly. Believers should come ready to contribute to one another’s growth. The contribution must serve others; participation is more than attending as a spectator or seeking a personal emotional experience.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 14:34-35
passages.section_title: What kind of silence is Paul requiring from women?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 34 Women are to be silent in the churches. They are not permitted to speak, but must be in submission, as the law says. 35 If they wish to inquire about something, they are to ask their own husbands at home; for it is dishonorable for a woman to speak in the church.
paragraphs: 34 Women are to be silent in the churches. They are not permitted to speak, but must be in submission, as the law says. 35 If they wish to inquire about something, they are to ask their own husbands at home; for it is dishonorable for a woman to speak in the church.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
These verses instruct women to be silent in the churches, refer to submission and the law, and direct those who want to inquire to ask their own husbands at home. They occur within Paul’s discussion of orderly speech, where a tongue-speaker and a prophet have also been told to be silent in specified circumstances.

The instruction must also be read alongside 1 Corinthians 11:5, which describes women praying and prophesying. Readers therefore need to explain what speech is restricted here and how the passages fit together.

The mention of husbands makes questions within marriage part of the immediate wording. It does not explain every woman’s situation or record a detailed scene of wives calling across a room. Paul also does not name a particular Old Testament verse when referring to the law. Those details should not be supplied as if they were stated.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians differ over the scope and setting of the restriction. Calvin’s exposition understands it as excluding women from public teaching and prophecy in the church’s ordinary ordered assembly, while allowing that an unusual necessity might require a woman to speak. Wesley’s note on verse 34 likewise restricts public teaching, but makes an exception for an extraordinary prompting of the Spirit.

The Catholic declaration Inter Insigniores, section 4, distinguishes the official function of teaching in the assembly from the prophetic speech Paul recognizes in women. It does not read this as a ban on every spoken word by a woman.

The Assemblies of God’s 2025 position paper on women in ministerial leadership supports women at every level of ministry. It reads these verses as a correction of wives questioning their husbands during the gathering, rather than a universal prohibition on women’s leadership.

A further question concerns the passage’s place in the letter. The USCCB study note discusses the proposal that verses 34–35 were added during the letter’s early transmission. This is a scholarly proposal discussed in a note, not a Catholic doctrinal ruling. The BSB includes the verses and notes that some manuscripts place them after verse 40. A change of location does not itself establish whether the proposed addition occurred.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 14:36-40
passages.section_title: What shows that a claim to spiritual authority is trustworthy?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 36 Did the word of God originate with you? Or are you the only ones it has reached? 37 If anyone considers himself a prophet or spiritual person, let him acknowledge that what I am writing you is the Lord’s command. 38 But if anyone ignores this, he himself will be ignored. 39 So, my brothers, be eager to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues. 40 But everything must be done in a proper and orderly manner.
paragraphs: 36 Did the word of God originate with you? Or are you the only ones it has reached? 37 If anyone considers himself a prophet or spiritual person, let him acknowledge that what I am writing you is the Lord’s command. 38 But if anyone ignores this, he himself will be ignored. 39 So, my brothers, be eager to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues. 40 But everything must be done in a proper and orderly manner.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul asks whether God’s word began with the Corinthians or reached only them. Their congregation is accountable to what it has received, rather than free to make its own preference the standard for everyone else.

Anyone claiming to be a prophet or spiritual person must acknowledge his written instruction as the Lord’s command. A claim to inspiration is to be tested by obedience, rather than used as a reason to avoid correction.

His closing instructions combine eagerness and restraint: be eager to prophesy, do not forbid tongues, and do everything properly and in order. The corrections are not a simple prohibition of all gifts, nor permission to use them without regard for the gathering.

The BSB’s warning in verse 38 states that the one who ignores this will himself be ignored. Paul’s authority is serious; it should not be borrowed by a modern speaker to treat every disagreement with that speaker as disobedience to God.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the conclusion as requiring spiritual claims to submit to apostolic instruction and the good order of the church. Calvin’s comment on verse 37 stresses Paul’s apostolic authority while warning that not every speaker may make that claim for himself. Wesley’s notes on verses 36–40 likewise connect recognition of spiritual gifting with receiving the instruction and acting considerately together.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Matthew 28:18–20, the risen Jesus sends His disciples to make disciples of the nations and teach them to obey what He commanded. Instruction and obedience belong within the mission, alongside the promise of His presence.

Paul’s correction fits that purpose: churches are being formed as communities accountable to the same Lord. Gifts serve His work when they help people receive His truth and live together faithfully, rather than establish a private authority beyond correction.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 15:1-4
passages.section_title: What is the good news on which Christian hope rests?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now, brothers, I want to remind you of the gospel I preached to you, which you received, and in which you stand firm. 2 By this gospel you are saved, if you hold firmly to the word I preached to you. Otherwise, you have believed in vain. 3 For what I received I passed on to you as of first importance: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, 4 that He was buried, that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures,
paragraphs: 1 Now, brothers, I want to remind you of the gospel I preached to you, which you received, and in which you stand firm. 2 By this gospel you are saved, if you hold firmly to the word I preached to you. Otherwise, you have believed in vain. 3 For what I received I passed on to you as of first importance: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, 4 that He was buried, that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures,

passages.context_html:
Paul turns to the resurrection by reminding the Corinthians of the gospel they received. Later in the chapter he will address some among them who deny the resurrection of the dead. He begins with the message that brought them to faith and on which they stand.

Gospel translates euangelion (yoo-an-GHEL-ee-on), εὐαγγέλιον, meaning good news; see Thayer’s entry. Paul gives its central content here: Christ died for our sins, was buried, and was raised on the third day, according to the Scriptures. The announcement concerns what God has done through Christ, rather than merely advice about improving our lives.

The burial affirms the reality of His death; the resurrection announces that death did not have the final word. Both belong to what Paul delivered as of first importance. His explanation will continue with the people to whom the risen Christ appeared.

The call to hold firmly to the message is part of the reminder. Paul does not separate being saved through this good news from continuing in the truth he preached. His warning about believing in vain asks the Corinthians to take the content of their faith seriously.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly recognize Christ’s death for sins, burial and resurrection as central to the gospel. They differ over how to understand the warning about holding firmly.

Calvin’s comment on verse 2 treats abandoning this fundamental teaching as exposing a shallow or unstable understanding. The Reformed Westminster Confession 17 gives the wider teaching that those truly accepted in Christ will be preserved to the end.

Wesley’s note on verse 2 emphasizes salvation reaching its completion as believers continue in faith. Methodist Article XII allows that people may fall from grace and be restored. The Catholic Catechism 162 likewise describes faith as God’s free gift that can be lost and must be nourished to persevere. These broader teachings inform the differing readings; this one sentence should not be made to carry each tradition’s entire account of salvation.
passages.current_position_html: In The Gospel According to Jesus, we take this passage as a direct statement of the gospel’s core: Christ died for our sins, was buried, and was raised on the third day in fulfillment of Scripture. This is the saving announcement of what God has done through Jesus, not simply a program for becoming a better person. Our statement here concerns that core message.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
In Luke 24:44–47, the risen Jesus explains that the Scriptures point to His suffering and resurrection on the third day, followed by repentance for the forgiveness of sins being proclaimed to all nations.

Paul’s summary belongs within that stated purpose. The death and resurrection are not isolated marvels; they stand at the center of God’s promised saving work and the message now carried to the nations. The Corinthians received that announcement, and their hope depends on the Christ it proclaims.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 15:5-11
passages.section_title: Why does Paul name the people who saw the risen Christ?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 and that He appeared to Cephas and then to the Twelve. 6 After that, He appeared to more than five hundred brothers at once, most of whom are still living, though some have fallen asleep. 7 Then He appeared to James, then to all the apostles. 8 And last of all He appeared to me also, as to one of untimely birth. 9 For I am the least of the apostles and am unworthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God. 10 But by the grace of God I am what I am, and His grace to me was not in vain. No, I worked harder than all of them—yet not I, but the grace of God that was with me. 11 Whether, then, it was I or they, this is what we preach, and this is what you believed.
paragraphs: 5 and that He appeared to Cephas and then to the Twelve. 6 After that, He appeared to more than five hundred brothers at once, most of whom are still living, though some have fallen asleep. 7 Then He appeared to James, then to all the apostles.

8 And last of all He appeared to me also, as to one of untimely birth. 9 For I am the least of the apostles and am unworthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God. 10 But by the grace of God I am what I am, and His grace to me was not in vain. No, I worked harder than all of them—yet not I, but the grace of God that was with me. 11 Whether, then, it was I or they, this is what we preach, and this is what you believed.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul continues the gospel summary by listing appearances of the risen Christ: to Cephas, the Twelve, more than five hundred at once, James, all the apostles, and finally himself. The BSB identifies Cephas as Peter. The list presents resurrection as something witnessed, rather than a symbol for the disciples feeling hopeful again.

Paul says most of the larger group were still alive when he wrote, although some had died. He does not give the location of that appearance or describe what Jesus said there. The Twelve is the group’s recognized name; it need not mean that exactly twelve people attended every appearance.

He describes his own appearance as an untimely birth and explains his sense of unworthiness by recalling his persecution of the church. He credits God’s grace for what he has become. That grace has led to strenuous work, yet he still gives God the credit rather than treating effort as something achieved independently of Him.

The final sentence returns to shared testimony: whether Paul or the other apostles preached, the message was the same one the Corinthians believed. His personal story supports the common proclamation rather than replacing it.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the list as testimony to Christ’s resurrection and Paul’s account as a confession of undeserved grace at work in his service. Wesley’s notes on verses 9–11 and the USCCB note on verses 9–11 both connect his past persecution, his calling and the work God enabled.
passages.god_plan_html:
Galatians 1:13–24 gives Paul’s own account of God revealing His Son to him so he might proclaim Him among the Gentiles. Churches that had known him as a persecutor glorified God when they heard what had happened.

That makes his appearance in the witness list more than a personal achievement. God’s grace turns an enemy of the church into a servant of the message he tried to destroy, and the benefit reaches other people. The gospel’s advance displays the mercy Paul confesses.
passages.current_position_html: On James’s place in verse 7, Who Shepherds the Church? sees his witness to the risen Jesus and service among the elders as likely factors in his recognized standing. The study distinguishes that personal standing from a transferable title making one person the institutional head of every church. This is our conclusion about the use of James’s example, rather than a new position on every detail of Paul’s witness list.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 15:7
passages.section_title: Why is James named among the resurrection witnesses?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 Then He appeared to James, then to all the apostles.
paragraphs: 7 Then He appeared to James, then to all the apostles.

passages.context_html:
Paul names James within 1 Corinthians 15:5–11, a list of appearances supporting the gospel’s claim that Christ rose from the dead. James is mentioned individually before the reference to all the apostles.

The verse does not describe their meeting, identify its location or record a conversation. Its immediate purpose is to identify another witness. Elsewhere Paul names James as the Lord’s brother (Galatians 1:19); the related church-leadership study connects the James mentioned here with the leader seen in Jerusalem.

Questions about James’s later role should be kept distinct from what this sentence itself says. Paul is recounting an appearance, not recording the creation of a church office or a process for appointing a successor.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as one of the appearances testifying to Christ’s resurrection. The USCCB note on verses 3–7 places the named appearances alongside His death, burial and resurrection in the gospel summary. The verse itself leaves the details of the encounter unstated.
passages.current_position_html: In Who Shepherds the Church?, we understand James’s standing as recognized personal authority likely connected with his witness to the risen Jesus and his service among other elders. We do not take this appearance as establishing a transferable office of institutional headship. The study distinguishes respect for a person’s maturity and knowledge from creating a title others must inherit.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
John 20:29–31 connects the testimony to the risen Jesus with faith among people who have not personally seen Him. The account is written so readers may believe in Him and have life in His name.

Naming witnesses such as James belongs within that wider purpose of making Christ known through testimony. Their experience serves people beyond those present at the appearance.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 15:12-19
passages.section_title: What would follow if the dead could not be raised?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 But if it is preached that Christ has been raised from the dead, how can some of you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? 13 If there is no resurrection of the dead, then not even Christ has been raised. 14 And if Christ has not been raised, our preaching is worthless, and so is your faith. 15 In that case, we are also exposed as false witnesses about God. For we have testified about God that He raised Christ from the dead, but He did not raise Him if in fact the dead are not raised. 16 For if the dead are not raised, then not even Christ has been raised. 17 And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile; you are still in your sins. 18 Then those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished. 19 If our hope in Christ is for this life alone, we are to be pitied more than all men.
paragraphs: 12 But if it is preached that Christ has been raised from the dead, how can some of you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? 13 If there is no resurrection of the dead, then not even Christ has been raised. 14 And if Christ has not been raised, our preaching is worthless, and so is your faith. 15 In that case, we are also exposed as false witnesses about God. For we have testified about God that He raised Christ from the dead, but He did not raise Him if in fact the dead are not raised.

16 For if the dead are not raised, then not even Christ has been raised. 17 And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile; you are still in your sins. 18 Then those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished. 19 If our hope in Christ is for this life alone, we are to be pitied more than all men.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul now names the problem: some Corinthians say there is no resurrection of the dead. He follows that claim through to its consequences. If the dead cannot be raised, Christ has not been raised either.

That would make the apostles’ proclamation worthless and their testimony about God false. The Corinthians cannot preserve the message that God raised Christ while rejecting the possibility on which that message depends.

The consequences reach beyond the preachers. Without Christ’s resurrection, the Corinthians remain in their sins, and those who have died in Christ have perished. Faith would not achieve what it promises simply because the people holding it are sincere.

Paul is stating the consequences of a denial he will reject, not announcing that the gospel has failed. The next section begins by affirming that Christ really has been raised. Here he makes clear why Christian hope reaches beyond benefits in this present life.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand Paul to make the real resurrection of Christ essential to the gospel’s saving hope. Wesley’s notes on verses 13–19 and the USCCB notes on verses 12–19 both explain that rejecting it undermines the proclamation, forgiveness and the future of those who have died in Christ.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Luke 20:37–38, Jesus appeals to God’s identification with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob when affirming the resurrection. God is the God of the living; death does not simply erase the relationship and hope His promises establish.

Paul’s reasoning likewise places resurrection within God’s saving purpose, rather than treating it as an optional addition to an otherwise complete message. The gospel offers a hope that reaches beyond the grave. The rest of this chapter will explain how Christ’s resurrection grounds that hope for His people.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 15:20-23
passages.section_title: Why does Christ’s resurrection give hope for ours?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 20 But Christ has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. 21 For since death came through a man, the resurrection of the dead comes also through a man. 22 For as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive. 23 But each in his own turn: Christ the firstfruits; then at His coming, those who belong to Him.
paragraphs: 20 But Christ has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. 21 For since death came through a man, the resurrection of the dead comes also through a man. 22 For as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive. 23 But each in his own turn: Christ the firstfruits; then at His coming, those who belong to Him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After tracing what would follow if resurrection were false, Paul firmly states what he proclaims: Christ has been raised. His resurrection is the firstfruits of those who have died, the beginning of a harvest that will include others.

The word firstfruits is aparchē (ah-par-KHAY), ἀπαρχή, the first portion of a harvest offered to God; see Thayer’s entry. Leviticus 23:9–14 describes bringing the first sheaf before using the harvest. Paul applies that picture directly to Christ: His resurrection points forward to the life of those who belong to Him.

The comparison with Adam explains why one person’s action can matter for many. Death came through a man, and resurrection also comes through a man. Paul places the human condition in Adam alongside the new hope found in Christ.

He then gives an order: Christ first, followed at His coming by those who belong to Him. Their future is connected to His victory. The passage is not merely saying that Jesus survived while everyone else’s death remains unchanged.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand firstfruits as connecting Christ’s resurrection with the resurrection of His people. Wesley’s note on verse 20 describes it as the assurance of what follows; the USCCB notes on verses 20–22 likewise emphasize that His resurrection reaches beyond Himself to those who share His life.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 8:11, 18–23 connects the Spirit who raised Jesus with life for believers’ mortal bodies, their future glory and the redemption of creation. Those who already have the Spirit still wait for the redemption of their bodies.

God’s purpose therefore includes more than release from guilt or survival as a memory. He is bringing His children into a life that shares in Christ’s victory over death. Paul’s harvest picture gives their waiting a foundation: the firstfruits have already appeared.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 15:24-28
passages.section_title: What is the goal of Christ’s victory over every enemy?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 24 Then the end will come, when He hands over the kingdom to God the Father after He has destroyed all dominion, authority, and power. 25 For He must reign until He has put all His enemies under His feet. 26 The last enemy to be destroyed is death. 27 For “God has put everything under His feet.” Now when it says that everything has been put under Him, this clearly does not include the One who put everything under Him. 28 And when all things have been subjected to Him, then the Son Himself will be made subject to Him who put all things under Him, so that God may be all in all.
paragraphs: 24 Then the end will come, when He hands over the kingdom to God the Father after He has destroyed all dominion, authority, and power. 25 For He must reign until He has put all His enemies under His feet. 26 The last enemy to be destroyed is death.

27 For “God has put everything under His feet.” Now when it says that everything has been put under Him, this clearly does not include the One who put everything under Him. 28 And when all things have been subjected to Him, then the Son Himself will be made subject to Him who put all things under Him, so that God may be all in all.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul widens the view from the resurrection of Christ’s people to the completion of His reign. Every opposing dominion, authority and power is to be overcome, with death named as the last enemy. The kingdom is handed to God the Father.

His language draws on Psalm 110:1, where enemies become a footstool, and Psalm 8:6, where God places everything under the feet of the one He appoints to rule. Paul explicitly applies that rule to Christ.

He also makes a distinction: the Father who subjects everything to the Son is not Himself one of the things placed under the Son. When the work is complete, the Son is subject to the Father, and the stated goal is that God be all in all.

The sequence emphasizes God’s final victory and the end of death’s dominion. These verses do not state the length of every stage or name every group that a fuller timeline might include. Their central reassurance is that no enemy will finally defeat God’s purpose through Christ.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand this as the completion of Christ’s victory and the defeat of death. They differ over the sequence of events surrounding that completion.

Wesley’s notes on verses 23–24 place the resurrection of the righteous and wicked together, followed by the final end. The Reformed Westminster Confession 32.2–3 describes all the dead being raised on the last day, with differing outcomes. Dallas Theological Seminary’s Articles XIX–XXI instead distinguish Christ’s gathering of His people, His return and millennial reign, and a final judgment of unbelievers after that reign. These are fuller accounts developed from other passages alongside this one.

The Son’s handing over of the kingdom is also read in light of His relationship to the Father. Wesley’s note on verse 24 understands it as the completion of His work as mediator while affirming that Father and Son continue to reign. The Reformed Westminster Confession 2.3 likewise affirms Father, Son and Spirit as sharing the same divine power and eternity. These readings do not treat the Son’s submission as His ceasing to be divine.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 1:9–10 describes God’s purpose to bring all things in heaven and on earth together in Christ. Paul’s account of every enemy being put under Him places resurrection within that larger purpose.

Revelation 21:1–4 describes the outcome in terms of life together: God dwells with His people, wipes away tears, and death and pain are no more. The defeat of death is not an abstract victory. It opens onto the promised life of God with His people in a renewed creation.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 15:29-34
passages.section_title: How should resurrection hope shape what we do now?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 29 If these things are not so, what will those do who are baptized for the dead? If the dead are not raised at all, why are people baptized for them? 30 And why do we endanger ourselves every hour? 31 I face death every day, brothers, as surely as I boast about you in Christ Jesus our Lord. 32 If I fought wild beasts in Ephesus for human motives, what did I gain? If the dead are not raised, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.” 33 Do not be deceived: “Bad company corrupts good character.” 34 Sober up as you ought, and stop sinning; for some of you are ignorant of God. I say this to your shame.
paragraphs: 29 If these things are not so, what will those do who are baptized for the dead? If the dead are not raised at all, why are people baptized for them?

30 And why do we endanger ourselves every hour? 31 I face death every day, brothers, as surely as I boast about you in Christ Jesus our Lord. 32 If I fought wild beasts in Ephesus for human motives, what did I gain? If the dead are not raised, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.” 33 Do not be deceived: “Bad company corrupts good character.” 34 Sober up as you ought, and stop sinning; for some of you are ignorant of God. I say this to your shame.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul continues testing the denial of resurrection against actual conduct. He first asks about people baptized for the dead. He does not explain the practice in enough detail to settle exactly what was happening, but his question makes its connection with resurrection hope clear.

He then turns to his own repeated danger. Why face death for the gospel if death ends the hope it proclaims? His reference to fighting wild beasts at Ephesus is often understood as a picture of violent opposition; this sentence alone does not give a detailed account of an arena encounter.

The saying about eating and drinking because tomorrow brings death comes from Isaiah 22:13. Paul voices the consequence of denying a future beyond death, rather than recommending that way of life.

He closes with a warning about corrupting influences and a call to stop sinning and come to a proper knowledge of God. Resurrection is not a detached theory. What people accept as true can shape their choices, their perseverance and the counsel they give one another.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The phrase baptized for the dead has several readings. The USCCB note on verse 29 leaves the practice unexplained and cautions that Paul’s use of it does not necessarily mean he approves it. Wesley’s note suggests baptism in hope of blessings after death, or new believers taking the place of Christians who have died.

The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints gives the verse a different practical application. Its own explanation of baptisms for the dead teaches living people being baptized on behalf of the deceased, who remain free to accept or reject what is offered. That should not be represented as automatically making someone a member or saving them against their will.

Identifying a possible ancient practice and endorsing a continuing religious practice are different questions. The clearer point in Paul’s surrounding discussion is that actions directed toward future life make little sense if resurrection itself is denied.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 6:3–11 explicitly connects baptism with Christ’s death and resurrection and with walking in newness of life. That connection does not by itself resolve the disputed phrase here, but it shows why resurrection hope belongs with present conduct.

God’s saving purpose changes the life His people are called to live now. Hope beyond the grave supports faithful service and resistance to sin, rather than making everyday choices irrelevant.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 15:35-41
passages.section_title: How can a body that dies be raised in a different form?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 35 But someone will ask, “How are the dead raised? With what kind of body will they come?” 36 You fool! What you sow does not come to life unless it dies. 37 And what you sow is not the body that will be, but just a seed, perhaps of wheat or something else. 38 But God gives it a body as He has designed, and to each kind of seed He gives its own body. 39 Not all flesh is the same: Men have one kind of flesh, animals have another, birds another, and fish another. 40 There are also heavenly bodies and earthly bodies. But the splendor of the heavenly bodies is of one degree, and the splendor of the earthly bodies is of another. 41 The sun has one degree of splendor, the moon another, and the stars another; and star differs from star in splendor.
paragraphs: 35 But someone will ask, “How are the dead raised? With what kind of body will they come?” 36 You fool! What you sow does not come to life unless it dies. 37 And what you sow is not the body that will be, but just a seed, perhaps of wheat or something else. 38 But God gives it a body as He has designed, and to each kind of seed He gives its own body.

39 Not all flesh is the same: Men have one kind of flesh, animals have another, birds another, and fish another. 40 There are also heavenly bodies and earthly bodies. But the splendor of the heavenly bodies is of one degree, and the splendor of the earthly bodies is of another. 41 The sun has one degree of splendor, the moon another, and the stars another; and star differs from star in splendor.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul voices the objection about how the dead are raised and what kind of body they will have. His sharp answer challenges the assumption that the limits of a decaying body also limit what God can do.

He begins with a seed. What is planted does not look like the grown plant that will emerge, yet God gives each kind its own body. The comparison holds together a connection with what was planted and a remarkable change in form.

He then points to the variety already visible in creation: different living creatures, the sun, the moon and the stars. God is not confined to producing only the kind of body the questioner currently knows.

The examples prepare for Paul’s description of resurrection in the next verses. They are illustrations of God’s power to give life and transform, rather than a technical account of which particles must be recovered or how a body is reconstructed.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the seed and creation examples as answering doubt about God’s power to raise the dead in a changed condition. Wesley’s notes on verses 35–41 and the USCCB notes on verses 35–41 both emphasize the difference between what is planted and what God brings forth.
passages.god_plan_html:
A related picture appears in John 12:23–26, where Jesus speaks of a grain of wheat falling into the ground and dying so it bears much fruit. He connects that image with His approaching glorification and the life of those who follow Him.

This is a parallel in the picture used, not a claim that Paul is quoting that conversation or explaining biological mechanics. Both passages turn attention toward life God brings through what looks like an ending. Resurrection belongs within the saving work of the Son whose death bears fruit for others.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 15:42-49
passages.section_title: What does Paul mean by a spiritual body?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 42 So will it be with the resurrection of the dead: What is sown is perishable; it is raised imperishable. 43 It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power. 44 It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual body. 45 So it is written: “The first man Adam became a living being”; the last Adam a life-giving spirit. 46 The spiritual, however, was not first, but the natural, and then the spiritual. 47 The first man was of the dust of the earth, the second man from heaven. 48 As was the earthly man, so also are those who are of the earth; and as is the heavenly man, so also are those who are of heaven. 49 And just as we have borne the likeness of the earthly man, so also shall we bear the likeness of the heavenly man.
paragraphs: 42 So will it be with the resurrection of the dead: What is sown is perishable; it is raised imperishable. 43 It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power. 44 It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual body.

45 So it is written: “The first man Adam became a living being”; the last Adam a life-giving spirit. 46 The spiritual, however, was not first, but the natural, and then the spiritual. 47 The first man was of the dust of the earth, the second man from heaven. 48 As was the earthly man, so also are those who are of the earth; and as is the heavenly man, so also are those who are of heaven. 49 And just as we have borne the likeness of the earthly man, so also shall we bear the likeness of the heavenly man.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul now applies the illustrations to resurrection itself. What is buried in decay, dishonor and weakness is raised to life that cannot decay or die, in glory and power. The contrast is a transformation of human life, not merely a return to the same condition of vulnerability and death.

The word translated natural is psychikos (psoo-khee-KOSS), ψυχικός, referring here to ordinary human life; see Thayer’s entry. Paul connects it with Adam becoming a living being. Calling the raised body spiritual does not mean he has stopped talking about a body: it belongs to the new life Christ gives.

His citation of Genesis 2:7 introduces Adam as the first man, formed from the earth. Christ is the last Adam and the life-giving one from heaven. Paul contrasts the life received in the first with the life given through the second.

The promise reaches to identity as well as survival: as people have borne the likeness of the earthly man, they will bear the likeness of the heavenly man. The point is the future Christ gives, rather than a detailed specification of a new material or a denial that the person raised is the person who died.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as real bodily transformation through Christ, rather than simply leaving embodied life behind. The Reformed Westminster Confession 32.2–3 affirms the raising of the same persons’ bodies with changed qualities, and Wesley’s note on verse 45 connects Christ’s life-giving work with the resurrection of their bodies.
passages.god_plan_html:
Genesis 1:26–28 gives humanity the calling to bear God’s image within His creation. Paul’s description of bearing Christ’s likeness places the hope of resurrection within God’s purpose for human life.

Philippians 3:20–21 explicitly promises that the Lord will transform His people’s lowly bodies to be like His glorious body. Their future is shaped by Him. Salvation’s goal includes people made fit for the life He gives, rather than the permanent defeat of their human existence by death.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 15:50-58
passages.section_title: Why can we keep serving when death seems to have the last word?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 50 Now I declare to you, brothers, that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable. 51 Listen, I tell you a mystery: We will not all sleep, but we will all be changed— 52 in an instant, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, the dead will be raised imperishable, and we will be changed. 53 For the perishable must be clothed with the imperishable, and the mortal with immortality. 54 When the perishable has been clothed with the imperishable and the mortal with immortality, then the saying that is written will come to pass: “Death has been swallowed up in victory.” 55 “Where, O Death, is your victory? Where, O Death, is your sting?” 56 The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law. 57 But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ! 58 Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast and immovable. Always excel in the work of the Lord, because you know that your labor in the Lord is not in vain.
paragraphs: 50 Now I declare to you, brothers, that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable. 51 Listen, I tell you a mystery: We will not all sleep, but we will all be changed— 52 in an instant, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, the dead will be raised imperishable, and we will be changed. 53 For the perishable must be clothed with the imperishable, and the mortal with immortality.

54 When the perishable has been clothed with the imperishable and the mortal with immortality, then the saying that is written will come to pass: “Death has been swallowed up in victory.” 55 “Where, O Death, is your victory? Where, O Death, is your sting?” 56 The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law. 57 But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ! 58 Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast and immovable. Always excel in the work of the Lord, because you know that your labor in the Lord is not in vain.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul explains that our present mortal condition cannot inherit God’s lasting kingdom. The change is necessary, but death will not be the route for every believer. Some will still be alive; all must be changed.

He describes an instant transformation at the last trumpet: the dead are raised imperishable, and the living are changed. Mortality is clothed with immortality. The passage reveals the promise and the suddenness of the change without supplying a date on the calendar.

Paul then draws on Isaiah 25:8 and Hosea 13:14 in his cry of victory over death. Sin gives death its sting, and the law exposes sin’s power to condemn; the victory is given by God through Jesus Christ.

The closing instruction follows from that hope: stand firm and keep giving yourselves to the Lord’s work. Paul does not end with a puzzle for calculating the future. He gives a reason for faithful service now: labor in the Lord is not wasted, even when its lasting result cannot yet be seen.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand this as the promised transformation of those who belong to Christ, whether they have died or remain alive. They differ over where it belongs in a fuller account of His return.

The Reformed Westminster Confession 32.2 places the change of the living and raising of the dead at the last day. Dallas Theological Seminary’s Articles XVIII–XIX instead connect these verses with Christ gathering His church before a future period of great distress. That gathering is often called the rapture. Both accounts affirm the transformation Paul announces; the further sequence comes from how they read other passages with it.

Wesley’s note on verse 58 draws out the practical result: steady faithfulness and love while looking forward to death’s defeat. The promise encourages service rather than making it pointless.
passages.god_plan_html:
The promise in Isaiah 25:6–9 places death’s overthrow alongside a feast for the peoples, tears wiped away and joy in God’s salvation. Paul explicitly identifies the coming transformation with the fulfillment of death being swallowed up in victory.

Revelation 21:1–4 also joins the end of death and tears with God dwelling among His people. The goal is a shared life with Him. Paul’s final encouragement gives present work its place within that hope: what is done faithfully in the Lord belongs to a future death cannot cancel.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 16:1-4
passages.section_title: How can a church prepare to help believers in need?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now about the collection for the saints, you are to do as I directed the churches of Galatia: 2 On the first day of every week, each of you should set aside a portion of his income, saving it up, so that when I come no collections will be needed. 3 Then, on my arrival, I will send letters with those you recommend to carry your gift to Jerusalem. 4 And if it is advisable for me to go also, they can travel with me.
paragraphs: 1 Now about the collection for the saints, you are to do as I directed the churches of Galatia: 2 On the first day of every week, each of you should set aside a portion of his income, saving it up, so that when I come no collections will be needed. 3 Then, on my arrival, I will send letters with those you recommend to carry your gift to Jerusalem. 4 And if it is advisable for me to go also, they can travel with me.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the long discussion of resurrection, Paul turns to a practical collection for believers in Jerusalem. He has already given the churches of Galatia instructions for the same undertaking. The Corinthians belong to a wider family whose needs call for action.

Each person is to set something aside on the first day of the week, according to their income. Regular preparation will keep the collection from becoming a hurried project when Paul arrives. This paragraph gives no fixed percentage.

The congregation will approve the people who carry the gift, and Paul will provide letters for them. He may accompany them if that is appropriate. Generosity and trustworthy handling of the money belong together; the gift is not simply placed beyond the givers’ concern.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as planned generosity toward believers in need, with contributions related to what people have received. Wesley’s note on verse 2 emphasizes giving as God has prospered a person; Calvin’s note on verse 3 emphasizes choosing trustworthy people to administer the gift. Neither point requires inventing a percentage that Paul does not state here.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 15:25–27 explains the wider significance of this collection. Gentile believers share material help with Jewish believers from whom spiritual blessings have come. The USCCB introduction to these verses also draws attention to this connection.

The gift makes the unity of Christ’s people visible across distance and background. God’s work of bringing people together takes practical form when one community accepts responsibility for the needs of another.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 16:5-9
passages.section_title: Can an open door for the gospel come with opposition?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 After I go through Macedonia, however, I will come to you; for I will be going through Macedonia. 6 Perhaps I will stay with you awhile, or even spend the winter, so that you can help me on my journey, wherever I go. 7 For I do not want to see you now only in passing; I hope to spend some time with you, if the Lord permits. 8 But I will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost, 9 because a great door for effective work has opened to me, even though many oppose me.
paragraphs: 5 After I go through Macedonia, however, I will come to you; for I will be going through Macedonia. 6 Perhaps I will stay with you awhile, or even spend the winter, so that you can help me on my journey, wherever I go. 7 For I do not want to see you now only in passing; I hope to spend some time with you, if the Lord permits.
8 But I will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost, 9 because a great door for effective work has opened to me, even though many oppose me.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul explains his travel hopes: he intends to pass through Macedonia before coming to Corinth, and he would like enough time with them for a substantial visit, perhaps through the winter. He hopes they can help him on the next stage of the journey.

His plans remain subject to the Lord’s permission. These are his intentions, not a promise that every detail of his itinerary has been revealed in advance.

For now he will remain in Ephesus until Pentecost because an important opportunity for work has opened there. There are also many opponents. Paul mentions opportunity and opposition together; difficulty has not automatically made the work pointless or closed the door.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand Paul to be weighing fruitful ministry, time with the congregation and the Lord’s permission as he makes plans. Wesley’s note on verse 9 explicitly observes that opposition can accompany opportunity. This is encouragement to discern faithfully, rather than a rule that every dangerous situation requires someone to remain.
passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 19:8–10 describes opposition to Paul’s teaching in Ephesus and his continuing work in another setting. The message of the Lord spread through the surrounding province of Asia.

This gives a concrete example of the mission continuing through resistance. God’s purpose to make Christ known is not measured simply by how comfortable a journey becomes. Paul’s plans serve that purpose while remaining open to the Lord’s direction.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 16:10-12
passages.section_title: How should believers receive people who serve the Lord?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 If Timothy comes, see to it that he has nothing to fear while he is with you, for he is doing the work of the Lord, just as I am. 11 No one, then, should treat him with contempt. Send him on his way in peace so that he can return to me, for I am expecting him along with the brothers. 12 Now about our brother Apollos: I strongly urged him to go to you with the brothers. He was not at all inclined to go now, but he will go when he has the opportunity.
paragraphs: 10 If Timothy comes, see to it that he has nothing to fear while he is with you, for he is doing the work of the Lord, just as I am. 11 No one, then, should treat him with contempt. Send him on his way in peace so that he can return to me, for I am expecting him along with the brothers.
12 Now about our brother Apollos: I strongly urged him to go to you with the brothers. He was not at all inclined to go now, but he will go when he has the opportunity.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul asks the Corinthians to make sure Timothy can be among them without fear. Timothy is doing the Lord’s work, as Paul is, and should not be treated with contempt. They are to send him on his way in peace.

Paul also explains that he strongly encouraged Apollos to visit with the brothers. Apollos was not inclined to come at that time and would come when he had an opportunity. Paul does not give his reason.

The letter began by challenging factions associated with teachers’ names. These travel arrangements show cooperation rather than a contest for an audience: Paul supports Timothy’s work and has encouraged Apollos to visit.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these instructions as a call to receive faithful workers with respect rather than judging them by personal preference. Calvin’s note on verse 12 points out that Paul himself encouraged Apollos to come. The text should not be made to say that Paul kept a rival away, or that it reveals Apollos’s private reason for delaying.
passages.god_plan_html:
Philippians 2:19–24 describes Timothy’s genuine concern for others and his tested service with Paul in the gospel. That is the kind of work the Corinthians are being asked to welcome.

Christ’s mission is carried forward through people who put His concerns ahead of their own status. Receiving such a worker well helps the wider work; it also resists the habit of turning servants into competing celebrities.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 16:13-14
passages.section_title: What does courage look like when everything is done in love?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 Be on the alert. Stand firm in the faith. Be men of courage. Be strong. 14 Do everything in love.
paragraphs: 13 Be on the alert. Stand firm in the faith. Be men of courage. Be strong. 14 Do everything in love.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
These brief instructions gather together concerns running through the letter. The Corinthians must stay alert, stand firm in the faith, act courageously and be strong. Their divisions and confusion call for steady faithfulness rather than drifting with pressure.

The next sentence governs how that strength is expressed: everything is to be done in love. Paul has already described love’s patience, kindness and refusal to seek its own advantage in chapter 13. Courage here cannot be used to excuse contempt or harshness.

The call addresses the congregation. The wording about men of courage in the BSB expresses the appeal to bravery; it does not turn love and steadfast faith into responsibilities belonging only to men.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these verses together as a call to firm faith expressed through love. Calvin’s notes on verses 13–14 explain both the need for strength and love’s direction of dealings with others. Firmness and care are meant to work together in the same life.
passages.god_plan_html:
2 Timothy 1:7–10 also joins courage with love. Timothy is encouraged to share in suffering for the gospel through God’s power, in keeping with the purpose and grace made known through Christ, who has abolished death.

That connection gives courage its setting. God’s saving purpose calls people to bear witness to Christ with strength and care for others, rather than to prove themselves through dominance.

passages.title: 1 Corinthians 16:15-18
passages.section_title: Whose service should a church learn to recognize?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 You know that Stephanas and his household were the first converts in Achaia, and they have devoted themselves to the service of the saints. Now I urge you, brothers, 16 to submit to such as these, and to every fellow worker and laborer. 17 I am glad that Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus have arrived, because they have supplied what was lacking from you. 18 For they refreshed my spirit and yours as well. Show your appreciation, therefore, to such men.
paragraphs: 15 You know that Stephanas and his household were the first converts in Achaia, and they have devoted themselves to the service of the saints. Now I urge you, brothers, 16 to submit to such as these, and to every fellow worker and laborer.

17 I am glad that Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus have arrived, because they have supplied what was lacking from you. 18 For they refreshed my spirit and yours as well. Show your appreciation, therefore, to such men.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul identifies the household of Stephanas as the first converts in Achaia and points to their devotion to serving the saints. He asks the Corinthians to submit to people like them and to everyone who joins in the work and labors.

Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus have brought Paul joy. Their presence has supplied what the congregation’s absence left lacking and has refreshed his spirit. He calls the Corinthians to recognize such people.

The commendation rests on actual service, shared labor and the help these people give. This paragraph does not provide a complete system of church offices or establish a lifelong authority that automatically transfers to every congregation.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the passage as a call to respect and cooperate with people devoted to serving the church. Wesley’s notes on verses 15–18 connect the appeal with their work and the refreshment they bring. Recognizing that contribution need not mean making claims about their precise office that Paul does not state here.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Mark 10:42–45, Jesus distinguishes greatness among His followers from the domination practiced by rulers. He places service at its center and points to His own giving of His life for many.

The commendation here follows that pattern: people are recognized for giving themselves to the good of others. This is a connection in the shape of service, not a claim that their work carries the saving role of Jesus’ death.
