passages.title: 1 Corinthians 16:19-24
passages.section_title: What holds distant churches together while they await the Lord?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 The churches in the province of Asia send you greetings. Aquila and Prisca greet you warmly in the Lord, and so does the church that meets at their house. 20 All the brothers here send you greetings. Greet one another with a holy kiss. 21 This greeting is in my own hand—Paul. 22 If anyone does not love the Lord, let him be under a curse. Come, O Lord! 23 The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you. 24 My love be with all of you in Christ Jesus. Amen.
paragraphs: 19 The churches in the province of Asia send you greetings. Aquila and Prisca greet you warmly in the Lord, and so does the church that meets at their house. 20 All the brothers here send you greetings. Greet one another with a holy kiss. 21 This greeting is in my own hand—Paul.
22 If anyone does not love the Lord, let him be under a curse. Come, O Lord! 23 The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you. 24 My love be with all of you in Christ Jesus. Amen.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul passes on greetings from the churches in the province of Asia, from Aquila and Prisca and the church in their house, and from the brothers with him. The Corinthians’ local troubles have not separated them from the wider family of believers.

The instruction to greet one another with a holy kiss expresses fellowship within that family. Paul then identifies the greeting written in his own hand. He does not say here who wrote the rest of the letter.

His closing words combine a solemn warning about not loving the Lord, a plea for the Lord to come, the grace of Jesus and Paul’s love for them all. The warning should not erase the grace and affection with which this difficult letter ends.

The plea translated Come, O Lord! carries an Aramaic expression into the Greek letter; see Thayer’s entry. The USCCB note on verse 22 explains the prayer reading followed by the BSB, while noting that dividing the expression differently gives another reading. The main text is kept as the BSB presents it.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly recognize the greetings as an expression of shared belonging and the closing appeal as looking toward the Lord. Wesley’s note on verse 22 explains the Aramaic expression in terms of the Lord’s coming; the USCCB note explains it as a prayer for Him to come. Those explanations share the focus on the Lord while describing the wording differently.
passages.god_plan_html:
Revelation 22:20–21 also closes with a plea for the Lord Jesus to come and with His grace. The hope reaches beyond the resolution of one congregation’s problems to the Lord Himself.

The greetings and that shared expectation belong together. Believers in different homes and regions look toward the same Lord and depend on His grace. Paul’s final love for the Corinthians includes the whole troubled congregation he has been working to restore.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 1:1-2
passages.section_title: Who is writing, and who belongs in this greeting?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, To the church of God in Corinth, together with all the saints throughout Achaia: 2 Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
paragraphs: 1 Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, To the church of God in Corinth, together with all the saints throughout Achaia: 2 Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul identifies himself as an apostle of Christ Jesus by God’s will and names Timothy as his brother. The greeting places his work under Christ’s calling while presenting Timothy as a fellow believer alongside him.

He addresses God’s church in Corinth and all the saints throughout Achaia, the surrounding region. Saints here are the believers he is addressing, not a small class singled out as unusually holy. The letter speaks to a local congregation within a wider family.

Paul wishes them grace and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. The difficult matters that follow begin with this greeting of God’s favor and peace, rather than with a withdrawal of fellowship.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these verses as Paul’s greeting to a congregation and the believers beyond it, grounding his apostleship in God’s will. Wesley’s note on verse 1 draws attention to his calling Timothy a brother. The greeting introduces the relationship Paul will seek to strengthen throughout the letter.
passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 18:1–11 describes the beginning of Paul’s work in Corinth: he teaches that Jesus is the Christ, people believe, and the Lord encourages him to keep speaking. The congregation addressed here grew through that work.

The greeting therefore belongs within the spread of the gospel and the formation of communities who belong to Christ. Their continued need for correction does not make them an abandoned project. This letter is part of caring for people after they first believe.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 1:3-7
passages.section_title: How can the comfort we receive help someone else?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 3 Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of compassion and the God of all comfort, 4 who comforts us in all our troubles, so that we can comfort those in any trouble with the comfort we ourselves have received from God. 5 For just as the sufferings of Christ overflow to us, so also through Christ our comfort overflows. 6 If we are afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation; if we are comforted, it is for your comfort, which accomplishes in you patient endurance of the same sufferings we experience. 7 And our hope for you is sure, because we know that just as you share in our sufferings, so also you will share in our comfort.
paragraphs: 3 Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of compassion and the God of all comfort, 4 who comforts us in all our troubles, so that we can comfort those in any trouble with the comfort we ourselves have received from God.

5 For just as the sufferings of Christ overflow to us, so also through Christ our comfort overflows. 6 If we are afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation; if we are comforted, it is for your comfort, which accomplishes in you patient endurance of the same sufferings we experience. 7 And our hope for you is sure, because we know that just as you share in our sufferings, so also you will share in our comfort.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul turns from greeting the Corinthians to praising God as the Father of compassion and the source of all comfort. He does not begin by pretending the troubles are small. He gives thanks for the help God provides within them.

The verb behind comforts is parakaleō (pah-rah-kah-LEH-oh), παρακαλέω. In this use it includes consoling and encouraging someone, helping them find strength; see Thayer’s entry. It is care that helps a person endure, not merely a request to stop feeling upset.

Comfort received has an outward purpose: it equips Paul and his companions to comfort others in trouble. He connects both their sufferings and their comfort with Christ. The Corinthians’ endurance matters to him, and their shared experience gives him hope for them.

Paul is describing how God’s help can be passed on. He does not require people to have experienced an identical loss before they can care for someone, nor does he say that continuing grief proves God has failed to comfort them.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as God’s comfort reaching people through their fellowship with Christ and then strengthening others. Wesley’s notes on verses 3–7 emphasize comfort during and after affliction and endurance through shared suffering. The USCCB notes on verses 3–7 likewise connect suffering and encouragement with union with Christ.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 8:17–25 places suffering with Christ alongside the hope of sharing His glory. It also describes creation’s groaning and believers’ waiting for the redemption of their bodies.

That wider hope gives present comfort its setting. God’s purpose reaches beyond helping people survive one crisis to the life He will bring to completion in Christ. In the meantime, care received becomes care given, helping others endure while they wait.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 1:8-11
passages.section_title: Where did Paul turn when the burden was beyond his strength?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 We do not want you to be unaware, brothers, of the hardships we encountered in the province of Asia. We were under a burden far beyond our ability to endure, so that we despaired even of life. 9 Indeed, we felt we were under the sentence of death, in order that we would not trust in ourselves, but in God, who raises the dead. 10 He has delivered us from such a deadly peril, and He will deliver us. In Him we have placed our hope that He will yet again deliver us, 11 as you help us by your prayers. Then many will give thanks on our behalf for the favor shown us in answer to their prayers.
paragraphs: 8 We do not want you to be unaware, brothers, of the hardships we encountered in the province of Asia. We were under a burden far beyond our ability to endure, so that we despaired even of life. 9 Indeed, we felt we were under the sentence of death, in order that we would not trust in ourselves, but in God, who raises the dead.

10 He has delivered us from such a deadly peril, and He will deliver us. In Him we have placed our hope that He will yet again deliver us, 11 as you help us by your prayers. Then many will give thanks on our behalf for the favor shown us in answer to their prayers.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul tells the Corinthians how severe the danger in the province of Asia had been. He and his companions were burdened beyond their ability to endure and despaired even of life. He does not give enough detail here to identify the event with certainty.

The experience left them expecting death. Paul describes its effect on their trust: they could not rest their hope on their own resources, but on the God who raises the dead. His honesty about being overwhelmed belongs within the testimony of faith, rather than being edited out of it.

God delivered them from deadly peril, and Paul continues to place his hope in Him. This confidence does not mean Paul expects never to die. His description of God as the one who raises the dead puts hope beyond the limits of escaping one danger.

The Corinthians also have a part through prayer. Paul connects their help with the favor received and the thanksgiving that many will offer. He presents people bringing their needs to God and thanking Him together, not prayer as a way to control Him.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a testimony of deliverance that teaches dependence on God and invites shared prayer. They do not all identify the danger in the same way. Wesley’s note on verse 8 suggests the events in Acts 19; the USCCB note on verses 9–10 leaves open whether the threat was an illness or an external danger. The passage’s lesson does not depend on settling that question.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 4:17–25 likewise describes faith directed toward the God who gives life to the dead. It connects Abraham’s hope with believers’ trust in the God who raised Jesus our Lord.

That connection places Paul’s rescue within a larger hope. God’s saving purpose is not exhausted by preserving a person’s present circumstances. The resurrection of Jesus gives reason to trust Him even when human strength has reached its limit.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 1:12-14
passages.section_title: Why does Paul ask the Corinthians to take his words plainly?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 For this is our boast: Our conscience testifies that we have conducted ourselves in the world, and especially in relation to you, in the holiness and sincerity that are from God—not in worldly wisdom, but in the grace of God. 13 For we do not write you anything that is beyond your ability to read and understand. And I hope that you will understand us completely, 14 as you have already understood us in part, that you may boast of us just as we will boast of you in the day of our Lord Jesus.
paragraphs: 12 For this is our boast: Our conscience testifies that we have conducted ourselves in the world, and especially in relation to you, in the holiness and sincerity that are from God—not in worldly wisdom, but in the grace of God. 13 For we do not write you anything that is beyond your ability to read and understand. And I hope that you will understand us completely, 14 as you have already understood us in part, that you may boast of us just as we will boast of you in the day of our Lord Jesus.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul turns from the danger he faced to the trust strained between him and the Corinthians. He appeals to the testimony of his conscience: he and his companions have acted with holiness and sincerity from God, relying on His grace rather than worldly wisdom.

He says his letters are not hiding another message beyond what they can read and understand. They have understood him in part, and he hopes for fuller understanding. The appeal concerns an honest relationship, rather than a claim that every sentence of Scripture requires no study.

Paul looks toward the day of the Lord Jesus, when they will have reason to rejoice in one another. His defense is not simply an attempt to win a personal dispute. He wants their shared life in Christ to end in joy.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as Paul’s appeal for mutual trust based on sincere conduct and open communication. Wesley’s notes on verses 12–14 emphasize integrity and shared rejoicing; the USCCB note on verses 12–14 likewise places the paragraph within Paul’s hope for growing understanding between himself and the church.
passages.god_plan_html:
Philippians 2:14–16 also connects a congregation’s faithful life with Paul’s joy on the day of Christ. Holding forth the word of life matters beyond the immediate moment.

God’s purpose includes people growing together toward that day. The lasting fruit of ministry is found in people belonging to Christ and living faithfully, giving workers and congregations reason to rejoice together.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 1:15-22
passages.section_title: Did changed plans mean that Paul’s message could not be trusted?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 Confident of this, I planned to visit you first, so that you might receive a double blessing. 16 I wanted to visit you on my way to Macedonia, and to return to you from Macedonia, and then to have you help me on my way to Judea. 17 When I planned this, did I do it carelessly? Or do I make my plans by human standards, so as to say “Yes, yes” and also “No, no”? 18 But as surely as God is faithful, our message to you is not “Yes” and “No.” 19 For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was proclaimed among you by me and Silvanus and Timothy, was not “Yes” and “No,” but in Him it has always been “Yes.” 20 For all the promises of God are “Yes” in Christ. And so through Him, our “Amen” is spoken to the glory of God. 21 Now it is God who establishes both us and you in Christ. He anointed us, 22 placed His seal on us, and put His Spirit in our hearts as a pledge of what is to come.
paragraphs: 15 Confident of this, I planned to visit you first, so that you might receive a double blessing. 16 I wanted to visit you on my way to Macedonia, and to return to you from Macedonia, and then to have you help me on my way to Judea. 17 When I planned this, did I do it carelessly? Or do I make my plans by human standards, so as to say “Yes, yes” and also “No, no”?

18 But as surely as God is faithful, our message to you is not “Yes” and “No.” 19 For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was proclaimed among you by me and Silvanus and Timothy, was not “Yes” and “No,” but in Him it has always been “Yes.” 20 For all the promises of God are “Yes” in Christ. And so through Him, our “Amen” is spoken to the glory of God.
21 Now it is God who establishes both us and you in Christ. He anointed us, 22 placed His seal on us, and put His Spirit in our hearts as a pledge of what is to come.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul explains that he had intended to visit Corinth on his way to Macedonia and again on his return, before traveling toward Judea. The change raised a question about his reliability. Had he made the plans carelessly, saying yes while meaning no?

His answer points beyond the itinerary to the message he, Silvanus and Timothy preached. Jesus Christ is not an uncertain promise that God makes and then takes back. God’s promises find their yes in Him, and believers respond through Him with their Amen to God’s glory.

God is also the one who establishes both the workers and the congregation in Christ. He has anointed them, placed His seal on them and given His Spirit in their hearts. Paul places himself alongside the Corinthians as someone dependent on God’s work.

The word translated pledge is arrabōn (ar-rah-BOHN), ἀρραβών: a first payment that assures the rest will follow; see Thayer’s entry. The Spirit is God’s gift and assurance of what is to come, not a human achievement Paul uses to elevate himself above them.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a distinction between a changed travel plan and the reliability of the gospel. Wesley’s notes on verses 18–22 emphasize the certainty of God’s promises in Christ and the Spirit as the beginning of the fullness still awaited. The USCCB notes on verses 18–22 likewise center the paragraph on God’s faithfulness and the Spirit’s assurance. The paragraph does not turn every human intention into an unconditional divine promise.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 1:9–14 sets the Spirit’s seal and pledge within God’s purpose to bring all things in heaven and earth together in Christ. Those who hear and believe the gospel receive the promised Spirit while awaiting their inheritance.

That wider statement shows why Paul grounds confidence in Christ rather than in a perfect travel schedule. The future God promises rests on His purpose and His gift. The Spirit gives believers a present share in the life whose completion they still await.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 1:23-24
passages.section_title: Why did Paul delay a visit he wanted to make?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 23 I call God as my witness that it was in order to spare you that I did not return to Corinth. 24 Not that we lord it over your faith, but we are fellow workers with you for your joy, because it is by faith that you stand firm.
paragraphs: 23 I call God as my witness that it was in order to spare you that I did not return to Corinth. 24 Not that we lord it over your faith, but we are fellow workers with you for your joy, because it is by faith that you stand firm.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul now gives a reason for not returning to Corinth: he wanted to spare them. He calls God as witness to the truth of that explanation. The following chapter will develop his concern about another painful encounter.

He immediately sets a limit on how his role should be understood. He and his companions do not lord it over the Corinthians’ faith; they work with them for their joy. The congregation stands by faith.

Paul can give serious correction while describing himself as a fellow worker. His concern is their good before God, rather than personal control over their trust in Him. This explanation should not become an excuse for every leader’s broken promise: Paul actually explains the purpose of his decision.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as Paul explaining a pastoral decision while rejecting domination over the congregation’s faith. Wesley’s note on verse 24 expressly describes ministers as helpers in faith and holiness, rather than people entitled to dictate belief by their own authority. The USCCB note on verses 23–24 connects the delay with the concern for pain and joy developed in chapter 2.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Mark 10:42–45, Jesus teaches His followers to serve rather than imitate rulers who dominate others. He gives His own service and His life given for many as the defining example.

Paul’s description of working for their joy fits that pattern. Care for Christ’s people is meant to help them stand in faith. A worker’s authority serves that purpose instead of taking the Lord’s place in their lives.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 2:1-4
passages.section_title: Can a painful letter be an expression of love?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 So I made up my mind not to make another painful visit to you. 2 For if I grieve you, who is left to cheer me but those whom I have grieved? 3 I wrote as I did so that on my arrival I would not be grieved by those who ought to make me rejoice. I had confidence in all of you, that you would share my joy. 4 For through many tears I wrote you out of great distress and anguish of heart, not to grieve you but to let you know how much I love you.
paragraphs: 1 So I made up my mind not to make another painful visit to you. 2 For if I grieve you, who is left to cheer me but those whom I have grieved? 3 I wrote as I did so that on my arrival I would not be grieved by those who ought to make me rejoice. I had confidence in all of you, that you would share my joy. 4 For through many tears I wrote you out of great distress and anguish of heart, not to grieve you but to let you know how much I love you.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul continues explaining why he did not return to Corinth as planned. He decided against another painful visit. The people whose fellowship should bring him joy were also the people who would be grieved by such an encounter.

Instead, he wrote with confidence that they would want to share his joy. He describes great distress, anguish of heart and many tears. The purpose of the letter was to make his love known, not simply to leave them feeling wounded.

The earlier painful visit and tearful letter are part of the relationship the original readers already knew. This paragraph does not identify that letter precisely enough to settle every proposed reconstruction of the correspondence.

Paul’s example shows why correction and love must be considered together. His distress is not proof that every harsh message a leader writes is loving; he is explaining his particular concern for these people and the joy he hopes they will share.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as Paul explaining the care behind a painful decision. Wesley’s notes on verses 1–4 emphasize faithful correction as an expression of love. The USCCB note on verses 3–4 likewise emphasizes Paul’s motive, while treating proposed identifications of the tearful letter as uncertain.
passages.god_plan_html:
In John 13:34–35, Jesus makes love for one another a defining mark of His disciples, grounding it in His own love for them.

Paul’s concern for a restored relationship belongs within that calling. Christ is forming a people whose dealings with one another make His love visible. Necessary correction should serve that shared life, rather than becoming an end in itself.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 2:5-11
passages.section_title: What should happen after discipline has done its work?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 Now if anyone has caused grief, he has not grieved me but all of you—to some degree, not to overstate it. 6 The punishment imposed on him by the majority is sufficient for him. 7 So instead, you ought to forgive and comfort him, so that he will not be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow. 8 Therefore I urge you to reaffirm your love for him. 9 My purpose in writing you was to see if you would stand the test and be obedient in everything. 10 If you forgive anyone, I also forgive him. And if I have forgiven anything, I have forgiven it in the presence of Christ for your sake, 11 in order that Satan should not outwit us. For we are not unaware of his schemes.
paragraphs: 5 Now if anyone has caused grief, he has not grieved me but all of you—to some degree, not to overstate it. 6 The punishment imposed on him by the majority is sufficient for him. 7 So instead, you ought to forgive and comfort him, so that he will not be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow. 8 Therefore I urge you to reaffirm your love for him.

9 My purpose in writing you was to see if you would stand the test and be obedient in everything. 10 If you forgive anyone, I also forgive him. And if I have forgiven anything, I have forgiven it in the presence of Christ for your sake, 11 in order that Satan should not outwit us. For we are not unaware of his schemes.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul turns to a person who has caused grief within the congregation. He avoids naming him or spelling out the offense. The harm has touched more than Paul alone; the community has also been affected.

The punishment imposed by the majority is now sufficient. Paul directs them toward forgiveness, comfort and a renewed expression of love, so that the person is not swallowed up by excessive sorrow. Continuing to press the punishment is not the response he asks for.

He joins the congregation in forgiveness, acting in the presence of Christ for their sake. The shared response is part of their obedience. Paul warns that Satan must not gain an advantage through the situation.

The direction is clear even though some background remains unknown: the congregation must move toward restoration. This paragraph does not describe every practical consequence of an offense or settle whether a particular person should return to a leadership role.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a call to restore someone rather than let discipline become endless rejection. The person’s identity is less certain. Wesley’s note on verse 11 connects him with the man earlier delivered to Satan in 1 Corinthians 5. The USCCB note on verses 5–11 leaves the offense unclear and reports the possibility that it involved rejection of Paul’s authority. Those explanations should not be presented as though Paul names the person here.
passages.god_plan_html:
Colossians 3:12–15 calls God’s chosen people to compassion, patience and forgiveness as the Lord forgave them. It joins that life with love and the peace of Christ within one body.

Restoring a brother or sister expresses something already received from the Lord. God’s work of gathering a people in Christ is meant to shape how they treat one another when relationships have been damaged. Forgiveness belongs to that shared life, rather than being a favor reserved for people who have never failed.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 2:12-13
passages.section_title: Why did Paul leave Troas when there was an opportunity to preach?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 Now when I went to Troas to preach the gospel of Christ and a door stood open for me in the Lord, 13 I had no peace in my spirit, because I did not find my brother Titus there. So I said goodbye to them and went on to Macedonia.
paragraphs: 12 Now when I went to Troas to preach the gospel of Christ and a door stood open for me in the Lord, 13 I had no peace in my spirit, because I did not find my brother Titus there. So I said goodbye to them and went on to Macedonia.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul resumes his account of traveling. At Troas he found an open door for the gospel of Christ. Even so, he had no peace in his spirit because he did not find Titus there, and he left for Macedonia.

The reason Titus mattered becomes clearer in 2 Corinthians 7:5–9. His arrival brought comfort and news about the Corinthians’ response. Paul’s concern was bound up with people and their relationship, not simply a choice between places to preach.

These verses record an opportunity alongside unresolved concern. They do not call Paul’s departure a sin or turn the phrase open door into a rule that a worker must stay in one place regardless of other responsibilities.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand Paul’s unrest as concern about Titus and the Corinthians, read together with the later account of their meeting. Wesley’s notes on verses 12–13 and the USCCB note on verses 12–13 both make that connection. The narrative itself does not give a complete rule for deciding between competing ministry needs.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 2:14-17
passages.section_title: How does God make Christ known through imperfect servants?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 But thanks be to God, who always leads us triumphantly as captives in Christ and through us spreads everywhere the fragrance of the knowledge of Him. 15 For we are to God the sweet aroma of Christ among those who are being saved and those who are perishing. 16 To the one we are an odor that brings death, to the other a fragrance that brings life. And who is qualified for such a task? 17 For we are not like so many others, who peddle the word of God for profit. On the contrary, in Christ we speak before God with sincerity, as men sent from God.
paragraphs: 14 But thanks be to God, who always leads us triumphantly as captives in Christ and through us spreads everywhere the fragrance of the knowledge of Him. 15 For we are to God the sweet aroma of Christ among those who are being saved and those who are perishing. 16 To the one we are an odor that brings death, to the other a fragrance that brings life. And who is qualified for such a task?
17 For we are not like so many others, who peddle the word of God for profit. On the contrary, in Christ we speak before God with sincerity, as men sent from God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul moves from his unsettled journey to thanksgiving. The BSB describes God leading him and his companions triumphantly as captives in Christ. Their place is under the victorious Lord, rather than that of independent conquerors displaying their own strength.

He adds the image of fragrance spreading the knowledge of Christ. The workers are a sweet aroma of Christ to God among both those being saved and those perishing. The message does not meet the same response in everyone who hears it.

For some the aroma brings death; for others it brings life. The weight of that task leads Paul to ask who is qualified for it. The question prepares for his explanation of dependence on God in the next chapter.

He contrasts sincere speech before God with peddling God’s word for profit. The issue is using the message for personal gain rather than faithfully speaking as someone sent by God. This sentence does not by itself prohibit every form of material support for a worker.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly see Christ’s victory and the spread of His message as the center of these images. Wesley’s note on verse 14 emphasizes sharing in a victory made visible. The USCCB note on verse 14 also draws attention to being led in captivity and submission, a sense explicit in the BSB wording. These readings place different weight on the picture; neither makes Paul’s difficult circumstances proof that Christ has failed.

Both Wesley’s notes on verses 16–17 and the USCCB note on verses 16–17 connect the task with dependence on God and sincere ministry. Paul is not presenting the message as merchandise to reshape for advantage.
passages.god_plan_html:
Colossians 2:13–15 connects forgiveness and life in Christ with His victory over the powers through the cross. The victory from which His servants work comes through His saving act, not their personal prestige.

Ephesians 5:1–2 also describes Christ’s self-giving love as a fragrant offering to God. This is a parallel in the image, not a claim that Paul’s ministry repeats Christ’s sacrifice. The knowledge of that Christ is what his servants carry into the world.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 3:1-3
passages.section_title: What makes the Corinthians a letter from Christ?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Are we beginning to commend ourselves again? Or do we need, like some people, letters of recommendation to you or from you? 2 You yourselves are our letter, inscribed on our hearts, known and read by everyone. 3 It is clear that you are a letter from Christ, the result of our ministry, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts.
paragraphs: 1 Are we beginning to commend ourselves again? Or do we need, like some people, letters of recommendation to you or from you? 2 You yourselves are our letter, inscribed on our hearts, known and read by everyone. 3 It is clear that you are a letter from Christ, the result of our ministry, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul has just described speaking sincerely before God. He now asks whether he needs to start recommending himself again or supply letters of recommendation to the people who already know his work.

The Corinthians themselves are his letter. He carries them in his heart, and their shared life is something others can see. He then takes the image further: they are a letter from Christ, brought about through the ministry but written by the Spirit of the living God.

The contrast moves from ink to the Spirit and from stone tablets to human hearts. Paul is not claiming to have produced changed people by his own skill. He points to God’s work among them as evidence of what the ministry has served.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the letter as a picture of people whose lives show Christ’s work through the Spirit. Wesley’s notes on verses 1–3 and the USCCB notes on verses 1–3 both connect the image with Paul’s relationship to the congregation and with God’s work in their hearts. The picture does not mean the Corinthians have replaced Christ Himself or become a new written Scripture.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ezekiel 36:22–28 promises cleansing, a new heart and God’s Spirit within His people. The promise is addressed to Israel and includes God making His holy name known among the nations.

Paul’s image of the Spirit writing on human hearts draws on that kind of promised inward renewal. The connection shows that God’s purpose involves more than outward identification with a community: He is at work changing His people so their life makes Him known. It does not require erasing the original promise’s address to Israel.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 3:4-6
passages.section_title: Where does the ability to serve the new covenant come from?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 4 Such confidence before God is ours through Christ. 5 Not that we are competent in ourselves to claim that anything comes from us, but our competence comes from God. 6 And He has qualified us as ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit; for the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.
paragraphs: 4 Such confidence before God is ours through Christ. 5 Not that we are competent in ourselves to claim that anything comes from us, but our competence comes from God. 6 And He has qualified us as ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit; for the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul follows the picture of a letter from Christ with a statement about confidence. His confidence is before God through Christ. He and his companions cannot claim that their ability or the fruit of their work comes from themselves.

God has qualified them to serve a new covenant: a new relationship established by His promise. Paul contrasts the letter that kills with the Spirit who gives life. The next verses identify the stone-engraved law and its condemning effect as the setting of that contrast.

The point is not that careful reading is harmful or that the Spirit makes the words of Scripture unimportant. Paul is explaining the difference between a written command that exposes and condemns sin and the life God gives through His Spirit.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as dependence on God for ministry and as a contrast between the Mosaic covenant and the life-giving work of the Spirit. Wesley’s notes on verses 4–6 identify the letter with the law written on the tablets. The USCCB notes on verses 4–6 connect new covenant with Jeremiah’s promise. Neither explanation makes the passage an instruction to stop studying Scripture.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jeremiah 31:31–34 promises a new covenant with Israel and Judah: God’s law written on hearts, a people who know Him, and sins forgiven. Paul’s language belongs within that promised renewal.

The goal is a relationship in which God is known and His people live as His own. His life-giving work supplies what people cannot produce by presenting their own qualifications. The promise joins inward change and forgiveness rather than treating them as unrelated needs.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 3:7-11
passages.section_title: Why does Paul say the new covenant has greater glory?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 Now if the ministry of death, which was engraved in letters on stone, came with such glory that the Israelites could not gaze at the face of Moses because of its fleeting glory, 8 will not the ministry of the Spirit be even more glorious? 9 For if the ministry of condemnation was glorious, how much more glorious is the ministry of righteousness! 10 Indeed, what was once glorious has no glory now in comparison to the glory that surpasses it. 11 For if what was fading away came with glory, how much greater is the glory of that which endures!
paragraphs: 7 Now if the ministry of death, which was engraved in letters on stone, came with such glory that the Israelites could not gaze at the face of Moses because of its fleeting glory, 8 will not the ministry of the Spirit be even more glorious? 9 For if the ministry of condemnation was glorious, how much more glorious is the ministry of righteousness!
10 Indeed, what was once glorious has no glory now in comparison to the glory that surpasses it. 11 For if what was fading away came with glory, how much greater is the glory of that which endures!

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul develops the contrast by pointing to the law engraved on stone. Its ministry came with glory: Moses’ face shone so brightly that the Israelites could not gaze at it. Exodus 34:29–35 provides the account he is drawing on.

He calls it a ministry of death and condemnation, then contrasts it with the ministry of the Spirit and of righteousness. The contrast is not between an evil God in the past and a good God now. Paul acknowledges the earlier glory while explaining the greater glory of what God is doing through the Spirit.

What was temporary is surpassed by what endures. The comparison supports Paul’s confidence in the ministry he has received, even when its workers do not look impressive. Its value comes from the life God gives, rather than the appearance of its messengers.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as a comparison between the glory of the Mosaic covenant and the greater, lasting glory of the new covenant. Wesley’s notes on verses 7–11 and the USCCB notes on verses 7–11 both emphasize the contrast. Paul’s recognition of the earlier glory should be retained alongside his description of its limits.
passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 8:6–13 explicitly describes Jesus’ more excellent ministry and the better covenant He brings into effect. It quotes Jeremiah’s promise of God’s laws written within His people and their sins forgiven.

That connection places the greater glory within Christ’s work of bringing the promised relationship into effect. God’s purpose advances toward lasting life with Him; it is not a contest between Moses’ personal worth and Paul’s personal worth.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 3:12-16
passages.section_title: What does Paul mean by a veil being taken away?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 Therefore, since we have such a hope, we are very bold. 13 We are not like Moses, who would put a veil over his face to keep the Israelites from gazing at the end of what was fading away. 14 But their minds were closed. For to this day the same veil remains at the reading of the old covenant. It has not been lifted, because only in Christ can it be removed. 15 And even to this day when Moses is read, a veil covers their hearts. 16 But whenever anyone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away.
paragraphs: 12 Therefore, since we have such a hope, we are very bold. 13 We are not like Moses, who would put a veil over his face to keep the Israelites from gazing at the end of what was fading away.

14 But their minds were closed. For to this day the same veil remains at the reading of the old covenant. It has not been lifted, because only in Christ can it be removed. 15 And even to this day when Moses is read, a veil covers their hearts. 16 But whenever anyone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The hope of an enduring ministry gives Paul boldness. He returns to Moses’ veil, then carries that picture from a covered face to a covered understanding when the old covenant is read.

In Exodus 34:33–35, Moses covers his face after speaking with the people and removes the veil when he enters before the Lord. Paul applies the image to recognizing what is found in Christ: the veil can be removed in Him.

His closing statement is an invitation, not a permanent barrier: whenever anyone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away. The paragraph should not be turned into a judgment about every Jewish person’s motives or an assertion that Jewish people cannot turn to Christ.

Paul is explaining the role of Christ in understanding the covenant, rather than saying that the Old Testament has no value. He is using its account of Moses as he explains the hope he proclaims.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the veil as an image of not recognizing Christ, and its removal as the understanding that comes in turning to Him. Wesley’s notes on verses 13–16 and the USCCB notes on verses 13–16 both explain the move from Moses’ face to the readers’ hearts. The image calls for attention to Christ rather than contempt for people.
passages.god_plan_html:
Luke 24:25–27 and 44–47 describes the risen Jesus explaining what Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms say about Him. He opens His disciples’ understanding of the Scriptures and connects His suffering and resurrection with the proclamation of repentance and forgiveness to all nations.

That gives a concrete New Testament connection to Paul’s point. Recognizing Christ brings Scripture’s saving message into view. The result is a message to be carried outward, rather than knowledge kept as a reason to feel superior to others.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 3:17-18
passages.section_title: What kind of freedom and change does the Spirit bring?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom. 18 And we, who with unveiled faces all reflect the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into His image with intensifying glory, which comes from the Lord, who is the Spirit.
paragraphs: 17 Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom. 18 And we, who with unveiled faces all reflect the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into His image with intensifying glory, which comes from the Lord, who is the Spirit.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul describes the removal of the veil in terms of the Lord’s Spirit and freedom. The setting is the Spirit’s life-giving work and release from the ministry of condemnation, not a claim that people are now free to disregard the Lord.

He then includes all the believers in the picture of unveiled faces. In the BSB they reflect the Lord’s glory and are being transformed into His image with intensifying glory. The change comes from the Lord, who is the Spirit.

This is God’s ongoing work in people, rather than a description of self-improvement achieved without Him. The language also reaches beyond one unusually gifted worker: Paul says all of them share in it.

The promise concerns a life increasingly shaped by the Lord. It should not be reduced to a demand that a faithful person must feel fearless or emotionally settled in every circumstance.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand these verses as freedom and transformation given through the Spirit in relation to Christ. Wesley’s notes on verses 17–18 connect freedom with release from sin and growing likeness in love. The USCCB notes on verses 17–18 connect it with release from condemnation and a change already begun in the community. Their focus is God’s work in His people, rather than permission to live without regard for Him.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 8:29–30 describes God’s purpose for His people in terms of being conformed to the image of His Son. 1 Corinthians 15:49 also looks ahead to bearing the likeness of the heavenly man in the discussion of resurrection.

These passages place present transformation alongside the future Christ promises. God’s purpose includes people becoming like His Son, with the Spirit already working in them as they await the completion of that hope.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 4:1-2
passages.section_title: Why must the message be shared openly and honestly?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Therefore, since God in His mercy has given us this ministry, we do not lose heart. 2 Instead, we have renounced secret and shameful ways. We do not practice deceit, nor do we distort the word of God. On the contrary, by open proclamation of the truth, we commend ourselves to every man’s conscience in the sight of God.
paragraphs: 1 Therefore, since God in His mercy has given us this ministry, we do not lose heart. 2 Instead, we have renounced secret and shameful ways. We do not practice deceit, nor do we distort the word of God. On the contrary, by open proclamation of the truth, we commend ourselves to every man’s conscience in the sight of God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul carries forward the discussion of the Spirit’s life-giving ministry. God has given him this work in mercy, so he continues rather than abandoning it. His confidence rests on what he has received, not a claim that the task is easy.

He describes the methods he has rejected: secret shameful practices, deceit and distortion of God’s word. In their place he sets an open proclamation of the truth, before people’s consciences and in God’s sight.

This is part of his explanation of trustworthy ministry. The message is not to be adjusted behind the scenes to serve the messenger’s advantage. Its truth is to be set out plainly for people to consider.

Not losing heart here describes continuing in the work God has given. It should be read alongside Paul’s earlier honesty about anguish and being burdened beyond his strength, rather than turned into a rule that faithful workers never feel distressed.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these verses as perseverance through God’s mercy joined with honest handling of His word. Wesley’s notes on verses 1–2 emphasize continuing the ministry and rejecting deceit or alterations that suit the hearers. The USCCB note on verses 1–2 likewise connects the ministry with confidence and openness.
passages.god_plan_html:
In John 17:17–20, Jesus prays for His followers to be sanctified in the truth, identifies the Father’s word as truth and sends them into the world. He also looks toward those who will believe through their message.

Honest proclamation serves that mission. God’s purpose of making Christ known calls for messengers who serve the truth they have received, rather than reshaping it to attract attention or secure their own standing.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 4:3-6
passages.section_title: Who brings the light that helps us see Christ?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 3 And even if our gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing. 4 The god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers, so they cannot see the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God. 5 For we do not proclaim ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, and ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake. 6 For God, who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” made His light shine in our hearts to give us the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.
paragraphs: 3 And even if our gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing. 4 The god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers, so they cannot see the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God.

5 For we do not proclaim ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, and ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake. 6 For God, who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” made His light shine in our hearts to give us the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul returns to the image of a veil. Where the gospel remains unseen, he describes unbelieving minds blinded by the god of this age. The light being obscured is the gospel of Christ’s glory, and Christ is the image of God.

The title god of this age is commonly understood as referring to Satan; see Wesley’s note on verse 4 and the USCCB note on verses 3–4. It does not make Satan equal to the Creator. Paul immediately turns to the God who brings light.

The workers proclaim Jesus Christ as Lord, not themselves. Their place is to serve the Corinthians for Jesus’ sake. The message and the messenger must not be confused.

God, who commanded light to shine out of darkness, has shone in their hearts to make His glory known in the face of Jesus Christ. Paul places the power to give that knowledge with God, while continuing to describe the message His servants openly proclaim.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the contrast as Satan’s blinding work and God’s giving of light through Christ, with the workers serving rather than taking Christ’s place. Wesley’s notes on verses 3–6 and the USCCB notes on verses 3–6 share those central points. This paragraph does not by itself set out every part of the different Christian accounts of how God’s grace and a person’s response relate.
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul explicitly reaches back to the creation of light in Genesis 1:1–5. The God whose word brought light into darkness is the one who makes Christ known within human hearts.

The connection presents the knowledge of Christ as God’s life-giving work, not simply a messenger’s persuasive achievement. It also links the glory seen in Christ with the Creator’s own glory. The light believers receive is meant to make Him known, rather than make the servant the center of attention.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 4:7-12
passages.section_title: Why would God place a treasure in fragile containers?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 Now we have this treasure in jars of clay to show that this surpassingly great power is from God and not from us. 8 We are hard pressed on all sides, but not crushed; perplexed, but not in despair; 9 persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed. 10 We always carry around in our body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be revealed in our body. 11 For we who are alive are always consigned to death for Jesus’ sake, so that the life of Jesus may also be revealed in our mortal body. 12 So then, death is at work in us, but life is at work in you.
paragraphs: 7 Now we have this treasure in jars of clay to show that this surpassingly great power is from God and not from us. 8 We are hard pressed on all sides, but not crushed; perplexed, but not in despair; 9 persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed.

10 We always carry around in our body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be revealed in our body. 11 For we who are alive are always consigned to death for Jesus’ sake, so that the life of Jesus may also be revealed in our mortal body. 12 So then, death is at work in us, but life is at work in you.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The treasure is the knowledge of God’s glory in Christ that Paul has just described. He and his companions carry it like valuable contents in ordinary clay jars. The picture points to their fragility, so the power at work is recognized as God’s rather than their own.

Paul describes pressure, bewilderment, persecution and being struck down. Each description is followed by a limit: they are not finally crushed, abandoned or destroyed. He is explaining how the work continues through people whose weakness is real.

He connects their repeated exposure to death for Jesus’ sake with the life of Jesus being shown in their mortal bodies. Carrying around His death means sharing the danger and suffering that accompany serving Him; it is not another sacrifice that completes an unfinished cross.

The cost reaches beyond the workers themselves. Death is at work in them, but life in the Corinthians: their costly service carries the message through which others receive life. The paragraph does not promise that a believer’s body can never be harmed or that faith prevents every feeling of despair.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read the clay jars as the weakness of human messengers carrying a treasure that comes from God. Wesley’s notes on verses 7–12 and the USCCB notes on verses 7–12 both connect the suffering with God’s sustaining power and the life of Christ. Their weakness is part of the picture, rather than evidence that the treasure has lost its value.
passages.god_plan_html:
Philippians 3:7–11 joins knowing Christ with the power of His resurrection and fellowship in His sufferings. Paul looks toward resurrection even as his present life is shaped by Christ’s death.

That connection gives the pattern here its larger setting. God’s purpose is life through Christ, reaching beyond the mortal weakness of His servants. Their suffering is not the source of salvation, but serving the crucified and risen Lord can carry a real cost while bringing His message to others.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 4:13-15
passages.section_title: Why does resurrection hope keep Paul speaking?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 And in keeping with what is written, “I believed, therefore I have spoken,” we who have the same spirit of faith also believe and therefore speak, 14 knowing that the One who raised the Lord Jesus will also raise us with Jesus and present us with you in His presence. 15 All this is for your benefit, so that the grace that is extending to more and more people may cause thanksgiving to overflow, to the glory of God.
paragraphs: 13 And in keeping with what is written, “I believed, therefore I have spoken,” we who have the same spirit of faith also believe and therefore speak, 14 knowing that the One who raised the Lord Jesus will also raise us with Jesus and present us with you in His presence. 15 All this is for your benefit, so that the grace that is extending to more and more people may cause thanksgiving to overflow, to the glory of God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul draws on Psalm 116:10 to explain why faith leads him to speak. The psalm itself describes distress, an appeal for rescue and thanksgiving to the Lord. Paul stands within that pattern of trusting God in trouble rather than waiting for all difficulty to disappear.

He identifies the assurance behind his continuing proclamation: the God who raised the Lord Jesus will raise them with Jesus and bring them with the Corinthians into His presence. The hope belongs to both the workers and the people they serve.

The work is for the Corinthians’ benefit, and its reach extends further as grace spreads to more people. The result is increasing thanksgiving to God. Paul’s focus moves from the workers’ perseverance to the shared future and praise that make the cost worthwhile.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand Paul’s speaking as sustained by faith in God’s resurrection promise, with the ministry benefiting others and bringing thanksgiving to God. Wesley’s notes on verses 13–15 and the USCCB notes on verses 12–15 both draw out that movement beyond the worker to the congregation and ultimately to God.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Corinthians 15:20–23 identifies the risen Christ as the firstfruits: His resurrection is the beginning of the harvest that will include those who belong to Him at His coming.

That explicit promise explains why Paul can look forward to being raised with the people he serves. The gospel forms a people with a shared future in Christ, not simply a collection of isolated experiences. As grace reaches more people, the circle of thanksgiving grows.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 4:16-18
passages.section_title: How can Paul call severe suffering light and momentary?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 Therefore we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, yet our inner self is being renewed day by day. 17 For our light and momentary affliction is producing for us an eternal weight of glory that is far beyond comparison. 18 So we fix our eyes not on what is seen, but on what is unseen. For what is seen is temporary, but what is unseen is eternal.
paragraphs: 16 Therefore we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, yet our inner self is being renewed day by day. 17 For our light and momentary affliction is producing for us an eternal weight of glory that is far beyond comparison. 18 So we fix our eyes not on what is seen, but on what is unseen. For what is seen is temporary, but what is unseen is eternal.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul returns to not losing heart. His outer life is wearing away, yet inward renewal continues day by day. He does not deny physical decline or say that trusting God makes a person’s body permanently strong.

Light and momentary are words of comparison with the eternal weight of glory. The same letter has described danger beyond his strength, and these verses follow a description of persecution and exposure to death. Paul is not saying the suffering feels small while it happens.

He says the affliction is producing a glory far beyond comparison. The future God promises gives him a way to understand a costly present without treating that present as the final outcome.

His attention rests on what is unseen and eternal rather than what is temporary. This does not mean that bodies, food, care for neighbors or other visible things have no value. It means the visible circumstances of the moment cannot show the whole future God has promised.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as endurance strengthened by the contrast between present affliction and lasting glory. Wesley’s notes on verses 16–18 and the USCCB notes on verses 16–18 both emphasize that the life God gives will outlast suffering and death. The comparison offers hope without requiring someone to call another person’s pain insignificant.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 8:18–25 makes the same comparison between present suffering and coming glory. It places believers’ waiting within creation’s longing for freedom from decay and the redemption of their bodies.

The promised future is therefore larger than a change of attitude toward hardship. God’s purpose includes release from decay and a completed life with Him. Present renewal gives reason to persevere while the fulfillment remains unseen.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 5:1-5
passages.section_title: What future does God promise beyond our fragile present life?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 For we know that if the earthly tent we live in is dismantled, we have a building from God, an eternal house in heaven, not built by human hands. 2 For in this tent we groan, longing to be clothed with our heavenly dwelling, 3 because when we are clothed, we will not be found naked. 4 For while we are in this tent, we groan under our burdens, because we do not wish to be unclothed but clothed, so that our mortality may be swallowed up by life. 5 And it is God who has prepared us for this very purpose and has given us the Spirit as a pledge of what is to come.
paragraphs: 1 For we know that if the earthly tent we live in is dismantled, we have a building from God, an eternal house in heaven, not built by human hands. 2 For in this tent we groan, longing to be clothed with our heavenly dwelling, 3 because when we are clothed, we will not be found naked.

4 For while we are in this tent, we groan under our burdens, because we do not wish to be unclothed but clothed, so that our mortality may be swallowed up by life. 5 And it is God who has prepared us for this very purpose and has given us the Spirit as a pledge of what is to come.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul continues the contrast between present decline and lasting glory. He pictures present bodily life as an earthly tent that can be dismantled, then speaks of a lasting dwelling from God, not built by human hands.

He adds the image of being clothed. The longing is not simply to shed the body and remain naked, but for mortality to be swallowed up by life. His hope reaches toward the life God gives beyond the weakness and burdens of the present.

God has prepared His people for this purpose and has given the Spirit as a pledge. Paul has used that image already in 2 Corinthians 1:21–22: the gift received now assures them of what is still to come.

The images give grounds for hope, but they should not be pressed into a detailed account of the materials of a future body or every step between death and resurrection. Paul’s concern is God’s promised life overcoming mortality.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly connect the tent, clothing and lasting dwelling with the promised life God gives beyond death. Wesley’s notes on verses 1–5 and the USCCB notes on verses 1–5 both emphasize bodily resurrection rather than a final existence without a body. They discuss details of the clothing image differently, but the longing for mortality to be overcome remains central.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Corinthians 15:50–54 explicitly describes the necessary transformation: what is mortal must be clothed with immortality, and death is swallowed up in victory.

That connection places Paul’s longing within the resurrection Christ promises His people. God’s purpose goes beyond helping them tolerate a failing body; it includes life in which mortality no longer has the final word. The Spirit’s present gift supports waiting for that completion.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 5:6-8
passages.section_title: How can Paul face death with confidence?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 Therefore we are always confident, although we know that while we are at home in the body, we are away from the Lord. 7 For we walk by faith, not by sight. 8 We are confident, then, and would prefer to be away from the body and at home with the Lord.
paragraphs: 6 Therefore we are always confident, although we know that while we are at home in the body, we are away from the Lord. 7 For we walk by faith, not by sight. 8 We are confident, then, and would prefer to be away from the body and at home with the Lord.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Because God has prepared His people for life and given the Spirit, Paul speaks with confidence. Present bodily life is described as being away from the Lord, and he would prefer to be away from the body and at home with Him.

The statement about walking by faith rather than sight belongs within that contrast. The Lord’s presence and the promised future are trusted before they are seen. Paul is not presenting faith as a reason to reject every form of observation or evidence.

His desire centers on being with the Lord. It gives the paragraph its hope without making present life worthless. The following verses describe the continuing ambition to please Him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The Reformed Westminster Confession 32.1–2 teaches that the righteous are consciously with God after death while awaiting bodily resurrection. Wesley’s note on verse 8 similarly understands being with the Lord as happiness that begins before resurrection.

Seventh-day Adventists teach a different account of the time between death and resurrection. Their official Belief 26 describes death as an unconscious state until Christ returns and the righteous are raised to meet Him. That should not be caricatured as denying resurrection or saying death permanently ends the believer’s hope.

The difference concerns what happens while resurrection is awaited. Both accounts look toward life with the Lord, but they should not be presented as the same explanation of the interval.
passages.god_plan_html:
Philippians 1:21–24 expresses the same desire to depart and be with Christ while recognizing the fruitful service still possible in bodily life. Paul holds both concerns together.

The future God promises is personal fellowship with Christ, and the present remains a place to serve others because of Him. Hope beyond death supports faithfulness here rather than making care for the people still around us pointless.
passages.current_position_html: In Should We Seek Signs From God?, we draw on verse 7 to describe trust in what God has revealed without needing repeated physical confirmations to keep that trust standing. Here that principle sits within Paul’s confidence about being with the Lord before he sees the promised future. The study does not establish our position on every detail of the time between death and resurrection.

deeper_study.title: Should We Seek Signs From God?

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 5:7
passages.section_title: What does it mean to walk by faith rather than sight?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 For we walk by faith, not by sight.
paragraphs: 7 For we walk by faith, not by sight.

passages.context_html:
This brief verse belongs inside 2 Corinthians 5:6–8. Paul contrasts present bodily life with being at home with the Lord and explains the confidence with which he awaits what he does not yet see.

Walking describes the way he lives in that interval. His confidence rests on the Lord and His promise, while the fullness of being with Him is still ahead. Read in its setting, the verse is about living by that trust rather than seeing the promised future already completed.

The wider application to trusting God matters, but it should not replace that immediate setting or turn faith into a rejection of careful thought and evidence.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the verse as present trust in the Lord before the fullness of the promised life is seen. Wesley’s note on verse 7 and the USCCB note on verses 6–9 both place it within the contrast between present life and being with Him.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Should We Seek Signs From God? applies this verse to faith that trusts what God has revealed without requiring a stream of new physical confirmations. We connect it with Jesus’ words to Thomas in John 20:27–29. Paul’s immediate setting remains the confidence of awaiting life with the Lord; the application does not remove that context.

deeper_study.title: Should We Seek Signs From God?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
In John 20:24–31, the risen Jesus meets Thomas and blesses those who have not seen and yet have believed. John then explains that the signs recorded in his Gospel are written so readers may believe and have life in Jesus’ name.

This is a connection between trusting Christ without personally seeing Him and receiving the witness God has provided. It does not make faith belief without any basis: the written testimony points readers toward the same living Lord.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 5:9-10
passages.section_title: Why does our present conduct matter if we hope to be with Christ?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 So we aspire to please Him, whether we are at home in this body or away from it. 10 For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, that each one may receive his due for the things done in the body, whether good or bad.
paragraphs: 9 So we aspire to please Him, whether we are at home in this body or away from it. 10 For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, that each one may receive his due for the things done in the body, whether good or bad.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul moves from his desire to be with the Lord to the ambition that governs his life: to please Him. Whether at home in the body or away from it, the relationship to Christ remains central.

He gives a reason for taking conduct seriously. All must appear before Christ’s judgment seat and receive their due for what was done in the body, whether good or bad. The workers who teach others are included in that accountability.

The paragraph states the reality of judgment without providing a numerical system for calculating rewards or an exact timetable of all future judgments. Hope in Christ does not make the way people live now irrelevant.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians affirm accountability to Christ, but differ over how this judgment fits within the larger account. The Catholic Catechism 1021–1022 teaches a judgment at death relating each life to Christ, including entrance into heaven immediately or through purification. Its paragraphs 1038–1040 also distinguish the final judgment following resurrection.

The Reformed Westminster Confession 33.1–2 places all people’s account of thoughts, words and deeds within the day Christ judges the world. Dallas Theological Seminary’s Article XVI instead emphasizes believers’ rewards for faithful service at Christ’s judgment seat after He receives His people, distinguishing those rewards from salvation. Article XXI separately describes unbelievers’ final judgment.

These are distinct accounts of timing and purpose. They share the conviction that Christ’s judgment gives present conduct lasting significance, rather than making it a matter no one will answer for.
passages.god_plan_html:
John 5:22–29 explicitly places judgment in the Son’s hands and joins His authority with the coming resurrection. Those who hear His voice are called from their tombs.

Paul’s concern therefore belongs within God’s purpose carried out through His Son, who gives life and judges. The future includes being brought before Christ; the person whose presence believers desire is also the one whose approval they seek.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 5:11-15
passages.section_title: What moves Paul to keep persuading people?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 Therefore, since we know what it means to fear the Lord, we try to persuade men. What we are is clear to God, and I hope it is clear to your conscience as well. 12 We are not commending ourselves to you again. Instead, we are giving you an occasion to be proud of us, so that you can answer those who take pride in appearances rather than in the heart. 13 If we are out of our mind, it is for God; if we are of sound mind, it is for you. 14 For Christ’s love compels us, because we are convinced that One died for all, therefore all died. 15 And He died for all, that those who live should no longer live for themselves, but for Him who died for them and was raised again.
paragraphs: 11 Therefore, since we know what it means to fear the Lord, we try to persuade men. What we are is clear to God, and I hope it is clear to your conscience as well. 12 We are not commending ourselves to you again. Instead, we are giving you an occasion to be proud of us, so that you can answer those who take pride in appearances rather than in the heart. 13 If we are out of our mind, it is for God; if we are of sound mind, it is for you.
