14 For Christ’s love compels us, because we are convinced that One died for all, therefore all died. 15 And He died for all, that those who live should no longer live for themselves, but for Him who died for them and was raised again.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul follows the statement about Christ’s judgment seat with his awareness of the fear of the Lord. He therefore seeks to persuade people. God knows what he is, and he hopes the Corinthians recognize his sincerity too.

He is not simply recommending himself again. He wants them to be able to answer people who take pride in appearances rather than the heart. Whether his conduct seems excessive or measured, he describes its purpose in relation to God and the people he serves.

The controlling reason is Christ’s love, made known in His death. One died for all, and Paul sees that death as involving those for whom He died. The stated purpose is a changed life: those who live should live for the one who died for them and was raised.

Persuasion is therefore part of Paul’s work, but personal prestige is not its goal. Reverence for the Lord and the love shown in Christ move him toward service.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand Christ’s death and resurrection as the ground of the changed life Paul describes. They differ in their wider accounts of the extent and effect of His saving work.

The Catholic Catechism 605 teaches that Christ died for every person without exception. John Wesley’s note on verse 15 likewise reads His death for all as intended for all to be saved. The Reformed Westminster Confession 3.6 instead describes redemption and its saving application as belonging to those God has chosen to save. That confession gives a wider doctrinal account, rather than a detailed commentary on this particular sentence.

These differences should not obscure Paul’s express aim here: the life given through Christ is to be lived for Him, rather than for ourselves. The paragraph does not say that everyone is automatically saved regardless of their response.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 6:3–11 explicitly connects belonging to Christ with His death and resurrection and with walking in newness of life. Those joined to Him are called to regard themselves as dead to sin and alive to God.

That connection places the changed direction of life within Christ’s saving work. God’s purpose is not simply to pardon people while leaving their allegiance untouched. The one who died and rose becomes the center of the life He gives.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 5:16-17
passages.section_title: How does being in Christ change the way we see people?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 So from now on we regard no one according to the flesh. Although we once regarded Christ in this way, we do so no longer. 17 Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away. Behold, the new has come!
paragraphs: 16 So from now on we regard no one according to the flesh. Although we once regarded Christ in this way, we do so no longer. 17 Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away. Behold, the new has come!

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Because Christ’s death and resurrection change the direction of life, Paul also describes a changed way of regarding people. He no longer judges them according to the flesh. The surrounding contrast with outward appearances helps explain the point: ordinary measures of status are not the final measure of a person in Christ.

He includes his former way of regarding Christ in that change of perspective. This does not mean Christ’s bodily life ceased to matter. Paul has just grounded the new life in His real death and resurrection.

Anyone in Christ is a new creation. The old has passed away and the new has come. Paul places that newness in belonging to Christ, rather than merely adopting an improved public image.

The declaration gives a basis for a changed life, not a claim that believers instantly have no struggle or that their whole past must be denied. The next verses identify God as the source of this reconciling work.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the new creation as a real change through belonging to Christ, affecting both life and the way others are seen. Wesley’s notes on verses 16–17 emphasize a new outlook and pattern of life. The USCCB note on verses 16–17 likewise relates the new way of seeing to Christ’s death and the new order He brings.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 2:10–18 describes people created in Christ for good works and Jews and Gentiles brought near through His blood. Christ makes peace, reconciling them to God in one body.

That gives new creation a shared dimension as well as a personal one. God’s work in Christ forms a people whose life and relationships are changed. Old measures of distance and standing cannot be the last word where He has brought people near.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 5:18-21
passages.section_title: What does it mean to be reconciled to God through Christ?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 All this is from God, who reconciled us to Himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation: 19 that God was reconciling the world to Himself in Christ, not counting men’s trespasses against them. And He has committed to us the message of reconciliation. 20 Therefore we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were making His appeal through us. We implore you on behalf of Christ: Be reconciled to God. 21 God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.
paragraphs: 18 All this is from God, who reconciled us to Himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation: 19 that God was reconciling the world to Himself in Christ, not counting men’s trespasses against them. And He has committed to us the message of reconciliation.

20 Therefore we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were making His appeal through us. We implore you on behalf of Christ: Be reconciled to God. 21 God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul identifies God as the source of the new life he has described. Reconciliation means a broken relationship being put right: God has brought them to Himself through Christ and entrusted them with that message for others.

The message concerns God’s work in Christ, not counting people’s trespasses against them. Paul and his companions serve as ambassadors, carrying an appeal on Christ’s behalf. They do not present themselves as the source of forgiveness.

The appeal is direct: be reconciled to God. Paul’s description of God’s initiative leads to a call to respond, rather than a declaration that no response matters.

The final verse holds Christ’s innocence and His work for others together. The one who knew no sin is made to be sin on their behalf, so that in Him they might become God’s righteousness. The BSB also notes sin offering as an alternative rendering. The verse does not describe Jesus committing sin.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand reconciliation as God’s saving work through the sinless Christ, but explain becoming God’s righteousness in different ways.

The Reformed Westminster Confession 11.1–2 describes God forgiving sins and counting believers righteous because of Christ’s obedience, received through faith. It distinguishes that acceptance from inward change while insisting that the faith receiving it is accompanied by love. The Catholic Catechism 1989–1991 includes forgiveness and inward renewal together in its account of being made right with God.

Wesley’s note on verse 21 speaks of Christ as a sin offering and of righteousness both credited and planted within the believer. These readings should be described in their own terms, rather than reduced to a contrast between Christians who value faith and Christians who try to earn salvation.
passages.god_plan_html:
Isaiah 53:4–6 describes the servant bearing others’ sorrows and iniquities, with peace coming through His suffering. 1 Peter 2:22–25 explicitly applies the sinless servant’s suffering to Jesus and says He bore sins so that people might die to sin and live to righteousness.

That explicit New Testament connection places Paul’s reconciliation appeal within God’s saving purpose through the innocent Son. The aim includes people brought back to God and a life turned toward righteousness, grounded in what Christ has done for them.
passages.current_position_html: Our study The Gospel According to Jesus affirms that Christ died for our sins and rose, bringing salvation from sin and the separation it produces as a gift of grace received through faith. That established gospel core supports the reconciliation announced here. The study does not settle every explanation of becoming God’s righteousness or the precise meaning of Christ being made sin in verse 21.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 6:1-2
passages.section_title: Why does Paul say the time to respond is now?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 As God’s fellow workers, then, we urge you not to receive God’s grace in vain. 2 For He says: “In the time of favor I heard you, and in the day of salvation I helped you.” Behold, now is the time of favor; now is the day of salvation!
paragraphs: 1 As God’s fellow workers, then, we urge you not to receive God’s grace in vain. 2 For He says: “In the time of favor I heard you, and in the day of salvation I helped you.” Behold, now is the time of favor; now is the day of salvation!

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul continues the appeal to be reconciled to God. As God’s fellow workers, he and his companions urge the Corinthians not to receive His grace in vain: the gift is to meet a real response, rather than leave life untouched.

He supports the appeal with Isaiah 49:8, where God speaks of hearing and helping in a time of favor and a day of salvation. Paul brings that promise into the present urgency of the message: now is the time of favor and salvation.

The warning calls for a response to God, not simply admiration of the message or confidence in having heard it before. The following account of the workers’ lives shows the seriousness with which they carry that appeal.

Paul does not give a date for the end of the world or explain every reader’s standing before God. His point is that God’s present offer should not be set aside for an imagined better moment.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as an urgent call for God’s grace to bear fruit in the life of those receiving it. Wesley’s note on verse 1 connects receiving grace by faith with persevering holiness. The USCCB notes on verses 1–2 likewise connect the appeal with living in keeping with the gift of new creation and reconciliation.
passages.god_plan_html:
The promise Paul quotes belongs to Isaiah 49:5–13, where the servant’s work includes restoring Israel and bringing God’s salvation to the ends of the earth. God’s care reaches prisoners, people in darkness and His afflicted people.

In Acts 13:46–48, Paul and Barnabas explicitly apply the same chapter’s light-to-the-nations promise to their gospel mission. The appeal here belongs within that outward reach of God’s salvation. Now is a summons to receive what God is making known, rather than merely a demand to become busier.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 6:3-10
passages.section_title: What does faithful service look like under pressure?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 3 We put no obstacle in anyone’s way, so that no one can discredit our ministry. 4 Rather, as servants of God we commend ourselves in every way: in great endurance; in troubles, hardships, and calamities; 5 in beatings, imprisonments, and riots; in labor, sleepless nights, and hunger; 6 in purity, knowledge, patience, and kindness; in the Holy Spirit and in sincere love; 7 in truthful speech and in the power of God; with the weapons of righteousness in the right hand and in the left; 8 through glory and dishonor, slander and praise; viewed as imposters, yet genuine; 9 unknown, yet well-known; dying, and yet we live on; punished, yet not killed; 10 sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; poor, yet making many rich; having nothing, and yet possessing everything.
paragraphs: 3 We put no obstacle in anyone’s way, so that no one can discredit our ministry. 4 Rather, as servants of God we commend ourselves in every way: in great endurance; in troubles, hardships, and calamities; 5 in beatings, imprisonments, and riots; in labor, sleepless nights, and hunger;

6 in purity, knowledge, patience, and kindness; in the Holy Spirit and in sincere love; 7 in truthful speech and in the power of God; with the weapons of righteousness in the right hand and in the left;

8 through glory and dishonor, slander and praise; viewed as imposters, yet genuine; 9 unknown, yet well-known; dying, and yet we live on; punished, yet not killed; 10 sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; poor, yet making many rich; having nothing, and yet possessing everything.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul describes how he and his companions carry out the appeal. They seek to put no obstacle in anyone’s way that would discredit the ministry. Their way of serving is meant to support the message rather than undermine it.

The list begins with great endurance. The Greek word is hypomonē (hoo-poh-moh-NAY), ὑπομονή: steady endurance that holds to its purpose through trials; see Thayer’s entry. Paul names troubles, beatings, imprisonment, sleepless nights and hunger. He is describing faithfulness through hardship, not an impressive life free of it.

He also names purity, knowledge, patience, kindness, the Holy Spirit, sincere love and truthful speech. Enduring pain is not his only evidence of service. The character shown within the difficulties matters too.

The closing contrasts distinguish outward impressions from what is true of the workers in God’s service. They can be called imposters while remaining genuine, be sorrowful while rejoicing, and be poor while enriching others. Paul does not admit to fraud or promise that everyone they help will become financially wealthy.

The picture holds costly circumstances and God’s resources together. It gives neither a guarantee that faithful people will avoid suffering nor a rule that suffering by itself proves someone is trustworthy.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as a description of sincere ministry sustained by God through hardship, rather than a claim that outward success proves faithfulness. Wesley’s notes on verses 3–10 and the USCCB notes on verses 3–10 both connect the trials, the workers’ character and the contrast between appearances and their true standing. Rejoicing does not erase the sorrow Paul also acknowledges.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Matthew 5:10–16, Jesus speaks of His disciples facing persecution for His sake and of their good deeds bringing glory to their Father. The people who suffer for belonging to Him are also called to be light in the world.

That connection gives the catalog here its larger purpose. God makes His character and message visible through people whose conduct remains marked by truth, kindness and love under pressure. The aim reaches beyond the worker’s reputation to others seeing reason to glorify the Father.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 6:11-13
passages.section_title: What does Paul mean by asking them to open their hearts?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 We have spoken freely to you, Corinthians. Our hearts are open wide. 12 It is not our affection, but yours, that is restrained. 13 As a fair exchange—I speak as to my children—open wide your hearts also.
paragraphs: 11 We have spoken freely to you, Corinthians. Our hearts are open wide. 12 It is not our affection, but yours, that is restrained. 13 As a fair exchange—I speak as to my children—open wide your hearts also.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After describing his service through hardship, Paul appeals directly to the Corinthians. He has spoken freely, and his heart is open wide toward them. The distance between them is not a withdrawal of his affection.

He asks for an answering openness from them. Speaking as to his children expresses the care of their relationship; compare his explanation of fatherly care in 1 Corinthians 4:14–15. It is not necessary to read the phrase as an insult to their intelligence.

The appeal concerns their relationship with Paul and the love he wants them to return. It should not become a general claim that every painful feeling is wrong or that a leader’s demand for acceptance can never be questioned.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these verses as an affectionate appeal for a renewed relationship. Wesley’s notes on verses 11–13 and the USCCB note on verses 11–13 both emphasize openness and mutual affection. Paul’s account of his ministry leads into a personal invitation rather than simply another claim of status.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 6:14-7:1
passages.section_title: How should belonging to God shape the loyalties we join?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. For what partnership can righteousness have with wickedness? Or what fellowship does light have with darkness? 15 What harmony is there between Christ and Belial? Or what does a believer have in common with an unbeliever? 16 What agreement can exist between the temple of God and idols? For we are the temple of the living God. As God has said: “I will dwell with them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they will be My people.” 17 “Therefore come out from among them and be separate, says the Lord. Touch no unclean thing, and I will receive you.” 18 And: “I will be a Father to you, and you will be My sons and daughters, says the Lord Almighty.” 1 Therefore, beloved, since we have these promises, let us cleanse ourselves from everything that defiles body and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God.
paragraphs: 14 Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. For what partnership can righteousness have with wickedness? Or what fellowship does light have with darkness? 15 What harmony is there between Christ and Belial? Or what does a believer have in common with an unbeliever? 16 What agreement can exist between the temple of God and idols? For we are the temple of the living God. As God has said: “I will dwell with them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they will be My people.”

17 “Therefore come out from among them and be separate, says the Lord. Touch no unclean thing, and I will receive you.” 18 And: “I will be a Father to you, and you will be My sons and daughters, says the Lord Almighty.”
1 Therefore, beloved, since we have these promises, let us cleanse ourselves from everything that defiles body and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul warns against being unequally yoked with unbelievers, then asks a series of questions contrasting righteousness and wickedness, light and darkness, Christ and Belial, and God’s temple and idols. Belial is a name for Satan; see Thayer’s entry. The contrast concerns loyalties that cannot be joined without conflict.

The temple statement addresses the people together: we are the temple of the living God. Paul supports the call with Scripture’s promises of God dwelling among His people, receiving them and being their Father. Leviticus 26:11–13 and Isaiah 52:11–12 help explain the dwelling and separation language.

The thought continues into 7:1. Because they have these promises, the beloved are called to turn from everything that defiles body and spirit and pursue holiness in the fear of God. The aim reaches through the whole person, rather than merely improving an outward image.

This warning should be read alongside Paul’s other instructions. In 1 Corinthians 5:9–13 he does not require withdrawal from all unbelieving people. In 1 Corinthians 7:12–16 he does not tell a believer to leave an unbelieving spouse willing to remain. The present warning cannot simply cancel those instructions.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand this as a call to loyalty to God that excludes participation in idolatry and incompatible allegiances. They differ in how widely they apply the yoke image. Wesley’s note on verse 14 applies it especially to marriage and extends it to other close ties. The USCCB notes on verses 14–18 focus on the incompatibility of Christian allegiance and pagan worship.

Church teaching on marriage also differs. The Reformed Westminster Confession 24.3 requires Christians to marry in the Lord and adds limits based on faith and conduct. Catholic canons 1086 and 1124–1125 distinguish marriage to another baptized Christian from marriage to an unbaptized person. They provide for permission or an exception under stated conditions, including safeguards for Catholic faith and the children’s upbringing.

These applications are not identical. The shared warning is against a joined life that compromises belonging to God; it should not be represented as contempt for unbelievers or a command to end every existing relationship.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ezekiel 37:26–28 promises God’s dwelling among His people in a covenant of peace. The parent-child language also recalls 2 Samuel 7:12–16, where God speaks about David’s promised descendant. Paul brings the promise of being God’s sons and daughters into his appeal to the community.

Revelation 21:3 and 7 explicitly join God dwelling with His people and the promise that He will be their God and the one who overcomes will be His son. The call to holiness here belongs within that hope of shared life with God. Separation from idolatry serves the relationship He promises, rather than being an end in itself.
passages.current_position_html: In What Is the True Church?, we affirm that God dwells in His people and that being His temple carries responsibility for how we live and relate to others. That established position applies to the community Paul calls God’s temple here. The study does not decide every marriage, friendship or business application of the yoke image.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 7:2-4
passages.section_title: Why is Paul still asking them to make room in their hearts?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 2 Make room for us in your hearts. We have wronged no one, we have corrupted no one, we have exploited no one. 3 I do not say this to condemn you. I have said before that you so occupy our hearts that we live and die together with you. 4 Great is my confidence in you; great is my pride in you; I am filled with encouragement; in all our troubles my joy overflows.
paragraphs: 2 Make room for us in your hearts. We have wronged no one, we have corrupted no one, we have exploited no one. 3 I do not say this to condemn you. I have said before that you so occupy our hearts that we live and die together with you. 4 Great is my confidence in you; great is my pride in you; I am filled with encouragement; in all our troubles my joy overflows.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul returns to the personal appeal heard in 2 Corinthians 6:11–13. He asks the Corinthians to make room for him and his companions, saying they have wronged, corrupted and exploited no one.

He immediately explains that he is not speaking to condemn them. They are so firmly held in his heart that he describes their relationship in terms of living and dying together. His defense of the ministry is joined with affection for the people.

Confidence, pride in them, encouragement and overflowing joy now come to the foreground, even while troubles continue. The following account of Titus will explain why Paul can speak this way. Reconciliation is beginning to change the relationship that had caused so much anguish.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these verses as a renewed appeal for trust and affection after conflict. Wesley’s notes on verses 2–4 emphasize Paul’s care and confidence. The USCCB note on verses 2–4 connects the appeal with 6:11–13 and treats its joy and encouragement as a bridge to the account that follows.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 7:5-7
passages.section_title: How did God bring comfort to Paul in Macedonia?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 For when we arrived in Macedonia, our bodies had no rest, but we were pressed from every direction—conflicts on the outside, fears within. 6 But God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the arrival of Titus, 7 and not only by his arrival, but also by the comfort he had received from you. He told us about your longing, your mourning, and your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced all the more.
paragraphs: 5 For when we arrived in Macedonia, our bodies had no rest, but we were pressed from every direction—conflicts on the outside, fears within. 6 But God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the arrival of Titus, 7 and not only by his arrival, but also by the comfort he had received from you. He told us about your longing, your mourning, and your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced all the more.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul resumes the travel account interrupted after 2 Corinthians 2:12–13. Arriving in Macedonia had not brought immediate relief. There were conflicts around him and fears within.

The comfort came through the arrival of Titus. Paul identifies God as the one who comforts the downcast and recognizes His care in this meeting. Titus also brings the comfort he received from the Corinthians themselves.

Their longing, mourning and zeal for Paul have made an impression on Titus, and hearing that report increases Paul’s joy. Comfort travels through the relationship: the congregation refreshes Titus, and his presence and news refresh Paul.

The passage gives a concrete account of God’s care through another person. It does not require a secret sign or deny that a faithful servant can experience fear and discouragement.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the arrival and report of Titus as the way God comforted Paul in this situation. Wesley’s notes on verses 5–7 connect the fears with concern for the church and its response. The USCCB notes on verses 5–7 likewise read the meeting as the resolution of the waiting described in chapter 2.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 12:4–5 and 15 describes believers as members of one body and calls them to rejoice with those who rejoice and weep with those who weep.

The meeting here gives a concrete example of that shared life. God’s purpose includes a people who carry care and encouragement to one another. Paul’s experience shows why another person’s presence and honest news can matter within that work.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 7:8-12
passages.section_title: What kind of sorrow leads to real change?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 Even if I caused you sorrow by my letter, I do not regret it. Although I did regret it—for I see that my letter caused you sorrow, but only for a short time— 9 yet now I rejoice, not because you were made sorrowful, but because your sorrow led you to repentance. For you felt the sorrow that God had intended, and so were not harmed in any way by us. 10 Godly sorrow brings repentance that leads to salvation without regret, but worldly sorrow brings death. 11 Consider what this godly sorrow has produced in you: what earnestness, what eagerness to clear yourselves, what indignation, what alarm, what longing, what zeal, what vindication! In every way you have proved yourselves to be innocent in this matter. 12 So even though I wrote to you, it was not on account of the one who did wrong or the one who was harmed, but rather that your earnestness on our behalf would be made clear to you in the sight of God.
paragraphs: 8 Even if I caused you sorrow by my letter, I do not regret it. Although I did regret it—for I see that my letter caused you sorrow, but only for a short time— 9 yet now I rejoice, not because you were made sorrowful, but because your sorrow led you to repentance. For you felt the sorrow that God had intended, and so were not harmed in any way by us. 10 Godly sorrow brings repentance that leads to salvation without regret, but worldly sorrow brings death.

11 Consider what this godly sorrow has produced in you: what earnestness, what eagerness to clear yourselves, what indignation, what alarm, what longing, what zeal, what vindication! In every way you have proved yourselves to be innocent in this matter. 12 So even though I wrote to you, it was not on account of the one who did wrong or the one who was harmed, but rather that your earnestness on our behalf would be made clear to you in the sight of God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul looks back on the painful letter and its effect. He had felt regret over the sorrow it caused, but he now rejoices in what followed. Causing pain was not the success he sought; the sorrow led the Corinthians to repentance.

The word translated repentance is metanoia (meh-TAH-noy-ah), μετάνοια. It describes a change of mind and course of life in response to wrong, rather than regret alone; see Thayer’s entry. The following list shows the change taking practical shape.

Paul distinguishes godly sorrow, leading toward repentance and salvation, from worldly sorrow that brings death. The difference is not simply who cries more or how intensely someone feels. He points to the direction and fruit of the response.

The Corinthians have shown earnestness, concern to put matters right, alarm, longing and zeal. Their response has cleared them in this matter. Paul is not claiming they have become incapable of any further sin.

He says his purpose reached beyond the individual who did wrong and the one harmed: their earnestness on his behalf was to become clear before God. The account concerns a congregation’s response to a real breach, not an unlimited permission for leaders to wound people and call the hurt beneficial.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the distinction as sorrow that turns people toward God and a changed life, rather than sorrow that remains trapped in the wrong direction. Wesley’s notes on verses 10–12 emphasize the response’s practical seriousness. The USCCB note on verses 8–12 places the change within the restoration of the relationship.

The offender’s identity is not settled here. Wesley connects the passage with the man in 1 Corinthians 5 and his father, but Paul does not name them. The positive lesson about repentance does not depend on treating that identification as certain.
passages.god_plan_html:
A related picture appears in Luke 15:17–24. The son recognizes his wrong, returns to his father and is welcomed with joy. This is a parallel in turning and restoration, not a claim that Paul is identifying the Corinthians with every detail of the parable.

Both passages place the changed response within a movement toward restored relationship. God’s saving purpose reaches beyond leaving people ashamed: turning from wrong opens toward the life and fellowship He gives.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 7:13-16
passages.section_title: How did the Corinthians restore confidence and joy?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 On account of this, we are encouraged. In addition to our own encouragement, we were even more delighted by the joy of Titus. For his spirit has been refreshed by all of you. 14 Indeed, I was not embarrassed by anything I had boasted to him about you. But just as everything we said to you was true, so our boasting to Titus has proved to be true as well. 15 And his affection for you is even greater when he remembers that you were all obedient as you welcomed him with fear and trembling. 16 I rejoice that I can have complete confidence in you.
paragraphs: 13 On account of this, we are encouraged. In addition to our own encouragement, we were even more delighted by the joy of Titus. For his spirit has been refreshed by all of you. 14 Indeed, I was not embarrassed by anything I had boasted to him about you. But just as everything we said to you was true, so our boasting to Titus has proved to be true as well. 15 And his affection for you is even greater when he remembers that you were all obedient as you welcomed him with fear and trembling. 16 I rejoice that I can have complete confidence in you.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul describes the effect of the Corinthians’ response on Titus and on himself. Their own encouragement is increased by seeing Titus’s joy, because his spirit has been refreshed by them.

Paul had spoken confidently about them to Titus. Their response has shown that confidence to be well placed, rather than leaving him embarrassed by an empty boast. Truth in what he said and truth in their response now belong together.

Titus remembers their welcome and obedience, expressed with fear and trembling, and his affection for them grows. The phrase communicates the seriousness of their reception; the passage does not present terror of a messenger as the goal of Christian fellowship.

The section ends with Paul rejoicing in renewed confidence. It is the fruit of a changed relationship after a painful episode, rather than a promise that every conflict will end immediately or that people can predict another person’s choices infallibly.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as joy over a relationship restored and confidence confirmed by the congregation’s response. The USCCB note on verses 13–16 draws together the encouragement, love and relief experienced by Titus and Paul. Their shared joy is the closing note of this account.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 8:1-5
passages.section_title: What made the Macedonian churches so eager to help?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now, brothers, we want you to know about the grace that God has given the churches of Macedonia. 2 In the terrible ordeal they suffered, their abundant joy and deep poverty overflowed into rich generosity. 3 For I testify that they gave according to their ability and even beyond it. Of their own accord, 4 they earnestly pleaded with us for the privilege of sharing in this service to the saints. 5 And not only did they do as we expected, but they gave themselves first to the Lord and then to us, through the will of God.
paragraphs: 1 Now, brothers, we want you to know about the grace that God has given the churches of Macedonia. 2 In the terrible ordeal they suffered, their abundant joy and deep poverty overflowed into rich generosity. 3 For I testify that they gave according to their ability and even beyond it. Of their own accord,

4 they earnestly pleaded with us for the privilege of sharing in this service to the saints. 5 And not only did they do as we expected, but they gave themselves first to the Lord and then to us, through the will of God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul turns from the restored relationship with Corinth to the collection for believers in need. 1 Corinthians 16:1–4 and Romans 15:25–27 identify the wider undertaking as help for the saints in Jerusalem. Here he begins with the example of the churches in Macedonia.

They were experiencing a terrible ordeal and deep poverty. Yet their abundant joy overflowed into rich generosity. Paul introduces their response as evidence of grace God has given them, so the story begins with His work among them.

Their contribution was willing. They gave according to their ability and beyond it, eagerly asking for the privilege of sharing in this service. Paul reports their extraordinary response without naming an amount or assigning everyone the same percentage.

Their giving grew out of giving themselves first to the Lord and then to the workers, through God’s will. The material gift expressed a deeper commitment to Him and to the good of His people.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as willing generosity flowing from God’s grace and a wholehearted commitment to Him. Wesley’s notes on verses 1–5 and the USCCB notes on verses 1–5 both emphasize the Macedonians’ eagerness and the giving of themselves. Their poverty and joy are both real parts of the account.
passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 4:32–35 describes the early Jerusalem believers sharing resources so that people’s needs were met. The collection here carries that care across the distance between congregations.

Romans 15:26–27 also explains the connection between Gentile believers and the Jewish believers they are helping. God’s work of bringing people together in Christ takes practical form when those who share spiritual blessings also share material help.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 8:6-9
passages.section_title: How does Christ’s generosity shape our own?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 So we urged Titus to help complete your act of grace, just as he had started it. 7 But just as you excel in everything—in faith, in speech, in knowledge, in complete earnestness, and in the love we inspired in you —see that you also excel in this grace of giving. 8 I am not giving a command, but I am testing the sincerity of your love through the earnestness of others. 9 For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though He was rich, yet for your sake He became poor, so that you through His poverty might become rich.
paragraphs: 6 So we urged Titus to help complete your act of grace, just as he had started it. 7 But just as you excel in everything—in faith, in speech, in knowledge, in complete earnestness, and in the love we inspired in you —see that you also excel in this grace of giving. 8 I am not giving a command, but I am testing the sincerity of your love through the earnestness of others.
9 For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though He was rich, yet for your sake He became poor, so that you through His poverty might become rich.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul asks Titus to help the Corinthians complete the work he had begun among them. Their faith, speech, knowledge, earnestness and love are to find expression in this grace of giving as well.

He explains his appeal as a test of sincere love, drawing on the earnestness of others. He expressly says he is not giving a command here. The question is whether the care they profess will take practical shape in a willing response.

The example at the center is the Lord Jesus Christ. Though rich, He became poor for their sake so that they might become rich through His poverty. His self-giving supplies the measure of generosity Paul wants them to consider.

The paragraph connects helping others with what believers have received through Christ. Completing the gift becomes an expression of love rooted in His grace.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read Christ’s riches and poverty as a picture of His saving self-giving and the riches His people receive through Him. Wesley’s note on verse 9 connects His poverty with becoming human, His life and His death, and the resulting riches with God’s favor and likeness. The USCCB note on verse 9 likewise places the contrast within Jesus’ saving work.
passages.god_plan_html:
Philippians 2:5–11 describes Christ taking the form of a servant, humbling Himself to death on a cross, and being exalted as Lord. Paul calls believers to share the mind seen in Him.

That explicit connection shows why Christ’s self-giving belongs in a discussion of a collection. God’s saving purpose through His Son shapes the kind of people He is forming: people whose care for others reflects the Lord from whom they have received life.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 8:10-15
passages.section_title: How can willing generosity become practical help?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 And this is my opinion about what is helpful for you in this matter: Last year you were the first not only to give, but even to have such a desire. 11 Now finish the work, so that you may complete it with the same eager desire, according to your means. 12 For if the eagerness is there, the gift is acceptable according to what one has, not according to what he does not have. 13 It is not our intention that others may be relieved while you are burdened, but that there may be equality. 14 At the present time, your surplus will meet their need, so that in turn their surplus will meet your need. This way there will be equality. 15 As it is written: “He who gathered much had no excess, and he who gathered little had no shortfall.”
paragraphs: 10 And this is my opinion about what is helpful for you in this matter: Last year you were the first not only to give, but even to have such a desire. 11 Now finish the work, so that you may complete it with the same eager desire, according to your means. 12 For if the eagerness is there, the gift is acceptable according to what one has, not according to what he does not have.

13 It is not our intention that others may be relieved while you are burdened, but that there may be equality. 14 At the present time, your surplus will meet their need, so that in turn their surplus will meet your need. This way there will be equality. 15 As it is written: “He who gathered much had no excess, and he who gathered little had no shortfall.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Corinthians had begun the collection and wanted to take part a year earlier. Paul now urges them to bring that willingness to completion. His advice concerns a gift already begun, within the wider collection for believers in Jerusalem described in 1 Corinthians 16:1–4.

The amount is to reflect their means. A willing gift is acceptable according to what a person has. Paul gives no fixed sum or percentage here, and he explicitly says the purpose is not to relieve others while burdening the Corinthians.

Their present surplus can meet someone else’s need. Another time, help may travel the other way. Paul pictures believers sharing responsibility for one another as circumstances change, with enough for people’s needs as the goal.

To explain that goal, he quotes Exodus 16:18. When Israel gathered manna in the wilderness, those who gathered more and those who gathered less each had enough to eat.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a call to complete a willing gift within one’s means and share resources so that others have enough. Wesley’s notes on verses 12–15 and the USCCB note on verses 12–15 both connect the giving with meeting need; the latter stresses that the aim is sharing rather than impoverishing the giver.
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul himself carries the story of God feeding Israel into the life of these churches. In Exodus 16:1–18, God gives bread to people who have come out of slavery and are learning to depend on Him in the wilderness.

Here, that picture of provision guides people who have resources they can share. God’s care for His people takes practical shape through their care for each other. The connection reaches across the two settings while preserving their difference: Israel gathered manna, and the Corinthians are preparing a collection.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 8:16-24
passages.section_title: Why send trusted people to handle the gift?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 But thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus the same devotion I have for you. 17 For not only did he welcome our appeal, but he is eagerly coming to you of his own volition. 18 Along with Titus we are sending the brother who is praised by all the churches for his work in the gospel. 19 More than that, this brother was chosen by the churches to accompany us with the gracious offering we administer to honor the Lord Himself and to show our eagerness to help. 20 We want to avoid any criticism of the way we administer this generous gift. 21 For we are taking great care to do what is right, not only in the eyes of the Lord, but also in the eyes of men. 22 And we are sending along with them our brother who has proven his earnestness to us many times and in many ways, and now even more so by his great confidence in you. 23 As for Titus, he is my partner and fellow worker among you. As for our brothers, they are messengers of the churches, the glory of Christ. 24 In full view of the churches, then, show these men the proof of your love and the reason for our boasting about you.
paragraphs: 16 But thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus the same devotion I have for you. 17 For not only did he welcome our appeal, but he is eagerly coming to you of his own volition. 18 Along with Titus we are sending the brother who is praised by all the churches for his work in the gospel. 19 More than that, this brother was chosen by the churches to accompany us with the gracious offering we administer to honor the Lord Himself and to show our eagerness to help.

20 We want to avoid any criticism of the way we administer this generous gift. 21 For we are taking great care to do what is right, not only in the eyes of the Lord, but also in the eyes of men. 22 And we are sending along with them our brother who has proven his earnestness to us many times and in many ways, and now even more so by his great confidence in you.

23 As for Titus, he is my partner and fellow worker among you. As for our brothers, they are messengers of the churches, the glory of Christ. 24 In full view of the churches, then, show these men the proof of your love and the reason for our boasting about you.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul introduces the people being sent to help with the collection. He thanks God for Titus’s devotion to the Corinthians and also describes Titus as eager to go of his own accord. God’s work in Titus and Titus’s willing response appear together in the account.

One companion is respected among the churches for his work in the gospel and has been chosen by them to travel with the gift. Another has repeatedly proved diligent and now has great confidence in the Corinthians. Paul leaves both men unnamed.

These arrangements serve a clear purpose: protecting the administration of a generous gift from criticism. Paul wants their conduct to be right before God and visibly honorable to other people. Trusted companions and the churches’ involvement give practical form to that concern.

Titus is Paul’s partner and fellow worker; the other brothers represent the churches. Paul asks the Corinthians to welcome this team with a response that shows their love and confirms his confidence in them. 1 Corinthians 16:3–4 likewise gives the Corinthians a role in approving people to carry their gift.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as responsible handling of a church collection, with trusted representatives and conduct others can examine. The USCCB notes on verses 16–24 emphasize the workers’ character and authority as church messengers; Wesley’s notes on verses 19 and 23–24 likewise describe their appointment and service. The passage gives the two brothers’ qualifications without supplying their names.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 9:1-5
passages.section_title: Why prepare a promised gift ahead of time?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now about the service to the saints, there is no need for me to write to you. 2 For I know your eagerness to help, and I have been boasting to the Macedonians that since last year you in Achaia were prepared to give. And your zeal has stirred most of them to do likewise. 3 But I am sending the brothers in order that our boasting about you in this matter should not prove empty, but that you will be prepared, just as I said. 4 Otherwise, if any Macedonians come with me and find you unprepared, we—to say nothing of you—would be ashamed of having been so confident. 5 So I thought it necessary to urge the brothers to visit you beforehand and make arrangements for the generous gift you had promised. This way, your gift will be prepared generously and not begrudgingly.
paragraphs: 1 Now about the service to the saints, there is no need for me to write to you. 2 For I know your eagerness to help, and I have been boasting to the Macedonians that since last year you in Achaia were prepared to give. And your zeal has stirred most of them to do likewise.

3 But I am sending the brothers in order that our boasting about you in this matter should not prove empty, but that you will be prepared, just as I said. 4 Otherwise, if any Macedonians come with me and find you unprepared, we—to say nothing of you—would be ashamed of having been so confident. 5 So I thought it necessary to urge the brothers to visit you beforehand and make arrangements for the generous gift you had promised. This way, your gift will be prepared generously and not begrudgingly.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul continues the collection discussion from chapter 8. He knows the Corinthians’ eagerness and has told the Macedonians that the believers in Achaia were ready to give a year earlier. Their enthusiasm has encouraged others to act.

Now he is sending the brothers ahead to help turn that eagerness into a prepared gift. He wants the confidence he has expressed in them to be supported by what actually happens. An unprepared collection would bring embarrassment if Macedonians arrived with him.

Paul explains why the advance visit matters: the generous gift they promised should be ready as a willing contribution. Preparing it beforehand gives their generosity room to take practical shape instead of becoming a reluctant response at the last moment.

The paragraph joins confidence in their goodwill with concrete arrangements. Paul both recognizes their desire to help and takes steps so they can follow through.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as preparation for a promised collection, with willing generosity as the goal. Wesley’s notes on verses 1–5 connect the brothers’ advance visit with the earlier promise and distinguish the gift from money extracted through persistent pressure.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 9:6-11
passages.section_title: What kind of harvest does generous giving produce?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 Remember this: Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows generously will also reap generously. 7 Each one should give what he has decided in his heart to give, not out of regret or compulsion. For God loves a cheerful giver. 8 And God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that in all things, at all times, having all that you need, you will abound in every good work. 9 As it is written: “He has scattered abroad His gifts to the poor; His righteousness endures forever.” 10 Now He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your store of seed and will increase the harvest of your righteousness. 11 You will be enriched in every way to be generous on every occasion, and through us your generosity will produce thanksgiving to God.
paragraphs: 6 Remember this: Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows generously will also reap generously. 7 Each one should give what he has decided in his heart to give, not out of regret or compulsion. For God loves a cheerful giver. 8 And God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that in all things, at all times, having all that you need, you will abound in every good work.

9 As it is written: “He has scattered abroad His gifts to the poor; His righteousness endures forever.” 10 Now He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your store of seed and will increase the harvest of your righteousness. 11 You will be enriched in every way to be generous on every occasion, and through us your generosity will produce thanksgiving to God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul uses sowing and harvesting to explain generosity. A person who sows sparingly reaps sparingly; a person who sows generously reaps generously. He immediately joins that picture to the giver’s own decision: each person should give what they have decided in their heart, freely and cheerfully.

The Greek word translated cheerful is ἱλαρός, hilaros (hi-lah-ROS). Thayer’s lexicon describes someone joyful and ready to act. Here it points to willing gladness in giving. Paul has already encouraged preparing the gift, so cheerfulness can accompany a thoughtful decision.

His confidence rests in God’s ability to supply what His people need so they can abound in good work. Paul quotes Psalm 112:9, where generosity to the poor belongs to a life that fears and trusts the Lord.

God supplies both seed for sowing and bread for food. Paul expects His provision to increase the harvest of righteousness and enable further generosity. The passage names the purpose of being enriched: having more to share, with thanksgiving to God flowing from the help received.

The picture includes real provision and real needs. Its direction is outward, toward the good that generosity makes possible. Paul describes that harvest in terms of righteous living, continued giving and gratitude to God.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand God’s provision here as enabling generous service. Wesley’s notes on verses 6–11 emphasize opportunities to help and the good effects of love for God and others. The USCCB note on verses 8–10 similarly connects God’s generosity with meeting needs and growth in righteousness.
passages.god_plan_html:
The seed and bread language recalls Isaiah 55:10–11. There, God describes rain bringing growth and food as a picture of His word accomplishing His purpose. The shared language forms a biblical parallel: God is the One who supplies life and fruitfulness.

The connection places the collection within a larger pattern: God gives, and His gifts bear fruit through His people. The harvest described here includes righteous action and thanksgiving, as the resources He provides become help for others.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 9:12-15
passages.section_title: How can practical help lead people to thank God?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 For this ministry of service is not only supplying the needs of the saints but is also overflowing in many expressions of thanksgiving to God. 13 Because of the proof this ministry provides, the saints will glorify God for your obedient confession of the gospel of Christ, and for the generosity of your contribution to them and to all the others. 14 And their prayers for you will express their affection for you, because of the surpassing grace God has given you. 15 Thanks be to God for His indescribable gift!
paragraphs: 12 For this ministry of service is not only supplying the needs of the saints but is also overflowing in many expressions of thanksgiving to God. 13 Because of the proof this ministry provides, the saints will glorify God for your obedient confession of the gospel of Christ, and for the generosity of your contribution to them and to all the others. 14 And their prayers for you will express their affection for you, because of the surpassing grace God has given you.
15 Thanks be to God for His indescribable gift!

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul describes what the collection will accomplish. It supplies the saints’ needs and also leads to many expressions of thanksgiving to God. The material help and the response of worship belong together.

Those receiving the gift will see evidence that the Corinthians’ confession of the gospel is shaping their conduct. Their generosity becomes a visible expression of obedience to Christ and care for other people.

The relationship grows in both directions. The recipients will pray for the Corinthians and feel affection for them because of God’s grace at work among them. The gift does more than move resources: it strengthens the bond between believers.

Paul ends by thanking God for His indescribable gift. The final praise gathers up the whole account, which began with grace given by God and has led to willing service, needs met, prayer and thanksgiving.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly see this as generosity producing thanksgiving and closer fellowship. Wesley’s notes on verses 11–15 and the USCCB note on verses 11–15 both follow the movement from God’s gifts, through service to others, back to praise directed to Him.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 15:25–27 identifies the collection as help for poor believers in Jerusalem and describes Gentile believers sharing material resources after receiving spiritual blessings. That gives these prayers and expressions of affection a wider setting: the gift strengthens ties across communities.

Ephesians 2:14–18 describes Christ bringing Jews and Gentiles near to God in one body. The collection does not create that unity; it gives an everyday expression to it as people help one another and thank their shared Father.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 10:1-6
passages.section_title: What does it mean to take every thought captive?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now by the mildness and gentleness of Christ, I appeal to you—I, Paul, who am humble when face to face with you, but bold when away. 2 I beg you that when I come I may not need to be as bold as I expect toward those who presume that we live according to the flesh. 3 For though we live in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh. 4 The weapons of our warfare are not the weapons of the flesh. Instead, they have divine power to demolish strongholds. 5 We demolish arguments and every presumption set up against the knowledge of God; and we take captive every thought to make it obedient to Christ. 6 And we will be ready to punish every act of disobedience, as soon as your obedience is complete.
paragraphs: 1 Now by the mildness and gentleness of Christ, I appeal to you—I, Paul, who am humble when face to face with you, but bold when away. 2 I beg you that when I come I may not need to be as bold as I expect toward those who presume that we live according to the flesh.

3 For though we live in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh. 4 The weapons of our warfare are not the weapons of the flesh. Instead, they have divine power to demolish strongholds. 5 We demolish arguments and every presumption set up against the knowledge of God; and we take captive every thought to make it obedient to Christ. 6 And we will be ready to punish every act of disobedience, as soon as your obedience is complete.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul turns from the collection to challenges against his ministry. Some people regard him as unimpressive in person and bold only from a distance. He appeals with Christ’s mildness and gentleness, asking them to respond before his arrival makes a firmer response necessary.

He acknowledges ordinary human life while explaining that his ministry draws on God’s power. The warfare picture describes a struggle against proud reasoning that stands against the knowledge of God. Paul names the strongholds he means: arguments and presumptions that resist that knowledge.

Taking every thought captive belongs first to this account of Paul and his fellow workers bringing opposition into obedience to Christ. The goal is that people’s thinking and allegiance come under Christ’s rule. Reading it in that setting helps us see why Paul speaks of strongholds being demolished and obedience replacing resistance.

The paragraph also contains a warning about disobedience. Paul is ready to act once the Corinthians’ obedience is complete. He begins with an appeal, giving them opportunity to respond, while making clear that persistent resistance will be addressed.

There is a personal application in allowing Christ’s truth to shape our thinking. That application grows from Paul’s stated goal of obedience to Him, with the gospel guiding what we accept and how we live.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the warfare as spiritual and the victory as bringing resistance to God’s truth into obedience to Christ. Wesley’s notes on verses 3–5 emphasize spiritual means and the mind yielding to Christ; the USCCB notes on verses 1–6 keep the imagery within Paul’s defense of his ministry and confidence in divine power.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Acts 26:16–18, Paul recounts Christ sending him to open people’s eyes, turning them from darkness to light and from Satan’s power to God. That commission gives a larger setting for the struggle described here: people are being called into a new allegiance through the gospel.

1 Corinthians 1:18–25 identifies the message of the crucified Christ as God’s power and wisdom. Together, these passages show why Paul can appeal with Christ’s gentleness and still trust that his message has power to change lives.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 10:7-11
passages.section_title: What is authority in Christ meant to accomplish?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 You are looking at outward appearances. If anyone is confident that he belongs to Christ, he should remind himself that we belong to Christ just as much as he does. 8 For even if I boast somewhat excessively about the authority the Lord gave us for building you up rather than tearing you down, I will not be ashamed. 9 I do not want to seem to be trying to frighten you by my letters. 10 For some say, “His letters are weighty and forceful, but his physical presence is unimpressive, and his speaking is of no account.” 11 Such people should consider that what we are in our letters when absent, we will be in our actions when present.
paragraphs: 7 You are looking at outward appearances. If anyone is confident that he belongs to Christ, he should remind himself that we belong to Christ just as much as he does. 8 For even if I boast somewhat excessively about the authority the Lord gave us for building you up rather than tearing you down, I will not be ashamed.

9 I do not want to seem to be trying to frighten you by my letters. 10 For some say, “His letters are weighty and forceful, but his physical presence is unimpressive, and his speaking is of no account.” 11 Such people should consider that what we are in our letters when absent, we will be in our actions when present.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul asks the Corinthians to look beyond outward appearances. Anyone confident of belonging to Christ should recognize that Paul and his fellow workers belong to Him too. The critics’ confidence in themselves gives them no basis for dismissing his relationship to Christ.

Paul then names the purpose of the authority the Lord gave him: building the Corinthians up. His confidence in that calling explains his firm words. The community’s good is the purpose he sets before them.

He quotes the criticism being made of him. Some find his letters forceful while describing his personal presence and speaking dismissively. These are their judgments, reported as part of the dispute.

Paul answers that his conduct in person will match his words from a distance. He wants them to take the letters seriously and respond, knowing that his authority will also be exercised when he arrives.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a defense of Paul’s authority and its purpose of strengthening the church. Wesley’s notes on verses 7–10 address judgments based on appearances; the USCCB notes on verses 7–10 likewise emphasize the intended good of Paul’s ministry for the community.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 4:11–16 describes Christ giving workers to equip His people and build up His body. The goal is maturity in Him, with the whole body growing in love as each part does its work.

That wider purpose helps explain the authority Paul describes here. Christ is forming a people who know Him, stand firm in the truth and serve one another. Leadership belongs within that work of growth.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 10:12-18
passages.section_title: Whose approval gives ministry its worth?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 We do not dare to classify or compare ourselves with some who commend themselves. When they measure themselves by themselves and compare themselves with themselves, they show their ignorance. 13 We, however, will not boast beyond our limits, but only within the field of influence that God has assigned to us—a field that reaches even to you. 14 We are not overstepping our bounds, as if we had not come to you. Indeed, we were the first to reach you with the gospel of Christ. 15 Neither do we boast beyond our limits in the labors of others. But we hope that as your faith increases, our area of influence among you will greatly increase as well, 16 so that we can preach the gospel in the regions beyond you. Then we will not be boasting in the work already done in another man’s territory. 17 Rather, “Let him who boasts boast in the Lord.” 18 For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends.
paragraphs: 12 We do not dare to classify or compare ourselves with some who commend themselves. When they measure themselves by themselves and compare themselves with themselves, they show their ignorance. 13 We, however, will not boast beyond our limits, but only within the field of influence that God has assigned to us—a field that reaches even to you. 14 We are not overstepping our bounds, as if we had not come to you. Indeed, we were the first to reach you with the gospel of Christ.

15 Neither do we boast beyond our limits in the labors of others. But we hope that as your faith increases, our area of influence among you will greatly increase as well, 16 so that we can preach the gospel in the regions beyond you. Then we will not be boasting in the work already done in another man’s territory.
17 Rather, “Let him who boasts boast in the Lord.” 18 For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul challenges a circle of self-approval: people who measure themselves against one another and commend themselves by their own standards. He explains his ministry instead in terms of the field God assigned him.

That field includes Corinth. Paul and his fellow workers really did reach the Corinthians with the gospel. Speaking about that work recognizes what happened among them and the responsibility God gave him.

His hope reaches further. As the Corinthians’ faith grows, he hopes his work can expand through them into regions beyond. He wants to bring the gospel to more people while respecting work already done by others.

Paul closes with the call to boast in the Lord. It echoes Jeremiah 9:23–24, where wisdom, strength and wealth give way to knowing the Lord who acts with loving devotion, justice and righteousness. The final measure is the Lord’s approval.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as a rejection of self-serving comparison and a recognition of work God has actually entrusted to someone. Wesley’s notes on verses 12–16 emphasize the assigned field and further gospel work; the USCCB notes on verses 12–18 distinguish self-commendation from boasting in what the Lord has accomplished.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 15:20–21 describes Paul’s ambition to preach where Christ has not yet been named, so people who have not heard can understand. That stated aim gives a wider setting for his hope of reaching regions beyond Corinth.

The growth of an existing congregation can help the message reach others. Paul’s defense of his work points forward to that continuing mission, with the Lord receiving the credit for what He brings about.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 11:1-6
passages.section_title: Why is Paul so concerned about their devotion to Christ?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 I hope you will put up with a little of my foolishness, but you are already doing that. 2 I am jealous for you with a godly jealousy. For I promised you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ. 3 I am afraid, however, that just as Eve was deceived by the serpent’s cunning, your minds may be led astray from your simple and pure devotion to Christ. 4 For if someone comes and proclaims a Jesus other than the One we proclaimed, or if you receive a different spirit than the One you received, or a different gospel than the one you accepted, you put up with it very easily. 5 I consider myself in no way inferior to those “super-apostles.” 6 Although I am not a polished speaker, I am certainly not lacking in knowledge. We have made this clear to you in every way possible.
paragraphs: 1 I hope you will put up with a little of my foolishness, but you are already doing that. 2 I am jealous for you with a godly jealousy. For I promised you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ. 3 I am afraid, however, that just as Eve was deceived by the serpent’s cunning, your minds may be led astray from your simple and pure devotion to Christ.

4 For if someone comes and proclaims a Jesus other than the One we proclaimed, or if you receive a different spirit than the One you received, or a different gospel than the one you accepted, you put up with it very easily. 5 I consider myself in no way inferior to those “super-apostles.” 6 Although I am not a polished speaker, I am certainly not lacking in knowledge. We have made this clear to you in every way possible.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul asks the Corinthians to bear with what he calls a little foolishness. He is about to speak about himself in order to answer people drawing them away from the message he brought. His deeper concern is their faithfulness to Christ.

He pictures the community as a bride promised to one husband. His godly jealousy is a protective concern that they remain devoted to Christ. The picture explains why he takes the threat seriously.

Paul recalls the serpent’s deception of Eve in Genesis 3:1–6. He fears a similar deception could turn their minds from simple, pure devotion to Christ. He then names the danger: tolerating another Jesus, a different spirit or a different gospel.

He answers the claims of the people he calls super-apostles by affirming that he is in no way inferior to them. He distinguishes polished speaking from knowledge and reminds the Corinthians that his knowledge has been made clear among them. The message they have received matters as they assess those now teaching them.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand Paul’s jealousy as concern for the church’s faithfulness to Christ. Wesley’s notes on verses 1–4 emphasize devotion directed to Him, while the USCCB notes on verses 2–4 connect the marriage picture and Eve’s deception with the danger of accepting a changed gospel.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 5:25–32 explicitly joins the marriage picture with Christ and the church. Christ loves the church, gives Himself for her and works to present her holy and blameless.

That gives Paul’s concern a larger setting. The church belongs to the Lord who has loved and given Himself for her. Faithful teaching serves that relationship by helping people remain devoted to the Christ proclaimed in the gospel.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 11:7-11
passages.section_title: Why did Paul preach to the Corinthians free of charge?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 Was it a sin for me to humble myself in order to exalt you, because I preached the gospel of God to you free of charge? 8 I robbed other churches by accepting their support in order to serve you. 9 And when I was with you and in need, I was not a burden to anyone; for the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied my needs. I have refrained from being a burden to you in any way, and I will continue to do so. 10 As surely as the truth of Christ is in me, this boasting of mine will not be silenced in the regions of Achaia. 11 Why? Because I do not love you? God knows I do!
paragraphs: 7 Was it a sin for me to humble myself in order to exalt you, because I preached the gospel of God to you free of charge? 8 I robbed other churches by accepting their support in order to serve you. 9 And when I was with you and in need, I was not a burden to anyone; for the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied my needs. I have refrained from being a burden to you in any way, and I will continue to do so.
10 As surely as the truth of Christ is in me, this boasting of mine will not be silenced in the regions of Achaia. 11 Why? Because I do not love you? God knows I do!

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
