Paul turns to another point of criticism: his decision to preach the gospel to the Corinthians without charging them. He asks whether humbling himself so they could be lifted up was somehow a sin. The question exposes the unfairness of treating his service as a reason to dismiss him.

Other churches helped support that work. Paul describes accepting their support with the striking word robbed, emphasizing the cost they bore while Corinth benefited. He also says brothers from Macedonia supplied his needs when he was among the Corinthians.

His practice therefore included receiving support, while deliberately keeping from being a financial burden to Corinth. Philippians 4:15–18 offers another account of churches sharing in his ministry through gifts.

Paul intends to continue his approach in Achaia. He closes by answering a possible misunderstanding: his refusal to take their support does not mean he lacks love for them. God knows that he loves them.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a defense of Paul’s decision to serve Corinth without taking support from them. Wesley’s notes on verses 7–11 and the USCCB notes on verses 7–12 both explain that decision within his response to criticism. His stated love and the support he received from elsewhere remain part of the picture.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 11:12-15
passages.section_title: Why can a convincing appearance be misleading?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 But I will keep on doing what I am doing, in order to undercut those who want an opportunity to be regarded as our equals in the things of which they boast. 13 For such men are false apostles, deceitful workers, masquerading as apostles of Christ. 14 And no wonder, for Satan himself masquerades as an angel of light. 15 It is not surprising, then, if his servants masquerade as servants of righteousness. Their end will correspond to their actions.
paragraphs: 12 But I will keep on doing what I am doing, in order to undercut those who want an opportunity to be regarded as our equals in the things of which they boast. 13 For such men are false apostles, deceitful workers, masquerading as apostles of Christ.

14 And no wonder, for Satan himself masquerades as an angel of light. 15 It is not surprising, then, if his servants masquerade as servants of righteousness. Their end will correspond to their actions.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul explains why he will continue his approach to support: he wants to undercut people seeking to be regarded as his equals in what they boast about. This follows his account of serving Corinth without becoming a financial burden to them.

He now identifies the people he means as false apostles and deceitful workers. They present themselves as apostles of Christ, while the message and conduct Paul has described expose a different reality. The issue concerns the truth of their claim to represent Him.

Paul uses Satan’s own disguise as an angel of light to explain how such deception can appear credible. A presentation that looks righteous can conceal service to a different master.

The paragraph ends with accountability: their end will correspond to their actions. An impressive religious appearance cannot determine the final verdict.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as a warning that religious appearance can conceal deception. Wesley’s notes on verses 14–15 and the USCCB note on verses 13–15 both connect the disguise with Paul’s exposure of false workers and their eventual judgment.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 John 4:1–6 also warns about false prophets and calls believers to test what they hear by the truth about Jesus and the apostolic message. It joins discernment with confidence that the One in God’s people is greater than the one in the world.

That wider setting gives both seriousness and hope to Paul’s warning. God’s people are called to remain faithful to Christ while relying on the God who is with them. The reality of deception belongs alongside His greater power.

Scripture supplies the standard by which an experience is tested. This applies the verse’s warning about disguise without making a feeling the proof of its source.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 11:14
passages.section_title: Can something seem like light and still deceive?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 And no wonder, for Satan himself masquerades as an angel of light.
paragraphs: 14 And no wonder, for Satan himself masquerades as an angel of light.

passages.context_html:
This verse belongs to Paul’s warning in 2 Corinthians 11:12–15. He describes deceitful workers presenting themselves as apostles of Christ and explains their disguise by pointing to Satan appearing as an angel of light.

The surrounding paragraph supplies the point of the comparison: apparent righteousness does not establish whose service someone is actually performing. Paul is exposing misleading claims to represent Christ.

Verse 15 then turns to their actions and their eventual end. Reading the verses together keeps the vivid image connected to discernment and accountability.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read the image as a warning about deceptive appearances. Wesley’s note on verse 14 describes an attractive disguise, and the USCCB note on verses 13–15 connects it with the false workers in the surrounding paragraph.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 11:16-21
passages.section_title: Why does Paul call this boasting foolish?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 I repeat: Let no one take me for a fool. But if you do, then receive me as a fool, so that I too may boast a little. 17 In this confident boasting of mine, I am not speaking as the Lord would, but as a fool. 18 Since many are boasting according to the flesh, I too will boast. 19 For you gladly put up with fools, since you are so wise. 20 In fact, you even put up with anyone who enslaves you or exploits you or takes advantage of you or exalts himself or strikes you in the face. 21 To my shame I concede that we were too weak for that! Speaking as a fool, however, I can match what anyone else dares to boast about.
paragraphs: 16 I repeat: Let no one take me for a fool. But if you do, then receive me as a fool, so that I too may boast a little. 17 In this confident boasting of mine, I am not speaking as the Lord would, but as a fool. 18 Since many are boasting according to the flesh, I too will boast.

19 For you gladly put up with fools, since you are so wise. 20 In fact, you even put up with anyone who enslaves you or exploits you or takes advantage of you or exalts himself or strikes you in the face. 21 To my shame I concede that we were too weak for that! Speaking as a fool, however, I can match what anyone else dares to boast about.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul again asks the Corinthians to bear with him as he speaks about himself. He labels the boasting foolish and says he is not speaking as the Lord would in this manner of boasting. He is taking up the kind of comparison others have brought into the dispute.

His words about the Corinthians being wise carry a pointed irony. They readily tolerate people who enslave, exploit, take advantage, exalt themselves and even strike them in the face. His list exposes what they are accepting from those who claim to lead them.

When he calls himself too weak for that, he is turning the charge of weakness back on the situation. The contrast helps them see how badly their standards for judging ministry have gone wrong.

He then prepares to answer the others’ claims. The account that follows will focus increasingly on labor, suffering and weakness in his service to Christ.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a deliberately ironic introduction to Paul’s defense. Wesley’s notes on verses 16–21 and the USCCB notes on verses 16–21 both highlight the Corinthians’ tolerance of abusive treatment and Paul’s pointed use of the charge of weakness.
passages.god_plan_html:
Mark 10:42–45 records Jesus contrasting rulers who exercise domination with the service He calls His followers to practice. He grounds that calling in His own coming to serve and give His life as a ransom for many.

That explicit pattern of service supplies a wider measure for the behavior Paul describes. Christ’s saving self-giving shapes the life of His people, including how they lead and how they recognize faithful service.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 11:22-29
passages.section_title: What has serving Christ actually cost Paul?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they descendants of Abraham? So am I. 23 Are they servants of Christ? (I am speaking as if I were out of my mind.) I am so much more: in harder labor, in more imprisonments, in worse beatings, in frequent danger of death. 24 Five times I received from the Jews the forty lashes minus one. 25 Three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, three times I was shipwrecked. I spent a night and a day in the open sea. 26 In my frequent journeys, I have been in danger from rivers and from bandits, in danger from my countrymen and from the Gentiles, in danger in the city and in the country, in danger on the sea and among false brothers, 27 in labor and toil and often without sleep, in hunger and thirst and often without food, in cold and exposure. 28 Apart from these external trials, I face daily the pressure of my concern for all the churches. 29 Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is led into sin, and I do not burn with grief?
paragraphs: 22 Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they descendants of Abraham? So am I. 23 Are they servants of Christ? (I am speaking as if I were out of my mind.) I am so much more: in harder labor, in more imprisonments, in worse beatings, in frequent danger of death. 24 Five times I received from the Jews the forty lashes minus one. 25 Three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, three times I was shipwrecked. I spent a night and a day in the open sea.

26 In my frequent journeys, I have been in danger from rivers and from bandits, in danger from my countrymen and from the Gentiles, in danger in the city and in the country, in danger on the sea and among false brothers, 27 in labor and toil and often without sleep, in hunger and thirst and often without food, in cold and exposure.
28 Apart from these external trials, I face daily the pressure of my concern for all the churches. 29 Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is led into sin, and I do not burn with grief?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul can answer the claims about Jewish identity: he too is a Hebrew, an Israelite and a descendant of Abraham. When he turns to service of Christ, his account centers on what he has endured in that service.

He names hard labor, imprisonment, beatings, danger of death, shipwrecks and a night and a day in the open sea. His journeys have exposed him to danger in many places and from many people. Hunger, thirst, sleeplessness, cold and exposure also belong to the account.

The list gives us more of his experience than Acts records in detail. It should be read as his own account here, with each reported event left within what he actually tells us.

Alongside those external troubles is his daily concern for the churches. Another person’s weakness or being led into sin affects him deeply. His care for people is part of the weight of ministry, as real to him as the dangers he has faced.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly see this as Paul’s account of costly service, ending with his concern for people. Wesley’s notes on verses 23–29 discuss both hardship and shared concern; the USCCB notes on verses 23–29 likewise connect the sufferings with service of the crucified Christ.
passages.god_plan_html:
Philippians 3:7–11 describes Paul valuing the knowledge of Christ above what he once counted as gain. His hope includes knowing Christ, the power of His resurrection and participation in His sufferings, looking toward resurrection from the dead.

That stated hope helps place these hardships within the larger purpose of belonging to Christ. The list records the cost of carrying His message, while Paul’s goal reaches through suffering toward life with Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 11:30-33
passages.section_title: Why end this account with an escape in a basket?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 30 If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness. 31 The God and Father of the Lord Jesus, who is forever worthy of praise, knows that I am not lying. 32 In Damascus, the governor under King Aretas secured the city of the Damascenes in order to arrest me. 33 But I was lowered in a basket through a window in the wall and escaped his grasp.
paragraphs: 30 If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness. 31 The God and Father of the Lord Jesus, who is forever worthy of praise, knows that I am not lying.
32 In Damascus, the governor under King Aretas secured the city of the Damascenes in order to arrest me. 33 But I was lowered in a basket through a window in the wall and escaped his grasp.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul states the direction of his boasting: he will speak of things that show his weakness. He calls on God, the Father of the Lord Jesus, as the One who knows he is telling the truth.

He recalls danger in Damascus. The governor under King Aretas secured the city to arrest him, and Paul escaped by being lowered in a basket through a window in the wall.

Acts 9:23–25 also describes a plot in Damascus and disciples helping him escape through the wall in a basket. Fellow believers provided the help he needed to get away.

The image fits the point Paul has just made. His account of service includes needing help and escaping danger in a vulnerable position. This is the story he chooses to tell as he turns toward boasting in weakness.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read the escape as an example of the weakness Paul has chosen to describe. Wesley’s notes on verses 30–33 explain the danger and escape; the USCCB note on verses 31–32 likewise connects the episode with weakness and deliverance.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 12:1-6
passages.section_title: Why does Paul speak so carefully about his vision?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 I must go on boasting. Although there is nothing to gain, I will go on to visions and revelations from the Lord. 2 I know a man in Christ who fourteen years ago was caught up to the third heaven. Whether it was in the body or out of it I do not know, but God knows. 3 And I know that this man—whether in the body or out of it I do not know, but God knows— 4 was caught up to Paradise. The things he heard were inexpressible, things that man is not permitted to tell. 5 I will boast about such a man, but I will not boast about myself, except in my weaknesses. 6 Even if I wanted to boast, I would not be a fool, because I would be speaking the truth. But I refrain, so no one will credit me with more than he sees in me or hears from me,
paragraphs: 1 I must go on boasting. Although there is nothing to gain, I will go on to visions and revelations from the Lord. 2 I know a man in Christ who fourteen years ago was caught up to the third heaven. Whether it was in the body or out of it I do not know, but God knows. 3 And I know that this man—whether in the body or out of it I do not know, but God knows— 4 was caught up to Paradise. The things he heard were inexpressible, things that man is not permitted to tell.

5 I will boast about such a man, but I will not boast about myself, except in my weaknesses. 6 Even if I wanted to boast, I would not be a fool, because I would be speaking the truth. But I refrain, so no one will credit me with more than he sees in me or hears from me,

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul continues his defense by turning to visions and revelations from the Lord. He describes a man in Christ who was caught up to the third heaven fourteen years earlier. He speaks of the experience in the third person while the surrounding discussion connects it with his own revelations and weakness.

He twice says he does not know whether it happened in the body or out of the body. God knows. Paul leaves the manner of the experience unexplained, even as he describes being caught up to Paradise and hearing things that cannot be told.

Paradise translates παράδεισος, paradeisos (pah-RAH-day-sos). Thayer’s lexicon includes the word’s use for a garden and for a heavenly place in this passage. The word helps connect the account with Scripture’s wider picture of life with God.

Paul could tell the truth about this experience, but he chooses restraint. He wants people’s judgment of him to rest on what they see in him and hear from him. When he speaks about himself, weakness remains the direction of his boasting.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the man as Paul speaking indirectly about his own experience. Wesley’s note on verse 2 and the USCCB note on verses 5–7 both make that connection. His restraint keeps the revelation from becoming a claim to personal greatness.
passages.god_plan_html:
Revelation 2:7 explicitly joins Paradise with Christ’s promise of access to the tree of life. That image reaches back to Genesis 3:22–24, where human sin leads to exclusion from that tree.

This gives Paradise a larger biblical setting of life with God and the hope Christ holds before His people. Paul’s brief account belongs within that hope while preserving the limits he places on what he can describe.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 12:7-9
passages.section_title: What answer did Paul receive when he asked for relief?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 or because of these surpassingly great revelations. So to keep me from becoming conceited, I was given a thorn in my flesh, a messenger of Satan, to torment me. 8 Three times I pleaded with the Lord to take it away from me. 9 But He said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness.” Therefore I will boast all the more gladly in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest on me.
paragraphs: 7 or because of these surpassingly great revelations. So to keep me from becoming conceited, I was given a thorn in my flesh, a messenger of Satan, to torment me. 8 Three times I pleaded with the Lord to take it away from me.
9 But He said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness.” Therefore I will boast all the more gladly in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest on me.

passages.context_html:
This passage follows Paul’s restrained account of revelations from the Lord. The first words continue his explanation of why he avoids being credited too highly. He then describes a thorn that keeps him from conceit, calling it a messenger of Satan that torments him.

He pleads with the Lord three times for it to be taken away. The account records the Lord’s response about sufficient grace and power perfected in weakness.

Paul responds by welcoming Christ’s power resting on him in his weakness. The fuller paragraph, 2 Corinthians 12:7–10, places that response among the hardships he endures for Christ.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as Christ sustaining Paul when the thorn remains. Wesley’s notes on verses 8–9 and the USCCB notes on verses 8–9 connect the repeated prayer with the answer of sufficient grace. The exact identity of the thorn remains uncertain.
passages.current_position_html: Our study What Does Prayer Look Like?, in its section on Paul’s thorn, understands this as an answer that supplies grace while the suffering remains. Its position is that hardship does not prove God is absent or inattentive. We can trust His care even when the answer takes a different form from the relief we asked for.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
2 Corinthians 4:7–12 describes the life of Jesus being revealed through His vulnerable servants. Their weakness makes clear that the power comes from God, and their costly ministry brings life to others.

That wider setting helps explain why Paul values Christ’s power resting on him. God’s work through him continues amid weakness, serving people through the gospel. The grace described here sustains him in that calling.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 12:7-10
passages.section_title: How does Christ’s power meet Paul in weakness?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 or because of these surpassingly great revelations. So to keep me from becoming conceited, I was given a thorn in my flesh, a messenger of Satan, to torment me. 8 Three times I pleaded with the Lord to take it away from me. 9 But He said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness.” Therefore I will boast all the more gladly in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest on me. 10 That is why, for the sake of Christ, I delight in weaknesses, in insults, in hardships, in persecutions, in difficulties. For when I am weak, then I am strong.
paragraphs: 7 or because of these surpassingly great revelations. So to keep me from becoming conceited, I was given a thorn in my flesh, a messenger of Satan, to torment me. 8 Three times I pleaded with the Lord to take it away from me.

9 But He said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness.” Therefore I will boast all the more gladly in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest on me. 10 That is why, for the sake of Christ, I delight in weaknesses, in insults, in hardships, in persecutions, in difficulties. For when I am weak, then I am strong.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The opening continues Paul’s explanation of why he avoids being credited too highly because of extraordinary revelations. He says he was given a thorn in his flesh to keep him from becoming conceited. He calls it a messenger of Satan that torments him, while describing a purpose that checks pride.

Paul gives no precise identification of the thorn. He tells us how he responded: he pleaded with the Lord three times for it to be taken away.

The Lord’s answer directs him to sufficient grace and power perfected in weakness. Paul then says he will gladly boast in his weaknesses so that Christ’s power may rest on him. The account moves from his request for removal to confidence in Christ’s sustaining presence.

Verse 10 places this response within the insults, hardships, persecutions and difficulties he faces for Christ. His strength comes through dependence on the Lord amid those weaknesses.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly see sufficient grace and Christ’s power in weakness as the center of the passage. Commentators differ about the thorn: Wesley’s note on verse 7 discusses a painful affliction; the USCCB note on verse 7 lists illness, temptation and ministry difficulties, including a possible opponent. Those are proposed identifications; Paul leaves the thorn unnamed.
passages.god_plan_html:
2 Corinthians 4:7–12 describes the life of Jesus being revealed through His vulnerable servants. Their weakness makes clear that the power comes from God, and their costly ministry brings life to others.

That wider setting helps explain why Paul values Christ’s power resting on him. God’s work through him continues amid weakness, serving people through the gospel. The grace described here sustains him in that calling.
passages.current_position_html: Our study What Does Prayer Look Like?, in its section on Paul’s thorn, understands this as an answer that supplies grace while the suffering remains. Its position is that hardship does not prove God is absent or inattentive. We can trust His care even when the answer takes a different form from the relief we asked for.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 12:11-13
passages.section_title: What evidence of Paul’s ministry had they already seen?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 I have become a fool, but you drove me to it. In fact, you should have commended me, since I am in no way inferior to those “super-apostles,” even though I am nothing. 12 The marks of a true apostle—signs, wonders, and miracles—were performed among you with great perseverance. 13 In what way were you inferior to the other churches, except that I was not a burden to you? Forgive me this wrong!
paragraphs: 11 I have become a fool, but you drove me to it. In fact, you should have commended me, since I am in no way inferior to those “super-apostles,” even though I am nothing. 12 The marks of a true apostle—signs, wonders, and miracles—were performed among you with great perseverance. 13 In what way were you inferior to the other churches, except that I was not a burden to you? Forgive me this wrong!

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul brings the discussion of his qualifications back to the Corinthians’ own experience. They should have commended him, yet their response has driven him into the foolish boasting he has repeatedly qualified.

He says he is in no way inferior to the super-apostles, while also saying he is nothing. His confidence concerns what God has done through his ministry. He points to signs, wonders and miracles performed among them with great perseverance.

Then he returns to his decision to serve without becoming a burden to them. His request that they forgive this wrong is pointed irony: they received his ministry while others bore the cost of supporting him. That difference is being treated as if he had deprived them.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read the signs and perseverance as evidence of Paul’s genuine ministry. The USCCB note on verse 12 places demonstrations of power alongside his weakness and endurance.

Christians differ over what this means for gifts today. Dallas Theological Seminary, article XVI, teaches that certain sign gifts ended with the founding apostles and prophets, while affirming that God can still perform miracles. The Pentecostal Assemblies of God statement, sections 7 and 12, teaches the continuing work of spiritual gifts and divine healing. These are the stated positions of those bodies; they do not represent every Christian in their wider traditions.
passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 2:1–4 describes salvation first announced by the Lord, confirmed by those who heard Him, and affirmed by God through signs, wonders, miracles and gifts of the Spirit.

That passage places such works within God’s confirmation of the message about His Son. Paul’s appeal to what happened among the Corinthians belongs within that larger setting of the gospel being proclaimed and confirmed.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 12:14-18
passages.section_title: What does Paul want from the Corinthians?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 See, I am ready to come to you a third time, and I will not be a burden, because I am not seeking your possessions, but you. For children should not have to save up for their parents, but parents for their children. 15 And for the sake of your souls, I will most gladly spend my money and myself. If I love you more, will you love me less? 16 Be that as it may, I was not a burden to you; but crafty as I am, I caught you by trickery. 17 Did I exploit you by anyone I sent you? 18 I urged Titus to visit you, and I sent our brother with him. Did Titus exploit you in any way? Did we not walk in the same Spirit and follow in the same footsteps?
paragraphs: 14 See, I am ready to come to you a third time, and I will not be a burden, because I am not seeking your possessions, but you. For children should not have to save up for their parents, but parents for their children. 15 And for the sake of your souls, I will most gladly spend my money and myself. If I love you more, will you love me less?

16 Be that as it may, I was not a burden to you; but crafty as I am, I caught you by trickery. 17 Did I exploit you by anyone I sent you? 18 I urged Titus to visit you, and I sent our brother with him. Did Titus exploit you in any way? Did we not walk in the same Spirit and follow in the same footsteps?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul is preparing to come a third time and again says he will avoid burdening them. He wants them, their good and their faithfulness to Christ. He explains his care through the picture of parents providing for their children.

He is willing to spend his resources and himself for their souls. The question about being loved less as he loves more expresses the pain of that costly care being met with suspicion.

The words about being crafty and catching them by trickery take up the suspicion he is answering. His next questions challenge it directly: did he exploit them through any of the people he sent?

He points specifically to Titus and the brother sent with him. Their shared conduct is something the Corinthians can consider. Paul asks whether Titus took advantage of them and whether they followed the same Spirit and footsteps.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as a defense of sincere care and honest handling of support. Wesley’s notes on verses 14–18 explain the trickery language as an accusation Paul rejects, and the USCCB note on verses 13–18 likewise connects his questions with rejecting secret self-enrichment.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 12:19-21
passages.section_title: Why does Paul’s love include a call to repent?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 Have you been thinking all along that we were making a defense to you? We speak before God in Christ, and all of this, beloved, is to build you up. 20 For I am afraid that when I come, I may not find you as I wish, and you may not find me as you wish. I fear that there may be quarreling, jealousy, rage, rivalry, slander, gossip, arrogance, and disorder. 21 I am afraid that when I come again, my God will humble me before you, and I will be grieved over many who have sinned earlier and have not repented of their acts of impurity, sexual immorality, and debauchery.
paragraphs: 19 Have you been thinking all along that we were making a defense to you? We speak before God in Christ, and all of this, beloved, is to build you up.

20 For I am afraid that when I come, I may not find you as I wish, and you may not find me as you wish. I fear that there may be quarreling, jealousy, rage, rivalry, slander, gossip, arrogance, and disorder. 21 I am afraid that when I come again, my God will humble me before you, and I will be grieved over many who have sinned earlier and have not repented of their acts of impurity, sexual immorality, and debauchery.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul explains the purpose of all he has been saying. He speaks before God in Christ, and his concern is to build up the people he calls beloved. His defense serves their good.

He fears that his arrival may expose a community neither he nor they want to see. He names quarreling, jealousy, rage, rivalry, slander, gossip, arrogance and disorder. These are problems affecting how people live together.

He also fears grief over those who have continued in impurity, sexual immorality and debauchery without repenting. His concern reaches beyond settling the dispute about his reputation to the life of the congregation itself.

The warning gives them opportunity to respond before he arrives. Building them up includes facing conduct that harms their faithfulness to Christ and their care for one another.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a loving but serious appeal for repentance. The USCCB notes on verses 19–21 connect Paul’s concern for building the community with its unresolved moral disorders. Wesley’s note on verse 19 likewise emphasizes that he speaks for their sake.
passages.god_plan_html:
Colossians 3:1–17 places changed conduct within life shared with the risen Christ. It describes the new self being renewed in the Creator’s image, then calls believers to compassion, forgiveness, love and peace as one body.

That wider purpose helps explain why the disorders at Corinth matter. God is forming a people whose common life reflects Christ. Turning from destructive conduct belongs to that renewal and makes room for the love and unity He calls them to practice.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 13:1-4
passages.section_title: Why does Paul give another warning before he comes?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 This is the third time I am coming to you. “Every matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses.” 2 I already warned you the second time I was with you. So now in my absence I warn those who sinned earlier and everyone else: If I return, I will not spare anyone, 3 since you are demanding proof that Christ is speaking through me. He is not weak in dealing with you but is powerful among you. 4 For He was indeed crucified in weakness, yet He lives by God’s power. For we are also weak in Him, yet by God’s power we will live with Him concerning you.
paragraphs: 1 This is the third time I am coming to you. “Every matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses.” 2 I already warned you the second time I was with you. So now in my absence I warn those who sinned earlier and everyone else: If I return, I will not spare anyone,

3 since you are demanding proof that Christ is speaking through me. He is not weak in dealing with you but is powerful among you. 4 For He was indeed crucified in weakness, yet He lives by God’s power. For we are also weak in Him, yet by God’s power we will live with Him concerning you.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul says he is coming a third time. He recalls the warning he gave when he was with them the second time and now warns those who sinned earlier, along with everyone else. The coming visit will bring unresolved disobedience into the open.

He cites the rule that a matter must be established by two or three witnesses. Deuteronomy 19:15–21 gives that rule in a setting that also calls for careful investigation of accusations. Paul places accountability alongside a standard for establishing what happened.

The Corinthians have demanded proof that Christ speaks through him. Paul answers by pointing to Christ’s power among them. His own apparent weakness does not exhaust what they will encounter when he comes.

Christ Himself was crucified in weakness and lives by God’s power. Paul places his own weakness and the power at work through his ministry within that pattern. The warning prepares them to take his appeal seriously before the visit.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as a serious warning about accountability, grounded in the power of the risen Christ. Wesley’s notes on verses 2–4 and the USCCB notes on verses 2–4 both connect Paul’s weakness and authority with that power.
passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 2:22–24 explicitly places Jesus’ death within God’s purpose and proclaims that God raised Him from the dead. The crucified Jesus is the living Lord through whom God is carrying out His saving work.

That gives the weakness-and-power pattern its larger setting. Paul represents this risen Lord, and his service depends on the power of the God who raised Christ.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 13:5-10
passages.section_title: What does Paul want their self-examination to lead to?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 Examine yourselves to see whether you are in the faith; test yourselves. Do you not realize that Jesus Christ is in you—unless you fail the test? 6 And I hope you will realize that we have not failed the test. 7 Now we pray to God that you will not do anything wrong—not that we will appear to have stood the test, but that you will do what is right, even if we appear to have failed. 8 For we cannot do anything against the truth, but only for the truth. 9 In fact, we rejoice when we are weak but you are strong, and our prayer is for your perfection. 10 This is why I write these things while absent, so that when I am present I will not need to be severe in my use of the authority that the Lord gave me for building you up, not for tearing you down.
paragraphs: 5 Examine yourselves to see whether you are in the faith; test yourselves. Do you not realize that Jesus Christ is in you—unless you fail the test? 6 And I hope you will realize that we have not failed the test.

7 Now we pray to God that you will not do anything wrong—not that we will appear to have stood the test, but that you will do what is right, even if we appear to have failed. 8 For we cannot do anything against the truth, but only for the truth. 9 In fact, we rejoice when we are weak but you are strong, and our prayer is for your perfection. 10 This is why I write these things while absent, so that when I am present I will not need to be severe in my use of the authority that the Lord gave me for building you up, not for tearing you down.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The people asking for proof about Paul are now called to examine themselves. He asks whether they are in the faith and whether they recognize Jesus Christ in them. The challenge turns their attention toward their own response to Christ.

Paul then explains what he prays for: that they do what is right, even if he appears to have failed their test. Their good matters more than an opportunity to demonstrate his authority through a severe response.

He rejoices when they are strong, even if he appears weak. His prayer for their perfection includes their strengthening and growth. The Greek word is κατάρτισις, katartisis (kah-TAR-tih-sis); Thayer’s lexicon describes strengthening or perfecting. The surrounding verses show his concern that their life in Christ be put right.

He writes while absent so that severity may be unnecessary when he arrives. He again names the purpose of the authority the Lord gave him: building them up. Self-examination is to lead toward a response that serves that growth.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a call to serious self-examination within Paul’s appeal for the Corinthians’ good. Wesley’s notes on verses 5–9 connect the test with Christ’s presence and faith working through love. The USCCB notes on verses 5–10 likewise connect their examination with Paul’s purpose of building up the community.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 4:11–16 describes Christ equipping His people to grow into maturity in Him. Truth, love and each person’s service belong to the growth of the whole body.

Paul’s prayer fits that larger purpose. The Corinthians’ strengthening is part of becoming a people whose shared life reflects Christ. His authority and his prayers serve that end.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Corinthians 13:11-14
passages.section_title: What holds this church together as the letter ends?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 Finally, brothers, rejoice! Aim for perfect harmony, encourage one another, be of one mind, live in peace. And the God of love and peace will be with you. 12 Greet one another with a holy kiss. 13 All the saints send you greetings. 14 The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with all of you.
paragraphs: 11 Finally, brothers, rejoice! Aim for perfect harmony, encourage one another, be of one mind, live in peace. And the God of love and peace will be with you. 12 Greet one another with a holy kiss. 13 All the saints send you greetings.
14 The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with all of you.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul closes by calling the believers to rejoice, encourage one another, seek harmony and live in peace. The God of love and peace is the One he holds before them as they respond.

The holy kiss and the greetings of all the saints give the closing a shared, personal character. After a letter full of strained relationships, Paul directs them toward fellowship with one another and the wider community of believers.

The final blessing names the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit. Paul ends by seeking these blessings for all of them. The last word over the community is a prayer of grace, love and fellowship.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly receive these words as a call to peace and a blessing that names Jesus Christ, God and the Holy Spirit together. Wesley’s closing note explains the grace, love and fellowship; the USCCB closing note likewise connects the ending with unity and recognizes its significance for the Christian confession of Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 2:14–18 describes Christ making peace, bringing people together in one body and giving them access to the Father through one Spirit.

That explicit connection helps explain why grace, love and fellowship belong at the end of this letter. The unity Paul urges grows from God’s work of bringing people near through Christ, with a shared life in the Spirit.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Galatians 1:1-5
passages.section_title: What does Paul put at the center of his greeting?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Paul, an apostle—sent not from men nor by man, but by Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised Him from the dead— 2 and all the brothers with me, To the churches of Galatia: 3 Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, 4 who gave Himself for our sins to rescue us from the present evil age, according to the will of our God and Father, 5 to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.
paragraphs: 1 Paul, an apostle—sent not from men nor by man, but by Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised Him from the dead— 2 and all the brothers with me, To the churches of Galatia:

3 Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, 4 who gave Himself for our sins to rescue us from the present evil age, according to the will of our God and Father, 5 to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul writes to the churches of Galatia with his authority and message already in view. He identifies himself as an apostle sent through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised Jesus from the dead. The brothers with him are included in the greeting.

He asks for grace and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. He then explains Christ’s self-giving: Jesus gave Himself for our sins to rescue us from the present evil age, according to the Father’s will.

These opening words establish what matters in the dispute that follows. Paul’s message concerns God’s gracious action through Christ, and his commission comes from the same Lord. The greeting ends by giving God glory.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read the greeting as a summary of Paul’s commission and Christ’s saving self-giving. Wesley’s notes on verses 1–5 and the USCCB notes on verses 1–4 both connect the opening with the authority and message Paul will defend.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 1:7–10 joins redemption and forgiveness through Christ with God’s purpose to bring things in heaven and on earth together in Him.

That gives the rescue named here a wider setting. Christ’s giving Himself for our sins belongs to the Father’s saving purpose, which reaches toward the fullness of all He will accomplish through His Son.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Galatians 1:6-10
passages.section_title: Why does Paul respond so strongly to a changed gospel?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 I am amazed how quickly you are deserting the One who called you by the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel— 7 which is not even a gospel. Evidently some people are troubling you and trying to distort the gospel of Christ. 8 But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be under a curse! 9 As we have said before, so now I say again: If anyone is preaching to you a gospel contrary to the one you received, let him be under a curse! 10 Am I now seeking the approval of men, or of God? Or am I striving to please men? If I were still trying to please men, I would not be a servant of Christ.
paragraphs: 6 I am amazed how quickly you are deserting the One who called you by the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel— 7 which is not even a gospel. Evidently some people are troubling you and trying to distort the gospel of Christ.

8 But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be under a curse! 9 As we have said before, so now I say again: If anyone is preaching to you a gospel contrary to the one you received, let him be under a curse! 10 Am I now seeking the approval of men, or of God? Or am I striving to please men? If I were still trying to please men, I would not be a servant of Christ.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the greeting, Paul moves immediately to his alarm. The Galatians are turning from the One who called them by Christ’s grace toward a message he calls a different gospel. He says this amounts to desertion of the One who called them.

Gospel translates εὐαγγέλιον, euangelion (yoo-an-GHEL-ee-on), meaning good news. Thayer’s lexicon explains its use for the good news of salvation through Christ. That meaning sharpens Paul’s point: a distorted message is losing the very good news it claims to offer.

He names people troubling the churches and trying to distort Christ’s gospel. His warning applies even if he himself, his fellow workers or an angel from heaven should bring a contrary message. The message already received supplies the measure for judging the messenger.

Paul repeats the warning, then asks whose approval he seeks. His loyalty is to Christ as His servant. Seeking favor from people cannot govern what he proclaims.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as a serious warning to preserve the gospel rather than accept a changed message on the strength of its messenger. Wesley’s notes on verses 6–10 and the USCCB notes on verses 6–10 both connect the warning with the churches’ departure from Christ’s gospel.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Corinthians 15:1–4 states the gospel Paul received and passed on: Christ died for our sins, was buried and was raised on the third day, according to the Scriptures.

That stated content gives the warning here a positive center. God’s saving work through His Son is the message being guarded, and its roots lie in what Scripture had promised.
passages.current_position_html: Our study The Gospel According to Jesus, in its discussion of Galatians 1:8–9, treats the gospel as a settled proclamation whose core must be preserved. That core includes Christ’s death for our sins and His resurrection. His saving work supplies the foundation for the love and obedience that follow from it.

passages.title: Galatians 1:8-9
passages.section_title: Why must even a messenger be tested by the gospel?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be under a curse! 9 As we have said before, so now I say again: If anyone is preaching to you a gospel contrary to the one you received, let him be under a curse!
paragraphs: 8 But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be under a curse! 9 As we have said before, so now I say again: If anyone is preaching to you a gospel contrary to the one you received, let him be under a curse!

passages.context_html:
These repeated warnings belong to Galatians 1:6–10. Paul is alarmed that the churches are turning from the One who called them by grace while people trouble them with a distorted message.

He includes himself and his fellow workers in the warning, then imagines even an angel from heaven bringing a contrary gospel. No messenger’s standing is allowed to change the message they already received.

The repetition shows how seriously he regards the danger. In the surrounding verses he connects this warning with his service to Christ and his responsibility to seek God’s approval.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these verses as making fidelity to the gospel the measure of a messenger. Wesley’s notes on verses 8–9 and the USCCB notes on verses 6–10 place the strong warning within Paul’s response to the distortion troubling the churches.
passages.current_position_html: Our study The Gospel According to Jesus, in its discussion of Galatians 1:8–9, treats the gospel as a settled proclamation whose core must be preserved. That core includes Christ’s death for our sins and His resurrection. His saving work supplies the foundation for the love and obedience that follow from it.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

1 Corinthians 15:1–4 states the gospel Paul received and passed on: Christ died for our sins, was buried and was raised on the third day, according to the Scriptures.

That stated content gives the warning here a positive center. God’s saving work through His Son is the message being guarded, and its roots lie in what Scripture had promised.

passages.title: Galatians 1:11-17
passages.section_title: How did Paul become a messenger of Christ?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 For I want you to know, brothers, that the gospel I preached was not devised by man. 12 I did not receive it from any man, nor was I taught it; rather, I received it by revelation from Jesus Christ. 13 For you have heard of my former way of life in Judaism, how severely I persecuted the church of God and tried to destroy it. 14 I was advancing in Judaism beyond many of my contemporaries and was extremely zealous for the traditions of my fathers. 15 But when God, who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me by His grace, was pleased 16 to reveal His Son in me so that I might preach Him among the Gentiles, I did not rush to consult with flesh and blood, 17 nor did I go up to Jerusalem to the apostles who came before me, but I went into Arabia and later returned to Damascus.
paragraphs: 11 For I want you to know, brothers, that the gospel I preached was not devised by man. 12 I did not receive it from any man, nor was I taught it; rather, I received it by revelation from Jesus Christ. 13 For you have heard of my former way of life in Judaism, how severely I persecuted the church of God and tried to destroy it. 14 I was advancing in Judaism beyond many of my contemporaries and was extremely zealous for the traditions of my fathers.

15 But when God, who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me by His grace, was pleased 16 to reveal His Son in me so that I might preach Him among the Gentiles, I did not rush to consult with flesh and blood, 17 nor did I go up to Jerusalem to the apostles who came before me, but I went into Arabia and later returned to Damascus.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul explains why the gospel he brought cannot be traced to a human invention. He says he received it through revelation from Jesus Christ. His account of his former life and calling supports that claim.

He had severely persecuted God’s church and tried to destroy it. He was advancing beyond many of his contemporaries in Judaism and was deeply zealous for his ancestral traditions. He describes his own former course, including the harm he did.

The turning point comes through God’s grace. God, who had set him apart from his mother’s womb, was pleased to reveal His Son in him so that he might preach among the Gentiles. The purpose of the revelation includes a mission to others.

Paul says he did not immediately consult human authorities or go to Jerusalem to the earlier apostles. He went to Arabia and later returned to Damascus. These details form part of his explanation of where his commission and message came from.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as Paul’s account of God’s gracious calling and his commission to proclaim Christ. Wesley’s notes on verses 11–17 and the USCCB notes on verses 11–17 both emphasize the revelation and the mission to Gentiles.
passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 13:46–48 describes Paul and Barnabas turning to the Gentiles and citing Isaiah 49:6, with its purpose of bringing salvation to the ends of the earth.

That explicit connection places Paul’s calling within the wider reach of God’s saving purpose. The Son revealed to him is the One he is sent to proclaim beyond his own people.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Galatians 1:18-24
passages.section_title: What happened when Paul finally visited Jerusalem?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 Only after three years did I go up to Jerusalem to confer with Cephas, and I stayed with him fifteen days. 19 But I saw none of the other apostles except James, the Lord’s brother. 20 I assure you before God that what I am writing to you is no lie. 21 Later I went to the regions of Syria and Cilicia. 22 I was personally unknown, however, to the churches of Judea that are in Christ. 23 They only heard the account: “The man who formerly persecuted us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy.” 24 And they glorified God because of me.
paragraphs: 18 Only after three years did I go up to Jerusalem to confer with Cephas, and I stayed with him fifteen days. 19 But I saw none of the other apostles except James, the Lord’s brother. 20 I assure you before God that what I am writing to you is no lie.

21 Later I went to the regions of Syria and Cilicia. 22 I was personally unknown, however, to the churches of Judea that are in Christ. 23 They only heard the account: “The man who formerly persecuted us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy.” 24 And they glorified God because of me.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul continues his account of the time after his calling. After three years he went to Jerusalem to confer with Cephas, whom the BSB footnote identifies as Peter, and stayed fifteen days. He also saw James, whom he calls the Lord’s brother.

He solemnly assures his readers before God that he is telling the truth. The details matter to his explanation of his limited early contact with the apostles in Jerusalem.

He later went to Syria and Cilicia. The churches in Judea did not know him personally. They heard the report that the man who had persecuted them was now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy.

Their response was to glorify God because of him. Paul’s account ends with the change in his life becoming a reason for other believers to praise God.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as an account of Paul’s early contacts with the Jerusalem leaders and the change others recognized in him. Wesley’s notes on verses 18–24 and the USCCB note on verses 18–24 both connect the reported events with Paul’s account of his ministry.

passages.title: Galatians 2:1-5
passages.section_title: Why was Titus’s freedom so important?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Fourteen years later I went up again to Jerusalem, accompanied by Barnabas. I took Titus along also. 2 I went in response to a revelation and set before them the gospel that I preach among the Gentiles. But I spoke privately to those recognized as leaders, for fear that I was running or had already run in vain. 3 Yet not even Titus, who was with me, was compelled to be circumcised, even though he was a Greek. 4 This issue arose because some false brothers had come in under false pretenses to spy on our freedom in Christ Jesus, in order to enslave us. 5 We did not give in to them for a moment, so that the truth of the gospel would remain with you.
paragraphs: 1 Fourteen years later I went up again to Jerusalem, accompanied by Barnabas. I took Titus along also. 2 I went in response to a revelation and set before them the gospel that I preach among the Gentiles. But I spoke privately to those recognized as leaders, for fear that I was running or had already run in vain. 3 Yet not even Titus, who was with me, was compelled to be circumcised, even though he was a Greek.

4 This issue arose because some false brothers had come in under false pretenses to spy on our freedom in Christ Jesus, in order to enslave us. 5 We did not give in to them for a moment, so that the truth of the gospel would remain with you.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul continues the account of his ministry by describing a later visit to Jerusalem with Barnabas and Titus. He says he went in response to a revelation and privately set before the recognized leaders the gospel he preached among the Gentiles.

His concern was that his work might be frustrated or come to nothing. The question involved the message being proclaimed and the place of Gentile believers within the community. Titus, a Greek, was not compelled to be circumcised.

Paul describes false brothers entering under false pretenses to spy on their freedom in Christ and bring them into slavery. He says he did not yield, so that the truth of the gospel would remain with the Galatians.

Titus’s case makes the issue concrete. A Gentile believer was among them, and the pressure to require circumcision was resisted. Paul presents that outcome as part of his defense of the gospel he had brought.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a defense of the gospel and Gentile believers’ freedom from a requirement to be circumcised. Wesley’s notes on verses 1–5 and the USCCB notes on verses 1–5 both connect Titus’s case with preserving the message Paul preached.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 2:11–18 describes people once far away being brought near through Christ, with Jews and Gentiles joined in one body and sharing access to the Father through one Spirit.

That explicit purpose gives the dispute about Titus a wider setting. The question concerns the place of people God is bringing together through His Son. The gospel announces a shared life in Christ across the boundary the dispute threatens to impose.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Galatians 2:6-10
passages.section_title: What did the Jerusalem leaders recognize in Paul’s ministry?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 But as for the highly esteemed—whatever they were makes no difference to me; God does not show favoritism—those leaders added nothing to me. 7 On the contrary, they saw that I had been entrusted to preach the gospel to the uncircumcised, just as Peter had been to the circumcised. 8 For the One who was at work in Peter’s apostleship to the circumcised was also at work in my apostleship to the Gentiles. 9 And recognizing the grace that I had been given, James, Cephas, and John—those reputed to be pillars—gave me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship, so that we should go to the Gentiles, and they to the circumcised. 10 They only asked us to remember the poor, the very thing I was eager to do.
paragraphs: 6 But as for the highly esteemed—whatever they were makes no difference to me; God does not show favoritism—those leaders added nothing to me. 7 On the contrary, they saw that I had been entrusted to preach the gospel to the uncircumcised, just as Peter had been to the circumcised. 8 For the One who was at work in Peter’s apostleship to the circumcised was also at work in my apostleship to the Gentiles.

9 And recognizing the grace that I had been given, James, Cephas, and John—those reputed to be pillars—gave me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship, so that we should go to the Gentiles, and they to the circumcised. 10 They only asked us to remember the poor, the very thing I was eager to do.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul says the recognized leaders added nothing to him. Their reputation does not determine God’s judgment of a person. What follows explains the agreement they reached about the work God had entrusted to them.

They recognized his commission to preach to the uncircumcised, just as Peter had been commissioned to the circumcised. Paul points to the same God at work in both ministries. The distinction concerns the people they are sent to reach.

James, Cephas and John, whom Paul calls pillars, recognized the grace given to him and extended fellowship to him and Barnabas. Their agreement affirmed the different fields of work within a shared gospel.

They also asked that the poor be remembered, something Paul was already eager to do. Care for people in need belongs beside the recognition of ministry and fellowship.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as recognition of God’s work through Paul and agreement in the gospel across different fields of ministry. Wesley’s notes on verses 6–10 and the USCCB notes on verses 7–10 both emphasize the shared work and fellowship. The latter also explains that these areas of work did not exclude either apostle from speaking to the other group.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 15:25–27 describes Gentile believers contributing to poor believers in Jerusalem. Paul connects their material help with the spiritual blessings they have shared.

That later collection gives practical expression to the fellowship recognized here. Different areas of ministry belong within a shared faith, and that relationship includes care for one another across the distance between communities.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Who Shepherds the Church?, in its discussion of James, recognizes the real authority and standing he had among the Jerusalem believers. It reads that standing alongside the other leaders and the shared decision-making described in Acts 15 and 21. The study distinguishes recognized personal standing from a separate rank meant to be reproduced in every church.

passages.title: Galatians 2:9
passages.section_title: What does the right hand of fellowship express?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 And recognizing the grace that I had been given, James, Cephas, and John—those reputed to be pillars—gave me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship, so that we should go to the Gentiles, and they to the circumcised.
paragraphs: 9 And recognizing the grace that I had been given, James, Cephas, and John—those reputed to be pillars—gave me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship, so that we should go to the Gentiles, and they to the circumcised.

passages.context_html:
This verse belongs to Paul’s account in Galatians 2:6–10. The Jerusalem leaders recognized the grace given to him and the work God was doing through his ministry.

Paul names James, Cephas and John as people regarded as pillars. They extended fellowship to Paul and Barnabas, recognizing their work among the Gentiles while continuing their own work among the circumcised.

The wider paragraph speaks of the same God at work through different workers and ends with a shared concern for the poor. Fellowship here has both a gospel foundation and practical responsibilities.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read the gesture as recognition of shared work in the gospel. Wesley’s note on verse 9 describes receiving Paul and Barnabas as fellow workers; the USCCB note on verses 7–9 likewise connects the fellowship with recognition of Paul’s mission.

It reads that standing alongside the other leaders and the shared decision-making described in Acts 15 and 21. passages.title: Galatians 2:11-14
passages.section_title: Why did Paul challenge Peter’s conduct in public?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 When Cephas came to Antioch, however, I opposed him to his face, because he stood condemned. 12 For before certain men came from James, he used to eat with the Gentiles. But when they arrived, he began to draw back and separate himself, for fear of those in the circumcision group. 13 The other Jews joined him in his hypocrisy, so that by their hypocrisy even Barnabas was led astray. 14 When I saw that they were not walking in line with the truth of the gospel, I said to Cephas in front of them all, “If you, who are a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you compel the Gentiles to live like Jews?”
paragraphs: 11 When Cephas came to Antioch, however, I opposed him to his face, because he stood condemned. 12 For before certain men came from James, he used to eat with the Gentiles. But when they arrived, he began to draw back and separate himself, for fear of those in the circumcision group. 13 The other Jews joined him in his hypocrisy, so that by their hypocrisy even Barnabas was led astray.

14 When I saw that they were not walking in line with the truth of the gospel, I said to Cephas in front of them all, “If you, who are a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you compel the Gentiles to live like Jews?”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul describes a later conflict in Antioch. Cephas had been eating with Gentile believers, but he withdrew after certain men came from James. Paul identifies fear of the circumcision group as the reason for the withdrawal.

The change affected others. The other Jewish believers joined Peter in the hypocrisy, and even Barnabas was led astray. A leader’s conduct was drawing the community toward separation.

Paul says they were not walking in line with the truth of the gospel. He challenged Cephas in front of everyone, asking how a Jew who had been living like a Gentile could pressure Gentiles to live like Jews.

The issue is how their shared faith is being lived out. Peter’s earlier table fellowship and later withdrawal send conflicting messages about who can be received as a fellow believer.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as Paul opposing conduct that contradicted the shared gospel. Wesley’s notes on verses 11–14 and the USCCB notes on verses 11–14 both identify the inconsistency and its effect on fellowship with Gentile believers.
passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 10:34–48 and 11:15–18 describe Peter recognizing God’s work among Gentiles. They receive the Holy Spirit, and the Jerusalem believers praise God for granting Gentiles repentance leading to life.

That earlier account places the Antioch dispute within God’s welcome of people beyond Israel. The fellowship being strained is fellowship God Himself has opened through Christ and the gift of the Spirit.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Galatians 2:15-21
passages.section_title: How can we be made right with God and live for Him?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 We who are Jews by birth and not Gentile “sinners” 16 know that a man is not justified by works of the law, but by faith in Jesus Christ. So we, too, have believed in Christ Jesus, that we may be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law, because by works of the law no one will be justified. 17 But if, while we seek to be justified in Christ, we ourselves are found to be sinners, does that make Christ a minister of sin? Certainly not! 18 If I rebuild what I have already torn down, I prove myself to be a lawbreaker. 19 For through the law I died to the law so that I might live to God. 20 I have been crucified with Christ, and I no longer live, but Christ lives in me. The life I live in the body, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave Himself up for me. 21 I do not set aside the grace of God. For if righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing.
paragraphs: 15 We who are Jews by birth and not Gentile “sinners” 16 know that a man is not justified by works of the law, but by faith in Jesus Christ. So we, too, have believed in Christ Jesus, that we may be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law, because by works of the law no one will be justified.

17 But if, while we seek to be justified in Christ, we ourselves are found to be sinners, does that make Christ a minister of sin? Certainly not! 18 If I rebuild what I have already torn down, I prove myself to be a lawbreaker.

19 For through the law I died to the law so that I might live to God. 20 I have been crucified with Christ, and I no longer live, but Christ lives in me. The life I live in the body, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave Himself up for me. 21 I do not set aside the grace of God. For if righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul moves from the dispute over fellowship to its foundation. Even those who are Jews by birth know that a person is justified by faith in Jesus Christ, through whom they have believed, rather than by works of the law. Being made right with God depends on Christ.

He then addresses the question of sin. Seeking to be justified in Christ does not make Christ a servant of sin. Rebuilding what has been torn down would expose the person doing so as a lawbreaker.

Paul describes the purpose of dying to the law as living to God. He speaks of being crucified with Christ and of Christ living in him. His present life is lived by faith in the Son of God who loved him and gave Himself for him.

The final statement returns to grace. If righteousness could come through the law, Christ’s death would have been needless. Paul places both acceptance before God and the life that follows within Christ’s self-giving.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read the passage as grounding our right standing with God in Christ and His grace, while calling us into a changed life. Traditions differ in how they explain justification and its relationship to that change.

The Catholic Church teaches that justification includes forgiveness and inward renewal, received through God’s grace and conferred in baptism. The Catechism, paragraphs 1987–1993, says grace comes first and enables a person’s free response in faith and love. This is understood as Christ’s gift, not something earned independently of Him.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 11, distinguishes God’s accepting someone as righteous from His work of inward renewal. It teaches that Christ’s obedience and saving work are credited to the believer, received through faith alone. The same chapter says this faith is living and works through love.

The Methodist Articles of Religion IX–X likewise teach justification through faith because of what Christ has done, with good works following as the fruit of living faith. Wesley’s notes on verses 16–21 emphasize both freedom from trying to be justified through the law and the new life of living to God.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 6:1–11 describes believers sharing in Christ’s death and resurrection so that they can walk in newness of life. Christ’s death and risen life become the pattern for their freedom from sin and life toward God.

That explicit connection develops the purpose expressed here in Paul’s desire to live to God. The Son who loved and gave Himself for him is also the source of the new life he now lives.
