passages.title: Galatians 3:1-5
passages.section_title: How did they receive the Spirit in the first place?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you? Before your very eyes Jesus Christ was clearly portrayed as crucified. 2 I would like to learn just one thing from you: Did you receive the Spirit by works of the law, or by hearing with faith? 3 Are you so foolish? After starting in the Spirit, are you now finishing in the flesh? 4 Have you suffered so much for nothing, if it really was for nothing? 5 Does God lavish His Spirit on you and work miracles among you because you practice the law, or because you hear and believe?
paragraphs: 1 O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you? Before your very eyes Jesus Christ was clearly portrayed as crucified. 2 I would like to learn just one thing from you: Did you receive the Spirit by works of the law, or by hearing with faith? 3 Are you so foolish? After starting in the Spirit, are you now finishing in the flesh?
4 Have you suffered so much for nothing, if it really was for nothing? 5 Does God lavish His Spirit on you and work miracles among you because you practice the law, or because you hear and believe?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul presses the question raised by the previous chapter: what place can works of the law have in a life received through Christ? He reminds the Galatians how clearly Jesus Christ had been presented to them as crucified.

He asks them to consider their own experience. Did they receive the Spirit by doing the works of the law, or by hearing with faith? His next question follows from the first: having started in the Spirit, are they now trying to finish in the flesh?

He also asks whether all they have suffered has been for nothing. The possibility makes the stakes of their change of direction clear.

The final question returns to God’s present generosity: He supplies His Spirit and works miracles among them. Paul asks again whether this comes through practicing the law or through hearing and believing. Their own experience is part of his appeal to hold to the gospel they received.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these questions as recalling the Spirit received through the gospel heard with faith. Wesley’s notes on verses 1–5 and the USCCB notes on verses 1–5 both connect the appeal to their experience with the need to continue depending on God’s Spirit.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 8:9–11 describes the Spirit of God dwelling in Christ’s people and connects His presence with the power of the God who raised Jesus from the dead.

That wider setting shows how much is at stake in the gift Paul names. The Spirit belongs to God’s work of giving life through His risen Son, with hope that reaches to life for mortal bodies. The Galatians are being called to continue in the life God has begun among them.

passages.title: Galatians 3:6-14
passages.section_title: How does Abraham’s blessing reach people through Christ?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 So also, “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness.” 7 Understand, then, that those who have faith are sons of Abraham. 8 The Scripture foresaw that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, and foretold the gospel to Abraham: “All nations will be blessed through you.” 9 So those who have faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith. 10 All who rely on works of the law are under a curse. For it is written: “Cursed is everyone who does not continue to do everything written in the Book of the Law.” 11 Now it is clear that no one is justified before God by the law, because, “The righteous will live by faith.” 12 The law, however, is not based on faith; on the contrary, “The man who does these things will live by them.” 13 Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us. For it is written: “Cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree.” 14 He redeemed us in order that the blessing promised to Abraham would come to the Gentiles in Christ Jesus, so that by faith we might receive the promise of the Spirit.
paragraphs: 6 So also, “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness.” 7 Understand, then, that those who have faith are sons of Abraham. 8 The Scripture foresaw that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, and foretold the gospel to Abraham: “All nations will be blessed through you.” 9 So those who have faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith.

10 All who rely on works of the law are under a curse. For it is written: “Cursed is everyone who does not continue to do everything written in the Book of the Law.” 11 Now it is clear that no one is justified before God by the law, because, “The righteous will live by faith.” 12 The law, however, is not based on faith; on the contrary, “The man who does these things will live by them.”

13 Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us. For it is written: “Cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree.” 14 He redeemed us in order that the blessing promised to Abraham would come to the Gentiles in Christ Jesus, so that by faith we might receive the promise of the Spirit.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul turns from the Galatians’ experience to Scripture. He recalls Genesis 15:6: Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness. Those who have faith are identified as Abraham’s sons.

He then brings in the promise of blessing for all nations. Paul says Scripture foretold the gospel to Abraham, looking ahead to God justifying Gentiles by faith. Those who believe share the blessing with Abraham.

The next verses explain the problem with relying on works of the law. Paul cites Deuteronomy 27:26, with its curse on failing to practice the law. He places Habakkuk 2:4, about the righteous living by faith, alongside Leviticus 18:5, about living by doing what the law commands.

The turning point is Christ’s redemption. He became a curse for us, and Paul connects His death with Deuteronomy 21:22–23, where an executed person’s body hung on a tree is described as under a curse.

Paul names the purpose of this redemption: Abraham’s promised blessing comes to Gentiles in Christ Jesus, and the promised Spirit is received through faith. Christ’s self-giving brings the account back to the gift of the Spirit with which the chapter began.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as connecting Abraham’s faith, Christ’s redemption and blessing for the nations. Wesley’s notes on verses 6–14 and the USCCB notes on verses 6–14 both follow that movement and emphasize that the promised blessing comes through faith in Christ.
passages.god_plan_html:
Genesis 12:1–3 begins Abraham’s calling with a promise that all the families of the earth will be blessed through him. Paul explicitly identifies the gospel’s reach to the Gentiles with that long-standing purpose.

Acts 10:44–48 gives a concrete account of Gentiles hearing the message of Christ and receiving the Holy Spirit. The promised blessing takes shape in people being welcomed into life with God through His Son and Spirit.

passages.title: Galatians 3:15-18
passages.section_title: Can the later law cancel God’s earlier promise?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 Brothers, let me put this in human terms. Even a human covenant, once it is ratified, cannot be canceled or amended. 16 The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. The Scripture does not say, “and to seeds,” meaning many, but “and to your seed,” meaning One, who is Christ. 17 What I mean is this: The law that came 430 years later does not revoke the covenant previously established by God, so as to nullify the promise. 18 For if the inheritance depends on the law, then it no longer depends on a promise; but God freely granted it to Abraham through a promise.
paragraphs: 15 Brothers, let me put this in human terms. Even a human covenant, once it is ratified, cannot be canceled or amended. 16 The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. The Scripture does not say, “and to seeds,” meaning many, but “and to your seed,” meaning One, who is Christ.

17 What I mean is this: The law that came 430 years later does not revoke the covenant previously established by God, so as to nullify the promise. 18 For if the inheritance depends on the law, then it no longer depends on a promise; but God freely granted it to Abraham through a promise.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul uses a human agreement to explain the lasting force of God’s promise. His illustration begins with a covenant already ratified, which cannot then be canceled or have new conditions added to it.

He says the promises were spoken to Abraham and his seed, and he identifies that seed as Christ. The promise therefore reaches its fulfillment through the One Paul has been proclaiming.

The law came 430 years later, but its later arrival does not revoke the covenant God had already established. Paul’s point concerns the continuing force of the promise.

He concludes by distinguishing an inheritance dependent on law from one granted by promise. God freely gave it to Abraham through a promise. The arrival of the law cannot turn that gift into something secured on a different basis.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as defending God’s promise against the claim that the later law displaced it. Wesley’s notes on verses 15–18 and the USCCB notes on verses 15–18 both connect the illustration with the inheritance given by promise and its fulfillment through Christ.
passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 6:13–20 also returns to God’s promise to Abraham and the oath confirming it. God’s unchanging purpose becomes a reason for hope, pictured as an anchor reaching into His presence, where Jesus has entered on our behalf.

That explicit connection shows why the certainty of God’s promise matters for believers. Their hope rests in the God who is faithful to what He has said and in the Son through whom they draw near to Him.

passages.title: Galatians 3:19-25
passages.section_title: Why did God give the law if it could not give life?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 Why then was the law given? It was added because of transgressions, until the arrival of the seed to whom the promise referred. It was administered through angels by a mediator. 20 A mediator is unnecessary, however, for only one party; but God is one. 21 Is the law, then, opposed to the promises of God? Certainly not! For if a law had been given that could impart life, then righteousness would certainly have come from the law. 22 But the Scripture pronounces all things confined by sin, so that by faith in Jesus Christ the promise might be given to those who believe. 23 Before this faith came, we were held in custody under the law, locked up until faith should be revealed. 24 So the law became our guardian to lead us to Christ, that we might be justified by faith. 25 Now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian.
paragraphs: 19 Why then was the law given? It was added because of transgressions, until the arrival of the seed to whom the promise referred. It was administered through angels by a mediator. 20 A mediator is unnecessary, however, for only one party; but God is one.

21 Is the law, then, opposed to the promises of God? Certainly not! For if a law had been given that could impart life, then righteousness would certainly have come from the law. 22 But the Scripture pronounces all things confined by sin, so that by faith in Jesus Christ the promise might be given to those who believe.

23 Before this faith came, we were held in custody under the law, locked up until faith should be revealed. 24 So the law became our guardian to lead us to Christ, that we might be justified by faith. 25 Now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul now asks the question raised by his defense of the promise: why was the law given? He says it was added because of transgressions, until the promised seed came. Its role belongs within the story leading to Christ.

He describes the law as administered through angels by a mediator, someone acting between parties, then points out that a mediator involves more than one party while God is one. The brief statement sits within his comparison of the law with God’s promise.

He directly rejects the idea that the law opposes God’s promises. The law cannot impart life. Scripture confines everything under sin so that the promise through faith in Jesus Christ may be given to those who believe.

Paul then pictures life under the law as a time of custody. The word translated guardian is παιδαγωγός, paidagōgos (pie-dah-go-GOSS), a child’s guide or guardian. Thayer’s lexicon explains that sense of supervision and applies it to the law preparing people for Christ.

His point concerns the change Christ brings. The law’s guardianship led toward being justified by faith. Now that faith has come, he says they are no longer under that guardian.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the law as exposing sin and preparing for Christ, while being unable to give the life He brings. The Catholic Catechism, paragraphs 1963–1964, explicitly uses the guardian picture: the law shows what is needed and prepares people for the Savior, while the grace of the Spirit supplies the strength it cannot itself give.

One common reading of the brief mediator statement contrasts the law’s mediated delivery with God’s direct promise. Wesley’s note on verse 20 and the USCCB notes on verses 19–20 both explain the contrast in that direction.

Christians differ in how they describe the law’s continuing place in life with Christ. The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 19, distinguishes ceremonies fulfilled in Christ from moral commands that continue to guide believers. Dallas Theological Seminary, article V, describes the Mosaic law and the present rule of grace as distinct periods with different responsibilities. Its statement also insists that salvation has always been by grace through faith. Both statements distinguish God’s instruction for His people from trying to earn salvation.
passages.god_plan_html:
Luke 24:44–47 records Jesus explaining that the Law of Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms find their fulfillment in Him. His suffering and resurrection lead to the proclamation of repentance and forgiveness in His name to all nations.

That explicit account places the law within God’s larger saving story. Its place is understood in relation to the Christ it points toward and the life and forgiveness being proclaimed through Him.

passages.title: Galatians 3:26
passages.section_title: How do we become God’s children in Christ?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 26 You are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus.
paragraphs: 26 You are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus.

passages.context_html:
This verse follows Paul’s explanation of the law as a guardian leading toward Christ. He now describes the believers’ standing as sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus.

The full paragraph, Galatians 3:26–29, connects that standing with baptism into Christ, shared belonging across human boundaries and inheritance according to Abraham’s promise.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as locating belonging to God’s family in faith in Christ. Wesley’s note on verse 26 connects sonship with the change from guardianship, and the USCCB note on verses 23–29 places the statement within the promise and inheritance described throughout the paragraph.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Baptism reads verses 26–27 as distinguishing sonship through faith from being clothed with Christ in baptism. Its position is that faith establishes the saved relationship with God, and water baptism follows as the appointed act in which the believer puts on Christ for a new life of obedience. The study sums up that distinction as faith saving and baptism clothing the believer with Christ.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 8:14–17 connects being God’s children with the Spirit’s witness, calling God Father and being heirs with Christ. That shared inheritance reaches through present suffering toward glory with Him.

The family language here therefore carries a future as well as a present hope. Those who belong to Christ share the promise and a life directed toward what God has prepared for His children.

passages.title: Galatians 3:26-27
passages.section_title: How do faith and being clothed with Christ belong together?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 26 You are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus. 27 For all of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ.
paragraphs: 26 You are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus. 27 For all of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ.

passages.context_html:
Paul moves from the law’s guardianship to the believers’ identity in Christ. He names sonship through faith and describes those baptized into Christ as having clothed themselves with Him.

The surrounding paragraph, Galatians 3:26–29, explains the shared family and inheritance that follow. People across the boundaries of Jew and Greek, slave and free, male and female are one in Christ and heirs according to the promise.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly see faith, belonging to Christ and shared life in God’s family at the center of these verses. They differ in how they explain the relationship between baptism and that belonging.

The Catholic Church teaches that baptism gives new birth, adoption and membership in Christ’s body. The Catechism, paragraphs 1265–1267, describes this as God’s gift of grace, enabling faith, hope and love.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 28, describes water baptism as a sign and pledge of being joined to Christ. It distinguishes the time of receiving the rite from the time the Spirit gives the grace promised. The 1689 Baptist Confession, chapter 29, describes baptism as a sign of sharing in Christ’s death and resurrection, given to those who profess repentance and faith.

Dallas Theological Seminary, articles XIII–XIV, distinguishes the Spirit’s work of joining believers into Christ’s body from water baptism as testimony. It describes water baptism as an act of testimony.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Baptism reads verses 26–27 as distinguishing sonship through faith from being clothed with Christ in baptism. Its position is that faith establishes the saved relationship with God, and water baptism follows as the appointed act in which the believer puts on Christ for a new life of obedience. The study sums up that distinction as faith saving and baptism clothing the believer with Christ.

passages.section_title: Who belongs to the family and the promise?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 26 You are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus. 27 For all of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ. 28 There is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus. 29 And if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed and heirs according to the promise.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.context_html:
After describing the law’s guardianship, Paul tells the believers who they are: God’s sons through faith in Christ Jesus. He connects their baptism into Christ with being clothed with Christ.

That belonging is shared. Jew and Greek, slave and free, male and female are all one in Christ Jesus. Paul includes people across these boundaries in the family and inheritance he is describing.

He then returns to Abraham’s promise. If they belong to Christ, they are Abraham’s seed and heirs according to the promise. Their place in God’s family rests in belonging to Christ.

The next chapter develops the inheritance picture through the comparison of a young heir with a son who has come into the freedom appointed by the father.

passages.title: Galatians 4:1-7
passages.section_title: How does God bring us into His family?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 What I am saying is that as long as the heir is a child, he is no different from a slave, although he is the owner of everything. 2 He is subject to guardians and trustees until the date set by his father. 3 So also, when we were children, we were enslaved under the basic principles of the world. 4 But when the time had fully come, God sent His Son, born of a woman, born under the law, 5 to redeem those under the law, that we might receive our adoption as sons. 6 And because you are sons, God sent the Spirit of His Son into our hearts, crying out, “Abba, Father!” 7 So you are no longer a slave, but a son; and since you are a son, you are also an heir through God.
paragraphs: 1 What I am saying is that as long as the heir is a child, he is no different from a slave, although he is the owner of everything. 2 He is subject to guardians and trustees until the date set by his father. 3 So also, when we were children, we were enslaved under the basic principles of the world.

4 But when the time had fully come, God sent His Son, born of a woman, born under the law, 5 to redeem those under the law, that we might receive our adoption as sons. 6 And because you are sons, God sent the Spirit of His Son into our hearts, crying out, “Abba, Father!” 7 So you are no longer a slave, but a son; and since you are a son, you are also an heir through God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul continues the picture of an inheritance from the end of chapter 3. A child may be the heir to everything, yet still live under guardians and trustees. The child cannot simply take charge of the inheritance; the father has set the time for that change.

Paul uses this picture to describe the earlier condition of bondage. Then comes the turning point: God sent His Son at the appointed time. Jesus was born of a woman and born under the law, entering the situation of those He came to redeem.

The purpose reaches beyond release from bondage. God acts so that we may receive adoption as His sons. Paul includes women in this family language, as he has already made clear in 3:26–29. The family shares an inheritance through God.

God also sends the Spirit of His Son into their hearts. The cry to God is that of children addressing their Father. The word Ἀββᾶ, Abba (ah-BAH), is an Aramaic form of address meaning Father. Thayer’s lexicon identifies its use in prayer to God.

Paul ends with the change in their standing: a son and an heir through God. His appeal rests on what the Father has done through His Son and Spirit.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this passage as describing the Father’s saving work through the Son and the Spirit, bringing believers into His family with the standing of heirs. Wesley’s notes on verses 1–7 and the USCCB notes on verses 1–7 both follow that movement from guardianship and bondage to belonging with God.
passages.god_plan_html:
The same address appears on Jesus’ lips in Mark 14:36, when He prays to His Father in Gethsemane. In Romans 8:15–17, believers also cry to God as Father through the Spirit and are described as heirs with Christ.

These connections show the depth of the welcome Paul describes. Through the Son and His Spirit, people are brought into a relationship with the Father that shapes their prayer and their hope. Romans also connects that shared inheritance with sharing Christ’s sufferings and future glory.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Galatians 4:8-11
passages.section_title: Why does Paul fear they are returning to slavery?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 Formerly, when you did not know God, you were slaves to those who by nature are not gods. 9 But now that you know God, or rather are known by God, how is it that you are turning back to those weak and worthless principles? Do you wish to be enslaved by them all over again? 10 You are observing special days and months and seasons and years! 11 I fear for you, that my efforts for you may have been in vain.
paragraphs: 8 Formerly, when you did not know God, you were slaves to those who by nature are not gods. 9 But now that you know God, or rather are known by God, how is it that you are turning back to those weak and worthless principles? Do you wish to be enslaved by them all over again?
10 You are observing special days and months and seasons and years! 11 I fear for you, that my efforts for you may have been in vain.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul turns directly to the Galatians’ earlier life. Before they knew God, they served things that were not gods by nature. Their former bondage was bound up with false worship.

Now their relationship with God has changed. Paul even corrects the direction of his wording: they know God, and more fundamentally they are known by Him. Against that background, their movement toward bondage again seems deeply troubling.

He points to their observance of special days, months, seasons and years. In the flow of the letter, this warning belongs with the pressure to place themselves under the law. The issue is serious enough for Paul to fear that his labor among them may have been in vain.

The BSB uses basic principles for the expression in verse 3 and principles in verse 9. Its footnotes also give elemental forces as a possible rendering. The phrase has been understood in more than one way, but Paul’s immediate concern is clear: people welcomed by God are turning toward something he describes as weak and unable to give them freedom.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley’s notes on verses 8–11 and the USCCB notes on verses 8–11 connect Paul’s warning with religious observances being pressed on the Galatians. Both understand him to be warning against renewed bondage.

They explain the underlying principles differently. Wesley’s note on verse 9 emphasizes the elementary instruction associated with the Mosaic law. The USCCB note on verse 3 considers the expression more likely to refer to heavenly powers understood in pagan circles to control the world. That difference concerns what lies behind Paul’s language; both readings recognize his urgent appeal to remain in the freedom God has given.
passages.god_plan_html:
Colossians 2:16–23 makes a related connection between religious regulations and Christ. Food rules and calendar observances are described as shadows whose reality belongs to Him. Paul also points to growth coming from Christ, the head of His body.

That wider picture helps explain why the warning matters. God’s purpose is a people receiving life and growth through Christ. Rules that appear impressive cannot supply that life or overcome the desires of the flesh by their own power.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Galatians 4:12-20
passages.section_title: What does Paul want to see take shape in them?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 I beg you, brothers, become like me, for I became like you. You have done me no wrong. 13 You know that it was because of an illness that I first preached the gospel to you. 14 And although my illness was a trial to you, you did not despise or reject me. Instead, you welcomed me as if I were an angel of God, as if I were Christ Jesus Himself. 15 What then has become of your blessing? For I can testify that, if it were possible, you would have torn out your eyes and given them to me. 16 Have I now become your enemy by telling you the truth? 17 Those people are zealous for you, but not in a good way. Instead, they want to isolate you from us, so that you may be zealous for them. 18 Nevertheless, it is good to be zealous if it serves a noble purpose—at any time, and not only when I am with you. 19 My children, for whom I am again in the pains of childbirth until Christ is formed in you, 20 how I wish I could be with you now and change my tone, because I am perplexed about you.
paragraphs: 12 I beg you, brothers, become like me, for I became like you. You have done me no wrong. 13 You know that it was because of an illness that I first preached the gospel to you. 14 And although my illness was a trial to you, you did not despise or reject me. Instead, you welcomed me as if I were an angel of God, as if I were Christ Jesus Himself. 15 What then has become of your blessing? For I can testify that, if it were possible, you would have torn out your eyes and given them to me. 16 Have I now become your enemy by telling you the truth?

17 Those people are zealous for you, but not in a good way. Instead, they want to isolate you from us, so that you may be zealous for them. 18 Nevertheless, it is good to be zealous if it serves a noble purpose—at any time, and not only when I am with you. 19 My children, for whom I am again in the pains of childbirth until Christ is formed in you, 20 how I wish I could be with you now and change my tone, because I am perplexed about you.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul’s appeal becomes personal. He asks the Galatians to become like him, reminding them that he became like them. This follows his defense of living through faith in Christ and his concern about their desire to come under the law.

He recalls the illness that led to his first preaching among them. Although his condition was a trial to them, they received him with extraordinary welcome. He remembers their willingness, if possible, to give him their own eyes. The passage describes both illness and affection, but it never names the illness.

Now he asks whether telling them the truth has made him their enemy. Other people are eagerly pursuing them, but Paul says their purpose is to isolate the Galatians so that their loyalty will turn toward those teachers.

Paul does not condemn enthusiasm itself. He welcomes zeal directed toward a good purpose, whether he is present or absent. The question is what that eagerness is producing.

He calls them his children and compares his concern to the pains of childbirth. What he longs for is Christ being formed in them. His wish to be present and change his tone reveals how troubled he is about their condition.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a deeply personal appeal from a teacher concerned for people he loves. Wesley’s notes on verses 12–20 and the USCCB notes on verses 12–20 both connect the memories of their first welcome with Paul’s distress over the influence now pulling them away. The goal stated in verse 19 is their growth in Christ.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 8:29 describes God’s purpose as His people being conformed to the image of His Son, who is the firstborn among many brothers. That gives a wider setting for Paul’s desire to see Christ formed in the Galatians.

The aim of his care reaches beyond gaining a hearing or restoring personal loyalty. Their lives are to take the shape of the Son in whose family they belong. Paul’s labor serves that larger purpose.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Galatians 4:21-31
passages.section_title: Why does Paul compare two mothers and two sons?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 Tell me, you who want to be under the law, do you not understand what the law says? 22 For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by the slave woman and the other by the free woman. 23 His son by the slave woman was born according to the flesh, but his son by the free woman was born through the promise. 24 These things serve as illustrations, for the women represent two covenants. One covenant is from Mount Sinai and bears children into slavery: This is Hagar. 25 Now Hagar stands for Mount Sinai in Arabia and corresponds to the present-day Jerusalem, because she is in slavery with her children. 26 But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother. 27 For it is written: “Rejoice, O barren woman, who bears no children; break forth and cry aloud, you who have never travailed; because more are the children of the desolate woman than of her who has a husband.” 28 Now you, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise. 29 At that time, however, the son born by the flesh persecuted the son born by the Spirit. It is the same now. 30 But what does the Scripture say? “Expel the slave woman and her son, for the slave woman’s son will never share in the inheritance with the free woman’s son.” 31 Therefore, brothers, we are not children of the slave woman, but of the free woman.
paragraphs: 21 Tell me, you who want to be under the law, do you not understand what the law says? 22 For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by the slave woman and the other by the free woman. 23 His son by the slave woman was born according to the flesh, but his son by the free woman was born through the promise. 24 These things serve as illustrations, for the women represent two covenants. One covenant is from Mount Sinai and bears children into slavery: This is Hagar.

25 Now Hagar stands for Mount Sinai in Arabia and corresponds to the present-day Jerusalem, because she is in slavery with her children. 26 But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother. 27 For it is written: “Rejoice, O barren woman, who bears no children; break forth and cry aloud, you who have never travailed; because more are the children of the desolate woman than of her who has a husband.” 28 Now you, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise.

29 At that time, however, the son born by the flesh persecuted the son born by the Spirit. It is the same now. 30 But what does the Scripture say? “Expel the slave woman and her son, for the slave woman’s son will never share in the inheritance with the free woman’s son.” 31 Therefore, brothers, we are not children of the slave woman, but of the free woman.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul addresses those who want to be under the law by asking them to listen to what it says. He turns to Abraham’s family in Genesis 16 and Genesis 21: one son was born to Hagar, a slave woman, and the other to Sarah, a free woman. Paul contrasts birth according to the flesh with birth through God’s promise.

He then explains the comparison he is making. The women represent two covenants. Hagar corresponds to Mount Sinai and the present Jerusalem, which he describes as in slavery with her children. The Jerusalem above is free and is the mother of those he addresses.

Paul brings in Isaiah 54:1, where a barren woman is called to rejoice over the many children she will have. He applies this promise-shaped picture to the Galatians: like Isaac, they are children of promise.

The comparison also addresses opposition. Paul says that the son born according to the flesh persecuted the son born according to the Spirit, and that something similar is happening now. He then cites the expulsion of Hagar and her son to explain that the inheritance does not pass through the slave woman’s son.

His conclusion prepares for the next chapter’s call to stand in freedom. The Galatians belong with the free woman. The comparison challenges their wish to place themselves under the law after receiving the promise through Christ.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley’s notes on verses 21–31 and the USCCB notes on verses 21–31 both read Paul’s comparison as supporting his earlier teaching about promise and freedom. They connect the inheritance with God’s promise and understand the Galatians to be included among its children.

The comparison follows the connections Paul himself identifies in this passage. It does not require treating every detail of Abraham’s family as a hidden code, and it gives no basis for treating Jewish people with contempt.
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul explicitly brings Isaiah 54:1 into this account. In its wider setting, verses 1–10 promise renewed life, an expanding family and God’s enduring compassion to a woman pictured as desolate. Paul uses its opening promise to help explain the family God is bringing into being.

Hebrews 12:18–24 also sets Sinai alongside the heavenly Jerusalem. It describes believers approaching that city, the gathered people of God, and Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant. This is an explicit New Testament connection between the heavenly city and the welcome made possible through Jesus.

Together these passages place Paul’s family comparison within the larger hope of God gathering His people through His promise and His Son. The connections are stated in Scripture; they do not depend on inventing an additional meaning for every person or place in the Genesis account.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Galatians 5:1-6
passages.section_title: Why must they stand firm in the freedom Christ gives?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 It is for freedom that Christ has set us free. Stand firm, then, and do not be encumbered once more by a yoke of slavery. 2 Take notice: I, Paul, tell you that if you let yourselves be circumcised, Christ will be of no value to you at all. 3 Again I testify to every man who gets himself circumcised that he is obligated to obey the whole law. 4 You who are trying to be justified by the law have been severed from Christ; you have fallen away from grace. 5 But by faith we eagerly await through the Spirit the hope of righteousness. 6 For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any value. What matters is faith expressing itself through love.
paragraphs: 1 It is for freedom that Christ has set us free. Stand firm, then, and do not be encumbered once more by a yoke of slavery. 2 Take notice: I, Paul, tell you that if you let yourselves be circumcised, Christ will be of no value to you at all. 3 Again I testify to every man who gets himself circumcised that he is obligated to obey the whole law. 4 You who are trying to be justified by the law have been severed from Christ; you have fallen away from grace.

5 But by faith we eagerly await through the Spirit the hope of righteousness. 6 For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any value. What matters is faith expressing itself through love.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul draws the conclusion of his comparison of the free woman and the slave woman: Christ has set His people free, and they must stand firm in that freedom. Taking on the yoke again would reverse the direction of the gospel he has been explaining.

His warning about circumcision belongs in that setting. Verse 4 identifies the issue as trying to be justified by the law. Accepting circumcision on those terms places a person under an obligation to keep the whole law, while treating Christ as unable to supply what is needed.

Paul uses severe language: those seeking justification that way have been severed from Christ and have fallen away from grace. The warning calls for a decisive return to dependence on Christ.

He then describes the hope of those who wait through the Spirit, by faith. Their future rests with God. In Christ, neither being circumcised nor being uncircumcised supplies the standing they need. What matters is faith expressing itself through love.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand this as a warning against seeking justification through the law and circumcision. Wesley’s notes on verses 1–6 and the USCCB notes on verses 1–6 both connect freedom in Christ with faith that acts through love.

Christians differ over how the warning about falling from grace relates to a believer’s final salvation. The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 17, teaches that those truly accepted in Christ will persevere to the end, while acknowledging that they can fall into serious sin and suffer its consequences. Within that framework, the warning cannot mean that God finally abandons someone He has truly saved.

The Methodist Articles of Religion, article XII, teach that people who have received the Holy Spirit may depart from grace and fall into sin, and that God’s grace makes repentance and restoration possible. The Catholic Catechism, paragraph 162, likewise teaches that faith is God’s free gift and can be lost. These teachings allow the warning to address a real turning away from grace already received. They also leave room for return and repentance.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 8:23–25 connects the Spirit’s presence with waiting for the redemption of our bodies. Hope concerns what God has promised and what His people do not yet see.

That larger horizon helps explain the waiting in verse 5. Life through the Spirit includes confidence in God’s coming completion of His work. The freedom Christ gives leads His people toward that hope, with faith taking visible shape in love now.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Galatians 5:7-12
passages.section_title: What has interrupted their progress in the truth?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 You were running so well. Who has obstructed you from obeying the truth? 8 Such persuasion does not come from the One who calls you. 9 A little leaven works through the whole batch of dough. 10 I am confident in the Lord that you will take no other view. The one who is troubling you will bear the judgment, whoever he may be. 11 Now, brothers, if I am still preaching circumcision, why am I still being persecuted? In that case the offense of the cross has been abolished. 12 As for those who are agitating you, I wish they would proceed to emasculate themselves!
paragraphs: 7 You were running so well. Who has obstructed you from obeying the truth? 8 Such persuasion does not come from the One who calls you. 9 A little leaven works through the whole batch of dough. 10 I am confident in the Lord that you will take no other view. The one who is troubling you will bear the judgment, whoever he may be.

11 Now, brothers, if I am still preaching circumcision, why am I still being persecuted? In that case the offense of the cross has been abolished. 12 As for those who are agitating you, I wish they would proceed to emasculate themselves!

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul pictures the Galatians as runners whose good progress has been obstructed. The persuasion turning them aside does not come from the God who called them. Like a small amount of leaven spreading through dough, the influence can affect the whole community.

His confidence is in the Lord: he expects them to return to the right understanding. At the same time, he says the person troubling them will bear judgment, whoever that person may be.

Paul then asks why he would still be persecuted if he were still preaching circumcision. His suffering gives the lie to the idea that circumcision as a requirement belongs to his message. A message that removed the offense of the cross would be a different message.

The final sentence is deliberately shocking. In the BSB, Paul wishes that those pressing circumcision would go on to emasculate themselves. His language exposes the destructive direction of their teaching and the intensity of his concern.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly see this as a warning about an influence spreading through the churches and pulling them away from the gospel. Wesley’s notes on verses 7–11 and the USCCB notes on verses 7–12 connect the obstruction, the leaven and the persecution with the pressure to add circumcision to the message of Christ.

The final expression has been explained differently. Wesley’s note on verse 12 takes the older wording about being cut off as removal from the church’s fellowship. The USCCB note understands a biting wish that the knife would go beyond circumcision, corresponding to the BSB’s explicit wording about emasculation.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Corinthians 1:18–25 explains why the cross can be an offense: what some regard as foolish or a stumbling block is the place where God’s power and wisdom are made known through Christ.

That connection gives a larger setting for Paul’s question here. The unwelcome part of his message belongs to God’s saving work through the crucified Christ. Making the message easier to accept by changing its basis would remove the very thing he has been sent to proclaim.
