passages.title: Galatians 5:13-15
passages.section_title: What is freedom meant to produce among us?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 For you, brothers, were called to freedom; but do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh. Rather, serve one another in love. 14 The entire law is fulfilled in a single decree: “Love your neighbor as yourself.” 15 But if you keep on biting and devouring one another, watch out, or you will be consumed by one another.
paragraphs: 13 For you, brothers, were called to freedom; but do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh. Rather, serve one another in love. 14 The entire law is fulfilled in a single decree: “Love your neighbor as yourself.” 15 But if you keep on biting and devouring one another, watch out, or you will be consumed by one another.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul returns to the freedom announced at the start of the chapter and explains how it is to be used. The flesh must not turn that freedom into an opening for self-indulgence. Love moves the believers to serve one another.

He sums up the law through the command to love one’s neighbor as oneself, quoting Leviticus 19:18. The command already appears in the law; Paul brings it forward to describe the kind of life the community is called to share.

His warning about biting and devouring one another shows what is at stake. Conflict can become mutually destructive. The freedom Christ gives is to be expressed in care for others, including how believers treat one another when tensions rise.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand these verses as joining freedom with loving service and warning against destructive conflict. Wesley’s notes on verses 13–15 and the USCCB notes on verses 13–15 both emphasize love of neighbor as the direction of a life freed through Christ.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Mark 10:42–45, Jesus teaches His disciples to serve and grounds that calling in His own coming to serve and give His life for many. In John 13:34–35, He makes love patterned after His own the identifying mark of His disciples.

These connections place the Galatians’ freedom within the life Jesus calls His people to share. Their service is shaped by the Son who gave Himself for them, and their love makes their belonging to Him visible.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Galatians 5:16-21
passages.section_title: What does walking by the Spirit turn us away from?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 So I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh. 17 For the flesh craves what is contrary to the Spirit, and the Spirit what is contrary to the flesh. They are opposed to each other, so that you do not do what you want. 18 But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law. 19 The acts of the flesh are obvious: sexual immorality, impurity, and debauchery; 20 idolatry and sorcery; hatred, discord, jealousy, and rage; rivalries, divisions, factions, 21 and envy; drunkenness, orgies, and the like. I warn you, as I did before, that those who practice such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.
paragraphs: 16 So I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh. 17 For the flesh craves what is contrary to the Spirit, and the Spirit what is contrary to the flesh. They are opposed to each other, so that you do not do what you want. 18 But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law.

19 The acts of the flesh are obvious: sexual immorality, impurity, and debauchery; 20 idolatry and sorcery; hatred, discord, jealousy, and rage; rivalries, divisions, factions, 21 and envy; drunkenness, orgies, and the like. I warn you, as I did before, that those who practice such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul now explains how the life of love is to be lived: walk by the Spirit. The Spirit and the flesh pull in opposing directions. Being led by the Spirit changes the believer’s relationship to the law and supplies a different direction for life.

He gives concrete examples of the flesh at work. Sexual wrongdoing, false worship and sorcery appear alongside hatred, jealousy, rage, rivalry and division. The list reaches into relationships throughout the community; the problem is much wider than bodily appetites alone.

The list ends with further examples and a warning Paul has already given them. Those who practice such things will not inherit God’s kingdom. The words carry the seriousness of the choice he is placing before his readers.

The next paragraph describes the fruit of the Spirit. The contrast shows why freedom cannot mean indifference to conduct. Life through the Spirit is meant to change the way people live together.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand this as a call to follow the Spirit and turn away from the conduct Paul names. Wesley’s notes on verses 16–21 and the USCCB notes on verses 16–25 connect the warning with the Spirit’s work in believers’ lives.

The wider difference over perseverance also affects how the kingdom warning is explained. The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 17, holds together God’s preservation of the truly saved and the real possibility of serious sins that grieve the Spirit. The Methodist Articles, article XII, allow for departure from grace and restoration through repentance. The warning is taken seriously within both frameworks; they differ over whether final falling away can occur after genuine salvation.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 8:9–13 also connects the Spirit’s presence with belonging to Christ and putting the body’s sinful deeds to death. It places this changed life within the hope of the God who raised Jesus giving life to mortal bodies.

That connection joins present obedience with God’s larger work of life and resurrection. The call to turn from the flesh belongs to the hope of sharing the life God gives through His risen Son.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Galatians 5:22-26
passages.section_title: What kind of life does the Spirit grow in us?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, 23 gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law. 24 Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires. 25 Since we live by the Spirit, let us walk in step with the Spirit. 26 Let us not become conceited, provoking and envying one another.
paragraphs: 22 But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, 23 gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law. 24 Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.
25 Since we live by the Spirit, let us walk in step with the Spirit. 26 Let us not become conceited, provoking and envying one another.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul turns from the acts of the flesh to the fruit of the Spirit. Love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control describe the character of the life the Spirit produces.

He says there is no law against these things. They fit the life of love he has called the community to practice. Their source is the Spirit at work in those who belong to Christ.

Belonging to Christ also means that the flesh, with its passions and desires, has been crucified. Paul then joins the gift of life through the Spirit with the call to walk in step with Him. What God gives is to shape the believers’ daily conduct.

The closing warning makes that conduct especially practical: they must turn from conceit, provoking one another and envy. The fruit Paul names is to be seen in how they live with each other.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the fruit as character produced through the Spirit’s work in Christ’s people, with the call to keep following His lead. Wesley’s notes on verses 22–26 and the USCCB notes on verses 19–25 connect this fruit with the changed life Paul describes.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus’ picture of the vine and branches in John 15:1–8 gives a related picture of fruitfulness. The branches bear fruit as they remain in Him, and their fruit glorifies the Father.

This is a parallel to Paul’s description, rather than a claim that Jesus lists the same nine qualities there. Both passages connect a fruitful life with God’s work and an ongoing relationship with Christ. The change in His people serves the Father’s glory.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Galatians 6:1-5
passages.section_title: How do we help someone who has fallen into sin?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Brothers, if someone is caught in a trespass, you who are spiritual should restore him with a spirit of gentleness. But watch yourself, or you also may be tempted. 2 Carry one another’s burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ. 3 If anyone thinks he is something when he is nothing, he deceives himself. 4 Each one should test his own work. Then he will have reason to boast in himself alone, and not in someone else. 5 For each one should carry his own load.
paragraphs: 1 Brothers, if someone is caught in a trespass, you who are spiritual should restore him with a spirit of gentleness. But watch yourself, or you also may be tempted. 2 Carry one another’s burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ.

3 If anyone thinks he is something when he is nothing, he deceives himself. 4 Each one should test his own work. Then he will have reason to boast in himself alone, and not in someone else. 5 For each one should carry his own load.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul carries the discussion of life by the Spirit into a situation where someone has been caught in a trespass. Those who are spiritual are to restore that person with gentleness. The quality just named as fruit of the Spirit in 5:23 is needed in the work of helping someone return.

The person offering help must also watch himself. Temptation is a danger for him too. Paul’s instruction calls for humility alongside the work of restoration.

Carrying one another’s burdens fulfills the law of Christ. The Greek word behind burdens is βάρος, baros (BAH-ross), meaning weight or burden. Thayer’s lexicon connects its use here with bearing another person’s troublesome faults. The surrounding passage brings that shared help into the setting of sin, temptation and restoration.

Paul then warns against self-deception and tells each person to test his own work. Comparing ourselves with someone else can give a false sense of importance. Each person has responsibility for his own conduct.

The call to carry one another’s burdens and the statement that each carries his own load belong together. Helping someone does not remove that person’s responsibility, and personal responsibility does not cancel the call to help.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as a call to restore others gently, remain humble about one’s own vulnerability and give practical help. Wesley’s notes on verses 1–5 and the USCCB notes on verses 1–5 both connect burden-sharing with Christ’s command of love and self-examination with the correction of pride.
passages.god_plan_html:
John 13:34–35 connects love among Jesus’ disciples with His own love for them. 1 John 3:16–18 makes the connection concrete: Jesus laid down His life for us, and love for others is to take shape in action, including help for a brother in need.

These passages show how mutual burden-sharing belongs to God’s larger work through His Son. The love shown in Christ’s self-giving becomes visible in a family that cares for its members. Helping one another is part of making that love known.
passages.current_position_html: Our study What Is the True Church?, in its section on bearing one another’s burdens, understands this as costly, practical care within God’s family. Sharing a burden means walking with someone through the struggle, offering sustained presence and help. The study treats that shared life as love in action, made possible by grace.

passages.title: Galatians 6:2
passages.section_title: What does carrying one another’s burdens look like?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 2 Carry one another’s burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ.
paragraphs: 2 Carry one another’s burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ.

passages.context_html:
This verse belongs to Galatians 6:1–5, where Paul tells believers to restore someone caught in sin with gentleness and to watch their own vulnerability to temptation.

Carrying another person’s burdens gives practical shape to the love described in 5:13–14. It helps explain what fulfilling the law of Christ looks like in shared life.

The surrounding warning against pride matters. The helper must examine his own work, and each person remains responsible for his own conduct. Paul brings mutual help and personal responsibility into the same paragraph.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the law of Christ here as the call to love expressed through practical help. Wesley’s note on verse 2 describes sympathy and assistance in weaknesses and trials, and the USCCB note on verse 2 connects it with serving one another through love.
passages.current_position_html: Our study What Is the True Church?, in its section on bearing one another’s burdens, understands this as costly, practical care within God’s family. Sharing a burden means walking with someone through the struggle, offering sustained presence and help. The study treats that shared life as love in action, made possible by grace.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
John 13:34–35 connects love among Jesus’ disciples with His own love for them. 1 John 3:16–18 makes the connection concrete: Jesus laid down His life for us, and love for others is to take shape in action, including help for a brother in need.

These passages show how mutual burden-sharing belongs to God’s larger work through His Son. The love shown in Christ’s self-giving becomes visible in a family that cares for its members. Helping one another is part of making that love known.

passages.title: Galatians 6:6-10
passages.section_title: Why should we keep doing good when the harvest takes time?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 Nevertheless, the one who receives instruction in the word must share in all good things with his instructor. 7 Do not be deceived: God is not to be mocked. Whatever a man sows, he will reap in return. 8 The one who sows to please his flesh, from the flesh will reap destruction; but the one who sows to please the Spirit, from the Spirit will reap eternal life. 9 Let us not grow weary in well-doing, for in due time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up. 10 Therefore, as we have opportunity, let us do good to everyone, and especially to the family of faith.
paragraphs: 6 Nevertheless, the one who receives instruction in the word must share in all good things with his instructor. 7 Do not be deceived: God is not to be mocked. Whatever a man sows, he will reap in return. 8 The one who sows to please his flesh, from the flesh will reap destruction; but the one who sows to please the Spirit, from the Spirit will reap eternal life.

9 Let us not grow weary in well-doing, for in due time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up. 10 Therefore, as we have opportunity, let us do good to everyone, and especially to the family of faith.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul continues with practical responsibilities in the community. Someone receiving instruction in the word is to share good things with the instructor. Giving and receiving within the family of faith includes supporting those who teach.

He then warns that God cannot be mocked. The picture of sowing and reaping makes the connection between a life’s direction and its outcome. Sowing to please the flesh leads to destruction; sowing to please the Spirit leads to eternal life.

Paul’s encouragement recognizes that doing good can become tiring. The harvest comes in its proper time, so he urges his readers to keep going. Perseverance matters in the life he is describing.

He ends with the opportunities in front of them: do good to everyone, especially the family of faith. Care within the church has a particular place, while the call to do good reaches beyond it.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read this as joining support for teachers, responsibility before God and patient persistence in doing good. Wesley’s notes on verses 6–10 connect the harvest of life with God’s free grace and power. The USCCB notes on verses 6 and 10 identify practical support for instruction and the wide reach of doing good, with particular responsibility toward fellow believers.

The sowing picture follows Paul’s contrast between flesh and Spirit. It does not supply a guaranteed financial return for a donation. The outcome he names is much larger than personal prosperity.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Corinthians 15:50–58 places perseverance within the hope of resurrection and God’s victory over death through Jesus Christ. Paul therefore urges believers to remain steadfast, knowing their labor in the Lord is not in vain.

That connection gives a wider reason to continue when doing good is costly or its results are hidden. The coming harvest belongs to the God who gives life through His risen Son. Present faithfulness is lived in the light of that future.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Galatians 6:11-16
passages.section_title: What counts when we belong to Christ?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 See what large letters I am using to write to you with my own hand! 12 Those who want to make a good impression outwardly are trying to compel you to be circumcised. They only do this to avoid persecution for the cross of Christ. 13 For the circumcised do not even keep the law themselves, yet they want you to be circumcised that they may boast in your flesh. 14 But as for me, may I never boast, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world. 15 For neither circumcision nor uncircumcision means anything. What counts is a new creation. 16 Peace and mercy to all who walk by this rule, even to the Israel of God.
paragraphs: 11 See what large letters I am using to write to you with my own hand! 12 Those who want to make a good impression outwardly are trying to compel you to be circumcised. They only do this to avoid persecution for the cross of Christ. 13 For the circumcised do not even keep the law themselves, yet they want you to be circumcised that they may boast in your flesh.

14 But as for me, may I never boast, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world. 15 For neither circumcision nor uncircumcision means anything. What counts is a new creation. 16 Peace and mercy to all who walk by this rule, even to the Israel of God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul calls attention to the large letters he is writing with his own hand. The personal note leads directly into his final contrast between the motives of those pressing circumcision and the message he has defended.

He says the teachers want an outwardly impressive result and are avoiding persecution for the cross of Christ. They do not keep the law themselves, yet want to boast about the Galatians’ circumcision.

Paul’s own boast is in the cross of the Lord Jesus Christ. Through it, the world has been crucified to him and he to the world. The relationship that matters is now centered on Christ and His self-giving.

Neither circumcision nor uncircumcision is decisive. What counts is a new creation. Paul pronounces peace and mercy on those who walk by this rule, using the expression the Israel of God.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly see the cross and new creation at the center of Paul’s closing appeal. Wesley’s notes on verses 11–16 and the USCCB notes on verses 11–16 connect this conclusion with the letter’s earlier warning against making circumcision the basis of belonging.

The expression the Israel of God is read in different ways. Wesley’s note on verse 16 identifies it with the church made up of people from every nation who follow this rule. The Catholic USCCB note on verse 16 allows the church as a possibility and also allows a reference to God’s ancient people, Israel. Its note recognizes the range of readings rather than defining one as the only Catholic position.

A dispensational reading, which keeps Israel and the church distinct, is explained in a faculty publication from Shepherds Theological Seminary. It understands the expression as Jewish believers within the churches, alongside Gentile believers who also follow Christ. This is the reading defended in that publication, rather than a statement that every evangelical Christian reads the verse that way.
passages.god_plan_html:
2 Corinthians 5:14–21 connects Christ’s death with a changed direction of life: those who live are to live for Him. It also explicitly describes anyone in Christ as a new creation and places that change within God’s work of reconciliation.

This connection brings the closing emphasis of Galatians into a larger picture. The cross leads to a people whose identity and way of life have been renewed through Christ. The new creation He brings is central to the peace and mercy Paul pronounces.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Galatians 6:17-18
passages.section_title: How does Paul bring his appeal to a close?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 From now on let no one cause me trouble, for I bear on my body the marks of Jesus. 18 The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen.
paragraphs: 17 From now on let no one cause me trouble, for I bear on my body the marks of Jesus. 18 The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul’s final request is that no one cause him further trouble. He points to the marks of Jesus that he bears on his body. After naming the desire to avoid persecution in verse 12, he directs attention to the bodily cost of his own service.

The letter then ends with a blessing: the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ with their spirit. Paul still addresses them as brothers. After the letter’s sharp warnings and urgent appeals, its closing word returns them to Christ’s grace.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand the marks as scars from Paul’s suffering in service to Christ. Wesley’s note on verse 17 takes them as the marks of affliction, and the USCCB note on verse 17 connects them with the sufferings described in his letters and Acts.
passages.god_plan_html:
In 2 Corinthians 4:7–12, Paul describes carrying the death of Jesus in his body so that Jesus’ life may also be revealed. Weakness and suffering become a setting in which God’s power is made known.

That explicit connection helps place the marks here within the pattern of service to the crucified and risen Lord. The scars point to the cost of Paul’s work, while the grace of Christ remains the gift he desires for the churches.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ephesians 1:1-2
passages.section_title: Who is this letter for, and what does Paul wish for them?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, To the saints in Ephesus, the faithful in Christ Jesus: 2 Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
paragraphs: 1 Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, To the saints in Ephesus, the faithful in Christ Jesus: 2 Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul introduces himself as an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God. His opening identifies both the One he serves and the source of his calling.

He addresses the saints in Ephesus, the faithful in Christ Jesus. Saints here names the people who belong to God. Their relationship with Christ is central to how Paul speaks about them throughout the letter.

The greeting asks grace and peace for them from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. The following blessing will explain the gifts of grace they have received in Christ, and the rest of the letter will show how that shared life is to be lived.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as identifying Paul’s calling and greeting God’s people in Christ. Wesley’s note on verse 1 emphasizes that his calling comes through God’s will rather than personal merit. The USCCB note on verses 1–2 places the greeting within the opening form of Paul’s letters.
passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 26:15–18 records Paul recounting Jesus’ commission to him. He is sent to open people’s eyes, turning them from darkness to light so that they may receive forgiveness and an inheritance among those sanctified by faith in Christ.

That explicit account gives a wider setting for the title apostle. Paul’s calling serves God’s purpose of bringing people to Christ, into forgiveness and shared belonging with His people. The letter’s opening addresses people already gathered into that life.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ephesians 1:3-6
passages.section_title: Why does Paul begin by praising God for choosing and adopting us?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 3 Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly realms. 4 For He chose us in Him before the foundation of the world to be holy and blameless in His presence. In love 5 He predestined us for adoption as His sons through Jesus Christ, according to the good pleasure of His will, 6 to the praise of His glorious grace, which He has freely given us in the Beloved One.
paragraphs: 3 Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly realms. 4 For He chose us in Him before the foundation of the world to be holy and blameless in His presence. In love 5 He predestined us for adoption as His sons through Jesus Christ, according to the good pleasure of His will, 6 to the praise of His glorious grace, which He has freely given us in the Beloved One.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul begins an extended blessing of God that continues through verse 14. He praises the Father for every spiritual blessing given in Christ. The gifts named in the paragraph include adoption, redemption, forgiveness and the promised Spirit.

He says God chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world, with the purpose that we should be holy and blameless in His presence. The blessing therefore reaches back beyond the believers’ own lifetimes and points toward the kind of people God intends them to be.

Paul then speaks of being predestined for adoption through Jesus Christ. The Greek word is προορίζω, proorizō (proh-or-ID-zoh), meaning to decide or appoint beforehand. Thayer’s lexicon gives that sense and identifies its use here with the purpose God has appointed for His people.

The purpose named is adoption as God’s sons through Jesus Christ. Paul speaks of God’s good pleasure and His freely given grace in the Beloved One. The passage is an expression of praise for that grace.

Holiness, belonging and praise all appear together. God’s choosing is described in relation to Christ and the family He is bringing into His presence.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly see God’s initiative, grace and purpose of adoption at the center of these verses. They differ over how His choosing relates to a person’s coming to faith.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 3, teaches that God chose particular people in Christ through His free grace and love, without basing that choice on foreseen faith or good works. In this reading, His choice is the source of their coming to faith and salvation.

In the Wesleyan reading, Wesley’s notes on verses 4–5 understand the chosen as those God foreknew as believing in Christ. He explains predestination here as God’s prior purpose that those who believe should enjoy adoption and inheritance with Christ. The Methodist Articles of Religion, article VIII, also insist that people cannot turn to faith by their own natural strength: God’s grace enables their response.

The Catholic Church describes God’s eternal plan as including each person’s free response to His grace in the Catechism, paragraph 600. Paragraphs 2012–2013 connect predestination and conformity to the Son with the call to holiness, lived through the strength Christ gives. This keeps God’s prior purpose and a grace-enabled human response together.
passages.god_plan_html:
Galatians 4:4–7 describes the Father sending His Son at the appointed time so that we might receive adoption, then sending the Spirit of His Son into our hearts. What Ephesians traces to God’s purpose before creation is also described as His work carried out through the Son and Spirit.

Romans 8:14–23 carries the family picture forward into shared inheritance with Christ, suffering, coming glory and the redemption of our bodies. Adoption belongs within that larger hope: God’s purpose brings His people into a life and future shared with His Son.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ephesians 1:7-10
passages.section_title: How does redemption belong to God’s larger purpose in Christ?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 In Him we have redemption through His blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of His grace 8 that He lavished on us with all wisdom and understanding. 9 And He has made known to us the mystery of His will according to His good pleasure, which He purposed in Christ 10 as a plan for the fullness of time, to bring all things in heaven and on earth together in Christ.
paragraphs: 7 In Him we have redemption through His blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of His grace 8 that He lavished on us with all wisdom and understanding.

9 And He has made known to us the mystery of His will according to His good pleasure, which He purposed in Christ 10 as a plan for the fullness of time, to bring all things in heaven and on earth together in Christ.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul continues the blessing that began in verse 3. After praising God for adoption through Jesus Christ, he names redemption through Christ’s blood and the forgiveness of our trespasses.

The Greek word for redemption is ἀπολύτρωσις, apolytrōsis (ah-poh-LOO-troh-sis). Thayer’s lexicon explains it as release obtained through a ransom payment and connects its use here with deliverance through Christ’s death. Paul’s words join the cost of that release with the riches of God’s grace.

God’s generosity also includes making His purpose known. The mystery in verse 9 is a purpose God has revealed in Christ. Thayer’s entry for mystery identifies this New Testament use with God’s saving purpose, once hidden and now made known.

Verse 10 states the reach of that purpose: all things in heaven and on earth brought together in Christ at the fullness of time. Forgiveness belongs within this larger Christ-centered purpose. The following verses continue with the place of God’s people and the promised Spirit.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand these verses as connecting forgiveness through Christ’s death with God’s revealed purpose to bring all things together in Him. Wesley’s notes on verses 7–10 and the USCCB notes on verses 3–14 and 9 both connect the gifts of grace with that larger purpose centered on Christ.
passages.god_plan_html:
Colossians 1:15–20 describes all things as created through the Son and for Him. It then connects reconciliation of things in heaven and on earth with the peace made through the blood of His cross. The same Son through whom creation exists is central to its reconciliation.

Romans 8:18–23 widens the hope beyond an individual’s forgiveness: creation itself waits for freedom from decay, alongside God’s children waiting for the redemption of their bodies.

Revelation 21:1–5 describes God dwelling with His people in a new heaven and new earth, with death and suffering removed. Revelation 22:1–5 adds the river and tree of life and the end of the curse. Read alongside the garden account in Genesis 3, these are strong connections between humanity’s broken beginning and the life God promises with Himself.

These passages give substance to the broad purpose named here. Christ’s redemption reaches toward a people and a creation freed to share life in God’s presence. That hope is grounded in the Son’s work, while each passage contributes its own part of the picture.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ephesians 1:11-12
passages.section_title: What is God’s purpose for those who first hoped in Christ?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 In Him we were also chosen as God’s own, having been predestined according to the plan of Him who works out everything by the counsel of His will, 12 in order that we, who were the first to hope in Christ, would be for the praise of His glory.
paragraphs: 11 In Him we were also chosen as God’s own, having been predestined according to the plan of Him who works out everything by the counsel of His will, 12 in order that we, who were the first to hope in Christ, would be for the praise of His glory.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul continues the same blessing of God, again locating His people’s standing in Christ. The BSB describes them as chosen as God’s own, according to the plan of the One who works everything by the counsel of His will.

The purpose is praise of His glory. Paul speaks of those who were the first to hope in Christ, then addresses his readers with you in verse 13. The movement will bring both groups into the same account of salvation, the Spirit and inheritance.

These verses therefore connect belonging to God with His continuing purpose. The people whose hope is in Christ are to be a living reason for His glory to be praised.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand these verses as joining God’s purpose, belonging in Christ and praise of His glory. Wesley’s notes on verses 11–12 identify those who first hoped as Jewish believers, in contrast with the Gentiles addressed next. The USCCB note on verse 12 also considers Jewish Christians the likely reference, while acknowledging other readings. On that common reading, Paul is preparing to describe the shared blessing of Jewish and Gentile believers.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Peter 1:3–9 also joins praise of the Father with new birth, living hope through Jesus’ resurrection and an inheritance kept for His people. It places that hope alongside present trials and the salvation to be revealed.

That explicit connection shows why the future God prepares matters for present life. Belonging to Him carries a hope that can sustain His people through suffering, with praise and glory reaching toward the revelation of Jesus Christ.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ephesians 1:13-14
passages.section_title: Why is the Holy Spirit called the pledge of our inheritance?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 And in Him, having heard and believed the word of truth—the gospel of your salvation—you were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, 14 who is the pledge of our inheritance until the redemption of those who are God’s possession, to the praise of His glory.
paragraphs: 13 And in Him, having heard and believed the word of truth—the gospel of your salvation—you were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, 14 who is the pledge of our inheritance until the redemption of those who are God’s possession, to the praise of His glory.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul now speaks directly to his readers: they too have heard the word of truth, the gospel of their salvation, and believed in Christ. He includes them in the blessing he has been describing.

They were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit. Thayer’s entry for sealing explains this use as God marking out His people through the gift of the Spirit. The image expresses belonging to Him.

The Spirit is also the pledge of their inheritance. The Greek word is ἀρραβών, arrabōn (ah-rah-BOHN), a down payment that pledges the full amount to come. Thayer’s lexicon identifies the Spirit’s gift here as both a foretaste and a pledge of future blessing.

Paul connects this gift with the coming redemption of those who are God’s possession. Their present life through the Spirit points toward what God will complete. The repeated purpose of the whole blessing returns once more: praise of His glory.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the Spirit as God’s gift marking His people and assuring them of the inheritance to come. They explain the sealing and its relation to faith, baptism and assurance in different ways.

The Catholic USCCB note on verse 13 connects the sealing with baptism. The Catechism, paragraphs 1272–1274, describes baptism’s permanent mark of belonging to Christ, while distinguishing that mark from sin’s ability to prevent the fruits of salvation. Paragraphs 1295–1296 also connect the seal of the Spirit with confirmation.

Wesley’s notes on verses 13–14 understand sealing in terms of God’s image impressed on the soul and fuller assurance of His promises, possibly after the first coming to faith. A different account of assurance appears in Dallas Theological Seminary’s statement, article X, which grounds the lasting security of every true believer in God’s purpose and the Spirit’s abiding presence. These are the teachings of the sources named, rather than one explanation shared by all Christians.
passages.god_plan_html:
2 Corinthians 5:1–5 also names the Spirit as God’s pledge. There Paul is speaking about mortal life being swallowed up by life and God preparing His people for that future.

That explicit connection gives a concrete horizon to the inheritance described here. The Spirit’s presence now belongs to God’s purpose of bringing His people into the life He has prepared, including the overcoming of bodily mortality.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Baptism, in its discussion of Ephesians 4:30, describes the Spirit as indwelling the believer at salvation. It distinguishes grieving Him through sin from ending that relationship: the study does not understand unconfessed sin as driving the Spirit away. Its emphasis is on honest confession and restored fellowship with God.

passages.title: Ephesians 1:15-19
passages.section_title: What does Paul ask God to help believers understand?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 For this reason, ever since I heard about your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love for all the saints, 16 I have not stopped giving thanks for you, remembering you in my prayers, 17 that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the glorious Father, may give you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in your knowledge of Him. 18 I ask that the eyes of your heart may be enlightened, so that you may know the hope of His calling, the riches of His glorious inheritance in the saints, 19 and the surpassing greatness of His power to us who believe. These are in accordance with the working of His mighty strength,
paragraphs: 15 For this reason, ever since I heard about your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love for all the saints, 16 I have not stopped giving thanks for you, remembering you in my prayers, 17 that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the glorious Father, may give you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in your knowledge of Him.

18 I ask that the eyes of your heart may be enlightened, so that you may know the hope of His calling, the riches of His glorious inheritance in the saints, 19 and the surpassing greatness of His power to us who believe. These are in accordance with the working of His mighty strength,

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the blessing of God in verses 3–14, Paul turns to thanksgiving and prayer for his readers. Their faith in the Lord Jesus and love for all the saints give him reason to keep thanking God.

He asks the glorious Father for wisdom and revelation in knowing Him. The prayer seeks a deeper understanding of the God whose grace Paul has just described.

He pictures that understanding as the eyes of the heart being enlightened. He wants them to know the hope of God’s calling, the riches of His glorious inheritance in the saints and the greatness of His power toward believers.

The next verses explain the power he has in view by pointing to Christ’s resurrection and exaltation. The prayer therefore seeks understanding rooted in what God has done and in the hope He gives His people.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a prayer for believers to grow in their knowledge of God and appreciation of His gifts. Wesley’s notes on verses 15–19 connect the prayer with the Spirit’s work of giving wisdom and understanding. The USCCB notes on verses 15–23 place the prayer within the blessings already described and God’s power shown in Christ.
passages.god_plan_html:
Colossians 1:9–14 records a closely related prayer for knowledge of God’s will, spiritual wisdom and understanding. It explains the purpose in daily life: conduct worthy of the Lord, fruit in good works, endurance and thanks to the Father.

That prayer also joins inheritance with rescue from darkness into the kingdom of God’s Son. The connection shows how growing understanding serves the larger life God is forming in His people. Knowing Him is meant to shape faithful, thankful conduct.

passages.title: Ephesians 1:20-23
passages.section_title: What does Christ’s resurrection show us about His authority?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 20 which He exerted in Christ when He raised Him from the dead and seated Him at His right hand in the heavenly realms, 21 far above all rule and authority, power and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in the present age but also in the one to come. 22 And God put everything under His feet and made Him head over everything for the church, 23 which is His body, the fullness of Him who fills all in all.
paragraphs: 20 which He exerted in Christ when He raised Him from the dead and seated Him at His right hand in the heavenly realms, 21 far above all rule and authority, power and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in the present age but also in the one to come.
22 And God put everything under His feet and made Him head over everything for the church, 23 which is His body, the fullness of Him who fills all in all.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul now identifies the mighty work behind his prayer about God’s power: the Father raised Christ from the dead and seated Him at His right hand in the heavenly realms.

Christ is far above every rule, authority, power and dominion, and above every name in the present age and the age to come. Paul’s description reaches beyond any single ruler or present circumstance.

God has placed everything under Christ’s feet and made Him head over everything for the church. The people Paul is praying for belong to the One whose authority he has just described.

He calls the church Christ’s body and speaks of His fullness. The closing description holds together the exalted Lord and the people who share life in relation to Him. It completes the prayer’s movement from their need for understanding to the greatness of the risen Christ.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand this as proclaiming Christ’s resurrection, supreme authority and relationship with the church as His body. Wesley’s notes on verses 20–23 emphasize His rule and the body’s dependence on Him. The USCCB notes on verses 15–23 likewise connect the church’s hope with the Father’s power in exalting Christ.

The closing expression about fullness has been explained in more than one way. Wesley’s note on verse 23 relates the fullness to Christ as the fullness of the Father. The USCCB note also discusses Christ filling the church, alongside other possible explanations of the sentence. These readings differ in where they place the emphasis: on Christ’s fullness from the Father or on the church receiving its fullness through Christ.
passages.god_plan_html:
Psalm 8:3–9 praises God for the place He gives humanity within His creation and speaks of all things being placed under human feet. Hebrews 2:5–9 takes up that wording and directs attention to Jesus, crowned with glory and honor after suffering death.

The New Testament itself therefore connects the creation theme of Psalm 8 with the crucified and exalted Jesus. Read alongside Ephesians, this places His authority within God’s larger purpose for creation and the world to come. The church’s life belongs under the Lord through whom that purpose is carried forward.

passages.title: Ephesians 2:1-3
passages.section_title: What condition were we in before God made us alive?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 And you were dead in your trespasses and sins, 2 in which you used to walk when you conformed to the ways of this world and of the ruler of the power of the air, the spirit who is now at work in the sons of disobedience. 3 All of us also lived among them at one time, fulfilling the cravings of our flesh and indulging its desires and thoughts. Like the rest, we were by nature children of wrath.
paragraphs: 1 And you were dead in your trespasses and sins, 2 in which you used to walk when you conformed to the ways of this world and of the ruler of the power of the air, the spirit who is now at work in the sons of disobedience. 3 All of us also lived among them at one time, fulfilling the cravings of our flesh and indulging its desires and thoughts. Like the rest, we were by nature children of wrath.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After describing God’s power in raising Christ, Paul turns to the condition of those who now belong to Him. He says they were dead in their trespasses and sins. The people he addresses were physically alive, yet lacked the life with God that the next verses will describe.

The Greek word for dead is νεκρός, nekros (neh-KROSS). Thayer’s lexicon recognizes its use here for spiritual deadness: a life given over to sin rather than devoted to God. The picture explains why the coming change must be a gift of life from Him.

Paul describes how they used to walk: following the ways of this world and the ruler of the power of the air, whose influence is at work among the disobedient. The language connects human wrongdoing with a spiritual power opposed to God.

He includes himself and others in the same condition. All of us once lived in the desires and thoughts of the flesh and were by nature children of wrath. The paragraph leaves no room for the believers to imagine they had always stood above those around them.

The sentence continues into the announcement of God’s mercy in verses 4–5. Remembering their former condition prepares the way for understanding what He has done through Christ.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand these verses as describing humanity’s need for God’s saving grace. Wesley’s notes on verses 1–3 and the USCCB notes on verses 1–10 connect the former condition with the life God gives through Christ. Traditions differ in how they describe the inherited condition behind verse 3.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 6, teaches that Adam’s guilt and a corrupted nature are passed to his descendants. Actual sins arise from that inherited corruption.

The Catholic Catechism, paragraphs 404–405, describes original sin as an inherited state of deprivation of original holiness, rather than a personal act committed by each descendant. It teaches that human nature is wounded and inclined to sin, while maintaining that it has not been totally corrupted.

The Methodist Articles of Religion, articles VII–VIII, describe human nature as fallen and continually inclined toward evil. They also teach that people cannot turn to faith by their own natural strength; God’s grace must enable their response. These explanations differ, while all recognize the need for God’s work of grace.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 5:12–19 places humanity’s condition within the larger account of Adam and Christ. Sin and death entered through one man’s disobedience; God’s gift through Jesus Christ brings the contrasting hope of righteousness and life.

That connection gives a wider setting for the condition Paul recalls here. The story reaches back to humanity’s fall, and God’s answer comes through His Son. The next verses of Ephesians will announce that answer in terms of mercy and being made alive with Christ.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ephesians 2:4-10
passages.section_title: What changes when God makes us alive with Christ?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 4 But because of His great love for us, God, who is rich in mercy, 5 made us alive with Christ even when we were dead in our trespasses. It is by grace you have been saved! 6 And God raised us up with Christ and seated us with Him in the heavenly realms in Christ Jesus, 7 in order that in the coming ages He might display the surpassing riches of His grace, demonstrated by His kindness to us in Christ Jesus. 8 For it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, 9 not by works, so that no one can boast. 10 For we are God’s workmanship, created in Christ Jesus to do good works, which God prepared in advance as our way of life.
paragraphs: 4 But because of His great love for us, God, who is rich in mercy, 5 made us alive with Christ even when we were dead in our trespasses. It is by grace you have been saved! 6 And God raised us up with Christ and seated us with Him in the heavenly realms in Christ Jesus, 7 in order that in the coming ages He might display the surpassing riches of His grace, demonstrated by His kindness to us in Christ Jesus.

8 For it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, 9 not by works, so that no one can boast. 10 For we are God’s workmanship, created in Christ Jesus to do good works, which God prepared in advance as our way of life.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul turns from the condition of death in sin to the God who is rich in mercy. His great love stands behind the change: He made us alive with Christ even while we were dead in our trespasses.

The description follows the resurrection and exaltation language of 1:20. God has raised His people with Christ and seated them with Him in the heavenly realms. Their belonging to Christ changes their standing and their future.

Paul also names God’s purpose for the coming ages: to display the riches of His grace in His kindness toward us in Christ Jesus. The life He gives is part of an unfolding display of that generosity.

Verses 8–9 summarize salvation as a gift of grace through faith. It does not originate in the recipients’ own achievements, and works provide no basis for boasting.

Verse 10 then describes the life God has created. The word translated workmanship is ποίημα, poiēma (POY-ay-mah), meaning something made or a work. Thayer’s lexicon identifies God as the maker in this use. His people have been created in Christ Jesus for good works He prepared as their way of life.

Paul therefore joins the gift with its purpose. The God who gives life also prepares a life of doing good for the people He has made new.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand salvation here as God’s gift through Christ and recognize that the new life is meant to bear good works. They differ in how they describe being made right with God and the relationship between faith, renewal and those works.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 11, describes justification as forgiveness and being counted righteous because of Christ’s obedience and work, received through faith alone. It also insists that this faith is living and acts through love.

The Catholic Catechism, paragraphs 1987–1993, describes justification as forgiveness together with inner renewal, given through Christ’s grace in baptism. It includes a response of faith and love enabled by grace, rather than treating human effort as an independent source of salvation.

The Methodist Articles of Religion, articles IX–X, teach that people are accounted righteous through faith because of Christ’s merit. Good works follow from living faith and please God, while being unable to remove sins. These accounts all appeal to God’s gift through Christ, while differing in how the gift and its effects are explained.
passages.god_plan_html:
Titus 3:3–8 gives a closely related account of the change from a former life of disobedience. God saves according to His mercy, through new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit, poured out through Jesus Christ. Those justified by His grace become heirs with the hope of eternal life.

Titus then calls believers to devote themselves to good deeds. The connection places the gifts described in Ephesians within God’s purpose of renewing a people through His Son and Spirit, giving them a future hope and a present life of doing good.
passages.current_position_html: Our studies The Gospel According to Jesus and Baptism read these verses as teaching salvation by God’s grace through faith, received as His gift rather than earned through religious effort or moral achievement. The Baptism study specifically distinguishes that saved relationship from the water baptism that follows: it understands salvation and the Spirit’s indwelling as received through faith, without waiting for baptism.

passages.title: Ephesians 2:8-9
passages.section_title: Why is there no room for boasting in salvation?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 For it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, 9 not by works, so that no one can boast.
paragraphs: 8 For it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, 9 not by works, so that no one can boast.

passages.context_html:
These verses summarize the saving action described in Ephesians 2:4–10. God, rich in mercy and love, has made people alive with Christ while they were dead in their trespasses.

Paul describes salvation by grace through faith as God’s gift. It is not from the recipients themselves or their works, so there is no basis for boasting about having achieved it.

The next verse describes the good works for which God created His people in Christ. Reading the whole paragraph keeps both truths in view: salvation is His gift, and the life He gives has a purpose in doing good.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand salvation here as God’s gift through Christ and recognize that the new life is meant to bear good works. They differ in how they describe being made right with God and the relationship between faith, renewal and those works.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 11, describes justification as forgiveness and being counted righteous because of Christ’s obedience and work, received through faith alone. It also insists that this faith is living and acts through love.

Good works follow from living faith and please God, while being unable to remove sins. These accounts all appeal to God’s gift through Christ, while differing in how the gift and its effects are explained.

The Baptism study specifically distinguishes that saved relationship from the water baptism that follows: it understands salvation and the Spirit’s indwelling as received through faith, without waiting for baptism.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?
