passages.title: Ephesians 2:11-13
passages.section_title: What does Paul want the Gentiles to remember?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 Therefore remember that formerly you who are Gentiles in the flesh and called uncircumcised by the so-called circumcision (that done in the body by human hands)— 12 remember that at that time you were separate from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers to the covenants of the promise, without hope and without God in the world. 13 But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far away have been brought near through the blood of Christ.
paragraphs: 11 Therefore remember that formerly you who are Gentiles in the flesh and called uncircumcised by the so-called circumcision (that done in the body by human hands)— 12 remember that at that time you were separate from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers to the covenants of the promise, without hope and without God in the world. 13 But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far away have been brought near through the blood of Christ.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul asks his Gentile readers to remember the distance that once marked their lives. The labels circumcised and uncircumcised identified a division in the flesh, marked by something done with human hands.

He names what they lacked: they were separate from Christ, outside the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise, without hope and without God in the world. The reminder sets their present belonging against their former condition.

Verse 13 gives the turning point. In Christ Jesus, those who were far away have been brought near through His blood. The change comes through the same Christ whose saving work Paul has been describing throughout the chapter.

The next paragraph explains how this nearness includes both reconciliation with God and a shared life between Jewish and Gentile believers. Remembering the former distance is meant to deepen their appreciation of the welcome they now share.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a reminder of the Gentiles’ former separation and their welcome through Christ. Wesley’s notes on verses 11–13 and the USCCB notes on verses 11–22 both connect nearness to God with the inclusion of Gentiles among His people.
passages.god_plan_html:
Genesis 12:1–3 gives Abraham the promise that all the families of the earth will be blessed through him. Galatians 3:6–14 explicitly connects that promise with the gospel reaching Gentiles and the blessing received through Christ.

Acts 10:34–48 shows that welcome taking place as Gentiles hear the message of Jesus and receive the Holy Spirit. Their inclusion belongs to God’s long-standing purpose of blessing the nations, now made known and accomplished through His Son.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ephesians 2:14-18
passages.section_title: How does Christ make peace between people and with God?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 For He Himself is our peace, who has made the two one and has torn down the dividing wall of hostility 15 by abolishing in His flesh the law of commandments and decrees. He did this to create in Himself one new man out of the two, thus making peace 16 and reconciling both of them to God in one body through the cross, by which He put to death their hostility. 17 He came and preached peace to you who were far away and peace to those who were near. 18 For through Him we both have access to the Father by one Spirit.
paragraphs: 14 For He Himself is our peace, who has made the two one and has torn down the dividing wall of hostility 15 by abolishing in His flesh the law of commandments and decrees. He did this to create in Himself one new man out of the two, thus making peace 16 and reconciling both of them to God in one body through the cross, by which He put to death their hostility.
17 He came and preached peace to you who were far away and peace to those who were near. 18 For through Him we both have access to the Father by one Spirit.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul identifies Christ Himself as the peace of Jewish and Gentile believers. He has made the two one and torn down the dividing wall of hostility.

The wall picture may recall the barrier within Jerusalem’s temple. Josephus, Jewish War 5.5.2, describes a stone partition with warnings against foreigners entering the inner sanctuary. That historical background helps explain the image of restricted approach; Paul’s concern is the hostility Christ has ended through His cross.

He connects that peace with the law of commandments and decrees abolished in Christ’s flesh. The purpose is one new humanity from the two groups and reconciliation of both to God in one body.

The cross therefore addresses both directions of the division. Those once separated from each other are brought together, and both are reconciled to God.

Paul then speaks of Christ announcing peace to those far away and those near. Through Him, both groups have access to the Father by one Spirit. Their shared approach to God rests in the work of the Son and the presence of the Spirit.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand these verses as describing reconciliation with God and the unity of Jewish and Gentile believers through Christ. Wesley’s notes on verses 14–18 and the USCCB notes on verses 11–22 both recognize the shared body and access to the Father.

Christians explain the law’s continuing place differently. Wesley’s note on verse 15 emphasizes the ceremonial commandments that separated the groups. The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 19, distinguishes ceremonies fulfilled in Christ from moral commands that continue to guide believers. Dallas Theological Seminary, article V, treats Mosaic and present Christian responsibilities as distinct. These accounts differ over continuing instruction, while agreeing that Gentiles are welcomed through Christ’s saving work.
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul’s language about peace for those far and near recalls Isaiah 57:14–19. In that passage, God promises to revive the humble and contrite, restore comfort and announce peace with healing.

Isaiah 56:3–8 also promises welcome to foreigners who join themselves to the LORD. God’s house is to be a house of prayer for all nations, and He promises to gather others alongside those already gathered.

These connections place the shared access described here within God’s larger purpose of gathering people into His presence. Ephesians identifies Christ’s cross and the one Spirit as central to that welcome, bringing Jewish and Gentile believers together before the Father.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ephesians 2:19-22
passages.section_title: How do former outsiders become God’s dwelling place?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 Therefore you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, 20 built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus Himself as the cornerstone. 21 In Him the whole building is fitted together and grows into a holy temple in the Lord. 22 And in Him you too are being built together into a dwelling place for God in His Spirit.
paragraphs: 19 Therefore you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, 20 built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus Himself as the cornerstone.
21 In Him the whole building is fitted together and grows into a holy temple in the Lord. 22 And in Him you too are being built together into a dwelling place for God in His Spirit.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul now describes the new standing of the Gentile believers. They are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household. The people once called strangers belong within the family.

The picture shifts from a household to a building. They are built on the foundation of apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus Himself as the cornerstone. The whole structure is fitted together in Him and grows into a holy temple.

The Greek word for temple is ναός, naos (nah-OSS). Thayer’s lexicon uses it for the sanctuary and explains its use here for the community in which God’s Spirit dwells. Paul is describing the people themselves as God’s holy dwelling.

His final words again address the Gentile readers directly: they too are being built together into that dwelling place through the Spirit. The emphasis is shared belonging and shared life in God’s presence.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand Christ as central to the foundation and the believers together as the dwelling of God’s Spirit. Wesley’s notes on verses 19–21 connect the foundation with God’s word declared by the apostles and prophets. The USCCB notes on verses 19–22 also identify the people of God as the temple in which His presence dwells.

The identity of the prophets is read differently. In his commentary on verse 20, the Reformed teacher John Calvin includes the Old Testament prophets and emphasizes the harmony of their teaching with the apostles. The Catholic USCCB notes understand prophets serving in the early Christian community, also mentioned in Ephesians 3:5. These are the explanations of the named sources, rather than a claim that every member of either tradition reads the detail identically.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Peter 2:4–10 gives a closely related picture. Christ is the chosen living stone, and those who come to Him are living stones being built into a spiritual house. The passage joins that house with a holy priesthood and offerings acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.

Peter also describes people called out of darkness to proclaim God’s virtues, once without belonging and now His people. That connection extends the building picture into the purpose of the gathered community: living in God’s presence, serving Him and making His goodness known.
passages.current_position_html: Our study What Is the True Church?, in its section We Are the Temple, understands God’s dwelling as His Spirit living in His people. It draws the practical conclusion that His presence calls for holiness in our thoughts, conduct and relationships, with reverence for the life He is forming among us.

passages.title: Ephesians 3:1-6
passages.section_title: What has God made known about the Gentiles’ place in Christ?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 For this reason I, Paul, the prisoner of Christ Jesus for the sake of you Gentiles... 2 Surely you have heard about the stewardship of God’s grace that was given to me for you, 3 that is, the mystery made known to me by revelation, as I have already written briefly. 4 In reading this, then, you will be able to understand my insight into the mystery of Christ, 5 which was not made known to men in other generations as it has now been revealed by the Spirit to God’s holy apostles and prophets. 6 This mystery is that through the gospel the Gentiles are fellow heirs, fellow members of the body, and fellow partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus.
paragraphs: 1 For this reason I, Paul, the prisoner of Christ Jesus for the sake of you Gentiles... 2 Surely you have heard about the stewardship of God’s grace that was given to me for you, 3 that is, the mystery made known to me by revelation, as I have already written briefly.

4 In reading this, then, you will be able to understand my insight into the mystery of Christ, 5 which was not made known to men in other generations as it has now been revealed by the Spirit to God’s holy apostles and prophets. 6 This mystery is that through the gospel the Gentiles are fellow heirs, fellow members of the body, and fellow partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul begins by describing himself as Christ Jesus’ prisoner for the sake of the Gentiles. His thought pauses while he explains the responsibility God gave him; the prayer he begins to introduce resumes in verse 14.

He describes that responsibility as a stewardship of grace given for their benefit. God made the mystery known to him by revelation, and he has already written briefly about it. He expects his readers to be able to understand his insight as they read.

The purpose once hidden has now been revealed by the Spirit to God’s holy apostles and prophets. Paul places his own service within that shared revelation.

Verse 6 states the content clearly: through the gospel, Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body and sharers in the promise in Christ Jesus. The explanation continues the shared household and dwelling described at the end of chapter 2.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the mystery here as God’s revealed purpose of shared belonging for Jews and Gentiles through Christ. They differ over how this new disclosure relates to what was already known.

In the Wesleyan reading, Wesley’s note on verse 5 understands the purpose as not previously known with the same clarity or fullness. The earlier prophets pointed toward what is now more fully revealed.

A dispensational reading, which distinguishes Israel and the church, appears in a faculty publication from Shepherds Theological Seminary. It understands the shared body of Jewish and Gentile believers as a new part of God’s purpose that had not been revealed as the church in the Old Testament. This is the account defended in that publication.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Acts 15:13–18, James responds to the report of God taking a people from among the Gentiles. He quotes the prophet Amos about the restoration of David’s fallen tent and Gentiles called by God’s name, saying the prophetic words agree with what has happened.

That explicit New Testament use of the prophets places Gentile welcome within God’s larger purpose. The shared belonging Paul explains is part of the gathering God has made known through His word and His work in Christ.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ephesians 3:7-13
passages.section_title: What is God making known through the church?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 I became a servant of this gospel by the gift of God’s grace, given me through the working of His power. 8 Though I am less than the least of all the saints, this grace was given me: to preach to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ, 9 and to illuminate for everyone the stewardship of this mystery, which for ages past was kept hidden in God, who created all things. 10 His purpose was that now, through the church, the manifold wisdom of God should be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly realms, 11 according to the eternal purpose that He accomplished in Christ Jesus our Lord. 12 In Him and through faith in Him we may enter God’s presence with boldness and confidence. 13 So I ask you not to be discouraged because of my sufferings for you, which are your glory.
paragraphs: 7 I became a servant of this gospel by the gift of God’s grace, given me through the working of His power. 8 Though I am less than the least of all the saints, this grace was given me: to preach to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ, 9 and to illuminate for everyone the stewardship of this mystery, which for ages past was kept hidden in God, who created all things.

10 His purpose was that now, through the church, the manifold wisdom of God should be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly realms, 11 according to the eternal purpose that He accomplished in Christ Jesus our Lord. 12 In Him and through faith in Him we may enter God’s presence with boldness and confidence. 13 So I ask you not to be discouraged because of my sufferings for you, which are your glory.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul describes his service to the gospel as a gift of grace working through God’s power. He calls himself less than the least of all the saints, placing his opportunity to serve in the setting of God’s generosity.

His task is to preach Christ’s unsearchable riches to the Gentiles and bring the previously hidden purpose to light. The Creator is the One who has held and now disclosed this purpose.

Paul then names a heavenly audience: through the church, God’s manifold wisdom is being made known to rulers and authorities in the heavenly realms. The word manifold comes from πολυποίκιλος, polypoikilos (poh-loo-POY-kih-loss). Thayer’s lexicon explains this use as richly varied, shown in many forms. The life of this shared people displays the richness of God’s wisdom.

This belongs to the eternal purpose accomplished in Christ Jesus. In Him, through faith, believers have confident access to God.

Paul therefore asks them not to become discouraged over his sufferings for them. His hardships belong to a service through which the Gentiles have received the blessings he has been describing.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as joining Paul’s grace-given mission with God’s purpose displayed through the church. Wesley’s notes on verses 7–13 emphasize the gift of service and the church as the setting where divine wisdom is shown. The USCCB notes on verses 1–13 likewise connect Paul’s mission, the inclusion of Gentiles and the making known of God’s purpose to heavenly beings.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Peter 1:10–12 describes prophets searching into the salvation and grace now announced through the gospel by the Holy Spirit. It adds that even angels long to look into these things.

This gives another explicit picture of God’s saving work having significance beyond its human hearers. The welcome of His people through Christ displays His wisdom, and the heavenly realm attends to the salvation He has brought about.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ephesians 3:14-19
passages.section_title: What does Paul pray will grow within God’s people?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 ... for this reason I bow my knees before the Father, 15 from whom every family in heaven and on earth derives its name. 16 I ask that out of the riches of His glory He may strengthen you with power through His Spirit in your inner being, 17 so that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith. Then you, being rooted and grounded in love, 18 will have power, together with all the saints, to comprehend the length and width and height and depth 19 of the love of Christ, and to know this love that surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God.
paragraphs: 14 ... for this reason I bow my knees before the Father, 15 from whom every family in heaven and on earth derives its name. 16 I ask that out of the riches of His glory He may strengthen you with power through His Spirit in your inner being, 17 so that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith. Then you, being rooted and grounded in love,

18 will have power, together with all the saints, to comprehend the length and width and height and depth 19 of the love of Christ, and to know this love that surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul resumes the prayer introduced in verse 1. He bows his knees before the Father, from whom every family in heaven and on earth derives its name. His posture gives a concrete picture of reverent appeal.

He asks the Father to strengthen the believers through His Spirit in their inner being, according to the riches of His glory. The strength he seeks is God’s gift at work within them.

He also asks that Christ may dwell in their hearts through faith. The Greek word is κατοικέω, katoikeō (kah-toy-KEH-oh), to dwell or settle. Thayer’s lexicon explains its use here in terms of Christ’s presence pervading and directing a person’s inner life.

The prayer joins that presence with being rooted and grounded in love. Paul wants them, together with all the saints, to grasp the length, width, height and depth of Christ’s love.

The love is greater than their knowledge, yet he prays for them to know it. He seeks a life filled with God’s fullness. The prayer moves from God’s strength within them toward a deeply shared understanding of the love of Christ.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these requests as a prayer for believers to be strengthened through the Spirit, established in Christ’s love and brought into a fuller life with God. Wesley’s notes on verses 15–19 and the USCCB notes on verses 14–21 both connect the prayer with growing understanding of God’s love and fullness.
passages.god_plan_html:
In John 14:15–23, Jesus promises the Spirit’s presence and speaks of the Father and Son making their home with those who love Him and keep His word. He connects shared life with God, love and obedience.

That explicit promise gives a wider setting for Paul’s prayer. The strength and love he asks for belong to the life Jesus promised His people through the Spirit. Paul is asking for that life with God to take deep root among them.
passages.current_position_html: Our study What Does Prayer Look Like?, in its discussion of Ephesians 3:16–19, treats this as an example of praying for others to know God more deeply, love more fully and live in a way that honors Him. The requests focus on strength through the Spirit, Christ dwelling in their hearts, being rooted in love and knowing His love more deeply.

passages.title: Ephesians 3:16-19
passages.section_title: What does it mean to pray for strength and Christ’s love?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 I ask that out of the riches of His glory He may strengthen you with power through His Spirit in your inner being, 17 so that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith. Then you, being rooted and grounded in love, 18 will have power, together with all the saints, to comprehend the length and width and height and depth 19 of the love of Christ, and to know this love that surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God.

Then you, being rooted and grounded in love, 18 will have power, together with all the saints, to comprehend the length and width and height and depth 19 of the love of Christ, and to know this love that surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God.

passages.context_html:
These requests belong to Paul’s prayer in Ephesians 3:14–19. He addresses the Father after explaining the shared place of Jewish and Gentile believers in God’s purpose.

He asks for strength through the Spirit in their inner being, Christ dwelling in their hearts through faith, and a life rooted and grounded in love.

The request reaches beyond an individual’s private understanding: he wants them to grasp Christ’s love together with all the saints. Knowing that love and being filled with God’s fullness are the direction of his prayer.

Wesley’s notes on verses 15–19 and the USCCB notes on verses 14–21 both connect the prayer with growing understanding of God’s love and fullness.

The requests focus on strength through the Spirit, Christ dwelling in their hearts, being rooted in love and knowing His love more deeply.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.title: Ephesians 3:20-21
passages.section_title: Why does Paul end his prayer with praise?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 20 Now to Him who is able to do immeasurably more than all we ask or imagine, according to His power that is at work within us, 21 to Him be the glory in the church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations, forever and ever. Amen.
paragraphs: 20 Now to Him who is able to do immeasurably more than all we ask or imagine, according to His power that is at work within us, 21 to Him be the glory in the church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations, forever and ever. Amen.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul closes the prayer of verses 14–19 by praising the God to whom he has been praying. God is able to do immeasurably more than all we ask or imagine, through the power already at work within His people.

The praise belongs in the setting of the requests for spiritual strength, Christ’s presence, love and fullness. Paul’s confidence rests in God’s ability to accomplish His work among them.

He gives glory to God in the church and in Christ Jesus throughout every generation, forever. The praise closes this part of the letter before chapter 4 turns toward living in a manner worthy of their calling.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as praise that expresses confidence in God’s power and gives Him glory through Christ and the church. Wesley’s notes on verses 20–21 connect the praise with confidence in the great things Paul has just prayed for. The USCCB notes on verses 14–21 likewise identify these verses as the prayer’s closing praise.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ephesians 4:1-6
passages.section_title: How do we live out the unity God has given us?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 As a prisoner in the Lord, then, I urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling you have received: 2 with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love, 3 and with diligence to preserve the unity of the Spirit through the bond of peace. 4 There is one body and one Spirit, just as you were called to one hope when you were called; 5 one Lord, one faith, one baptism; 6 one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all.
paragraphs: 1 As a prisoner in the Lord, then, I urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling you have received: 2 with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love, 3 and with diligence to preserve the unity of the Spirit through the bond of peace.

4 There is one body and one Spirit, just as you were called to one hope when you were called; 5 one Lord, one faith, one baptism; 6 one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul now urges a way of life worthy of the calling his readers have received. The appeal grows out of the grace, shared belonging and hope described in the first three chapters. He writes again as a prisoner in the Lord.

He names the qualities needed in that shared life: humility, gentleness, patience and bearing with one another in love. They are to be diligent in preserving the unity of the Spirit through the bond of peace.

The unity has a foundation deeper than the believers’ immediate feelings toward each other. Paul names one body, one Spirit and one hope of their calling, then one Lord, one faith and one baptism.

He concludes with one God and Father, over all, through all and in all. The Father, Lord and Spirit stand at the center of the shared life he is describing. The call to treat one another with love rests in what they already share through God’s grace.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand this as a call to preserve the Spirit-given unity of Christ’s people through humble, patient love. Wesley’s notes on verses 1–6 and the USCCB notes on verses 1–16 both connect the shared body and faith with the way believers live together.

The expression one baptism is understood differently. Wesley’s note on verse 5 takes it as outward baptism. The Catholic Catechism, paragraph 1271, describes properly received baptism as a foundation of Christian communion even where churches are not fully united. The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 28, likewise describes water baptism as a sign and pledge of grace and belonging to Christ.

Another reading understands the baptism here as Christ’s work of joining believers to His body through the Holy Spirit. Evangelical writer Hampton Keathley IV develops that reading in One Baptism in Ephesians 4:5, connecting the verse with 1 Corinthians 12:13. This is a teacher’s reading of the passage, rather than an official explanation shared by all evangelical churches.
passages.god_plan_html:
In John 17:20–23, Jesus prays for those who will believe through the apostles’ message to be one. He connects their unity with the relationship of the Father and Son and with the world recognizing that the Father sent Him.

That explicit prayer gives a larger purpose to the unity Paul asks them to preserve. Their life together bears witness to the Christ who gathers them and to the Father’s love. Humility, patience and peace therefore serve more than the comfort of a congregation; they belong to its witness in the world.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ephesians 4:7-10
passages.section_title: Why does the risen Christ give gifts to His people?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 Now to each one of us grace has been given according to the measure of the gift of Christ. 8 This is why it says: “When He ascended on high, He led captives away, and gave gifts to men.” 9 What does “He ascended” mean, except that He also descended to the lower parts of the earth? 10 He who descended is the very One who ascended above all the heavens, in order to fill all things.
paragraphs: 7 Now to each one of us grace has been given according to the measure of the gift of Christ. 8 This is why it says: “When He ascended on high, He led captives away, and gave gifts to men.”
9 What does “He ascended” mean, except that He also descended to the lower parts of the earth? 10 He who descended is the very One who ascended above all the heavens, in order to fill all things.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After describing what all believers share, Paul turns to the grace given to each person according to Christ’s gift. The unity of the body includes His generosity toward its members.

Paul brings in the victory picture of Psalm 68:18: ascending on high and leading captives away. The psalm speaks of receiving gifts, while Ephesians emphasizes Christ giving gifts to people. Paul applies the victory language to the One who supplies His church.

He then pauses over the word ascended. The One who ascended is also the One who descended to the lower parts of the earth. Paul identifies the same Christ in both movements and describes Him as ascending above all the heavens to fill all things.

The next paragraph will name people Christ gives to equip His people and build His body. These verses introduce that service by directing attention to the authority and generosity of the risen Lord.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand this as connecting Christ’s victory and exaltation with the gifts He gives His church. Wesley’s notes on verses 7–10 and the USCCB notes on verses 1–10 both place the giving of gifts within that movement.

The descent is explained in different ways. The Reformed teacher John Calvin’s note on verse 9 understands the lower place as the earth compared with heaven: the Son came down into human life. The Catholic USCCB notes also consider His coming to earth the more likely meaning of this verse.

The Reformed Westminster Larger Catechism, question 50, explains the creed’s language of descent into hell as Christ’s burial and His remaining in the state of death until the third day. The Catholic Catechism, paragraph 631, connects these verses with His descent into the realm of the dead. Paragraphs 632–637 teach that He truly experienced death and freed the righteous who awaited Him, distinguishing this realm from the hell of final condemnation. These teachings and explanations give different accounts of the descent; the shared emphasis is Christ’s real death and triumphant life.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Acts 2:32–36, Peter connects Jesus’ resurrection and exaltation to the Father’s right hand with the promised Holy Spirit being poured out. The risen Christ is actively giving to His people.

Acts 2:42–47 shows the life that follows: devotion to the apostles’ teaching, fellowship, prayer, shared meals and practical care for those in need. The gift serves the formation of a people who learn, worship and care for one another together. This gives a concrete picture of the larger purpose behind Christ’s generosity.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ephesians 4:11-12
passages.section_title: Who is being prepared to serve?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 And it was He who gave some to be apostles, some to be prophets, some to be evangelists, and some to be pastors and teachers, 12 to equip the saints for works of ministry and to build up the body of Christ,
paragraphs: 11 And it was He who gave some to be apostles, some to be prophets, some to be evangelists, and some to be pastors and teachers, 12 to equip the saints for works of ministry and to build up the body of Christ,

passages.context_html:
Paul has just described the generosity of the risen Christ. He now names people Christ gives to help His church: apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers.

Verse 12 explains their purpose. They equip the saints, meaning God’s people, for works of ministry and for the building up of Christ’s body. The service of those named in verse 11 prepares others to serve.

The sentence continues through verse 13, and verses 14–16 explain the desired growth: steadiness in teaching, truth spoken with love and each part contributing under Christ. Read the whole connected passage for that fuller picture.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read these verses as Christ providing people who teach, guide and prepare His church for service. The USCCB note on verse 12 explicitly understands the whole people of God as those being equipped for ministry.

Christians differ over how the apostles’ and prophets’ ministries continue. The Catholic Catechism, paragraphs 857–862, distinguishes the apostles’ unique role as witnesses and foundation from the pastoral care continued by bishops as their successors.

Among evangelical Christians, Dallas Theological Seminary’s doctrinal statement, article XVI, teaches that the foundational offices of apostle and prophet ended with the New Testament period, while evangelists, pastors and teachers continue. It also affirms that God can perform miracles today.

The Pentecostal Assemblies of God distinguishes the original apostles’ unique authority from ongoing apostolic work, such as missionary work and starting churches, without requiring an apostolic title or office. It also affirms prophecy as a continuing gift, with messages tested by the church against Scripture. These are distinct accounts of continuing ministry, rather than a single view shared by all Christians.
passages.current_position_html: Our study What Is the True Church? recognizes the leadership roles described here. Their purpose is to prepare believers to take part in ministry. Leaders serve and equip the community, while the whole community shares responsibility for its life and service. The study calls for active participation by believers and affirms the need for spiritually mature leadership.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
1 Corinthians 12:4–7, 21–27 places different gifts within the work of the same God and directs them toward the common good. It also calls the members to care for one another, including those who appear weaker.

This is a supported parallel to the purpose stated here. Christ prepares a people whose members contribute to one another’s life. The ministry of leaders belongs within that shared calling.

passages.title: Ephesians 4:11-16
passages.section_title: How does the whole church grow toward Christ?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 And it was He who gave some to be apostles, some to be prophets, some to be evangelists, and some to be pastors and teachers, 12 to equip the saints for works of ministry and to build up the body of Christ, 13 until we all reach unity in the faith and in the knowledge of the Son of God, as we mature to the full measure of the stature of Christ. 14 Then we will no longer be infants, tossed about by the waves and carried around by every wind of teaching and by the clever cunning of men in their deceitful scheming. 15 Instead, speaking the truth in love, we will in all things grow up into Christ Himself, who is the head. 16 From Him the whole body, fitted and held together by every supporting ligament, grows and builds itself up in love through the work of each individual part.
paragraphs: 11 And it was He who gave some to be apostles, some to be prophets, some to be evangelists, and some to be pastors and teachers, 12 to equip the saints for works of ministry and to build up the body of Christ, 13 until we all reach unity in the faith and in the knowledge of the Son of God, as we mature to the full measure of the stature of Christ.

14 Then we will no longer be infants, tossed about by the waves and carried around by every wind of teaching and by the clever cunning of men in their deceitful scheming. 15 Instead, speaking the truth in love, we will in all things grow up into Christ Himself, who is the head. 16 From Him the whole body, fitted and held together by every supporting ligament, grows and builds itself up in love through the work of each individual part.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
These verses explain the purpose of the gifts introduced in verses 7–10. The risen Christ gives apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers so His people are prepared for ministry and His body is built up.

The word translated equip is katartismos (kah-tar-tis-MOSS). Thayer’s lexicon connects it with a word for strengthening or perfecting, also used for training and instruction. In this sentence, the preparation has a purpose: God’s people are to serve.

Paul describes the goal as all of us growing in faith and knowledge of the Son of God, with Christ as the measure of maturity. He then shows what that growth looks like. Believers become steadier when faced with misleading teaching and learn to speak truth with love.

The body picture brings the paragraph together. Christ is the head, and growth comes from Him as each part contributes. Paul is describing the health of the whole community, including what its members say, believe and do for one another.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read these verses as Christ providing people who teach, guide and prepare His church for service. The USCCB note on verse 12 explicitly understands the whole people of God as those being equipped for ministry.

Christians differ over how the apostles’ and prophets’ ministries continue. The Catholic Catechism, paragraphs 857–862, distinguishes the apostles’ unique role as witnesses and foundation from the pastoral care continued by bishops as their successors.

Among evangelical Christians, Dallas Theological Seminary’s doctrinal statement, article XVI, teaches that the foundational offices of apostle and prophet ended with the New Testament period, while evangelists, pastors and teachers continue. It also affirms that God can perform miracles today.

The Pentecostal Assemblies of God distinguishes the original apostles’ unique authority from ongoing apostolic work, such as missionary work and starting churches, without requiring an apostolic title or office. It also affirms prophecy as a continuing gift, with messages tested by the church against Scripture. These are distinct accounts of continuing ministry, rather than a single view shared by all Christians.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 8:29 describes God’s purpose for His people as being conformed to the image of His Son. The growth described here belongs to that larger purpose: God is shaping people to resemble Christ.

1 Corinthians 12:21–27 develops the same body picture by emphasizing the care owed to members who seem weaker and the sharing of suffering and joy. This parallel helps explain why maturity includes making room for the contribution and needs of others. A community’s growth is more than the knowledge or prominence of a few members.
passages.current_position_html: Our study What Is the True Church? recognizes the leadership roles described here. Their purpose is to prepare believers to take part in ministry. Leaders serve and equip the community, while the whole community shares responsibility for its life and service. The study calls for active participation by believers and affirms the need for spiritually mature leadership.

passages.title: Ephesians 4:17-24
passages.section_title: What changes when we learn to live in Christ?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 So I tell you this, and insist on it in the Lord, that you must no longer walk as the Gentiles do, in the futility of their thinking. 18 They are darkened in their understanding and alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them due to the hardness of their hearts. 19 Having lost all sense of shame, they have given themselves over to sensuality for the practice of every kind of impurity, with a craving for more. 20 But this is not the way you came to know Christ. 21 Surely you heard of Him and were taught in Him—in keeping with the truth that is in Jesus— 22 to put off your former way of life, your old self, which is being corrupted by its deceitful desires; 23 to be renewed in the spirit of your minds; 24 and to put on the new self, created to be like God in true righteousness and holiness.
paragraphs: 17 So I tell you this, and insist on it in the Lord, that you must no longer walk as the Gentiles do, in the futility of their thinking. 18 They are darkened in their understanding and alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them due to the hardness of their hearts. 19 Having lost all sense of shame, they have given themselves over to sensuality for the practice of every kind of impurity, with a craving for more.

20 But this is not the way you came to know Christ. 21 Surely you heard of Him and were taught in Him—in keeping with the truth that is in Jesus— 22 to put off your former way of life, your old self, which is being corrupted by its deceitful desires; 23 to be renewed in the spirit of your minds; 24 and to put on the new self, created to be like God in true righteousness and holiness.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul turns from the growth of the body to the way its members live. His readers once belonged to the life he now tells them to leave behind. Earlier he called them Gentiles who have been brought near in Christ (2:11–13). Here, walking as the Gentiles do describes the way of life apart from God that they are to stop following.

The problem reaches into both understanding and desire. Paul describes darkened thinking, hardened hearts and a loss of shame that makes room for impurity and a craving for more. He then contrasts this with what they learned in Christ and the truth found in Jesus.

The picture is like changing clothes: put off the old self, be renewed in the mind and put on the new self. Paul ties the new life to God’s creative work and describes its character as righteousness and holiness. Changed conduct belongs with a changed understanding of who they are in Christ.

The following verses make this practical through truthfulness, honest work, helpful speech, kindness and forgiveness. These instructions continue the concern for the whole body: the way each person lives affects the others.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read this passage as a call for the new life in Christ to reshape thinking, desires and conduct. Wesley’s notes on verses 17–24 and the USCCB notes both emphasize leaving the former life and living in holiness.

The connection with baptism receives different emphasis. The Catholic USCCB note links putting on the new self in verse 24 with baptism. The Catholic Catechism, paragraphs 1227–1228, teaches that baptism joins a person to Christ’s death and risen life and, through the Holy Spirit, purifies, justifies and sanctifies.

The Reformed teacher John Calvin’s comments on verses 22–24 explain the change through turning from the old nature and being renewed by Christ’s Spirit, who restores God’s image. Wesley likewise explains the new self as holiness in God’s image. These comments focus on the change in the person; the Catholic explanation also explicitly places that change within baptism. The passage’s call to a changed life is shared.
passages.god_plan_html:
Genesis 1:26–27 introduces humanity as made in God’s image. Colossians 3:9–11 connects the new self with renewal in the image of its Creator. That is a supported connection between the beginning of humanity’s story and the renewal described here.

Colossians also places people from different backgrounds together in this new life, with Christ in all. Ephesians has already described Jews and Gentiles becoming one new humanity in Him (2:14–18). The renewal reaches beyond private improvement: God is forming a people whose shared life reflects His character across former divisions.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ephesians 4:25-32
passages.section_title: What does the new life look like between us?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 25 Therefore each of you must put off falsehood and speak truthfully to his neighbor, for we are all members of one another. 26 “Be angry, yet do not sin.” Do not let the sun set upon your anger, 27 and do not give the devil a foothold. 28 He who has been stealing must steal no longer, but must work, doing good with his own hands, that he may have something to share with the one in need. 29 Let no unwholesome talk come out of your mouths, but only what is helpful for building up the one in need and bringing grace to those who listen. 30 And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption. 31 Get rid of all bitterness, rage and anger, outcry and slander, along with every form of malice. 32 Be kind and tenderhearted to one another, forgiving each other just as in Christ God forgave you.
paragraphs: 25 Therefore each of you must put off falsehood and speak truthfully to his neighbor, for we are all members of one another. 26 “Be angry, yet do not sin.” Do not let the sun set upon your anger, 27 and do not give the devil a foothold. 28 He who has been stealing must steal no longer, but must work, doing good with his own hands, that he may have something to share with the one in need.

29 Let no unwholesome talk come out of your mouths, but only what is helpful for building up the one in need and bringing grace to those who listen. 30 And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption. 31 Get rid of all bitterness, rage and anger, outcry and slander, along with every form of malice. 32 Be kind and tenderhearted to one another, forgiving each other just as in Christ God forgave you.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul now makes the call to put on the new self concrete. Falsehood gives way to truth because believers belong to one another. Anger must be kept from becoming sin or taking root, and the devil must be given no foothold.

The person who stole is to work honestly and become able to share with someone in need. Speech is to help the person who hears it. The Greek word behind unwholesome is sapros (sah-PROSS). Thayer’s lexicon describes what is rotten, poor in quality or unfit for use. Paul contrasts such speech with words that build someone up.

The warning against grieving the Holy Spirit stands within these instructions about relationships. Paul reminds the readers that they were sealed in Him for the day of redemption. Their conduct toward one another matters to the Spirit who marks them as God’s people.

The paragraph ends by replacing bitterness, rage, slander and malice with kindness, tenderness and forgiveness. God’s forgiveness in Christ supplies the pattern. This continues the chapter’s concern for a body whose members care for one another.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand these commands as practical expressions of life in Christ: honesty, generosity, helpful speech and forgiveness. Wesley’s notes on verses 25–32 and the USCCB notes connect the instructions with the church’s shared life. The warning about anger calls for prompt attention rather than allowing resentment to settle.

Christians understand grieving the Spirit as a serious warning about conduct that harms the life God gives His people. They differ over how the seal relates to the possibility of finally falling away.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 17, teaches that those truly called and sanctified will finally be saved, while recognizing that serious sin grieves the Spirit and damages their comfort and others’ lives. The Wesleyan Methodist Articles of Religion, article XII, teach that people who have received the Holy Spirit can depart from grace and fall into sin, and can rise again through God’s grace.

The Catholic Catechism, paragraphs 1272–1274, teaches that baptism’s spiritual mark cannot be erased, while also teaching that sin can prevent it from bearing the fruits of salvation. An enduring mark is therefore understood differently from an unconditional assurance of final salvation. These teachings frame the warning in distinct ways; all take the call to faithfulness seriously.
passages.god_plan_html:
The day of redemption points forward. Romans 8:11, 23 connects the Spirit’s presence now with God’s future giving of life to mortal bodies and the redemption believers still await. The community is learning to live together in light of that promised future.

Matthew 5:14–16 also connects the good works of Jesus’ followers with others giving glory to their Father. This provides a supported parallel to the practical change described here: honesty, generosity and care make the Father’s character visible in the lives of His people.
passages.current_position_html: On verse 30, our study Baptism teaches that sin grieves the Holy Spirit without driving Him out or cancelling the believer’s salvation. It distinguishes that secure standing from the harm sin does to fellowship with God. The study calls for honest confession and a renewed walk with Him.

passages.title: Ephesians 4:30
passages.section_title: What does it mean to grieve the Holy Spirit?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 30 And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.
paragraphs: 30 And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.

passages.context_html:
This warning appears in instructions about life together. Immediately before it, Paul calls for speech that helps those who hear. Immediately after it, he calls believers to put away bitterness and malice and practice kindness and forgiveness.

The Spirit is grieved by conduct that conflicts with that life. At the same time, Paul reminds the readers that they were sealed in Him for the day of redemption. Both the warning and the future hope belong to the sentence.

Read Ephesians 4:25–32 to keep the warning connected with the relationships and choices Paul is addressing.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians understand grieving the Spirit as a serious warning about conduct that harms the life God gives His people. They differ over how the seal relates to the possibility of finally falling away.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 17, teaches that those truly called and sanctified will finally be saved, while recognizing that serious sin grieves the Spirit and damages their comfort and others’ lives. The Wesleyan Methodist Articles of Religion, article XII, teach that people who have received the Holy Spirit can depart from grace and fall into sin, and can rise again through God’s grace.

An enduring mark is therefore understood differently from an unconditional assurance of final salvation. These teachings frame the warning in distinct ways; all take the call to faithfulness seriously.

It distinguishes that secure standing from the harm sin does to fellowship with God. The study calls for honest confession and a renewed walk with Him.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 8:11, 23 places the Spirit’s presence within the hope of resurrection and the redemption of our bodies. The promised day reaches beyond a present feeling or experience.

This is a supported connection with the future redemption named here. God’s people are called to live faithfully together while awaiting the completion of His saving work.

passages.title: Ephesians 5:1-2
passages.section_title: What does it mean to love as God’s children?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Be imitators of God, therefore, as beloved children, 2 and walk in love, just as Christ loved us and gave Himself up for us as a fragrant sacrificial offering to God.
paragraphs: 1 Be imitators of God, therefore, as beloved children, 2 and walk in love, just as Christ loved us and gave Himself up for us as a fragrant sacrificial offering to God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The word therefore carries forward the call to forgive as God forgave in Christ (4:32). Paul now calls believers to imitate God as children who are loved by Him. God’s love is the starting point for their response.

Walking in love describes the way they are to live. Christ supplies the pattern: He loved us and gave Himself for us. Paul describes His self-giving as an offering and sacrifice pleasing to God.

This short passage connects the practical kindness and forgiveness of chapter 4 with the warnings that follow. Loving others belongs with turning from conduct that uses or harms them.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a call to reflect the Father’s love through the pattern of Christ’s self-giving. Wesley’s note on verse 1 and the USCCB note connect imitating God with forgiving and loving others. The passage grounds that love in what Christ has already done for His people.
passages.god_plan_html:
The pleasing-aroma language has a clear scriptural background. Exodus 29:15–18 describes a burnt offering to the Lord with that language. Ephesians explicitly applies sacrificial language to Christ’s gift of Himself. This is a connection the passage makes, rather than a claim that every detail of that offering supplies a separate symbol here.

2 Corinthians 5:14–15 connects Christ’s death with His people living for the One who died and rose for them. His saving work gives direction to their life: received love becomes the reason for loving service.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ephesians 5:3-7
passages.section_title: Why does Paul warn against treating sin lightly?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 3 But among you, as is proper among the saints, there must not be even a hint of sexual immorality, or of any kind of impurity, or of greed. 4 Nor should there be obscenity, foolish talk, or crude joking, which are out of character, but rather thanksgiving. 5 For of this you can be sure: No immoral, impure, or greedy person (that is, an idolater) has any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God. 6 Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of such things the wrath of God is coming on the sons of disobedience. 7 Therefore do not be partakers with them.
paragraphs: 3 But among you, as is proper among the saints, there must not be even a hint of sexual immorality, or of any kind of impurity, or of greed. 4 Nor should there be obscenity, foolish talk, or crude joking, which are out of character, but rather thanksgiving.

5 For of this you can be sure: No immoral, impure, or greedy person (that is, an idolater) has any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God. 6 Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of such things the wrath of God is coming on the sons of disobedience. 7 Therefore do not be partakers with them.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul has just called believers to walk in the love shown by Christ. He now names conduct that conflicts with that calling: sexual immorality, impurity, greed and degrading speech. Thanksgiving is the positive alternative he names for their speech.

The warning about inheritance gives these instructions weight. Paul connects greed with idolatry and says that the immoral, impure or greedy person has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God. He tells the readers not to be deceived by empty words or become partners in these things.

The contrast continues in verse 8: they were once darkness, but now are light in the Lord. Paul is calling people who belong to Him to take that change seriously. The text gives no permission to excuse harmful conduct as unimportant to God.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand these verses as a serious warning that sexual sin, greed and degrading speech conflict with life in God’s kingdom. They differ in how they relate the warning to perseverance and the possibility of falling away.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 17, teaches that those truly called and sanctified will finally be saved, while recognizing that they can fall into serious sins that grieve the Spirit and hurt others. The warning is therefore taken seriously within an account of God preserving His people.

The Wesleyan Methodist Articles of Religion, article XII, teach that those who have received the Holy Spirit can depart from grace and fall into sin, and can be restored through God’s grace. The Catholic Catechism, paragraphs 1272–1274, teaches that baptism’s spiritual mark endures while sin can prevent it from bearing saving fruit. These documents give differing accounts of security and faithfulness; none treats this conduct as harmless.
passages.god_plan_html:
Calling greed idolatry connects this warning with the Bible’s larger concern about what people worship. Romans 1:21–25 describes the disorder that follows when people exchange the truth about God for devotion to created things.

Colossians 3:5 also explicitly identifies greed as idolatry. This parallel helps explain why the warning reaches beyond outward respectability: the issue includes what claims our trust and devotion in place of God.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ephesians 5:8-14
passages.section_title: How do we live as children of light?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light, 9 for the fruit of the light consists in all goodness, righteousness, and truth. 10 Test and prove what pleases the Lord. 11 Have no fellowship with the fruitless deeds of darkness, but rather expose them. 12 For it is shameful even to mention what the disobedient do in secret. 13 But everything exposed by the light becomes visible, for everything that is illuminated becomes a light itself. 14 So it is said: “Wake up, O sleeper, rise up from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.”
paragraphs: 8 For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light, 9 for the fruit of the light consists in all goodness, righteousness, and truth. 10 Test and prove what pleases the Lord.

11 Have no fellowship with the fruitless deeds of darkness, but rather expose them. 12 For it is shameful even to mention what the disobedient do in secret. 13 But everything exposed by the light becomes visible, for everything that is illuminated becomes a light itself. 14 So it is said: “Wake up, O sleeper, rise up from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul describes a change in who the readers are: once darkness, now light in the Lord. Their conduct is to agree with that new life. He names its fruit as goodness, righteousness and truth, with a call to test what pleases the Lord.

They must take no part in the fruitless deeds of darkness, but expose them. The verb is elegchō (eh-LENG-khoh). Thayer’s lexicon includes bringing wrongdoing to light and correcting it, including correction through words. The call involves truthful conduct and the refusal to let evil remain disguised.

Paul also says that the hidden wrongdoing is shameful even to mention. His instruction does not call for enjoying or celebrating its details. The closing appeal pictures a sleeper rising into Christ’s light.

The next paragraph carries this forward through wise use of time and understanding the Lord’s will. Walking in light is expressed in daily choices about what is good and true.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the light as life in the Lord that bears goodness, righteousness and truth. Wesley’s notes on verses 8–14 call for both avoiding and correcting evil. The USCCB notes connect the awakening language with Christ’s life-giving work.

The closing lines are often explained as an early Christian hymn, possibly used at baptism, as the USCCB note suggests. Wesley connects their sense with God’s scriptural call to awaken. The precise origin is uncertain; the call to rise into Christ’s light is clear in the passage itself.
passages.god_plan_html:
Isaiah 60:1–3 pictures Zion rising into the Lord’s light while darkness covers the peoples, with nations drawn to that light. There is a strong parallel with the call to awaken and receive Christ’s light here, without needing to treat Ephesians as an exact quotation of Isaiah.

John 8:12 identifies Jesus as the light of the world and connects following Him with the light of life. Ephesians places the readers’ new life in the Lord. The larger connection points to Christ as the source of the light they are to reflect; it does not turn them into their own source of salvation.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ephesians 5:15-17
passages.section_title: How can we make wise use of the time we have?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 Pay careful attention, then, to how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, 16 redeeming the time, because the days are evil. 17 Therefore do not be foolish, but understand what the Lord’s will is.
paragraphs: 15 Pay careful attention, then, to how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, 16 redeeming the time, because the days are evil. 17 Therefore do not be foolish, but understand what the Lord’s will is.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
These verses draw a practical conclusion from the call to live as children of light. Paul tells the readers to pay careful attention to their walk, using the contrast between wisdom and foolishness.

Redeeming the time means making good use of the opportunity before them in days marked by evil. Paul directs their attention to understanding the Lord’s will. The preceding instructions already show its moral direction: goodness, righteousness, truth and turning from darkness.

The next sentence contrasts drunkenness with being filled with the Spirit, followed by worship, thanksgiving and submission to one another. Wise living belongs within that shared life before God.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these verses as a call to thoughtful, faithful living and the use of present opportunities for good. Wesley’s notes on verses 15–17 emphasize using time well and attending to God’s will in the circumstances of life. The USCCB notes also connect the wording with the call to wise conduct in Colossians 4:5. No separate denominational breakdown is needed for that shared point.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 13:11–14 also connects awakening, the passing night and putting aside the works of darkness. There the reason includes the approaching completion of salvation.

This parallel adds a future horizon to the call to use the present well. Christian hope gives direction to ordinary choices now: believers are to live in keeping with the Lord they await.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ephesians 5:18-21
passages.section_title: What does life filled with the Spirit look like together?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 Do not get drunk on wine, which leads to reckless indiscretion. Instead, be filled with the Spirit. 19 Speak to one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs. Sing and make music in your hearts to the Lord, 20 always giving thanks to God the Father for everything in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. 21 Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ.
paragraphs: 18 Do not get drunk on wine, which leads to reckless indiscretion. Instead, be filled with the Spirit. 19 Speak to one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs. Sing and make music in your hearts to the Lord, 20 always giving thanks to God the Father for everything in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. 21 Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul continues the call to wise living with a contrast: drunkenness leads to reckless conduct, while believers are to be filled with the Spirit. The verses that follow describe a shared life of song, thanksgiving and submission out of reverence for Christ.

The singing has two explicit directions. Believers speak to one another through psalms, hymns and spiritual songs, and sing and make music in their hearts to the Lord. The text keeps mutual encouragement and praise to Him together.

Thanksgiving is offered to God the Father in the name of Jesus Christ. The paragraph then calls believers to submit to one another. Paul places their treatment of each other within their reverence for Christ.

This last instruction also leads into the following discussion of households. The whole movement belongs within the letter’s concern for a community shaped by Christ’s love.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read this paragraph as contrasting drunkenness with life directed by God’s Spirit, expressed through worship, gratitude and regard for others. Wesley’s notes on verses 18–20 connect the Spirit’s work with heartfelt singing and thanksgiving. The USCCB notes connect the following household instructions with mutual responsibility under Christ.

On the shared point, the passage itself names the practices rather than leaving Spirit-filled life as an undefined feeling. Its instructions include both the heart’s response to the Lord and what believers do for one another.
passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 2:13–18 records an accusation of drunkenness at Pentecost. Peter explains what is happening through God’s promised outpouring of the Spirit. This is a useful parallel to Paul’s contrast, rather than proof that the two passages describe an identical outward experience.

The shared life that follows in Acts 2:42–47 includes teaching, fellowship, prayer, practical care and praise to God. God’s gift forms a people who learn, give thanks and care for one another. That larger purpose helps connect the practices named here.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Worship as the Early Church Knew It emphasizes the purpose of speaking to one another in song: communicating truth that helps others grow in faith. It distinguishes that service from a song’s emotional effect on an individual. Personal feeling by itself does not show that the gathering is being built up. The study also recognizes praise and thanksgiving directed to God.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

passages.title: Ephesians 5:19
passages.section_title: How can our singing help one another?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 Speak to one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs. Sing and make music in your hearts to the Lord,
paragraphs: 19 Speak to one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs. Sing and make music in your hearts to the Lord,

passages.context_html:
This verse is part of the description of being filled with the Spirit in 5:18–21. Paul names singing alongside thanksgiving to the Father and submission to one another out of reverence for Christ.

Believers are to speak to one another through psalms, hymns and spiritual songs. They also sing and make music in their hearts to the Lord. Both directions belong to the verse: words shared with fellow believers and heartfelt praise to Him.

The parallel instruction in Colossians 3:16 connects teaching and admonishing one another with singing in gratitude to God. It helps explain how song can serve the life of the community.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this verse as joining heartfelt praise to the Lord with song that serves fellow believers. Wesley’s note on verse 19 includes the voice as well as the heart in singing to the Lord. Colossians 3:16 supplies the explicit parallel of teaching and admonishing one another.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Worship as the Early Church Knew It emphasizes the purpose of speaking to one another in song: communicating truth that helps others grow in faith. It distinguishes that service from a song’s emotional effect on an individual. Personal feeling by itself does not show that the gathering is being built up. The study also recognizes praise and thanksgiving directed to God.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 2:42–47 places praise within the shared life formed after the gift of the Spirit: learning, prayer, fellowship and care for those in need. Praise belongs within the life of a people gathered around Christ.

This is a supported parallel to the song described here. The Spirit’s work gives the community reasons to thank God and ways to strengthen one another as they live together.

passages.title: Ephesians 5:22-33
passages.section_title: How does Christ’s love shape marriage?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 Wives, submit to your husbands as to the Lord. 23 For the husband is the head of the wife as Christ is the head of the church, His body, of which He is the Savior. 24 Now as the church submits to Christ, so also wives should submit to their husbands in everything. 25 Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her 26 to sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing with water through the word, 27 and to present her to Himself as a glorious church, without stain or wrinkle or any such blemish, but holy and blameless. 28 In the same way, husbands ought to love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself. 29 Indeed, no one ever hated his own body, but he nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the church. 30 For we are members of His body. 31 “For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and the two will become one flesh.” 32 This mystery is profound, but I am speaking about Christ and the church. 33 Nevertheless, each one of you also must love his wife as he loves himself, and the wife must respect her husband.
paragraphs: 22 Wives, submit to your husbands as to the Lord. 23 For the husband is the head of the wife as Christ is the head of the church, His body, of which He is the Savior. 24 Now as the church submits to Christ, so also wives should submit to their husbands in everything.

25 Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her 26 to sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing with water through the word, 27 and to present her to Himself as a glorious church, without stain or wrinkle or any such blemish, but holy and blameless. 28 In the same way, husbands ought to love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself. 29 Indeed, no one ever hated his own body, but he nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the church. 30 For we are members of His body.

31 “For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and the two will become one flesh.” 32 This mystery is profound, but I am speaking about Christ and the church. 33 Nevertheless, each one of you also must love his wife as he loves himself, and the wife must respect her husband.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
This passage follows the call to submit to one another out of reverence for Christ (5:21). Paul addresses wives and husbands, placing marriage within the life of a community learning to walk in Christ’s love.

Wives are told to submit to their own husbands, with the church’s relation to Christ providing the comparison. Husbands are told to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave Himself for her. Both sets of instructions belong to the same connected passage.

Paul describes Christ’s purpose as making His church holy and presenting her to Himself without stain or blemish. His care for the church gives the husband a pattern of nourishing and cherishing his wife as his own body.

Paul then quotes Genesis 2:24 about the two becoming one flesh. He connects that union with Christ and the church, before returning to the husband’s love and the wife’s respect. The passage moves between the marriage relationship and the saving love of Christ that gives it a pattern.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand this passage as calling for faithful marriage shaped by Christ’s self-giving love. They differ over how the husband’s headship and the instruction to submit describe decision-making and responsibility within marriage.

The Southern Baptist Baptist Faith and Message, article XVIII, affirms the equal worth of husband and wife while giving them distinct responsibilities. The husband is called to loving leadership, provision and protection, and the wife to gracious submission to that servant leadership. This is the confession’s stated Baptist position, rather than a description of every Baptist congregation.

CBE International’s own statement, family point 11 and its applications, reads headship as self-giving service within mutual submission and responsibility, with leadership shared in the home. This represents a Christian equality reading found across several denominations, rather than one denomination’s official teaching.

In the Catholic apostolic letter Mulieris Dignitatem, paragraph 24, John Paul II emphasizes that the spouses’ submission is mutual, while the church’s submission to Christ is one-sided. He explains the husband’s headship through Christ’s giving of Himself. The accounts share an emphasis on love and dignity, while describing the responsibilities of the spouses differently.

On the washing in verse 26, Wesley’s note connects the water with baptism, joined with inward grace and the word. This is an interpretation of the phrase in context. The Greek word for water does not by itself settle every question about baptism or cleansing.
passages.god_plan_html:
The connection with God’s larger purpose is explicit: Paul quotes Genesis 2:24, then says that he is speaking about Christ and the church. The union described at the beginning of the Bible becomes a picture through which he explains Christ’s committed love for His people.
