Revelation 19:6–9 looks forward to the marriage of the Lamb and the readiness of His bride. This gives a supported future connection to Christ preparing His church to be holy and without blemish. The picture directs hope toward His completed work.

The comparison has limits: the husband does not become his wife’s savior or replace Christ. The saving work belongs to Christ, whose self-giving love supplies the pattern for the care described here.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ephesians 6:1-4
passages.section_title: How should children and parents treat one another?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right. 2 “Honor your father and mother” (which is the first commandment with a promise), 3 “that it may go well with you and that you may have a long life on the earth.” 4 Fathers, do not provoke your children to wrath; instead, bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.
paragraphs: 1 Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right. 2 “Honor your father and mother” (which is the first commandment with a promise), 3 “that it may go well with you and that you may have a long life on the earth.”
4 Fathers, do not provoke your children to wrath; instead, bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
These instructions continue the discussion of household relationships begun in chapter 5. Children are addressed directly and told to obey their parents in the Lord. Paul then quotes the command to honor father and mother, including its promise of well-being and long life.

Fathers are also addressed directly. They must not provoke their children to wrath, but bring them up in the Lord’s discipline and instruction. The command to children stands beside an obligation on those who raise them.

The Lord is central to both instructions. Children’s conduct is related to Him, and their upbringing is to be shaped by His teaching. Paul treats the home as part of the community’s life in Christ.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand this as joining children’s respect and obedience with parents’ responsibility to teach and care for them. Wesley’s notes on verses 1–4 limit obedience to what is lawful and describe upbringing through Christian teaching with tenderness. The Catholic Catechism, paragraphs 2217 and 2222–2223, likewise rejects morally wrong commands and emphasizes respect, good example and care.

The continuing duty to honor parents is distinguished from a child’s obedience while dependent on them; the Catechism explains that distinction in paragraphs 2217–2218. Applications of the long-life promise also receive different emphasis. Wesley’s note on verse 3 gives it a spiritual dimension under the gospel. The promise is a reason to value honoring parents, rather than a timetable by which readers can calculate a particular child’s lifespan.
passages.god_plan_html:
Deuteronomy 6:4–9 places love for the Lord and teaching His words within the ordinary rhythms of home: sitting, walking, lying down and rising. This is a supported parallel to bringing children up in the Lord’s instruction.

The larger theme is the passing on of the knowledge of God across generations. Family care and teaching belong within that purpose. Ephesians places responsibility on those who teach as well as those who are learning.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ephesians 6:5-9
passages.section_title: What does answering to the same Lord change?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 Slaves, obey your earthly masters with respect and fear and sincerity of heart, just as you would obey Christ. 6 And do this not only to please them while they are watching, but as servants of Christ, doing the will of God from your heart. 7 Serve with good will, as to the Lord and not to men, 8 because you know that the Lord will reward each one for whatever good he does, whether he is slave or free. 9 And masters, do the same for your slaves. Give up your use of threats, because you know that He who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and there is no favoritism with Him.
paragraphs: 5 Slaves, obey your earthly masters with respect and fear and sincerity of heart, just as you would obey Christ. 6 And do this not only to please them while they are watching, but as servants of Christ, doing the will of God from your heart. 7 Serve with good will, as to the Lord and not to men, 8 because you know that the Lord will reward each one for whatever good he does, whether he is slave or free.
9 And masters, do the same for your slaves. Give up your use of threats, because you know that He who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and there is no favoritism with Him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul now addresses slaves and masters. He calls those who are enslaved to serve sincerely, with their attention on Christ rather than only on pleasing a master who happens to be watching.

The promise of the Lord’s reward names both slave and free. Their earthly standing does not determine whether the Lord sees the good they do.

Masters are then told to act from the same responsibility to Him and give up threats. Paul reminds them that the One in heaven is Master of both groups and shows no favoritism. The instructions place those exercising power under His judgment too.

This completes the household instructions. It is important to read the whole group: the command to serve and the command to stop threatening stand together under the authority of the same Lord.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the central point as sincere service to Christ and accountability to Him on both sides of the relationship. Wesley’s notes on verses 5–9 connect service with the Lord’s will and explain the command to masters through gentleness and humane treatment.

The USCCB note on the household instructions beginning at 5:21 also emphasizes responsibility on both sides and the judgment facing slave owners in 6:9. The passage addresses slavery directly; drawing lessons about other relationships of work or authority requires keeping that original setting in view.
passages.god_plan_html:
Galatians 3:26–29 places slave and free together in belonging to Christ and sharing the promised inheritance. That is a supported connection with the same Lord seeing and rewarding good without favoritism here.

In Philemon 15–17, Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus as a beloved brother and as he would receive Paul himself. This provides a concrete parallel of how belonging to Christ changes the way one person is to regard another. The other person’s dignity cannot be measured merely by their earthly status.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ephesians 6:10-17
passages.section_title: How do we stand firm in the Lord’s strength?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 Finally, be strong in the Lord and in His mighty power. 11 Put on the full armor of God, so that you can make your stand against the devil’s schemes. 12 For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the powers of this world’s darkness, and against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms. 13 Therefore take up the full armor of God, so that when the day of evil comes, you will be able to stand your ground, and having done everything, to stand. 14 Stand firm then, with the belt of truth buckled around your waist, with the breastplate of righteousness arrayed, 15 and with your feet fitted with the readiness of the gospel of peace. 16 In addition to all this, take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming arrows of the evil one. 17 And take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.
paragraphs: 10 Finally, be strong in the Lord and in His mighty power. 11 Put on the full armor of God, so that you can make your stand against the devil’s schemes. 12 For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the powers of this world’s darkness, and against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms. 13 Therefore take up the full armor of God, so that when the day of evil comes, you will be able to stand your ground, and having done everything, to stand.

14 Stand firm then, with the belt of truth buckled around your waist, with the breastplate of righteousness arrayed, 15 and with your feet fitted with the readiness of the gospel of peace. 16 In addition to all this, take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming arrows of the evil one. 17 And take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul closes his main instructions by directing believers to the Lord’s strength. He describes a struggle against the devil’s schemes and spiritual powers of evil, and tells them to take up God’s full armor so they can stand firm.

The armor gives a concrete picture of what God supplies: truth, righteousness, readiness associated with the gospel of peace, faith and salvation. Paul identifies the Spirit’s sword as the word of God. These belong together in the call to resist evil.

The statement that the struggle is not against flesh and blood matters. Paul directs the community’s attention to spiritual opposition rather than making other people the targets of its warfare.

The paragraph continues into prayer in verses 18–20. Remaining alert and praying for one another belong with taking up the armor. Paul then asks for prayer for his own gospel witness while he is in chains.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the armor as God’s provision for resisting spiritual evil through faith, truth, righteousness, salvation and His word. Wesley’s notes on verses 10–17 emphasize the need for His power and the completeness of the armor. The USCCB note likewise identifies spiritual opposition and connects the picture with Isaiah.

The imagery describes faithful resistance under the Lord’s strength. It gives no schedule of enemy movements or test for assigning a particular inconvenience to a demon. The text’s emphasis falls on what believers are to take up and the Lord in whom they are to stand.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Isaiah 59:15–20, the Lord acts when justice is absent. He wears righteousness as a breastplate and salvation as a helmet. Ephesians’ armor has a strong scriptural parallel: believers are told to stand in the Lord’s strength with qualities associated with His saving action.

Isaiah 11:1–5 describes the ruler from Jesse’s line with righteousness and faithfulness as His belt. Isaiah 52:7–10 connects the feet of the good-news messenger with peace, salvation and God’s reign. These parallels place the armor within the larger story of His faithful rule and rescue.

The details are not all transferred unchanged: Ephesians calls for the gospel of peace and identifies a spiritual struggle. The connection directs believers to God’s provision as they resist evil and bear witness to His good news.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Ephesians 6:18-20
passages.section_title: What should we pray for as we stand together?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 Pray in the Spirit at all times, with every kind of prayer and petition. To this end, stay alert with all perseverance in your prayers for all the saints. 19 Pray also for me, that whenever I open my mouth, words may be given me so that I will boldly make known the mystery of the gospel, 20 for which I am an ambassador in chains. Pray that I may proclaim it fearlessly, as I should.
paragraphs: 18 Pray in the Spirit at all times, with every kind of prayer and petition. To this end, stay alert with all perseverance in your prayers for all the saints. 19 Pray also for me, that whenever I open my mouth, words may be given me so that I will boldly make known the mystery of the gospel, 20 for which I am an ambassador in chains. Pray that I may proclaim it fearlessly, as I should.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The call to prayer continues the instructions about God’s armor. Paul tells believers to pray in the Spirit at all times, with every kind of prayer and petition, while staying alert and persevering in prayer for all the saints.

He then includes himself in their prayers. His request is specific: words to make the mystery of the gospel known and boldness to speak as he should. He describes himself as an ambassador in chains.

His imprisonment has not removed his calling to proclaim the gospel, and his role as an apostle has not removed his need for others’ prayers. The community’s prayer includes those who lead and speak as well as the wider body.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as a call to persistent prayer for fellow believers and for the clear, courageous proclamation of the gospel. Wesley’s notes on verses 18–20 explain prayer in the Spirit through the Spirit’s influence and emphasize intercession. The USCCB note on 6:10–20 also gives prayer a central place in the call to stand firm. The passage names both the broad concern for all God’s people and Paul’s particular request.
passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 4:23–31 supplies a close parallel. After threats against the apostles, the believers recognize God’s authority and purposes, ask for boldness to speak, and ask Him to act through healing and signs in Jesus’ name.

The account then describes them being filled with the Spirit and speaking God’s word boldly. Prayer supports witness as God’s people depend on Him together. Paul’s request here belongs within that larger pattern of the gospel being made known despite opposition.
passages.current_position_html: Our study What Does Prayer Look Like? uses Paul’s request here as an example of prayer for faithfulness under pressure. He asks for words and courage to make the gospel known while in chains. The study emphasizes seeking God’s strength to carry out His purposes in the circumstances we face.

passages.title: Ephesians 6:19-20
passages.section_title: Why does Paul ask others to pray for his courage?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 Pray also for me, that whenever I open my mouth, words may be given me so that I will boldly make known the mystery of the gospel, 20 for which I am an ambassador in chains. Pray that I may proclaim it fearlessly, as I should.
paragraphs: 19 Pray also for me, that whenever I open my mouth, words may be given me so that I will boldly make known the mystery of the gospel, 20 for which I am an ambassador in chains. Pray that I may proclaim it fearlessly, as I should.

passages.context_html:
Paul has just called for persevering prayer for all God’s people. He now asks the readers to include him, naming his need for words and boldness to proclaim the gospel.

He is an ambassador in chains: a messenger of Christ whose imprisonment is real. His request concerns how he will speak within that situation. The need for prayer is shared by the messenger and the community he serves.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as a call to persistent prayer for fellow believers and for the clear, courageous proclamation of the gospel. Wesley’s notes on verses 18–20 explain prayer in the Spirit through the Spirit’s influence and emphasize intercession. The USCCB note on 6:10–20 also gives prayer a central place in the call to stand firm. The passage names both the broad concern for all God’s people and Paul’s particular request.
passages.current_position_html: Our study What Does Prayer Look Like? uses Paul’s request here as an example of prayer for faithfulness under pressure. He asks for words and courage to make the gospel known while in chains. The study emphasizes seeking God’s strength to carry out His purposes in the circumstances we face.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 4:23–31 also connects opposition, shared prayer and bold gospel witness. The believers ask for courage as well as God’s work of healing and signs, and the account ends with Spirit-filled proclamation.

This provides a supported parallel to Paul’s request. God’s people take part in the spread of the gospel through their dependence on Him and their prayers for those who speak.

passages.title: Ephesians 6:21-24
passages.section_title: How does Paul encourage the church as he closes?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 Tychicus, the beloved brother and faithful servant in the Lord, will tell you everything, so that you also may know about me and what I am doing. 22 I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know about us, and that he may encourage your hearts. 23 Peace to the brothers and love with faith from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. 24 Grace to all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with an undying love.
paragraphs: 21 Tychicus, the beloved brother and faithful servant in the Lord, will tell you everything, so that you also may know about me and what I am doing. 22 I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know about us, and that he may encourage your hearts.
23 Peace to the brothers and love with faith from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. 24 Grace to all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with an undying love.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After asking for prayer, Paul explains that Tychicus will bring news about him and his circumstances. He calls him a beloved brother and faithful servant in the Lord, and says his visit will encourage their hearts.

The letter ends with peace, love with faith, and grace. Paul names God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ as the source of these gifts and closes with grace for those who love Christ with an undying love.

The practical sharing of news belongs beside the blessing. The readers are to know how Paul is doing, and he wants them encouraged in the life they share in the Lord.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as personal encouragement and a closing blessing. The USCCB note on verses 21–24 identifies Tychicus as the bearer of news and points to the parallel in Colossians 4:7–8. Wesley’s notes connect the news with encouragement and the final blessing with continuing faithfulness to Christ. The shared emphasis is care for the community and the grace that sustains it.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Philippians 1:1-2
passages.section_title: How does Paul greet the believers at Philippi?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Paul and Timothy, servants of Christ Jesus, To all the saints in Christ Jesus at Philippi, together with the overseers and deacons: 2 Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
paragraphs: 1 Paul and Timothy, servants of Christ Jesus, To all the saints in Christ Jesus at Philippi, together with the overseers and deacons: 2 Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul opens with Timothy beside him, describing them both as servants of Christ Jesus. The word is doulos (DOO-loss). Thayer’s lexicon gives its ordinary meaning as slave and explains its use here for people serving Christ and His cause. Their belonging to Him comes first in the greeting.

The letter is addressed to all the saints in Christ Jesus at Philippi, together with the overseers and deacons. Saints here names the community of believers. Paul includes its recognized leaders within his greeting to the whole church.

He wishes them grace and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. The next paragraph will show the affection and gratitude behind that greeting. Later in the chapter, Paul will describe his imprisonment and their shared commitment to the gospel.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a greeting to the whole believing community, including its leaders, from fellow servants of Christ. Wesley’s note on verse 1 emphasizes Paul’s placing Timothy beside himself under the shared description of servants. The USCCB note likewise understands it as stressing their service to Christ. The greeting’s shared focus is their relationship to Him and the grace and peace that come from God.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Mark 10:42–45, Jesus teaches His followers to understand greatness through service and points to His own coming to serve and give His life. This is a supported parallel to the service named at the beginning of the letter.

Philippians will develop that pattern in 2:3–8, connecting concern for others with Christ’s humility and His taking the form of a servant. The opening greeting fits within the larger purpose of a people learning to treat one another in the way of their Lord.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Philippians 1:3-8
passages.section_title: Why does Paul thank God for their partnership?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 3 I thank my God every time I remember you. 4 In every prayer for all of you, I always pray with joy, 5 because of your partnership in the gospel from the first day until now, 6 being confident of this, that He who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion until the day of Christ Jesus. 7 It is right for me to feel this way about all of you, since I have you in my heart. For in my chains and in my defense and confirmation of the gospel, you are all partners in grace with me. 8 God is my witness how I long for all of you with the affection of Christ Jesus.
paragraphs: 3 I thank my God every time I remember you. 4 In every prayer for all of you, I always pray with joy, 5 because of your partnership in the gospel from the first day until now, 6 being confident of this, that He who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion until the day of Christ Jesus.

7 It is right for me to feel this way about all of you, since I have you in my heart. For in my chains and in my defense and confirmation of the gospel, you are all partners in grace with me. 8 God is my witness how I long for all of you with the affection of Christ Jesus.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul remembers the Philippians with gratitude and prays for them with joy. He gives a reason: their partnership in the gospel from the first day until now. The Greek word is koinōnia (koy-nohn-EE-ah). Thayer’s lexicon includes sharing, participation and fellowship, and directly connects this use with the bond between Christians.

Their partnership is practical. Later, Philippians 4:14–18 describes gifts sent for Paul’s needs and their sharing in his affliction. Here he calls them partners in grace during his chains and his defense and confirmation of the gospel.

His confidence looks beyond the present: God began a good work among them and will carry it to completion until the day of Christ Jesus. Paul places their continuing life and service within God’s work.

The paragraph also shows personal affection. Paul has them in his heart and longs for them with the affection of Christ Jesus. Shared gospel work includes care for the people involved.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand Paul’s gratitude as a response to genuine gospel partnership and his confidence as resting in God’s faithful work. The USCCB notes on verses 3–11 connect their partnership, Paul’s affection and preparation for Christ’s return.

Christians differ in how they relate this confidence to final perseverance. The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 17, teaches that those truly called and sanctified will be preserved to final salvation. Wesley’s comments on verses 6–7 also affirm God’s work toward completion, while grounding Paul’s confidence about these readers in their actual sharing in grace and his affections for them.

The Wesleyan Methodist Articles of Religion, article XII, allow that people who have received the Spirit can depart from grace and be restored through grace. The Catholic Catechism, paragraph 2016, describes final perseverance as a grace for which believers rightly hope. These are distinct accounts of perseverance; the passage’s emphasis on God’s work and the readers’ continuing partnership should both remain in view.
passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 16:13–15, 25–34 gives concrete beginnings for this community: Lydia and her household receive the message, and later the jailer and his household hear it in the aftermath of Paul and Silas’s imprisonment. Hospitality, witness and care appear together in the account.

Philippians 4:14–18 then shows the community supporting Paul’s gospel work. This is a supported connection across the story: people reached by the gospel become participants in its continuing spread. Their giving is one visible part of that partnership.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Philippians 1:9-11
passages.section_title: What kind of growing love does Paul pray for?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 And this is my prayer: that your love may abound more and more in knowledge and depth of insight, 10 so that you may be able to test and prove what is best and may be pure and blameless for the day of Christ, 11 filled with the fruit of righteousness that comes through Jesus Christ, to the glory and praise of God.
paragraphs: 9 And this is my prayer: that your love may abound more and more in knowledge and depth of insight, 10 so that you may be able to test and prove what is best and may be pure and blameless for the day of Christ, 11 filled with the fruit of righteousness that comes through Jesus Christ, to the glory and praise of God.

passages.context_html:
After thanking God for the Philippians and expressing his affection, Paul tells them what he prays for. He wants their love to keep growing in knowledge and depth of insight, so they can recognize what is best.

The Greek word translated insight is aisthēsis (EYE-sthay-sis). Thayer’s lexicon explains its use here as moral discernment: understanding that helps a person recognize what is right. Paul joins love with the ability to make good judgments.

The goal is a life pure and blameless for the day of Christ, filled with righteous fruit that comes through Jesus Christ. The prayer moves from growing love to discerning choices and a life that brings glory and praise to God.

This is prayer for the growth of people already sharing in the gospel. It belongs beside Paul’s confidence that God is at work among them and his desire for their continuing faithfulness.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as prayer for love that grows with knowledge, sound judgment and a life pleasing to God. Wesley’s notes on verses 9–11 connect growing love and discernment with righteous fruit coming through Christ. The USCCB notes on verses 3–11 likewise connect Paul’s prayer with the community’s growth in readiness for Christ’s return. No separate denominational breakdown is needed for that shared emphasis.
passages.current_position_html: Our study What Does Prayer Look Like? uses this passage as an example of praying for others to know God more deeply, love more fully and live in a way that honors Him. We draw that positive emphasis from the study: ask for growing love, discernment and righteous fruit through Christ.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
In John 15:1–12, Jesus connects remaining in Him with bearing fruit, glorifying the Father and loving one another. Paul’s prayer belongs within that same larger pattern: the fruitful life comes through Christ and expresses itself in love.

This is a supported parallel, rather than a new explanation of every detail of the vine picture. It directs attention to the source and purpose of the growth Paul seeks: life sustained by Christ that honors God through what His people become and do.

passages.title: Philippians 1:12-18
passages.section_title: How can the gospel advance while Paul is in chains?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 Now I want you to know, brothers, that my circumstances have actually served to advance the gospel. 13 As a result, it has become clear throughout the whole palace guard and to everyone else that I am in chains for Christ. 14 And most of the brothers, confident in the Lord by my chains, now dare more greatly to speak the word without fear. 15 It is true that some preach Christ out of envy and rivalry, but others out of goodwill. 16 The latter do so in love, knowing that I am appointed for the defense of the gospel. 17 The former, however, preach Christ out of selfish ambition, not sincerely, supposing that they can add to the distress of my chains. 18 What then is the issue? Just this: that in every way, whether by false motives or true, Christ is preached. And in this I rejoice. Yes, and I will continue to rejoice,
paragraphs: 12 Now I want you to know, brothers, that my circumstances have actually served to advance the gospel. 13 As a result, it has become clear throughout the whole palace guard and to everyone else that I am in chains for Christ. 14 And most of the brothers, confident in the Lord by my chains, now dare more greatly to speak the word without fear.

15 It is true that some preach Christ out of envy and rivalry, but others out of goodwill. 16 The latter do so in love, knowing that I am appointed for the defense of the gospel. 17 The former, however, preach Christ out of selfish ambition, not sincerely, supposing that they can add to the distress of my chains. 18 What then is the issue? Just this: that in every way, whether by false motives or true, Christ is preached. And in this I rejoice. Yes, and I will continue to rejoice,

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul turns from thanksgiving and prayer to news about his circumstances. His imprisonment has served the advance of the gospel. People throughout the palace guard and beyond know that he is in chains for Christ, and most of the fellow believers have become more courageous in speaking.

He also acknowledges mixed motives among those preaching. Some act from goodwill and love, while others are moved by envy and selfish ambition and intend to add to his distress. Paul does not describe these motives as equally good.

His reason for rejoicing is that Christ is being proclaimed. The passage distinguishes the message being made known from the personal motives of its messengers. The following paragraph will explain his hope that Christ will be honored whether he lives or dies.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read these verses as an example of gospel witness continuing despite suffering and imperfect messengers. Wesley’s notes on verses 12–18 and the USCCB notes on verses 14–18 both distinguish the preachers’ motives while recognizing Paul’s joy that Christ is proclaimed.

This is not the same question as whether a different gospel should be accepted. In Galatians 1:6–9, Paul warns strongly against changing the gospel. Here his stated joy concerns Christ being preached, even by people whose personal motives he names as selfish.
passages.god_plan_html:
2 Timothy 2:8–10 gives a close parallel: Paul suffers in chains, but God’s word cannot be chained. The focus is the saving message of the risen Jesus reaching others despite the messenger’s confinement.

The ending of Acts 28:23–31 also places Paul under restraint while people come to hear him speak about God’s kingdom and Jesus Christ. These accounts show the larger purpose served by his witness. They do not require the claim that every hardship will produce the same visible result.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Philippians 1:19-26
passages.section_title: Why can Paul hope in Christ whether he lives or dies?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 because I know that through your prayers and the provision of the Spirit of Jesus Christ, my distress will turn out for my deliverance. 20 I eagerly expect and hope that I will in no way be ashamed, but will have complete boldness so that now as always Christ will be exalted in my body, whether by life or by death. 21 For to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain. 22 But if I go on living in the body, this will mean fruitful labor for me. So what shall I choose? I do not know. 23 I am torn between the two. I desire to depart and be with Christ, which is far better indeed. 24 But it is more necessary for you that I remain in the body. 25 Convinced of this, I know that I will remain and will continue with all of you for your progress and joy in the faith, 26 so that through my coming to you again your exultation in Christ Jesus will resound on account of me.
paragraphs: 19 because I know that through your prayers and the provision of the Spirit of Jesus Christ, my distress will turn out for my deliverance. 20 I eagerly expect and hope that I will in no way be ashamed, but will have complete boldness so that now as always Christ will be exalted in my body, whether by life or by death.

21 For to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain. 22 But if I go on living in the body, this will mean fruitful labor for me. So what shall I choose? I do not know. 23 I am torn between the two. I desire to depart and be with Christ, which is far better indeed. 24 But it is more necessary for you that I remain in the body.

25 Convinced of this, I know that I will remain and will continue with all of you for your progress and joy in the faith, 26 so that through my coming to you again your exultation in Christ Jesus will resound on account of me.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul expects the prayers of the believers and the provision of Christ’s Spirit to serve his deliverance. His stated hope is that he will not be ashamed, but that Christ will be exalted in his body, whether by life or death.

That explains his next statement: living means Christ, and dying means gain. Continued life would bring fruitful work, while departing would mean being with Christ. His desire to be with Him stands beside his concern for the people who still need his service.

Paul then expresses confidence that he will remain and continue with them for their progress and joy in the faith. Their growing confidence is to center on Christ. His reflection holds together personal hope, concern for others and the value of the work still before him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand Paul’s central hope as Christ being honored and the assurance that being with Him is better. Wesley’s notes on verses 20–26 describe life as knowing and following Christ and death as fuller union with Him. The USCCB notes on verses 19–25 likewise keep Christ central in both outcomes.

The deliverance in verse 19 receives different emphasis. Wesley relates it to Paul’s final good and glory. The USCCB notes include his expectation of release and continued service while also connecting the wording with God bringing suffering toward an ultimate good end. Thayer’s entry for deliverance includes rescue, preservation and salvation; the word alone does not require choosing only one event.

Paul’s hope in Christ remains clear while he considers both life and death. His confidence is not expressed as a demand that God grant only the outcome he personally prefers.
passages.god_plan_html:
2 Corinthians 5:6–10 also connects being at home with the Lord, walking by faith and seeking to please Him. It provides a close parallel to Paul’s desire to be with Christ and his concern for faithful service now.

1 Corinthians 15:20–23, 58 grounds the hope of God’s people in Christ’s resurrection and concludes that their labor in the Lord is not in vain. This places both the future hope and the present work within the saving victory of the risen Christ, without supplying an extra timetable here.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Philippians 1:27-30
passages.section_title: How can the church stand together when it faces opposition?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 27 Nevertheless, conduct yourselves in a manner worthy of the gospel of Christ. Then, whether I come and see you or only hear about you in my absence, I will know that you stand firm in one spirit, contending together as one for the faith of the gospel, 28 without being frightened in any way by those who oppose you. This is a clear sign of their destruction but of your salvation, and it is from God. 29 For it has been granted to you on behalf of Christ not only to believe in Him, but also to suffer for Him, 30 since you are encountering the same struggle you saw I had, and now hear that I still have.
paragraphs: 27 Nevertheless, conduct yourselves in a manner worthy of the gospel of Christ. Then, whether I come and see you or only hear about you in my absence, I will know that you stand firm in one spirit, contending together as one for the faith of the gospel, 28 without being frightened in any way by those who oppose you. This is a clear sign of their destruction but of your salvation, and it is from God.

29 For it has been granted to you on behalf of Christ not only to believe in Him, but also to suffer for Him, 30 since you are encountering the same struggle you saw I had, and now hear that I still have.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul turns from his own circumstances to the way the Philippians are to live. Whether he visits or remains absent, their conduct should be worthy of Christ’s gospel. He wants to hear of them standing in one spirit and contending together for the faith.

The word translated conduct carries the idea of living as a citizen. Thayer’s lexicon also explains its use for living according to a rule of life. Here the standard Paul names is the gospel of Christ.

The call to courage is communal. They are to stand together rather than be frightened by their opponents. Paul names both faith in Christ and suffering for Him as gifts granted to them, and connects their struggle with his own.

The next paragraph will develop the unity this requires through humility and concern for others. Standing firm for the gospel belongs with the way they treat one another.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand this as a call to united, faithful witness despite opposition. Wesley’s notes on verses 27–30 emphasize shared effort and steadfastness. The USCCB notes likewise connect the instructions with congregational unity and suffering for Christ.

The contrast between salvation and destruction places their struggle within God’s judgment. It is not a reason to celebrate another person’s suffering. The passage’s own instruction is for the believers to remain faithful and united, with their confidence in God.
passages.god_plan_html:
Philippians 3:20–21 explicitly describes the believers’ citizenship as heavenly and directs their hope toward Christ’s return and the transformation of their bodies. That fuller statement in the letter supplies a supported connection with the conduct called for here.

Acts 5:40–42 gives a concrete parallel: the apostles suffer for Jesus’ name and continue teaching and proclaiming Him. The Philippians’ struggle belongs within that continuing witness to Christ.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Philippians 2:1-11
passages.section_title: How does Christ show us the way of humility?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Therefore if you have any encouragement in Christ, if any comfort from His love, if any fellowship with the Spirit, if any affection and compassion, 2 then make my joy complete by being like-minded, having the same love, being united in spirit and purpose. 3 Do nothing out of selfish ambition or empty pride, but in humility consider others more important than yourselves. 4 Each of you should look not only to your own interests, but also to the interests of others. 5 Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus: 6 Who, existing in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be grasped, 7 but emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in human likeness. 8 And being found in appearance as a man, He humbled Himself and became obedient to death— even death on a cross. 9 Therefore God exalted Him to the highest place and gave Him the name above all names, 10 that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, 11 and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.
paragraphs: 1 Therefore if you have any encouragement in Christ, if any comfort from His love, if any fellowship with the Spirit, if any affection and compassion, 2 then make my joy complete by being like-minded, having the same love, being united in spirit and purpose. 3 Do nothing out of selfish ambition or empty pride, but in humility consider others more important than yourselves. 4 Each of you should look not only to your own interests, but also to the interests of others.

5 Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus: 6 Who, existing in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be grasped, 7 but emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in human likeness. 8 And being found in appearance as a man, He humbled Himself and became obedient to death— even death on a cross.

9 Therefore God exalted Him to the highest place and gave Him the name above all names, 10 that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, 11 and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul has called the Philippians to stand together for the gospel. He now appeals to the encouragement, love, fellowship and compassion they share in Christ. He asks them to make his joy complete through unity of love and purpose.

That unity has practical demands. They are to leave behind selfish ambition and empty pride, consider others more important than themselves and attend to others’ interests alongside their own. Paul then directs them to the mind of Christ.

The movement of verses 6–8 is downward: Christ, existing in the form of God, empties Himself, takes the form of a servant and humbles Himself in obedience as far as death on a cross. His self-giving supplies the pattern for how they treat one another.

The movement of verses 9–11 is upward: God exalts Him, and every knee bows and every tongue confesses Jesus Christ as Lord, to the Father’s glory. Paul brings the community’s ordinary relationships into view of the One they confess as Lord.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Catholic, Reformed and Wesleyan readings commonly understand Christ’s humility as real self-giving in human life while affirming His divinity. The Catholic Catechism, paragraphs 464–469, the Reformed Westminster Confession, 8.2, and Wesley’s comments on verses 6–7 affirm that He became truly human while remaining truly God. His taking a servant’s place is read within that confession.

The wording about equality in verse 6 is explained in more than one way. Wesley emphasizes equality as Christ’s rightful possession; the BSB footnote also offers the sense of something to be exploited, emphasizing His refusal to use His status for selfish advantage. In the paragraph, both questions lead into His freely taking the servant’s place and obeying to the cross.

The USCCB notes on verses 1–11 emphasize the connection between this account of Christ and the community’s life together. The doctrinal confession and the practical call belong together: people who share life in Him are to serve one another.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Isaiah 45:20–25, the Lord calls the ends of the earth to turn to Him for salvation and declares that every knee will bow before Him. Philippians draws on that language in describing every knee bowing at Jesus’ name and every tongue confessing Him as Lord.

This is a strong scriptural connection between the call to the nations and the honor given to Christ. The Father’s glory is the stated goal of the confession. The One who took the servant’s place and went to the cross is the One whose lordship is acknowledged throughout creation.

John 17:1–5 also connects Jesus’ completion of the Father’s work with His glorification and the glory He shared with the Father before the world existed. These passages place His humility and exaltation within the Father’s saving purpose, giving depth to the call for His people to follow His pattern of care.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Philippians 2:12-18
passages.section_title: How does God’s work shape the way we live?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 Therefore, my beloved, just as you have always obeyed, not only in my presence, but now even more in my absence, continue to work out your salvation with fear and trembling. 13 For it is God who works in you to will and to act on behalf of His good purpose. 14 Do everything without complaining or arguing, 15 so that you may be blameless and pure, children of God without fault in a crooked and perverse generation, in which you shine as lights in the world 16 as you hold forth the word of life, in order that I may boast on the day of Christ that I did not run or labor in vain. 17 But even if I am being poured out like a drink offering on the sacrifice and service of your faith, I am glad and rejoice with all of you. 18 So you too should be glad and rejoice with me.
paragraphs: 12 Therefore, my beloved, just as you have always obeyed, not only in my presence, but now even more in my absence, continue to work out your salvation with fear and trembling. 13 For it is God who works in you to will and to act on behalf of His good purpose.

14 Do everything without complaining or arguing, 15 so that you may be blameless and pure, children of God without fault in a crooked and perverse generation, in which you shine as lights in the world 16 as you hold forth the word of life, in order that I may boast on the day of Christ that I did not run or labor in vain.
17 But even if I am being poured out like a drink offering on the sacrifice and service of your faith, I am glad and rejoice with all of you. 18 So you too should be glad and rejoice with me.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul draws a conclusion from Christ’s obedience and exaltation. The Philippians are to continue obeying in his absence and work out their salvation with fear and trembling. He immediately gives the reason: God is at work in them, both in their willing and their action, for His good purpose.

The next instructions show what this involves in community. They are to do everything without complaining or arguing, live as God’s children and shine as lights while holding forth the word of life. Paul hopes to see that his labor among them has borne lasting fruit.

He then pictures his own life as a drink offering poured out alongside the sacrifice and service of their faith. Exodus 29:38–42 gives a scriptural example of a drink offering accompanying an offering to the Lord. Paul uses sacrificial language to describe his costly service.

Even in that prospect, he calls for shared joy. The paragraph keeps God’s work, the believers’ conduct and their life of service together, preparing for the examples of Timothy and Epaphroditus that follow.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand these verses as joining God’s enabling work with the believer’s active response. Wesley’s notes on verses 12–13 emphasize serious, diligent obedience encouraged by God’s power. The USCCB notes likewise read the passage as practical consequences of the salvation God works in Christ.

Traditions describe the place of these works differently. The Reformed Westminster Confession, 16.2–6, calls good works the fruit and evidence of faith, enabled by Christ’s Spirit and accepted in Him, while denying that they merit forgiveness or eternal life. The Wesleyan Methodist Articles, article X, likewise describe them as fruits of faith that follow justification and cannot remove sins.

The Catholic Catechism, paragraphs 2001–2002, teaches that God’s prior grace enables human cooperation. Paragraphs 2008–2010 distinguish the unearned initial grace of forgiveness from the merit of later works done through grace and love, including toward growth and eternal life. Here merit means a value God grants to grace-enabled works, rather than an achievement independent of Him. These accounts differ while each affirms the need for His grace.
passages.god_plan_html:
The description of a crooked and perverse generation echoes Deuteronomy 32:3–6, where God is faithful and upright while His people act corruptly. Philippians calls the community to live as His children without that fault. This is a supported connection with the long scriptural concern that God’s people reflect the character of their Father.

Matthew 5:14–16 connects the light of Jesus’ followers with good works that bring glory to the Father. Romans 12:1 describes lives offered to God in response to His mercy. These parallels place the practical obedience and sacrificial service here within the larger purpose of a people whose life makes His goodness known.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Philippians 2:19-24
passages.section_title: Why does Paul want to send Timothy?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 Now I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you soon, that I also may be cheered when I learn how you are doing. 20 I have nobody else like him who will genuinely care for your needs. 21 For all the others look after their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ. 22 But you know Timothy’s proven worth, that as a child with his father he has served with me to advance the gospel. 23 So I hope to send him as soon as I see what happens with me. 24 And I trust in the Lord that I myself will come soon.
paragraphs: 19 Now I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you soon, that I also may be cheered when I learn how you are doing. 20 I have nobody else like him who will genuinely care for your needs. 21 For all the others look after their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ. 22 But you know Timothy’s proven worth, that as a child with his father he has served with me to advance the gospel.
23 So I hope to send him as soon as I see what happens with me. 24 And I trust in the Lord that I myself will come soon.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul hopes in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy so he can learn how the Philippians are doing. This travel plan is an expression of care: he wants someone to attend to their needs and bring reliable news.

He describes Timothy as a person who genuinely cares for them and whose service they already know. He has worked alongside Paul to advance the gospel, like a child with his father.

The contrast with those pursuing their own interests continues the chapter’s earlier call to look to others’ interests. Timothy gives the community a concrete example of that concern.

Paul intends to send him when his own circumstances become clearer, and also expresses trust in the Lord that he himself will come. The plans are held within that dependence on Christ.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as both a practical travel plan and a commendation of faithful care. Wesley’s notes on verses 19–22 explain Timothy’s concern and service alongside Paul. The USCCB notes also place the notice within Paul’s arrangements to visit and encourage the community. The emphasis is on proven character, concern for others and the gospel work they share.
passages.god_plan_html:
2 Timothy 2:1–2 calls Timothy to be strong in Christ’s grace and entrust what he has learned to faithful people able to teach others. This adds a wider purpose to the pattern of Paul and Timothy serving together.

Careful teaching and faithful service can continue through others. Timothy’s mission to the Philippians belongs within that larger pattern of the gospel being passed on and communities being strengthened beyond one person’s immediate presence.

passages.title: Philippians 2:25-30
passages.section_title: Why should Epaphroditus be welcomed with joy?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 25 But I thought it necessary to send back to you Epaphroditus, my brother, fellow worker, and fellow soldier, who is also your messenger and minister to my needs. 26 For he has been longing for all of you and is distressed because you heard he was ill. 27 He was sick indeed, nearly unto death. But God had mercy on him, and not only on him but also on me, to spare me sorrow upon sorrow. 28 Therefore I am all the more eager to send him, so that when you see him again you may rejoice, and I may be less anxious. 29 Welcome him in the Lord with great joy, and honor men like him, 30 because he nearly died for the work of Christ, risking his life to make up for your deficit of service to me.
paragraphs: 25 But I thought it necessary to send back to you Epaphroditus, my brother, fellow worker, and fellow soldier, who is also your messenger and minister to my needs. 26 For he has been longing for all of you and is distressed because you heard he was ill. 27 He was sick indeed, nearly unto death. But God had mercy on him, and not only on him but also on me, to spare me sorrow upon sorrow.

28 Therefore I am all the more eager to send him, so that when you see him again you may rejoice, and I may be less anxious. 29 Welcome him in the Lord with great joy, and honor men like him, 30 because he nearly died for the work of Christ, risking his life to make up for your deficit of service to me.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul explains why he is sending Epaphroditus back. He describes him as a brother, fellow worker and fellow soldier, and as the Philippians’ messenger who ministered to his needs. Philippians 4:18 identifies him as the person who brought their gifts.

Epaphroditus had been seriously ill, close to death. He was distressed because the Philippians had heard about his illness. Paul describes his recovery as God’s mercy toward both Epaphroditus and himself, sparing him further sorrow.

Sending him back is meant to bring joy to the community and ease Paul’s concern. Paul asks them to welcome him in the Lord and honor people like him because he risked his life in Christ’s work to provide the service they could not personally give.

The account makes the chapter’s concern for others tangible. Gifts, travel, illness, worry, recovery and a welcome home are all part of this shared service.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand Paul’s commendation as honoring costly, faithful service and the concern shared between this messenger and the church. Wesley’s notes on verses 25–30 explain the gifts, recovery and service offered on the community’s behalf. The USCCB note on verse 25 likewise identifies him as their messenger sent to help Paul. His illness and recovery are described within the real affection and care of this relationship.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Corinthians 12:24–27 describes God arranging the body so its members care for one another: when one suffers, the others share the suffering, and when one is honored, they share the joy. That is a supported parallel to the concern and welcome described here.

The larger purpose includes a community that values and cares for the people who serve within it. Epaphroditus’s practical help matters to Paul’s gospel work, and his own needs matter to the community. God’s people are being formed into a body whose members belong to one another.

passages.title: Philippians 3:1-6
passages.section_title: Where should our confidence before God rest?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Finally, my brothers, rejoice in the Lord. It is no trouble for me to write the same things to you again, and it is a safeguard for you. 2 Watch out for those dogs, those workers of evil, those mutilators of the flesh! 3 For it is we who are the circumcision, we who worship by the Spirit of God, who glory in Christ Jesus, and who put no confidence in the flesh— 4 though I myself could have such confidence. If anyone else thinks he has grounds for confidence in the flesh, I have more: 5 circumcised on the eighth day, of the people of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin; a Hebrew of Hebrews; as to the law, a Pharisee; 6 as to zeal, persecuting the church; as to righteousness in the law, faultless.
paragraphs: 1 Finally, my brothers, rejoice in the Lord. It is no trouble for me to write the same things to you again, and it is a safeguard for you. 2 Watch out for those dogs, those workers of evil, those mutilators of the flesh! 3 For it is we who are the circumcision, we who worship by the Spirit of God, who glory in Christ Jesus, and who put no confidence in the flesh—

4 though I myself could have such confidence. If anyone else thinks he has grounds for confidence in the flesh, I have more: 5 circumcised on the eighth day, of the people of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin; a Hebrew of Hebrews; as to the law, a Pharisee; 6 as to zeal, persecuting the church; as to righteousness in the law, faultless.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul again calls the believers to rejoice in the Lord and says that repeating his instruction is a safeguard. He then warns sharply against teachers whose emphasis on circumcision would lead people to put confidence in outward standing.

His contrast names three marks of the community to which he belongs: worship by God’s Spirit, glorying in Christ Jesus and no confidence in the flesh. The Greek verb for worship is latreuō (lah-TREW-oh). Thayer’s lexicon includes religious service and worship, and connects this verse with service prompted by God’s Spirit.

Paul can speak about outward credentials from experience. He lists his circumcision, Israelite ancestry, tribe, Pharisaic commitment, zeal and record under the law. This is the background against which the next paragraph will describe what he has come to value above those advantages: knowing Christ.

The warning targets the misplaced confidence being taught. Paul’s own identification as an Israelite is part of his explanation, and the passage should be read through that contrast rather than as contempt for an entire people.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a warning against resting one’s confidence before God in ancestry, ritual standing or personal credentials. Wesley’s note on verse 3 and the USCCB notes on verses 2–11 both connect the identity of God’s people with life in Christ, worship by the Spirit and a confidence that comes from God.
passages.god_plan_html:
Deuteronomy 30:1–10 speaks of Israel returning to the Lord and of God circumcising the hearts of His people so they will love Him. The concern for the heart is already present in the earlier Scriptures.

Romans 2:28–29 also connects circumcision of the heart with the Spirit. Galatians 3:26–29 describes people from different backgrounds belonging to Christ and sharing the promised inheritance through faith. These are supported connections with Paul’s emphasis here on what God’s Spirit does and the confidence found in Christ.
passages.current_position_html: On verse 3, our study Worship as the Early Church Knew It understands worship by the Spirit as sacred service to God expressed in daily obedience. The study emphasizes a life led by His Spirit rather than reading this verse as an instruction about music. Its focus is the service of people whose confidence is in Christ.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

passages.title: Philippians 3:3
passages.section_title: What does worship by God’s Spirit mean here?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 3 For it is we who are the circumcision, we who worship by the Spirit of God, who glory in Christ Jesus, and who put no confidence in the flesh—
paragraphs: 3 For it is we who are the circumcision, we who worship by the Spirit of God, who glory in Christ Jesus, and who put no confidence in the flesh—

passages.context_html:
Paul is warning against teachers who would turn circumcision and outward standing into a basis for confidence. He identifies his own community through worship by the Spirit, glorying in Christ and no confidence in the flesh.

The word translated worship is latreuō (lah-TREW-oh). Thayer’s lexicon explains religious service and worship and identifies God’s Spirit as prompting that service here. The verse describes who these people are and whom they trust.

The surrounding passage matters: Paul goes on to name his own inherited and religious credentials, then explain why knowing Christ has become his greater gain. Read Philippians 3:1–6 for the immediate contrast.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as describing God’s people through Spirit-led worship and confidence in Christ. Wesley’s note emphasizes inward holiness, and the USCCB note connects the description with belonging to God and the promise to Abraham. The shared emphasis reaches into the heart and the source of a person’s confidence.
passages.current_position_html: On verse 3, our study Worship as the Early Church Knew It understands worship by the Spirit as sacred service to God expressed in daily obedience. The study emphasizes a life led by His Spirit rather than reading this verse as an instruction about music. Its focus is the service of people whose confidence is in Christ.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Deuteronomy 30:6 describes God circumcising His people’s hearts so they will love Him. Romans 2:28–29 also describes circumcision of the heart by the Spirit.

This supported connection helps place the verse within the larger scriptural concern for God’s people to love and serve Him from the heart. Paul directs the readers’ confidence to Christ and the work of God’s Spirit.

passages.title: Philippians 3:7-11
passages.section_title: Why does knowing Christ change what Paul values?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 But whatever was gain to me I count as loss for the sake of Christ. 8 More than that, I count all things as loss compared to the surpassing excellence of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord, for whom I have lost all things. I consider them rubbish, that I may gain Christ 9 and be found in Him, not having my own righteousness from the law, but that which is through faith in Christ, the righteousness from God on the basis of faith. 10 I want to know Christ and the power of His resurrection and the fellowship of His sufferings, being conformed to Him in His death, 11 and so, somehow, to attain to the resurrection from the dead.
paragraphs: 7 But whatever was gain to me I count as loss for the sake of Christ. 8 More than that, I count all things as loss compared to the surpassing excellence of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord, for whom I have lost all things. I consider them rubbish, that I may gain Christ 9 and be found in Him, not having my own righteousness from the law, but that which is through faith in Christ, the righteousness from God on the basis of faith.
10 I want to know Christ and the power of His resurrection and the fellowship of His sufferings, being conformed to Him in His death, 11 and so, somehow, to attain to the resurrection from the dead.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul has just listed the inherited and religious advantages that once gave him confidence. He now explains his changed judgment: what had counted as gain is loss compared with knowing Christ Jesus as Lord.

The word translated rubbish is skubalon (SKOO-bah-lon). Thayer’s lexicon includes refuse and dung. It is a strong comparison of value: those former grounds of confidence cannot compare with gaining Christ and being found in Him.

Paul contrasts righteousness derived from the law with righteousness from God through faith in Christ. His desire reaches into his whole relationship with the Lord: knowing His resurrection power, sharing His sufferings and being conformed to His death.

The paragraph looks toward resurrection from the dead. The next verses make clear that Paul has not reached the end of that pursuit. Knowing Christ gives direction to his present life and his future hope.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand Paul as receiving righteousness from God through Christ rather than resting on his former credentials. Traditions describe that righteousness and its relationship to renewed life in different ways.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, 11.1–2, teaches that God accepts people as righteous because Christ’s obedience is credited to them and received through faith. It also teaches that this faith is accompanied by other graces and acts in love.

The Catholic Catechism, paragraphs 1987–1993, describes justification as forgiveness together with inner renewal through the Spirit. It grounds this gift in Christ’s saving death, received through faith and baptism. John Wesley’s note on verse 9 also emphasizes righteousness worked inwardly by God’s Spirit through faith, and understands the passage to concern growth in holiness as well as acceptance before God.

The BSB footnote to verse 9 also allows the wording through Christ’s faithfulness. The main translation reads through faith in Christ. Both belong to the discussion of how Paul describes righteousness received from God; neither wording supplies a reason to return to boasting in personal credentials.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 6:3–11 connects participation in Christ’s death with a new way of life and the promise of sharing His resurrection. It supplies a close parallel to the death-and-life pattern Paul desires here.

1 Corinthians 15:20–23 identifies the risen Christ as the firstfruits of those who have died and connects His coming with the resurrection of those who belong to Him. Knowing Christ reaches into God’s purpose to give His people life beyond death. That future hope gives weight to the present pursuit.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Philippians 3:12-16
passages.section_title: What does it mean to keep pressing on toward Christ?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 Not that I have already obtained all this, or have already been made perfect, but I press on to take hold of that for which Christ Jesus took hold of me. 13 Brothers, I do not consider myself yet to have taken hold of it. But one thing I do: Forgetting what is behind and straining toward what is ahead, 14 I press on toward the goal to win the prize of God’s heavenly calling in Christ Jesus. 15 All of us who are mature should embrace this point of view. And if you think differently about some issue, God will reveal this to you as well. 16 Nevertheless, we must live up to what we have already attained.
paragraphs: 12 Not that I have already obtained all this, or have already been made perfect, but I press on to take hold of that for which Christ Jesus took hold of me. 13 Brothers, I do not consider myself yet to have taken hold of it. But one thing I do: Forgetting what is behind and straining toward what is ahead, 14 I press on toward the goal to win the prize of God’s heavenly calling in Christ Jesus.

15 All of us who are mature should embrace this point of view. And if you think differently about some issue, God will reveal this to you as well. 16 Nevertheless, we must live up to what we have already attained.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul has expressed his desire to know Christ and attain the resurrection. He now says plainly that he has not already obtained all this or been made perfect. His pursuit begins with something Christ has done: Christ Jesus took hold of him.

He uses the picture of reaching toward a goal. Rather than treating what lies behind as the end of the story, he presses toward the prize of God’s heavenly calling in Christ. The direction of his life is forward toward Him.

Paul then includes the community in this way of thinking. The mature are to embrace it, while he trusts God to bring understanding where they think differently. They are to live up to what they have already attained.

The passage holds together real progress and continuing growth. Paul offers himself as someone still pursuing Christ, preparing for the following call to follow faithful examples together.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a call to persevere in the life Christ has begun, with humility about what remains to be completed. Wesley’s notes on verses 12–16 distinguish readiness for the race from its completed prize. The USCCB note likewise emphasizes that belonging to Christ does not mean a person has already reached the end of spiritual maturity. Both keep continued growth and trust in God in view.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 8:29–30 describes God’s purpose as conforming His people to the image of His Son and bringing them to glory. The growth Paul pursues serves that larger purpose.

The confidence expressed earlier in Philippians 1:6 also looks to God completing the work He began. The continuing effort described here belongs within that dependence on Him and the hope of completed life in Christ.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Philippians 3:17-21
passages.section_title: How does our heavenly citizenship shape life now?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 Join one another in following my example, brothers, and carefully observe those who walk according to the pattern we set for you. 18 For as I have often told you before, and now say again even with tears: Many live as enemies of the cross of Christ. 19 Their end is destruction, their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame. Their minds are set on earthly things. 20 But our citizenship is in heaven, and we eagerly await a Savior from there, the Lord Jesus Christ, 21 who, by the power that enables Him to subject all things to Himself, will transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body.
paragraphs: 17 Join one another in following my example, brothers, and carefully observe those who walk according to the pattern we set for you. 18 For as I have often told you before, and now say again even with tears: Many live as enemies of the cross of Christ. 19 Their end is destruction, their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame. Their minds are set on earthly things.

20 But our citizenship is in heaven, and we eagerly await a Savior from there, the Lord Jesus Christ, 21 who, by the power that enables Him to subject all things to Himself, will transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul asks the believers to follow his example together and observe others who walk in the same way. The pattern has already been made concrete through Christ’s self-giving and the service of Timothy and Epaphroditus.

He then warns, with tears, about people whose lives are hostile to Christ’s cross. He describes their end as destruction, their appetites as their god and their attention as fixed on earthly things. His sorrow belongs with the seriousness of the warning.

The believers’ citizenship, by contrast, is in heaven. They await the Savior from there, the Lord Jesus Christ. The hope Paul names is bodily: Christ will transform their lowly bodies to be like His glorious body.

This transformation rests on the power by which Christ can subject all things to Himself. The paragraph joins a pattern for present conduct with the future they await from Him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the closing hope as Christ’s return and the transformation of His people’s bodies, giving direction to their present life. Wesley’s notes on verses 20–21 emphasize heavenly belonging and likeness to Christ’s glorified body. The USCCB notes likewise connect heavenly citizenship with the future coming of Christ and the pattern of a life centered on His cross and resurrection.

The exact identity of the opponents is not named in these verses, and the USCCB notes discuss more than one explanation. The description Paul gives and his call to faithful imitation remain the center of the warning.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Corinthians 15:20–28 connects the resurrection of Christ’s people with His reign, the subjection of His enemies and the defeat of death. This supplies a wider picture of the power named in Philippians 3:21.

Romans 8:18–25 joins the redemption of believers’ bodies with the hope that creation itself will be freed from decay. The promise reaches into God’s larger work of rescue and renewal. The bodily transformation awaited here belongs within that hope, while believers continue to follow Christ in their present lives.
