passages.title: Philippians 4:1-3
passages.section_title: How do we stand together when believers disagree?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Therefore, my brothers, whom I love and long for, my joy and crown, that is how you must stand firm in the Lord, my beloved. 2 I urge Euodia and Syntyche to agree with each other in the Lord. 3 Yes, and I ask you, my true yokefellow, to help these women who have contended at my side for the gospel, along with Clement and the rest of my fellow workers, whose names are in the Book of Life.
paragraphs: 1 Therefore, my brothers, whom I love and long for, my joy and crown, that is how you must stand firm in the Lord, my beloved.

2 I urge Euodia and Syntyche to agree with each other in the Lord. 3 Yes, and I ask you, my true yokefellow, to help these women who have contended at my side for the gospel, along with Clement and the rest of my fellow workers, whose names are in the Book of Life.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After describing the coming Savior and the transformation of His people, Paul tells these dearly loved believers to stand firm in the Lord. Calling them his joy and crown expresses how deeply their life in Christ matters to him.

He then appeals to Euodia and Syntyche to agree in the Lord. Their disagreement is real, but its subject is not given. Paul speaks to both women and asks a trusted companion to help them.

He also remembers their work beside him for the gospel, alongside Clement and his other coworkers. The appeal seeks reconciliation among valued fellow workers. It does not erase their service or turn their dispute into their whole identity.

The companion’s identity is uncertain. The BSB footnote allows the possibility of the name Syzygus. The text does not tell us that this helper was the pastor, nor does it identify Clement as the later bishop of Rome.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as a call to reconciliation and practical help within the church. Wesley’s notes on verses 1–3 emphasize Paul’s tender personal appeal; the USCCB notes connect it with his earlier call to humility in Philippians 2:2–4. Their shared emphasis is on standing together in the Lord, without enough information to reconstruct the disagreement.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus prays in John 17:20–26 for those who will believe through His disciples’ message. He connects their unity with the world knowing that the Father sent Him, and He desires that they be with Him. Reconciliation serves that wider purpose of a people whose life together bears witness to Him.

The mention of the Book of Life also reaches beyond the present dispute. Revelation 21:22–27 describes the final city lit by God’s glory and the Lamb, entered by those named in the Lamb’s Book of Life. Paul addresses these coworkers in light of their belonging to God’s people, not merely the tension between them.

passages.title: Philippians 4:4-7
passages.section_title: Where can we bring our worries?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 4 Rejoice in the Lord always. I will say it again: Rejoice! 5 Let your gentleness be apparent to all. The Lord is near. 6 Be anxious for nothing, but in everything, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God. 7 And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.
paragraphs: 4 Rejoice in the Lord always. I will say it again: Rejoice! 5 Let your gentleness be apparent to all. The Lord is near.

6 Be anxious for nothing, but in everything, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God. 7 And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul calls the believers to rejoice in the Lord and let their gentleness be seen by everyone. The joy he describes is rooted in the Lord, amid the difficulties the letter has already acknowledged.

He adds that the Lord is near. The USCCB note understands this most likely as His approaching return, while also noting the reading that emphasizes His present nearness. The preceding chapter has explicitly looked toward His coming.

Paul closes the letter with instructions for a community facing disagreement and difficulty. He has called them to rejoice in the Lord and show gentleness to everyone. He now tells them to bring their concerns to God.

The invitation is broad: in everything, they are to pray, make requests and give thanks. Paul directs their worries toward the One they can approach, rather than telling them to hide those worries or pretend nothing is wrong.

The promise is that God’s peace will guard their hearts and minds in Christ Jesus. The Greek verb is phroureo (froo-REH-oh). Thayer’s lexicon explains its use for guarding or protecting, including this figurative use in verse 7. The picture is protection for their inner life.

The passage promises that peace without saying every requested change will occur. Paul has already described genuine sorrow, danger and suffering in this letter. Prayer belongs within those experiences.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these verses as a call to a life marked by joy in the Lord, gentleness toward others and prayerful dependence on God. Wesley’s notes on verses 5–7 connect gentleness with the Lord’s nearness and encourage bringing concerns to Him freely. The promised protection is God’s peace guarding the heart and mind; Paul does not promise that every request will receive the outcome desired.
passages.god_plan_html:
In John 14:25–31, Jesus promises His disciples the Holy Spirit and gives them His peace as He prepares them for His departure. He distinguishes that gift from what the world gives. This is a close parallel: peace comes from belonging to Him even as trouble lies ahead.

That gift belongs within God’s work of bringing people into life with His Son. It looks forward to the completed hope described in Philippians 3:20–21, where the returning Savior transforms His people’s bodies. Present peace and future rescue have the same Lord at their center.
passages.current_position_html: In What Does Prayer Look Like?, we understand this passage as an invitation to bring our requests to God with thanksgiving. The promise attached to those requests is His peace guarding our hearts and minds in Christ. It does not promise the particular outcome we ask for.

passages.title: Philippians 4:6-7
passages.section_title: What does God promise when we bring Him our concerns?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 Be anxious for nothing, but in everything, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God. 7 And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.

Wesley’s notes on verses 6–7 encourage confident prayer about both great and small concerns and describe God’s peace as guarding the heart and mind. Neither the command to pray nor the promise of peace requires treating a particular requested outcome as guaranteed.

The promise attached to those requests is His peace guarding our hearts and minds in Christ. It does not promise the particular outcome we ask for.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

In John 14:25–31, Jesus promises His disciples the Holy Spirit and gives them His peace as He prepares them for His departure. He distinguishes that gift from what the world gives. This is a close parallel: peace comes from belonging to Him even as trouble lies ahead.

passages.title: Philippians 4:8-9
passages.section_title: What should shape our thoughts and actions?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 Finally, brothers, whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is right, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is admirable—if anything is excellent or praiseworthy—think on these things. 9 Whatever you have learned or received or heard from me, or seen in me, put it into practice. And the God of peace will be with you.
paragraphs: 8 Finally, brothers, whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is right, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is admirable—if anything is excellent or praiseworthy—think on these things. 9 Whatever you have learned or received or heard from me, or seen in me, put it into practice. And the God of peace will be with you.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After encouraging prayer and promising God’s guarding peace, Paul turns to what should occupy their minds. He names what is true, honorable, right, pure, lovely and admirable—what deserves careful attention.

The next verse carries thought into action. They are to practice what they learned and received from him, including what they heard and saw in his life. The letter has already supplied examples of service, endurance and putting others first.

This is more than imagining pleasant outcomes. Paul joins attention to what is good with the work of living it. The passage ends with the promise that the God of peace will be with them.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand these verses as a call to direct both thought and conduct toward what is good. Wesley’s notes on verses 8–9 connect reflection with practice and emphasize God Himself as the source of peace. The USCCB notes connect Paul’s appeal to the faithful example he commends in 3:17. The focus is a formed way of life, rather than thought detached from action.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 12:1–3 places the renewing of the mind within a whole life offered to God in response to His mercy. It connects changed thinking with recognizing His will and living humbly among others.

That renewal belongs within God’s purpose to make His people like His Son, stated in Romans 8:29–30. The thoughts and habits described here are part of a life being shaped toward Christ, with its completion still ahead.

passages.title: Philippians 4:10-19
passages.section_title: How do contentment and generosity belong together?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 Now I rejoice greatly in the Lord that at last you have revived your concern for me. You were indeed concerned, but you had no opportunity to show it. 11 I am not saying this out of need, for I have learned to be content regardless of my circumstances. 12 I know how to live humbly, and I know how to abound. In any and every situation I have learned the secret of being filled and being hungry, of having plenty and having need. 13 I can do all things through Christ who gives me strength. 14 Nevertheless, you have done well to share in my affliction. 15 And as you Philippians know, in the early days of the gospel, when I left Macedonia, no church but you partnered with me in the matter of giving and receiving. 16 For even while I was in Thessalonica, you provided for my needs again and again. 17 Not that I am seeking a gift, but I am looking for the fruit that may be credited to your account. 18 I have all I need and more, now that I have received your gifts from Epaphroditus. They are a fragrant offering, an acceptable sacrifice, well-pleasing to God. 19 And my God will supply all your needs according to His glorious riches in Christ Jesus.
paragraphs: 10 Now I rejoice greatly in the Lord that at last you have revived your concern for me. You were indeed concerned, but you had no opportunity to show it. 11 I am not saying this out of need, for I have learned to be content regardless of my circumstances. 12 I know how to live humbly, and I know how to abound. In any and every situation I have learned the secret of being filled and being hungry, of having plenty and having need. 13 I can do all things through Christ who gives me strength.

14 Nevertheless, you have done well to share in my affliction. 15 And as you Philippians know, in the early days of the gospel, when I left Macedonia, no church but you partnered with me in the matter of giving and receiving. 16 For even while I was in Thessalonica, you provided for my needs again and again.

17 Not that I am seeking a gift, but I am looking for the fruit that may be credited to your account. 18 I have all I need and more, now that I have received your gifts from Epaphroditus. They are a fragrant offering, an acceptable sacrifice, well-pleasing to God. 19 And my God will supply all your needs according to His glorious riches in Christ Jesus.

passages.context_html:
Paul thanks the Philippians for renewing their practical support. He does not accuse them of having stopped caring: they were concerned before, but lacked an opportunity to show it.

He has learned contentment in very different conditions, including hunger and need as well as plenty. The Greek word is autarkes (ow-TAR-kays). Thayer’s lexicon includes being content with one’s circumstances and means. Paul immediately names the strength Christ gives, so his contentment is not a claim that he needs no one.

Verse 13 belongs to that explanation. The things he can face through Christ include the difficult circumstances he has just named. He then affirms their help: sharing in his affliction was good. Dependence on Christ and receiving help from others belong together.

The church’s repeated gifts supported him while he was in Thessalonica, and Epaphroditus has now delivered their gift. Paul desires the fruit of their generosity, describes the gift as a sacrifice pleasing to God and assures them of God’s provision. His thanks keeps both their practical care and their relationship with God in view.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read this paragraph as teaching contentment through Christ, generous partnership and confidence in God’s care. Wesley’s notes on verses 10–19 connect contentment with both scarcity and abundance and link the promise of provision with the Philippians’ care for Paul. The USCCB notes likewise keep the gift, the church’s growth and God’s provision together.

These readings place verse 13 within Paul’s changing circumstances and verse 19 within his thanks for their support. The paragraph itself includes hunger and affliction, alongside generosity and abundance.
passages.current_position_html: In Prayer and Faith, we read the promise of verse 19 within Paul’s thanks for this church’s generous support of gospel work. He assures these believers of God’s care as they have shared in his need. We do not treat the verse as a general prayer formula or a guarantee of comfort or wealth. The surrounding passage teaches contentment and dependence on Christ through difficulty as well as plenty.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Paul’s description of the gift as a pleasing sacrifice belongs to a wider biblical pattern. Ephesians 5:1–2 calls believers to walk in love after Christ’s self-giving, described as a fragrant offering to God. This is a supported parallel in sacrificial language: their giving reflects His love; it does not repeat His saving work.

Hebrews 13:10–16 joins Jesus’ sacrifice, hope for the coming city and the sacrifices of praise, doing good and sharing. Practical support thus belongs within a life offered to God through Christ. The gift helps gospel work while expressing the kind of love He forms in His people.

passages.title: Philippians 4:19
passages.section_title: What does the promise of God’s provision mean here?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 And my God will supply all your needs according to His glorious riches in Christ Jesus.
paragraphs: 19 And my God will supply all your needs according to His glorious riches in Christ Jesus.

passages.context_html:
This promise comes at the end of Paul’s thanks for the Philippians’ support. They have shared in his affliction, sent help more than once and now supplied him through Epaphroditus. He has called their gift an acceptable sacrifice pleasing to God.

Paul assures these givers that his God will supply their needs from His riches in Christ Jesus. The direction of the sentence is from their care for him to his confidence in God’s care for them.

The surrounding verses keep that assurance connected with contentment in need as well as plenty. Paul’s strength in Christ does not mean he has never been hungry or suffered. The promise belongs within that lived dependence and generous gospel partnership.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as assurance of God’s provision to the church Paul is thanking. Wesley’s note on verse 19 explicitly relates their needs to the needs they met for him. The USCCB note on verses 10–20 likewise reads it within the gift, the believers’ spiritual growth and God’s care through Christ. The context gives no promise of personal wealth.
passages.current_position_html: In Prayer and Faith, we read the promise of verse 19 within Paul’s thanks for this church’s generous support of gospel work. He assures these believers of God’s care as they have shared in his need. We do not treat the verse as a general prayer formula or a guarantee of comfort or wealth. The surrounding passage teaches contentment and dependence on Christ through difficulty as well as plenty.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The preceding verse describes practical giving as a sacrifice pleasing to God. Hebrews 13:10–16 places doing good and sharing within a life of worship through Jesus, alongside hope for the city to come. Meeting another believer’s need belongs within God’s work of forming a people who live for Him.

The same pattern appears in 2 Corinthians 9:8–12: God supplies what is needed for good works, generosity meets needs and thanksgiving goes to God. Provision serves that fruitful life together, rather than becoming an end in itself.

passages.title: Philippians 4:21-23
passages.section_title: What do these final greetings tell us about life in Christ?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 Greet all the saints in Christ Jesus. The brothers who are with me send you greetings. 22 All the saints send you greetings, especially those from the household of Caesar. 23 The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.
paragraphs: 21 Greet all the saints in Christ Jesus. The brothers who are with me send you greetings. 22 All the saints send you greetings, especially those from the household of Caesar. 23 The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul closes with greetings to all the saints in Christ Jesus. The brothers with him and the wider group of believers send greetings in return. The letter ends by connecting people who are apart but belong to the same Lord.

Those sending greetings include people from Caesar’s household. The USCCB note on verse 22 explains that the expression can include imperial employees, slaves and freed people. It does not require that Caesar’s relatives or Caesar himself had become believers.

Paul finishes with the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ. The opening of the letter wished grace and peace to these believers; the ending returns them to the grace of the Lord whose example, strength and coming have shaped the whole letter.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this closing as an expression of fellowship among believers and a blessing of Christ’s grace. The USCCB notes emphasize the breadth of the greetings. The closing addresses saints in Christ as a living community; it does not use the term only for a few unusually distinguished believers.
passages.god_plan_html:
The greetings from Caesar’s household stand alongside Paul’s earlier report that his imprisonment has helped advance the gospel in Philippians 1:12–14. The closing gives another glimpse of believers in places associated with imperial power, without explaining how each came to faith.

Ephesians 2:13–22 describes Christ making people who were far apart into members of God’s household and a dwelling for His Spirit. That larger purpose helps explain why these simple greetings matter: people in different places belong together in Him. This is a parallel in their shared belonging to Christ.

passages.title: Colossians 1:1-8
passages.section_title: What does Paul thank God for in this church?

versions.label: BSB

section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul opens as an apostle of Christ Jesus by God’s will, with Timothy named alongside him. He addresses the believers at Colossae as saints and faithful brothers in Christ and wishes them grace and peace from God the Father.

His thanksgiving centers on their faith in Christ, love for the saints and hope stored up in heaven. This hope came to them through the gospel, which he calls the word of truth.

The gospel is bearing fruit among them as it is elsewhere. Their community belongs to a larger work of God’s grace; the message they received is not a private discovery reserved for their city.

They learned from Epaphras, whom Paul commends as a faithful minister of Christ. His report of their love in the Spirit provides the immediate setting for the prayer that follows.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this opening as thanksgiving for faith, love and hope produced through the gospel. Wesley’s notes on verses 2–8 connect their love with the Spirit’s work. The USCCB notes likewise emphasize the report of their faithful response and the growth of the gospel beyond their own community.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 3:5–6 describes Gentiles sharing the promise in Christ through the gospel as members of the same body. The spread of the message to this community belongs within that wider welcome.

The hope Paul thanks God for also points forward. Colossians 3:1–4 connects their life with the risen Christ and the promise of appearing with Him in glory. The gospel’s present fruit is joined to a future held in Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Colossians 1:9-11
passages.section_title: What does Paul ask God to grow in His people?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 For this reason, since the day we heard about you, we have not stopped praying for you and asking God to fill you with the knowledge of His will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding, 10 so that you may walk in a manner worthy of the Lord and may please Him in every way: bearing fruit in every good work, growing in the knowledge of God, 11 being strengthened with all power according to His glorious might so that you may have full endurance and patience, and joyfully
paragraphs: 9 For this reason, since the day we heard about you, we have not stopped praying for you and asking God to fill you with the knowledge of His will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding, 10 so that you may walk in a manner worthy of the Lord and may please Him in every way: bearing fruit in every good work, growing in the knowledge of God, 11 being strengthened with all power according to His glorious might so that you may have full endurance and patience, and joyfully

passages.context_html:
The report of the Colossians’ faith and love moves Paul from thanksgiving into a continuing prayer for them. He asks God to fill them with the knowledge of His will, with spiritual wisdom and understanding.

The purpose of that knowledge is a life pleasing to the Lord. Paul describes good works, growing knowledge of God, endurance and patience. Knowing and living belong together: the prayer reaches into what they do and how they persevere.

The power he asks for is God’s power. Its stated purpose here includes patient endurance. Paul does not equate strength with escaping every difficulty; he asks for what will sustain a faithful life through it.

The sentence continues into thanksgiving in the following verses. Paul grounds their growing life in what the Father has already done to bring them into His Son’s kingdom.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as prayer for knowledge that bears fruit in a changed life. Wesley’s notes on verses 9–11 connect understanding God’s will with conduct and patient endurance. The USCCB note on verses 9–14 also describes the interaction between knowing God and living according to the gospel. This is an active life of dependence on Him.
passages.current_position_html: In What Does Prayer Look Like?, we draw attention to what Paul asks for here: deeper knowledge of God’s will, a life that honors Him, good fruit and strength to endure. This passage gives us a positive pattern for praying for another person’s growth in Christ.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Paul describes the purpose of his teaching later in Colossians 1:27–29: Christ among His people, hope of glory and people brought to maturity in Him. The prayer for knowledge and endurance serves that larger goal.

Romans 8:29–30 names God’s purpose of making His people like His Son and bringing them to glory. Growth in faithful conduct is part of that work, sustained by His power and directed toward its completion.

passages.title: Colossians 1:9-14
passages.section_title: How does knowing God shape the way we live?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 For this reason, since the day we heard about you, we have not stopped praying for you and asking God to fill you with the knowledge of His will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding, 10 so that you may walk in a manner worthy of the Lord and may please Him in every way: bearing fruit in every good work, growing in the knowledge of God, 11 being strengthened with all power according to His glorious might so that you may have full endurance and patience, and joyfully 12 giving thanks to the Father, who has qualified you to share in the inheritance of the saints in the light. 13 He has rescued us from the dominion of darkness and brought us into the kingdom of His beloved Son, 14 in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins.
paragraphs: 9 For this reason, since the day we heard about you, we have not stopped praying for you and asking God to fill you with the knowledge of His will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding, 10 so that you may walk in a manner worthy of the Lord and may please Him in every way: bearing fruit in every good work, growing in the knowledge of God, 11 being strengthened with all power according to His glorious might so that you may have full endurance and patience, and joyfully

12 giving thanks to the Father, who has qualified you to share in the inheritance of the saints in the light. 13 He has rescued us from the dominion of darkness and brought us into the kingdom of His beloved Son, 14 in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The report of the Colossians’ faith and love moves Paul from thanksgiving into a continuing prayer for them. He asks God to fill them with the knowledge of His will, with spiritual wisdom and understanding.

The purpose of that knowledge is a life pleasing to the Lord. Paul describes good works, growing knowledge of God, endurance and patience. Knowing and living belong together: the prayer reaches into what they do and how they persevere.

The power he asks for is God’s power. Its stated purpose here includes patient endurance. Paul does not equate strength with escaping every difficulty; he asks for what will sustain a faithful life through it.

The prayer leads into thanksgiving to the Father, who has qualified them to share in the saints’ inheritance in the light. He has rescued them from darkness and brought them into His beloved Son’s kingdom. Their life of growth rests on His saving action. In the Son they have redemption, explained here as the forgiveness of sins. The passage moves from prayer for a worthy life to the reason for grateful confidence: God has acted to bring them to Himself through Christ.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read this as prayer for knowledge that bears fruit in a changed life. Wesley’s notes on verses 9–11 connect understanding God’s will with conduct and patient endurance. The USCCB note on verses 9–14 also describes the interaction between knowing God and living according to the gospel. This is an active life of dependence on Him.

The closing verses are commonly read as thanksgiving for God’s rescue and forgiveness through His Son. They supply the basis for the growing life Paul asks God to sustain.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Acts 26:15–18, the risen Jesus sends Paul to the Gentiles so they may turn from darkness to light, receive forgiveness and share an inheritance among those sanctified by faith in Him. The same connected themes appear here in a community that has received the gospel.

This rescue reaches beyond an individual improvement project. God is bringing people into His Son’s kingdom and forming their lives in keeping with that belonging. Paul’s stated aim in Colossians 1:27–29 is to present people mature in Christ, with the hope of glory. The prayer and the thanksgiving belong to that one work.
passages.current_position_html: In What Does Prayer Look Like?, we draw attention to what Paul asks for here: deeper knowledge of God’s will, a life that honors Him, good fruit and strength to endure. This passage gives us a positive pattern for praying for another person’s growth in Christ.

passages.title: Colossians 1:15-20
passages.section_title: Why is Christ at the center of creation and reconciliation?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 The Son is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn over all creation. 16 For in Him all things were created, things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities. All things were created through Him and for Him. 17 He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together. 18 And He is the head of the body, the church; He is the beginning and firstborn from among the dead, so that in all things He may have preeminence. 19 For God was pleased to have all His fullness dwell in Him, 20 and through Him to reconcile to Himself all things, whether things on earth or things in heaven, by making peace through the blood of His cross.
paragraphs: 15 The Son is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn over all creation. 16 For in Him all things were created, things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities. All things were created through Him and for Him. 17 He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together.

18 And He is the head of the body, the church; He is the beginning and firstborn from among the dead, so that in all things He may have preeminence. 19 For God was pleased to have all His fullness dwell in Him, 20 and through Him to reconcile to Himself all things, whether things on earth or things in heaven, by making peace through the blood of His cross.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul has just described rescue into the kingdom of God’s beloved Son. He now turns to who the Son is: the image of the invisible God, before all things, the One through whom and for whom all things were created.

The word firstborn is prototokos (proh-TOH-toh-koss). Thayer’s lexicon discusses both birth priority and uses associated with supreme rank. The title needs its context. Here the following verses place all created things in relation to the Son as their creator, goal and sustainer. In Psalm 89:24–29, God also uses firstborn for the exalted position He gives His appointed king.

The paragraph then names Christ as the head of the church and firstborn from the dead. Creation and the church are held together under His preeminence. The fullness dwells in Him, and peace comes through the blood of His cross.

The scope extends to things on earth and in heaven. Paul immediately brings this vast account of reconciliation into the Colossians’ own story in the following verses: they too were alienated and have been reconciled through Christ’s death.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The major historic Catholic, Reformed and Wesleyan traditions share the reading that the Son is truly God, before creation, rather than one created being among others. Their own statements include the Catholic Catechism, paragraphs 464–469, the Westminster Confession, chapter 8, and the Methodist Articles of Religion, article II. Within that shared reading, this paragraph declares Christ’s supremacy and His work of reconciliation through the cross.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 1:9–10 describes God’s purpose to bring all things in heaven and on earth together in Christ. It is a close parallel to the scope named here: God’s purpose reaches the creation, with Christ at its center.

1 Corinthians 15:20–28 connects Christ’s resurrection with the resurrection of His people, His reign and the defeat of death. The One called firstborn from the dead leads His people into that promised life. Creation’s Lord is also the Lord who brings God’s restoring purpose to its goal.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Colossians 1:21-23
passages.section_title: What does reconciliation mean for the life ahead?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 Once you were alienated from God and were hostile in your minds, engaging in evil deeds. 22 But now He has reconciled you by Christ’s physical body through death to present you holy, unblemished, and blameless in His presence— 23 if indeed you continue in your faith, established and firm, not moved from the hope of the gospel you heard, which has been proclaimed to every creature under heaven, and of which I, Paul, have become a servant.
paragraphs: 21 Once you were alienated from God and were hostile in your minds, engaging in evil deeds. 22 But now He has reconciled you by Christ’s physical body through death to present you holy, unblemished, and blameless in His presence— 23 if indeed you continue in your faith, established and firm, not moved from the hope of the gospel you heard, which has been proclaimed to every creature under heaven, and of which I, Paul, have become a servant.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After describing Christ’s supremacy and the peace made through His cross, Paul addresses the believers’ own change. They were once alienated, hostile in mind and doing evil. Now God has reconciled them through Christ’s physical body in death.

The purpose is to present them holy, unblemished and blameless in His presence. Reconciliation is directed toward that completed life with Him.

Paul attaches a serious appeal: continue established and firm in the faith, holding to the gospel’s hope. He places their local hearing of that message within its worldwide proclamation and names himself as its servant. The next paragraph explains the work and suffering this service involves.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians agree that the passage calls believers to remain in the gospel’s hope. Traditions differ over how this condition relates to the possibility of finally falling away.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 17, teaches that those truly accepted in Christ will persevere because God preserves them. It also allows for serious falls into sin. On that account, continuing faith belongs to the life God sustains, rather than earning reconciliation.

The Catholic Catechism, paragraph 162, teaches that faith is God’s free gift and can be lost; it calls believers to nourish faith through God’s word, prayer and love.

The Methodist Articles of Religion, article XII, teach that people who have received the Spirit may depart from grace, while also affirming repentance and restoration by grace. Wesley’s note on verse 23 reads the condition as a real warning about losing blessings already received. These readings all take the appeal seriously, but understand its relationship to final salvation differently.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 5:25–27 describes Christ giving Himself for the church so that He may present her holy and without blemish. It supplies a close parallel to the purpose of His death named here: a people made ready for life with Him.

Romans 8:29–30 likewise describes God’s purpose of likeness to His Son and glory. That is the future toward which Paul directs this call to remain in faith.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Colossians 1:24-29
passages.section_title: Why does Paul suffer and work for the church?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 24 Now I rejoice in my sufferings for you, and I fill up in my flesh what is lacking in regard to Christ’s afflictions for the sake of His body, which is the church. 25 I became its servant by the commission God gave me to fully proclaim to you the word of God, 26 the mystery that was hidden for ages and generations but is now revealed to His saints. 27 To them God has chosen to make known among the Gentiles the glorious riches of this mystery, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory. 28 We proclaim Him, admonishing and teaching everyone with all wisdom, so that we may present everyone perfect in Christ. 29 To this end I also labor, striving with all His energy working powerfully within me.
paragraphs: 24 Now I rejoice in my sufferings for you, and I fill up in my flesh what is lacking in regard to Christ’s afflictions for the sake of His body, which is the church. 25 I became its servant by the commission God gave me to fully proclaim to you the word of God, 26 the mystery that was hidden for ages and generations but is now revealed to His saints. 27 To them God has chosen to make known among the Gentiles the glorious riches of this mystery, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory.

28 We proclaim Him, admonishing and teaching everyone with all wisdom, so that we may present everyone perfect in Christ. 29 To this end I also labor, striving with all His energy working powerfully within me.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul has just called himself a servant of the gospel. He now describes what that service costs and what it seeks: he suffers for the church and works to proclaim God’s word fully.

His statement about filling up what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions needs the surrounding context. The previous paragraph already located reconciliation in Christ’s death. Here Paul describes his own suffering for Christ’s body, the church, as he carries out his commission.

The message once hidden has now been made known among the Gentiles: Christ in them, the hope of glory. Mystery here is explained as something God has revealed, so Paul makes Christ known openly.

The goal is to present everyone mature in Christ. Paul warns and teaches toward that end, laboring with the energy Christ powerfully supplies. His effort and his dependence on the Lord belong together.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand Paul’s suffering as service for the church, while affirming the sufficiency of Christ’s saving sacrifice. Wesley’s note on verse 24 distinguishes the suffering of Christ’s members from the work by which Christ reconciled them to God. The Catholic Catechism, paragraph 618, likewise calls Christ’s sacrifice unique and describes His invitation to share in His suffering. These readings keep Christian suffering in relation to His work rather than treating the cross as a failed or incomplete sacrifice.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Acts 9:1–6, Jesus identifies Saul’s persecution of His disciples as persecution of Himself. This supplies a clear parallel to the relationship between Christ and His suffering body here.

Ephesians 3:4–12 explains the revealed mystery as Gentiles sharing the promise and the same body through the gospel. It places that welcome within God’s eternal purpose in Christ and the display of His wisdom through the church. Paul’s costly service helps make that purpose known and bring people to maturity in Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Colossians 2:1-5
passages.section_title: How does knowing Christ help a church stand firm?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 For I want you to know how much I am struggling for you and for those at Laodicea, and for all who have not met me face to face, 2 that they may be encouraged in heart, knit together in love, and filled with the full riches of complete understanding, so that they may know the mystery of God, namely Christ, 3 in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. 4 I say this so that no one will deceive you by smooth rhetoric. 5 For although I am absent from you in body, I am present with you in spirit, and I delight to see your orderly condition and firm faith in Christ.
paragraphs: 1 For I want you to know how much I am struggling for you and for those at Laodicea, and for all who have not met me face to face, 2 that they may be encouraged in heart, knit together in love, and filled with the full riches of complete understanding, so that they may know the mystery of God, namely Christ, 3 in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.

4 I say this so that no one will deceive you by smooth rhetoric. 5 For although I am absent from you in body, I am present with you in spirit, and I delight to see your orderly condition and firm faith in Christ.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul continues describing his labor for believers, including those in Laodicea and others who have not met him. His distance from them does not diminish his concern.

He wants their hearts encouraged and their lives knit together in love, with the understanding that leads to knowing Christ. In Christ are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. The knowledge Paul seeks is joined to love and confidence in Him.

This prepares the warning in verse 4: persuasive speech can deceive. Paul wants their understanding of Christ to help them recognize that danger. He rejoices in the order and firmness of their faith, even while writing to strengthen it.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as concern for a community to be strengthened in love, understanding and faith in Christ. Wesley’s notes on verses 1–2 emphasize Paul’s prayerful concern and fuller understanding of the gospel. The warning concerns teaching that draws them away from the Christ in whom wisdom is found.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 3:8–12 describes God’s wisdom being made known through the church according to His eternal purpose in Christ. It also connects Christ with confident access to God. The understanding and love Paul desires here serve that wider work of a people brought near to God together.

The goal is a growing community, as Ephesians 4:11–16 explains: believers grow toward maturity in Christ and become less vulnerable to deceptive teaching. This is a close parallel to the combination of love, knowledge and stability in these verses.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Colossians 2:6-15
passages.section_title: What has God already given us in Christ?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 Therefore, just as you have received Christ Jesus as Lord, continue to walk in Him, 7 rooted and built up in Him, established in the faith as you were taught, and overflowing with thankfulness. 8 See to it that no one takes you captive through philosophy and empty deception, which are based on human tradition and the spiritual forces of the world rather than on Christ. 9 For in Christ all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form. 10 And you have been made complete in Christ, who is the head over every ruler and authority. 11 In Him you were also circumcised, in the putting off of your sinful nature, with the circumcision performed by Christ and not by human hands. 12 And having been buried with Him in baptism, you were raised with Him through your faith in the power of God, who raised Him from the dead. 13 When you were dead in your trespasses and in the uncircumcision of your sinful nature, God made you alive with Christ. He forgave us all our trespasses, 14 having canceled the debt ascribed to us in the decrees that stood against us. He took it away, nailing it to the cross! 15 And having disarmed the powers and authorities, He made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them by the cross.
paragraphs: 6 Therefore, just as you have received Christ Jesus as Lord, continue to walk in Him, 7 rooted and built up in Him, established in the faith as you were taught, and overflowing with thankfulness. 8 See to it that no one takes you captive through philosophy and empty deception, which are based on human tradition and the spiritual forces of the world rather than on Christ.

9 For in Christ all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form. 10 And you have been made complete in Christ, who is the head over every ruler and authority. 11 In Him you were also circumcised, in the putting off of your sinful nature, with the circumcision performed by Christ and not by human hands. 12 And having been buried with Him in baptism, you were raised with Him through your faith in the power of God, who raised Him from the dead.

13 When you were dead in your trespasses and in the uncircumcision of your sinful nature, God made you alive with Christ. He forgave us all our trespasses, 14 having canceled the debt ascribed to us in the decrees that stood against us. He took it away, nailing it to the cross! 15 And having disarmed the powers and authorities, He made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them by the cross.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul asks the believers to continue living in the Christ they received as Lord: rooted in Him, built up in faith and overflowing with thanks. He warns against being carried away by deceptive teaching grounded elsewhere.

His reason is what they have in Christ. The fullness of deity dwells in Him bodily; He is above every ruler and authority. Their completeness rests in Him.

Paul describes a circumcision performed by Christ rather than human hands, then burial and resurrection with Him in baptism through faith in God’s power. God made them alive with Christ and forgave their trespasses. These descriptions all direct attention to what God has done.

The canceled record is called a cheirographon (khay-ROH-grah-fon). Thayer’s lexicon explains its use for a handwritten acknowledgment of debt. Paul uses that image for the debt that stood against them: God has taken it away at the cross.

The paragraph ends with the powers disarmed and publicly defeated. The cross that dealt with their debt also displays Christ’s triumph. This leads directly into Paul’s warning against accepting the judgments and religious demands of the following verses.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly see this as a declaration of Christ’s sufficiency, forgiveness and victory. They differ in how they describe the baptismal participation in His death and resurrection.

The Catholic Catechism, paragraph 1213, teaches that through baptism people are freed from sin, reborn as God’s children and incorporated into Christ and His church.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 28, calls baptism a sign and seal of grace, union with Christ and forgiveness. It also teaches that baptism’s effectiveness is not bound to the moment it is administered and that not everyone baptized is necessarily reborn.

The Baptist 1689 Confession, chapter 29, explicitly cites Colossians 2:12 when describing baptism as a sign of fellowship in Christ’s death and resurrection. It limits baptism to those professing repentance and faith.

The Methodist Articles of Religion, articles XVI–XVII, describe sacraments as means by which God strengthens faith and baptism as a sign of new birth, retaining infant baptism. Wesley’s note on verse 12 stresses the inward new life God works. These descriptions distinguish the traditions’ teachings about baptism while keeping God’s action and Christ at the center.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 6:3–11 gives a close parallel: burial with Christ, new life with Him and the hope of resurrection lead into living for God. The pattern of death and life reaches into both present conduct and the future.

Hebrews 2:10–18 places Christ’s death and defeat of the devil within God’s purpose of bringing many children to glory and freeing them from slavery through fear of death. The victory named here serves that larger rescue, rather than being a reason to seek protection from rival powers.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Colossians 2:16-19
passages.section_title: Why does Paul point from the shadow to Christ?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 Therefore let no one judge you by what you eat or drink, or with regard to a feast, a New Moon, or a Sabbath. 17 These are a shadow of the things to come, but the body that casts it belongs to Christ. 18 Do not let anyone who delights in false humility and the worship of angels disqualify you with speculation about what he has seen. Such a person is puffed up without basis by his unspiritual mind. 19 He has lost connection to the head, from whom the whole body, supported and knit together by its joints and ligaments, grows as God causes it to grow.
paragraphs: 16 Therefore let no one judge you by what you eat or drink, or with regard to a feast, a New Moon, or a Sabbath. 17 These are a shadow of the things to come, but the body that casts it belongs to Christ.

18 Do not let anyone who delights in false humility and the worship of angels disqualify you with speculation about what he has seen. Such a person is puffed up without basis by his unspiritual mind. 19 He has lost connection to the head, from whom the whole body, supported and knit together by its joints and ligaments, grows as God causes it to grow.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Because of what God has done in Christ, Paul tells the believers not to let others judge them over food, drink or religious dates. He calls these a shadow and identifies Christ as the reality to which the shadow belongs.

He also warns about false humility, angel worship and claims about visions. The person he describes is proud and disconnected from the head, Christ. The details of the teachers’ practices are not fully explained.

The alternative is a body nourished and held together through its connection with Christ. Growth comes from God. The warning protects that relationship from demands that displace the One who gives the church life.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read the shadow-and-reality comparison as directing attention to Christ. They differ over what this means for continuing Sabbath observance.

Wesley’s note on verses 16–17 includes the weekly Jewish Sabbaths among the ceremonial observances Paul names. In the Reformed tradition, the Westminster Confession, 21.7–8, nevertheless teaches an enduring one-day-in-seven command, observed on Sunday as the Christian Sabbath.

The Catholic Catechism, paragraphs 2175–2176, distinguishes Sunday from the Sabbath and describes Sunday worship as fulfilling its spiritual truth and moral call to worship.

The Seventh-day Adventist Church’s Fundamental Belief 20 affirms continued seventh-day Sabbath observance. A Biblical Research Institute explanation reads the Sabbaths in this passage as annual ceremonial rest days, rather than the weekly Sabbath. That is a named reading within the tradition; the official belief statement itself does not give this detailed interpretation of Colossians.
passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 10:1–14 also uses the picture of a shadow for earlier worship, then points to Christ’s once-for-all offering. It is a supported parallel in how earlier patterns direct attention to His accomplished work; it does not by itself settle every dispute about the calendar.

Ephesians 4:15–16 describes the church growing from Christ its head as every part contributes in love. The purpose goes beyond freedom from another person’s judgment: God is forming a people whose growth comes from their union with His Son.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Colossians 2:20-23
passages.section_title: Can strict rules give us a changed heart?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 20 If you have died with Christ to the spiritual forces of the world, why, as though you still belonged to the world, do you submit to its regulations: 21 “Do not handle, do not taste, do not touch!”? 22 These will all perish with use, because they are based on human commands and teachings. 23 Such restrictions indeed have an appearance of wisdom, with their self-prescribed worship, their false humility, and their harsh treatment of the body; but they are of no value against the indulgence of the flesh.
paragraphs: 20 If you have died with Christ to the spiritual forces of the world, why, as though you still belonged to the world, do you submit to its regulations: 21 “Do not handle, do not taste, do not touch!”? 22 These will all perish with use, because they are based on human commands and teachings. 23 Such restrictions indeed have an appearance of wisdom, with their self-prescribed worship, their false humility, and their harsh treatment of the body; but they are of no value against the indulgence of the flesh.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul carries forward the believers’ death with Christ. If they have died with Him to the spiritual forces of the world, why submit as though they still belong to that world?

He names restrictive commands about handling, tasting and touching. Their objects are used up and perish, and the regulations rest on human commands and teachings.

Such practices can look wise and humble. Yet Paul says that self-made worship and harsh treatment of the body do not overcome the indulgence of the flesh. An impressive appearance of discipline is not the same as the inward change he seeks.

The next chapter supplies the positive direction: seek the things above with Christ and put away the old way of life. Paul’s criticism of these restrictions leads toward a changed life, not indifference to how people live.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these verses as a warning that outward severity cannot produce the holy life it claims to achieve. Wesley’s notes on verses 20–23 describe the danger of religious rules that feed self-will and pride even while appearing to restrain them. The warning does not turn every practice of fasting or self-discipline into the condemned system; it concerns the commands and claims Paul is addressing.
passages.god_plan_html:
Galatians 5:13–26 gives the positive counterpart: freedom serves love, and life by the Spirit produces fruit including patience, gentleness and self-control. The change God seeks grows from His Spirit’s work rather than the appearance of strictness.

That life belongs within the new humanity described in Colossians 3:9–11, renewed in the Creator’s image and centered on Christ across old divisions. God’s purpose reaches beyond a list of forbidden objects to a people made new in Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Colossians 3:1-4
passages.section_title: How does life with the risen Christ change our direction?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Therefore, since you have been raised with Christ, strive for the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God. 2 Set your minds on things above, not on earthly things. 3 For you died, and your life is now hidden with Christ in God. 4 When Christ, who is your life, appears, then you also will appear with Him in glory.
paragraphs: 1 Therefore, since you have been raised with Christ, strive for the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God. 2 Set your minds on things above, not on earthly things. 3 For you died, and your life is now hidden with Christ in God. 4 When Christ, who is your life, appears, then you also will appear with Him in glory.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul turns from the ineffective restrictions of the previous paragraph to the believers’ life with Christ. Since they have been raised with Him, they are to seek the things above, where He is seated at God’s right hand.

Their life is hidden with Christ in God. Its full glory is not yet visible, but Paul connects its future with Christ’s appearing: they will appear with Him in glory.

This hope gives direction to present life. The following paragraphs explain what seeking the things above looks like through changed desires, truthful speech, forgiveness and care for others. Life with Christ reaches into the way they live now.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these verses as connecting present life in the risen Christ with the future glory believers will share with Him. Wesley’s notes on verses 1–4 emphasize life held with Christ and its coming disclosure. The USCCB note likewise relates their present belonging to their future life with Him in God’s presence.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 8:18–25 connects future glory with the redemption of believers’ bodies and creation’s freedom from decay. It widens the horizon of this hope: the glory to be revealed belongs within God’s renewing purpose.

1 Corinthians 15:20–23 ties the resurrection of those who belong to Christ to His own resurrection and His coming. The life now hidden with Him will have a public, bodily future in His victory over death.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Colossians 3:5-11
passages.section_title: What belongs to the old life, and what is being made new?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 Put to death, therefore, the components of your earthly nature: sexual immorality, impurity, lust, evil desires, and greed, which is idolatry. 6 Because of these, the wrath of God is coming on the sons of disobedience. 7 When you lived among them, you also used to walk in these ways. 8 But now you must put aside all such things as these: anger, rage, malice, slander, and filthy language from your lips. 9 Do not lie to one another, since you have taken off the old self with its practices, 10 and have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge in the image of its Creator. 11 Here there is no Greek or Jew, circumcised or uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, or free, but Christ is all and is in all.

8 But now you must put aside all such things as these: anger, rage, malice, slander, and filthy language from your lips. 9 Do not lie to one another, since you have taken off the old self with its practices, 10 and have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge in the image of its Creator. 11 Here there is no Greek or Jew, circumcised or uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, or free, but Christ is all and is in all.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Because their life belongs with Christ, Paul tells the believers to put to death the practices of their earthly nature. He names sexual immorality, impurity, lust, evil desires and greed, identifying greed as idolatry.

He then addresses the damage done through anger and speech: rage, malice, slander, filthy language and lying. These are things to put aside, not qualities that define the new life.

The clothing picture explains the change. They have taken off the old self and put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge in the Creator’s image. Paul joins a real change of identity with an ongoing renewal.

This renewed life is shared across divisions of people and status. Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, slave and free are brought into a life centered on Christ. The next paragraph describes the compassion and love to put on together.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as a call to leave sinful practices behind because of the new life in Christ. Wesley’s notes on verses 5–11 apply the call to desires as well as speech and conduct. The USCCB notes likewise read the taking-off and putting-on language as a changed way of life flowing from union with Christ. The call concerns living out that renewal, rather than harming the physical body.
passages.god_plan_html:
The language of the Creator’s image reaches back to Genesis 1:26–28, where God makes humanity in His image. This is a supported connection in the image language: God’s work in Christ renews human life toward its created purpose.

Ephesians 2:13–22 describes Christ making people once divided into one new humanity, God’s household and a dwelling for His Spirit. Renewal thus includes a people learning to live together under Christ across former divisions.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Colossians 3:12-17
passages.section_title: What does a community shaped by Christ look like?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 Therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, clothe yourselves with hearts of compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience. 13 Bear with one another and forgive any complaint you may have against someone else. Forgive as the Lord forgave you. 14 And over all these virtues put on love, which is the bond of perfect unity. 15 Let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, for to this you were called as members of one body. And be thankful. 16 Let the word of Christ richly dwell within you as you teach and admonish one another with all wisdom, and as you sing psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs with gratitude in your hearts to God. 17 And whatever you do, in word or deed, do it all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through Him.
paragraphs: 12 Therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, clothe yourselves with hearts of compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience. 13 Bear with one another and forgive any complaint you may have against someone else. Forgive as the Lord forgave you. 14 And over all these virtues put on love, which is the bond of perfect unity.

15 Let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, for to this you were called as members of one body. And be thankful. 16 Let the word of Christ richly dwell within you as you teach and admonish one another with all wisdom, and as you sing psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs with gratitude in your hearts to God. 17 And whatever you do, in word or deed, do it all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through Him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul addresses these believers as God’s chosen, holy and loved people. He describes what to put on in keeping with that belonging: compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience.

They are to bear with one another and forgive as the Lord forgave them. Love binds these qualities together. The peace of Christ is to rule among people called into one body, with thanksgiving.

Christ’s word is to dwell richly among them through wise teaching and admonition, including psalms, hymns and spiritual songs. The singing includes gratitude in their hearts to God. Learning, care for others and thanksgiving are woven together.

The paragraph reaches beyond a meeting: every word and deed is to be done in the Lord Jesus’ name, with thanks to the Father through Him. The household instructions that follow bring that whole-life call into particular relationships.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand this as a call for the community’s life and singing to be filled with Christ’s message. Wesley’s note on verse 16 stresses the word’s lasting, active place in believers. The USCCB note on verses 5–17 includes the congregation’s hymns and prayers within its response to God through Christ. The verse joins wisdom, mutual instruction and gratitude to God.

The instructions to forgive and bear with others belong to the same shared life. Christ’s forgiveness supplies the stated pattern, and the peace of the one body is a community concern.
passages.god_plan_html:
John 13:34–35 connects love patterned on Jesus with the world recognizing His disciples. The relationships Paul describes belong within that public witness to the Lord they follow.

Ephesians 2:19–22 places their life together within God’s purpose of a household and dwelling for His Spirit. Compassion, forgiveness, peace and shared teaching serve the building up of that people. The church’s life together displays more than individual moral improvement.
passages.current_position_html: In Worship as the Early Church Knew It, we emphasize the mutual purpose named here: songs should teach, admonish and build up the people beside us. Clear, meaningful content matters to the gathered church. The verse also names gratitude to God; thanksgiving and care for one another belong together in this life shaped by Christ’s word.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

passages.title: Colossians 3:16
passages.section_title: How should Christ’s word shape our singing and teaching?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 Let the word of Christ richly dwell within you as you teach and admonish one another with all wisdom, and as you sing psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs with gratitude in your hearts to God.
paragraphs: 16 Let the word of Christ richly dwell within you as you teach and admonish one another with all wisdom, and as you sing psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs with gratitude in your hearts to God.

passages.context_html:
Paul has called the believers to compassion, forgiveness, love and the peace of Christ as one body. He now describes how Christ’s word should make its home among them.

Teaching and admonishing are mutual activities. The community is to help one another understand and live the message, with wisdom. Psalms, hymns and spiritual songs belong within this shared life.

The verse also directs gratitude toward God. The surrounding paragraph repeatedly calls for thanksgiving and ends by placing every word and deed under the name of the Lord Jesus. Singing serves both a grateful relationship with God and the building up of His people.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 5:18–21 closely parallels the shared singing and thanksgiving here, placing them within a community filled by the Spirit. The Spirit’s work shapes how believers speak to one another and give thanks to the Father through Christ.

Ephesians 4:11–16 supplies the wider purpose: the whole body grows toward maturity in Christ as its members contribute in love. Songs that carry His message belong within that work of forming and strengthening His people.

passages.title: Colossians 3:18-4:1
passages.section_title: How does belonging to Christ shape responsibilities at home?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 Wives, submit to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord. 19 Husbands, love your wives and do not be harsh with them. 20 Children, obey your parents in everything, for this is pleasing to the Lord. 21 Fathers, do not provoke your children, so they will not become discouraged. 22 Slaves, obey your earthly masters in everything, not only to please them while they are watching, but with sincerity of heart and fear of the Lord. 23 Whatever you do, work at it with your whole being, as for the Lord and not for men, 24 because you know that you will receive an inheritance from the Lord as your reward. It is the Lord Christ you are serving. 25 Whoever does wrong will be repaid for his wrong, and there is no favoritism. 1 Masters, supply your slaves with what is right and fair, since you know that you also have a Master in heaven.

It is the Lord Christ you are serving. 25 Whoever does wrong will be repaid for his wrong, and there is no favoritism.
1 Masters, supply your slaves with what is right and fair, since you know that you also have a Master in heaven.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul applies the call to do everything in Jesus’ name to relationships within the household. He addresses each group directly: wives and husbands, children and fathers, slaves and masters.

Wives are called to submit as fitting in the Lord. Husbands are called to love and avoid harshness. Children are called to obey, and fathers are warned not to provoke them into discouragement. The instructions place real responsibilities on those with authority as well as those under it.

Paul is addressing actual enslaved people and their masters, rather than simply modern employees and employers. He directs their service toward Christ and promises an inheritance from Him. He also states that wrongdoing will be repaid without favoritism.

The instruction to masters continues in 4:1. They must supply what is right and fair, remembering that they too have a Master in heaven. Keeping this verse with the preceding instructions preserves Paul’s address to both sides of the relationship.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read these instructions as bringing household responsibilities under Christ’s lordship. They differ in how they describe authority and mutual responsibility in marriage.

The Southern Baptist Baptist Faith and Message, article XVIII, affirms equal worth while assigning the husband loving leadership and the wife gracious submission to that servant leadership. This is its stated confessional account, not a description of every Baptist church.

CBE International’s statement, family points 11–12, reads the marriage relationship through mutual submission and responsibility, with both parents sharing leadership in raising children. It represents a Christian equality reading across denominations.

In the Catholic apostolic letter Mulieris Dignitatem, paragraph 24, John Paul II reads the spouses’ relationship through mutual submission and Christ’s self-giving. These accounts share the call to love while explaining the pattern of responsibilities differently.

The commands to slaves and masters address an existing condition of slavery. They hold both accountable to the heavenly Lord and do not make a master’s earthly power the final measure of right and wrong.
passages.god_plan_html:
Galatians 3:26–29 identifies those in Christ as God’s children and heirs of the promise, across distinctions including slave and free. The inheritance promised to enslaved believers here belongs within that larger standing in Him.

Philemon 15–17 provides a concrete parallel: Paul asks that Onesimus be received as a beloved brother and as Paul himself. The call to live under one heavenly Master reaches into how people recognize and treat one another in Christ.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Colossians 4:2-6
passages.section_title: How do prayer and gracious speech serve the gospel?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 2 Devote yourselves to prayer, being watchful and thankful, 3 as you pray also for us, that God may open to us a door for the word, so that we may proclaim the mystery of Christ, for which I am in chains. 4 Pray that I may declare it clearly, as I should. 5 Act wisely toward outsiders, redeeming the time. 6 Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how to answer everyone.
paragraphs: 2 Devote yourselves to prayer, being watchful and thankful, 3 as you pray also for us, that God may open to us a door for the word, so that we may proclaim the mystery of Christ, for which I am in chains. 4 Pray that I may declare it clearly, as I should.
5 Act wisely toward outsiders, redeeming the time. 6 Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how to answer everyone.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul calls the believers to devoted prayer, watchfulness and thanksgiving. He then asks for prayer for himself and his coworkers: an open door for the word and clarity in proclaiming Christ.

His chains are part of the setting, but the request centers on the message reaching others. Prayer supports the work of speaking it clearly.

The believers also have responsibilities toward outsiders. They are to act wisely, make good use of their opportunities and speak graciously, with the care needed to answer each person. The paragraph connects their shared prayer with the way they meet and speak to people beyond the community.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as a call to persistent, thankful prayer and wise witness. Wesley’s notes on verses 3 and 6 connect the open door with opportunity to speak and emphasize gracious conversation. The request is for a clear message, joined with conduct and speech that serve the people hearing it.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Acts 1:8, Jesus sets the direction of His witnesses’ work from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth through the Spirit’s power. The prayer for an open door belongs within that wider mission.

Ephesians 3:5–6 explains the gospel’s purpose of bringing Gentiles into the same body and promise in Christ. Gracious, clear speech serves that welcome: the message is to reach people who are still outside the believing community.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Colossians 4:7-18
passages.section_title: What does the closing tell us about serving Christ together?
