Remember my chains. Grace be with you.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Tychicus and Onesimus will bring news and encouragement. Paul calls both valued servants and brothers in the Lord, and identifies Onesimus as one of the Colossians.

The greetings name fellow workers who have supported him. Epaphras continues the concern described at the start of the letter, laboring in prayer for their maturity and confidence in God’s will. Paul also commends his care for neighboring communities.

The greetings extend to Nympha and the church meeting in her house. Paul asks that this letter be read in Laodicea and that the Colossians also read the letter from there. The identity of that other letter is not established here.

Archippus is reminded to complete the ministry he received in the Lord. Paul closes with a greeting in his own hand, a request to remember his chains and a blessing of grace. These are people connected by shared service, prayer, hospitality and the message they receive together.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this closing as a picture of fellowship and shared service across connected communities. Wesley’s notes on verses 12 and 17 emphasize maturity and ministry as service. The USCCB notes on the closing likewise identify the personal greetings and encouragement. The letter supplies names and responsibilities without giving a complete biography or office description for each person.
passages.god_plan_html:
Philemon 8–21 fills out the significance of calling Onesimus a beloved brother. Paul appeals for him to be received in a new relationship of love and fellowship. The new humanity described earlier in Colossians takes shape in particular people and costly acts of welcome.

Ephesians 2:13–22 describes people brought near through Christ and built together as God’s household. The Jewish coworkers named here, the wider community of believers and the churches sharing the letter belong within that larger purpose of life together in Him.

passages.title: 1 Thessalonians 4:3

versions.label: LSB
versions.text: "For this is the will of God, your sanctification..."

passages.context_html: 1 Thessalonians 4:3 should be read within the flow of its chapter and the larger argument of 1 Thessalonians.
passages.common_interpretations_html: God's revealed will centers on the salvation of souls, the sanctification of believers, gratitude in all circumstances, and eternal life for those who believe. These are not mysteries — they are stated plainly and repeatedly throughout Scripture. God's providential will — His specific purposes for individual circumstances, situations, and events, which we often cannot know in advance. This is what Paul could not see when he asked three times for the thorn to be removed. This is what Abraham tried to engineer in Egypt instead of trusting. It is the path God is clearing that Proverbs 3:5-6 tells us we are not equipped to navigate on our own.
passages.current_position_html: No defined position is stated here yet beyond the common interpretations above. As related study develops, this section will be updated where the text warrants a clearer conclusion.

passages.title: 1 Thessalonians 5:17-18
passages.context_html: In 1 Thessalonians 5, Paul closes the letter with a rapid series of exhortations for sober, watchful, Spirit-sensitive Christian living. The chapter binds prayer, gratitude, discernment, testing, and holiness together, so its short commands belong to a larger picture of a church living in readiness for the Lord.
passages.common_interpretations_html: If prayer were primarily a matter of asking for things, praying without ceasing would be an absurd command — no one can spend every waking moment making requests. But if prayer is relational communion, an ongoing orientation toward God, an awareness of His presence running underneath everything else in the day, then praying without ceasing is simply what it looks like to live in that posture. This is where Romans 8:26-27 matters again. The Spirit intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words, searching our hearts and knowing what is there even when we have not said it. If God already knows the heart this intimately, then praying without ceasing is not about constantly generating words — it is about staying oriented toward Him closely enough that what is in your heart is, in a sense, already being prayed. The folded hands and spoken words are one expression of prayer. They are not the only one.

passages.title: 1 Thessalonians 5:20-21

versions.label: LSB
versions.text: "do not despise prophetic utterances. But examine everything carefully; hold fast to that which is good."

passages.context_html: In 1 Thessalonians 5, Paul closes the letter with a rapid series of exhortations for sober, watchful, Spirit-sensitive Christian living. The chapter binds prayer, gratitude, discernment, testing, and holiness together, so its short commands belong to a larger picture of a church living in readiness for the Lord.
passages.common_interpretations_html: These two passages work together. The first says we're not supposed to dismiss everything out of hand — but we are supposed to test it. The second is a sobering reminder of what the standard for that test can't be: how something feels. Something can feel peaceful, timely, encouraging, and "right" and still not be from God. That means the feeling itself can never be the proof. There has to be something outside the feeling — namely, Scripture — that the experience is tested against. Observation: "Test everything" only works if there's a fixed standard to test against. For the Christian, that standard is Scripture — not the emotional weight of the experience itself.
passages.current_position_html: No defined position is stated here yet beyond the common interpretations above. As related study develops, this section will be updated where the text warrants a clearer conclusion.

passages.title: 1 Thessalonians 5:21
passages.context_html: In 1 Thessalonians 5, Paul closes the letter with a rapid series of exhortations for sober, watchful, Spirit-sensitive Christian living. The chapter binds prayer, gratitude, discernment, testing, and holiness together, so its short commands belong to a larger picture of a church living in readiness for the Lord.
passages.common_interpretations_html: It's worth being careful here in both directions. Scripture does record God communicating through dreams to specific people at specific moments tied to His larger plan — Joseph, Daniel, Cornelius in Acts 10, Paul in Acts 16. Those accounts are firsthand, specific, and tied to pivotal moments in the story of redemption. Whether God continues to communicate through dreams and visions today is a question Christians genuinely debate — Peter's citation of Joel 2 in Acts 2 is a passage continuationists appeal to legitimately, and that debate does not need to be resolved here. What is much easier to defend is this: regardless of one's position on that question, no serious biblical framework treats every dream or impression as reliable divine communication requiring no testing. "Test all things" (1 Thessalonians 5:21) applies equally in either direction. A secondhand story, repeated through several layers of retelling, that can't be verified, sits in a very different category — even if the underlying claim might be true. Asking God for a feeling of peace, an "open door," or a general "sense" before making a decision — and then treating whatever happens afterward as God's answer. This often comes with a hidden bias: the times it "worked" get remembered and retold, while the times the feeling was wrong, or nothing happened, or the door that seemed "open" led nowhere, tend to be quietly forgotten.
passages.current_position_html: No defined position is stated here yet beyond the common interpretations above. As related study develops, this section will be updated where the text warrants a clearer conclusion.

passages.title: 1 Timothy 1:1-2
passages.section_title: What is the foundation of Paul’s charge to Timothy?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the command of God our Savior and of Christ Jesus our hope, 2 To Timothy, my true child in the faith: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.
paragraphs: 1 Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the command of God our Savior and of Christ Jesus our hope, 2 To Timothy, my true child in the faith: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul introduces himself as an apostle of Christ Jesus by the command of God our Savior and Christ Jesus our hope. His authority to give the coming charge rests in the Lord who appointed him.

Timothy is addressed as Paul’s true child in the faith. This describes their close relationship in the gospel. Paul wishes him grace, mercy and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus the Lord.

The following verses explain Timothy’s immediate responsibility in Ephesus. This greeting places that work within a relationship of faith and dependence on God’s saving care.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as Paul affirming his commission and encouraging Timothy in their shared faith. Wesley’s notes on verses 1–2 connect Christ with the ground of their hope and mercy with the needs of the person serving. The greeting gives the coming instructions a setting of grace, mercy and peace.
passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 9:10–16 describes the Lord appointing Paul to carry His name before Gentiles, kings and Israel. Timothy’s work belongs within the mission Paul received, rather than a private project detached from the spread of Christ’s message.

Titus 2:11–14 connects God’s saving grace and the hope of Christ’s appearing with a people He redeems and forms for good works. The Savior and hope named in the greeting point toward that larger purpose for the community Timothy serves.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Timothy 1:3-7
passages.section_title: What should sound teaching produce?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 3 As I urged you on my departure to Macedonia, you should stay on at Ephesus to instruct certain men not to teach false doctrines 4 or devote themselves to myths and endless genealogies, which promote speculation rather than the stewardship of God’s work, which is by faith. 5 The goal of our instruction is the love that comes from a pure heart, a clear conscience, and a sincere faith. 6 Some have strayed from these ways and turned aside to empty talk. 7 They want to be teachers of the law, but they do not understand what they are saying or that which they so confidently assert.
paragraphs: 3 As I urged you on my departure to Macedonia, you should stay on at Ephesus to instruct certain men not to teach false doctrines 4 or devote themselves to myths and endless genealogies, which promote speculation rather than the stewardship of God’s work, which is by faith.

5 The goal of our instruction is the love that comes from a pure heart, a clear conscience, and a sincere faith. 6 Some have strayed from these ways and turned aside to empty talk. 7 They want to be teachers of the law, but they do not understand what they are saying or that which they so confidently assert.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul reminds Timothy why he urged him to stay in Ephesus: certain people must stop teaching false doctrines and devoting themselves to myths and endless genealogies. These pursuits produce speculation rather than furthering God’s work by faith.

The goal Paul names is love flowing from a pure heart, a clear conscience and sincere faith. Teaching is meant to serve that life. Confidence and a wish to be recognized as a teacher do not replace understanding.

Some have turned from these qualities into empty talk. They want to teach the law but do not understand the matters about which they speak so confidently. Paul’s next paragraph explains that the problem is its misuse, rather than the law being bad.

The passage does not identify the full content of the myths or genealogies. It tells us their effect and gives a positive test of the instruction the community should receive.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a charge to protect the church from teaching that distracts from faith and love. Wesley’s notes on verses 3–7 contrast fruitful faith and love with empty religious disputes. The USCCB note likewise emphasizes the community’s growth in love. The warning does not condemn careful study simply because it involves difficult questions.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 3:8–12 describes God’s wisdom being made known through the church according to His eternal purpose in Christ. The community is meant to bear witness to that wisdom through its shared life.

Ephesians 4:11–16 connects teaching with a body growing toward maturity in Christ, stable in the truth and active in love. This is a supported parallel to Paul’s concern here: teaching serves God’s formation of a people who live together under His Son.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Timothy 1:8-11
passages.section_title: What does it mean to use the law rightly?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 Now we know that the law is good, if one uses it legitimately. 9 We realize that law is not enacted for the righteous, but for the lawless and rebellious, for the ungodly and sinful, for the unholy and profane, for killers of father or mother, for murderers, 10 for the sexually immoral, for homosexuals, for slave traders and liars and perjurers, and for anyone else who is averse to sound teaching 11 that agrees with the glorious gospel of the blessed God, with which I have been entrusted.
paragraphs: 8 Now we know that the law is good, if one uses it legitimately. 9 We realize that law is not enacted for the righteous, but for the lawless and rebellious, for the ungodly and sinful, for the unholy and profane, for killers of father or mother, for murderers, 10 for the sexually immoral, for homosexuals, for slave traders and liars and perjurers, and for anyone else who is averse to sound teaching 11 that agrees with the glorious gospel of the blessed God, with which I have been entrusted.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul has criticized people who want to teach the law without understanding it. He immediately affirms that the law is good when used legitimately. His criticism concerns what the teachers are doing with it.

He explains its relation to lawlessness by naming serious wrongs: violence, sexual sin, slave trading, lying and false testimony. The list ends broadly with whatever else is opposed to sound teaching.

That sound teaching agrees with the glorious gospel entrusted to Paul. The paragraph places the proper use of the law alongside the gospel, while exposing wrongdoing rather than supplying a stage for a teacher’s confident self-display.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand Paul as defending the law’s goodness and its exposure of wrongdoing while rejecting its misuse. Wesley’s notes on verses 8–11 describe the moral law as exposing sin and guiding believers in holy living. The Reformed Westminster Confession, 19.5–7, similarly distinguishes guidance in God’s will from using the law as the basis of a person’s acceptance or condemnation before Him. These readings do not treat the gospel as permission for the conduct Paul condemns.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 3:19–26 connects the law’s knowledge of sin with God’s gift of righteousness through faith in Jesus Christ. The law’s exposure of wrong belongs within a message that points sinners to God’s grace.

Galatians 3:23–29 places the law within the movement toward Christ and the promise shared by God’s children in Him. This provides a wider setting for its good purpose without turning moral instruction into a way to earn that inheritance.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Timothy 1:12-17
passages.section_title: What does Paul’s story show about Christ’s mercy?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 I thank Christ Jesus our Lord, who has strengthened me, that He considered me faithful and appointed me to service. 13 I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and a violent man; yet because I had acted in ignorance and unbelief, I was shown mercy. 14 And the grace of our Lord overflowed to me, along with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus. 15 This is a trustworthy saying, worthy of full acceptance: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the worst. 16 But for this very reason I was shown mercy, so that in me, the worst of sinners, Christ Jesus might display His perfect patience as an example to those who would believe in Him for eternal life. 17 Now to the King eternal, immortal, and invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.
paragraphs: 12 I thank Christ Jesus our Lord, who has strengthened me, that He considered me faithful and appointed me to service. 13 I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and a violent man; yet because I had acted in ignorance and unbelief, I was shown mercy. 14 And the grace of our Lord overflowed to me, along with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus.

15 This is a trustworthy saying, worthy of full acceptance: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the worst. 16 But for this very reason I was shown mercy, so that in me, the worst of sinners, Christ Jesus might display His perfect patience as an example to those who would believe in Him for eternal life. 17 Now to the King eternal, immortal, and invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After speaking of the gospel entrusted to him, Paul thanks Christ for strengthening him and appointing him to service. He remembers that he had been a blasphemer, a persecutor and a violent man.

He does not hide that past. He says he acted in ignorance and unbelief and received mercy, with the Lord’s grace overflowing in faith and love in Christ Jesus.

The trustworthy message is that Christ came into the world to save sinners. Paul counts himself the worst. The Greek word is protos (PROH-toss); Thayer’s lexicon includes first in rank or chief and specifically lists verse 15. His words stress the seriousness of his sin and the greatness of the mercy shown to him.

Paul then states why his case matters to others: Christ’s patience toward him provides an example for those who will believe for eternal life. His account ends in praise to the eternal, immortal and invisible God.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this as testimony to Christ’s mercy toward a former persecutor and encouragement to sinners who hear the gospel. Wesley’s notes on verses 12–17 emphasize abundant grace and hope for others. The USCCB note likewise connects Paul’s experience with Jesus’ saving purpose and the praise it produces. Paul’s past is evidence of the mercy he received, rather than a reason to minimize his wrongs.
passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 9:10–16 gives the striking setting: the man feared for harming believers is appointed to carry Jesus’ name to others. Mercy makes a former persecutor a servant of the message he opposed.

Titus 2:11–14 connects the appearing of saving grace with Christ’s purpose of redeeming a people for Himself and teaching them a new way of life as they await His glory. Paul’s story displays that work in a particular person, with a purpose that reaches those who will believe after him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Timothy 1:18-20
passages.section_title: Why must Timothy hold on to faith and a good conscience?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 Timothy, my child, I entrust you with this command in keeping with the previous prophecies about you, so that by them you may fight the good fight, 19 holding on to faith and a good conscience, which some have rejected and thereby shipwrecked their faith. 20 Among them are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I have handed over to Satan to be taught not to blaspheme.
paragraphs: 18 Timothy, my child, I entrust you with this command in keeping with the previous prophecies about you, so that by them you may fight the good fight, 19 holding on to faith and a good conscience, which some have rejected and thereby shipwrecked their faith. 20 Among them are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I have handed over to Satan to be taught not to blaspheme.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul returns to the charge he has entrusted to Timothy. He reminds him of earlier prophecies concerning him and calls him to fight the good fight while holding on to faith and a good conscience.

The warning is concrete: some have rejected a good conscience and shipwrecked their faith. Paul names Hymenaeus and Alexander as examples and says he has handed them over to Satan.

The stated purpose of this severe action is that they learn not to blaspheme. Paul describes a serious failure and a disciplinary aim, without giving a complete account of what happened to them afterward. The charge concerns Timothy’s conduct as well as what he teaches.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read this as a serious warning against rejecting faith and conscience, with discipline aimed at correction. They differ about what shipwrecked faith implies for a person’s final salvation.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 17, teaches that people truly accepted in Christ will finally persevere, though they may fall into grievous sin for a time. That account distinguishes serious failure from the final loss of saving grace.

Wesley’s note on verse 19 understands these people as genuine believers who fell away. The Methodist Articles of Religion, article XII, allow departure from grace and also affirm restoration through repentance by grace. The Catholic Catechism, paragraph 162, likewise teaches that the free gift of faith can be lost. These sources differ over final perseverance without diminishing the warning.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Corinthians 5:1–5 uses the same handing-over language in another disciplinary setting, with a stated hope of salvation on the day of the Lord. The parallel helps keep correction and the final horizon in view, rather than treating discipline as an end in itself.

Hebrews 12:5–11 describes God’s discipline as directed toward His children sharing in His holiness and bearing righteousness and peace. This is a broader parallel in purpose; it does not identify every painful circumstance as the same disciplinary act.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Timothy 2:1-7
passages.section_title: Why should our prayers reach beyond our own circle?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 First of all, then, I urge that petitions, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgiving be offered for everyone— 2 for kings and all those in authority—so that we may lead tranquil and quiet lives in all godliness and dignity. 3 This is good and pleasing in the sight of God our Savior, 4 who wants everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. 5 For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, 6 who gave Himself as a ransom for all—the testimony that was given at just the right time. 7 For this reason I was appointed as a preacher, an apostle, and a faithful and true teacher of the Gentiles. I am telling the truth; I am not lying about anything.
paragraphs: 1 First of all, then, I urge that petitions, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgiving be offered for everyone— 2 for kings and all those in authority—so that we may lead tranquil and quiet lives in all godliness and dignity. 3 This is good and pleasing in the sight of God our Savior, 4 who wants everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.

5 For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, 6 who gave Himself as a ransom for all—the testimony that was given at just the right time. 7 For this reason I was appointed as a preacher, an apostle, and a faithful and true teacher of the Gentiles. I am telling the truth; I am not lying about anything.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul calls for petitions, prayers, intercessions and thanksgiving for everyone, explicitly including kings and all in authority. He connects this with the hope of a tranquil, quiet life marked by godliness and dignity.

The reason reaches beyond the community’s immediate well-being. God our Savior wants everyone to be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth. Paul places the breadth of prayer within that saving concern.

There is one God and one mediator between God and humanity, Christ Jesus, who gave Himself as a ransom. Paul’s commission to teach the Gentiles belongs to the same message. Neither social position nor national background supplies a separate Savior or a different route through another mediator.

The paragraph invites prayer for people who may hold power over the church as well as those near to it. It describes prayer shaped by God’s saving purpose rather than confined to familiar names.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians agree that prayer should reach beyond our own circle, including rulers and people unlike us. They differ in how they understand everyone in the statement about God’s saving desire.

Calvin’s comments on verses 3–4 read the passage as including every rank and nation, especially rulers and Gentiles. He understands the emphasis as all kinds of people, rather than a statement about God’s purpose for every individual. This is a named Reformed reading, not a claim that every Reformed teacher phrases the distinction identically.

Wesley’s notes on verses 3–6 read God’s saving desire as extending to every person, while distinguishing that desire from compulsion. The Catholic Catechism, paragraph 851, also expressly describes God as willing everyone’s salvation through the knowledge of the truth. These readings give a wider individual scope to the desire described here.

The difference does not remove the practical instruction to pray broadly. Paul places that instruction beside the one God, Christ’s mediation and His self-giving for others.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jeremiah 29:4–7 provides an earlier parallel: God tells the exiles to seek Babylon’s welfare and pray for the city where they live. Prayer for the wider society already belongs within the faithful life of God’s people amid people who do not share their faith.

Ephesians 3:5–6 describes Gentiles sharing the promise and the same body through the gospel. Paul’s mission to the Gentiles, named in verse 7, serves that wider purpose. Prayer crosses the boundaries of rank and nation because the message of Christ is to reach beyond them.
passages.current_position_html: In Prayer and Faith, we identify God’s stated desire for everyone to be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth as part of His revealed will. That gives our prayer a clear direction: seek people’s salvation and their knowledge of Him, in keeping with what He has made known.

passages.title: 1 Timothy 2:3-4
passages.section_title: What does God’s saving desire tell us about prayer?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 3 This is good and pleasing in the sight of God our Savior, 4 who wants everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.
paragraphs: 3 This is good and pleasing in the sight of God our Savior, 4 who wants everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.

passages.context_html:
These verses give a reason for the instruction just before them: prayer for everyone, including kings and those in authority. Paul calls that prayer good and pleasing in God our Savior’s sight.

He describes God as wanting everyone to be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth. The following verses connect that concern with the one mediator, Christ Jesus, His self-giving and Paul’s mission to the Gentiles.

The statement belongs to an appeal for broad prayer and the proclamation of Christ. It is not presented here as a guarantee that every person will finally be saved, nor as a reason to exclude particular groups from prayer.

Calvin’s comments on verses 3–4 read the passage as including every rank and nation, especially rulers and Gentiles. These readings give a wider individual scope to the desire described here.

The difference does not remove the practical instruction to pray broadly. Paul places that instruction beside the one God, Christ’s mediation and His self-giving for others.

That gives our prayer a clear direction: seek people’s salvation and their knowledge of Him, in keeping with what He has made known.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Jeremiah 29:4–7 provides an earlier parallel: God tells the exiles to seek Babylon’s welfare and pray for the city where they live. Prayer for the wider society already belongs within the faithful life of God’s people amid people who do not share their faith.

Ephesians 3:5–6 describes Gentiles sharing the promise and the same body through the gospel. Paul’s mission to the Gentiles, named in verse 7, serves that wider purpose. Prayer crosses the boundaries of rank and nation because the message of Christ is to reach beyond them.

passages.title: 1 Timothy 2:8-10
passages.section_title: What should mark the people who gather to pray?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 Therefore I want the men everywhere to pray, lifting up holy hands, without anger or dissension. 9 Likewise, I want the women to adorn themselves with respectable apparel, with modesty, and with self-control, not with braided hair or gold or pearls or expensive clothes, 10 but with good deeds, as is proper for women who profess to worship God.
paragraphs: 8 Therefore I want the men everywhere to pray, lifting up holy hands, without anger or dissension. 9 Likewise, I want the women to adorn themselves with respectable apparel, with modesty, and with self-control, not with braided hair or gold or pearls or expensive clothes, 10 but with good deeds, as is proper for women who profess to worship God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul moves from the breadth of the community’s prayer to the conduct of those praying. He wants the men everywhere to pray with holy hands, without anger or dissension. The condition of their relationships and conduct belongs with their public prayer.

He then addresses women’s appearance, calling for respectable dress, modesty and self-control. Braided hair, gold, pearls and expensive clothing are set alongside the different adornment of good deeds.

The passage directs attention from displays of appearance to a life fitting the profession of devotion to God. The next verses continue with learning and teaching in the community; these instructions are part of the letter’s concern for its shared life.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read these instructions as calling for holy, peaceable prayer and conduct that shows devotion to God. Applications of the clothing list differ.

Wesley’s note on verse 9 treats the named ornaments as explicit prohibitions. Calvin’s comments on verses 9–10 instead understand the instruction as requiring modesty and moderation rather than forbidding every use of gold or jewels. These are named teachers’ readings, rather than a claim that every church in either tradition has one identical dress rule.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Peter 2:9–12 describes a people called out of darkness to proclaim God’s goodness. Their honorable conduct and good deeds are meant to lead others to glorify Him. This supplies the wider purpose behind a life that visibly matches devotion to God.

Matthew 5:14–16 similarly connects good deeds with giving glory to the Father. The goal of the community’s visible life is to direct attention toward Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Timothy 2:11-15
passages.section_title: How do Christians understand Paul’s instructions about learning and teaching?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 A woman must learn in quietness and full submissiveness. 12 I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; she is to remain quiet. 13 For Adam was formed first, and then Eve. 14 And it was not Adam who was deceived, but the woman who was deceived and fell into transgression. 15 Women, however, will be saved through childbearing, if they continue in faith, love, and holiness, with self-control.
paragraphs: 11 A woman must learn in quietness and full submissiveness. 12 I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; she is to remain quiet.

13 For Adam was formed first, and then Eve. 14 And it was not Adam who was deceived, but the woman who was deceived and fell into transgression. 15 Women, however, will be saved through childbearing, if they continue in faith, love, and holiness, with self-control.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul continues his instructions about the community’s shared life. He says that a woman must learn in quietness and submission, then states a restriction on teaching or exercising authority over a man. The BSB footnotes also allow wife and husband in these verses.

The verb behind exercise authority is authenteo (ow-then-TEH-oh). Thayer’s lexicon gives governing or exercising dominion over someone. Christians differ over the kind of authority Paul has in view and how widely the instruction applies. The word alone cannot answer both questions.

Paul gives reasons from Genesis: Adam was formed first, and Eve was deceived and fell into sin. He then speaks of being saved through childbearing, joined to continuing in faith, love, holiness and self-control.

The paragraph does not give a full account of the particular people or events behind it. The wider letter warns about false teaching. How those circumstances relate to the scope of this instruction, and how verse 15 should be understood, are questions on which Christians differ.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
One reading takes this as an enduring restriction on women teaching or governing men in the church. The Southern Baptist Baptist Faith and Message, article VI, cites this passage and reserves the office of pastor/elder/overseer for qualified men, while affirming that women and men are gifted for service. This describes that confession’s rule for the office; it does not state that women may never teach in any setting.

The Catholic Church reserves sacred ordination to baptized men in the Catechism, paragraph 1577. It also recognizes women’s teaching ministry: Antiquum Ministerium, paragraph 8, explicitly includes women in the instituted lay ministry of catechist. Its distinction between ordination and other ministry is important when describing this position.

Another reading holds that this passage does not exclude women generally from church teaching and leadership. CBE International’s statement, points 8–9 and its applications, calls for women’s and men’s gifts to serve the whole church and reads restrictive passages within the wider teaching of Scripture. This represents a Christian equality reading across denominations. The United Methodist Church’s own explanation of women’s ordination likewise affirms women’s leadership at every level; it should not be confused with a claim that every Methodist body takes the same position.

The childbearing sentence also has different readings. Calvin’s comments on verse 15 describe hope of salvation through God’s grace while women faithfully endure the work and difficulties of motherhood; he expressly rejects treating childbirth as earning salvation. Wesley’s note includes preservation through childbirth’s danger and final salvation in continuing faith. These readings differ in what saved refers to and how childbearing relates to it. The faith, love, holiness and self-control in the sentence remain part of the discussion.
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul explicitly brings the story of creation and human sin into the discussion, drawing on Genesis 2:18–25 and Genesis 3:1–19. The wider New Testament carries that story toward restoration: Romans 5:12–19 contrasts Adam’s disobedience and the reign of death with Christ’s obedience and God’s gift of life.

Galatians 3:26–29 identifies women and men who belong to Christ as God’s children and heirs of the promise. The larger purpose is a people receiving life in Him and learning to live in faith and holiness together. The questions about teaching roles are considered within that shared belonging.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Timothy 3:1-7
passages.section_title: What should we look for in someone who cares for the church?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 This is a trustworthy saying: If anyone aspires to be an overseer, he desires a noble task. 2 An overseer, then, must be above reproach, the husband of but one wife, temperate, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach, 3 not dependent on wine, not violent but gentle, peaceable, and free of the love of money. 4 An overseer must manage his own household well and keep his children under control, with complete dignity. 5 For if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how can he care for the church of God? 6 He must not be a recent convert, or he may become conceited and fall under the same condemnation as the devil. 7 Furthermore, he must have a good reputation with outsiders, so that he will not fall into disgrace and into the snare of the devil.
paragraphs: 1 This is a trustworthy saying: If anyone aspires to be an overseer, he desires a noble task. 2 An overseer, then, must be above reproach, the husband of but one wife, temperate, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach, 3 not dependent on wine, not violent but gentle, peaceable, and free of the love of money.

4 An overseer must manage his own household well and keep his children under control, with complete dignity. 5 For if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how can he care for the church of God? 6 He must not be a recent convert, or he may become conceited and fall under the same condemnation as the devil. 7 Furthermore, he must have a good reputation with outsiders, so that he will not fall into disgrace and into the snare of the devil.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul calls the work of an overseer a noble task. He then describes the character and readiness that must accompany the desire to serve.

The Greek word is episkopos (ep-ISS-koh-poss). Thayer’s lexicon explains it as an overseer or someone charged with watching over others. Here the duty is care for the church, made explicit in verse 5.

The list joins public and private life: faithfulness in marriage, self-control, hospitality and the ability to teach, together with gentleness and freedom from greed. The person must not be dependent on wine or violent.

Care in the household provides a test of readiness to care for the church. Paul also warns against appointing a recent convert and requires a good reputation with outsiders. The concern is a person’s tested life and capacity for the work, not aspiration alone.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand this list as requiring tested character, faithful conduct and the ability to teach. They differ in how the office is related to other church offices.

The Baptist 1689 Confession, 26.8–9, identifies bishops or elders and deacons as the church’s appointed officers. The Catholic Catechism, paragraph 1554, describes bishops, priests and deacons as three degrees of ordained ministry. The shared call to character stands within different accounts of church order.

The marriage phrase also needs careful application. The BSB footnote offers faithful to his wife. Wesley’s note on verse 2 reads it as excluding unfaithful marriage practices, rather than requiring every overseer to marry or banning every second marriage. Catholic practice likewise does not require marriage: Catechism 1579–1580 describes the Latin Church’s normal celibacy rule and the different Eastern practice of ordaining married men. These examples do not settle every church’s rules about divorce, remarriage or selection.
passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 20:17, 28–32 connects the elders’ oversight with care for the church God obtained, protection from harmful teaching and the word of grace that builds His people and gives an inheritance. The qualifications here serve that larger care for a people belonging to Him.

1 Peter 5:1–4 places the elders’ service under Christ the Chief Shepherd, with His appearing ahead. Leaders are to be willing examples, rather than ruling for greed or control. Their work prepares and cares for His people in light of that future.
passages.current_position_html: In Who Shepherds the Church?, we emphasize that rejecting a titled hierarchy does not mean rejecting qualified teaching. Those caring for the church must be able to explain Scripture and correct teaching that departs from it. Shared leadership needs people equipped to keep the community’s study anchored in the text.

passages.title: 1 Timothy 3:2
passages.section_title: Why do character and the ability to teach belong together?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 2 An overseer, then, must be above reproach, the husband of but one wife, temperate, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach,
paragraphs: 2 An overseer, then, must be above reproach, the husband of but one wife, temperate, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach,

passages.context_html:
This verse begins the detailed qualifications for an overseer. Paul places the ability to teach alongside a life marked by faithfulness, self-control, respectability and hospitality.

Above reproach is a character requirement, not merely a title given to someone who wants the role. The following verses extend the picture to gentleness, freedom from greed, household care, maturity and reputation.

The word translated able to teach is didaktikos (dee-dak-tee-KOSS). Thayer’s lexicon describes aptitude and skill in teaching. Paul’s concern includes a real ability to help the community understand, alongside a life consistent with that instruction.

The Catholic Catechism, paragraph 1554, describes bishops, priests and deacons as three degrees of ordained ministry. The shared call to character stands within different accounts of church order.

passages.title: 1 Timothy 3:8-13
passages.section_title: What makes a person ready for trusted service?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 Deacons likewise must be dignified, not double-tongued or given to much wine or greedy for money. 9 They must hold to the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience. 10 Additionally, they must first be tested. Then, if they are above reproach, let them serve as deacons. 11 In the same way, the women must be dignified, not slanderers, but temperate and faithful in all things. 12 A deacon must be the husband of but one wife, a good manager of his children and of his own household. 13 For those who have served well as deacons acquire for themselves a high standing and great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus.
paragraphs: 8 Deacons likewise must be dignified, not double-tongued or given to much wine or greedy for money. 9 They must hold to the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience. 10 Additionally, they must first be tested. Then, if they are above reproach, let them serve as deacons.

11 In the same way, the women must be dignified, not slanderers, but temperate and faithful in all things. 12 A deacon must be the husband of but one wife, a good manager of his children and of his own household. 13 For those who have served well as deacons acquire for themselves a high standing and great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus.

passages.context_html:
Paul turns from overseers to deacons. The Greek term is diakonos (dee-AH-koh-noss). Thayer’s lexicon includes servant or minister and recognizes its use for an appointed role of service in the church.

The qualifications concern a trustworthy life: dignity, honest speech, freedom from dependence on wine and greed, faith held with a clear conscience. Those serving are to be tested first.

Verse 11 gives qualifications for women, with their wives as the BSB footnote alternative. Paul then mentions marriage and household care and commends those who serve well for gaining standing and confidence in the faith.

The paragraph does not describe service as a lesser spiritual concern. Faith, conscience and conduct matter to this work, and faithful service receives explicit recognition.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand these as qualifications for trusted service. One difference concerns the women in verse 11. The Greek word can mean woman or wife, so its reference must be considered in context.

Calvin’s comment on verse 11 reads the reference as the wives of deacons and bishops. The USCCB notes prefer women serving in the role while acknowledging the wives reading. This is a difference in interpretation of the ancient passage. Catholic teaching on ordination is a separate point: the Catechism, paragraph 1577, reserves sacred ordination to baptized men.

The standing gained in verse 13 also receives different explanations. Wesley’s note understands a step toward a higher office. Calvin’s comment on verse 13 instead emphasizes the honor of faithful service itself. Thayer’s entry for standing describes dignity and wholesome influence; the word alone does not promise a promotion.
passages.current_position_html: In Who Shepherds the Church?, we understand the deacon’s role as recognized practical service, distinct in function from the work of elders. We do not treat it as a lower rung on a ladder to eldership. Its value lies in the faithful service it provides to the body.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Mark 10:42–45 connects greatness among Jesus’ followers with serving others, grounded in the Son of Man’s own service and self-giving. It supplies a wider setting for the honor attached to faithful service here.

1 Corinthians 12:4–7 places different gifts and forms of service under the same Lord and the Spirit’s work for the common good. Trusted service belongs within God’s care for the whole body, rather than a competition for importance.

passages.title: 1 Timothy 3:14-16
passages.section_title: What holds the household of God together?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 Although I hope to come to you soon, I am writing you these things 15 in case I am delayed, so that you will know how each one must conduct himself in God’s household, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth. 16 By common confession, the mystery of godliness is great: He appeared in the flesh, was vindicated by the Spirit, was seen by angels, was proclaimed among the nations, was believed in throughout the world, was taken up in glory.
paragraphs: 14 Although I hope to come to you soon, I am writing you these things 15 in case I am delayed, so that you will know how each one must conduct himself in God’s household, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth.

16 By common confession, the mystery of godliness is great: He appeared in the flesh, was vindicated by the Spirit, was seen by angels, was proclaimed among the nations, was believed in throughout the world, was taken up in glory.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul explains why he is writing: he hopes to come soon, but Timothy needs these instructions if his visit is delayed. They concern conduct in God’s household, the church of the living God.

Calling the church the pillar and foundation of the truth describes a serious responsibility. The instructions about leaders, service and conduct belong to a community entrusted with the truth.

Paul then centers the confession on Christ: His appearing in flesh, vindication by the Spirit, being seen by angels, proclamation among the nations, belief throughout the world and being taken up in glory. The church’s life is bound to the Lord it confesses.

The BSB footnote records God appeared as a textual alternative to its main He appeared. The main passage clearly describes Christ’s appearing and glory. Identifying the variant does not require replacing the verified quotation.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read the closing confession as a summary of Christ’s person and work. They differ in how they describe the church’s authority in guarding the truth.

The Catholic Catechism, paragraphs 2032–2035, uses this pillar language in explaining the church’s teaching responsibility. It affirms the pope and bishops’ teaching authority and God’s protection from error in the church’s definitive teaching of faith and morals.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, 25.3 and 31.2–3, likewise gives the church a real teaching responsibility, but says that councils can err and their decisions must agree with God’s word. The difference concerns the authority of the church’s teaching, alongside the shared responsibility to proclaim and preserve the truth about Christ.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 1:9–10 describes God’s purpose of bringing all things in heaven and on earth together in Christ. The confession here places His earthly appearing, worldwide proclamation and heavenly glory within one connected account.

Philippians 2:6–11 likewise joins Christ’s coming in human likeness and obedient death with His exaltation and the confession of His lordship to the Father’s glory. The church carries a message centered on the One through whom God accomplishes His purpose.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Timothy 4:1-5
passages.section_title: Why does Paul defend marriage and God’s good creation?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now the Spirit expressly states that in later times some will abandon the faith to follow deceitful spirits and the teachings of demons, 2 influenced by the hypocrisy of liars, whose consciences are seared with a hot iron. 3 They will prohibit marriage and require abstinence from certain foods that God has created to be received with thanksgiving by those who believe and know the truth. 4 For every creation of God is good, and nothing that is received with thanksgiving should be rejected, 5 because it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer.
paragraphs: 1 Now the Spirit expressly states that in later times some will abandon the faith to follow deceitful spirits and the teachings of demons, 2 influenced by the hypocrisy of liars, whose consciences are seared with a hot iron. 3 They will prohibit marriage and require abstinence from certain foods that God has created to be received with thanksgiving by those who believe and know the truth.
4 For every creation of God is good, and nothing that is received with thanksgiving should be rejected, 5 because it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After describing the church’s confession of Christ, Paul warns that some will abandon the faith in later times, following deceitful spirits and demonic teachings. The influence works through people who speak falsely and whose consciences are seared.

The teaching named here prohibits marriage and requires abstaining from foods God created to be received with thanks. Paul answers by affirming the goodness of God’s creation and its thankful reception.

The word behind abandon is aphistemi (ah-FISS-tay-mee). Thayer’s lexicon includes departure and falling away, explicitly citing this verse. The warning is serious. How it relates to a person’s earlier profession or possession of saving faith is part of the wider discussion of perseverance.

God’s word and prayer frame the reception of His gifts. Paul’s answer to the false teaching is grateful dependence on the Creator, rather than a claim that His gifts are inherently unclean or incompatible with faithful life.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly see a warning against teachings that displace the truth and reject God’s good gifts. Their wider accounts of falling away differ: the Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 17, affirms the final perseverance of true believers; Catholic Catechism 162 and Methodist article XII allow a real loss of faith or departure from grace.

Applications to celibacy and religious food rules also differ. Calvin’s comment on verse 3 applies the warning to compulsory religious restrictions on marriage and food. The Reformed Westminster Confession, 22.7, rejects monastic vows of lifelong celibacy.

The Catholic Catechism, 1618–1620, affirms both marriage and voluntary celibacy for God’s kingdom as good gifts from the Lord. It also commends penitential fasting in paragraph 1438. On that account, these practices express devotion rather than a judgment that creation is evil. The dispute concerns which restrictions fall under Paul’s warning, not whether God’s creation is good.

On verse 5, Wesley’s note understands God’s word as His creating and giving food, while the USCCB note understands the phrase as invoking God’s name in blessing. Both keep prayer and grateful reception in view, with different explanations of the phrase.
passages.god_plan_html:
Genesis 1:26–31 places humanity and its food within God’s good creation. Genesis 2:18–25 similarly presents the union of man and woman as His provision. The warning here protects a thankful response to the Creator’s gifts.

2 Thessalonians 2:1–12 supplies a broader parallel in its warning about rebellion and deception. It also names Christ’s victory at His coming. God’s purpose does not end with false teaching taking hold; the returning Lord brings opposition to its end.

passages.title: 1 Timothy 4:6-10
passages.section_title: What kind of training has lasting value?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 By pointing out these things to the brothers, you will be a good servant of Christ Jesus, nourished by the words of faith and sound instruction that you have followed. 7 But reject irreverent, silly myths. Instead, train yourself for godliness. 8 For physical exercise is of limited value, but godliness is valuable in every way, holding promise for the present life and for the one to come. 9 This is a trustworthy saying, worthy of full acceptance. 10 To this end we labor and strive, because we have set our hope on the living God, who is the Savior of everyone, and especially of those who believe.
paragraphs: 6 By pointing out these things to the brothers, you will be a good servant of Christ Jesus, nourished by the words of faith and sound instruction that you have followed. 7 But reject irreverent, silly myths. Instead, train yourself for godliness. 8 For physical exercise is of limited value, but godliness is valuable in every way, holding promise for the present life and for the one to come.

9 This is a trustworthy saying, worthy of full acceptance. 10 To this end we labor and strive, because we have set our hope on the living God, who is the Savior of everyone, and especially of those who believe.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Timothy is to point these matters out to the believers and be nourished by the words of faith and sound instruction. Paul contrasts that nourishment with irreverent, silly myths.

He calls Timothy to train for godliness. The Greek verb is gymnazo (goom-NAH-zoh). Thayer’s lexicon includes vigorous exercise of body or mind and specifically applies it here to earnest pursuit of a godly life. The training picture gives weight to steady practice.

Paul gives physical exercise a limited value, then describes godliness as carrying promise for both present life and the life to come. His comparison directs Timothy’s priorities toward what lasts.

The work is sustained by hope in the living God, named as Savior of everyone and especially of believers. The paragraph joins real effort with dependence on Him. It prepares the following instructions about Timothy’s teaching, example and perseverance.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly read these verses as a call to sustained growth in devotion to God, with a hope that reaches beyond this life. Wesley’s notes on verses 7–10 emphasize earnest training and the promised life that sustains the effort.

On Savior of everyone, Calvin’s comment on verse 10 reads God’s preserving kindness toward all people as a reason to trust His particular care for believers. Wesley also includes God’s preservation of people in this life, while emphasizing His desire to save all eternally and the salvation received by believers. These readings distinguish God’s care for humanity and the particular relation of those who believe, rather than treating the sentence as a declaration that every person is already finally saved.
passages.god_plan_html:
Titus 2:11–14 connects saving grace with instruction in a godly present life while believers await Christ’s glory. Training serves His purpose of a people redeemed for Himself and ready for good works.

Philippians 3:20–21 places future bodily transformation in the hands of the returning Savior. The lasting hope is grounded in Him, with present faithfulness directed toward the life He will bring to completion.

passages.title: 1 Timothy 4:11-16
passages.section_title: How should Timothy’s life support what he teaches?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 Command and teach these things. 12 Let no one despise your youth, but set an example for the believers in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity. 13 Until I come, devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, and to teaching. 14 Do not neglect the gift that is in you, which was given you through the prophecy spoken over you at the laying on of the hands of the elders. 15 Be diligent in these matters and absorbed in them, so that your progress will be evident to all. 16 Pay close attention to your life and to your teaching. Persevere in these things, for by so doing you will save both yourself and those who hear you.
paragraphs: 11 Command and teach these things. 12 Let no one despise your youth, but set an example for the believers in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity. 13 Until I come, devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, and to teaching.

14 Do not neglect the gift that is in you, which was given you through the prophecy spoken over you at the laying on of the hands of the elders. 15 Be diligent in these matters and absorbed in them, so that your progress will be evident to all. 16 Pay close attention to your life and to your teaching. Persevere in these things, for by so doing you will save both yourself and those who hear you.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul tells Timothy to command and teach these things. His youth is to be answered through an example in speech, conduct, love, faith and purity. The way he lives must support the instruction he gives.

His work includes public reading of Scripture, exhortation and teaching. He is also to use the gift connected with the prophecy over him and the laying on of the elders’ hands.

Paul calls for diligence and visible progress. Timothy must attend both to his life and his teaching and persevere. The closing statement gives this work its weight: his faithful ministry concerns both himself and the people hearing him.

The paragraph combines dependence on God’s gift with careful practice. God’s gift and the elders’ recognition lead into ongoing service and a life that reflects the message.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand this as a call for a teacher’s conduct, use of gifts and perseverance to match the message. Calvin’s comment on verse 16 understands the saving language as God using faithful gospel ministry to bring people to Christ. He expressly identifies God as the source of salvation, with human ministers serving as His instruments.

Churches describe the laying on of hands in different ways. The Catholic Catechism, paragraph 1556, describes the Spirit’s gift being passed on through the laying on of hands in ordained succession. The Baptist 1689 Confession, 26.9, describes the church setting apart a person already fitted and gifted by the Spirit. These are the traditions’ own accounts of the practice, rather than an assumption that everyone describes Timothy’s gift and recognition identically.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 10:13–17 connects people calling on the Lord with hearing the message through those sent to preach it. Faithful teaching serves God’s saving mission by making Christ known.

Ephesians 4:11–16 places teachers and other gifts within the growth of the whole body toward maturity in Christ. Timothy’s attention to both life and teaching serves that larger purpose: people equipped to live and grow together in Him.

passages.title: 1 Timothy 5:1-2
passages.section_title: What does correction look like within God’s family?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Do not rebuke an older man, but appeal to him as to a father. Treat younger men as brothers, 2 older women as mothers, and younger women as sisters, with absolute purity.
paragraphs: 1 Do not rebuke an older man, but appeal to him as to a father. Treat younger men as brothers, 2 older women as mothers, and younger women as sisters, with absolute purity.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul has urged Timothy to watch his life and teaching. He now turns to the way Timothy should address different people in the community.

An older man is to be approached as a father, younger men as brothers, older women as mothers and younger women as sisters, with purity. The family language gives Timothy a pattern of respect and care.

The reference to older men here is part of a contrast between age groups. Later in the chapter Paul specifically discusses the elders who lead and teach. The call to respectful appeal does not remove the need for the correction and accountability he goes on to describe.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read these verses as instruction in respectful, family-like treatment of believers. Wesley’s note on verse 1 relates the tone of correction to Timothy’s youth. The USCCB notes likewise place the advice within the community’s life and care. The instruction changes how Timothy addresses people, rather than telling him to ignore conduct that needs attention.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Mark 3:31–35, Jesus describes those who do God’s will as His brother, sister and mother. This supplies a close parallel to the family relationships Paul names within the believing community.

Ephesians 2:19–22 describes those brought near through Christ as God’s household and a dwelling for His Spirit. Respectful care belongs within the life of that new family.

passages.title: 1 Timothy 5:3-8
passages.section_title: Who should care for widows who need help?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 3 Honor the widows who are truly widows. 4 But if a widow has children or grandchildren, they must first learn to show godliness to their own family and repay their parents, for this is pleasing in the sight of God. 5 The widow who is truly in need and left all alone puts her hope in God and continues night and day in her petitions and prayers. 6 But she who lives for pleasure is dead even while she is still alive. 7 Give these instructions to the believers, so that they will be above reproach. 8 If anyone does not provide for his own, and especially his own household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.
paragraphs: 3 Honor the widows who are truly widows. 4 But if a widow has children or grandchildren, they must first learn to show godliness to their own family and repay their parents, for this is pleasing in the sight of God. 5 The widow who is truly in need and left all alone puts her hope in God and continues night and day in her petitions and prayers.

6 But she who lives for pleasure is dead even while she is still alive. 7 Give these instructions to the believers, so that they will be above reproach. 8 If anyone does not provide for his own, and especially his own household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul begins his instructions about widows with honor for those truly in need. Where children or grandchildren are present, they are to learn godliness toward their own family and repay the care their parents gave them.

The word for showing godliness is eusebeo (yoo-seh-BEH-oh). Thayer’s lexicon includes acting piously or reverently, with this verse applying it to one’s household. Faithfulness to God takes a practical form in care for family.

The widow left alone is described as hoping in God and continuing in prayer. Paul contrasts that life with living for pleasure, then instructs the community so it may be above reproach.

Verse 8 gives the family duty strong emphasis: neglect of one’s own household contradicts the faith professed. The paragraph brings family responsibility and the church’s care for those left without help into the same discussion.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as assigning family members a real responsibility to care for dependent relatives, while the community supports those left alone. Wesley’s notes on verses 3–8 emphasize provision and repayment of parents’ earlier care. The USCCB notes likewise distinguish the family’s responsibility from the community’s care for a widow without that support. The warning concerns a failure of care, not the claim that religious activity can substitute for it.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Mark 7:9–13, Jesus challenges a use of religious dedication that leaves parents without the help they should receive. Honoring God includes honoring the family responsibilities He has given.

James 1:26–27 likewise connects devotion before God with care for widows and orphans in distress. The wider biblical purpose is a people whose faith shows His care through what they do for others.
passages.current_position_html: In Worship as the Early Church Knew It, we understand this as godly devotion expressed through everyday relationships: caring for aging parents and grandparents. Devotion to God includes the practical care we give at home. This passage gives that care a clear place in a faithful life.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

passages.title: 1 Timothy 5:4
passages.section_title: How does caring for parents show devotion to God?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 4 But if a widow has children or grandchildren, they must first learn to show godliness to their own family and repay their parents, for this is pleasing in the sight of God.
paragraphs: 4 But if a widow has children or grandchildren, they must first learn to show godliness to their own family and repay their parents, for this is pleasing in the sight of God.

passages.context_html:
This instruction belongs to Paul’s discussion of support for widows. Before the church carries the need, children and grandchildren are to recognize their responsibility toward their own family.

The word translated show godliness is eusebeo (yoo-seh-BEH-oh). Thayer’s lexicon includes pious or reverent conduct and specifically applies it here to the household. Paul brings devotion into the relationship between generations.

Repaying parents recognizes the care already received from them. Paul calls this pleasing in God’s sight. The following verses retain the community’s responsibility toward the widow left alone, so family duty and church care belong together.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly understand this verse as making practical family care part of a godly life. Wesley’s note on verse 4 points to the parents’ earlier care and expense. The USCCB notes likewise place the first responsibility within the family circle. The act of care, rather than a particular religious ceremony, is the instruction here.
passages.current_position_html: In Worship as the Early Church Knew It, we understand this as godly devotion expressed through everyday relationships: caring for aging parents and grandparents. Devotion to God includes the practical care we give at home. This passage gives that care a clear place in a faithful life.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
In Mark 7:9–13, Jesus challenges a use of religious dedication that leaves parents without the help they should receive. Honoring God includes honoring the family responsibilities He has given.

James 1:26–27 likewise connects devotion before God with care for widows and orphans in distress. The wider biblical purpose is a people whose faith shows His care through what they do for others.

passages.title: 1 Timothy 5:9-16
passages.section_title: What does Paul ask of widows enrolled for support?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 A widow should be enrolled if she is at least sixty years old, faithful to her husband, 10 and well known for good deeds such as bringing up children, entertaining strangers, washing the feet of the saints, imparting relief to the afflicted, and devoting herself to every good work. 11 But refuse to enroll younger widows. For when their passions draw them away from Christ, they will want to marry, 12 and thus will incur judgment because they are setting aside their first faith. 13 At the same time they will also learn to be idle, going from house to house and being not only idle, but also gossips and busybodies, discussing things they should not mention. 14 So I advise the younger widows to marry, have children, and manage their households, denying the adversary occasion for slander. 15 For some have already turned aside to follow Satan. 16 If any believing woman has dependent widows, she must assist them and not allow the church to be burdened, so that it can help the widows who are truly in need.
paragraphs: 9 A widow should be enrolled if she is at least sixty years old, faithful to her husband, 10 and well known for good deeds such as bringing up children, entertaining strangers, washing the feet of the saints, imparting relief to the afflicted, and devoting herself to every good work.

11 But refuse to enroll younger widows. For when their passions draw them away from Christ, they will want to marry, 12 and thus will incur judgment because they are setting aside their first faith. 13 At the same time they will also learn to be idle, going from house to house and being not only idle, but also gossips and busybodies, discussing things they should not mention.

14 So I advise the younger widows to marry, have children, and manage their households, denying the adversary occasion for slander. 15 For some have already turned aside to follow Satan. 16 If any believing woman has dependent widows, she must assist them and not allow the church to be burdened, so that it can help the widows who are truly in need.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul moves from the community’s care for widows to enrollment on a list. He gives an age threshold of sixty and describes a woman known for marital faithfulness, hospitality, help for those in distress and other good works.

He cautions against enrolling younger widows, describing a conflict between the commitment involved and the desire to marry. The warning also addresses idleness, gossip and interference in matters that do not concern them.

Paul advises the younger widows under discussion to marry, raise children and manage their households. He says some have already turned aside, then returns to the family responsibility to support dependent widows so the church can help those truly in need.

The paragraph connects the use of the community’s support with faithful, active life. It does not give a complete description of the list’s organization or the wording of the commitment associated with it.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Several commentators understand enrollment as organized service alongside support. Wesley’s note on verse 9 calls these women deaconesses serving others. Calvin’s comments on verses 9–10 describe widows supported by the church and engaged in caring for the poor and sick. These are interpretations of the list, rather than a complete surviving rulebook for it.

The qualifications receive different applications. Wesley allows successive lawful marriages in his reading of the wife-of-one-husband phrase. The USCCB note instead understands it as married only once. The BSB main text renders the requirement faithful to her husband.

First faith in verse 12 is also read differently. Thayer’s entry for faith lists the verse under pledged faith or faithfulness. Calvin’s comment on verse 12 expressly rejects limiting it to a promise of remaining unmarried and reads it as departure from Christian faith. Wesley describes abandoning trust in God and the earlier commitment to dedicated service. The precise nature of the warning should not be assumed from one reading alone.
passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 9:36–42 gives a concrete parallel in Tabitha’s acts of charity and the widows who show the clothing she made. The account joins practical care within the believing community with a work of God that leads others to faith. It does not identify Tabitha as a member of this later enrollment list.

Galatians 6:9–10 places continuing good works within the hope of a harvest and calls for good toward all, especially the household of faith. The ordered care described here belongs within that wider life of doing good together.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.
