passages.title: 1 Timothy 5:17-25
passages.section_title: How should leaders be honored and held accountable?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 Elders who lead effectively are worthy of double honor, especially those who work hard at preaching and teaching. 18 For the Scripture says, “Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain,” and, “The worker is worthy of his wages.” 19 Do not entertain an accusation against an elder, except on the testimony of two or three witnesses. 20 But those who persist in sin should be rebuked in front of everyone, so that the others will stand in fear of sin. 21 I solemnly charge you before God and Christ Jesus and the elect angels to maintain these principles without bias, and to do nothing out of partiality. 22 Do not be too quick in the laying on of hands and thereby share in the sins of others. Keep yourself pure. 23 Stop drinking only water and use a little wine instead, because of your stomach and your frequent ailments. 24 The sins of some men are obvious, going ahead of them to judgment; but the sins of others do not surface until later. 25 In the same way, good deeds are obvious, and even the ones that are inconspicuous cannot remain hidden.
paragraphs: 17 Elders who lead effectively are worthy of double honor, especially those who work hard at preaching and teaching. 18 For the Scripture says, “Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain,” and, “The worker is worthy of his wages.”

19 Do not entertain an accusation against an elder, except on the testimony of two or three witnesses. 20 But those who persist in sin should be rebuked in front of everyone, so that the others will stand in fear of sin. 21 I solemnly charge you before God and Christ Jesus and the elect angels to maintain these principles without bias, and to do nothing out of partiality. 22 Do not be too quick in the laying on of hands and thereby share in the sins of others. Keep yourself pure.

23 Stop drinking only water and use a little wine instead, because of your stomach and your frequent ailments. 24 The sins of some men are obvious, going ahead of them to judgment; but the sins of others do not surface until later. 25 In the same way, good deeds are obvious, and even the ones that are inconspicuous cannot remain hidden.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul calls for honor toward elders who lead effectively, especially those laboring in preaching and teaching. He supports that instruction with Scripture about the working ox and the worker’s wages, bringing material support into the discussion.

Honor is joined to accountability. Accusations require witness-supported grounds, and those persisting in sin are to be corrected publicly. Timothy receives a solemn charge to act without bias or favoritism.

The warning against laying on hands too quickly fits the concern for careful judgment and shared responsibility. The closing verses explain why patience matters: some sins are obvious, others appear later, and good deeds also come to light.

Paul also briefly gives personal advice about Timothy’s stomach and frequent ailments, telling him to use a little wine. The larger instruction remains careful care for the community, its servants and the truth they teach.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the honor to include practical support for faithful leaders, alongside fair correction. Wesley’s note on verse 17 speaks of more generous provision. Calvin’s comments likewise include support and discuss how the comparison with honor for widows bears on the phrase. Neither the office’s name nor a claim to it replaces faithful work.

The laying on of hands is commonly read as appointment to ministry. Wesley’s note on verse 22 stresses prior testing; the USCCB notes also record the alternative reading of reconciliation after public sin. Both readings connect the warning with responsibility and careful judgment. The letter keeps honor, correction and impartiality together.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Corinthians 9:7–14 explicitly applies the working-ox instruction to support for gospel workers. Provision for ministry serves the sharing of spiritual good with the community.

1 Corinthians 4:1–5 describes servants accountable to the Lord, who brings hidden things and motives to light. That future judgment gives weight to present faithfulness and to the refusal of favoritism. Human judgment must be careful in view of the Lord who knows fully.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Timothy 6:1-2
passages.section_title: How should believers live under the yoke of slavery?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 All who are under the yoke of slavery should regard their masters as fully worthy of honor, so that God’s name and our teaching will not be discredited. 2 Those who have believing masters should not show disrespect because they are brothers, but should serve them all the more, since those receiving their good service are beloved believers. Teach and encourage these principles.
paragraphs: 1 All who are under the yoke of slavery should regard their masters as fully worthy of honor, so that God’s name and our teaching will not be discredited. 2 Those who have believing masters should not show disrespect because they are brothers, but should serve them all the more, since those receiving their good service are beloved believers. Teach and encourage these principles.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After speaking about family care and church leaders, Paul addresses people living in slavery. Their conduct is to honor God’s name and the teaching they have received. If their master also believes, their shared faith is a reason for devoted service rather than disrespect.

These are enslaved people, with a master’s authority over their lives. The passage does not say how each person became enslaved. Roman slavery cannot simply be equated with an ordinary job or a loan someone freely chose: the Roman jurist Gaius, Institutes 1.82, records that children could be born into slavery through their mother’s status.

Paul calls believing masters brothers, even while addressing a relationship of unequal power. The reason he gives for the slaves’ conduct is the reputation of God’s name and teaching. He does not say that their social position measures their worth before God.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Calvin and Wesley read the instructions as a call to faithful conduct within the slaves’ existing circumstances. Both recognize that sharing faith with a master establishes a real spiritual kinship, while Paul still asks the enslaved believer to serve faithfully. The immediate concern is how God’s people live and bear witness in that situation.
passages.god_plan_html:
Paul’s appeal concerning Onesimus gives another view of what this shared family means. In Philemon 1:15–17, he asks Philemon to welcome Onesimus as a beloved brother and receive him as he would receive Paul. This is a related passage, rather than a claim that both letters describe the same household.

Galatians 3:26–29 places slave and free together among God’s children and heirs through Christ. That belonging gives the instructions their wider setting: social power does not determine a person’s place in God’s family.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Timothy 6:3-10
passages.section_title: What is the difference between true gain and chasing wealth?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 3 If anyone teaches another doctrine and disagrees with the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and with godly teaching, 4 he is conceited and understands nothing. Instead, he has an unhealthy interest in controversies and disputes about words, out of which come envy, strife, abusive talk, evil suspicions, 5 and constant friction between men of depraved mind who are devoid of the truth. These men regard godliness as a means of gain. 6 Of course, godliness with contentment is great gain. 7 For we brought nothing into the world, so we cannot carry anything out of it. 8 But if we have food and clothing, we will be content with these. 9 Those who want to be rich, however, fall into temptation and become ensnared by many foolish and harmful desires that plunge them into ruin and destruction. 10 For the love of money is the root of all kinds of evil. By craving it, some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows.
paragraphs: 3 If anyone teaches another doctrine and disagrees with the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and with godly teaching, 4 he is conceited and understands nothing. Instead, he has an unhealthy interest in controversies and disputes about words, out of which come envy, strife, abusive talk, evil suspicions, 5 and constant friction between men of depraved mind who are devoid of the truth. These men regard godliness as a means of gain.

6 Of course, godliness with contentment is great gain. 7 For we brought nothing into the world, so we cannot carry anything out of it. 8 But if we have food and clothing, we will be content with these.

9 Those who want to be rich, however, fall into temptation and become ensnared by many foolish and harmful desires that plunge them into ruin and destruction. 10 For the love of money is the root of all kinds of evil. By craving it, some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul returns to teaching that departs from Jesus and the godly life. He describes its fruit: pride, disputes, suspicion and friction. At the center is an attempt to turn religion into a source of profit.

He then turns the idea of gain around. A faithful life joined with contentment is great gain, because possessions cannot follow us beyond death. Food and clothing give him a concrete way to speak about enough, rather than an endless demand for more.

The Greek word for contentment, autarkeia (ow-TAR-kay-ah), describes being satisfied with one’s lot. The word for love of money, philargyria (fil-ar-goo-REE-ah), names greed for money. Paul’s warning concerns that craving, which can draw people from the faith into harmful choices and deep sorrow. Verse 17 will address wealthy believers directly, so possessing money and loving money are not treated as the same thing.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley both read this as a serious warning against greed and a call to contentment. Calvin explains that Paul is describing the many evils money-love produces, rather than claiming that every sin has this one cause. Neither reads godliness as a promise that believers will become wealthy.

Traditions differ over how departure from faith relates to final salvation. The Reformed Westminster Confession 17 teaches that those truly saved will be preserved, though they may fall seriously. The Methodist Articles, Article XII, allow that a person may depart from grace and also return through God’s grace. Both approaches take the warning seriously; they differ over whether a truly saved person can finally fall away.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Luke 12:15–21, Jesus tells of a man who builds up his possessions but is unprepared to meet God. The parallel is the mistake of treating stored wealth as lasting security.

Matthew 6:19–24 places treasure, the heart and serving God together. These passages widen Paul’s warning: God is forming people whose deepest hope and loyalty rest in Him, beyond what they can accumulate in this life.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Timothy 6:11-16
passages.section_title: What should Timothy pursue while he waits for Christ?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 But you, O man of God, flee from these things and pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, perseverance, and gentleness. 12 Fight the good fight of the faith. Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called when you made the good confession before many witnesses. 13 I charge you in the presence of God, who gives life to all things, and of Christ Jesus, who made the good confession in His testimony before Pontius Pilate: 14 Keep this commandment without stain or reproach until the appearance of our Lord Jesus Christ, 15 which the blessed and only Sovereign One—the King of kings and Lord of lords—will bring about in His own time. 16 He alone is immortal and dwells in unapproachable light. No one has ever seen Him, nor can anyone see Him. To Him be honor and eternal dominion! Amen.
paragraphs: 11 But you, O man of God, flee from these things and pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, perseverance, and gentleness. 12 Fight the good fight of the faith. Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called when you made the good confession before many witnesses.

13 I charge you in the presence of God, who gives life to all things, and of Christ Jesus, who made the good confession in His testimony before Pontius Pilate: 14 Keep this commandment without stain or reproach until the appearance of our Lord Jesus Christ, 15 which the blessed and only Sovereign One—the King of kings and Lord of lords—will bring about in His own time. 16 He alone is immortal and dwells in unapproachable light. No one has ever seen Him, nor can anyone see Him. To Him be honor and eternal dominion! Amen.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul turns directly to Timothy: leave greed behind and pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, perseverance and gentleness. Fighting the good fight belongs with those qualities. It is a call to faithful endurance, rather than another invitation to the quarrels just condemned.

Timothy has publicly confessed his faith. Paul now charges him before the life-giving God and Christ Jesus, who bore witness before Pilate, to keep his calling faithfully until Christ appears.

The closing praise lifts his eyes beyond present pressures to God’s rule and life. Christ’s appearing will come in God’s own time. God’s unapproachable light and unique immortality emphasize His greatness beyond human power or sight.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley suggests Timothy’s public confession may have occurred at baptism. Calvin understands it more broadly as the witness of Timothy’s ministry. The occasion is not named in the passage. Both read the charge as a call to persevere in faith and faithful service.

Major Christian readings agree that God is the source of life. Calvin and Wesley understand His unique immortality to mean that He has life in Himself; whatever life creatures have comes from Him.

Where traditions differ is what happens to a person at death. The Catholic Church teaches that the soul survives bodily death and will be reunited with the body at the resurrection (Catechism 366). The Reformed Westminster Confession 32.1–2 likewise teaches conscious life after death and a future bodily resurrection. Seventh-day Adventists instead teach that death is an unconscious state until resurrection, when God gives eternal life to His redeemed (Belief 26). These readings all depend on God giving life; they differ over the soul’s condition between death and resurrection.
passages.god_plan_html:
The passage itself connects Timothy’s endurance with Jesus’ witness before Pilate and His future appearing. In John 18:33–37, Jesus speaks of His kingship and His coming into the world to bear witness to the truth. Timothy serves under that King while he waits for the King’s return.

2 Timothy 1:8–10 places suffering for the gospel within God’s gracious purpose and Christ’s victory over death. The life Timothy is called to hold onto has its foundation in what God has done through Christ, rather than in the security wealth can offer.
passages.current_position_html: In Who is The Angel of the Lord?, we understand the unseen One in this passage as the Father. Read alongside John 1:18, this helps explain how people in the Old Testament could encounter God visibly: our study identifies those appearances with the eternal Son, who makes the Father known. This is the position developed in that study, rather than a conclusion supplied by the word light on its own.

deeper_study.title: Who is The Angel of the Lord?

passages.title: 1 Timothy 6:16
passages.section_title: Why does Paul praise God as the source of immortal life?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 He alone is immortal and dwells in unapproachable light. No one has ever seen Him, nor can anyone see Him. To Him be honor and eternal dominion! Amen.
paragraphs: 16 He alone is immortal and dwells in unapproachable light. No one has ever seen Him, nor can anyone see Him. To Him be honor and eternal dominion! Amen.

passages.context_html:
This verse closes Paul’s charge to Timothy in 6:11–16. Timothy is to persevere until Christ appears at the time God appoints. Praise for God’s unmatched rule, immortal life and unapproachable light brings the charge to its conclusion.

The verse should stay connected with that encouragement. Timothy’s life and future rest with the God whose power is greater than the pressures he faces.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Major Christian readings agree that God is the source of life. Calvin and Wesley understand His unique immortality to mean that He has life in Himself; whatever life creatures have comes from Him.

Where traditions differ is what happens to a person at death. The Catholic Church teaches that the soul survives bodily death and will be reunited with the body at the resurrection (Catechism 366). The Reformed Westminster Confession 32.1–2 likewise teaches conscious life after death and a future bodily resurrection. Seventh-day Adventists instead teach that death is an unconscious state until resurrection, when God gives eternal life to His redeemed (Belief 26). These readings all depend on God giving life; they differ over the soul’s condition between death and resurrection.
passages.current_position_html: In Who is The Angel of the Lord?, we understand the unseen One in this passage as the Father. Read alongside John 1:18, this helps explain how people in the Old Testament could encounter God visibly: our study identifies those appearances with the eternal Son, who makes the Father known. This is the position developed in that study, rather than a conclusion supplied by the word light on its own.

deeper_study.title: Who is The Angel of the Lord?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
John 1:18 connects the unseen God with the Son who makes Him known. Colossians 1:15–20 likewise describes the Son as the image of the invisible God and places creation and reconciliation through Him together.

These passages give a wider setting for knowing the God whom human sight cannot reach. God makes Himself known through His Son, and 2 Timothy 1:9–10 connects life and immortality with Christ’s appearing and the gospel.

passages.title: 1 Timothy 6:17-19
passages.section_title: How should people with wealth use what God has given?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 Instruct those who are rich in the present age not to be conceited and not to put their hope in the uncertainty of wealth, but in God, who richly provides all things for us to enjoy. 18 Instruct them to do good, to be rich in good works, and to be generous and ready to share, 19 treasuring up for themselves a firm foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of that which is truly life.
paragraphs: 17 Instruct those who are rich in the present age not to be conceited and not to put their hope in the uncertainty of wealth, but in God, who richly provides all things for us to enjoy. 18 Instruct them to do good, to be rich in good works, and to be generous and ready to share, 19 treasuring up for themselves a firm foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of that which is truly life.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul has warned against wanting to become rich. He now addresses believers who already have wealth. They are not to become proud or place their hope in something so uncertain. Their hope belongs in God, who provides generously and gives good things to enjoy.

Their resources bring an opportunity to do good. Paul asks for generosity, a readiness to share and a life rich in good works. Present wealth is to serve a future that lasts, rather than become a substitute for trusting God.

This is not an instruction to despise every gift or refuse all enjoyment. Enjoyment, humility and generosity belong together under the God who gives.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley both understand the passage as a call to replace pride and trust in wealth with trust in God and practical generosity. Both connect the future treasure with God’s gracious reward, rather than treating donations as a purchase of eternal life.

They describe that connection in different terms. Calvin emphasizes God’s acceptance and reward of service by grace, without human merit. Wesley likewise denies that giving can obtain eternal life, while warning that failure to give can accompany a loss of grace and salvation. Those are their own explanations of how the warning and promise work.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus tells His disciples in Matthew 6:19–21 to store up treasure in heaven, connecting their treasure with their hearts. Paul’s instructions share that future direction: possessions can be used now in service of what lasts.

Acts 4:32–35 shows believers sharing their resources so that people in need receive help. It is a concrete example of the generous life described here, rather than a command that every believer must use that community’s exact arrangement. God’s gifts become a means of care for others.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Timothy 6:20-21
passages.section_title: What has Timothy been entrusted to guard?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 20 O Timothy, guard what has been entrusted to you. Avoid irreverent, empty chatter and the opposing arguments of so-called “knowledge,” 21 which some have professed and thus swerved away from the faith. Grace be with you all.
paragraphs: 20 O Timothy, guard what has been entrusted to you. Avoid irreverent, empty chatter and the opposing arguments of so-called “knowledge,” 21 which some have professed and thus swerved away from the faith. Grace be with you all.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The letter ends with a personal appeal to Timothy to guard what has been entrusted to him. That charge gathers up the letter’s concern for faithful teaching and a life that agrees with it.

The Greek word paratheke (par-ah-THAY-kay) means a deposit or something placed in another’s care. Timothy is responsible for preserving what he has received, rather than replacing it with impressive claims to knowledge that lead away from the faith.

Paul ends with grace for them all. The work of guarding and teaching belongs within dependence on God’s grace, even in this firmly worded closing.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley relates the trust to the charge already given to Timothy. Calvin emphasizes the grace and gifts entrusted to him for ministry. Both read the warning as a call to preserve faithful ministry and reject empty teaching that damages the church. The charge includes a responsibility to pass on what is sound, rather than to pursue controversy for its own sake.
passages.god_plan_html:
2 Timothy 1:13–14 returns to this trust, joining sound teaching with faith and love and telling Timothy to guard it with the Holy Spirit’s help. That is a direct connection within the New Testament.

The wider purpose is the faithful passing on of the gospel. In 2 Timothy 2:1–2, Timothy is to entrust what he has heard to reliable people who can teach others. Guarding the message serves its continued life in God’s people.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Timothy 1:1-5
passages.section_title: What holds Paul and Timothy together in difficult days?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, according to the promise of life in Christ Jesus, 2 To Timothy, my beloved child: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord. 3 I thank God, whom I serve with a clear conscience as did my forefathers, as I constantly remember you night and day in my prayers. 4 Recalling your tears, I long to see you so that I may be filled with joy. 5 I am reminded of your sincere faith, which first dwelt in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice, and I am convinced is in you as well.
paragraphs: 1 Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, according to the promise of life in Christ Jesus, 2 To Timothy, my beloved child: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.

3 I thank God, whom I serve with a clear conscience as did my forefathers, as I constantly remember you night and day in my prayers. 4 Recalling your tears, I long to see you so that I may be filled with joy. 5 I am reminded of your sincere faith, which first dwelt in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice, and I am convinced is in you as well.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul opens with the promise of life in Christ Jesus and addresses Timothy as his beloved child. Later in the chapter he speaks of his chains in Rome. This greeting comes from a prisoner who still holds onto that promise of life.

He remembers Timothy in prayer, longs to see him and recalls his tears. Their relationship includes deep affection as well as shared work. Paul’s thanksgiving also reaches back through Timothy’s family: sincere faith lived in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice before him.

The reference to Paul’s forefathers connects his service with the God his ancestors worshiped. The letter introduces Timothy’s faith as something real and personal, with a family history behind it.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley understand Paul’s thanksgiving as an expression of enduring care for Timothy and gratitude for sincere faith. The family references show faith lived across generations; they do not make family ancestry a substitute for Timothy’s own faith.

They differ over how far Paul’s clear conscience reaches back. Wesley includes Paul’s conscientious worship before and after conversion. Calvin limits the pure conscience here to his service after the gospel changed him, while affirming that he worships the same God as his ancestors. Both recognize the continuity with Israel’s God.
passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 16:1–3 introduces Timothy as a disciple with a believing Jewish mother, whom Paul takes along in the work. The letter now shows that shared mission through the affection of a spiritual father for his child.

Later, 2 Timothy 3:14–15 connects Timothy’s childhood knowledge of Scripture with the wisdom leading to salvation through faith in Christ. The larger purpose of teaching faith in the home is coming to know Christ, not merely keeping a family custom.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Timothy 1:6-7
passages.section_title: How is Timothy to use the gift God has given him?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 For this reason I remind you to fan into flame the gift of God, which is in you through the laying on of my hands. 7 For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control.
paragraphs: 6 For this reason I remind you to fan into flame the gift of God, which is in you through the laying on of my hands. 7 For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Because Paul recognizes Timothy’s sincere faith, he urges him to put God’s gift fully to use. He recalls the laying on of his hands and uses the picture of a fire stirred into flame. Thayer’s entry confirms the sense of kindling or rekindling. The picture calls for active care; it does not tell us exactly how far Timothy’s zeal had declined.

Power belongs with love and self-control. Courage in ministry is not permission to become harsh or reckless. The word translated self-control includes moderation and disciplined judgment (Thayer). Verse 8 will show what this strength is for: bearing witness without shame and enduring suffering for the gospel.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley read the fire image as a call to exercise God’s gifts rather than let them lie unused. Both connect courage with love and a disciplined life. Calvin particularly emphasizes God’s Spirit equipping ministers for their calling; Wesley applies the encouragement to Christians more broadly.

Traditions explain the laying on of hands differently. The Catholic Church describes apostolic laying on of hands as transmitting the Spirit’s gift in ordination (Catechism 1556). The Baptist 1689 Confession 26.9 describes setting apart a minister already fitted and gifted by the Spirit. Both recognize a calling from God and a public act of setting someone apart.
passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 4:23–31 gives a related picture of believers facing threats. They turn to God, ask for boldness and speak His word through the Holy Spirit’s power. Their courage serves the spread of the message.

In 1 Corinthians 12:4–7, the Spirit’s varied gifts are given for the common good. Timothy’s gift belongs within that purpose: God equips people so that others can be helped and the church built up.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Timothy 1:8-12
passages.section_title: Why can Paul face suffering without shame?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 So do not be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, or of me, His prisoner. Instead, join me in suffering for the gospel by the power of God. 9 He has saved us and called us to a holy calling, not because of our works, but by His own purpose and by the grace He granted us in Christ Jesus before time began. 10 And now He has revealed this grace through the appearing of our Savior, Christ Jesus, who has abolished death and illuminated the way to life and immortality through the gospel, 11 to which I was appointed as a preacher, an apostle, and a teacher. 12 For this reason, even though I suffer as I do, I am not ashamed; for I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that He is able to guard what I have entrusted to Him for that day.
paragraphs: 8 So do not be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, or of me, His prisoner. Instead, join me in suffering for the gospel by the power of God. 9 He has saved us and called us to a holy calling, not because of our works, but by His own purpose and by the grace He granted us in Christ Jesus before time began. 10 And now He has revealed this grace through the appearing of our Savior, Christ Jesus, who has abolished death and illuminated the way to life and immortality through the gospel,

11 to which I was appointed as a preacher, an apostle, and a teacher. 12 For this reason, even though I suffer as I do, I am not ashamed; for I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that He is able to guard what I have entrusted to Him for that day.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul asks Timothy not to be ashamed of the Lord’s testimony or of Paul as a prisoner. Instead, he is to share in suffering for the gospel through God’s power. Paul grounds that appeal in what God has already done: saved them and called them to a holy life by grace, rather than because of their works.

That grace belongs to God’s purpose before time began and has now been revealed through Christ’s appearing. Christ has defeated death and brought life and immortality into the light through the gospel. The message Paul was appointed to preach is also the reason he suffers.

His confidence rests in the One he has believed. The BSB main text describes Paul entrusting something to God for safekeeping until that day; its footnote also records the reading of something entrusted to Paul. The object is explained differently, but the declaration centers on God’s ability to guard.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Major Christian traditions agree that God’s grace comes before any claim to have earned salvation. They differ over how His eternal purpose relates to human response. The Reformed Westminster Confession 3.5–6 teaches an election that does not depend on foreseen faith. Wesley’s notes on Ephesians 1:4–5 instead describe God’s settled purpose to adopt those whom He foreknows as believing. Both locate salvation in God’s grace and Christ, while explaining that choosing differently.

For verse 12, Wesley understands the entrusted thing as Paul’s soul, and Calvin as his eternal life. The USCCB note also records the possible reading of the faith entrusted to Paul. These readings emphasize either God keeping Paul’s life and future or God preserving the message committed to him.
passages.god_plan_html:
The passage itself gives the wider story: grace purposed before time, revealed through Christ’s coming, and announced through the gospel. Ephesians 1:3–10 similarly places God’s saving purpose in Christ before the foundation of the world and looks toward all things being brought together in Him.

1 Corinthians 15:20–26, 50–57 connects Christ’s resurrection with the final defeat of death and the resurrection of His people. Paul’s present chains do not cancel that future. The confidence he commends is grounded in Christ’s victory, rather than a promise that faithful service will avoid suffering.

passages.title: 2 Timothy 1:13-14
passages.section_title: How should Timothy guard the teaching he has received?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 Hold on to the pattern of sound teaching you have heard from me, with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus. 14 Guard the treasure entrusted to you, with the help of the Holy Spirit who dwells in us.
paragraphs: 13 Hold on to the pattern of sound teaching you have heard from me, with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus. 14 Guard the treasure entrusted to you, with the help of the Holy Spirit who dwells in us.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul moves from confidence in God’s keeping to Timothy’s responsibility to keep what he has received. Timothy is to hold onto the pattern of sound teaching he heard from Paul, with the faith and love found in Christ Jesus.

He is not left to guard it by determination alone. The Holy Spirit who dwells in them supplies the help. The teaching is a treasure to preserve and live by, rather than material to reshape for convenience or popularity.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Calvin and Wesley understand the trust here as faithful teaching to be preserved. Calvin emphasizes keeping its substance and faithful form, rather than distorting it; Wesley describes a pattern of wholesome doctrine. Both take Paul’s instruction as care for the truth received, with faith, love and God’s help.
passages.god_plan_html:
2 Timothy 2:1–2 explains how the message is to continue: Timothy is to pass it on to reliable people who can teach others. Guarding serves that future transmission; it is more than keeping something private.

Ephesians 4:11–16 describes the wider goal of teaching and speaking truth in love: a whole body growing toward maturity in Christ. Faithful teaching is entrusted to the church for that shared growth.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Timothy 1:15-18
passages.section_title: What does faithfulness look like when others turn away?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 You know that everyone in the province of Asia has deserted me, including Phygelus and Hermogenes. 16 May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, because he has often refreshed me and was unashamed of my chains. 17 Indeed, when he arrived in Rome, he searched diligently until he found me. 18 May the Lord grant Onesiphorus His mercy on that day. You know very well how much he ministered to me in Ephesus.
paragraphs: 15 You know that everyone in the province of Asia has deserted me, including Phygelus and Hermogenes.

16 May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, because he has often refreshed me and was unashamed of my chains. 17 Indeed, when he arrived in Rome, he searched diligently until he found me. 18 May the Lord grant Onesiphorus His mercy on that day. You know very well how much he ministered to me in Ephesus.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul describes desertion by people from the province of Asia and names Phygelus and Hermogenes. He then recalls Onesiphorus, who refreshed him, was unashamed of his chains and searched diligently until he found him in Rome.

The contrast gives a concrete example of the loyalty Paul has just asked Timothy to show. Paul asks mercy for Onesiphorus’s household and for Onesiphorus himself on that day. He also recalls service in Ephesus that Timothy knows well.

The passage does not tell us that Onesiphorus later deserted Paul. His help is remembered with gratitude. Nor does it explicitly state whether he was living when the letter was written.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin reads Onesiphorus as an example of generous, courageous help and Paul’s prayer as grateful dependence on God’s mercy. Wesley understands the household prayer as including Onesiphorus himself. The USCCB note instead suggests he had died, partly because Paul addresses his household here and in 4:19. That is an inference from the wording, rather than a death report in the text.

That question connects with a genuine difference over prayer for the dead. The Catholic Church teaches that such prayer can help the departed (Catechism 958). The Reformed Westminster Confession 21.4 excludes prayer for the dead. These are the traditions’ stated positions; neither tells us with certainty whether Onesiphorus had died.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Matthew 25:34–40, Jesus connects care for His brothers, including visiting them in prison, with service to Himself. Onesiphorus’s help is a concrete parallel to that kind of care, without identifying him as a character in Jesus’ description.

Hebrews 13:1–3 joins brotherly love with remembering prisoners and those who are mistreated. Faithfulness to Christ includes staying close to His people when association with them is costly.

passages.title: 2 Timothy 2:1-7
passages.section_title: How can Timothy keep serving and prepare others to teach?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 You therefore, my child, be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus. 2 And the things that you have heard me say among many witnesses, entrust these to faithful men who will be qualified to teach others as well. 3 Join me in suffering, like a good soldier of Christ Jesus. 4 A soldier refrains from entangling himself in civilian affairs, in order to please the one who enlisted him. 5 Likewise, a competitor does not receive the crown unless he competes according to the rules. 6 The hardworking farmer should be the first to partake of the crops. 7 Consider what I am saying, for the Lord will give you insight into all things.
paragraphs: 1 You therefore, my child, be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus. 2 And the things that you have heard me say among many witnesses, entrust these to faithful men who will be qualified to teach others as well.

3 Join me in suffering, like a good soldier of Christ Jesus. 4 A soldier refrains from entangling himself in civilian affairs, in order to please the one who enlisted him. 5 Likewise, a competitor does not receive the crown unless he competes according to the rules. 6 The hardworking farmer should be the first to partake of the crops. 7 Consider what I am saying, for the Lord will give you insight into all things.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul calls Timothy to draw strength from the grace found in Christ Jesus. What Timothy heard from Paul is to be entrusted to reliable people who can teach others. The work is meant to continue beyond either of them.

Three everyday pictures show the kind of commitment involved. A soldier stays focused on pleasing the one who enlisted him. An athlete competes according to the rules. A hardworking farmer is to receive a share of the crop.

The pictures join focus, faithful effort and the prospect of fruit from the work. Paul asks Timothy to consider them, while also trusting the Lord to give understanding. Reflection and dependence on God belong together.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley read these pictures as encouragement to devoted, patient service. The soldier is not to be pulled away by competing concerns; the athlete must compete faithfully; the farmer’s work comes before the harvest. The comparisons call for perseverance, rather than promising easy results.

Calvin makes a particular point that the Christian soldier’s hardship is endured patiently, rather than inflicted on others. The imagery serves Timothy’s teaching and witness; it does not turn the church’s mission into permission to use force.
passages.god_plan_html:
Passing the message from Paul to Timothy, then to reliable teachers and those they teach, gives a concrete picture of the gospel continuing through generations. Matthew 28:18–20 likewise connects making disciples with teaching them to keep Jesus’ commands.

1 Corinthians 3:5–9 places the work of planting and watering under God, who gives the growth. Timothy’s effort and the service of later teachers have that same larger purpose: God’s people growing through the message entrusted to them.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Timothy 2:8-13
passages.section_title: Why does remembering Jesus give strength to endure?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 Remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead, descended from David, as proclaimed by my gospel, 9 for which I suffer to the extent of being chained like a criminal. But the word of God cannot be chained! 10 For this reason I endure all things for the sake of the elect, so that they too may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus, with eternal glory. 11 This is a trustworthy saying: If we died with Him, we will also live with Him; 12 if we endure, we will also reign with Him; if we deny Him, He will also deny us; 13 if we are faithless, He remains faithful, for He cannot deny Himself.
paragraphs: 8 Remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead, descended from David, as proclaimed by my gospel, 9 for which I suffer to the extent of being chained like a criminal. But the word of God cannot be chained! 10 For this reason I endure all things for the sake of the elect, so that they too may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus, with eternal glory.

11 This is a trustworthy saying: If we died with Him, we will also live with Him; 12 if we endure, we will also reign with Him; if we deny Him, He will also deny us; 13 if we are faithless, He remains faithful, for He cannot deny Himself.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul brings Timothy back to the center of his message: Jesus Christ, raised from the dead and descended from David. Paul is chained for proclaiming Him, but God’s word cannot be chained. He endures so that others may receive salvation in Christ and eternal glory.

The trustworthy saying then joins dying and living with Christ, endurance and reigning, denial and being denied. Its final line declares that Christ remains faithful because He cannot deny Himself.

Both promise and warning are present. The saying gives hope in fellowship with Christ while calling Timothy to take faithfulness seriously. Christ’s character does not change with human failure.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Major Christian readings recognize both the hope of life with Christ and the seriousness of denying Him. Calvin understands denial here as a rejection with real consequences before Christ, rather than simply receiving a smaller reward. He reads Christ’s faithfulness as including faithfulness to His warning. Wesley likewise connects denial with avoiding suffering and explains verse 13 as God keeping His promises to those who believe.

Traditions differ over whether someone truly saved can finally depart from faith. The Reformed Westminster Confession 17 teaches that God preserves those He has saved. The Methodist Articles, Article XII, allow departure from grace and restoration; the Catholic Church teaches that the gift of faith can be lost (Catechism 162). These differences shape how the warning is applied, without removing the call to endure.
passages.god_plan_html:
The passage itself connects present suffering with the risen Christ, the promise associated with David’s line and future life with Him. Acts 2:29–36 likewise brings God’s promise to David together with Jesus’ resurrection and exaltation.

Romans 6:3–11 explains dying and living with Christ as the basis for a new life no longer ruled by sin. Romans 8:16–25 places suffering with Christ alongside future glory and creation’s hope. Paul’s endurance belongs within that larger story of life overcoming death.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Timothy 2:14-19
passages.section_title: How does faithful teaching differ from destructive disputes?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 Remind the believers of these things, charging them before God to avoid quarreling over words, which succeeds only in leading the listeners to ruin. 15 Make every effort to present yourself approved to God, an unashamed workman who accurately handles the word of truth. 16 But avoid irreverent, empty chatter, which will only lead to more ungodliness, 17 and the talk of such men will spread like gangrene. Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus, 18 who have deviated from the truth. They say that the resurrection has already occurred, and they undermine the faith of some. 19 Nevertheless, God’s firm foundation stands, bearing this seal: “The Lord knows those who are His,” and, “Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord must turn away from iniquity.”
paragraphs: 14 Remind the believers of these things, charging them before God to avoid quarreling over words, which succeeds only in leading the listeners to ruin. 15 Make every effort to present yourself approved to God, an unashamed workman who accurately handles the word of truth.

16 But avoid irreverent, empty chatter, which will only lead to more ungodliness, 17 and the talk of such men will spread like gangrene. Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus, 18 who have deviated from the truth. They say that the resurrection has already occurred, and they undermine the faith of some. 19 Nevertheless, God’s firm foundation stands, bearing this seal: “The Lord knows those who are His,” and, “Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord must turn away from iniquity.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul asks Timothy to remind people of the teaching just given and stop destructive disputes over words. He contrasts that conduct with the careful work of someone who seeks God’s approval and handles the message of truth faithfully.

The Greek word orthotomeo (or-thoh-toh-MEH-oh) has the picture of cutting straight. In this verse, Thayer explains it as teaching the truth correctly and directly. The point is faithful handling of the message, rather than a license to force a preferred meaning into it.

Paul gives an example of the damage false teaching causes: Hymenaeus and Philetus say the resurrection has already happened and undermine people’s faith. Against that instability, God’s foundation stands. The two sayings on its seal join God’s knowledge of His people with their responsibility to turn from wrongdoing.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley read verse 15 as a call to explain and apply the truth faithfully, with God’s approval in view. Both see a real contrast between teaching that helps people and disputes that damage them.

The exact account of the false resurrection teaching is not supplied. Wesley suggests it may have reduced resurrection to a spiritual change already experienced. The USCCB note also explains it as denying a future bodily resurrection in favor of an already realized spiritual rising. These are explanations of the error; the passage itself states its claim and harmful effect without giving a full system.

On the foundation, Calvin particularly emphasizes God preserving His chosen people despite others’ desertion. Wesley emphasizes God’s unchanging truth together with the necessity of turning from sin. Both keep the assurance and the call to holiness together.
passages.god_plan_html:
The first saying on the seal echoes Numbers 16:1–7, where a challenge to Moses and Aaron is met by God’s declaration that He will show who belongs to Him. In that same account, the people are told to move away from the rebels’ tents (16:23–27). God’s knowledge and His people’s response belong together in both settings.

This is a connection with that event, not a promise that every later dispute will end with the same judgment. 1 Corinthians 15:20–26 sets the hope threatened by the false teaching in its wider setting: Christ has risen, His people will be raised, and death will finally be defeated.
passages.current_position_html: In The Berean Standard, we understand this verse as a call to honest, daily and humble engagement with Scripture. We should examine words in their context, test what we are taught and remain willing to be corrected by the text. The goal is a faith that knows what it believes and why, rather than correctness for its own sake.

passages.title: 2 Timothy 2:15
passages.section_title: What does it mean to handle the word of truth accurately?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 Make every effort to present yourself approved to God, an unashamed workman who accurately handles the word of truth.
paragraphs: 15 Make every effort to present yourself approved to God, an unashamed workman who accurately handles the word of truth.

passages.context_html:
This instruction belongs to Paul’s warning in 2:14–19 about destructive disputes and false teaching. Timothy is to be a careful worker whose handling of the truth can stand before God.

The Greek verb orthotomeo (or-thoh-toh-MEH-oh) uses the picture of cutting straight. Thayer explains its use here as teaching the truth correctly and directly. Accuracy serves the people who hear; the surrounding verses show the damage caused when the message is distorted.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Calvin emphasizes seeking God’s approval and explaining the message in a way that builds people up. Wesley emphasizes explaining and applying the whole of Scripture faithfully to those who hear it. Their shared concern is honest teaching, rather than verbal display or careless claims.
passages.current_position_html: In The Berean Standard, we understand this verse as a call to honest, daily and humble engagement with Scripture. We should examine words in their context, test what we are taught and remain willing to be corrected by the text. The goal is a faith that knows what it believes and why, rather than correctness for its own sake.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Paul earlier tells Timothy to entrust the teaching to reliable people who can teach others (2 Timothy 2:1–2). Accurate handling serves that continuing transmission of the gospel.

Ephesians 4:11–16 gives the wider goal: people equipped to serve, protected from misleading teaching and growing together toward maturity in Christ. Careful teaching matters because it helps build that shared life.

passages.title: 2 Timothy 2:20-26
passages.section_title: What makes someone useful to the Master?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 20 A large house contains not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and clay. Some indeed are for honorable use, but others are for common use. 21 So if anyone cleanses himself of what is unfit, he will be a vessel for honor: sanctified, useful to the Master, and prepared for every good work. 22 Flee from youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace, together with those who call on the Lord out of a pure heart. 23 But reject foolish and ignorant speculation, for you know that it breeds quarreling. 24 And a servant of the Lord must not be quarrelsome, but must be kind to everyone, able to teach, and forbearing. 25 He must gently reprove those who oppose him, in the hope that God may grant them repentance leading to a knowledge of the truth. 26 Then they will come to their senses and escape the snare of the devil, who has taken them captive to his will.
paragraphs: 20 A large house contains not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and clay. Some indeed are for honorable use, but others are for common use. 21 So if anyone cleanses himself of what is unfit, he will be a vessel for honor: sanctified, useful to the Master, and prepared for every good work.

22 Flee from youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace, together with those who call on the Lord out of a pure heart. 23 But reject foolish and ignorant speculation, for you know that it breeds quarreling. 24 And a servant of the Lord must not be quarrelsome, but must be kind to everyone, able to teach, and forbearing. 25 He must gently reprove those who oppose him, in the hope that God may grant them repentance leading to a knowledge of the truth. 26 Then they will come to their senses and escape the snare of the devil, who has taken them captive to his will.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul pictures a large household with different vessels for different purposes. He urges cleansing from what is unfit so that a person can be set apart, useful to the Master and ready for good work.

The instructions that follow show what that readiness looks like: turning from youthful passions and pursuing righteousness, faith, love and peace alongside others who call on the Lord sincerely. It includes refusing foolish disputes without becoming a quarrelsome person.

Timothy must still teach and correct. He is to do so with kindness, patience and gentleness, hoping that God will grant repentance and release people from the devil’s trap. The aim of correction is their recovery into the truth.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley both connect the vessels with the church and the call to separate from wickedness. Calvin recognizes a mixture of good and bad people in the visible community; Wesley notes that a vessel intended for honorable use may be put to a bad use. The picture calls hearers to a life fit for God’s service.

Both read the final instructions as requiring patient, gentle teaching and dependence on God for repentance. Refusing a quarrel does not mean abandoning every person who disagrees. Calvin particularly stresses continuing to seek the recovery of people who now appear resistant, because God can change them.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 2:8–10 joins salvation by grace with being made in Christ for good works. That gives the wider setting for becoming useful to the Master: a life shaped by grace and prepared for service.

Galatians 6:1–2 calls for gently restoring someone caught in wrongdoing and bearing one another’s burdens. Timothy’s correction shares that purpose of recovery and care within God’s people, rather than winning a contest at someone else’s expense.

passages.title: 2 Timothy 3:1-5
passages.section_title: What makes these difficult times spiritually dangerous?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 But understand this: In the last days terrible times will come. 2 For men will be lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boastful, arrogant, abusive, disobedient to their parents, ungrateful, unholy, 3 unloving, unforgiving, slanderous, without self-control, brutal, without love of good, 4 traitorous, reckless, conceited, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, 5 having a form of godliness but denying its power. Turn away from such as these!
paragraphs: 1 But understand this: In the last days terrible times will come. 2 For men will be lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boastful, arrogant, abusive, disobedient to their parents, ungrateful, unholy, 3 unloving, unforgiving, slanderous, without self-control, brutal, without love of good, 4 traitorous, reckless, conceited, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, 5 having a form of godliness but denying its power. Turn away from such as these!

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul has just instructed Timothy to teach patiently while refusing quarrels. He now warns of terrible times marked by people’s conduct: self-centeredness, greed, pride, broken relationships, cruelty and a love of pleasure that displaces love for God.

The warning reaches into religion itself. A person can maintain the appearance of godliness while denying its power. Timothy is told to turn away from such people, rather than be drawn into their pattern of life.

The description is meant to help him recognize danger. Verse 6 immediately points to people already acting this way, so Paul is not speaking only of a remote future Timothy could never encounter.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley understand the last days as the era of the gospel and the church, rather than only a brief final interval. Both apply the warning to people who can be found within the religious community. Outward claims to godliness do not excuse a life that contradicts it.

They read the list as a reason for vigilance and faithful conduct. It does not supply a date for Christ’s return or turn every troubling event into a separate prediction to decode.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Matthew 7:15–23, Jesus warns that impressive religious claims can conceal a life that does not do His Father’s will. The fruit of a life matters when claims of belonging to Him are tested.

Romans 12:1–2 describes the positive direction for God’s people: lives offered to Him and minds renewed so they can discern what pleases Him. Paul’s warning belongs within that purpose of forming people whose worship and conduct agree.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Timothy 3:6-9
passages.section_title: How do deceptive teachers exploit people who are vulnerable?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 They are the kind who worm their way into households and captivate vulnerable women who are weighed down with sins and led astray by various passions, 7 who are always learning but never able to come to a knowledge of the truth. 8 Just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so also these men oppose the truth. They are depraved in mind and disqualified from the faith. 9 But they will not advance much further. For just like Jannes and Jambres, their folly will be plain to everyone.
paragraphs: 6 They are the kind who worm their way into households and captivate vulnerable women who are weighed down with sins and led astray by various passions, 7 who are always learning but never able to come to a knowledge of the truth.

8 Just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so also these men oppose the truth. They are depraved in mind and disqualified from the faith. 9 But they will not advance much further. For just like Jannes and Jambres, their folly will be plain to everyone.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul gives a concrete example of the danger: people gain access to households and captivate vulnerable women weighed down by sins and driven by different desires. Repeated exposure to teaching is not bringing them to a settled knowledge of the truth.

This describes the particular women being exploited, rather than declaring every woman unable to learn faithfully. The same letter has already praised the sincere faith of Lois and Eunice and acknowledged Timothy’s childhood instruction.

The opposition is compared with Jannes and Jambres resisting Moses. Paul says that the false teachers’ folly will become plain, just as theirs did. Deception may gain a hearing, but it is not given an unlimited future.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley, Calvin and the USCCB note associate Jannes and Jambres with the Egyptian magicians who opposed Moses. The Exodus account does not give the magicians these names. The comparison draws attention to resistance against God’s truth and the eventual exposure of that resistance.

Wesley and the USCCB note read the repeated learning as a failure to arrive at the truth, despite an appearance of religious interest. The concern is the hold of deception, not a condemnation of careful learning itself.
passages.god_plan_html:
The New Testament itself makes the connection with Moses. In Exodus 7:8–13, the magicians imitate the sign, but Aaron’s staff swallows theirs. In Exodus 8:16–19, they cannot reproduce what God does and acknowledge His power.

Those events belong to God’s work of freeing His people from Egypt. Paul uses the opposition to Moses as a comparison for present resistance to the truth. The parallel points to the limits of that resistance; it does not promise that every teacher’s error will be exposed on a schedule we can set.

passages.title: 2 Timothy 3:10-13
passages.section_title: What can Timothy learn from Paul’s life and suffering?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 You, however, have observed my teaching, my conduct, my purpose, my faith, my patience, my love, my perseverance, 11 my persecutions, and the sufferings that came upon me in Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra. What persecutions I endured! Yet the Lord rescued me from all of them. 12 Indeed, all who desire to live godly lives in Christ Jesus will be persecuted, 13 while evil men and imposters go from bad to worse, deceiving and being deceived.
paragraphs: 10 You, however, have observed my teaching, my conduct, my purpose, my faith, my patience, my love, my perseverance, 11 my persecutions, and the sufferings that came upon me in Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra. What persecutions I endured! Yet the Lord rescued me from all of them. 12 Indeed, all who desire to live godly lives in Christ Jesus will be persecuted, 13 while evil men and imposters go from bad to worse, deceiving and being deceived.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul sets his life alongside the pattern he has warned against. Timothy knows his teaching, conduct, purpose, faith, patience, love and perseverance. The example includes how he suffered, especially in Antioch, Iconium and Lystra.

He remembers both persecution and the Lord’s rescue. His difficult circumstances do not mean the message has failed or that God has abandoned him. Paul says godly living in Christ will meet persecution, while deceivers continue to deceive and be deceived.

Timothy is being prepared to remain faithful, rather than to judge the truth of his calling by whether life becomes comfortable.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley read the passage as preparation for opposition that comes with following Christ. Calvin stresses that suffering should not be taken as proof that God has rejected His servant. Wesley likewise treats persecution as something believers should expect as they follow Christ.

God’s rescue gives confidence in His faithfulness; it is not a promise that every believer will always escape injury or death. The letter will shortly have Paul speak of his own approaching death in 4:6–8.
passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 13:44–52 and 14:1–23 give the setting of the named persecutions. Opposition did not stop the mission: Paul and Barnabas continued proclaiming the gospel and strengthened disciples to remain in the faith. The Antioch account specifically connects the message with light reaching the Gentiles.

In John 15:18–21, Jesus prepares His disciples to face the opposition directed against their Master. Paul’s experience belongs within that shared witness to Christ, rather than an isolated story of one person’s hardship.

passages.title: 2 Timothy 3:14-17
passages.section_title: How does Scripture equip us to live faithfully?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 But as for you, continue in the things you have learned and firmly believed, since you know from whom you have learned them. 15 From infancy you have known the Holy Scriptures, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus. 16 All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness, 17 so that the man of God may be complete, fully equipped for every good work.
paragraphs: 14 But as for you, continue in the things you have learned and firmly believed, since you know from whom you have learned them. 15 From infancy you have known the Holy Scriptures, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus.

16 All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness, 17 so that the man of God may be complete, fully equipped for every good work.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After describing deception and recalling his own example, Paul tells Timothy to continue in what he has learned. Timothy has known the sacred writings from infancy; those writings lead to wisdom for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus.

Paul then describes both Scripture’s source and its use. The Greek word theopneustos (theh-oh-PNYOO-stos) means inspired by God, expressed in the BSB as God-breathed. It identifies Scripture as coming from God.

The uses are practical: instruction, conviction, correction and training in righteousness. Verse 17 states the goal—someone fully equipped for good work. Scripture is to shape a faithful life, not simply provide information to collect.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Major Christian traditions receive Scripture as inspired by God and authoritative for faith and life. Wesley emphasizes the Spirit’s help both in the writers’ work and in readers being taught through it. The Catholic Church likewise teaches that God inspired real human authors who used their own abilities (Catechism 105–107).

Traditions differ over Scripture’s relationship to the church’s other received teaching. The Reformed Westminster Confession 1.6 holds that everything necessary for God’s glory, salvation, faith and life is stated in Scripture or follows from it. The Catholic Church teaches that Scripture and apostolic Tradition together transmit God’s revelation, distinguishing that Tradition from later changeable customs (Catechism 80–83). Both affirm Scripture’s divine source; they differ over whether Scripture alone supplies the church’s certainty about revealed truth.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus explains in Luke 24:25–27, 44–47 how the Scriptures point to His suffering, resurrection and the proclamation of repentance for forgiveness to the nations. That gives a larger setting for the wisdom leading to salvation through Christ in verse 15.

Romans 15:4–6 says earlier Scripture was written for instruction, endurance, encouragement and hope, within a people learning to glorify God together. God’s purpose in giving Scripture reaches into the shared life and faithful service it forms.
passages.current_position_html: In Is the Bible the Inerrant Word of God?, we understand God-breathed as a claim about Scripture’s origin in God. Our study applies inerrancy to the original writings as God inspired them. It distinguishes those writings from later translations, which are human works to be examined carefully against the Hebrew and Greek. This verse does not declare every later translation free from error. In Should We Seek Signs From God?, we also understand verses 16–17 as teaching that Scripture equips believers for good work. We should let its teaching guide our judgment and conduct, rather than treat everyday events as personal omens that supply a new message.

deeper_study.title: Is the Bible the Inerrant Word of God?
Should We Seek Signs From God?

passages.title: 2 Timothy 3:16
passages.section_title: What does it mean that Scripture is God-breathed?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness,
paragraphs: 16 All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness,

passages.title: 2 Timothy 3:16-17
passages.section_title: What is Scripture meant to do in a person’s life?
