passages.title: 2 Timothy 4:1-5
passages.section_title: What must Timothy keep doing when people resist the truth?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 I charge you in the presence of God and of Christ Jesus, who will judge the living and the dead, and in view of His appearing and His kingdom: 2 Preach the word; be prepared in season and out of season; reprove, rebuke, and encourage with every form of patient instruction. 3 For the time will come when men will not tolerate sound doctrine, but with itching ears they will gather around themselves teachers to suit their own desires. 4 So they will turn their ears away from the truth and turn aside to myths. 5 But you, be sober in all things, endure hardship, do the work of an evangelist, fulfill your ministry.
paragraphs: 1 I charge you in the presence of God and of Christ Jesus, who will judge the living and the dead, and in view of His appearing and His kingdom: 2 Preach the word; be prepared in season and out of season; reprove, rebuke, and encourage with every form of patient instruction.

3 For the time will come when men will not tolerate sound doctrine, but with itching ears they will gather around themselves teachers to suit their own desires. 4 So they will turn their ears away from the truth and turn aside to myths. 5 But you, be sober in all things, endure hardship, do the work of an evangelist, fulfill your ministry.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul has described Scripture’s usefulness for equipping a person for good work. He now gives Timothy a solemn charge before God and Christ Jesus, the Judge: proclaim the word and remain ready to do so, whether the circumstances seem favorable or not.

The verb for preach means to announce or proclaim, like a herald (Thayer). The task includes reproving, rebuking and encouraging, with patient instruction. Firmness and patience belong together.

Paul warns that hearers can choose teachers who suit their desires and turn toward myths instead of truth. Timothy must keep a clear head, endure hardship, do the work of an evangelist and fulfill the ministry entrusted to him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley read this as a call to persistent proclamation rather than waiting for an easy or popular moment. Calvin connects it directly with the previous chapter: Scripture is to be both read and taught. Wesley emphasizes readiness to speak even when an obvious opportunity is lacking.

Both read the teachers and hearers in verses 3–4 as mutually reinforcing a preference for pleasing messages. The answer is faithful teaching joined with patience, rather than reshaping the message to secure approval.
passages.god_plan_html:
The charge itself places Timothy’s work before the coming Judge and His kingdom. Acts 10:39–43 likewise joins testimony to Jesus’ death and resurrection with His role as Judge and the promise of forgiveness through His name.

Romans 10:13–17 explains why proclamation matters: people hear the message, believe and call on the Lord. Timothy’s patient work belongs within God’s purpose of bringing the gospel to those who need to hear it.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Timothy 4:6-8
passages.section_title: What hope does Paul have as his death approaches?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 For I am already being poured out like a drink offering, and the time of my departure is at hand. 7 I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. 8 From now on there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous Judge, will award to me on that day—and not only to me, but to all who crave His appearing.
paragraphs: 6 For I am already being poured out like a drink offering, and the time of my departure is at hand. 7 I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. 8 From now on there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous Judge, will award to me on that day—and not only to me, but to all who crave His appearing.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul gives urgency to Timothy’s charge by speaking of his own approaching departure. He pictures his life being poured out like a drink offering. His service has reached its closing stage, and he looks back on the fight, the race and keeping the faith.

He also looks ahead. The Lord is a righteous Judge, and Paul expects the crown of righteousness on that day. The hope is shared with all who long for Christ’s appearing; it is not reserved for Paul alone.

The confidence is spoken by someone still in chains. His assessment of a faithful life reaches beyond how successful or secure it looks at its end.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Calvin and Wesley read Paul’s departure as approaching death and his crown as a future gift from the Lord. Calvin explicitly joins God’s gracious acceptance with the rewarding of faithful service. Wesley describes a righteousness God has both credited to Paul and worked within him. Both hold out the same hope to others who look for Christ’s appearing.
passages.god_plan_html:
The drink-offering picture draws on worship in which an offering is poured out to God, as in Numbers 28:1–8. It is a comparison for Paul’s life given in service, rather than a claim that his death supplies another atoning sacrifice.

Paul uses the same image in Philippians 2:17–18, joining his possible death with the Philippians’ faithful service and shared joy. 1 Corinthians 15:50–58 places steadfast work within resurrection hope: labor in the Lord has a future because death does not have the final word.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Timothy 4:9-15
passages.section_title: What do Paul’s requests reveal about ministry and friendship?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 Make every effort to come to me quickly, 10 because Demas, in his love of this world, has deserted me and gone to Thessalonica. Crescens has gone to Galatia, and Titus to Dalmatia. 11 Only Luke is with me. Get Mark and bring him with you, because he is useful to me in the ministry. 12 Tychicus, however, I have sent to Ephesus. 13 When you come, bring the cloak that I left with Carpus at Troas, and my scrolls, especially the parchments. 14 Alexander the coppersmith did great harm to me. The Lord will repay him according to his deeds. 15 You too should beware of him, for he has vigorously opposed our message.
paragraphs: 9 Make every effort to come to me quickly, 10 because Demas, in his love of this world, has deserted me and gone to Thessalonica. Crescens has gone to Galatia, and Titus to Dalmatia. 11 Only Luke is with me. Get Mark and bring him with you, because he is useful to me in the ministry. 12 Tychicus, however, I have sent to Ephesus. 13 When you come, bring the cloak that I left with Carpus at Troas, and my scrolls, especially the parchments.
14 Alexander the coppersmith did great harm to me. The Lord will repay him according to his deeds. 15 You too should beware of him, for he has vigorously opposed our message.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul asks Timothy to come quickly. Demas has deserted him because he loves this world. Crescens and Titus have also gone elsewhere, but the verse does not give them Demas’s stated motive. Paul says that he himself sent Tychicus to Ephesus.

Luke is with him, and he wants Timothy to bring Mark because Mark is useful in ministry. He also asks for the cloak left at Troas and for his scrolls, especially the parchments. Faithful service includes ordinary needs and dependence on other people’s help.

The warning about Alexander is different from those travel updates. Alexander has actively opposed the message and caused harm. Timothy should beware of him; Paul places repayment in the Lord’s hands.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley distinguish Demas’s desertion from the other coworkers’ departures, which they understand as legitimate ministry travel. Both also recognize Mark’s present usefulness after his earlier departure from Paul’s work.

Calvin does not take the statement about Demas as proof that he completely renounced Christ. The USCCB note allows either abandonment of ministry for worldly concerns or departure from faith itself. The text identifies his love of the world and desertion, without giving his later history.
passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 13:13 records John Mark leaving the journey, and Acts 15:36–40 records the disagreement between Paul and Barnabas over taking him again. Paul’s present request shows that the earlier conflict was not the last word on Mark’s usefulness.

Colossians 4:7–11 also places Tychicus and Mark among coworkers who serve and encourage the church. These connections show a mission carried through real relationships, in which help is shared and earlier failure need not end a person’s service.

passages.title: 2 Timothy 4:16-18
passages.section_title: How did the Lord sustain Paul when no one stood with him?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 At my first defense, no one stood with me, but everyone deserted me. May it not be charged against them. 17 But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the message would be fully proclaimed, and all the Gentiles would hear it. So I was delivered from the mouth of the lion. 18 And the Lord will rescue me from every evil action and bring me safely into His heavenly kingdom. To Him be the glory forever and ever. Amen.
paragraphs: 16 At my first defense, no one stood with me, but everyone deserted me. May it not be charged against them. 17 But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the message would be fully proclaimed, and all the Gentiles would hear it. So I was delivered from the mouth of the lion. 18 And the Lord will rescue me from every evil action and bring me safely into His heavenly kingdom. To Him be the glory forever and ever. Amen.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Paul recalls standing without human support at his first defense. He asks that the abandonment not be charged against those who failed him. He then names the support that remained: the Lord stood by him and gave him strength.

That strength served a purpose beyond his own survival. The message was proclaimed so that the Gentiles could hear. Paul describes his rescue as deliverance from a lion’s mouth.

He trusts the Lord to bring him safely into His heavenly kingdom. Since he has just spoken of approaching death, this confidence is larger than a promise to avoid physical harm indefinitely.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin understands the lion’s mouth as a picture of severe danger rather than necessarily a literal lion or one specific ruler. He reads the final rescue especially as God keeping Paul faithful and bringing him into the kingdom. Wesley likewise distinguishes that final safety from merely escaping death.

The shared encouragement is that human abandonment does not leave Paul outside God’s care. His trust rests in the Lord who strengthens and keeps him, even when faithful service remains costly.
passages.god_plan_html:
Daniel 6:19–27 offers a related picture: God rescues His servant from lions, and that rescue leads to a proclamation of His enduring kingdom among the nations. This is a biblical parallel, not a claim that Paul is reporting a literal lions’ den.

Paul directly connects his own rescue with the Gentiles hearing the message. Acts 23:11 similarly records the Lord standing near Paul and assuring him of witness in Rome. God’s keeping serves His mission, while the letter’s final hope reaches into His heavenly kingdom.

passages.title: 2 Timothy 4:19-22
passages.section_title: How does Paul close a letter written in difficult circumstances?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 Greet Prisca and Aquila, as well as the household of Onesiphorus. 20 Erastus has remained at Corinth, and Trophimus I left sick in Miletus. 21 Make every effort to come to me before winter. Eubulus sends you greetings, as do Pudens, Linus, Claudia, and all the brothers. 22 The Lord be with your spirit. Grace be with you all.
paragraphs: 19 Greet Prisca and Aquila, as well as the household of Onesiphorus. 20 Erastus has remained at Corinth, and Trophimus I left sick in Miletus. 21 Make every effort to come to me before winter. Eubulus sends you greetings, as do Pudens, Linus, Claudia, and all the brothers. 22 The Lord be with your spirit. Grace be with you all.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The letter closes with greetings, coworkers’ locations and another request for Timothy to come before winter. Prisca and Aquila are remembered along with the household of Onesiphorus. Others send greetings from where Paul is.

Paul reports that Erastus remained at Corinth and that he left Trophimus sick in Miletus. These are real limits and needs within the life of the mission, rather than a picture in which every faithful worker is always healthy and always together.

The last words turn again to the Lord’s presence and grace. The personal appeal to Timothy is held within a blessing that includes them all.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley reads Trophimus’s illness as a reminder that the apostles did not work miracles whenever they chose; their exercise depended on God. The verse itself reports the illness without naming its cause or later outcome.

The closing greetings and request for a visit are generally read as ordinary expressions of fellowship and practical care. They complete the letter’s call to faithfulness with dependence on the Lord and His grace.

passages.title: Titus 1:1-4
passages.section_title: Why does Paul join truth, godliness and hope in his greeting?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Paul, a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ for the faith of God’s elect and their knowledge of the truth that leads to godliness, 2 in the hope of eternal life, which God, who cannot lie, promised before time began. 3 In His own time He has made His word evident in the proclamation entrusted to me by the command of God our Savior. 4 To Titus, my true child in our common faith: Grace and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Savior.
paragraphs: 1 Paul, a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ for the faith of God’s elect and their knowledge of the truth that leads to godliness, 2 in the hope of eternal life, which God, who cannot lie, promised before time began. 3 In His own time He has made His word evident in the proclamation entrusted to me by the command of God our Savior.
4 To Titus, my true child in our common faith: Grace and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Savior.

passages.context_html:
Paul introduces himself as God’s servant and an apostle of Jesus Christ. His work serves the faith of God’s people and their knowledge of a truth that leads to godly living. From the beginning, knowing the message and living by it belong together.

That life rests on hope in the God who cannot lie. God’s promise and His timing come before Paul’s entrusted work of proclamation. Paul speaks as someone responsible for a message he has received, rather than one he has invented.

He addresses Titus as his true child in their common faith. Their relationship and shared message stand behind the work Titus has been left to do in Crete, which the next paragraph explains.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Calvin read the greeting as tying the apostolic message to godliness and the hope of eternal life. God’s truthfulness makes that hope dependable; the message is meant to shape a faithful life.

They explain the promise’s timing differently. Wesley understands the promise before the world began as made to Christ, the Head of His people. Calvin considers that reading but favors God’s promise given to people in ancient times, including the promise to Abraham. These are named interpretations of the timing; the displayed BSB keeps its before time began wording.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 16:25–27 likewise joins God’s purpose hidden for long ages with its present proclamation to the nations, so that they may respond in faith. Paul’s entrusted message belongs within that wider work.

Later in this letter, Titus 2:11–14 explains how saving grace trains people to live godly lives while they await Christ’s appearing. The greeting introduces that connection between God’s saving promise, present conduct and future hope.

passages.title: Titus 1:5-9
passages.section_title: What kind of people should care for the church?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 The reason I left you in Crete was that you would set in order what was unfinished and appoint elders in every town, as I directed you. 6 An elder must be blameless, the husband of but one wife, having children who are believers and who are not open to accusation of indiscretion or insubordination. 7 As God’s steward, an overseer must be above reproach—not self-willed, not quick-tempered, not given to drunkenness, not violent, not greedy for money. 8 Instead, he must be hospitable, a lover of good, self-controlled, upright, holy, and disciplined. 9 He must hold firmly to the faithful word as it was taught, so that he can encourage others by sound teaching and refute those who contradict it.
paragraphs: 5 The reason I left you in Crete was that you would set in order what was unfinished and appoint elders in every town, as I directed you. 6 An elder must be blameless, the husband of but one wife, having children who are believers and who are not open to accusation of indiscretion or insubordination.

7 As God’s steward, an overseer must be above reproach—not self-willed, not quick-tempered, not given to drunkenness, not violent, not greedy for money. 8 Instead, he must be hospitable, a lover of good, self-controlled, upright, holy, and disciplined. 9 He must hold firmly to the faithful word as it was taught, so that he can encourage others by sound teaching and refute those who contradict it.

passages.context_html:
Paul explains why he left Titus in Crete: to complete what remained unfinished and appoint elders in every town. The instructions move from their household life to their conduct and their grasp of the teaching.

The elder in verse 5 and overseer in verse 7 are described within the same set of qualifications. The person is God’s steward, responsible for something belonging to God. Hospitality, self-control and a love of good stand against arrogance, anger, violence and greed.

The final requirement serves the people who hear: holding firmly to the faithful word enables a leader both to encourage sound belief and to correct teaching that contradicts it. Character and the ability to teach belong together.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The USCCB note recognizes that elder and overseer refer to the same people here. Traditions differ over how those roles developed and should be organized. The Catholic Church teaches three degrees of ordained ministry—bishop, priest and deacon (Catechism 1554). The Baptist 1689 Confession 26.8–9 instead describes elders or bishops and deacons within a local church.

Household qualifications also receive different readings. Calvin understands the children as believers. A Bible.org question-and-answer article reads the requirement as reliable, well-disciplined children, connecting it with 1 Timothy 3:4–5. The Greek pistos (pis-TOS) can mean faithful or believing; Thayer lists this verse under believing. The word’s range alone does not remove the contextual question. The BSB reads children who are believers.

Calvin also reads the one-wife wording as marital faithfulness that does not exclude remarriage after a spouse’s death. Catholic practice generally requires celibacy of Latin-rite priests while allowing married priests in Eastern Catholic traditions (Catechism 1579–1580). These are distinct applications, rather than one uniform Christian rule.
passages.current_position_html: In Who Shepherds the Church?, we understand elder and overseer here as descriptions of the same work of caring for the church. Our study calls for plural leadership among the people, marked by character, maturity and the ability to teach and correct. Rejecting elevated ranks does not remove the need for qualified teachers who keep the gathering anchored to Scripture.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 14:21–23 likewise joins strengthening disciples, appointing elders and entrusting them to the Lord. The aim is the continued care of people who have received the gospel.

In 1 Peter 5:1–4, elders shepherd God’s flock without greed or domination, as examples under the Chief Shepherd. That gives the larger setting for these qualifications: the people belong to Christ, and their leaders serve under His care and authority.

passages.title: Titus 1:10-16
passages.section_title: Why must harmful teaching be corrected?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 For many are rebellious and full of empty talk and deception, especially those of the circumcision, 11 who must be silenced. For the sake of dishonorable gain, they undermine entire households and teach things they should not. 12 As one of their own prophets has said, “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons.” 13 This testimony is true. Therefore rebuke them sternly, so that they will be sound in the faith 14 and will pay no attention to Jewish myths or to the commands of men who have rejected the truth. 15 To the pure, all things are pure; but to the defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure. Indeed, both their minds and their consciences are defiled. 16 They profess to know God, but by their actions they deny Him. They are detestable, disobedient, and unfit for any good deed.
paragraphs: 10 For many are rebellious and full of empty talk and deception, especially those of the circumcision, 11 who must be silenced. For the sake of dishonorable gain, they undermine entire households and teach things they should not.

12 As one of their own prophets has said, “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons.” 13 This testimony is true. Therefore rebuke them sternly, so that they will be sound in the faith 14 and will pay no attention to Jewish myths or to the commands of men who have rejected the truth.

15 To the pure, all things are pure; but to the defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure. Indeed, both their minds and their consciences are defiled. 16 They profess to know God, but by their actions they deny Him. They are detestable, disobedient, and unfit for any good deed.

passages.context_html:
The reason for leaders able to correct becomes clear: rebellious teachers are undermining households for dishonest gain. Paul singles out those of the circumcision as a particular concern, rather than saying every person of Jewish background is an opponent.

He quotes a severe saying about Cretans and applies it to the need for firm correction. The stated goal is that people become sound in faith instead of following myths and human commands that turn from the truth.

The closing contrast concerns purity and the life that reveals it. Outward religious claims do not make a corrupt mind and conscience clean. The opponents say they know God, but their actions deny that profession. The correction addresses a real danger to people’s faith and conduct.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Calvin understand the statement that all things are pure in the setting of food and purity restrictions. The point is not that every action becomes morally acceptable to a believer. They connect true purity with faith and the inner life, rather than reliance on religious restrictions alone.

The USCCB note similarly connects the opponents with ritual-purity requirements and harmful speculation. The shared emphasis is that religious claims must agree with truth and conduct. The aim of rebuke is sound faith, rather than humiliation as an end in itself.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
In Mark 7:14–23, Jesus locates defilement in the evil that comes from the heart rather than in food entering a person. That is a related teaching which helps explain why outward purity rules cannot cure a corrupt inner life.

Acts 10:34–48 gives the wider setting of God receiving people from the nations through Christ. Peter proclaims forgiveness through Jesus, and the Spirit is given to the Gentile hearers. God’s saving work calls people into faith and a new life; human barriers cannot supply or replace that cleansing.

passages.title: Titus 2:1-10
passages.section_title: How should sound teaching shape everyday relationships?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 But as for you, speak the things that are consistent with sound doctrine. 2 Older men are to be temperate, dignified, self-controlled, and sound in faith, love, and perseverance. 3 Older women, likewise, are to be reverent in their behavior, not slanderers or addicted to much wine, but teachers of good. 4 In this way they can train the young women to love their husbands and children, 5 to be self-controlled, pure, managers of their households, kind, and submissive to their own husbands, so that the word of God will not be discredited. 6 In the same way, urge the younger men to be self-controlled. 7 In everything, show yourself to be an example by doing good works. In your teaching show integrity, dignity, 8 and wholesome speech that is above reproach, so that anyone who opposes us will be ashamed, having nothing bad to say about us. 9 Slaves are to submit to their own masters in everything, to be well-pleasing, not argumentative, 10 not stealing from them, but showing all good faith, so that in every respect they will adorn the teaching about God our Savior.
paragraphs: 1 But as for you, speak the things that are consistent with sound doctrine. 2 Older men are to be temperate, dignified, self-controlled, and sound in faith, love, and perseverance.

3 Older women, likewise, are to be reverent in their behavior, not slanderers or addicted to much wine, but teachers of good. 4 In this way they can train the young women to love their husbands and children, 5 to be self-controlled, pure, managers of their households, kind, and submissive to their own husbands, so that the word of God will not be discredited.

6 In the same way, urge the younger men to be self-controlled. 7 In everything, show yourself to be an example by doing good works. In your teaching show integrity, dignity, 8 and wholesome speech that is above reproach, so that anyone who opposes us will be ashamed, having nothing bad to say about us.

9 Slaves are to submit to their own masters in everything, to be well-pleasing, not argumentative, 10 not stealing from them, but showing all good faith, so that in every respect they will adorn the teaching about God our Savior.

passages.context_html:
Paul contrasts Titus’s teaching with the harmful teaching just described. He addresses older men, older women, younger women and younger men, then people living in slavery. Faithfulness is to become visible across the whole community, rather than remain a concern only for its leaders.

Older believers are called to maturity and self-control. Older women have an active teaching role in helping younger women care for their families and live faithfully. The household language in verse 5 concerns working at and caring for the home (Thayer); the BSB renders it managers of their households.

Titus must model the good work and trustworthy speech he teaches. Slaves are asked to serve faithfully rather than steal or be argumentative. They are enslaved people under masters, so the relationship should not be reduced to an ordinary freely chosen job.

The reasons Paul gives repeatedly concern witness: God’s word is not to be discredited, opponents should have no sound charge against their conduct, and their lives are to make the teaching about God our Savior attractive.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Calvin read the paragraph as practical teaching for the community’s different relationships, with the teacher’s own example included. Older women’s instruction helps younger women put faith into practice; age alone is not a substitute for a faithful life.

Traditions differ over how a wife’s submission relates to shared responsibility. The Southern Baptist Faith and Message, Article XVIII affirms equal worth together with distinct leadership and household roles. Christians for Biblical Equality instead teaches shared marital leadership and responsibility under mutual submission. These are stated approaches to applying household passages, rather than claims that every Christian in either tradition describes every household the same way.

Wesley qualifies obedience to husbands and masters by what is lawful and can be done without sin. His reading does not make a human authority’s every demand morally right. His account of care at home also allows going out for necessity, devotion and mercy. The passage’s instructions should be considered with their actual concern for faithful conduct and the reputation of the message.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
In John 13:34–35, Jesus says His disciples’ love for one another will identify them as His followers. The cross-generational care and faithful conduct in this paragraph give that witness everyday form.

1 Peter 2:9–12 places honorable conduct among the nations within the calling of a people brought into God’s light. Paul likewise connects ordinary relationships with the way others hear and see the message about God.

passages.title: Titus 2:11-15
passages.section_title: How does God’s grace teach us to live while we wait for Christ?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to everyone. 12 It instructs us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live sensible, upright, and godly lives in the present age, 13 as we await the blessed hope and glorious appearance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ. 14 He gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for Himself a people for His own possession, zealous for good deeds. 15 Speak these things as you encourage and rebuke with all authority. Let no one despise you.
paragraphs: 11 For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to everyone. 12 It instructs us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live sensible, upright, and godly lives in the present age, 13 as we await the blessed hope and glorious appearance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ. 14 He gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for Himself a people for His own possession, zealous for good deeds.
15 Speak these things as you encourage and rebuke with all authority. Let no one despise you.

passages.context_html:
The word for at the beginning explains the instructions just given. God’s saving grace has appeared, and that grace teaches people to leave ungodliness and worldly passions behind and live rightly now.

The verb for instructing, paideuo (pie-DYOO-oh), carries the idea of teaching and training. Grace is doing more than overlooking wrong: it forms a different way of life.

Paul joins two horizons. Christ has given Himself to redeem and purify a people who belong to Him, eager for good work. Those people now live in hope of His glorious appearing. Titus is to teach, encourage and correct on that foundation.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley both read saving grace as leading to godly living and hope, rather than permission to continue unchanged. They differ over the scope of everyone in verse 11. Calvin explicitly reads people of every rank or class, including slaves. Wesley emphasizes grace’s saving purpose and its instruction of those who do not reject it. The Catholic Church also affirms God’s desire for everyone’s salvation through knowledge of the truth (Catechism 851). These readings do not require saying that every person is finally saved.

On verse 13, Wesley reads great God and Savior as referring together to Jesus Christ. Calvin considers both that reading and one distinguishing the Father and Christ in the phrase, while affirming the divine glory revealed in Christ. This is a difference over the sentence’s wording, rather than a claim that one of them denies Christ’s deity. The displayed BSB reads our great God and Savior Jesus Christ.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The passage itself connects Christ’s self-giving, a people made His own, present good works and His future appearing. In Exodus 19:3–6, God likewise brings a delivered people to Himself and calls them His treasured possession and a holy nation. This is a parallel in the purpose of deliverance: people belonging to God and living as His people.

1 Peter 2:9–10 uses that people-and-possession language for those who have received mercy and are called to declare God’s praises. Ephesians 2:8–10 likewise joins salvation by grace with good works prepared for a new life in Christ. The work follows His saving gift; it is the life for which He has redeemed His people.

passages.title: Titus 3:1-8
passages.section_title: Why should people saved by mercy show gentleness to everyone?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Remind the believers to submit to rulers and authorities, to be obedient and ready for every good work, 2 to malign no one, and to be peaceable and gentle, showing full consideration to everyone. 3 For at one time we too were foolish, disobedient, misled, and enslaved to all sorts of desires and pleasures—living in malice and envy, being hated and hating one another. 4 But when the kindness of God our Savior and His love for mankind appeared, 5 He saved us, not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy, through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit. 6 This is the Spirit He poured out on us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior, 7 so that, having been justified by His grace, we would become heirs with the hope of eternal life. 8 This saying is trustworthy. And I want you to emphasize these things, so that those who have believed God will take care to devote themselves to good deeds. These things are excellent and profitable for the people.
paragraphs: 1 Remind the believers to submit to rulers and authorities, to be obedient and ready for every good work, 2 to malign no one, and to be peaceable and gentle, showing full consideration to everyone. 3 For at one time we too were foolish, disobedient, misled, and enslaved to all sorts of desires and pleasures—living in malice and envy, being hated and hating one another.

4 But when the kindness of God our Savior and His love for mankind appeared, 5 He saved us, not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy, through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit. 6 This is the Spirit He poured out on us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior, 7 so that, having been justified by His grace, we would become heirs with the hope of eternal life.

8 This saying is trustworthy. And I want you to emphasize these things, so that those who have believed God will take care to devote themselves to good deeds. These things are excellent and profitable for the people.

passages.context_html:
Paul moves from relationships within households to conduct in the wider community. Believers are to respect rulers and authorities, be ready for good work, avoid slander and quarrels, and show gentleness to everyone.

The reason begins with remembering their own past. They too were once deceived, disobedient and ruled by destructive desires. God’s kindness met them there. They have no basis for treating other people as though they had earned a superior standing.

God saved them by mercy, not by righteous deeds they had already done. Paul describes the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit, poured out through Jesus Christ. By His grace they are put right with Him and become heirs who look forward to eternal life.

Good deeds return at the end of the paragraph as the result to cultivate. They are not the reason God first showed mercy; they are part of the useful, fruitful life believers are now called to live.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley reads the civil instructions as obedience within the bounds of conscience, joined to gentleness toward people who need the mercy believers themselves received. He and Calvin both distinguish salvation by God’s mercy from the good works that follow it.

Traditions differ over the washing in verse 5. The Catholic Church identifies it with baptism as God’s means of bringing about new birth (Catechism 1215). Luther’s Small Catechism, Holy Baptism, also applies Titus 3 to baptism, stressing God’s word with the water and the faith that trusts His promise.

The Reformed Westminster Confession 28.1, 5–6 describes baptism as a sign and assurance of new birth through which the Spirit truly gives grace, while denying that every baptized person is renewed or that its effect is confined to the moment of administration. The Baptist 1689 Confession 29.1–2 describes baptism as a sign of union with Christ, forgiveness and new life for those already professing repentance and faith. These accounts differ over the relationship between the outward act and the Spirit’s renewing work; none describes water acting independently of God as a payment for salvation.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Ezekiel 36:25–27 promises cleansing, a new heart and God’s Spirit dwelling within His people so they can walk in His ways. It provides a biblical parallel for the washing, renewal and changed life described here.

Acts 2:14–18, 32–33 connects the promised outpouring of the Spirit with the risen and exalted Jesus. Paul likewise says the Spirit is poured out abundantly through Jesus Christ. God’s saving mercy forms a renewed people with an inheritance of life and a calling to do good.

passages.title: Titus 3:9-11
passages.section_title: How should Titus respond to persistent divisiveness?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 But avoid foolish controversies, genealogies, arguments, and quarrels about the law, because these things are pointless and worthless. 10 Reject a divisive man after a first and second admonition, 11 knowing that such a man is corrupt and sinful; he is self-condemned.
paragraphs: 9 But avoid foolish controversies, genealogies, arguments, and quarrels about the law, because these things are pointless and worthless. 10 Reject a divisive man after a first and second admonition, 11 knowing that such a man is corrupt and sinful; he is self-condemned.

passages.context_html:
Paul contrasts useful good work with disputes that produce no good result. Titus is to avoid foolish controversies, genealogies and quarrels about the law, rather than let them consume the community’s attention.

A persistently divisive person is first to receive a warning and then another. If the pattern continues, Titus is to reject that person. The instruction addresses repeated destructive conduct after correction, rather than a sincere question or a single difference of opinion.

The Greek adjective hairetikos (high-reh-tee-KOS) describes someone factious or divisive, including a follower of false teaching. In this setting, the person’s own persistence makes his wrongdoing evident.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley reads the instruction as a response to someone obstinately generating factions through pointless disputes. Calvin likewise warns against immediately branding everyone who disagrees as a heretic. He emphasizes that correction must precede rejection.

The shared reading recognizes both an opportunity to respond to correction and a boundary against ongoing damage. The instruction does not make every unresolved question an act of division or require endless repetition of the same fruitless controversy.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
1 Corinthians 1:10–13 confronts factions by bringing the community back to Christ, who is not divided. That gives a larger purpose for addressing divisiveness: the people belong together in Him, rather than becoming rival followings.

Ephesians 4:1–6 likewise joins humility, patience and bearing with one another to preserving unity in the Spirit. Titus’s warnings belong within care for that shared life, not a goal of making every person agree with a leader’s private preferences.

passages.title: Titus 3:12-15
passages.section_title: How can the church put good works into practice?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 As soon as I send Artemas or Tychicus to you, make every effort to come to me at Nicopolis, because I have decided to winter there. 13 Do your best to equip Zenas the lawyer and Apollos, so that they will have everything they need. 14 And our people must also learn to devote themselves to good works in order to meet the pressing needs of others, so that they will not be unfruitful. 15 All who are with me send you greetings. Greet those who love us in the faith. Grace be with all of you.
paragraphs: 12 As soon as I send Artemas or Tychicus to you, make every effort to come to me at Nicopolis, because I have decided to winter there. 13 Do your best to equip Zenas the lawyer and Apollos, so that they will have everything they need.

14 And our people must also learn to devote themselves to good works in order to meet the pressing needs of others, so that they will not be unfruitful. 15 All who are with me send you greetings. Greet those who love us in the faith. Grace be with all of you.

passages.context_html:
Paul closes with practical arrangements. When Artemas or Tychicus is sent, Titus is to come to him at Nicopolis, where Paul intends to spend the winter. He is also to equip Zenas and Apollos for their journey so that they have what they need.

The request becomes an instruction for the community as a whole: learn to devote themselves to good works that meet pressing needs. Fruitfulness takes a concrete form in providing help, rather than remaining an idea discussed in the gathering.

The letter ends with greetings from those with Paul, love shared in the faith and grace for them all. The teaching about God’s saving kindness has led back to a people learning to show kindness in practice.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin reads the request as an opportunity for believers to exercise generosity instead of remaining unfruitful. Wesley likewise connects their learning with Titus’s instruction and example and the need to help Zenas and Apollos. The practical provision is part of living out the teaching.

Wesley understands Artemas or Tychicus as taking over Titus’s work while he visits Paul. The passage names the alternatives but does not say which one was ultimately sent.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Philippians 4:14–20 describes practical giving as partnership in gospel work and fruit in the givers’ lives. The help requested here belongs within that same pattern of people using their resources to support others in the mission.

Ephesians 4:28 also connects honest work with having something to share with someone in need. God’s renewed people learn a different use for their resources: meeting needs becomes part of the life they share in Christ.

passages.title: Philemon 1:1-3
passages.section_title: Why does a personal appeal begin by addressing a church?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, and Timothy our brother, To Philemon our beloved fellow worker, 2 to Apphia our sister, to Archippus our fellow soldier, and to the church that meets at your house: 3 Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
paragraphs: 1 Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, and Timothy our brother, To Philemon our beloved fellow worker, 2 to Apphia our sister, to Archippus our fellow soldier, and to the church that meets at your house: 3 Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

passages.context_html:
Paul introduces himself as a prisoner of Christ Jesus and names Timothy alongside him. He writes to Philemon as a beloved fellow worker, then includes Apphia, Archippus and the church meeting at Philemon’s house.

The letter will appeal for the welcome of Onesimus as a brother in Christ. Naming the gathered community gives that personal matter a setting within their shared faith. Paul’s request concerns how people who belong to Christ will treat one another.

He begins with grace and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. The appeal is made within that shared dependence on God, rather than simply as a private business settlement.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley, Calvin and the USCCB note recognize that Paul’s identity as a prisoner gives a particular weight and personal tone to the appeal that follows. His words address fellow believers, with the gathering in the home included.

Wesley and Calvin understand Apphia as Philemon’s wife. That is a traditional identification, rather than a relationship expressly named in these verses. Archippus is called a fellow soldier; the letter does not identify him as their son. Those household relationships should not be treated as certain details of the story.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.title: Philemon 1:4-7
passages.section_title: What does Paul pray for in Philemon’s shared life of faith?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 4 I always thank my God, remembering you in my prayers, 5 because I hear about your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love for all the saints. 6 I pray that your partnership in the faith may become effective as you fully acknowledge every good thing that is ours in Christ. 7 I take great joy and encouragement in your love, because you, brother, have refreshed the hearts of the saints.
paragraphs: 4 I always thank my God, remembering you in my prayers, 5 because I hear about your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love for all the saints. 6 I pray that your partnership in the faith may become effective as you fully acknowledge every good thing that is ours in Christ.
7 I take great joy and encouragement in your love, because you, brother, have refreshed the hearts of the saints.

passages.context_html:
Paul thanks God for what he hears of Philemon’s faith in Jesus and love for the saints. The thanksgiving identifies a good already at work before Paul asks for another act of love.

He prays that Philemon’s partnership in faith will become effective through recognizing every good thing they share in Christ. The Greek word koinonia (koy-noh-NEE-ah) means fellowship or shared participation. Here it points to a faith lived in relationship, rather than something held privately.

Paul has already received joy and encouragement from Philemon’s love, because others have been refreshed through him. That language prepares for the later appeal to refresh Paul’s heart by receiving Onesimus.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin reads the prayer as asking for faith to show its effectiveness through good works. Wesley emphasizes faith becoming known to others through the love they see. Both connect the knowledge and sharing language with a life that benefits people, rather than information acquired for its own sake.

The prayer builds on Philemon’s existing love while asking for further fruit. The displayed BSB’s partnership wording emphasizes the life believers share. In the letter that follows, this partnership will be tested through the way Philemon receives Onesimus.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Philippians 1:9–11 similarly joins growing knowledge with love, discernment and the fruit that comes through Jesus Christ. Paul’s prayer here belongs with that purpose of a faith which becomes fruitful in relationships.

Acts 2:42–47 gives another picture of shared faith taking visible form: teaching, fellowship, prayer and practical provision. These are related examples of God forming a people whose life together expresses the good they have received in Christ.

passages.title: Philemon 1:8-22
passages.section_title: What does it mean to welcome Onesimus as a brother?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 So although in Christ I am bold enough to order you to do what is proper, 9 I prefer to appeal on the basis of love. For I, Paul, am now aged, and a prisoner of Christ Jesus as well. 10 I appeal to you for my child Onesimus, whose father I became while I was in chains. 11 Formerly he was useless to you, but now he has become useful both to you and to me. 12 I am sending back to you him who is my very heart. 13 I would have liked to keep him with me, so that on your behalf he could minister to me in my chains for the gospel. 14 But I did not want to do anything without your consent, so that your goodness will not be out of compulsion, but by your own free will. 15 For perhaps this is why he was separated from you for a while, so that you might have him back for good— 16 no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother. He is especially beloved to me, but even more so to you, both in person and in the Lord. 17 So if you consider me a partner, receive him as you would receive me. 18 But if he has wronged you in any way or owes you anything, charge it to my account. 19 I, Paul, write this with my own hand. I will repay it—not to mention that you owe me your very self. 20 Yes, brother, let me have some benefit from you in the Lord. Refresh my heart in Christ. 21 Confident of your obedience, I write to you, knowing that you will do even more than I ask. 22 In the meantime, prepare a guest room for me, because I hope that through your prayers I will be restored to you.
paragraphs: 8 So although in Christ I am bold enough to order you to do what is proper, 9 I prefer to appeal on the basis of love. For I, Paul, am now aged, and a prisoner of Christ Jesus as well. 10 I appeal to you for my child Onesimus, whose father I became while I was in chains. 11 Formerly he was useless to you, but now he has become useful both to you and to me.

12 I am sending back to you him who is my very heart. 13 I would have liked to keep him with me, so that on your behalf he could minister to me in my chains for the gospel. 14 But I did not want to do anything without your consent, so that your goodness will not be out of compulsion, but by your own free will. 15 For perhaps this is why he was separated from you for a while, so that you might have him back for good— 16 no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother. He is especially beloved to me, but even more so to you, both in person and in the Lord.

17 So if you consider me a partner, receive him as you would receive me. 18 But if he has wronged you in any way or owes you anything, charge it to my account. 19 I, Paul, write this with my own hand. I will repay it—not to mention that you owe me your very self. 20 Yes, brother, let me have some benefit from you in the Lord. Refresh my heart in Christ.

21 Confident of your obedience, I write to you, knowing that you will do even more than I ask. 22 In the meantime, prepare a guest room for me, because I hope that through your prayers I will be restored to you.

passages.context_html:
Paul moves from thanking Philemon for his love to asking him to show that love toward Onesimus. He could issue a command, but chooses an appeal. He wants Philemon’s response to be willing rather than forced.

Onesimus has become Paul’s child in the faith during his imprisonment. The word translated child can describe the relationship between a teacher and a disciple. Paul is speaking about coming to faith through his ministry, not a physical birth. Onesimus’s name means useful or beneficial, and Paul plays on that name: the man formerly described as useless has become useful to them both.

Paul is sending him back, although he would gladly have kept him nearby to help. His request changes the terms of the welcome: Philemon is to receive Onesimus as a beloved brother, and to welcome him as he would Paul himself. Paul suggests that their separation may have led to a lasting good. His word perhaps matters; he does not claim to know every reason God allowed it.

If Onesimus has caused a loss or owes anything, Paul offers to pay. The verb translated charge it to my account means to put a charge against someone’s account. Paul makes that offer personally, in his own handwriting. The sentence is conditional; it does not tell us exactly what Onesimus did or how much he owed.

Paul expects a generous response and asks for a guest room, hoping to be restored to them through their prayers. The letter gives the appeal and the hope, but does not report Philemon’s answer or Paul’s eventual visit.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley both emphasize Paul’s affectionate appeal, the change in Onesimus and the welcome now owed to him as a fellow believer. Both understand Paul’s offer to pay as removing an obstacle to that welcome. The appeal asks Philemon to act on the faith and love Paul has already commended.

The question of legal freedom needs care. Calvin reads the letter as requiring a forgiving reception without removing the master’s existing civil authority. Wesley’s introduction suggests that Philemon may actually have freed Onesimus, although his note on verse 16 still describes service alongside Christian brotherhood. These are named teachers’ readings, not a complete statement of every Reformed or Wesleyan view. Paul explicitly requires the welcome of a beloved brother; the letter does not record a formal release or its outcome.

Calvin also reads the request for lodging as a real hope of release, subject to God’s will, rather than a guarantee. Wesley likewise understands verse 22 as restoration to liberty. Their readings allow the prayer to concern Paul’s actual circumstances without promising that every requested outcome will occur.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Galatians 3:26–29 says that those who belong to Christ share the standing of God’s children, including slave and free. Colossians 3:11 likewise places both within the new life in Christ. Philemon shows what that shared belonging asks of a particular relationship: the person being sent back is to be welcomed as a brother.

Paul’s offer to bear a cost so Onesimus can be received provides a limited parallel to the reconciliation described in 2 Corinthians 5:18–21. There God reconciles people to Himself through Christ and entrusts a message of reconciliation to His servants. Paul is helping two people be reconciled; his promise to pay a possible debt is not another sacrifice for sin.

There is also a parallel with Joseph’s story in Genesis 50:15–21: God can bring good through events which caused real harm. Joseph states what God accomplished in his story. Paul speaks more cautiously about Onesimus’s separation. Neither passage turns the harm itself into something good or promises that every loss will soon have an explanation.

passages.title: Philemon 1:23-25
passages.section_title: Who joins Paul in his final greeting?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 23 Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, sends you greetings, 24 as do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow workers. 25 The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.
paragraphs: 23 Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, sends you greetings, 24 as do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow workers. 25 The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.

passages.context_html:
Paul closes by naming the people who send greetings with him. Epaphras is called his fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus. Mark, Aristarchus, Demas and Luke are named as fellow workers.

The names show that the appeal comes from within a wider circle of Christian relationships. Paul ends where he began: with the grace of Jesus Christ. After such a personal request, the final blessing includes the community addressed at the start of the letter.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
These verses are generally read as greetings and a closing blessing. The USCCB notes connect the named workers with their appearances in Colossians, Acts and 2 Timothy. Those links help identify the people, but the greeting itself does not describe their later lives or the result of the appeal.

Calvin draws a warning about perseverance from Demas’s later desertion in 2 Timothy 4:10. That is a connection with another letter, rather than something Philemon’s closing greeting says has already happened. Here Demas is still included among Paul’s fellow workers.
