versions.text: 23 So it was necessary for the copies of the heavenly things to be purified with these sacrifices, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these. 24 For Christ did not enter a man-made copy of the true sanctuary, but He entered heaven itself, now to appear on our behalf in the presence of God. 25 Nor did He enter heaven to offer Himself again and again, as the high priest enters the Most Holy Place every year with blood that is not his own. 26 Otherwise, Christ would have had to suffer repeatedly since the foundation of the world. But now He has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to do away with sin by the sacrifice of Himself. 27 Just as man is appointed to die once, and after that to face judgment, 28 so also Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many; and He will appear a second time, not to bear sin, but to bring salvation to those who eagerly await Him.
paragraphs: 23 So it was necessary for the copies of the heavenly things to be purified with these sacrifices, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these. 24 For Christ did not enter a man-made copy of the true sanctuary, but He entered heaven itself, now to appear on our behalf in the presence of God.

25 Nor did He enter heaven to offer Himself again and again, as the high priest enters the Most Holy Place every year with blood that is not his own. 26 Otherwise, Christ would have had to suffer repeatedly since the foundation of the world. But now He has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to do away with sin by the sacrifice of Himself.

27 Just as man is appointed to die once, and after that to face judgment, 28 so also Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many; and He will appear a second time, not to bear sin, but to bring salvation to those who eagerly await Him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The writer carries the comparison from the earthly copies to the heavenly reality. Christ has entered heaven itself to appear before God on our behalf. The greater cleansing rests on His own offering.

His entrance does not begin an endless repetition of His suffering. He appeared once to deal with sin through the sacrifice of Himself. The contrast is with the high priest’s yearly entrance carrying another creature’s blood.

The comparison then joins our one earthly life and coming judgment with Christ’s one offering and coming return. He will appear again to bring salvation to those who eagerly await Him, rather than to bear sin through another sacrifice. This does not imply He was personally sinful at His first coming.

The passage states that the heavenly things require the greater cleansing, but it does not describe a hidden incident that polluted heaven or give the movements of blood through an unseen building. Its clear emphasis is Christ’s sufficient offering and His presence before God for us.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin, Wesley and the USCCB notes agree that Christ’s offering is once for all and that His return brings its saving outcome rather than another death.

They explain the heavenly things in verse 23 differently. Calvin speaks of Christ’s spiritual kingdom. Wesley identifies them with believers’ heaven-born spirits and acknowledges that there may be more here than we yet understand. The USCCB notes emphasize the heavenly realities to which the earlier rites pointed. These readings do not all require an account of a sinful act inside a heavenly temple.

Christians also differ about judgment after death. The Catholic Catechism, 1021–1022, teaches a personal judgment at death. Wesley’s comment on verse 27 instead refers judgment to the final day and denies a separate immediate judgment, while saying that a person’s final state is determined at death. His view is an individual commentator’s reading; the Catechism states official Catholic teaching.
passages.god_plan_html:
Isaiah 53:10–12 describes the servant offering His life and bearing the sins of many. Acts 8:30–35 explicitly connects Isaiah’s servant passage with Jesus. Hebrews’ language about bearing the sins of many belongs within that larger scriptural account of His mission.

1 Corinthians 15:20–26 connects Christ’s return with the resurrection of those who belong to Him and the final defeat of death. Waiting for Him is therefore hope for the completion of His saving work, rather than waiting for a sacrifice that still needs to be made.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Hebrews 10:1-10
passages.section_title: Why could repeated sacrifices never finish the work?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 For the law is only a shadow of the good things to come, not the realities themselves. It can never, by the same sacrifices offered year after year, make perfect those who draw near to worship. 2 If it could, would not the offerings have ceased? For the worshipers would have been cleansed once for all, and would no longer have felt the guilt of their sins. 3 Instead, those sacrifices are an annual reminder of sins, 4 because it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins. 5 Therefore, when Christ came into the world, He said: “Sacrifice and offering You did not desire, but a body You prepared for Me. 6 In burnt offerings and sin offerings You took no delight. 7 Then I said, ‘Here I am, it is written about Me in the scroll: I have come to do Your will, O God.’” 8 In the passage above He says, “Sacrifices and offerings, burnt offerings and sin offerings You did not desire, nor did You delight in them” (although they are offered according to the law). 9 Then He adds, “Here I am, I have come to do Your will.” He takes away the first to establish the second. 10 And by that will, we have been sanctified through the sacrifice of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.
paragraphs: 1 For the law is only a shadow of the good things to come, not the realities themselves. It can never, by the same sacrifices offered year after year, make perfect those who draw near to worship. 2 If it could, would not the offerings have ceased? For the worshipers would have been cleansed once for all, and would no longer have felt the guilt of their sins. 3 Instead, those sacrifices are an annual reminder of sins, 4 because it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.

5 Therefore, when Christ came into the world, He said: “Sacrifice and offering You did not desire, but a body You prepared for Me. 6 In burnt offerings and sin offerings You took no delight. 7 Then I said, ‘Here I am, it is written about Me in the scroll: I have come to do Your will, O God.’”

8 In the passage above He says, “Sacrifices and offerings, burnt offerings and sin offerings You did not desire, nor did You delight in them” (although they are offered according to the law). 9 Then He adds, “Here I am, I have come to do Your will.” He takes away the first to establish the second. 10 And by that will, we have been sanctified through the sacrifice of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The writer continues the contrast between repeated animal offerings and Christ’s one sacrifice. Repetition showed the earlier offerings could not finally remove sin. Each year brought another reminder of the need they could not bring to an end.

He then presents Christ speaking the words of Psalm 40:6–8. The central movement is from sacrifices to a willing person who comes to do God’s will. Christ fulfills that obedience by offering His own body.

There is a difference in wording worth noticing. The BSB of Psalm 40:6 speaks of ears God has opened; Hebrews speaks of a body prepared. Hebrews follows the ancient Greek form of the psalm here. The writer applies that wording to Christ’s obedient offering; we should read each passage as it stands rather than silently making their wording identical.

God had commanded the earlier offerings, as verse 8 recognizes. The contrast does not make those commands a mistake. It shows that Christ accomplishes the purpose they could not complete. Through His willing offering, people are set apart for God once for all.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin, Wesley and the USCCB notes understand Christ’s obedience and bodily offering as the fulfillment toward which the earlier sacrifices pointed. Animal blood could not itself accomplish what His offering does.

Calvin stresses that this does not leave faithful people before Christ without grace: their hope also depended on Him. Wesley emphasizes the greater holiness and reconciliation made possible through Christ. Their comments share the passage’s movement toward His sufficient offering without making the earlier ceremonies worthless in their own appointed time.
passages.god_plan_html:
Philippians 2:5–11 describes Christ’s willing obedience even to death, followed by His exaltation. Romans 5:18–19 connects the obedience of the one man, Christ, with righteousness for others.

God’s purpose is carried forward through the Son who willingly does His will. Hebrews’ use of the psalm belongs within that larger account of Christ’s coming and obedience, rather than a story of an unwilling Son forced to act against His purpose.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Hebrews 10:11-18
passages.section_title: What does Christ’s one offering accomplish?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 Day after day every priest stands to minister and to offer again and again the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. 12 But when this Priest had offered for all time one sacrifice for sins, He sat down at the right hand of God. 13 Since that time, He waits for His enemies to be made a footstool for His feet, 14 because by a single offering He has made perfect for all time those who are being sanctified. 15 The Holy Spirit also testifies to us about this. First He says: 16 “This is the covenant I will make with them after those days, declares the Lord. I will put My laws in their hearts and inscribe them on their minds.” 17 Then He adds: “Their sins and lawless acts I will remember no more.” 18 And where these have been forgiven, an offering for sin is no longer needed.
paragraphs: 11 Day after day every priest stands to minister and to offer again and again the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. 12 But when this Priest had offered for all time one sacrifice for sins, He sat down at the right hand of God. 13 Since that time, He waits for His enemies to be made a footstool for His feet, 14 because by a single offering He has made perfect for all time those who are being sanctified.

15 The Holy Spirit also testifies to us about this. First He says: 16 “This is the covenant I will make with them after those days, declares the Lord. I will put My laws in their hearts and inscribe them on their minds.” 17 Then He adds: “Their sins and lawless acts I will remember no more.” 18 And where these have been forgiven, an offering for sin is no longer needed.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The daily standing service of the priests is contrasted with Christ seated at God’s right hand. Their offerings were repeated; His one sacrifice has lasting effect. His seated place also expresses His authority as He waits for His enemies to be made His footstool.

The passage holds completed work and ongoing holiness together: one offering has made perfect for all time those who are being sanctified. This assurance does not claim that believers have already stopped needing growth or that the following calls to obedience are unnecessary.

The Holy Spirit’s testimony comes through Jeremiah’s promise of inward renewal and forgiveness. The writer returns to the new covenant already discussed in chapter 8. Once sins are forgiven through Christ’s offering, another offering for sin is unnecessary.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin, Wesley and the USCCB notes read this as a declaration of the lasting sufficiency of Christ’s offering. Calvin also warns against treating His seated position as inactivity: He reigns and continues to act for His people.

Christians differ over how this relates to the Lord’s Supper. The Catholic Catechism, 1366–1367, teaches that the one sacrifice is made present in the Eucharist, the church’s celebration of the Lord’s Supper, without another death of Christ. The Westminster Confession, 29.1–2, describes the Supper as remembrance of the one offering and rejects offering Christ there for the forgiveness of sins. Both appeal to His one sacrifice, while differing over the meaning of the church’s celebration.
passages.god_plan_html:
Psalm 110:1 supplies the picture of the exalted Lord with His enemies under His feet. 1 Corinthians 15:24–28 develops the expectation that Christ’s reign ends in the defeat of every enemy, including death.

The sacrifice is complete while the full display of His victory is still awaited. That distinction helps us understand why Hebrews can assure believers about forgiveness and still direct them toward a future Day.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Worship as the Early Church Knew It identifies Christ’s sacrifice as the once-for-all offering that fulfills the earlier sacrifices. It distinguishes that saving work from believers offering their lives in grateful service, as in Romans 12:1. Our obedience responds to His completed offering; it does not make another payment for sin.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

passages.title: Hebrews 10:12
passages.section_title: Why does the writer emphasize that Christ sat down?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 But when this Priest had offered for all time one sacrifice for sins, He sat down at the right hand of God.
paragraphs: 12 But when this Priest had offered for all time one sacrifice for sins, He sat down at the right hand of God.

passages.context_html:
This verse belongs to the comparison in 10:11–18. Priests stand day after day offering sacrifices that cannot take away sins; Christ offers one sacrifice with lasting effect and sits at God’s right hand.

The seated position joins completed sacrifice with royal honor. The next verse points toward His enemies becoming His footstool, drawing on Psalm 110:1. It does not mean He has stopped caring for His people or that His continuing priestly ministry has ended.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley emphasize the contrast between repeated offerings and Christ’s sufficient sacrifice, together with the honor of His place beside God. Calvin explicitly rejects the idea that Christ is now idle.

Christians differ over how this relates to the Lord’s Supper. The Catholic Catechism, 1366–1367, teaches that the one sacrifice is made present in the Eucharist, the church’s celebration of the Lord’s Supper, without another death of Christ. The Westminster Confession, 29.1–2, describes the Supper as remembrance of the one offering and rejects offering Christ there for the forgiveness of sins. Both appeal to His one sacrifice, while differing over the meaning of the church’s celebration.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Worship as the Early Church Knew It identifies Christ’s sacrifice as the once-for-all offering that fulfills the earlier sacrifices. It distinguishes that saving work from believers offering their lives in grateful service, as in Romans 12:1. Our obedience responds to His completed offering; it does not make another payment for sin.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 8:34 joins Christ’s death, resurrection, place at God’s right hand and intercession for His people. Completed sacrifice and continuing care belong together.

1 Corinthians 15:24–28 looks toward the defeat of death under His reign. Christ’s seated authority directs hope toward that lasting victory.

passages.title: Hebrews 10:19-20
passages.section_title: Who has opened the way into God’s presence?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 Therefore, brothers, since we have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus, 20 by the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body,
paragraphs: 19 Therefore, brothers, since we have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus, 20 by the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body,

passages.context_html:
These verses introduce the response called for in 10:19–25. The confidence to approach God comes through Jesus’ blood and the new, living way opened through His body. The image returns to the curtain that restricted entrance into the sanctuary.

The next verses identify Jesus as the great priest over God’s house and call believers to draw near, hold to hope and encourage one another. Access through Christ leads into faith and care for others, rather than independence from the people He gathers.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley understand Jesus Himself as opening the way to God. Their explanations of the curtain center on His humanity and saving work, rather than a new physical sanctuary Christians must enter.

Traditions distinguish that access from the responsibilities of church ministers in different ways. The Catholic Catechism, 1544–1547, teaches that ordained priesthood participates in Christ’s one priesthood while all believers share a common priesthood. The Reformed Westminster Confession, 27.3–4, reserves administering baptism and the Lord’s Supper to ordained ministers while attributing their effectiveness to the Spirit and Christ’s promise. These accounts should be distinguished from a claim that a minister supplies a second saving sacrifice.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Who Shepherds the Church? understands these verses as direct access to God through Christ. Believers do not need a human priestly class standing between them and God. The study also preserves the work of elders who teach, correct and care for people; that service does not replace Christ’s unique role.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 2:18–22 describes both Jewish and Gentile believers having access to the Father through Christ in one Spirit and belonging to one household. The opened way serves God’s purpose of gathering His people together.

Romans 8:31–39 grounds confidence in God’s gift of His Son and Christ’s continuing intercession. Drawing near depends on that saving love, rather than achieving a standing Jesus has failed to provide.

passages.title: Hebrews 10:19-25
passages.section_title: How should we respond to the access Christ has opened?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 Therefore, brothers, since we have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus, 20 by the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body, 21 and since we have a great priest over the house of God, 22 let us draw near with a sincere heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled to cleanse us from a guilty conscience and our bodies washed with pure water. 23 Let us hold resolutely to the hope we profess, for He who promised is faithful. 24 And let us consider how to spur one another on to love and good deeds. 25 Let us not neglect meeting together, as some have made a habit, but let us encourage one another, and all the more as you see the Day approaching.
paragraphs: 19 Therefore, brothers, since we have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus, 20 by the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body, 21 and since we have a great priest over the house of God, 22 let us draw near with a sincere heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled to cleanse us from a guilty conscience and our bodies washed with pure water.

23 Let us hold resolutely to the hope we profess, for He who promised is faithful. 24 And let us consider how to spur one another on to love and good deeds. 25 Let us not neglect meeting together, as some have made a habit, but let us encourage one another, and all the more as you see the Day approaching.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The writer now calls for a response to Christ’s priesthood and sacrifice. Because Jesus has opened the way into God’s presence, believers are invited to draw near sincerely and with assurance. The confidence rests on Him.

Three calls shape the paragraph: draw near, hold firmly to hope, and consider how to encourage one another toward love and good deeds. The second call explicitly rests on God’s faithfulness to His promise.

The third call gives meeting together a purpose. Believers need one another’s encouragement as the Day approaches. The passage addresses a habit of abandoning the gathering; it does not reduce Christian care to having one’s attendance recorded.

The sprinkling and washing language recalls cleansing for access to the sanctuary. Christ opens that access for people whose hearts and lives are being cleansed, rather than inviting a performance that hides an unchanged heart.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin, Wesley and the USCCB notes understand the paragraph as a call to sincere approach, enduring hope and mutual care. Confidence in Christ strengthens life together.

They differ over the bodies washed with pure water in verse 22. The USCCB notes understand a reference to baptism. Calvin acknowledges that common reading but favors cleansing by God’s Spirit, drawing on Ezekiel 36:25. Wesley emphasizes a holy way of life in place of merely outward washings. These readings share an emphasis on cleansing while differing over the water image.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 2:18–22 joins access to the Father through Christ with believers becoming one household and a dwelling for God. Access is personal, and it also brings people together.

Ephesians 4:11–16 describes the whole body growing as its members serve one another. Hebrews’ call to encourage love and good deeds fits that purpose: a people growing together toward Christ while awaiting Him.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Who Shepherds the Church? understands these verses as direct access to God through Christ. Believers do not need a human priestly class standing between them and God. The study also preserves the work of elders who teach, correct and care for people; that service does not replace Christ’s unique role.

passages.title: Hebrews 10:26-31
passages.section_title: Why is rejecting Christ’s sacrifice so serious?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 26 If we deliberately go on sinning after we have received the knowledge of the truth, no further sacrifice for sins remains, 27 but only a fearful expectation of judgment and of raging fire that will consume all adversaries. 28 Anyone who rejected the law of Moses died without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses. 29 How much more severely do you think one deserves to be punished who has trampled on the Son of God, profaned the blood of the covenant that sanctified him, and insulted the Spirit of grace? 30 For we know Him who said, “Vengeance is Mine; I will repay,” and again, “The Lord will judge His people.” 31 It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.
paragraphs: 26 If we deliberately go on sinning after we have received the knowledge of the truth, no further sacrifice for sins remains, 27 but only a fearful expectation of judgment and of raging fire that will consume all adversaries.

28 Anyone who rejected the law of Moses died without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses. 29 How much more severely do you think one deserves to be punished who has trampled on the Son of God, profaned the blood of the covenant that sanctified him, and insulted the Spirit of grace? 30 For we know Him who said, “Vengeance is Mine; I will repay,” and again, “The Lord will judge His people.” 31 It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The warning follows the invitation to draw near, hold to hope and encourage one another. Verse 29 describes the rejection in severe terms: trampling on the Son, treating the covenant blood as unholy and insulting the Spirit of grace. The concern reaches beyond a believer discovering another failure and sincerely seeking help.

No further sacrifice remains because the letter has identified Christ’s offering as the sufficient one. The warning cannot be answered by finding a different sacrifice to replace Him. It speaks of judgment rather than minimizing the rejection.

The comparison with Moses’ law moves from a lesser case to a greater one. Deuteronomy 17:2–7 describes the two-or-three-witness requirement in a case of turning to other gods. The writer then draws on Deuteronomy 32:35–36 to underline that judgment belongs to God.

The person is described as having received knowledge of the truth and as sanctified by the covenant blood. Those descriptions help explain why Christians differ over whether the warning concerns someone who was truly saved. Both the descriptions and the threatened judgment matter to understanding it.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians differ over the status of the person described and the judgment threatened. Calvin reads the offense as a total repudiation of Christ, rather than every particular sin, and the outcome as eternal loss. He also speaks of God separating hypocrites from the truly faithful. The Reformed Westminster Confession, 17, teaches that those truly brought into saving faith are preserved to the end, while still capable of grave sin and discipline.

Wesley also understands a deliberate, total abandonment of Christ. He takes the person described as having previously been justified and reads the warning as a real danger of losing that saving relationship. This differs from the Reformed account of final perseverance.

In a Free Grace reading, J. Paul Tanner understands the people warned as genuine believers who can abandon their confession yet remain eternally saved. He proposes severe consequences at Christ’s judgment, including lost reward and a forfeited role in the coming kingdom. His paper presents this as an interpretation requiring explanation, rather than a view shared by all Christians.

The Catholic Catechism, 162, teaches that faith can be lost. It also teaches the possibility of reconciliation after serious post-baptismal sin in 1446. That is relevant doctrinal context, rather than the Catechism’s direct explanation of every phrase here. The warning should not be turned into a claim that every knowingly committed sin makes repentance impossible.
passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 12:22–25 later joins the new covenant, Jesus and His blood with another warning not to refuse the One who speaks. Grace and the call to heed God’s voice appear together within the letter’s purpose.

Romans 12:19–21 uses the same statement about God’s vengeance to forbid personal revenge and call believers to overcome evil with good. A warning about divine judgment does not give people permission to punish others in God’s name.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Hebrews 10:32-39
passages.section_title: What helps faith endure when following Christ is costly?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 32 Remember the early days that you were in the light. In those days, you endured a great conflict in the face of suffering. 33 Sometimes you were publicly exposed to ridicule and persecution; at other times you were partners with those who were so treated. 34 You sympathized with those in prison and joyfully accepted the confiscation of your property, knowing that you yourselves had a better and permanent possession. 35 So do not throw away your confidence; it holds a great reward. 36 You need to persevere, so that after you have done the will of God, you will receive what He has promised. 37 For, “In just a little while, He who is coming will come and will not delay. 38 But My righteous one will live by faith; and if he shrinks back, I will take no pleasure in him.” 39 But we are not of those who shrink back and are destroyed, but of those who have faith and preserve their souls.
paragraphs: 32 Remember the early days that you were in the light. In those days, you endured a great conflict in the face of suffering. 33 Sometimes you were publicly exposed to ridicule and persecution; at other times you were partners with those who were so treated. 34 You sympathized with those in prison and joyfully accepted the confiscation of your property, knowing that you yourselves had a better and permanent possession.
35 So do not throw away your confidence; it holds a great reward. 36 You need to persevere, so that after you have done the will of God, you will receive what He has promised.

37 For, “In just a little while, He who is coming will come and will not delay. 38 But My righteous one will live by faith; and if he shrinks back, I will take no pleasure in him.” 39 But we are not of those who shrink back and are destroyed, but of those who have faith and preserve their souls.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The writer turns from warning to encouragement by reminding the readers of their earlier faithfulness. They endured public abuse, stood beside others who suffered, cared for prisoners and accepted the loss of property because they knew they had something lasting.

The call is to keep that confidence and persevere in doing God’s will. Earlier courage is a reason to continue, rather than a reason to assume the remaining journey no longer matters.

The closing words draw on Habakkuk 2:3–4: God’s promise calls for waiting and a life of faith. Hebrews directs that expectation toward the One who is coming. Its final contrast is between shrinking back to destruction and faith that preserves life.

The writer places himself alongside his readers in the hopeful final sentence. He expects faith to endure, while his call to endurance remains real. That prepares for chapter 11’s examples of people who trusted God before receiving everything He promised.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley both read the passage as a serious call to continuing faith with eternal life in view. Calvin explains that receiving reward is consistent with relying on God’s mercy, and recognizes that joy in God’s promise can coexist with real grief over loss.

Their broader accounts of perseverance differ, as in the preceding warning. The Free Grace reading represented by Tanner instead emphasizes the lasting reward and inheritance a believer can forfeit without losing eternal salvation. These differences should not hide the shared call to endure, help those suffering and trust God’s promise.
passages.god_plan_html:
Matthew 6:19–21 directs disciples toward lasting treasure rather than possessions that can be taken away. Romans 8:18–25 describes present suffering alongside hope for the redemption still to come.

The next chapter develops the same connection through earlier believers: some received remarkable help, and others suffered without receiving the final promise in their lifetime. God’s purpose gives hope beyond immediate relief, without calling present cruelty good.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Hebrews 11:1-3
passages.section_title: How does faith help us trust what we cannot yet see?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now faith is the assurance of what we hope for and the certainty of what we do not see. 2 This is why the ancients were commended. 3 By faith we understand that the universe was formed at God’s command, so that what is seen was not made out of what was visible.
paragraphs: 1 Now faith is the assurance of what we hope for and the certainty of what we do not see. 2 This is why the ancients were commended.
3 By faith we understand that the universe was formed at God’s command, so that what is seen was not made out of what was visible.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Chapter 11 continues the call to enduring faith at the end of chapter 10. The writer describes confidence in what God promises and certainty about realities beyond our present sight. The people who follow illustrate that trust through their choices.

The word translated assurance can describe firm confidence. The word translated certainty can express proof or conviction. Here they describe reliance on God, rather than a wish made true by the strength of a person’s feelings.

The first example concerns creation: by faith we understand that the universe was formed at God’s command. Faith concerns more than the future alone; this verse also looks back to an act of God the readers did not witness. The visible world depends on Him.

This introduction is followed by people who acted on God’s word, waited for His promises and sometimes suffered for trusting Him. The chapter’s concern is faith that endures through those circumstances.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin, Wesley and the USCCB notes read these verses in connection with the endurance the readers need. Faith shapes their response to God’s promises before the final outcome is visible.

There is a difference in how Calvin and Wesley explain the last part of verse 3. Wesley emphasizes God creating without first needing any existing material, then forming the world. Calvin instead understands the visible creation as displaying God’s invisible power and character. The BSB retains the wording that what is seen was not made out of what was visible; the commentators’ explanations should be distinguished from the translation itself.
passages.god_plan_html:
Colossians 1:15–20 connects creation with Christ and then with reconciliation through His cross. Hebrews 1:1–3 likewise joins God speaking through the Son with His creating and sustaining work.

The God whose promise invites faith is the God who made and sustains the world. Creation and redemption belong within His purpose, giving the chapter’s hope a foundation beyond the changing circumstances of its readers.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Hebrews 11:4-6
passages.section_title: What do Abel and Enoch show us about pleasing God?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 4 By faith Abel offered God a better sacrifice than Cain did. By faith he was commended as righteous when God gave approval to his gifts. And by faith he still speaks, even though he is dead. 5 By faith Enoch was taken up so that he did not see death: “He could not be found, because God had taken him away.” For before he was taken, he was commended as one who pleased God. 6 And without faith it is impossible to please God. For anyone who approaches Him must believe that He exists and that He rewards those who earnestly seek Him.
paragraphs: 4 By faith Abel offered God a better sacrifice than Cain did. By faith he was commended as righteous when God gave approval to his gifts. And by faith he still speaks, even though he is dead.

5 By faith Enoch was taken up so that he did not see death: “He could not be found, because God had taken him away.” For before he was taken, he was commended as one who pleased God. 6 And without faith it is impossible to please God. For anyone who approaches Him must believe that He exists and that He rewards those who earnestly seek Him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The first named examples are Abel and Enoch from Genesis 4 and Genesis 5. Abel’s offering was accepted through faith, and his witness continues after his death. Enoch was taken by God without seeing death and was commended as pleasing Him.

Their outcomes are strikingly different. Abel was killed by his brother, while Enoch was taken away. Both are presented as people of faith. The way a person’s earthly life ends is therefore not a simple measure of whether God approves of that person.

Verse 6 explains what unites them: drawing near to God requires believing that He exists and that seeking Him is not in vain. The word translated earnestly seek can describe seeking God and His favor. It is a personal response of trust, rather than merely agreeing that some divine being exists.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley both connect Abel’s acceptable offering with faith, while explaining its significance differently. Calvin emphasizes that Abel himself was accepted by God, rather than imagining that an animal offering pleased God on its own. Wesley understands the offering as expressing hope in the coming Redeemer and His sacrifice.

They also discuss Abel’s continuing voice. Calvin connects it with God responding to his blood crying from the ground. The USCCB note considers that possibility but favors the continuing witness of Abel’s story. Both readings recognize that his death did not erase his testimony.

Enoch’s example then leads to the shared point of verse 6: God is approached in faith, with confidence that He responds to those who seek Him. The passage does not promise that every faithful person will escape Abel’s suffering.
passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 12:22–24 explicitly brings Abel into its account of the new covenant, saying that Jesus’ sprinkled blood speaks a better word than Abel’s. The connection is made by Hebrews itself; it does not require treating every detail of Abel’s death as a prediction of Christ.

Enoch’s escape from death offers a related parallel to the hope in 1 Corinthians 15:51–54, where God’s people are changed and death is overcome. That is a parallel about God’s power over death, rather than a timetable drawn from Enoch’s story.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Prayer and Faith connects this verse with trusting and seeking God rather than finding the right wording for a request. It draws on Jesus crediting faith when people came to Him in different ways. Prayer is an expression of that trust, rather than a technique whose wording controls God’s response.

passages.title: Hebrews 11:6
passages.section_title: What does it mean to seek God in faith?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 And without faith it is impossible to please God. For anyone who approaches Him must believe that He exists and that He rewards those who earnestly seek Him.
paragraphs: 6 And without faith it is impossible to please God. For anyone who approaches Him must believe that He exists and that He rewards those who earnestly seek Him.

passages.context_html:
This verse explains why Enoch’s life pleased God and states a principle that runs through the chapter. Anyone approaching God must believe that He exists and that He rewards those who earnestly seek Him.

The word translated earnestly seek can describe seeking God and His favor. The verse joins belief with turning toward Him. It is more than a statement that God exists while He remains irrelevant to one’s life.

The surrounding examples keep the promise from becoming a guarantee of immediate comfort. Abel pleased God and was killed; Enoch pleased God and escaped death. Later in the chapter, some receive deliverance and others endure suffering while still awaiting what God promised.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Calvin, Wesley and the USCCB note connect the verse with approaching the real God in trust, rather than treating belief as a detached opinion. Calvin stresses confidence in God’s goodness; Wesley explicitly applies the approach to prayer and worship. The shared emphasis is that seeking Him matters and is not empty.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Prayer and Faith connects this verse with trusting and seeking God rather than finding the right wording for a request. It draws on Jesus crediting faith when people came to Him in different ways. Prayer is an expression of that trust, rather than a technique whose wording controls God’s response.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
In Luke 18:1–8, Jesus teaches continued prayer, speaks of God bringing justice and asks whether the Son of Man will find faith when He comes. Trust in God and waiting for His action belong together.

Hebrews 11:35–40 shows why that waiting matters: some faithful people suffered and died without receiving the final promise in their lifetime. God’s response reaches beyond present circumstances into the completion He has prepared for His people.

passages.title: Hebrews 11:7
passages.section_title: How did Noah respond before the flood was visible?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 By faith Noah, when warned about things not yet seen, in godly fear built an ark to save his family. By faith he condemned the world and became heir of the righteousness that comes by faith.
paragraphs: 7 By faith Noah, when warned about things not yet seen, in godly fear built an ark to save his family. By faith he condemned the world and became heir of the righteousness that comes by faith.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Noah continues the examples drawn from early Genesis. God warned him about a judgment still to come, and he responded with godly fear by building the ark. His faith took the form of action before the danger arrived.

Genesis 6:13–22 records both the warning and God’s provision for Noah’s household. Hebrews connects his response with the righteousness that comes by faith. The ark was not a project Noah invented to make God accept him.

His obedience also exposed the unbelief of the world around him. That is the sense in which his faith condemned the world: the contrast became visible through his response to God. The verse does not describe Noah carrying out private punishment against other people.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Calvin and Wesley understand Noah’s preparation as the visible response of faith to God’s warning. Calvin emphasizes obedience flowing from trust in God’s promise of deliverance; Wesley emphasizes the contrast with those who neither believed nor feared. The shared point is that Noah took God seriously before seeing the flood.
passages.god_plan_html:
Matthew 24:37–39 explicitly connects Noah’s days with the coming of the Son of Man. Jesus uses the example to call people to readiness when ordinary life can conceal the seriousness of a coming reckoning.

The connection concerns heeding God’s warning. It does not give readers Noah’s date or a calculation for Christ’s return. Faith prepares by listening and responding to God.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Hebrews 11:8-12
passages.section_title: How did Abraham and Sarah trust a promise still unfolding?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 By faith Abraham, when called to go to a place he would later receive as his inheritance, obeyed and went, without knowing where he was going. 9 By faith he dwelt in the promised land as a stranger in a foreign country. He lived in tents, as did Isaac and Jacob, who were heirs with him of the same promise. 10 For he was looking forward to the city with foundations, whose architect and builder is God. 11 By faith Sarah, even though she was barren and beyond the proper age, was enabled to conceive a child, because she considered Him faithful who had promised. 12 And so from one man, and he as good as dead, came descendants as numerous as the stars in the sky and as countless as the sand on the seashore.
paragraphs: 8 By faith Abraham, when called to go to a place he would later receive as his inheritance, obeyed and went, without knowing where he was going. 9 By faith he dwelt in the promised land as a stranger in a foreign country. He lived in tents, as did Isaac and Jacob, who were heirs with him of the same promise. 10 For he was looking forward to the city with foundations, whose architect and builder is God.

11 By faith Sarah, even though she was barren and beyond the proper age, was enabled to conceive a child, because she considered Him faithful who had promised. 12 And so from one man, and he as good as dead, came descendants as numerous as the stars in the sky and as countless as the sand on the seashore.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Abraham obeyed God’s call without knowing where the journey would lead. Even after reaching the promised land, he lived there as a stranger. Isaac and Jacob shared the promise and the same life in tents. The promise was real before they possessed its fullness.

His expectation reached beyond a temporary campsite to a city whose builder is God. That expectation helps explain why living as a foreigner did not make God’s promise meaningless to him.

Sarah’s example brings the same trust into a different difficulty. Though barren and beyond the usual age for bearing a child, she considered the One who promised faithful. The account is grounded in Genesis 18:9–15 and 21:1–7, where her initial laughter and Isaac’s birth are both recorded.

The many descendants came from a beginning that seemed humanly impossible. Hebrews celebrates God’s faithfulness and the trust that received His promise. It does not give every couple the particular promise made to Abraham and Sarah.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley read Abraham’s journey and life in tents as faith continuing beyond a first act of obedience. Both connect the city with the lasting home God provides.

Both also recognize the question raised by Sarah’s earlier laughter. Calvin understands her faith as overcoming the unbelief exposed by God’s rebuke; Wesley likewise notes that she first laughed at the promise. They do not treat a moment of doubt as the whole story of her response to God.
passages.god_plan_html:
Galatians 3:6–9, 13–14 connects Abraham’s promise with the gospel reaching the nations through Christ. Romans 4:16–25 joins Abraham’s confidence in God’s life-giving power with faith in the God who raised Jesus.

The family’s unlikely beginning therefore belongs within a purpose larger than their own household. God’s blessing reaches others through Christ, and the promise teaches trust in His power to give life.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Hebrews 11:13-16
passages.section_title: What were they still waiting for when they died?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 All these people died in faith, without having received the things they were promised. However, they saw them and welcomed them from afar. And they acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth. 14 Now those who say such things show that they are seeking a country of their own. 15 If they had been thinking of the country they had left, they would have had opportunity to return. 16 Instead, they were longing for a better country, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for He has prepared a city for them.
paragraphs: 13 All these people died in faith, without having received the things they were promised. However, they saw them and welcomed them from afar. And they acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth. 14 Now those who say such things show that they are seeking a country of their own.

15 If they had been thinking of the country they had left, they would have had opportunity to return. 16 Instead, they were longing for a better country, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for He has prepared a city for them.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The writer pauses to reflect on the patriarchs just described. They died in faith without receiving the full reality of what God had promised. This does not deny that Isaac had been born or that God had already helped them; it distinguishes the beginning of fulfillment from its completion.

They acknowledged being strangers and exiles. If their hope had simply been a return to the country they left, they could have gone back. Instead, they longed for the better, heavenly country God had prepared.

The assurance at the end is personal: God is not ashamed to be called their God. Death did not cancel the relationship or make His promise empty. Their hope rested on what He would provide, beyond what their present circumstances could show.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley understand the better country as the heavenly home promised to God’s people. Both read the patriarchs’ unsettled earthly lives in light of that lasting hope.

Calvin places particular emphasis on the difference between their distant view of Christ’s kingdom and the clearer knowledge available after His coming. Wesley emphasizes their expectation of eternal glory. These emphases allow for real blessings already received while recognizing that the promised completion was still ahead.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Luke 20:37–38, Jesus appeals to God calling Himself the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob when explaining resurrection. The same enduring relationship named here becomes part of Jesus’ case that death is not the final word.

Revelation 21:1–5 describes the city from God and His dwelling with His people, where death and mourning are removed. This supplies a larger picture of the lasting home for which Hebrews teaches believers to hope, without requiring a complete timetable from these four verses.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Hebrews 11:17-19
passages.section_title: How could Abraham trust God when Isaac’s life was at stake?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac on the altar. He who had received the promises was ready to offer his one and only son, 18 even though God had said to him, “Through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned.” 19 Abraham reasoned that God could raise the dead, and in a sense, he did receive Isaac back from death.
paragraphs: 17 By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac on the altar. He who had received the promises was ready to offer his one and only son, 18 even though God had said to him, “Through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned.” 19 Abraham reasoned that God could raise the dead, and in a sense, he did receive Isaac back from death.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The account returns to Abraham’s test in Genesis 22:1–18. Isaac was the son through whom God had promised descendants, yet Abraham was asked to offer him. The tension concerned God’s own promise, as well as Abraham’s love for his son.

The word translated one and only can describe someone unique or the only one of a kind. Abraham also had Ishmael; here Isaac’s unique place as the promised heir is in view. The phrase does not erase the earlier account of his family.

Hebrews supplies Abraham’s reasoning: God could raise the dead. His trust did not depend on knowing how God would resolve the test. It depended on God being able to keep His promise even beyond death.

Isaac was not actually killed. God stopped Abraham and provided a ram instead. Hebrews describes receiving Isaac back as, in a sense, a return from death. The word behind that expression can describe a comparison or figure; it has prompted the readings below.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley emphasize that Isaac’s rescue was like receiving him back from death, although he had not literally died. Both understand Abraham’s trust in resurrection as the key to the test.

The USCCB note takes the picture further by understanding Isaac’s return as a symbol of Christ’s resurrection, while acknowledging the reading that it simply describes Isaac’s rescue figuratively. Calvin allows a connection with Christ but distinguishes that broader parallel from what he takes as this phrase’s immediate meaning.
passages.god_plan_html:
A supported parallel connects the beloved son in this account with God giving His Son. Romans 8:32 describes God not sparing His own Son but giving Him for us. John 10:17–18 describes Jesus willingly laying down His life and taking it up again.

The difference matters alongside the likeness: Isaac was spared, while Jesus actually died and rose. Hebrews explicitly states Abraham’s trust in God’s power to raise the dead; the father-and-son connection is a parallel drawn alongside that statement. It does not establish every detail of Isaac’s age, thoughts or response.
passages.current_position_html: Our related study Who is The Angel of the Lord? reads the Angel who stops Abraham in Genesis 22 as the eternal Son acting before His earthly life as Jesus. That is the study’s conclusion about the Genesis account behind these verses. Hebrews itself concentrates here on Abraham trusting God’s promise and His power to raise the dead.

deeper_study.title: Who is The Angel of the Lord?

passages.title: Hebrews 11:20-22
passages.section_title: How did their faith look beyond their own lifetimes?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 20 By faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau concerning the future. 21 By faith Jacob, when he was dying, blessed each of Joseph’s sons and worshiped as he leaned on the top of his staff. 22 By faith Joseph, when his end was near, spoke about the exodus of the Israelites and gave instructions about his bones.
paragraphs: 20 By faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau concerning the future. 21 By faith Jacob, when he was dying, blessed each of Joseph’s sons and worshiped as he leaned on the top of his staff. 22 By faith Joseph, when his end was near, spoke about the exodus of the Israelites and gave instructions about his bones.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The final examples from the patriarchs concern blessings and instructions given near the end of life. Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau concerning the future. Jacob blessed Joseph’s sons and worshiped. Joseph spoke of Israel’s coming departure from Egypt and gave instructions about his bones.

These actions treated God’s promise as something that would continue beyond the speaker’s lifetime. Joseph’s instructions in Genesis 50:24–25 are especially clear: God would attend to His people and bring them from Egypt to the land He had promised.

Hebrews draws together Jacob’s blessings in Genesis 48 and his worship near death. There is a wording difference to notice: Genesis 47:31 in the BSB describes the head of his bed, while Hebrews describes the top of his staff. The common emphasis is his worship, with his hope turned toward God’s continuing promise.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley understand these blessings and burial instructions as faith looking beyond present possession. The fathers did not control the future, but they trusted the God who had promised it.

Calvin emphasizes Joseph’s instructions as encouragement to his people to expect deliverance from Egypt, rather than a belief that one burial location had power in itself. Wesley likewise connects the bones with the land of promise. The point is the testimony to God’s promise, rather than a new rule about where every believer must be buried.
passages.god_plan_html:
Exodus 13:19 records Moses carrying Joseph’s bones when Israel left Egypt. The instruction given in faith becomes part of the later account of God’s deliverance.

Galatians 3:16, 29 connects the promise to Abraham with Christ and those who belong to Him. God’s purpose extends beyond one generation’s experience: later people share in the promise on which earlier believers relied.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Hebrews 11:23-27
passages.section_title: Why did Moses choose the people of God over Egypt’s treasures?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 23 By faith Moses’ parents hid him for three months after his birth, because they saw that he was a beautiful child, and they were unafraid of the king’s edict. 24 By faith Moses, when he was grown, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter. 25 He chose to suffer oppression with God’s people rather than to experience the fleeting enjoyment of sin. 26 He valued disgrace for Christ above the treasures of Egypt, for he was looking ahead to his reward. 27 By faith Moses left Egypt, not fearing the king’s anger; he persevered because he saw Him who is invisible.
paragraphs: 23 By faith Moses’ parents hid him for three months after his birth, because they saw that he was a beautiful child, and they were unafraid of the king’s edict.

24 By faith Moses, when he was grown, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter. 25 He chose to suffer oppression with God’s people rather than to experience the fleeting enjoyment of sin. 26 He valued disgrace for Christ above the treasures of Egypt, for he was looking ahead to his reward. 27 By faith Moses left Egypt, not fearing the king’s anger; he persevered because he saw Him who is invisible.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The account of Moses begins with his parents’ faith. They protected him for three months despite the king’s command. Hebrews then turns to Moses as an adult, choosing identification with God’s oppressed people over the privileges of Pharaoh’s household.

The contrast concerns what he valued. Passing enjoyment and Egypt’s treasures were weighed against disgrace for Christ and the reward ahead. Hebrews reads Moses’ solidarity with God’s people in relation to Christ, long before Jesus’ earthly life.

The reference to leaving Egypt has prompted discussion because Exodus 2:14–15 describes Moses being afraid and fleeing, while the later exodus shows him confronting Pharaoh and leading Israel out. The readings below explain the difference.

He persevered as seeing the invisible God. That recalls the chapter’s opening concern with what cannot presently be seen: faith gave God’s reality more weight than the king’s anger.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley understand Moses’ departure in verse 27 as the later departure with Israel. Calvin considers the earlier flight before favoring the later event; Wesley explicitly distinguishes the earlier occasion when Moses feared Pharaoh. The USCCB note instead highlights the difference between Hebrews’ reason for leaving and the flight described in Exodus 2.

They also explain disgrace for Christ with different emphases. Calvin speaks of the suffering shared by Christ’s people and their Head. Wesley understands Moses as acting in expectation of the coming Messiah. Both connect his costly choice with God’s purpose, rather than treating suffering as valuable merely because it hurts.
passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 7:35–37 places Moses within the larger story of God sending a deliverer and recalls his promise of a prophet like him. Hebrews 3:1–6 distinguishes Moses’ faithful service in God’s house from Christ’s authority over it as Son.

Moses belongs within that movement toward Christ. His example calls readers to value belonging to God’s people when it carries a cost, while recognizing the greater One to whom their faith now looks.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Hebrews 11:28-31
passages.section_title: What joined the Passover, the sea crossing and Rahab’s rescue?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 28 By faith he kept the Passover and the sprinkling of blood, so that the destroyer of the firstborn would not touch Israel’s own firstborn. 29 By faith the people passed through the Red Sea as on dry land; but when the Egyptians tried to follow, they were drowned. 30 By faith the walls of Jericho fell, after the people had marched around them for seven days. 31 By faith the prostitute Rahab, because she welcomed the spies in peace, did not perish with those who were disobedient.
paragraphs: 28 By faith he kept the Passover and the sprinkling of blood, so that the destroyer of the firstborn would not touch Israel’s own firstborn. 29 By faith the people passed through the Red Sea as on dry land; but when the Egyptians tried to follow, they were drowned.

30 By faith the walls of Jericho fell, after the people had marched around them for seven days. 31 By faith the prostitute Rahab, because she welcomed the spies in peace, did not perish with those who were disobedient.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The examples move through Israel’s departure from Egypt and entrance into the promised land. Moses kept the Passover in reliance on God’s word about the firstborn. The people then passed through the Red Sea, while the pursuing Egyptians drowned.

At Jericho, the people followed God’s instructions before the walls fell. Joshua 6:1–5 records the promise and the unusual marching instructions. The result is credited to faith in God, rather than to the strength of their siege methods.

Rahab supplies a personal example from within the city facing judgment. Joshua 2:8–14 records her confession that Israel’s God rules heaven and earth, and her appeal for mercy for her family. She protected the spies, and Joshua 6:22–25 records her rescue.

These events join trust with response: people acted on God’s word before seeing the outcome. Rahab’s inclusion also shows that the chapter’s account of faith reaches beyond Israel’s leaders and patriarchs.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley understand these events as faith expressed through action. Calvin distinguishes the immediate point about the Passover—trusting God’s promised protection—from the further connection with Christ. He accepts that connection while keeping the writer’s immediate example in view.

Both recognize Rahab’s faith in her welcome of the spies. Calvin emphasizes the grace shown to an outsider whose former life did not make her an obvious candidate for honor. The chapter commends her trust and response without offering a blanket judgment that every action in her history was right.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Corinthians 5:7 explicitly identifies Christ as the Passover lamb. 1 Corinthians 10:1–6 likewise connects the sea crossing with Israel’s relationship to Moses and uses that history to instruct Christians. These connections come from the New Testament itself.

Rahab is also named in Matthew 1:5, within the family line leading to Jesus. James 2:25–26 names her protection of the messengers when explaining faith expressed in action. Her rescue belongs within the larger account of God’s mercy and the people He gathers.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Hebrews 11:32-38
passages.section_title: Does faith always end in visible victory?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 32 And what more shall I say? Time will not allow me to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets, 33 who through faith conquered kingdoms, administered justice, and gained what was promised; who shut the mouths of lions, 34 quenched the raging fire, and escaped the edge of the sword; who gained strength from weakness, became mighty in battle, and put foreign armies to flight. 35 Women received back their dead, raised to life again. Others were tortured and refused their release, so that they might gain a better resurrection. 36 Still others endured mocking and flogging, and even chains and imprisonment. 37 They were stoned, they were sawed in two, they were put to death by the sword. They went around in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, oppressed, and mistreated. 38 The world was not worthy of them. They wandered in deserts and mountains, and hid in caves and holes in the ground.
paragraphs: 32 And what more shall I say? Time will not allow me to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets, 33 who through faith conquered kingdoms, administered justice, and gained what was promised; who shut the mouths of lions, 34 quenched the raging fire, and escaped the edge of the sword; who gained strength from weakness, became mighty in battle, and put foreign armies to flight.

35 Women received back their dead, raised to life again. Others were tortured and refused their release, so that they might gain a better resurrection. 36 Still others endured mocking and flogging, and even chains and imprisonment. 37 They were stoned, they were sawed in two, they were put to death by the sword. They went around in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, oppressed, and mistreated. 38 The world was not worthy of them. They wandered in deserts and mountains, and hid in caves and holes in the ground.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The writer says there is not enough time to tell every story. He names judges, David, Samuel and the prophets, then gathers examples of victory, justice, deliverance and strength given in weakness.

Some descriptions recall well-known accounts: God protecting Daniel from lions in Daniel 6:19–23, and the three men from the furnace in Daniel 3:21–28. Women receiving their children back recalls 1 Kings 17:17–24 and 2 Kings 4:32–37. Hebrews does not attach a name to every item.

The direction then changes. Others were tortured, imprisoned, killed or driven into poverty and hiding. They are included among the faithful, alongside those who received remarkable deliverance. Their suffering does not put them outside God’s approval.

The better resurrection sets their hope beyond a temporary escape from death. The world rejected people whom the writer calls worthy of honor. Faithfulness could be sustained without the visible outcome others had received.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley both emphasize faith enduring through suffering as well as faith receiving deliverance. Calvin notes the striking contrast between people rescued by miracles and those who seemed abandoned, while recognizing faith in both groups.

They explain the better resurrection with different emphases. Calvin connects it with lasting life rather than accepting deliverance at the cost of denying God. Wesley emphasizes a greater reward in the resurrection. Neither reads the sufferings as proof that these people lacked faith.
passages.god_plan_html:
John 11:25–26 locates resurrection and life in Jesus Himself. 1 Corinthians 15:20–26 distinguishes His resurrection as the beginning of a victory that ends in death’s defeat.

The earlier restorations of children to their mothers were real mercies, while the lasting hope reaches further than returning to another span of mortal life. Hebrews’ sufferers trust the God whose purpose is completed through Christ, even when their own story contains no rescue before death.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Hebrews 11:39-40
passages.section_title: How does God bring their story and ours together?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 39 These were all commended for their faith, yet they did not receive what was promised. 40 God had planned something better for us, so that together with us they would be made perfect.
paragraphs: 39 These were all commended for their faith, yet they did not receive what was promised. 40 God had planned something better for us, so that together with us they would be made perfect.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The chapter closes by gathering all its examples into one statement. These people were commended for faith, yet they had not received the promised completion. Their lives were part of a purpose that also includes the writer and his readers.

This does not contradict verse 33, where some gained what was promised. God truly fulfilled particular promises along the way, while the full completion remained ahead. The earlier gifts did not exhaust everything He intended.

The phrase together with us keeps their story from becoming a separate history of spiritual achievement. God has provided something better that joins His people across generations. The next paragraph turns that shared history into a call to endure while looking to Jesus.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin, Wesley and the USCCB note explain the timing of this completion differently. Calvin emphasizes the fuller revelation and fulfillment brought by Christ’s coming, through which God unites the earlier faithful with later believers. Wesley looks toward the perfected life they will share together in heaven.

The USCCB note emphasizes the earlier faithful receiving their recompense through Christ’s completed saving work, while Christians still struggling have yet to possess that fullness. These readings all connect the generations through God’s purpose, but they should not be flattened into one agreed timetable for every part of the promise.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 1:9–10 describes God’s purpose to bring all things together in Christ. Ephesians 2:14–22 shows that purpose bringing Jewish and Gentile believers into one household with access to the Father.

Hebrews places earlier and later believers within the one story God is bringing to completion. The call that follows is to run with endurance while looking to Jesus, whose own suffering and exaltation give that shared hope its center.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Hebrews 12:1-3
passages.section_title: Where do we look when the race becomes hard?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Therefore, since we are surrounded by such a great cloud of witnesses, let us throw off every encumbrance and the sin that so easily entangles, and let us run with endurance the race set out for us. 2 Let us fix our eyes on Jesus, the author and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy set before Him endured the cross, scorning its shame, and sat down at the right hand of the throne of God. 3 Consider Him who endured such hostility from sinners, so that you will not grow weary and lose heart.
paragraphs: 1 Therefore, since we are surrounded by such a great cloud of witnesses, let us throw off every encumbrance and the sin that so easily entangles, and let us run with endurance the race set out for us.

2 Let us fix our eyes on Jesus, the author and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy set before Him endured the cross, scorning its shame, and sat down at the right hand of the throne of God. 3 Consider Him who endured such hostility from sinners, so that you will not grow weary and lose heart.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The therefore draws the chapter 11 examples into the readers’ own lives. They have a great cloud of witnesses whose stories show faith enduring. Now they are called to put aside whatever weighs them down, reject entangling sin and continue the race set before them.

The focus then moves to Jesus. The word translated author can describe a leader or one who goes before others. He is both the One to whom faith looks and the supreme example of endurance, having faced the cross and its shame before taking His place beside God.

The call to consider His suffering is meant to keep weary people from losing heart. The passage directs attention toward His faithfulness; it does not ask readers to measure their pain against one another to decide whose struggle deserves care.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley emphasize the earlier believers’ witness to the power of faith and the encouragement their examples supply. Jesus remains the center of the race.

The place of the saints in prayer is understood differently. The Catholic Catechism, 2683, uses the cloud-of-witnesses picture when teaching that saints continue to care and pray for those on earth, and that Christians should ask for their intercession. The Reformed Westminster Confession, 21.2–3, directs religious worship, including prayer, to God alone through Christ. Both honor earlier believers, while differing over their continuing role in prayer.

Calvin also offers a different reading of the joy in verse 2. He prefers the sense that Jesus accepted suffering instead of the earthly ease He could have chosen, while allowing the reading that He endured for the joyful outcome ahead. Wesley emphasizes that future joy. The BSB presents the latter wording.
passages.god_plan_html:
Philippians 2:5–11 joins Christ’s willing obedience and death with His exaltation. Endurance belongs within the Son’s saving mission, rather than making suffering an end in itself.

2 Timothy 4:7–8 uses the race picture for a life brought to its finish while looking toward the Lord’s righteous judgment. The One who endured and now reigns gives the readers a lasting reason to keep following Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Hebrews 12:4-11
passages.section_title: How can God’s care be present in painful discipline?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 4 In your struggle against sin, you have not yet resisted to the point of shedding your blood. 5 And you have forgotten the exhortation that addresses you as sons: “My son, do not take lightly the discipline of the Lord, and do not lose heart when He rebukes you. 6 For the Lord disciplines the one He loves, and He chastises every son He receives.” 7 Endure suffering as discipline; God is treating you as sons. For what son is not disciplined by his father? 8 If you do not experience discipline like everyone else, then you are illegitimate children and not true sons. 9 Furthermore, we have all had earthly fathers who disciplined us, and we respected them. Should we not much more submit to the Father of our spirits and live? 10 Our fathers disciplined us for a short time as they thought best, but God disciplines us for our good, so that we may share in His holiness. 11 No discipline seems enjoyable at the time, but painful. Later on, however, it yields a harvest of righteousness and peace to those who have been trained by it.
paragraphs: 4 In your struggle against sin, you have not yet resisted to the point of shedding your blood. 5 And you have forgotten the exhortation that addresses you as sons: “My son, do not take lightly the discipline of the Lord, and do not lose heart when He rebukes you. 6 For the Lord disciplines the one He loves, and He chastises every son He receives.”

7 Endure suffering as discipline; God is treating you as sons. For what son is not disciplined by his father? 8 If you do not experience discipline like everyone else, then you are illegitimate children and not true sons.

9 Furthermore, we have all had earthly fathers who disciplined us, and we respected them. Should we not much more submit to the Father of our spirits and live? 10 Our fathers disciplined us for a short time as they thought best, but God disciplines us for our good, so that we may share in His holiness. 11 No discipline seems enjoyable at the time, but painful. Later on, however, it yields a harvest of righteousness and peace to those who have been trained by it.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The readers have endured real hardship, as chapter 10 described, but their struggle has not yet reached the shedding of their blood. The writer recalls Proverbs 3:11–12, where God addresses the one He corrects as a loved son.
