The word translated discipline includes training and correction. The writer invites them to receive their difficult course as children being formed by a caring Father, rather than conclude from suffering that they have been abandoned.

The comparison also distinguishes God’s care from human judgment. Earthly parents disciplined as they thought best; God acts for His children’s good, so that they may share His holiness. His purpose is their growth toward righteousness and peace.

The passage calls discipline painful, rather than asking people to pretend it feels good. Its fruit comes through being trained by it. The writer states God’s good purpose without giving a separate explanation for every tragedy a person might experience.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin, Wesley and the USCCB notes understand the passage as assurance of fatherly care within the call to endurance. God’s discipline aims at His children’s good and holiness, rather than showing that He has stopped loving them.

Calvin distinguishes different purposes: suffering may correct sin, restrain it or train believers while they face persecution for the gospel. He does not describe every instance of suffering for Christ as punishment for a particular offense. Wesley also recognizes that earthly parents can err, in contrast with God’s good purpose.
passages.god_plan_html:
James 1:2–5 connects tested faith with endurance and maturity, while inviting people who need wisdom to ask God. Growing through difficulty includes dependence on Him.

Romans 8:28–29 places God’s work for His people’s good within His purpose of conforming them to His Son. Hebrews’ harvest of righteousness and peace belongs within that larger goal of a people shaped by Christ.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Hebrews 12:12-17
passages.section_title: How do we help one another keep going?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 Therefore strengthen your limp hands and weak knees. 13 Make straight paths for your feet, so that the lame may not be disabled, but rather healed. 14 Pursue peace with everyone, as well as holiness, without which no one will see the Lord. 15 See to it that no one falls short of the grace of God, and that no root of bitterness springs up to cause trouble and defile many. 16 See to it that no one is sexually immoral, or is godless like Esau, who for a single meal sold his birthright. 17 For you know that afterward, when he wanted to inherit the blessing, he was rejected. He could find no ground for repentance, though he sought the blessing with tears.
paragraphs: 12 Therefore strengthen your limp hands and weak knees. 13 Make straight paths for your feet, so that the lame may not be disabled, but rather healed. 14 Pursue peace with everyone, as well as holiness, without which no one will see the Lord.

15 See to it that no one falls short of the grace of God, and that no root of bitterness springs up to cause trouble and defile many. 16 See to it that no one is sexually immoral, or is godless like Esau, who for a single meal sold his birthright. 17 For you know that afterward, when he wanted to inherit the blessing, he was rejected. He could find no ground for repentance, though he sought the blessing with tears.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The response to discipline includes renewed strength and care for those struggling. The writer draws on Isaiah 35:3 and the straight-path picture in Proverbs 4:26–27. The aim is healing and a steady course, rather than allowing weakness to become a departure from the way.

Peace and holiness are to be pursued together. Care for people does not mean treating destructive conduct as harmless, and pursuing holiness does not make peace with others unimportant.

The warning about a root of bitterness recalls Deuteronomy 29:18–19, where a person turns toward other gods while imagining that stubborn disobedience will still bring peace. The concern is a corrupting influence that can spread through the community, beyond the ordinary hurt feelings the English word bitterness may suggest.

Esau supplies the example of treating something valuable as expendable for an immediate appetite. Genesis 25:29–34 records the birthright bargain, and 27:34–38 his later tears over the blessing. The warning urges care now, before a careless choice brings consequences that cannot simply be undone.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley understand the strengthening and watchfulness as responsibilities that involve the community, rather than permission to abandon those who struggle. They take the pursuit of holiness seriously.

They place different emphases on Esau’s tears. Wesley says no change could regain the lost blessing. Calvin distinguishes sorrow over loss from a sincere return to God, and explicitly says God welcomes the repentant sinner. He does not read Esau as proof that genuine repentance is always refused.

The USCCB note connects Esau with the warning about repentance after falling away. That is a commentary reading; the Catholic Catechism, 1446, also teaches reconciliation for serious sin after baptism. Neither the wording here nor that note should be made into a claim that every failure leaves someone unable to seek God.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 5:25–27 describes Christ loving the church and giving Himself to cleanse it and present it holy. The holiness pursued here belongs within His purpose for the people He loves.

1 Corinthians 12:25–27 describes members of one body sharing care, suffering and joy. Strengthening a weakened person serves that common life, rather than treating the Christian journey as a private contest against everyone else.

passages.title: Hebrews 12:18-24
passages.section_title: What kind of gathering has Jesus brought us into?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 For you have not come to a mountain that can be touched and that is burning with fire; to darkness, gloom, and storm; 19 to a trumpet blast or to a voice that made its hearers beg that no further word be spoken. 20 For they could not bear what was commanded: “If even an animal touches the mountain, it must be stoned.” 21 The sight was so terrifying that even Moses said, “I am trembling with fear.” 22 Instead, you have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem. You have come to myriads of angels 23 in joyful assembly, to the congregation of the firstborn, enrolled in heaven. You have come to God the Judge of all, to the spirits of the righteous made perfect, 24 to Jesus the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.
paragraphs: 18 For you have not come to a mountain that can be touched and that is burning with fire; to darkness, gloom, and storm; 19 to a trumpet blast or to a voice that made its hearers beg that no further word be spoken. 20 For they could not bear what was commanded: “If even an animal touches the mountain, it must be stoned.” 21 The sight was so terrifying that even Moses said, “I am trembling with fear.”

22 Instead, you have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem. You have come to myriads of angels 23 in joyful assembly, to the congregation of the firstborn, enrolled in heaven. You have come to God the Judge of all, to the spirits of the righteous made perfect, 24 to Jesus the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The writer contrasts the gathering at Sinai with the heavenly gathering believers have approached through Jesus. Exodus 19:10–22 and 20:18–21 describe the fire, boundaries, thunder and fear surrounding the giving of the law.

The words you have come then introduce Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, angels, God’s enrolled people, the righteous made perfect and Jesus as mediator. The contrast describes access to God and belonging among His people through the new covenant.

God is still named as Judge of all within this joyful gathering. The comparison does not replace a formerly harsh God with a different, kind God. Jesus brings people into the presence of the holy God whose authority remains real.

His sprinkled blood speaks a better word than Abel’s. Genesis 4:10 describes Abel’s blood crying from the ground after his murder. Christ’s offering opens the way for cleansing and access to God, as Hebrews has explained throughout its account of His priesthood.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley understand the gathering as a present privilege of believers through Christ, joining them with God’s heavenly people. Both connect Jesus’ blood with access and forgiveness, in contrast with Abel’s blood crying for vengeance.

They differ over the firstborn enrolled in heaven. Calvin especially identifies them with the patriarchs and honored saints of the earlier people of God. Wesley includes the whole body of true believers, on earth and in paradise. The USCCB note records several possibilities, including the earlier faithful and the whole new-covenant assembly. These readings concern the groups described; all recognize that access rests on Jesus.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 2:13–22 connects being brought near through Christ’s blood with the joining of Jewish and Gentile believers into one household. The access celebrated in Hebrews belongs within that gathering purpose.

Revelation 21:1–5 looks toward the holy city and God dwelling with His people when death and mourning are removed. The fellowship believers now approach in faith has a promised completion beyond their present struggles.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Hebrews 12:25-29
passages.section_title: How do we respond to a kingdom that cannot be shaken?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 25 See to it that you do not refuse Him who speaks. For if the people did not escape when they refused Him who warned them on earth, how much less will we escape if we reject Him who warns us from heaven? 26 At that time His voice shook the earth, but now He has promised, “Once more I will shake not only the earth, but heaven as well.” 27 The words “Once more” signify the removal of what can be shaken—that is, created things—so that the unshakable may remain. 28 Therefore, since we are receiving an unshakable kingdom, let us be filled with gratitude, and so worship God acceptably with reverence and awe. 29 “For our God is a consuming fire.”
paragraphs: 25 See to it that you do not refuse Him who speaks. For if the people did not escape when they refused Him who warned them on earth, how much less will we escape if we reject Him who warns us from heaven? 26 At that time His voice shook the earth, but now He has promised, “Once more I will shake not only the earth, but heaven as well.” 27 The words “Once more” signify the removal of what can be shaken—that is, created things—so that the unshakable may remain.
28 Therefore, since we are receiving an unshakable kingdom, let us be filled with gratitude, and so worship God acceptably with reverence and awe. 29 “For our God is a consuming fire.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The invitation to the heavenly gathering is followed by a warning: do not refuse the One who speaks. Greater access through Christ gives greater reason to listen, rather than making God’s voice unimportant.

The writer recalls Sinai’s shaking, then quotes Haggai 2:6 about a further shaking of heaven and earth. He draws the distinction between created things that can be removed and the unshakable kingdom believers receive.

The response is gratitude expressed in acceptable worship, with reverence and awe. The final description of God as a consuming fire comes from Deuteronomy 4:23–24, where Israel is warned against forgetting the covenant and turning to idols.

The paragraph holds assurance and warning together. God’s kingdom is dependable, and His holiness calls for a serious response. The writer moves from that response into practical instructions about love, hospitality and faithful living in chapter 13.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley both connect the shaking with Christ’s kingdom, though their explanations emphasize different stages. Calvin emphasizes the change brought through Christ’s coming and the gospel’s reach, while recognizing the need for created things to be brought into a better state. Wesley sees the shaking as beginning with Christ’s first coming and reaching its completion at His return, with the new heaven and earth.

They also handle verse 28 differently. Calvin favors the sense that receiving the kingdom gives believers grace for worship. Wesley urges holding fast the grace through which they serve. The BSB expresses the response as being filled with gratitude. These readings connect God’s gift with reverent service, rather than making the kingdom an achievement of human effort.
passages.god_plan_html:
2 Peter 3:10–13 likewise joins the passing of the present order with holy living and the expectation of a new heaven and earth where righteousness dwells. Future hope shapes present conduct.

1 Corinthians 15:24–28 describes Christ’s victory over every enemy and the kingdom brought to its appointed completion. The lasting kingdom of Hebrews belongs within that purpose, rather than the security of something people can build for themselves.

passages.title: Hebrews 13:1-3
passages.section_title: What does continuing in love look like?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Continue in brotherly love. 2 Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for by so doing some people have entertained angels without knowing it. 3 Remember those in prison as if you were bound with them, and those who are mistreated as if you were suffering with them.
paragraphs: 1 Continue in brotherly love. 2 Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for by so doing some people have entertained angels without knowing it. 3 Remember those in prison as if you were bound with them, and those who are mistreated as if you were suffering with them.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The call to grateful worship at the end of chapter 12 now becomes practical. Love is to continue among believers, extend hospitality to strangers and identify with people who are imprisoned or mistreated.

The reference to welcoming angels recalls accounts such as Genesis 18–19, where visitors received hospitality before their full identity was understood. The point gives ordinary welcome a depth people may not see at first.

The readers had already shown sympathy to prisoners, as 10:34 recalls. They are asked to continue that care by imagining themselves beside those who suffer, rather than treating imprisonment as someone else’s remote problem.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley both connect hospitality with Abraham and Lot, and read remembering prisoners as active compassion. Wesley specifically includes prayer and practical help.

They explain the shared bodily condition behind verse 3 differently. Calvin emphasizes members of the one body of the church. Wesley emphasizes that the readers themselves are bodily people exposed to suffering. The BSB expresses the intended sympathy as caring as though they were suffering with those mistreated.
passages.god_plan_html:
Matthew 25:35–40 connects welcome and care for prisoners with service to Jesus in caring for His brothers. Ordinary acts of mercy belong within how His people respond to Him.

1 Corinthians 12:25–27 describes one body whose members share suffering and honor. The love called for here makes that shared life visible.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Hebrews 13:4-6
passages.section_title: How do faithfulness and contentment shape our lives?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 4 Marriage should be honored by all and the marriage bed kept undefiled, for God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterers. 5 Keep your lives free from the love of money and be content with what you have, for God has said: “Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you.” 6 So we say with confidence: “The Lord is my helper; I will not be afraid. What can man do to me?”
paragraphs: 4 Marriage should be honored by all and the marriage bed kept undefiled, for God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterers.

5 Keep your lives free from the love of money and be content with what you have, for God has said: “Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you.” 6 So we say with confidence: “The Lord is my helper; I will not be afraid. What can man do to me?”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The instructions turn to marriage and money. Marriage is to be honored, with faithfulness in sexual conduct. The warning about God’s judgment gives those relationships moral weight; they are not merely private preferences.

The readers are also called to freedom from the love of money and to contentment. The reason given is God’s promise not to abandon His people. Confidence rests on His presence, rather than on being able to accumulate enough to control every risk.

The promise recalls Deuteronomy 31:6–8, and the confession of help draws on Psalm 118:6–7. These Scriptures supply assurance for trust. The surrounding letter, with its accounts of confiscated property and suffering, does not make that assurance a promise that faithful people never face material need.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley both emphasize the honor of marriage and the call to trust God rather than love money. Both also apply the marriage statement to clergy, rejecting the idea that marriage is inherently beneath a minister’s calling.

The Catholic Church’s discipline differs here: the Catechism, 1579–1580, describes the Latin Church’s normal choice of priests committed to remaining unmarried, while recognizing married priests in Eastern Catholic churches. That is not a teaching that marriage itself is immoral.

Christians also differ over divorce and remarriage in applying marriage’s permanence. The Catholic Catechism, 1649–1650, permits separation in some circumstances but does not recognize a new marriage while the first valid marriage remains. The Reformed Westminster Confession, 24.5–6, allows divorce for adultery or certain cases of willful desertion, and remarriage after lawful divorce. Hebrews’ brief instruction does not itself set out all those cases.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 5:25–33 connects marriage with Christ’s faithful love for the church. Honoring marriage belongs within a life shaped by that love, rather than using another person for one’s own satisfaction.

1 Timothy 6:6–10, 17–19 likewise connects contentment and trust in God with generosity. Freedom from money’s rule makes room to use what one has for the good of others.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Hebrews 13:7-9
passages.section_title: What keeps faith steady when teachers and circumstances change?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 Remember your leaders who spoke the word of God to you. Consider the outcome of their way of life and imitate their faith. 8 Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever. 9 Do not be carried away by all kinds of strange teachings, for it is good for the heart to be strengthened by grace and not by foods of no value to those devoted to them.
paragraphs: 7 Remember your leaders who spoke the word of God to you. Consider the outcome of their way of life and imitate their faith. 8 Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever. 9 Do not be carried away by all kinds of strange teachings, for it is good for the heart to be strengthened by grace and not by foods of no value to those devoted to them.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The readers are to remember leaders who brought God’s word to them and consider the outcome of their lives. They are directed to imitate faith, rather than treat a title or personality as the source of truth.

Jesus Christ’s constancy stands at the center of the paragraph. Teachers may pass from the scene, but He remains. That steadiness gives the warning against strange teachings its setting.

The particular contrast is between a heart strengthened by grace and reliance on foods. The passage does not identify every rule being promoted. It challenges the idea that such observances can supply the spiritual strength found in God’s grace.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin, Wesley and the USCCB notes understand the remembered leaders as earlier teachers whose faithful lives had reached their end. Calvin especially considers martyrdom while allowing a broader reference to faithful perseverance.

Calvin and Wesley connect the food teaching with Jewish ceremonial observances. The USCCB note considers food laws and also the possibility of sacrificial meals. The exact practice is discussed, while the main contrast remains grace rather than dependence on food observance for spiritual strength.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 4:11–16 connects sound teaching with a body growing into maturity, rather than being carried about by changing doctrines. Christ’s gifts serve the community’s stability in Him.

Colossians 2:16–23 also weighs food regulations and human rules against holding to Christ. Together these passages direct growth toward the living Head, rather than searching for an additional system that supplies what He lacks.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Hebrews 13:10
passages.section_title: What is the altar the writer says we have?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 We have an altar from which those who serve at the tabernacle have no right to eat.
paragraphs: 10 We have an altar from which those who serve at the tabernacle have no right to eat.

passages.context_html:
This verse belongs to 13:9–16. The writer contrasts strength through grace with reliance on food observances, then speaks of the altar and the earlier tabernacle service.

The next verses explain the connection through sin offerings whose blood entered the sanctuary and whose bodies were burned outside the camp. Jesus likewise suffered outside the gate. The contrast concerns participation in His sacrifice, rather than a claim that a Christian object can replace the need for Him.

The comparison concerns the specific offerings described in Leviticus 6:30 and 16:27. It should not be expanded into a claim that priests never ate any sin offering; Leviticus 6:26–29 describes offerings they did eat.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Calvin, Wesley and the USCCB note understand the altar in relation to Christ’s sacrifice, with Wesley naming the cross directly. The USCCB note does not identify the verse with the Eucharist. In these readings, the contrast directs people to the benefits of Christ’s offering rather than reliance on the earlier sanctuary service.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Worship as the Early Church Knew It identifies the altar here with the cross of Christ. His sacrifice fulfills the earlier offerings. The study distinguishes that saving work from the grateful response of believers offering their lives in service to God; their service does not add another payment for sin.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 10:10–18 explains why Christ’s one offering does not need to be supplemented by another offering for sin. That is the wider setting for what believers have in Him.

1 Peter 2:4–5 then describes the spiritual sacrifices offered by God’s people through Jesus. Hebrews itself names praise, generosity and doing good in 13:15–16. God’s purpose brings a people into grateful service through the sacrifice Christ has already made.

passages.title: Hebrews 13:10-16
passages.section_title: What sacrifices do we offer through Jesus?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 We have an altar from which those who serve at the tabernacle have no right to eat. 11 Although the high priest brings the blood of animals into the Holy Place as a sacrifice for sin, the bodies are burned outside the camp. 12 And so Jesus also suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood. 13 Therefore let us go to Him outside the camp, bearing the disgrace He bore. 14 For here we do not have a permanent city, but we are looking for the city that is to come. 15 Through Jesus, therefore, let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess His name. 16 And do not neglect to do good and to share with others, for with such sacrifices God is pleased.
paragraphs: 10 We have an altar from which those who serve at the tabernacle have no right to eat. 11 Although the high priest brings the blood of animals into the Holy Place as a sacrifice for sin, the bodies are burned outside the camp. 12 And so Jesus also suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood.
13 Therefore let us go to Him outside the camp, bearing the disgrace He bore. 14 For here we do not have a permanent city, but we are looking for the city that is to come.

15 Through Jesus, therefore, let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess His name. 16 And do not neglect to do good and to share with others, for with such sacrifices God is pleased.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The altar statement continues the contrast with reliance on the earlier sanctuary. The writer recalls a specific kind of sin offering whose blood entered the holy place and whose body was burned outside the camp. Leviticus 6:30 and 16:27 describe that arrangement.

Jesus’ suffering outside the city gate is connected with that earlier pattern. The writer then turns the comparison into a call to join Him outside the camp, bearing His disgrace. Belonging to Him matters more than keeping a secure place within the order that rejects Him.

The lasting city is still ahead. This carries forward the hope of chapter 11 and helps explain why public rejection need not make the readers abandon Christ.

The sacrifices now named are praise through Jesus, doing good and sharing. These responses please God. They belong alongside the letter’s repeated assurance that Christ’s one offering has dealt with sin; they do not begin a new series of offerings to make His death sufficient.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin, Wesley and the USCCB note direct the altar statement to Christ’s sacrifice. Wesley specifically identifies the altar with the cross. The USCCB note explicitly distinguishes it from a reference to the Eucharist, the Lord’s Supper.

Calvin and Wesley understand the passage’s praise and generous action as the sacrifices believers offer in response. Calvin includes prayer and thanksgiving, and connects kindness toward people with service offered to God. These responses are made through Christ.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Peter 2:4–10 describes people coming to Christ, the rejected living stone, and being built into a spiritual house and holy priesthood. Their spiritual sacrifices are acceptable through Jesus. That connects Christ’s rejection with the people and worship His work makes possible.

Revelation 21:1–5 carries the city theme toward God’s dwelling with His people. Bearing disgrace now is held within that lasting hope, rather than treated as an additional price that purchases forgiveness.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Worship as the Early Church Knew It identifies the altar here with the cross of Christ. His sacrifice fulfills the earlier offerings. The study distinguishes that saving work from the grateful response of believers offering their lives in service to God; their service does not add another payment for sin.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

passages.title: Hebrews 13:17-19
passages.section_title: How do leaders and the community care for one another?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they watch over your souls as those who must give an account. To this end, allow them to lead with joy and not with grief, for that would be of no advantage to you. 18 Pray for us; we are convinced that we have a clear conscience and desire to live honorably in every way. 19 And I especially urge you to pray that I may be restored to you soon.
paragraphs: 17 Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they watch over your souls as those who must give an account. To this end, allow them to lead with joy and not with grief, for that would be of no advantage to you.
18 Pray for us; we are convinced that we have a clear conscience and desire to live honorably in every way. 19 And I especially urge you to pray that I may be restored to you soon.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The writer calls for obedience and submission to leaders who watch over the community’s souls. He also says they must give an account. Their responsibility and the community’s response belong together; leadership is a charge to care, rather than ownership of other people.

The word translated obey can include listening and yielding, and the word translated submit describes giving way to authority or admonition. The call is stronger than ignoring counsel whenever it is unwelcome. It does not make leaders the source of an authority above God.

The appeal then turns to prayer. The writer says he and his companions desire to live honorably, and asks especially to be restored to the readers soon. This is a request for a real reunion. The paragraph does not tell us the exact circumstances that have kept him away.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley read the command as a serious responsibility to receive the guidance of faithful leaders. Both also place limits around its misuse. Calvin distinguishes genuine care from having a title while harming the church. Wesley explicitly distinguishes submitting one’s will in ordinary matters from surrendering conscience or judgment.

Calvin considers several possible circumstances behind the requested reunion, including persecution, and allows that the writer could have been free. Neither the request itself nor its wording proves imprisonment. The shared point is the community’s prayerful support for honorable service.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Peter 5:1–4 places elders’ care under the Chief Shepherd and calls for willing service and example rather than domination. Acts 5:29 makes obedience to God the final standard when human demands conflict with Him.

The leadership and prayer described in Hebrews serve a people being cared for under Christ. They strengthen His body’s life and faithfulness, while the leaders themselves remain accountable to Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Hebrews 13:20-21
passages.section_title: Who equips us to live the life this letter calls for?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 20 Now may the God of peace, who through the blood of the eternal covenant brought back from the dead our Lord Jesus, that great Shepherd of the sheep, 21 equip you with every good thing to do His will. And may He accomplish in us what is pleasing in His sight through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.
paragraphs: 20 Now may the God of peace, who through the blood of the eternal covenant brought back from the dead our Lord Jesus, that great Shepherd of the sheep, 21 equip you with every good thing to do His will. And may He accomplish in us what is pleasing in His sight through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The closing blessing turns from what the readers are called to do to the God who equips them. He is the God of peace who brought Jesus from the dead, the great Shepherd of the sheep, through the blood of the eternal covenant.

The writer asks God to equip them for His will and work in them what pleases Him through Jesus Christ. Their response is real, and the help that makes it possible comes from God.

The blessing gathers the letter’s themes into a prayer: Christ lives, His covenant endures and His people are to live in a way that pleases God. Glory belongs to Jesus, rather than to the leaders or readers for sustaining themselves.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Calvin and Wesley understand the blessing as dependence on God’s continuing work through Christ. Calvin emphasizes God fitting and strengthening people for good, while Wesley emphasizes the enduring covenant and the holiness God produces. Both connect the life being asked for with the help God supplies.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ezekiel 34:11–16, 23–24 joins God’s promise to seek and care for His flock with the promise of one shepherd from David’s line. In John 10:11–18, Jesus identifies Himself as the good Shepherd who lays down His life and takes it up again.

Ephesians 2:8–10 connects salvation by grace with a people created in Christ for good works. The final prayer of Hebrews places those works within the risen Shepherd’s saving and equipping care.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Hebrews 13:22-25
passages.section_title: How does the letter leave its readers?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 I urge you, brothers, to bear with my word of exhortation, for I have only written to you briefly. 23 Be aware that our brother Timothy has been released. If he arrives soon, I will come with him to see you. 24 Greet all your leaders and all the saints. Those from Italy send you greetings. 25 Grace be with all of you.
paragraphs: 22 I urge you, brothers, to bear with my word of exhortation, for I have only written to you briefly. 23 Be aware that our brother Timothy has been released. If he arrives soon, I will come with him to see you. 24 Greet all your leaders and all the saints. Those from Italy send you greetings. 25 Grace be with all of you.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The writer asks the readers to bear with the word of exhortation. The letter’s teaching has been meant to be received and acted upon, not only admired from a distance.

The news about Timothy points toward a hoped-for visit. If he arrives soon, the writer expects to come with him. The greeting from those from Italy connects the readers with other believers, without by itself identifying the writer or the place of composition.

Leaders and all the saints are greeted, and the letter ends with grace for everyone. The practical concern and personal warmth belong beside its serious warnings and sustained teaching about Christ.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley understand the ending as an appeal to receive the exhortation, together with personal news and greetings. They do not agree on authorship: Wesley assumes Paul, while Calvin considers other possibilities. The closing details alone do not establish an author.

The BSB says Timothy has been released. Beyond that notice, these verses do not supply an account of his detention or prove that the writer shared it. The hoped-for visit expresses a continuing relationship with the readers.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: James 1:1-4
passages.section_title: How can trials become a reason for hope?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, To the twelve tribes of the Dispersion: Greetings. 2 Consider it pure joy, my brothers, when you encounter trials of many kinds, 3 because you know that the testing of your faith develops perseverance. 4 Allow perseverance to finish its work, so that you may be mature and complete, not lacking anything.
paragraphs: 1 James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, To the twelve tribes of the Dispersion: Greetings.

2 Consider it pure joy, my brothers, when you encounter trials of many kinds, 3 because you know that the testing of your faith develops perseverance. 4 Allow perseverance to finish its work, so that you may be mature and complete, not lacking anything.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
James introduces himself as a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ. He addresses the twelve tribes of the Dispersion, using the language of Israel living scattered abroad. The letter speaks to people who confess faith in Christ and asks what that faith looks like in everyday life.

The writer is traditionally identified with James, the Jerusalem leader called the Lord’s brother in Galatians 1:19. The letter itself does not settle the questions about its authorship and date. The USCCB introduction describes both the traditional identification and other proposals.

The first instruction concerns trials of many kinds. James gives a reason for joy: tested faith can develop perseverance, and perseverance is to keep working toward a mature, complete life. The word translated mature has the sense of completion and full growth. The emphasis is on becoming steady in faith, rather than escaping every difficulty.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as encouragement to remain faithful through hardship, trusting God to bring growth from it. Calvin explicitly allows grief alongside joy, while Wesley emphasizes giving perseverance room to complete its work.
passages.god_plan_html: 1 Peter 1:3–9 sets tested faith within the hope opened by Jesus’ resurrection: an unfading inheritance and salvation to be revealed. Peter speaks of grief and rejoicing together. The larger hope gives endurance a destination; it does not require pretending that suffering feels pleasant.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: James 1:5
passages.section_title: What kind of help does God promise to give?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 Now if any of you lacks wisdom, he should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault, and it will be given to him.
paragraphs: 5 Now if any of you lacks wisdom, he should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault, and it will be given to him.

passages.context_html:
This verse sits between the call to persevere through trials and the call to ask in faith. James does not shame people for needing wisdom. He directs them to a generous God who welcomes the request.

The immediate need is to know how to live faithfully in difficulty. Reading the promise together with verses 6–8 keeps the request connected with trust in God, rather than treating it as a formula for discovering an answer to every private decision.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Calvin and Wesley both connect the wisdom promised here with facing trials well. They understand God’s generosity as a reason to ask Him confidently, rather than withdraw because of one’s need.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Should We Seek Signs From God? understands the promise here as wisdom: sound judgment for navigating circumstances, rather than a sign revealing a predetermined answer. It places prayer alongside Scripture and the counsel of believers as ways God guides His people. Circumstances are to be understood through Scripture, rather than treated as coded personal messages.

deeper_study.title: Should We Seek Signs From God?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html: Jesus likewise encourages His followers to ask their Father, comparing His goodness with a parent giving good things to a child in Matthew 7:7–11. Wisdom is one expression of that fatherly care: help for a life of trust and obedience.

passages.title: James 1:5-8
passages.section_title: What should we ask God for when we do not know how to respond?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 Now if any of you lacks wisdom, he should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault, and it will be given to him. 6 But he must ask in faith, without doubting, because he who doubts is like a wave of the sea, blown and tossed by the wind. 7 That man should not expect to receive anything from the Lord. 8 He is a double-minded man, unstable in all his ways.
paragraphs: 5 Now if any of you lacks wisdom, he should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault, and it will be given to him. 6 But he must ask in faith, without doubting, because he who doubts is like a wave of the sea, blown and tossed by the wind. 7 That man should not expect to receive anything from the Lord. 8 He is a double-minded man, unstable in all his ways.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The call to become complete, lacking nothing, leads directly to a need the readers may recognize: lacking wisdom. James tells them to ask God, whose generosity makes it possible to come honestly with that need.

The promise concerns wisdom in the setting of trials. It is help for understanding and living faithfully through difficulty, rather than a promise that prayer will deliver whatever outcome someone imagines.

The warning is serious: the person asking must trust God. The word translated doubting can mean hesitating or being at variance with oneself. The next verse describes a double-minded person, pulled in conflicting directions. James calls for steady trust in the God being asked, rather than prayer that leaves His trustworthiness continually in question.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Calvin and Wesley read wisdom as God’s help for responding to trials, and faith as confidence in Him. Calvin distinguishes that confidence from never experiencing a struggle: even rooted faith can be shaken without being uprooted.
passages.god_plan_html: This belongs with Jesus’ invitation to ask the Father for good gifts in Matthew 7:7–11. God’s generosity makes dependent prayer possible. The wisdom sought here is part of learning to live as His children, trusting His goodness while putting His teaching into practice.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Should We Seek Signs From God? understands the promise here as wisdom: sound judgment for navigating circumstances, rather than a sign revealing a predetermined answer. It places prayer alongside Scripture and the counsel of believers as ways God guides His people. Circumstances are to be understood through Scripture, rather than treated as coded personal messages.

deeper_study.title: Should We Seek Signs From God?

passages.title: James 1:9-11
passages.section_title: What do poverty and wealth really say about a person?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 The brother in humble circumstances should exult in his high position. 10 But the one who is rich should exult in his low position, because he will pass away like a flower of the field. 11 For the sun rises with scorching heat and withers the plant; its flower falls and its beauty is lost. So too, the rich man will fade away in the midst of his pursuits.
paragraphs: 9 The brother in humble circumstances should exult in his high position. 10 But the one who is rich should exult in his low position, because he will pass away like a flower of the field. 11 For the sun rises with scorching heat and withers the plant; its flower falls and its beauty is lost. So too, the rich man will fade away in the midst of his pursuits.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
James now puts lowly circumstances and riches beside each other. The poor believer has a high standing to celebrate, while the rich person must face the lowliness that wealth can hide. Money cannot stop a human life from fading.

The flower makes the point concrete: its beauty does not keep the heat from withering it. James applies that passing beauty to the rich person in the midst of ordinary pursuits. The image recalls Isaiah 40:6–8, where human frailty stands beside God’s enduring word.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The shared emphasis is that poverty does not erase a believer’s dignity, and wealth provides no lasting reason for pride. Calvin and Wesley both connect the poor believer’s high position with belonging to God and receiving His promised inheritance.
passages.god_plan_html: Jesus’ message to Smyrna in Revelation 2:8–11 makes a similar contrast: He knows the church’s poverty yet calls it rich. The risen Christ sees a value that its outward circumstances cannot measure. That parallel helps explain why James can speak of a high position while the believer remains poor.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: James 1:12-15
passages.section_title: How is enduring a trial different from giving in to temptation?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 Blessed is the man who perseveres under trial, because when he has stood the test, he will receive the crown of life that God has promised to those who love Him. 13 When tempted, no one should say, “God is tempting me.” For God cannot be tempted by evil, nor does He tempt anyone. 14 But each one is tempted when by his own evil desires he is lured away and enticed. 15 Then after desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is full-grown, gives birth to death.
paragraphs: 12 Blessed is the man who perseveres under trial, because when he has stood the test, he will receive the crown of life that God has promised to those who love Him.

13 When tempted, no one should say, “God is tempting me.” For God cannot be tempted by evil, nor does He tempt anyone. 14 But each one is tempted when by his own evil desires he is lured away and enticed. 15 Then after desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is full-grown, gives birth to death.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
James promises the crown of life to the person who perseveres under trial, then immediately guards against blaming God for temptation to sin. The Greek word behind trial can also refer to temptation; the surrounding sentences show the distinction James makes.

Testing may become an occasion for endurance. Enticement to evil does not come from God. James instead makes each person face the pull of his or her own evil desires. Desire here is broader than sexual desire: it includes craving what is forbidden.

The picture of conception and birth traces a destructive development. Desire gives birth to sin, and fully grown sin brings death. James is warning readers about where sin leads, rather than giving them someone else to blame for it.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley read the crown as God’s promised blessing for those who endure and love Him. Both reject making God the source of enticement to evil; Calvin understands the final death in verse 15 as eternal ruin.

Traditions differ over how to describe the inward desire before a person consents to it. The Catholic Church teaches that the inherited inclination toward sin is not itself a personal offense, though it inclines people to sin (Catechism, 2515). The Reformed Westminster Confession, 6.5, calls the remaining corruption of nature and its sinful movements themselves sin. Wesley also warns that James’ sequence does not make an evil desire innocent simply because it has not yet become an outward act. These distinctions concern inward sin; they do not make every experience of being tempted the same as choosing evil.
passages.god_plan_html:
The contrast between sin producing death and God giving life appears again in Romans 6:20–23. Eternal life is God’s gift in Jesus Christ. James’ warning makes the need for that saving gift concrete, while the promised crown points beyond the present struggle.

In Revelation 2:10–11, Jesus promises the crown of life to people facing imprisonment and possible death. Faithfulness can carry them through suffering without preventing their physical death. Their hope rests with the One who died and returned to life.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: James 1:16-18
passages.section_title: What does God bring into our lives?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 Do not be deceived, my beloved brothers. 17 Every good and perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of the heavenly lights, with whom there is no change or shifting shadow. 18 He chose to give us birth through the word of truth, that we would be a kind of firstfruits of His creation.
paragraphs: 16 Do not be deceived, my beloved brothers. 17 Every good and perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of the heavenly lights, with whom there is no change or shifting shadow. 18 He chose to give us birth through the word of truth, that we would be a kind of firstfruits of His creation.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After describing desire giving birth to sin and death, James turns to another kind of birth. God chose to give His people birth through the word of truth. His giving brings life, rather than the evil that the previous verses refused to attribute to Him.

The Father of the heavenly lights is contrasted with change and shifting shadow. James directs attention to God’s dependable goodness: His character does not swing between generosity and an intent to lure people into evil.

The firstfruits image draws on the first portion of a harvest offered to God. Calling believers a kind of firstfruits places their new life within His purposes for His creation, rather than treating it as a merely private improvement.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Calvin and Wesley understand the birth as the new life God gives through the gospel. Both emphasize that His goodness and initiative stand behind it; the image of firstfruits describes a people set apart for Him.
passages.god_plan_html: 1 Peter 1:22–25 also connects new birth with God’s living, enduring word and calls the resulting people to sincere love. James’ image can be read alongside the wider hope in Romans 8:18–25: God’s children await bodily redemption, and creation itself awaits freedom from decay. That is a supported connection in theme, rather than a timetable supplied by James for every stage of creation’s renewal.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: James 1:19-21
passages.section_title: What helps us receive God’s word?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 My beloved brothers, understand this: Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to anger, 20 for man’s anger does not bring about the righteousness that God desires. 21 Therefore, get rid of all moral filth and every expression of evil, and humbly accept the word planted in you, which can save your souls.
paragraphs: 19 My beloved brothers, understand this: Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to anger, 20 for man’s anger does not bring about the righteousness that God desires. 21 Therefore, get rid of all moral filth and every expression of evil, and humbly accept the word planted in you, which can save your souls.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The word that gives new birth in verse 18 is now the word the readers must humbly receive. Listening, speaking and anger all matter to that response. James asks them to be ready to listen and restrained in speech and anger.

Anger does not produce the righteousness God desires. The response is to put away evil and welcome the planted word. James’ picture joins receiving God’s message with allowing it to take root in life.

The promise that the word can save their souls gives this instruction its weight. It concerns their lives before God, rather than merely becoming more agreeable in conversation. The term for souls has a range including life, persons and the soul’s salvation; the word alone does not restrict James to saving someone from present inconvenience.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Calvin and Wesley both connect these instructions with receiving the gospel humbly and turning from evil. They read the word’s saving work as God’s work through the gospel, rather than a benefit gained by simply hearing sounds or attending a religious meeting.
passages.god_plan_html: The sequence reflects the wider movement from God giving life to a changed way of living. Ephesians 2:8–10 places good works after God’s saving gift: His people are created in Christ for them. Receiving the word is therefore meant to shape their treatment of others as well as their understanding.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: James 1:22-25
passages.section_title: What is the difference between hearing and doing?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 Be doers of the word, and not hearers only. Otherwise, you are deceiving yourselves. 23 For anyone who hears the word but does not carry it out is like a man who looks at his face in a mirror, 24 and after observing himself goes away and immediately forgets what he looks like. 25 But the one who looks intently into the perfect law of freedom, and continues to do so—not being a forgetful hearer, but an effective doer—he will be blessed in what he does.
paragraphs: 22 Be doers of the word, and not hearers only. Otherwise, you are deceiving yourselves. 23 For anyone who hears the word but does not carry it out is like a man who looks at his face in a mirror, 24 and after observing himself goes away and immediately forgets what he looks like. 25 But the one who looks intently into the perfect law of freedom, and continues to do so—not being a forgetful hearer, but an effective doer—he will be blessed in what he does.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
James follows the call to receive the word with a call to act on it. Hearing without doing can leave a person deceived about the state of his or her life.

The mirror illustrates that failure. Someone looks, walks away and forgets; the encounter changes nothing. The contrasting person looks intently, continues and acts. The blessing is connected with putting the teaching into practice.

The perfect law of freedom belongs within this picture of attentive, continuing obedience. James does not present freedom as permission to ignore what God says. The next verses make its demands concrete in speech, care for vulnerable people and personal conduct.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Calvin and Wesley both understand genuine reception of God’s word to bear fruit in conduct. Calvin describes God’s teaching written on the heart by the Spirit, while Wesley calls it the law of love established by faith; both connect freedom with a changed life.
passages.god_plan_html: Jesus makes a close parallel in Matthew 7:24–27. Two people hear His words, but only one acts on them; the difference appears when the storm comes. Read beside James, that picture brings the chapter back to perseverance: a life grounded in Jesus’ teaching must actually be lived.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: James 1:26-27
passages.section_title: What does a life of faith look like to God?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 26 If anyone considers himself religious and yet does not bridle his tongue, he deceives his heart and his religion is worthless. 27 Pure and undefiled religion before our God and Father is this: to care for orphans and widows in their distress, and to keep oneself from being polluted by the world.
paragraphs: 26 If anyone considers himself religious and yet does not bridle his tongue, he deceives his heart and his religion is worthless. 27 Pure and undefiled religion before our God and Father is this: to care for orphans and widows in their distress, and to keep oneself from being polluted by the world.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
James ends the chapter by testing a person’s view of his or her own religion against everyday conduct. An uncontrolled tongue can expose self-deception beneath a religious appearance.

Care for orphans and widows means responding to people in distress, while keeping unstained by the world concerns the character of one’s own life. These instructions put outward mercy and personal integrity together.

The examples bring the earlier command to do the word into ordinary relationships. James is not offering a way to replace faith with a list of charitable accomplishments. He is showing the inconsistency of claiming devotion to God while disregarding what He asks.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Calvin and Wesley read this as practical mercy, disciplined speech and a life kept from evil. Calvin explicitly treats widows and orphans as examples of people needing help, rather than an exhaustive list of everyone Christians should care for.
passages.god_plan_html: Care for vulnerable people continues an established theme in Scripture. Deuteronomy 10:17–19 describes God defending the fatherless and widow and loving the foreigner, then calls His people to reflect His care. James places that same kind of visible mercy beside the confession of faith in Jesus.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: James 2:1-7
passages.section_title: Why does favoritism conflict with faith in Jesus?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 My brothers, as you hold out your faith in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ, do not show favoritism. 2 Suppose a man comes into your meeting wearing a gold ring and fine clothes, and a poor man in shabby clothes also comes in. 3 If you lavish attention on the man in fine clothes and say, “Here is a seat of honor,” but say to the poor man, “You must stand” or “Sit at my feet,” 4 have you not discriminated among yourselves and become judges with evil thoughts? 5 Listen, my beloved brothers: Has not God chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith and to inherit the kingdom He promised those who love Him? 6 But you have dishonored the poor. Is it not the rich who oppress you and drag you into court? 7 Are they not the ones who blaspheme the noble name by which you have been called?
paragraphs: 1 My brothers, as you hold out your faith in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ, do not show favoritism. 2 Suppose a man comes into your meeting wearing a gold ring and fine clothes, and a poor man in shabby clothes also comes in. 3 If you lavish attention on the man in fine clothes and say, “Here is a seat of honor,” but say to the poor man, “You must stand” or “Sit at my feet,” 4 have you not discriminated among yourselves and become judges with evil thoughts?

5 Listen, my beloved brothers: Has not God chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith and to inherit the kingdom He promised those who love Him? 6 But you have dishonored the poor. Is it not the rich who oppress you and drag you into court? 7 Are they not the ones who blaspheme the noble name by which you have been called?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The call to care for people in distress now becomes a test of the congregation’s welcome. A well-dressed visitor receives an honored seat; a poorly dressed visitor is left standing or placed at someone’s feet. James exposes the judgment behind the difference.

The word translated favoritism concerns preferring people because of outward status. Their clothes and money have become a measure of their worth. The word for meeting can refer to an assembly, including a Christian gathering; the word alone does not tell us the building’s ownership or exact setting.

James contrasts the congregation’s treatment of the poor with God’s choice of people rich in faith and heirs of His kingdom. He also reminds the readers of rich oppressors who drag them into court and dishonor the name they bear. Giving wealth automatic honor has blinded them to both God’s welcome and the conduct in front of them.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Christians commonly read this as a rejection of giving people greater worth or a better welcome because they have money or status. Calvin and Wesley both distinguish God’s honor for the lowly from the congregation’s preference for appearances; neither makes every poor person faithful or every rich person an unbeliever.
passages.god_plan_html: 1 Corinthians 1:26–31 explains why God’s calling overturns ordinary rankings: no one is to boast before Him, and Christ is the source of His people’s righteousness and redemption. Welcoming believers on that basis makes God’s grace visible in a community, rather than rebuilding a ladder of human importance.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: James 2:8-13
passages.section_title: Can we love our neighbors while choosing whom to value?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 If you really fulfill the royal law stated in Scripture, “Love your neighbor as yourself,” you are doing well. 9 But if you show favoritism, you sin and are convicted by the law as transgressors. 10 Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles at just one point is guilty of breaking all of it. 11 For He who said, “Do not commit adultery,” also said, “Do not murder.” If you do not commit adultery, but do commit murder, you have become a lawbreaker. 12 Speak and act as those who are going to be judged by the law that gives freedom. 13 For judgment without mercy will be shown to anyone who has not been merciful. Mercy triumphs over judgment.
paragraphs: 8 If you really fulfill the royal law stated in Scripture, “Love your neighbor as yourself,” you are doing well. 9 But if you show favoritism, you sin and are convicted by the law as transgressors. 10 Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles at just one point is guilty of breaking all of it. 11 For He who said, “Do not commit adultery,” also said, “Do not murder.” If you do not commit adultery, but do commit murder, you have become a lawbreaker.
12 Speak and act as those who are going to be judged by the law that gives freedom. 13 For judgment without mercy will be shown to anyone who has not been merciful. Mercy triumphs over judgment.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The royal law is stated in Scripture: love your neighbor as yourself. James does not allow favoritism to be excused as a harmless preference. It breaks that command.

The illustrations about adultery and murder explain why selective obedience is insufficient. The same God gave both commands. Keeping one does not cancel breaking the other, and a good record elsewhere does not make mistreating a poor neighbor acceptable.

The coming judgment gives speech and action their weight. James joins the law of freedom with mercy: people who need God’s mercy must take seriously their treatment of others. The warning continues the call to put the word into practice.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Calvin and Wesley both understand the commands as the will of one Lawgiver, requiring consistent love rather than selective obedience. Calvin explicitly distinguishes becoming a lawbreaker from a claim that every offense is equally serious, and both connect the judgment warning with the need to show mercy.
passages.god_plan_html:
The command comes from Leviticus 19:15–18, where fair judgment stands beside love of neighbor. James carries that concern into a community confessing Jesus.

Jesus’ account of the forgiven servant in Matthew 18:21–35 connects receiving mercy with extending it. The servant’s failure makes clear why mercy is more than polite feeling: what someone has received is meant to shape how that person treats another.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: James 2:14-17
passages.section_title: What good is a claim to faith that leaves a neighbor hungry?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 What good is it, my brothers, if someone claims to have faith, but has no deeds? Can such faith save him? 15 Suppose a brother or sister is without clothes and daily food. 16 If one of you tells him, “Go in peace; stay warm and well fed,” but does not provide for his physical needs, what good is that? 17 So too, faith by itself, if it does not result in action, is dead.
paragraphs: 14 What good is it, my brothers, if someone claims to have faith, but has no deeds? Can such faith save him? 15 Suppose a brother or sister is without clothes and daily food. 16 If one of you tells him, “Go in peace; stay warm and well fed,” but does not provide for his physical needs, what good is that? 17 So too, faith by itself, if it does not result in action, is dead.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
James moves from mercy to a concrete claim: someone says he has faith but has no deeds. He asks whether such faith can save. The example makes the problem visible: a brother or sister lacks food and clothing, but receives only reassuring words.

The failure is not a shortage of religious language. The person’s physical need remains unmet. James compares that useless response with faith left by itself, producing no action.

The word translated save can refer to rescue from danger or to salvation in Christ. Its range does not by itself decide the question here. That is one reason readers must consider James’ whole discussion, including the examples that follow.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The major readings agree that words of concern do not replace helping a person in need. They differ over what James’ description of dead faith means for salvation.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, 11.1–2, and the 1689 Baptist Confession, 11.1–2, teach that God accepts people as righteous through faith in Christ alone, while that faith is never left without love and other signs of new life. Calvin reads James as exposing an empty claim to faith. Wesley likewise distinguishes living faith from a claim that never becomes active love.

The Catholic Church teaches that saving faith belongs with hope and love. The Council of Trent, session 6, chapters 7–8, explicitly uses James’ description of dead faith, while also teaching that nothing preceding a person’s justification earns that initial grace. Its view is not that unaided good deeds can purchase salvation.

A different reading appears among Free Grace interpreters. Keith Pesce, writing for the Grace Evangelical Society, understands the warning as concerning believers’ rescue from deadly consequences in this life, rather than whether their faith brings eternal life. On his reading, genuine believers can have faith that remains unproductive. This is a distinct interpretation, rather than the shared conclusion of the traditions above.
passages.god_plan_html: Ephesians 2:8–10 places God’s saving gift and a life of good works together: His people are created in Christ for such a life. Galatians 5:6, 13–15 likewise joins faith, freedom and loving service. These passages supply a wider setting for James’ hungry neighbor: the saving work of Christ has a purpose that reaches into the treatment of other people.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: James 2:18-20
passages.section_title: Is knowing that God exists the same as living by faith?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 But someone will say, “You have faith and I have deeds.” Show me your faith without deeds, and I will show you my faith by my deeds. 19 You believe that God is one. Good for you! Even the demons believe that—and shudder. 20 O foolish man, do you want evidence that faith without deeds is worthless?
paragraphs: 18 But someone will say, “You have faith and I have deeds.” Show me your faith without deeds, and I will show you my faith by my deeds. 19 You believe that God is one. Good for you! Even the demons believe that—and shudder. 20 O foolish man, do you want evidence that faith without deeds is worthless?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The discussion now takes the form of an exchange about showing faith. James places a claim that cannot be seen beside conduct that makes faith visible. The challenge is followed by an unsettling example: even demons recognize that God is one, and they shudder.

That example prevents agreement with a true statement from being treated as the whole response God seeks. The passage ends by pressing the question again: faith without deeds is worthless.

The example does not say the demons trust Christ for salvation. Nor does it give an account of their origin. James uses their recognition of God to make the reader examine what his or her own confession amounts to.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley both understand the example as showing the inadequacy of mere knowledge of God without a changed response to Him. They read the challenge to show faith through deeds as exposing a profession without living faith.

Readers who understand the wider passage as warning already-saved believers, such as Keith Pesce, frame the issue differently: whether faith is fruitful and protects a believer from sin’s consequences. The disagreement concerns the force of James’ warning, while the call to act rather than rest in religious claims remains serious.
passages.god_plan_html: Titus 2:11–14 describes Jesus giving Himself to redeem and purify a people eager for good deeds. Grace teaches a changed way of living as they await Him. That purpose goes beyond recognizing facts about God: it concerns the kind of people Christ is forming.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: James 2:21-26
passages.section_title: What do Abraham and Rahab show about faith in action?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 Was not our father Abraham justified by what he did when he offered his son Isaac on the altar? 22 You see that his faith was working with his actions, and his faith was perfected by what he did. 23 And the Scripture was fulfilled that says, “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness,” and he was called a friend of God. 24 As you can see, a man is justified by his deeds and not by faith alone. 25 In the same way, was not even Rahab the prostitute justified by her actions when she welcomed the spies and sent them off on another route? 26 As the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without deeds is dead.
paragraphs: 21 Was not our father Abraham justified by what he did when he offered his son Isaac on the altar? 22 You see that his faith was working with his actions, and his faith was perfected by what he did. 23 And the Scripture was fulfilled that says, “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness,” and he was called a friend of God. 24 As you can see, a man is justified by his deeds and not by faith alone.

25 In the same way, was not even Rahab the prostitute justified by her actions when she welcomed the spies and sent them off on another route? 26 As the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without deeds is dead.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
James gives two examples from Israel’s Scriptures. Abraham acted when he offered Isaac, and Rahab acted when she received the messengers and sent them away safely. Their circumstances and backgrounds differ greatly, but both entrusted themselves to God in a way that affected what they did.

The reference to Abraham brings together Genesis 15:6, where his faith is credited as righteousness, and Genesis 22, where that faith is tested. James says his faith worked with his actions and was perfected by them.

Rahab’s actions are recorded in Joshua 2. James closes with the body without the spirit: faith without deeds is dead. The comparison is meant to give weight to the whole discussion, not leave the readers satisfied with words alone.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Traditions agree that Abraham and Rahab acted on faith. They differ over how those actions relate to being justified—being accepted or shown to be righteous.

Calvin reads Abraham’s obedience as demonstrating the righteousness he already received through faith. This fits the Reformed Westminster Confession, 11.1–2, and 1689 Baptist Confession, 11.1–2: faith alone receives Christ’s righteousness, and living faith is accompanied by love.

The Catholic Church sees more than evidence of an unchanged standing. The Council of Trent, session 6, chapter 10, cites James 2:24 in teaching that people already justified grow in the righteousness received through Christ’s grace as faith works with good deeds. Its chapter 8 says the initial gift is not earned by preceding faith or works.

Wesley distinguishes Abraham’s earlier acceptance through faith from his later growth in righteousness when offering Isaac. He describes obedience as the fruit of faith that also strengthens and completes it, rather than the source from which faith first receives life.
passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 11:17–19, 31 also presents Abraham and Rahab as examples of faith. Abraham trusted God’s ability to raise the dead; Rahab received the spies instead of sharing the fate of those who refused to believe. Their actions belong within the history of people relying on God’s promises, across differences of background and standing.

Paul draws on Abraham in Romans 4:1–8 to explain God’s gift of righteousness. Reading those passages beside James keeps both the promise and the response in view; the tradition differences above concern how that relationship should be explained.
