deeper_study.title: Who is The Angel of the Lord?

passages.title: James 3:1-2
passages.section_title: Why should teaching be approached with care?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers, because you know that we who teach will be judged more strictly. 2 We all stumble in many ways. If anyone is never at fault in what he says, he is a perfect man, able to control his whole body.
paragraphs: 1 Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers, because you know that we who teach will be judged more strictly. 2 We all stumble in many ways. If anyone is never at fault in what he says, he is a perfect man, able to control his whole body.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The discussion of faith expressed in deeds now turns to words. James warns against many people becoming teachers because those who teach face stricter judgment. Speaking about God’s ways brings responsibility for what others are taught.

He immediately places that warning beside human weakness: we all stumble in many ways. Control of speech would mark a person able to govern the whole life. The warning gives teachers reason for humility, rather than a basis for treating themselves as above those they teach.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley reads this as a warning against pressing into the teaching role without God’s call. Calvin notes that this is the usual reading but proposes a different emphasis: people setting themselves up as harsh judges of everyone else’s conduct. Both readings take seriously the danger of claiming authority over others while failing to govern one’s own words.
passages.god_plan_html: Jesus connects greater responsibility with what a person has been entrusted in Luke 12:47–48. Teaching belongs within that accountability to the Master. Knowledge is a trust to use faithfully, rather than a title that places someone beyond examination.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: James 3:3-8
passages.section_title: How can such a small part of us cause so much harm?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 3 When we put bits into the mouths of horses to make them obey us, we can guide the whole animal. 4 Consider ships as well. Although they are so large and are driven by strong winds, they are steered by a very small rudder wherever the pilot is inclined. 5 In the same way, the tongue is a small part of the body, but it boasts of great things. Consider how small a spark sets a great forest ablaze. 6 The tongue also is a fire, a world of wickedness among the parts of the body. It pollutes the whole person, sets the course of his life on fire, and is itself set on fire by hell. 7 All kinds of animals, birds, reptiles, and creatures of the sea are being tamed and have been tamed by man, 8 but no man can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison.
paragraphs: 3 When we put bits into the mouths of horses to make them obey us, we can guide the whole animal. 4 Consider ships as well. Although they are so large and are driven by strong winds, they are steered by a very small rudder wherever the pilot is inclined. 5 In the same way, the tongue is a small part of the body, but it boasts of great things. Consider how small a spark sets a great forest ablaze.

6 The tongue also is a fire, a world of wickedness among the parts of the body. It pollutes the whole person, sets the course of his life on fire, and is itself set on fire by hell. 7 All kinds of animals, birds, reptiles, and creatures of the sea are being tamed and have been tamed by man, 8 but no man can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
A horse’s bit and a ship’s rudder show how something small can direct something much larger. James uses those examples to explain the tongue’s influence, then turns to a spark that sets a forest ablaze. Words can set consequences in motion far beyond the moment they are spoken.

The fire image grows more severe: the tongue pollutes the whole person and is itself set on fire by hell. The description gives destructive speech a moral and spiritual seriousness, rather than dismissing it as an unfortunate habit.

People have tamed all kinds of animals, yet cannot tame the tongue. Calling it a restless evil emphasizes how persistently it escapes control. The passage exposes the need for more than confidence in one’s own restraint; it does not excuse the harm caused.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Calvin and Wesley read the images as showing the tongue’s far-reaching power for evil. Wesley explicitly adds that controlling it requires God’s help; neither understands the difficulty as permission to stop resisting harmful speech.
passages.god_plan_html: Galatians 5:22–25 includes gentleness and self-control in the fruit of the Spirit and calls believers to walk in step with Him. Read beside James, that gives a positive direction to the warning: God’s work is meant to shape what comes out of a person’s mouth, as well as other parts of life.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: James 3:9-12
passages.section_title: Can we honor God while speaking with contempt for people?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 With the tongue we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse men, who have been made in God’s likeness. 10 Out of the same mouth come blessing and cursing. My brothers, this should not be! 11 Can both fresh water and salt water flow from the same spring? 12 My brothers, can a fig tree grow olives, or a grapevine bear figs? Neither can a salt spring produce fresh water.
paragraphs: 9 With the tongue we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse men, who have been made in God’s likeness. 10 Out of the same mouth come blessing and cursing. My brothers, this should not be! 11 Can both fresh water and salt water flow from the same spring? 12 My brothers, can a fig tree grow olives, or a grapevine bear figs? Neither can a salt spring produce fresh water.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
James names the contradiction plainly: the same tongue blesses the Lord and Father, then curses people made in God’s likeness. The way we speak about another person cannot be separated from the God whose image that person bears.

A spring and fruit trees make the contradiction visible. A spring does not naturally produce both fresh and salt water, and a tree does not grow the fruit of another kind. James calls the readers to a consistency their mixed speech lacks.

The examples do not simply report what people do. The words this should not be call for change. Praising God cannot make contemptuous speech toward people harmless.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Calvin and Wesley both connect the wrong of cursing people with the dignity they have from their Creator. They understand the natural images as a rebuke to inconsistent speech, rather than a reason to be content with it.
passages.god_plan_html: The likeness language reaches back to Genesis 1:26–28, where humanity receives its place from God. Colossians 3:8–14 carries that theme into renewal in Christ: putting away slander and lies belongs beside being renewed in the Creator’s image and putting on compassion and love. Honoring the Creator thus reaches into the words used about His creatures.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: James 3:13-18
passages.section_title: How can we recognize wisdom that comes from God?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 Who is wise and understanding among you? Let him show it by his good conduct, by deeds done in the humility that comes from wisdom. 14 But if you harbor bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your hearts, do not boast in it or deny the truth. 15 Such wisdom does not come from above, but is earthly, unspiritual, demonic. 16 For where jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there will be disorder and every evil practice. 17 But the wisdom from above is first of all pure, then peace-loving, gentle, accommodating, full of mercy and good fruit, impartial, and sincere. 18 Peacemakers who sow in peace reap the fruit of righteousness.
paragraphs: 13 Who is wise and understanding among you? Let him show it by his good conduct, by deeds done in the humility that comes from wisdom. 14 But if you harbor bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your hearts, do not boast in it or deny the truth. 15 Such wisdom does not come from above, but is earthly, unspiritual, demonic. 16 For where jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there will be disorder and every evil practice.

17 But the wisdom from above is first of all pure, then peace-loving, gentle, accommodating, full of mercy and good fruit, impartial, and sincere. 18 Peacemakers who sow in peace reap the fruit of righteousness.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
James asks the person who claims wisdom to show it through good conduct and humble deeds. The question continues the chapter’s concern with speech: impressive words are not enough to establish that someone is wise.

Bitter jealousy and selfish ambition reveal a different source. They produce disorder and evil practices, even when someone calls the result wisdom. James tells readers to judge the claim by the life and relationships it produces.

Wisdom from above has a different character: purity, peace, gentleness, mercy, good fruit, impartiality and sincerity. The word behind accommodating points to being willing to listen or yield, rather than insisting on one’s own way. Peacemaking is joined with righteousness, not used as a reason to abandon it.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Calvin and Wesley both read the contrast as a test of wisdom by its fruit. Calvin emphasizes correcting wrongdoing peacefully rather than using cruelty, and Wesley describes gentleness as a willingness to be persuaded rather than remain stubborn.
passages.god_plan_html: Jesus calls peacemakers sons of God in Matthew 5:9. The peaceable wisdom James describes fits that family likeness. Galatians 5:22–23 likewise describes peace, gentleness and goodness as the Spirit’s fruit: the character of God’s people is part of His work among them.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: James 4:1-3
passages.section_title: What do our quarrels reveal about what we want?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 What causes conflicts and quarrels among you? Don’t they come from the passions at war within you? 2 You crave what you do not have; you kill and covet, but are unable to obtain it. You quarrel and fight. You do not have, because you do not ask. 3 And when you do ask, you do not receive, because you ask with wrong motives, that you may squander it on your pleasures.
paragraphs: 1 What causes conflicts and quarrels among you? Don’t they come from the passions at war within you? 2 You crave what you do not have; you kill and covet, but are unable to obtain it. You quarrel and fight. You do not have, because you do not ask. 3 And when you do ask, you do not receive, because you ask with wrong motives, that you may squander it on your pleasures.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The peaceable wisdom described at the end of chapter 3 stands in sharp contrast to the quarrels now addressed. James directs attention from the outward conflict to the competing desires within the people involved.

Craving, coveting, killing and fighting show the destructive course of desires that cannot be satisfied. James then brings prayer into the same picture. Some do not ask God; others ask with the purpose of spending what they receive on their pleasures.

This is a rebuke of self-seeking conflict and prayer, rather than a diagnosis of every disappointed request. The question is what the people want God to serve, as well as whether they are asking Him.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Calvin and Wesley both connect the quarrels with desires allowed to rule the heart and read the prayer warning as a rebuke of wrong motives. Wesley understands the language of killing as hatred in the heart; James supplies no account of a particular incident here.
passages.god_plan_html:
Galatians 5:13–15 contrasts using freedom for the flesh with serving one another in love. God’s purpose for the community is not satisfied by religious language added to rivalry.

1 John 5:14–15 describes confidence in prayer in relation to God’s will. Beside James, it directs asking toward trust in Him rather than an attempt to enlist His power for whatever the heart happens to crave.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Prayer and Faith identifies two failures here: not asking God, and asking with motives directed toward self-gratification rather than His purposes. It also keeps the limit of the passage clear: James does not promise that sincere motives guarantee the outcome someone wants. His warning calls for examining the desire beneath the request.

deeper_study.title: Should We Seek Signs From God?

passages.title: James 4:2-3
passages.section_title: Why might asking God still leave our desires unfulfilled?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 2 You crave what you do not have; you kill and covet, but are unable to obtain it. You quarrel and fight. You do not have, because you do not ask. 3 And when you do ask, you do not receive, because you ask with wrong motives, that you may squander it on your pleasures.
paragraphs: 2 You crave what you do not have; you kill and covet, but are unable to obtain it. You quarrel and fight. You do not have, because you do not ask. 3 And when you do ask, you do not receive, because you ask with wrong motives, that you may squander it on your pleasures.

passages.context_html:
These verses belong to James’ rebuke of quarrels and competing desires in the community. The people seek what they want through conflict, and even their asking can remain directed toward self-indulgence.

James identifies both a failure to ask and a failure in the purpose of asking. Prayer is not detached from the conduct and desires surrounding it. The wider passage calls the readers back to humble dependence on God.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Calvin and Wesley both read the passage as exposing self-serving desires beneath prayer. It calls for turning toward God with those desires brought under His will, rather than using prayer to justify them.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Prayer and Faith identifies two failures here: not asking God, and asking with motives directed toward self-gratification rather than His purposes. It also keeps the limit of the passage clear: James does not promise that sincere motives guarantee the outcome someone wants. His warning calls for examining the desire beneath the request.

deeper_study.title: Should We Seek Signs From God?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html: In 1 John 5:14–15, the confidence of asking rests in God and concerns requests according to His will. That fits James’ larger concern with allegiance: prayer belongs to a life dependent on God, rather than a method of gaining control over outcomes.

passages.title: James 4:4-6
passages.section_title: Why does divided loyalty matter so much?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 4 You adulteresses! Do you not know that friendship with the world is hostility toward God? Therefore, whoever chooses to be a friend of the world renders himself an enemy of God. 5 Or do you think the Scripture says without reason that the Spirit He caused to dwell in us yearns with envy? 6 But He gives us more grace. This is why it says: “God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”
paragraphs: 4 You adulteresses! Do you not know that friendship with the world is hostility toward God? Therefore, whoever chooses to be a friend of the world renders himself an enemy of God. 5 Or do you think the Scripture says without reason that the Spirit He caused to dwell in us yearns with envy? 6 But He gives us more grace. This is why it says: “God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
James describes friendship with the world as hostility toward God. In this setting, the world is the pattern of self-seeking desires that produces rivalry, rather than simply the existence of other people or the goodness of creation.

The language of adultery gives divided allegiance the weight of a broken relationship. James then refers to Scripture, the spirit dwelling within, and envy. The wording of verse 5 has been understood in several ways, as the readings below explain.

The next statement supplies a clear direction: God gives more grace, opposes the proud and gives grace to the humble. The rebuke is followed by an invitation to turn, not a command to remain trapped in pride.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The main disagreement concerns verse 5. One reading takes it as describing the human spirit’s tendency toward envy. Calvin reports that reading but instead takes the verse as a question about the Holy Spirit: does He produce envy? Calvin’s answer is no; the Spirit gives generously.

Wesley also understands the Holy Spirit but reads the sentence as describing His opposition to envy. The USCCB notes identify further possibilities: the Spirit longing jealously for believers, or God longing jealously for the spirit He placed in them. Those readings emphasize God’s claim on His people rather than attributing sinful envy to Him.

These are differences in understanding a difficult sentence, rather than settled positions held uniformly by whole denominations. The surrounding warning against divided loyalty and the promise of grace remain central.
passages.god_plan_html: 2 Corinthians 11:2–4 also uses the picture of faithfulness to one husband, applying it to the church’s devotion to Christ. That gives a clear New Testament setting for James’ relationship language. It supports the seriousness of allegiance to God without deciding every question about the wording of verse 5.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: James 4:7-10
passages.section_title: What does returning to God look like?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 Submit yourselves, then, to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. 8 Draw near to God, and He will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners, and purify your hearts, you double-minded. 9 Grieve, mourn, and weep. Turn your laughter to mourning, and your joy to gloom. 10 Humble yourselves before the Lord, and He will exalt you.
paragraphs: 7 Submit yourselves, then, to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. 8 Draw near to God, and He will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners, and purify your hearts, you double-minded. 9 Grieve, mourn, and weep. Turn your laughter to mourning, and your joy to gloom. 10 Humble yourselves before the Lord, and He will exalt you.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
God’s grace to the humble leads to a series of direct calls: submit to God, resist the devil, draw near, cleanse the hands and purify the heart. The turn involves both outward conduct and the desires beneath it.

To resist is to stand against or oppose. The command belongs with submission to God, rather than confidence in an independent spiritual power of one’s own.

The mourning concerns the sin and divided loyalty James has exposed. It calls for taking that failure seriously, rather than treating it lightly. Humbling oneself before the Lord leaves the lifting up to Him.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Calvin and Wesley both understand this as a call to repentance, humble dependence and resistance to evil. Calvin explicitly connects sorrow with turning from sin, while Wesley connects drawing near with prayer; the passage does not make permanent misery the goal of Christian life.
passages.god_plan_html: Philippians 2:5–11 calls believers to the mind of Christ and describes His humility, obedience and exaltation. This is a useful parallel in direction: life before God is not a competition to lift oneself above others. Jesus’ unique exaltation as Lord is not a promise that every humble person receives His place, but His self-giving life supplies the pattern for His people.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: James 4:11-12
passages.section_title: What happens when we set ourselves up as judges of one another?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 Brothers, do not slander one another. Anyone who speaks against his brother or judges him speaks against the law and judges it. And if you judge the law, you are not a practitioner of the law, but a judge of it. 12 There is only one Lawgiver and Judge, the One who is able to save and destroy. But who are you to judge your neighbor?
paragraphs: 11 Brothers, do not slander one another. Anyone who speaks against his brother or judges him speaks against the law and judges it. And if you judge the law, you are not a practitioner of the law, but a judge of it. 12 There is only one Lawgiver and Judge, the One who is able to save and destroy. But who are you to judge your neighbor?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
James returns to harmful speech between believers. Slandering a brother or sister sets the speaker against the law that calls for love of neighbor. Instead of doing that law, the person assumes a position over it.

The contrast is with the one Lawgiver and Judge, who can save and destroy. The speaker must remember his or her own place before God, rather than treat a personal verdict about another person as the final authority.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Calvin and Wesley both read the warning as a rejection of presumptuous condemnation and speech that places the speaker above God’s law. Calvin distinguishes judging by personal preference from submitting to what God actually commands.
passages.god_plan_html: Romans 14:1–4, 10–13 applies a similar concern to disputed practices: believers belong to the Lord and each will give an account to God. 1 Corinthians 4:3–5 adds that the Lord will expose hidden motives. The church’s life is therefore shaped by His authority and knowledge, rather than claims to know everything about another person’s heart.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: James 4:13-17
passages.section_title: How should we make plans when we do not control tomorrow?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 Come now, you who say, “Today or tomorrow we will go to this or that city, spend a year there, carry on business, and make a profit.” 14 You do not even know what will happen tomorrow! What is your life? You are a mist that appears for a little while and then vanishes. 15 Instead, you ought to say, “If the Lord is willing, we will live and do this or that.” 16 As it is, you boast in your proud intentions. All such boasting is evil. 17 Anyone, then, who knows the right thing to do, yet fails to do it, is guilty of sin.
paragraphs: 13 Come now, you who say, “Today or tomorrow we will go to this or that city, spend a year there, carry on business, and make a profit.” 14 You do not even know what will happen tomorrow! What is your life? You are a mist that appears for a little while and then vanishes. 15 Instead, you ought to say, “If the Lord is willing, we will live and do this or that.” 16 As it is, you boast in your proud intentions. All such boasting is evil.
17 Anyone, then, who knows the right thing to do, yet fails to do it, is guilty of sin.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The merchants’ confident announcement covers a destination, a year of business and a profit. James challenges the assumption beneath it: they do not even know what tomorrow will bring, and their own lives are brief.

Acknowledging the Lord’s will changes the posture of planning. Both being alive and carrying out a plan depend on Him. The problem is arrogant confidence in control, rather than the ordinary act of preparing for the future.

The final sentence brings knowledge back to action: knowing the good and failing to do it is sin. The readers cannot treat an acknowledgment of God as a substitute for living accordingly.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Calvin and Wesley read this as a warning against planning as though life were in one’s own hands. Calvin explicitly distinguishes the attitude from a rule that every sentence about the future must include a particular phrase; the point is real dependence on God.
passages.god_plan_html:
Proverbs 27:1 already warns against boasting about tomorrow. James carries that wisdom into the plans of people who confess the Lord.

Luke 12:47–48 connects knowing the Master’s will with responsibility to act on it. The future’s uncertainty gives weight to present faithfulness, rather than excusing inaction until everything can be known.

passages.title: James 5:1-6
passages.section_title: What does God see when wealth is built on another person’s suffering?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Come now, you who are rich, weep and wail over the misery to come upon you. 2 Your riches have rotted and moths have eaten your clothes. 3 Your gold and silver are corroded. Their corrosion will testify against you and consume your flesh like fire. You have hoarded treasure in the last days. 4 Look, the wages you withheld from the workmen who mowed your fields are crying out against you. The cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of Hosts. 5 You have lived on earth in luxury and self-indulgence. You have fattened your hearts in the day of slaughter. 6 You have condemned and murdered the righteous, who did not resist you.
paragraphs: 1 Come now, you who are rich, weep and wail over the misery to come upon you. 2 Your riches have rotted and moths have eaten your clothes. 3 Your gold and silver are corroded. Their corrosion will testify against you and consume your flesh like fire. You have hoarded treasure in the last days.

4 Look, the wages you withheld from the workmen who mowed your fields are crying out against you. The cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of Hosts. 5 You have lived on earth in luxury and self-indulgence. You have fattened your hearts in the day of slaughter. 6 You have condemned and murdered the righteous, who did not resist you.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The warning about proud plans now becomes a warning to the unjust rich. James pictures wealth decaying and testifying against its possessors. What had seemed to offer security instead becomes evidence of how they have lived.

The accusations are concrete: withheld wages, luxury and self-indulgence, condemnation and the killing of the righteous. The harvesters’ cries have reached the Lord of Hosts. Their lack of earthly protection does not mean their suffering has escaped His notice.

The warning concerns wealth joined with exploitation and disregard for God. It does not say that every possession is evil or that every rich person has committed each offense listed.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Calvin and Wesley both read the passage as a severe warning to oppressors and an encouragement to those suffering under them. Wesley sees the righteous person’s suffering as including Christ; Calvin emphasizes the innocent poor harmed by the powerful.
passages.god_plan_html: Deuteronomy 24:14–15 forbids withholding a needy worker’s wages and warns that the worker may cry to God. Malachi 3:5 names defrauding laborers among the wrongs the Lord of Hosts will judge. James continues that account of God’s justice: power and wealth do not place someone beyond His hearing or judgment.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: James 5:7-11
passages.section_title: What can keep us steady while we wait for justice?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 Be patient, then, brothers, until the Lord’s coming. See how the farmer awaits the precious fruit of the soil—how patient he is for the fall and spring rains. 8 You, too, be patient and strengthen your hearts, because the Lord’s coming is near. 9 Do not complain about one another, brothers, so that you will not be judged. Look, the Judge is standing at the door! 10 Brothers, as an example of patience in affliction, take the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord. 11 See how blessed we consider those who have persevered. You have heard of Job’s perseverance and have seen the outcome from the Lord. The Lord is full of compassion and mercy.
paragraphs: 7 Be patient, then, brothers, until the Lord’s coming. See how the farmer awaits the precious fruit of the soil—how patient he is for the fall and spring rains. 8 You, too, be patient and strengthen your hearts, because the Lord’s coming is near. 9 Do not complain about one another, brothers, so that you will not be judged. Look, the Judge is standing at the door!

10 Brothers, as an example of patience in affliction, take the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord. 11 See how blessed we consider those who have persevered. You have heard of Job’s perseverance and have seen the outcome from the Lord. The Lord is full of compassion and mercy.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
James turns to the brothers and calls them to patience until the Lord’s coming. The farmer waits for a harvest that cannot be forced into immediate existence. The readers likewise need strengthened hearts while the outcome is still ahead.

Waiting also concerns their treatment of one another. They must not turn their hardship into complaining against their brothers and sisters, forgetting that they too stand before the Judge.

The prophets and Job show that suffering does not mean a person has been abandoned by God. James directs attention to endurance and to the Lord’s compassion and mercy in the outcome.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley both understand patience as sustained hope in the Lord’s judgment and care. They differ over the immediate reference of His nearness: Calvin prefers the final deliverance at Christ’s coming, while Wesley also connects it with judgment on Jerusalem, alongside the final coming.

Calvin also observes that Job’s endurance was not the absence of every troubled word or failure. The example encourages perseverance through weakness, rather than requiring a sufferer never to express grief.
passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 11:32–40 places faithful people who experienced deliverance beside others who continued to suffer. Their common hope extends beyond what happened during their lifetimes.

Job 42:7–17 shows God correcting Job’s friends, accepting his prayer and restoring him. James draws attention to the Lord’s merciful outcome; that account does not promise every reader an identical sequence of losses and material recovery.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: James 5:12
passages.section_title: Why should our ordinary word be trustworthy?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 Above all, my brothers, do not swear, not by heaven or earth or by any other oath. Simply let your “Yes” be yes, and your “No,” no, so that you will not fall under judgment.
paragraphs: 12 Above all, my brothers, do not swear, not by heaven or earth or by any other oath. Simply let your “Yes” be yes, and your “No,” no, so that you will not fall under judgment.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
James returns to speech, warning against swearing by heaven, earth or another oath. The positive instruction is simple: let yes and no be reliable. Truthfulness is to characterize ordinary dealings, not depend on finding a stronger-sounding promise.

The warning about judgment gives the instruction weight. A claim of devotion to God must not coexist with speech that misleads others.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians agree on truthful speech but differ over whether every solemn oath is forbidden. The Reformed Westminster Confession, 22.1–4, permits lawful oaths in serious matters while rejecting rash or deceptive swearing. The Catholic Catechism, 2154, likewise permits oaths for grave and right reasons. Wesley allows a solemn oath before a magistrate.

The Mennonite Church USA Confession, article 20, instead calls for avoiding oaths, including affirming the truth in legal matters without swearing. Its reading applies James’ instruction directly to both ordinary speech and formal assurances.
passages.god_plan_html: This closely parallels Jesus’ teaching in Matthew 5:33–37. Both direct people toward dependable speech before God. The connection places James’ practical instruction within the way of life Jesus teaches His followers.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: James 5:13-16
passages.section_title: How should we care for one another in suffering and sickness?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 Is any one of you suffering? He should pray. Is anyone cheerful? He should sing praises. 14 Is any one of you sick? He should call the elders of the church to pray over him and anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord. 15 And the prayer offered in faith will restore the one who is sick. The Lord will raise him up. If he has sinned, he will be forgiven. 16 Therefore confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous man has great power to prevail.
paragraphs: 13 Is any one of you suffering? He should pray. Is anyone cheerful? He should sing praises. 14 Is any one of you sick? He should call the elders of the church to pray over him and anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord. 15 And the prayer offered in faith will restore the one who is sick. The Lord will raise him up. If he has sinned, he will be forgiven.
16 Therefore confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous man has great power to prevail.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
James calls suffering people to pray and cheerful people to sing praises. Neither condition is to leave God out of the picture. When someone is sick, the community’s elders are to be called to pray and anoint the person with oil in the Lord’s name.

The Lord is the One who raises the sick person up. James also speaks of forgiveness if the person has sinned, then calls believers to confess and pray for one another. The care embraces a person’s life before God as well as the condition that prompted the request.

The word translated sick can describe weakness or physical illness, and the word behind restore can describe physical rescue or salvation. Those words do not by themselves exclude bodily healing or settle every question about the promise. The conditional statement about sin does not say that every illness is punishment for a personal offense.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The Catholic Church understands this anointing as a sacrament for the sick (Catechism, 1510–1513). It describes spiritual strengthening and bodily healing if God wills (1520). This is not an unconditional guarantee of physical recovery.

Calvin reads the anointing as a sign associated with the early church’s temporary gift of healing. Wesley instead thinks the healing practice was intended to continue, and understands verse 16’s healing to include spiritual diseases. Their different accounts should not be treated as one Protestant view.

On confession, Wesley emphasizes the instruction’s mutual character: believers may confess to others who can pray for them, rather than only to elders. Catholic teaching also recognizes confession and forgiveness within the church’s priestly ministry (Catechism, 1441–1448); it teaches that the forgiveness itself comes from God.
passages.god_plan_html:
Mark 6:12–13 connects repentance, the disciples’ mission and anointing sick people with oil. James brings prayer and care into the ongoing life of the community.

John 9:1–3 prevents a simple diagnosis of every illness as someone’s personal sin. 2 Corinthians 12:7–10 also shows Christ sustaining a servant through weakness after a request for its removal. Together these passages keep care, restoration and trust in Christ’s strength in view.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Prayer and Faith reads this passage as a call to seek spiritual restoration and renewed fellowship with God, with physical recovery remaining in His hands. It understands faithful prayer as dependence on God’s will, rather than an unconditional promise of healing produced by the strength of someone’s belief. Our study Baptism understands the mutual confession here as accountability and healing among believers, rather than a priestly requirement for receiving God’s forgiveness.

passages.title: James 5:14
passages.section_title: Why call the elders when someone is sick?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 Is any one of you sick? He should call the elders of the church to pray over him and anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord.
paragraphs: 14 Is any one of you sick? He should call the elders of the church to pray over him and anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord.

passages.context_html:
This instruction follows the call to pray in suffering and sing in cheerfulness. The sick person is to seek the elders’ care, and they are to pray and anoint with oil in the Lord’s name.

The following verses speak of the Lord raising the person up, forgiveness, confession and mutual prayer. The verse should therefore be read as part of a community caring for someone before God, rather than as an isolated technique.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The Catholic Church treats the anointing as a sacrament for the sick (Catechism, 1510–1513), administered by priests (1516).

Calvin understands it as a sign belonging to the early gift of healing, which he considers temporary. Wesley instead understands the practice as intended to remain. These readings differ over the continuing place and form of the anointing, while agreeing that the sick person should receive prayerful care.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Prayer and Faith reads this passage as a call to seek spiritual restoration and renewed fellowship with God, with physical recovery remaining in His hands. It understands faithful prayer as dependence on God’s will, rather than an unconditional promise of healing produced by the strength of someone’s belief.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html: The disciples anoint sick people with oil in Mark 6:12–13. The connection places the instruction alongside Jesus’ mission of compassion and restoration. The prayer is offered in His name; neither the oil nor the elder is presented as an independent source of healing.

passages.title: James 5:14-16
passages.section_title: What are prayer, healing and confession doing together?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 Is any one of you sick? He should call the elders of the church to pray over him and anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord. 15 And the prayer offered in faith will restore the one who is sick. The Lord will raise him up. If he has sinned, he will be forgiven. 16 Therefore confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous man has great power to prevail.
paragraphs: 14 Is any one of you sick? He should call the elders of the church to pray over him and anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord. 15 And the prayer offered in faith will restore the one who is sick. The Lord will raise him up. If he has sinned, he will be forgiven. 16 Therefore confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous man has great power to prevail.

passages.context_html:
James joins elders’ prayer, anointing, the Lord’s raising up, forgiveness and the confession of sins. The person in need is not left to carry the condition alone, and the believers are told to pray for each other.

The wording if he has sinned keeps the connection with personal sin conditional. James calls for honesty and restoration without making every sick person guilty of a particular hidden offense.

The words for sickness and restoration allow bodily as well as spiritual concerns. The promise cannot be explained simply by declaring that the Greek rules physical healing out.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The Catholic Church understands the anointing as a sacrament (Catechism, 1510–1513), bringing spiritual help and bodily healing if God wills (1520). It also teaches a priestly ministry of reconciliation in which God forgives (1441–1448).

Calvin connects the oil with the early church’s temporary gift of healing, while Wesley understands the practice as intended to continue. Both see mutual confession as prompting believers to pray for one another; Wesley explicitly refuses to confine that confession to elders.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Prayer and Faith reads this passage as a call to seek spiritual restoration and renewed fellowship with God, with physical recovery remaining in His hands. It understands faithful prayer as dependence on God’s will, rather than an unconditional promise of healing produced by the strength of someone’s belief. Our study Baptism understands the mutual confession here as accountability and healing among believers, rather than a priestly requirement for receiving God’s forgiveness.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Mark 6:12–13 places anointing and healing beside repentance in the disciples’ mission. John 9:1–3 also shows why care must not become an automatic accusation of personal sin.

2 Corinthians 12:7–10 brings another part of Christ’s care into view: strength given through continuing weakness. His saving purposes encompass more than the immediate removal of every painful condition.

passages.title: James 5:16
passages.section_title: Why confess and pray for one another?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 Therefore confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous man has great power to prevail.
paragraphs: 16 Therefore confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous man has great power to prevail.

passages.context_html:
The mutual confession and prayer follow James’ instructions about care for the sick. They extend the concern beyond a person privately carrying a need: believers are to be truthful with one another and seek healing together.

The following example of Elijah emphasizes that prayer has real effect even when the person praying shares ordinary human weakness. James directs confidence toward prayer before God, rather than toward a supposedly untouchable religious class.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley both understand confession as helping fellow believers pray with knowledge of one another’s needs. Wesley says it is not restricted to confession to elders and describes the healing here in spiritual terms.

The Catholic Church also teaches a distinct priestly ministry of reconciliation, while locating the source of forgiveness in God (Catechism, 1441–1448). That broader teaching differs from reading mutual confession here as the whole pattern for the church’s practice.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Prayer and Faith reads this passage as a call to seek spiritual restoration and renewed fellowship with God, with physical recovery remaining in His hands. It understands faithful prayer as dependence on God’s will, rather than an unconditional promise of healing produced by the strength of someone’s belief. Our study Baptism understands the mutual confession here as accountability and healing among believers, rather than a priestly requirement for receiving God’s forgiveness.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html: Galatians 6:1–2 calls for gentle restoration and carrying one another’s burdens as the law of Christ. That supplies a fitting wider setting for confession and prayer: helping someone return and heal, rather than using knowledge of a fault to humiliate or control that person.

passages.title: James 5:17-18
passages.section_title: Why does James use Elijah as an example of prayer?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 Elijah was a man just like us. He prayed earnestly that it would not rain, and it did not rain on the land for three and a half years. 18 Again he prayed, and the heavens gave rain, and the earth yielded its crops.
paragraphs: 17 Elijah was a man just like us. He prayed earnestly that it would not rain, and it did not rain on the land for three and a half years. 18 Again he prayed, and the heavens gave rain, and the earth yielded its crops.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After speaking of the power of a righteous person’s prayer, James names Elijah and immediately puts him within reach: he was a man just like us. The example encourages people who might otherwise imagine effective prayer belongs only to a different kind of human being.

James recalls prayer for the withholding of rain and prayer followed by its return. The land’s renewed fruitfulness makes the effect concrete.

The background is 1 Kings 17–18. In 18:1, God announces that He will send rain, and later Elijah bows before Him before the rain returns. The story presents God acting in relation to His prophet’s prayer, rather than Elijah independently controlling the weather.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Calvin and Wesley both understand Elijah as an encouragement to prayer by ordinary people dependent on God. Calvin explicitly warns against presuming that the example tells everyone to ask for the same drought; it teaches confidence in prayer, rather than imitation of every request.
passages.god_plan_html: In 1 Kings 18:36–39, Elijah asks that the people know the Lord is God and that their hearts are turned back. The rain belongs within that larger account of God confronting divided worship and calling His people back to Himself. James’ example therefore reaches beyond personal achievement to the Lord’s work of restoration.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Prayer and Faith understands Elijah’s example as prayer in agreement with God’s declared purposes. Its emphasis is on confidence in His will, rather than belief strong enough to produce a private outcome independently of Him.

passages.title: James 5:19-20
passages.section_title: What is at stake when someone wanders from the truth?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 My brothers, if one of you should wander from the truth and someone should bring him back, 20 consider this: Whoever turns a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover over a multitude of sins.
paragraphs: 19 My brothers, if one of you should wander from the truth and someone should bring him back, 20 consider this: Whoever turns a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover over a multitude of sins.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The letter closes with responsibility for one another. If someone wanders from the truth, another person may help bring that sinner back. James presents this as a work of rescue, not an opportunity for superiority.

The language of saving a soul from death and covering sins gives restoration its seriousness. The conclusion returns to the letter’s concern that truth be lived, with believers caring about the direction of one another’s lives.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin reads this as rescue from eternal death through God’s use of another believer’s help. Wesley likewise emphasizes the soul’s value and sins no longer remembered in condemnation. The USCCB note describes forgiveness and return to the life of grace.

A distinct Free Grace reading, represented by Keith Pesce, understands the rescue as preserving a believer’s earthly life from sin’s deadly consequences. These readings differ over the death in view, while sharing the call to help a wandering person return.
passages.god_plan_html: Galatians 6:1–2 describes restoration carried out gently by people who remember their own vulnerability. The saving work belongs to God, yet care within Christ’s people can be one of the means by which a sinner is brought back. James ends by directing his readers toward that active concern for one another.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Peter 1:1-2
passages.section_title: What gives these scattered believers their identity?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, To the elect who are exiles of the Dispersion throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, chosen 2 according to the foreknowledge of God the Father and sanctified by the Spirit for obedience to Jesus Christ and sprinkling by His blood: Grace and peace be yours in abundance.
paragraphs: 1 Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, To the elect who are exiles of the Dispersion throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, chosen 2 according to the foreknowledge of God the Father and sanctified by the Spirit for obedience to Jesus Christ and sprinkling by His blood: Grace and peace be yours in abundance.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The letter opens in Peter’s name as an apostle of Jesus Christ and addresses believers scattered through five regions of Asia Minor. They are described both as chosen people and as exiles: their difficult place in the world does not exhaust who they are before God.

The word behind exiles describes people living as strangers in a place. The letter will return to that picture as it considers how believers should live among their neighbors.

Their identity is described in relation to the Father, the Spirit and Jesus Christ. They are chosen according to the Father’s foreknowledge, set apart by the Spirit for obedience to Jesus, and sprinkled by His blood. The greeting joins God’s saving work with the life to which His people are called.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Readers differ over the audience’s background. Calvin and Wesley emphasize Jewish believers living outside their homeland. The USCCB introduction sees clues elsewhere in the letter pointing to a largely Gentile audience. Both approaches recognize the letter’s concern with people living as God’s own among a surrounding society.

Christians also differ over how God’s choice relates to faith. The Reformed Westminster Confession, 3.5–6, teaches that God chooses people for salvation from His free grace, rather than because He foresees their faith, and brings those chosen to faith and obedience.

Wesley instead describes God’s appointment in terms of His gracious promise to save those who believe and persevere. Faith remains God’s gift, while the person’s continuing response matters to the final outcome.

The Catholic Catechism, 600, says God’s eternal plan includes each person’s free response to grace. These readings all speak of God’s initiative, but explain the relationship between His purpose and human response differently.
passages.god_plan_html: The sprinkling language recalls Exodus 24:3–8, where blood marks the people’s covenant relationship with God alongside their commitment to obey. Hebrews 12:24 explicitly speaks of Jesus as the mediator of a new covenant and of His sprinkled blood. That connection places the greeting within God’s work of bringing a people into relationship with Himself through Christ.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Peter 1:3-5
passages.section_title: What makes this hope secure?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 3 Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ! By His great mercy He has given us new birth into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, 4 and into an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, reserved in heaven for you, 5 who through faith are shielded by God’s power for the salvation that is ready to be revealed in the last time.
paragraphs: 3 Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ! By His great mercy He has given us new birth into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, 4 and into an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, reserved in heaven for you, 5 who through faith are shielded by God’s power for the salvation that is ready to be revealed in the last time.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The greeting becomes praise. God’s great mercy has given His people new birth into a living hope through Jesus’ resurrection. The hope has a foundation in what God has done, rather than in a prediction that their present circumstances will become easier.

The inheritance is described through what cannot spoil it: it does not perish, become defiled or fade away. It is reserved in heaven. The readers themselves are also described as guarded by God’s power through faith for the salvation still to be revealed.

The word behind shielded has the sense of guarding and protecting. God’s care for the heirs belongs beside His keeping of their inheritance. The next verses make clear that this protection can coexist with grief and trials.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians commonly understand the living hope as God’s merciful gift grounded in Christ’s resurrection. They differ over whether a person who has received this grace can finally abandon it.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, 17.1–3, teaches that those truly called and accepted by God will be preserved to the end, although they can fall seriously and suffer for it. Calvin reads God’s guarding here as the reason their future salvation need not rest on their own strength.

Wesley emphasizes that salvation is received and retained through faith, in keeping with his call to continue responding to grace. The Catholic Catechism, 162, likewise calls faith a free gift that can be lost and must be nourished. Neither account makes perseverance a matter of unaided human strength.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Corinthians 15:20–23, 50–55 connects Christ’s resurrection with the future resurrection and transformation of those who belong to Him. The inheritance reaches beyond surviving the present life: God’s victory over death includes His people’s future embodied life.

Romans 8:18–25 places that hope alongside creation’s longing for freedom from decay. The unfading inheritance belongs within God’s larger work of renewal, while believers still wait patiently for what they do not yet see.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Peter 1:6-9
passages.section_title: How can joy and grief exist together?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 In this you greatly rejoice, though now for a little while you may have had to suffer grief in various trials 7 so that the proven character of your faith—more precious than gold, which perishes even though refined by fire—may result in praise, glory, and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ. 8 Though you have not seen Him, you love Him; and though you do not see Him now, you believe in Him and rejoice with an inexpressible and glorious joy, 9 now that you are receiving the goal of your faith, the salvation of your souls.
paragraphs: 6 In this you greatly rejoice, though now for a little while you may have had to suffer grief in various trials 7 so that the proven character of your faith—more precious than gold, which perishes even though refined by fire—may result in praise, glory, and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ.

8 Though you have not seen Him, you love Him; and though you do not see Him now, you believe in Him and rejoice with an inexpressible and glorious joy, 9 now that you are receiving the goal of your faith, the salvation of your souls.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Peter does not erase the readers’ grief. They rejoice in the hope just described while suffering trials. The temporary hardship is placed beside the lasting salvation and inheritance, rather than treated as the whole measure of their future.

The comparison with gold explains the value of tested faith. Fire proves and refines a precious metal, yet even gold perishes. Faith’s proven character looks toward praise, glory and honor when Jesus is revealed.

These believers love Jesus although they have not seen Him. Their relationship with Him is real in the present, with joy that anticipates the salvation toward which their faith is directed.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Calvin and Wesley both understand grief and joy as able to coexist in a believer’s life. Calvin explicitly says joy does not remove human feeling, while Wesley places present trials beside hope that reaches into eternity.
passages.god_plan_html:
In John 20:29–31, Jesus blesses those who believe without having seen Him, and the Gospel’s written testimony is given so people may believe and have life in His name. Peter addresses just such a life of trust and love.

The wider hope is also expressed in Romans 8:18–25: present suffering does not have the final word over the glory to come. Grief can therefore be honestly acknowledged while the believer continues looking toward Christ.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Peter 1:10-12
passages.section_title: How does the gospel complete what the prophets were looking toward?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 Concerning this salvation, the prophets who foretold the grace to come to you searched and investigated carefully, 11 trying to determine the time and setting to which the Spirit of Christ in them was pointing when He predicted the sufferings of Christ and the glories to follow. 12 It was revealed to them that they were not serving themselves, but you, when they foretold the things now announced by those who preached the gospel to you by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven. Even angels long to look into these things.
paragraphs: 10 Concerning this salvation, the prophets who foretold the grace to come to you searched and investigated carefully, 11 trying to determine the time and setting to which the Spirit of Christ in them was pointing when He predicted the sufferings of Christ and the glories to follow. 12 It was revealed to them that they were not serving themselves, but you, when they foretold the things now announced by those who preached the gospel to you by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven. Even angels long to look into these things.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The salvation the readers now receive had a history before their own experience of it. The prophets foretold grace to come, then searched to understand the time and setting of the sufferings of Christ and the glories that would follow.

The Spirit of Christ worked in that earlier testimony, and the Holy Spirit is also named in the gospel’s proclamation. Peter connects the earlier promise and its later announcement, giving the readers reason to value what has reached them.

The angels’ desire to look into these things adds a final note of wonder. The word behind look into can describe careful, intent attention. The readers are hearing news of a saving work that reaches far beyond their immediate circumstances.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Calvin and Wesley both read this as showing the privilege of receiving the gospel’s fuller revelation of Christ. Calvin explicitly distinguishes the prophets’ looking toward fulfillment from a claim that they themselves had no share in God’s salvation.
passages.god_plan_html: Jesus gives a direct explanation of the same movement in Luke 24:25–27, 44–49. He connects Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms with His suffering and resurrection, then with repentance and forgiveness proclaimed to all nations. Peter’s readers stand within that announced fulfillment: what the prophets looked toward has become good news carried outward through the Holy Spirit.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Peter 1:13-16
passages.section_title: How should hope change the way we live?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 Therefore prepare your minds for action. Be sober-minded. Set your hope fully on the grace to be given you at the revelation of Jesus Christ. 14 As obedient children, do not conform to the passions of your former ignorance. 15 But just as He who called you is holy, so be holy in all you do, 16 for it is written: “Be holy, because I am holy.”
paragraphs: 13 Therefore prepare your minds for action. Be sober-minded. Set your hope fully on the grace to be given you at the revelation of Jesus Christ. 14 As obedient children, do not conform to the passions of your former ignorance. 15 But just as He who called you is holy, so be holy in all you do, 16 for it is written: “Be holy, because I am holy.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The hope described in the first half of the chapter now leads to action. Peter calls the readers to prepare their minds, remain sober-minded and set their hope fully on the grace to come when Jesus is revealed.

The word behind sober-minded points to calm, watchful self-control. The instruction reaches into the direction of thought and desire, rather than being limited to avoiding drunkenness.

As obedient children, they are to leave their former passions behind and reflect the holiness of the God who called them. The call concerns all their conduct. Peter grounds it in God’s own character, quoting the earlier command to be holy because He is holy.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Calvin and Wesley both understand these commands as the response of people who have received grace and now await Christ. They connect readiness and self-control with a changed life shaped by God’s holiness.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Leviticus 19:1–2, 9–18, the call to holiness includes leaving food for the poor, paying workers honestly, fair judgment and love of neighbor. Holiness reaches into ordinary treatment of other people.

Jesus likewise calls His followers to reflect their Father’s character in Matthew 5:43–48, including love for enemies. Read alongside Peter, that gives practical shape to living as God’s children: His character is to become visible in their conduct.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Peter 1:17-21
passages.section_title: What does the cost of our redemption ask of us?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 Since you call on a Father who judges each one’s work impartially, conduct yourselves in reverent fear during your stay as foreigners. 18 For you know that it was not with perishable things such as silver or gold that you were redeemed from the empty way of life you inherited from your forefathers, 19 but with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot. 20 He was known before the foundation of the world, but was revealed in the last times for your sake. 21 Through Him you believe in God, who raised Him from the dead and glorified Him; and so your faith and hope are in God.
paragraphs: 17 Since you call on a Father who judges each one’s work impartially, conduct yourselves in reverent fear during your stay as foreigners. 18 For you know that it was not with perishable things such as silver or gold that you were redeemed from the empty way of life you inherited from your forefathers, 19 but with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot.

20 He was known before the foundation of the world, but was revealed in the last times for your sake. 21 Through Him you believe in God, who raised Him from the dead and glorified Him; and so your faith and hope are in God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The God the readers call Father also judges impartially. Their relationship with Him calls for reverent fear during their life as foreigners, taking seriously how they live before Him.

The reason reaches back to their redemption. Silver and gold could not free them from the empty way of life received from their forefathers. The price named is Christ’s precious blood, pictured as that of a lamb without blemish or spot. The word translated redeemed carries the sense of release or deliverance.

Christ was known before the world’s foundation and revealed for their sake. Through Him their faith and hope are directed to the God who raised and glorified Him. The appeal to holy living therefore rests on the saving work already described, not simply on fear in isolation.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Calvin and Wesley both connect reverent conduct with the Father’s impartial judgment and the cost of Christ’s redeeming work. Calvin emphasizes that God sees the heart beyond outward appearance; Wesley describes the fear as humble and loving, accompanying hope.
passages.god_plan_html:
The unblemished lamb recalls Exodus 12:1–13, where the Passover accompanies deliverance from Egypt. John 1:29 directly identifies Jesus as the Lamb of God who takes away the world’s sin.

Peter connects that saving work with deliverance from an empty way of life. The purpose includes a people learning to live before God through Christ, with their faith and hope placed in the One who raised Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Peter 1:22-25
passages.section_title: Why does new birth lead to sincere love?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 Since you have purified your souls by obedience to the truth so that you have a genuine love for your brothers, love one another deeply, from a pure heart. 23 For you have been born again, not of perishable seed, but of imperishable, through the living and enduring word of God. 24 For, “All flesh is like grass, and all its glory like the flowers of the field; the grass withers and the flowers fall, 25 but the word of the Lord stands forever.” And this is the word that was proclaimed to you.
paragraphs: 22 Since you have purified your souls by obedience to the truth so that you have a genuine love for your brothers, love one another deeply, from a pure heart. 23 For you have been born again, not of perishable seed, but of imperishable, through the living and enduring word of God.

24 For, “All flesh is like grass, and all its glory like the flowers of the field; the grass withers and the flowers fall, 25 but the word of the Lord stands forever.” And this is the word that was proclaimed to you.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Peter turns from the cost of redemption to the readers’ life together. Their purification through obedience to the truth is directed toward genuine brotherly love, and he calls them to love deeply from a pure heart.

New birth provides the reason. Their new life comes through God’s living and enduring word. Peter places that lasting source beside the fragility of human life and glory, using Isaiah’s picture of withering grass and falling flowers.

The final sentence identifies the word as the gospel proclaimed to them. The message they received is meant to form a community of sincere love, rather than remain something they have only heard.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Calvin and Wesley both connect the new life God gives with active love. Calvin stresses continuing purification and growing sincerity; Wesley starts from the gift already received and calls for deeper love. Both understand the enduring word as the ground of a life that should bear its character.
passages.god_plan_html:
Isaiah 40:1–11 places the enduring word within God’s promise of comfort, His coming and His shepherding care. Peter applies that word to the gospel his readers have heard.

Jesus makes mutual love a visible mark of His disciples in John 13:34–35, giving His own love as their pattern. The new birth Peter describes is therefore connected with a shared life that shows whose people they are.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Peter 2:1-3
passages.section_title: What helps a new life grow?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Rid yourselves, therefore, of all malice, deceit, hypocrisy, envy, and slander. 2 Like newborn babies, crave pure spiritual milk, so that by it you may grow up in your salvation, 3 now that you have tasted that the Lord is good.
paragraphs: 1 Rid yourselves, therefore, of all malice, deceit, hypocrisy, envy, and slander. 2 Like newborn babies, crave pure spiritual milk, so that by it you may grow up in your salvation, 3 now that you have tasted that the Lord is good.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The new birth and sincere love described at the end of chapter 1 now lead to putting away malice, deceit, hypocrisy, envy and slander. These habits damage the very shared life the readers are called to cultivate.

The newborn’s appetite for milk gives the positive picture: crave nourishment that will bring growth in salvation. The word behind spiritual describes what nourishes the soul. The image follows Peter’s description of the enduring word through which they have received new life.

The appeal rests on having tasted the Lord’s goodness, recalling Psalm 34:8. Growth is a response to the One whose goodness they have begun to know.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley identifies the milk with God’s word nourishing faith, love and holiness. Calvin gives the picture a wider emphasis on the sincere, God-shaped life fitting the new birth. Both read the call as ongoing growth, rather than permission to remain immature.
passages.god_plan_html:
Psalm 34:1–10 joins tasting God’s goodness with refuge, praise and fear of the Lord. Peter draws the readers into that continuing life of dependence.

Ephesians 2:19–22 describes believers growing together into God’s dwelling place. The move from newborns to living stones in Peter’s next paragraph likewise places growth within a people being formed together.
