passages.title: 1 Peter 2:4-8
passages.section_title: What is God building around Christ?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 4 As you come to Him, the living stone, rejected by men but chosen and precious in God’s sight, 5 you also, like living stones, are being built into a spiritual house to be a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ. 6 For it stands in Scripture: “See, I lay in Zion a stone, a chosen and precious cornerstone; and the one who believes in Him will never be put to shame.” 7 To you who believe, then, this stone is precious. But to those who do not believe, “The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone,” 8 and, “A stone of stumbling and a rock of offense.” They stumble because they disobey the word—and to this they were appointed.
paragraphs: 4 As you come to Him, the living stone, rejected by men but chosen and precious in God’s sight, 5 you also, like living stones, are being built into a spiritual house to be a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.

6 For it stands in Scripture: “See, I lay in Zion a stone, a chosen and precious cornerstone; and the one who believes in Him will never be put to shame.” 7 To you who believe, then, this stone is precious. But to those who do not believe, “The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone,” 8 and, “A stone of stumbling and a rock of offense.” They stumble because they disobey the word—and to this they were appointed.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
As believers come to Christ, the picture changes from a newborn receiving milk to living stones being built together. Jesus is the living stone: rejected by people, yet chosen and precious to God.

The readers are being formed into a spiritual house and a holy priesthood, offering sacrifices acceptable through Jesus Christ. The image concerns their joined life before God; they receive their place and service in relation to Him.

The quotations bring together Isaiah 28:16, Psalm 118:22 and Isaiah 8:14. Christ is the cornerstone for those who believe and the stone over which the disobedient stumble. Human rejection does not overturn God’s choice of Him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley understand the spiritual house as believers joined together in Christ and the sacrifices as lives offered in service, including prayer and grateful obedience.

Christians differ over the relation between this shared priesthood and ordained ministry. The Catholic Catechism, 1546–1547, affirms that the whole community is priestly, while distinguishing the ordained priesthood as a distinct participation in Christ’s one priesthood, serving the faithful. Reformed churches also recognize particular ministerial duties: the Westminster Confession, 27.4, reserves administering baptism and the Lord’s Supper to lawfully ordained ministers. A shared priesthood is therefore not read by every tradition as the removal of all distinct ministry roles.

The last sentence raises a further difference. Calvin prefers to understand the appointment as extending to unbelief itself, while Wesley understands it as God’s appointed judgment on those who do not believe. The Reformed Westminster Confession, 3.1, 3.7, relates judgment to God’s purpose while explicitly denying that God is the author of sin.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 2:19–22 gives a closely related picture: Christ as cornerstone, believers joined into one holy temple and God dwelling among them by His Spirit. The building image brings identity and service together. God is forming a people whose shared life has its foundation in Christ.

The spiritual offerings also fit Hebrews 13:15–16, which connects praise, doing good and sharing with sacrifices pleasing to God through Jesus. The people built around Christ have a life to offer.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Returning to the Word identifies the church as the people in whom God’s Spirit dwells and the priesthood as a calling shared by every believer. Who Shepherds the Church? connects that shared life with direct access to God through Christ, without a necessary human mediating class between Him and His people.

passages.title: 1 Peter 2:9
passages.section_title: What does it mean to share in a royal priesthood?
passages.note: Every believer as priest: a royal priesthood, not a clerical class.

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 But you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession, to proclaim the virtues of Him who called you out of darkness into His marvelous light.
paragraphs: 9 But you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession, to proclaim the virtues of Him who called you out of darkness into His marvelous light.

passages.context_html:
This verse follows the picture of believers as living stones built together around Christ. The description is addressed to the people who believe: their calling is to belong to God, serve Him and proclaim His virtues.

The titles recall Exodus 19:4–6, where God calls the people He delivered His treasured possession, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. Verse 10 immediately adds the mercy through which they have become His people.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley apply this priesthood to the believing people, whose lives and words are to declare God’s goodness. It gives the whole community a calling before Him.

The Catholic Catechism, 1546–1547, affirms this common priesthood while also teaching a distinct ordained priesthood serving it in Christ. Reformed churches also assign particular responsibilities to ministers, as in Westminster Confession, 27.4, on baptism and the Lord’s Supper. These differences concern the form of ministry within the people, rather than whether the people have any priestly calling.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Returning to the Word identifies the church as the people in whom God’s Spirit dwells and the priesthood as a calling shared by every believer. Who Shepherds the Church? connects that shared life with direct access to God through Christ, without a necessary human mediating class between Him and His people.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Isaiah 43:20–21 connects the people God forms for Himself with declaring His praise. Peter carries that purpose into the life of believers who have been called from darkness into light.

The next verse’s reference to mercy belongs with Hosea 2:23, also used in Romans 9:24–26 for God’s calling from Jews and Gentiles. Their privilege is a reason for grateful witness rooted in received mercy.

passages.title: 1 Peter 2:9-10
passages.section_title: Why has God called a people His own?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 But you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession, to proclaim the virtues of Him who called you out of darkness into His marvelous light. 10 Once you were not a people, but now you are the people of God; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy.
paragraphs: 9 But you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession, to proclaim the virtues of Him who called you out of darkness into His marvelous light. 10 Once you were not a people, but now you are the people of God; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The contrast with disobedience now becomes a description of the readers’ calling: a chosen people, royal priesthood, holy nation and God’s own possession. These titles are joined with a purpose—to proclaim the virtues of the One who called them into His light.

The language recalls Exodus 19:4–6 and Isaiah 43:20–21. Peter draws on God’s earlier descriptions of His people to explain the dignity and responsibility of those who belong to Christ.

The movement from no people to God’s people, and from no mercy to mercy, recalls Hosea 2:23. Their identity rests in mercy received, giving them reason to declare God’s goodness.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley both understand the priesthood as belonging to the believing people and the proclamation as extending through their conduct as well as their words.

Traditions differ over distinct ordained ministry within that people. The Catholic Catechism, 1546–1547, affirms the whole community’s priesthood and also an ordained priesthood serving it through participation in Christ’s one priesthood. The Reformed Westminster Confession, 27.4, assigns administering baptism and the Lord’s Supper to ordained ministers. The shared calling is not the same question as who carries out every particular task.
passages.god_plan_html:
God’s call at Exodus 19:4–6 follows His deliverance of Israel and gives that people a vocation before Him. Isaiah 43:20–21 likewise connects the people He forms with declaring His praise.

Romans 9:24–26 also applies Hosea’s people-and-mercy language in speaking of those called from Jews and Gentiles. The connection shows the breadth of God’s mercy as He brings people into a shared life before Him.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Returning to the Word identifies the church as the people in whom God’s Spirit dwells and the priesthood as a calling shared by every believer. Who Shepherds the Church? connects that shared life with direct access to God through Christ, without a necessary human mediating class between Him and His people.

passages.title: 1 Peter 2:11-12
passages.section_title: How can our daily lives point people toward God?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 Beloved, I urge you, as foreigners and exiles, to abstain from the desires of the flesh, which war against your soul. 12 Conduct yourselves with such honor among the Gentiles that, though they slander you as evildoers, they may see your good deeds and glorify God on the day He visits us.
paragraphs: 11 Beloved, I urge you, as foreigners and exiles, to abstain from the desires of the flesh, which war against your soul. 12 Conduct yourselves with such honor among the Gentiles that, though they slander you as evildoers, they may see your good deeds and glorify God on the day He visits us.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Peter turns from describing God’s people to how they live among their neighbors. Calling them foreigners and exiles recalls the letter’s opening: they belong to God while living in a world that does not always welcome their faith.

The desires they must resist wage war against the soul. The concern reaches beyond outward appearances to what is shaping them within. Their conduct among others should be honorable even when they are falsely accused.

The hope is that people who speak against them will see their good deeds and glorify God. Being slandered is not itself evidence that the accusations are deserved. Peter calls for faithful conduct in the face of hostility.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley both connect honorable conduct with neighbors coming to recognize God’s work. They understand the day of visitation as an occasion of God’s mercy that can turn those observers toward Him.

Calvin also discusses the reading that places this recognition at the last judgment, although he prefers the merciful-visitation reading. The Greek word for visitation can refer to God’s gracious care or His examination and judgment. The word alone does not settle which occasion Peter has in view.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus connects visible goodness with the Father’s glory in Matthew 5:14–16. His followers’ lives are to shine so that people see their good deeds and glorify their Father. Peter applies that purpose to believers whose neighbors are suspicious of them.

Their witness therefore includes the everyday life people can observe. God’s people proclaim His goodness, as verse 9 says, and their conduct should agree with that proclamation.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Peter 2:13-17
passages.section_title: How do we honor authority while serving God?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 Submit yourselves for the Lord’s sake to every human institution, whether to the king as the supreme authority, 14 or to governors as those sent by him to punish those who do wrong and to praise those who do right. 15 For it is God’s will that by doing good you should silence the ignorance of foolish men. 16 Live in freedom, but do not use your freedom as a cover-up for evil; live as servants of God. 17 Treat everyone with high regard: Love the brotherhood of believers, fear God, honor the king.
paragraphs: 13 Submit yourselves for the Lord’s sake to every human institution, whether to the king as the supreme authority, 14 or to governors as those sent by him to punish those who do wrong and to praise those who do right. 15 For it is God’s will that by doing good you should silence the ignorance of foolish men.
16 Live in freedom, but do not use your freedom as a cover-up for evil; live as servants of God. 17 Treat everyone with high regard: Love the brotherhood of believers, fear God, honor the king.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Peter now applies honorable conduct to public life. The king and governors make clear that the human institutions in view include civil authority. Submission is offered for the Lord’s sake, with doing good as the answer to ignorant accusations.

Freedom in Christ is not a cover for evil. These believers are free people who live as God’s servants. Peter ends with four short instructions: honor everyone, love the brotherhood, fear God and honor the king. The ruler receives honor; the fear that governs their lives belongs to God.

The instruction describes the public purpose of government in punishing wrongdoing and commending good. It does not declare every ruler’s action good. The letter will immediately address the reality of unjust treatment.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian teaching commonly joins respect for civil authority with a higher allegiance to God. The Catholic Catechism, 2238–2242, teaches service to the common good, allows just criticism and requires refusal of commands contrary to the moral order, basic human rights or the Gospel. The Reformed Westminster Confession, 23.4, calls for prayer, honor and obedience to lawful commands even when a ruler’s religion differs from the believer’s.

Wesley likewise explains obedience as offered for God’s sake. Respect for rulers is not permission to treat them as a higher authority than God.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Acts 5:27–32, Peter and the other apostles continue the witness to Jesus when authorities forbid it. Their answer puts God’s command first. That episode helps us read the call to honor authority alongside the mission God has given His people.

1 Timothy 2:1–6 connects prayer for rulers and peaceful, godly lives with God’s desire for people to be saved and know the truth. Public conduct serves a larger purpose: a life that honors God while His saving message is made known.

passages.title: 1 Peter 2:18-20
passages.section_title: Does God see those who suffer unfairly?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 Servants, submit yourselves to your masters with all respect, not only to those who are good and gentle, but even to those who are unreasonable. 19 For if anyone endures the pain of unjust suffering because he is conscious of God, this is to be commended. 20 How is it to your credit if you are beaten for doing wrong and you endure it? But if you suffer for doing good and you endure it, this is commendable before God.
paragraphs: 18 Servants, submit yourselves to your masters with all respect, not only to those who are good and gentle, but even to those who are unreasonable. 19 For if anyone endures the pain of unjust suffering because he is conscious of God, this is to be commended. 20 How is it to your credit if you are beaten for doing wrong and you endure it? But if you suffer for doing good and you endure it, this is commendable before God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Peter addresses household servants, including enslaved people. The Greek word identifies service within a household; this is not simply a description of a modern job. He speaks to people who may be beaten and who do not control how their masters treat them.

The instruction includes masters who are harsh. The word behind that description can mean crooked or unfair. Peter names the treatment as unjust, rather than pretending that a master’s power makes every action right.

He distinguishes suffering for wrongdoing from suffering while doing good. The latter can be endured with an awareness of God, whose judgment of the servant’s conduct matters more than the master’s approval. The following verses place Christ’s own unjust suffering before them.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley understand this as a call to faithful conduct under unjust treatment because the believer seeks to please God. Both connect it with Christ’s patient response in the next paragraph.

Calvin expressly limits human obedience by God’s authority. The passage speaks to sufferers about their conduct; it gives no instruction authorizing masters to mistreat them. Elsewhere, 1 Corinthians 7:21–23 tells enslaved believers to take the opportunity for freedom when it is available.
passages.god_plan_html:
Peter will connect this endurance directly with Christ, who suffered without wrongdoing and entrusted Himself to the righteous Judge. God sees people whose suffering others overlook, and their faithfulness is not measured by the powerful person’s verdict.

Romans 12:17–21 likewise joins doing good with refusing personal vengeance and trusting God’s judgment. The aim is to overcome evil with good, while leaving judgment in God’s hands.

passages.title: 1 Peter 2:21-25
passages.section_title: How does Christ’s suffering change our lives?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 For to this you were called, because Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example, that you should follow in His footsteps: 22 “He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in His mouth.” 23 When they heaped abuse on Him, He did not retaliate; when He suffered, He made no threats, but entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly. 24 He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree, so that we might die to sin and live to righteousness. “By His stripes you are healed.” 25 For “you were like sheep going astray,” but now you have returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls.
paragraphs: 21 For to this you were called, because Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example, that you should follow in His footsteps: 22 “He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in His mouth.” 23 When they heaped abuse on Him, He did not retaliate; when He suffered, He made no threats, but entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly.

24 He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree, so that we might die to sin and live to righteousness. “By His stripes you are healed.” 25 For “you were like sheep going astray,” but now you have returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Christ is the example for people suffering without deserving it. He committed no sin, used no deceit and answered neither insults with insults nor suffering with threats. He entrusted Himself to the One who judges justly.

Peter then moves beyond an example to what Christ accomplished for them. He bore their sins in His body on the cross so that they might die to sin and live to righteousness. They are not being asked to pay for their own sins through mistreatment; their new life rests on what Christ did for them.

The language draws repeatedly on Isaiah 53: the innocent sufferer, the bearing of sins, healing through His wounds and wandering sheep. The readers have now returned to the Shepherd and Overseer who cares for their souls.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley both distinguish Christ’s example from His saving work. His suffering gives a pattern of patience, while His bearing of sins brings forgiveness and a life freed from sin’s rule.

Both connect the healing language with that rescue from sin and return to Christ. In this paragraph, the stated purpose is a righteous life under the Shepherd’s care. It does not state that every believer will immediately recover from every bodily illness.
passages.god_plan_html:
Peter explicitly identifies Jesus with the suffering Servant described in Isaiah 53:4–12. The Servant’s innocent suffering and bearing of others’ sins become the basis for their restored relationship with God. The connection is made by the New Testament itself.

The closing shepherd picture also fits Jesus’ words in John 10:11–18. The good Shepherd lays down His life for the sheep and gathers them to Himself. Christ’s death both rescues a people and calls them into a new way of living under His care.

passages.title: 1 Peter 3:1-6
passages.section_title: How can faith be seen within a marriage?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Wives, in the same way, submit yourselves to your husbands, so that even if they refuse to believe the word, they will be won over without words by the behavior of their wives 2 when they see your pure and reverent demeanor. 3 Your beauty should not come from outward adornment, such as braided hair or gold jewelry or fine clothes, 4 but from the inner disposition of your heart, the unfading beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is precious in God’s sight. 5 For this is how the holy women of the past adorned themselves. They put their hope in God and were submissive to their husbands, 6 just as Sarah obeyed Abraham and called him lord. And you are her children if you do what is right and refuse to give way to fear.
paragraphs: 1 Wives, in the same way, submit yourselves to your husbands, so that even if they refuse to believe the word, they will be won over without words by the behavior of their wives 2 when they see your pure and reverent demeanor.

3 Your beauty should not come from outward adornment, such as braided hair or gold jewelry or fine clothes, 4 but from the inner disposition of your heart, the unfading beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is precious in God’s sight.

5 For this is how the holy women of the past adorned themselves. They put their hope in God and were submissive to their husbands, 6 just as Sarah obeyed Abraham and called him lord. And you are her children if you do what is right and refuse to give way to fear.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The call to honorable conduct now reaches marriages in which a husband may refuse to believe the word. Peter addresses wives about the witness of their lives: their husbands may be won over as they see pure and reverent conduct.

The word for submitting describes placing oneself under another’s authority. Peter’s instruction concerns their own husbands. It does not tell every woman to submit to every man, and the next verse addresses the husband’s responsibility to honor his wife.

Peter turns attention from outward display to the lasting beauty of the heart. The holy women’s hope was in God. Sarah’s calling Abraham lord recalls Genesis 18:12; Peter’s closing description joins doing right with refusing to give way to fear.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians agree that faith should shape conduct within marriage, but differ over how the responsibilities are shared. The Southern Baptist Baptist Faith and Message, XVIII, teaches equal worth before God together with a husband’s servant leadership and a wife’s gracious submission. CBE International’s statement, family point 11, reads these verses alongside Ephesians 5:21 as mutual submission and responsibility, with headship expressed through self-giving love. CBE speaks as an organization, not for every church.

The outward-adornment instruction also has different readings. Calvin understands it as rejecting vanity and excessive display, rather than every ornament. Wesley takes a stricter view, forbidding ornamental gold, elaborate hair and costly dress. Both emphasize the inward character precious to God.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Corinthians 7:12–16 also addresses marriages in which only one spouse believes. It leaves room for the unbelieving spouse’s salvation while declining to guarantee that one spouse will save the other. Faithful witness is meaningful without placing another person’s response under the believer’s control.

Ephesians 5:21–33 sets marriage beside Christ’s self-giving love for the church. Read together, these passages bring everyday married life into the wider calling to reflect Christ’s character.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Peter 3:7
passages.section_title: Why must a husband’s faith show in how he treats his wife?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 Husbands, in the same way, treat your wives with consideration as a delicate vessel, and with honor as fellow heirs of the gracious gift of life, so that your prayers will not be hindered.
paragraphs: 7 Husbands, in the same way, treat your wives with consideration as a delicate vessel, and with honor as fellow heirs of the gracious gift of life, so that your prayers will not be hindered.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Peter now addresses husbands directly. They must live with consideration and give their wives honor as fellow heirs of the gracious gift of life. Their treatment of their wives belongs to their life before God, including their prayers.

The BSB’s delicate vessel expresses a comparison using the Greek word for weaker. The verse does not call a wife less valuable to God: it expressly places her alongside her husband as an heir. Vulnerability is a reason for honor and care.

The warning about hindered prayers makes the responsibility serious. A husband cannot separate devotion to God from the way he treats the person who shares his life.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley both connect consideration with tender treatment and the honor due to a wife who shares in God’s gift. Both take the warning about prayer as a reason to put away marital strife, rather than treating domestic conduct as spiritually unimportant.

The USCCB’s note on this verse likewise emphasizes consideration and wives’ equal reception of salvation. These readings share the central call to honor, even while Christian accounts of family leadership differ.
passages.god_plan_html:
Galatians 3:26–29 describes those who belong to Christ as God’s children and heirs according to the promise, without making male or female a barrier to that standing. Peter’s fellow-heir language brings that shared inheritance into the home.

The husband is therefore called to recognize in his wife someone who receives God’s gift alongside him. The family’s daily life should reflect the grace in which both share.

passages.title: 1 Peter 3:8-12
passages.section_title: How do God’s people respond to hurt with good?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 Finally, all of you, be like-minded and sympathetic, love as brothers, be tenderhearted and humble. 9 Do not repay evil with evil or insult with insult, but with blessing, because to this you were called so that you may inherit a blessing. 10 For, “Whoever would love life and see good days must keep his tongue from evil and his lips from deceitful speech. 11 He must turn from evil and do good; he must seek peace and pursue it. 12 For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and His ears are inclined to their prayer. But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil.”
paragraphs: 8 Finally, all of you, be like-minded and sympathetic, love as brothers, be tenderhearted and humble. 9 Do not repay evil with evil or insult with insult, but with blessing, because to this you were called so that you may inherit a blessing.

10 For, “Whoever would love life and see good days must keep his tongue from evil and his lips from deceitful speech. 11 He must turn from evil and do good; he must seek peace and pursue it. 12 For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and His ears are inclined to their prayer. But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Peter widens the address from particular household relationships to all the readers. Shared purpose, sympathy, family love, tenderness and humility are to characterize their life together.

The word for sympathetic carries the idea of sharing another person’s feelings or suffering. These believers are to care about what others endure, rather than looking only at their own circumstances.

Their response to evil and insult is to give a blessing. Peter grounds the appeal in Psalm 34:12–16: guard the tongue, turn from evil, do good and actively pursue peace. The Lord watches over the righteous and hears their prayer, while opposing evil.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley read the passage as a call to compassionate life together and a refusal to repay hostility in kind. Calvin includes praying for those who insult them; Wesley connects their blessing of others with the blessing God gives them.

The promise is read alongside the letter’s repeated acknowledgment of unjust suffering. Peter’s next paragraph expressly allows that people may suffer for doing right. These verses do not describe a life in which faithful people never encounter harm.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 5:6–11 shows God giving His love through Christ while people were still sinners and enemies. Peter’s call to bless those who mistreat them fits that pattern: received mercy shapes the way they treat others.

Jesus likewise calls His followers to love enemies and pray for persecutors in Matthew 5:43–48, reflecting their Father’s goodness. The blessing they have received is to become visible in the good they offer.

passages.title: 1 Peter 3:13-17
passages.section_title: How do we speak about our hope when faith is challenged?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 Who can harm you if you are zealous for what is good? 14 But even if you should suffer for what is right, you are blessed. “Do not fear what they fear; do not be shaken.” 15 But in your hearts sanctify Christ as Lord. Always be prepared to give a defense to everyone who asks you the reason for the hope that is in you. But respond with gentleness and respect, 16 keeping a clear conscience, so that those who slander you may be put to shame by your good behavior in Christ. 17 For it is better, if it is God’s will, to suffer for doing good than for doing evil.
paragraphs: 13 Who can harm you if you are zealous for what is good? 14 But even if you should suffer for what is right, you are blessed. “Do not fear what they fear; do not be shaken.”

15 But in your hearts sanctify Christ as Lord. Always be prepared to give a defense to everyone who asks you the reason for the hope that is in you. But respond with gentleness and respect, 16 keeping a clear conscience, so that those who slander you may be put to shame by your good behavior in Christ. 17 For it is better, if it is God’s will, to suffer for doing good than for doing evil.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Peter asks who will harm those eager to do good, then immediately allows that they may suffer for doing right. His encouragement is not a promise that faithful conduct prevents every injury.

The response to intimidation is to honor Christ as Lord in their hearts. The language recalls Isaiah 8:12–13, where God’s people are told whom to fear. Christ’s authority, rather than the threat, is to govern their response.

They must be ready to explain their hope. The word for defense concerns a spoken answer or explanation. Gentleness, respect and a clear conscience belong with that answer, so their behavior supports what they say. Peter again distinguishes suffering for doing good from suffering for wrongdoing.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley both connect readiness to answer with trust in God and a calm, respectful manner. Calvin expressly says this is not a demand that every believer be able to solve every theological question. Wesley warns that anger damages the witness as well as the speaker.

Both understand the hope in light of God’s lasting care. The passage acknowledges real suffering while calling believers to a response shaped by Christ, rather than retaliation.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 8:31–39 also places confidence in God alongside real persecution, danger and death. Hope rests in His love through Christ, rather than freedom from all present trouble.

In Acts 4:7–13, 18–20, Peter and John explain their witness to Jesus under questioning. The episode gives a concrete example of speaking about salvation in the risen Christ when authorities challenge that witness.
passages.current_position_html: Our study I Am a Disciple understands this as a call to be ready to explain the hope we have in Christ. Our witness includes words as well as conduct, and the explanation should be given with gentleness and respect.

passages.title: 1 Peter 3:15
passages.section_title: How can we be ready to explain our hope?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 But in your hearts sanctify Christ as Lord. Always be prepared to give a defense to everyone who asks you the reason for the hope that is in you. But respond with gentleness and respect,
paragraphs: 15 But in your hearts sanctify Christ as Lord. Always be prepared to give a defense to everyone who asks you the reason for the hope that is in you. But respond with gentleness and respect,

passages.context_html:
This verse sits within encouragement to believers who may suffer for doing right. Honoring Christ as Lord in the heart comes before answering those who question their hope.

The Greek word for defense means a spoken answer or defense. Peter expects them to be ready to explain, and he names gentleness and respect as part of that readiness. The next verse joins their explanation with a clear conscience and good conduct.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Calvin and Wesley read this as readiness to acknowledge faith and hope without being ruled by fear or anger. Calvin distinguishes a basic explanation of faith from being able to settle every question. Wesley emphasizes the damage anger can do to both the witness and the person speaking.
passages.current_position_html: Our study I Am a Disciple understands this as a call to be ready to explain the hope we have in Christ. Our witness includes words as well as conduct, and the explanation should be given with gentleness and respect.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 4:7–13, 18–20 shows Peter and John answering questions by pointing to Jesus’ resurrection and the salvation found in Him. The same risen Christ is the ground of the hope believers are called to explain.

The witness is therefore more than describing a personal outlook. It points people to the One through whom God has acted to save.

passages.title: 1 Peter 3:18-20
passages.section_title: How does Christ bring the unrighteous to God?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 For Christ also suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God. He was put to death in the body but made alive in the Spirit, 19 in whom He also went and preached to the spirits in prison 20 who disobeyed long ago when God waited patiently in the days of Noah while the ark was being built. In the ark a few people, only eight souls, were saved through water.
paragraphs: 18 For Christ also suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God. He was put to death in the body but made alive in the Spirit,

19 in whom He also went and preached to the spirits in prison 20 who disobeyed long ago when God waited patiently in the days of Noah while the ark was being built. In the ark a few people, only eight souls, were saved through water.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Christ’s suffering gives the reason for the preceding encouragement. He suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring them to God. His death serves a purpose that reaches beyond showing people how to endure hardship.

The movement from death to life leads into a difficult statement about preaching to spirits in prison. Peter connects their disobedience with the days of Noah and God’s patience while the ark was being built. He names the few who were brought safely through the water: eight people.

The paragraph does not state everything readers may want to know about the identity of the spirits, the timing or the content of the preaching. The account leads into baptism, Christ’s resurrection and His authority over heavenly powers.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
There are several established readings. Wesley understands Christ to have preached by His Spirit through Noah to people who were disobedient then and are now held for judgment. The editor’s note in Calvin’s commentary also favors that reading.

Calvin himself takes a different view: Christ’s life-giving work was made known to faithful people who had died awaiting Him. He acknowledges difficulty in fitting the following reference to disobedience into that reading.

The Catholic Catechism, 632–635, connects the passage with Christ’s descent to the realm of the dead, proclaiming salvation and freeing the righteous who awaited Him. It expressly distinguishes this from freeing the damned.

The USCCB’s note on verse 19 also reports another reading: the spirits are hostile angelic powers overcome by Christ. This is an interpretive possibility in its study note, not a declaration that every Catholic must identify the spirits that way.
passages.god_plan_html:
The reference to Noah connects judgment with God’s preservation of a few people who trust Him. 2 Peter 2:4–9 explicitly uses Noah’s rescue to show that God knows how to rescue the godly while holding the unrighteous for judgment.

The outcome of Christ’s suffering is life and authority, not defeat. The chapter ends with all powers subject to Him; Ephesians 1:20–23 likewise presents the risen Christ above every authority and as head over everything for His church. That larger outcome supplies hope amid present opposition.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Peter 3:21
passages.section_title: What does Peter mean when he says baptism now saves?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 And this water symbolizes the baptism that now saves you also—not the removal of dirt from the body, but the pledge of a clear conscience toward God—through the resurrection of Jesus Christ,
paragraphs: 21 And this water symbolizes the baptism that now saves you also—not the removal of dirt from the body, but the pledge of a clear conscience toward God—through the resurrection of Jesus Christ,

passages.context_html:
The preceding verse recalls Noah’s family brought safely through the floodwater. Peter now connects that rescue with baptism, using a word for a corresponding picture.

His statement includes its own clarification: the saving matter is not bodily dirt being washed off. The BSB speaks of a pledge of a clear conscience toward God; the Greek expression is also understood as an appeal to God for a good conscience. Peter grounds the connection in Jesus Christ’s resurrection.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The Catholic Catechism, 1213, teaches new birth and incorporation into Christ through baptism. The Lutheran Small Catechism, Baptism, links forgiveness and salvation with God’s word joined to the water and received in faith.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, 28.1, 28.5–6, teaches a sign and seal of grace while rejecting the claim that every baptized person is necessarily born anew. The 1689 Baptist Confession, 29.1–2, emphasizes the sign of union with Christ, administered to those professing repentance and faith. Wesley distinguishes the outward sign from inward grace. The traditions therefore relate baptism and salvation differently, rather than agreeing on every part of the verse.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Baptism understands baptism here as the appointed expression of genuine faith, in which that faith is formally pledged before God. The water has no saving power of its own. The saving power belongs to Christ and His resurrection, received through faith.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 6:3–5 links baptism with sharing in Christ’s death and resurrection and walking in new life. That connection helps keep Peter’s language centered on Christ’s saving work, rather than on an isolated washing.

The following verse places the risen Jesus at God’s right hand over every authority. The rescue pictured here rests on the Savior who has passed through death and now lives and rules.

passages.title: 1 Peter 3:21-22
passages.section_title: How is baptism connected with Christ’s resurrection?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 And this water symbolizes the baptism that now saves you also—not the removal of dirt from the body, but the pledge of a clear conscience toward God—through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, 22 who has gone into heaven and is at the right hand of God, with angels, authorities, and powers subject to Him.
paragraphs: 21 And this water symbolizes the baptism that now saves you also—not the removal of dirt from the body, but the pledge of a clear conscience toward God—through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, 22 who has gone into heaven and is at the right hand of God, with angels, authorities, and powers subject to Him.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Peter connects the water in Noah’s story with baptism through a word meaning a corresponding picture. The comparison belongs to his movement from judgment and rescue to the believer’s relationship with the risen Christ.

He says that baptism now saves, then distinguishes it from removing dirt from the body. The BSB calls it the pledge of a clear conscience toward God. The Greek expression is also read as an appeal or request to God for a good conscience; its precise sense is discussed by interpreters.

The saving connection is through Jesus Christ’s resurrection. Peter closes with Christ in heaven at God’s right hand, with angels, authorities and powers subject to Him. The One in whom believers place their hope is risen and rules.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians differ over how baptism conveys or expresses God’s saving gift. The Catholic Catechism, 1213, teaches that baptism frees from sin, gives new birth and incorporates a person into Christ. The Lutheran Small Catechism, Baptism, teaches forgiveness and salvation through God’s word joined with water, received in faith.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, 28.1, 28.5–6, calls baptism a sign and seal of grace, while denying that everyone baptized is necessarily born anew or that salvation is impossible without baptism. The 1689 Baptist Confession, 29.1–2, describes it as a sign of union with Christ in death and resurrection, given to those who profess repentance and faith.

Wesley distinguishes the outward sign from inward grace. These readings do not all make baptism work in the same way, but none of these documents assigns saving power to ordinary water acting apart from God.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 6:3–5 connects baptism with Christ’s death and resurrection and the call to walk in new life. Peter likewise directs attention through the outward act to the risen Christ and the life received through Him.

Ephesians 1:20–23 joins Christ’s resurrection and place at God’s right hand with His authority over every power for the church. The final word here is the authority of the Savior to whom believers belong.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Baptism understands baptism here as the appointed expression of genuine faith, in which that faith is formally pledged before God. The water has no saving power of its own. The saving power belongs to Christ and His resurrection, received through faith.

passages.title: 1 Peter 4:1-3
passages.section_title: What does living for God change?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Therefore, since Christ suffered in His body, arm yourselves with the same resolve, because anyone who has suffered in his body is done with sin. 2 Consequently, he does not live out his remaining time on earth for human passions, but for the will of God. 3 For you have spent enough time in the past carrying out the same desires as the Gentiles: living in debauchery, lust, drunkenness, orgies, carousing, and detestable idolatry.
paragraphs: 1 Therefore, since Christ suffered in His body, arm yourselves with the same resolve, because anyone who has suffered in his body is done with sin. 2 Consequently, he does not live out his remaining time on earth for human passions, but for the will of God. 3 For you have spent enough time in the past carrying out the same desires as the Gentiles: living in debauchery, lust, drunkenness, orgies, carousing, and detestable idolatry.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Christ’s suffering now becomes the starting point for a change in the readers’ purpose. The word translated arm yourselves pictures equipping oneself. They are to face life with the same resolve, ready to do God’s will even when that brings suffering.

The statement about being done with sin is followed by its practical direction: use the remaining time for God’s will rather than human passions. The contrast is between the old way of life and the new purpose that belongs to following Christ.

Peter says they have already spent enough time in the former life. He names uncontrolled desires, drunkenness, sexual excess and idolatry. The appeal is to leave that course behind, rather than keep postponing obedience.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin connects being done with sin with sharing in Christ’s death so that sin no longer rules one’s life. Wesley likewise relates it to being made inwardly like Christ in His suffering and delivered from sin. Both direct the reader toward a changed life lived for God.

The following instruction to live differently is part of their explanation. This is more than enduring pain as an isolated experience; it concerns the purpose and conduct of the life that remains.
passages.god_plan_html:
Romans 6:6–14 connects Christ’s death and resurrection with freedom from sin’s rule. Those brought from death to life are to offer themselves to God rather than let sin reign.

This gives a wider setting for Peter’s appeal. Christ’s saving work is meant to produce a new direction in daily life, including the choices a believer makes when obedience becomes costly.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Peter 4:4-6
passages.section_title: What if others reject the change in our lives?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 4 Because of this, they consider it strange of you not to plunge with them into the same flood of reckless indiscretion, and they heap abuse on you. 5 But they will have to give an account to Him who is ready to judge the living and the dead. 6 That is why the gospel was preached even to those who are now dead, so that they might be judged as men in the flesh, but live according to God in the spirit.
paragraphs: 4 Because of this, they consider it strange of you not to plunge with them into the same flood of reckless indiscretion, and they heap abuse on you. 5 But they will have to give an account to Him who is ready to judge the living and the dead. 6 That is why the gospel was preached even to those who are now dead, so that they might be judged as men in the flesh, but live according to God in the spirit.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
People who shared the readers’ former way of life now find their refusal to join in strange. Surprise turns into abuse. A changed life does not always bring immediate approval from old companions.

Peter directs attention from their verdict to the One who judges the living and the dead. Those who speak against the believers must themselves give an account. The judging authority is not held by the crowd.

The Gospel’s purpose reaches beyond the verdict people pass on a person’s bodily life. The BSB speaks of those who are now dead and of life according to God in the spirit. How this relates to preaching and death is one of the passage’s disputed details.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands the Gospel to have been preached to people who have since died. Human judgment against them did not cancel the life God gave. The USCCB’s note on verse 6 reports this reading alongside a possible connection with the dead mentioned in 3:19.

Calvin connects the verse with the reach of Christ’s saving work to the dead, as he did in chapter 3. The Catholic Catechism, 634, uses the verse in explaining Christ’s descent to the dead and the reach of His redemption. These readings differ over when and to whom the preaching occurred.
passages.god_plan_html:
In John 5:24–29, Jesus speaks both of people passing from death to life through hearing and believing, and of the future resurrection of those in the graves. He has authority to give life and to judge.

Peter’s encouragement belongs within that larger hope. Those who receive His life are not deprived of that hope by human rejection or bodily death. The final account belongs to Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Peter 4:7-9
passages.section_title: How should hope for the end shape life today?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 The end of all things is near. Therefore be clear-minded and sober, so that you can pray. 8 Above all, love one another deeply, because love covers over a multitude of sins. 9 Show hospitality to one another without complaining.
paragraphs: 7 The end of all things is near. Therefore be clear-minded and sober, so that you can pray. 8 Above all, love one another deeply, because love covers over a multitude of sins. 9 Show hospitality to one another without complaining.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Peter’s statement that the end is near leads straight to ordinary faithfulness: clear thinking, prayer, deep love and cheerful hospitality. He does not give a date or tell the readers to stop caring for daily needs.

The saying about love covering many sins recalls Proverbs 10:12, where love is contrasted with hatred that stirs up conflict. Love changes how people respond to one another’s faults.

Hospitality gives that love a practical form. Welcoming others without complaining makes room for them in one’s life, rather than treating them only as a burden.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley connect watchfulness with prayer and read the covering of sins in terms of generous love toward others. Calvin stresses forgiving rather than spreading faults; Wesley describes patient care and prayer for the other person.

Both take the approaching end as a reason for faithful living. Hope draws believers toward God and one another, rather than making mutual care less important.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Matthew 24:42–51, readiness for the Lord’s return is pictured through a servant faithfully caring for the household. Watching includes doing the work of care entrusted to him.

Romans 12:9–13 likewise joins sincere love, patience in affliction, persistent prayer and hospitality. These are ways the hope God gives takes shape in a community’s present life.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Peter 4:10-11
passages.section_title: What are God’s gifts for?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 As good stewards of the manifold grace of God, each of you should use whatever gift he has received to serve one another. 11 If anyone speaks, he should speak as one conveying the words of God. If anyone serves, he should serve with the strength God provides, so that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom be the glory and the power forever and ever. Amen.
paragraphs: 10 As good stewards of the manifold grace of God, each of you should use whatever gift he has received to serve one another. 11 If anyone speaks, he should speak as one conveying the words of God. If anyone serves, he should serve with the strength God provides, so that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom be the glory and the power forever and ever. Amen.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Each person who has received a gift is to use it to serve others. Peter describes believers as stewards: people entrusted with something that belongs to God and responsible for using it well.

He names speaking and serving as examples. Speaking carries responsibility to convey God’s words faithfully; serving depends on the strength God supplies. The emphasis is on the source and purpose of the service, rather than the importance of the person doing it.

The goal is that God be glorified through Jesus Christ in everything. The paragraph ends in praise, bringing the readers’ varied contributions back to the One who gave them.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley understand the gifts as entrusted for the good of others. Both stress dependence on God and giving Him the honor, rather than claiming His gifts as personal grounds for superiority.

Calvin gives particular attention to the responsibility of those teaching God’s word. Wesley applies the speaking instruction more broadly to speech shaped by God’s truth, especially public teaching. Neither treats the instruction as permission to label any personal opinion God’s word.
passages.god_plan_html:
1 Corinthians 12:4–7 describes different gifts, services and workings coming from the same Spirit, Lord and God. Each receives a manifestation of the Spirit for the common good.

Peter’s stewardship picture serves that same purpose. God’s varied grace meets the needs of His people as they serve one another, and the credit returns to Him through Christ.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Peter 4:12-16
passages.section_title: What does suffering for Christ mean?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery trial that has come upon you, as though something strange were happening to you. 13 But rejoice that you share in the sufferings of Christ, so that you may be overjoyed at the revelation of His glory. 14 If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the Spirit of glory and of God rests on you. 15 Indeed, none of you should suffer as a murderer or thief or wrongdoer, or even as a meddler. 16 But if you suffer as a Christian, do not be ashamed, but glorify God that you bear that name.
paragraphs: 12 Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery trial that has come upon you, as though something strange were happening to you. 13 But rejoice that you share in the sufferings of Christ, so that you may be overjoyed at the revelation of His glory. 14 If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the Spirit of glory and of God rests on you.
15 Indeed, none of you should suffer as a murderer or thief or wrongdoer, or even as a meddler. 16 But if you suffer as a Christian, do not be ashamed, but glorify God that you bear that name.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Peter tells his beloved readers not to treat their fiery trial as something entirely unexpected. The suffering tests them and joins their experience with Christ’s, while their hope looks toward the revelation of His glory.

Insults for Christ’s name do not mean God has abandoned them. Peter says the Spirit of glory and of God rests on them. The judgment of those who ridicule them is not the measure of their standing before Him.

He again distinguishes suffering for Christ from suffering for wrongdoing. Murder, theft, evil and meddling give no reason to claim persecution as a Christian. But those suffering because they belong to Christ need not be ashamed of His name.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley read these trials in relation to suffering for Christ, rather than as approval of whatever behavior brings criticism. Both connect present endurance with the hope of sharing His glory.

Calvin explicitly allows present joy and grief to exist together. The promise of glory is consolation within suffering, rather than a demand to pretend that pain is not real.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus tells His disciples in John 15:18–21 that the world’s hostility to them follows its hostility to Him. Peter’s description of sharing Christ’s sufferings carries that connection into the life of these churches.

The letter places this experience on the way to Christ’s revealed glory. Their hope is grounded in belonging to the risen Lord even while others reject His name.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Peter 4:17-19
passages.section_title: Why entrust ourselves to God while we keep doing good?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 For it is time for judgment to begin with the family of God; and if it begins with us, what will the outcome be for those who disobey the gospel of God? 18 And, “If it is hard for the righteous to be saved, what will become of the ungodly and the sinner?” 19 So then, those who suffer according to God’s will should entrust their souls to their faithful Creator and continue to do good.
paragraphs: 17 For it is time for judgment to begin with the family of God; and if it begins with us, what will the outcome be for those who disobey the gospel of God? 18 And, “If it is hard for the righteous to be saved, what will become of the ungodly and the sinner?” 19 So then, those who suffer according to God’s will should entrust their souls to their faithful Creator and continue to do good.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Peter sets the readers’ trials within God’s judgment, beginning with His own household. He asks what the outcome will be for those who disobey the Gospel if God’s people themselves pass through such difficulty.

The saying about the righteous being saved with difficulty echoes Proverbs 11:31, although its wording differs from the BSB translation of Proverbs. Peter uses it to make the contrast serious, rather than to describe salvation as casual or opposition as harmless.

His conclusion is active trust: entrust one’s soul to the faithful Creator and continue doing good. God’s faithfulness is the reason to persevere; suffering is not an invitation to answer evil with evil.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin understands judgment beginning with God’s people as His fatherly correction and care, distinguished from the final outcome for those who reject Him. He relates the difficulty of salvation to the hazards of the believer’s present course.

Wesley also describes God visiting His church in justice and mercy. He reads the difficulty primarily in terms of present deliverance, while applying the warning to eternal matters as well. Both conclude with trusting God’s care and continuing to do good.
passages.god_plan_html:
2 Thessalonians 1:4–10 likewise puts believers’ present persecution beside God’s righteous judgment. It looks toward relief for the afflicted and accountability for those who afflict them when Christ is revealed.

The connection places present suffering within a story whose outcome belongs to God. His people can leave judgment with Him while remaining faithful to the good He calls them to do.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Peter 5:1-2
passages.section_title: What work is entrusted to the elders?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 As a fellow elder, a witness of Christ’s sufferings, and a partaker of the glory to be revealed, I appeal to the elders among you: 2 Be shepherds of God’s flock that is among you, watching over them not out of compulsion, but willingly, as God would have you; not out of greed, but out of eagerness;
paragraphs: 1 As a fellow elder, a witness of Christ’s sufferings, and a partaker of the glory to be revealed, I appeal to the elders among you: 2 Be shepherds of God’s flock that is among you, watching over them not out of compulsion, but willingly, as God would have you; not out of greed, but out of eagerness;

passages.context_html:
After encouraging believers to entrust themselves to God while doing good, Peter addresses their elders. He speaks as a fellow elder, sharing both the reality of Christ’s sufferings and the hope of His revealed glory.

The word for fellow elder identifies a shared responsibility. The task is to shepherd God’s flock among them, watching over people willingly and eagerly. Compulsion and greed are set against the motives that fit this care.

The following verses clarify how the work is carried out: by example, under Christ the Chief Shepherd. The people remain God’s flock rather than a leader’s possession.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley understand the charge as active care through faithful teaching and conduct, offered willingly rather than for gain.

The Reformed Baptist 1689 Confession, 26.8–9, treats bishop and elder as names for the same office. The Catholic Catechism, 1554–1558, distinguishes bishops, priests and deacons within ordained ministry. The shared call to shepherd is therefore read within different accounts of church leadership.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Who Shepherds the Church? understands elder, overseer and shepherd here as descriptions of the same work: mature, qualified believers caring for the people among whom they serve. It reads this alongside Acts 20 and Titus 1 as a pattern of plural leadership, rather than separate ranks of spiritual standing.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
John 21:15–19 shows the risen Jesus entrusting care of His sheep to Peter. Here that responsibility is shared with the elders as they care for people who belong to God.

Acts 20:17, 28–35 gives the same joined description of elders, oversight and shepherding, with protection and generosity directed toward the people Christ has gathered.

passages.title: 1 Peter 5:1-4
passages.section_title: How should leaders care for God’s people?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 As a fellow elder, a witness of Christ’s sufferings, and a partaker of the glory to be revealed, I appeal to the elders among you: 2 Be shepherds of God’s flock that is among you, watching over them not out of compulsion, but willingly, as God would have you; not out of greed, but out of eagerness; 3 not lording it over those entrusted to you, but being examples to the flock. 4 And when the Chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the crown of glory that will never fade away.
paragraphs: 1 As a fellow elder, a witness of Christ’s sufferings, and a partaker of the glory to be revealed, I appeal to the elders among you: 2 Be shepherds of God’s flock that is among you, watching over them not out of compulsion, but willingly, as God would have you; not out of greed, but out of eagerness; 3 not lording it over those entrusted to you, but being examples to the flock.
4 And when the Chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the crown of glory that will never fade away.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Peter turns from the trials facing the whole church to those caring for it. He addresses the elders as a fellow elder, a witness of Christ’s sufferings and someone sharing the hope of coming glory. The word for fellow elder emphasizes the work they share.

The flock belongs to God. The elders must watch over it willingly and eagerly, rather than from compulsion or greed. They are to lead by example instead of lording it over those entrusted to them.

Their care is carried out under Christ, the Chief Shepherd. His appearing and the unfading crown of glory give them a reason to remain faithful beyond whatever recognition the present work brings.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley both emphasize willing care, freedom from greed and an example the leaders themselves live. Their authority does not put them above the conduct they ask of others.

Christians differ over the structure of that ministry. The Reformed Baptist 1689 Confession, 26.8–9, uses bishop and elder for the same office, alongside deacons. The Catholic Catechism, 1554–1558, distinguishes bishops, priests and deacons and teaches that bishops receive the fullness of Holy Orders. Both accounts describe real responsibilities of care, although they understand the offices differently.
passages.god_plan_html:
In John 21:15–19, the risen Jesus charges Peter to care for His sheep and calls him to follow even through a costly future. Peter now passes that care on to others under the Chief Shepherd.

Acts 20:17, 28–35 likewise addresses elders as overseers charged to shepherd God’s church. Paul connects protecting the flock with warning, generosity and helping the weak. The people Christ has gathered are to receive that kind of care.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Who Shepherds the Church? understands elder, overseer and shepherd here as descriptions of the same work: mature, qualified believers caring for the people among whom they serve. It reads this alongside Acts 20 and Titus 1 as a pattern of plural leadership, rather than separate ranks of spiritual standing.

passages.title: 1 Peter 5:3
passages.section_title: What does leading by example look like?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 3 not lording it over those entrusted to you, but being examples to the flock.
paragraphs: 3 not lording it over those entrusted to you, but being examples to the flock.

passages.context_html:
This instruction belongs to the charge to elders in verses 1–4. They must care for the flock willingly, without greed and without treating those entrusted to them as people to dominate.

The word behind lording it over describes exercising mastery over others. Peter sets being examples against that use of power. A leader’s life should show the character being taught.

The next verse names Christ as the Chief Shepherd. Those caring for the flock remain accountable under Him; they do not take His place as its owner.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley both reject domineering leadership. Calvin insists that leaders live under the same standard as those they serve; Wesley specifically rejects treating people’s consciences as a pastor’s domain.

The Catholic Catechism, 1551, likewise describes ordained ministry as service entirely dependent on Christ and measured by His example of becoming the servant of all. Different accounts of church offices do not remove the common responsibility to serve in Christ’s manner.
passages.current_position_html: Our studies What Is the True Church? and Who Shepherds the Church? understand leadership as mature, qualified service among the people, exercised through teaching, care and example. Recognized leaders equip believers to serve; they do not become a spiritual class with exclusive access to God or permission to dominate His people.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
In Mark 10:42–45, Jesus contrasts rulers lording it over others with the service required among His followers. He grounds that instruction in His own coming to serve and give His life for many.

Peter’s instruction carries that pattern into the care of the church. Leadership is to reflect the self-giving character of the Savior whose people are being served.

passages.title: 1 Peter 5:5-7
passages.section_title: How can humility and trust help us carry our cares?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 Young men, in the same way, submit yourselves to your elders. And all of you, clothe yourselves with humility toward one another, because, “God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” 6 Humble yourselves, therefore, under God’s mighty hand, so that in due time He may exalt you. 7 Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you.
paragraphs: 5 Young men, in the same way, submit yourselves to your elders. And all of you, clothe yourselves with humility toward one another, because, “God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” 6 Humble yourselves, therefore, under God’s mighty hand, so that in due time He may exalt you. 7 Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Peter addresses young men about submission to their elders, then turns to everyone: all are to clothe themselves with humility toward one another. The saying about God opposing the proud and giving grace to the humble recalls Proverbs 3:34.

Humility before other people is joined with humility under God’s mighty hand. The promise of being lifted up comes in His time, rather than through grasping at status or control.

The readers are also invited to cast all their anxiety on Him because He cares for them. Trust rests in His concern for them, not in pretending that the pressures they face are small.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley understand elders in verse 5 as those older in years. The USCCB’s notes read the passage within the community’s relationship to its pastoral leaders and also note a possible ministry-related sense for the younger members. The immediate instruction to everyone still requires humility across the whole community.

Calvin explicitly says that giving cares to God does not mean becoming unfeeling or abandoning responsibility. It is trust that steadies faith. Wesley applies the invitation to every kind of need and pressure.
passages.god_plan_html:
Psalm 55:22 also calls people to place their burden on the Lord who sustains them. Peter’s instruction continues that life of dependence on God’s care.

Philippians 4:4–7 connects gentleness and prayer about every concern with God’s peace guarding hearts and minds in Christ. Entrusting cares to God belongs within the life and peace He gives His people.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Peter 5:8-11
passages.section_title: How can we stand firm when faith is under pressure?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 Be sober-minded and alert. Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour. 9 Resist him, standing firm in your faith and in the knowledge that your brothers throughout the world are undergoing the same kinds of suffering. 10 And after you have suffered for a little while, the God of all grace, who has called you to His eternal glory in Christ, will Himself restore you, secure you, strengthen you, and establish you. 11 To Him be the power forever and ever. Amen.
paragraphs: 8 Be sober-minded and alert. Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour. 9 Resist him, standing firm in your faith and in the knowledge that your brothers throughout the world are undergoing the same kinds of suffering.

10 And after you have suffered for a little while, the God of all grace, who has called you to His eternal glory in Christ, will Himself restore you, secure you, strengthen you, and establish you. 11 To Him be the power forever and ever. Amen.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Trust in God’s care goes together with sober attention. Peter pictures the devil as a prowling lion seeking someone to devour. His instruction is to resist by standing firm in faith.

The readers are not alone: believers throughout the world face the same kinds of suffering. Their hardship belongs to a shared struggle, rather than proving they have been singled out and forgotten.

The final emphasis falls on the God of all grace. He has called them to eternal glory in Christ and will restore, secure, strengthen and establish them after their suffering. Peter answers the picture of danger with confidence in God’s power and purpose.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley both join watchfulness with resistance through faith and dependence on God’s grace. They read the little while of suffering beside the lasting glory to which God calls His people.

Both emphasize God’s work in sustaining the believer. The call to resist is active, while confidence rests in His ability to strengthen and establish them, rather than in personal toughness alone.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 6:10–18 likewise calls believers to stand against the devil’s schemes in the Lord’s strength. Faith, God’s word and persevering prayer belong together in that resistance.

Romans 8:35–39 puts real persecution and danger beside the assurance that nothing in creation can separate believers from God’s love in Christ. That lasting relationship gives them a reason to keep going.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 1 Peter 5:12-14
passages.section_title: What does Peter want his readers to hold on to?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 Through Silvanus, whom I regard as a faithful brother, I have written to you briefly, encouraging you and testifying that this is the true grace of God. Stand firm in it. 13 The church in Babylon, chosen together with you, sends you greetings, as does my son Mark. 14 Greet one another with a kiss of love. Peace to all of you who are in Christ.
paragraphs: 12 Through Silvanus, whom I regard as a faithful brother, I have written to you briefly, encouraging you and testifying that this is the true grace of God. Stand firm in it. 13 The church in Babylon, chosen together with you, sends you greetings, as does my son Mark. 14 Greet one another with a kiss of love. Peace to all of you who are in Christ.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The closing names Silvanus as a faithful brother through whom the letter has been written. Peter states its purpose plainly: to encourage the readers and testify to God’s true grace. His final instruction is to stand firm in it.
