Greetings come from the church in Babylon and from Mark, whom Peter calls his son. These greetings place the readers within a wider fellowship, sharing the same calling even across distance.

The letter ends with a loving greeting and peace to those in Christ. The closing returns to the shared life and hope that have supported its instruction through suffering.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley take Babylon as a literal location. The USCCB’s note understands it as a symbolic name for Rome. The identification therefore differs among interpreters; the verse itself does not give a travel history that settles every question.

Calvin and Wesley understand Mark’s being called a son in terms of a relationship in the faith. Both read the closing as encouragement to remain in the grace already received and to express sincere fellowship.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Peter 1:1-2
passages.section_title: What do believers share with the apostles?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Simon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, To those who through the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ have received a faith as precious as ours: 2 Grace and peace be multiplied to you through the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord.
paragraphs: 1 Simon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, To those who through the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ have received a faith as precious as ours: 2 Grace and peace be multiplied to you through the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The letter opens in the name of Simon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ. The word translated servant can mean a slave belonging to another. Here it expresses his service under Christ alongside the responsibility of being His apostle.

The recipients have received a faith as precious as that of the writer and his companions. The word behind as precious speaks of equal worth or honor. Their standing does not depend on having been present during Jesus’ earthly ministry.

This faith is received through the righteousness of Jesus Christ, named their God and Savior. The greeting then asks for increasing grace and peace through knowing God and Jesus their Lord. Knowing Him will remain central as the letter turns to growth and warns against error.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley both understand this faith as God’s gift, rather than something earned by human achievement. Calvin explains its equal worth through believers sharing the same Christ and salvation, while allowing differences in the measure of faith. Wesley emphasizes that those who have not seen Jesus share a faith as precious as that of the apostles who did.

Both connect growing knowledge of God with grace and peace. The knowledge is directed toward the God who saves, rather than being only a collection of facts to possess.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus describes eternal life in John 17:1–5 in terms of knowing the Father and the Son whom He sent. The knowledge sought in this greeting belongs within that saving relationship.

Ephesians 2:13–18 describes those once far away being brought near through Christ, with Jews and Gentiles sharing access to the Father by one Spirit. This gives a wider picture of the common standing God grants through the same Savior.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Peter 1:3-4
passages.section_title: What has God given us for a life that reflects Him?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 3 His divine power has given us everything we need for life and godliness through the knowledge of Him who called us by His own glory and excellence. 4 Through these He has given us His precious and magnificent promises, so that through them you may become partakers of the divine nature, now that you have escaped the corruption in the world caused by evil desires.
paragraphs: 3 His divine power has given us everything we need for life and godliness through the knowledge of Him who called us by His own glory and excellence. 4 Through these He has given us His precious and magnificent promises, so that through them you may become partakers of the divine nature, now that you have escaped the corruption in the world caused by evil desires.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Before calling the readers to make every effort, the letter begins with what God has already given. His divine power supplies what they need for life and godliness through knowing the One who called them by His glory and excellence.

His precious promises are connected with sharing in the divine nature and escaping the corruption caused by evil desires. The contrast is practical as well as hopeful: life received from God is set against the desires that ruin life in the world.

The next paragraph will describe the character that should grow from this gift. The readers’ effort responds to God’s provision; it is not the starting point from which they must somehow create His power.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley connect sharing in the divine nature with renewal in God’s image and life in fellowship with Him. Calvin expressly rejects the idea that people become part of God’s very being. The Catholic Catechism, 460, likewise relates this passage to the Son becoming human so that people may share His life as God’s children.

They differ somewhat over the scope of life in verse 3. Calvin focuses on the new spiritual life and what is needed for godliness. Wesley includes God’s provision for ordinary life as well as growth in spiritual life. Both place the gift before the call to diligent growth.
passages.god_plan_html:
In John 17:20–26, Jesus prays for later believers to share in life with the Father and Son, to know the Father’s love and to be with Him in His glory. That prayer helps place Peter’s promise within God’s purpose to draw people into life with Himself through Christ.

Romans 8:29–30 describes God’s purpose in terms of making His people like His Son and bringing them to glory. Sharing God’s life includes being changed to reflect the One to whom they now belong.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Peter 1:5-7
passages.section_title: What character should grow from our faith?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 For this very reason, make every effort to add to your faith virtue; and to virtue, knowledge; 6 and to knowledge, self-control; and to self-control, perseverance; and to perseverance, godliness; 7 and to godliness, brotherly kindness; and to brotherly kindness, love.
paragraphs: 5 For this very reason, make every effort to add to your faith virtue; and to virtue, knowledge; 6 and to knowledge, self-control; and to self-control, perseverance; and to perseverance, godliness; 7 and to godliness, brotherly kindness; and to brotherly kindness, love.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The call to make every effort follows God’s gift of power and promises in verses 3–4. The readers are to respond to what He has supplied by cultivating the character that fits their faith.

Peter names virtue, knowledge, self-control, perseverance, godliness, brotherly kindness and love. The word for self-control concerns governing one’s desires and passions. Perseverance means remaining steady in faith and purpose through trials.

The movement reaches beyond knowing what is right to living it toward God and other people. Knowledge belongs with self-control, endurance and love. The next sentence will speak of these qualities being present and continuing to grow together.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley both call for active effort in response to God’s gifts. Calvin treats the qualities as companions of living faith rather than a rigid staircase. Wesley sees a fitting order in which the qualities strengthen one another, while distinguishing that order from a timetable in which each must be completed before the next begins.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, 16.2–3, also joins good works with dependence on Christ’s Spirit and expressly calls for diligence. The instruction to act is therefore not a point on which Reformed teaching simply denies human responsibility.
passages.god_plan_html:
Galatians 5:22–25 describes love, patience, kindness and self-control as fruit of the Spirit. Those who live by the Spirit are also called to walk in step with Him. God’s gift and a changed way of living belong together.

This places Peter’s list within God’s work of forming people who reflect Him. The growth is seen in how they govern their desires, endure difficulties and love others, rather than only in how much they can say about their faith.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Peter 1:8-11
passages.section_title: Why does growth in faith matter?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 For if you possess these qualities and continue to grow in them, they will keep you from being ineffective and unproductive in your knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. 9 But whoever lacks these traits is nearsighted to the point of blindness, having forgotten that he has been cleansed from his past sins. 10 Therefore, brothers, strive to make your calling and election sure. For if you practice these things you will never stumble, 11 and you will receive a lavish reception into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.
paragraphs: 8 For if you possess these qualities and continue to grow in them, they will keep you from being ineffective and unproductive in your knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. 9 But whoever lacks these traits is nearsighted to the point of blindness, having forgotten that he has been cleansed from his past sins.

10 Therefore, brothers, strive to make your calling and election sure. For if you practice these things you will never stumble, 11 and you will receive a lavish reception into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The qualities just listed are to be present and increasing. Peter connects them with fruitful knowledge of Jesus Christ. The person who lacks them is described as blind or shortsighted, having forgotten the cleansing of past sins.

He therefore calls the readers to make their calling and election sure. The encouragement includes a promise about not stumbling as they practice these things and a lavish reception into Christ’s eternal kingdom. Both the seriousness of the call and the generosity of the promise belong to the paragraph.

The passage does not leave knowing Christ at the level of words alone. It asks what is growing from that knowledge and directs the readers toward the kingdom of the Lord and Savior who called them.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Traditions differ over how the warning and assurance relate. Calvin reads holy living as evidence of God’s calling and election, rather than their cause. The Reformed Westminster Confession, 17.1–3 and 18.2–4, teaches that God preserves true believers to the end while their assurance may be strengthened or shaken; good works are part of the evidence of grace.

Wesley reads the warning as addressed to people who can cast away benefits they have received, and the promise as assurance against finally falling while they continue in this diligence. The Catholic Catechism, 162, likewise teaches that faith is God’s gift, can be lost and must be nourished through a life of faith and love.

A different Free Grace reading appears in Bob Wilkin’s explanation. He understands making the calling sure as demonstrating it to others, with assurance resting on Christ’s promise. He relates the lavish reception to reward for faithfulness, while holding that all believers enter the kingdom. This is an individual reading, rather than a shared conclusion of all Protestant churches.
passages.god_plan_html:
In John 15:1–8, Jesus connects fruitfulness with remaining in Him and His words. The Father is glorified as His disciples bear fruit. Growth serves that larger purpose, beyond answering questions about one’s own standing.

Peter’s promise also keeps the destination in view: the eternal kingdom of Jesus Christ. The life being cultivated now belongs to the Savior whose people are called to live with Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Peter 1:12-15
passages.section_title: Why do we need reminders of what we already know?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 Therefore I will always remind you of these things, even though you know them and are established in the truth you now have. 13 I think it is right to refresh your memory as long as I live in the tent of my body, 14 because I know that this tent will soon be laid aside, as our Lord Jesus Christ has made clear to me. 15 And I will make every effort to ensure that after my departure, you will be able to recall these things at all times.
paragraphs: 12 Therefore I will always remind you of these things, even though you know them and are established in the truth you now have. 13 I think it is right to refresh your memory as long as I live in the tent of my body, 14 because I know that this tent will soon be laid aside, as our Lord Jesus Christ has made clear to me. 15 And I will make every effort to ensure that after my departure, you will be able to recall these things at all times.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Peter turns from the call to growth to why he keeps repeating it. The readers already know the truth and are established in it, yet he considers reminders necessary. Knowing something once does not make continued attention unnecessary.

He describes his body as a tent that will soon be laid aside. Jesus has made his approaching departure clear to him. The concern is how best to use the time he has left, so that the readers can remember these things after he is gone.

The letter itself serves that purpose. The message is to remain available beyond the life of the person teaching it, supporting the readers as they continue in faith.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley understand the reminders as ongoing care for believers, rather than evidence that the readers have never learned the truth. Both read the tent and departure language as referring to Peter’s coming death.

They differ over how the notice from Jesus relates to John 21:18–19. Wesley connects it with that prediction while allowing a further indication that the time was near. Calvin emphasizes a disclosure of the approaching time. Neither reading requires inventing the details of an unrecorded conversation.
passages.god_plan_html:
Matthew 28:16–20 joins making disciples with teaching them to obey what Jesus commanded. Peter’s effort to leave lasting reminders belongs within that continuing work of teaching.

2 Timothy 2:1–2 similarly calls for the message to be entrusted to faithful people who can teach others. God’s work of forming His people continues as the apostolic teaching is preserved and passed on.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Peter 1:16-18
passages.section_title: Why does Peter point to Christ’s glory?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 For we did not follow cleverly devised fables when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of His majesty. 17 For He received honor and glory from God the Father when the voice came to Him from the Majestic Glory, saying, “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” 18 And we ourselves heard this voice from heaven when we were with Him on the holy mountain.
paragraphs: 16 For we did not follow cleverly devised fables when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of His majesty. 17 For He received honor and glory from God the Father when the voice came to Him from the Majestic Glory, saying, “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” 18 And we ourselves heard this voice from heaven when we were with Him on the holy mountain.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The assurance Peter gives is grounded in testimony. He denies following cleverly devised stories and says that he and his companions were eyewitnesses of Jesus’ majesty. They heard the Father declare Him the beloved Son.

The account recalls the event commonly called the transfiguration, when Jesus’ appearance was changed and His glory became visible to Peter, James and John. Matthew 17:1–9 recounts the cloud and the Father’s voice. The account describes a high mountain without naming it.

The witness supports the message about Christ’s power and coming. The readers are being directed to what God made known about His Son, rather than asked to build their hope on an invented story.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley both identify the event with the transfiguration and emphasize the authority of the Father’s testimony to His Son. They differ over the coming in verse 16: Calvin relates it to Christ’s arrival and saving work in the world, while Wesley understands the powerful coming in future glory.

In either reading, the eyewitness account matters because it concerns who Jesus is and the glory that belongs to Him. It is not a command that every later believer must receive the same experience before trusting the message.
passages.god_plan_html:
Luke 9:28–36 adds that Moses and Elijah spoke with Jesus about the departure He would accomplish at Jerusalem. The glimpse of glory is therefore connected in the Gospel itself with the saving work He was about to undertake.

After His resurrection, Jesus explains the same movement from suffering to glory through the Scriptures in Luke 24:25–27. The glory witnessed on the mountain belongs within God’s purpose carried out through His Son’s suffering and victory.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Peter 1:19-21
passages.section_title: Why should we keep listening to Scripture?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 19 We also have the word of the prophets as confirmed beyond doubt. And you will do well to pay attention to it, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts. 20 Above all, you must understand that no prophecy of Scripture comes from one’s own interpretation. 21 For no such prophecy was ever brought forth by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.
paragraphs: 19 We also have the word of the prophets as confirmed beyond doubt. And you will do well to pay attention to it, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts. 20 Above all, you must understand that no prophecy of Scripture comes from one’s own interpretation. 21 For no such prophecy was ever brought forth by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The eyewitness testimony is joined with the word of the prophets, described as confirmed beyond doubt. The readers do well to attend to it as they would to a lamp in a dark place. The image gives them a reason to keep listening while they await the dawn.

Peter then addresses the source of scriptural prophecy. The word translated interpretation concerns explanation; the next sentence connects the point with origin. Prophecy was not brought forth by human will. People spoke from God as His Spirit carried them.

The word behind carried along can describe being moved or prompted. Here the Holy Spirit supplies that direction. Human speakers are present, but the message is not presented as their own invention.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley both prefer to read verses 20–21 in terms of prophecy’s origin in God. The Reformed Westminster Confession, 1.4, grounds Scripture’s authority in God as its author, and the Catholic Catechism, 105–106, affirms the Spirit’s inspiration through genuine human authors.

The dawn and morning-star image has different readings. Calvin looks toward the fuller sight of God beyond the present life. Wesley connects it with the light of the Gospel and Christ being revealed in the heart. Both treat the prophetic message as a light that directs believers toward Christ.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Luke 24:25–27, 44–49, the risen Jesus explains the Scriptures in relation to His suffering, resurrection and the proclamation of forgiveness to the nations. The prophetic word belongs to that unfolding saving purpose.

Its role is therefore more than supplying isolated predictions. It directs people to the Christ through whom God has acted and to the message His witnesses are to carry.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Is the Bible the Inerrant Word of God? understands this passage as describing Scripture’s origin in God: His Spirit carried the human speakers as they spoke from Him. The study applies inerrancy to the original texts as God inspired them. English translations are human works that must be examined against those texts; this passage does not promise that every translation choice is without error.

deeper_study.title: Is the Bible the Inerrant Word of God?

passages.title: 2 Peter 1:20-21
passages.section_title: Where does Scripture’s authority come from?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 20 Above all, you must understand that no prophecy of Scripture comes from one’s own interpretation. 21 For no such prophecy was ever brought forth by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.
paragraphs: 20 Above all, you must understand that no prophecy of Scripture comes from one’s own interpretation. 21 For no such prophecy was ever brought forth by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.

passages.context_html:
These verses explain why the prophetic word deserves attention. Prophecy was not produced by human will; people spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.

The word for interpretation concerns explanation. The contrast in the next verse helps explain the emphasis: the message is not simply the speaker’s own account of what God might mean. Its source is God’s Spirit.

The carried-along language describes the Spirit’s direction while people genuinely speak. Peter’s concern is confidence in that message within the larger call to attend to God’s word.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley understand the main point as divine origin, rather than a blanket prohibition on individuals reading Scripture. Calvin prefers the sense that prophecy did not arise from a person’s own suggestions; Wesley explains it as God making known what had been unknown.

The Catholic Catechism, 105–106, and the Reformed Westminster Confession, 1.4, both affirm God as Scripture’s author. Agreement on that point does not mean every tradition has the same account of how disputed passages should be interpreted.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Is the Bible the Inerrant Word of God? understands this passage as describing Scripture’s origin in God: His Spirit carried the human speakers as they spoke from Him. The study applies inerrancy to the original texts as God inspired them. English translations are human works that must be examined against those texts; this passage does not promise that every translation choice is without error.

deeper_study.title: Is the Bible the Inerrant Word of God?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
Luke 24:44–49 shows Jesus opening the Scriptures in relation to His death, resurrection and the announcement of forgiveness to all nations. God’s speaking through the prophets leads toward that saving message.

2 Timothy 3:14–17 also connects Scripture with salvation through faith in Christ and a life equipped for good work. Its divine origin serves God’s purpose of bringing people to Christ and shaping their lives.

passages.title: 2 Peter 1:21
passages.section_title: What does it mean to be carried along by the Spirit?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 For no such prophecy was ever brought forth by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.
paragraphs: 21 For no such prophecy was ever brought forth by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.

passages.context_html:
This sentence explains the preceding statement about scriptural prophecy. It contrasts human will as the source of a message with people speaking from God under the Holy Spirit’s direction.

The Greek word behind carried along can describe being moved or prompted. The speakers are human, and the directing action is God’s. Peter offers this as a reason to take the prophetic word seriously.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Calvin and Wesley both emphasize the Spirit’s initiative. Calvin expressly says the speakers did not lose the use of their minds. The Catholic Catechism, 106, likewise describes God working through people who use their human faculties as actual authors. These explanations keep the message’s divine source and its human speakers in view.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Is the Bible the Inerrant Word of God? understands this passage as describing Scripture’s origin in God: His Spirit carried the human speakers as they spoke from Him. The study applies inerrancy to the original texts as God inspired them. English translations are human works that must be examined against those texts; this passage does not promise that every translation choice is without error.

deeper_study.title: Is the Bible the Inerrant Word of God?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
2 Timothy 3:14–17 gives the purpose alongside the source: Scripture makes people wise for salvation through faith in Christ and trains them for lives of good work.

God’s speaking is directed toward a people who know His Son and are equipped to live faithfully. The authority described here supports that saving and forming work.

passages.title: 2 Peter 2:1-3
passages.section_title: What makes false teaching destructive?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Now there were also false prophets among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you. They will secretly introduce destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them—bringing swift destruction on themselves. 2 Many will follow in their depravity, and because of them the way of truth will be defamed. 3 In their greed, these false teachers will exploit you with deceptive words. The longstanding verdict against them remains in force, and their destruction does not sleep.
paragraphs: 1 Now there were also false prophets among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you. They will secretly introduce destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them—bringing swift destruction on themselves. 2 Many will follow in their depravity, and because of them the way of truth will be defamed. 3 In their greed, these false teachers will exploit you with deceptive words. The longstanding verdict against them remains in force, and their destruction does not sleep.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The warning follows the account of people speaking from God by the Holy Spirit. Just as false prophets appeared among God’s people in the past, false teachers will arise among the readers. The danger can come from within their own fellowship.

Peter describes teaching that denies the Master who bought them. The word for Master emphasizes the authority of one to whom servants belong, and the word for bought describes purchase. Their denial rejects His claim over their lives.

The harm extends into conduct and relationships. Many follow their depravity, the way of truth is defamed, and greed turns deceptive teaching into a means of exploiting people. Peter warns that God’s verdict against such evil has not become idle.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley both understand denial of the Master as reaching into conduct as well as teaching. Calvin especially connects it with turning redemption into permission for an immoral life.

The words who bought them raise a further difference. Wesley understands Christ to have bought with His blood even people who finally perish. The Catholic Catechism, 605, also teaches that Christ died for every person without exception, although this does not make its whole account of salvation identical to Wesley’s.

A Reformed reading in Ligonier’s exposition understands being bought here as being brought into the visible church, without necessarily possessing saving faith. The Westminster Confession, 3.6 and 8.8, relates Christ’s saving redemption to those God elects and brings to salvation. This broader doctrinal difference helps explain why the same phrase receives different readings.
passages.god_plan_html:
Acts 20:28–32 joins care for the church purchased by Christ’s blood with a warning that people will arise from among its leaders and distort the truth. Paul entrusts the believers to God and the word of His grace, which builds them up and gives an inheritance.

The warning therefore belongs within God’s care for the people He gathers through Christ. They are to be protected and built up by His truth rather than used for someone else’s gain.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Peter 2:4-9
passages.section_title: What do these examples show about judgment and rescue?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 4 For if God did not spare the angels when they sinned, but cast them deep into hell, placing them in chains of darkness to be held for judgment; 5 if He did not spare the ancient world when He brought the flood on its ungodly people, but preserved Noah, a preacher of righteousness, among the eight; 6 if He condemned the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to destruction, reducing them to ashes as an example of what is coming on the ungodly; 7 and if He rescued Lot, a righteous man distressed by the depraved conduct of the lawless 8 (for that righteous man, living among them day after day, was tormented in his righteous soul by the lawless deeds he saw and heard)— 9 if all this is so, then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials and to hold the unrighteous for punishment on the day of judgment.
paragraphs: 4 For if God did not spare the angels when they sinned, but cast them deep into hell, placing them in chains of darkness to be held for judgment; 5 if He did not spare the ancient world when He brought the flood on its ungodly people, but preserved Noah, a preacher of righteousness, among the eight; 6 if He condemned the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to destruction, reducing them to ashes as an example of what is coming on the ungodly;

7 and if He rescued Lot, a righteous man distressed by the depraved conduct of the lawless 8 (for that righteous man, living among them day after day, was tormented in his righteous soul by the lawless deeds he saw and heard)— 9 if all this is so, then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials and to hold the unrighteous for punishment on the day of judgment.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Peter supports the warning with three examples: angels who sinned, the world in Noah’s day, and Sodom and Gomorrah. None was beyond God’s judgment. The angels are held for judgment; the ancient world and the cities met destruction.

The examples also include rescue. God preserved Noah with seven others and delivered Lot, whose life in Sodom brought distress at the lawlessness around him. Genesis 19:16 explicitly attributes Lot’s being brought out to the Lord’s compassion.

The conclusion holds both sides together: the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials and how to hold the unrighteous for judgment. Present delay does not mean evil has escaped His notice or that those trusting Him have been forgotten.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley understand these examples as assurance that God can judge evil and care for His people. Calvin emphasizes leaving the timing of rescue and judgment to God, rather than assuming His silence means inaction.

Calvin also cautions against inventing details about the angels’ sin, since Peter does not name its time or circumstances. The USCCB’s study notes link the angelic example with Jude 6 and Genesis 6, while emphasizing the paragraph’s joined themes of judgment and rescue. The central conclusion is clearer than every detail readers may ask about.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus Himself brings Noah and Lot together in Luke 17:26–33, comparing their days with the day the Son of Man is revealed. The earlier judgments are used by the New Testament to call people to readiness for God’s final accounting.

Peter’s examples carry warning and hope together. God’s ability to preserve His people is part of the same account that insists evil will be judged. They give believers reason to trust Him while taking His call seriously.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Peter 2:10-16
passages.section_title: What happens when teachers are ruled by pride and greed?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 Such punishment is specially reserved for those who indulge the corrupt desires of the flesh and despise authority. Bold and self-willed, they are unafraid to slander glorious beings. 11 Yet not even angels, though greater in strength and power, dare to bring such slanderous charges against them before the Lord. 12 These men are like irrational animals, creatures of instinct, born to be captured and destroyed. They blaspheme in matters they do not understand, and like such creatures, they too will be destroyed. 13 The harm they will suffer is the wages of their wickedness. They consider it a pleasure to carouse in broad daylight. They are blots and blemishes, reveling in their deception as they feast with you. 14 Their eyes are full of adultery; their desire for sin is never satisfied; they seduce the unstable. They are accursed children with hearts trained in greed. 15 They have left the straight way and wandered off to follow the way of Balaam son of Beor, who loved the wages of wickedness. 16 But he was rebuked for his transgression by a donkey, otherwise without speech, that spoke with a man’s voice and restrained the prophet’s madness.
paragraphs: 10 Such punishment is specially reserved for those who indulge the corrupt desires of the flesh and despise authority. Bold and self-willed, they are unafraid to slander glorious beings. 11 Yet not even angels, though greater in strength and power, dare to bring such slanderous charges against them before the Lord.

12 These men are like irrational animals, creatures of instinct, born to be captured and destroyed. They blaspheme in matters they do not understand, and like such creatures, they too will be destroyed. 13 The harm they will suffer is the wages of their wickedness. They consider it a pleasure to carouse in broad daylight. They are blots and blemishes, reveling in their deception as they feast with you. 14 Their eyes are full of adultery; their desire for sin is never satisfied; they seduce the unstable. They are accursed children with hearts trained in greed.

15 They have left the straight way and wandered off to follow the way of Balaam son of Beor, who loved the wages of wickedness. 16 But he was rebuked for his transgression by a donkey, otherwise without speech, that spoke with a man’s voice and restrained the prophet’s madness.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Peter now develops the description of the false teachers. They indulge corrupt desires, despise authority and speak arrogantly about what they do not understand. Their presumption is contrasted with the restraint of angels who are greater in power.

The picture of irrational animals exposes lives driven by appetite rather than understanding. They openly pursue pleasure while sharing the community’s meals. Lust and practiced greed make other people targets. The word behind entice pictures luring with bait.

Balaam supplies the example of seeking wrongful gain. Numbers 22 describes Balak offering him honor and reward to curse Israel, and God confronting him through the donkey and the angel of the Lord. Peter uses that rebuke to expose the madness of letting gain rule one’s response to God.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The identity of the glorious beings in verse 10 receives different readings. Calvin and Wesley understand the insults as directed toward people in authority. The USCCB’s study note considers angelic beings more likely, especially alongside Jude 8–10. These readings share the warning against arrogant contempt, while differing over its immediate objects.

Calvin and Wesley both connect Balaam with the desire for wrongful gain and understand the teachers’ conduct as leading toward judgment. Peter connects their teaching with greed, seduction and disregard for God.
passages.god_plan_html:
In Revelation 2:12–17, Jesus also uses Balaam’s example in warning a church. He identifies the counsel that led Israel into idolatry and sexual immorality and calls His people to repent. The earlier story remains a warning within Christ’s care for His churches.

Titus 2:11–14 states the larger purpose: Christ gave Himself to redeem people from lawlessness and make them His own, eager for good work. Peter’s warning protects that calling against teaching that uses people to feed a leader’s desires.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Peter 2:17-22
passages.section_title: Can a promise of freedom lead back into slavery?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 These men are springs without water and mists driven by a storm. Blackest darkness is reserved for them. 18 With lofty but empty words, they appeal to the sensual passions of the flesh and entice those who are just escaping from others who live in error. 19 They promise them freedom, while they themselves are slaves to depravity. For a man is a slave to whatever has mastered him. 20 If indeed they have escaped the corruption of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, only to be entangled and overcome by it again, their final condition is worse than it was at first. 21 It would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than to have known it and then to turn away from the holy commandment passed on to them. 22 Of them the proverbs are true: “A dog returns to its vomit,” and, “A sow that is washed goes back to her wallowing in the mud.”
paragraphs: 17 These men are springs without water and mists driven by a storm. Blackest darkness is reserved for them. 18 With lofty but empty words, they appeal to the sensual passions of the flesh and entice those who are just escaping from others who live in error. 19 They promise them freedom, while they themselves are slaves to depravity. For a man is a slave to whatever has mastered him.

20 If indeed they have escaped the corruption of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, only to be entangled and overcome by it again, their final condition is worse than it was at first. 21 It would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than to have known it and then to turn away from the holy commandment passed on to them. 22 Of them the proverbs are true: “A dog returns to its vomit,” and, “A sow that is washed goes back to her wallowing in the mud.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Peter closes his warning about false teachers with pictures of disappointment: a spring that gives no water and mist swept away by a storm. Their impressive words offer what their lives cannot supply. They promise freedom while being mastered by the very corruption they encourage.

The people being lured are only just escaping from those who live in error. That makes the danger especially serious. Verse 18 describes their movement away from error; it does not say they narrowly escape a future sentence of judgment.

Verses 20–22 describe becoming entangled again after escaping the world’s corruption through knowing Jesus Christ. Peter says this return leaves people worse off than before. The dog proverb comes from Proverbs 26:11; the washed pig supplies a second picture of returning to what was left behind. The warning reaches beyond knowing the right words to the direction a life takes.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley both understand the promised freedom as permission to follow sinful desires. They also take the return to corruption seriously. Their disagreement concerns what that return tells us about a person’s relationship with God.

Wesley reads the escape in verse 20 as escape through faith in Christ. He describes the return in verse 22 as receiving grace and then making shipwreck of faith. This is a reading in which people can turn away from a faith they genuinely had.

The Reformed Westminster Confession, chapter 17, and the 1689 Baptist Confession, chapter 17, teach that those God has truly called and made His own will finally persevere. Both allow that believers can fall into serious sin. Calvin’s comments on this passage distinguish falling under sin’s rule and abandoning the gospel from the sins of believers who continue resisting it. These confessions represent their subscribing churches, rather than every Baptist or every reader of Calvin.

The Catholic Church also teaches that faith is God’s gift and that it can be lost; see Catechism 162. That is its broader teaching about remaining in faith, rather than a line-by-line ruling on these verses. The point at issue is whether this return follows genuine saving faith or an escape that did not become lasting faith. None of these sources treats corruption as the freedom Christ gives.
passages.god_plan_html: John 8:31–36 connects Jesus’ work with freedom from slavery to sin. Romans 6:15–23 develops the same theme: grace leads people into obedience to God, with holiness and eternal life as its fruit. These passages show why Peter’s warning matters within God’s saving purpose. A message that keeps people under sin’s control contradicts the freedom the Son gives.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Peter 3:1-7
passages.section_title: Does the passing of time mean Christ will not return?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Beloved, this is now my second letter to you. Both of them are reminders to stir you to wholesome thinking 2 by recalling what was foretold by the holy prophets and commanded by our Lord and Savior through your apostles. 3 Most importantly, you must understand that in the last days scoffers will come, scoffing and following their own evil desires. 4 “Where is the promise of His coming?” they will ask. “Ever since our fathers fell asleep, everything continues as it has from the beginning of creation.” 5 But they deliberately overlook the fact that long ago by God’s word the heavens existed and the earth was formed out of water and by water, 6 through which the world of that time perished in the flood. 7 And by that same word, the present heavens and earth are reserved for fire, being kept for the day of judgment and destruction of ungodly men.
paragraphs: 1 Beloved, this is now my second letter to you. Both of them are reminders to stir you to wholesome thinking 2 by recalling what was foretold by the holy prophets and commanded by our Lord and Savior through your apostles.

3 Most importantly, you must understand that in the last days scoffers will come, scoffing and following their own evil desires. 4 “Where is the promise of His coming?” they will ask. “Ever since our fathers fell asleep, everything continues as it has from the beginning of creation.”

5 But they deliberately overlook the fact that long ago by God’s word the heavens existed and the earth was formed out of water and by water, 6 through which the world of that time perished in the flood. 7 And by that same word, the present heavens and earth are reserved for fire, being kept for the day of judgment and destruction of ungodly men.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After warning about corrupt teachers, Peter returns to the purpose of his letters: helping his readers remember what they have received. The words of the prophets and the Lord’s command through the apostles give them a foundation for clear thinking.

The scoffers challenge the promise of Christ’s coming. They point to the continuing course of the world as though the passing of generations proved that God will never intervene. Peter connects their scoffing with following their own desires.

Peter answers from creation and the flood. Genesis 1:1–10 describes God speaking, separating the waters and bringing dry land into view. Genesis 7:17–24 records the flood’s judgment. The world’s continued existence depends on God’s word; it gives no guarantee against His future judgment.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin, Wesley and the USCCB’s study notes agree that Peter answers the denial of Christ’s return by recalling God’s past action. The passage calls readers to trust God’s promise rather than assume that familiar conditions will continue forever.

The fathers in verse 4 are understood differently. Calvin and Wesley connect them with earlier ancestors; the USCCB note understands the first Christian generation. Both readings recognize the same objection: people have died and time has passed, yet the promised coming has not occurred.
passages.god_plan_html: Jesus Himself draws the connection between Noah’s day and His coming in Matthew 24:36–44. People went about ordinary life without recognizing the approaching judgment. Jesus uses that history to call His followers to readiness. Peter’s appeal to the flood belongs to that same warning: God’s past judgment helps readers take the promised coming seriously.

passages.title: 2 Peter 3:8-10
passages.section_title: Why does God give people time to repent?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 Beloved, do not let this one thing escape your notice: With the Lord a day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years are like a day. 9 The Lord is not slow in keeping His promise as some understand slowness, but is patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance. 10 But the Day of the Lord will come like a thief. The heavens will disappear with a roar, the elements will be destroyed by fire, and the earth and its works will be laid bare.
paragraphs: 8 Beloved, do not let this one thing escape your notice: With the Lord a day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years are like a day. 9 The Lord is not slow in keeping His promise as some understand slowness, but is patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance.
10 But the Day of the Lord will come like a thief. The heavens will disappear with a roar, the elements will be destroyed by fire, and the earth and its works will be laid bare.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Peter now addresses his beloved readers directly. The comparison between a day and a thousand years recalls Psalm 90:1–6, where God’s enduring life is set beside human frailty. It corrects the way people measure His faithfulness; it supplies no conversion formula for calculating the date of Christ’s return.

The apparent delay is described as patience that gives room for repentance. The warning about the Day of the Lord remains: it will arrive unexpectedly, like a thief. God’s patience is therefore a reason to respond to Him now.

The BSB ends verse 10 with the earth and its works being laid bare. Other translations read that they will be burned up. The USCCB note records this difference in the surviving texts. The passage’s fire and judgment language remains clear; the wording in the Scripture panel follows the verified BSB.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The main difference concerns the scope of anyone and everyone in verse 9. Wesley understands God’s patience as expressing His desire that no human soul perish. The Catholic Church uses this verse in teaching that God predestines no one to hell and that the Church appeals to His mercy; see Catechism 1037. Neither source treats that desire as a prediction that everyone will finally be saved.

One Reformed reading, presented in Ligonier’s The Lord Is Patient, links anyone and everyone to the believing audience addressed as you. On this reading, the passage concerns God bringing all His chosen people to repentance. The broader Reformed teaching about God’s choice appears in Westminster Confession, chapter 3. Ligonier’s explanation is a particular application of that teaching to this verse.

Calvin’s own comments express the distinction differently: he sees an invitation to all humanity in the gospel while distinguishing that invitation from God’s hidden purpose in choosing people. Reformed writers therefore should not all be assigned one explanation of these words. Across these readings, God’s patience calls for repentance, and His promised coming remains certain.
passages.god_plan_html: Romans 2:1–5 also places God’s kindness and patience beside His coming judgment. His kindness leads toward repentance; a hard heart can instead store up judgment. Together the passages show that the time God gives has a saving purpose. The proper response is to turn toward Him rather than treat the passage of time as proof that He will never act.

passages.title: 2 Peter 3:11-13
passages.section_title: How should the promised new creation shape life now?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 Since everything will be destroyed in this way, what kind of people ought you to be? You ought to conduct yourselves in holiness and godliness 12 as you anticipate and hasten the coming of the day of God, when the heavens will be destroyed by fire and the elements will melt in the heat. 13 But in keeping with God’s promise, we are looking forward to a new heaven and a new earth, where righteousness dwells.
paragraphs: 11 Since everything will be destroyed in this way, what kind of people ought you to be? You ought to conduct yourselves in holiness and godliness 12 as you anticipate and hasten the coming of the day of God, when the heavens will be destroyed by fire and the elements will melt in the heat. 13 But in keeping with God’s promise, we are looking forward to a new heaven and a new earth, where righteousness dwells.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Peter turns the promise of coming judgment into a direct question about daily life. Knowing that the present order will pass away should lead to holiness and devotion to God. His concern is the kind of people his readers become while they wait.

The hope reaches beyond destruction: God promises a new heaven and a new earth where righteousness dwells. Isaiah 65:17–19 already speaks of new heavens and a new earth in connection with joy in what God creates.

The Greek word translated elements can refer to the basic constituents of the world; Thayer lists these verses under that meaning. Peter’s language describes creation under God’s judgment without explaining a modern physical process.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin understands the fire as cleansing and renewing creation. The Catholic Church likewise teaches a transformation of the visible universe while acknowledging that its manner and timing are unknown; see Catechism 1042–1048. Calvin’s published commentary also includes an editor’s note cautioning that the promise of a new creation does not by itself settle whether the present creation is renewed. That note is the editor’s observation, rather than Calvin’s own conclusion.

The word translated hasten in verse 12 also receives different explanations. Calvin emphasizes eager, active waiting; Wesley connects it with earnest desire and prayer. The USCCB note also considers conduct helping bring the promised day. Thayer lists earnest desire as the word’s sense here. These explanations agree that waiting should shape life now, while differing over how that waiting relates to the day’s arrival.
passages.god_plan_html: Revelation 21:1–8 develops the same new-creation hope. God dwells with His people, wipes away their tears and brings an end to death and pain. The holy city is pictured as a bride prepared for her husband. This is more than escape from a damaged world: it is life with God in the creation He makes new, with His people belonging to Him.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: 2 Peter 3:14-16
passages.section_title: How do we handle Scripture that is hard to understand?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 Therefore, beloved, as you anticipate these things, make every effort to be found at peace—spotless and blameless in His sight. 15 Consider also that our Lord’s patience brings salvation, just as our beloved brother Paul also wrote you with the wisdom God gave him. 16 He writes this way in all his letters, speaking in them about such matters. Some parts of his letters are hard to understand, which ignorant and unstable people distort, as they do the rest of the Scriptures, to their own destruction.
paragraphs: 14 Therefore, beloved, as you anticipate these things, make every effort to be found at peace—spotless and blameless in His sight. 15 Consider also that our Lord’s patience brings salvation, just as our beloved brother Paul also wrote you with the wisdom God gave him.

16 He writes this way in all his letters, speaking in them about such matters. Some parts of his letters are hard to understand, which ignorant and unstable people distort, as they do the rest of the Scriptures, to their own destruction.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Because his readers expect God’s promised future, Peter urges them to make every effort to be found at peace, spotless and blameless. He again connects the Lord’s patience with salvation, then points to Paul as a beloved brother whose wisdom comes from God.

Peter openly acknowledges that some things in Paul’s letters are difficult. The danger he identifies is people distorting those things, just as they distort the other Scriptures. Difficulty calls for care and steadiness; it does not make manipulation harmless.

The reference to the rest of the Scriptures places Paul’s letters alongside Scripture. The passage does not identify which particular letter Paul had written to these readers, nor does it provide a list of all the books they possessed.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Calvin, Wesley and the USCCB note recognize Paul’s letters as being treated here as Scripture. Calvin and Wesley also stress that misuse of difficult passages gives no reason to stop reading them. The warning concerns distortion; readers are called to approach the writings with care and a willingness to learn.
passages.god_plan_html: 2 Timothy 3:14–17 explains the positive purpose of Scripture: it gives wisdom for salvation through faith in Christ and equips God’s servant for good work. That helps show what is at stake in Peter’s warning. God gives His word to teach and form His people; distorting it turns a gift meant for their good into an occasion for harm.

passages.title: 2 Peter 3:17-18
passages.section_title: How do we stay steady and keep growing in Christ?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 Therefore, beloved, since you already know these things, be on your guard so that you will not be carried away by the error of the lawless and fall from your secure standing. 18 But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To Him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen.
paragraphs: 17 Therefore, beloved, since you already know these things, be on your guard so that you will not be carried away by the error of the lawless and fall from your secure standing. 18 But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To Him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Peter ends with both a warning and a direction for growth. His readers have been told about the danger ahead, so they should guard against being carried away by the error of lawless people. Their secure standing is something to protect.

The closing direction is to grow in the grace and knowledge of Jesus Christ. This returns to the letter’s opening emphasis on knowing Him and receiving what He gives for a godly life. The final praise gives Christ glory now and forever.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Calvin understands the warning as awakening believers to watchfulness while leaving their confidence in God’s promises intact. Growth in Christ is part of how they persevere. Wesley gives the closing call a stronger warning about the possibility of spiritual life declining toward death when growth and the putting away of sin are neglected. Both call for active growth, while differing over what a final failure to continue would mean.
passages.god_plan_html: Ephesians 4:11–16 describes Christ giving people to equip His church so that it grows toward maturity. That growth protects believers from being carried about by deceptive teaching and builds the whole body in love. Peter’s closing direction belongs within that larger purpose: people who know Christ increasingly learn to stand together under His care.

passages.title: 1 John 1:6-7

versions.label: LSB
versions.text: "If we say that we have fellowship with Him and yet walk in the darkness, we lie and do not practice the truth; but if we walk in the Light as He Himself is in the Light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus His Son cleanses us from all sin."

passages.context_html: In 1 John 1, John opens the letter by grounding fellowship with God in the apostolic witness about the Word of life. The chapter contrasts walking in the light with false claims about sinlessness, so its statements about confession, cleansing, and fellowship must be read within that truth-versus-falsehood framework.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Fellowship — the closeness, the clarity, the active walking with God — is what is at stake here, not salvation itself. Walking in darkness while claiming fellowship is self-deception. Walking in the light — which includes the honesty of confession — is what keeps the relationship close and the cleansing ongoing.
passages.current_position_html: No defined position is stated here yet beyond the common interpretations above. As related study develops, this section will be updated where the text warrants a clearer conclusion.

passages.title: 1 John 1:9

versions.label: LSB
versions.text: "If we confess our sins, He is faithful and righteous to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."

passages.context_html: In 1 John 1, John opens the letter by grounding fellowship with God in the apostolic witness about the Word of life. The chapter contrasts walking in the light with false claims about sinlessness, so its statements about confession, cleansing, and fellowship must be read within that truth-versus-falsehood framework.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Two words matter here. Forgive — ἀφίημι (aphiēmi (ah-FEE-ay-mee)), the same root as aphesis — the releasing of the debt. And cleanse — καθαρίζω (katharizō (kah-thah-RID-zoh)) — a purifying word, the same family as the apolouō of baptism. Both realities baptism accomplished at the start — cancelling the debt, washing the person — remain available through confession. Not through repeated baptism, but through an ongoing posture of acknowledgment before God. This is the mechanism for what happens after baptism. Confession is not a formality or a ritual phrase — it is the believer's continual turning back to God, naming what is true, and receiving both the forgiveness and the cleansing that flow from Christ's finished work. Notice also who confession is made to. John does not say "to a priest" or require confession "to one another" as a precondition for forgiveness — he says "if we confess our sins," addressed directly to God, who is "faithful and righteous to forgive." No human intermediary stands between the believer and the Father here. Every believer, clothed with Christ at baptism, already has direct access — there is no priesthood of a select few standing in between. The mutual confession James 5:16 commands — confessing faults and praying for one another — is a separate practice aimed at accountability and healing among believers, not a sacramental requirement for receiving God's forgiveness. 1 John 1:9 is addressed to the individual believer and to God alone. Sin that goes unconfessed does not undo salvation. The debt remains cancelled — that was settled once, by faith, and is not revisited. But unconfessed sin does something else: it accumulates. It sits on the believer like a stain that was never washed out. The Spirit who indwells the believer at salvation is not driven out by sin — but He can be grieved. The word pictures a relationship under strain, not a relationship ended. A believer carrying unconfessed sin is not cut off from God, but their ability to hear, to discern, to walk in step with the Spirit is diminished. The stain does not change their standing before God; it changes their experience of walking with Him.
passages.current_position_html: No defined position is stated here yet beyond the common interpretations above. As related study develops, this section will be updated where the text warrants a clearer conclusion.

passages.title: 1 John 5:7-8
passages.context_html: In 1 John 5, John is drawing the letter toward its conclusion by stressing life in the Son, assurance, and confidence before God. The chapter ties prayer, obedience, and discernment together, so verses here should be read in light of the whole letter's concern for abiding in Christ and walking in the truth.
passages.common_interpretations_html: What remains is a genuinely small list of notable places where manuscripts differ in a way that affects the reading — the Comma Johanneum in 1 John 5:7-8 (an explicit Trinitarian formula found only in a handful of late manuscripts), the ending of Mark's Gospel after 16:8, and the story of the woman caught in adultery in John 7:53-8:11. These are worth knowing about, and good study Bibles typically flag them with a footnote. But even here, the core teaching involved — the Trinity, the resurrection, grace toward sinners — is affirmed clearly and repeatedly elsewhere in passages no one disputes. No textual variant anywhere in the manuscript tradition puts a single core doctrine of the faith at risk. That claim isn't ours alone — it's close to a consensus statement among textual critics across the theological spectrum, whatever position they hold on which text family is best. (For a genuinely exhaustive, manuscript-by-manuscript treatment of this subject, Berean Patriot's "Majority Text vs. Critical Text vs. Textus Receptus – Textual Criticism 101" is the most complete single resource we've found. It doesn't land firmly on any one camp, but it does the work of walking through the evidence in full. We link it here for anyone who wants to go deeper than this document is trying to.)

deeper_study.title: Is There a Source of Truth?

passages.title: 1 John 5:14
passages.context_html: In 1 John 5, John is drawing the letter toward its conclusion by stressing life in the Son, assurance, and confidence before God. The chapter ties prayer, obedience, and discernment together, so verses here should be read in light of the whole letter's concern for abiding in Christ and walking in the truth.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Notice the structure of the promise. It is not "ask and you will receive." It is conditional at every step: if we ask according to His will, then He hears us; if we know He hears us, then we know we have what we asked. The entire promise depends on alignment with His will, not on the sincerity, persistence, or emotional intensity of the request. This is the lens through which every other prayer passage in Scripture should be read. Whenever a verse seems to promise that God will give us whatever we ask, this conditional clause is already built into it, whether stated explicitly or not. The contrast with Paul's two examples is instructive. All three prayers are specific. All three name something. The difference is what the something serves. Paul's requests aimed at his own relief and comfort, and were met with patient denial. The believers in Acts 4 aimed at God's purpose being accomplished through them regardless of what happened to them personally, and were met with an immediate yes. This is the distinction 1 John 5:14-15 draws: "if we ask anything according to His will, He hears us." It is not a prohibition on specific requests. It is a definition of what makes a request rightly aimed. Pray specifically. Pray earnestly. But pray for what serves His purpose, not what serves personal comfort or preference — and hold even the most earnest request the way Christ held His own in Gethsemane: "not as I will, but as You will." Paul learned to stop asking and trust a plan he could not see. Genesis gives us the picture of what happens when a man does not. When the famine came, Abraham did not inquire of God about what to do. He took matters into his own hands, went down to Egypt, and devised a plan built on deception to protect himself — a plan that nearly cost him his wife and ended with a pagan king rebuking the father of faith for his dishonesty. God still intervened and protected Sarah, but the intervention happened in spite of Abraham's lack of trust, not because his plan had worked.

passages.title: 1 John 5:14-15
passages.note: The governing principle of prayer: we approach God on His terms, not ours.

versions.label: LSB
versions.text: Now this is the confidence which we have before Him, that if we ask anything according to His will, He hears us. And if we know that He hears us in whatever we ask, we know that we have the requests which we have asked from Him.

versions.label: NKJV
versions.text: Now this is the confidence that we have in Him, that if we ask anything according to His will, He hears us. And if we know that He hears us, whatever we ask, we know that we have the petitions that we have asked of Him.

versions.label: NABRE
versions.text: And we have this confidence in him, that if we ask anything according to his will, he hears us. And if we know that he hears us in regard to whatever we ask, we know that what we have asked him for is ours.

passages.context_html: 1 John 5:14-15 comes near the close of the letter, where John is drawing together his pastoral purpose: that believers may know the life they have in the Son and live with confidence before God. The immediate context matters. In 1 John 5:13, John says he is writing so that believers may know they have eternal life. Then in verses 14-15 he moves straight into confidence in prayer, and in verses 16-17 he applies that confidence to a concrete case involving prayer for a brother in sin. The passage is therefore not an isolated slogan about getting what one wants from God. It sits inside a larger argument about abiding in the Son, walking in truth, and praying in a way consistent with God's own life and character. That wider setting also guards against cherry-picking. Throughout 1 John, John contrasts truth and falsehood, obedience and disobedience, love and hatred, life and death. By the time chapter 5 arrives, confidence before God is already tied to remaining in Him, believing rightly about Christ, and keeping His commandments. Verses 14-15 belong inside that whole framework.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The promise is conditional at every step. The text does not say, 'ask and you will receive' without qualification. It says that if we ask according to His will, then He hears us; and if He hears us, then we know we have what we asked. That means the controlling issue is not sincerity, repetition, or emotional force. The controlling issue is alignment with God's will. John places confidence in prayer under God's rule, not under human desire. Read that way, the verse becomes a boundary for other prayer passages. Acts 4:29-31 shows believers asking for boldness so the word of God may go forward, and the request is granted. By contrast, 2 Corinthians 12:7-9 and Romans 15:30-32 show that even earnest, specific requests are not granted simply because they are heartfelt. The issue remains whether the request serves God's purpose rather than personal relief or preference. The same principle fits naturally with John 15:7, where abiding in Christ shapes what is desired and asked, and with Romans 8:26-27, where the Spirit intercedes according to the will of God when believers do not know how to pray as they should. Taken together, 1 John 5:14-15 presents prayer as confidence under God's will, not leverage for securing personal outcomes.
