passages.title: 2 John 1:1-3
passages.section_title: What holds truth and love together?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 The elder, To the chosen lady and her children, whom I love in the truth—and not I alone, but also all who know the truth— 2 because of the truth that abides in us and will be with us forever: 3 Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and from Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father, will be with us in truth and love.
paragraphs: 1 The elder, To the chosen lady and her children, whom I love in the truth—and not I alone, but also all who know the truth— 2 because of the truth that abides in us and will be with us forever: 3 Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and from Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father, will be with us in truth and love.

passages.context_html:
The writer introduces himself as the elder and addresses the chosen lady and her children. Before giving any warning, he speaks of love grounded in the truth they share. This truth lives among them and will remain with them.

The word translated abides means remains or continues. Here it describes the truth’s lasting presence. Grace, mercy and peace come from the Father and from Jesus Christ, the Father’s Son, within this life of truth and love.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The main difference is the identity of the lady. Wesley understands an individual Christian woman and takes the term as her name, Kyria. The USCCB study note understands a local church, with its members pictured as children. The closing greeting from an elect sister fits that church reading, though it does not name either community.

Both readings recognize a greeting to people joined by Christian truth and love. The letter itself does not give their location or explain why the writer uses the title elder.
passages.current_position_html: Our study The True Church According to Jesus places Christ at the foundation of the church and identifies self-giving love as the mark of His people. From that study, we understand truth about Christ and love for one another as belonging together in the life of the church.

deeper_study.title: The True Church According to Jesus

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html: In John 14:15–24, Jesus joins keeping His word with love for Him and the presence of the Father, the Son and the Spirit of truth. This provides a wider biblical setting for the letter’s opening: God gathers people into life with Him, and His abiding truth shapes their love for one another.

passages.title: 2 John 1:4-6
passages.section_title: What does walking in love look like?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 4 I was overjoyed to find some of your children walking in the truth, just as the Father has commanded us. 5 And now I urge you, dear lady—not as a new commandment to you, but one we have had from the beginning—that we love one another. 6 And this is love, that we walk according to His commandments. This is the very commandment you have heard from the beginning, that you must walk in love.
paragraphs: 4 I was overjoyed to find some of your children walking in the truth, just as the Father has commanded us. 5 And now I urge you, dear lady—not as a new commandment to you, but one we have had from the beginning—that we love one another. 6 And this is love, that we walk according to His commandments. This is the very commandment you have heard from the beginning, that you must walk in love.

passages.context_html:
The elder rejoices that some of the children are walking in the truth. Walking describes the way they live. His joy comes from seeing the Father’s command expressed in their conduct.

He then returns to the command they have already received: love one another. Verse 6 connects that love with walking according to God’s commandments. Truth, obedience and love belong together throughout the letter.

The reference to some children tells us whom he has found walking faithfully. By itself it does not tell us the conduct of every other member of the family or community.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley and the USCCB notes connect love with obedience expressed in daily life. They recognize the call to love as teaching already received. This passage gives a practical description of love through conduct rather than treating the command as a claim that warm feelings alone fulfill it.
passages.current_position_html: Our study I Am a Disciple describes discipleship as learning from Jesus and following His way of life. It identifies self-giving love in action as the mark of a disciple. We therefore read this call to walk in love as something to practice through obedience, rather than simply a statement of admiration for Jesus.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html: Jesus gives His disciples the command to love one another as He has loved them in John 13:34–35. He says that their love will identify them as His disciples. The letter carries that purpose into community life: obedience and love make allegiance to Jesus visible.

passages.title: 2 John 1:7-11
passages.section_title: When does welcoming a teacher support a lie?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 For many deceivers have gone out into the world, refusing to confess the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh. Any such person is the deceiver and the antichrist. 8 Watch yourselves, so that you do not lose what we have worked for, but that you may be fully rewarded. 9 Anyone who runs ahead without remaining in the teaching of Christ does not have God. Whoever remains in His teaching has both the Father and the Son. 10 If anyone comes to you but does not bring this teaching, do not receive him into your home or even greet him. 11 Whoever greets such a person shares in his evil deeds.
paragraphs: 7 For many deceivers have gone out into the world, refusing to confess the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh. Any such person is the deceiver and the antichrist. 8 Watch yourselves, so that you do not lose what we have worked for, but that you may be fully rewarded. 9 Anyone who runs ahead without remaining in the teaching of Christ does not have God. Whoever remains in His teaching has both the Father and the Son.
10 If anyone comes to you but does not bring this teaching, do not receive him into your home or even greet him. 11 Whoever greets such a person shares in his evil deeds.

passages.context_html:
The reason for the warning now becomes explicit: deceivers refuse to confess Jesus Christ’s coming in the flesh. John calls such a person the deceiver and the antichrist. In this sentence the description applies to the person promoting that denial; the passage gives no name or date for a future world ruler.

The readers must watch themselves, hold to Christ’s teaching and seek a full reward. The person who runs ahead without remaining in that teaching does not have God. Claiming to advance beyond the received teaching is therefore no proof of spiritual maturity.

The command against receiving or greeting such a teacher is tied to sharing in that person’s evil work. The issue is how a welcome can help teaching spread. Third John 5–8 supplies the positive counterpart: supporting faithful messengers makes believers fellow workers for the truth.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The Catholic Church and Reformed confessions affirm that Christ truly became human while remaining truly God; see Catechism 464–465 and Westminster Confession 8.2. The denial described in verse 7 concerns that real coming in the flesh.

Readers differ over how to understand not having God in verse 9. Wesley treats it as not having God as one’s Father and God. The USCCB note connects fellowship with God to holding the teaching about Christ. A Free Grace reading presented by the Grace Evangelical Society understands the warning as loss of fellowship and God’s support in a believer’s work, while distinguishing that from loss of eternal life. That is this organization’s reading, rather than the position of all evangelicals.

Wesley understands the forbidden greeting as encouragement of the teacher’s work; the Grace Evangelical Society likewise distinguishes supporting a traveling teacher from ordinary conversation. The USCCB note describes a more complete avoidance of dangerous traveling teachers. These explanations differ in how widely the restriction applies, while sharing the concern that hospitality can assist deception.

The truth about His real human life belongs to how God has made Himself known, rather than being an optional detail that a teacher can discard.

passages.title: 2 John 1:12-13
passages.section_title: Why does the elder hope to speak face to face?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 I have many things to write to you, but I would prefer not to do so with paper and ink. Instead, I hope to come and speak with you face to face, so that our joy may be complete. 13 The children of your elect sister send you greetings.
paragraphs: 12 I have many things to write to you, but I would prefer not to do so with paper and ink. Instead, I hope to come and speak with you face to face, so that our joy may be complete. 13 The children of your elect sister send you greetings.

passages.context_html:
The elder has more to say, but he hopes to visit and speak face to face so that their shared joy may be complete. The letter gives what is needed now while looking toward a fuller personal conversation.

The closing greeting comes from the children of the elect sister. It echoes the opening address and ends the letter with a relationship between the people sending and receiving it.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley reads the greeting in terms of an actual sister’s children; the USCCB note reads it as a greeting between churches. Both recognize the desire for personal conversation. Neither the wording here nor the reference to paper and ink states that persecution is the reason for postponing the rest.

passages.title: 3 John 1:1-4
passages.section_title: What brings joy when someone is growing in the truth?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 The elder, To the beloved Gaius, whom I love in the truth: 2 Beloved, I pray that in every way you may prosper and enjoy good health, as your soul also prospers. 3 For I was overjoyed when the brothers came and testified about your devotion to the truth, in which you continue to walk. 4 I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth.
paragraphs: 1 The elder, To the beloved Gaius, whom I love in the truth: 2 Beloved, I pray that in every way you may prosper and enjoy good health, as your soul also prospers.

3 For I was overjoyed when the brothers came and testified about your devotion to the truth, in which you continue to walk. 4 I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth.

passages.context_html:
The elder writes personally to Gaius, whom he loves in the truth. He prays for Gaius’s well-being and good health alongside the well-being of his soul. The greeting shows concern for his whole life.

The word translated prosper can mean to fare well or succeed. Thayer lists this verse under that broader sense. The prayer expresses a desire for Gaius’s welfare; its wording does not guarantee that every faithful believer will become wealthy or remain physically healthy.

The reason for the elder’s joy is the report brought by other believers: Gaius continues to walk in the truth. The elder speaks of his children with affection and delights in seeing their faith shape their lives. The letter does not identify Gaius with any other man of the same name in the New Testament.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley and the USCCB notes understand walking in the truth as Christian faith expressed in life. Wesley suggests that Gaius may be the man Paul knew in Corinth, but presents that identification as a possibility. It is not supplied by the letter itself. Their shared emphasis is the encouragement given by Gaius’s faithful conduct.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html: John 13:34–35 says that the disciples’ love will make their connection to Jesus known. Gaius’s conduct illustrates that purpose: the truth becomes visible enough for other believers to report it. The comparison is a parallel in the life of disciples, rather than a claim that Jesus was predicting this particular report.

passages.title: 3 John 1:5-8
passages.section_title: How does practical support make us fellow workers?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 5 Beloved, you are faithful in what you are doing for the brothers, and especially since they are strangers to you. 6 They have testified to the church about your love. You will do well to send them on their way in a manner worthy of God. 7 For they went out on behalf of the Name, accepting nothing from the Gentiles. 8 Therefore we ought to support such men, so that we may be fellow workers for the truth.
paragraphs: 5 Beloved, you are faithful in what you are doing for the brothers, and especially since they are strangers to you. 6 They have testified to the church about your love. You will do well to send them on their way in a manner worthy of God.
7 For they went out on behalf of the Name, accepting nothing from the Gentiles. 8 Therefore we ought to support such men, so that we may be fellow workers for the truth.

passages.context_html:
The elder commends Gaius for helping fellow believers, including people he did not previously know. Their report confirms his love. He is encouraged to help them continue their journey in a way worthy of God.

These messengers have gone out for the sake of the Name and accept nothing from the Gentiles. The word used for Gentiles here refers to people outside the worship of the true God. It does not imply that every Christian of non-Jewish ancestry is excluded from supporting them.

Verse 8 states the result of supporting such people: the helpers become fellow workers for the truth. Gaius does not have to make the same journey to share in the work. His material help has a part in its progress.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley and the USCCB notes understand these travelers as messengers of the gospel and the requested help as practical provision for their onward journey. Hospitality and support express Gaius’s faith. The passage concerns support for these faithful workers; it does not promise a financial return to every donor.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?

passages.god_plan_html: In Matthew 10:40–42, Jesus connects receiving His messengers with receiving Him and speaks of God recognizing even a cup of cold water given to a disciple. First Corinthians 9:7–14 likewise connects gospel work with material support. These passages place Gaius’s hospitality within a larger pattern: God advances the work through both those who go and those who help them.

passages.title: 3 John 1:9-12
passages.section_title: Whose example should we follow when a leader wants control?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 I have written to the church about this, but Diotrephes, who loves to be first, will not accept our instruction. 10 So if I come, I will call attention to his malicious slander against us. And unsatisfied with that, he refuses to welcome the brothers and forbids those who want to do so, even putting them out of the church. 11 Beloved, do not imitate what is evil, but what is good. The one who does good is of God; the one who does evil has not seen God. 12 Demetrius has received a good testimony from everyone, and from the truth itself. We also testify for him, and you know that our testimony is true.
paragraphs: 9 I have written to the church about this, but Diotrephes, who loves to be first, will not accept our instruction. 10 So if I come, I will call attention to his malicious slander against us. And unsatisfied with that, he refuses to welcome the brothers and forbids those who want to do so, even putting them out of the church.

11 Beloved, do not imitate what is evil, but what is good. The one who does good is of God; the one who does evil has not seen God. 12 Demetrius has received a good testimony from everyone, and from the truth itself. We also testify for him, and you know that our testimony is true.

passages.context_html:
Diotrephes provides a sharp contrast to Gaius. He loves to be first, rejects the elder’s instruction, speaks maliciously against him and refuses the visiting brothers. He also blocks those who want to receive them and puts them out of the church.

The elder plans to call attention to this conduct if he comes. He then tells Gaius to imitate good rather than evil. The contrast concerns actual conduct: the one doing good is of God, while the one doing evil has not seen God.

Demetrius receives a good testimony from others, from the truth itself and from the elder. He offers a positive example after the warning about Diotrephes. The letter commends his reputation without explicitly telling us his office or saying that he carried it.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and the USCCB notes see Diotrephes as exercising authority in the community and understand verse 11 as warning against following his conduct. Wesley suggests he may have been its pastor. The USCCB introduction discusses several possible reasons for the conflict. Those reconstructions do not change what the letter states about his slander and exclusion of others.

Wesley understands not having seen God as being a stranger to Him. The warning directs readers to recognize the seriousness of evil conduct and follow the good example commended to them. It gives no procedure here for determining every individual’s final standing before God.
passages.current_position_html: Our studies Who Shepherds the Church? and The True Church According to Jesus describe recognized leadership as mature, accountable service among believers. We read the warning about Diotrephes in line with that conclusion: wanting to be first and controlling others conflicts with the kind of care these studies describe.

passages.god_plan_html: In Mark 10:42–45, Jesus answers the desire for greatness by calling His followers to serve. He points to His own service and the giving of His life. Philippians 2:1–11 likewise grounds care for others in Christ’s humility. These passages explain why a church leader’s desire to be first conflicts with the pattern Christ gives His people.

passages.title: 3 John 1:13-15
passages.section_title: How does a difficult letter end with personal care?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 I have many things to write to you, but I would prefer not to do so with pen and ink. 14 Instead, I hope to see you soon and speak with you face to face. Peace to you. The friends here send you greetings. Greet each of our friends there by name.
paragraphs: 13 I have many things to write to you, but I would prefer not to do so with pen and ink. 14 Instead, I hope to see you soon and speak with you face to face. Peace to you. The friends here send you greetings. Greet each of our friends there by name.

passages.context_html:
The elder has more to write, but hopes to visit soon and speak face to face. The letter closes with peace and greetings between friends. Asking that each friend be greeted by name gives the ending a personal warmth.

The BSB places the peace and final greetings in verse 14. Editions that number them as verse 15 cover the same closing material; the Scripture panel here follows the BSB numbering.

The writer does not explain why he prefers to finish the conversation in person. His closing expresses that preference without telling readers that letters are inadequate or that a specific threat prevented him from saying more.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley emphasizes greeting the friends individually, as though they had each been named. The USCCB note recognizes friends as members of the connected Christian community. The emphasis is personal fellowship and peace at the end of a letter that has addressed a painful conflict.

passages.title: Jude 1:1-2
passages.section_title: Where does confidence begin when the church faces danger?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James, To those who are called, loved by God the Father, and kept in Jesus Christ: 2 Mercy, peace, and love be multiplied to you.
paragraphs: 1 Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James, To those who are called, loved by God the Father, and kept in Jesus Christ: 2 Mercy, peace, and love be multiplied to you.

passages.context_html:
Jude introduces himself as a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James. He addresses people who are called, loved by God the Father and kept in Jesus Christ. Before describing the danger facing them, he reminds them of their relationship with God.

The prayer for multiplied mercy, peace and love sets the tone for the letter. Its strong warnings will serve people who are beloved. Jude will return to God’s keeping power and to praise at the end.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley and the USCCB note understand the greeting as reassurance of God’s care for those He has called. Wesley explicitly connects the opening with the later call to remain in God’s love. The letter places God’s care before its warnings and the readers’ response.

passages.god_plan_html: Ephesians 1:3–14 describes the Father’s purpose, redemption through Christ and the promised Holy Spirit as the pledge of the inheritance. It gives a fuller account of the saving work within which Jude’s greeting belongs: God gathers a people in Christ to live before Him and praise His glory.

passages.title: Jude 1:3-16
passages.section_title: How can grace be turned into an excuse for corruption?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 3 Beloved, although I made every effort to write to you about the salvation we share, I felt it necessary to write and urge you to contend earnestly for the faith entrusted once for all to the saints. 4 For certain men have crept in among you unnoticed—ungodly ones who were designated long ago for condemnation. They turn the grace of our God into a license for immorality, and they deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ. 5 Although you are fully aware of this, I want to remind you that after Jesus had delivered His people out of the land of Egypt, He destroyed those who did not believe. 6 And the angels who did not stay within their own domain but abandoned their proper dwelling—these He has kept in eternal chains under darkness, bound for judgment on that great day. 7 In like manner, Sodom and Gomorrah and the cities around them, who indulged in sexual immorality and pursued strange flesh, are on display as an example of those who sustain the punishment of eternal fire. 8 Yet in the same way these dreamers defile their bodies, reject authority, and slander glorious beings. 9 But even the archangel Michael, when he disputed with the devil over the body of Moses, did not presume to bring a slanderous charge against him, but said, “The Lord rebuke you!” 10 These men, however, slander what they do not understand, and like irrational animals, they will be destroyed by the things they do instinctively. 11 Woe to them! They have traveled the path of Cain; they have rushed for profit into the error of Balaam; they have perished in Korah’s rebellion. 12 These men are hidden reefs in your love feasts, shamelessly feasting with you but shepherding only themselves. They are clouds without water, carried along by the wind; fruitless trees in autumn, twice dead after being uprooted. 13 They are wild waves of the sea, foaming up their own shame; wandering stars, for whom blackest darkness has been reserved forever. 14 Enoch, the seventh from Adam, also prophesied about them: “Behold, the Lord is coming with myriads of His holy ones 15 to execute judgment on everyone, and to convict all the ungodly of every ungodly act of wickedness and every harsh word spoken against Him by ungodly sinners.” 16 These men are discontented grumblers, following after their own lusts; their mouths spew arrogance; they flatter others for their own advantage.
paragraphs: 3 Beloved, although I made every effort to write to you about the salvation we share, I felt it necessary to write and urge you to contend earnestly for the faith entrusted once for all to the saints. 4 For certain men have crept in among you unnoticed—ungodly ones who were designated long ago for condemnation. They turn the grace of our God into a license for immorality, and they deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ.

5 Although you are fully aware of this, I want to remind you that after Jesus had delivered His people out of the land of Egypt, He destroyed those who did not believe. 6 And the angels who did not stay within their own domain but abandoned their proper dwelling—these He has kept in eternal chains under darkness, bound for judgment on that great day. 7 In like manner, Sodom and Gomorrah and the cities around them, who indulged in sexual immorality and pursued strange flesh, are on display as an example of those who sustain the punishment of eternal fire.

8 Yet in the same way these dreamers defile their bodies, reject authority, and slander glorious beings. 9 But even the archangel Michael, when he disputed with the devil over the body of Moses, did not presume to bring a slanderous charge against him, but said, “The Lord rebuke you!” 10 These men, however, slander what they do not understand, and like irrational animals, they will be destroyed by the things they do instinctively.

11 Woe to them! They have traveled the path of Cain; they have rushed for profit into the error of Balaam; they have perished in Korah’s rebellion. 12 These men are hidden reefs in your love feasts, shamelessly feasting with you but shepherding only themselves. They are clouds without water, carried along by the wind; fruitless trees in autumn, twice dead after being uprooted. 13 They are wild waves of the sea, foaming up their own shame; wandering stars, for whom blackest darkness has been reserved forever.

14 Enoch, the seventh from Adam, also prophesied about them: “Behold, the Lord is coming with myriads of His holy ones 15 to execute judgment on everyone, and to convict all the ungodly of every ungodly act of wickedness and every harsh word spoken against Him by ungodly sinners.” 16 These men are discontented grumblers, following after their own lusts; their mouths spew arrogance; they flatter others for their own advantage.

passages.context_html:
Jude explains why he is writing urgently. People have entered the community unnoticed, use God’s grace as a license for immorality and deny Jesus Christ as Master and Lord. He calls the readers to contend for the faith entrusted to the saints. The word translated contend describes striving for something; here the concern is faithfulness to the received faith.

Three examples show the seriousness of rebellion: the unbelieving people after the deliverance from Egypt, angels who abandoned their proper place, and Sodom and Gomorrah. The BSB names Jesus as the one who delivered His people from Egypt in verse 5. Jude’s point is that earlier privilege gives no protection to persistent unbelief and rebellion.

The present offenders likewise defile their bodies, reject authority and slander what they do not understand. Michael provides the contrast. In the dispute over Moses’ body, he appeals to the Lord’s rebuke rather than making a slanderous charge. Jude does not explain the reason for that dispute or describe what the devil planned to do with the body. Deuteronomy 34:1–12 records Moses’ death and burial without giving those details.

Cain, Balaam and Korah provide further examples. Genesis 4:1–16 describes Cain’s anger and murder of Abel. Numbers 31:16 identifies Balaam’s counsel that led Israel into unfaithfulness; Jude emphasizes his pursuit of profit. Numbers 16 describes Korah and his companions rebelling against the authority God had given Moses and Aaron.

The pictures from nature expose danger and empty promises: hidden reefs, clouds without water, fruitless trees, shameful waves and wandering stars. The teachers share the community’s meals while caring for themselves. Belonging visibly to a gathering gives no assurance that a person is nourishing it.

Enoch’s prophecy announces judgment on ungodly deeds and words. Its wording also appears in 1 Enoch 1:9. Jude applies it to people whose grumbling, arrogance and flattery serve their own desires. The warning addresses both what they teach and how they live.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The received faith is central to the passage, though traditions differ over how it is preserved and interpreted. The Catholic Church teaches that the apostolic faith is entrusted to the church in Scripture and Tradition; see Catechism 84. The Reformed Westminster Confession 1.6 locates the necessary rule of faith and life in Scripture and what follows from it. Both claim continuity with the apostolic faith; they differ over the authority of received church teaching alongside Scripture.

The angels in verse 6 also receive different readings. Calvin and Wesley emphasize their abandonment of their original place and dignity. Calvin understands the chains as the misery that accompanies their fall, rather than confinement to one place. The USCCB note connects the verse with the heavenly beings and women in Genesis 6, and reads the strange flesh of verse 7 in relation to the angelic visitors at Sodom.

The glorious beings in verse 8 are understood as human rulers by Calvin, honored Christian ministers by Wesley, and angels in the USCCB note. Michael’s restraint stands against the offenders’ arrogance in these readings. The passage does not itself rank Michael below the devil or explain the reason for his restraint in terms of an angelic hierarchy.

Readers also differ over the wider book associated with Enoch’s prophecy. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church lists Enoch among its Scriptures. The Westminster Confession’s list in chapter 1 does not include it. Calvin favors a prophecy handed down orally; the USCCB note identifies a citation of the written book. These are distinct questions about the prophecy’s transmission and the status of the whole book. Jude uses the prophecy here to warn of God’s judgment.
passages.current_position_html: Our study The Berean Standard calls believers to examine teaching against Scripture, even when the speaker is respected. We apply that standard here by testing what is taught and taking seriously the conduct it encourages. The church’s responsibility is to hold faithfully to the truth it has received.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html: First Corinthians 10:1–13 explicitly connects Israel’s wilderness history with Christ and with warnings for the church. Paul identifies the spiritual rock as Christ and says that these events were written as examples for later believers. Jude’s examples serve that same purpose: God’s saving acts call for continuing trust and obedience, while the failures of earlier generations warn His people against turning privilege into presumption.

passages.title: Jude 1:17-23
passages.section_title: How do we stay faithful and help people who are being misled?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 But you, beloved, remember what was foretold by the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ 18 when they said to you, “In the last times there will be scoffers who will follow after their own ungodly desires.” 19 These are the ones who cause divisions, who are worldly and devoid of the Spirit. 20 But you, beloved, by building yourselves up in your most holy faith and praying in the Holy Spirit, 21 keep yourselves in the love of God as you await the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ to bring you eternal life. 22 And indeed, have mercy on those who doubt; 23 save others by snatching them from the fire; and to still others show mercy tempered with fear, hating even the clothing stained by the flesh.
paragraphs: 17 But you, beloved, remember what was foretold by the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ 18 when they said to you, “In the last times there will be scoffers who will follow after their own ungodly desires.” 19 These are the ones who cause divisions, who are worldly and devoid of the Spirit.

20 But you, beloved, by building yourselves up in your most holy faith and praying in the Holy Spirit, 21 keep yourselves in the love of God as you await the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ to bring you eternal life.
22 And indeed, have mercy on those who doubt; 23 save others by snatching them from the fire; and to still others show mercy tempered with fear, hating even the clothing stained by the flesh.

passages.context_html:
Jude turns from the conduct of the intruders to the response of his beloved readers. They should remember the apostles’ warnings about scoffers who follow ungodly desires. The divisive people he describes are worldly and lack the Spirit.

The positive response involves growing on the foundation of their holy faith, praying in the Holy Spirit, keeping themselves in God’s love and awaiting Christ’s mercy. The Father, the Spirit and Jesus Christ are named within a life of faith, prayer and hope.

The readers also have responsibilities toward people caught in danger. They should show mercy to those who doubt, rescue others and exercise care while helping those affected by sin. The call to hate even the stained clothing expresses a serious rejection of the corruption while mercy remains part of the response.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Calvin and Wesley understand praying in the Spirit as prayer enabled and guided by God’s Spirit. The Pentecostal Assemblies of God also includes prayer in tongues within this expression; its Baptism in the Holy Spirit position paper cites Jude 20 and describes a prayer language as one element of praying in the Spirit. That explanation includes a particular spiritual gift without equating the entire phrase only with that gift.

The wording and grouping of verses 22–23 differ among surviving texts, as the USCCB note explains. Calvin’s comments work with two groups and emphasize gentleness toward some and stronger correction for others. Wesley describes help suited to differing needs, with care against being drawn into sin. The BSB used here names mercy toward doubters, rescue from the fire and mercy tempered with fear. The shared concern is restoration with discernment.

section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html: Zechariah 3:1–5 gives a useful biblical parallel. Joshua the high priest is described as a firebrand rescued from the fire; his filthy clothes are removed as God takes away his iniquity. Jude’s pictures of rescue and stained clothing echo that combination of mercy and cleansing. This is a connection between the images, rather than an identification of every person in Jude with Joshua. God’s mercy rescues people from corruption and calls them out of it.

passages.title: Jude 1:24-25
passages.section_title: Who can bring God’s people into His presence with joy?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 24 Now to Him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you unblemished in His glorious presence, with great joy— 25 to the only God our Savior be glory, majesty, dominion, and authority through Jesus Christ our Lord before all time, and now, and for all eternity. Amen.
paragraphs: 24 Now to Him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you unblemished in His glorious presence, with great joy— 25 to the only God our Savior be glory, majesty, dominion, and authority through Jesus Christ our Lord before all time, and now, and for all eternity. Amen.

passages.context_html:
The letter ends in praise to the God who is able to keep His people from stumbling and present them unblemished in His glorious presence. After urging the readers to guard themselves and help others, Jude directs their confidence toward God’s power.

The praise is offered to the only God our Savior through Jesus Christ our Lord. Glory, majesty, dominion and authority belong to Him before all time, now and forever. The closing gathers the letter’s warnings and instructions into worshipful dependence on God.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Calvin emphasizes that the readers’ efforts depend on God’s power working with them. Wesley likewise identifies God as the one able to keep people from the errors and sins described and present them faultless. The USCCB note recognizes the return to the opening themes of divine care and preservation. These comments share the passage’s emphasis on God’s keeping power, without treating the call to vigilance earlier in the letter as unnecessary.
passages.current_position_html: Our studies Prayer and Faith and What Does Prayer Look Like? place trust in God at the center of prayer. The latter highlights Jesus’ prayer that the Father would keep His people and sanctify them in the truth. We read Jude’s closing praise in that same dependence: confidence rests in the God who keeps and brings His people into His presence.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html: Ephesians 5:25–27 describes Christ loving the church and giving Himself for her so that He may present her holy and without blemish. That passage gives a wider setting for Jude’s closing hope. God’s work reaches toward a people brought into His presence, with Christ’s self-giving love at the heart of that purpose.

passages.title: Revelation 1:1-3
passages.section_title: Why are we given the revelation of Jesus Christ?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 This is the revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave Him to show His servants what must soon come to pass. He made it known by sending His angel to His servant John, 2 who testifies to everything he saw. This is the word of God and the testimony of Jesus Christ. 3 Blessed is the one who reads aloud the words of this prophecy, and blessed are those who hear and obey what is written in it, because the time is near.
paragraphs: 1 This is the revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave Him to show His servants what must soon come to pass. He made it known by sending His angel to His servant John, 2 who testifies to everything he saw. This is the word of God and the testimony of Jesus Christ.
3 Blessed is the one who reads aloud the words of this prophecy, and blessed are those who hear and obey what is written in it, because the time is near.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The book begins by naming its source and purpose. God gives the revelation to Jesus Christ to show His servants what must soon take place. Jesus makes it known through His angel to John, who bears witness to what he saw.

The word translated revelation means an uncovering or disclosure. The opening presents something God makes known. It calls the readers and hearers to respond: the blessing is attached to hearing and obeying the prophecy, because the time is near.

The reference to one person reading aloud and others hearing fits a message received by a community. The book is meant to shape their faithfulness, rather than merely supply material for speculation.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Readings differ over how the promised events relate to history. Wesley understands their fulfillment as beginning soon after the book was given and extending toward the end of the world. The USCCB introduction emphasizes the message to first-century Christians facing pressure while also affirming its continuing hope for the church.

John Walvoord’s preface to his commentary presents a reading that places the great final conflict and victory in the future, while finding encouragement for earlier generations awaiting it. These examples show why readers can agree on Christ’s final victory while differing over which events had begun in John’s time and which remain ahead. They are particular explanations, rather than one uniform position shared by every Protestant or Catholic.
passages.god_plan_html: Ephesians 1:9–10 describes God making known His purpose to bring all things in heaven and on earth together in Christ. That gives a wider setting for this opening. The future God reveals belongs to His purpose centered on Christ, and is given to help His people live faithfully within that purpose.

passages.title: Revelation 1:4-8
passages.section_title: Who loves, frees and gathers God’s people?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 4 John, To the seven churches in the province of Asia: Grace and peace to you from Him who is and was and is to come, and from the seven spirits before His throne, 5 and from Jesus Christ, the faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead, and the ruler of the kings of the earth. To Him who loves us and has released us from our sins by His blood, 6 who has made us to be a kingdom, priests to His God and Father—to Him be the glory and power forever and ever! Amen. 7 Behold, He is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see Him—even those who pierced Him. And all the tribes of the earth will mourn because of Him. So shall it be! Amen. 8 “I am the Alpha and the Omega,” says the Lord God, who is and was and is to come—the Almighty.
paragraphs: 4 John, To the seven churches in the province of Asia: Grace and peace to you from Him who is and was and is to come, and from the seven spirits before His throne, 5 and from Jesus Christ, the faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead, and the ruler of the kings of the earth. To Him who loves us and has released us from our sins by His blood, 6 who has made us to be a kingdom, priests to His God and Father—to Him be the glory and power forever and ever! Amen.

7 Behold, He is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see Him—even those who pierced Him. And all the tribes of the earth will mourn because of Him. So shall it be! Amen. 8 “I am the Alpha and the Omega,” says the Lord God, who is and was and is to come—the Almighty.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
John addresses seven churches in the province of Asia. The greeting brings grace and peace from the eternal God, the seven spirits before His throne and Jesus Christ. The seven churches are named later in verse 11.

Jesus is called the faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead and the ruler of the earth’s kings. The praise then names what He has done for His people: He loves them, has released them from sin through His blood and has made them a kingdom of priests to God.

The announcement of His coming reaches every eye, including those who pierced Him. The Lord God identifies Himself as the Alpha and the Omega—the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet—and as the Almighty who is, was and is to come.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands the seven spirits as the one Holy Spirit in the fullness of His work. He takes seven as expressing completeness here, rather than seven separate divine spirits. He also understands Christ’s people as sharing in His kingdom and offering themselves to God as priests.

The Catholic Church likewise affirms the priesthood of the whole believing community in Catechism 1546–1547, while distinguishing that shared calling from its ordained ministry. The text’s language of a kingdom and priests therefore should not be presented as something the Catholic Church simply denies. Traditions differ over ordained ministry while recognizing that Christ gives His people a shared calling.
passages.god_plan_html: The coming with clouds recalls the Son of Man receiving an everlasting kingdom in Daniel 7:9–14. The mourning over the pierced one recalls Zechariah 12:10–14, language also applied to Jesus’ crucifixion in John 19:31–37. Revelation brings these biblical threads together around Jesus: the One who was pierced is the One whose coming and kingship concern the whole earth.
passages.current_position_html: Our studies Returning to the Word and The True Church According to Jesus identify the priesthood of believers as the calling of all Christ’s people. We read the kingdom and priests language here in line with that understanding: those He has redeemed share responsibility to serve God, rather than leaving the whole work of ministry to a separate group.

deeper_study.title: The True Church According to Jesus

passages.title: Revelation 1:9-11
passages.section_title: Who receives this vision, and who needs to hear it?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 I, John, your brother and partner in the tribulation and kingdom and perseverance that are in Jesus, was on the island of Patmos because of the word of God and my testimony about Jesus. 10 On the Lord’s day I was in the Spirit, and I heard behind me a loud voice like a trumpet, 11 saying, “Write on a scroll what you see and send it to the seven churches: to Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea.”
paragraphs: 9 I, John, your brother and partner in the tribulation and kingdom and perseverance that are in Jesus, was on the island of Patmos because of the word of God and my testimony about Jesus. 10 On the Lord’s day I was in the Spirit, and I heard behind me a loud voice like a trumpet, 11 saying, “Write on a scroll what you see and send it to the seven churches: to Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
John identifies himself as a brother and partner with his readers in the tribulation, kingdom and perseverance found in Jesus. He is on Patmos because of God’s word and his testimony about Jesus. His introduction joins him to the people who will hear the message.

On the Lord’s day, while in the Spirit, he hears a voice like a trumpet. The command is to write what he sees on a scroll and send it to seven named churches. The revelation is given to be shared with communities, rather than kept as a private experience.

The seven destinations are Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia and Laodicea. The instruction prepares for the messages to those churches in the following chapters.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and the USCCB note understand the Lord’s day as Sunday, connected with Christ’s resurrection. The Greek adjective means belonging to the Lord; its form does not itself mean an unusually spiritual day.

Both sources recognize John as receiving a vision for the churches. John names himself and describes his circumstances here, while the identification with the apostle and the precise date involve historical questions beyond these verses. The tribulation he shares with the churches is already part of their experience; this sentence does not itself supply a timetable for the final events.

passages.title: Revelation 1:12-20
passages.section_title: What does the risen Christ reveal about His care and authority?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 Then I turned to see the voice that was speaking with me. And having turned, I saw seven golden lampstands, 13 and among the lampstands was One like the Son of Man, dressed in a long robe, with a golden sash around His chest. 14 The hair of His head was white like wool, as white as snow, and His eyes were like a blazing fire. 15 His feet were like polished bronze refined in a furnace, and His voice was like the roar of many waters. 16 He held in His right hand seven stars, and a sharp double-edged sword came from His mouth. His face was like the sun shining at its brightest. 17 When I saw Him, I fell at His feet like a dead man. But He placed His right hand on me and said, “Do not be afraid. I am the First and the Last, 18 the Living One. I was dead, and behold, now I am alive forever and ever! And I hold the keys of Death and of Hades. 19 Therefore write down the things you have seen, the things that are, and the things that will happen after this. 20 This is the mystery of the seven stars you saw in My right hand and of the seven golden lampstands: The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches, and the seven lampstands are the seven churches.

And having turned, I saw seven golden lampstands, 13 and among the lampstands was One like the Son of Man, dressed in a long robe, with a golden sash around His chest. 14 The hair of His head was white like wool, as white as snow, and His eyes were like a blazing fire. 15 His feet were like polished bronze refined in a furnace, and His voice was like the roar of many waters. 16 He held in His right hand seven stars, and a sharp double-edged sword came from His mouth. His face was like the sun shining at its brightest.

17 When I saw Him, I fell at His feet like a dead man. But He placed His right hand on me and said, “Do not be afraid. I am the First and the Last, 18 the Living One. I was dead, and behold, now I am alive forever and ever! And I hold the keys of Death and of Hades.

19 Therefore write down the things you have seen, the things that are, and the things that will happen after this. 20 This is the mystery of the seven stars you saw in My right hand and of the seven golden lampstands: The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches, and the seven lampstands are the seven churches.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
John turns and sees seven golden lampstands and One like the Son of Man among them. The robe, golden sash, white hair, fiery eyes, bronze-like feet and powerful voice present a vision of majesty and authority.

The language recalls earlier visions. Daniel 7:9–14 describes the Ancient of Days with white hair and the Son of Man receiving dominion. Daniel 10:4–12 includes a golden belt, fiery eyes, shining limbs and an overwhelming voice. These are connections between the descriptions; they do not require every detail in the two earlier visions to have one identical meaning.

John falls as though dead, but the speaker touches him and tells him not to fear. He identifies Himself as the First and the Last, the Living One who died and now lives forever. His authority extends to Death and Hades, the realm of the dead.

He commands John to write, then explains two features of the vision: the stars are the angels of the seven churches and the lampstands are the churches themselves. The opening vision therefore places the living Christ among His churches and shows them held within His care and authority.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and the USCCB notes read the description as a portrayal of Christ’s divine majesty, with royal and priestly features. Wesley explicitly distinguishes the vision’s symbolic appearance from a complete description of how Christ appears in heaven. Both find reassurance in His victory over death.

The angels of the churches receive different explanations. Wesley understands each as the church’s pastor or ruling minister. The USCCB note favors heavenly spirits connected with the churches, while also recording the possibilities of a pastor or a symbol for the congregation itself. Verse 20 identifies the stars as angels, but does not itself explain which of those senses is intended.
passages.god_plan_html: Hebrews 2:14–18 explains that Christ shared human life and passed through death to free people from slavery to its fear. The One who tells John not to fear is that same crucified and living Savior. His majesty and His care belong together: His victory over death serves the people He came to save.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Revelation 2:1-7
passages.section_title: Can a church defend the truth and still lose its first love?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 “To the angel of the church in Ephesus write: These are the words of Him who holds the seven stars in His right hand and walks among the seven golden lampstands. 2 I know your deeds, your labor, and your perseverance. I know that you cannot tolerate those who are evil, and you have tested and exposed as liars those who falsely claim to be apostles. 3 Without growing weary, you have persevered and endured many things for the sake of My name. 4 But I have this against you: You have abandoned your first love. 5 Therefore, keep in mind how far you have fallen. Repent and perform the deeds you did at first. But if you do not repent, I will come to you and remove your lampstand from its place. 6 But you have this to your credit: You hate the works of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate. 7 He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. To the one who overcomes, I will grant the right to eat from the tree of life in the Paradise of God.
paragraphs: 1 “To the angel of the church in Ephesus write: These are the words of Him who holds the seven stars in His right hand and walks among the seven golden lampstands. 2 I know your deeds, your labor, and your perseverance. I know that you cannot tolerate those who are evil, and you have tested and exposed as liars those who falsely claim to be apostles. 3 Without growing weary, you have persevered and endured many things for the sake of My name.

4 But I have this against you: You have abandoned your first love. 5 Therefore, keep in mind how far you have fallen. Repent and perform the deeds you did at first. But if you do not repent, I will come to you and remove your lampstand from its place. 6 But you have this to your credit: You hate the works of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate.
7 He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. To the one who overcomes, I will grant the right to eat from the tree of life in the Paradise of God.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Ephesus was a Roman port city with a renowned sanctuary of Artemis; see UNESCO’s account of the archaeological site. Acts 19:8–12, 23–41 records Paul’s ministry there and the conflict stirred by tradesmen whose livelihood depended on Artemis worship.

Jesus addresses the church as the One who holds the stars and walks among the lampstands. He knows its labor, perseverance and testing of people who falsely claim to be apostles. Its refusal to accept evil and its endurance for His name receive real praise.

His complaint concerns its abandoned first love. He calls for remembrance, repentance and a return to the deeds done at first. The warning about removing the lampstand concerns the church’s place as His witness. The letter does not report how this community later responded.

Jesus also commends its rejection of the Nicolaitans’ works. The group appears again in Revelation 2:14–15, beside the warning about idolatry and sexual immorality. The appeal then reaches everyone able to hear what the Spirit says to the churches, with a promise of the tree of life to the one who overcomes.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands the first love as the warmth and vigor of love the church had earlier. John Gill explicitly includes love for God, Christ and one another. Both see the remedy as a real return to faithful action, rather than simply remembering an earlier feeling.

Readings differ over whether the seven churches also represent successive periods of history. Gill reads Ephesus as representing the apostolic age. Wesley explicitly rejects a sequence of ages and understands the seven churches as examples of conditions found throughout the church in every age. The direct address to the historic church and its continuing relevance are recognized in both readings.

The Nicolaitans’ precise identity is uncertain. Wesley suggests a connection with Nicolas in Acts 6:5; the USCCB note cautions that there is little evidence for that connection. The letter gives little detail about the group’s origins.

Gill understands the tree of life as a picture of Christ giving life to His people. Wesley emphasizes its promise of eternal life with God. These explanations share the hope of life given by Christ, while explaining the picture in different ways.
passages.god_plan_html: The tree of life appears in Genesis 2:8–9, with access to it barred after human rebellion in Genesis 3:22–24. In Revelation 22:1–5, it appears again beside the river from God’s throne, where the curse is gone and His servants see His face. Christ’s promise to Ephesus belongs to that larger hope: the life with God lost through sin is the life He holds out to His people.
passages.current_position_html: Our study The True Church According to Jesus places Christ at the foundation of the church and identifies self-giving love as the mark of His people. Alongside the call in The Berean Standard to test teaching against Scripture, this gives us the pattern for reading Ephesus: care for truth and lived love belong together in following Christ.

passages.title: Revelation 2:8-11
passages.section_title: What hope does Jesus give a church facing death?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 To the angel of the church in Smyrna write: These are the words of the First and the Last, who died and returned to life. 9 I know your affliction and your poverty—though you are rich! And I am aware of the slander of those who falsely claim to be Jews, but are in fact a synagogue of Satan. 10 Do not fear what you are about to suffer. Behold, the devil is about to throw some of you into prison to test you, and you will suffer tribulation for ten days. Be faithful even unto death, and I will give you the crown of life. 11 He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. The one who overcomes will not be harmed by the second death.
paragraphs: 8 To the angel of the church in Smyrna write: These are the words of the First and the Last, who died and returned to life. 9 I know your affliction and your poverty—though you are rich! And I am aware of the slander of those who falsely claim to be Jews, but are in fact a synagogue of Satan.

10 Do not fear what you are about to suffer. Behold, the devil is about to throw some of you into prison to test you, and you will suffer tribulation for ten days. Be faithful even unto death, and I will give you the crown of life. 11 He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. The one who overcomes will not be harmed by the second death.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Smyrna receives encouragement in suffering. Jesus introduces Himself as the One who died and returned to life. That matters for people facing prison and possible death: the One speaking to them has already passed through death and lives.

He knows their affliction, poverty and the slander directed against them, yet calls them rich. The contrast shows that their circumstances do not tell the whole story of their standing before Him. The letter contains no rebuke of this church.

The warning is specific: some will be imprisoned, their faith will be tested, and their suffering will last ten days. Jesus calls them to remain faithful even when doing so costs their lives. He promises the crown of life and protection from the second death. The comfort rests on His life and promise; He does not promise to prevent every imprisonment or execution.

The severe language in verse 9 concerns the people slandering this community. It should be read within that accusation, without turning it into a description of every Jewish person.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings broadly recognize this as encouragement to remain faithful under persecution. Differences concern particular details. Wesley takes the ten days literally, as a brief persecution of this community. John Gill also considers a wider historical reading: ten Roman persecutions, or ten years of persecution represented by ten days. Those are different explanations of the number, rather than dates supplied by the letter itself.

The identity of the slanderers is also read differently. The USCCB notes identify Jewish opponents of the local Christians. Gill understands people falsely claiming to be God’s people while professing Christianity. Neither identification gives grounds for assigning the letter’s accusation to an entire people across history.

Wesley describes the crown of life as a particular reward for faithfulness unto death. Gill includes eternal life itself in the promise. The Greek word for crown, stephanos, can describe a victor’s wreath, but its range also includes honor and royal rank. Thayer’s entry reads this phrase as life given as a crown. The word alone does not settle every question about salvation and rewards.
passages.god_plan_html: The promise reaches beyond whether the Christians survive the coming trial. In Revelation 20:4–6, 11–15, those who belong to Christ share His life, while the second death is identified as the lake of fire. The risen Jesus can therefore offer hope that execution cannot take away. This passage connects the costly faithfulness of a small, suffering church with God’s final defeat of death and judgment of evil.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Revelation 2:12-17
passages.section_title: Can a church stand firm under pressure and still accept harmful teaching?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 To the angel of the church in Pergamum write: These are the words of the One who holds the sharp, double-edged sword. 13 I know where you live, where the throne of Satan sits, yet you hold fast to My name. You did not deny your faith in Me, even in the days of My faithful witness Antipas, who was killed among you where Satan dwells. 14 But I have a few things against you, because some of you hold to the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to place a stumbling block before the Israelites so they would eat food sacrificed to idols and commit sexual immorality. 15 In the same way, some of you also hold to the teaching of the Nicolaitans. 16 Therefore repent! Otherwise I will come to you shortly and wage war against them with the sword of My mouth. 17 He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. To the one who overcomes, I will give the hidden manna. I will also give him a white stone inscribed with a new name, known only to the one who receives it.
paragraphs: 12 To the angel of the church in Pergamum write: These are the words of the One who holds the sharp, double-edged sword. 13 I know where you live, where the throne of Satan sits, yet you hold fast to My name. You did not deny your faith in Me, even in the days of My faithful witness Antipas, who was killed among you where Satan dwells.

14 But I have a few things against you, because some of you hold to the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to place a stumbling block before the Israelites so they would eat food sacrificed to idols and commit sexual immorality. 15 In the same way, some of you also hold to the teaching of the Nicolaitans. 16 Therefore repent! Otherwise I will come to you shortly and wage war against them with the sword of My mouth.

17 He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. To the one who overcomes, I will give the hidden manna. I will also give him a white stone inscribed with a new name, known only to the one who receives it.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus addresses Pergamum as the One with the sharp, double-edged sword. The image comes from Revelation 1:16 and returns in the warning that He will confront the false teachers with the sword of His mouth. He has authority to judge the teaching and conduct of His church.

The church has remained loyal to His name, even when His witness Antipas was killed among them. The letter describes their surroundings as the place of Satan’s throne, but does not identify a particular building or explain how Antipas died.

The same church nevertheless tolerates teaching compared with Balaam’s. Numbers 25:1–3 describes Israel joining in idolatrous meals and sexual immorality; Numbers 31:16 connects that unfaithfulness with Balaam’s counsel. Jesus says a similar trap is being set here. The warning about the Nicolaitans follows alongside it.

The call to repent addresses the church, while the threatened confrontation falls on those promoting the corrupt teaching. Courage against outside pressure does not excuse accepting corruption within. The promise of hidden manna, a white stone and a new name gives those who overcome something better than participation in the practices Jesus condemns.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill both connect the warning with Balaam’s influence on Israel and read the call to repentance seriously. Their wider settings differ: Wesley reads the local church’s correction, while Gill also applies Pergamum to the church’s growing worldly power after Constantine. That historical application is Gill’s reading, rather than an explanation shared by all Protestant churches.

The white stone has several explanations. Wesley suggests acquittal: a favorable verdict pictured by a white voting stone. Gill discusses that reading but favors an association with priestly acceptance and the stones connected with Israel’s high priest. The USCCB note suggests a name-bearing amulet, used here to picture victory and joy. These are proposals about the image’s background; the letter itself does not explain the custom.

The Greek word psephos means a small, smooth stone or pebble. Thayer’s entry records its use in voting and discusses the acquittal explanation, while acknowledging disagreement. A proposed ancient custom should help explain the promise without being treated as something John explicitly states. The giver, the new name and the personal nature of the gift are clear in the passage.
passages.god_plan_html: The manna recalls God feeding Israel in the wilderness and commanding that some be preserved for later generations; see Exodus 16:31–35. Jesus takes up that history in John 6:30–35, directing people to the Father’s gift of true bread from heaven and identifying Himself as the bread of life. This is a scriptural parallel that helps explain the promise: God provides lasting life for His people. Against the pressure to seek satisfaction at an idol’s table, Christ holds out provision that belongs to Him.
passages.current_position_html: Our study The Berean Standard calls for teaching to be tested against Scripture, even when the speaker has a respected name. That principle applies to Pergamum’s warning: loyalty to Christ includes examining what a church accepts and teaches. The church’s courageous witness does not remove that responsibility.

passages.title: Revelation 2:18-29
passages.section_title: What does Jesus see when good works and false teaching exist together?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 To the angel of the church in Thyatira write: These are the words of the Son of God, whose eyes are like a blazing fire and whose feet are like polished bronze. 19 I know your deeds—your love, your faith, your service, your perseverance—and your latest deeds are greater than your first. 20 But I have this against you: You tolerate that woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess. By her teaching she misleads My servants to be sexually immoral and to eat food sacrificed to idols. 21 Even though I have given her time to repent of her immorality, she is unwilling. 22 Behold, I will cast her onto a bed of sickness, and those who commit adultery with her will suffer great tribulation unless they repent of her deeds. 23 Then I will strike her children dead, and all the churches will know that I am the One who searches minds and hearts, and I will repay each of you according to your deeds. 24 But I say to the rest of you in Thyatira, who do not hold to her teaching and have not learned the so-called deep things of Satan: I will place no further burden upon you 25 than to hold fast to what you have until I come. 26 And to the one who overcomes and continues in My work until the end, I will give authority over the nations. 27 He will rule them with an iron scepter and shatter them like pottery —just as I have received authority from My Father. 28 And I will give him the morning star. 29 He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.

20 But I have this against you: You tolerate that woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess. By her teaching she misleads My servants to be sexually immoral and to eat food sacrificed to idols. 21 Even though I have given her time to repent of her immorality, she is unwilling. 22 Behold, I will cast her onto a bed of sickness, and those who commit adultery with her will suffer great tribulation unless they repent of her deeds. 23 Then I will strike her children dead, and all the churches will know that I am the One who searches minds and hearts, and I will repay each of you according to your deeds.

24 But I say to the rest of you in Thyatira, who do not hold to her teaching and have not learned the so-called deep things of Satan: I will place no further burden upon you 25 than to hold fast to what you have until I come.

26 And to the one who overcomes and continues in My work until the end, I will give authority over the nations. 27 He will rule them with an iron scepter and shatter them like pottery —just as I have received authority from My Father. 28 And I will give him the morning star. 29 He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus addresses Thyatira as the Son of God, with eyes like blazing fire and feet like polished bronze. As the letter unfolds, He says that He searches minds and hearts. His knowledge reaches beneath a church’s appearance and reputation.

This church receives genuine praise for love, faith, service and perseverance. Its later deeds exceed its earlier ones. Yet it tolerates a woman called Jezebel, who claims to speak for God and leads Christ’s servants into sexual immorality and eating food sacrificed to idols. The name recalls Ahab’s wife, whose influence led him further into idolatry; see 1 Kings 16:29–33 and 21:25–26.

Jesus has given her time to repent, but she refuses. He announces severe judgment on her and on those who continue in her deeds, while still calling her followers to repentance. This is a specific warning from Christ; the letter does not tell us the later events by which it was carried out.

He also distinguishes the people who have rejected her teaching. They are to hold fast until He comes. The promise then looks beyond the present struggle: the one who overcomes and continues in His work will share authority over the nations and receive the morning star. Good works, truthful teaching and continuing faithfulness all matter in His assessment.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Interpretations differ over the reach of the name Jezebel. Wesley understands a woman deceiving the church in Thyatira, named for her resemblance to the Old Testament queen. Gill also reads her as a picture of the Roman Catholic Church within his account of successive church ages. This is an identification made by Gill; Revelation does not name that later institution in this letter. Wesley explicitly rejects reading the seven churches as a sequence of historical ages.

Wesley and Gill both understand the bed as an image of affliction, but their wider applications differ with their identification of the woman. Her children can be understood as followers shaped by her teaching; Wesley also allows her actual children. The letter’s distinction between her adherents and those who rejected her teaching should remain visible in either reading.

The promise of authority is also explained differently. Wesley emphasizes sharing in Christ’s victory over the nations. Gill includes the spread of the gospel and the defeat of opposition through the Reformation and beyond. Both identify the morning star with Christ. These teachers share confidence in His final victory while proposing different ways the promised rule unfolds.
passages.god_plan_html:
The promise of an iron scepter and shattered pottery directly takes up Psalm 2:7–9, where God gives the nations to His Son. Jesus says that He shares authority received from His Father with the one who overcomes and continues in His work. The future of His people is bound to His own victory.

The morning star becomes clearer when Jesus identifies Himself that way in Revelation 22:16. The hope offered here includes Christ Himself. The warning also echoes Jeremiah 17:9–10: God searches the heart and judges deeds. Together these connections show that hidden corruption will not escape His judgment, and that present faithfulness belongs within His larger purpose to establish His Son’s rule.
