passages.title: Revelation 3:1-6
passages.section_title: What if a church looks alive but Jesus says it is dead?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 “To the angel of the church in Sardis write: These are the words of the One who holds the seven spirits of God and the seven stars. I know your deeds; you have a reputation for being alive, yet you are dead. 2 Wake up and strengthen what remains, which is about to die; for I have found your deeds incomplete in the sight of My God. 3 Remember, then, what you have received and heard. Keep it and repent. If you do not wake up, I will come like a thief, and you will not know the hour when I will come upon you. 4 But you do have a few people in Sardis who have not soiled their garments, and because they are worthy, they will walk with Me in white. 5 Like them, he who overcomes will be dressed in white. And I will never blot out his name from the Book of Life, but I will confess his name before My Father and His angels. 6 He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.
paragraphs: 1 “To the angel of the church in Sardis write: These are the words of the One who holds the seven spirits of God and the seven stars. I know your deeds; you have a reputation for being alive, yet you are dead. 2 Wake up and strengthen what remains, which is about to die; for I have found your deeds incomplete in the sight of My God. 3 Remember, then, what you have received and heard. Keep it and repent. If you do not wake up, I will come like a thief, and you will not know the hour when I will come upon you.

4 But you do have a few people in Sardis who have not soiled their garments, and because they are worthy, they will walk with Me in white. 5 Like them, he who overcomes will be dressed in white. And I will never blot out his name from the Book of Life, but I will confess his name before My Father and His angels. 6 He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Sardis has a reputation for life, but Jesus sees a different reality. He holds the seven spirits of God and the seven stars, images already introduced in chapter 1. The church’s reputation cannot substitute for His assessment of its deeds.

His instructions give a way forward: wake up, strengthen what remains, remember what they received and heard, keep it, and repent. Something remains that can be strengthened, but the danger is urgent. If they ignore Him, His coming upon them will be as unexpected as a thief.

Jesus distinguishes a few who have not soiled their garments. Their faithfulness is known to Him even within this failing church. They will walk with Him in white. The one who overcomes receives the promises of white clothing, a name retained in the Book of Life, and Christ’s acknowledgment before His Father and the angels.

The letter holds warning and encouragement together. It calls a complacent community to repentance while giving faithful people reason to continue. It does not report the church’s later response.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill both see a contrast between outward reputation and spiritual reality. Wesley understands the remaining things as knowledge, desires and convictions that need strengthening. Gill includes gospel truths and struggling members, while denying that God’s saving work itself can die. Both call for an active response to Christ’s warning.

They differ over the promise about the Book of Life. Gill connects the book with God’s certain choice of His people and says their names can never be erased. Wesley treats the promise as belonging to those who overcome and contrasts it with the failing leader at Sardis. These readings reflect a wider difference over whether a believer can finally fall away. The promise to the one who overcomes should be heard alongside the call to repent in either reading.

Gill also applies Sardis to the churches of the Reformation and their later decline. Wesley reads the seven churches as conditions found across ages, without assigning each one a successive historical period. Those applications should be distinguished from what the letter directly says to Sardis.
passages.god_plan_html: Christ’s promise to acknowledge the faithful before His Father echoes His teaching in Matthew 10:32–33. The Book of Life appears again in Revelation 21:22–27, where it identifies those admitted to the holy city. Sardis therefore brings a church’s present response into view against its ultimate hope: being known by Christ and sharing life in God’s presence. A public reputation is temporary; His acknowledgment reaches into that lasting future.
passages.current_position_html: Our study I Am a Disciple describes following Jesus as a life shaped by His teaching, conduct and self-giving love. That gives us a direct point of application here: the name or appearance of discipleship must be accompanied by actually following Him.

deeper_study.title: The True Church According to Jesus

passages.title: Revelation 3:7-13
passages.section_title: What can a church with little strength expect from Christ?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 To the angel of the church in Philadelphia write: These are the words of the One who is holy and true, who holds the key of David. What He opens no one can shut, and what He shuts no one can open. 8 I know your deeds. Behold, I have placed before you an open door, which no one can shut. I know that you have only a little strength, yet you have kept My word and have not denied My name. 9 As for those who belong to the synagogue of Satan, who claim to be Jews but are liars instead, I will make them come and bow down at your feet, and they will know that I love you. 10 Because you have kept My command to persevere, I will also keep you from the hour of testing that is about to come upon the whole world, to test those who dwell on the earth. 11 I am coming soon. Upon him I will write the name of My God, and the name of the city of My God (the new Jerusalem that comes down out of heaven from My God), and My new name. 13 He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Philadelphia receives encouragement from the One who is holy and true and holds the key of David. The language recalls Isaiah 22:20–22, where Eliakim receives authority over David’s house. Here Jesus has authority that no opponent can overturn: what He opens stays open, and what He shuts stays shut.

The church has little strength, yet has kept His word and remained loyal to His name. Its limited strength does not prevent Him from placing an open door before it. He promises that the opponents described in verse 9 will come to recognize His love for this community. The accusation concerns those opponents, without making every Jewish person its target.

Jesus also promises protection from an approaching hour of testing and calls the church to hold fast so no one takes its crown. The promise encourages continued faithfulness. It does not make the need to persevere disappear.

The final images emphasize belonging and permanence: a pillar that remains in God’s temple, God’s name, the name of the new Jerusalem, and Christ’s new name. The church’s future rests on the authority and love of the One addressing it.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The open door is commonly connected with access granted by Christ. Wesley includes both entrance into the Lord’s joy and opportunity for faithful work. Gill emphasizes opportunity to proclaim the gospel. The image can carry more than one closely related application without reducing Christ’s authority to a technique for getting the results someone wants.

The hour of testing receives substantially different explanations. Wesley connects it with persecution under Trajan within the Roman Empire. Gill places it in a later conflict affecting the churches and describes Christ preserving His people amid the distress. John Walvoord’s own commentary, representing a reading in which Christ gathers the church before a future worldwide tribulation, understands it as deliverance from that period. This is a real difference over the setting and manner of protection, not a teaching on which every church agrees.

The Greek verb tereo means to guard or keep. Thayer’s entry places this promise alongside John 17:15, where Jesus asks that His people be kept from evil while remaining in the world. The word supports the promise of protection; deciding exactly how that protection happens requires the passage’s wider context. A word definition alone does not establish an entire end-times timetable.
passages.god_plan_html:
The key from David’s house in Isaiah becomes part of the picture of Christ’s authority over His people. The destination named in the promise is the new Jerusalem. In Revelation 21:1–4, that city descends from God, and God dwells with His people as death and mourning pass away.

The pillar and written names express a lasting place with God. Revelation later says that God and the Lamb themselves are the city’s temple; see 21:22–27. These pictures carry the hope beyond a fragile community’s present security to life permanently shared with Him. They do not require us to settle every disputed detail about the intervening trial.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Revelation 3:14-22
passages.section_title: What if we think we need nothing, but Christ sees our need?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 To the angel of the church in Laodicea write: These are the words of the Amen, the faithful and true Witness, the Originator of God’s creation. 15 I know your deeds; you are neither cold nor hot. How I wish you were one or the other! 16 So because you are lukewarm—neither hot nor cold—I am about to vomit you out of My mouth! 17 You say, ‘I am rich; I have grown wealthy and need nothing.’ But you do not realize that you are wretched, pitiful, poor, blind, and naked. 18 I counsel you to buy from Me gold refined by fire so that you may become rich, white garments so that you may be clothed and your shameful nakedness not exposed, and salve to anoint your eyes so that you may see. 19 Those I love I rebuke and discipline. Therefore be earnest and repent. 20 Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears My voice and opens the door, I will come in and dine with him, and he with Me. 21 To the one who overcomes, I will grant the right to sit with Me on My throne, just as I overcame and sat down with My Father on His throne. 22 He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.”
paragraphs: 14 To the angel of the church in Laodicea write: These are the words of the Amen, the faithful and true Witness, the Originator of God’s creation. 15 I know your deeds; you are neither cold nor hot. How I wish you were one or the other! 16 So because you are lukewarm—neither hot nor cold—I am about to vomit you out of My mouth!

17 You say, ‘I am rich; I have grown wealthy and need nothing.’ But you do not realize that you are wretched, pitiful, poor, blind, and naked. 18 I counsel you to buy from Me gold refined by fire so that you may become rich, white garments so that you may be clothed and your shameful nakedness not exposed, and salve to anoint your eyes so that you may see. 19 Those I love I rebuke and discipline. Therefore be earnest and repent.

20 Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears My voice and opens the door, I will come in and dine with him, and he with Me. 21 To the one who overcomes, I will grant the right to sit with Me on My throne, just as I overcame and sat down with My Father on His throne. 22 He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Laodicea receives a searching correction from Jesus, the faithful and true Witness and the Originator of God’s creation. His truthful assessment stands against the church’s confidence that it is wealthy and needs nothing.

The picture of lukewarmness expresses His rejection of its present condition. He describes a community that does not recognize its own poverty, blindness and nakedness. Its own account of success has left it unable to see what He sees.

The remedies come from Him: refined gold, white clothing and salve for the eyes. These pictures answer the needs He has just named. He then explains that His rebuke and discipline come from love, and calls for earnest repentance. The warning is severe, but the invitation remains open.

Jesus stands at the door and knocks, offering a shared meal to the person who hears and opens. The letter is addressed to a church and reaches each hearer within it. It closes with the promise of sharing His throne, just as He overcame and sat down with His Father. The final appeal again asks everyone able to hear to listen to the Spirit’s message.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill understand lukewarmness as a complacent profession of faith lacking warmth and commitment. They explain the preference for cold or hot comparatively: open indifference is more readily recognized than self-satisfied religion. Gill nevertheless allows that members possess spiritual life while lacking fervor. The description does not produce a unanimous conclusion about every member’s salvation.

The clothing and meal receive different emphases. Wesley explains the white garments as true holiness and the supper as Christ sharing His grace now and life with Him eternally. Gill favors Christ’s righteousness as the clothing and reads the supper especially in connection with His return and the kingdom. Both direct the hearer toward receiving from Christ what self-sufficiency cannot supply.

Wesley and Gill also understand Jesus as the source and author of creation. The Greek arche can mean beginning, origin or rule; Thayer’s entry places Revelation 3:14 under origin or active cause. That supports the BSB’s wording, Originator. The same connection with creation through the Word appears in John 1:1–3.
passages.god_plan_html:
The purpose of loving discipline appears elsewhere in Scripture. Hebrews 12:5–11 describes God correcting His children for their good, so they may share His holiness. Laodicea’s correction belongs within that larger pattern of love calling people away from a destructive course.

The meal and throne also recall Jesus’ promise to His disciples in Luke 22:28–30: sharing His table and kingdom after standing with Him through trials. This is a scriptural parallel, not a claim that the two passages describe every detail in the same way. Christ’s purpose reaches beyond exposing the church’s failure to bringing those who respond into fellowship with Him and participation in His victory.

passages.title: Revelation 4:1-6
passages.section_title: What does John see when heaven is opened to him?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 After this I looked and saw a door standing open in heaven. And the voice I had previously heard speak to me like a trumpet was saying, “Come up here, and I will show you what must happen after these things.” 2 At once I was in the Spirit, and I saw a throne standing in heaven, with someone seated on it. 3 The One seated there looked like jasper and carnelian, and a rainbow that gleamed like an emerald encircled the throne. 4 Surrounding the throne were twenty-four other thrones, and on these thrones sat twenty-four elders dressed in white, with golden crowns on their heads. 5 From the throne came flashes of lightning, rumblings, and peals of thunder. Before the throne burned seven torches of fire. These are the seven spirits of God. 6 And before the throne was something like a sea of glass, as clear as crystal. In the center, around the throne, were four living creatures, covered with eyes in front and back.
paragraphs: 1 After this I looked and saw a door standing open in heaven. And the voice I had previously heard speak to me like a trumpet was saying, “Come up here, and I will show you what must happen after these things.” 2 At once I was in the Spirit, and I saw a throne standing in heaven, with someone seated on it. 3 The One seated there looked like jasper and carnelian, and a rainbow that gleamed like an emerald encircled the throne.

4 Surrounding the throne were twenty-four other thrones, and on these thrones sat twenty-four elders dressed in white, with golden crowns on their heads. 5 From the throne came flashes of lightning, rumblings, and peals of thunder. Before the throne burned seven torches of fire. These are the seven spirits of God. 6 And before the throne was something like a sea of glass, as clear as crystal. In the center, around the throne, were four living creatures, covered with eyes in front and back.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the letters to the seven churches, John sees an open door in heaven. The voice he heard before, compared with a trumpet, calls him to come and see what must happen next. He immediately describes himself as being in the Spirit. The vision moves from the churches’ circumstances to the throne at the center of heaven’s court.

John describes the One seated there through the brilliance of precious stones and an emerald-like rainbow. The comparisons convey overwhelming glory. He then describes twenty-four elders on surrounding thrones, dressed in white and wearing gold crowns.

Lightning, rumblings and thunder come from the throne. Seven burning torches stand before it, identified as the seven spirits of God. Something like a clear sea of glass lies before the throne, and four living creatures appear around it. Their description and worship continue in the following verses.

The scene recalls earlier visions of God’s glory. Ezekiel 1:22–28 includes a crystal-like expanse, a throne, radiant light and a rainbow. The thunder and lightning also recall God’s appearance at Sinai in Exodus 19:16–20. These connections help us recognize the majesty of the One John sees before trying to assign a separate meaning to every detail.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings broadly recognize a vision of God’s authority and glory. They differ over how its details relate to the church and the events that follow. Wesley understands John’s ascent as an experience in the Spirit. John Walvoord places the scene after Christ gathers the church to heaven, but explicitly says the invitation to John is not itself a direct description of that event. The words address John; their connection with a timetable for the whole church is an interpretation.

The elders receive several explanations. Wesley sees representatives of the saints and also considers an association with the Jewish people of God. Gill favors the whole gospel church, linking twenty-four with the priestly divisions. The USCCB notes understand the number as the twelve tribes together with the twelve apostles. These readings agree on the importance of God’s people while differing over precisely whom the elders represent.

The seven spirits are also understood differently. Wesley and Gill read them as the Holy Spirit in the fullness of His work. The USCCB notes identify seven angels attending God. The torches are expressly identified with the seven spirits in the passage, but the text does not go on to explain that phrase in the same detail.

The sea of glass has several proposed meanings. Wesley considers the life-giving work of the Spirit; Gill favors the gospel’s clarity and peace. The USCCB notes connect the image with the crystal-like expanse in Ezekiel’s vision. The comparison with crystal is explicit; a complete explanation of the image is not supplied here.
passages.god_plan_html:
The heavenly throne has already appeared in Daniel 7:9–14, where earthly violence is brought before God’s court and the Son of Man receives an everlasting kingdom. That provides a scriptural parallel for the perspective Revelation now gives: events on earth unfold before the God whose rule outlasts every earthly power.

The rainbow can also recall Genesis 9:12–17, where God gives it as the sign of His covenant with Noah and living creatures. Reading that alongside the throne’s thunder brings His faithfulness and authority into the same picture. This is a connection between scriptural images, not a claim that John explains every part of the rainbow’s meaning. The vision prepares readers to hear the difficult events ahead in the presence of the One who remains sovereign and faithful.

passages.title: Revelation 4:7-11
passages.section_title: Why does heaven never stop worshiping God?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 The first living creature was like a lion, the second like a calf, the third had a face like a man, and the fourth was like an eagle in flight. 8 And each of the four living creatures had six wings and was covered with eyes all around and within. Day and night they never stop saying: “Holy, Holy, Holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come!” 9 And whenever the living creatures give glory, honor, and thanks to the One seated on the throne, who lives forever and ever, 10 the twenty-four elders fall down before the One seated on the throne, and they worship Him who lives forever and ever. They cast their crowns before the throne, saying: 11 “Worthy are You, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honor and power, for You created all things; by Your will they exist and were created.”
paragraphs: 7 The first living creature was like a lion, the second like a calf, the third had a face like a man, and the fourth was like an eagle in flight. 8 And each of the four living creatures had six wings and was covered with eyes all around and within. Day and night they never stop saying: “Holy, Holy, Holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come!”

9 And whenever the living creatures give glory, honor, and thanks to the One seated on the throne, who lives forever and ever, 10 the twenty-four elders fall down before the One seated on the throne, and they worship Him who lives forever and ever. They cast their crowns before the throne, saying: 11 “Worthy are You, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honor and power, for You created all things; by Your will they exist and were created.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The description of the four living creatures continues from verse 6. John sees likenesses of a lion, a calf, a human face and a flying eagle. Each creature has six wings and is covered with eyes. These are images within a vision of God’s throne, with close connections to earlier Scripture.

Ezekiel 1:5–14 describes four living creatures with related faces, though their arrangement and wings differ. Ezekiel 10:20–22 identifies those creatures as cherubim. The six wings and repeated declaration of God’s holiness also recall the seraphim in Isaiah 6:1–3. John’s scene brings these familiar images together.

The creatures continually praise God as holy, almighty and eternally living. The elders respond by falling before Him, worshiping and placing their crowns before His throne. Whatever honor they possess is offered back to the One they worship.

Their spoken reason is creation: all things owe their existence to God’s will. Before the vision moves into the opening of the seals, it fixes attention on the worthiness of the Creator. Heaven’s worship gives a perspective from which to hear the difficult scenes ahead.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Interpretations differ over what the creatures represent. The USCCB notes understand them as representing creation, with the lion, calf, human and eagle expressing its varied strengths. Wesley connects them with heavenly powers and considers their representation of the Christian church. Gill favors gospel ministers, applying their features to courage, patient service, understanding and readiness. These are different explanations of the imagery; the creatures’ worship of God is clear in all of them.

Wesley hears the repeated holiness as praise of the triune God: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Gill likewise applies the praise to all three. Both understand the elders’ action as humble acknowledgment that God deserves the honor He has given His people. The scene directs attention toward Him, even where readers differ about the identity of those around the throne.
passages.god_plan_html:
Psalm 148 calls the heavens, angels, earth, living creatures and peoples to praise the LORD because He created them. Revelation’s throne-room worship belongs to that larger movement: creation acknowledging the One to whom it owes its life.

The vision does not begin with earthly evil as the center of reality. It begins with the Creator’s throne and the worship He deserves. That prepares for the next chapter, where the song will also celebrate the Lamb’s work of redemption. Creation and redemption come together in the unfolding vision, giving reason for worship before the judgments begin.

passages.title: Revelation 5:1-5
passages.section_title: Who is worthy to open the sealed scroll?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then I saw a scroll in the right hand of the One seated on the throne. It had writing on both sides and was sealed with seven seals. 2 And I saw a mighty angel proclaiming in a loud voice, “Who is worthy to break the seals and open the scroll?” 3 But no one in heaven or on earth or under the earth was able to open the scroll or look inside it. 4 And I began to weep bitterly, because no one was found worthy to open the scroll or look inside it. 5 Then one of the elders said to me, “Do not weep! Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has triumphed to open the scroll and its seven seals.”
paragraphs: 1 Then I saw a scroll in the right hand of the One seated on the throne. It had writing on both sides and was sealed with seven seals. 2 And I saw a mighty angel proclaiming in a loud voice, “Who is worthy to break the seals and open the scroll?” 3 But no one in heaven or on earth or under the earth was able to open the scroll or look inside it. 4 And I began to weep bitterly, because no one was found worthy to open the scroll or look inside it.
5 Then one of the elders said to me, “Do not weep! Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has triumphed to open the scroll and its seven seals.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The throne-room vision continues. The One seated on the throne holds a scroll written on both sides and sealed with seven seals. A mighty angel asks who is worthy to open it. No one in the realms named can do so, and John weeps.

The picture recalls Ezekiel 2:8–10, where the prophet receives a scroll written on the front and back. That scroll contains lamentation, mourning and woe. The connection helps place John’s scroll within the biblical pattern of God revealing what He will bring about.

The Greek word biblion can mean a book, scroll or written document; see Thayer’s entry. The word alone does not tell us the precise kind of document John sees. Its meaning must be considered through its place in the vision and what follows as the seals are opened.

An elder interrupts John’s grief with news that someone has triumphed: the Lion of Judah, the Root of David. The focus moves from the inability of others to the unique worthiness of Christ. The next verses show Him taking the scroll as the slain yet living Lamb.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley and Gill broadly agree that the scroll represents God’s purposes and the events unfolded through the rest of the vision, which Christ alone is worthy to reveal and bring about. Both connect the titles Lion of Judah and Root of David with the promised Messiah. Their wider accounts of the timing of the events differ, but the central emphasis here is shared: hope rests on Christ’s victory.
passages.god_plan_html:
The titles reach back to promises already given. Genesis 49:8–10 joins Judah with the image of a lion and the expectation of rule. Isaiah 11:1–2, 10 speaks of the shoot from Jesse and the Root of Jesse whom the nations seek. The elder identifies the victorious One through those promises.

The next scene shows how the victory has come: the Lion is seen as a Lamb who has been slain, and His blood has purchased people for God. The movement from royal titles to sacrificial death ties God’s promised rule to the work of Christ. Revelation presents His suffering and triumph within the same saving purpose.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Revelation 5:6-10
passages.section_title: How has the slain Lamb become worthy to rule?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 Then I saw a Lamb who appeared to have been slain, standing in the center of the throne, encircled by the four living creatures and the elders. The Lamb had seven horns and seven eyes, which represent the seven spirits of God sent out into all the earth. 7 And He came and took the scroll from the right hand of the One seated on the throne. 8 When He had taken the scroll, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb. Each one had a harp, and they were holding golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints. 9 And they sang a new song: “Worthy are You to take the scroll and open its seals, because You were slain, and by Your blood You purchased for God those from every tribe and tongue and people and nation. 10 You have made them to be a kingdom and priests to serve our God, and they will reign upon the earth.”
paragraphs: 6 Then I saw a Lamb who appeared to have been slain, standing in the center of the throne, encircled by the four living creatures and the elders. The Lamb had seven horns and seven eyes, which represent the seven spirits of God sent out into all the earth. 7 And He came and took the scroll from the right hand of the One seated on the throne. 8 When He had taken the scroll, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb. Each one had a harp, and they were holding golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints.

9 And they sang a new song: “Worthy are You to take the scroll and open its seals, because You were slain, and by Your blood You purchased for God those from every tribe and tongue and people and nation. 10 You have made them to be a kingdom and priests to serve our God, and they will reign upon the earth.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
John hears about the victorious Lion and then sees a Lamb standing, bearing the appearance of having been slain. The two pictures refer to the same Christ. His death has not ended His life or His victory.

The seven horns and seven eyes belong to this powerful, seeing Lamb. The eyes are identified with the seven spirits of God sent throughout the earth, recalling the eyes of the LORD surveying the earth in Zechariah 4:10. The Lamb approaches and takes the scroll from the One seated on the throne.

The creatures and elders fall before Him. The harps accompany a scene of worship, while the bowls of incense are expressly identified as the prayers of the saints. Psalm 141:1–2 already compares prayer offered to God with incense.

The new song gives the reason for His worthiness: He was slain and purchased people for God with His blood. Those people come from every tribe, language, people and nation. He makes them a kingdom and priests, with a future of reigning on the earth. Their identity and calling begin with what He has done for them.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Gill understand the slain yet standing Lamb as the crucified and risen Christ. Both see His death as the basis for the praise and the redeemed people’s place with God. Their readings differ over the setting and some of the people represented in the vision, but both keep Christ’s saving work central.

The bowls of prayers touch a real difference over who prays for the church. The Catholic Church teaches that saints in heaven pray to the Father for those on earth through Christ, the one mediator; see Catechism 956. Gill does not read this scene as support for addressing prayers to departed saints: in his reading, the figures represent earthly believers and their own prayers. Wesley understands the bowls as representing the prayers of other saints still on earth. These explanations should be distinguished from the passage’s explicit identification of the incense as prayer.

The BSB song speaks of the redeemed as those Christ purchased and made a kingdom, using them and they in verse 10. Older commentaries sometimes reason from wording with us and we. That difference matters when assessing a claim that the song proves exactly who the singers must be. The page retains the BSB wording throughout.
passages.god_plan_html:
The Lamb connects with John 1:29, where Jesus is identified as the Lamb of God who takes away sin, and 1 Peter 1:18–21, where redemption is tied to His precious blood and resurrection. Revelation shows the crucified and risen Christ receiving worship and authority in heaven.

The kingdom of priests also recalls Exodus 19:3–6, where God brings Israel to Himself and gives it a priestly calling. Here the Lamb gathers people from every nation for service to God. Their worship and future rule are grounded in redemption, bringing Christ’s sacrifice and God’s purpose for a people who serve Him into the same picture.
passages.current_position_html: Our studies Returning to the Word and The True Church According to Jesus describe priesthood as a calling shared by the whole community of believers, with access to God through Christ. That is the principle we draw on here: the Lamb makes His redeemed people a kingdom and priests to serve God.

deeper_study.title: The True Church According to Jesus

passages.title: Revelation 5:11-14
passages.section_title: Why does all creation join in praising the Lamb?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 Then I looked, and I heard the voices of many angels encircling the throne, and the living creatures and the elders. And their number was myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands. 12 In a loud voice they were saying: “Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and riches and wisdom and strength and honor and glory and blessing!” 13 And I heard every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea, and all that is in them, saying: “To Him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be praise and honor and glory and power forever and ever!” 14 And the four living creatures said, “Amen,” and the elders fell down and worshiped.

And their number was myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands. 12 In a loud voice they were saying: “Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and riches and wisdom and strength and honor and glory and blessing!”

13 And I heard every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea, and all that is in them, saying: “To Him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be praise and honor and glory and power forever and ever!” 14 And the four living creatures said, “Amen,” and the elders fell down and worshiped.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The circle of praise widens. John hears a vast company of angels surrounding the throne, the living creatures and the elders. Their praise centers on the Lamb who was slain. Power, riches, wisdom, strength, honor, glory and blessing are declared His due.

The wording recalls the great heavenly company before God’s court in Daniel 7:9–10. John then hears praise from every creature in heaven, on earth, under the earth and in the sea. The vision brings the whole created order into the acknowledgment of God and the Lamb.

The One seated on the throne and the Lamb receive praise together. The creatures answer Amen, and the elders fall down in worship. This closes the chapter’s movement from John’s grief over the sealed scroll to the shared celebration of the One worthy to open it. The first seal is opened in the next chapter.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Wesley and Gill both understand the shared praise as honoring the Lamb together with God. They include the acknowledgment of Christ by His enemies within the universal scope of the scene, while distinguishing that from the willing joy of His people. The passage’s central emphasis is His worthiness and the breadth of the praise He receives.
passages.god_plan_html:
Philippians 2:9–11 looks toward every knee bowing and every tongue acknowledging Jesus Christ as Lord, to the Father’s glory. Revelation’s widening song gives a corresponding picture of that universal acknowledgment.

The contrast within the chapter is striking: no one else can open the scroll, yet the Lamb who was slain receives the worship of creation. His death is not a detour from His victory. It is the reason the song gives for His worthiness. God’s purpose moves forward through the crucified and risen Christ, and the vision places the coming events beneath His authority.

passages.title: Revelation 6:1-8
passages.section_title: What happens when the Lamb opens the first four seals?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then I watched as the Lamb opened one of the seven seals, and I heard one of the four living creatures say in a voice like thunder, “Come!” 2 So I looked and saw a white horse, and its rider held a bow. And he was given a crown, and he rode out to overcome and conquer. 3 And when the Lamb opened the second seal, I heard the second living creature say, “Come!” 4 Then another horse went forth. It was bright red, and its rider was granted permission to take away peace from the earth and to make men slay one another. And he was given a great sword. 5 And when the Lamb opened the third seal, I heard the third living creature say, “Come!” Then I looked and saw a black horse, and its rider held in his hand a pair of scales. 6 And I heard what sounded like a voice from among the four living creatures, saying, “A quart of wheat for a denarius, and three quarts of barley for a denarius, and do not harm the oil and wine.” 7 And when the Lamb opened the fourth seal, I heard the voice of the fourth living creature say, “Come!” 8 Then I looked and saw a pale green horse. Its rider’s name was Death, and Hades followed close behind. And they were given authority over a fourth of the earth, to kill by sword, by famine, by plague, and by the beasts of the earth.
paragraphs: 1 Then I watched as the Lamb opened one of the seven seals, and I heard one of the four living creatures say in a voice like thunder, “Come!” 2 So I looked and saw a white horse, and its rider held a bow. And he was given a crown, and he rode out to overcome and conquer.

3 And when the Lamb opened the second seal, I heard the second living creature say, “Come!” 4 Then another horse went forth. It was bright red, and its rider was granted permission to take away peace from the earth and to make men slay one another. And he was given a great sword.

5 And when the Lamb opened the third seal, I heard the third living creature say, “Come!” Then I looked and saw a black horse, and its rider held in his hand a pair of scales. 6 And I heard what sounded like a voice from among the four living creatures, saying, “A quart of wheat for a denarius, and three quarts of barley for a denarius, and do not harm the oil and wine.”

7 And when the Lamb opened the fourth seal, I heard the voice of the fourth living creature say, “Come!” 8 Then I looked and saw a pale green horse. Its rider’s name was Death, and Hades followed close behind. And they were given authority over a fourth of the earth, to kill by sword, by famine, by plague, and by the beasts of the earth.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lamb begins opening the scroll He received in chapter 5. With each of the first four seals, a living creature calls out and a horse and rider appear. The repeated pattern brings the four scenes together, while each adds a different feature.

The white horse’s rider carries a bow, receives a crown and goes out conquering. The red horse’s rider takes peace from the earth and receives a great sword. People turn against one another in bloodshed. The black horse’s rider holds scales as a voice announces grain prices and a command concerning oil and wine.

The price of wheat is a denarius for a quart. In Matthew 20:1–2, a vineyard worker agrees to a denarius for a day’s work. That comparison helps convey the hardship in the vision: a day’s earnings buys only a small amount of staple food. Leviticus 26:26 similarly pictures scarce bread being measured out by weight.

The fourth horse is pale green, and its rider is explicitly named Death, with Hades following. The Greek color word chloros can describe green or a yellowish, pale shade; see Thayer’s entry. Hades refers to the realm of the dead; see Thayer’s entry. Death and the gathering of the dead are pictured together.

The authority given them extends over a fourth of the earth, with killing by sword, famine, plague and wild beasts. The scene is devastating, but the riders act with authority that is given and bounded. The Lamb’s opening of the seals remains the setting for everything John sees.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The first rider has several major readings. Gill understands Christ advancing through the gospel. Wesley reads imperial conquest, particularly under Trajan. The USCCB notes also emphasize conquering power. Walvoord favors a future ruler opposed to Christ. These explanations differ over the rider’s identity and whether the scene concerns earlier history or future events.

The later horses are widely connected with war, scarcity and death. Wesley reads the preserved oil and wine as a limit on the shortage; Gill contrasts those supplies with the scarcity of basic bread. Their particular historical applications differ, but both hear an actual restraint in the command not to harm them. The verse itself does not identify a country exempted from the crisis.

The absence of arrows from the description of the first rider does not by itself prove that he has no weapons to use or must conquer peacefully. Likewise, the crown and white horse do not name him for us. Each proposal needs to be considered alongside the whole group of riders and the wider book.
passages.god_plan_html:
The colored horses recall Zechariah 6:1–8, where heavenly agents go out from before the Lord of all the earth. The parallel places the movement of earthly events under His authority, without requiring every horse in the two visions to have an identical meaning.

The sword, famine, plague and wild beasts also recall the four judgments named in Ezekiel 14:21–23. Revelation draws on language already used to show that violence and judgment are not beyond God’s knowledge or rule. These connections help locate the terrifying scenes within the larger biblical account of His authority over evil and His right to judge.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Revelation 6:9-11
passages.section_title: Does God hear those who have suffered for His word?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 And when the Lamb opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God and for the testimony they had upheld. 10 And they cried out in a loud voice, “How long, O Lord, holy and true, until You judge those who dwell upon the earth and avenge our blood?” 11 Then each of them was given a white robe and told to rest a little while longer until the full number of their fellow servants, their brothers, were killed, just as they had been killed.
paragraphs: 9 And when the Lamb opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God and for the testimony they had upheld. 10 And they cried out in a loud voice, “How long, O Lord, holy and true, until You judge those who dwell upon the earth and avenge our blood?” 11 Then each of them was given a white robe and told to rest a little while longer until the full number of their fellow servants, their brothers, were killed, just as they had been killed.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The fifth seal changes the scene. There is no new horse. John sees beneath the altar the souls of people killed because of God’s word and the testimony they maintained. Their deaths have not placed them beyond God’s care.

They ask the holy and true Lord how long it will be before He judges and avenges their blood. This is an appeal for justice to the One entitled to give it. The vision lets their suffering be named and their question be heard.

Each receives a white robe and is told to rest a little longer. Others will still suffer as they have. The answer assures them of a place with God while acknowledging that the wrongs on earth have not yet all been brought to an end. The passage does not name the victims or give a calendar date for the end of their waiting.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Readings differ over the historical setting. Gill includes the earlier Christian martyrs, especially those associated with Diocletian’s persecution, and allows later martyrs within the continuing account. Wesley also reads earlier and later periods of persecution. Walvoord instead places these deaths in a future tribulation after the church has been gathered to Christ. The identification depends in part on how each reads the book’s sequence.

Wesley and Gill both distinguish the cry for justice from malicious personal revenge. They understand the white robes as honor, acceptance and joy given to those who suffered. Their explanations point toward confidence in God’s judgment while leaving its execution with Him. The scene does not instruct the church to carry out violence against opponents.
passages.god_plan_html:
The cry reaches back to Genesis 4:9–10, where Abel’s blood cries out to God. Scripture’s story does not treat a victim’s death as the disappearance of the wrong done. The God who heard then also hears here.

Jesus addresses persistent appeals for justice in Luke 18:1–8, encouraging His people to keep praying and not lose heart. Romans 12:17–21 entrusts vengeance to God and calls believers to overcome evil with good. Read together, these passages give a larger frame for the martyrs’ waiting: God’s people can appeal to Him for wrongs to be put right while trusting Him with the outcome.

passages.title: Revelation 6:12-17
passages.section_title: Who can stand when the day of judgment comes?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 And I watched as the Lamb opened the sixth seal, and there was a great earthquake, and the sun became black like sackcloth of goat hair, and the whole moon turned blood red, 13 and the stars of the sky fell to the earth like unripe figs dropping from a tree shaken by a great wind. 14 The sky receded like a scroll being rolled up, and every mountain and island was moved from its place. 15 Then the kings of the earth, the nobles, the commanders, the rich, the mighty, and every slave and free man hid in the caves and among the rocks of the mountains. 16 And they said to the mountains and the rocks, “Fall on us and hide us from the face of the One seated on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb. 17 For the great day of Their wrath has come, and who is able to withstand it?”
paragraphs: 12 And I watched as the Lamb opened the sixth seal, and there was a great earthquake, and the sun became black like sackcloth of goat hair, and the whole moon turned blood red, 13 and the stars of the sky fell to the earth like unripe figs dropping from a tree shaken by a great wind. 14 The sky receded like a scroll being rolled up, and every mountain and island was moved from its place.

15 Then the kings of the earth, the nobles, the commanders, the rich, the mighty, and every slave and free man hid in the caves and among the rocks of the mountains. 16 And they said to the mountains and the rocks, “Fall on us and hide us from the face of the One seated on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb. 17 For the great day of Their wrath has come, and who is able to withstand it?”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The sixth seal brings a great earthquake and a vision of upheaval in the heavens and on earth. The sun becomes black, the moon turns blood red, stars fall, the sky recedes like a scroll, and mountains and islands are moved. The imagery strips away the things people normally regard as stable.

The language has close biblical precedents. Isaiah 34:1–4 pictures judgment with the skies rolled up and the stars falling like leaves. Hosea 10:8 pictures people calling on mountains and hills to cover them. John’s scene draws these images into the vision of the Lamb opening the seals.

People from every rank seek shelter: rulers and commanders, wealthy and powerful people, slaves and free people. Their differences in status do not remove their fear. They ask to be hidden from the One seated on the throne and from the Lamb’s wrath.

The chapter ends with their question about who can withstand the great day. Chapter 7 follows with the sealing of God’s servants and a multitude standing before His throne. That next scene matters when reading the question: this chapter is not the vision’s final word about those who belong to Him.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
There is a substantial difference over how the upheaval is fulfilled. Gill reads the imagery chiefly as the overthrow of pagan rule and worship in the Roman Empire. Wesley understands it as a vision of judgment shown to the wicked dead. Walvoord favors future physical disturbances in heaven and on earth. The USCCB notes emphasize prophetic pictures of the cosmic upheaval attending divine judgment. These readings share the seriousness of judgment while differing about the events pictured.

The text’s own comparisons—sackcloth, falling figs and a rolled scroll—should remain visible in each explanation. It does not provide a scientific account of every event or identify a particular modern eclipse. Its stated focus is the fear of facing God and the Lamb, not a calculation that enables readers to date the end.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jesus takes up the cry for the mountains to fall in Luke 23:27–31, warning the women of Jerusalem about judgment to come. Revelation uses that same biblical language to show the failure of every earthly refuge before God.

The Lamb praised for His redeeming death in chapter 5 is also named here in connection with judgment. The vision holds those truths together. God’s purpose includes both rescue through Christ and the reckoning with evil that His people have asked Him to bring. The question of who can stand leads into the following chapter’s account of His servants and their hope.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Revelation 7:1-8
passages.section_title: Whom does God mark as His own before judgment falls?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 After this I saw four angels standing at the four corners of the earth, holding back its four winds so that no wind would blow on land or sea or on any tree. 2 And I saw another angel ascending from the east, with the seal of the living God. And he called out in a loud voice to the four angels who had been given power to harm the land and the sea: 3 “Do not harm the land or sea or trees until we have placed a seal on the foreheads of the servants of our God.” 4 And I heard the number of those who were sealed, 144,000 from all the tribes of Israel: 5 From the tribe of Judah 12,000 were sealed, from the tribe of Reuben 12,000, from the tribe of Gad 12,000, 6 from the tribe of Asher 12,000, from the tribe of Naphtali 12,000, from the tribe of Manasseh 12,000, 7 from the tribe of Simeon 12,000, from the tribe of Levi 12,000, from the tribe of Issachar 12,000, 8 from the tribe of Zebulun 12,000, from the tribe of Joseph 12,000, and from the tribe of Benjamin 12,000.
paragraphs: 1 After this I saw four angels standing at the four corners of the earth, holding back its four winds so that no wind would blow on land or sea or on any tree. 2 And I saw another angel ascending from the east, with the seal of the living God. And he called out in a loud voice to the four angels who had been given power to harm the land and the sea: 3 “Do not harm the land or sea or trees until we have placed a seal on the foreheads of the servants of our God.”

4 And I heard the number of those who were sealed, 144,000 from all the tribes of Israel: 5 From the tribe of Judah 12,000 were sealed, from the tribe of Reuben 12,000, from the tribe of Gad 12,000, 6 from the tribe of Asher 12,000, from the tribe of Naphtali 12,000, from the tribe of Manasseh 12,000, 7 from the tribe of Simeon 12,000, from the tribe of Levi 12,000, from the tribe of Issachar 12,000, 8 from the tribe of Zebulun 12,000, from the tribe of Joseph 12,000, and from the tribe of Benjamin 12,000.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Before the seventh seal is opened, John sees a pause in the threatened harm. Four angels hold back the winds, and another angel comes from the east with the seal of the living God. The command is to wait until God’s servants have been sealed on their foreheads.

The scene answers the fear raised at the end of chapter 6 with attention to people who belong to God. The harm is restrained while His servants are identified. The description calls them His servants before speaking of their sealing.

John hears a number: 144,000, with 12,000 from each named tribe of Israel. Judah comes first. Levi and Joseph appear, while Dan and the name Ephraim do not. The passage gives the list without stating the reason for every inclusion or omission.

The number is followed by the vision of an uncountable multitude from every nation. How the two groups relate is a major question in interpretation. The text first lets us hear the numbered list and then see the multitude, and both scenes deserve to be read in their full setting.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christian readings differ over the identity and number of those sealed. Walvoord reads 144,000 Israelites protected during a future tribulation. Wesley also understands Israelites secured from coming calamities, while explaining that the number does not include every Israelite who will ever be saved. These readings take the tribal identification as referring to Israel’s people.

Gill instead understands the number as representing God’s people across nations and ages. The USCCB notes likewise read it symbolically, as the new Israel embracing people from every nation. This is a genuine difference over how the tribal list functions in the vision, rather than a disagreement that can be resolved simply by assuming one meaning for every number in Revelation.

The identity of the angel bearing the seal is also interpreted differently. Gill identifies him with Christ acting for His people; Wesley understands a good angel carrying out God’s commission. The passage calls him an angel and describes his authority without giving a name. Both readings emphasize that the servants’ security comes from God.
passages.god_plan_html:
The mark on the forehead recalls Ezekiel 9:1–6, where those grieving over Jerusalem’s wrongdoing are marked before judgment. The parallel draws attention to God knowing His people amid the evil around them.

Ephesians 1:13–14 also uses sealing for believers’ relationship with God, identifying the Holy Spirit as the pledge of their inheritance. That does not make every detail of these passages identical, but it places Revelation’s scene within a wider biblical theme: those who belong to God are known to Him and held within His purpose. The following vision will show His people brought out of suffering into His presence.

passages.title: Revelation 7:9-17
passages.section_title: What future does the Lamb give people who have suffered?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 After this I looked and saw a multitude too large to count, from every nation and tribe and people and tongue, standing before the throne and before the Lamb. They were wearing white robes and holding palm branches in their hands. 10 And they cried out in a loud voice: “Salvation to our God, who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!” 11 And all the angels stood around the throne and around the elders and the four living creatures. And they fell facedown before the throne and worshiped God, 12 saying, “Amen! Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanks and honor and power and strength be to our God forever and ever! Amen.” 13 Then one of the elders addressed me: “These in white robes,” he asked, “who are they, and where have they come from?” 14 “Sir,” I answered, “you know.” So he replied, “These are the ones who have come out of the great tribulation; they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb. 15 For this reason, they are before the throne of God and serve Him day and night in His temple; and the One seated on the throne will spread His tabernacle over them. 16 ‘Never again will they hunger, and never will they thirst; nor will the sun beat down upon them, nor any scorching heat.’ 17 For the Lamb in the center of the throne will be their shepherd. ‘He will lead them to springs of living water,’ and ‘God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.’”
paragraphs: 9 After this I looked and saw a multitude too large to count, from every nation and tribe and people and tongue, standing before the throne and before the Lamb. They were wearing white robes and holding palm branches in their hands. 10 And they cried out in a loud voice: “Salvation to our God, who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!” 11 And all the angels stood around the throne and around the elders and the four living creatures. And they fell facedown before the throne and worshiped God, 12 saying, “Amen! Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanks and honor and power and strength be to our God forever and ever! Amen.”

13 Then one of the elders addressed me: “These in white robes,” he asked, “who are they, and where have they come from?” 14 “Sir,” I answered, “you know.” So he replied, “These are the ones who have come out of the great tribulation; they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.

15 For this reason, they are before the throne of God and serve Him day and night in His temple; and the One seated on the throne will spread His tabernacle over them. 16 ‘Never again will they hunger, and never will they thirst; nor will the sun beat down upon them, nor any scorching heat.’ 17 For the Lamb in the center of the throne will be their shepherd. ‘He will lead them to springs of living water,’ and ‘God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.’”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
John now sees a multitude too large to count, drawn from every nation, tribe, people and language. They stand before God’s throne and the Lamb, wearing white robes and holding palm branches. They praise God and the Lamb for salvation, and the surrounding angels join in worship.

One of the elders asks John who these people are and where they came from. John leaves the answer to him. The elder identifies them as those who have come out of the great tribulation and washed their robes in the Lamb’s blood. Their cleansing and their place before God are bound to Christ’s death.

The final description moves from their suffering to God’s care. They serve in His presence, sheltered by Him. Hunger, thirst and scorching heat no longer afflict them. The Lamb becomes their shepherd, guiding them to living water, and God wipes away their tears.

This scene should be heard beside the question at the end of chapter 6 about who can stand. Here a multitude is standing before the throne. The vision of judgment is accompanied by a vision of salvation and lasting care for people from across the nations.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The scope of the great tribulation is read differently. Walvoord identifies the multitude as people martyred during a future tribulation. Wesley explicitly includes the righteous across history who have passed through many kinds of affliction, rather than limiting the group to martyrs. The USCCB notes connect the distress with Roman persecution. These readings locate the suffering in different settings.

Gill also includes God’s people across ages, but places the scene especially in Christ’s future reign with His people on earth. Wesley emphasizes the righteous in God’s heavenly presence. Their difference concerns the setting of the promise, alongside their shared confidence that the suffering will end.

Wesley and Gill both connect the white robes with cleansing through the Lamb’s blood. The praise attributes salvation to God and the Lamb. Both direct attention to Christ’s death as the basis for their place with God and to the care He gives His people.
passages.god_plan_html:
The promise of no hunger, thirst or scorching heat takes up Isaiah 49:8–13, where God has compassion on His afflicted people and guides them beside springs. The removal of tears recalls Isaiah 25:6–9, where God swallows up death and comforts His people. Revelation places those promises within the Lamb’s care for this multitude.

The Lamb who gave His life is also the shepherd who leads them. That connects with Jesus’ own description of the good shepherd laying down His life for His sheep in John 10:11–18. Revelation 21:1–4 will return to God dwelling with His people and wiping away their tears. The larger hope is more than surviving a crisis: it is life with Him, where the suffering that made those tears necessary has ended.

passages.title: Revelation 8:1-6
passages.section_title: What follows the silence when the seventh seal is opened?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 When the Lamb opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour. 2 And I saw the seven angels who stand before God, and they were given seven trumpets. 3 Then another angel, who had a golden censer, came and stood at the altar. He was given much incense to offer, along with the prayers of all the saints, on the golden altar before the throne. 4 And the smoke of the incense, together with the prayers of the saints, rose up before God from the hand of the angel. 5 Then the angel took the censer, filled it with fire from the altar, and hurled it to the earth; and there were peals of thunder, rumblings, flashes of lightning, and an earthquake. 6 And the seven angels with the seven trumpets prepared to sound them.
paragraphs: 1 When the Lamb opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour. 2 And I saw the seven angels who stand before God, and they were given seven trumpets.

3 Then another angel, who had a golden censer, came and stood at the altar. He was given much incense to offer, along with the prayers of all the saints, on the golden altar before the throne. 4 And the smoke of the incense, together with the prayers of the saints, rose up before God from the hand of the angel. 5 Then the angel took the censer, filled it with fire from the altar, and hurled it to the earth; and there were peals of thunder, rumblings, flashes of lightning, and an earthquake. 6 And the seven angels with the seven trumpets prepared to sound them.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The Lamb opens the seventh seal, and heaven becomes silent for about half an hour. The pause stands out after the great chorus of praise in chapter 7. Seven angels before God receive trumpets, but their sounding is delayed while John sees another scene at the altar.

An angel holds a golden censer, a vessel for burning incense. Much incense is given to him to offer with the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar before the throne. The smoke and prayers rise before God. The vision gives those prayers a place in heaven’s activity before the next judgments begin.

The angel then fills the censer with fire from the altar and throws it to the earth. Thunder, rumblings, lightning and an earthquake follow. The movement from prayers before God to fire cast upon the earth connects the altar scene with the judgments about to unfold.

The seven angels prepare to sound their trumpets. This passage carries the vision from the seventh seal into the trumpet sequence. The warning and judgment that follow are introduced in the presence of God and alongside His people’s prayers.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands the silence as heaven’s reverent expectation before what God will do. Gill, within his historical reading, connects it with a brief period of peace for the church under Constantine. Walvoord reads it as a solemn pause before future judgments. All recognize a pause of significance, while differing over its setting.

They also differ over the angel at the altar. Wesley understands a created angel serving God, while Gill identifies the figure with Christ acting for His people. Walvoord discusses both possibilities without claiming the question can be settled with certainty. The passage describes the angel’s work and the prayers rising before God without naming the figure.

The incense is closely connected with the prayers in each reading. The differences should not obscure what the scene makes plain: those prayers come before God, and the coming judgments belong to His authority. The text does not set out a new set of prayer words or a ritual that readers must perform.
passages.god_plan_html:
Silence before God already appears in Zephaniah 1:7, as the Day of the LORD draws near, and Habakkuk 2:20, where the earth is called to be silent before Him in His temple. These are scriptural parallels for hearing heaven’s pause as an acknowledgment of His majesty and judgment.

The fire cast from the altar also recalls Ezekiel 10:1–2, where burning coals are scattered over Jerusalem. Revelation places judgment alongside prayers already heard before God. The martyrs’ question in Revelation 6:9–11 has not been forgotten: God’s purpose includes answering evil with justice. The scene gives His people reason to bring their suffering to Him and await His action.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Revelation 8:7-13
passages.section_title: Why do the first trumpets strike the world that sustains life?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 Then the first angel sounded his trumpet, and hail and fire mixed with blood were hurled down upon the earth. A third of the earth was burned up, along with a third of the trees and all the green grass. 8 Then the second angel sounded his trumpet, and something like a great mountain burning with fire was thrown into the sea. A third of the sea turned to blood, 9 a third of the living creatures in the sea died, and a third of the ships were destroyed. 10 Then the third angel sounded his trumpet, and a great star burning like a torch fell from heaven and landed on a third of the rivers and on the springs of water. 11 The name of the star is Wormwood. A third of the waters turned bitter like wormwood oil, and many people died from the bitter waters. 12 Then the fourth angel sounded his trumpet, and a third of the sun and moon and stars were struck. A third of the stars were darkened, a third of the day was without light, and a third of the night as well. 13 And as I observed, I heard an eagle flying overhead, calling in a loud voice, “Woe! Woe! Woe to those who dwell on the earth, because of the trumpet blasts about to be sounded by the remaining three angels!”
paragraphs: 7 Then the first angel sounded his trumpet, and hail and fire mixed with blood were hurled down upon the earth. A third of the earth was burned up, along with a third of the trees and all the green grass.

8 Then the second angel sounded his trumpet, and something like a great mountain burning with fire was thrown into the sea. A third of the sea turned to blood, 9 a third of the living creatures in the sea died, and a third of the ships were destroyed.

10 Then the third angel sounded his trumpet, and a great star burning like a torch fell from heaven and landed on a third of the rivers and on the springs of water. 11 The name of the star is Wormwood. A third of the waters turned bitter like wormwood oil, and many people died from the bitter waters.

12 Then the fourth angel sounded his trumpet, and a third of the sun and moon and stars were struck. A third of the stars were darkened, a third of the day was without light, and a third of the night as well. 13 And as I observed, I heard an eagle flying overhead, calling in a loud voice, “Woe! Woe! Woe to those who dwell on the earth, because of the trumpet blasts about to be sounded by the remaining three angels!”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The first four trumpets form a connected group. They affect the land and vegetation, the sea, the fresh waters, and the lights of heaven. The repeated third emphasizes the judgments’ reach while also describing limits to the destruction.

The first trumpet brings hail and fire mixed with blood, burning a third of the earth and trees and all the green grass. At the second, something like a burning mountain is thrown into the sea. A third of the sea becomes blood, with a corresponding loss of sea life and ships. John gives a comparison to a mountain, without identifying the object more precisely.

The third brings a burning star named Wormwood upon rivers and springs. The waters become bitter and many people die. The name belongs to biblical language of bitter judgment: Jeremiah 9:13–16 joins wormwood and poisoned water with the consequences of unfaithfulness.

The fourth affects the sun, moon and stars, leaving part of the day and night without light. An eagle flying overhead then announces three woes connected with the remaining trumpets. The Greek word for its position, mesouranema, describes the high or middle sky, where it can be seen and heard; see Thayer’s entry. The announcement directs attention toward the even more severe scenes still to come.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Readings differ over how the trumpet scenes are fulfilled. Wesley applies them to calamities affecting Judea and the Roman world, including invasions and conflicts over teaching. Gill especially connects the first four with invasions and the collapse of the western Roman Empire. Walvoord favors future judgments affecting the physical world. The difference concerns the events pictured as well as their timing.

The named star illustrates the difference. Wesley applies Wormwood to Arius and the spread of his teaching. Gill favors the destructive effects of invading powers. In a future physical reading, the star brings actual contamination of water. The text itself supplies its name, the bitterness of the waters and the deaths that follow; it does not directly name a later teacher or ruler.

The final announcement makes clear that the first four trumpets are not the end of the sequence. The three woes warn of what remains. The BSB reads eagle here; older commentaries sometimes discuss a text reading angel. That difference should be recognized when comparing their explanations with the passage quoted on this page.
passages.god_plan_html:
The judgments recall the plagues of Egypt. Exodus 9:22–26 describes hail, fire and ruined vegetation. Exodus 7:19–21 describes water turned to blood and fish dying. Exodus 10:21–23 describes darkness over the land. These parallels connect Revelation’s judgments with the earlier account of God confronting oppression and bringing His people out of bondage.

The repeated pattern does not identify every modern place or prescribe the physical mechanism of each event. It shows the authority of the same God over the things on which earthly life depends. The vision calls readers to take His judgment seriously while the wider story continues toward the rescue, worship and life with Him already pictured in chapter 7.
