passages.title: Revelation 9:1-12
passages.section_title: Why are the locusts allowed to torment people but kept within limits?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then the fifth angel sounded his trumpet, and I saw a star that had fallen from heaven to earth, and it was given the key to the pit of the Abyss. 2 The star opened the pit of the Abyss, and smoke rose out of it like the smoke of a great furnace, and the sun and the air were darkened by the smoke from the pit. 3 And out of the smoke, locusts descended on the earth, and they were given power like that of the scorpions of the earth. 4 They were told not to harm the grass of the earth or any plant or tree, but only those who did not have the seal of God on their foreheads. 5 The locusts were not given power to kill them, but only to torment them for five months, and their torment was like the stinging of a scorpion. 6 In those days men will seek death and will not find it; they will long to die, but death will escape them. 7 And the locusts looked like horses prepared for battle, with something like crowns of gold on their heads; and their faces were like the faces of men. 8 They had hair like that of women, and teeth like those of lions. 9 They also had breastplates like breastplates of iron, and the sound of their wings was like the roar of many horses and chariots rushing into battle. 10 They had tails with stingers like scorpions, which had the power to injure people for five months. 11 They were ruled by a king, the angel of the Abyss. His name in Hebrew is Abaddon, and in Greek it is Apollyon. 12 The first woe has passed. Behold, two woes are still to follow.
paragraphs: 1 Then the fifth angel sounded his trumpet, and I saw a star that had fallen from heaven to earth, and it was given the key to the pit of the Abyss. 2 The star opened the pit of the Abyss, and smoke rose out of it like the smoke of a great furnace, and the sun and the air were darkened by the smoke from the pit. 3 And out of the smoke, locusts descended on the earth, and they were given power like that of the scorpions of the earth.

4 They were told not to harm the grass of the earth or any plant or tree, but only those who did not have the seal of God on their foreheads. 5 The locusts were not given power to kill them, but only to torment them for five months, and their torment was like the stinging of a scorpion. 6 In those days men will seek death and will not find it; they will long to die, but death will escape them.

7 And the locusts looked like horses prepared for battle, with something like crowns of gold on their heads; and their faces were like the faces of men. 8 They had hair like that of women, and teeth like those of lions. 9 They also had breastplates like breastplates of iron, and the sound of their wings was like the roar of many horses and chariots rushing into battle. 10 They had tails with stingers like scorpions, which had the power to injure people for five months. 11 They were ruled by a king, the angel of the Abyss. His name in Hebrew is Abaddon, and in Greek it is Apollyon. 12 The first woe has passed. Behold, two woes are still to follow.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The fifth trumpet begins the first of the three woes announced at the end of chapter 8. John sees a star that has fallen from heaven and is given the key to the Abyss. The star acts as a person, opening the shaft. Smoke rises and darkens the sun and air, and locusts emerge from it.

The Greek word abyssos refers to a deep, unfathomable place; in this setting it is connected with imprisoned evil powers. Thayer’s entry connects its use here with Luke 8:30–33, where demons beg Jesus not to send them into the Abyss. The word helps explain the scene’s spiritual setting without giving us a map of the unseen world.

These locusts behave differently from the insects that destroy crops. They are forbidden to harm vegetation and may torment only people who lack God’s seal. Their power lasts five months, and they may not kill. The repeated restrictions matter: the terrifying beings do not decide for themselves whom they may attack or how far they may go.

John describes them through a series of comparisons: battle-ready horses, human faces, women’s hair, lions’ teeth, iron breastplates and scorpion-like tails. Their king is the angel of the Abyss. The Hebrew name Abaddon is associated with destruction, and the Greek name Apollyon means destroyer; see Brown–Driver–Briggs and Thayer. The first woe ends with a warning that two remain.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Readers differ over the identity of the star. Wesley understands a holy angel carrying out God’s command. Walvoord favors Satan as a fallen angel who receives permission to open the Abyss. Both recognize that the key is given; the figure does not possess unlimited authority of his own. John does not name him.

The locusts also receive different explanations. Wesley connects the first woe with Persian persecution of Jewish people. Gill relates the imagery especially to medieval Arab conquests, alongside a reading concerning corrupt religious power. Walvoord understands a future outbreak of demonic torment. These are the readings of particular teachers, rather than positions that every member of their traditions shares.

These differences affect the five months as well. A future reading may take them as ordinary months, while historical readings connect them with longer periods. Each explanation should be distinguished from the passage’s direct description: the attack is severe, it is limited, and those bearing God’s seal are protected from it.
passages.god_plan_html:
The locusts recall Exodus 10:12–20, where God confronts Pharaoh through a plague that destroys Egypt’s vegetation. Joel 1:4–7 and 2:1–11 also combine locust devastation with the language of an invading army. Revelation uses familiar pictures of judgment, while changing their target from plants to people. These are scriptural parallels, not a claim that every detail describes the same event.

The limits placed on the attackers also fit the distinction God makes between judgment and rescue. Second Peter 2:4–9 brings together imprisoned rebellious angels, judgment on evil and God’s care for the godly. Revelation’s sealing scene in chapter 7 prepares for that distinction here. Evil is frightening, but it cannot erase God’s knowledge of His people or take control of His purposes.

passages.title: Revelation 9:13-21
passages.section_title: Why do the survivors still refuse to turn from their sins?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 Then the sixth angel sounded his trumpet, and I heard a voice from the four horns of the golden altar before God 14 saying to the sixth angel with the trumpet, “Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates.” 15 So the four angels who had been prepared for this hour and day and month and year were released to kill a third of mankind. 16 And the number of mounted troops was two hundred million; I heard their number. 17 Now the horses and riders in my vision looked like this: The riders had breastplates the colors of fire, sapphire, and sulfur. The heads of the horses were like the heads of lions, and out of their mouths proceeded fire, smoke, and sulfur. 18 A third of mankind was killed by the three plagues of fire, smoke, and sulfur that proceeded from their mouths. 19 For the power of the horses was in their mouths and in their tails; indeed, their tails were like snakes, having heads with which to inflict harm. 20 Now the rest of mankind who were not killed by these plagues still did not repent of the works of their hands. They did not stop worshiping demons and idols of gold, silver, bronze, stone, and wood, which cannot see or hear or walk. 21 Furthermore, they did not repent of their murder, sorcery, sexual immorality, and theft.
paragraphs: 13 Then the sixth angel sounded his trumpet, and I heard a voice from the four horns of the golden altar before God 14 saying to the sixth angel with the trumpet, “Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates.” 15 So the four angels who had been prepared for this hour and day and month and year were released to kill a third of mankind. 16 And the number of mounted troops was two hundred million; I heard their number.

17 Now the horses and riders in my vision looked like this: The riders had breastplates the colors of fire, sapphire, and sulfur. The heads of the horses were like the heads of lions, and out of their mouths proceeded fire, smoke, and sulfur. 18 A third of mankind was killed by the three plagues of fire, smoke, and sulfur that proceeded from their mouths. 19 For the power of the horses was in their mouths and in their tails; indeed, their tails were like snakes, having heads with which to inflict harm.

20 Now the rest of mankind who were not killed by these plagues still did not repent of the works of their hands. They did not stop worshiping demons and idols of gold, silver, bronze, stone, and wood, which cannot see or hear or walk. 21 Furthermore, they did not repent of their murder, sorcery, sexual immorality, and theft.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The sixth trumpet brings a voice from the golden altar before God. Four angels bound at the Euphrates are released at the appointed hour, day, month and year. Their release leads to the death of a third of mankind. The scene returns to the altar already associated with the prayers of God’s people in chapter 8.

John hears the number of the mounted troops: two hundred million. He then describes riders with fiery red, dark blue and yellow breastplates, and horses with lion-like heads. Fire, smoke and sulfur come from their mouths. Their serpent-like tails also do harm. The vision presents destructive power from both the front and the rear.

The movement from the fifth trumpet to the sixth is a serious escalation. The locusts were forbidden to kill; this army does kill. The passage identifies the deadly agents as the fire, smoke and sulfur, but it does not directly identify a modern nation, weapon or military technology.

The final verses turn attention from the army to the survivors. They continue worshiping demons and lifeless idols, and they refuse to turn from murder, sorcery, sexual immorality and theft. The chapter ends with the condition of their hearts. Surviving a judgment has not brought them to abandon what is wrong.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Historical readings connect the army with different conquests. Wesley relates this woe to early Arab expansion, while Gill favors the Ottoman Turks. Their explanations treat the imagery and its timing as referring to events in history, although they disagree about which events.

Future readings also differ. Walvoord sees a future destructive force and considers whether the imagery could describe modern warfare. David Guzik discusses that possibility but favors a demonic army. The USCCB notes explain the vision as a diabolical attack pictured through the threat of a Parthian invasion. These readings should not be merged into a single agreed identification.

The two hundred million may be understood as an exact number or as a way of expressing an overwhelming force. The closing refusal to repent remains central across the readings. Identifying the army does not remove the warning about people who cling to false worship and destructive conduct even when confronted with judgment.
passages.god_plan_html:
The horses and fire have a scriptural parallel in Joel 2:1–11, where an overwhelming force advances amid darkness and devastation. The resemblance places this vision within the Bible’s larger warnings about the Day of the LORD. It does not, by itself, establish that Joel and John are describing the very same army.

The survivors’ response also recalls Pharaoh in Exodus 9:27–35: even after acknowledging wrongdoing during a plague, he returns to resistance. Psalm 115:4–8 exposes the helplessness of idols made by human hands. Revelation brings those themes together: people can witness great power and still keep trusting what cannot save them.

Romans 2:4–8 connects God’s patience with the call to repentance and warns against a hard, unrepentant heart. The wider purpose is more than bringing calamity to an end. It calls for a real turning toward God, including a change in worship and conduct. The passage presses that question on its readers while describing the refusal of the people in the vision.

passages.title: Revelation 10:1-7
passages.section_title: What does the mighty angel announce about God’s purpose?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then I saw another mighty angel coming down from heaven, wrapped in a cloud, with a rainbow above his head. His face was like the sun, and his legs were like pillars of fire. 2 He held in his hand a small scroll, which lay open. He placed his right foot on the sea and his left foot on the land. 3 Then he cried out in a loud voice like the roar of a lion. And when he cried out, the seven thunders sounded their voices. 4 When the seven thunders had spoken, I was about to put it in writing. But I heard a voice from heaven saying, “Seal up what the seven thunders have said, and do not write it down.” 5 Then the angel I had seen standing on the sea and on the land lifted up his right hand to heaven. 6 And he swore by Him who lives forever and ever, who created heaven and everything in it, the earth and everything in it, and the sea and everything in it: “There will be no more delay! 7 But in the days of the voice of the seventh angel, when he begins to sound his trumpet, the mystery of God will be fulfilled, just as He proclaimed to His servants the prophets.”
paragraphs: 1 Then I saw another mighty angel coming down from heaven, wrapped in a cloud, with a rainbow above his head. His face was like the sun, and his legs were like pillars of fire. 2 He held in his hand a small scroll, which lay open. He placed his right foot on the sea and his left foot on the land. 3 Then he cried out in a loud voice like the roar of a lion. And when he cried out, the seven thunders sounded their voices. 4 When the seven thunders had spoken, I was about to put it in writing. But I heard a voice from heaven saying, “Seal up what the seven thunders have said, and do not write it down.”

5 Then the angel I had seen standing on the sea and on the land lifted up his right hand to heaven. 6 And he swore by Him who lives forever and ever, who created heaven and everything in it, the earth and everything in it, and the sea and everything in it: “There will be no more delay! 7 But in the days of the voice of the seventh angel, when he begins to sound his trumpet, the mystery of God will be fulfilled, just as He proclaimed to His servants the prophets.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Before the seventh trumpet sounds, the vision pauses for another scene. A mighty angel descends from heaven with a cloud, a rainbow, a sunlike face and legs like pillars of fire. He holds an open small scroll and stands with one foot on the sea and the other on the land. The scene presents a messenger of extraordinary authority.

The Greek word biblaridion means a little book or scroll; see Thayer’s entry. The description tells us that it is small and open. It does not give its full contents or explicitly say that it is the same scroll seen in chapter 5.

When the angel cries out, seven thunders speak. John is ready to write their words, but a voice from heaven tells him to seal them up and leave them unwritten. Revelation therefore includes an express limit on what is disclosed. Readers are told that the thunders spoke, but are not given their message.

The angel raises his right hand and swears by the eternal Creator of heaven, earth and sea. There will be no more delay: in the days of the seventh angel’s trumpet, God’s mystery will be fulfilled as He announced to His prophets. The focus turns from the withheld words to the promise that God will complete His purpose.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The angel’s identity is disputed. Gill understands the figure as Christ, pointing to His majesty and authority. Wesley and Walvoord favor a created angel serving God, noting especially his oath by the Creator. The description has features associated with divine glory, but the passage itself calls the figure an angel and does not name him.

Readers also differ over the scroll. Gill and Wesley connect it with the earlier sealed scroll, now open and with much of its message already unfolded. Walvoord sees no certain identification with that scroll. The difference should be kept open rather than settled simply by the use of the word small.

The older wording about time being no more has sometimes been read as the end of time itself. Gill and Walvoord instead explain an end to delay before God’s purpose is fulfilled, although they place that fulfillment within different accounts of the coming kingdom. Wesley offers a historical calculation involving a long prophetic period. That calculation belongs to his interpretation, rather than to the BSB wording quoted above.
passages.god_plan_html:
The raised hand and oath closely parallel Daniel 12:4–10. There, a figure above the river raises his hands and swears by the One who lives forever, while Daniel is told that words are sealed until the time of the end. Revelation draws on that earlier picture of God’s authority over the completion of events. The resemblance does not require us to identify the angel by name or imagine a physical scroll passed from Daniel to John.

The promise that God’s mystery will be fulfilled also belongs within the larger purpose stated in Ephesians 1:9–10: God intends to bring all things in heaven and on earth together in Christ. Revelation’s announcement gives confidence that His purposes will reach their goal. It does not disclose what John was forbidden to write or supply a date for readers to calculate.

passages.title: Revelation 10:8-11
passages.section_title: Why does John eat a scroll that tastes sweet but turns bitter?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 Then the voice that I had heard from heaven spoke to me again, saying, “Go, take the small scroll that lies open in the hand of the angel standing on the sea and on the land.” 9 And I went to the angel and said, “Give me the small scroll.” “Take it and eat it,” he said. “It will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be as sweet as honey.” 10 So I took the small scroll from the angel’s hand and ate it, and it was as sweet as honey in my mouth. But when I had eaten it, my stomach turned bitter. 11 And they told me, “You must prophesy again about many peoples and nations and tongues and kings.”
paragraphs: 8 Then the voice that I had heard from heaven spoke to me again, saying, “Go, take the small scroll that lies open in the hand of the angel standing on the sea and on the land.” 9 And I went to the angel and said, “Give me the small scroll.” “Take it and eat it,” he said. “It will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be as sweet as honey.” 10 So I took the small scroll from the angel’s hand and ate it, and it was as sweet as honey in my mouth. But when I had eaten it, my stomach turned bitter.
11 And they told me, “You must prophesy again about many peoples and nations and tongues and kings.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The voice from heaven now tells John to take the open scroll from the angel. John goes to him and asks for it. He is then told to eat it, with a warning that it will taste like honey but make his stomach bitter.

John obeys, and both parts happen as promised. The sweetness does not cancel the bitterness, and the bitterness does not make the message untrue. His experience joins the pleasure of receiving a message from God with the difficulty of what that message contains and what delivering it may involve.

The scene ends with a renewed task: John must prophesy again about many peoples, nations, languages and kings. Eating the scroll prepares for speaking. He receives the message before being sent to deliver it, and the scope reaches well beyond one local community.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The main explanations share a common picture: John must take God’s message to heart before proclaiming it. Wesley connects the sweetness with the good things promised and the bitterness with coming evils. Gill includes the joy of God’s kingdom alongside suffering and resistance to the message. Walvoord likewise emphasizes both the preciousness of God’s word and the grief associated with its judgments and the messenger’s trials.

The USCCB notes connect the sweetness with God’s people finally overcoming and the bitterness with their suffering. These explanations place the emphasis somewhat differently, but they do not require a denomination-by-denomination division. The central movement is the same: John receives the message, experiences both sweetness and bitterness, and is commissioned to speak again.
passages.god_plan_html:
The direct scriptural parallel is Ezekiel 2:8–10 and 3:1–11. Ezekiel receives a scroll containing lamentation, mourning and woe, yet finds it sweet as honey. He is then sent to speak God’s words to Israel, whether they listen or refuse. Revelation presents John in that recognizable pattern of a prophet receiving a message before carrying it to others.

There is also a difference in the stated scope. Ezekiel is sent to the house of Israel; John is told to prophesy about many peoples, nations, languages and kings. God’s dealings with the world include making His message known across human boundaries. The messenger’s responsibility is to receive and faithfully deliver it, including the parts that bring sorrow as well as those that give hope.

passages.title: Revelation 11:1-6
passages.section_title: What do the measured temple and the two witnesses show?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then I was given a measuring rod like a staff and was told, “Go and measure the temple of God and the altar, and count the number of worshipers there. 2 But exclude the courtyard outside the temple. Do not measure it, because it has been given over to the nations, and they will trample the holy city for 42 months. 3 And I will empower my two witnesses, and they will prophesy for 1,260 days, clothed in sackcloth.” 4 These witnesses are the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth. 5 If anyone wants to harm them, fire proceeds from their mouths and devours their enemies. In this way, anyone who wants to harm them must be killed. 6 These witnesses have power to shut the sky so that no rain will fall during the days of their prophecy, and power to turn the waters into blood and to strike the earth with every kind of plague as often as they wish.
paragraphs: 1 Then I was given a measuring rod like a staff and was told, “Go and measure the temple of God and the altar, and count the number of worshipers there. 2 But exclude the courtyard outside the temple. Do not measure it, because it has been given over to the nations, and they will trample the holy city for 42 months.

3 And I will empower my two witnesses, and they will prophesy for 1,260 days, clothed in sackcloth.” 4 These witnesses are the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth. 5 If anyone wants to harm them, fire proceeds from their mouths and devours their enemies. In this way, anyone who wants to harm them must be killed. 6 These witnesses have power to shut the sky so that no rain will fall during the days of their prophecy, and power to turn the waters into blood and to strike the earth with every kind of plague as often as they wish.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
John is given a measuring rod and told to measure God’s temple and altar and count the worshipers. The outer courtyard is excluded because it has been given to the nations, who will trample the holy city for forty-two months. The vision distinguishes what is measured from what is handed over to hostile powers.

The focus then turns to two witnesses who receive authority to prophesy for 1,260 days. They wear sackcloth, clothing associated with mourning. Their task is to speak during a period of opposition, with power to defend their testimony.

The witnesses are called two olive trees and two lampstands standing before the Lord of the earth. This language points back to Zechariah 4, where olive trees stand beside a lampstand and God promises to complete His work by His Spirit. Their strength comes from the One they serve.

Fire destroys anyone seeking to harm them. They can prevent rain, turn water into blood and strike the earth with plagues. The description recalls powers associated with Elijah and Moses. It shows that resistance cannot silence their testimony before its appointed work is done.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The temple receives different readings. Wesley expects a temple in Jerusalem connected with Ezekiel’s vision. Gill understands it as the church being ordered according to Scripture. The USCCB notes understand the temple and worshipers as pictures of God’s faithful people. These explanations differ over whether the scene concerns a building or uses temple imagery to describe a community.

The witnesses are likewise understood as either two individuals or a larger body of witnesses. Wesley expects two prophets but rejects certainty that they are Moses and Elijah. Gill understands a continuing succession of faithful churches and ministers. The USCCB notes favor the church bearing witness, especially through its martyrs.

Walvoord favors a future temple and two individual prophets whose names are not disclosed. He also acknowledges disagreement over which half of a future seven-year period their ministry occupies, favoring the latter half. The passage’s stated periods should be distinguished from the larger timelines teachers build around them.
passages.god_plan_html:
Zechariah 4:1–14 supplies more than a visual resemblance. Its message to Zerubbabel connects the olive trees and lampstand with work accomplished by God’s Spirit. Revelation draws on that picture as it presents witnesses equipped to speak in the face of opposition. The connection highlights God’s provision for His work, without settling every question about the witnesses’ identity.

The powers given to them also recall Elijah’s announcement of drought in 1 Kings 17:1 and the water turned to blood in Exodus 7:19–21. These are scriptural parallels with earlier confrontations between God’s messengers and resistant rulers. The resemblance places the witnesses in that larger story of God making His authority known; it does not by itself prove that Moses and Elijah have returned.

passages.title: Revelation 11:7-14
passages.section_title: What happens when the witnesses are killed and God raises them?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 When the two witnesses have finished their testimony, the beast that comes up from the Abyss will wage war with them, and will overpower and kill them. 8 Their bodies will lie in the street of the great city—figuratively called Sodom and Egypt—where their Lord was also crucified. 9 For three and a half days all peoples and tribes and tongues and nations will view their bodies and will not permit them to be laid in a tomb. 10 And those who dwell on the earth will gloat over them and celebrate and send one another gifts, because these two prophets had tormented them. 11 But after the three and a half days, the breath of life from God entered the two witnesses, and they stood on their feet, and great fear fell upon those who saw them. 12 And the witnesses heard a loud voice from heaven saying, “Come up here.” And they went up to heaven in a cloud as their enemies watched them. 13 And in that hour there was a great earthquake, and a tenth of the city collapsed. Seven thousand were killed in the quake, and the rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven. 14 The second woe has passed. Behold, the third woe is coming shortly.
paragraphs: 7 When the two witnesses have finished their testimony, the beast that comes up from the Abyss will wage war with them, and will overpower and kill them. 8 Their bodies will lie in the street of the great city—figuratively called Sodom and Egypt—where their Lord was also crucified. 9 For three and a half days all peoples and tribes and tongues and nations will view their bodies and will not permit them to be laid in a tomb. 10 And those who dwell on the earth will gloat over them and celebrate and send one another gifts, because these two prophets had tormented them.

11 But after the three and a half days, the breath of life from God entered the two witnesses, and they stood on their feet, and great fear fell upon those who saw them. 12 And the witnesses heard a loud voice from heaven saying, “Come up here.” And they went up to heaven in a cloud as their enemies watched them. 13 And in that hour there was a great earthquake, and a tenth of the city collapsed. Seven thousand were killed in the quake, and the rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven. 14 The second woe has passed. Behold, the third woe is coming shortly.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The witnesses’ death comes only after they finish their testimony. The beast from the Abyss wages war against them and kills them. Their bodies remain exposed in the street of the great city for three and a half days, while people from many nations look on and refuse them burial.

The city is figuratively called Sodom and Egypt and is described as the place where their Lord was crucified. Those names connect the setting with rebellion and oppression. The witnesses’ opponents celebrate their deaths and exchange gifts, believing the prophets who tormented them have been removed.

The celebration ends when God gives the witnesses life. They stand, hear a voice calling them upward, and ascend to heaven in a cloud while their enemies watch. The power that killed them cannot prevent God from raising and receiving them.

An earthquake then destroys a tenth of the city and kills seven thousand people. The survivors are terrified and give glory to the God of heaven. The second woe ends, and the third is announced as coming soon. John records the survivors’ response without spelling out every question about their subsequent lives.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley reads the deaths, return to life and ascent as events involving two prophets in Jerusalem. Gill understands the witnesses more broadly as faithful churches and ministers; he reads the great city in terms of Rome and its religious power. The USCCB notes also understand the city symbolically, relating it to Rome’s opposition to God and His witnesses.

The survivors’ response is also disputed. Wesley and Gill understand their giving glory to God as genuine conversion. Walvoord, while expecting an actual resurrection and earthquake, understands the response as acknowledgment of God’s power rather than clear evidence of faith in Christ. The passage’s words should remain visible alongside that difference: the survivors fear and give God glory.

The vision’s broad reach has prompted suggestions about how people see the bodies, including modern broadcasting. Such suggestions concern the means by which the event might be witnessed. John describes the public exposure and international response without naming a communication technology.
passages.god_plan_html:
The breath entering the witnesses and their standing on their feet closely parallel Ezekiel 37:1–14. In Ezekiel, God explains the dry bones as the house of Israel, whose hope has been lost, and promises to give His people life. Revelation uses a recognizable picture of life restored by God. The parallel does not erase Ezekiel’s own explanation or make the two passages identical in every detail.

The larger pattern is that human opposition does not have the last word over God’s servants. The witnesses finish their task, suffer death and are publicly received by God. Their enemies’ celebration proves premature. This part of the vision prepares for the next announcement: the kingdom belongs to the Lord and His Christ, rather than to the powers that oppose them.

passages.title: Revelation 11:15-19
passages.section_title: What does heaven celebrate when the seventh trumpet sounds?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 Then the seventh angel sounded his trumpet, and loud voices called out in heaven: “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ, and He will reign forever and ever.” 16 And the twenty-four elders who sit on their thrones before God fell on their faces and worshiped God, 17 saying: “We give thanks to You, O Lord God Almighty, the One who is and who was, because You have taken Your great power and have begun to reign. 18 The nations were enraged, and Your wrath has come. The time has come to judge the dead and to reward Your servants the prophets, as well as the saints and those who fear Your name, both small and great— and to destroy those who destroy the earth.” 19 Then the temple of God in heaven was opened, and the ark of His covenant appeared in His temple. And there were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, an earthquake, and a great hailstorm.
paragraphs: 15 Then the seventh angel sounded his trumpet, and loud voices called out in heaven: “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ, and He will reign forever and ever.” 16 And the twenty-four elders who sit on their thrones before God fell on their faces and worshiped God, 17 saying: “We give thanks to You, O Lord God Almighty, the One who is and who was, because You have taken Your great power and have begun to reign. 18 The nations were enraged, and Your wrath has come. The time has come to judge the dead and to reward Your servants the prophets, as well as the saints and those who fear Your name, both small and great— and to destroy those who destroy the earth.”

19 Then the temple of God in heaven was opened, and the ark of His covenant appeared in His temple. And there were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, an earthquake, and a great hailstorm.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The seventh trumpet is answered by loud voices in heaven announcing that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of the Lord and His Christ. The announcement brings the promise of completion in chapter 10 into focus: His reign will endure forever.

The twenty-four elders fall before God and give thanks that He has taken His great power and begun to reign. They name the conflict between the enraged nations and God’s judgment. Their praise includes the judgment of the dead, the reward of God’s servants and the destruction of those who destroy the earth.

The people named for reward include prophets, saints and all who fear God’s name, small and great. The vision does not restrict God’s recognition to people of public importance. The same scene announces accountability for those who bring destruction.

God’s heavenly temple opens, revealing the ark of His covenant. Lightning, rumblings, thunder, an earthquake and hail accompany the scene. The chapter moves from a threatened holy city and slain witnesses to heaven’s declaration of God’s enduring rule and His covenant.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The main readings agree that this trumpet announces God’s victory and enduring reign. Wesley understands the proclamation as introducing events unfolded through the remainder of the book. Walvoord likewise sees an announcement of the coming kingdom before all the judgments leading to it have been narrated. Heaven celebrates the certain outcome while the vision still has more to disclose.

Teachers differ over how to arrange the later judgments and the thousand years mentioned in chapter 20. Those questions should be distinguished from the shared emphasis here: God judges evil, honors His servants and reigns through His Christ. The covenant ark is read as assurance of God’s faithfulness, rather than permission to identify a present earthly location for the lost ark.
passages.god_plan_html:
The nations’ anger and the rule of God’s Anointed One recall Psalm 2. There, rulers gather against the LORD and His Anointed, but their resistance cannot overturn His purpose. Revelation’s announcement carries that conflict toward its promised outcome: earthly rebellion will not determine the world’s final ruler.

The everlasting kingdom also corresponds to Daniel 7:13–14, where one like a son of man receives dominion over all peoples, nations and languages, and His kingdom will never be destroyed. These connections explain why the scene is a reason for worship. God’s larger purpose includes justice, the vindication of His servants and a reign that hostile powers cannot bring to an end.

passages.title: Revelation 12:1-6
passages.section_title: Who are the woman, the child and the dragon?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 And a great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed in the sun, with the moon under her feet and a crown of twelve stars on her head. 2 She was pregnant and crying out in the pain and agony of giving birth. 3 Then another sign appeared in heaven: a huge red dragon with seven heads, ten horns, and seven royal crowns on his heads. 4 His tail swept a third of the stars from the sky, hurling them to the earth. And the dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, ready to devour her child as soon as she gave birth. 5 And she gave birth to a son, a male child, who will rule all the nations with an iron scepter. And her child was caught up to God and to His throne. 6 And the woman fled into the wilderness, where God had prepared a place for her to be nourished for 1,260 days.
paragraphs: 1 And a great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed in the sun, with the moon under her feet and a crown of twelve stars on her head. 2 She was pregnant and crying out in the pain and agony of giving birth.

3 Then another sign appeared in heaven: a huge red dragon with seven heads, ten horns, and seven royal crowns on his heads. 4 His tail swept a third of the stars from the sky, hurling them to the earth. And the dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, ready to devour her child as soon as she gave birth.

5 And she gave birth to a son, a male child, who will rule all the nations with an iron scepter. And her child was caught up to God and to His throne. 6 And the woman fled into the wilderness, where God had prepared a place for her to be nourished for 1,260 days.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
John sees two great signs: a pregnant woman clothed in the sun, with the moon beneath her feet and twelve stars on her head, and a red dragon with seven heads, ten horns and seven royal crowns. The scene presents a conflict around the birth of her child.

The dragon sweeps a third of the stars from the sky and waits to devour the child. The attempt fails. The woman gives birth to a son destined to rule the nations with an iron scepter, and he is caught up to God and His throne. The language of royal rule echoes Psalm 2:7–9.

The woman then escapes into the wilderness, where God has prepared a place to nourish her for 1,260 days. The passage moves quickly from the threatened birth to the child’s place with God and the woman’s protection. Its purpose is to show the conflict and God’s provision, rather than retell every event in the child’s life.

The dragon’s identity is made explicit later in the chapter: he is the devil and Satan. The woman’s identity is expressed through pictures that readers connect with other biblical passages, and that is where the main differences in interpretation arise.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Walvoord understands the woman as Israel, from whom the Messiah comes, and the child as Christ. He connects her sun, moon and stars with Joseph’s family in Genesis 37. Wesley understands her as the church rooted in Israel and enlarged through Gentile believers; he reads the child especially in terms of Christ’s kingdom.

The USCCB notes understand the woman as God’s people across the Old and New Testaments. In Catholic teaching, a further connection is made with Mary. Benedict XVI explains the woman as representing both the mother of the Redeemer and the whole church. In that reading, the personal and community meanings belong together.

The central difference is therefore not simply whether someone notices that Jesus was born to Mary. It concerns how the woman’s whole story—giving birth, fleeing and having other children—represents Mary, Israel and the church. The readings should be compared on that wider basis rather than reduced to a choice between a real woman and a symbol.
passages.god_plan_html:
The heavenly lights recall Genesis 37:9–11, where Joseph dreams of the sun, moon and stars, and Jacob recognizes a reference to his family. This is a genuine biblical parallel behind the connection with Israel. It supplies context for the picture without, on its own, answering every question about the woman’s meaning.

The conflict between the dragon, the woman and her child also recalls Genesis 3:14–15, with its hostility between the serpent and the woman and between their offspring. Revelation identifies its dragon as the ancient serpent and presents the child as the ruler promised in Psalm 2. Read together, these passages connect the vision with the larger biblical story of opposition to God’s purpose and the triumph of His appointed ruler.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Revelation 12:7-12
passages.section_title: How is the accuser defeated, and why does his defeat bring a warning?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 Then a war broke out in heaven: Michael and his angels fought against the dragon, and the dragon and his angels fought back. 8 But the dragon was not strong enough, and no longer was any place found in heaven for him and his angels. 9 And the great dragon was hurled down—that ancient serpent called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world. He was hurled to the earth, and his angels with him. 10 And I heard a loud voice in heaven saying: “Now have come the salvation and the power and the kingdom of our God, and the authority of His Christ. For the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down— he who accuses them day and night before our God. 11 They have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony. And they did not love their lives so as to shy away from death. 12 Therefore rejoice, O heavens, and you who dwell in them! But woe to the earth and the sea; with great fury the devil has come down to you, knowing he has only a short time.”
paragraphs: 7 Then a war broke out in heaven: Michael and his angels fought against the dragon, and the dragon and his angels fought back. 8 But the dragon was not strong enough, and no longer was any place found in heaven for him and his angels. 9 And the great dragon was hurled down—that ancient serpent called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world. He was hurled to the earth, and his angels with him.

10 And I heard a loud voice in heaven saying: “Now have come the salvation and the power and the kingdom of our God, and the authority of His Christ. For the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down— he who accuses them day and night before our God. 11 They have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony. And they did not love their lives so as to shy away from death. 12 Therefore rejoice, O heavens, and you who dwell in them! But woe to the earth and the sea; with great fury the devil has come down to you, knowing he has only a short time.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
War breaks out in heaven. Michael and his angels fight the dragon and his angels, and the dragon loses. He and his angels are thrown down to the earth, with no place remaining for them in heaven. John explicitly names the defeated dragon as the ancient serpent, the devil and Satan.

A loud voice announces salvation, God’s kingdom and the authority of His Christ. It also explains one reason for heaven’s joy: the one who accused God’s people day and night has been thrown down. The battle concerns more than force; it includes accusations made against those who belong to God.

The victory of God’s people is attributed to the Lamb’s blood and to their faithful testimony. They remain faithful even when faced with death. In this vision, overcoming evil can include suffering martyrdom; victory is not defined simply as escaping harm.

Heaven is called to rejoice, but earth and sea receive a warning. The devil comes down in fury because he knows his time is short. His defeat is certain, yet his remaining activity brings danger to those he opposes.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Readings differ over when this heavenly conflict takes place. Walvoord expects a future expulsion connected with the great tribulation. Wesley relates the vision to the advance and trials of Christ’s kingdom in church history. Both take the ending of Satan’s role as accuser seriously, but place it within different timelines.

The USCCB notes connect the serpent with Genesis and the expulsion with Jesus’ words about Satan falling from heaven. Such connections encourage readers to understand the scene alongside the wider biblical account of his defeat, rather than as an isolated description of heavenly warfare.

The passage itself states the foundation of the believers’ victory: the blood of the Lamb and their testimony, maintained even in the face of death. It does not give readers a new set of words for commanding angels or promise that faithful believers will never suffer.
passages.god_plan_html:
In John 12:31–33, Jesus connects the judgment of the world’s ruler with His own coming death. Revelation likewise places the Lamb’s blood at the heart of victory over the accuser. This connection keeps attention on what Christ has accomplished while readers consider the vision’s disputed timing.

Romans 8:33–39 asks who can bring a charge against God’s people when God declares them righteous and Christ, who died and rose, speaks for them. It also names persecution and death without treating them as separation from His love. That gives fuller meaning to Revelation’s picture of overcoming: the enemy may bring suffering, but cannot overturn what God has done through Christ.

passages.title: Revelation 12:13-17
passages.section_title: How does God protect the woman when the dragon pursues her?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 13 And when the dragon saw that he had been thrown to the earth, he pursued the woman who had given birth to the male child. 14 But the woman was given two wings of a great eagle to fly from the presence of the serpent to her place in the wilderness, where she was nourished for a time, and times, and half a time. 15 Then from his mouth the serpent spewed water like a river to overtake the woman and sweep her away in the torrent. 16 But the earth helped the woman and opened its mouth to swallow up the river that the dragon had poured from his mouth. 17 And the dragon was enraged at the woman and went to make war with the rest of her children, who keep the commandments of God and hold to the testimony of Jesus. And the dragon stood on the shore of the sea.
paragraphs: 13 And when the dragon saw that he had been thrown to the earth, he pursued the woman who had given birth to the male child. 14 But the woman was given two wings of a great eagle to fly from the presence of the serpent to her place in the wilderness, where she was nourished for a time, and times, and half a time.

15 Then from his mouth the serpent spewed water like a river to overtake the woman and sweep her away in the torrent. 16 But the earth helped the woman and opened its mouth to swallow up the river that the dragon had poured from his mouth. 17 And the dragon was enraged at the woman and went to make war with the rest of her children, who keep the commandments of God and hold to the testimony of Jesus. And the dragon stood on the shore of the sea.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Thrown down to the earth, the dragon turns against the woman who bore the child. She receives the wings of a great eagle and escapes into the wilderness, where she is nourished away from the serpent for a time, times and half a time. This develops the earlier account of her flight and care in verse 6.

The serpent sends water like a river after her, seeking to sweep her away. The earth helps her by opening its mouth and swallowing the river. The attack is powerful, but it fails to remove the protection given to her.

The dragon then makes war on the rest of her children. John describes them as people who keep God’s commandments and hold to the testimony of Jesus. Both descriptions belong to the group named in the verse. Protection of the woman does not bring an end to all suffering among those associated with her.

The BSB includes the dragon’s position on the shore of the sea at the end of verse 17. That closing detail prepares for the next chapter’s beast rising from the sea. Some Bibles number the shoreline sentence separately as verse 18.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The woman’s identity continues to shape the explanation. Walvoord understands God preserving Israel during future persecution, with the remaining children especially identified as Jewish believers in Jesus. Wesley understands the protection and attacks through the history of the church, including Christians living under hostile rulers.

The details of the escape are also read differently. Wesley connects the eagle’s wings with the help of imperial powers. Walvoord favors a symbolic understanding of the flood as the enemy’s attempt to destroy Israel. The USCCB notes understand the eagle as a picture of swift divine help and distinguish God’s preservation of the church from the suffering individual Christians may endure.

The text names no modern aircraft, country or desert refuge. Proposed locations and political identifications should therefore be presented as interpretations. What is clear in the scene is the failure of the dragon’s attempt to sweep away the woman, followed by his continuing hostility toward her children.
passages.god_plan_html:
The eagle’s wings have a strong parallel in Exodus 19:3–6. God describes bringing Israel out of Egypt as carrying His people on eagles’ wings and bringing them to Himself. Revelation reuses that recognizable picture of rescue as a woman escapes a hostile pursuer and is sustained in the wilderness.

The parallel connects the woman’s preservation with God’s earlier rescue and care for His people. Yet the final verse also keeps persecution in view. God’s larger purpose is not defeated by the enemy, even while His people face danger. The vision holds protection and costly faithfulness together as the story moves toward the dragon’s further attempts to oppose God.

passages.title: Revelation 13:1-10
passages.section_title: Why does the beast’s power lead people into false worship?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then I saw a beast with ten horns and seven heads rising out of the sea. There were ten royal crowns on its horns and blasphemous names on its heads. 2 The beast I saw was like a leopard, with the feet of a bear and the mouth of a lion. And the dragon gave the beast his power and his throne and great authority. 3 One of the heads of the beast appeared to have been mortally wounded. But the mortal wound was healed, and the whole world marveled and followed the beast. 4 They worshiped the dragon who had given authority to the beast, and they worshiped the beast, saying, “Who is like the beast, and who can wage war against it?” 5 The beast was given a mouth to speak arrogant and blasphemous words, and authority to act for 42 months. 6 And the beast opened its mouth to speak blasphemies against God and to slander His name and His tabernacle—those who dwell in heaven. 7 Then the beast was permitted to wage war against the saints and to conquer them, and it was given authority over every tribe and people and tongue and nation. 8 And all who dwell on the earth will worship the beast—all whose names have not been written from the foundation of the world in the Book of Life belonging to the Lamb who was slain. 9 He who has an ear, let him hear: 10 “If anyone is destined for captivity, into captivity he will go; if anyone is to die by the sword, by the sword he must be killed.” Here is a call for the perseverance and faith of the saints.
paragraphs: 1 Then I saw a beast with ten horns and seven heads rising out of the sea. There were ten royal crowns on its horns and blasphemous names on its heads. 2 The beast I saw was like a leopard, with the feet of a bear and the mouth of a lion. And the dragon gave the beast his power and his throne and great authority. 3 One of the heads of the beast appeared to have been mortally wounded. But the mortal wound was healed, and the whole world marveled and followed the beast. 4 They worshiped the dragon who had given authority to the beast, and they worshiped the beast, saying, “Who is like the beast, and who can wage war against it?”

5 The beast was given a mouth to speak arrogant and blasphemous words, and authority to act for 42 months. 6 And the beast opened its mouth to speak blasphemies against God and to slander His name and His tabernacle—those who dwell in heaven. 7 Then the beast was permitted to wage war against the saints and to conquer them, and it was given authority over every tribe and people and tongue and nation. 8 And all who dwell on the earth will worship the beast—all whose names have not been written from the foundation of the world in the Book of Life belonging to the Lamb who was slain.

9 He who has an ear, let him hear: 10 “If anyone is destined for captivity, into captivity he will go; if anyone is to die by the sword, by the sword he must be killed.” Here is a call for the perseverance and faith of the saints.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The dragon’s hostility now takes shape through a beast rising from the sea. It has seven heads, ten horns and royal crowns, with names that dishonor God. Its body combines a leopard, a bear and a lion. These features recall the beasts in Daniel 7, where violent kingdoms oppose God’s people.

The dragon gives the beast power, a throne and authority. One head appears mortally wounded, yet the wound is healed. The world marvels and follows the beast. Admiration becomes worship of both the beast and the dragon behind it, expressed in the question of who could possibly defeat such a power.

The beast’s character appears in what it says and does. It speaks arrogantly against God, slanders His name and dwelling, and wages war on the saints. Its authority reaches across peoples and nations, but its stated period of action is forty-two months. The vision describes a fearsome power within an appointed limit.

Those who worship it are contrasted with those whose names are written in the Lamb’s Book of Life. The slain Lamb remains the point of belonging for God’s people, even when the beast appears successful against them. The closing call is to hear and endure faithfully through captivity and death.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The main differences concern the beast’s identity and timing. The USCCB notes understand the first beast as the ancient Roman Empire and connect its heads with emperors. Wesley, reading the vision through later church history, identifies it with papal political power. These are different historical explanations, rather than a single shared identification of Rome.

Walvoord expects a future ruler and revived Roman Empire. He favors understanding the healed wound as the empire’s recovery. David Guzik instead favors a ruler who suffers a mortal wound and is healed, presenting an imitation of Christ’s death and resurrection. Thus even readers expecting a future fulfillment differ over the wound.

The final warning concerns perseverance under oppression. Older commentaries sometimes discuss wording about the captor becoming a captive or the killer being killed. The BSB quoted here speaks of those destined for captivity or death. That wording matters when comparing an explanation about judgment on persecutors with one about the endurance of persecuted believers.
passages.god_plan_html:
Daniel 7:1–8 and 21–27 provides a strong scriptural parallel: beasts, horns, arrogant speech and war against the saints. Daniel’s vision also gives the outcome. The hostile power loses its dominion, and God gives an enduring kingdom to His people. Revelation’s beast should be read against that larger promise, rather than as a power capable of overthrowing God’s purpose.

There is also a contrast with the Lamb in Revelation 5:6–10. The Lamb was slain and stands before God, receiving praise because He purchased people for God. The beast’s healed wound attracts a different worship, directed toward the dragon. This is a literary parallel and contrast: impressive power must be judged by the one it serves and the worship it demands.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Revelation 13:11-18
passages.section_title: How do signs, an image and a mark enforce worship of the beast?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 Then I saw another beast rising out of the earth. This beast had two horns like a lamb, but spoke like a dragon. 12 And this beast exercised all the authority of the first beast and caused the earth and those who dwell in it to worship the first beast, whose mortal wound had been healed. 13 And the second beast performed great signs, even causing fire from heaven to come down to earth in the presence of the people. 14 Because of the signs it was given to perform on behalf of the first beast, it deceived those who dwell on the earth, telling them to make an image to the beast that had been wounded by the sword and yet had lived. 15 The second beast was permitted to give breath to the image of the first beast, so that the image could speak and cause all who refused to worship it to be killed. 16 And the second beast required all people, small and great, rich and poor, free and slave, to receive a mark on their right hand or on their forehead, 17 so that no one could buy or sell unless he had the mark—the name of the beast or the number of its name. 18 Here is a call for wisdom: Let the one who has insight calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man, and that number is 666.
paragraphs: 11 Then I saw another beast rising out of the earth. This beast had two horns like a lamb, but spoke like a dragon. 12 And this beast exercised all the authority of the first beast and caused the earth and those who dwell in it to worship the first beast, whose mortal wound had been healed. 13 And the second beast performed great signs, even causing fire from heaven to come down to earth in the presence of the people. 14 Because of the signs it was given to perform on behalf of the first beast, it deceived those who dwell on the earth, telling them to make an image to the beast that had been wounded by the sword and yet had lived.

15 The second beast was permitted to give breath to the image of the first beast, so that the image could speak and cause all who refused to worship it to be killed. 16 And the second beast required all people, small and great, rich and poor, free and slave, to receive a mark on their right hand or on their forehead, 17 so that no one could buy or sell unless he had the mark—the name of the beast or the number of its name.
18 Here is a call for wisdom: Let the one who has insight calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man, and that number is 666.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
A second beast rises from the earth. It has horns like a lamb but speaks like a dragon. Its appearance and voice point in different directions. Its actions reveal its purpose: it exercises the first beast’s authority and leads people to worship that beast.

Its signs include fire descending from heaven in public view. These displays deceive people and support the making of an image of the first beast. The image is given breath and can speak, and those who refuse to worship it face death. The account links the signs with the false worship they promote.

The pressure also reaches ordinary economic life. People of every social standing are required to receive a mark on the right hand or forehead, and buying or selling depends on having it. The Greek word charagma means a stamped or impressed mark; see Thayer’s entry. Here its meaning is supplied by the surrounding scene: it identifies people with the beast’s name or the number of its name.

The chapter ends by calling for wisdom and understanding to calculate the number, 666. The number belongs within the account of the beast, its name and the allegiance it demands. John gives a challenge to discernment rather than an explanation of the mark’s physical manufacture.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Walvoord expects a future false prophet supporting the first beast, with the mark identifying its worshipers. Wesley connects the mark with acknowledgment of papal authority and succession. The USCCB notes place the second beast within the setting of false prophecy and pressure to worship the emperor. These readings differ over the setting while recognizing the connection between deception, worship and coercion.

The number also receives different explanations. The USCCB notes favor a calculation using Caesar Nero’s name in Hebrew letters. Wesley takes 666 as a period of years. Walvoord favors its significance as a human number falling short of divine perfection. These are proposed explanations; the passage itself gives the number and the instruction to calculate.

An early Christian discussion shows why caution is appropriate. In Against Heresies 5.30, Irenaeus considers several Greek names that total 666, but declines to pronounce a certain name. Letter values were therefore not confined to Hebrew, and obtaining the total does not by itself establish an identification.
passages.god_plan_html:
The forced worship of an image recalls Daniel 3:4–6 and 16–18. There, a ruler commands people of many nations and languages to worship his statue under threat of death. Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego refuse, whether or not God delivers them. Revelation continues that recognizable conflict between imposed worship and faithfulness to God.

The deceptive signs also fit the warning in 2 Thessalonians 2:8–12, where satanic power and wonders accompany rejection of the truth. The same passage promises the lawless one’s defeat by Jesus. The wider picture joins discernment with hope: a display of power does not establish that its message comes from God, and the power opposing Him will not endure.
