deeper_study.title: Should We Seek Signs From God?

passages.title: Revelation 14:1-5
passages.section_title: What sets the Lamb’s followers apart from the beast’s followers?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then I looked and saw the Lamb standing on Mount Zion, and with Him 144,000 who had His name and His Father’s name written on their foreheads. 2 And I heard a sound from heaven like the roar of many waters and the loud rumbling of thunder. And the sound I heard was like harpists strumming their harps. 3 And they sang a new song before the throne and before the four living creatures and the elders. And no one could learn the song except the 144,000 who had been redeemed from the earth. 4 These are the ones who have not been defiled with women, for they are virgins. They follow the Lamb wherever He goes. They have been redeemed from among men as firstfruits to God and to the Lamb. 5 And no lie was found in their mouths; they are blameless.
paragraphs: 1 Then I looked and saw the Lamb standing on Mount Zion, and with Him 144,000 who had His name and His Father’s name written on their foreheads. 2 And I heard a sound from heaven like the roar of many waters and the loud rumbling of thunder. And the sound I heard was like harpists strumming their harps. 3 And they sang a new song before the throne and before the four living creatures and the elders. And no one could learn the song except the 144,000 who had been redeemed from the earth.

4 These are the ones who have not been defiled with women, for they are virgins. They follow the Lamb wherever He goes. They have been redeemed from among men as firstfruits to God and to the Lamb. 5 And no lie was found in their mouths; they are blameless.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the beast’s mark and demands for worship, John sees the Lamb with 144,000 on Mount Zion. They bear the Lamb’s name and His Father’s name on their foreheads. The contrast is immediate: their identity and allegiance belong to God and the Lamb.

John hears a mighty sound from heaven, like waters, thunder and harpists. A new song is sung before the throne, the living creatures and the elders, and only the 144,000 redeemed from the earth can learn it. The scene presents their relationship with God through worship, rather than through the beast’s coercion.

They are described as virgins, as followers of the Lamb wherever He goes, and as people whose mouths contain no lie. These descriptions stand against the unfaithfulness and deception surrounding the beast. They are also called firstfruits to God and the Lamb. The Greek word aparche draws on the first portion of a harvest offered to God; see Thayer’s entry. Here the picture expresses their being set apart for Him.

The passage describes their faithfulness and belonging. It does not narrate their deaths or explicitly explain how they came to stand with the Lamb. Those questions belong to the differing readings of the scene.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley understands Mount Zion here as heavenly and the group as a company distinguished by holiness. Walvoord understands a future scene on earthly Zion, with the same 144,000 from chapter 7 preserved through the tribulation. The USCCB notes understand the number as representing the whole Christian people gathered with the Lamb.

The description of virginity is read either as literal abstinence from sexual relations or as a picture of spiritual faithfulness. The USCCB notes favor the latter, connecting it with refusal of idolatry. Walvoord discusses both possibilities. Wesley emphasizes purity of life. In each reading, the description belongs with following the Lamb and refusing falsehood.

The shared emphasis is loyalty to the Lamb. The readings differ over the group’s identity, location and circumstances; the vision itself identifies whose names they bear and whom they follow.
passages.god_plan_html:
Hebrews 12:22–24 brings together Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, the joyful assembly of God’s people and Jesus. That is an important scriptural connection for understanding Zion as a place of belonging and worship. It gives context to the heavenly reading without making every mention of Zion refer to the same location.

The firstfruits picture also appears in James 1:18, where those given birth through God’s word are called a kind of firstfruits of His creation. Revelation’s faithful company belongs within that wider picture of people set apart for God. The image does not, by itself, prove that they were the first group to suffer martyrdom.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Revelation 14:6-13
passages.section_title: What do the three angels announce, and what hope do the faithful receive?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 Then I saw another angel flying overhead, with the eternal gospel to proclaim to those who dwell on the earth—to every nation and tribe and tongue and people. 7 And he said in a loud voice, “Fear God and give Him glory, because the hour of His judgment has come. Worship the One who made the heavens and the earth and the sea and the springs of waters.” 8 Then a second angel followed, saying, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great, who has made all the nations drink the wine of the passion of her immorality.” 9 And a third angel followed them, calling out in a loud voice, “If anyone worships the beast and its image and receives its mark on his forehead or on his hand, 10 he too will drink the wine of God’s anger, poured undiluted into the cup of His wrath. And he will be tormented in fire and sulfur in the presence of the holy angels and of the Lamb. 11 And the smoke of their torment rises forever and ever. Day and night there is no rest for those who worship the beast and its image, or for anyone who receives the mark of its name.” 12 Here is a call for the perseverance of the saints, who keep the commandments of God and the faith of Jesus. 13 And I heard a voice from heaven telling me to write, “Blessed are the dead—those who die in the Lord from this moment on.” “Yes,” says the Spirit, “they will rest from their labors, for their deeds will follow them.”
paragraphs: 6 Then I saw another angel flying overhead, with the eternal gospel to proclaim to those who dwell on the earth—to every nation and tribe and tongue and people. 7 And he said in a loud voice, “Fear God and give Him glory, because the hour of His judgment has come. Worship the One who made the heavens and the earth and the sea and the springs of waters.”
8 Then a second angel followed, saying, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great, who has made all the nations drink the wine of the passion of her immorality.”

9 And a third angel followed them, calling out in a loud voice, “If anyone worships the beast and its image and receives its mark on his forehead or on his hand, 10 he too will drink the wine of God’s anger, poured undiluted into the cup of His wrath. And he will be tormented in fire and sulfur in the presence of the holy angels and of the Lamb. 11 And the smoke of their torment rises forever and ever. Day and night there is no rest for those who worship the beast and its image, or for anyone who receives the mark of its name.”

12 Here is a call for the perseverance of the saints, who keep the commandments of God and the faith of Jesus. 13 And I heard a voice from heaven telling me to write, “Blessed are the dead—those who die in the Lord from this moment on.” “Yes,” says the Spirit, “they will rest from their labors, for their deeds will follow them.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Three angels announce messages that answer the beast’s demand for worship. The first carries the eternal gospel to every nation, tribe, language and people. He calls them to fear God, give Him glory and worship the Creator, because the hour of His judgment has come.

The second announces the fall of Babylon, which has drawn the nations into its unfaithfulness. The third warns those who worship the beast, its image and receive its mark. The wine of Babylon’s immorality is answered by the wine of God’s anger. The warning describes fire, sulfur, rising smoke and the absence of rest.

The call to the saints is perseverance: keeping God’s commandments and the faith of Jesus. The passage then gives a blessing to those who die in the Lord. The Spirit affirms that they will rest from their labors and that their deeds follow them.

The contrast is between the worship demanded by the beast and faithfulness to God, including faithfulness through death. The warning is severe, while the promise of rest assures suffering believers that their labor is not forgotten.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Readers differ over the angels and their setting. Wesley understands them as messengers of God whose work is carried out through human proclamation. The USCCB notes present the announcements as impending judgment on the pagan world and identify Babylon with Rome. In Walvoord’s future reading, the announcements lead toward the defeat of the beast and its kingdom.

The duration and nature of the punishment are a substantial difference among Christians. The Catholic Church affirms the eternity of hell in Catechism 1035. The Reformed Westminster Confession 33.2 teaches eternal torment. Wesley reads this passage’s torment as continuing forever.

The Seventh-day Adventist Church instead teaches final destruction of the wicked in its official belief on the end of sin. Adventist writer Samuele Bacchiocchi understands the rising smoke in Revelation 14:11 as evidence of destruction with a permanent result. That position affirms final judgment while differing from the reading of suffering that continues without end.

These explanations should be weighed alongside the passage’s own wording, including both the smoke rising forever and the absence of rest. The encouragement to the faithful remains clear: those who die in the Lord are blessed, and their labor has not been wasted.
passages.god_plan_html:
The announcement about Babylon recalls Isaiah 21:9, where Babylon’s fall is announced and its idols are shattered. The cup of anger recalls Isaiah 51:17. Revelation draws on those earlier pictures of God bringing proud powers and unfaithfulness under judgment.

The call to worship the Creator reaches every people, answering the beast’s claim over every people in chapter 13. Alongside judgment, the promise of rest gives a reason to remain faithful. God’s larger purpose includes the defeat of powers that demand false worship and the recognition of those who belong to Him, even when their service has cost them their lives.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Revelation 14:14-20
passages.section_title: What do the harvest and the winepress reveal about judgment?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 14 And I looked and saw a white cloud, and seated on the cloud was One like the Son of Man, with a golden crown on His head and a sharp sickle in His hand. 15 Then another angel came out of the temple, crying out in a loud voice to the One seated on the cloud, “Swing Your sickle and reap, because the time has come to harvest, for the crop of the earth is ripe.” 16 So the One seated on the cloud swung His sickle over the earth, and the earth was harvested. 17 Then another angel came out of the temple in heaven, and he too had a sharp sickle. 18 Still another angel, with authority over the fire, came from the altar and called out in a loud voice to the angel with the sharp sickle, “Swing your sharp sickle and gather the clusters of grapes from the vine of the earth, because its grapes are ripe.” 19 So the angel swung his sickle over the earth and gathered the grapes of the earth, and he threw them into the great winepress of God’s wrath. 20 And the winepress was trodden outside the city, and the blood that flowed from it rose as high as the bridles of the horses for a distance of 1,600 stadia.
paragraphs: 14 And I looked and saw a white cloud, and seated on the cloud was One like the Son of Man, with a golden crown on His head and a sharp sickle in His hand. 15 Then another angel came out of the temple, crying out in a loud voice to the One seated on the cloud, “Swing Your sickle and reap, because the time has come to harvest, for the crop of the earth is ripe.” 16 So the One seated on the cloud swung His sickle over the earth, and the earth was harvested.

17 Then another angel came out of the temple in heaven, and he too had a sharp sickle. 18 Still another angel, with authority over the fire, came from the altar and called out in a loud voice to the angel with the sharp sickle, “Swing your sharp sickle and gather the clusters of grapes from the vine of the earth, because its grapes are ripe.” 19 So the angel swung his sickle over the earth and gathered the grapes of the earth, and he threw them into the great winepress of God’s wrath. 20 And the winepress was trodden outside the city, and the blood that flowed from it rose as high as the bridles of the horses for a distance of 1,600 stadia.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
John sees a white cloud and One like the Son of Man seated upon it, wearing a golden crown and holding a sharp sickle. An angel comes from the temple and announces that the earth’s crop is ripe. The sickle is swung, and the earth is harvested.

A second harvest follows. Another angel with a sickle receives a call from an angel at the altar to gather the ripe grapes of the earth. The grapes are thrown into the great winepress of God’s wrath. This second picture explicitly identifies the harvest with judgment.

The winepress is trodden outside the city, and blood flows as high as the horses’ bridles over the distance John records. The picture is deliberately overwhelming. It conveys the severity and reach of judgment rather than giving readers a description of an ordinary agricultural harvest.

The two scenes bring the chapter’s warnings to a climax. The time for reaping is announced from God’s temple and altar. Earth’s apparent strength does not put it beyond His judgment.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The identity of the first reaper is disputed. Wesley understands an angel in human form, sent by Christ. Walvoord understands Christ Himself. The phrase Son of Man and the crowned figure support the latter reading; the message delivered by another angel has led some readers toward the former.

The first harvest is also explained differently. Wesley understands a gracious gathering of the righteous, followed by judgment on the wicked in the grape harvest. The USCCB notes likewise distinguish the gathering of the elect from the doom of the ungodly. Walvoord favors two pictures of judgment, with the second presenting its climax. The text explicitly names wrath in the winepress scene, while leaving the first harvest less fully explained.

The blood and distance are understood with different degrees of literal detail. The main readings recognize an extraordinary picture of judgment. A proposed battlefield, channel of blood or physical calculation should be distinguished from what John actually records.
passages.god_plan_html:
Joel 3:12–14 places the sickle, ripe harvest and overflowing winepress together in a scene of judgment on the nations. That close parallel helps explain why Revelation uses harvest language for the moment when God deals with evil.

Isaiah 63:1–6 also pictures the LORD’s judgment through a winepress and blood-stained garments. Revelation’s scene belongs to that larger biblical picture of God acting against wickedness. The judgment answers the apparent success of the beast; its authority and violence will not continue forever.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Revelation 15:1-8
passages.section_title: Why do the victors sing before the final plagues are poured out?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then I saw another great and marvelous sign in heaven: seven angels with the seven final plagues, with which the wrath of God is completed. 2 And I saw something like a sea of glass mixed with fire, beside which stood those who had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name. They were holding harps from God, 3 and they sang the song of God’s servant Moses and of the Lamb: “Great and wonderful are Your works, O Lord God Almighty! Just and true are Your ways, O King of the nations! 4 Who will not fear You, O Lord, and glorify Your name? For You alone are holy. All nations will come and worship before You, for Your righteous acts have been revealed.” 5 After this I looked, and the temple—the tabernacle of the Testimony—was opened in heaven. 6 And out of the temple came the seven angels with the seven plagues, dressed in clean and bright linen and girded with golden sashes around their chests. 7 Then one of the four living creatures gave the seven angels seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God, who lives forever and ever. 8 And the temple was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from His power; and no one could enter the temple until the seven plagues of the seven angels were completed.
paragraphs: 1 Then I saw another great and marvelous sign in heaven: seven angels with the seven final plagues, with which the wrath of God is completed.

2 And I saw something like a sea of glass mixed with fire, beside which stood those who had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name. They were holding harps from God, 3 and they sang the song of God’s servant Moses and of the Lamb: “Great and wonderful are Your works, O Lord God Almighty! Just and true are Your ways, O King of the nations! 4 Who will not fear You, O Lord, and glorify Your name? For You alone are holy. All nations will come and worship before You, for Your righteous acts have been revealed.”

5 After this I looked, and the temple—the tabernacle of the Testimony—was opened in heaven. 6 And out of the temple came the seven angels with the seven plagues, dressed in clean and bright linen and girded with golden sashes around their chests. 7 Then one of the four living creatures gave the seven angels seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God, who lives forever and ever. 8 And the temple was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from His power; and no one could enter the temple until the seven plagues of the seven angels were completed.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
John sees another great sign in heaven: seven angels with seven final plagues. Before those plagues are poured out, the vision turns to people who have conquered the beast, its image and the number of its name. They stand beside something like a sea of glass mixed with fire, holding harps from God.

Their victory is expressed in worship. They sing the song of God’s servant Moses and of the Lamb, praising God’s great works and His just and true ways. The song looks toward all nations worshiping Him because His righteous acts have been revealed. The beast’s demand for worship has not determined their allegiance.

The heavenly temple, described as the tabernacle of the Testimony, then opens. Seven angels emerge in bright linen and golden sashes, and a living creature gives them golden bowls filled with God’s wrath. The Greek word phiale means a broad, shallow bowl; see Thayer’s entry. These are vessels for the pouring out described in the next chapter.

Smoke from God’s glory and power fills the temple, and no one can enter until the seven plagues are completed. The scene presents the coming judgment in connection with God’s holiness and the praise of people who have remained faithful. Their worship comes before the account of the bowls reaching the earth.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley, Walvoord and the USCCB notes understand this as a heavenly scene of victory and worship before the plagues. They connect the singers with people who have resisted the beast. The encouragement is that the beast’s apparent success has not deprived God’s people of their place with Him.

The song’s relationship to Moses is explained with different emphases. The USCCB notes point especially to Exodus 15, after Israel’s escape through the sea. Wesley connects its language with both Exodus 15 and Deuteronomy 32 and understands the song as belonging to Moses and the Lamb together. Walvoord favors two songs and gives particular weight to Deuteronomy 32. The readings share the themes of God’s faithfulness, rescue and justice.

The bowl sequence is generally understood as bringing the judgments toward their climax, although teachers differ over how it fits with the seals, trumpets and later events. The word final describes these plagues in the vision; it should be read alongside the later judgment scenes that Revelation still presents.
passages.god_plan_html:
The reference to Moses makes the connection with Israel’s earlier rescue explicit. In Exodus 15:1–18, the people sing after God defeats the pursuing army and brings them through the sea. Revelation places the victors over the beast beside a glassy sea and names the song of Moses and the Lamb. The earlier rescue helps readers understand the larger pattern: God overcomes the power that oppresses His people and receives their worship.

Deuteronomy 32:3–4 and 35–36 likewise joins God’s greatness, just ways, judgment and compassion for His servants. These scriptural parallels give substance to the song’s praise of His justice. His people’s rescue and His judgment of evil belong within the same story.

The temple filled with glory also recalls Exodus 40:34–35 and 1 Kings 8:10–11, where God’s presence prevents ordinary entry or ministry. Revelation draws on that recognizable sanctuary imagery. Hebrews 9:23–24 helps explain the wider connection between the earthly sanctuary and heaven, where Christ appears before God on behalf of His people.

deeper_study.title: Worship as the Early Church Knew It

passages.title: Revelation 16:1-11
passages.section_title: What do the first five bowls reveal about judgment and resistance?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then I heard a loud voice from the temple saying to the seven angels, “Go, pour out on the earth the seven bowls of God’s wrath.” 2 So the first angel went and poured out his bowl on the earth, and loathsome, malignant sores broke out on those who had the mark of the beast and worshiped its image. 3 And the second angel poured out his bowl into the sea, and it turned to blood like that of the dead, and every living thing in the sea died. 4 And the third angel poured out his bowl into the rivers and springs of water, and they turned to blood. 5 And I heard the angel of the waters say: “Righteous are You, O Holy One, who is and was, because You have brought these judgments. 6 For they have spilled the blood of saints and prophets, and You have given them blood to drink, as they deserve.” 7 And I heard the altar reply: “Yes, Lord God Almighty, true and just are Your judgments.” 8 Then the fourth angel poured out his bowl on the sun, and it was given power to scorch the people with fire. 9 And the people were scorched by intense heat, and they cursed the name of God, who had authority over these plagues. Yet they did not repent and give Him glory. 10 And the fifth angel poured out his bowl on the throne of the beast, and its kingdom was plunged into darkness, and men began to gnaw their tongues in anguish 11 and curse the God of heaven for their pains and sores. Yet they did not repent of their deeds.
paragraphs: 1 Then I heard a loud voice from the temple saying to the seven angels, “Go, pour out on the earth the seven bowls of God’s wrath.” 2 So the first angel went and poured out his bowl on the earth, and loathsome, malignant sores broke out on those who had the mark of the beast and worshiped its image.

3 And the second angel poured out his bowl into the sea, and it turned to blood like that of the dead, and every living thing in the sea died. 4 And the third angel poured out his bowl into the rivers and springs of water, and they turned to blood. 5 And I heard the angel of the waters say: “Righteous are You, O Holy One, who is and was, because You have brought these judgments. 6 For they have spilled the blood of saints and prophets, and You have given them blood to drink, as they deserve.” 7 And I heard the altar reply: “Yes, Lord God Almighty, true and just are Your judgments.”

8 Then the fourth angel poured out his bowl on the sun, and it was given power to scorch the people with fire. 9 And the people were scorched by intense heat, and they cursed the name of God, who had authority over these plagues. Yet they did not repent and give Him glory.

10 And the fifth angel poured out his bowl on the throne of the beast, and its kingdom was plunged into darkness, and men began to gnaw their tongues in anguish 11 and curse the God of heaven for their pains and sores. Yet they did not repent of their deeds.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
A voice from the temple commands the seven angels to pour out their bowls. The first brings painful sores on people who bear the beast’s mark and worship its image. The judgment directly confronts the allegiance demanded in chapter 13.

The second turns the sea to blood like that of the dead, and every living thing in it dies. The third turns rivers and springs to blood. An angel explains the justice of this judgment: those who spilled the blood of saints and prophets are given blood to drink. The altar answers by affirming that God’s judgments are true and just.

The fourth affects the sun, which scorches people with intense heat. They recognize God’s authority over the plagues, yet curse His name instead of repenting and giving Him glory. Knowledge of who is acting does not produce a change in their response.

The fifth strikes the beast’s throne, plunging its kingdom into darkness. People gnaw their tongues in anguish and curse God over their pains and sores. The continuing sores connect this scene with the earlier bowl. Once again, John records that they do not repent.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The main difference concerns whether the plagues describe physical events or picture judgments on religious and political powers. Wesley expects future physical plagues. Walvoord likewise expects severe future judgments. Gill understands the bowls through the downfall of powers associated with the papacy, interpreting the sea especially in terms of Rome’s authority and its maritime territories.

Gill did not simply regard these bowls as already fulfilled in the Reformation; he expected judgments still to come. His reading differs from a physical reading in what the plagues represent, as well as in the powers he identifies. It should not be presented as the position of all Baptists or Reformed Christians.

The USCCB notes emphasize the plagues’ modeling on Exodus and understand the beast’s throne as the forces of evil. Across these explanations, the blood of God’s servants and the refusal to repent remain central. The chapter presents a moral reckoning, not merely a sequence of disasters.
passages.god_plan_html:
The bowls recall the plagues of Egypt: boils in Exodus 9:8–11, water turned to blood in Exodus 7:19–21, and darkness in Exodus 10:21–23. In Exodus, God confronts an oppressive power and brings His people out. Revelation’s repeated imagery places the beast’s rule within that larger pattern of opposition that God will overcome.

The explanation about shed blood also connects with the martyrs’ appeal for justice in Revelation 6:9–11. Their suffering has not been forgotten. The angel and altar affirm the righteousness of God’s answer to their appeal.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Revelation 16:12-16
passages.section_title: Why are the kings gathered, and why does Jesus interrupt with a warning?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 12 And the sixth angel poured out his bowl on the great river Euphrates, and its water was dried up to prepare the way for the kings of the East. 13 And I saw three unclean spirits that looked like frogs coming out of the mouths of the dragon, the beast, and the false prophet. 14 These are demonic spirits that perform signs and go out to all the kings of the earth, to assemble them for battle on the great day of God the Almighty. 15 “Behold, I am coming like a thief. Blessed is the one who remains awake and clothed, so that he will not go naked and let his shame be exposed.” 16 And they assembled the kings in the place that in Hebrew is called Armageddon.
paragraphs: 12 And the sixth angel poured out his bowl on the great river Euphrates, and its water was dried up to prepare the way for the kings of the East. 13 And I saw three unclean spirits that looked like frogs coming out of the mouths of the dragon, the beast, and the false prophet. 14 These are demonic spirits that perform signs and go out to all the kings of the earth, to assemble them for battle on the great day of God the Almighty.

15 “Behold, I am coming like a thief. Blessed is the one who remains awake and clothed, so that he will not go naked and let his shame be exposed.” 16 And they assembled the kings in the place that in Hebrew is called Armageddon.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The sixth bowl dries the Euphrates, preparing the way for the kings of the East. John then sees three unclean spirits like frogs coming from the dragon, the beast and the false prophet. He identifies them directly as demonic spirits that perform signs and draw the world’s kings toward battle.

Their gathering is for the great day of God Almighty. The powers are deceived into assembling, yet the day is still named for God. The vision does not suggest that their combined strength places the outcome beyond His authority.

In the middle of the scene, Jesus warns that He is coming like a thief and blesses the person who remains awake and clothed. The warning addresses readiness and faithfulness while the world is being drawn into deception. Attention shifts briefly from what the kings are doing to how His people should live.

The gathering place is called Armageddon. The name is commonly linked with Megiddo, although its exact derivation is debated; see Thayer’s discussion. The passage names the gathering but does not yet narrate the battle itself.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The kings from the East receive different identifications. The USCCB notes relate them to the Parthians in the setting of the Roman world. Walvoord expects future eastern rulers approaching the final conflict. Wesley also expects an eastern advance, while connecting it with his wider account of the powers opposed to God. The passage itself does not name a modern nation.

The unclean spirits need less reconstruction: John identifies them as demons and explains their deceptive signs and mission. The name Armageddon is variously understood as pointing to a future military gathering around Megiddo or as a picture of the final overthrow of hostile powers, drawing on the place’s biblical associations.

The warning about coming like a thief is understood as a call to watchfulness. It does not give a date for the gathering or invite readers to calculate one from a current event. Faithful readiness remains the stated blessing.
passages.god_plan_html:
The drying of water recalls Exodus 14:21–28, where a path opens through the sea but the pursuing army meets destruction. This is a scriptural parallel rather than an identical event: in Revelation, the opened way brings hostile rulers toward the day of God’s reckoning. Their movement does not amount to victory over Him.

The interruption also repeats the warning Jesus gave in Matthew 24:42–44, where the unexpected thief illustrates the need to be ready for the Son of Man. The same theme appears in Revelation 3:3. Within the larger picture of judgment, His people are called to remain awake and faithful.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Revelation 16:17-21
passages.section_title: What happens when the seventh bowl is poured into the air?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 Then the seventh angel poured out his bowl into the air, and a loud voice came from the throne in the temple, saying, “It is done!” 18 And there were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, and a great earthquake the likes of which had not occurred since men were upon the earth—so mighty was the great quake. 19 The great city was split into three parts, and the cities of the nations collapsed. And God remembered Babylon the great and gave her the cup of the wine of the fury of His wrath. 20 Then every island fled, and no mountain could be found. 21 And great hailstones weighing almost a hundred pounds each rained down on them from above. And men cursed God for the plague of hail, because it was so horrendous.
paragraphs: 17 Then the seventh angel poured out his bowl into the air, and a loud voice came from the throne in the temple, saying, “It is done!” 18 And there were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, and a great earthquake the likes of which had not occurred since men were upon the earth—so mighty was the great quake. 19 The great city was split into three parts, and the cities of the nations collapsed. And God remembered Babylon the great and gave her the cup of the wine of the fury of His wrath.

20 Then every island fled, and no mountain could be found. 21 And great hailstones weighing almost a hundred pounds each rained down on them from above. And men cursed God for the plague of hail, because it was so horrendous.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The seventh angel pours the bowl into the air. A voice from the throne in the temple announces completion. Lightning, rumblings, thunder and an earthquake follow. John describes the earthquake as greater than any since human beings were on the earth.

The great city splits into three parts, and the cities of the nations collapse. Babylon is remembered before God and receives the cup of His fierce wrath. Remembered here leads directly to action: the judgment already announced against Babylon is being carried forward.

Islands flee and mountains cannot be found. Enormous hailstones fall, described in the BSB as weighing almost a hundred pounds each. The scene depicts upheaval reaching beyond a single city. Yet the human response at the end of the chapter is still to curse God.

The bowls have reached their climax, but the story has more to disclose. The next chapters explain Babylon’s character and downfall in greater detail. The chapter ends with judgment underway and resistance still exposed.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The great city is a point of disagreement. Wesley identifies the divided city as Jerusalem, distinguished from Babylon. The USCCB notes understand it as Rome and its empire. Gill understands the wider domain of Roman religious power rather than the city alone. The phrase should therefore not be treated as an agreed code for one location in every passage.

Walvoord discusses both Jerusalem and Babylon in explaining the divided city, while expecting a future physical judgment. He does not claim that the wording removes every uncertainty about the geography. All these readings recognize Babylon as a particular object of the judgment.

The earthquake, disappearing mountains and great hail are read with different degrees of physical and symbolic detail. The central point is the overthrow of powers and places that seemed secure. The passage does not supply the geological mechanism or a complete map of the changed world.
passages.god_plan_html:
The hail recalls Exodus 9:22–26, another judgment confronting a ruler who resists God. The repeated language of thunder, lightning and earthquake also connects this bowl with the earlier heavenly scenes in Revelation 8:5 and 11:19. The final bowl belongs to the same unfolding account of divine authority.

Hebrews 12:26–29 gives a related biblical theme: what can be shaken is removed, while God’s kingdom cannot be shaken. That is a parallel, not an exact identification of the earthquake’s physical effects. It directs attention toward what endures when earthly power and security fail, and toward worship marked by reverence for God.

passages.title: Revelation 17:1-6
passages.section_title: What does the woman called Babylon reveal about corrupt power?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then one of the seven angels with the seven bowls came and said to me, “Come, I will show you the punishment of the great prostitute, who sits on many waters. 2 The kings of the earth were immoral with her, and those who dwell on the earth were intoxicated with the wine of her immorality.” 3 And the angel carried me away in the Spirit into a wilderness, where I saw a woman sitting on a scarlet beast that was covered with blasphemous names and had seven heads and ten horns. 4 The woman was dressed in purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold and precious stones and pearls. She held in her hand a golden cup full of abominations and the impurities of her sexual immorality. 5 And on her forehead a mysterious name was written: BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF PROSTITUTES AND OF THE ABOMINATIONS OF THE EARTH. 6 I could see that the woman was drunk with the blood of the saints and witnesses for Jesus. And I was utterly amazed at the sight of her.
paragraphs: 1 Then one of the seven angels with the seven bowls came and said to me, “Come, I will show you the punishment of the great prostitute, who sits on many waters. 2 The kings of the earth were immoral with her, and those who dwell on the earth were intoxicated with the wine of her immorality.”

3 And the angel carried me away in the Spirit into a wilderness, where I saw a woman sitting on a scarlet beast that was covered with blasphemous names and had seven heads and ten horns. 4 The woman was dressed in purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold and precious stones and pearls. She held in her hand a golden cup full of abominations and the impurities of her sexual immorality. 5 And on her forehead a mysterious name was written: BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF PROSTITUTES AND OF THE ABOMINATIONS OF THE EARTH. 6 I could see that the woman was drunk with the blood of the saints and witnesses for Jesus. And I was utterly amazed at the sight of her.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
One of the angels with the bowls invites John to see the punishment of a woman called the great prostitute. She sits on many waters, has relationships with the earth’s kings, and intoxicates its inhabitants with her immorality. The next scene begins to explain Babylon’s judgment announced in chapter 16.

Carried in the Spirit into a wilderness, John sees her riding a scarlet beast with seven heads, ten horns and names that dishonor God. The woman and the beast are connected, but remain distinct figures. She is carried by the same kind of hostile power already described in chapter 13.

Her clothing and ornaments display wealth and splendor: purple, scarlet, gold, precious stones and pearls. Her golden cup, however, is filled with abominations and impurity. What looks magnificent carries corruption. The name on her forehead identifies her as Babylon the Great, a mother of prostitutes and abominations.

The final description exposes the cost of that power: she is drunk with the blood of saints and witnesses for Jesus. John’s amazement is met by the angel’s promise to explain. The vision’s own explanation will identify the waters as peoples and nations and the woman as a ruling city.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The USCCB notes identify the woman with Rome in its ancient imperial setting, connecting her wealth and unfaithfulness with idolatry and the persecution of Christians. Wesley also identifies her with the city of Rome, but distinguishes her from the beast as papal power. His reading concerns a later history of the city and its religious and political rule.

Walvoord expects a future corrupt religious system allied with the beast’s political power. He distinguishes the woman’s downfall from the fall of Babylon described in chapter 18.

These identifications should remain attributed to the teachers and documents that hold them. The chapter itself establishes the relationship with rulers, the corruption beneath the wealth, and the violence against God’s people. Those features provide the basis on which proposed identifications must be tested.
passages.god_plan_html:
The cup and waters recall Jeremiah 51:7 and 13, where ancient Babylon intoxicates the nations and dwells beside many waters with great wealth. Verses 24–25 announce God’s reckoning for the evil done against Zion. Revelation reuses those pictures to show that worldly splendor does not place an oppressive power beyond judgment.

Nahum 3:4–7 likewise describes a city, Nineveh, through the picture of a seductive prostitute whose conduct harms nations. This is a biblical parallel for the kind of imagery John sees. The wider theme is God confronting power that enriches itself, leads others into corruption and brings suffering, rather than allowing its success to continue without an answer.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Revelation 17:7-14
passages.section_title: What does the angel explain about the beast, the kings and the Lamb?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 “Why are you so amazed?” said the angel. “I will tell you the mystery of the woman and of the beast that carries her, which has the seven heads and ten horns. 8 The beast that you saw—it was, and now is no more, but is about to come up out of the Abyss and go to its destruction. And those who dwell on the earth whose names were not written in the Book of Life from the foundation of the world will marvel when they see the beast that was, and is not, and yet will be. 9 This calls for a mind with wisdom. The seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman sits. 10 There are also seven kings. Five have fallen, one is, and the other has not yet come. But when he does come, he must remain for only a little while. 11 The beast that was, and now is not, is an eighth king, who belongs to the other seven and is going into destruction. 12 The ten horns you saw are ten kings who have not yet received a kingdom, but will receive one hour of authority as kings along with the beast. 13 These kings have one purpose: to yield their power and authority to the beast. 14 They will make war against the Lamb, and the Lamb will triumph over them, because He is Lord of lords and King of kings; and He will be accompanied by His called and chosen and faithful ones.”
paragraphs: 7 “Why are you so amazed?” said the angel. “I will tell you the mystery of the woman and of the beast that carries her, which has the seven heads and ten horns. 8 The beast that you saw—it was, and now is no more, but is about to come up out of the Abyss and go to its destruction. And those who dwell on the earth whose names were not written in the Book of Life from the foundation of the world will marvel when they see the beast that was, and is not, and yet will be.

9 This calls for a mind with wisdom. The seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman sits. 10 There are also seven kings. Five have fallen, one is, and the other has not yet come. But when he does come, he must remain for only a little while. 11 The beast that was, and now is not, is an eighth king, who belongs to the other seven and is going into destruction.

12 The ten horns you saw are ten kings who have not yet received a kingdom, but will receive one hour of authority as kings along with the beast. 13 These kings have one purpose: to yield their power and authority to the beast. 14 They will make war against the Lamb, and the Lamb will triumph over them, because He is Lord of lords and King of kings; and He will be accompanied by His called and chosen and faithful ones.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The angel begins the explanation with the beast. It was, is no more, will come from the Abyss and will go to destruction. The world marvels at its reappearance. Its apparent return to power should be read alongside the destination the angel names: destruction.

The seven heads are explained as seven mountains and also seven kings. Five have fallen, one is, and another is still to come for a short time. The beast is also an eighth king who belongs to the seven. The passage gives a sequence, but does not supply the rulers’ names.

The ten horns are ten kings who have not yet received a kingdom. They receive a brief period of authority with the beast and unite to give it their power. These kings are described together, in contrast to the sequence associated with the heads.

The alliance makes war against the Lamb, but the outcome is stated in advance. The Lamb will conquer because He is Lord of lords and King of kings. His companions are called, chosen and faithful. The explanation leads beyond the difficulty of identifying the rulers to the certainty of His victory.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The USCCB notes connect the seven mountains with Rome’s hills and the kings with Roman emperors, while acknowledging little agreement over the exact sequence. They connect the beast’s return with expectations about Nero returning to power. Wesley instead places the sequence within his account of papal power and its different periods.

Walvoord reads the heads in terms of successive imperial kingdoms leading to a future world empire. He favors the revival of imperial power over the personal return of a dead ruler.

The angel explicitly identifies the horns as kings and gives the alliance’s purpose and outcome. A proposed list of rulers should therefore be distinguished from those stated explanations. The difficulty of the list does not make the Lamb’s promised triumph uncertain.
passages.god_plan_html:
The horns, kings and war against God’s people recall Daniel 7:21–27. Daniel sees hostile rule prevailing for a time, followed by God’s judgment and an everlasting kingdom. Revelation develops that same conflict and names the Lamb as the victorious ruler.

The title King of kings and Lord of lords also appears in 1 Timothy 6:15–16, in praise of God’s supreme sovereignty. Revelation applies that royal authority to the Lamb as the reason He conquers. The vision’s larger purpose is to assure His people that no coalition of earthly rulers can overturn His rule.

passages.title: Revelation 17:15-18
passages.section_title: Why do the beast and its allies turn against the woman?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 Then the angel said to me, “The waters you saw, where the prostitute was seated, are peoples and multitudes and nations and tongues. 16 And the ten horns and the beast that you saw will hate the prostitute. They will leave her desolate and naked, and they will eat her flesh and burn her with fire. 17 For God has put it into their hearts to carry out His purpose by uniting to give their kingdom to the beast, until the words of God are fulfilled. 18 And the woman you saw is the great city that rules over the kings of the earth.”
paragraphs: 15 Then the angel said to me, “The waters you saw, where the prostitute was seated, are peoples and multitudes and nations and tongues. 16 And the ten horns and the beast that you saw will hate the prostitute. They will leave her desolate and naked, and they will eat her flesh and burn her with fire.

17 For God has put it into their hearts to carry out His purpose by uniting to give their kingdom to the beast, until the words of God are fulfilled. 18 And the woman you saw is the great city that rules over the kings of the earth.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The angel explains that the waters beneath the woman represent peoples, multitudes, nations and languages. Her influence is broad. But the powers carrying her do not remain loyal: the beast and ten horns will hate her, strip her and destroy her with fire.

The reversal exposes the fragility of her apparent security. The alliance with rulers that supported her splendor becomes the means of her ruin. The vision uses violent imagery to describe a downfall brought about by the very powers associated with her.

The angel then states that God has put it into their hearts to carry out His purpose by uniting under the beast until His words are fulfilled. Their actions do not take the story beyond His authority. The chapter closes by identifying the woman as the great city ruling over the kings of the earth.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The USCCB notes understand the hostile kings as powers that bring judgment on Rome while unwittingly fulfilling God’s will. Wesley likewise sees the destruction of the woman as the fulfillment of God’s judgment, within his reading of Rome and papal power. The shared feature is the reversal of an alliance and the woman’s loss of the wealth and support on which she depended.

Walvoord expects the beast to destroy a future religious system and replace it with worship of himself. He distinguishes that event from Babylon’s later political and commercial downfall.

The passage’s own explanation is that the rulers’ common purpose serves God’s stated purpose until His words are fulfilled. Their alliance brings about the woman’s downfall while God’s words are fulfilled.
passages.god_plan_html:
Jeremiah 51:11–13 and 28–29 describes God stirring rulers against ancient Babylon to accomplish His announced judgment. Revelation’s account has a similar pattern: a powerful city is brought down through other rulers, while God’s purpose governs the outcome. This is a scriptural parallel, not a claim that every ruler in the two passages is the same.

Isaiah 10:5–7 and 12 adds another aspect of that larger theme. Assyria serves a purpose in God’s judgment while pursuing its own destructive ambitions, and is itself held accountable for arrogance. Revelation likewise presents hostile powers acting within a purpose they do not control. Their temporary usefulness does not make their rule permanent or put them beyond judgment.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Revelation 18:1-8
passages.section_title: Why must God’s people come out of Babylon?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 After this I saw another angel descending from heaven with great authority, and the earth was illuminated by his glory. 2 And he cried out in a mighty voice: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great! She has become a lair for demons and a haunt for every unclean spirit, every unclean bird, and every detestable beast. 3 All the nations have drunk the wine of the passion of her immorality. The kings of the earth were immoral with her, and the merchants of the earth have grown wealthy from the extravagance of her luxury.” 4 Then I heard another voice from heaven say: “Come out of her, My people, so that you will not share in her sins or contract any of her plagues. 5 For her sins are piled up to heaven, and God has remembered her iniquities. 6 Give back to her as she has done to others; pay her back double for what she has done; mix her a double portion in her own cup. 7 As much as she has glorified herself and lived in luxury, give her the same measure of torment and grief. In her heart she says, ‘I sit as queen; I am not a widow and will never see grief.’ 8 Therefore her plagues will come in one day— death and grief and famine— and she will be consumed by fire, for mighty is the Lord God who judges her.”
paragraphs: 1 After this I saw another angel descending from heaven with great authority, and the earth was illuminated by his glory. 2 And he cried out in a mighty voice: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great! She has become a lair for demons and a haunt for every unclean spirit, every unclean bird, and every detestable beast. 3 All the nations have drunk the wine of the passion of her immorality. The kings of the earth were immoral with her, and the merchants of the earth have grown wealthy from the extravagance of her luxury.”

4 Then I heard another voice from heaven say: “Come out of her, My people, so that you will not share in her sins or contract any of her plagues. 5 For her sins are piled up to heaven, and God has remembered her iniquities. 6 Give back to her as she has done to others; pay her back double for what she has done; mix her a double portion in her own cup. 7 As much as she has glorified herself and lived in luxury, give her the same measure of torment and grief. In her heart she says, ‘I sit as queen; I am not a widow and will never see grief.’ 8 Therefore her plagues will come in one day— death and grief and famine— and she will be consumed by fire, for mighty is the Lord God who judges her.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
An angel descends from heaven with great authority, lighting the earth with his glory. He announces Babylon’s fall. The city that drew the nations, rulers and merchants into its luxury and immorality is described as a dwelling place of demons and unclean creatures. Splendor gives way to desolation.

A second voice calls God’s people to come out of her so they will not share in her sins or plagues. The warning joins two concerns: refusing participation in corruption and escaping its judgment. Babylon’s sins have piled up to heaven, and God remembers what she has done.

The punishment is described as repayment for her deeds. Her self-glorification and luxury are answered by torment and grief. In her heart she treats herself as a secure queen who will never experience loss. The judgment overturns that confidence.

Death, grief, famine and fire come upon her. The reason given is that the Lord who judges her is mighty. Her apparent strength cannot protect her when He acts.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The USCCB notes understand Babylon as Rome, with prophetic images expressing judgment on its idolatry and persecution. Wesley also identifies Babylon with Rome, especially in its later religious power. Walvoord expects a future collapse of political and commercial Babylon, discussing a rebuilt Babylon as a possible location. The setting is disputed; the connection between corruption and judgment is shared.

The command to come out is also read differently. The USCCB notes emphasize separation from sin rather than evacuation of a city. Walvoord includes actual departure from the place facing destruction, alongside separation from its wrongdoing. These explanations differ over the action pictured while taking the call to reject Babylon’s sins seriously.

The repayment language presents God’s judgment. The chapter’s first direct call to His people is to leave Babylon’s corruption behind.
passages.god_plan_html:
The call echoes Jeremiah 51:5–9 and 45–50, where God’s people are told to flee Babylon and not perish in its punishment. Babylon’s wealth and influence do not make its conduct safe to share. Revelation draws on that earlier warning as it calls God’s people away from a power that stands under judgment.

The boast of a queen who will never know widowhood or loss recalls Isaiah 47:7–9. The desolate city also recalls Isaiah 13:19–22. These scriptural connections show a recurring theme: a power that treats its prosperity as permanent must still answer to God.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Revelation 18:9-20
passages.section_title: Why do the rulers and merchants mourn while heaven is called to rejoice?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 Then the kings of the earth who committed sexual immorality and lived in luxury with her will weep and wail at the sight of the smoke rising from the fire that consumes her. 10 In fear of her torment, they will stand at a distance and cry out: “Woe, woe to the great city, the mighty city of Babylon! For in a single hour your judgment has come.” 11 And the merchants of the earth will weep and mourn over her, because there is no one left to buy their cargo— 12 cargo of gold, silver, precious stones, and pearls; of fine linen, purple, silk, and scarlet; of all kinds of citron wood and every article of ivory, precious wood, bronze, iron, and marble; 13 of cinnamon, spice, incense, myrrh, and frankincense; of wine, olive oil, fine flour, and wheat; of cattle, sheep, horses, and carriages; of bodies and souls of slaves. 14 And they will say: “The fruit of your soul’s desire has departed from you; all your luxury and splendor have vanished, never to be seen again.” 15 The merchants who sold these things and gained their wealth from her will stand at a distance, in fear of her torment. They will weep and mourn, 16 saying: “Woe, woe to the great city, clothed in fine linen and purple and scarlet, adorned with gold and precious stones and pearls! 17 For in a single hour such fabulous wealth has been destroyed!” Every shipmaster, passenger, and sailor, and all who make their living from the sea, will stand at a distance 18 and cry out at the sight of the smoke rising from the fire that consumes her. “What city was ever like this great city?” they will exclaim. 19 Then they will throw dust on their heads as they weep and mourn and cry out: “Woe, woe to the great city, where all who had ships on the sea were enriched by her wealth! For in a single hour she has been destroyed.” 20 Rejoice over her, O heaven, and you saints and apostles and prophets, because God has pronounced for you His judgment against her.

For in a single hour your judgment has come.”

11 And the merchants of the earth will weep and mourn over her, because there is no one left to buy their cargo— 12 cargo of gold, silver, precious stones, and pearls; of fine linen, purple, silk, and scarlet; of all kinds of citron wood and every article of ivory, precious wood, bronze, iron, and marble; 13 of cinnamon, spice, incense, myrrh, and frankincense; of wine, olive oil, fine flour, and wheat; of cattle, sheep, horses, and carriages; of bodies and souls of slaves. 14 And they will say: “The fruit of your soul’s desire has departed from you; all your luxury and splendor have vanished, never to be seen again.”

15 The merchants who sold these things and gained their wealth from her will stand at a distance, in fear of her torment. They will weep and mourn, 16 saying: “Woe, woe to the great city, clothed in fine linen and purple and scarlet, adorned with gold and precious stones and pearls! 17 For in a single hour such fabulous wealth has been destroyed!” Every shipmaster, passenger, and sailor, and all who make their living from the sea, will stand at a distance 18 and cry out at the sight of the smoke rising from the fire that consumes her. “What city was ever like this great city?” they will exclaim. 19 Then they will throw dust on their heads as they weep and mourn and cry out: “Woe, woe to the great city, where all who had ships on the sea were enriched by her wealth! For in a single hour she has been destroyed.”
20 Rejoice over her, O heaven, and you saints and apostles and prophets, because God has pronounced for you His judgment against her.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Three groups mourn Babylon: the kings who shared her luxury, the merchants who sold her goods, and those who profited from shipping. They stand at a distance because they fear her torment. The repeated cry about a single hour emphasizes how quickly the wealth they trusted has collapsed.

The cargo list moves through precious metals, jewels, fine fabrics, luxury materials, spices, food, animals and transport. It ends with the bodies and souls of slaves. Human beings have been included among the goods that sustain the city’s abundance.

The Greek word translated souls can refer to lives or persons. Thayer’s entry specifically connects its use here with enslaved people, as in Ezekiel 27:13. The list makes the human cost of Babylon’s commerce visible; its wealth includes people treated as merchandise.

The merchants’ stated reason for grief is that no one buys their cargo anymore. The sailors likewise lament the loss of the city by which they were enriched. Their cries look back to its former splendor and influence.

Heaven, the saints, apostles and prophets are then called to rejoice because God has judged on their behalf. The contrast is between mourning the loss of a profitable order and rejoicing that its victims have received justice.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The main explanations recognize the economic character of the lament. The USCCB notes emphasize its irony: the merchants mourn their lost market. Walvoord likewise understands the grief in terms of dependence on Babylon’s wealth and trade. The passage itself gives that reason rather than recording repentance for the city’s wrongdoing.

Wesley applies the merchandise to Rome’s luxury and religious commerce. Walvoord emphasizes a future political and economic order. These settings differ, while both explanations connect the apparent riches with a power that will face judgment.

The call to rejoice concerns God’s judgment for the saints, apostles and prophets. It marks His answer to the persecution and bloodshed described in the chapter.
passages.god_plan_html:
The lament closely parallels Ezekiel 27:12–14 and 27–36. Tyre’s goods, trade in enslaved people, shipping and wealth are followed by the cries of seafarers and merchants at its downfall. Revelation reuses that pattern to expose how a wealthy power can draw many others into dependence on it.

The rejoicing also answers the martyrs’ appeal for justice in Revelation 6:9–11. The loss celebrated in heaven is the overthrow of a power responsible for harm, not the disappearance of ordinary work or trade as such. Within God’s larger purpose, His people’s suffering is neither invisible nor permanently unanswered.

passages.title: Revelation 18:21-24
passages.section_title: Why does the angel throw a millstone into the sea?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 21 Then a mighty angel picked up a stone the size of a great millstone and cast it into the sea, saying: “With such violence the great city of Babylon will be cast down, never to be seen again. 22 And the sound of harpists and musicians, of flute players and trumpeters, will never ring out in you again. Nor will any craftsmen of any trade be found in you again, nor the sound of a millstone be heard in you again. 23 The light of a lamp will never shine in you again, and the voices of a bride and bridegroom will never call out in you again. For your merchants were the great ones of the earth, because all the nations were deceived by your sorcery.” 24 And there was found in her the blood of prophets and saints, and of all who had been slain on the earth.

Nor will any craftsmen of any trade be found in you again, nor the sound of a millstone be heard in you again. 23 The light of a lamp will never shine in you again, and the voices of a bride and bridegroom will never call out in you again. For your merchants were the great ones of the earth, because all the nations were deceived by your sorcery.” 24 And there was found in her the blood of prophets and saints, and of all who had been slain on the earth.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
A mighty angel casts a stone the size of a great millstone into the sea. He explains the action: Babylon will be thrown down violently and will not be found again. The visible sign makes the announcement of her downfall unmistakable.

The loss is then described through the silence and darkness of everyday life. Music stops. Craftsmen and the sound of grinding grain disappear. Lamps no longer shine, and the voices of bride and bridegroom are no longer heard. The city’s bustle and apparent permanence have come to an end.

The closing charges return attention to why judgment has come. Its merchants possessed great power, its sorcery deceived the nations, and it was found responsible for the blood of prophets, saints and those slain on the earth. The chapter closes by exposing the violence beneath the wealth.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley, Walvoord and the USCCB notes connect the sinking-stone action with Jeremiah’s earlier sign against Babylon. The shared emphasis is decisive judgment and the end of the city’s former power, despite differences over Babylon’s identity and the physical or symbolic details of its downfall.

The final bloodshed charge is read as a statement of Babylon’s guilt in persecution and violence. The proposed historical identifications seek to explain how a city or power fits that description.
passages.god_plan_html:
The sign directly recalls Jeremiah 51:61–64. Jeremiah tells Seraiah to read the prophecy against Babylon, tie a stone to the scroll and throw it into the Euphrates as a picture of Babylon sinking and not rising again. Revelation’s millstone in the sea uses a closely related picture to announce the finality of the downfall.

The silence of this corrupt city also forms a contrast with the city introduced in Revelation 21:1–4. There, the new Jerusalem is prepared as a bride, God dwells with His people, and death and sorrow pass away. Babylon’s end is part of a larger purpose that reaches beyond destruction to life with God, free from the powers that deceived and shed blood.

passages.title: Revelation 19:1-5
passages.section_title: Why does heaven answer Babylon’s fall with praise?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 After this I heard a sound like the roar of a great multitude in heaven, shouting: “Hallelujah! Salvation and glory and power belong to our God! 2 For His judgments are true and just. He has judged the great prostitute who corrupted the earth with her immorality. He has avenged the blood of His servants that was poured out by her hand.” 3 And a second time they called out: “Hallelujah! Her smoke rises forever and ever.” 4 And the twenty-four elders and the four living creatures fell down and worshiped God who sits on the throne, saying: “Amen, Hallelujah!” 5 Then a voice came from the throne, saying: “Praise our God, all you who serve Him, and those who fear Him, small and great alike!”
paragraphs: 1 After this I heard a sound like the roar of a great multitude in heaven, shouting: “Hallelujah! Salvation and glory and power belong to our God! 2 For His judgments are true and just. He has judged the great prostitute who corrupted the earth with her immorality. He has avenged the blood of His servants that was poured out by her hand.” 3 And a second time they called out: “Hallelujah! Her smoke rises forever and ever.”

4 And the twenty-four elders and the four living creatures fell down and worshiped God who sits on the throne, saying: “Amen, Hallelujah!” 5 Then a voice came from the throne, saying: “Praise our God, all you who serve Him, and those who fear Him, small and great alike!”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The scene moves from the cries over Babylon to the sound of a great multitude in heaven. They praise God for salvation, glory and power, and explain the reason: His judgments are true and just. The power that corrupted the earth and shed His servants’ blood has faced His judgment.

The repeated Hallelujah is a call to praise the LORD. Thayer’s entry traces the word’s Greek form to that Hebrew expression. Its repetition gives the scene the character of a great response of worship after the laments in chapter 18.

The twenty-four elders and four living creatures fall before God and join the praise. A voice from the throne then calls all His servants, those who fear Him, small and great alike, to praise. The invitation reaches across differences of status.

The celebration answers what the chapter itself names: corruption has been judged and the blood of God’s servants avenged. The vision’s attention is on God’s faithfulness and justice after the long experience of suffering and opposition.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The main readings understand the praise as a response to God’s judgment of Babylon and His faithfulness to His people. Wesley connects the multitude especially with those whose blood Babylon shed. The USCCB notes describe the victory song as the worship of the church. Their explanations share the passage’s movement from oppression to praise.

Walvoord particularly associates the multitude with martyrs of the tribulation, while recognizing the broad call to all God’s servants. The precise grouping depends partly on each teacher’s reading of earlier visions. The words small and great make clear that public rank does not determine who belongs in the call to praise.
passages.god_plan_html:
The response follows the call in Revelation 18:20 for heaven and God’s people to rejoice over His judgment. It also answers the martyrs’ appeal in Revelation 6:9–11. Their question about how long justice will be delayed has been carried through the vision to this response.

The earlier prophecy in Jeremiah 51:48–49 likewise joins heaven’s rejoicing over Babylon with accountability for bloodshed. Psalm 115:1 and 13 gives a related pattern of glory belonging to God and blessing for those who fear Him, small and great. These connections place the scene within the Bible’s wider hope that God’s justice and faithfulness will be made known.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Revelation 19:6-10
passages.section_title: What does the marriage supper of the Lamb celebrate?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 And I heard a sound like the roar of a great multitude, like the rushing of many waters, and like a mighty rumbling of thunder, crying out: “Hallelujah! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns. 7 Let us rejoice and be glad and give Him the glory. For the marriage of the Lamb has come, and His bride has made herself ready. 8 She was given clothing of fine linen, bright and pure.” For the fine linen she wears is the righteous acts of the saints. 9 Then the angel told me to write, “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb.” And he said to me, “These are the true words of God.” 10 So I fell at his feet to worship him. But he told me, “Do not do that! I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers who rely on the testimony of Jesus. Worship God! For the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.”
paragraphs: 6 And I heard a sound like the roar of a great multitude, like the rushing of many waters, and like a mighty rumbling of thunder, crying out: “Hallelujah! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns. 7 Let us rejoice and be glad and give Him the glory. For the marriage of the Lamb has come, and His bride has made herself ready. 8 She was given clothing of fine linen, bright and pure.” For the fine linen she wears is the righteous acts of the saints.

9 Then the angel told me to write, “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb.” And he said to me, “These are the true words of God.” 10 So I fell at his feet to worship him. But he told me, “Do not do that! I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers who rely on the testimony of Jesus. Worship God! For the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The great multitude’s praise grows to the sound of rushing waters and thunder. God reigns, and the marriage of the Lamb has come. The bride has made herself ready and is given bright, pure linen. John explains the clothing as the righteous acts of the saints.

The scene holds together a gift and the faithful life of God’s people. The clothing is given to the bride, and the vision identifies what it represents. The image presents a prepared people celebrating their relationship with the Lamb.

An angel tells John to write a blessing on those invited to the marriage supper, assuring him that these are God’s true words. John then falls to worship the angel, who immediately refuses. He is a fellow servant, and God is the One to worship.

The closing statement connects the testimony of Jesus with the spirit of prophecy. The messenger directs attention toward God and the witness concerning Jesus, rather than toward himself. The next scene will reveal the rider named the Word of God.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The bride is broadly understood as the church in relationship with Christ. The Catholic Catechism 796 uses the bride of the Lamb image for the church. The Reformed Westminster Confession 25.1 describes Christ’s church as His spouse and includes His people across the ages.

There is a difference over how the bride and guests relate. Wesley understands the bride as the whole company of faithful people belonging to Christ. Walvoord distinguishes the church of the present age as bride from Old Testament and tribulation believers as guests. That distinction belongs to his account of God’s people and is not a list of guest categories supplied in the verse.

The linen also receives different emphases. Wesley connects it with God making His people right with Him and holy in life. Walvoord emphasizes their righteous deeds. The BSB explicitly calls it the righteous acts of the saints and also says that the clothing was given.

The angel’s refusal of worship is clear across these readings. He is a servant, and the command directs worship to God. Interpretations of the wedding’s timing should be distinguished from that direct instruction and from the passage’s promise of blessing.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ephesians 5:25–32 explicitly connects marriage with Christ and the church. Christ loves her, gives Himself for her and prepares her to be holy and without blemish. Revelation’s prepared bride and pure clothing belong within that larger purpose of His self-giving love and the holiness of His people.

The blessing on the invited also recalls Jesus’ teaching about the kingdom as a great banquet in Luke 14:15–24. That parable includes an invitation reaching people who lack wealth or public standing. This is a scriptural parallel, rather than an exact seating plan for Revelation’s feast. The larger picture is fellowship with God made possible through Christ, received with readiness and faithfulness.
passages.current_position_html: On the angel’s correction, our study Who is The Angel of the Lord? distinguishes ordinary angels, who refuse worship and redirect it to God. We understand this angel’s response in the same way: he is a fellow servant, and worship belongs to God.
