passages.title: Revelation 19:11-16
passages.section_title: Who is the rider called Faithful and True?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 Then I saw heaven standing open, and there before me was a white horse. And its rider is called Faithful and True. With righteousness He judges and wages war. 12 He has eyes like blazing fire, and many royal crowns on His head. He has a name written on Him that only He Himself knows. 13 He is dressed in a robe dipped in blood, and His name is The Word of God. 14 The armies of heaven, dressed in fine linen, white and pure, follow Him on white horses. 15 And from His mouth proceeds a sharp sword with which to strike down the nations, and He will rule them with an iron scepter. He treads the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty. 16 And He has a name written on His robe and on His thigh: KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS.
paragraphs: 11 Then I saw heaven standing open, and there before me was a white horse. And its rider is called Faithful and True. With righteousness He judges and wages war. 12 He has eyes like blazing fire, and many royal crowns on His head. He has a name written on Him that only He Himself knows. 13 He is dressed in a robe dipped in blood, and His name is The Word of God.

14 The armies of heaven, dressed in fine linen, white and pure, follow Him on white horses. 15 And from His mouth proceeds a sharp sword with which to strike down the nations, and He will rule them with an iron scepter. He treads the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty. 16 And He has a name written on His robe and on His thigh: KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Heaven stands open, and John sees a rider on a white horse. His names identify Him: Faithful and True, the Word of God, and King of kings and Lord of lords. This is Christ, coming as the righteous judge. The many royal crowns express His authority above the rulers who have opposed Him.

The blazing eyes recall the vision of Jesus in chapter 1. His robe is dipped in blood, and armies in pure white linen follow Him. John also mentions a name known only to the rider. The vision reveals who He is while leaving that name unexplained.

The sharp sword comes from His mouth. The Greek word rhomphaia refers to a large sword, as Thayer’s entry explains. Here its location matters: the picture connects His judgment with what He speaks. The armies follow, while the action of striking the nations and treading the winepress is assigned to Him.

The iron scepter and winepress draw on earlier biblical pictures of royal authority and judgment. The passage brings those images together around one person. The powers that demanded allegiance in earlier chapters now face the One whose right to rule exceeds their own.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
These readings agree that the rider is Christ and that His victory rests on His authority. They differ over how the vision relates to His return. Walvoord reads it as Christ’s future return to earth. Gill instead understands this scene as Christ overcoming opposition through His power and the spread of His gospel, before the final judgment. Gill does not take the heavenly armies here to mean glorified believers returning from heaven.

The blood on the robe has more than one proposed explanation. Gill mentions Christ’s own blood, the blood of His persecuted people, and the blood of His enemies, preferring the last. Wesley also connects it with conquered enemies through Isaiah 63. The verse names the bloodied robe without directly identifying whose blood it is.

Readers also differ about the accompanying armies. Gill identifies believers; Walvoord includes saints and angels. The clothing recalls the bride’s linen in verse 8, but this passage does not give a complete list of everyone in the armies. In either reading, Christ is the central figure who judges and wins.
passages.god_plan_html:
The ruler promised in Isaiah 11:1–10 judges the poor with righteousness and defeats the wicked by the breath of His lips. Psalm 2:1–12 describes rebellious kings confronting God’s appointed King, who receives the nations and an iron scepter. Revelation places those promises around Jesus. His rule brings the world’s competing claims to authority before God’s judgment.

The title Word of God also recalls John 1:1–5, where the Word is with God, is God and is the One through whom all things were made. The One who judges creation is already connected with its beginning.

The bloodied clothing and winepress recall the divine warrior in Isaiah 63:1–6, where judgment and redemption belong to the same scene. That is a supported connection in the imagery. A detailed route for Christ’s return would require further interpretation beyond what John gives here.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Revelation 19:17-21
passages.section_title: What becomes of the beast and its armies?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 17 Then I saw an angel standing in the sun, and he cried out in a loud voice to all the birds flying overhead, “Come, gather together for the great supper of God, 18 so that you may eat the flesh of kings and commanders and mighty men, of horses and riders, of everyone slave and free, small and great.” 19 Then I saw the beast and the kings of the earth with their armies assembled to wage war against the One seated on the horse, and against His army. 20 But the beast was captured along with the false prophet, who on its behalf had performed signs deceiving those who had the mark of the beast and worshiped its image. Both the beast and the false prophet were thrown alive into the fiery lake of burning sulfur. 21 And the rest were killed with the sword that proceeded from the mouth of the One seated on the horse. And all the birds gorged themselves on their flesh.
paragraphs: 17 Then I saw an angel standing in the sun, and he cried out in a loud voice to all the birds flying overhead, “Come, gather together for the great supper of God, 18 so that you may eat the flesh of kings and commanders and mighty men, of horses and riders, of everyone slave and free, small and great.”

19 Then I saw the beast and the kings of the earth with their armies assembled to wage war against the One seated on the horse, and against His army. 20 But the beast was captured along with the false prophet, who on its behalf had performed signs deceiving those who had the mark of the beast and worshiped its image. Both the beast and the false prophet were thrown alive into the fiery lake of burning sulfur. 21 And the rest were killed with the sword that proceeded from the mouth of the One seated on the horse. And all the birds gorged themselves on their flesh.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
An angel calls the birds to a dreadful feast. Earlier in the chapter, people were blessed to be invited to the Lamb’s marriage supper. Here the invitation is to birds that will consume the defeated armies. Kings, commanders, mighty men, slaves and free people all appear in the announcement; rank cannot shield them from the outcome.

The beast and the kings gather to fight the rider and His army. John moves directly from that gathering to their defeat. The beast and the false prophet are captured, and the false prophet is identified by the signs that deceived people into receiving the beast’s mark and worshiping its image. This brings the deception of chapter 13 to its end.

The two are thrown alive into the fiery lake of burning sulfur. The rest of the assembled force are killed by the sword from the rider’s mouth, and the birds feed on their flesh. The scene ends with Christ’s victory. Chapter 20 will turn to the dragon, whose power stood behind the beast.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The main readings agree that the gathering against Christ fails and that the beast’s deceptive power cannot save it. The USCCB notes connect the birds’ feast with Ezekiel 39 and emphasize the certainty of Christ’s victory. The imagery makes the defeat complete and public.

The identity of the defeated powers affects how teachers explain their end. Wesley, despite identifying the beast with Rome’s religious power in his wider reading, takes the beast and false prophet here as two men cast into punishment without first undergoing bodily death. Gill understands the pair as hostile civil and religious powers, particularly the papal order in his account of history. He reads their fate as the severe judgment of those powers and those who belong to them. These are the teachers’ particular identifications, rather than an agreed Christian identification of a present church or government.

The passage explicitly distinguishes the pair thrown alive into the lake from the remaining army killed by the sword. A proposed death, visit to the realm of the dead and resurrection of the pair before their casting is an added sequence; John does not describe those intervening events here.
passages.god_plan_html:
The call to the birds closely parallels Ezekiel 39:17–22: birds and beasts are summoned to feed on defeated warriors, horses and rulers, and God makes His judgment known among the nations. Revelation draws on that picture to show the overthrow of the beast’s assembled force. The connection in the imagery is clear even where readers differ over how the two prophecies fit on a timeline.

A related rescue appears in 2 Kings 19:14–19 and 32–36. Hezekiah brings an enemy’s threats before God, and the LORD delivers Jerusalem by striking the invading force. This is a parallel in God’s defense of His people and the failure of a seemingly overwhelming army, rather than a claim that the Assyrian invasion and Revelation’s battle are the same event.

2 Thessalonians 2:8–12 likewise joins deceptive signs, opposition to truth and the defeat of the lawless one by the Lord Jesus at His arrival. Together these passages direct attention to Christ’s authority over the forces that deceive and oppress.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Revelation 20:1-3
passages.section_title: What does the binding of Satan accomplish?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then I saw an angel coming down from heaven with the key to the Abyss, holding in his hand a great chain. 2 He seized the dragon, that ancient serpent who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years. 3 And he threw him into the Abyss, shut it, and sealed it over him, so that he could not deceive the nations until the thousand years were complete. After that, he must be released for a brief period of time.
paragraphs: 1 Then I saw an angel coming down from heaven with the key to the Abyss, holding in his hand a great chain. 2 He seized the dragon, that ancient serpent who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years. 3 And he threw him into the Abyss, shut it, and sealed it over him, so that he could not deceive the nations until the thousand years were complete. After that, he must be released for a brief period of time.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the beast and false prophet are defeated, John sees an angel descend with a key and a great chain. The angel seizes the dragon, whose identity is made explicit: the ancient serpent, the devil and Satan. The enemy behind the beast’s power is now restrained.

The angel throws him into the Abyss, closes it and seals it over him. The passage states the purpose: Satan cannot deceive the nations until the thousand years are complete. The Abyss is his prison in this scene. His final fate in the lake of fire comes later, in verse 10.

The restraint has a stated limit. After the thousand years, Satan must be released for a brief time. John announces that release before describing the reign of those who belong to Christ. The vision presents the enemy as subject to a limit on both his activity and his time.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Christians differ over when the thousand years occur and what the binding prevents. Walvoord reads this as a future confinement after Christ’s return, with Satan removed from activity in the world for a literal thousand years. He points to the sequence after chapter 19 and to the repeated statements about confinement and its duration.

The Catholic USCCB notes understand the thousand years as the period between Christ’s resurrection victory and the end of the world. Augustine, City of God 20.7–8, explains the binding as a restraint that allows people among the nations to be brought to Christ. His reading allows continuing temptation and persecution during this period; he does not understand the binding as an end to every activity of evil.

Wesley also places the binding in the future, after the beast’s overthrow, though his account of the following reign differs from Walvoord’s. He is cautious about deciding exactly how literally to take every feature of the chain and seal. These differences concern the vision’s timing and imagery; each reading recognizes God’s authority over Satan.
passages.god_plan_html:
The binding belongs within the Bible’s larger account of Christ overcoming the enemy. In Mark 3:22–27, Jesus answers an accusation about His authority over demons by describing a strong man who must be bound before his house can be plundered. The picture connects the defeat of Satan’s hold with the rescue Jesus brings.

Colossians 2:13–15 connects forgiveness and the cross with Christ’s triumph over hostile powers. Revelation carries the story through restraint, a final release and eventual judgment. Readers connect these stages differently, but the larger purpose is consistent: evil does not keep its dominion, and God brings His work of rescue to completion.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Revelation 20:4-6
passages.section_title: Who shares in the first resurrection?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 4 Then I saw the thrones, and those seated on them had been given authority to judge. And I saw the souls of those who had been beheaded for their testimony of Jesus and for the word of God, and those who had not worshiped the beast or its image and had not received its mark on their foreheads or hands. And they came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years. 5 The rest of the dead did not come back to life until the thousand years were complete. This is the first resurrection. 6 Blessed and holy are those who share in the first resurrection! The second death has no power over them, but they will be priests of God and of Christ and will reign with Him for a thousand years.
paragraphs: 4 Then I saw the thrones, and those seated on them had been given authority to judge. And I saw the souls of those who had been beheaded for their testimony of Jesus and for the word of God, and those who had not worshiped the beast or its image and had not received its mark on their foreheads or hands. And they came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years.

5 The rest of the dead did not come back to life until the thousand years were complete. This is the first resurrection. 6 Blessed and holy are those who share in the first resurrection! The second death has no power over them, but they will be priests of God and of Christ and will reign with Him for a thousand years.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
John sees thrones and people given authority to judge. He then sees the souls of those killed for their testimony about Jesus and God’s word, along with those who refused the beast’s worship and mark. They come to life and reign with Christ for a thousand years.

The vision reverses the apparent outcome of the beast’s persecution. Those who suffered for faithfulness now share in Christ’s reign. John distinguishes their coming to life from the rest of the dead, who do not come back to life until the thousand years are complete.

He calls this the first resurrection and pronounces those who share in it blessed and holy. The second death has no power over them. They will be priests of God and of Christ and reign with Him. Later in the chapter, verse 14 identifies the second death with the lake of fire.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The central difference is whether the first resurrection is a future bodily raising or the life believers already receive in Christ. Walvoord understands it as bodily resurrection before an earthly thousand-year reign. He includes it within the raising of the righteous, with different groups raised at different points before that reign.

Augustine, City of God 20.6–10, understands the first resurrection as passing from death in sin to life in Christ. He also includes the departed faithful sharing in Christ’s reign while awaiting the resurrection of their bodies. The USCCB notes connect this reign with the life God’s people receive through Christ’s resurrection and baptism.

Wesley understands the martyrs’ coming to life as their souls and bodies being reunited, and locates their reign in heaven. He proposes two distinct thousand-year periods, with Satan’s binding beginning and ending earlier than the martyrs’ reign. That is his particular reading, rather than a timetable shared by every Wesleyan Christian.

Across these readings, the blessing honors faithfulness to Christ in the face of the beast. The assurance that the second death has no power over those who share in this resurrection is central to the passage. The location and sequence of their reign remain points of interpretation.
passages.god_plan_html:
The thrones and judgment recall Daniel 7:9–14 and 21–22. There, a beastly power wages war against God’s people until judgment is given in their favor and they receive the kingdom. Revelation develops that reversal around Jesus and those who bear witness to Him. The promise in 2 Timothy 2:11–13 likewise joins endurance with reigning alongside Christ.

The resurrection language also belongs with Daniel 12:1–3 and John 5:24–29. Daniel speaks of the dead awakening; Jesus speaks both of a present passage from death to life and of those in their graves coming out at His voice. These passages help explain the questions readers bring to Revelation without by themselves resolving every interval in its sequence.

1 Corinthians 15:20–28 places the resurrection of those who belong to Christ within His victory over every enemy, including death. That larger hope gives this scene its weight: the beast’s violence cannot determine the lasting future of Christ’s people.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

deeper_study.title: The True Church According to Jesus

passages.title: Revelation 20:7-10
passages.section_title: How does Satan’s final rebellion end?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 7 When the thousand years are complete, Satan will be released from his prison, 8 and will go out to deceive the nations in the four corners of the earth—Gog and Magog—to assemble them for battle. Their number is like the sand of the seashore. 9 And they marched across the broad expanse of the earth and surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city. But fire came down from heaven and consumed them. 10 And the devil who had deceived them was thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur, into which the beast and the false prophet had already been thrown. There they will be tormented day and night forever and ever.
paragraphs: 7 When the thousand years are complete, Satan will be released from his prison, 8 and will go out to deceive the nations in the four corners of the earth—Gog and Magog—to assemble them for battle. Their number is like the sand of the seashore. 9 And they marched across the broad expanse of the earth and surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city. But fire came down from heaven and consumed them.

10 And the devil who had deceived them was thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur, into which the beast and the false prophet had already been thrown. There they will be tormented day and night forever and ever.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The release announced in verse 3 now takes place. Satan again deceives the nations, gathering a vast force from the four corners of the earth. John calls them Gog and Magog, names drawn from Ezekiel’s account of an attack on God’s people.

The army surrounds the camp of the saints and the beloved city. Fire comes down from heaven and consumes the attackers. As in chapter 19, the gathered opposition does not become a close contest between equal powers. The vision moves swiftly to its defeat.

The devil is then thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur, where the beast and false prophet have already been thrown. John describes their torment as day and night forever and ever. The temporary imprisonment and release are over; this scene gives no further release for the deceiver.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The final defeat of Satan is shared ground, while the setting depends on the reading of the thousand years. Walvoord places the rebellion after Christ’s future earthly reign. The Catholic USCCB notes describe a symbolic final attack at the end of the period between Christ’s resurrection and the end of the world.

The connection with Ezekiel is also read differently. Wesley understands John as referring back to the war described in Ezekiel 38–39. Walvoord distinguishes the two battles while recognizing the repeated names and pattern of attack. The shared imagery establishes a connection; whether both accounts describe one event is a further question.

There is a difference over the lasting punishment. Wesley reads the torment as continuing without interruption, and the Reformed Westminster Confession 33.2 teaches enduring conscious punishment of the wicked. The Seventh-day Adventist Church’s Belief 27 and its accompanying explanation teach permanent destruction of Satan and the wicked, understanding the punishment’s permanence as the meaning of its lasting forever. This differs from reading the torment itself as unending. The passage’s wording is retained in full above.
passages.god_plan_html:
The attack recalls Ezekiel 38:1–9 and 14–23, where Gog leads a great force against God’s people and God intervenes so that the nations will know Him. Revelation expands the gathering to the nations in the four corners of the earth. The connection places this final assault within the Bible’s account of God preserving His people and making His authority known.

The description of the beloved city also recalls God’s love for Zion in Psalm 78:67–69. The city is surrounded, yet the surrounding army does not determine its future.

Paul’s promise in Romans 16:20 looks toward God crushing Satan under the feet of His people. Revelation gives a final scene of the deceiver’s defeat. That hope directs attention to God’s faithfulness after a long history of deception and opposition.
passages.current_position_html: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.

passages.title: Revelation 20:11-15
passages.section_title: What is revealed at the great white throne?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 11 Then I saw a great white throne and the One seated on it. Earth and heaven fled from His presence, and no place was found for them. 12 And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne. And books were opened, and one of them was the Book of Life. And the dead were judged according to their deeds, as recorded in the books. 13 The sea gave up its dead, and Death and Hades gave up their dead, and each one was judged according to his deeds. 14 Then Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire. This is the second death—the lake of fire. 15 And if anyone was found whose name was not written in the Book of Life, he was thrown into the lake of fire.
paragraphs: 11 Then I saw a great white throne and the One seated on it. Earth and heaven fled from His presence, and no place was found for them. 12 And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne. And books were opened, and one of them was the Book of Life. And the dead were judged according to their deeds, as recorded in the books. 13 The sea gave up its dead, and Death and Hades gave up their dead, and each one was judged according to his deeds.

14 Then Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire. This is the second death—the lake of fire. 15 And if anyone was found whose name was not written in the Book of Life, he was thrown into the lake of fire.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
John sees a great white throne and the One seated on it. Earth and heaven flee from His presence, and no place is found for them. The scene brings the dead, great and small alike, before the throne. Social standing gives no exemption from this judgment.

Books are opened, including the Book of Life. The dead are judged according to their deeds, recorded in the books. John names the Book of Life but does not give titles for the other books. Both the record of deeds and the presence or absence of a name in the Book of Life belong to the description.

The sea, Death and Hades give up their dead. Hades is the Greek name used here for the realm of the dead; Thayer’s entry also notes its portrayal as a power in this verse. The vision presents Death and Hades as giving up those they held, then being thrown into the lake of fire themselves.

The lake of fire is identified as the second death. Anyone whose name is not found written in the Book of Life is thrown into it. The chapter ends with judgment and the removal of Death and Hades; the next scene reveals a new heaven and earth where death will be no more.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The main readings understand this as the final judgment, though they differ over who is standing in this particular scene. The Catholic Catechism 1038–1040 and the Reformed Westminster Confession 33.1 describe a final judgment of all people. Wesley likewise reads John’s vision as including every age and condition.

Walvoord understands those judged here as the unbelieving dead, with the righteous already raised and rewarded before the thousand years. That conclusion depends on his reading of the first resurrection and the sequence of judgments. John’s wording identifies the assembled people as the dead, great and small, and states the consequence for anyone absent from the Book of Life.

The books are commonly understood as expressing God’s complete knowledge and the justice of His judgment. Wesley connects them with God’s knowledge, conscience and the standards God has made known. These explanations develop the picture; John’s own account emphasizes that people are judged according to their deeds and that nothing held by the sea, Death or Hades remains beyond the judgment.
passages.god_plan_html:
The court and opened books recall Daniel 7:9–14, where judgment answers the arrogance of a beastly power and dominion belongs to the Son of Man. John 5:24–29 connects resurrection and judgment with the Son’s authority. Revelation’s scene belongs within that larger account of God bringing human history before His judgment.

The judgment according to deeds also appears in Romans 2:5–11. Paul joins it with God’s impartiality. Great and small standing before the throne gives a vivid picture of that same accountability.

The removal of Death and Hades reaches beyond the punishment of individual wrongs. 1 Corinthians 15:20–28 names death as the last enemy to be destroyed. Here even the powers that held the dead are brought to an end. The promise of no more death in Revelation 21:1–4 follows directly from that victory.

passages.title: Revelation 21:1-8
passages.section_title: What will life with God be like?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and earth had passed away, and the sea was no more. 2 I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband. 3 And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them. They will be His people, and God Himself will be with them as their God. 4 ‘He will wipe away every tear from their eyes,’ and there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, for the former things have passed away.” 5 And the One seated on the throne said, “Behold, I make all things new.” Then He said, “Write this down, for these words are faithful and true.” 6 And He told me, “It is done! I am the Alpha and the Omega, the Beginning and the End. To the thirsty I will give freely from the spring of the water of life. 7 The one who overcomes will inherit all things, and I will be his God, and he will be My son. 8 But to the cowardly and unbelieving and abominable and murderers and sexually immoral and sorcerers and idolaters and all liars, their place will be in the lake that burns with fire and sulfur. This is the second death.”

This is the second death.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
After the judgment, John sees a new heaven and a new earth. The former heaven and earth have passed away, and the sea is no more. The holy city, the new Jerusalem, comes down from God, prepared like a bride for her husband.

The voice from the throne explains the heart of the scene: God will dwell with His people. He wipes away their tears, and death, mourning, crying and pain will be no more. The promise reaches the griefs that have marked their lives throughout the book.

The One on the throne declares that He makes all things new and tells John to write because His words are faithful and true. He identifies Himself as the Alpha and Omega, the Beginning and the End. He gives the water of life freely to the thirsty, and promises an inheritance and the relationship of a son to the one who overcomes.

The closing warning names the second death as the fate of the cowardly, unbelieving and those characterized by the evils listed. The comfort and invitation stand alongside a serious distinction between life with God and the judgment described in the previous chapter.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Wesley and Walvoord understand this as the lasting new creation after the final judgment. Gill places the chapter’s vision within the thousand-year reign instead. Their difference concerns where John’s description belongs in the sequence of visions.

The Catholic Catechism 1042–1048 describes the universe as renewed and transformed, with humanity and creation brought to their fulfillment in Christ. Walvoord emphasizes a new creation replacing the former heaven and earth. Both readings affirm a lasting home with God, while explaining its relationship to the present world differently.

The sea receives different emphases. Walvoord reads its absence as a feature of the new world. The USCCB notes connect its disappearance with the removal of the dragon’s home. These explanations draw attention respectively to the world John sees and to the meaning of the imagery within Revelation.
passages.god_plan_html:
The promise of God dwelling among His people recalls Ezekiel 37:26–28, where His dwelling, His people and His enduring covenant belong together. Revelation brings that relationship to the center of the new creation.

Isaiah 25:6–9 joins the swallowing up of death with God wiping tears from every face. Isaiah 65:17–19 speaks of new heavens and a new earth, Jerusalem’s joy and an end to weeping. John’s vision draws these promises together into a picture of God’s faithful care.

The freely given water also recalls Isaiah 55:1–3 and Jesus’ offer of living water in John 4:10–14. Life with God is presented as His gift to the thirsty, with an invitation to receive what He gives.

passages.title: Revelation 21:9-14
passages.section_title: Why does the city bear the names of Israel and the apostles?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 9 Then one of the seven angels with the seven bowls full of the seven final plagues came and said to me, “Come, I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb.” 10 And he carried me away in the Spirit to a mountain great and high, and showed me the holy city of Jerusalem coming down out of heaven from God, 11 shining with the glory of God. Its radiance was like a most precious jewel, like a jasper, as clear as crystal. 12 The city had a great and high wall with twelve gates inscribed with the names of the twelve tribes of Israel, and twelve angels at the gates. 13 There were three gates on the east, three on the north, three on the south, and three on the west. 14 The wall of the city had twelve foundations bearing the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb.
paragraphs: 9 Then one of the seven angels with the seven bowls full of the seven final plagues came and said to me, “Come, I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb.” 10 And he carried me away in the Spirit to a mountain great and high, and showed me the holy city of Jerusalem coming down out of heaven from God, 11 shining with the glory of God. Its radiance was like a most precious jewel, like a jasper, as clear as crystal.

12 The city had a great and high wall with twelve gates inscribed with the names of the twelve tribes of Israel, and twelve angels at the gates. 13 There were three gates on the east, three on the north, three on the south, and three on the west. 14 The wall of the city had twelve foundations bearing the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
One of the angels who carried the final bowls invites John to see the bride, the wife of the Lamb. He then shows John the holy city coming down from God. The city shines with God’s glory, with a radiance John compares to a clear and precious jewel.

The invitation recalls chapter 17, where an angel with one of the bowls showed John Babylon. The new scene sets another city and another relationship before him: the holy city belongs to the Lamb.

Twelve angels stand at twelve gates, arranged three on each side. The gates bear the names of Israel’s twelve tribes, and the city’s twelve foundations bear the names of the Lamb’s twelve apostles. The vision joins these names within one city; John does not list the individual names or identify a particular apostle’s place in the foundations.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The bride and city are closely linked in the main readings. The Catholic Catechism 1045 identifies the holy city and bride with the community redeemed in Christ. The USCCB notes likewise read the description as a picture of the church. Walvoord understands it as a real dwelling place for God’s people across the ages, described with the beauty and relationship of a bride.

Wesley connects the apostolic foundations with the faith delivered through the apostles. These readings give different weight to the city as a place and as a picture of its people, but they recognize the importance of its relationship with God and the Lamb.
passages.god_plan_html:
Ezekiel 48:30–35 also describes gates named after Israel’s tribes, three on each side, and ends by naming the city for the LORD’s presence there. The repeated pattern connects the city John sees with God’s earlier promise to dwell among His people.

Ephesians 2:19–22 describes believers as members of God’s household, built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets with Christ as the cornerstone. The purpose is a dwelling place for God in His Spirit. Revelation’s named foundations belong within that larger picture of God gathering a people around Christ.

The tribal names also recall the covenants, promises and human descent of the Messiah through Israel in Romans 9:4–5. The vision remembers that history as it presents the Lamb’s city.

passages.title: Revelation 21:15-21
passages.section_title: What do the city’s measurements and precious stones show?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 15 The angel who spoke with me had a golden measuring rod to measure the city and its gates and walls. 16 The city lies foursquare, with its width the same as its length. And he measured the city with the rod, and all its dimensions were equal—12,000 stadia in length and width and height. 17 And he measured its wall to be 144 cubits, by the human measure the angel was using. 18 The wall was made of jasper, and the city itself of pure gold, as pure as glass. 19 The foundations of the city walls were adorned with every kind of precious stone: The first foundation was jasper, the second sapphire, the third chalcedony, the fourth emerald, 20 the fifth sardonyx, the sixth carnelian, the seventh chrysolite, the eighth beryl, the ninth topaz, the tenth chrysoprase, the eleventh jacinth, and the twelfth amethyst. 21 And the twelve gates were twelve pearls, with each gate consisting of a single pearl. The main street of the city was pure gold, as clear as glass.
paragraphs: 15 The angel who spoke with me had a golden measuring rod to measure the city and its gates and walls. 16 The city lies foursquare, with its width the same as its length. And he measured the city with the rod, and all its dimensions were equal—12,000 stadia in length and width and height. 17 And he measured its wall to be 144 cubits, by the human measure the angel was using.

18 The wall was made of jasper, and the city itself of pure gold, as pure as glass. 19 The foundations of the city walls were adorned with every kind of precious stone: The first foundation was jasper, the second sapphire, the third chalcedony, the fourth emerald, 20 the fifth sardonyx, the sixth carnelian, the seventh chrysolite, the eighth beryl, the ninth topaz, the tenth chrysoprase, the eleventh jacinth, and the twelfth amethyst. 21 And the twelve gates were twelve pearls, with each gate consisting of a single pearl. The main street of the city was pure gold, as clear as glass.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The angel measures the city, its gates and its wall with a golden rod. Its length, width and height are equal: twelve thousand stadia. The wall measures one hundred and forty-four cubits, using a human measure. The repeated twelves continue the pattern of the tribes, apostles, gates and foundations.

The city is pure gold, clear like glass, and its wall is jasper. Twelve precious stones adorn its foundations. Each gate is a single pearl, and the main street is pure gold, again described as clear as glass.

John presents an abundance of beauty and order. The measurements and materials belong to a city shining with God’s glory. The description gives more attention to that glory than to the practical details of how a city of this kind would function.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Readers differ over how directly the dimensions and materials describe physical construction. Walvoord understands a real city of immense dimensions, while allowing more than one possible shape consistent with equal length, width and height. The Catholic USCCB notes emphasize completeness, the repeated twelve and the picture of the church’s beauty.

Wesley treats the gold, pearls and precious stones as figures expressing glory, while affirming a real dwelling for people with real resurrection bodies. His reading illustrates that an emphasis on the imagery’s meaning can still include a lasting place to live.
passages.god_plan_html:
The equal length, width and height recall the inner sanctuary of Solomon’s temple in 1 Kings 6:19–22. That room was also a cube and overlaid with gold. The comparison is a scriptural parallel: the city as a whole now carries features associated with the place of God’s presence.

The jewels also recall Isaiah 54:11–14, where God promises an afflicted city foundations and walls of precious stones, established in righteousness and free from terror. Revelation’s beauty belongs with that hope of restoration.

The twelve named stones on the priest’s breastpiece in Exodus 28:17–21 provide another parallel linking precious stones and Israel’s tribes. The comparison does not require assigning a hidden meaning to every stone or matching each foundation to a named apostle.

passages.title: Revelation 21:22-27
passages.section_title: Why is there no temple in the city?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 22 But I saw no temple in the city, because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple. 23 And the city has no need of sun or moon to shine on it, because the glory of God illuminates the city, and the Lamb is its lamp. 24 By its light the nations will walk, and into it the kings of the earth will bring their glory. 25 Its gates will never be shut at the end of the day, because there will be no night there. 26 And into the city will be brought the glory and honor of the nations. 27 But nothing unclean will ever enter it, nor anyone who practices an abomination or a lie, but only those whose names are written in the Lamb’s Book of Life.
paragraphs: 22 But I saw no temple in the city, because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple. 23 And the city has no need of sun or moon to shine on it, because the glory of God illuminates the city, and the Lamb is its lamp. 24 By its light the nations will walk, and into it the kings of the earth will bring their glory.

25 Its gates will never be shut at the end of the day, because there will be no night there. 26 And into the city will be brought the glory and honor of the nations. 27 But nothing unclean will ever enter it, nor anyone who practices an abomination or a lie, but only those whose names are written in the Lamb’s Book of Life.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
John sees no temple in the city because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple. Their presence defines its worship. The city also has no need of sun or moon to illuminate it: God’s glory gives light, and the Lamb is its lamp.

The nations walk by that light, and the kings bring their glory into the city. Its gates remain open, with no night there. The honor of the nations is brought in, so the scene includes both the city and peoples coming into it.

The open gates belong with holiness. Nothing unclean, no one who practices abomination or falsehood, enters. Entrance belongs to those whose names are written in the Lamb’s Book of Life. This returns to the distinction made at the judgment and to the earlier blessing on those who belong to the Lamb.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The main readings understand the absence of a temple as a statement about God’s presence with His people. Wesley emphasizes God filling and sanctifying the city. The USCCB notes connect the image with Christ’s presence throughout the church. The emphasis is on access to God, His light and the holiness of the people who live with Him.
passages.god_plan_html:
The nations, kings, open gates and light recall Isaiah 60:1–5, 11 and 19–22. There the LORD’s glory rises over His people, nations come to the light, and God becomes their everlasting light. Revelation gathers these promises into its description of the Lamb’s city.

Jesus’ teaching in John 4:21–24 looks beyond worship tied to one mountain or Jerusalem and toward worship of the Father in spirit and truth. The city with God and the Lamb as its temple gives a final picture of fellowship centered on God Himself.

passages.title: Revelation 22:1-5
passages.section_title: What does the river of life bring to God’s people?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 1 Then the angel showed me a river of the water of life, as clear as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb 2 down the middle of the main street of the city. On either side of the river stood a tree of life, bearing twelve kinds of fruit and yielding a fresh crop for each month. And the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations. 3 No longer will there be any curse. The throne of God and of the Lamb will be within the city, and His servants will worship Him. 4 They will see His face, and His name will be on their foreheads. 5 There will be no more night in the city, and they will have no need for the light of a lamp or of the sun. For the Lord God will shine on them, and they will reign forever and ever.
paragraphs: 1 Then the angel showed me a river of the water of life, as clear as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb 2 down the middle of the main street of the city. On either side of the river stood a tree of life, bearing twelve kinds of fruit and yielding a fresh crop for each month. And the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations.

3 No longer will there be any curse. The throne of God and of the Lamb will be within the city, and His servants will worship Him. 4 They will see His face, and His name will be on their foreheads. 5 There will be no more night in the city, and they will have no need for the light of a lamp or of the sun. For the Lord God will shine on them, and they will reign forever and ever.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The angel shows John the river of the water of life, clear as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb. The tree of life stands on either side, bearing twelve kinds of fruit with a fresh crop each month. Its leaves are for the healing of the nations.

There is no longer any curse. God’s servants worship Him, see His face and bear His name on their foreheads. The marks of belonging to the beast have given way to a picture of people openly belonging to God.

God gives them light, with no night in the city and no need of lamp or sun. They reign forever and ever. This is also a life of worship and service in His presence; the vision does not describe their future as empty or inactive.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The main readings connect the river and tree with life supplied by God and with the garden and river imagery elsewhere in Scripture. Wesley understands the leaves as maintaining the nations’ health in a world without sickness. The USCCB notes point to the fruit and healing leaves in Ezekiel 47.

The word translated healing can be checked in Thayer’s entry, which lists this verse under curing or healing. Explaining how that picture relates to the promise of no more pain is a matter of interpretation. The vision itself holds together God’s life-giving provision and the removal of the curse.
passages.god_plan_html:
The tree of life and river recall Genesis 2:8–10. After human disobedience, the ground was cursed and access to the tree barred in Genesis 3:17–24. Revelation answers those scenes with life, access to God and no more curse. The ending reaches back to the beginning while showing what God has brought to completion.

Ezekiel 47:1–12 describes water flowing from the sanctuary, bringing life, with fruit each month and leaves for healing. John’s vision places the source at the throne of God and the Lamb. The repeated picture directs attention to God as the giver of life.

The promise that His servants see His face also recalls Jesus’ blessing in Matthew 5:8 on the pure in heart who will see God. The goal is a restored relationship with Him, alongside the renewal of the world in which His people live.

passages.title: Revelation 22:6-7
passages.section_title: How should we respond to this prophecy?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 6 Then the angel said to me, “These words are faithful and true. The Lord, the God of the spirits of the prophets, has sent His angel to show His servants what must soon take place.” 7 “Behold, I am coming soon. Blessed is the one who keeps the words of prophecy in this book.”
paragraphs: 6 Then the angel said to me, “These words are faithful and true. The Lord, the God of the spirits of the prophets, has sent His angel to show His servants what must soon take place.” 7 “Behold, I am coming soon. Blessed is the one who keeps the words of prophecy in this book.”

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The account of the city gives way to the book’s closing assurances and instructions. The angel calls these words faithful and true. The Lord who speaks through the prophets has sent His angel to show His servants what must soon take place.

Christ announces that He is coming soon and gives a blessing to the one who keeps the prophecy’s words. The response includes taking the message to heart and living by it. The promise echoes the opening blessing on those who hear and keep what is written.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The readings agree on the call to trust the message and keep it. They differ over how soon relates to fulfillment. Wesley says the events begin to be fulfilled immediately. Walvoord emphasizes events that remain impending and will unfold swiftly, connecting Christ’s coming here especially with His coming for the church.

Thayer’s entry for the expression in verse 6 includes quickly, shortly and soon. The word’s range helps explain the question, but a full timetable depends on how readers understand the visions as a whole.
passages.god_plan_html:
Revelation 1:1–3 introduced the same movement from God’s revelation to a blessing on hearing and keeping it. The ending returns to that purpose after the visions: the book is given to shape the faithfulness of those who receive it.

Jesus likewise blesses those who hear God’s word and obey it in Luke 11:27–28. The promise here belongs within that wider call to receive God’s message through a life responsive to Him.

passages.title: Revelation 22:8-9
passages.section_title: Why does the angel refuse John’s worship?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 8 And I, John, am the one who heard and saw these things. And when I had heard and seen them, I fell down to worship at the feet of the angel who had shown me these things. 9 But he said to me, “Do not do that! I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers the prophets, and with those who keep the words of this book. Worship God!”
paragraphs: 8 And I, John, am the one who heard and saw these things. And when I had heard and seen them, I fell down to worship at the feet of the angel who had shown me these things. 9 But he said to me, “Do not do that! I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers the prophets, and with those who keep the words of this book. Worship God!”

passages.context_html:
John identifies himself as the one who heard and saw these things. He falls at the feet of the angel who showed them to him, but the angel immediately refuses his worship.

The angel calls himself a fellow servant with John, the prophets and those who keep the book’s words. His command is direct: worship God. The messenger shares the work of service; he does not receive the worship that belongs to the One whose message he brings.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The central reading is shared: the angel refuses worship and directs John to God. Wesley connects the passage closely with the similar scene in Revelation 19:10, and the USCCB notes also cross-reference that scene. The instruction gives God the worship while placing the angel alongside the other servants.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Who is The Angel of the Lord? uses this passage to distinguish ordinary angels from the Angel-of-the-LORD encounters it examines. Here the angel refuses worship immediately and identifies himself as a fellow servant. We understand his correction plainly: worship belongs to God.

deeper_study.title: Who is The Angel of the Lord?
Worship as the Early Church Knew It

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The scene follows the same pattern as Revelation 19:10, where the angel also refuses worship and points John toward God. Its repetition keeps the reader’s attention on the source of the revelation.

Jesus’ response to temptation in Matthew 4:8–10 likewise directs worship and service to the Lord God alone. The authority of a messenger never becomes a reason to replace God as the One worshiped.

passages.title: Revelation 22:10-15
passages.section_title: Why must the prophecy remain open?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 10 Then he told me, “Do not seal up the words of prophecy in this book, because the time is near. 11 Let the unrighteous continue to be unrighteous, and the vile continue to be vile; let the righteous continue to practice righteousness, and the holy continue to be holy.” 12 “Behold, I am coming soon, and My reward is with Me, to give to each one according to what he has done. 13 I am the Alpha and the Omega, the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End.” 14 Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have the right to the tree of life and may enter the city by its gates. 15 But outside are the dogs, the sorcerers, the sexually immoral, the murderers, the idolaters, and everyone who loves and practices falsehood.
paragraphs: 10 Then he told me, “Do not seal up the words of prophecy in this book, because the time is near. 11 Let the unrighteous continue to be unrighteous, and the vile continue to be vile; let the righteous continue to practice righteousness, and the holy continue to be holy.”

12 “Behold, I am coming soon, and My reward is with Me, to give to each one according to what he has done. 13 I am the Alpha and the Omega, the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End.” 14 Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have the right to the tree of life and may enter the city by its gates. 15 But outside are the dogs, the sorcerers, the sexually immoral, the murderers, the idolaters, and everyone who loves and practices falsehood.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
John is told not to seal the prophecy because the time is near. The message is to remain available. The next statement sets the unrighteous and vile alongside the righteous and holy, followed by Christ’s promise to come with His reward and repay each person according to what he has done.

Christ again identifies Himself as the Alpha and Omega, the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End. A blessing follows for those who wash their robes: they have access to the tree of life and enter the city through its gates.

The contrast is with those outside, described by practices including sorcery, sexual immorality, murder, idolatry and love of falsehood. The city’s life is joined to cleansing and holiness, as in the closing verses of chapter 21.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
Readers understand verse 11 in light of the approaching judgment, rather than as a simple invitation to do evil. Wesley emphasizes the final condition of people after judgment. Walvoord emphasizes the lasting consequences of rejecting the warning or continuing in faithfulness. Both take the surrounding promise of judgment seriously.

There is also a difference in the wording readers encounter in verse 14. The BSB speaks of washing robes, while Wesley comments on an older reading about keeping Christ’s commands. The difference comes from the underlying textual readings. The BSB’s wording recalls the robes washed in the Lamb’s blood in Revelation 7:14.
passages.god_plan_html:
The command to leave the prophecy open contrasts with Daniel 12:4 and 9–10, where words are sealed until the time of the end. Daniel also contrasts the conduct of the wicked with the purification of the wise. Revelation brings those themes into its urgent closing appeal.

Christ’s reward accompanying His coming recalls Isaiah 40:10–11, where the Lord comes with might and reward while tending His flock. The promise joins His authority to judge with His care for His people.

The blessing also completes the promise of access to the tree of life given to the overcomer in Revelation 2:7. What the churches were encouraged to seek is now described as entrance into the Lamb’s city.

passages.title: Revelation 22:16-17
passages.section_title: Who is invited to receive the water of life?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 16 “I, Jesus, have sent My angel to give you this testimony for the churches. I am the Root and the Offspring of David, the bright Morning Star.” 17 The Spirit and the bride say, “Come!” Let the one who hears say, “Come!” And let the one who is thirsty come, and the one who desires the water of life drink freely.
paragraphs: 16 “I, Jesus, have sent My angel to give you this testimony for the churches. I am the Root and the Offspring of David, the bright Morning Star.” 17 The Spirit and the bride say, “Come!” Let the one who hears say, “Come!” And let the one who is thirsty come, and the one who desires the water of life drink freely.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
Jesus personally confirms that He sent His angel to give this testimony for the churches. He calls Himself the Root and Offspring of David and the bright Morning Star. The message ends with attention on His identity and on the communities receiving it.

The Spirit and the bride say Come, and the hearer is called to join them. The invitation then reaches the thirsty and anyone who desires the water of life. They may drink freely. After the visions of judgment and renewal, the book still speaks directly to those who hear its message.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The bride is understood as the church, as the USCCB notes explain. Wesley reads the first Come as a longing for Christ to fulfill the prophecy, followed by an invitation for the thirsty to receive His blessings. Walvoord emphasizes the open invitation to receive life. These emphases recognize both the hope for Christ and the gift offered to those who hear.
passages.god_plan_html:
The Root and Offspring of David recalls the promised ruler from Jesse’s family in Isaiah 11:1–2. The star image also recalls the star and scepter arising from Israel in Numbers 24:17. The titles connect Jesus with the earlier promises of God’s appointed ruler.

The free water returns to Isaiah 55:1–3, where the thirsty are called to receive without money, and to the promise of life-giving water in John 4:10–14. The final invitation carries forward God’s purpose to give life through Christ.

passages.title: Revelation 22:18-19
passages.section_title: Why must these words be preserved faithfully?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 18 I testify to everyone who hears the words of prophecy in this book: If anyone adds to them, God will add to him the plagues described in this book. 19 And if anyone takes away from the words of this book of prophecy, God will take away his share in the tree of life and the holy city, which are described in this book.
paragraphs: 18 I testify to everyone who hears the words of prophecy in this book: If anyone adds to them, God will add to him the plagues described in this book. 19 And if anyone takes away from the words of this book of prophecy, God will take away his share in the tree of life and the holy city, which are described in this book.

passages.context_html:
The warning is addressed to everyone who hears the prophecy in this book. Adding to it brings the plagues described in it; taking away its words brings the removal of a share in the tree of life and the holy city.

The warning matches the actions and their consequences: adding brings added plagues, and removing brings removal from the promised blessings. Its immediate subject is the book of prophecy John has delivered. The words are to be received and passed on faithfully.
passages.common_interpretations_html:
The readings agree that the warning protects the integrity of the prophecy. Wesley also applies its force to the wider New Testament, comparing the warning with Moses’ protection of the law. That wider application should be distinguished from the immediate wording about this book.

Walvoord understands deliberate tampering as evidence of unbelief, rather than the loss of salvation by someone truly born of God. Wesley stresses the removal of blessings expressed in the warning. The consequence is serious in either account; the passage should be read alongside the rest of Scripture when considering how it relates to perseverance in faith.
passages.current_position_html: Our study Returning to the Word, also reflected in Is the Bible the Inerrant Word of God?, treats this warning as part of Scripture’s recurring call not to add to or subtract from what God has said. We apply that principle here by keeping the prophecy’s words intact and testing our explanations against what they actually say.

deeper_study.title: Is the Bible the Inerrant Word of God?

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.god_plan_html:
The warning recalls Deuteronomy 4:1–2, where Israel is told not to add to or subtract from God’s commands so that they may keep them. Proverbs 30:5–6 likewise joins trust in God’s word with a warning against adding to it.

These connections place Revelation’s closing warning within a recurring biblical responsibility: people receive God’s message rather than make themselves its author. The prophecy’s invitation, comfort and warning are all part of what its hearers are charged to preserve.

passages.title: Revelation 22:20-21
passages.section_title: How does Revelation end?

versions.label: BSB
versions.text: 20 He who testifies to these things says, “Yes, I am coming soon.” Amen. Come, Lord Jesus! 21 The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all the saints. Amen.
paragraphs: 20 He who testifies to these things says, “Yes, I am coming soon.” Amen. Come, Lord Jesus! 21 The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all the saints. Amen.

section_headings.common: How is this passage commonly understood?
section_headings.plan: Where does this fit in God's plan?
section_headings.deeper: Where can I study this further?

passages.context_html:
The One who testifies repeats His promise to come soon. John answers with Amen and the prayer Come, Lord Jesus. The book closes with the grace of the Lord Jesus for all the saints.

The final response is personal and shared: hope in Christ’s coming, prayer directed to Him and dependence on His grace. The visions leave their hearers with that promise and prayer.
passages.common_interpretations_html: The closing words are broadly read as a promise of Christ’s return, a prayer for Him to come and a blessing on His people. Wesley emphasizes the church’s desire for the fulfillment of Christ’s promise. The USCCB notes connect the prayer with the similar appeal at the end of 1 Corinthians. Both explanations emphasize hope for Christ and His grace for His people.
passages.god_plan_html:
The prayer and blessing recall 1 Corinthians 16:22–24, where a call for the Lord to come stands beside the grace of Jesus and love for His people. Revelation’s ending belongs within that wider hope and dependence.

Titus 2:11–14 joins grace with waiting for Christ’s glorious appearance and living faithfully in the present. The last words of Revelation direct its hearers toward the same response: receive His grace, remain His people and look for His coming.

passages.title: Didache 7:1-3

versions.label: LSB
versions.text: "Concerning baptism, baptize in this way. Having said all these things beforehand, baptize in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit in living water. But if you do not have living water, baptize in other water. And if you are not able to use cold water, use warm water. And if you do not have either, pour water three times on the head in the name of the Father and Son and Holy Spirit."

passages.context_html: The Didache is an early Christian church document, not part of the biblical canon, but historically useful for seeing how some early believers described practice. Chapter 7 concerns baptismal instruction and therefore belongs in a historical, not scriptural, supporting context.
passages.common_interpretations_html: Living water — ὕδωρ ζῶν (hudōr zōn (HOO-dor zohn)) — means flowing water: a river, stream, or spring. This was the clear preference. The hierarchy of options — flowing water, still water, pouring as a last resort — confirms that full immersion was the norm. Pouring is offered only when immersion is not possible. The fact that an alternative is needed at all confirms immersion as the default. At the same time the Didache explicitly validates pouring under certain circumstances — written within living memory of the apostles. This directly challenges any position that declares immersion the only valid mode under all circumstances. The conclusion the evidence supports is this: immersion is the clear and intended mode of baptism, rooted in the meaning of baptizō, confirmed by the burial and resurrection imagery of Scripture, and reflected in the practice of the earliest church. It should be the mode whenever possible. However Scripture never explicitly declares other modes invalid, and the Didache — our earliest practical church document — permits pouring when immersion is not available. The mode matters because of what it represents. What makes baptism valid is not the quantity of water but the genuineness of the faith of the one being baptized.
passages.current_position_html: No defined position is stated here yet beyond the common interpretations above. As related study develops, this section will be updated where the text warrants a clearer conclusion.
